--- Page 2 ---
<meta>This page contains the formal dedication of the 1580 Basel edition of Plotinus’s works. It follows the title page and is addressed to the governing council of Nuremberg, a major center of learning and printing in the Holy Roman Empire.</meta>

# TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED CONSULS
## AND ILLUSTRIOUS SENATORS
### OF THE REPUBLIC OF NUREMBERG <note>Nuremberg was a Free Imperial City known for its wealth and patronage of humanist scholars.</note>

->Greetings.<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'P' depicting a central human figure amidst dense foliage, scrolls, and other decorative figures.</image-desc>

**P**lato’s famous saying is well known, most distinguished Fathers, that Republics will only then be happy if either **Philosophers** rule, or kings **philosophize**. For since the correct administration of **Politics** <note>original: "Politice̅"</note> depends entirely upon the perfect use of reason, and—according to the opinion of **Aristotle**—the person most excellent in virtue and wisdom is, by the silent consensus of all nature, most worthy of the empire of the universe: just as this perfect honor belongs to God alone and to the man **Christ**, the Best and Greatest, so it is granted by a certain participation to those whom He willed to be His vicars <note>representatives</note> on earth, and whom He honored with the name of **"Gods."** <note>A reference to Psalm 82:6, "I have said, Ye are gods," often used in this period to describe the divine right or responsibility of civil magistrates.</note> Moreover, He is accustomed to stir up, call, and instruct these very men for the task of ruling rightly by a certain peculiar fate, as the examples of **Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, the Maccabees,** and similar figures teach us. 

Then indeed, by a common principle, that good Author of good nature is accustomed to unfold and illuminate the rules of right living—inscribed in the minds of all men—through the efficacy of His spirit in certain people born to rule. These individuals, possessing **"golden souls"** <note>original: "aureas animas" — a reference to Plato’s "Myth of the Metals" in the *Republic*, where those fit to lead are said to have gold in their nature.</note> according to the opinion of Plato, are made participants in His truth and virtue as much as is divinely permitted, just as they share in His essence. 

Truly, there are two standards of virtue and truth: **Sacred Authority**, consisting of eternal reason, and **secular reason**, relying on mortal authority. The former, enjoying the unadorned name of **Theology**, is like a most brilliant sun that can, by itself, dispel and illuminate all the darkness of the human mind; but this is granted only to those who, by the singular kindness of the Divine Power, have obtained the revelation of the divine oracles—sketched out first in the **Mosaic law**, and subsequently explained by the **Gospel law**. 

The latter standard, which they have called **Philosophy** in imitation of the Wise God, "collects the remnants of the human shipwreck" and investigates the law of uncorrupted nature. While it understands and laments the acquired depravity of man, it strives to escape toward the idea of native beauty—if not through action, then at least through contemplation. But even in this effort it is frustrated; while it recognizes what it lacks, it remains ignorant of the cause of the disease and sees no way to dispel it. It turns itself entirely toward the good Author of nature, whose goodness envies no one, so that it might humbly and devoutly seek the help for its restoration and preservation from the one to whom it owes the principles of its origin. This is the end [goal] of its philosophy...

<summary>In this dedication, the author praises the leaders of Nuremberg by invoking Plato’s concept of the "Philosopher King" and "golden souls." He distinguishes between Theology (divine revelation) and Philosophy (human reason) as two paths toward truth and virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Nuremberg, Plato, Aristotle, Philosopher King, Theology, Philosophy, Golden Souls, Civil Governance</keywords>

# PREFACE

...[reason], **Socrates**, judged by the oracle of **Apollo** as the wisest of all mortals, established this rule when he taught that all things should be referred back to that highest good and beauty. He defined **philosophy** as a preparation for death. Indeed, he did not hesitate to assert that philosophy holds the primary place among all those gifts we have received from the Gods. In this one matter he was deceived: through his ignorance of **Divine Authority**—even if he perhaps silently hinted that this authority itself was placed beyond the reach of human gifts—he assigned the first rank to **reason**, which ought only to be counted in the second place. 

For indeed, human reason itself—for divine reason utterly dulls and darkens the eyes of men with its brilliance, much like the sun does to **owls**—derives universal theory and contemplation from the history and observation of individual cases. Furthermore, such observation cannot be performed in a short time or by a single person. To acquire the "equipment" of reason, so to speak, the constant order of nature persuades us that **experience** must serve as a handmaid and midwife. Therefore, we must place the highest value on the **Authority** of those who found things through observed reason, established what they found, and taught what they established. 

For this reason, that admirable initiate and interpreter of nature, **Aristotle**, who asserted that nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses, pronounced that <gloss>it is necessary for [a concept] to exist in the senses</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ton mē en aisthēsei tis einai"</note>. For although the freedom of reason and speech—devoted to no authority but dedicated to truth alone—is becoming to a philosopher, such freedom can only belong to those few whom "just **Jupiter** has loved," and who have surpassed all authority by the piercing insight of a divine mind. Meanwhile, for the average sort of people, who make up the greatest part, it is much more advisable to serve the opinions of their predecessors than to seize upon the tyranny of <gloss>new opinions</gloss> <note>original Greek: "neodoxias"</note> through an inconsiderate zeal for liberty, thereby repudiating the authority of the ancestors. 

Even if we omit the **Gymnosophists** <note>"Naked wise men" or Brahmans</note> and **Brahmans** of the Indians, the priests of the **Egyptians**, the **Chaldeans** of the Babylonians, the **Tarabostes** <note>An aristocratic class of priests or warriors</note> of the Scythians, and the **Druids** of the Germans and Gauls, the two most famous schools of the ancient Greek philosophers certainly attributed a great deal to authority. Whether we look at the **Ionic** school from **Thales** down to **Epicurus**, or the **Italic** school from **Pythagoras** all the way to **Socrates**, they frequently turned aside into the realms of authority while following the tracks of reason. This is more than proved by that famous Pythagorean saying: <gloss>He himself said it</gloss> <note>original Greek: "autos epha," Latin: "ipse dixit"; a phrase used by disciples to indicate that the master's word is final authority</note>. 

Indeed, when **Socrates** set out to restore the neglected state of philosophy to its integrity, and to investigate not only the obscurity of nature but also the wickedness of morals—seeking a way to repair them—he produced various "colonies" of later philosophers because of the elegance of his teaching and the holiness of his life. His skillful disciples sought either to understand more rightly or to cultivate more diligently those natural seeds of virtue and truth they had drawn from him.

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of balancing human reason with historical authority, arguing that most people should follow established traditions rather than radical new ideas. It cites various ancient philosophical schools—from the Druids to Pythagoras—to illustrate that even the greatest thinkers relied on the authority of their predecessors.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Aristotle, Divine Authority vs Reason, history of philosophy, Pythagoras, neodoxia, pedagogical tradition, ancient schools of thought</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the historical narrative of the Greek philosophical schools, transitioning from the foundational figures of Socrates and Plato to the development of the Academy and the life of Plotinus. It establishes continuity with the previous discussion of "Authority" by showing how philosophical traditions were preserved and eventually moved to Rome. Catchword: "dis" (likely for "disputaverunt" or "discipuli").</meta>

# PREFACE

* 3

From this very source, the sect of Academic philosophers was established by **Plato**, and that of the **Cynics** by **Antisthenes**—which soon gave rise to the **Stoics** as well. **Aristotle**, the disciple of **Plato**, led the **Peripatetic** <term>Peripatetic: Derived from the Greek word for "walking about," referring to Aristotle's habit of teaching while walking with his students.</term> colony from its "metropolis" into the **Lyceum**, a school in no way inferior to the original due to the clarity of its order and method, continuing through a perpetual succession for so many centuries. Meanwhile, **Speusippus** and his successors preserved the name and dignity of the **Old Academy**, while **Arcesilaus** introduced the **Middle Academy**, and **Lacydes** the **New**.

After the constitution of the Athenian school was later disturbed along with the empire, the **Academy**—having been roused from its birthplaces—began to spread its branches across all of Greece and then through Italy, more so than any other sect. So great was the kindness of the climate and soil that those living roots grew into the most vast forests. And after "captured Greece took captive its fierce conqueror," <note>original: "Græcia capta, ferū victorē cepit" — a famous quote from the Roman poet Horace, noting how Greek culture dominated Rome after the military conquest.</note> as the saying goes, the harvest of **Platonic** philosophy became most abundant, especially in Rome. This was attested and celebrated marvelously not only through living tradition but also by the writings of the most learned men.

**Plotinus of Lycopolis**, whom we produce here upon a more refined and elegant literary stage, can testify to this. He was a diligent pupil of the supreme philosopher **Ammonius of Alexandria** for eleven years, starting from his twenty-eighth year when he first approached philosophy. He was a fellow student of **Origen** <note>This refers to Origen the Neoplatonist, a contemporary and fellow student of Plotinus, often distinguished by scholars from the Christian Church Father of the same name.</note> and **Herennius**. It had been agreed among them long ago that they would not publish the master’s **acroamatic** <term>acroamatic: From the Greek for "things heard"; secret or oral teachings intended only for initiated disciples, rather than for the general public.</term> doctrines, but would instead preserve the authority of the school by communicating them only by word of mouth to legitimate listeners.

However, first **Herennius** and then **Origen** broke this faith. Furthermore, because **Plotinus's** students—of whom he had many learned ones in Rome over twenty-six years—were following a disorganized oral tradition without a written record of the doctrines, **Plotinus** finally turned his mind to writing. He was then just over forty years old and continued until his sixty-sixth year, which was the second year of the Emperor **Claudius II** <note>reigned 268–270 AD</note>—a year certainly fatal to both.

Since **Porphyry** has followed the life of **Plotinus** diligently and at length, there is no reason for us to "do what has already been done." <note>original: "actū agamus" — a Latin idiom similar to "reinventing the wheel."</note> We should, however, observe this one thing: that **Plotinus** lived in those times when "profane" <note>In this context, "profane" (profana) refers to secular or non-Christian philosophy.</note> philosophy was stirred by competition with the **Christian religion**, which was then emerging far and wide. Philosophy, compelled by the truth of Christian doctrines, could have very easily submitted to the "yoke of Christ," had it not been for the ambition and wickedness of those who were philosophers only as far as their beards and cloaks. <note>original: "barba pallioq; tenus" — a common critique of hypocritical philosophers who adopted the appearance (the long beard and philosopher's cloak) without the actual wisdom.</note> Swollen with the reputation of wisdom, they thought it most shameful to obey the "unskilled" and "ignorant." <note>Referring to how the intellectual elite viewed the early Christians, who were often from lower social classes.</note>

For while they sought to protect the authority of secular wisdom, they observed that **Christian piety** relied not so much on the subtlety of arguments as on the holiness of character and the frequency of miracles. They did not hesitate to "move Acheron itself" <note>original: "Acheronta mouere" — a phrase from Virgil’s Aeneid meaning to stir up the underworld or resort to any means necessary, however dark or supernatural.</note>—that is, to call upon **Magic** for assistance under the pretext of human philosophy. Thus, after **Apollonius of Tyana** (whose marvelous tricks the most cunning demon [mimicked] the miracles of Christ the Best and Greatest)...

<summary>This page traces the genealogy of the Platonic Academy and the Peripatetic school, eventually focusing on Plotinus's life in Rome and his decision to break his vow of secrecy to record his teachings. It also frames the conflict between late Neoplatonism and the rising Christian faith as a battle between philosophical pride/magic and Christian piety.</summary>

# PREFACE

...to weaken the authority of the **Apostles**, and attempted to oppose him as a sort of antagonist to them.) <note>The text likely refers to the "authority of the Apostles" or "Gospels," which pagan philosophers tried to undermine by presenting their own figures as rivals to Christ.</note> **Julian the Chaldean**, known as the "Wonder-worker," **Iamblichus of Chalcis**, **Maximus of Ephesus**, **Libanius** the sophist, **Amelius** and **Sopater of Apamea**, **Aedesius of Cappadocia**, **Chrysanthius of Lydia**, and that impious **Porphyry of Tyre**, along with the blasphemous **Proclus of Lycia**, introduced the mask of philosophy over impious magic. Indeed, this situation led **St. Paul** to seriously command the faithful to abstain from "empty philosophy." <note>A reference to Colossians 2:8, where Paul warns against being "spoiled through philosophy and vain deceit."</note> Consequently, the followers of the Christian religion in that century condemned not only the philosophers (and rightly so), but also philosophy itself—though it was undeserving—as an act of impiety. Matters reached a point where, out of a hatred for magic, divine Theology was almost entirely stripped of the honorary and necessary service and ministry of pure Philosophy.

But since the more excellent a thing is, the worse its abuse tends to be, these two should have been carefully distinguished from one another; the faults of men should not have been attributed to the art itself. Those who acted more rightly included **Melito**, Bishop of Sardis (a disciple of the philosopher **Fronto**), **Pantaenus** the Alexandrian Stoic, along with his disciples **Clement of Alexandria** and **Alexander**, Bishop of Jerusalem; likewise **Quadratus**, **Aristides of Athens**, **Justin Martyr**, **Cyprian of Carthage** (who was a magician before he became a bishop), and furthermore **Origen the Egyptian**, among many others. These men rejected philosophical vanity but compelled philosophical truth to serve as a handmaid to revealed truth. In this way, they translated the otherwise forbidden use of "Egyptian gold" <note>original: "auri Aegyptij" — a common metaphor in early Christian writing, referring to the Israelites taking gold from the Egyptians to build the Tabernacle. It signifies using pagan learning for holy purposes.</note> into the worship of the true God. They did this with such success that **Julian the Apostate** <note>The Roman Emperor who attempted to revive paganism.</note> believed the only way to uproot Christianity was to bar the faithful from the literature of the heathens; he feared that if they were instructed in these works, they would defend the Truth more plausibly and effectively, defeating the impious with their own weapons.

Now, although it seems absurd that men turned away from God and professing themselves enemies of true piety could reach any knowledge of sincere truth (even if it is "profane"), great is the indulgence of that eternal Giver of Good things. Just as He illuminates the impious and the pious alike with His sun, so too, by a wonderful counsel, He gave to various heathens much clearer revelations of the **Messiah** (as can be established from the **Sibylline Oracles**) than He gave even to the prophets of the Jews themselves. Therefore, although **Plotinus** may have felt impiously regarding our revealed religion—and perhaps even attacked it through magical attempts (though **Porphyry** trifles when he claims that a God of the Egyptians, rather than a demon, appeared to the priest who summoned **Plotinus's** guiding spirit)—nevertheless, in that branch of philosophy which is consistent with human reason and seeks to rival nature (that is, the works of God) in knowing and expressing every kind of being, he was the most excellent after **Plato**. Indeed, if, as a certain man said, "the Platonists can become Christians with only a few things changed," then **Plotinus** certainly...

<summary>This page discusses the conflict between Neoplatonist "magicians" and early Christian thinkers, arguing that while some used philosophy to attack the Church, the great Church Fathers successfully used philosophical truths (the "Egyptian gold") to support Christian theology.</summary>

# PREFACE

...him <note>original: "te," likely referring to Plotinus, as the previous page was discussing the lineage of philosophers.</note>, who has scrutinized and interpreted the Platonic dogmas much more accurately and diligently, would deserve the first place among these. For if he were compared with others of the same profession, he would seem no less worthy of the name **divine** <note>original: "theos"</note> than Plato once was when compared to the **inspired** <note>original: "daimonia," often translated as "divine" or "spirit-like," here used to contrast Aristotle's genius with Plato's.</note> Aristotle. Even if he was either unwilling, or perhaps because he was deprived of the deity's kindness and could not reach the knowledge of eternal piety: yet we, upon whom a more generous grace of the divine spirit has shone, should compel his philosophy—which is rightly consistent with nature, and so far not foreign to divine Authority—to serve as a handmaid to Theology. Let us learn to refer those very treasures of nature, unearthed from these inner shrines through both contemplation and action, to the glory of the one God, and to find rest in the light of Him who illuminates every man, though in a different manner.

With this very intention, most distinguished gentlemen, we wished to present **Plotinus**—who had come forth from our printing house several years ago in the translation of **Marsilio Ficino**—now speaking in his own tongue <note>The editor is presenting a Greek-Latin bilingual edition, allowing Plotinus to "speak" in his original Greek.</note> and in an enlarged and corrected form. This was made possible through the reliability and assistance of four Greek manuscript copies: three from Italy, and a fourth provided by the literary generosity of **Johannes Sambucus** of Trnava, the Imperial Historian—a man to be preferred over all private collectors and even compared to many princes. Our goal was to grant students of both languages the power to know, judge, and apply to the use of true piety the **Platonic philosophy**—that is, the one most closely related to the Christian religion. For his work overflows with such richness of thought and brevity of words that it can sometimes be understood more correctly from the Greek than from the Latin—not through any fault of the translator, but due to the obscurity of the subject itself and the particular character of the language.

Moreover, I wished to offer this same author especially to your Republic <note>Referring to the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg.</note>, most honorable Fathers, so that since similarity breeds friendship, this prince of philosophers—who is also an outstanding teacher of truth and virtue in his own way—might come forth under the title and patronage of that Republic which

> *Has raised its head as high among the cities of Germany,*
> *As cypresses are wont to do among the bending osiers* <note>A quote from Virgil's Eclogues (1.24–25), comparing the majesty of a city—originally Rome, here Nuremberg—to a tall tree among shrubs.</note>

and which, through a constant succession of many years, has expressed both the wealth of **Corinth** and the best discipline—far holier than that of **Sparta**—in the heart of **Germany**, and has bravely preserved it with long-standing kindness among so many who lie in wait for liberty. But just as these are the ancestral praises of your city, so what must now be said is specific to you, the noble posterity of good parents: that with a mind no less royal than philosophical, at this time when we see most people brooding over politics in either shameful or empty idleness (to say nothing more serious), you have established the **Academy of Altdorf** <note>The University of Altdorf was founded by the city of Nuremberg in 1575.</note>, and the most learned...

<meta>This page concludes the preface, transitioning from a general defense of Plotinus’s philosophy to a specific dedication to the leaders of Nuremberg. It emphasizes the city's role as a center of both commerce and high culture.</meta>

# P R E F A C E

...of the most distinguished men summoned by stipends <note>original: "stipendijs euocatorum," referring to the scholars and professors whose salaries were paid by the city to ensure the quality of the local Academy</note>, you have taken such care to preserve learning through erudition and virtue, that in the future the Christian world will both admire and celebrate famous **Nuremberg** in Germany, not only as a marketplace of the most esteemed and precious goods, but also of the best and most praiseworthy arts. In the manner of the ancient Roman military, a soldier of a good name and a good omen was accustomed to be chosen first and enrolled in the camp's register. Likewise, most illustrious men of all ranks, receive **Plotinus**, the prince of the Academicians, with your customary kindness. Let him stand as a witness and a guarantor of my long-standing respect toward your Republic <note>original: "Rempublicam," referring here to the city-state of Nuremberg</note> and my new goodwill toward your Academy. Furthermore, receive me—the common midwife <note>original: "obstetricatorem," a Socratic metaphor for a printer or editor who assists in the "birth" of intellectual works</note> of all Academicians—into your patronage from this time forward.

Farewell, you lights and pillars of Germany. 

At Basel, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September <note>August 27th</note>, in the Christian year 1580.

->Your Devoted<-
->*Most Devotedly,*<-
->*Petrus Perna, Printer of Basel.*<-

He uses the metaphor of a 'midwife' to describe his role in publishing these philosophical works for the benefit of the German Academy.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded the printer Petrus Perna’s 1580 dedication to the city of Nuremberg. This page begins the original 15th-century preface written by Marsilio Ficino himself, addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici ("the Magnificent"), explaining the origins of the Platonic Academy in Florence and how this translation of Plotinus came to be.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO
## THE FLORENTINE, ON PLOTINUS
### TO THE MAGNIFICENT LORENZO
### DE' MEDICI, SAVIOR OF THE FATHERLAND <note>original: "Patriae Servatorem," a title echoing the classical "Pater Patriae" given to his grandfather Cosimo</note>

### Preface.

<image-desc>A large ornamental historiated drop cap 'M' featuring classical or foliate decorative motifs within a square frame. The letter begins the word 'Magnus'.</image-desc>**Cosimo the Great**, named "Father of the Fatherland" by decree of the Senate, at the time when the Council between the Greeks and the Latins was being held in Florence under Pope Eugenius, frequently listened to a Greek philosopher named **Gemistus**, surnamed **Pletho** <note>a Byzantine scholar who inspired the Renaissance revival of Plato</note>, who spoke as if he were a second Plato on the Platonic mysteries. From his fervent speech, Cosimo was so immediately inspired and encouraged that he conceived the idea of a certain **Academy** <term>Academy: a school of higher learning modeled after the one founded by Plato in ancient Athens</term> in his high mind, intending to bring it to birth at the first opportune moment. Later, while that great Medici was, in a sense, nurturing this conception, he destined me—the son of his most favored physician, Ficino—while I was still a boy, for this great work, and he educated me daily for this very purpose. Furthermore, he took care that I should have all the Greek books not only of **Plato**, but also of **Plotinus**. After this, in the year 1463, when I was thirty years old, he commissioned me to translate first **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Mercurium Termaximum," a legendary figure associated with ancient wisdom and magic</note> and soon after, Plato. I completed Hermes in a few months while he was still living; I then also began Plato. Although he also desired Plotinus, he did not say a word about translating him, lest he seem to weigh me down with too heavy a burden all at once. Such was the kindness of so great a man toward his associates, and such was his modesty toward everyone. And so, I myself did not think of approaching Plotinus for some time. But meanwhile Cosimo, what he once sang while living on earth, he finally expressed—or rather impressed—from on high. For at the time I gave the Latin Plato to the public to read, that heroic spirit of Cosimo somehow spurred the heroic mind of **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** to come to Florence, though he himself hardly knew how he arrived. He was born, indeed, in the very year I had begun Plato; then, coming to Florence on the very day and almost the same hour I published Plato, he asked me about Plato immediately after our first greeting. To him I said, "Indeed, our Plato has just this day crossed our threshold." At this, he congratulated me vehemently, and then—I know not with what words he spoke or I replied—he did not just lead me, but rather incited me to translate Plotinus. Truly it seems to have been brought about by divine will that while Plato was being reborn, the hero Pico was born under his own **Saturn** occupying **Aquarius** <note>an astrological reference; both Ficino and Pico shared this planetary alignment, which was thought to favor deep, melancholic, and philosophical intellects</note>, under which I too had been born thirty years earlier. And arriving in Florence on the day our Plato was published, he wonderfully inspired in me that same ancient wish of the hero Cosimo concerning Plotinus—a wish entirely hidden from me, but inspired in him from heaven. Since we have now touched upon **Divine Providence** in the duty of philosophizing, it seems worthwhile to pursue this a little more broadly. One must certainly not think that the sharp and, in a sense, philosophical minds of men can ever be enticed and led toward perfect religion by any bait other than philosophical discourse. For sharp minds usually commit themselves to reason alone, and when they receive this reason from a religious philosopher, they readily admit a common religion; once imbued with this, they are led to a better form of religion contained within that genre...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino recounts how Cosimo de' Medici was inspired by Gemistus Pletho to found a new Platonic Academy and commissioned Ficino to translate the works of Plato and Plotinus. He highlights the "divine" timing of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's arrival in Florence, which spurred the completion of the Plotinus translation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's preface to Lorenzo de' Medici, following the account of how his grandfather, Cosimo de' Medici, commissioned the translation of the Platonic corpus. Here, Ficino outlines the genealogy of "Pious Philosophy" and explains why translating Plotinus is necessary to combat the secular Aristotelianism of his day.</meta>

->### PREFACE.<-

...are more easily transmitted. Therefore, it was not without divine providence—which wishes, of course, to wonderfully recall all people to itself according to their individual talents—that it came to pass that a certain **pious philosophy** was born once among the Persians under **Zoroaster**, and among the Egyptians under **Hermes** <note>original: "Mercurio," referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, consistent with itself in both places. It was then nourished among the Thracians under **Orpheus** and **Aglaophemus**. It soon grew to adolescence under **Pythagoras** among the Greeks and Italians, and at last was reached its full maturity in Athens by the divine **Plato**. 

It was the ancient custom of these theologians to shroud divine mysteries in both mathematical numbers and figures, as well as in poetic fables, lest they be cheaply exposed to just anyone. Finally, **Plotinus**—who delighted in this veiled theology—was the first and only one, as **Porphyry** and **Proclus** testify, to penetrate the divine secrets of the ancients. But because of his incredible brevity of words, his abundance of thoughts, and the depth of his meaning, he requires not only a translation into another language, but also commentaries. 

We, therefore, have labored in translating and explaining these higher theologians in the works of Plato and Plotinus. We did this so that, once this theology comes to light, poets may stop impiously counting the mysteries of piety among their myths, and the many **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking in the Lyceum</term>—who comprise nearly all philosophers today—may be warned that one should not think of our common religion as if it were merely "old wives' tales." 

For nearly the whole world is now occupied by the Peripatetics, who are divided into two main sects: the **Alexandrian** <note>followers of Alexander of Aphrodisias, who argued the individual soul is mortal</note> and the **Averroist** <note>followers of the Andalusian philosopher Averroes, who argued there is only one collective human intellect</note>. The former believe our intellect is mortal; the latter contend that it is only one for all mankind. Both equally undermine all religion at its foundation, especially because they seem to deny divine providence regarding human affairs, and in both cases, they have even defected from their own teacher, **Aristotle**. Today, few interpret his mind with that same piety shown of old by **Theophrastus**, **Themistius**, **Porphyry**, **Simplicius**, **Avicenna**, and recently **Plethon**—with the exception of our sublime **Pico della Mirandola** <note>original: "Picum Camplatonicum," a playful Latinization of Pico's name, suggesting his mastery of Platonic philosophy</note>. 

If anyone thinks that such widespread impiety, fortified by such sharp wits, can be erased among men by a simple preaching of faith alone, he is clearly proven wrong by the reality of the situation. There is need here of a much greater power: either through divine miracles appearing everywhere, or at least through a certain "philosophical religion" that might eventually persuade philosophers, who would listen to it more willingly. It pleases divine providence in these times to confirm religion itself through philosophical authority and reason, until at a certain appointed time, it may confirm the truest form of religion through miracles among all nations, as it once did.

Led, therefore, by divine providence, we have interpreted the divine **Plato** and the great **Plotinus**. We sent Plato himself to you long ago, so that he might one day live again in your presence—the same Plato in whom your grandfather **Cosimo** lived again, and in whose care you grew up according to his wishes, and now happily flourish in your maturity. We are now, and always will be, sending Plotinus to you; or rather, we do not so much "send" him as watch him hurry to your house of his own accord and with alacrity. He is drawn from Plato himself, like iron by a **Herculean stone** <note>a magnet</note>, so that he may live most happily with his Plato in your care, O magnanimous **Lorenzo**, unique patron of men of letters. 

Hear Plotinus, then, speaking happily with you and Plato about all the mysteries of philosophy. But before you listen to him, you must listen to **Porphyry**, his pious disciple, who recounts the life, character, and deeds of his master most briefly and truly. Our student **Angelo Poliziano**, your protégé—a man of the sharpest judgment—deems this history to be as much a work of oratory as of philosophy; for that reason, it will please you greatly. Finally, do not only listen happily, but also live most happily. And as much as you love us, dearest Lorenzo, I pray that you love our **Filippo Valori** <note>a Florentine nobleman and friend of Ficino who funded the printing of this book</note>, an excellent man and a student of Platonic wisdom, who loves you ardently.

# EXHORTATION OF MARSILIO FICINO
## THE FLORENTINE TO THE AUDIENCE AND READERS OF PLOTINUS.

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or philosopher, within a classical architectural frame surrounded by foliage.</image-desc>First, I advise all of you who approach here to hear the divine Plotinus: consider that you are about to hear Plato himself speaking through the mask <note>original: "persona"</note> of Plotinus. For either Plato once lived again in Plotinus—which the **Pythagoreans** <term>Pythagoreans: followers of Pythagoras who believed in the transmigration of souls, or reincarnation</term> will easily grant us—or the same **Spirit** <term>Spirit: or "Dæmon," a divine intermediary or guiding genius that inspires great thinkers</term> first inspired Plato and then later Plotinus, which no Platonists will deny. In every way, the same inspirer breathes through the Platonic mouth as through the Plotinian. 

Yet, in inspiring Plato, the spirit poured out more abundantly; but in Plotinus, the breath was tighter—though I should not say tighter, but rather no less majestic <note>original: "augustũ"</note>, and sometimes nearly more profound. Therefore, the same divinity pours out divine oracles for the human race through both mouths. In both cases, a very sharp interpreter is required: one who, in the former [Plato], might labor in unwrapping the coverings of his fables, and in the latter [Plotinus], might work more diligently both in expressing the most secret meanings everywhere and in explaining his very brief words. 

Remember, moreover, that you will penetrate the sublime mind of Plotinus not with the senses as your companion nor with human reason as your guide, but by a certain higher **mind** <note>The "higher mind" or *Mens* refers to the intuitive faculty above discursive logic</note>. Indeed (to speak in the Platonic way), we call other men "rational souls," but Plotinus we call not a "soul" but "Intellect." So all philosophers of his age, especially the Platonists, used to name him. 

And would that the help of **Porphyry**, or **Eustochius**, or **Proclus**—who arranged and explained the books of Plotinus—were here with us in interpreting these mysteries. I hope, however, for that which is far more fortunate: that divine help will not fail Marsilio Ficino in translating and explaining the divine books of Plotinus. But now, with heavenly auspices, let us happily proceed to translate the first book of Plotinus, to explain its argument briefly, and then the rest in order. And you should imagine Plato himself shouting thus toward Plotinus: "Run here to my beloved disciple and hear him!"

->MARSILIO FICINO<-
->To the Great-Souled Piero de' Medici<-
->Greetings<- <note>original: "S," abbreviation for "Salutem," a standard Latin greeting</note>

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental initial 'C' featuring dense floral and acanthus leaf scrollwork.</image-desc>*When I was walking together with Lorenzo the Magnificent <note>original: "Magno Laurentio Medice," Ficino's patron</note> at the Careggi estate <note>the Medici villa where the Platonic Academy met</note> on the Ides of November, and we were interpreting many mysteries of Plato back and forth, the conversation happened to fall from wisdom into **fortune**, and I began to blame the latter more sharply for obstructing Plato’s light for so many centuries. Then he said: "Marsilio, do not call our Plato unfortunate, unless perhaps you think that I am going to be unfortunate." We concluded our conversation then with these words.*

*But is it permitted to think Lorenzo unfortunate because death followed afterward? And that Plato’s fortune has collapsed entirely? Far be it from me to think that soul less happy, which, flying out from the shackles of the body, the joyful upper air <note>original: "æther"</note> received with a new sort of applause. For a great star fell upon the roofs of the Medici, and wondrous flames from on high flashed through the Careggi fields for three days. But two days before his death, Jupiter <note>a reference to lightning</note>, with his reddening right hand, struck the sacred towers <note>likely the lantern of the Florence Cathedral</note> and terrified the world—soon to be orphaned of such a father. He terrified the enemies, lest they perhaps attempt anything grave against the invincible Medici house.* 

*Therefore, neither the Hero Lorenzo, nor the heroic Piero, son of Lorenzo, is to be judged less happy hereafter because of what has recently happened; nor for that reason is our Plato unfortunate. His head was until now sheltered by the truly healthy shade of the **Laurel** <note>original: "Lauri," a pun on Lorenzo's name</note>. Now his feet rest upon a most firm **Rock** <note>original: "petra," a pun on Piero’s name</note>. Finally, Plotinus, now held in your hands, was meanwhile supporting the elder Plato on his pious shoulders, and under your leadership, he will lead him into the light.*

# THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS, AND THE ORDER
## OF HIS BOOKS, BY PORPHYRY,
### with Marsilio Ficino the Florentine as translator.
### Porphyry on the life of Plotinus, and the arrangement of his books.

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<language>English</language>

<margin>Plotinus despised a life of delicacies and empty glory; a dragon appeared everywhere.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> Plotinus, the philosopher who lived in our times, seemed to be affected by a singular sort of shame because his soul was in a body. Because of this disposition, he could not bear to talk about his lineage, <margin>A</margin> nor his parents, nor his homeland, nor did he ever mention the year in which he was born. 
<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, he so strongly disdained handing over his physical likeness to be expressed by painters or sculptors that when Amelius begged him to allow an image of himself to be made, he replied: "Is it not enough to bear this image <note>Original Greek: *eidolon*; refers to the physical body as a mere shadow or reflection of the true soul.</note> which nature has already wrapped around us from the beginning? Must we also consent to leave behind a longer-lasting image of an image for posterity, as if it were a work worthy of being seen?" Since he firmly refused this and would not sit still for a painter’s work, <margin>B</margin> Amelius commanded his friend Carterius—the finest painter of those times—to attend Plotinus’s lectures. (For anyone who wished was allowed to attend these gatherings of disputation). 

Amelius then accustomed the painter, through long and close attention, to conceive the most vivid mental images from his observations. <margin>C</margin> Then, while Carterius rendered the likeness correctly from the image committed to his memory, and while Amelius simultaneously corrected the lines to achieve a closer resemblance, the painter’s skill produced a portrait of Plotinus that was a perfect likeness, without Plotinus even knowing it. 

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, as he was often troubled by a colonic disease, he always refused enemas, saying it was not fitting for an old man to undergo such treatments. Nor did he ever accept <term>theriaca</term><note>A famous ancient "universal" medicine or antidote made of many herbal and animal ingredients.</note> antidotes, saying that he did not even take food from the bodies of tame animals <note>Plotinus was a vegetarian, believing that eating animals weighed down the soul.</note>. He also abstained from baths, but used daily massages at home. <margin>E</margin> However, when a plague grew beyond measure and those who performed his massages died of the disease, he entirely neglected such treatments and gradually fell into <term>angina</term><note>A severe inflammation of the throat; the Greek text uses "cynanche," literally "dog-strangle."</note>. 

Indeed, while I was present, that malady never gave any indication of itself. But after I had departed, the plague of this disease grew so strong (as my friend Eustochius later told me upon my return—he who never left Plotinus’s side until his death) that all the vigor of that clear, sonorous, and rounded voice departed through extreme hoarseness. <margin>F</margin> His vision became blurred, and his hands and feet became ulcerated. For this reason, because his friends no longer greeted him—since he had the habit of addressing everyone personally <unclear>with his own mouth</unclear>—

<column-break/>

<margin>F</margin> ...the disease had progressed. <note>The text here transitions into the physical toll of his final illness, emphasizing the Neoplatonic theme of the body's decay compared to the soul's endurance.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the biography of the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus, detailing his extreme modesty regarding his physical existence and his refusal to have his portrait painted, which led his student Amelius to have one made in secret.</summary>

<header>PLOTINUS’S LIFE.</header>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>

He departed from the city and secluded himself in Campania, brought to the estate of his old friend Zethus, who had already passed away. His needs were supplied by the heirs of Zethus, and provisions were also brought from the lands of Castricius in Minturnae. Castricius indeed held estates in Minturnae. As the death of Plotinus approached—as reported to us by Eustochius <note>Eustochius was a physician and one of Plotinus's most devoted students, who attended him in his final illness.</note>, who lived in Puteoli and arrived to see him somewhat late—Plotinus said: "I am still waiting for you; I am even now striving to lead back the divine within us to the divine that flourishes in the universe." With these words, he released his spirit. Meanwhile, a serpent <note>Original: *draco*. In antiquity, a house-snake was often seen as a protective spirit or a symbol of the soul's liberation.</note> that had been under the bed where he lay crawled away and hid itself in a hole in the wall. Plotinus was then sixty-six years old (as Eustochius reported), with the second year of Emperor Claudius's reign <note>Claudius Gothicus, roughly 270 AD.</note> having just concluded. At the time Plotinus departed from this life, I, Porphyry, was staying in Lilybaeum; Amelius was in Apamea in Syria; but Castricius was in Rome. Only Eustochius was present at the end. Now, if we calculate back sixty-six years from the second year of Emperor Claudius, the time of his birth coincides with the thirteenth year of Emperor Severus <note>Septimius Severus, placing Plotinus's birth around 204 or 205 AD.</note>. He never declared to anyone the month or the day he was born, for he thought it was by no means fitting that his birthday be celebrated with sacrifices or banquets. However, he himself used to perform sacred rites on the traditional birthdays of Plato and Socrates, and would host his friends at a banquet; there, it was expected that all friends who were able should recite a formal discourse before the assembled company. The things he himself often told us in our conversations regarding his own life are as follows:

<margin>
On the education of Plotinus, and the disciplines under Ammonius, from which he was afterward inspired.
</margin>

He recalled that when he was in his eighth year of age, and already attending school, he was still in the habit of going to his nurse and greedily uncovering her breasts to suckle. But when he was eventually told how troublesome a boy he was being, he stopped out of a sense of shame. After this, when he was completing his twenty-eighth year, he was set on fire by a powerful love for philosophy. He was recommended to those who were then considered the most excellent teachers in Alexandria; but he came away from their schools deeply saddened, and declared the cause of his grief to a certain friend. This friend, clearly understanding the desire of his mind, led him to Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, the mysterious "self-taught" philosopher whom many consider the father of Neoplatonism.</note>, whom Plotinus had not yet tried. When he entered Ammonius's school and heard him speak, he said to his friend: "This is the very man I was looking for!" From 그날 on, he listened to Ammonius diligently for eleven years. He made such progress in that philosophy that he desired to make a trial of the philosophy practiced by the Persians, and even determined to pursue the wisdom especially esteemed among the Indians. Therefore, when Emperor Gordian <note>Gordian III, who led an ill-fated campaign against the Sassanid Persian Empire.</note> was about to set out for Persia to bring war to those people, Plotinus joined the army, being then about thirty-nine years old. But after Gordian was killed near Mesopotamia, Plotinus barely escaped with his life and reached Antioch in safety. Later, during the reign of Philip, he came to Rome at the age of forty.

<column-break/>

**A** He departed from the city. Coming into Campania, to the estate of Zethus, an old friend of his who had died, he stayed there. His necessities were brought to him from the heirs of Zethus and from Castricius in Minturnae (for Castricius had his possessions in Minturnae). When he was about to die, as Eustochius related to us—since he was living in Puteoli and arrived somewhat

**B** slowly to see him—Plotinus said, "I have been waiting for you," and said he was trying *to lead the divine in you* <gloss>the divine in us</gloss> <note>The Greek text notes a variant: the original scribe wrote "in you," but the correction "in us" is provided in the margin/gloss.</note> back to the divine in the universe. A serpent passed under the bed on which he lay and went into a hole that was in the wall, and he gave up his spirit. He was, as Eustochius said, sixty-six years old, the second year of Claudius's reign being completed. When he died, I, Porphyry, happened to be dwelling in Lilybaeum; Amelius

**C** was in Apamea of Syria; Castricius was in Rome; only Eustochius was present. Counting back sixty years from the second year of Claudius's reign, the time of his birth falls in the thirteenth year of Severus's reign. He did not reveal to anyone which day he was born, nor the day of the new moon, nor

**D** did he care to come to his own birthday celebrations. Yet on the traditional birthdays of Plato or Socrates, he would sacrifice and feast his companions, where he required those companions who were able to read a discourse; and these things he himself often related from his own memory in our meetings, and they are as follows.

**E** He said that in the eighth year of his age, while already going to a grammar-teacher, even until the eighth year from his birth, he would go to his nurse and desire to suckle her breasts. But hearing that he was being a nuisance to the children, he desisted out of shame. In his twenty-eighth year, he was impelled to pursue philosophy. He was introduced to those who were highly regarded in Alexandria, but he came away from their lectures downcast and full of grief. He told one of his friends what he was feeling, and the friend, understanding the will of his soul, took him to Ammonius, whom he had not

**F** yet tried. Having entered and heard him, he said to his companion, "This is the one I was seeking." And from that day he remained continuously with Ammonius, and acquired such a habit in philosophy that he was impelled to gain a trial of the knowledge of the Persians and that which is practiced among the Indians. When Emperor Gordian was about to go against the Persians, Plotinus gave himself to the camp and followed, being now thirty-nine years old. And when he was in Greece,

**G** the teachings of Ammonius remained with him; but after Gordian was killed in Mesopotamia, he barely escaped by flight and was saved in Antioch. And when Philip had seized the throne, being forty years old...

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s biography of Plotinus, specifically detailing his early years in Rome, his relationship with his teacher Ammonius Saccas, and the beginning of his career as a writer and teacher.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS’S LIFE.</header>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>

...having become forty years of age when he was introduced to Ammonius. <margin>7 a</margin> Origen <note>This refers to Origen the Pagan, a contemporary philosopher, not the famous Christian theologian of the same name.</note> and Erennius likewise kept the agreements they had made with Plotinus: not to disclose the doctrines of Ammonius, which had been thoroughly clarified for them in his lectures. Plotinus also remained faithful to this, even with those who approached him, keeping the doctrines received from Ammonius unpublicized. However, Erennius was the first to violate the agreements. Origen then followed the example of Erennius, who had preceded him. Yet Origen wrote nothing more than a treatise *On Demons* and, during the reign of Gallienus, a work titled *That the King is the Only Creator*. <note>Original: *hoti monos poiētēs ho basileus*. This may refer to Emperor Gallienus's interest in the arts or a metaphysical point regarding the 'First Principle' as King.</note> Plotinus, for his part, continued for ten years without writing anything, conducting his sessions based on the time spent with Ammonius. Even though he continued for these ten years, though healthy in mind, he wrote nothing. But since his classes were entirely (at that time) full of the zeal of those approaching him, they were full of disorder and much idle chatter, as he allowed them to spread out in a somewhat careless manner. Amelius <note>Plotinus’s chief assistant and student for over two decades.</note> came to him when Plotinus was in his third year in Rome, during the third year of Philip's reign. <note>Emperor Philip the Arab, approx. 246 AD.</note> Having remained until the first year of Claudius’s reign, he spent twenty-four years in total with him. When he first arrived, he came from the school of Lysimachus. Surpassing all his contemporaries in his love of labor, he either transcribed or collected nearly all the works of Numenius <note>Numenius of Apamea, a philosopher whose blend of Platonism and Pythagoreanism was a major influence on Neoplatonism.</note> and committed most of them to memory. Taking notes from the lectures, he compiled one hundred books of these notebooks, which he left as an inheritance to Hesychius of Apamea, whom he had adopted as his son. In the tenth year of Gallienus’s reign, I, Porphyry, having come from Greece with Antonius of Rhodes, found Amelius already in his eighteenth year of association with Plotinus. He had not yet dared to write anything beyond the great number of notebooks he had issued in a disorganized fashion. Plotinus himself, in the tenth year of Gallienus’s reign, was about fifty-nine years old. I, Porphyry, first joined him when I was thirty years old. From the first year of Gallienus's rule, Plotinus had been encouraged to write on the subjects that occurred to him; thus, by the thirteenth year of Gallienus's rule, when I, Porphyry, first became known to him, he was found to have written twenty-one books, which I received as they had been distributed to only a few. For their publication was not yet easy, nor was it done in a prepared way, nor simply at random, but they were received only after careful judgment. For this reason, and because he did not provide titles himself, different people gave different titles to each work. However, the titles that prevailed are as follows:

| On the Beautiful. | On the Immortality of the Soul. |
|-------------------|--------------------------------|
| On Fate. | On the Essence of the Soul. |

On Intellect, the Ideas, and Being.
On the Descent of the Soul into Bodies.
How that which follows the First comes from the First; and On the One.
Whether all Souls are One.
On the Good, or the One.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Being now forty years of age. But since Erennius, Origen, and Plotinus had long ago agreed among themselves not to publish the doctrines of Ammonius, which they had heard from him and which they had first purified and thoroughly approved. Plotinus indeed stood by his promises, receiving several people in a similar way, yet preserving the secret and intact teachings of Ammonius. <margin>Note on Origen: Not the Christian.</margin> Erennius, however, was the first to break the pact: and Origen followed Erennius who had gone before him: but he wrote nothing except a certain book *On Demons*. <margin>B</margin> And under the reign of Gallienus, a book in which he perhaps proved that the King alone is [maker]. Plotinus, however, entirely desisted from writing, and for ten years straight he introduced into his conversations only those things which he had formerly received from his association with Ammonius; and so he persevered for ten whole years. While admitting several to his conversation, he wrote nothing. But because he had permitted or invited his friends to question him at their discretion, Amelius said that those sessions were full of a certain confusion and trifles. Nevertheless, this Amelius <margin>C</margin> came to him at Rome when he had already been there for three years, in the third year of Emperor Philip: and he persevered with him until the first year of Emperor Claudius: and so he lived with him for twenty-four whole years. When he first brought himself to Plotinus, he was possessed only of that training which he had conceived from his friendship with Lysimachus. In his endurance of labor, he surpassed all his fellow-disciples, because he wrote down and brought together almost all the doctrines of Numenius, and committed most of them to memory. <margin>D</margin> From his very zeal for hearing, he gathered certain scholarly notebooks and composed about one hundred books from them, which he gave as a gift to a certain Hesychius of Apamea, his adopted son. In the tenth year of Emperor Gallienus, I, Porphyry, came to Rome from Greece together with Antonius of Rhodes. There I found Amelius, who had already been in familiar association with Plotinus for eighteen years, yet had not yet dared to write anything except certain notebooks as I have said, <margin>E</margin> which had not yet grown to the number of one hundred. Accordingly, in the tenth year of Emperor Gallienus, Plotinus was now about fifty-nine years old: but I, Porphyry, when I first attached myself to him, had then completed thirty years. Plotinus indeed in the first year of Emperor Gallienus turned himself to writing whatever questions occurred to him: but by the tenth year of the same, when I, Porphyry, became known to Plotinus, he had already written <margin>F</margin> twenty-one books: which I found had been handed over to a few people. For as yet publication was not easy, nor was anyone aware of them: for nothing was published easily or rashly: but only those received them who were approved by a certain mature judgment. These things had already been written, which <unclear>certainly</unclear> different people had inscribed with different titles. The titles, therefore, which more widely prevailed, are of this sort.

**A** **On Providence, the second book.**

**B** These then, in the first year of the reign of Emperor Claudius <note>Claudius II Gothicus, who reigned from 268 to 270 AD.</note>, or the beginning of the second—shortly before he died—he sent these following works:
**On what are evils.**
**Whether the stars act.**
**What is the living being, and what is man.**
**On the first good, and other goods.**

**C** These, together with the forty-five books previously sent to me, make fifty-four in total. Just as some were written in his early youth, others in his prime, and others when his body was worn down, so too do the books reflect these varying powers. For the first twenty-one are of a lighter strength, not yet having reached the height of intensity and greatness; but those of the middle period show the peak of his power. These are the books found in the <term>Enneads</term> <note>The 'Enneads' (meaning 'Groups of Nine') is the name given to the collected works of Plotinus as organized by Porphyry.</note>, except for a few short ones. The late works and the final four show a more relaxed faculty, even more so than the five preceding them.

**D** He had many listeners, but those who were his true followers and lived with him for the sake of Philosophy included Amelius from Tuscany, whose proper name was Gentilianus. He himself, however, preferred to be called **Amerius** with an 'R', as if from 'indivisibility' <note>original: "ἀμερείας" (amereias). A play on words between the name Amelius and the Greek word for 'indivision' vs 'neglect'.</note>, rather than Amelius with an 'L'. There was also Paulinus of Scythopolis, whom Amelius nicknamed 'Miccalus' <note>Meaning 'The Little One'.</note>.

**E** Furthermore, there was Eustochius of Alexandria, another physician, who came to know him toward the end of his life and remained caring for him until his death. Devoting himself only to the teachings of Plotinus, he took on the character of a true Philosopher. There was also Zoticus, a critic and poet, who corrected the works of Antimachus and turned the Atlantic history into verse <note>Likely referring to the story of Atlantis mentioned in Plato’s works.</note>; he later suffered from failing eyesight and died shortly before Plotinus. Paulinus also died before his companion. There was also Theodosius, who took the daughter of Ammonius <note>Plotinus's own teacher</note> in marriage.

**F** There was also Zethus, a physician of Arabian descent, who was very dear to Plotinus. Since Zethus was involved in politics and had political influence, Plotinus tried to lead him back [to philosophy]. He was on such familiar terms with him that he would even retreat to Zethus's estates in the countryside.

**G** Castricius, called Firmus, possessed estates sixty miles away. He was, in our time, the greatest lover of beauty and excellence, and he revered Plotinus. He served Amelius in all things like a good servant, and he treated me, Porphyry, in every way as a true...

On the knowing substances, and those above them.

**B** These books, therefore, he sent to me in the first year of the Emperor Claudius; or rather, between the beginning of the second year and shortly before he departed from this life. He also sent these:
**What are evils.**

**What is man; What is the animal.**
**On the first good, and other goods.**

**C** These books, together with the first forty-five written over time, are calculated as fifty-four in total. Just as some were written in his first age, some in the very vigor of his life, and finally some when his body was weak, so the books declare a similar strength. For the first twenty-one, if compared with those immediately following, seem to have a gentler power, not yet possessing a sufficiently constant strength. But those composed in the middle period show the flower of his virtue at its summit. Such are the twenty-four (except for a few) of perfection. Finally, the last nine reflect a more relaxed faculty, and the final four show this more than the five preceding them.

**D** He had many listeners indeed, but his imitators and those very familiar with him for the sake of philosophy were Amelius the Tuscan and others. Also Paulinus of Scythopolis, very studious of medicine, whom Amelius called 'Miccalus'.

**E** Moreover, Eustochius of Alexandria was also a physician, who was born to Plotinus <note>Meaning he became his 'spiritual son' or student.</note> near the last period of his life and remained with him, diligently admiring and caring for Plotinus; by the institutions of Plotinus alone, he took on the habit of a legitimate philosopher. But by that time, Zoticus was also with him, a critic and poet, who corrected the works of Antimachus and translated the Atlantic history into a poetic style; after this, he fell into darkness of the eyes <note>original: "caliginé incidit oculoru" - he went blind.</note>, and died a little before the death of Plotinus.

**F** Paulinus also died a day before Plotinus. Furthermore, Zethus was very familiar to Plotinus, deriving his race from Arabia, who had also married the daughter of a certain Theodosius, a familiar of Ammonius. He was also skilled in medicine and very dear to Plotinus; Plotinus used to strive to call him back from the weights of civil government and used him familiarly, so much so that they would retreat to his lands at the sixth milestone before Minturnae, which Castricius possessed.

**G** Surnamed Firmus, he was truly a man most studious of all the good arts of our age, and more observant of Plotinus and Amelius; he even served with the devotion of a servant, and to me, Porphyry, in all things no differently than to a legitimate...

<margin>
Plotinus’s remarkable speed of composition: for with his mind intensely focused, he wrote things down with a certain negligence of hand.

**A** ...devoted to his brother. Although he chose a civic life, he nonetheless venerated Plotinus above all others. Not a few Senators also diligently listened to Plotinus: among whom Marcellus Orontius applied himself most studiously to philosophy and made the greatest progress; then there were Sabinillus and likewise Rogatianus from the same senate. Rogatianus so far removed himself from the concerns of this life that he neglected the care of his own property, dismissed all his servants, and rejected his honors. Indeed, when he was about to go forth as a <term>Praetor</term> <note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate</note> and the <term>lictors</term> <note>Bodyguards and attendants who carried the symbols of a magistrate's power</note> were already standing by, he neither went forth nor took any account of his public duty. He did not even live in his own <term>lares</term> <note>Original: "lares"; referring here to his ancestral home or household</note>, but staying with various friends and associates, he spent his time <unclear>among</unclear> <unclear>soldiers</unclear> <unclear>and</unclear> judges <unclear>as if</unclear> in enlightenment <unclear>and those</unclear> <unclear>matters</unclear> <unclear>which</unclear> <unclear>externally</unclear> <unclear>hindered</unclear> him. By this way of life, though he had been so afflicted by gout that he had to be carried in a litter and could not walk, he finally regained his strength; furthermore, whereas he previously could not extend his hands, they recovered through his moderate lifestyle so that he could use them more skillfully than those who practice manual crafts every day. **C** Plotinus, therefore, embraced this man above all others, extolled him with wonderful praises, and held him up as a distinguished example for those intending to practice philosophy. There was also Serapion of Alexandria: formerly a rhetorician, but thereafter devoted to philosophical disputes, though he was not yet able to free himself from the vices of greed and meanness. He also had me, Porphyry, a Tyrian by birth, numbered among his closest friends, whom he appointed to correct his writings.

---

**D** For when he had written something, he could not bear to look over it a second time, nor even to read it through once, because his eyesight was not sufficient for reading. While he was writing, he did not even form the letters beautifully, nor did he distinguish syllables exactly, nor did he apply any care to orthography <note>Correct spelling and punctuation</note>; he was clearly focused only on the intellect of his mind, and to the wonder of us all, he continued to do this until the end of his life. **E** For once he had conceived a whole arrangement from beginning to end in his mind, and then committed what he had conceived to writing, he connected his thoughts so continuously as he wrote that it seemed as if he were transcribing from a book placed before his eyes. Even if he happened to be talking with guests, or composing matters pertaining to human business, he never <unclear>departed</unclear> from the internal action of his mind; thus he could simultaneously take care of a friend's business and keep the things he had conceived in his thoughts, **F** preserving his mental focus perpetually intent. Therefore, when the person who had been speaking with him had left, he did not re-read what he had written, since his sight (as we have said) was not at all up to the task; yet he would connect the subsequent parts as if he had not interrupted his original purpose for even the slightest moment while listening to and dealing with human affairs. Thus, he was both with himself and with others at the same time, and he never interrupted that focus of the mind directed toward himself, except perhaps while he slept—though even sleep he largely shook off through his meager diet (often abstaining even from bread) and his constant turning of himself toward the Mind.

->(For this often... ) and the [attention] toward himself.<-

<column-break/>

**A** ...his brother, to whom he attended in all things... to venerate Plotinus, even though he had chosen a political life. Not a few of the Senators also made it their work to be his friends, especially Marcellus Orontius and Sabinillus. Among these was Rogatianus, who also came from the Senate and turned away from the <unclear>shame</unclear> of a pragmatic life, so that he gave up all his possessions, and these things he gave to Plotinus. So much so that when he was about to proceed as a Praetor and the attendants were standing by, he neither came forward nor cared for the liturgy <note>Public service or office</note>, but choosing not even to have his own house, he went to stay with certain friends or acquaintances. There he lived and ate only every other day, and from this **C** departure and unconcerned way of life, though he had previously been unable to walk and had to be carried in a chair, he appeared restored. His hands, which he had not been able to use, he could now use much more easily than those who follow crafts with their hands. Plotinus received him and continued to praise him greatly, setting him up as a good example for those who study philosophy. Serapion the Alexandrian was also with him, a rhetorician at first, but later coming to philosophy through discourses, though he was still hindered by matters of money. And there was us, Porphyry, who was especially his companion, and he tasked me with the duty of correcting his writings as he produced them.

---

**D** For having written, he was unable to look over his handwriting so as to see it clearly. He would not read it through even once because his vision did not serve him for reading. He wrote without forming the letters beautifully, nor dividing the syllables, nor caring for orthography, but only holding to the meaning, which we all marveled at. This he continued to do until the end. **E** For having gathered the whole subject in himself from the beginning to the end, he then committed to writing what he had contemplated, and he wrote as if the thoughts were being joined in his soul as if from a book. Even while talking to someone and joining in conversations, he was able to fulfill the necessity of the talk while keeping his mind uninterrupted in those matters which were set before him in his contemplation. **F** When the person he was talking to had left, he did not need to go over the written parts, because his vision (as we said) was not sufficient for re-reading, but he would join the next parts as if no time had passed between the conversation. He was therefore with himself and others at the same time, and the attention toward himself **G** never relaxed, except only in sleep, which he kept at bay through the small amount of food he took and his constant turning toward his own mind.

->A<-
He also had several women who were deeply devoted to him. Among their number was Gemina, in whose household he actually lived. There was also her daughter, likewise named Gemina. Another was Amphicleia, the daughter of Ariston and wife of the son of Iamblichus <note>A significant later Neoplatonist philosopher; his son was likely part of this intellectual circle</note>. Many noble men and women, when they were near death, would bring their children to him—both boys and girls—and entrust them to him along with all their property, as if to a certain holy and divine guardian. 

<margin>Women devoted to Plotinus.</margin>
<margin>Among whom was Gemina, in whose home Plotinus lived. He was a diligent guardian of the orphans' estates, ensuring they were well-managed.</margin>

->B<-
Thus, you could see Plotinus’s house filled with youths and maidens. Among them was Potamon, whom Plotinus educated with great care; he would even listen attentively whenever Potamon was about to change something <note>Likely referring to revisions in his studies or exercises</note>. Nor did he find it tedious to hear the reports of the orphans' trustees or to review the accounts of their administration. He applied a diligent thriftiness to their care, affirming that as long as they were not yet practicing philosophy, it was only just that they should possess their property and receive their income without any loss.

->C<-
And although he provided for the necessary expenses of so many orphans with such diligence, he never—while he was awake—relaxed the intensity of his mind, which remained turned toward his inner spirit. He was also exceedingly mild-tempered and available to anyone who sought his company in any way. For this reason, although he lived in Rome for twenty-six full years and acted as an arbiter in many disputes, he never had a single enemy among the citizens.

->D<-
<margin>Plotinus overcame the influence of a rival: he shows the power of fate to the gods: he commands with confidence.</margin>
However, among those who claimed to study philosophy, there was one Olympius of Alexandria. He had been a student of Ammonius for a short time, and because he desired to claim the first rank in philosophy for himself, he looked down on Plotinus and tried to make others despise him as well. With such intense malice, he attacked Plotinus, attempting to "star-strike" <note>original: "siderare"; referring to a form of baleful astrological magic or a "blasting" spell</note> him through certain magical machinations. But after he felt his efforts recoiling back upon himself, he said to his associates that the power of Plotinus’s soul was so great that it could immediately turn attacks aimed at him back upon the evildoers. 

->E<-
Indeed, Plotinus noticed as soon as Olympius began his magical attempts, and he said to his friends: "Right now, Olympius’s body is being contracted like a purse <note>original: "marsupiorum"; a drawstring bag or purse</note>, and all his limbs are being crushed together." When Olympius had experienced many times, at his own peril, that Plotinus was repelling his strikes back at him, he finally ceased his malice. And truly, from the very beginning, Plotinus possessed something greater than others by his very nature. 

->F<-
For a certain Egyptian priest who had come to Rome became acquainted with Plotinus through a friend. Wishing to give a demonstration of his own wisdom in Rome, he persuaded Plotinus to join him so that he might summon Plotinus’s "companion spirit" <note>original: "Dæmonem"; in the Greek sense of a personal guardian or guiding spirit, not an evil entity</note> so that they might see it. Plotinus easily agreed. This invocation of the spirit took place in the Temple of Isis, for the Egyptian said he could find no other "pure" place in Rome. 

->G<-
But when the spirit was summoned to appear before their eyes, a God appeared instead of a mere spirit. At this, the Egyptian suddenly cried out: "Blessed are you, O Plotinus, you who have a God for a guardian spirit, rather than one from the lower orders!" <note>The hierarchy of being suggested that Plotinus’s soul was so refined it was guided by a divine being (theos) rather than a subordinate spirit (daemon)</note>
