<meta>This page continues Porphyry's biography of his teacher, Plotinus. The previous page concluded with Plotinus’s role as a guardian to orphans and his constant state of intellectual focus.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS

<column-break/>

...of a superior kind, you have been allotted a divine spirit as a companion. Plotinus related that it was not permitted then to ask any further questions, nor to see the spirit present for any longer; for a certain companion who was watching there with them <note>likely a reference to an Egyptian priest or a temple official mentioned earlier in the narrative</note> strangled the birds he was holding in his hands for protection, whether led by envy or terrified by fear. Therefore, since Plotinus possessed a companion spirit from the more divine order of Spirits <term>daemons: in the Neoplatonic sense, these were personal guardian spirits or tutelary divinities, not "demons" in the modern sense</term>, he rightly and always raised the divine eye of his mind more sublimely toward it. For this reason, he later composed a book concerning the spirit companion allotted to each of us, wherein he certainly attempts to diligently present the causes for the differences among these companion deities. Furthermore, when Amelius—who was a diligent observer of sacred rites and performed sacrifices on the new moons—once asked Plotinus to join him in visiting the gods, Plotinus replied: "It is for those gods to come to me, not for me to go to those gods." In what state of mind he spoke such lofty words about himself, we ourselves could neither understand nor did we dare to ask. He was also exceptionally shrewd and tireless in perceiving character. Thus, when a certain woman named Chione, who lived with him along with her children and lived a life of chaste widowhood, had a very precious necklace stolen, and all the servants and household members were summoned into Plotinus’s presence, Plotinus looked at each one and picked one out, saying: "This man stole the necklace." Though the man denied it for a long time even under beating, he eventually confessed and restored the stolen item. Similarly, he would wonderfully predict what the future would be for each of the boys in the household. For instance, he predicted of Polemon: "This one will be more prone to lust and will not reach a mature age." And so it happened. At one time, I [Porphyry] was contemplating taking my own life, which he perceived in a miraculous way. While I was walking at home, he stood before me and said that such a thought was not from a sound mind, but rather from a soul raging with black bile <term>melancholy: ancient medicine attributed suicidal depression to an excess of black bile</term>. Therefore, he ordered me to go to Rome. Obeying him, I set out for Sicily, especially since I heard that a certain virtuous and refined man was then living near Lilybaeum. By this deed, I was freed from that perturbation of mind, but meanwhile I was prevented from leading my life alongside Plotinus until his death.

<margin>
He wished to build Platonopolis.
</margin>
Accordingly, the Emperor Gallienus and his wife Salonina honored and greatly esteemed Plotinus. Relying on their goodwill, he prayed that they might restore a certain ruined city in Campania that had once been suitable for philosophers, and grant the surrounding region to the restored city, allowing the city to be governed by the laws of Plato for those who would live there. He asked that the city itself be called Platonopolis, and he promised he would move there to live with all his friends. 

<margin>
A sharp debater, with flowing and lovely speech; though careless in some pronunciations, he was profound in meaning.
</margin>
The Philosopher would have easily obtained his wish, had not certain of the Emperor’s associates—driven by envy, indignation, or some other unfair reason—sharply opposed it. In debates, he was vigorous in speaking, skillful in invention, and most ready to perceive the opportune point. However, he perhaps slipped in some of his pronunciations; for instance, he did not say *meminisse* <note>to remember</note> correctly, but said *meminille*; and he similarly misused certain other words. 

<margin>
He abundantly combined Platonic ideas with Peripatetic ones.
</margin>
Indeed, he followed this same flaw in his writing. Furthermore, while he was speaking, his mind shone forth...

<column-break/>

...of a lesser kind, he has been allotted a companion. He related that he could not ask anything because he who was present could not see it any longer, for the friends who were watching with them strangled the birds they held for protection, either out of envy or out of some fear. Since he had a companion from the more divine spirits, he himself continued raising his divine eye toward it. Indeed, for this reason and through such a cause, he also wrote a book about the spirit that has been allotted to us, where he tries to bring forth the causes for the difference of these companions. Amelius, having become a lover of sacrifices, observed the sacred rites at the new moon and the festivals in rotation. Once, when he asked Plotinus to visit the temples with him, Plotinus said: "It is for those ones to come to me, not for me to go to those ones." With what kind of thought he spoke so loftily, we ourselves were not able to understand, nor did we dare to ask him. There was in him such an abundance of understanding of character that he could find who was stealing even from a man's home. And once, when the oil of one of the children was spoiled, he predicted it. When a certain Chione's very expensive necklace was stolen, and the servants were gathered under Plotinus himself, he looked at them all and pointed one out. And though he was whipped and denied it more at first, he later confessed, brought the stolen thing, and returned it. He also foretold about each of the present children how they would turn out, as he said of Polemon that he would be amorous and short-lived, which also came to pass. And once when I [Porphyry] was thinking of taking myself out of life, he suddenly stood over me while I was staying in the house and said that this impulse was not from a sound state, but from some melancholic disease, and he ordered me to go abroad. Being persuaded, I went to Sicily, hearing that a certain famous man was staying near Lilybaeum. And so I was kept from such an impulse, but I was also hindered from being present with Plotinus until his death.

The Emperor Gallienus and his wife Salonina honored Plotinus most of all. He, being graced by their friendship, asked that a certain city of philosophers said to have existed in Campania, but otherwise in ruins, should be rebuilt, and the surrounding land gifted, and that those about to inhabit it should live according to the laws of Plato, and the name of the city should be called Platonopolis. There he promised he would withdraw with his companions. And it would have been most beautifully and easily accomplished for the Philosopher, if some of those who were with the King, envying or for some other wicked cause, had not hindered it. 

He was sufficient in his discourses, bold, and most capable of finding what was fitting; but in some words he made mistakes, and did not always remember correctly, but used certain strange names, which even in writing he was already accustomed to use.

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS

...until his face was lit up with light <note>This concludes the story from the previous page where Plotinus identified a thief through a piercing gaze; the light refers to the moment of revelation or the thief’s subsequent confession</note>. He was lovely to behold, but he was most beautiful to look upon when he was in the heat of a discussion. At those times, a light sweat would break out upon him. His gentleness shone through, and his kindness was evident in the way he handled questions. Indeed, when I, Porphyry, once questioned him for three days on how the soul is joined to the body, he persevered in his demonstration. This prompted a man named Thaumasius, who had entered the school and wished to hear general lectures, to say that he wanted to hear him speak from books <note>Thaumasius preferred a formal reading of texts over the back-and-forth questioning between Plotinus and Porphyry</note>. But when Porphyry continued to ask and answer, and Thaumasius could not endure it, Plotinus said: "If we do not resolve the difficulties raised by Porphyry’s questions, we shall not be able to say anything at all that can be written into a book." 

When he wrote, he was dense and full of thought, using more ideas than words, often expressing himself with a kind of divine inspiration <term>enthusiasm: from the Greek "enthousiasmos," meaning to be inhabited by a god or divine spirit</term> and deep emotion. He spoke not from mere tradition but from a sympathetic connection to the truth. Hidden within his writings are the doctrines of the Stoics <note>A school of philosophy that emphasized virtue, reason, and endurance</note> and the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching</note>. Indeed, Aristotle’s *Metaphysics* <note>original: "meta ta Physika," referring to Aristotle's "After the Physics"</note> is condensed within his work. No theorem of geometry, arithmetic, mechanics, optics, or music escaped him, though he did not devote himself to the practical execution of these arts. In his gatherings, the commentaries of Severus, Cronius, Numenius, Gaius, or Atticus were read aloud, as well as those of the Peripatetics, such as Aspasius, Alexander, and Adrastus. However, he never simply repeated what was in these books; he was unique and independent in his contemplation, bringing the mind of his teacher Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, the self-taught philosopher of Alexandria who was Plotinus’s primary influence</note> to his investigations. He reached his conclusions quickly and with few words. He would immediately grasp the theoretical heart of a matter. When Longinus’s work *On Principles* and his *Lover of Antiquity* were read to him, Plotinus remarked: "Longinus is a philologist <note>original: "Philologos." Plotinus means Longinus is a lover of words and scholarship, but not a true philosopher</note>, but certainly not a philosopher." When Origen <note>This refers to Origen the Platonist, a contemporary, not the famous Christian Father Origen</note> once came to his gathering, Plotinus turned red and wished to stand up. When Origen asked him to continue speaking, Plotinus replied that the desire to speak ceases when the speaker knows he is addressing those who already understand what he is about to say. After speaking briefly, he stood up and left.

Once, when I read a poem at the feast of Plato’s birthday concerning the "Sacred Marriage" <note>A mystical concept representing the union of the soul with the divine</note>, and someone present remarked that Porphyry must be mad because much of the poem was spoken in a mysterious and inspired manner, Plotinus said in the hearing of everyone: "You have shown yourself to be at once a poet, a philosopher, and a hierophant <term>hierophant: a priest who reveals holy mysteries</term>." On another occasion, the orator Diophanes read a defense of Alcibiades <note>A famous and controversial Athenian general who appears in Plato's "Symposium"</note>, arguing that for the sake of learning virtue, a student should submit himself even to sexual union with a teacher who is in love with him. Plotinus stood up several times during the reading as if to leave the assembly, but he restrained himself;

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...diffusing an inner light all the way to his face. He was indeed lovely in appearance, but while he was disputing, he seemed far more beautiful; for then a thin sweat, like dew, would distill from his face. Then a kindly gentleness would shine forth; then he appeared most placid in receiving questions, and sharp in resolving and loosening them. Indeed, when I, Porphyry, questioned him for three days on the specific condition of how the soul remains with the body, he continued to persevere in his demonstration. <margin>B</margin> When a certain man named Thaumasius entered the school and introduced the idea of a general discourse, saying he wished to hear Plotinus’s opinions in the form of written expositions, and Porphyry was instead asking and answering, Thaumasius could not tolerate such a dispute. But Plotinus objected: "Unless we dissolve the doubts by answering Porphyry’s questions, we shall not be able to put anything into a book in the form of a continuous commentary." He wrote with a certain intense sharpness and a manifold intellect. <margin>C</margin> He is indeed brief, but everywhere more abundant in sense than in words. He pours out many things while inspired by a divine power. Often he is wonderfully affected by the very subject he treats; nor does he speak with a simple discipline, but with a mind more ardently inspired by the thing itself. Inserted in his books are the hidden doctrines of the Stoics and the Peripatetics likewise; but especially the sentences of Aristotle collected in his *Metaphysics* press upon us there more frequently. Nothing escaped him at all that pertained to <margin>D</margin> geometry, arithmetic, mechanics, perspective, or music, although he did not settle down to execute these works as if they were his own primary task. In his schools, the commentaries of Severus, Cronius, Numenius, Gaius, and Atticus were read, along with those of the Platonic and Peripatetic philosophers such as Aspasius, Alexander, Adrastus, and whatever other commentaries might happen to fall into their hands. But nothing was said from these in a continuous drawl. For he was a law unto himself, and different from these in his contemplation. In discussing matters, he brought the intellect of Ammonius. <margin>E</margin> He would emerge from a reading quickly imbued with the text, and rising up, he would bring a fuller understanding of contemplation in a few words. When the book of Longinus and Phylarchaeus *On Principles* was read, Plotinus said: "Longinus is indeed a man of letters <note>original: "literarum studiosus," translating the Greek "philologos"</note>, but by no means a philosopher." When Origen once came into the schools, Plotinus, immediately having his cheeks suffused with a red blush, wished to rise. When asked by Origen to continue his sermon, he replied: "The zeal for speaking ceases when he who speaks perceives that he is addressing those who already know the very same things." And so, when he had discussed a <margin>F</margin> few things, he rose from that place.

***

When I had recited a poem about the "Sacred Marriage" on the birthday of Plato, and a certain person present <margin>He celebrates the birthday of Plato. He was the most modest of all.</margin> objected that Porphyry was insane, seeing that many things had been said there with a certain divine inspiration and the mystery of a secret thing, Plotinus said openly in the hearing of all: "You have demonstrated yourself to be at once a poet, a philosopher, and a priest." At one time, the orator Diophanes read a <margin>G</margin> defense for Alcibiades, who was reveling in Plato’s *Symposium*, attempting to prove that for the sake of learning virtue, one should expose oneself to a lover, even if that lover should affect a venereal union, to one who was about to demonstrate this very virtue. During the reading, Plotinus rose several times, as if he were about to suddenly depart from that gathering; nevertheless, he restrained himself;

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS

Soon after the assembly was dismissed, Plotinus ordered me to address the points made, so that I might refute the orator <note>original: "refellerẽ oratorem." This refers to Diophanes, who had given a speech arguing that a student should be willing to submit to sexual advances from a teacher for the sake of learning—a view Plotinus found abhorrent</note>. Since that man, Diophanes, would not allow me to have his book to read, I relied on the power of my memory to recall his arguments and wrote a rebuttal. Soon after, I recited it to the same audience. This brought Plotinus such joy that during the gathering he repeatedly called out: "Strike thus, that you may be a light to men!" <note>original: "Βάλλ᾿ οὕτως, αἴκεν τι φῶς εἴ ἄνδρεσσι γέναι." A quote from Homer’s Iliad (8.282), where Agamemnon encourages the archer Teucer</note>. Eubulus, a follower of Plato, wrote from Athens and sent writings to Rome concerning certain Platonic questions. Plotinus ordered these to be handed to me, instructing me to consider each point and report back to him. He also devoted effort to the principles of astronomy, though not in a strictly mathematical fashion <note>meaning he focused on the philosophical implications of the heavens rather than calculating planetary positions</note>; however, he applied himself more diligently to the claims of the astrologers. When he discovered that their predictions were not worthy of trust, he did not hesitate to frequently refute their omens in his own writings.

->A<-

->B<-

->C<-

<margin>
He wrote against certain Christian heretics, Adelphius and Aquilinus; and these others wrote against them as well.
</margin>
There were many Christians at that time, as well as others—heretics who had drifted away from the ancient philosophy. These included followers of Adelphius and Aquilinus. They possessed many books by Alexander of Libya, Philocomus, Demostratus, and Lydus, and they produced certain "revelations" attributed to Zoroaster <note>An ancient Persian prophet</note>, Zostrianus, Nicotheus, Allogenes, Mesus, and others of that kind. They deceived many, having already been deceived themselves, by asserting that Plato had not truly penetrated the depths of the <term>intelligible essence: the realm of pure thought and reality, as opposed to the physical world</term>. For this reason, Plotinus brought many arguments against them in his lectures. He also wrote a book against them, which we have titled *Against the Gnostics* <note>original: "contra Gnosticos." The Gnostics believed the physical world was an evil creation of a lesser god, a view Plotinus rejected in favor of the world's inherent beauty and order</note>, and he left the rest for us to examine and judge. Amelius, for his part, composed forty books in response to the book of Zostrianus. I, Porphyry, showed through many arguments that the book they titled "Zoroaster" was a modern forgery, fabricated by those who established this heresy to make it seem as though their doctrines were those of the ancient Zoroaster.

->D<-

<margin>
Many falsely accused Plotinus of following Numenius; very few truly understood his depth. Testimony of Amelius and Porphyry concerning the excellence of Plotinus's books.
</margin>
Many of the Greeks falsely accused Plotinus, claiming that he secretly usurped the doctrines of Numenius <note>Numenius of Apamea, a 2nd-century philosopher who combined Plato and Pythagoras</note>. Very few of them truly penetrated the meaning of his work. Because of this, Amelius wrote a book which we have titled *On the Difference Between the Doctrines of Plotinus and Numenius*. Amelius dedicated the book to me, Porphyry—or rather, he addressed me as "Basileus" <note>Greek for "King"</note>. This was because of my original name; in my native language <note>Syriac/Phoenician</note> I was called Malchus, which was also my father's name. "Malchus," when translated into the Greek language, is called "King" <note>original: "Basileus"</note>. This is why Longinus, when he dedicated his writings *On Impulse* to Cleodamus and me, addressed me as: "O Cleodamus and Malchus." But Amelius, translating the name just as Numenius had called Maximus "the Great" <note>Greek: "Megalos"</note>, likewise called Malchus "King." Amelius wrote: "Amelius to Basileus, greetings. Know for certain that I would never have sent a word on behalf of these illustrious men—regarding what you say is being spread about, that our friend's doctrines are traced back to Numenius of Apamea—had I not been moved by their own claims. It is clear that this talk arises from their own boastful talkativeness..."

->E<-

->F<-

->G<-

<column-break/>

After the assembly was dismissed, he ordered me, Porphyry, to write a refutation, as Diophanes was unwilling to give me the book. Recalling the arguments from memory, I wrote the response and read it aloud before the same gathered listeners. This gave Plotinus such great joy that even in his classes he would continually quote: "Strike thus, if you would be a light to men!" Eubulus, the successor of the Platonic school, sent commentaries on Platonic questions from Athens; he gave these to me, Porphyry, to look over, examine, and report back on what was written. He also paid attention to the rules regarding the stars, though not in a purely mathematical way, but more accurately to the results claimed by the casters of horoscopes. Detecting the lack of a guarantee in their promises, he frequently refuted their claims in his writings.

There were many Christians in his time, and others—heretics who had been led away from the ancient philosophy—such as those around Adelphius and Aquilinus. They owned a great many writings of Alexander the Libyan, Philocomus, Demostratus, and Lydus, and they brought forward revelations of Zoroaster, Zostrianus, Nicotheus, Allogenes, Mesus, and others of that sort. They deceived many, and were deceived themselves, claiming that Plato had not reached the depth of the intelligible essence. Therefore, he himself made many refutations in his lectures and wrote a book, which we titled *Against the Gnostics*, leaving the rest for us to decide upon. Amelius went as far as forty books in writing against the book of Zostrianus. And I, Porphyry, made frequent refutations against the book of Zoroaster, demonstrating that the book was a forgery and a modern invention by those who founded the heresy, designed to make people believe that the doctrines they chose to honor were the ancient teachings of Zoroaster.

Among those from Greece who said that he was presenting the ideas of Numenius as his own, and those around Amelius who reported these things, and those who secretly said his Platonic views were taken from Numenius, Amelius wrote a book which we titled *On the Difference of the Doctrines of Plotinus Compared to Numenius*. He addressed it to me, Basileus. For "Basileus" is the name given to me, Porphyry, according to my native dialect, in which I was called Malchus. This was the name of my father, and "Malchus" would have the interpretation of "King" <note>original: "Basileus"</note> if someone wished to translate it into the Greek dialect. This is why Longinus, addressing his work *On Impulse* to Cleodamus and me, Porphyry, wrote "Cleodamus and Malchus." But Amelius, interpreting the name—just as Numenius had Maximus as "the Great"—so he called Malchus "the King" and wrote: "Amelius to Basileus, greetings. Since you say—on account of those men among you who have made it a common rumor against him—that the doctrines of our companion are traced back to Numenius of Apamea, know clearly that I would not have uttered a word. For it is obvious that this talk has proceeded from their own boastful talkativeness..."

<meta>This page continues Porphyry's biography of Plotinus, specifically addressing the early criticisms and misunderstandings of Plotinus's work. It includes a letter from Amelius—Plotinus’s long-time assistant—regarding accusations of plagiarism and Porphyry’s own journey from critic to devoted follower.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS

<margin>A</margin> At one moment they say his work is "broad nonsense," <note>original: "πλατὺς φλήναφος." This was a common insult used by critics to describe Plotinus’s dense and difficult prose style.</note> and at another that it is counterfeit. Thirdly, they claim that the poor elements were stolen from others, and that he merely criticized them while repeating them. It is necessary for you to have this defense ready against such claims, so that everything is at hand for my argument, through which it is best not to rejoice in my name alone, but in manliness and great wealth. Even if these things have been said of old, there is nothing else to know <margin>B</margin> than that they have come to me; I am returning to you what was promised within three days, as if they were produced by a sudden impulse—not because they are my own from a collection of those treatises, or even modeled after chosen excerpts, but because they are filled with the ancient life breathed into them, or as if each was being formed for the first time. Having been arranged here in this way, they should justly receive <margin>C</margin> pardon from you, as if it were my intention to send forth the things brought under our agreement. For it is the part of a man to be ready to show favor, because of the choice to speak of the same things to another again. But if you have anything that seems forged from the image, correct it kindly or at once. For it seems we are compelled, as the tragedy reveals, O Busy-body <note>original: "Φιλοπράγμον" (Philopragmon). Amelius is likely using a playful nickname for Porphyry here.</note>, by the desire to do something; therefore, take what is yours, be joyful, and may you be successful in all things. Farewell.

<margin>D</margin> I have brought forward this letter from Amelius, not only for the sake of establishing trust—since some boasted that his famous praise of Plotinus was a pretense—but because they thought him a "big talker," a rustic, and a madman because they did not understand what he said. He appeared to all the <term>sophists</term> <note>professional teachers of rhetoric who often prioritized style over philosophical truth</note> as if he were attacking them from a stage, but in his gatherings, he seemed like one in common conversation, or one who did not quickly show the logical necessities contained within his discourse. Since I, Porphyry, <margin>E</margin> thought the same when I first attended his lectures, I brought forward counter-arguments, as if he were intoxicated, trying to show that the "thought" stands outside of the intellect <note>A major technical dispute: Porphyry initially argued that the objects of thought (intelligibles) existed outside the divine Mind, whereas Plotinus taught they were internal to it</note>. Having made these readings, he sat down and told Amelius to solve the difficulties into which I had fallen through ignorance of our current views. Amelius wrote a small book <margin>F</margin> regarding my difficulties, and when I wrote back against his writings, and Amelius replied again, I, Porphyry, having barely understood what was being said on the third attempt, changed my mind and wrote a "palinode" <note>original: "παλινῳδίαν" (palinodian), a poetic term for a retraction or "re-singing" of a previous statement</note>, which I then read in the school. After that, I was entrusted with Plotinus’s books and I encouraged the master himself to the ambition of writing down his views in an articulated and structured way <margin>G</margin> for me. Indeed, this also made Amelius eager to write. See also the opinion that Longinus held regarding Plotinus’s work, from what he wrote:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Now indeed they call his works mere trifles, and now they call them counterfeit. Again, they accuse him as if he were putting forward the most worthless things; and they attack him wrongly with lying talkativeness. But since you think this occasion should be used—namely, that I should return to you those things that seem more prompt for remembering—you also think I should act for the glory of a friend, especially one as great and admirable as Plotinus, although the mysteries sung of old have become more fully known. <margin>B</margin> I have considered that I must comply with you, and so I return to you the promised things within three days, worked out by us as is right. Truly, it is fitting for you to forgive our writings, seeing that they were not composed or selected by a final comparison of those works, but repeated from an old collection; and wherever the first things occurred to me, they have been arranged here for the present. Pardon must also be given to me because that man’s divine nature—which has been brought into the dispute of our judgment by some—cannot easily <margin>C</margin> be grasped, because he speaks differently at different times about the same things, just as it pleased him. I, however, know for certain that you will kindly correct it if anything has been marked by us here beyond the familiar character of our Plotinus. Indeed, now I seem compelled, as is said in tragedies, like a busy man, and therefore more distant from the clear doctrine of our leader, to undergo the judgment of a corrector and to revise; only the ardent will to please you has such power over me. Farewell.

<margin>D</margin> I have been led to bring this letter here <margin>Confirmation of the former points</margin> not only to create trust that some of those times even lived to suspect that Plotinus took pride in the inventions of Numenius <note>original: "Numenij." Numenius of Apamea was a 2nd-century philosopher whose work predated Plotinus and shared some similarities</note>, but also because they thought and viewed him as a great trifler for the reason that they by no means understood his sayings. Plotinus himself was a stranger to all sophistic ostentation and pride, and in the very assemblies of those disputing, he seemed to behave no differently than in <margin>E</margin> familiar conversations, nor did he always reveal the necessary strengths of his arguments lying hidden in his speech. The same happened to me, Porphyry, when I first heard Plotinus. Therefore, I even attempted to provoke him by writing against him, trying to show that what is understood exists outside the intellect. But when he had ordered Amelius to read my writings, and he had read them through, he said, smiling: "It is for you, Amelius, to dissolve those doubts into which he has fallen through a certain ignorance of our opinion." After <margin>F</margin> Amelius had composed a book of no small size against my objections, and I had again contradicted his writings, and Amelius had replied to me a second time, at the third stage, having at last barely suspected Plotinus's mind, I changed my opinion. So much so that, rewriting a "palinode," I recited it in the assembly of all. And thereafter I judged Plotinus’s books to be most worthy of trust, and I urged the teacher himself with all zeal to distinguish his opinion in an articulated way and to describe it more broadly. Indeed, <margin>G</margin> it happened from this that he made Amelius also very inclined toward writing. But what Longinus felt about Plotinus, learn through those things which he wrote.

It highlights the transition from Plotinus as an oral teacher to a prolific author of philosophical treatises.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Plotinus written by his student Porphyry. The previous page discussed accusations of plagiarism against Plotinus and the defense mounted by his circle. This page transitions to the testimony of Longinus, a renowned literary critic and philosopher, who initially struggled with Plotinus's difficult style and poor manuscript copies but eventually came to recognize his genius.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS

<margin>Testimonies of Longinus regarding the excellence of Plotinus's books</margin>
Especially those things which I indicated to him when writing, as a part of the letter written to me in this sequence will declare. Since it was judged worthwhile for me to travel from Sicily to him in Phoenicia, and to bring Plotinus's books with me, he says thus:

"You, indeed, send those things to us when they please you, or rather bring them with you. Truly, I shall not easily cease to plead with you to prefer the journey to us over every other journey. And if for no other reason (for I know not what new wisdom you might hope for in coming to us), at least for the sake of our old friendship and the healthiness of the air, which would benefit the bodily weakness of which you complain. But if you think to achieve anything else with me, do not expect anything new, nor even anything old, much of which you say has perished. 

Now, there is such a shortage of transcribers <note>original: "trascriptorū" (transcriptorum). Professional copyists were essential for distributing philosophy before the printing press.</note> here that, by the gods, it took all this time—while you were restoring the missing parts of Plotinus—for me to find a scribe for these works. I had to pull him away from his usual duties and order him to focus solely on this one task. 

I have many books there, so you may see I have nearly all of them since receiving those you sent; but I confess I do not have them in a perfect state. For these books are significantly full of errors. And though I had thought our friend Amelius had corrected the errors of the copyists throughout, other matters were of greater concern to him than the diligence of proofreading. 

For this reason, I have no idea how to make use of these books; even though I desire beyond measure to consider what Plotinus writes *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note> and *On Being* <note>original: "de ente"</note>. But these books in particular are corrupted by the scribes' faults. Therefore, I greatly desire to receive those same books from you, written with the highest diligence, so that I may read them through, correcting my own copies from them, and then I shall return them at once. 

But again, I repeat the same thing I said from the beginning: do not merely send them, but bring them here yourself. And do not bring only these, but if there is anything else remaining that escaped Amelius. For those which he brought here, I possess through the greatest effort. Why indeed should I not seek out the writings of that man with the highest diligence, as they are worthy of all honor and veneration? 

This I have always indicated to you, both when you were present and when you were far away, and when you lived in Tyre: that I do not fully grasp many of the arguments in Plotinus's books; but the form of the writing itself, the density of the ideas, and the philosophical arrangement of his questions I love and venerate beyond measure. Indeed, I judge that seekers of truth should bring forward Plotinus's books to be compared only with the works of the most excellent authors."

> You speak of the density of the man’s ideas, and I extraordinarily admire and love the philosopher's arrangement of questions, and I judge his books should be brought forward to be compared only with the works of the most excellent [authors]. <note>This is a Greek translation of the preceding Latin praise, emphasizing the same sentiment for Greek-speaking scholars.</note>

<margin>Confirmation of the above.</margin>
I have been somewhat lengthy in the previous narration for this reason: to demonstrate what that man [Longinus]—possessed of the sharpest judgment in our age, who discussed and refuted nearly all the works of the writers of his time—judged regarding Plotinus. Initially, having been influenced by others, he despised Plotinus for a long time. He thought the works of Plotinus which he had received from Amelius were corrupted by the scribes' faults, because he did not at all understand that man’s unusual style of expression. If there were any others, certainly those which were in the possession of Amelius...

**A** Especially those things I indicated to him when writing, as a part of the letter written to me in this sequence will declare. For it was worthy for me to go down from Sicily to him in Phoenicia, to bring the books of Plotinus. He says:

**B** "And you, send these things when it seems best to you, or rather bring them; for what I might send, I would often need to ask of you, to prefer the road to us over the other, even if for no other reason (for what wise thing would you expect from us in coming?) than our old friendship, and the air, which is very temperate, for the weakness of your body, even if you happen to find other ease. From me, expect nothing newer, nor of the old things, as many as you say have been lost by those who wrote the same. All [work] here has...

**C** ...stalled, so that by the gods, for this whole time, regarding the remaining works of Plotinus, I have barely managed to get a scribe, drawing him away from his usual tasks and ordering him to be assigned to this one thing. I have acquired as many as seemed [necessary], and I have all those sent by you now. But they are incomplete and moderately full of errors. For I thought our companion Amelius would have corrected the slips of the scribes. But to him...

**D** ...other things were more urgent than such a dedicated sitting. I do not know in what way I shall converse with these [books], though I desire beyond measure to look into those *On the Soul* and those *On Being*. For these in particular are full of errors, so I am quite eager for the accurately written ones to come from you for me to read alongside mine. I will send them back again. On the other hand, how...

**E** ...I myself might say, that they should not be sent, but rather that it is more worthy for you to have them yourself, those remaining things that escaped Amelius. For those he brought, I acquired all of them with haste. How was I not going to acquire the memoirs of a man worthy of all respect and honor? Indeed, whether you were near or departing far, or spending time around Tyre, I happen to have sent to you. For most of the themes happen to have truly attracted me, and I extraordinarily admire and love the style of the writing, the density of the ideas, and the philosopher’s arrangement of questions, and I judge his books should be brought forward to be compared only with the works of the most excellent authors."

**F** Writing these things, I set them forth as coming from one who was most critical in our time, and who refuted almost all others of his day, to show what the judgment was regarding Plotinus. At first, from the ignorance of others, he continued to have a contempt toward him. For he thought, from the copies he took from Amelius, that they were full of errors because he did not at all understand the man's usual way of interpreting. For if any others, even those with Amelius...

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS
-> γ <- <note>Original: "γ". This is a signature mark used by printers to keep the pages in the correct order.</note>

Those copies belonging to Amelius were the most corrected, having been transcribed from Plotinus’s own original manuscripts. For it is necessary to compare what Longinus wrote in his work concerning Plotinus and Amelius, who were the philosophers of his own time, so that a full judgment concerning them might be formed, as it was by a most distinguished man. The book is titled *Longinus to Plotinus and Gentilianus Amelius, On the End* <note>original: "περὶ τέλους" (peri telous). In ancient philosophy, "The End" refers to the ultimate goal or highest good of human life.</note>; and it begins as follows:

<margin>Pe</margin> Many philosophers have emerged in our time, O Marcellus, and especially during the first years of our youth—for it is impossible to say how great a scarcity of the matter there is in the present time. However, when we were young men, not a few excelled in the study of philosophy. It was my fortune to see all of them, due to the travels I made with my parents from childhood through many lands. I associated with those who survived into my time as I moved through various nations and cities. Some of them attempted to treat their doctrines in writing, leaving behind the benefits of their work for posterity; others thought it sufficient to lead their associates toward an understanding of their favored views. Of the former group, the Platonists were Euclides, Democritus, and Proclinus (who lived in the Troad <note>The region around ancient Troy.</note>), and those who even now teach publicly in Rome, Plotinus and Gentilianus
<margin>Log</margin> Amelius. A prominent man of that circle, Themistocles, and Phoebion, flourished for a long time; and among the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school.</note>, Heliodorus of Alexandria. In the second group were the Platonists Ammonius and Origen, with whom we studied for a great deal of time—men who significantly excelled the philosophers of their day in intelligence—and also the successors at Athens, Theodotus and Eubulus. Some of these have written, such as Origen, who wrote two books *On Daemons*, and Eubulus, who wrote commentaries on the *Philebus* and *Gorgias*. There is also his work against the *Republic* of Plato. These works are of little weight compared to the arguments they used to assign more precisely by voice <note>Longinus suggests that their written work was casual and did not reflect the depth of their oral teaching.</note>. Indeed, they do not seem to have written with serious study, nor did they choose the task of writing as their primary duty. Among the Stoics were Herminus and Lysimachus, and those who lived in the city, Athenaios and Musonius. Among the Peripatetics were Ammonius and Ptolemaeus. Both were the most learned of their time, especially Ammonius, for no one seems to have come close to him in the abundance of his learning. Amelius, though he wrote on technical ideas, also composed poems and demonstration-speeches, which I do not think will be preserved among the most important works, as I believe they did not intend to be known by posterity through such books, having neglected to commit their deeper thoughts to more exact writings.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Those belonging to Amelius were the most corrected: indeed, since they had been transcribed from the handwritten books of Plotinus himself. Accordingly, it is worthwhile to relate what Longinus wrote in his work about Plotinus, Amelius, and the other philosophers of his time: so that it may be more certain to us what opinion that most elegant man, so ready to judge talents, held concerning them. Indeed, the book is inscribed *On the End*, addressed to Plotinus and Gentilianus, surnamed Amelius; its prologue is of this kind:

<margin>B</margin> While many philosophers have emerged in our times, O Marcellus, surely a greater number of them appeared in the first years of our age. For it is impossible to say how few the present time possesses. But while we were youths, not a few excelled in the studies of philosophy, all of whom it was our fortune to see: since from our tender years we traveled through many regions everywhere with our parents. There, truly, the opportunity was given to me to meet those who were still among the living,
<margin>C</margin> since I often visited the same places they were in among many nations and cities. But from their number, some committed their opinions to letters, intending to benefit posterity by writing; others, however, thought they had done enough if they made their present friends and associates sharers of their counsel. In the first group, then, were the Platonists Euclides, Democritus, and Proclinus, who lived in the Troad. Besides these are those who even now live in Rome, Plotinus and Gentilianus
<margin>D</margin> Amelius, the associate of Plotinus. Of the Stoics <note>A school of philosophy focused on virtue and endurance.</note>, Themistocles and Phoebion: and those who flourished until quite recently, Annius and Medius. From the Peripatetics, Heliodorus of Alexandria. But in the second group, among the Platonists, were Ammonius and Origen, with whom we were long associated—men who surely surpassed the philosophers of their century by no small interval in intelligence; likewise those who succeeded them at Athens, Theodotus and Eubulus. Truly, if anything was written by any of them—as a certain book *On Daemons* by Origen,
<margin>E</margin> or a certain exposition of the *Philebus* and *Gorgias* by Eubulus, or those things which he opposes to the *Republic* of Plato and by what reasons these are refuted—these are certainly of little weight if you wish to compare them with the reasons which they were accustomed to assign more exactly by voice. Nor indeed do they seem to have written with any serious study, nor to have chosen the duty of writing as a principal office for themselves. Furthermore, from the number of Stoics, Herminus and Lysimachus; and those who lived in Athens, Athenaios and
<margin>F</margin> Musonius. But among the Peripatetics, Ammonius and Ptolemaeus: both most full of all learning in their time, especially Ammonius; for no one seems to have approached him in the abundance of his learning. Nevertheless, they constructed nothing very systematic, but only certain poems and demonstration-speeches. These writings I believe have been preserved among posterity against the will of their authors. For I do not think they desired to become known to
<margin>G</margin> posterity through books of that kind, since they neglected to entrust their opinions to more exact writings.

### THE LIFE OF PLOTINUS

Of those who have written, some composed nothing more than a collection or a certain transcription of those things which the ancients had already composed; such were Euclides, Democritus, and Proclinus. <note>These are likely minor Platonists of the 2nd and 3rd centuries, not the famous mathematician Euclid or the atomist Democritus.</note> Others, committing very few things from the history of the ancients to memory, followed the same path and set out to compose books, such as Annius, Medius, and Phoebion. This last one [Phoebion] clearly sought to acquire glory for himself more through the arrangement of his speech than through the concepts of his mind alone. Among these, one might also number Heliodorus, who himself, beyond those things heard from the ancients, seems to have contributed nothing at all to a distinct structure of discourse.

Plotinus, however, and Gentilianus Amelius are filled with a wealth of propositions which they handle with great zeal; they chose the task of writing seriously, using their own particular manner of contemplation. And Plotinus, as it seems, explained the Pythagorean and Platonic principles more clearly than those who came before. Certainly, the writings of Numenius, Cronius, Moderatus, and Thrasyllus, <note>Earlier Middle Platonists and Pythagoreans whose work influenced Plotinus.</note> when Plotinus writes on the same subjects, do not come close to his exact diligence in any part. Amelius, for his part, chose to follow in the footsteps of Plotinus and pursues many of his discoveries; but while he is more prolix <note>wordy or lengthy</note> in explaining matters, and wanders with a wider range of interpretation, he takes on a form contrary to that of Plotinus.

We consider only the books of these men to be worthy of consideration. For why should anyone strive to read the others, neglecting meanwhile to investigate those from whom these writers received the things they committed to their own letters? They themselves added nothing to these works—not the main points of the matters, nor even any argument. They cared for nothing further than to gather what had belonged to the majority, or to diligently select the better parts from many. Indeed, we have achieved the same through other means: for instance, where we spoke against Gentilianus [Amelius] regarding justice in Plato's *Republic*, and where we considered Plotinus’s book treating the Ideas. <note>The Platonic "Ideas" or "Forms" are the eternal, non-physical templates for all things in reality.</note> I speak of our companion, the Tyrian Basileus <note>original: "Basileem". This is Porphyry himself; his original name "Malchus" means "King," which is "Basileus" in Greek.</note>, who as a disciple treated many things by imitating Plotinus. He, approving Plotinus himself more than our own way and rule, attempted through the composition of a certain book to show that the Platonic opinion on Ideas was truer than our own. We seem to have refuted him moderately in a certain written reply, as one who had not correctly recanted. In these works, we have certainly examined many of the opinions of these men, as also in the letter to Amelius, which grew to the size of a book. It was a response to several things he had sent to us from Rome and had written concerning "Plotinian Philosophy." We, however, were content with only the common title of the book, labeling the book itself as an "Epistle to Amelius."

<margin>Testimonies.</margin>
<margin>Longinus, the wisest man of his age, preferred Plotinus and Amelius for their wealth of propositions and questions, and noted that they used a manner of contemplation that was specifically their own.</margin>
In these words, therefore, Longinus confessed that Plotinus and Amelius were to be preferred over all the wise men of his century for their wealth of propositions and questions, and that they used a manner of contemplation that was specifically their own. Neither...

<sig>I</sig>

<column-break/>

Of those who have written, some made nothing more than a collection and a certain transcription of the compositions of their elders, just as Euclides, Democritus, and Proclinus did. Others, having memorialized only very small matters from the history of the ancients, attempted to compose books using the same arrangements as those others, just as Annius, Medius, and Phoebion did. The latter [Phoebion] preferred to be known for the construction of his style rather than for the composition of his thought. To these, one might also add Heliodorus, who contributed nothing more to the articulation of reason than what had been said by the elders in their lectures. 

But those who, through the multitude of problems they handled, went beyond their contemporaries in writing—using their own particular way of contemplation—were Plotinus and Gentilianus Amelius. The former [Plotinus] established an explanation of Pythagorean and Platonic doctrines that was, as it seemed, clearer than those who preceded him. Indeed, the works of Numenius, Cronius, Moderatus, and Thrasyllus do not come close to the precision of Plotinus’s writings on the same subjects. Amelius, choosing to follow in the footsteps of Plotinus, held to most of the same doctrines, but was extensive in his elaboration, being led by the circuitous nature of his interpretation toward a zeal for the former [Plotinus]. We think that only the writings of these men are worth our investigation. 

As for the rest, if someone were not to be moved by them, it would be because of those sources from which they examined and under whose names they wrote; they added nothing of their own, neither in terms of main headings nor even in terms of arguments, nor did they even care for a collection that was better or superior to that of the majority. Now, we have also done these things through others, just as we spoke against Gentilianus regarding justice according to Plato; and regarding Plotinus, having examined the work on the Ideas. Our common companion, Basileus the Tyrian <note>Porphyry.</note>—who himself has produced a few works in imitation of Plotinus—did not accept our guidance, but instead attempted through a treatise to demonstrate that the opinion concerning the Ideas held by Plotinus was better than the one we favored. We might seem to have censured him moderately. In turn, we have disturbed many of these men's opinions, just as in the letter to Amelius—which was the size of a treatise—responding to the things he sent to us from Rome. He himself did not write a letter concerning the method of Plotinian philosophy. We were satisfied only with the common title of the treatise, addressing it as the "Letter to Amelius."

In the end, we shall agree that Plotinus and Amelius excelled all those of their time in the multitude of problems they addressed, and that these two especially used their own particular manner of contemplation.

<margin>A</margin> In this oracle it is contained that Plotinus was good, and mild, and especially gentle, and sweet, just as we ourselves have confirmed by true experience. Moreover, that he was vigilant, and always pure in soul, with his mind raised upward toward the divine itself, which indeed he loved ardently with his whole soul. Likewise, that he strove with all his strength to tear himself away from the bitter wave of this life and to emerge entirely. Therefore, by this reason and by this blessed light—since he often raised himself with his whole mind to the first God who is superior to the mind, through all the steps arranged by Plato in the *Symposium* <note>Referring to the "Ladder of Love" in Plato's *Symposium*, a philosophical ascent from physical beauty to the Idea of Beauty itself.</note> so that he might ascend to divine things—that very God immediately shone upon him, who has neither form nor any idea, but is above the intellect and the entire intelligible world, consisting in himself. To whom I, Porphyry, once approached and was joined, when I was already completing my sixty-eighth year. Therefore, that end appeared very close to Plotinus. For the end and the goal for Plotinus was to draw near and be joined to the God who is present to all things everywhere. Four times during the time I spent with him, he attained this end, not merely in potentiality, I say, but attained it by a certain ineffable act. Furthermore, the oracle adds: that the gods, often seeing Plotinus wandering, took hold of him and directed him onto the right path, while they kindly extended the most abundant rays of divine light to the light of his eyes; so that it may truly be said that Plotinus composed his books by the contemplation of visions, shining by divine grace. Now indeed, because of his intuition, which was vigilant both within and without, he is said by the oracle to have seen many and most beautiful things with his own eyes; things which indeed no other professor of philosophy easily inspected. For the contemplation of men can indeed be superior to human contemplation; but compared to divine knowledge, though it may be graceful, it still lacks the power to penetrate the depths which the heavenly beings penetrate. Thus far the oracle shows what sort of things Plotinus performed while he was enclosed in the body, and what he attained. In these verses it is said that he was good and mild, and especially gentle and sweet, just as we were conscious of him being. It is also said that he was vigilant, keeping his soul pure and always looking toward the divine, which he loved with his whole soul; and that he did everything to escape the bitter wave and to flee the blood-nourished life <margin>B</margin>. Thus, especially by the divine light, he frequently led himself by his thoughts toward the first God who is beyond, following the paths shown by Plato in the *Symposium*. To him appeared that one who has neither form nor any idea, but is established above the intellect and all the intelligible. To whom indeed I, Porphyry, say that I once approached and was joined, being in my sixty-eighth year. Thus, the goal appeared to Plotinus <margin>C</margin> dwelling nearby. For his end and goal was to come near and approach the God over all. Seven times <note>The Latin text says "quater" (four), while the Greek here says "ἑπτάκις" (seven). And it says that the gods often directed him as he was being carried along, frequently providing a ray of light, so that he might look upon the things they gave and write down what he saw. It is said that from his vigilance toward <margin>D</margin> outward sights, "you saw," it says, "with your eyes many <margin>E</margin> and graceful things" which none of those men who applied themselves to philosophy could easily see. For the contemplation of the heavenly ones might be better than human contemplation. Though it might be graceful compared to divine knowledge, we are not able to reach the depth in the same way the gods lift us up. Thus far has been told in a historical manner concerning the life of Plotinus. Since he himself entrusted to us the arrangement and the correction of his books, and I promised him while he was living—and pledged to my other companions—that I would provide some care for them, I decided first that it would be a worthwhile effort not to allow the books to remain in a confused state, just as they were composed in the sequence of time. <sig>B</sig> It pleased us to arrange these first three Enneads together in a single volume. Now, in the Third Ennead, we have included the material regarding our allotted spirit, because that subject is treated there in a general sense. Furthermore, this proposition or question is well-suited to the type of inquiry that investigates human horoscopes <note>original: *genituras* / γενετας. This refers to the study of the stars' influence on a person's life-lot.</note>. Similarly, the proper place for the discussion on Love is also found here. We have also rightly placed the treatise on Eternity and Time here because of the specific arguments regarding time. Moreover, it pleased us to number the discussion on Nature, Contemplation, and the One in this section because of the word "Nature" in its title.

On Intelligible Beauty.
On Intellect, Ideas, and Being.

We have constructed these three Enneads by arranging them into a single volume. In the Third Ennead, we placed the treatise on our allotted spirit, because its subject is considered generally, and the problem or inquiry is consistent with those studies regarding the births of men. Similarly, the place for the treatise on Love is here. The treatise on Eternity and Time we placed here because of the discussion of time. We have thus arranged the fifty-four books into six Enneads. However, we found among the books certain commentaries without a certain order, because the friends who were with us at the time urged us to set them out, particularly those which most required explanation for them. Moreover, we have made chapter headings for all the books according to the times of their edition, except for the one *On the Beautiful*. For here the notice of the time was missing for us. But in this volume, not only the chapters are set out according to the measure of each book, but also the arguments which are numbered in the manner of chapters. Now, running through the individual books, we shall endeavor to apply even marks and signs, and if there has been an error in the wording anywhere, to amend it; and if anything else moves us, the work itself will be able to signify it.

# MARSILIO FICINO OF FLORENCE
## COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE FIRST ENNEAD.

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK

*The rational soul is the middle between divine and natural forms; it is not "in" the body, but "present to" it, and it propagates life from itself, which exists in the body: from this life and the body, a single composite animal is formed.*

**Chapter one.**

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' containing floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>
**P**ROPITIOUSLY, this first book of all meets us, in which we may contemplate ourselves as if in a mirror, lest we, being overly curious about foreign things, seek others before our own. For it will teach us that we—that is, the true human—are this very thing which we properly are, and not the body: because we use this as an instrument. We are not the life that is entirely the body's own and bound to it, since we share this life with the beasts; <margin>D</margin> for often the very reason through which we exist opposes and commands this life. We are not something composed of the body and its own life, for the very same reasons we have assigned here. For this "animal" is not ultimately joined from the rational soul and the irrational living thing, since one cannot be made from the indissoluble and the dissoluble. Rather, the human is the soul—that is, an incorporeal rational substance, existing from the divine intellect, subsisting in itself, not inherent in the body, but rather standing by <note>original: *assistentem*. Ficino distinguishes between being "in" something like a physical ingredient and "standing by" or presiding over it as a higher principle.</note> it, and by its very presence producing this life in the body, from which and the body the composite is called an "animal."

That our soul is indeed present to the body, but not "in" it, we shall briefly show in this way. There are three kinds of forms. The lowest forms are natural; the highest are divine; and the middle are rational souls. Natural forms, such as those of the elements and mixtures, are said to be present to matter insofar as they affect it and effect something in it; they are also said to be "in" matter because they suffer <note>original: *patiuntur*. In philosophy, "to suffer" means to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> in the same way along with the matter itself. But divine forms—that is, the divine intellect, the craftsman of the world, and the Ideas of things—are present by the act of the first divine intelligence and as the patterns of things, but they are not "in" matter; otherwise, nothing could even be imagined as separate from matter. Furthermore, they are not present *to* matter in the sense of location—for doubtless they are everywhere—but they are not present according to any kinship of nature or any affection toward matter. For who would not notice that the divine intellect is sequestered from all commerce with matter? Since even the human intellect cannot expedite and perfect its own proper action of intelligence otherwise than by segregating itself from matter. 

Therefore, between the natural forms which are simultaneously present to and "in" matter, and the entirely divine forms which are neither "in" nor even present to it <note>In the sense of being bound to it.</note>, there must exist a middle form of nature: which is not "in" matter, so that it does not suffer with matter, nor by suffering with it act imperfectly upon it; for if it acted imperfectly, it could not sustain this very form until the vigor of life. However, it is present to matter—that is, it favors it with natural providence and cherishes it with a certain love of affinity; by cherishing it, it forms it; and by forming it, it vivifies it; and by vivifying it, it gives birth to the human animal, subjected to the human, that is, the generating soul. It is clearly evident that the rational soul is such a thing; it appears that it is indeed not "in" the body, where bodies...

<meta>This page continues the introductory commentary by Marsilio Ficino on Plotinus's first book of the First Ennead. It establishes the philosophical framework for understanding the hierarchy of the soul's faculties.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

[The soul] resists and commands; it also appears to be present where it naturally loves the union with the body. It possesses a specific character when it reasons—that is, when it adapts its assent through arguments from effect to cause over time and motion; where, having proposed an end, it deliberates on the choice of paths through a variety of discovered means. This entire faculty is called reason <note>original: *ratio*</note>, and this deliberation is named as that which is most characteristic of a human being. Again, it has something as if in common with the divine intellect: an understanding <note>original: *intellectum*</note> that is not discursive, but attains truth through a direct gaze <note>original: *intuitu*</note>. By the gaze of this stable contemplation, the wandering discourse of reason is governed; there is its beginning, and there it finally ends. It also has something in common with the brute animal: imagination, which is the innermost and simple sense of the soul, and the judge that follows the senses. Therefore, the middle power itself, which is defined by the term "reason," is called the "reasoning faculty" <note>original: *ratiocinatrix*</note> or counsel. But where it takes its beginnings from the intellect through discourse, it is called intelligence, wisdom, and science. Yet, where it leans toward the course of imagery, it is called conjecture, faith, and opinion. This substance, endowed with these three powers, is properly called the "Soul of Plato," insofar as it is so affected that it pours a certain life into the human body; it is also called "Man." This is the soul proper. However, the life poured out from here should properly be called "animal" and "vivification" <note>The process of giving life to the body.</note>. Nevertheless, taking some liberty, we shall call that soul the "first soul," and this one the "second soul." For from the first, where the powers are situated... in the first soul, reason proceeds from the intellect, and imagination proceeds from reason. In the second soul, there are also three principal powers: imagination (that is, a certain common sense), then the external sense divided into five parts, and finally the generative power, which is also called "nature," the origin of generation, growth, and nutrition. Imagination exists in the second, animal soul. For from it and the body, the human animal is formed; it represents the intellect to the primary soul, and reason to the external sense. Finally, the vegetative nature reflects the imagination to the first soul. Again, the imagination which belongs to the prior soul is the lowest part, and is called "phantasy," because it does not judge based on sensuality alone, but follows reason entirely. However, the imagination of the following [animal] soul holds the highest place in it; it is usually called "confused phantasy," and perceives only accidents, being led mostly by natural instinct. Therefore, the lowest sense in this animal pertains both to external sensible things and to the passions <note>In this context, "passions" refer to things undergone or felt by the body, not just emotions.</note> of the body brought on by external things, which it feels most closely as the body itself suffers. But the sense—that is, the imagination of the higher soul—does not direct itself to sensible things, but to the senses of the subject animal; it does not feel the passions of the body directly, but immediately notices the shared feelings of the senses, and is generally occupied with the images, actions, and passions of the lower sense. It does not merely perceive or receive passions from there, but is very often touched by a certain paternal affection toward it. Thus far, let this be a general outline of the argument for the whole book.

->Division of the book into thirteen parts.<-

**I** We divide the whole book into thirteen chapters or sections. But up until the seventh, it only inquires; in the seventh, it begins to bring forth questions, and thereafter investigates and defines them equally. In the first chapter, therefore, where the disturbances are, it first establishes what is to be tracked down. In the second, where the actions and effects mainly accompanying them are. In the third, where thought and opinion are. In the fourth, where intelligence is. In the fifth, what this very thing is that considers these matters. In the sixth, what it is that wishes to be prone [to things], and where the sense is. Seeking, however, where these are and to whom they belong, it asks whether the soul is simple, or whether it is the whole body entirely, or whether it comes from both mixed together, or if a mixture has been made. This inquiry and those following it tend toward finding out what "man" is and what "animal" is. This, then, is the purpose and order of the book.

The rational soul is the same as the rational nature of the soul itself, which, although it is separate from the body according to its being, nevertheless produces a life joined to the body, which is the "animal" life. Therefore, Plotinus's opinion is a middle ground between the opinions of Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, an Aristotelian commentator who saw the soul as more tied to the body.</note> and Averroes <note>Averroes, the Islamic philosopher who posited a single, universal intellect for all humans.</note>.

**II** In the second chapter of the book, he begins thus: If the soul is a simple form consisting in itself, it receives neither any passions, nor those things which precede or follow passions. However, when it is either something composed of matter and form, or a form that is a specific part of a composite, I would know that it easily received such things. There you will note what he says: "If the soul is one thing, and its being an soul is another" <note>original: *Si aliud anima sit, aliud ipsius esse anima*</note>. Read this as: not only the "being of the soul" itself, but even if the "soul being" is the same, they signify exactly the same thing in Plotinus. "Soul" indeed signifies this soul demonstrated in some way, or found by event, which, whatever it may be, is present somewhere or sometime. But "the being of the soul" itself, or "that which is the being of the soul," knows such a special nature of the soul (so to speak), in which neither the life necessary for this earthly soul is defined, nor is there anything superfluous. He makes them the same. He declares this in the book *On the Will of God*, saying: "The soul and the very thing that is the being of the soul are the same." If indeed the soul is a simple form and is not spoken of as being "of" something else: it should not be said to be about a composite, nor about the specific form of a composite (which itself appears to be composed into some sort of being in a certain way). This thing and its very being are the same, or the being itself and life itself. For this human is one thing, and human nature itself is another, since nothing is lacking from nature, but it is entirely human; nor does anything superfluous happen to it, but in this man, by a certain goodness of fate, he is a part of the universe and one. (To speak in a Platonic way) because there are certain things in him foreign to the lowest man, just as this man, because of his very location here, does not degenerate from integrity. Moreover, forms separated from matter, which are both simple and exist in themselves, lose nothing of their ideal reason and undergo nothing foreign. They judge the substance of the rational soul to be such; in his book *On the Soul*, he demonstrates its immortality. And in the book *On Happiness*, he signifies this by saying: "That the soul is one part of the composite, tossed out from the body, yet through reason it understands separation in two ways: one through suitable philosophy by which it segregates itself from the disturbances of the human body; the other through contemplation, by which it separates itself from the senses and imagination." Truly, because the soul does not become a part of the composite, it can therefore be turned back into its own primary causes, and resolve itself into any equals—that is, into simple parts, and those powers into simple forms already existing within itself. It is found that Plotinus's opinion is a middle ground between Alexander and Averroes. For Alexander conjectures that the intellect is a small nature present in the body. Averroes, however, neither grants that it is the life of the body nor that it pours any life into the body. Finally, Plotinus says that the intellectual nature is indeed the life of the body; however, he denies altogether that it propagates a more familiar life in the body through its presence, from which life and the body not just "man" but the "human animal" is made. You, however, must remember to investigate with much study what a man is and what an animal is, not only in this book but in those books where the question of the "Idea" is known. Here he says the sense either looks at or perceives the body as impassive, and soon [discusses] opinion regarding the conjecture of the sense: for where he wants the sense to receive only corporeal images, others [perceive] certain corporeal things... such are they, as where [it is] suspected...

<meta>catchword: from the sense</meta>

<summary>Marsilio Ficino outlines the hierarchy of the soul's faculties, distinguishing between the higher rational soul and the lower animal life. He interprets Plotinus's view of the soul as an immortal, simple form that manages the body without being corrupted by it, placing this theory between the views of Alexander of Aphrodisias and Averroes.</summary>
