<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically investigating how the soul can be present in a body without being "stained" or changed by it. It builds on the previous discussion of the soul’s various powers—reason, intellect, and imagination.</meta>

### ON THE FIRST BOOK OF THE FIRST ENNEAD.

...from sense, provided it is judged correctly, nor do they <note>The objects of sense</note> themselves suffer in the meantime—that is, they are not changed from what they are by the sense—nor does the sense suffer similarly from them.

->The rational soul, although it exists within itself, nevertheless turns in some way toward the body, which is least appropriate for an intellectual substance.<-

**III** Since he had indicated that the soul exists within itself, lest anyone should think it does not differ at all from the Mind <note>original: *mens*; in Neoplatonism, the Mind or 'Nous' is a higher level of reality than the Soul</note>, he adds that the soul, although it exists in itself just as the Mind does, nonetheless "flows" into the body, nourishing it, forming it, and filling it with life—which the Mind itself certainly does not do. Next, he considers the soul or its vivification <note>the act of giving life</note> as using the body as a kind of natural and conjoined instrument. After this, he investigates whether, while using the body as an instrument, it receives the same sensations and passions. He gradually leans toward the view that it does *not* receive them, because it uses the body not like a craftsman <note>who works on something external</note> but like a ruler. Then he indicates that the nature of the soul is separable from the body, a fact proven most strongly through philosophy. Finally, he asks: if it is joined to the body, in what manner is it then separated? Is it like a certain temperament <note>a physical mixture or balance</note> of the body? Or is it because the soul itself extends through the whole body? Or because it is a form hidden within the body, or a "species" <note>a guiding principle or appearance</note> presiding over it? Or is it partly separate, insofar as it uses the life of the Mind (as the rational soul), and partly joined, insofar as it is a "living instrument," as Iamblichus <note>a later Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the soul's descent into the body</note> wishes? Or is it by some other irrational method, such that the "animal" is constituted from the soul and the body together? The philosopher <note>referring to Plotinus</note> ought to distinguish both the instrument and the mover of the instrument according to reason, so that he might be entirely free to recall reason itself from this use of the body, the better to be at leisure for contemplation.

->A double reason shows that the soul is not mixed with the body.<-

**IIII** In the fourth chapter of the book, he inquires into this matter, saying: if the soul were a certain mixture or form lying within the body, just as it would not truly be the soul itself but the "composite" <note>the soul-body unit</note>, so it would not feel, or act, or suffer; rather, the composite would do so, while the soul would be, so to speak, something else entirely. But if it is an essence possessing its own being within itself—not mixed, not lying within, but unfolding itself through the body only out of its own abundance and vivifying it by its presence—it will never admit any passions <note>physical disturbances or emotions</note> of the body, much like light does not admit the disturbances of the air. Now, he demonstrates that the soul is not mixed with the body (and therefore not "lying" within it) by a double reason. First: If the soul, which is that which vivifies the body, were mixed with the body at the beginning, it would be thoroughly "infected" and degraded by the mixture, and it would fall away from life at the very moment it was meant to give life; therefore, it would not perfectly vivify or form the body. Indeed, life mixed into a body already living is not so much "life" as it is a certain "vivification" received in the manner of a passion; however, in the manner of an action, it belongs to life itself, which is separable. Just as any form in matter is a certain "passion" <note>an effect produced in the recipient</note>, with the matter depending on an action from some effective form that exists separately—and light in the air is an "illumination" rather than the Light itself—so too, the task of perfectly vivifying and forming the body is not the duty of this imperfect "life" lying in the body, nor is it the duty of the true Intellect; rather, it is the duty of the intellectual and rational soul. The second reason: Things are not mixed into one unless they meet in a common matter and agree in their genus. But the soul, especially the intellectual soul, is further removed from the body than a line is from the color white, yet these two <note>geometry and color</note> are not mixed. Therefore, neither is the soul mixed with the body.

->Unless it is known how the soul is joined to the body, it will not be known which actions or passions belong to the soul alone, and which to the composite.<-

**V** Since he touched upon the Aristotelian opinion <note>Ficino refers to the followers of Aristotle as the Peripatetics</note> which says that passions and affections belong not so much to the soul as to the "animal" <note>the living being</note>, he shows again that it is difficult to say how this conjunction or communion occurs—that is, how things belong to the animal as a whole. For whether you say these things proceed from the body into the soul through sense, it is not yet clear what part of the sense belongs to each. Or whether you say they descend from the soul into the whole body through opinion or a certain judgment, it is not yet established whose opinion it is. Likewise, the appetite for the "common good" of knowledge and eternal glory can belong to the soul alone. Again, the opinion that something is "evil" does not necessarily cause pain in such a living body. Similarly, the opinion of "urging efforts" does not necessarily provoke lust or desire in this or that body toward a specific work. Furthermore, if it is said that "perturbations" <note>emotions like anger or fear</note> belong to the powers of desire and anger themselves, and that these are rooted and founded in the soul, and thus the perturbations are "common," he similarly examines this suspicion. Finally, if the Peripatetics assert that such affections relate to the soul not as an "imitator" but in some other way, he brings this into doubt as well, indicating that such ambiguities happen to us primarily because we do not yet sufficiently understand how the soul is joined to the body and how the "composite animal" is made.

->If the rational soul is said to be a part of the composite animal, the doubts are not resolved.<-

**VI** In the sixth chapter, he brings the solution to the preceding Peripatetic doubts into the open. For they say: since in a living animal, "being" belongs not to a part but to the whole, the passions rightly relate to the whole. Thus it seems that the soul and the power of the animal are that by which the animal acts; but the "animal" is chiefly what acts and suffers. Plotinus will perhaps concede that this is manifest in actions and passions that pass into external matter; but regarding the sense which is internal, and regarding the life which is innermost, he says it must be questioned why the soul itself does not feel and live. This entire controversy, as I said, tends toward this: that we understand that these ambiguities cannot be clarified unless it is first established how the soul relates to the body, and the body to the soul—what remains simple, and what is composed and how. Thus far, as I said at the beginning, he is only questioning; nothing is defined in the meantime.

->The rational soul exists in itself and has its own rational actions and a certain sense free from passion; however, it produces irrational life in the body, the sense of which is concerned with the passions of the body.<-

**VII** In the seventh chapter, he begins to define his opinion little by little and brings forward his own view. He wants it to be clear that this view is primarily true because the doubts about the soul cannot be solved unless it is posited. And indeed, unless one distinguishes these things, one will find it very difficult to assign reasons, partly for our divinity and partly for those things in us which seem alien to divinity. This is not only the opinion of Plato and Pythagoras—as is clear from the *Timaeus*—and of the Egyptians, as Iamblichus teaches, but even Themistius <note>a 4th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> asserts that Aristotle felt this way. This is the opinion: That there are two lives in us...

<summary>In this section, Ficino analyzes Plotinus's inquiry into the soul's relationship with the body, arguing that the soul is not physically "mixed" with the body but governs it as a separate, higher essence. He critiques the Aristotelian view that emotions belong solely to the "composite" animal, suggesting instead a dual-life model where the rational soul remains distinct from physical suffering.</summary>

### THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...of which the second comes from the first and is its image. But the first subsists within itself, while the second inheres in the body; the first is a whole something in itself, while the second is a part of a composite—namely, the living creature <note>original: *animalis*; in this context, 'animal' refers to the 'living creature' formed by the union of soul and body</note>. This is because the first is the foundation of life. No one doubts that there is a certain life inherent in the body; but reason proves that another life presides over this one, subsisting in itself, suggesting that a life lying within another thing depends on a perfect life, as an imperfect thing depends on the perfect. In the same way, the intellect situated in the soul flows from an intellect flourishing in itself, and the good in the intellect flows from the Good itself existing in itself. Furthermore, intellectual good is not only created by the Good itself, but is also preserved by it, and does not depart from it. Similarly, the intelligence infused into the soul is both created and preserved by the pure Intellect, and is not separated from it. By the same reasoning, the life or soul enslaved to the body is produced and preserved by the Soul that always remains in itself and stays contiguous to it. Just as a ray of the sun is on one side continued with its own sun, but on the other side touches and forms the subject matter below. For this reason, the first life is, as it were, a certain form of the living creature; the second is the form of the natural body endowed with instruments <note>organs or physical tools</note> adapted for the use of the living creature. This is also what Aristotle says; and after he called the soul the "form" or "act," he added that the intellectual soul is an act in one way, and the other life in another way. But to return to our own points: with this distinction proposed, Plotinus attributes sensation accompanied by passion <note>or 'suffering/emotion'</note> to the living creature, but he assigns sensation free from passion to the soul. Again, he assigns the discourses of reason to the same soul, whether they incline toward the senses or rise toward the intellect. The remaining points of this chapter will be clear to anyone who considers them diligently for themselves.

->The rational soul is joined through its intellect to the Divine Mind, and through that to God; thus also the<-
->irrational life is linked to the rational soul. Moreover, the Intellect is both "proper" <note>individual</note> and "common."<-

**VIII** The eighth chapter inquires how the soul relates to all things both above it and below it; but first, in what way it relates to the Divine Intellect, the father of rational souls, which presides over the soul almost exactly as the soul presides over the living creature. Know, however, that the One itself, or the Good itself—which is the highest God—has no "respect" <note>no relative relationship or dependence on other things</note>. But the Intellect, the "son of the Good" according to Plotinus, has at least two respects: the first insofar as it comes from the One, and thus is itself one; the second insofar as it exists in itself, and thus is derived into a multitude of Ideas—which, however, it possesses and beholds all at once as one in actuality. The soul then has three respects. For it has the power of knowing from the Intellect, but this very power, as it depends most closely on the Intellect, is itself also intellect; always continuous with its father, under his form and act, it always understands all things at once. But insofar as it is taken according to the nature of the soul, it now acts in time and runs through a succession from potentiality to act; this is called "reasoning" and "thought," and thus it seems to hold the species <note>the forms or mental images</note> of things as distinct from one another. Finally, as it turns toward the living creature, it descends from universal reason to the imagination of particulars. But this life of the living creature seems to undergo four respects. Insofar as it depends on the soul, like an image from a substance, it has imagination. Insofar as it is something in itself, it is derived into its own multitude. Insofar as it rules the body, it exercises vital power. Insofar as it adheres to the body, it turns out to be a part of the living creature and is rendered liable to passions. Therefore, this life is the form of the body, but the soul is rather the form of the living creature, and the Intellect is the form of the soul. God is, in a certain way, the form of the Intellect itself, and the lower grade always acts by being constituted under the act of the higher grade as if under a form. Furthermore, the Divine Intellect itself is called "common" insofar as it is indivisible and whole everywhere, and "proper" insofar as it is received by individual souls in their own individual ways. From this, different modes of reasoning follow in different souls, and different modes of imagining. But no one has said that the intellect which is a certain form in the soul—not only presiding but also implanted—is common. If there were many eyes, many might report souls to it; furthermore, many visual rays might be naturally present in the eyes; these represent the intellects naturally implanted in souls. But the one common light of the sun, present everywhere, represents the Divine Intellect, the father of souls and intellects. Finally, the one light of the Sun consisting in the Sun itself shows us the Good itself, the Father. Therefore, the intellects innate to souls, even if they are not a single intellect, are nevertheless one—namely, one according to intellectual being, rendered in the act of understanding by that one light of the Mind. In that light, as if in a common form and object, they are one, even though they are many according to the multitude of souls. Just as visual rays or sights are numbered according to the number of eyes and are not one, yet they are one in the one light by running together; they would especially seem to be one if they existed in themselves, freed from the eyes, just as intellectual souls remain absolute from bodies. Themistius seems to adapt this opinion of Plato and Plotinus to Aristotle and Theophrastus, and Avicenna and Al-Ghazali follow it. Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note>, however, agrees with Plotinus in this: that besides the one Intellect, he also attributes many to us; but he disagrees in asserting that these many are mortal. But Averroes agrees with Plotinus in asserting that every intellect is immortal; yet he disagrees when he assigns us only a single one <note>the 'unicity of the intellect' doctrine</note>. You, however, should take from Alexander the number of human intellects, and from Averroes the immortal gift of all intelligence, and you will have the complete opinion of our Plotinus. Furthermore, know that regarding the nature of the intellect, Plotinus is to be believed above all others; his life, deeds, and writings testify that he always lived by the intellect. I wish to advise you of this now, so that Alexander and Averroes do not disturb you. He concludes finally that "we"—that is, the human being—are properly the soul using rational discourse, whether it discourses through universals or through particulars. Those things which are above or below reason are "ours": the former because we always depend on them, the latter because they depend on us. He adds, in the manner of Plato, that the intellectual nature—both that which presides over us and that which resides in us—is indivisible; but the life diffused as far as the body is said to be divisible. Because although it is one and whole in any member, it is nevertheless affected toward different things and vivifies in various ways. It varies in many things, whether in members or vehicles at once, or in bodies to be vivified in succession. The rational soul does not consist of itself and the body as one thing, but of the body and a certain life attributed to it as a certain image of the soul itself. Finally, he teaches that one power of the soul depends on another in succession.

->The cause of sinning is in the irrational soul and our living creature; in the soul, however, there is consent.<-
->Likewise, the rational circuit is the middle between rest and straight motion. Again, how intelligence<-
->and reason relate to each other and to the imagination. Likewise, the allegory of Adam and Eve.<-

**IX** The higher distinctions teach us in the ninth chapter that the beginning of sins is in the living creature, but the middle is in the imagination of the higher soul; specifically because the soul obeys the incitements of the living creature before reason has clearly judged whether the thing should be pursued or fled. Hence, the "inner man" complains about the "outer man."

### ON BOOK I OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

Sense perception flows into the members of the mind by the law of nature, guided by the counsel of the mind. But even reason itself, when it is occupied with practical affairs, draws upon images from its own mind to establish itself, so that it is less carried away by animal appetite. As long as reason directs itself toward the intellect, it conforms itself entirely to that form by which the intellect administers the mind’s commands in an orderly fashion. For this reason, it is entirely free from fault. 

But we—that is, through rational choices, actions, and studies—reach toward that very intelligence; I mean that receptive contemplation which was first in the divine mind. We perceive this most clearly as it exists within our own mind. It is present in our reason when it has been prepared, but it is always active in the higher mind. Plotinus spoke of the "separation of reason" from us—meaning that the soul is most truly itself when it stands in the middle between divine things, which always remain constant, and natural things, which fall into decay. Reason defines itself in a circular way <note>Ficino refers to the Neoplatonic idea of "circular motion," where the soul proceeds from God and returns to Him through contemplation.</note> between the higher mind and discursive reason—that is, the mind's own essence. 

Intelligence is sometimes said to exist without reason, not because of its nature, but because it does not understand things through the instrument of the body. In this way, the soul discerns even without that discursive reason. This occurs in the mind; what is called the "act of meditation" is not sustained by the body, although it almost always holds some images from the senses before its eyes. The mind is naturally drawn toward reason; however, true intelligence neither uses the body’s instruments nor is it carried by such images. Furthermore, when reason turns itself entirely toward the intellect, it perceives universals <note>General concepts or essences, as opposed to specific, individual things.</note> without the involvement of particulars. But we discuss these matters more fully in our *Platonic Theology*. 

At this point, the words indicate that the author <note>Plotinus</note> does not disagree with Aristotle or Plato. He adds that the discourse of reason, the intellect, and the imagination do not touch the passions of the body. Rather, they are occupied with a certain "passive sense" of the image—that is, the primary imagination—even though reason, when acting without lower thought, is a kind of intellectual act. For true thought is a certain intelligence explained more broadly: when the mind reaches the intellect, it gazes upon universal species <note>The eternal "Forms" or "Ideas" in the mind of God.</note>. When the mind inclines toward the imagination, it derives those universal species down into the particular living creature. It then discerns and judges by comparing these particulars with the universals, seeing where they agree or differ. If reason is exercised by the intellect and descends from there, it descends to individual things by "composing" them. But if it takes its occasion from the imagination and rises higher, it ascends from individuals to universals by "resolving" them. 

You should observe this order in the soul: remember that it holds species in the mind that are both universal and stable. In reason, the species are universal but in a way mobile; in the imagination, however, they are particular and changeable. Plotinus considers passions, disturbances, and the causes of sin to belong properly to the <term>animal</term><note>original: *animalis*; here meaning the "living creature" or the composite of body and lower soul, rather than just a beast.</note>. Yet reason is the true observer of these things and often gives them its consent. 

You, however, should notice a **Mosaic allegory** in the words of Plotinus: namely, two personae. One is the man himself, who is like **Adam**; the other is the human part drawn toward the animal life and degenerating, who is like **Eve**. Add to this the "drawing out" from the sleeping soul. For the soul propagates from itself when, sliding from its former wakefulness near God toward natural things and forgetting divine things, it now sleeps and dreams. Thus, it then generates the corporeal life, which is like Eve. Consider her as the one who first sins, and the man as the one who then consents. Yet the intellect stands over them like a presiding angel, and Moses <note>Ficino implies that the story in Genesis is a coded philosophical truth about the soul's descent.</note> represents the one rebuking them, and the angel represents God. Finally, one must consider "two in one flesh"—as if there were two souls in the same body. This is how **Moses**, **Plotinus**, **Origen**, and **Ammonius** understood it. Let us proceed to the rest.

---

->**How the living creature within us relates to the soul, and whether any life perishes.**<-

<margin>X</margin> The tenth chapter of the book teaches that the things proper to our "animal" nature also pertain to us in a certain way. Likewise, in the rational soul, there are virtues sought through reason; in the animal, there are virtues acquired through habit. Furthermore, the life granted to the body by the rational soul is not extinguished when the body is dissolved; rather, it follows its own soul just as a light seems to follow a candle. **Numenius** <note>A 2nd-century philosopher who influenced Neoplatonism.</note> held this same view.

---

->**How the soul relates to the intellect, through which it always understands, although reason does not always notice it. Also concerning children and brutes.**<-

<margin>XI</margin> After discussing in the previous sections how we relate to the animal nature below us, he now discusses in the eleventh chapter how we relate to the intellect within us—that is, the "higher reason." He says, therefore, that our intellect always acts within itself regarding divine things and always contains all intelligible things in perpetual intellection. **Iamblichus** asserts that it would be deceptive to think otherwise. But how does it act in children? He believes Plotinus understood it this way: the "little gates" are never closed to those who see the face of their fatherland. For **Ammonius** and **Origen**, in the manner of Plato, were accustomed to interpreting the sacred scriptures this way. 

He says that in children, the powers of the animal nature work with great intent for the necessary task of building up the body. The imagination of the higher soul is mostly occupied with these same powers. Only the smallest sparks of reason flash out there, as they are turned toward opposing things. It follows that the act of reason, when free from these lower things, operates meanwhile around the intellect; for since it is so effective, it cannot be entirely idle. Nevertheless, neither that intellect (concerning intelligible things) nor the act of reason (concerning the intellect) is recognized by us at that time. This is because the imagination proper to the higher soul—whose service in us is "noticing"—is entirely deluded by the work of the opposites. It does not receive those intellectual images which it would reflect like a mirror to the eyes of reason. It is by such reflection that reason looks back, and thus we notice the actions of the intelligence and reason. 

They call this imagination in us the "middle." For it stands between our rational and irrational parts. It is a medium through which both are said to be received. Imagination is the "gathering place" of the minds, especially when something from the animal nature is brought near. Through these two "middles," noticing usually occurs. For imagination is like a mirror in which reason itself, through reflection, sagaciously apprehends things. Therefore, after speaking of children, he rightly speaks of "brutes" (beasts), as being those in whom only a few sparks appear. Wherever there is life in any body, the soul that contains that life is not dissolved when the body is. Furthermore, it is necessary that a life remains in itself, by whose power the "giving of life" is supplied without any loss of reason. It is preserved just as reason is preserved from change, and it always enjoys its own light. Since nothing in its genus is called "imperfect" unless it depends on the "perfect," it is very easy for life in beasts to be held from the soul itself. Just as nature herself does not decline from true perfection, so too it does not lack any soul; though not from a rational soul, it is supplied with life from another power close to reason. 

<meta>catchword: XI After-</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's hierarchy, using the allegory of Adam and Eve to represent the Fall of the human intellect into sensory life. He argues that even in children and animals, a spark of the higher soul remains, though it is often obscured by the physical demands of the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book I. The previous page discussed how the rational soul mediates between divine intelligence and the physical body. This section examines whether the rational soul can truly "sin" or "suffer," the nature of animal life, and the relationship between the individual mind and the "common intellect."</meta>

->### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

...to be supplied by one rational <term>soul</term><note>Ficino uses "soul" (anima) to refer to the animating principle of a living being, which in humans has a rational capacity.</note>, but in the meantime, it is said to be present itself, and yet not present. It is present indeed, insofar as it provides life, but not truly present: because it does not carry out the effect of "merging" there, as intelligence does in the higher realms, and the substance of the rational soul itself remains within itself, nor does it become a part of the <term>composite</term><note>The "composite" refers to the union of soul and body that makes up a physical living creature.</note>. This view was pleasing to Ficino, and before him to Porphyry, who denied that the rational soul of a man becomes the actual soul of a brute beast, though he allowed that the souls of animals possess a certain cleverness and a bit of reason, and that they live forever. Origen also attempted the same; indeed, when he heard that demons frequently insinuate themselves into men, and were once sent into pigs, he dared to suggest that the souls of men might be sent into animals, perhaps for the sake of purging them. But let them look to these matters themselves. One must observe, however, that Plotinus tempers his judgment here, saying: *if our souls are in brutes*. Likewise, where he says, *If it is carried along*, namely by <term>Adrasteia</term><note>original: "Adragstis." Adrasteia is the Greek goddess of inescapable destiny or fate, often associated with the laws of reincarnation in Platonic thought.</note>, and again when he adds: *Those which have sinned*: as if speaking of a place of purgatory. Finally, he denies that the soul becomes the proper form of the brute or a part of the composite. But we shall correct this opinion in what follows. Indeed, we have declared how Platonic sayings should be refined in the books of our *Theology*, especially the final ones.

*In the rational soul, there is neither sin nor punishment, strictly speaking; rather, these exist in the irrational life, which is the image of the soul. Although this life is no longer an image once the soul departs from here, it is nonetheless a certain vital act rooted in the soul.*

### XII Chapter Twelve
Chapter twelve raises and solves doubts concerning these statements, saying that in the essence of the soul itself there is, properly speaking, neither sin nor punishment, because it is a simple form subsisting in itself and, strictly speaking, does not fall into the lowest things. Instead, these occur in the life flowing from it, and strictly in the <term>animal</term><note>The "animal" (animalis) refers to the biological entity composed of the lower life-force and the physical body.</note> which is composed of this life and the body. He says in one place that the soul sins, and in another that it does not: it "sins" in the sense that it slackens its intention, which was previously turned toward higher things; but it "does not sin" in the sense that it neither loses its natural qualities nor admits foreign things within. Then he declares how the generation of the animal occurs: that is, when a certain life reflects from the soul into a body already prepared in a certain condition. This is something natural, not a sin; nor does the soul "fall" in a strict sense, but rather gives its nod and favor. Furthermore, this life—which is an act and a kind of image of the soul—does not perish when the soul departs from here, insofar as it is an act of the soul, but it ceases to be an image. This is just as if an image is made in a mirror from a face: when the face departs, a certain act remains in the face that was effective in making the image shine, but the image itself does not remain. Truly, this act of the soul ceases to be an image when the body lacks the preparation to reflect that image, and the soul is entirely turned toward the <term>intelligible</term><note>The "intelligible" refers to the realm of pure thought and divine forms, beyond the physical world.</note>. Nevertheless, its act does not cease, for such is the vigor of life; just as when a hand is cut off, the life-giving act itself does not cease, which would be equally ready to return if the hand were restored, as is seen in hair that grows back. Remember that Numenius and Plotinus thought that no part of life ever perishes, because life is a part of eternity—that is, the splendor of the First Intelligence and the indissoluble bond of the universe.

*The rational soul reasons through itself, not through the instrument of the body; it also understands through its own intellect, and through the common intellect, which is like a form of any individual intellect.*

### XIII Chapter Thirteen
Chapter thirteen explains the final point proposed in the inquiry: namely, what it is that considers these things at present. He asserts that it is not some "composite" that considers these things through the soul as if it were a mere part, but the soul itself, existing in itself, meditates on such things. Therefore, the soul is not changed in the same way the body is changed, but its motion is its own, an essential act of life, or a vital and perennial act of its essence. He adds: just as rational consideration is ours (that is, belonging to the soul's own nature) and is not driven through the body, so too intelligence is the soul's own. For clearly the soul is intellectual, so much so that intelligence in the soul is life, and the highest life of the soul. Thus, that which is a part of us acts upon us—that is, upon the reason most proper to us—just as the "common intellect" acts upon our own. Note here that life in all things is almost the final splendor of the mind; but the Supreme Mind is the highest degree of life. Hence that prophetic saying: *Give me understanding, and I shall live* <note>original: "intellectum da mihi, & viuam." A quote from Psalm 119:144.</note>. He adds that the soul understands both through its own intellect and through the common and divine intellect, and that reason strives toward our intellect, and our intellect finally toward the divine. Both are parts of us, but in different ways. Our own intellect is a part of us because it is, in a way, the apex of the soul; but the divine intellect is seen as a part because our intellect is subject to the divine as "matter" is to "form," and it understands through the divine and the divine itself. Indeed, through this form common to all, individual intellects—though not a single one—are nonetheless "something one." And so that part of us seems to be like a form—a form, I say, providing the very intellectual being and the act of understanding to our intellects. To this point tends that prophetic saying: *The Lord is the portion of my inheritance* <note>original: "Dominus pars hæreditatis meæ." A quote from Psalm 16:5.</note>. Whatever we have omitted in this commentary can be clear to those who consider it diligently; partly they will be explained more broadly in what follows, and partly we have explained them in our *Theology* and in the arguments already published on the whole of Plato. Now, concerning how the intellect is ours, and whether it is a part of us or not, you will learn in the fifth book of the third *Ennead*.

<summary>Ficino explains that the rational soul is inherently pure and does not sin; rather, "sin" is a turning away from the divine. He also describes the soul's relationship to the body as an image in a mirror and introduces the concept of a "common intellect" that illuminates individual human minds.</summary>

And this third thing might be understood in two ways: for it is either the mixture itself, <margin>B</margin> * or something else different derived from the mixture. Similarly, we must investigate the things that arise from these <term>passions</term><note>original: "pathemata." In Greek philosophy, "passions" refers to anything the soul "undergoes" or experiences, including emotions and physical sensations.</note>—actions, opinions, and even thought and belief; do these belong to the same source as the passions, or are some one way and others another? And how should we <margin>* that</margin> * regard contemplations: of what kind are they, and to whom do they belong? And indeed, what is this very thing that is looking into these matters, performing the inquiry and the judgment? And what is it that perceives? <margin>C</margin> For it is proper to begin from there, <margin>* since</margin> * since the passions are either types of perceptions, or at least cannot exist without perception.

FIRST, then, we must consider the soul: is "soul" one thing, and the "essence of soul" another? If so, the soul would be a composite, and it would not be strange * for it to receive and possess such passions, if the argument should allow it, and altogether to have habits and dispositions, both better and worse. But if the soul and the essence of soul are the same, the soul would be a certain <term>form</term><note>original: "eidos." A "form" here refers to a pure, non-material principle that gives structure and life but is not made of "stuff" that can be changed or damaged.</note>, incapable of receiving all these activities which it imparts to another, but having its own activity <margin>D</margin> within itself, whatever reason may show it to be. For in this way, it would be true to say that the soul is immortal, if indeed that which is immortal and incorruptible must be <term>impassible</term><note>original: "apathes"—unable to be affected, changed, or harmed by outside forces.</note>, giving something of itself to another, but receiving nothing from elsewhere, or only what it receives from the higher principles from which it is not cut off. For what could such a thing fear, being incapable of receiving anything from the outside? <margin>* in another</margin> * That thing, then, might fear, * which is able to suffer. Nor would it be daring; for daring belongs to those for whom fearsome things are not present.

<margin>1</margin>
<margin>Concerning man's disturbances, senses, opinions, intellect, soul, or the composite, etc.</margin>
PLEASURES and pains, fears and disturbances, likewise both boldness, desires, and flights, and torments—whose are they? Are they of the soul itself rather using a body? or of some third composite? This can be understood in two ways: for it is either the thing that is mixed, or the mixture itself: or something else arising from the mixing. Similarly, we must ask about those things which are made from these passions, and are acted upon, and thought. Again, we must inquire about thought and opinion, whether they belong to the same things as the passions: or if some are one way, and others are handled differently. Furthermore, we must investigate intelligence, to whom it belongs, and in what manner it holds itself. And even about this very thing, which considers and provides the inquiry and judgment concerning these matters, what it may be. And first, to whom does it belong most of all to perceive? For from here it seems we must begin: since the passions themselves are either certain senses, or at least are not without sense.

<margin>II</margin>
<margin>If the soul is a simple form in itself, it is not suffering. If the soul is form, it will not suffer.</margin>
BUT FIRST we must think about the soul, whether the soul is one thing, and the essence of the soul is another. For if it is different, the soul will be a certain composite: nor will it be absurd for it to receive forms now, and other things later, and for such passions of it to exist, if only reason allows it, and altogether habits and better or worse affections. But if the soul and the essence of the soul are the same, the soul will surely be a certain form, not receiving actions of that kind, which it imparts to another: but having in itself a related action, whatever reason shall demonstrate. For thus it will be true to say it is immortal. Since it is necessary that what is immortal and incorruptible is also impassible, imparting some of itself to another, but itself receiving nothing from another, unless it receives anything from superior things, from which indeed, being more excellent, it is by no means separated. What therefore would such a thing fear, since it receives nothing from the outside? Certainly that might fear, which can also suffer. Nor again will it be daring; for daring is present to those for whom things that would be feared are not yet present.

It argues that if the soul is a pure, immortal form, it must be "impassible," meaning it cannot be harmed or changed by physical sensations.</summary>

**N**EVERTHELESS, one must place the soul in the body, whether it is said to be "over" this or "in" this, from which, together with the soul itself, the whole animal is named. Therefore, using the body as an instrument, it will not be compelled to receive bodily <term>passions</term><note>original: "passiones." For if the soul must use an instrument, it must know those passions from the outside through sensation; for to use the eyes is to see. But even the injuries that happen concerning vision will happen to it: and therefore also distress and pains, and in short, whatever happens concerning the body; for which reason the soul also has desires, clearly while caring for its own instrument. But in what way will the passions enter from the body into the soul? A body, indeed, can pass something of its own to another body: but how can a body to a soul? For this would be as if one thing suffered while another were the sufferer. For insofar as one is the user and the other is that which is used, they are each separate. Therefore, he who grants that the soul is the user separates it. But before it is separated through philosophy, how did it hold itself? Was it perhaps mixed? But if it was mixed, it was either a certain blending and tempering, or as if diffused and unfolded through the body, or as a form not at all separate, or as a form touching it, like a <term>governor</term><note>original: "gubernator" or "κυβερνήτης." A classic Platonic metaphor comparing the soul to a pilot steering a ship.</note>, or partly separate (which is the user) and partly mixed (whatever is in the order of that which is used): so that philosophy might turn this back toward the user, and lead the user away from there, except so far as the highest necessity compels, so that as far as possible, it conducts itself as if it does not always use it.

### VI

<margin>*VI It is brought into doubt whether it is true what is said, that the soul is <term>impassible</term><note>original: "impassibilem". In Neoplatonism, this means the soul cannot be changed or harmed by physical experiences.</note>; and that, being joined to the living being, it provides life to it by nature. But if it is so, they suffer and act—not the soul, but the composite itself: which feels, acts, or suffers.*</margin>

**B**UT perhaps it is better to say generally, from the fact that the powers are present, those things which have them act through them, while the powers themselves remain immobile, providing their possessors the force of acting. But if it is so, while the living being suffers, it is necessary that the soul—which gives the cause of living to the <term>composite</term><note>original: "coniuncto". The "composite" refers to the union of body and soul.</note>—must live and suffer, yet remain impassible, since the passions and actions belong to the possessor. But if so, then living also will not belong to the soul at all, but to the composite. Or living will not belong to the soul of the composite, but to itself. Neither will it be the power of sensing, but that which possesses it will sense. But if sensation, which is a movement through the body, reaches as far as the soul and ends there, how will the soul not sense? Or will it sense by the presence of the sensory power, because it is there? But what indeed will it sense? For it is the composite. But if the power is not moved, how then is it already the composite, and without the soul, nor the force of the soul, coming together for this very purpose?

### VII

<margin>*VII The rational soul presiding over the heavy soul in which is the sense: let the passions and senses be in this passive part of the composite living being.*</margin>

**B**UT let the composite itself belong to the soul: namely, from the fact that it is present there: the soul itself, being such as it is, not handing itself over into the composite, or into another part of it, but producing from such a body—and by a certain light as if handed down from itself—the nature of the <term>living being</term><note>original: "animalis". Plotinus distinguishes between the "Living Being" (the body animated by a reflection of the soul) and the higher "Soul" itself.</note>, which exists as something else: to which indeed belongs sensing, and the other passions of the living being which we have described. But how do we sense? Perhaps because we are not separated from such a living thing. And if other more excellent things belonging to the whole essence of man—constituted from many things—are present to us: it is necessary that the sensory power of the soul perceives not the sensible things themselves, but their images impressed upon the living being through the sense, for these forms are in a certain way intelligible. Wherefore the exterior sense is a phantom of this sense; but this sense is truer in essence: since it is a perception of images only, without passion. From these forms, at least, from which the soul now receives the sole command of the living thing, opinions and thoughts and understandings proceed. This is where we truly are. But the things before us are ours, but we are that which follows from here on, presiding over the living being from above. Yet nothing will prevent us from calling this whole thing the "living being," but saying that what is lower is mixed. What remains is the true man. Although the lower part is partly lion-like and partly brute, it is called altogether manifold. For when man concurs together with the rational soul, whenever he reasons, it is surely "us" who reason: because the discourses of reason are the actions of the soul.

...and it is everywhere the same property, because each person possesses the soul in its entirety. For instance, the **Primary Soul** <note>original: "Ψυχὴ τὴ πρώτη". This refers to the higher, celestial soul that remains in the divine realm.</note> contains the **Forms** <note>original: "τὰ ἤδη" (eide). These are the perfect archetypes or blueprints of all things.</note> in a twofold way: in the Soul they are, as it were, unrolled and separated, but in the **Intellect** <note>original: "νῷ" (Nous). In Plotinus's system, the Intellect is the realm of pure, unified thought above the Soul.</note> they are all together as one. We receive a third reflection from that **indivisible nature** (as Plato says) which is above, and from the nature that is **divisible** <note>original: "μεριστῆς". This refers to how the soul's influence is spread out across the physical parts of a body.</note> regarding bodies. We must not think of it as being divided among bodies in the sense that it distributes itself into the physical dimensions of whatever living thing it occupies; rather, it is present to the whole of the universe as a unity. It appears to be present in bodies by illuminating them, making them "living beings" not by merging its own substance with the body, but by remaining itself while giving out **images** <note>original: "εἴδωλα" (eidola). Like shadows or reflections.</note> of itself, just as a face appears in many mirrors. The first of these images is **sensation** <note>original: "αἴσθησις".</note>, which resides in the common part of the being; then follow all the other powers of the soul, one after another, down to the powers of reproduction, growth, and the general capacity for action—all of which are directed toward the work being produced, while the soul’s creative power remains fixed upon its source.

<column-break/>

**A** And it is everywhere the same, its own property because each person possesses it whole in the primary soul. We possess the **Forms** in a twofold manner: in the soul, they are, as it were, explained and set apart, but in the intellect, they are all together. We have a certain close connection: perhaps as one who begins the nature of the intelligible and truly real essence; we, however, are third in line from that **indivisible nature** (as Plato says), the celestial nature, and from the nature that is divisible among bodies. **B** It is necessary to understand this "divisibility" among bodies in this way: the soul gives itself over to the dimensions of the body so far as each thing is a living being, while it remains one in the whole and in the universe. Furthermore, it appears to be present to bodies by illuminating them: making them living things, I say, not by coming out of itself into the body, but by remaining itself while providing **images** of itself, just as the image of a face appears in many mirrors. The first image is **sensation**, **C** which flourishes in the common part of the being; then, from here, every other "species" or power of the soul is mentioned, one always following the other, reaching down to the nature of generating and increasing, and even to the performance of other works, while the power that does the acting is turned toward the work to be accomplished.

**D** Therefore, the nature of that higher soul will be for us free from the cause of evils, which a human being both commits and suffers. For these things belong to the "common" living being—"common," I say, as has been stated. But if **opinion** and **thought** belong to the soul itself, how will it be free from the fault of sin? For opinion is often false, and many evils are committed because of it. Perhaps evils are committed by us because we are overcome by our "inferior part." For we often succumb to **desire** or **anger**, or we yield to an evil image. That which is called "fallible thought," which is also the **imagination** <term>original: "phantasia". In this context, it refers to the mental power that receives and stores sensory images, which can be misleading.</term>, often does not wait for the judgment of the deliberating mind; instead, we follow along, obeying our lower parts, just as happens with sensation **E** before the power of reason can discern the truth. It happens that we "see falsely" through the common sense. Has the **Intellect** <note>The highest part of the human mind that communicates with divine truth.</note> perhaps not reached us? Thus, it remains innocent. Perhaps it should be said that we either have or have not grasped the "intelligible" thing itself which is in the Intellect, or that which is within us. For it is possible to "have" it, and yet not have it ready and at hand. We have distinguished the "common" properties from the "private" ones by this: that some are corporeal **F** and do not happen without a body, while others do not require a body for their action and are therefore judged to be the soul's own properties. We consider **reasoning** <note>original: "Excogitationem".</note> to be the soul's own work—specifically the power that judges and distinguishes the images coming from the senses. This power looks upon the Forms and perceives them with a kind of internal sense; this is the true reasoned thought of the soul itself. For true thought is the act of the higher intellects, and it is often a likeness and a communion between the external and internal.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS BOOK I.

...the body of ours, we say that *we* suffer. We are, therefore, spoken of in two ways: either including the **brute** <note>original: "bruto" / "θηρίου". In Plotinian philosophy, this is the animal nature or the "composite" of body and the lower trace of the soul.</note> added to us, or as that which stands above it. The brute is the body made alive. The **true man**, however, is distinct from these; he is pure, possessing the **virtues** <note>original: "virtutes" / "ἀρετὰς".</note> that exist in the intellect, which are rooted in the separate soul itself—separate, I say, and separable even while it is here in the world. For when the soul is absent entirely, those things which shine forth from it depart as well, following it. But the virtues that come not from wisdom <note>original: "prudentia" / "φρονήσει". This refers to practical or intellectual wisdom.</note> but from habit and practice seem to belong to the **composite being**. For these are human, as are the vices—envy, emulation, and pity. But to whom does friendship belong? Perhaps partly to the composite, and partly to the inner man.

<margin>
XI
In children, the animal nature and the imagination of the rational soul reign. This is also true in sleep and in mental ecstasy; but when our reason moves to the center, it acts by itself.
</margin>

AS LONG AS we are children, the powers within the composite are active, but only a few things shine down upon it from the higher realms. When these higher powers are "idle" in relation to us, they are still active toward the higher world. They act upon us only when they reach the center. What then? Are we not also that which exists before this? Indeed, but we must turn our attention toward it. We do not constantly use everything we possess, but only when we turn our "center" toward the higher things or their opposites, or when we bring something from potentiality into action. How do **brutes** possess a "living being"? Perhaps if a human soul is in them (as it is said of souls that have sinned), that soul does not belong to the brute as a separable part, but it is present without being fully "there"; instead, the communion of its senses possesses an **image of the soul** <note>original: "simulachrum animae" / "εἰδώλου". A reflection or trace of the true soul, rather than the soul itself.</note> together with the body. The body, I say, is made such as it is by the "coloring" of this soul-image. But if a human soul has not entered it, then the animal nature is produced by an illumination from the **Soul of the All** <note>original: "totius animae" / "τῆς ὅλης". Often called the World Soul, which provides the life-force for the entire physical cosmos.</note>.

<margin>
XII
In the essence of the soul, no one sins, nor is there punishment; but sin and punishment occur in the animal nature generated by the soul, in whatever way it is punished.
</margin>

BUT IF the soul is not the sinner, how can there be judgments and punishments? This discourse seems to contradict all tradition, which says the soul sins, is purified, pays penalties in the underworld, and migrates through bodies. We must hold to whichever view is preferred. But perhaps someone might find a way for them not to conflict. For the one who claims the soul does not sin posits a single, entirely simple thing, taking "soul" and "the soul's essence" to be the same. But the one who says it sins joins to it another form of soul that possesses heavy passions. Let the soul itself, then, be a composite of all these, and it certainly suffers as a whole, and the **composite** sins; it is this composite that pays the penalty, not that higher soul. Hence Plato says: "For we see it as those who would look upon the sea-god **Glaucus**." <note>original: "marinumer Glaucum". In Plato’s Republic (10.611), Glaucus is a sea-god whose original form is hidden by seaweed, shells, and rocks; Plotinus uses this to illustrate how the soul's true nature is obscured by physical attachments.</note> If one wishes to see its nature, one must strip away the additions and look at its "philosophy"—what it touches and what it is related to—to see what it truly is. Thus, there is one life and one set of actions, and another thing that is punished. The withdrawal and separation must be not only from this body, but from every added part. Indeed, in the process of **generation** <note>original: "generatione" / "γενέσει". The process of coming into physical existence.</note>, an addition occurs, or rather the generation of another species of soul. As for the question of how this generation occurs, the answer would be that the soul descends...

<column-break/>

Or if the thing is our body, we say that we are suffering. Thus "we" is twofold: either including the brute, or that which is already above it. The brute is the body made alive. But the true man is another, pure of these things, having the virtues in thought which are established in the soul that is separate—separate, I say, or even separable while still here. Since when that soul has completely withdrawn, the virtues established as a reflection or echo of its illumination also depart—those virtues not of wisdom, but clearly of habit and exercise, for they do not belong to the vice of this world, since envy, jealousy, and pity—or even some friendships—belong to whom? Are some of the human being and others not?

WHILE WE ARE CHILDREN, the activities are those of the composite, and little of the things from above shines into it. But when it is idle toward us, it acts toward the things above. It acts toward us when it comes as far as the center. What then? Are we not that which is before this? But we must add "we," or rather not everyone uses that which is before this at all times. But only when we set the middle parts toward the things above, or toward the opposites, or as many of the powers or habits as we lead into activity.

How do the brutes have the living being? If, as you say, human souls are in them—as it is said, having sinned—the soul becomes to the brute that which is separable, yet present or providing for it; but the shared perception, through the image of the soul together with the body, has a body produced as if by the image of the soul. But if it is not a human soul, such a living being has an illumination produced by the Whole Soul.

But if the soul sins, how are there punishments? But this argument disputes with everything that says souls both sin and are purified, and pay penalties in Hades, or are reincarnated. One must speak against this in whatever way one wishes. But perhaps someone might find a way that they do not conflict. For to attribute sins to the soul is one argument, positing it as entirely one and simple. It equates the soul and the soul-like. But the one who allows it to sin joins it together, placing around it another form of soul, which has the terrible passions, and the whole is from both.

And the whole sins, that is, the composite. And it is this which gives the penalty, not that. Whence he says, "we see it as those who see the sea-god Glaucus." He says those who wish to see its nature must scrape away the additions and look to its philosophy, to see what it touches and to what it is akin. And there is another life, and other activities, and that which is punished is different. But the withdrawal and the separation are not only from this body, but from every addition. For those things occur in generation. The question of how generation occurs is answered by saying that the soul descends...

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>It happens through itself.</margin>
But if this image is produced from the soul itself, how does it descend? If what the soul sends forth is an image, how is its thinking not a sin? <note>Plotinus is addressing whether the soul's "downward" focus into the body constitutes a "fall" or a moral failure.</note> But if this thinking is merely an illumination directed toward what is below, it is not a sin, just as a shadow is not a sin. The cause of the shadow is that which is illuminated; for if there were nothing there to receive the light, the soul would have nowhere to shine. Therefore, the soul is said to "descend" or "incline" only in the sense that the thing illuminated by it exists alongside it. 

<margin>A</margin> The soul, then, lets go of the image only if there is nothing nearby to receive its light. It lets go not because it is being torn apart, but because the image is no longer there. It is no longer "here" below if the soul looks entirely toward the heights. 

The poet <note>Referring to Homer in the Odyssey, Book 11.</note> seems to separate these two aspects in the case of Hercules, placing his **image** <note>original: "simulachrum" / "εἴδωλον". Often translated as 'shade' or 'phantom'.</note> among the dead in Hades, but placing Hercules **himself** among the gods. He maintains both accounts: that Hercules is among the gods, and that he dwells among the dead. 

<margin>A part is divided.</margin>
Perhaps this explanation is persuasive: because Hercules possessed **active virtue** <note>original: "virtutem actiuam". Practical excellence in worldly affairs.</note> and was judged worthy to be a god because of his noble character—since he was a man of action rather than a man of contemplation—he is not entirely in the higher realm. While he himself is among the gods, a part of him remains below.

<margin>XIII. It is not a composite in the soul, but the soul itself that reasons and understands, both through its own intellect and through the common intellect.</margin>
BUT CONCERNING THESE MATTERS, who is it that investigates? Is it not "we" in the soul? Perhaps it is us, but through the soul. And how through the soul? Do we investigate by "possessing" the soul? Or is it the soul itself that investigates? 

<margin>D</margin> If it is the soul, will it not be moved? Or must we grant it a motion that is not like the motion of bodies, but is the soul’s own **life**? Furthermore, intelligence is ours in the sense that the soul is intellectual; this intelligence is a higher form of life, active both when the soul thinks and when the intellect acts upon us.

<column-break/>

<meta>Continuity note: This column continues the Latin translation of the Greek concepts regarding the "inclination" of the soul.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> ...descending; and then, something else is created by the soul, occurring in the very inclination of the soul toward the body, as if by a "nod" or a gesture. Does the soul then dismiss the image? And how is this inclination, even without a "nod," not a sin? If to "nod" is simply to illuminate that which is lower, it is certainly not a sin, any more than a shadow is. The cause of the shadow is the object being illuminated. If this object did not exist, the soul would have no way to shine. Therefore, the soul is said to "descend" and "incline" because that which is illuminated by it is connected to it. 

<margin>B</margin> It dismisses the image, then, unless there is something close by to receive it. It dismisses it not by being split, but because the image is no longer present here. It is no longer here if the soul looks back entirely toward the heights. The poet appears to distinguish this in Hercules, sending his image to the underworld while counting Hercules himself among the gods. He observes both in his words: that he is among the gods and that he stays among the dead. He divided them. 

<margin>C</margin> Perhaps this reasoning is likely: Since Hercules possessed active virtue and was considered a god because of his moral uprightness—being an active man rather than a contemplative one—he would not be entirely among the higher beings. And so, while he is indeed among the higher beings, a part of him remains meanwhile among those below.

<margin>
XIII
The soul is not a composite, but the soul itself reasons and understands, both through its own intellect and through what is shared.
</margin>
IN TRUTH, regarding who considers these things: are we not in the soul? Perhaps it is we, but through the soul. But how through the soul? Does one consider them by "having" a soul, or is it the soul itself? Will it not then be moved? Or must we admit a motion that is not of bodies, but is the soul's own life? Moreover, understanding is ours because the soul is intellectual, and this understanding stands as a better life—both when the soul understands and when the intellect acts within us.

# MARSILIO FICINO'S
# ARGUMENT ON THE
# BOOK ON VIRTUES

-> SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK. <-

-> We must strive to flee from here, to become like God through virtue. <-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' featuring floral and leaf motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
**T**HE PURPOSE of this book is for the soul to become like God. Its subject matter is **virtue**, through which such a likeness is gained. Finally, the form of the book is its division into seven chapters: the first is an exercise in discovering virtue; the following chapters define and distribute it. 

The first chapter begins with a "golden saying" of Plato from the book on Knowledge (the *Theaetetus*): "That we may avoid evils, we must flee from here immediately." To "flee from here" means to become like God. The soul becomes like God through virtue. But lest anyone err in knowing this goal, he argues that the soul becomes like God through virtue not because there is virtue in God in the same way as in the soul, but because God is the principle, the exemplar, and the very essence of virtue. By "God," I mean the **Divine Mind**, the craftsman of the world, presiding over both the world and its soul. 

Although at the start of the discussion he suggests we become like the Soul of the World and its Mind through virtue, as the argument progresses, he shows that the goal of this likeness extends higher—to the Divine Intellect itself. The soul reaches this goal, the "fourth level" where the archetypes of virtues exist, through three prior stages: first, the **civil virtues**; second, the **purifying virtues**; and third, the virtues of the **already purified soul**. This is the summary of the entire book.

*Although the soul becomes like God through virtues, God himself does not "have" virtue; rather, He is the exemplar of virtue. What is a "quality" in the soul is "essence" in God. Likewise, the existence of the Ideas <note>The Platonic Forms.</note> is confirmed here.*

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically focusing on the nature of virtue and how the human soul achieves likeness to God. While the previous page used the myth of Hercules to distinguish between the lower "image" and the higher "true self," this section provides a philosophical breakdown of different levels of virtue.</meta>

# 8 THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO

<margin>I</margin> **I**n the first chapter, he first says: If any human virtues are present in God, it is more probable that **prudence** and **justice** are present than others that deal with disturbances <note>original: "perturbationes" / "passions" or "emotions".</note>. Next, he says that none of the human virtues are civil virtues <note>original: "ciuiles" / referring to social or political virtues practiced in a community.</note>; and meanwhile, he brings forward the definitions of these virtues placed by Plato in the books of the *Republic*. In the meantime, however, he confesses that through these we attain a certain divine likeness. Yet he denies the logic that someone might use—namely, "the soul becomes like God through virtues; therefore, God has virtue." He also rejects the solution where someone might say God has virtues, but in some superior form. For he casts this aside: If the soul is granted to be made like God, even if the virtues in God are not finite but distantly superior, one could also grant that the soul can be made like a God who possesses no virtues at all. Indeed, although the air receives heat through the presence of light, the sun (from which the light flows) receives no heat from the living air; nor is fire heated simply because it heats something else. And yet these things become similar to those sources. Thus, the soul receives virtue from God, through which it becomes like God, yet God himself does not "possess" virtue <note>Ficino is arguing that God is the *source* of excellence, and therefore is "above" the category of virtue itself.</note>. 

Nor should anyone suggest: "Just as heat is accidental in water but native in fire, so virtue is foreign in the soul but naturally implanted in God, so that virtue exists in both, but is more excellent in God." For virtue is necessary for someone and exists *in* someone, in whom it acts as a form within a subject. But nothing is like this in God. Truly, the gift the soul receives from God retains nothing of the same nature in the soul as it has with God; for there, it is the very essence of God, but here it is something like a "qualitative essence." There, then, is the **exemplar** <note>The perfect original pattern or prototype.</note> and principle; here is a certain imaginary effect. Indeed, although an image performs the duties of that which it represents, it seems to retain nothing of the same nature. For here, virtue is something distinct and composite, but there it is nothing of the sort. Rather, the soul reflects the **Ideas** <note>The divine archetypes in the Mind of God.</note> through a certain disposition, just as a house reflects the intelligence of the architect. 

It is truly the opinion of many philosophers that things which are "accidents" <note>Non-essential qualities that can change, like being tan or cold.</note> in the order of bodies can be "substances" in that same corporal order. Thus, heat and light, which are accidents in water, are not accidents in the sphere of fire or in the heavens, but are substances. Here they are qualities that happen to change, but there they are (so to speak) essential and entirely unmoving qualities. From this, the Platonists will argue: things that proceed from the imperfect are finally perfected into the more perfect by the same power by which they proceeded, and they reach the most perfect; by whose power whatever is not most perfect is ruled and entirely completed as if it were in need. Therefore, the condition of **Forms**—which is led from a changing quality to an unmoving quality and an entirely essential property—finally leads to forms that are now "essences" rather than existing "in an essence." 

Truly, in an incorporeal thing—indeed, he shows that only an incorporeal thing can exist in this way—these exist differently than natural forms. There, heat, light, and the rest are the essence of the form; and to be and to act are themselves the essence. Likewise, the soul is an Idea, and an entirely perfect Idea. Therefore, the Idea of virtues (by which the soul itself is perfected) is also virtue from that source, both naturally implanted and continually preserved—though the Ideas of virtues are there in another way, as will appear in what follows. However, the exemplar of virtue is in God, namely God himself; but a certain form of virtue is in the substance of the rational soul itself; and the image of virtue is in the part of the soul lacking reason. Furthermore, in our soul, virtue is an added quality; in higher souls, it is an inborn and unmoving quality. In the Divine Mind, virtue is the very essence of the Mind and the act of being.

->How the soul becomes like God through virtue. And how civil virtue belongs to the purificatory stage of the purified soul.<-
->Exemplars are distinguished among themselves. And concerning the first and second movements of the soul.<-

<margin>II</margin> The second chapter of the book approaches the definitions of virtue and the virtues, specifically toward the same end we were speaking of: so that we may know the reason for our likeness to God and, having known it, compare it. He brings forward two main modes of likeness to the Principle in this way. When two things established under one principle both receive a quality from it, they agree in species or genus: like two things that are white or at least colored. Then, just as this is said to be like that, so in turn that is easily said to be like this. But when two things are different in genus (or more than genus), and one is from the other and under it like an image from a substance (or like what happens in a mirror), then the image is indeed like the exemplar where there is one nature of the same communion; yet the exemplar of virtue is not said to be "like" the image. Under this condition, the soul becomes like God through virtue, insofar as it receives virtue from there, which is the image of the divine exemplar. 

After this, he distinguishes the defined virtues. But you, to understand these, must understand which movements in us are "first" and which are "second." For the **first movements** are certain sudden impulses in our animal nature, stirred by external impulses through the animal’s senses and the natural instinct of its imagination, before the rational soul consults reason about them or perhaps notices with the imagination whether they should be pursued or rather fled—whether these be terrors or certain incitements. The **second movements**, however, consist in pursuing or declining, following either the observation of the higher imagination or even the counsel of reason, whether it be rash or mature. 

Therefore, the virtue that cuts off the second movements as they decline toward sensible things is called **civil virtue**; whether it be courage, temperance, prudence (consulting thus far), or justice (preserving thus). For we think enough has been done thus far by a citizen. But the virtues that not only cut off the second movements but uproot them are called **purificatory** <note>original: "purgatoriæ". Virtues that "cleanse" the soul from worldly attachment.</note>. Finally, the virtues that have already tamed the second disturbances and, moreover, either eradicate the first impulses (if that can even be done by a human) or at least moderate them by some reason and habit, are the virtues **of the purified soul**. 

Therefore, of these virtues which are in a triple genus, there are exemplars in God. But virtues are not in God at all. For there are no movements or business there in which our virtues are engaged. Through these three steps, then, together with Paul, we are "transformed into the same image," drawn "from glory to glory" <note>Ficino is quoting 2 Corinthians 3:18 to link Neoplatonism with Christian scripture.</note> by the spirit of the Lord. That is, having set out for that place, we apply our virtues like images to the divine exemplar and are reformed—which Plotinus, as if imitating Paul, will declare in the following. 

In this second chapter of the book, however, he performs only the duty of the **civil virtues**, which he calls certain "moderations" and "measures"—both regarding the passions and regarding the stirring of opinion, having established prudence in the place of knowledge. He adds that **Matter**, since it is by its own nature devoid of all measure and moderation, is most dissimilar to God, but appears similar only insofar as it receives measures and forms from that source. And since these things, though naturally most remote from God, can nevertheless appear somewhat similar to God under this condition, he wants the soul (which is by nature much closer to God) to acquire a certain divine likeness even through the civil virtues, which determine and moderate it like matter—although God has neither measure nor form. 

But you, regarding what is said—that He has no "form"—understand this of the **Father** himself, as existing above form and shapes. Regarding his **Intellect** (the Son), understand that He does not have a form distinct from His essence, but is already the Form itself and the fullness of all forms; from which we all receive, insofar as we advance toward the Virtue infused in us from there when we turn toward it; through which "He gave us power to become the sons of God" <note>Quoting John 1:12.</note>. But from God...
