<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically the second book of the first Ennead, which examines the nature of virtues and how the soul ascends to the divine. Having previously discussed "civil virtues," Ficino now moves into the higher "purifying" virtues and the intellectual relationship between the soul and God.</meta>

# ON BOOK II OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

In this way, let the soul be like God. It is as if someone, having looked deep within a soul so affected, would think that he immediately sees God. But you, in this chapter, when you read "Our Better part" <note>original: "Meliori nostro"</note>, you can understand it as **reason**; you might also read "to the better things," meaning those which introduce a better opinion, or by bringing oneself forward through a superior **virtue**. Likewise, where he says: "May you be entirely of God here" <note>original: "Totam Dei hîc sis"</note>, this refers to such a constitution of the soul, or that it should be entirely a turning toward divinity, or that it belongs entirely to God. Often in Plotinus, the same speech—as Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and editor</note> confesses—equally admits several meanings.

->To understand according to a certain **analogy** is spoken of regarding both the divine intellect and the soul. Likewise, the discussion concerns the **Word** <note>original: "sermo" or "verbum"</note>, whether in the voice, in the soul, or in the mind.<-

<margin>I II</margin>
*After the civil virtues, he approaches the greater ones in the third chapter of the book, and he properly defines the **purifying virtues** <note>virtues that "cleanse" the soul from material attachment</note>, and collectively with these, the virtues of a soul already purified. Meanwhile, he shows that the civil virtues ought to be called "dispositions toward virtue" rather than virtues themselves; and similarly, through them, we are "disposed and prepared" for divine likeness rather than actually being made like God. Furthermore, he does not want the **Ideas** <note>the perfect eternal patterns of things</note> to be in God in the sense of being affections, qualities, or reflections of the soul, for such things cannot exist in God. The basis for this claim is that our understanding is situated in a temporal progression <note>original: "discursione," meaning step-by-step reasoning</note>, whereas such understanding cannot exist in God. Truly, we say both God and the soul "understand" by a common name, yet this is not a purely accidental or chance name, nor is it based on a reason where the definition of understanding is exactly the same in species or genus for both. Rather, it is based on this condition: that this understanding in the soul is like a possession and an **image**, and it is preserved by the understanding of God as if by a far superior **Exemplar** <note>the original model</note>, to which the soul’s understanding refers as a representation. This condition is usually called **analogical**. He then compares them through analogy in this manner: just as the word in the voice is related to the word in the soul, so too is the word in the soul related to the word in the mind. When we say "word," you may also say "reason" or "logos." The word in the voice is the image and interpreter of the word in the soul; the word of the soul is the image and interpreter of the word in the mind. Finally, Plotinus says elsewhere that the **mind** is the image and word of God, whom he also calls the father of mind and intelligence. Here, surely, both Plotinus and Origen—and as I believe, their teacher Ammonius—thought that the divine intellect and the "Son" are related to "God the Father" (that is, the Good itself) just as **radiance** <note>original: "lumen"</note> is related to **light** <note>original: "lucem"</note>. They also thought the **Spirit** (that is, the life of the world) is related to the intellect as **color** is to radiance. Now, although they seem to bring an essential difference between these three, they nevertheless prove that there is such unity among them in other respects that no more singular unity could be imagined. Thus far did the geniuses of the philosophers proceed, especially in that era. But their judgment must then be referred to the councils of the Holy Fathers. Let us now conclude the chapter. The word in the voice requires air, which the form of the soul does not. Likewise, it is divided into more parts and longer times than the word of the soul; the word of the soul itself passes in time. However, the word of the mind, or reason, is not distracted by any time. Likewise, this reason or notion of the mind often fulfills through a single form and a single act what the word or reasoning of the soul is forced to perform through many forms and acts. Finally, the Good itself stands above all limits of forms and intelligence: from which it appears that one proceeds from multitude and lack, step by step, toward a greater and ever greater unity and self-sufficiency.*

->The soul is neither the Good itself, nor that which is properly called **Boniform** <note>having the "form of the Good"</note>. Likewise, the steps by which the Ideas are shared. Again, proof of the Ideas, and concerning the divinity of the soul. And how the forms of things are in the divine mind, how they are in ours, and how they are in reason and imagination.<-

<margin>I III</margin>
*Turning now from the virtues that are still purifying to those that are in the already purified soul, he says that the effect of purity itself is the goal of the purification, and these virtues are more excellent goals, the highest degree of human virtue, and the chief and nearest vessel of divine likeness. For this purity, restored through the service of cleansing, is not the soul's Good itself: for the soul is not content with itself as its end, since it had its beginning from elsewhere. Certainly, this nature which is now freed from foreign and evil things through purification cannot be the Good itself; otherwise, it would not have been subject to evil. Furthermore, it is not even what the Platonists call **Boniform**: for that is what is always equally a participant in the Good itself from the start; but a nature in need of this kind of purification is not always equally a participant, and therefore is not a participant in the Good in the primary way. For the order of goods rises necessarily from those things that participate in the Good either not always or not equally, to that which always participates equally, and finally from this to that which is simply the Good through itself, by the participation of nothing else. Thus, there is an ascent from the soul to the Intellect, and from the Intellect to the Good itself: just as one ascends from the decaying forms which participate unequally in elementary matter, to the forms in celestial matter which always participate equally, and finally to those forms in the "intellectual heaven" <note>the realm of pure thought</note> which are not in another through participation, but are now the intellectual heaven itself, simple, uniform, and likewise "all-form." Yet the first, equal, and eternal participation in the Good is what is properly called "Boniform," and it is the eternal splendor of the Good itself. Since the effect proceeds from its cause first as more similar, and then gradually becomes more dissimilar, it rightly depends first upon the simple and eternal Good itself, which it always participates in equally, and then upon that which participates unequally at times. Then he signifies the divinity of the soul when he says: "The evil of the soul is to cling to foreign things" (that is, the decaying), but its good is to cling to its own domestic and kindred things. Since, therefore, the Good—that is, life free from passions, uncorrupted truth, solid vigor, and full joy—happens to the soul only when it clings to divine things, it is clear that its origin is very close to that realm. Hence the saying: "For me, to cling to God is good." Since the soul, by purification alone (that is, by restoration to its own nature), suddenly turns toward the Good itself and by that turning alone suddenly possesses it, it is clear its nature is divine. Indeed, our soul is more vehemently affected toward the Good than toward the True: for it seeks the True as a good, and the Good itself is more powerful than the True, since power itself belongs to the Good rather than the True. Therefore, when the soul, having shaken off the mists of errors, suddenly follows the True, surely the purification from evils is followed immediately by the Good. After this, he says that the purity of the soul and its turning toward the Good is the virtue of the soul—that is, the third degree of virtue belonging to the purified soul. He adds that it is much more "virtue" what the soul attains from that turning: he now signifies the **Exemplary Virtue**, to...*

# COMMENTARIES OF MARSILIO FICINO
<sig>B iiij</sig>
<meta>catchword: So</meta>

As the soul ascends through the three steps toward the aforementioned lights, it then sees by means of forms. And indeed, just as there are three steps, so there are three kinds of **Exemplary Virtues**. The first is when the soul turns its **imagination** toward the **reason** that has already been illuminated by the **mind**, or is to be formed from it. The second is when it hands over the <term>formulas</term> <note>original: "formulas" — here referring to the rational blueprints or "logoi" of things</note> of reason to the forms implanted in its own **intellect**, so that it may know them better there. The third is where it perfectly accommodates its own intellect to the **Divine Mind**, and conforms its understanding to the very character of the Divine Mind: this it achieves through a certain eternal contact. From this, it follows that in time they can apply reason or, in turn, properly conform the imagination. There are primary forms of all things, namely in the one Intellect that produces all things; there is a supreme gathering of forms in the one matter that is subject to all things. Next, he wishes for them to be distinct and formed by the difference of natural forms among themselves: which is neither from formless matter, nor by chance (since it is always most ordered), nor from any one single species among these forms, since it is ordered toward the one thing most common to all. Therefore, since the formal distinction of all forms proceeds from the one producer of all, it is necessary that the principle of distinction be present there, through which there are certain forms distinguished from one another by reason. Therefore, that intellect is both **uniform** and **omniform** <note>Meaning it is both a single unity and contains the forms of all things simultaneously</note> at once. But there, a most close union also occurs; for the forms are one because they are of one essence, though diverse in their rational principle. 

But in every intellect after that one, forms are certain essential contacts of the **Ideas**, eternally and deeply implanted. From this contact, thereafter in the soul—that is, in the rational faculty—the <term>formulas</term> of the Ideas are conceived, as if in a shared living, always present in their placement, but passing from a state of habit into action, one by one in time. These are the universal formulas, designating both what each thing is and for what purpose. Furthermore, from these, formulas soon flow into the **imagination**, falling away into specific instances for individual things; these show "of what kind" a thing is rather than "what" it is, and they scarcely reveal the reason "why" it is so. 

Now, when Plotinus denies elsewhere that the figures of things are received by the soul, do not think he contradicts this book; understand rather that figures are not "stamped" into the soul by lower, material things, nor do they arrive recently, only to recede into a third state and be utterly erased. For these forms, which the soul draws from its inmost fountain, are as it were the very nature of the soul—whether it be a single natural soul, or something added and applied. For the soul proceeds from the Author of its own nature. It comes forth near to others from another nature, always endowed with its own duty. Remember, Plotinus is speaking here specifically about the intellect as the "goods" of the soul; for he thinks this belongs to the virtues: that the entire soul may emerge from there as an **intellectual world**, the end of which is the "simply blessed" state itself. For just as the soul underlies what is corporeal, and is the very "length" of the soul <note>An analogy for the soul's extension or reach</note>, so above the understanding of the mind is that same "Intellect simply," and above the intellectual good stands the "Good Simply" itself. 

Regarding the words to be explained, where he says that the figures or "impressed forms" ought to be accommodated to their own **exemplars**—now led into action and in a suitable brilliance—understand these to be the formulas of the imagination [accommodated to] the forms of reason and the brilliances of reason. Likewise, the formulas of reason [are accommodated] to the intellect’s own forms, or rather to be applied to the formations themselves. For here, there is always the presence of the Divine Mind. When he says that being an intellect is "alien" to the soul, understand this to mean that the soul has its own implanted intellect, and its own proper intellect is always joined to the divine, and indeed joined in a way peculiar to itself. Truly, that the forms of the soul are natural within it, and that our intellect is always conformed to the divine, we have sufficiently proven in our **Theology** <note>Referring to Ficino's major work, "Platonic Theology"</note>.

->In the specific imagination of the rational soul, images are often stirred according to the first movements of the imagination, which exists in an animal before it deliberates or notices.<-

<margin>V</margin>
He defines the virtues of the **purified soul** in a sufficiently manifest order. As for what he calls "pre-figured fantasy" here, understand it as those images which, from the first stirrings, are prone to press upon and speak within our imagination before reason fully takes notice.

->Wisdom in the Divine Mind is like a **touch**; in our mind, it is like a **contact**; in reason, it is like a **visible figure**.<-

<margin>VI</margin>
He confirms that the goal of the soul is not mere "innocence," but to **become God**. He says that the person in whom only the "first movements" remain is both a certain god and a <term>daemon</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, a "daemon" is a guiding spirit or a being between mortal and divine, not a "demon" in the modern sense</note>. For daemons are touched by some affections, while the one in whom even those first movements are seen to have vanished is simply a **god**—that is, an entirely intellectual soul of the number of those who properly accompany the Divine Mind. He adds that when the soul is turned entirely toward itself (following a preceding purification), it is such as it had proceeded from the Divine Mind: and suddenly it is there, inward and divine. For just as it set out to come here, it did not entirely depart from there. Indeed, reason clings to its own divine intellect at will, and the intellect is naturally coupled with the Divine Mind. After this, he defines the **Exemplary Virtues** insofar as they are somehow accommodated to us. For insofar as they are in the Divine Mind, they are not so much virtues, but Truth itself. **Wisdom** in the soul is the "impression" of those things which the intellect possesses; but the intellect has wisdom by a certain "touch." Understand the intellect here to be twofold: namely, our own and the divine. Wisdom in the divine is called "touch"—that is, the possession and rather the existence of the thing itself, not of some image. In our intellect, however, it is better called "contact"—that is, a real (so to speak) coupling, not an imaginary notion. For in the rational nature which is properly called "soul," possession is more imaginary; but in the intellect, it is (as it were) **substantial**. But this possession is first in the Divine Mind, and then it is translated into our own.

->The Divine Intellect is primarily the very things it possesses; our intellect is secondarily the things it possesses; reason is not similarly the things it possesses. Likewise, a comparison is made here of the virtues, and several precepts are handed down.<-

<margin>VII</margin>
He aligns the **Exemplary Virtues** accommodated to the soul in a certain order corresponding to the divine exemplars. He explains what each virtue is in God, and in what way the exemplary virtues in the soul rightly respond to the divine examples of the virtues. And where he says the soul "is not similarly" those very things it possesses (unlike the intellect), it is clear he understands the soul as different: in the soul, essence is one thing, forms or images are another, and habit and act are another. But in the Divine Mind, **essence** is reduced to **act** from eternity; and that essential act overcomes all things that are carried out through "additions" in the soul. Furthermore, our intellect, in a certain way, *is* what it possesses, to speak according to the mind of Plotinus.

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's ascent to God through grades of mental "light," defining how virtues exist as divine archetypes (Exemplary Virtues) that the human intellect can "touch" or "contact" through purification. He distinguishes between the Divine Mind, where being and knowing are identical, and the human soul, where knowledge is a reflected image or a rational formula.</summary>
<keywords>ascent of the soul, Exemplary Virtues, Divine Mind, imagination, reason, formulas, logoi, purification, Marsilio Ficino, Plotinus, theosis, Intellect</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Marsilio Ficino’s introductory commentary on the second book of Plotinus’s first Ennead and begins the primary text of Plotinus himself. Ficino has been discussing how the soul conforms to the Divine Mind through different grades of virtue. This page transitions from Ficino's summary to the actual treatise "On Virtues," where Plotinus explores the Platonic idea of "becoming like God."</meta>

For he is brought into activity by an eternal and intimate contact with all the **ideas**: the divine mind goes forth from eternity into the activity of these ideas. After this, he compares the virtues to one another in a way, and hands down certain precepts, or solves doubts. Let it be thus: Those things which precede the perfected purity of the soul are paths to virtue, rather than virtue itself. Likewise, purity is not to be considered virtue unless it is referred to God, both to be imitated and attained according to one's strength. Again, in the lower grades of virtues, the higher ones are present only through an **image**. In the higher ones, however, the lower are contained through the **exemplar** <note>original: "exemplar" — the divine archetype or perfect model of a thing</note> and the virtues themselves. Likewise, where the principles change, the types of virtues also change. I mean two principles, namely the specific end of each virtue, and its own rules and laws to which it is formed: especially where the principles of **prudence** are changed, which is judged the rule of the other virtues. From this it follows that <term>civil temperance</term> is of one type, <term>purifying temperance</term> <note>original: "purgatoria" — virtues that cleanse the soul from material attachments</note> is of another, <term>purified temperance</term> is of another, and <term>exemplary temperance</term> is of another; and the same applies to the other virtues. Finally, he concludes that the common end of all virtues is the One, which is the supreme good, found not in external things, nor in virtue, nor in the soul, but in God. Indeed, no conclusion more holy than this can be stated. It testifies to us the divine mind of our Plotinus.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD I
### BOOK II

->ON VIRTUES.<- ->On virtues<-

<margin>A</margin>
Since evils are here and necessarily revolve around this place, and the soul wishes to flee evils, one must undoubtedly flee from here. What then is this flight? He says, according to Plato, to become **like God**. This will happen if we become just and holy with **prudence**, and live entirely with virtue. If, therefore, we are made like Him through virtue, do we then become like a God who possesses virtue? And indeed, which God? Is it perhaps that God who more clearly seems to possess these things? Namely, the **World Soul** and its inner leader, in whom there is a wonderful prudence.
<margin>B</margin>
Truly it is probable that we, living here, become like him. But perhaps it is first ambiguous whether all virtues are present in him—for instance, being temperate and brave—to whom nothing is terrifying. For nothing happens to him from external things, nor does anything pleasant approach him whose desire might provoke him in its absence, so that he might wish to have or grasp it. But if he himself desires the **intelligible things** <note>original: "noētōn" / "intelligibilia" — the higher realities accessible only to the mind</note> just as our souls do, it is clear that from that source also come beauty and virtue to us.
<margin>C</margin>
Does he himself also possess these virtues? Perhaps it is not probable that he possesses the <term>civil virtues</term> <note>original: "politikas" — the social and political virtues of everyday life</note>, namely **prudence** concerning the power of deliberation, and **fortitude** concerning the impulse of anger, and **temperance** in a certain consensus and concord of the desiring nature with ra[son]...

<column-break/>

<margin>3 The soul becomes like the divine exemplar of virtues through virtue, insofar as it becomes an image.</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
Since evils are here and necessarily revolve around this place: and the soul wishes to flee evils: one must undoubtedly flee from here. What then is this flight? To become like God, says Plato. This will happen if we become just and holy with prudence, and live entirely with virtue. If, therefore, we are assimilated by virtue, do we then assimilate to one who has virtue? But to what god? Is it not to that god who seems more likely to have these? Namely, to the soul of the world and its innermost leader, in whom there is marvelous prudence.
<margin>B</margin>
Certainly it is probable that we, living here, become like him. But perhaps it is first ambiguous whether all are present to him, such as being temperate and brave, to whom nothing is terrifying. For nothing happens from external sources, nor does anything pleasant approach, the desire for which would trouble him when it is absent, so that he might have or grasp it. But if he himself desires the intelligible things in the same way our souls do: it is clear that from there beauty and virtue also fall to our lot.
<margin>C</margin>
Does he himself also have these? Perhaps it is not probable that he has the civil virtues, namely prudence concerning the power of deliberation: and fortitude concerning the impulse of anger: and temperance in a certain consensus and concord of the desiring nature with ra[son]...

It establishes a hierarchy of virtues, from social (civil) virtues to higher divine archetypes (exemplars), and questions whether the World Soul possesses these same human traits.</summary>

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK I.

<column-break/>

**[Translation of the Greek Column]**

They [the civic virtues] define and participate in the desires, and generally the passions, and they remove false opinions altogether for the better. By defining the soul to be outside of the immeasurable and the indefinite, and by being measured and defined itself, this measurement in the soul—as if in matter—is made like to the **Measure** <note>original: "μέτρῳ" (metron) — the divine standard or proportion that brings order to chaos</note> that exists in the divine realm, and they possess a trace of the Best that is there. For that which is completely immeasurable, being **matter** <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle) — the raw, formless potential that Plotinus views as the source of "evil" because it lacks order</note>, is completely unlike the divine. But insofar as it receives **Form**, it becomes like the Formless [the One]. The soul, being nearer to the body and more akin to it, participates more closely. Yet, it participates in such a way that it can be deceived, so that it imagines that the whole is not God, and that things remained in...

But since he [Plato] indicates another likeness, as belonging to the **greater virtue**, we must speak of that. In this, it will become clearer what the essence of **civic virtue** <note>original: "πολιτικῆς" (politikēs) — the social virtues like justice and temperance used in governing a city</note> is, and what the virtue is that is greater according to its essence, and generally if there is another kind beyond the civic virtues. Indeed, **Plato** says that "likeness to God" is a "flight from the things of this world" <note>This is a reference to Plato's *Theaetetus* 176b</note>, and he does not call the virtues used in civic life simply "virtues," but adds the qualification "civic." Elsewhere, he calls all virtues **purifications** <note>original: "καθάρσεις" (katharseis) — the process of stripping away material attachments to reveal the soul's divine nature</note>, not as if he were making the likeness consist only in civic virtue. How then do we call these "purifications," and how is it that by being purified we are most especially made like God? Is it because the soul is evil when it is thoroughly mixed with the body, sharing its passions and agreeing with all its opinions? It would then be good and possess virtue if it did not share those opinions, but acted alone (which is the act of **intellection** and wisdom), and if it did not share those passions (which is **temperance**), and did not fear being separated from the body (which is **courage**), and if reason and intellect led while the other parts did not resist (which would be **justice**). Such a disposition of the soul, in which it thinks and is thus free from passion, if one were to call it a "likeness to God," would not be mistaken; for the Divine is pure, and its activity is such that whatever imitates it possesses wisdom. What then? Is the Divine itself also disposed in this way? No, it is not "disposed"; a disposition belongs to a soul. The Divine thinks, but our thinking is different; of the things that are there, some are different than here, and others are not there at all. We use the word "thinking" for both, but for the Divine it is primary, while for us it is derived. Just as the word in speech is an imitation of the word in the soul, and the word in the soul is an imitation of that in another [higher] thing, as if divided from it. So also, virtue belongs to the soul, but it does not belong to the **Intellect**, nor to that which is **beyond** the Intellect.

ONE MUST INQUIRE whether **purification** is the same as this kind of virtue, or does purification come first, followed by virtue? Or does virtue consist in the very process of being purified? Or in having been purified? Or is it less perfect while being purified, as if the end were already in sight, but having been purified is the removal of the alien—

<insert>

</insert>

**[Translation of the Latin Column]**

A. They [the virtues] affect the desires and all other immoderate perturbations, and in this way remove false opinions, because they define the soul and place it outside of the immoderate and the undue, and they themselves take up a measure. The parts of measure in the soul, acting as matter, are like the measure that is there [in the divine realm], and they obtain a trace of the best that is there. For that which is entirely immoderate, since it is matter itself, is entirely dissimilar. But insofar as B. it receives **form** <note>original: "speciem" — the Greek "eidos," the defining shape or essence of a thing</note>, to that extent it is like that which has no [material] form. The things that are near participate more. The soul, however, is nearer and more akin than the body, and therefore it becomes a greater participant of that divine thing: so much so that it may deceive, appearing as a god, inducing a suspicion that it is the whole of this [the divine]: thus, in this way, they are similar.

<margin>
III. Definitions of the virtues which have already been spoken of regarding others: and by what things that virtue which is now superior differs from the inferior ones.
</margin>
C. BUT since he [the author] signifies that there is another likeness, which pertains to a greater virtue, we must speak of that. In this matter it will be more manifest both what the essence of **civic virtue** is, and what the virtue is that is more excellent through its essence, and it is established that there is entirely another virtue besides the civic. **Cicero** <note>The Latin text here says "Cicero," but the Greek original correctly identifies the author as "Plato." Ficino often compared Platonic thought to Roman philosophy.</note> says thus, when he says that "likeness to God" is a certain "flight from lower things": furthermore, he attributes the name not simply of virtues, but of "civic virtues" to those which befit citizens: and elsewhere he calls all virtues **purifications**; he plainly seems to propose a double nature, D. and that the likeness to God itself is not perfected through civic virtue. How then do we call these "purifications"? Likewise, how are we, having been purified, thoroughly made like [to God]? Perhaps because the soul is indeed evil if it be mixed with the body, and suffers together with it, and consents with it in opinion through all things: it will be most truly good and endowed with virtue if it is not so consenting, but acts alone, which is indeed to understand and to be wise; and if it is not a sufferer of similar things [to the body], which is to be **temperate**: and if it does not fear to be secluded from the body, E. which is to be **brave**. Let reason and intellect lead, while the other parts do not resist, which indeed will be to be **just**. Truly, if one calls this state of the soul in which it understands and lives so far from perturbation a "likeness to God," he has not erred. For the divine is pure, and its action is such that that which imitates it possesses wisdom. What then? Is the Divine itself not also affected in this way? Perhaps it is not even "affected" at all. For affection or F. disposition belongs to the soul: and the soul understands in a different way than God does. Of those things which are said to be there [in the divine], they are partly different than they are here, and partly they are not there in any way. Again, therefore, "to understand" is an **equivocal** term <note>original: "equivocum" — a word that has the same sound but different meanings; Plotinus warns that human "thinking" is not the same as divine "thinking"</note>: not in one way only, but that [divine] is as the primary: while this [human] proceeds from that and holds itself differently. For as the word which is in the voice is an imitation of that which is in the soul, so that which is in the soul is of that G. which remains in the superior. 

<margin>
IIII. Purification helps the soul toward wisdom and the mind; it also leads it back to the things of the mind and superior properties.
</margin>
Just as the word in speech is separated and divided from the word of the soul, so the word in the soul is divided from the superior, and is its interpreter. Virtue belongs to the soul, but not to the Mind: nor to that which is superior to the Mind.

<margin>
Whether it is fitting to count this among the virtues: and if not it, which one follows it?
</margin>
G. IT MUST BE ASKED truly whether that purification is such a virtue? Or does purification indeed precede, and virtue follow? Or is virtue in the act of purifying: or does virtue consist in that which is already purified and perfected? The virtue still laboring in the purifying is certainly more imperfect: for the end of this is that which has already purified. Truly pu.

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK I

...to have been purified <note>original: "purificatum" / "κεκαθάρθαι"</note> is the removal of everything foreign. But the **Good**, **A** beyond this very thing, seems to be something else. Perhaps if the soul was good before it lost its purity, purification would be sufficient; indeed, purification is enough, and the result is the Good, but purification itself is not the Good. In that case, we must ask what that "remaining thing" is. For perhaps the nature left behind is not the Good; otherwise, it would never have fallen into evil. Should we then call it "good-formed"? Or rather, is it something not quite sufficient to remain in that which is truly Good? For by nature, it tends **B** toward both. Its Good, therefore, is to adhere to its kin, and its evil is to adhere to opposites. It is necessary, then, for the purified soul to adhere; and it will adhere by having been turned around <note>original: "conversa" / "ἐπιστραφεῖσα" — a key Neoplatonic concept of the soul "turning back" toward the divine source</note>. Does it turn after the purification? Or after the purification is it already turned? This "turning," then, is its virtue—or rather, the thing that follows from the turning. What then is this? It is a vision, and the impression of the thing seen, imprinted and active, just as sight acts around the visible. Did the soul not have these things, nor remember them? Or perhaps it had them, but **C** they were not active, but rather lying dormant and obscure? But so that they may be illuminated, and the soul may then recognize these inherent things, it must move toward the illuminator. The soul did not have the things themselves, but rather their forms; it must therefore perfectly harmonize these forms to the true things of which they are images. Perhaps it is thought to possess them in this way: because the **Intellect** <note>original: "intellectus" / "νοῦς" (Nous) — the divine Mind or realm of pure thought</note> is not foreign, and especially not foreign when the soul looks toward it; otherwise, even when present, the Intellect is foreign, just as sciences **D** are foreign to us if we do not use them in any way.

<margin>
V
The virtues of the purified soul are defined, and their duties are handed down.
</margin>

**FURTHERMORE**, it remains to be said how far purification should proceed. In this way, it will become clear to which god the soul becomes similar and identical. This is primarily to ask: to what extent is it possible to purify anger, desire, pleasure, pain, and the like, and to separate the soul from the body? To separate from the body is, perhaps, for the soul to collect itself as if from diverse places, being altogether segregated from disturbances, and ensuring that **E** necessary pleasures are merely sensations and certain "remedies" or calms for labor, so that no interruption occurs. It will remove pains; but if it cannot, it will bear them moderately, diminishing them by not suffering alongside the body. It will remove anger, so far as possible, from its midst—altogether, if that can be done; if not, it will at least not be angry alongside the body. It will surely ensure that the anger belongs to "the other" <note>the "other" refers to the lower, animal part of the human, distinct from the higher soul</note>, occurring without deliberation and suddenly; and even this unpremeditated, sudden movement will be **F** very small and weak. Furthermore, it will expel fear entirely, for it will fear nothing; though a sudden movement might occur as a kind of warning. Regarding the desire for base things, the soul will undoubtedly have none. As for food and drink for the relief of pain, the soul itself will not have the desire, nor will it have sexual desires. But if it does, they will be only natural ones, I believe, and even those will not have an unpremeditated impulse. And if **G** they do, they will only go as far as the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note>, having been pre-figured there. Entirely, the soul itself will be pure of all these things, and it will wish also to make the irrational part pure, so that it is not even moved, or at least that its movements are minimal and can be immediately calmed by the soul’s proximity; just as if someone, by being near a wise person, might benefit from that very proximity...

...all seek. But the Good is different from it. Or, if it [the soul] was good before its impurity, then purification was necessary. But purification is sufficient both to be the most beautiful thing and to be before the Good, yet purification is not that which remains. We must seek: for perhaps the nature that is left behind is not the Good **A** itself; for then it would not have been in evil. Should we then say it is "good-formed"? Or <margin>* or persistence</margin> * is it not somehow bad, or does it remain in that which truly **B** is? It is natured toward both. Its own good, therefore, is to be with its kin, and its evil is to be with opposites. It must therefore, having been purified, be with it; and it will be with it having turned. Does it then turn after purification? Or after purification is it already turned? Is this then its virtue, or that which happens to it from the turning? Or is it this: the vision and the impression of the seen thing placed within, and acting, as sight acts around the visible? It did **C** not, therefore, have them—or does it remember them? Or did it have them not as active, but lying away un-illuminated? But so they may be illuminated, and it may then know them as being within, it must cast itself toward the illuminator. It did not have the things themselves, but something like them; it must therefore fit the impressions to the true things of which they are impressions. Perhaps it is said to have them in this way, because the **Intellect** is not foreign, and especially not foreign when it **D** looks toward it. Otherwise, even when present, it is foreign; since even sciences, if we do not act at all according to them, are foreign.

But it must be said how far purification goes. For thus the likeness to someone will be clear, as well as the identity with some god. This is especially to seek: how to separate from the body, as far as **E** possible, anger and desire and all other things—pain and its kin. From the body indeed, perhaps by the soul collecting itself into itself as if from certain places, being altogether without passion, and making only the sensations of necessary pleasures as healings and releases from labor, so it is not troubled; and removing pains, or if not possible, bearing them mildly, and making them less by not suffering with them; and removing anger as much as possible, or if possible, altogether not—at least not being angry along with it, but let the unpremeditated be of the other part; and let the unpremeditated be small **F** and weak. And fear, altogether. For it will fear nothing; except for the unpremeditated in it as a warning. And as for desire, it is clear: of nothing base. And of food and drink for relief, the soul itself will not have it, nor of sexual things. If then it does, I think they are natural, and not even **G** having the unpremeditated. Or if they do, only as far as the imagination, and even that unpremeditated. Altogether, the soul itself will be pure of all these, and it will wish also to make the irrational part pure, so that it is not struck by anything, or at least not violently, but its strikes are few and immediately dissolved by the proximity, just as if one, being a neighbor to a wise man, might benefit...

## SECOND BOOK.

...perceives; or having been made like that [divine being], or out of reverence, so that he dares to do nothing which the good man would not permit. There will, therefore, be no struggle. For the presence of reason <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"</note> is sufficient: which the lower part of the soul will revere; so much so that it will even be angry with itself if it is moved in any way and does not remain quiet in the presence of its master, and it will rebuke its own inconstancy.

<margin>
He confirms that the goal of virtue is to purify the soul, so that virtue may finally be obtained.
</margin>

Such things, then, are not a sin for the man, but a correction of the man, and his duty. For the true aim and desire is not merely to be free from sin, but to be a god. <note>original: "deum esse" / "θεὸν εἶναι"</note> If, therefore, any of these [lower impulses] should occur without prior deliberation, such a man would be both a god and a divine spirit <note>original: "demon" / "δαίμων"</note>, existing as a double being: or rather, he is a god who has another god with him, one endowed with a different kind of virtue. If he has nothing of the sort, he is simply a god. I mean a god from the number of those who follow the First [Principle]. For he is the one who proceeds from there. And if he maintains his own nature, just as he came from there, he remains there; but having traveled here, he is joined to the Intellect, and through its power he will assimilate this [lower part] to himself. He does this so that, if possible, it will not be moved, or at least it will not perform any act that is not pleasing to its master.

What then is each of these virtues to such a person? Wisdom <note>original: "sapientia" / "σοφία"</note> is the contemplation of those things which the Intellect possesses. The Intellect, however, possesses them through a kind of contact. But each of these is twofold: one exists in the Intellect, and the other in the soul. In the Intellect, it is not properly called "virtue," but in the soul, it is virtue. What then is it in the Intellect? It is the Intellect's own action and what it essentially is; here in the soul, however, what comes from there into another thing is virtue. For neither Justice itself, nor Temperance itself, nor any such thing is strictly a virtue in the divine realm, but rather a paradigm or "model." That which is produced by the model in the soul is the virtue. For virtue belongs to someone; but each thing in the divine realm belongs to itself and not to another.

As for Justice <note>original: "iustitia" / "δικαιοσύνη"</note>, if it is the performance of one's own duty, does it always require a multitude of parts? No, only in a multitude where there are many parts. Simply put, it is the performance of one's own duty even if it were of a single thing. True Justice, therefore, is the soul’s activity toward itself, in which there is no distinction between one thing and another. Therefore, the greater Justice for the soul is to direct its activity toward the Intellect. Temperance <note>original: "temperantia" / "σωφροσύνη"</note> is the internal turning toward the Intellect. Fortitude <note>original: "fortitudo" / "ἀνδρεία"</note> is a state free from passion, achieved by becoming like that toward which it looks, which is naturally beyond passion. The soul, by virtue, overcomes passion so that it does not suffer alongside its inferior companion [the body].

<column-break/>

<margin>
In a clear explanation of the virtues, he speaks in a certain order of how they are first used to purify, then the virtues are prepared before the self; finally, he proves the end of virtue is in the divine.
</margin>

These virtues in the soul, therefore, follow one another in turn, just as in the Intellect there are the "exemplars" which exist before the virtues. For in the Intellect, knowledge and wisdom are found; to be turned toward itself is temperance; the soul's own work is its own activity, which is called justice; and in place of fortitude, there is immateriality and remaining pure within itself. 

In the soul, therefore, the vision directed toward the Intellect is wisdom and prudence, which are its virtues. For the soul is not these things themselves in the same way the Intellect is. Other virtues follow in a similar way, and likewise purification. Since all virtues are a kind of purification, it is necessary that they result in a completed state of purification; otherwise, no virtue would be perfect. Furthermore, whoever possesses the "greater" [purifying] virtues necessarily possesses the "lesser" [civic] virtues potentially; but the reverse is not true—one who has the lesser does not necessarily have the greater. This, then, is the life of the person endowed with virtue. But whether he possesses the lesser in active...

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE
## BOOK CONCERNING THE TRIPLE RETURN
### OF THE SOUL, UNTO THE DIVINE PRELUDE.
#### THE ARGUMENT.

->In which he treats of the Trinity that produces, converts, and perfects,<-
->and of the ninefold number in divine matters.<-

Those who titled this book "On Dialectic" judged that it should be named from its more prominent part. Although (as I believe) they would have titled it much more correctly if they had called it "On the Return of Souls to the Divine." For this is the greatest, indeed almost the only desire to be sought first in this proposition: this results from every part of the discussion. Because Plotinus here delights in the number three, leading us to God by a triple path, it seemed right, as if enticed, to wander a little more freely through the number three. The higher principles of the universe produce those things that follow; the produced things they lead back; the led-back things they perfect. While they produce, they bestow being; while they convert <note>In Neoplatonism, "conversion" (conversio) refers to the soul turning back toward its source, God.</note>, they preserve being; when they perfect, they reform it into a better being. These three, however, with their seemingly concrete affections, are counted in a triad to that absolute trini<gloss>ty</gloss> of the three affections: namely the producing, the converting, and the perfecting. 

In the producing trinity, the first is the Good itself; the second is the Intellect (or the Son); the third is the Soul, both being the spirits of the world as if of divine intelligence. Since these three once produced all things together with their substance, they are often distinguished from one another. There follows the converting trinity, or the one that leads back to the supernal realms: in which Mercury holds the first rank, recalling souls to the heights through reason; second is Venus through a higher vision of the supernal; third is Phoebus <note>Apollo, the Sun-god.</note> accomplishing the same through hearing. And if each of the three calls us to all things above, Mercury calls especially to the Good itself; Venus to the Intellect in which the first beauty shines; Phoebus to the Soul to which harmony especially pertains—as we have discussed in the compendium on the *Timaeus* and in Latin theology. Indeed, these three individual planets act both by their intellect upon our reason, by their animal power upon our imagination, and by their body upon our body to entice us toward the same goal. Finally, all three lead first to the planet Saturn, the leader of intelligence; then to the Saturn superior to the planet, the father of intelligence and the first intellect; and at last to the Good itself, the father of Saturn. The Mercurial, Venereal, and Phoebean spirits—and finally the Saturnian spirits—similarly serve this same office. 

There remains the perfecting trinity, distributed thoroughly into a ninefold <note>original: "nouenarium"</note> order: for the soul, whether it is brought back to the soul of the world, or higher to the mind reigning over the world, or more loftily to the Good itself, the father of the intellect, it certainly recognizes the Father himself as the principle, the middle, and the end of all things (which is more clearly opened in the fourth book of the *Laws*). It recognizes the Divine Mind as essence, as life, and as intellect. Finally, it recognizes the Soul as life, as motion, and as reason—describing it as living, mobile reason. Again, it accommodates each thing it finds in lower things to each thing that exists in higher things by a certain proportion. Therefore, it refers the reason in the soul to the intellect reigning in the Mind and to the end considered concerning the Good. Similarly, it refers the motion of the soul to the life of the guardian, the middle point in the Good itself. Finally, it refers the life of the soul to the essence of the Mind and to the very principle of the universe. 

But let us set aside these other trinities for the present. For in this book, the trinity is treated primarily as converting, and especially in what manner the soul may be brought back to the Divine Mind, insofar as it is thought of as Intellect and as something intelligible. For one never arrives suddenly at the Good itself. In this Intellect, moreover, are contained the Ideas, which Plotinus elsewhere calls certain "numbers." Therefore, the soul, called toward these, considers a trinity in each one. For it contemplates them as Truth, as Concord (or commensuration), and as Beauty—which Plato discusses in the *Philebus*: Mercury leading toward Truth, Apollo toward Concord, and... <note>The text cuts off at the catchword "ad."</note>

It then begins Marsilio Ficino’s introduction to "On Dialectic," where he uses a complex system of trinities and planetary influences (Mercury, Venus, Apollo) to explain the soul's return to the Divine.</summary>

--- Page 52 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, moving from the nature of virtues in Ennead I.2 to the "Triple Way" of ascent and the nature of the ultimate Good as discussed in Ennead I.3 and related sections. It uses the Platonic imagery of the "wing of the soul" to describe the spiritual journey.</meta>

...leads the soul to the beauty of the **Wing**. <note>A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul grows wings to fly back to the divine realm.</note> In the truth of the soul, he recognizes the perpetual firmness of nature, as well as a purity that tastes nothing foreign, and an integrity that never abandons its own essence. He considers Harmony in a similar **triad**, insofar as any given Idea is consistent with itself, agrees with higher things, and is related to lower things. He also views Beauty as a **triad**: for a true and fitting Idea, when it returns to us as beautiful, approaches the soul like **Venus** accompanied by the three **Graces**. It arrives to be admired, joins the soul to be loved, and enters it to bring delight. Thus, the ideal trinity is duly expanded into a grouping of nine. Similarly, this conversion toward the Idea is derived from a trinity into a ninefold structure, since **Mercury** does not only convert things by his own reason, but in this duty he agrees partly with **Venus** and partly even with **Apollo**. By the same reasoning, **Venus** both calls souls back in her own way, and agrees in one way with **Mercury** and in another with **Apollo**. Finally, **Apollo** exists in his own right, yet here he accords with **Mercury**, and there with **Venus**.

### That the goal of the soul is beyond the intellectual nature, toward the Good itself

<margin>1</margin> This book is divided into three chapters, just as there are three ways to the divine. The third chapter, being the most important, is further distributed into three sections. In the first chapter, he describes the goal that must finally be reached: that the soul finds rest not in some "intellectual good" or "intelligible good" <term>intelligible: things that can be understood by the mind but not seen by the eyes</term>—which are nearly the same thing—but in the **Absolute Good** itself, the highest principle. For the desire for the Good proceeds as far as the light of the desired Good extends. But just as the most keen-scented hounds find by the power of smell what they do not yet see with their eyes (nor could their sight reach it, for the scent was closer to them than the prey's body was), so the soul, by a certain marvelous sagacity of its higher intellectual nature, "prophesies" that the Good exists, even though it transcends all the eyes of intelligence. Indeed, just as we find nothing above the sensible by means of the senses, so we find nothing above the intelligible by means of the intellect. But just as we find the intelligible above the sensible by means of an intellect superior to the senses, so by a certain power of the soul superior to the intellect, we equally predict and desire the **Absolute Good** itself, which is above the intelligible (or the "intellectual good"). For once you have said "the Good itself," to then add "intellectual" or "intelligible" is nothing other than to speak of "a certain good" or "a part of the good." It either remains silent regarding the intellect, or is at least narrowed to the limits of intelligence itself, or is restricted to the intellect by some specific property. But above this—which is, as it were, imperfect, narrow, and fading—is the **Absolute Good** in itself, without limit. Its most ample faculty produces both the "intellectual good" and the "non-intellectual good"; it produces both the "sensible good" and the "good of the senses." Toward these opposites, as it were, the **Absolute Good** without limit pours itself out everywhere. This is what the soul desires as the ultimate end, which it enjoys not through some perception of an imaginary intelligence, but through a certain true and substantial contact of a power superior to the intellect. There, the soul does not merely fly, but also "tastes and touches how sweet the Lord is." <note>original: "gustat etiam atque tangit quàm suauis sit dominus" — a paraphrase of Psalm 34:8.</note> David, I believe, meant this as a great and entirely hidden multitude of sweetness. Because the **Absolute Good** is above all cognition and above the "knowable good," the natural affection of the soul carries it toward cognition, yet as if toward a dream; otherwise, the goal would be a mere accident of our substance, and no knowledge would ever fail us. Often, some imaginary figure of the good offering itself to our knowledge would satisfy the nature's desire. Therefore, the natural affection seeks cognition, not for the sake of cognition alone, but so that through it, it may seek, find, and apprehend in whatever way possible the **Good**. It is not so much the nature of this Good to be "known," as it is to truly agree with us, flow into us, and sweetly refresh and help us. In this state, which is far more excellent than the intellect and the intelligible, the soul finally rests, as if in the ultimate end of all things, through its nature that is superior to the intellect. The **Apostle Paul** calls such an affection a "love" that is higher than the limits of sense and intelligence. <note>original: "amorem... intelligentiæ limitibus altiorem" — likely referencing Ephesians 3:19.</note> Let enough be said for now regarding the goal.

### On the intelligible and sensible world, and on the triple way and natural disposition toward the intelligible.

Let us proceed now to the "ways," and to those who may more easily progress through these ways or be led through them to this goal. The Platonists posit two primary worlds: first, the **Intelligible World**, which is the Divine Mind, the principle and exemplar of this world; second, the **Sensible World**, which is this world manifest to the senses, an image of the divine exemplar. Plotinus thinks our **soul** is always in the former through the intellect, but always in the latter through its vegetative nature, just as a ray of the sun touches both the earth here and the sun there. Through its middle nature, however, which is placed in a primary—and therefore perpetual and circular—motion, the soul acts perpetually; it lives one life in the intelligible world and another, in turn, in the sensible. This does not strictly happen by a change of location; rather, when the soul turns its whole focus from the imagination to reason, and from reason to the mind, then he says the soul has "ascended" to the intelligible world. But when reason bends itself toward its imagination, and this imagination bends toward the lower imagination—either of the animal already born or of the one to be generated—then a "fall" into the sensible world is indicated. He teaches that there are three types of souls: some are always in the higher world, such as the souls of the spheres, stars, and higher **daemons** <note>In the Platonic sense, "daemons" are intermediary spirits or guardians, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>; others are only in the lower world, such as those of plants or those purely addicted to sensory passions; but the middle ones—that is, the **rational souls**, whether they are ours or those of lower daemons—carry out perpetual cycles from here to there and back again. Accordingly, our souls in the higher world contemplate or are affected sometimes more attentively, sometimes more loosely, just as in this world we see them affected more or less by certain things. Now, those souls that work more readily there contemplate either all divine things or most of them. Therefore, when such souls, having completed certain cycles of time, gradually slip back toward sensible things, they remain ready for the remembrance of divine things. Those who are the most ready of all are judged to be endowed with a **philosophical** disposition; those who are ready in the second degree have a primarily **amatory** (loving) disposition; and finally, those in the third degree are more suited to **music**. For those who are enslaved to entirely corporeal things through touch, taste, and smell are judged to be furthest removed from that incorporeal world, as they do not seem to have descended from that world into this one, but rather to have migrated here from somewhere else. As for how these dispositions work: the **philosophical** mind investigates the reasons of natural things through reason; these reasons are primarily derived from the Ideas, and thus the philosopher glimpses the divine Ideas. Consequently, **sight** and **hearing** are rightly judged to be the closest servants of our reason. Because they belong to the whole body and yet seem to deal with things that are, in a way, less corporeal, they manifest a certain most exact order in the things offered to the eyes and ears. For this reason, we are usually more easily provoked from these two senses toward the intellect and intellectual reasons, from which all order is arranged. Thus, while reason hastens toward the wisdom of divine things, sight meanwhile supplies the mind with discovery as best it can, and hearing suggests learning. Therefore, in a triple...

...we proceed to more divine seats by means of reason, sight, and hearing. Three types of souls are more readily carried up to that place: the **philosophical** type devoted to reason; the **amatory** <note>the lover</note> devoted to the eyes; and the **musical** type devoted to hearing, as Plato testifies in the *Phaedrus* and the *Phaedo*.

### On the three contemplations in the intelligible world, and then the three natural dispositions.

<margin>I</margin> Furthermore, in the divine world, three things are chiefly contemplated: **Form** <note>original: *Species*</note>, **Number**, and **Mode** <note>measure or proportion</note>. For the divine mind itself is the primary Form, and every "Idea" is a form or shape. There is a fixed Number there, both of the forms themselves and of the properties belonging to each form. There is also a fixed Mode or measure of power and a certain proportion, both of the forms within themselves or in relation to other forms, and in relation to the counts of numbers. Although these three are distinguished from each other by a certain logic, nevertheless, within the Form itself, both Number and Mode are contained, though under a formal logic. Likewise, in Number, there is both Form and Mode, especially under a numerical condition. Again, in Mode and measure, there are similarly both Form and Number, existing in what I might call a "mensural" proportion. 

For this reason, the souls who contemplate divine things—even though they each behold and love all things—nevertheless, some refer the remaining two aspects to the **Form** itself, through both knowledge and affection. Others refer them to the logic resembling **Number**; and finally, others refer them to **Mode** and measure itself. From the first group comes the **philosophical** disposition; from the second, the **musical**; and from the third (which is by no means inferior), the **amatory** disposition. 

However, these three dispositions are as fervently joined to one another as Form, Number, and Mode are interconnected. The **Philosopher**, therefore, in thinking out numbers and measures, admires the Form itself and its nature above all. The **Musician**, in natures, modes, and measures, is powerfully moved by tuneful numbers. Finally, the **Lover** ardently pursues the Mode and measure in all things. In short, all three (according to Plato) are raised to sublime beauty—that is, to the divine mind, which is the primary beauty and the eternal splendor of the Good itself. In this divine mind, Form, Number, and Mode, like the **three Graces** embracing one another, contribute equally to an integral beauty and full grace. 

He likewise says that one person is awakened in one way, and another in a different way. Furthermore, after they have risen to the divine mind, which is also the **intelligible world** <note>the realm of pure thought and Ideas</note>, they progress through all the classes of Ideas in their own specific order, and finally exit from that world to reach the **Good** itself, which is the beginning and end of that world. 

After this, he explains the logic by which the musical disposition is enticed by nature and carried along by art. For by nature, it is inclined toward beauty, specifically in such a way that it is primarily moved through beautiful voices to the universal beauty of proportion. This person must therefore be taught that the very thing he admires in the melodies of voices is not the vocal or similar material—otherwise, all sounds would please him equally everywhere—but rather the proportional and numerical logic, which is like a form within the material of the voice and sound. Therefore, if any material could be stripped away from it, so that such a form remained either in itself or in the mind, the form alone would then please him; and it would please him more, because the proportion of numerical logic there would be more perfect and the "One" <note>the principle of unity</note> more absolute, for the sake of which proportion is pleasing. 

He must therefore be led from the beautiful voice to the beauty that exists *in* the voice; from here, again, to that beauty which consists in a certain proportion within the rational soul; then from this and that proportion (which are merely "something beautiful" or "a certain beauty") to the Beauty of this order and Beauty itself—that is, the **Idea**. From the Idea, he is led first to the very number and "vocal-ness" of Beauty, then to the simple logic of Beauty, and finally to the **Good** itself, from which beauty (that is, its splendor and grace) shines forth almost in this way: just as external shapeliness shines from internal health, or as outermost light shines from an innermost glow.

### The Philosophical, Musical, and Amatory dispositions easily coincide.

<margin>II</margin> In the second chapter of the book, he says that the **Musician** often harmonizes with the **Lover**, and both with the **Philosopher**, and not without reason. For the inspirations of these are closest in both position and motion: the **Sun** <note>associated with the Philosopher/Apollo</note>, **Mercury**, and **Venus**. Closest again are hearing, sight, and the imagination serving reason. Likewise, he who naturally loves the beautiful, loves it everywhere for the reason that it is beautiful: whether in the true logic of any thing (as the Philosopher), or in those things which are seen (as the Lover), or in those things which are heard (as the Musician). All remaining points of this chapter are explained very extensively in the *Symposium* <note>original: *Convivio*</note> regarding love.

### The philosophical disposition is more free than the others, and needs only a leader through mathematical discipline to metaphysical wisdom.

<margin>III</margin> The third chapter of the book describes the disposition and education of the one practicing philosophy. This person, like the lover, has a disposition naturally inclined toward beauty. But the difference is this: the Musician and the Lover hunt for beauty in the body; but he who is a Philosopher by nature is seen to be, in a way, released from the body. This is because he possesses more moderate affections, and he always reduces particular things into universal notions through resolution, while investigating separate causes through argumentation. Therefore, he does not need someone to release him from matter, but someone to show the goal to a disposition already released and flying, and to show a more certain way. Concerning this disposition, and by what levels of discipline it must be led to sublime things, it is sufficiently discussed in the fifth, sixth, and seventh books of the *Republic*: namely, how he is instructed in morals and in mathematical disciplines that are somewhat separated from matter, and finally led to the **metaphysical** faculty.

### The duty of the Metaphysician is to travel through all beings by dividing, composing, defining, and demonstrating, and finally to progress beyond beings; likewise, what is below beings and what is above them.

<margin>IIII</margin> Among most **Peripatetics** <note>followers of Aristotle</note>, the subject of **metaphysics** is "Being" itself, according to the broadest notion of Being among them, in which all those beings are included: thus, it is common to things separated from matter and things joined to matter. However, among **Platonists**, the subject of metaphysics seems to be broader: namely, either "Being and Non-being," or at least Being endowed with a fitting relationship—a relationship, I say, both to that which is higher than Being and to that which is lower. 

Higher than Being is the **One** and the **Good** itself, which is the principle and end of Being. Lower than Being is any form changeable in matter, and matter itself. But such a form is an image of Being, while matter is the shadow of Being itself. The Platonists call true beings "substances" <note>original: *substantias*</note>: in which either there is no inclination toward "non-being" (the opposite of being), or that inclination does not rule. It is not present, I say, as in substances separated from matter (or those to be separated); or it does not rule, as in the spheres of the world, where the perfection of the form always overcomes the defect of the matter. Through all these things, the metaphysical faculty proceeds, which Plato calls **Dialectic**, using **Logic** as an instrument. For Logic concerns...

questions, concepts, propositions, and syllogisms. Metaphysics, however, deals with the things themselves, while using **logical tools** <note>original: "logicis machinis"</note> in the process. Indeed, the duty of the Metaphysician is to analyze, divide, synthesize, define, and demonstrate. By doing this, he proceeds through all beings, especially toward the **incorporeal** <note>immaterial realities</note>, because those are the truly existing beings. Then, he proceeds toward the very principle and end of these things. After this, he observes the process of beings from the highest to the lowest, returning again through all the ranks of beings until he returns to the highest, and there he rests. Meanwhile, you can recognize how the Platonic division is made in Plotinus's three books on the *Genera of Being*; likewise in the *Parmenides*, the *Sophist*, the *Statesman*, and the *Philebus*.

->The Metaphysician possesses principles that are innate in the intellect, but he brings them into<-
->actuality through reason, and by the rules of truth, he refutes sophistries<-
->and holds the rules of logic.<-

**V** The fifth chapter of the book teaches that the **Intellect** itself—which always exists in a state of activity and similarly possesses the principles of all sciences—sometimes hands these over to the reason that has turned toward it. Through these principles, the mind becomes "metaphysical" while the reason is formed by the intellect and perfected within it. Furthermore, it says that Metaphysics, through the rule of truth itself, detects and refutes the lies and quibbles of the **sophists** <note>philosophers who use clever but fallacious arguments</note>. It does not merely dwell on the literal or technical rules of logic, but because it understands the very movements of souls and the harmony or discord of things among themselves, it rightly discerns the power of propositions and the consistency of affirmations and negations.

->All faculties draw their principles from metaphysics, without which sciences<-
->do not exist and moral characters are imperfect.<-

**VI** He says further in the sixth chapter that the other faculties—whether mathematical, physical, or moral—take their principles from metaphysics. Likewise, metaphysics holds the universal laws of morality, which it hands over to **Prudence** <note>practical wisdom</note> as if to a geometer or an architect. Prudence, in turn, serves the other virtues as if in the act of building. He concludes that the other virtues are imperfect without **Wisdom** <note>original: "sapientia"</note>, and vice versa. For Wisdom and the other virtues grow together almost equally. The natural beginnings of virtues in the soul, when Wisdom is added, turn into perfect virtues, whether Wisdom arises before the others or vice versa; for wherever you begin, one virtue leads to the other. Finally, the natural starting point in a rational nature toward Wisdom or Prudence is like an imperfect eye; but Wisdom is the **right eye**, while Prudence is the **left**. Again, the natural starting point for the other virtues is called an imperfect "custom" or "habit." The true principle of the various types of virtues is drawn mostly from those things which we naturally possess in the mind, the reason, or even the imagination.

...the second [path] is for those who have already advanced to the things above. The first path ascends from the lower things; the second belongs to those who are already in the **intelligible realm** <note>The world of pure ideas and forms, beyond physical sensation</note> and have fixed their footsteps there. It is necessary for them to progress further until they reach the very summit. This end of the journey occurs when one reaches the height of the intelligible world; but let this departure remain for the present. We must first attempt to speak of the ascent and the "reduction" <note>The process of leading the soul back to its divine source</note>. First, we must distinguish between these men, beginning with the **musician**, [and ask] what his nature might be. We must surely define him as easily moved and as one who, being full of wonder, is more inclined toward the beautiful, yet is not able to be moved sufficiently by himself. He is easily incited by those figures he encounters; and just as a timid man is stirred by noise, so is he stirred by harmonious sounds. He rushes toward the beauty that appears in sounds and everywhere flees from dissonance. He follows what is true in songs and rhythms—that which is rhythmic and harmonious. Therefore, after these sensible <note>perceptible by the senses</note> sounds, rhythms, and figures, he must be led in this way: namely, by separating the matter in which the proportions and their comparisons exist, and by leading him back to the beauty that is within them. Furthermore, he must be taught that the things by which he is so vehemently affected with wonder are not these [physical] things, but rather an **intelligible harmony** <note>The mathematical and spiritual order underlying music</note>, and the beauty within it, and beauty itself in its entirety—not merely some particular beauty. Finally, the principles of philosophy must be applied to these things, through which he may be led to a firm belief in those things which he possesses but does not yet know. What these principles are, we shall declare in the following.

<margin>How the nature of the lover must be accustomed to the beauty of the body, then to the love of incorporeal things, and so finally to the mind.</margin>

## II

The **LOVER** is he into whom the Musician might happen to change, and having so changed, he either remains with you or passes beyond. He remembers beauty in a certain way, but because he is separated from it, he cannot fully grasp it. Struck by the beauties that are open to his sight, he is vehemently moved by them. He must be taught not to revolve around a single body as if he were falling into it, but rather, persuaded by every reason, he should properly direct himself to all bodies: considering that which is the same in all of them, and noticing that beauty itself is distinct from the bodies, and that it proceeds from elsewhere, and exists more truly in other things—such as beautiful pursuits and beautiful laws. For through these things, the lover's zeal already becomes accustomed to loving **incorporeal things** <note>Immaterial realities like justice or wisdom</note>. It must also be shown that beauty exists in the arts, sciences, and virtues, and that the beauty in all of them is one, regardless of how it arrives. Finally, from the virtues, one must reach the **Intellect** and Being itself; and there, the journey to even higher things must be completed.

<margin>The philosophical nature is naturally released from matter and only needs a guide to divine beauty through certain steps of discipline.</margin>

## III

The **PHILOSOPHER** is naturally ready and, as it were, "winged" <note>A reference to the soul's wings in Plato's Phaedrus</note>. He does not need the separation from matter required by those we mentioned just before—namely, for the exit to the things above. He is in a state of wonder, and therefore only needs a guide. Thus, it is worthwhile to demonstrate [the truth] to him and to lead the man who, by nature, wishes to be led and who has long been released [from the body]. Therefore, **mathematics** <note>original: "mathematica"</note> must be employed so that he may become accustomed to thinking about and believing in the incorporeal. For he will perceive it easily, since he is eager for learning; and his naturally noble character must be led toward the perfection of the virtues.

<column-break/>

[Right Column]

<margin>A</margin>The first [path] is from the things below, while the second is for those who are already in the intelligible [realm], and who have, as it were, made a footprint there. It is necessary for all to go until they reach the furthest part of the place, which happens to be the end of the journey, when one arrives at the peak of the intelligible. But let that wait; regarding the ascent, we must try to speak of it in another way. A distinction must be made between these men, beginning with the **musician**,
<margin>B</margin>who he is by nature. One must define him as easily moved and captivated by the beautiful, yet unable to be moved by himself, but ready [to be moved] by the impressions he happens upon—just as the fearful are moved by noises, so is he [moved] by sounds and the beauty ready in them. Always fleeing from the unharmonious, he pursues that which is
<margin>C</margin>in songs and rhythms, seeking the rhythmic and the well-formed. Beyond these sensible sounds, rhythms, and forms, he must be led to separate the matter upon which the proportions and ratios [depend]. He must be taught that the cause of the beauty in them was that **intelligible harmony**, and the beauty within them, and beauty as a whole; and he should be introduced to the discourse and arguments of philosophy,
<margin>D</margin>from which he is led to a trust in the things he possesses but does not know. What those arguments are must be said later.

THE LOVER, into whom the musician might change—and having changed, he might either stay there or move on—possesses a certain memory of beauty. Being separate from it, he is unable to fully understand it. Struck by the beauties in his sight, he is captivated by them. He must therefore be taught not to be captivated by one body, but he must be led by reason to all bodies, showing that the [beauty] in all is the same, and that it is different from the bodies, and must be described
<margin>E</margin>as coming from elsewhere, and that it exists more in other things, such as beautiful practices and beautiful laws. The lover must be accustomed to incorporeal things, and in the arts, and in the sciences, and in
<margin>F</margin>virtues. Then, it must be shown that the beauty in all is one, and he must be taught how they come to be. From the virtues, he must then ascend to the Intellect, to Being, and there walk the upward path.

THE PHILOSOPHER is by nature ready and, as it were, winged, and not needing the separation [from matter] that these others do, as he is already moved toward the heights. Being in doubt, he
<margin>G</margin>needs only a guide. One must show him the way and release him, for he wishes it and has by nature long been released. Thus, the mathematical sciences must be given to him to accustom him to the understanding and belief in the incorporeal. For he will receive them easily, being a lover of learning; and being naturally virtuous, he must be led to the final perfection of the virtues.
