-># THIRD BOOK.<-

...and after mathematical studies, one should impart dialectical reasoning, or indeed make the student a true dialectician.

<margin>III</margin>
**WHAT** then is dialectic, and by what principles is it handed down? It is, indeed, the logical examination of the power concerning each thing: what each thing is, how it differs from others, what they have in common, where each of these is found, whether a thing exists as it is, how many "beings" <note>true, eternal realities</note> there are, and conversely, what things are "non-beings" <note>things that change or pass away, like physical matter</note> as distinct from true beings. 

**B** This science also discusses the Good itself and the non-good; it examines everything that falls under the Good and its opposite, as well as what is eternal and what is not. It treats all these matters with certain knowledge <note>original: *scientia* / *episteme*</note> rather than mere opinion. It rests the soul from the wandering caused by the physical world and fixes it upon the **intelligible** <note>that which can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</note>. There, it occupies itself with real things, leaving falsehood behind and nourishing the soul in what is called the "Plain of Truth" <note>original: *ἀληθείας πεδίῳ* (alētheias pediō). This is a reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*</note>. 

<margin>Dialectic, that is, pure physics: for it contains everything most broadly: in few words, it is that from which divine progress moves as a tool.</margin>

To do this, it employs the Platonic method of division to distinguish various forms or "Ideas." It also uses this method to define what a thing is and to reach the **primary genera** <note>the most basic categories of reality, like Being, Sameness, and Difference</note>. From these, it weaves together an intellectual understanding until it has traversed the entire intelligible world. **C** Then, it reverses the process, analyzing and breaking things down until it returns to the very beginning. At that point, the soul keeps still; for as long as it remains in that high place, it is at rest. It no longer busies itself with many things but, having become unified, it looks down upon what is called "logic"—the study of propositions and syllogisms <note>formal rules of argument</note>. It views these rules as if they were the art of writing; it considers some of them necessary as a preliminary craft, but it judges them just as it judges anything else, seeing some as useful and others as superfluous or merely belonging to the mechanical side of debate.

<margin>* That which is precious</margin>
**E BUT** where does this science get its principles? Perhaps the **Intellect** <note>the divine Mind or *Nous*</note> provides clear principles which the soul is then able to receive. Then, the soul composes, connects, and divides these truths until it reaches a perfect intellectual state. For Dialectic is, as has been said, the purest part of intelligence and wisdom. Since it is the most excellent "habit" <note>a stable quality or disposition of the soul</note> within us, it must deal with the most excellent reality: **Being**. 

<margin>The Metaphysician receives principles from the intellect, and with truth refutes sophisms, and comprehends truth itself.</margin>

Wisdom is concerned with Being, while the Intellect is concerned with that which is even higher than Being <note>The One, or the absolute source of all</note>. What then is Philosophy? It is the most precious thing of all. Or rather, are Philosophy and Dialectic the same? Dialectic is the most precious *part* of philosophy. We must not think of it merely as a tool for the philosopher to use; it does not consist of empty theorems and rules. Instead, it deals with actual things and has real Beings as its subject matter. It proceeds along its path possessing the things themselves alongside its theories. It recognizes falsehood and sophisms <note>deceptive or fallacious arguments</note> only as an accidental byproduct. It judges them as something alien, recognizing the lie by the truth it already possesses. Whenever someone brings forward an argument that deviates from the rule of truth, Dialectic knows it is false. 

**G** Strictly speaking, Dialectic does not concern itself with the formal "proposition"—for these are merely letters and words. But because it knows the truth, it also knows what people call a "proposition." More generally, it knows the movements of the soul: what it affirms and what it denies, and whether it denies the same thing it affirms or something else. It sees whether things are different or the same when they are presented, just as the physical senses perceive objects by coming into contact with them. However, it leaves the technicalities of these movements to another faculty that finds them more important.

<column-break/>

<summary>This page defines Dialectic as the highest part of Philosophy, which leads the soul from the physical world to the "Plain of Truth" in the intelligible realm. It distinguishes true philosophical Dialectic, which deals with reality (Being), from mere formal logic, which deals with the structure of arguments.</summary>

...demanding exact precision, or it grants that precision to another branch of study.

<margin>A</margin> **PHILOSOPHY** also has other parts that are held in honor. For there is the contemplation of nature <note>Physics</note>, which takes aid from dialectic, just as arithmetic is used by other arts. However, dialectic itself brings its own principles closer to the truth. <margin>B</margin> Ethics is treated in a similar way: we contemplate it from the perspective of dialectic, but it adds habits and exercises, from which the virtues themselves proceed. The rational virtues possess their own habits—becoming, as it were, the soul's own properties derived from dialectic—even though they involve many things in conjunction with practice and matter. Other virtues involve reasoning within their own specific passions and actions. But **Prudence** <note>original: *phronesis*. This refers to practical wisdom or the ability to make right choices in daily life.</note> is a special kind of primary reasoning, and is concerned more with the universal. <margin>C</margin> Dialectic and Wisdom <note>original: *sophia*. Theoretical wisdom or the understanding of eternal truths.</note> provide everything to Prudence for its use, in a universal and immaterial way. It might be asked whether lower concerns can exist without dialectic and wisdom; perhaps they can, but only in a very imperfect way. It is possible for a person to be a dialectician and wise in this manner, or perhaps these things grow together. Perhaps one has "natural virtues" <note>instinctive or biological tendencies toward good behavior</note> from which the perfect ones are formed once Wisdom is added. After the natural virtues, Wisdom appears and then perfects the character, or rather, it grows alongside the natural qualities as they exist; for both are perfected together. <margin>D</margin> Or perhaps one, coming first, perfects the other. For a natural virtue has an "imperfect eye" <note>a limited vision of the truth</note> and a limited character before the application of **intellection** <unclear>thinking/reasoning</unclear>, and the principles of both mostly come from what we already possess.

<column-break/>

...providing exact diligence in these matters.
<margin>Pl</margin>
<margin>Metaphysics <note>the study of ultimate reality</note> provides rules for all other faculties, both speculative and moral; they do not exist except through it, and without it, morals remain imperfect.</margin>
Therefore, this PART is to be honored. For philosophy has other faculties besides. It also contemplates nature, taking help from dialectic, just as all other arts use arithmetic. But it draws its own principles more closely from dialectic. The faculty of morals <note>Ethics</note> likewise contemplates from that same source: but it joins to it habits and exercises, from which the habits themselves proceed. The Rational virtues also have their habits, and as it were, their own properties which lead from there; for they have much to do with matter. And other virtues indeed have their reasonings within their own passions and further actions. But **Prudence** is a certain chief reasoning, and is occupied with the more universal: it considers whether something should be restrained or abstained from in the present, or for the future, or whether something else is entirely better; and it notices what follows in turn and what does not. Dialectic and wisdom, moreover, provide everything in a universal and immaterial way for the use of prudence. Whether lower things can be without dialectic and wisdom might be asked; perhaps they are quite imperfect. It can happen that one is wise and a dialectician without them. Or it does not happen quite like that, but they grow together either before or at the same time. And perhaps someone will have natural virtues, from which perfect ones are made, provided that wisdom is applied. Therefore, wisdom comes after the natural ones; then it perfects the character, or rather grows together with the existing natural ones: for both are finally perfected together. Or perhaps one, anticipating the other, perfects it. For altogether a natural virtue has an imperfect eye and character; and the principles for both mostly happen from those things we have.

# MARSILIO FICINO'S
## PREFACE TO THE
### BOOK ON HAPPINESS.

->SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.<-
->The blessed man is he who lives by the mind alone.<-

He begins the *Book on Happiness* from that opinion in which everyone agrees. Indeed, everyone proclaims that happiness <note>original: *felicitas* / *eudaimonia*</note> is "living well." However, because they are completely ignorant of what life is and what the good is, they define "living well" however they please, and are thus forced to err just as often. Plotinus detects their errors in the first and second chapters of the book, warning us to make the definition itself the beginning of our discussion. Thus, in the third chapter of the book, he describes life, the good, and happiness. In the fourth, he raises and solves various doubts: asking whether a blessed life is possible for man. Also, in what way it might be hindered—meanwhile indicating that it cannot be hindered. In the following chapters, he brings forward similar questions and finally solves them: proving from all these points that only he is blessed who lives by the mind alone; now being entirely centered in the intellect, depending on nothing else but the divine intellect and the Good itself, which is the beginning and end of all things. This is the purpose of the whole book.

->Various opinions on what it means to "living well."<-

1 The first chapter therefore examines the circuitous paths of those who, being ignorant of what life itself is and what the good itself is, meanwhile strive to define "living well," saying for instance: Living well is to pass through life without hindrance; or to be in a good state; or again to complete one's own proper work; or furthermore to achieve the end naturally desired by one's appetite; or to live tranquilly; or finally to live according to nature. In all these matters, he leads those who are ignorant of the true definition to the point where they are compelled to grant the divine gift of happiness to the lowliest little beasts, and even to plants, and to attribute happiness—which is the peak of life—to those things that have the least amount of life.

Just as in the first chapter, so in the second he deals with false opinions and selects some truth from them: in which note the discussion on sense-perception in animals and plants.

Marsilio Ficino provides a summary, arguing that true happiness consists only in the life of the mind and the divine intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous discussion on dialectic and the virtues into a specific commentary on Plotinus’s treatise regarding happiness (Ennead I, Book 4). It addresses whether life and well-being can be attributed to all living things, including plants.</meta>

# ON BOOK III, ENNEAD I.

### II.
In the second chapter of this book, while achieving nearly the same goal as in the first, he attempts to find the path toward true **happiness** <note>original: *beatitudinem*</note> by examining the errors or doubts of others. Some had claimed that happiness is a certain "disposition of nature" <note>This refers to the Stoic or Peripatetic idea that happiness is living according to one's natural design.</note> by which someone is said to be "faring well." Following this, some among them denied that happiness exists in **plants**, even though they attributed it to all animals. On this point, Plotinus says: Those who deny happiness to plants because they do not "feel" or have sensation would also seem to deny it to certain animals—such as oysters and similar creatures—which seem barely to possess sensation at all. 

Indeed, the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for believing all living things possess a soul.</note> thought that the more "perfect" plants possess sensation in almost the same way as animals, so that the highest grade of plant life matches the lowest grade of animal life. Furthermore, there is a distinction of sex in plants; plants placed near their "mates" sprout more fruitfully. They also turn toward moisture and heat by some unknown sense, and they wither when pruned or handled with violence. 

However, we consider sensation to be twofold: There is a **lower sensation** <note>original: *stupidus sensus*. This refers to a dull, non-conscious awareness, like a reflex or a plant's growth toward light.</note> which does not discern the nature of a thing or any quality, but only feels a certain impression brought upon it; this is a "dull" sense, like that found in those who sleep or in plants. There is also a **superior sensation** which perceives both nature and quality, and this is proper to animals alone. 

But to return to those who said that happiness was a certain disposition or a habit of the body suitable to its nature: they certainly were not right to strip happiness from plants simply because they lacked sensation, since such a "habit" or state exists even before sensation does. But if they say the **supreme good** consists not in such a habit, but in sensation and knowledge, they are immediately refuted. For if the true nature of the good is found in sensation itself, then surely whatever is felt, and in whatever way it is felt, would have to be proven as "good." Yet the opposite is true: we often reject the act of sensing and that kind of knowledge when we realize—or fear—that it will be harmful to us. 

Furthermore, if they then argue that the supreme good is a mixture of the state and the perception of it, they are again proven wrong. If you join something indifferent to the good with another thing that is also indifferent, the "good itself" will not be created from the two of them. Therefore, if they concede that both parts are indifferent to the good, the supreme good will certainly not result from them. 

Perhaps they will say that a certain habit is the supreme good, but only when it is known to be present. To this, Plotinus argues as follows: "Living well" belongs to someone not simply because a certain thing happens to be present, but primarily because they **truly judge** it to be good. For only then does one truly enjoy it as a good. Now, judging the nature and reason of the good is no longer the duty of sensation, but of **reason** and **mind**. Therefore, it is not the habit of pleasure, nor the sensation of it, but reason and the mind that are the causes of living well and blessedly. 

If a disposition of the bodily nature, or a pleasure of that kind, is something devoid of reason, then reason and mind are superior to it, acting as its judge and more excellent "charioteer." If reason is superior, then its natural and primary action is directed toward a more excellent goal. Those who attribute "living well" to all animals or even to plants certainly imply—when they add that these "live well" when they live more perfectly in a certain way—that they are prophesying. They seem to suggest that the life of the senses and the vegetative life "live well" not because they are simply what they are, but because they sometimes live "better." It is as if above such life (which is never always perfect, and indeed always imperfect) there exists another life that is always most perfect. 

Therefore, those who place happiness in the "more perfect" form of living—namely the **rational**—judge more correctly. But virtue in that rational life is not necessary for making people blessed simply because it provides what is needed for the first impulses of the physical nature; for these can be provided or be present even without virtue. Likewise, it would be absurd if the rational nature served only the inferior nature. For the superior nature must have a superior duty and its own proper function leading toward a superior goal. And just as the physical and sensual nature sometimes reaches its goal, the rational nature must reach its own; its perfection does not consist in dealing with imperfect things, but in dealing with things even more perfect than reason itself. For whatever is to be perfected by virtue can only be perfected by the attainment of that very perfection. 

Finally, since the rational nature can never be satisfied by compatible physical things, nor ever rest in the possession of such things, it is clear that it is located in another and more excellent order, and is perfected and made blessed from elsewhere—namely, from **on high**.

->There is one supreme life, namely the supreme intellect;<- 
->others depend on it through many degrees.<-

### III.
The third chapter of the third book now establishes the definition: if the same reason and an equal condition of life were in everything that is said to "live," then everything would eventually reach a blessed life equally. But since this is not the case—since **true life is the Intellect**, while others are but "images" of life—blessed life exists in the Intellect alone. In others, there appears to be a certain "imaginary" happiness, just as they possess an image of the Intellect. Therefore, those who place happiness in **reason** are indeed close to the truth, since reason is closest to the mind; yet they do not judge entirely correctly. Since reason is involved in "motion" <note>Discursive thought that moves from one premise to another.</note>, the nature of pure virtue (which is like a state of supreme rest) does not properly belong to it, as it is quite removed from motion. 

Furthermore, the blessed life is the most absolute life of life itself. Therefore, they say that happiness is not simply "life," but a certain "habit of rational life." First, they deny that the blessed life is Life itself; then they place it in a certain accidental quality; and again in "discursive thought" which, while it is always involved in motion, is never a life that is entirely absolute. 

Plotinus concludes, therefore, that the **Blessed Life** must be placed in another "species" of life—one distinct from the sensual and distinct from the rational. However, he immediately corrects himself for using the word "species." He does not want the Intellect itself to be counted in the same category as a plant, or sensation, or reason, as if it were a species distributed equally alongside them by specific differences. Instead, he wants the **Intellect to be Life itself**, the principle and archetype of all living things. The other living things flow from it through various degrees: first the rational, then the sensual, and finally the vegetative. They are connected only in such a way that in a rational animal there is also something "intellectual"; in a sensual being, there is something "rational"; in a plant, there is something "sensual"; and finally, in mixed bodies, there is something "vital" and "vegetative." In this way, the fertility of the Principle is declared, the condition of the subsequent things is preserved, and the entire universe is perfectly connected on all sides. But now, let us ascend by these arranged steps to Life and Mind itself, and to the Blessed Life.

->The first essence, the first life, and the first intellect are the same.<-

In the very order of things, we see that **essence** strives toward **life**, insofar as whatever exists is inclined toward motion and generation. Motion and generation manifest something "vital." Likewise, **life** strives toward **knowledge**, insofar as that which lives generates "forms" within itself; in this, it imitates the nature that knows, which conceives within itself the forms to be known. From this it is clear that life is the perfection of essence, and knowledge is the perfection of life, although all of this falls under the category of
<meta>catchword: life</meta>

# THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

### III.
...of life can be considered. For it seems that **essence** <note>original: *essentia*; the basic "being" or "what-ness" of a thing</note> is that which is already life being born, and knowledge—especially intellectual knowledge—is life itself fully grown. We see, moreover, certain traces of these three things extended through all things that exist. For everywhere a trace of essence is found under the aspect of **form**; for each thing seems to exist through its form. Likewise, a trace of life is found under that same aspect; for through form, there is inclination, movement, and generation. Again, a trace of intelligence appears by the same logic: since through form, order is now everywhere, which is the proper sign of intelligence. Since, therefore, these things are extended through all things by means of one thing—that is, through form—it is necessary that there be one primary form of all things: which is itself the first essence, and similarly the first life, and the first intellect. For in truth, through one living form, these three are produced through all things: because life stands as a form above all things, embracing these three within itself.

Now, that the first form is the first essence is clear from the fact that through form, essence and being are produced everywhere; and as there is more form, so there is a greater gift of being. Likewise, we gather that the same first form is both the most perfect life and the most perfect intellect from the fact that from a single essence and intellect, the most perfect life is made. Thus, the highest perfection of life and intellect now concurs with the highest perfection of essence. Let the most perfect essence possess its own most perfect attribute. Life, however, is thus the act of essence; likewise, the most absolute life is joined to the most perfect essence. That, indeed, is nothing other than essence led back into itself through intelligence. Therefore, just as in the sensible world—which is an image of the **intelligible world** <note>original: *mundus intelligibilis*; the realm of pure ideas and divine forms</note>—essence is formed as if by matter through life, and life is formed fruitfully through intellect (or whatever kind of cognition represents intelligence), so in the intelligible world, the intellect is a certain act of life, and life is an act of essence. 

Although these three are distinguished among us by a certain formal order, they are therefore distinguished by a certain reason: so that the first form is the principle, the model, and the end of the entire formal order. We gather this distinction in a certain way from the fact that among us, although traces of those three are everywhere, in things which most people say merely "exist," a clearer sign of essence appears than of life or mind. However, in those things which are said only to "live," a more certain trace of life meets us than of mind. And since essence there also seems to be something "unformed" if it is viewed in relation to life, and life similarly if it is compared to mind—and the unformed cannot form itself—therefore, the **One** and the **Good** <note>The highest principle in Neoplatonism, above even Being and Intellect.</note> reigns over these three in which these three are conceived. By its power and efficiency, a thing progresses better as it passes into life, and from life into mind, until it is fully perfected in the mind. This mind, therefore, is the **blessed life**: that is, the most absolute life brought to the summit of its nature by its own additions, reflected back into itself, turned toward the Good itself, and filled with its overflowing goodness. 

But the Good itself, being so simply true, is not essence. Life and intellect are the "middle" of form, but are so exceedingly excellent that they exist through themselves where reason resides. That which is most closely beneath goodness in this way exists through form. **The Soul** <note>original: *Anima*; specifically the World Soul or the human soul in its higher state</note> then possesses these three through true participation. But what is subjected to the **rational soul** <note>The human mind's capacity for logic and reasoning.</note> is judged to possess these three through a kind of imaginary participation—just as light pours out its brightness: in invisible vessels they are through themselves without reason; in the visible heaven by way of form; in the ether by true participation; and thereafter, by a condition that is entirely imaginary. You know that **Proclus** <note>A later Neoplatonist (412–485 AD) known for his very complex and rigid hierarchies of divine "hypostases."</note> wanted these to be distinct substances, and for essence to be superior, and life to be more excellent than mind; we do not easily approve of this. For in that case, the traces of the Good would have to behave similarly—namely, that which only *is* would be more excellent than that which *lives*, and again, that which *is* and *lives* would be more excellent than that which *understands*. We, therefore, say that the more noble substances of the Good contain fewer "gifts," while the less noble ones fall to many. For many perfect things are prepared in small matters to receive a more excellent gift.

->Intellect itself is the highest peak of life.<-

We describe life in a general sense as a certain first emergence of essence, and its departure into its own act, and that first act itself, and that inward and perennial motion which is the principle of all motions. By this, it is brought about that act and motion are everywhere a trace of life, and a more perfect motion and act is a clearer sign of the perfection of life. Since that is the highest grade of life toward which every motion seems to tend as if to an end, we gather that intellect itself is the highest life from the fact that the entire motion of the world finally ends in intellectual form. It begins generation with the forms of the elements, then the forms of mixtures, then of plants, and from there of animals, finally proceeding to the very form of man, which already participates in intelligence. Similarly, in generation itself, it comes forth from the matrix from a unified form to a certain plant-form, from this to a sensory form, and from this to an intellectual form. 

But indeed, because of the power of receiving motion, generation offers itself to a general order of such a habit and property, which series is in itself an image of the intellect. Likewise, the arts also try to imitate this: starting from instruments, matter, and things, they finally define themselves in the intellectual form of the artist's craft itself. Since, therefore, we wish to see the intellect appear in the order of "middle lives," who would not see that intelligence is the highest life? Especially if we consider it as the efficient and exemplary cause of the universe. For everywhere, by the power of that mind, all things are reduced, as if to an end, to the likeness of that mind through their appearances. This, therefore, is life itself. Truly, besides this, there is no life "simply," but only a certain birth or participation in life. **Rational life** is a certain image of this life; an image of rational life is the life called **sensory**; and the likeness of this seems to be **vegetative life**. Finally, a trace of vegetative life is any form in matter, while it is inclined and inclines toward motion, while it generates as if in the manner of a living thing, and while it thins or condenses, in which the condition of growth and decay appears. 

Thus, there is a descent from the substance of life to others one after another through a defect of life: just as if a craftsman were to fashion a very similar statue of his living self, and then reproduce a painting of it, and then place that image before a mirror, from which a final mirror-image would appear. Only the craftsman is the man; none of the images are the man. Only the intellect is the life which is true; those things participated thereafter, which are made later, are judged to be certain images of life rather than life itself. Not only because they degenerate from life itself by a long interval, but because they seem to have an admixture similar to changeable death, while they fail in some degree of life, possess a certain deprivation in moving from potentiality to act, and passing as if out of time, they are now ignorant and suffer forgetfulness. Therefore, this exterior mind is an indicator: and life has now become weaker as if departing from its own fountain. Elements, if they are mixed, are moved; but they generate only from the influence of matter. Plants, however, are now moved from within and fight against the instability of matter. Indeed, by this soul, the power from the One, besides such generation, conceives forms in itself by imagining. Then, by the power of Reason, just as the imagination borrows the beginnings of its conception from the senses, it draws them together from an inward seed, and embraces its own concept by observing it. Finally, the intellect itself now generates within itself, so that it...

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of Being, Life, and Intellect, arguing that they are unified traces of the "First Form" found in all things. He distinguishes his view from Proclus and describes life as a descending series of images, from pure Intellect down to the vegetative life of plants and the forms of matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Enneads, specifically exploring how the soul achieves the "blessed life" (happiness) by aligning itself with the Divine Intellect. It transitions from discussing the nature of life in the previous page to the specific mechanics of human reason and its ultimate goal.</meta>

->ON BOOK IV OF THE FIRST ENNEAD<-

...so that it appears in a way to have begotten itself. For in that state where being, living, and understanding are truly one and the same, while the mind understands itself, it seems meanwhile to begetting, or unfolding, or preserving something essential and vital within itself. From all these points, we can conclude that the most perfect soul, motion, and generation flourish within the mind; and therefore, this is the most perfect life. I mean this flourishes in the Divine Mind primarily and through itself, but in our mind, it flourishes secondarily and through the Divine.

Therefore, we consider the **blessed life** <note>original: *beatam vitam*; often translated as "happiness" or "well-being" in a philosophical sense</note> to be not just any kind of life, as if it required some external addition, but life itself flourishing at the highest level of abundance. I mean life that is the act of the **first essence** <note>The primary source of all being</note> directed naturally toward the Good itself, and thus made perfect. And at this very level of perfection, we consider all understanding to take place, and life itself to be entirely completed by that understanding. In this Intellect, living, understanding, and willing are the same thing. Although in our rational nature living is one thing, thinking another, and choosing another—just as in celestial light, to shine, to sparkle, and to warm are the same—nevertheless, in the light of our air, to gleam is one thing, to reflect another, and to burn another. For what an inferior nature is forced to do through diverse parts, a superior nature fulfills through a single unity.

In the same way, one who acts through the five instruments of the external senses does not perform those acts through a single imagination. And what the imagination contrives through many individual forms, the **reason** <note>original: *ratio*; the discursive faculty of the soul</note> collects into one universal species. Finally, what reason runs through in a manifold act, the **intellect** <note>original: *intellectus*; the higher, intuitive faculty that sees truth all at once</note> possesses in a single, stable act of intuition—one perpetual act. For the Intellect, to live is to understand; to understand is to will. Or if perhaps some distinction is made in the will, it is still said to "will" naturally by its own instinct (so to speak) while it strives toward the Good; it is said to "understand" when it attains the Good; and again, it is judged to "will" when it embraces the Good it has attained. This first life and first mind, always enjoying the Fatherly Good, is considered the blessed life. From this, any mind is perpetually blessed by the First Mind, and by clinging always to the Good through it. From this also, reason becomes happy as often as it is joined to its own mind, and through its own mind to the Divine Mind.

### The rational nature can achieve the blessed life specifically when it is formed by and acts through the intellect.

<margin>IV</margin> Since, therefore, the blessed life is the perfect life, and the perfect life is true intellect and perfect act, the next question is: Whether man—that is, the rational soul—can attain this mind and this life through his own rational power. This question is answered in the fourth chapter of this book, stating that it can sometimes be attained; a point we have opened up more widely in our *Theology* and in our book *On the Mind*.

This rational power has two principal acts: namely, **intuition** and **argument**. Through intuition, it resolves and abstracts forms from the conditions of matter; it withdraws from the individual forms of the imagination to universal forms; and again, from those universals to even more universal ones until it reaches the most common forms, which are proper to the intelligence itself. Here, reason seems to find its end in the Mind, from which it also draws the power of arguing; it prescribes to itself the primary rules of the sciences and arts—naturally implanted in the intellect—as the principles for its arguments. Thus, by intuiting, it places its end in the Mind, and by arguing, it draws its beginning from the Mind. This is fitting, since that which comes later naturally depends on its source. Therefore, the end of reason is to take possession of the Mind to the best of its ability. From this, it strives—as far as it is not hindered—to be formed by the Mind more and more, step by step.

Since this power is not in vain (as it is natural to this species), it can eventually attain the Mind and finally be perfected by that power. When the rational power has proceeded to the ideal forms and rules of the intelligence, it will then be clothed by and formed by the Mind itself as if by a form, and it will then act under the Mind. And so, finally, it will live that life and live blessedly. If it cannot acquire these things here in this life while occupied with other matters, it attains them in the next; and he likewise attains it who has more readily prepared himself for it.

You will note in Plotinus's words that there is a certain "intellect" of the soul, which is a proper part of the soul itself. Before the whole reason is turned toward the Mind, there are still "intellect" and "reason" as two separate parts of the soul; but after it has been turned, the intellect is no longer a part, but the soul itself then becomes Intellect. Certainly, the soul is not happy until it entirely becomes Intellect in act. This is much like how the high air under the **sphere of fire** <note>In ancient cosmology, the region of fire above the air</note> becomes fiery and acts like fire. Indeed, a being is not even a "human" unless he has intellect at least in potential. I believe this was said because of the **brute animals**; if there is any argumentative power in their imaginations, it still cannot be formed by the Mind. Since the forms of the Mind itself are entirely stable and universal, the imagination of a brute—dealing only with particular and mobile forms—can never be formed by the Mind. Reason, however, though its forms are in some way mobile, can eventually be led to the forms of intelligence because they are universal.

After this, he argues that this kind of happiness is not at all disturbed by the care of the animal body or its inconveniences. This is because the soul (or the higher affection) does not consider the "animal" to be part of itself, but rather something either made from it or entrusted to its providence. Plotinus affirms that among these things, the soul so affected exists as a good for itself, namely through the intellectual form which the rational soul has put on. It dwells within, as if under its own intellect, just as its own intellect was clothed from the beginning by the Divine Intellect. And entirely through both its own and the Divine Intellect, the soul enjoys the Good itself. That which is simply "the Good" in itself becomes in the Intellect an essential, vital, intellectual, and intelligible good.

### What the Peripatetics might object.

<margin>V</margin> The fifth chapter of the book briefly lists what a **Peripatetic** <note>A follower of Aristotle</note> would object to this definition of happiness, and what they would count as necessary for happiness. Among these, you will note that **magical poisons** <note>original: *magica veneficia*; refers to both literal poisoning and spiritual "binding" or charms</note> can have some effect on the body and soul, as Porphyry also asserts. This is especially true for souls that are in some way weak—that is, addicted to the imagination and not fortified by the Intellect as if by the **shield and spear of Pallas** <note>Athena/Minerva, goddess of wisdom</note>. But we deal sufficiently with poisonings and fascinations in our *Theology* and in our *Symposium on Love*.

### The ultimate end is the One Good, namely the highest, intelligible or more than intelligible.

<margin>VI</margin> To these objections, he responds in the sixth chapter: If we placed happiness in the prosperity and tranquility of human affairs, it would follow—as the Peripatetics object—that someone who encounters adversity is not happy. But since we place the blessed life in the possession of the First and Divine Good, he does not think the other things called "goods" should be counted toward this; nor does he think their opposites take happiness away from us, provided that in the meantime we are not separated from Divinity itself.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s First Ennead, Book 4. Having established that the "blessed life" consists of the soul's union with the Divine Intellect, Ficino now explores how this happiness remains stable despite physical suffering or mental distraction, and details the hierarchy of the soul's powers.</meta>

...let us depart from this as little as possible. Indeed, as long as the soul is joined to this <note>The Divine Intellect or Mind</note>, Plotinus calls it equally blessed, even if the body is meanwhile racked with pains. I believe that Plotinus learned this—not so much from the words of the Stoics, but from the spirit of the Christian martyrs, whose works were becoming more frequent in his era. Furthermore, he denies that happiness should be placed in a greater accumulation of "lesser goods"; he instead calls these lesser things "necessities" rather than "goods." Surely God, the author of nature, willed that our animal nature—that is, the living body, as something imperfect—be subject to the soul. 

From there, he subordinates imagination to reason, reason to the mind, and finally the mind to Himself. By this same logic, he established that the good and the specific goal of souls should serve the ultimate goal and good of the soul's source. He commanded that the specific goal of the imagination in the soul serve the goal of reason, and likewise that the familiar goal of reason serve the goal of the mind. Truly, just as this is the specific goal of the intelligence, so it is the common goal of everything that follows it—the "End of Ends." For this reason, the goal of the rational soul is not composed of diverse goods, but is the very "Good of Intelligence" in its entirety. Subsequent goods are referred to this as their final goal. This is especially true since the soul is judged most blessed when it is not distracted by **external things** into many directions, but rather—with its other powers and duties set aside or at least greatly relaxed—it is now entirely transferred into the mind. 

Therefore, the entire good of the soul is one: the good of intelligence itself. Then, even the remaining things which are called "goods," if the soul chooses them, it does not choose them for their own sake, but as certain remedies, so that all inconveniences might be avoided. Such inconveniences might otherwise seem to pull the soul down to care for inferior things, causing it to work more sluggishly regarding the Divine Good. Moreover, one's ultimate and most desirable goal must not only be the greatest good in itself, but also the most intimate to the soul compared to all others. For a good is most beneficial if it becomes deeply internal; thus it is the soul's greatest good. Conversely, that which is the greatest good in itself, if it is joined to our soul, becomes more intimate than all else—both because it most effectively reaches and penetrates itself, and because the soul is most vehemently moved toward it. Such a thing is the only <term>intelligible</term><note>Objects of pure thought, accessible to the mind rather than the senses</note> and "more-than-intelligible" good. 

For other things called "goods" are either outside our "animal" (our physical being)—such as riches, honors, and power—or they are within our physical being, like the pleasures of the senses. Or, if they are in the soul, they look toward external things, like the delights of the imagination or the concerns of reason occupied with doing business. Even if they do not look at external things, they are still (so to speak) imaginary and in constant motion, like the wandering thoughts and concepts of the speculative reason. But only the good that stands above the motion of reason is deeply intimate to the mind and is, if I may say so, stable and **accessible**, and at the same time a complete whole. Therefore, it is both the greatest good in itself and the greatest good of the soul.

->*The happy man desires a single good; he chooses others for its sake.*<-

**VII & VIII** In the seventh chapter of the book, he admits that the happy man chooses comforts rather than their opposites. He chooses comforts not for themselves, but to avoid inconveniences. If he prefers that inconveniences be far away, it is not because their arrival would destroy his happiness, but because they might take away his ability to be focused (though he subsequently considers these things of no value) if they strive to interrupt his pursuit of contemplation. He concludes that the blessed man, full of divinity, considers all other things to be nothing; therefore, he cannot be deflected from his state by any of them. He accomplishes the same argument in the eighth chapter.

->*Eternal wisdom is in the mind; when reason reaches it, the soul is happy.*<-

**IX** In the ninth chapter, a doubt is raised once more: Will he who has already been defined as blessed remain so if he suffers from <term>phrenesis</term> <note>original: *phrenesim*; a state of delirium, mental distraction, or madness</note> due to some very grave disease or injury? The answer is: he remains blessed even while he sleeps and dreams in his imagination. Even then, he is awake and acts perfectly with his mind. This is said regarding the whole soul: both the "higher reason" (which is called "reason" because of contemplation and is in a way an "understanding" that is **already** formed in the mind of the blessed man) and the fact that the mind **might use** its power according to the universal species of things and the principles of action. For it is not so perfectly formed according to individual things, as these are more distant from the mind. 

Furthermore, the remaining power of reason, which is more refined in action, even if it is distracted or idle during delirium, is nevertheless most ready to be reflected back toward the higher power of reason and the mind once the impulse of delirium has passed. After this, he distinguishes eternal knowledge from temporal knowledge, which we believe must be examined more deeply. Since in the **first essence** <note>The highest level of reality/God</note> to live is to act internally, and to understand is to act upon itself and reflect upon itself in the knowledge of itself—an act that in no way leans toward the body—we rightly think that the intellectual nature extends as far as knowledge is a certain separation from matter. 

Therefore, in the rational nature, although a certain image of the mind shines through in its action, it nevertheless appears as an intellectual nature. For reason both notices itself and often separates forms from the conditions of matter. Thus, there are three grades of intellectual nature: the **Common Intellect** (Universal Mind), the **Intellect proper to the soul**, and **Reason**. There are also three natures within those images: first, the **Senses**; second, the **Vegetative power**; third, the **Form of the body**. But we speak of these elsewhere. 

Now, in the First Intellect, "to understand" is "to be." In the second, "to understand" is like "being" and (so to speak) "existing." For it is to act—to act, I say, with a certain essential act, and as something **final** and perpetual, much like "shining" or "sparkling" is to light. In the third, finally, "to understand" is "to argue" or reason; that is to operate through motion, much like "reflecting" is to light. Between the eternal "understanding" (which is "to be" simply, without participation, but entirely through essence) and the "understanding" which is "to act through motion," there is a middle "understanding" which is "to act entirely without motion." 

The first intelligence exists by essence; the second by participation, yet entirely immobile; the third becomes through mobile participation. Just as the sphere of fire is hot by essence, and the highest air is hot by simple perpetual participation, but the lower air is hot by changeable participation. Not only does reason show us that there is a proper intellect in the soul that operates stably, but it is further confirmed by this: that the rational nature is a certain potential that is in a way passive while it is formed by motion and comes into action from rest—which many call the "passive" or "formable" intellect. 

It is necessary, therefore, that this intellect, being imperfect in itself, be led from potential into an act of perpetual change by something more perfect that is always "in act" <note>Actualized or fully functioning</note>. Not only must the Common Intellect always be "in act," but also the intellect proper to the soul, lest the rational nature lack an effective, intimate, and sufficient principle for its own understanding. Even the vegetative nature does not lack its own <term>seminal reason</term> <note>original: *ratio seminalis*; the internal blueprint or "seed-logic" that directs growth</note>, which is an intimate, effective, and continuous principle of generation. Therefore, just as universal nature (the entire "seed-logic" of the universe) presides over particular nature (the "seed-logic" of each living thing), and this perpetually presides over the moving duty of generation; so too the Common and Active Intellect presides over the soul's own Active Intellect, and this in turn over Reason (which is as if "passive"). Thus, between the Common Active and the Particular Passive, the soul's own Active Mind is stationed as a middle. From this it happens that the soul, whenever it is recalled to its highest self, immediately finds...

He outlines a hierarchy where the soul's internal active intellect acts as a bridge between the Universal Mind and human reason.</summary>

# ON BOOK IV OF THE FIRST ENNEAD.

...and he may often prophesy and perform works that everyone wonders at. This happens because he suddenly returns into his own mind, which flourishes with a certain divine power to which all things are open. But we discuss these matters at great length in our *Theology* <note>original: "Theologia"; likely referring to Ficino's own work, *Platonic Theology*</note>. Plotinus would perhaps say that Paul ascended to this very Intellect as if to a "third heaven"—that is, an intellectual heaven above the imaginary and rational heavens—and that Moses ascended this same mountain, and that an angel of this kind announced many things to the prophets. For it is not fitting for the divine beings to descend to us, nor is it necessary for the soul that is about to see divine things to change its physical location; it is enough for the soul to be turned toward the mind and toward divine things. But let Plotinus see to these matters himself.

->The previous points are confirmed: that eternal wisdom is in every mind,<-
->and how the rational nature ascends to it.<-

The soul often considers many things, either by intuition or by logical argument, not only that things are eternal, but also by what principle they are eternal; it even conceives (so to speak) the very logic of the property of eternity. Nature, however, is the very logic or "mode" for a thing moving toward eternity. Since there is such great power in the soul that it can think about eternal things and eternity itself in an eternal way, there is by much more reason a power in the soul which considers eternal things in a certain eternal manner—that is, eternally and always. Thus, above the act of **imagination** (which is a moving faculty concerned with moving things), there stands the act of **reason** (which is a moving faculty concerned with unmoving things). Above this is the act of the **intellect**, which is entirely unmoving and concerned with unmoving things. Just as the act of the soul progresses toward the better, so it is perfected in the absolute best. 

Tell me, from where does our reason derive its power, so that while it withdraws itself from individual shapes to universal ones, it can gaze upon those very forms released from this or that place, motion, or time? It must come from a certain power presiding over reason, whose own act is released not only from place, but also from motion and time. Otherwise, reason itself—as long as it acts in a moving and temporal way—could never, by its own act, release forms from motion and time. I am speaking of an **innate power**. For even if someone were to deny that reason achieves this under the "common intellect" <note>The universal divine mind</note>, they would still be forced to confess that a specific act cannot be performed without a specific power, since such action follows such a faculty. Therefore, a certain power that operates stably proceeds from the common intellect to our reason; through this power, even if reason moves, it nevertheless turns itself toward things that do not move. 

This stable power we call the **proper intellect** <note>The individual's highest mental faculty</note>. It is necessary that the most common and certain axioms of the sciences (the first principles) and the very "patterns" of things exist within it. This allows reason to pour out its chains of argument there, to rightly distinguish true and good things and opinions from their opposites, and—through the power of that intellect which always contains everything by "habit" <note>A permanent state or disposition</note>—to ensure that reason itself is never without something to gaze upon. When we say that "intelligible things" <note>Ideas that can be understood by the mind</note> are in the intellect, understand it this way: the intellect *is* the intelligible itself. For this is how the order works: **Sense perception** neither is nor possesses the "sensible" object, but turns itself outward toward it. **Thought**, though it is not the thing being thought, nevertheless possesses it internally. Finally, the **Intellect**, being superior to reason, does not merely "have" the intelligible, but *exists* as it. 

Where Plotinus says that the "Wisdom of the happy soul" is situated in a certain essence—or rather, in Essence itself—he means that the act of understanding is the same as Being itself. This is true both in the "proper intellect" (which is a specific essence) and in the "common intellect" (which is Essence itself). He added "or rather," because the act of the individual intellect is created and preserved by the act of the universal one. Furthermore, just as in a light it is the same thing to *be* light as it is to *shine* (though it is not the same thing to be light as it is to reflect or to give off heat), so in the intellectual soul, it is the same thing to be intellectual as it is to understand—though it is not the same to "be" as it is to reason or to imagine. 

But remember: according to Plotinus, we must place two types of reason between the intellect and the imagination. One is **speculative reason**, which rises toward the intellect; the other is **active reason**, which declines rather toward the imagination. Otherwise, since one person cannot be more blessed than another through the intellect alone (since the intellect always acts similarly in everyone), one would not be happier than the other unless the speculative reason—which is naturally closest to the intellect—were turned entirely toward the mind. This cannot be said of active reason, because it is further from the mind, occupied with labor, and in a way stretched outward toward external things. It is clear that these two types of reason differ in kind, not only because speculative reason works properly with nature while active reason thinks about deeds, but also because it is very rare—perhaps impossible—for a natural talent for both to occur in the same person.

->Not everyone notices that their mind is always acting upon divine things;<-
->nor does the blessed person always notice that their higher reason is<-
->acting upon the mind.<-

Even if in a blessed person the speculative reason acts under the form and activity of the mind, it does not always notice that it is doing so; just as others do not always recognize that our mind is constantly acting upon the Divine Mind. For just as in our "animal" nature, living according to the **vegetative power** is almost the same as the act of vegetating (that is, nourishing, growing, reproducing, and preserving), yet we do not recognize that this power is doing these things or how it performs them—because no image of this action reaches our imagination—so too in our mind, living is the same as understanding. Yet, we do not notice its eternal action unless a certain image of it is conceived in our imagination. 

Indeed, not even the blessed person always recognizes that the speculative reason within them is already acting alongside their intellect upon the Divine Mind. This is because an image of such an action is not always formed in their imagination, and it is through the imagination that the soul is usually alerted to what its higher or lower powers are doing. 

**Note here:** it belongs to our **intellect** to always know through direct action; it belongs to our **reason** to somehow "recollect" things known as it moves from potential habit into actual thought regarding forms; and finally, it belongs to the **imagination** to somehow "learn" new things. For if the imagination turns away from reason and toward the animal body, it immediately notices what the animal sees or hears; but it does not recognize what the internal reason or intellect is doing. Conversely, if it is ever free from the animal and turns entirely toward reason, then through this very imagination, the soul perceives that reason is already performing some act. 

But if reason is turned toward the mind—which happens in the blessed person—then the soul immediately notices both that reason is "awake" regarding our mind, and our mind regarding the divine. Since the imagination is free from the animal body and is not constructing anything corporeal, certain images appear there from the very act of the mind and reason. Through these, the soul is "admonished" (whether in speculative or active reason) that both the intellect and speculative reason are at work. But you must remember: in the intellect itself, just as living and knowing are the same, so knowing thoroughly and "acknowledging" (that is, noticing that one knows) are the same. But in reason, since living and knowing are not entirely the same—because the former is eternal while the latter is perpetually changeable—it is rightly not the same thing to know as it is to acknowledge what one knows or does...

# 18 MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY

...whom he follows. Here, **recognition** <note>original: "agnitio"</note> follows **knowledge** <note>original: "cognitionem"</note> as something subsequent, perhaps as a consequence or companion, often causing the prior action to become somewhat weaker due to a distraction of the mind. Therefore, not without reason does Plotinus say that this kind of recognition and notice is carried out through a subsequent and secondary faculty and form. We do not doubt that this accompanying secondary faculty is the **imagination** itself. Similarly, we call the form that accompanies the prior form an "image." Let there be, therefore, natural forms in the mind, or in reason; though there they are eternal, here they are perpetual. Let there then be "adventitious" <note>Added from the outside or acquired rather than innate</note> forms in the imagination—images of the natural forms—through which the soul, as if in wonder, might attend to and notice what is being done in the reason and the mind as if they were new things.

Indeed, just as linear rays of a face are directed into a mirror positioned toward us in a certain way, and are reflected from there at similar angles to the eye, and the mirror thus displays an image (if it currently holds one); in a similar way, **reason**, like an eye, neither sees the **mind** nor notices its action—even though the mind is always acting—unless its act affects the imagination, which is of a different nature but turned toward it. By this act, an image of the higher action is reflected from the imagination into the reason.

Here you should first note where Plotinus says that *we* are not the act of the vegetative faculty <note>The lowest part of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition</note>, but rather the act of the intelligence. This is especially true of the **blessed** person; it is also true in every soul, which Plotinus considers more closely joined to the intellect than to the animal nature. 

Next, where he says that the act of understanding occurs without **phantasia** <note>The Greek term for imagination or the faculty of forming mental images</note> when no image is formed or reflected there, he means not that pure intelligence depends on imagination, but rather that imagination depends on intelligence. However, rational intelligence—that is, thought and the "mobile" reason—is often stirred by imagination, especially the "active" reason. Aristotle says that this active reason always needs imagination, as Themistius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> and Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator</note> wisely interpret. 

Finally, know that Plotinus agrees, while reviewing certain words of Aristotle, that this was Aristotle's own opinion regarding the mind: where, in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de Anima"</note>, he writes that the **Intellect** always understands, and that understanding is its very substance, and that it exists as truly immortal. For immortality is not so "true" in the lower powers; for even if some are perpetual, they are nevertheless involved in motion. As for his denial that we "remember" (that is, the rational power) after death, Plotinus will examine this carefully elsewhere.

Lastly, remember that Averroes <note>The famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle</note>, though not saying the exact same thing, introduced something similar when he said our intellect has a double intelligence within it: one eternal, the other temporal. The former acts through its own being, while the latter acts through our images. We never notice the eternal one because it shares nothing with our imagination; however, we recognize the temporal one because its forms agree with the images of our imagination. Since he places a "twin" intellect in the same substance—namely, the **formative** and the **formable**—he says that this formable intellect does not recognize what the formative one is doing through us until it has been perfectly formed by the other through us. Only then, and together with the formative intellect, will it be happy within us. 

But let us leave Averroes aside; for even Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and biographer</note> and Proclus <note>A major late-antique Neoplatonist</note> left Plotinus behind on this point, not approving of the idea that the intellect of our soul always acts in the way Plotinus says. We have explained this in the preceding sections, not so much approving of it as interpreting it. Yet we must think there is enough stability and excellence in our mind if the essence and form of things remain implanted there, along with the principles of the sciences.

He contrasts this view with other philosophers like Aristotle, Averroes, and Proclus to clarify the unique Neoplatonic stance on the soul's immortality and intellectual life.</summary>

Plotinus begins his investigation into the nature of happiness (eudaimonia), questioning whether it is a state exclusive to rational beings or if it can be attributed to all living things, including animals and plants.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD 1.
### TREATISE 4.

# PLOTINUS
## FIRST ENNEAD
### BOOK IV.

-> ON HAPPINESS <-
<note>original Greek: "Peri Eudaimonias"</note>
-> On Beatitude <-
<note>original Latin: "De Beatitudine"</note>

---

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial T containing a scene with a man seated outdoors near foliage.</image-desc> Since we identify **living well** <note>The Greek "eu zen" and Latin "bene viuere" refer to a life of flourishing, not just survival.</note> and **being happy** as the same thing, shall we grant these to other living creatures as well? For if they are permitted to live their lives according to their nature without hindrance, what prevents us from saying they too "live well"? Indeed, one might either grant "living well" to all living things, or only to those with the power of sensation. For a proper activity that reaches its fulfillment—both of these <margin>B</margin> will be present in other living creatures. If it is granted that they feel, and that they have tasks according to their nature, there are also "musical" animals, such as those that sing to others; and certainly, pleasure is natural to them, and they choose things that are desirable to them. Furthermore, if we establish that the goal of happiness is the final point of a natural desire, we would also grant happiness to them in this way, as they reach that final point <margin>C</margin> when their inner nature has passed through its whole life and fulfilled it from beginning to end. But if someone finds it troublesome to lower happiness to other animals—claiming that in this way it would be granted even to the lowliest of them, and even to plants—since they also live and have a life that unfolds toward an end: first, he might <margin>D</margin> seem absurd if he says other animals cannot "live well" simply because he thinks they are of little value. He would not be forced to grant to plants what he grants to other living creatures, because they lack sensation. However, perhaps someone might even grant happiness to plants, since living is present in them. Life can happen "well" or, on the contrary, "poorly"; just as it is given to plants to be in a good state, to bear fruit or not to bear fruit. Therefore, <margin>E</margin> if pleasure is the goal, and "living well" consists in this, it is absurd to deny the other animals a "good life." And if the goal is tranquility <note>original: "ataraxia," a state of being undisturbed</note>, the same follows. Likewise, if "living well" is said to be "living according to nature."

THOSE WHO deny happiness to plants because they lack sensation...

<column-break/>

<margin>Various opinions on what it means to live well, and to whom it applies.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial C set in a circular frame depicting a figure in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc> Since we establish that **living well** and **being happy** are the same thing, shall we concede this to other living creatures as well? For if they are given the ability to spend their life without hindrance according to the way they were born: what prevents them from also living well—that is, happily? For whether one places "living well" in a state of being well off, or <margin>B</margin> in the perfection of one's own work, both will apply to other animals. For it will be possible for them to be in a good state and to perform their best natural work: such as "musical" animals <note>Plotinus refers to birds and other creatures that produce melodic sounds as a natural function.</note> which are in a good state in other respects and sing just as they are naturally suited; and in this way, it seems possible for them to achieve a desirable life. Furthermore, if we establish that happiness is a certain goal, which is indeed the extreme point in the appetite of nature, we shall confess that they too will be <margin>C</margin> happy in this way—namely, when they arrive at that extreme point. When they have proceeded there, the movement of nature stops in them, having already completed their whole life and fulfilled it entirely from the beginning to the end. But if anyone finds it troublesome that happiness is transferred to beasts, asserting that it would thus apply even to the most abject things, and to plants besides—since they too are living and lead their life to its own end—he might indeed <margin>D</margin> seem absurd, saying that other animals cannot "live well" because they do not seem to him to be of much value. He will not be forced to grant to plants what he gives to all animals, for the reason that they lack sensation. And perhaps there will not be wanting someone who hands over happiness even to plants, since living is also present in them. Moreover, living happens partly well, and partly the opposite: just as it is given to plants to be in a good state and bear fruit, or not to bear fruit. Accordingly, <margin>||</margin> if pleasure is the goal, and "living well" <margin>He refutes the false opinions of those who inquire whether living well consists in pleasure, or in the absence of pain, or in the constitution of natural movement.</margin> <margin>E</margin> consists in this, he who takes "living well" away from the brutes will be absurd. If tranquility <note>original: "tranquillitas"</note> is the goal, the same will happen. Likewise, if "living well" is said to be "living according to nature," he will seem to be saying the same thing.

BUT WHOSOEVER denies that happiness is present in plants because they do not feel...

<summary>Plotinus investigates whether happiness (eudaimonia) can be attributed to animals and plants, arguing that if happiness is defined simply as pleasure, tranquility, or fulfilling a natural life cycle, then all living things could be considered "happy." This serves as a rhetorical starting point to eventually argue for a higher, specifically human or rational form of happiness.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> ...nor would they be willing to grant it to all living creatures. Or, when they say that "to sense" this is for the state <note>original Latin: "affectionem"; Greek: "pathos". In this context, it refers to a physical or mental state or "feeling".</note> not to be hidden, then the Good itself must be that very state even before it is said "not to be hidden"—just as being in a state **according to nature** <note>original Latin: "secundum naturam". This is a Stoic technical term for living in harmony with the natural order.</note> exists even if it remains hidden, and it is one’s own even if you do not yet recognize it as your own. Indeed, even a sweet thing must be sweet before you perceive it to be so. Therefore, since that is the Good, and that which possesses it is present, it is already in a "well" state. <margin>B</margin> So why is it necessary to add "sensation"? Unless, perhaps, they do not place the Good in a certain present state or constitution, but rather in the knowledge and sensing of it. But if so, they will be saying that sensation itself, and the sensual activity of life, is the Good; and thus they will be forced to admit that the Good is present to anything that perceives. But if they say the Good is composed of both—namely, a certain thing/state and the perception of it—how can they assert that the result of both is "Good" when each part, taken individually, is indifferent? <margin>C</margin> But if they say the Good is the state itself, and that **living well** is that condition when someone recognizes the Good as present to them, we must ask them: Does he "live well" simply by knowing that what is present is present? Or must he know not only that it is sweet, but that this very thing is the Good? Truly, if he must know it is the Good, that will no longer be the work of sensation itself, but of some virtue or a more excellent faculty. Therefore, "living well" will not belong to those drenched in pleasure, but to him who is able to recognize that pleasure is the Good. And so, the cause of "living well" will not be pleasure, but rather that which is able to judge that pleasure is the Good. <margin>D</margin> And that which judges is more excellent than the state or the passion: for it is **reason**, or **intellect**, while pleasure is merely a passion. In no way is that which is irrational more excellent than reason. How then could reason, dismissing itself, place something else from an opposite genus as being more excellent than itself? <margin>E</margin> But it seems that those who attribute [this state] to plants, and those who seek "well-being" in a specific kind of sensation, are unaware that they are seeking "living well" as something less than it is; they place that which is called "the best" in a certain more complete life. Again, those who say it exists in a **rational life**, and not in life simply (not even if it were a sensory life), might perhaps speak correctly. But as to why they place happiness only around the rational animal, <margin>F</margin> one must ask them: Do you add "rational" because reason is more skillful and sagacious, and can more easily investigate and seize the **primary things according to nature**? <note>original Latin: "prima secundum naturam". This refers to basic biological needs like health and strength.</note> Would it still be so if reason were able neither to investigate sagaciously nor to achieve them? But if reason is preferred only for its power of discovery, then happiness will be present even to those lacking reason, provided that they naturally attain those primary things of nature without reason. Thus reason would be a servant, and in no way to be chosen for its own sake; nor would its perfection, which we call **virtue**, be chosen for itself. <margin>G</margin> But if you say that reason does not have its dignity because of the primary things of nature, but is to be cherished for itself, then you must state what its other work is, and what its nature is, and what makes it perfect. Surely it must become perfect not from its inspection of these [natural] things, but its perfection must consist in something else, and another nature must be within it; it should not be in the number of these primary things of nature, nor from those things from which the primary things...

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...giving, they will risk not giving pleasure to all animals. If, however, they define sensing as "the state not being hidden," the state itself must be good before it is "not hidden"—as in having it **according to nature** <note>original Greek: "kata physin".</note> even if it is hidden, and it being one's own even if one does not yet know it is one's own, and it being sweet. For it must be sweet; so if this is somehow existing and present, the "well-being" is already in the having of it. <margin>Β</margin> So why must sensation be added? Unless, perhaps, they do not place the Good in the state or constitution produced, but in the knowledge and sensing. But in this way, they will say that sensation itself is their Good, and the activity of a sensory life; so that for those perceiving anything at all [the Good is present]. If they do not say the Good is from both—for instance, of such a sensation—how, if each is indifferent, do they say the Good is from both? <margin>C</margin> If the state is the Good, and such a constitution is "living well" when one knows the Good is present to him, they must be asked: if this knowledge is what is present, or if it is present <unclear>but he does not know it</unclear>. If it is to know, then is it only that it is sweet, or that this is the Good? But if this is the Good, this is no longer the work of sensation, but of another power greater than sensation. If, therefore, "living well" belongs to those experiencing pleasure, it belongs to him who is able to know that pleasure is the Good. <margin>D</margin> And the cause of "living well" will not be pleasure, but the ability to judge that pleasure is the Good. That which judges is better than the state [of pleasure]; for it is **reason** <note>original Greek: "logos".</note> or **intellect** <note>original Greek: "nous".</note>; while pleasure is a state. Nowhere is the irrational better than reason. How then could reason, letting itself go, set another thing lying in an opposite genus as better than itself? <margin>E</margin> But it seems that those who do not grant [this] to plants, and those who place "living well" in a certain sensation, are unaware that they are seeking a "living well" that is something greater, and are placing the "best" in a clearer life. And those who say it is in a **rational life**, but not simply in life (even if it were sensory), would perhaps speak well. But as to why they place **happiness** <note>original Greek: "eudaimonein".</note> only in the rational animal, <margin>F</margin> it is proper to ask them: Do you add the rational because reason is more mechanical <note>meaning "resourceful" or "instrumental".</note>, and can easily track down and provide the primary things according to nature, or even if it were not able to track them down or obtain them? But if it is because it is more able to find them, happiness will belong also to those not having reason, if they attain the primary things of nature through their [own] nature. Reason would then be the servant, and would not be chosen for itself, nor would its own perfection, which we say is **virtue**. <margin>G</margin> But if you will say it does not have its value because of the primary things of nature, but is to be welcomed for itself, one must say what its other work is, and what its nature is, and what makes it perfect. For except for [being used] through itself more than for contemplation or concerning these things, but another [nature] is that which makes its nature perfect, and it is not itself one of the primary things of nature, nor from those things from which the primary things of nature [come], nor...

<summary>Plotinus argues that happiness (eudaimonia) cannot be defined merely as pleasure or the sensation of a natural state, as this would imply that reason is merely a tool for achieving physical needs. He concludes that for happiness to be truly "good," it must be judged by a higher faculty—reason or intellect—which is valuable for its own sake rather than just as a servant to bodily sensations.</summary>
