# FOURTH BOOK.

...nor to be of this kind at all, but rather better than all of these: otherwise, I do not think they would be able to explain how it is to be honored, and what it means to be honorable. But indeed, as long as these people find a better nature in those things they currently focus on, they must be permitted to linger there wherever they may find honor, wandering about what it means to live well, to whom it can belong, in what way, and in which of these things it can be found.

<margin>B</margin> Let us, however, resume from the beginning: what do we consider happiness <note>original Greek: εὐδαιμονεῖν (eudaimonein); Latin: felicitas. In Greek philosophy, this refers to "flourishing" or "living well" rather than just a fleeting emotion.</note> to be? Certainly, if we place happiness in "life," and if we were to assume that "living" means the same thing for everyone, then we would grant the capacity for happiness to all living creatures. We would then think that "living well" is an activity present to all those who share in that one and the same thing that all animals are naturally capable of.

In that case, we would not distinguish between types of life; we would not grant happiness to the rational <note>original Latin: rationali. Referring to humans as "rational animals."</note> faculty while denying it to the irrational. Life itself would be the common denominator, which should be capable of achieving blessedness <margin>C</margin> if indeed happiness consisted in a certain kind of life. Therefore, those who say that happiness occurs in a "rational life" do not place it in life as a whole. I believe they do not sufficiently realize that they are defining happiness as something other than life itself. They will be forced to say that the "Good" <note>The ultimate goal or purpose of existence.</note> is a quality—the rational power—around which happiness is established. But for them, the subject is "rational life": for happiness revolves around this whole. Therefore, it seems we must place it in another species of life. <margin>D</margin> I say this not as if other species are distinguished as being "against reason" on equal terms, but as we have analyzed: one thing is prior, and another is posterior. Since, therefore, "life" is spoken of in many ways, having differences according to what is primary and what is secondary, and so on—and "living" is used as an equivocal <term>equivocal (aequivoca): a word that has multiple, distinct meanings depending on the context, like "bank" (a river bank vs. a money bank).</term> term—it is used one way for a plant, another for a brute animal. Life differs in its fullness and its scarcity; and certainly, by a certain analogy, both "living well" and "living" are spoken of regarding all <margin>E</margin> these things. And if one living thing is a mere image of another living thing, then similarly, one habit of "living well" must be judged as a mere image of another "living well." But if happiness belongs to whoever has a sufficient amount of life—that is, that which does not fail in any part of life—then surely happiness will belong only to the one who lives "sufficiently." For to this one belongs the "best": since in the very order of beings, the best is that which truly exists in life, and that is the "perfect life." In this way, the Good will not be something added from the outside; <margin>F</margin> nor will anything else coming from elsewhere cause the subject to be placed in the Good. For what must be added to a perfect life for it to be the best? If someone says that the nature of the Good itself must be added, our argument will be more specific: however, we are not seeking the cause, but that which is within us. It has often been said that the perfect and true life flourishes in that intellectual <note>original Greek: νοερὰν φύσιν (noeran physin); Latin: intellectuali natura. This refers to the highest form of reality or consciousness in Plotinus's system.</note> nature; while others are imperfect lives, images of life, neither living perfectly nor purely—indeed, they are no more "lives" than they are "non-lives." <margin>G</margin> And now, to put it briefly: insofar as all living things live from one principle, yet do not live equally, it necessarily follows that the principle of living itself is the "first life" and "perfection."

IF, therefore, a man is able to have this perfect life, then certainly the man having this is happy. Otherwise, we would attribute happiness only to the gods, if such a life belongs to them alone. But since we declare that happiness exists also among men...

A In what way this is so, we have already recognized. I say it this way: that a human being possesses a perfect life, not if they possess only the life of the senses, but if they also possess reason and true intellect <note>original: *intellectum verum*; Greek: *νοῦν ἀληθινὸν*. For Plotinus, the Intellect is the highest level of human consciousness, connected to the Divine.</note>, as can be clear from other arguments. But does he possess this as something else, existing as if he were someone else? Or is he certainly not a human being at all, unless he possesses this either potentially or in act <note>original: *potentia... actu*. Technical Aristotelian terms meaning the "capacity for something" versus "actually doing it."</note>, which is what we call being happy? But shall we place this "perfect form of life" in him as if it were a part of him? B Or rather, we shall say that another kind of human being possesses it as a part, having it by a certain potential; but that the truly happy man is the one who already exists in this "act," and has reached the point where he is the same as this intellect. As for other things, they now simply surround him; one would not call them his parts, for they surround him against his will; yet they would be his own if he wished them to be connected to him. C To such a person, then, what is the "good"? Perhaps it is he himself, through what he possesses. For that which was above him is the cause of the good that thrives in him. And while that higher Good is good in itself in one way, it is present to him in another. A testimony for this can be found here: that someone who is in this state desires nothing further. For what should he seek? Certainly nothing of the lower things, for he is joined to the best. He who lives this way, therefore, has a sufficient life. And if he is endowed with virtue, he is sufficient for happiness and for the possession of the good. D For there is no good that he does not have. Whatever he seeks as "necessary," he seeks not for himself, but for something belonging to him—he seeks it for the body that is attached to him. And even if he makes use of the living body, he certainly seeks what pertains to the body, not what is proper to the "inner man" <note>original: *interioris hominis*. A concept familiar to Platonists and later Christian thinkers (like St. Paul) referring to the soul or spiritual self.</note>. Indeed, he knows these things clearly, and he gives what he gives in such a way that he in no way falls away from his own life; for this reason, he will be nonetheless blessed even in adverse fortunes: for a life of this kind remains constant. Furthermore, E in the death of family and friends, he is not ignorant of what death is. Those who suffer such things, if they are upright, know the same thing clearly. If his family members and close associates suffer and cause any trouble, they do not bring it upon the man himself, but rather upon that part of him which is lacking in mind <note>original: *mente captum*; Greek: *νοῦν ἔχον*. Referring to the irrational part of the soul or the body.</note>, whose private troubles the happy soul will not receive.

Although someone looking at these things will perhaps oppose us and bring the calamities of Priam <note>original: *Priamique calamitates*. Someone might easily say they accept this, since the passions of the body are transferred to the soul itself, and conversely, for the sake of the body, a human being pursues or avoids individual things. Therefore, since pleasure is necessary for a happy life, how can it be found in such narrow straits?

<column-break/>

A How we must consider this is as follows: I say it thus, that it is clear from other arguments that the life we speak of as "perfect" does not belong to one who has only the sensory life, but also reason and true intellect. But does he, being someone else, have this as something else? Or is he not a human being at all, unless he has this either potentially or in actuality—the very thing we say is being happy? Shall we say this very thing is in him as a part? B Or rather, that while another kind of human has this as a part (possessing it potentially), the happy man is he who is already this in actuality, and has transitioned so as to be the same as this? The other things merely surround him, which one would not even place as parts of him, as they surround him without his choosing; but they would be his if they were joined to him according to his will. For such a person, then, what would be the C good? He is his own good through what he has. But that which is beyond him is the cause of the good in him, and is good in another way, being uniquely present to him. A witness of this being the case is that the one who is in this state would not seek anything else; for of the inferior things he seeks nothing, and for the superior things his life is self-sufficient. To the one who has D such a life, if he is virtuous, it is self-sufficient for happiness and the acquisition of the good; for there is no good which he does not have. What he seeks, he seeks as a necessity, and not for himself, but for something of his own; for he seeks it for the body attached to him, and while the body lives, he seeks the things of this living body, not the things that belong to the human being that he is. And he knows these things, and gives what he gives without taking anything away from his own life, nor is he any less happy even in bitter and contrary fortunes; for such a life remains. And when E relatives and friends die, he knows what death is. Those who suffer also know it, if they are virtuous. And if his family or those close to him suffer this, and if it brings any distress, it is not they who bring it, but rather the part in them that possesses [only] mind <note>This translation of the Greek follows the manuscript's flow regarding the "distress" of the irrational part.</note>, which does not accept these pains into itself.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's inquiry into whether happiness (eudaimonia) can be maintained in the face of physical suffering and external misfortune. He argues that the "perfect life" resides in the intellect and is not diminished by bodily pain.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin>
...and if one is surrounded by sorrows and pains, will they be happy? This would be the case even if the one pressed by such adversity is a good person. And yet, who indeed would deny that the perfect habit of the mind alone is happy and self-sufficient? For a human being, in whose soul another, lower element is joined <note>original: *deterius aliud est adiunctum*; referring to the physical body or the irrational soul</note>, happiness must be sought concerning the whole composite being, not just one part—even if that part is the more excellent one. For as often as the other part fares ill, the superior part is necessarily hindered from carrying out its duties. Otherwise, one must either cast off the body or the senses of the body, and thus seek self-sufficiency for our happiness in that state.

<margin>VI</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
BUT if reason were to place happiness in not grieving, not being sick, not facing danger, and not falling into great adversities, then no one could be happy when the opposites of these things are imminent. But if happiness is instead placed in the possession of the true Good <note>original: *veri boni possessione*; Plotinus identifies the True Good with the Intellect and the One</note>, why should it be necessary to overlook this and judge a person's happiness by looking at the things that happen to them besides? Why seek other things which are not even counted toward happiness?

<margin>C</margin>
<note>He would answer that the goal (finis) is the simple supreme and therefore is a thing of the mind; other things are not the goal, but are merely toward the goal.</note>
For if happiness were an accumulation of both goods and necessary things—whether we speak of greater goods or lesser ones, which are called "goods" only because they are necessary—then these too would need to be present. But if it is necessary for the "End" <note>term: *Finis/Telos* — the ultimate purpose or highest state of a being</note> to be one single thing and not many—for otherwise a person would seek not an "End" but "Ends"—then only that which is ultimate and most excellent should be joined to it, which is exactly what the soul seeks to make internal to itself.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>*consequent. *superimposed.</margin>
This inquiry and will does not mean that the soul wishes to be in this state of misfortune. For the turning away from hardships is not driven by the primary desire of our nature; rather, the soul simply flees their presence through the discourse of reason and pushes them away, or seeks to add comforts instead. The primary appetite itself is directed toward that which is best; when that is present, the soul is filled and finds rest. This is the life that is sought after with the highest will. To have some of the necessary things present is not a matter of "will" in the proper and primary sense, nor even by a loose use of the word. We think these things ought to be present because we turn away from evils as much as we can; yet this act of turning away is not itself the primary thing to be desired. It is more desirable to have never needed such turning away at all. This is proven by these very things when they are present, such as health and freedom from pain. For which of these things draws the soul to itself with wonder? Indeed, present health and the absence of pain are usually ignored.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>G</margin>
Things which, when present, have no charming power to turn the soul toward them, add nothing to our happiness. When they are absent, they are required only because of the presence of their painful opposites. It is consistent with reason, then, to judge them as "necessities" rather than "goods." Therefore, they should not be counted as part of the End; even when they are absent and their opposites are imminent, the End must be preserved whole.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
And if he is surrounded by pains, will he be happy? Even if he is a good man, whom such adversity has pressed. And yet, who indeed would deny that the perfect habit of the mind alone is happy and self-sufficient? For a human being, in whose soul something lower is joined, happiness must be sought concerning the whole composite, not however concerning only one part, even if it is the more excellent: which, as often as the other part fares ill, is necessarily prohibited from carrying out its duties. Otherwise, one must cast away the body, or the sense of the body, and so seek self-sufficiency for our happiness.

<margin>VI</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
BUT if reason placed happiness in not suffering, and not being sick, and not being in danger, nor in falling into great adversities, no one could be happy while the opposites were imminent. But if it is placed in the possession of the true good itself: why is it necessary to pass over this and, looking at what happens besides, judge the happy man, seeking other things in addition which are least of all numbered in happiness?

<margin>The happy man wants only the intelligible good; he does not depend on other things, whether good or bad.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
For if happiness were an accumulation of goods as well as necessities, whether of greater goods and lesser, which are called not only necessary but even "goods," these would furthermore need to be present. But if it is necessary for the end to be one certain thing, and not many—otherwise a man would seek not an end but ends—that alone ought to be joined which is ultimate and most excellent, and which the soul seeks to become internal to itself.

<margin>D</margin>
This inquiry and will does not go so far as to mean that it is in this state [of pain] at all. For the turning away from inconveniences is hardly driven by the chief vow of nature, but the reason merely flees their presence by its discourse and drives them away: or even seeks to add comforts. But the principal appetite itself is directed toward that which is best: by whose presence it is filled and rests. And this is the life which is desired by the chief will. That some necessary things be present will not be "will" properly and chiefly, nor even by an abuse of the word "will": since we even think these things ought to be present because we obviously turn away from evils according to our strength: and yet this duty of turning away is not itself chiefly to be desired: for it is more desirable to have not needed this turning away at all. Moreover, these same things bear witness when they are present, such as health and the absence of pain. For which of these things wonderfully draws the soul to itself? For present health and absence of pain are accustomed to be neglected.

<margin>E</margin>
Those things which when present by no means have a charming power of turning the soul to themselves, add nothing to our happiness.

<margin>F</margin>
When they are absent, they are required because of the presence of the offending opposites; it is consistent with reason to judge them as necessities rather than goods. Therefore they do not seem to be numbered with the end, but even when they are absent, and their opposites are imminent, the end is to be kept whole.

<margin>VII</margin>
<margin>G</margin>
FOR what reason, then, does the happy man desire these things to be present and reject the opposites? Perhaps we shall say, not because they contribute to being blessed, but rather to being itself; while the opposites of these either lead toward not-being, or because they interrupt the one who has obtained the goal with their occurring inconveniences, not by taking away the end, but because he who is the best...

<summary>Plotinus argues that true happiness (eudaimonia) is an internal state of the Intellect and remains "whole" even during physical suffering. He distinguishes between "goods," which constitute happiness, and "necessities" like health, which the wise person prefers but does not require for their ultimate fulfillment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the "blessed life" (eudaimonia). Having previously established that happiness is an internal state of the soul rather than a reaction to external events, he now addresses specific worldly tragedies—loss of family, status, and physical pain—to prove they cannot extinguish the wise man's inner light.</meta>

## PLOTINUS, ENNEAD I

<margin>A</margin> He enjoys [the Good], and desires to have it alone, and nothing else along with it; for if something else should occur, it does not take away his goal, which remains present even in the midst of other things. In no way does a happy man fall from his blessed state simply because something happens to him that he did not wish for. Otherwise, he would be changed and fall from happiness every single day—for instance, if he were to lose a son or suffer the loss of his household goods.

<margin>B</margin> Truly, there are countless things that happen contrary to one's wishes, yet they take nothing away from the presence of the ultimate goal. They say that great adversities do not change a man's happiness through any ordinary chance. But what human affair is so great that it cannot be looked down upon by one who has raised himself to things higher than all these, and no longer depends on any of these lower things?

<margin>C</margin> For why should he consider worldly successes, of whatever kind they may be, to be great? Such things as kingdoms, or the rule over cities and nations, or the founding of cities? Even if he himself should lose this power or see his homeland destroyed, would he consider it a heavy evil? If he were to judge such a thing as a massive evil, or any evil at all of that kind, he would have to be considered ridiculous. He would no longer be a man of integrity, for he would be valuing mere wood and stones—and by Jove, the transitory habits of mortals—as something great. We maintain that such a man ought to consider death to be altogether better than life in a body.

<margin>D</margin> If he himself is to be sacrificed, will he think death is an evil to him because he is to be slaughtered next to the altars? <note>original: *iuxta aras sit iugulandus*; Plotinus is likely referencing the Stoic idea that the manner of death does not affect the soul's virtue.</note> Unless this is granted, his body will be dissolved just the same, whether above or below the earth. Will he also be troubled if he is buried without expense or honor, having been judged unworthy of a tall monument? To value such things is the mark of a small-minded man. Furthermore, if he is led away as a captive, the means of freeing himself is available <note>A veiled reference to the "open door" policy of ancient philosophy—the option of suicide if the life of virtue becomes impossible.</note> if it is not possible to be happy there. If his family members are led into captivity—his daughters or granddaughters—will he be any less happy? What then shall we say? If he departs from life without seeing such things, did he leave life believing that these things could not happen? To think so would be absurd.

<margin>E</margin> Will he then not believe it possible for his own people to be overwhelmed by such fortunes? Surely he will not lose his happiness because of the mere opinion that such a thing might happen? On the contrary, even holding such an opinion, he can be happy; for even if it happens in his presence, he will reflect upon the nature of the universe <note>original: *vniuersi naturam*; referring to the cosmic order or "The All."</note>, seeing that it draws things along this way and that it is necessary to follow.

<margin>F</margin> Many, indeed, even after being led into captivity, fare better than before. Furthermore, it is within the power of those who are bound to free themselves; but if they remain, they remain for a reason, and so it is not an altogether heavy thing. Or if they stay for some other reason, it is not fitting that they themselves should be the cause of their own distress. Truly, the man of integrity will never be crushed by evil on account of the ignorance of his own people, nor will he be diverted into the misfortunes or successes of others.

<margin>
<insert>
VIII
The blessed man
keeps his own
goods whole 
within himself
in any
misfortune.
</insert>
</margin>

<margin>G</margin> **WHEN** his pains are violent, he will bear them as long as he is able; but if they should become excessively great, they will carry him away <note>original: *efferent*; meaning they will cause him to lose consciousness or lead to death.</note>. He will not be miserable even when placed in the midst of pains; instead, his own light will shine steadily within his innermost chambers, like a torch in a lighthouse, even while the winds blow outside, howling with whirlwinds and storms. But if he should be less steady in himself, or if perhaps—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...having the best within himself, he wishes only to have that, and nothing else with it; or if something else is present, it is not that thing he seeks, though it is present nonetheless. For if he did not wish for something, and yet it was present, it does not take away from his happiness. If it were to change every day, he would not fall from happiness, as for example if he should lose a child or some piece of property.

<margin>B</margin> There are ten thousand things which, if they turn out contrary to his mind, would take nothing from the presence of the goal. For they say that great things, not just any things, [make the man]. But what among human things is so great that it would not be looked down upon by one who has ascended to the things above <note>original: *ἀναβεβηκότος πρὸς τὰ ἀνωτέρω*; the Platonic ascent of the soul to the Intelligible realm.</note> all these, and no longer hangs upon any of the things below?

<margin>C</margin> Why indeed should he consider misfortunes, however great they may be, to be significant? Such as the loss of kingdoms, or the rule of cities and nations, or the founding or ownership of cities? If he loses these through his own actions, or sees his city razed to the ground, why should he think it a great thing? If he thinks it a great evil, or an evil at all, he would be a ridiculous person, or one who holds false dogmas. He would no longer be held in high esteem if he thought wood and stones—and by Zeus, the deaths of mortals—to be something great. For we say he must hold the dogma that death is better than life with a body.

<margin>D</margin> And if he himself is sacrificed, will he think death is an evil to him because he is placed by the altars? But even if he is not buried, his body will rot entirely, whether above the earth or below it. And if he is buried without great expense and without a name, not being deemed worthy of a high monument, that is merely small-mindedness. But if he is taken captive, there is always a way to go out, if it is not possible to be happy. If his relatives are taken captive—for instance, his daughters—what then? We say, if they died without him seeing any of these things, would he depart with the opinion that such things could not happen to us? He would be absurd not to realize that such fortunes can happen to one's kin.

<margin>E</margin> Or if he does not think that what will happen is a cause for unhappiness, or thinks that while living he is happy, then even when it happens he will know that the nature of the whole is such that it is produced to be borne, or one must endure it.

<margin>F</margin> Many indeed have fared better after becoming captives. The power is in those who are burdened to either stay or leave; if they stay without reason, that is no terrible thing, but if they stay without reason, they should not make others the cause. For he will not be in a bad state because of the folly of others who are his kin, nor will he be disturbed by the misfortunes and distresses of others.

<margin>G</margin> **BUT** when violent pains come upon him, he will bear them as long as he can; if they exceed his strength, they will carry him out. He will not be pitiable in his suffering, but the light within him—like a light in a lantern—will shine while much wind blows outside in a great storm of winds and tempests. But if we should not happen [to be steady]...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the wise man’s happiness is entirely internal and intellectual, remaining untouched by external tragedies such as the loss of family, status, or even physical torture. He uses the striking metaphor of the "inner light" in a lighthouse to describe how the soul's reason remains calm despite the "storms" of bodily experience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "wise man" or "man of integrity" (the spoudaios). Having established that external losses do not destroy happiness, Plotinus now tackles the most difficult challenges: physical torture and the loss of consciousness through illness or sleep.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> ...if pain should be so prolonged and intense that it even kills the animal part of us <note>original: "θηρίον" (beast/animal part); referring to the biological body</note>, what shall we say? Truly, if it is prolonged, he will deliberate on what must be done; for in these circumstances, his power of self-determination <term>original: "αὐτεξούσιον" (autexousion); the innate freedom of the soul to choose its own state</term> is not taken away. One must realize that things do not appear to the man of high character in the same way they appear to others. <margin>B</margin> None of these things reach the inner depths of the man: neither hardships, nor tortures, nor pains, even when others are overwhelmed by such distress. To feel otherwise would be a weakness of our soul. This is clearly shown when we think it is better for certain things to be hidden from us, or if we think it would be better for imminent death to remain unknown. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, when we wish for the misfortunes of our loved ones to be hidden from us, we are looking out for ourselves so that we do not suffer the distress. This is entirely a fault of our own frailty, which we ought to push far away; we should not yield to weakness or fear that some trouble might happen.

If someone objects that we are so constructed by nature that we must grieve over the misfortunes of our family, let him understand first that not everyone is affected this way. Secondly, it is the duty of virtue to lead our common natural condition toward that which is better and more honorable, rising above the common opinion of the crowd. <margin>D</margin> It is honorable not to yield to those things which seem terrible to our common nature. A man should not be like a raw, uneducated person, but like a disciplined athlete manfully repelling the blows of fortune. For he knows that while such things are terrifying to our common nature, his own inner character must endure them—not as things that are truly heavy, but as things that are "frightening to children." Did he wish for these things? Perhaps not; but when they happen, he opposes them with virtue, through which the soul is made difficult to move and difficult to make suffer.

But what if he is not following his own mind, being "submerged" <note>original: "βαπτισθεὶς" (baptized/submerged); a metaphor for being overwhelmed</note> by illness, or by the arts of magicians? <margin>E</margin> If we grant that he retains his own virtue in such a state, even as one who is sleeping, what prevents him from being happy? For we do not take away his happiness even in his sleep, nor do we judge that time as a separate moment that prevents us from calling his whole life happy. But if they say such a man is no longer a "man of integrity" <note>original: "σπουδαῖον" (spoudaios); the sage or virtuous person</note>, then they are no longer talking about the man of integrity at all. We, however, assuming he is a man of integrity, are asking whether he is always happy insofar as he is such a man. <margin>F</margin> "But if he possesses virtue," they say, "yet does not sense it and does not act according to virtue, how can he be happy?" 

Well, if a man does not sense that he is healthy, he is nonetheless healthy; if he does not notice he is beautiful, he is no less beautiful. If a sage does not sense he is wise, will he be any less wise? <margin>G</margin> But perhaps someone will say that wisdom requires self-awareness and conscious attention <gloss>original: "παρακολουθεῖν" (parakolouthein); to follow along with or be conscious of one's own states</gloss>, for they claim happiness consists in the active exercise of wisdom. If wisdom and its actions were something brought in from the outside, this argument might have some weight. But if the substance of wisdom is found in our very essence—or rather, is our essence—and this essence does not perish in the sleeper or in the one who is said to be unaware of himself, then the activity of that essence continues within him. Such an activity is perpetually awake; surely then also the man of integrity, insofar as he is a man of integrity, acts even if he is asleep or infirm. It will be hidden...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...if the pain is stretched out so vehemently that it even kills the animal part, what shall we say? Certainly, if it is prolonged, he will consult what ought to be done. For here, his free will is not taken away from him. It is necessary to know that things do not appear the same to men who excel in virtue as they appear to others; <margin>B</margin> nor do these individual things reach into the man’s innermost parts: not these other things, nor tortures, nor pains, nor again when others are oppressed by narrow straits. Otherwise, this would be a certain weakness of our soul. This indeed appears clearly when we judge that it would be worthwhile for these things to be hidden from us; similarly, if we should think it better for an imminent death to be hidden from us. Moreover, when we desire the troubles of others to be hidden from us, we are looking out not for them, but for our very selves, lest we be affected by the annoyance. <margin>C</margin> This is entirely the vice of our own imbecility, which we ought to drive far away; nor should we, yielding to imbecility, dread lest any trouble should happen.

If anyone should object that we are so instituted by nature that we grieve at the misfortunes of our household, let him understand first that not everyone is so affected. Second, it is the office of virtue to lead the common condition of nature to that which is better, and to something more honorable beyond the opinion of the common people. It is honorable to by no means concede to those things which seem heavy to our common nature. <margin>D</margin> For it does not befit him to be as if he were unrefined, but like a bridle or a wrestler manfully repelling the blows of fortune. Since he knows that such things are displeasing to our common nature, but must be endured by his own genius—not as if they were truly heavy, but as if they were terrifying to boys. Did he, then, want these things? Perhaps indeed he did not want them; yet when they happen, he opposes virtue to them, through which the soul is not easily changed or made to suffer.

<margin>IX / Happiness [comes from] the superior eye of eternal intelligence, whence he is blessed even if the inferior eye of reason is afflicted by these things.</margin>
<margin>E</margin> BUT when he is overwhelmed by a divine power, or by diseases, or by the arts of magicians, what then shall we say? But if we concede that he retains his own virtue even in that state, as if he were sleeping, what prohibits him from being happy? Since they do not take away his happiness even in sleep, nor do they estimate that time as any moment that prevents them from confessing him to be happy throughout his whole life. But if they deny he is a man of integrity, they are no longer speaking of the man who has been proven. We, however, conceding that he is a man of integrity, ask whether he is always happy insofar as he is a man of integrity. <margin>F</margin> "But if he is endowed with virtue," they say, "yet not sensing it, and not acting according to virtue, how then will he be happy?"

Truly, even if he does not sense himself to be healthy, he will nonetheless be healthy; again, if he does not notice himself to be beautiful, he will be no less beautiful. If, however, he does not sense himself to be wise, will he be any less wise? But perhaps someone will say that for wisdom, it is necessary to have a sense of oneself and an observation of it: for they say happiness is present in the act of wisdom. <margin>G</margin> But if his wisdom and its action were something adventitious <note>Coming from the outside</note>, such a discourse might perhaps be somewhat convincing. But if the substance of wisdom is in a certain essence—indeed, rather, is situated in essence—and this essence itself does not perish in the sleeper, or in him who is denied to be consistent with himself or conscious, then the act of the essence itself is in him; and such an act is perpetually wakeful. Surely then also the man of integrity, insofar as he is a man of integrity, will act, even if he be sleeping or weak. It will be hidden...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the sage's happiness and virtue are essential, internal qualities of the soul that persist even during extreme physical suffering, unconsciousness, or illness. He maintains that while the "animal" body may suffer, the true self remains undisturbed because happiness is an eternal activity of the soul's essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "wise man" (the spoudaios) and his internal state of happiness. Having previously discussed physical suffering, Plotinus now explores why we are not always consciously aware of the high-level intellectual activity that constitutes true happiness.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD I

A
However, an activity of this kind is not the whole of the person, but rather some part of him. This is much like how, when the vegetative activity <note>original: "vegetali actu"; referring to basic biological growth</note> is in full force, the awareness of such action does not pass into the rest of the man through his sensory nature. If we were entirely identical with our vegetative faculty, we would undoubtedly be "acting" whenever it was active. But in truth, we are not that faculty; rather, we are the activity of the thinking intellect itself. Therefore, when the intellect acts, we act.

<margin>
**X**
Why a person’s intellectual activity may be hidden and how it can be noticed.
</margin>
B Perhaps it remains hidden because it does not reach the faculty of perception. For there must be a medium, like a sense-organ, for us to act through regarding these external things. But why does the intellect itself not act? And again, why does the soul, which precedes sensation and awareness, not act? For there must be some action before there is awareness—if indeed "to think" and "to be" are the same thing. Awareness, it seems, only exists and comes into being when the act of intelligence is reflected back; just as when that which acts according to the life of the soul is, as it were, struck back again, like an image in a mirror resting upon a smooth, bright, and calm surface. For just as in such things, when a mirror is present, an image is produced; but when it is absent or not in the right state, the activity which would have produced the image is still present, though the image is absent. So it is with the soul: when that part of us which reflects the images of thought and intellect is in a state of calm, then those images <note>original: "imaginationes"; here meaning mental representations or phantasia</note> are seen within us. D In this way, we recognize—in a manner almost like physical sensation—that the intellect and thought are active, alongside our prior knowledge. But when this "mirror" is disturbed because the harmony of the body is thrown into turmoil, then the thought and the intellect still think without an image, and the act of intellection then takes place without a mental representation <term>original: "phantasia"; the faculty of creating mental images</term>. Therefore, one might consider that intellection is accompanied by a mental image, even though the act of intelligence is by no means the same as the image itself. Indeed, one will find E many noble contemplations and actions even in those who are awake, in which we do not notice ourselves contemplating or acting. For it is not necessary for one who reads to realize that he is reading, especially when he reads with the greatest attention; nor does he who acts bravely necessarily know that he is acting bravely. There are many other similar cases, so much so that conscious awareness seems to make the actions they accompany weaker. When actions are alone, they are then pure, and they seem to possess more activity and life. Now, when men of high character live in that state, it is certain that they live more fully; for at that time, life is not scattered into the senses, but is gathered into itself in a constant flow.

<margin>
**XI**
The happy man lives most of all, and why.
</margin>
But if any should object that such a man is not even alive, we shall surely affirm that he is indeed living. Their happiness is hidden from such objectors, just as his life is hidden. But if they will not believe it, we shall think it fair that they first grant he is alive and a man of integrity, and on that basis inquire whether he is happy. They should not first strip him of life and then ask if he lives well; nor should they remove the man from the equation and then deliberate on the happiness of a man; and finally, they must concede that the man of integrity has turned his attention toward his innermost self.

<column-break/>

This activity of the soul is not the whole of him, but a part of him, just as when the <margin>Plant-like</margin> natural activity is acting, the perception of such activity does not reach the rest of the man through the sensory part. If we were our <margin>Plant-like</margin> <gloss>Plant-like</gloss> natural part, then we would be acting [when it acts], but I say we are not; rather, we are the activity of the thinking part, so that when that part acts, we "ourselves" act.

It is hidden, perhaps, because it does not act through the senses—as if through a medium—concerning external sensible things. For it seems to <gloss>act</gloss> act concerning all things, but there is no one who [externally] sees it acting, nor the soul acting concerning them, whether in sensation or in general perception. If there is some activity prior to sensation—since to think and to be are the same—then perception exists and comes into being when the thought is reflected back, and when that which acts according to the life of the soul is reflected back as if from a mirror, on a smooth and bright and quiet surface. Therefore, just as in such cases the image is produced when the mirror is present, but when it is not present or not in such a state, the activity from which the image would have come is still there; so too regarding the soul: when that part in us is at rest, the images of the mind and the intellect are reflected. These are seen and known as if by the senses, along with the prior knowledge that the intellect and the mind are active. But when this is confounded because the harmony of the body is disturbed, the mind and the intellect still think, but the thinking is then without a mental image <term>original: "phantasia"</term>. Thus, one might think that thinking occurs with a mental image, even though the thinking is not itself a mental image. One might find many beautiful activities, contemplations, and deeds among those who are awake, where we do not have a conscious following-along <term>original: "parakolouthein"; a consciousness that monitors one's own actions</term> while we contemplate or act. For it is not necessary for the one who reads to <gloss>consciously follow</gloss> <gloss>be aware</gloss> be aware that he is reading. <margin>Awareness</margin> And truly, the one acting bravely is not aware that he is acting bravely, or that he acts according to courage. There are a myriad of other cases, so that conscious awareness risks making the very activities it follows along with more dim. But when they are alone, they are pure, acting more and living more. And indeed, when the men of high character are in such a state, their life is more intense, not being poured out into sensation, but gathered together in the same place within itself.

If you say that such a person does not even live, we say that he does live; but his happiness is hidden from them, just as his life is. If they are not persuaded, we shall ask them to assume he is living and a man of integrity, and then seek to know if he is happy. They should not diminish his life and then seek to know if life is present, nor should they take away the man and then seek the happiness of the man. Nor should they grant he is a man of integrity and then [fail to see him] turned toward the inner...

<summary>Plotinus argues that true happiness depends on the activity of the Intellect, which continues even when we are not consciously aware of it. He uses the famous "mirror" analogy to explain that consciousness is merely the reflection of this deeper intellectual life on the faculty of imagination.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "good man" (the spoudaios). Having established that true intellectual activity can occur without our conscious awareness, he now argues that this internal state of "happiness" is entirely independent of external circumstances, physical pleasure, or even intense bodily pain.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

They must not seek him in external actions, **A**
nor assume his will is placed in things outside himself.
Otherwise, there would be no substance to his happiness if
his will were fixed on external things, and if you claimed the
good man seeks such things. He certainly wishes
that all people live well, and that no evils
befall anyone. However, even if these things do not happen,
he will nonetheless be happy. If someone should say that he
is deceived and wanders from reason if he wishes for such
things (since it is impossible for evils not to exist), then **B**
that person will certainly agree with us when we turn his
will toward his innermost self.

<margin>
**XII**
The happy man does not need any external pleasures.
</margin>
But if you require pleasure in this man’s life, surely you
will not demand the pleasures of the intemperate, or
bodily pleasures at all. For it is impossible that these
be present without contaminating happiness.
Nor, on the other hand, does he require the restless
motions of joy. For why would he demand such things?
Rather, he requires only those pleasures which necessarily
accompany the presence of the Good itself. These are **C**
not placed in motion, nor are they newly arrived. For
the Good is already present; he is present to himself, and
his pleasure and serenity remain constant. The good man is
always serene; his state is quiet and his disposition is
self-sufficient. No matter what "evils" (as they are called)
occur, none can disturb him, provided he is truly a good man.
If someone seeks another kind of pleasure in the life of the
good man, they are no longer seeking the life of the good man.

<margin>
**XIII**
Eternal action remains even if external reasons are hindered.
</margin>
Nor will his actions be entirely hindered by the force of
fortune; rather, different actions will occur under **D**
different fortunes. Yet all are similarly honorable, and
perhaps those are then most honorable which are properly
composed within difficult circumstances. Those actions
situated in contemplation <note>original: "θεωρίας"; the act of intellectual vision or study</note>, if they concern individual matters,
will perhaps be such that, having sought and considered
them, he will prefer them. But the greatest part of his
learning is always ready at his hand—even more so
if he is placed inside the Bull of Phalaris <note>A legendary torture device; a hollow bronze statue of a bull in which victims were roasted alive. Philosophers used it as the ultimate test of the sage's happiness.</note>. It is said
foolishly that such a thing is pleasant; that is stated
twice over in vain. For that which is spoken of there
is the part that is situated in torture. **E**
But the part that feels pain is one thing; the part that dwells
with itself is another. Insofar as it necessarily dwells
with itself, it will never fall away from the contemplation
of the total Good.

<margin>
**XIIII**
Why man, as a happy being, is not hindered by the external.
</margin>
The fact that a man—especially the good man—is not
some composite of soul and body is witnessed by his
very separation from the body and his contempt for those
things called "bodily goods." It would be ridiculous if
someone said that happiness also belongs to that part **F**
of us which is the animal. Since happiness is the "good life,"
which indeed consists in the soul itself, and since this
happy life is an activity—and yet not an activity of the
<margin>* Vegetative</margin>
whole soul, not even the vegetative <note>original: "φυτικής"; the lowest part of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition</note> part, so that it
does not even touch the body. For happiness is not
situated in the magnitude or healthy state of the body,
nor again in the sharpness of the senses. Indeed, an
excess of bodily and sensory prosperity weighs down the
soul and twists the man toward itself. On the contrary,
it is fitting to use a certain compensation and diversion **G**
to lead one toward the best, and in a way to "thin out" the
body, so that it may appear that the man himself is different
from external things. Let the man among us be both
beautiful and great and wealthy, and a ruler of all men—
since he is considered a citizen of this region—but let

**G**

<summary>Plotinus argues that the happiness of the wise man (the spoudaios) is an internal state of contemplation that remains undisturbed by external misfortune or physical torture. He emphasizes that the "true man" is the intellectual soul, which must distance itself from the body's sensations and "vegetative" needs.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, Happiness, Contemplation, Bull of Phalaris, Soul-Body Dualism, Stoicism, Neoplatonism, Ethics, Eudaimonia</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument that the "happy man" (the *spoudaios* or sage) possesses a happiness that is entirely internal. He now addresses how this man interacts with his own body, the experience of pain, and the concept of "natural advantages" like health and beauty.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS I.

...if anyone is deceived by these external things, they are to be pitied. Regarding the wise man himself, perhaps such misfortunes would not even occur from the start; but if they do appear, he will diminish them through the care he takes for his own soul. He will wear down luxury and the gifts of the body through a deliberate negligence. He will lay aside positions of power. Furthermore, while he will care for his bodily health, he does not wish to be entirely inexperienced with illness, nor similarly with pain. Indeed, if they have not yet happened, he will wish to learn of them in his youth; but in old age, he wishes to be disturbed neither by these nor by pleasures, nor by any bodily thing, whether pleasant or troublesome. He does this so that he is not forced to incline his attention toward the body. When placed in the midst of pains, he will oppose them with the virtue that is present and sufficient within him for such things. He will so prepare himself that he does not consider himself "more happy" in times of pleasure, health, and rest from labor, nor "less happy" in their opposites. For since the former do not increase his true happiness, certainly their opposites cannot diminish it.

<margin>
**XV**
Nothing can be added to or taken away from a happy man.
</margin>

But if there were two wise men—one of whom possessed everything judged to be in accordance with nature <note>original: *naturae consentanea*. These are "preferred indifferents" in ancient philosophy, like health or wealth, which are natural to want but not essential for virtue.</note>, and the other the opposite—should we say they are equally happy? We shall certainly say so, provided they are equally wise. For if the one has a beautiful body and possesses all other things that contribute neither to wisdom, nor to virtue, nor to the contemplation of the Highest, nor to the best life—I do not see what extra weight he gains from them. Indeed, he who possesses such things will not boast, as if he were happier than the man who lacks them. Furthermore, an abundance of instruments does not help a flute-player <note>original: *tibicinis*. Plotinus uses the analogy of a musician to show that while you need an instrument to play, having "more" or "prettier" instruments doesn't make you a better master of the art itself.</note> achieve his goal. However, we, out of our own weakness, consider such a man happy by judging those things to be "heavy" or "horrible" which the happy man himself does not judge so. Otherwise, he would not yet be wise or happy, unless he first chased away all such fallacies of the imagination and, having become entirely transformed, trusted in himself as one who can suffer no true evil. In this way, he will live without fear in all circumstances. If he fears anything, he is not yet perfect in virtue, but seems to possess only half of it. As for sudden fears that occur before one can judge them, if they happen while the wise man is intent on other things, he will try to repel them. Feeling the part of himself that is joined to the body—like a child moved by pain—he will restrain it with either threats or reason. I say "threats" without him being personally disturbed, just as a child might be immediately restrained by the mere sight of a respected elder. Yet, such a man will not be lacking in friendship or gratitude. Since he attributes the same things to his friends as he does to himself, he will be a friend above all, and will live with a shared mind.

<margin>
**XVI**
A wise man, happy in his own happiness, is not crushed by adversity nor elated by riches, but content with the circumstances of the time, he governs without disturbance.
</margin>

But if someone does not place the good man in this exalted state of mind, but subjects him to the blows of fortune and fears these blows on his behalf, then they are certainly not bringing forward the "good man" as we believe he ought to be. Instead, they present a mediocre man, a mixture of good and evil, leading a "middle life" composed of both. This middle state is neither easy to find, nor, if it were found, would it be worthy of the name "happy." For such a man would have nothing great within him, neither in the excellence of wisdom nor the purity of the Good. Therefore, happiness is not found in a "mixed" life <note>original: *vita coniuncta*. A life tied too closely to the union of soul and body.</note>. For Plato rightly judged that the Highest Good must be sought from above.

# BOOK FOUR.

<note>The top of this page contains the concluding passage of Ennead I.4 in both the original Greek and the Latin translation by Marsilio Ficino.</note>

And looking toward that <note>The "Good" or the "End"</note> most of all, there should be zeal and happiness, striving to be made like it and to live according to it. This alone, therefore, must be held toward the perfection of the end itself. As for other things, the wise man will consider them merely like changes of place; he receives no increase in happiness from his location, but regards them as other things surrounding him from the outside. It is as if they were arranged either here and in this way, or there and differently. He grants to the body whatever necessity demands and his ability allows, but he himself lives as another <note>He identifies with his soul, not his body</note>, not hindered from letting go of that which is joined to him. Nature too will grant this in its own time, and he will let go of it easily; he can also consult his own judgment regarding this departure. For this reason, his duties will partly lead toward happiness, and partly be undertaken neither for the sake of the end nor for himself, but only for the sake of that which is joined to him <note>The body</note>. He will care for it as long as he can and endure it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Just as a musician <note>original: *musicus*</note> cares for his lyre as long as he is able to use it; but when it becomes useless, he either changes it or gives up the use of the lyre altogether, abstaining from actions involving the lyre, because he has another duty to perform without it. Thus, he may look down upon the lyre lying nearby, singing himself without the service of the instrument. Yet the instrument was not granted to him in vain from the beginning, since he has already used it often.

### MARSILIO FICINO ON BOOK V: WHETHER HAPPINESS INCREASES WITH TIME.

->What eternity is; what happiness is; how all minds enjoy eternity forever, but rational natures <note>Such as human souls</note> only sometimes; and while these enjoy it, they act with stability.<-

<margin>I</margin> Above being itself, the Platonists place the principle of being itself; and they name it the **One** and the **Good**. Within being, however, they contemplate the first essence, the first life, and the first mind. We can call that life both eternal and blessed, but for different reasons. For the first life is the perpetual act of essence. Therefore, insofar as such an act of essence is present to itself entirely at once, and all essence is present to it simultaneously over and above each other, it is called "eternal life," or rather **Eternity** itself. But insofar as the same act, as if departing from its source, is reflected toward external things, it is called **Mind**; and being thus most closely joined to the Good, it is deservedly called "blessed life," or rather **Happiness**. Because all minds enjoy this mind, this eternity, and this happiness directly, they do so forever. Rational natures <note>Humans</note>, however, because they possess a following rank, do indeed possess eternity and happiness of this kind, but (to speak in the manner of Plato, or rather Plotinus) they do not enjoy them eternally. Thus, they are happy at some times, and at other times they are not happy. Nevertheless, while they are happy, they no longer act changeably, but act with stability. Since the first eternity and happiness are in reality one, rational natures follow eternity just as they follow happiness. Since the most proper characteristic of eternity is stability, for as long as they possess eternity as happy beings, they act immovably, and embrace all actions at once in a single, as it were, intuition. To speak according to my own views: the soul cannot enjoy eternity unless it enjoys it eternally. Therefore, as soon as it reaches the state of eternity, being placed there outside of time and motion, it acts so stably that it can no longer be moved from there in any part. Our opinion having been set down once, let us follow the Plotinian interpretation.

->Rational nature lives happily in the sublime spheres for much longer ages than it lives unhappily around the earth.<-

<margin>II</margin> Accordingly, they judge that the souls of humans living on earth, or in the thicker air, are for the most part not happy but miserable, situated as they are in a place of sin, punishment, and <term>purgatory</term> <note>Ficino uses the term *purgatory* here to describe the Platonic idea of the soul being purified through various lives or states before ascending.</note>. But then all will be blessed when they have ascended from here to the pure <term>spheres</term> <note>The celestial layers of the cosmos</note> with a pure body, or to the more sublime air, or the ether and the heavens. Now, just as the power and amplitude in the higher spheres are greater than in the lower ones, and the virtue of the soul living there is more excellent than here, so they think that souls live there for a much longer time than here. Therefore, they are happy for a much longer duration than they are miserable, which **Plato** testifies in the *Phaedo* when he discusses the long-lived, and which **Olympiodorus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and commentator</note> confirmed. Added to this is the fact that, just as the mind which lifts one to sublime things is more powerful than the animal imagination which tends toward the opposite, so the life of the rational soul through the mind, raised to such sublime things, is longer than its life through the imagination directed to the lower...

### COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

...bent downwards. Furthermore, the **Mind** <note>Latin: *mens*; in Ficino's philosophy, this refers to the highest, intuitive part of the soul that mirrors the Divine Intellect</note> consists solely of identity and stability; therefore, it always acts steadily in the same way. **Imagination**, by contrast, is always changing and fashioning diverse images. The **Rational faculty**, however, is composed of all these elements: for within it, stability and motion concur with diversity. For this reason, it operates both changeably and stably; it revolves through various things and then collects them together again.

Insofar as the nature of identity and stability is more excellent than the nature of diversity and motion, the soul lives longer in eternity when it has turned toward it, than it lives in time when it has fallen into time. But since this is fulfilled less in this life, it is necessarily compensated for in the next. Certainly, they believe that just as the intellect in no way declines toward the body, while the life entirely devoid of intelligence declines completely, so too the intellectual soul, in that part which is intellectual, is never inclined toward the body; but in that part which is not possessed of natural intelligence, it is turned toward bodies. 

Likewise, if it is true that the rational soul is the mean between eternal and temporal things, and the **indissoluble bond of the universe** <note>A central theme in Ficino’s *Platonic Theology*: the soul as the "center of nature" connecting the physical and spiritual realms</note> (as we often prove in our *Theology*), they wish it to follow that it never departs entirely from either side. Instead, holding both at once, it reconciles both within itself in a fitting proportion. Wherefore, through the intellect, it is always awake in eternity; through the life-giving power, it always acts in some way in time; through the imagination, which is close to the divisible nature, it dwells mostly in time; through reason, being close to the mind, it lives as much as possible in eternity; through the other imagination immediately subject to reason, it alternates equally between the two, and offers us images now of eternal things, now of temporal things. 

Indeed, as long as reason leads a happy life, so too does the imagination; and if it occasionally brings forth images of temporal things happily, it nonetheless brings those images into the open. Finally (to speak briefly), if out of the entire circuit of the world—which some think is completed in thirty-six thousand years <note>The "Platonic Year" or Great Year, the time it takes for all heavenly bodies to return to the same relative positions</note>—the soul dwells here as an exile for perhaps three hundred years (though at different times), they think it conversely dwells in its ancestral seats for at least three thousand years. They believe those souls dwell here for a shorter time and there for a longer time who, either from the beginning were suited to the more excellent stars and commended to **daemons** <note>Guardian spirits or intermediaries between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>, or who, being fortified by a more effective virtue, looked down upon fleeting things and cherished the eternal. 

They believe that not only human souls, but also many daemonic souls—both those of the air and those of the ether—change bodies and levels of happiness. However, they believe those daemons descend only as far as our thick air, while our souls descend all the way into the burning body; both types of souls lead a happier and much longer life in the higher regions. But more on these matters elsewhere.

->How the rational nature is formed by its own mind, and how the mind is formed by the common mind.<-

III. It is also possible that this reason, in this life, by segregating itself from matter and the lowest imagination more than others and recalling itself to the mind, may in some way taste the happiness of that other life. And indeed, insofar as it possesses that happiness, as something already formed by the intellect, it enjoys it in an eternal way—that is, in a stable act, entirely whole and simultaneous. We prove that this can and should happen sometimes by tracing the matter back to its deeper roots. 

When two different things flow together into one, it is because of a cause: such as solid dimensions on both sides from the beginning, or dimensions of any kind, or opposing forms on both sides. Iron is melted into fire, even if both the solidity of the iron and its coldness seem to hinder it; and it is so melted that the iron, now formed by the fire, acts as fire rather than as iron—that is, it glows, shines, heats, and illuminates. Air is ignited more easily, where neither density nor such great diversity of qualities hinders it further. This same air becomes bright under the sun even more easily, since no dimension in the light retards their union. Most easily and closely of all is a naturally prepared body formed by the soul, and through it, the body now acts as a living thing. 

Finally, the soul is formed by the mind most easily and joined most tightly. For since it is the property of form to shape and perfect, and the property of matter to bind itself to its own form, surely the more excellent the form is, the more easily and closely it shapes and binds the subject accommodated to it. Therefore, the soul is formed more absolutely by the mind than the body is by the soul—inasmuch as the mind is a more perfect form than the soul, and the soul is a more perfect subject than the body. Since, therefore, the divine mind is everywhere, and the essence of the rational soul is perpetually created and preserved by a flow from there, and its essence is thus perpetually turned toward the mind by instinct, nothing prevents the soul, so suspended and so turned, from being always formed from that source. 

Since this formation is effected both by the essential instinct of the soul and by the essential act of the mind, it is rightly an essential formation on all sides. Just as in the mind, essence is the same as intellect, and being is the same as understanding, so in the soul, the intellect becomes the same as its essence, and understanding becomes the same as being. This is especially true because the divine intellect itself forms the soul by the very act of intelligence. To be formed by the act of understanding is nothing other than to understand—just as to be formed by the act of seeing is to see. Or at least, just as in the air, becoming bright and shining happen entirely at once, and in the body under the soul, becoming alive and living happen at once, so in the soul, by essential reason, becoming intellectual and understanding happen at once. For the soul to be perfectly formed by the intellect is nothing other than to exist under the form of the intellect and to act under the act of the intellect. In the intellect itself, its form and its act are the same. Therefore, as soon as the soul exists under the form of the intellect, it already acts under the act of the intellect and thoroughly understands. 

Hence that saying of **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who emphasized ritual and theurgy</note>, spoken according to the mind of the **Egyptians**: "For the intellectual soul, to be is to understand God and divine things." For just as we perceive temporal things through a certain temporary act, so we diligently contemplate eternal things through an eternal and essential act, since both exist eternally. So says he. But enough and more than enough has been said regarding the intellect.

->The rational nature both can and should be formed at some time by the mind, and then it possesses all things in a single act.<-

IIII. The same reasons indicate to us that the rational faculty can also be formed by the intellect in almost the same way at some time, especially since it exists in the same essence as the intellect. We have shown elsewhere that it *should* be so, lest natural appetite be in vain. Since in every rational nature there is an everlasting appetite for intelligence, the Platonists maintain that everyone eventually reaches happy intelligence. And if one departs from there, one can return again; and in that age, as long as one acts as a mind and lives blessedly, one imitates the eternal intelligence of the mind—so that all things exist together in a single act, whether one tastes this in this life or rather feeds upon it in the next. Indeed, the intellect itself gazes upon the entire circuit of things all at once, just as the eye gazes upon a certain sphere...

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's hierarchy, noting that while the Mind is eternal and stable, Reason bridges the gap between eternity and time. He argues that the soul can achieve a state of "essential formation" where its very being becomes synonymous with understanding divine truths.</summary>

Specifically, it concludes a comparison between discursive reason and intuitive intellect before moving into a systematic summary of Ennead I, Book 4 (though the header identifies it as Book V), which investigates whether the duration of time adds anything to the quality of true happiness.</meta>

<page-num>41</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK V, ENNEAD I.</header>

...constructs a certain whole all at once. **Reason**, however, not yet turned toward the **intellect** <note>Ficino distinguishes between *ratio* (discursive, step-by-step reasoning) and *intellectus* (the higher, intuitive grasp of truth)</note>, approaches things part by part, one after the other. It is like the touch of a blind man’s finger which, by gradually feeling a sphere, eventually judges it to be a sphere, whereas the eye judged it instantly. Finally, we believe that **reason**, once it has been turned [toward the intellect], embraces all things together with the mind, just as the hand of a seeing man, guided by the eye, grasps a small sphere with his whole fist and immediately perceives its true nature. Indeed, the soul in a state of heightened affection <note>referring to a state of spiritual or emotional intensity</note> knows and possesses as much in a single moment as another does over a long period. Similar to this is that prophetic saying: *A single day in your courts, Lord, is better than a thousand years of others.* <note>original: *Dies vna in atriis tuis Domine plus, quam mille aliorum anni*; a reference to Psalm 84:10.</note>

## Who is blessed: and how happiness consists in a certain possession of the present good: to which the prolongation of time adds nothing by reason of the past or future, but only by reason of the present.

*We consider him to be happy in the highest degree who already beholds all true things and possesses all goods. But he sees all true things together in a single form of truth, that is, in the **Divine Mind**; likewise, he enjoys all goods in a single fountain of goods, that is, in **the Good** itself. Since, therefore, there is one form and one fountain through which he beholds the true and draws out the good, he perceives both with a single gaze—all true things joined together—and similarly drinks in all goods with a single draught. Whoever has not yet reached this point is not yet happy in the highest degree. But he who has reached this point can no longer be happier simply because of the length of time.*

*But suppose such happiness lasts for a year in one soul, and only for a day in another: is the former more blessed than the latter? Certainly not because of that specific day on which the latter is blessed, for each possesses all of his own things equally. As for the remaining days, the one is not "happier" than the other; rather, one is blessed for a time, while the other is no longer blessed. Let us then compare a year's happiness and a day's happiness. Is the year judged to be greater or "more" of a happiness than the day? It is certainly of longer duration or longer in time, but it is not greater in degree. Just as a certain heat can last for a year, yet it is not more fervent in degree than a day’s heat. But is a year's happiness not more desirable to us than a day's? It is, beyond a doubt. But that length of time is not more desirable for its own sake—just as no one would choose a year-long fever over a brief one. Rather, it is desired for the sake of the happiness itself. For the good of anything seems to pertain to its quality rather than its quantity.*

*Now, the soul desires quantity for the sake of the good; if quantity is joined with the good, the soul desires it more as the quantity increases; if joined with evil, the more there is, the less the soul chooses it. Why, then, do we think a life of happiness for a year is to be chosen over one of a day? Certainly not because of the temporal succession itself, which becomes longer in a year; for even in a day's happiness, we do not prefer a whole day over an hour because of the mere succession of moments. For it is the **present** itself within happiness that we deeply desire. This is what we seek: to be "one," while we seek to be happy. We primarily wish for this same "present" to be realized and to remain entirely, which is the unique property of **eternity**, in the enjoyment of which we are blessed. We enjoy this continually through the intellect, and sometimes through reason when it has been shaped by the intellect. But if we distrust that this "present" can remain firmly the same for us, we then choose as a second best that another moment of the present, and then another and another, should succeed it—always directing our affection and gaze toward the "present" itself rather than toward the succession. For in succession there is always some mixture of privation and evil. This shows us that as long as we live in this motion, we cannot be truly blessed, although insofar as we draw near to eternity, we may taste something of beatitude. Plotinus deals with this in the ten questions of this book.*

### Question one.

*Whether happiness is increased by time? He concludes that happiness consists in a certain affection or disposition of life through which someone is actually in a blessed state. This state is present, and the memory of the past adds nothing to it.*

### Question two.

*Since every man desires to live forever: whether attaining this perpetual perseverance is the chief happiness. He concludes that happiness is not increased by this perpetual succession; otherwise, time, rather than virtue, would measure happiness. Nor would happiness ever be absolute, even among the gods, because it would always be increasing in this way. He confirms the same: because natural appetite properly desires only what it can actually attain, and it attains only what is present, whenever it attains it. Therefore, it does not desire what is not, but only what is. Only the present exists; the past is no longer, and the future is not yet. Therefore, it desires only the present, and prefers that this very present be fixed deeply and remain the same, rather than having another succeed it.*

### Question three.

*Whether one who has contemplated longer is happier? He concludes that if he saw the same things and with the same clarity, he has gained nothing in happiness by the length of time; if, however, he eventually knew more things and knew them better, he was not happy before, but only then.*

### Question four.

*Whether a longer-lasting pleasure increases happiness. He concludes that if "pleasure" here signifies a certain motion or act distinct from the act of intelligence itself, it is not to be counted as part of happiness. But if it signifies the very act of intelligence, free from all hindrance, and thus unhampered, absolute, and pleasing to us, then the soul is happy only when the intelligence is such, and time brings nothing greater to it—especially since it is now in eternity rather than in time. Also, the motion of pleasure is desired only because of what is present within it.*

### Question five.

*Whether one who is happy throughout his whole life is happier than one who is happy only for a part of life. He concludes that if they are compared according to the same part of life, they are equally happy; if according to different parts, one is blessed and the other is not.*

### Question six.

<sig>d 5</sig> <note>This is a "signature mark" used by early printers to keep the folded sheets of a book in the correct order.</note>
