<meta>This page continues the commentary by Marsilio Ficino on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically focusing on the relationship between happiness (felicity) and time. Ficino is exploring why the duration of time does not increase the "amount" of happiness in the same way it seems to increase the weight of misery.</meta>

<page-num>42</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

*Since a miserable person seems to become more miserable over a longer period of time, why shouldn't a happy person become happier for the same reason? He <note>Ficino is referring to Plotinus</note> concludes that evil happens to a subject that is changeable, liable to suffering, and weak, and thus it continues to infect that subject more and more. If the subject always remained exactly the same and no greater harm occurred, the evil would only be judged by its present state. However, if the subject persists in such narrow distress that the evil within it increases, then the misery is judged to be heavier—not so much because the time is longer, but because a more massive degree of evil has been added. Highest happiness, however, possesses a certain limit <note>original: "terminum"; here meaning a peak or a state of completion</note>, which is to say, the highest degree in the Good. Likewise, it always possesses that same limit—namely the summit itself—neither greater nor lesser than it was at first or for as long as the happiness lasts; otherwise, it would not be the "highest" happiness. Finally, the state of evil exists in time and is subject to time, where diversity occurs; but happiness exists in Being <note>original: "ens"</note> and in an eternal subject, to which identity and stability properly belong. That eternal state also belongs to the rational part of the soul once it has been made happy; otherwise, it would neither be sufficiently happy nor live securely if it thought it might one day depart from that state.*

### Question Seven.

*Since in time we count the past and the future together with the present, and thus call it a "longer" space of time, why do we not do the same regarding happiness? He concludes that it is permissible for us to count one thing with another across the length of time, because the very nature of time consists in a certain number and flux. Even things that no longer exist, but passed away long ago, are counted. Likewise, in every flux, "being" is joined, as it were, with "non-being"; for the present moment, which is in some way called "being," falls in the middle between the past (which is no longer) and the future (which is not yet). He denies, however, that this happens in the nature of happiness itself, since its essence consists in a present life and a stable act of eternity, which is already perceived as a whole. Otherwise, if it still ran through a certain motion and time, it would not yet be a perfected habit <note>original: "habitus"; a settled and permanent state of character or soul</note>, and the soul would not yet have reached its goal. Therefore, since the essence of happiness includes the "present" itself and a state of stability, it excludes all temporal calculation far from itself. Now, since eternity is the primary essence and the very life of Being itself—whether it is in the Primary Mind <note>referring to the Divine Intellect</note> or already communicated to some other mind—it admits nothing of "non-being" in any way; it thus utterly expels temporal flux from itself. In eternal life, therefore, there is one stable act; but in time—whether in the soul or then in the body—acts are many, succeeding one another in a certain flux. This is just as in the center of a circle there is a single, stable point, from which various moving points are produced along the length of lines toward the circumference. There, one sees the "one" dispersed into "many," and stability progressed into motion. In short, he concludes that the blessed life is the best life: and this is the life of Being itself. This is true whether it exists by itself in the Universal Mind, or is always communicated from there into each person's own mind, or is eventually communicated again into the rational faculty. Everywhere it preserves its eternal condition, especially since the best degree of life (which serves as the goal) is no longer placed in motion, but in stability. Finally, the "present" of eternity is not the same as the "present" of time; for in time there are many present and individual moments arranged so that one is outside the other. In eternity, however, the "present" is unique, including all the "presents" of time simultaneously—just as the center point in a circle concludes all the points of the lines coming from the circumference, whereas the signs on the circumference are distant from one another.*

### Three Questions.

*The remaining three questions are easily understood and resolved, both on their own and through those discussed above. From all of them, it is finally gathered that the perfectly blessed life is a life not occupied with exterior actions, but*

->collected in the mind itself: not gathered from<-
->many thoughts and things, whether<-
->past or present, but into a<-
->wholly present and stable act of its<-
->own mind: an act, I say, formed by the<-
->Divine Mind, and through the<-
->Divine Mind enjoying<-
->the Good which is<-
->above the mind.<-

<meta>catchword: OF PLOTINUS</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains that true happiness is a stable, eternal state of the mind that does not increase with time, unlike misery which worsens as the subject weakens. He uses the analogy of a circle's center to illustrate how eternity contains all moments of time in a single, unchanging "present."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of happiness (felicity). On the previous page, the commentary established that while misery might feel heavier over time because it weighs down a changing, weak subject, true happiness is a state of completion in the "Good" and therefore remains constant. Here, Plotinus himself (through this Greek and Latin parallel text) asks whether the mere duration of time adds anything to the quality of being happy.</meta>

### PLOTINUS ENNEAD ONE, BOOK FIVE.

->On whether happiness increases with time.<-
<note>original Greek: ΠΕΡΙ τοῦ εἰ ἡ εὐδαιμονία ἐπίδοσιν χρόνῳ λαμβάνει. Latin: Utrum beatitudo tempore suscipiat incrementum.</note>

<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Large decorative initial E containing a scene of a seated man in a study, possibly a scholar or philosopher.</image-desc> Does being happy <term>Eudaimonein; the state of flourishing or living well</term> receive an increase from the passage of time, or is happiness always something perceived in the present moment? Certainly, we do not believe that the *memory* of being happy constitutes happiness itself; if it were so, happiness would exist in having been happy once, but it would not be a current reality. Nor does the activity of life <note>original: ἡ ἐνέργεια τῆς ζωῆς</note> exist in the past.

<margin>B</margin> If, on the other hand, someone says that to live and to act is a matter of desire, and that happiness is rather the attainment of each thing desired: first, in this view, tomorrow's happiness would be greater than today's, and the next day's greater still, and happiness would no longer be measured by virtue <margin>* being happy</margin> <note>original: εὐδαιμονεῖν</note>. Furthermore, the gods would then become "happier" as time went on, and their state would never be a finished or perfect end. Besides, when the will chooses <margin>* to be</margin> <note>original: τὸ εἶναι</note> a certain state, it has already captured the "present"; it does not seek a "present" that is yet to come. The search for happiness—which is the longing for the "to be" of life—ceases when that life is present to the person. If "to be" is found in the "now," then seeking a future or a sequence of moments is merely seeking to receive more and more, not the past, but a continuous present. It is not a matter of how long the whole duration is, but that the state of "being" must be here, now; to be is to be now.

<margin>D</margin> What then shall we say of the man who has been happy for a longer time? If someone looks at the same object with his eyes for a longer period, does he see it more accurately? The length of time adds nothing to the sight unless he sees it better; if he sees the same thing equally throughout, does the one who watches for a long time gain more than the one who looked just once?

<margin>E</margin> One might say that duration is an "infiniteness," but it is not logical to count happiness as a numerical sum. We do not say an activity is greater because of its length, for it is the same activity as the one that just happened <margin>* in the same way</margin>. Pleasure <margin>* in the same way</margin> <note>original: ὡσαύτως</note> exists only in the present; what has passed of it has vanished. Why then should someone who has happiness all at once <note>meaning, in its entirety</note> seek it to have an end in time?

<column-break/>

<margin>Question 1.</margin>
<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Large decorative initial Q depicting a man being attacked by a lion or beast.</image-desc> It must be asked whether happiness receives an increase from time, since "to be blessed" is always understood according to the present? Certainly, the remembrance of past happiness has no weight; happiness does not consist in the telling of it, but in a certain disposition. This disposition is placed in the present quality of being, as is the activity of life itself.

<margin>Question 2.</margin>
<margin>B</margin> But if someone should say that because we always desire to live and to act, happiness is rather the attainment of these things, we must respond as follows. First, if this were so, tomorrow's happiness would be greater, and each subsequent day greater than the one before; thus virtue itself would no longer be the measure of happiness. Next, the gods would now be happier than they used to be; there would be no perfect happiness, nor could it ever be perfect. Furthermore, the appetite of the will has already attained something present, and it always strives toward that very present: as long as it exists, it requires to remain in happiness. The appetite for living is a seeking, and it undoubtedly seeks something present; for "to be" is the opposite of "not being" in the present. If it should desire the future and what follows next, it desires what it already has—the "now"—not what has passed, nor truly what is to come, but that which is already here. It seeks existence itself: not an eternal stretching out or a procession, but <margin>D</margin> that what is now present, remains present.

<margin>Question 3.</margin>
What then shall we say of the man who has lived happy for a very long time? And has gazed upon the same spectacle for a great duration? Surely if he saw more clearly over a longer time, the length of time brought him something extra; but if he saw the same thing throughout the whole time, he certainly gains nothing more than the man who looked upon it only once.

<margin>Question 4.</margin>
<margin>E</margin> But someone might say that the other person was delighted for longer. Yet one is not permitted to count this as part of happiness, unless perhaps one defines "pleasure" as the unimpeded activity of the intelligence. For it is here that the person would say what we are seeking. Consequently, a longer pleasure always possesses only the present; for whatever of it is said to be past has already utterly vanished.

<sig>d 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: MOREOVER</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that happiness (eudaimonia) is a complete activity of the soul that exists entirely in the present moment, meaning its value is not increased by how long it lasts. He compares this to sight, noting that looking at a beautiful object for a longer time does not make the vision "more" than the initial perfect glimpse.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into whether the duration of time adds to the quality of happiness (felicity). Plotinus now tests this by comparing happiness to its opposite, misery, and examining the relationship between time and eternity.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD I.

<margin>A</margin> ...but another only for the future? And finally, what if one who was once happy has now ceased to be happy? Are they equally happy? Certainly, a comparison of this kind is not drawn among those who are all happy. Rather, those who are not happy—specifically at the times when they lack happiness—are compared with someone who is happy. If the happy person possesses something "more," they certainly possess it only in the sense that a happy person is compared to unhappy people; it happens that he surpasses others by the reality of his present state.

<margin>Question 6.</margin> <margin>B</margin> WHAT then? Does a miserable person not become more miserable over a longer period of time? And do not all other troublesome things bring a greater calamity over a longer time: such as distress, long-lasting pains, and other things of that kind? If these things increase an evil through time, why does the opposite not also increase happiness? Perhaps regarding pains and distress, it is fair to say that an increase happens over time, as in the case of diseases. For a disease becomes a *habit* <term>habitus; a settled physical or mental disposition</term>, <margin>C</margin> and the body itself is more deeply infected over time. Otherwise, if the disease remained exactly the same and no greater harm were added, even here the present moment would always be the same troublesome thing, unless one were to count the past. You would be looking, evidently, at what has been done and what remains. Thus, even in the "habit" of a miserable person, the evil is increased over a more extended time because the wickedness increases in that which remains, for as long as it remains. Therefore, greater misery seems to arise not from the length of time itself, <margin>D</margin> but rather from the addition of a greater degree of suffering. But this "more" perhaps does not exist all at once; nor should we say there is "more" at all when that which *is not* [the past] is counted alongside that which *is* [the present]. However, the very nature of happiness possesses a certain and always identical limit. Now, if progress comes here from the length of time itself—so that by progressing in virtue, one also progresses in happiness—we do not praise happiness as if it were long-lasting by counting many years, but rather we call it "greater" at that time when it exists more fully.

<margin>Question 7.</margin> <margin>E</margin> BUT why then, if we ought to look only at the present and not count things together, should we not do the same with time that has passed? Why do we count the past together with the present and call it a "longer span of time"? Why then do we not say that happiness is as great as the time is long? For perhaps one might divide blessedness <margin>F</margin> according to the divisions of time itself. For if we measure by the present alone, we make it indivisible. But perhaps it would not be absurd to count time even when it does not yet exist. Indeed, since we compute the number of those things that have passed and are no longer—such as the number of the dead—it would be a mistake if someone called past happiness (which no longer exists) "greater" than the present, as if it were still present. For they would be claiming that blessedness had "happened" to them in the past. But a longer time beyond the present must be said to be nothing other than "not yet being." <margin>G</margin> In every way, an extension of a time interval somehow contrives the *dispersion* of that "one" thing which is in the present. Therefore, time is rightly called the "image of eternity" <note>original: æternitatis imago / εἰκὼν αἰῶνος; a reference to Plato's Timaeus, where time is a moving, changing reflection of the stillness of eternity</note>, desiring to destroy through its own dispersion that which remains eternal. And so, if that which remains is taken away from eternity and becomes...

<column-break/>

...but another for the later time, and another who was happy previously has changed? Do they have an equal share? Or should these comparisons not be made, even if one were to say that all are happy? For one should not be called happy if they are not currently happy. How could they be happy? If one has something "more," they have as much as the happy person has compared to those who are not happy, by which it happens that they have an advantage over them in the present.

WHAT then? Is the miserable person not more miserable in a longer time? And all other difficult things, in a longer time, do they not give a greater calamity? For example, pains and griefs and such things? If, therefore, time increases the evil, why not also the opposite? Or is it enough that it stays the same? Perhaps in the case of grief or pain, it makes sense to say that the persistence of diseases provides a perception of strength, for it becomes a *habit* <note>original: ἕξις / hexis</note>, or the body brings upon itself more evil over time, or at least no less harm. And here, the "present" is always that which is painful, unless we include the past in what is happening and remaining. In the "habit" of misery, the evil is intensified over a longer time, the wickedness increasing by its permanence. Thus, the magnitude [of misery] becomes "more" in a longer time. But "more" itself is equal from its own parts, and one should only speak of "more" by counting that which no longer exists with that which does. For the nature of happiness has a limit and a boundary, and is always the same. But if one also makes progress here over a longer time, so as to be more happy by progressing toward a greater virtue, we do not praise the many-yeared happiness in number, but rather that which has become "more" at the time when it exists more.

BUT why, if we must consider only the present and not count it with what has happened, do we not do the same regarding time? Why do we count the past with the present and speak of "more"? Why do we not measure happiness by however long the time is? Or would we divide happiness according to the divisions of time? And if we do not measure it by the present, we would make it indivisible. <margin>to itself</margin> Or we count time even if it is no longer, since we make a count of things that have happened but are no longer, such as the dead. But it is absurd to count happiness that is no longer existing as "more" than what is present; it would be claiming that not being happy is a property of happiness. A longer time beyond the present is simply that which no longer exists. "More" in respect to time is a certain dispersion of a nature that exists in the present. Therefore, it is reasonably called the "image of eternity," wishing to vanish in its own scattering that which remains in eternity. If it departs from eternity, or if the "remaining" falls away from it, it loses that same...

<meta>catchword: of time (temporis),</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that happiness (eudaimonia) is a complete state of being in the present that does not increase by the mere accumulation of time. He contrasts this with misery or disease, which can feel "greater" over time because they wear down the subject, whereas true happiness is a stable participation in eternity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether duration increases happiness. Plotinus has previously argued that happiness (felicity) is an activity of the soul that exists in the present. Here, he deepens the argument by contrasting the "eternal now" of the soul with the linear "passing time" of the physical world.</meta>

# FOURTH BOOK.

<margin>*, the things preserved</margin>
<margin>A</margin> The *things being preserved <note>original: τα σωζόμενα</note>, how are they in a certain way lost? Or is the whole identifying mark within it; which is not even to be happy? Is it in life, or in reason? It is not in the inquiring; or in itself, but fire, and numerical things are always most eternal in time, or more, in less, no longer, but fire, and the indivisible; or to be timeless, or participating in the honorable intellect, nor time to eternity, nor the temporal through eternity, nor extended indivisible, but the whole must be taken as a whole, if ever you take it by taking, nor the indivisible by time, but by eternity, or life, from many times, but by eternity following all time.

<margin>B</margin> If anyone should say that the memory of past things—remaining in the past—provides something more to those who have been in a state of happiness for a longer time, what would be said of memory? Is it memory of wisdom <note>original: φρονήσεως</note> regarding actions that have happened, so that one might be called wiser, and not contrary to the hypothesis? For does pleasure through memory, as if many things had been done, truly make one happy? And not being satisfied with the present, what more would you have of pleasant or intellectual things? Just as, again, if someone were to remember that yesterday there was a tasty dish, or ten years ago, it is even more ridiculous. Or as for wisdom, it is even more superfluous to have been wise.

<margin>C</margin> If the memory were of beautiful things, how would it not be called good fortune? But it is a sensory impression <note>original: αἰσθητικὴ</note> for those lacking beautiful things in the present, or because they do not have them now, seeking the memory of things that have happened.

<margin>E</margin> **BUT** does the long-lived person perform many beautiful actions, of which the person happy for only a short time is deprived? If he says this, he speaks of the divine <term>daimon; here referring to the guiding spirit or state of happiness</term> entirely. What would come through the experiences of beautiful things? Or does being happy come from many things? He speaks of both times and actions, from things that no longer exist, but from those that have passed. Or is it from one "now"? Or is being happy entirely in the present? For being happy is not measured by the present, if we seek whether being happy in more things is greater. It must be sought whether actions in more things gain an advantage in being happy. First, then, it is possible not to place happiness in actions, and not less, but more than the one who has acted. Since actions do not give the "well-being" from themselves, but the dispositions <term>diatheses; internal states or characters</term> also make the actions beautiful. And the wise man harvests the good and acts, not for the sake of acting, nor from the things that happen, but from what he possesses. Even as the safety of the fatherland—either it is a base thing or for the sake of safety—and that for the safety of the fatherland is pleasant, and other actions are pleasant? Or itself, what then is it that makes one happy now? Pleasure, but...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...saved, insofar as it is preserved in a certain way in eternity <note>original: æternitate</note>: but vanishing if it becomes entirely within time. If therefore happiness consists in the good life: surely the good life itself must be placed in existing life or in the being itself. For this is the best; it is not to be numbered by time, but to be judged by eternity. That indeed is neither more nor less: nor does it consist in any length, but in that which is itself, and indivisible, and exists beyond time. Wherefore neither existing
<margin>B</margin> things from non-existence can be joined into one, nor time to eternity, nor that which is sempiternal in time to eternity, nor can the indivisible be stretched into different parts; rather, if you ever grasp it, the whole must be grasped. When, I say, you grasp it, you grasp not an individual part belonging to time, but the life of eternity—not heaped up from many times, but all at once from the universal age.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Question 8.</margin> **IF ANYONE** however says that the memory of the past, remaining in the present, brings something more to that man who has lived a longer time in bliss: he must be asked what is meant by that memory? For either the memory of wisdom already past is signified here: for which reason he would call this man wiser, and his proposition would not hold; or it is the memory of pleasure, just as if one were blessed by many delights. But he would not be content with present joy.
<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, what iucundity <note>delight or pleasantness</note> does the memory of past pleasure bring? As if someone remembered he had tasted a side-dish <note>original: oblonium, likely obsonium</note> with pleasure yesterday: and if it were ten years ago, he would be even more to be laughed at. Similarly also if he remembered that he possessed wisdom in the year past.

<margin>Question 9.</margin> **BUT IF** the record of good and honest things is what is meant, why should it not contribute something? Yet that is the mark of a man lacking good or honest things in the present; and because he does not have them now, he seeks the memory of those things which have passed away.
<margin>E</margin> <margin>Question 10.</margin> **BUT** a long time provides the occasion for many and famous actions: of which he who has lived happily for a short time will be deprived. To this it must certainly be said that a man is not happy because of many and famous actions. Otherwise, whoever says happiness must be accumulated from many times as well as actions, has heaped up happiness from things which are no longer, but are finished, and from some single present moment. Therefore, we have placed blessedness in the present
<margin>F</margin> moment. Then we asked whether that which is called "more" consists in a greater quantity, and so a greater happiness occurs? This therefore must be asked: does the happiness of a long time excel only in this, that it abounds in many actions? First, indeed, it can happen that he who applies himself to no actions is blessed—and not less indeed, but truly more than he who has been occupied
<margin>G</margin> in actions. Secondly, actions do not bring the good from themselves, but the dispositions <term>affectiones; the internal state of the soul</term> themselves make the actions good. Now truly the wise man possesses the good even while acting, not because he is acting, nor from those things which happen to him, but from that which he possesses. For even the safety of the fatherland can proceed from some wicked person. Indeed, even in the saving of the fatherland, one can perceive that one is doing something else. Therefore, this is not what creates the pleasure of the happy man; rather...

<summary>Plotinus argues that happiness is a quality of the soul found in the "eternal now" rather than a quantity of time or actions. He rejects the idea that memory of past joy or a long duration of virtuous acts increases the essence of a person's current happiness.</summary>

PLOTINUS: ENNEAD I

<margin>A</margin> Truly, the habit <note>The "habitus" or disposition of the soul.</note> itself both produces such pleasure and excels in happiness. And if anything pleasant happens, the soul makes it so through its own nature. To place happiness in external actions is nothing other than to place it in those things which are outside of virtue and outside the soul. For the soul’s own proper action consists in wisdom, so that it acts within itself: and this is what it means to act happily.

<column-break/>

<note>This Greek text is the original source for the Latin passage to the left.</note>
The disposition itself is happiness, and if it produces anything pleasant, it does so through itself. To place being happy in external actions is to place it in things outside of virtue and the soul. For the activity of the soul lies in the exercise of wisdom, and in acting thus within itself; and this is the state of being happy.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE
# BOOK OF BEAUTY
### ARGUMENT

->*From the first essence, life, and mind, influences emanate through all things, like rays, voices, and words, through six levels.*<-

---

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'I' showing a figure standing in a landscape next to a tree.</image-desc>
Certain influences flow from Being itself through all beings everywhere: but in the way that essence exists in that source, they flow out chiefly in the manner of a solar ray; in the way that life exists there, they break forth in the manner of a fountain and a voice; and finally, in the way that intellect exists there, they are carried in the manner of a meaningful word. Where they are like rays, they are seen to move the sight; where they are voices or sounds, they strike the ears; where they are like words, they especially provoke the souls. Everywhere, however, they encounter us as certain beauties, or some forms of beauty: for they proceed from the very form of Beauty itself. When we name Beauty itself, we wish it to be understood properly in the manner of a "form"—that is, as formal beauty; but in the manner of a "cause"—that is, as the cause of beauty itself—we wish it to be thought of as the Good itself. For we consider the Good to be the light itself, or the fountain of flashing beauty flowing from it. Beauty, however, is the splendor emanating from that light of the Good: that is, Being itself depending on the One and the Good.

From Being itself, as I was saying, we do not doubt that influences proceed through all things like rays, voices, and words. Such influences are first in the divine Idea of the mind; secondly, they are perceived in any mind thereafter; through universal providence they are in the mind of the World-Soul; thirdly, in the reason of that same soul; fourthly, in its primary imagination; fifthly, in the secondary imagination; sixthly, in the vegetative power, which is also called "universal nature." Thus far, they retain a certain <term>ideal</term> <note>From the Greek 'idea,' meaning a divine blueprint or pattern.</note> reason within themselves. For up to this point, they are living, effective, eloquent, and eternal. Indeed, in this last level of divine things are the "seed-reasons" of all things, by which the species of things themselves are propagated. Since the first life and the first formal reason of all things exist in the first Essence—the principle of each thing, in which principle, reason, and life were one—it is right that insofar as the influences flowing from it preserve life and formal reason pure, whole, and effective within themselves, they are called essential, ideal, and divine reasons. They are preserved only slightly less even in nature (that is, the vegetative power of the soul); therefore, on this "sixth day" <note>An allusion to the biblical creation story, mapping it onto Neoplatonic emanations.</note> they are understood to become the proper works of God. 

Subsequently, those influences strike the matter lying beneath the soul. But since they can neither proceed further, nor retain the nature of true essence and life in matter (which is "next to nothing"), they pass from being forms into being mere images. Images, I say, which are likenesses of the true and divine forms. These, under the reproductive nature of the soul acting upon matter, result from that same passive matter; they are reflected back from the matter like a ray from a mirror, or echoed like a voice from a vault, or returned like a word from a garden wall—just like an Echo. To this lowest level of formal outflowing, the Moon seems to grant favor, as the final mistress of generation; but to the "seed-reasons" flourishing in nature and nourishing matter, Venus; to those same reasons in the lower imagination hastening toward motion, Mars; to those same reasons reigning in the imagination, the Sun; but to those flourishing in reason, Mercury; to those dominating the gentle part of the soul, Jupiter; and finally, to those resting in the divine mind, Saturn. In this seventh level, as if on the day of Saturn, the maker of the world rests—that is, the Idea itself, the offspring of the whole. For he does not refer this Idea to other things made from it, but refers other things to it as their exemplar.

->*Formal beauty itself is the mind: with its charms are mixed*<-
->*wonder, power, diffusion, and pleasure.*<-

Because this exemplar is the "all-formed" reason of all forms, it is judged to be the Idea, the form, and the primary and universal species. And for that reason, it is the first "formal beauty": which is why we are accustomed to calling beauty everywhere both "form" and "species," and the beautiful "well-formed"; the opposite of which we call deformity and the deformed. From this it is clear that matter, being by its nature entirely without form, is rightly judged to be deformity itself. But more on this elsewhere. Formal beauty itself arises with the first essence; it grows as essence proceeds into life; and it is finally judged mature when life is completed in the mind. For through the very act of the mind, essential life is perfectly formed and becomes an "all-formed" form. Therefore, in the order of things, there is the most beauty where there is the most mind—whether it be some nature of the mind present, or its own proper craftsmanship, or a trace, or a judgment. And everything moves us more vehemently where it encounters us more vividly. For the true form of beauty is life itself, made completely absolute through the act of the mind. The proper quality of beauty is to attract and to seize at the same time: hence in Greek it is called <term>Calon</term> <note>original: "κάλλος" (kallos), which Ficino connects etymologically to "kalein" (to call or summon).</note>, as if it were "the provoker" or "the caller." And since beauty exists as an intellectual gift, it attracts only those who know: those who know, I say, whether by some intellectual reason, or by sight or hearing, which are the chief servants of reason. Moreover, wonder is mixed with the charms of beauty,

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's commentary on Plotinus’s famous treatise "On Beauty" (Ennead I.6). It distinguishes between the universal desire for the "Good" and the more specific desire for the "Beautiful," while critiquing the classical definition of beauty as mere physical proportion.</meta>

# ON THE SIXTH BOOK OF ENNEAD I.

...and a certain sharper power, and a longing that diffuses itself. Therefore, remember what we prove in the *Theology* <note>referring to Ficino’s own major work, *Platonic Theology*</note>, that all things indeed seek the Good, but not all seek the Beautiful—only those that possess a certain judgment of beauty. Furthermore, these latter always seek the Good, yet they do not always strive after beauty. Since, therefore, the appetite and draw toward the Good is most universal, it follows that the Good itself is the most universal principle and the most powerful of all, and that Beauty is its form, standing closest to the Good. And since the summons from beauty to beauty is like something new—occurring only from certain things, at certain times, and after nature and cognition have developed—it is right that a certain wonder is mixed with the allurements of beauty. Likewise, there is a certain "violence" (if I may call it that); for although the appetite for the Good, which is universal and perpetual, is inward by nature and draws from within, the appetite for the Beautiful seizes as if from the outside, necessarily following upon cognition. Therefore, because it is less "natural" <note>in the sense of being an instinctive biological drive like survival</note>, it seems to have something violent about it, and finally, it diffuses the lover in a certain way. For once it has snatched the lover away from himself, it does not immediately restore and reintegrate him into a unity, since it draws from without and seizes through the mode of cognition—which involves making distinctions—and thus it scatters him. 

Finally, the amatory affect, whether it be mild or sharp, always remains with pleasure, just as there is delight not only in sweet, deep sounds, but also in certain sharp flavors and high-pitched voices. We have found that the soul is affected by pleasure whenever it is touched by something congruent to itself and is led toward the Good. But Beauty, wherever it meets us, approaches as something congruent, and for that reason it pleases and is approved: because it responds to the idea of beauty innate within us and matches it in every way. Again, by its own nature, it always leads the soul to the Good; for our participation in beauty calls the soul toward that same intellectual form, and through that form, finally to the Good itself—just as brilliance leads to light, and light leads to the source of radiance. But let it suffice for now to have run through Plotinus's most beautiful book on beauty with "freer feet" <note>original: *liberioribus pedibus*; a poetic way of saying he is summarizing or paraphrasing rather than translating word-for-word</note>. Next, the chapters of this new book must be recounted by us in order, and these also briefly, as we have disputed more extensively about these matters in the *Symposium* <note>Ficino’s *De Amore*, a commentary on Plato's *Symposium*</note> concerning love.

->Beauty is a certain grace, which exists more in those things which are seen than those which are heard, and even more in those which are thought; it is not merely proportion.<-

<margin>
The effect of beauty
</margin>
I. We conceive by a common notion that Beauty is something gracious, or a certain grace alluring us through sight, or hearing, or reason. Indeed, insofar as it exists in things that are seen, heard, and thought, it is called "Beauty," and it represents to you the three Graces. But insofar as it consists in sight, hearing, and reason, it is named "delight" and "pleasure"—a "becoming" pleasure, I say. For a becoming pleasure properly follows a becoming thing in itself, and a becoming appetite follows this: namely, Love itself. A base disturbance, however, happens perhaps from other causes. Therefore, the first chapter inquires into what this grace and beauty chiefly is, and assigns what it is not.

<margin>
Beauty is in the voice and thought
</margin>
Meanwhile, he signifies that beauty pertains more to sight than to hearing, because sight and light are more familiar to the intelligence than hearing and sound. Furthermore, he signifies that the habits of the soul are more beautiful than the bodies which are called "comely"; and that they are more beautiful in the voice, because they are similarly more akin to the mind. Indeed, the habits of the soul, both in morals and in learning, can rightly be called not only beautiful, but even "Beauties" themselves. For they are forms—forms, I say, close to the mind. Bodies, however, might be called "beautiful," but they cannot be called "Beauties." For although Beauty itself ought not to be called now beautiful and now not beautiful, the same body is beautiful today, but tomorrow, by a slight change, it is not beautiful. Similarly, the matter in us remains nearly the same, but by a change in proportion, it turns from beautiful to ugly. Nevertheless, since beauty pertains more to those things which are beheld than those which are heard, and again more to those which are thought, we must investigate whether there is something common to all these things, or what that very thing is by which all these things are called beautiful. But first he investigates this in bodies that are seen, as it will be more manifest that way.

<margin>
Bodily proportion
</margin>
In the beginning, he refutes the common opinion concerning these things, which says that the beauty of the body is a certain proportion of the parts among themselves and to the whole, together with a harmony of color. He refutes this with four arguments.

<margin>
The falsity of the opinion on proportion based on four of Plotinus's reasons
</margin>
First, if beauty itself is proportion or a certain symmetry, then certainly it is only a composite thing; therefore, no simple thing, however gracious it may be, would be called beautiful <note>e.g., the sun, or a single color</note>. Second, again, if only the composite is beautiful, no part—especially the simple ones—will be beautiful; indeed, no part at all, since beauty is placed only in that proportion measured against another. From this it would follow that the beautiful is made out of non-beautiful things; yet we have found that nothing gracious is ever created from things lacking all grace. Third, the same face, often with the same figure and proportion remaining, sometimes appears beautiful to us and sometimes not beautiful; thus, beauty must be something other than mere measurement. Fourth, it is necessary that beauty in bodies refers us back to a higher beauty. We must, therefore, accommodate this bodily beauty to that higher one as much as possible; yet it must exist there in an altogether more excellent way than in bodies. But in what way there could be a "measurement" there—namely, in the soul or the intellect—cannot easily be explained.

<margin>
The soul's merits in beauty
</margin>
And in the soul, we cannot understand how morals and sciences could be "measurements" or proportions if we follow Plotinus. For he does not want habits in the soul to ever be heaped up from figures—namely, many of them—which might be called habits of morals or sciences; rather, he wants the simple act of moral virtue to shine forth as soon as the clouds of incidental vices are shaken off, and the simple form of science to glow once false opinions are finally expelled. For the soul in a certain sense "vanishes" and then most truly knows the thing itself, when, having been stirred by arguments, it now becomes in act the very thing which it was previously, but only by a certain fertile power and strength. But these things will be disputed more opportunely elsewhere.

->Beauty in bodies is the absolute perfection and grace of form especially,<-
->which dominates both the matter and the other forms within it, and reports<-
->the ready victory of divine art and reason over matter,<-
->and clearly represents the Idea itself.<-

II. The second chapter examines what beauty itself is in bodies. It asserts that it is something that offers itself readily at first sight. For since beauty is an "intelligible form" shaped in the intelligible world, and similarly in the body it is a "form being formed," it rightly moves the intellect there and the sight here, first and most readily—as Plato testifies in the *Phaedrus*. Plotinus adds that the soul vehemently rejects the ugly and is affected by the beautiful, and not without reason: for ugliness is a certain foul face of evil, while beauty is the charming face of the good. Furthermore, the rational soul depends most closely upon the Divine Mind and keeps the idea of beauty impressed within itself from that source; with which idea, indeed, beauty harmonizes, as if with its own paternal kin...

<summary>Ficino explains Plotinus’s view that beauty is an innate spark of the Divine, rejecting the idea that it is merely physical symmetry (proportion) and instead defining it as a "grace" that mirrors the Good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On Beauty" (Ennead I.6). Having previously discussed the universal desire for the Good versus the specific desire for the Beautiful, Ficino now delves into the metaphysical nature of "Form" and how the human soul recognizes beauty through innate divine blueprints.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...gladly embraces it. Furthermore, that form is fitting in bodies which is composed according to the very norm and rule of the *Idea* <note>In Platonic philosophy, an "Idea" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing existing in the Divine Mind</note>. This occurs while the *seminal reason* <term>ratio seminalis: a "seed-logic" or formative power implanted in nature that directs the growth and shape of physical things</term>, which is the shaper of bodies within nature, dominates the matter to the greatest extent. It renders the form within that matter not "material" in the lowly sense, but "formal" in the highest sense. Indeed, as we learn from the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe</note>: the Divine Intellect itself is the father of forms, and matter is the mother. But the "kindling" or reason of forms flourishing in nature can rightly be called the paternal and effective seed, while the form generated from it is the offspring. 

Beauty (*formositas*) is nothing other than the character of this offspring, more expressively reflecting the image of the father. Deformity, on the other hand, is both a certain lack of likeness in a failing form compared to the father’s form, and the matter itself which is the origin of this defect. This happens especially when, due to some impeding chance, the subject is not overcome by the shaping reason—that is, it either cannot sustain the act of the shaper or receives it most poorly. Accordingly, although there are many accidental forms in any element, there is nonetheless one *substantial form* <note>the essential core that makes a thing what it is</note> that is primary. Similarly, in mixed things like stones and metals, even if many substantial forms are present in potential, one is principal in act and common to the whole. So too in plants and animals: if many substantial forms exist in each through certain actions, one is primary in act, ruling over the others. Everywhere, beauty is a certain absolute perfection, or grace, and as it were a certain "flower" of that primary form ruling over the other forms. It is, therefore, something divine and imperial: because it signifies the command of the reigning form, reflects the victory of divine art and reason over matter, and clearly represents the *Idea* itself.

->Beauty in bodies is a more expressive likeness of the Idea; indeed, if the matter is taken away, it is the Idea itself. Likewise, the beauty of any species is judged by the soul through a "formula" of that same Idea implanted within itself, according to which the species was established.<-

### III. Who then is a beautiful man? Or a beautiful lion? Or a beautiful horse? 

Certainly, it is the one who is specifically so formed and so born as the Divine Mind established through its own *Idea*, and as universal nature then conceived through its "seed-like" power (*seminaria virtus*). Now, our soul possesses the formula of that *Idea* inborn in its mind; it likewise possesses the *seminal reason* in its own nature. Therefore, by a certain natural judgment, the soul is accustomed to judge concerning a man, a lion, a horse, and other things—concluding that this one is not beautiful, while that one is. This is because the former disagrees with the internal formula and reason, while the latter agrees. Moreover, among beautiful things, the soul judges one to be more beautiful than another because it agrees with the formula and reason more than the other does. And truly, since this judgment is natural and cannot be more conveniently explained than through the formulas and reasons innate to us, it is probable that Divine Providence, disposing all things, impressed such "characters" upon us from the beginning. 

When we judge beauty, we approve above all else that which is animate and rational, and so formed that it satisfies the formula of beauty we hold in our mind (through the soul) and corresponds to the *seminal reason* of beauty we possess in our fertile soul (through the body). The form in a beautiful body is the "kindling" of its Idea, just as the shape of a building in matter is like the model in the architect’s mind, or as a spoken word is like the speech held in the soul. Therefore, if you take away the matter of a man but leave the form, this very form remaining to you is that very *Idea* according to which the man was formed. Just as if you removed the matter from a building while leaving the shape, or if you took away the sound from a speech while preserving the meaning: certainly, the remaining shape is nothing other than the model residing in the architect, and the preserved meaning is nothing other than the thought of the speaker. Hence, he who gathers such meaning is said to "have the mind" of the speaker and to "interpret" it. 

Thus, we too, in beautiful things, ought to set matter aside and, by loving the forms and order, suspect the Ideas within them, and so interpret the divine art and mind. He <note>Plotinus</note> considers the beauty of the body to consist of a harmony of forms, such that individual forms overcome the uniformity of matter, and a common form altogether excels the individual forms. However, he places the beauty of a "simple body" (where a single substantial form is in act, such as gold or silver) in a likeness to the greatest portion of light. Indeed, he wants light to be the form of fire—that is, of heaven—which is a certain image of the life of heaven; so much so that what is *intellectual* in celestial life is *luminous* in the celestial body. Likewise, he considers light beneath the moon to be an act and (so to speak) an image of the celestial form or light. From this, it is clear how great the power of heaven is, since its form—as an image—produces and preserves all things among us. He also considers the fire beneath the moon to be a fiery or ignited body rather than "pure fire." Nevertheless, because it is more like heaven—existing as something clear and as a form for other bodies, and close to the incorporeal—it is therefore most beautiful, and by participation in it, other things become most beautiful, especially those that carry light from it. Such things are those that have the least amount of "earth" or have a most tempered nature. For that which is most earthy or least tempered, being far different from heaven, is most unsuited to receiving light and luminous color, which are celestial qualities. 

What has been said regarding bodies that appear beautiful applies similarly to things that are heard as beautiful, whether it be a single voice or a pleasing composition of voices. And just as the beauty of a visible form proceeds from its ideal and seminal reason, so the beauty of voices and "concord" <note>musical harmony</note> is perfected both by the breath (*spiritus*) and by the harmonic conception of the mind. Everywhere, beauty is the empire of form over its subject, and the corporeal form proceeds from an incorporeal form.

->Beauty that is seen represents the beauty of the mind; beauty that is heard reflects the beauty of the soul. Likewise, no one ought to, or can, speak of the beauty of the mind and soul unless he possesses it himself.<-

### IIII. Beauty is twofold: namely, incorporeal and corporeal. 

And just as corporeal beauty is again twofold (one in things seen, the other in things heard), so too is incorporeal beauty twofold: one in the intellect, the other in the soul. The beauty of intellectual light is represented to us primarily by that which is seen in physical light, as if in an image. In turn, the beauty of the soul, which is established in a certain harmony, is rightly reflected by that which is heard as musical beauty, as if in an image. 

In every way, just as no one can speak of corporeal beauty unless he has known it through the senses, so neither can one speak of incorporeal beauty unless the soul has perceived it. But while the knowledge of the corporeal is carried outside itself, he who is about to perceive the incorporeal must be brought back within himself. Yet, once recalled to himself, he will not perceive it unless he *possesses* it. Therefore, be beautiful in both intellect and soul before you dare to dispute concerning incorporeal beauty. Remember that he who delights in sensible beauty—which is an image of insensible beauty—will receive a much greater pleasure if he perceives the latter.

<summary>Ficino explains that beauty is the victory of "Form" (divine blueprints) over "Matter," and that humans recognize beauty because our souls contain innate versions of these divine Ideas. He categorizes beauty into corporeal (seen and heard) and incorporeal (intellectual and soulful), arguing that one must be internally beautiful to truly understand beauty.</summary>

# ON BOOK VI OF ENNEAD I

You will experience pleasure when you recognize the beauty of the mind and soul itself—or rather, when you come to possess it. Matter possesses a natural deformity, while its "formality" <note>the quality of having a defined shape or essence</note> is something foreign to it. But for the soul, foulness is the foreign element, while beauty is its native state. Furthermore, the beauty of the **Divine Mind** is like **light**. The beauty of the **human mind**—specifically in its intellectual power—is like a **brilliant color**. The beauty of the **soul**—specifically in its moral power—is like a **figure or shape**.

Since beauty (that is, shapeliness) is the very flower, vigor, and grace of form, it follows that just as matter is formlessness itself, it is also deformity itself. To matter, therefore, deformity is natural, while beauty becomes a "foreigner" insofar as matter receives form from elsewhere. But for the soul, the opposite is true: beauty is native to it because by its own nature it is a true form—that is, a certain "act" or power existing within itself. Indeed, all other forms ranked below the soul are "formations" rather than "forms"; they are the actions of the soul upon matter, and in turn, the "passions" <note>original: "passiones"—meaning the way matter is affected or acted upon</note> of matter. Therefore, for the soul, beauty is natural and deformity is accidental. Just as matter seems to become beautiful when it borrows something formal from the soul, the soul conversely becomes deformed when it receives something formless from matter. It receives this formlessness to the degree that it yields to the body through its emotions and concedes to it through its understanding. Thus, the soul does not become beautiful by acquiring some new gift, but through **purification** alone, by which it is restored to its original nature. In that state, its own *Idea* and the Divine Intellect formed it. The beauty of that Divine Intellect is like light; the beauty of our own intellect flowing from it—called intellectual virtue—is like a brilliant color; but moral beauty, proceeding from both, is like a figure or shape.

->Virtue and beauty in the soul are natural; they are the soul's own purity restored to it.<-
->Immediately, the soul shines with the beauty of the Divine Mind and enjoys the Good itself most happily.<-
->Likewise, the first form, the first mind, and the first being are one and the same.<-

VI. An ancient oracle, cited by both Plato in the *Phaedo* and by Plotinus here, teaches that all virtue—both intellectual and moral—is a certain purification and purity. Consider this also said of beauty under the name of virtue: that virtue and beauty are native to the soul, while foulness and wickedness are foreign. Thus, a soul purged of bodily filth does not merely become beautiful, but becomes **Beauty itself**—that is, a form existing by itself, an "ideal ratio" <note>a mathematical or logical blueprint in the mind of God</note>, and an expression of the Divine Countenance. This happens when the soul ascends from being merely rational to being intellectual, and finally becomes "Intellect" itself. For the "First Beauty" exists according to form, where the "First Form" resides; and the First Form is the Intellect. The First Form must be both "uniform" (simple) and "omniform" (containing all forms), being the origin of all other shapes. Just as "First Matter" is utterly formless and a receptacle for forms, only the "First Intellect" can be the source, which is also "Being" itself. For if being everywhere exists through form, surely the First Being coincides with the First Form. Furthermore, just as in matter natural evil coincides with natural deformity, so in the First Being (the First Mind), native Goodness (which is "Good-form") coincides with native beauty. Yet, above Being and Mind is the **Good itself**; if it is ever called "Beauty," it is understood as the *source* of beauty, from which the Intellect flows as the first form of beauty. From the Intellect, the soul is born as the first "participation" in beauty; other things below the soul receive beauty in second or third-hand participations. Finally, we conclude that the soul is beautiful and divine by nature because beauty shines most clearly in those bodies where the **seed-power** <term>seminaria virtus: the life-force or "logic-seed" that organizes physical matter</term> of the soul finds a submissive subject, whether in the universe as a whole or in any specific individual nature.

->How the Gods are distinguished from the daemons, and how their bodies are seen.<-
->Also, the six differences between the sight of gods and the spectacles of daemons.<-
->Conclude: if you labor to contemplate divine beauty,<-
->be beautiful and divine yourself.<-

VII. There is no need to interpret Plotinus’s meaning at great length; for as divinely as he speaks—and he speaks most divinely—he also speaks with great clarity. He strives everywhere not so much to lead the soul to *look* at beauty as to *possess* it. As for what he briefly hints at regarding the appearance of gods and daemons <note>original: "dæmonibus"—in the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or "guardian angels," not "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>, understand it thus: He signifies the higher beings and daemons similarly, as those who naturally have invisible bodies and are benevolent, and who sometimes reveal themselves to our eyes as a benefit to us. Distinguish the Gods from the daemons in this way: in the "God of Gods" <note>The One or Supreme Source</note>, providence is entirely universal, for He provides all things for everyone. Providence is also universal in a way in the Divine Mind and the Soul of the World. In the subsequent gods—whether invisible or visible—providence is also somewhat universal, but with a specific condition. They either give some gifts to all things, or they give all things to some specific things. In the daemons, however, providence is both particular and restricted by specific conditions. They distribute certain gifts only to certain kinds of things and regions. Nor are they, like the gods, entirely separated from all passion, worry, or emotion; for they seem to "incline" toward the very things they care for. Furthermore, many daemons follow each god (whether celestial or sub-celestial) as their leader. But how do those who are invisible by nature become visible? I do not think a god or daemon necessarily contracts their vast, subtle body into a small space to be grasped by your eyes, reflecting your eye-beams back to you. They do not wish to be seen through their own "passion" (being acted upon), but perhaps by a powerful virtue they move your visual rays, repelling them or terminating them within themselves, thus making themselves known to you. But we shall discuss vision according to Plotinus elsewhere. You can also perceive them in another way, not with outer sight, but with an internal and "celestial" sight, if you ever gather yourself inward from all sides. As for the differences between the forms of a god and a daemon—whether both are ethereal, or fiery, or airy—Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote "On the Mysteries"</note> briefly reveals them according to the Egyptians: the appearance of a god is pleasant and offers us a simple figure; that of a daemon is complex. A god’s appearance is stable; a daemon’s is subject to total variety and change. Likewise, a god's form is at once venerable and propitious, and entirely kind; a daemon's is not just to be revered, but to be feared. Furthermore, a divine spectacle seems to fill the whole world suddenly; a daemonic one shows itself in a specific place. Again, a divine "flash" (so to speak) strikes with the very blow of intelligence...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On Beauty" (Ennead I.6). Ficino concludes his introductory remarks by describing the mystical ascent to the "Father" or the Source of Beauty, before providing the bilingual text of Plotinus’s original treatise.</meta>

[The soul] is faster and acts more swiftly: the demonic is indeed fast, but it does not quite surpass the speed of the mind. Finally, whatever the size, quality, or kind of form and beauty a demon might present to you, you can express it in some way; but God's beauty, you cannot. Plotinus himself perceived how venerable and gracious both are through his own senses, though he does not fully explain it; Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and biographer</note>, who was likely present, testifies to this in his *Life of Plotinus*. He concludes the whole book thus: "Just as the eye, to see the sun, must be and become sun-like, so you, to look upon beauty itself—which is the divine intellect itself—must leave behind matter, leave behind the senses, and leave behind reason as well. Become intellectual <note>meaning, move into the realm of pure Mind/Intellect</note>: first your own intellect, then the divine." Then at last, like an eagle's eye rejoicing as it flies into the sky, it will behold the solar and celestial splendor near the sun’s innermost light, surrounding it like a single beauty combined with the light itself. So too will you, having progressed through your intellect to the divine intellect—flashing with a wondrous series of Ideas <term>Ideas: the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in the mind of God</term> and flowing from the light of the Father's goodness—behold at first glance an intellectual splendor continuous with the Father's light, as one and the same. Soon, however, noticing that the light is entirely uniform, but that the splendor pours out in a multiform way within the light—shining is an outpouring—you will surely discern (to speak in the Platonic way) that this mind, the very form of beauty, is the true Good, and that the Mind is the Father, the progenitor of beauty. Thus you will admire the Son in the Father, and love the Father in the Son, and rejoice in the mutual love of both.

### THE SIXTH BOOK.

->On Beauty.<- ->On Beauty.<-

<margin>
Beauty is found in those things which are seen, which are heard, and which are known, and it is not merely proportion.
</margin>

<image-desc>Two decorative drop caps begin the columns: a 'P' for the Latin text and a 'Τ' (Tau) for the Greek text, both featuring scrolling floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

Beauty is found mostly in the sense of sight. It is also in the sense of hearing, in the arrangement of words, and in all music; for songs and rhythmic harmonies are beautiful. Furthermore, if we ascend from the senses to that which is above the senses, we find that studies, duties, actions, habits, and sciences are also beautiful, as is the beauty of the virtues. Whether there is any beauty above these, the matter itself will reveal as we proceed. What is it, then, that makes bodies appear beautiful, and causes the ear to approve of voices as beautiful, and everything else pertaining to the soul? In what way, then, do all these things become beautiful? Are all things beautiful by one and the same principle <term>original: "ratione" — meaning a guiding logic or formal cause</term> of beauty? Or is beauty one thing in a body and another in something else? Again, what are these things, if they are two? What exists if it is one? For some things, like bodies, are surely not beautiful by their own nature, but rather by some participation <term>participation: the Platonic idea that material things share in a higher, perfect reality</term>. Others, however, are beauties themselves, like the nature of virtue itself. For the same bodies appear beautiful at one time and not at another, as if being a body were one thing and being beautiful were another. What, then, is this primary thing that makes bodies beautiful by its presence? This is what we must consider first. Tell me: what is it that most attracts the eyes of onlookers, turns them toward itself, seizes them, and delights the viewer? If we find this, perhaps we can use it like a ladder to see other things. For almost everyone teaches that beauty consists of a certain proportion <note>original: "commensurationem"</note> of parts, both to each other and to the whole, along with the grace of color, pertaining

Beauty is found mostly in sight, but it is also in sounds according to the composition of words, and it is in all music; for melodies and rhythms are beautiful. And as for the beauty before these—if indeed there is any—it will show itself from them. What then is the thing that makes even bodies appear beautiful, and charms the hearing with sounds as beautiful, and all that follows regarding the soul—how are all these things beautiful? <meta>This page transitions from Marsilio Ficino’s introductory commentary into the primary text of Plotinus’s treatise "On Beauty" (Ennead I.6). The text challenges the common ancient definition of beauty as "symmetry," arguing instead that beauty is a divine quality recognized by the soul.</meta>

### BOOK SIX.

Beauty for the sight is judged by almost everyone to consist in the symmetry <note>Greek: *symmetria*; the balanced proportion of parts to a whole</note> of parts in relation to each other and to the whole, combined with the attractiveness of color. For those who hold this view, beauty is necessarily found only in composite things, and nothing simple can be beautiful. In their view, only the whole will be beautiful, while the individual parts will not possess beauty on their own, but only contribute to the beauty of the whole. Yet, if the whole is beautiful, the parts must surely be beautiful as well; for beauty cannot be composed of ugly things, but must pervade everything. Furthermore, for them, beautiful colors—like the light of the sun—being simple and not deriving beauty from symmetry, would be excluded from being beautiful. And how, then, would gold be beautiful? Or the flash of lightning at night, or the sight of the stars? Similarly, in the case of sounds, the beauty of a single tone would vanish, even though many individual sounds within a beautiful whole are often beautiful themselves. Moreover, when the same symmetry remains but the same object appears beautiful at one time and not at another, how can we avoid saying that beauty is something other than the symmetry itself, and that the symmetrical object is beautiful because of something else? If these thinkers then move on to beautiful practices and beautiful discourses, citing symmetry as the cause, what kind of symmetry could be said to exist in beautiful practices, or laws, or lessons, or sciences? How could theorems be symmetrical to one another? If they say it is because they are "in harmony," then even among evil things there is a certain agreement and harmony: for the claim that "temperance is stupidity" and "justice is a noble ignorance" are in harmony and agreement with one another. Thus, all virtue is the beauty of the soul—a beauty more true than those mentioned before. But how are these things "symmetrical"? They are not symmetrical in the way of magnitudes or numbers. Since the soul has many parts, in what ratio would the composition or the blending of these parts or theorems consist? Finally, what would the beauty of the Intellect itself, isolated and alone, be?

<margin>* The terms "shrinks" and "recoils" [used below] refer to the soul not being in harmony with, or being alienated from, the object. We say that the soul, being what it is by nature and belonging to the superior order of reality, feels joy and is stirred when it sees anything akin to itself or a trace of its kin.</margin>

**Ficino's Translation:**

**A** [Beauty is thought] to be produced for the eyes, and in it the beauty of all things is placed, such that they are moderate and well-proportioned. But according to those who hold this opinion, nothing simple but only the composite will necessarily be beautiful, and the whole itself will be the most beautiful. Indeed, the individual parts will have no beauty of their own; they will be called beautiful only insofar as they contribute to the whole. However, it is necessary that if the whole is beautiful, the parts must also be handsome; for beauty does not consist of ugly things.

**B** It is necessary, therefore, that all parts have received beauty. Furthermore, beautiful colors—just like the light of the sun—since they are simple and do not have beauty from proportion, would be left excluded from beauty by those thinkers. In what way will gold be beautiful to them? Or the nightly flash of lightning, or the spectacle of the stars? Similarly, in voices, that which is simple will be alien to beauty. Although any whole in these

**C** songs, which are beautiful as a whole, is itself beautiful. Accordingly, when the same proportion remains but the same face appears beautiful at one time and not at another, must we not say that beauty is something other than that which is proportionate, and that proportion is something else? And that the proportionate thing is beautiful because of something else? If, however, they turn themselves to beautiful studies and beautiful discourses, and

**D** assign the proportion of measure as the cause of beauty in these things as well, what kind of proportionate measure will be spoken of in beautiful studies, or laws, or disciplines, or sciences? Furthermore, in what way are the contemplations <note>Latin: *speculationes*; referring to intellectual or scientific insights</note> themselves said to be mutually proportionate? If anyone assigns this to the fact that they are, evidently, in agreement, we shall say that there is also a certain consensus and agreement among evil things. For these two things agree with each other (as it is said): namely,

**E** that temperance is stupidity and that justice is a noble ignorance. Therefore, the beauty of the soul is every virtue, and this very beauty is much more excellent in appearance than the things mentioned above. But in what way will proportion be here? For it is not such as exists in magnitude, nor such as exists in number. And since there are several parts of the soul, in what ratio will the composition or tempering of the parts or the contemplations be placed? Finally, what will the beauty of the Intellect itself—namely, the segregated and solitary intellect—be in itself?

<margin>From where beauty in bodies flourishes: and what it is, namely a Form <term>Species: In Platonic thought, an eternal archetype or "Form"</term> descending from the higher world down to this one.</margin>

**F** LET US REPEAT again from the beginning, asking what is this beauty in bodies? In the beginning, it is indeed something revealing itself to the sense at first glance; and the soul, apprehending it and recognizing it as something familiar, looks up to it, and approves and embraces it as most suitable. But encountering the ugly, it recoils; and as if shrinking in discord, it rejects it and treats it as alien. Being

**G** indeed the soul, which is what it is naturally, and nearly the most excellent in the order of things according to its essence, whenever it looks upon anything kindred or a trace of its kin, it rejoices and is struck with awe, and refers it back to itself: and it remembers itself and its own. <summary>This page presents Plotinus's argument against the "symmetry" theory of beauty, suggesting instead that beauty is a divine quality the soul recognizes through an innate "kinship." Plotinus uses examples like light, gold, and the stars to prove that simple, non-composite things can be beautiful, and he extends this logic to the beauty of the soul and the intellect.</summary>
