<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "On Beauty" (Ennead I.6). Having previously dismissed the idea that beauty is merely physical symmetry, the text now explains that beauty arises when a divine "Form" (Idea) organizes formless matter into a unified whole. The soul recognizes this beauty because it possesses a similar "Form" within itself.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK I

<margin>
III. The soul, through an innate pattern of beauty within itself, recognizes beauty in physical bodies. This form is applied to matter; both the idea and the matter are involved. Therefore, even among the lowliest sights, the path of art leads into the matter.
</margin>

...though there may be thousands. But in what way are both these things and those things beautiful at the same time? We say that these things are beautiful by participating in a **Form** <note>original Latin: *species*; Greek: *eidos*. In Neoplatonism, this refers to the divine blueprint or "Idea" that gives shape to reality.</note>. For everything that is naturally formless but capable of receiving shape and form, insofar as it lacks **Reason** <note>original Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*</note> and form, is ugly and removed from divine reason. That which is entirely removed from form is completely ugly; likewise, that which is not fully mastered by form and reason is also ugly, because the matter did not fully submit to being shaped.

Therefore, when the Form approaches, it organizes and coordinates the many parts that are to become a single composition; by this very harmony, it creates a "One," since the Form itself was already a "One." It was necessary for the shaped object to become one, as far as something composed of many parts can be called one. Beauty, then, is established within the object once it has been reduced to a unity, and the Form imparts itself to both the parts and the whole. But when the Form encounters something that is already a single unit with uniform parts, it gives itself entirely to the whole. Sometimes it does this, for example, to an entire building and its parts together; at other times, it is given to a single stone. In the former case, it happens through **art** <note>original Latin: *ars*; Greek: *techne*</note>, while in the other, it is through nature. In this way, a beautiful body is produced through communion with the Reason that descends from the divine.

The soul recognizes this beauty through a certain power appointed for this task, than which nothing is more capable of judging its own concerns, especially when the rest of the soul joins in the judgment. Perhaps this power speaks by adapting the Form it possesses within itself, using it for judgment just as one uses a ruler to judge what is straight. But how does that which is in the body harmonize with that which is above the body? Tell me: how does the architect judge a building to be beautiful by adapting the external structure to the form of the building that is in his mind? Perhaps because if you take away the stones, the external building is nothing other than the internal form, though divided by the external mass of matter; it remains indivisible in itself, even if it appears in many parts. Therefore, when the senses perceive the Form dwelling in bodies—binding and overcoming the contrary nature of formless matter—and see the shape shining out elegantly upon other shapes, the soul gathers together the beauty that appeared scattered, brings it back to itself, and introduces it to the indivisible Form within. It renders it harmonious, congruent, and friendly to that inner form. Just as the character of virtue appearing in a young man is pleasing to a good man, because it harmonizes with the true virtue that exists within him. The beauty of color, however, is simple; it arises when the darkness of matter is mastered by the presence of light, which is itself incorporeal and a kind of Reason and Form. For this reason, fire itself is beautiful beyond all other bodies; for if compared with other elements, it holds the rank of Form. It is more eminent than the others and the most subtle of all, as if it were already close to an incorporeal nature. It alone does not receive other things into itself, though other things receive it. For other things are heated, but fire itself does not receive cold. Furthermore, fire possesses color primarily and fundamentally.

<column-break/>

->A<- ...are similar. But how are both those and these beautiful? We say they are beautiful by participation in a Form. For all that is formless, though born to share in shape and form, is ugly and outside of Divine Reason as long as it has no share in Reason and Form. This is the completely ugly. And that which is not mastered by shape and Reason is also ugly, because the matter does not endure being shaped entirely according to the Form.

->B<- Therefore, the Form, approaching those things that are to be made of many parts into a completion, coordinates them and brings them into a single completion; by this agreement, it makes them fitting by being itself a unity, so that the shaped object may be a single Form as much as is possible for something made of many parts. Thus, beauty is established upon it.

->C<- Once it has been composed into a unity of <insert>elements</insert>, the Form gives itself both to the parts and to the wholes. But when it takes hold of something that is one and uniform, it gives the same beauty to the whole. For instance, sometimes nature gives beauty to an entire house with its parts, and sometimes to a single stone; at other times, art does this. In this way, the beautiful body comes into being through communion with the Reason that comes from the divine.

->D<- The power appointed for this task recognizes it, and nothing is more authoritative than this power in judging its own things, when the rest of the soul also joins in the judgment. And perhaps the soul speaks by harmonizing the object with the Form within itself, using that internal Form for judgment as a rule for straightness. But how does that which concerns the body harmonize with that which is prior to the body? How does the architect, by harmonizing the house outside with the form of the house inside, say that it is beautiful? It is because the house outside, separated into stones, is the internal form divided by the external mass of matter; though it is indivisible, it is imagined in many parts.

->E<- Therefore, when the sense-perception sees the Form in bodies, binding and mastering the contrary nature (which is formless), and sees a shape riding exceptionally upon other shapes, <insert>being composed</insert> it brings together that which is scattered, brings it back, and introduces it to the now-indivisible interior, giving it to the internal Form as something harmonious, fitting, and

->F<- friendly. Just as the trace of virtue appearing in a young man is pleasant to a good man, harmonizing with the truth within him. The beauty of color is simple in form, mastering the darkness in matter by the presence of light, which is incorporeal and is both Reason and Form.

->G<- Hence fire itself is beautiful beyond the other bodies, because it holds the rank of Form relative to the other elements; it is high in its position and is the most subtle of the other bodies, being close to the incorporeal. It alone does not admit the others into itself, but the others receive it. For those things are heated, but this is not cooled. It possesses color primarily.

<summary>Plotinus explains that beauty is the result of divine Form organizing formless matter into a unified whole, a process the soul recognizes because it contains these same Forms within itself. He uses the examples of an architect's design, the recognition of virtue in others, and the elemental beauty of fire to illustrate this "kinship" between the soul and beautiful objects.</summary>

A And other things receive the form of color from this [light] when it shines and glitters as if it were a **Form** <note>original Greek: *eidos*. A divine blueprint that gives shape to reality.</note>. But that which is not mastered [by the form], becoming faded by the light, is no longer beautiful, as if it did not participate in the form of color *at all*. B Moreover, the hidden harmonies in sounds create those which are manifest, and in this way they make the soul conceive of beauty, showing the same principle in a different medium. One might also count among sensory things those measured by numbers in **proportions and rhythms** <note>original Greek: *en logō kai rhythmō*</note>. * But as forms are in matter, so they act toward the production of [other] forms and toward mastery [over matter]. And so much for the beauties in the realm of sense, which are like images and shadows that have run out into matter, decorating it and appearing as such great things.

C BUT concerning the higher beauties, which it is no longer the lot of the senses to see, but which the soul sees and speaks of without instruments, one must contemplate them by ascending, leaving sense perception lying far below. D Just as with the beauties of sense, it was not possible for those who had neither seen them nor perceived them as beautiful to speak of them—such as those who have been blind from birth—in the same way, one cannot speak of the beauty of **pursuits** <note>original Greek: *epitēdeumatōn*; refers to the practices or habits of a virtuous life</note> if one has not accepted the beauty of pursuits and sciences and other such things. Nor can one speak of the light of virtue, if one has not imagined how beautiful is the face of justice and temperance, and that neither the **evening star nor the morning star** <note>original Greek: *hesperō kai tō heōō*. A reference to a famous saying that Justice is more wonderful than the stars.</note> is so beautiful. But it is necessary to see these things with that by which the soul looks at such things, and having seen them, to be delighted and stunned, and to be shaken much more than by those previous beauties, because one is now touching upon true things. For these are the passions that must occur around what is <margin>* Idea</margin> E truly beautiful: wonder and a sweet amazement, longing and love, and a trembling accompanied by pleasure. It is possible for souls to experience these things even concerning things that are not seen—all souls, so to speak, but especially those more **erotic** <note>original Greek: *erōtikai*. In the Platonic sense, "erotic" refers to a soul's intense, driving desire for truth and beauty.</note> toward these things, <margin>* erotically / delight / [unclear] / of this</margin> just as in the case of bodies, everyone sees them, but not everyone is moved equally; rather, it is those who are most "in love" who are said to be moved.

And when you see your own internal beauties, what do you feel? How are you **inspired to frenzy** <note>original Greek: *anabakkheusesthe*; literally "to be driven into a Bacchic madness." For these are the things that true lovers feel. But what is it for which they feel these things? It is not a shape, nor a color, nor a certain size, but it is for the soul, which is itself colorless, and which possesses a **temperance** <note>original Latin: *temperantia*; Greek: *sōphrosynē*. A Other things, however, receive the appearance of color from this. It flashes, therefore, and shines as if it were a form. But when the subject is not overcome, like a participant in a meager light, it does not come forth as beautiful: inasmuch as it does not receive the appearance of color in its entirety. Furthermore, harmonies which are in voices—those which lie hidden in the soul—create and produce them as far as the senses, and thus they act so B that the soul perceives the concept of the beautiful, demonstrating the same thing in another medium. Truly, it finds in the harmonies that are sensed that they are measured by numbers—not in every ratio of number or voice, but only in that which pertains to the production of the form and the victory of the form that obeys it. But so much for the beauties in the sense realm, which, like images and shadows flowing into matter, have adorned it: and encountering the senses, they have stirred up an admiration for themselves.

<margin>(Chapter III)
If we wish to become beautiful, we must now devote ourselves more to the enjoyment of the knowledge of beauty than to bodily beauty.</margin>
C BUT truly, those beauties which are superior to these and are not at all open to the eyes—but which the soul itself, without instruments, discerns and proclaims—we ought to contemplate by a certain ascent, leaving sense at the lowest point. Just as D we would not have been able to express in words the beauties offered to the senses unless we had seen them at some time and perceived them as beautiful (a gift which those born blind are deprived of), so also we cannot speak of the beauty of duties and sciences and other things of the same kind unless we possess these very things. Similarly, we cannot speak of the brightness of virtue unless we have somehow reflected upon how beautiful is the face of justice and temperance: and in what way neither the evening star nor the morning star is so fair. Rather, it is necessary to see these things only by that [faculty] with which the soul itself gazes upon such things. Moreover, those who see are greatly delighted and vehemently affected, and admire it much more than bodily beauty: as they are now touching upon true things. Such affections, I say, ought to be E excited concerning whatever is beautiful: namely, admiration and a sweet stupor, longing also, and love, and a joyful agitation. Certain things of this sort happen to souls concerning those things that are not seen: to all souls indeed (so to speak), but more so to those which are more inclined toward the love of those things: just as happens regarding the beauty of the body. For everyone sees equally, yet they are not equally incited, but the lovers most of all.

<margin>Beauty shines forth naturally in souls and beams upon us: as soon as they have emerged from deformity and have overcome matter.</margin>
F MOREOVER, concerning the amorous affections that rise above the senses, one may inquire in this manner. Come, what do you feel regarding honorable studies and duties, and honest ways, and temperate characters, and regarding all the works of virtue, and the affections, and habits, and the beauty of souls? What, I say, do you feel when you look upon your own inner beauties? And in what way (if I may say so) are you driven wild and stirred up? And do you desire to join with yourselves, gathering yourselves G apart from your bodies? For true lovers are affected in this way. But what is it toward which they are thus utterly affected? It is not a figure, not a color, not a size, but toward the soul itself, which is devoid of all color, and similarly possessing a temperance removed from color, and the splendor of the rest of the virtues...

...splendor: <note>original: "dorem" - the end of "splendorem" (splendor)</note> as often as you look within yourselves <margin>A</margin> or contemplate in another the greatness of soul and a just character; pure temperance; and furthermore, fortitude with a noble and venerable countenance; and finally modesty, and a venerable honor, walking with a certain fearless, tranquil, and serene step: and the divine mind illuminating these things from above. By what reasoning, then, shall we say these things are beautiful? For they are, and they are apparent; and no one who sees them will ever say they are anything other than <margin>B</margin> truly existing things. But what are truly existing things? Perhaps they are the beautiful. But reason still desires to know what makes these existences—so that the soul is lovable—and what is the light, as it were, upon all the virtues? Do you wish, by taking the opposites, which are clearly the base things in the soul, to compare them? Perhaps if we know what the base is, and <margin>C</margin> for what reason it is base, it will contribute to what we seek. Let there be, then, a base soul, which is intemperate and unjust, overflowing with many desires, and vexed by a great many disturbances because of fear, and suffering through <unclear>anxious</unclear> narrowness and avarice, laboring under envy: thinking of nothing but the mortal and the abject, always revolving crooked thoughts in the mind, enslaved to impure pleasures, leading a life proper to itself, whatever it may be that it suffers through the body: gladly taking its baseness through the body as something to be relished. And <margin>D</margin> shall we not say that this very baseness comes to the soul under the pretext of an external beauty, like an external evil? Which indeed, with heavy detriment, renders it impure, mixed with much wickedness, so that it neither <unclear>lives</unclear> further, nor feels endowed with purity, but through the mixture of evil, it now <unclear>sees</unclear> a meager life, worn down by much death, no longer seeing what <unclear>its own</unclear> things are for the one seeing; nor is it allowed to dwell with itself anymore, because it is always <margin>E</margin> snatched away toward external, lowest, and dark things. Indeed, becoming thus impure, snatched everywhere by those things which fall upon the senses, full of the stain of the body: namely, when it has given itself over to much of matter and has contracted a material nature into itself, surely falling into a worse state because of this sort of mixture, it has now changed its own appearance into another form: just as if someone <margin>F</margin> rolled in mud and filth no longer displays beauty. Indeed, let that be seen which he has contracted into himself from the mud and filth. Truly, to this one, baseness seems to have happened by the addition of a foreign nature. But if it desires to recover its former beauty, it will be worth the effort to wash away the stains: and by that very purgation to be again what it was. Therefore, if we say the soul becomes base by mixture, confusion, and commerce with the body and matter, we shall (I believe) be asserting correctly. For this is the baseness of the soul: namely, not to be <margin>G</margin> pure and sincere. Just as baseness happens to gold if it is covered with earthy clods: which if someone shakes off, pure gold suddenly remains; and that is now beautiful, when it has been separated from foreign things, so indeed it is content with the purity of beauty. In the same way, the mind, separated from these desires which it conceived in itself from too much commerce with the body, and from other disturbances...

<column-break/>

...the light of virtues, whenever you see something in them, or even behold in another the greatness of soul and a just character, and pure self-control, and courage having a stern face, and majesty, and modesty coming upon a steady, waveless, and passionless state; and above all these, the god-like intellect <note>original: "theoeidē noun" - the Divine Mind or Intellect, the highest part of the soul's reality</note> shining upon them. These things, being led and loved, how do we say they are beautiful? For they are, and they appear, and never would the one seeing them say they are anything else than the things which truly exist <margin>these things</margin>. What truly exists? Or the beautiful. But reason still longs to know: what makes the soul lovable? What is that light upon all the virtues? For instance, let it cast light even by taking the opposites: what would be the base things that arise around the soul? For perhaps it would contribute to what we seek—what the base is, and why we call it so. Let there be, then, a base soul: both intemperate and unjust, full of many desires, and of the greatest turmoil in fears; because of cowardice, in envies; because of small-mindedness, thinking all those things which it indeed thinks—mortal and lowly; crooked everywhere; a friend of impure pleasures; living a life of whatever it suffers through the body, as if having received the base as sweet, and it striking into her—shall we not say it is like an external beauty, or shall we say that which, coming upon something with it, has made it impure, and thoroughly fouled with much evil, no longer having life, nor pure sensation, but using a dim life by the mixture of evil, and mixed with much of the mortal, no longer seeing what a soul ought to see, no longer being allowed to remain in itself, by being dragged always toward the outside, and the bottom, and the dark? Being impure, I think, and carried everywhere by pulls toward the things that fall upon the senses, having much of the bodily mixed in, being much with the material, and having received another form into itself, it has changed by the mixture with the worse; as if someone [fell] into mud or filth, the beauty he had, he would no longer <margin>to result</margin> present this to be seen; but that <margin>wiped away</margin> which the mud or filth <margin>off</margin> showed upon him. To him, indeed, baseness came as a foreign addition, and it is a task for him, if indeed he is to be beautiful again, to wash and cleanse himself to be what he was. Thus, calling the soul base by mixture and blending and pollution with the body and matter, we would be speaking correctly. And this is the baseness for a soul: not to be pure and unmixed, just as if gold were filled with earth. If someone takes this away, the gold is left behind, and it is beautiful, isolated from other things and being only itself. In the same way, the soul, isolated from desires which it had because of the body with which it consorted too much, and freed from the other...

<summary>Plotinus discusses the beauty of the soul through its virtues—such as justice and temperance—noting that this beauty is intrinsic to the soul's true nature. He explains that vice and ugliness are not inherent to the soul, but are "foreign" additions caused by its entanglement with material concerns, much like mud covering gold.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of beauty. After describing the "base" or "ugly" soul on the previous page—one weighed down by material desires—he now describes the process of purification. He identifies the four classic virtues as tools for this cleansing, leading the soul back to its divine origin in the Intellect and the Good.</meta>

<header>BOOK SIX.</header>

<columns>

...freed from passions: those stains wiped away, which familiarity with the body had previously burned in: and thus, left alone to itself, it has undoubtedly purged away every ugliness <note>original: "αἰσχρὸν" (aischron) - meaning the base or ugly</note> that was thoroughly soaked in from a foreign nature.

**VI.** FOR INDEED, as the ancient saying goes, **temperance**, **fortitude**, and every **virtue**—and **wisdom** itself—are a certain purification. This is why the sacred mysteries <note>A reference to the Orphic or Eleusinian mysteries, which used rituals to symbolize the soul's journey.</note> rightly hint, though obscurely, that the unpurified soul lies in mud in the underworld. For that which is impure is, through its own depravity, a friend to the "mud"; just as pigs, being dirty in body, delight in such filth. For what else would true temperance be, if not to refuse indulgence in bodily pleasures, but to flee them as being neither pure nor belonging to the pure? **Fortitude**, truly, is not to fear death. And what is death but the separation of the soul from the body? He does not fear this who desires to be alone. Furthermore, **magnanimity** <note>Also called "greatness of soul."</note> is the contempt for mortal things. **Wisdom**, finally, is the act of the mind turning away from lower things and leading the soul toward the things above. The soul, having been purified, thus becomes a certain "form" and "reason" <term>Logos; the organizing principle or rational structure of a thing</term>, and is entirely incorporeal, intellectual, and wholly divine: from whence the fountain of beauty flows, and all things akin to it. Therefore, the soul, led back into the <term>Intellect (Nous); the realm of pure thought and eternal forms</term>, improves wonderfully in beauty. But the Intellect, and whatever flows from it, is not a foreign beauty, but the soul's own proper glory; for then alone is it truly a soul. Rightly, therefore, is it said that the "good" and "beautiful" for the soul consist in being like God: for from Him comes beauty and the true lot of existing things. Rather, that which is called "being" and "essence" is beauty itself. The opposite nature is the "ugly," and the primary evil; therefore, that same thing is the "Good" and the "Beautiful." Perhaps, indeed, the Good and Beauty are the self-same thing; therefore, the Beautiful and the Good are to be sought by a similar path, as are the ugly and the evil. In the first rank, Beauty itself must be placed, which is the same as the Good; from which the Intellect immediately flows as the "beautiful." The soul is beautiful through the Intellect, but other things—whether in actions or in studies and duties—are already made beautiful by the soul which gives them form. Now, whatever bodies are called beautiful are made so by the soul, which, being a divine thing and a portion of beauty itself, renders whatever it touches and masters beautiful, according to the capacity of their nature.

<margin>VI When the soul is pure, it allows the possessor to enjoy beauty itself.</margin>

**VII.** WE MUST ASCEND, therefore, again to the Good itself, which every soul desires. If anyone has seen it, he knows what I say: in what way it is beautiful. For it is desirable as the Good, and our desire tends toward it. But those who climb to the things above follow it, turning toward it as they strip off the garments they put on while descending. Just as those who enter the "holy of holies" of the temples are first purified, and strip off their previous clothes, and proceed naked, until someone, progressing in the ascent and having dismissed everything foreign to God, might see by himself alone that Divine itself: sincere, simple, and pure, upon which all things depend, and toward which all things look, and are, and live, and think. For He is the cause of life, and mind, and being.

<margin>* He might go up naked, until he reaches... [textual variant]</margin>

<column-break/>

...freed from passions: those stains wiped away, which familiarity with the body had previously burned in: and thus, left alone to itself, it has undoubtedly purged away every ugliness from a foreign nature that it had thoroughly absorbed.

<margin>VI When the soul is pure, it allows the possessor to enjoy beauty itself.</margin>

INDEED, just as the ancient oracle <note>Ficino translates the Greek "logos" as "oraculum," emphasizing the divine nature of the teaching.</note> tells us, **temperance**, **fortitude**, and **wisdom** itself, and altogether every virtue, is a kind of purification. For this reason, the sacred mysteries rightly, though quite obscurely, prophesy that the soul which is not purged lies in the mud among those in the lower world. For the impure soul, on account of its depravity, is a friend to the mud—just as pigs, filthy in body, take delight in filth. For what else is true temperance but not to indulge in bodily pleasures, but to flee far from them as things that are neither pure nor for the pure? **Fortitude** is truly not to fear death. For death is a certain separation of the soul from the body. He does not fear this who desires to be alone. Furthermore, **magnanimity** is the contempt for mortal things. **Wisdom**, finally, is intelligence turning away from lower things and raising the soul to the higher. The soul, therefore, having now been purified, becomes a "species" and a "reason," and entirely incorporeal, intellectual, and wholly divine: from whence the fountain of beauty flows, and all such kindred things. On this account, the soul, having been brought back into the **Intellect**, advances marvelously in beauty. Moreover, the Intellect and whatever flows from the Intellect is not a foreign ornament, but becomes the soul’s own proper glory; since it is then only that it is truly a soul. Rightly, therefore, is it said that the "good" and the "beautiful" for the soul consist in this: that it be like unto God. For from this source comes the beauty of the soul and the lot of existing things. Nay, even more: that which is called "being" and "essence" is beauty itself. The different nature is "ugliness," the primary evil; and therefore that same thing is the "good" and the "beautiful." Perhaps, indeed, the Good and Beauty are the very same; for which reason the beautiful and the good must be sought by a similar path, and likewise the ugly and the evil. In the first rank, Beauty itself must be placed, being the same as the Good itself; from which flows the Intellect as the "beautiful." The soul is beautiful by the Intellect; but other things are made beautiful by the soul that forms them, whether they be in actions or in the studies of duties. Now indeed, whatever bodies are called beautiful are made so by the soul, which, being a divine thing and a portion of beauty itself, makes whatever it has touched and mastered beautiful, according to the capacity of its nature.

<margin>VII The soul's affections toward matter are cast far away like clouds; it is flooded with pleasure at the light of invisible beauty, through examples found in things, which it then expresses.</margin>

WE MUST ASCEND, therefore, again to the Good itself, which every soul desires. If anyone has known it, he knows what I mean, in what way it is beautiful. It is indeed desirable as the Good, and toward it our desire tends. But he follows it who climbs to the higher things and turns toward it, insofar as he strips off what he had put on in descending. Just as those who penetrate into the "holy of holies" of the sacred places are first purified, and strip off their clothes, and proceed naked, until someone, progressing and having dismissed all things foreign to God, may by himself alone behold that Divine itself: sincere, simple, and pure, upon which all things depend, toward which they look, and are, and live, and think. For He is the cause of life, of mind, and of being.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion on the soul's ascent. Having established that the soul must be purified of material stains to see true beauty, Plotinus now describes the overwhelming experience of beholding the "Primary Beauty" and the specific method for beginning this inward journey, famously warning against the "Narcissus-like" trap of physical reflections.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK I.

Whoever has seen this [divine Beauty], by Jupiter, <margin>A</margin> with how great a love they burn, with what desire they are inflamed, longing vehemently to be united with it: how wonderfully they mix pleasure with a holy awe. For it is so ordained by nature that he who does not yet see it, seeks it as the **Good**; but he who already sees it, is delighted by it as the **Beautiful**, and is filled equally with admiration and pleasure. He is struck by a certain healing stupor; he is moved by the true and highest love. He laughs at sharp passions and other lesser loves, and <margin>B</margin> despises those things which were previously held to be beautiful. This is exactly what happens to those who, having met with the forms of gods or spirits <note>original: "daemonum" — in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary beings between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense</note>, no longer care for the beauty of other bodies. What then do we think he would do, who has contemplated Beauty itself? I mean Beauty itself, pure in its own nature: not weighed down by flesh, nor by any body; not confined by earth, nor by heaven; so that it exists in its purity. For all these other things are added from the outside and are mixed, <margin>C</margin> and are not primary, but proceed from it. If anyone, therefore, should ever behold that which offers gifts to all, yet remains meanwhile in itself while it gives, and receives nothing from another—remaining in the intuition of it and so enjoying it that he becomes like it—how much more beauty could he possibly need? For that, being the chief and primary Beauty itself, <margin>D</margin> makes its lovers beautiful and lovable. Here, truly, is the greatest and final struggle <note>original: "certamen" — a reference to the athletic contests of Greece; the soul's journey is the "Olympic games" of the spirit</note> proposed to souls, for the sake of which we must labor entirely, lest we be left without a share of that best contemplation. He who attains this is blessed by a happy vision; but he who does not attain it is unhappy. For a man is not wretched because he lacks beautiful colors or handsome bodies; nor he who fails to gain power, office, or a kingdom; but he who lacks this possession alone, <margin>E</margin> for the sake of which alone one should cast away kingdoms and empires of the whole earth, the sea, and the sky: if, by leaving all these behind and scorning them, one might turn toward it and behold it.

<margin>
VIII
How the
soul may see
Beauty.
</margin>
**WHAT** then is the way? What method? What reasoning allows one to contemplate this inestimable beauty: a beauty, I say, established in sacred inner chambers, not coming out into the open where the profane might see it? Let him enter, therefore, and let whoever is able proceed into <margin>F</margin> the innermost parts, leaving behind the sight of the eyes and not looking back at the accustomed spectacles of the senses. For he who looks upon this must look at no bodily beauty at all, but recognizing that these bodily things are images, footprints, and shadows, he must not flee toward those things of which these are merely representations. For if <margin>G</margin> anyone should rush toward these as if they were real—just as beautiful images appear on the water—he will undoubtedly suffer what (as the myth tells) he suffered who, trying to catch a shadow, plunged into the water and perished. For in a similar way, he who embraces the forms of bodies and does not let go, is plunged into the dark depths, hateful to the mind, not so much in body as in soul; where, remaining blind even in the underworld, he will dwell among shadows both here and there. Let us therefore flee to our

<column-break/>

Who then, if they saw it, what kind of loves would they feel, <margin>* in this manner</margin> what kind of longings, wishing to be blended with it, <margin>A</margin> and how would they be struck with pleasure? For it is possible for one who has not yet seen it to desire it as the Good; but for one who has seen it, it is his to wonder at its beauty and be filled with awe combined with pleasure, and to be struck without harm, and to love with a true love and sharp longings, and to laugh at other loves, and to look down <margin>B</margin> upon those things previously thought beautiful. This is the experience of those who have seen the forms of gods or spirits, for they would no longer accept the beauties of other bodies in the same way. What then do we think if someone were to see Beauty itself, by itself, pure, not full of flesh, not full of body, not on earth, not in heaven, but pure? From which <margin>C</margin> all these things are mixed, and are not primary, but come from that. If then one should see that which supplies everything, yet staying in itself gives and does not receive, if one should see it, staying in the contemplation of it and enjoying it, becoming like it, what more of beauty would he need? For this is itself the highest beauty, which being the first, makes its lovers beautiful and makes them lovable. This is indeed the greatest and ultimate struggle <margin>D</margin> set before souls, for the sake of which all our labor is spent: not to be left without a share of the best vision, which he who attains is blessed, having seen a blessed sight; but he is unfortunate who does not attain it. For he is not wretched who does not attain beautiful colors or bodies, or power, or offices, or a kingdom, but he who fails in this and this alone. For the sake of this, one should let go of kingdoms and rule over the whole earth, and sea, and heaven, <margin>E</margin> if by leaving these behind and overlooking them, one might turn toward that and see it.

What then is the way? What device? How may one see the incredible beauty which remains within in the holy sanctuaries and does not come out to the exterior, lest some profane person see it? Let him go then and follow into the interior, he who is able, leaving behind the sight of the eyes, and not turning himself back to the previous splendors of bodies. <margin>F</margin> For having seen the beauties in bodies, one must not run toward them, but knowing that they are images and traces and shadows, one must flee to that of which these are images. For if one should run to them, wishing to seize them as true—as beautiful images carried on water—he who wished to seize them, as some myth (I think) hints, <margin>G</margin> by sinking into the depth of the stream, vanished. In the same way, he who clings to beautiful bodies and does not let go, will sink not in his body, but in his soul, into the dark and unpleasant depths, where remaining blind in the underworld, he lives with shadows both here and there. Let us flee to our dear fatherland! As someone might more truly exhort us,

<meta>This page continues the famous conclusion of Plotinus's treatise "On Beauty" (Ennead I.6). Having warned against the soul becoming trapped by physical reflections—like Narcissus—Plotinus now provides the practical instructions for the "flight" to the divine fatherland, introducing the celebrated metaphor of the soul as a sculptor of its own character.</meta>

# BOOK SIX. <note>original: "LIBER SEXTVS" — Referring to the sixth treatise of the first Ennead, "On Beauty."</note>

What then is this flight? And how shall we be led back? Just as it is said of **A** Odysseus—which I believe is a riddle—fleeing from Circe or Calypso, for he was not willing to remain, even though he had pleasures for his eyes and lived with great beauty perceived by the senses. Our fatherland, however, is the place from which we came, and our Father is there. What then is this flight? It is not accomplished by **B** feet, which carry the legs across the earth from one land to another; nor do you need to prepare a carriage for horses or ships for the sea. Instead, you must let all these things go and not look back; rather, as if closing your eyes, you must exchange your physical sight for another kind of vision, and awaken that sight which everyone possesses, but which very few use.

What, then, does that inner eye behold? Just as it is **C** awakening, it is not yet able to look upon very brilliant things. Therefore, the soul must be accustomed first to look at beautiful pursuits; then at beautiful works—not those produced by the arts, but those performed by men who are called "good." Next, behold the soul of those who perform these beautiful works. How then might you see the beauty of a good soul? **D** Withdraw into yourself and look. And if you do not yet see yourself as beautiful, then act like the creator of a statue that is to be made beautiful: he cuts away some parts, scrapes others, makes this part smooth and that part clean, until he reveals a beautiful face in the statue. In the same way, you too must cut away whatever is superfluous and straighten whatever is crooked; by purifying what is dark, make it work to be bright, and never stop "sculpting" your own statue until the godlike splendor of virtue shines out upon you—until you see **Temperance** <note>original: "σωφροσύνην" (sophrosyne) — the virtue of self-control and harmony</note> standing firmly in her holy and pure majesty. If you have become this, and have seen it, and have joined with yourself in purity—having no obstacle toward becoming one in this way, nor having anything else mixed in with you inside, but being entirely yourself, a true and solitary light, not measured by magnitude, nor restricted by any shape into a smaller form, nor increased into a great size through a lack of limit, but everywhere unmeasurable, as being greater than any measure and superior to any quantity— <insert>or his own</insert> 

<margin>
His own perfection
</margin>
if you see that you have become this, you have now become Sight itself. Having gained confidence in yourself and having **F** already ascended to this point, you no longer need one to show you the way; fix your gaze and look. For this is the only eye that beholds that Great Beauty. But if the

<margin>
Cowardice
</margin>
eye goes to the spectacle while infected by the filth of vices and not yet purified, or if it is weak through a lack of courage <note>original: "ἀνδρίᾳ" (andreia) — manly courage or fortitude</note> and unable to look at very bright things, it sees nothing, even if someone else points out the spectacle as being present and perfectly prepared to be seen. For the one who sees must be made kindred and similar to the thing seen before they may apply themselves to the vision. **G** For the eye would never have seen the sun had it not first become sun-like; nor can the soul see Beauty unless it has become beautiful itself. Therefore, let everyone first become godlike and beautiful if they intend to behold God and Beauty. For thus, first, in his ascent, he will come to the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦν" (Nous) — the divine Mind or first emanation in Neoplatonism</note>.

<column-break/>

<meta>The Latin column follows the Greek text almost exactly, serving as a translation and commentary for the reader of the era. The following is the English rendering of the Latin column's specific phrasing.</meta>

...fleeing to the sweet fatherland. What then is the method of fleeing? And by what way shall we avoid the enchantments of Circe and Calypso? This is indeed what the obscure fable of Ulysses signifies: it depicts him as unwilling to stay, even though sights pleasing to his eyes met him, and other things that delight the senses were promised. Our fatherland is truly there, from whence we came, and our Father is in that same place. What fleet, then, or what flight shall we use? Surely we must not flee on feet. For feet carry us only from one land to another. Nor again should we prepare horses for carrying us, nor ships for sailing for this purpose; rather, we must dismiss all these things and not even look toward them. Instead, with the sight of the body closed, we must assume another sight in its place, one which shines from within. Everyone has this, but very few use it.

<margin>
IX. How the soul tends toward that conspicuous and spiritual splendor, from which its beauty had previously shone forth.
</margin>
What then does that innermost eye behold? Surely, having been suddenly awakened, it cannot yet look upon bright things. The soul must therefore be accustomed first to consider beautiful studies, then beautiful works—works, I say, not produced by the arts, but those performed by upright men. After these things, you must behold the soul of those who perform such deeds. By what means, then, will you behold the beauty of a good soul? Come, call yourself back into yourself and contemplate; and if you do not yet recognize yourself as beautiful, imitate the statuary <note>a sculptor</note>. For when he desires a beautiful statue, he cuts away some parts, directs others, and by polishing he scrapes away, making it smooth and clean until he expresses a lovely face in the statue. So you also: take away what is superfluous, direct what is crooked, and by purging the dark things, make them bright. Do not cease working on your statue until the divine glow of virtue shines upon you, until you see Temperance sitting firmly in pure and holy majesty. If you have escaped into this state, and have inspected it and yourself at the same time, and now live purely within yourself—having clearly no impediment to being made one—and having nothing else mixed with you inside, but being yourself entirely a true and solitary light: a light, I say, not measured by magnitude, not circumscribed by some confining shape, not swollen by magnitude (though it is immense), but immeasurable everywhere, as being greater than every measure and superior to every quantity—if, I say, you see yourself having become that, you have now become Sight itself. Relying on yourself, and having progressed to the point where you no longer need a guide or an indicator: fix your gaze now. For only this eye beholds the vast beauty. But if by chance the eye is infected with filth and not yet purged, or is weak from cowardice when it is directed toward the most lucid spectacle, it will immediately grow dark and discern nothing, even if someone demonstrates a spectacle that is otherwise able to be seen. For it is necessary that the one who is to see be first made kindred and similar to the thing seen before he is applied to the viewing. Truly, the eye would never see the sun unless it had been made sun-like. Nor again will the soul behold Beauty itself unless it has been made beautiful. Therefore, let anyone become divine, or "deiform," and beautiful, if he is to behold God and Beauty. For thus he will first ascend into the Intellect.

# MARSILIO FICINO’S ARGUMENT ON BOOK VII: ON THE FIRST GOOD AND OTHER GOODS.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->*The Good itself is beyond essence, life, and intellect.*<-

<margin>I</margin>
In the universal order of things, no <term>essence</term> <note>original: "essentia" — referring to the fundamental being or nature of a thing.</note> rests within itself, but everything naturally and always strives with its whole power toward action. This natural and proper function of all essences is granted by none other than the "First Essence," because that First Essence itself comes forth into action in a nearly similar way. Every essence, and Essence itself, proceeds into action so that it may be better off as a result. Neither these steps, nor the things taken in them, are the Good itself, since they do not rest in themselves but advance toward the "better" through acting. For an essence is better off if it acts than if it does not. Furthermore, its action is not the Good itself, nor the highest end of essence; for action depends on the power of the essence, while the action of essence simultaneously depends on the Good. It acts always so that it may be better through acting; and it would not be better unless it were always acting toward the Good. For a thing was well-off initially when its action proceeded from the Good, and it is well-off again—and even better—when it turns itself with all its effort toward the Good itself. 

Now, from the fact that essence and its act (which is <term>life</term> and <term>intellect</term>) are perfected by the Good itself as their goal, we can infer that they are produced by the Good as their principle. For from wherever a thing is produced, it is also there that it is perfected. Human nature also bears witness to this: men do not desire "to be" and "to live" simply for their own sake, but so that they may be *well* and live *well*. It is as if they desire these things only for the sake of the Good itself. By a certain natural judgment, they prefer the gift of the Good over the gift of "being" or "living" alone. Just as they sometimes reject being and living—not simply, but for the sake of avoiding evil, so that they do not exist or live miserably—so too they embrace these things for the sake of the Good, so that they may be well and live as excellently as possible. 

Therefore, the innermost action of essence—whether it be called life, motion, or knowledge—is not the Good in itself. If it were to depend on evil, or fall toward evil by chance or error, it would undoubtedly be evil. It exists and becomes "good," therefore, through something higher: specifically, by proceeding naturally from the Good it possesses something similar to the Good, and by rightly turning itself back toward the Good, it is made similar to it again. He concludes, therefore: just as individual essences relate to their own specific goods, so too Essence itself relates to the Good itself. The Good is preferred by essence, and the Good itself is placed before essence. That the Good and the "One" are entirely the same, and that the One is superior to essence, will be discussed more appropriately elsewhere. But let this be the summary of this book so far. He treats the Good briefly here, as if preparing an "argument" for his other books in which he discusses the Good most diligently. There are three chapters in this book or argument. In the first, he proves that the Good is that toward which all things are carried, while the Good itself is carried toward nothing. In the second, he shows how other things are carried toward it and referred to it. In the third, he raises and solves three questions concerning the matters above.

---

### The good proper to each thing is a natural action, readily directed toward the universal Good itself, which is the principle and end of all things.

<margin>I</margin>
In the first chapter, he teaches that action is a certain good for everyone—action, I say, not simply, but with a twofold condition. First, it must be a **natural action**; that is, not forced and not accidental. Second, it must not fail in any part; that is, it must be neither weak nor crooked, but must be carried powerfully and rightly toward the end. But why is such an action "the good"? Because it is natural precisely because it was implanted by the Good itself, the author of nature. Likewise, because while it tends rightly toward its end, it is necessarily carried toward the Good itself. For the Good, as the principle of all nature, has established every nature toward itself as its goal. Among these things, he signifies that those which are below the rational soul are led by nature properly toward certain "goods" of their own. Toward the first and highest Good itself, nature does not lead them properly, but in attaining their own specific goods, they bring back a certain likeness of it. But the soul, which through the intellect can conceive the common reason of the whole of being outside of the whole, and can sense the fountain of the Good itself, rightly leads you toward the <meta>Good...</meta>

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of Beauty in Ennead I.6 to the nature of the Good in Ennead I.7. Marsilio Ficino continues his commentary, synthesizing Plotinus's Greek philosophy with a theological framework, focusing on how all things originate from and return to the "First Good."</meta>

# ON BOOK VII OF THE FIRST ENNEAD

It is proper for the first and highest <term>Principle</term><note>The "Principle" (principium) refers to the source or origin of all existence.</note> to be able to proceed continuously and finally to arrive at its goal. But so that we may understand what the Good itself is, two things especially must be understood first: First, that there is a certain principle of things, and that it exists as one. Second, that this very thing is the end <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing’s existence.</note> of all things. Indeed, in our <term>Theology</term><note>Ficino often uses "our Theology" to refer to the Platonic tradition which he viewed as compatible with Christian truth.</note> we assert this whole point with many arguments. We conclude that if a first and highest principle were not granted, but if things instead proceeded from one to another in succession without any end, whatever you found would depend on something else, and would by its own nature be changeable and wavering. There would be no stable foundation for changing things, nor any fixed axis for the mutable. Consequently, there would be no stability in things, no order, no reason, and no harmony. 

However, since all things perpetually maintain a certain stable order and lead everywhere to a single form of the universal work and to one common universal end, it is established that there is a certain highest principle of all things, existing everywhere. Moreover, that it is also the end of all things is clear from this: since the highest principle depends on nothing, it neither looks toward nor acts toward anything else, nor does it establish all things for any end other than itself. Therefore, the principle of the universe and its own end are the same. This is nothing other than the **Good itself**. 

For if it is the highest principle, surely all things are made, perfected, and restored by it; therefore, it is the highest good of all. Likewise, if it is the highest and ultimate end of all, it follows that it is that for the sake of which individual things always act. Indeed, all things do whatever they do for the sake of the Good itself. From both sides, therefore, it is established by fate that the Good of all is the same as the principle and the end of all. This same point is confirmed by the fact that no better gift can be shown to things than what is handed down from the highest principle; again, no better gift than what is offered by the Good itself. 

From this, it is clear that the principle of all and the Good are the same, and the end is the same. For all things are affected in the best possible way in their principle; again, all things are in the best possible state in their desired end. Finally, since individual things are turned back toward the place from which they proceeded by desiring it with all their strength, and since all things are thus turned toward the Good as toward an end, it is clear that all things proceeded from the Good as from a principle. 

Other things are judged to be "good" by a certain action—by a double action, I say: first, that which flows from them as good (which is nothing other than the Good itself on one hand, and on the other, the essence and vital act of the things made from it); and second, that which is carried toward the Good. This latter is appetite, inclination, movement, and generation. But the principle and end of all is not "good" by any action at all, but by its own first and simple nature; just as the primary light or heat shines and warms by nothing other than itself. I say "not by any action" because it is neither extrinsic (for it does not concern itself with another thing, nor acquire anything from elsewhere) nor intrinsic: for it is not good by any essential, vital, or intellectual act. 

First, because if it is <term>above-essence</term><note>original: "super-essentiam." This is the Neoplatonic concept that the One/Good is so transcendent that it cannot even be called "Being" or "Essence" in the way we understand those terms.</note>, which we shall prove, it is much more above and before all such acts which follow essence. Second, because the definition of the Good is one thing, and that of essence is another. For essence is sought for the sake of something else—that is, for the sake of the Good—but the Good itself is sought only for its own sake. Again, the definition of the Good is one thing, and that of life and intellect another; for the Good itself exists by its own necessity simply. Life and intellection, however, are judged to be choices only if they are good and happy—if you live well, if you understand good things, if the act of understanding is good for you. Otherwise, they are sometimes rejected. But the nature of the Good itself cannot be rejected by anyone. Furthermore, the logic and gift of the Good are propagated through all things; but the logic of life and the nature of intelligence cannot be extended through all things. 

Since, therefore, the nature of the Good is both different from, and prior and superior to, the nature of essence, life, and intelligence, it is certainly "good" by none of their acts, but only by itself. For this reason, at the end of this chapter, Plotinus compares the Good itself to a center and the sun, while other things are compared to the circumference and the lines, or to light and its rays. For the Good, remaining simple and stable, produces all things, while the rest are manifold and, in a sense, mobile, continually revolving around it through natural desire. But concerning this comparison and light itself, we shall speak more carefully elsewhere.

->Those things below the soul do not have true unity, essence, or form,<-
->and therefore lack true goodness; but the soul and higher<-
->things possess those three truly, as well as true goodness.<-

**11** In the second chapter, it is taught that different things turn toward the Good itself by desiring it in different ways. Things that are below the soul receive life from the soul; and if they are separated from life by any force, they are separated with difficulty and some pain; and they strive to be joined again however they can. This can be seen more clearly in the parts of plants and animals. While these things capture life from the soul with all zeal, they are meanwhile proceeding toward the Good; for they proceed toward the better as they approach the soul, which is closer to the Good itself. 

But the soul proceeds toward the Good through the intellect; for through that which is highest in itself, it rightly rises to the highest of the universe. And lower souls look out for the Good for themselves, some through sense-perception, others through imagination; and finally, our souls through reason. Sense-perception is a trace of intelligence; imagination, again, is a confused image of intelligence. Reason, finally, is a distinct image of the same. 

Accordingly, something of the Good is inserted into all things; and not without cause, since the Good itself is the principle of all. Three things especially are seen as gifts of the Good itself in things. The first is **unity**; the second is **essence**; the third is **form** (species). But why is unity first? Because the Good itself and the <term>One itself</term><note>original: "ipsum vnum." In Plotinian thought, the One and the Good are identical names for the ultimate source.</note> are entirely the same. For nothing can be thought of as simpler than unity itself; again, nothing simpler than goodness itself. Since nothing is prior to it, it alone is the principle of all. I pass over the fact that just as all things perish by dispersing into a multitude, so they are preserved by union, and being preserved, they are perfected from that point. Since, therefore, all things are preserved by unity and proceed toward the better—and this can only happen by goodness alone—it follows that the first unity and goodness are the same. 

The second gift of the Good follows, which is essence, which must necessarily come after the One. For the One itself admits no multitude or composition within itself; but essence and "being" do admit them. For although nature forbids something to exist as unity itself and yet have multitude within it at the same time, nothing forbids a thing to be considered "being" and "essence" even if it is composed of many parts. Since, therefore, the One itself is simpler than being and essence, it is necessarily both prior and superior. And unity is rightly placed as the first gift of the highest principle, while essence is the second. For unity is more widely present in things than essence. For "to be" (existence) does not truly belong to matter or to privation <note>Privation refers to the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like darkness being the privation of light.</note>. For those things which lack form, in which "being" consists, rightly lack "being." However, matter can be called "one" even though it is formless. And blindness can be called "one privation," just as a habit is one. Matter can also be called "good" in a way, insofar as it desires the good and proceeded from the Good. Nor does anything prevent it from being indicated as good in some way, even though in Plotinus's view it is evil itself. For if the Good itself admits nothing in itself...

<summary>This page explains that the "Good" is the source and goal of all existence. Ficino argues that for the universe to have order, there must be a single, stable principle (the One) that provides the gifts of unity, essence, and form to all things.</summary>

### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

of evil; nevertheless, evil itself (if it is even right to speak of evil itself) is compelled under the immense empire of the Good to desire the good, and even to be named after the good. The third gift of the Good is <term>Form</term><note>The Latin *species* refers to the specific form, appearance, or defining essence of a thing.</note>. For this is a certain determination, or distinction, or act of essence. But when you hear here that the gift of the One and the Good is propagated more widely than the gift of Being and Essence, conclude that the One and the Good themselves are superior to Being. Furthermore, just as there is unity, essence, and form in things, so too is there a <term>participation</term><note>In Platonic thought, "participation" is the way lower, material things share in the qualities of higher, divine Realities.</note> in the Good. Certainly, from the First Mind, in other minds, and in animals endowed with reason, there is a true participation in the Good because there is true unity, essence, and form. For even if the unity in them has admitted a certain multitude, it nevertheless produces a "one" there, because it overcomes the multitude and renders the "one" indissoluble. Therefore, true essence exists there as well, since at no time can it cease to be. There is also true form, since the form there cannot be resolved into something formless. In the lower things of the soul, however, unities are often overcome by multitude, and therefore they can for the most part be dissolved; in their essence there is a certain privation and a sliding toward non-being; and the form is mixed with a subject that is entirely formless, into which it falls. For this reason, there is no true "one" in these things, no true essence, and no true form—and therefore, there is no true participation in the Good, but only an imaginary one.

->Just as life is not a good simply in itself, but rather is a good if it is directed toward the highest principle,<-
->so death is not an evil simply in itself, but rather is a good if it separates the soul from evil—that is, from matter.<-

III. The third chapter brings three questions into the middle of the discussion. The first is of this kind: If life is a good, is living a good for anyone and in any way they might live? Certainly not: because life itself is not the first and simplest good in its own right, but rather life becomes perfect only insofar as it rises powerfully and directly toward that first Good. But if it limps and wanders, falling away from the Good itself, it simultaneously degenerates from the perfection of life. Hence that saying of Democritus: "To live imprudently, intemperately, and impiously is not so much to live badly as it is to die for a long time." <note>original: "Viuere imprudenter, intemperanter, impie non tam malè viuere est, quàm diu mori."</note> The second question: Since life becomes a certain evil for the soul when it is mixed with mortality and disturbed by it—even though it may be a good for the body and for the universe—is death not an evil, given that what is mortal makes life evil by its proximity? In responding, he asks: To whom is death an evil? Certainly, since evil is either an <term>accident</term><note>An "accident" is a quality that is not essential to a thing's nature, like the color of a shirt.</note> or even weaker than an accident, and therefore cannot stand by itself, it must necessarily happen to something. It does not happen to that which in no way exists, nor to that which by nature can exist without life. Again, it does not happen to the soul if the soul is immortal; and in whatever other way it might happen, it will benefit the eternal soul, which will perform its own proper actions more perfectly without the hindrance of the body. If, after the death of the body, the soul does not perform its own proper actions so much as common ones—acting as a colleague to the Soul of the World—much less can any evil happen to it there, where it already lives with the universal life. On the contrary, for a soul that is gravely ill with disturbances, whether here or in the lower world, death is rather to be desired, and life is the evil. Here that question is solved: Whether souls that are supremely miserable would prefer to die rather than live. And without a doubt, nature teaches this; for those who are gravely tormented, on her advice, prefer to lose their senses rather than feel dire pains. Finally, since the soul has its own life, and is by its essence a certain life living in itself, it neither borrows life from elsewhere nor undergoes death. If, however, someone defines "living" as being joined to the body and "death" as being separated from the body, both will happen to the soul in this sense, but neither will properly change its substance. The third question: If life is good, why is death not also evil? He responds that death is not simply an evil because life is not simply a good. For life is judged to be similar to a certain motion; and motion, whatever kind it may be, ought to be named from the goal toward which it properly tends. Therefore, insofar as that vital motion perhaps slides toward evil—that is, toward matter—to that extent it is judged to be an evil. Insofar as it directs itself toward the Good itself—that is, toward the highest principle of the universe—to that extent it is judged to be a good.

<summary>Ficino explains that life's value is not intrinsic but depends on its orientation toward the "First Good," arguing that death can be a benefit if it frees the soul from the corruption of matter. He concludes that the soul's essential nature is life itself, meaning it cannot truly die even when separated from the body.</summary>

->ON the first good, and other goods.<-
->Concerning the first good and other goods.<-

<image-desc>The page features two columns of text, each beginning with a decorative woodcut drop-cap 'A'. The left column is in Ancient Greek and the right column is in Latin. The drop-caps depict floral or classical motifs. Marginal notes are present in both margins.</image-desc>

Is it enough to suppose that the good for each being is the <term>activity</term><note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia). In Plotinus, this refers to the "actualization" or the "working" of a thing's nature.</note> of its life according to its nature? And if a thing is composed of many parts, is its good the preservation of the better part within it—an activity that is always its own, natural, and never failing? The activity of the soul, then, is its natural good. But if the soul also acts toward the best—provided it is the best of things—then its good is not only relative to itself, but is the Good in an absolute sense. For if a thing does not act for the sake of any other, and is the most excellent of all beings—indeed, is "beyond" beings—and all other things act toward it, then it is clearly the Good itself, through which all other things become participants in the good. I mean other things in relation to that 
<margin>not</margin>
\*then the good\* which is achieved by being likened to it and by directing one's activity toward it. For the desire and the activity are directed toward the best as the Good. Indeed, the Good itself must not look toward another, nor desire any other thing; it must be fixed, the fountain and source of activities that are according to nature, making other things "good-like" because they act toward it. For that First Principle is good not by its activity, nor by its thought, but by its very being. For if it exists beyond activity, and beyond mind <unclear>and</unclear> thought, then it is the Good upon which all things are suspended, while it is suspended from nothing. For this is how the saying is true: "that which all things desire." Therefore, it remains still, and all things turn back toward it, just as a circle turns toward its center, from which all lines radiate. The sun serves as an example: it is like a center for the light that hangs from it; the light is joined to it from all sides and is not cut off; even if you try to cut it off on one side, the light remains with the sun.

<column-break/>

<margin>The good proper to each thing is set before it and is found by acting according to its nature.</margin>
Can anyone say that the good for each thing is anything other than the natural action of its life? And if something is composed of many parts, is its good the very action of its better part—an action that is always its own, in harmony with nature, and lacking in no respect? 
<margin>It is good not by action, but as an end in itself.</margin>
The soul’s action according to its nature is therefore its good. But if it acts further toward the best—provided it is itself at its best—then not only is that which pertains to itself good, but it exists as the Good simply. If, therefore, something acts in no way for another, since it is itself the most excellent of all things and above all things, while all other things act toward it, it is clear that this itself is the Good, by whose virtue other things also become participants in the good. Other things possess the good in two main ways: both because they are made similar to it, and because they operate toward it. Accordingly, if the desire and action toward the best is good, it follows that the Good itself does not look toward another, and desires nothing else. It is the fixed and entirely peaceful principle of all natural actions: indeed, it makes other things good by their likeness to itself. It makes them so, I say, not by any action upon them, but because they act toward it. Thus it is clear that it exists as the Good not through any intelligence or action at all, but solely by itself. For because it stands above essence, it stands above action, and transcends both intellect and intelligence. Furthermore, one must assert that this is the very Good to which all things are referred, while it is referred to no other. Thus, it is clearly true that the Good itself is what all things desire. It must, therefore, remain firmly fixed and turn all things toward itself, just as a circle revolves around a center, from which each individual line is produced. The Sun can be an example for us; it is like a center for the light that depends on it and is simultaneously joined to it; thus, the light exists everywhere along with it and is never separated from it. And even if—

<meta>The bottom line serves as a catch-line for the Latin text flow.</meta>
you should wish to separate it on the other side, the light meanwhile remains strong within the sun.

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK I
<page-num>62</page-num>

<margin>
II
In all things there is something of the Good itself: accordingly, and following this, each thing is in some way a true good.
</margin>

But how do all other things refer back to the Good itself? Truly, insofar as they are reduced to the soul; and the soul is reduced to the Good itself through the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦς" (nous). In Neoplatonism, the Intellect is the first emanation from the One/the Good, containing the eternal Forms.</note>. However, everything possesses something of the Good, insofar as each thing is in a certain way "one" and a "being," and a participant in a **Form** <note>original: "speciei" / "εἴδους" (eidous). These are the ideal patterns or blueprints of all things.</note>. By the same reasoning that it participates in these, it also participates in the Good; therefore, it is a participant in the image. For those things which participate are considered images of the "one being." Forms are similarly so. But in the soul, which is first and closest to the intellect, to live is nearer to the truth, and it obtains the "shape" of the Good through the intellect—it obtains it, I say, if it receives the Good itself; for the intellect holds its seat after the Good itself. Therefore, life must be judged a good for those to whom it is given to live; likewise, the intellect is a good for all whom intelligence suits. Thus, wherever life flourishes together with the intellect, the Good is present in a twofold way.

<margin>
III
Three questions about evils. 1. Is death an evil for the living? 2. Is death itself an evil? 3. Is it in itself simply a good or an evil?
</margin>

But if life is a good, does it perhaps belong to every living thing? No, indeed it does not. For life in a wicked man is "lame," no different than an eye that does not see clearly; indeed, it does not perform its proper work. Furthermore, if life—insofar as it is mixed within us—is a "evil-good" <note>This refers to the "mixed" nature of human life, combining spiritual good with bodily hardship.</note>, why should death not be an evil? But for whom would it be an evil? For an evil must happen to *someone*. But that which is called "dead" no longer exists; or if it does exist, it lacks life, and even then it is no more an evil than it is for a stone. But if life and the soul continue after death, then death will surely be a good; all the more so because the soul performs its actions without a body. If the soul becomes a companion to the **All-Soul** <note>original: "totius animae". The cosmic soul that governs the universe.</note>, what evil can happen to a living being there? Just as among the gods the Good exists without any mixture of evils, so within the soul nothing at all is evil, provided it preserves its purity. If it does not preserve it, then not death, but life is the evil for it. Moreover, if punishments are paid in the **underworld** <note>original: "apud inferos". The place of the dead or the lower spiritual realms.</note>, then life there is again an evil for the soul, because it is not life alone. But if life is the coupling of the soul and the body, and death is their dissolution, the soul can experience both. Yet if life is good, why will death not be an evil? Certainly, life is good for those who possess the Good, not indeed by reason of the "coupling" [with the body], but because they repel evil through virtue. Death is, in fact, the greater good. In summary, it must be said that life in the body is itself an evil, but the soul is established in the Good through virtue—not by preserving and giving life to the composite [of body and soul], but by now segregating itself from its commerce with the body.

<column-break/>

But how do all other things relate to it? Either all things, or the soulless things toward the soul, and the soul toward it. And through the intellect and [the Good] itself, by each being "one" in a way and "being" in a way, and by participating in a **Form**. As it participates in these, so it participates in the Good; they are reflections, then, of what they participate in—reflections of being and of existing, and of "faring well" in the same way.

<margin>B</margin>
For the soul, to live—for the first soul which follows the intellect—is closer to the truth and is of the nature of the intellect; it is "good-formed," and it would possess the Good if it looked toward it. For the intellect comes after the Good. They would say, then, that for the living thing, life is a good, and the intellect is a good for that which participates in the intellect; so that for whatever possesses life together with the intellect, it is twofold in its relation to the Good.

If indeed life is a good, does it belong to every living thing? Or is life "lame" in the wicked man, just as in an eye that does not see clearly? For its work is [impaired]. If indeed life for us—whether or not it is mixed 
<margin>C</margin>
evil with good—how is death not an evil? And to whom? For evil must happen to someone. But that [which is dead] is not the cause. Or if it is a turning away from life, is it then an evil for a stone? Or if there is life and soul after death, it would already be a good, insofar as the soul acts more according to its own nature without the body. And if it becomes part of the **Whole** <note>original: "τῆς ὅλης" (tēs holēs). Refers to the World Soul or the Universal Being.</note>, can there be any evil there? And entirely, just as for the gods there is good and no evil, so it is for the soul which preserves its 
<margin>D</margin>
purity. But if it should not preserve it, death would not be the evil for it, but life, or the lack of true life. And if there are injustices [and punishments], then life itself there is an evil—not only the lack of life, but the life that is present. If life is the life of the soul and body, and death is the dissolution of these, the soul is receptive to both. But if life is good, how is death not evil? Or is life good for those for whom it is good, not according to the 
<margin>E</margin>
union [of body and soul], but because through virtue it wards off evil? Thus death is the greater good. Or it must be said, that life in the body is an evil in itself; but the soul comes to be in the Good through virtue, not by saving the composite [being], but by already separating itself.
