# MARSILIO FICINO'S ARGUMENT ON BOOK VIII: WHAT EVILS ARE, AND WHENCE THEY COME.
f 2

### Four questions concerning good and evil.

This entire book seems to be concerned with how we might avoid evils to the best of our strength and pursue goods: that is, that we might flee from **matter** <note>original: "materiam." In Neoplatonism, matter is not just physical "stuff" but the absolute limit of existence, often associated with the absence of light or "form," and thus the source of evil.</note> and follow divine things separated from matter. We are to recognize that the very principle of the universe is the **Good** itself, but the "last" part of the universe—that is, matter—is **evil** itself. It teaches how evil affects us and by what reasoning we may finally avoid it. The first chapter of the book raises these questions: What things are truly evil, and from where do they proceed? However, in order to find these, the author inquires into what things are good; and to find these in turn, he sets out to track down what the Good itself is, or what evil is. He also asks how we can know evil, since, due to its inherent weakness, it is entirely foreign to the **form** <note>original: "forma." Here meaning the structural essence or "blueprint" of the mind.</note> of the knowing soul. He teaches that the weakness of evil is discerned through the very form and light of the good. Finally, he asks in what way evil is contrary to the good—whether, perhaps, it is like a defect of the universe compared to the universe's primary cause, or a total poverty compared to a total abundance. 

Where he says that the power of knowing is very similar to the thing being known, you should understand this as being similar both by nature and by a certain new effect. For there is no reason why sight should seek out and recognize light rather than a voice, except that it is naturally more compatible with light than with sound, and conforms itself to the former rather than the latter. Truly, since the senses seem only to touch the external aspects of things in perceiving them, while the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectus." The higher, divine part of the mind that grasps eternal truths directly.</note> penetrates even the innermost parts, it is clear that the intellect is more compatible with the intelligible and divine than the senses are with the sensible and fleeting. From this, a more certain argument can be held by us: that the intellect is divine, just as the senses are fleeting. Furthermore, regarding his statement that the perfect necessarily precedes the imperfect, and that the **species** <note>original: "speciem." Meaning the "Form" or "Idea."</note> is prior to the privation, be careful not to understand this in the order of our own physical generation—in which things are first begun and imperfect, then gradually acquire a more perfect form. Instead, take this to refer strictly to the order of things and causes, and the levels of the universe: where whatever is imperfect, since it cannot exist or be preserved through itself, depends on a higher perfection which exists and is preserved through itself. Since that higher thing is already composed of its own form and species, the lower thing is rightly subjected to it; and the lower, being powerless to form itself, is led toward forms by appropriate stages. Truly, because an "agent" acts through its own nature and thus renders the effect similar to itself, and because the subject is led toward form and **actuality** <term>Actuality: (original: "actum") The state of being fully realized or functional, as opposed to "potentiality."</term> under superior agents, we conclude that the superior causes exist actively as forms within themselves.

->The universe has a beginning and an end, and that itself is the Good; likewise the intellect, both human and divine, is always in "act," although reason progresses from potentiality into act.<-

II. In the second chapter, he signifies what the Good itself is, and designates how far pure goods proceed. He says the Good is the principle and the end of the universe: here he says that the Good depends on nothing, but all things depend on it; likewise, it is the measure and limit of all things. In any given moment, wherever parts achieve their own—that is, their natural—perfection, there also the whole which the parts serve achieves its own end. When the eyes see clearly, when the hands grasp something promptly, when the feet walk most expeditiously, they possess their own proper end. Much more truly does the whole body sometimes enjoy its natural perfection. In the same way that these parts of the body relate to the whole body in a physical thing, so do the parts of human life relate to the whole of life. By "parts of life," we mean here choices, faculties, and all the arts. Individual choices and arts have a certain "extreme" goal by which they are rightly perfected, beyond which they require nothing more. Thus, medicine has health as its extreme goal; military strength has victory. Just as the parts of life pursue their own ends, so much more does the whole of life finally look toward a certain ultimate common Good, by which it may at last be perfected, so that the whole life is more perfect than its parts. 

Similarly, as in man, one may argue in the other species of animals and all things. For natural appetite is a certain necessary inclination of nature, from the deficiency of one who lacks something toward fullness: and fullness and the ultimate end are the same thing. If no ultimate end were prescribed for our seeking, but nature progressed from end to end without any final stop, it could never be sufficiently filled; it would therefore strive to be filled in vain—indeed, it would not even strive at all. For no species of thing is moved toward that which is entirely impossible. Indeed, to be moved "naturally" is to progress gradually from a natural **potentiality** <note>original: "potentia." The capacity to become something or do something that hasn't happened yet.</note> into actuality. This natural progression, which advances step by step by some faculty, is at some point perfected when the ultimate end is attained. Otherwise, nature would everywhere struggle in vain, and the Author of nature himself would move it rashly and to no purpose. Therefore, if the species of things, which are parts of the universe, are not cheated of their own perfection, much less is the striving of the universe itself frustrated by chance. For the universe also strives toward a common end, since it constantly leads the parts toward their own ends (which serve the common end), and it obtains the ultimate end, lest perhaps the whole be more imperfect than its parts. Thus, the world will at some time achieve an end of this sort, or it may be said to have achieved it already in its present state. 

However, if there were no "best" end, but the world were imagined to proceed toward the "better" without any final stop, certainly, since it cannot pass through infinite degrees, it could never reach the best. Wherefore—though it is a crime to say so—this universe, constructed beyond doubt with the best form, would strive toward the best end in vain. Moreover, the "best habit" and end stands before all things so that they may be conformed in every way to their principle and Author. For the fact that this heap of things in the world, so diverse and mutually repugnant, should meet in one common form of the whole, and be rightly placed toward one common Good as an end, does not arise from the nature of the diverse things themselves, but rather from the one form and will of the superior Craftsman. Just as the world is formed under the "form" of its Author as its principle, so it is always being re-formed and conformed to Him as its end. Plotinus names this Author of all things the "Good itself": since by the same thing this universe was both brought into being and perfected. This he calls the measure of all...

<summary>Ficino introduces Plotinus's exploration of evil, defining it as the absence of form (matter) while identifying the Good as the ultimate goal and source of order in the universe. He argues that all natural strivings must lead to a final, perfect end, otherwise nature and its divine Creator would be acting in vain.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Ennead I.8. The previous page established the quest to define Good and Evil. # THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...call it the limit <note>original: "terminum." Ficino is completing a sentence from the previous page regarding God as the boundary of all things.</note>: just as Plato names it in the *Philebus* <note>A Platonic dialogue concerning the nature of pleasure and the "Highest Good."</note>. God measures all things as their principle; He likewise limits all things as their end. If God is the measure of all things, then certainly the order of things does not ascend from a principle to a principle without some first principle of all. To think otherwise would be to wander aimlessly through principles without any logic of a "first" principle; for the logic of a "beginning" is that it must be first. By using God as a measure, we rightly judge that the intellect is better than the soul, and the soul better than the body, because the former is closer to God (as the supreme Good) than the latter. Indeed, if the first and highest goodness did not stand somewhere, but one were imagined to proceed through countless steps, there would truly be no logic, measure, or rule by which one thing could be preferred over another; for one thing would not be closer to the measure than another. Let God, therefore, be the principle and the measure. Furthermore, let Him be the limit of all things because He is the end: a limit, I say, which marks out the forms of subjects and the motions of forms, and finally the enjoyment of Himself, so that nature does not wander from end to end without a final purpose. That would be nothing other than wandering through ends without any logic of "The End." The chief logic of an end is that it is the ultimate and the extreme.

After these things, in the second degree of goods, he places **Essence**, and within essence, the **Mind** <note>original: "mentem." In Ficino’s Neoplatonism, the Mind or Intellect is the first thing that emanates from the One/God.</note>. In the third degree, he places the **Soul**, and within the soul, **Life**. He says all these are good because they come from the Good itself and because they act around the Good by the power of the Good. He wishes for a fourth place of goods to be held only by those forms of bodies that never fail from the soul, which themselves never cease from God. Such things are the celestial bodies, the families of the heavens. 

To these points, he adds a difference between the divine intellect and the rational intellect: namely, that the divine is itself the fullness of all things, while the rational intellect strives to be filled from that source. Therefore, when you hear here that our intellect is called "empty," do not take it to mean our simple intellect <note>The "higher" soul that is always in contact with the divine.</note> which is always filled by the divine, but rather our **rational intellect**—that is, the power of the soul running through universal types. This power is, in a way, the potential of the intellect; it comes forth into act through the power of a superior intellect which always exists in act. It becomes active, I say, by the power of both the divine intellect and our own higher intellect. Just as a human being living in act is produced not only by universal nature (which holds the seed-reasons <term>seminariae rationes: the latent blueprints or "seeds" of physical things held within the soul or nature</term> of all animals reigning in act), but also by its own specific human nature, so too must this power (the human intellect in potential) become a human intellect in act through a human intellect that is always flourishing in act. This is what the generation of perfect things requires, and this is everywhere the opinion of *Plotinus*.

He adds that the divine intellect holds all things in itself in such a way that it is itself all things. Take this example: If all sorts of vessels of different shapes were submerged in the sea, the water would immediately fill them all. By filling them, it would take on the logic and similar shapes of as many vessels as it conceived. Such shapes would be nothing other than the water itself, adapted in various ways. Thus, the Intellect is all the "species" <note>original: "species." Here meaning the formal blueprints or Ideas of things.</note> it is thought to have; and it is its own species much more than the sea is the water of the shapes. This is because no novelty, no dimension, and no distance hinders their union there; and because these "waters" are not from another nor in another, but the Intellect brings forth, produces, or entirely exists as these species from itself and in itself. (We have often discussed elsewhere how species are distinguished from one another in the mind and yet all are in each one). 

He adds that whatever participates in the divine mind does not have all species flourishing in act at once: understand this as the **rational power**, which is accustomed to sometimes become a participant in the divine mind. For the intellectual nature itself, even in us, does not "sometimes" participate (as *Plotinus* intends it), but is always in possession of the divine mind. Furthermore, he calls the divine mind the "first act" of the Good itself and the "first essence." For he does not wish for there to be any act in God through which God acts—that is, some act distinct from the substance of God himself, at least by some logic. Every difference and every number must be absent from the primary Unity. Therefore, he considers the act of God itself to be "outside" God, just as light is outside the source of light. God is of such great power that His act is not a motion or an accident, but the first substance and essence. There, the act and the thing acted upon are the same; that is, it is the most full fountain of the essence of all things. Thus, while one thing seems to be made by the divine Unity, all things are made together in the One. Rightly so, for from the Unity which is above all and which regards all things, this "One" is made proximately, which is equally all things. Finally, he wishes the act of this essence around God to be His life, and its absolute state to be the Mind.

He adds that the pure soul does not stain the light of the Good through the Mind—taking the soul's own mind as a stain <note>Likely referring to the soul's individual perspective as a "spot" compared to the pure light of God.</note> and the divine Mind as light. Up to this point, nothing [of evil] happens. If either the soul or nature itself stopped at this step of descending, there would be no evil. However, the very fertility of nature brings it about that many degrees of things exist beneath the soul and nature. Because the portion of the Good is diminished little by little in this gradual descent (for effects cannot equal their causes), one finally arrives from the universal Good into **evil**. 

When he says that all things are "around God," he means they are equally from God and toward God. Thus, the first orders of things (the Ideas) are around God, from whom they come into the mind and into whom they are reflected by the mind. The second orders (rational notions) are around the second, which is the Intellect, from which they flow into the soul. Furthermore, the third orders (the seed-reasons) are around the third, which is the soul, from which they flow into nature and through which they flow back into the soul. Finally, he wants the fourth orders to be understood as being around the fourth—that is, natural forms around Nature—from which they slide into **matter**, and into which they slide back as much as they are able. All of this, I say, we have said more fully elsewhere and shall say again.

## Chapter III
### Chapter three disputes what evil is, and how many evils there are and where they are. 

He denies that evil exists in that which stands above being <note>i.e., God/The One.</note>; for that is the Good itself. This is known to be above being because the very nature of desiring and choosing not only desires to be many things, but often wishes things not to be, not to have been, or not to be in the future; yet one always chooses under the logic of the "good." From this, it is clear that the Good does not only belong to "being," but even pertains to "not-being" <note>Meaning the Good is so universal it exists even where specific "being" does not.</note>, and therefore the Good itself exists as something more common and higher. Because the first essence has been justified as good, and therefore the goods are derived through it into other things, it follows that as far as the participation in true essence extends, so far does the true portion of the good extend, and thus far there are no evils—just as wherever true heat flourishes, coldness is absent. But the portion of true essence extends all the way to the substances of the spheres of the world, in whose essence no deprivation is found. In these, therefore, evils cannot exist.

<summary>Ficino describes the hierarchy of the universe as a descent from the perfect "Good" (God) through Intellect and Soul down to Nature. Evil is defined not as a positive force, but as the point where the Good is most diminished, specifically occurring when one reaches the level of "matter" and "deprivation."</summary>

-># ON BOOK VIII OF THE FIRST ENNEAD<-

Whatever is eventually dissolved among composite things <note>Things made of multiple parts, like physical bodies.</note> is not truly called "being." This is because its existence was preceded by a long period of privation <note>original: "privatio"; here meaning the absence of a particular form or existence.</note>, and a similar state follows it. Furthermore, the very flow of its existence, as it passes through motion and time, possesses only a fleeting "present" moment in terms of what properly belongs to "being"; yet, in terms of "non-being," it suffers a long past and a long future. Therefore, a composite of this kind, in which so much "privation of being" is mixed, is called "not truly being," just as something is called "not truly hot" if a tiny amount of heat is applied to a great deal of cold.

Evil, then, happens to these things because they are "not truly being." As they fall too far from the First Essence, they slip away from the lot of the Good itself and are meanwhile plunged into evil. Truly, evil itself is that which is most distant from the Good: that is, the formless matter of the world itself. In the second place, evil is suffered by the form or quality lying within matter, which is called a certain "passion" or "affection" of matter stirred up from the outside. In the third place, the soul admits evil insofar as it is inclined toward matter by a certain sharp craving. 

But there is a difference: matter can be called, in a certain way, the *substance* of evil; composite things (made of matter and falling form) *suffer* evil into their substance; and finally, the soul receives evil not in its substance, but in a certain quality or accident. Amidst these points, Plotinus understands that which is called "non-being" in three ways:
1. First, as "absolute non-being," which is **nothingness**.
2. Second, as "truly non-being," which is the **prime matter** of the world.
3. Third, as "not truly being," which is the **form inherent in matter**, the falling composite, and its properties and accidents.

Also, when he calls the sensible universe "not true being," he refers chiefly to the composite realm below the moon <note>original: "sub luna"; in ancient cosmology, the region of earth characterized by change and decay.</note>. He wishes for the form (which depends on the "Idea") to be an image of being, representing a true shadow of being; but matter—which does not depend on the Idea insofar as it is an Idea, but rather is not represented by it as a formal essence—is different. For no one looking closely into matter will suspect the specific face of any Idea, nor judge that matter is anything but "non-being"—not indeed like nothingness, but like a "not-nothing" most distant from the First Being. 

Furthermore, form and the composite thing are distant from the First Being not only by that space of "rest" and "motion" found in the First Being, but by a much greater distance. In what manner those things which are essence—motion, rest, the same, and the different—exist in Being itself, we shall discuss elsewhere. Certainly, there, motion is not Being itself; otherwise, there would be no rest in things. Nor, again, is rest Being itself; otherwise, nothing would ever move. Rather, these are different properties and acts of Being. 

But for the present, Plotinus sets aside the properties of Being itself. He happens upon "non-being" (that is, matter’s own properties) which are opposed to those he numbered as properties of the Good itself. Therefore, he judges that this matter, as it is most distantly discrepant from the Good, should be named "Evil itself." The Good itself is "measure," but matter (to use his words) is called "measurelessness." Likewise, the Good is "limit"; matter is the "infinite." Furthermore, matter is "formless," while the Good is the "former" (the giver of form); matter is "needy," while the Good is "sufficient"; and so on.

Just as the properties of the Good are the same as each other and are the Good itself insofar as they are within the Good (though they seem to differ when referred to subsequent things), so too the properties of matter are one and are matter itself insofar as they are logically within matter. But when they are looked at in comparison to higher things, they are judged as diverse—much like the figures of lines, which are one at the center but many at the circumference. 

Furthermore, in things composite—located between God and matter—there is a certain infinity and a limit, a formlessness and a beauty. The composite thing itself is not merely one of these opposites; otherwise, the thing would not have both, or at least one would have to be both. If the thing were "limit" itself, it would have no infinity; if it were "infinity," it would have no limit. If, finally, the thing were both of these by its very nature, then both would remain the same. But the nature of things does not allow "limit and form" to be the same as their opposites, "infinity and formlessness." 

Since all things mixed from opposites are not "perfectly" such, they must be reduced to things that are simple and "supremely" such. Therefore, above the form and limit which are mixed in another thing <note>Meaning, mixed within a physical body or composite.</note>, one must ascend to the Form and Limit which are in themselves and are most pure. Conversely, beyond the formlessness and infinity which are joined as opposites in another thing, one must descend to formlessness and infinity subsisting simply in themselves. 

Hence, where Plotinus says, "That which happens to something must itself be something before it happens," he did not say it exists in or by itself before it happens, lest you should believe an "accident" <note>A property that is not essential to a thing's nature, like the color of a shirt.</note> is actually a "substance." Remember this example: the heat which sometimes happens to water is reduced to the heat of fire (because it is in something else and belongs to it by accident). Even though the fire's heat is in "something else," it is not said to be there by chance, but by nature. Finally, this heat is reduced to the very "Idea of Heat," which consists both by and in itself. Thus, just as that which exists by accident is referred to that which exists according to nature, so that which lies in another is referred to that which consists in itself. 

Finally, remember that evils happen to the forms of things. They do not come by mere chance—for they come continually and perpetually—nor do they come from the nature of the form itself (which ultimately proceeds from the First Form, the Divine Mind, through the logic by which the Mind is turned toward the Good). Therefore, know that evils flow in from the outside, and indeed from a certain determined principle—certainly not a principle like a "form," but a "formless something"; therefore, from matter. Thus, matter is the First Evil, just as the Good is from the First Principle; that Principle, therefore, is the Good itself.

The higher points are confirmed again: we see in the order of things that individuals are composed of a certain potentiality and act—that is, they consist of a "formable nature" and a "formal act." Those things which hold the middle ground are rightly mixed with an equal portion of these opposites. But above the middle of the universe, the "formable potentiality" is gradually exceeded by the "formal act." Conversely, moving toward the middle, the act decreases, and the potentiality for suffering <note>original: "potentiam patiendi"; the capacity to be acted upon or changed.</note> and the deformed nature increase. Therefore, the increase of the "act" reaches the supreme and pure Act through very orderly steps, while its decrease descends gradually to the "lesser act" of a form. Immediately following this is a certain supreme formlessness and infinity—a nature entirely passive, always exposed to forms coming from above as if to measures and limits.

But observe this meanwhile: just as the descent of this order goes beyond the "least form" into matter, so the ascent goes beyond the "highest form" (that is, the first essence and mind) to the Good itself. Conversely, just as something exists *above* being (the Good itself), so something subsists *underneath* being (Evil itself), a middle ground between being and nothingness, entirely opposite to the Good. For the Platonists place matter as the middle between "being" and "nothing" (or "non-being"); it is called both "non-being" and "not-nothing." 

This matter, like a universal potentiality, precedes the act of the world in its origin and order of generation, just as specific potentialities everywhere precede their own specific acts. Since matter, because of an extreme defect of virtue, always needs a support and cannot lean upon any lower foundation (for nothing is lower than it), it is born only to hang from a support from above—that is, Nature; just as Nature similarly hangs from the Soul. Matter depends on the essence of Nature and from the essence of the Mind itself. The forms born in matter come from the "seeds" of Nature and the "Ideas" of the Mind. Matter is clearly like the shadow of the intellectual essence...

He argues that while matter is "non-being," it is not "nothingness," but rather a formless potentiality that sits at the very bottom of the cosmic order.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead I, Book 8, which investigates the nature and origin of evil. This section follows the previous discussion on non-being and the hierarchy of existence.</meta>

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

then of nature; however, the forms are like images of the Mind itself and of the generative seeds <note>original: "seminum," referring to the *logoi spermatikoi*, the formative principles that shape the physical world</note>. Matter, indeed, seems to be sustained from above by the form in the manner of a suspension, just as iron is suspended by a magnet above it.

->Three degrees of evils: how evil exists in the soul, and how matter possesses nothing of the good.<-

**IIII** In the fourth chapter, Plotinus pursues the degrees of evils. He places matter in the first degree, and in the second degree, he places the form of corporeal matter. Plotinus briefly indicates here—and we demonstrate more extensively in our *Platonic Theology*—that this corporeal form is not "true" form. In the third degree, he establishes the evil of the soul. He says that the soul itself is not evil by its own nature; otherwise, every soul would be evil, and it would have been evil from the beginning and for all time. He believes that the "second soul"—that is, the life <gloss>the vital faculty</gloss> sometimes granted to the "first soul" for the body—becomes depraved immediately at the beginning of its accommodation to the body. For when it is so bound to the body that one single animal is composed of both soul and body, it is understandably infected by matter soon after. This goes so far that it becomes subject to passions and undergoes immoderate movements in both excess and deficiency, following the nature of the body. The Platonists think that every such life becomes this way, though it can finally, with great effort, be tempered. However, they judge that before the effect of moderation takes hold, those passions are involuntary because they are, in a sense, "natural." Even the higher soul—because it willingly consents to the lower—receives false opinions from it. Through these, it judges with too little consideration, believing that things that are truly good for it are becoming bad, or whatever the lower soul pursues or flees from by a certain natural impulse.

Therefore, just as the lower soul becomes evil by natural impulse, so the higher soul becomes evil through love, consent, or opinion. But there is this difference between this lower life and the corporeal form: this form is a certain "passion" <note>in the sense of a passive quality or something "suffered" by matter</note> of matter, whereas life is rather an action or an "act" of the soul. Therefore, while the corporeal form is an incurable evil, life is a curable one. As for his statement that matter has "nothing of the good," understand this to mean nothing of formal, intrinsic, or absolute good. Since the very essence of the first Good is something "formal"—that is, the Divine Mind, the Form of Forms—then wherever the formal nature is missing, the intrinsic nature of the good is also missing. 

But because matter is the "first subject" <note>the underlying substratum of all physical things</note>, equally exposed to all forms, it claims no form as its own, and almost no evil. Therefore, nothing of formal, intrinsic, absolute good is its own. And yet, it does not lack the desire for the good. For matter is the height of poverty <note>original: "indigentiæ summa"</note>, naturally most ready to capture formal abundance. Therefore, it naturally desires this; therefore, it affects the good. This desire can be called "good" in a certain way—not absolutely, but because it looks toward and leads to the good; to an external good, I say. For that which is received never becomes matter's own. Consequently, the principle of the effect from which the appetite and motion of matter toward the good is produced is not in matter itself (for there is no essence where there is no form), but in Nature acting as the instrument of God. Yet, such desire and motion are not driven by violence. For matter does not resist this pull; rather, it is most capable of it, and the more beneficent the thing it undergoes, the more easily it is formed. 

Finally, matter itself, because it is formless, is evil; indeed, because it is "formlessness" itself, it is evil itself. Yet it can be called good in a certain way, insofar as it can be formed by the Good. Since Plotinus often calls form a "limit" <term>terminus: a boundary that gives a thing its specific identity</term> and a "measure," know that it is called a limit because it terminates the nature of matter (which is equally indifferent to any appearance) within the certain limits of a species. For example, through the form of a man, it obtains the species of a man; through the form of a horse, it is contracted into the species of a horse. Again, he calls it a "measure" because matter by its own nature has no proper magnitude or figure, but while a certain form limits it to a certain species, it requires a certain proper magnitude and figure. Just as the form of the body is the measure and limit of matter, so the intellectual form is the measure and limit of the soul. The Good itself is the measure and limit of the Mind and of all things. 

Finally, the soul that is turned toward the Mind through all its powers is composed by its measure and limit, and it neither receives nor looks back at anything of evil. But the soul that has departed from the Mind and proceeds with an inclination toward matter already sees evil and is, as it were, fascinated by a certain gaze. But after it pours the strength of its nature (which should be felt) into matter—like the arm of its soul's breast—it is then said to have "touched" evil. When at last it has conceived a habit through which it suffers alongside and consents with the suffering material body, it then seems to languish under such a poisonous spell <note>original: "veneficio," suggesting a magical or medicinal poisoning</note>.

->In what defect evil consists: how matter is evil itself: and how this is evil in the soul.<-

**V** Chapter five introduces and solves two questions. The first question is this: it has been said that the rational power takes care of imperfection and is its image; similarly, the natural power is the image of rational imperfection. Is such a "defect" <note>a falling short or lack</note> therefore evil, either here or there? By no means. For evil does not consist in just any defect of the good, such as when something is found to be surpassed by a different, higher good and yields to it. For these are certain degrees of goods arranged by divine providence. Rather, evil is involved in a "proper" defect: when something is seen to be robbed of some good belonging to its own species or its own particular gift. 

Supreme evil is weighed in a "universal" defect—that which lacks all the goods of a species by its own nature and is deprived of every formal gift. He says matter is of this kind, having no portion of the good—that is, within itself and as its own. For since Being itself primarily receives the good within itself as something near to itself, the intrinsic good is rightly attributed to things through the gifts of Being itself—namely, through essence. Matter, however, has no "being" of its own, since it is not a form, nor does it have its own form. It exists, therefore, through the being of a substantial form (just as an accidental form exists through the being of a substance); nor, again, does it have an essence. For since the first essence is something formal in itself (especially if compared to other essences), matter, which is nothing formal, is rightly not even an essence. Nevertheless, it is something "similar" to essence, although it has nothing similar to being itself. 

Consequently, that in which there is some defect (of whatever kind) is not the Good itself; where a defect falls away from a certain "proper" good, there is already some evil. Where all defects meet, there is evil itself, and that is matter. Moreover, a defect that degenerates from its own proper good—in which there is a potential and a proclivity that eventually falls into evil—is a worse defect than a simple lack of some good. For the latter consists of a "lesser good," but the former consists of "evil." For that proclivity, especially when it is already leaning, verges toward evil itself, which is already evil even before the proclivity. And that proclivity in the soul, when it has once been made more primary, is already evil before the habit of falling headlong is confirmed. Now, the "first evil" of the soul is not this or that vicious habit, but the very proclivity that is more prone toward matter itself: the matter around which it turns—either by touching it with certain of its parts (namely, by its nature and the powers that serve nature) or by affecting it...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword is "habitu" (by habit).</meta>

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains Plotinus's hierarchy of evil, identifying prime matter as absolute "evil itself" due to its total lack of form and being. He describes how the soul becomes evil not by nature, but by turning away from the Divine Mind toward matter, eventually falling under a "poisonous spell" of physical sensation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead I, Book 8. Having previously discussed the three degrees of evil, Ficino now examines how the soul interacts with matter and why evil must exist as a "contrary" to the Good.</meta>

# ON BOOK VIII OF ENNEAD I.

whether through the counsel of the rational part choosing toward matter, or through the command of the higher imagination; or by falling into matter—specifically through the affection of the lower imagination; or finally by "suffering," which occurs through the lowest sense. Indeed, since all such things are judged according to something else, insofar as they are referred to that which is simply "such," Plotinus rightly weighs all things as evil through some relation to matter, which is evil itself. This applies both to the soul, because it is rightfully distant from the Good, and to the body and its forms, as he shows next when he raises and solves the second question. He concludes from these points that the soul is not the principle of evil itself. Because its nature is not inherently evil—since it is of an intellectual nature and, through the intellect itself, is very close to the Good—the soul, through the intellect, turns back toward the Good and the Intellect which is nearest to it. 

Here he warns that souls do not fall away from God by a fixed, rebellious purpose, but rather from a certain accidental consequence <note>original: "consequentia contingenti," suggesting the fall is a side-effect of the soul's involvement with the physical world rather than a deliberate act of malice</note>. This happens insofar as they are affected by matter and material things; from this state, the soul is hiddenly turned away from God while it willingly turns toward the opposite. Truly, if in this defect of wickedness the soul departs from a greater good into evil, it does so with a certain proposal—but under the appearance of good—using less caution outside of that body, as if it prefers a manifest evil over a manifest good. 

Therefore, he wants the beginning of evil in the soul to be accidental, occurring as it inclines too eagerly toward something less good—that is, toward the service of the cycle of generation <note>original: "lapsu generationis," referring to the soul's descent into physical birth and rebirth</note>. But meanwhile, evil also creeps in, which sometimes holds the soul even against its will. Thus, one might be struck by the inevitable momentum of fate and shut for a long time within these "prisons" <note>a common Platonic metaphor for the physical body</note>, partly because the soul does not know from the start how much damage follows from its affection for and habituation toward the body. Plotinus alone thinks that those who can still avoid evil in some way are the ones who, before the bodily habit is confirmed, recognize the danger and withdraw themselves entirely into the mind. Truly, since not all people can be corrected at all times, it is clear that depravity does not reside in nature itself, nor is the soul evil by its own nature. Finally, he concludes that the soul deviates, or repels and overcomes the depravity sprouting from matter, or proceeding toward matter; thus, only the nature within the soul that is segregated from matter is divine. Even though it is divine, because it is so close to natural things, it still admits evil through the senses. 

This is not like a corporeal form, which falls from its own good because it inheres in matter and is mixed with contrary forms, so that its evil follows from within. Rather, the soul seems to degenerate from its own good and admit evil because it enters into commerce with a lower nature. From this kind of "rooming together" <note>original: "contubernio," a word used for sharing a tent or living quarters</note>, there follows anxiety and an impediment to its higher duties, rather than total destruction.

### How something may be contrary to the Good, namely Matter; and how forms separated from matter are contraries.

**P I** The sixth chapter explains what Plato means when he says in the book *On Knowledge* <note>original: "libro de Scientia," referring to Plato's dialogue, the *Theaetetus*</note> that evils cannot be entirely deleted; for there must be things that are necessarily contrary to the Good, and these evils dwell in mortal nature. Among these points, understand that there is nothing properly contrary to the Good itself in the sense that it is divided as an opposite within the same category. For the Principle of things cannot share a category with anything else, nor can it be distinguished from anything by added differences. But something is said to be "sub-contrary" to the Good—that is, placed outside the company of the Good—by being most distant from it and entirely most dissimilar: namely, the lowest matter of the world. 

Furthermore, he teaches that in other contraries, it is not necessary that if one exists, the other must immediately exist; but if the Good itself exists, its sub-contrary necessarily follows. That is, if there is a First Principle of the universe, a lowest degree of the universe is necessarily given. In this, he accepts "contrariety" differently than those who define it as a simple repugnance of two qualities in the same category (which would imply that substances are not contrary to each other). Here, he wants contrariety to be the greatest possible distance between things, making them opposites and producing opposites. Thus, matter will be sub-contrary to God. For matter is not essence, while He is the principle of being. Matter is the origin of evils; He is the origin of goods. Matter is the cause of formlessness and deformity; He is the principle of forms. These two are much more contrary to each other than heat and cold, for heat and cold share a category (quality) and a substrate, whereas God and matter share nothing. He adds that if fire and water were to keep their species even if matter were removed, they would still be contrary—that is, the essence of water to the essence of fire. In them, heat and cold would not just be essential properties, but in a way, they would be essences themselves, or acts of essence, most distant as contraries and causes of the whole. Also, no portion of one would be in the other, since common matter would be missing. Again, these two would differ by their whole selves and would be distant by "otherness" itself.

### How, if the Good exists, it is necessary for Evil to exist; and how the universe consists of matter and form, from Mind and Necessity.

**P II** After this, in the seventh chapter, he shows why it is necessary that if the Good exists, evil will also exist. Indeed, the work commanded and made by God himself would never have been made in its present effect and act unless it *could* have been made. Therefore, two things are conceived: both the "power" <note>potentiality</note> and the "act" of being. These are indeed contrary or opposite to each other; for that which already exists in act can no longer be "made," and by the reason it was able to be made, it was not yet in act. Likewise, potentiality is the starting point from which the making of the world proceeds, and act is the terminal point toward which it goes. 

If you ask what the first potentiality of the world-to-be was, I will answer: it was not "something" already existing (for then it would have been in act), but it was not "nothing" either (for nothing is founded upon nothing). I will say, therefore, that it was "not-nothing"—namely, the potentiality of existing and matter itself. This was not founded in God (for nothing happens to God as an accident), nor was it founded in nothing, but was rather the foundation itself. It was not the first thing in the intention of the divine Architect, but rather the last. For the first and chief thing in God's judgment is the Form of the world; the matter, hiding beneath the world’s form, is later. But in the execution of the work, matter is first, and the form follows. Therefore, the universe consists, as Plato says, of Mind (that is, the formal act, which is the chief image of the divine mind) and of Necessity (that is, matter, which is taken into this work not so much by its own intention as by a certain necessary condition). If, therefore, the Good itself is most efficacious...

<summary>Ficino explains that evil in the soul is an accidental result of its involvement with matter rather than an inherent trait. He also defines matter as the "sub-contrary" to God, arguing that evil is a necessary consequence of the existence of the Good and the process of creation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead I, Book 8. Ficino is exploring why matter and evil must exist if the universe begins from a perfect Good.</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

of all things, Plotinus necessarily maintains that the work of the world follows from it. If the world exists, matter necessarily exists, which is evil. If, therefore, the Good exists, evil necessarily follows. Furthermore, since the Good itself possesses an inestimable efficacy, it spreads its power and its outpouring as far and as wide as possible. If it extends itself to the furthest distance, it certainly produces a series of innumerable steps, so that the final step—being most distant—is contrary to the highest Good, and is entirely different and most dissimilar to it. This, then, will be evil: evil, I say, in a simple and common sense. Likewise, if it spreads its power most widely, many degrees of things are produced across that breadth, so that one thing is most different from another, and often truly contrary and evil—not evil in a simple sense, but rather evil in relation to one another. 

Therefore, if the Good exists, it follows that evil has crept in, both at the far end of the vertical line <note>original: "in longum," referring to the vertical hierarchy of being from God down to matter</note> and in the horizontal line <note>original: "in latus," referring to the horizontal diversity and conflict between physical things</note> where certain things happen to be harmful to one another. From the inestimable fertility of the Good itself, a second most fertile thing necessarily follows among the good things. And from the fertility of this next thing, another follows, and then another. But once the goodness of the cause begins to fade through its effects, a continuous diminishing of the good arises; and from this diminishing, evil finally follows. Thus, the effect of the good is both good, because it comes from the Good, and "less good," because it is outside and below the Good; and finally, it suffers evil after a very long loss of the good. 

Because matter itself is evil, and the entire world is composed of it, evil lies hidden in every small part of the world, even if the usual effects of evil do not occur in the higher spheres of the world. Indeed, there the deficiency of matter is overcome by the excessive perfection of the form; nevertheless, a certain continuous privation <term>privation: the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</term> seems to display something similar to evil, which the perpetual motion of the world brings into the past and future. The matter of the heavens, too, because its potential is indifferent to all forms, would sometimes change its substantial forms if it were not held back by a certain wonderful power of its present form, as if by a bridle. It is perhaps to this bridle that matter clearly yields, not so much because it is simply matter, but because it is the matter of such a specific form. For this reason, Plato says in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the physical world</note> that the spheres and stars of the world could be dissolved—specifically because of the nature of matter—unless they were bound together by divine power, that is, by the wonderful goodness of their form. 

Thus, separate forms <term>separate forms: abstract ideas or souls that exist independently of physical bodies</term> cannot be dissolved; for even if these too are preserved by the gift of the Good itself, nevertheless this very gift of the Good belongs to the form. While any form separated from matter is preserved, it seems meanwhile to be preserved by itself, since it truly is a form in its own right. But if anyone should wonder why the human body is not kept indissoluble by its own form—that is, the soul, which is divine—let him hear Moses teaching that this body could also be held indissoluble, if only the soul would preserve its own dignity. The Persian Magi followed this as well, promising perpetual health of the body to a soul that recovers its original health.

### How matter is the cause of evil, first to its own forms, and then to the soul; also that all good things are referred to one Good, and all evil things to one evil.

VIII. In the eighth chapter of the book, he wonders whether matter is the cause in the soul of both ignorance and wickedness, or whether it is rather a certain form and "complexion" of forms. He answers soon after: if any bodily form is said to be the cause of evil in the soul, it is the cause of evil precisely because this form is addicted to matter; it is an entirely material effect. It is not a true form, but a certain image of a form and a "passion" <term>passion: here meaning a passive state or something acted upon</term> of matter. 

Since it is necessary that the mobile region below the heavens—which wavers unsteadily, as if by itself—be ruled and led by the celestial region (which is mobile, but stably mobile, meaning it revolves perpetually with the same rhythm), so too must the celestial region be governed by something entirely immobile. We rightly trace the lower forms in our matter back to the forms that are in the heavens, and we refer the celestial forms again to those which are in the Master Craftsman and Leader <note>The Demiurge or Divine Intellect</note>. There, these forms are nothing other than the intelligence of the Craftsman and Leader himself. Therefore, they are judged to exist in themselves. 

Indeed, the forms below the heavens degenerate far from the celestial ones; for there they are pure, whole, effective, free from passion, and not combative. Here, however, they are stained by some mixture, maimed, ineffective, subject to innumerable passions, and if they do anything, they fight among themselves unto destruction. Nevertheless, these forms agree with the celestial ones both in the genus of the body and in matter and motion. Therefore, these forms degenerate much more from those that are entirely incorporeal (which stand by themselves far from matter and all motion) than they do from the celestial forms. It has reached the point where those sublime ones are "Forms," while these are now merely "deformed" marks, or very small and inserted vestiges of forms in a completely formless matter. Matter, I say, now overcomes the forms, just as in the heavens the forms overcome the matter containing them, and above the heavens, the forms eliminate all matter far from themselves. 

Consider again light in itself, and in it all the powers and degrees of colors, which nevertheless are nothing other than the light itself. Then notice the colors transferred into plants; you will immediately recognize how far these colors that exist in matter fall away from those that exist in light—or rather, in light itself. I will pass over the fact that these colors are already shadowed and polluted by a nature contrary both to light and to each other. Do you not see that they have turned out so ineffective that they do nothing when the light departs? Perhaps they are so much "nothing" that while they seem to exist when light is present, this very existence is perhaps the existence of the light itself. Certainly, this very act of working and moving the eyes is the work of the light acting within them. 

Remember that the comparison of our forms to the divine ones is just like that. For matter infects all forms lying within it with its own formlessness much more than a cold subject infects a weak heat that approaches it. For there is a greater diversity between a form and an entirely weak subject than between any form and a subject that is already shaped in some way. If, therefore, it is not "true heat" when mixed with cold, certainly it is not a "true form" when immersed in an entirely formless subject—or (to speak more truly) immersed in "formlessness." Take four colors—white, saffron, green, and red; mix any of these with another, and you will not stain any of them by mutual mixing as much as if you mixed any of them with blackness. Blackness, compared to the other colors, represents matter compared to the forms. 

Remember, furthermore, that forms in matter become needy and subject to dangers because they have been made material; therefore, they struggle with one another so that they may be nourished by another’s loss and be safer once their contrary is extinguished. Forms separated from matter, however, although they are quite different from one another, nevertheless fight each other in no way. Yet they generate contraries in the universe: the "Idea" of fire generates fire, and the "Idea" of water generates water. Because there is an unconfused property of each one among the different Ideas, here on earth it becomes a hostile repugnance. 

Conclude finally that forms entirely shadowed in matter become so weak that, being "sickly" by the grace of matter, they are in a way poisonous and come too close to the soul. By what reasoning the different characters and habits of men exist due to the diversity of humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile—thought to determine temperament</term>, and whether and how these inconveniences can be overcome and tempered, we often dispute in our *Theology* <note>Ficino’s "Platonic Theology"</note>, where we also frequently assert that forms in matter are not "true" forms. And

He argues that physical forms are mere shadows or "sickly" versions of divine Ideas because they are submerged in the darkness of matter, leading to conflict and decay.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead I, Book 8. Having established that the Good is the source of all things, Ficino now explains how we categorize various "goods" and "evils" based on their distance from the source, and how the soul can perceive formless matter.</meta>

# ON BOOK VIII OF THE FIRST ENNEAD.

However, so that you may grasp the summary of what Plotinus introduces here and in the preceding sections regarding the good, the evil, and the degrees of both, consider it in this way. We call different goods in every category by the common name of "good"; we do this not by chance, but led by a certain condition. For we sense a common lot in all of them, a nature in species or genus; indeed, in all categories, however diverse, we perceive and name the good. Therefore, this name is one because of a certain identity—namely, a union—since they are from the same principle, possess something of it, and are carried toward and contribute to the same end. Similarly, through all categories, we find something of evil; we mark all evil things not only with the same name of "evil," but by a certain logic. This can be done more truly than if we were to refer all things to one supreme evil—specifically, because they happen to come from there, or possess something of its likeness, inclination, or nature, or because they are carried toward it. Since that which is good is the highest degree of the universe, let Evil itself be the ultimate degree of all things. It is not truly fitting to judge evil things solely by their departure and distance from the Good itself; rather, it is much more correctly judged by their approach to Evil itself. For we do not immediately judge whatever is distant from the first <note>meaning the "First Principle" or the Good</note> to be evil, but after long intervals, we detect evils which, through their proximity to the ultimate <note>matter</note>, are already hideous and destructive. For it is very probable that those things closer to the Good than to Evil are judged as good, while those closer to Evil are thought to be evil. But if it were to fall away without any limit, there would be no bottom, nothing most distant from the Good itself. Once this is established, let it be permitted to consider one thing closer to this bottom than to the Good, and to weigh another as closer to this by any reasoning. To refer the judgment of evils solely to a certain distance from the Good would be the same as if someone referred every judgment of goods solely to their distance from Evil.

->How that which is formless can be known by the soul, which is form, and<-
->is accustomed to know through forms.<-

**IX** In chapter IX, he asks how that which is formless is known, since the power of knowing is a form, the soul is active through form, and the object must meet the power through a form. He responds that the soul knows darkness through light—that is, by imagining all light to be absent, it thinks of the extreme darkness. By imagining a part of light to be missing here, which we see elsewhere, it recognizes something dark. Similarly, by removing every form, the soul senses <term>matter</term> <note>In Plotinus’s philosophy, matter is the absolute "lack" or "privation" of form, making it difficult for the mind—which works with forms—to grasp.</note>; but by removing only some forms, you think of something deformed. But something strange happens here. For just as we see nothing without light, nor can we see darkness without light, so too we understand nothing without form, nor do we understand matter through form or in form. Finally, just as the soul knows the Good itself above the intellectual light, so it imagines matter below such light. We sense both kinds of knowledge through a sort of intuition rather than through the pursuit of logic.

->That matter is evil, not because of what kind it is, but because it is not of any kind; just as God is the Good without<-
->quality; likewise that matter is entirely formless,<-
->and what form is.<-

**X** After this, in the remaining chapters of the book, he raises and solves questions. The first question in chapter X is whether matter, if it is not "of a certain kind," can be evil. For the categories of virtue and vice, goodness and malignancy, usually pertain to qualities. He responds that things mixed from a certain subject and a form are usually judged as either good or evil. But those things that are most simple are not judged in this way, but otherwise. Thus, the very principle of things, when it is called "Goodness," is not a quality, and when it is called "the Good," it is not "of a certain kind." For it is Goodness itself, superior not only to quality but to substance and essence. Thus, the ultimate end of things—that is, matter—when it is called "Malignancy," is not a quality; otherwise, it would exist in another subject, it would not be the ultimate, and through its formal nature, it would possess some formal good. Likewise, where it is named "evil" by God, it is not so named because it is something composed of a subject and quality; otherwise, it would not be the ultimate, for it could be resolved into simpler things and a subject. Furthermore, its quality would not be consistent with other possibilities of qualification, for then matter would not be equally ready to receive all qualities; nor would it be a quality equally indifferent to all qualities, for then it would already be drawn toward the nature and lot of matter. And if anything were judged to be "formal" <note>possessing a specific form or definition</note>, it would follow at the very least that what is called the subject of all things would still be composed of form and subject. However, to prevent an infinite regression, one must arrive at a subject that is entirely simple and formless. Matter, therefore, is considered evil not because it has a quality, but because it does not have one. If, therefore, a quality is sometimes called good, it is not because it is "of a certain kind," but because it is a quality; thus, matter is evil, not because it is "of a certain kind," but because it is matter, possessing no quality in itself. For quality and form in a subject are nothing other than the measure and determination of the subject—an expression from the Good itself, impressed through the primary form (that is, the Mind) as if by its own seal, reflecting the Good itself. We can imagine matter as something depending on the Good, though through a mode of "procession" rather than "constitution" <note>meaning it flows out from the source but lacks the structure of higher beings</note>, not yet regarded by the Good, nor signed by any specific seal. Thus, everything that follows is ruled by the common power of the celestial nature, depending on it all the way to the center of the earth. But the common nature of heaven itself, through light as if through a seal like itself, expresses nothing further than the surface of the earth and forms nothing similar to itself. That which follows is therefore similar to formless matter; that which stands above is similar to forms and to the beautiful. Let that light represent the Divine Mind to you, while the simple light, which is prior to the nature of heaven, represents the Good itself.

->Whether evil is the ultimate privation; and whether it can exist through itself and in itself?<-
->The answer is given by making a distinction.<-

**XI** The second question in chapter XI asks: Since a "privation" cannot exist in itself due to its defect, it follows that the extreme privation—because of its extreme defect—can least of all exist through itself and in itself. In what way, then, is evil the "ultimate privation," or if it is such, how does it consist through itself or in itself? We respond to this that the ultimate privation—that is, the pure emptiness of all forms—cannot be in another, otherwise there would not be extreme emptiness there; nor truly in itself, in the sense that it depends on nothing, but rather because it is sustained by nothing as its subject. Therefore, let no one say that the first and primary evil is either the soul or in the soul; otherwise, there would be no intellect in the soul, no life, no essence, and the soul itself would no longer be a soul.

Here, he moves into the specific nature of "Primary Evil" and how the human soul interacts with it, focusing on the concept of matter as a "pure void."</meta>

<header>MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY.</header>

### Whether Evil itself is not a small evil, and whether it resides in the soul * The answer is that it is pure evil, and does not reside in the soul.

XII. The third question in chapter 11 examines whether one may designate the "First" or "Primary Evil" as something other than purely evil, and thus place it within the soul. I respond: First, among the followers of Plotinus, the highest evil is understood as the extreme emptiness of forms. Insofar as it pertains to forms, it is a pure void and is "Prime Matter" <note>The fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe</note>. Indeed, if this matter possessed anything formal within itself, it would not be true matter, just as a thing is not a "true form" if it admits something material into itself. Conversely, if it is not true matter if any internal form escapes from it, so too it is not true form if any part of it becomes material. This is especially true because if matter—while it is being shaped toward the better (that is, being translated into a formal state)—ceases to be "true matter," then much more does a true form cease to exist as a form when it is transferred toward the worse (that is, into matter). Therefore, so that we may arrive at the truth from that which is not true, we must show both the pure forms existing above matter and the pure matter existing below forms. For this reason, matter is always a "pure void." For even while it seems to possess all forms, it actually possesses none; this is partly because such forms are not "true" in that state, and partly because matter neither contracts any form as its own nor preserves any trace of them. Perhaps, in the manner of a mirror, it shows itself to have what it does not actually possess.

### Whether Evil itself is an impediment in the soul * The answer is that Primary Evil and Primary Good are outside the soul, and the soul descends into evil (namely matter) through four stages.

XIII. The fourth question in chapter 13: Whether Primary Evil should be placed in the soul in such a way that "evil" here is not so much a privation as an impediment to achieving one's own good. Plotinus denies that such an impediment—namely, vice—is the "Primary Evil." This is because vice is called evil specifically because, by hindering the good, it leads one *toward* evil; therefore, vice itself is not the First Evil. Likewise, just as virtue is not the "Supreme Good," neither is wickedness the "Supreme Evil." It is clear that virtue is not the first and highest point in goodness, both because it is occupied with labor and does not fully satisfy the appetite of nature, and because it proceeds into effect from a certain idle potential, and the course of time moves it from the lesser to the greater. Furthermore, virtue can admit some degree of composition <note>meaning it is made of parts, whereas the highest principles are simple</note>. These characteristics cannot apply to the "Good" in its simple essence. Therefore, just as the Good itself is more excellent than virtue, so Evil itself is lower than vice and far worse. Certainly, for the soul, "evil" consists in turning itself toward matter, which Plato in the *Theaetetus* calls the "region of dissimilarity"—that is, the region most unlike divinity in every way. The soul glides down into this "Lethean depth" <note>Referring to Lethe, the mythological river of forgetfulness</note> through four stages, which are like four rivers. In the first stage, it imagines this bodily fabric too intently; in the second, it desires it too ardently; in the third, now joined to it, it builds within it; in the fourth, it turns the pleasure of that "deathly union" into a habit. Thus far, the soul seems to be cast headlong through four rivers to the underworld. Once cast down, it is further entangled there by four more turns: first, when judgment is completely blinded by imagination; second, when the affections change from human to beast-like; third, when this union renders the soul "corporeal" or body-like; and finally, when the habit of the soul’s commerce with the body becomes entirely indelible, unless perhaps it is deleted by divine power. At this stage, Plato says that the soul "slumbers" after it has fallen to the underworld.

### How evil in the soul is a weakness, and what kind of weakness, and how it comes from matter; how the soul is joined to the body; how it is separated; how matter depends on the soul, and how it also depends from above.

XIIII. The fifth question in chapter 14 investigates whether the evil that occurs in the soul—that is, vice—is a weakness <term>imbecillitas</term>? He concedes this, saying that a similar weakness occurs in the soul as in the body, though they are not the same. Both are called "weak" when they easily suffer influence from elsewhere and perform their own functions with difficulty. But weakness in the body is twofold: it occurs either when the body loses what is its own, or when it is burdened by something foreign. In the soul, however, weakness happens only from a "foreign weight." The soul is said to "receive the foreign" insofar as it occasionally admits matter, which is present to it everywhere on the outside. I say "present" because wherever the soul is, matter is also there. I say "outside" because matter hangs, as it were, outside the soul; the soul in no way resides in matter, but in itself, even while matter hangs from it. This matter—partly because it exists from the soul, partly because it is utterly destitute, and partly because it is drawn by the soul like a servant—seems to strive to penetrate into the soul, where it might be perfected by forms. It is just as if a cloud, by its own movement or draw, subjects itself to light and receives a "redness" from it, as if it were a form. In that case, the light does not seem to exist in the cloud so much as in itself, but the redness is in the cloud. The light is not divided there so that one part is in itself and another in the cloud; rather, the light exists entirely in itself. However, a power or glow <note>original: rubor, literally "redness" or "blush"</note> of the light is in the cloud. Because this glow is received by a nature lower than ours, it is much weaker than the light itself, and it seems to obscure the gift of light as far as our sight is concerned. Let such a cloud be matter; let the light be the soul; and let the "redness" be that which is received by the capacity of matter. It becomes a meager and weak life, ineffective for action and subject to passions. Meanwhile, the intellect shines in the soul from above, just as light shines from above, even while the glow in the cloud degenerates from that splendor, and the cloud takes away from us the sight of the true light. Remember that Plotinus hints to us, both here and elsewhere, that matter is generated by "nature"—that is, by the lowest power of the soul. I say it is from the soul without the soul being "passive" <note>meaning the soul is not changed or harmed by creating matter</note>, or rather, while the soul is "present," which I think is a more accurate way to speak. For matter, while not yet born, causes the soul to suffer nothing—unless one understands that the soul is affected in some way by its inclination to generate something. Since natural things are subject to divine things, it is probable that the subject of generation itself—matter—depends upon the lowest of divine things, which is "nature" as the natural generator. And just as specific natures create specific subjects for their works (disposed in a certain way), so does universal Nature create a universal subject. It is as if the same architect who constructs the building also creates the foundation. But if you should guess that matter proceeds from even higher than nature, we shall concede it, but only on the condition that this subject (which is most common to all forms) depends most closely on nature—insofar as nature is conceived as not yet formed, but submitted to the "reasons" <note>logoi or formative principles</note> by which it is to be formed. Next, it comes from the essence of the Mind, insofar as that essence is a formable Idea; finally, it is derived from the highest Principle of all things, though not properly by the logic of that Good...

<meta>Catchword: itself</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains that "Primary Evil" is identical to Prime Matter (a formless void) and describes the soul's moral decline as a "descent" into material concerns, likened to the rivers of the underworld. He uses the analogy of a cloud catching light to show how matter depends on the soul without the soul losing its divine essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Ennead* I, Book 8. Having established that "Primary Evil" is identical to "Primary Matter" (the pure absence of form), Ficino now explains how the higher Good generates lower levels of reality, and how the human soul becomes entangled with the "unruly" nature of matter.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK VIII OF ENNEAD I</header>

[The Good] is itself <note>original: "ipsum est"</note>, that is, communicating itself abundantly, but rather insofar as it is the One itself, that is, wonderfully separated from all things. Thus matter emerges as utterly needy and unformed, separated from all gifts. Thus, again, matter is called "a certain unity" rather than "good," because it has an intrinsic unity, while its goodness only appears from the outside. Completely, however, since all effects of the highest principle [the One] are both from it and yet are compelled to exist outside and below it, certainly insofar as they are from it, they bring back forms and acts from that source. But insofar as they are outside it and lower, they suffer (so to speak) a certain material lot mixed within them. They exist under the condition of a lesser good, and finally, in matter, they represent every extreme and infinite subject, and the origin of evils. Now indeed, that which is ensouled <note>The generative power of the soul</note> generates matter; this power is not yet evil, but good, nor yet weak, but fertile, and therefore it is able to generate. But when it embraces this fertile matter too much, it becomes weaker from here, as if by a burden, and falls away. Now, both the poverty and desire of matter, and the fertility of the soul, cause it to embrace matter. Therefore, this very embrace, insofar as it happens from the fertility of the soul, is in a certain way good and produces good, such as certain species and forms. But insofar as it is composed of a certain unruly boldness <term>procacitate: an impudent or forward nature attributed to matter</term> of matter, it is evil and partakes of evil—that is: the weakness of life, impediments to knowledge, and the innumerable passions of the soul.

->good; How evil is made in the soul; How matter is intrinsic,<-

XV. The sixth question in chapter 15 wonders whether, in this kingdom of the Good—so good and so beautiful—there can be matter that is utterly unformed <note>original: "materia prorsus informis"</note> and evil that is entirely deformed. It is necessary that matter exists, as we prove in earlier sections and in my *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his work *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of the Soul*</note>, and we confirm it again here with Plotinus; and for the present, we briefly confirm it. The form of each individual thing, whether made by art or nature, is resolved everywhere into its own proper matter. These matters, as far as they pertain to the forms to be acquired later, are unformed, although they might already possess another form. It is clear, then, that if the form of worldly things—which is the universal form—is reduced to utterly unformed matter, one might imagine this matter (of which the universe is made) still has some form besides the worldly one. At least a form of that kind would finally be led into "matter per se" as something lacking form. This is true unless someone perhaps imagines that under this form another, and again another, lies beneath without end. This indeed cannot happen: first, because since any subsequent form taking the place of matter is a worse form than the one before it, certainly by proceeding through things that gradually fail into the worse, one cannot reach infinity. Second, because if a "first form" were given without any "prior matter" ever existing, no beginning would be given to the work of creation; indeed, an innumerable crowd of matters and forms would stand in the way of the principle of the work to be constructed and would be utterly opposed to union. Furthermore, because if matter, due to its own defect, cannot form itself and is therefore formed by another, it receives a limit of forms on both sides—both the first and the last—from a higher Creator. Finally, when we come to the first principle and the ultimate end of the universe, it is rightly not permitted to proceed without beginning or end through matters and forms, which are usually led by an efficient principle to a certain end.

Therefore, beneath the order of forms lies matter that is in itself utterly unformed; thus evil is beneath the Good, which follows the defect of the Good by necessity. A "defect of the Good," however, necessarily follows a lesser degree of the Good. Finally, a lesser good belongs to the Good itself (for it undoubtedly accompanies it). Therefore, just as from the Good itself evil finally follows necessarily by the necessity of nature, so conversely, if you take away evil, you will necessarily—that is, by logical necessity <note>original: "necessitate consequentiæ"</note>—take away the Good. If nothing ever occurs to us as good or evil, but all things are indifferent as some dreamers imagine, our appetite will never be moved either by pursuing or fleeing. Sensation, which was granted by nature for the sake of this service, will cease, and the intellect will cease. For just as the senses serve the sensible good, so the intellect serves the intelligible good. From which it is also clear that the Good itself is simply more excellent than the intellect, since the intelligible good is also in a certain way higher than the intellect. 

When, therefore, in the very order of things we see many things, partly good and partly evil (the former being virtuous, the latter not virtuous), and likewise some better and others worse, it is necessary to rightly resolve these composite things into a simple, First Good and a simple, First Evil. After this, he confirms again that the evil of the soul happens from elsewhere, namely from matter. For since the soul suffers only for the sake of the body, it fears for the body, it desires for the body, it grieves for the sake of the body; it is disturbed by the imagination at the impulse of the body, and while it is disturbed in its imagining, it holds false opinions. Finally, evil happens to the soul from the outside, just as good happens to matter from the outside. Conversely, the good of the soul arises from within, from the intellectual form of the soul, just as the evil of matter hides within, arising from the very emptiness of the intellectual form and image.

<summary>Ficino explains that matter is the "unformed" foundation of the physical world and the source of evil, which exists as a necessary "falling away" from the Good. He argues that the soul only experiences evil when it becomes overly preoccupied with the body and the "unruly" nature of matter.</summary>

<meta>This page begins Book 8 of the First Ennead. The previous discussions in the Enneads have focused on the nature of the Soul and the Intellect; here, Plotinus shifts his focus to the problem of "Theodicy" (the origin of evil in a world governed by the Good).
