# OF PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD I
### BOOK VIII.

->ON WHAT EVILS ARE AND WHENCE THEY COME.<-

---

<margin>
Four questions concerning good and evil.
</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' depicting a seated figure in a garden or landscape setting.</image-desc>WHOEVER seeks to investigate the source of evils—whether they have fallen among existing things or into some specific class of beings—should make the proper starting point of their inquiry a definition of what evil actually is, and the nature of evil. For in this way, it will become clear from where it came, where it is seated, and to whom it happens; and indeed, it will be established whether it even exists at all within the nature of things.
<margin>B</margin>
However, there is a doubt: by which of the powers within us do we perceive the nature of evil? This is because the knowledge of individual things is achieved through a certain similarity <note>A fundamental Platonic principle: "Like is known by like."</note>. For since the Intellect and the Soul are certain "Forms" <note>original: "species"</note>, they also recognize other Forms and naturally desire them. But truly, no one can imagine evil under the logic of a Form, since it is conceived as the total absence of the Good. But if, because the science of opposites is the same, and evil is the contrary to the good, then the knowledge of both good and evil would be the same. 
<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, it is strictly necessary for those who would know evils to first discern the Good; for indeed, better things rightly precede the worse, and Forms precede those things which are judged not to be Forms, but rather "privations" <term>privations: the lack or absence of a quality that should naturally be present</term>. Again, it is a question worthy of study: in what way is the good contrary to the evil? Perhaps it is because the former is the "first" while the latter is the "last"; or certainly that the former is like a Form, and the latter like a privation. But we shall speak of these things 
<margin>D</margin>
more opportunely in what follows.

<margin>
II. Description of the Good: from which all things exist; how Intellect is directly moved by the Good, but the Soul through Intellect.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'I' depicting a winged putto or cherub playing a horn.</image-desc>AT present, we must state what the nature of the Good is, as much as this current discussion requires. It is that upon which all things depend, and which all things desire—taking their beginning from it and being utterly in need of it. But the Good itself lacks nothing; it is self-sufficient, desiring nothing at all. It is the measure and the boundary of all things, producing from itself the Intellect, Essence, Soul, and Life; and in turn, the activity surrounding the Intellect. Up to this point, all things are beautiful, and the "Beautiful Itself" <note>The highest principle of beauty, which Plotinus identifies with the Good</note>, being above the best of things, reigns in the intelligible world. This is the Intellect: an Intellect, I say, not of the sort one might perhaps suppose, thinking it to be similar to those we call "intellects" among ourselves, which are filled by 

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'O' (Omicron) depicting a landscape with figures under a tree.</image-desc>THOSE who inquire whence evils come—whether they have crept into the realm of beings or around some genus of beings—would make a proper beginning to their search if they first posited what evil is and what the nature of evil is. For from this, it would be known where it has come from, where it is established, and what it has happened to, and overall, it would be agreed whether it is among the things that exist. But how might one know the nature of evil by the power within us? For since knowledge of each thing happens through similarity, those things which are Intellect and Soul—being "Forms" <note>original: "eide"</note>—would perform the knowledge of Forms and would have a desire for them. But how could one imagine evil as a Form, when it is understood as the absence of all good? But if the same science applies to opposites, and evil is contrary to the good, then there will be one knowledge of both. It is necessary, then, for one who is to know evil to first know the beautiful things <note>The "kaloi" or the Good/Beautiful</note>; since indeed, we are naturally inclined toward better things over worse, and towards Forms rather than what are instead "privations" <term>privations: sterēseis; the Greek term for the loss or lack of a natural form</term>. It is a similar question as to how evil is contrary to the good. Or is it perhaps that one is the "beginning" <note>archē</note> and the other the "extreme" <note>eschaton</note>? Or one as a Form, and the other as a privation? But this we shall discuss later.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'H' (Eta) depicting a figure, possibly a shepherd or traveler, in a pastoral setting.</image-desc>WHAT then should we say is the nature of the Good, as far as is fitting for the present arguments? It is that to which all things are joined, and which all beings long for—having it as their principle and needing it. But that itself is without need, sufficient unto itself, needing nothing; the measure of all things and the limit. It gives from itself Intellect and Essence and Soul and Life, and the activity concerning Intellect. And up to this point, all things are beautiful; it is the "Super-Beautiful," and beyond the best of things, reigning in the intelligible realm. That one there is the Intellect; not such as those called intellects among us, which are filled by way of propositions <note>original: "ek protaseōs" - referring to discursive or logical reasoning, which Plotinus considers inferior to the direct intuition of the divine Intellect</note>...

<summary>This page introduces Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of evil, defining it not as a positive force but as a "privation" or absence of the Good. Plotinus argues that to understand evil, one must first understand the Good, which is the self-sufficient source and measure of all existence, Intellect, and Life.</summary>

# BOOK EIGHT.

...those who are able to understand what is said, and who attempt to grasp things by following the words and the sequence of thought, as if observing realities through analogy. For those who do not possess these things, but are in a state of emptiness regarding what they must learn... but that Intellect is of such a kind that it is not just one thing among all, but it is with all things, being all things, and possessing all things without "having" them in a possessive sense. For it does not possess them as if they were different from itself, nor is he himself something else; nor is each of the things within him separated from the whole. For all existing things are wholes, and everywhere is the all, yet they are not confused, but are again distinct.

Therefore, that which participates in this does not participate in the whole at once, but participates as it is able. And there is the first activity of that one, and the first essence, while that one remains in itself. But the activity itself is around that one, like a life dancing around it from the outside. The soul, looking toward him and contemplating his interior, sees God through him. And this is the life of the gods, free and blessed, and evil is nowhere there. And if nature had stopped here, no evil would have existed.

But there are first, second, and third goods around the King of all <note>original: "regem vniuersorum." A reference to Plato's Second Letter, describing the hierarchy of the One, the Intellect, and the Soul.</note>; everything is around him, and he is the cause of all beautiful things, and all those things exist because of him—the second things around the second, and the third things around the third.

If these are the beings, and if that which is above beings is the Good, then certainly evil will be nowhere in the beings; and much less in that which transcends beings. For all these things are good. It remains, therefore: if evil exists anywhere, it is to be found in the things which "are not," <note>original: "τὰ μὴ ὄντα / non-ens." This refers to Matter, which Plotinus views not as "nothing," but as a lack of Form.</note> like a certain form of non-being, and around something of those things which are mixed with non-being, or in whatever way they have commerce with non-being. "Non-being," I say, not as that which is completely non-existent, but only different from Being. 

It is not non-being in the sense of motion or rest, which are said to exist around Being, but as an image of Being, or even more remote from Being. And this is the sensible universe, and whatever passions <note>affections or movements of the soul/body</note> are around the sensible; or something following these, and as if an accident to them, or the principle of these, or one of those things which complete it: such a thing, indeed, as I shall now describe. For one may think of it as a kind of immoderation if referred to a measure, and an infinity compared to a limit, a formlessness compared to a former <note>the "former" is that which provides the "Form" or blueprint</note>; likewise always needy compared to the self-sufficient, always indeterminate, never entirely at rest, suffering all things from every side, insatiable, absolute and total poverty. 

And such things do not happen to it as accidents, but seem to be its very essence; furthermore, whatever portion of it you see, you will find all these things together in any part. But other things which participate in it and are assimilated to it, become evil, but are not themselves "Evil Itself." Therefore, these things exist in a certain foundation, not as something different from it, but as itself. For if evil happens to another, it is necessary that there be something which is "Evil Itself" beforehand, even if it possesses no essence. For just as there is one "Good Itself" and another which is good by accident to others, so it is with evil: this is "Evil Itself," while that is evil according to those things...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...are usually filled by a proposition, and are able to perceive what is gathered by reasoning. Likewise, those who reason are those who think out what follows from each point, and speculate on things through their consequences: as those who did not have them before. But before they learned, they were one: although even then the intellect existed. That intellect, I say, is not such a thing, but it has all things and is all things; it dwells with itself, entirely united to itself, having all things without "possessing" them: for it does not possess them as other things, nor <margin>B</margin> does he himself exist as something else; nor are the things in him separated one from another: on the contrary, anything there is the universe, and everywhere is the whole, yet all things are not confounded, but rather each is distinct. Therefore, that which is a participant in this does not participate in all things at once, but participates in what it can. It is the first act of that one, and the first essence, while that one remains within itself. It acts surely around him, living as if around him. Accordingly, the soul moving around this from the outside, <margin>C</margin> since it clearly inspects his inner parts, sees the source and God: and this is the sacred and happy life of the gods, entirely removed from evils. Indeed, if nature stood still here for a moment, evil would be nowhere. But truly there are first goods, and second, and third: and all things are around the king of the universe. And the king himself is the cause of all goods, and for his sake all things exist. Finally, around the second are the second things, and the third around the third.

<margin>III. Evil is in those things which are not, but in those things which are [so] that they are inclined toward those things which truly are not.</margin>

<margin>D</margin> If these are the beings, and if that which is above beings is the Good, then certainly evil will be nowhere in the beings: and much less in that which transcends beings. For all these things are good. It remains, therefore: if evil exists anywhere, it is to be found in the things which are not, as if a certain species of non-being: and around something of those things which are mixed with non-being, or in whatever way they have commerce with non-being. Non-being, I say, not as that which is completely non-existent, but only different from Being. <margin>E</margin> Not non-being in the sense of motion or rest, which are said to exist around Being, but as an image of Being, or even more remote from Being. And this is the sensible universe, and whatever passions are around the sensible: or something following these, and as if an accident to them, or the principle of these, or one of those things which complete it: such a thing, indeed, as I shall now describe. For one may think of it as a kind of immoderation if referred to a measure, and <margin>F</margin> an infinity compared to a limit, a formlessness compared to a former: likewise always needy compared to the self-sufficient, always indeterminate, never entirely at rest, suffering all things from every side, insatiable, absolute and total poverty. And such things do not happen to it as accidents, but seem to be its very essence: furthermore, whatever portion of it you see, you will find all these things together in any part. But other things which participate in it and are assimilated to it, become evil, <margin>G</margin> but are not themselves "Evil Itself." For if evil happens to another, it is necessary that there be something which is "Evil Itself" beforehand, even if it possesses no essence. <summary>This page explores the hierarchy of being, moving from the divine Intellect (where all things are unified and good) down to the sensible world. Plotinus identifies evil not as a positive force, but as "Non-Being" or "Matter"—a state of total lack, immoderation, and poverty that sits at the furthest point from the Good.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, Non-Being, Matter, Evil Itself, Hierarchy of Being, The King of All, Sensible Universe, Immoderation, Plotinus, Neoplatonism</keywords>

--- Page 109 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the origin of evil. Having established that the "Intellect" is perfectly good, he now argues that evil is not a positive force, but a "lack" or "un-measuredness" found in matter (hyle). He explores how the soul, though not evil by nature, can become "darkened" when it turns away from the light of the Intellect and toward the formless void of matter.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK I.

A This happens to one through the other. Since, therefore, immoderation <note>original: "immoderatio" (Latin) / "ametria" (Greek). This refers to a lack of limit or measure, a state of chaos.</note> is said to be a thing, does it exist only in that which is immoderate? Conversely, does measure exist only in the thing measured? But just as a certain measure exists even when nothing is being measured, so also immoderation exists outside of any immoderate subject. For if it were in another, it would either be in that which is immoderate—but this thing does not need immoderation, since it is already immoderate itself—or it would be in a measured thing. But truly, that which is measured, insofar as it is measured, cannot undergo immoderation.

B Indeed, there must be something that is infinite <note>original: "infinitum" / "apeiron." In Neoplatonism, the "infinite" often implies a lack of boundaries or form, rather than "eternal."</note> in itself, and formless by its own nature, and possessing all those qualities we mentioned previously when describing the nature of evil. Moreover, if anything else is such, it either has it mixed in, or at least, because it looks toward it, it has turned out that way, or because it is the cause of such a thing. On this account, a nature that is subject to figures, species, forms, measures, and limits, and is endowed with an external ornament, possessing no good of its own:

C a phantom <note>original: "simulachrum" / "eidolon." An image that lacks the reality or substance of the original.</note> once again, if compared with real beings—indeed, even the "essence" of evil itself, if indeed an essence of evil can be said to exist—this reasoning rightly proves that this is the primary evil, and evil in itself.

<margin>The three degrees of evil: how they exist in animals; how matter possesses no good.</margin>

D The nature of bodies, insofar as it participates in matter <note>original: "materia" / "hyle." The fundamental, formless "stuff" that Plotinus identifies as the source of evil.</note>, is indeed evil, though it is not the primary evil. For it possess a certain form, though not a true one. It is also deprived of life; it carries within itself a mutual corruption among bodies, and an unordered clashing between them. Furthermore, it brings an impediment to the soul’s own activity. Moreover, by its perpetual flux, it flees from essence <note>original: "essentiam" / "ousian." True, unchanging reality.</note>, and therefore, by its own nature, it reaches a degree of evil. But the soul is not evil in itself, nor is every soul depraved. But which one is depraved? Clearly, as Plato says, the one that serves that thing in which the depravity of the soul can naturally dwell; as if the rational species of the soul underwent evil, immoderation, excess, and defect, from which intemperance, turmoil, and other depravities of the soul arise like involuntary passions:

E from which also arise false opinions, through which one might think things are good or evil, which he then pursues or flees. But what joins this depravity to the soul? And how can you trace it back to that source and cause? First, it will be said that its soul is not outside of matter, nor is it such according to itself; and so it is mixed with immoderation and deprived of the form that provides ornament and brings it to measure. For it is immersed in a body that possesses matter.

F Furthermore, the rational power is obstructed, prevented from discerning because it is obscured by perturbations and buried in the darkness of matter; for by its inclination, it slips into matter. It does not look toward essence at all, but toward generation <note>original: "generationem" / "genesin." The world of change, birth, and decay, as opposed to the eternal world.</note>, the origin of which is the nature of matter—a nature so evil that even that which is not yet within it, but merely looks toward it, is filled with its evil.

G For since it is entirely devoid of good, and is a privation of good, and a pure defect, surely whatever touches it in any way, it renders like unto itself. Therefore, the perfect soul, turning toward the intellect, is always pure: driving matter far away from itself, along with everything indeterminate, immoderate, and evil. It neither approaches these things nor even looks at them; for this reason, it remains pure, fixed in the intellect—

<column-break/>

A —and in that one. What then is un-measuredness, if not in the un-measured? Or measure, if not in the measured? But just as there is measure not in the measured, so there is un-measuredness not in the un-measured. For if it is in another, it is either in the un-measured—but it would not be un-measuredness itself, being itself the un-measuredness of the un-measured in the measured—but it is not possible for the measured to have un-measuredness insofar as it is measured, and there must be some thing that is infinite in

B itself, and formless in itself, and all the rest, which we spoke of first, which possesses the character of the nature of the [absence of] beauty. And if anything should come after those things, it either has filth mixed in, or it still looks toward it as being of such a kind, or it has produced something of such a kind. But that substrate <note>original: "hypokeimenē." The underlying "stuff" or matter.</note> which is not color, and has no forms, nor shapes, nor measures, nor limits, and is adorned with a foreign world, having nothing good from itself,

C but is a phantom compared to the things that exist, and the essence of evil—if one can even say there is an essence of evil—this the argument has determined to be the primary evil, and evil in its own right.

D The nature of bodies, insofar as it participates in matter, would be an evil, but not the primary evil. For they have certain forms, though these are phantoms of the true ones, deprived of life, and in their mutual movement, they are disordered. They will be an impediment to the soul regarding its own activities. It flees from essence, always flowing—another evil. The soul in itself is not evil, nor is every soul evil. But which is the evil one? It says <note>Referring to Plato.</note> it is the one that has been enslaved, in which the vice of the soul is naturally born, as in the irrational form of the soul, receiving evil, un-measuredness, and excesses and deficiencies. From which also come licentiousness and cowardice, and the rest of the soul’s vice, being involuntary

E sufferings, producing false opinions, making one think certain things are evil or good, which it then flees or pursues. But what is it that produces this vice, or how will you trace that cause back to the principle? First, the soul is not outside of matter, nor is it [the evil one] in itself. The first [soul] is mixed with un-measuredness, and is without a share of the form that adorns and leads to measure. For it has been mixed into a body that has matter.

F Then, as for the reasoning part, it might be harmed; it is hindered from seeing both by the passions and by being darkened by matter, and by its inclining toward matter, and generally not toward essence, but toward generation. From where the principle, the nature of matter, being so evil, that even what is not yet in it, but only looks toward it, is filled with evil from it. For being entirely without a share of the

G good, and being a privation of it, and a pure deficiency, it makes like to itself everything that touches it in any way. The perfect soul, therefore, which inclines toward the intellect, is always pure, and has turned away from matter, and all that is indeterminate, and the un-measured and evil; it does not see it, nor does it approach it. It remains pure, therefore, being made like—

<summary>Plotinus defines primary evil as matter (hyle), characterized by a total lack of measure, form, and goodness, acting as a "phantom" that darkens any soul that inclines toward it. He argues that while bodies are secondary evils due to their material nature, the soul only becomes depraved when it turns away from the Intellect and becomes entangled with the formless void of matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of evil. Having previously defined the "Intellect" as the source of all light and goodness, Plotinus now moves to define evil not as a competing power, but as the "darkness" that remains when the light of the Good is completely absent. This specific section focuses on matter as the ultimate form of this absence.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

...is entirely determined. But that which does not sustain this duty, but proceeds out of itself existing in a certain degree—neither perfect, nor primary—is like an image of that other thing. Because of its own failure, and to the extent that it fails, it is filled with a sort of formlessness and looks toward the darkness. And now it possesses matter <note>original: "ὕλην" (hyle) / "materiam." In this context, matter is the formless "stuff" that remains when all divine order is removed.</note>, looking into that which it does not see: and as the saying goes, it "sees the darkness."

B HOWEVER, if a defect of the good is the cause why the soul sees the darkness and is submerged in it, then the evil would be in the soul’s deficiency. This would be the "first" evil. The second evil would be the darkness itself—the nature of evil—which exists not just in matter, but even before it. Or, certainly, evil does not consist in just any deficiency, but in a total and universal defect. That which fails only slightly from the good is not yet evil; for according to its own nature, it can still be perfect. But that which fails entirely, such as matter <note>original: "ὕλη" / "materia"</note>, is truly evil, possessing no portion of the good. For matter does not even possess "being" (by which it might have a share of the good), but "being" is said of it only equivocally <term>Equivocally: when the same word is used for two different things, like "bank" (of a river) and "bank" (for money). Plotinus argues that matter "exists" in a way that is actually a form of non-existence.</term>.

<margin># In what evil consists: how matter is itself evil: and how evil is produced in the soul.</margin>

C Therefore, it is the lot of deficiency that it is not good, but it is the lot of *universal* deficiency to be evil itself. A "middle" deficiency is the potential to fall into evil, which is already a state of evil. From this, one must investigate <unclear>investigare</unclear> evil—not this or that specific evil, such as injustice or any other vice, but that "primary" evil which is not yet any of these things. Rather, these specific vices are like species or types of that primary evil, distinguished by

<column-break/>

D certain additions: just as in the soul there is vice, and then the various species of vice, either according to the matter it deals with, or according to certain parts of the soul. Thus, the soul partly "looks" at evil, is partly incited by its own desires, and finally suffers from it. But if someone should place evils outside the soul as well, one must ask: how do we trace things like disease, ugliness, or poverty back to that primary nature of evil? They will say that disease is a defect or an excess in bodies composed of matter, when they cannot sustain order and measure.

E Ugliness, truly, is matter that has been very little overcome by form <note>original: "εἶδος" / "forma." In Neoplatonism, "form" is the organizing principle that gives beauty and purpose to raw matter.</note>. Finally, poverty is the need and deprivation of those things we require because of the matter to which we are joined—matter which is so naturally gaping and hollow that it is essentially "neediness" itself. Therefore, if these things are said correctly, it must not be said that we are the *source* of evils, as if we were evil by our own original nature, but rather that these things exist before us. As for the vices that occupy men, they are held by them unwillingly. Nevertheless, an escape from these evils of the soul is provided to those souls who are capable of it, though not all are able. The presence of matter in physical bodies is a natural evil; for the "evil itself" is not the vice of men, since vice is not in all men (for the faculty to overcome it is given). Those who are more excellent are certainly those to whom this does not happen. They overcome it, finally, because that which is within them is segregated from matter.

G IT IS WORTHWHILE to understand by what reasoning Plato mainly said that "All evils cannot be destroyed," but come about by necessity. And that they are not among the gods, but travel about mortal nature and this lower place.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Plotinus’s "Ennead I, Book 8" concerning the origin of evil. Having established that matter is a "total defect" of the Good, Plotinus now addresses Plato’s famous passage from the *Theaetetus* regarding the necessity of evil and the "flight" from this world to the divine.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD I

<margin>A</margin> Is it free from evils? <note>Referring to the heavenly or divine realm.</note> Since it moves in a perpetual order and is carried along as a beautiful ornament, no injustice or iniquity is found there, nor do the celestial bodies inflict injury upon one another, being guided by an ordered moderation. On the earth, however, there is injustice and an iniquity devoid of order. For this is the nature of mortality and the "lower place." But when he <note>Plato, in the *Theaetetus*.</note> says that one must "flee from here," it is by no means spoken of leaving terrestrial locations. For "flight," he says, does not mean departing from the earth, <margin>B</margin> but even while living on the earth, becoming "just and holy with wisdom." It is as if he were saying that one must flee from wickedness, as if evils for a human are both wickedness itself and the things that spring from wickedness. 

Furthermore, when Theodorus suggested that evils could be removed from our midst if only men could be persuaded of what he said, Socrates denied this could happen. For he says that evils must exist by necessity, since it is necessary for there to be something "sub-contrary" <term>Sub-contrary: A logical term here meaning an opposite that exists on a lower level of reality.</term> to the Good. <margin>C</margin> But by what reasoning can it be that human evil—that is, wickedness—is contrary to the Good itself? Surely this wickedness is contrary to virtue. Virtue, however, is not the "Absolute Good," but a "certain good" <note>original: "quoddam bonum"</note> which enables us to master matter. How then will anything be contrary to the Absolute Good itself? For it has no "quality" <note>In Platonic thought, the One or the Good is beyond all categories, including quality.</note>. 

Furthermore, what force requires that if one of a pair of contraries exists, the other must also exist? It may indeed be possible for a contrary to exist if its opposite exists—for instance, while health exists, disease can also exist—<margin>D</margin> yet it does not follow by necessity. Perhaps Plato does not think this kind of necessity applies to every order of contraries, but only to the contrary of the Good itself. 

But if the Good itself is "Essence" <note>original: "essentia" / "ousia"</note>, or rather "Beyond Essence," what can possibly be contrary to it? That nothing is contrary to essence is manifest enough through an induction of individual existing things. But can there be a contrary to "Essence" in the absolute sense, and generally to the first principles of the universe? <margin>E</margin> Perhaps "Non-Essence" will be the contrary to Essence itself, and if there is a nature and principle of evil, it will be the contrary to the Nature of the Good. For both are principles—one of good things, the other of evil things. And all things that exist within either nature are contrary to one another; therefore, the wholes themselves are contrary, and more contrary than anything else. 

Other contraries are placed either in the same species or the same genus, and they share something in common <margin>F</margin> in whatever things they reside. But those things that are separate, and which are constituted in such a way that they fulfill the nature of the "other," are the contraries of those that fulfill the nature of the "divine." What prevents them from being the most extreme contraries, provided they are things that are distant from one another by the greatest possible interval? 

To the "Limit" and "Measure" and the other things that are proper to the divine nature, there are the contraries of "Infinitude" <margin>G</margin> and "Immoderation," and whatever else is said to reside in the nature of evil. Therefore, the whole is contrary to the whole. One side possesses a most deceptive existence, being primarily a "falsehood" and a "lie"; the other side possesses "True Being." Thus, the falsity of the former resists the truth of the latter. Again, that which exists according to the essence of the former is opposed to that which exists according to the essence of the latter. From these points, it is sufficiently clear...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it is pure of evils, and is always carried along in order and in a cosmic arrangement, with neither injustice being there, nor any other vice, nor things doing wrong to one another, but being carried along in order. But on earth, there is injustice and disorder, for this is the mortal nature and this "here-place." But when he says one must "flee quickly," it is not spoken of fleeing the things on earth. For flight, he says, is not <margin>B</margin> <margin>judgment / maxim</margin> to depart from the earth, but even while being on earth, to be "just and holy with wisdom," so that this is what is meant. One must flee vice, since vice and the things arising from vice are the cause of evils. 

And regarding what was said before—that one might think there could be a removal of evils if one could persuade men—he says this is not possible, but that evils must exist by necessity. For it is necessary that there be something <margin>C</margin> [opposed] to the Good. To the [Absolute Good], not as the vice concerning humans—how are such things contrary to that Absolute Good? For vice is contrary to virtue, but virtue is not "The Good," but a good such as that which masters matter. 

But how is this [matter/vice] contrary to that Absolute Good? And how can the Good itself [have a contrary]? If there is a necessity everywhere that if one of the contraries exists, the other must also, it might be granted that the contrary exists because of the existence of the other—just as where there is health, <margin>D</margin> it is possible for disease also to exist, though not by necessity. One need not say this is true of every contrary, but it was said regarding the Good. 

But if the Good is Essence, how can there be anything contrary to it, or to that which is "Beyond Essence"? <note>Plotinus refers to the One/Good as "Beyond Being" (epekeina ousias).</note> That there is nothing contrary to essence is a point demonstrated by induction regarding particular essences. But regarding Essence as a whole, what will be <margin>E</margin> contrary to universal Essence? And generally to the Firsts? To Essence, "Non-Essence" is contrary; to the Nature of the Good, the nature and principle of Evil is contrary. For both are principles, one of evils, the other of goods. And all things in each nature are contrary. So the wholes are contrary, and more contrary than others. For other <margin>F</margin> contraries are either in the same species or the same genus, and they have shared in some common thing. 

But as for those things that are separate, and which are the "completion" of the nature of the "other," how could they not be the most extreme contraries, if indeed contraries are those things which are most distant from one another? To the "Limit" and "Measure," and the other things in the divine nature, "Infinitude" and "Immoderation" and the other things in the evil nature <margin>G</margin> are contrary. So the whole is contrary to the whole. And its "being" is a lie, and is primarily and truly a "falsehood," whereas the other is "True Being." So the "truly false" is contrary to the "true," or essence to that which is according to its essence, as we have declared.

Plotinus clarifies that "fleeing the world" means attaining virtue and wisdom rather than physical departure, and explores how the principle of Evil (Matter/Non-being) serves as a total opposite to the principle of Good (Essence/Being).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of evil, specifically responding to Aristotelian logic regarding contraries and Platonic cosmology. It examines whether matter is the primary source of evil and explains why evil must exist as a necessary consequence of the "descent" from the Absolute Good.</meta>

### BOOK EIGHT

<column-break/>

It is not everywhere true that "nothing is contrary to essence" <note>original: "nihil essentiæ contrariũ esse"; This refers to Aristotle’s *Categories*, where he argues that substances/essences like "man" or "horse" do not have opposites.</note>; for we would admit that fire and water are contraries even if there were no common matter underlying them. In these cases, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness are accidents. But if these qualities alone, without a common subject, fulfilled their essence, they would still be contraries—one essence against another essence. Therefore, things that are entirely segregated from one another, sharing nothing in common and having the greatest possible distance between them, are contrary by their very nature. For contrariety is not merely a quality or any specific class of things, but rather the fact that they are as far apart from each other as possible, consist of opposites, and produce contrary effects.

<margin>VII. How, if the Good exists, it is necessary for Evil to exist; how matter is connected to necessity.</margin>
Moreover, why must evil exist if the Good exists? Is it because matter is necessary for the universe? For this universe necessarily consists of contraries; otherwise, it would not exist if matter were not present. The nature of this world is therefore mixed from both necessity and intellect <note>original: "ex necessitate, simul atque mente"</note>. Indeed, whatever comes into this world from God is good; but evils come from the "ancient nature," as Plato says <note>original: "ex antiqua natura inquit Plato"; referring to the *Politicus* or *Timaeus*.</note>, meaning the underlying matter which has not yet been adorned. But why does he call it a "mortal nature"? In the passage where he says that "evils revolve around this place" <note>A reference to the *Theaetetus*.</note>, let us grant that he designates the universe. Perhaps this is confirmed by what he says in the *Timaeus*: "But since you have been born, you are not indeed immortal; yet you shall never be dissolved, being preserved by my will." If this is so, it is rightly said that "evils cannot be destroyed." How then shall one flee from evils? He says one does not flee by moving to a different place, but rather by acquiring virtue and removing oneself from the body. For in this way, one separates oneself from matter, since sticking to the body is sticking to matter. He himself explains how "to separate" or "not to separate" works. Furthermore, to be "among the gods" means to be in the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure forms and intellect, above the physical world.</note>; for that is where the immortals are. One may also consider the necessity of evil by this reasoning: since the Good does not remain alone, it is necessary that by a certain departure from it, evil must finally occur at the furthest distance. Or if one prefers to put it this way: there is a perpetual descent and distance until a final point is reached, beyond which nothing further can be produced—and that very point is evil. It is necessary that something exists after the First <note>The "First" refers to the Absolute Good or the One.</note>, and therefore there must also be a Last. This Last is matter, which possesses nothing further of the First. And this is the necessity of evil.

<margin>How matter is not the cause of evil primarily by its forms, and how all evils are ultimately referred back to one primary evil.</margin>
Someone might perhaps object that we do not become evil because of matter; for neither ignorance nor wicked desires proceed from matter. If someone goes astray because of a "wicked affection" of the body, the principle of that affection is not the matter, but rather the *form*—such as heat, cold, hardness, bitterness, saltiness, and other qualities of the humors <term>Humors: In ancient medicine, the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance determined health and temperament.</term>; furthermore, states of being "filled" or "emptied." I mean "fillings" not of just anything, but of certain specific things; and that it is entirely this *quality* that creates the difference in desire, and if you wish, the discrepancy in false opinions. Thus, it would appear that *form* rather than matter is the evil. However, even by this argument, one is nonetheless compelled to admit that matter is evil...

<sig>g 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: nonetheless</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that evil is the "extreme distance" from the Good and identifies it with matter, which acts as the final boundary of existence. He maintains that while the divine realm is perfect, the physical world's "mortal nature" necessitates the presence of evil as a lack of form and goodness.</summary>
<keywords>contraries, essence, matter, necessity, Plato, Timaeus, Theaetetus, descent from the Good, intelligible world, humors, form vs matter</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus’s discussion from the previous page regarding whether matter is the primary source of evil and how the "ancient nature" of the material world interacts with divine intellect.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS I.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to confess. Indeed, whatever quality does while lying within matter, it does not achieve by existing separately, just as the shape of an axe does not cut without the iron. Furthermore, the forms that are in matter are not the same as they would be if they existed in themselves; rather, they are "material reasons" <note>original: "rationes materiales" / "logoi enyloi"; these are the formative principles or "blueprints" of nature as they exist within the physical world.</note> already corrupted in matter and filled with its material nature. For fire itself, if separated from matter, does not burn; nor does any other thing that exists in itself perform the actions that forms are said to perform once they have entered into matter.

<margin>B</margin> For since matter is the mistress over what appears within it, she depraves and dissolves it, bringing her own nature against it as its contrary. I do not mean that she brings cold against heat, but rather that she opposes her own lack of form <note>original: "orbitatem" / "aneideon"</note> to the species of heat, and her own formlessness to form. She opposes excess and defect to a measured nature, until she finally brings it to pass that the form no longer belongs to itself, but belongs entirely to matter.

<margin>C</margin> Just as in the nourishment of animals, that which is taken in does not remain as it was when it entered; rather, in a dog it becomes blood and everything else specific to a dog, and all the humors turn into the nature of the recipient. For this reason, if the body is the cause of evils, then matter is judged to be the cause of evils for this very reason.

<margin>D</margin> Perhaps someone might say that one ought to overcome such things; but that which is able to overcome is not pure unless it flees. Indeed, the more vehement desires arise from a certain temperament of the bodies; different desires come from different temperaments, so that not just anyone can easily be overcome. What then of the fact that some people are duller than others and unfit for judgment, seeing as they are cold by nature and unfit for movement? Others, by contrast, are carried away by an unbridled levity. Our own habits, which vary according to the times, bear witness to this. For when we are full, we desire and think in one way; but when we are empty, we do so differently. Indeed, when we are replenished, we are accustomed to being affected in one way, and in another way when we are not.

<margin>E</margin> Finally, to speak in summary: first, evil is that which is entirely devoid of measure; but that which exists in a nature entirely devoid of measure—whether by similarity or by participation—becomes evil in a secondary sense, because of what has happened to it. Again, darkness is evil in the first degree, but in the next degree, that which is darkened is likewise evil. In the same way, since vice is a lack of knowledge and a lack of measure in the soul, it holds the second place of evil, and is not evil itself; just as virtue is not the primary good, but is considered good insofar as it becomes either similar to or a participant in the Good itself.

<margin>IX. How that which is formless can be known by the soul, which is accustomed to knowing through forms.</margin>

<margin>F</margin> **BY WHAT MEANS**, then, do we know these things? And first, by what means do we know vice? We know virtue, indeed, by the mind and by prudence, for virtue knows itself. But how do we know vice? Is it perhaps like a rule by which we discern the straight from the crooked, so that we know vice as that which does not align with virtue? But do we know vice by looking at it directly? Certainly, we do not perceive vice in its entirety, for it is infinite <note>original: "infinitum" / "apeiron"; meaning without limit, boundary, or definition.</note>. Therefore, we know it by a kind of removal, when we say it possesses absolutely nothing of virtue; and as for vice that is not total, we [discern] that which falls short of virtue.

<margin>G</margin> Therefore, by seeing a part, and because of the part that is present, we suspect the remainder which is absent—the part which is contained in the whole form, but is missing here. In this way, we judge vice in the [soul]... <meta>catchword: inde / there</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> [it is forced] to be evil. But quality in matter does not act without matter; just as the shape of the axe does not act, but the iron does. And all the things that act in conjunction with form are not the same as they would be if they were by themselves, but are material reasons <note>original: "logoi enyloi"</note> destroyed in matter, and filled with the nature of the latter. For fire itself does not burn, nor does any other of the things existing in themselves perform these works, but <margin>* happening</margin> they are said to act when they are *produced in matter. 

<margin>B</margin> For matter, being mistress of the image that appears in her, destroys it and drives it out of its own state by being contrary to its nature: not by bringing "cold fire" to the heat, but by bringing her own formlessness to the thing that makes form, and her own lack of shape to the shape, and excess and deficiency to the measured, until she makes it her own, 

<margin>C</margin> and no longer an image of the former, just as in the food of animals, that which enters no longer works as that thing. But it becomes the blood of a dog and all the canine humors are those which exist in the recipient. If indeed the body is the cause of evils, matter would be the cause of all evils. But that which is able to rule it ought always to rule it in the pure state, or it will not [rule] naturally; but desires are more violent [due to] some mixture from bodies, some in some people, others in others, 

<margin>D</margin> so that the weakness in each does not rule. The flow toward the worse is labored through bodies, being chilled, and the activities are hindered, and there is the noise of dispersion; and the seasons and diets bear witness to these things. For some people are different in their desires and thoughts when they are full, and others are different when empty and regarding their affairs. 

<margin>E</margin> And this is so. Primarily, the unmeasured is evil; and that which happens in unmeasurement, either being made like it or participating in it, is evil by accident to itself, because of the primary evil. And darkness is primary, while that which is darkened is secondary in the same way. Vice, being ignorance and unmeasurement regarding the soul, is a secondary evil. For it is not <margin>* image</margin> *evil itself; for virtue is [not] the first good, but because it has been made like it or has participated in it.

<margin>F</margin> **BY WHAT** then did we recognize these things? And first, vice by what? By virtue, by the mind itself and by wisdom; for she knows herself. But how do we know vice? Just as by a rule we know the straight and the not-straight, so also do we know vice as that which does not fit with virtue? Do we look at it itself, or do we not look at it—I mean vice? Or do we not look at total vice, for it is infinite; and so we know it by removal or 

<margin>G</margin> in no way how? But [we know] that which is not total vice by its lacking something. Seeing therefore a part, and taking the part present as the whole, which is indeed in the whole form, but is absent there, thus we also speak of vice, leaving that which is deprived to the indefinite.

<summary>Plotinus explains that matter acts as a corrupting force on divine forms, comparing the process to how a body transforms food into its own substance. He defines primary evil as a total lack of measure (matter) and secondary evil as the resulting ignorance and lack of measure within the soul.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the philosophical inquiry into the nature of matter as the primary cause of evil. Having previously discussed how forms are corrupted when they enter matter, Plotinus now examines how the human intellect can even "see" or conceive of something as formless as matter.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

(A) Starting from what is defined, we leave behind that which is deprived of form. Indeed, when we look upon matter itself, we see it as a kind of deformed face; because the Reason-Principle <note>original: "λόγου" (logou) / "ratio"; the divine ordering principle of the universe.</note> does not rule there, it cannot hide the ugliness of matter. Thus, we imagine deformity as a certain lack of form. But how do we recognize that which has no share of form at all? Perhaps by removing every form, we say that the total remainder—which contains no forms—is matter. We ourselves take on a kind of formlessness within us when we strip away every form in order to behold the whole.

(B) If we are to behold matter, the intellect must become something other than itself; it must no longer be an "intellect" in the strict sense when it dares to look upon what does not belong to it. It is like an eye turning away from the light so that it might see the darkness; by leaving the light, it does not see, yet it "sees" the darkness in the only way possible—by not seeing. For without light, it cannot see anything, yet it seeks to see the darkness as best as it can.

(C) In the same way, when the intellect hides its own light within its inner chambers and goes out, as it were, into things foreign to itself, it does not bring its own light with it. It then experiences a condition contrary to its own nature, standing naked so that it may behold its opposite.

(D) And so much for that. But from where does this essence come, and how is it evil? It is called "without quality" <term>without quality: the Greek 'apoios' describes something that has no inherent properties like color, heat, or weight before form acts upon it.</term> because it possesses none of those qualities itself which it is about to receive. These qualities will exist in matter as if in a subject, but matter itself does not have a nature of its own. If it does have a nature, what prevents that nature from being evil? Yet I do not mean evil in the sense of a quality; for a "quality" is that by which something else is described through its presence.

(E) But the nature that is contrary to every form is "privation" <term>privation: 'sterēsis', the total absence of a quality or form that should naturally be present.</term>. Privation is always found in something else and has no substance of its own. Therefore, if evil is situated in privation, then evil must exist in that which is deprived of form, meaning it cannot exist by itself.

(F) If, then, evil exists in the soul, it is the privation within the soul that is the evil and the vice, and there is nothing outside it. Since other arguments completely do away with the existence of matter, one should not look for evil elsewhere, but place it in the soul as the absence of good; but this privation is something that falls upon the soul from itself.

<column-break/>

(A) Leaving behind the defined, we look at that which is deprived of form. Yet in matter itself, we behold a kind of deformed face, because Reason does not rule there, nor can it cover the foulness of matter. Thus, we conceive of deformity as a result of a certain defect of form <note>original: "speciei defectu"; Plotinus uses 'species' here as the Latin equivalent of 'eidos' or 'form'.</note>. But in what way do we know that which has obtained no form from any side? Perhaps by taking away form entirely, we claim that the whole of what remains—which lacks form—is matter, and we admit a total formlessness into ourselves while we strip away the universal form.

(B) This is how we must be if we are to inspect matter. Therefore, this intellect becomes something else, a sort of "non-intellect," while it dares to look at things above <note>In this context, 'supra' (above) refers to looking beyond the boundaries of defined reality into the abyss of matter.</note> its own nature. It is like an eye turning away from the light to see the darkness, and yet it does not see; for to see darkness, it leaves the light. It cannot see darkness together with light, nor can it see anything without light; yet it happens that it "sees" in such a way that it can see as much as possible.

(C) Similarly, the intellect, hiding its own light in its inner depths and progressing as if outside of itself, goes away into those things which are foreign to it. In the meantime, it does not apply its own light; and therefore, it undergoes a condition contrary to its nature so that it may inspect what is contrary to itself.

<margin>Why matter is evil: not because of what type it is, but because it is never the end until it is the Good without quality; thus matter is entirely formless; and what form is.</margin>

(D) **SO MUCH** has been said of these things. Since matter is entirely void of quality, under what condition is it said to be evil? Perhaps it is said to be void of quality because it possesses none of the qualities it is destined to receive within itself as a subject; yet it is not called "without quality" as if it had no nature at all. If it has some nature, what prevents us from saying this nature is evil? I do not mean "evil" as if it were endowed with a specific quality; for a quality is that by which another thing is named.

(E) A quality, therefore, is an accident <term>accident: 'accidens', a property that belongs to a thing but is not part of its essential definition.</term>, and it happens in something else. Matter, however, is not in something else, but is the subject around which every accident turns. Since that which is called a quality has the nature of an accident, matter is said to have no share in being "of a certain quality." Furthermore, if quality itself is "without quality," how can matter—which has not obtained a quality—be called "of a quality"? It is correctly said to be both "without quality" and "evil."

(F) For it is not judged to be evil because it has a quality, but rather because it has no quality. If it were a form, it might perhaps be evil in some way, but it would not be a nature contrary to form.

<margin>The first is total privation: whether it can exist by itself in itself. Let the answer be given by making a distinction.</margin>

(G) **BUT** the nature contrary to the whole form is privation. Privation, however, is always in another thing; it is not a substance in itself. Therefore, if evil is situated in privation, evil will certainly be in that which is deprived of form. Thus, it cannot exist by itself. If, then, evil is in the soul, the privation in the soul is the evil and the depravity, and one need not receive anything from the outside. For other reasons also completely remove matter; and these do not even think it is evil when it is present. Therefore, nothing is to be sought elsewhere as if it were evil; but he who places evil in the soul must conclude that it is the absence of good.

<summary>This page discusses how the human mind perceives matter—the "formless" substrate of the universe—by stripping away all light and quality. Plotinus argues that matter is essentially "evil" not because it has bad traits, but because it is a "privation" or total absence of form and goodness.</summary>

<keywords>matter, form, privation, evil, intellect, quality, Plotinus, Enneads, soul, substance</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of evil. Having previously explored whether matter itself is the "primary evil," he now examines whether vice or wickedness within the human soul can be considered "pure evil" or if it is merely a secondary effect of the soul's contact with matter.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS. BOOK I

...and if the privation of good exists in the soul—which indeed produces wickedness within it by its own reason-principle <note>original: "sua quadā... ratione" / "τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἑαυτῆς"; the organizing principle that gives a thing its nature.</note>—it follows that the soul would possess nothing of the good. If that were so, it would no longer have life, even while remaining a soul. But if it lacked life, the soul would be empty; thus, even while it was a soul, it would not truly be a soul. Therefore, the soul possesses life by its very nature. For this reason, it does not possess the privation of good within itself. The soul is therefore uniform, insofar as it possesses some trace of the Intellect, and it is not evil of its own accord. Therefore, the soul is not the "primary evil." Furthermore, that which is primarily evil is not an "accident" <note>An "accident" in philosophy is a property that a thing may or may not have without losing its essential identity.</note> of the soul, since the soul is never entirely devoid of all good.

<margin>XII
Vice itself is not pure evil in the soul, but rather a kind of mixed reason. The response is that it is not pure, even in the soul.</margin>
**WHAT** then if someone suggests that wickedness is not a total privation of good, but that the soul, possessing evil and yet partially lacking it, would have a mixed perception rather than pure evil? In that case, we would not yet have found "pure evil" itself. The good of the soul would reside in its very essence, while evil would be considered a mere accident.

<margin>XIII
How vice itself may be evil when present in the soul: how the soul is said to be among evils, namely matter.</margin>
**UNLESS** perhaps evil is said to be an impediment to the soul, just as an obstruction is to the eye for seeing. If this were the case, evil would certainly be the *cause* of evil, implying that "evil itself" is something else entirely. If vice is an impediment to the soul, then vice is not evil itself, but the cause of evil. For virtue is not the Good itself, but rather something that contributes to it. If virtue is not the Good, then vice is not Evil. Accordingly, just as virtue is neither the "Beautiful itself" nor the "Good itself," so vice is neither the "Ugly itself" nor "Evil itself." We have said that virtue is not the Beautiful or the Good because the Beautiful and the Good exist before and above virtue. Therefore, virtue is deemed good and beautiful only by a kind of participation. Just as the Beautiful and the Good meet the mind as it ascends above virtue, so too does Evil itself meet the soul as it descends below wickedness—provided the soul starts from wickedness and is then able to "view" evil (if indeed any "view" of evil itself is possible). Finally, once the soul has descended, it enters into evil; it goes deep into the "region of dissimilarity" <note>original: "dissimilitudinis regionem" / "ἀνομοιότητος τόπῳ"; a famous Platonic concept describing the state of being unlike God or the divine order.</note>, where, submerged, it is said to have fallen into "dark mire" <note>original: "cœnum tenebrosum" / "βόρβορον σκοτεινὸν".</note>. If the soul falls completely into total wickedness, it no longer possesses mere wickedness, but takes on another, lower nature. For wickedness is still something human, being mixed with its opposite. A wicked man "dies," therefore, in the only way a soul can die. The death of the soul is twofold: while still plunged in the body, it sinks into matter <note>original: "materiam" / "ὕλῃ"</note> and is filled by it; and after it has laid aside the body, it wallows in the same mud until it finally returns to the higher realms and lifts its gaze from the filth. Otherwise, its fate is to slumber in the underworld.

<margin>XIIII
How evil in the soul is a weakness. How the soul can certainly suffer weakness; how it is when separated.</margin>
**PERHAPS** someone might say that wickedness is a weakness of the soul. For a "bad" soul is easily affected and moved by anything, and is easily carried toward every evil, toward lusts...

<column-break/>

**A** ...the privation of the good in the soul: how can vice be in it? If the soul, by its own reason-principle, has no good, it would never have life while being a soul. The soul would thus be soulless. It would be as if it had no life, so that while being a soul, it would not be a soul. But the soul has life by its own reason, so it does not have the privation of the good from itself. It would then have something of the nature of the good. **B** If it has the nature of the good, evil would not come from itself. Therefore, the soul is not immediately the "primary evil," nor is the primary evil an accident of it, unless some good is absent from it.

**C** What then if one does not call vice or evil in the soul a total privation of the good, but a certain privation of it? If this were so, the soul would have some part and be deprived of another; it would have a mixed perception, and the evil would not be "unmixed" <note>original: "ἄκρατον" (akraton); pure or undiluted.</note>. Thus, "primary and unmixed evil" has not yet been found. The good for the soul lies in its essence, while evil is an accident.

**D** Unless, then, it is evil in this way: as an impediment, just as it is for the eye in regard to seeing. But in this way, the "evil of the soul" is a producer of evil, or it is a producer in the sense that it is different from "evil itself." If vice is an impediment to the soul, it is affected by evil. But if vice is vice, and virtue is not the Good but rather a "cooperator" <note>original: "συνεργόν" (synergon); a helping force.</note>, then if virtue is not the Good, neither is vice Evil. If virtue is the "Beautiful" for the soul, but not the "Good itself," then vice is not the "Ugly itself" nor the "Evil itself." We said that virtue is not the "Beautiful itself" nor the "Good itself," for the Beautiful itself and the Good itself are prior to it and beyond it. **E** Participation in them is how a thing becomes good and beautiful. Just as people ascend from virtue to the Beautiful and the Good, so they descend from vice to Evil itself. Starting from vice, they view it—if a "view" of evil itself is possible—and by participating in it, they come to be entirely in the "region of dissimilarity." **F** Having plunged into it, the soul falls into "dark mire." For if the soul were to fall completely into total vice, it would no longer have vice, but would have exchanged its nature for another, worse one. For vice is still something human, mixed with a certain opposite. Thus the soul dies, as a soul might die. And death for it—even while still immersed in the body—is to sink into matter and be filled with it. And even after departing the body, it lies there until it runs back up and somehow removes its vision from the mire. This is what it means to go to Hades and fall asleep there.

**G** If one were to call vice a "weakness" <note>original: "ἀδυναμίαν" (adynamian); lack of power or strength.</note> of the soul, noting that it is passive and easily moved, being carried by everything toward every evil...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul cannot be "pure evil" because its very essence is life and reason, which are goods; instead, evil in the soul is a "weakness" or an "impediment" caused by its immersion in matter, which he metaphorically describes as falling into a dark, muddy mire.</summary>
<keywords>soul, nature of evil, privation of good, matter, virtue and vice, region of dissimilarity, death of the soul, Neoplatonism, Plotinus</keywords>

# BOOK EIGHT.

</margin>
If the soul is moved as if by desire, easily provoked to anger, headlong in its assents <note>original: "συγκαταθέσεις"; in Stoic and Neoplatonic thought, this is the internal "yes" we give to a perception or impulse.</note>, and yielding easily to dim fantasies—like the weakest of things made by art or nature—it is easily struck by the winds of corruption. Therefore, this weakness of the soul is worthy of investigation. For if there is weakness in the soul just as there is in bodies, we must ask if it is the same. Just as bodily weakness is an inability to perform one's work and a susceptibility to suffering, so here, a certain analogy of weakness holds the name, unless perhaps the same matter is the cause of the weakness in both cases.

But we must look closer with reason to see what this so-called weakness of the soul actually is. For it is not caused by density or rarity, or a thinning or thickening, nor is it a disease like a fever that makes it psychically infirm. It is necessary that such weakness of the soul exists either in those souls that are completely separate from matter, or in those involved with matter, or in both. 

But if weakness were in those without matter, how could they all be pure and—as the saying goes—"winged" <note>original: "ἐπτερωμέναι"; a reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, where a healthy soul has wings to soar toward the divine.</note> and perfect, with their work unhindered? It remains then that weakness belongs to those souls that have "fallen." For these are neither pure nor purified. Their weakness is not the removal of something, but the presence of something foreign, just as phlegm or bile exists in a sick body. 

If we grasp the cause of why the soul "falls," the object of our search—the weakness of the soul—will become clearer. There is, indeed, earthly matter, and there is the soul. Matter, while present, acts like a bold intruder, desiring to enter within. But the entire place is sacred, and nothing is devoid of soul. Matter is thus illuminated by the soul as it submits to it, yet it cannot truly grasp that which illuminates it. For that divine source does not tolerate the presence of matter; the soul does not "see" it because of its own vice. 

Instead, the soul’s light is darkened by the mixture, and its desire is made weak by the very act of entering into matter. This is the "fall" of the soul: to enter into matter in this way and become weak, because all its powers are not present for action. Matter prevents them from being present by occupying the place the soul holds, causing the soul to become cramped or "contracted." What the soul has taken from there—as if by theft—it renders evil, until it is able to run back upward. Matter, then, is the cause of the soul's weakness and the cause of its wickedness.

<column-break/>

A soul prone and headlong toward anger and impulses, inconsiderately yielding to the slightest signs of the imagination, is no different than those things made very weak by nature or art. For these are easily corrupted by winds and whirlwinds.

In truth, it is worthwhile for one who speaks thus to ask: what and from where is the soul’s lack of strength? For the weakness in the soul is not altogether like that in bodies, but just as bodily weakness consists in not being able to execute its own proper work and being very easy to affect, so roughly here a certain similarity of proportion has introduced the name of "debility," <note>original: "debilitatis"; meaning a lack of power or a state of being crippled.</note> unless perhaps the same matter is the cause of weakness for both. 

But we must approach closer with reason and examine what is the cause of this thing that has received the name of "infirmity" in the soul. For it is not some nature that is dense, or rare, or thin, or fat, nor some disease like a fever that renders the soul infirm. Furthermore, it is necessary that this kind of weakness of the soul be either in souls entirely segregated from matter, or in those joined to it, or in both. 

But if weakness is not in those segregated—for they are all pure and (as it is said) winged and perfect, and they perform their actions without hindrance—it remains that weakness exists in those souls that have fallen. Indeed, these are neither pure nor expiated. Their weakness is not the removal of something, but the presence of something foreign: like phlegm or bile in the body. 

Accordingly, if we can clearly and rightly comprehend the cause for which the soul falls, we will have found what we seek: namely, what the weakness of the soul is. There is surely matter in the order of things, and there is soul: and it is as if they were truly in one place. For the place of matter is not separate, nor is the place of the soul separate—as if the place of matter were on the earth and the place of the soul were in the air. Rather, the "place" of the soul, which is said to be separate from matter, signifies that the soul is not *in* matter. This indicates that it is not united to matter; it shows that the soul and matter do not become a single thing. Finally, it hints that the soul is not in matter as if in a "subject" <note>term: "subject" (subjectum); in Aristotelian logic, the underlying thing in which qualities or "accidents" reside.</note>; and that is precisely what is meant when it is said that the soul is separate from matter. 

The powers of the soul are many. For the soul has a beginning within itself, as well as middle and last parts. But matter, being present, affects it and, like a bold woman, demands and desires to penetrate within; but the entire place is sacred, and nothing is devoid of soul. Matter is therefore illustrated <note>original: "illustratur"; meaning to be lit up or made visible by light.</note> by submitting itself to the soul. Yet it cannot grasp that by which it is illustrated. For that source does not sustain matter, even though it is present, because the soul does not even see it due to its depravity. 

The light and illumination proceeding from there is obscured by matter through mixture; matter renders it weak, especially since matter itself provides the occasion for the "entrance" into generation. For the soul would never approach unless matter were present. And that is the fall of the soul: to slip into matter in this way and become weak. Because not all the soul's powers are present for action, since matter prevents them from being present: because it occupies the place it contains, and it causes the soul to be, as it were, contracted. But what the soul snatches from there, as if by theft, it makes evil, until it is able to flee from that place. Matter, therefore, is the cause of both the soul’s weakness and its malice.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul is not naturally evil, but becomes "weak" and susceptible to vice when it comes into contact with matter. This contact is described as a "fall" where matter, though illuminated by the soul, prevents the soul's full powers from acting, leading to moral failure.</summary>
<keywords>soul (psyche), matter (hyle), weakness (asthenia), the fall of the soul, Plato's Phaedrus, illumination, Marsilio Ficino, Neoplatonism, the nature of evil</keywords>
