<meta>Continuity: Following the previous discussion on the nature of evil and its relationship to matter, Ficino now transitions to a specific ethical and metaphysical question: whether the soul can ever be rightfully separated from the body by force (suicide) or whether it must wait for a natural release.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
## BOOK IX: CONCERNING THE WITHDRAWAL
## OF THE SOUL FROM THE BODY.
### ARGUMENT.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a floral or classical motif.</image-desc>

Whether it is ever permitted to release the soul from the body by force or not is a matter of dispute among certain Platonists: on both sides they bring forward either the causes or the patrons of the arguments, namely Plato and Plotinus; but two in particular, Olympiadorus and Macrobius, seem to disagree. Macrobius indeed favors that side of the argument found in certain parts of Socrates's speech in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the immortality of the soul and the final hours of Socrates.</note> and in many other places in Plato. The argument of Socrates relies primarily on Orphic authority <note>References to Orpheus, the legendary poet and prophet, whose "Orphic Mysteries" deeply influenced Pythagorean and Platonic thought.</note>. Specifically, Orpheus places the universal providence of Jupiter—that is, the world-soul—over Dionysus, which represents providence, or nature itself. To him, he assigns the Titans—that is, the Daemons <note>term: Daemons (original: "Daemones"); in this context, these are intermediary spirits or forces of nature, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>—to serve him. These Titans, persuaded by Juno—that is, the care for progression and generation—are imagined to tear Dionysus apart. This is because they divide his common office of begetting and moving all things equally among themselves into different lots, and they lead the species of things down into individual generation. Orpheus further imagines that the Titans, because they tore Dionysus apart, were struck by lightning as a punishment—that is, they were turned toward higher things by Jupiter—and that humans were born from their ashes: that is, they were procreated from their divine mystery. And because humans were born from the Titans, who had been nourished by the body of Dionysus, he therefore calls them "Dionysians," as if they were certain members of Dionysus sprouting again from the germinating Titans. Thus, even the human body is a part of Dionysus—that is, of the world-body—and human nature and life are a certain portion of that universal nature and life. And if there is anything of a private form within us, or anything belonging to the whole that exists strictly within us, it ought to comply with the common whole. For this reason, being guarded by the providence of Dionysus—that is, universal nature—we ought to remain in this guardianship <note>original: "custodia"; a reference to the Platonic idea that the soul is in a "guard-post" or "prison" which it must not desert.</note>; nor should we depart from here before God commands it. Likewise, we must preserve what we have received from there, in the manner we received it to be preserved: neither dissolving what God himself has bound, nor bringing violence upon the members of God himself. Socrates first introduces this Orphic opinion in the *Phaedo*, and then confirms it by the authority of Philolaus the Pythagorean. For Philolaus says: "Do not divide the bond on the road," <note>original: "Ne diuidas in via liganum"</note> that is, do not divide the body from the soul in the very span of life while the path still leads toward its end. Again: "When you have arrived at the sacred, do not look behind you," that is, once a life of the highest contemplation has been achieved, do not turn back again to lower things. In the first precept, he commands that just as nature bound the body to the soul, so you should permit nature to release the body from the soul. In the second, he instructs that just as our will bound the intention of the soul to the body, so the will should release this intention from the body, so that once released, it does not allow itself to be bound to further things. Plotinus follows these Pythagorean and Platonic mysteries, weaving in the final clause with a poem of Zoroaster, and confirms it thus: The soul, being divine, ought to retain its own proper dignity after the manner of divine things; and meanwhile, by no envy or other disturbance, should it prevent that which it commands—that is, the body—from receiving some small gift from it, namely some degree of life, however it can. Therefore, the soul should remain within itself, and never by any disturbance should it disconnect the body's flow from itself. For that same disturbance would soon be turned back either toward the same body or toward something similar; since motion itself draws one toward bodies, and disturbance precipitates one even more toward lower bodies. But if the soul dwells within itself according to its strength, and meanwhile does not grudge life of any sort to the body, and waits until the body itself, by its own defect alone, can no longer preserve the life it has received, the soul—distracted by no internal motion and carried away by no downward impulse—will stand out entirely within itself outside the body. It will no longer wander from this body to that one, but will be translated from a baing of animal nature into an intellectual nature. After this, Plotinus asks how the body fails the soul. He answers in this way: When the body loses a certain proportion through which it reconciled life to itself under the soul, then it fails the soul. Just as if a certain solid, green wood were placed near a concave mirror, and a certain flame had been applied through oil to the sun's rays: once the oil is consumed, it soon loses the flame as well; but the light of the sun remains in itself just as before. Surely universal nature acts earlier and longer upon the seminal matter of this kind of generation in the manner of a universal cause than does this particular human nature. For this proper nature—that is, the human power—acts within the power of the common nature, and nature in turn acts according as it is directed by the man's own nature toward the particularity of this human body. Therefore, in the fetus of this man about to be born, universal nature, directed through the proper nature of the parents, agitates and forms the seminal matter. It affects it with a certain proportion of humors and vital qualities through which the fetus, like bait, reconciles to itself a certain life from the rational soul already present; through which it retains that same power. However, the ability to retain it for a certain span is granted from the beginning, to the extent that the reconciling power flourishes in the body. This 

<margin>
MARSILIO
</margin>

elective power was inserted by universal nature so that the life of the man might be prolonged there for a course of time fitting for the universe. If anyone, while this power is still reigning and would otherwise preserve life in the body, violently breaks this bond, they frustrate the counsel of universal nature as much as is in them, intercepting the course of nature which would have seen further according to a certain order. He therefore sins against the god Dionysus—that is, against the nature of the universe itself—and against Jupiter, the soul of the world and ruler of common nature. He also sins against Saturn—that is, the divine mind—which commands our soul to be tranquil. But this man, stirred by some disturbance, rages against the body; or at least, while he is occupied with such a service, he is distracted from simple and exalted contemplation. He sins again against Coelus <note>The Roman name for Uranus, the personification of the Sky and father of Saturn.</note>, the father of Saturn—that is, against the Good itself—while he grudges the bodily good to the body entrusted to him. Finally, he sins against himself: both because the soul had fashioned this living being and then unsews its own handiwork, which was destined to fall by its own proper fault eventually; and because we have need of a long time to purge from the soul the stains of vice mixed in from tender years, so that it may depart pure from the body and thus attain a pure state of life thereafter. Therefore, no one ought to take away from themselves the span of time in which they might purge the soul, prove themselves more and more, and profit through moral virtue and discipline. For the ancient theologians hand down in the secrets concerning the return of the soul that those souls who sin in this life are very similar to those who have fallen upon a level floor: to whom the ability to rise again is granted without difficulty.

--- Page 119 ---
<meta>Continuity: Following the previous discussion on the nature of evil and the "Orphic" metaphor of Dionysus being torn apart by the Titans, Ficino moves from metaphysical allegory to a concrete ethical debate: whether a philosopher is ever permitted to end their own life.</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO.
<page-num>64</page-num>

Moreover, those souls who have departed from this life weighed down by the filth of their sins are compared instead to those who, having fallen headlong from a height into a precipice, lack the power to rise again. They warn, therefore, that one should use the granted spans of life, so that the opportunity for perfect purgation <note>The process of purifying the soul from earthly desires and sins.</note> is not lacking. Macrobius, persuaded by these arguments of Plato and Plotinus, interprets their mind on both sides such that they would not grant to anyone, under any condition, the right to lay hands upon themselves <note>original: "manus inferre"; to commit suicide.</note>. Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a major Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> feels the same in his book *On Abstinence*. It appears that Olympiodorus <note>A later Neoplatonist commentator who often offered more flexible interpretations of Plato’s rules.</note> understands and approves of these same reasons, yet from their very words, both here and elsewhere, he maintains that this might sometimes be permitted.

To prove this point, he brings forward certain words of Socrates in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue depicting the final hours of Socrates before his execution.</note>. First, indeed, where he says: "The philosopher perhaps <note>original: "fortè"</note> would not bring force upon himself." Since he used the word "perhaps," he seems to have left a suspicion that it is sometimes lawful. Next, because he added in this manner: "Philosophers ought not to inflict death upon themselves, unless God has brought about a great necessity, such as he has brought upon me in the present." As if to say: A philosopher, caught in a certain necessity of fate, can rightfully extract himself from it by death.

He brings forward again the testimony of Plato in the *Republic*, where it seems to be permitted for a man utterly overwhelmed by a long-lasting and incurable disease to release himself from here, because he is useless to the city. For it is necessary that a citizen live not for himself, but for the city. Likewise, he adds the testimony of Plato in the *Laws*, saying: for a man seized by an incurable crime—such as lust for his mother, or the greed of sacrilege, or a similar impulse which he sees he cannot restrain—it is fitting to remove himself from the midst.

Similarly, Olympiodorus seems to have understood some of Plotinus's words. First, where Plotinus says: "If someone were to endure madness as death is imminent, then this very thing is not to be sought for its own sake, but is to be chosen under a necessary condition." Olympiodorus seems to have taken this to mean that it is better to drive the soul away from here than to live with madness—which, if it persists, means the man no longer lives as a man but as a brute, and no opportunity for progress is given. Someone might further confirm these points through what Plotinus says in his book *On Happiness* <note>original: "de Beatitudine"</note> in this manner: "If a happy man should happen to be led captive, the way is prepared for his exit; if not, it is granted to live happily there."

Macrobius could respond to these things así: First, that Plato used the word "perhaps" (as is his custom) for the sake of modesty. Then, regarding his statement "unless God has brought a necessity," he would say it is permitted for the philosopher not to kill himself, but rather, out of many cases and conditions placed in his choice, to select which one he prefers. Furthermore, he would explain Plato's words in the *Republic* and *Laws* thus: that Plato does not so much wish to permit the ability to kill oneself as to provoke a great love for the fatherland and to sharply recall one from impious crime. He will also take Plotinus's words in such a way that in the book *On Happiness*, he releases the happy man from his fetters by separating the mind from the senses rather than life from the body. Finally, concerning what he says in this book—that it should be chosen as a necessity—someone might explain that enduring madness is the necessary thing to be borne, rather than bringing force upon nature.

This opinion will be confirmed again by Plotinus's words at the end of his disputation *Against the Gnostics*, where he forbids leaving here before the natural time. Olympiodorus, in opposition, will argue again that the words of Plato and Plotinus are being too twisted; indeed, it is proper to undergo a certain death voluntarily, or by one's own hand, for the safety of the fatherland, for honor, or for truth. Likewise, it is sometimes better to separate the soul from the body through starvation <note>original: "inedia"; voluntary fasting to death.</note> than to permit it to live uselessly—or rather, with detriment to oneself and others, and far from every duty of reason—through long-lasting madness and utterly incurable disease. For in this way, although one might not follow the order of the lower nature, he will nevertheless follow the order of the higher nature; and the more perfect thing is always to be preferred to the less perfect—and that not by impulse, but by deliberation. These arguments they assert back and forth, and the dispute is still before the judge <note>original: "sub iudice lis est"; a Latin idiom meaning the case is undecided.</note>.

<summary>Ficino examines the debate between Neoplatonists like Macrobius and Olympiodorus on whether suicide is ever permissible, weighing Plato's and Plotinus's views on "necessity," madness, and the soul's duty to the state.</summary>

<margin>He does not lead out</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'O' depicting a putto/cherub holding a flowering branch.</image-desc>
A person does not lead the soul out <note>original: "ἐξάγει" (exagei); a common philosophical term for committing suicide</note>, so that it does not depart [prematurely]. For if it departs by force, it will go out still carrying something of the body with it. To "depart" means to move across into another <gloss>place</gloss>. Instead, the soul must wait for the body to stand apart from it entirely, rather than the soul moving itself away. In that case, the soul is entirely "outside" the body already. How, then, does the body stand apart? It happens when nothing of the soul is bound to it any longer—when the body is no longer able to bind the soul because its "harmony" <note>The physical balance or health of the body that allows it to hold life.</note> has been lost. What if someone schemes to dissolve the body? He has used force, and he has torn himself away rather than letting the body release him. And when he dissolves the bond, he is not free from passion; rather, he acts out of distress, or pain, or anger. But one must do nothing of this kind. What if a man begins to lose his mind? This would perhaps not happen to a serious man <note>original: "spoudaios"; the virtuous philosopher</note>; but if it should occur, it must be counted among those things that are considered necessary—things chosen because of circumstances, rather than chosen for their own sake. Furthermore, the administration of drugs <margin>to lead it out</margin> <note>original: "prosexagoge"; a variant reading or addition referring to the act of inducing death</note> to hasten the soul's exit is perhaps not beneficial to the soul. And if there is a fated time <note>original: "heimarmenos chronos"</note> granted to each person, it is not fortunate to leave before that time, unless (as we have said) it is a matter of necessity. If each person maintains the same rank in the next life according to how they departed this one, one must not lead the soul out while there is still a possibility for further progress.
<margin>to stand apart from her entirely</margin>

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'N' depicting a putto reclining within a landscape or foliage.</image-desc>
<margin>A</margin>
Let no one thrust the soul out of the body by force, lest it should perhaps depart only to migrate into a similar place [of bondage]. Otherwise, it will go out carrying something of the corporeal with it, through which it will migrate to similar things. For to migrate is to pass from one place to another. Instead, one ought to wait until the entire body fails by itself from the soul; for then the soul does not require a "transmigration," but is entirely outside. <margin>B</margin> In what way, then, does the body fail from the soul? Specifically, when no power of the soul is bound within it any longer, since the body can no longer bind the soul itself, having lost the harmony which, while it possessed it, also possessed the soul. What then, if someone takes care that the body is dissolved from the soul? Truly, in this way he inflicts force: and the body would not then be dismissing the soul, but rather the soul would be abandoning the body. <margin>C</margin> Added to this is the fact that when someone dissolves the body, he is not free from passion, but is compelled by either anguish, or pain, or anger. But nothing of this sort should be done. And if someone should endure imminent insanity, what then shall he do? Perhaps this will not happen to a man of integrity. But if it should happen, it must be placed in the category of things called "necessary": and chosen because of the surrounding circumstances, but not to be chosen simply on its own. Indeed, the contriving of poisons to compel the exit of the soul is perhaps not expedient for the soul. And yet, even if a fated time has been given to each,

---

it will hardly be done happily before that time, unless (as we have said) it is considered as a necessity. Finally, if each person retains the same rank or order there as when they exited here, the soul must not be extracted from the body while there may still be an opportunity for making progress.

MARSILII FICINI IN LIBR. I ENNEAD. SECVNDAE, DE CAELO, COMMENTARIVS.
<note>Marsilio Ficino's Commentary on Book I of the Second Ennead, "On the Heaven."</note>

# SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK

The discussion by Plotinus regarding the heaven contains eight chapters. In the first and second, he raises several doubts and, in the meantime, brings forward certain points conducive to solving these questions. In the third, resuming the doubts, he begins to unravel the difficulties little by little, and does similarly in the rest. He concludes summarily from all of them that the heaven is fire, and this fire is pure and most refined, possessing a sensible form. Its first form is light, and its second is a harmless and vital heat. But he maintains that this twin form proceeds from the non-sensible <note>intelligible or spiritual</note> form of that same heaven: he holds that the heat comes from life, while the light comes from the intellect, which constitutes its everlasting substance. He further asserts that the intellectual life—that is, its soul, which never departs from divinity—is the cause of this immortality and perpetual motion. As for the corporeal nature of the heaven itself, insofar as it is not strictly the cause of immortality, it nevertheless contributes to perpetual perseverance through a certain suitability, as it aptly, opportunely, and willingly obeys the cause that constantly preserves it. Thus far is the summary of the entire book.

---

->Since the world is corporeal, it is neither from itself, nor is it eternal through itself, but through a cause that is entirely incorporeal.<-

1 In the beginning, he seems to marvel at how the world, being a body, is able to be everlasting, as many wise men have agreed. For this universal body cannot be perpetual through itself, since it cannot even exist through itself—a point we have sufficiently proved in our *Theology* <note>original: "Theologia"; referring to Ficino’s own work, *Platonic Theology*</note>. Nor is it easily demonstrated how it is everlasting through another cause, especially under such a singularity of substance that, by its very dimension and motion, it appears destined to undergo division and, eventually, a change of substance. Furthermore, the matter of the whole world is also the single work of the total Creator. One work, I say, through its matter and form, being everywhere consistent with itself and sharing a common nature. Indeed, the form and matter themselves bring about this communion of acting and suffering <note>experiencing impact/change</note> among all parts. Finally, since the nature of matter itself is utterly formless, and distinction usually occurs through forms, there seems to be no reason why matter should ever be distinguished from matter. Since matter is the infinite subject of all things and is entirely without form, it is equally greedy for all forms—even those that clash with one another—and is thus perpetually changeable. Therefore, just as it is below the moon, so too in the heaven there is a potentiality for the change of form that always lies hidden in matter, since the matter is the same everywhere. 

This happens because the motion flourishing in the soul is the primary motion, and thus there is "action" there; but motion in the body becomes secondary, and thus there is "passion" <note>the state of being acted upon</note>. Truly, this passion threatens the body with destruction, especially because motion in the soul, as in an indivisible thing, does not tend toward dissolution, whereas in the body, as something divisible, it does tend that way in a certain manner. Nor is it permissible to follow the path of Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher Ibn Rushd</note> and place dimensions in the heaven without matter. For if the very first forms—that is, the Ideal forms—have something quasi-material joined to them (namely, the "formable" essence of the mind), then much more do the lowest forms—that is, material dimensions—have something, or rather something entirely material, always with them. And if substantial forms are placed within a subject, then dimension much more requires a subject, since dimension is rather accidental and entirely ineffective on its own. Indeed, any corporeal form is nothing other than a "passion" of matter, or the way this matter is affected from elsewhere; nor is dimension anything other than the extension of matter itself, while it is extended by the same source from which it is formed, so that each may be formed more distinctly. 

Therefore, the foundation of the world is matter and division simultaneously: from matter it is changeable, from dimension it is divisible, and from both it is ineffective and passive, necessarily depending on something else. The world, therefore, is not eternal by the power of its own body, but rather by the soul as an intrinsic cause of immortality, and by the divine will as an extrinsic principle and end. If its nature is considered in God, existing always in a high unity, clean from all variety and change, it is said to have always been and always to be. Hence Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> and Plotinus, because for divine beings "to be" and "to act" are the same, and the effect follows that action immediately, judge the world to be eternal for all. 

But if the free Will in God is considered and this is indicated as the beginning of the world—which Hermes, Plato, and Plotinus also believe—it seems the world could be made by God not without a "newness" of divine nature or a "new" will. Thus Plato, Archytas, Severus, and Atticus <note>various Platonist and Pythagorean philosophers</note> think of a "new" world, taking it in the sense of the words of Timaeus of Locri, where he says: "God created the soul of the world, prior to its body both in power and in time." A little later, Plato also says in the *Timaeus*: "the soul of the world was created prior to its body, both in virtue and in generation." However, Plotinus, Porphyry, Proclus, and others explain these words of Timaeus and Plato in this way: that the "time" and "generation" by which the soul precedes the body is not an external interval of time, but rather that a certain "aspect" in the soul, in the very discourse of forms, precedes the motion of the world's origin. Thus, this motion comes from that one, and that one is the "age of ages" <note>eternity</note>. 

Add now the opinion of Heraclitus: that every body of the world, even of the spheres and the stars, is always flowing out and flowing back; therefore, it either ends or is perpetually renewed. Plato also touched on this when he said the world is "always becoming, but never is." Plotinus here, and Proclus in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, and Phileton <note>likely referring to a Renaissance commentator or a late antique figure</note> do not deny this is probable, and we ourselves prove in our *Theology* that the same can happen. But if the entire body of the world thus flows and ebbs forever, while the substance of the soul remains, then not without reason will the soul be prior in time and generation to any "new" body of the world, if the world is always being made new from the old. Hence perhaps the Prophets and Evangelists say: "I saw a new heaven and a new earth." Likewise, the Evangelist says: "the world indeed passes away." 

But let us return now to Plotinus. Since the matter in the heaven is the same as that below the heaven, Plotinus asks whether celestial things are changed just like others, and whether the species <note>types/kinds</note> remain stable while any particular stars remain always the same, or whether the singular nature of each is changed little by little and renewed in a way, just as happens below the moon? To these things, if someone should answer that the universe is perpetual because nothing can flow out of it or into it, since... 

<summary>Marsilio Ficino introduces Plotinus's work on the heavens, arguing that the universe's immortality stems from an incorporeal divine will and soul rather than its physical matter, which is inherently changeable.</summary>
<keywords>Cosmology, immortality of the soul, divine will, matter and form, Plotinus, Plato, Timaeus, Averroes, celestial bodies, Heraclitus</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's "On the Heaven" (Ennead II, Book 1). The previous page established that the heaven's immortality comes from the soul, not its own material nature. This page delves into the physical mechanics of the cosmos and the arrangement of the four elements.</meta>

IN BOOK I OF ENNEAD II.

it happens, since it encompasses all things: if it has not yet sufficiently discovered whether any sphere whatsoever, and any star, are everlasting. For not every sphere and star contains all things; nor would it have granted a sufficient eternity to the whole world. For the world could still be changed from above—if not outside itself, then within itself—in such a way that, much like the manner of our own living bodies, it often changes its individual substance, while nevertheless retaining its eternal nature as a <term>species</term> <note>Ficino distinguishes between the "species" (the eternal blueprint or form) and the "individual" (the specific material instance that can change or decay).</note>. Finally, a doubt remains: whether this universe, or at least something in it, is so everlasting; and for what reason and why the species and the individual remain together in the heaven, whereas below the heaven only the species itself remains while individual things are transformed.

->The Soul is indeed the cause of the heaven being immortal; yet the heaven, for its part, does not resist the Soul in this.<-

## II
In the second chapter, therefore, he doubts again whether anything mundane can remain perpetual by its own nature. You should remember that all these things are created and preserved from elsewhere. As for what the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked while discussing philosophy.</note> say—that the heaven is everlasting because it is a "fifth body" <note>original: "quintum corpus." Also known as the quintessence or ether, distinct from earth, water, air, and fire.</note> beyond the four elements—he passes over it here as he touches upon it. For by the very fact that it is a body, since it is not simply from itself, it certainly is not always through itself, especially since its nature is divisible and changeable. Finally, if anything is to be the cause for a life of immortality, I maintain it is the soul itself, which is simply the cause of life; but the celestial body and the Universe are naturally prepared, if not to produce an immortal life, at least to receive it—or at least to offer no resistance to receiving it.

->The causes by which the world is everlasting, and the distribution of the four elements.<-

## III
But in the third chapter he asks: how does this body contribute to a state of stability when it is naturally inclined toward motion? He responds that it is because it does not flow outward, but flows within. Therefore, perpetual perseverance in such motion is not resistant, but rather conducive to stability. For if any animal, as long as it lives, is said to be "the same" because a similar nature and figure are preserved under the same form of the soul (even though there is a daily "outflow" of matter), how much more can the world be said to remain the same in substance as long as the same figure perseveres under the same soul? Especially since nothing flows out of the whole. Even if one imagines an alternating flow and reflux in any part of the world, it happens within such a vast community that nothing flows outside the whole, nor flows in from elsewhere; thus the entire body of the world seems to contribute to its eternal perseverance. The parts also seem to lead to the same end. For even the spheres of the elements remain firm at least in their mass. The four individual seats of the elements, disposed separately in the world, contribute to this same end, for they are arranged according to their natures; thus the elements, although contrary, are so separated that they never dissipate or confound each other. That there are indeed four elements of the world, and that the heaven is pure fire, we shall discuss based on the signs in the *Summary of the Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the world.</note>, in the fourth book of the *Theology*, and again briefly concerning the <unclear>absode</unclear>. Since, therefore, the greatest amount of fire is distant from the earth in its qualities, both are distant from each other as much as possible in space: they are thus in the sphere of the world, where the earth is driven to the center, and so in its stability the fire is extended to the outermost edge. And if the earth is always stable, that which is most distant from it is surely most mobile; but no motion in a straight line is everlasting. Therefore, fire is by its nature always mobile in a circle. Finally, if the proper characteristics of fire are the greatest distance from the earth, a perpetual circuit, and light, then the whole [heaven] is undoubtedly fire. Just as the nature and power of the world are bounded under a certain higher salvation, so too through its amplitude and figure—which is the measure of all things and encircles all things—it is similarly shaped into a circle. Thus, by its figure, it is not equal to itself [in all directions], and similarly it is also more capable and fit for motion. Fire seems to rise toward fire; indeed, while it stretches itself out in every direction from the center, it is forced to come to a halt somewhere "upward"—that is, at the perimeter—where it extends and revolves in a circle. And its figure reflects its circuit for its own cause: the figure stands for the circuit in knowledge, while the motion is not in the cause but completed in the action. They lead, however, to making the fire serve the stability of the world because of its "amplifiable" nature; it claims this amplifiable power for itself as fire that is quite effective, naturally rare, bright, and utterly foreign to any resisting or restraining solidity. Maximum solidity, which is proper to earth, hinders amplification most of all. Hence earth contributes to making the center of the world, while air and water, as mediums by nature, fill the middle. Let no one disagree that fire, because it is most rare and thus appears susceptible to change, is actually subject to no such passions. For that which seems to yield with wonderful agility, if you apply your mind, is seen to divide; it penetrates and divides, and immediately escapes every blow. Finally, let us add that the Divine Mind willed many forms in its work, just as it is itself "all-formed." But since from many things one work was to be made (I do not say one "greater" thing, but one most perfectly formed work), He willed in this work forms whose natures were far distant from each other, so that from their blending, various formal things might coalesce in a vast space. Think, then, of these things, diverse both in rarity and quality, made together from the beginning. These suddenly drive each other away and flee. Then the most subtle things flee first and fastest because they are more agile for motion and penetration, and because liquid things can float more conveniently upon solid things than vice versa. Thus, by a surer reason, the distinction was made—matter, of course, obeying the plan of the Author. But meanwhile, a spirit was commanded to be preserved everywhere within each part, even inside the densest things, not so much by the density restraining it, but by the very Soul of the whole containing the spirit everywhere, with animals and other things conspiring toward that same office of breathing.

->The heaven is spirit, and breath, and the word of the world soul: and it is everywhere, though hidden.<-

This kind of spirit carries us further. In the beginning, the celestial soul is not joined to the heaven as if it were already made; rather, by its own fecundity—which is both superior to and closest to the heaven yet to come—it gives birth to the heaven everywhere, while it itself, being most alive, breathes everywhere. But what does it breathe? A vital and sensory breath: not one that feels itself or is felt by another, but that by which the soul both gives life and senses other things. Because a breath of this kind proceeds from the soul, it penetrates her entire power, and insofar as it penetrates the universe, it is the salvation of all. Hence the saying: *The spirit nourishes from within.* <note>original: "Spiritus intus alit." A famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (VI.726) often used by Neoplatonists to describe the World Soul.</note> It imitates, again, the containing power of the soul, insofar as it—by its own "vision," so to speak—floats and circles above other things like oil. To this, perhaps, the following also points: *The Spirit of God was moved over the waters,* or brooded upon them <note>Reference to Genesis 1:2.</note>.

<sig>h z</sig>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

water, fostering matters that are cold in themselves, which are vitalized although secretly warmed by it; and from this, they obtain a certain hidden power of health. By this breath, by this first soul, the "Word" <note>original: "verbum." In the Platonic sense, this refers to the *Logos* or the rational, organizing principle of the universe.</note> (as far as one may speak Platonically) is the "face" of heaven; indeed, a spirit of this kind is the heaven itself. Spirit—that is, fire—is at least as much more subtle and effective than our fire here as our fire is sharper and more powerful than the air. This spirit is like a kind of wine and a leap of nature, having no proportion to our sight or our own movement. It is also the "Word" of the soul itself, now brought forth externally. For the first word of the soul is in the Mind, entirely simple; the second is in the Reason, already distinct there; the third is in the Imagination and Nature, now receiving motion and affection; the fourth is in the utterance—that is, the heaven—now admitting dimension together with motion. For the magnitude of power in the soul, among its forces which are far distant from one another, creates the magnitude of dimension in the heaven. The motion of the soul creates movement in the heaven; its affection creates efficacy toward an effect. Indeed, the rational power generates other forms in the heaven, while intellectual clarity provides light. Therefore, the heaven is like a spirit breathed out from the mouth of a more divine soul, and thus it vivifies and nourishes all things. It is, again, like a certain eye and the sight of the soul, by which the soul's affection and counsel are often indicated to us; by its rays and gaze, all things grow together. Light in the heaven, insofar as it is in the transparent, represents the intellect of the soul; insofar as it is in motion, it represents joy. Light alone is the image of intelligence itself; but the other forms, whether they be in the heaven or in other things through the heaven, reflect other "Ideas" conceived in the intellect itself. These are conceived and discerned through intelligence there, just as qualities are discerned through the light existing here. And just as the act of intelligence is the same throughout the whole intelligible world, so throughout this whole transparent realm, a certain pleasant image of the spirit from there produces and discerns forms everywhere, just as that intelligence does. Hence Julian the Platonist <note>Julian the Apostate (331–363 AD), whom Neoplatonists like Ficino regarded as a philosopher-king.</note> says, from the theology of the [Phrygians?], that a certain nature has been diffused through the universe and implanted in all things, which is translucent and shining in itself. This nature is tempered from the transparent and the light, and is never subject to any foreign mixture or any passions; it is surely a certain act of pure intelligence—pure, indeed, but proceeding outward in a certain way. It possesses both an invisible and incorporeal light, which is the cause of this visible but incorporeal light. These are his words. The Soul of the World, under the act of the first Mind, produces a light of this kind conceived by its own mind into its own nature; it joins and effects it everywhere with motion, whence it produces it like a breathed-out spirit. Now it extends it by dimension, yet does not disperse it; rather, it restrains itself by its own circuit in an orbital flight. Insofar as it pours itself beneath itself, it pours itself around itself, and brings forth from its first origin a continuous, single spirit, as it were, of a single breather. But other souls, following this one in succession, each similarly breathing a spirit by their own breathing power into this spirit that thrives so strongly, bring each one to the form and figure of the circuit of their own proper soul. For this reason, other spheres are subsequently distinguished in different ways, arranged here much as the breathing souls are arranged by nature. But all souls always border upon the common, perpetual breathing of the first soul. Such spiritual orbs, however, made narrower near the center of the world, turn out denser, and in turn generate denser things around themselves. And that which is densest remains infused in the orb of the earth; yet if it is compared to the earth, it will be judged as very thin, and agile for motion, and vivifying dense things. Do not ask, therefore, for what reason dense things descend to the middle. For the idea of the dense is there, because from the beginning they have obtained the middle. Again, consider how much rarefaction and condensation avail in turn for the generation of elements, lest perhaps you deny that, through the various density of the primary spirit, various elements occur besides itself. But meanwhile remember that rarity and density serve the actions and formations of the "Ideas" <note>The eternal archetypes or blueprints of all things in the mind of God.</note> in the things to be generated. Conclude, then, that a certain vital spirit <note>original: "animalem spiritum." This refers to the "spirit" as the third element connecting soul and body, not "animal" in the modern sense.</note> always sprouts from the Soul of the World like an inner offshoot of life, and that this is fire; and that this, like a vital light now stretched out into dimensions, a spirit lucid in act and hot in potential, is the fuel of generation everywhere—the heaven, I say, not only poured around all things but also infused into all. It is the "heaven of heavens." It is the breath of a more divine soul flying forth immediately under a certain form closest to the soul—that is, celestial, fiery, translucent, lucid, and hot—soon swelling into air (which is sometimes less like the soul), and then compacted into water and earth. However, in these three, the celestial spirit is everywhere present as the effecter and preserver of all things: closest indeed to flame and to the veiling soul; the nourishment for every soul. Wherever other things are, therefore, the celestial spirit is present beneath them; yet wherever this spirit is, other things are not immediately present. Just as all things are governed most closely by this heaven, I say that the very substance of the heaven is present not only by celestial power, which now necessarily demands presence everywhere. Thus even under the earth certain things are generated as if they were celestial. Thus all things live by heat alone, and they live by a certain hidden heat which manifest heat seems to have abandoned. Thus where extreme cold appears, fire is kindled: as it is produced in the mutual collision of cold things, the heaven, of course, producing it. Similarly, in any animal, the soul contains and brings forth a spirit infused into all the members, but in some places it inhabits a [son?], while in others it is fortified by humors, and in others by the members besides. But particular souls produce this spirit—which is the vapor of blood—by which they rule the body from heated blood. Rational souls, however, produce a celestial spirit, with which they wrap themselves as if most closely, so that they may be supported by the substance of heaven present everywhere. Plotinus confesses elsewhere that this is received even by the soul of the earth; Plutarch, John the Grammarian <note>John Philoponus (c. 490 – c. 570), a Christian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note>, Proclus, and Plethon <note>George Gemistos Plethon, the Byzantine scholar who reintroduced Plato to the West in the 15th century.</note> bear witness that Aristotle also thought our eyes possessed this. From this it is clear that heaven is everywhere, so that it may bear the whole and individual things perfectly and continuously, and that they may be ruled with wonderful ease by the heaven. And rational souls, wherever they receive or possess a celestial body, have and possess it in a place natural to celestial things. Truly, this celestial fire, of which [the poet] says: "A fiery vigor belongs to them, and a celestial origin" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing the divine spark within living things.</note>—though infused in all, it is mixed with none; nor is the visible light proceeding from it mixed anywhere; nor does manifest fire easily allow for mixture. Moreover, celestial fire is the only pure fire, neither suffering force nor inflicting it; shining wonderfully, but most sweetly warming beyond what can be seen, if in any way it is touched. But manifest fire both burns and consumes; it is not pure fire, but rather an "ignited element," which surely has everything from the heaven (which thrives everywhere), because it is more easily generated than others, and it generates and amplifies itself, and shines the farthest, and draws all things to itself, and is born everywhere. Hence Theophrastus <note>Successor to Aristotle, author of a treatise *On Fire*.</note> admires the power of fire in an entire book. Hence perhaps is that "spirit" which the Egyptians call the parent of nature, infused into all things. Truly, the nature of this spirit will best appear if someone should portray—which is perhaps permissible—that there are not many spheres of the heavens, but a single one, both filling all things and also poured around them, which has that motion which they wish to be the "First Mover." All the stars are then both led by this motion and also run through it by their own progression, with the heaven yielding everywhere without any offense, if indeed there is need for yielding. In this way, the Stars will most especially seem to have their own lives, if they move forward in the manner of animals, and are not merely fixed in the manner of plants. Thus, besides their own souls, there will be a single soul of the whole sphere. I, for my part, would perhaps defend these things as probable, were I not restrained by the authority of great men.

He also explores the radical possibility that the heavens consist of a single fluid sphere rather than multiple solid ones, allowing stars to move like animals rather than being fixed like plants.</summary>

### ON BOOK I, ENNEAD II.

->The heaven is the image of the soul, and the individual things that are in the heaven correspond to the individual things that are in the soul.<-

But let us repeat the whole matter again from another beginning. If you consider the heaven—which fills the entire world in its form and motion—to be entirely apart from external matter, you will undoubtedly be thinking of the World Soul itself. Of this Soul, the heaven is indeed the image, while the rest of the world is merely its shadow. That Soul, therefore, is an indivisible heaven; the heaven, in turn, is a soul already extended in space. Thus, I assign individual parts to one another, as if moving from the image back to the original model. The Soul is a simple form; similarly, this celestial body is a simple body. The Soul has no parts; this heaven is never separated into parts. The Soul is unique in its action—that is, it fulfills its primary duty through self-awareness—while the heaven performs all its tasks through a perpetual revolution back upon itself. Furthermore, the Soul is an unchangeable essence, although it is in some way changeable due to a certain formal shift in its own discourse. Similarly, the heaven does not change in its substance, even while it revolves in action. The Soul always acts in a similar manner; even within the dissimilarity of its own forms, it restores similar cycles of revolutions. The heaven likewise moves unchangeably, and while it seems to change certain configurations and outward appearances, it meanwhile preserves its center and circumference, and repeats the same and similar things through the same circuits of time. In the soul, the light of intelligence comes first; then, as if it were heat, comes the affection of the will. In the heaven, light everywhere precedes heat. And just as there the will is, as it were, the very boundary of the intellect—and to understand is to will—so here heat is, as it were, a certain boundary of light; to shine and to be hot are joined, for as purely and widely as it shines, so in turn does it heat. From this it happens that in materials similar to heaven—that is, diaphanous and translucent ones—illumination precedes the presence of heat, while in opaque materials it is the reverse. For these must first be heated, purged by heat, and made translucent, as it were, before they become bright. Moreover, of this celestial and hidden fire that flourishes everywhere, the rays of the stars are a more manifest and higher expression; and the ether—that is, that sublime air closest to the heavens, an "igneous air," I say—is its image. For now the heaven alone is fire; the rest are called "ignited." But the heaven and the air—especially that sublime air where there is either no solid resistance or very little, but a great deal of breadth—shine more purely and heat more gently. Water and earth, and terrestrial things, being heated by force, heat others by force. Since the fire kindled among us is still more similar to heaven than the other elements, it has been made a participant in light (which is something incorporeal) and is the most powerful of all things. It is as if it were alive with perpetual motion, dividing all things without being divided itself, assuming all things into itself, and fleeing any foreign mixture; and suddenly, when it is set free, it flees back into the celestial fire that is hidden everywhere. This is perhaps why the ancients were afraid to extinguish fire, lest they should seem to take away the power of a nature that lives by heavenly means. Just as ignited matter is suddenly converted into the very act and form of fire, so too does this fire flee from here into the form of heaven; and the form of heaven is considered to have always been converted into the form and act of life, while the matter of heaven seems to have been converted into form. It is exactly as in a burning vapor or a comet: the very matter of the vapor is so reduced to the proper act of fire that no condition or act appears there anymore except fire. In this way, the celestial form so completely overcomes and absorbs its own matter that no manifest condition of matter is seen. This is what most people mean when they say the heaven lacks matter—that is, it lacks the manifest sufferings and conditions of matter. Similarly, those who say that the vehicle <note>The "astral vehicle" or *ochema* was believed by Neoplatonists to be a subtle, quasi-immaterial body that carries the soul.</note> of our celestial soul is devoid of matter. This is what Iamblichus and Proclus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) and Proclus (412–485 AD) were influential Neoplatonist philosophers who explored the relationship between the soul and the cosmos.</note> believe. Now, since the nature of form is ultimately more powerful than matter, it rightly makes form the lowest thing—that is, quantity—which is so absorbed into matter that it seems to be matter itself, doing nothing and suffering infinite division; indeed, it is nothing other than a certain passive extension of matter itself. Thus, the most excellent of corporeal forms—that is, the celestial—occupies and hides its matter entirely, and the whole results there as form. I say a corporeal form, but so corporeal that it is as if it were not a body, but a kind of flashing light shining forth from an incorporeal life and a more hidden power, especially through the "eyes of heaven," which are the stars. Therefore, Iamblichus does not speak wrongly when he says that the body of heaven has been so reduced into life that it is life itself, and its nature is now in some way incorporeal, having only this much of a body: that its parts are distant and thought of as separate from one another. Indeed, just as in us this tangible body differs greatly from the soul, but the spirit itself—which many call the most subtle vapor of the blood—is like a kind of soul (so much so that the Epicureans and others, deceived by the proximity, judged this spirit to *be* the soul); so too does the rest of the body of the world differ more clearly from the World Soul. But the celestial nature flourishing everywhere is surely a "nourishing spirit" <note>original: "spiritus almus."</note> fostering all things. This spirit, by its closeness, deceived the Stoics and Strato <note>Strato of Lampsacus (c. 335–269 BC), a Peripatetic philosopher who emphasized natural forces.</note> into thinking it was the divine soul and God. That Platonist Marcus <note>Ficino attributes the following quote to "Marcus," but it is famously from Virgil's *Aeneid* (6.726). He likely views Virgil as a poetic mouthpiece for Platonic wisdom.</note> seems to have seen this more correctly when he said: *A spirit nourishes all things from within.* So that the spirit, which is by itself dissipatable and haphazard, might be ruled by a stable and organizing nature, he added: *And Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass.* And when he named "limbs" and "members," he signified that the world is one single living animal, living by a certain single spirit everywhere, and ruled similarly by a single intelligence. Ruled, I say, most easily and always; for that spirit, the more it is near to the soul through its purity, the more easily it obeys the divine soul for the sake of perseverance and order. And the rest of the body, being easily penetrated by the spirit, is supported by it, and it does not know how to be scattered from its natural place, while the Soul, being far more powerful, arranges and contains each of its own places. By its own motion, the Soul anticipates all motions, and according to the rule of its own revolution, it resolves individual things in certain places and times.

->The world, although called infinite in its perseverance, is not however infinite in its power, magnitude, or number.<-

The universe, therefore, remains for an infinite time, although it is not infinite in magnitude. For if the World Soul is very close to eternity—that is, to the divine Mind—and is therefore eternal and vivifies with an essential life, it certainly always supplies life, and from that source, its body continuously draws everlasting life. Furthermore, if the Soul always conforms this world to the very Ideas of the divine Mind, it certainly preserves all the species of things as motionless as the Ideas themselves (even while individual things are continually changed), and thus it contains this whole work as indissoluble as its entire Model. For just as any species in the universe of things is referred back to its own Ideas, so this whole world is referred to this whole Model. Here, however, individual things under a species are changed due to a certain cycle of "seminal reasons" <note>term: "rationes seminales" (seminal reasons). These are the productive, formative principles or "seeds" implanted in nature by the World Soul that cause physical things to grow and develop.</note>, which is carried out in nature and in a certain imagination joined to nature within the World Soul, with the celestial motion meanwhile contributing steadily to the same end. Nevertheless, the same species is preserved everywhere because of the eternal perseverance of the Ideas in the Mind, and of similar forms also flourishing in the Soul, with the always similar celestial restoration aiding the same. But the world, although infinite in time, is not...

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...either in number or in magnitude, we briefly conjecture as follows. We conceive of a fourfold infinity. The first is the highest infinity of both power and perseverance, found especially in God. The second is an infinity of perseverance at least in His divine works, which remain perpetually in their seat. The third is an infinity of number. The fourth, finally, is an infinity of bulk <note>original: "molis," referring to physical mass or size</note>. Indeed, an infinity of number seems to arise gradually through a certain perpetual succession of individual things, yet it never exists all at once in actuality. For even a species is defined by unity as its limit, and an unnumerable multitude admits of no order in actuality. Yet all things are defined by a certain order, both under a first principle common to all and under principles proper to some. If there is no crowd devoid of order among infinite things, much less is it found in the highest things, where order is supreme. For this reason, there are neither innumerable worlds, nor are the various parts of the world innumerable. 

Furthermore, an infinite bulk is more distant from the divine mind than an infinite number. Since the divine mind by no means desires an unnumerable number, much less will it tolerate an immense bulk; otherwise, this bulk would receive no order or limit from God. Nor is it permitted to imagine that a corporeal mass exists entirely of itself, or from several causes that are completely different from one another—a point we frequently refute in Theology. Neither is it necessary that there be more than one work under the single cause of all things, nor multiple worlds, one disconnected from the other. For we reject that idea in the *Timaeus* <note>referring to Plato's dialogue on the creation of the world</note>. Nor, again, could the bulk of the single world be so entirely immense that it would be divided into many members, or exist as a single mass everywhere. If it were cut into many parts innumerably, there would be no infinity of bulk anywhere, but rather of number; and the work would not be one or ordered, but rather scattered and accidental. But if there were a single immense bulk, no variety of things would remain at all, and this very bulk would not receive order or figure. 

And if such a machine were imagined to extend through an immense circuit on all sides, then toward the center (if any center could be imagined) it would be gradually reduced into a narrow space. Therefore, if it were moved, innumerable circuits would be imagined in that bulk: they would be arranged so that around the center one would always revolve more slowly than another, while toward the outer edge, in turn, one would be driven continually faster than another. Thus, on one side we would look toward an infinite slowness, and on the other toward an infinite velocity that would wander on forever. From this, the circuit of an immense bulk would be completed in a moment. From the other side, it would not even move; indeed, there would be no motion at all. For both infinite velocity and infinite slowness seem finally to coincide in a state of rest. <gloss>Someone</gloss> might object otherwise: that there would be an immense space everywhere, both of the whole and of the parts to the parts, because through lines projected at length from the center, they would turn out to be continually wider and more distant. Thus, the space of neither the parts nor the whole could ever be traversed. Therefore, it would move in vain, or rather, it would not move at all. 

What more? The fact that the worldly bulk has within itself a distinction of members is clearly declared by the differences of forms, the repugnance of qualities, and the opposition of motions. That this machine is not immense is shown by the limit of each single revolution and the defined order of the whole. That it is spherical in its highest parts is demonstrated by its inner spheres, which clearly imitate the most ample one. That causes are connected to one another by a single cause is proved by the wonderful concord of discordant things. Finally, the fact that it lives by the life of a most free breath of spirit is shown by a certain mutual communion of acting and suffering, through which lower things easily receive gifts from higher things everywhere, and higher things seem to hear the prayers of lower things, to bless their vows, and through which wonderful results often spring from any part of the world to any other far distant part, provided it is rightly prepared.

### It is confirmed that the heaven is eternal, first by the benefit of the soul, then by that of the body.

IIII. In the fourth chapter of the book <note>referring to Plotinus, Ennead II.1</note>, following doubt after doubt, he proves the immortality of the heaven both by the reason of the soul and by the reason of the body. Surely the summit of the corporeal order is present—the heaven—with which the incorporeal nature of divine things (that is, the soul) harmonizes so closely that it cannot be dissolved. Just as the highest air touching the fire is always ignited, so the very life of the soul, since it hangs most closely from eternity and does not depart from it, is eternal. Because the soul itself, due to its natural proximity, becomes the bond of temporal things (as we show in Theology), it is rightly joined to the eternal which it lives out. 

Likewise, since it has not grown weary in governing and moving this bulk for so many ages—a fact to which I abundantly testify—it will never grow weary. This is especially true since the soul does not drive the body through violence, for the body is naturally balanced for motion in this way; nor can violence be brought upon it from elsewhere, nor are the parts of the world worn down, but rather they are preserved by one another. Finally, if the soul, through its own eternal life—the nature of which is always to give life—has always provided life to the world, it will provide it always. Nor does it "sin" here, as if this most divine soul did a favor to the world by mistake, as if it did not begin to do good intentionally, or will cease because of its "sins." This he refuted in his books against the Gnostic heretics. 

But as for what Aristotle says in his own opinion regarding the parts of the purest fire, take it thus: This fire of ours, with a certain voracity, suddenly devours all matter, and then, luxuriating, vomits forth flame as if it were fierce; by this, it consumes objects even further away. Since fire, because of its thin, expansive, and mobile nature, is easily dissipated when placed and mixed among foreign things, it is granted by nature to easily devour nearby things so that it does not perish. Again, lest it destroy all things like an all-powerful force, it is granted in turn that it be more quickly extinguished. But truly, lest such a noble nature be lacking to the world, it is arranged that it may be easily recreated everywhere and quickly grow from the smallest bits into something ample. But celestial fire consumes nothing, because it is not itself consumed; for it is not dissipated at all, since it never changes its place, nor is it ever deserted by life.

### Why celestial things remain eternal both in species and in the individual; composite things, however, only in species; also concerning twin souls.

V. The fifth chapter signifies that for the very partitioning of the world, one must judge not only the first Intellect as its maker, but also the World Soul and the souls of the spheres, insofar as they are entirely joined to that Intellect and always, like colleagues, agree together with the first Intellect in this work. It signifies, again, that if composite bodies were made directly from the substance of any celestial soul, they would be indissoluble. For there both the substance and the action (that is, intelligence) remain, and from a completely stable cause, a stable effect is produced. 

But because any such soul pours into another from itself as if it were a soul, and pours out an image of itself externally and instills it into matter—whereby that kind of life becomes weak—therefore, this life preserves celestial and simple bodies as always undissolved, seeing as they seem to not oppose harmony and perseverance at all. However, it cannot exercise this against the repugnance of composite things. Here you will note that the celestial spheres remain permanent both in their whole and in their parts; other simple spheres <note>referring to the four elements</note>, however, remain permanent as a whole, but not in all their parts everywhere; finally, composite things ought to remain permanent neither in their whole nor in their parts. Nor should anyone object regarding

# ON BOOK I OF ENNEAD II.

...especially in rational animals, the soul remains after death, and among the Platonists, the parts of the animal will remain in <term>primary matter</term> <note>original: "primâque materia," the fundamental, formless substance that underlies all physical reality</note>. For this soul is not so much a part of the animal as its cause, and primary matter is the subject through which the animal exists. Thus, I say, [the parts] of its own specific matter are already entirely adapted to its own specific form. However, where he says that the things within the heavens are not parts of heaven: understand this as being "below," not so much in physical location as in rank. For the heaven, although it flourishes everywhere, is never separated from itself. Where he says that the heaven extends as far as the moon, understand this as "as far as the lunar condition." The lunar lot is also the last in the grades of celestial dignity. For the ancients call the region above the moon "solar," and the following region "lunar." Finally, he declares that in the whole of humanity, life is infused into the already formed <term>matrix</term> <note>The womb or the formative environment of the fetus</note> by the "animal stars" <note>The Platonists believed stars were living divine beings or "animals"</note>. The souls of these stars—while the soul of the mother herself, along with the father's power, contributes happily to the same end—draw the life of the rational soul toward the body. In a way, she contracts that life to herself, preserves it under action, and leads it; indeed, she would do so again if the generation were ever to cease. In that state, the lower soul gives the quality of being "simply an animal" by way of form; but to be a "rational animal," the higher soul itself grants this, though it contributes only slightly to the "being" in the manner of a form. And that indeed comes from the rational power or act, since it seems to contribute not to "being" simply by reason of form, but to being "such a kind of thing." And it contributes to being "such a kind" to the same extent that the other soul contributes to "being" simply. It can perhaps be said to contribute to being by way of an efficient cause.

->Individual elements are pure in themselves. Heaven is fire alone.<-
->Also concerning metals and demons.<-

### VI
The sixth chapter brings forward two doubts again: whether there is only fire in heaven, and whether anything flows out from there. He solves the first in both this sixth and the seventh chapters, and the second in the eighth. I say that fire is there, and at the same time not earth; indeed, Timaeus <note>referring to Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus*</note> thinks there is a certain solidity or resistance, or a consistency as if of earth, so that through fire, clarity might be seen, and through a solidity as if of earth, it might be touched. But by whom is it sensed in this way? Not properly by others. For since the whole world is constituted for the sake of its parts and particular things, and since it is the most perfect of all these and their end, it must first depend on itself to be sensed. For when the <term>World Souls</term> <note>original: "animæ mundanæ," the animating spirits of the cosmos</note>, born in a certain way beforehand, fashion the body: its offspring would not be so common unless it were such that it would be most clear and well-known to the soul. Recognize that where a body is properly conceived under the condition of a body, it is nothing other than being sensed. Therefore, the body of heaven obtained light from itself so that it might be sensed by its own souls by way of intelligence (which is to be seen); it also had a certain resistance from solidity or a consistency as if of earth, so that it might be sensed again by way of essential life (which is to be touched, namely by itself first, and consequently by others). Indeed, it could not even be seen through light unless solidity was also present for the reflection of the visual ray, so to speak; nor could it be touched through solidity unless it were again quickened by fire. Among these points, Plotinus indicates that if the heaven is touched, either by itself or by another, a gentle heat is felt. He conjectures that the "earth-like solidity" exists for the sake of "being" rather than for the nature of earth itself—which is opaque and therefore opposite to light, and very dense. Therefore, he by no means wants the nature of earth to be in the brightest and swiftest heaven, as earth is the most unsuited of all things for such motion. Likewise, he excludes water, because of its coldness and contrariety (since fire is the primary heat); and again, he excludes air. For nothing is more easily changed into something else than air; and if it approached a heaven so powerful, it would suddenly be transformed into the form of heaven. While he strives to prove that there is nothing in heaven besides fire, he brings into doubt that opinion of the *Timaeus*: namely, that two solids always require two means between them <note>Plato argued that to link two solid numbers or elements, two intermediate terms are needed for a perfect geometric proportion</note>. Perhaps this is more manifest in the "solid numbers" and dimensions of the mathematicians, as we explained in our argument on the *Timaeus* back then. In the elements, however, it is not so manifest, except perhaps in the distinct composition of the whole world and in distinct places. Plotinus indicates, however, that fire or air can penetrate the earth without water, and water can penetrate the earth and glide into it without the benefit of fire and air. But if someone proves that both earth and water are always present in the other two, Plotinus responds that these two would still not be necessary for the purpose of uniting them. But while Plotinus argues this, we must remember that water congeals into ice far from the fuel of air and fire, and becomes crystal; thus it cannot easily penetrate anything without them. But these points are nothing to Plotinus, whose intention is to refute the common saying—as if from the mind of Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) famously claimed that "everything is in everything," meaning every substance contains a small part of every other substance</note>—that there is never anything pure in the earth, nor can the thing and its essence consist in itself without the essence of another. As if someone were to say: there is no earth unless it is glued together by the moisture of water; there is no water unless it is liquid through air; there is no air unless it is bright, rare, and light through fire; and conversely, that fire never lives unless it is fed by moisture, nor does moisture hold together unless it is contained within the earth. But surely the formed <term>ratio</term> <note>The governing principle or "logic" of a thing's nature</note> of each thing seems to be such that what a thing is, it can consist of without the addition of a foreign nature. Since it can and ought to be understood rightly even without this; otherwise, if things are nothing in themselves, they will consequently be nothing in others, nor will anything be constituted from several things. Furthermore, since imperfect things (because they do not exist by themselves) depend on perfect things (which do exist by themselves), and the form of the whole is more perfect than the forms of the parts, the elements are rightly arranged above the compound things. These elements, which exist as parts in a mixture, existed as "wholes" in themselves. They exist, I say, as whole elements, though not as the "whole body" [of the universe]. Therefore, the form of the whole body precedes them as something more perfect; and if it does not precede them in the finished work, it precedes them at least in the Mind of the Creator. In Him, the community of the form of the whole and the attention to the parts are fused together in His art according to this sequence of precedence. Finally, just as in the <term>exemplar</term> <note>The divine "blueprint" or world of Ideas</note> of the world the principle of each species is distinct from the others, so are things distinguished from each other in the physical work. They are distinguished, I say, by both reason and existence simultaneously, especially since the diversity is greater here than there. This is also evident to the senses, because contraries flee from one another insofar as they flourish as contraries. Therefore, just as composite bodies are composed internally of simple elements, so are they governed externally by simple ones. Also, the celestial fire (the simplest of all things) governs many simple things, such as ether, air, water, and earth. This fire is governed most closely by the Soul, and through this—as if through a spirit—other bodies (first the simple, then the composite) are governed by the Soul. For it is necessary that many bodies, even those most unlike the Soul, be inspired and moved by the one World Soul through one body, and that one most similar to her. But to return to our purpose: it is necessary that each element be something in itself, at least internally, without the mixture of another. For either some small portion of earth is granted which is properly the same thing as earth, or none is. If any is granted, it is possible for earth to consist without water.
