# THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIUS FICINO

If there were no earth, then earth would be nowhere, and water would not be able to bind together the earth which is found nowhere. Likewise, the nature of air is one thing, and the nature of earth is another; indeed, their natures are very different. If anyone should say that earth, in order to be earth, requires air within it, he would be saying that cold, dryness, density, and weight require their opposites in order to be what they are. Furthermore, air is something in itself before it is poured into the earth; similarly, earth is something in itself before it draws in the air. Then indeed, air exists in its own <term>rarefaction</term> <note>The state of being thin or less dense, the opposite of condensation</note> before it is condensed into earth; and earth exists in itself before it condenses air—which, if condensed by another, namely water, would pass into water. For this reason, *Timaeus* <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue *Timaeus*, which describes the creation of the universe</note> did not say that earth, in order to be earth, requires fire, lest cold and weight be said to require heat and lightness as their roots in order to be cold and weight; rather, he said fire is required so that earth might be visible. For by light the eyes see, and the things themselves are seen, which are also colored by a certain participation in light. 

Indeed, light is the proper quality of fire. Since earth is naturally opaque and neither shines by itself nor receives light within, while water and air, being <term>diaphanous</term> <note>Transparent or translucent</note> (that is, clear and permeable to light), do not possess light themselves but receive it suddenly, it follows that fire possesses light by its very nature. This is especially clear since other things obviously receive light from fire, and fire itself leaves its light to nothing else as if it were its own when it departs, although it may leave heat behind for a time. From this it is established that fire is the "heaven." Since fire provides light—which is its chief and proper quality—earlier, more quickly, and further than it provides heat, it can apply this light of its own as a "nourishment," and through this it produces an effect, which is color, especially bright to others, through which they may be seen, even if fire does not mix itself with them. Indeed, it provides light and visibility more to moist things, as they are more familiar to the heavens, while to drier things it provides color, and this is a consuming color, made by the sun through dryness, narrowness, and violence. Thus far we have shown that earth is this very thing which it is, without an intimate mixing of fire, air, and water.

That water, in turn, can be water without the participation of earth is evident through similar arguments. Surely when water is forced into an earthy density, it ceases to be water and becomes <term>crystal</term> <note>Ancient philosophers often believed rock crystal was water frozen so intensely it could never melt</note>, clearly after it has received a new and substantial form; for before that, it becomes ice. Earth, therefore, does not make it to be water, but rather to be "not-water." In the same way, anyone who considers that nothing is softer, more yielding, or more penetrable than air—and nothing is less so than earth—will find that air does not participate in earth. Therefore, earth does not make air to be air, since it has a repugnant property. But if the lower things are something by themselves apart from others, much more so is the "heaven" itself, which is most excellent of all and intolerant of mixing. 

Nor does the heaven need earth to acquire dimensions and continuity; for because of its nature, which is most effective in matter, it expands its own matter into dimensions in a wonderful way. Likewise, since it least tolerates mixing, it preserves its own continuity for itself. It possesses a certain resistance and consistency, which they call "solidity" in it, not because of earth (as earth simply has it due to three-fold dimension), but through a density now proper to itself, by which it not only reflects the rays of the eyes but also accommodates the powers of higher things to the lower and more kindred ones. Truly, it is clear that nothing earthy underlies these flashing lights, because nowhere in heaven is such a color seen as exists in the color of clouds, which have something earthy in them; rather, the color is such as either a frequent flame or a gathered paleness of saffron is accustomed to produce. 

Indeed, *Plotinus* <note>The Neoplatonist philosopher whose work Ficino is commentating upon</note> wishes for solidity, which resists in whatever way, to be one way in earth and another way in other things. In earth, it exists along with a certain rough appearance and a hardness proper to earth, which nevertheless is most distant from the heaven, which is the smoothest and most agile of all things. Elsewhere, in fire, there is its own solidity through a certain proper compacting, certainly not through earth, but through a density proper to it in some place. Just as in water, often not through earth but through its own coherence and coming together, crystal is made, and metal, namely gold. He [Plotinus] seems to think that gold does not participate in earth, but is made only from water in the manner of crystal, but more tightly compressed within itself, in which there is some viscous substance similar to oil. From this it happens that gold, both because of its very tight hardening, is indissoluble, and because of its viscous moisture, it is cast in fire and liquefied; and because it does not participate in earth, it does not draw rust. It obtains its brilliance from its <term>species</term> <note>Its formal appearance or essence</note> and is therefore yellow-gold; and the form of silver behaves similarly, except that it follows the *Moon* rather. 

For the authors of <term>alchemy</term> <note>The medieval and Renaissance precursor to chemistry, focused on the transmutation of matter</note> attribute gold to the *Sun*, but silver to the *Moon*; lead to *Saturn*, tin to *Jupiter*, iron to *Mars*, [copper] to *Venus*, and silver which they call "living" [quicksilver/mercury] to *Mercury*. Indeed, I approve more of this opinion of *Plotinus* at present than the one I followed in the compendium of the *Critias* <note>Another Platonic dialogue on which Ficino wrote</note>. It seems that *Plotinus* received these purest opinions about metals from the *Timaeus*, where metals are called products of condensed and fusile water; gold is said to emerge like a flower from water compacted within veins of adamant. It is also added that because it [other metal] participates in earth, it is converted into rust by age as the earth separates. *Plato* therefore also seems to place nothing of earth in gold, and similarly in silver; however, it can probably be understood from the opinion of others that what is earthy in gold is so tempered with the other elements and so perfectly mixed that it can never be separated from them. 

Moreover, gold and every metal are said to be made from water by a certain glutinous moisture, from which, as if from a mother, all metals are made; this they name the "first and hidden quicksilver," which they think is cooked and formed by "sulphur," as if by the father of metals. And from there all metals are made, and they are diverse insofar as in a single coming-together there is more of one or the other, and according to whether this or that of the two is purer or more impure there, and according to whether the cooking is lesser or greater. These two [quicksilver and sulphur] are therefore purest in gold, most equally tempered, and highly mixed; almost similarly in silver. In other things, these behave far differently. Indeed, all metals liquefy in fire because their "mother" is a great, oily, and viscous moisture. But stones do not liquefy because they have a great deal of earth; yet they do not have a moisture so fatty or glutinous like oil. In this way we can explain *Plato*. 

And where *Plotinus* says: "Gold, since water thus constrains it in itself without earth," it can be taken thus: that is, when it is melted at the fire like water, it hardens again in itself without the addition of earth when removed from the fire. But let anyone take these things however he wishes. Finally, let us return to the instruction. If condensation alone in moisture either completes the form of crystal or restores the form of metal, why should not the soul, like ice, keep the fire continuous, bind it to itself, and keep it continuous under the form of life? Indeed, there are also the fiery bodies of <term>daemons</term> <note>Spiritual beings that inhabit the air and fire, acting as intermediaries between humans and the divine</note>, not through earth, nor through a hardening forced like frost, but through the connecting power of the soul into their own held form, and reduced to a spherical shape. For the daemons are above us, each in its own sphere like stars; although for the most part they are hidden from us, they bestow a naturally circular shape through the interior circle of the mind, expressing it with the same affection and in the same place in their bodies. Although they often show us whatever figures they please, they either easily transfigure the agile matter of their body into various modes and then very easily re-figure it into the former shape; or through the effects of imagination and its intensity—like pregnant women—they fashion whatever forms they wish in a tenderer body. I leave aside that they often do not so much change their own body as they excite various images in our vast imagination. Moreover, although daemons are properly airy animals, he [Plotinus] often names them both fiery and watery. For three...

He also explains the alchemical origins of metals and the mutable, fiery nature of daemonic bodies held together by the soul.</summary>

### ON BOOK I OF THE SECOND ENNEAD
<note>original: "IN LIBR. I. ENNEAD. II." This refers to Plotinus’s second set of books, known as the Enneads, specifically the first book of that set regarding the world.</note>

Properly speaking, there are orders of demons assigned to the three regions of the air. The first inhabit the sublime air closest to the Moon, which is warmed and made radiant by the motion and light of the heavens; these they call the "ethereal" ones. The second group inhabits the middle region, and the third group the third. The highest air is named "fiery," the middle "aerial," and the lowest is "aqueous." Similarly, a certain aerial <term>triplicity</term> <note>In astrology, a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note> of the stars presides over these three distributed demons (as they say). Over the highest region of air is Gemini; over the middle, Libra and Aquarius; and over the lowest, similarly, the <unclear>Scorpions</unclear>. The ancients sometimes call these "gods"—not simply gods, but divine demons. Just as they call certain similar living beings in heaven "demons"—not simply demons, but demonic gods. I personally believe that the celestial demons are not in the region of the fixed stars, but in the region of the planets, acting as companion stars to the planets; following the motions of the stars and planets while maintaining their proportions, these demons in the pure air complete their celestial dance in an appropriate progression. For perhaps one might think that just as with demons, so the stars and planets walk through the heavens with their own motions, in the manner of living animals.

<margin>
Orders of demons
</margin>
VII. The seventh chapter confirms the answer to the previous doubt using Platonic authority: namely, that the heavens are pure fire, and that any element is pure somewhere—meaning that what it is exists even without the others—although they mutually borrow and lend their gifts as if from the outside. Likewise, in any element there exists, I do not say the very nature of the others (otherwise all things would be utterly confused), but a certain quality somewhat similar to the qualities of the other elements. For since the world is a single "animal" <note>A living, breathing organism</note>, living everywhere by one primary soul and made of one matter, every limb necessarily has something in common with the others due to this union and participates in the qualities of others. This is just as physicians have discovered in the human body. 

<margin>
The world as a living animal.
</margin>
Thus, the celestial fire possesses not earth, nor air, nor water, but a consistency or a certain resistance somewhat similar to earth; likewise, it has a fluid liquidity or agility suitable to air; and finally, a smooth, gentle, and slippery equality very similar to water. It possesses something of the remaining elements in a similar way, yet they are not confused by that method of mixing in which the whole is usually mixed with the whole, nor are only certain qualities fused, but the very natures and matters themselves. Thus, where Plato says in the *Timaeus*: "God kindled a light around the second sphere from the earth," he declared that in the heavens there is only fire, and of the qualities of fire, only light. 

<margin>
Only fire in heaven.
</margin>
I say light alone—that is, primarily and chiefly. For under this light are all other qualities that exist there: namely, a vital and gentle heat, in which resides the moving and forming action of all things. When Plato says "light," he understands the very body of the sun, shining by itself with a manifest light—namely, through an internal light which is of a different kind from the light that flows from it through all things like an image of the sun. But even its internal light shines most closely from an incorporeal light; otherwise, it would not itself be incorporeal, nor could the light flowing from it be incorporeal. For that which is incorporeal in a body, or exists around a body as light does, is created by the incorporeal which exists in itself. 

It is clear that light is not corporeal, because it illuminates the whole suddenly and fills the whole without obstruction; and more lights join together instantly into one without resistance, nor are they stained by filth. The light of the sun itself belongs to no sudden thing; for it remains in nothing for a time, nor does it require the proper quality of an element in a subject to be present, but rather a purity very similar to the heaven and the soul. This same light, without collision, condensation, rarefaction, or delay, pours itself as easily through a vast space as it immediately pours itself back into a narrow one. 

<margin>
What the light of the sun is.
</margin>
Thus, one ascends from a coal to a flame, which is already departing from thicker matter; from a flame, one arrives again at light, which leaves behind whatever thin matter remains—it is no longer poured *into* matter but rather poured *through* matter. Finally, from this light which is seen, one proceeds to the light of the celestial soul; by its vigor, motion and matter are extended through dimensions, and through those dimensions, its light is poured out, just as if from the spark of a certain wheel, a bright circle of the whole orb should flash out. But enough of this in Theology. 

As for placing the globe of the sun nearest above the moon, this is not only the opinion of Plato but of Aristotle, the Egyptians, and many other philosophers, both ancient and more recent. It is clear that there is a great distance between Saturn and Jupiter, and between Jupiter and Mars, from the fact that Saturn completes its circle in thirty years, Jupiter in twelve, and Mars in two. It is also manifest that there is a great interval from Mars to the planets that run through their spaces in a year. Finally, we have clearly found a great gap between these and the moon, which completes its course in a month. Therefore, since the Sun, Mercury, and Venus revolve in a one-year period and are thus close to one another, it is asked which of these three is closer to the Moon. 

It is indeed probable that the one in whose sphere the diameter is longer is closer, whereby the greatest distance to the Moon is made. It is likely that the longer diameter is in the sphere of the Sun, so that it may be more accommodated to a grander planet. But what mathematical reasoning may hold regarding these things, others have treated sufficiently. Certainly, physical reasoning seems to require that the source of heat and the source of moisture—namely, the Sun and the Moon—be joined most closely above this region of the world dedicated to generation <note>The birth and growth of living things</note>, which primarily requires moisture as its material and heat as its nurturing force. Furthermore, the Sun and Moon possess adjacent houses <note>Astrological signs where a planet is most "at home"</note>: the Moon has Cancer, and the Sun has Leo. They also have contiguous exaltations: the Moon in Taurus, the Sun in Aries. 

<margin>
The order of the planets.
</margin>
Rightly, therefore, they also have contiguous spheres. Finally, from this order, Mercury will hold the middle position among the planets, like a wise man; and deservedly so, since it must be turned toward all equally and easily conformed, so that it may more quickly facilitate the actions of all. If, moreover, one were to believe one's eyes, I would say that the sun and the moon appear largest because they are both closest to us. Their proximity is further demonstrated by the fact that they clearly act upon us the most—so much so that the remaining planets, compared to these, seem to do almost nothing. Finally, the Moon, which alone of the stars does not possess a manifest light of its own, is deservedly alone under the sun and nearest to the sun, so that it may more conveniently borrow manifest light from the most radiant one. It borrows, however, in the manner of a mirror, and similarly reflects the image of the light. They call the celestial body "white"—that is, luminous; and while they say "white," they mean "most brilliant." For what whiteness is among colors, brilliance is plainly that there. 

Through these things, he hints that the form of paleness or redness is not actually in the stars, but appears so to us because of certain vapors. For we know that the purer the light of a fire is, the more brilliant it is. On the contrary, it grows red in thick matter and pale in medium matter, but in the thinnest matter, it shines. A suddenly burning flame is neither in the heavens, nor does it reach all the way to heaven; but it is either extinguished by the wind, or if it occurs in drier and more tenacious matter, it is reflected downward as lightning; or if it should fly even higher, it creates comets; but if the flame remains there longer, it is amplified through the ether and becomes milder,

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page's discussion on the hierarchy of demons and the tripartite division of the air, Ficino now expands on the nature of celestial light, the vital spirit of the world, and how these concepts relate to both Platonic philosophy and alchemical traditions.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
<page-num>94</page-num>

...knows the celestial light as well. If you say that this whole heaven is light—though invisible to our eyes due to its thinness—yet you say stars appear in it with light because of a certain density. Purely visible light cannot be seen on its own, but only when mixed with or spread through the heaven of an external matter, or when meeting a certain solidity and resistance in the heaven as if encountering a boundary. I do not mean "solidity" in the heaven in the way some do, as something that resists touch (for this is an earthly property), but rather a quality that either gathers or reflects rays. Indeed, this light extends even invisibly, as is taught in the tenth book of the *Laws* <note>Plato’s *Laws*, Book X, discusses the soul's movement of all things</note>, throughout the entire universe, like the vision of the **World Soul**, which sees, touches, and preserves its whole self. The Platonists think that each sphere of the Sun is the vision of its own soul, and likewise, other spheres and globes are the visions of other celestial souls. Hence we see in the eyes of all creatures that vision is nothing other than a ray, and the shape and quality of the eyes are most similar to the heavens; and that which is seen is either light itself or a primary participant in light, namely, colors. But the stars and planets are eyes that are not only "seeing" but "visible," through which animals may see and by which they are then guided; for through these more distinct rays, their powers are more easily adapted to us. The remaining spheres, however, are "invisible eyes"—invisible, I say, to earthly eyes—for they can be perceived by "ethereal eyes," that is, by the sense that flourishes in our own ethereal body. Plato proves in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue on the creation of the physical world</note> that this hidden light, or vital fire and spirit, is diffused throughout the universe. He says: "The circuit of nature, having embraced the genera of the rest in its circular path, and striving to meet with itself, constricts all things and never allows a vacuum to be left." Therefore, fire has penetrated most greatly through all things; then air, as it is closest to fire in its thinness; and so on for the others by a similar logic. 

Here he seems to think that the nature of this **hidden fire** first proceeded from a certain breath of the World Soul, and flowed into the elements from the motion fixed within that soul; by its power, the remaining elements hold together. These are soon encompassed by the circuit of the fire itself and, as if restrained, leave no vacuum between them. Thus, when that fire, expanded into a sphere, contains them, then everywhere within itself it meets itself, leaving nothing empty anywhere; it penetrates all things, most especially the highly-penetrating air, and similarly penetrates water, and finally earth. So much so that if we move from the center through the middle spheres to the waters where the earth is, the presence of fire is found remaining there, however mixed it may be. Next, where there is water, there are the other two; where there is air, there is also fire. Thus the spheres of the four elements are compared among themselves: the narrowest sphere is that of earth; wider is that of water, both filling the gaps of the earth and towering over its surface; the sphere of air is similarly wider than both earth and water; finally, fire, by a similar logic, is the widest of all, uniquely warming from the outside and nourishing from within. 

**Danaldus** <note>Possibly a reference to an alchemical author like Bernard of Trevisan</note> and **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a philosopher and alchemist</note>, thinking this fire and vital spirit is implanted in all things, call it the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>The "quintessence," a celestial element beyond the four earthly ones</note>. They investigate most diligently by what machines it might be separated from foreign matter, and once segregated, which studies might best apply it to uses that they hope will be <unclear>fruitful</unclear> for all. Many also hope that if they carefully receive this spirit from wine—since it is so celestial—they might apply it because its <unclear>virtue</unclear> is so heavenly; then gold might drink it up as its closest relative, and retain an eternal state as **potable gold** <note>Gold in a drinkable form, believed to be a universal medicine and elixir of life</note>. But these things are for you to judge. I, for my part, know certainly that unless a spirit of this kind were present in all things, many could not perform what they promise; nor could that Platonic word be true: that the fire of the visible world is one. It is indeed probable that the center and hinge of the universe is an earthly hearth, but rather of fire. This is proven again in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato's dialogue on the soul</note>, where he treats of mountains, clouds, and airs, and says that tubes of earth lie hidden equally in the part of heaven where the stars are; this cannot be true unless either the lowest part of the air is heaven, or rather heaven is there, as if there were one sphere above the clouds. 

But the entire world is denoted in the present context. Perhaps that "Supreme Theologian" <note>Likely St. John the Apostle</note>, when he says he has a **Celestial Jerusalem**, understands by that city this vital spirit reigning everywhere; its twelve foundations being the twelve spheres of the divided world, not (as some do) placing them only above the ethereal ones, but accepting them among the ethereal, namely air, water, and earth. He distributes twelve parts: three from the East, three from the West, three from the South, and three again from the North, so that there would be the <term>triplicities</term> <note>Groups of three zodiac signs</note> of the four signs. One is Eastern, that is, fiery, containing Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius. Another is Western, which he calls "watery," comprising Libra, Gemini, and Aquarius <note>Ficino here uses a non-standard elemental assignment for these signs, which are usually "Air"</note>. Another is Southern, of the earth: namely, Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn. The last is Northern, embracing Pisces, Cancer, and Scorpio. It is probable that when he says the whole city is made of pure gold, he means this fiery splendor is diffused through all things. He adds that this gold is like pure and transparent glass, that is, both <term>diaphanous</term> <note>transparent or translucent</note> and shining at once. For if you take the transparency of glass and add to it light as if it were its own, or if you take the brightness of native gold and add transparency as if it were its own, you will have the substance of heaven: which is indeed everywhere translucent and bright at once, even if it does not appear so to us everywhere. Where the theologian adds a variety of precious stones, he signifies the lights of the stars, whether appearing to us or not. For in any supreme sphere of the world, there are certain stars of great power and wonder, even if they are not visible everywhere. It is necessary for light to shine in a mirror in heaven everywhere, if light is proper to heaven, and if light is the most excellent quality of all other forms. That it shines differently in different stars happens not from some other mixture, as usually happens in our colors, but from the specific degrees of rarity, density, and distance. Thus the color of fire, when gathered, is red; when diffused, it is pale; and when most scattered, it shines. Consider how much our sight is deceived in these things from a distance through different media. But in addition to light, add to celestial things various virtues as well, from which both various colors and actions proceed—not the kind of actions that come from elements, but from a certain more hidden property, namely of a specific form, just as iron is drawn by a magnet. For things that act this way among us are said to act by celestial virtue.

->**It is confirmed that the heaven is eternal, both in soul and body: and although it is fire, it nonetheless moves naturally in a circle.**<-

The **Philosopher** <note>Likely referring to Plotinus or Aristotle in a specific context, though Ficino is commenting on Plotinus here</note> responds to the head of a doubt that asks: "Does anything flow out of or into the heaven?" He responds that nothing flows out, unless it is possible for the soul to contain its spirit everywhere; and the spirit willingly obeys the soul, nor can a most powerful violence be brought upon it from elsewhere. Everything is turned into itself before it is turned into another. Since, therefore, nothing flows out from there, it is rightly necessary that nothing flows in to preserve it. Nor is it permitted to imagine that heaven is anything other than fire, so that its circuit may be natural. For every natural event occurs to a spherical body placed in its own location insofar as it is moved; but straight motion is either violent (which is a disturbance from a natural place) or a return to a place (which is a natural return). Between these, where it is best for the action of fire to be heat, understand that power of elemental fire for the action. For the primary action of celestial fire is that which [is] the primary action...

He argues that the heavens are made of a transparent, golden, fiery substance that moves eternally and naturally in a circle.</summary>

Finally, at the conclusion of the book, you will observe that nature, in those things composed below the moon <note>original: "sub luna"; the "sublunary" realm refers to Earth and its atmosphere, where things are subject to decay, unlike the eternal heavens</note>, is either weaker, situated in a weaker place, or surrounded by weaker things. Consequently, it does not preserve perpetual life within a single individual compound. In this, it follows the celestial power, which preserves both the species and the individual together. <margin>He asks whether the heaven itself is eternal in each singular or individual substance, as well as in its species.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' with floral motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc>
When we say that the world has a body A and has always existed and will always be, if we attribute the cause of this perpetuity to the divine will, we might perhaps be speaking the truth at first, though we do not provide a clear explanation. Furthermore, while the mutual B exchange of the elements and the death of earthly animals preserves the eternal species <note>the "form" or "type" of a thing that remains constant even when individuals die</note>, it remains ambiguous whether perhaps the same thing happens in the universe as a whole. It is as if the divine will were able to do this: namely, while the body is always escaping and flowing away, it imprints the same species upon different parts at different times. In this way, the world would remain one perpetually not in number <note>individual identity</note>, but in species. Nor is it without reason that one doubts why some things in the world possess only an eternal species, while the things that are in heaven, and the C heaven itself, are said to remain always the same as individual things. If, however, we suggest the cause of its perpetuity is that the world embraces all things within itself, and nothing remains outside into which it could ever be changed, nor can anything external fall upon it to destroy it, we shall be assigning a fitting cause of eternal preservation to the "whole" and the "all." But the Sun and the substance of the other stars, since D they are individual parts and not the "whole" or the "all," do not yet receive certain proof from this line of reasoning that they can endure for all time. Instead, just as it is fitting for fire and other such elements to persist only according to their species, it would seem to fit these stars as well—and indeed, even the universe itself. For nothing prevents it, even if it is not harmed from the outside, from suffering eternal destruction as its parts destroy one another, all while E preserving the same species for itself. Thus, while the nature of the underlying matter <note>original: "natura subiecti"; the material substance of a thing</note> is always flowing, it receives its species from something else. The same thing would then happen in this universal living being that happens to a man, a horse, and other creatures. For "man" always exists

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' within a square frame featuring floral and architectural elements.</image-desc>
When we say that the world has both a pre-existence and an eternal body, if we trace the cause back to the will of God, we might perhaps be speaking the truth, but we would provide no clarity. Furthermore, the change of the elements and the destruction of the animals upon the earth preserves the species <margin>...these things</margin>; however, one might ask if this also occurs in the case of the whole. It is as if the will of God were capable of this: namely, just as the body is fleeing and flowing, the will imposes the same species upon it, so that it is not preserved as one in number <note>numerically identical</note> for all time, but the species is always preserved. Why then are some things only worthy of being eternal according to their species, while the things in heaven, and the heaven itself, are eternal according to each individual part? If we give the cause for its lack of destruction as the fact that it encompasses all things and there is nothing into which a change could be made, nor can anything from the outside fall upon it and destroy it, we will be giving a good reason for the "whole" and the "all" not to be destroyed. But as for our Sun and the essence of the other stars—they are parts and not each a whole—how can we have faith in this <margin>...as they</margin> reasoning, that they are preserved for all time? Or perhaps they remain according to their species, just as fire and the things produced from the earth seem to do, and even the whole world itself. For nothing prevents the parts from destroying one another even if they are not destroyed from the outside; thus, while always undergoing destruction, only the species remains. As the underlying nature <term>Substrate: the "subject" or material that underlies physical forms.</term> is always flowing, it gives way to another species, and the same thing happens to the whole living being as happens to a man, a horse, and the others. # BOOK ONE.
<i>i</i>

**A** exists, and a horse exists, though not the same one. It is not the case, then, that one part of the world—the heaven—will remain eternal, while the other part—the earthly realm—suffers destruction. Instead, all things are similarly eternal, differing only in the span of time they endure. For the things in heaven are far more long-lasting. If we were to grant that "eternity" applies to the whole universe and its parts in this way, there would be less difficulty for this opinion. Indeed, we would be entirely free of doubt if one believed that the universe is held together perpetually by the divine will <note>original: "βουλήσεως" / "diuinam voluntatem"</note> in such a manner. But if we say that this specific underlying subject possesses eternity in its own substance, we must show whether the divine will is sufficient to accomplish this. The problem remains: why are some things eternal in this way and others in that? Why are some eternal only in species <note>original: "εἴδει" / "specie"; the "form" or "type" of a thing, like "humanity" remaining even as individuals die</note>, while the parts in heaven are themselves permanent and exist in every respect as the same individuals?

<column-break/>

**A** exists, and a horse exists, though not the same individual. Therefore, it is not as if one thing in the world will persist as everlasting—namely, the heaven—while another—the earthly kind—suffers death. Rather, all things will behave similarly, differing only by the space of time: for heavenly things are more durable. If, therefore, we accepted the "everlasting" on this condition, both in the universe and in its parts, less ambiguity would follow this opinion. In fact, all doubt would be far removed if we demonstrated that the divine will is sufficient, and if it is so in such a way as to hold the universe together perpetually. But if we say that something in the world possesses perpetuity within its own proper substance, it remains for us to demonstrate whether the divine will can effect that. The doubt will also persist as to why some things remain everlasting both in species and in number <note>meaning as unique, individual entities</note>, while others remain so only in species. **C** For we must ask by what reason the parts in heaven are perpetually the same, whereas here on earth, animals are only the same in type.

<margin>
He doubts in a similar way, and you should know he is preparing to respond.
</margin>

**D** If we admit this opinion and discern that the heavenly realm and all things within it possess an everlasting endurance according to a singular and identical substance, while those things beneath the sphere of the moon possess it only according to species, we must demonstrate how a thing that has a body can preserve the same nature always under a singular property, since the nature of the body itself is in constant flux. For this is an ancient opinion, held by others who argued about nature and by Plato himself: that there is a perpetual flux not only in other bodies, but even in the celestial bodies themselves. For he says: how can things that are bodies and are visible be able to preserve an immutable nature that is always the same? In this, he clearly agrees with Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher famous for the idea that "everything flows"</note>, who said that even the sun is constantly coming into being. For Aristotle, **E** this would not be a difficult matter if one granted his suppositions regarding the "fifth body" <note>original: "quinto corpore"; also known as the aether or quintessence, which Aristotle believed was the incorruptible material of the heavens</note>. But for those who do not posit this, and who believe the heaven is made of the same elements as the animals here on earth, how can they account for this? Furthermore, it is much more to be doubted regarding the sun and the other parts in heaven. **F** Truly, since every animal is composed of a soul and the nature of a body, it is necessary that the heaven—if it is indeed always the same in number—possesses this quality either through both or through one of the two within it: that is, through the body or through the soul. Whoever attributes incorruptibility to the body would have no need of the soul for this purpose, except perhaps so that the soul is always with the body to constitute the living being. But for one who **G** posits that the body is of itself corruptible, yet attributes the cause of eternal safety to the soul, they must strive to show that the nature of the body is not at all repugnant to such a constitution and endurance. For in those things established by nature, nothing is discordant; rather, it is proper that the matter itself be entirely suited to the intention of the result.

<summary>Plotinus explores whether the heavens are eternal as individuals (by number) or only as a collective type (by species), contrasting his views with Plato, Heraclitus, and Aristotle's theory of the "fifth element." He questions whether the soul or the body is the primary cause of the heavens' permanence.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ON THE ENNEADS, BOOK II

<margin>
III.
The answer is that the soul is everlasting, both by its own nature and through the benefit of the body.
</margin>

**A** In what way, then, does the matter of the body <note>original: "materia corporis" / "ἡ ὕλη ἡ τοῦ σώματος"</note> which belongs to the universe contribute to the immortality of the world, since it is in a state of perpetual flux? Or shall we say it is preserved for the very reason that it does not flow out beyond the world? If something flows within itself, and not away from itself, it surely remains the same, neither increasing nor decreasing; therefore, it does not grow old. It is worthwhile to observe the earth, which always remains in the same shape and mass, and the air, which never fails, and the water likewise. **B** However, that which is changed within these elements does not change the nature of the living being as a whole <note>The "whole living being" refers to the universe itself, which Neoplatonists viewed as a single, giant organism.</note>. For even in us, while the parts are constantly changing and flowing outward, each of us lives for a long time; but where nothing exhales to the outside, the nature of the body does not disagree with the soul, so that a single living being is fashioned from both and remains forever. Contributing to this very state is fire—sharp and swift—insofar as it does not rest upon the earth, just as the earth does not rest upon anything else. **C** Once fire has ascended to the heights, where it must stop and remain, it certainly ought not to become sluggish. Nor should we think that, being settled in its own proper seat, it seeks to expand in every direction any less than other things do. It cannot ascend to higher regions (for nothing higher exists), and its nature does not allow it to be carried to lower ones. Therefore, it remains for it to be easily led into a wide expanse, and by a natural pull **D** from the soul, it is led toward life; thus, in an altogether beautiful region—namely, in the soul itself—it is moved. If anyone perhaps fears lest the fire should fall: he will find reason for confidence if he considers how the rotation of the soul <note>original: "circuitus animae" / "ἡ τῆς ψυχῆς περιαγωγή"</note> there prevents every downward inclination, guiding it strongly and sustaining it. But if the fire has no natural momentum toward descent, it certainly does not resist staying there. The parts within us, **E** joined into our form, cannot maintain their own constitution and so seek to borrow parts from others to be preserved in their habit. But if nothing flows away from heaven, there is no need for any nourishment at all; if, however, something did flow out from there and was extinguished, then another neighboring fire would need to be lit. And if it receives something from another that falls away, then another thing must be supplied in its place. But for that reason, the whole living being will not remain the same, even if things were so.

<margin>
IIII.
The world is continuously eternal through the participation of the soul and the body.
</margin>

**F** **HOWEVER**, this matter should now be considered on its own, not just in relation to the question, but in itself. Does anything exhale from there, so that the celestial bodies seem to require a kind of nutrition (even if not strictly called that)? Or perhaps, are they arranged there in an order where they naturally rest and suffer no outflow? Furthermore, **G** is only fire present there, or is fire the most abundant element, while the other elements are lifted high and carried through the heights by the fire that completely dominates them? For if one adds the most important cause—namely, the soul—together with bodies so pure and entirely superior (since even in other living beings, nature chooses the better parts for the principal members), he will certainly seem to have brought forth a solid opinion regarding the immortality of the heaven. For Aristotle also rightly says,

<column-break/>

**A** How then could the matter of the whole body be a co-worker toward the immortality of the world, if it is always flowing? Or do we say that it does not flow out, but flows within itself, and staying within itself, it remains the same? It would neither increase nor decrease, nor would it be born or grow old. One can see the earth also remaining always in the same shape from eternity, and in mass, and the air never fails, nor the water. Nature and the **B** living being change within themselves; there is no alteration of the nature of the whole living being. For indeed in us, while the parts are changing and going to the outside, each remains for a long time; if nothing flows out, is it not the case that the same falls <note>The Greek text here is slightly fragmented or contains OCR errors compared to the Latin, but refers to the harmony between body and soul.</note>? Nature is toward the souls, toward being the same living being, and remaining forever. And fire, being sharp and fast, by not staying here just as the earth does not stay elsewhere, but roaring there, it must be; and one should not think it is so **C** established in its own place as to not seek to move like other things. For it would not be carried higher, for nothing is above it; and it is not its nature to go down. What remains for it is a way of life, being drawn by a natural pull by the soul toward living, and it moves beautifully within the soul. And if you fear it might fall, the **D** rotation of the soul is already ahead of it, proving itself the strongest defense against every disease. And if it has no impulse toward the lower parts from itself, it remains without reclining. Our parts, having come into a form, are well-preserved in their own essences; they take parts from others so that they may remain. But if nothing flows away from there, would it need any nourishment? If it flows away and is extinguished from there, another fire must be kindled, and **E** if it has anything from another, and it flows away from there, it must also come from that; but because of this, the whole living being would not remain the same, even if it were so.

But this must be considered by itself, not just regarding the thing sought: whether there is an outflow from there, such that those things need what is (not strictly) called nourishment; or whether the things fixed there once according to nature remain, suffering no outflow? **F** And whether there is fire alone, or more fire, and it is possible for the others to be suspended and raised up by that which dominates? For if someone proposed even the most sovereign cause, the soul, along with such pure bodies—since even in the most important parts of other living beings, **G** nature selects the better things—he would grasp a firm opinion concerning the immortality of the heaven. For Aristotle also rightly says,

# BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin> That a flame is a living being and that fire can be insolent through its own excess; but the fire there <note>referring to the celestial realm</note> is even and quiet, and is mixed with the light and motion of the stars. Since it is moved by a soul that is next to the highest and best, and is endowed with wonderful power, how could anything once placed within it ever escape into non-existence? Unless one were to deny that the bond ordained by God is stronger than any other link, one must recognize it as the cause of all causes, which holds all things together. <margin>B</margin> Indeed, is it not absurd to think that the soul, which is able to hold the heavens together for a time, could not do so forever? It is as if one believed the universe were held together by force, rather than by what is natural to it, or that its stability in the "all" and in its beautiful arrangement were somehow temporary. Truly, only a violent force could dissolve this constitution, acting like a rebellion against a kingdom or a rightful rule, thus destroying the nature of the soul. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, this very fact—that the world never had a beginning (or at least began from something incorruptible)—gives us faith in its future perseverance. For what could cause the world to end at some point? The elements of the world are not worn away like wood or other such materials; since the elements remain forever, the whole remains. Even if the whole changes, it remains, for the cause of the change itself persists. <margin>D</margin> We have shown elsewhere that any "repentance" or change of mind by the soul regarding the world is a vain thought, especially since the governance of the world is free from all labor and harm. Even if the entire body <note>the physical universe</note> could be destroyed, nothing alien or harmful would happen to the soul itself.

   But why, then, do the parts in heaven remain, while the elements and certain living things here among us do not? <margin>p. 1. 2. He resolves the doubt of why celestial things remain, while sub-celestial things do not.</margin> <margin>F</margin> As Plato says: it is because those celestial things were made by the God <term>Demiurge</term> <note>the "Craftsman" or Divine Architect of the universe in Platonic thought</note> himself; but these animals here among us were made by the "generated gods" who were themselves produced by Him. And it is not lawful for that which is made by God himself to perish. <margin>E</margin> This is the same as saying that the celestial soul is closest to the Architect of the world, and our souls are similar; but from that celestial soul, a certain "image" is produced, which, flowing down from the higher realms, creates the animals on earth. Since this "imaginary" soul <note>original Latin: "imaginaria anima"</note> imitates the superior one as best as it can, yet cannot fully achieve that state—because it uses inferior bodies for its work and acts in an inferior place—it attempts to bring together things that are difficult to unite. These things, once joined, remain together unwillingly, and thus these animals cannot live forever. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, these earthly bodies are not held by a similarly powerful force, since they are governed by a different, more immediate soul. Therefore, if the whole heaven must endure, it is necessary that its parts—the stars—must also endure; for how could the whole remain if the parts did not likewise persist? <margin>G</margin> For the things below the heavens are no longer considered parts of the heaven; otherwise, the heaven would not extend only as far as the moon. We, however, are formed by a soul handed down by the celestial gods, and we are linked to the heaven itself by our bodies according to that soul. For the other soul through which we exist <note>the higher, rational soul</note> is the cause not just of our being, but of our well-being. And...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **A** flame is a certain heat, and a fire that is, as it were, injurious and luxuriant due to its satiety. The celestial fire, however, is equal and quiet, adapted to the nature of the stars. But what is most important is that since it is joined to a soul closest to the best things and endowed with wonderful power, by what way could anything that has been once placed in it escape this soul toward destruction? If anyone does not declare the soul flowing from God <note>original Latin: "animam ex Deo manantem"</note> to be stronger than every bond, he will surely seem to be ignorant of the cause that contains all things. <margin>B</margin> It is certainly absurd to suppose that the soul, which can contain the heaven for a time, cannot also do so always: as if it held it together by violence, whereas that which is held is in accordance with nature, and whatever is beyond this itself is situated in the nature of the universe and consists of those things which are most beautifully arranged. It is as if some force, introduced like an assault, could dissolve the constitution of the world, and like a collapse of a kingdom and sovereignty, could undermine the nature of the soul. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, the very fact that the world never began (otherwise it would be absurd) gives faith regarding its future perseverance. For what could be the cause for the world to cease at some time? For the elements of the world are not consumed in the manner of wood and other such things. Since they therefore always remain, the universe surely remains. Furthermore, if it is continually changed, the universe nevertheless persists: since the cause of the change persists. <margin>D</margin> We have demonstrated elsewhere that it is vain to suppose any change or "repentance" <note>original Latin: "pœnitentia"</note> of the soul regarding the future world; especially since the government of the world is placed far from all labor and detriment. Furthermore, if at any time the whole body could be dispersed, nothing alien would nevertheless happen to the soul because of this.

   BUT why do the parts in heaven persist, while the elements among us, and the animals, <unclear>threaten</unclear> to perish? <margin>F</margin> For as Plato says: it is because those things indeed were made by God himself; but these animals among us were made by the gods born of God. It is a sin <note>original Latin: "nefas"</note> for things made by God himself to perish. This is the same as if it were said that the soul is celestial, being the next after the Architect of the world, and our souls similarly; but from that celestial soul itself a certain image is produced, and as if flowing down from the higher beings, it makes the earthly animals. Since, therefore, this imaginary soul imitates the superior one according to its strength, and yet cannot entirely attain it—because it uses inferior bodies for its work, and again in an inferior place—it tries to reconcile into one those things which scarcely come together, and having come together into one they remain unwillingly; thus, these animals cannot always live. And these bodies are not held by a similarly strong power, since another soul dominates them more closely. Therefore, if the whole heaven ought to persevere, it is necessary that its parts also—namely the stars—persevere: otherwise, in what way would it remain, unless those similarly endured? <margin>G</margin> For the things which are below the heaven are no longer parts of the heaven: otherwise, the heaven would not be extended only as far as the moon. We, however, are formed by the soul which is handed down by the celestial gods, and we adhere to the heaven itself by our bodies according to that soul. For the other soul through which we exist is the cause not of [the soul's] being, but of its well-being. And...

PLOTINUS ENNEAD II.

...for it withdraws once the body has been formed, contributing little to existence by way of reason <note>original: "parum ratione simula ad esse conducens," suggesting that while reason/form is the blueprint, the physical existence requires the "body" to be manifest</note>.

VI
Whether fire alone is in heaven, and how much a part of it exists in itself; but also whether earth is composed within it, and likewise for the other parts of the world.
</margin>

### VI

->A<-

**NEXT** it remains to be considered whether fire alone exists in the heavens, and whether anything flows out from there so that it requires nourishment. Since *Timaeus* <note>Referring to Plato’s dialogue "Timaeus," the foundational text for ancient Greek cosmology</note> first composes the body of the world from fire and earth—so that it might be seen through fire and be solid and tangible through earth—it seems consistent that the stars are not entirely fire but contain mostly fire, especially since the stars appear to possess solidity.

->B<-

Perhaps this view is indeed correct, as Plato confirms this opinion with probable and apparent reason. Certainly, through the senses themselves—both by sight and by the perception of touch—the heaven appears to have mostly, or even entirely, the nature of fire. But for those considering it through reason itself, it will be thought to contain earth as well, since solidity cannot exist without earth. But why would it need water and air? For it might seem absurd for water to exist in such great fire. As for air, if it were present there, it would immediately be transformed into the nature of fire. But if two solids <note>Referring to fire and earth as the "extreme" elements in Plato's geometric model of the universe</note> having the ratio of extremes require two means <note>In Platonic mathematics, two cubic numbers (representing 3D solids) require two geometric means (air and water) to be linked in a continuous proportion</note>, one might wonder whether this is also the case in natural things. For one might mix earth and water without needing any medium to reconcile them. If we say that the remaining elements are already present in the earth and water, we might seem to be saying something plausible; but another will object that those remaining elements do not conspire at all to reconcile the two. Nevertheless, we shall say they are now reconciled to each other because each possesses all the others. Furthermore, it must be considered whether earth cannot be seen without fire, and conversely, whether fire cannot be solid without earth. For if it were so constituted by nature, perhaps nothing would have its own essence in itself, but all things would be confused. Yet each thing will be named for that which prevails within it. For they say that earth cannot hold itself together without moisture, for the moisture of water is the "glue" <note>original: "glutinum," a common ancient metaphor for how the elements are held together</note> of the earth. But even if we grant this, it would still be absurd to say that while each thing is something, it does not provide its own constitution to itself, but only does so together with the others—where, evidently, nothing would exist as its own thing. For in what way will the nature of earth exist, or the very essence of earth, when no portion of earth is that which earth is unless water is also present to serve as glue? Moreover, what could glue things there where there is no magnitude <note>size or volume</note> to connect one part to the next in continuation? For if there is any magnitude of earth itself, it must be that earth by its own nature consists without water; otherwise, there would be nothing left to be glued by the water. Likewise, why would the mass of earth need air in order to be earth, with the air remaining as air before it is transformed? Truly, it is not said that earth needs fire to be earth, but it is granted that it needs fire so that it and these other things can be seen. For it is consistent with reason to grant that sight is brought about by light. For they do not see darkness; rather, we must say that darkness is "not being seen," just as silence is "not being heard." But it is by no means necessary for fire to be in the earth; for light is sufficient. Indeed, snow and many very cold things are bright without fire.

<column-break/>

...body; it comes into being, having been gathered in a small way from reasoning toward conviction.

->Α<-

**BUT** whether there is fire only, and if there is an outflow from each [star] and it needs nourishment, must now be examined. To *Timaeus*, then, who made the body of the universe first from earth and fire—so that it might be something visible through fire and solid through earth—it seemed consistent to also make the stars not entirely, but having the most part, of fire; since the stars appear to have solidity, and perhaps this might be correct, with Plato also confirming this with the likelihood of these views. For by the perception of sense, both through sight and through the apprehension of touch, it appears to have the most part, or the whole, of fire. But through reason they inquire whether, if earth were the cause of solidity, it would also contain earth. But of water and air, what need would there be? For it would seem strange for water to be in so much fire; and if air were there, it would change into the nature of fire. But if two solids having the ratio of extremes require two means, one might be at a loss whether it is so in natural things as well. For they might mix earth and water, needing no medium; and if we should say that the others already coexist in the earth and the water, we shall perhaps seem to be saying something. But they do not—not by themselves—constitute the two coming together; but nonetheless we have them already disposed together so that each has all. But one might again be at a loss, as fire is visible and earth is tangible, but fire is not solid <note>original: "οὐ στερεὸν πῦρ"</note>. For if this were so, perhaps nothing would have its own essence by itself, but all things have been mixed. And each is named according to that which prevails. Since they say not even earth can be constituted without moisture, for they say the moisture of the waters is the "being" <note>original: "εἶναι," or essence</note> for the earth. But even if we grant it so, yet if each thing—while being called something—does not give constitution to itself by itself, then when together with the others, each thing will be nothing. For how could there be a nature of earth, and the "being something" of earth, if no part of earth is earth unless water were present and making a "glue" <note>original: "κόλλησιν," referring to the binding quality of moisture</note>, which is prevented if it [the glue] does not exist—at least as a magnitude which holds a part to other parts? For how will the earth and any magnitude of it exist, having a nature? But if one does not make water exist [within it], there will be nothing that will be glued by the water. And of air, why would the bulk of earth have need for its existence, remaining in itself before changing? Or of fire, so that it may be earth, it has not been said; but as for being visible, both it and the others—for it is unreasonable to grant [fire as necessary for existence]—but as for visibility coming from light, for surely darkness is not seen, but one must say it is not seen just as voicelessness is not heard. But fire at least does not necessarily have to be present in it. For light suffices. For snow and many of the coldest things shine without sensible fire.

† To be constituted [means] to be assisted.
</margin>

But it was poured out, someone says, and it arrived before it departed. But we must also wonder about water: if it is not water, what part of earth might it take? <margin>nobly</margin> Or is it because it is a human being? Does fire always need earth so that it may have continuity from it? For without it, it could not even hold walls together. But its solidity is not according to its three-dimensional extension, but clearly according to its resistance. Therefore, if it is a physical body, there will be hardness, which belongs to earth alone; since even the cold does not overcome flowing water—it is not a frozen kind of earth, but comes from density or freezing and from fire itself. Therefore, has the soul provided this, rather than the body? But it provides it as its power; and there are living beings of a fiery nature, like the spirits <note>original: "δαιμονίων" (daimonion), often referring to intermediary spirits or divine beings in Neoplatonism</note>. But shall we move fire as a living being having its constitution from all elements? He who speaks of things on earth will call them earth, or even call the heaven "aether," but will say it is not a nature, and that each of the things stationed in the aether includes those things concerning the movement. Dead bodies are not natural; they appear as something obstructing or walking, and they fall short of the fire that is there.

Perhaps it would be better to listen to Plato when he says that in the whole world—which is of such a different kind—the causes make the earth, which is established in the middle, a foundation for those who walk upon it for safety; and the living beings upon it must necessarily have such solidity. But the earth has its continuity from itself; it is illuminated by fire and participates in water so as not to be parched, and its parts have the ability not to be prevented from coming together. Air mainly supports the masses of the earth. But fire is mixed with all things, because the constitution of the airy things is earth, but they do not use a world there; and fire, having received something of earth, is like the earth in the fire. And each of those things exists, not as if they were to enjoy a friendly exchange, each not sharing itself entirely, but according to the community in the world. For it is not possible to take it with itself, but only what belongs to it: for example, not air itself, but the softness and sweetness of air; not fire itself, but the brilliance of fire. But the mixture must certainly provide everything and then make the combination of both—not just the sweetness and the nature of the seed, but the solidity of the fire and the density. And he himself bears witness to the plants, saying: "God kindled a light around the second circuit from the earth," <note>A reference to Plato's Timaeus 39b, describing the creation of the Sun</note> meaning the Sun. He says it shines by itself, but he leads us away from the same thing without interruption, naming it by another name, or saying it is fire. But he gives the cause to neither of its forms, but to the light, which he says is different from flame; it is of heat, but only refined. This light is a body, and there shines from it the light of the same name, which we say is incorporeal. This is how it is.

<column-break/>

->A<-
Although someone might say that fire was present there, and that it colored those things before it departed. Furthermore, one must wonder about water, whether it can be water unless it participates in earth. In what way will air be called a participant in earth, since it is most soft and penetrating, yielding as easily as possible? But regarding fire, it is doubted whether it needs earth, since it clearly does not have continuity from itself; nor does it have a triple dimension insofar as it is a natural body. But solidity in fire is perhaps placed not ->B<- through a triple dimension, but through a certain resistance. Hardness and roughness, however, belong only to earth: since density belongs to gold (which is "water" <note>In ancient alchemy and Platonic physics, metals were often classified as a dense form of "water" or "liquefiable" element</note>), not because of earth, but because of density and a congealed glue-like quality. Therefore, why should fire itself not be connected to the power of the soul, since the soul is present with it? For there are also fiery animals of the spirits. But in this way, we will ->C<- change what is said—that the "universal animal" is composed of all things. Perhaps one might argue that earthly animals are composed this way: but to raise earth into heaven, he will say, is against nature and contrary to those things arranged in the order of nature. Now, it seems in no way probable that the swiftest course of the heavenly bodies should carry earthly bodies along by force. Finally, earth would be a hindrance to the brightness and splendor of the celestial fire.

->D<-
PERHAPS it is worthwhile to hear Plato saying that there must be such a solid thing in the universe which is resistant, so that the earth, placed in the middle, might be a stable foundation for all those walking upon it: and earthly animals must necessarily have a certain solidity. But the earth possesses this very quality of being thin <note>original: "tenuina," perhaps a transcription error for "tenax" (tenacious) or "continua" (continuous)</note> from itself: but it is illuminated by fire, and it also participates in water to avoid excessive dryness. It possesses, moreover, a faculty by which its parts are not prevented from breathing together with other parts. Finally, air supports the mass of the earth with a certain lightness. ->E<- But one must remember that earth is not mixed in the heights in such a way that it is built into the very composition of the stars. But since individual things are placed in the one body of the world, fire surely has something of the earthly; just as the earth has something of the fiery. And each of the luminaries has something of each other—not indeed so that they are constituted of both (that is, from themselves and from that in which they participate)— ->F<- rather, in the community of the world itself, it is rightly arranged that one receives not so much the other thing itself, but something *of* the other. Just as it receives not air itself, but the liquidity of air; so too the earth receives not fire itself, but fiery clarity. But the mixture itself employs all things and melts both into one—not just earth and the nature of fire, or fire and the nature of earth, but a certain solidity and density of that kind. Plato himself bears witness to these things, saying: "God kindled a light around the second sphere from the earth," ->G<- certainly meaning the Sun, which elsewhere he calls the most splendid and the most shining. By these words, he drives away from us every opinion suspecting that there is anything else there besides fire. He also signifies that no other quality of fire is present except light, which he says is different from flame: in terms of heat, it is only mild, and from it comes the "equivocal" light, which we say is incorporeal.

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD II
### VIII

...from that light it depends, shining from it like its flower and its brilliance, which is truly said to exist as a "white body." We, however, are accustomed to taking what is called "earthy" in a worse sense; for although Plato <note>Plato discusses the composition of the world from the four elements in his dialogue, the *Timaeus*.</note> takes "earth" to mean a certain solidity, we usually call only one specific thing "earth," even though he considers those different qualities within the earth. Since, therefore, such a fire provides the purest light, and resides itself in a sublime seat, and naturally dwells there, we must not think that our earthly flame is mixed with those superior things. Instead, our flame, running through a certain space, is utterly extinguished, evidently because it encounters so much air. But as it proceeds, it is often cast down to the earth, since it is almost unable to pass higher; rather, it stops below the moon, where they say the air becomes thin. And if a flame remains there, it certainly becomes more subtle and less brilliant; in this state, it does not possess what pertains to heat, but only as much as it is illuminated by the light from above. Truly, celestial light is partly distributed in various ways among the stars, in which it differs as much in appearance as in magnitude; and partly it flourishes in the rest of the heaven outside the stars in a similar manner. And if it does not appear to our eyes because of the thinness and transparency of its body, which offers no resistance to the sight—just as happens in pure air—the great distance of the intervals also contributes to this.

<margin>That nothing flows out of heaven, and nothing flows into it.</margin>
Since, therefore, such light flourishes on high, where it is naturally established, it will appear pure; and being most pure in itself, by what way could any outflow happen from there? For a nature so sublime does not flow down of its own accord, nor is there anything there that might cast it down by force. Add to this that every body behaves far differently when it is joined to a soul than if it were separated from it; and the celestial body is by no means destitute of soul. Likewise, whatever approaches heaven is either air or fire. First, if it is air, I do not see how it could act upon heaven. Secondly, if it is fire, it does not fit at all, nor does it touch heaven in such a way as to act upon it. Furthermore, it is suddenly transformed into the celestial nature before the heaven can suffer anything from it. Also, it is much smaller in size and yields far behind in strength. Moreover, the most powerful action of fire is heating. But that which is to be heated must not be hot of its own accord. If anything is dissolved by fire, it is moved by heating out of its natural condition. For this reason, heaven has absolutely no need of any other body to preserve its nature; nor does it need one for its circular motion to be natural, although this has not yet been demonstrated. Nor does the natural motion of heaven tend in a straight line; for their own nature commands celestial things either to remain at rest or to revolve; other motions would pertain to violence. Therefore, celestial things do not even need nourishment. Consequently, it is not fitting to judge sublime things by the condition of our own affairs; since they neither have the same containing soul, nor a similar region, nor is the cause present there which compels inferior composite things to require nourishment due to their continuous flowing away. Far be it...

<column-break/>

...the light is provided from that, shining out from it like a flower and a sheen, which would properly be called a "white body" in this way <margin>in this way</margin>. We, following a worse habit of taking the worse part, whereas Plato took "earth" according to its solidity, if he shows "earth" as a single living thing, we name the differences he placed there. Since such a fire provides the purest light, being situated in the upper place and established there according to nature, we must certainly assume the flame here is not mixed with those things there. Instead, it is extinguished before reaching a certain point, encountering mostly air. Always living with the earth, it is thrown downward, not being able to transcend to the upper regions, but standing below the moon, so that it makes the air there thinner; and the flame, if it remained, would fade away, as it happens to what is seasoned, and it would not have brilliance as much as belongs to life, but only insofar as it is illuminated by the light from above. The light there, being reasonably varied among the stars, works a difference in colors just as it does in sizes; as for the rest of the heaven, even if it is of such a kind <margin>of such a kind</margin>, it is manifest that it is light and not ash. Because of the thinness and transparency of the body, it offers no resistance to the sight, just like the lower air provides this, and also because of the distance.

Since this sweetest light remains above in that pure place, and being pure, what manner of outflow could come from it? For it is not the nature of light to flow downward, nor is there any nature among the things there to push it down by force. For every body, when with a soul, is different and not the same as when it is alone. And one might say it is likely, not being alone, that that which is neighboring, whether air or fire, approaches; what could it do to fire which, even if it is placed toward the whole, does not have the strength <margin>strength</margin> to act upon them by touch? Strength for living and wondering, not for being affected by that lesser fire occurring here. Furthermore, it is possible for the whole to be heated. Because the thing being heated is not hot from itself; if something is heated again by fire, it is fitting for it to be heated. And its nature does not consist in being heated, nor is it always so, so that its revolution may be according to nature; for it has not been shown to all, nor <margin>or stable positions</margin> will it be wondered at, whether its motion is according to nature or whether it is natural for them to stay still or revolve. Other motions are of those being forced. Therefore, one must say the things there do not need nourishment, nor are they always wasting away. They do not have the same soul containing them, nor the same <margin>to those</margin> manner, since there is a cause there through which the things here, being composite and flowing, are nourished. In every way, the change of the things here...
