# MARSILIO FICINO’S COMMENTARY ON THE SECOND BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD, CONCERNING THE MOTION OF THE HEAVEN.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->The heaven is moved by its own soul, which is rational and intellectual, and it is driven in a circle: because the soul and the intellect perform circular revolutions within themselves.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'M' featuring a figure in classical dress pointing toward an architectural structure with a column and pediment.</image-desc> THE heaven is MOVED not by some elemental or similar nature, but by life: and indeed, not by an external life, but an internal one, through which the heaven lives. I mean a rational life, and even an intellectual one. Likewise, Plotinus disputes here why it is moved in a circle and in what manner, a topic we treat more extensively in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of the Soul*.</note>. It shall be enough now to have touched upon it briefly. That the heaven lives is demonstrated by the matter of that most excellent form of all living things: a motion most natural and intimate to itself, never deserting itself; a perpetual action naturally giving life to all things. Likewise, the wonderful order in the movements and in all things produced from them indicates that the heaven lives a rational life. Furthermore, the constancy in changing things, always remaining immobile in the production of such diverse effects, declares that it flourishes with an intellectual life. 

Therefore, we shall not think that a work disposed with such admirable and perpetual reason is driven and moved by some rash chance; or perhaps that it is driven and governed by a "blind" nature, as it were, devoid of reason, in the same way that limbs are formed in an animal or parts in a plant by a vegetative power or "seminal reasons" <term>seminal reasons: *rationes seminariae*, the Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of formative principles latent in matter</term>. For such natures are, so to speak, irrational and blind, since they have no account of themselves, nor do they ever possess themselves by noticing themselves. Thus, as something imperfect, such a nature is ruled by a more perfect reason which flourishes in the power of the soul, discoursing rationally if need be; and this in turn, being mobile, is ruled by the most perfect reason which reigns immobile in the mind. Finally, that reason is the **Word of God**, by which, as if by a primary hinge, the heaven is simultaneously moved and made firm. 

But let us now return to the soul: the Mother of the world, conceiving the world through reason in nature, while the Intellect is the Father of the world, defending it from above through the intellect. Finally, from a natural breath, a certain imagination and affection together contribute for a long time toward the birth; the world is born, an image of the mind, an expression of reason, a progeny of life necessarily living. Hence Orpheus calls Jupiter <note>referring to Zeus/Jupiter as the Demiurge or world-maker</note> the maker of the world both male and female. Plato also in some places understands the architect of the world to be simultaneously mind and soul, as if he were both the father and mother of the world. 

We have said—and shall say—in our *Theology* and our commentary on the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the cosmos</note> that the soul is constituted of five genera of things, and for what reason: namely, Essence, the Same, the Different, Rest, and Motion. Therefore, the essence of the world represents the essence of the soul; the "Same" in the soul is mirrored by the common matter and form in the world. Conversely, the "Different" of the soul is represented here by the extension of this matter and the distinction of forms. The motions of the world are like the motion of the soul; the state of the world in motion represents the state of the soul. For since the motion of the world must "stand" in such a way that it neither changes its substance nor leaves its natural place, it is rightly revolved around the same point. Thus, even while it moves, it does not depart from its state at all, and it represents the revolution of the soul. For the soul, beginning from the Good and the Intellect together, revolves back again to the same through the intellect and the will; and if it discourses by reason, it returns through the same forms to those same forms from which it began to discourse. The reproductive parts of nature and the imagination, the companion of nature, also bring forth the seeds of things and motions to be generated from potentiality into act, so that a most ordered and perpetual succession occurs, and finally a return to the same or similar things in certain cycles of time. The revolution of the world follows this revolution of the soul at least as easily as motion and formation in our own spirit follow the effective instinct of a prepotent nature and the affection of a similar imagination. This, then, is the summary of the entire book.

->The heaven, while it moves in a circle, is as much as possible whole in every part of itself, and thus attains the whole soul everywhere. It remains fixed through an indivisible center, just as the soul does through intellect and substance.<-

I. Plotinus intends in the first chapter, according to the opinion of our Plato, that the heaven is moved in a circle because it imitates intelligence: most closely the intelligence of the celestial soul, and even more deeply the intelligence of the divine mind. For this is the first circuit: then having returned from the good into the good through the very light of the good, then from the intellect into the same intellect through...

returned to their own proper forms. Therefore, a circuit occurs in the soul by the power of the mind, and in the heaven, it is carried out through an imitation of the mind.
But in the mind, understanding occurs in an eternal moment; in the discourse of the soul, however, it happens in a specific <note>original: "particulari," referring to fragmented or sequential time</note> time; and finally, in the heaven, as a body, it is even compelled to require a place, whatever that place may be. It is
asked, however, what produces such motion? Not the body of the heaven itself, for a body, by the very reason that it is a body, does nothing; the soul,
therefore, produces motion from itself into the body, yet the motion is not of the same kind in the soul and the body simultaneously. For
in the body, our spirit <term>spiritus: a subtle substance connecting soul and body</term> undergoes expansion through pleasure and contraction through pain, according to a certain motion of the soul
which can be neither expansion nor contraction within the soul itself, as the soul is indivisible. There is, moreover, a "second soul" <note>The "lower" aspect of the soul that governs physical life</note> from
which motion most directly arises, being so continuous with the body that from it and the body one single animal—namely, the heaven—is fashioned. And toward
these things, it is rolled by a certain formal motion—that is, from one act of a form into another act of a form—and is rolled back again; meanwhile, the heaven is shaped differently and differently by a motion that is, as it were, local. If, therefore, the soul stood still, the body would also stand still, although
the body is moved in a different way than the soul's motion. Now indeed, the body, insofar as it is extended through different parts of dimension,
has obtained this: that it is led through different parts of the body as well. It would also have a tendency to be dragged in a straight line, and thus
perhaps be dissipated, had it not been reduced to a spherical shape by the intellectual soul, whence it was made naturally inclined toward a circle.
In this way, the body of the heaven constrains the spirit, which flows out from the "breathing out" <note>original: "exspirante," the soul's outward creative act</note> of the soul as if dispersed in a straight line, making it entirely subject to it; but in turn, the "breathing in" <note>original: "respirans"</note> soul immediately restrains it. And since it cannot rest while the soul remains active, it
necessarily twists it back into an orb around the soul, or rather within the soul. Remember, therefore, that its motion is not entirely local.
For it never changes its place, which is nowhere from the beginning; nor does the whole ever pass from here to there, but while certain parts
pass through in a way, the whole meanwhile remains at rest. Therefore, circular motion is local only "by accident" <term>per accidens: a secondary or non-essential property</term>; that is, it passes
through parts of a place according to its own parts incidentally, not from the primary purpose of the soul. What, then, is the primary
purpose of the soul and, especially, the instinct of this body? Motion in the soul is certainly a transition from one thing
always to another. For since its lower part is not so powerful as the upper part (which grasps all things together in act), but yet wishes to bring all its own things into act, it does by perpetual succession what it cannot achieve all at once. When it
finishes the species of acts, it eventually consumes them all; but because it still desires them similarly, it repeats them all again.
Thus it acts very swiftly, so that by the very speed of resuming, it seems as if it has not yet lost them. By the same reason and
likeness, the heaven changes all its configurations in perpetual succession and alternation. In this, therefore, the chief desire
both of the soul and the heaven is not to pass away, but to embrace all things at once in act as far as possible; and if they
pass through them, to resume those things as soon as they have passed, so as to continue the act of all things. Therefore, the motion of the soul is a vital,
reasoned judgment; but it is such that it simultaneously affects to have all acts and forms of living, sensing, and thinking at once, and to
perceive absolutely all of them. Likewise, it strives to live together through its whole self, to sound out all its duties everywhere at once,
to know each thing simultaneously, so that the life of the whole is everywhere: sense, self-consciousness, not proceeding from without but from within. Similar to this is the motion
of the heaven. Imagine a certain space equal to the heaven in which it rotates. Whether this space is something other than the heaven, or rather is the
very nature of the heaven, let us divide that space, like the heaven, into a hundred portions, produced in length from the circumference to the middle,
marked out by lines on all sides from the wide to the narrow in equal order. This, then,
as the foundation of nature, the heaven desires to possess in its entirety with its whole self—with its whole self, I say, meaning to touch every part of that space with every one of its own parts. It cannot, however, touch them all at once, for the proportion of space
prohibits it; it therefore hurries by succeeding quickly through all its own parts, soon to touch each of its parts, so that by such a
natural bond it may equally enjoy the space, or rather the fate of its own nature. And this is, as it were, a common and mutual conspiracy of
life everywhere, and a most infinite communion of knowledge. Now indeed, the soul appears thus, which through this very space
is safe everywhere at once, to imitate it as far as its powers allow, while it also exists as quickly as possible everywhere, noticing the whole and everything everywhere
thus, namely by a certain motion. The soul which is moved, is moved, I say, not only by a formal instinct, as I said, by effort, but in a certain way also by local
motion, insofar as it does not reside in a narrow space but diffuses itself everywhere through the whole space. For it could not
form an extended and mobile body with life in any other way than by a certain diffusion of itself into each part. For the life of the body is a certain motion, and the body only becomes a living thing when extended, insofar as the
spirit diffuses and acts through it; and the spirit itself lives insofar as the soul similarly propagates itself through it. That which is
foremost in an animal, whether particular or mundane, that is, the soul, connects the rest—that is, its spirit most closely,
that is, the heaven. It connects, I say, the heaven both to the soul herself and to itself; through the heaven, as through a spirit, it also connects the remaining elements together. And according to Plutarch <note>Plutarch of Chaeronea, whose views on the soul and fire Ficino is synthesizing</note>, the circuit of fire belongs by the providence of nature to
necessity. For the divine mind, foreseeing that fire would be a body, and rising because it is extended into parts outside of parts by its substance,
would therefore proceed by action in a moment, with one thing following another, which is indeed to be
moved; and indeed from the primary nature of the body, it wills to be moved. And therefore, knowing the fiery body would be dissipable,
rightly, to avoid destruction, it soon joined a second nature to the primary nature of the body—that is, to the naturally mobile dimension—namely,
the spherical figure of dimension. Therefore, the whole nature of fire was granted by providence: through the first,
when it is placed outside its natural place, it seeks its own seat by the straightest and shortest path; through the second
and first together, after it has returned to its own seat, it rests most willingly. But while it remains in its own place,
it also remains in its nature, which is indeed to be moved; there, motion rests in motion. Which surely is nothing other
than to be revolved around the same center and circumference, with both this very nature (which is to be moved) and
following providence contributing to this; for even there it naturally desires to be moved, or even if it should wish to go in a straight line from
its primary nature, yet since it cannot go in a straight line, it falls back by the same necessity. I say it cannot go in a straight line, for
no such infinite space is given. For in such a space, dispersed in a straight line through parts outside of parts, the
natural power of the space, weakened little by little through the immense distance, cannot remain vigorous. Nor should it be thought that the celestial body
repeats its turns back and forth through a certain space produced straight in length. For those motions would be opposite to each other,
and therefore a rest would intervene between them everywhere. Thus the first motion would not be uniform and perpetual, but
immediately deformed and interrupted. Therefore, the celestial fire, placed in its own proper place, is always rotated in a perfect and perpetual orb,
especially since for it to be moved in this place is nothing else than to be moved within itself. For the parts of the universal body are in a place in others besides
themselves. But the universal body, especially through its outermost circumference, is the universal place, just as

# ON BOOK II OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

Individual motions are carried out in specific times, but the first universal motion is essentially the same thing as time itself, just as the "first state" <note>original: "status primus," referring to a state of being at rest or stability</note> is eternity. Therefore, it is clear that in this perfect and continuous sphere—which is moved perfectly in a circle—something of it remains stationary. This is evident because the sphere possesses no linear motion, nor does it change its location as a whole. It is also established that a part of this circular and solid dimension can remain still while the whole moves, because it is not broken by the motion, but remains complete and continuous everywhere. Here you may ask: what remains still in the sphere while it is agitated? It is the **indivisible**. And that indeed seems to be the center. For since the speed decreases gradually as it approaches the center from either side, it stands to reason that the center itself is entirely at rest. 

And if you imagine that some dimension in the middle—a point—is the center, surely this center, as far as it can be grasped, will be shaped like a sphere. Then I would ask: does this tiny sphere remain entirely still or not? If you say the whole remains still, the entire orb is now broken, for while the outer edge revolves, the center stays at rest. I will then ask about the center again. If you say it is divisible, the previous question returns, and you are forced to wander infinitely and will never find the center. Instead, you must confess it is **indivisible**; you must admit that only an indivisible "something" in a continuous sphere remains at rest. This center is not so much a geometric figure or a point as it is the very soul of the whole sphere, its power, or rather the soul itself. Because the whole orb rushes with natural desire toward this indivisible point—as if toward a life-giving foundation—it revolves rightfully so that it does not lose its natural shape by trying to collapse into that indivisible point. 

In this way, the whole sphere gradually inserts itself through every point and line marked within it; and thus, it seems to become indivisible and "whole everywhere," just like the soul, and from every side, the whole sphere gazes upon the whole soul. Furthermore, I believe you will not deny that this whole universe lives, when you consider that even the smallest things live within its womb and by its power. If these live, the whole lives; and the heaven lives most of all, for it is the greatest part of the whole, and is indeed the whole. If you say the heaven is an instrument of a more divine life for generating living things, you must still admit that this natural and immediate "generative instrument" (if I may call it that) of the divine life lives with its own life. By its warmth, and in its womb, all things grow together into one. In this way, and no other, the benefit of living is passed on to the rest of the world through this already-living being. This life proper to the heaven is the very nature of the heaven and the universe. Through this life, the motion of the heaven—acting as the leader of all natural motions—is full of vitality and spirit, and is voluntary in the highest degree. The heaven desires to be moved in this way as eagerly as it desires to contemplate, or as the proper life of the heaven, in harmony with the higher life, decides to move. 

Hence, this motion is the easiest and most perpetual: both because in a sphere, any point you mark as an "end" will similarly be in the "beginning," and because the power and act of moving within the soul is the very natural life of the soul itself. Therefore, by this life and this soul—which is entirely present everywhere and remains as if still—the heaven renders itself present everywhere, just as light does in an instant. The heaven also, as far as it is able, makes itself "whole everywhere" through revolution alone; through motion, it enjoys the moving soul. It only catches up to the soul insofar as it follows it, yet it never catches up except in each passing moment. Thus, the heaven revolves eternally toward the soul, just as the soul itself revolves eternally in its own way. Similarly, the whole orb enjoys every part of its own state and nature through its various parts; and every smaller sphere enjoys the vast "ocean" of the superior convex sphere that surrounds it, as it applies all its parts to each of the larger parts through perpetual revolution. And it does this always out of **love**. Even the larger orbs gaze upon and nourish the regions of the lower orbs through all their own regions. Thus, finally, as the figures of motion vary above, the forms among us are varied, and individual things are multiplied; through the sweet return of these revolutions, all species of things are preserved.

->The rational soul moves by free motion; the irrational soul follows the universe.<-
->Also, in the universe, the circumference desires the center and enjoys it through its circular path.<-
->Also, from the circuit of the soul and mind around God, the circuit in the heaven is produced.<-

### II
In the second chapter, he raises and solves questions concerning the matters above. 

**In the first question**, you will note that the heaven is indeed diffused through all things, and all bodies are either proper parts of the heaven or attached to its parts; therefore, they are moved by the "touch" of the heaven. 

**In the second question**, you will consider that every rational soul exists as a "whole" within itself, or is a part of the universal soul. This is evident to anyone for three reasons: First, because no part that is continuous with a whole turns back on itself by its own motion; second, no part can equal the whole; and third, no part resists the whole. Yet the rational soul *does* turn back into itself through self-awareness; it measures the order of the universe and transcends it to reach the Cause of the universe. Preceding itself, it often leads itself in a different direction than the nature of the whole might pull—whether it rises toward the better or falls toward the worse. However, that which is "of us"—whether the body or the life of our specific body—is a certain part of the world-body and the world-life; therefore, it follows the pull of the universe for the most part. 

**In the third question**, it is discussed how the body of the world wanders perpetually through the heaven so that, according to its capacity, it is "whole" everywhere, just as the soul is whole everywhere at once, and is enjoyed by the soul everywhere in the same way. 

From this, certain conclusions are brought forward: 
**First Conclusion:** Since the power of the soul—namely the life force—thrives most in the center of the world, like the heart in an animal, and spreads from there everywhere, this world-body, desiring life, rightfully turns itself around the center. Specifically, it is led by the soul to the side. For by bringing its whole self toward any lines drawn from the circumference to the center, it seems to touch the center from every side. It is not by chance that both the extension and the propagation of life happen from the center. For the center is necessarily first, because it is indivisible and completely immobile. Every thing standing in itself is thought to *be* what it is before it is extended; and that which is indivisible and stable precedes all things that are divisible and unstable. 

**Second Conclusion:** Just as there is a center in the body of the world upon which the rest depends, so in the soul there is an intellectual substance from which all other power and "secondary life" <note>the lower soul that governs biological functions</note> proceed. And from this, you will note that the substance of the heaven must be placed no less—and indeed more—in the center and near it than in the circumference. 

**Third Conclusion:** Just as the body revolves around the soul, so the soul revolves around God. It revolves, I say, as much by a certain perpetual natural instinct (though hidden from us) as by the study of meditation and love. While any soul remains near God as its end, each nonetheless returns to God at certain times. Likewise, if a soul cannot perceive or "touch" God in a single glance, it at least turns toward God through a multifaceted variety of gazes. After these things, it is asked: Do all rational souls perform the same action? He responds immediately: They all perform it always.

<summary>Ficino explains that the circular motion of the heavens is a physical expression of the soul's love and desire for the "indivisible center," which represents divine stability. He argues that the world is a living animal whose soul centers it, just as the human soul revolves around God through meditation and reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Ennead* II, Book 2. Having established that the center of a rotating sphere remains still and represents the "indivisible," Ficino now transitions to how the Soul uses this stability to turn toward God.</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

For all things, through a certain perpetual act of intelligence—though it remains hidden from us—perpetually enjoy the divine mind and God. All things, through a certain rational discussion, either perform the same act or strive to perform it. Now, noticing that the act of the soul proceeds from one point to another, even if it happens suddenly and without a middle step, you might call this "motion." Thus, you will, in a sense, name the intelligence proceeding from the divine mind into God Himself as "motion" and a "circuit." However, an act that proceeds from one thing to another suddenly, but through a middle point, you will more properly call "motion." Through this circuit of rational nature, the soul is turned around God via the divine intellect as a kind of medium. Finally, an act that passes from one thing to another both through a medium and over time, you will most properly call "motion." Through this circuit of rational nature, the soul is both revolved within itself around the "forms" <note>The "forms" or "ideas" are the perfect archetypes of all things existing in the divine mind</note> and turned from itself toward its own intellect, and through the divine, it turns toward God.

Next, it is asked whether our bodies revolve in accordance with the revolution of our souls, just as the body of the world revolves according to the circuit of its own soul? The answer is: a solid and composite body does this least of all, because it is moved in a straight line, both because the things within it are placed outside their natural location, and because it is drawn toward external things out of necessity. However, the celestial body, which is hidden within us <note>original: "corpus celeste, quod est in nobis occultum," referring to the *spiritus* or "astral body," a subtle vapor that Ficino believed connected the soul to the physical flesh</note>, restored its spherical shape from the beginning to match the shape of the containing body into which it was placed, since we received it suddenly upon coming into existence here. Meanwhile, that circular motion can be hindered in a way; indeed, it is attempted and driven according to its strength, as far as the shape of the earthly body allows. Regarding this earthly body, the soul's first body, that body is most nimbly driven and agitated by every nod of the soul. There is also a certain "eye of the soul," but our soul is more easily noted by the movement of our visual power than by the eye itself. He adds that God is in all things like the center of His own being, and like "bait" <note>original: "esca," implying that God's beauty lures or attracts minds</note>, He draws minds and souls entirely to Himself. And these are turned around God not so much by birth as by affection, and by that same affection, they turn the body toward the same goal as much as they are able. For it is not knowledge, but affection, that is the principle of motion. For the former [knowledge] seems to be imaginary, while the latter [affection] is substantial and receptive; the former rests within itself, while the latter is transferred to another.

Among these things, if you ask about the motion of the stars, Plotinus answers along with Plato that they are not only moved by the sphere, but also revolve with their own motion around their own center. Since those things which are, as it were, "half-carried" possess their own substance and life, they should also have their own motion. Indeed, the globes of the stars are moved according to the motion of the soul, so that just as the soul circles around God, so the globe revolves around its own soul. When he says that the soul, enjoying God, immediately leaps with joy, he signifies that the globe there grows warm; for it is rolled by the soul's desire rather than by joy, just as in our own minds the spirits are dilated and the limbs exult with joy. As for his statement that the circuit there happens not by deliberation but by the necessity of nature, understand that the Good itself ravishes the contemplating souls with a certain necessary pull. Since the Good itself is all that is good, containing every reason for willing, the soul cannot "not will" it. Furthermore, souls thirsting for it do not stop to deliberate. Then, whether they choose or not, and whether they move the body in this way or another—first, they desire by a sudden instinct, they rejoice, they are moved, and they remain. This is especially true since in any mind, its natural being and its understanding are the same thing; and understanding is almost the same as willing. Similarly, in the vegetative nature <note>term: "vegetali natura" — the lowest level of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition</note> which follows the mind there, to live, to give life, and to be moved are the same. These three necessarily accompany those three [being, understanding, and willing].

## That there are powers in the world soul, and how the lower spheres are moved toward the circle of the higher ones, and finally how the lowest heaven circles.

III. The third chapter of the book confirms the points above in this manner. The primary soul in the world, reigning as if in its own animal body, seems to propagate vital power from the center like a heart throughout the whole. However, it begins the sensory matrix from the upper spheres as if from a head, communicating it from there to the rest; it exercises reason within itself, and mind within the divine mind. This mystery seems to have been received from Orpheus <note>Orpheus was the legendary Greek poet and musician whom Ficino considered a primary source of ancient, "pious" philosophy</note>. Now, just as the upper sphere of a seer contains and moves the lower one, so the substance of the world soul embraces and leads around the life communicated to its body. Similarly, the powers within the substance itself are rolled together with the powers in this life. In the substance itself, there is intellect, reason, and "first imagination"—which is the first and common sense—and all that is often called "opinion" when joined to reason, just as "opinion" is alternately called various things when joined to imagination. This reason and this imagination are such by their own nature that they carry out their duties through the passage of time, unless they are strengthened and ruled by their own mind. Yet, although they act in the moment of the circuit just like a visual ray, almost every moment it flashes out and is reflected back to the same point.

From this substance of the world soul, then—which by its own nature and dignity is separated from the body—the world body is nourished and fed in no other way than through that "life" (as we have said) which is entirely dedicated to the body. This life possesses the ability to nourish from the higher substance insofar as it is substance, and it moves as it nourishes. Insofar as that substance is knowing, it has the capacity to know through imagining. In this life, therefore, the duty of procreation <note>term: "genituræ" — the generative or reproductive power of nature</note> concurs with imagination in such a way that they move each other. Just as it is prepared for procreation, so it entirely imagines; and as it imagines in turn, it becomes more ready for procreation. In us, indeed, a power of this kind is not open to our higher power, and it remains hidden while acting, since it depends not so much on us as on the nature of the world. This is partly because when our soul first descends into the body, the body already lives with another life, and partly because this life of the universal body rightly follows the life of the universe. Yet it gives specific traits to the body; and since our body is a part of the universal body, it rightly follows the life of the universe from that source.

But in the life of the world, it accompanies the imagination joined to it by nature, and vice versa; and this life, together with that power, proceeds as one from the substance of the soul, flashes from the soul’s powers, and is moved from there. But since this life is the "generator" of individual things, it imagines from each individual; and so that it may rightly imagine the order of the universe, it is led by a prior imagination that thinks of each thing rationally, as it is most closely joined to reason. Universal reason, in turn, looks back at individual things; and finally, the intellect comprehends the individuals within the universals. For this reason, the motion of the heaven in a circuit follows the motion of its own life, insofar as that life is encompassed by the higher power and substance—as if by a sphere—and is twisted back into a circle. Indeed, in any corporeal sphere, whatever part is continuous with the whole and is moved, it drags the whole with it, while it pushes the forward parts with motion and meanwhile pulls the trailing parts. Thus, in the sphere, the higher part undoubtedly vibrates the lower with its motion. Finally, just as when our mind rejoices and is moved in its own way by a sudden opinion of something good, the body—especially the "spirit"—is also moved in its own way (though by a different, local motion), so too the generative life in the world, enjoying the Good and exulting through its imagination directed by the higher imagination, suddenly excites its own body and leads it in a dance <note>original: "tripudio," a ritual or celebratory dance</note>. The higher imagination, directed toward the Good by reason, also rejoices <note>meta: catchword "congratulari" (rejoice/congratulate) indicates the next page continues this thought on the soul's joy in the Good.</note>

<summary>Ficino describes celestial motion as a physical manifestation of the Soul's "affection" and "joy" in God, using the metaphor of a dance. He explains the internal hierarchy of the World Soul, linking the powers of intellect and reason to the physical generative forces that shape the material world.</summary>

IN BOOK II, ENNEAD II.

...rejoicing, it is moved with exultation: because it desires to be occupied around the Good, and because the Good itself is everywhere, the soul surely performs a dance everywhere. <note>The "dance" (Greek: *choreia*) is a common Neoplatonic metaphor for the harmonious movement of the soul or stars around the Divine.</note> Similarly acts the reason directed toward the good intellect: and similarly acts the intellect joined most closely to the Good. But because it is closest to the Good, and while it acts toward it, it does not need any formal medium—and much less a temporal medium—therefore while it is moved (that is, while it acts around the Good), it is said and permitted to be at rest. In this state, certainly, the "first state" <note>original: "primus status"</note> is thought to exist, through which the soul stands firm in the First Principle. Therefore, whatever things are said to "stand still" at the same time they are "in motion"—which is to be moved in a circle—are judged to have obtained that gift from the Intellect. 

But now conclude the argument with this observation: remember that the higher substance and virtue of the soul, if compared with the lower life and virtue, is judged to be both the center and the circumference. It is the center insofar as this higher part is more stable and simpler; the rest of the soul proceeds from this center and returns to it through desire. It is the circumference insofar as the higher part undoubtedly exceeds the lower by many degrees of virtue. By this excess of power, as if by some wider circuit, it stands above that lower, narrower part; it embraces, preserves, leads it forth, and brings it back alike.

### ON THE MOTION OF THE HEAVEN.
### On the motion of the heaven.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'A' (Alpha) set within a square frame featuring a triangle. Inside the triangle are three figures: one seated and two standing, appearing to engage in study or discussion. The frame is decorated with scrollwork and floral patterns.</image-desc> WHY does it move in a circle? Because it imitates the Intellect. To what does this motion belong? To the soul or the body? What then? Is it because the soul is in it and always strives to go toward itself according to its essence? Or is it in it <unclear>*</unclear> not being continuous, or being carried along, does it contribute? But it ought to be carried along, not carrying. But should we consider them to be parts? Or perhaps it is not even local motion, this circular movement, and it will also stand still; or if it moves, it is not local in any way. How then does it move locally, if it moves itself in another way?
<margin>by the same</margin>
Or perhaps circular motion is not local. Or is it by accident? What kind of motion is it then? It is a motion toward itself, self-sensing, self-thinking, and vital, and in no way directed outward; nor is the whole anywhere else, for it must embrace the whole. For how is life the sovereign principle, self-willed and such that it will embrace things vitally rather than locally? Perhaps those things within are governed so. It has a body, and indeed the life of a body is motion. If then it is also a natural motion, how will it be able to move? Not only as a soul, but as an animated body, and as a living being, so that the motion is a mixture of the bodily and the psychic.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'Q' containing a circular motif with interlaced vines and floral designs.</image-desc>
<margin>The motion of the heaven comes from the soul but the intellect rules it; it occurs in a circle both because it is congruent with the soul and intellect that they act upon themselves, and because the centers in the figure of the heaven agree with the circuit of the body.</margin>
WHY is the heaven's motion rolled in a circle? Because it is done by the soul imitating the mind. But of whom is that motion? Of the soul or of the body? What then? Is it because the soul is in the sphere, and the sphere hastens to proceed around the soul? Likewise, is the soul in it as if not continuous, or rather in such a way that the soul, being moved, communicates it? But perhaps it was necessary for the soul, while prompting movement, to no longer move it, but to have already moved it. That, however, is rather to cause it to remain, and not to always agitate it in a circuit. For perhaps it will stand by itself, or if it is moved, it will not change its place. In what way, therefore, does that move through a location which is itself moved in some other way? Perhaps circular motion may not seem to anyone to be local. But if such a motion happens by accident, what sort of motion is this per se? Surely it is a certain conspiracy <note>In the sense of "breathing together" or harmony</note> consenting within itself, conscious of its own parts and vital, in no way turning outward or elsewhere, in which it is necessary for all things to be comprehended. For that which is the principle in a living being comprehends all things in itself and consists as one. It will not, however, embrace things vitally if it rests, nor will it preserve the interior things when it has a body; for the life of the body is a certain motion. But if such motion also becomes local, it will be agitated however it can: not as a soul alone, but as an animated and living body, so that such agitation is made from a mixture of bodily and animal motion.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.

<margin>
II
The questions are resolved: 
How the soul is moved, and why it is a part of man. 
Again, how the heaven moves in a circle.
</margin>

->**A** Since indeed the body is carried by its own nature in a straight line, but the soul contains it: and thus from both is produced a certain motion, in which it happens both to move and to remain at the same time. If, however, the motion of the body is said to be circular, in what way will this be correctly stated when every body—even fire itself—is carried by a straight motion? <note>According to ancient physics, the four elements (earth, water, air, fire) move naturally in straight lines toward their "natural places."</note> Perhaps indeed it must be said that it proceeds in a straight path until it arrives at that place where it is naturally ordained to be. For as it has been ordained by order, so it is seen both to remain according to nature and to be carried toward that which has been ordained. **B** Why, then, does fire not rest after it has attained its own proper seat? Is it because the very nature of fire is to be engaged in motion? And so, unless it is fenced in, it will surely be scattered and dissipated directly in a straight line; does it then remain for it to be agitated in a circle? But truly, is that now the task of providence? Let it be so indeed: for fire itself was placed within itself by providence itself. Therefore, if it comes to be there, it will revolve circularly from itself. It desires a straight motion toward its author <note>original: "auctori suo," referring to the source of its being</note>, but where it has no further place to be carried, it necessarily revolves as if in a circle; in those places where it can, it now unfolds. **C** For no place lies open to it beyond itself. For this is the outermost place. Therefore, it runs around in that seat which it possesses; indeed, it is its own place, thus naturally established, not indeed to remain still, but to be carried. Furthermore, in a circle the center rests by nature, but if the exterior circumference should rest, the center would be immense. Rather, therefore, it will be present around the center, namely in a living body that behaves naturally. **D** For thus it will conspire toward the middle itself with a continuous inclination, not by settling down—otherwise it would lose its circuit—but when it is not able to do that, at least by circling around. For by this reason alone will it thoroughly fulfill its appetite. But if the soul revolves, it is never exhausted, for neither does the soul pull it along, nor is the body driven against its nature. For that very thing is nature, which has been ordained by the soul of the universe. **E** Moreover, the soul of the world, existing everywhere and not divided into parts, but giving itself as a whole everywhere to the heaven so that the heaven, as far as it is able, may be everywhere. But it is able to do this only by passing through and proceeding through all things. It would surely rest if the soul should rest anywhere, having finally reached the soul. But now, since the soul itself, which the heaven desires, pours itself as a whole through the whole, the heaven surely follows the soul everywhere. **F** What then, will it never overtake the soul? Perhaps indeed it always overtakes it here; or rather, the soul always drawing the heaven toward itself, by always acting, moves it, and always. Moving it not elsewhere, but toward itself and in the same place; leading it not indeed in a straight line, but in a circuit, and therefore it grants to it that wherever it arrives, it finds the soul there. But if the soul should rest, as if it remained only there where any thing rests, the heaven would also come to rest. **G** If therefore the soul is not only in some place but everywhere, the heaven is surely moved through all things. And although it is not carried outside, it is rightly turned back into a circle.

BUT in what way are other things conquered? <note>Referring to how individual parts of the world are governed compared to the whole.</note> Certainly not every thing is a whole, but each thing is a part and contained in its own place: but the heaven is the whole and is like a place, nor does anything prohibit it, for it is itself the universe. In what way, then, are men moved? Perhaps by the reason that each one is a part depending on the whole: but in that which we ourselves are, each is a proper whole. Thus, if a body finds the soul wherever it is, why is it compelled to wander? Perhaps because it does not flourish only in one place...

<column-break/>

**A** While bodies move by nature, the soul holds them back: and from both a movement arises, being carried and yet remaining. But if the movement of bodies is said to be in a circle, how would this be entirely consistent? Even of fire: its nature is to act until it comes to where it is ordained: but as it is ordained, so it seems both to remain according to nature and to be carried to where it was ordained. Why then does it not remain when it has come? **B** Is it because the nature of fire is in motion? Or if not in a circle, it will be dispersed. It must therefore move in a circle: but is this a work of providence? But it is already in itself a work of providence: so that from that source it is moved in a circle by itself or by desiring that which gives it. <note>original Greek: "tou didos," meaning the giver or source.</note> It has no further place, so just as if falling short it turns back in those places where it is as a body, since it has nothing after itself, thus **C** within itself. Because there is no place where it may go. And of this cause <gloss>of the giver</gloss>, not in order that it remain as it becomes, but in order that it may be carried. And in a circle, by being moved, it remains according to nature; if it should happen that the circumference remains, the center would lead, and again the center would seek the way, and this is for a body having a natural state. For thus having come together toward the center, not by stopping does it lose the circle, **D** but since this is not the body containing it <margin>the body containing it</margin> in that alone will it receive its release. But the soul being unharmed, it does not fail. For the soul does not drag it, nor is it against nature: for nature is that which is ordained by the whole soul, being everywhere. The soul is a whole, and not divided from the whole according to parts, it gives also to the heaven, as it is able, to be everywhere. And it is able by **E** being present to all and going around. If then the soul were standing still somewhere, the heaven having come there would rest. But now, since all things are hers, it stands over all things. Will it then never cease? Or rather, as it may happen, it is always led toward itself, in leading, it led, and will move not elsewhere, but toward itself in the same place, not **F** toward the second <note>original: "deu," likely an abbreviation for "deuteros," the second or subsequent place</note>, but leading in a circle, it gives to it, wherever it comes, to have itself there. But if it remains as if the soul were only there, where each thing remains, or it stops or because it is not only in one place, it will move everywhere, and thus in the outer circle. **G** AND what of the other things? Or is not each whole a part? And a part contained by something particular. But that is the whole and as if a place, and nothing hinders it being the whole itself. What do men experience? Either as much as they receive a part of the whole: but there is also a certain proper whole. If it is not everywhere, where it may be, it has it, why then must it move? Or because it is not only there, if it were...

**B** a spherical one: for just as that [the soul], so this [the body] is around itself. But since they do not remain fixed beside Him, they at least move around Him: why then do not all things effect this course? Indeed, everything does this wherever it is. But why does our body also not do the same? Because, clearly, that which proceeds by straight motion is joined to it, 

**C** and moreover, impulses tend toward other things. That which again is spherical in us cannot easily be twisted back into an orb: for it has already become earthly; but there [in the heavens] follows that which is thin and easily moved. For I do not sufficiently see by what reason it should rest, by whatever motion the soul is moved. Perhaps in us also the spiritual body <term>spiritale corpus: the "pneuma" or airy vehicle of the soul</term> which is diffused around the soul, effects the same. For if God is in all things, it is necessary for the soul, desiring to meet with Him, to pour itself out around Him. For He is not only 

**D** in some particular place. Accordingly, Plato attributed to the stars not only motion together with the whole universe in a circle, but also to each a motion revolved around its own center. For every globe, wherever it is, in some way encircling God, utterly exults—not indeed by some deliberate counsel, but moved by a certain natural necessity.

<margin>III The above are confirmed; for it turns the world into order through its lower power; through the higher, only the heaven.</margin>

**III** L E T THE SAME be considered moreover by this reason. The last power of the soul, starting from the earth, pours itself through the universe; but the sensitive power of the soul, and that which possesses the reasoning of opinion, flourishes among the higher things in the spheres, brooding over the lower power, and reaching out from itself a more vital and vivifying force to this one. This [lower power] is therefore agitated by that [higher power] which embraces it circularly and sits upon the whole, as much as it recurs into the spheres. Therefore, since the latter encompasses the former in a circle, the former is deservedly reflected back into itself. But the reflection of this [soul] twists the body together with which it is 

**F** an island. For in a sphere, whatever part is moved, if only it is moved while remaining in place, it necessarily shakes the sphere in which it is, from which the motion of the sphere proceeds. For in our bodies, when the mind is moved—even if it is moved far differently, as if exulting with joy at the thought of something good—a local motion of the body is also effected from there. From there, therefore, the soul escaping [the material] and becoming nearest to the good, and having been made more sharp in its sense, is moved around the good, and incites the body according to its nature toward a local motion. The sensitive virtue follows; and since it is everywhere, it deservedly brings all things together through itself. But what does the Intellect <term>Intellectus: the "Nous," the second hypostasis in Neoplatonism</term> do? It is certainly moved in this way. For it remains at the same time as it is moved: for it is reflected into itself. In a similar way, therefore, the universe is moved in a circle and remains at the same time.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads. Having previously discussed the metaphysical relationship between the soul and the physical motion of the heavens, Ficino now moves to Book III of the Second Ennead, which addresses the specific influence of the stars on earthly events and human character.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S
# COMMENTARY ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD:
# WHETHER THE STARS ACT AT ALL.

### SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

*Species and individual members within those species are generated primarily by the seminal powers <note>original: "virtutibus seminalibus" – the hidden blueprints or formative forces within nature</note> inherent in those species and individuals; the celestial bodies, however, merely dispose matter in one way or another.*

Porphyry writes in his *Life of Plotinus* that although Plotinus had devoted diligent effort to astrology, he discovered that the judgments of astrologers were not to be trusted; he frequently refuted them both in speech and in writing. This he did in his book *On Fate*, as well as in his books *On Providence*. But finally, in this book, *Whether the Stars Act*, he seems to investigate the matter more thoroughly. In this work, Plotinus’s intent is primarily to assert that whatever things are born or moved by nature are produced and guided chiefly by the "seminal reasons" <note>original: "rationibus seminariis"</note> of universal nature, and by those most specific seminal reasons which are in no way discordant with the whole of nature. He argues at length that neither the motions and divine natures of the stars (being too universal), nor the temporary configurations of the heavens (being too fleeting), are the specific causes of these individual earthly events; rather, they sometimes happen to act as signs. Furthermore, he argues that because these signs are so general, any judgment based on them is prone to error and likely to result in an uncertain conclusion. Indeed, general principles must be distinguished by specific ones, and moving things must be ruled and guided by stable things—or at least by some form of providence—lest things everywhere happen merely by chance. He admits, however, that through the daily encounter of celestial and inferior causes, things may be changed in their *quality* (how they appear) but not in their *species* (what they fundamentally are); a similar change occurs through art and experience. He attributes the causes of our affairs partly to higher things, partly to the circumstances surrounding us, and partly to our own counsel, experience, and opportunity. He believes, moreover, that just as the body is ruled by the soul, so the soul is ruled by the intellect, and that through the gift of intelligence, the soul can be liberated from the common impulses of fate and fortune.

->The nature of the planets is not malicious, nor is it changeable by a change of location; nor are natural things primarily generated from their rays and motions, but rather from their own specific natures everywhere, and from the common nature.<-

<margin>1</margin> In the first chapter, therefore, he recounts how astrologers—not all of them, I say, but many—think that every individual thing is both signified and caused by the powers and motions of the stars. This includes external events, the state of the body, and the soul and its actions, whether they be good and honorable or, conversely, evil and base. But you should remember that the primary authors of astrology did not pass down such teachings; rather, certain "plebeian" astrologers, who were entirely ignorant of astronomy, spread these ideas. He notes, furthermore, that Plotinus perhaps concedes right from the beginning, for the sake of argument, that *some* events are signified, though not all are *caused*; and that even then, many things (though not all) are signified, and those that are can hardly be discerned. 

In the course of this narrative, he mocks the astrologers on two counts. First, because they say the stars change their natures according to their change of position and their "aspects" <term>aspects: the geometric angles between planets, such as a square or trine</term>. Certainly, such a change does not happen even to earthly things, which are most unstable, simply from a change of location or a difference in how they are viewed. Second, because they say the stars, which are in the best possible state, are made evil, and that they "benefit" as if by providence yet often harm innocent men. He especially detests the fact that while all stars are ensouled and endowed with intelligence and obey the will of God (which Ptolemy himself admits), these astrologers do not hesitate to call some "good" and others "evil." 

Thus, they claim that the planets they call "evil" often bestow good things: for instance, Saturn can sometimes bring stability; and the Moon, which aids Jupiter in some cases, can also be helped by Saturn when it is placed in its "house" or "exaltation" <term>exaltation: a specific sign of the zodiac where a planet's influence is thought to be most powerful</term>. They say Mars provides greatness of soul and fortitude, and when joined with others, it becomes merciful. He mocks them again because they admit that the planets they call "good" sometimes do harm—namely, that Venus mixed with Mercury hinders prudence, and Jupiter mixed with Mercury establishes tyranny. 

Then these astrologers say the planets are changed either by looking at one another or by not looking, as if a thing were one way and then suddenly changed by such a tiny action. Thus they believe that the Moon, if it "regards" Mercury, produces an appetite obedient to the laws of reason; but if it does not look at it, it produces unbridled lust, especially if Venus or Mars influences the "womb" <note>likely referring to the astrological "house" of beginnings or biological origins</note>. He mocks their claim that Mercury, while it influences Saturn or Mars, becomes like them, but then by a glance from the Moon, it becomes "Jovial" (like Jupiter)—as if it were a chameleon with no constant nature of its own, even though nothing among us is so utterly uncertain and changeable. 

He wonders, moreover, how it can be true that the "gaze" of the planets upon each other is so unstable that whenever they form a high figure <note>a complex geometrical configuration</note>, that gaze is forced to change its nature. Such a change does not occur even in our own sight when we look at each other now from one position, now from another. He seems to suggest, however, that due to the various "affections" of the stars, even if their own natures do not change, some natural variety can occur in earthly things; this is a topic we investigate in our book *On Life* <note>Ficino refers here to his own famous work, "De Vita Libri Tres"</note>. 

Finally, he addresses the claim that from the containment of all celestial rays, a form and power is produced in the combined rays themselves—just as water, wine, and oil differ according to their types and locations. Plotinus seems to condemn the idea that a single form arises from different mixed liquids in this context because rays are neither bodies (like liquids) nor qualities inherent in bodies (like the natures of liquids). Instead, they are certain vital and sensory "acts" of the stars, or visual rays flashing out from the stars as if from the eyes of the heavens, miraculously beholding all things. These rays do not take on qualities or character from any external subject; therefore, they are not "infected" by them, nor are they changed from their prior state, nor are they merged into a form common to all. This is just as the visual rays of many animals that see at night are not made specific to the objects they see, nor are many rays confounded into a single form. 

But although Plotinus has not approved of the astrologers thus far, he might perhaps approve if they were to say that from rays diffused everywhere (even if not specific to any one subject), specific qualities are nevertheless created—just as heat is created from light—and these are reduced to a single form within a subject. And just as in a mixture of liquids a new quality is formed more quickly when the mixing cause is more powerful, so too a quality is suddenly granted to subjects from the common gathering of rays, and these are reconciled into one.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether the stars are the causes of earthly events or merely signs. It specifically addresses the "seminal reasons" (formative blueprints) and the debate over whether the celestial bodies possess souls and intelligence.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK III OF ENNEAD II.</header>

<margin>
...and more learned judgments are found not in the stars, but in the seminal reasons.
</margin>
Because the causes are vast and powerful, and their movement is most effective and swift, Plotinus will grant that qualities coming together into such a form are brought forth from a single, stable cause that is active everywhere. This is clearly the power of the **seminal reasons** <note>original: "seminaria ratio" — the internal biological or metaphysical blueprints that guide growth and development</note> which thrives in the life of the world, so that one does not arrive at a result by chance or through instability. However, rays of light flowing together in one way or another either affect matter in different ways, or they provoke the acting cause—that is, the seminal reason—to produce its own effect. Yet, from the confluence of rays (which is always changing from one moment to the next), a new form cannot be produced from many elements if that form requires a specific amount of time to develop. Perhaps such a form is begun and perfected not merely by that specific confluence of light, but also by the preceding disposition of the matter, and finally by what the seminal reason—both the specific one and that of universal nature—decrees for such a condition. In short, however the matter stands, it is extremely difficult to judge the future. For if it is hidden from us what new thing arises from the mixing of natural elements which we handle daily, it will be much more hidden to us what new communion and form is forged by the casting of rays. Indeed, since they admit that from the union of two celestial rays something else is produced than from the two individually, then something far different must happen from the confluence of all the stars. But the more causes flow together into the acting force, the more difficult the judgment becomes: because neither are all the causes understood, nor, if they were understood, is it immediately weighed what new thing is produced from them all. This is especially true since, for the sake of judging, one must look around at the confluence not only of celestial causes, but also of elemental causes and contingent things—which even **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and author of the *Tetrabiblos*</note> admits and commands.

## How the heavens signify even what they do not cause; and that the heavens are alive. Many things cannot be produced by celestial bodies and their motions.

<margin>
The sequence of future events exists within the celestial souls; the stars do not cause these events, but signify them.
</margin>
In the second chapter, he treats the idea that not all things are produced by the heavens. For if they are inanimate, they do not do the things that properly belong to the soul; if they are animate—possessing, clearly, a divine soul—they do not do evil. The authors of astronomy concede to us that the heavens are animate, especially **Ptolemy**, **Abu Ma'shar**, and **Sahl ibn Bishr**. This is also confirmed by the Italians, who mock those following Ptolemy's opinion who said the heavens are alive because they do not wander about like our animals. For he says, along with Ptolemy, that the celestial animals, possessing the best motion, preserve it perpetually once it has been chosen. **Aratus** and **Manilius** think similarly. They understood, I believe, that if the stars act upon the soul, they cannot act upon it except through a soul, and a superior one at that. Furthermore, if something is signified to us through them which cannot be referred to a bodily cause, this could not happen unless the series of future events were described in the celestial souls, which they occasionally explain to us through the stars as if by "nods of the eyes." Plotinus thinks this explanation, whenever it occurs, also happens in many things of which not the star, but we and our own causes, are the future authors. Nor, indeed, where there are signs, are there necessarily continuous causes: just as a father's favorable nod toward a son is not the *cause* of a future benefit, but a *sign*. Thus, when astrologers predict that a child will be wise because **Mercury** is positioned in a certain way, the body of the planet itself is not the cause of that wisdom. For that which does not create a soul does not, in turn, produce wisdom, which is proper to the soul. Rather, it indicates to us, as both a cause and a sign, that the body of the newborn will be tempered to be obedient to wisdom. And like a sign, it portends that the soul (to speak in the Platonic manner) descending into the body at that time is a familiar of the Mercurial soul and divinity, and is governed by a certain Mercurial or similar **daemon** <note>A guiding spirit or intermediary divinity, not a "demon" in the modern sense</note>. **Porphyry** indeed says: a person will know what kind of daemon he has obtained if he learns the figure of his birth and who was the ruler within it. However, as to who is the chief ruler in the birth chart, although some profess they can know, Porphyry says in his *Letter to Anebo*—by the testimony of **Chaeremon** and other astronomers—that this is uncertain. 

But if any deny that the celestial bodies are alive, they will be forced to admit that their bodily natures produce nothing among us other than the service of the elemental bodies. Therefore, they would offer only the qualities of bodies, and nothing beyond that. But they would not even offer all the qualities of bodies. For just as in art, the artistic form of a work—even if it seems to be made through a tool—is nevertheless produced by the skill and the intelligent form, which alone it imitates; so the forms of natural things, arranged by a reason more than artistic, do not so much imitate and follow the mass or qualities of celestial bodies as they do the **notions** <note>The divine ideas or thoughts</note> of celestial souls. Furthermore, heat in souls does not reduce food into the form of life simply because it is heat (whose function is to dissolve), but insofar as it is guided by life. Nor do the heat of the humors in the world or other qualities perform a work toward a most choice end in a certain order insofar as they are drawn by their own nature or the impulse of the celestial mass, but insofar as they are tempered within themselves and among each other by the very reason of the celestial movers, and are conveniently directed toward a prescribed end. For this reason, Plotinus says: Let the flow from the celestial globes be the same—namely, that in the way they are bodies, they are everywhere bodily; and in the way they possess fiery heat, they are nourishing. Although, in addition, other stars may bring moisture with heat, others thinness, others some density, others swiftness, others firmness, and other things similarly. Hence, from a common condition, all stars in some way provide heat, and by their own specific reason (such as that which moistens or that which thins) they always moisten or thin. Whatever comes from there, whether by common or specific reason, happens more or less in one place or another. No other variety arises from this than in certain qualities of matter and accidents and the degrees of those accidents. However, the variety of specific shapes, forms, and virtues will not be primarily from the natural intention of the heavens, but—as far as the heavens are concerned—will happen by chance, or at least be given from elsewhere. For that which is by "artistic reason" is done only by art and by a living reason, especially if it is alive itself. 

Nor indeed shall we grant to astrologers, if any should say, that the bodies of the **fixed stars** provide the specific differences of things, while the daily configurations of the **planets** bring differences to each individual thing, even if the heavens have no soul. For the bodies of the fixed stars can indeed bestow other qualities of bodies everywhere, being uniform just as they themselves are uniform. But they can only provide the shapes proper to species and the order toward an end if they possess a soul and a mind—especially because in many species of precious herbs and stones there are certain singular powers by which they act wonderfully upon the **spirit** <note>The "pneuma" or subtle vapor that links the body and soul</note>, and through the spirit they seem to bring wonderful things to the soul as well. These bodies could not have received such a great gift from the celestial bodies alone, but only from their souls. Now, truly, the bodies of the stars themselves are much less able to bring us those differences which pertain to arts, fortunes, and necessities. For just as there is no nature of your body, so there is no nature of a celestial body, that would design you to be a theologian rather than an orator, or that you should be designated a Magistrate at a certain time in... or that you should have such a father or brother; rather, we are compelled to investigate the causes of these things elsewhere. In short, all the stars...

<summary>Ficino explains Plotinus's view that the stars act more as signs than as direct causes of human character and destiny. He emphasizes that for the heavens to influence the soul or create complex life, they must themselves be animate and guided by divine intelligence rather than just physical heat or motion.</summary>

Likewise, to reconcile agents that are diverse from one another under a common leader, we surely believe that one **Life** <note>Ficino refers to the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul—the vital force that animates the entire universe.</note> reigns everywhere, chiefly performing all things and using celestial and earthly instruments for that purpose.

**III Chapter three** pursues the same points as follows: Perhaps astrologers admit that the planets are indeed alive and not evil by nature, but that they are made harmful <note>original: "maleficos" — the technical term for "malefic" planets like Saturn and Mars, traditionally thought to cause misfortune</note> by a certain degree of the signs or by a certain configuration and figure among themselves, and that they change their nature along with their location. However, this is disproved for five reasons. **First:** because that degree of the signs, or the one affected by it, would have to be evil by nature if a planet placed in that degree, or looking at that planet, were to turn out evil. Yet they admit that no part of the heavens is naturally evil. **Second:** if a degree and figure of this kind had evil in itself by nature, all planets placed in that degree or figure would similarly be rendered evil. Yet astrologers do not grant this. **Third:** surely it must be asked how this or that planet could turn out different in different degrees—so different, in fact, that it becomes malefic. First, no planet is actually *in* a degree of the Zodiac, but is at a vast distance from it; so even if that degree were perhaps harmful, the planet could not be infected by it from so far away. Furthermore, wherever it may be, it is in heaven. Heaven is the most excellent body, closest to divinity; therefore, every single part of heaven is utterly excellent and divine. **Fourth:** since heaven is mostly uniform in its motion and locations, and does not abound in the necessary changing nature of earthly things, it is ridiculous to think that a planet undergoes a different nature in one region of the heaven than in another—especially since it is a powerful and eternal substance, and must necessarily be "at home" living among long-lived things wherever it may be. **Fifth:** it is also absurd to say, as they do, that a planet has one nature when it is in an "angle" <term>Angle: one of the four cardinal points of a horoscope—the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Lower Midheaven</term> and another nature when it declines from the angle. For at the same time, the same planet is "angular" to us, but is "declining" to distant nations, and vice-versa; therefore, it would have to possess different natures at the exact same time. Astrologers imagine four angles in the figure of the sky: those in the East, in the West, in the Midheaven, and the one below; and they say a planet is "angular" when it holds an angle within five or at least three degrees of the sign. For instance, the very point of the East, or the West, or the Midheaven—the highest point of the sky—I mean that very point or a certain space near the point. But as soon as it proceeds from there, they say it "falls away" from the angle. They dread Mars above all others in the angles, especially in the West. They also do not desire Saturn to be angular. For since they think these planets are harmful, they do not believe they should be placed in an angle lest they be more powerful, unless perhaps Saturn is in Aquarius (his own home) or Libra (his exaltation), especially in a daytime birth. Therefore, they place Saturn in the twelfth house <note>original: "duodecima signi... domo"</note> of the sign and Mars in the sixth. They call that region of the sky the "twelfth" which precedes the Eastern part, and they want this twelfth to be the "Evil Spirit" <note>original: "coaculē", likely a corruption of the Greek-derived *Cacodaemon*, the traditional name for the 12th house</note>, even though it actually rises upward. They call the "sixth" that which seems to fall from the angle of the West. I pass over other things now, but in placing Saturn in the twelfth and Mars in the sixth, they seem to contradict themselves. For in this way, they make those planets opposed to each other, whose appetites they know are sharply detested. Add to this that they equip the sixth house, by which diseases are signified, both with the opposition of Saturn and the presence of Mars, so that all diseases would be incurable. Truly, reason does not allow one to pass from the strongest to the weakest without a middle point; no one would dare to say that a planet, if it is in an angle, is strongest, but immediately after the angle will be weakest, especially since as long as a star acts upon us, it acts effectively. Again, because they call the twelfth a richer land over us than the angular ascending part has drawn, they admit it acts more upon us than the Ascendant (the angle), which nevertheless could not happen. Again, since Ptolemy usually calls a planet or sign in the Midheaven the most powerful location, how can it be true that the Ascendant is the strongest, which is far from the middle? Why do the twelfth and eleventh regions of the sky, which are between the Ascendant and the Midheaven, seem less powerful the closer they are to the middle, if the middle is the strongest? Furthermore, since they say the lights <note>The Sun and Moon</note> are darkened in the twelfth and eighth by the vapors of the earth and water together, and are therefore weakened: so when the eighth is nearly as close to the West as the twelfth is to the East, they are compelled to say they are much more obscured in the angles of the East and West, being hindered everywhere by great earthly obstacles. But they will never be able to assign a reason why they make any angle most significant when they are most fleeting and seem hardly to pertain to us, while other parts pertain to us longer, for any part occupies thirty degrees. What then? When they admit angles, why do they claim that planets they think are beneficial "rejoice" elsewhere than in the angles? The Sun in the ninth, the Moon in the third, Jupiter in the eleventh, and finally Venus in the fifth. They call the "ninth" that which somewhat precedes the Midheaven above the earth towards the West. The "eleventh" is that which follows the Midheaven toward the East. The "third" is that which precedes the Midheaven below the earth near the East. The "fifth" is that which follows immediately after the lower Midheaven and is closer to the West. They call the ninth the seat of great religion. The third they call a "gift" and of the gods, though they are not angular. The eleventh they call the foundation of hope and friendship; the fifth, the seat of joy and children. I pass over the fact that while they want the Sun to rejoice in the ninth and the Moon in the third, they meanwhile make them opposites—yet they are accustomed to dread opposition. I pass over that while they say Mercury rejoices in the East rather than the West, and Venus in turn rejoices in the West rather than the East, they will be forced to admit they rejoice and grieve equally at the same time. For while a planet is rising for some men, it is setting for others, and vice-versa. Since they think the angle of the East is the beginning angle of life, and death is its opposite, why do they not designate the angle of the West (opposite the East) for death? Instead, they assign this to the "eighth seat" near the West, and they commit it to Saturn. But why do they also commend the first house, the origin of life, to Saturn? As if both death and life were in his hand! But I see what they will resort to. They attribute the first house to Saturn, the first of the planets; the second house to Jupiter, the second of the planets, following the sign ascending in the East. To Mars the third; to the Sun the fourth; to Venus the fifth; to Mercury the sixth; and finally to the Moon the seventh, which is the sign located in the West. Then they repeat the beginning of the planets from Saturn again in the eighth,

# ON BOOK III OF THE ENNEADS, CHAPTER II.

But since, after Saturn, they have assigned the ninth house to Jupiter, the tenth to Mars, the eleventh to the Sun, and the twelfth to Venus, there will be nothing left to dedicate to Mercury and the Moon in a similar succession; yet the effects of these two are the most manifest of all to us after the Sun. Unless, perhaps, they accommodate the Ascendant to Mercury and the Moon just as they did for Saturn—which would be the act of a fabricator rather than a teacher. Furthermore, why do they not designate the ages of a person already born with that same continuity? To be sure, in a preserved order, they destine the first age to the Moon, the second to Mercury, and so on. But to arrive at all these things is quite "pretty" <note>Ficino uses "perbella" sarcastically here to mean "neat" or "convenient."</note> and entirely arbitrary, confirmed by no reasons at all. It is similarly arbitrary that they place Mercury—whom they think is easily converted from a deceitful evil to a good—in the joyful beginning of life as if in a state of "rejoicing." Why not the Sun instead, or Venus, or Jupiter? Why also do they consider Mercury to be both the author of reason and yet so slippery toward evil? But I seek a reason from them in vain for this or that matter, for they never rely on any reason,
