but most often upon some imaginary similarity and empty comparison. Who does not see that they compare things too ineptly? When they accommodate Saturn to the ascending sign because he is the highest of the planets and signifies darkness and absence; for because of his height, the Midheaven <note>term: "medium cœli" (Midheaven). The highest point in the sky at the moment of birth, associated with career and public life.</note> fits him better than the Ascendant, and because of darkness and absence, the signs below the earth fit Saturn better than the one ascending from the earth. Now truly, it is too childish to say that Saturn portends the absence of some thing to someone for the reason that he himself is distant—just as if the Moon, by a similar folly, refers to a present matter because she is near, and the middle planets refer to middle matters by a similar degree. Nor is it less insane to assign darkness to Saturn, who, being a star of immense magnitude and very close [to the heavens], necessarily flashes with a wonderful clarity of light; rather, it must be confessed that the eye is deceived in judging his light, rather than that Saturn shines less. But as I was saying, they flee in all things to empty similarity, having no regard for causes. Why does the ascending star from the East signify the beginning of life? Because, they say, at the same time the star emerges from the darkness of the earth, and the newborn emerges from the darkness of the womb. O, what a utterly hollow mechanism! In the same way, someone might say: a father now leaving the city signifies a son entering the house at the same time, and moreover a daughter leads the one leaving. Likewise, if anything is to be signified this way, the position that ascends when the fetus first begins to live in the womb should rather signify life and the beginning of life; but they neither observe this, nor can they observe it by any logic. Why also does the region of the Midheaven portend dignity to those being born? Is it because the highest seat signifies the height of dignities? So also the fourth house <note>term: "domicilium quartum" (fourth house). Located at the bottom of the astrological chart, associated with foundations, home, and hidden things.</note>, because it is the angle entering under the earth, they dream signifies treasures hidden under the earth. If they are so delighted by this fabricated similarity, they ought to have described marriage through the sign joined to the Ascendant as well. Yet they predict this through the seventh house, far removed from the Ascendant; but what has the West to do with the East regarding marriage? Because, they say, the rays from each region are joined. Let it be so, indeed. But why is it also that through this seventh house manifest enemies are signified? They say that the planets nearer the Ascendant rule the youthful age, while those more remote rule old age. Truly, this is too childish: as if this local transition, like a dance of players, suddenly causes—through others—these to rule first, while those delay, and only then act when they are at last most remote in condition from the first. Let them say further, since they are so eager for similarity, why the twelfth region, into which the Ascendant arrives at the light, signifies prison and hidden things rather than fertile ones, from which one must emerge as if from darkness? In short, they rave similarly in all things, and they compel others—either those laughing at them or those disputing with them at length—to rave in nearly the same way, as Abu Ma'shar <note>original: "Abumazar" — a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note> shows even unwillingly.

For when he struggles to assign the causes why the twelve houses are distributed with their duties, he says that astrologers disagree among themselves, and others designate them far differently. Then truly, in assigning the reasons why such signs are the houses of such planets, they disagree widely among themselves; for the ancients assign them one way, Ptolemy another, Ammon another, and Hermes another: clearly because they are fictions rather than reasons. Abu Ma'shar hands down that Jupiter signifies riches and Mercury signifies wisdom. But because the desires for these things are opposite, therefore he says both houses of Jupiter and Mercury are opposite: namely, Pisces to Virgo, and Sagittarius to Gemini. O Abu Ma'shar, if it pleases you to distribute them thus, why did you not also oppose the houses of Venus and Mercury to each other? Since Venereal lust and Mercurial contemplation are much more opposed than what we have mentioned? But you confess them to be harmonious with each other: Libra with Gemini, and Taurus with Virgo. Likewise, since Jovian equity and Martial violence are most greatly opposed to each other, why do you not allow their seats to fight? But instead you allow the East to agree entirely with Sagittarius, and Scorpio with Pisces? Furthermore, when they ascribe other regions of the earth to other signs, they are carried by uncertain opinion. For they do not distribute them because a sign passes perpendicularly over such a region; for if that were so, Cancer will signify nothing in Europe, since the whole of it exists beyond Cancer, turning toward the North; nor is there any harmonious property. Nay, they say the sign is cold, yet they judge it to preside over Spain, a hot region. With similar rashness, they set signs over the limbs of the body; for they often put hot signs over cold limbs, and cold over hot. Significations that are too repugnant to each other are also joined to the same planets. They want Saturn to signify the worship of the one God and also gluttony; Jupiter to signify piety and also intemperance in coitus; Mercury to signify wisdom and the oracles of prophets, and moreover superfluous amusements. You let pass many things published together with rashness, such as that Saturn designates rain, though they confess him to be dry. Likewise, they call him masculine, whom they say is cold. Finally, they say he portends slowness because he himself is slow, though he is certainly the fastest in terms of the length of his path. What of the fact that he dreams of the Head and Tail of the Dragon? <note>term: "caput Draconis" (Head of the Dragon). These are the Lunar Nodes, the points where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic; the "Head" is the North Node and the "Tail" is the South Node.</note> For these are only imaginary. The Head is thought of as an imaginary line left in our mind from the motion of the Moon from the South to the North, which can indeed be imagined in any degree of the Zodiac. And where the head is imagined now, there at some point the tail will also be imagined. What can that imaginary line do? When the Moon has departed from there, why is the tail evil rather than the head? Why is the tail cold and feminine, when the northern region is colder than the southern? And so the head, in which the Moon declines toward the North, ought to be cold rather than hot; and the tail the opposite. They call a planet retrograde when it proceeds toward the East in the lower part of its epicycle. From this similarity, they dream that the business of men is retarded, and again accelerated, as if both motions were not equally natural to the planets. Furthermore, they are accustomed to say: because Taurus or Leo have such powers in themselves, therefore those who are born under these lots obtain a similar nature. Although these animals are falsely imagined in the sky; nor is there there any figure or nature of that kind similar to our bulls and lions. The ancients placed the Bull among the stars in honor of Jupiter, because he was fabulously turned into a bull. Hercules killed a huge Lion; they (as it is said) established it among the signs. They designated the Ram as the head of the signs because of Jupiter Ammon, on whose head the ancients used to imagine the horns of a Ram. After the Ram, they say they soon fashioned the Bull, because then the earth was arable and desired cultivation. The Gemini [Twins]...

<summary>In this passage, Ficino systematically deconstructs the symbolic logic of medieval and ancient astrology, arguing that the meanings assigned to houses, planetary motions (like retrograde), and zodiac signs are arbitrary human inventions rather than physical realities. He mocks the "similarity" principle—where a planet's physical distance or a sign's mythical name dictates its influence—as unscientific and contradictory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s critique of the literal-mindedness of many astrologers. He argues that the names given to the zodiac signs are merely human inventions based on seasonal changes on Earth, rather than reflecting actual animal natures present in the stars.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...because then, by budding, all things are "doubled" <note>Ficino is connecting the name Gemini (the Twins) to the Latin *geminare*, to double or repeat, referring to the abundance of spring growth</note>. They named it Cancer <note>the Crab</note> because from that point the Sun begins to move backward like a crab; Leo <note>the Lion</note> because the Sun heats most intensely there; Virgo <note>the Virgin</note> because the earth, exhausted by the Sun, then produces nothing from its trees; Libra <note>the Scales</note> because the Sun then makes the nights equal to the days; Scorpio because the air then stings with the first cold; Sagittarius <note>the Archer</note> because of the sharper stings of cold and winds, and other signs for similar reasons. What is more foolish, then, than to attribute specific animal natures and personal outcomes to people born or acting under this or that sign, when nothing of the sort exists in the sky, but is constituted by a far different logic? You would not, therefore, refuse to give medicine when Taurus <note>the Bull</note> or Capricorn <note>the Goat</note> is rising on the grounds that these animals chew their cud <note>original: "ruminant"</note> and you would instead provoke vomiting. As if there were actually a goat chewing its cud in the sky, and Capricorn were not instead a fiction—named because the Sun begins to ascend again from that point in the manner of a climbing goat. And after these come Aquarius <note>the Water-Bearer</note> and Pisces <note>the Fish</note>, because then more abundant rains pour down, and at that time fish are most prolific. Would someone then craft an image of a fish in silver when the Moon is in the rising sign of Pisces, expecting to catch fish at will, relying, of course, on a false figure of a Fish in the sky and a fictional nature? 

But to return at last to Plotinus: he maintains that the celestial bodies are led by a soul, and truly live by divine intellect, having no emotional attachment to lower things. Since their bodies are not sent down to lower matters, they neither lack anything nor are they disturbed; therefore, they are never touched by pain or any new joy, nor do they do harm out of hatred, nor do they simply do harm, nor do they signify things to us by their own choice. Rather, perhaps from their own self-contained "dance" <note>term: "coream" (dance). A common Neoplatonic metaphor for the orderly, circular motion of the heavens</note>, a signification sometimes follows for us. For if birds, which are closer to us in nature and place, signify things to us without any choice on their part (if there is indeed any truth in augury <note>term: "augurio" (augury). The ancient practice of predicting the future by observing the flight or sounds of birds</note>), but their sign happens to reach us while they are simply flying or chirping, much less do the stars deliberate to portend our affairs. 

Surely it was not in vain that our ancestors taught the vanity of augury, consisting only in the worship of demons—auspices, auguries, soothsaying, and the inspection of entrails. For demons, the rulers of the misty air, kept their worshippers bound by this divination, or rather, by this deception. But if any conjecture about the future happens through the movement of the stars, where are those future things "prescribed," so that such or such a constitution of the sky follows or accompanies that prescription? Truly, they are prescribed in the celestial minds, which move their own celestial "face"—that is, their appearance—while their thoughts judge things in one way or another. But in their minds, these notes are eternal; not only of those things which they themselves will do, either by themselves or through the heavens, but also of those things which elemental causes will follow and do by their own nature. Furthermore, they contain the things which rational souls—sisters to the celestial souls—will do by a common nature, by chance, or by counsel. 

I say "common" because these things are not designated in the celestial minds for lower conditions in every specific detail down to the smallest bit. Instead, they are arranged according to a general providence, summarized by the "headings" of things, which are then further divided through the specific natures, emotions, opportunities, and counsels of lower beings, and are led, in a way, into a different quality. For this reason, individual things cannot be known for certain from that source; but for the most part, only certain generalities, which even Ptolemy asserts. One must look into the individual natures and imaginations to see the specific conditions of individuals. Thus, to be occupied daily with such predictions (if we believe Origen and Porphyry <note>Two influential ancient scholars: Origen was a Christian theologian; Porphyry was a Neoplatonist philosopher</note>) is the work not of men, but of demons—and I mean the more clever demons. For they believe most demons are often deceived by conjecture regarding these matters and lie to us. 

Ancient astrologers doubted which matters were signified to us from the sky. Thus Abumazar <note>original: "Abumazar" (Abu Ma'shar), a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note>, where he treats judgments, says that some astrologers believe the planets predict only universal things—namely, concerning the elements and the species of natural things—but show nothing at all concerning individuals and their specific parts or acts (such as moving, resting, and the like). Others think the stars show only what is necessary (for instance, that fire is hot and water is cold), but not things that are contingent (such as whether a man speaks or is silent). Finally, the pious believe the planets portend changes of the seasons, and Abumazar says they portend what happens to bodies through these changes. He says all later astrologers follow the ancients, yet none of the sayings of the ancients lead to this intention of "judging" <note>The practice of "judicial astrology," or making specific predictions about human lives</note>, since they said it would be impossible even for wise astronomers to find anything in the science of judgments. In these passages, Abumazar admits that the causes and rules of judgments had not yet been found; even Ptolemy, who came much later, offers no rational basis for judgments, but only childish similarities. Ptolemy also, in his book on *Judgments*, hints that there is very little truth in these sayings. Even if it happens that prediction fails us for the most part, it would still be worthwhile to investigate these things subtly, because some truth does reside within them.

### On the five aspects of the planets, and how astrologers err in these, being deceived in the qualities and actions of the celestial bodies.

IIII. After this, he descends to the loves and hates of the planets, and their aspects and effects. It would be tedious, and quite absurd, to recount the loves and hates between planets, and what is even more shameful, to record how this one loves that one, while that one does not love in return, but rather hates. As if they were not all kindred, placed most excellently in a uniform and divine region! Certainly, since similarity in our world creates mutual love between two parties, much more does it create mutual charity in the heavens, where a closer similarity and bond flourish. 

To understand more clearly what is said about "aspects," one must remember that astrologers present five aspects: a **conjunction** occurs when a planet moves directly under another planet on a perpendicular line; an **opposition** is when they are at their maximum distance (for example, if one is in Aries and the other in Libra, the seventh sign from Aries). A **sextile** aspect occurs when a sixth portion of the twelve signs falls between them (a measure of two signs); for example, if the Sun is seen in the middle of Aries and the Moon in the middle of Gemini, or one at the start of Aries and the other at the start of Gemini. For between them falls the whole of Taurus, plus parts of Aries and Gemini. Then the fourth aspect, **quadrature** <note>Also known as a "square" aspect</note>, where a fourth part of the Zodiac falls between them (three signs); such as when the Sun is in the middle of Aries and the Moon is in the middle of Cancer. For three signs are seen between the Sun and Moon: the whole of Taurus and Gemini, plus parts of Aries and Cancer. Three signs constitute a fourth portion of the twelve signs. A **trine** aspect is when four signs intervene, which is a third part of the Zodiac; for example, if the Sun is under Aries and the Moon is similarly under Leo. Ptolemy says the reason there are only these aspects is because shapes can be made from the twelve signs: they have **hexagons**, where each side contains two signs; there, the aspect of one angle to another will be sextile, containing a sixth part of the figure. A **square** figure can also be described, as can a **triangle**. In the square, the quadrature aspect arises; in the triangle, the trine.

<meta>catchword: Non</meta>

<summary>Ficino critiques the literal interpretation of zodiac signs as animal natures and argues that stars signify general providential patterns rather than micro-managed human fates. He explains the geometric basis for planetary "aspects" (conjunction, opposition, sextile, square, and trine) while remaining skeptical of their use in specific "judicial" predictions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Enneads, specifically Book 3, Ennead 2. Having previously argued that zodiac signs are human-named conventions rather than literal celestial animals, Ficino now moves to critique the mathematical and physical assumptions of astrologers regarding "aspects" (the geometric angles between planets).</meta>

# ON BOOK III OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

A five-sided figure <note>a pentagon</note> cannot be formed from twelve whole signs. However, it seems it can be asserted that this can be done in another way. For there are three hundred and sixty degrees in the Zodiac which, when divided into five parts, will produce a figure possessing five angles. In the same way, one angle will "look at" <note>the Latin *aspiciet* refers to an "aspect," or an astrological angle</note> another angle, just as happens in the trine aspect. Therefore, just as with those pentagons, a square aspect can be considered. Furthermore, a figure of eight, nine, or ten angles can be made from all the degrees of the Zodiac, and thus there would be an eighth, ninth, and tenth aspect. For this reason, to assert that there are only five aspects is more the work of someone inventing things than someone truly calculating them. Indeed, the circle of the Zodiac itself is continuous; stars are everywhere, and signs are inserted into one another. We should not only be able to make aspects through the twelve signs—as if they were separate from one another—but through the degrees everywhere in the Zodiac. 

Accordingly, if we inquire truly, we do not say this star looks at that one, or planet looks at planet, for any other reason than that it casts these rays into that one. Moreover, any star casts rays into any other; therefore, any star, wherever it may be, beholds any other. From this kind of "beholding" of rays, a star reaches and looks at a nearby one more than a remote one, which is indeed evident in lit candles. Shall a neighboring sign then say it does not behold the next one, but only one removed by a certain distance? Or that it looks at a distant star but not a nearby one? For this opinion—or rather, this error—arises because they measure the celestial bodies (or rather, they lie about them) based on our own limitations. For a human in a dance usually has more difficulty looking at a person right next to them than one further away, because the head does not have eyes on every side with which to see everywhere with equal ease. But in the celestial face, whatever exists are eyes; whatever is "eyed" is entirely an eye, entirely sight in every direction. 

They say that the **sextile** aspect <note>an angle of 60 degrees</note> is of moderate love, the **trine** <note>120 degrees</note> of perfect love, the **square** aspect <note>90 degrees</note> of moderate [enmity], and the **opposition** <note>180 degrees</note> of the highest. They say conjunction with good planets is good, but with bad ones it is bad. Yet they cannot assign the reason why one aspect differs from another in being good or bad solely from the figure or the number. For good or evil does not pertain to quantity, but to quality. Furthermore, action or passion does not pertain to a figure or number, but to forms and qualities. These figures or numbers either follow or accompany these forms. Nor, again, is it permitted to say that Aries is contrary in some quality to Cancer, and therefore the square aspect arising from the two is contrary and hostile. For there are no contraries in heaven, where there is no battle, no transgression, and no destruction. 

On the contrary, if figures in a specific work of art are in some way clashing with each other, they do not clash in the mind of the artist; if natural forms clashing with each other do not disagree in the mind of the observer; if opposing limbs do not oppose each other in the seed—then certainly the effective powers of these forms do not disagree in heaven. These powers only struggle in the lower, baser matter because it is not capable of reconciling what it receives. Indeed, not only does Cancer not disagree with Aries, but it harmonizes with it; for they are parts of a body that is mostly uniform, and things that disagree among us are harmonically tempered by their own nature there. Everything harmonizes in heaven no less than in a musical song, and perhaps from this celestial harmony one might be able to devise human music; for the Pythagoreans called the heaven the **Lyre of God** <note>original: "Dei lyram", though the text reads "Delyram"</note>. 

Therefore, let the assembly of the planets represent for us the harmony of the eighth voice <note>the octave</note>, for this seems to unite with the first. The opposition of the celestial bodies, which occurs in the seventh [sign], is represented by the seventh voice <note>the interval of a seventh</note> among us, which is similarly the most dissonant of all. The **sextile** aspect, which occurs in the third sign, is represented by the third voice; the **square** by the fourth; the **trine**, which occurs in the fifth sign, by the fifth. Just as in our independent harmony a fourth voice, or sometimes a seventh, which would be dissonant by themselves, nevertheless contribute to the grace of the harmony when joined with the others—so, even more so in the celestial harmony, all aspects are judged necessary for absolute concord. 

This is why the wiser astronomers do not only not dread the square aspect when joined to either a sextile or a trine, but they even desire it. It also happens that the number seven—whether of days in diseases or years in life, in which the squares of either the Moon or Saturn soon arrive—brings changes in us that are not always for the worse, but sometimes for the better. Meanwhile, it is pleasing to laugh at the astrologers, who, while they say Cancer is more contrary in quality to Aries than Libra is, nonetheless judge the opposite aspect (such as results from Libra to Aries) to be worse than the square. But why do they chatter that Cancer is cold and moist, when the Sun positioned there increases the heat for us? Why say Sagittarius is hot, under which the Sun does not protect us from the cold or even from illness? From this it is clear that heat and cold are intensified and relaxed in turn by the approach and departure of the Sun rather than by the "quality" of the stars. 

Nor should they cast at us the idea that the Moon or Mercury changes the quality of the air in different signs because there is supposedly a different quality there. For, first of all, they do not produce this everywhere; summer never arises among the Scythians <note>an ancient people of central Eurasia, used here to represent a cold northern climate</note>, nor does cold and moisture ever arise for the Indians. Secondly, even if they do happen to change it, it is not immediately proven that there are qualities there clashing with each other in that way; for these things proceed from there by a different power, far different from our own. Do not contrary qualities arise immediately in the body both from various affections of the soul and from a certain contraction and dilation of the spirit, even though those qualities are not in the soul or spirit? From light reflected too much, heat arises, which does not exist in the light itself. From light, both dryness in wax and liquidity in mud arise simultaneously, yet there is no "dry" or "liquid" passion in the light. Thus, by the position or repulsion of the stars, vapors and winds are raised on the earth, yet winds do not blow there, nor do vapors cloud things there. 

That the powers in heaven are very foreign to these clashing elements we can guess from the fact that in all things mixed from elemental qualities, there are certain marvelous forces, both beyond and above the natures of the elements, which they call **specific properties** <note>term: *speciales proprietates* — unique occult powers that cannot be explained by the four elements (hot, cold, wet, dry)</note>, attributed to species from heaven. I pass over countless other examples. Thus the magnet follows its Arctic pole, and iron follows the magnet; thus chaff follows amber. The latter perhaps follows the Antarctic pole. Through such powers as these—and those which purge bile in scammony <note>a medicinal plant used as a purgative</note> and black bile in hellebore—Albumasar <note>the famous Persian astronomer Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD)</note> proves that the principal actions of the heavens are fulfilled. Whether such fixed powers are in the stars, or are prepared for them by their daily relationships to one another and then sent to lower things. 

Rightly, therefore, Almasar and Albius <note>likely Al-Battani</note> everywhere rebuke Ptolemy because he often attributed elemental and clashing qualities to the stars, and they prove that such natures do not exist in heaven. I pass over now the fact that not only those I mentioned disagree with Ptolemy and others, but Ptolemy himself disagrees with others when he speaks of the "terms" <note>term: *terminos* — specific subdivisions of zodiac signs ruled by different planets</note> of the planets, and he recounts that others disagree among themselves. For the Egyptians were most accustomed to receiving the terms from the lords of the houses, but the Chaldeans from the lords of the triplicity, and he refutes this very extensively. I pass over the fact that they disagree on the "dignities" and "exaltations." For Ptolemy measures simply from sign to sign; others, however, measure from degree to degree. Ptolemy thinks the exaltations of the planets should be taken in a whole sign; some others from a certain specific space in the sign. Similarly, they disagree about the **significator of life** <note>term: *significatore vitae* — also known as the Hyleg, a planet or point used to determine lifespan</note> and the **giver of years** <note>term: *annorum datore* — the Alcochodon, a planet used to calculate the length of life</note>. 

I return briefly to the qualities. Since they think Mars is fiery, why do they not say it "falls" <note>is weakened</note> in Pisces rather than in Libra? They say it is because Libra is furthest from Aries, the home of Mars. But surely the distance of nature is greater than the distance of position; thus, Pisces (which they say is watery) differs more from Aries than the airy Libra does.

<meta>This page continues Ficino's critique of astrological systems. Having dismissed the arbitrary nature of zodiac signs and aspects on the previous page, he now examines the physical contradictions in how astrologers assign "cold" or "hot" qualities to planets like Saturn and Mars. He argues instead for a more unified, life-giving celestial physics where the heavens provide only life-sustaining qualities.</meta>

<page-num>116</page-num>
->COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO<-

Why indeed do they want Saturn to be exalted <term>exaltation: a specific sign in the zodiac where a planet is thought to have its most powerful influence</term> in Libra, a planet they otherwise consider to be "earthy"? It would be tedious to review other inconsistencies of this same kind. Let us return now to Plotinus’s conclusion. He notes first that astrologers believe each star acts individually on its own, yet from all of them conspiring together, something new is produced from the rest. From this, it is clear that no one can judge with any clarity what these stars are primarily announcing. Next, he indicates that astrologers have no explanation for the *way* in which planets act to bring about whatever they are said to cause. For they do not indulge in action either by their own individual deliberation or by a collective plan. After all, natural causes below the moon <note>the "sublunary" realm of Earth where change and decay happen</note> are sufficient by their own nature for action, and they do not require a "plan" from those things beyond nature. Furthermore, since the stars perform these things by way of nature, they cannot act differently or do other things than what is possible within the course of nature—even if they do so more excellently and produce more excellent things by virtue of their superior nature. Therefore, they do not produce prophets, nor miracles (which must be done by divinity), nor theologians, nor geometers (who are made by mind and art), nor wealth, nor kings; nor do they produce those things' opposites, which are made or hindered by prudence, opportunity, and favor.

---

## Errors of the astrologers concerning Saturn, Mars, and the Moon.

VI. In the fifth chapter, he pursues and attacks the errors of astrologers more extensively. They claim that Saturn, because he is cold, is harmful to nature; for this reason, they separate him from the Ascendant <note>the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>, which they call the principle of life. And so that they might separate him from it as much as possible, they foolishly place him in the "Twelfth House." This seat, although it seems most remote from the first house according to their method of calculation, is actually the closest. For it is continuous with the East, moving upward; whatever star ascends soon hastens into the twelfth house. Thus, they would have more probably placed Saturn in the "Seventh House" <note>the Western horizon, opposite the Ascendant</note> as the most distant of all. But they do not want that either, lest he be positioned directly opposite those being born. In both cases, they seem to contradict themselves: for they usually assign Saturn and the Ascendant to the beginning of the first conception for another reason. Furthermore, they say that Saturn and Mars harm us when they are either joined together or positioned opposite one another. It would perhaps have been more correct to say that Saturn’s coldness is best tempered by the heat of Mars, and Mars’s fire by Saturn’s cold. They also claim that if Saturn is "above the earth" for others being born, or near the East, tempered by the heat of the day, he then turns out to be favorable to us. And even if he rises in this way, especially in Aquarius <note>Saturn's traditional zodiac home</note>, he does not harm nature. They say Mars, however, being of a fiery nature, should be placed in the night, or under the earth, so that he does not burn too vehemently with the heat of the sun. In this, as often, they are raving. Since the shadow of the earth, from which night comes, barely reaches as far as the moon, all the lights of all the stars above the moon are continuously in contact with one another with nothing intervening. Likewise, they are always "in the day" and never "under the night." Saturn, most of all, is separated from the shadow and coldness that are proper to the earth; thus, nothing seems more absurd than to call him "dark" and "cold." Furthermore, they are accustomed to disparaging the meeting of the Moon with Saturn or Mars. However, if she commands Saturn while "full of light" <note>a full moon</note>, or Mars while "empty" <note>a new moon</note>, they do not dare to condemn it. For if she is placed with Saturn while full, they say she then nourishes him with her light and that he does not chill her. Conversely, if she joins Mars while full, they say they then burn up together; if she is "empty," they are tempered in turn. Here too, as elsewhere, they err quite boldly. First, celestial bodies, being always in harmony, never "burn" or "chill" one another. Secondly—even if we concede the point—the opposite should be done: when the Moon is "full" to us looking at this wonder, she is meanwhile "empty" to the other planet, and vice versa. Therefore, to avoid that discomfort, they should have placed her under Saturn when she is "empty" to us; for then she would be "full" to him. But she should be with Mars when she is "full" to us, for then she shows herself "empty" to him. 

Between these points, it is helpful to warn that many clauses in the Greek manuscript <note>Ficino was translating Plotinus from Greek into Latin</note> seem to have been transposed, and words very often swapped. I have diligently corrected these to the best of my ability, relying on reason (if I may say so) rather than merely the duty of a translator. Therefore, what follows soon in the text can admit a double meaning. Either it means that Saturn does not help us much sometimes because he is far away, and therefore the Moon must be full toward us then so that she at least might help us; or rather it means that Saturn does not oppose the Moon because he is far from the Moon, nor she him in turn if she is "empty" toward him, and therefore she must extend herself "full" to him. In that case, her half-circle facing us would be enough for us, even if she were "empty" to us, and even though Saturn is far from us. The first sense seems to follow the words more clearly, but I fear they are corrupted. It does not seem to fit the preceding or following statements of Plotinus, but rather seems to contradict them.

---

## That in heaven there is only light, heat, and moisture; while cold and dryness are around the center; and nothing celestial brings cold through itself, or dryness, or anything harmful to life.

VI. Since heaven is closest to life, and therefore most alive and most life-giving, we must believe that it primarily warms and moistens. For these two qualities are properly conducive to life. It never chills or dries out through its own nature, as these are naturally contrary to life. And if they do contribute anything, they contribute it "by accident" <term>accidentally: in philosophy, a property that is not essential to a thing's nature</term>—cold, perhaps, so that excessive rising heat does not suddenly dissolve the moisture; dryness, so that the moisture does not flow away too much. These two qualities are sufficiently supplied to us by the earth. This is further confirmed if what most people believe is true: just as death is nothing other than the privation <note>the total absence or loss of a quality</note> of life, so the deadly qualities of cold and dryness are nothing other than the privations of heat and moisture. Plotinus himself indicates this elsewhere. It is also probable that, just as darkness occurs at the greatest distance from the light of heaven as a mere privation, so cold and dryness perhaps occur from an excessive distance from heaven due to the absence of heat and moisture. That the whole heaven is hot is clear because it is entirely fire; and its loftiness, mobility, light, and heat (or a hidden warmth nourishing all things) show that it is entirely fire. Moreover, this very abundant heat, suffering no violence from its vast spaces, possesses a familiar moisture. Indeed, in the soul, the most celestial things are life, intellect, and motion. For the soul is a certain life that is both intellectual and mobile, and all of this is one. Therefore, what is "life" in the soul exists as "heat" in heaven. What is "intellect" there, is "light" here. What is "vital motion" there, is "vital moisture" here. Thus, moisture is nothing other than an agility (if I may put it that way) for motion. Celestial fire, therefore, can be called not only hot but also moist—that is, liquid, fluid, agile, slippery, smooth, and mild. For in "dryness" we understand a harsh rigidity, just as a more vehement cold brings. For this reason, nothing in heaven is in any way similar to our qualities except heat, moisture, and light. Light, I say, is there in place of intelligence; heat is there as the efficacy of life; moisture is the motion and food of life. Nor is that heat felt there otherwise than as a vapor, a nourishment, a recreation, and a vigor; nor is moisture felt otherwise than as growth, amplification, agility, and abundance. All these...

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s exploration of celestial physics. On the previous page, he argued that stars act by their nature rather than by a conscious "plan." Here, he refines this by arguing that the heavens are inherently life-giving and warm, and that "cold" is merely a relative absence of heat or an accidental effect of distance and earthly density.</meta>

# ON BOOK III OF THE ENNEADS, II.

Certain similar things exist within us. To these—which lack the moist heat and the temperate warmth of a grove—the spirit, heat, and humor <term>humor: in Renaissance physics, a fluid or vaporous substance that carries life and qualities through the body or the cosmos</term> of one’s age is in some way similar. This is seen more clearly in animals or hidden in plants, implanted everywhere from the heavens—from a heaven, I say, implanted in all things. If anyone should argue that the cold of our world certainly happens from here and not from there: let it be known that this is due to the very narrowness and dense nature of this place [Earth], and the resistance of the spirits to the formation of movement, and the unfitness caused by the distance of the thing by nature from the whole heaven, and especially the greatest possible distance from the stars. Regarding cold, therefore, we have strongly proved the author right who says: the celestial bodies bring no cold, but suggest heat; those which are said to offer cold are those which heat less. <margin>The opinion of Aristotle.</margin> This is Aristotle’s own opinion in his book *On the Heavens*. <margin>Abraham Avenezra</margin> Abraham Avenezra <note>A 12th-century Jewish polymath and astrologer</note> calls Saturn "cold" because its heat is more remiss <note>meaning "weak" or "reduced"</note> than ours. The whole heaven, therefore, is like a lucid humor, but it is a certain effective life, most ample in honor, agile, and formable. I say formable easily through its translucent humor by the archetype <note>the divine original pattern</note>, again easily forming the interior parts through what is clear and bright.

But in some places in heaven there is a little more heat, in others humor, in others conversely; in some places the portion is equal on both sides, and similarly regarding light. Through the different proportions of these three among themselves, there are different things there, just as here various things coalesce everywhere under the rays of heaven from the varied mixing of heat and humor. It happens meanwhile that something may suggest cold more, perhaps by hindering itself, or even by helping somewhat. We must remember, however, that this celestial heat is of a far different genus than ours—much more so than even the natural heat in wine differs from the burning of a furnace, or the Sun's own warmth in the air differs from this flame itself. From this, however, when the Sun's heat is sometimes forced into a hollow in hard or dry matter, a flame is straightway kindled. Finally, the humor in heaven is dry and non-distilling, and its heat is not consuming. The humor differs from aerial humor at least as much as aerial humor differs from water. Therefore, cold and dryness, or hard solidity, are rashly imagined to be in heaven. Indeed, since dryness is fled and cold is completely left behind as one ascends from the earth, one soon arrives at humor and lightness together: in the heights, there is such a mild heat from the light.

Therefore, the cold, the dry, and the hard together arise from nature and extreme distance from the heaven, while those things which are in the middle are moist according to the likeness of heaven, and the rest are bright and easily moved. In the heaven, which is most mobile, there is nothing of cold or dryness, nothing hard hindering motion—if indeed anything can be imagined under the heaven similar to the inhabitant of heaven. In that region, conspicuous to all eyes, a vital vegetation is seen in which vigorous heat, with much but tenacious humor, produces a restless motion. The structure of the more subtle and translucent parts will have a bright nature, and so will the heaven. That it is not hard seems to be confirmed by what is said by physicists and astronomers who, asserting doubts when they dispute about circles, centers, distances, and motions, give rise to a manifold and insoluble controversy. The physicists indeed accuse the astronomers of imagining impossibilities; the astronomers accuse the physicists because they cannot assign reasons. But how can theologians and others attack these things unless the others yield? I pass over the "Vehicles" <note>the 'astral body' or spirit-vessel of the soul</note> among the ancients, described as being given for the happiness of souls through a sudden community, where no natural substance or force of quality follows from hardness; it is not becoming to call it evil.

But let us now return to other qualities of the celestial bodies. Although nothing there is cold or dry, we call a star that is less celestial "cold": perhaps because while it travels, its rays open our passages so that earthly cold enters more easily. We may also call a star "dry" which moistens less: perhaps also because by moistening little, it often exposes chaff to the fire, whence the matter is dried more fervently. All stars everywhere heat, however, not by motion alone, but also from the nature of their nature—especially the nature of light. <margin>Avicenna.</margin> Which *Avicenna* <note>the Persian philosopher Ibn Sina</note> also proves, saying: where there is more light, there is also more heat. <margin>Hippocrates.</margin> Indeed, *Hippocrates* says: the air becomes healthier and more subtle by the action of the stars, and sometimes warm, suited for generation and life. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> *Aristotle* also, where he doubts concerning the parts of animals, says: nights during the full moon are warmer because of the Moon's light. The Moon indeed is very little hot, and very moist. If she is said not to heat in a certain place, it is because she moves more slowly than the Sun; perhaps she ought to compensate for the slowness of motion with her proximity to us, and thus finally heat by motion just as the Sun does. Likewise, if the fixed stars, although they move most swiftly, are nevertheless said not to heat by motion because they are very distant, they ought perhaps to compensate for the distance with their very swift motion, and therefore heat in the end. 

Truly, if motion itself were simply the cause of heat, then no motion would extinguish heat and flame, and at least the swifter would be the origin of a more vehement heat, and the slower of a more lukewarm one. Again, if it is not motion itself that simply begets heat, but a certain velocity, I truly do not see in the first place what distance or proximity can do, provided the motion itself is swift. Then, it is clear enough here that the effect of heat must rightly be referred to another cause besides motion, since motion—whether of the will—requires before it a form of imagination and nature; or if it is of natural inclination, nature requires a preceding form. Therefore, motion itself does not generate heat or any other form: but form is sometimes produced through motion, such and such by such and such forms, although the form is prior and more excellent by nature. Finally, who would assert that local motion, which is inferior to every form and belongs to external things, generates heat by its own nature? Often, by the hard collision of a body, it breaks the middle air and only rarefies it, and the thinned air, brought to a condition competent for fire, is clothed with the form of fire by the seminal idea of generation as if by a path. 

The Moon, therefore, heats less than the Sun because she is less hot. The superior stars [the outer planets] also heat less than the Sun, because they are either less hot, or smaller than the Sun, or at a great distance, or very separated from each other. Moreover, the Sun seems to dry by accident: not because there is in it a dry nature or any other power of desiccating—otherwise it would not naturally increase all things, but rather decrease them in the manner of fire—but because the Sun’s rays are either too constricted in very hard hollows, or being struck directly, they are reflected more strongly toward us: for then, through the violence of pouring out, new things happen. But because all rays, being as if immaterial, most liquid, and immaculate, are neither collected nor do they break their own things, nor are they broken, but are either gathered or returned from a region, it appears that heat is in them by nature, which is intensified by its own gathering and acts more vehemently. The Moon also, if she seems to bring cold by accident, it is because her light opens our passages by motion and meanwhile drives out the nocturnal cold, whereby it happens that the cold enters more freely and subtly through the opened entries. Indeed, the nature of cold is to kill and compress; but the light of the Moon truly begets and increases by the warmth it has, and heat with humor. Similarly, the Sun's light is the cause of cold by accident or never: whether it calls forth the natural heat of our body outward, or if you expose the body to the vice of cold soon after the heat of the Sun. 

Furthermore, it is a localized sin to call Saturn cold in any way, and therefore death-bringing. For nothing in him, which is so great and vital, can be in any way cold or lethal. It is enough to know that in Saturn, heat is overcome by humor. And since he is such, and moreover most remote from us, he brings very little heat, and not much humor: because besides these two, there is in him a power of naturally contracting, halting, containing, and compelling. Whence, although he never dries out...

He explains that perceived cold or dryness is merely a relative lack of heat or an accidental physical effect of distance, light reflection, and earthly density.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Ficino’s defense of the planets as inherently life-giving. ### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...just as the Moon does not seem to dry things out, even though it draws moisture into itself, much like the Moon does when its light decreases or when it descends. Truly, it is difficult to deny that Saturn is humid when authorities say it often increases rainfall and stimulates the flow of the bowels. Nor is it right to call this planet "pestiferous" <note>meaning "deadly" or "bringing plague"</note>; for Providence, which disposes all things, has honored it with such an ample sphere and willed it to be closest to the vital rays of innumerable stars. I will pass over the fact that the ancient Theologians attributed the Mind itself to Saturn, and dedicated the first and eternal life to that very Mind. Do not the Astrologers, for this reason, calculate its rising as the beginning of life? Do they not entrust the first month of conception to Saturn? Surely it would not be fitting to begin life under a deadly omen?

What then? First, if they commit the Mind to Saturn for this reason, it is so that he may gather the seed by his cold dryness and stop it from flowing away. Indeed, he halts and gathers it, not by a cold or dry power—otherwise the beginning of life would be sought from the opposite of life—but by a certain wonderful virtue of contracting, collecting, and containing. For there are many things that curdle milk and other liquids by a power other than cold. Thus, Saturn does not bind things together through chill or dryness—otherwise, from the very beginning, he would render life entirely unfit for generation—but rather through a virtue that draws everything from the circumference back to the center. It does not act merely by cold, but in the manner of a hand or a fist, or like the nature of rennet <term>rennet: a substance used to curdle milk into cheese; Ficino uses it as a metaphor for the formative "clumping" of biological matter</term> pressing tightly together, just as Mars, in turn, stretches outward from the center to the circumference. 

As for the fact that a child usually does not survive if born in the eighth month <note>original: "non vivat... mente" [likely a typo for "mense", month]</note>—if indeed that always happens, for it happens differently in Egypt and in some places among the Greeks—the cause is not the coldness or dryness of Saturn, but a certain violence inflicted from elsewhere at that time, which expels the child at the very moment Saturn was still holding it within the womb. For while he retains it, no one is born unless expelled from on high by an overly violent cause. Even the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note> and physicians assign reasons for this from sources other than Saturn, and astrologers report that in the regions of India subject to Saturn, lives are exceptionally long. 

But shall we not say that a dry or cold nature occasionally arises from Saturn, at least by accident? It might seem so if Saturn’s ray is caught in cold or dry matter. For then, it can even slightly warm or benefit things by itself, and it halts the excess of matter that is being frozen by the frost. But in more humid or especially in warmer matter, it seems to contribute the most. For by its own humor <term>humor: in this context, a celestial fluid or vapor that tempers planetary qualities</term>, it tempers the excess of heat, and by its very virtue of binding, it restrains the flowing out of moisture. 

Mars, on the other hand, moderates its effect in colder or more humid matter; but in warmer matter, it rushes headlong, acting more through an excess of heat than by the vigor of movement. But since we have now mentioned the seminal matter, it is worthwhile to point out that the power of the Sun and Moon in the fetus is universal toward vital heat and humor. The power of Saturn is to collect and deeply strengthen the seminal matter. Jupiter's office is to subsequently provide guidance and nourishment. Mars's action is to move toward external things. Mercury’s gift is to shape the spirit and limbs according to the senses. Venus’s ministry is to conform everything toward affection and the production of offspring. 

These are the gifts pertaining chiefly to the body, derived from the bodies of the planets and signs. Furthermore, from their "souls" <note>the animating spirits of the planets</note> acting upon our minds:
* From Saturn, **contemplation**, **caution**, and **diligent preservation** are increased. 
* From Jupiter, **civil and prudent governance** most of all. 
* From Mars, **magnanimity** and the **expulsion of injuries**. 
* From Mercury, **inquiry** and **expression** of any kind. 
* From Venus, **charity** and **humanity**. 
* From the Sun, **good stature**, **modesty**, and the **study of true glory**. 
* Finally, from the Moon, the **care and diligent providence for the necessities of life**. 

But lest anyone perhaps condemn us for arranging the planets in this Platonic order, remember that Divine Providence established that the Sun should wander the least through the latitude of the Zodiac; for its entire deviation comes to less than the estimation of a single degree. Because the Sun might perhaps confound the planets that approach it too closely in height or latitude, and might entirely overwhelm them by the excellence of its power, it was decreed that the Moon and Venus, between which the Sun moves, should wander more widely; for the ancients held that they wander nearly twelve degrees. Mercury, being further from the Sun than Venus, protects itself by a narrower wandering, for it runs to about eight degrees, and Mars and Jupiter to five. Saturn, being the most remote, runs out to three degrees in latitude. Thus the opinion of those who place Mercury before Venus is confirmed, although those who do the opposite defend themselves by the order of the zodiac signs. For just as house follows house, they wish the planets to be arranged. Therefore, Cancer holds the Moon first; Leo the Sun second; Virgo Mercury third; Libra Venus fourth; Scorpio Mars fifth; Sagittarius Jupiter sixth; Capricorn Saturn seventh. Then they are placed in reverse order—but let them see to that.

---

->Such are the compositions of the natures of the planets, their diverse powers and<-
->actions, and from them all, the wonderful tempering of the heavens.<-

*But I return to Plotinus. Since he maintains that everything in heaven is warm and nothing is cold, yet in certain things heat is tempered more or less, he seems to join humor there with heat, by the mixing of which tempering occurs. For there, heat is not repressed by coldness, nor is it restrained by itself, nor does pure heat reign there alone; otherwise, it would not dominate more in one place than another. Humor, therefore, is there—that is, a certain light and agile tenderness, a sort of mixed liquidity and life-giving fertility. Humor, I say, of this kind nourishes like nectar, just as heat nourishes light like ambrosia. Then it restrains the fire, lest the heat itself be destroyed by the blaze; then it prevents the mutual collision of the spheres, which would otherwise occur from their most rapid motion and immediately burn up the spheres and everything else; and finally, it softens and soothes the motions and rays, so that they may touch the lower things more mildly. Humor accomplishes all these things; and it is so necessary to its own familiar heat that it never drips away or flows out, nor does it dull or suffocate the heat itself. Furthermore, just as in the soul the vital motion depends on the animal life, and this in turn depends on and is preserved by the intellect; so in heaven, liquidity depends on heat, and heat on light. Thus, for example, compose the celestial things: in Saturn, humor greatly exceeds heat; in Mars, heat far conquers humor; Jupiter, in the middle of these, tempers heat almost equally with humor. Next, to arrange them in the Platonic manner, Mercury succeeds, reflecting the nature of Saturn; Venus follows him, representing a Jupiter-like proportion. I say "as if," because of the opinion of those who think Jupiter inclines somewhat toward heat, but Venus rather toward humor, yet from both a most perfect temperament is created. Then the Sun, like Mars, has heat far conquering humor; the Moon finally, just as Saturn and Mercury, possesses much more humor than heat. But the humor of these three seems to relate to one another thus: Saturn's humor always returns to the center; the Moon's humor moves toward the circumference after it expands with increasing light. Mer-*

He details the specific physiological and psychological gifts of each planet and explains the Platonic arrangement of the cosmos based on planetary movement and "humoral" balance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*. ON BOOK III OF THE ENNEADS, TRACTATE II.

<margin>The Moon</margin>
Ultimately, she creates a balance between both. But to return to the Moon: when she wanes in light, the more learned astronomers say she does not actually diminish the substance of her moisture <note>original: "humoris substantiam"; in ancient science, "humors" or fluids were the building blocks of life</note>, but rather draws it back toward her center. Likewise, as she waxes, she expands it, which is visible in the sea: its breadth expands while the Moon seeks the middle of the sky from the East, but as she moves from the middle toward the West, it recedes into a narrow space. Meanwhile, it is not likely that she could be so easily or suddenly increased or diminished in herself. Furthermore, the heat of the Sun and of Mars are moved and move under different conditions: that of Mars moves, as if in a pyramid from the Sun, in a circle. In two of them, therefore—that is, Jupiter and Venus together—the portion of moisture and heat is roughly equal. But since in the other two—namely the Sun and Mars—heat far exceeds the rest, are there not again three—Saturn, Mercury, and the Moon—in which moisture exceeds? This is because heat is more effective than moisture, and the combined mass of the Sun and Mars is immense. There, the two are balanced by the works of the three from the opposite side. Indeed, so great is the efficacy of heat upon moisture that if the Craftsman of the world himself <note>The "Demiurge" or Creator</note> willed to balance them in the coils of the spheres that contain the stars, the moisture would exceed the portion of heat; so that by its portion, or rather its weight, the moisture might equal its nature to the efficacy of the heat. By this reasoning, all the spheres above the earth are called "waters." Just as the sea is water and liquid compared to the earth, so the air is a "moisture" to the sea; so the circuit of the Moon is a "liquid" to the air; and so the higher spheres seem to relate to the lower ones in succession, so that the higher things always cherish and fruitfully nourish the lower.

<margin>Waters above the firmament</margin>
There are, therefore, waters below the firmament; there are also waters in the firmament—not in the stars themselves shining in the firmament, but in its very tempered substance—and likewise the planets are composed by a proportion of these. There are even waters above the firmament itself, which astronomers have posited so that a completely simple motion might rule and lead the double and opposing motion of the firmament.

<margin>Empyrean fire</margin>
Above these waters, the Theologians have placed fire—that is, the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest heaven in medieval cosmology, believed to be made of pure light or fire</note>, a further Christian concept. And this, perhaps, is the light which, according to Moses, God kindled before the Sun, the Moon, and the stars. For this reason, the Crystalline heaven is judged to precede it, just as rest precedes motion, and heat precedes moisture. But is moisture a companion to heat in the Empyrean? It does accompany it, but it is absorbed into the heat. Again, does heat accompany moisture in the Crystalline? It does indeed, but it is drawn into the moisture.

<margin>Heat and moisture in the spheres</margin>
And so, following this, moisture gradually increases in the spheres until, beneath the middle region of the air, it becomes damp and flows out and scatters like something superfluous, as if tossed about by the heat. Above, however, each is so necessary and domestic to the other that the moisture tempers and moderates the neighboring heat, and the heat cherishes and transforms the moisture; and in both, light is preserved. But where there is more heat, the light is more effective and quite manifest to the eyes; whereas where moisture abounds, the light is less effective and whitening, like a flame that presents itself more intensely to the sight of the eyes. Meanwhile, I want you to remember that light and heat in the more "moist" stars—even if it affects us less regarding the star itself—nevertheless affects us much more and longer in succession, unless perhaps moisture or cold coming from elsewhere from the start resists it. This is because there is no dissolution of its matter, and primarily because since this star is of almost the same temperament as the sphere it rules, it will surely draw the influx of the entire sphere’s abundance toward us along with its own gift. Thus, as much as the other stars are powerful by their own individual virtue, these are pre-eminent by a collective virtue—especially the stars in the largest spheres. For a larger circle, being the container and the leader, is always more excellent in power, and it implants a wonderful and hidden power into its star.

<margin>Saturn, Mars, Jupiter, Venus, Moon, Mercury, Fixed Stars</margin>
But to return to Plato: Mars does not harm us by the sharpness of its heat, but rather tempers the matter of more moist things. Nor is Saturn harmful; but because it is the most distant, its influence is like a "stranger" to us, which is why it does not easily harmonize with us, especially with the young—unless it is properly mixed with the other lights, or if Saturn itself, sitting in a "human" constellation <note>Signs like Aquarius or Gemini, often depicted as humans</note> where it has its home or is exalted, acts as the author of the work. Nor is Mercury ever "evil," but since he is in the middle, he easily becomes very similar to all the others in their arrangement. Finally, just as in our bodies individual members with different qualities contribute both to each other and to the whole for the sake of the good, so in the heavens—which live by a common life—Mars holds the place of the gall <note>the gallbladder</note>, Jupiter the liver, and Venus and the Moon the genital membranes (if I may call them that). Mercury holds the place of the tongue and the face; Saturn the head, the spleen, and the stomach. The Fixed Stars represent the eyes, and those things that appear in this manner contribute to the overall balance.

<margin>Soul of the world</margin>
I have said that the universe thrives by a certain "common life," through which all the members of the world share in experience with one another; that is, influence is easily transferred from one thing to another, and a certain hidden sense is excited, and affection is incited. When I speak of a "common life," I mean, along with Plotinus, an "irrational life" <note>meaning the natural, instinctive life-force of the cosmos, rather than a thinking intellect</note>. There, the souls of the world, granted to the universe in a living communion, share a hidden consensus of actions and passions in all things. But we wish these lives not to be confused, but "conjoined"—lives similar to those of stars, demons, and men—just as the lives of our limbs harmonize deeply with the common life of the whole animal. Thus, it is no wonder that these things happen to one another through a certain proportion of "figures"—that is, from other members of the world-animal by a similar proportion, just as in us certain signs are provided to indicate the effects of others.

---

<margin>VI</margin>
### Five signs that the stars do not do everything.

<margin>1</margin>
The sixth chapter confirms by five signs that the stars do not do everything. First, it is established by the dignity of their nature, the sublimity of their location, and the amplitude of their power, that even the least "good" of the stars must be considered better than even the best of men. Therefore, the crimes that the best man would not commit, the stars certainly do not perpetrate—especially since all things regarding the stars are instruments of the Divine Craftsman. This is asserted by Ptolemy, and reason teaches it: both because individual things have been formed through them for so long by such a skillful plan (so that all this seems to be according to their strength, yet no other power could ever do it), and because the celestial bodies, though endowed with such great power, never seem to wander freely. Instead, under the condition of instruments, they are led through a certain path and limit toward a prescribed end, revolving always through the same cycles and in a similar way. Whatever, therefore, is carried out through the celestial instruments of the Divine Craftsman proceeds chiefly from God Himself. Since that is supremely good, it cannot become an evil falling away from order. Certainly, despite what some astrologers prattle, that through Mars joined with Jupiter and Taurus crimes are invented, adulteries are never committed among us because of them.

<margin>2</margin>
The second sign: Since the divine things above the heavens do not change in nature or in mode, while the things below the heavens change in both, it follows that the celestial bodies act as a middle ground; even if they seem to change always in their "mode" <note>their position or appearance</note>, they never change in their "nature." Does God rule whatever planets are at this hour, so that from this very conception they obtain such a nature, only for them to undergo another nature in the following hour from another conception? Similarly, do they have no limit or specific nature of their own or in relation to others in time, but like a Chameleon, are they always changed by the objects they face? <note>Ficino is arguing against the idea that planets are "fickle" or change their essential character</note>

<margin>3</margin>
Third: the stars are quite separate from our affairs; they are the most general causes, and they are limited in nature and number.

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

The <term>influx</term> <note>original: "influxus"; the Neoplatonic idea that celestial power "flows" down into the material world</note> of the stars, in whatever arrangement of celestial motions it is sent to us, reaches us in a more general and defined manner. Therefore, the uncertain multitude of effects and their infinite diversity cannot be carried out by the stars without an intermediary. Instead, intermediate causes and opportunities must fall between the celestial bodies and the lower effects; these intermediaries are more diverse in nature and perhaps vary daily, allowing the stars to descend into even the smallest and most innumerable effects. 

Thus, the stars do not arrange every tiny detail by a conscious "plan" of intimidation—otherwise, they would be miserable with such great anxiety. Nor do they descend from their very general nature directly into every specific detail by a purely natural condition. 

Fourthly, astrologers are accustomed to say that a planet, when placed in a certain <term>term</term> <note>A "term" is a specific subdivision of a zodiac sign governed by a particular planet</note> of a sign, progresses through a certain number of degrees. Likewise, they say a planet does not fulfill what it promised until that same sign rises again for us in a birth revolution; and that it rises again in the birth revolution after as many years as the degrees it had ascended for us from the beginning. Furthermore, they claim the effect differs more or less depending on where individual planets and other stars reside for those being born. 

All of this, however, belongs to a man who calculates according to his own whim, inventing rather than teaching. Even if one can more probably imagine that a planet does the same thing when it returns to the same position, nonetheless, what it could not do the first time, it will not be able to achieve the second time. Nor do I clearly see why it would not act based on its first position, which is much stronger in us than the second. What is said regarding the simple delay of action is entirely fabricated; for if the cause itself does not produce an effect while it is present, it will do so much less when it is absent. They might perhaps offer some specific reason for this: that the influence is "preserved" until that time. But I would ask where it is preserved? For it must be preserved either in causes closer to us, or in matter. Suppose it is preserved in this way. Certainly, if it is preserved, it is kept according to the condition of the things that preserve it, and it is gradually drawn toward their nature and distinguished according to their own distinctions. Therefore, whatever finally happens will occur under our own specific character rather than a general celestial one. 

Fifthly: as we have proved in *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his major work, *Platonic Theology*</note> and will repeat elsewhere: the whole crowd of causes depends on one first cause, so that from there it exists, is preserved, and is guided. Otherwise, the diversity of causes would not lead to a single end unless they were led to one by the One. Therefore, whatever comes from above, hanging as it were from the Highest Good, is both most beautifully made and comes as the best. Let no one, therefore, dare to confess that the stars are either entirely or even partially evil.

---

->Five proofs that the stars signify our affairs rather than cause them.<-

VIII. Plotinus and Origen, fellow students under Ammonius of Alexandria and always friends, agree on this matter as in most others: the stars neither do everything, nor, where they do act, do they complete everything entirely. Likewise, they signify many things that they themselves do not cause. I say they "do not do everything" so that, if they were to do evil, either God would seem not to provide for the world, or He would be unjust, and the stars would be unjust as well. Nor, again, do they do "everything entirely," lest the actions of natural things become empty and <term>free will</term> <note>original: "liberum arbitrium"</note> cease to exist, should the stars themselves carry out every single detail to the exact degree. 

With similar consensus, they willingly grant the stars a frequent "signification" even where they do not act, because divine providence is greatly confirmed by this. Indeed, they could not present signs of past and future things in this present variety of appearances unless things were woven together with other things, and times with other times, in a certain and consequent order. From this it is clearly evident that all things do not wander by uncertain chance, but are ruled by a certain reason and providence. 

If you consider the perpetual lights of the stars, and their approach toward us and retreat from us, Plotinus and Origen would concede that only as much is effected among us as proceeds from the natural order and pertains to the <term>affections</term> <note>The physical states or dispositions</note> of bodies—and that indeed by a general condition, which can be changed by things closer to us. But if you look again at the daily positions of the stars and their mutual <term>aspects</term> <note>The geometric angles between planets, like "square" or "trine"</note>, know that according to these philosophers, our affairs are signified rather than enacted. 

Origen proves this in his *Commentary on Genesis*, where it is said that the stars were made "for signs," and Plotinus proves it here and in his book *On Fate*, primarily with five invincible arguments. 

**First:** That which comes later cannot exist as the efficient cause of that which preceded it. Yet astrologers promise to indicate from the hour of birth not only what will happen to the newborn, but what has already happened: whether it is male or female, whether it is crippled or whole. Indeed, they even profess to reveal many past things to us through today's stellar position, things which preceded not only the birth but even the conception of the child—the natures and fortunes of parents and grandfathers, as well as elder brothers and others joined to us by necessity. You must grant that a later configuration of the heavens cannot be the cause of prior things; rather, let it be a sign, if indeed it declares anything. 

But if someone should concede that the past is only represented by these signs, while the future is additionally "caused," they will be forced to show us the difference and assign a cause for this distinction. Why, if the present configuration is not the cause of the past, should it be the cause of the future? If the position of Mars in the fourth house demonstrates both that the parents will die soon and that the child's inheritance will be squandered—just as this position does not kill the parents, so too it does not squander the inheritance. Furthermore, astrologers profess to predict certain future things through this configuration whose cause this configuration cannot be: namely, the fates of a wife, brothers, and friends, which have their own causes elsewhere and not in this specific birth chart. Finally, those things which will happen thirty years later certainly cannot be "perfected" by the present state of the heavens, even if they can be portended. Rightly, indeed, they often say that this child will be the cause of his own misfortunes, and another of his own advantages. 

**Second Proof:** If they say someone is destined to die on the <term>gallows</term> <note>original: "patibulo"</note>, they think this can be understood not only from his own birth, but also from the births of his parents, brothers, children, and other relations—and even from the birth of his killers. If there is any cause for this gallows, it is either one cause or several; certainly they are joined and exist within the event itself. But where these causes are dispersed among different people, they appear not as causes, but as signs. Finally, if the child's fate is predicted through the configuration of the heavens at birth as something "already made" long ago, this configuration does not *make* the fate, but declares it; just as the child is not *made* at that moment, but is declared to have been made. But the Platonists will say that fate was conceived even before conception, namely when the soul chose its body. 

**Third Proof:** Since there are thought to be many ways of foreseeing—oracles, augury, <term>haruspicy</term> <note>Divination by inspecting animal entrails</note>, the interpretation of dreams, the presages of doctors and farmers, omens, and <term>physiognomy</term> <note>Judging character or future from facial features</note>—in all of these, signs are perceived, not causes of the future. Why, then, in the inspection of the celestial figure alone, do they think it is not just a sign but a cause? Is it because that configuration is "higher" than us? But they also say that the flights of birds and thunder are higher, yet they are not accustomed to hunt for the future through these as causes, but as signs. Finally, it has already been established what and how a cause for effecting these things might be in the heavens. Are not God and the divine minds also superior? Yet oracles and the words of prophets, pronounced or written by divine inspiration, are portents of future...

<summary>Ficino argues that stars are "signs" created by Divine Providence rather than direct "causes" of human fate, using arguments from Plotinus and Origen to preserve human free will and God's justice. He points out the logical inconsistency of astrology claiming to predict the past (which the current stars couldn't have caused) while simultaneously claiming to cause the future.</summary>
