## ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

<margin>l 1</margin>

omens are not judged as causes. Similarly, the face of the heavens can be seen as a book in which divine figures are written to display things, not to enact them. This is especially true if, by observing the celestial bodies, we can foreknow things that the physical powers of that bodily nature could not possibly produce: namely, the specific honors or failures of men at certain times, the discovery of treasures, the secrets of human thoughts, and the changes of fortune—both our own and those of our kin. 

**The fourth piece of evidence:** If the present arrangement of the stars or dreams portend crimes or the specific works of divinity, it is far more probable to say that the stars declare omens rather than suggesting that these stars (which are inherently good) actually perpetrate evil acts, or that, being physical bodies, they produce effects in other bodies that are either against or beyond physical nature. 

**The fifth piece of evidence:** The inquiries that are made daily to astrologers—whether about the past (did such things happen?), the future (will they happen?), or the present (are they happening?)—concerning matters that are foreign to us and far distant, confirm that whatever is answered from the hour of the inquiry is answered through a sign, not a physical cause. 

From this, the points above are confirmed once more: that all things happening to us occur because of us. When we look at manifest causes, we find them within ourselves—in the specific nature of our own kind, in habit, in emotion, in effort, and in the convergence of surrounding circumstances. Nothing ever happens from the sky without these causes. It is foolish to search for causes in heaven that are clearly visible on Earth but cannot be found in the sky. 

Yet, if the celestial patterns always produced something in us every hour, we would admit it, but we would say it pertains only to the affections of the body and our first impulses—and even then, it would be of little importance, since you are driven by a momentary cause. Conversely, things are taken up according to their own nature, as if our more stable parts are resistant to change. 

Furthermore, because the arrangement of the stars signifies rather than causes just any event, the outcomes of divinity, nature, and higher art are confirmed. Therefore, whether a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn portends a new religion, it will nevertheless be clear that either a true religion is being perfected by God in the meantime, or it is being touched by the destiny of man. Or, if through celestial motions the things that happen in nature <term>below the Moon</term> <note>The "sublunary" realm: the Earth and its atmosphere, which ancient science believed was subject to change and decay, unlike the "incorruptible" heavens.</note> are sometimes disrupted, nature nevertheless does such things and carries them out by its own natural course. Likewise, if human actions of the mind are portended by these same motions, they nevertheless proceed by human counsel and according to our own free will. Signs are occasionally given when an effective cause signifies a cause changed within itself. 

Accordingly, as both *Plotinus* and *Origen* <note>Origen (c. 184 – c. 253 AD) was an early Christian scholar who, like the Neoplatonist Plotinus, struggled with the relationship between divine foreknowledge and human freedom.</note> say: the "letters" of the future were either written in the sky from the beginning and are openly unfolded, or they are written perpetually. Thus they link the stars and the patterns formed from stars (both real and imaginary), as well as the degrees of the signs and the minute parts—and finally, the aspects and motions of the planets—to these consequences. 

But you should understand "heaven" here as the entire universe. For heaven is everywhere, and *Timaeus* <note>A reference to the character in Plato's *Timaeus* who describes the creation of the universe.</note> calls the universe "heaven." Above the Moon, there are common causes of lower things, and thus common signs; but below the Moon, there are specific causes. Once these are known, the common signs are derived into specific indications, and this whole world exists as if it were the body of a single living creature. 

Therefore, in this living world, one must look around at everything both above and below the Moon and weigh them against each other. Just as there are diverse things acting among themselves—above, below, and sometimes the higher upon the lower—so too are signs scattered everywhere and often diverse. Just as in any animal there are contrary natures, diverse members, and signs in those members that conflict with others: so *Rhazes* <note>original: "Rasis"; Abu Bakr al-Razi, a famous Persian physician and philosopher.</note> warns in <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of judging a person's character or future from their physical features.</note> not to trust a single sign, but to grasp them all, to balance the mind, and where there are contradictions, to follow those that are more numerous and certain. 

Likewise, one must observe divinations within the world from the world itself. *Aristotle*, in his book *On Sleep and Waking*, warns that one must be cautious in judging with these words: "There are often signs in bodies, even from heaven, such as of rains and winds; yet the event signified is not produced when another more violent motion occurs." For this reason, *Origen* and even *Porphyry* <note>Porphyry was a student of Plotinus who edited his works.</note> attributed this kind of divination to <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, *daemons* are not "demons" in the modern evil sense, but intermediary spirits or intelligences that bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note>, conceding that the "celestial book" is open for them to read. 

I say this applies neither to daemons nor to souls alone; for in Porphyry's book *On Oracles*, it is clear how much he approved of the fact that whichever gods are prophetic through oracles then predict by the observation of stars. He adds that even the gods often lie, and that the precise knowledge of the future is not only uncertain for men, but even for many gods. From this, it can be understood that the knowledge of the gods is perfected at any given hour. Thus, as far as the present is concerned, the daemons "arrange" the book; and if they deal with new things, they contemplate celestial omens more than earthly ones. But daemons who dwell in the weak parts of things hunt for evidence from our affairs more than from celestial ones. 

The <term>Magi</term> <note>Wise men or practitioners of high astrology and natural magic.</note> finally perceive signs in both ways, and therefore they are much more suited for prophecy among us. From these, *Origen* says, men would have acknowledged that they received omens. However, whether they received them from these spirits or learned them by observation, they proceed from causes alone, and they hallucinate in a certain darkness.

---

### The judgment of the future is most difficult for many reasons.

As to why only an inspection of celestial things allows a human or daemon to see every tiny detail among us, we argue this point: Just as any celestial nature is more stirred than any earthly nature, so any boundary of heaven is much more "common" <note>Meaning "universal" or "general" rather than "specific."</note> than any earthly thing. Therefore, things cannot be rendered one-to-one from heaven to earth down to the smallest detail. Nor, therefore, can every tiny thing here be clearly discerned from there. For often a celestial motion vanishes, as it were, and is indifferent to the many motions here. Unless you look at our affairs here in addition to the heavens, you cannot weigh by what specific "fortification" this celestial motion is caught, or in which part it is defined. 

Suppose you take the figure of the heavens at your birth. You will see in it certain defined notes, few in number, by which you see certain common and few effects noted in you. But your "deaths"—which are innumerable, occurring not just in your whole life but every year and month—you can never perceive from there. Not even if you unroll the revolution of your birth every year, nor if you observe diligently every day. 

Furthermore, regarding what daemons can do in the present, men certainly cannot. No wise man will deny that all the stars, which are innumerable to us, contribute something to an effect, and from their counsel comes something common—and that is fashioned according to the nature of the place and the matter. But astrologers observe only 1,025 stars out of the others, or at most, just over 1,476. 

The result is that, since they hold nothing of the number of causes and do not yet know them perfectly, they cannot judge the absolute condition of the effect—especially since there are very many stars above the planets, marvelous in both size and splendor. There are also innumerable stars in the Milky Way, entirely hidden from our eyes. They will not be able to know how the planets are affected in different ways by the aspects of those stars. I pass over the fact that the philosopher *Favorinus* <note>original: "Phauerinus"; a Roman skeptic philosopher.</note> argues not only that other stars exist besides the known ones, but even that there may be other planets, unknown either because of their great brilliance or the vastness of their height—without the observation of which a perfect knowledge of things perhaps cannot be had. To this, wherever the figures [signify], the stars and their emissions act upon a person born under this very horizon, and differently upon others...

122 COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

Let us grant that the stars, wherever they may be, all cast their rays upon one another—with the shadow of the earth never hindering this—and that these rays pass from every side all the way down to us. Yet, only a very few stars in the hemisphere have been noted by men. Indeed, even if the number of stars were calculated at the very minimum, certainly not all their powers have yet been recorded. Furthermore, their individual motions have not yet been fully grasped, neither by the eye, nor by instruments, nor by any span of time sufficient to observe them all. What of the fact that it is most difficult to believe that the size, height, and motion of Mercury have been perceived <note>original: "ad unguem," meaning "to the fingernail" or with perfect precision</note> perfectly? For it is seen only very rarely, and even then, it presents itself obscurely and almost in an instant, not waiting for sufficient diligence. Since, therefore, what *is* in the heavens and what is *happening* there has not yet been fully perceived, it is no wonder that we also do not know what is being *produced* by the heavens. 

Furthermore, astrologers do not rely on reason, but on experience and practice; yet experience very often fails unless all the surrounding circumstances on both sides are similar. Was it truly because Mars was in Aries at the eastern angle during the birth of Romulus <note>The legendary founder of Rome</note> that he performed such great deeds? This was based on the stars known to human ingenuity happening to coincide in that way at that time. Since, therefore, such a Romulus emerged once under such a sky, will Hannibal—for whom Mars also ascended in Aries—necessarily follow the exact same outcome? Not at all. For even if you imagine all the planets to be similarly arranged in both cases, the other stars and parts of the firmament do not hold the same positions they once did. For the signs that are in some way manifest to our eyes have already shifted their position toward the east from the time of Romulus to Hannibal; while running beneath the hidden and more stable signs, they complete one degree every hundred years. <note>Ficino is referring to the precession of the equinoxes, where the physical constellations shift away from the fixed mathematical zodiac signs</note> In this span of time, the position of the signs is permuted, and at the same time, the relationship of the visible signs to the hidden signs changes, which surely produces different effects. 

Even astronomers confess that all things must be referred to the invisible sign. For perhaps the manifest Aries, which then coincided with the hidden Aries, now aligns with Taurus, or at least with a different degree or minute of that Aries. Thus, the other signs respond to the signs in a different following order. Whence, if the signs exchange their powers through other signs, the planets also change through the signs. When the world has run its course, and in what state these signs appear compared to those, it is not even permitted for a human to suspect. How much the diversity regarding the eighth sphere <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note> matters is seen from the fact that, although for many thousands of years the planets have frequently returned to the same positions relative to each other, they still do not produce entirely similar effects. The knot of the world’s former face is not renewed; empires do not return in the same place, nor do similar laws and customs. We speak of the diversity of the eighth sphere, not only regarding its motion from west to east, but also its access and recess <note>The theory of trepidation, an imagined oscillation of the equinoxes</note>, through which the constellations approach the north in some ages and the south in others. 

Therefore, astrologers could not have established certain rules to be confirmed by experience while they conjectured similar effects for men born at different times, even if they had a somewhat similar position of certain stars. For the exact same face of the universe will not return until thirty-six thousand years have been consumed. <note>The "Great Year" or Platonic Year, after which the stars supposedly return to their original positions</note> Added to this is the fact that, just as the rules of physicians must be observed differently in different places if they are to be health-giving, so the rules of astrologers admit change under different regions. For the system of observation used by the Chaldeans cannot stand if one wishes to use the same system for figures under different regions of the sky. For the same stars do not stir up frost everywhere, nor similarly heat, winds, and rains; rather, they change and vary the weather, moving calm air in one place and violent storms in another at the same time, or none at all in a third. Why should human events not also be different in Chaldea, and different in Getulia and Scythia? <note>Ancient regions in Mesopotamia, North Africa, and Central Eurasia</note> Surely, just as the habit of the body is different under a different curve of the sky, so in all other human affairs you cannot conjecture the exact same thing if you view the stars from different parts of the earth.

But even granted that nothing stands in the way of astrologers knowing what is best suited to come from heaven in certain ages in individual regions—which to this day no one has properly observed—they certainly cannot fully explore the celestial figure they usually designate as "fatal" for each individual. First, they concede that in the fates of a newborn, the state descends not from his own figure alone, but from the figure of his parents and ancestors, and even from the time of the marriage itself. It is not possible to explore so many configurations, nor is it given to collect the fatal causes of a birth which are so widely dispersed and the signs so distracted. Nor, even if they should notice some things, can they weigh the weightier moments of matters; and if anyone could comprehend those, he still would not see every event in the life of the newborn from these alone. For they say that universal causes often come which are so powerful that they change the specific traits of an individual, for better or for worse. 

But let us return to the figures pertaining to the birth. Ptolemy, in his *Quadripartitum*, says: "A brief time can make a very great change in the thing, and therefore judgment is extremely difficult." To this, Abu Ma'shar <note>A famous Persian astrologer known in the West as Albumasar</note> adds in his *Book of Judgments*: "It is necessary for judgment to know the courses of the planets perfectly at any hour, and to hold the degrees and minutes of the signs with the utmost certainty." Indeed, the six signs starting from Cancer, because they proceed straight, occupy two hours or a little more in ascending; the remaining six, which begin from Capricorn, because they arise obliquely, ascend in less than two hours. Therefore, the hour must be divided on both sides into parts, and the figures distributed among the parts of the hour. In the straight signs, five degrees of the signs fill almost a fifteenth part of an hour; in the oblique ones, almost a twentieth. But just as there are thirty degrees in the signs, and sixty minutes in each degree, and sixty seconds in each minute, so it is necessary to distribute the parts of the hour—whether the fifteenth or twentieth—into sixty parts, and again into sixty, and to accommodate each part to each. 

Since, therefore, astrologers assert (as Origen also says) that not only degrees, but even minutes and the minutes of minutes must be known—where the planets are, and which are ascending or descending—who can grasp such minutiae? (For in the smallest thing is the greatest difference, which Nigidius demonstrated with the turning of a potter’s wheel.) <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar, reportedly argued that just as two drops of ink placed on a spinning potter's wheel land in different spots, two twins born in rapid succession are born under different celestial points.</note> Now, since for the most part one half of a sign occupies an hour in ascending, how can you find those few ascending minutes when you cannot observe such a minute division of time? For it is necessary to know not only the hour, but even at which five-minute interval of the hour the boy was poured out from the womb. In Pisces and Aries, due to the oblique ascension of the hours (for they seem to ascend in almost an hour and a third), they do not doubt that the smallest part of time brings a great change, so that even a twentieth part of one hour changes the degree of the ascendant. 

Since, therefore, they assert that even a tiny amount of time falling between births—whether of twins or of any two men born of different parents but at almost the same time—brings the diversity which is perceived in their effects, Augustine asks them: "Does that tiny interval bring a tiny discrepancy between them, or a great one?" If they say a tiny one, we point to the twins Jacob and Esau, born with no interval of time, yet they were greatly dissimilar. If they say a great one, since those seconds, thirds, and fourths of minutes can be grasped by no instrument, they certainly cannot judge. I have experienced that a small time can bring great differences in my own family. In our household, twin sisters were born without any interval: one was killed by a specific disease after seven weeks; the other was suffocated by a negligent nurse after seven months. Similarly, twins were born: one was killed by fire within a few days; the other was suffocated by water after fourteen years. And in our neighborhood, twins were born without intermission...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s systematic deconstruction of astrological determinism. Having previously argued that the vastness and complexity of the stars exceed human observation, he now addresses the "problem of the moment"—the impossibility of pinpointing a single instant of birth or conception to which a specific fate can be attached.</meta>

### ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.

*...those who are already adults, and who are extremely diverse in their bodies, characters, and fortunes. I pass over how different is the lot of brute animals that are born many at once, especially those fostered together in eggs. Truly, if the moment of time in which a human being is born and receives a fate is so small and rapid that in that very same point under the same point of the celestial circle several people can hardly be born to the same destiny, it follows that even twins are not made with the same lot in life, since they were not born at the same moment. Let them answer, I pray—so that I may ask along with Favorinus <note>A Roman-era philosopher known for his skeptical arguments against astrology</note>—how they can possibly grasp that course of flying time, which can scarcely be understood by the mind’s thought, when they say that in such a headlong whirling of the heavens, even the smallest moments bring about massive changes? Indeed, there is a greater delay in the birth of a single child than there is between twins who quickly follow one another in labor. If, therefore, the celestial constitution and fate are changed in the blink of an eye, it will surely be necessary for them to claim as many fates as there are limbs being born. Here, too, it is asked in what proportion the series of fate is unfolded: at the first moment the child begins to emerge from the womb? Or rather when he is halfway out? Or perhaps when he is entirely out? For even on this point they disagree among themselves. But it seems the matter must be taken up again from a deeper beginning.*

*Although some profess that they will discover the very configuration of the heavens at that time, and indeed from the chart of birth, yet since they hold this birth-chart to be uncertain, then surely that earlier one <note>The conception chart</note> is much more uncertain. But let us grant them that they hold this as certain; by what means, finally, will they be able to catch a royal fate from it? Some will perhaps say that the degree of the Moon at the ascending birth was the degree at conception, and conversely, the degree of the ascendant at birth was the degree of the Moon when the fetus was conceived in the womb. But even this cannot be firmly established; indeed, it is entirely arbitrary. Now they also seek answers from elsewhere, and as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who integrated theurgy and astrology</note> reports, some are accustomed to use five laws for this, others fewer, and others still more. Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus who often debated the technicalities of astrology</note> says that even with astronomers conceding the point, it is altogether uncertain. But suppose someone does happen to find the first beginnings of the fetus: we ask whether that first tempering of the sky, when the human work is first begun, alone influences the work, or whether the remaining celestial harmonies that follow—which, like the first, were momentary and vary with every passing second—also have an influence? If the first moment alone is said to be effective, it is a wonder that a momentary figure of the sky completes a long-lasting work, and continues to act when it is no longer there. But they will claim that from the first configuration a certain power is left in the fetus, surviving and acting as it were. Let it be so, then, however marvelous it may be; yet do the figures that continually follow afterward do nothing to the fetus? On the contrary, these also act and impress their own marks. And since they are received according to the nature of what came before, they nevertheless flow in with their own nature and gradually change the prior things, confounding the signs and deceiving judgments.*

*A very great change of preceding things and a beginning of following things occurs when the soul first flows into the small body of the fetus, which has been prepared for the soul; this moment is uncertain even to the daemons <note>original: "dæmonibus"; intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences</note>. Iamblichus, following the mind of Plato, proves that the lot and the daemons that guide life are assigned to the soul even before conception, from the universal disposition of the whole world, insofar as the soul first desires a body, relates itself to the universe, and connects to it. Therefore, it would be necessary first to know and weigh that time, which he thinks can only be grasped by divine inspiration. Besides these things, in judging the effects of men, five times/moments seem necessary to observe:*

*First, indeed, the time of fertility, when the seed is cast into the womb. The condition of this contact follows the voluntary motion of the parents, and the present nature of both, and the accompanying imagination, rather than the present constitution of the sky. For the beginning of the motion was the will of both; the lot in such a motion happens chiefly according to their nature and imagination, while the heavens favor it somewhat in the meantime. How much imagination can do is apparent from what pregnant women hear, and in animals that are born white from parents imagining white things, as is told of peacocks.*

*Second, the time when, the aforementioned motion having ceased, the seed collected in the womb begins the fetus; it starts to be transformed from what it was, and perhaps first to congeal. The beginning and lot of such congealing and distinction follow the condition of the seed and the parents more than the sky, because what is being made is very material, and it was and is a part of the parents. In its birth, it follows its own near and proper lot. Thus we see such a species and such an individual coalesce from such seed; meanwhile, the heaven contributes.*

*Third, the time when the fetus is first formed into life; they say this happens in the "fecund month," and Jupiter acts most of all. But it is uncertain whether life is present as soon as it has filled the middle of its month, or some days after, when it has reached the forty-ninth day from conception—since nature frequently rejoices in the number seven <note>The "septenary" theory of development common in ancient medicine</note> in our affairs—and whether all happens otherwise is obscure. For perhaps just as in the ninth month, which they attribute to Jupiter again, not every infant is brought forth into the light in the same way, so too not everyone receives life in the same way in the second month. For they say that females are not tempered to receive it in the same way as males; thus it is probable that males among themselves and females among themselves do not receive it at the same intervals. What of the fact that others will perhaps say the rational soul descends not in the month of Jupiter (in which they say the vegetative power is given), nor in the month of Mars (in which the sensory power is given), but in the month of the Sun, or perhaps of Mercury? But leaving these opinions aside, let us consider simply the beginning of one's own life; the auspice of life is chiefly drawn from this day and hour. For from conception it was rather an auspice of essence and mass until now, for it lived no other life than that of the parents and existed as a part of another; but now it claims its own life for itself and is now a whole, and will soon use its own motion. Therefore, such a life seems to borrow a lasting external life from the universe. The lot of life—I mean in the body—chiefly follows the present constitution of the sky. Then also the habit of the body; I say the present habit, for it is now different than it was at conception. And rightly so: just as that which was material followed a more material cause, so that which is most formal follows a primarily formal cause—that is, the celestial, and especially the super-celestial.*

*Fourth: the time when the grown infant in the womb strives with all its might to release itself from maternal bonds. The lot of such a release follows, first, the present strength of the child and the condition of the mother; then the habit of the sky, contributing more or less to it.*

*Fifth: the time when the entirely released child breaks forth from the womb. The condition of the one breaking forth follows the preceding condition of the one looking on <note>The observer or the state of the heavens</note>. But what the future condition of this one will be, who now comes forth from another, if it is indeed indicated by the celestial constitution in which he comes forth, it is weighed not as a cause, but as a sign. For they will say it is probable that the preceding prosperity of the heaven led to a consequent prosperity of the heaven. But remember, perhaps it cannot be weighed at all, both because the times are unknown, and because the causes are unknown (how many or of what kind they are), and because it is not known what is chiefly produced from the concurrence of all things. By "concurrence," I mean both of present causes among themselves, and of subsequent causes with preceding ones. For there was one troop of stars when the human was first conceived, another later when the soul was infused, and another when he was brought out into the light. If one arrangement and course of stars after another promises different fortunes, who will choose the most important among these when judging a lot? Who, in any given tempering...*

<summary>Ficino argues against the precision of astrology by highlighting the "problem of the moment," noting that the rapid movement of the heavens and the multiple stages of development (conception, animation, and birth) make it impossible to identify a single point of "fate." He suggests that celestial configurations act more as signs than as direct causes, and that parental imagination and biological nature play a primary role in formation.</summary>

Ficino highlights that while "signs" exist in nature, interpreting them as "causes" is a common error. # COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

of the heavens, it will remain uncertain how much good or evil is asserted, taken away, increased, or diminished here or there by the comparison of diverse influences. What new result, finally, is forged from the mixture of all things—in which mixture there is no doubt the greatest power resides? For even planetary aspects that are perhaps thought to be discordant on their own, when joined in harmonious combinations, produce a more pleasing and agreeable effect. When I speak of a mixture of all things, I consider not only the celestial lights but also the powers of the lower worlds and the <term>matter of the place</term> <note>The physical environment where an event occurs</note> to contribute greatly to such a mixture. To grasp all these things perfectly is surely a property of divinity alone. Hence Isaiah says: "Tell me the things that are to come, and I will call you gods." <note>Isaiah 41:23</note> Hence Plato attributes certain knowledge to God, but to us only opinion. Hence Ptolemy says that judgments about the future fall midway between necessity and contingency, and nothing should be affirmed as certain or discovered as a personal truth. Hence Avicenna, in his *Metaphysics*, denies that astrologers should be believed, because they do not grasp all celestial things, nor the natures of the lower things necessary for judgment, nor do they use demonstration, but rather a kind of experience, or prophecy, and oratorical or poetic proofs. For the human genius is hidden from both the number and quality of causes; experience fails us, and signs deceive us. Indeed, since many causes can often concur toward the same effect, it is scarcely discerned from which cause primarily such or such an effect has proceeded. Furthermore, an experiment is not consistent unless it is conducted in entirely similar materials and times. Deception in judging also increases because there are frequently many and dissimilar signs for the same effect due to different causes; and conversely, sometimes similar signs point to the events of dissimilar things. Finally, the judgments of things vary at different times; thus the astrologer fails unless he is compelled to observe the <term>revolution</term> <note>The annual return of the sun to its position at birth</note> of each year; just as the physician predicts a future outcome by circumspectly watching the "accidents" <note>Symptoms or external changes</note> of the sick person at various hours. Similarly, if there is any truth in the <term>augur</term> <note>One who interprets signs from birds</note> and the <term>haruspex</term> <note>One who interprets signs from animal entrails</note>, they must catch all other things everywhere at every single moment. Similarly, if there is any truth in the <term>physiognomist</term> <note>One who reads character and fate from facial features</note>, his evidence of health and character is perfected in each of the seven-year periods of human life. For just as new indications are primarily taken from the sick on every seventh day, so too in every seventh year certain new accidents and features, a new shape, new colors, and gestures either arise in us or at least are more clearly demonstrated. But remember that in whatever way or ritual truths are spoken concerning the future or things hidden from men, it often happens by chance, especially among those who speak a great deal. Often, too, something similar to this occurs because many things in life are common to almost everyone and happen daily in many ways from all sides. Sometimes what seems to be perceived by chance or art was actually brought forth by a natural, demonic, or divine instinct. By "natural instinct," I mean when nature in us is so tempered that it is easily moved by universal nature. "Demonic," when the imagination is so affected that it is opportunely struck by a <term>daemon</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, a mediating spirit or guardian, not necessarily an evil entity</note>. "Divine," when the reason or intelligence is so situated that it is most fitly subjected to its own divine mind, even if this is hidden from us. Whoever possesses these modes of predicting—by art, chance, nature, daemon, or God—it follows that many who are either idle or less learned in the arts excel through a guided presage. Hence Porphyry, before recounting how Plotinus wonderfully surpassed the example of Socrates, says that he had something wonderful in his very nature beyond other men, and had not only a daemon but also a God as his teacher. Hence that astrological judgment from the stars is made not only through the inspection of them but also from the very nature of the one who judges. Hence Ptolemy says these judgments are ambiguous to him who considers the natures of things and the stars, but those who know the future from a "better part" are closer to the truth because of the power of the soul dominating in them, even if they do not have much skill in this art. Conclude finally: if farmers and doctors are very often deceived in predicting more serious matters, other predictors are deceived most often of all. All the most learned astronomers, detecting this fallacy, neglected judgments. I pass over others known to me. Paolo of Florence, a singular astronomer, used to laugh at these things; he completed eighty-five years of life, yet having most diligently contemplated his own <term>genesis</term> <note>Birth chart or horoscope</note>, he could find nothing in it that contributed to such a long life.

### How great the communion of things is in the universe: and how there are certain hidden indications in things.

Although the judgment of future and hidden things is most fallible—and if it is ever truthful, it proceeds more often by a natural, demonic, or divine instinct than by art—nevertheless, there are certain indications of things within things, by which a more sagacious nature, being warned, explains all things by its own or a higher faculty, which the indications only lightly suggest. Plotinus wishes that signs are in turn implanted in things for other things because of the "communion of nature" itself: from which one thing signifies the event of another, and one thing signifies something mutual to another, similarly in a similar way, and similarly within us. Certainly, if elements are thoroughly mixed in things, so that an element is in any given thing, much more so in an animal, which is composed of a series of limbs just as a mixture is forged from elements; in any limb, all things are present. For a composite that is better by nature is surely compacted by a better reason. No composite structure is perfectly connected unless, just as the parts are in the whole, so in turn the whole is in the parts. But the whole is not in the parts if it is only through one or some parts while other parts are stripped away; rather, it is through all parts entirely that the whole is in any part: that is, if all are in any part. It is added further that in the generative faculty of the soul, the whole man is present at once, such that he is whole in any limb. Similarly, in the formative power of the seed, wherever any limb is conceived, the rest follow at the same time; thus far there is no distinction of place among the limbs, but only of reason. Therefore, since the animal visible to the eyes springs forth from both the soul and the seed under this condition of union, it follows that it receives a similar union in some way. For this reason, even if the head seems to be in one place and the hands and feet elsewhere, yet by a certain common participation, perhaps all things are in all: as if in the brain there is something of the heart and liver; so in the heart, something of the liver and head; so in the liver, in turn, the hands and feet are in the face; in the hands perhaps both the face and feet; in the feet perhaps the face and hands. In any limb, therefore, although something of the others is naturally present, so besides its own indications, the indications of others sometimes lie hidden. You, therefore, after you have contemplated the forehead and especially the eyes first, look around at all signs everywhere. For what is either hidden from you somewhere or is least brought forth due to an impediment, you will perhaps find elsewhere. By a similar reason, the <term>world-animal</term> <note>The 'Anima Mundi' or Soul of the World, which Neoplatonists believed animated the entire universe</note> once sprouted from its soul and its seed, namely by that reason that the whole is in any of its members: thus in any sphere, all spheres are present in their own certain way. All stars are in any star; living beings in living beings; all mixed things lie hidden in mixed things: so much so that an influx easily happens from all into all, and almost in individual things, besides their own signs, certain indications for the rest lie hidden. I pass over how in Saturn there is not only a certain nature of Mercury and the Moon, but also of the others. In Jupiter, not only the nature of Venus, but additionally of the others. In the Sun, the nature of Mars and of all. I pass over how, similarly in us, the lungs and stomach and the rest in succession are referred to the head. To the heart, the spirit and bile, and the rest; to the liver, the blood and generative members, and so forth. Gather finally: just as in our body

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of the microcosm and macrocosm. Having previously argued that precise astrological prediction is nearly impossible for humans, he now moves to the philosophical core of the matter: how the human soul relates to the "signs" of the universe and how wisdom can overcome the mechanical necessity of fate.</meta>

# ON BOOK III OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

parts correspond to parts for their duty and perhaps for the overall argument: so the whole world, of which the human body is a part, provides judgments here and there for our own benefit. For just as in us all members follow a single generative and formative power <note>The "virtus genitalis atque formatrix" is the internal force believed to shape the embryo and maintain the body's structure</note> which is preserved within them, so all bodies, along with their various powers, accompany the body of the universe and its similar power. Thus, it is perhaps not surprising that signs suited to us can be perceived from the whole of things. But while those signs are provided from that source, they seem more general; in us, however, they approach a specifically human quality. For from that source they pertain in a certain way to everything, but in us they are drawn toward the human. Truly, just as things designated in the heavens do not always happen—sometimes because a different cause stands in the way, or because the matter is adverse—so the signs implanted in us are cheated of their outcome, hindered by other causes that fight back either openly or secretly. For although all causes and indications in us may be more specific to man, they are nevertheless usually most uncertain. This is partly because they have become too manifold and are confused by their own crowd and opposition; partly because our matter is not only subject to many things, but is also unstable, often hindered, and deceptive; partly because the imaginative remnants of our own thoughts often confuse the likenesses; and finally, because the power of the soul, both natural and acquired, often changes many things. But since we have arrived quite opportunely at the soul—that is, our own—we must note in Plotinus's words that the soul does not view all things by only one path. Indeed, he says: If our individual members have their own powers and actions, even though they are not whole things but parts, how much more must those animals which are rational in the world possess them. For these remain what they are and are not only parts, but are moreover also wholes. From this it is clear that, beyond a common fate, certain gifts belong to them, either so that their lot differs from the fatal one, or so that their own unique qualities apply beyond fate. Finally, he confirms that in the universe there is not a mere heap of wandering things, but a perpetual series of things and motions disposed by a certain natural and divine art, because each thing is directed toward a fixed end, and all things contribute to a common one, and the resulting order of succession is always enacted and repeated in the same way.

->*What the principles of things are, and how our soul also has the character of a "principle" <note>A "principle" or "arche" is a starting point or governing cause</note>, overcomes fate, yields to fate, and is punished by divine law. Likewise, how it can perform wonders and even free the body from fate in a certain way.*<-

IX. There are three primary principles of the world: the Good, the Intellect, and the Soul. Thus the world, established under the Good and directed toward the Good, is led toward it by providence as an intellectual animal. Again, all souls, which through intelligence and reason create orbits within themselves and both imitate and follow the world-souls and the mundane orbits, are themselves also thought to have the character of a principle. This is especially true because they are received as colleagues, as it were, into the very differentiation of the world, even though the other rational souls fulfill through many revolutions, as far as they are able, that duty which the Soul of the World performs in a single revolution. Therefore, the rational soul is not only led in the "choral dance" <note>original: "choream" – a common Platonic metaphor for the harmonious movement of the heavens and souls</note> of the world, but it also leads. For it begins its own work as an active agent when it proceeds from itself both to contemplate the intelligible <note>The realm of pure ideas and divine truth</note> and to govern the sensible <note>The physical world perceived by the senses</note>. I say it proceeds rightly toward the sensible when it conducts itself toward it in such a way that it does not at all abandon the intelligible for its sake. This is what it means to proceed "straight," for in this way it tends properly toward that end where providence is directly aimed; but it "prevaricates" through oblique paths whenever it places a sensible good too far above an intelligible one. Now, Plotinus seems here, in the manner of Plato, to touch upon the force of "rectitude" in measurements through the names of the "straight" and the "oblique." A straight column stands firm under a great weight, while one that is not straight breaks or falls. Light rays that are straight and perpendicular are seen to strike back; they do not slip away in different directions but return to themselves. When they are plunged from the easy air into the difficulty of water, they are not broken, but proceed straight and are not twisted from the course they began. But oblique rays both depart from themselves in solids, where they are forced to be reflected, and are broken when descending in liquids from the air, or vice versa. One can quite properly transfer each of these points to the straightness or obliquity of the soul. But I return to the beginning. Truly, in the judgment of divine providence, a soul that conforms itself to what is inferior is justly transformed into something worse, to that level in the order of things which providence has already provided. Even if it was not intended primarily, it follows as a consequence: as each person departs from the first rank, they proceed by right into the second. And the soul, which had been free in a certain way until then, follows thereafter as if a miserable slave to those things which it loved too passionately, until it releases itself from that burning love. But divine judgment is never absent, nor is it ever escaped. Indeed, by the law of that same all-powerful providence by which things are adapted to each person in natural objects everywhere, things suitable and their own are also rendered to souls. The stars seem to serve this law of providence in three primary ways. First, they make this universe almost as beautiful as the divine mind first conceived it as beautiful through the "ideals" <note>The archetypal forms or patterns in the Mind of God</note>. Second, they contribute to natural effects, which we clearly see are nourished by the rays of the stars. Third, they provide "demonic signs" <note>Signs intended for "daemons," intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note> of future and hidden things to both demons and men. If these are said to portend all things that arise in the sensible world, "all things" should be understood in a general sense, especially everything that proceeds by sensible reason. Finally, "all things" for demons rather than for men: for it seems God proposed the "celestial volume" <note>The sky viewed as a book or scroll</note> to be read by them. If anything is transferred from there to us, whether by instinct or by argument and omens, it is clear that this too was done by divine institution. And if we are not warned there in vain, it is certain that we can for the most part avoid evils and attain the goods that are shown in advance through our own industry. Hence Abumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, an influential 9th-century Persian astrologer and philosopher</note>, against those who say the science of the future is useless, says: "It will perhaps be clear to you to take precautions by changing the place in which a plague is to occur; it will even sometimes be possible to repel the whole thing from yourself, and by foreseeing a future infirmity, or an invasion of enemies and similar things, to avoid them." Hence also Ptolemy says: "The wise man shall rule the stars" <note>original: "Sapiens dominabitur astris"</note>, insofar as once warned, he can turn aside a looming danger. Likewise, the wise man joins his work to the work of the stars, just as a prudent farmer joins his to the natural power of the earth, insofar as he himself completes through his own industry the good things sometimes indicated from heaven. For as a prudent farmer is related to the earth and the sky, so a physician and a prudent man are related to both. Therefore, just as the farmer perfects what nature began, and heaven in turn finishes what the farmer starts, so the farmer changes many things regardless of the nature of the sky and the Sun: he defends certain things, sometimes relieving them from dryness by watering, sometimes protecting them from cold, sometimes supporting them against a fall. In the same way, the physician and the prudent man can conduct themselves specifically toward the heavens and our body. How much the diligence of medicine is worth in these matters, I have discovered both often at other times and in the case of a boy who was born in the eighth month of conception, at night, under the station of Saturn the Calculator...

He argues that the stars provide signs that a wise person can interpret to avoid harm, much like a doctor or farmer works with nature to improve its outcomes.</summary>

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

...with the first degree in Sagittarius <note>The "ascendant" or rising sign at the moment of birth, which astrologers believe determines physical health</note> ascending, the child was indeed half-dead, and it seemed he would barely live for three days. However, having been most diligently cared for by us, he gradually recovered his strength and has now completed many years. I pass over the fact that I assisted the heart, brain, liver, and stomach of the newborn—and those of the nurse as well—with remedies applied both externally and internally, while observing the more favorable days and hours for their application. 

Indeed, Plotinus thinks that the rational soul does not only defend its own body and those things entrusted to it from a common fate by such arts, but that, like the celestial souls, it can sometimes exercise command over the lower materials of the world. This is because the soul is a sibling to the celestial souls, and thus may act in all things as if possessing a certain principle of leadership. When and how it can do this, we discuss more extensively in our *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's major work, *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of the Soul*</note>. 

I also pass over how much power one may have through magic that is both astronomical and physical: how one might draw the wonderful powers of the stars through certain "images" <note>Talismans or figures engraved under specific planetary alignments</note>, just as a concave mirror often gathers the rays of the Sun. From this, the mirror reflects and burns a piece of wood placed in front of it, and sometimes blinds those looking on. In the same way, in certain materials prepared for the stars by both nature and art, the soul may conceive certain stellar rays and influences, which it can both keep for itself and direct toward others. Porphyry relates that Olympus of Alexandria <note>A rival of Plotinus who allegedly tried to use magic against him</note> was accustomed to doing this; he says that Plotinus’s soul possessed such great power that he was able to deflect the "stellar stings" directed at himself back onto others. 

The Jews, through their Kabbalistic wisdom <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note> and their intimate skill in the sacred scriptures, confess that the fatal lot hanging over us from the heavens can often be broken. Iamblichus says this is done through the effective worship of the high gods; Porphyry says it is through magical wisdom, citing the oracle of Apollo as a witness. For Porphyry says in his book *On Oracles* that when someone asked why he had been judged by Apollo as unfit for a certain matter, and what should be done to be accepted as fit, the oracle replied: "He is hindered by the force of the Fates, which he could have escaped through magical arts." From this it is clearly evident that the art of magic was granted to men by divine gift so that they might, in some way, repel fate. This is the view of Porphyry. 

Plato, in the *Charmides*, signifies that the health of the mind and body can be cured through magic, and finally that immortality can be acquired through temperance, especially when prepared through the virtue of wisdom; for he proves by the testimony of the Magi <note>Ancient Persian sage-priests</note> that the health of the body proceeds from the health of the soul. But let us hear Zoroaster <note>The legendary founder of the Magi, to whom Ficino attributed the "Chaldean Oracles"</note> singing divinely: "If you focus your mind entirely on the duties of piety, you will also preserve the fading body." From this, it is handed down that the Pythagoreans agreed to expel the diseases of minds and bodies with "made songs" <note>Incantations or rhythmic chants</note>. 

If the soul has such great power, is it any wonder that it is naturally free from fatal servitude, until it embraces the body with too much love beyond the measure of providence? For thereafter the soul obeys the body, and the body serves the law of fate, until the soul turns its love away from the body and back toward the Mind <note>The "Intellect" or higher divine reason</note>. Thus, it first exempts itself from fate by fleeing; then it defends the body, since the soul is now strengthened by the Mind, usually protecting it from fate through a certain hidden power related to the celestials, and sometimes through art revealed by divine means. 

This chapter concludes that the stars signify many things, but they do not *cause* them <note>original: "significare, non facere"</note>. Therefore, they do not cause riches or poverty, which happen to us from the meeting and occasion of various causes among us. They do not cause virtues, which are made from reason in the senses, and perfected from the Mind in reason. They do not cause vices, since the efficient cause of fate is one's own, or perhaps a "deficient" cause; that is, insofar as the sensual life fails to follow reason, and reason degenerates from the Mind. It can indeed happen from the stars, through a certain defect of matter in the living body, that there is some prompting toward vice; but the love of the higher soul for the animal part provides the occasion for vice to be conceived from this. Otherwise, the soul lives externally free from fate, insofar as it is dedicated to the Mind, and through its own mind consents to the law of the first Divine Mind. Hence that prophetic saying: "My soul is always in my hands, because I have not forgotten your law" <note>Psalm 119:109</note>.

->How the rational soul is not subject to fate, but the irrational is: how the life of our body specifically depends on the life of the heavens and on our soul. Also, that there are twin souls in all celestial beings. Concerning demons, and from where evils happen.<-

### IX
Regarding the previous points where it is asserted that the stars do not do everything for us, even though they can signify many things, someone might perhaps object with the words of Plato, especially in the *Republic* and the *Timaeus*. For he says in the *Republic* that souls go forth into bodies under the fatal "dice of Necessity" and the revolutions of her daughters, the Fates. He also says in the *Timaeus* that a corporeal life is infused into us; in these words, he seems to subject us quite heavily to fate. 

The answer to the first point is this: souls chose this specific life and form of living of their own accord before they came into the body under the fatal revolution. Therefore, they have not so much lost their original virtue and self-governing authority as they have suspended it for a time; finally, they can recover it because they themselves partly decreed it, were partly helped by divine means, and were partly warned by laws. 

The answer to the second point is this: according to the *Timaeus*, a corporeal life is given to us by the stars, from which disturbances arise; yet the intellectual soul, the ruler of this life, is refreshed by the Divine Intellect. Just as the soul, while it loves this life in this world too much, loses itself along with this life in fate, so by loving it as little as possible, it meanwhile recovers itself above fate in eternity. 

Zoroaster teaches that the rational soul can enslave itself to fate and, in turn, set itself free, commanding this sentiment: "Do not increase your fate." Regarding this, Plotinus says: "You"—that is, the human being itself—are the rational soul, which by natural right should preside over the animal. He added: we must take care lest we accidentally become "this animal." For he thinks that through the fulfillment of imagination and the consent of affection, one "living thing" can be made out of the soul and the animal together: namely, when both imagine the same thing in the same way, and are affected toward the same thing in the same way. This is much like how one thing is made from fire and wood through the communion of light and heat. 

He adds again that in the "animal"—that is, the animated body—the nature of the body prevails. For there the body is truly a body because it is formal to the highest degree and brought to the peak of corporeal form; but its specific life is not a true soul, nor a true life, because it is heavily corporeal and holds almost the last place in the order of life. Therefore, just as this life acts upon the body naturally by forming it—or rather, is acted upon in the body while the body is formed by it from above—so the body in a certain way acts upon life while it conforms this life to itself. 

For this reason, just as there appear to be four principal alterations in the body—through heat and cold, through moisture and dryness—so four principal disturbances arise in the corporeal life. Likewise, what is expansion and contraction in the body, is pleasure and pain in the life of the body. But just as the rational soul, joined with the animal through the affection of imaginations, is touched by these passions and struck by a fatal lot, so when it finally subdues this animal to the laws of reason, it first resolves itself from disturbances and fate. It does this while it recognizes that it is one thing and the animal is another, and therefore that fate belongs to the "other." Then, it defends this animal entrusted to it by nature from the most atrocious wounds of fate or fortune. Where indeed Plotinus...

### ON BOOK III. ENNEAD II.
<sig>I 4</sig>

He says that of the twin souls of humans, the higher one is sent from the divine intellect, while the lower one is infused by the gods who are carried through the heavens. You should understand "gods" here to mean the souls of the celestial spheres and stars, which act in harmony with the soul of the world. For all these are said to be moved, whether they are carried by a specific local movement or a formal one. But in what way does life overflow into the body from the conspiracy of all these things? For just as a single harmony results from many voices sounding under a vaulted ceiling, or again, as a certain common splendor is created in a hall from many lamps—it is not quite like that. For in those cases, the harmony and the splendor are a "one" by assembly rather than by form. But a soul, whatever its nature, is a simple substance, and the form of a single living being is one, even if the separated soul might be judged as a secondary quality <note>original: "accidens"</note> in relation to the more excellent soul. In what way then? Perhaps it is like how a single voice with a distinct meaning comes from a single imagination through many different vocal instruments. Or again, as a single light from one sun, penetrating through glass stained with various colors, does not thereafter split into many lights, but remains one, even though it is shaped by the power of the varied colors. In almost this same way, a certain single form of life, manifold in its power, results in the body: one form arising from the power of the life of the world, and another manifold form arising from the communion of many souls besides this one, all breathing life together.

The "character" most proper to the animal is imprinted chiefly in the spirit <term>spiritus: a subtle, vaporous substance that medieval and Renaissance thinkers believed connected the physical body to the immaterial soul</term> by the generating soul. By the specific quality of this imprint, either all the "breathing holes" <note>referring to the pores or channels of the body</note> are brought into harmony with the familiar soul, or the body is made capable of being animated by such a specific soul. One might perhaps guess that this life could be infused into us by the common soul and the shared celestial souls without the benefit of our own individual soul, judging by those living things that are born spontaneously <note>Aristotelian idea that small creatures like insects could be born from decaying matter without parents</note>, and those which arise from all things without the nurturing of their own parent. On the other hand, reason seems to dictate that our soul—that is, the superior one—must conspire together with the superior powers to breathe life. This is both because the human being is the most perfect creature and obeys reason, and because just as many common natures are defined by their own specific natures to fulfill specific effects in nature, so too it seems a specific work of the soul is needed for its own life—provided that the form is perfect in its powers and distinct—beyond the common souls.

Therefore, one might perhaps say that in some cases a specific influence is added beyond the common influx, while in others it is not at all. In the former, the human animal is more perfect and more obedient to reason; in the latter, it is less so—specifically where the rational soul finds a body already made living from elsewhere. I will pass over the fact that if, by chance, the rational soul does not approach a body living in this way, a "brute animal" will be born in the shape of a human, and it will be a monster of the soul, just as bodily monsters are sometimes born. Therefore, when Plotinus says in one place that the second life flows from our first life, and in another place from elsewhere, it can be understood as we have described.

Remember indeed that what Plotinus discusses regarding the twin souls is confirmed by Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized ritual and theurgy</note> based on the mind of Hermes <note>original: "Mercurij," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage</note>. He says that the higher soul in us, because it is created by the highest Intelligible, has a creative power within the world, such as the power by which it may transcend the world and save itself and its own, especially with the help of the gods; and that this solution, insofar as it seems to transcend the order of nature, is nevertheless contained within the order of Providence. 

Accordingly, where Plotinus distinguishes one soul from the other, he says that whatever the ministries of the inferior soul are, they are corporeal. For all its passions and motions are incited by the body, they serve the body, they accompany the motion of the body, and vice versa. But the duty of the other soul, which comes from "without," is to raise itself higher. Note in this place that Plotinus interprets that famous Aristotelian saying—"the intellect comes from without"—in its legitimate sense. "Intellect," that is, the superior soul; not the single shared intellect of Averroes' interpretation <note>Ficino is refuting the idea of a single collective human mind, arguing instead for individual immortal souls</note>, but each individual intellectual soul. Likewise, "from without" means not from the seminal spirit or heat, nor from the life of the world thus far, but from the divine Mind, which, being as it were "exterior" (meaning not contained like a physical form), rules over all things. 

From this it follows that the intellectual soul, both by thought and also by will, can seek at its own discretion those things which are above the body, nature, and corporeal life, and can overcome the body, nature, and fate whenever it has fully decided to do so. For insofar as it is separated from temporal things, it is joined to eternal things and, together with them, in a certain way rules over temporal things. Both occur through thought, but especially through the will. For just as we are joined to temporal things, so we are joined to eternal things—not so much by considering them as by loving them. And rightly so, since consideration stays rather within the mind, but love turns the lover into the beloved. In the same way, any matter reaches the nature of fire more by undergoing heat than by receiving light. It is from this, therefore, that the soul becomes a master of eternal things and, together with them, a mistress over temporal things: because it both loves them ardently and, by loving, imitates them in life as much as it can; by living in imitation, it attains them, and having attained them, it imitates their authority in its works. 

From this, finally, amazing works upon the body sometimes proceed beyond the usual course of fate. Because in fate, the soul is counted as an agent; it does not so much break fate as claim it for itself. This, too, is designated in the laws of Providence, upon which fate depends. Therefore, if by the benefit of a skillful intelligence—through art, namely the use of images and medicine—the mind is sometimes received into the company of fate as a colleague and actor, how much more can it achieve by the order of a more divine intelligence, or most especially, by the will. For the act of the will is more effective than knowledge, and freer, being the beginning, middle, and end of action. Therefore, by mere thought, nothing happens; but by mere affection—even if hidden and natural—many things are done. There is, moreover, a natural appetite which seems able to emulate the will; it is constant, prior to the imagination, naturally more sublime, and closer to efficacy. We have touched upon the power of art within fate in the sections above, but we will demonstrate it elsewhere. 

But to return to the previous points: the soul lives in Providence above fate in that part where the animal is formed by reason, reason by the mind, and the mind finally by God. In that part where, conversely, the formation takes place, it lives in fate under the judgment of Providence; not as an agent, but as a "patient" <note>one who is acted upon</note> it is counted in the number of the fated. If, therefore, anything is portended for this person by the messenger stars, it can simply happen as it is portended, unless it is resisted by this soul. But if evils occur, they are not sent from on high, but result in the lowest things. Plotinus says that the inferior soul in us is, in a way, a part of the universe, because it both depends on the universal soul and follows its common instinct—almost as the members of our body are, in a way, part of the universal body. Thus our "animal" nature is connected to the "World Animal," and from this it is brought about that the superior soul in us, acting together with the World Soul and the other celestial beings, contributes most to creating the inferior life within us. This life is not made by the mother’s soul: for just as the mother’s seed cannot produce the body of the child to be born, so the mother’s soul cannot procreate the soul. Nor, again, is the soul of the child born from the soul of the father (who might be far away), nor does it proceed from the power of the seed itself, which is both inferior and secondary. It remains, therefore, that it is procreated by the soul of the world with the celestial souls concurring—and with the superior soul of the human about to be born also concurring, if indeed it is already present through its life-giving act. If anywhere Plotinus says that the rational soul does not contribute to the "animal" being of the person, or contributes very little, he is denying the mode of form, not the mode of an efficient cause. For although it is the cause of life for the animal, it is not the specific "form" of the body, even if it is sometimes called the form of the animal when it contributes to the animal’s well-being. What sort of thing, furthermore, exists in us from the twin souls and the body...

--- Page 163 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically discussing the hierarchy of souls within the cosmos and how they influence the human condition and the concept of fate.</meta>

...there is a harmony, he indicates that such a harmony exists in the world itself, in the spheres, and in the stars. For everywhere the intellectual soul rules the body through a life closer to the body that flows forth from the soul. For just as the intellectual part is separate, and its higher part stands distant from the body, so much more does it approach through something else, which—within the soul or from the soul—degenerates just enough from the intellect <note>Ficino explains that the "lower" part of the soul is a stepped-down version of the "higher" intellect, allowing it to interface with physical matter.</note>. I say "from the soul": since if an elemental nature, such as fire, being a nearby subject, does not only move its substance where it goes but also inserts a quality similar to itself, how much more does the soul, as a more powerful nature, infuse a certain vital faculty into the body by the presence of its vital substance.

Let there be, then, in the world, in the spheres, and in the stars, twin souls everywhere. Let the first ones hold the place of good angels and gods everywhere, following the truth; let the ones that follow, which have grown into bodies, seem to play the part of demons <note>original: "dæmonum." In Neoplatonism, "daemons" are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil, though Ficino notes they are more "entangled" with the physical world.</note>. All angels of this first kind—that is, the angelic attendants of the world-soul—always cling to God. Similarly, all demons of the second kind everywhere follow the "demon" of the world-soul, which departs further from God and leans entirely upon the body. Again, the angels draw souls toward the Mind <note>original: "mens" / "Nous"</note>, while the demons draw them toward bodies, or as far as the souls can be lured. Therefore, the angels release souls from fate, but the demons bind them to fate. The nearby command of this corporeal world is placed in the demons. Whence, if a comparison is made from here to the angels, this world may rightly be said to be "placed in the power of the evil one." <note>Ficino is referencing 1 John 5:19 here to bridge Neoplatonism with Christian scripture.</note> From this, the error of the Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement that believed the physical world was inherently evil and created by a dark god.</note> easily arose.

Just as he asserts our intellect always enjoys divine intuitions even while the reason is meanwhile occupied with human affairs, so he affirms that the reason and the entire higher soul in the celestial beings enjoys the perpetual contemplation of divine things. The lower souls of the celestial beings rule the bodies; their imaginings also rule the bodies. He judges, therefore, that "demonic" affects are in these; divine affects are in the first ones; human affects are in our souls, which are often carried toward the truth, but they are "demonic" there only insofar as...? 

He imagines a wise man busily occupied with divine contemplations, but in whom, meanwhile, an affection for the body's nourishment thrives in his vegetative nature: the itch of hunger occasionally creeps into the stomach, and he is tickled by the natural general desire. But the reason of the wise mind, meanwhile dedicated to separate things, in no way notices such acts; even the imagination hardly feels them stupidly. It happens almost as it usually does for one in whom these things are incited during sleep without dreams. Such, therefore, are the "demonic" affects toward these things in heaven. 

Therefore, nothing evil—or hardly anything—proceeds from the prior souls. From the subsequent souls, however, not truly "evils" but certain vices and "lesser goods" follow; insofar as from them, sometimes ordered changes occur in the bodies of the world, and in souls. For souls enslaved to a bodily nature, incitements frequently arise; through these, even if the souls do not necessarily become wicked, they nonetheless indulge the body's licenses, or at least they cherish the body more readily and care for it more accurately every day. 

He says, moreover, that the superior souls of the stars are not parts of this universe. For since they are turned entirely toward the intellectual world, they can be seen as parts of that world instead. But he calls the inferior souls of the stars parts of this universe because they are enslaved to the bodies of the world—which are situated among themselves out of the same matter—and under the same common form of the whole, they are thought to be parts of the universe. In this common matter and form of the world, all such souls conspire together into one body everywhere with the world-soul, and they communicate with each other through a sense, however occult, and they communicate through a certain latent compassion. 

Now, indeed, whatever works are done by these exist as individual parts of the world, or pertain to the parts and the whole. Nothing proceeds from them anywhere that is separate from the natural condition of this world. Whatever of "fate" they perform, they do so by a nature of the soul, just as elements act by elemental nature, or plants by vegetative soul, with absolutely no choice involved. For since choice is something other than life, and is a "later" life, if a soul performs its duties of an inferior life or action through itself, how much more does the life of the superior beings absolute its own affairs through itself? If there is any choice of intellect or reason there, this superior office does not choose "ministry" <note>i.e., menial labor or direct governance of matter</note>. And from before that choice, they follow what they procreate from life out of life and from prior choice. Altogether, everywhere it consists of necessity alone, even if some imagination accompanies them; and from the first soul there proceeds the second, and from the second a similar particular way of life in the body, and from the body light, and in the light a power generating and governing the lower things. 

Many steps, therefore, separate the things that are generated and happen daily in this world from the Intelligible World. It should not seem surprising, then, if these things happen with less happiness in their actions and turnings. For if such things followed directly from the divine intellect, or at least from the intellectual souls, they would be perfect; but now they are acted out through time and through souls living rationally, and through the forces they emit into the body. Therefore, if anything occurs in the world that is troublesome, laborious, or not right, remember that all of it happens from our "flame" <note>original: "flamina" - breath or spirit</note>—that is, from the soul enslaved to the body, from the matter of the body, and again from the conflict of elemental qualities.

### What things are done by stars, what are not, and how signification happens. By what instinct the soul enters the body, by what fate, and how it loves the body before fate.

The tenth chapter of the book proceeds with the world, the spheres, and the stars thus composed, discussing the lot of signifying and acting. It states that from the stars and their movements—insofar as only corporeal life and the body are considered in them—those things which are naturally generated occur. Nor are these things properly done by the first souls of the stars, which tend entirely toward separate things; nor are all things here done by the stars. For those things which surpass corporeal life cannot be produced by the body of the stars or by corporeal forces. Again, those things which are done by us through counsel and art, or by chance and fortune, are not carried out from there, where whatever is done is done through corporeal qualities and the long-lasting tenor of nature. Finally, no truly evil thing is committed through these divine instruments. 

The stars, therefore, do not "make" all things, but only the passions and motions that belong to the mundane body, and those things which are necessarily generated from these. They do these things, however, by a "common condition"; for a "proper condition" seems to belong to the proper causes of things. They also signify many things, yet not all things equally. For it is probable that if most things surpass or escape the efficiency of the stars, some things even surpass their signification. It is probable, again, that those things which are portended through common causes are portended only by a common condition. 

But Plotinus thinks the soul approaches this body not because it is compelled by a certain configuration of the stars. Indeed, he says that before any new figure of the heaven, it is the nature of the soul itself to animate the body; it is also its nature to transcend corporeal and temporal fate. For every instinct of the soul, by its own natural office, can resolve the entire corporeal nature into an incorporeal essence, and all of time into eternity—as if into a beginning and an end. Certainly, it can exist both before and after any body and time, and through any temporal motion whatsoever. Therefore, the position of the stars does not impel the soul...

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of the soul, distinguishing between higher intellectual souls (angels) that free humans from fate and lower souls (demons) that bind them to the material world and necessity. He argues that while stars signify and influence bodily conditions, the soul's essential nature exists prior to and above the influence of astrological fate.</summary>
