<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book III, Ennead II. Having previously discussed how souls are distributed throughout the cosmos, Ficino now moves to explain how the soul’s internal choice interacts with the movements of the stars (astrology) and why the "evils" of the world are not the fault of the heavens.</meta>

# ON THE THIRD BOOK OF ENNEAD II

...toward the body: but first, it brings certain natural cares of the soul toward this end. Next, a certain disposition <term>affectio: a state of being or inclination</term> is acquired from preceding actions; and finally, a choice of reason eventually consents with nature and disposition. Nature and disposition incline most strongly toward the body when they harmonize most opportunely with the universal nature; yet they are not compelled by force to harmonize. It is just as those dancing in a triple-step <note>original: "tripudio," a rhythmic or ritualistic dance</note> harmonize with the song and the sound—they are in accord not by necessity, but by will. Indeed, to receive this or that form of life consists in the soul’s own choice. But however that great passion or disposition occurs by which the soul is inclined to the body, it is not provoked by the stars, but originates from the soul itself. At the time it enters a new body, it is thought to obtain this or that fortune based on the present position of the stars; yet the choice of life already made can approach the coming circumstances in various ways. Therefore, the present harmony of the stars effects something in us by its service, contributing to the fulfillment of that lot in life which most fits the universe. For any daily configuration of the heaven is a part of the total harmony, just as a part obeys the universal nature with which every individual nature—both bodily and animal—is born. For this reason, individual things are carried out by the nature of the world itself together with the specific nature of each thing; by the motion and figure of the heavenly bodies, they are disposed in different ways and are portended through a certain concord with nature. Since, however, individual natures concur with the universal nature to produce any effect, the specific character of the outcome is judged only very obscurely by astrological judgments.

->The evils that happen here are not sent as evils from heaven.<-

### Chapter Eleven

**XI** Chapter eleven defends the dignity of heaven in all things which are said to be done or signified from there. This is because the things which happen here because of the heavens are not like that when they are *there*, nor do they arrive in themselves as they later result here. You might say our fire here is procreated by celestial fire. However, this fire is so different from that one that nothing could be more perverse: nothing, in turn, is more unstable than our fire, which barely lasts a moment without outside fuel. Nothing is more healthy than celestial fire; nothing more pestilential than ours, which devours everything most greedily. I leave aside the fact that celestial fire is almost entirely light, while ours is almost entirely smoke. Surely, as far as the name "fire" is concerned, you can perhaps understand that whatever is given from celestial fire is something fiery in itself, but it results in a degenerate, meager form among us. You can also weave Plotinus's words another way: that the fiery nature within us, degenerating from the celestial, together with our own disposition toward loving—which also falls far short of the celestial principle of benevolence—will often overcome a lesser good through lust; and this is to be observed regarding the nature itself. Soon he introduces an example regarding the changes in nature, then regarding reason placed in action, and finally regarding reason in a contemplative mode, to show that everywhere a thing is received differently in us than how it was granted by heaven. 

Thus, Venus is instilled as the sense that either supplies or increases necessary affection, until it has made men lustful; yet the affection offered through her turns into wanton lust among us. So too with Mars: he might make the wild more fierce, or the tamed more timid (as with the Sun), and Jupiter makes men ambitious and vain. So too Mercury makes them too clever and deceptive; so too Saturn makes them more solitary and sluggish. Yet Mars intended to provide magnanimity <note>original: "magnanimitatem," or greatness of soul</note>, Jupiter and the Sun intended a zeal for honesty, Mercury industry, and Saturn contemplation and gravity—if only we had not contaminated these gifts through a nature or habit that has been corrupted. 

Among these things, remember that the gifts of the soul are not given, increased, or favored by the motions or bodies of the planets, but by their *souls*. Evils, however, are brought upon us neither by the souls nor the bodies of the celestial beings. For it is a wicked thing to say that those stars harm us with an emotion in the same way a serpent does; it is pious, however, to believe that all stars naturally foster all things by the gaze of their rays, in the manner of an Ostrich <note>A common medieval and Renaissance belief was that the ostrich hatched its eggs simply by staring at them with a powerful, nurturing gaze.</note>, just as in a living creature the principal life of the whole and of the members fosters and helps all the limbs. Thus the light of the Sun, by its own nature, contributes to life and to sense, even though it sometimes seems to harm us because of the weakness of the subject or a lack of moisture. Just as the heat of the liver naturally helps the stomach; but when there is either too little moisture or the barest minimum of liquid nourishment in the stomach, it sometimes perhaps weakens it. 

It seems, therefore, that Mars has falsely brought about fury, or Saturn, on the contrary, stupor or fear. Remove the excess of bile from me, take away the abundance of black bile, and neither the aspect of Mars nor of Saturn will make me furious, or stupid and fearful. Again, that slander against Mars and Saturn—that they make men unfortunate—happens because when people are Saturnine (contemplatives), they neglect external things or are slower to action; especially if they receive that influence in colder matter, which results in them attempting nothing at the right time. Martian types, on the contrary, if they receive the instinct of Mars in hotter matter, disturb everything with headlong motion. Perhaps also the Saturnine demons <note>Ficino refers to the spiritual intermediaries associated with the planet Saturn.</note>, being contemplatives, act more negligently regarding our affairs if we are commended to them; but Martian demons urge the minds of their followers too importunately. 

In short, as much as a lower nature differs from a superior nature, so much does the condition of what is received differ. If, therefore, the often-inferior matter—when it is deserted by heat—receives the containing and stabilizing power of Saturn, it takes it on as a condition that is too compact or frozen by frost. So too, the subject receives the moving force of Mars somewhat too hotly, as an impulse through the agitation of inflammation. What more? Who does not understand that even the mild heat of heaven becomes gluttonous among us, and the heavenly moisture becomes suffocating and immediately diluting among us? 

And therefore, I shall say in summary: just as the heaven visible to us relates to the intellectual heaven, so this tangible region of ours relates to the visible heaven. The forms of things in the intellectual heaven are free from matter, dimension, and motion; but in the visible heaven, these three necessarily occur. But there, the matter is far from suffering <term>passio: being acted upon or undergoing change</term>; the dimension is without division; the motion is likewise apart from any transgression of order or transmutation of substance. Finally, in our region, things naturally suffer these three. Therefore, what is a good on all sides in the first heaven through entire participation, becomes a "lesser good" in the second heaven, and in our region, it is now "evil." Let no one, therefore, impute evil to the celestial beings. For just as the fact that you speak or walk is held from the soul and the moving power, but the fact that you speak or walk awkwardly happens from a fault of the tongue or the foot; whatever is sent down to you from the soul and the celestial body proceeds in a right order, but in you, it is often compelled to limp. 

We conclude this whole matter, along with Plotinus and Iamblichus, in this way. The gifts attributed from heaven degenerate for five reasons: 
1. Because that which proceeds from a cause, especially a higher one, fails by the very fact that it exits from it. 
2. Because while it is being received in viler matter, it is taken according to the vileness of the matter. 
3. Since the nature of the recipient is far different, it rightly renders what it receives not only worse, but different by an excessive degree. 
4. While the subject receives various other things from elsewhere besides the celestial gift, those things—being both repugnant to each other and different from heaven—deservedly not only infect the celestial gift but greatly confound it, often rendering it subject to passions. 
5. Because from all causes acting together, something new results that is very unlike its first origin, and altogether inferior; the weakness of a nature subject to passion often cannot sustain a celestial good and, lacking a competent proportion for it, suffers uncomfortably even under that which acts healthily.

<summary>Ficino argues that the stars are not the source of evil, but rather provide a neutral celestial harmony that is corrupted by the "limping" nature of the material world and human choice. He outlines five specific reasons why divine gifts degenerate into "evil" or "vice" once they reach the earthly realm.</summary>

### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

### Things generated here have their own nature more from their own specific causes than from celestial ones.

### XIII
The twelfth chapter shows that various influences coming from the heaven flow together into one here among us, although differently in different places; and from that confluence, whatever is born under it carries away something of that influence. Certainly, whatever is born is aided in its birth by the common favor of the heaven in a general way. However, that a human or a horse is born is not obtained from that common influence—which favors all equally—nor is it allotted from this or that specific celestial influence. For under any given celestial configuration, humans and horses are born alike. A human, therefore, comes forth because he is born from a human, and a horse because it is born from a mare. 

But as to why a human is of a certain type—such as being sanguine or choleric, more or less beautiful, bold or short, and so on—he seems to have this partly from the heaven, but certainly mostly from his parents. Even Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and geographer whose 'Tetrabiblos' was the foundational text for Western astrology.</note> confesses this, compelled by the evidence. Hence, he forbids judging the newborn solely by the observation of the celestial bodies; instead, he commands one to diligently consider the nature of the parents, the nourishment, the location, and the customs. For the present, let us set aside how much variety the imagination of those generating children brings to their offspring. 

Certainly, regarding the specific property of the substance and its natural quality, the nature of both the species and the generating individual is much more powerful than the celestial influence. Manifest experience teaches this in all things, especially from the very likeness by which the one being born reflects the species and the person of the generator at the same time. Therefore, common and celestial causes have the greatest authority over the most general conditions; however, near and specific causes are undoubtedly much more powerful regarding specific traits. This is especially true because what is brought down from higher causes is received according to the nature of the subject and the place, and through the determination of the nearby causes, it is transformed into another form. 

Hence Ptolemy says—and even Aristotle <note>Ficino often seeks to harmonize Aristotle's physics with Neoplatonic metaphysics.</note>—that celestial effects can be changed due to the matter and nature of inferior things, and they do not occur inevitably. A human, therefore, in his countenance and cause, is made from the human <term>seminal reason: a formative, seed-like principle that directs the growth of a physical body according to its species</term>, which is indeed in the soul and its own nature, and is ruled under the ideal reason of "Human" which, flourishing in the common nature and soul, is finally ruled by the Idea itself in the Divine Mind. 

While a human is conceived through the power of the seed, in the meantime, either from the heaven, or from the nearby or surrounding matter, an impediment or an aid can be brought, by which the one to be born receives either a more perfect or a more degraded quality. Nevertheless, the offspring usually comes forth similar to the generator, always in species and frequently in person. While an impediment can happen either from the heaven or from the matter, that which happens from the matter is much greater, for it often produces defective things. But the greatest impediment is that which happens to the imagination, for this is accustomed to bring forth <note>original: "monstra," meaning biological anomalies or "monsters" in the classical sense</note>. If, therefore, the greater impediment comes from the matter and the circumstances of the causes near us, then surely the greatest help also comes from there. Entirely no celestial influence, but the seminal reason possesses the authority of generating; for even where living creatures seem to arise spontaneously under the Sun and moisture, they necessarily arise from the seminal power which the life of the world possesses, which we declare more at length in our *Theology* <note>Referring to his major work, 'Theologia Platonica' (Platonic Theology).</note>.

---

### All things are generated from the common life of the world and its seminal reasons, together with the specific reasons of each thing. Likewise, besides the common action of the world soul, there are specific actions in many things, while the influence of celestial motions seems to come, as it were, from the outside.

### XIII
Since he had already descended to the causes of things, both common and specific, he therefore pursues the principles of the life of things in the thirteenth chapter of the book. Just as in every living thing, so in the world—as if it were the greatest animal—the entire body is formed under the "form of the whole" from the seminal reason which exists in the vegetative power of the soul and the natural and vital spirit. The members are also formed by the specific forms of the members, and each is conformed both by mutual communion among themselves and by a relation to the form and end of the whole. 

Since, therefore, all things are contained formally in the form of the whole, but in the forms of individuals, other things are not formally included (although they seem to be present by a certain participation), whatever is done, or acts, or is acted upon in the world—as if it were a familiar and specific part of it—conduces to its good. However, not everything that happens from one part comes to another part as something equally "domestic" or fitting. For that which comes from one part of the world to another part far distant either in location or nature seems to offend it like a stranger; while that which comes otherwise seems to help. 

But truly, in whatever way all things act upon each other, beyond the fact that they consist in themselves and act by their own faculty, they undoubtedly conspire everywhere toward the common spirit of the life of the whole. Therefore, distinguish the agents in this way: Those things in this living body of the world which, besides a certain small trace of common life, possess no life of their own, are not properly "agents," but are the instruments of agents—namely, of the world itself and its principal mundane parts. And no wrong is done to them. For natural action depends on motion, and the principle of motion is life. For in this way, just as the first internal perpetual motion of essence is the principle of any motion, so it is the origin of natural action. 

Therefore, in those things where specific life is lacking, motion is surely absent and specific action is absent; where they seem to act, they are being acted upon. Thus, heavy and light things that heat you and similar things are drawn to motions and actions by the life of the world itself, no differently than iron is drawn by a magnet, or heat or moisture in an animal is led and drawn by the vital power. But those things which, beyond the common life of the world, have obtained some gift of their own life, these seem to have something of their own motion and action. 

But distinguish these living things: Since the principle of motion is in all living things, it is either indifferent to different motions among themselves, or it is determined to a certain condition of motion by another, or rather by itself. By another: namely, plants, by the universal nature and by a certain daily indulgence, opportunity, occasion, and the concurrence of surrounding causes. By another again: namely, brutes, by the encounter of those things which are sensed, while they drive the imagination here or there, serving, moreover, the necessity of nature. 

The rational animal, however, often defines the internal principle of its motion toward certain motions by its own notion and choice conceived through itself. And the more it proceeds by intelligence, the more it is counted in the order of agents and is separated from those who are merely passive <note>original: "patientibus," those who receive action or are passive</note>. Both types of animals—those having reason and those lacking it—conduce as certain parts of the world to the beauty of the world. Again, distinguish animals: celestial and ethereal animals are said rather to act simply, than to suffer. Brutes, however, have the least action and the most passion. But indeed, daemons <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil.</note> and humans occupy almost a middle ground between action and passion. From these three kinds of animals, the beauty of the mundane animal is produced and completed. And the highest genus holds itself in the world just as intelligence does in us; the middle, just as reason (either universal or particular) does in us; and finally the lowest...

### ON BOOK III OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

*...just as that which is most just exists within us. Everywhere in the universe, the higher souls of the spheres and stars provide more excellent things to the whole than do their lower souls; these are called by Plato "Joves," <note>Ficino refers to the Platonic idea of "Zeus" or "Jove" as the governing cosmic intelligence.</note> that is, colleagues of the mundane intelligence. In truth, everything everywhere in the world lives in some way—either by its own life or by a shared life—no less than anything that exists within any animal. I say they live, and all things are living according to life, I mean, in part: principally by the benefit of the World Soul, in whose <term>seminal reason</term> <note>original: seminaria ratione; the formative, biological blueprint or 'seed-logic' that guides the growth of a living thing.</note> all the reasons of living things are contained. And everywhere the seminal reason, flourishing in the soul—both in the common soul and in any specific one—is the primary principle of motion, generation, and formation.*

*For as to why certain "specific powers" <note>original: storiales virtutes; these are unique properties of plants or minerals that seem to bypass the usual laws of the four elements.</note> exist in things which cannot be referred back to elemental causes, this happens simply from the confluence of many factors; otherwise, they would happen either by chance or would not be firm. It arises, therefore, from the animal and seminal reason. Thus, Peony hung around the neck helps those who fall <note>a historical remedy for epilepsy, the "falling sickness."</note>; Polypody <note>a type of fern.</note> purges black bile; Coral drives away fear; Laurel repels lightning; the Torpedo fish numbs a person who touches it even from the outside with a rod; the small suckerfish <note>original: echinus pisciculus; here referring to the legendary Echeneis or Remora, believed to be able to stop ships in their tracks.</note> stops a ship. Now indeed, specific powers of this kind exist from the same source as the species themselves. Various species of natural things are referred not only to different <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and stars, but also to their own seminal reasons reigning everywhere in the life of the world itself.*

*For concerning any species, many agents concur here and there for its effect, which would never lead properly to a single end by a common and firm order unless they were governed by one leader present everywhere. Surely, just as many species of things lead to certain genera, and these finally to one genus everywhere, so many agents are necessarily reduced step by step to one agent everywhere. I mean agents either as instruments—like the lower bodies to the higher ones, and those perhaps to the sun by the benefit of light present everywhere—or as principal agents, such as the rational souls of a lower order to the rational souls of a higher order, and those finally to the one ruling equally everywhere.*

*Indeed, he <note>Plotinus</note> wishes there to be such power in the nature of an animal and its seminal reasons that he thinks no part or motion of the world, however great, can be thoroughly disturbed from its order, preventing certain species and properties of things from arising from specific reasons, just as the order of the whole animal nature prescribes and any nature following that order duly pursues. What then of the stars? What will their daily motion effect? Certainly, it will neither create a species, nor change one, nor twist their outcomes away from the species; but perhaps it will affect them with certain qualities for better or worse, whether according to the body or according to the soul when it is utterly immersed in the body, or according to certain actions for which the higher soul requires instruments. All of that celestial influence is said to act "by accident," <note>a philosophical term meaning "coincidentally" or as a secondary effect, rather than as the primary essence.</note> because it acts both from the opportunity it finds from the concurrence of lower things, and because it does not act upon deformed things by its own tenor, nor does it move the soul, unless perhaps when the body is moved by the heaven, the soul is moved by accident or consents to the motion.*

*If anyone should doubt whether seminal reasons or species are changed because of occasional monstrous births, let him observe that the principal part and the root of the species are always preserved, even if something has been added or taken away. I say "added or taken away" not so much by celestial influence as by a fault of the matter, the location, or the imagination, or by some fortuitous confluence of different things. The principal thing is always preserved, or certainly as much as possible, because the principal and containing agent there is the seminal reason; if this were removed, things would happen by chance rather than by nature. We have proved in our *Theology* that this is necessary even in those things which seem to be born spontaneously. For since these are formed so skillfully, and endowed with life and living as are those born by propagation, surely these, like the others, are formed by a living, hidden seminal reason. This reason, reigning everywhere in the life of the world, forms matter that is prepared here and there opportunely, both most skillfully and most swiftly; as that which has the most excellent and divine power, through which it produces the most beautiful moments from the most base things, while it directs diverse agents toward one end and distinguishes general influences into special and proper effects according to the disposition of the matter.*

->In the individual things that happen to humans, we find sufficient causes among us<-
->besides celestial motions.<-

*XIII. Thus far he has discussed how celestial influences do not have much authority in things pertaining to the body and the soul; next, he declares they have even less power over those things called "external." In all things, he brings forward the highest causes existing and manifest under the heaven: whether they are the determined causes of things, or certain occasions happening from the concurrence of many factors, or human arts and choices. Among these, note that the nature of the parents and the quality of the place and nourishment have much more power over the health of the body than the common, remote, and momentary motions of the heavens; therefore, those things which are sufficiently acted upon by proximate causes are sometimes signified by the stars rather than effected by them. He says, moreover, that there is a mutual consequence in things, through which they can provide mutual signs—provide them, I say, as far as the connection of the universe itself is concerned—and certainly to signify at least to him who, looking around at all things, sees how much consequence he may behold.*

*Then, in the generation of a human, he says the seminal reason and power is the principal cause, indeed the whole cause from close at hand. The fact that certain species arise from certain seeds and in their own proper ways, and that there is neither mutual confusion nor transgression, consists entirely in the seminal natures. He declares that they have all authority in generation: where, if nothing hinders it, the fetus is duly formed according to the norm of the seminal reason. It is said to be "hindered" when it does not allow the absolute image of the seminal power to be expressed. He indicates that such a hindrance proceeds not so much from the motions of the planets properly (as they are remote and momentary) as from a fault of the mother or from a quality of the air that is dissonant to the conception.*

->On fate, and the fates: and how the soul, before it is touched by fate, is touched by love of the body.<-
->On the daemon as the guide of life. On liberation from fate. On the principles of<-
->beings. How our soul also holds<-
->the status of a principle.<-

*VI. After he explained what part of the fates—that is, only the daily revolution of the heaven—is capable of, he now explains what the whole of fate is capable of. "Universal Fate" is the entire series of all moving causes, whether they be animal causes, corporeal, superior, or inferior. Since, therefore, the subsequent connection of moving causes is fate, clearly the rational soul is entangled in the snares of fate to the extent that it departs from intellectual stability and is spread out more widely in motion. On the contrary, while the whole soul lives by a perfectly stable intelligence, it is entangled in no nets of fate. Think, therefore...*

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, moving from the biological "seminal reasons" of the previous page to the metaphysical descent of the soul. Ficino explores how the soul transitions from a purely intellectual existence into the realm of "Fate" (fatum) and the role of the personal guardian or "daemon."</meta>

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

### ON THE SOUL’S DESCENT AND FATE

The rational faculty within the soul, after it has lived for a long time in the realm of the Mind, finally begins to lean toward the vegetative nature beneath it through a certain new motion. The imagination, in a sense, communicates with nature when it perceives "imaginations" or patterns within nature itself. This type of affection then instills itself into the noble and final corporeal part of the soul. At that point, the soul, leaning more propensically toward changeable things by a new motion of its own, chooses a "mobile life" <note>A life subject to change, time, and physical movement.</note> and consequently falls into fate—in a way, even before it enters an earthly body. 

Indeed, before that body is even conceived in the womb, the soul perhaps undergoes a sympathetic lot, and most especially a "fatal lot," which the soul itself had partly chosen shortly before, and which was partly favored by the shifting occurrence of the whole and of every rational fortune. It first receives the "guide of its remaining life" <note>The personal spirit or *daemon*.</note> at the moment it first affects and chooses such a life. Similarly, when it subsequently affects and chooses an earthly body, it is thought to receive its form of life—partly by choice, and partly by the governance of the heavens at the time of choosing and entering—and to be guided in this manner.

Regarding the name of the **daemon** <term>daemon</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, a *daemon* is not an evil spirit, but a tutelary "genius" or guardian spirit that acts as an intermediary between the divine and the human.</note>, the Egyptians maintain that the daemon proceeds from God himself toward the chosen way of life, and toward the harmony of the universe containing the time of election—not from some other source, and not from a planet. Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus.</note> thinks differently, placing more weight on the actual configuration of the birth chart. Therefore, in terms of the "concord of the world," the daemon is properly said to accommodate the soul to its fate (if I may put it that way). Yet, because it is given by God according to the soul's own choice, it is also said to belong to fate because it can, in turn, free the soul from fate. I mean that the soul, turned toward the daemon, is eventually turned through the daemon toward God. For this reason, that Pythagorean song prays to Jove <note>original: "oret Iovem"; a reference to the Golden Verses of Pythagoras praying to Jupiter/Zeus for deliverance.</note> that he might either release us from these evils or at least show us which daemon we should use. 

Finally, he responds that the solution must be hoped for through a certain **divination** <note>A natural intuitive spark or prophetic ability.</note> implanted in us, leading us upward toward divine remedies. Primarily, however, it must be committed to memory: 
1. First, that the life and the lot of living do not begin from fate, but from the choice and election of the soul; and through the daemon it receives, it is in a sense set free. 
2. Second, that the lot and form of living are received or completed—as I said—by the entire worldly disposition which suits each person, both when the soul affects and chooses the body, and when it enters the body. 
3. Third, that the disposition of life is not made solely as choice determines, but as the preparation of the lower matter allows, as well as the nature of the parents, the imagination, and other things that concur with the celestial revolutions. 
4. Fourth, it follows from all these that we receive different outcomes based on the manifold disposition of each person being born. 

Because various factors before birth or even before conception pull one into the beginnings of fate, and because fate is fulfilled by the addition of the daemon through the concurrence of these turns, no one can easily look over or surpass it, or change everything, or perfectly understand what is enfolded and follows within that "complexion." <note>The "complexion" refers to the specific physical and spiritual temperament of an individual.</note> 

Sixth, the judgment is confirmed by the signs of the prophets: because of the different origins of our lot, the opposing causes, and contrary things, many judgments differ and are pulled apart. Indeed, from some "footprints," other stories are told, so that one judging the lot of a person is more a matter of careful observation than of certain science. 

After these things, **Lachesis** <note>One of the three Fates (Moirai).</note> flies toward us, signifying the lots and forms of living. By the name **Clotho**, the "convolving and evolving" of these things through the universe is shown. Finally, **Atropos** signifies the necessary effect of this explanation—necessary, I say, insofar as it consists in the nature of fate. And however much of the soul has fallen into fate, I say it is "necessary" because Plato properly places his kingdom in the heavens; therefore, among the celestial things themselves, the outcome is always necessary. 

If the aforementioned "concord of the lower things" also flowed together in deep harmony, it would necessarily follow the decree of fate. But perhaps it does not harmonize. For perhaps this lower air flows together in such a way that, even if it is bound to the celestial things, the fates may still be diverted. Furthermore, even if celestial and lower bodies were to flow toward the same outcome, and that outcome seemed entirely inevitable in this "conspiracy" of all bodies—and though fortune were already firmed by fate—nevertheless, the Soul still has its right. In the Soul, motion is rather free, just as the universe proceeds rightly as the ancients defined it. 

For just as in heaven is the kingdom of Fate, but beneath heaven is the power of Fortune (and both collect together), so in the "balance of reason" <note>original: "rationis aqui"</note>—which runs through opposites—God has placed the judgment of counsel and choice. Hence Plato in the *Statesman* <note>original: "in Politico"</note> judged the soul to be either under the jurisdiction of fate or free. Plotinus, from the borders of both, suggests that the "worse" part can be changed. 

Regarding the three Fates <note>The Parcae: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos.</note>, we have said enough in the commentary on the tenth book of the *Republic*. Now we must consider what Plotinus brings up next: that some men become such—whether by nature, by habit, or both—that they are dragged away by various allurements, while others are such that they eventually turn back from them. They become such by nature, both in the soul (through prior choice and life) and in the body (through natural causes). They also become such through habit. Plotinus says that most are **fascinated by worldly things in a magical manner** <note>original: "mundanis more quodam magico fascinari"; Ficino's famous concept that the material world acts as a "glamour" or spell on the soul.</note>. He declares that the soul is ensnared in no other way than by love—either natural or habitual—and by the bait of pleasure. 

He declares that the nature of the universe has instilled not only a beautiful appearance but also a certain "infernal" quality into dull bodies and souls. Enjoying this form like an idol, the soul is enticed as if by bait, and by these lower attractions, it is led along. He signifies, meanwhile, that souls can eventually "fortify themselves against fate" through the divine allurements of world-contempt, rising to an intellectual nature superior to the whole body and corporeal life. From this, the soul dissolves itself insofar as it loves the higher world; by loving that primary and chief nature, the soul returns into its own Mind—I mean, into the reason formed by the Mind. 

Certainly, all natural things have their own nature and action within them, regardless of the conditions daily received from outside. Much more does the soul possess this gift, for it holds the "principle of initiation." I mean the principle of natural and mobile things; for nature and motion depend upon the soul. I speak of the **Intellectual Soul**, for the efficient principle under the Good is the Intellect, under which the Intellectual Soul is the efficient and, as it were, the forming principle. The Soul of the Universe is the principle of formation for all natural things. All rational souls, insofar as they possess the nature of a principle, just as they form this body, so in a sense they can—at the very least—affect other things. Just as it forms and leads that body as a principle, so it can do not only other things but even greater things, provided it is similarly...

### PAGE 133
<sig>m</sig>
<meta>catchword: in</meta>

In reason, being is something actual, so to speak, and formal; but the soul is the principle of being insofar as it is mobile. And if it is the principle of forms, is it primarily the origin of those that emerge immediately? As for other forms, if the soul is their principle, it possesses them not so much as a living animal, but insofar as it is similar to the Intellect. However, the One and the Good itself, which is superior to the intellect, is the principle of all beings and of "becoming" <note>original: *fieri*; the process of coming into existence in the physical world</note>, in whatever way a thing is understood, whether in potentiality, in act, in "first act" or "second act," and whether the world is mobile or immobile. Most especially, it is the principle of being and becoming insofar as being is one and good. It is also the supreme principle of being, just as it and being are one, fertile, and this itself is the Good.

But of these things we speak elsewhere. Let us return to the soul. We are accustomed to argue that the rational soul is an essence—namely, a form and species firmly consistent within itself, having its own being and existence entirely within itself—based on the fact that it has certain specific desires and actions, sometimes separated from the body and often opposed to the body. Plotinus, in turn, takes it as a settled fact here that the soul exists as such an essence; through this, he argues that it possesses certain unique functions. But from where does he take this as settled? Perhaps from the fact that it is the principle of mobile being, which moves in an orderly and perpetual way. Therefore, it is a fixed essence, as if stable, yet mobile from itself, living its own life just as it is mobile by its own internal motion. For this motion and act is internal. Therefore, if the soul seems sometimes to be moved or formed by external things, this happens because the soul itself has voluntarily yielded and continues to yield to bodies; but meanwhile, it maintains its own form and its being far off in its essence. Indeed, it moves toward the body by natural instinct, not as something mobile and passive, but as a mover and an agent. How our soul is also a principle of motion, and in its capacity as a principle is a colleague of the **World Soul** <term>anima mundana</term>, we prove in our *Theology*. Now, however, let us grant that the soul, in its duty of movement, lives almost equally with the celestial beings; it is fitting to know that it agrees with them in a higher duty—that of contemplation—by which it also transcends nature, rising back toward eternal things. Finally, Plotinus concludes that our "animal nature" <note>The "animal" here refers to the composite of the lower soul and the physical body.</note> depends on the World Animal, namely from the beginning, as he has explained there, and daily in many ways. But just as it daily depends on our soul, so from the beginning it also depended on ours; and conversely, just as it was in the beginning, so it is now. Such, then, is the primary "animal" in us, just as the World Animal is: namely, having a soul that naturally cares for the use of the body, acting together with the body, and in us at least, being in some way passive. Likewise, every day certain marvelous influences of the World Soul result in our animal nature according to the different disposition of the world, both for those who sleep and those who wake. And this animal often consents and suffers along with the World Animal, except insofar as the higher soul in us is also the master of this one, and from here—being separable and a sibling to the World Soul—moves and stops this animal differently. For this soul is separated from the beginning by its essence and being, and can be even more separated by study through the opposing actions of its affections and acts; it has its own actions, as if it can tame the animal entrusted to it and turn it toward itself. As Plotinus says elsewhere, it can even sometimes rescue it from these evils by a marvelous virtue, just as the soul rescues itself, while it sometimes regards the things pertaining to the animal as alien and of no value.

->Concerning the two souls within us. Also, how all things are generated from the common seminary of the world; and how those things that are produced are contained within it, and how they degenerate upon exiting, and fail over the ages from their origins.<-

---

After he demonstrated in the preceding sections which things are not truly the causes of events, and designated in some way those that are true, he now defines the true causes in the three following chapters of this book. You, however, should especially note where he says that the soul is inseparable when it is in the body; perhaps Plotinus means that the life dedicated to the body—which he often calls the "second soul"—is inseparable from the body, that is, it acts inseparably from this individual body while it is within it. However, it can finally be led away from here along with the higher soul. For it depends on the higher soul like its act or "breath" <note>original: *afflatus*</note>, which is then joined to the body through the flow of the World Soul, just as a visual ray penetrates the air through the act of a solar ray. And just as neither ray vanishes according to Plotinus, but both are folded back into their own source, so also here both vitalities—the common one from the World Soul and the proper one from our own—return to their own source. Nor perhaps does this duality of life prohibit the union of the sight and the unity of the animal, since one is common and the other is proper; and that which is proper naturally conspires with the common toward the same end, sometimes determining the common toward specific ends, and sometimes aided by it for its own work in harmony with the common work of the whole. But of this, more carefully elsewhere. He maintains that the primary causes of natural things are their **seminal reasons** <term>rationes seminales</term> in the Vegetative part of the World Nature, to which the seminal reasons in individual species always correspond with the most certain order. But he investigates through many questions how all things sprout from the universal "seminary" <note>The "seminarium mundi" or world-nursery, the source of all biological and physical blueprints.</note> of the world. 

First, he asks: does the World Soul make individual things, as if in a certain straight succession? Namely, in the order of stages and temporal occasions: first the elements according to their origin, then those things composed of them, then man first according to dignity, then the beasts. I ask, does it do these things and provide for them only as far as the species of things, their propagation and safety, while not attending to the things that happen daily to individuals? 

Second question: Does the soul also cause the singular things that happen daily to individuals because the things generated by it subsequently act, and other things follow? As if the World Soul is said to act upon any contingencies, if not through itself, then through intermediate causes everywhere. 

Third question: Does the soul have prescribed within itself, in its seminal reasons, the individual actions and passions of every single thing, so that nothing happens by chance, but all are led by fatal necessity? 

Fourth question: If the soul thus contains individual things within itself, do the seminal reasons of the soul effect these things, or do they (or the soul through them) only know them? To the extent that they daily behold not only individual things generated by them, but also their actions, passions, and all outcomes; while they comprehend all present things, the soul concludes by argument whatever follows from them. Whether it contemplates many things in the past as if present, or whether it never embraces the future summarily, but always addresses individual things in their own hours. 

Fifth question: Is it entirely wrong to imagine the World Soul as being so solicitous <note>Meaning "worried" or "anxious" about details.</note>, or should we think rather that all these things were foreknown once in its notions, or even destined by the seminal reasons? 

Sixth question: Can the life and the defects of natures be destined and come about from the seminal reasons of nature? For perhaps that from which an evil distraction arises contributes to the good of the universe. 

Finally, he solves the questions, denying that anything is contained in the seminal reasons of natural things that is against the order of nature; just as in the reasons of an art, insofar as they are such, nothing is contained outside that art. Whatever is formal in things...

He introduces six metaphysical questions regarding how "seminal reasons" govern individual events and whether the World Soul is actively "solicitous" or simply follows a divinely ordered blueprint.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically addressing how the "reasons" (blueprints) within the soul relate to the physical world's imperfections and the cyclical nature of time. It transitions from the metaphysical structure of the soul to the practical manifestation of beauty, decay, and the astrological "Great Year."</meta>

<page-num>114</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO.</header>

That which is beautiful is contained within the reasons <note>original: *rationibus*; these are the "seminal reasons" or formative principles that act as blueprints for nature</note> by themselves and proceeds properly from them. Whatever deformity happens, however, seems to arise primarily from chance and matter, or consequently from those things which have been infected by them. But what does he mean when he says that the defects of things are contained in the reasons not according to act, but according to potentiality? Certainly not according to act, because we would then be the ones causing those defects; for there is no proper "form" of a defect existing there. Rather, it is said to be there only according to potentiality because from the perfect form—as if from a master model—one can certainly determine in what way or to what degree something might fall short. Thus, while evil or "lesser good" things can indeed be foreknown <note>original: *præscita*</note> there, they cannot be predestined <note>original: *prædestinata*</note>. 

For whatever is determined there is defined by form. But what is produced from there does not turn out in matter exactly as it is possessed by the soul; instead, because it is produced "outside," it degenerates. Because it is produced in formless matter, it becomes deformed, and is further confused by the mixing of different things. Therefore, the soul acts through these reasons only as long as things match the reasons in beauty. Beyond that—that is, where deformity can take hold—the soul generates not by specific intelligence or reason, nor by some imagination continued from nature, but in those things not so much by running through each detail as by a general summary. Or rather, forms in matter fall short of the forms of nature by a certain "habit"—that is, partly because they seem to depart from the reasons, partly because they are influenced by the forms of the matter, partly because they are mixed with opposites, and partly because natural things gradually degenerate from their original dignity. 

Plotinus says in the previous sections that natural things gradually degenerate through the ages, as does Plato in the *Statesman*, *Protagoras*, *Critias*, and *Athenoxenus* <note>original: *Politico Protagora, Critia, Athenoxeno*</note>, which we have assigned there and assign here briefly. There is a certain long-lasting degeneration of things, stretching from the beginning of the world's circuit to its end; another is less long-lasting, persisting from one destruction of lands to another. Consider, therefore, the twelve signs <note>the Zodiac signs</note> which are seen in the firmament to lie beneath the twelve signs marked in the ninth sphere—a sphere which Plato, though he did not state it clearly, thought could exist, since he does not deny the possibility. Thus, certain signs corresponded to signs everywhere: Aries to Aries, Taurus to Taurus, Gemini to Gemini, Cancer to Cancer, Leo to Leo, Virgo to Virgo, Libra to Libra, Scorpio to Scorpio, Sagittarius to Sagittarius, Capricorn to Capricorn, Aquarius to Aquarius, and finally Pisces to Pisces. 

At that time, there was a happy omen for the "Age of Ages" <note>original: *seculi seculorum*; the Great Year</note>, a happiness that lasted as long as these signs remained in agreement. But later, through movement toward the east, Aries moved past Aries, and the following signs moved past those following them; meanwhile, the things of nature began to degenerate by a similar degree. Nevertheless, in certain ages they can flourish and seem to be able to recover for a time, specifically when these signs—even if not exactly at the same points—at least come to similar ones: Aries to Leo, or at least to Gemini; or Leo to Sagittarius, or to Libra; Gemini to Libra, or Libra to Aquarius, and others similarly. Or at least when those aspects <note>astrological relationships like trines or sextiles</note> arise which astronomers teach are more harmonious. Meanwhile, certain great conjunctions of planets contribute to this, since from nearby alignments they sometimes happen to flourish. 

Similarly, the movement of images through their approach to the south and their retreat leads to changes in things; they restore many faculties, but things will not recover their original happiness until the same signs return to the same positions. Indeed, the movement of the signs manifest to us verges toward the east at a rate of one degree every hundred years, passing the higher signs. Thus, the "Age of Ages" is completed in thirty-six thousand years <note>Ficino is calculating the Great Year based on the precession of the equinoxes</note>. Meanwhile, there is another change of the age, when the earth is either washed away by a flood of waters or stripped bare by a fire of flames. Just as after the waters the sun’s power settles upon the moisture (and after fire, in turn, rain overflows), the earth soon becomes more fertile from the moisture on both sides and brings forth most beautiful things, until, drying out due to the stars, it provides less and finally requires a "senile flood" or a fire as a remedy. By observing the mutations of the heavens, we see things pertaining to the generation of forms—which properly occurs through the seminal reasons—rather than to matter or its different disposal. 

The third cause of degeneration pertains especially to human affairs: that in the mental world itself, whether the soul is made through creation or through its prior exit, there was a new way of seeing the higher powers of man, who are governed by the diligent providence of "shepherds" <note>a reference to the divine rulers mentioned in Plato’s *Statesman*</note>. For being born weak everywhere and unskilled in arts, humans entirely need the governance of the higher powers. Providence, however, never deserts its own in necessary matters. For it is most false to say that nature fails in this use. Therefore, nature labors more in the body of an animal for the necessity of some member of matter. Thus, all human affairs of the worthy proceeded rightly and divinely, too much from the divine; but eventually, as human ingenuity seemed sufficiently cultivated by time and less in need of the constant care of demons <note>original: *dæmonum*; intermediary spirits, not evil entities</note>, they began to be governed more negligently by the demons and the angels were set aside. From this, human affairs slide daily into the worse, until human sickness, becoming incredible in itself, provokes the necessary care of the divine back to itself. In what way the world is continued from the variety of degenerating steps, or made more beautiful by some deformity of parts, we have said enough elsewhere and will say again.

XVII. The seminal reasons, just as they are in any soul, are not certain "notions"; otherwise, they would generate continuously by knowing, and they would know the things to be generated. So it is not even in the Soul of the Universe, whose life is more effective than any other life, and therefore can generate by a simple power of life without the help of a notion. First, such reasons of intelligence do not exist: for Intelligence separates both itself and, if necessary, the thing to be understood from matter. But that which is effective, such as the natural seed, since it is to produce offspring only in matter, approaches matter first and enters it deeply. 

Second, they are not "reasonings" <note>discursive thoughts</note>: for these are, as it were, accidental and imaginary, and therefore cannot make things that are substantial and vital. They usually act in the manner of art from the outside and with the help of external instruments, creating something imaginary. Seminal reasons, however, act from within, and through themselves and through joined instruments in the manner of any nature, they create substances. Furthermore, they are not "imaginations": for these, as appears in us, effect nothing in the body without the effectiveness of an emotion <note>original: *affectus*</note>. For emotion is not sufficient for the imagination to generate forms, but perhaps for local motion. For from the imagination wrapped in emotion, a local motion occurs instantly in the spirit and the heart. From this motion, in turn, qualities which have long been in the body...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, Ennead III, Book 2, concerning Divine Providence. Having previously discussed how deformity arises from matter, Ficino now explains the mechanism of creation: how the World-Soul uses "seminal reasons" and imagination to shape the physical world without the need for conscious deliberation.</meta>

<page-num>155</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK III OF THE SECOND ENNEAD.</header>

Now they are stirred up, from which they create either an additional quality or a passion. Similarly, in the **World-Soul**, imagination does not generate forms by itself—since it seems to be something imaginary even more so than reasoning—but when joined with an effect, it leads to the local motion of the world. Before this motion, the forms of things already exist in the world, having long been generated by the world’s generative power through **seminal reasons** <note>original: *seminales rationes*; these are the biological and metaphysical "blueprints" or "seeds" that determine how a living thing grows and takes shape</note>. Therefore, from the nature of this kind of reasoning inherent within it, the primary forms of things are procreated in the world. From there, individual things are generated from the underlying imaginations through specific motions, as it were. These individual motions occur as the forms of things are stirred toward a change of movement; by this change, matter—erroneously thought to be passive—is rightly prepared to receive new forms daily according to these reasons. 

Imagination and nature are thus companions in the soul; they are companions because change and generation are constant throughout the universe. Yet, nature—the parent of individual things—does not employ imagination in a way that distracts it among particulars. Nor does it use immediate reason (which flees to universals), nor the intellect (which always persists in universals). Rather, if the intellect is the reason that perfects individual things, it does so as a consequence. Primarily, however, it remains focused on universals. Therefore, generation, alteration, and motion—which belong only to individuals—seem to exist just after "nature" and close to imagination, which deals solely and chiefly with individual things. 

Since all generation occurs entirely around matter, if a formative power is to be found, it is forced to descend to matter, recognizing it in some way. For every power of knowing possesses a form and an action that makes it separate from matter. Just as the light in a dream is its own light, appearing in the midst of splendor, so there is heat, and as heat generates, so the soul acts as a splendor. In the soul, which exists somewhat below the highest intellectual level, it moves in the middle; finally, at its lowest level, it is merely vital and life-giving. It does not generate and give life as something intellectual or discursive, but simply as something vital. Even if the things it does are intentional and known, it does not do them *because* it knows, but because it is of such a nature and is naturally affected; thus, it acts in such a way. 

I say it acts "not because it knows," meaning it does not think of things as separate from its essence. For in its highest part, to understand is the same as to be. Therefore, this vital essence and intelligence exist naturally as forms—that is, seminal reasons—through essential and ideal notions, just as nature shapes forms in matter through them. Just as a circle in water arises from the touch of a pebble, and another circle arises after it, and so on: so from the sphere of the ideal Divine Mind hangs the soul of the world, and from there it emanates into nature, and from nature into matter. 

Thus, a formula is made from the highest intelligence of the soul into the generative nature of the soul. These formulas are essential and efficient, and they must create substance. Forms exist so essentially in the Divine Mind and in the soul's mind that there, to understand is the same as to be; and to understand is to form nature by the very act of understanding. In nature, to be is the same as to live, and in a way, to give life to matter is the same as to live. 

But it is asked: *Does the animal intelligence shape nature through some rational or imaginary discourse, like a material craftsman does?* Not at all. For even the most perfect art does not consult further but acts in the manner of nature, insofar as it has imitated skill. Furthermore, if it were determined to shape nature by a discourse of thought, it would be referring the forms it must make to others—like a fixed model or a spectacle upon which it focuses its wandering reason, comparing its work to a stable measure. 

It is therefore asked: *Are there certain external spectacles proposed as fixed models, and does it have the forms of the lowest things within?* Certainly not external and corporeal ones (for these do not yet exist, being still to be generated by nature and formed by the intellect). Therefore, it possesses the forms within. What is possessed intrinsically and naturally is not to be sought through wandering. If, therefore, nature forms and contains matter without the service of any counsel, how much more does the Mind form the nature joined to it without counsel, and vice versa? 

He concludes that he has perceived more keenly through these steps that there is something everywhere beyond essence—something accidental and corrupted in these things—which, as it appeared in parts, suddenly vanished. Thus, these things cannot be firm and substantial through themselves, but for such an effect, there is need for the firm and essential efficacy of another nature. Thus, not with anxiety or labor, but with untiring ease, both natural things sprout from nature herself, and the "seeds" of nature sprout from the intelligence. 

Conclude from above: in the heavens, native light and a most stable heat remain, while their configuration changes daily in their circuit. Thus, in the way of the world, intelligence and nature remain stable in their reasons; they act through them, even if a universal or particular discourse is carried out. 

Since the fertile World-Soul—that is, a certain life distributed through the world-animal from the intellectual soul to the body—is the final vestige of the divine, it seems to happen that the soul possesses certain vestiges of the **Ideas** <note>The "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal forms in the mind of God/The One, of which physical things are only shadows</note>. Undoubtedly, the world composed of this life and body degenerates far from divinity. Often its "seeds" seem hindered in their work, and such an animal, compared to higher things, seems to be turned toward them. 

For in what way, while its intellect gives sparks by a certain perpetual presence to its soul, does this animal receive the manifestation? Yet, because this animal is something later and secondary to the intellectual soul, one may consider the soul itself as distinct from the wilder animal. This is what **Plato** meant when discussing the "acting" of thought in the <term>Politicus</term> <note>The dialogue *The Statesman*</note>, the <term>Timaeus</term>, and the <term>Laws</term>: what this vast and robust animal would become if the reins of intelligence were removed. Truly, although we can call this power of fire a luminous citadel, we can also call it naturally cold and dark. Again, iron gradually loses its coldness, and air clearly declares its darkness. 

By a certain condition of Fate, **Plotinus** seems to depict this animal as rather ferocious. From such an origin, if you please, imagine a man with a body entirely choleric or melancholic, or one using a rustic bodily habit. If you place this animal under a wise mind, it might seem to cultivate quietness for a while, but meanwhile, it is most ready for anger and grief. If it were of a sanguine nature, it would be prone to lust—an affection which, even if he barely shows it while awake, he indicates more easily in his sleep. This animal is almost to be pitied: from fire (like bile) it is prone to wrath and pride; from earth, it is moved to sorrow; from air (like blood), to joy and lust; from water (like phlegm), it is more inclined to torpor; and from primary matter, which is a kind of flux underlying these natural things, it meets with bitterness and pain. 

For from the dregs of dryness and cold, it is saturated with bitterness and acidity. This animal will therefore seem most ferocious due to vices and sins, and due to the poverty of matter, it will be too small-minded, envious, and complaining about its own usefulness and changeability. Finally, you will cease to wonder at an animal so affected, in which not everything is according to the ideal, and many things happen even beyond reason.

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

### On the Causes of the Universe and the Nature of Evil

Next, he encompasses the causes of the universe. The cause of evils, however, is considered in two ways: one by the logic of consequence, and the other by the logic of the end <note>The "logic of the end" refers to *teleology*, the idea that everything has a purpose or final goal.</note>. For just as many things follow from the "good" that are "less good," and again, far down the line, the "least good," so too certain things happen in relation to evil. Furthermore, just as in a musical harmony the fourth, or even the second and seventh intervals—which do not harmonize when heard in isolation—create a more pleasing consonance when combined with the others, so in the order of things, lesser goods, and even vices, being the smallest things among the rest, and evils among the least goods, render the common good of the whole more admirable. What then? You will find that those things which seem evil in this part or toward this end are actually good in another part or toward another end; finally, all things lead to the common good of the universe.

After this, he proposes three "craftsmen" <term>artifices</term> <note>original: *artifices*; refers to the creative principles or "architects" of reality</note> of the worlds. The first is indeed the **Divine Intellect**; the second is the **Animal Intellect** and the **Intellectual Soul**; the third is the **image of this Soul**, which is the life dedicated to the body. In this matter, as Proclus testifies, Porphyry agrees with Plato. But why does he not call the "Good itself" a craftsman? Because within a craftsman there are the "exemplars" <note>Models or blueprints of all things</note> of the works, but since the simplest unity exists in the Good itself, he does not dare to place the exemplar of the world—which is multiple—there. Instead, Plato and Plotinus call the Good itself both the **Father** of the worldly craftsman and the **Sun** of the worldly work. It is as if the **Son** <note>Ficino is here identifying the Platonic "Intellect" with the Christian "Son/Word," a common move in Renaissance Neoplatonism</note>, shining while "pregnant" with the love of the Father, procreates the world for the sake of the Good and conforms it to the Good.

Thus, the Good itself generates the Intellectual world; this world procreates the Animal world; this in turn procreates the Natural world; and the Natural procreates the Corporeal world. For others, it flows from one to the next almost like a circle in water depends on a previous circle, or as light comes from a source, splendor from light, heat from splendor, and generation comes from heat. The Intellect, in the process of procreating the Intellectual Soul, in no way departs from the Father; rather, through its union with the Father, it possesses creative power and action. Similarly, the Intellectual Soul, insofar as it rests upon its own Intellect, abounds from it and overflows into the other—that is, the corporeal life. This life, in turn, insofar as it depends on the Soul of which it is the image, is filled with "seeds" <term>seminal reasons</term> and fills the matter of this world with forms. 

The Good itself exceeds "status" <note>original: *status*; a state of standing still or fixed being</note>. For status occurs in the Good and for the sake of the Good, but the Intellect itself exists as status. The Intellectual Soul is judged to be the first "stable" thing. But the life that is the image of this soul is stable only insofar as it exists from those higher things, yet it is mobile "by accident" insofar as it is joined to the body, which is properly mobile. Plotinus calls a life of this kind the **"seedbed world"** <note>original: *mundum seminarium*; a nursery or place where the seeds of all things are kept</note>, which the ancients called the "Image," which is always occupied with becoming like the original. For this is called not so much the Soul, as the *image* of the Soul. To the extent that it approaches matter—which is foreign to the intellectual source—to that same extent it degenerates from the Intellectual Soul. The seeds within it are also not so much "reasons" as they are "images of reasons." For if reason properly consists of the form in the ideal Intellectual Soul, then in the lower life there is deservedly only an image of reason. For who would call something "true reason" which, being ignorant of itself, has no account <note>original: *rationem*; a play on words: "reason" also means "an account" or "understanding"</note> of itself? 

This life is therefore an image, full only of images; this image is always moved by a desire for the likeness of its exemplar, and it always pursues it. Again, it is always being shaped and is perpetually formed; by this logic, the acts of the seeds themselves seem to flourish differently at different times. Yet they always agree with the exemplar. Through this, the life revolves as if as one with the body of the world; finally, along with the celestial revolution, the mind and the imaginative faculty are affected in various ways, and externally it is always clothed in other figures. Perhaps Plotinus also touches upon the opinion of Heraclitus and Timaeus with these words, when they say that this world, manifest to the eyes, never truly "is" but is perpetually "becoming." 

Altogether, just as water is shaped under a seal, but the shape does not remain once the seal is removed—and therefore the shape seems not so much to have been made once, but to be made always, especially if the water flows beneath it—so matter relates to nature, and nature in turn to the soul fertile with intellect. Plotinus intends that this world "becomes" or "is" only insofar as it is the image of the soul flowing from the soul, and the soul proceeds from the mind, and the mind is generated from the Good. And finally, the "goods" remain as long as that which is Good exists; the intellect remains as long as that which is Intellect exists. While these things remain, the following things naturally either remain or flow forth from them, just as light flows from the sun, and light from light thereafter. Regarding these things, we can say for the sake of religion: if we consider eternity in divine matters, the procession of the world from there rightly appears eternal; but if we consider...

->the will, the world proceeds by that limit which the divine<-
->will has decreed, by whose judgment the limit of power<-
->and magnitude is fixed in the world, and thus<-
->THE END.<-

<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of the World-Soul to a specific investigation into astrology and the influence of the heavens. In the previous section, Ficino explored how the Divine Intellect and the Soul organize the universe. Here, Plotinus (via Ficino’s Latin translation) begins Ennead II, Book III, questioning whether the stars are actual causes of human events or merely signs of what is to come.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
->ENNEAD TWO<-
->BOOK III.<-

# PLOTINUS

->ON WHETHER THE STARS EFFECT ANYTHING.<-

<margin>Section 1</margin>
That the movement of the stars signifies <note>original: "σημαίνει" (sēmainei); Plotinus emphasizes that stars are signs, not causes.</note> what will happen to each individual, but does not itself cause everything as many people believe, has been stated elsewhere regarding the heavens and in related arguments. However, we must now speak more accurately and at greater length, for it is no small matter to hold a correct opinion on this. Indeed, many say that the wandering stars <note>The "planets."</note> in their courses cause not only other things, such as poverty and wealth, health and disease, but often even the shameful and the beautiful. And—what is most significant—they claim the stars cause vices and virtues, and even the specific actions of every moment, as if the stars were angry with humans, just as one man might be with another. They suggest that humans do them no wrong, yet we are so influenced by them that they give us what are called "goods" or "evils." They do not do this out of love for those receiving them, but because of their movements or their positions, which they call "aspects," or because of the way their minds change as they move through different locations. They claim that when stars are in "angles" <term>kentrōseis</term> <note>original: "κεντρώσεις"; astrological houses that are considered points of high power in a chart.</note> or are "declining," it changes everything. Most importantly, they call some stars "evil" and others "good." Yet, they say that even the so-called "evil" stars give good things, and the "good" ones can become harmful. They add that planets act differently when they "see" each other <note>original: "ἰδόντας"; a reference to "aspects," or the geometric relationships between planets.</note> and differently when they do not, as if they were not their own masters. They say a star is good when it looks at one planet, but if it looks at another, it becomes different. Furthermore, the way they look—whether in this "figure" or that "sight"—affects the "blending" <note>original: "κρᾶσιν" (krasin); the mixture of planetary influences.</note> of the whole, just as different liquids produce a different mixture when combined. Having considered these and similar opinions, let us discuss each point accurately to persuade others of the truth.
<margin>The destiny that soon follows...</margin>
<margin>PLOTINUS</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Various opinions of the stars regarding mutual planets: and by what things the movement of the planets [is affected].</margin>
The movement of the stars regarding each person signifies future events, but does not cause everything, as many believe—a point we have touched upon elsewhere. However, we must speak on this presently with more exacting and numerous arguments. For it is of no small importance to think of these things in one way or another. Many astrologers hand down the idea that the planets, by their movements, cause not only external things like poverty and riches, or favorable and adverse health, but even the base and the beautiful, and—what is greatest of all—vices and virtues as well. Likewise, they claim that individual actions arising at specific times come from the stars, as if the stars were moved to anger against humans, even in cases where the humans themselves have done no injury; they are simply such as they were fashioned to be by the planets. They add, moreover, that the stars bring what are called "goods" not because they care for the recipients, but because they themselves are affected either well or poorly by the diversity of their motion and position.
<margin>C</margin>
Again, they argue that the stars change their "intentions" <note>original: "sententias"; used here to describe the planetary 'will' or 'influence' as if they were conscious actors.</note> according to the change of their course, and they turn out different from themselves when they are either in the "angles" or when they "decline" <note>original: "declinationes"; astronomical terms for the strength of a planet's position in the sky.</note>. But what is most significant is that while they say some among them are "bad" and others "good," nevertheless the "bad" ones often grant goods, and the "good" ones sometimes turn out "bad."
<margin>D</margin>
They add that the planets do some things when they "behold" one another and other things when they do not, as if they were not in control of themselves, but became one way by looking and another way by not looking. Finally, they claim a planet becomes "good" when it gazes upon a certain other planet, but when it gazes upon a different one, it is suddenly changed. They even assert that they "look" differently if the gaze happens in a certain "figure" <note>A geometric "aspect," like a square or trine.</note> and differently if the figure of the gazing changes. Then, from all these things conspiring together, another "mixture" <term>mistionem</term> is produced, just as from various liquids a different sort of blend is brewed beyond the individual parts. Since they hold these and other similar opinions, it is worthwhile to discuss each one accurately. A suitable beginning would be as follows.
<margin>E</margin>

He argues that while celestial movements may signify the future, they do not dictate human character or act out of human-like emotions such as anger.</summary>
