<meta>This page continues the investigation into the influence of the stars from Ennead II, Book III. While the previous page introduced the astrological claim that planets in "angles" determine human fate, this page begins a systematic refutation, questioning whether stars are physical bodies or divine souls, and arguing that their changing positions cannot reasonably cause changes in their character or our morality.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
# SECOND ENNEAD

<margin>
II
If the stars are inanimate, they only affect physical bodies; if they possess souls, they do not produce evil.
</margin>

**IN THE FIRST PLACE**, we must consider whether <margin>A</margin> the celestial bodies are animate <note>original: "animata"; meaning they possess a soul or life-force.</note> or the opposite. For if those things which are so moved lack a soul, they will be able to provide nothing other than heating and cooling, and perhaps bring about similar physical effects—provided we even concede that any of the stars are cold. Thus, they will extend their actions and duties only as far as the nature of our own bodies. Indeed, since only a physical impulse would proceed from them to us, not even much diversity of bodies would result from it. For the destination <margin>B</margin> of each would be the same, and they would be mixed together into one on the earth, where diversity arises only according to the variety of locations. This diversity is born from the fact that something is exposed either more closely or more distantly to the celestial influence, and thus it is received differently. The same logic applies if "coldness" is admitted among these influences. However, how they could produce wise men and the ignorant, or make some men grammarians, others rhetoricians, others lyre-players <note>original: "citharædos"; refers to professional musicians in antiquity.</note>, and others <margin>C</margin> skilled in various arts, or how they make some rich and others poor, I do not see at all. Similarly, there are other things that can in no way have their cause through the mere mixing of physical bodies: for instance, why you have such a brother, such a father, or that specific wife; or finally, that prosperous things occasionally happen to you, and now you are designated a leader of an army or obtain a kingdom. But if the celestial bodies are animate and act by counsel <note>original: "consilio"; meaning with intent or rational planning.</note>, tell me, I pray: what injury have they received from us that <margin>D</margin> they would willingly harm us every day? Especially since they are placed in a divine seat and are themselves divine. For those things which cause humans to become evil do not happen to them; nor does any good or evil happen to them at all from human prosperity or adversity.

<margin>
III
The stars are not changed by their movements, locations, or emotions.
</margin>

**THEY WILL PERHAPS SAY** that the stars do not do <margin>E</margin> such things willingly, but are compelled by their locations and "aspects" <note>The geometric relationships between planets in astrology.</note>. But if they acted by compulsion, then everyone ought to do the same thing when they are in the same locations and aspects. Now, however, what difference would this planet suffer while it passes through this degree or again through that part of the zodiac circle? Or what difference would that other planet suffer? For it is not in the zodiac itself, but far distant below it, and through whatever portion it passes, it is similarly in the heaven. For it is ridiculous <margin>F</margin> that a planet should become of one nature or another according to whatever tiny portion of the sky it traverses, and exhibit different effects. Likewise, it is ridiculous to say a planet has one nature when it rises and is in an "angle" <term>angle</term> <note>original: "angulo"; refers to the four "cardinal" points of an astrological chart (Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli), which were thought to be points of peak power.</note>, and another when it declines. For it does not then "rejoice" when it is in an angle, nor is it then "pained" or "sluggish" when it declines. Nor again does it favor someone when it rises, or become gentle when it sets. But one of them is said to be "better" when it is setting. In reality, any planet is continually "angular" for some people, but "falling" for others; it falls for some, and in turn is angular for others. Yet it is not at the same time delighted, grieving, angry, and pacified. As for the claim that some rejoice at their setting and others conversely at their rising, this seems absurd. For it would happen that the same planet would be delighted and grieved at the same time. Furthermore, why should their grief bring evil to us? But we must not concede that they either feel pain or experience temporary delight; rather, they are always the same.

<column-break/>

<margin>
II
* Whether they produce bodies.
</margin>

**WHETHER** we must consider these moving things to be animate <note>original: "ἔμψυχα" (empsycha); literally "en-souled."</note> or inanimate. If indeed they are inanimate, they provide nothing except heating or cooling—or perhaps also cold, if we shall say it comes from the stars—but certainly not from the nature of our own bodies. The gift would be rare, some physical flows happening unto us, such that there would not even be a great change in our bodies, the influence of each being the same. And indeed, these are mixed together upon the earth, so that difference arises only according to the turns caused by their movement, resulting from being near or far, giving differently to the different recipient; and the coldness likewise. But how do they make the wise and the ignorant, and some grammarians, and others lyre-players, and the other arts, and furthermore the rich and the poor? And the other things that do not have the cause of their becoming from the mixing of bodies—such as having such a brother and father, and land, and a wife, and the chance of becoming a lover or a king? But if, being animate, they are said to act, what have they suffered from us that each planet acts against us? And this while they are established in a divine lot, and are themselves divine. For those things through which men become evil do not belong to them, nor does any good or evil come to them at all from us being unfortunate or suffering evils.

<margin>
III
* movement
</margin>

But they do these things not willingly, but compelled by their locations and figures <note>astrological configurations.</note>. But if they were compelled, then everyone surely ought to do the same things when they are in the same locations and figures. Now, however, from where does the difference arise? Furthermore, is this segment of the zodiac circle the cause? Or again that one? For indeed, the planet is not in the zodiac itself, but much further below it. Then, also, in whatever part of the sky it might be? For it is ridiculous that, according to each part as it is contained, the planet becomes one thing or another, and gives different things; and that it is different when it has come to an "angle" <term>kentro</term> <note>original: "κέντρου" (kentrou); the Greek term for the "angle" or pivot point in a horoscope.</note> and when it has declined. For does it then rejoice when it is upon the angle, and then is pained when it declines, or becomes "right-handed"? And this one is "angry" at the gate of another. But one of them, even when declining, will be better. For indeed each one is both "upon" for some and "declining" for others, "falling" for some and "upon" for others. And it would seem that at the same time it rejoices and is pained, and is angry, and is gentle... it is irrational to say they "rejoice" in such a rhythm... being undisturbed, how is it not illogical? For thus it happens that they are pained and rejoice at the same time. Then, why would paining that planet hinder it? In general, we must not grant them either to be pained or to rejoice according to the occasion, but that they are always equally rejoicing in the good...

<summary>Plotinus argues against the idea that stars are the causes of human character and fate, asserting that if they are physical they only affect physical heat/cold, and if they are divine they would not have the petty emotions or motives to harm humans.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's critique of astrology from Ennead II, Book III. Following the previous page’s argument that celestial bodies, if they are divine, would not intentionally cause human suffering, this section specifically targets the logic of "aspects" (the geometric angles between planets) and the supposed "friendships" or "hostilities" that astrologers attribute to the stars based on their positions in the zodiac.</meta>

### BOOK THREE

[The stars are] tranquil, rejoicing in their present goods, both those which they enjoy themselves and those they foresee. For there, the life of each consists in itself, and in that very activity each possesses its own good. This good, however, does not incline toward our affairs. Indeed, the work of those living beings who have no commerce with us is not primarily, but rather as a consequence—or rather, not at all—directed toward our concerns. For just as birds provide omens to the augurs <note>original: "augures"; Roman priests who interpreted the will of the gods through the flight and behavior of birds.</note> by coincidence, so too do these celestial bodies happen to portend the future.

<margin>!!! Astrologers do not truly assign the cause of effects.</margin> FURTHERMORE, it seems absurd that one planet should be pleased by a certain aspect <term>aspect</term> <note>The geometric angle between two planets in the zodiac.</note>, while another is offended by that same view. What discord can there be between them, and concerning what matter? Furthermore, for what reason do they behave differently when they gaze upon each other in a trine aspect <term>trine aspect</term> <note>original: "trino aspectu"; a 120-degree angle, traditionally considered harmonious.</note>, but differently when they look from an opposite or square aspect <term>square aspect</term> <note>original: "quadrato"; a 90-degree angle, traditionally considered a source of tension.</note>? Also, why does a planet look one way when configured thus, but upon moving to the next sign in the sequence and being closer, it is said to refuse to look? In short, what could be the method for producing those things said to happen because of them? And how does each of them act separately, while all of them acting together produce something different from the sum of their parts? For they do not meet as if by consultation to carry out what they have deliberated upon us, with each one relaxing something of his own duty; nor again does one prohibit the function of another by force; nor will one yield to another, persuaded to hand over his duty to the other. <margin>*from themselves</margin> Finally, what they say—that one planet is delighted when placed in the houses of another, while conversely another is affected when received in its house—seems just as if someone were to grant that two people are friends, but then assert that one loves the other, while the other, in turn, hates the first.

<margin>!!! Error thus concerning the nature of planets.</margin> THEY TEACH that one of them [Saturn] is cold, and being placed slightly further from us, is more good to us, precisely because in that cold evil he would place his evil against us <note>Plotinus is critiquing the traditional astrological view of Saturn as a "greater malefic" whose cold nature is harmful unless tempered by distance or position.</note>; even though it ought to be that in opposite signs of the zodiac, a good should exist for us. They further claim that a cold planet opposite a hot one makes both of them oppressive, even though a temperate state <term>temperantia</term> <note>A balanced mixing of qualities, like hot and cold, which in Greek medicine and philosophy was the ideal state of health.</note> ought to have resulted from such a mixture. Furthermore, they say one planet is delighted by the day and becomes propitious through the heat of the day, while another, being fiery, rejoices in the night—as if there were not perpetual day there (that is, light) or as if another were obscured by night, when it is actually very far removed from the shadow of the earth. As for what they say—that the moon is good when full of light and approaching a planet, but evil when empty of light—if such a thing were to be granted, one should say the opposite. For when it is full toward us, it is empty toward the one walking above it (in the other semicircle). But when it is diminished toward us, it is filled from that side; wherefore the opposite effects ought to result when it is diminished, namely when it looks upon that planet with light. Therefore, it makes no difference to the moon how it is situated, since it is always half-full; but perhaps it matters to that planet which they say is heated from there. Indeed, it will perhaps be heated if the moon is devoid of light toward us. While it is said to be "bereft of light," it is actually full toward the planet above it, though empty toward us. Consequently, when that planet does not help because it is far away, it seems to be in a worse state; but when it is full, it suffices for what is below, even if it is far off; but when it is bereft of light toward the fiery one, it seems to be good toward us. For its own power is sufficient by itself.

<meta>catchword: in</meta>

<summary>Plotinus systematically dismantles the logic of astrology, arguing that the technical definitions of planetary "aspects" and "friendships" are inconsistent and ignore the physical and divine reality of the stars. He particularly mocks the idea that planets are "pleased" or "offended" by their geometric positions in the zodiac.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the heavens. Having previously argued that the stars are divine and tranquil beings, Plotinus now addresses the "temperament" of the planets (Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, etc.) and begins a vigorous critique of judicial astrology—specifically the idea that planets "cause" human vice or that their positions can be calculated like a mathematical ledger to predict individual fortunes.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS: BOOK II.

...as it is more fervent <note>original: "feruentius"; implying both heat and a kind of vital intensity.</note>, if compared to another. Indeed, the bodies of living beings that flow from that source are more or less warm, but none is entirely cold: a fact that the very region of the heavens testifies. Furthermore, the planet they call **Jupiter** is well-tempered with fire; the **morning star** <note>original: "lucifer" (Latin) / "heosphoros" (Greek); both refer to the planet Venus when it appears before sunrise.</note> is similar. Therefore, through a certain likeness, they seem to be in harmony with one another. As for the one called "the fiery one" <note>original: "igneus" (Latin) / "pyroeis" (Greek); a common epithet for the planet Mars.</note>, we must think that he contributes to a certain tempering of the whole. Regarding **Saturn**, finally, because he is so far distant, he must be said to behave as an outsider. **B** Lastly, what they say of **Mercury**—that he is indifferent to all—must be understood to mean that he easily becomes similar to all. Yet all these planets contribute to the universe; thus, they relate to one another in a way that is advantageous to the whole, just as the individual parts are arranged within a single living being. It is for the sake of this whole that they are primarily positioned, just as **bile** <term>bile</term> <note>original: "bilis" (Latin) / "chole" (Greek); in ancient medicine, one of the four humors. Plotinus uses it here as an example of a "bitter" or "unpleasant" part of a body that nonetheless serves a vital purpose for the health of the whole organism.</note> serves both the whole body and its immediate part. For it was necessary to arouse the **C** soul and not allow either the whole or the nearest part to be affected by injuries. Moreover, in the universe, such a thing was necessary, and another part besides had to be applied to create a sweeter temperament. Other parts are like eyes; and all the irrational aspects of their lives suffer or feel together in turn. For in this way the whole is one, and the harmony of the whole is one. Thus, then, how shall they not be certain signs according to the proportion that one considers?

<margin>VI The actions of the wandering planets.</margin>
FURTHERMORE, when they say that **Mars** or **Venus**, when arranged in a certain way, produce **adulteries**, **D** this is far removed from reason. For that would be nothing other than those stars themselves ardently filling their own mutual greed and lack, as if they shared in human intemperance. Consequently, when they say that a certain configuration or "aspect" is pleasing to them, but that they have no limit at all in their effects, this seems to be granted by no sound logic. Likewise, since there are countless thousands of animals constantly being born, how is it that the planets always manage each one individually, bestowing **E** glory and riches, or making men poor and incontinent, and effecting the individual actions of every single person? What kind of life would those stars have to lead, or how could they possibly accomplish so many and such diverse things? It is also said quite absurdly that they wait for the "ascensions" <note>The rising of specific points of the zodiac over the horizon.</note> and returns of the signs, and only then complete their assigned duty; or that for however many degrees each sign ascends, there are just as many years of ascension or return—as if they were **F** counting on their fingers when they are to act, and were not permitted to do anything before that time. Finally, they ascribe the authority of governance to no single being, but attribute everything to these planets, as if there were not one presiding **Prince** <note>original: "princeps"; referring to the One or the supreme Governing Intellect.</note> upon whom the universe depends, and who distributes to each their own natural duties; in which, thereafter, all things are coordinated in a similar fashion. To believe otherwise is the mark of a man who dissolves the very order in which he himself is numbered, and who is ignorant of the nature of the universe—a nature that has a first principle and cause **G** whose power propagates thoroughly through all things.

<margin>VII The signs of the stars occur because of the wonderful connection of things in the world.</margin>
HOWEVER, if the stars portend the future, just as we are accustomed to observe many other signs of future events, by what means does this happen, and by what logic is the order maintained? For unless they proceeded in a certain order, individual things could not be signified. Let them be, therefore, like **letters in the sky**, which are either being written continually or have already been inscribed and move.

<column-break/>

...more fiery, or being in relation to that. But the bodies existing there are of living things, but some others are more or less hot, and none is cold. The place itself bears witness, because of which they speak. The power is fiery and <margin>equal</margin> the morning star <gloss>this one</gloss>; therefore they also seem to be in harmony, by a certain likeness, by which the fiery one will shine; by the temperament, but the other is of a different kind, being alien to the cutting <note>Perhaps referring to the "section" or "orbit" of the planet.</note> because of the distance. But [Mercury] is indifferent toward all, as if being made like that one. But all contribute toward the whole, so that they relate to one another in the way it benefits the whole. Just as the individual parts of some living being, which were not born before, especially like bile, both for the whole, and for what is near, and for the need, and to rouse spirit [anger], and the whole, and not to allow the neighbor to be treated with insolence. And indeed in the complete [universe], it was necessary for some to be, and another for what is pleasant, joined together, and others <gloss>not</gloss> and for all to be entirely in sympathy because they are irrational <note>In the sense of "without discursive reason," acting by natural instinct or soul-harmony.</note>; for thus there is also one harmony. How then would these not be signs based on analogy?

But that this **Ares** [Mars] or **Aphrodite** [Venus] being joined, produce adulteries, if they are in this way—as if the licentiousness of men were overflowing onto them— <margin>difficulty</margin> just as they have need of each other, how could this not hold much irrationality? And while they have this relation to each other, if it is so: but as for there being nothing for them, how could it be? And while countless thousands of animals are being born, and of these <margin>objection</margin> each one always completes what is necessary. If you happen to be giving: to be rich in everything, poor, licentious, and they themselves complete the activities of each, what is their life? Or how is it possible to do so many things? But as for waiting for the parts [degrees] of the zodiac, and not completing them, and in the parts themselves <margin>absurdly</margin> if indeed there is a fulfillment, that the years of the ascension are so many, and not to be able to do it sooner: if one were not to be persuaded that the same thing is before all for the need. But altogether to give the authority of administration to no one thing, but for all things to give all, as if no one <gloss>one</gloss> were commanding from whom the whole is arranged <gloss>it is</gloss>, each giving according to nature the things from itself to bring along and arrange the things of itself, being arranged in turn with them—this is the mark of one who dissolves and is ignorant of the nature of the world, which has a first principle and cause, going through all things.

But if they signify the things that will be, just as we say many other things are significant of the things to be, what would be the source of trust and how is the order? For it would not <margin>signs</margin> be signified in an orderly way, unless each thing happened, if anything of all things were like **letters written in the sky** always, or having been written and moving. <summary>Plotinus argues that the planets are part of a unified cosmic "organism" where even "harsh" elements like Mars serve a purpose, much like bile in a body. He rejects the astrological belief that planets cause human immorality, asserting instead that they are "signs" or "letters" that reveal a pre-existing cosmic order governed by a single First Principle.</summary>

# THIRD BOOK

Everything follows a sequence, or rather, there are signs from these things. In a way, both the sign and the signified belong to a single living being. But this is not only true for the parts, but also for the long-range connections. For even we sometimes sense something in our eyes, or in another part of the body, regarding dangers or safety, and those very parts feel it too. These are our parts, but we are also parts of others; everything is full of signs, and the wise person is one who learns one thing from another. For all knowledge regarding what occurs is understood through the mutual conspiracy <note>original: "sympnoia" (Greek); literally a "breathing together," a term Plotinus uses to describe the organic, interconnected harmony of the universe.</note> of all things. In this way, the practice of bird-divination is rational, as are the other animals from which we take signs for each thing; all things have been made to belong to one another. And this single conspiracy exists not only in the specific details mentioned, but much more and primarily in the Whole. Before any single principle, the entire living being was created, and it consists of all things; and just as in the specific parts, where each part has received a sacred function, so in the Whole, each thing has its own works, and more so than these, as they are not only parts, but also wholes and greater entities. Each thing will be acted upon by the one, and each will contribute something to another; for the one is not separate from the others. Indeed, it is one and all-encompassing. Each part perceives the states of the others, and is either pained or pleased. It will be acted upon not by chance or by accident, but according to a sequence following its nature.

<margin>From causality</margin>
And indeed, the soul, having been urged to perform its own work—the soul that makes all things—clings to the principle and then later ceases, and something follows it in sequence. Then, how is what is done a kind of justice for the Whole? If it is not destroyed, it remains, being set right by the order of the Whole and the power of that which governs. The stars, as non-negligible parts of the heavens, work together toward the end and exist for the purpose of signifying. Thus, all things that arise from sensible things signify; but other things produce results, such as the imagination and the work of our soul, and the things we do according to nature, as long as we are not in error. If anyone strikes at the Whole, when we err, we pay the penalty. And the error itself, and the portion in the underworld <note>original: "charoni" (Charon); the ferryman of the dead, used here to represent the afterlife or the consequences of the soul's descent.</note>, come afterward. Wealth and poverty, and the fortunes of external things, are one thing; but virtues and vices are another. Virtues come from the reception of the soul, while vices are the coincidence of the soul with external things. But concerning these, it has been said elsewhere.

<margin>it has been said</margin>
But for now, let us recall the spindle which the Fates <note>original: "Moirae"; the three sister-goddesses of destiny.</note> spin and twist. In Plato's work <note>A reference to the Myth of Er at the end of Plato's *Republic*.</note>, the spindle represents the celestial revolutions, both of the wandering and the fixed stars, and the Fates and Necessity, their mother, turn them, and at the birth of each person, they spin their threads...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...should be explained first, producing something else beforehand, from which the significance of things follows as a result. Just as in a single living being from a single principle, one can judge one member from another: for instance, one can guess the character of a person from their eyes, or by properly considering another part of the body, recognizing dangers and the warnings of dangers. These are parts of our body, and we likewise are parts of the world. Thus, some things lend themselves to others. But all things are full of 
<margin>B</margin>
signs, and a wise person argues one thing from another. Indeed, many familiar signs are known to everyone daily. How, then, is there a mutual order of all things? It is in this way that it is consistent for prophecy to be valid in bird-omens, and also in other animals from which we predict individual events. It is necessary, therefore, that all things be ordered together and follow in sequence. For not only in each thing that is perfectly connected does a single conspiracy <note>original: "conspiratio" (Latin translation of "sympnoia"); implies a "breathing together" or harmonized action.</note> flourish, but much
<margin>C</margin>
more so and primarily in the universe. There, it is necessary that from one principle the living being itself becomes one manifold entity, one, I say, constituted from all things. And just as in each individual, any part has its own proper work, so also in the universe, individual works are allotted to individual parts: and much more so because these are not only parts, but are also wholes and greater things. Each thing, therefore, proceeds from one principle performing its own duty, while other things everywhere are 
<margin>D</margin>
conducive to others. For nothing is ever separated from the total form itself: they act and are acted upon in turn, and something is added to each thing, by which it is either helped or harmed. They proceed, however, not at random, nor as chance allows: for something else is produced from these, and another thing naturally follows, and another succeeds it.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>VIII. The World Soul is the principle of natural things; Fate belongs to the World Soul; rational beings possess freedom of choice.</margin>
Now indeed, while the soul performs its own duty, having begun its work—for the soul does all things—it possesses the rational principle of its origin and proceeds for the most part rightly. But if it should wander, being led away by others, it follows the course of those things that are produced in the world by a certain judgment, unless perhaps it is released. For its judgment always remains: since the universe is ruled and directed by the power and order of the ruling principle. The stars serve this and contribute to it, as significant parts of heaven, both for the beauty of the whole form and for the duty of signification. Thus, they portend all things that arise in the sensible world, and 
<margin>F</margin>
they truly perform whatever they clearly do. We, however, perform the works of the soul according to nature, as long as we do not wander or fall into that multitude of the whole. But when we wander, we pay the penalty to judgment: namely, the error itself, and a certain worse fate that will come to us in the future. Let it be said, therefore, that poverty and such things happen by the coincidence of external events; but how do virtues and vices happen? 
<margin>G</margin>
<margin>IX. The soul that descends into us from heaven is subject to fate; but that which is given to us by God is free from fate and can liberate us.</margin>
Virtues, indeed, arise because of that which is older and more excellent in the soul. Vices, however, come from a certain commerce of the soul with external things. But concerning these, it has been said elsewhere.

At present, it is worthwhile to recall that spindle which the Fates twist in the ancient stories, through which Plato signifies the celestial circuit, which is called either wandering or non-wandering. In his work, the Fates and Necessity, the mother of the Fates, turn this spindle, and they entwine it with the generation of each person. And through...

<summary>Plotinus explains that the universe is a single, interconnected living organism where every part reflects the whole through "cosmic sympathy." He argues that the stars act as signs of future events and that while the soul is subject to fate when it identifies with external things, it possesses an inherent freedom when it acts according to its higher nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s examination of the relationship between the human soul, the stars, and fate. Having established that the universe acts as a single living organism where parts signify the states of other parts, Plotinus now addresses Plato’s Timaeus to reconcile the influence of the "wandering gods" (the stars) with human free will and the nature of the higher soul.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.</header>

<margin>A</margin>From this circuit and revolution, whatever is marked out proceeds into generation <note>original: "generationem"; in Platonic thought, this refers to the physical world of change and birth as opposed to the eternal realm of Being.</note>. In the *Timaeus* as well, God, the craftsman of the world, hands over the principle of souls; but the gods who are carried along <note>original: "dii verò qui perferuntur"; referring to the planetary deities or stars</note> apply heavy and necessary passions: angers, lusts, pleasures, pains, and another species of soul from which perturbations of this kind arise. These words of Plato certainly seem to bind us to the stars, as we clearly receive our souls from them; <margin>B</margin> likewise, they suggest that we, falling down into this realm, are subject to necessity. He also says that we derive our characters from them, and according to those characters, our actions and passions proceed from a certain passive habit. Therefore, we must investigate what else we might be.

Perhaps, in truth, the remainder is what we truly are: those to whom nature gave the power to dominate the passions. For besides the fact that we were surrounded by these evils because of the nature of the body, God granted a virtue that is entirely free from servitude. For we do not need virtue when we are placed in a safe state, but when, in the absence of virtue, danger from <margin>C</margin> evils looms. For this reason, it is necessary to flee from here, and to segregate ourselves from those things which are joined to us in generation; and effort must be given so that we are not, by chance, that very thing which is the "compound"—namely, the animated body. In this compound, the nature of the body prevails more, having obtained a certain trace of the soul, so that this common life belongs primarily to the body; for whatever belongs to this life is corporeal. <margin>D</margin> But the other soul, which exists from the outside <note>original: "extrinfecus extat"; the transcendent, higher soul that does not fully descend into the body</note>, pertains more deeply to the sublime—that is, to the beautiful and the divine, over which nothing foreign dominates. On the contrary, the mind uses its powers so that it may escape; and according to this, it lives itself when it receives itself back into itself. But whoever is devoid of the soul established here already lives in fate. In this state of life, the stars do not only signify for the man, but he himself becomes as a part of the universe, and not unjustly serves the whole of which he is a part. <margin>E</margin> For every person is twofold: partly indeed encompassing both in himself, and partly existing as that which he truly is. The whole world also is partly a certain compound of a body and a soul enslaved to that body, and partly the Soul of the whole itself, which is not in the body, but instead imprints certain traces upon the soul that lies within the body. <margin>F</margin> Even the sun and the rest of the celestial bodies are similarly twofold. One soul, which is pure, brings nothing depraved or base; but those things which happen throughout the universe from them, insofar as they are parts of the universe—namely, both because they are a body and because they are an animated body—proceed as certain parts. Meanwhile, the choice of the star and its true soul looks toward that which is best. Other things follow from this very thing; or rather, not so much from the soul itself as from those things which are around it, which become many and various from the heat diffused everywhere from there, and if anything flows from one soul into another kindred soul. But troublesome things, if they are difficult and adverse, are born in the world because of a certain mixture; for the nature of this world is mixed. And if anyone were to somehow separate its separable soul from it, he would see that the remainder is not great. Thus, let the separable soul be numbered in its own substance. For the remainder is a daemon <note>original: "dæmon"; a spiritual being or intermediary power, here referring to the lower, governed part of the cosmic soul</note>, which Plato called the "Great Daemon," and the affections in it are daemonic.

<column-break/>

Those things which come into being are directed toward generation by the soul itself. In the *Timaeus*, God the creator gives the beginning of the soul, but the gods who travel [the stars] provide the terrible and necessary passions: rages, and desires, and pleasures, and pains. This is another form of soul, from which these very sufferings arise. These arguments bind us to the stars, suggesting we receive a soul from them and have fallen under necessity, if indeed we travel through them. Our characters, then, come from them, and according to those characters our actions and passions arise from a passive state. What then remains for us? Or is it that which we are in truth—those to whom nature gave the power to master the passions? For likewise, while we are caught in foul evils because of the body, God gave an invisible, glowing character <note>original: "atheatōn zeston ēthos"</note> in whose goodwill we exist, and which provides us with virtue. But when one is in danger of being in evils, virtue is present. <margin><unclear>good con...</unclear></margin> Therefore, one must flee from here, and separate oneself from the things that have been assigned to us; and one must not be the "compound," the body * animated with life, in which the nature of the body rather prevails, having taken a trace of the soul, so that the common life belongs more to the body. For all things are corporeal, as many as belong to this. But the other soul, which is outside, is directed toward the things above, and the beautiful, and the divine, which no one masters; rather, the soul either clings to it, or is that thing, or lives according to it, having withdrawn from the desert <note>original: "erēmos"; perhaps referring to the lack of the higher soul</note> of this lower soul. But fate, even here, and the stars do not only signify for him, but he himself becomes like a part. And he follows the whole, of which he is a part. Thus each of us is twofold: both the compound and the self. The world itself is also such: one part is that from body and a certain soul <margin><unclear>necess...</unclear></margin> bound to the body; the other is the soul of the whole, which is not in the body, but shines its traces upon the soul in the body. The sun and the others are also double in this way: the one soul, which is pure, gives nothing base; but those things that happen to the whole from them, insofar as they are parts of the whole—a body, and * the body as an animated part—give to the part according to the choice of the star and the soul which is truly itself looking toward the best. But the other things follow it. Or rather, <margin><unclear>wicked...</unclear></margin> not it itself, but the things around it: like the circle of heat from fire into the whole, * and from the other soul into another soul that is kindred. But the difficult things are due to the mixture, for the nature of this whole is mixed. And if someone were to separate the separable soul from it, the remainder is not great. It is a god, then, when that soul runs with it. But the remainder is a daemon; if it is a part, then the passions in it are daemonic.

### BOOK TWO

<column-break/>

**A** If this is so, then we must now grant the significance [of the stars]. Yet we should not grant them influence over all things, nor over the entirety of the souls themselves, but rather over those things that depend on Fortune <note>original: "τύχης" (Tyche); the random or external circumstances of life</note>, and as much of the soul as remains tied to them. The soul, even before it enters into generation <note>The realm of birth, death, and physical change.</note>, when it comes from the Circuit <note>The celestial rotation of the stars.</note> to enter the body, does not possess a great capacity for suffering. However, when it enters into the circumstances of life, something returns upon it from that very circuit, and by acting upon that circuit, it cooperates even in a subservient way; for most things occur when each individual part takes its place within the whole.

**B** We must also consider this: that which comes from the stars is not the same in the receiver as it was in the source. For example, the fire that comes from them is not simply fire, but something else entirely. Even a friendly disposition in them becomes something different in us. Nor do we receive their qualities in a purely good way; for instance, anger may be received without its proper measure, as if it were happening by chance. Idleness may produce despondency. In general, while the forms there always possess beauty, they are not the same in those who receive them; and even if judgment stumbles, it is not because the stars are malicious. Where craftiness is found, it is perhaps because the mind is striving for something it cannot attain. Each of these things is not evil in its source, for evil is not there. The things that arrive here do not remain as they were, but are altered by being mixed with bodies, with matter, and with one another.

**C** Furthermore, existence is not merely a joining together; rather, each thing produced is brought forth from a mixture, so that in the act of becoming, it is not just the father who exists, but that which is given according to his nature. For a horse is born from a horse, and a man from a man; the star does not enter into the seed itself, but the child is born according to the rational principle <note>original: "λόγου" (Logos); the formative blueprint of a species.</note> of the man. However, external additions can hinder or help this; a son is born similar to the father, yet often he improves by grace, or he may fall away entirely. At times, matter <note>original: "ὕλη" (Hyle); the raw, formless substance of the world.</note> prevails over nature, so that the soul’s form does not reach perfection.

**D** It is necessary, then, to distinguish that which is caused, since some things come from the celestial circuit, while others come from <unclear>...</unclear> and negligence and <unclear>...</unclear>. The soul governs this entire universe according to reason, just as in any individual animal there is a principle of life from which each part is formed and directed toward the whole. The parts are thus: in the whole, all things exist; but in the parts, there is only as much as each part requires. Of those things happening from without, some are contrary to the will of Nature, while others are in harmony with the plan; yet all things, being parts, harmonize with Nature as a whole, fulfilling the life of the entire universe.

<column-break/>

<margin>
The stars do not corrupt every soul in every way: nor do the souls follow their fortune.
</margin>
If the matter stands thus, we must now also grant the significance [of the stars]. However, the passions <note>Internal movements of the soul like anger or desire.</note> should be granted neither to the souls themselves, nor to them in their entirety: but only insofar as they belong to what remains of them. We must admit again that the soul, even before it reaches generation, slides down, carrying something from the celestial spheres; nor would it come into the body unless it had some capacity for suffering, and a great one at that. We must admit that the fortunes of one entering a body happen for this very reason: that it enters the world when **B** certain rulers are in dominion. Finally, we must admit that the course of the world flows in such a way that it leads simultaneously in its work, and fulfills from itself those things which are to be carried out by the universe; for indeed, those things which are in the course of the universe itself obtain the order of parts.

<margin>
**XI**
Those things which emanate from the celestial bodies are corrupted by our vices.
</margin>
Nor truly should it be hidden from us that what proceeds from the celestial bodies does not turn out to be the same in those who receive it as it was when it departed from the higher beings. Just as if fire in us were to degenerate far from the celestial **C** source, and a disposition inclined toward love were made weaker among us and gave birth to something bitter and dishonorable: so also courage, when it happens to occur beyond measure in relation to fortune, creates—by necessity—anger, madness, or sluggishness. Thus, the study of true honor brings a desire for things that seem beautiful and honorable. Thus, a downward flow of the mind produces craftiness; for craftiness emulates the mind because it wishes to attain what it cannot. Therefore, although these individual things are not evil among the higher beings, **D** they happen to be evil among us. For those things which proceed from there are neither the same as those, nor do they remain as they proceeded, being mixed with bodies and matter and with each other.

<margin>
**XII**
A thing is generated from corporeal and seminal rational principles of nature, with infinite accidents of matter arranged.
</margin>
Furthermore, that which comes from there meets with the mind, and from this joining, whatever is born contracts something from which it is, exists, and turns out to be such a thing. For the celestial influx does not create a horse, but it gives something to the horse: **E** for a horse is generated from a horse, and a man from a man. The Sun, however, approaches this formation as a helping force. A man is made from the seminal reason <note>original: "seminaria ratione"; the biological and spiritual blueprint of a human.</note> of a man; yet in such a way that what is external either hinders or helps: for a son is produced similarly to the parent, but often for the better, and sometimes it happens for the worse, yet never is he led away from the <unclear>original</unclear> subject. Sometimes matter prevails over nature, so that the effect does not turn out absolute—namely, when the species is overcome by matter.

<margin>
**XIII**
Concerning the common life and action of the world: and likewise how each individual has his own proper life and actions.
</margin>
**F** It is necessary hereafter, since some things flow from the mundane motion while others do not, to distinguish now, judge, and explain from where exactly each thing truly comes. The principle, therefore, shall be of this kind: The soul governs this whole by reason, just as in any animal the principle of life itself is that from which the individual members of the living being are formed, and are ordered toward the whole of which they are parts. In the whole, indeed, all things are present; but in the parts, there is only as much as is in each one. As for those things which approach from the outside, some are **G** then truly in agreement; yet all things harmonize with the whole from every side as its members. Nature, having obtained what they possess, simultaneously fills the entire life of the universe in its own way.

<summary>Plotinus argues that while stars provide the "raw material" of passions and physical conditions, they do not corrupt the higher soul; rather, these influences are altered by the receiver's own nature and matter.</summary>

### PLOTINUS ENNEAD II.

<margin>
XIII.
Fate is assigned to both—that is, in these things and in those that follow.
</margin>
Those things which are inanimate in the world are **A**
entirely the instruments of others, and are driven
to action from the outside. But those things which 
are animate, if they lack reason, have an indeter-

chariot before the charioteer prescribes their

The nature of a rational living being, however, has
a charioteer within itself; if it has a skilled one, 
it is carried mostly in a straight line and does not, as **B**
tends to happen, wander by chance. Both, however, 
are within the world and contribute to the whole: 
and those things among them which are greater and
more excellent in rank perform many great things, 
and contribute from all sides to the life of the whole, 
having received a rank of acting rather than of 
suffering <note>In this context, "suffering" means being acted upon by external forces.</note>. But many things are occupied in suffering, 
having little power for action. Those in the middle 
indeed suffer from others, but frequently act upon 
others, since they have the principle of acting and 
doing within themselves. On which account the **C**
whole world is a universal and perfect life, 
while those things which are best perform the best 
actions, insofar as the "best" exists in each. This 
best part must be considered a colleague to the 
leader of the whole, like fellow soldiers to a 
general, who are said by Plato to follow Jupiter <note>original: "Iovem" (Zeus), referring to the King of the Gods as the cosmic mind.</note> 
as he marches into the intelligible nature. But 
those things which are established in a lower rank

universe, and are roughly such as the secondary **D**
powers of the soul are in us; other things 
similarly hold themselves like the final parts in 
us, for not all things in us are equal. Therefore, 
all things are living, or exist according to the 
entire reason of the universe—both all things in 
heaven and whatever things are distributed through 
the whole. Nor does any part, even a massive one, 
have the power either to disturb the "seminary reasons" <note>original: "rationes mundi seminarias" (logoi spermatikoi); the formative blueprints that govern natural growth.</note> 
of the world from their order, or to change 
the things that proceed according to such reasons 
from their own species. And although it can bring 
about a certain change, sometimes for the better **E**
and sometimes for the worse, it cannot, however, 
thrust a thing out of its own nature. Indeed, it 
makes things worse either by bringing weakness 
to the body, or to the soul, insofar as it becomes 
the cause of some accidental depravity in that 
soul which is "sympathetic" and passed down from 
the superior to the inferior—or when, the body 
being poorly composed, a hindrance is brought 
against the soul's action to be fulfilled through 
the body, just as if a lyre were not so composed **F**
and tuned that it could sustain a perfect 
harmony to complete musical sounds.

**CONCERNING** poverty, however, and riches, and 
glory, and power, what should be said? Perhaps if 
riches come from parents, the celestial signs 
indicated that one would be wealthy, just as they 
only declared the noble man who derives glory 
from his lineage. But where riches are acquired 
by the excellence of virtue, if the body supplied **G**
the strength for it, then surely those who provided 
strength to the body contribute to the amassing of 
wealth. Parents indeed first, then whatever region 
has a propitious sky; to this is added the 
wholesome fertility of the earth. But if virtue, 
without the benefit of the body, increased wealth 
through its own efforts, the most must be 
attributed to virtue alone in this matter—and to 
whatever divine fortune may have happened from 
those things which are exchanged and repaid in 
turn. But where men have given riches, if indeed 
they are good, it contributes to virtue...

<margin>...and the rest.</margin>
...Nor are all inanimate things within it merely instruments 
and, as it were, pushed from the outside into acting. 
But of the animate things, some have an 
indeterminate motion, like horses under an impulse 
before the charioteer has defined the course for 
them, since they are managed by the lash. 
The nature of a rational animal, however, has 
the charioteer from itself; and having a 
knowledgeable one, it is carried straight, 
not frequently as it might happen by chance. 
Both are within the whole, and contribute 
toward the whole; and some of them, being 
greater and more earnest, do many and 
great things, and contribute toward the 
life of the whole, having a rank that is productive

infinite, have little power toward acting. 
The things in the middle somewhere, suffering 
indeed from others, yet doing many things 
at certain times, have the beginning of 
conduct and production from themselves. And 
the whole becomes a complete life, with the

is in it—the guide of each—is coordinated with 
the leading principle, like soldiers to a

But those things using nature to a lesser 
degree, only as much as the parts of the whole, 
are like the other parts of the soul in us. 
And the other things are analogous to our final 
parts. For not all our parts are equal. 
All things are therefore living beings according 
to the reason of the whole universe; everything 
in heaven, and all other things as many as 
are divided into the whole. And none of the 
parts, not even the greater ones, have the power 
to work a change of the things spoken of 
that occur according to the reasons—nor to 
alter them. But they can work something 
toward both sides, both making regions better, 
yet they cannot [change] those things 
from their proper nature. They will work 
worse things according to the passive body, 
either by the use of the bodily part, or 
when it receives within itself the cause of

cause, so that in all things a certain 
steady activity remains in it, just as the 
whole itself did not <unclear>seize</unclear> the lyres 
in such a way that they might have the 
accuracy of harmony for the purpose of 
musicians completing the sounds.

CONCERNING poverty, and wealth, and glory, 
and rule, how [is it]? Either the stars of 
the whole signify that some will be handed

well-born man from such ancestors. 
For by having that which is glorious, 
it [the star] only pointed it out. But if 
virtue being present has become a co-worker 
with the body, then those providing strong 
bodies contribute: parents first, then 
the place, if indeed the heavenly things

virtue is without the body, she alone

things from the ever-shining ones <note>The stars.</note> 
contribute; but if we were good, having given

# BOOK THREE.

<column-break/>

A similar cause must be assigned to these things. If **A** men are wicked, yet they have received gifts justly, it must be considered that this benefit came from something within them that acts according to what is best. But if the one who has gathered riches is evil, it must be judged that the primary cause is his own wickedness, as well as whatever cause led to that wickedness. Furthermore, those who contributed the wealth should be included in the order of causes. Consequently, if a 
plenty of goods arises from labor, as happens in **B** agriculture, the cause must be referred to the farmer, as well as the fertility of the soil and the mildness of the sky. But if one finds a treasure, it should be thought that something from the whole universe <note>original: "ex vniuerso"; Plotinus refers to the "All" or the Cosmic Soul.</note> concurred to that end; nor is it a wonder if these things are signaled by certain signs. For all things absolutely follow one another in turn, and therefore can be signaled everywhere. If someone produces wealth for himself, he is the cause. If it is snatched away, the robber is the cause; if a loss is made by shipwreck, many factors which constitute the cause of the loss have contributed. Glory is held either justly **C** or otherwise; if justly, it is gained both by one’s duties and by the fairness of those judging; if unjustly, it proceeds from the injustice of those bestowing the honor. The reasoning is the same regarding power <note>original: "imperio"; here meaning political command or rule.</note>. For it is possessed either honorably or the opposite. And one side has its cause in the fairness of those who chose the leader, or pertains to the one who attained it through the gathering of others and the favor of friends, or however else the matter stands. Marriage produces offspring, either through **D** choice or chance, and by a concurrence of all factors. The generation of children follows these, and the fetus is formed either according to the proper proportion of the women without any hindrance, or it turns out worse due to some internal impediment, or by a flaw in the one conceiving, or by a disposition of the father <note>original: "cotinentis"; likely referring to the male seed or the "holding" principle.</note> that is adverse to this conception.

<margin>
XV
On the primary power of souls: what power they have over the best things, and how they change according to... they signify properties in fate, for even power can be subject to fate.
</margin>

**Plato**, when he brought forward certain **E** Lots and choices joined together before the rotation of the worldly spindle <note>This refers to the "Spindle of Necessity" from the Myth of Er in Plato's Republic, representing the celestial spheres.</note>, subsequently described the powers of the Lot in the spindle itself, by which those things which had been chosen are completed; since a guardian spirit <note>original: "dæmon"</note> also approaches as a confirmer to fulfill these same things. But what are the Lots? Perhaps by the Lots is signified the disposition of the universe, as it was then, when the souls set out to enter a body. Likewise, it is signified **F** that they enter into this or that kind of body, and under such certain parents. Furthermore, it signifies being born in such a certain region, or what I was saying in summary: the concurrence of external things. All things are indeed made at the same time, and as if wound together <note>original: "conuoluta"</note> by one of the Fates named **Clotho** <note>The "Spinner" who weaves the thread of life.</note>: this is demonstrated in the whole as much as in the individuals. **Lachesis** <note>The "Allotter" who determines the length of the thread and the lot of life.</note>, however, brings the Lots themselves into the center: finally, **Atropos** <note>The "Inflexible" or "Inevitable" who cuts the thread.</note> necessarily effects that all these recurring events are carried out. Among men, however, some become **G** so fascinated by the whole and by external things that they are their own masters in few things, or in none at all. But others dominate external things, and lifting their heads toward the heights <note>original: "ad sublimia"; referring to the divine or intellectual realm.</note>, they surely preserve that which is best in the soul and the ancient character of its essence. For it must not be thought that the soul is such that it only carries back a nature such as whatever passion it has received from external things, as if it did not possess a nature of its own; rather, it is necessary that the soul itself, much earlier than other things—seeing as it holds the principle of reason—meritously exercises many of its own powers toward its natural actions.

[...to be] fulfilled. For it is impossible that, since it is an **A** essence, it does not also possess, along with that essence, desires and actions, and the capacity for living well. <margin>
The definition of the world soul, while the soul is distributed through seeds and reasons through individual things.
</margin>
**B** MOREOVER, we must next inquire—taking a new starting point—what that "together" <note>The composite of soul and body.</note> is, and what is not; what is separable and what is inseparable when it is in the body; and what an animal is in general. For not all thinkers have agreed on this matter. For the present, then, let us repeat what we were seeking in the previous sections: namely, how the order of things proceeds while the soul governs all things through a <term>seminal reason</term> <note>original: "seminariâ rationem"; these are the "logoi spermatikoi," the formative principles or blueprints that guide the development of the natural world.</note>. Does the soul then produce each individual thing in a kind of direct succession—for example, a human, then a horse, then another animal, and all the wild beasts? **C** Does it first see fire and earth, and then, seeing all these things concurring, either threatening or helping one another, does it only perceive the complexity made from all these and the resulting accidents in summary? Indeed, it does not notice or act upon the things that usually happen to these individually afterward; rather, it merely regenerates the prior animals again and leaves those that are born subject to the passions they inflict upon one another. **D** Or shall we say that the soul is the cause even of effects that arise in this way, because they are born from it and act accordingly? Does the <term>seminal reason</term> of the soul perhaps also contain within itself something of this sort: the power to do and to suffer such things individually? If so, then none of these things happens by chance or coincidence, but necessarily. If this is the case, do the "reasons" <note>The divine principles or blueprints.</note> themselves do these things? Or are the reasons not like agents, but rather like observers? **E** Nay, the soul, containing such reproductive reasons, knows whatever proceeds from all its works. For when the conditions and circumstances are the same, it is consistent that the same effects are produced. Grasping or foreseeing these, the soul determines and connects those things that follow. It therefore observes and cares for the preceding and following things, and again in those that come next, the preceding and following are connected as if from what came before. Thus, perhaps, the things that follow are continuously coming to an end: just as some men existed once, and others now, while in the meantime the "reasons" yield to the passions of matter through a certain perpetual distance and the necessity of degeneration. **F** Does it therefore always follow some things and then others, and diligently follow the passions of each of its works and lead such a life? Is it never free from the instant care of its individual works, nor does it impose a prescribed end on its work, as one who did not think out just once how its handiwork should always proceed correctly? Is it like a farmer who not only sows and plants, but also constantly corrects and restores what the winter rains, or the cold, or the blasts of the winds have devastated? **G** But if these things are absurd, perhaps it must be said that these things are already foreknown, or even...

<column-break/>

**A** Since that nature is a certain thing, it is not possible for it to be foreign, not having along with its being both desires and actions and the possession of what leads toward the good. That which is the "both-together" <note>The composite of soul and body.</note>, therefore, comes from the "both-together" of Nature, and is of such a kind, and has such works. But the soul which is separated acts in a separate and private way, and the passions of the body do not fail to be absent from it; but it already sees that one is one thing, and the other is another.

**B** But what the "mixed" is, and what is not, and what is separable and inseparable when it is in a body, or what the "living being" <note>Greek: "zoon"</note> is at all, we must seek later, taking a different starting point; for not all have set down the same opinion about them. But in the present, let us speak of how, while the soul manages the whole according to a "reason" <note>Greek: "logos"</note>, the details regarding each thing follow. For instance, **C** having made [one thing], does it then make an animal, then a horse, and another animal, and indeed the wild beasts? And fire and earth first, or seeing these things falling together, or the things here with one another? Or is it helped by the entanglements of all things, seeing only them, and the things that happen to it and occur afterward? Will it contribute nothing to what follows? Or does it only make the births of animals again in succession, and allow them to yield to one another through their passions? Or do we say it is the cause also of the things happening here, **D** because they are produced from it and work out the sequence? Or does the "reason" <note>logos</note> have the cause for this particular thing happening to that one? Nothing of these things happens randomly, nor by chance, but out of necessity in this way, as if the reasons themselves were doing them. Or are the reasons not "doing" them, but "knowing" them? Rather, the soul, having the generative reasons, knows the things that result from all its works. **E** For when the same things fall together and stand apart, the same things happen again. The soul, seeing those things which have proceeded further, finishes and weaves together the sequence with them. Preceding and following things are thus entirely [ordered], and again the preceding and following things are in sequence, as if from the present circumstances; whence perhaps the following things are always worse, such as men of old and men now, with the interval and the always necessary [decline], as the reasons give way to the passions of matter. **F** Does it then always follow some things and others, and following along with the passions of its own works, does it have such a life? And is it not released from the cares over its works... will it give an end to the poem and how it follows? Or **G** having contrived everything... like a farmer who, having sown or planted, always corrects the things that happen by storms or harm or frost? Or if these things are absurd—but if these are absurd—then we must say that it is already known, or...

# BOOK THREE

<column-break/>

...destined by the **A** rational principles <note>The "Logoi"—the divine blueprints or formative laws of the universe.</note>, namely destruction and those effects proceeding from vice. But if this is the case, we must say that even vices themselves arise from these rational principles, even though in the arts and the principles of the arts there is no error, nor is anything lacking in art, nor is there a destruction of the thing crafted. To this, someone will respond that nothing evil or contrary to nature happens to the universe as a whole, but that what seems "worse" must be conceded as ultimately being for the "better." What then, if even that which is worse **B** serves the universe, and it is not necessary for all things to be beautiful? Since even contraries contribute to the perfection of the whole, the world could not exist without them; indeed, nature holds itself in a similar balance within individual living beings. Certainly, reason itself necessarily brings forth and forms the things that are better; but those things which are less good lie in the rational principles according to a certain potentiality, but manifest in actual deed within the things that are born. Therefore, it is no longer necessary for the soul to do anything further, or to sustain the rational principles; for while the soul returns the material **C** world to a lower state through a certain jarring of the principles coming from preceding causes which it holds, it is nonetheless overcome by those same rational principles so that it might conceive better things. For this reason, a single beauty is created out of everything, while individual things result from matter itself in one way, and are contained and created within the rational principles in another.

<margin>XVI. Whether the seminal reasons are intelligent, or in what way they are reasons.</margin>

### **D** IT MUST BE ASKED, however, whether these <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original Latin: "seminales rationes"; Greek: "logoi spermatikoi." These are the life-principles that act like DNA or spiritual seeds to "program" the development of matter.</note> which exist in the soul are forms of intelligence. But in what way would the soul act through acts of intelligence? For the rational principle acts upon matter; and that which it effects naturally is neither an act of intellect nor a vision, but a certain power that stirs matter—not indeed knowing, but only acting, like a shape or figure forming in water. Just as from a circle made in one place, another circle might redundantly form elsewhere; for since it is the office of the natural and generative power to create, the principal power of the soul leads to this end, insofar as it moves and forms the material, generative soul. But does it move and form it by a certain **E** wandering of reason <note>original: "discursione"; refers to "discursive thought," the step-by-step logic humans use, as opposed to the instant intuition of the divine.</note>? If it acted by rational discourse, it would be a secondary thing. Is it then something else? Or rather, does it act upon those things which are within itself? Truly, if it acts upon what is within, there is no need for a wandering of reason. For it does not form things by moving them, but because it contains the rational principles within itself: for that is more powerful and more effective for acting upon the soul; therefore, it creates according to the <term>species</term> <note>The "Forms" or "Types" of things.</note>. It is necessary, therefore, that the soul itself, receiving the species from the Intellect, should pass them on. For the Intellect grants them to the Soul of the Universe; **F** and the Soul, being closest to the Intellect, passes them on from itself to the soul that follows after it, illuminating and forming it. This latter soul, being led by the order of the higher soul, creates species; but it creates some without hindrance, and others while being impeded, and for that reason, they are worse. Therefore, when it has received the power to act, and has not been previously imbued with the rational principles, it does not only act according to what it had received, but there arises from itself a "nothingness," and that is undoubtedly worse. And it will live indeed, but now more imperfectly and bearing its own life heavily, as if it were **G** most base, difficult, and wild; a thing composed of worse matter, like a sort of dreg settling from preceding things. This matter is bitter, and it makes things bitter; and such things it also brings into the universe. <margin>XVII. From where evils come, and what are "ill-begotten births" <note>original: "kakogenesiai".</note>.</margin>

<margin>A</margin> ...causes follow. Perhaps also because if these things <note>referring to the hardships or "evils" mentioned on the previous page</note> did not exist, the whole would be imperfect. For many evils—or rather, all of them—provide utility to the whole, just as venomous creatures do, even if the use and purpose of most of them remains hidden from us. Indeed, it is well established that wickedness itself contains much that is useful and produces many beautiful things in the manner of an intricate art. It often rouses men toward **prudence**, and does not permit them to grow sluggish through a license for luxury. If these things are correctly stated, it is necessary for the **Soul of the All** <note>The World Soul</note> to contemplate the highest things from another source, rising toward the **B** intellectual nature and God. And when she is filled and has become full, she overflows into her own image; this last and lowest part of her is a certain maker. Wherefore, this is the final producer; over this presides that which is first filled by the **Intellect** within the soul; and finally, the **Artificer Intellect** <note>The Demiurge or Divine Mind</note> presides over all things, who indeed pours forms into the soul closest to him, the traces of which are imprinted in the <margin>C</margin> third <note>The material world</note>. This world is rightly called an **image**, which is always in a state of becoming like its original. Thus, the first and second stand firm; the third also stands firm, but in matter; and therefore it becomes mobile, as if by accident. For as long as Intellect and Soul exist, so long do the **seminal reasons** <note>original: "rationes seminales" — the formative spiritual blueprints</note> flow into this image of the soul. Just as long as the sun itself thrives, all lights flow forth from it.
*The soul, just as long as the sun exists, so too these lights proceed from it.* <note>original: Ψυχῆς, ωστερ εως αύ ηλιοσ, ταυτα τα απ' αυτου φωτα.</note>

...if these things were not, the All would be incomplete. For the need for most of them is clear. And if the **Rational Principle** <note>The Logos</note> provides all things, even those of the lowest degree, then such things are revealed. Why? Because even through wickedness it <margin>that which</margin> holds many useful things for the whole, and is the maker of many beautiful things, such as the beauty of the art of the <margin>all-encompassing</margin> whole, and it rouses us toward wisdom, not allowing us to give way to fear. If these things are correctly said, then the soul of the All must always see the best things, going toward the **intellectual nature** and God. Being filled by this and having been made full, it is as if it overflows from itself, and that which comes from it is necessarily its lowest part, which is also a maker. This is the final maker; since indeed this part of the soul <margin>singular</margin> is that which is abundantly filled; and that which is over all is our leader, which also gives to the soul that comes after it, the traces of which are in the third. Thus it is rightly said that the world is an **image**, always being imaged. While the first and second stand, the third also stands, but in **matter** or moving by accident. For as long as Intellect and Soul exist, the Rational Principles flow into this form of the soul...

# MARSILIO FICINO’S COMMENTARY ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD CONCERNING MATTER.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut letter Q depicting a seated scholar or saint in a study, surrounded by books and a desk.</image-desc>
Since Plotinus nowhere speaks more beautifully, more clearly, nor more distinctly than when he disputes concerning the **formless**, the **obscure**, and the **indefinite** subject of things <note>Matter</note>, this book on matter does not seem to require an exact commentary so much as certain brief reminders. He will prove, therefore, that in both worlds—the **intellectual** as well as the **corporeal**—there is a certain matter of its own, and that in both realms it is one thing underlying all others. This matter differs as much from that as the forms of this world differ from the forms of that one. He will refute false opinions concerning matter; he will most diligently confirm the true ones. He will conclude that matter in both realms is a certain **infinity**, that is, a nature or power that does not set a limit to form but is only terminable and formable from another source. Furthermore, he concludes that matter in the divine world is indeed a "being," but one formable by an intellectual act. However, matter in the **sensible world** <note>The physical world we perceive</note> is not indicated to be truly a being, but rather a shadow of that higher being, perpetually subjected to the images of natural form as if to the shadows of that being.

### Diverse opinions of the philosophers concerning matter and that a certain matter exists even in incorporeal things.

<margin>1</margin> In the first chapter, he sets down a very general description of matter by way of its relation to forms: through which all have agreed that matter is the **receptacle of forms**, though different thinkers have explained the details in different ways. The **Stoics**, **Cynics**, and **Cyrenaics**, imagining nothing above the body, wished matter to be merely a substance. They held that forms were nothing other than certain "passions" or qualities of matter, and that matter itself was a body extended in three dimensions. We have refuted these thinkers extensively in the first book of our *Theology* <note>Ficino's "Platonic Theology"</note>. The **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists**, however, understood a certain matter even in incorporeal things. For just as they place something "formal" in both corporeal and divine things, so they grant in a certain way that there is something "material" in divine things, so that these lower things may be more aptly fitted to those higher ones, and that this order might exist from their order. For they have reasoned that the corporeal nature is derived from the animal nature, and the animal from the intellectual, and is composed by a certain similar proportion. Truly, we always find composition in bodies to be most perfect when it consists of matter and form. For in this alone is there the greatest union; since matter is something belonging to form, and form in turn is something belonging to matter. Indeed, matter is like **form in potentiality**, and form is like **matter in position**. Therefore, this union is similar to the dissonance in the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> arising from a double proportion, where the high voice joins with the low as form joins with matter to become one. If, therefore, there is any composition in the animal and intellectual nature—which there certainly is, since they exist after the "One" itself—it is surely a composition of this kind, in which there is both form and, moreover, something like matter. Regarding this matter, we dispute more widely in the seventeenth book of our *Theology* and in our commentary on the *Philebus*.

<summary>This page concludes Plotinus's argument that the physical world is a necessary and beautiful image of the divine realm, even including "evils" that serve the whole. It then begins Marsilio Ficino's commentary on the nature of matter, introducing the Platonic concept that matter exists in both the spiritual and physical worlds.</summary>
