# ON BOOK IV OF ENNEAD II.

### That there are not multiple equally first principles, and that matter originates from God

II. In the second chapter, he <note>Plotinus</note> asks whether there is any matter within the **intellectual nature**: and he brings forward five reasons why matter would seem not to exist there, which he will refute in what follows. You, however, will note among these points that there cannot be multiple principles that are entirely and equally "first," a point which we demonstrate sufficiently in our *Platonic Theology* <note original="Roman Theology">The transcription reads "Roman Theology," likely a reference to Ficino's *Theologia Platonica de immortalitate animae*</note> insofar as it pertains generally to principles. But regarding **God** and **matter**, and why they cannot be equal principles, pay attention here. The **Stoics** and their followers, and in a certain way even **Plutarch**, posited that matter was not alone: they claimed it existed from itself from eternity, alongside **God** the artificer of the world. They held matter to be alive but void of reason, tossed about inordinately by its own impulse, until it finally received reason from the divine, from which it began to be formed and moved by reason. Thus, they believe the world was once a "complication" which also existed before it was reduced into **chaos**, and conversely, it will one day be reduced into chaos again, having been reformed by **God** once and to be reformed by **God** again. Truly, those who seem to have taken the words of **Plato** in the *Timaeus* and the *Statesman* <note original="Politico">The Statesman</note> exactly as they sound to the ears have fallen into this opinion. **Porphyry** refutes these men abundantly in his commentary on the *Timaeus*: but out of the many arguments he brings forward, only three need to be reported at present, by which it is refuted that matter exists entirely from itself like **God**, as if these two were equal principles of all things, meeting each other from opposite directions. Thus he says: If neither **God** is from matter, nor matter exists from **God**, but both are equally principles: we ask, what is the cause of this difference by which they so differ? For **God** is indeed good and active, while matter is evil and passive. The cause of this difference cannot come from either of them, nor from both (since neither is more excellent than the other), nor again from some third thing above both, since nothing is placed higher. Therefore, since they differ from each other entirely, and there is no rational cause for the difference, it happens that the principle of such things is perhaps irrational. It certainly happens by chance that there are two; it happens by chance that they are principles. For their concurrence in being equally "first" has no cause—neither from one to the other, nor from a third determined thing—they concur by chance: and therefore, everything following this concurrence happens by chance. Furthermore, if **God** is fit for adorning matter, and matter is fit to be adorned by **God**, we ask: From where does this mutual fitness arise? For there must be something that reconciles them to each other; since these are greatly differing and opposite things, they would never be made fit for union by themselves. Divine things are not reconciled by a third party, nor do I admit **Fortune** as a reconciler. Finally, since matter is not sufficient by itself for its "well-being" <note>original: "bene esse," a technical term for a thing's perfection or flourishing</note>, but utterly needs **God** for this, while **God** is sufficient unto Himself for both "being" and "well-being," who does not see that **God** is superior to matter? And that matter itself could in no way provide for its own "being"? Otherwise, it would also provide for its own "well-being." Therefore, matter must come from the same **God** by whom it is not denied to be perfected.

---

### How God is infinite, and how there is a certain infinity in all things after God, like matter: and how composition differs in incorporeal and corporeal things.

III. He solves the reasons denying that there is matter in the incorporeal world in the third chapter. The **Good** itself <note>The One or God</note> is often called **infinite**, not because it is made of parts where one is bounded by another, nor because it is surpassed from without, nor constrained by any underlying limits, nor does it reach a boundary of power: hence it likewise reaches no boundary of perfection. **Matter** is also called infinite, not indeed as surpassing all things in power like **God**, but as being in need of boundaries, which it demands from above. Again, the **Good** itself is said to be **formless**, because it is superior to form; matter is also formless, because it is inferior to form. Yet it is not altogether nothing: for if order surpasses all things through itself, so that nothing is lacking, but is brought into entirely pure **actuality**; the thing formed ceases to be from the lowest level, present not as nothing, but as a similarly pure **potentiality** and a capacity for forms. We can conceive of such a subject not only in the corporeal world for the forms of bodies, but also in the incorporeal world, where it may support incorporeal forms. These we call "fountains" in that realm, and we do not begrudge them that name, since they are most obedient to forms and are always formed from the whole. Thus we are accustomed to praise the affection of the **irrational soul** when it offers itself spontaneously to be formed by the **rational soul**. We also praise the rational soul when it is similarly formed by the **Mind** <note>Intellect</note>. Composition also exists among those things, appearing to be something equal. Here, the material effect is produced; there, on the contrary, matter is always formed. Furthermore, we would condemn the composition in those things if it were a matter in which a certain form arises from parts after the parts; as is most common in bodies. But that there are many things there which do not so much "make one" as "act as one," befits divine matters. Indeed, matter and form there do not produce a third thing, nor is form properly compared to matter there as a habit to a potentiality, or a quality to a subject, but as **actuality** to a habit, and a higher act to a lower step. Therefore, they do not constitute the **Mind** as if they were parts, but they exist as something of the Mind, in which the Mind itself depends from eternity. There, therefore, form does not so much happen to matter as matter itself is proceeding into eternal **actuality**. Just as the whole of a living soul is one, in which many forms of parts are contained: so also the **Seminal Power** <term>Virtus seminalis: the formative principle or "seed-reason" that guides growth</term> is one power, but in it are many powers that form the many parts of the limbs. Meanwhile, a body is given where a secondary power is composed: for a common form does not arise from pure forms but from particular forms. In the **Seminal Power**, the form is then propagated into the forms of the parts. Here, then, it is not so much one made from many, as many propagated from one: otherwise, in the body, many things would never be so rationally led back to one, unless many preceded the one in the seminal reason, and similarly in the mind. Indeed, we ought not to reject composition either in the soul or in the mind. On this matter where **Plotinus** speaks of such composition, let these **English** <note>original: "Latina," referencing the translated text provided by Ficino</note> words represent the form: he suggests that the higher parent is the Mind, and that it is similarly composed of form. For since such a power does not consist in itself alone but gives birth in matter, and does not so much exist and act in itself as in matter and around matter, it is clear that it depends on another, leaning on something higher—that is, depending on the **Intellect**. And from there, he made it exist not only in the manner of something present, but to be preserved in the manner of a constant image; and he says the manifold reason and power of forms comes from the manifold **Intelligence**, although in a certain way the mass borrows from the immobile. He concludes, finally, that the thing which holds the place of matter in the soul and divine things may never change forms, since it possesses them all at once: all together in one, since they are entirely in the same—if I may say so—sign of themselves, by which it is made so that the whole is everywhere in a quiet possession of all. Furthermore, since the [catchword: itself]

<summary>Ficino argues against the Stoic view of eternal, independent matter, asserting instead that God is the sole first principle and the source of matter. He also explains the concept of "intellectual matter," describing it as a pure potentiality in the divine realm that is eternally and perfectly filled by forms.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II, Book 4. Ficino is exploring the paradox of "intelligible matter"—the idea that even in the perfect, divine realm of the Mind, there must be a kind of "substrate" that allows for the variety of different Ideas.</meta>

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO
<meta>catchword: videtur (it seems)</meta>

matter, on account of its extreme poverty <note>original: *inopiam*; a reference to the Platonic idea that matter is a "beggar" lacking its own form</note> and its unquenchable desire for change among us, is rightly called the origin of mutability here. Wherever there is matter, there is change; only where matter is entirely absent is there no evil. Nor indeed, from the fact that matter and form are found together there <note>in the higher, divine realm</note>, should we think any less of that place where order resides (so to speak), just because we imagine matter to precede form. This pertains to order, not to time; matter is prior in "origin" rather than in time, for time measures the order in motion from what comes before to what comes after. There could, therefore, be a certain original order in the higher realms of these things to those: of the things of a certain "matter" to form, just as in this world substance sustains light with no intervening interval of time. Nor again, because the matter of each individual thing seems to be something to shrink from, should the name of "matter" be dreaded among the higher beings. For even in bodies, the origin of dimensions arises from the "form of the body," and it is within the body itself, yet it is not truly judged to be "corporeal" <note>Ficino is distinguishing between the physical "stuff" and the mathematical or metaphysical extension that underlies it</note>.

->*That in the intelligible world there is something similar to matter, and concerning the Idea.*<-

<margin>III</margin> In the fourth chapter, he <note>Plotinus</note> proves that in the intellectual world <note>the realm of pure thought and divine ideas</note> there is something in some way similar to matter. It would have the same relationship to what follows it in that same genus, a point which we prove abundantly in our *Theology* <note>Ficino's *Platonic Theology*</note>. Certainly, from the fact that there are many **species** <note>original: *species*; here meaning "distinct types" or "Ideas"</note> in the Mind, it is established that the essence of the Mind—which is the first power of the Mind—exists as something else besides the Ideas, and therefore it underlies them here as a kind of matter for some form. That there are different **reasons** <note>original: *rationes*; the formative principles or "blueprints" of things</note> or formal structures between them is clear, because from that source—that is, from the first variety of forms—distinct forms proceed in the order of things. They do not come from the lowest matter, for things are not divided into parts by chance, nor finally from various agents, unless there is one directing all things toward one end. This one end is known as the "reason" in a uniform mind, pertaining to the necessary order of the universe. The distinction here is produced from the scattered things, but in what way? This has been said elsewhere and remains to be said. Now we observe that the Mind does not employ its breadth like a painted tablet, but rather as if it were applying species; otherwise, it would not be a "one," but a congregation and an aggregation. In truth, the intellectual nature is a "one" that, so as to obey the intellect, might be called "the rest," meeting in species from a single source. That is, the Ideas agree as if belonging to a general nature, but differ among themselves through various habits of the intellect. This nature of intelligence is not only rational (so to speak) but also possesses varieties of formative efficacy, like formal modes. These particular forms approach the general nature of intelligence itself to complete the ideal species. Indeed, **Dialectic** <note>the philosophical art of logical division and synthesis</note>, which sorts that "genus" (as I might call it) into species, does not seek it from a source outside of the innermost parts. That natural thing which is distributed—namely, the essence—is like an "animal": that into which it is distributed are like the parts of the animal. But that which performs the distribution is the very power of intelligence, strengthened by the Good, like a creative power through which various divine powers are pursued. Because they are distinguished, they bring forth another most absolute form; certainly, the nature itself, the norm of the mind toward things, behaves as matter. Thus, let the corporeal world be an image of the higher world, reflecting the corporeal world as a model: if our speech refers to the multiform, then this matter refers to that <note>intelligible matter</note>. But in this case, things are indeed in a "one," not a whole cast into parts. There, however, that entire intellectual nature is contained in any Idea, but in different ways, as will be declared elsewhere. Then, truly, as things in that world are further distant from each other in parts, it will have the same matter as our world. <gloss>Namely</gloss> for this is the passion <note>experience or state</note> of our matter; but he notes that although matter properly admits sectioning, matter does not admit division into parts from itself, nor would quantity suffer that again if it were far from matter, separated by form. Thus, matter is read as "how much" <note>quantitative</note> of a part, when there is quantity or matter alone. But if any of those things which are joined there are like many things within themselves, and the rest are simply simple, so that the whole is nowhere seen by itself: again there was distance. There is, however, something from afar that seems to be there, but something else finding its way to the others, which is the "matter" when many primary things are observed, they are contemplated as one under many numbers. Indeed, the multiple and multiform first offer themselves there. He says the former is involved in the same way as a mover; how could I deny that the material itself becomes prior? How great a thing it is for the "matter" of things to be the very acting forms, whereby what is material here becomes actual there. Now, since "being" simply precedes this essence in reality, weight is rightly considered to be there when being is multiple and formal.

### *Confirmation of the above concerning the penetrative and resolutive power of the mind: what the similarity of lower matter to higher matter is, and what the dissimilarity is, and how it is constituted from "otherness" and motion.*

<margin>IV</margin> In the fifth chapter, he resolves the objections that could be made against what was said, and at the same time confirms his statements. He warns us not to deny that there is some matter in the higher realms just because essence there always possesses these forms and is simultaneously a "one." For even here, where our matter is always formed, it constitutes a "one" with form. Matter is no less hidden there than it is always hidden here. The intellect devises this; the intellect finds this by <unclear>investigating</unclear>. Truly, the powers of intelligence, being most effective, naturally penetrate and resolve all things like fire. Because it is similarly simplified, it never rests until it reaches the simplest order. In analyzing living things, the mind conjectures that what lies beneath the formal reasons of things—least hidden to them—is matter, like a "depth" <note>original: *profundum*; the Greek *bathos*, a term for the underlying substrate</note>. He says the formal reason is the substance, while those things that surpass them are placed as if between the sublime and the deep. Indeed, if you see the formal reasons of things entirely segregated from matter, and yet turning their efficacy toward matter, you will see these very things in nature, and nature itself. Furthermore, if you imagine such formal reasons not only segregated but turning their efficacy toward themselves, you will immediately contemplate the **Mind**. For the **Divine Mind** is the exemplary reason of the universe, effective through a connection to itself, knowing and making all things at once. Then, indeed, any mind born from there is full of formal reasons and the essence of forms for things. These formal reasons are like certain rays of divine intelligence, matching their own reasons. Therefore, just as the eye, created and greeted by the sun, looks at colors everywhere in the solar light, and is accustomed to call what lies beneath them "darkness," so any intellect created by the Divine Mind, and imbued with the lights of the Ideas from there, always hunts for ideal similarities in the formal reasons of things. It gladly recognizes them and, beneath the forms—which are like the lights of divine intelligence—it prophesies that matter lies hidden, just as in the things of the lower world. And because matter is by itself devoid of forms (the ideal reasons), it is therefore "dark." Remember, however, that corporeal matter does not agree in "genus" with that incorporeal matter of the world, but rather in a certain "relationship" <note>original: *habitudine*; an analogy of proportion</note>; for each relates similarly both to its own forms and to the "One" itself.

<summary>Ficino explains that "matter" exists even in the divine Mind as a metaphysical substrate (intelligible matter) that allows for the diversity of Ideas. He describes the intellect's power to "penetrate" through forms to find this hidden depth, comparing the process to how light reveals color but leaves the underlying subject in darkness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, Ennead II, Book 4, which investigates the nature of "matter" in both the divine (intelligible) and physical (sensible) realms.</meta>

# ON BOOK 4 OF ENNEAD II.

It seems, therefore, that it is defined almost similarly through its forms in act: both are, as it were, similarly referred back to the One. Thus, indeed, it flows from there to the One in the same way: I say that this proceeds entirely even far from here: now from here over the circumference through the middle; then it becomes inferior. For that which is determinable with knowledge is an excellence; again, between themselves, these and those are something else. For just as these two parts we mentioned become one, so too that [higher realm] in turn holds them as one in the mind. Therefore, the soul seems to have the rational principles <note>original: *rationes*; the formative blueprints or "Logoi"</note> of bodies within itself, as well as certain affections <note>original: *affectus*; the ways a thing is moved or influenced</note>, directed toward this matter like passions <note>original: *passiones*; the state of being acted upon</note>. This is what happens: just as they hold the place of forms there, so it is carried from here and presently they call it from there: and it is one. For from the One comes conversion, affection, and firmness, now downward, and they seem presently to terminate both matters. 

But they also differ from each other: these [lower] from those [higher], because these are produced proximately by the soul, while those are from the Intellect, or God. This matter also differs from that one, because this [lower] matter is an "imaginable depth," while the other is a "depth of forms." In this matter, they seem to differ: for those higher forms are certain, and are only of matter; without forms, those forms are nowhere by themselves apart from matter, but are essence. And those things which are in the soul, he calls this matter "essence." Yet this thing too—from which it is called essence—is clearly so if these essences are compared to the perfection of the highest things. After this, he will observe to what extent this and that are the same: always indeed the same, but again always in act, for the form was presently joined in that higher realm. In matter, however, the world comes from itself; it is no longer in another, but either exists or is always becoming from it, and again from it, mobile—as they say of light in the air. That which flows below the moon sometimes perishes; thus, a cloud <note>original: *nimbus*</note> fills all eternity, and likewise the light always does; but those things under it fill a certain part. 

Thus, the things from here in the intelligible world have essence and a "formable" quality: this very thing proceeds as something formed in a certain order—I say by order, not by time—for the form is more truly the fullness and the lot of these things. We consider also the One of that Father as both One and as the Good in unity: the most eminent simplicity in goodness, and a fecundity that is entirely communicable. We think that what is in the intelligible world hangs from the Unity—wonderfully segregated from all things—holding the place of matter that is solitary and as yet indistinct. It is segregated from the following forms; but from the Good, it has that which is formable and cooperative by the communication of that second level. On the side of that world, we distinguish unity and goodness by this relation; thus in that world, instead of essence, we distinguish the formable from the ideal form, and we distinguish the ideal forms among themselves by reason. 

But we have suspected poorly until now, unless we finally arrive at such a distinction of matter: thus by matters, places, and times of distance. Where there is matter here, let form follow form. But we recall matter to this point again. After what follows: the essence and substance of the thing itself depends somewhat on that which is not itself. Therefore, this thing which is "by itself" is not the thing itself. And because it is not the One itself, it clearly comes from the One. It depends indeed from there: according to which this seems to be, yet is not true, because it seems to be of another and diverse. These two therefore follow each other: since there is a rational principle, but in it, thus in both. For not everywhere is whatever comes from something immediately and completely such as its source. Then indeed, matter has no rational principle from the forms or ideals, but is called "toward matter." This rational principle participates in this very "being"—namely, in "depending"—just as another thing comes from light and something else from fire. 

The Pythagoreans <note>Ancient followers of Pythagoras who saw numbers as the fundamental reality</note> called this "primary matter." Just as the rational principles are first from themselves, so they are toward unity and thereafter: thus in the first things of the world, primary matter is again a procession from goodness. There is also a certain cause from the elements of the genus and the qualities, namely those dependent on certain things, which strive toward one from an equal; just as whatever was aiding here as a formed image might lie by itself, where matter again prevails toward perfection, they might be converted back to that place from whence they proceeded. These are the tertiary and rare apparatuses it seems to fill. To what end would they persist effectively in matter? Yet it does not lack "conversion" <note>original: *conversio*; the Neoplatonic return of the soul or matter toward its divine source</note>, if only this conversion happens opportunely: since its appetite follows from the state of the property of matter. What they truly acquire through this appetite seems to be what was below, which is properly turned toward form. 

After this, a "five" <note>the Pentad</note> follows from Lucanus <note>likely Ocellus Lucanus, a Pythagorean philosopher</note>, which again pertains to the "seven" <note>the Septenary</note> toward the end, the minimum of action. The seven leads to the ultimate end; had it not likewise been an act. Here again, it flows together in numbers: thus also again that from the agent which was likewise absolute: again the lower, and it acts in the superior rest. But lest these things perhaps disturb you, remember that where there is already some being in act, consider that this evil is not a being in nature, which is being itself: which is by consensus, before it becomes from another, or is not another. Matter itself: by what formal and ideal reason it lacks, even though it depends on another; depending from there, it is almost not that from which it depends, except under an absolute reason. For this too is its rational principle: namely, dependency itself, and negation itself; finally, it is considered the most vile of all things. Therefore, what Plotinus says—that matter consists of change and alteration—you can understand in what way we say it. One can also understand it otherwise from that which is in each thing again: and again its condition exists as a certain determined perfection; where, because nothing further is required. But an indeterminate and imperfect condition properly pertains to matter: since from that which is in some thing, there is alterity and diversity; if only a true union is made there, one thing is in the place of act and form, and another in the place of power and matter: indeed, and the effect of it also is "not to be that." This very thing which is said "not to be that," turning as if toward a negative and indeterminate condition, pertains to matter.

### Proof that matter exists in bodies.

He begins the sixth <note>chapter</note> with arguments by which he shows that matter is in bodies. **First**, from the mutual commutation of the elements, which neither makes something out of nothing, nor leads anything into nothing; therefore it is necessary on both sides that matter be subject to the mutation of forms. **Second**, from a certain dissolution of the compound. **Third**, from resolution reduced all the way to the extreme. **Fourth**, he confirms the same from the nature of elements. For in vain does air come from water, perhaps because they change in "where": nor does whatever was in the water perish, as if something were being led into nothing, since the intention of nature is not toward evil, nor otherwise would it be created from nothing. For certainly something does not come from just anything, much less does something realistically come from nothing. There remains, therefore, something which, putting off the form of water, in turn puts on the form of air: this contains the subject of matter, which can subsist as neither that which leaves nor that which approaches, and yet mutation, as the weakest accident, indicates the foundations. **Fifth**, lest he deny that matter is subject to natural forms, remember: since form is the principle of action, it is rightly judged to be a certain act; but act, by the reason that it is act, cannot properly suffer <note>original: *pati*; to be the passive recipient of an action</note> since it acts. Since, therefore, natural things mutually suffer from one another, it is established that besides the forms by which they act...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, Ennead II, Book 4. Having previously discussed the existence of "intelligible matter" in the divine realm, he now focuses on the nature of physical matter in the sensible world, defining it through its relationship to form and potentiality.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...to have matter, that is, an essential potentiality <term>potentiality: the capacity to become something or be acted upon, as opposed to "actuality"</term> through which they might be acted upon, and that this matter underlies all things as one, so that they may more easily be acted upon by one another and be exchanged. But this path certain of our arguments in the *Platonic Theology*, Book I, chapter five, finish in a more popular <note>original: *plebius*; simplified for a general audience</note> way; and here we confirm it again with a new reason. Among mathematicians, a body is limited at the boundaries which, if they are absent from external things—namely in two surfaces, one of depth and the other of height—are neither bodies themselves, and are certainly something other than nothing. So among the physicists, a body is limited by an internal boundary, which is neither a body nor nothing, namely, that which is raised into form from the infinite into matter. For the order of beings in their descent, before it is thought to end in nothingness (which seems the external extreme), must be limited by a certain boundary joined to itself. This is nothing other than one of the beings: for beneath any act lies that which can be made and which can be acted upon by the act. Therefore, this extreme is a potentiality capable of acts and subject to being acted upon. But potentiality toward action, or toward their acts, is not indeed altogether nothing, but is indicated rather as the lowest of beings. This lowest, being as it were indefinite and seeking a boundary from another, reflects the infinity and matter of the superior world—the infinity also in any intellect, the infinity again in the soul of the world, and in nature itself, which Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the role of the divine in the material world</note> testifies is a material infinity everywhere. And since the wise call it (to use his words) essentiality itself <note>original: *essentialitatem*</note>, through which that one matter is produced into bodies, and as Proclus <note>One of the last major Greek Neoplatonists who systematized the philosophy</note> concedes, nature itself also acts toward this, as we have declared elsewhere. Finally, since nothing can look toward the ideal reasons <term>ideal reasons: the divine blueprints or "Logoi" in the mind of the Creator</term> except formal things, and therefore matter is not an idea, it is clear that since the world is a necessary work produced by some power, the ideas and the ideal craftsman lead the first origin in the beginning—namely, from the essence itself of the craftsman, which in a certain order precedes the ideas and the property of craftsmanship, and finally is itself one above essence, through which variety is most simple and wonderfully separated from all things. But from these things, it is indicated that matter is produced not only through the formal act in the craftsman, but also through the formable essence in the soul of the world and nature through continuation. I say matter is like one infinite thing—not just those things which exist by themselves, but the fruit by which they are born. Just as the One itself is superior to both. Thus in the *Parmenides* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the nature of the "One" and the "Many"</note>, whatever is said about the One simply, without the existence of those things following it, is denied of the imperfect one as far as it is in unity; those things which truly exist are affirmed properly through form. Concerning matter, about the one which is in those things being born, it seems to be affirmed partly according to form and partly according to participation. But the same things again are denied of the one matter of all things, as if responding from the opposite, primarily because of a defect of the exterior: so much so that nothing can be found (so to speak) more similar to the One than this last One, provided that assimilation is thought through dissimilarity, and comparison is made through negation, and an infinite defect is referred to an infinite excess.

->False opinions about matter are refuted.<-

VII. In the seventh chapter, he reproves four false opinions about matter. First, that of Empedocles, who splits matter and element, thinking the four elements are the ultimate result of resolution. This is false because an element is dissipated, but matter is by no means a "what-ness" <term>quiddity: the essence or "what-ness" that makes a thing what it is</term>, as we proved in *Theology* I, chapter five. The second is usually ascribed to Anaxagoras; for some say (if it is right to believe it) that Anaxagoras posited two principles of things: intellect and matter, and that matter is neither from intellect nor born from it, and that it already has the forms themselves within it, but confusedly, though they are discerned by the intellect. This mixture is confirmed by the fact that all things are imperfect and hindered by each other. Matter is also imperfect, seeking its own: this is not valid. Since all these imperfect things cannot be made except by themselves, but have being through a certain participation, it follows that there is a prior essence above this essence, and confused by a similar condition, lest a higher thing be forced to need something again. Now, the essence of the craftsman is superior to matter, so that he can dominate matter and by dominating it, perfect the forms. Similarly, the superiority and ease with which he moves matter from another and forms the craft would be lost if matter already contained the forms within itself. If matter had from a primary force an essence entirely formless in itself, it would yield to all things with wonderful ease; whereas if forms were already in it, he would be drawing them out from within the matter, and his labor in discerning the confused forms would be like a struggle. Against this and after these is the opinion of Anaxagoras, or (as they say) of Anaximander (as it is reported), who says matter is infinite. He calls this "learned" <note>original: *eruditum*</note> because it cannot be traversed, or this will be primarily infinite through itself and in itself—that is, formal infinity itself, which contains all things in act within another. Not in the first way, certainly, for that which is thus infinite consists of wholes, with infinite parts, so that those things which are purely in it are only together as part of motion, nor does part differ from part or from the whole. Nor also in the second way by chance, that which happens to be infinite, nor would it be immense before this addition, so that it would not contain the infinite. And whatever it may be, matter is not that which happens, because it is in another. Again, matter is not that from which it happens, if it were already one of the opinions already posited, nor is this whole composite prime matter, because it is not simple, but something separable in the wholes. But there was also among those Anaximenes, positing air as the matter of things—that is, a certain infinite and entirely formable vapor <note>original: *vespida*; likely a corruption or specific term for 'mist/vapor'</note>. But neither is any body an individual, nor is magnitude corrected from the number of individuals, nor does continuity and the moisture of bodies coalesce from things seen discretely which lack them, nor is life created from a single rarity, nor does order happen by chance, belonging rather to intelligence and art. Neither art, whether natural or acquired, can ever fashion anything from materials that naturally flee continuity.

->Matter is not quantity, nor does it have its own quantity. Likewise, the formal reason draws a certain quantity with it, not the other way around.<-

VIII. Concerning this same matter, which is the one vessel of the world, it is also continuous—that is, everywhere whole through itself—and not like atoms; there is a difference, and being devoid of all form, he says, it becomes something especially: so that if anything now exists without any "what," it is thought of as most powerful. In the beginning, it is not a body, as if it lacked form; if a body is resolved into matter and form, matter does not have it, even if it seems to penetrate bodies as if naked. If matter is only form, it is not matter as a "what," but because of its own qualities, from which it becomes otherwise, and Plotinus here treats how to bring this about. Finally, the agent making it is "how much" <term>quantity: the extension or size of a thing</term> before that "how much" which underlies it from matter is prior, just as nature, which is prior to art, is subjected to matter first. But this is once again as if matter were first subjected to the first; I am entirely formless just as that is all-formed. Since, however, quantity is first of all formal, and like matter it is ineffective and most subject to being acted upon, and this exists with difficulty from matter, he therefore examines more carefully both here and in what follows whether matter is quantity, or at least has its own...

<summary>Ficino defines matter as the ultimate potentiality and the lowest level of being, serving as a boundary before nothingness. He refutes the views of early philosophers like Empedocles and Anaxagoras, arguing that matter must be formless and void of quantity to be properly shaped by the divine craftsman.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Ennead II, Book 4, "On Matter." Having established that matter exists in both the divine and physical realms, Ficino here argues that physical matter must be entirely devoid of its own "quantity" (size and shape) so that it can perfectly receive the forms imposed upon it by the divine Artisan.</meta>

->ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD. 151<-

...should possess quantity. Indeed, it is clear that matter does not have its own quantity, since it is indifferent to being great or small; rather, it becomes a "quantified thing" from an external source. Since quantity is one thing, and the "quantified" <term>quantified: something that has been given a specific size or dimension</term> is another, there are two types of quantified things: one belonging to matter and the other to the composite <note>original: *compositi*; a thing made of both matter and form</note>, both of which will be indicated here. Pious reason suggests that something must be joined to it first, and so it is not the case that primary matter possesses quantity of its own; for in order for it to be primary matter, the first thing capable of being formed, and the first thing capable of receiving, it must be completely formless throughout. Just as you have accepted that the Author <note>The "Artisan" or Creator (Demiurge)</note> of forms is the first "Fullness," He does not simply make a form within matter out of all forms; rather, in the manner of a seal-maker, He expresses and impresses a seal upon matter from every side, using the forms He holds within Himself. When I speak of forms, I also include quantity as something formal, existing in matter that has been prepared to be one; it seeks unity, whether it is extended, asserted, or <unclear>closed</unclear>. Likewise, He is the artisan of all things because He is the universal and primary <unclear>artisan</unclear>. Furthermore, this matter must not oppose its own quality (if it had any) to the quality of the artisan. Nor, if it possessed its own quantity or shape, would it resist the artisan like something imperfect—or at least force Him to grant forms according to its own limits rather than by His own authority. 

Now, truly, since He is the one who first gives what He bestows, and hands it over to an empty matter, it rightly faces no obstacle; nor does He necessarily bring quality to a pre-existing quality, nor again in accordance with a pre-existing quantity, since the First Being bestows the first quantity. You should consider these words to be spoken concerning the universal Artisan of nature and the primary formation of things through that first Artisan. We consider, moreover, in our minds, that the will of the universal Artisan is not bound by a certain magnitude of matter during the process of thickening <note>original: *concretionis*; the process of becoming solid or physical</note> and appearing, to the point that the mode of the form would be forced to follow the mode of the quantity. For if those two should meet by chance, then "luck" <note>original: *fortuna*</note> would be the foundation of order. That which exists in things by accident would then be prior and superior to that which exists through itself. 

Again, do not think that the first Author, in His primary action, depends upon a certain quantity of matter; much less upon a certain shape, otherwise He would be hindered in many actions. But know that this Artisan, who precedes matter in order and power, dominates matter with the highest liberty and labors not at all in forming it, lest any error should ever occur in the work. Therefore, He moves the primary things and forms matter according to His own nature, reason, and will, rather than according to the mode of some quantity. Since He moves and acts not through quantity, but through effective form, the movement first responds to His action in matter as a form of that kind; then, an attached quantity accompanies the form. Indeed, matter is moved and stretched toward the formal impulse of the action and the entry of the effective form—it is extended, I say, specifically to the extent that the form penetrating it then stirs it with an impulse; then the Ideal Reason itself prescribes it; and finally, the formal or "seminal" reason <term>seminal reason: the internal blueprint or "seed" within matter that directs its growth</term> demands it. 

It is not without reason that a certain quantity or shape follows a certain species, rather than the other way around. For these two <note>quantity and shape</note>, being less perfect, depend on form as if flowing from it; and as though they were not effective themselves, they serve the effectiveness of the form, are encompassed by the logic of that form, and are brought into being. Do not doubt that quantity is contained by form. For quantity is a kind of form; and as something less "formal" in its appearance, it is contained by a more "formal" reality; like something folded up there, it is soon unfolded within the matter. Hence it happens that certain species of living things have certain magnitudes and shapes. That quantity pertains to form and is not matter itself is clear from the fact that it possesses the principle of unity where it <unclear>is known</unclear> and counted in determining things. Matter, however, is clearly only that which is capable of being determined and serves as a <unclear>basis</unclear>. I pass over how much the forms of things, as they are brought in everywhere, either differ among themselves or frequently promote changes in both quantity and shape. This would surely never happen to pure matter. Our minds often truly recoil from the effects created by shapes and numbers in the body. Certainly, it is posited that form exists before the "quantified"; <unclear>for</unclear> something would not be quantified unless it simply *was*. Moreover, to "be" and to "be one" comes before "to be quantified." It seems, therefore, that "being simply," which precedes being quantified, is first extended in thought, and only then becomes quantified after it has been made into something extended. This very portion of being which is stretched out is matter already made corporeal and is a quantity of a certain <unclear>vastness</unclear>. Extension indeed understands the subject; since it is an accident <term>accident: a property that a thing has, but which is not essential to its being what it is</term>, and a certain passion not necessarily following the formal reason. Now, something might be extended and yet not stretch itself out by its own nature: this very thing which is stretched out is the matter subject to extension, being prior to the extension itself. Unless it is somehow stretched toward the One, it cannot prevail. 

Nor is it permitted to stop here and say that form is the subject of quantity. For any other form, being incomparably more effective than quantity, does not submit to it, but rather subdues quantity. Finally, what is called "body" in the intelligible world is a power present before all things and exempt from the lower; through this, matter is reflected in the sensible world as if it were an image of that power. Whatever abundance of virtue is there, appearing as "matter," seems to be reflected through this matter here. Since, therefore, quantity and matter do not look toward the same thing, they are certainly not judged to be the same essence. But who does not see that numbers exist even in things separated from matter? And that points, lines, and even surfaces are neither matter nor have a necessary requirement for matter? Conclude, then, that quantity is something formal, depending on the Agent rather than on the matter. And since it is the least among formal things, it is rightly bestowed everywhere just as the more excellent form requires.

### Confirmation of the above.

**IX** Indeed, lest you perhaps wonder that no quantity is contained in the very principle of matter, and that matter is not "quantified" by itself, remember: since there are many things besides quantity—such as substances and qualities and the like—the reason of "being" is rightly different from the reason of "quantity," and it is both more fitting and prior. Therefore, many things can both be and be understood, even if they do not exist or are not understood as being quantified. If we generate quantity from all that is quantified, then neither is the matter "quantified" (which precedes bodies), nor is quantity itself "quantified," lest we go on into infinity. Since the "quantified" is posited so that it may *become* quantified; just as something becomes "qualified" by a quality. From this it is also confirmed that quantity is something formal. Just as a <unclear>living thing</unclear> becomes colored by a natural color, yet the color itself is not "colored." Nor again is the whole formative power, which creates the natural color in an animal, itself a color. Similarly, neither the quantity nor the shape suitable for a living thing is itself "quantified" or "shaped," nor is the seminal virtue of such a shape and quantity another quantity or shape. Then, truly, just as a quality (as an accident) coming to matter makes that which was not yet "qualified" suddenly "qualified," so also quantity, by approaching matter, makes that which was not yet "quantified" simply "quantified." Nor should you think that matter, upon the arrival of the first quantity, is stretched out into something wider from something narrower. For "narrowness" and "width" are certain modes of the existence of quantity. Before the first arrival of quality, quantity is not in the matter, and therefore the modes of quantity are not there either.

->COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

And from this, the formal definition <term>formal definition: the essential logic or "blueprint" of a thing</term> of quantity is neither large (otherwise it would not fit small things) nor, on the other hand, is it small (otherwise it would not be able to accommodate itself to large things). Similarly, matter itself is not properly "this much" or "that much," so that it remains equally indifferent to undergoing all modes of quantity. Nor, again, is it "quantity" in a simple sense, lest it possess something formal within itself without being a composite <note>original: *composita*; a thing made of both matter and form</note>.

### How matter may be known, since it is formless.

It is therefore doubted how matter can be known, since it lacks all forms. It is usually necessary for the thing to be known to move the knower through its form, and then for the knowers to act upon the thing to be known through a form that matches it. Since cognition occurs through forms, we seem consequently destined to think of things with form, not formless things—unless, perhaps, by a mental effort, we strip away all forms from the soul and attempt to grasp something in objects that is likewise stripped of all forms. But while we make this effort, we certainly do so through a certain form; thus, many of us struggle with a form even while we think of it as formless—specifically, when we imagine the "indefinite" to the best of our ability. Under such a form, we suspect there is an indefinite matter. Thus, through a certain indefiniteness of our own conception, we think of the indefiniteness of matter. A certain indefiniteness helps toward this, existing naturally as a sort of material hidden beneath the soul's form. 

If an infinite circle were imagined, the definition and logic of the circle would be finite and certain, but the act of the eye or a similar act of the imagination would wander infinitely through that infinite circle. Similarly, if someone were to strip away all forms and direct the sharp edge of the mind toward matter, just as the eye does toward an object, they would see absolutely nothing—just as the eye sees nothing when light and color are removed from everywhere. But here, the soul conjectures that an obscure body lies beneath when light is removed. Does it not also conjecture there that a formless thing lies beneath when forms are taken away? It conjectures as best it can; yet this kind of conjecture is neither a legitimate reasoning (which usually conceives forms by following the mind's ideal reasons derived from forms) nor is it a legitimate act of the imagination (which usually views forms either from the mind or the senses). Therefore, this grasping of matter is a mixture of "spurious reason" and "adulterous imagination" <note>original: *spuria ratione et adulterina imaginatione*; terms Ficino borrows from Plato’s *Timaeus* to describe the "bastard logic" used to perceive matter, which has no true form to hold onto</note>. 

But this very indefiniteness of the soul regarding the suspicion of matter’s indefiniteness still contains something defined, insofar as the soul acts through forms and defines something about matter. Yet, the soul does not "understand" it in the strict sense; for understanding is the contemplation of Ideas, or at least of ideal things. Nor is it properly "reasoning," for reasoning is a kind of gathering or collection of thoughts. Here, however, the soul does not so much gather as scatter, while it denies all things of matter. For if it affirms anything, it stands as a denial of internal traits. When it affirms that matter is the receptacle of all flowing things, it confirms that matter is formless in itself. And since the soul—being a species <term>species: here meaning a formal essence or type</term> and a true essence—denies forms and essence to matter, it must reject everything. Just as it first knows by denying, so it then knows by referring. In this way, the knowledge of the lowest of things <note>matter</note> and the knowledge of the highest <note>God/The One</note> seem similar in some way. But you, when Plato says "like is known by like," must understand that a thing capable of being known is something akin to the knower before the act of knowing, and in the act of cognition itself, it produces a form or undergoes the condition of the object. Conclude again: where cognition is more effective, there the similarity is greater. And since intelligence is that which not only touches a thing externally (as the senses do) but also penetrates it most effectively, it follows that this logic and knowledge of essence exist more truly than physical location in a body.

### Matter is not quantity, nor does it have its own quantity; Likewise the reception of forms is not by reason of quantity, but by reason of matter. Likewise form precedes quantity.

Accordingly, he confirms that matter is not "something quantified" against those who claim there is nothing else in things called "matter" besides the dimension underlying quality—a view Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century philosopher whose interpretations of Aristotle often clashed with Ficino’s Platonism</note> seems to hold regarding the heavens. He refutes them. Others thought that because dimension is present in things and is suited to the wise, matter itself was dimension. These people respond to Plato, who proves that dimension is also necessary for the very reception of form, since the mind and soul grasp things without dimensions. Furthermore, since "to be" simply precedes "to be quantified," quantity rightly happens to a being later. It follows that matter does not receive form because of quantity. Similarly, matter receives quantity without a preceding quantity; therefore, its ability to receive anything else is not because it is quantified, but because it is matter—since matter was the first thing to which other things were added. 

It happens, however, that matter receives forms within dimension, because just as it receives the forms of different things, quality is extended in it when space is produced, and contracted when space is narrowed. But from the very intent of nature, the species <note>the formal type or essence</note> and its primary properties seem to be prior to its quantity or shape. Therefore, matter is naturally established such that its most powerful preparation is for the species rather than for any specific quantity. I speak of simple and "prime" matter; for "secondary" matter <term>secondary matter: matter that has already been given some basic form, like the four elements</term>, already prepared in a certain way for some species, cannot help but receive a size suitable to it. But even before magnitude, a certain quality of the future bodily spirit surely undergoes a change; the power of this quality gradually adapts the magnitude and shape to the species. 

Thus, a certain form in a way precedes a certain quantity. Even if you imagine that an indeterminate quantity precedes certain forms, we shall likewise imagine that this indeterminate quantity is preceded by an indeterminate form, whose efficacy stretches matter into quantity. Thus, the command and action of the prepared form over matter will immediately follow the preceding forms in matter: namely, quantity, which is further distant from the separated form. Then, since acting and moving is the property of quality, not of quantity, it is rightly not quantity that acts upon quality, but quality that acts upon and moves quantity through a secondary change. Thus, it is not magnitude that makes a thing hot, but heat that extends a thing into magnitude. For it makes fewer things colder, but cold drives them into a small space. Why say more? The virtues and power of seeds, without having their own final magnitude, define certain sizes and growths, in which the species is immediately present and always the same, though the required magnitude or shape is not there immediately. These proceed through the power of the species at certain times, and from potentiality, the species gradually enters into act. Wherefore matter also receives form for this reason: because it is matter subject to natural art, and it was first made to receive form from an agent form. Therefore, it does not receive form because it is a "bulk" <note>original: *moles*; physical mass or volume</note>, but because it is "formable" matter. It receives form in a bodily way because matter becomes a bulk in the meantime, while through both the power and grace of the form, it displays a quantity suitable to that form. And even if it did not have bulk, it would still receive quality, though not yet a bodily one.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On Matter" (Ennead II, Book 4). Ficino is currently explaining how matter acts as a substrate for forms and dimensions, and why the human mind often confuses matter with empty space.</meta>

->ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD<-

For just as many qualities exist simultaneously in the same space without that space scattering them, so too—unless another space is established—many more things can exist together in matter. Most people think of matter as space, and indeed as a vacuum or emptiness itself; this is because when the mind focuses on matter, it cannot direct its attention toward any specific shape or figure. Thus, it finds nowhere to rest its gaze. Wandering aimlessly, distracted here and there, the mind seems to roam through an empty interval, one that appears infinite. If one were to veil this matter, or bend it, or mark it with lines, the mind would be forced to think of shapes. In reality, just as space itself is the capacity for other things, so matter (without having its own space) is the capacity for space itself. And although matter lacks size in its own right, just as the ideal forms <term>ideal forms: the perfect, non-physical blueprints of things in the divine mind</term> do, no specific form appears to one contemplating space. This is because a form defines its own limit and preserves itself as an individual unit. 

Matter, however, appears to be space because it underlies that space and defines no mark for itself. It never rests within itself, but while it puts on various forms, it also casts them off in turn. In losing these shapes to the flow of forms, matter itself seems to us to be "flowing"—just as the shore itself seems to move when viewed from a moving ship <note>original: *sicut ad nauis motum littus ipsum nauis moueri videtur*; a classic ancient analogy for relative perception</note>. Whoever considers the long stretch of matter beneath a vast variety of forms is rightly compelled to think of matter as space, and specifically as a "mobile" space.

### XII The previous arguments are confirmed.

You have heard quite often that all forms of natural things exist according to "seminal reasons" <term>seminal reasons: Latin *rationes seminales*; the latent 'seeds' or formative principles within nature that guide the growth of physical things</term> within the very nature of the World Soul. And since there is no division there, any form exists within any other, and all exist everywhere at once; such a "seedbed" of the world is called both animal <note>meaning "living" or "ensouled"</note> and incorporeal. Imagine, then, that dimension <note>extension in space</note> were to arise there at some point. Suddenly, the nature of length, breadth, and depth would be amplified, and form would extend outward. Thus, those things which were previously incorporeal within nature without space, would then—having found space in that same nature—become corporeal and separated from one another in space. 

Think of this entire corporeal world as having propagated from the incorporeal in this way, perhaps only by the addition of dimension. If you subtract dimension, the seminal forms will still remain, which once preceded dimension in nature; but the world would cease to be a body and would instead become incorporeal. I wish to remind you, however, that nature intends for the world of the "seedbed" to transition into this corporeal world through matter. For it seems it can only propagate there into this world if matter sprouts immediately from nature—matter being the only place where dimension can arise by the command of the all-powerful Nature. 

Indeed, we think that dimension is bestowed upon bodies, not because dimension is the actual "matter" of bodies, but because it is the same matter that exists both under dimension and as the matter of dimension itself. Furthermore, dimension is not strictly necessary for forms to simply *be*, but rather for them to become corporeal. That they are forms, they possess from being in the seedbed; that they are corporeal, they obtain from being extended in matter. 

This is the point Plotinus makes: "Forms are not properly the powers of magnitude, but they arise around matter." For even if magnitude were taken away, forms could remain—perhaps in the seminal reasons, or perhaps even in matter itself, though not in a corporeal way. This is further confirmed by the opinion of those who argue that during the arrival of a substantial form <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the 'soul' of a human or the 'nature' of gold)</term>, everything is resolved down to prime matter. In this way, the substantial form and "being" in its simplest sense come to exist within that which is substantial and potential in its simplest sense. 

Such a thing would exist before quantity (which is an accident) <term>accident: a non-essential property, like color or size, that can change without the object's core identity changing</term> could attach itself to matter. If quality preceded it there, then the fortunate substantial form would cross the limits of quantity and infuse itself into the very levels of matter. For this reason, perhaps, some think substantial forms are indivisible: because no quantity of matter intervenes to prevent them from infusing themselves entirely, even though they are accompanied by the dimension that precedes accidental forms. Therefore, this is an effective distinction. 

Plotinus seems to touch on this when he says: "If a substantial form were to enter into a dimension, it would undergo it, and the form would perish entirely." Yet a form can remain there, albeit invisible, whether it is founded in matter proper or in nature. Perhaps it can even remain indivisible in matter, for it is conceived of as existing before it is extended. I should also mention that even when quantity is changed over a long period, the form remains the same; however, the form would not remain the same if the matter were changed. From this, it is clear that form is not created around quantity, but around matter. Many bodies are easily gathered into one body because they concur in the same matter, which is equally prepared for all things and equally greedy for all things; matter does not have dimension by its own nature, which would otherwise force many things to be distant from one another. 

Now, since division in some way hinders the union of bodies while matter reconciles it, it is established that dimension is one thing and matter is another. Matter itself neither has dimension by its own nature, nor do forms receive dimensions, but rather they receive themselves. This is especially true because the primary reason for "receiving" consists in that which is the "first receptacle" <term>first receptacle: the ultimate underlying 'stuff' that receives all form and extension</term>. Surely that which can receive all things everywhere at once seems the most capable of all. 

Furthermore, we confirm that matter is not dimension in this way: If dimension were matter itself, it would be the foundation of all things and would be "substance." But since quantity is everywhere an "accident," quantity cannot be "substance" at the lowest level of things; for those things which are accidents among us are judged to be substances in the higher realms. Moreover, just as substance does not necessarily change when a quality changes, it does not change when quantity changes; from this, it is clear that both are equally accidents. For this reason, when defining a thing, one does not usually use quantity in the definition, as if quantity does not belong to the natural logic of the thing as a part, but rather arrives as an accident. 

Indeed, quantity seems no less "contingent" than quality—in fact, quality seems to agree more with the logic of form through its efficacy, act, and property. Therefore, if quantity is not substance, it is certainly not matter; for matter is rightly judged to be the subject of all things, just like substance. But who cannot see that quantity is not matter? Matter, which is entirely indefinite, is immediately determined by quantity just as it is by quality—namely, "how much" and therefore "of what kind." Even if you take dimension as something determined in itself, it still determines matter—at least to the extent that matter is not just matter simply, but is extended in length, depth, and breadth so that it occupies a place. This allows it to be divisible, to have parts within itself, for one part to be different from another, for one part to be bounded by another, and for parts to be bounded by the whole. 

Finally, you will be compelled to admit that dimension exists *in* matter, which is nothing other than confessing that matter relates to any dimension indifferently, just as it does to any quality. Therefore, just as it is granted that matter lacks quality, you must concede it lacks dimension. No one should deny that matter exists simply because we judge it to be invisible and indivisible. For even quantity, if considered in itself without quality, would be invisible; and quality, if taken apart from quantity, would immediately be indivisible. Yet they are still "something," even though they are accidents. Therefore, matter, which sustains such things in the manner of a substance, [continues...]

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

<note>original catchword: vnum (one)</note>

[Matter] is not entirely a fiction. But indeed, although it is perceived by no sense, it must nevertheless be posited as something. For we assert that nature itself and the mind are something, even though they cannot be sensed. We know matter not only through reason. Even if it is not known by the kind of reasoning full of intelligence—that is, reasoning founded on ideal forms <term>ideal forms: the perfect, non-physical archetypes of things in the divine mind</term>—it is nevertheless known by an argument partly denying forms and partly referring matter to forms. Furthermore, the words of Plotinus can be understood here: namely, that matter is known by a certain reasoning—not, I say, a reasoning of the void itself, but in a "void-like" way <note>original: *vacuo modo*</note>. It is as if he forbids matter to be called the void itself, or nothingness and emptiness. Let him concede, however, that it is known in a certain void-like manner—that is, by thinking of it as void of forms. 

Since it has been proved that matter is neither quantity, nor possesses quantity by its own nature, nor quality, it is clear that it is neither body, nor (if I may say so) the function of corporeity <term>corporeity: the quality or state of being a physical body</term>—if corporeity is taken as a certain form mixed with dimension; otherwise, matter would be a body. Nor again can it be a body if corporeity itself is taken as an ideal or seminal privation <term>privation: the lack or absence of a quality that should naturally be there</term> that produces the body. For these are far different from matter, since they consist in the soul and mind. Finally, one ought to say that a body can exist without matter [in a specific sense]: by a certain property of action it seems to exist without matter. For the actions and behaviors of bodies are composed together; nor are they generated from one thing to another like bodies. Rather, the substance of the agent or the patient itself, which is composed of matters, acts as the place of matter for those actions.

### Matter is neither quality, nor does it possess its own quality.

XIII Just as in the previous sections he showed that matter is neither quantity nor "quantified" <note>original: *quantam*</note>, so at present he shows it is neither quality nor "qualified" <note>original: *qualem*</note>. For it is absurd to say that the subject of all things is a quality, or that a quality exists within the subject if it were its own quality. Furthermore, if a subject is said to be defined by a certain fixed and certain nature, matter—which must necessarily be indefinite—cannot be that subject; if it were an uncertain and indefinite nature, then it would indeed be matter, but by no means a quality. For it is the specific property of quality to determine and distinguish something. 

Someone will object that matter either is or has a quality because it lacks the qualities of all other things, as if this very privation were the property and quality of matter, through which it is thought to differ from others. We indeed concede that this very "vacation" <note>original: *vacationem*; meaning being vacant or free from other properties</note> is a property of matter. But meanwhile, we shall deny that it is a quality. For the privation of quality is more different from quality than quantity is. Or if substance and its privation are called "quality" because of those qualities, it is much more probable that substance or quantity could be named quality. Furthermore, it is foolish to say that something becomes "qualified" <note>original: *quale*</note> not by the quality of nature itself, but by the "bereavement" of quality <note>original: *orbitu qualitatis*</note>, that is, by the very privation of qualities. 

Surely, because matter is different from the qualities of others, they might say it is "qualified" by this very fact: do they then want matter to be "otherness" <term>otherness: the state of being different or distinct; Latin: *alteritas*</term>? If they think so, it will not happen that it becomes "qualified"; nor is its quiddity <term>quiddity: the essence or "whatness" of a thing</term> judged as you wish. Or perhaps they want matter then to be like something "other"? If they think so, certainly although it is other by otherness, so also it is qualified by quality—a quality, I say, of another nature besides itself. There will therefore be some other quality through which matter becomes qualified. If it becomes something other than qualified, matter is not quality. 

Then indeed, just as the privation of quality from wine is not that specific quality, so the complete bereavement of qualities is no quality at all: but it is individual and does not function as "qualified," since it is vacant of qualities on all sides. Likewise, just as negation is not affirmation, so privation is not quality. For that privation consists in denying; quality consists in affirming. Again, not every property is to be judged as a quality. For just as privation is opposed to quality, so they are opposed to each other by their property. And just as there is something proper to affirmation and quality, so also something is proper to negation and privation; yet that will not be quality, but rather the opposite of quality. 

Added to this is that just as the property of quality is not matter, so the property of matter is not quality but the privation of qualities. If anyone says matter is "qualified" because of this privation, he will err no less than one who says matter is "great" because of the privation of magnitude. Then truly, if the property of matter were some "affirmed being" <note>original: *affirmatum esse*</note> as an opposite, it would undoubtedly behave as a quality. But in fact, the property of matter itself is the subject of matter itself; thus we are also accustomed to think concerning the principle of things. 

Matter, therefore, is judged to be different from others not through another property but through itself. Matter is therefore something like "different-in-itself" <note>original: *se diuersum*</note> or a certain otherness; it would not be different by itself, but it is different from different things besides itself. Let it hold this truth which seems to signify two things especially: namely, both a common negation of other things (through which it agrees in no way with generated things), and a universal power of receiving, referring itself to other things by a certain natural habit. Truly, it is proper to matter to be "diversity" in both ways: both because the "one" of other things is denied of it, and because it is naturally referred to others. For thus it is necessary: it is both "other" than those, and as affinity is opposed through negation. 

He concludes therefore for the present that matter itself is its own property: and this property is namely that it is "other" than other things—that is, that it is neither other things nor anything similar to other things. For other things agree among themselves either by communion or similarity. Matter, however, is entirely set apart, just as the first principle <note>meaning God or the One</note> is set apart. Again, it makes other things to be diverse either from each other or from matter, so that they have something according to species within themselves. Matter, however, is not one thing through one part and diverse through another: but rather it is diversity itself; or rather something entirely secret from the communion of others. Since Plotinus fears lest, by pronouncing about matter in the singular number as either "diversity" or "the other," matter might appear too formal for some definition: Therefore he suggests we should speak in the plural number, saying that matter is "others" or "diverse things," so that through this we may better contemplate its infinity.

### Matter is entirely the same as the privation of all forms, if privation signifies a certain infinity and formal power.

XIIII So far we have treated how matter relates especially to those things which are more remote from it, namely to quality and quantity. Next, we compare how it relates to those things which are closer, namely to privation and the infinite—but first concerning privation. He discusses, therefore, that claim of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who was known for walking while teaching</term>: "matter and privation are one thing in subject or reality, but two in reason." When the Peripatetic said these two are distinct in reason, he ought first of all to assign the "reasons"—that is, the definitions: one proper to privation, and the other proper to matter. Unless this is done, it cannot be proved that they are two in reason. But if two definitions are brought forward in turn, we ask whether they are such that neither of the two is placed in the definition of the other. If it happens thus, they will not be one in subject or reality.

<summary>Ficino explains that matter is not a physical body or a quality, but rather a "void-like" subject that is defined by its "otherness" and lack of qualities. He critiques the Aristotelian (Peripatetic) view that matter and privation are the same thing viewed from different logical perspectives.</summary>
