# ON BOOK IV OF ENNEAD II.

...whether one, or rather both, should be placed in the definition of the other: just as is usually said regarding a "snub nose" and "snubness" itself. If they remain distinct, then there are two things: namely, the nose and the quality of snubness. Or perhaps one of them exists within the definition of the other, but not vice versa—much like heat is in the definition of fire, but fire is not necessarily in the definition of heat. If it is spoken of in this way, there are still two things: the subject <term>subject: the underlying "stuff" or *subiectum* that receives qualities</term> and the quality itself. After this, he discusses whether matter and privation <term>privation: the lack or absence of a specific form or quality</term> are called one thing: because privation adds no actual thing to matter, but simply denies everything else of matter. In this case, however, it remains ambiguous how there can be two "reasons" or definitions—one pertaining to the subject (that is, matter), and the other pertaining to the relation created by the privation of other things. It is indeed probable that not only the definition of privation, but also that of the subject, is properly referred to other things. Those things which are above matter are not only referred to an end <term>end: the "telos" or ultimate purpose/perfection of a thing</term>, but they also have the quality of being the ends of other things. But since matter alone is the end of nothing—which no one would serve by natural order, but which itself serves all things—and since everything it is remains empty of the role of an "end," it is naturally directed toward an established end from every side, being always needy and desiring. Therefore, it is rightly said that its nature is referred to other things by its very own definition. Just as in the highest of things the entire definition of the "end" exists, but is not directed *toward* an end; so conversely, in the lowest thing, there is no definition of an "end" at all, but everything is directed *toward* an end. Do not, in the meantime, dream of mere dialectical relations here. For we wish the relation of nature itself to be understood here as part of divine providence. Nothing is further from matter than a mere logical relation. For such a relation is founded either in opinion, or in some thing, or in a subject. Matter, on the contrary, is purely the subject and the foundation. Furthermore, it is probable that here, by the name of "privation," a certain relation is signified: that is, the indefiniteness of this subject, and its neediness naturally established and longingly turning toward other things. And therefore, one cannot easily discern how there are two distinct definitions—one of privation and the other of matter. For they are one, not only in reality, but also in definition. No one would say that matter is a "privation" in the same way we usually speak of other privations—that is, as certain defects in a subject. For matter itself is the subject of all things. Again, let no one think of matter as privation in the sense of "nothingness"; for when bodies are either composed of matter or resolved back into matter, it is far from the case that they are made from nothing or reduced to nothing.

---

->Infinity does not happen to matter, but is matter itself.<-

XV. This privation, which is called "unlimitedness" or "infinity"—that is, a capacity that is only formable by itself and possessing no formal limits within itself—this infinity, I say, does not merely happen to matter as an accident, but *is* matter itself. Consider the "reasons" and the numbers. I mean the formal reasons <note>original: *rationes formales*; these are the shaping principles or "logoi" that give things their specific nature</note> depending on the seminal and ideal reasons. I mean the numbers of such reasons: both of the properties within them, the degrees of their power, and the differences between them. Reasons indeed limit and order by flowing. Numbers, however, order and limit by the act of ordering. Likewise, reasons terminate each of the forms; they terminate "genera" (acting as matter) into "species," and they terminate the wandering appetite of matter toward an effect. Do they not also order and limit the series of things and the subject matter beneath them? Likewise, they define the quality of motion, and through these, they seem to limit matter as well. Since, therefore, reasons and numbers of this kind provide the limit, there is certainly a subject that is limited by them. That primary subject is matter itself. For those things which are composite <note>original: *composita*; things made of both matter and form</note> possess through matter the need to be limited from elsewhere; and nature, or the soul, or the mind, through their own "matter," have the power to urge the limit of forms. Therefore, since matter is this very thing which is limited from elsewhere, it is undoubtedly infinite by its own nature. Just as that which is illuminated from elsewhere is, by itself, dark. Therefore, somewhere—or rather, everywhere—an infinite nature lies beneath, or rather, infinity itself. For just as an infinite thing corresponds to a finite one, so also the "end" or limit corresponds to the infinite. I say a "substantial" limit; that infinity of substance does not stop. I say an infinity not in another thing; just as the primary limit and end is not in another thing. If anyone were to say that this infinity is not matter itself, but merely happens to it, they would be forced to admit that infinity has something "formal" <note>original: *formale*; defined or structured</note> within itself; for it would be in a subject, and would determine the subject under such a condition—which is certainly seen to be against the nature of infinity. Now, infinity itself is not any formal reason. For it is the extreme of "formability" <note>original: *formabilitas*; the capacity to receive form</note>. If there were anything uniquely "formal" in it, it would not be formable in that part. However, so that it may look toward the supreme Form-Giver, it is necessary to attribute all forms to Him, while the subject responding in proportion to Him must have none at all. Furthermore, if matter is infinite by itself, it is not necessary for infinity to "happen" to it as an accident. But if it is called "limited," then it is not "primary matter" <term>primary matter: *materia prima*, the most basic, formless level of existence</term>. Finally, if matter is imagined as a kind of formal limit, and that infinity—that is, the mere aptitude for being formed—happens to it, then whatever formal element was imagined in matter is suddenly lost. For nothing actually formal is left under "extreme formability." That the matter of the corporeal world is infinity is confirmed by the fact that the matter of the incorporeal world is also infinity. For infinity does not happen to it as an accident; for whatever is in it exists by its own nature. But this physical matter depends on that higher matter through a similar mode of infinity. Think, therefore, of that which is simply the "One" above "Being." Consider infinity in "Being" <note>original: *Vuo ente*, likely *Uno ente*</note>, which is the power formable by the One itself. Insofar as it is extended into formal limits there, it is called "power" and "infinity." Insofar as it is called a limit outside the duration of perseverance, it is named "eternity." That infinity, named in a way according to a "defect," follows the infinity of the One according to its thought-out "supereminent existence." And insofar as the one exceeds the other, so far does the mundane infinity of matter take its beginning: just as much under the nature of the formable as that higher one is under the Good. But the two infinities introduced here do not belong to the same genus, under which they might differ by specific differences. And yet, each is most simple: and while this one depends on that one, it seems to agree with it by referring back to it, and yet it is not that one, because it was not born for similar forms. But this is also to differ from oneself. Because that formable power, although it is like matter in relation to the Ideas, is nevertheless considered as "form" in itself and in relation to us. Therefore, it is not designated as "indefinite" in the same way as the matter of bodies. Especially because that formable nature is always similarly reduced to the height of form. This physical matter, however, is reduced gradually; and the height is lost. That higher matter also becomes "formal." Here, conversely, the form turns out "material." Therefore, the condition of the "indefinite" is found more in this than in that. The condition of the "limit" dominates there; here, it necessarily fails. Accordingly, if you consider the composite of matter and form, you will say this is in some way "infinite," namely, by reason of its matter. You will not, however, say this infinite thing is the nature of infinity itself. Which is indeed said to belong to the infinite itself, by which reason it is infinite: for this pertains to matter. When, however, considering this matter as if separately, you say "this infinite," this "infinite" is certainly the same as infinity itself, which we were just calling the [unlimited] itself...

<summary>Ficino explores the ontological status of matter, arguing that matter and "infinity" are essentially the same. He distinguishes between the "intelligible matter" of the divine realm (which relates to eternity) and the "physical matter" of our world (which is the extreme of formlessness and need).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On Matter" (Ennead II, Book 4). Having previously discussed how matter is perceived through a "bastard reasoning," Ficino now moves into a metaphysical definition of matter as the "infinite" and its status relative to being and non-being.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...end; being, insofar as it is infinite. But when you speak of matter, which is the very nature of infinity, stop at this point: do not add that it is the "reason" <term>reason: *ratio*, here meaning the formal definition, logical structure, or the "Logos" of a thing</term> of infinity. For "reason"—whether it signifies form, definition, or Idea—includes a limit, and does not suit what is essentially indefinite matter. Likewise, when you say that this infinite thing is the "natural state of the infinite," it is the same thing; only do not understand under this name of "being" any limit, act, or mode of that indefinite essence. For these things pertain to reason—that is, to the rational, ideal, and formal aspect. Indeed, no such "reason" fits the nature of the infinite itself. If you attempt to define it, you will labor in vain; it will slip from your hands as you define it, and you will be forced to define infinity merely by its relationship to limits which it does not yet possess. In this case, infinity does not have a "reason" pertaining to itself internally, but rather externally toward something else, and so on; this is what it truly means to be infinite. For if you were to place anything in this as its own so that it was not referred to something else, that which was not directed toward an end would itself be an end. But an end is repugnant to infinity. Therefore, we shall consider infinity further: defining it internally, but referring it to reason itself externally. I mean reason (as we have often said) in the ideal, seminal, and formal sense. To this, as to an end and to that which "knows," we oppose matter as that which is directed toward an end, is indefinite, and is "to be known." We oppose the one to the other, I say, the most simple to the most simple. Whence we rightly conclude that just as reason itself is reason, end, and form not by any other gift but by itself, so matter is utterly indefinite not by anything added to it, but by its own nature: for whatever you add to it will be a limit, and its infinity will cease.

### Four questions about matter are solved concerning otherness, privation, the infinite, and evil.

XVII Chapter, the last of the book, raises and solves four questions about matter: concerning otherness <term>otherness: *alteritas*, the quality of being different or 'other' than the Forms</term>, privation, the infinite, and evil. You should note among these that otherness (or diversity) itself is common to both the formable subject and matter. For there is always some difference between the two. Matter, therefore, is the same as otherness—not in a simple sense, but as an otherness furthest removed from those things which truly *are* (that is, the Ideal Reasons). If matter is sometimes called "non-being" because it is furthest from the First Being, it can meanwhile be called a "certain being"—that is, something most distantly segregated from the first things. Similarly, "privation" is not used in a simple sense as if it were "nothing," but as the extreme opposition to the First Being and the Ideal Reasons within Him. Therefore, this kind of privation is not "lost" (that is, the nature of formable matter does not vanish from elsewhere) when it receives form. Instead, the nature of the subject remains ever the same, perpetually alternating between forms or modes of forms, being formed in turn. If matter were infinite in *quantity*, it would lose its nature entirely upon receiving a limit. But since it is infinite by *formability* <term>formability: the capacity or potential to receive a form</term>, the more it is formed, the more it seems to exercise its formability and perform its proper duty as a formable subject. Furthermore, since it remains "unformed" even after receiving "goods" (that is, forms)—because it contracts nothing as its own personal property, and the nature of forms is prone to change—it is rightly still called "evil." Finally, you will consider three grades here. First, the One itself, which is superior to being. Second, Being itself, in which "intelligible matter" is placed (which nothing prevents from being called "being"). Third, the matter of the corporeal world: since it is inferior to being by the furthest degree, it is called "non-being" by this condition. I do not mean "nothingness," but "as if non-being," if compared to the beauty of true being itself. For all things are judged by those limits of being which belong to the nature of true being. The "form" of bodies, which flows from nature into matter, is also truly a "being." Matter, finally, is "true non-being." This is because it falls away not only from the being of nature itself, but even from its image—the sort of image found in natural forms. For matter is neither a true being nor an image; rather, an image represents being somewhere else.

### Although being, essence, or "to be" is not properly said of matter, it should not be called nothing, but something, and that in the manner of substance.

XVIII Among the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching</term>, if someone called matter "non-being," they would mean it is entirely nothing. But among the Platonists—who extended the nature of the One more widely than the nature of being and produced it further downwards—even though they call matter "non-being," you should not take it for "nothing." Just as you do not take the "Good" for nothing, even though it is judged to be "non-being" <note>original: *non ens*</note>. But the Good is "non-being" in such a way that it is *superior* to being; whereas matter is "non-being" because it is *inferior* to being in its power. Just as the Highest God is called "Pure Act" <term>Pure Act: *actus purus*, existence without any potential for change or unfulfilled capacity</term> by most, having no "formable potential" in himself but responding to that act as a parent-like source, so too matter becomes "Pure Potency," to which no proper "act" corresponds—at least, the act of other things seems to respond in place of its own act. Although we call it the "ultimate state of loss" because it looks toward formal vigor (which we by no means grant as belonging to matter), yet when we encounter an act—when we attribute the truth of a present act to matter as if it were its own—we shall call it, in a way, the "being" of matter. This "act of being" does not prevent matter from being called "pure potency." For the present and primary truth of matter’s potency makes it more truly "pure" and more firmly "potency." You should not judge this potency by the conditions of other potencies. For other potencies exist within subjects, but this is the subject of all natural things. Therefore, this potency is (if I may say so) "subject-like" and "substantial." Add also "essential," provided "essence" can be named within the limits of being. For we might speak of the essence of matter as "potential essence" or "essential potency." For while potencies and acts in things are accidental and lie in another, they become parts of the rest in a pre-existing "first act"; so in a "first subsisting potency," whose "to be" is perhaps "to be under" <note>original: *subesse*</note>, just as for forms "to be" is "to be in" <note>original: *inesse*</note>. But here, furthermore, some theologians say that "being simply" <note>original: *esse simpliciter*</note> naturally precedes "being such-and-such" by reason, as if it were then fit to be thus or otherwise, here or there. Therefore, just as a form cannot exist in itself unless it first *is* simply in itself, so matter cannot be rightly understood as a subject unless it is understood to "be simply" first in some way. This they call the "being of essence" <note>original: *esse essentiae*</note>, to which they soon add the "being of existence" <note>original: *esse existentiae*</note>. Through the first, they say a thing exists in its own essence and from it. Through the second, they say a thing exists in effect and in the order of things, depending on something else. For this reason, they grant to matter a "first being" through itself, but a "second being" through form. Perhaps the Platonists...

<summary>Ficino defines matter as the extreme opposite of the One, characterizing it as "pure potency" and "non-being" not because it is nothing, but because it is the furthest remove from the perfection of true Being. He contrasts the Platonic view of matter as a substantial potency with the Aristotelian view of matter as nothingness.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Marsilio Ficino’s preliminary commentary on the nature of matter and begins the actual text of Plotinus’s Ennead II, Book 4. It bridges the philosophical discussion of matter as an "image of essence" to the historical overview of how different schools (like the Stoics and Peripatetics) defined it.</meta>

...they take away the primary "to be" <term>to be: *esse*, referring to the act of existing or actualized existence</term> from matter; especially when they hear Plotinus forbidding that "to be" be assigned to matter itself. Therefore, just as many theologians place "to be" without essence in the first principle of things <note>referring to God as pure existence without being limited by a specific essence</note>, so these thinkers will consider matter as a kind of essence without "to be"; yet they will not call it nothing, but rather something. For Plotinus also calls matter the "image of essence." Just as other things have their own images—which, although they are not the things themselves, are nonetheless something—so too we shall call the image of essence "not-nothing" and "something," even if it is not a true essence. 

Although matter can be called "not-nothing" and "something," they usually deny that it is strictly "something," lest perhaps the mind, while hearing the word "something," suspect it to be something formal <note>possessing a specific form or definition</note>, as is most common. Indeed, since the mind is itself form and is prompted by forms to think, it thinks through forms. Truly, however, matter is judged in reality to be "not-nothing" and something like a substance <term>substantial: *substantiale*, here meaning it acts as the underlying foundation</term>. 

Hence Plotinus says in the preceding sections that matter is necessary for bodies. Nor is it a hollow name, but some underlying subject, however hidden; and this subject persists much more than quantities and qualities do. This is also indicated by Timaeus <note>referring to Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus*</note> when he says that before the world there was the architect of the world like a father, and matter like a mother; and he calls matter the subject, the receptacle, and the place. From these words it appears that matter is a thing subsisting beyond our concepts and relations. The Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note> also confirm this when they divide substance into matter, form, and the composite. 

Although we name matter "substance" because it stands under bodies and does not reside in another, we nonetheless think it depends perpetually from above, so much so that it has no vigor in itself to preserve itself. It depends, therefore, on Nature itself as if bound to it by a certain spring-like connection. Furthermore, it is continually gathered together by forms cast from Nature into matter, as if by steady sinews <term>sinews: *nervos*, used metaphorically here for the binding power that holds physical reality together</term>. Matter replaces form in the manner of a depth. And while it falls away from "Being"—that is, from Nature, which is the lowest of true beings—it meanwhile serves as the foundation for the images of Being, namely natural forms. 

Wherefore, even if among some thinkers matter is said to have something in itself proper to its own essence—which indeed precedes its formal being and existence—nevertheless, the "first being" attributed to it is preserved for it by Nature itself; thereafter its "secondary being" and existence are preserved by the forms of bodies. But this happens sequentially, from one form and then another, as if Nature applies various sinews at different times to conquer the thoughts directed toward matter. But let us now put an end to this dispute. For in the book where Plotinus argues that incorporeal things suffer nothing, and elsewhere, many things concerning matter will be treated.

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK II.

...and to extend the gods. Finally, they say that the supreme, prior God strips this matter, which exists in a certain state. They <note>The Stoics, who believed everything real was a body</note> further hand down the concept of "body," saying that this matter is a body void of quality, and they attribute magnitude to it. However, those who have argued for an incorporeal essence <term>incorporeal essence: *incorporea essentia*, a reality that does not consist of physical matter</term> do not all posit a single matter; rather, some of them say that one type of matter is subject to bodies—as those earlier thinkers mentioned—but that there is another, prior matter in the realm of intelligible things, which underlies the forms <note>Platonic "Ideas" or blueprints of reality</note> and the incorporeal essences found there.

<margin>II. Reasons proving that there is matter in the intelligible world.</margin>
## CHAPTER II
CONCERNING this very matter, we must first inquire whether it exists, what it is, and in what manner it exists. If matter must be something indefinite and formless, and if in the highest and best things <note>The Intelligible realm or the world of Forms</note> there is nothing indefinite and nothing formless, then matter would not exist there. Furthermore, if every thing there is "one" and "simple," it would have no need of matter, from which—with something else added—a composite thing might be made. Matter is needed more rarely in things that are generated, and among those things that are generated from one another; it is least needed for those things that are not generated at all. Indeed, in sensible things <note>Physical things perceived by the senses</note>, matter seems to be produced from the very process of generation and mutual change. Finally, from where would matter proceed and exist among those eternal things? For if it was made, it was certainly made by someone; but if it is eternal, then there are multiple first principles. Moreover, that which is first, if it is added to that which is so composed, will be a body. Thus, there would be a body in the realm above.

<margin>III. Solutions to objections against intelligible matter.</margin>
## CHAPTER III
IN THE BEGINNING, it must be said that not everywhere is that which is "indefinite" to be entirely despised, nor that which is formless in its own nature—provided it offers itself to be shaped by the higher and best things. In the same way, the soul is related by its own nature to the intellect and reason; it is formed by these and led toward a better form. Added to this is the fact that in the intelligible world, what is called "composite" <term>composite: *compositum*, a thing made of parts, like matter and form</term> behaves differently than it does in physical bodies. Since even the "reasons" <note>The formative principles or *logoi*</note> are themselves composite, and in their activity they create a certain composite—namely, the very nature that acts toward a form. If, however, it is drawn toward another and depends on another, it is even more so. Likewise, the matter of things that are generated always takes on a different form. But the matter of eternal things always possesses the same form. Indeed, the matter here in our world behaves almost the opposite of the matter there. For our matter takes on different states by turns, and different things at different times; therefore, nothing in it remains the same, as one thing is pushed out by another. For this reason, nothing is ever the same. But in the higher realm, matter is all things at once. And since it possesses all things, it has nothing into which it could change. Therefore, matter there is never formless, just as our matter is never truly empty. But in this regard, the two behave differently. As for what was said about whether it is eternal or generated, that will finally be clear to us after we have shown what it is.

<margin>IV. Proof that there is matter in the intelligible.</margin>
## CHAPTER IV
TO BEGIN, since it has been shown elsewhere that "Ideas" <note>The eternal archetypes of all things</note> exist, let us proceed with our plan, admitting for now that Ideas exist. Surely, if there are many species <term>species: *species*, here used synonymously with the Platonic Forms or Ideas</term> there, it is necessary that there be something common in them, and again something unique by which one is distinguished from another. This unique quality and this separating difference is certainly the proper form.

<column-break/>

...gods and the eternal, and finally that the end is in him. Of the gods, except for those who are in a certain state toward him. He also teaches that matter is a body, for those who call it a body make it void of quality and give it magnitude, which must be incorporeal; and in some way, there is not just one idea for them, but they themselves say this one is underlying bodies, about which the earlier thinkers spoke. Yet there is another, prior matter in the intelligible realm, underlying the forms there and the incorporeal essences.

WHEREFORE we must first seek concerning it, if it is, and what it happens to be, and how it is. If indeed the nature of matter must be something indefinite and formless, and if among the best things there <note>in the divine realm</note> nothing is indefinite or formless, then matter would not be there. And if each thing is simple, there would be no need of matter, so that from it and another thing a composite might be made; and things being generated, this very thing, and some things made from others, and those which have their generation in change with one another; but in that realm, nothing comes from another. If that is the case, it would not need matter. And there would be more principles, and the first things would be by chance; and if it approached them, that which is saved would be a body, so that there too would be a body.

FIRST, then, it must be said that not everywhere is the indefinite to be dishonored, nor that which is formless in its own nature, if it is to provide itself to the things before it and to the best things; in which way also the soul is naturally disposed toward intellect and reason, being formed by them and led to a better form. Furthermore, in the intelligible realm, the composite is otherwise than in bodies. Since even the "reasons" <note>the formative principles</note> are composite, and the activities are those of a composite nature, the nature acting toward form. But if by nature it follows another, and is around another, it is even more so. And the matter of things that are generated always holds a different form. But eternal things hold the same things; it is the reverse of how it is here. For there, the whole is all things together, even if each is something. But they are not becoming, but are another thing suddenly. Because the "all" is always there, they are all things; therefore, it is not near and does not change, for it has all things. Therefore, it is never formless, neither the matter there nor the matter here. But each is in a different way. Whether it is eternal or generated, once we grasp what it is, it will be clear.

That it is clear in us, having now hypothesized that the forms exist—for it is shown elsewhere—that if the forms are many, it is necessary that there be something common in them, and also something unique, by which one differs from another; and every unique thing and the separating difference is also the form.

<summary>Plotinus introduces the concept of "Intelligible Matter," arguing that even the perfect realm of divine Ideas requires a substrate to account for the diversity and composition of the Forms.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter II of Book 4, where Plotinus investigates the existence of "Intelligible Matter." Having previously established that matter acts as a substrate for forms in the physical world, he now argues by analogy that the Intelligible world—the realm of pure thought and divine "Ideas"—must also possess a kind of matter to serve as a foundation for its various forms.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR
## V I

<margin>It is a monad <note>original: "μονάς ἔστι"</note></margin>
But if there is form, there is also that which is being formed, which is the subject of the differentiation. For all matter would receive form, and the substrate is always present. Furthermore, if the intelligible world exists there, and this world is an imitation of that one, and this world is a composite made of matter, then there must also be matter there. Otherwise, how can we speak of a "world" <note>The Greek *kosmos* implies an ordered arrangement</note> if we do not see matter being shaped into form? Or how could there be a form, unless it were received by something? For that realm is not entirely simple or without height; it is composed of parts.
<margin>From secondary things</margin>
Even if the parts are distinct from one another, the "cut" or differentiation exists across the whole substrate. If there were many things, they could not exist without a division among the many; and if there is a "One," and these forms are existing things—for this One contains variegated things—then just as the variegated and multiform must be indivisible prior to their variety, so too within the infinite varieties of forms, reasons, and thoughts, there must be something that is unformed in relation to them. This something would be nothing of the things that exist upon it or within it.

But if someone objects that because the realm there always possesses these forms, and both exist together as one, it follows that there is no matter there, then by that logic there would be no matter for bodies here either. For here, too, matter is never found without form, but is always a complete body; nevertheless, it remains a composite. The intellect discovers this "double nature," for it divides until it reaches that which is simple and can no longer be resolved into anything else. As far as it can reach into the depth, it proceeds, and the depth of each thing is its matter. Therefore, all matter is "dark," because the rational principle <term>Reason: *Logos*, the ordering principle of the universe</term> is light; and the intellect itself is light. Thus, when the intellect looks upon the reason within each thing, it considers that which lies beneath the light to be dark. Just as an eye, being light-like, looks toward the light and 
<margin>colors</margin>
sees colors—which are themselves a kind of light—and then says that what lies beneath the colors is dark and material, hidden by the bodies. However, there is a great difference between the darkness of the intelligible world and the darkness of the sensible world. Matter differs as much as the forms that are placed upon it differ in both realms. For divine matter, when it receives that which defines it, possesses a life that is defined and intellectual; but physical matter becomes something defined, yet it is neither living nor thinking; it is a "decorated corpse." Furthermore, the form here is a mere image <note>original: "εἰδώλων" (eidolon), a ghost or phantom</note>, so the substrate is also an image. But there, the form is a true reality, and consequently the substrate is a true essence. 
<margin>vain things</margin>
Therefore, those who say that matter is "essence"—if they are speaking of that intelligible matter—should be understood to see correctly. For the substrate there is essence; or rather, it is conceived together with what is in it, as a totally illuminated essence. As for the question of whether this intelligible matter is eternal, it is the same as asking whether the "Ideas" <note>The Platonic blueprints of reality</note> are eternal. 
<margin>generated things</margin>
They are "generated" only in the sense that they have a principle of origin, but they are "un-generated" because they do not exist in time.

<column-break/>

But if form is there, there is also that which is formed, in which the difference exists. Let matter therefore undergo that form which it receives, acting as a perpetual subject. Furthermore, if an intelligible world exists there, and this world of ours is an imitation of it and is composed of matter, then there too it is necessary for matter to exist. Otherwise, by what logic will you call it a "world" or an "arrangement" unless you contemplate species <note>The Latin *species* here refers to the outward form or appearance of the divine Ideas</note>? In what way will you perceive the species, unless you also grasp that in which the species exists? To be sure, that higher world is entirely indivisible everywhere, yet in another sense it is divisible. And if its parts are dispersed among themselves, that very sectioning and dispersion is a certain experience of matter. For it is matter that is properly said to undergo "sectioning." But if those many things there are a "one" and indivisible being, then surely those many things existing in the One are in that One as if in matter, and they are its forms. For the One itself, which must first be considered as a unity, is variegated and multiform. It must be considered again as "unformed" before it is "variegated." For if you remove the variety, the forms, the reasons, and the intelligences by thought, undoubtedly that which precedes these occurs as something unformed and undefined; nothing appears of those things which exist through it and within it.

<margin>A solution showing the relationship to secondary things and the distinction.</margin>
But if, because an essence of this kind always possesses these forms and both are one together, it is said that there is no matter there, it would follow that there is no matter for bodies here either. For this matter is never without form, but is always a whole body; nonetheless, it is a composite. And the intellect finds this "duplicity." For it divides until it arrives at that which is simple—that which cannot be further resolved. As far as it can be referred to something else, it proceeds by penetrating into its depth. Finally, the depth of each thing is its matter. For this reason, all matter is "shadowy" or "dark," since the reason itself is light, and the intellect itself is reason. Therefore, perceiving the reason in each thing, the intellect concludes that what is lower, as if beneath the light, is obscure. Just as the eye, since it is luminous, looks into light and into colors (which are themselves certain lights) and brings itself to say that those things which lie hidden beneath the colors remain dark and material, covered by colors. Nevertheless, there is a wide gap between what we guess to be dark in intelligible things and what is dark in sensible things; and that matter differs from this matter as much as the species inherent in that one differs from the species inherent in this one. For divine matter, receiving that which terminates it, acquires a determined, intellectual life. This physical matter, however, becomes something determined, yet it is neither living nor intellectual, but a certain thing void of life, however much it is decorated. Furthermore, this form is imaginary; therefore, the subject is imaginary. There, however, the form is a true thing, and consequently the subject is true essence. Therefore, those who say matter is essence—if they are speaking of that matter—must be thought to judge correctly. For what is the subject there is essence; or rather, it is considered together with what is in it. For that whole is truly essence, already full of light. As for the question of whether that intelligible matter is everlasting or not, it is the same as asking whether the "Ideas" are everlasting. They are "generated" in the sense that they have a principle. But they are "un-generated" because they are not in time...

<summary>Plotinus argues that even the divine, intelligible realm must contain a form of "matter" to act as a substrate for the diversity of divine Ideas. He distinguishes this "divine matter," which is full of life and light, from the "dead" and "imaginary" matter of the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the nature of matter. Having previously discussed "Intelligible Matter"—the underlying substrate for divine ideas—he now transitions into discussing physical matter, the "receptacle" for the bodies we see in the sensory world. He concludes the argument that even in the perfect realm of thought, there must be a principle of "Otherness" that allows for distinction between ideas.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.

they have a beginning, but they exist always from another; not in the sense of things that are constantly being "made" as this world is, but existing eternally, as that world does. For the **Otherness** <note>original: "alteritas" / "ἑτερότης"</note> which is found there flows eternally into matter. This Otherness is the principle of matter, and it is the "first motion." For this reason, it is called Otherness: because motion and otherness sprang forth from the First together.

But both motion and otherness are **indeterminate** <note>original: "indeterminata" / "ἀόριστον"; meaning lacking limit, boundary, or definition</note> because they depend upon the First <note>The "First" refers to The One, the ultimate source of all existence in Plotinus's system</note>, and they require the First to give them a limit. They receive their limit when they turn back toward it. Before that turning, however, matter is indeterminate; it is "the other," and it is not yet "the good," but rather a thing devoid of the light of the Good. For if light shines out from the Good, then surely that which receives the light does not possess light before it receives it. And insofar as it has light, it holds it as something else, since the light itself proceeds from another source. Thus far we have discussed the matter of the **intelligible world** <note>The realm of pure thought and forms, as opposed to the physical world</note>, perhaps at greater length than this inquiry required.

<margin>VI. He proves that there is a primary matter in bodies.</margin>
CONCERNING the **receptacle** <note>original: "susceptaculo" / "ὑποδοχῆς"; a term borrowed from Plato’s Timaeus to describe matter as a vessel or "nurse" for forms</note> of bodies, let us next speak as follows. To begin with, the mutual change of elements into one another shows us that there must be some substrate for bodies, which is something distinct from the bodies themselves. For that which is transformed is not entirely destroyed; otherwise, an essence would vanish into utter non-being. Nor, on the other hand, is that which is "made" produced from that which in no way exists. Rather, a change occurs from one form into another. That which receives the form of the thing being made remains, while it sheds the previous form. This is further proven by **destruction** <note>Death or decay</note>. For destruction applies to a composite thing. If this is so, every perishable thing consists of matter and form. **Induction** <note>Logical reasoning from specific examples to general rules</note> also testifies that whatever is dissolved is a composite. **Resolution** <note>Breaking a thing down into its constituent parts</note> shows us the same thing. For example, if a bowl is resolved into gold, and gold is resolved into water <note>Following the ancient theory that metals are a form of "fusible water"</note>, then the water, as it perishes, requires something proportional to remain. Furthermore, the elements must be either forms themselves, or primary matter, or a composite of matter and form. It is impossible for them to be forms alone. For how could they have bulk and magnitude without matter? But they are not primary matter either, for they are dissolved. Therefore, they are composed of both matter and form. Form relates to quality and shape, while matter relates to the indeterminate substrate, because it is not yet a form.

<margin>VII. He refutes false opinions regarding matter.</margin>
FURTHERMORE, the very destruction of the elements argues against **Empedocles**, who posits that the elements themselves are matter. **Anaxagoras**, meanwhile, introduces a certain "mixture" <note>Anaxagoras taught that "everything is in everything," a primordial soup of all substances</note>—like water—saying that this has a certain aptitude for all things, but actually contains all things within it. By doing this, he effectively removes the **Intellect** <note>Mind or Nous</note> he had introduced. For he does not say that Intellect bestows shape and form, nor that Intellect is prior to matter, but rather that they exist together. But it is impossible for them to be simultaneous. If the mixture participates in existence, then Existence itself is more ancient. And if Existence itself is a kind of mixture, it requires some third thing beyond these. Therefore, if it is necessary for the **Craftsman** of the world to be prior, why was it necessary for the forms to exist as tiny particles within matter? Why must the Intellect then distinguish them through some inexplicable labor? Since it is matter's role—if it is to be of any quality—to be imprinted with quality and form...

<column-break/>

it has a beginning, but always from another; not as things that are constantly being "produced" as this world is, but existing eternally, as the world is there. For the **Otherness** that is there eternally sinks into matter. For this is the principle of matter: the "first motion." Therefore, this was also called Otherness, because motion and otherness sprouted forth together. Both motion and otherness are **indeterminate**, originating from the First and needing it to define them. They are defined when they are turned back toward it; but before then, both matter and "the other" are indeterminate, and not yet good, but unlit and shadowy. For if light is from that source, then that which receives the light, before receiving it, does not have it eternally. Rather, it would have it as something else, since the light is from another. Concerning intelligible matter, if we have mentioned it more than was fitting, let these things be said.

CONCERNING the **receptacle** of bodies, we must speak thus. That there must be some substrate for bodies, something other than the bodies themselves, is shown by the transformation of the **elements** <note>original: "στοιχείων"; earth, air, fire, and water</note> into one another. For the destruction of things that change is not total. Otherwise, a substance would be consumed into non-existence, and that which is "becoming" would arise from total non-existence. Rather, there is a change of form; one form arises from another, while the thing that receives the form of the becoming remains, having cast off the other form. This is also shown by destruction in general. For destruction is of a **composite** <note>original: "συνθέτου"; a thing made of multiple parts, specifically matter and form</note>; each thing consists of matter and form. Induction also bears witness, showing that what is destroyed is a composite, as does resolution. For example, if a bowl is resolved into gold, and gold into water; and the water, being destroyed, requires something analogous. It is necessary that the elements are either forms, or primary matter, or from matter and form. But they cannot be forms. For how, without matter, could they exist in bulk and magnitude? Nor are they primary matter, for they are things that are destroyed. Therefore, they are from matter and form. Form is according to quality and shape, while matter is according to the **infinite** <note>original: "ἄπειρον"; meaning the boundless or undefined</note> substrate, because it is not form.

IF **EMPEDOCLES** posits the elements as matter, their very transformation contradicts him. **Anaxagoras** makes the "mixture" like water, saying it does not merely have the potential for all things, but contains all things in actuality. This destroys the purpose of the Intellect he introduced, for he does not make Intellect the giver of shape and form. Nor is Intellect prior to matter, but simultaneous with it. Yet it is impossible for them to be simultaneous; for if the mixture shares in being, **Being** is prior. And if Being itself is also the mixture, they both need some third thing. If, then, it is necessary for the **Demiurge** <note>The divine "Craftsman" or creator</note> to be the cause, why was it necessary for the forms to be in matter in tiny fragments? Is it because the Intellect is blamed for distinguishing them through a lack of resources? Since it is possible for matter, if it does not already possess qualities and forms...

<summary>Plotinus argues that both the spiritual and physical worlds require "matter" as an underlying substrate. He uses the logic of transformation—elements turning into one another—to prove that a permanent, formless "receptacle" must exist beneath the changing physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section where Plotinus distinguished between "Intelligible Matter" (the substrate of the divine realm) and the matter of our physical world. He is now examining whether physical matter can be considered "infinite" or "atomic," and ultimately arguing that matter must be a completely characterless substrate—devoid of quality, size, or shape—in order to receive the forms of the physical universe.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin>For one might say that it is shaped by them; but how is it possible for it to be in everything? This seems impossible. He who posits the **infinite** <note>original: "ἄπειρον" / "apeiron"</note> as matter in the universe must explain what this means. And if it is infinite in the way we have understood it—such that nothing of it can be fully traversed—then we must remember that such a thing cannot exist among real objects; it cannot be infinite in and of itself, nor can it exist in another nature as an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has, but which is not essential to its nature—like the color of a shirt.</note> of a body. For if it were the infinite itself, it would necessarily be subject to infinite division. <margin>B</margin>If it were an accident, then the thing it belongs to would not be infinite by its own nature. It would be neither simple, nor matter <note>original: "ὕλη" / "hyle"</note>, <unclear>la</unclear> and it would not even rank as matter in the order of numbers.

Furthermore, if it were composed of all things in this way, it would first have to be incorporeal. Yet the continuity of bodies, their fluidity, and the fact that each individual thing cannot exist without **Mind** <note>original: "νοῦ" / "nous"</note> and **Soul** would prove it otherwise. It is also impossible for it to be made of **atoms**; rather, its nature must be such that the atoms are crafted from it. A creator would make things from both body and form; to say that matter is not continuous, or to speak of "marrow" <note>A reference to Plato's *Timaeus*, where marrow is described as the fundamental substance of life.</note> in relation to this hypothesis, has already been discussed. Therefore, we should allow that infinity exists in these things only in a different sense.

<margin>C</margin>What, then, is this thing which is called "one," "continuous," and "without properties" <note>original: "ἀπαθὴς" / "apathes"; literally "impassive" or "incapable of suffering change."</note>? It is clear that if it is without properties, it is not a body, for a body has quality. We say that this is the matter of all **sensible things** <note>Things that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>. We do not mean that it is the matter for white things only, and some other matter for other forms—the way we say clay is matter for the potter, but not matter in an absolute sense. When we speak of the matter of the whole universe, we do not attribute to its own nature any of the things seen by the senses. If we did, we would have to include other qualities like heat, cold, bitterness, weight, density, or thinness. It would have no color, and therefore no size. For size is one thing, and that which is endowed with size is another; shape is one thing, and that which is shaped is another. If it were a composite, it would be something else, not simple. If everything is removed from its nature, including that which we give to form, then even size must be stripped away. If we take away all "beings" from it, it is clear that size is among those things. Matter must receive whatever size the creator wills, but only as much as the matter can take. Some Greeks say its size is a mere fiction; if the "maker" precedes all matter, then matter is everywhere, and the maker directs it into all things, including sizes. If it has size by nature, it must also have shape, which would make it even more difficult for the craftsman to work with. Therefore, form enters into matter bringing all things with it; every form contains size and a measure of quantity, governed by a rational principle <note>original: "λόγου" / "logou"</note>. This is why in every produced thing, the quantity is determined along with the form, as is the case with a human being.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...to extend through the whole. Finally, I truly do not see how it is possible for all things to be in anything at all. He who puts the **infinite** <note>original: "infinitum"</note> in the place of matter must explain what this itself is. And if it is infinite in such a way that one cannot pass through it, it is necessary to remember that nothing of this kind can exist in reality—neither if it is infinite by and in itself, nor if it is in another nature as an accident to some body. Indeed, it is not <margin>B</margin>immense in itself, because a part of it would also necessarily be immense. Nor is the infinite an accident to another thing, because that to which it happens would not be infinite by its own nature. It is not simple; and certainly it is not matter; but even **atoms** <note>The "atomists" (like Democritus or Epicurus) believed the world was made of tiny, indivisible particles; Plotinus argues here that these cannot be the "primary matter" because matter must be continuous.</note> will not hold the rank of matter, which are indeed nothing at all. For every body is divisible throughout. This same idea is refuted by the continuity and fluidity of bodies. Again, it is refuted by the fact that individual things cannot exist without mind and soul, <margin>C</margin>which nature does not allow to come from atoms. Likewise, because no nature at all has been discovered besides atoms that can fabricate anything out of atoms; for no craftsman <note>original: "artifex"</note> is able to create anything out of matter that is not continuous. Many other things could be said, and have been said, against this opinion; therefore it is a waste of time to dwell on them any longer.

<margin>D</margin>**WHAT**, then, is this thing which is said to be one, continuous, and devoid of quality? In the first place, it is manifest that this is not a body, if it is truly devoid of quality; otherwise, it would possess quality. When we say that this very thing is the matter of all sensible things, we do not mean that it is the matter of only certain things, while for others it is a species—as we are accustomed to say that clay is the matter for the potter, but it is not matter simply and absolutely. Since we do not distinguish the matter of the world in this way, but refer it to all things simply: we shall attribute to it <margin>E</margin>nothing at all of those things which are perceived in the sensible genus according to its own nature. If this is so, besides other qualities such as colors, heat, and cold, we must not ascribe to matter lightness, nor gravity, nor density, nor rarity, nor figure: therefore, not even **magnitude** <note>original: "magnitudinem"; size or physical volume.</note>. For magnitude is one thing, and that which is great is another. Again, shape is one thing, and that which is shaped is another. It is necessary that this substrate be nothing composite, but something simple and one by its own nature. For only then will it be empty of all things. And whoever is to hand over form to it, will hand it over <margin>F</margin>as something else existing besides the matter. He will grant it magnitude and all things from those that exist, as if offering and bringing them to it: otherwise, he would be a slave to the magnitude of the matter itself, and would produce a work not as great as he himself decided, but only as much as the matter itself could hold. Moreover, that which some claim—that the will of the craftsman coincides with the magnitude of the matter—seems to be a fiction. If the **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being (like the carpenter making a table).</note> precedes the matter, then the matter will behave exactly as the efficient cause wants, and it will be easy to lead it to all things, and therefore even to <margin>G</margin>magnitude. But if it already possessed magnitude, it would also have shape; for which reason it would be even more difficult to be worked upon by the craftsman. Therefore, the **species** <note>original: "species"; here meaning the "form" or "ideal pattern" of a thing.</note> enters the matter bringing all things with it: and every species contains magnitude, and every mode of quantity together with reason and under reason. For this reason, in each individual kind of thing, the quantity is designated along with the species. For one thing is the prescribed size of a human...

<margin>
**CONCLUSION.**
Because that thing which is the lowest <note>Referring to primary matter, which is at the bottom of the hierarchy of existence.</note> has no forms, and how it relates to forms.
</margin>

<summary>Plotinus argues that primary matter must be a "formless" and "quality-less" substrate. He refutes the idea that matter is made of atoms or has its own inherent size, as this would limit the creative power of the divine Craftsman (the Demiurge).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the nature of matter (hyle). Having previously argued that matter is not a body or a "thing" with properties, he now addresses whether matter possesses any inherent size or "magnitude." This is part of his larger project in the *Enneads* to define matter as a pure, characterless substrate that underlies the physical world but originates from the intelligible realm.</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD II.

<margin>IX
That matter has no magnitude, however great.</margin>
...magnitude, others say: indeed it would be absurd to claim that producing a certain bird's own quantity <note>original: "quantitatem"</note> is different from impressing its own quality. For we should not say that quality is a certain **formative principle** <note>original: "ratio" / Greek: "logos". In Neoplatonism, this refers to the rational structure or "blueprint" that shapes a thing.</note>, while quantity is not: for there exists a certain measure and number belonging to the species.

BUT by what reasoning could one grasp something that has no magnitude at all? Perhaps, indeed, "being" is not the same as being "of a certain size." For Being and Quantity are not identical; there are many other things besides quantity. In every way, we must place all incorporeal nature far from quantity; and matter is incorporeal. Furthermore, quantity itself is not "quantified." For that which is "of a certain size" is that which participates in quantity; for this reason, it is also manifest that quantity is a kind of form <note>original: "speciem"</note>. Just as, therefore, by the presence of "whiteness," something becomes white; but that which creates whiteness in an animal, and the various colors, is not itself a varied color but a certain **formative principle** of variety. Thus, that which makes a thing "of such a size" is not itself of such a size, but is Magnitude itself, or Quantity itself, or the formative principle of quantity that effects it. When quantity itself approaches matter, does it then unfold and extend the matter into a broad expanse? By no means. For matter had not been squeezed into a narrow space; rather, quantity brings a magnitude that was not there before, just as it brings a quality that did not previously exist.

<margin>X
By what means and in what way matter, devoid of quantity and every form, may be known.</margin>
WHAT then? Shall I understand matter in itself to be devoid of magnitude? And how will you understand that which is formless? What kind of intellection is this, or what gaze of thought? Perhaps it is an **indefiniteness** <note>original: "indefinitas". Plotinus argues that to know the "infinite" or "indefinite," the mind must make itself indefinite.</note> itself. For if like is grasped by like, then the indefinite is perceived by the indefinite. A definition <note>original: "Ratio"</note> can indeed be "definite" about the indefinite; but the mental gaze into the indefinite itself ends up being indefinite. But if everything is known by reason and intelligence: here the reason says whatever it says about it; but the intelligence that strives to be there is not intelligence at all, but rather a kind of "orbit" <note>original: "orbitas" / Greek: "anoia" (mindlessness)</note> of intelligence; or rather, it is a **bastard imagination** <note>original: "imaginitio... spuria" / Greek: "nothon logismon". This is a famous reference to Plato's *Timaeus*, where he says matter is perceived by a "bastard reasoning" because it is neither truly "being" nor "non-being."</note> concerning matter, not legitimate, composed partly of that which is not true, and partly of reason. Looking toward this, Plato said that matter is perceived by a "bastard reasoning." What then is this indefiniteness of the soul? Is it total ignorance, like a kind of oblivion? Perhaps it consists rather in a certain negation joined with a certain infinite affirmation. Just as to the eye there is the darkness of shadows, which is the "matter" of every invisible color: so too the soul, by removing everything that is like light in the realm of the senses, and being unable to define what remains, becomes like the eye situated in the darkness. It becomes the same as that which it, in a sense, sees. Does it then see? Perhaps it sees as if seeing nothingness: something devoid of figure, color, and light. Moreover, it has no magnitude, for otherwise it would already be reduced to a form. When, therefore, the soul understands nothing at all, is that state not the same as this experience? Not at all. For when it understands nothing, it "says" nothing, or rather, it experiences nothing. But when it thinks of matter, it undergoes such an experience as if it were receiving a "form" of a formless thing. For indeed, even when it understands things that are formed and have magnitude...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...If another bird <note>original: "ὄρνις" / "ornis"</note> makes a bird. It is more marvelous to introduce quantity to matter than to clothe it in quality; nor is quality a "reason" <note>original: "λόγ@ " / "logos"</note> while quantity is not; for it is also measure and a certain number.

<margin>B</margin>HOW then will someone grasp anything of these beings which has no magnitude at all? For "being" and "quantity" are not the same thing, and there are many other things besides quantity. In general, all incorporeal nature must be placed far from quantity; and matter is incorporeal. Since even quantity itself is not quantified, but rather that which participates in it; so from this it is clear that quantity is a kind of form <note>original: "εἶδός" / "eidos"</note>. <margin>C</margin>Just as, then, something becomes white by the presence of whiteness. And that which produces a white body in a living thing, and the other various colors, is not itself a varied color, but a varied **formative principle** <note>original: "λόγ@" / "logos"</note>, if you will. So also that which makes a thing "of such a size" is not itself of such a size, but is magnitude itself, or quantity, or the "reason" that produces it. Does quantity itself, then, upon arriving, unroll the matter as if it were magnitude? Not at all. For it was not previously **contracted** <note>original: "συνεπέσταλτο" / "synepestalto"</note> in a small space, but quantity gave it magnitude, which was not there before, just as it gave quality, which was not there before.

<margin>D</margin>WHAT then? Will you think of that which is in matter as without magnitude? How will you perceive it? And what is the intellection, and the application of thought? Is it "indeterminacy"? For if like is known by like, and the indeterminate by the indeterminate, then a "reason" <note>original: "λόγ@"</note> might become a definition concerning the indeterminate; but the application of the mind toward it becomes indeterminate. If each thing is known by reason and intellection, <margin>E</margin>but here the reason says what it says about it, the intellection that wishes to be there is not intellection, but a kind of "not-thinking" <note>original: "ἀνοία" / "anoia"</note>, or rather a shadow of it, and not a legitimate one, composed of the other which is not true, and with the other "reason." And perhaps looking at this, Plato said it was graspable by a **bastard reasoning** <note>original: "νόθον λογισμὸν" / "nothon logismon"</note>. What then is the soul's indeterminacy? Is it complete ignorance like a kind of forgetfulness? <margin>F</margin>Or is the indeterminate a kind of affirmation, like the darkness to the eye, which is the matter of every invisible color? Thus also the soul, having removed all things in the sensible world which are like light, and no longer having the power to define what is left, is made like the eye in the darkness. Does it then see? Or does it see in such a way as to see neither form nor light, or like the quantity that has magnitude? But what if it has none? <margin>G</margin>Perhaps it is **unseen** <note>original: "ἅδη" / "hade" (likely a reference to Hades/invisible)</note> when it understands nothing; or is this experience of the soul not the same? Indeed, when it understands nothing, it says "nothing," or rather it experiences nothing. But when it thinks of matter, it undergoes an experience like an impression <note>original: "τύπον" / "typon"</note> of the formless, since even when it thinks of things that are formed and divided...

<meta>catchword: χρη (chré) - "it is necessary"</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter is inherently devoid of magnitude and quantity, existing as an incorporeal substrate that only gains size when the form of quantity is applied. He explains that we perceive this formless matter not through standard logic, but through a "bastard reasoning" akin to the eye trying to see in total darkness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's inquiry into the nature of matter (hyle), specifically focusing on why matter cannot possess inherent size or "mass" (moles/onkos). It concludes Chapter 10 and begins Chapter 11 of Ennead II.4. The translator, Marsilio Ficino, here aligns the Greek concept of matter with the "void" or "empty dimension."</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

...and as something passive <note>original Greek: "patheton"</note> and not affirmative, and moreover, indistinct. It could not even be conceived, unless by some absurdity of those who think of it; nor could it be anything shapeless lying alongside. For the shapeless is already connected to something else. But again, it is like an image and a kind of debt <note>original: "chreoston". This suggests matter is "beholden" to form for its existence.</note> that reason <note>original: "logos"</note> leaves behind. **B** This reason is faint; faint, and darkly dark. One must therefore conceive it so. And since matter itself remains there entirely formless, but within the myths <note>original: "memythologemenois"</note> and the things that have been shaped, even the soul—as if it had lost its form <note>original: "eidos"</note>—feels shame before the indefinite. It is as if it fears being outside of the order of existing things, not enduring to remain in that which is nothing.

<column-break/>

**A** One thinks of it as a kind of composite. For how can it be distinct or colored if it is considered as something infinite? One understands something of it, yet at the same time anxiously and perplexedly; it is a type of understanding or perception of things inherent within it. This "shadowy" understanding of the formless is false and suspicious, for it is not a **species** <note>In Neoplatonism, "species" refers to the intelligible Form or outward appearance that gives a thing its identity and makes it knowable.</note>. Whenever, therefore, in the whole and the composite, the mind perceives the subject together with those things that are in it, it may resolve and separate the consequences. That which remains—which reason leaves behind as a residue—is a kind of thin thing, **B** thinly suspected and darkly seen; it understands without understanding. And since matter itself does not remain formless, but is continually being formed in things, the soul suddenly applies to it the form of things, feeling distress at its indefiniteness—just as if it feared it might fall out of the order of things, not tolerating to linger too long in that which is not.

<margin>XI. That matter is not quantitative mass.</margin>
BUT why is there need for something else to compose bodies besides magnitude and all the qualities? **C** Is there perhaps a need for that which receives all things? Therefore, that receiver will not be **mass** <note>original: "moles" / Greek: "onkos". This refers to bulk or physical volume.</note>. For if it were mass, it would also be magnitude. But if it is devoid of magnitude, perhaps it will have no place to receive the rest. Indeed, since it lacks magnitude, how would it be useful if it contributes neither to form and quality, nor to distance and magnitude? These things, wherever they may be, seem to happen to bodies from matter itself. But in general, just as actions, effects, **D** times, and motions—although they have no physical impression in matter—are nevertheless in the order of things: so it is not necessary for the primary bodies to have matter, but for them to exist as a whole, individually, as that which they are. These existing things, through a varied mixture, have their constitution from many forms. Therefore, the name "matter," which in sacred texts <note>likely referring to Plato's *Timaeus* or the Pythagorean traditions</note> is called magnitude, seems to be a vain term. Furthermore, it is by no means necessary **E** for that which receives everything to be a mass or to have dimension, unless perhaps it is an acquired magnitude. For even the soul, which receives all things, possesses all things at once. If magnitude happened to the soul, it would rightly hold each thing within that magnitude. But matter receives what it receives within a certain space for this very reason. Just as animals and plants, while they are extended by magnitude, meanwhile receive the production of quality; where, even when the quantity is contracted, the quality is also contracted. But if anyone should say, because in such things a **F** certain magnitude precedes and is subject to the Form-giver, that magnitude is simply required, he would not be speaking correctly. For in the making of these things, it is not simply matter itself, but a "thing of such a kind" that is thought of as matter. But that which is simply matter must receive its magnitude from something else. Thus, it is not necessary for that which is to receive form to be a mass; **G** rather, while it is a mass, it must receive another quality. It must have no visible appearance or image, since, as it is the primary thing, it is a certain "aptitude" <note>original: "aptitudo". In this context, it means a potentiality or readiness to receive forms.</note> for them. Whether it be like a certain mass or an empty dimension: for this reason, some have said that matter is the same as the "imagination of dimension," or rather, the void.
->they handed down that it is the same as the void.<-

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter is a formless, dimensionless substrate that the soul perceives with "spurious reasoning." He concludes that matter is not a physical mass, but rather a potentiality or "void" that receives magnitude and form from a higher source.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's inquiry into the nature of matter (hyle). Having established that matter is formless and indefinite, Plotinus now explores how the soul perceives "mass" or "bulk" (moles/onkos) when it encounters this indefinite subject. This corresponds to Ennead II.4, Chapter 11 and the beginning of Chapter 12.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

Since the soul, when it can determine nothing, wanders, whenever it applies itself to matter, it pours itself out into a state of infinity. It neither circumscribes itself nor directs itself toward a specific point; otherwise, it would already be defining something. For this reason, this subject should not be called "large" in itself, nor "small" again; rather, it is both "the large and the small." In this way, it is both a mass and yet lacks magnitude—because, clearly, it is the *matter* of mass. If it is contracted from a wide state into a narrow one, and conversely stretched from a narrow state into a wide one, it traverses mass, as it were. Such a mass is its own indefiniteness—a capacity for magnitude within itself, I say—but in the imagination, it appears in the manner we have described. For other things that lack magnitude, which are indeed **forms** <note>original: "species". In this context, these are the intelligible blueprints or "Forms" that give objects their identity.</note>, are such that each is defined; therefore, no suspicion of mass falls upon them. But because matter is indefinite and never rests within itself, but is transferred here and there into every form, and by its slipperiness is diverted into anything at all, it certainly becomes "many" through its derivation and birth throughout all things. Under this condition, it seems to have acquired a certain nature of mass and dimension.

<margin>
XII. The recipient of matter: if the forms resided within it in the same way they are seated there, they would be a single matter.
</margin>

**SPACES THEREFORE CONTRIBUTE** to bodies. For the forms of bodies exist here in dimensions; however, they are not created around magnitude as if it were a subject, but rather around that which *becomes* quantitative. Indeed, if they were to arise around magnitude itself rather than around matter, they would similarly lack mass and substance, or they would be nothing more than "reasons" <note>original: "rationes". Here meaning conceptual principles rather than physical realities.</note>. These, however, are concerned with the soul, and therefore they would not be bodies. It is necessary, then, that many things here revolve around a single thing—a single thing, I say, which *becomes* quantitative. This thing must be something other than magnitude itself. For whatever things are mixed together come together into the same thing because they possess matter, and they do not need another thing around which they stand. For each of those things which are mixed runs together, bringing its own self and its own matter with it. Nevertheless, there is a need for a simultaneous receptacle, that is, a vessel or a place. But place is posterior to matter and to bodies; therefore, bodies require matter first. Nor does it follow that because actions and effects are immaterial, bodies are also without matter. For bodies are composites, while actions are not. Matter itself provides the subject for those who act when they perform an action, remaining within them. Yet it does not offer itself into the action itself—for the agents themselves do not seek that—nor is one action transformed into another, which would necessitate matter being within them; rather, the agent itself passes from one action to another, so that it is consistent for the agent to be the "matter" for the actions. Matter is therefore necessary both for quality and for magnitude, and thus for bodies. Nor is it a vain name, but a certain subject, although it is invisible and devoid of magnitude. Otherwise, we would have to deny the existence of qualities and magnitude by the same logic. For if any of these were taken only in itself, it would be said to be nothing; but if these exist, and if each of them exists in a faint way, then much more will matter exist, even if it is not clear, and certainly not perceptible to the senses. For it cannot be seen by the eyes, as it is colorless; nor by hearing, for it lacks sound; nor even by sm—

<column-break/>

**A** Since the soul can define no mass when it associates with matter, it pours it out into infinity, neither circumscribing it nor arriving at a point. Because it can show everything, it should not be called "large" separately, nor "small" again, but "large and small." Thus it is mass, and thus it is without magnitude, because it is the matter of mass. Contracting from the large to the small, and from the small to the large, it runs through mass, as it were. Its indefiniteness is such a mass: a <term>reception</term> <note>original: "hypodoche". Plato's term in the *Timaeus* for the "nursing mother" or "receptacle" of all generation.</note> **B** of magnitude within itself. In the imagination it is perceived that way, and not like the other things without magnitude which are forms, where each is defined. Thus there is no likelihood of mass unless it is indefinite and not yet entirely present. Because it is carried into every form, it moves like water, and being stirred up everywhere, it becomes "much" by its leading into and generation of all things, and **C** it holds its current manner, as a nature of mass.

**SIZE THEREFORE CONTRIBUTES** to bodies. For the forms of bodies, if they were in magnitude, but not *around* magnitude, would not exist. For all things that come to be around magnitude, or around matter, would likewise be without magnitude and without substance, or they would be only "reasons" <note>original: "logoi". Rational principles or formative seeds.</note>. These are around the soul, and **D** not bodies. Through which it must be that many things are around one; and this thing, having been made quantitative, is second to magnitude and to the body. It has the greatest relation to matter. So that everything is in one... <insert>but that around which each of the things being mixed arrives, bringing its own matter</insert>... it is seen through it nonetheless as a servant... **E** ...second from matter and bodies... bodies need matter. Nor are they like productions and actions which are immaterial; because of this, bodies also [require it]. For all bodies [are composite], but actions are not. And to those who act, matter gives a subject when they act, remaining in them. It does not give the acting itself; for actions do not transfer or change into one another in one **F** another. For they are matter for themselves, but the one who acts changes from some actions into others, so that he himself is the matter of the actions. Matter is therefore necessarily in both quality and magnitude; thus it is in bodies, or it is an empty name. But it exists as a subject, and it is invisible and without magnitude. Otherwise we shall not even speak of qualities and magnitude as the same in reason. **G** None of those things would be said to exist if taken only by themselves. But if these exist and each is a faint being, much more is there matter, even if it does not exist clearly, being invisible, not to the senses—for it is not for the eyes, being colorless, nor for hearing; not by <term>sound</term> <note>original: "psopho". Meaning any kind of noise or resonance.</note>.

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter (hyle) serves as an indefinite "receptacle" for magnitude and quality, allowing the soul to perceive "mass" even though matter itself is incorporeal and invisible. He differentiates between immaterial actions and composite bodies, asserting that matter is a necessary substrate for physical existence.</summary>
<keywords>matter, hyle, magnitude, mass, moles, onkos, soul, psyche, receptacle, hypodoche, form, eidos, Neoplatonism, perception, imagination, phantasia</keywords>
