<meta>This page continues the translation of Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically the Fourth Book of the Second Ennead (II.4.12). Plotinus is examining the nature of "prime matter" and whether it can be said to have any qualities or properties of its own.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

**A** Matter is not perceived by taste or smell, for it possesses neither moisture nor vapor. But can it be felt by touch? Not at all, since it is not a body. Touch reaches a body when it perceives it as dense or rare, soft or hard, moist or dry. Yet none of these belong to the nature of matter. Matter, therefore, cannot be known by the senses, but only by a certain reasoning—and I do not mean a reasoning full of intellect, but one that is empty. For this reason, this type of logic is called "bastard reasoning" <note>original: "ratio adulterina" / "logos nothos". Plotinus uses this Platonic term to describe how we try to think about matter: since matter has no form, our mind has to "think nothing" to reach it.</note>.

**B** Furthermore, corporeity <term>corporeity: the state of being a physical body</term> itself is not a property of matter. If corporeity is a kind of definition or ratio, it certainly differs from matter. Matter is something else entirely; if it were to bridge the gap and become something active, it would immediately be a "body" and no longer "matter" alone.

<margin>XIII. Matter is neither a quality, nor does it possess a specific quality.</margin>

**C** **IF** one were to say that a certain quality is the underlying subject of things—a quality common to all elements—they must first explain what kind of quality it is. Then, they must explain how a quality can be the "subject" (the foundation) and how something that lacks magnitude <note>original: "magnitudine caret". Matter is considered to have no size or dimension until form is applied to it.</note> can be perceived as having a quality, since it possesses neither matter nor size. Lastly, if this quality is defined, how can it be matter? And if it is indefinite, it is not a quality at all, but is instead the very subject and matter we are looking for.

**D** But perhaps someone will object that nothing prevents matter from being "without quality," in the sense that by its own nature it shares in no qualities of other things. Yet, by the very fact that it shares in **none** of these things, it is already "qualified" in a way. It possesses a property that distinguishes it from others, like a certain "privation" <term>privation: the absence or lack of a quality that should normally be present</term>. For a person who suffers a privation is described as having a certain quality—such as a blind man.

**E** If, therefore, this privation is a condition of matter, why is matter not "qualified"? If privation is present within it, it follows even more clearly that privation is a type of quality. But whoever says this makes everything into qualities! By this logic, even "quantity" would be a "quality," and "essence" would be the same. If everything is a quality, then quality itself must be present. It is ridiculous to claim that a thing is "qualified" by something that is not itself a quality.

**F** If it is argued that matter is "Otherness" itself, then it is not "qualified," since "Otherness" is not itself a "quality." But if it is simply "other," we must answer that it is not made "other" by itself, but by "Otherness" (just as a thing is made identical by Identity). Neither is privation a quality, nor is it "qualified"; rather, it is the lack of a quality, or the absence of something else—just as silence is the absence of voice. For privation is a negation, whereas being "qualified" consists in an affirmation.

**G** Added to this is the fact that the property of matter is not a **form**. Its "property" is simply the fact that it is not qualified. To call it "qualified" because it lacks quality is like saying it "possesses magnitude" because it has no magnitude. Therefore, its property is nothing other than what it is: "matter." This property is not something added to it, but rather resides in its relationship to other things—namely, that matter is "other" than them. While other things are not only "other" but also "something" (a species or form), matter is appropriately called "only other." Perhaps it is more fitting to call it "Others" in the plural, so that by using the plural, you do not accidentally define matter as a single "Other," but instead demonstrate its indefinite nature.

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter is not a "quality" and has no inherent properties; even its "otherness" or "lack of quality" should not be mistaken for a defining characteristic, as matter is fundamentally indefinite.</summary>
<keywords>Matter, Hyle, Quality, Privation, Otherness, Bastard Reasoning, Corporeity, Plotinus, Metaphysics</keywords>

--- Page 203 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of "Prime Matter" from Ennead II.4. Having established that matter lacks quality and magnitude, Plotinus now explores its relationship to "privation" (the absence of form) and "the infinite."</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD II.

<margin>
**XIII. Whether matter is privation itself, or if privation is a property predicated of matter.**
</margin>

But we must now investigate whether matter is the same thing as **privation** <term>privation: in philosophy, this refers to the absence or lack of a specific quality or form that something could potentially have</term>, or if privation is instead something said about matter. If one claims that matter and privation are one in their underlying subject, but two in their logical definition, they ought to explain the specific definition of each. We should provide a definition of matter that touches on nothing regarding privation, and a definition of privation in the same way. Either neither definition exists within the other, or both exist in each other, or one exists only within the other, whichever that may be. 

If, therefore, each is defined separately and neither requires the other, then they are two distinct things, and matter will be something other than privation, even if privation happens to belong to it. In such a definition of one, the other should not be visible, even as a potentiality. But if they are related in the way we are born and exist, then each becomes a double and there are two. If, however, they are like fire and heat—where heat exists within fire, but fire is not necessarily implied when we speak of heat—and if matter is privation in the same way fire is hot, then privation would be a "species" or form of matter, while the underlying subject would be something else, which must be the matter. Thus, in this way, they would not be one. 

Furthermore, could they be one in subject but two in definition in the sense that "privation" does not denote the presence of anything, but rather an absence? In this view, privation would be a negation of being, as if one were to say "non-being." For a negation adds nothing, but simply states that something does not exist; thus, privation would be like non-being. If "non-being" is used in this way—meaning it is not "being" but something else—would there then be two definitions? One looking at the subject, and the other at the privation, signifying a certain relationship to other things? Or rather, does the definition of matter look toward other things, and the definition of the subject first look toward others? The definition of privation shows its indeterminacy, perhaps even touching its very nature—except perhaps for the claim that both are one in subject, but two in definition. But if matter is the same as that which is indeterminate, undefined, and formless, how can there still be two definitions?

<margin>
**XV. How matter is called "the infinite," whether it is the "indefinite," or "privation."**
</margin>

**AGAIN**, we must examine whether "the infinite" and "the indeterminate" exist as an accident <term>accident: a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature</term> within some other nature, and how this accident occurs, and whether privation is such an accident. Certainly, if the ratios <note>original: "rationes" / "logoi"</note> of number that exist are outside of infinity—since they are limits and orders, and order itself descends from these into other things—then that which is ordered must be something other than the "orderer." Since it is the "limit," the "end," and the "ratio" that perform the ordering, it is necessary that what is being ordered and limited is, by its own nature, **infinite**. 

Matter is what is being ordered, or indeed anything that is not matter but is called such because it either participates in matter or takes on its condition. Therefore, it is necessary that the infinite itself is matter. We should not say the infinite is "accidental" to matter, as if infinity were just a property that happened to matter. First, because whatever happens to something must be a "ratio" or definition, but the infinite is not a ratio. Secondly, to what already existing thing would the infinite happen? To a limit or a thing already limited?

<column-break/>

**A** But we must ask that question: whether it is privation, or if privation is *about* it <note>original: "περὶ αὐτῆς" / "peri autēs"</note>. He who says they are both one in the underlying subject but two in definition should be prepared to teach the definition of each. He should give a definition of matter while assuming nothing <gloss>as nothing</gloss> regarding privation, and a definition of privation likewise. Either neither should be in the definition of the other, or each in each, or one only in the other. **B** <gloss>whichever of these</gloss> If each is separate and does not seek the other, both will be two, and matter will be different from privation, even if privation happens to it. In the definition, it must not be revealed <gloss>unless perhaps</gloss> that it is like a snub nose and "snubness"—in which case each is double and two. If it is like fire and heat, and if heat is the essence of fire, **C** and if heat is taken from the fire, and matter is privation as fire is hot, then privation will be a kind of form for it, and the subject will be something else, which must be the matter. It is not in this way, then, that they are one in the subject and two in definition. For "privation" does not signify something present, but rather something *not* present; privation is, as it were, a negation of beings, as if one were to say "non-being." **D** If non-being is a negation, but one says that it *is* something, or if privation is "non-being" in such a way that it is indeed something, but something *else*, then there would be two definitions: one looking to the subject, and the other to the privation, which they say reveals its relationship to other things—or rather, it reveals what matter is in relation to other things, and the subject in relation to other things. The definition of privation shows its indeterminacy <note>original: "ἀόριστον" / "aoriston"</note>, or perhaps this is its very nature; except if they are one in the subject and two in definition. If being indeterminate, and being infinite, and being formless <note>original: "ἀπόρων" / "aporon"</note> are the same as matter, how are there still two definitions?

**E** **AGAIN**, therefore, we must investigate if the infinite and the indeterminate are "accidental" to another nature, and how they are accidental, and if privation is accidental. If the ratios and limits of number are outside of infinity—for they are limits and orders—then <gloss>to order</gloss> is to bring order to other things. **F** These things that bring order are not in the thing being ordered; the thing ordered is different from the thing ordering. Limit and ratio are the orderers. It is necessary that the thing being ordered and defined is, in itself, infinite. Matter is what is ordered, and whatever is not matter is said to be so by participating in matter. **G** Is it therefore necessary for matter to be the infinite itself? He did not mean it in this way, as if it were accidental, or that being infinite happened to it. For first, that which happens to something must be a ratio, but the infinite is not a ratio. Secondly, to what existing thing will the infinite happen? To a limit or to the limited?

<summary>Plotinus explores the metaphysical relationship between matter, privation, and infinity, arguing that matter is not just "accidentally" infinite or lacking form, but is essentially the indeterminate "non-being" that receives order from external ratios.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, matter, privation, infinity, non-being, metaphysics, Neoplatonism, form and substance, Aristotle's categories</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation of "Prime Matter" from Ennead II.4. Having previously discussed whether matter is synonymous with "privation," Plotinus now examines the "infinite" (the indefinite) nature of matter and its relationship to "otherness" and "evil."</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> ...not limited, but the most infinite. For the infinite does not come to matter as a quality or a source coming to something already limited. Rather, is this its very nature, or is the infinite merely an accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing happens to have, but which is not essential to what that thing is.</note> of matter? It must be the infinite itself. For even in the intelligible realms <note>The "intelligible realms" refer to the higher world of Divine Mind and the Forms, as opposed to the physical world.</note>, matter is the infinite, being generated from the infinity or power of the One there—or whatever it might be. It is not without infinity in that realm, but it is of a certain kind. How then is it there, and how is it here? Perhaps there is a double infinite.
<margin>B</margin> In what way will they differ? As archetype and image. Is the infinite here then "less" infinite? On the contrary, it is more so. For insofar as an image flees from true being, it is more infinite; for infinity consists more in being less defined. That which is "more" in the realm of the Good is "more" in the realm of the Evil. The infinite there, having more "being," is an image tending toward non-being, or insofar as it flees from 
<margin>C</margin> being and truth. * It falls into the nature of an image and becomes a more true infinity. Is the infinite, then, the same as the "essence of the infinite"? Where there is both a reason-principle <term>reason-principle: translated from "logos," this refers to the formative, organizing power that gives shape to matter</term> and matter, they are distinct; but where there is only matter, one must say they are the same—or better yet, that matter here is not even to be assigned "being" as its own. For some reason-principle existed in the higher infinite, but here there is none, if it is to be truly infinite.
<margin>D</margin> One must say, therefore, that matter is infinite of itself, as something standing in opposition to the reason-principle. Just as the reason-principle is nothing other than reason-principle, so matter, standing opposite to it according to its infinity, is nothing other than infinity itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For indeed, matter is neither a limited thing nor a limit itself. Likewise, if the "infinite" were to be added to a limited thing, it would destroy its nature; therefore, the infinite is not an accident of matter. Matter itself is the infinite; since even in the intelligible world, matter is the infinite itself. This was perhaps generated from the very infinity of the One, or from its power or eternity; so that in the One itself there is no infinity, but the One is the author of infinity. By what reasoning, then, is the infinite both there and here?
<margin>B</margin> Perhaps the infinite is twofold. But how do they differ? Truly, as archetype <note>original: "exemplar"</note> and image. Is that which is among us "less" of an infinite? Perhaps it is actually "more." For insofar as the image falls short of existence and truth, it is to that extent more infinite. For infinity is found more in that which is less defined. That which is "less" in the realm of the Good is "more" in the realm of evil. Therefore, the infinite that is there, because it exists more as a "being," is like an imagined 
<margin>C</margin> infinite. But the being here, which is "less," insofar as it recedes from "being" itself, falls and slides into the nature of an image, and is more truly infinite. Consequently, is "the infinite" the same as "being infinite"? Perhaps where there is both reason-principle and matter, each is different; but where there is only matter, one must say either they are the same, or—what is more correct—that "being" is not to be assigned to the infinite there at all: for some reason-principle existed there, which is entirely absent in the infinite here, if it is to be truly infinite. 
<margin>D</margin> One must therefore say that matter is infinite from itself, as something positioned in opposition to the reason-principle. For just as a reason-principle is nothing other than a reason-principle, so matter, opposed to reason according to its infinity, must be called infinite in such a way that it is nothing else besides matter itself.

### XVI. Questions concerning matter itself regarding otherness, privation, and evil.

<margin>A</margin> And is matter the same thing as "otherness"? <note>original: "alteritas"</note> Perhaps it is not the same as otherness in a general sense, but a part of otherness: namely, that part which is opposite to the things that truly "are," which exist as reason-principles. For this reason, that which is called "non-being"
<margin>E</margin> can be something, namely privation <term>privation: the absence of a quality or form that should naturally be present</term>, if indeed privation is a certain opposition to those things that consist in the reason-principle itself. Will privation then be destroyed when that thing arrives of which it is the privation? Not at all. For the recipient of a "habit" <note>In ancient philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) refers to a stable quality or state of being.</note> is not the habit itself, but the privation of it. Likewise, the recipient of a limit is neither a limited thing nor a limit, but the infinite, insofar as it is infinite. But how can it be that the arriving limit does not destroy the nature of the infinite? Especially since this infinite is not said to be an accident. Perhaps if this infinite were a quantity, it would be destroyed; but as it is, it does not happen that way, but rather the limit preserves it in being. 
<margin>F</margin> For that which it was fashioned for by nature, it is brought into act and perfection; just as that which was not yet "destined" <note>original: "fatum"</note>, when it is struck, or like the female when she is joined with the male. For then the female nature is not lost, but becomes more "feminine"—that is, that which it is, is made more so. But 
<margin>G</margin> does matter become evil by obtaining good? Perhaps because it was already in want; for it did not possess it. For that which lacks something and then obtains it, holds a middle position between good and evil, if it stands equally toward both. But that which possesses nothing, as if weighed down by poverty—or rather, since it is poverty itself—must necessarily be evil.

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes between the "intelligible infinite" of the higher realms and the "true infinite" of physical matter, which is more infinite because it is further from Being. He concludes that matter is not just lacking in form, but is "Poverty" and "Otherness" itself, identifying it with the root of evil.</summary>

Having concluded the discussion on the nature of matter in Book 4, he now moves to Book 5 (which he titles Book 1 of a new section), focusing on the Aristotelian and Platonic concepts of "Act" and "Potency"—essentially the difference between what something is currently and what it has the potential to become.</meta>

<margin>B</margin> For this is not a lack of riches or of strength, but a lack of wisdom, a lack of virtue, of beauty, of value, of shape, of appearance, and of quality. What, then, prevents this from being misshapen, and entirely base, and entirely evil? Indeed, among the higher beings, "matter" is said to be "being." For that which stands above matter itself is judged to be superior to being; but among us, that which is above matter exists as "being." Therefore, when "non-being" is said of this matter, it is understood as a "different being" compared to the beauty of being itself. <note>Ficino is explaining that in the divine realm, even "matter" has a form of existence, whereas in our physical world, matter is the lowest rung of reality, often called "non-being" because it lacks inherent form.</note>

<column-break/>

<note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἢ πλάτῳ πενία τοῦ παρ’ ἐκείνῳ..." This is the original Greek text of Plotinus (Ennead II.4.16) that Ficino translated into Latin in the left column.</note> But is it a poverty of breadth compared to what is there? Rather, it is a poverty accompanied by mindlessness, a poverty of virtue, beauty, strength, shape, form, and quality. How then is it not ugly? How is it not entirely shameful? How is it not entirely evil? But that matter there, which exists in its own form, is "beyond being"—for there must be something prior to it—whereas here, the thing surrounding matter is different from it, just as light is different from the beautiful being.

# MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY ON BOOK I: ON THAT WHICH IS IN ACT AND THAT WHICH IS IN POTENCY.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->Also concerning act and potency. Also concerning metals and stones.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' featuring floral and scrolling foliage patterns.</image-desc>
THE BOOK on potency and act confirms by this summary those things which were said in the book on matter, and through these it is more fully understood. It is divided, however, into five chapters. In the first, you will note—after certain doubts—that whatever is said to be "in potency" <term>potency: the capacity or potential to become something else, like a seed having the potency to be a tree</term> is necessarily referred to something else, namely to that which comes from it or exists "in act" <term>act: the completed reality or state of being, like the tree itself</term>. Likewise, potency is properly referred to act. Furthermore, it is rare that something which is in potency toward something else remains the same substance; for when something new arrives, it is sometimes changed, whether the variation happens for the better or for the worse. You will consider, moreover, that in the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" is the realm of divine ideas or forms, which Platonists believe is more real than our physical world.</note> there is no potency that is not also act, or which needs to be drawn out or acquired; otherwise, if it never reached act, it would be judged to be in potency in vain, or if it did eventually reach act, there would be a temporal change within eternal things. Therefore, lest these absurdities follow, every potency there is reduced to its total act from eternity. Next, you will observe that the "potency of acting" should not be called "being in potency," but "being able to suffer/undergo" can be called "being in potency." Finally, you will observe the Platonic view here—which he has already opened up twice elsewhere—that he thinks metal is "cooked water," whether he thinks it is simply water in the manner of crystal, or mostly water. For it is the opinion of the Physicists <note>The "Physicists" refers to natural philosophers, often Aristotelians.</note> that in composing mixtures, heat and cold approach rather as agents than as matter, for they cannot be easily mixed due to their vehemence. Indeed, the "dry" and the "moist" underlie them as matter. Physically, where the dry prevails over the moist, stone hardens; but where the moisture of the liquid exceeds, metal is formed, which melts in fire because of the exuberance of the liquid, whereas the dryness in stone prevents such melting.

->Concerning the two matters, and act, and potency, both in bodies and in the soul.<-

II IN the second chapter, you will observe a twofold matter. First, indeed, is "composite natural matter," which is taken up for the form of art, such as when a statue is made from bronze. Second is "natural matter" as well, but "simple," which is taken up for a similarly natural form, as when air is made from water. In the first case, that which is said to be a "statue in potency" is the bronze itself; this is opposed to what is called a "statue in act," which is neither the bronze alone, nor the figure fashioned in the bronze, but something composed of both. This "composite" thing, existing in act, is opposed to the bronze insofar as the bronze was "this" in potency; yet it is not predicated of the bronze in that way. Therefore, the bronze does not "become" a statue, but a statue is made *from* bronze. Here, certainly, insofar as the matter remains the same—that is, the substance of the bronze remains under the figure—nevertheless, it is something other than the figure or the composite. But matter is more distinct from form and the composite where, upon the arrival of a new form and for the generation of a new composite, the substance of the prior composite is necessarily transformed, as when air is made from water. For there, "prime matter" <term>prime matter: the most basic, formless "stuff" of the universe that can become anything</term> underlies it, in which there is nothing of form, so that it can deservedly be said to be "nothing in act." But "secondary matters," as composites, possess something of form; they add that they are in potency toward one thing, while being in act according to another. In the higher things, therefore—since from a preceding matter and an arriving form something else is made, namely a composite, and that is not the same as the matter or even the form—that which is "in potency" is deservedly called "something other" than that which exists "in act" in the matter (that is, the composite). But truly, in the soul, it seems it should not be said this way. For when the soul acquires a habit <note>In this context, a "habit" is a stable quality or learned skill, like knowing how to speak a language.</note>, a third composite essence does not emerge from the soul and the habit. Therefore, the same soul which was called "knowing in potency" is soon called "knowing in act." It becomes knowing in act, however, not by the reason that it was "ignorant," but by the reason that it was "rational and teachable"; for even when it is already "taught in act," it still preserves the aptitude for knowledge, but it does not preserve the ignorance. But it is "in potency" in one way toward acquiring a habit, and in another way "in potency" toward the act once the habit is acquired. That it does not become "learned" by the reason that it is "ignorant" is clear, since not just any ignorant person is easily made learned, but only the one who is apt. Neither does "privation" <term>privation: the simple absence of a quality</term> contribute to a habit, but "potency" does.
Conclude everywhere that what is called "in potency" is the "subject," while what is "in act" is the "composite" or "quasi-composite." Indeed, the form in a subject is named "act"—not simply, but the act of the subject. Finally, besides the form or habit (which is a certain form), the action itself which proceeds from the form or habit is also named "act." Action is most especially called "act" because it is more manifest in its activity; for the sake of this, form or habit is acquired, and the whole...
<meta>Catchword at bottom: "vis forma" (the power of form)</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the distinction between being "in potency" (having the potential) and "in act" (being the realized reality), applying these concepts to the physical world, the creation of art, and the learning process of the human soul.</summary>

On the previous page, Ficino began discussing how these concepts apply differently to the physical world versus the divine or "intelligible" realm.</meta>

<page-num>171</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK V OF ENNEAD II.</header>

...the power of form or disposition is brought forth to the efficacy of action. Again, observe here that the act which is form, or takes the place of form—because it approaches a subject that is as yet unformed and powerless—requires some benefit from an external cause. Otherwise, an act would proceed from the internal power of the form or disposition itself.

->How potency and act differ below the heavens, in the heavens, and again in the intelligible world.<-

III After these things, however, he <note>Plotinus</note> prohibits anything in the intelligible world from being "in potency," indicating: "in potency," I say, in a way that might proceed to a new act, where the thing’s nature is one thing and its act is another. He says, however, that because the potency there is a fruitful thing, it is not only always in act, but is itself the very act. Furthermore, because what is designated there as "material potency" is actually a certain form, it is therefore also an act; this is because this potency and the act it looks toward are not two different things by nature, but one. We should not, however, say that exactly the same thing exists just because that matter always has the same form; for even if God continued the form in the matter of a body for eternity, the form would still be something other than the matter—as we believe happens in the celestial bodies. 

Again, just as in someone who has already learned something, the potency of learning itself does not perish—for the "teachable" potential is not removed by education, but perfected—so in the intellectual world, alongside the formal act, there also lies hidden a potency. Yet, one would not say that something exists there "in potency" because of this, nor is this a different substance from the act; they differ only by reason. 

Certainly, just as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Aristotle argued that in the "sub-lunar" world (Earth), matter and form are distinct, while in the heavens they are more unified.</note> held that matter and form below the Moon were two natures and different substances, but perhaps in heaven there is one nature of that body which acts as matter or a subject for its own light—which light is not some other nature besides the nature of that body, but is the property and act of that nature—so Plotinus thinks concerning matter and form in the corporeal and incorporeal world. For here <note>in our physical world</note> there are two natures, but there <note>in the intelligible realm</note> one. 

Here they differ just as light diffused through the air (acting as form) differs from the airy matter; but there they are like a glow from light, or shining from light, or at least like light within a flame. For light in the air is a different nature than the air; but in a flame, it does not add another nature, but is a certain property and the act of the perpetual flame. Therefore, just as this light is to the flame as form and act are to potency, so form (the formal) seems to relate to that which is called "material" in the intelligible world. 

A similar distinction appears between the "concave" and the "convex": if you consider a spherical surface where there is no underlying depth, then the concave and convex conditions differ neither in place, nor subject, nor nature, but perhaps only by logical definition. For a single surface by nature will seem "convex" to those outside the circle, but to those inside it will be called a "concavity"—just as the intellect and will differ within the soul. 

But to speak briefly: in this whole corporeal world, matter and form are two natures—except for heaven, where matter exists for the nature of form. In the incorporeal world, however, matter is the essence and nature of form, while form is the "being" and "act" of matter. Again, matter there is not "in potency" toward form, nor is it a potential for form; rather, it is the very potency *of* the form. Form, likewise, is not some act *in* matter or potency, but rather the very "potency-act" itself. 

Since, when he names the "intelligible world," he does not want only the Divine Intellect to be understood, but also all intellects and souls capable of intelligence, he therefore also denies that the intellectual soul is "in potency" toward anything new. He says that in its vegetative part, it is the power that produces life, and in its rational part, it is the power that produces knowledge. Then he adds that any Idea or thing separated from the body is entirely what it is "in act," because it is a species and form completely absolute from time. 

Here you will also note that for us, not only is a thing "in potency" (needing something higher to bring it to work), but wherever potency and act are two distinct natures, there is a need for a higher principle, even if the potency is perpetually joined to the act. For a nature that is "formable" in itself is not led to a formal nature except by the benefit of some single and simple nature. Above anything composed of two natures stands a simple nature, performing a perpetual act. Because this nature always brings forth the act from itself, it is rightly called "The Act." 

Accordingly, where he says that the soul, as intellect, is in the intelligible world, but as reason, it is in matter: notice that the soul is distinct by nature from the intelligible world, even if joined by action—just as light is a different nature from matter, even if it touches it by spreading over it. The soul is not the act of matter, but rather the act of the "Higher Soul" acting upon matter, and serving as a kind of form for matter. The "First Soul" is chiefly called "act" because nothing new is added to its nature nor taken away, and it exercises its own act within itself. Through the intellect, it enjoys eternal action; through its discursive power, it conceives nothing from external things, but rather gives birth within itself. 

The "Second Soul" too, although it seems to change its various actions, nevertheless, insofar as it is itself, it forms the flowing and ebbing matter through a single act—or at least through the vigor of giving life. Just as fire burns different things with the same heat, it is as if someone were to shape the flowing waves beneath with a diligent succession of the same seal. I omit the fact that some argue the soul always perceives and wills through a single continuous act of cognition and will, seeing things as they fall into this act of the soul—much like someone who, with eyes wide open, sees many things at once, and sees not only a continuous view but also the preceding traces in succession. 

What he later signifies regarding the "Ideas"—saying they are all "lives" and "acts"—will be explained elsewhere. Certainly, remember that the "Primary Essence" in which the Ideas exist is life itself. For life does not come to that essence from the outside like a form comes to a body; it proceeds from within as an act. Therefore, that essence is perfect, and its life is perfect; it exists "in act" in a perfect way. Thus, what is "in act" there, exists as the Act itself. Just as essence’s innermost act is life, so life’s innermost act is intellect. From that life, the "True Soul" proceeds; from that intellect, in turn, the "Intellect" flashes forth into the soul.

->Matter is not something in act.<-

IIII He asks in the fourth chapter: whether primary matter is anything "in act." He first explains that it is not any of those things that are entirely above it (the "true beings"), nor is it any of those things generated within it (the "untrue beings"). He wonders meanwhile if it could be something else "in act." Certainly not something "above-being," nor "true being," lest it be mistaken for being again. What then? Will matter be something even lower "in act"? Certainly nothing. Since it fails to meet the whole nature and name of "being," and thus does not have "being," it surely does not have "being in act."

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical distinction between "actuality" and "potentiality," arguing that in the divine/intelligible world, these two are unified, whereas in the physical world, they are separate natures requiring a higher cause to unite them. Ficino uses analogies of light, fire, and geometry (concave/convex) to explain how the Soul and Intellect operate as pure acts compared to the "non-being" of primary matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically addressing the nature of "matter" and its relationship to "potency" (potentiality) and "act" (actuality). While the previous page (171) concluded the discussion of intellectual potency, this page (192) transitions into the fifth book of the second Ennead. There appears to be a gap in the page numbering provided in the source, but the thematic continuity regarding the transition from the intelligible realm to the nature of "non-being" or matter remains intact.</meta>

<page-num>192</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO. He confirms the previous points.</header>

He <note>Ficino referring to Plotinus</note> questions again in the fifth chapter: If matter is nothing in "act" <note>actuality</note>, in what way are we able to speak of this very thing? And he confirms the things already said through debate. Now, matter is called the "matter of beings" precisely because it exists in potency <note>potentiality</note> toward those beings, or toward receiving their images; or rather, it is itself the very potency that can be formed from them. Indeed, in any art, to name "matter" as being under a craftsman is nothing other than to introduce something that possesses nothing of the craft itself, yet is capable of receiving all things. In nature, however, to place matter under the "Architect of all things" <note>God or the Demiurge</note> is not so much to assert something that is in potency toward forms in a specific way, as it is to assert a potency that is entirely "formable." Such a potency, although it is thought to precede the effect of the form in a certain order, nevertheless—because the very definition of this potency is nothing other than "formability"—necessarily depends on the "act" <note>the reality</note> of the form.

Where, even if the form still appears to be in the future, that potency already appears present—driving out, as it were, the actual effect of the form. Yet, that which is called the "presence" of this potency is nothing other than possibility (if I may put it that way) and the "futureness" of the form; or, as someone might imagine, it is a certain confused beginning of the form. Now, if you compare the form to the efficient cause, the fact that the form is future depends on the presence of the cause. But if you compare matter to the nature of the form itself, whatever "presence" is imagined to be in the matter depends on the future status of the form—indeed, even on its present status. For the form is seen as being included in the "inspiration" <note>the breathing into or shaping</note> of matter, so long as matter is defined as "formability."

Likewise, if you relate this lowest thing <note>matter</note> to the supreme "One," and you say that just as that One is pure Act, the Shaper of all, so this matter is pure Potency, formable only under all other things; then, surely, if you were to attribute anything of that supreme status to this formable potency, you would immediately destroy its nature. Conversely, whatever "act" <note>actual being</note> of any kind you dedicated to this lowest thing as its own, you would also suddenly lose its nature. For the "being" of this thing is judged to be "being in potency," and the act proper to it is specifically "formability." Its presence is nothing other than the "future-state" of the form.

Matter is so separated from the nature of "being" <note>true reality</note> that it neither adheres to being as its property or passion, nor does it represent being like an image, nor is it so impressed under its image that it is affected by it, or retains a trace or footprint. It is always, by its nature, casting off any specific "acts" while preserving its possibility. It provides aid only there where the grade of true beings is at its lowest—that is, in nature itself—and there it submits itself to the images of beings, without gaining anything familiar to itself from them. Nothing can be said of it, insofar as it pertains to beings, except that it is the "shadow of nature." Since it is further distant from "being" than even an image of being is, it should in no way be thought of as either "a being" or "to be."

Now we must judge concerning being and its opposite, non-being. A "being in act" <note>an actualized thing</note> has more "being-ness" than a "being in potency." Conversely, then, what is called "non-being in act" has less being (or more non-being) than what is called "non-being in potency." Since matter is further removed from the first essence and truth than can be thought, and is therefore "falsehood" itself and truly "non-being," if you imagine this matter in its own "act" <note>as a completed reality</note>, you would assert all the more that it is non-being. And the more truthfully matter is called "possibility," the more falsely it will be thought of as "act," and vice-versa. Conclude the book with this sentiment: Truth itself allows even false things to live; otherwise, unless it were true that a thing is false, it would not be false. And the more "truly" it is false—or the more true it is that "this is false"—the more "false" it is without a doubt. So, in the way that matter is "truer" matter (that is, the truer the possibility is toward beings), the more "false" it is in actuality, and vice versa.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD TWO
### BOOK FIVE.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD TWO
### BOOK FIVE.

->Concerning that which is in potency, and that which is in act.<-
-><note>original Greek: ΠΕΡῚ τῶ͂ ο' δυνάμει καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ.</note><-

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>
1.
What is said to be "in potency" is referred to that which is "in act"; potency itself is referred to act.
</margin>

It is customary to say that something is "in potency," something else in turn is "in act," and something else again is "act" within the order of things. We must consider, therefore, what exactly is that which is "in potency," and what is that which is "in act"; and whether "being in act" is the same thing as "the act" itself. Likewise, if something is an "act," whether it is also "in act," or whether each is different, so that what exists "in act" is not necessarily also "an act."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' (originally Greek Lambda 'Λ') at the start of the Greek text column.</image-desc>

It is said that one thing is in potency, while another is in act; it is also said that there is "act" among beings. We should therefore consider what "in potency" is, and what "in act" is. Is "being in act" the same as "the act"? Or if there is "act," is this also "in act," or is each one different? And is it not necessary that a thing being "in act" is also "an act"?

<summary>Ficino explains the fifth book of Plotinus's second Ennead, defining matter as "pure potency" or the "shadow of nature" that lacks its own actual being. He argues that matter's very reality consists in its "formability" and its status as a possibility for future forms.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "potency" (potentiality) and "act" (actuality or reality), moving into the Fifth Book of the Second Ennead of Plotinus. While the previous page examined how matter relates to the "Architect of all things," this page delves into the technical definitions of how a thing transitions from a mere possibility to a completed reality.</meta>

### BOOK FIVE. 173

<margin>A</margin> That there is something "in potency" <note>original: δυνάμει (dynamei); the state of being a potentiality or possibility</note> within the world of the senses is obvious. But whether there is also something "in potency" within the world of the mind <note>the "intelligible" realm</note>, or whether only that which is "in act" <note>original: ἐνεργείᾳ (energeia); a thing that is fully realized or active</note> exists there, is something we must investigate. If there is indeed potentiality there, is it always merely potential and never coming into actualization? They might exclude actualization because of the lack of time in that realm. But first, we must state what "in potency" actually means. For if what is "in potency" is not spoken of simply—or if it is nothing unless it relates to something else—then we might say, for example, that 
<margin>B</margin> brass is a statue "in potency." But if nothing was ever going to be made from it, or if it wasn't within its power to change, or if nothing was ever going to happen beyond what it already was, and if it were impossible for it to become anything beyond its current state, then how could it be anything other than what it was? If it was already present and nothing else was going to happen, what else could it be other than itself? It could not be called "in potency." Therefore, for something to be "in potency," it must be something else already, yet also have the potential to become something after its current state. Either it remains what it is while 
<margin>C</margin> producing something else, or it offers itself up to become that which it is capable of becoming, so that its previous state passes away. For we say "brass is a statue in potency" in one sense, but we say "water is brass in potency" or "air is fire" in another. Among these, can we also call the "potency" a "power" <note>original: δύναμις (dynamis)</note> directed toward the future thing? For example, is brass the "power" of the statue? Perhaps not, if "power" is understood as the capacity to *act* or produce. We would not call it "in potency" 
<margin>D</margin> if we were considering "power" only in terms of production. If "in potency" is not only spoken of in relation to being "in act" <note>the completed state</note>, but also in relation to the "activity" <note>the process of acting</note>, then "power" itself would also be "in potency." It is better and clearer to say that "in potency" refers to the state of being "in act," while the "potential" refers to the "activity." Indeed, that which is "in potency" is like a subject for various experiences, shapes,
<margin>E</margin> and forms which it is naturally suited to receive, or which it hastens to follow—sometimes toward a better state, and sometimes toward a worse or destructive state, while each of them is something else "in act."

We must also examine matter: whether it is something existing "in act," or if it is always "in potency" toward those things by which it is formed or toward its activity. In general, other things we call "in potency" become "in act"
<margin>F</margin> <margin>lesser.</margin> when they receive a form and remain the same underlying thing. Or perhaps the term "in act" will be said of the statue itself, such that the "actual statue" is opposed to the "potential statue." However, the term "in act" would not then be predicated of that same thing of which we said it was a "potential statue." If this is the case, the potential does not *become* the actual, but rather, from that which was previously "in potency," something else later comes to be "in act." For that which is said to exist "in act" is the composite whole <note>the combination of matter and form</note>, not the matter itself. If it were the matter itself, it would have to be of equal value. But a brass statue is a different substance,
<margin>G</margin> as it is a joined whole. In those things that do not remain the same at all, it is clear that the "potential" state will not exist in the end.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is clear, therefore, that in the realm of the senses, there is something "in potency." We must inquire whether this is entirely true, and whether something "in potency" also exists in the realm of the mind. Or perhaps only that which is "in act" is there? And if by chance there is something "in potency" there, is it always only "in potency"? If it exists forever, does it never proceed into act because it is not completed by time? But first, we must explain what it means to be "in potency." For "in potency" is not a simple term. It cannot be that what is called "in potency" refers to nothing else; for example, brass is said to be "in potency" to a statue being made. Otherwise, if nothing were to be made from it or within it, and nothing was to be beyond what it already was, it would simply be what it was. Since it was already there and present, and nothing else was to be, what else could it be besides its present self? Therefore, it could not be said to be "in potency." It is necessary, then, that something "in potency" is already something "in act," from which it is said to be "in potency" because it can become something else later—either by the prior thing remaining as it is, or by offering itself up so that what can be made from it comes to be, while the prior thing perishes. For brass is a statue in potency in one way, but water is brass in potency in another, and air is similarly fire. Therefore, since it is "in potency" in this way, can it also be called a certain "power" <note>Latin: *potentia*; here meaning a capacity or force</note> toward the future? For instance, is brass a certain power of the statue? Perhaps if "power" is taken as the capacity for *doing* or *making*, it should not be said this way at all. For a power considered in terms of making is not said to be "in potency." But if that which is "in potency" is not only referred to that which is "in act" <note>the result</note>, but also to the *act* itself <note>the process</note>, then the power itself will also be "in potency." One can refer to this more rightly and clearly: that which is "in potency" refers to the state of being "in act," while "power" refers similarly to the "act" or "activity." Truly, that which is "in potency" is of such a kind—like a subject for passions, forms, and species which it is suited by its nature to receive, or even hastens to obtain. These are partly toward the better, and partly toward the worse and the destruction of those things, each of which is also something else "in act."

It questions whether matter has any reality of its own or exists only as a capacity to become something else.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the philosophical concepts of potentiality and actuality. Having previously established that physical objects like brass have the potential to become statues, Plotinus now moves to more abstract examples, like the human mind (the grammarian) and the soul, to see if these rules apply to the eternal, divine realm of ideas.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS II.

**A** But when a person who is a grammarian in potency <note>original: "potentia"; referring to someone who has the capacity to learn grammar but hasn't yet</note> becomes a grammarian in act <note>original: "actu"; actually practicing or possessing the knowledge</note>, why isn't this "potential" version of the person the same as the "actual" version? After all, Socrates is the same person whether he is potentially wise or actually wise. Is it the case, then, that the ignorant person is also the knowing person? He was, in fact, potentially knowing; but it is rather by accident <note>a philosophical term meaning a non-essential quality</note> that the ignorant man becomes a knower. It is not by virtue of being ignorant that he is potentially knowing; rather, it just so happened that he was ignorant.

**B** The soul, however, existing by its own nature, remains "in potency" even insofar as it is knowing, and it still preserves what is called "in potency." Thus, someone who is already a grammarian does not stop being a "potential" grammarian. Perhaps nothing prevents a thing from being one way and then another. In the first case, it is called "in potency" alone; in the second, it is in potency while already possessing the form <note>the actualized quality</note>. Therefore, let us say that what is called "in potency" is the subject <note>the underlying material or person</note>, while what is "in act" is the combined whole—like a statue. But how shall we name the "form" <note>the "statue-ness" or "knowledge-ness"</note> that exists within the thing?

**C** Perhaps it is not out of place to call the state where the subject is "in act" an "actuality." But when it is only "in potency," we should call it the "form" or "species," rather than simply an "act"—or rather, the act *of this specific thing*. For we can also name another kind of "act" in a more primary sense: the actuality that stands in opposition to that power <note>potentia</note> which leads something into action.

**D** For that which is called "in potency" receives its "actuality" from something else, from the outside, in order to become active. But that power through which something is able to act produces an act from within itself, in a way that is opposite to itself—much like a habit <note>a settled disposition</note>, such as "courage" and the "acting courageously" that follows from it. But enough of these matters for now.

<margin>
In the intelligible world <note>the realm of pure thought and forms</note> nothing exists in potency relative to something else, even though a certain power exists there; rather, it is always in act, so that the whole is said to exist as actuality.
</margin>

**E** We must now explain for what purpose these things have been said. All of this was leading to a clear conclusion: in what way should we speak of "actuality" in the intelligible world? Is only that which is "in act" found there, or is every single thing there an "act"? And if everything there is an "act," how can we say anything there is "in potency"? Surely, if there is no matter there (which is where potentiality resides), and if nothing there is "going to be" something it isn't already, and if nothing changes into something else, or generates something else while remaining the same, or steps away from itself to let something else take its place—then certainly there will be nothing there called "in potency." That is the kingdom of true beings: not temporal things, but eternal ones.

**F** If someone, then, posits that there is "matter" in the intelligible world, they must answer: how can matter exist there if there is no "potentiality" associated with that matter? (For even if matter exists there in a different way, there will still be one part that is like matter, another like form, and a third that is the combined whole.) What will they answer?

**G** Perhaps they will say that what is called "matter" there is actually "form," since even the soul is a form in itself, but acts as matter relative to something else. Is it, then, "in potency" relative to that other thing? Not at all. For the soul is its own form, and it is not a "future" form; it is distinguished only by logic, and thus it has matter only in the sense that it is a dual concept. But both are a single nature—just as Aristotle asserted that the "immaterial body" <note>the aether or fifth element</note> was still a body. But what shall we say of the soul? It is an animal "in potency" when the animal is not yet born but is about to be. Likewise, it is musical "in potency," and other things it becomes. But as for the eternal things, they always remain.

<column-break/>

**A'** But when the grammarian in potency <note>original Greek: δυνάμει (dynamei)</note> becomes one in actuality <note>original: ἐνεργείᾳ (energeia)</note>, how is the potential not the same as the actual? Is the potential Socrates the same as the actually wise Socrates? Is the ignorant one therefore the wise one? For he was potentially wise; or is the unlearned one wise by accident? For he is not potentially wise because he is unlearned; it just happened to him to be unlearned.

**B'** The soul, having its own nature, is "in potency" in a way, even when it was wise, since it preserves that power. Even one who is already a grammarian is a grammarian "in potency." Or nothing prevents it from being another way: there, it is "in potency" alone; here, the potency possesses the form. Let the "in potency" be the substrate, and the "in actuality" be the composite, like the statue.

**C'** What then shall the bronze be called? Is it strange to call the "actuality" that by which it is in act, and to call the shape and form "potential" only in a certain sense? We might call it "the act" not simply, but "the act of this." For we might more properly call another thing "actuality": the one opposite to the power that brings about the act. For the thing "in potency" has its "actuality" from another; but the power itself can produce actuality from within itself—like a habit <note>ἕξις - hexis</note>, and the act said to follow it, like courage and the acting bravely. These things are so.

<margin>specifically</margin>

**D'** Why these things are said must now be stated by us: how "actuality" and "in act" are spoken of in the intelligible realms. Is each thing there an actuality, are all things actuality, or is there also "potency" there? For if there is no matter there with which potency resides, and nothing there is about to be what it is not already, nor changes into another, nor remains while generating another, nor departs from itself to let another be in its place, then "potency" would not be there. For that realm consists of beings that are eternal, not those held by time. If someone asks about the matter placed there in the intelligible world, whether "potency" exists there according to that matter—even if matter is there in another way—then **F'** each thing will be one part as matter and another as form, and a third as the composite. What will they say?

**G'** In a way, the "matter" there is "form," since the soul, being a form, could be "matter" relative to another. Is it then "in potency" to that? Not at all. For its form is not for the future. It is distinguished only by reason <note>λόγος - logos</note>, having matter as if thought of as double, yet both are one nature, as **E'** Aristotle says the fifth body is immaterial. But of the soul, how shall we speak? It is **Z'** a living being "in potency" when it is not yet so but is about to be, and musical "in potency," and all other things that come to be, while those that are eternal always exist.

<summary>Plotinus explores the technical definitions of potentiality (potency) and actuality (act), concluding that while potentiality defines the physical world of change, the divine "intelligible" world is composed of pure actuality where everything exists eternally and fully realized.</summary>

# BOOK FIVE

How is it regarding the things in the intelligible realm <note>The world of Ideas or Forms, existing beyond the physical sense-world.</note>, whether the "in potency" or "the potential" exists among them? But the soul is the "potency" of these things, while the "in act" <note>original: "energeia"; the state of being fully realized or active.</note> is something else; so how does it stand? Is it that each thing has been assigned its place in potency before it exists in act, or is it that each thing is already complete? For the intellect <note>original: "nous"; the divine Mind.</note> does not proceed from a potency of thinking into an act of thinking; rather, if something were to be carried along, it would still require potency, but if it is the whole itself, it must be act. For that which is "in potency" wishes to pass over into that other thing, to be led into "act," and for the act
<margin>in itself.</margin>
to be born within it. But whatever is entirely from itself and always remains the same is already "act." For all
the primary things are "act"; they possess what they ought to possess, both from themselves and through themselves. And so too is the soul;
or rather, the soul that is not in matter but in the intelligible world. But the soul in matter
<margin>the natural soul.</margin>
is another kind of act, such as the natural soul <note>The "vegetative" or lowest level of soul that governs physical growth.</note>; for even
<margin>act before potency.</margin>
this is an act. Yet it is an act directed toward external things, whereas all act truly so-called is that which remains according to itself. If indeed that nature is rightly called "sleepless," unceasing, and the best and most beautiful life, then there would be "acts" there. And therefore everything there is "act," and all things are "life." And the place there is the origin and source of life, and truly the source of soul and mind.

**D** All other things that are something "in potency" also have the quality of being something else "in act"; but when something is itself, it is said to be something else "in potency." But concerning what is called "matter," which we say is all beings "in potency," how is it possible for it to be any of the beings "in act"? For if all beings were "in potency," and nothing were "in act," there would necessarily be nothing in it that is a kind of act. If then there is no act even in this, but rather
**E** it is the "impotence" of the things that come from it; then something else might hinder it, or neither all beings are directed toward matter, nor is any one of these things upon it actually "these things." Perhaps it would not even exist; or it is either a truth or an imagining—an image—whether it exists in a likeness or in a substance; and it is not even from both.
<margin>fabrication.</margin>
Therefore, it is entirely a "non-being." * It will therefore be
**F** a "non-being" if it flees from the nature of the truly existing things. Or it is able to
<margin>phantom.</margin>
underlie them; but those things said to be false are so because they are not even a lie—there is a reason for these things, of which being is the cause. But if it is in no way "being," then it would be all "act." <note>This is a paradoxical argument: if matter has no potential to be anything else, it must be "stuck" in its own state, but Plotinus concludes it is actually a phantom of being.</note>

HOW then do we speak of it? And in what way is it the "matter" of beings? Perhaps because it is something "in potency," because there the "potency" <note>original: "dynamis"; meaning power or capacity.</note> or the "life" is according to what it is about to be; but its "being" is only this: promising what is to come, as if its being is deferred into that which it will be.
**G** That which is becoming is "in potency." All other things are "in potency"... <note>The Greek text cuts off here, continuing in the Latin translation.</note>
not in it, its future is considered: But for its very being to be alone, its nature is referred to and deferred to that which it will be.

<column-break/>

**A** Therefore, in the intelligible kind it will be thus: that which is usually called "in potency." But the soul is not these things in potency; rather, the soul is the power <note>original: "potestas"</note> of these things. But that which is usually called being "in act," by what reason can it exist among those above? Is it perhaps as a statue is a composite "in act," and so it is there, since every intelligible thing possesses its own species <note>original: "speciem"; here meaning its Form or essential nature.</note>, or rather because every thing is a species, and that which it is, is a perfect species? For the intellect by no means proceeds from a
**B** potency that is able to understand into an "act" of understanding; otherwise it would have need of some other prior thing that does not burst forth from potency into act, but already possesses the whole in itself. For that which is "in potency" requires another thing, by whose approach it may be led to "act," so that it may finally become something in act. But that which is always thus by itself, is "act." Therefore all primary things exist as "act": for they have whatever they ought to have, and that indeed from themselves and always. Now indeed the soul
**C** is also thus, especially the one which is not in matter, but in the intelligible world. And yet even that which is in matter is another act, namely the vegetative: for it is an act by the very fact that it exists. But since all things are in act, in what way are they all acts? Surely if it is rightly said that the intelligible nature is "ever-watchful" and the "best life": the life of the best are undoubtedly "acts" there. And therefore all things there consist both "in act" and as "acts," and they are all of "life."
**D** And that place is the place of life, the principle and source of the true soul and of the mind.

<margin>IV. Matter is the first [distanced] from others; what evil is.</margin>
ALL OTHER things which are something "in potency" have this quality: that they are also something else "in act." When a thing already exists, yet leans toward something else, it is judged to be "in potency." But as for matter itself, which we judge to be all beings "in potency," by what condition can we affirm it to be any of the beings "in act"? Otherwise all beings would no longer be "in potency." If therefore it is none of the beings, it is necessary that it is not even "being" itself. Thus, since it is none of the beings, how can it be anything "in act"? Perhaps indeed it is none of these things which are in it. Yet what prevents this from being something else? For not all beings are in matter. Certainly if nothing of those things which are in it exist, and these things are "beings," it will be called "non-being." Likewise, insofar as it is thought of as something unformed, it is not a species: therefore it will not be numbered among those as a being. Therefore, and by this reason further, it will be judged "non-being." When therefore it is judged by both. If then it flees the nature of true beings, nor yet can it achieve this—to be from the number of those things which are falsely said to be—since it is not even an image of reason as these things are handed down: in what kind of being can this be apprehended? But if in none, what will it be able to be "in act"?

HOWEVER, if it is so, how do we speak of it? And by what condition is the matter of beings indicated? Perhaps because it is "in potency." <summary>This page explores the distinction between potentiality and actuality in the divine realm and in physical matter. --- Page 211 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of "potency" and "act," focusing specifically on the nature of Matter. He argues that Matter is the absolute limit of reality—a "pure potentiality" that never actually becomes anything fixed, remaining a "shadowy image" of true Being.</meta>

<page-num>176</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD II.</header>

<margin>A</margin>...anything, or rather all things: it is not any being according to itself, but that which it is, is matter; therefore it is rightly said not to be "in act" <note>original: "in actu"; meaning fully realized or having reached its final form.</note>. For if it were something in act, that very thing which is in act would not be matter: it would therefore not be matter at all, but would behave as a being. It is therefore judged to be "non-being," not as something different from being (such as motion). For motion clings to being as something that comes from it and exists within it. Matter, however, is like something rejected and utterly separated, unable to change itself: but what it was from the beginning—which was non-being—it always remains. Moreover, <margin>B</margin> from the beginning it was not anything in act, since it falls so far short of all beings: nor has it ever become anything. For those things which it perpetually sought to put on, it could never be colored by them: instead, it continually remains leaning toward something else, existing in potency <note>original: "in potentia"; the capacity or possibility to become something, without yet being it.</note> toward those things that follow. And since this matter appears where the order of beings ends and is constrained by those things that come after it, the extremity of both the former and the latter sinks down: and while it is constrained by both, it is in act toward neither. It resides only in <margin>C</margin> potency, left as a weak and shadowy image <note>original: "umbratile simulachrum"; a phantom or ghostly reflection.</note> unable to be formed. Is there not, then, a "falseness" in act? This is the same as saying it is truly a falsehood, and truly non-being. If, therefore, it is non-being in act, it is even more non-being, and truly non-being. It is far, then, from being anything among beings in act, as it retains its truth only in non-being itself. Wherefore, if it must exist, it must not exist in act, so that by turning away from that which truly exists, it may have its being in non-being itself: since if you take away the falseness from those things that are false, you suddenly take away whatever essence they had. Similarly, if you introduce "act" to those things that <margin>D</margin> have their essence in being in potency, you have simultaneously removed the cause of their substance: because their "to be" was to be in potency. Therefore, if it is necessary to preserve matter as incorruptible, it is necessary to preserve it as matter. It is necessary, therefore, as it appears, to say that it exists only in potency, so that it may remain what it is, or to accurately discuss such arguments.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is nothing in itself, but what is matter, is not in act. If there were any act, it would be an image of act, not matter. For if it were something in matter—like bronze—it would be a being. But as non-being, it is not "other" than being like motion is, for motion is from being, like an appearance. But matter is entirely separated, unable to change itself; if it was from the beginning <margin>B</margin> non-being, it would be so. It was not in act from the beginning, being far from all beings, nor did it become so. What it wished to undergo, it could not be colored by, but remains directed toward another, in potency toward things that follow. When the stages of beings have ended, it appears; since it cannot rest or have truth in itself, it is brought into this state, mastered by both [the higher and lower], being in act toward neither, but remaining in <margin>C</margin> potency, left as something weak, a dim image, unable to be shaped. Is not the image then an act? Or is it a "falsehood in act," which is the same as "true falsehood" and "truly non-being"? If then it is non-being in act, is it not more non-being and truly a false non-being? How then can there be any act of being in that which has its truth in not being? Therefore, it must be that it is not in act, lest it depart from its true state, which <margin>D</margin> is to have its being in non-being. Since if it is false, and you take away the falseness from it, you take away its existing substance. If being consists in potency and in "seeming to be," then by introducing act, you have destroyed the cause of its substance, because its being was in potency. If therefore one must keep matter undestroyed, one must keep it as matter. Therefore, it seems one must only say it is "in potency," so that it remains what it is, or this reasoning must be tested.
