# THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO 
## ON THE SIXTH BOOK OF THE SECOND ENNEAD
# ON ESSENCE AND QUALITY.
### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

On essence, how it is constituted from being, motion, rest, the same, and the other, and what distinction is there, and concerning substantial form, formal reason, and accidents.

WE BEGIN the disputation on essence and quality rightly from the first essence. There, from the One itself, proceeds the "One Being" <note>original: "hen on"; a Platonic term for the first level of generated reality.</note>—not simply one, but one being: one insofar as it comes from the One, but being insofar as it is under the One. Because the origin of being itself is a certain procession, that which is born lives in a perpetual procession—an internal procession. For internal progress signifies fertility, whereas external progress would signify need. We are accustomed to call such a procession a "motion," which we do not call local <note>Moving from place to place.</note>, but as it were "vital" <note>The internal movement of life or thought.</note>. If any motion is there, there is also diversity, which for the sake of argument you may call "alterity" <note>The state of being "other" or different.</note>. For in every motion, one passes from one limit to another. Now, therefore, we have applied motion and alterity to being itself. But because its procession does not depart from its own ground, and thus is not transmuted into another nature, "rest" and "identity" are rightly recognized there: for while it does not depart, it remains; and while it is not transmuted into another, it remains the same.

<meta>This section establishes the "Five Greatest Kinds" of Being from Plato's Sophist—Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference—as the structural pillars of the divine Mind.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus defines Matter as "pure potentiality" and "true non-being," arguing that it must never become "actual" to remain matter. Marsilio Ficino's commentary introduces the five basic categories of reality—Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference—within the divine Intellect.</summary>
<keywords>Matter, Potentiality, Actuality, Non-being, Marsilio Ficino, Essence, Quality, Motion, Stability, Identity, Alterity, Plotinus</keywords>

--- Page 212 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded a discussion on Matter as a "shadowy image" and pure potentiality. This page shifts focus toward the structure of true Being and Essence, specifically exploring the "Five Great Kinds" (Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Otherness) derived from Plato’s *Sophist* as they exist within the divine Intellect.</meta>

### ON BOOK V, ENNEAD II.

We call this entire progression of being itself, and its stable identity within that progression, **essence**, a name rightly derived from "being." In a similar way, in any subsequent essence, these five are found: **being, motion, otherness, rest** (so to speak), and **identity**. For any essence that proceeds externally also proceeds internally in a similar way before that external progression. Here again, we can designate five aspects within the *formal reason* <note>original: "ratione formali"; the logical definition or blueprint of a thing.</note> of any thing, which is captured by its definition: for in a definition, we place **genus** and **difference**. By its *genus*, a thing is defined insofar as it agrees with others and is in some way the same as them; but by its *difference*, it is defined insofar as it disagrees with others, is "other" than them, and meanwhile remains the same as itself. 

In this primary essence of a thing, designated by its genus and difference, its natural and proper **power** <note>original: "virtus"; the inherent strength or capacity of a thing.</note> remains, through which the thing itself persists in duration and continues its efficacy in acting. In this stability, not only does **rest** <note>original: "status"; stability or being at a standstill.</note> shine forth, but **motion** moreover flashes out—namely, the natural inclination or the dexterity for acting. All these seem to be included in a definition, though perhaps some more clearly than others. 

Therefore, these five categories we have numbered agree much more with Essence than they do with one another. For they spring from Essence itself rather than from each other. First, motion and otherness differ from being itself as a process differs from the starting point from which it proceeds. Since rest and identity are opposed to motion and otherness, they are something other than being; yet being is not opposed to them in the same way. No one doubts that motion is something other than rest, and identity something other than otherness, since they are opposites. It is also clear that motion differs from otherness because rest is also something other than identity. For one can remain in diversity just as one remains in identity; yet these do not differ so much from essence. For each of them is essence, though in different ways—especially if considered from their foundation. For in the same foundation, they differ from each other by their *formal reasons*.

However, although motion is in some way called essence, essence itself does not conversely exist as motion; otherwise, rest would not suit it at all. Nor, again, is essence simply rest, for then it would not agree with motion. One may argue similarly regarding "the other" and "the same." Thus, essence becomes **one**, and within it there are also **many**; these are not so much "many essences" as they are (so to speak) many **essentials**. I mean essential reasons, properties, and acts, much like light, heat, and lightness in a fire. And yet (as some think), neither these nor those are qualities "in a subject," but are rather certain **acts** in an acting principle, proceeding from the very same source.

Indeed, since the primary essence is most effective as the first form, naturally almost innumerable essential powers and acts spring from it and exist in it, differing from one another in their formal reason and efficacy. There, all are like certain "differences" which seem to constitute essences under one single Essence, while they constitute essential species there. You will not wonder that there are many things there which are formally diverse from one another—even though they are founded as one— if you consider how various are the *seminal reasons* <note>original: "seminalia rationes"; the invisible "seeds" or formative principles that guide the growth of physical things.</note> of limbs within the single power of a seed; or how various are the powers in the soul germinating from the soul, all at once. Likewise, consider how much lines distance themselves from each other outside the center, yet they do not differ in the center. You might think of a circle as a single thing, in whose center the lines are one (as if in their essence and foundation), but through the circumference (as if through their form) they are many and distant. You should imagine the primary essence in a similar way.

No one doubts how much things that are joined in a **cause** are discrete in their **effect**. For things that in their cause are not only joined in place and time, but are moreover one in essence, are distinguished in their effects by the distance of places, intervals of time, and moreover by their essences. For a weaker essence cannot, like the primary one, supply the same many powers at once to many forms, nor suffice for many actions that proceed from various forms. 

Remember, however, that what is said here about essence and those five categories is *attempted* rather than finished. For these matters will be treated more diligently in the books *On the Genera of Being* <note>Referring to Enneads VI.1-3.</note>. Remember, moreover, that no qualities should be assigned to divine things by their proper name. For what appear to be qualities there are those *special differences* by which the species themselves are necessarily constituted and discerned, and the intimate and perpetual acts of essence. Among us, too, special differences and similar acts ought not to be called qualities. For **qualities** are those things which happen to a specific nature that is already complete in itself—whether they happen inseparably (like certain properties accompanying a species or individual) or whether they arrive separably (which are called "common accidents"). 

And this is indeed the correct naming, although it is sometimes conceded that those primary differences and intimate properties be called "essential qualities." But where we use names correctly, we call heat in water a "quality" and a "passion" <note>original: "passionem"; a state of being acted upon or changed.</note>. Likewise, we call heat manifest to the senses in a mass of fire a "quality"—specifically a proper one and an act. But the *heating power*, or the generator of heat, which is included in the substantial nature of fire and in its definition, we call not a quality, but the *producer* of a quality.

We must think, therefore, that whatever is included in the *reason* <note>original: "ratione"; here meaning the logical or ontological definition.</note> itself exists as entirely substantial or essential. We understand this "reason" here in three ways:
1. First, as **Ideal** in the mind.
2. Second, as **Seminal** in nature.
3. Third, as **Formal** wherever it may be—namely, that which is weighed by a definition.

To this formal reason in natural things corresponds the *substantial form*, which is specific to its matter; in its power lies the origin of its proper qualities. Effects manifest to the senses are taken as qualities, whereas in the reasons themselves, they are substantial. Hence Plato says in his *Letters* <note>Referring to the Seventh Letter.</note> that we fail in defining whenever we use things that encounter our senses to define what is substantial in things. For all these are accidents. Substance is not perceived by the sense by which it is sought; and since the substantial form does not necessarily imitate dimension, many think it is indivisible and reduce it to the intelligible genus. 

Plotinus says that the things the senses openly reach are not essences, but "passions of matter" proceeding from the efficacy of the essential form; thus the sense is in a way "acted upon" by them, while the reason argues from them. No one, therefore, ought to include in the definition of water "this coldness" or "liquid" manifest to the senses. This is both because "cold" and "liquid" designate *what kind* of body this is, but do not define *what* it is; and because even if it is heated, it is still water; and if it is frozen solid and does not appear liquid, it is still water. 

Furthermore, a collection of many qualities is not to be considered a substance, or an essence, or an essential reason. For there is one form of one thing, and one formal reason, which precedes the heap of accidents. It is absurd to assemble the proper nature of a thing from many qualities at once, especially where any one of them is common elsewhere. Otherwise, an essence would be made of things that are not essence and are far inferior to essence. 

But if anyone asks how that first essence of all things is composed: first it is answered that the thing constituted need not be exactly the same as those things from which it is said to be constituted. Then, it is not wrongly called that essence which is made from being, which is there the first and simple—

It distinguishes between essential "acts" and accidental "qualities," warning that true substance cannot be defined by sensory data like temperature or state of matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically Ennead II, Book 6, "On Quality and Form." The previous page discussed the five primary categories of Being (Essence, Motion, Rest, Sameness, Otherness). Here, Ficino transitions into how these categories constitute a specific "essence" and begins a detailed investigation into the distinction between an object's core "essence" and its "qualities."</meta>

...of it: to which, while its various acts are added—through which certain internal differences arise—the essence is completed. It is not perfected in its "first being" <note>original: "primo esse"; the basic existence of a thing before it takes on specific characteristics.</note> simply insofar as it is essence; for it would be a certain section of being, or a temporary departure from the first unity which primarily reflects itself as "one," and it would lack the parts of which it is composed—if indeed composition can properly be spoken of in that realm. Thus far let it be said concerning essence as it is compared to being and the one. However, how it compares to life and mind must be sought elsewhere.

### What Essence properly is in things. What Quality is besides.

II In the second chapter of the book, he inquires what quality is, and whether it pertains in any way to the essential nature <note>original: "essentialem rationem"; the defining logic or blueprint of an essence.</note>. He admits that quality does not belong to essence taken simply, but to *such* an essence. For if the definition of essence for a constant fire is "that which heats," you will rightly conclude that heat is there; but perhaps heat, in that context, ceases to be properly called a "quality." If, however, you define the absolute substance of fire, which precedes such a substance, you will not clearly place heat there. 

Indeed, he intends the substance of fire to be not merely a body, but a body situated in a certain species. Within its essence, he perceives a primary, hidden part of its <term>substantial form</term> <note>The "substantial form" is the internal principle that makes a thing what it is (e.g., "fireness" rather than just "hot stuff").</note>, endowed with hidden powers, while its second part is its matter. The form holds the first place because it situates the thing in its species and gives being to the matter. Here and elsewhere, he often calls the substantial form the **reason** <note>original: "rationem"; referring to the formative principle or "Logos" of the thing.</note>: primarily because it corresponds to the ideal and "seed-like" reason, through which the thing itself is understood, then chiefly defined, and known by its own proper logic. 

Meanwhile, he touches upon the opinion of some who say that the qualities which meet our senses are not anything firm in themselves, but are certain flowing **passions** <note>original: "passiones"; in philosophy, this means something "acted upon" or a secondary effect, rather than a feeling.</note> of subjects or opposites, brought about by the actions of substantial forms lurking everywhere. From these forms, whatever flashes out continually into its own matter is a form: acts and actions of this kind include heat, light, and lightness in fire. However, whatever passes from there into a foreign matter is a "passion," just as heat passes from fire into water. 

Among these things, he repeats that those which necessarily complete the essence of the thing itself ought not to be named "qualities" there—whether they complete such an essence, or whether heat completes a "heating essence," or an essence simply as a specific difference, or the first power in fire that also precedes heat. He adds that neither the triangle nor "triangularity" itself in a triangle is a quality (that is, an accident); but for a paper to become triangular happens in the manner of a quality. 

He concludes that **quality**, accepted in its proper name, happens after the absolute essence itself, whether that quality becomes separable from it or, conversely, inseparable. These things seem to be confirmed by the fact that some **Theologians** <note>Ficino likely refers to Scholastic thinkers like Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus, who used similar logical divisions.</note> dispute concerning essence or nature, which they call **quiddity** <note>original: "quidditatem"; the "what-ness" or the definition of a thing.</note> or formal reason. For they establish four "signs" <note>Logical stages or priorities of understanding a thing's nature.</note> regarding it: 
1. In the first sign, "man is a rational earthly animal": which is indeed the formal reason of man. 
2. In the second, they apply to this reason the negations of everything, even of things that properly follow from it. I say "negations" that look upon the formal reasons: for a man [in this abstract stage] is neither <term>risible</term> <note>original: "risibilis"; the capacity to laugh, traditionally used in logic as the classic example of a "property" unique to humans.</note> nor not risible, neither learned nor not learned. 
3. In the third sign, his properties are added to the man: such as that a man is "capable of learning" and "capable of laughter." 
4. In the fourth sign, common accidents flow together. 

It is necessary, however, that before common accidents, there be something proper to each part, because changeable things must necessarily cling to firm ones. Furthermore, he puts forward that if there are many qualities, they should be reduced to one that is most proper. Again, if he recently considered qualities to be "being such or such," even if he attributes this continually, it is resolved into the substantial form: which, as something more perfect, excludes "being" simply. This indeed precedes "being such," just as the power itself simply precedes "such a power." And a resolution of its accompanying features into the essence takes place: in the essence itself, the essential power, naturally sent forth, is resolved into the essence; one may, by thinking, place the essence before the power, and from this power proper "passions" arise. After these, common things mostly happen from elsewhere.

### Confirmation of the above.

III Chapter three confirms the above and concludes that quality, wherever it may be, is a certain "passion" of the subject depending on a hidden power of the essence, an essential efficacy. However, in the essences and formal reasons of things, in the place of qualities, there are "specific differences" and (so to speak) "essential properties," by which the species of things are both constituted in themselves and distinguished from others. These are indeed certain essential acts, especially in essences separated from matter. 

He adds that the **reason** itself—both the "seed-like" and the formal one—propagates substantial efficacy from what is proper in them (and hidden from us) into the qualities manifest to the senses on the surface. When he says that the heat innate to fire is not a quality, but an "act of the species," we must first understand this heat to be both the substantial form of the fire and its property, from which manifest heat is exercised; this manifest heat is received not so much in the form of the fire itself as in some subject. 

Among these points, where he says that in the principles and patterns of qualities there are certain "acts" in place of the qualities that appear openly in subjects, it can also be read this way: the exemplary principles of qualities are the acts of those things in which they primarily reside. Nor, again, would it be absurd where he says that nature is indeed a "just essence," a species of itself or an act, but a "distributed quality" is an affection passing into something else. One may understand such a passage in two ways: 
1. First (as we said), that the property lurking in the species itself is its own difference and act, while the quality is what appears in matter. 
2. Second, that the "affection" proper to this species, flourishing continually in its own matter (like heat in fire), should be considered not so much a quality as an "act of fire"; but it is a "quality" especially when it passes into water.

<summary>Ficino distinguishes between the "substantial form" (the hidden, essential power of a thing) and "qualities" (the outward, sensible manifestations). Using fire as an example, he argues that heat is an internal "act" of fire's essence, but becomes a "quality" or "passion" when it affects another substance like water.</summary>

<margin>He raises doubts concerning essence and quality throughout the entire solution.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> IS Being something other than Essence, and is Being spoken of even when other things are excluded? Is Essence truly Being joined together with other things, namely motion, rest, sameness, and otherness? And are these the elements of Essence? Therefore, the whole is Essence. Any one of those others, however, is Being; another is motion, and others are similar.
<margin>B</margin> Motion, therefore, is Being by accident. But is it also Essence by accident? Or perhaps it completes the Essence? Rather, it is itself Essence, and all things that exist in divine matters are Essence. Why then is the matter not the same among us? Perhaps it is because there, all things are one; but here, since the images are already distinct, this thing is one and that is another. Just as in a seed all things are present at once, and any part is the whole. Neither the hand nor the head is separate there; but in the actual result, they are distinguished from one another. For they are not true things, but images.
<margin>C</margin> Shall we say then that qualities there are essences? Which are indeed differences around Essence or around Being. Differences, I say—shall we call them efficient causes, so that essences are different from one another, and are altogether essences? Perhaps that is not absurd to say; but it would be said absurdly regarding these qualities that are among us, of which some are differences of essences, such as being "two-footed" and "four-footed." Others are by no means differences, and for this reason alone they are called qualities. Although the same thing can seem to be a difference where
<margin>D</margin> it completes the essence, and yet not a difference in another case where it does not fulfill the essence. For instance, whiteness completes the nature in a swan or in white lead <note>original: "cerussa"; white lead pigment.</note>, but in a human it is merely an accident. Or perhaps whiteness, insofar as it is in the formative principle <note>original: "in ratione"; within the rational definition of the thing.</note>, is a completion; but insofar as it is on the surface, it is a quality. Perhaps indeed one thing is essential, existing as a certain property of the essence; while another is only "the such," according to which the essence is named "qualified." Furthermore, as one might say, the visible whiteness in a swan does not complete its essence <note>term: "essence" (ousia/essentia): the core nature that makes a thing what it is; its "what-ness."</note>, for a swan can exist even if it is not white. Therefore, these same things will complete the essence and will not be mere qualities. And it is absurd to say that where they complete the essence they are one thing, but where they do not complete it they are something else, even though their nature remains the same. Perhaps, however, it should be said that the formative principles <note>original: "rationes" / "logoi"; the rational blueprints or codes that organize matter.</note> themselves, which produce these things, exist as entirely essential; but these effects, which are substantial within the principles themselves, are brought forth no longer as substantial things, but as "qualities." From this, it happens that we always err in assigning "what" a thing is, straying in our inquiry into substance and sliding into quality. For we must not think that fire is merely this thing we call "fire" when we look at its quality; rather, it is essence itself. But the things we now see, and which we speak of as we look at them, lead us away from "what" a thing is, and what is correctly designated in the sensible world is merely a "sort of thing" <note>original: "quale quiddam" / "poion ti"; a quality rather than a substance.</note>. For none of these things are essence, but are instead the experiences or "affections" of essence. Hence the question arises: how can essence be composed of non-essences? We have said, therefore, that what is produced need not be the same as those things from which it is composed; but now we must say that it is a denial <note>original: "negantiam"; the text explores the idea that the manifested thing is a step down or a "negation" of the pure essence.</note> of what substance is. But how do we say that what we called essence in the higher realm is constituted from non-essence? We shall say that essence there possesses being in a more primary and pure way, as if constituted in the differences of Being itself; or rather, we shall think that it is called essence when actions are added to it, which appears to be the perfection of Being. But perhaps, because of this addition, it should be judged as more lacking, since it departs from simplicity and declines from Being itself.

<margin>11 What quality is, and whether it pertains to essence or essential use in any way.</margin>

BUT we must consider what quality is in general. For perhaps once we know what it is, we will dispel such doubts. First, we must inquire whether we should think that the same thing is sometimes merely a quality and sometimes also completes the essence, so that we do not struggle too hard to prove which quality simply completes the essence, but rather what *sort* of essence it completes. It is necessary, therefore, in such an essence, for the essence to exist—the "what it is"—before it becomes a "certain sort." What then? In fire, before it is a "certain sort" of essence, is it simply essence? Perhaps it follows from this that it is "body." Therefore, the genus itself, which is "body," will be the essence; fire, then, will be a "hot body," and the whole of it will not be essence, but heat will be in it just as a shape is in a statue. For this reason, if heat, and brightness, and lightness—which seem to be qualities—are taken away, and the resistance is removed, and what is called "extension in three dimensions" and matter are left behind, that which remains would be the essence. But that does not seem likely. For the Form <note>original: "Species" / "Eidos"; the intellectual shape or structure of a thing.</note> is more...

But if one were to say that "fire-ness" is the essence, and the same by analogy for white lead, nonetheless the visible things—"fire-ness" or whiteness or heat—complete it. And if whiteness in a swan is essence-completing for it, then it is both a quality and essence-completing. And it is absurd to say it is one thing in cases where it completes the essence, and another thing where it does not, when it is of the same nature. But perhaps the formative principles <note>original: "logoi"</note> that made them are entirely essential, while the results produced—which are close to what is produced there—act and are produced in a certain way, and we err concerning the "whatness," leaving it behind in our inquiries and falling down into "qualities." And fire is not what we say it is, looking at it as a "certain sort" of fire, but rather it is essence; but the things we see now, and which we speak of, lead us away from the "whatness," and toward that "quality" in the world of the senses; and by analogy none of them is essence, but rather the passions <note>term: "passions" (pathē): not emotions, but things that "happen" to a substance or properties it undergoes.</note> of essence. From this comes that other question: how is essence not made of non-essences? It was said, then, that the thing produced is not the same as those things from which it comes; but we must also say that the things produced are not essence. But how did we call those things there "essence," while saying they do not come from essence? For he says that there, Being is held more purely and essentially, as if it were truly in its differences, or rather with the addition of activities, the whole being called a "perfection"; yet perhaps it is more deficient because of the addition and because it has already departed from the simple.

BUT we must consider what quality is as a whole. For perhaps if it is known what it is, it will more likely stop the difficulties. First, then, we must seek whether the same thing is in one way only a quality, and in another way completing the essence—if we are uneasy about what sort of thing "essence-completing" is—but rather of what sort of essence it becomes a part, or the "what it is." What then, in the case of fire, before it is a certain sort of essence, is it essence or body? The "whatness," therefore, is the essence, the body. Fire is a "hot body." The whole is not yet essence. But the heat will be in it, as the shape is in the image. Therefore, when the heat is taken away, and the brightness and the lightness—which seem to be qualities—and the density, the three-fold extension is left behind, and matter is the essence. But the Form <note>original: "eidos"</note> does not seem...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the categories of Being, specifically distinguishing between "Essence" (what a thing fundamentally is) and "Quality" (the attributes it possesses). Following the previous page’s discussion on whiteness in lead versus whiteness in a swan, Plotinus now explores whether the "formative principles" that define a thing are themselves qualities or activities of essence.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

Is it rather essence <note>original: "ousia"</note>, but in what way? Is it a conviction where the quality exists, or the formative principle <note>original: "logos"</note> of the "what-it-was-to-be"? Does this not come from the principles and the underlying subjects? What is it? For to chill and to burn—what kind of things are these? Unless one were to say that burning is an activity <note>original: "energeia"</note> arising from the principle, as is heating and whitening; these would then be actions. If so, as for quality, we will have nothing left to define. Or perhaps we should not call those things qualities which are said to complete an essence, since they are the activities of the formative principles and the powers that move within essences. Rather, qualities are those things that exist outside of all essence, which sometimes appear as qualities and sometimes not.
The "odd," for example, follows after the essence.
Just as virtues and vices, ugliness and beauty, health and disease shape a thing, so too do the triangle and the square; in themselves
<margin>every triangle <unclear>...</unclear></margin>
they are the "of what sort." <margin>the always odd</margin> But that which is always "triangularized" or shaped—how should we speak of it? We should not call it "triangularity," but rather the formation. Arts and aptitudes are also like this. Thus, quality would be a certain disposition <note>term: "disposition" (diathesis); a temporary or permanent state or arrangement of a thing.</note> added to essences that already exist, whether it is introduced later or exists alongside it from the beginning; even if it were not preserved, the essence would be no less than it was. We say this disposition is either stable or easily changed, just as God is different—one part being stable, the other remaining within itself.
What then? Is the whiteness in you a position or a quality? It is clearly an activity arising from the power of whitening. In that realm, all so-called qualities are activities that have taken on the role of "making." Now, our opinion is that each is a certain property <note>term: "property" (idiotes); a characteristic specific to a particular thing.</note> that distinguishes essences from one another or within themselves, having their own character. Or how can the activity there be a quality? Is it quality insofar as it is itself, or insofar as it belongs to nothing else? Is it a departure from the subjects, or the character itself? But because only one of the so-called qualities there is an activity, it is obvious that when you speak of properties, you speak of "of what sort." But when the reason separates that which is specific to them and takes it away, or rather, when it receives it and generates something else, it brings forth a "quality." It is like taking a part of the essence that appears on its surface. In this way, nothing prevents heat from being the innate form <note>original: "eidos"</note> of fire, and not a quality of fire, but its activity. Yet it is called a quality when it is grasped in something else; there, it is no longer the form of the essence, but only a trace and a shadow and an image, leaving behind that essence of which it is the activity.
<margin>more manifest</margin> Therefore, whatever things are accidents <note>term: "accidents" (symbebekos); attributes that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist.</note> and are neither activities nor forms of essences, but provide certain shapes, these are the "qualities."
For example, habits and dispositions belonging to subjects should be called qualities. That which...

<column-break/>

**A** is essence. But is the species <note>original: "species"; the specific form or kind.</note> a quality? Perhaps it is not a quality, but the formative principle <note>original: "ratio"</note> is the species itself. What, then, is that which consists of the principle and the subject? It is the name for that which appears visible and burning. But what sort of thing is that? Unless someone should say that combustion itself is an act flowing from the formative principle; and thus heating, whitening, and others of this kind are understood as actions. Therefore, we will find no place to put quality. Perhaps indeed we **B** ought not to call those things qualities which are said to complete essences: since they are actions or acts arising from the formative principles and essential powers. Rather, we should only call those things qualities which are outside the total essence. These are things that do not appear as qualities in one place and not in another, but seem to bring something extra after the essence: such as virtues and vices, beauty and ugliness, and health and the arrangement of shape. Just as a Triangle and a **C** Square are not in themselves a "quality," but the fact of becoming triangular, insofar as it is so formed, must be called a "quality." We cannot call "triangularity" a quality, but rather the formation of the whole. We can also call arts and aptitudes for studies qualities. Thus, quality will be a certain disposition in essences that already exist, whether this is added later or accompanies it from the beginning. If it had not accompanied it, would the essence have been any less? We can say this is partly **D** easily moved and partly difficult to move, so that two species of it appear: one stable, the other mobile.

<margin>They manifest quality to be a passion of sight from the action of color; that which exists entirely within its own essence is its act and special property; that which stands apart from the essence is quality.</margin>
WHITENESS, therefore, appearing in you, is said to be not so much a quality as a certain act proceeding from the power of whitening. In that realm, it must be said that all things named qualities are effects. Yet they receive the name of quality from our opinion, because they are properties, as if they were distinguishing **E** essences from one another and having a character proper to themselves. Since, therefore, the quality that is there differs from our own, are these also acts? Perhaps because they do not show "of what sort" a thing is, nor the difference of subjects, nor the character, but only that which is called quality, which is indeed an act there. For this reason, when it has the property of essence, it is clearly established that it is not a quality. But when the reason has made what is proper in these things—not by taking away or cutting off, but rather by **F** receiving and generating—it procreates another "of what sort," as if taking a part of the essence appearing to it on the surface. Because it is so placed, nothing prevents heat from being a form innate to fire and an act of fire, rather than a quality of fire. But it is only then a quality when it is received in something else, where it is no longer the form of the essence, but only a trace and a shadow and an image, leaving behind that essence of which it is the act. **G** Therefore, as many things as are accidents, and are neither acts nor species of essences, but provide only certain forms through which they make the subjects "of a certain sort"—such as habits and dispositions, or other affections—these are to be called qualities. The acts in their primary examples are the principles of those things which are named qualities in these subjects.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the essential characteristics of a thing (like the heat of fire) are "activities" or "acts" of its nature rather than mere qualities. A "quality" is properly defined as a secondary attribute or a "shadow" of an essence that appears when an essential power acts upon a different subject.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary of Marsilio Ficino on Plotinus's Second Ennead. Having previously discussed the categories of quality and essence, Ficino now transitions to Book VII, which investigates "Mixture"—specifically how different substances or qualities combine into a single entity.</meta>

Nor would the same thing be a quality in one place and not a quality in another; rather, what is abandoned by essence <note>original: "essentia"; the fundamental "whatness" of a thing</note> becomes a quality. What remains with essence, however, is surely essence, or species, or act. For no nature is the same as it exists in its source and as it exists in another; where it is already destitute of its origin, it does not retain the dignity of species and act. However, what is never the species of anything, but always an accident <note>term: "accident" (accidens); a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing, like being tanned or sitting down</note>, is now purely a quality, and only a quality.

<column-break/>

<note>This column contains the original Greek text of the passage translated in the preceding column.</note>
Those things which are in themselves activities of those [essences], and in which these become a quality or a unity, together with being stripped of essence, are themselves a certain quality, and not merely an activity. But those things which are the same in themselves as they are in another, only fall away from being a species or activity; yet those which are never one thing and then another, but always an accident, are purely quality and nothing else.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
## BOOK VII OF THE SECOND
### ENNEAD.
### COMMENTARY.

->SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.<-

->How composition and mixture take place in numbers and in nature:<-
->Also concerning the three opinions on mixture.<-

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial letter 'Q' featuring a swan or large aquatic bird within a circular medallion, set against a background of foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>

JUST AS in numbers one thing is to be added, but another to be multiplied: so in natural things, one thing is to compose, another to mix thoroughly. Indeed, there is a similar proportion: just as in the order of numbers a unit is added to a unit, and thus a pair <note>original: "binarius"</note> is made, so in nature matter is added to form, and thus a body is created. Where again a unit or a pair proceeds to a trinity <note>original: "ternarium"</note>: so similarly a single being <note>likely referring to the soul or a vital principle</note> is joined to the body to effect motion; and thus a mobile body. There again, number is applied to number, as two to two, from which four is made, or even three is added to four to compose seven. In a similar way, in nature, a body already made mobile brings itself to another equally mobile body, and vice versa, whence bodies are composed of bodies just as numbers are composed of numbers. 

Hence, just as in numbers multiplication occurs beyond addition, so in nature, beyond composition or juxtaposition, thorough mixture <note>term: "commixtio"; a deep blending where parts become indistinguishable, as opposed to "compositio," which is mere stacking or placing side-by-side</note> occurs. You see four created by addition, where one says "two and two"; you see mixture in the same, where "twice two" produces four. Again, nine is created by addition while four is added to five. You find mixture in the same while you say "three times three is nine." Similarly, bodies are mixed and, in a way, even infused into one another, so that they are completely confounded into one. In this confusion, it is not possible to discern one part of the mixed body here and another there, but the whole is contained in each individual part; and so the universe is enclosed in any part whatever. Just as when you multiply a number—suppose three in any unit—you comprehend the whole three in any unit <note>original: "ternario totum ternarium comprehendis"</note>, otherwise you could not calculate "three times three." 

Then truly, as in numbers, whatever is fused by multiplication is also produced by addition, but not vice versa; so in nature, wherever there is an exact mixture of things, composition already occurs, but it does not happen the other way around. Altogether, therefore, just as in numbers you cannot have this kind of fusion in which the whole is contained in any part unless it comes from a new form to be procreated—as the whole three multiplied in any of its parts leads to the form of nine—so you should not deny a similar mixture in nature. For both in nature and in numbers there is this kind of fusion, which exists in vital nature, and in that ideal life itself where there is a mutual conspiracy <note>original: "conspiratio"; literally a "breathing together" or harmony of forms</note> of formulas or ideal reasons. 

Plotinus, then, about to treat this at present, brings forward three opinions: 
First, the opinion of those who, in reconciling bodies with each other, mixed neither the matters nor the qualities thoroughly, but placed matters next to matters and qualities next to qualities; he immediately rejects this opinion. 
Second, the opinion of those who, although they did not mix the matters but rather moved them close together, nevertheless confounded the qualities with each other. He declares their sentiment to be more probable. 
Third and finally, the opinion of those thinking that both matters with matters and qualities with qualities can be most exactly fused; he admits this also as probable. 

In the beginning, he uses the example of oxymel <note>term: "oximel"; a medicinal drink made of vinegar and honey</note>: if we mix vinegar with honey so far that no small portion is left in this composite which does not have the taste of both; by this, those are refuted who consider it a mere juxtaposition, just as if whole grains of panicum <note>term: "panicum"; a type of wild grass or millet</note> were gathered with whole grains of millet. Others will crush the grains of both equally, and say that with the grains on both sides now crushed into the smallest particles of their nature, the individual particles on both sides do indeed draw near, but the matters are not entirely confounded, although the qualities are confounded with each other. For everywhere in any smallest bit of millet there is a certain taste of panicum, and vice versa. 

But others, applying more care to this, will crush them more diligently; and therefore will mix the things more exactly, so that the matters, being not only crushed but even liquefied, are no longer merely placed next to each other, but—nothing prohibiting it—are thoroughly confounded. Hereafter, in every part of each, there are not only the qualities, as the sense itself declares, but also the fused matters. They conclude that such a thing can be fused by nature much more perfectly than by art—matters not foreign, but their own; not occasionally, but always from the beginning; not from without, but tempering from within. 

Plotinus, however, for the present brings forward no reason for the first opinion, but three for the second. The first reason is of this kind: Two bodies cannot be entirely equal to each other in the same place; for if they must be entirely in the same place, it is necessary first that they be divided into parts; then the parts in turn must apply themselves to parts. If these parts are indivisible, then those bodies have been resolved into individual units <note>original: "individua"; referring to atoms or the smallest possible components</note>. And since they were composed of the same things into which they are dissolved, it follows that the magnitude of the bodies themselves came together from certain individual units; which can never happen, because indivisible units gathered together produce no magnitude. If, however, those parts of bodies are divided <note>meta: catchword "biles" completes "diuisibiles" (divisible)</note>

<summary>Ficino introduces Plotinus's investigation into the nature of "mixture" (commixtio), using the analogy of mathematical multiplication to explain how two substances can blend so thoroughly that the whole is present in every part. He outlines three historical theories on how bodies and qualities combine, using the example of honey and vinegar (oxymel) to illustrate the difference between simple juxtaposition and total fusion.</summary>
<keywords>mixture, composition, multiplication, Marsilio Ficino, Plotinus, oxymel, essence, quality, matter and form</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II, moving into Book VII. While the previous page dealt with the metaphysical distinction between essence and quality, this page shifts to the physical and philosophical problem of "mixture"—how two distinct bodies or substances can occupy the same space or combine into one.</meta>

# ON BOOK VII OF ENNEAD II.

If they were separate, each would be a body by itself, and would have its own proper place apart from others. Therefore, two bodies will not be in exactly the same place; rather, they would be in many places if there are many small bodies. **The second reason.** When two bodies are mixed, they almost always occupy a larger space together than either one did alone; from this, it appears that the dimensions were not fully penetrated to the highest degree on both sides. **The third reason.** When a much smaller body is introduced into a much larger one, the smaller itself cannot be made exactly equal to the larger. But if someone objects that sometimes, after the mixing of two things, a larger space is not occupied, the answer must be that the air exits from there as the new body enters. After these points, an argument is made for the opposing opinion: that sweat trickles out from the entire body, and yet no "fraction" <note>original: "fractionem"; a breaking or tearing of the physical tissue</note> occurs there. Whether the adversaries say that passages were established by nature there through which sweat might flow without a tear, others will respond that oil penetrates through plates that are often made thin by art—such as horn or ivory—and even through very dense membranes, and it fills them entirely, neither increasing the mass nor splitting it. Then they will prove that materials are entirely made equal to one another from the fact that often, after their mixing, the prior mass does not seem to have increased. The adversaries will object again that two bodies cannot penetrate each other to the highest degree without an incision; but these thinkers, by penetrating each other most exactly, would cut each other most exactly and be entirely destroyed. Furthermore, the space is often not increased because an internal evaporation of subtler parts accompanies the process. The authors of the third opinion will respond: even where a larger space is required after mixing, there was an exact mixture of the two bodies there. For why should it be a wonder that their magnitude is increased, when many powers [virtues] have also grown together from the blending of many things? For perhaps the prior dimension does not perish fundamentally, but from many qualities another quality grows together, and from many dimensions another magnitude increases. They will still object that no increase can happen if materials are not placed next to materials, or a line added to a line along its length; instead, they are inserted into each other, and a line is entirely infused into a line, whether you imagine it inserted fundamentally from the end or joined from the side. Likewise, where it is clear that the mixture was complete, it cannot be understood how the smallest body there could equal the greatest quantity. We respond: either they diminish the body to the extent that it is mixed with the greatest, as far as it can be; or it is even able to spread itself through the whole, specifically when the prior quantity is extended. For they will perhaps say that extension is not itself properly quantity, but a "passion" <note>term: "passion" (passio); in a philosophical sense, this refers to a way in which a thing is acted upon or a state it undergoes, rather than an emotion</note> and mode of quantity; and so the same quantity, like matter, receives various modes of extension. Plotinus says such a response is not safe when it is assigned by those who say that several bodies, while they are mixed, preserve their prior substances, forms, and qualities. For then the smallest body, while it preserves its prior form, perhaps cannot be fundamentally extended in quantity to the greatest degree; but if it has received a new form, it is no wonder if it receives another quantity, just as when air is made from water.

->Discussion of the opinions on mixture, in which he seems to approve that in a perfect mixture the whole body is confused on both sides throughout the whole.<-

## II
In the second chapter he tests what should especially be said in these doubts. First, indeed, he seems to concede that a liquid body enters entirely through another both in matter and in quality, just as water through silk <note>original: "bombice"; likely referring to silken or fine cotton cloth</note>. And after such a mixture, the magnitude there can be equal to what it was before, especially where, as the liquid enters, the fibers become air; the magnitude can also be increased where one is entirely hindered by the other. For why is it a wonder if, as it receives new qualities from that source, it receives new magnitudes in the meantime? And just as it receives quality throughout the whole, so it introduces its dimension through the life of that thing, and thus they grow together? But since quality is more opposed to quality than quality is to quantity, or quantity to quantity, it is right that in a mixture some prior quality either yields to the new one or is obscured, while quantity seems to remain more. Indeed, the more exact the mixture is, the more the prior forms yield to the following form; this is accomplished both by art and by nature. Perhaps, indeed, a dimension can enter a dimension without a "section" <note>original: "sectione"; a cutting or physical division</note>, just as a quality and matter often enter matter. For nothing prohibits this from entering entirely where by its own nature it is incorporeal. But where entry is hindered, it is not hindered simply because it is a body, but because density and hardness resist. For it is this which properly keeps things from yielding, and therefore it does not know how to let in or to enter. No one is ignorant that hardness is one thing and dimension is another. Entry, however, is usually hindered not only by a hard quality, but also by a hostile quality; but where neither is present, entry is not usually hindered. Let it suffice that Plotinus has tested all these things rather than settled them. Unless someone should perhaps say that because this body is entirely infused into that one—just like an alteration in the meantime—if the magnitude does not grow, the prior dimension ceases along with its own form, while both become new. For dimension itself is the cause of distance in things; but if those things exist as two certain things in some dimension, then there is distance and mass between them, and they are extended. Plotinus perhaps signified this here by saying that matter by its own nature does not reject mixture, especially when it has neither its own quantity nor rejects any quantity; and when it finds one body penetrating through another, it does not seek dimensions, but qualities and matter. Nevertheless, he does not seem to think it impossible for dimension to penetrate dimension without a break between very liquid bodies; for a break usually occurs between hard ones. And perhaps he would concede that a flame similarly penetrates iron and is at the same time entirely made equal to it.

->What body is, what corporeity is, and concerning the ideal, seminal, and formal reason.<-

## III
Indeed, he defines the "natural body" in the third chapter as a substance affected by three dimensions and qualities; but by "corporeity" <note>term: "corporeity" (corporeitas); the essential quality or state of being a physical body</note> he means a certain formative principle <note>original: "rationem"; often translated as "reason," but in this Neoplatonic context, it refers to a formative, organizing principle or "Logos"</note> that effects dimensions and qualities. He certainly accepts "reason" here both as the "seminal" principle in nature and as the "substantial form" in matter, in whose specific power its familiar species, dimensions, and qualities are contained. He wished these to be contained in it when he said: "A body is composed of matter and reason." Among these things, he says that in the definition of substance, matter is included; but in the definition of substantial form, matter is not included, since it does not sprout from matter but is impressed by a "seminal reason" <note>term: "seminal reason" (ratio seminalis); a Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of "seed-like" principles that govern the development and form of living things</note>. He also touches upon a threefold reason: the highest and **ideal** in the intellect, which is the intellect itself, whose being and action are not in matter. The second is the **seminal** in the soul of nature itself, whose action (more than its being) is in matter. The third is the **formal**, that is, the form of the substantial body, whose being and action are simultaneously in matter. It can, however, be understood in a way without the addition of matter, since it does not then proceed from matter, but rather from a separate cause; it seems in that very first step of proceeding to have some formal reason in itself, in which it can be thought of before it applies itself to matter. From here it can perhaps be confirmed what many argue: that "distractions" <note>original: "distractiones"; likely referring to the spreading out or spatial extension of matter</note> and degrees do not originate from matter at all, but all these, as formal things, are reduced to the power of the form, just as material conditions are reduced to matter.

# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>A</margin> ...of artificial things, whenever they are fine and continuous to the sight, they are produced as a whole through themselves and flow everywhere just like a liquid. But as these are physical bodies, how is it possible for these things to occur—to pass through one another without cutting or dividing—it is not easy to conceive. <margin>B</margin> To cut through everywhere would clearly result in them destroying one another. When the Stoics say that an increase in volume does not occur in many cases of mixture, they grant an opportunity for others to attack their logic. One might question how the growth of forms <note>original: "τύπων" (typon)</note> occurs—it is difficult, yet nothing prevents us from saying that, as each body is brought together, the magnitude <note>original: "μέγεθος" (megethos)</note> is increased along with the other properties. <margin>C</margin> This growth happens by necessity; nor is it lost, just as the other qualities are not. And just as a new quality is altered there, arising from both, so too is there a new magnitude which the mixture connects with both original magnitudes. But others complain not about the qualities, but say that if matter <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle)</note> is adjacent to matter, and bulk <note>original: "ὄγκος" (onkos)</note> to bulk, then magnitude is preserved. This would be our view; but if matter, along with the primary magnitude upon it, exists through the whole of the other, this is not possible. <margin>D</margin> For if a line were placed next to another line, joining their points at the ends, growth would happen; but in the other case, where one line is superimposed on another, it is as if they become the same, and the volume would be smaller—indeed, the smallest. <margin>the smallest</margin> In every way, the larger * and the largest * would contain the smallest, and this is where motion is most visible. <margin>the smallest</margin> For even of things unseen, one can say they do not reach into everything; but in those cases where it clearly happens, one might speak of an extension of the bulks, speaking very persuasively, as if <margin>E</margin> the smallest bulk were extended to such an extent *. Or it must be that as the body changes, they grant it a larger magnitude, just as if air were produced from water.

->THIS itself must be investigated on its own:<-
what happens when that which was a specific bulk of water becomes air—how the larger volume comes from what was produced. And here, while many other things are said by each side, let us consider <margin>F</margin> what must be said about this. What opinion is consistent with what has been said, or what other view exists besides those mentioned concerning death <note>The Greek "θανάτου" (thanatou) here may be a transcription error for "thinning" or "passing through," or refers to the "death" of the original substance in a mixture</note>, when water is examined in this way? Or if a book does not contain any water in itself, how can the entire body of water pass through it? Or even when it does not flow, how shall we join matter to matter and bulk to bulk? Shall we grant that only the qualities <margin>G</margin> are mixed, and not by a total blending, or indeed...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since even sweats <note>original: "sudores"; ancient philosophers used the passage of sweat through skin to debate whether bodies had "pores" or were solid</note> do not cause incisions in the body, nor is anything perforated there. But indeed, if anyone objects that nothing prevents nature from being so structured that sweat flows out more easily, they will yet add regarding certain artificial things that when they are thin and continuous, they often appear soaked through with moisture and dripping, and the liquid flows through from there to the other side. But since these are bodies, it is not easy to understand by what reasoning it can happen that one <margin>B</margin> passes through the other without an incision. If, however, they are mutually divided through the whole, they will undoubtedly destroy each other. Next, when they say that an increase in bulk <note>original: "mole"</note> often does not occur from the meeting of two bodies, they seem to concede to others the assignment of the exhalations of air as the cause. But regarding the increase of places, though it is difficult, nothing prevents saying that where each body is mutually insinuated, the magnitude <note>original: "magnitudinem"</note> must also necessarily <margin>C</margin> increase along with the other qualities. Nor is this lost, just as the other qualities are not; and just as a new kind of quality arises there from both mixed together, so too another magnitude, where surely the mixture produces the magnitude. But here perhaps our adversaries would say this to us: "If matter is adjacent to matter, and bulk to bulk, which magnitude accompanies, then you are citing this in support of your own opinion." But if matter, along with the magnitude <margin>D</margin> that was in it before, enters into the whole of the other bulk, it would happen to both, not in the same way as a line is joined to another line by their endpoints (where growth can happen), but rather in that way, I say, as if one line were applied to another so that no increase results. Finally, it was argued against these: it seems impossible for a smaller body to stretch itself through one larger than itself, especially the smallest through the largest, where a mixture <margin>E</margin> would have been completed. Surely where it is not sufficiently proven that such things are entirely confounded together, one may object that the smallest does not run through the whole of the largest. But where it is clearly found to happen, certain extensions of the bulks themselves can be assigned: although they do not speak with enough probability who attempt to stretch the smallest bulk into the largest bulk, especially since they attribute a larger magnitude to the body without actually transforming it, <margin>F</margin> as when air is made from water.

<margin>II. Bodies being sent into a mixture; then the qualities of the bodies are mingled.</margin>
->THIS itself requires its own inquiry:<-
what happens when what was a bulk of water becomes air: namely, in what way a larger bulk is produced in that which is created. For the present, let these few things out of many be said, which could be brought forward for each opinion. We, however, should investigate in these matters what is most important to assert, which opinion is more consistent with reason, and <margin>G</margin> whether any other opinion besides those mentioned appears. In the first place, when water flows through wool, or when wool or paper drips out the water it has soaked up, why does the whole body of water not pass through it by flowing through? Or even when it does not flow out, by what means shall we join matter to matter, and bulk to bulk? Shall we concede that only the qualities are confounded with one another? Surely the matter of the water is not outside the silk...

### PLOTINUS, ENNEADS II.

<margin>A</margin>
...is placed there, and not merely in certain intervals: for the whole is soaked, and nowhere is the matter <note>original: "materia"</note> void of quality. But if matter is everywhere present along with quality, then surely the water is throughout the whole of the silk <note>original: "bombicem" - likely referring to silk or fine cotton fabric used as an example of absorption.</note>. Or if the water itself is not there, but rather the quality of the water, we must ask where that quality resides if the bulk <note>original: "moles"</note> is absent? Perhaps that which is added extends the silk; for it received magnitude <note>original: "magnitudinem"</note> from that which entered it. But if it received it, some bulk was added; and if it was added and placed alongside, it was by no means soaked into the other: it is therefore necessary for the matter to be in one position and the other matter in another.

<margin>B</margin>
Perhaps, indeed, nothing prevents one body from receiving magnitude from another, just as it receives quality. To be sure, when a different quality meets another quality, because it has already been fused with the other, it by no means remains pure, nor is it entirely what it was, but is now erased or obscured; 

<margin>C</margin>
but magnitude <note>original: "magnitudo"</note> meeting with magnitude is not erased or obscured. Regarding the claim that a body proceeding through another body causes sections <note>original: "sectiones" - divisions or "cuts" in the physical structure</note> throughout, one might object: for we also concede that qualities propagate themselves through bodies, yet they do not cause sections.

<margin>D</margin>
But perhaps someone might say they do not do so because they are incorporeal. Yet if matter itself is also incorporeal—just as qualities are incorporeal—what prevents a few qualities, together with matter, from penetrating deep through another body? Whereas solids do not penetrate because they possess such qualities as hinder that very penetration. Or perhaps we shall say that many qualities together with matter cannot achieve this. 

<margin>E</margin>
Truly, if a multitude of qualities produced the body, then the multitude would be the cause. But if density is a specific quality of its own, just as "corporeity" <note>original: "corporeitas" - the state of being a body</note> itself is a specific quality, then perhaps qualities do not produce a mixture by virtue of being qualities, but by being *certain kinds* of qualities. Nor again does matter, as matter, reject mixture, but only when it is joined with such a quality; especially if it has no magnitude of its own, so that it neither claims its own space nor rejects any that comes to it by nature. Let these doubts concerning these matters suffice for now.

---

### III. How he defines body and corporeity.
<margin>F</margin>
SINCE we have made mention of corporeity, we must investigate whether corporeity itself is something composed of all the qualities together, or rather if it is a specific form and principle <note>original: "species & ratio" / "εἶδος καὶ λόγος" (eidos kai logos) - the defining blueprint or essence of a thing.</note> which, when it enters into matter, produces a body. Certainly, if the body is this very thing gathered from all the qualities together with matter, then that will be "corporeity." But if it is a principle <note>original: "ratio" / "logos"</note> which, by its approach, produces the body, then clearly that principle encompasses and contains all the qualities.

<margin>G</margin>
It is necessary for such a principle—if it is not simply a defining formula of what each thing is, but rather a principle that *makes* the thing—not to encompass the matter within itself, but rather to exist around the matter and, by being present, to produce the body. Furthermore, the body is matter and the indwelling principle <note>original: "λόγον ἐνόντα" (logon enonta)</note> together. ...to be a principle, and by entering in to complete the body, and that the body is matter and the principle existing within.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...in the book <note>original: "βίβλῳ" (biblō) - likely a transcription error for "βύμβυκι" (silk) as seen in the Latin column.</note>, or how the matter of the water is likened to it. For it is as if it were stretched through all of it; for the whole would be watery. And indeed quality is material. If matter is everywhere with quality, then the water is everywhere in the silk. Or is it not the water itself, but the quality of the water? But where would the quality of the water be? For how could the same bulk or extension of the silk be that which is affected? 

<margin>B</margin>
But if magnitude is added to that which has passed through, and if it received it, there is some addition of bulk. And if it is placed alongside, then it is in all those places. But if the matter is in one and then another, does anything prevent it from receiving magnitude from this other body, just as it gives quality? For when quality comes together with quality, it is no longer that same quality, but is with another; they are not 

<margin>C</margin>
pure when with another, nor are they entirely themselves, but are obscured by magnitude. But magnitude coming together with another magnitude does not disappear. As for the claim that a body passing through a body makes "cuts" <note>original: "τομὰς" (tomas)</note> in all things, how is it said? For we ourselves say that qualities go through bodies, and do they make cuts, or is it because they are incorporeal? But if matter is also incorporeal, 

<margin>D</margin>
why can a few qualities not pass through bodies in the same way with matter? But do solids perhaps stop the qualities, as they prevent them from passing through? Or is it impossible <margin>Impossible.</margin> for many things to do this together with matter? If we say it is the multitude of qualities that makes a body, then the multitude would be the cause. But if density is a private quality, 

<margin>E</margin>
just as what is called "corporeity" <note>original: "σωματότης" (somatotēs)</note> is a private quality, then qualities do not produce it insofar as they are qualities, but insofar as they are *such* qualities. If matter as matter does not mix, but only insofar as it is with such-and-such a quality, and especially if it has no magnitude—it does not have it, unless it were to lose that magnitude. Let these things be thus debated.

<margin>F</margin>
SINCE we have mentioned corporeity, we must consider whether corporeity is that which is composed of all things, or is it a certain form <note>original: "εἶδός" (eidos)</note> and a certain principle <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note> which, by entering into matter, makes a body? If, therefore, the body is this thing made of all the qualities with matter, this would be corporeity. And if it is a principle which, by approaching, makes the body, it is clear that the principle, by embracing them, holds 

<margin>G</margin>
all the qualities. But it is necessary for the principle in this way—if it is not entirely like a definition of what a thing is, but a principle making the thing—not to have embraced the matter within itself, but to be around it.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON
# BOOK VIII: ON SIGHT, AND
## WHY THINGS THAT ARE FAR AWAY
## APPEAR SMALL,
## A COMMENTARY.

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

*Two reasons from others, and two from Plotinus: why more remote things appear smaller.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a circular medallion depicting a bird, possibly an eagle or a phoenix.</image-desc>
**T**WO things are investigated in this book: First, why objects further from the eyes usually appear smaller. Second: for what reason do two very distant sights that are separated from each other—by a stadium <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet or 185 meters.</note>, for instance—appear to be separated by an even smaller distance than if they were closer to us. To these questions, some respond that the very light by which we see, as it comes from the object and approaches the eye, accommodates itself more to the eye and the pupil, just as liquid bodies accommodate themselves to their containers. This response is specifically valid if the light spoken of is a visual ray sent from the eye and then reflected back from the object to the eye; for in this way, perhaps, it would return to the size of its origin by a certain natural vigor. 

There are also those who say that this light, proceeding from the eye, reaches the object to be seen in a pyramidal shape, and suddenly dilates through it; then, from that object as if from a pyramidal base, it reflects the shape back toward the eye, touching the pupil with its point (the "cone") in a similar pyramidal nature. According to their opinion, such a response was appropriately applied. For some might say it holds true generally: because the primary luminous thing—that is, the sun—pours out light from its entire circumference, but this light gathers itself into a cone from every side so that it does not vanish by flowing too far from its source. In this way, it acts more powerfully, and the whole is more easily present everywhere; and while the entire base is narrowed into a cone, the whole sun and all its power will be present through that angle and will act everywhere. Thus, its entire magnitude can be seen within that angle. Likewise, since there is both a center and a circumference in the sun, its light imitates the circumference insofar as it flows from the sun's whole ambit; but insofar as it is gathered into a narrow space, they say unity and a center are created. From this, they argue that from any illuminated body, light gathers itself toward other things and toward the eyes in roughly the same shape. This concludes the first response.

Others respond with a different reason: that the form <term>forma</term> of the thing to be seen has a material nature in the thing itself; but when taken up by spiritual light, it suddenly strips off its matter and travels by a certain spiritual rational principle, so long as it seems to maintain a certain proportion to its own matter over a distance. But as soon as it begins to lose this proportion, it appears smaller; and finally, when all proportion to its own matter is consumed, it is no longer seen by the eyes. To the eyes, these things appear just as the formal, seminal, and ideal principles <term>rationes formales, seminales, ideales; the invisible "blueprints" of nature</term> of natural forms are themselves not seen. These are the responses according to the opinions of others. To what extent these opinions and responses contain the truth will be discovered elsewhere.

After this follows Plotinus’s own response to the same problem. Surely, we fully measure how great a distance is only when we look more piercingly at its individual parts, step by step. Therefore, when a thing is placed far away and many tiny parts are hidden from us, the measurement of the whole naturally escapes us, and it appears smaller. This is especially true because the quality of light—since it is both more effective than quantity and more proper to the sense of sight—presents itself to the eyes more effectively and sooner than quantity does. Therefore, we first see what kind of thing it is <note>Its "quality," such as color or brightness.</note>, and only secondly how big it is, specifically while we are perceiving its quality. 

Therefore, since the visual ray poured out from us toward the object is eventually weakened by a longer journey, it discerns the quality—that is, the color and the luminous nature—less clearly; consequently, it measures the quantity confusedly as well. Now, what is more perfect or less perfect in substantial forms, and more intense or relaxed in accidental forms, is the same as "greater" and "smaller" in quantity; "faster" and "slower" in motion; and "longer" and "shorter" in time. Since "greater" and "smaller" (which are proper to quantity) have a certain proportion to "more intense" and "more relaxed" (which are proper to quality), and since quantity follows quality in the order of our recognition, it is no wonder that when the sight perceives a quality at a "relaxed" (weaker) degree, it meanwhile perceives the quantity as a "smaller" measure. 

Among these points, one should remember that color is the proper object of sight, just as voice is the proper object of hearing; likewise, the vehemence and power of color belong properly to sight, and the vigor of voice to hearing. Magnitude, however, is perceived by several senses, and it is not so much the power of the sensible thing itself as it is a certain diffusion of that thing through a multitude of space. We do not know this magnitude primarily, but rather through the quality and effectiveness of the thing. Thus it happens that where quality is less apparent, quantity remains hidden. This is confirmed by three main signs. 

The first is this: if you look at hills full of the shapes of various things, and you see those shapes clearly, you will measure the magnitude of the hill more correctly than if you did not see such shapes at all—as if magnitude is revealed through shapes. Second: if you look at a table placed nearby that is impressed with various figures, unless you look at the figures individually, you will not judge the size of the table to be as great as if you had clearly seen them all individually and as a whole. Third: if on a wall depicted only with green color...

<sig>q 4</sig>
