<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II, Book 8, specifically focusing on the second question posed at the end of the previous page regarding the perception of distance between two far-off objects.</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

<meta>catchword: PLOTINUS</meta>

If you turn your gaze toward a painted surface, such a wall will not appear as large to you insofar as it has been marked with many different colors. For you can scarcely discern the parts of a dimension between themselves where a variety of forms does not distinguish them; rather, you suddenly slip away from any given part of the dimension unless a difference in quality halts your gaze. Through these points, a response can be given to the second question: namely, for what reason two buildings on an opposite hill, situated very far away and distant from each other by a stadium <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>, appear to be less distant from each other than they are. Likewise, if they are separated from us by a hundred stadia, they seem to be at an even shorter interval from us. For where we discern the variety of forms more confusedly, we certainly do not discern the magnitude of the interval either.

---

### That those things which are more remote do not appear smaller on account of smaller angles.

II In the second chapter, he refutes the response of those who think that a pyramidal shape is extended from the visible object toward the eye via lines of rays, touching the pupil at a certain cone. They argue that the more remote the object is, the more gradually sharper the cone becomes. Thus, while we perceive the thing little by little through a narrower angle, we also conjecture a narrower magnitude—especially when the process has gone so far that the angle is already smaller than the pupil. What should be said regarding the rest, we shall discuss elsewhere along with Plotinus. For the present, however, this idea is especially rejected: that they say a body appears smaller for the reason that the angle has now turned out smaller than the pupil. For this reasoning would allow that certain other things might then be seen by the pupil when a single thing cannot fill the pupil with its own angle; but indeed, where an object is so vast that nothing further can be perceived in a single glance, it even then appears smaller than it is, although the angle by which it is said to be seen has not turned out smaller than the pupil. For the entire hemisphere is perceived by the whole sight, which fills the pupil to such an extent that it can perceive nothing else besides. Therefore, that something is thought to be smaller than it is does not happen because it is discerned through a narrower angle than the pupil. Among these things, he notices a judgment which confirms, according to Plotinus, that it is not the form of the object that reaches the eyes, but the ray of the eye that reaches the object. For vision is performed like a certain action according to the very mode of the visual form. If, therefore, the object conformed itself to the narrowness of the pupil (as they say), it would never be judged larger than the pupil; but now it is judged far larger, because the visual ray <term>radius visualis; the concept that the eye emits a beam to "touch" the object</term> stretched outward diffuses itself through the very magnitude of the thing. But surely we cannot deny that rays reach the eyes from luminous bodies in a certain pyramidal shape, and with this very shape they carry the spiritual solar quality of the thing, or its power <term>virtus; the inherent capability or essence</term>, or its act, all the way to us. That sight also emits rays from the eyes is testified by the radial nature of sight, especially in animals that see at night. Some see things close at hand by emitting rays, others further away; nor do we see very thin things, nor very close clouds, because they do not terminate the still-powerful rays of the eyes. I pass over the fact that humans and certain animals affect things outside themselves by the gaze of their eyes. Finally, more light is necessary near the object than near the eye; for where our ray is emitted, it is strong. Nor is it additionally useful for light to be scattered in abundance here, but it is better that the object be cherished by a much weaker light, as the ray is immediately diffused through the object. For it seems probable that the visual ray of the eye is extended through the pyramidal breadth of the meeting light, with the help of that same light, toward the breadth of the thing to be seen, insofar as it is able to proceed. And when it is thus terminated, the effect of vision is completed. Indeed, both Plato in the *Timaeus*, and Galen and Chalcidius in the same place, teach—and the experts in perspective confirm—that vision is produced by a certain commerce <note>original: "commercio"; a reciprocal interaction or "meeting"</note> of both the visual ray and the more abundant light. This light is either innate to the visual ray or applied from the outside.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino discusses the optical theories of Plotinus, refuting the idea that objects look smaller simply due to the geometry of the visual angle. He argues for the "extramission" theory, where the eye emits a visual ray that interacts with external light to perceive the true scale of distant objects.</summary>
<keywords>optics, visual ray, perspective, Plotinus, geometry of vision, extramission theory, perception of distance, Timaeus, Chalcidius</keywords>

->On vision, or why distant things appear small.<-

->On sight, or why things far removed from us seem small.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A featuring two human figures in conversation within a scenic or interior background.</image-desc>DO distant things appear smaller, or do those separated by a great distance seem to have little space between them, while those nearby appear as large as they truly are, or as far apart as they truly are? To those watching, distant things seem smaller because the light comes to the sight and to the size of the pupil in a gathered way. And to the extent that the matter of the thing seen is far away, its form arrives as if it were isolated, and many parts of it merge into the same qualities, so that only its rational principle <note>original: "λόγον" (logos) — here meaning the essential form or identifying characteristics</note> arrives. Furthermore, magnitude is not present to the observer in a way that passes through and encounters each individual part of the form as if perceiving it directly, nor is it close enough to be known in itself; rather, magnitudes are seen as an accidental property <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a quality that is not essential to the nature of a thing, like its size or color.</note> of the colors, which are the first things known. Thus, as much as a thing is separated nearby, it is known. But far away, because the parts and the whole are poured together, it does not provide an accurate diagnosis of their quantities. For even the colors themselves arrive faintly. What then? Is it any wonder if magnitudes, just like voices, appear smaller to the extent that their form flows away in a faint <margin>*</margin> manner? Or perhaps the sense of hearing does not seek size poorly, but perceives magnitude only as an accidental property. But where does hearing stand if magnitudes are accidental? For magnitude belongs primarily to the form of the voice, <margin>*</margin> just as what is seen appears * to the voice <note>The Greek text here is somewhat corrupted or difficult, comparing the visibility of sight to the audibility of sound</note>; but even if hearing perceives magnitude, it is not according to quantity, but according to the "more" or "less," and as an accident. For example, a "strong" sound is like the "strong" sweetness of taste. Or is even this accidental? <margin>specifically</margin> And what if someone were to speak of it as magnitude, as much as the half...

<margin>He gives the reason why things appear smaller when they are perceived from a distance.</margin>

And why is it that things separated by a long space appear to us to be distant by only a small space? Whereas those things that meet us from nearby appear as large as they are, and show the true extent of their interval? Do things far away seem smaller to those looking at them because the light somehow requires itself to be gathered toward the sight and the size of the pupil?

<insert>B</insert> And as far as the matter of the visible thing is remote, to that extent the species <note>original: "species" — the visible form or appearance of the object</note> arrives as if it were the form alone without the matter. Yet both quantity and quality are a kind of species. And thus, as it were, only the reason <note>original: "ratio" — the conceptual proportion or definition of the object</note> of this thing arrives. Or perhaps also because we sense how great a magnitude is through a certain mental traversal made across every part? Therefore, it is necessary for the object to be present, and present nearby, so that its size may be known.

<insert>C</insert> Is it also because magnitude is perceived as an accidental property? Since color is what is perceived first? Thus, from nearby, the full extent of the colored object is discerned; but from a distance, only that it *is* colored is discerned: the parts arranged according to quantity do not bring an exact knowledge of that quantity. Since the colors themselves arrive weak and thin, what wonder is it if magnitudes also appear smaller, just as voices do, to the extent that their form arrives meager and weak. Indeed, there too, the hearing strives for the form. But magnitude is perceived by accident.

<insert>D</insert> But as far as hearing is concerned, if magnitude is felt as an accident, to what power is the magnitude that exists in a voice first exposed? # PLOTINUS ENNEAD II.

<column-break/>

A It happens that they are designated; however, not exactly. Truly, the intensity of each nature is the same as the nature itself. But the progression into multitude is considered according to the extension into every place which is filled. Yet, these are not small colors, but weak ones; and the magnitudes are small. Perhaps there is something common to both, which is usually said to be "less" in that which exists. A color is said to be "less" in that B it is weak and fading. A magnitude—that is, a dimension—has that which is called "less" in that it is small. Indeed, magnitude, following color, is diminished by a certain consequent proportion. This kind of experience becomes more manifest in sights that are varied; as in the sight of mountains having many dwellings and trees and many other things: if any of these are perceived, it allows you to measure the whole from the individual things inspected. But when the C visible form <note>original: "species" (Latin) / "εἴδους" (Greek) — in Neoplatonic optics, this refers to the 'sensible form' or image that travels from the object to the eye.</note> from the individual parts does not reach the eye, the eye has no way to know how great the whole is, since it usually measures the underlying magnitude according to each presented form. Since even things that are nearby, because they are varied, may cause the gaze to turn suddenly toward all of them at once, so that not all forms are discerned, they tend to appear smaller in proportion, insofar as any form escapes the viewer. But when individual forms are clearly discerned, D then the measure of the magnitude is rightly judged. However, whatever magnitudes occur as uniform in a single color most greatly deceive the indication of quantity. This is because the sight cannot easily measure them discretely by parts; but in measuring, it suddenly slips beyond the part, having no way of difference by which it can halt its progress in individual parts. Something far remote seems to be situated nearby E because the middle space, for the same reason, is usually gathered as to how great it is. For what is near does not hide how great it is, for the same reasons. But where the sight does not discern the length of the distance as it is according to the visible form, it certainly cannot measure how great it is in magnitude.

<margin>
II
That they do not appear smaller because of smaller angles; seek why they are smaller.
</margin>

G As for what is said by some—that things far distant appear smaller for the reason that they are seen through smaller <term>visual angles</term> <note>The 'visual angle' is the angle formed by two rays of light coming from the extremities of an object and meeting at the eye; early optics taught that the size of this angle determined the perceived size of the object.</note>—it has been stated elsewhere that this is false, and it must be refuted here at present. Surely, he who says an object is seen through a smaller angle leaves the rest of the vision—either the angle, or something else outside the viewer that is visible, or at least something external like the air. Therefore, when nothing is left over because the mountain is huge, but the vision is either equal to it or no other thing can be perceived by sight—since the power of the space itself is accommodated to the object—or even exceeds the object on both sides of the visual gaze. How will anyone respond here? Since the object itself appears much smaller than it is, and yet it is perceived by the whole sight. If someone looks up into the heaven, anyone will understand this without a doubt. For otherwise, no one could behold the whole hemisphere all at once in a single glance;

Color is "less" when it is faint; B magnitude is "less" when it is small and the magnitude, staying with the color, is fashioned proportionally. This experience becomes clearer in the case of variegated things. For example, mountains having cities, dwellings, and a multitude of trees, and many other things; each of which, if seen, provides a certain way of the individual defined things to measure the whole. But when the form of each part is withdrawn, it is prevented from C measuring the underlying magnitude by each form, [and thus] from knowing how great the whole is. Since even things that are nearby, if they are variegated, and the application [of sight] toward them happens all at once and not all forms are seen, they would appear smaller in proportion, by as much as each [form] was stolen from the eye. But when all are seen accurately, they are measured and known. Whatever magnitudes are of the same form or same color, these also deceive as to D quantity, as the sight itself is not at all able to measure them by parts, because it slips past the part in measuring, because it has no place to stop at each part by means of a difference. Things far away [seem] nearby because the intervening [space] is passed over in silence, for the same reason. For the nearby (how great it is in itself) is not hidden, for the same reasons; but the distance of the far-off thing through the interval, if it does not stand according to form, one could not say, or tell how great it is in magnitude.

# MARSILIO FICINO’S COMMENTARY ON BOOK IX OF THE SECOND ENNEAD: AGAINST THE GNOSTICS.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK

->The One and the Good are the same and the first of all things. Likewise, there are three principles: The Good itself, the Mind, and the Soul.<-

<image-desc>A large woodcut decorative initial 'P' begins the main text, featuring ornate floral scrollwork within a square border.</image-desc>

We can gather that the mind of Plotinus was not entirely foreign to the Christian law from the fact that he was a disciple of Ammonius—who was always a Christian—and always a friend of the very Christian Origen. It is said that he agreed, along with Origen and Herennius, that they would never depart from the teachings of Ammonius; and he is said to have kept this promise just as he had pledged. Furthermore, his own disciple Porphyry bears witness that Plotinus at one time looked down upon the worship of the pagan gods with a lofty spirit, even when Aurelius exhorted him to it. Finally, being frequently provoked by many heretics who partly corrupted and partly even despised his beloved Plato, he responded at great length. Yet, in responding, he inserted nothing hostile to the common Christian faith, but only addressed those things peculiar to the heresy—even though it was permitted to attack Christians with impunity at that time, and the occasion was offered. Porphyry, in describing the life of Plotinus, recounts who the authors of this heresy were and what those heretics—who were called "Gnostics" <note>literally "those who know"—a group of early religious movements that claimed secret, salvific knowledge</note>—professed. It is certainly clear from their opinions that this heresy, although they worshipped Christ, disagreed no less with the common consensus of Christians than they did with the Platonists.

But since it pertains to the work at hand, these are their chief errors: Above the "One Good" itself, they dreamed up some unknown thing. Furthermore, they distinguished the Intellect into many separated parts. Between the Intellect and the Soul, they inserted some middle thing. They thought the Soul was corrupted and that the world was an evil thing created by an evil principle. 

That there is nothing superior to or prior to the Good itself in goodness, nor to the One itself in unity, is shown thus: In the beginning, one must remember that what is not "First" is not "Simple" <note>In Platonic philosophy, "Simple" means something that is not made of parts and cannot be broken down further</note>; and conversely, what is not simple cannot be First. For if any thing were not the first of all, it would certainly depend on others; therefore, there would be two things in it—namely, something of a cause, and something else of its own differing from that cause. Thus, while it is not First, it deservedly cannot be Simple. Again, if a thing is not simple, it will necessarily have both "this" and "that" within itself. We must ask, therefore, whether "this" comes only from "that," or whether both come equally from each other, or neither from neither, or whether both come from some third thing. 

If you answer that "this" depends on "that," then "that" will certainly be First, and "this" will be second; nor will it be permitted to say that a composite thing is First here. Nor, again, will it be permitted to say that both are made equally from each other; otherwise, the same thing compared to itself will be both cause and effect, both prior and posterior. But if you say that both are made from a third thing, then not the composite, but that third thing will be the First and the Principle. Furthermore, it is a sin to place two things in the highest realms where neither is from the other, nor both from a third; otherwise, they would come together not by a determined law of causation, but perhaps by chance. But reckless chance cannot exist in the highest realms; otherwise, there would be no order in the things that follow. 

Wherefore, just as we have said that what is not First is not Simple, so we also say that what is not Simple cannot be First. Therefore, the more prior a thing is, the simpler it is, and vice versa. That which is First is the most simple, and vice versa. For primality itself (so to speak) is simplicity itself, and the opposite is also true. Since, therefore, the Supreme holds the highest degree in simplicity and divinity, it is certainly the same as the One, and the First of all, and the Principle. 

Goodness is surely most simple; otherwise, it would be composed of many things, and therefore it would lack parts and a composer, and thus it would be least self-sufficient. Yet it is necessary that Goodness itself be not only the most self-sufficient, but be sufficiency itself. For this is what is desired as the "Good." Thus, since the Good itself is the most self-sufficient, it is also the most simple. It is therefore First, especially because if it were not First, whatever was superior to the Good itself would also be better than Goodness—even though nothing better than Goodness can be imagined, for only by Goodness is whatever is better made better. 

Now we ask whether the Good itself desires that which is perhaps placed before it, or not. If it does not desire it, it is a marvel that an effect does not desire the cause by which it is perfected. If it does desire it, it is again a marvel that the Good itself should long for something outside itself, since all desire ends in the Good. Furthermore, we ask similarly about other things: whether they desire what is imagined to be above the Good, beyond the limits of the Good, or not. It is indeed a sin to suggest that all things do not desire the First Principle. It is a sin, again, to desire anything beyond the Good. From all this, it is concluded that the Good itself is the most simple of all things, and the First. Truly, no one doubts that Unity, or the One itself, is the most simple. For in every essence, composition or number can either exist or be imagined; but in Unity alone it cannot. Otherwise, it would not be Unity itself, but "a certain one thing" and a multitude. Division, furthermore...

<summary>This page contains Ficino's introduction to Plotinus's critique of Gnosticism, arguing that Plotinus's philosophy of the "One" as the simple, primary principle is compatible with Christian thought and serves to refute Gnostic dualism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Book 9 of Plotinus’s Second Ennead. Ficino transitions from the introductory remarks about Plotinus’s background into a deep metaphysical analysis of the "Three Primary Hypostases" (The One/Good, Mind, and Soul) and why they cannot be further subdivided or considered in a state of potentiality.</meta>

...cannot happen to unity. For if anyone strives to divide this, he will not indeed divide it, but will only find unity again. Surely you cut one piece of wood <note>original: "Lignum certe vnum secas"</note> and again wood into smaller pieces of wood. But the unity that was conceived in the wood, you could not divide into any parts of unity—otherwise it would be less than unity—rather, you have multiplied or rather propagated unity in such a way that what was previously in one was subsequently the same whole in two. Since, therefore, unity is the most simple and the first, it is rightly the same as the Good. Could it be that there are perhaps two primary principles of things and they happen to meet by chance? Or that a duality exists before unity? Yet when we say that goodness and unity are utterly simple, we do not mean a "simple thing" that exists inside something else, or from which something else is composed. For if it were in another, and could not sustain itself, it would certainly depend on that other. Again, if something else were composed from it, it would by no means be a perfect thing, but would strive further to be reduced into the form and act of the composite. Therefore, the Good itself, or the One itself, is entirely the same, most simple, and first; it does not reside in anything else, nor is it considered in such a way that something else is prior to it—as if it were first a "thing" and then "good" and "one." Otherwise, one quality would be added to another, and there would be some prior imperfect thing, and a composition would be created. Therefore, we ought to contemplate goodness or unity itself from the most simple intuition of the mind, not predicating one thing of another, but perceiving that very simplicity with the first and total strike of the mind.

Since after this Plotinus treats the three principles of the world <note>These are the three "Hypostases" or levels of reality in Neoplatonism: The One, the Divine Intellect, and the World Soul.</note>—namely the Good itself, the First Mind, and the First Soul—we must remember that where the common principles of the world are concerned, we ought to contemplate those things which are common in the world above all others. Unity is everywhere the most common of all things, and it is linked to the Good. For that gift extends even to things not yet formed. In the second degree of community or origin is "Form," as the formal degree teaches; finally, in the third degree is placed "Vital Motion" itself. Since a function that is more common belongs to a prior cause, the first cause of all is rightly the Good itself, or the One, upon which unity and the striving toward the good depend. The second cause of things is the First Mind, to which formal order belongs. The third is the First Soul, by which a vital motion is returned to all things everywhere. Therefore, when we behold the universe, both at its most formed in the order of forms and at its most effective in vital motions everywhere, we rightly think that Mind governs everywhere and Soul breathes everywhere. And since the order of forms exists for the sake of the good as one, and vital motion strives toward the good, it is not without reason that we wish both the Mind, which thus orders all things, and the Soul, which thus moves them, to depend on the One-Good itself.

If, therefore, this corporeal universe, which is moved by another, is first reduced to the Soul (which is movable by itself and moves all things by its own motion), then the Soul is led to the Mind, which is entirely stable and leads all things by its own stability. But both—namely Mind and Soul—are referred back to the Good, for whose sake the Mind appears to be moved stably <note>Ficino uses "moved stably" to describe the Mind's internal, eternal activity which does not change its essence.</note> and the Soul to be moved changeably; in the Good the Mind itself finds rest, and around the Good the Soul revolves. Truly, whether the Soul is moved or moves, it is moved and moves toward the Good. Whether the Mind rests or makes firm, it certainly rests and stays in the Good. Hence, nature has granted to all things that just as they are moved toward the Good, so they also rest in the Good. And indeed, just as the Good itself is something other than those things which are moved toward it and other than motion itself, so it is also something other than those things which stand in it and other than "state" or "rest" itself—otherwise they would have rested in themselves from the beginning.

After the Good, the Mind follows most closely; the Soul accompanies the Mind most closely. For since every agent acts toward the Good, the Mind—which while it acts, acts stably toward the Good and is revolved back into itself by its acting—is shown to be closest to the Good. But the Soul, which moves through its essence and is moved again by itself in things to be done, then completes its circle after a progression, and is entirely closest to the Mind, which is entirely stable and turned entirely toward itself. But who does not see that the Soul, being always and truly a sharer in intelligence, is closest to the Intellect? Therefore, that which happens in the world in a greater and higher way, contributing finally to life, proceeds from the Soul. But that such motion is ordered and stable, restored in a circle, and expresses forms, is obtained from the Mind. Finally, that the Mind has certain principal ends everywhere, and that various forms elsewhere lead to one another, results from the Good itself, which alone Mind and Soul represent in essence, light, mobility, and goodness. Below the heavens, the final cause seems to refer to the Good, the formal cause to the Mind, and the efficient cause to the Soul.

However, since we dispute more extensively concerning the three principles of all things throughout our arguments on Plato and in our *Theology*, it must suffice to have touched upon these things briefly. After this, however, he [Plotinus] refutes those who distinguish divine things among themselves either because some are in "potentiality" and others in "actuality." For nothing in eternal things is in potentiality <note>In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic thought, "potentiality" implies a lack or a need to become something else. Divine things are "pure act," meaning they are already fully everything they can be.</note>. Nor [does he accept] that one intellect remains still while another is moved. For the intellect is not any kind of motion, but rather the first motion is in the Soul. Nor [does he accept] that this intellect understands a certain substance—whether its own or even another's—while that other intellect understands only the action of another intellect, by which that other (to whom the action belongs) does not understand. Such a distinction in the nature of souls certainly does not divide the substance of souls. Since the soul is the same thing that understands either itself or anything else, it understands itself by itself. Therefore, the substance of minds is even less divided in this way; and much more can the same mind fulfill both.

Now we do concede that "to understand" simply differs by a certain reasoning from the "observation of intelligence." For the former has some essence as its object, while the latter seems to look at an action as its object. And in us, he who knows does not always also recognize that he knows. Nevertheless, any Mind separated from commerce with the body understands so readily that, insofar as it understands something, it thoroughly recognizes that it understands itself. Especially since the condition of understanding there is such that the mind looks to its own essence in order to understand. For if perfect intelligence is there, it has its "intelligible" <note>term: Intelligible — an object of pure thought, rather than a physical object of the senses.</note> as something most inward and certain, and it depends on nothing. Thus it happens most of all if it looks to its own essence as its object. While it contemplates its own essence, placed in its own intellectual being and in a perpetual act of intelligence, it knows itself to be an intellectual essence and always understanding. Insofar as it understands itself, it understands that it understands. Especially since, just as in light "to shine" is the same as "to be," so in the intellect itself "to be" is the same as "to understand." Therefore, while it knows itself to be, it also thoroughly recognizes that it understands itself. For this reason, any absolute intellect, just as it always understands, so it always notices that it understands; especially since no exterior occupation diverts it from that self-observation. Moreover, the act of intelligence there is the same by which it simply understands something and by which it always recognizes that it understands it. For if such acts were distinguished there, we would then say that a second, third, and fourth act, and so on infinitely, are distinguished there, insofar as an innumerable number of subsequent acts would be imagined to understand the preceding one. But philosophers consider it a crime to place infinite acts—and indeed superfluous ones—there in the presence [of the divine]; especially if infinite substances were said to be multiplied through them. Among these things, you will note that he places in blessed minds a perpetual observation of their own essence and action, and by the same act and intelli-

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of the One, Mind, and Soul, arguing that these divine principles are "pure act" without potentiality and possess perfect self-knowledge without infinite regression.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II. Here, Ficino examines the nature of intelligence, the hierarchy of providence, and a refutation of the Gnostic view that the physical world was created as a result of a "fall" or an evil impulse of the soul.</meta>

# ON BOOK 8 [9] OF ENNEAD II. <note>While the header reads "Book 8," this text actually comments on Ennead II, Book 9, "Against the Gnostics."</note>

...that the essence of intelligence is filled by knowledge and recognition. If he [Plotinus] ever says that the simple "First" <note>The One</note> is distracted from the act of intelligence by attention, you should explain it thus: namely, when attention is an action differing in reality from intelligence, and when attention happens through the service of a certain imagination—which differs too much from the intellect and distracts it toward external things in the meantime. He immediately refutes those who say there is a middle substance between the mind and the soul, which they call "intellectual reason" itself; they say the soul receives reason from this. In this way, no soul would have true and perpetual intelligence. For true and perpetual intelligence is either in the mind itself or in that which is the most immediate participant in the mind. According to their opinion, the soul would receive some intelligence not in the first degree, but in the second, and would receive its image rather than its nature. Thus, it would neither observe itself—which is the duty of intellectual nature—nor could the intellect devise the substance of another thing from its nature, which follows the absolute; nor could it comprehend the formal reason <term>formal reason: the essential definition or "Logos" of a thing</term>, or embrace the definitions themselves even unto the truth. For such things properly belong to the Mind.

->Different modes of Providence: first, in the three principles; second, in the stars; third,<-
->in demons; fourth, in humans.<-

II In the second chapter, therefore, he gathers the three principles of things: namely, the Good itself, and its son, the Intellect, flowing from the paternal light in the manner of a light; and additionally, the Soul of the World from the divine Intellect, flowing through all things like a spirit. But it provides for lower things on the condition that, in the meantime, it does not decline from divine things in any part. Rather, he says that the more attentively it clings to divine things, the more powerful and fertile it is rendered toward the things that follow—and as if already pregnant from that source, it gives birth to the things that follow. Universal providence belongs to these three principles, by which they provide for all things and in all ways. A less universal providence belongs to the souls of the spheres and stars; for any of these provides for all things, but not in all ways. For each one bestows its own properties, even if to everyone. An even less universal providence exists in demons: for each one cares for certain kinds of things, to which they also bestow certain properties. There is also a particular providence in our souls toward lower things, even with a more pressing concern than that with which demons care for their own—so much so that it would be foolish to compare human providence with the providence of the World Soul. For since from the first soul the most powerful universal providence is made, outside of which there is nothing that resists its duty, Plotinus says not without justice that while it provides, it neither labors nor is it less blessed. But our soul is so occupied with ruling bodies that it sometimes departs from higher things. It departs, I say, first through its lowest part—that is, through the imagination and its affect, which inclines more readily toward lower things. This part may then drag with it the middle part of the soul, whose property it is to run to and fro by reason. However, the Intellect, which he also names a part of the soul, he affirms (as he often does) never ceases from divine intelligence. This opinion about the intellect seems to have been not only Plotinus's but also that of his teacher, Ammonius of Alexandria. Plotinus is said to have followed him in all things. We have heard that certain other students of Ammonius remained in the same opinion, which Iamblichus also seems to count among the dogmas of the Egyptians. You will note in the meantime that our soul, although it is called a "particular soul" because it has a particular providence, is in no way a part of the World Soul. Again, our soul is anxious and labors in ruling the body because it neither holds the highest grade of the soul—which the World Soul obtained—nor does it remain entirely in the highest when it provides for lower things. He certainly thinks it is the condition of particular souls that they do this or that in turns—at least as far as reason and imagination are concerned—but as far as the intellect is concerned, they take no turns. For every intellect is established entirely in eternity. Indeed, in the property of the soul that follows immediately, there is the first movement and the first time.

->The world was not at some point new because of a new depravity of the soul,<-
->nor will it ever perish.<-

III In vain, therefore, did the heretics <note>Ficino refers to the Gnostics, whom Plotinus attacks in this specific book</note> imagine that the first soul once fell from divine blessedness, and that, degenerating into worse things, it fabricated the world. Too rashly they gave the world a beginning for the reason that its maker had recently been changed into evil. It was much better to say that the world always proceeded from a certain natural necessity of the soul—just as the form of a body proceeds from vegetative power, and heat and light from fire. For we see that all the most perfect things always act in natural generosity, not out of the poverty of evil, but rather out of the goodness of abundance. If they always act—even those things whose power and action are determined only toward certain specific things, like any element or composite—how much more do those three principles of things, whose power is common to all, always act? It is therefore better to say that the maker of the world, out of the abundance of eternal goodness, brought forth the world from eternity, rather than a "new" world from a "new" depravity. Certainly, if we consider the nature of the principles to be always absolute in act, and thus compare the work to it, it seems an everlasting work follows from it. Although, if you look to the will of divine goodness or intelligence itself, you might be able to conceive of the world as new without a new depravity in the maker, and without a novelty in the divine counsel. Truly, since in the divinity of nature the "same" becomes "will," the will does not take away from nature what is proper to nature, nor does nature take away what is proper to the will. Then indeed he refutes those who thought the world would eventually perish. For only those things that can be resolved into something else seem able to perish. For the very goodness of nature does not allow anything to vanish into nothingness, since it does not permit a vacuum anywhere. Into what, then, can the world be resolved? Perhaps into matter? Let it be so. But then we ask whether that matter has a form or not. If it has, it will still be a composite resolvable into matter. Then that matter can neither vanish into nothingness nor persist in forms. For existence is given everywhere through form. But if you imagine it remaining without form, then matter will be in one place, and divine things in another, separated by boundaries—since nothing would shine forth from them into the matter. Thus, divine things would not be everywhere. We have proven that saying this is a sin in my *Platonic Theology*, and we will prove it elsewhere. Nor is it permitted to imagine that matter can be resolved into nothing. For no agent strives to resolve simply to resolve, but to increase or propagate itself. That can only happen from something and into something. Furthermore, if matter were reduced to nothing, it would certainly be established that matter from the beginning had necessity from no preceding subject from which it was made, since thus no other...

<summary>This page outlines the hierarchy of providence—from the universal reach of the Three Principles to the particular care of human souls—and refutes the Gnostic claim that the world was created through a "fall" or a sudden onset of evil, arguing instead for the world's eternal and necessary existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s defense of the physical world’s creation, refuting the Gnostic belief that the world was created by a "fallen" or "ignorant" deity. He uses the philosophy of Plotinus and Porphyry to argue that the universe is a stable, necessary, and beautiful reflection of divine intelligence.</meta>

...when the subject preceded it, just as "none" follows in the end. It exists, therefore, from the beginning by a certain necessity of consequence from a higher and efficient cause. By that same following necessity, it will always exist.

### The Architect of the world made the world not by a downward leaning, but by his own stability.

IIII He again rejects what they <note>The Gnostics, whom Plotinus attacks in this treatise</note> say: that the first soul procreated the world not because it remained in its own dignity, but because it had degenerated. But before I pursue Plotinus's refutations, it is helpful to review the words of Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> on the same subject, from his books titled *The Ways to the Intelligible*. <note>Originally the *Sententiae ad Intelligibilia Ducentes*</note> Thus he says: "No substance in which all things are universal and perfect turns toward generation <note>the process of physical birth and becoming</note> itself. Rather, every perfect substance is led back toward its generating sources, even down to the cosmic body. This cosmic body, since it is indeed perfect, is led back toward the soul—the intellectual soul, I mean—and therefore it moves in a circle. The Soul of the World, however, is lifted up toward the Intellect, and the soul of the whole is raised toward the Principle." He adds a little later: "In particular substances, however, which are capable of falling toward many things, there is a propensity leaning toward generations, and therefore in these, a 'falling away' is said to have occurred; in these, unfaithfulness is condemned. These are contaminated by matter itself, because they can be diverted toward it, even though they are meanwhile able to turn themselves back toward divine things. Therefore, perfection exists as something secondary to the prior things, preserving those same things when they are turned toward better things. A defect also somewhere turns certain prior things toward posterior ones, and by this very diligence it causes a temporary diversion." This is what he says. In these words, he confirms that certain demons or the souls of men create bodies by degenerating from divine things. But the world was established by a certain divine soul that perseveres in divine things. For to produce such a great, beautiful, and lasting work, to lead it without transgression, and to move it with such miraculous reason, is not the power of something that sometimes leans away, but of something always standing firm in the best state, making the structure not just so it *seems* best, but because it is naturally best itself. But if that power is the best, and (as appears from its motion) is tireless, it will never destroy what it has so excellently built out of regret, nor will it cease to preserve it out of exhaustion. Truly, to claim the world was instituted poorly—and to argue from this that the nature of the world is evil and its author is evil—belongs to men who are either wicked or utterly ignorant. It is also a mistake to think that that power requires deliberation in order to act. For if it was in its very nature to give birth, it required no deliberation at all for this. If it were a task requiring effort, then that power was not naturally sufficient for the effect of generation. Therefore, no nature and no power could generate or make anything by itself.

### Neither is the soul corporeal, nor was the world established by an evil principle.

V He furthermore refutes what they said: that the architect of the world (the soul by which the world lives and moves) was compacted from the elements of the world, and that it is corporeal, irrational, and mortal. First of all, it is a sacrilege to believe the universe has a soul inferior to a human soul; secondly, it is impossible for the soul to be composed of elements as if they were prior to it, since the soul, as the unifying power of conflicting things, must be prior, simpler, and more constant. Finally, a nature compacted from elements produces nothing except what is corporeal, nor does it reflect upon itself. Let it also be added that they think they will be happy when they enjoy the "Model" <term>the Archetype or the World of Ideas</term> of the world, yet they are not afraid to detest the Maker here who was established according to such a model—especially since they say the Architect of the world first thought of the world's model only when he turned himself toward worse things. They added that the structure of this world was for the purpose of guarding souls, which was an attempt made in vain. But regarding the care they thought he has for us: did he have this care before the world, or did he begin to care after the world was made? If before, he cared in vain (as they say) if he could soon lose that care. Then perhaps he received the disposition of the world from the "species" <term>the ideal form or appearance</term> of the world itself, by separating it from matter or from souls. But if he perceived the condition of caring from the species of the world itself, the soul could similarly have perceived it through itself; if he got it from souls, it is quite ridiculous—indeed, both are ridiculous. Furthermore, regarding the souls being restrained, he touches upon an opinion which you may find in the third book of Origen <note>A 3rd-century Christian theologian who theorized that God created all souls equal and they "fell" into bodies based on their choices</note>: namely, that all spirits were equal from the beginning, but because of diverse movements of the will (either turning toward God or away from Him), they then received various degrees of spirit, and the bodies of the world were established in various degrees, and finally the subject spirits were assigned to bodies. The error of this opinion is proven by the fact that this distinction of the world, consisting in the very distinction of degrees, is highly formal and final <term>final: relating to the ultimate purpose or "Final Cause"</term> and is the best thing in the universe—and thus is rightly the first thing in the intention of such principles. Therefore, it does not happen because of a diversity of merits; especially since if rational natures were equal from the beginning, one would not depend on another. Thus, the conversion of various wills would have happened by chance; therefore, the order both in spirits and in the world would be accidental. Likewise, since special differences and species are natural and essential in rational things, it is a sacrilege to say they are accidental in higher beings. They would be accidental if they did not exist from the beginning, but happened later through free movements of the wills. Moreover, it is very difficult to assign spirits that were so equal to such diverse movements. For if they were "naked" before the moment of willing, they were surely distinct through the division of quantity, and not yet differing by any accident. Therefore, they differed from each other through certain formal and essential things, insofar as something was in one that was not in the other. Such a distinction cannot exist without a diversity of degrees, since it is reduced to privation and form. Therefore, before the variety of the many, there was a variety of natural things. But we will discuss these things more opportunely elsewhere.

### The Maker of the world is the First Intellect acting through the soul; likewise, there are three principles: the Good, the Mind, and the Soul. Also, the First Intellect and the First Intelligible are the same.

VI There was an ancient opinion that forms result in matter from a certain impression made by divine forms, while matter reflects the influx of the Ideas like a mirror; and therefore, instead of the true forms of the Ideas, it reports or renders or simulates things that are merely "like the truth" <note>original: "verisimiles," referring to images or likenesses rather than the things themselves</note>. Thus, they say souls are deceived once they have fallen from the supernal world, until they are finally moved by repentance to return to their fatherland from this "colony" or "exile." The heretics, usurping this ancient opinion, often obscured these passions of the soul with the names of certain substances. After this, you will observe that among the ancient Christians, the heretics took the "transcorporation" <term>transcorporatio: the transmigration or reincarnation of souls</term> of souls from the ancients, but I believe they only meant from human to human.

He maintains that the Soul of the World is stable and divine, unlike the fluctuating wills of individual souls.</summary>

Ficino aligns Plotinus’s thought with that of the "Hebrew doctors" and Plato’s *Timaeus* to defend the dignity of the physical cosmos.</meta>

# ON BOOK VIII OF THE SECOND ENNEAD

...whether earthly or airy, he did not, however, believe that the souls of men were transferred into beasts. Indeed, it is said that the <term>doctors of the Hebrews</term> <note>Referring to Jewish scholars or Kabbalists whom Ficino often synchronized with Platonic thought</note> accepted this as well. Regarding the words on the "craftsmanship of the world," Plotinus indicates he perceived this: since they take three words from the <term>*Timaeus*</term> <note>Plato's dialogue on the creation of the universe</note> as three substances, which nevertheless signify three properties of the same substance according to Plotinus. Specifically, that God himself, the craftsman of the world, "conceived"—that is, decreed—and by naturally decreeing, he brought it to pass, so that the species of things in the world, as many as there are in the intellect itself, might be in that very "living being"—that is, he would contemplate the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes of all things</note> in his own living essence. 

And the heretics <note>The Gnostics</note> used to say that the "Living Being" itself is the intelligible being itself, the first spirit-intellect of all. But they say that he who contemplates the Ideas in that being is the "first intellect" in a formal sense; while he who conceived of making the world is the "first soul," and they claim she did this with a certain "bad counsel," or "evilly," namely after she had degenerated from the heights. 

Plotinus, however, will prove that the "first Intelligible" and the "first Intellect" are the same. If the first Intellect understands its own perfect things in a perfect way, it holds the "Intelligible" <note>The object of thought</note> within itself. Therefore, he is understood by himself, just as if he were the Intelligible itself, just as he is the Intellect. Likewise, because the first and perfect Intelligible must be understood in a perfect way, it is understood by a perfect reason if it is understood by itself. Therefore, whether the "species" <note>The forms or types</note> follows the intellect, the intimate Intelligible follows immediately; or if the Intelligible is three-fold, the intimate Intellect immediately accompanies it. And rightly so, since there is a far greater proportion of the Intelligible to the Intellect and to life than there is of the visible to the sight. For the Intellect penetrates, touches, and defines the very thing to be understood—something which no sense achieves regarding a sensible thing. Since, therefore, there is this proportion between the Intelligible and the Intellect, it follows that because the power of this Intelligible reaches a point of being the "highest Intelligible," it likewise follows that it is the "highest Intellect," and vice versa. 

Plotinus thinks this is the primary architect of the world; yet he does not wish to exclude the "First Soul" from the duty of the craftsman, but he denies that she makes the world by "counsel" or leads it with "anxiety." Otherwise, neither the substance of the worldly work could stand, nor its order endure, if it were made and moved by some shifting, and especially laborious, action of a craftsman. He detests even more the claim that they say the "architect soul" is void of mind, subject to disturbance, and worse than our own souls; whereas in this craftsmanship, nothing is done ignorantly, and nothing appears disturbed. Accordingly, he distributes their order in this manner: 

The most absolute unity or simplicity of God so far surpasses all things that he has no relation to anything, either by likeness or respect. Therefore, he does not affect this thing before that; certainly, he either effects nothing, or all things at once. But indeed, the highest goodness rightly effects all things above all else; the highest unity immediately effects "the One." What, then, flows most closely from that—namely, from the Unity that is above all things? Surely it is the "One-All": that is, one Being that is all beings; this is the Intelligible itself, which is all intelligible things. This is the First Intellect, which, since it is all intellect—I say, absolute intellect—contains all the Ideas. This is the **Intelligible World**, generated by the One who is above all things: the "One-All" generated by the "One." From here is born the First Soul, now "One and All," which in a certain way movingly unfolds the whole things which the First Intellect holds stably. Indeed, then the world exists from the Intellect through the Soul, not so much as "One and All," but as "One out of All." Truly, both in the Mind and in the Soul, their own unity precedes the multitude. But in the corporeal world, the unity of forms follows the multitude in a certain way. 

You can, however, collect it thus: all the members and natures of the world belong to the one nature of the World Soul; all individual souls belong to the one World Soul as their leader; and all the intellects that are in those souls belong to the one Intellect existing above the souls, like eyes toward the light of the sun. Finally, the pure Intellect looks toward the paternal light and goodness. <note>original: "bar exfernalis"</note> Though many people posit that intellects are entirely separate from bodies, Plotinus places intellects only in souls, which he calls "animal intellects" and "intellectual souls." These intellects can surely be judged as free from bodies because, although they are in souls, they are nevertheless not in bodies; for while souls are in bodies, intellects of this kind have no commerce with the body. As Plotinus often confirms, according to him, they are always joined with the Divine Mind. The opinion of the Christian theologians among the Greeks <note>The Eastern Church Fathers</note> seems to hardly differ from this view, even though they attribute bodies to angels. 

But where Plotinus allows for multiplication to a great degree in lower things, he forbids introducing a similar multiplication in higher things. Understand that multiplication is forbidden there which occurs through tiny and, as it were, superfluous divisions, as usually happens among us; but not that which occurs into species or necessary things, or is gathered summarily into one. He specifically forbids multiplying the "principles" and "heads" of things. That he wishes there to be many intellects, he shows where he says that intellects are the highest parts of rational souls, and that the souls themselves differ from one another in their passions and nature.

->The World Soul binds its own body to itself, and through this, it binds other souls. Likewise, how the individual soul also gives life to the body.<-

VII. He rejects again the claim that the soul who is the "mother of the world" labors in this construction in the manner of our own soul, and is distracted by it from the duty of contemplation. For he says: Since the whole machine is subject to the World Soul, nothing there resists it, nothing of its own flows away, and nothing foreign happens to it. Likewise, the entire mass of bodies is both bound together and devoted to the soul by the life infused from the soul itself, and is entirely subordinate. Our soul, however, approaches the body as a certain member of the world so far, and as something already living in the lap of the entire soul, so closely connected to it as a fetus in the womb. Thus, the soul coming from without is "bound" to a living being that is, as it were, already made, and does not rule it completely. 

But the World Soul generates the living being for herself, and binds it to herself rather than herself to it; therefore, she never suffers along with the passions of the living being. For that which is connected as the "inferior" to the "superior" usually suffers if the superior suffers, but it does not happen the other way around. But remember, although our soul vivifies the body as something living, nothing prevents it from also applying life to the body as "light to light." For here, the prior life is easily drawn to the act and property of the life coming after; for this is placed in its own body, and if compared to the other, it seems to have the relation of a substantial thing to an accidental one. He finally concludes that the universe is well-disposed everywhere, led toward the common good. If any inconvenience happens to certain parts in the meantime, it occurs because, by their own weakness, they cannot rightly follow the order of the whole, or sustain its force, or avoid it. 

I have observed, however, that in Plotinus's comparison, the "intellectual soul" can both escape the fatal order itself (since it hangs from a higher principle) and also willingly and diligently obey this order; and finally, it can conform this body committed to it with the order so that it may sometimes avoid inconveniences.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s refutation of Gnostic doctrines, specifically addressing the motivations of the "Craftsman of the World" (the Demiurge) and defending the goodness of the physical universe against the claim that it was created due to a "fall" or "bad counsel."</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

->*The craftsman of the world made the world as a statue of God, not through a change in himself, but through the abundance of natural power.*<-

## VIII
When the heretics <note>Referring to the Gnostics, a group of early mystical thinkers whom Plotinus and Ficino both opposed</note> are asked why the craftsman of the world constructed the universe, they respond: because he fell from contemplation, and, as if driven by ambition, turned himself toward action and command. However, it would have been better to assign this to a natural fertility rather than to a perversity of will, and thus to answer those questioning: Just as heat, by the very nature of being heat, naturally warms, and light, by being light, naturally illuminates and similarly gives life, so does that most powerful agent act by the presence of his natural power. Indeed, it seems entirely contrary to all religion and philosophy, as the heretics used to say, that the maker of the world was first formally changed within himself in order to make the world, or that the exercise of his powers—which is eternal, or rather, is the same thing as eternity itself—had a beginning at some point, namely when that maker became weaker due to a fall from better things.

It is also against religion to revile the world as if it were evil. For even in <term>Genesis</term> <note>The first book of the Hebrew Bible</note>, Moses says that the craftsman of the world made both the individual things in the world good, and the whole together "very good." To this also belongs that saying: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands* <note>original: "Coeli enarrant gloriam Dei, & opera manuum eius annuntiat firmamentũ." A quote from Psalm 19:1.</note>. Thus, the magnitude, power, and character of the universe show us the wonderful power of the divinity; the order preserved—especially in such a great variety of things—shows a miraculous wisdom; and its use, leading everywhere to the best end, declares a provident goodness. I say power, wisdom, and goodness, not only as it exists in the craftsman, but as it has also been communicated to the craft; otherwise, we could not judge such things about the craftsman by contemplating his work. 

Indeed, it would be far better, in the manner of <term>Plato</term>, to honor this universe as a "statue of God," and to regard the more excellent things within it as more certain "statues of the <term>Ideas</term>" <note>The perfect, eternal archetypes of all things</note>, rather than to revile it in the manner of the heretics. The Platonists judge it an act of impiety to cast down—let alone to accuse—the living statues of God fabricated by Him and placed in the worldly temple to demonstrate legitimate worship to everyone. For we should not neglect the meaning of that verse: *He placed his tabernacle in the sun* <note>original: "In sole posuit tabernaculum suum." From Psalm 19:4.</note>. Therefore, the world does not only imitate the divine mind in a dissimilar way, as the heretics claim, but it also imitates it in a similar way. "Dissimilar imitation" is understood where things are compared by opposition: those divine things are immaterial, indivisible, and immobile, while this world in turn is material, divisible, and mobile. Therefore, just as that is good, so this would be evil. 

But there is, moreover, a certain "similar imitation" in the world toward the divine mind, which represents to us His essence, life, intelligence, Ideas, and even Unity itself and Goodness through His work. Therefore, this world is also good, as it is an imitation of the Good. Plotinus believes that this world emanates from there by a certain natural and most exuberant overflowing of that Goodness, which a cause cannot fail to match. After this, he argues that the Earth is full of immortal animals <note>Ficino uses "animals" in the sense of "living beings" or "souls"</note>. Similarly, the spaces all the way to heaven, and much more so heaven itself. There are mortal living beings on earth; beyond the earth itself, there are at least souls like ours, and in the celestial bodies, there are souls joined to bodies. 

Furthermore, he maintains that the <term>Orphics</term> <note>Followers of the mystical teachings attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus</note> introduce even terrestrial <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, these are intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense</note>. There are immortal daemons in the air as well as in the ether, at least as far as their celestial body is concerned. In the higher circuits of the heavens, there are such divine beings, which are living beings in themselves, namely the stars. There are also those who place daemons in the spheres of the planets, beyond the planets themselves, so that they are subject to the planets just as stars; just as in the <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>, the smaller stars are ruled by the larger ones. I pass over the fact that there are all the Ideas, which they are accustomed to call "intelligible living beings." Finally, we have treated, and will treat elsewhere, in Theology how any intellectual substance can be everywhere in a similar way. 

But if anyone seeks to convince <unclear>donnanum</unclear> and even that the souls of daemons can at some point lay down their celestial vehicle—from which it would follow that a living being of that kind is not immortal—we say first that this is not easily admitted. Then, if it were admitted, the laying down of such a body should not properly be called death, because it would happen neither by a fatal nature, nor by force, nor by violence brought from without or within, but by a certain easy laying down, as if by vow and will. Finally, if they concede that earthly things live (though perhaps they deny that celestial things live), let them hear <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A student of Aristotle and successor in the Peripatetic school</note> saying that he is no philosopher who denies that the celestial bodies live. If indeed the celestial bodies enjoy reason—as they always proceed by a wonderful reason—let these heretics realize that they themselves are sometimes devoid of either eyes or reason. If they deny that the world is from a good author, the world itself cries out against them twice over: "While I constantly provoke you by my order to divine wisdom and life, my happiness depends upon the divinity."

->*The errors of the Gnostics are no less opposed to Christians than to Platonists.*<-

## IX
In the following parts, while he refutes the foolish accusations of the heretics against the world, notice that there are three primary levels in the world. In the first is placed the sphere of the stars and their movers. In the second, the spheres of the planets. In the third, the sublunary things <note>The realm of the four elements below the moon, including Earth</note>. Yet, because of the good distinction of each level, the world is beautiful. Similarly, there are three levels of human life: there are divine men, there are human men, and there are, in a way, brutish men. Similarly, a diversity of reason appears even in a most rightly constituted city. Remember that in such distinction and order lies the beauty of both life and the city. 

You will note, meanwhile, that the celestial gods provide for each of the lower things, and that there are many good daemons under the moon who wish well to men. He acknowledges, however, that some daemons are evil. Furthermore, there was such foolish arrogance in the Gnostic heretics that they said no kind of virtue could exist except in those who submitted themselves to that same heresy; likewise, they claimed that all daemons and angels are evil, and that the rulers of the celestial spheres are wicked, as is the very life of the whole world. Finally, they claimed that no divinity anywhere was to be honored or acknowledged in any way, but only the First [God] should be prayed to without a mediator. And for the purpose of obtaining what is asked, they claimed the mere profession of their heresy and certain words and rituals were sufficient, and that an exact purity of life and morals was not necessary for this. Finally, they judged that even the worst follower of their heresy should be considered better than the entire universe. 

Thus, it is no wonder that Plotinus here is even more sharply indignant. You will note, finally, that just as the greatest power of the sun shines out to us if we are convinced that most things are "solar"—that is, the lights of all things everywhere—so also the power of God shines if from the One many things are made and depend on Him. After this, he says that God inspires men with things that please both the superior God and themselves. Take "God" here to mean the souls of the stars, as well as the good daemons. For the souls of the stars, which are governed by the decrees of the Mind of the World-Soul and the Divine Mind, inspire the daemons as well as us. 

But you, while Plotinus inveighs more broadly against the heretics, remember that neither the legitimate Christian kind is being touched upon here, nor the person of Christ himself. For the errors of the Gnostics are no less alien to Christ than they are to the Platonists. And indeed, if <term>Porphyry</term> <note>A student of Plotinus who famously wrote "Against the Christians"</note>, who took up the cause against the Christians, judged Christ to be wise, pious, and blessed according to the confirming oracles, then Plotinus, who acts only against certain heretics, rightly judges that Christ should be excluded from these curses. Nor does he unjustly pursue those who asserted the world...

He distinguishes between the radical Gnostics and "legitimate" Christians, noting that even the anti-Christian Porphyry respected Christ's personal piety.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II, specifically the eighth and ninth books, where he systematically dismantles the doctrines of the Gnostics. The previous page discussed the "Craftsman" (the Demiurge) creating the world out of natural abundance rather than a "fall" or mistake.</meta>

<page-num>197</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK VIII OF ENNEAD II.</header>

...that the world is evil by nature and comes from an evil source. They claim that our souls are better than the souls of the world and even become better than the angels—and this, indeed, without any labor or duty of purification, but solely by the confession of that heresy <note>The Gnostics believed salvation came through "Gnosis" or secret knowledge/confession rather than through moral works or traditional religious practice</note>, certain rituals, and a specific pronunciation of words; they say it is not permitted for anyone to become good in any other way. Finally, they claim that God himself cares only for the human race, and that there is no divine providence at all for the rest of the world and worldly things. 

These claims are no less opposed to the Christian law than they are to the Platonists. For on this point you may hear Paul [the Apostle] writing to the Romans, where he says that God is one, and not for one group only but for all, including the Gentiles; or you may recognize from the Gospel that God provides for the whole universe down to the smallest things. Likewise, the Prophets are confirmed when they say that all can be called "gods" and "children of the Most High" <note>original: "dii, et filii excelsi omnes," a reference to Psalm 82:6</note>. Lastly, the Prophet places angels above living creatures. Their arrogance is the greatest of all. God is to be adored in spirit and truth alone; favor is to be earned through purity of character alone. Indeed, this is achieved with much less labor.

### Confirmation of the above.

XII. In the twelfth chapter, you will again see more clearly that it is not the Christian law that is being rejected in any part, but the superstitious heresy of the **Gnostics** <term>Gnostics</term> <note>A diverse group of early mystical thinkers who generally viewed the physical world as a prison created by a lesser, often ignorant deity</note>, who rely on the false books of **Zoroaster**, professing the height of philosophy while arrogantly placing themselves above **Plato** in wisdom. Many practitioners of philosophy—even those quite <unclear>eloquent</unclear>—were deceived by them, as were all those close to Plotinus before they became his intimate associates. 

But what they say (where they also cling to that most foolish point) is that they call the "Wisdom" and the "Soul" the "desire of the craftsman of the world": Wisdom, insofar as it lived before intellect; Soul, insofar as it is inclined toward the work of building. Furthermore, they debate which of its powers first declined toward the construction of the world. They add that the rest of the souls subsequently descended into bodies then, as if bound to this by a fatal law, and at the same time assigned "members of wisdom" (that is, **demons** <note>In the Platonic sense, "daimones" are intermediary spirits between humans and gods, not necessarily evil</note>) to the bodies. Then, they say the craftsman infused something imagined into matter, and thereafter from this material-imaginary power of the image, other various results followed, as if further removed from substance—and perhaps yet another, until the very edge of the world. All this is shown to be entirely vain.

### Life which depends on the soul in the body is immortal, as it is an act of the soul.

XIII. You will observe in the thirteenth chapter that the irrational life which depends on the rational substance (like its image and act) is in no way sustained by matter; nor does it become a quality of any subject or exist solely from the soul as if merely flashing out—like a visual ray from the eye of an animal that sees at night. Even if it does not happen to be extinguished, it sometimes happens not to flash out, or it flashes out while depending solely on the eye.

### In the intention of nature itself, the whole is prior to the parts of the work, and the whole is begun at once.

XIIII. In the fourteenth chapter you will note that, since nature acts through form, and acts with the total force of the whole form to propagate the whole entirely, the form of the whole and the integral parts are primary in the natural intention of the agent. Thus, the whole is begun from the bottom in all parts at once, as it were, by a vigor acting from within. In this way, the species of plants and animals are begun; in this way, from the divine cause, the entire world flowed out at once.

### The heavens are indeed hot and they warm things, yet they do not live, nor are they absent.

XV. In the fifteenth chapter, remember that the heavens are hot and they warm things, but they do not "live" in the way the heretics added. If in every living body heat is born together with innate life, the body certainly first lives and first grows hot. And by warming everything together, it happens that while it increases and nourishes all things, it burns nothing. That it warms not by motion alone but by nature is clear: because it warms by rays diffused through all things without motion. And if it were restricted to the collision of many rays upon themselves, it would warm nothing more vehemently; nor does it naturally burn, <unclear>however much</unclear> it might be moved, so that it would suddenly consume everything else by the speed of its motion. 

As for fires being kindled on high, this does not come from the heat of the heavens but perhaps from the narrowness of that air. In that place, heat—at first gently kindled from the heat and motion of the heavens—becomes a little sharper due to the narrowness of the location. When a subtle, dry, and sulfurous vapor applies itself to this, the heat becomes far more vehement in the vapor. There, the heat is also intensified by the motion shaking the vapor. Nevertheless, there is still more light there than heat. Lightning, however, is sent down from a lower seat for a more violent cause. 

After this, you will note that since the celestial nature generates, vivifies, and preserves all things, it is naturally good. Furthermore, those things which are judged within it occur for the sake of significance. God and those things which occur among us under the common influence of the celestial bodies are made different from one another—partly because of differences in the flow, and partly because of the various fortunes affecting individuals. Various, I say, as they pertain to the seasons of the year, locations, and the diverse dispositions of minds. Therefore, these differences do not exist because of the heavens, but rather what is given from the heavens by a common influence is received differently because of these factors. 

Moreover, it is a sin to disparage as "evil" the grades of goods proceeding from greater to lesser through the very breadth of the Good, and thus to reject the nature of the universe itself. It is also ridiculous to introduce a "principle of malice" simply because something evil occasionally creeps in while things proceed in order—as if there were an "efficient" cause of evils rather than a "deficient" one <note>A classic Platonic and Augustinian argument: evil is not a positive "thing" (efficient cause) but a lack or failure of good (deficient cause)</note>, or as if they accompanied a purpose rather than happening by chance. 

While certain forms are generated by the intention of nature proceeding from the very principle of things (and therefore they are made good), other forms consequently give way, which appears to be "evil." Since, therefore, by the same motion by which good is made through itself, evil also happens by accident, no one ought to punish certain contrary principles because of the difference between goods and evils, nor introduce an evil principle alongside the good principle—and much less a principle that is evil by its first nature and essence. Otherwise, that which is evil by essence would be desired as if it were good, and its opposite would be rejected as if it were evil. Furthermore, a principle acts upon what follows it insofar as it is effective and in act, and it acts through form. These things are good. Therefore, that principle is not evil; nor does it make evil things through itself, but things similar to itself (that is, formal things), and therefore good things. Evil, however, pertains to the **privation of form** <note>Evil is defined here as the absence or loss of the proper "shape" or "form" of a thing</note>, which happens but is not intended. Through these arguments, therefore, the error of both the Gnostics and the **Manichaeans** <note>Followers of Mani, who believed in two equal and opposing powers of Good and Evil</note> is refuted.

### Prayer does not change the adored God or the divinity, but the one who adores.

XVI. The sixteenth chapter mocks the heretics because they think that the celestial bodies—and the souls of the heavens, the divinities superior to the heavens—can be turned from their state by human words and rituals. Likewise, they think all the power of prayer is in the melodies of voices and...
