<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Ennead II, Book 9, titled "Against the Gnostics." Ficino is contrasting Gnostic views on the world and the soul with both Platonic philosophy and Christian theology.</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...with odors and symbols. Furthermore, [he notes] that they [the Gnostics] believe all diseases are nothing other than demons <note>The Gnostics often attributed physical illness to demonic possession rather than natural causes.</note>. But Gospel doctrine commands that God be adored in spirit and truth; it does not wish for God to be changed, but for the person adoring Him to be changed. Moreover, He heals many who are sick but not possessed by a demon.

### Not ritual worship, but virtue obtains a divine gift from God.

**XVII** The gift proper to providence shines forth in the excellent arrangement of the universe and in the perfect state of the world’s Creator. The heretics foolishly took all this away when they accused the Lord and Author of providence by finding fault with the world's arrangement. Now, in order to convince people that there is nothing good in the world, they claimed that no laws of nature or of goodness were truly good. They said that what are called "virtues" are nothing, and they themselves spoke nothing of virtues, nor did they have any understanding of the purification of souls. For they preached that if anyone merely thought of God and invoked Him with specific prayers, they would obtain everything—even if they did not expel the disturbances of the senses. Certainly, nothing is more foreign to Gospel doctrine than this. For "not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord,'" and what follows <note>original: "Domine domine"; a reference to Matthew 7:21: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father."</note>. Remember, however, what he says: "Absolute virtue reveals God to us." Just as the perception of fire's heat, when brought to its peak, immediately fills matter with light and makes it fire; so too the imitation of God through virtue eventually makes the soul divine and a "god"; and the soul, by seeing itself in this way, also sees God.

### Platonists more easily accept Christian dogmas than those of the Gnostics.

**XVIII** Suppose Plotinus had heard from the Greek Christians—especially from John of Damascus <note>Ficino likely refers to the synthesized angelology found in the works of John of Damascus or Pseudo-Dionysius.</note>—that a certain final order of angels fell away from God and were afterwards enclosed in bodies made of thicker air; he would not reject this, but would adapt it to Plato's views. Indeed, Egidio of Rome <note>original: "Romanus Egidius," a 13th-century Augustinian theologian.</note> teaches that this does not contradict Christian law. However, Plotinus cannot help but be sharply indignant when he hears that the whole world was created as "worst" by some "worst angel" <note>The Gnostic "Demiurge," whom they often viewed as a bumbling or evil lesser deity.</note>. Likewise, he is indignant that the heretics claim to be most welcome to the divinities above the heavens, while they detest the celestial rulers—who depend upon those higher divinities and are most like them—as if they were evil. They curse the whole world, which is arranged in a most divine order, as something evil; and they preach that God cares only for the human race, but does not even look upon the whole world in which man exists and to whose order human affairs are connected. These claims are so ridiculous that they are sufficiently refuted by their own absurdity.

### On the animate world, demons, beauty, and how beauty proceeds from goodness and is a sign of goodness.

<margin>On the animate world</margin>
**XIX** Separate the soul, if you can, from worldly dimension and matter; leave the rest, and you will have an "intelligible sphere"—that is, one that is animate and manifold. In this sphere, the first soul corresponding to the universe will be greater than the second power of the orb. Successive orbs are, as it were, narrower in power; the remaining intellectual souls in their order are able to embrace others, just as in the visible world one orb embraces another. But in the "animate world," because no physical dimension pulls things apart, the whole is found everywhere within any part. There is movement and rotation there, of the kind suited to the souls of the intellects, but dimension exists not in act, but in a certain potentiality very close to act. For from the power of the soul, a bodily species is immediately produced, requiring from the soul a certain quantity and shape in matter. And as far as the soul's proceeding power extends itself, so far is physical quantity extended in the body according to its strength.

Truly, if anyone inspects the internal motion of the soul, he will see both a formal diversity there and, because of the motion, a temporal interval from one act to another. In this diversity, in this interval of the soul’s circuit, one will begin to suspect the dimension of the future body and its orbs, just as one suspects a continuous circle from the frequent vibration of a spark. That universe is a spherical living being: stable in its intellectual faculties, like centers, but mobile in its subsequent powers. From the vigor of that state and motion, the corporeal world is made, and it stands and moves. From its clear and wonderful beauty, Plotinus teaches that its natural and internal goodness exists; and from these two, one can infer the beauty and goodness of the soul.

Therefore, when he says that demons can be perceived and are most beautiful: understand that they can be perceived just as we said in the book *On Beauty*. Furthermore, they are most beautiful, whom Basil the Great <note>A 4th-century Church Father who wrote on the Holy Spirit and the Hexameron.</note> calls "good demons" or angels, having bodies partly of fire and partly of air, most bright and beautiful; as Daniel indicated by saying the angels of God are ministers of spirit and flame <note>A reference to Psalm 104:4, often cited in angelic descriptions.</note>. Thus Basil thinks Angels can change their appearances, and can rest, enter, and offer themselves to the senses without deception. Finally, Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and demonologist.</note> asserts this was the opinion of the Apostle Paul. In this way, whether you prefer to call them "good demons" or "angels," they are beneficial divinities in bodies, worthy of some honor and worship, according to the opinion of both Platonists and Christians, and contrary to the opinion of the Gnostics. For the Gnostics remove beneficial divinities from the world, subvert the order of the universe, and deprive themselves of the mediators through whom they could conveniently be served by the highest beings.

In summary, whatever things are truly beautiful on the outside come from things that are naturally good within; for external beauty arises from the internal perfection of form and the victory of the "seminal reason" <note>The Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of 'logoi spermatikoi', the formative principles that organize matter.</note> over matter. But if the internal species is lacking, then the thing itself is diminished in its better parts—that is, the internal ones—and it falls short of the better things that are higher in rank. It is not absolutely beautiful, but mutilated in its beauty. Hence Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and biographer.</note> says that demons whose souls are wicked also have deformed bodies; but those whose souls are upright have beautiful bodies. And Origen <note>An early Christian theologian who attempted to synthesize Platonism and Christianity.</note> argues from the light of the celestial order that spirits are present in them that are closer to God, bright and capable of intelligence; and together with the Apostle Paul, he includes spirits that degenerate far from God as being enclosed in bodies composed of dark air.

Certainly, if the body depends on the soul, then a certain disposition of the body arises from a certain affection of the soul—whether natural, or contracted through habit, or conceived through a prompt inclination. This is especially true when the foundations of the body are given and as long as it grows. Therefore, a beautiful body is a sign of a beautiful soul—that is, one that is thoroughly harmonious, shining, and entirely well-composed and healthy, as much in regards to thought and imagination as to affection and seminal nature. A base or ugly body is a sign of a disordered soul, one that has already fallen into a discordant habit or affection. Since the world is most beautiful, the Soul of the World is simultaneously most beautiful and best; and likewise the souls of all the spheres and stars. Among us, it can perhaps happen, though rarely, that a soul that is currently not beautiful resides in a beautiful body, because a soul that was beautiful at the very beginning of conception later gradually became deformed.

<summary>Ficino argues against the Gnostics by asserting that physical beauty is an outward sign of internal moral goodness and divine order. He aligns Platonic thought with Christian authorities like Basil and Origen to defend the world's inherent goodness and the existence of beneficial angelic mediators.</summary>

Since, therefore, the nature of the Good itself has appeared to us as the primary nature—for everything that is primary is not composite, nor does it have anything within itself, but is a certain "One"—this nature is either called "the forms" or something else, or else the "being" here is one thing and the "good" is another. When we speak of "being" and when we speak of "the Good," we should then consider that nature to be one and the same. Nothing is separated from it, for it reveals itself to us as far as possible as the primary "One" in a secondary way, because it is simply One. And it is self-sufficient, since it is not <margin>clearly</margin> of another and not from another, because everything that exists is either in another or from another. If, then, it is neither from another nor in another, and there is no multiplicity in it, it is necessary that nothing exists above it. And from certain things it must go toward other <margin>prophesy</margin> souls, but these are joined to itself, whether it be the Intellect after it (and the act of thinking primarily), or the Soul after the Intellect. For this is the order according to nature: that neither more than these nor fewer should be placed in the intelligible realm. For if they place fewer, they will say either that the Soul and the Intellect are the same, or the Intellect and the First. But that they are different from one another has been shown in many ways. It remains...

<column-break/>

<margin>There are only three: the Good itself, Intellect, and Soul.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'Q' featuring a seated figure amidst classical architectural and floral motifs.</image-desc>
<margin>A</margin> SINCE from other discussions it is established for us that the nature of the Good itself is simple and first—for unless it were first, it could not be simple—it consists in itself, having nothing [added], but is only "the One." And the nature of that which is called "the One" is the same. For this is not first one thing and then "One" additionally; nor is <margin>B</margin> the Good itself one thing and then "Good" besides. Since, I say, it is so, certainly when we say "the One" and when we say "the Good," it must be understood that we mean one and the same nature. We do not predicate anything of it at all, but rather we designate it to ourselves as best we can. And it is called "First" because it is the most simple; likewise, it is self-sufficient because it does not consist of many parts; otherwise, it would be traced back to those things from which it is composed. Again, it is not in another, because <margin>C</margin> whatever is in another is also from another. Therefore, if it is neither from another nor in another, and there is no composition in it, nothing can be higher than it. For this reason, one must not try to resort to other principles, but with this [The One] established, we must then place the Intellect (or that which primarily understands) and then the Soul after the Intellect. For this is the natural order. Therefore, it is fitting to enumerate neither more nor fewer than these in the intelligible category. Indeed, if fewer were placed, they would say either that the soul and the intellect are entirely the same, but that they are different from each other has often been demonstrated...

Ficino’s commentary emphasizes that while the human soul is "sister" to the World Soul and can escape fate, it remains a distinct intellectual entity.</summary>

Having established that there are only three primary divine levels—the One, the Intellect, and the Soul—Plotinus now argues against the Gnostic idea that the Soul "fell" or created the world through a flawed or complicated process of deliberation.</meta>

### BOOK NINE.

The soul, by the act of thinking, does not see the things being thought, but rather sees the intermediate steps of the Reason <note>original: "λόγου" (Logos). In Neoplatonism, the Logos is the formative principle that bridges the gap between the higher Intellect and the material world.</note>, and an image of that Reason; for the one who possesses Reason and thinks entirely does not think through sensation, or entirely through a single intuition.

**THUS**, one should not devise more unnecessary levels among those divine beings, which they <note>The Gnostics, whom Plotinus is criticizing for multiplying the number of divine "Aeons."</note> do not accept; but when the Intellect thinks, it remains the same and in the same state, unwavering in every way, imitating the Father <note>The "Father" here refers to the One, the absolute source of all existence.</note> as much as possible. Our soul has one part always directed toward those higher things, another part directed toward these earthly things, and a part stationed in the middle. Since there is a single nature with many powers, sometimes the whole soul joins with its best part and the true **Mind** <unclear>mind</unclear>; but when the part dragged down to the lower realm pulls the middle part with it, we would not say that the "whole" soul is there; rather, this suffering happens to the soul because it did not remain in the most beautiful state. Where the soul remains—or does not remain—as we do in part, it has given to the whole body of the world as much as it can receive from the soul without the soul itself becoming troubled. It does not govern through a process of reasoning, nor by making constant corrections, but by <margin>how is it not this</margin> its own **Mind** <unclear>mind</unclear>, it brings order to what is below it through a marvelous power. For the more it stands fixed toward itself, the more beautifully and powerfully all things are maintained, being taught by it and, as if by a radiance, it illuminates but is not itself reflected back.

**ALWAYS**, therefore, being illuminated and possessing a lasting light, it gives to the things that follow; these things are always held together and nourished by that light and enjoy life as much as they are able, just as a fire placed in the center warms whatever can be warmed, and the whole is kept in measure. Since these are powers that are not measured out, nor taken from those that stand firm, how is it possible for them to exist without any of them participating in it? For it is necessary for each thing to give of itself to another; otherwise, the Good would not be good, the Intellect would not be intellect, or the Soul would not be the whole, unless it lived after the primary life. * <margin>from it</margin> Since the first life is primary, it is necessary for all things to exist sequentially for one another, both the things that are generated and the ultimate things. * They exist in relation to each other, and again are generated, but were generated, and are generated—at least those things said to be "generated." Others will be destroyed, but pleasure holds them; and if they are not held forever, they will be destroyed. If someone speaks of matter, why even matter? If he says even matter is generated, what necessity shall we say there was for it to be made? But if we say it follows by necessity, then we say it exists now as well. If it were left alone, or entirely so, then divine things would be restricted to a specific place, and as if locked away. But if it has a kind of <margin>therefore</margin> radiance extending through it.

<column-break/>

**A** If it sits in the middle, it forces the soul to lack intelligence: for if it receives its reason not from the intellect itself, but from some other intermediate thing, it will not possess the reason itself, but a certain image of reason. Ultimately, it would neither know the intellect itself, nor understand anything at all.

<margin>
II
He confirms that higher beings always act, since there is no part of the world's mind that does not have a part in the higher realm.
</margin>
**B** THEREFORE, one should not posit more things in the intelligible world, nor place there superfluous meditations which they do not admit; rather, one should posit one intellect, always behaving in the same way, entirely unwavering, which imitates its father to the best of its ability. Our soul, indeed, lives with one part of itself near those higher things, with another part turning toward these earthly things, and finally with a part placed in the middle. Since there is one nature in many powers, sometimes the whole soul, along with its best part and that of the universe, betakes itself to the higher realms. At other times, however, that which is in the soul's <unclear>whole</unclear> is drawn to lower things, dragging the middle part down with it. Yet it is not permitted for the "whole" of the soul to be cast down anywhere into the lower regions. Such a passion **C** happens to the soul because it did not remain in the "best" of the universe—that state in which the soul exists as something that is not a part, and of which we are not parts either. In that state, the soul granted to the whole body of the world the gifts of receiving power. Meanwhile, the soul itself lives completely free from all anxiety, governing clearly with no deliberation, nor correcting anything with obsessive care; but from its own gaze toward the higher realms, it adorns the whole world with a miraculous power. For the more it fixes its gaze upon its own source, the more beautiful and powerful it becomes, and from there, drawing from the **D** heights, it pours into the lower things; and as if always divinely illuminated, it shines through all things.

<margin>
III
The world proceeds always, not by chance or by a mind from behind without change; and so it is eternal.
</margin>
**E** ALWAYS, therefore, being illuminated and possessing eternal light, it transmits it thereafter to lower things. These lower things are both always contained and made to flourish by this light, and they receive life from it according to their own capacity; just as if they were warmed by a certain fire placed somewhere in the middle, from which whatever can be warmed is warmed—even if the fire is restricted in some measure. But when powers are not restricted by measure, and are not lacking in the universe, by what logic can it be that these powers exist, yet there is nothing anywhere that participates in them? Truly, it is necessary for each thing to bestow something of its own upon the rest. Otherwise, the Good itself will not be good, the intellect itself will not be intellect, and the soul again will not be soul—unless, after that which primarily lives, something else lives consequently as long as the first also lives. For this reason, it is necessary that all things after the first exist consecutively and always, and that they **F** are engaged in a kind of "generation," <note>original: "generatione" (Greek: *genesis*). In this context, Plotinus refers to the continuous flow of existence from the divine source, rather than a single event in time.</note> because they depend on something else. Therefore, they were not made at some specific time, but were being made and will be made—as many things as are said to be in the process of generation. Nor will they be destroyed, except for those things that have something into which they may be dissolved; but that which has nothing into which it may be resolved cannot perish. But if someone says it must be resolved into matter, let him answer why he does not likewise concede that matter is also resolvable. If he further admits matter is resolvable, we will ask: what was the necessity for it to be made? But if they say it was necessary for it to follow consecutively, we will assert **G** that it is similarly necessary now. But if matter were to be left alone, it would follow that divine things are not everywhere, but are in a certain determined place, as if separated by a certain limit. But if that cannot happen, it follows that the world is perpetually illuminated.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the world was not created through a flawed "fall" or stressful deliberation, but flows eternally and effortlessly from the divine Intellect like light from a sun. He asserts that the soul governs the material world simply by looking toward the divine, thereby maintaining the world's beauty and existence forever.</summary>

## PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II.

<margin>IV. He confirms the previous points, proving that the world is not evil, nor did it come from an evil source.</margin>

**A** IF, however, they should say that the soul created the world after having fallen, as if its wings were already broken <note>original: "confractis alis." A reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul loses its "wings" and falls from the divine realm into a physical body.</note>, we would object that the Soul of the World itself cannot suffer such a thing. But if they bring forward the idea that the soul at some point deviated <note>original: "praevaricata." In a legal or moral sense, to step out of line or fail in duty.</note>, they are compelled to explain the cause of this deviation and error. Furthermore, at what time did it go astray? For if it was from eternity, then by the same logic it surely remains in error even now. But if it began at a certain time, one must inquire why it did not go astray before that time. We, however, do not believe that a "downward inclination" of the soul is the creator of the world; rather, it is its very nature, which is not inclined toward falling at all. But if it did incline, surely **B** it did so because it had already forgotten the things that are in that higher realm. And if it has forgotten, by what faculty does it fashion the universe? And from where and how does it make it? Perhaps from those things which it had glimpsed there? But if it makes the world while remembering those things, it has not turned away from them at all; for it does not hold that memory weakly. If it is not further inclined, I will say it clearly: why would it not wish to return immediately, while still **C** retaining the memory of those things? Furthermore, what did it imagine would come to it from the construction of the world? For it is a ridiculous thing to say that it produced the world so that it might be honored—this is the opinion of those who transfer the emotions of our own sculptors to the divine beings. Since even if it acted by thought, and it was not in its nature to act so, yet it still belonged to its power to produce it, in what manner did it produce this world? Furthermore, **D** when will it destroy the world? For if it did so because it repented of its work, what difference does it make? If it has not yet fully repented, it will never be moved by repentance, seeing as it has already grown accustomed to it and has been made more indulgent toward the work by the long passage of time. But if it waits for the souls of individuals, it ought to have long since ceased for souls to enter into <term>generation</term> <note>The process of being born into the physical, changing world.</note> again, specifically those souls not ignorant of the evils they endured in their previous life; for this reason, they should have stopped descending long ago. Therefore, as for their claim that the world was badly established, and that for this reason many adverse things have grown within it, this must not be admitted. For this view is flawed, ascribing more dignity to the world than is proper; let them judge clearly that this world is <term>intelligible</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, the "Intelligible World" is the realm of perfect, eternal Ideas, whereas the visible world is its reflection.</note>, as if **E** this visible one were not its image. Yet truly, what more beautiful image of that realm could have been made? For what other fire could be a better image of the "intelligible fire" than our fire here? Likewise, what other earth besides this one after that higher earth? And what sphere could be more perfect and venerable, or more orderly in its movements, than this one, which contains within itself the structure of the intelligible world? Finally, what other sun could be imagined after that one, beyond this visible sun?

<margin>V. Neither are souls corporeal, nor was the world established from an evil principle.</note>

**F** IT IS altogether absurd that while they themselves have a body—just as other men have—and have desires, pains, and anger, they nevertheless do not make little of their own power, but assert that it is permitted for them to touch the Intelligible itself; yet they claim that in the sun there is no power more removed from passion, even though it stands in a greater order and stability, and they claim it does not possess a wisdom superior to ours—we who were born only recently and are hindered by countless deceptions from attaining the truth. Nor is it fitting to assert that only our soul is immortal and divine, **G** even the souls of the most worthless of men, while claiming that the whole heaven and the stars lack immortality of life, even though they are composed of things far more beautiful and pure...

<column-break/>

**A** IF they say the soul created [the world] as if it had lost its feathers, and the whole suffers those things which they call "slips," let them state the cause of these slips. Where did it slip? For if from eternity, it will remain slipped according to the same reasoning. If it began, why not before? We say it is not a "downward inclination" that creates, but rather a "non-inclination." But if **B** it is by inclination, clearly it is by having departed from the things there and having forgotten them; how then does it create? From where does it make, if not from the things it saw there? But if it makes while remembering those things, it did not incline at all. <margin>*</margin> If it remembers nothing, it remains there. Or rather, the Mind does not imagine, so that it might not see dimly. Why then did it not wish to return at some point, or why does the memory not return now? For what would it have reasoned would happen to itself from **C** the making of the world? For it is laughable [to say] it was so that it might be honored—they are transferring [motives] from the statue-makers here. Since even if thought creates, and it is not in [its] nature to create, and the power is the creating force, how did it create this world, and when will it destroy it? For if it changed its mind, why does it wait? But if it will never change its mind again, has it already become pleased? And with time having become more **D** accustomed [to it]. But if it waits for each soul, it would have been necessary for them to no longer come into generation again, having suffered in the prior generation the evils here. So they would have already departed, knowing what they know. As for those who say this world was made badly because many things in it are **E** difficult: this assumption is greater than is fitting for them, if they assume the world itself is <margin>*</margin> the Intelligible, rather than an image of that. <margin>*</margin> Or what other image could have become more beautiful than that one? How could there be another fire than that one, or from fire, or indeed the bodies... what other earth after the earth there? What sphere more accurate and venerable, or more orderly in its motion, after the one there that contains the intelligible things within itself? What other sun after that one, compared to the things seen? Who?

**F** BUT while they themselves have a body, such as men have, and desires and pains and angers, they do not dishonor their own power, but say it is possible to touch the intelligible things; yet [they say] there is not in the sun a power more passionless, being in a greater order and not in [a state of] change? Or that it does not have a wisdom better than ours, who were just born and are dissolved by so many things that deceive us from coming to the truth? Or to say that their own soul is **G** immortal and divine, even that of the most base men, but the whole heaven and the stars there have no share in immortality, even though they are from many more beautiful and purer things, seeing...

# BOOK NINE.

<margin>God is blameless; the blame lies with the one who chooses. <note>original: "ὁ δὲ θεὸς ἀναίτιος, αἰτία δὲ ἑλομένου." A famous quote from Plato’s *Republic* (617e), used here to argue that the Divine is not responsible for the perceived "evil" in the world; rather, it is a matter of the soul's choice.</note></margin>
**A** In seeing what is avoided, ill-omened, and unbecoming—especially among those who speak of the disorder of the earth and blame it—it is as if the immortal souls chose the worse path on earth by necessity, or as if the better things must retreat. In this way, they speak of a mortal soul having chosen this; but is the cause for the introduction of this second soul not irrational? **B** Do they compose it from the elements? If so, how could such a thing have life? For a composition of elements is either a mixture of them, or it is heat, or cold, or bitterness, or dryness, or moisture, or a blend of these. Furthermore, how can the soul be the bond that holds the fathers together if it was born after them? When they assign to it perception, and "the best," and a thousand other things, what would he himself say? But those who do not honor this craftsmanship, **C** nor even the earth, now say that a "new earth" has been made for them, into which they will go when they depart. But if this world is governed by Reason, why do they hate it and yet wish to live in a "model world" that is patterned after it? When was this model made? According to them, these animals already existed when the Father had already made the model. If, therefore, these things are not the same as the one who made them, **D** there is much concern as to why, after the Intelligible World, he would have the desire to make another world different in form. If it was so that the souls might be guarded, how then were they not protected? How was it that they had to learn something? He who took from the world after the world, receiving from the world’s radiance—as if receiving a spark—did he himself fail to guard those souls that were turned away? Why did he not grant this to the souls, if they deserve the world, or the evil that comes by Reason?

<margin>Transfusion and decanting. <note>original: "μεταγγισμὸς καὶ μετακέντωσις." These are technical terms Plotinus uses to mock the Gnostic view of the soul being "poured" from one body to another like liquid between vessels.</note></margin>
**E** What more should I say of the other substances they introduce, which they call "dwellings," "reflections," and "repentances"? <note>Plotinus is critiquing Gnostic technical terminology: *paroikeseis* (dwellings/sojourns), *antitypiai* (reflections/oppositions), and *metanoia* (repentance).</note> If they say these are passions of the soul when it feels repentance, or "reflections" when it contemplates the images of beings rather than the beings themselves, then this is all empty talk introduced to bolster their own sect. Since they have not grasped the ancient Greek wisdom, **F** they invent these fictions. The ancient Greeks knew these things clearly and described them without pride or arrogance: the ascents from the cave, and the gradual progress more and more toward a truer contemplation. Indeed, it is clear that they have stolen most of their ideas from Plato, and whatever they have "innovated" to establish their own philosophy is found to be far from the truth. For the judgments and the rivers in Hades and the transmigrations from one body to another are all taken from Plato. **G** Likewise, when they posit a multitude in the Intelligible World—namely, Being itself, and then the Intellect, and after these another "Creator"—they have usurped this for themselves from the words of the *Timaeus*. consent: especially since we suspect that whatever is there is most orderly and beautiful, particularly when they themselves complain of the confusion that turns around the earth, as if souls do not choose this place by a lower organ, but choose magic by a studious effort, the mortal soul obeying that more excellent one. Furthermore, there is an absurdity among them regarding the introduction of this other soul, which they think is composed of the elements. For in what way can any composition from elements have any life? For a mixture of these makes either heat or cold, or a mixture of dry or moist, or some composition from these. Furthermore, how is the soul the power connecting the elements, if indeed it exists from them and is posterior to them? Finally, when they add to the soul observation and counsel, and other private sins, who could say by what reason such things can be assigned to the soul? Moreover, since they do not at all venerate this mundane craftsmanship, nor honor this earth, they assert a new earth is reserved for them, into which an ascent may finally be made from here: that this is the very Reason and Model of the world. Truly, why is it worth their effort to dwell there in the model of a world which they hold in hatred? Likewise, from where does this model come? For it shines forth among them only when the one who conceived this model has already declined toward these things of ours. If, therefore, in the creator himself there is much care for the world, namely to produce another world beyond the Intelligible World which he possesses, why was that expedient for him? And if he already cared for it before the world, for whose sake did he decree it? Perhaps so that the souls themselves might be guarded? By what reason, then, were they not guarded? Hence the world was made in vain; but if after the world, taking from the world, as if plundering the species of matter, his skill was sufficient for the guardianship of experienced souls. But since they have not reached the ancient wisdom of the Greeks, they comment on fictions of this kind. Certainly, the ancient Greeks both knew correctly and described without swelling boastfulness the ascents from a certain cave, and the souls proceeding from there little by little into a truer contemplation. ### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD II.

The Intellect beholds the ideas existing within it insofar as it is a "living being," and to that extent, as the architect of the world, it conceives of them as being comprised within the world. <note>original: "vivens est... architectus mundi." Plotinus refers to the *Timaeus*, where Plato describes the Demiurge looking at the "Eternal Living Being" to craft the universe.</note> But they, by no means understanding Plato, imagined a certain deity that contains all things within itself in a kind of quietude; then they imagined another intellect following that one which looks upon what is in the first, and yet another which thinks. Frequently, in their system, that which is said to "think" is the Soul, the artisan of the universe; they think such a thing is the world-maker in Plato's view, entirely failing to understand who the world's maker is, or the reason for its making. Furthermore, they are caught lying in their interpretation of Plato, twisting his opinions for the worse—as if they alone had attained the intelligible nature, while Plato and other blessed men of old were unable to reach it. Then, by the multitude of "intelligible entities" <term>Intelligible entities: the realm of pure thought and forms, beyond the physical senses</term> they name, they confidently hope to appear as if they have reached the summit of the divine, even though this very multiplication actually drags the intelligible nature down into a likeness with the lower, sensible nature.

<margin>B</margin>
It is indeed proper for the intelligible nature to be gathered into as small a number as possible—ideally just three. One should attribute all things to the one that follows the First, and not number the intelligibles further. For that [second] level is all things: the primary Intellect, the primary Essence, and whatever other beautiful things are considered after the First Nature. One should then place the species of "Soul" as the third rank.

<margin>C</margin>
Furthermore, one ought to investigate the differences between souls in terms of their passions or their nature, rather than quibbling with divine men. Instead, one should interpret the mysteries of the ancients with kindness, accepting from them what they say correctly: the immortality of the soul, the intelligible world, and the First God. Likewise, that it is necessary for the soul to flee from commerce with the body, and again, that the separation of the soul from the body is nothing other than the soul turning itself away from the world of "becoming" toward true "essence."

<margin>D</margin>
In these matters treated by Plato, if they say them clearly, they do well. For those who wish to disagree, there is no resentment from those of us speaking; however, it is a sacrilege to confirm one’s own dogmas to listeners by using quibbles and insults against the Greeks. Rather, they ought to demonstrate that their own views are correct—whatever unique things they have found beyond the opinions of the ancients—and they should introduce those opinions with kindness and philosophical integrity. Where they disagree, they should look justly for the truth, and not hunt for popular approval by disparaging those men who have been approved for many centuries by no ordinary people.

<margin>E</margin>
It is altogether ridiculous to claim that they are superior to the ancients. Truly, what was handed down by the ancients regarding the intelligible order is spoken much better and more learnedly; this will be easily recognized by those who have not been deceived by the fallacies currently invading mankind.

<margin>F</margin>
Indeed, in the things these people have received from the ancients, one finds certain additions attached that are in no way fitting; certainly, in those areas where they strive to oppose the ancients, they introduce multiple "generations" and "corruptions." <note>Plotinus is likely criticizing the complex Gnostic mythologies involving the "fall" of Wisdom (Sophia) and the creation of the world by a flawed deity.</note>

<margin>G</margin>
Furthermore, they find fault with this universe and criminalize the soul's association with the body; they blame the very one who arranges the whole, the world...

<column-break/>

[The Intellect] beholds the ideas within the [True] Living Being; and he who makes the whole <term>The Demiurge: the craftsman-god of Plato's *Timaeus*</term> intended the world to contain just as many. But they, not understanding, took one to be not in quietude, possessing all things in himself; and the next as a second intellect beholding the one from itself, and another as the one who thinks. Often for them, the thinking one is the Soul that creates. And according to Plato, they think this is the creator...

<margin>B</margin>
...they have wandered from the truth regarding the creator and the entire manner of creation. They tell many other lies against him, and in this way they drag his opinions toward their own liking. As people who have understood the intelligible nature, they should consider the other blessed men...

<margin>C</margin>

By naming a multitude of intelligibles, they <insert>seem to</insert> think they have discovered exact truth; but by this very multitude, they bring the intelligible nature into a likeness with the sensory and lesser nature. It is necessary to seek as small a number as possible and to attribute all things to that which is after the First, since that First is all things. The first and the essential are not different things after the First Nature; but Soul is the third.

<margin>D</margin>
One should track the movements of souls in their passions or their nature, and not talk nonsense about divine men, but rather receive their works kindly as being from the ancients. Having taken from them what they say well—the immortality of the soul, the world, the First God, and that the soul <insert>and the world</insert> must flee from intimacy with the body—and that the separation from it is a flight from the world of "becoming" into "essence." For these things are wearying...

They should show that their own findings are correct, and when they choose to speak of the opinions of the ancients, they should present those opinions kindly and philosophically. Or if they are easily proven...

# BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

...blaming everything, and reducing the Creator and the Soul to the same status. To the Creator, they attribute the same passions <note>original: "passiones." In ancient philosophy, "passions" refers to being acted upon or suffering, which the Gnostics attributed to the world-maker.</note> which they also attribute to the souls of particular animals. 

It has been stated elsewhere that this world never had a beginning, nor will it ever have an end, but it exists as long as the divine things exist. Furthermore, it has been previously said that the communion of our soul with the body is not for the better of the soul. 

<margin>VIII. How the World Soul rules the world more easily than our soul rules the body.</margin>

But to judge the Soul of the All <term>Soul of the All: The "Anima Mundi," the divine life-force that governs the entire universe</term> by our own is much like a person in a well-ordered city who, observing the status of the potters or the smiths, proceeds to blame the entire city. It is worthwhile to consider how much more differently the World Soul governs; for its mode is not the same, nor does it govern as if it were tied down.

For besides other differences which have been listed elsewhere, one must also consider that we are bound by the body, as if a bond had already been fashioned. But in the universe, the Soul—which has already bound the nature of the body—binds whatever it takes hold of, yet the Soul of the All is by no means bound by the things it binds itself. For it acts as the mistress and provides the starting point; therefore, it is produced neither by them nor with them. We, however, are not the masters of these things. Insofar as the Soul is raised toward the divine which is above it, it remains pure and simple and is not hindered. But insofar as it grants life to the body, it receives nothing back from it. Generally, that which exists in another must necessarily receive the passions <note>original: "passivēm" / "πάθημα." Here meaning the influences or sufferings of the environment.</note> of that in which it resides. But the World Soul does not grant anything further to that which possesses its own life. 

It is as if something alien were inserted: while the host suffers, the insert shares the feeling; but if the host should dry up, the Soul allows it to have its own life. Indeed, if this fire within you is extinguished, the whole fire of the universe is not extinguished; moreover, even if all fire were extinguished, that Soul would not suffer at all, but rather the physical constitution of the body. Even if another world could exist through the remaining elements, there would be no care for it from that Soul, because its constitution is not like that of the world, nor like any individual soul. But there, the Soul stands over it, commanding it to stay consistent, while here, the elements are like things sliding away, which must be brought back into the prior order by a secondary bond. But in the higher realm, they have no place to flee. Therefore, it is not necessary to hold them in from within, nor to push them back to the interior by restraining them from without. Rather, wherever the nature of the thing was strong from the beginning, there the individual parts naturally remain. If any of them should move naturally, those things meanwhile suffer whose natures do not at all suit such a movement. But the things that move by nature are carried rightly, as they are members of the whole. Some things are destroyed here because they cannot sustain or they turn away from the order of the whole. It is as if a great dance <note>original: "chorea." A choreographed group dance, often used as a metaphor for the harmony of the spheres.</note> were performed in order, and in the middle of its path a tortoise <note>original: "testudo" / "χελώνη." Used here as a symbol of something slow or out of place in a fast, divine movement.</note> was caught somewhere and stepped upon, since it could not escape the order of the dance. Yet, if it had joined itself to the order of the dance, it would have suffered nothing from it.

Regarding the question commonly asked—for what reason did he make the world?—it is the same as asking: why is there a Soul? Or why is there a Creator?

<margin>VIII. The world was made not by error, but by the power of nature, because it is similar to the natural divine and is of such a quality.</margin>

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the World Soul governs the cosmos effortlessly and without suffering, unlike the human soul which is "bound" by its body. He uses the metaphor of a choral dance to explain how perceived "evils" or accidents (like a tortoise being stepped on) are simply the result of individual parts being out of sync with the grand, divine order.</summary>

# BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

<margin>
IX
All things are justly dispensed in the world: good names and good things are in it; and they are not achieved without effort.
</margin>

**A** Indeed, the fact that it is possible to acquire wisdom even while in this world, and that those living here can live in the likeness of supernal <note>original: "supernorum," referring to the higher, celestial, or intelligible realms</note> things, undoubtedly testifies that the world depends upon the realm above.

**B** If anyone should complain about the world because of the state of wealth and poverty, criticizing it because an equal distribution does not occur, they are entirely ignorant that the virtuous man <note>original: "probum virum," the Greek "spoudaios," meaning the serious or morally excellent person</note> does not demand equality in these matters. Nor does he believe that those possessing more money have more of what is truly "good," nor does he judge that those in power possess more than private citizens. Instead, he deliberately leaves the pursuit of such things to others. The virtuous man knows that there is a twofold life here: one of the virtuous, and another of the many. The life of the virtuous is raised toward the highest degree and the supreme nature; but the life of those who are more humble is likewise twofold. One part, being mindful of virtue, rightly shares in some good; the other is like a base and 

**C** **mechanical** <term>mechanical: "mechanica," referring to the laboring classes or those focused solely on physical survival and material tasks</term> crowd that provides the necessary things for more honorable men. If homicide is committed, or if the mind is overcome by pleasures due to its own weakness, it should not seem surprising. These are sins occurring not in the higher Mind, but in souls that are like children or youths who have not yet reached maturity. If this world is a kind of training ground <note>original: "gymnasium"</note> for those who conquer and those who are defeated, then in this respect also, the world is well-ordered. If you suffer an injury, nothing 

**D** grave will happen to that which is immortal within you. Furthermore, if you are killed, you will have what you [as a Gnostic] claimed to desire <note>Plotinus is being ironic here: if the Gnostics truly hate the body and wish to leave the world, death should be seen as a gift, not a tragedy</note>. If you still complain about such things, nothing forces you to remain any longer in this "city" [of the world]. It is also established that judgments and punishments exist here, which makes it unjust to accuse this "city" for distributing to each according to their merit. In this world, virtue is honored, and wickedness receives its deserved disgrace. 

**E** There are not only statues of the gods here, but the gods themselves, looking down from on high. As it is said, they easily escape or avoid the faults of men, leading all things in order from the beginning to the end, and distributing to each a fitting lot <note>original: "sortem," their portion or destiny</note> according to the cycles of their various lives. This lot, I say, follows from their previous actions. Whoever is ignorant of this lot is, above all men, reckless and unlearned in divine matters. One must strive with all one's strength to eventually become the best oneself; but do not 

**F** think that you alone can become the best. Otherwise, you would not yet be "best" if you did not recognize that other men can be best too, and that there are good spirits <term>spirits: "dæmones," in the Neoplatonic sense of intermediary divine beings, not evil "demons"</term> and, much more so, gods. These gods, inhabiting this world, look up toward the superior world. Above all of these is the most blessed Soul, the leader of the entire world. From here, one should worship the intelligible gods, and finally, among them all, one should venerate the great King of all who dwells there. We should certainly judge that this King demonstrates his excellence most of all through the multitude of gods. For it is not the role of those who have known the power of God to 

**G** suddenly contract everything into a single point, but rather to unfold that great divine abundance, just as He himself has unfolded it. Inasmuch as He is seen as the One who is permanent, He produces the many who all depend upon Him, because they exist through Him and from Him. Truly, this world is also through Him, and the whole world looks up toward Him.

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS: BOOK II.

### THE ARROGANCE OF THE CHOSEN

<margin>A</margin>
*Every one of the gods respects [the First], as do those who announce the decrees of God to men: they declare through oracles and responses what is pleasing to those divine beings. If these secondary gods <note>original: "sequentes hi dij," referring to the stars and celestial intelligences</note> are not the same as the First God, this is entirely in accordance with nature. But if one chooses to despise these higher things, and to think of oneself as no worse than them, one must remember that the better a person is, the more kindly and*
<margin>B</margin>
*modest they are toward others, both toward men and toward the celestial beings. Therefore, one ought to maintain their own dignity with moderation, far removed from any bitter rudeness. We should lift ourselves up only as far as our nature allows, and we must realize that the path to God is open to others as well. One should not imagine they are flying alone toward God, as if in a dream, or that they alone are placed nearest to Him. Above all, one must take care not to deprive oneself of the very capacity that has been given to our souls to become godlike.*
<margin>C</margin>
*A soul can become godlike only as far as the Mind <term>Mind: "mens," translating the Greek "Nous," the realm of pure intellectual forms</term> leads it. To try to transcend the Mind is nothing else than to fall away from it. Yet foolish men believe such words when they first hear: "You will be more excellent than all others, not only than men, but even than the gods." For a great deal of arrogance reigns among men. A person who was previously modest, humble, and simple is now puffed up with pride when he hears: "You are indeed a son of God, but the others whom you previously*
<margin>D</margin>
*admired are not sons of God." Nor are the beings they worship according to ancestral rites considered sons of God: "But you, without any struggle or labor, are more excellent than heaven itself." Others join in this shouting, much like someone who does not know how to count, hearing in a crowd of people who are equally ignorant that his height is exactly one thousand cubits. What happens then? If he thinks himself a thousand cubits high, and believes others do not exceed five cubits, he doesn't*
<margin>E</margin>
*actually know how large those numbers are; he simply imagines he is much greater because of the number he was given. Furthermore, they <note>Plotinus is referring to the Gnostics</note> admit that God has care for human affairs, but they claim He has no care for the whole world in which humans live. But why would He neglect the world? If He neglects it because He does not have the leisure to look after the universe, then surely it would be forbidden for Him to care for the "lower" human affairs. Also, while He looks after humans, why does He not also look at the environment that surrounds them?*
<margin>F</margin>
*And thus He would look at the world in which humans exist. If He does not look "outside" to avoid seeing the world, then He does not see humans either. But they will say that humans do not need that, yet the world does. On the contrary, God knows the order of the world—who is in it, what their condition is, and how they came to be there. Therefore, whoever among men are friends of God will endure with a calm mind whatever happens to them from the world, and they will rightly bear whatever necessarily results from the*
<margin>G</margin>
*movement of the whole. This is not done without reason: for one ought to look not at one's own individual wishes, but at the whole itself, honoring each thing according to its worth. One should strive with all their might, but recognize that there are many things—indeed, all things—striving toward that higher place, and those that follow it are blessed. Some things, as far as their nature allows, attain a lot that is suitable for them. Truly, a virtuous man does not claim for himself alone the power to achieve happiness. For it does not come from...*

# BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

<margin>Isocrates</margin>
*A promise to know implies that one possesses what they speak of; but many, though knowing they lack it, boast that they have it. Others believe they possess it when they do not, or they are mad to think they have it, or they are the only ones who do not have it.* <note>This quote is attributed to Isocrates, an ancient Greek rhetorician, used here to highlight the gap between Gnostic claims of "secret knowledge" and actual truth.</note>

If one were to examine many other points—indeed, all of them—one would find an abundance of evidence in every argument to show how things truly are. I am moved by a sense of shame for certain friends who, before they became our friends, happened upon these Gnostic doctrines. For some reason, they persist in them, even though they have not benefited their own lives. They hope these ideas are true, or perhaps they believe them to be credible, or they feel compelled to defend them as they are. However, we address our words to the underlying ideas, not to the individuals themselves. Perhaps we can achieve nothing more toward persuading them, for they do not spend their leisure time considering proofs, nor do they care how we have discovered these truths through a different way of life. Instead, they boldly attempt to smear the teachings of the ancient and divine men <note>original: "παλαιῶν καὶ θείων ἀνδρῶν," likely referring to Plato and Pythagoras</note>, who spoke beautifully and held fast to the truth. We must let those men be examined, for even if one were to accurately grasp what was said before, there are always things from others that can strengthen the argument. 

But let us speak of those claims that surpass all absurdity. They say that the Soul and a certain Wisdom <term>Wisdom: "Sophia," in Gnostic myth, a divine being whose "fall" or "error" led to the creation of the material world</term>—whether this "inclination" <note>original: "νενευκέναι," meaning a downward movement or "leaning" toward matter</note> began from the <margin>* Outflow</margin> Soul or from Wisdom sensing its own richness—either they want both to be the same, or they say that while other souls descended as members of Wisdom, and that these souls entered bodies like those of humans, the one for whose sake they descended did not herself descend. They claim she did not "fall," so to speak, but only shined into the darkness, so that an image of her was produced in matter. Then, having fashioned an image of an image <note>original: "εἴδωλον εἴδωλον," emphasizing how far removed the material world is from the divine source in their view</note>, they claim it persuades the whole, giving names to things—this to one, that to another—using many obscure names for the one they call the "Maker" <term>Maker: "demiurge," the Gnostic term for a lower, often ignorant creator of the physical world</term> born from the Mother. They call this "fire" or something of the sort, so that the author of this writing might mock the world as the lowest of images.

NOW, if she <note>Sophia</note> did not descend, but only illuminated the darkness, how can she be correctly said to have "inclined"? For if a light flowed from her, she cannot be said to have inclined herself toward it, unless something was already positioned below <margin>then</margin> and she, staying in herself, merely shone upon it. But if she remained in herself while shining, performing nothing * intentional toward the work,

<column-break/>

By the fact that he professes to possess something, he already "possesses" it: indeed, many who know they have nothing boast that they do, and even those who do not have it think they have it, and that they alone possess it, when they are actually the only ones who do not.

FURTHERMORE, anyone discussing many other things—indeed, everything—will easily and abundantly find reasons to show, point by point, the nature of their discourse. I cannot help but feel a sense of shame for certain friends who, before entering into a friendship with us, fell into speeches of this kind. They still <margin>X
How greatly they err who say the world was fashioned when they do not yet know how it could be possible.</margin> persevere in them, I know not how. They are not ashamed, but rather they urge others more intensely, so that their opinions might undoubtedly appear true. Or, perhaps, they themselves believe the matter to be so. We, however, address our words only to those we know, and not at all to the many who listen to them; for we would gain nothing by persuasion, attempting to convince them not to permit themselves to be perverted by those people. What power would demonstrations have? They would only boast more stubbornly. Since there is another way for one to write and refute those who do not fear to cavil at the most noble and true mysteries of the ancient and divine men, let us set aside that mode of discussion for the present. Since they have perfectly understood the things just said, they will clearly be able to judge the nature of the rest. I also set aside for now that saying which surpasses all in absurdity—if it is even fitting to call this "absurdity." For they say that the Soul and Wisdom, by a certain "nod" toward that which is inferior—whether the Soul began this movement or Wisdom was the cause of the nodding, or if they want both to be the same—they say other souls descended, as if they were limbs of Wisdom, and entered human-like bodies. But she, for whose sake the souls fell, they say she did not fall at all, as if she had not actually "nodded," but had only illuminated the darkness. They claim an image resulted in matter from this; and then, forming an image of an image here through matter—or "materiality," or whatever they wish to call it—calling one thing this and another that, and inventing many names for the sake of obscurity, they bring about what they call the "Maker of the World" <note>original: "mundi opifex"</note>. Falsely claiming he broke away from the Mother, they derive the world from him down to the lowest of images, so that the one who wrote these things might more bitingly heap abuse upon it.

BUT TRULY, if that soul did not fall but only illuminated the darkness, how can it be correctly said that she "nodded" toward the inferior? For it should not be said she "nodded" simply because something like a light flowed out from her—unless there was something else <margin>XI
He refutes the claim that the Soul, by her shining, made another soul within matter, and that this one fabricated everything.</margin> placed below, and she, moving as if from place to place, descended and shone by becoming closer. But if, while remaining in herself, she poured out light, she was not performing anything more intimately in this work. Why then do they say...

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK II ###

-> Page 310 <-

For only the soul gave light, but not those beings who, in the actual order of things, are more powerful than the soul. But if they say that the soul, because it encompasses the rational notion <note>original Latin: "rationalem mundi notionem," likely translating the Greek "logos"</note> of the world within itself, was able to illuminate the world through that very rational discourse: what is to prevent it, at the very moment it first illuminated, from simultaneously creating the world? Why did it wait for the further birth of "images" <note>term: "simulachrorum" or "eidola," referring to the Gnostic idea that the physical world is a mere phantom of the divine</note>? Furthermore, this very rational notion of the world—which they call the "alien and hospitable land" <note>This refers to a specific Gnostic myth where the lower world is a foreign place to the divine spark</note>—even if produced by higher beings (as they claim), did not at all force the creators to look downward in a fall. Moreover, what is the reason that matter, once illuminated, does not produce the nature of bodies, but instead produces the "images" of souls? Indeed, it seems the image of a soul requires neither darkness nor matter; but if anything is created, that which is made will immediately accompany its creator and remain attached to you. Also, regarding that which is first infused into matter, is it an essence, or rather (to use their words) a thought-construct <note>original: "excogitamen" / "ennoema"</note>? For if it is an essence, what will be the difference between this and that from which it flowed? But if it is another species of soul—provided the higher one is rational—perhaps this one is the vegetative and generative soul. If this is so, how can it be true that the effect <note>the world</note> was honored? And how did it create through "audacity" and "pride," and entirely through what is called a sort of "imagination"? Much more so is the claim that it created through reasoning thus refuted. Or again, why was it necessary for the creator to work within from matter and an image? But if it is said that what is first infused is a "thought-construct," one must first interpret where such a name is derived from; then by what reasoning it exists, unless one grants a power of creation to this thought-construct. But how shall the power of creation reside in this figment? They will surely say that this happens first, and another thing happens next. But they say this by their own whim. Why, then, was fire created first, and then the rest?

<margin>
XII
He refutes the same ideas and proves the world was made according to the outlines of the whole.
</margin>

SIMILARLY, one must ask by what reasoning that "image," having been recently born, would attempt creation through a certain memory of the things it had known before. For there was no way at all for it to know them; nor was that "image" the one they claim is its mother. Added to this is the fact that they descended into this world not as mere images of souls, but as true souls; and yet, scarcely one or at most two among them, being moved by the world and calling themselves back to memory, finally resume some small part of their observation of the things they had seen. Is it not, therefore, beyond measure marvelous that either this "image"—even if (as they say) it is a faint one—could immediately upon being born "imagine" the higher realms? Or even that its mother could suspect the same things, she who is an entirely material image? And not only consider those things and receive a notion of this world and that one, but even comprehend from what elements they are made? From where did it first think to make fire <note>original Greek: "πῦρ"</note>, deeming it necessary for that to be made first? Why not similarly something else? But if it could create because its notion was marked by fire, why was it not marked by the "world"? For it ought first to have been marked by the whole; it should have created the whole world at once. For in the thought-construct itself, the mark of the whole—

<column-break/>

For why did she alone shine? But not the things more powerful than her among existing beings. If it was by her receiving a "reasoning" <note>logos</note> of the world, from where? If she shone out from the reasoning, why did she not make the world at the same time as she shone? Why did she wait for the generation of "images" <note>eidola</note>? Then, the reasoning of the world—or what is called by them the "alien land"—being produced by the greater beings as they say, did not pull the creators down into an "inclination" <note>term: "neusis," the Gnostic term for the soul's downward turn or fall toward matter</note>. Then how, when matter was illuminated, does it produce "psychic images," but not the nature of bodies? An image of a soul would have no need of darkness or matter; but having been produced, if it were produced, it would follow the creator, being joined to it. Then, is that which first enters <note>matter</note> an essence, or as they say, a "thought-concept" <note>ennoema</note>? If it is an essence, what is the difference from that from which it came? If it is another form of soul, the searching and rational kind, perhaps it is the vegetative and generative soul itself. If it is this, how would it still be most honorable? And how could "arrogance" and "audacity" <note>term: "tolma," often used in Gnosticism to describe the daring or fall of Sophia</note> be attributed to it, and in general, creation through "imagination" <note>phantasia</note>? And even more so, how could it be through "reasoning"? It is most foolish to think the creator produces from matter and an image. If it is a "thought-concept," from where is this name applied? Then how is there a "making," unless one gives the "making" to the thought-concept? But how will this "figment" create? They say one thing is first, and another after that; but speaking as if by their own authority, they say: "Why was fire <note>pur</note> first?"

AND how could it, having just been born, attempt to "imitate" <note>mimesis</note> what it saw? For it was not at all in a state of remembering, if indeed it is itself, or its "mother," whom they teach to it. So how—for most of them do not come into this world as "images" of souls, but as "true souls"—could they, or barely two of them, be moved by the world, coming into "remembrance" <note>anamnesis</note>, and barely ever receive a strike of what they once saw? But how could the "image," in a typical and dim way as they say, having just been born, "think" upon those higher things? Or even the mother herself, a material image, not only think upon those things and receive a notion of that world, but even learn from what it might be made? Why indeed did it make fire first? And if it was first for this reason, why not something else? But if it was able to create because fire was conceived, why did it not conceive the world together with it? For it was necessary first to think upon the whole; not a world piece by piece—

# BOOK NINE #

<margin>Sophistical arguments.</margin>
Next, let us consider how those things are interwoven in the logical reasoning; for it is certainly more natural this way, and not like the arts which came later. For arts are posterior to nature and the cosmos. Since even now, the things that come into being part by part through natural processes do not happen by fire being first, then each other thing individually, and then their nature; rather, there is a surrounding and an outlining—the whole being produced for those who have grasped that the animal is a whole. Body, then, is not evil, nor is the matter that was outlined in some way within the world, * from the place where earth and fire and the others are. But perhaps they themselves, when they made the world—acting as if they possessed a truer soul—hesitated @ in how it should be made, both its encompassing boundary and its magnitude. They judged rather that it should be of such a size, and the carving out of the living beings, <margin>the things brought forth.</margin> and the difference of the things under them; and they spoke of the causes of why the tongue is such as it is, as if they knew. This was not the work of an image <note>term: "eidolon," a mere shadow or reflection</note>, but entirely from the power coming from the eternal beings, which they themselves must admit, even if unwillingly. And as for the illumination toward the darkness, let it be examined. It forces one to admit the true causes of the world. And the <margin>Illumination.</margin> illumination sings, * though not entirely as it should. For that nature is the same as the lower nature; but while one is according to nature, this one is in a certain way; but the Nature among the things there is the first Nature, and the evils concerning this world. And the world is not the cause of evils, but the things down here and in the soul—not from the higher beings, but from the soul itself. For the rational principle <note>term: "logos," the governing reason of the universe</note> governs the world through the primary things; but if matter appeared from somewhere, or the soul that saw it <margin>Darkness.</margin> saw it in the darkness. They say * it also shone forth, or these things were generated; if nature itself produced an image, it would be clear that wherever it looked, or if the darkness was within it. Let the cause be in the seeing, but the nature of the soul itself. This is the same as the necessities that have been explained, since the primary things are the causes.

THEREFORE, HE who finds fault with the nature of the world does not know what he does, nor how far his audacity goes. This happens because perhaps they are ignorant of the order of the things that follow—the first, the second, and the third, and so on until the last. One should not revile the first among the lower things, but rather gently yield to the nature of all things, being less harsh toward the primary beings. One should cease the tragedy of terrors, as they imagine them to exist in the spheres of the world, which indeed—

<column-break/>

**A** —acle <note>meta: completing "spectaculo" (spectacle) or "miraculo" (miracle) from the previous page</note> those things also are marked. Thus it will certainly be judged to have been effected more naturally. Nor should it be thought that he fabricated it in the manner of craftsmen, especially since arts are posterior <note>term: "posterior," meaning coming after in time or logical order</note> to both nature and the world. Since those things which are naturally generated in each individual species do not happen in such a way that fire is made first, then the rest one by one; but rather, as a mixture of all things—or indeed, the configuration of the whole living creature at once—embracing the necessary connection of the limbs to the whole, it **B** coalesces in the power of the mind. What then prevents the matter from being marked with the figure of the whole world simultaneously in the very order of things? In which figure, earth, and fire, and the rest would have been necessarily connected. Perhaps they would have procreated the world in such a way as those who are born with a better soul. But the Craftsman of the world did not "not know" how to make the world, even though he foresaw the magnitude of the heaven, its certain measure, the slanted weaving of the celestial circles <note>original: "lignorum" is likely a typo in the OCR for "signorum," referring to the zodiacal signs</note>, and **C** the paths driven beneath them; and he foresaw the earth and all these things, so that the reason for each—by which they are as they are—is maintained. This is not the task of any mere image <note>term: "simulachrum," a representation or phantom</note>, but rather of some power that proceeds from the best things. Which indeed they themselves will confess, even if unwillingly. For that illumination, diffused through the darkness, if examined diligently, will make them admit the true causes of the world. For why was it necessary to illuminate, if it were not necessary at all? For that necessity was either according to **D** nature or contrary to nature. But if it was according to nature, it would certainly be so always; but if it was contrary to nature, and something contrary to nature happened to those higher beings, then undoubtedly evils existed before this world. Nor is this world the cause of evils, but the higher things are the cause of evil to this world; nor does the evil of the soul happen because of this world; but rather to this world from the soul. And thus, reason running its course rightly will lead this world back to the supreme **E** things. But if they say that matter is also the cause of evil, from where then did matter come? For the soul, turning toward the lower things, saw and illuminated the darkness (as they say) which already existed. From where then shall we say the darkness came? If they say the soul, turning toward lower things, brought them into the open, it follows that before the soul inclined, there was no darkness; and thus the cause of the inclination is not in the darkness, but consists in the nature of the soul itself. This is nothing other than assigning the cause from preceding necessities; wherefore the cause of this kind is referred back to their own principles.

<margin>XIII
Things are not separated by reason in the machine of the world all the way to the extremes, but all things are bound together, one from another.</margin>
**F** **HE THEREFORE** who blames the nature of the world, is utterly ignorant of what he does, nor does he understand where his rash arrogance leads him. In this, many err, because they do not know the perpetual order from the first things through the middle to the third; and thus always necessarily descending even to the extremes. Nor do they consider that it is not fitting for **G** the lower to accuse the supreme, or to impute to the supreme the things that follow; but it is necessary always to obey the nature of the universe with a calm mind, and to refer oneself to those higher things: utterly despising the tragic terrors, which some people imagine for mortals from the spheres of the world, which indeed—

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s "Against the Gnostics" (Ennead II, Book 9).
