# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II. #

[...they] strike. Yet these celestial bodies bring all things beneficial to mankind. For what do they contain within themselves that is to be feared? This is a question for those who use fear to terrify men unskilled in reason and lacking in sound doctrine and true knowledge. For even though the bodies of the celestial spheres are made of fire, they are not to be feared, since they are perfectly adapted for the good of the universe and the earth. It is fitting, however, to consider their souls; it is because of these souls that they [the stars] are considered of great value. Even if their bodies wonderfully surpass our own in magnitude and beauty, they also contribute to the production and preservation of all things born of nature. Otherwise, as long as these primary things exist, these secondary things [on earth] would not come to be. They certainly complete the universe and are its massive members. If humans are to be honored above other living creatures, how much more so these stars, which do not exist in the world to exercise tyranny, but rather create ornament and order. As for the things said to be caused by them, it should be judged that such things are *signified* by them rather than *enforced* by them. Moreover, the things that happen result from differences in fortune. For it is impossible for the same outcomes to happen to every individual, given the differences in the times of their birth, the diversity of their locations, and the widely differing dispositions of their souls. Again, one must not demand that everyone in the world be good, nor, if that is impossible, should one suddenly find fault with the order of the world. Nor should one require that these inferior things differ in no way from the superior ones, nor judge that to be "evil" which is merely less suited for prudence or less good, proceeding always toward the lesser. It would be as if one asserted that nature is evil because it is not sensation; or that the world of the senses is evil because it is not reason. Otherwise, they will be forced to admit that there is evil even among the higher beings. For even there, the soul is inferior to the Mind <note>term: "Mind" or "Nous," the second hypostasis in Plotinus's philosophy, representing pure intellect</note>, and the Mind is inferior to another [The One].

<margin>
XIII.
One can refute the claim that certain sounds of words can bend higher beings, and that diseases are demons, and that these are expelled by certain words and ways of living.
</margin>
**MOST ESPECIALLY** do they [the Gnostics] act in this way again, making it seem as if the higher beings are not inviolable. They compose certain incantations <note>original: "cantilenas," literally songs or chants used as spells</note> to move those higher powers at their will—not just bodies and souls, but even things superior to these. But what do they actually achieve through these? They will answer that they compose charms, enchantments, and persuasions, so that the higher beings might hear their words and be drawn down. This assumes that if one of us knows how to pronounce such things with great skill, and can produce certain chants and sounds in a specific way—using breathy tones, or hisses, or whatever else they have written down—they contain magical power. But if they do not wish to say this, but rather that their voices signify certain incorporeal things, it follows that while they wish to make their art appear more honorable, they unwittingly destroy their own glory. Furthermore, they boast that they expel diseases. If they promised to do this through temperance and a right rule of life, they would certainly speak rightly and in the manner of philosophers. But as it is, they say diseases are demons <note>term: "dæmones," here referring to malevolent spirits believed to possess the body</note> and profess to expel them with words, and they spread this abroad to the common people...

<column-break/>

A ...that one might say they possess most for the sake of knowing them, or rather that they have nothing to fear, though they terrify those who are inexperienced in reason, and who perhaps do not know the powers reasonably and harmoniously. Even if their bodies are made of fire, one should not fear them, for they are proportionate to the whole and to the earth. One must <margin>behold</margin> behold their souls, by which they themselves surely claim to be honorable. B And their bodies, differing in magnitude and beauty, act together and cooperate with those things that happen according to nature. These things would not happen otherwise, nor would the primary things [the stars] be what they are, being completions and great parts of the whole. If humans are honorable compared to other animals, much more so are these, being in the universe not for the sake of tyranny, but providing ornament and C order. <margin>what</margin> As for what is said to be produced by them, it signifies what is to come. The things that happen occur through differences in souls, and it is not possible for the same things to happen to each person, given the timing of their choices, the great distance of their locations, and the dispositions of their souls. And <margin>concerning</margin> one must not demand that all things D in the world be good, and if this is not possible, one should not blame the things that follow, nor again demand that these [lower things] differ in no way from those [higher things]. One should not consider it "evil" but rather something less apt in prudence, and a lesser good, and so on toward the smaller. For example, if someone were to call nature "evil" because it is not sensation, or the sensory world "evil" because it is not reason. Otherwise, they will be forced to call E the higher things evil. For even there, the soul is inferior to the Mind, and the Mind is less than another.

**MOST ESPECIALLY** they do this in another way, making the things there [in the heavens] not unswayable. For when they write incantations, speaking as if to those powers—not only to the soul, but even to all things—they say they perform sorceries, enchantments, and persuasions, and that [the powers] obey their word and are led, if one of us is more skillful in speaking these things, or F certain songs and sounds, or according to some mystical strings <margin>the same</margin> of the voice, and all the other things that their magicians write. But if they do not wish to say these things, but rather how incorporeal things are [affected] by voices, so that their words might seem more venerable, they have failed to notice that they are stripping those beings of their dignity and making them the objects of sorcery. <margin>disease</margin> Regarding disease: if they said they resulted from a lack of temperance and could be cured by a G disciplined life, they would speak rightly, just as the philosophers speak. But now, by assuming diseases are demons, and claiming they can remove them by a word, or by reporting such things, they might seem to be more venerable...

<summary>Plotinus refutes Gnostic claims that the stars are malevolent, arguing instead that they are beautiful, orderly parts of the divine cosmos. He further critiques Gnostic "magic" and their belief that diseases are caused by demons that can be exorcised through spells, advocating instead for philosophical temperance and natural medicine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s polemic against the Gnostics. Having previously defended the physical beauty of the cosmos and the stars, he now turns to the Gnostic practice of "exorcism" and their claim that diseases are caused by demons rather than natural biological processes. He contrasts his own philosophical pursuit of virtue with the Gnostics' "insolent" rejection of the world's order.</meta>

# BOOK NINE. #

Just as children <note>original: "ὥσπερ παῖς"</note> admire the many tricks of magicians, so the common people are struck by their wonders. However, they could not persuade the prudent that diseases do not have natural causes—such as exhaustion, or overindulgence, or deficiency, or decay, and generally from changes originating either internally or externally, or from several of these meeting together. This is made clear by their treatments: for through the clearing of the bowels or the administration of drugs, the disease is expelled through secretions, and it is cured by bloodletting and fasting. Or perhaps the demon is hungry <note>Plotinus uses biting sarcasm here to mock the Gnostic idea that a physical cure affects a spiritual demon.</note> and the drug causes it to waste away and melt? 

<margin>
So also the Divine.
</margin>

But if the demon suddenly departs, or remains as a phantom—if it does not remain, how is it a phantom? Is the person no longer sick? If the demon has departed, why does the person still suffer the same thing, or why was the sickness permitted? Is the disease something natural, which holds back the demon? ... Why is the person not always sick? If there is a natural cause, why is a demon needed for the person to be ill? For the cause—the fever—is sufficient by itself to produce the effect. It is ridiculous to think that as soon as the cause arises, a demon stands by like a servant <note>Plotinus finds it absurd that a spiritual being would wait for a physical trigger like a "fever" to act.</note> because the demon is supposedly the cause. But how and why they say these things is quite difficult.

<margin>
That spirit is not without breath.
</margin>

It is clear then that they no longer hold to the truth, and they mock the things of the demons. <note>original: "ἐμυκτήρισαν" — literally "to turn up one's nose at" or sneer.</note> The rest I leave for you who read to consider. Observe this everywhere: that our own courage is immediately pursued by philosophy, along with all other good things, and simplicity of character is bound together with pure thinking. Dignity is pursued without pride, 

<margin>
As if because of this even God is destroyed.
</margin>
<margin>
This is it.
</margin>

and boldness is joined with reason and great safety and piety. This is the full persuasion that brings forth <term>sophrosyne</term> <note>often translated as temperance or sound-mindedness—a core Greek virtue of self-restraint.</note> and the rest. The views of the others, however, have overturned all things through opposition. For even if one says more about them, one would not be exhausted.

BUT THIS above all we must not fail to grasp: what their words produce in the souls of those who hear them—persuading them to despise the world and the things in it. For there are two sects regarding the "end" <note>the *telos* or ultimate goal of life.</note>: one places the end in the pleasure of the body, while the other chooses the beautiful and virtue, whose desire depends on God and is referred back to God. How this is to be understood regarding God must be explained elsewhere. Epicurus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (341–270 BC) who taught that the highest good was pleasure (the absence of pain) and that the gods do not intervene in human affairs.</note> took away providence and commanded the pursuit of pleasure and enjoyment as what remains. But the discourse of the Gnostics is even more insolent; they blame providence itself and its authority, dishonoring all the laws here and the virtue that has been revered throughout all time. They make a mockery of <term>sophrosyne</term>, as if nothing beautiful could be seen to exist here. They would destroy temperance or the innate justice <note>original: "δικαιοσύνην"</note> in characters, which is perfected by reason and practice.

<column-break/>

[They] are considered more excellent. For the common people are accustomed to admire the powers of magicians too much; however, they cannot persuade wise men that human diseases lack causes—namely, arising from labor, or satiety, or deficiency, or some sort of putrefaction, and in short from certain changes originating either internally or externally. The cures themselves of the diseases show this to us: for by a flux of the belly and by drugs, the disease is usually led out through the lower parts; 
furthermore, it is often cured by bloodletting and fasting. Perhaps the demon is hungry then, and the drug, by its power, causes the demon to melt away and waste away? If ever someone recovers suddenly, it is achieved either by the demon departing or remaining within. But if it remains, why does the person not fall ill while it still reigns within? But if it has gone out, what was the cause? For what did the demon itself suffer? Was it because it was being nourished by the disease? Therefore, the disease was something other than the demon itself.
Moreover, if a demon enters even when no cause exists, why is the person not always sick? But if it only enters when a cause is present, why is a demon needed for the person to be sick? For the cause itself is sufficient to ignite a fever. It is truly ridiculous that as soon as a cause occurs, a demon is suddenly present as if diligently prepared for the task. But in what way and for whose sake such things are boasted by them, we have sufficiently understood. It is for this reason no less than any other that we have just made mention of these demons.
The rest I leave to you readers to consider: and this especially must be noticed everywhere, that our kind of philosophy, when rightly perceived, embraces simplicity of character along with purity of intelligence above all other goods; it does not choose vain boasting but the dignity of elegance. It contains courage along with reason and caution and circumspect providence. But the other things prepared for that end, and those things in turn, appear to be entirely contrary in every part. For nothing more can be said. It seems fitting for us to speak of them in this way.

<margin>
That it is a crime for those living to measure death, even regarding the world and whatever is born in the world, as is done by these men.
</margin>

Above all, it must not escape us what their speeches bring forth in the minds of those who hear them—they who persuade men to despise the world and the things that are in it. Truly, the choice and the sect regarding the "end" is twofold: one indeed places the end in the pleasure of the body, but the other prefers honesty and virtue; the pursuit of which depends on God and is referred back to God. In what manner that happens must be contemplated elsewhere. Epicurus indeed, since he had removed providence, commanded that what remains—pleasure and delights—be followed. But the speech of the Gnostics is even more insolent, blaming the very lordship and authority of providence, and providence itself; it strips of honor all the laws here, and virtue which has been proven over many centuries, and it considers temperance ridiculous, so that nothing of the good might appear to exist among us. It roots out temperance and the justice innate in characters which must be acquired through reason and practice.

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Gnostic belief that diseases are caused by demons, arguing instead for natural medical causes like diet and exhaustion. He further attacks Gnostic ethics, claiming their contempt for the world leads to the destruction of traditional virtues like temperance and justice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of the Gnostics in Ennead II.9. On the previous page, Plotinus mocked the Gnostic belief that illnesses are caused by demons that can be exorcised. Here, he pivots to a more profound philosophical critique: that the Gnostic rejection of the physical world (the cosmos) and its inherent order leads to a rejection of virtue itself. He argues that true piety is found through moral discipline, not through a "shortcuts" to God that involves despising the natural world.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK II #

...and indeed every path by which one might attain **virtue** <term>virtus: moral excellence and philosophical discipline</term>: so much so that nothing else remains for them but to follow pleasure, and to attend only to their own affairs, deserting the common fellowship of the human race to study only their own personal utility—unless, perhaps, someone is by their own nature superior to such talk. For of those things which we consider good and honorable, nothing is esteemed as good by them, but rather something else entirely, whatever it is they may pursue. Although it would be more fitting for those who have already known the divine to pursue it from this starting point, and as they follow, to correct these primary things of ours by approaching them from the perspective of the divine nature. For it belongs only to that nature which neglects the pleasures of the body to understand what is truly good and honorable. But those who are entirely devoid of virtue can in no way approach the higher realms. This is also evidenced by the fact that they never speak of virtue, and they entirely abandon all discourse regarding those things that pertain to virtue. They do not strive to define what virtue and the good are, nor how many types there are, nor any of those many noble things contained in the discussions of the ancients; nor, again, do they discuss the means by which the good is acquired and possessed, nor how the soul is cultivated and purified. For their habit of saying, "Look toward God," is of no use at all unless they clearly teach *how* one is to look. For as one might say, nothing prevents a person from looking, while nonetheless abstaining from no pleasure and failing to restrain their anger; such a person, while merely reciting the name of God, remains a slave to all disturbances and makes no effort to drive them away. **Virtue**, truly acquired through **prudence** <term>prudentia: practical wisdom or phronesis</term> and progressed to the highest degree, reveals God to us; but if someone speaks of God without true virtue, they possess nothing but a name.

<margin>XVI
Those who say there is no good divinity in the bodies of the world pervert the order; yet they [claim] to become like others [unclear] the world is the medium of those evils through which they could reach the higher things.</margin>

**XVI**
LET NO ONE think that they will turn out good from the mere fact that they despise the world, the gods who reign in the world, and the other beautiful and noble things of the world. Indeed, it is the primary mark of an entirely evil man to despise the gods; no one is truly evil until they despise the celestial beings. But even if a person is not yet evil in all other respects, they become evil in everything through this one act. Furthermore, what they say about worshiping the "intelligible gods" <note>Plotinus refers to the Gnostic claim that they only honor the spiritual deities, not the physical stars or the creator of this world.</note> has nothing consistent or kindred about it. For whoever loves something also pursues with affection whatever is related to the object of their love. For you also love the children whose father you love. But every **soul** <term>anima: the life-force or psyche</term> is the daughter of that Father. And the souls in the spheres of the world are intellectual and good, and far more closely related to the higher realms than our own souls are. For how could this world be severed from that one, or how could the gods who are in the world be separated? But we have spoken of these things in the preceding sections. Now it must be affirmed that those who despise what is related to the higher divinities do not even know those divinities themselves, but only grasp them in words. Furthermore, how can it be pious to say that **providence** <term>providentia: the divine care for the universe</term> does not reach all these things, or even any part of them? Likewise, how is this consistent with their own views? For they claim that God cares only for humans. But is it only for humans while they are there [in the divine realm], or also while they are on earth?
<meta>catchword: earth</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>*According to which...*</margin>
**A** ...and generally, *according to the principles they accepted*, one might be found lying, so that pleasure is left to them and to their eternal selves, and the concern for other humans is only for their own needs, unless someone by their own nature were superior to these words. For of the things here, they consider nothing among the beautiful, but rather something else, whatever they might pursue; and they think that those who have already known [the divine] must immediately pursue it, and in pursuing it, first set these things right, having come from the divine nature. For it is the part of that nature to understand the beautiful, **B** while despising the pleasure of the body. But those who have no share in virtue would never be moved at all toward those higher things. The evidence for them is this: that they have made no account of virtue among themselves, and they have abandoned the contemplation of it; they do not speak of what it is, nor how many kinds there are, nor the many noble things found in the discourses of the ancients, nor by what means it is obtained or acquired, nor how the soul is tended or purified. For indeed, to say **C** "Look toward God" is a trivial task unless they teach how one should look. For what prevents someone from looking, while yet abstaining from not a single pleasure, or being unrestrained in anger—remembering the name, but suffering under the passions of the gods <note>original: "θεῶ πεπονθόμενον"; Plotinus may be mocking the idea of "divine" passions or suffering</note> and not withdrawing from any of them? Virtue, then, proceeding to the end and being born in the soul along with **prudence** <term>phronesis: practical wisdom</term>, reveals God; but without true virtue, God is merely a spoken name.

**D** **THUS**, it is not through despising the world and the gods within it and the other beautiful things that one becomes good. For every evil man would first <margin>*before*</margin> despise the gods; he is not evil *before* he despises them, and even if he is not evil in all other things, he would be evil by this very thing. For even the things said to be not [honored] by them regarding the intelligible gods would be inconsistent with their honor. For the one who loves something embraces that which is related to the thing loved. If you love the **E** children, you love the father. And every soul is a *child* <note>original: "παῖ;"</note> of that One. The souls in these [celestial bodies] are both intellectual and good, and far more in harmony with the things there than our own are. For how could this world be cut off from that one? Or how could the gods in it be? But these things were discussed before. Now, we say that since they despise what is related to those higher beings, they do not even know those things, except **G** in words. Since they do not recognize *providence* <margin>...the... providence...</margin> as reaching the things here, or *as they* say, how <margin>*as they*</margin> is that pious? And how is it consistent with themselves? For they say he [God] provides for them alone—is it only when they have become [divine] there, or for those who are here?

# BOOK NINE #

<margin>Not</margin>
**A** If [the souls] were not there <note>original: "ἐκεῖ" (ekei) — referring to the intelligible or divine realm</note>, how did they come here? Or how are they still here? And how are they present to the things that are here? For from where will [the Divine] know that they are here? And how, if they did not enter by walking, did they not forget the Divine and become evil? If he knows those who have not become evil, he will surely also recognize those who have, so that he may distinguish them from the others. Therefore, he shall be present to all, and he will be in this world in whatever way he is present.

<margin>Day.</margin>
**B** Therefore, the world will participate in him. If, however, he is absent from the world, he is also absent from us, and you would have nothing to say about him or about the things that follow after him. But whether some providence flows to you from that place, or whatever you wish to claim, certainly this world also possesses things from there in the same way; it is neither abandoned by God, nor will it ever be abandoned. For God has much more care for the whole than for the parts, and the whole world is a participant in divinity much more than any single part.

**C** Furthermore, the Soul of the All <term>World Soul: the animating principle of the entire universe in Platonic thought</term> is cared for and adorned by God even more. This demonstrates that the world truly *is*, and that it exists wisely. And who among those who are foolishly proud <note>Plotinus is targeting Gnostic "intellectuals" who looked down on the physical world</note> is as orderly and wise as the universe? Indeed, it is ridiculous and altogether absurd to bring these into comparison. If anyone compares them for any reason other than for the sake of argument, they cannot be far from impiety. Truly, it is in no way the mark of a prudent man to doubt these things, but rather of one who is blind, lacking both sense and mind, and removed far from the 

<margin>Impiety.</margin>
<margin>Foolish.</margin>
<margin>The World.</margin>
knowledge of the **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world: the higher realm of pure forms and ideas, accessible only through the intellect</term>, since he does not even see this visible world. 

**D** For what musician will there be who, having understood the intelligible harmony, is not then moved when he hears the harmony resonating in audible voices? Or who is so skilled in geometry and numbers that, when he sees with his eyes a spectacle composed with fitting proportion, symmetry, and order, is not greatly delighted? Indeed, those who look through artistic eyes do not see these things in the same way even in drawings and paintings.

**E** Rather, they recognize in that which is perceived by the senses an **imitation** <note>original: "μίμημα" (mimēma)</note> of that which is placed in the intellect. Thus, they are struck with wonder and brought back to the **recollection** <term>anamnesis: the philosophical "remembering" of divine truths the soul knew before birth</term> of the truth. From this state of feeling, loves also arise. But he who sees beauty shining aptly in a face is raised toward the intelligible. 

<margin>Recollection.</margin>
**F** He, therefore, would be altogether lazy in mind and never incited toward anything else, who, seeing all the beautiful sights in this world, its absolute order, and the bond of perfect proportion in its measurements—and that form which shines so wonderfully in the stars, however far removed—does not then contemplate and revere these things with the most intense admiration, wondering what sort of things they are and from what source they proceed. Otherwise, he has neither considered these things nor known those higher ones.

**XVII**
Above the corporeal world is the soul-filled world, which is mobile and possesses and produces corporeal dimensions; it is the invisible world, most beautiful itself, creating this most beautiful world.
</margin>

<margin>But.</margin>
<margin>From the obstacles.</margin>
**G** And if by chance they were provoked to a hatred of the body by Plato, where he complains about the body because it hinders the soul, and where he judges the entire corporeal nature to be far inferior to the soul, one must nevertheless read the nature of the body with the intellect; removing the lesser parts, one must behold the remainder: the intelligible sphere containing the worldly form within itself, and souls in their order without the magnitude of bodies.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument against the Gnostic view of the world. ### BOOK TWO OF THE ENNEADS ###

Regarding magnitudes <note>original: "μεγεθῶν" (megethōn) — referring to the physical dimensions or sizes of things</note>, some things under the intelligible principle are led out into distance, so that by its magnitude, that which is generated might be made equal to the indivisible principle of the model there <note>original: "ἐκεῖ" (ekei) — the "there" refers to the higher Intelligible Realm</note>, according to its proportion or power. For what is great there in power becomes great here in bulk. And if one considers this sphere, he should think of it as moved by a divine power, which possesses the beginning, middle, and end of the whole. One would have a correct conception if they thought of this universe as being governed by a soul. Even if someone were to add a body to it <note>referring to the physical manifestation of the World Soul</note>, so that you would suffer nothing, no one should begrudge the gods for having what they are or what they can be. One must grasp each thing as he himself understands it, by looking at the world or that same soul’s power, and seeing how well it has made the nature of the body—insofar as the body itself is capable of participating in beauty. Does it not move all divine souls? Unless, perhaps, they say they no longer sing, and that you are led here to see ugly and beautiful bodies alike. But there is a difference between seeing the ugly and the beautiful. Beautiful studies and such contemplations belong to all the gods; for Zeus is not the first, but after him these things are shown to be beautiful. But when they say they despise the beauty here, they would do well to despise the beauty in children and women, or that of shameful and unrestrained men. But one must know that they do not boast by despising the ugly, but by saying that it is proper to despise the beautiful and everything that one might set forth <margin>Which indeed ought rather to be in the whole.</margin> as an accusation of beauty. I think, entirely and in every way, that things are either altogether beautiful or full of clumsiness; for even in the magnitude of the spirits <term>daemons: intermediate spirits between gods and humans</term>, as of the body that has been made, they either persuade us or act clumsily. In matters beyond reach, to speak of the beauty there is not to be held by these things. But they are skeptical if those things exist, yet they do not stop their insults. And if the things here are beautiful, they would say they are in harmony with each other. <margin>* The opposite is true.</margin> If, however, the things here are base, how can the best things be defeated? But nothing here is ever truly beautiful if the outside is ugly on the inside. For either the outside is entirely beautiful because the inside has conquered it, or if they are called beautiful while being ugly within, then the beauty on the outside is a lie. If someone says that they are accidentally beautiful in this way, but ugly here, I think <margin>* Censure.</margin> he has not seen them, but thinks other things are the beautiful ones. But if the ugliness is inherited by them, though they are beautiful in nature—for many things here are obstacles to reaching the end—in the whole...

<column-break/>

**A** Regarding magnitude under an intelligible principle, they produce it and lead it into distance, so that the magnitude of that which is created may be made equal to the indivisible proportion of the model according to its strength. For what is great there in power, becomes great here in mass. And whether they wish to consider this very sphere as agitated, or as being led around by a divine power containing the beginning, middle, and end of the whole sphere: or as staying still, like a knot governing anything else, they will certainly arrive at a right **B** way of thinking about the soul that governs the world. And if they then attach a body to the soul, it is clearly not so that the soul suffers anything, but rather that it grants something to the other; because it is a sin to suggest there is any envy among the gods. Lest each part should perceive things according to its capacity, they will be judged to think quite rightly about the world. They think of a vast power in the world’s soul, because it makes the nature of the body—which is by itself not at all beautiful—**C** a participant in beauty according to its capacity. This beauty indeed draws souls to itself as if they were divine. Unless, perhaps, they say their own minds are not at all incited by this, nor do they look at ugly and beautiful bodies with any different reasoning. But if that is admitted, it follows also that they are not affected by any difference between shameful and honorable pursuits. They would neither prefer beautiful teachings to others, nor therefore contemplation itself, nor therefore God himself. For these things are good or beautiful because of the primary things. **D** If, therefore, these things are not good and beautiful, we conclude that those primary things are not good or beautiful either, and so after those, these are no longer deemed good or beautiful. Accordingly, whenever they say that they value this beauty as nothing, if they despise it in the forms of boys and women, let them not appear in the same place, for they act rightly. Nevertheless, it should not escape us that they will by no means boast if they were to value something ugly as nothing. But they boast in this very thing: that they despise what they previously **E** conceded to be beautiful, and they themselves were affected in some way. Furthermore, beauty is not the same in a part as it is in the whole, or in all things and the universe. Finally, many things are so beautiful even in things that are sensed and are particular—as in the order of the spirits <term>daemons: intermediate spiritual beings</term>—that we often marvel at their author from this, and easily believe these things were made by him. And from this we can praise the author’s inestimable beauty. If only we are by no means **F** consumed by these things: but let us fly from these to those, and let us not vituperate these works of his. Certainly, if the internal things are also beautiful, just as the external things are, we ought to affirm that they agree among themselves. But if the internal things are evil, they must have been diminished in better things. But certainly, it cannot happen that what is truly beautiful on the outside is deformed on the inside. For that which is entirely beautiful on the outside becomes such because it is conquered by what is interior. He who is said to be beautiful in appearance, but is ugly within, would **G** falsely object that he has seen those who are beautiful in body but ugly in soul; I think, for my part, that he has not seen them, but considers certain others to be beautiful. But if perhaps he has seen them, I assert that the ugliness is adventitious <note>original: "aduentitiā" — something added from the outside, not part of the essential nature</note> to those who are beautiful by nature. For there are many obstacles among us to following the end. But in the whole world, to the sight...

### BOOK NINE. ###

To that which is beautiful <note>original: "καλῶς ὄντι" (kalōs onti)</note>, what impediment was there to it being beautiful on the inside as well? Indeed, for those whom nature did not grant perfection from the beginning, there may be a reason for them to eventually reach a goal; and thus it is possible for things to become flawed. But for the Universe, it was never a child <note>original: "παῖς" (pais) — implying the world did not undergo a developmental stage of incompleteness or growth</note> such as to be imperfect; nor did it grow as it went along, nor was its body added to it later. For from where could such a thing come? For it already possessed all things. But if it fashioned itself like a soul; if indeed it is by the grace of that same soul, then it is not a thing of evils.

<margin>* perhaps</margin>
But perhaps they will say that by their own doctrines they flee the body by way of reason, hating it from afar, while our doctrines hold our souls fast to it. This would be as if two people were living in the same beautiful house; the first person blames the builder <note>original: "κατασκευασάντων" (kataskeuasantōn) — refers to the craftsman or architect of the world, often called the Demiurge</note> and the materials used, yet stays in it nonetheless; the other person does not blame it, but says the craftsman made it with the greatest skill, and waits for the time to come when he shall depart and no longer need a house. The former might think himself wiser and readier to leave because he knows how to say that the walls are made of lifeless stones and wood and fall far short of a "true" dwelling; he is ignorant that the difference lies only in his inability to bear the necessary things, provided he does not make himself suffer, while moderately loving the beauty of the stones. We must remain as long as we have a body in the dwellings built by a soul that is our sister <note>The "Sister Soul" is the World Soul, which Plotinus views as an equal to the human soul, rather than a fallen or evil entity as the Gnostics did</note>, which has great power to create without effort. Or do these people think even the most wretched humans are worthy of being called "brothers," yet they refuse to call the Sun and the other heavenly bodies brothers? Even the soul of the whole world they separate from "brotherly" fellowship with an insane mouth. Truly, as long as we are wicked, it is a sin to claim kinship with the beings above; but when we become good, not being bodies but souls in bodies, we are able to dwell in them in a way that comes as close as possible to the manner in which the World Soul dwells in the whole body of the universe. To this end, <margin>* and also</margin> <margin>* the small</margin> the small part of us should not obey the pleasures or sights that fall upon us from without, nor be troubled by harsh things. That World Soul is not struck, for it has nothing by which it can be struck. We, however, living here, can repel the blow through virtue, so that by greatness of mind some blows become lighter and others do not touch us at all. When we have come close to that which cannot be struck, only then will we imitate the soul of the universe and the stars; having reached the closest likeness to them, we shall converge into the same goal. Then the same sights will be offered to us which have been present to the beings above from the beginning, and are not lacking to us—provided we are well-disposed by nature and prepared by study. If some, however, boast that they alone—

<column-break/>

From a most beautiful appearance, what obstacle could there have been to prevent it from being beautiful on the inside as well? Then indeed, for those to whom nature did not give perfection from the start, it happens by chance that they do not reach the goal; and therefore they can become corrupt. But it did not happen to the world that it was ever like a child, and not yet perfected; nor did anything coalesce into the world as it progressed further, nor was anything added to its body. For from where could that have happened? Since it already possessed all things. Nor is it permitted to imagine anything subjected to its soul. And if perhaps one grants this to the Gnostics <note>original: "Gnosticis" — Plotinus’s students gave this treatise the title "Against the Gnostics," though Plotinus usually refers to them as "friends" who have gone astray</note>, one still cannot admit any evil.

<margin>
**XVIII.**
*It is not fitting to blame the craftsman of the world: and to depart from here, if allowed: yet to bear the fates, and moreover to take care of the new building. Since then the soul will escape from those things by its delay.*
</margin>
Perhaps they will say that by their own words they effect an escape from the commerce of the body, and hold it in utter hatred; while our words detain the soul in the body. This is like a comparison where two people inhabit the same beautiful house: one blames the construction, the furnishings, and the builder, yet continues to live there; the other does not blame it at all, but says the builder of the home constructed it most skillfully. He waits for the time of his stay to end, until he shall depart; as one who then will no longer require a dwelling. The former might seem wiser and more ready for his exit because he knows how to say the building is constructed of inanimate stones and wood, and is far from a true dwelling—ignoring that the great difference lies in tolerating the necessary things, or not bearing them at all; for he will not depart with difficulty from a building he thinks is beautiful, if he loves the beauty of the stones with moderation. Certainly, we must remain while we have a body in the dwellings which were fabricated by our sister soul, which has the greatest power, through which she creates without labor. Or do those men deign to call even the worst people "brothers" daily, yet utterly disdain to call the Sun and other heavenly beings "brothers"? Indeed, with an insane mouth they even segregate the soul of the whole world from brotherly fellowship. Certainly, as long as we are wicked, it is a crime to join ourselves in kinship with those above; but only then, when we are good, we are not bodies, but souls in bodies, and thus able to inhabit them so that we approach as closely as possible to that manner of dwelling by which the soul of the world inhabits the whole body. That means not to be cast down from one's rank, nor to indulge in external allurements, nor to be broken by hardships. That Soul, indeed, is not struck, nor is there anything from which it could be struck. We, however, dwelling here, can repel the blow by virtue, so that by magnitude and strength of mind some blows become lighter, and others do not touch us at all. When we have approached closely to that which cannot be struck, only then shall we imitate the soul of the world and the stars. Likewise, when we have attained the closest similarity, we shall finally breathe together in the same purpose. Then truly the same spectacles will be offered to us which are present to the beings above from the beginning, and are not lacking to us; namely, to those well-instituted by nature and prepared by study. If some, however, boast that they alone—

He uses an analogy of a house to criticize the Gnostics, suggesting that one can appreciate the world's craftsmanship while still preparing for the soul's eventual departure.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Plotinus’s argument against the Gnostics in Ennead II.9 and begins Marsilio Ficino's commentary on Ennead III.1, which shifts the focus toward the nature of Fate and the relationship between eternal being and temporal action.</meta>

<page-num>818</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS’S ENNEAD II.</header>

Even if they are able to contemplate divine things, they possess no greater capacity for contemplation because of this; nor even for the reason that they boast that they will depart from their bodies through death, while claiming that the souls which forever govern the world are never permitted to do so. For they say these things out of a certain lack of experience <note>original: "imperitia" — a lack of practical or philosophical skill</note>, being ignorant of what is meant by "outside," and furthermore, not knowing in what manner the soul of the whole governs that which is inanimate. A faculty has been given to us, therefore, by which we should not indulge the body, but rather become pure in due time. Let us despise death; let us understand higher things with our intellect and follow them. Let us not envy those among them who can follow and always do follow, nor should we disparage them as if they were unable. Neither should we ever suffer the same error as many who think the stars do not move simply because their senses report that they are at rest. For because of this, they themselves do not think the nature of the stars looks upon the things which are "outside," since they do not see the soul of the stars existing externally <note>Plotinus argues that just because we see the physical body of a star, we shouldn't assume its soul is trapped within it; its soul transcends the physical body while still governing it.</note>.

<column-break/>

Whatever they are able to contemplate, it would not result in more contemplation for them. Or because they say it is for them to depart when they die, but for those [souls] who forever care for the world, [they say it is not possible]; for they speak these things through inexperience of what that truly is. Or [they do not know] the way in which the soul of the universe takes care [of the world]. * <note>original: "πού τι" (pou ti)</note> somehow it does not allow those who are lovers of the body to become pure and to despise the things that are present. B Rather, one should choose those things, and pursue those which others who are able to pursue—or who pursue them always—do, and not envy them as if they did not pursue them. Nor should one suffer the same as those who think the stars do not run, because their sense-perception says they stand still. For because of these things, they also think the nature of the stars does not see the things outside, because they do not see their soul existing from the outside. C

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE
## FIRST BOOK OF THE THIRD EN-
## NEAD CONCERNING FATE.
### COMMENTARY.

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

**Concerning eternal things and their action: Concerning the causes of those things which come to be: Concerning four opinions regarding fate.**

<margin>302</margin>
In the order of things, some things merely "are," while others "become." Likewise, those which only "are" are either principles themselves or come from principles. Again, those which "become" either do so always or only at certain times. Indeed, those things which are primary, insofar as they are primary, cannot be referred back to other causes. For that which is simply first, simply has no cause. But that which is first in a specific category has no cause within that category. Thus, in the category of moving things, that which is moved by itself, insofar as it is the "prime mover," has no higher cause through which it is moved; however, it does have a cause through which it is intellectual. Similarly, the First Intellect is not properly an intellect through a higher cause, but insofar as it stands outside the One and the Good, it possesses its life from the higher things. The Good itself, however, has nothing from any cause.

Therefore, those things among the eternal that exist from a cause have their essence from that cause, which their action also perpetually accompanies. Which action is one thing (to speak from Plato’s view) and yet the same as "being" <note>original: "esse" — the fundamental existence of a thing</note>. Certainly, where action passes outside [to an external object], it is undoubtedly different from "being." Likewise, where action—even that which remains inside—proceeds from an added form <note>original: "adventitia forma" — a quality that is not part of a thing's core nature</note>, it is also different from "being." But where it is internal and perpetual, and comes only from the essential form, it is certainly the same as "being," or at least what is called "existing." For from that form and in that same form, "being" is both the source from which it arises and the place where the act resides. Thus, heating proceeding from fire into water is undoubtedly different from the "being" of fire. Again, the heat in glowing iron is different from the "being" of iron, because it comes from an added form. But in fire, being hot is nothing other than being fire.

Therefore, since in entirely eternal substances there is no added form, and because acting and being come from and exist in the same natural form—and so closely—rightly is acting the same as being. For we call "being" the act of essence and of essential form. This act is truly internal, and an utterly inward action. For this reason, since in the soul life is not an added form, "to live" is the "being" of the soul. Similarly, in the intellect itself, "to understand" <note>original: "intelligere"</note>, flowing naturally from the intellectual form, is the "being" of the intellect itself—especially since intellection is the primary action. Therefore, since it is most divine and ultimate in itself, it does not differ from "being." The Platonists certainly place this first: they do not properly place action in the Good itself, since all action is directed toward the Good. Thus far has been said concerning those things which properly "are"—which we wish to be neither under fate nor in fate.

But those things which "become"—if they become at a specific time—we consider subject to Fate. If they become always (that is, if they revolve perpetually), we place them not so much "under fate" as "in fate." In summary, we ought to refer every action placed in motion in any way (as if not entirely perfect) to a cause, and ultimately to a permanent one. Concerning that which is moved by another, there is no doubt that its motion and action proceed from another. Furthermore, that which is moved by itself—that is, by its own nature—has it by its own nature that it acts through movement; but that it acts and becomes "simply," it obtains from elsewhere. For a movable action, since it is more imperfect than a stable one, signifies that the essence in which it exists proceeds from another. But an action of this sort is guided by a certain stable power of the same essence. Surely, since motion, like a certain accidental thing, is in need of determination, and suffers from lack, scattering, and loss, it is rightly dependent to the highest degree. For this reason, it is prompted by the subject in which it exists, the efficient power from which it is produced, the end for whose sake it happens, and by a certain occasion...

Ficino transitions from Plotinus's critique of the Gnostics to a systematic investigation into the nature of necessity and the various philosophical schools' views on what governs the universe.</meta>

<page-num>219</page-num>
<header>ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ENNEADS</header>
<sig>i 2</sig>

depends on an instigator. Therefore, let no one dream that some "inclination" or collision of atoms, or a sudden movement of some body, or a similar inclination of the soul depending on no cause, gave a beginning to things. Instead, let everyone consider every action or passion <note>original: "actionem, vel passionem" — in a philosophical sense, "action" is doing something, while "passion" is having something done to you</note> of this kind to be produced by some higher cause, or even managed by all existing beings. 

Since, therefore, whatever happens at any time happens from a cause, we possess immediate and manifest causes in most cases. But where the immediate causes are not sufficiently clear, or are not enough to produce the effect, we rightly investigate more remote causes—especially when, under the same imminent immediate cause, an effect follows in one case but not in another. And when similar results do not happen to everyone from similar human works. Likewise, where fortune and the coincidence of things favor someone beyond the merits of their actions, or the opposite. Finally, the diversity of talents, characters, and fortunes—which cannot be so great solely from the causes known to us—compels us to track down more hidden and superior causes. 

In the investigation of hidden causes, the opinion regarding Fate arose among philosophers. Indeed, they define Fate by a certain common notion as a certain necessity imposed upon things from above. Since, therefore, there are four principal opinions concerning principles, there are naturally four opinions concerning Fate. For some insert necessity into things from certain bodies which they take to be principles; some of these warned against randomness, whether it be from atoms and collisions, as **Democritus** <note>A Greek philosopher who proposed that the universe is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms</note> held, or whether necessity is inserted by the nature and motions of certain other bodies, as they say was pleasing to **Thales**, **Anaximenes**, and **Anaximander**. Others think that a single life-principle is infused into all things, by which individual things are moved everywhere by fatal necessity, which some **Stoics** <note>Philosophers who believed in a world-soul and that all events are strictly determined by a rational, divine chain of cause and effect</note> wanted. There are also those among the **Astronomers** who think the revolutions of the celestial bodies are the principle and fate of all things. Nor are there lacking among the physicists and metaphysicians those who think individual things happen daily from a certain series and connection of all causes to one another, whether celestial, superior, or even inferior. And from this, they believe Fate hangs over all things, whether such a heap of causes has one single beginning or not.

### Neither are all things forced or made by bodies: nor would there be fate or prophecy if the principles of things were random.

III. We have sufficiently shown in our *Theology* <note>original: "Theologia" — Ficino refers to his own work, *Platonic Theology*, where he argues for the immortality of the soul</note> that the nature of bodies proceeds from an incorporeal cause, and that all things ultimately come from one cause providing for all. Again, we proved in the book *On Love* that the common beauty of bodies consists in order, measure, and form <note>original: "ordine et modo specieque"</note>, and that these three, and beauty itself, are something incorporeal. **Democritus** himself admits that the motion of atoms lacks order. Thus, one cannot easily produce the highest order of the universe from things that are inferior in order to those that are always continuous. 

Furthermore, it is clear that the mass of all bodies, by the very fact that it is corporeal, does not maintain order, because order, measure, form, and beauty in the mass of the world are more excellent than the mass itself; moreover, they are incorporeal. For this reason, they are propagated into the body from a more excellent, incorporeal, rational, and living nature. And that which is most immediate is the Soul, the driver of bodies, the Mind, and the Good itself, which is the beginning and end of the universe. Therefore, order itself, and the Reason from which order comes, and the Soul in which Reason resides, do not follow bodies, but precede them. 

Now, truly, whoever derives all things from the disordered motion of bodies cannot assert a fatal necessity for things. To introduce a contingency <note>original: "contingentiam" — the idea that things happen by chance or could be otherwise</note> devoid of order into the principles is nothing other than to exclude Fate from things. For in this way, no thing at all will come forth determinately and necessarily if there is no order from which one thing follows another in succession. 

Now, however, what has been done, at least after it has been done, is said to have been done necessarily: because, clearly, while it was happening in the present, it happened by a certain necessity. And all this conditional necessity, whether concerning the past or the present, proceeds from a certain superior nature which is simply Necessity itself. From this, it is established that not fortune, but rather necessity, should be placed in the principles. I omit the fact that if there were no order in things, in which one thing properly follows another, there could be no accurate prediction of the future, whether it be done by art, by some natural instinct, or by any other divine means. 

Moreover, from atoms or other bodies, there cannot proceed into the soul—by that path and motion—the vital and sensory vigor by which the soul moves itself and is moved; by which it suddenly and artistically imagines such varied things; by which it transcends the genus of bodies by contemplating and loving; by which it opposes the perturbations of the body; by which some souls are better suited than others for different disciplines, and indeed incorporeal ones; and which, finally, as if they were free and acting for the future, discern liberty from necessity. We have disputed more extensively in our *Theology* that the soul possesses a certain freedom.

### There is not only one agent in the universe.

IIII. Nor again should it be thought that the world is only one "animal" in such a way that there is only one soul and one body in it, and that all movements and effects everywhere are necessarily the proceeding works of only that same soul, and that there is no other cause besides it, and finally no other agent. For in this way, both the order of the whole chain of causes—in which people commonly think Fate consists—and the highest dignity would be taken away from the world if there were only one agent and mover in it, while all other things merely suffered and were moved. For the perfection of the world consists mostly in this: that this universe be maximally formal and active, and that in it there be the greatest possible order of forms and agents. 

Furthermore, since the whole nature of the First Agent is itself an altogether immense efficacy, it propagates many effective things, and therefore agents, from itself; since indeed even fire as an agent generates fire as an agent. Likewise, whatever the first mover alone acts upon and moves, it performs as well as possible. Yet many things seem to happen here and there outside of the most exact and best order, as far as individual natures are concerned. From this, it is clear that subsequent natures do not lack their own duty for acting. Finally, when the intellectual soul turns toward itself; when it distracts itself into opposite conjectures by deliberating; when it imitates, corrects, and restores the works of nature; when it progresses rightly in some things but transgresses in others; when it surmounts the order of both bodies and souls; it certainly declares that it is neither a part of the universal "animal" nor necessarily subject to it.

### Neither are we forced by the heavens, nor are all other things made only and necessarily by the heavens.

V. The third proponents of Fate are the astrologers—not all of them, I say, but many—and they say that Fate is that which is decreed for each person by the necessity established by their stars. They confirm that each person's lot is destined from there because...

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

<warning>Heavy staining and tape residue on the left margin; text slightly faded in some areas.</warning>

By the observation of the stars, future events for individuals are foretold. Furthermore, many changes occur in bodies due to the approach, departure, and arrangement of the celestial lights. Plotinus, however, can in no way tolerate the idea that a human being is necessarily driven by the shameful commands <note>original: "flagitis nutibus" — likely referring to the "shameful" or "wicked" dictates that astrologers claimed the stars imposed on human behavior</note> of rays flowing from the heavens. This is because the human body is not a continuous part of the world, nor is the human soul a part of the Soul of the World, nor is it created by the Soul of the World. Therefore, the human body possesses its own internal mover <term>motor: the principle or power that initiates movement or action within a being</term> besides its own shape, and it has its own progress. I say "mover" in the intellectual sense, which certainly transcends the body and the life of the world through its intellectual nature; for it is not just a part of the universe, but is something in itself through its own experience. And since our soul holds this common notion of the whole simply for the sake of all things, and within this notion individual goods are understood, the movement of the soul is not necessarily destined to this or that thing as if by a god, but can turn itself toward anything according to the variety of objects presented to it.

Indeed, long consideration of individual things, careful weighing of opposites in turn, and a precise choice—which soon results in a revocation to other consultations—declares that the soul is not driven by some natural force, or by a single power or natural instinct, but rather by a universal and free faculty of living and acting. Since, therefore, we have our own nature and efficacy, and consequently our own action, we do not merely suffer under celestial action. Instead, we receive the force of the heavens within us according to the character of our own property; unless we are doing something specific from that source, we likewise perform something within ourselves by our own property. 

The celestial influences around us also change according to the nature of places. For under the same signs and parts of the climates, where the influence of the stars is the same, diverse things are born at the same moment and time; these things happen differently according to the diversity of the site, the earth, the air, the water, the winds, the vapors, the customs, and the laws. Furthermore, offspring <note>original: "semines" — seeds or offspring</note> are for the most part like their parents and authors in whatever hour they are born and nourished, inasmuch as they receive much more from their own lineage than from the hour of birth. Even when they share a common place, generation, and nourishing nature, and are similar in form, they nevertheless often differ greatly in character and talent. This is because the diversity of souls, differing in both talent and character, arises from elsewhere than from these bodily causes. 

Finally, when the soul acts and the mind opposes the body—and does so for the sake of its own intelligence—it declares that it operates freely and does not depend on its own body, and therefore not on the celestial body. It seems that the celestial body can only act upon us through our body; however, we can rightly resist our body through both virtue and grace, and choose a life agreeable to the mind, even if it is unfavorable to the body. Often, while nature and ignorance remain in the body, some seeds <note>referring to children or people of the same lineage</note> choose differently among themselves simply because of the variety of their social circles. Even where nature has turned out differently in these individuals, they nonetheless choose similar things if a similar habit of reason has grown within them. At that point, we do not depend so much on the influx of bodies as on the abundance of intelligence and reason. 

As for the claim made by some that it is pointless for these things to be "caused" by the stars if they are merely "signified" by the stars, this has been refuted more diligently elsewhere. You, however, should conclude this: at any moment, and even in the same stadium, many different things can be born at once—different not only in particulars and accidents, but even in species and genus. To these, a very different fate falls, which is not drawn solely from the hour of birth, the nature of things, and fortune. This is also confirmed by the fact that very many people often perish together in the same common destruction, yet they were not born at the same hour, nor did they flow to the place of their destruction at the same time.

## How individual things are generated by their own natures with the heaven contributing. How celestial things signify, and how daemons <term>daemons: in the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</term> know and execute them.

THEREFORE, as we have argued elsewhere, in the specific generation of things, lower causes—as the proximate and proper causes—can do the most. Thus, this man is born, or that horse, not because of the time of birth, but because this one comes from a man and that one from a horse. Similarly, that this man is born in a certain way proceeds from the specific disposition of the parents rather than from some external, common, accidental, and completely momentary arrangement of the heavens. Nevertheless, the celestial influences joined to that process are very influential in providing a species or quality to the parents and the offspring. This is certainly true for the body, since it is produced by bodies in bodies, and is received according to the natural condition of the recipients. 

But the gifts of the soul—which do not obey the body, nor follow from the body, looking instead toward incorporeal things—cannot leap from the body of the heaven into the soul, nor can they be made through the most certain flow from one neighboring body to another. Having introduced these arguments, they skillfully investigate the incorporeal reasons of things. These do not follow the bodies of the heaven, but rather the incorporeal nature of the human mind, which is perhaps moved to this by the souls and minds of the stars themselves through the ministry of the contemplating daemons. 

Elsewhere we have demonstrated that it is wrong to say the stars, which are divine by nature, move toward evil by their motion in any way. It is better to say that when evil or imminent things are foretold by the observation of the heavens, these things are not *caused* by those good and orderly bodies, but are *signified* by them—just as people say things are signified by the flight and chatter of birds or other portents. The ability to signify consists in a certain mutual connection of things; daemons themselves, rather than men, can know this connection. This is what Origen argues and what Plotinus says here when he mentions those who "read the letters in the heaven." Plato also means this in the *Timaeus* when he indicates what happens or is signified by the arrangement of the heavens. 

To truly know these things is impossible without a diligent inspection of those "images." How much those images can accomplish is not for us to know, but for the daemons; for we lack the age, the eye, and the talent for it. Just as it is the primary duty of the daemons to hold the celestial signs and suggest them to us—whether we are sleeping or waking—so too it is often their role to execute what the heavens have portended at certain times. Better daemons execute better things, and worse daemons execute worse things. Through these spirits, after long cycles of time, those things can be fulfilled which that arrangement of the heavens—which has long since passed and can no longer act—once signified. 

Yet daemons do not move us in such a way that they compel us by necessity (as Plato says), for they lead the imaginative soul much more than the body. Although they act upon us not only by choice but also by a certain property of nature—just as stars appear to our eyes—they also act upon lower things through their own movements and affections, insofar as they accompany the celestial dance. But because they apply something of their own duty, the action and judgment of the heavens within us are combined. In this way, the things that the visible stars portended are subsequently suggested to us by "invisible stars"—that is, the daemons—and are partly executed by their powers. Hence that saying of Plato: They lead souls sliding into generation...

He explains that stars act as signs rather than direct causes of human character or "evil," with intermediary spirits (daemons) playing a role in interpreting and executing these celestial patterns.</summary>

### ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ENNEADS

daemons <note>original: "demones" — intermediate spirits between gods and humans</note>, once the life of the lot has been chosen, act as the executors of fate. Saturnian daemons indeed rule Saturnian souls and carry out Saturnian duties; Jovian daemons do the same for Jovian souls, and so on for the others. And just as there are men in any region who are partly Saturnian and partly Jovian, so too are there various daemons dwelling in any sphere of the world. Among the Saturnians, the better ones perform the better duties of Saturn, while the worse among them tend to carry out the worse outcomes under that same influence; and the same holds true for the Martians and the rest. But where Plotinus says that the daily motions of the celestial bodies are useful beyond the common welfare of the world—in that they signify the future to those capable of understanding—he shows that signified evils can be avoided, and signified goods can be further assisted. This is much more than a doctor is able to assist health based on the signs found within us; otherwise, the observation of signs in both astrology and medicine would be useless, and God, who prescribed the signs in the heavens to look out for the welfare of those below, would have warned us in vain.

->Those who introduce a necessary series of things, where every single event happens inevitably, take away both the contingency of this world and the freedom of counsel.<-

VII. The fifth opinion on fate, which we take up for consideration, agrees with the second opinion in that it thinks individual things are generated through seminal reasons <term>seminal reasons: "rationes seminales," the internal formative powers or "blueprints" that direct the growth of all living things</term> by a single vital principle infused in all things, which was chiefly proven by Strato. It differs, however, in that they think not only is such a vital principle effective, but many other things besides it possess some efficacy of action. Yet, they act only as they are pulled by what came before. They add that causes follow one after another in a continuous chain and are so connected that many things are necessarily deduced and pronounced from those prior, and whatever they do, they do by necessity. Whatever happens there, happens necessarily. They suggest causes for every event everywhere, though they may establish them differently in different places; this seems to have been primarily the opinion of Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus was a major Stoic philosopher who argued for a deterministic universe where everything is linked by cause and effect</note>. For the present, let it be said that this openly takes away contingency from things—a contingency which all the most learned men believe occurs at least in the lowest parts of the world. Plotinus seems to detest this above all, because it deprives the rational soul of its freedom of choice and its authority over action in the present doubt—if indeed it were true, as they say, that any volition of the soul proceeds necessarily from some impulse, appetite from imagination, and imagination from a series of preceding events acting either within us or around us. But how shameful it would be to subject the intellectual soul—incorporeal, separate from the body, and looking up to the divine—to the necessity of bodies, as we have shown sufficiently in our *Platonic Theology*. Moreover, the doctors and others who speak of "interrogations" <note>In astrology, an "interrogation" is a question asked to the stars to determine a specific outcome</note> show that not every movement of the mind is driven by the heavens. For they say that an interrogation and judgment only have an effect when the seeker asks with a certain vehement anxiety, as if only then does the seeker seem to be moved by something external in the heavens. But when the interrogation is not anxious, the answer is most deceptive, as if the interrogator were then not being moved by the heavens. What more? Our study and industry in opposing fate is not given to us by fate. The worship of the super-celestial God is finally resolved in a cause higher than the heavens.

->How the soul is above fate, in fate, and under fate.<-

VIII. The common opinion of philosophers concerning fate is that it is a certain necessity brought upon things by the conspiracy <note>original: "conspiratione" — here meaning a "breathing together" or harmonious cooperation of causes</note> of corporeal causes. But since both the motion of bodies proceeds from the soul, and the order of corporeal forms proceeds from the intellect, we rightly judge that the intellectual soul is naturally free from the necessity usually imposed by bodily motion and order. So far is the soul from being subject to fate that she herself is the principle of fate itself—if indeed fate is a series of bodies, and this series depends on intellectual souls. By the Soul of the Universe, I say, the entire series is contained; and by other souls endowed with a similar intelligence, the series is contained elsewhere, partly in general and partly in particular. There are, therefore, two kinds of causes in fate: I call them "animal" <note>from "anima" (soul)</note> causes, such as the principles of fate, which are souls adapting themselves to ruling bodies; and again, corporeal causes, which are like the complex of fate. Furthermore, there is a triple order: of all bodies toward the first body, of corporeal souls toward the first Soul, and of bodies toward souls—and through souls to the first Soul, and through that intellectual soul to the first Intellect. Thus, the entire series of fates is finally reduced to divine providence. If, therefore, the soul is entirely outside the body, she is likewise outside of fate; if she is in the body, insofar as she naturally indulges the body, she suffers under fate, and she herself suffers within fate to that extent. But if she separates herself from the body as much as possible, and having been freed, now adapts her vegetative power <term>vegetative power: the basic biological functions of growth and nutrition</term> to it, she is counted in fate only as an agent. She acts, however, according to the condition of fortune; some things she herself changes by her natural faculty, or corrects and amends by some art, or most easily tolerates through magnanimity. That the soul undergoes fate only insofar as she involves herself in the body is shown by Timaeus <note>The speaker in Plato's "Timaeus"</note> when he says that souls first learned the laws of fate when they were joined to their "vehicles" <note>In Platonic thought, the "vehicle" is a subtle, quasi-physical body the soul inhabits before birth</note>; for from this point the beginnings of fate are drawn. But meanwhile, Plato declares in both the *Timaeus* and the tenth book of the *Republic* that the soul approaches fate by free fear and can release herself whenever she chooses, saying that God gave souls both the laws of fate and the reason of divine and human law alike, so that God might exist without blame, and he adds that virtue and reason are free.

->How the soul is in fate as an agent, and how as a patient; likewise on the contingency of things.<-

IX. To those, however, who were saying that whatever exists happens necessarily and inevitably because all causes are connected at once—and once all causes are positioned everywhere, the effect necessarily follows—it is now objected in this way: Even if that were granted to you, the mind can still retain its authority. For the mind itself is in the order of causes: both natural causes, insofar as it does not suffer but acts upon the body through its vegetative power, and those causes which act by will, and therefore move freely from within themselves. When, therefore, the mind has decreed to move the tongue or an arm, the movement in the limb happens necessarily, provided that all causes concur—namely, along with choice and purpose, all surrounding circumstances, which is to say whatever exists besides the mind, the concurrence of which is here called "fortune." This means, of course, that the limbs must be fit and nothing stands in the way. Also numbered among the external causes designated by the name of fortune is anything from the motion of the universe that, along with subsequent causes, contributes to the work. Thus, the work proceeds by necessity, but not as if souls were...

<summary>Ficino explores the relationship between the human soul and fate, arguing that while the body and lower biological functions may be subject to celestial necessity, the intellectual soul remains free and can even act as a cause of fate. He refutes Stoic determinism by asserting that God granted souls free will and the ability to transcend bodily constraints through reason and virtue.</summary>
