--- Page 257 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book III. It develops the distinction between "acting" (active, internal movement) and "suffering" (passive, external movement). Ficino is explaining how the wise soul maintains its freedom from the stars and fate by retreating into contemplation, while also addressing why this freedom is sometimes lost through physical illness or demonic influence.</meta>

[The soul] when compelled is moved to its work, if it neither follows an impulse creeping in from the body by choice, nor thinks about external convenience or inconvenience regarding bodily things. It does not look at external things at all, nor is it deceived by false opinion, but it possesses intellect and certain reason, free from passion, as its guide; it directs all things toward its own best state as if toward a goal. From the fact that the wise soul directs its actions toward itself as toward an end, it is certain that it possesses an internal rather than an external principle of action. To this extent, the soul is judged to act, because it operates through its own proper, intimate, and principal form, and for its own sake. 

But when the soul itself first degenerates from its own nature, or acts out of ignorance, or is incited from the outside and marked by the body, it approaches something by looking toward things other than the soul; then it is judged not so much to act as to suffer <note>original: "pati" — to be passive or acted upon</note>. However, it acts most of all when it not only operates from itself for its own sake, but also acts within itself through itself alone without instruments—that is, when it exercises the duty of contemplation. 

Truly, when it either lives a life of pleasure without moderation or follows an active life without prudence, it serves and suffers most heavily. Yet, as often as it leads an active life with prudence, it partly acts itself and is partly acted upon, insofar as it is incited to motion by external things and performs its service according to the condition of those around it. Remember, however, that Plotinus is speaking here of the things that closely surround us, which he calls "fortune"; he thinks this should not necessarily be reduced in every case to celestial fates, as if fate arranged things to the fingernail <note>idiom: "ad unguem" — perfectly or precisely</note> in the same way that celestial things arrange themselves. For order in these lower things is not as exact as in those higher things, nor is their stability equal, nor their harmony similar. 

Hence that saying of Plotinus: The effects of the celestial bodies upon us occur according to the condition of the lower causes. Just as natural effects have a far greater similarity with nearby causes than with remote ones. Furthermore, the influences of the celestial bodies are often not so much causes as signs; for this reason, he speaks with a certain qualification when he says: "And if anything besides from the motion of the heavens contributes to the work." Finally, he thinks that the soul, through human diligence and virtue, can sometimes change the order that might perhaps proceed from there to here.

### Intellectual nature acts freely, but its effect is sometimes hindered in reason.

X He concludes, therefore, that things are not driven by chance, but that there is an order in things following through causes, from which things can be skillfully made and signified. Nor, again, are all things always struck by external necessity; for it is necessary that there be not only things moved from the outside, but also those moved from within. And of those moved from within, some are moved by a certain determined instinct of nature, but others by an absolute, ample, and free principle. Otherwise, the order of movable things will either be nonexistent or will not be reduced to the highest principle; and those things which are movable through another would not be referred back to that which is movable by itself (which must, however, exist). 

For that which is carried solely by the instinct of nature does not move itself, but is either driven by the one imprinting that nature—in the manner of an arrow—or is drawn by something kindred, just as iron is drawn by a magnet. For this reason, the intellectual soul performs all things with a certain best, that is, intellectual reason. By "reason," he means that in whatever the soul produces through a totally universal and absolute reason, it acts from an intellectual principle and does not suffer. For according to Plotinus and most of the great philosophers, the intellectual [act] of the wise man does not have an external cause (as if inciting it from things encountered), but it shines from within itself and sparkles internally, with absolutely nothing hindering it up to this point. It also flashes into the reason nearest to the intelligence, using that intelligence as long as it is not hindered. 

However, it is commonly hindered due to a certain distraction of the soul toward many things, and specifically in those who are either born insane or become so. These become insane in three main ways: they become either dull, or forgetful, or senseless, or furious. The cause of this insanity is sometimes the foulness of the senses and the physical instruments, sometimes the rising of vapors <note>historical medical theory: "vapores" — gases produced by bodily fluids that affect the brain</note>, sometimes an overly intense focus of the imagination by which the act of reason is weakened, sometimes the excessive occupation of nature with the cure of a disease, and finally a certain demonic occupation. 

Perhaps, indeed, just as monstrous actions in our behavior usually proceed from us at the instigation of weak daemons <note>original: "demonum" — intermediate spirits, here suggesting lower or "bad" spirits</note>, so insanity often occurs through a certain mixed engine of daemons. Just as they stir up the sensible vapors of the humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament</term> and images to incite vices, so they sometimes provoke both vapors and images in the phantasy <note>imagination</note> to incite and thoroughly strengthen it, so that from there reason is either weakened or mocked. 

Indeed, the elder Serapio and Avicenna <note>Serapio and Avicenna were highly influential medieval medical authorities</note> do not deny that insanity is caused by daemons wonderfully irritating the humors, and the Gospel testifies to this everywhere: where those seized by a daemon are healed, the insane are cured. For it is not likely that a soul participating in divinity would either sin so wickedly or be so insane unless it were moved additionally by a demonic nature. This is perhaps why he said in the second chapter that the immense diversity of talents and characters does not come from manifest and nearby causes alone. Therefore Paul the Apostle said that our struggle is not merely against the body, but against the "dark daemons" <note>reference to Ephesians 6:12</note> destined for this air. 

Therefore, a prosperous disposition of the humors and limbs, or the position of the stars, does not *create* wisdom, but signifies that the *use* of wisdom is not hindered by an opposite disposition or position. Once this hindrance is removed from us, the light of wisdom flashes forth by itself. What we have said about daemons is also confirmed by Porphyry in his book *On Oracles*: "The bodies of men," he says, "are full of malignant daemons, especially those who live on more delicate banquets. For while we are eating, they approach and cling to the body; therefore fasting and chastity are greatly praised. Not because God, who is properly good, is pleased by them in that way, but so that those who rejoice in blood and impurity might depart—those who enter the bodies of the voluptuous so that they too may enjoy these things." 

For it is certain that the vehement desire for these same things and the force of a lustful spirit grow excessively strong from no other source than the presence of malignant daemons. Therefore, when the appetite is more vehemently inflamed, and the heat of pleasure so tosses the soul that every thought wanders toward external things, then know that daemons of this kind are present; their presence causes the spirit, which is naturally greedy in us, to grow. He says these things there, which he also confirms in his book *On Abstinence* in almost the same words.

<summary>Ficino explains that the human soul is truly "active" only when it operates through internal reason and contemplation, independent of external fate. He also attributes madness and vice to a combination of physical humors and the interference of malignant daemons who are attracted to bodily excess.</summary>

## MARSILIAN SUMMARY.

### That not everything arises from fatal necessity.

### I.

<image-desc>A large woodcut ornamental initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or philosopher, within a circular frame surrounded by decorative foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>

Since you truly desire, Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron</note>, to understand separately what Marsilio Ficino thinks about these matters, I shall take up the subject again from its highest beginning. It is established that the Good itself <note>referring to God or the Neoplatonic "One"</note> provides for all things, arising from the order of all things marvelously established toward a certain end. In this order, individual things are everywhere directed toward their own specific good, and all things together contribute to the common good. And if it seems surprising that the Good itself, in the order of its providence, permits evil, it must be admitted that it often permits it for the sake of the good; specifically, it permits the destruction of things so that infinite faces of new forms may thereafter be generated. The conflict between forms does not allow these to exist at the same time, nor does physical space admit them. Since God is simply goodness itself, yet not simply necessity itself, but rather gives himself to the good, he is opposed to God—if I may put it this way—more by will than by contingency. Therefore, if He permits evil, he certainly also permits contingency <note>original: "contingentiam" — events that happen by chance or choice, rather than by fixed necessity</note>, since he everywhere brings back good into good. 

For a contingent experience reduces back into the necessary. Whatever has been done by acting could have happened or not have happened; yet the whole of it, while it already exists, is necessary to exist; since it is of the past, it is necessary that it be present. And when all circumstances are gathered from every side through a conclusion, the necessary often seems to emerge from the contingent. Furthermore, one should not think that the opposite of the "necessity of fate," according to formal reason, is that which is called "the impossible." For in that which is formally necessary, no opposition ought to be included; for that is necessary in which it is included that the opposite is impossible. Indeed, even that which cannot be is false. That which cannot be is necessarily non-existent. Likewise, the impossible seems to be included in the necessary itself; for that which is necessary is also "impossible not to be." 

Therefore, "necessary" and "contingent" are placed in opposition. For just as necessity itself is the ratio <note>reason or principle</note> for healthy being, or for being alone if it is finite, so a single principle of contingency verges toward being and non-being equally. But between the necessary and that which happens equally either way, the "frequent contingent" <note>original: "contingens vt plurimum" — things that usually happen but aren't guaranteed</note> seems to be the middle ground, the opposite of which happens more rarely. Thus, it is necessary for the human species to exist; but it happens equally that a man will be manly or upright by himself. That the human hand has five fingers happens for the most part; it is rarer to have only four. The order requires a "true contingency" that is equal toward both outcomes, so that if the necessary is given, its opposite is also given. In this opposition, a distinction is found in what is called "being" itself; thus, by that very fact, an opposite to formal necessity must be given, and it is necessary that the contingent exist equally toward both outcomes. 

Again, if we must give that which is opposite by reason of matter, we say to that which is necessary—as it opposes it—that it is impossible to exist. Between these, however, we shall place the "possible" as a middle, and that is the contingent; sometimes it is more frequent, approaching closer to the necessary, and sometimes rarer, appearing to decline toward the impossible; and sometimes it is indifferently "to be" or "not to be" contingent, which must certainly be granted as true and equally distant, and by this reasoning, a middle between the necessary and the impossible. 

Contingency is born by the very order of things descending through many continuous steps. In this order, the things that are closer to the beginning are entirely immobile—namely, the Intellects. Then, those things just a little further away are moved only by a "formal motion" while the substance does not change; these are those substances <note>referring to the celestial spheres or stars</note> which give of their substance while they move themselves, and are meanwhile rolled by a certain local motion, and again from a formal motion insofar as they are changed in turn through certain configurations in their orbit. But they move (if I may say so) immovably, insofar as they are always revolved in the same necessary order. Following this, it results that those things which are "under the heavens" <note>sublunary or terrestrial things</note> are now moved in a mobile way. 

In this wandering lot of motions, contingency is born, because things that move this way seem to diverge and stray from their own specific order, although they cannot cross the common order of the universe. For since the effective power is diminished through many successive steps of agents, and a multitude of many conflicting forms flows together, it certainly follows that every specific nature sometimes fails in its duty, while its power—weakened by the offering—is sometimes more easily hindered by the incursion of different things. Thus, the seeds <note>original: "seminaria"</note> of a plant or animal do not always produce their natural offspring, nor do they produce them everywhere at the right time, nor do they produce them perfectly. Therefore, although—as far as the celestial nature is concerned—this offspring of a plant or animal would come forth as an absolute and undoubtedly necessary thing in its proper time, it nevertheless happens sometimes that it happens imperfectly, or does not come forth at all, because the specific or intrinsic nature of the parent fails, or is hindered from the outside. 

Often the present disposition of the heavens seems just about to produce a certain quality in this matter, but the quality of a different matter, contracted from nearby causes and conditions, changes the effect of the heavens in one way or another. Nor should anyone object to us that this quality of matter also happened from the celestial bodies because the "proximate" <note>immediate or local</note> causes are moved by the celestial ones. Let it be that they are indeed moved, but they move according to their own nature. For neither does God, while he acts through the heavens upon lower things, take away his gifts from the heavens; nor does the heaven, when it acts through lower causes upon our affairs, meanwhile withdraw the proper and natural powers and actions of these causes. 

Therefore, since the effect and condition of every form usually arises alongside the "affection" <note>disposition or state</note> of matter, and this state of matter comes from the celestial bodies in a general way, but from the proximate causes in a specific way, it follows that the specific effect of a created earthly thing comes forth as the proximate cause requires the matter to be affected, rather than how the remote cause <note>the stars</note> seems to tempt or incline it. For if the remote cause is necessary, it does not mean that every event follows necessarily from it, unless the proximate cause was also necessary. Now it is manifest, as we have often said, that individual effects turn out more similar to their own proximate causes than to remote ones; just as any plants and animals are judged not so much by their similarity to celestial bodies as to their own parents and the seeds from which they are born. From this it is clear that effects of this kind sort their nature and follow their seeds rather than the celestial ones; and according to the condition of familiar causes and all surrounding circumstances (all of which are changeable), they happen changeably, not necessarily according to the condition of the heavens. And rightly so, because nature does not retain its being as a necessity, but can fail from it; it should also be noted that power is not necessary, but sometimes falls away from action. For which reason, things that were perhaps necessary...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical defense of human free will against strict astrological determinism. Following the previous page’s introduction on providence and contingency, Ficino now explains how the pure, orderly influence of the heavens becomes distorted and varied as it descends into the "greedy" and "conflicting" realm of matter.</meta>

COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

indicated from heaven, those same things occur among us in this material region contingently <note>that is, by chance or without absolute necessity</note>. Matter, I say, which is always greedy for all forms equally. In this region, I say, because here innumerable and conflicting qualities flow together. Therefore, although the celestial influx <note>the spiritual and physical influence of the stars</note> proceeds according to a definite order toward a certain goal, it becomes confused by this matter—which is easily susceptible to other influences—and loses its form as it prepares to receive another. Furthermore, this region, being full of discordant qualities, immediately mixes and transforms that influence, so that a certain result rarely arises here from heaven exactly as intended. It can hardly be guessed what will be born unless, perhaps, you have surveyed the whole universe: considering how many and what kind of conditions and causes flow together at any given moment from above, from the middle, and from the lowest depths, and what might arise from the combination of all these things. 

Accordingly, if corporeal nature—which is more obviously subject to the celestial body and seems determined toward one particular thing—does not necessarily receive celestial influences exactly as they are sent from heaven, then much less does the rational soul. The soul’s capacity and movement are both intimate and vast; it often transcends the physical category and resists the body. It does not necessarily follow celestial instinct. Indeed, nature would have given the soul the power of daily deliberation in vain—allowing it to propose many opposing choices based on different conjectures—unless it could lead itself to the truth by choosing as it pleases. It could not turn toward either side of a choice if it were compelled toward a fixed path by the daily constitution of the heavens. Added to this is the fact that since divine providence permits a degree of contingency in natural things arising from their defects, it permits it much more in voluntary beings <note>humans</note>, where this contingency arises from perfection. This is truly more characteristic of them, since natural things are moved only by an impressed form, while voluntary beings are moved and act based on a conceived notion as well.

Add to this that every celestial influx, insofar as it comes from heaven as the nearest instrument of divine providence and is thus marvelously ordered, always leads toward a certain order. Therefore, if we often wander without right order and stray from the best form, this happens not because of heaven, and much less because of the mover of heaven <note>God</note>, but from the lingering condition of our own race or the state of fortune. Now, if the disposition of our race can pervert the celestial influx from its ordinary and good state into its opposite, it can much more easily turn itself from one quality to another. Nature intended all things to descend by degrees through their weight. All things will therefore descend by a certain heavy impulse of nature unless they are perhaps impeded. They can undoubtedly be impeded from moving; often they are even cast down by a sharp and more rapid force than nature usually bears. Then they produce themselves according to either a natural or artificial shape—one slides down a slope, another is thrown into disorder. For one will slide as a square, another as a cylinder, and another as an angular figure; this is what that famous Chrysippus <note>original: "Chrysippus ille" — a Stoic philosopher known for his "cylinder" analogy to explain how fate and character interact</note> confesses, though he was a great advocate of the heavens. 

Therefore, in a similar way, the present constitution of the heaven at this hour seems likely to bring heat to the bodies and vehemence to the souls of those being born. But in one person, the cold and moist nature of the parents, the place, the time, and the nourishment tempers the prevailing power of heaven and perhaps turns it to the opposite. In another, the hot and dry nature of those same factors leads the moderate quality coming from heaven into a mixed state. Again, the specific and varied natures of the parents and the children, as well as different laws and customs, might distinguish that impulse of mind and body descending from heaven through various moderations of degrees. Thus it happens, as we have often said, that effects usually arise not so much according to the nature of the distant agent <note>the stars</note> as according to the condition of the proximate agents <note>the parents or environment</note> and, finally, according to the affection of the matter and the layout of the place. 

What more? The same ray of the Sun acts differently in different ways: if it strikes directly rather than obliquely; if it passes through clear air rather than through thick fog. It is terrestrial things, not celestial ones, that make the air foggy. Likewise, it acts one way if it encounters wax and another if it encounters mud; for it liquefies the former and dries out the latter. Again, if it hits ice rather than crystal: it sometimes melts the ice, but never the crystal. If it shines on snow on a mountain peak rather than snow in a mountain hollow: for it melts the latter more quickly. One may often see on the same peak that snow fallen at the same time melts away more quickly on the side facing south, while on the northern side it lasts longer. Although one part is hardly distant from the other, even a brief discrepancy in position produces such a result. Finally, if the ray acts for a short time, it often gathers mists, but over a long time, it disperses them. It acts one way through open spaces and another through hollows; it benefits some at the same time, while harming others even in the same place. 

The powers of superior things are so changed by place and matter that, while the waters mostly rise and fall according to the movement of the Moon, not all do so equally. For even the sea does not suffer this everywhere or equally; and where it seems to observe this most, it is often prevented from rising by a contrary wind. There are specific qualities of places under every star: some of marshes, others of fields, others of inhabited hills, and others of forests. Likewise, due to the variety of heat, cold, dryness, moisture, winds, vapors, rivers, and valleys, the qualities are vastly different regardless of which star hangs over them. From this arise different lifespans, various bodily habits, and different capacities of intellect. No matter at what moment they are born, many born at the same time do not fall ill at the same time because they live in different places. Many not born at the same time fall ill together because of a similar path, cloud, or vapor; and regardless of when they were born or what age they have reached, they fall into disease together if they have converged in a contagious region. 

In short, although universal superior causes have a broad, intimate, and long-lasting power over effects, the intermediate causes mixed with the birth and the proximate factors can contribute very much to the specific qualities of events. Thus, the effects turn out to be much more similar to the proximate causes. For the most common influences of distant causes are gradually determined and distinguished by succeeding causes. Just as the life-giving power of heaven favors all newborns in common, it is narrowed down to those very species in different types of plants and animals; and in each individual within a species, it is contracted to singular properties. Natural actions and passions then take on specific characteristics—following the two principles <note>likely form and matter</note> first, and then the special principles rather than the most universal ones everywhere. This is especially true when the most universal principles are "equivocal" <note>producing different effects from the same cause</note> and are very different in kind from their effects; no one denies that celestial things are such. 

However, lest someone should object that whatever is in the secondary cause comes from the first, and whatever is found in the third is attributed entirely to the second—and thus nothing comes from subsequent causes that does not likewise come from the superior ones—remember that the nature of a subsequent cause is not only similar to the superior one, insofar as it receives from it, but also...

<meta>Catchword: "also" (Latin: etiam) indicates the text continues on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains that celestial influences are universal and orderly, but their actual effects are determined by local conditions, the "greed" of matter, and human choice. He uses the analogy of the sun's rays acting differently on wax and mud to illustrate how the same heavenly cause produces diverse terrestrial results.</summary>

Ficino is arguing that while the heavens provide a general influence, the specific outcomes on Earth are shaped by local nature, biological processes, and human choice, rather than a rigid, fatalistic necessity.</meta>

...it even becomes dissimilar, insofar as it has proceeded outward; it has not only degenerated from its source, but has moreover become something else, differing by a certain quality of its own. It is just as a ray of light is soothing in the heavens but becomes varied on the earth; likewise, it is shining in the heavens but turns red in a cloud. Thus, it is no wonder if something happens here from time to time that does not properly proceed from the heavens themselves. Therefore, many things can be brought about by causes lower than the heavens—things of a sort that are not produced by the heavens. Remember again that these causes below the Moon are driven with a stronger force by the "life of the world" <note>the *Anima Mundi*, or World Soul, which animates the entire universe</note>, not only through themselves, but also carried directly through the vegetative soul <note>the *anima vegetalis*, the basic level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition</note>, a power flourishing everywhere. Just as the life of an animal gives many things to the feet and hands through the principal limbs—not only through itself—those things it gives through the principal limbs are also transformed within them. Finally, nutrients conceive a power from the concurrence of unified causes which is properly found in none of them individually; just as from a flow of materials and qualities, a certain new material and quality results. 

Nor indeed should we here entirely place contingencies <note>events that happen by chance or could be otherwise</note> under the rule of necessity. Only a man of reason can rightly contemplate a line emerging under a changing state from a multitude of unities, and see things themselves under a simple unity and state through a certain multitude. For mobile things, through a long stretch of degrees, eventually arrive at a nearly innumerable number and an uncertain mobility; it is in this most ample distinction of degrees and downward order that the things of the universe consist. For this reason, all these individual motions and passions, which vary into an infinitely multiple multitude and mobility, cannot be properly distributed or led by celestial powers and motions. These celestial motions are defined by a certain number and proceed in a certain order, such that they do not vary in that way—unless perhaps someone were so delirious as to assign every single movement of madmen or playing children, at every moment, to individual celestial shifts. According to such a person, a fingernail, feet, limbs, joints, eyes, senses, or imagination would move in no other way at any given moment than as that celestial influx dictates. To such people, even the flight of flies across innumerable leaps of space, and any accidental stumbles whatsoever, would be so dictated. 

But surely not all things are done entirely or compelled by heaven; indeed, even the works and actions of the elements, mixtures, plants, and animals would not exist without their own input. Fire heats under any star and <unclear>uarrat</unclear> <note>original: "uarrat," likely a typo for "narrat" or "servat" (preserves)</note> it by a property of nature, which under that star makes or generates water and other similar things. For this reason, however the heavens may hold themselves, as long as natural law remains constant, both non-living and living things act—or rather, are acted upon—through motion, appetite, indulgence, and imagination. They are clearly carried toward those things so that, because they exist and live in common, they can act and move in common, just as celestial bodies are moved. However, that they exist in such a species and with a singular property, they have from their parents and from the place, and from those who in turn perform such actions. That there are so many and such species in the universe results both from the illustrious fruits of the Divine Mind and from the "seminal reasons" <note><term>seminal reasons</term>: *rationes seminales*, the latent formative principles in nature that guide development</note> of the soul. For the species themselves are the definitions of things, and it does not happen by chance that there is always a most ordered beauty within them, even when they come from formless matter. This beauty is subject to form, and is equally superior to the movement of the celestial state. For form is immobile and prior to its own eternal state; or rather, it is granted by celestial forms and figures, which cannot be described as species in heaven in that way. Many species of things are incorporeal, and their formal order is skillfully directed toward an end by a certain intelligence proceeding from that end.

### Confirmation against celestial fate by Alexander, Oenomaus, Diogenianum, and Ptolemy.

II Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A famous commentator on Aristotle (c. 200 AD) who defended free will</note>, in his book *On Fate* addressed to Antonius, refutes the opinion of Chrysippus <note>The Stoic philosopher who argued for a strict chain of causal fate</note> regarding fate. With many arguments, he shows that fate or the "fatal" is nothing other than what nature is. He shows that some things happen contrary to the ritual of nature, as it sometimes happens that an impediment holds nature back. Therefore, since certain things happen contrary to nature, surely if "to happen by nature" is fate, then things also happen "contrary to fate." Let us see if human works are separated from that fate, and if something else exists according to their particular nature. We know that a natural habit of the body of this kind can be turned toward the better by a diligent rule of living, by the art of physicians, and by the counsel of the gods. Similarly, souls that are driven—not without their own natural inclination, which they have as if from the complexion of the body—often become better through exercise and art. 

Whence, when the physiognomist <note>One who judges character from facial features</note> Zopyrus said certain foul things about Socrates that were foreign to his virtue, and many people wanted him to be mocked, Socrates responded: "Zopyrus is not wrong. For I would have been such by nature, had I not overcome nature through philosophy." Therefore, such are those things over which nature presides; do these natural things differ at all from fatal ones? But in truth, those things happen by fortune <note>luck or chance</note> which are in no way intended. When certain things happen for the sake of one thing, and something else occurs that was expected from intuition: such as if someone digging a field finds a treasure, when he was not digging for that reason; these are certainly not done by fate. There are, however, certain causes entirely unknown to men. For some things suspended from heaven are said to cure certain diseases, for which we certainly have no known cause. It is also uncertain what cause magical incantations and arts may have. 

But besides these, there are some things which are named as "likely contingencies," which we deny happen by fate at all—such as living, sleeping, standing, speaking, and other such things that occur freely and can in no way be forced by fate. For what is fatal cannot happen contrary to what is hoped. Furthermore, the counsel of man ought not to be entirely in vain. It would be in vain if whatever we did, we did by necessity. Without doubt, man possesses this above all other animals: he does not follow imagination everywhere in the same way, but possesses reason, by which he judges what must be done. He knows by experience those things which they even tell to the uncertain or examine; if indeed he approves by examining, he grants it to his imagination and is then moved to act. But if he disapproves, he rejects and expels those things, obeying reason. Therefore, we are accustomed to deliberate about such things as we are able to do or not do; and if ever we do not use counsel, but commit something through headlong desire, we later accuse ourselves of the crime of despising counsel and of rashness. We also blame everyone who acts rashly, and we urge them to use counsel, as if the power of acting were in our hands. That the opinion held about fate is completely false is clear from this: that even the authors of such an opinion teach, discuss, urge, and advise; they even rebuke and punish their own people as if they sinned by their own will. Therefore, even according to them, there is no necessity of fate. Our liberty is therefore naturally in all of us; yet we concede that many things are not in our power, such as those which belong to nature or fortune, which no one will dare to say are subject to no fate. These are the words of Alexander. Oenomaus the philosopher <note>A Cynic philosopher known for his vitriolic attack on oracles and fatalism</note> relates almost similar things against Chrysippus, excluding brute animals.

<summary>This page argues against strict astrological determinism, asserting that while celestial influences exist, they are modified by material conditions and overcome by human reason and philosophy. Ficino cites Alexander of Aphrodisias and the famous anecdote of Socrates and Zopyrus to prove that character and fate can be mastered through the intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument that human affairs are not strictly governed by the stars. He draws on various historical authorities to show that reason, custom, and law allow humans to act independently of celestial "necessity."</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...by a certain appetite of its own, it happens to move at any given moment, rather than by some necessary chain of causes. This is much more true for human beings, who live by their own counsel; through their own industry, they are able to alter many of the causes that contribute less directly to a final result. The philosopher Diogenianus <note>A 2nd-century Epicurean philosopher known for his critiques of Stoic determinism</note> confirms these same points in his book against Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus was a leader of the Stoic school who argued that everything happens by fate</note>. He proves that not everything happens through a necessary chain of inevitably concurring causes; rather, some things happen by a specific and singular nature, others by fortune <note>random chance</note>, others by our own counsel, and others by the will of the gods. Ptolemy also confirms this in many places, and specifically in his *Quadripartitum* <note>original: "Quadripartito"; also known as the *Tetrabiblos*, the foundational text of Western astrology</note>, saying that while effects proceed from God to the heavens and among the heavens themselves in an unbreakable chain, they do not always proceed from the heavens to the lower world inevitably or in the exact order begun in the sky. For these effects can be changed or hindered, sometimes by the resistance of lower natures, and sometimes by human skill and counsel. Furthermore, in his *Book on Judgments*, he says that humans do not always follow the general instincts ordained by the heavens because of the particular natures of their locations and their parents, and because of various customs and the opportunities of their regions which specifically provoke or assist certain outcomes.

### Confirmation of the above by Bardesanes the Syrian, by others, and by Marsilio himself.

III. Bardesanes the Syrian <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic scientist and philosopher</note>, whom they say was the wisest of all the Chaldeans in astronomy, argues in a long dialogue that while brute animals are driven individually to certain ends by the instinct of nature, humans possess a mind and the speech that proceeds from the mind in addition to natural instinct. By the gift of this mind, they are not entirely driven by nature; hence, human life is varied. They do not share one diet, nor the behaviors of beasts, nor the same clothing, nor similar customs and laws, nor a single desire for things. Instead, by their own judgment, different choices are made, and various ways of life are established. From this, he proves that man is not driven everywhere by nature, since nature is the same in all people, yet their pursuits are diverse. He then recounts at great length how diverse the laws and customs of nations are—how certain actions are forbidden to some or even permitted to others. These institutions are kept by those people regardless of the hour they were born or which region they have migrated to; they are not compelled to act otherwise by any position of the stars, either in their birth chart <note>original: "genesi"</note> or in the ruling sign of their location. It is as if the authority of laws and customs is firmer as a rule for living than the authority of the stars. 

After many points, he adds the following: All Jews, according to the Mosaic law, circumcise their boys on the eighth day. They are not compelled to such a thing by the power of any star, nor forced by the nature of their region, nor ever led by foreign customs to do otherwise. Indeed, wherever they are, they keep their law, which could in no way happen by the necessity of birth. For it is not possible for all Jews to have the same birth chart, such that being born at the same time they would similarly shed blood on the eighth day, or likewise rest on the seventh day. And what shall we say of the sect of Christians, who are found in every part of the world, indeed in every city? Wherever they are, they cannot be forced to live by foreign laws and customs. They are not compelled by the necessity of their horoscope <note>original: "genesios"</note> nor by the command of any prince to think they must do the things their Master deemed unspeakable; instead, they endure poverty, labor, disgrace, and intolerable tortures. Therefore, if everything were in our own power, we would be those who could avoid nothing of what is right or lawful; otherwise, we would be mere instruments and do nothing by our own will. By God's will, however, nothing can be hindered, for His power subjects all things. Yet to every nature something special has been given; to man, He gave this excellence: that he might use the freedom of his will and judgment. 

He shows among these things that the globe of the earth is indeed divided into seven climates <note>the ancient geographic zones used to map the world</note>, and that some say a different planet dominates in each climate—by whose power laws are established everywhere. Yet, even if the globe is divided into seven parts, there are many laws in each part, not just seven (matching the seven planets), nor twelve (matching the signs of the zodiac), nor thirty-six (matching the number of the "faces" of the zodiac). Rather, he asserts that innumerable differences in laws are found, by whose institutions different people live differently, to whichever region they have migrated. Clement of the Apostles <note>referring to the *Clementine Recognitions*, an early Christian text attributed to Clement of Rome</note> confirms the very same things in almost the same words; the experience of customs confirms it too. For where it is permitted to sin with impunity, even the more modest people sin; but where and when sinners are punished more sharply, even those who are naturally instigated toward crimes are restrained. Often, also, people sin more or less, or even act rightly, depending on greater or lesser opportunity and convenience. 

Aristotle and Plutarch confirm the same, most notably through the authority of Lycurgus <note>the legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>. They say that Lycurgus, wishing to show how much law, custom, and education prevail over other things, raised twins from the same birth. Insofar as they were raised differently by Lycurgus, they turned out to be different from each other. If education in brute animals overcomes the similarity of their birth and parents, it can do so much more in humans. Indeed, Plutarch shows how much custom and diligence are worth through a long narrative, where he writes that many who were always sickly by nature fulfilled a long old age by diligence alone. I pass over what he wrote concerning the poet Philitas, Maecenas, and very many others. Aristotle certainly writes that a certain Herodicus, a learned man but quite sickly, lived to a hundred years solely by the diligence of his diet. Plato is also a witness to this matter in his *Republic*. 

But what need is there for witnesses? We have known similar things from ourselves, and we have frequently experienced the miraculous fruits of medicine and diligence. We know that from different custom, education, and discipline, the greatest diversity proceeds in bodies, characters, and talents. As all natural philosophers <note>original: "Physici"</note> agree, we have found in many cases that custom itself is a "second nature." Yet we know that custom does not consist of some natural necessity, but arises from public laws, manners, or private example and discipline, or from some fortune and opportunity, or even from one’s own counsel and opinion—or is gathered from all of these. Frequently, the custom of a region or a time and the example of some excellent person makes many people musicians, poets, orators, painters, or even hunters, rather than a certain birth chart. And when a birth chart begins something, it is nonetheless not completed except according to the capacity of those being born and the region and the times. Often a military or royal house produces soldiers and kings rather than a birth chart doing so. By the imitation of good men, many daily become good, and evil men are made by the imitation of the wicked, under whatever star they were born—just as from the contagion of one person, many soon fall ill, infected not so much by the stars as by the poison of the contagion. What more? The extent of the power of a region and human institution is declared by the fact that Judea produces no fishermen or hunters, where there is no capacity or custom for fishing and hunting; and conversely, almost everyone born under any star fishes and hunts where opportunity, use, and necessity provide for it. Since and where humans have become accustomed to eating animals, entirely innumerable animals are daily [slaughtered] before the institution...

<summary>Ficino argues against astrological fatalism by citing various historical and philosophical authorities, including Bardesanes and Plutarch, to show that human will, law, education, and local custom have more influence over a person's life than their birth chart.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically challenging the idea of absolute astrological determinism. Ficino argues that human will, local environment, and education can override the supposed "necessity" of the stars.</meta>

->### ON BOOK I OF THE THIRD ENNEAD. 127<-

Laws and time are destroyed in the interval; on the contrary, the same animals grow old regardless of the star under which they are said to be born. Similar things occur regarding the devastation of crops and fruits; at whatever time they grew together, one can argue this happens according to human custom and whim, not by a fatal sequence. Indeed, observe daily the boundaries and emotions of the planets; explore diligently what they portend. It happens much that on a day said to be "unfortunate," prosperous things happen to many; on a "fortunate" day, adversity happens to many; and among those competing at any given moment, some indeed overcome, while others are overcome. Certainly, the "unfortunate" days of the astrologers are often the most serene and calm, while "fortunate" ones are often scorching. But I have found through experience that the qualities of both bodies and souls are affected differently by variations in the air, rather than by the different aspects of the stars.

Finally, I have discovered that the shifts in the planets' effects turn out to be vastly different according to the diversity of regions and people. If rain is promised, it rains a lot in one place, a little in another, and not at all in another, according to the differences of the regions. If discords or lusts are signified, some are incited to these more vehemently, others more mildly, others not at all; and I see this happens differently not only according to the natural variety of bodies, but also according to the diversity of ages—and indeed even according to the difference of education and discipline, habit and opportunity.

We see, and it is certain, that daily events do not seem to be fulfilled exactly as they were destined from the heavens, but happen one way and then another. And what truly matters to that determined moment is that from the very moment of birth, a certain quality is brought from heaven and infused into us. I similarly assert that this infusion did not strictly obey the exact celestial rule expressed in our souls, since many things beneath the heaven, both from the beginning and daily, apply their own efficacy or passion to confound this expression. These things, which surely have a nature far different from celestial things, also have a cause for their own progression that does not entirely agree with the celestial orders.

Therefore, many things flow together under the heaven in a way more profound than the celestial order might reconcile; just as rational souls often act otherwise than the supreme reason of God dictates. Many things also concur contingently <note>By chance or coincidence</note>, such as the goodness of beauty combined with talkativeness; for these two have no such order between them, from which it is clear they do not flow together from any single determined cause. However, from this concurrence, a more abundant persuasion commonly arises among the people. That someone might be a beautiful person can happen from a certain cause. Likewise, that they are eloquent, from a certain cause, however different. But that both should be present at once—from which a persuasive person easy of access is born—seems to happen from no determined cause; otherwise, they would have a necessary relationship to each other. Now, however, it happens by chance that a beautiful person is eloquent; for conversely, one is not necessarily eloquent because they are beautiful or fair-skinned, nor vice versa. Therefore, you cannot refer this kind of concurrence, which is like a fluke, to a determined cause.

It is false, therefore, that all events proceed from a certain determined cause. It is also false that, once a certain determined cause of something is established, it must soon be necessarily completed. For impediments fall from various sources below, partly from things struggling against each other, partly from those resisting the celestial order of the heavens, while hard things give way and join with those coming together and flowing in. Added to the changing of natural things is both animal motion and the counsel of rational nature—either of one person or even many—whether they agree among themselves or disagree.

Therefore, since those two points are false by which the proponents of fate chiefly argue, it is clear that not everything happens by fate—that is, by a necessary series of causes depending from the heavens. It is helpful to conclude the present dispute with a certain prophetic and royal authority. In Synesius the Platonic <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop who synthesized Neoplatonism and Christianity</note>, the King of the Egyptians—who was also, as he says, a prophet and most powerful in divine matters—when handing over the empire to his son Osiris <note>In Egyptian myth, Osiris represents order and kingship; Ficino uses him here as an example of a ruler exerting will over destiny</note>, warned him to remove his brother Typhon <note>original: "Typhonem"; Typhon (or Set) represents chaos and destructive fate</note> from their midst, saying: "If you think rightly, take care to remove your brother like a certain plague and an unjust fate; so that you may seize your own fate and that of all Egyptians from adversity, and by counsel prevent him from invading; for it is permitted and possible to do so."

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' featuring a complex circular geometric knot-work and floral pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>
The order of those things which come into being and those which simply exist <note>Plotinus distinguishes between eternal "Being" (like the Soul or Intellect) and the world of "Becoming" (physical events and objects)</note> must be of such a kind that either everything that happens and exists is through a cause, or both happen without a cause; or in both categories, some things happen without a cause and others from causes; or all things that exist come from a cause, while those that come into being partly have a cause and partly do not; or nothing that exists is referred to a cause, while all things that exist are from a cause; or things that come into being happen partly one way and partly another; or none of them come from a cause. 

In the beginning, within the order of eternal things, whatever things are "first," by the very fact that they are first, cannot be referred to other causes. However, whatever things depend on these first things receive their existence from them. You will also rightly assign specific actions to individual things if you refer them to their essences <note>original: "essentias"; in Neoplatonism, a thing’s actions naturally flow from its fundamental nature or "essence"</note>. For it is the nature of their being to produce such an act. 

But in the category of things that come into being—or those things that always exist but do not always produce the same action—one must affirm that everything happens according to causes. We must in no way admit that anything happens without a cause. To do so would open the door to "random swerves" <note>original: "παρεγκλίσεσι" (paregklisesi); a reference to the Epicurean theory that atoms randomly "swerve," which Plotinus rejects as unscientific</note> and vain inclinations, or to a sudden motion of bodies proceeding with no preceding leader to guide them, or to a rash and sudden impulse of the soul where nothing incited the soul to act in a way it was not acting before. 

Perhaps, indeed, a greater necessity will touch the soul from this very fact: that it is not its own guardian and its own cause in the things that happen to it. For either something from the outside or something from within incited the soul to want something, or provoked it to desire something. Otherwise, if nothing had moved it to pursue a goal, it would not have been moved at all. Since all things happen according to causes, we can easily find the "proximate" <note>meaning the immediate or direct</note> causes for each thing and trace the effects back to them. For example, the proximate cause of going to the market 

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Π' (Pi) depicting a seated male figure in classical attire (likely a philosopher) in a landscape with trees and a distant building.</image-desc>
All things that come into being and all things that exist either come into being according to causes, and existing things are those that have come into being; or both happen without cause; or some without cause and some with cause; or all things that come into being are with cause, while for existing things, some are with cause and some without; or the reverse: all existing things are with cause, while for things that come into being, some are with cause and some without. 

Regarding eternal things, the first things are eternal as they are without cause, being "first" <note>The "One" or the "Good" in Plotinus’s system is the ultimate source and has no cause above it</note>. But as many things as depend on the first things have their being from them. One might assign the activities of each to their essences, for this is their being: to provide such an activity. 

But in the case of things that are always coming into being, or things that always exist but do not always act in the same way, one must say that all happen according to causes. One must not accept the "uncaused," nor give space to "empty swerves" <note>again, a critique of the Epicurean 'clinamen' or random atomic movement</note>, whether it be a sudden movement of bodies without a preceding guide, or a sudden impulse of the soul toward whatever happens, with nothing moving it. For even these things have a greater cause within them. It is necessary that the soul is not its own master, but that such movements—unwilled—have causes, either in that which is desired (whether outside or the desiring faculty moved it) or if nothing moved the object of desire, it would not have moved at all. Since all things happen according to causes, it is easy to grasp the proximate causes for each and lead them back to these: such as the cause of walking to the market...

# FIRST BOOK.

<column-break/>

One might suppose a certain idea for us: that, in general, some things are set in motion by the impulses of free men, while others persuade everyone according to the imagination of each. Of these, some are necessary because of the **arts** <note>The Greek term *technai* refers to specialized knowledge or skills like medicine or engineering.</note>, whether it be medicine or other skills, or the seeking of wealth through chosen paths, or receiving gifts, or money made from labor or boxing; and the father is the cause of everything. <margin>once for the bad things</margin> And if there are outside helpers for the procreation of children. * There are also other sources: for example, certain foods are made to be easily digestible, providing seed for procreation, as they have been requested for birth and altogether for nature.

Until these points, you would not think it worthy, even if everything happened within them; you might try, but it would be for the very lazy or the sleepy; because these are the primary things both for the arts and for those things derived from living. But because in these defined things—for instance, as the moon appears, or the sun is infinite, or the stars are held in the ether for each, some for stability and others for wandering <note>The "wandering" stars are the planets.</note>. From which, as if from the same works and turns and rages, the results and fortunes are different, they demand a look further away * by necessity; and because those standing there, some perhaps create bodily pleasures, others misfortunes, as well as the movements, blows, and entanglements with one another, each making them so, and it is and happens as those things are composed, to act and to suffer, and that our impulses and dispositions are held this way, as those things might act, it is a necessity that it be this way, not as if this should seem to lead into things. And to teach other things from the principles of bodies, from which everything comes to be; or from these things it is a necessity to happen. And if somehow the bodies themselves are the principles or reins for the things among them, all things are held by it through the cause visiting through all things, or only of the living and of movement, but also saying that which makes each is **Fate** <note>original: "heimarmene"</note>, and setting this as the most sovereign cause, it itself being all living things. And that the other animals come from it, but also that our thoughts are not ours but from those things moved, like one life and one moving for each from them, both in the leading part of each of the animals; especially the movement of the whole containing it, and making everything by its movement, and by the circuits of the wandering stars, and their configurations to one another. And trusting in the predictions from these, they think that each thing happens from there. This is also the entanglement of causes with one another and the thread from above, and the sequence where later things always follow the earlier, and these are causes because of them, or from those from the mind, showing how everything is for it. If anyone should say these things, he would call Fate another way—

<column-break/>

**A** is the judgment <note>original: "existimatio"</note> through which we decide that something must be found, or a debt must be collected, and altogether to choose these or those things and pursue them. Finally, the cause of ends is opinion, in which it seems to each that such things must be brought about. And some we refer to the **arts** as causes, such as healing in medicine; others to the physician. And others to a treasury of recently accumulated causes found by chance, or a gift made by someone, or labors, or any art whatsoever. Similarly, a father is the cause of a son, and if there is anything else that contributes from the outside to the procreating of children: while clearly one thing proceeds from another, such as certain foods, or things somewhat prior and more remote, contributing to the generation of sons, such as a woman more fit for offspring and birth. And altogether we refer these to nature.

**B** But to have progressed this far and suddenly stop, not wishing to proceed to higher things, might perhaps seem the mark of a sluggish man, and of one who has not lent his ears to those ascending to sublime causes. <margin>‡ Because causes are so close that they are often insufficient, therefore above each person in their actions there seems to be some other Fate present, or an opinion distributed as a judgment.</margin> For what is the cause that, with the same circumstances occurring, **C** such as the moon appearing, one person indeed seizes something, while another does not? And with similar things coming from the surrounding heaven, or the air, one person indeed falls ill, but another not at all? Furthermore, from the same works does this man turn out rich, but that one poor? Moreover, the various modes of character, differing manners, and diverse fortunes warn us to examine more remote causes. Therefore, since philosophers never wished to rest in proximate causes, whoever positioned corporeal principles, **D** such as **atoms** <note>The "atomos" refers to the school of Epicurus, who believed the world was made of tiny, indivisible particles.</note>, by whose delay, impulse, and mutual complications they make individual things, they said that things happen and each thing holds itself in that condition in which those principles come together, and they make and suffer even our own impure affections: that they are such as those principles make them. These men, therefore, introduce this necessity into the principles and into those things which are from them, throughout all things: and whoever else says that other bodies are the principles, and that all things are made by them, he surely thinks that all things serve a certain necessity founded in these. **E** Others indeed, ascending to the very principle of the universe, derive all things from it: and they think that this first cause diffuses itself through all things, and not only moves them, but even makes individual things. This indeed they also call **Fate**, considering Fate to be the most powerful cause moving all things, so that not only whatever else happens, but even our thoughts proceed from its motions; not otherwise than in an **F** animal the individual parts are moved, not indeed by themselves, but by that which holds the leadership in any animal. Others, moreover, judge that the circuit of the whole world, embracing all things and making each thing by its motion, and by the mutual habits and configurations of the stars—both wandering and non-wandering—is Fate. And relying on predictions made through celestial things, they think individual things are made from there. **G** Someone might furthermore describe Fate by another reason, saying that it is the mutual complication of causes, and a connected series emanating from above, through which later things always comply with the prior: and these very later things are reflected back into the preceding, seeing as they are made through them, and cannot be brought about without them: by which—

...be carried. If anyone, however, distinguishes these two ways, he will perhaps not wander from the truth. Namely, some will think that all things depend on a single principle; others, however, by no means think so. These matters will be discussed in what follows. But for the present, we must first debate with the primary views; then we must consider the sayings of the others in succession.

### IT IS CERTAINLY IMPOSSIBLE and absurd
<margin>III. That all things are neither forced nor created by bodies; nor will there be any foreknowledge if the principles of things were based on compulsion.</margin>
to entrust everything to corporeal causes, whether atoms or elements, or to subject order, reason, and the leading soul to the unorganized motion of bodies. It is especially impossible to subject things to atoms; many true arguments have been handed down to refute them. Even if one posits such principles, it does not follow that fate exists through necessity in all things, or by some other agreement. Suppose first that there are atoms: these would move partly downward—if indeed there is any "downward"—and partly sideways, however they happen to fall. Since no order exists, nothing would happen according to a plan. Because of this, there would be no prediction, no prophecy, nor any foreknowledge from art <note>The term "art" here refers to *technē*, a systematic skill or science, like medicine or navigation.</note>. For in what way can there be any art in disordered things? Nor could there be divination from oracles and divine inspiration, or by the instinct of the mind. For in these cases, the future must already be determined. Bodies might happen to suffer whatever the atoms bring by necessity from their clashing. But the actions of the soul—whether through the descent or any kind of collision of atoms—to what movements of atoms could you attribute its passions? What impulse in the soul produces such rational discourses, or such drives? Or how could distinctions, or impulses, or movements necessarily arise, or arise in any way at all? Furthermore, when the mind resists the disturbances of the body, what do atoms contribute to that? Tell me again, by what differences of atoms are men compelled so that some are geometers, others arithmeticians and astronomers, and others wise? Overall, the freedom of our will <term>libertas arbitrij</term> <note>Original Latin: *libertas arbitrii*. This refers to the capacity of the human mind to make independent choices regardless of physical pressures.</note> and our own work would be removed, and that through which a living being exists. For we would be carried wherever bodies drag us, like inanimate bodies pushing us. The same can be similarly objected to those who believe that other bodies are the causes of all things: which can further heat us, cool us, and dissolve us, and whatever other miseries they can inflict. But the kinds of actions the soul produces cannot be made by these; instead, they must be made by some other principle.

### BUT DOES PERHAPS a single soul,
<margin>IIII. That there is not only one active power in the universe.</margin>
running through all things, perform everything? So that any individual thing is carried along like a part to where the whole leads? Do the resulting causes follow from there by necessity? And should we call the continuous connection of all these things "Fate"? Just as in a plant having its beginning from a root, someone might call "fate" the disposition diffused from the root itself through all parts of the plant, as if governing them, and their mutual conspiracy, and...

<column-break/>

...for it will appear. Again, if one posits these two ways, one would not miss the truth. Some hang all things from one source, others do not. This is spoken of, but let us go to the first arguments, then examine the others in order.

### TO ENTRUST EVERYTHING to bodies,
<margin>B</margin>
whether atoms or so-called elements, and to their disordered motion—denying order, reason, and the soul’s leadership of us—one might argue is impossible, or rather, more than impossible to say it comes from atoms. Many arguments have already been made about this. But if one posits such principles, does necessity follow, or fate? Suppose first that 
<margin>C</margin>
atoms exist. They move downward—suppose there is a downward—or sideways, however it happens, with no order. If something happens, when will it happen? There would be no divination or 
<margin>D</margin>
art. How can there be art in the disordered? Nor from enthusiasm or divinity, for there the future is defined. Bodies would suffer from the striking of atoms. But the works and 
<margin>F</margin>
passions of the soul—to what atom-movements would you assign them? What blow or motion produces calculations or impulses, or thought, or action? When the soul resists the passions of the body, what atom-flow makes one a geometer, an arithmetician, or a seeker of astronomy, or a wise man? Our own work and the freedom of life are lost if we are carried where bodies lead us like soulless things. The same applies to those who make other bodies the causes. These can heat and cool us, or destroy the weaker parts, but no work that the soul performs comes from them. They must come from another principle.

### BUT DOES PERHAPS ONE Soul
pervade everything and accomplish all? Does it lead every part as a piece of the whole? 
<margin>G</margin>
And from there, does the necessity of following causes—their sequence or weaving together—constitute Fate? Like a plant starting from a root, where the management from there over all the parts and their weaving together...

# BOOK ONE.

...action and passion for all things, a single administration, or a kind of **fate**. Or if someone says these things exist, some by one cause and others by another, then the extreme power of such a necessity and fate utterly removes fate itself, and the chain and entanglement of causes. For those things which move in our own parts according to the **leading principle** <note>original: "ἡγεμονικόν" (hēgemonikon) — the governing or rational part of the soul in Stoic and Neoplatonic thought</note>, it is irrational to say they move according to fate. For if one thing gives the motion and another receives it, and uses the impulse from itself, but that first thing is what moves the leg—in the same way, if in the universe the "All" will not be one thing acting and suffering, or one thing in relation to another, then we cannot trace causes back. But if in other cases we have the truth that all things happen by causes, then all things are within themselves. Thus our affairs, coming from our own power, are said to have their own causes. It is not reasoning, or things thrown out, or things done, just as children do not kick by themselves, but we kick through parts of ourselves. But the reality is that in each person there exist our own actions and thoughts, and the honorable and shameful actions of each person come from themselves; one must not attribute the generation of shameful things to the "All" <note>Plotinus is arguing for moral responsibility; if the Universe/God causes everything, then God is the author of evil, which he rejects.</note>.

<margin>self-moving</margin> But perhaps, as actions are different, their course and administration—that is, the motion of the stars—is placed there as the cause of their mutual relationship. They provide accurate evidence through settings and risings, and observations of their positions. Again, they say how someone among those in the universe will be affected, concerning each person's affairs, and how you will fare in fortune and thought based on these. One can see that other animals and plants increase and decrease by their connection <note>original: "συμπαθείας" (sympatheias) — the 'sympathy' or interconnectedness of all parts of the cosmos</note> with these stars, and suffer all other things from them. The climates on earth differ from each other according to the air influenced by them, and especially follow the sun. It is not only the places or other plants and animals, but already the size of men, or their colors, or angers and desires, pursuits and habits, and these things themselves are the movement of everything. In response to these things, this must first be said: that if we assume our affairs—impulses, passions, and vices—are attributed to them in another way, as if they were a fountain or flowing through a pipe, then they would not belong to men. But we are from them and of the same nature; yet one must grant that our own belongs to us. Into our affairs, those things that are images of ourselves from the "All" run toward us, so that while we work through what we suffer by necessity, not everything should be attributed to them and their movements.

<column-break/>

**A** action and passion contained in one arrangement. But truly, this excessive height of necessity and the constitution of fate of this kind utterly takes away fate itself and the sequence of causes, along with their connection. For just as in our parts which are moved by our **leading principle**, it is absurd to say they are agitated according to a fatal sequence. For it is not one thing that passes on the motion and another that receives it, itself also having a certain proper impulse, but that first thing **B** is what moves the limbs. In the same way, if in the universe the "All" will be one thing acting and suffering—and not one thing entirely distinct from another according to causes continuously reduced to another—certainly it will not be true that all things happen according to causes, but all things will be one. Therefore, neither will we ourselves be ourselves, nor will any work be ours; we ourselves will not reason, but the reasoning will belong to some other, and the counsel will belong to another. Likewise, we ourselves would not act, just as our feet then **C** kick, but we are said to kick through our feet as our parts. It is necessary, however, for each of us to exist properly as what we are, and for our actions and thoughts to be our own. And the honorable or shameful actions of each individual must proceed from that individual; nor is it fitting to ascribe shameful actions to the universe.

->PERHAPS, TRULY, INDIVIDUAL MATTERS ARE NOT CARRIED OUT IN THIS WAY.<-

Instead, the circuit of the heavens governs all things, <margin>Neither indeed are they ruled by heaven, nor are the stars the total cause of these things being done by necessity.</margin> **D** and the motions of the stars dispose individual things according as they stand in relation to one another, according to the time and position of the meridian, and the risings, settings, and conjunctions. From these things, those who foretell the future predict what will happen concerning the universe and concerning each individual. Not only what kind of fortune there will be, but also what kind of thought will occur in a matter. It is possible to see other animals and plants both increase and decrease by that very constitution of the stars, and **E** suffer all other things from them. Furthermore, regions on the earth differ from each other according to a certain relationship to the universe, especially through their aspect to the sun. It appears that not only plants and beasts follow the nature of the place, but even the species and sizes of men, their colors, angers, desires, pursuits, and habits. Thus, the authority over all things seems to consist in the circuit of the universe itself. **F** To these things, therefore, it must first be said that this discourse also—although in another certain way—subjects all our affairs, wills, passions, vices, and impulses to the things above. It assigns nothing of ours to us, but considers us to be moved like stones, rather than as humans who have a certain proper duty arising from ourselves and our nature. Nevertheless, it is right to concede what is ours to ourselves, and to think besides that certain things reach our affairs from the universe, which are already something in themselves and proper to us. **G** Indeed, a distinction must be made as to which things we ourselves do, and which things we suffer by necessity; all things must not be granted to the heavenly bodies. We ought to think that from the different regions and circles of the air...

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

...necessity many things happen to us: just as in the constitution <note>original: "complexione" — referring to the physical makeup or "complexion" of the body's humors</note> of the body, cold and heat occur; they also occur from the condition of those who beget us. Do not children often resemble their parents, both in form and figure, and in certain passions of the irrational soul? Indeed, they are often similar in form because of the common nature of the place: yet there is a very great difference in their habits and thoughts, as if these arise from some other principle. Furthermore, the resistance of reason against the constitution of the body and its lusts serves to refute these things similarly. 

But if, because those who look up at the position of the stars predict future things for individuals, it is thought that these things are also caused by them: it would be just as if birds were the causes of what they signify; and similarly if all things, by the inspection of which diviners foretell, were said to also cause what they signify. Likewise, from these things one may more perfectly consider the same, which the astrologer predicts for the newborn, looking up at the arrangement of the stars established when they are born; which, if they say they are not only signified by the present arrangement, but caused by it, they will more often be lying. 

For when they judge a noble lineage, saying the newborn is descended from noble fathers or mothers: how can it be said that those things which were in the parents before such an arrangement of stars came about (by the contemplation of which it is predicted) were caused by this? For he also declares the fortunes of the parents from the birth of the children. Again, they portend the future conditions and fortunes of children from the parents themselves regarding those who are not yet born. From a brother also, death is predicted for his siblings; likewise, the fates of wives from the woman: and vice versa he judges the former from the latter. By what reason, then, does the arrangement of the stars cause each person's properties, which are said to be future from the fathers in a certain fixed condition? For either those prior things are the efficient causes: or if those are not the causes, neither will these be the causes. 

Moreover, the likeness of children's forms to their parents is restored; beauty and deformity proceed from the lineage itself, not from the motions of the stars. It is probable, furthermore, that at the same time animals of all kinds and humans are born together: in which exactly the same things ought to happen to whoever the same arrangement of stars hangs over. In what way, then, do humans and the rest arise at the same time through the same figures of the heaven?
