VI
Here, individual things receive their own quality in generation from their own natures more than from the heavens, although they are signified by the heavens.
</margin>

# VI
BUT indeed, each thing must happen according to its own nature. A horse, indeed, is born from a horse, and a human from a human; and a certain kind of horse or human because it comes from such a kind. Let the motion of the heaven also be a fellow-worker <note>original: "συνεργὸς" (synergos) — a secondary or contributing cause rather than the primary one</note> in the whole, yet yielding very much to the parents and the ones born. Let the celestial things indeed grant many things to the body, in a bodily way, providing heat and cold, and the resulting temperaments of bodies: but how can they grant habits and pursuits, especially those which do not seem to serve the temperaments of bodies? Such as if someone is a grammarian, or a geometer, or a gambler, or an inventor of this or that thing. Now, how can wickedness of character be given by the celestials, who are gods? And

<column-break/>

...passions [come] to us, such as heat or cold from the temperament <note>original: "κράσει" (krasei) — the blending of bodily elements</note>, and others from those who begot us. For who are not like their offspring? Since many things are [the same], and the passions of the irrational part of the soul are similar to them in their forms <note>original: "ειδεσι" (eidesi)</note>, yet their character <note>original: "τροπάς" (tropas)</note> changes; if there is a change everywhere in habits; it will be in the thoughts, as if such things come from another principle. 

And again, the resistances against the temperaments of the bodies, and against the desires, would certainly be spoken of here. But if, because they look at the sight of the stars and speak of things that happen, they conclude they are causes from those things, it would be as if birds were the ones making the signs, or even all things which diviners see and speak of. But if from these things it were believed by them concerning these things always because of the relations of the stars, even when each person was born, would they not fail if they said these things happen because of them? 

Or is it only signified, but they [the stars] are not the causes of what they say concerning each person, such as from what fathers and mothers [they come]? How can one say these things to the child, which pre-existed concerning the births? Concerning the fortunes that happen to the parents, from which they trace back the fortunes of the parents from the birth of the children; and of the children from the parents, they similarly divine the opposite, and from the parents, they speak of the greatest things. And from brothers the deaths of brothers, and from wives, those things concerning them, and vice versa from those things. 

How then will each be saved through the stars, since they say they are such from the fathers? Or are those things from the fathers? If not those, neither these. Or the likeness in forms toward the births is not, he says, from the stars, such as beauty and deformity. But if humans and animals of all kinds [are born] at the same time, all having the same [star] positions... How then at the same time is there a human, and at the same time other animals from the [same] figures?

# VI
BUT indeed, each thing must happen according to its own nature. A horse, indeed, is from a horse, and a human because it is from a human, and a certain kind because it is from such a kind. Let the motion of the "All" be a fellow-worker, yielding much to those being born. Let them grant much to the body in a bodily way, such as heats or colds, and the resulting temperaments of bodies. How then are habits and pursuits [given], especially those which do not seem to serve the temperament of bodies? Such as if someone is a grammarian, or a geometer, or a gambler, or of some such virtue? How can wickedness of character be given by those who are gods? And

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of astrological determinism. Having previously argued that stars are not the direct causes of human character, he now explains that they act as signs or "letters" within the natural world. He then transitions to a philosophical discussion on the nature of Fate and the role of the Soul in preserving free will against total determinism.</meta>

BOOK ONE.

...altogether, in whatever way they are said to grant "evil" things—becoming, as it were, evil themselves—it is simply because they set or are carried beneath the earth. It is as if they were undergoing something different when they "set" for us, whereas they are always carried around the celestial sphere and, as far as they are concerned, they look upon the earth in the same way. Nor should it be said that one of the gods <note>original: "deorum" — Plotinus refers to the stars and planets as visible, divine beings</note> becomes better or worse based on looking from this or that position, as if they would do us good when well-disposed and harm us when poorly disposed. It is better to say that the celestial bodies traverse their paths for the safety of the whole universe, but in the meantime serve another purpose: nature reads those positions like letters. Those who know this kind of "literacy" <note>original: "literatura" — here meaning the ability to read the signs of nature</note> can investigate the meaning from the celestial figures themselves through a certain analogical comparison. It is just as if one were to say that a bird flying through the heights signifies certain healthy actions.

### VII.

<margin>How the arrival of things does not inevitably take away the freedom of individual persons through the innate connection of things.</margin>
It remains to consider the opinion which says that all things are simultaneously implicated and connected, from which a condition is assigned to individuals. This view posits a single principle from which all things are generated through "seminal reasons" <term>seminal reasons (rationes seminales): the formative principles or "blueprints" in nature that determine how things grow and develop</term>. This opinion is very similar to the one that says every state and every motion of ours proceeds from the Soul of the Universe. And even if one wishes to grant us and individuals the ability to effect something by ourselves, this view still holds that everything is bound by an excessive necessity. Indeed, if all things are encompassed by a single cause, it is impossible for each thing not not be enacted. For there is nothing left that could either prohibit it or cause it to happen differently; all things would be swallowed up by Fate. When such things depend on a single finite principle, nothing remains for us but to be carried wherever those causes drive us. For our imaginations would follow preceding causes, and our impulses would follow those imaginations; "freedom of choice" <note>original: "arbitrij libertas"</note> would be an empty name. We would not have more choice simply because we approach something with a certain impulse, since that entire impulse would have fallen upon us from preceding events. Our condition would be like that of other animals, infants, or the insane who run about driven by certain blind stings <note>original: "caecis quibusdā stimulis" — refers to instinctive or irrational drives</note>, for even in these there is an impulse. And by Jupiter, there is a similar impulse in fire, and in all things which are driven by their own instinct. Everyone who looks at this clearly can see it. But those who search for other causes of this impulse do not rest satisfied with this principle.

### VIII.

<margin>How the soul is in fate, and fate is under the soul.</margin>
What other cause, then, remains besides these? One that, while arriving, leaves nothing without a cause, preserves the order and sequence of things, yet permits us to be "something," and does not do away with predictions and prophecies. This must be the Soul, which is another principle introduced into the order of things. We mean not only the Soul of the Universe, but also the individual soul of any person. Along with the Soul of the All, the individual soul is a principle of no small importance for weaving all things together—provided, of course, that the soul does not arise from "seeds" like other things, but is placed in a preceding order in the generation of causes. For this reason, when the soul lives apart from the body, it is most truly mistress of itself, free, and outside the causes of the world.

<column-break/>

A altogether, in whatever way they are said to grant "evil" things, even those that are "set" <note>original: "κείμενοι" — referring to the setting of stars below the horizon</note> because they go down and are carried under the earth, as if their appearance changed when they set in relation to us. But those beings are always carried in the same sphere, and they hold the same relation to the earth. Nor should it be said that those who see the sun at different times and in different places are made to rejoice or be harmed as if the sun changed toward them; it is wrong to blame it for anything. Rather, these things move for the preservation of the whole, but provide another use: that those who look at the things in them as if they were letters—those who know this kind of grammar—may read what is to come from the figures by analogy. <margin>just as they say a bird [signifies] what is to come by its flight</margin> They track the things signified, just as someone says that because a bird is high up, it signifies certain "high" or noble actions.

C It remains to see the "co-alteration" or how all things are woven together, from which it follows for each person... so that all things are accomplished from one principle according to * <margin>seminal</margin> seminal reasons. Since this opinion is close to the one <margin>from without</margin> that says each of our actions and all things happen according to the nature of the Soul of the All. If someone wants D to grant us something from ourselves, everything about us is still held by necessity, and these causes being taken together, it is impossible for anything else to happen. For what is there to prevent it, or for it to happen otherwise, if all things are taken up in Fate? Such things being determined from one principle, nothing is left to us but to be pushed wherever those things drive. For imaginations follow preceding causes, and impulses follow the imaginations. E And as for "what is up to us," if we do not only act from impulse, there is something more, since impulse happens according to those things * <margin>we know</margin>. But this "ours" will be like that of other animals, and children, and those who go like blind beasts, or the impulse of the insane. F For those, and even fire, are carried by their constitution according to this. And all who see this do not dispute it, but seeking other causes for these impulses, they are not satisfied with this one.

What other cause then, coming upon these, will leave nothing uncaused, will maintain the sequence of beings, will grant us everything [as agents], and will not overturn predictions and divinations? We must again bring in the Soul as another cause G into the realm of beings—not only the Soul of the All, but also the soul of each individual with it. As a principle, though it be small, it weaves all things together. It does not come into being, like other things, from seeds, but is a primary acting cause. When it is outside the body, it is most sovereign of itself and free, and outside the worldly cause.

### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD III.

<margin>
IX
How the soul is within fate and how it acts. Also concerning the contingency of things.
</margin>
...power: but once infused into a body, it no longer has the authority to dominate or the freedom in all things, as it has now been ordered alongside other things. As for the matters of Fortune—namely, those surrounding circumstances with which the soul coincides when cast into the midst of life—they have a very great power, to the point that the soul does many things haphazardly <term>atoma</term> <note>original: "atoma propter circumstantiam" — referring to things that happen without a rational plan due to external accidents</note> because of its circumstances, though it may act with a certain command in whatever it has decreed. Indeed, the soul dominates in more things if it is of a better nature, and in fewer if it is of a worse nature. For it is either compelled to desire or be angry by obeying the temperament <term>complexionis</term> <note>the "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors in the body, which was thought to influence personality</note> of the body; or, succumbing to poverty, it becomes more humble; or, admiring riches, it becomes puffed up; or, exulting in power, it practices tyranny. However, a soul relying on the goodness of its nature, if it falls into these same circumstances, resists and dominates them; it rather changes the things that would change it, partly altering them and partly allowing them to happen without fault on its own part.

<margin>
X
Intellectual nature acts freely, but its effect is sometimes hindered in its reasoning.
</margin>
Therefore, those things are NECESSARY which are completed by the combination of purpose and fortune. For what could exist besides these? When all causes are grasped together, absolutely everything happens. Among those things which are external is also counted whatever from the motion of the universe, together with subsequent causes, contributes to the work. Whenever, therefore, the soul—already changed by external things—acts and undertakes something as if using a blind motion, we must call neither that action nor that affection voluntary and free. Similarly, when the soul itself, being in a worse state of its own accord, does not use right or primary beginnings for its movements. But whenever it undertakes something while having pure reason <note>original: "rationem puram"</note> and freedom from passion as its own guide, we must judge this undertaking alone to be placed in our own choice <term>arbitrio</term> and to be truly free. This is our own work, which is not derived from elsewhere, but from within the pure soul—from a soul, I say, proceeding from the first and most principal beginning, not wandering through ignorance or being overcome by the violence of lust. For vehement lusts, occupying the soul, lead and drag it; they do not permit our actions to be in our own power, but rather turn them into passions <note>in the classical sense, "passions" are things that happen *to* you, rather than things you *do*</note>.

REASON finally concludes in summary that all things are signified and happen according to causes, but that these causes are twofold: partly pertaining to the soul and partly to the surrounding circumstances. Likewise, when souls act according to right reason, they do all things from themselves; but in other cases, they are hindered from executing their own work, and therefore they suffer <term>pati</term> <note>to "suffer" here means to be the passive recipient of an action</note> rather than act. Therefore, when the soul lacks wisdom, it must be thought that there are other causes, and in such a state it might rightly be said to act according to fate—especially according to those who think fate is an external cause. But the best things are to be judged as being done by us ourselves. For it is the light of the best nature that the virtuous act and do honest things freely from themselves; others act freely and honestly only insofar as they have "taken a breath" and been set free from external pressure. They do not obtain wisdom from elsewhere when they are wise; rather, they are wise as soon as they are not hindered from using their own wisdom.

<column-break/>

A * But once it has entered into a body, it is no longer mistress in every way, as if it had been ranked with other things. All the surrounding things are fortunes <note>original Greek: "τυχαι" (tychai) — chances or luck</note>, which it encounters upon entering the center; these lead to many results, so that it does some things, but in others it is mastered, and it does not always lead these things where it wishes. It masters more if it is better, and less if it is worse. For either by the temperament of the body, or by lack, or by punishment or anger, it is B compelled to suffer, or it is made humble by poverty, or vain by prosperity, or a tyrant by powers. But the soul resists these same things if it is good by its nature, or rather together with its nature, so that it either changes the things that flow in or yields without wickedness.

C These things are NECESSARY, as many as happen when mixed with choice and fortunes. For if there were yet other things, since causes have been taken... all things happen through causes, those from without, and those that are woven together from the cosmic rotation. Whenever, therefore, the soul is altered by external things and does something or moves as if using a blind impulse, one must not call the disposition of each of these actions voluntary; even when the soul, through its own fault, sees things through springs that are not right, or D uses impulses that are not the masters. Therefore, only whenever it moves having the master of the pure and impassive soul—which is its own—must we say that this impulse is in our power and voluntary; and this is our own work, which did not come from elsewhere, but from within, from the pure soul, from a primary, leading, and sovereign principle. It does not suffer from wandering out of ignorance, E nor is it led and dragged by the force of desires which, being brought in, lead it away. These are no longer voluntary works, but rather passions of our own.

F FINALLY, the argument says that all things are signified and happen, all according to causes, but these causes are twofold: some from the soul and others from the surrounding causes. And those from the soul, whatever it does, doing them according to right reason, it does from itself; but when doing other things, it is hindered from acting for itself, so it suffers rather than acts. Thus, not being wise, but acting through ignorance—it is perhaps right to say these things happen according to fate, especially for those who think fate is an external cause. But the best things are from us, as many of us as remain in our true nature, and the virtuous do noble things from themselves. G And others, as many as may "breathe again" <note>original Greek: "αναπνεύσωσι" (anapneusosi) — a metaphor for recovering one's senses or gaining a respite</note> and be permitted, do noble things; they do not receive wisdom from elsewhere when they are wise, but are merely no longer prevented from it.

ON BOOK II OF THE THIRD ENNEAD.

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO ON THE SECOND BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, CONCERNING PROVIDENCE.
## SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

->Order in the world does not happen by chance.<-

We are accustomed to attribute **Chance** only to those things that are capable of being otherwise than they are. However, the possibility for things to be "otherwise" arises solely from the indeterminate nature of **Matter** <term>materia</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, "matter" is seen as a chaotic, formless substrate that lacks its own stability.</note>, which is always sliding from one state to another; it does not arise from the nature of **Form**, which always determines a thing toward a specific, certain state. But in the order of the universe, there is both "prime matter" (which does not come from other matter) and "forms" naturally subsisting in themselves (which also cannot arise from matter). Therefore, neither these substances nor their distinctions from one another can happen by chance. 

For perhaps the distinction between certain individuals—distinct from each other only by the division of their physical bulk—might happen by some accident. But the distinction between the species themselves, which is a **Formal** distinction <note>A "formal" distinction refers to the essential nature of a thing (e.g., what makes a human different from a horse), rather than just two different physical examples of the same thing.</note>, cannot have happened by any stroke of luck at all. It was necessary for things to have been produced from the beginning along with their specific distinctions, especially since there are many things in the universe that are neither generated from each other nor from some common source, seeing as they do not share the same matter. 

Therefore, neither this formal distinction nor the production of things could have occurred by any chance—particularly because a cause that exists "through itself" is prior to a cause that exists "by accident." Since later things proceed mostly from a cause determined by itself, it is a sacrilege to say that the higher things arose from a fortuitous cause, and that "Luck" was the principle of the most noble and stable things. On the contrary, it is necessary that moving things are always ruled and led by stable things, and ordered out of their own motions. Furthermore, since it has been proven elsewhere that the universe is made by the **Divine Intellect**—which is evident from the highly artistic order of things proper to intelligence—it is necessary that the common form of the universe be both conceived by the Intelligence of God and established by His Will, which no event can frustrate. 

Since, therefore, the form of the world is not outside the intention of the agent <note>The "agent" here refers to the Creator or the Divine Mind.</note>, it rightly does not happen by chance. And since the form of the whole consists in the distinction and order of its parts, the distinction of those things could not have been accidental. Finally, that which is best in a work must be judged as the "End" (the purpose) of that work. The "Best" of the whole world is located in the mutual order of its parts. Order, however, cannot exist without distinction; through such an order, the world is established in its integrity, which is its highest good. Thus, the order of the parts of the universe and their distinction is the "best" end of its production; for this reason, the order and distinction of things cannot have happened by chance.

->The worldly order does not arise from matter.<-

If the distinction of species does not result from chance, it follows that it does not result from matter either. Since matter is naturally indeterminate toward many possibilities, if anything were to come from it on its own, it would flow forth randomly—especially if the intention of a higher agent were not introduced. If you were to say that there are "diverse matters" and that various forms proceed from them for that reason, you would be forced to admit that matters (since they have the most imperfect condition of being) must depend not on themselves, but on a higher principle. Therefore, they receive both their existence and their distinctness from elsewhere. 

Thus, matters are not the primary cause of distinction in the world, especially since there are many distinct things that consist of no matter at all; even matter itself is separated from immaterial things not by other matter, but by something else. Add to this that every agent, since it acts through a form, intends that form as its goal. Therefore, forms were not introduced into the universe for the sake of matter; rather, matter exists so that natural forms may exist, and matters are affected here and there so that they are shaped by the power of form. The distinction of things according to species is through forms. This distinction, therefore, should not be referred to matter as its primary cause, but matter should be referred entirely to forms. Matter is moved in one way or another by a cause acting through form and intending form; and rightly so, since matter is more base than form. Forms are not for matter as if for a goal; instead, matter is referred to forms, while it is made, moved, and variously affected in every way by the forms of the supreme agent. Therefore, distinction in the universe proceeds from the "formulas" (the blueprints) of the author’s intention, not primarily from the condition of matter. Whatever follows matter declines toward the "deformed" rather than the "formal," and matter's quantitative division does not change a thing's specific form.

->The worldly order is not from a diversity of principles.<-

If anyone, admiring the diversity of things, should introduce a diversity of "primary agents" as the cause, they must consider whether those diverse agents have an order among themselves or not. If they have a common order, they possess it from a single higher source. From that one source they exist, are distinct, and are united; to that source the distinction of all things is finally reduced as to its cause. But if those agents were said to have no order, they would concur by chance, and no perpetual order would be preserved in things.

->The order of things does not happen merely from the succession of things, but from the intention of One.<-

There are those who cannot derive the diversity of multiple things from a single immediate cause, but think that the multitude grows step-by-step: from the One into two, from two again into three, then four. They argue that because the First Cause is entirely simple and strictly One, it makes one thing, which (unable to equal the purity of its cause) slips into potentiality and action. But this opinion assigns determined causes to individual effects, yet it cannot assign a single cause to the entire universe of things. Instead, it suggests the whole results "opinionably" from the concurrence of all causes, and thus happens by a fortuitous luck. Consequently, that which is best in the universe—namely, the common to—

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "On Providence." On the previous page, Ficino established that the formal order of the universe cannot be a product of chance or the random movements of matter, but must originate from a higher principle.</meta>

### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

The ultimate good, which consists in the order and distinction of all parts, must be traced back to the best cause of all things. Therefore, the distinction and arrangement of things proceeds not merely from the subsequent levels of secondary causes, but from the first cause, which is **Providence** <term>prouidentia</term>. But who does not see that it would be a sacrilege to reduce this very thing—which is the best in all things—to a certain defect of causes? This would imply that a secondary cause degenerates from the prior simplicity of the primary cause. Indeed, if the form and arrangement of the world, which is situated in the order of all its parts, received this order through its distinctions, such an arrangement (as the ultimate form of the world) requires the best and most formal cause of all. It corresponds entirely and rightly to the First Cause; deservedly, the causes following after God serve this arrangement. Therefore, this order does not result from the gradual action of secondary causes as if by accident, but those following causes do whatever they do for the sake of this constitution and preservation, as if acting toward an end prescribed for them by the mind of the First Cause. Since this arrangement is designated in that Mind, certainly all things are necessarily described there. If that **Intelligence** <term>intelligentia</term> produced these things, many things can proceed from it simultaneously: especially since divine power can act through more than one <unclear>way</unclear>, being most ample. It is not defined or limited to a single thing as if it were constrained, because it is simpler and (so to speak) more unified, stronger, and more powerful for procreating many things. Finally, since there are many things which, because of the wondrous simplicity and perfection of their essence, cannot proceed directly from anywhere else but the First Cause, it is necessary that the distinction and arrangement among them follows from the providence of the First Cause. Since this Intelligence is capable of many things and understands what it is capable of, it ultimately made a work for itself as if it had produced something manifold and various; for example, it represents the essence of the cause piecemeal across many things, which it could not represent in one or only a few. And since there is such goodness in God, his diffused goodness necessarily preserves the divine composition in the work. If God is Good, and if goodness passed into itself, it would be diffused from the whole into other things; indeed, this diffusion cannot happen unless there is a diversity and inequality of things—inequality, I say, according to their **Species** <note>Ficino means that the world is better because it contains a variety of types of beings (humans, animals, plants) rather than just many identical things.</note>. For in this way, the multitude in the world will be most perfect and most fully formed if the species are as numerous as possible.

### ->The purposes of things and their motions declare that they are made, arranged, and moved by divine providence.<-

First, it has been established among Physicians and other natural philosophers that if the assignment of a **Purpose** <term>finis</term> <note>Latin: "finis" refers to the "end" or "goal" toward which a process moves.</note> is taken away, no cause can be assigned for any arrangement of things or natural motions. Therefore, the entire arrangement of nature and the logic of science consists primarily in looking toward the end, toward which no cause would be destined if there were no purpose. But no end is found in things that are accidental and haphazard; nor could things be made unless they were moved by the intention of a certain end of causes, through which any parts in a thing preserve each other in turn; they are parts that both serve the form itself and the well-being of the whole. Tell me, I pray, why are seeds not driven into plants in various ways, but only through tender little buds? Is it not because these alone need a support to which they may be bound by their neighbors? Thus nature neither allows for the superfluous nor lacks anything necessary. For if a plant reaches out as if extending a hand toward a part of its goals, where a support is placed, and if that support is not offered, it seeks to move longingly until it is given; then it entwines itself more extensively. Do we not see here that nature has a mind, and eyes? Come, tell me why the end itself of nature moves the causes, and thus in a way precedes them all, unless it is established by that art in which Mind appears everywhere preceding nature, toward which all such things are destined? To be sure, matter precedes and goes before in motion; but place the end before the matter here, because it is designated for an end, wherever the eternal nature of the form is concerned. There is, therefore, a supreme Reason of natures in the **Mover** and the Mind, which thus commands the parts to serve each other for the sake of the whole in anything, and calls them back to the good of the whole. By the reciprocal motion of the parts, each part everywhere adapts to the whole and, like parts of the universe, leads toward the good of the universe, and never allows a vacuum to occur. And for the sake of avoiding this vacuum, as if by the intention of an end, wonderful things can be done and moved, so that a natural impulse stops contrary to the mode of nature, as if led by a guide far superior to nature. How much more wonderfully now might one transfer to the good of a living creature—beyond the condition of the elements—the light things upward and the heavy things downward; with what miraculous art does it figure each thing. I pass over with what caution water (which by the proper order of elements seems to cover the earth) is restrained by nature from totally submerging the earth, for this reason alone: so that many species of things might be generated on the land. I pass over how for all things that are born, limbs, and ligaments, and all necessary things are provided everywhere; these are divinely established for us in various and diverse ways, and even decorated wonderfully beyond necessity. But the highest point in this is that the "end" is nothing other than some boundary toward which something is moved by the intention of art, and in which cause it would rest; certainly, the ends of natural motions are prescribed by unity. For things are not moved toward just anything at will, nor in any way they please, but by a certain reason which fits their nature, as is evident in things that are neither stirred up rashly nor wander by fortune. Thus heat, by its own reason, seeks a place suitable to its nature where it may be preserved, and flees the unsuitable, and flees cold, sometimes even contrary to its own law and mode so that it is not extinguished. Since, therefore, the motions of natural things are certain and seek a boundary in which they may rest firmly, the compositions of natural things (from which certain motions are produced) would be even more certain unless the arrangement was like a work of art; natural things are directed toward their end much more artificially than man-made crafts, and it is necessary that they be made by some art more excellent than human crafts. And just as the most perfect art in us does not deliberate about those things but acts as if in the manner of nature, so the natural and divine art acts for the sake of a reason and an end; it does not need to be practiced with any divine efforts which a consummate art would not need: especially if human art does not exist (as is now said) merely to handle matter, but is imagined to be moved from within in the manner of divine art.

### ->How this world is made from the supernal world and how it degenerates: what the intelligible world is like.<-

**I** What is said in the first chapter—that if God made the world "new" at some time, he therefore previously consulted whether and how he should make it—does not follow. It is only a consequence that it is possible for us to think that God consulted in this way: which we are not permitted to think if it is posited that the world never had a beginning in time. Second, note that the primary essence, life, and mind (which are the same thing) are the cause of the world—namely the **Efficient and Exemplary Cause** <term>efficientem & exemplarem</term> <note>The "efficient" cause is the one that brings something into being; the "exemplary" cause is the model or blueprint it follows.</note>—but the end is the Good. Indeed, the world is made from there because the world is that very thing, just as fire comes from itself. In the bodily world, formal order is one thing, but dimension and motion are another. If, therefore, you subtract dimension and motion and leave the order, you are contemplating the Mind which is the craftsman of this world: in which Mind, indeed, are the levels of all forms.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the third Ennead of Plotinus, specifically focusing on how the perfect, unchanging "Intellectual World" gives rise to the physical, changing "Sensible World." In the previous section, Ficino discussed how divine Providence orders the universe.</meta>

...if indeed it is a formal order. But since motion and time do not exist there <note>original: "ibi," referring to the Intellectual World</note>, nothing of the present form is lost to the past, nor is anything lacking in the future. Again, because there is no dimension through which one part is usually separated from another, all things are present in every part. Therefore, every form is **all-formed** <term>omniformis; the Platonic idea that every part of the divine mind contains the whole</term>, though in various ways. For formal distinction itself is not removed, even though dimension and time are taken away. For even where dimension and time exist, many very different qualities are present together in the same thing, and all are in every part of it. 

Since, therefore, in the intellectual world all things are in each thing, and nothing is lacking to anyone there, it is rightly said that there is no motion there, no impulse from one thing to another, and no new intention or generation. For no part is contrary to the whole, nor is one part there contrary to another. Indeed, even if they were contraries, one would not make an impulse against the other, since nothing is lacking to anything, and every single thing is entirely **in act** <term>in actu; fully realized and active, not merely potential</term>, so that nothing new can be produced from it. In general, because it is proper for a body to be in motion, but for the incorporeal to be in a state of rest, it is right that just as this heaven <note>the physical sky</note> acts and generates more on earth the more it moves, so that higher realm—the more truly it remains still—the more truly it makes this whole world, and makes all things within it.

### How the world is made from the higher realm, and how it degenerates.

**II** In what way, then, does this world proceed from that one? Surely, just as from a relatively simple seed a manifold power naturally sprouts into a bud, then that fertility results in a great progression here. There, that entire immense act is unified and simultaneous; here, it passes into the movement of the degenerate, and eternity passes into time. From the distance of form and position, origins arise; from division, however, comes need; and from both come appetite, motion, and impulse. Since all nature is from the **Good** <note>the ultimate source of being in Neoplatonism</note>, and therefore its intention is not toward evil but toward the good, natural things do not act through hatred or dissent from one another, but through the very diligence and love of themselves, lest they be severed from their source. 

But since nature in each primary genus produces those things that follow as if it were most fertile in itself, much more does that Essence—which, being first, needs no support besides its own essential life—generate the essences and lives of things. By the very fact that it lives its own life, all other things obtain their essence and life from there. But if you also attribute this to divine intelligence and will, nothing is thereby added to the source. For there, intelligence and will are nature itself. Insofar as nature acts, it acts by necessity; but insofar as nature there is intelligence, it acts also by will. Since it acts both through a voluntary nature and a natural will, it certainly does not need investigation or counsel to act. 

Accordingly, if you distinguish Essence and Intelligence by reason, you will see the matter of this world born from Essence, but its form from Intelligence. And just as Essence is thought to precede Intelligence in a certain order there, so here you will think of matter preceding form. But before that Intelligence provides form to the world—a corporeal form far distant from itself—because the incorporeal has its own end first from its own life, they procreate the **World Soul** <term>anima mundi</term> as a middle between Essence and Intelligence. This is a "vegetable" life composed with the intellectual, acting as a medium between the Intellect and the corporeal form, just as life there holds the middle between Essence and Intelligence. And this very thing is the **seminal reason** <term>ratio seminaria; the spiritual blueprint or "seed" that governs physical growth</term> of the world, and like a certain word of the divine intelligence which, having struck matter, took on the worldly ornament. 

When you read that "the intellect infuses reason into matter," interpret the intellect not only as the simple intellect itself, but also as the "animal" intellect <note>the soul's intellect</note>, which is first formed by the higher intellect. From that higher one through this soul, and from the soul's power, the genital power sprouts into matter, depending on the essence of both. Similarly, it is often said: "The Sun generates natural things," which it nevertheless does with the light flowing from it. There, the solar light and the radiance together produce these things through heat. He compares both intellects to the male. For he generates with a power separate from the offspring. He compares the seminal nature of the world to the seminal virtue of the male, which acts on things from within. He compares the world to the generated offspring. In both cases, members are distributed among themselves, and parts are so conflicting that in the seed they were together and did not fight. The world consists of necessity—that is, matter and the defect occurring from matter—and also of intelligence, that is, the formal order reflecting intelligence. It is resolved into parts, as if into limbs: that is, into matter and the seminal and formal reason. But the very essence of the intellectual soul is not an innermost part of the world, but presides over it.

### Four stages after the Good: the Intellectual, the Animate, the Seminal, and the Sensible; and how procession and judgment occur.

**III** If anything in considering the world should offend you, do not accuse God, as if he did not consult well or choose poorly in the construction of the world. For he does not bring it together by deliberation, but nature itself acts sufficiently. Nor should you argue against nature in the first principle of things. For it is goodness itself; from goodness it does the simply best in the closest proximity—namely, the intellectual world. And it does this by its first purpose. For if it acts by goodness, it acts also by will. For in the first principle, will concurs with goodness. Therefore, the intelligible world existed by the first will (so to speak); but the animate world <note>the world of the Soul</note>, which follows next from the intelligible by a certain necessity, he wills in a way by a "necessity of consequence." For it does not escape him that the second follows from the work, nor does he reject it, but he does not approve it as the first. 

Similarly, that intellectual world generates the animate world not by counsel, but by nature. Since its nature is intelligence, and intelligence is will, while nature acts, intelligence and will also act. I say it generates the first animate world, and consequently the seminal world in nature, which it knows must necessarily follow the animate. By the same logic, the animate world—that is, the intellectual soul—by a certain natural intelligence and will generates life and a genital nature, namely the seminal world, the final trace of the divine things. By a necessity of consequence, it generates the types of sensible things following the seminal world—I say following, because from the living seminal world life must still be poured out, but not by the intelligence or will which the sensible lacks. 

For it acts by living, just as the intellectual soul and the first intellect act by understanding. Conversely, the intellect acts naturally by understanding, and in the manner of nature, just as nature generates by living, and builds in the order of intelligence. Therefore, do not estimate or weigh the dignity of the marvelous Good itself, or pure intellect, or the animate intellect entirely from the sensible world. Instead, from the sensible world look to the dignity of the seminal; from this to the nature of the soul; from the soul to the excellence of the mind; and finally from the mind to the Good. Then, in contemplating the sensible world, do not fix your whole attention on the parts, but behold the whole. Do not refer the whole to the parts, but the parts to the whole. Nor should you demand this work to be simply the best, but the best that...

### COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...to that extent it occupies the ranks of the world, just as nature follows the Good. You will note, meanwhile, where the world is imagined to speak: for sometimes it governs many kinds of living things as one; there are also many things above, and the whole is joined together according to its own dignity as an image of the divine life itself. The first of these it calls **gods**; the following, **demons** <term>daemones; in the Platonic sense, these are not "evil" spirits, but spiritual intermediaries between the divine and the human</term>; the third, **particular lives**, which are transferred into demons. Where he placed the populations of demons, he showed that they are distributed throughout the air above us and have their own leaders who follow the stars and specific regions. We suspect the bodies of demons everywhere follow the motions of the stars by their own movement. In those places, they everywhere perform a **dance** <note>original: "choram," likely referring to the "cosmic dance" of the heavens</note>. 

They press upon the stars according to their strength, size, shape, and manner of acting: just as the stars act by the gaze of their rays, an effective frequency of the imagination. You will note, moreover, that the ether is of an aerial nature, and therefore its reasons depend on the Good, since that part desires the Good in all things. Finally, life itself is simply mind itself: where he says that the intelligible nature alone possesses the whole of life. Thus you may infer that whatever ranks of things exist are participants in life only insofar as they possess something intellectual. It should be observed from **Porphyry** <note>OCR reads "Psophycis," likely a corruption of Porphyrius, the student of Plotinus</note>—not by deliberation, but by nature—as **Porphyry** confirms in his commentary on the *Timaeus*: "Action indeed requires instruments, insofar as it provides for the service of matter, and they do not dominate entirely, but labor from the outside. But natural powers, insofar as they belong to perfection, are intimate to it; they act as much as they are." For thus, being always from the soul, essential life moves, increases, generates, breathes, feels, and so on. Even in the imagination, it is so powerful that by the sole variety of its act it affects the body with various qualities and motions. Lastly (as theologians hand down), demons perform wonders by their imaginations without any instrument or outward act; they produce effects by their will alone, emitting rays from there, as if sending out forms from their imagination to affect the world. How much more, then, is the being of the world itself—that is, the spiritual substance—able to rule the whole division of the world? For whom is it a marvel that something is propagated from the incorporeal by its excess of power? Since from the smallest seed a living animal sprouts forth, with so many and such diverse members composed from it? And if in a small seed that seminal power is so vast while it produces great things, why should it not be great while it is whole in any seed? But while divine power needs nothing, it builds all things while remaining in its own nature; it produces and moves all things. Thus far **Porphyry**.

->Whatever things seem evil whether concerning bodies or souls, are reformed into good.<-

IIII. While this element here lends its parts to other elements elsewhere, meanwhile other parts are borrowed by others: and the two elements seem to undergo almost nothing of evil. Similarly in the composition, while it is given to that matter—namely, itself. For when the elements then return to their spheres, or another composite is generated, and generation itself, while it takes parts from the elements, adorns them with new forms: this perpetual change of generation is necessary for the world. For since mundane matter both can and ought to receive innumerable forms of things for its perfection, yet cannot hold them all at the same time—because the matter from which they are made is not enough for innumerable composites at once, nor does the space hold them, nor do such diverse things agree—it follows that by perpetual exchange, it induces innumerable figures and new powers by its motion. These do not all arise at the same time where they might admit conflicting things; and meanwhile, by motion, it contributes to transforming the lower matter. Therefore, by this reasoning, transmutation—both of place and of form—contributes to the best: it preserves the "habit" of the universe. We should judge individual things as good insofar as they contribute to the order of the whole. 

Hence, where things appear to be broken by another force, one might argue from the rectitude of another discipline that they are sometimes destroyed by one thing so as to be built into others. Meanwhile, whatever is deteriorated or corrupted regarding certain souls—and even evil itself—is not permitted to happen except for other equally numerous and better benefits, so that it may rightly complete the order of the universe. Furthermore, right order requires (as is clear from the wonderful abundance of the earth) that many subsequent ranks should arise, and that they should decline gradually from the state of the first unity. Thus, the breath of life is mitigated, as if the essence were immediately mobile before it is bent by itself or by other moving things. Since motion is derived from the state of minds, then it distinguishes us in its distribution. Therefore, many things are stable through others and are returned to others in a certain way; and those that have motion from themselves are finally restored. But truly, just as those things which are stable through themselves must be superior and established in a certain common power, lest the inferior things seem to succeed through many particular valleys. Since the procession of things must be continuous, and nothing left empty in this succession, it is right that after the universal and self-moving things, we descend to their opposites—namely, the particular and immobile. Between these are interposed certain things which are particular, but have a nature that is stable in itself. But the condition of such particular natures can sometimes be contracted into a certain habit: but because of that self-moving faculty, they can sometimes move from their own habit. The condition of particular nature also brings about another change of life by parts, with free motion meanwhile contributing to this. Thus they may sometimes obtain a nearer habit, sometimes a superior one, and sometimes an inferior one. They can easily turn to either side, as they occupy a middle nature; they fill the other things which the superior common things embrace in a universal tract. 

Meanwhile, the nature of the universe enjoys this circular change of motions. In this genus of particular substances, souls are placed by a mobile law; these, **Plotinus** says, take turns in changing bodies—that is, the souls of lower men, inhabiting this turbulent air. Indeed, he desires that rational souls inhabit even here; yet intellectual natures do not always inhabit a region in a way that is discordant or contrary to the happiness of life and intelligence. Hence the **Platonists** confirm the "alternation" of souls <note>original: "vicissitudinem animarum," referring to metempsychosis or reincarnation</note>. And since a harder province falls to such souls, and they even slip into worse states, it is providently compensated that they can eventually return not only to the next superior ranks, but even to the highest things—that is, to transcend even to heaven. They believe that such souls, having laid aside the body, leave the turbulences of both earth and air...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically focusing on the descent of the soul, the nature of "mobile" versus "immobile" life, and the philosophical justification for why evil exists in a world governed by divine providence.</meta>

# ON BOOK II. ENNEAD III.

...for a time to be counted among the ethereal **demons** <term>daemones; in Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that inhabit the air</term> in a body of purer air, and even to be made colleagues of universal souls—that is, the souls of the heavens—within a celestial body, which Plotinus says is placed beyond the realm of generation. Finally, if they should furthermore lay aside the celestial body, they live a life not so much with the celestial soul as with the "idea" of the celestial soul, which we call the **mind**. Here Plotinus calls this a "completely immobile life," namely, a stable intellectual life belonging either to the first Mind <note>referring to the "Nous" or Divine Intellect</note> or those that follow. He calls "mobile life," on the other hand, the collective animal effects, whether they are found in the discourse of the imaginary reason or in the service of generation. Specifically, he calls the generative power "mobile life" here, which flows continually from the very consistency of that higher life, just like its breath—much like the motion in our vital pulse arises from our soul. He calls this kind of generative faculty, which arises from the **Soul of the World** <term>anima mundi; the spirit that animates the entire universe</term> and from the souls of all the worldly spheres at once, and which is implanted in matter and rules over it, the **worldly reason**, the mother of the animals produced. He says that the forms of these animals consist in the higher heaven, that is, the intellectual realm. From there, they have come into matter through **seminal reason** <term>rationem seminariam; the spiritual "seeds" or blueprints that direct the growth and form of physical things</term>, just as many say that the forms of earthly things proceed from celestial forms through the lights shining from them. For one must not think that forms arise from this formless matter, nor order from unmixed chance, nor stability from a nature that is entirely unstable.

But to return to the order of the universe—to which whatever harmonizes in any way must be judged as good, since the order is the best—such an order requires that particular souls, which are mobile of themselves and possess free motion, and are akin not only to intelligence but also to alternating generation, should be able to choose both the intelligible and the sensible good. And this very choice of alternatives is good for the universe; in this way, ministries are fulfilled and natural works proceed simultaneously, provided that souls do not postpone the intelligible good by choosing the sensible good. For the soul is something that chooses everything by reason of the "good," and if it prefers a lesser good to a greater one, it may be an evil for the one choosing, yet it is still a good for the universe. This is especially true because a harmony immediately reflects back upon such a choice: so that the soul which turns toward worse things is itself made worse and undergoes a worse life. This state is certainly judged as good because it harmonizes with the order of natural justice. It even turns out to be a good for the soul, insofar as the distress of a delinquent mind sometimes leads it to repentance for a wicked choice. Thus, the goodness of divine providence transforms a nascent evil into a good; and it accomplishes this stably in the motions of both the highest and lowest things.

It happens by chance that air is made from this water, or water from this air; however, the water of that matter could not take on lightness, nor the matter of air contain a destined heaviness, nor that matter ascend to the place of the air, nor this one descend to the thirst of the water, except that forms are already implanted naturally, and they necessarily seek congruent places by the law of nature and the divine law, which the law of nature perpetually follows. Similarly, by the faculty of the soul's own free will, it happens that it first turns toward such or such things; then it inclines toward them more frequently; finally, once a habit is formed, souls are carried toward them as if by nature and by natural and divine law simultaneously, and thus they obtain this or that kind of life. But He who sanctioned the law of nature was not led to sanction the law and establish order by deliberating over the transgression of law and order, as men are usually accustomed to do. For before the first simple law itself, which is the first order, there can be no transgression of law; nor can the first order be procreated from the privation of order. Our human lawmakers are warned by the transgression of natural law to write laws for the people, but the essential form of the divine mind itself is the law and order of all things, and then the law of nature follows. Therefore, whatever falls away from this best order due to weakness immediately falls by that same order from good into evil—evil, I say, for itself, but good for the world; insofar as it falls there only as and to the extent that order requires. Indeed, "evil" and what is proper to it is nothing other than a defect of this kind. 

Thus **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: "Trism[egistus]"</note>, following (as I believe) **Dionysius the Areopagite**, explains: Evil is not in intellectual things, for they are closest to the Good itself, nor is it in universal souls and bodies, for universal form and authority belong to their own good. It remains, therefore, that evil is in particular souls and bodies. Yet it is not in their essences born from God, nor again in their natural powers, for these also depend on God. Evil, therefore, happens only to their actions. But as far as it concerns souls, it is not in their rational actions, for all seek the good; nor again in their actions lacking reason, for they are carried by a good nature; but it is in a certain incongruity between them, which they call **asymmetry** <note>original: "asymmetriam," meaning incommensuration or lack of proportion</note>. Furthermore, as far as it concerns bodies, evil is not in the form (for it wishes to rule over matter), nor again in the matter (for it desires to be adorned), but in the unfitness of the matter for the form. From this he concludes that all evil is "beyond subsistence" <note>meaning it has no independent existence of its own</note>, and whatever it may be, it is colored by a divine condition as something suspended under the condition of the Good. Since generation exists, it is necessary that this [evil] also be present as something conducive to worldly perfection; but since divine providence overcomes all things and wills the good, it is wonderfully shaped into good. But if He uses the destruction of some things as a "bad" thing for the construction of others as a "good" thing, and for the restoration of the world as the "best" thing, how much more does He use a certain defect of the soul wonderfully for that perfection. 

At the end of this chapter, you will note three habits contracted into evil: the causes. The first is that very beginning which the soul takes even before this present life, to turn toward such a life and gradually become more inclined to it. The second is the body so affected that it provokes the soul to such things—incautious from the very start, and thereafter gradually accustomed to them. The third is the habit of meeting sensible things through the senses into the soul, as if effecting her before reason either notices or matures in deliberation, and altogether the negligence of the mind in its own consultation. Punishment, however, necessarily follows. For the choice itself and the perverse motion is both a sin and a punishment sharply piercing the soul, until providence, in the manner of a physician, heals the soul through the stings of such affliction; while it thus provokes a hatred for the perverse habit, repentance for the iniquitous choice, and an most useful love for the contrary choice. Similarly, a right choice is simultaneously the beginning of both a reward and a virtue. Both, however, are as **Proclus** says, works of divine providence, which acts as a healer for those doing just things, delighting the soul, but wonderfully afflicting madness.

---

It is fitting for intelligible beings, as stable things close to the Good itself, to be happy; but for souls, as noble but more remote things, it is fitting that they be *made* happy—but because they are mobile of themselves, they become so through their own effort. Now, for more common souls, blessedness is obtained through a certain brief effort. But for particular souls...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically focusing on how divine providence governs a world where adversity and "evil" appear to exist. Ficino reconciles the suffering of the good with a perfectly ordered universe.</meta>

# COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO

...hard-won happiness was obtained: indeed, they consider themselves blessed, but labors make them so over a long time. And since everyone can eventually achieve this, it is a sin to complain about our condition; nor is it permitted to lose faith in divine providence because of adversity. Hear **Synesius the Platonist** <note>original: "Synecium Platonium"; Synesius of Cyrene was a 4th-century philosopher-bishop who combined Neoplatonism with Christianity</note> speaking divinely on this matter: "Adversity, even that which seems to happen to us beyond our merits, contributes greatly to rooting out that anxious affection we feel for fleeting things. Certainly, among those who possess a mind, fortune of this kind is confirmed by providence, though those who are mentally blind usually lose faith in providence because of it. For no place would be left for souls to flee from matter and return to their fatherland if they encountered no evil here." Therefore, one must consider that the lower governors of provinces <note>referring to lesser spiritual entities or "daemones" managing the physical world</note> devised common prosperities as if they were traps for souls. Thus, one might say that for souls migrating from here, they encounter the drink of forgetfulness; certainly, for souls entering this life, a certain sweet and bland fortune of life brings the drink of oblivion <term>drink of oblivion; a reference to the mythological River Lethe, which caused souls to forget their divine origin</term>. Thus far Synesius.

Accordingly, it is necessary—as the order of things runs—that adversity happens to many, not unlike how a certain part might seem to sound discordant in a grand harmony. But just as that which seems to clash in a single part of a concert fits perfectly within the total order of the world, so too adversity—whether in the body or in fortune—serves as an exercise and progress for the good, and as punishment and purging for the evil. Indeed, even wickedness itself contributes to the order, insofar as it is not only punished in an orderly fashion, but also provides the material for justice and an example for men. Furthermore, when it is weighed down by heavy misery, it deters others from vice and demonstrates, by comparison, how great the happiness is in virtue. After this, observe that evils—which have their "idea" <term>idea; the perfect, archetypal form in the divine mind</term> even in the higher regions of the world—do not proceed from any intention of those higher things, but happen at the very end of the long chain of goods, at the point where the good finally fails. Although these things happen as if by chance, it was nevertheless in the intention of the rulers and in the nature of virtue from the beginning to use the evils that happen in any way for good, and to reform them everywhere into justice.

-> He confirms the same points and raises doubts. <-

VI Since everything is received according to the nature of the recipient <note>original: "pro natura suscipientis"; a fundamental philosophical rule that the effect of an influence depends on the capacity of the thing receiving it</note>, it is certain that whatever happens to the good turns out good in the end, and to the evil, bad. Likewise, since man is the soul itself, and the entire good of the soul consists in virtue, while the entire evil consists in wickedness: it follows that for a man perfected through virtue and already blessed, subsequent comforts or discomforts outside the soul mean nothing, even if they sometimes help or diminish. Similarly, for a man—that is, a soul—confirmed in vice and already miserable, subsequent things add nothing and take nothing away. Yet, it will seem more fitting to most people that prosperity happens to the good and adversity to the evil, so that the outstanding works of the good are increased, while the public crimes of the evil are suppressed. But before responding to these things, you will consider that the universe, down to its smallest parts, depends on wisdom, so that the power and action of intellectual providence spreads itself down to the smallest things and leaves nothing unordered.

-> He provides the principles for responding. <-

VII No one should desire absolute beauty in every way in this world, which is not the "first world" but the fourth, and has degenerated far from the first. Do not, again, blame God for the actions of rational souls—which, being mobile by themselves, seem to be the cause of their own actions—as if He were properly the cause of such actions; nor should you think that souls are arbitrarily compelled by the very nature of the world to choose such a life and action. For since the essence of souls is superior to and prior to the nature of the world, it is not from the world, but from the souls themselves, that it happens that they live in the world and are more or less affected by it. Finally, do not demand from souls, while they are in the nature of bodies and so much flesh, the height of all perfection. Beware lest the less-ordered race of men should seem outside it, or that divine providence does not reach down to men—for it is fitting that it descends even below man to the smallest things, seen in the highly artistic arrangement and motion of them all. This can only be effected by the **seminal and vital reason** <term>rationem seminariam; the divine "seeds" or blueprints that guide the growth and function of living things</term> from the divine breath of the mind, just as in an animal, by a similar reason of nature, not only the higher and middle members but even the lowest parts are made and governed.

-> He responds to the doubts above and touches upon new opinions. <-

VIII About to respond to the doubts, he says it is no wonder there is not the same order among us on earth as there is in the highest realms; far from being a trivial thing, the human race is not the highest of animals, but the middle between beasts and gods—that is, the **demons** <term>daemones; intermediary spirits</term>. Therefore, humans err because it belongs to the order of the universe that a middle nature, mixed from both sides and mobile by itself, sometimes keeps the middle and then turns itself toward either extreme. Among these things, to express the insignificance of our affairs, he says the earth is like a point compared to the universe, or like a tiny star among the rest. 

Perhaps he touches here upon the opinion of certain **Pythagoreans**, who say that the globe of the earth, surrounded by water, if seen from the wider heavens, appears like a moon struck by the rays of the sun. Because it moves continually in the manner of a star, we do not perceive it because the heavens and the stars move together consequently. Thus, in any star there is something solid, and again something liquid and transparent, just as in the "earthly star" <note>the Earth</note>, and perhaps not a little is molten, as in the moon, but from a distance it appears minimal. The whole space is like air, and the globe is one unit surrounded everywhere by stars—as if by worlds—and the stars move by their own progression, as befits such living beings, and they are full of inhabitants, just like the earthly star, though some are more excellent than others and are inhabited by more excellent beings. 

After this, you will observe the new response of Plotinus: that among the "goods of the soul" one should not count only those pertaining to contemplation, temperance, and justice, but also those pertaining to all skill brought about by talent, habit, and dexterity. Therefore, it is just that those who are more excellent in this kind of good should surpass others in the things properly acquired by it, and gain something more from it. Conversely, it is fair that those who are more excellent in contemplation, temperance, and justice should similarly surpass others in receiving the rewards proper to their virtue. The rewards of the latter are divine, while the rewards of the former are fleeting. Meanwhile, it is justly punished if their unbridled will and more idle life often neglect necessary things. Finally, providence and justice cannot be defended to the highest degree through this and similar arguments if we only consider this present life; things which are frequently missing here in the present—whether reward or punishment—must be compensated for either from another life or elsewhere.

He argues that humans occupy a middle state in the universe and that true justice may only be visible when considering the soul's journey across multiple lives.</summary>
