<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically exploring the relationship between divine providence and the independent actions of worldly things. It addresses the philosophical problem of how a singular First Cause can allow for secondary causes and free will.</meta>

ON BOOK II OF ENNEAD III.

### That divine power in acting does not prevent lower things from acting, especially rational ones.

IX Some people imagine that all effects—no matter what things they seem to be produced by, whether inanimate or rational—are so overtaken by the First Cause <note>original: "causa prima"; the ultimate source of all existence, which for Ficino is God</note> that they happen only through this one agent, while all others are merely passive. They believe no action proper to the things themselves intervenes. If the proper actions of things were thus removed, their own powers would be empty, or rather, they would be non-existent. Similarly, their own essences would be destroyed, and nothing would remain but a bare, common result or effect; or rather, nothing would exist at all after the First. In this view, every event—even the most vile, those lacking all order, and even evil events—would be produced directly by the Highest Good alone. 

Furthermore, after the first act of the Primary Agent, no further act or action would persist, but only a most common and extreme passivity. It would be as if nothing bright or hot proceeded from the light or heat of the elements, except that which mimics its origin by illuminating or heating; instead, the work would be entirely dark. Certainly, if the work of God were compiled only from passive slaves <note>original: "mancipijs"; suggesting entities with no agency of their own</note>, it would in no way be divine, but utterly abject. God would not be rightly called the First Cause or the First Agent if there were no secondary agents after Him. Such things cannot be agents unless they produce something through an act; otherwise, a thing that is not acting, but is only passive, would be "acting" out of passivity. 

Finally, just as a thing is not seen to exist everywhere through certain objects, so too it would seem that effects result from God everywhere instantly without the need for objects. It would be as if the Sun, without the help of the elements, were to complete the works of all mixed bodies, plants, and animals at all hours. But in truth, God gave natures to things and granted them their own power of acting. It is only right that simple acting belongs to the First, which is simply Pure Act <term>Pure Act; "actus purus," a philosophical term for a being with no unfulfilled potential, traditionally identifying God</term>. Other things, which derive from the First so that they exist in a certain state of activity, are also granted the ability to act. Because they receive from the Immense Good the capacity to be as good as possible in all things, they diffuse their own goodness into others by working. Thus, the Good itself, while communicating its likeness to a power, does so both that the things might exist as participants and that they might be causes for others. For as their cause, the Good gave them the ability to be causes themselves. 

An effect proceeds from each thing, both moved by another and as its own; yet it is as close to God as it is to its own cause. This is as close as the power of a vine <note>original: "uitis"; a classic Neoplatonic metaphor for the chain of being where the source flows through the branches</note> is to the vine itself, though it is not equal to it. Nor is one part of a work produced by a proper cause and another part by a common cause; rather, the whole is produced by both, though differently—from one as a principle and immediate cause, and from the other as an instrument. We consider, therefore, in any agent both its essence and its power. This power depends on the power of a superior agent, insofar as it is given, preserved, or moved to its work from there. And just as an effect is made equally by the essence of a lower cause and its power, so it is made by this very power together with the power of the superior. This continues further to the power of the Highest, always with an equal closeness, insofar as the following agent always acts by the power of the preceding one. 

By these most powerful reasons, we affirm that after the one most common Agent, there are many things which act through themselves and by themselves. They fulfill certain proper tasks with their own powers, provided they are led by the common action of the First Agent—just as agents beneath the Moon act through themselves and also through the Sun. If such a duty (or tribute) is granted to things even below man, how much more is it given to man, through a soul that is self-moving, to act by himself—and to act differently and more often than if he were merely being pulled from on high? 

Just as in the works of nature, whatever is found to be more common and better is often a tribute from higher causes, whereas whatever is more specific or less good is added from proximate causes. So in human actions and works, the common act is effective, such as that which comes to us more rightly from divine sources. However, the specific condition of acting "thus or so," or in a worse manner, happens because of us and our circumstances. This is no different than how, in a lame person, the limping comes from the crookedness of the leg, but the ability to walk comes from the soul. 

Since divine providence does not take away the natures and proper actions of things—which it gave and preserves—and since defects and evil occur in a work when these grades fail over a long stretch, evil is rightly not so much "removed" by providence as it is suddenly "transferred" into good. Just as in music, a somewhat discordant voice is not removed, nor is a middle silence often taken away, but the harmony of both is applied as a fitting and pleasing perfection. Therefore, if providence does not remove evil from the midst, it rightly does not remove fortune <note>original: "fortunam"; chance or luck</note>, which is less contrary to the goodness of providence than evil is. 

Providence has established under itself a long order of causes; the superior causes, endowed with greater power, act further and wider than the inferior ones. Because natural power extends only as far as the intention of nature reaches, many things happen in effects far removed from the First. These arise from the power of the action and the intention of higher causes, to which the intention of the lower causes does not extend, since their power is propagated only so far. Such things, therefore, happen "beyond the intention" of lower causes, yet they occur by the intention of higher souls. To the former, they are fortuitous; to the latter, they are not. Even those things called "monstrous" <note>original: "prodigiosa"; unnatural occurrences or omens</note>—which happen beyond the intention and order of a particular nature—nevertheless follow the order and purpose of the higher ones. 

Providence does not remove chance, lest it lose the long order of causes. It does not remove evil, lest it take away the abundance of good things, or rather, lest it break the order of various species. While these species are distinguished by their own differences, they are equally separated by grades of goodness. Whoever removes the different grades of goodness removes the wonderful abundance of various species. From the long production of grades of goodness, evil finally arises at the end, where something either already fails from its own good or is able to fail. 

If the goodness of divine providence does not remove evil, and if its reason does not destroy chance, then certainly its freedom does not take away our freedom. Indeed, if providence rules fate <note>original: "fatum"</note>, it does not want souls to be forced to sin by fates, lest providence itself be the cause of sins. If God were to compel the rest, He would certainly impel human powers with the power of things, so that they might act everywhere divinely and from on high. But since the divine power, while acting in all things, does not prevent them from acting in their own way and in their own time, certainly divine knowledge, while considering the proper natures of things, will not deprive a thing of its own property. For this knowledge, together with the power that exists from it, is the cause of all things in such a way that they are brought forth with their own natures. 

It is because of this cause that intellectual and rational natures lead themselves in acting toward the divine likeness, rather than being dragged. It is because of this cause that lower natures, more dissimilar to God, are led in acting by something else, but are led according to their own properties. This ensures that things are not dragged everywhere against their natures under the order of God, the institutor of natures, lest there be a kind of perpetual violence where all things are arranged by the wonderful will of the Good itself—and the Good is sought not violently, but naturally. Providence calls souls back to God: the ingenious ones through wonder at the beauty and order of things, and the slower ones at least through their marvelous convenience. It cares for and chastises all, like both a doctor and a father.

<summary>This page argues that divine providence does not negate the independent actions of secondary causes or human free will, but rather incorporates them into a harmonious universal order. Ficino explains that evil and chance are not removed by God because doing so would destroy the diversity of nature and the chain of causality.</summary>
<keywords>divine providence, primary cause, secondary causes, free will, nature of evil, harmony, chain of being, fate, rational souls, Marsilio Ficino, Plotinus</keywords>

--- Page 277 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically continuing the discussion of how the soul relates to divine providence and whether human actions are compelled by external forces like the stars or internal biological drives.</meta>

### Rational souls are not compelled to shameful actions by either superior or inferior forces.

**X** Since it was said in the previous sections that humans are free under the care of providence, Ficino now questions how we should understand Plato’s frequent claim that "no one is evil voluntarily." <note>original: "homines non sponte fieri malos"; a central Platonic paradox suggesting that people only choose evil because they mistake it for a good, or are blinded by passion.</note> If this is true, it would seem humans are forced to sin, whether by the influence of the heavens, some fatal internal instinct, or by "seminal reasons" <note>original: "seminali ratione"; the formative biological and spiritual blueprints that shape an organism's development.</note>. The answer given is that when people sin, they are moved voluntarily toward the action they have chosen, even if they do not "voluntarily" fall into the perverse habit that grows secretly and gradually through repeated actions. Thus, the movement begins with the will; however, as they proceed far enough down that path, they slide into such a habit by necessity, and from that habit, they are necessarily delivered into punishment. 

It is clear that humans are not always driven to act by inferior bodies (physical urges), because they often choose and perform actions that reason proves to be beyond or even contrary to their physical condition. Furthermore, it is clear they are not compelled by superior bodies (the stars/planets) or their rulers, because they often act perversely against the very dignity and order of those higher powers. Similarly, humans perform virtuous movements starting from their own rational principle. Whenever multiple principles of action are counted together, the rational faculty itself is always included in that number of acting principles.

---

### Beyond the qualities of bodies, there is everywhere an incorporeal life ruling all things rationally, and this universal nature dominates particular natures.

**XI** The eleventh chapter asks whether every outcome of events arises solely from a "fated" conjunction of physical bodies, or if there is another providence beyond that. We have shown elsewhere, and sufficiently in our *Theology*, that beyond physical causes there is a certain life infused everywhere in things, naturally crafting all things according to fixed reasons. This life imposes a limit on physical qualities that would otherwise rush forward with total force. It reconciles conflicting elements, and stamps specific forms and shapes onto matter that is, by itself, uncertain and wandering. It creates living things from the non-living. 

Just as a human craft builds from the outside, this "natural art" <note>original: "ars naturalis"; Ficino views nature as God’s artistry working from within the objects themselves.</note> builds from within, more easily and successfully. It moves plants (which are otherwise motionless) and even the most sluggish animals at set times and in wondrous ways to propagate their species. It also skillfully equips plants from within—roots to seek moisture, and fruits and leaves to seek heat. It moves heavy and light objects in straight lines according to "geometric" laws, and it guides even the lowliest animals toward what they need through "prophecies" <note>original: "vaticinijs"; here meaning natural instincts that seem like divine foreknowledge</note>, sagacity, and natural arts. They are led by reasons that often surpass human reason, for they are led divinely. 

This is a kind of "breath" <note>original: "spiraculum"; a vital spirit or spark</note> of the air and the power of the World Soul, universally and rationally striking and shaping matter. It has two boundaries: it hangs from the intellectual substance of the soul itself, but it ends in matter. Insofar as it ends in matter, it is simply called "seminal reason." But insofar as it proceeds from the intellect—either the soul's own or through the soul from the First Cause—it is called "intellectual and law-giving reason." Again, as it is seminal, it creates physical things; as it is law-giving, it sets the degrees of change and action for the movements of souls. 

Truly, because it is both seminal and law-giving at once, it disposes the entire order of the universe according to its ranks. It is exactly like a seal from the intellectual principle, stamping matter with precision. This is "Universal Nature." Many things happen according to its intention which often go against the "particular intention" of an individual nature. For example, while the reproductive power in any animal (acting as the male) strives to procreate a perfect version of its own kind, Universal Nature sometimes wants a female—so that through male and female animals, the propagation of the universe is more perfect. 

Similarly, while any individual thing intends only to continue itself, Universal Nature meanwhile intends to dissolve that thing to compose another, and then another, looking out for the good of the whole. Thus, while individuals of any species would naturally look out for themselves rather than the species, this force secretly impels them to care for the species as much as or more than themselves, and to provide for their offspring more diligently than for themselves. They are led not so much by their own qualities as by universal providence. Finally, while specific species would naturally only be born from their own kind, this nature produces the mule from the horse and the donkey; and it prevents the propagation of mules, even though particular nature equips mules with reproductive organs. In short, it wants the whole universe to be filled with diverse and very different things, enriched by a wondrous abundance of various forms. From all this, "evil" may seem to appear—that is, the admission of a "lesser good" in some places—but it is done for the sake of a greater, universal good.

---

### Because Universal Nature is "all-formed," it makes the universe "all-formed" and does not compel souls.

**XII** Human artists who work with external qualities, and natural qualities that work like "seeds," usually "make themselves" in a way—just as an artist’s imagination and spirit are formed into the image of a horse before he creates a physical horse. If natural things (which act through natural qualities) also "make themselves" by propagating their form outward, and if the heavens (acting through light and motion) act upon the elements by gifting them celestial qualities, then surely this Nature that rules all things acts in a similar way. In making the world, Nature expresses itself; it makes the world "all-formed" <note>original: "omniformem"; containing the archetypes or blueprints for every possible form of life.</note> because Nature itself is all-formed. 

I say "all-formed" because it flows from an all-formed intelligence. However, the forms of things in this Nature are further apart from each other than they are in the Divine Mind. This is because Nature is further from "the One" (unity) and cannot reconcile its parts as the Mind can. Furthermore, being lower in power, Nature needs more tools and forms to act. Finally, because it must accommodate itself to matter (where countless things must be replaced as they perish), Nature is greatly distracted or spread out. 

Therefore, many things result in the matter of the world from the specific condition of Nature itself, rather than from the property of the Divine Mind; in these cases, it is wrong to blame the Divine Mind as if it were the immediate craftsman. Note that rational souls are not compelled to fall into a worse fate by this "seminal reason" of the world. Indeed, the soul is like a colleague of the World Soul and possesses its own authority and duty in worldly affairs. Therefore, souls move up or down on their own "hinge" <note>original: "cardine proprio"; their own axis or center of choice.</note>.

<meta>catchword: non</meta>

<summary>This page argues that human souls possess free will and are not forced into evil by the stars or biology, explaining that "Universal Nature" acts as an internal divine blueprint that prioritizes the balance of the whole universe over individual parts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s "Enneads," specifically expanding on the mechanisms by which Providence governs the world, administers justice across multiple lifetimes, and manifests divine craftsmanship even in the smallest details of nature.</meta>

### ON THE BOOKS OF THE THIRD ENNEAD

...not indeed compelled by the nature of the world, but rather harmonizing opportunely with nature itself. For nature herself fits and matches such seats and lots to the souls who have prepared themselves for this or that way of living.

->By what order providence punishes, and how it acts.<-

XIII After this, Plotinus descends to the Platonic, Pythagorean, and Egyptian opinion that there is a cycle of all things. Therefore, those crimes which providence does not punish in one life are punished in another life by the penalty of retaliation <note>original: "talionis pœna"; the principle of "an eye for an eye," where the punishment matches the crime.</note>. In this sense, Origen accepted that Gospel saying, *He who strikes with the sword, perishes by the sword* <note>original: "Qui ferit gladio, gladio perit"; see Matthew 26:52</note>. But let Origen see to that himself. The Kabbalists, the teachers of the Hebrews, also approve of such a condition of punishment, believing that the souls of men often return to this life in a human form; in this way, curable sins are purged, but they can return here only three times. For they believe these turns are sufficient for testing, and the soul which has been purged through these cycles deserves to become more blessed than it was before its descent. But the soul which utterly casts aside reason remains forever in a certain grade lower than reason—that is, in the imagination and brutal affection of an animal. They add, so that no one may excuse their own sin, that all souls were present when God gave the Law to Moses. However, they do not sufficiently prove a perpetual cycle. For they judge that a transformation of this kind can occur until the end of the world’s motion, which will be followed by at least eternal rest and the eternal happiness of the good. They judge that David's saying points to this: *An unfading inheritance forever* <note>original: "Immarcescibilem hereditas in æternum"; likely a paraphrase of Psalm 37:18 or 1 Peter 1:4</note>. Likewise, *the holy shall be preserved forever*. 

But let us return to Plotinus. He confirms that all human actions and habits are observed by providence and are arranged in a certain order according to merit, based on the fact that providence cares most diligently for things even much lower than us—indeed, even the lowest things—and arranges them most orderly. For if providence were to be neglected even down to the level of smoke, it would surely be a most vile and weak thing. Yet in these small things, a craftsmanship appears no less admirable than in the most precious things, looking both to necessity and to adornment. Indeed, the skill and diligence of the powerful Craftsman <note>Ficino uses "Artifex" to refer to the divine creator as a master artist or architect.</note> is even greater to the degree that this matter and these places seem to resist order. 

The order established in the universal matter of the world and the actions of worldly things, which always results from divinity, does not indicate some deliberation through which an order is sought, but rather results from the very essence of divinity, which is itself Order. Understand "Divinity" here not only as the divine intellect but also the intellect of the world (the World Soul); and furthermore, the intellectual "nursery" or "seed-bed" of this world, the breath of life in the world's matter. 

As for what was said about the cycle of things, nature seems to warn us in a way through the viper, when the newborn offspring kill the mother who had previously killed the father during mating. From this, perhaps, it is signified why the ancient laws suffocate parricides <note>those who kill their parents or close relatives</note> enclosed in a leather sack with a viper <note>original: "culleo inclusos"; refers to the Roman "Poena Cullei," where a parricide was sewn into a sack with a dog, a rooster, a viper, and a monkey, then thrown into the sea.</note>. And truly, just as it is right that the harmless genus of animals, which are easily devoured by others, should multiply as easily as possible, so too the pestiferous genus should have a more difficult time increasing.

->The works of nature are crafted by providence in the manner of an acting art and nature. Likewise, minds are not properly parts of this world.<-

XIIII we are accustomed to guess the qualities of the virtues in the actors from the quality of their works and actions. By this reasoning, we detect the heat-giving or moisture-giving power in the sun or moon, just as we do in fire and water, through their works and actions. Since, therefore, the work of nature is limited and is always specifically such a thing, and is made in such a way as is always accustomed to be made and governed by art and providence, we rightly conjecture that an artificial and providing power exists within and presides over nature—a power that is not wavering, not capable of fatigue, and not vacillating. Indeed, the work is carried out correctly and continuously, and unless something is retracted, the accustomed order is never deserted. 

And truly, since no discourse of human reason, however great, can fully attain the habit of nature's craftsmanship through either work or thought, we have a sign here that this is the work not merely of discursive thought, but of something entirely intellectual. I say an "Intellect" superior to the discourse of reason, at least as much as that work stands above the work of human art. For this Intellect does not act by seeking, but rather by the acting tenor of nature; indeed, it acts no differently than anything acting naturally. It acts with a stable intellect, without a doubt; otherwise, there would be no stability in things, no union, and no perpetual order of things and actions would be preserved. Finally, with this intellect, which understands all things at once more easily and happily than natural intelligences, and which makes things capable of being understood, just as the sun touches and acts upon the universe and individual things at once with its rays. 

The "Word" <term>Verbum; here meaning the formative expression or "Logos"</term> and nature of this intelligence belongs both to the absolute and the animal spirit, and by its "striking" <note>or "pulsing" influence</note>, they generate and move individual things, and interpret the secrets of the intelligence to those who understand. In the meantime, this is produced under the condition that in this "voice," individual things are more distantly separated from each other than they are in the originating concept. For there, because of the marvelous unity, all things are contained in any single nation; but here, because of discrepancy, they are more distant and are not all deeply present in every single thing. Therefore, neither here nor in the world should the ultimate perfection be required in the parts, nor should the property of one be expected in another part; rather, the power and wisdom of nature should be admired, because it has propagated itself so orderly through so many steps and such disparate grades. 

After this, understand the obscure end of this chapter thus: Men and daemons <note>intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil</note>, according to their bodily life, are parts of the universe. Again, according to their rational action, they are in a way something particular, because while their discourse is distracted by motion through many things, "before" or "after," it determines itself specifically to one thing or another. But according to the Mind, they are at the same time universal; because the Mind possesses all things at once, and is not fixed to one side rather than another, nor does it have an affection contiguous to the world. Finally, just as stars shine in the sky, so minds shine in daemons and men, a gift more excellent than merely having parts. Nor do the minds of these beings, even if considered as parts, detract from the universe. For they are considered excellent to the extent that they are judged similar to the Mind of the whole, and to the intellectual order of the whole.

->The seminal reason of the universe itself, which is universal nature, has pre-designated in itself even those things called evil, and confirms these for the good of the universe. Also, all worldly things are empty like games.<-

XV The defect and destruction of things brought upon them by one another is thought to happen not only from matter and the condition of material things—for they have a perpetual order—but also from the very intention of universal nature. For it is from her purpose that things fail by degrees, while she establishes disparate grades. It is her purpose that they perish either spontaneously or by others; while...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's "Enneads," specifically transitioning from the discussion of reincarnation and providence into a deeper metaphysical explanation of "seminal reasons" (the divine blueprints in nature) and the hierarchy of reality from pure intellect down to physical matter.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...he wishes to form the future from the present: so that with us, he may henceforth follow that right number which he was once unable to follow. Among these things, you will note four points concerning the <term>seminal reason<note>original: "ratio seminalis"; in Neoplatonism, these are the formative, life-giving principles or "blueprints" through which the divine intellect shapes the physical world.</note></term>, that is, concerning universal nature. First, indeed, that this is the efficient principle of all things capable of being generated. Second, that these are rational, insofar as they embrace the seeds of all things. Third, that individual things which are produced are made through it specifically—that is, according to its own effective and exemplary power. Fourth, that the entire natural distribution and the alternation among things are pre-marked within it: and through these, they go forth outwardly just as they are impressed within, to such an extent that nothing is left outside of providence. For even that which happens contingently in its works is contingent to reason itself, but already pre-marked and immovable in the divine mind. Among these things, he touches upon the opinion of those who think that the souls of all living beings can be separated from their present bodies and not be resolved into the soul of the universe, but subsist in their own property and return again to bodies. He also touches upon the opinion of those saying that the souls of brutes, which flow forth from the Soul, also flow back into that same universal soul. Truly, he thinks that many such universal lives exist: many, I say—that is, powerful and manifold according to the various rational substances of souls. Indeed, all these propagate corporeal lives from themselves everywhere, and by that very propagation, they make animals as if they were a kind of play or pastime. Otherwise, if no animated things were made from there, then matter would be entirely devoid of life, and life itself, staying in something other than matter—that is, in its own source—would seem as if sterile and powerless. Indeed, it is the settled opinion of Plotinus that rational life, of whatever kind and wherever it may be, proceeds from rational life insofar as it exists and in whatever way it is made, just as the imperfect necessarily depends on the perfect.

Certainly, just as in a naturally bright body you consider three things: first, the form itself—that is, the light according to its essence; second, the act within itself while it sparkles; and third, the action proceeding outside itself while it illuminates something (where "to illuminate" depends on "to sparkle," and this likewise on "to be light"). In the same way, consider that the sensual life depends on that rational life, and this rational life depends on the intellectual life. For the <term>Reason of Nature<note>original: "Ratio naturae"</note></term> is something from the intellectual substance, like light in a window, or into itself as if from the light of the world. But the sense is like a light that would already be directed by a command. Therefore, just as images flow from bodies which are like bodies themselves, so from souls (which are living beings) flow animal images which are like souls; and once these are accommodated to suitable bodies, living animals are made. And since these things are seen in this way, whatever pertains to it in terms of advantage or disadvantage has no more weight toward good or evil than what an opinion brings when it deceives and disturbs us.

->That there is a seminal reason of the world: how it acts; also concerning the four grades of plenitude: in what way the reasons of things are contrary in common reason.<-

XVI. If all things exist by a certain intention of the reason of universal nature, then all things seem to happen naturally and reasonably; therefore, nothing would happen against nature, nor would there be any sin. To solve this, it must be considered thus: just as at night the moon and the fixed stars derive not two lights from the sun, but the sun emits one light—not a small amount of solar light, but as it descends from there to our realm, it becomes inferior—so from the intellect itself, and from the intellectual soul made there, the seminal reason proceeds into nature alone. Now indeed both are inferior: the animal reason being more so than the intellectual, and degenerating again in matter from both, which indeed coalesce like rational things placed in light. Because this reason depends on animal substance, it is life; but because it depends on the intellectual through the discursive, it is reason. Where it is discursive, since it is essential reason, it acts rationally through its essence—even if it does not perceive what it acts upon, although it accompanies the imaginative part of the work. Because its action penetrates into matter, it is called motion; but it acts upon and moves all things. I say it does not act like an agent determined to something specific by its whole impetus, but first in various ways, and with a certain moderation, toward a certain end, limit, figure, and work—variously and in different ways. I say it acts by various commands like a fire, which can also do various things by accident or consequence and through something else. It also moves things not simply by driving force, but as we are accustomed to be formed. Its "moving," however, is to "form," not to alter; it holds its seat more as reason and act. For there, art is reason itself, and there, reason is nature itself. From there, the body is moved by nature in the same way as a judgment is moved by the art of responding—especially if art were not something that occurs only sometimes, but was so naturally ingrained that it was nature itself. This art, formed in itself in various ways, is complete and moves the "dancer" from within by measure and figure. This natural action of forming and moving is itself a form and a quality, or a motion and action within the same thing. It is, as it were, both: for it is a high effect already possessing the truth of form and the efficacy of the soul, like a certain quality without accident; it is motion without passage; it is life and the vigor of substance standing from the soul into matter, a perennial liveliness acting upon all things and doing so rationally. It does many things—indeed, even contrary things first, many present and nearly contrary things at the same time.

Here you must understand a fourfold multitude or <term>plenitude<note>original: "plenitudinem"; the state of being full or complete, used here to describe the different levels of reality's "fullness."</note></term>: Pure Intellect, Animal Intellect, Natural Soul, and Material Nature. Pure Intellect, standing immediately under Unity itself, becomes so united that it formally constitutes all things, being whole in any part of itself. Therefore, all its things are comprehended in any part of itself. Thus, in its presence, all parts are in any given part, not by power alone, but by act. They differ formally, however, because they exist through one act or another, and in one way or another, without being "more" or "less." The plenitude of the Animal Intellect (or the intellectual soul) is indeed a multitude of the entire universe, though not entirely united; therefore, even if all its parts are comprehended in any given part, they are contained not so much by act as by power. The Natural Soul, which is universal reason and pure nature, is moreover a plenitude of the whole multitude, but departing further from unity; this whole is no longer contained in any of its parts, neither by act nor by power. From this, it happens that certain parts are contrary to others, since one can no longer admit the other. Finally, Material Nature—that is, the corporeal machine—is seen to be distracted in such great multitude and contrariety that one thing not only no longer admits another, but also differs by its very approach. This surely would not happen in the parts of the higher nature; returning to which, let us say that nature itself, by its own diversity, is in a certain way the origin of the diversity and the conflict arising among the parts of the world. Thus, this world is said to be "set in malice," <note>original: "in maligno"; a reference to the Vulgate translation of 1 John 5:19, "mundus totus in maligno positus est," often interpreted as the world being under the sway of the evil one or inherent physical imperfection.</note> having no peace, nor giving peace to anyone; it has been shown, however, that the primary cause of this is very near. Let us conclude, therefore, that when unity in universal nature degenerates further from that higher unity, and at the same time plenitude degenerates, the parts differ from one another and fall short.

### ON BOOK II OF THE THIRD ENNEAD

What is present to some is meanwhile lacking in others: and so they may now seem to fight among themselves, so that what they lack themselves they claim from elsewhere, while individual things desire to emerge as the whole. Yet the whole itself is not so vast that it can utterly expel contrariety from itself. Hence it happens that the corporeal world cannot, for the time being, expel either contrariety or mutual destruction from things. Meanwhile, however, universal nature itself—just like a word of a higher intelligence brought forth by <term>musical reason<note>original: "musica ratione"; the idea that the universe is structured according to harmonic proportions, similar to a musical scale or a symphony.</note></term>—renders opposing voices friendly by the power of its proportions. And thus the whole is "one" in the same way that a whole musical piece or a whole tragedy is composed of contraries into a single harmony of elegance and beauty. Moreover, this reason of the world, the queen of things, is more similar to musical reason than to poetic reason. For the poetic art receives its characters and false events from elsewhere, and it is not necessarily composed of contraries. But music itself brings forth tones—necessary and contrary—for there is no harmony unless it is composed of deep and high notes, of tense and relaxed ones, of ascending and descending ones, and even of discordant and concordant sounds. Therefore, the reason of harmony itself is not a common thing unless it consists of the reasons of these opposites, which are similarly opposed to one another. 

In the same way, understand that the "nursery" <note>original: "seminarium"; the storehouse of seminal reasons or life-seeds.</note> of the world is constituted from contrary reasons, through which it produces contrary forms in the world. For since the formal discrepancy between these things arises neither from one another, nor from matter, nor by chance, it is expressed in a friendly and exact manner from formulas that are contrary in their reasoning. Indeed, the <term>Ideal Forms<note>original: "Formæ ideale"; the perfect, unchanging archetypes in the Divine Mind.</note></term> of contraries in the Mind are not contrary; rather, in opposites, things placed together are often recognized. But the <term>seminal formulas<note>original: "formulæ seminales"; the active, formative powers in nature derived from the higher Ideas.</note></term> in nature that produce contraries are themselves contrary. For in a seed, the "seed of fire" cannot be the "seed of water," just as fire cannot be in water. Remember that in the divine mind, there exists the Idea of Identity itself, and the Idea of Alterity <note>original: "alteritatis"; "Otherness" or "Difference," one of the five Great Kinds from Plato’s *Sophist*.</note>, and of Rest and Motion. You should refer intellectual substances to Identity and Rest rather than to opposites; but refer rational powers rather to the Idea of Alterity and Motion, especially the final reason which is now contiguous with matter. 

Thus, everywhere the office of the Mind consists more in union, while the office of Reason is more concerned with description <note>original: "descriptione"; the process of laying out, mapping, or diversifying.</note>. Nor could there be reason unless it were quite manifold, because it exists in parts that are contrary within themselves. I speak of the seminal reason of the world, the lowest of divine things, in which as much discrepancy of parts is found as can possibly happen to divine things. Therefore, since there is a final dissonance in that divine genre, it rightly received the name of contrariety. Furthermore, since Identity and Rest belong more to the perfect, while Alterity and Motion act toward the imperfect: rightly, as much as one descends from the Idea of Identity and Rest, to that extent things participating in those Ideas gradually have less identity and rest. On the contrary, the further one descends from the Idea of Alterity or Motion, the more the things participating therein admit alterity (that is, diversity) and mobility into themselves. Therefore, Alterity and Diversity, inserted into the seminal reason of the world, render it the most "other" within itself and the most diverse of divine things. Since the condition of this reason looks especially toward the Idea of Alterity itself, it is said that the "way" prevails far in this, while that Idea or power propagates reason from here into extreme diversity; it seems by this very reason to propagate itself no differently than the root of a plant into the trunk and branches and the rest: which nevertheless acts by a certain vigor of vegetal life. And indeed, those things which lack a "way" do not seem to act within, but to effect things without; but living things act also within themselves, and much more do they act by an interior life, and propagate themselves from one certain thing into many produced within themselves. And so the seminal reason of the world—a life indeed, but the last of the divine and universal lives—seems, under that very Idea of diversity, to diffuse itself within itself through diverse, articulated, and contrary parts.

->As power decreases from higher to lower things, it is compensated by number; also how human<-
->natures are and are ordered in intellectual and natural providence.<-

XVII Nature contains more seeds of things within itself than the Mind contains Ideas. For since the power of nature and the seed is weaker, it cannot comprehend or do through one seed everything that a single Idea possesses in power. Therefore, the vigor of one Idea is distributed through many seeds, and the weakness of its power is compensated by number. By the same logic, matter is led into many forms under each individual seed. Added to the innumerable multitude of this world is dimension (which is always subject to division), motion (which varies individual things), and also the multiple convergence between them, and the heap of powers and gifts necessarily proceeding from individual higher causes everywhere. Finally, lest the species of mutable things should ever perish, the substituted number of individuals—both in succession and simultaneously—is increased more enduringly beyond mere permanence. 

Furthermore, in such a crowd of things, because of the greatest discrepancy and dissonance, some things become harmful to others, and because of their need, they try to protect, preserve, and recreate themselves through the destruction of others. Yet, amid many things discordant with one another, providence inserts such a vehement love into individuals—both toward themselves and toward the whole—whereby individuals everywhere lay snares for each other and are in turn avoided by each other, and finally [serve] the whole. After this, it is doubted whether good or evil men are pre-marked by the very reason of the universal form, and how. This is answered by the long example of comedies: just as actors bring with them their own figures, voices, gestures, and characters besides those which the poet commands—the poet who assigns to each the appropriate duties and places according to the property of each—so rational souls, even before these bodies, become "such and such" by certain inclinations of their own. Then, the reason of the world accommodates such bodies to them, and insofar as they persevere and follow through, such fortunes and finally such seats [are given]. From this disparity on both sides, and the mutual agreement of proportions in the meantime, the world is most beautiful and most just. 

We have this entire concept similarly from a similar origin; and it is reported by many concerning angels, either those not falling, or those falling more or less. But you, whenever "mundane reason" is named, understand it often as that seminal power joined to the intelligence of the world soul, upon which seminal nature continually depends and is ruled according to the pattern. Therefore, the proper and self-moved <note>original: "autotedenter," from Greek *autexousios*; refers to the soul's free will or self-initiated movement.</note> motions of souls are not prescribed in the nursery, but in the intellectual "fatherly book," yet they are not compelled from there. For they are written there everywhere just as they themselves are—that is, arising from their own sources—so that their lots, fortunes, and seats are foreknown from there at the same time and destined according to their merits. In the nurseries, however, with the antecedent motions of the souls excepted, the remaining things which follow in due order are impressed not intellectually, but naturally and effectively. Just as the nursery corresponds to the intellectual, so too the effective formulas in the nursery correspond to the reasons which are there. Thus it happens that the nursery always fits the consequences to the antecedent motions of the souls, although [the nursery knows these] not for itself but for the marks of intelligence: just as a powerful motive force in art executes to a hair’s breadth what it does not itself know, but which the imagination knows. In the antecedent things, the soul always acts specifically; God, however, acts commonly. In the consequences, the soul in turn operates commonly, [God] specifically...

<header>THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

truthfully, God and nature. However, there must be some proper action inherent in souls beyond the influence drawn from the universal whole; otherwise, if they possessed no action of their own, they would be unable to achieve a rational understanding of the principle of the universe—which is without form—or of things more excellent than this world. Unless, indeed, it is necessary for those souls to have some degree of individual character within the very influence of the universe. For in this way, they themselves assert their own proper natures, and the principle that makes all things has most effectively made them similar to itself, if it makes them as "makers" <note>original: "facientia facit"; the idea that God, the ultimate Creator, creates beings that are also capable of creating or acting autonomously.</note>: for that principle itself acts through the process of making. If, therefore, that action is the very thing from which they originate, it is probable that the things arising from there will be agents; and so that they may have something to act upon, there will also be "patients" <note>beings that receive action or undergo change</note>: and there will also be matter, the primary foundation for these experiences.

---

->**On the orders, types, and differences of souls, and how each**<-
->**is designated in divine providence.**<-

XVIII Plato, in the *Timaeus*, distributed the orders of souls into three primary grades, extending them thus for this reason, as I believe: because in a soul we consider either the elements from which it is composed, its power, or its action. By **reason of the elements**, it is conveniently distributed into three grades. In the first order of souls, the "Same" and the "Stable" overcome the "Different" and the "Mixed"; in the second, they are equalized; in the third, there is a turning back toward the first. Similarly, through three grades, essence penetrates into their being.

Again, as far as **powers** are concerned: in the first grade, the <term>Intellect<note>The highest part of the soul, capable of direct spiritual intuition.</note></term> prevails; in the second, **Reason**; in the third, only **Imagination**.

As far as **actions** are concerned: in the first grade, the action is entirely and universally providing—namely, providing all things to all; in the second, it is universal in a certain way—namely, either some things to all, or all things to some; in the third, however, it is particular—namely, regarding certain things and certain people. We place the "balanced souls" <note>original: "animas librari"; likely referring to the primary world-souls that maintain cosmic equilibrium.</note> in the first grade, the souls of the **stars** in the second, and the souls of **daimons** <note>In the Platonic tradition, "daimons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and **humans** in the third. 

Indeed, in the souls of these daimons and humans, the *Timaeus* places as many types as there are stars in the heaven, each type differing among themselves. Just as they enjoy an order within themselves, so too do the corresponding daimonic and human souls. But here **Aristotle** thinks there is a difference: that in the type of a star, there is only one individual <note>each star is its own unique species</note>, but in the types of the subsequent souls, there are many individuals in each. Furthermore, there are more individuals in each type of human soul than in any type of daimon. For always, a lesser power is compensated by a greater number. This directs the nature of any "Idea" through the power or unity of one (so to speak) toward the blessedness of the manifold universal order. 

Furthermore, the types of stars, being essential, possess within themselves the splendor of the most perfect things; and the soul, being wise, arouses the type from the divine **Idea**; the type is the absolute effect of the Idea. But the type of souls, being less perfect, possesses fewer perfect individuals, because it cannot by itself sufficiently explore or demonstrate the various types of the Idea. Therefore, through many individuals here, the various effects of the species from the Idea are fulfilled. However, in the human type, there must be even more individuals than in the daimonic type, through which the various gifts of the Idea are distributed without end; and the minds of many consist of what neither one nor a few could manage from the one. 

Furthermore, it is clear to the **Platonists** that there are many types of human souls from the fact that there is such a great diversity of <unclear>disposition</unclear> among men, so that some seem divine, others brutish, and others human. Such diversity is not found in any other species of animal, whether regarding the soul or the body. For example, the Platonists think it is incredible to attribute this immense diversity of souls solely to the diversity of earthly bodies as a cause—especially since those who are most similar in body are often most dissimilar in talent and character, and vice versa. 

Moreover, someone might be able to refer the fact that a soul is sometimes faster or slower in talent, or more prone to anger or gentleness, to these bodily qualities in a certain way. But the fact that some are naturally more inclined and much more fit for certain sciences and arts, no one will be able to explain from the differences of bodies; since such arts and sciences often seem to regard an incorporeal rather than a corporeal nature. I pass over the mathematical and physical disciplines, the prudence of governing, and the wondrous subtleties of the arts, in which some differ most distantly from others by nature. Certainly, that this man seems to be a **Theologian** by nature, that one a **Prophet**, another an author of miracles and a founder of eternal laws, while others are not at all—though they do not differ much from these others in body—cannot be assigned to their bodies. Nor is it a proper characteristic, I say, of the physical gatherings of elements, which seem to instruct our minds only through their own proper structures. 

For this reason, the Platonists gather the souls of men under a "subalternate" type, in which there are many "most specialized" types (if I may speak thus), and also many individuals under each type, so that certain souls are naturally very similar and friendly to one another, while others are the opposite. Entirely, however, individual types of souls are reduced to their corresponding stars and to similar types of stars: thus **Solar souls** correspond to Solar daimons and Solar things, **Venereal souls** to Venereal daimons and Venereal things, and so on similarly. 

So far, we have treated the differences of souls which **Plotinus** asserted as primary—namely, those which are from nature itself, either according to type or according to a singular property under a type. Secondly, he thinks differences are asserted by some from others after they have begun to be received or inclined differently by free motion, perhaps even before they entered the body. It happens more often that the same soul, at different times, acts and lives through various shifts of itself, so that it becomes dissimilar not only to others but even to itself. 

Thirdly, he thinks diversity happens in animals from the body; first indeed from the "spiritual body" <note>the 'astral' or 'aethereal' vehicle of the soul</note> and then from the solid one. For it matters a great deal from which part of the mundane sphere the soul has obtained its spiritual or familiar vehicle—whether celestial or ethereal—and it matters most of all under what course and configuration of the stars it was received. For many and varied things flow into such bodies from the heights, and from there they flow into the souls. Such differences are increased by the various "guides" of souls accepted from the daimons at that time—different guides for different souls. Finally, these solid bodies, along with birth, time, and place, bring no small weight to certain differences of souls. 

Lastly, he wants the difference in animals to occur from varying education, custom, and discipline. He maintains that the entire distribution of souls through unequal grades and parts is described within the intellectual reason of the world itself. Furthermore, he thinks the entire distribution of various bodies, fortunes, and boundaries is marked in the "seminal reason" in a certain congruent proportion to the differences of souls, and that individual things are thus fittingly adapted to individuals. He adds that **Providence** could not return fitting duties, rewards, and punishments to the properties of minds unless it also thoroughly embraced these properties within itself. Just as a poet cannot assign fitting roles and gestures to individual actors unless he understands their natural and proper faculties. Therefore, everywhere, both the things that come before and the things that follow are parts of Providence, both human and divine. But the preceding things are especially primary, not so much in the nurseries...

...to be threatened, rather than in examples: let one understand that book of divine providence <note>Ficino uses the metaphor of a "book" to describe how God's plan is written into the structure of reality.</note> in which parts are read that are not entirely brought about from there, just as human providence acts. Truly, the subsequent parts are often also in the book of seminal providence <note>original: "prouidentiæ seminariæ"; referring to the "seed-like" principles or *logoi spermatikoi* that govern natural growth and development.</note>, where those things understood in the higher realm are imprinted and expressed from there. In another way, through antecedents always being followed by ordered consequences, individual things are arranged. For example, when adultery is committed out of disordered lust: immediately in the book of nature, the ordered propagation of offspring follows from the sexual act. Meanwhile, in the total intelligent book, from the disturbed commotion of the soul and the subsequent choice, the disturbed life and worsened condition of the adulterer follow in due order. Thus, the natures of things, as well as whatever seems to happen—whether bad or perhaps by chance—are entwined by a certain common consequence into the orders of the universe. In this way, the wicked habits of souls and evil works are called parts of the worldly reason, and the reason itself is said to have communion with these evils. This is not because they are properly drawn here from there, but because they are noted there to be kept from doing other things, and are bent by the fates. Therefore, when providence is considered either as the exemplars of all things without a maker, sins are indeed parts of it insofar as it is an exemplar rather than a maker; yet, as for those who sin, they are parts under both conditions. Furthermore, whether evils there have their own proper exemplar <note>The "Exemplar" is the perfect divine blueprint or Idea of a thing in the Mind of God.</note> insofar as they are evil, or whether they are instead judged by the exemplar of good things, is more appropriately discussed elsewhere. Let us now conclude that providence is not only "vegetable" <note>governing the basic growth of plants</note>, but indeed extends even to the smallest things, in an intellectual manner through art and providence, yet by way of nature.

## ->Confirmation of the first and second of these: that God makes, understands, and cares for individual things.<-

**XIX** It is worthwhile to briefly confirm those things which are transferred from these points into the following book concerning providence. Since "to be" is everywhere through form, and to the extent that one possesses form, one also possesses being; and conversely, we rightly confess that the primary essence is also the primary form. We believe it necessary for the primary form to be both most simple and most eminent, insofar as it surpasses all things and gives birth to the universe. The intellect is said to possess uniform simplicity and equal-form commonality only when composite things are referred entirely back to simple ones; then it comprehends individual things under the most universal forms. Therefore, the primary essence is the primary form, and the primary form is the primary intellect. If that essence is in fact the intellect, then to be and to understand are surely the same thing there universally. Then, just as such an essence everywhere, or the first of its kind, makes the following thing by the addition of its own state—just as the sun illuminates by shining, or fire heats everywhere by being hot—so the essence itself, simply by being, procreates all beings. But if it is the cause, so that all things simply have being, it is furthermore the cause so that all things have "this" or "that" kind of being. For being "such a way" depends on "being" itself; and it proceeds with a form common to it, with the distinctions of this or that, not from matter, but from that very primary Uniform form of all things, whatever it may be. Therefore, insofar as it brings all things about by being, it also does so by understanding; since for it, to understand is nothing other than to be. Because it makes all things by understanding, it is marvelous that it also understands all things by making. It understands, I say, not only those things most common to all, but also individual things, the proper characteristics by which each thing stands in its own being. Otherwise, it would proceed to understand in too confused a manner, and would by no means retain intellect in actuality, but rather would know things in a remote and confused potentiality. 

Add to this that if its own proper action is intelligence—as something most eminent, most ample, and at the same time most intimate—it understands exactly as far as it acts, and vice versa. Moreover, it acts in the performance of individual and even the smallest things; for the influence of the first being is most ample through all individual beings following in certain orders, and those things which act after it are moved and act everywhere by its virtue. Truly, it is not the species of things themselves (which are eternal and which God himself makes) that are acted upon everywhere, but individuals. Either, then, God understands and acts on nothing outside himself (which is false), or by acting on individuals, he understands those same things, which would never come to be unless they were first understood by God—just as nothing is produced by the sun except what is seen by the sun. Therefore, God himself understands individual things, not distracted by the many, but collected within himself. He contains all things as a rare exemplar and the cause of causes, through which the cause of all causes is contained, and by containing them, he cares for them. He also provides for them, directing individual things toward their end, and subjects them in whatever way to the good; he procreated all things through the form of the good itself for the sake of the good. That he cares for all things as easily as he does diligently is proven by this: that from God himself, things possess not only that they "are," but also that they are "causes." For they have it from there that they exist, insofar as he is the cause. If, therefore, they have essence, then insofar as he is the cause, they possess the proper office of a cause. This office is to preserve its own things and care for what it makes. Therefore, if the first cause and all causes have this property, insofar as they are certain causes, this power rightly possesses this most of all: to care for all things and individuals, insofar as it is the greatest cause. 

And since in individuals, again, each proper form contains within itself all things that are maintained in the individuals, and the whole is by no means preserved when it is composed of necessary parts, the universal order of the whole is not excluded, which necessarily stands in grades descending down to the smallest things. This order, which is the more distinct as it has certain properties as an order (and likewise as chance), cannot exist except as it proceeds from the intention of some agent. Nor does it proceed so much from the necessity of the agent's nature—whose intention is determined toward one thing rather than many insofar as they are distinct—but rightly proceeds from a certain intention of an intelligent being, for intelligence is of a certain and particular cause. For all distinctions are counted in an instant in a single number of works. Therefore, from the intention of the primary and most common intelligence proceeds the universal distinction of things. For those things are distinguished from others by themselves, and he distinguishes the rest among themselves by his own most known norm; and insofar as he knows them most distinctly, he cares for them most distinctly. Finally, if providing proceeds from an abundant and penitent <note>original: "penitenti"; likely meaning a "penetrating" or "overflowing" goodness in this context.</note> goodness and leads governing things toward the good, it rightly belongs to the best cause of causes to provide for individuals most exactly.

## ->Confirmation of the same. Also that God certainly knows even contingent things, yet without taking away the freedom of choice.<-

**XX** We do not doubt that God provides for things especially as they are his own, as far as he sees them; we also assert that God sees things insofar as they follow from certain orders of causes—whether of subsequent agents or of necessary concurring viewpoints. For indeed, we see that philosophers sometimes see many things far in the future as if they were present. They see these things, I say, in causes which they themselves neither act upon nor establish. How much more, then, does God foresee what...

He asserts that God’s knowledge of the world is inseparable from His act of creation, ensuring that every part of the universe is cared for according to its own nature.</summary>

Here, Ficino explores the distinction between human discursive reasoning—which moves through time—and the divine "gaze" which sees all events, even contingent ones, as eternally present.</meta>

<page-num>248</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO</header>

causes: what arises from the properties of causes, and what comes from their union. For God himself, by the act of seeing, brings causes into being; he grants them their properties and binds them into one. If philosophers are more clever, they are able to gather information about absent things more quickly from present causes or signs. Although they rely on a certain temporal progression of reason, they nevertheless bring future things back to the present, as if instantly. Surely that stable and entirely outward-reaching gaze of the eternal mind embraces the entire distance of things—whether in space or even in time—in a certain indivisible and present-making stroke, so that things which are distant from each other and in the future are, to that mind, deeply close and present. Thus, the effect is contained not so much in its causes as in the mind itself. Now, from this very fact—that he does not look upon events as if they were standing in their causes, nor as if they were future, but rather as present—it follows that while philosophers hesitate when they hunt for contingent <note>original: "contingentes"; events that may or may not happen, as opposed to "necessary" events which must happen.</note> future events, God himself does not hesitate. For those things which we call "contingencies," as long as they are still in the future, have the possibility of not emerging from their causes; but as soon as they are present, they cannot *not* have emerged. Nor can they "not be" while they actually exist. In these contingent things, insofar as they exist in the present, it is not possible for them "to be" and "not to be" at the same time, but they only "are"—even though they have the potential not to exist in the future. For this reason, they seem to have already obtained the condition of necessary things. Therefore, God holds contingent things just as firmly as those that are naturally necessary, since he sees them as present. For anyone is certain that these contingent things are happening in the present, even if they were previously uncertain whether they would happen in the future. Furthermore, just as it can be known with certainty from a necessary cause that an effect will follow, so all things are grasped by a science of impending things from elsewhere, whether from contingent causes or not. But since God, as the archetype, the maker, and the mover of all, embraces all things, he is just as certain of the outcome following from contingent things as he is from necessary ones—indeed, he sees them following already. He does not understand mutable things in a mutable way, nor does he see divisible things divisibly; rather, through his own indivisible and immobile nature, he holds firmly and simultaneously things that are, in themselves, scattered and wandering. Just as the sight often perceives many moving things in a single indivisible glance, so too things that are naturally mutable are not made "firm" simply because he grasps them firmly, just as they do not become immaterial because he embraces them immaterially (so to speak). For by his own intelligence—that is, by his own action—he imposes the lot of contingency upon contingent things just as he shows the law of necessity to necessary things. Yet, he also most firmly holds any movements of our voluntary intelligence, however free they may be. He understands them, I say; for the First Essence is the cause of being for all things in whatever way they exist, just as he is the cause for intellects to rightly understand and will in whatever way they do. Thus, he understands direct movements as the one who moves them, but oblique <note>original: "obliquos"; referring to "crooked" or sinful actions that deviate from the straight path of divine order.</note> movements as being in opposition to, and falling away from, the right ones. He also understands "certain" movements which, in themselves, seem "uncertain," since he sees each one as already happening, not as "about to be." For to Eternity, all time is present at once, just as the entire stretch of a circumference is equally present to its center. And although one who is moved by this will now can afterwards be moved in another way or differently, God does not think of this in different ways at different times. For he has anticipated each movement and its mode once and from the beginning; he steadies the mutable progression by means of the indivisible tension within himself. As for what many are accustomed to argue here: "If God is certain that the soul will act, the soul will necessarily do it"—this does not follow. For God is certain that the soul will do it *freely*—indeed, he sees it doing so freely. For he sees in himself as present those things which, to the objects, are in the future. Since he already sees events as present, it is not permitted to ask again whether the soul can change its choice in the meantime, after God has seen that the soul would so choose. For "in the meantime" does not apply to the time when he saw the soul would not choose; rather, he sees the person *in the act* of choosing. Do not object further: "If God firmly sees the choice, therefore the soul chooses by compulsion." For what prevents the soul from favoring its own will now, which God, by his own nature, firmly sees? Just as God by his own will always ordains that gold should function as gold, he also ordains that the soul should act with a free will. Finally, as some have been accustomed to argue: "It is necessary for the soul to do it if God knows it will do it"—they mean, to do it *willingly*. We can argue similarly: if a human were said to know the same thing, the necessity is placed not so much in the consequence as in the relationship of the logic; it is found not in the thing itself, but in the one arguing. This is a certain conditional necessity, not an absolute one. And a conditional necessity is not at all accustomed to drag an absolute one along with it.

Through these doubts we have resolved those matters which were raised at the end of the previous book, and we now approach the second book on Providence. Certainly, rational souls are designated as parts in Providence—I do not mean parts of the physical nature or the bodily machine, but rather partners and colleagues in governing. Hence, even lower movements are permitted, once a certain authority has been granted to these roles. But since he says that the "seminal nature" <note>original: "seminariam naturam"; referring to the "seed-like" formative principles that govern the growth and development of the natural world.</note> of the universe is a certain soul, remember that just as a vocal reason <note>original: "uocalis ratio"; likely referring to the spoken word or *logos* which carries meaning.</note> signifies distinctly, proceeding not only from an intellectual notion but also being a certain notion itself, so the living and all-formed seed-bed of the world, budding from the soul of the world itself, is a certain soul. And if it is called an instrument of either pure intelligence or of the soul's intelligence, it is certainly such that the mover himself provides not only the motion, but also the form of the workmanship. For an instrument is most closely related to its master, and is subject to the craftsman...
