*But they act not as if they were hands, but as if they were imaginative or formative powers—stern and rational. In the second book, he adds the rationale of that God, by which He is a living being in a completed world. For if the characters of things were first designated in this state, then privations <note>original: "privationes"; the absence of a quality that should be present, often used to explain the existence of "evil" as a lack of good.</note> were also consequently marked down. If the better things were described, so too were the worse; and in the long process of proceeding, the boundaries were also written down—at least in such a way that, having been traversed from wherever they were sought, they are explained in the world through the body and the causes of their own condition, as if they were begun and prepared all along. Indeed, all the grades and orders of this universe are so woven together in one divine reason <note>original: "ratione"; here meaning the 'Logos' or the rational blueprint of the cosmos.</note> that there is nothing outside the First that contains them within itself, down to the very last things, just as it was expressed with its parts of that kind and by the intellect or seal, even while it might escape and then perish. For many things from this very order of worldly reason are considered perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem"; literally 'to the fingernail,' a Roman expression for sculptural perfection.</note> by the movements of souls; these surely agree not only from this reason alone, but so that it might subsist by movements, and also it appears that certain anomalies moved from every side by the intelligence have been foreknown and pre-defined by the higher powers. Truly, the quantity of these in the seed-bed of the world neither generates parts in that way, nor is a part joined from the beginning; the whole corporeal machine of the world germinates from the seed-bed all at once. It does not generate its own parts from which it is composed, nor among its necessary parts did one procreate another: light does not make a star, nor did fire make the earth from the beginning, nor does man make the law. It is so brought about that no part of the world has been entirely produced by others: but rather, it responds to the whole, so that the whole exists through itself from its own parts, from its own worldly seed; and the seed is from the mind, or as he testifies, the generative seed of plants and animals. There, a part does not make a part, but the parts together with the whole sprout little by little from the seed: just as the reasons <note>original: "rationes"; referring to the 'seminal reasons' or 'logoi,' the formative principles that guide growth.</note> of all the parts, as of the whole, are contained in the seed. Similarly, the worldly reasons are in the nature of things born, and in the soul, and the reasons of the soul are altogether in the mind. Therefore, as the whole machine is the seminal soul in act, it allows, as it were, the spirit of the entire union of the world; and both parts in it are certain acts, and like certain breathing-holes of the parts similar to the property of the soul, in a certain order this whole world is about to act as a whole seed-bed and of the parts equally. But since the machine agrees on all sides with the seed-bed—and this with the soul of the world, and the soul with the mind—it follows that in the machine all things are dispensed according to the movement of the mind. It is also probable that particular souls are like sisters of the World Soul, and as colleagues they entirely harmonize with the movements and circuits of the World Soul: so much so that the turns of choices and actions which the souls perform are accommodated everywhere to the turns of the World Soul in performing natural things. By this connection, certain lots, fate, and specific bodies, and similar outcomes rightly respond in the universe to the specific choices, actions, and lives of souls. Amidst these things, let no one think that this care of ordering is difficult because innumerable and contrary things happen in it: for all things, however many or few, are brought together into one form. The authors wish them to obey by this relaxation: if in many elements contrary things fight against each other, do not the contrary qualities of the members in plants and animals maintain the one condition of the living thing? And in us, whatever the duty of a particular nature may be, to whom should it seem a wonder that the contrary parts of the world are kept together in one form hidden from us? Certainly, I say, they are the works of universal nature, which is why particular natures help each other everywhere. If, therefore, you join individual works to individual natures everywhere,* <margin>by universal reason</margin> *and these to this universal reason connected to the intelligence, and the intelligence to the one whole, you will clearly recognize that the intelligence, out of one love, moves all creatures according to its nod and moves the following things with wonderful ease: for it is seen to be far beyond intellects, as is pious to believe.* The examples which Plotinus brings *from the order of the categories <note>original: "praedicamentorum"; the Aristotelian categories of being.</note> he recalls to a multitude to be reduced finally into one; they become clear. Among these, you will note this argument: that the One itself is the cause of all things; that all things, even contraries in the universe, are reduced into one, namely the pre-destined one, joined into one by unity. You will note by what rationale you may resolve being itself into a higher cause: for whether you say the essence of each thing is a body, you would be forced to resolve it into simple things; or whether you say it is that which is actually reduced into an effect, the foundation of the last; or whether you say you will see this essence first as imperfect, unless you look up to the act of the one over this, the One itself—that is, known to be of ineffable simplicity—upon which essence and the act of essence depend. Or the One itself is diffused through all things: it gathers you from all, as if through members and nerves; which, while it seems to be stretched out, the One itself is contracted into the one, which in truth is simply everywhere; it collects all things into one. However, insofar as it is such a one from there, it also appears to be diffused, but in such a way that meanwhile it is necessarily bound back to that very simplicity of the One. Nor is the One itself found in all things in this way, like a single species from individuals, or one genus in species: but according to prior and posterior, more and less, just as unity is served everywhere in numbered things. Therefore, the simplicity of Plato himself makes a one, as if it derives into a "one being," namely the one Intellect: by which he makes the whole world properly and as a ruler who, from the multiple concept conceived in himself, completes the world; and from the unity in himself surpassing the multitude, he collects the many members of the world into one living animal. In which, surely, whatever exists is both a certain part of the whole from the common nature, and moreover, from its own proper nature, it is something whole and employs a proper action besides the common passion <note>original: "passionem"; here meaning 'experience' or 'influence' received from the outside.</note> brought upon all things from the universe. From which it appears* that God, *by the wonderful actions of His power, does not take away actions from the things' own properties; I say from the smallest things, such as from fire or a horse, and much less does He take them away from more excellent things, namely from souls, which are not determined to one thing by the condition of nature, but turn themselves towards many and opposite things. And they do this according to their own nature through diverse movements, but meanwhile* God *ordering it, such as the souls have rendered themselves, such outcomes are always rendered to them.*

->Nothing happens by chance. For Providence orders even the smallest things.<-

---

II Consider *firstly that the whole machine of the world surrounding the lands is always most ordered in every disposition of movement. Secondly, that earthly things, highly adorned, are born and proceed most orderly. Thirdly, that the earth is like a point compared to the rest of the world. Through these, fourthly, you will conclude: in this point of immense mass, wonderfully ordered and enclosed by that mass, nothing can be left unordered; so that even those things which sometimes seem to float by a certain chance, you may know for certain that by the order of the universe they do not lack their own certain order—I say, by the intellect that is the orderer of the whole world. For order always accustomed to be born from intelligence. For by the simple and entirely immobile nod of that Mind, the machine, composed of so many diverse moving parts, stands and is ruled most orderly. Furthermore, since in any governance, insofar as it is a greater gradation of a greater thing, there is intelligence and power in the governor, to that extent less happens there by chance; certainly, if a supreme power and intelligence governs the world, and the whole is entirely subject to it, nowhere...*

<summary>Ficino explains that the universe functions as a single living organism (the world-machine) guided by a "seminal" World Soul and Divine Intellect. He argues that even seemingly random or contrary events are part of a perfect, providential order where individual free will and natural properties are preserved but harmonized by God.</summary>

It reconciles the appearance of "chance" or "luck" with a deliberate divine order, explaining that what seems accidental to humans is actually part of a complex chain of causes managed by higher spiritual beings and, ultimately, by God.</meta>

<page-num>153</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...no place is left for rashness. For an unexpected or alien event usually happens to a pilot <note>original: "gubernatori"; Ficino uses the metaphor of a ship's captain to represent a ruler or coordinator who lacks total control.</note> because he either does not see everything or does not rule everything alone when struck from the outside. But the Universe is entirely comprehended under the command of a single divine mind, so that nothing can escape or violate its law. This is especially true because, just as the life of the world is whole in every part, so too is intelligence in this living body whole and everywhere at once. It does not treat external materials as alien, nor is it distracted by many things; rather, it directs its own focus and the whole from a single hinge. It rules the world as easily through understanding as life gives life through living, or as a body acts through its being. For that which is "being" in the body—received through form from life and intelligence—is "living" in life, and in turn is "understanding" in the intellect. Indeed, from the whole intelligence, the whole flows forth; through the entire life, a common form shines out to the whole body. By a similar proportion, the various forms in the world-machine result from the various seeds <term>seminal reasons: "semina"; Neoplatonic "seeds" or formative principles that bridge the gap between abstract divine ideas and physical matter.</term> in life. The differences of the seeds are brought in from the different notions in the intelligence. Therefore, the notions of the intellect itself reach down to the individual forms of things through these seeds. They are a single seed while generating many individual forms; the intellect does not act confusedly but distinctly in each thing, otherwise it would not form each thing perfectly. Thus, one intelligence and one notion expresses many forms in individual things through the many seeds of life. It does not act indefinitely, but determinately in each thing; otherwise, it would act imperfectly, nor would its power reach all the way to the specific actions of natural life. Nevertheless, it is necessary for the power and action of the higher and always wider "eye" to proceed further and more broadly than the service of the lower office. From this it follows that the primary power and action of essence itself, by which intelligence exists, is extended through every individual thing. 

Then, if you believe that various individual effects arise everywhere in things solely from their own forms and powers, you must most vainly believe that the powers proper to forms—which belong to the formal order of the universe—proceed from the first ordered thing, and that all things are preserved and moved by it. Since, therefore, individuals exist within these forms and powers, it is necessary that through these very powers and forms, every individual effect everywhere belongs deeply to the bringer, preserver, and mover of all powers and forms—I mean powers and forms whether they be specific or even individual. For even in individual physical things, they have found marvelous gifts which are often not granted among others of the same species. Finally, if (as the Platonists think and the astrologers somehow admit) there is sense-perception here in the heavens, and a ray is extended everywhere from its light to perceive individual things, and to make things to be felt and to feel things to be made—and nothing lies hidden even under the earth that it does not feel where such an intention is present everywhere in the rays (otherwise celestial things would not be generated even under the earth)—then surely the rays of the first intelligence are extended through all things. Insofar as they derive down to individuals, they procreate and perfect individual things everywhere by procreating them, since they procreate by looking upon them. It is just as if you were to say that the stars, by their aspects and turnings, wonderfully foster the rational plan of things and form their offspring. Since, therefore, nothing divine is hidden from the intellect, and order is proper to intelligence, nothing can happen anywhere in this workshop of intelligence that is not ordered by the ordainer of the whole—both before it happens and when it arrives suddenly as something annexed to the rest, reduced into the order of the universe. Surely this order is only most absolute if even the smallest things are most providently ordered. Likewise, it is most excellent if it is completed not only from things ordered, but also from the ordainers themselves. 

Therefore, many in this ordered world—governed under the First—may disagree under various laws, but the power and action of the First, as the most powerful, is spread through all the governors under Him, even beyond their own duties. Thus, many things that are accidental to us are foreseen by the governors. Even if some things come about outside the intention of the [local] governors, they are from the providence of the First, to whom nothing ever happens unseen; for to the most perfect and best belongs the most consummate providence in the intellect. It is true that He who ignores nothing permits nothing to be unforeseen. Truly, unexpected chances that happen to us from the clash of diverse causes, if they are ordered by some cause, are not governed by a cause acting only in the manner of nature. For a purely natural cause, since it acts through a single form, is determined toward one thing. It cannot, therefore, by itself bring together several scattered causes of an unexpected event, nor any order among themselves, toward a single effect. But a cause acting by knowledge alone can restrain multiform causes into one, which, conceiving many forms in itself, is rightly the principle of multiform things, and gathers diverse causes into one form of an unexpected event. Hence Proclus, in his commentary on the *Timaeus*, defining fortune, says it is not a rash or blind thing, but is a divine or daemonic <note>original: "demoniacam"; refers to *daemons*, spiritual intermediaries between gods and men, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> power, gathering diverse causes into one outcome. Therefore Plato, where he treats a certain accidental event in his letters, suddenly brought in the name of a *daemon* after the name of fortune. And so, often by a certain hidden persuasion, daemons send one man here by this way, and another there, so that meeting each other there, they produce an event unforeseen by them, but foreseen by the higher beings. Sometimes, too, the higher beings do not so much move different people toward one thing, as they use those already moved by themselves for something else—unexpected indeed to men, but foreseen by the higher beings. 

Furthermore, whether the higher beings first move our minds, or use a motion already present: the superior daemons act upon reason primarily through reason, by persuading simply and tranquilly; but the inferior ones act mostly through imagination and spirit, by arousing certain disturbances in our spirit and imagination, and consequently they act upon the will. God, however, acts directly upon the will. Finally, in whatever way and wherever we fall into unexpected chances, whether prosperous or adverse, these always happen to us in accordance with our merits—whether present, past, or future—and they sometimes contribute to us universally. For in this way God tempers the harmony of the universe: so that he who can behold the entire space of the world, and every individual thing in it, and all of time in a single intuition, would see that just rewards are repaid to each person; and that although certain sounds may seem out of place, they harmonize perfectly with the whole.

->Although individual things are marked in the mind of the provident God, the soul nevertheless acts freely.<-
->Likewise, it was necessary for the universe to have unequal degrees.<-

III. Within the Creator himself and the first model of the world, just as souls are numbered, so too are bodies. Thus, of what sort the souls are from the beginning, so similarly are the bodies; and again, what sort of souls they make themselves, and subsequently what fates are to be repaid to them according to their merits. All things, therefore—both who acts and how, and what they will suffer, and in what way—are comprehended in the very order of providence. Because the human soul, affected in this or that way by its character, proceeds...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains that nothing in the universe happens by chance; even "accidents" are coordinated by Divine Providence and spiritual intermediaries (daemons) according to a perfect rational plan and individual merit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the third book of Plotinus's Enneads. The previous page established that the universe is governed by a single divine intelligence and that "chance" is merely a human perspective on a complex causal chain. This page delves deeper into the specific nature of the soul’s agency and why the world is organized into a hierarchy of different beings.</meta>

<page-num>251</page-num>
<header>ON THE THIRD BOOK OF THE ENNEADS</header>
<meta>catchword: to become</meta>

...to proceed is the cause, because it is so and whenever it is so. However, that it began in this way is the cause only because it was able to begin in this or that manner. Truly, the fact that it was able to do both you cannot resolve into any other cause. For this is its very nature: namely, a life that is freely mobile and rational. But if anyone should further inquire into the cause of why the soul was such from the beginning, he would be no less ridiculous than if he were to inquire why the soul itself is a soul, or why fire itself is fire. Certainly, you can assign a cause for why fire ascends, penetrates, and dissolves—because it is light, subtle, and hot. But to ask why it is this very thing is nothing other than to ask why fire is fire. Each species of things is defined from eternity by internal, known boundaries. Thus, all species, determined within themselves from the eternal age, seem to be nothing other than certain determinations by which the first intelligence is primarily constituted. And it is discerned by the senses as if in parts, so much so that the Mind itself consists of such intellectual definitions by a necessity of nature. A similar arrangement of things follows subsequently in vegetable nature; and the **world-machine** <term>world-machine: "machina mundi," a common Renaissance term for the universe as a complex, divinely-ordered system</term> is similar, arising from a cause that does not indeed deliberate or choose through counsel, but is so naturally disposed within itself: so naturally germinating. The arrangement of such species in nature is nature itself; in the machine, it is likewise the **world-machine** itself. To ask, therefore, why the world consists of so many and such diverse levels of things is to ask for what reason the world itself is the world. It is as if one were to ask why a plant has life but not sensation, and has roots and branches; or why an animal has sensation but not reason, and has feet and a head; or why a human has human intelligence and not divine. To wish for a plant to be an animal, an animal to be a human, and a human to be God, is nothing other than to leave God alone and destroy the world. It is just as if someone wanted a foot to be a hand, or desired the hand to be an eye; in this way, he would destroy the individual members, and finally the whole.

But to descend to the condition more proper to us: man ought not to complain that he was not made more excellent from the beginning. For he has been given himself, and as some maintain, he can in a certain way make himself more excellent, which things lower than man cannot do. Therefore, he has within himself a certain **principle of beginning** <note>original: "principij rationem"; the capacity for self-initiated action or moral choice</note>: for he can add some good to the good he had from the beginning. That he is able to do so, we infer from the fact that he can also sometimes fall into a worse state, which lower things cannot do. But God would not have made the human species—which is better than plants and brutes—such that it could fall into a worse state, unless He had also made it such that it could move toward a better state, especially since it is closer to the **First Good** <note>The "First Good" refers to the Neoplatonic One or God, the ultimate source of all value.</note>. Among these things, however, remember that either the exemplar of the universe itself, or the Universe, consists of all things arranged by degrees. In the first and pure form, many different things cannot exist, nor can they differ except formally; there, they are distinguished from each other in two ways: first, by various modes of forms, as if through *breadth*; and then by diverse degrees of forms, as if through *length*. Clearly, because the Mind received its formation under the Good through a certain conception, and by proceeding similarly within itself, it put on various degrees of its own form like faces. From this it follows that in the world, too, a procession occurs successively through unequal degrees, and some things consequently make or produce others. Again, in the arrangement of plants and animals, parts are distributed in unequal degrees. Such an arrangement in the world is said not to be "simply the best" in the sense of being perfect like God, because it stands at the furthest distance from the Good, to which the first **World-Maker** <note>original: "mundi faber"; the Demiurge or creator-god who fashions the physical world</note> is nearest, and to whom the **World Soul** <term>World Soul: "anima mundi," the spiritual principle that animates and governs the entire physical universe</term> is subject. Below this is placed the **seminal reason** <term>seminal reason: "ratio seminalis," the formative spiritual power that acts as a "seed" to organize matter</term> of the world, from which the world becomes a living animal at the same time as the body of the world; the form of the world's body is subject to this reason. However, a reason of this kind does not become "animated"—that is, it is not called "living" in the same way the World Soul is. Rather, the vigor of the soul is derived into this reason just as heat turns into lukewarmness, or as light turns into paleness. By a similar proportion, degenerating from the lives that remain everywhere within themselves, certain lives are dedicated from there to bodies, whether that is considered in the spheres and stars, or in demons and men. Everywhere, the higher naturally provides for the lower in nature; and the higher it is, the more it provides, and by providing, it remains more firmly within itself. For from this very firmness of its own, the perpetual tenor of providence proceeds, precisely because it is not affected or inclined toward other things, but **overflows** <note>original: "exuberat"; a key Neoplatonic concept where the higher levels of reality produce the lower through an abundance of being without losing their own essence.</note>.

## On Intellect, Reason, and Imagination. Why humans do not always use reason.
### Why the soul becomes worse, though it does not pass into beasts.

**IIII** In the following chapter, you will consider again that there is a double common reason of the world. The first is present to the world as an **artificer**; the second is within it as a **form**, through which, as if it were kin to the artificer, the artificer also seems joined to the world. The presiding artificer is the intellectual substance itself; the residing form is the **seminal reason**, by which the intellect seems to unite with the matter of the world and generate. Collect the rest of Plotinus's opinion briefly in this way: There are two principles of action in our soul: the free **intellect** and **reason**. By their work, the soul can progress beyond that which it had from the beginning. But through the intellect, the progress is sudden, and the soul is immediately made divine from human. Through reason, it progresses in time, and similarly fails; so that it is either human, or divine, or demonic and beast-like. Intellect and reason are always present to all souls of men, but not all live by reason; and indeed, very few live by the intellect. For many live rather by **imagination** and **sensation**. In their imagination, the sparks of reason itself either rarely flash or sometimes do not flash at all, since imagination is turned rather toward opposites. Just as the intellect, except in the blessed, hardly seems to sparkle into human reason. That intelligence and a proper reason are present to human souls even when they are not using them will not be doubted by anyone who knows that common intelligence and reason flourish everywhere and are present to even the smallest things.

Meanwhile, you will note that the intellect is not so separate that it is not a part of the soul. Likewise, just as fire is always hot, so the intellect is always understanding, and the power of the soul placed in discourse is always discoursing in whatever way it discourses—whether through reasons or through images, even in the manner of a dreamer—just as the vegetable power is constantly vegetating. Furthermore, while the soul lives in a human, both the mind and reason are proper to humans, although both do not always overflow into action in men, and the mind shines much more rarely than reason. But if ever the soul is in "brutes" <note>Ficino uses "brutes" to refer to irrational animals.</note>, he does not want either mind or reason to be anything belonging to the brutes; instead, only imagination and vegetation can be shared with them. As for the fact that not only common intelligence but even the flash of reason sometimes does not seem to sparkle in souls at all, the cause is either an excessively perverse composition of the body—frequently so inept for talent and ready for disturbance—or perhaps the seminal reason of the soul itself has been turned for so long into a brutal habit, and consequently the body in matter as...

<summary>Ficino explains the hierarchical order of the universe, arguing that diversity is necessary for the world-machine to function. He discusses the components of the human soul—Intellect, Reason, and Imagination—and explains that while higher faculties are always present, their use depends on the individual's condition and the body's influence.</summary>

On the previous page, Ficino established that the soul possesses a free and rational nature, and that its actions are not merely a result of chance but are rooted in its eternal definition. Here, he explores how the soul's character is shaped by its choices and its relationship with the physical body, as well as the mathematical order that underlies the universe's structure.</meta>

...opportunity almost conforms it to a brutal <note>original: *brutale*; referring to animal-like or irrational behavior</note> state: if the generative power brings the first quality to the body in such a way that the soul does not then turn out entirely as the body is born, but rather shapes a body for itself according to what nature itself has already received, so that by its own merit it casts itself down into a worse transfer of life or into a strong one. After this, you will observe four causes by which the soul can sometimes turn out much worse. First, because it was placed from the beginning after the second order of souls. Second, because a minimum momentum from the beginning becomes a maximum by falling gradually. Third, because two of the souls happen to meet by some other soul or thing, or rather while one prior affection in the soul coincides with a later one, a new force results from such a meeting, and it produces a new effect from there—just as is discovered in the mixing of other substances. Fourth, because preceding actions in a past life initiated such a habit in the present life. 

Truly, where Plotinus seems to want the seminal reason of the soul to degenerate so much from preceding actions that the very generative power, which was in the proper species of man, now becomes a vital power in the species of a brute—and thus conceives or receives these "brutish" things of this kind—this must be understood as spoken under a condition. That is, *if* ever the natural power itself could change its species within itself, then the form would consequently be transferred to such a species. But surely, he soon shows us that this can rarely happen. First, indeed, because since the proper essence of no thing, even a potential one, can be the essence of another species as long as it exists, it certainly cannot undergo the essential nature of that other. Unless nature, which is much more excellent than things, could fall so far from its own species that it puts on the species of others, and sometimes worse ones. 

Second, because since Plotinus says that the act of understanding and the act of vegetating <term>vegetating: "vegetare," referring to the basic biological functions of growth and nutrition</term> are entirely substantial and that intelligence is not transformed by the soul’s actions, it follows that he must also admit that the vegetative power is not transformed by any actions—which is evident from experience. For it does not become bad through a bad habit, nor good through a good one. Reason itself demonstrates that a mobile accident <term>accident: a non-essential quality that can change without changing the thing's essence</term> does not transform a permanent substance, especially those intrinsic to the species. Wherefore the vegetative essence itself will never be transmuted into the species of a brute through accidental imaginations that are somewhat similar to a brute, nor will it desert its own species of its own accord. Rather, it remains the same forever, but perhaps a certain habit is instead contracted in the actions and affections of the imagination itself—a habit, I say, which further affects the rational power, specifically when it frequently consents to the imagination. This habit, like a kind of chain, long twists the soul away from the contemplation of divine things and from life. 

Third, because transmigration into such a thing is the worst degree of the grace of purgation. If the rational species itself were cast headlong into a brute, the entrance to the mind's repentance would be closed, even though the repentance of others leads them back from their misdeeds. Added to this is the fact that in our own genus there are such diverse degrees that it is not necessary for the figure of the body to change for the sake of justice or fitting grace. For under this very human figure, there are men who are human, and those who are brutish (in their life, I should say), and those who are demonic. If Plotinus feels this way so far, he will not disagree with Timaeus the Pythagorean, and perhaps he will not be at odds with Aristotle, nor will he be disapproved of by the Hebrews <note>Ficino often references "the Hebrews" to align Platonic thought with Jewish Kabbalistic or scriptural traditions</note>. For all these will easily concede that our soul can be revolved only through the bodies of men, but can by no means be accommodated to brutes. It can, however, flee to be accommodated to the demonic; for from the beginning, it has a spiritual body very similar to the bodies of demons.

---

->That there must be different levels of things; that providence dispenses each thing with the<-
->equality of geometric proportion; that fate serves<-
->providence concerning free will.<-

Just as the divine mind has within itself the formal reasons <term>formal reasons: "rationes," the eternal blueprints or ideas of things in the mind of God</term> of things, distinct in their species and degrees (for otherwise there could be no distinction in pure form), so too, configuring such a distinction in the world, it preserves an equal number everywhere. Thus, whatever powers and of what kind this thing has in itself, that thing has just as many and of the same kind. Otherwise, perhaps one single thing would suffice, and the rest would be superfluous, adding nothing—they would seem to be many by a fiction of dimension rather than by a form of essential difference. Therefore, those things which God does not make equal to one another in number and weight, he at least makes equal by the fitness of proportion. 

As if you were to proceed in length, you would see the first creature surpass the second by a double proportion; and furthermore, just as the second is surpassed by the first by a double proportion, so the second similarly surpasses the third by a double, and thereafter the third surpasses the fourth. Similarly, by whatever proportions natures surpass other natures, the related actions and passions of those natures in turn exceed the actions and passions of others. If you turn again to breadth, you will see if a joined creature exceeds the first by a sesquialterate ratio <note>original: *sexquialtera*; a 3:2 ratio</note>, or rather by a sesquitertian ratio <note>original: *sexquitertia*; a 4:3 ratio</note>, the following creatures are surpassed by a similar proportion. 

Therefore, providence delights not in arithmetic but rather in geometric equality <note>Geometric equality is proportional/distributive justice (to each according to their worth), whereas arithmetic equality is simple numerical identity (the same for everyone)</note>. For this is the proper justice by which civil prudence governs a house, a city, and a kingdom. Plotinus compared divine providence to a prudent law, and likewise to both poetry and music; finally, he even more willingly compared it to vegetative nature, like a soul ruling a plant. For nature is the instrument of providence. By this comparison he teaches that, just as each animal is dispensed everywhere by one nature, being as present in the lowest members as in the highest, so also this mundane animal <note>the universe as a living being</note> is ruled by one providence, which is present everywhere in every single part. 

Among these things, you will observe that individual things in the world, like members in an animal, possess certain powers and proper actions beyond their common condition. Likewise, just as in any animal the parts, because of their common nature, immediately communicate with other parts through sense and passion, so easily do individual things in the world (as members of this animal) suffer together and serve one another because of the communion of one nature—not only those which are close in position, but even those which are very far apart. For just as from the head to the feet, so from the highest parts of the world to the lowest, motion and affection leap forth instantly. 

Indeed, the seminal life of the world, by which this whole is one animal as if by a form, he calls **Fate**, the explanation of which is a certain series of celestial causes and motions. In this explanation, **Atropos** is sometimes named the firmament; **Clotho** the very revolving region of the planets; and **Lachesis** that which is transferred from there by lots under the Moon. This entire dispensation and disposition of things everywhere is simply **Providence**, but because it depends on the Mind and is carried out everywhere by the nod of the Mind, it is called Providence. However, because it proceeds through the vegetative nature of the soul and subsequently through the celestial bodies, it is also called **Fate**. Whatever things are done by fate, therefore, are done by providence—although providence does many things besides which are not enclosed within the boundaries of fate: namely, whatever pertains to intellectual things, and those which intellectual substances themselves similarly do. Not otherwise...

<summary>Ficino explains the soul's relationship to animalistic behavior and the mathematical harmony of the universe. He argues that while souls may take on "brutish" habits, their human essence remains, and the universe is governed by a proportional "geometric" justice acting through Providence and Fate.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the soul's relationship with the cosmic order. It moves from the internal habits of the soul to the broader governance of the universe, specifically how human choices interact with Divine Providence and Fate.</meta>

<page-num>255</page-num>
-> # ON THE SECOND BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD <-

In truth, fate depends on providence just as heat depends on light. Where heat acts, light also acts, but the reverse is not always true. For there are marvelous powers hidden in light that are not present in heat. Similarly, the spirit depends on the soul; it does nothing without the soul, nor does the soul do anything without the spirit acting as its vehicle. Thus far, he has established providence and fate as the common principles of all things and actions. 

However, the specific principles of motion are the effective natures found everywhere, especially that of the rational soul. This soul is not merely uniform or strictly determined to one path, but is multiform <note>original: *multiformis*; meaning the soul has many capacities and can choose different paths</note> and deliberately directs itself toward diverse things. Therefore, whatever comes from fate likewise comes specifically from providence. But what arises from our rational nature does not strictly arise from providence alone, although it agrees with it through a certain influence. When a soul's counsel precedes its choice toward the best end along a chosen path, that action proceeds according to the very order that providence itself preserves. Otherwise, it would neither come from providence nor follow the primary rules of providence. 

No matter how our affairs turn out, they are neither hidden from providence nor neglected by it; instead, they are woven into the order of providence. Through the very rules of providence, they are always disposed in a condition and place appropriate to their merits. Right actions are directed by the primary rules of providence, while crooked actions are managed by the secondary rules. This is no different than how nature acts in a living body: it guards the health of the limbs, restores health when it is lost through change, and cleanses or assigns the humors <note>humors: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—once thought to determine health and temperament</note> to their proper places. 

That we sometimes transgress the order of providence happens either solely from our ignorance—occurring through negligence when we yield to it—or from a leaning of the senses and nature, conceding too much to external pleasures. Even though things offered to us from the outside move us not so much by their own nature as by our own quality, a new and hidden effect often occurs when a certain person meets another person or thing. This happens for a reason unknown to us but known to providence, whether it arises from our own properties flashing outward and generating a "third property" through their meeting, or from the power of our guardian spirits <note>original: *daemonum*; referring to personal tutelary spirits rather than "demons" in the modern sense</note>, or from the influences of the stars flowing within and from us in various ways. Plato testifies in the *Theages* <note>Theages: a Socratic dialogue concerning the "divine sign" that guided Socrates</note> that such things happened marvelously and fortunately to many because of Socrates.

## By what order of consequence can evils be foreseen from goods? How signs of the future exist in the present.

**Pi** <note>This "Pi" likely marks a section of Plotinus's text being commented upon</note> If evils are not according to the order of providence, they seem to lack order; therefore, it seems they cannot be foreseen. Yet many people do foresee them. How, then, can they be predicted? It is because they eventually follow the order of providence itself, or, if they happen through divine intervention, they are marvelously drawn into the established order of providence. 

Just as a "multitude" falls away step by step from the First Principle until the extreme descent into the physical world occurs, it is necessary that what is "power" in the higher world becomes "matter" in the lower world. While this power is compared to the most absolute Act, it is distinguished from it by a certain reason; in the physical world, it is already matter, separated from the form of nature both in reality and distance. Thus, by itself, it remains formless and "evil." Furthermore, the mind can see and foresee the order of consequences: from form it sees matter, and from good it sees evil. 

Moreover, the order of providence establishes various states of qualities in the world, which proceed as a fertility of nature propagated far and wide. From this order of progression, many things are forced to stand far from their source, and thus they possess a worse condition. You see again by what series of providence privations and defects can be known from established states. Just as the world itself and the things in it are composed of the beautiful and the deformed, and move from perfection toward defect, so too do the actions of all things. Therefore, from the very vigor of a right action as it descends further, its "crookedness" can be sensed in advance. 

This does not mean that God or divine beings are the cause of the defect, but rather that such a prediction arises from the study of ultimate principles. These observers foresee future things in the present, not through hidden causes, but through the signs that openly accompany those causes. It is like someone who knows what a friend will do in the future because they have become certain of that friend's character through their previous generosity. 

The preceding causes of things, in which future effects are contained, act everywhere as if writing for future generations in a fitting manner, so that wise seekers may predict the future as if by reading. Since all these things are members of a single living world <note>original: *animalis vnius mundi*; the "World Soul" concept where the universe is a single organism</note>, the motions of the lower members often follow or imitate the motions of the higher members. Thus, signs of the lower are presented in the higher. By these signs, through a certain preparation and proportion rather than exact reason, future events are known. 

In this way, the bird-diviner <note>original: *auspex*</note> predicts: this bird flies high, while that one is raised or lowered only slightly. Similarly, the augur promises happy things from the joyful chirping of birds and warns of sad things from the somber. Similarly, astrologers designate high status through the height of the planets. After this, whether in birds or other things, the "seminal reasons" <note>seminal reasons: the rational blueprints or seeds implanted in nature that direct the growth and development of all things</note> of the world are a single power gathered from many seeds. This power makes us what we are; but here, it proceeds through influences, conspiring so that this world, along with its members, sprouts from there like a single animal. It does not "make" its members, but the members "become." Nor do the members make the world, but they are moved, and in turn, each acts or suffers according to its nature, signaling to others in its own way and being signaled to by others.

---

## That in the providence of God, artificial and natural action is the same, governing the world like life governs a plant.

**Pii** <note>Marks the next section of Plotinus's text</note> We should not listen to those who quibble: "If there is providence, then there is no evil; but if there is evil, then there is no providence." In truth, by the very fact that the Highest Good acts by providing, it provides by acting, and it cares for even that which is "less good." Step by step, through the "less and less good," one arrives at "evil." If you remove evil, you subvert providence. 

Do you wish to see providence? Remember that the gifts distributed among the lower things are gathered together in the higher. Thus, astronomers recognize heat and moisture—which are dispersed separately through Mars and the Moon—as joined together in Jupiter. You believe the Divine Mind is superior to both nature and art. For you admit that nature acts from within but without its own intelligence, while art uses instruments and builds from the outside. Therefore, you find each to be imperfect on its own. Thus you are compelled to return to a Perfect Principle, which builds from within through understanding, and understands by building. In this way, you grasp Divine Providence, where those things which are separate in the world are joined in one.

<meta>This page concludes Ficino’s commentary on the preceding section and begins Plotinus’s famous treatise on Providence (Ennead III, Book 2). Ficino’s commentary uses the analogy of a tree and the sun to explain how divine unity produces a diverse world.</meta>

<page-num>254</page-num>
-> # COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO <-

in things, they are two—that is, separated by nature and by art—whereas in the Divine they are gathered into exactly one and the same power. In your own soul, these are divided into two powers: through one power you understand and reason, while through the other you nourish your body, and you generate and manage the individual parts within the body. Therefore, you do not generate by means of the things you understand, nor, conversely, do you understand the things you generate. But think of my Divine Being <note>Ficino refers to the "Divine Mind" or God</note> as generating and understanding in exactly the same act and in the same way. Just as shining and heating, which exist in fire as two distinct qualities, exist in the sun as a single power; so too, understanding and generating are two acts in you through two different forces, but in God they are a single act. Under this single act lies a certain intelligence of the World Soul, which acts like an art, and the power of the World Soul’s vegetative life, which takes the place of nature. Beneath these is the body of the world, so animated and so directed that it is like a living body joined together. For as these three—the Divine Mind, the World Soul, and Nature—breathe together in turn, all worldly things exist within them in such a way that the whole is contained in each part. Therefore, the harmony <note>original: *conspiratio*; literally a "breathing together"</note> of these is called the "root of the world-tree," or the "root-like vitality" <term>radicalis vigor</term> <note>The life-force that sustains the universe from its source</note> diffused everywhere throughout the tree. In this world-tree, things are already so distinct that from the root comes the trunk, from the trunk many branches, from these more twigs, and from these many leaves and fruits; yet in all of these, even the furthest extremities, the vitality of the root itself is preserved, ready for propagation. In these things, one may first consider that all worldly things, however much they seem separated from one another, are nevertheless connected to each other and dependent on the same principle; thus, they can easily communicate with one another in action and passion <note>In philosophy, "passion" refers to being acted upon</note>. Furthermore, all things are very easily ruled by that same principle which remains everywhere, binding everything together deep within into a single articulated structure, much like a nerve.

### First [Treatise] on Providence.
### De Prouidentia.

<margin>1 The arrangement of the world is produced by the providence of the divine mind, not by a reasoning process that comes first in time, but by a prior order of causes from the first mind, shaping the world like a seal.</margin>

Indeed, many arguments have already been brought forward concerning this very point. However, taking up the discussion from the beginning, we must consider the very manner <margin>B</margin> in which all these things are made and have been made. This is especially necessary since, because some things seem not to happen rightly, it happens that people doubt the providence of the whole. From this, some have come to deny providence entirely, while others assert that the world was established by an evil craftsman <note>A reference to Gnostic beliefs that the material world was created by a flawed deity</note>. Instead, let us assume for now that providence which we call the "providence of the universe," and let us connect what follows in a consistent manner. # BOOK TWO

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If we were to posit a "providence" <note>Greek: *pronoia*</note> of the same kind that we speak of in the production of individual things—namely, a certain foresight and a process of reasoning—we would be imagining a God who deliberates over the best possible conditions under which the universe might be made, and how it might be constituted as well as possible. However, since we believe this world has always existed and will never cease to be, we must rightly assign providence to the world in a different way: specifically, that the world exists according to Mind <note>Latin: *mens*; Greek: *nous*</note>. This Mind does not precede the world in time, but because the world comes from Mind, Mind is prior by nature. Mind exists as the cause of the world—its principal form and archetype—while this world exists as an image existing through that archetype, subsisting from it perpetually in the same way.

<margin>C</margin> The nature of Mind and Being is the true and primary world; it is not distant from itself, nor is it weakened by any divided condition, nor is it lacking in its parts due to any defect. Indeed, no part is severed from the whole; rather, its entire life and entire Mind live as one, simultaneously understanding. This ensures that every part acts as the whole, and the whole is friendly to itself. There, one thing is not segregated from another, nor is anything solitary or destitute of the rest. <margin>D</margin> Thus, one part does not harm another, even if they appear contrary. Since it is everywhere, it remains perfect everywhere; it admits no change at all. One thing does not act upon another, for what reason would it have to act when nothing is lacking? <margin>E</margin> Why would one "reason" <note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*</note> produce another reason there, or one intellect produce another? Could it be because something might be hidden from it? If that were so, it would not have been well-ordered to begin with. But a being that lacks nothing has no need to act; it would only be moved if there were something inferior within it. It is entirely sufficient for the blessed ones to remain within themselves, existing simply as what they are. To be "busy" with affairs is not entirely safe, for those who are busy are forced to go out from themselves. That archetype of this world is so blessed that it accomplishes the greatest things without "doing" them, and by remaining within itself, it achieves no small task.

<margin>II. This world consists of many different animals and matter originating from the proximal intellect: hence discord is born within it. In this world, animals lacking reason are foreign to intelligence.</margin>

<margin>F</margin> From that true and unified world, this world depends. However, this world is no longer truly one; it is manifold and divided into a multitude, in which one thing is distant and foreign from another. No longer does friendship alone flourish here; because of the distance, discord is born, and in their very deficiency, things now necessarily oppose one another. For no part is sufficient unto itself; while it seeks its own safety from elsewhere, it brings war upon that which preserves it. <margin>G</margin> This world was made not by a concluding chain of reasoning that it *ought* to be made, but by a certain necessity that forced a "secondary nature" to follow the "first nature." For the intelligible world was not of such a kind that it could be the "limit" of existing things. It was the "First," and it possessed the greatest power—indeed, the total power—to produce something else, far removed from the anxiety of one who seeks to act. Otherwise, it would not have possessed this power by its own nature if it had to seek it out. Nor would its production come from its own essence; it would be like a craftsman who does not have within himself the thing he makes, but acquires it as something external through learning.

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III

<margin>A</margin> Intellect, therefore, by infusing something of itself into matter, while remaining itself unmoving and quiet, has fashioned all things. This infusion is the Reason-Principle <note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. In this context, it refers to the formative power that flows from the divine Mind into the physical world.</note> proceeding from Intellect. Indeed, that which flows from Intellect is Reason, and it flows perpetually so long as Intellect itself remains within the order of reality. Just as in the Reason-Principle inherent in a seed, all parts exist together in the same place and nothing fights with another, nor differs, nor stands in the way; yet, meanwhile, something is produced in the physical mass <note>Latin: *mole*; Greek: *onko*. Refers to the bulk or volume of matter.</note> where one part is in one place and another elsewhere, and one thing is hindered or harmed by another. <margin>B</margin> In this same way, from the one Intellect and the Reason-Principle flowing from it, this universe has blossomed forth, now distant from itself. By necessity, some things were born friendly and beneficial to one another, while others are hostile and destructive. Whether willing or unwilling, they damage and destroy each other, and through their mutual destruction, they work toward the generation of new things. Simultaneously, the Craftsman <note>Latin: *faber*. A reference to the Demiurge or the creative power of the Soul.</note> established a single harmony among these things that act and suffer, so that while each individual part sounds its own note, the Reason-Principle <margin>C</margin> contains the consonance within them and establishes a single overarching order throughout the whole. For this universe is not like the Intellect and Reason-Principle found in the higher realm, but it is a *participant* in that Intellect and Reason. Therefore, it required a harmony, specifically because Intellect and Necessity <note>Greek: *ananke*. The brute, irrational forces of the physical world.</note> concur here. While Necessity draws things toward the worse and deflects them into a lack of Reason—since Necessity itself lacks reason—Intellect <margin>D</margin> nevertheless dominates over Necessity. For the Intelligible World is Reason alone, and it is impossible for another world to exist that is purely Reason. If anything else was to be made after that perfect realm, it had to be less than it; neither pure Reason, nor again merely Matter (otherwise it would lack all order). Thus, it came forth as a mixture. And indeed, that in which the world ends is Matter and Reason; but that from which it begins and is ruled is the Soul, perfected by this mixture. We should not think that the Soul toils, for she governs the whole with the greatest ease by her very presence.

<margin>III How the corporeal world was made, how it is to be understood, and whether its unity is evident if the whole is considered together.</margin>

<margin>E</margin> **NOR** can anyone rightly disparage this world as if it were not beautiful, or as if it were not the best of all things that could exist with a body. Nor, again, can one accuse the Cause through which the world exists. First, because the world exists by necessity, not constructed by the deliberation of logic, but by a superior nature generating a work similar to itself according to its own nature. Secondly, even if deliberation were the cause, the manner of it would not bring shame upon the author. For he <margin>F</margin> made the whole as a thing entirely beautiful, sufficient, and friendly to itself. Furthermore, it is equally fitting in its parts, both great and small. Whoever, therefore, censures the whole based on the parts, censures it foolishly. For it is proper to consider the parts in comparison to the whole to see if they are suitable and accommodated to that whole. When considering the whole itself, one should by no means look only at the smallest particles. Otherwise, that would not be the act of a man criticizing the world, but of one taking certain parts of the world in isolation from the others. <margin>G</margin> It is as if someone were to look only at a single hair or a toe of a complete animal, neglecting to contemplate the wonderful spectacle of the whole human being, and by Jove—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Intellect, then, by giving something of itself to matter, remaining tranquil and quiet, worked all things. This is the Reason-Principle flowing from Intellect. That which flows from Intellect is Reason, and it always flows as long as Intellect is present among existing things. It is like the reason in a seed: all things are in the same place, and nothing in that same being is brotherly-fighting <note>Greek: *adelphos machomena*. A poetic way of describing internal conflict between related parts.</note> or differing or acting as an obstacle. However, something now comes to be in bulk, where <margin>B</margin> one part is in one place and another in another; and indeed they might hinder one another or one might consume another. So indeed from the one Intellect and the Reason-Principle from it, the whole arose, and because it is divided, it is necessary that some things become friendly and mild, while others are hostile and warlike; some willingly, others unwillingly, they ruin each other. And being destroyed, they work toward the generation of each other. And among them, as they do <margin>C</margin> and suffer such things, He introduced one harmony. While each sounds their own sounds, the Reason-Principle makes of them a harmony and produces one arrangement for the whole. For this whole is not like the Intellect and Reason over there <note>Greek: *ekei*. A common Platonic term for the higher, intelligible realm.</note>, but it participates in Intellect and Reason. Therefore, by the coming together of harmony, Intellect and Necessity—the one pulling toward the worse and leading toward irrationality, <margin>D</margin> being itself devoid of reason—nevertheless, Intellect rules over Necessity. For the world over there is Reason alone. And there could not be another that is only Reason. But as another has already come to be, it had to be less than that one, and neither Reason alone nor again a certain Matter, which would be un-ordered. It was mixed, then. And again, the Reason-Principle is a mixture of Reason and Matter. But that from which it begins is the Soul standing over the mixture; she is without toil because she is present by her very being, having fashioned the whole by her presence with it.

<margin>E</margin> And one could not reasonably find fault with this mixed world as not being beautiful, or as not being the best possible of those with a body, nor could one blame the cause of its being. First, because it exists from necessity; it did not come from a calculation of logic, but from a better nature generating something like itself according to nature. Then, even if calculation were what made it, one could not blame the maker for the whole <margin>F</margin> that he made. For it is beautiful, and again sufficient, and friendly to itself, and its parts—both the more dominant and the smaller—are suited to their roles. Therefore, he who blames the whole because of the parts would be absurd in his blame. For one must look at the parts in relation to the whole itself, to see if they are harmonious and fitting to it. And when looking at the whole, one must not look toward certain small <margin>G</margin> parts. For this is not the act of one blaming the world, but of one taking some of its parts separately—as if someone, looking at a hair or a toe on the ground belonging to a living creature, were to neglect the divine sight of the whole man—

# BOOK TWO

<margin>Ὡς εἴποι <note>original Greek: "As one might say"</note></margin>
It is as if someone, completely ignoring all other living things, were to take the most abject one—or perhaps, dismissing an entire species, were to bring forward someone like Thersites <note>In Homer’s Iliad, Thersites is portrayed as the ugliest and most insolent of the Greek soldiers; Plotinus uses him here as a symbol of human imperfection.</note> as the representative of the human race. However, since the world that has been created is a single whole, if you were to incline the "ears of your mind" to it, you might perhaps hear it crying out: "Without a doubt, God made me, and I was made perfect, composed of all living things. I am sufficient unto myself and fully satisfied within myself, in need of nothing. For all things are within me: animals and plants, the nature of all general types, many gods, <margin>B</margin> crowds of spirits <note>Latin: *daemonum*; Greek: *daimones*. In this philosophical context, these are intermediary beings between the divine and the human, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, armies of good souls, <margin>κόσμος <note>original Greek: "world" or "order"</note></margin> and men happy in their virtue.

"For it is not only the earth that is adorned with all plants and every kind of living creature, nor has the power of the soul spread itself only as far as the sea. Does the entire air, the ether, and the whole of heaven lack soul and life? On the contrary, souls are also there, all of them good, providing life to the stars and to the celestial revolution in the most orderly and eternal way. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, in imitation of the Mind <note>The "Divine Intellect" or *Nous*.</note>, they move in a circle, wisely acting always around the same center; for the world seeks nothing from the outside. Moreover, all things within me truly desire the Good, and each attains it according to its own particular capacity. For the entire heaven depends upon that Good, as does my entire soul.

"Furthermore, there are the gods who rule in my various parts, and all animals and plants alike; finally, even whatever seems to be inanimate within me. <margin>D</margin> For indeed, some things seem to participate only in 'being,' others in 'living,' others more in 'sensing,' others already possess 'reason,' and others, finally, possess 'total life.' For one should not require equal things everywhere in unequal objects; nor is it fitting for a finger to see—that task is assigned to the eye. Instead, one should require something else from the finger. I believe that requirement is that it should be a finger and perform its own proper function."

<column-break/>

<margin>
IIII
Nature's view of evil: for even there, among bodies and souls, good is mixed in.
</margin>

No one should wonder that fire is extinguished by water, or that fire itself often consumes other things. <margin>E</margin> For something else brought this fire into its own state of being; since it was not produced by itself but by another, it is not unjust that it is also destroyed by another. Indeed, its very entrance into being proceeded from the corruption <note>In ancient philosophy, "corruption" is the technical term for the change or breaking down of one substance so that another can be born.</note> of something else, and thus its own destruction brings no unfairness to it. Likewise, when one fire is extinguished, another sometimes flourishes in its place. 

Certainly, in the incorporeal heaven, each thing remains as it is. But in this physical heaven, the whole indeed lives forever, and whatever parts are honored and primary remain. <margin>F</margin> But souls, by turns, exchange bodies, taking on different forms in different ones. Whenever a soul is able to be placed outside the cycle of generation, it lives together with the Universal Soul. But bodies, according to their form and as individual wholes, clearly will both exist and be nourished from these souls; for life here is in motion, while life there is immobile. <margin>G</margin> It was truly necessary for motion to come forth from an immobile nature, and for another life to flow from the life flourishing within itself—like a kind of vital breath, somewhat unstable, which is a sort of expiration of the quiet life. # PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. III.

### BOOK TWO
->Chapter 4<-

**A** These things happen by necessity, for they were not born to be eternal. They were born, however, because the Reason-Principle <note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. In Plotinus’s philosophy, this is the formative power that emanates from the Divine Mind to shape the material world.</note> occupied all matter, possessing within itself all things—even the sterile ones—just as they exist there in the celestial heaven above. For where else could they have come from, if they did not exist there? Furthermore, the mutual injuries men inflict on one another perhaps arise from the very desire for the Good; specifically, when they are unable to attain the Good, they wander astray and attack others. But those who have acted unjustly must pay the penalty, both because they carry away a depraved soul from their wicked actions, and because they are moved into a worse place by a certain fixed order. For nothing can ever escape what has been ordained in the Law of the Universe.

**B** However, order was not established because of the transgression of order, nor was the law made because of the breaking of the law—as some might think—as if those higher things were created for the sake of the worse things, just to make them apparent to us. On the contrary, order exists here because it is a consequence of the higher order; and because there is order, the transgression of order finds a place. Because of law and the Reason-Principle, **C** and because the Reason-Principle exists, the transgression of law and reason occurs. This does not happen because the better things made the worse things; rather, it happens because those things that are in need and ought to look up to the better things are unable to receive them—whether by their own lapse, or by their nature, or by chance, or by some other obstacle that has been raised. For that which employs a secondary order perhaps fails to reach its goal, either through an internal vice or because of something else happening from the outside. It also suffers many things from others, sometimes when they do not intend it, and sometimes **D** when they aim for it. Truly, those living beings that possess a spontaneous motion of their own <note>Latin: *spontaneum... motum*; Greek: *kinesis autexousios*. This refers to self-willed or voluntary movement, the basis of moral responsibility.</note> sometimes strive toward better things, and at other times slide toward the worse. It is perhaps not right to seek the cause of this inclination or fall toward the worse within the Reason-Principle itself; for once a small momentum toward falling is given at the beginning, the error proceeds along that same path and constantly makes the mistake both larger and more significant. The body is also present, and by necessity, desire is within it.

**E** Moreover, that which occurs first and suddenly, and is not immediately noticed or caught, creates a choice in favor of that toward which one was first inclined. Nevertheless, punishment follows under divine judgment. It is not unjust for a soul that has become such to suffer things that match its own disposition; nor should it be required that those who have done nothing worthy of happiness should be happy. Only the good are happy; for it is for this very reason that the gods are also blessed.

<margin>
V.
This same teaching confirms that no one can complain about providence. And where evil comes from.
</margin>

**F** If, therefore, every power is given to souls in this world to attain happiness, no one is permitted to complain about this region because some are not happy, but rather to blame their own weakness—that they are not strong enough to struggle vigorously where the prizes of virtue are set forth. For who could justly complain that those who have not yet become divine do not lead a divine life? Furthermore, poverty and disease have no weight for good men, but for the wicked, they are useful.

**G** Moreover, it is sometimes necessary to be sick, since we have bodies. Nor are these things entirely useless for the common order and the fullness of the universe; for just as when certain things are destroyed, the Reason-Principle of the world, the craftsman of things—

**A** These things happened as non-eternal. They happened because the Reason-Principle <note>original Greek: *logos*</note> took hold of all matter and held all things in itself, just as they are there, the things of the heavens; for whence would they have come, if they were not there? The injustices of men against one another might all have a desire for the good <note>original Greek: *ephesin tou agathou*</note>, but failing to attain it through weakness, they turn to other things. Those who do injustice pay the penalty by having their souls made worse through the practice of vice, and indeed by moving into a worse condition. For what they do results in—

**B** —escaping nothing that is according to the law of the same [universe]. It is not that order exists because of disorder, nor law because of lawlessness, as someone might think, so that the higher things might be known through the worse, and so that they might appear. Rather, it is because of the order that disorder follows; and because there is order, there is disorder; and because of the law and the Reason-Principle; and because there is the Reason-Principle, there is lawlessness. **C** This lawlessness does not come from the better having made the worse, but from those things that need to receive the better things being unable to receive them, either by their own nature or by chance and the hindrance of others. For why should they be allotted to always succeed? Either they do not have everything from themselves, or one thing is instructed by another. Some things are as they are, acting from themselves and striving toward other things, while **D** animals have a self-governing motion <note>original Greek: *kinesin autexousion*</note> through themselves. It leans sometimes toward the better, and sometimes toward the worse. One should perhaps not seek the cause itself of the turns toward the worse. For a small turn occurring at the beginning, making the error along this path, constantly makes the mistake more and larger. The body is present and desire is a necessity, and that which is first and sudden is passed by, and not being recovered immediately, **E** it made a choice toward that which it fell into. Indeed, justice follows, and it is not an unjust suffering for one who has become such to suffer things consistent with their disposition. Nor should it be demanded that happiness belong to those who do not do works worthy of happiness. The good alone are happy; because indeed, the gods are happy.

If, then, the souls in this universe are placed **F** to be happy, those who are not happy should not blame the place but their own weaknesses, or their failure to enter well into the struggle where the prizes of virtue <note>original Greek: *athla aretes*</note> are set forth. Or is it a terrible thing that those not becoming gods do not have a god’s life? Poverty and diseases are nothing to those who share in [virtue], but to the wicked, they are beneficial.

**G** Or it is a necessity to be ill, for those having bodies; nor are these things altogether useless for the order or the fulfillment of the whole. For as some things are destroyed, the Reason-Principle in the whole according to—
