# SECOND BOOK.

<margin>Opinion concerning the corruptible <unclear>cause</unclear></margin>
Leave aside those corruptible and fleeting causes, or say rather that they are no causes at all. Or, if you grasp the nature of the order, see that even those things which are considered "evils"—such as the weaknesses of the body or the soul—are part of the design. These things happen to those who suffer them, yet they are encompassed by the overarching cause just as the cosmic order is. For the sufferers themselves, these "evils" like poverty and disease can be a means of salvation. For even **depravity** produces something useful for the whole; it serves as an example of justice and works many beneficial ends. Indeed, it makes men vigilant, rouses the mind and understanding, and turns them away from the paths of wickedness. It teaches us what a great good virtue is by comparison with the evils that the wicked endure. Nor did these evils come into being for this reason; rather, because they exist and arose from necessary causes, the highest power makes use of them. It is the mark of the greatest power to be able to use even evil things well, and to be able to use the "formlessness" that has arisen to generate other forms. In general, one must define **evil** as a deficiency of the good. It is necessary for a deficiency to exist within the good because the good is present in "another" <note>Original: ἐν ἄλλῳ (*en allo*). In Plotinian thought, this refers to the material world, which is "other" than the pure, undivided Good.</note>; for that which is "other" than the Good will not be the Good itself. Thus, as Plato says, it is impossible for evils to be destroyed, because things are inferior to one another in relation to the nature of the good; and since these other things take their existence from the Good, those that have moved furthest away from the source become such as they are.

As for the fact that "evils" happen to the good contrary to their merit, while the wicked receive the opposite: it is rightly said that nothing truly bad happens to the good, nor anything truly good to the wicked. But why are some things distributed according to nature, and others contrary to nature for the wicked? How is this a "good" distribution? But if things "according to nature" <note>term: *secundum naturam* (according to nature). This refers to external comforts like health and wealth, which the Stoics and Platonists considered "indifferents" rather than true moral goods.</note> neither create happiness 
<margin>useful things</margin>
for the happy, nor do things "contrary to nature" take away the evils of the wicked, what does it matter whether it is this way or that? It is just as if one man were beautiful in body and another ugly, while the first were good. Yet, what is fitting and proportional, and what is "according to merit," ought to be present. While it is rarely absent, that most excellent "fittingness" is required there. Is it not fitting for the "god-like" to be the rulers of cities, rather than for the refined to be dragged away by the unjudging? This should be fitting; but if one does not consider the possession of these things as "good" or "evil," then perhaps a wicked ruler would not even be performing the most shameful acts. Or shall the wicked prevail in wars? Or commit shameful deeds when they take captives? These are the very things that cause us to doubt how these things happen if Providence exists. Or, if the whole is well-ordered, must not the parts also be in a state that follows logically, especially when they are living souls?

<column-break/>

**A** Just as he uses [matter] for the generation of others (for nothing can ever escape being encompassed by this very order), so too with corrupted bodies and the languid passions of the soul that have been seized by disease and vice: they are soon brought under the control of the order. These conditions bring certain benefits to the sufferers, such as poverty and illness. Indeed, see how depravity brings something to the whole; it becomes, as it were, **B** an example of justice itself, and produces many useful things from itself. It renders souls vigilant and makes them consider carefully how they might best avoid the heights of wickedness. Again, it allows us to recognize how great a good virtue is by comparing it to the evils that afflict vicious souls. Nor were these evils made for this purpose; rather, it has been said that the very Designer <note>original: *artificem*; likely referring to the Reason-Principle or Demiurge.</note> of the world is accustomed to use evils opportunely once they have come into being. This is the greatest sign of **C** power: to be able to use even evils for a good end, and to be able to use things that have become formless to generate other forms. Truly, we ought to consider **evil** as a deficiency of the good. It is necessary for a deficiency of good to occur here, because it exists in "the other." Because that in which the good resides is different from the Good itself, it brings about a deficiency; yet it was never the case that the Good itself was not. For this reason, as Plato says, it is impossible for evils to be entirely rooted out, because some things are inferior **D** to others in relation to the nature of the Good, and some are different from the Good, having received the cause of their existence from there. Such things have turned out this way because they have proceeded to the furthest point from the Good.

<margin>He confirms these same points, and will soon teach us more.</margin>
As for that which often seems to happen contrary to merit—when either the good suffer evil or the wicked report success—it will be rightly answered that nothing truly evil happens to the good man, nor does anything truly good befall the wicked man. However, one might ask: why do many things "contrary to nature" happen to the good **E** man, while many things "according to nature" occur for the wicked? By what logic can this distribution be correct? But if that which is "according to nature" neither adds to the happiness of the good nor removes the misery of the wicked, and if that which is "contrary to nature" takes nothing from the good, then what does it matter whether things go this way or that? It is just as if a wicked man had a beautiful body and a good man had an **F** ugly one. Nevertheless, what is fitting and proportional, and what can be said to be "according to merit," should ideally happen in the best way possible, which currently seems not to be the case; yet it was the role of the best Providence to have instituted it so. Furthermore, it does not seem fitting that the wicked should be lords and rulers of cities while the upright are servants—not even if these things add nothing to the "good" or "evil" of the soul—especially when an unjust ruler commits the most loathsome deeds. What of this: that the wicked triumph in battle and commit the foulest acts against their captives? **G** All these things compel us to doubt the reason why they happen while Providence reigns. For if parts belong to the whole, the parts also ought to obtain what is advantageous to them, especially when they are animated with life.

f 4

<summary>Plotinus addresses the "Problem of Evil," arguing that evil is not a positive force but a deficiency of good that the Reason-Principle utilizes to create cosmic balance and highlight the value of virtue. He acknowledges the difficulty of understanding why the wicked prosper but maintains that external circumstances do not affect the true happiness of the soul.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

...they possess, especially reason. Finally, it is probable that **Providence** <note>Original: *providentia*. For Plotinus, Providence is not a divine person making decisions, but the natural, rational ordering of the universe stemming from a higher intelligence.</note> extends itself through all things, and that its function is to ensure that absolutely nothing is neglected anywhere. For this reason, if we concede that this whole world depends on the **Intellect** <note>Original: *intellectu*. The *Nous*, or Divine Mind, which contains the perfect blueprints for all things.</note>, and that the power of that mind pours itself through all things, we must try in every way to demonstrate how each of these individual things is well-constituted.

<margin>
VII
He gives the principles and answers. He also treats the condition of the human world, regarding those who first degenerate, and the choices made by deliberation.
</margin>
**IN PRINCIPLE**, we must not ignore the fact that when we seek beauty in a "mixed" thing <note>Original: *in mixto*. A "mixed" thing is a physical object composed of both spiritual Form and physical Matter.</note>, we must not demand all the same qualities that constitute beauty in an "unmixed" nature. Nor should we look for the primary perfections in secondary things. Instead, since the world possesses a body, we must concede that some things happen to the universe because of the very nature of that body. Likewise, we must judge the rational principle only insofar as a "mixed" thing is capable of receiving it; it should be considered sufficient if nothing is lacking of those qualities it is actually capable of holding. 

It is just as if someone on earth were to contemplate a most beautiful man: he should not think it necessary for this man to be identical to the "Ideal Man" who exists in the Mind. Rather, he should think the Creator has done enough if, even though this man is made of flesh, nerves, and bones, he has nevertheless been encompassed by a **Rational Principle** <note>Original: *ratione*. Used here to mean the formative blueprint or "Logos" that gives shape to matter.</note> to such a degree that even these physical parts are rendered beautiful, and the principle is made to spread itself over the matter. Having conceded these points, we must then proceed to our inquiries. For perhaps in these things we will be able to find the wonderful gift of Providence and the miraculous power of the Craftsman of this world.

Certainly, regarding those actions of souls which are situated within the souls themselves—such as when wicked souls do harm to others, or when the wicked harm the wicked—unless someone wants to claim that Providence is the cause of their depravity, it is not right to demand an account or a retraction of the deed from Providence itself. Rather, one should refer the cause to the one who chose the action. For it has been said that souls, too, must have their own individual motions. Furthermore, we are not just dealing with souls now, but with **living animals** <note>Original: *animalia*. In the sense of "animated beings" or "living creatures" existing in the physical world.</note>. It is not surprising that when they are of a certain character, they have a life that follows accordingly. For they did not come here because of the world’s existence, but they existed before the world; it was their nature that they would one day belong to the world, to care for worldly things, to be the causes of stability, to govern, and to act in whatever way they might—whether by presiding over it and contributing something from themselves, or by immersing themselves within it. We are not debating how that happens at this moment, but however it may be, Providence is not to be blamed. 

But when someone considers the comparison of evils to their opposites—namely, that the good are poor while the wicked are rich, and that the worse people often possess much more of the things necessary for human nature, or that they dominate and occupy cities and nations—what shall he say? Will he say that Providence does not reach down to the earth at all? Yet, since all other things happen according to Reason, this is itself testimony that Reason descends even to the earth; for animals and plants participate in Reason, Soul, and Life. Perhaps it reaches this far, but...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...which possess also reason. It is necessary, then, for **Providence** <note>Original: πρόνοια (*pronoia*)</note> to reach through all things; its work is to be, and to neglect nothing. If we say that this whole world is suspended from it and that its power has reached into all things, we must try to show how each of these things is in a good state.

<margin>B</margin>
**FIRST**, then, let it not be ignored that those seeking the "well-ordered" in a mixed thing should not demand exactly the same degree of beauty as in the unmixed, nor should they seek the primary things in the secondary. But since it also has a body, one must concede that things come into the whole from the body itself, and demand only as much as the **Rational Principle** <note>Original: λόγος (*logos*)</note> was able to give, and as much as the mixture was able to receive, so that nothing is lacking in this. 

It is as if someone were examining a physical man to see how beautiful he is; he would surely not expect him to be the same as the Man in the Mind, but would accept him as he is, even if he consists of flesh, nerves, and bones, provided that he is grasped by the Rational Principle so that even these parts are made beautiful <margin>C</margin> and the Rational Principle is spread throughout the matter. Having laid these foundations, we shall go through the rest. We may happen upon the wonder of Providence and its power in how this whole world is constituted. 

As for the works of souls, which originate in the souls themselves when they perform worse actions—such as when wicked souls harm others, or the wicked harm each other—unless you could say they are not souls at all, why is it right to demand an account of Providence as if it were the cause, rather than <margin>D</margin> giving the cause to the one who chose? For it has been said that it was necessary for souls also to have their own motions. And they are not just souls, but already living beings. Indeed, one should not wonder that those who are such as they are have a corresponding life. For they did not come into being because of the world, but were before the world; they had it in them to be of the world, to take care of it, to sustain it, to manage it, and to act in some manner—whether they stand over it and give all of themselves, or whether they do it in some other way, <margin>F</margin> or whether they are themselves in all these things. But however it may be, it is not possible to blame Providence. 

But when one considers the life of the wicked in contrast to their opposites—good people being poor, and the wicked being rich and having more, even over themselves, or over nations or cities—is it because Providence does not reach the earth? Yet all other things that happen are witnesses <margin>G</margin> that it does indeed reach the earth. For animals and plants also partake of Reason, Soul, and Life... reaching them, it may not dominate, but...

...it does not dominate. But since this whole universe is one single liv...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of Providence from Ennead III, Book 2. Having established that the universe is a singular, rational organism, he now addresses why "evils" or imbalances exist within the physical world and why human suffering often results from a lack of self-discipline.</meta>

# SECOND BOOK.

<margin>
I think it is easier <note>original: "Ῥᾷον οἶμαι..."</note> to say that the whole is well-ordered, rather than saying the head and face of a man were made by a governing Nature and Reason, while the rest was left to other causes—whether by necessity or chance—and turned out poorly due to nature’s weakness. Indeed, it would be neither holy nor pious to suggest that these things are not beautifully arranged, for that would force one to find fault with both the craftsmanship and the Creator.
</margin>

A **IT REMAINS**, then, for us to ask how these things are rightly ordered and hold their proper place; or, if they do not, how they might still be considered "not bad." In every living creature, the upper parts—which we call the head and the face—are the most beautiful, while the middle and lower parts are less so. B Humans, however, occupy the middle and lower positions. But in the heights is the Heaven, where the gods of the heavens dwell, occupying the greatest part of the world and the entire surrounding sky. The Earth, meanwhile, sits like a center point, appearing as just one among the many stars.

C Most people are astonished that men live unjustly; they think this because they believe man is the most venerable thing in the universe, as if nothing were wiser than he. But in truth, man is midway between the gods and the beasts, and he leans toward both. Thus, some men become more like gods, while others become more like beasts; but the majority maintain a middle ground. Therefore, those who have degenerated and approached the quality of beasts seize those in the middle and do them violence. D These victims are better than their oppressors, yet they are overcome by those who are worse, insofar as they themselves are also "worse"—meaning they are not truly good, nor have they prepared themselves so that they cannot be harmed.

For example, if certain boys have exercised their bodies but, through ignorance, have left their souls in a worse state than their peers, they might be defeated in the wrestling school <term>palæstra: an ancient Greek wrestling school or gymnasium</term> by those who have exercised neither body nor soul. If the winners then snatch their food and strip them of their soft clothes, E should this seem harsh or ridiculous? For why would it not be right for a lawmaker to permit such things to happen to them, so they might pay the penalty for their lazy and pampered lives?

Indeed, since the gymnasiums were available to them, and they—through laziness, softness, and neglect—ignored their own training, they have rendered themselves like fat lambs, a ready prey for wolves. For those who commit such crimes, the first punishment is that they become wolves and unhappy men; afterward, it is ordained what such people must suffer. For one does not simply die after becoming evil; rather, F there is always a consequence following from what came before, according to reason and nature. Worse things follow the worse, and better things follow the better.

The world is not merely a wrestling school. For there is a "game" <note>Original: "Ludus". Plotinus often refers to human life as a drama or a game to emphasize that the soul remains unharmed if it maintains its higher perspective.</note> being played here. It was necessary that once boys have grown up, they should arm themselves with justice and take up weapons and adopt a character superior to that of those merely wrestling in a gym. But as it stands, some are unarmed, and those who are armed prevail. In such a case, G it is not right to expect God himself to fight for those who are cowardly. For the Law says that safety is to be sought not through prayers <note>Original: "votis". Refers to vows or religious petitions.</note>, but through courage in war. Nor is it fitting for those...

<meta>catchword: ...those (eos)</meta>

<column-break/>

A ...it would be just as if someone were to say that the head and face of a man are made by nature, with the "seed-reason" <term>ratione seminaria: the "Logoi Spermatikoi" or formative rational principles that shape matter</term> clearly prevailing, but that the rest was attributed to other causes, whether accidental or necessary, and is therefore inferior; or that such things arise because of the frailty of nature. But truly, it is neither holy nor pious to admit that these things are not beautifully arranged, whereby you would be forced to find fault with the work and the workman at the same time.

<margin>
He answers some points quite well.
</margin>

B **IT REMAINS** for us to inquire how these things are rightly constituted and hold their order; or if in some way they do not, or rather, why they are not bad. In every animal, the highest parts—namely the head and face—are more beautiful, while the middle and lowest parts are less so. Humans, however, are in the middle and lower parts. But in the heights is the heaven, and the celestial gods, and that which holds most of the world, and all the heaven in its circuit. The earth is like a center, and like one of the number of stars.

C Indeed, many wonder that men live unjustly, because they think that man is the most to be honored in the universe, as if there were nothing wiser at all. But in reality, man is midway between gods and beasts, and inclines toward both. Thus, some indeed turn out more like gods, others more like beasts, but most occupy the middle between these. Therefore, those who are depraved and approach the quality of beasts seize the middle ones and do them violence. These are better than those who compel them, yet they are overcome by the D worse ones, insofar as they themselves are also worse; they are not good, nor have they so prepared themselves that they could not suffer.

Thus, if certain boys have exercised their bodies, but have souls worse than these due to ignorance, and therefore in the wrestling school they defeat those who have been exercised neither in body nor in soul, and they seize their food and strip them of their soft clothes—ought this to seem either harsh or ridiculous? For why would it not be right that the lawgiver himself allow them to suffer such things, E paying the deserved penalties for a lazy and luxurious life?

Since gymnasiums were already shown to them, but they, through laziness, softness, and neglect, so neglected their own cultivation that they rendered themselves like fat lambs and the prey of wolves. For those who have perpetrated such crimes, the first punishment is imminent: that they be wolves and unhappy men; then it is prescribed what such people should suffer. For it is not permitted here for those who have been made evil to simply die, but to the prior things F there always follow those things which are according to reason and nature. Specifically, worse things follow the worse, and better things follow the better. Nor is the world simply such a wrestling school. For a "play" or "game" is held there. For it was necessary, after the boys have grown up, that both should be girded with justice, and now be equipped and have weapons, and better habits than those of the wrestlers in the gym are accustomed to be. But now, these are indeed unarmed, and the armed prevail; where G it certainly is not right for God himself to fight for those who are weak. For the Law says that safety is sought not by prayers, but by courage in war. Nor is it fitting for those...

Having previously discussed the hierarchy of beings, Plotinus now addresses the relationship between individual effort and Divine Providence, arguing that humans cannot expect the gods to do for them what they are capable of doing for themselves.</meta>

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEAD III.

<margin>
IX
The Providing God knows how humans act, and especially how they provide for their own lives through providence.
</margin>

A [Those who merely] wish [do not gather fruit], but those who cultivate the earth gather its fruits; nor are those healthy who neglect the care of their health. One should not take it poorly if the wicked accumulate more fruit, provided they have been more effective in their farming. Furthermore, it is ridiculous to perform all other matters pertaining to life according to one’s own judgment—even if one does not act in a way <note>original: "ut placet diis"</note> pleasing to the gods—and then demand safety and salvation from the gods alone, especially when one has not done the very things through which the gods command men to be saved. Indeed, death B is better for such people than a life of the sort that the laws of the universe themselves do not wish to sustain. If, through the persistence of folly and wickedness, things were to be preserved for a long time despite contrary actions, then Providence could be accused of negligence for allowing the worse to overcome the better. In truth, the evil of the subjects is mastered by their own cowardice <note>The Latin *ignavia* and Greek *anandria* imply both laziness and a lack of manly spirit.</note>; for this is more just than the alternative.

C **PROVIDENCE** should not exist in such a way that we ourselves become nothing at all; for if Providence were everything and existed alone, it would no longer be Providence. For whom would it provide? It would simply be the totality of the Divinity. In reality, the Divinity exists and confers its influence upon another, yet not in such a way as to make that "other" disappear. Rather, when it approaches a human being, for example, it preserves him in that which constitutes being human. Now, to be preserved by the law of Providence is to live according to it, which means doing whatever the law prescribes for a person. D The law prescribes that those humans who have become good shall henceforth remain in a good life, even one established after death, while the wicked shall have the opposite. It is a sacrilege to think that those who have turned to evil should be protected by others as their saviors while they themselves remain idle and trust only in prayers. Nor is it right for the gods to set aside their own lives to manage every single detail of the lives of the wicked. It is not fitting for upright men—who lead a different life, one better than the human standard—to be burdened with governing the worse sort. E For if they did so, they would never have time to care for the path by which they themselves became leaders of others, nor to meditate on how that status belongs to them; instead, they should invite anyone who is willing to become good of his own accord. Indeed, more people would have already become good if they had seen these leaders as their guardians.

The human race was thus made as a certain kind of living creature—not the most excellent of all things, but occupying and choosing a middle rank. Yet, at the same time, in the place where it is positioned, it is by no means abandoned by the benefit of Providence; rather, it is continually called back to the higher realms. By all the various mechanisms which the Divinity employs, it F constantly restores virtue as the prevailing power. By this means, it has come to pass that the human race has never lost its rational faculty; on the contrary, man is a participant in mind, art, and justice—even if he is not supremely wise. In the justice that individuals practice among themselves, they believe they are acting justly, for they judge that those they harm are deserving of such treatment. Man is truly as beautiful a piece of workmanship G as can possibly be, and he is so situated in the world that he has a better lot than the other animals that are upon the earth; for even those animals inferior to man...

<column-break/>

...to gather fruits, not by wishing, but by caring for the earth; nor to be healthy, without caring for health. Or to be annoyed that other fruits go to the wicked rather than to those who farm them, is already absurd. Then it is also ridiculous to do all other things in life according to one's own judgment—and not to do those things which are pleasing to the gods—yet seek to be saved by the gods alone, without even doing the things they command if one wishes to be saved. And indeed, it does not turn out better for them than to be living thus, just as they live not according to how the laws in the universe willed. So that when the opposites occur, there is a reckoning of both vice and the cessation of vice. When it is guarded carelessly, Providence increases, so that the worse does not truly prevail. But wickedness rules through the cowardice of those held by it. For this is just, not the other.

AND indeed, let it not be that Providence must be such that we are nothing. If all things were of that Providence alone, or of it only, would it then belong to anyone? It would only be the Divine. But then, as it is now, it has willed to be toward another, not in order to take away the other; but by being present, as in a man or in himself, to preserve the being of a man. This is living by the law of Providence, which is doing as many things as the law itself says. And it says to those who have become good, a good life follows from there, both now and later; but to the wicked, the opposite. To think that those who have become wicked should have others as their saviors while they offer nothing but prayers is not lawful. For the gods do not rule their individual affairs by abandoning their own life. And as for good men living another life, one better than the human one, to then choose them to rule [the wicked]—they themselves would not care to be the start of rewards for others, just so that they might care for them; but a good man flees [to be] by himself. So they grow by their own nature toward the multitude. If there were some good people standing over everything, then such a living being would be produced that is not the best, but holds a middle rank and chooses it; nevertheless, it does not fall away. Nor was it better to perish from Providence, but being always brought back toward the things above, by all kinds of devices which the Divine uses, it makes virtue called upon, so that the human race does not lose being rational, but participates even if it is not at the peak of wisdom; but there is art, and justice, at least that which they have toward one another, and they do not act unjustly, or they think they do something justly. For man is a worthy and beautiful creation, as much as possible... like the whole, he has a share of the other living things, as many as are better upon the earth; since among others which are less...

<summary>Plotinus argues that Providence does not override human agency or the laws of nature; individuals must exert effort (like farming or self-care) rather than relying solely on prayer. He defines humanity as a "middle" being that possesses reason and a path toward the divine, provided they live according to the rational laws of the universe.</summary>

Having argued that humans must take responsibility for their own welfare, Plotinus now expands his scope to the natural world and the internal causes of human behavior, defending the complexity and variety of the created order.</meta>

### BOOK TWO.

<margin>Of Plato.</margin> No wise person censures those living beings that bring beauty and ornament to the earth. **A** For it would be ridiculous if someone were to disparage the nature of animals because they bite or harm humans, as if it were proper for humans to live in a state of absolute, secure laziness <note>original: "ignavia"</note>. It is necessary, however, for these things to exist as well. The benefits that can come from them are, in part, completely self-evident; in other parts, though they may be less manifest, the long passage of time eventually demonstrates them, so that nothing in them—either regarding themselves or regarding humans—is in vain. **B** It is truly laughable if someone disapproves because many animals are wild, especially since many humans are also wild. If they do not obey humans but resist out of mistrust, it should not be seen as a marvel.

<margin>**X** Although the wicked are not evil through their own choice in these vices, their madness is nonetheless voluntary.</margin> BUT if humans are evil against their will, and are such without wanting to be, someone might argue that one should not blame either those who commit an injury or those who suffer it, as if they suffer such things through their own fault. Truly, if it is necessary for them **C** to become evil in this way—whether by celestial motion or by a certain principle <note>original: "principium" / "archē"</note> that brings about consequences in sequence—can it not be argued that this is the natural state of things? And if Reason <note>original: "Logos"</note> itself is what does this, how is it not committing an injustice? Perhaps, indeed, they are said to sin "not by choice" because the sin itself is not a voluntary goal. Yet this does not prevent the actions from proceeding from the people themselves. Because they are the ones doing the acts, they are the ones who sin. Otherwise, they would not have sinned at all if they were not the authors of such actions. When it is said that they become evil **D** by necessity, this should not be understood as coming solely from an external force, but because they sin within a certain shared condition. Likewise, what is said about celestial motion should not be taken as if nothing were placed in our own power. For if everything were done solely by an external force, then things would surely happen exactly as the authors intended; therefore, humans would not have committed acts contrary to them. Indeed, humans would not even be impious if the gods themselves performed all these deeds. In reality, the action proceeds from the **E** humans themselves. Once a principle is given, that which follows is carried out; you must understand this as the consequence of all those things which act as principles. And humans, too, are principles. Therefore, a person is moved toward honorable things by their own nature, which is a principle of spontaneous action. <margin>* If the gods were doing these things.</margin>

<margin>**XI** The Reason of the world, as an artist, would have distinguished various ranks in the world for its perfection.</margin> WHETHER each thing happens through certain natural necessities and consequences, and they happen as rightly as they possibly can, is one question. But perhaps it is not quite like that; rather, the dominant Reason <note>original: "Logos"</note> itself **F** does all these things and wills them so. Even those things called "evils," Reason itself performs rationally, not wishing for all things to be equally good. For just as an artist does not make every part of an animal an eye, so too Reason did not make all things gods. Instead, it decreed that some things should be gods, and others should be spirits <note>original: "daemones"</note> of a secondary nature, and after these, humans and other animals in succession. This was not done out of envy, but through a reason that possesses an intellectual variety. We, however, are affected like those who are **G** ignorant of the art of painting, who condemn the painter because he has not placed beautiful colors equally everywhere. But the painter attributed to each part what was fitting for it. Well-ordered cities, too, are not arranged with equality in all their parts. Furthermore...

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD II
<note>While the header says Ennead II, this text is traditionally categorized as Ennead III, Book 2, Sections 15–17 in modern editions.</note>

Who would find fault with a comedy or a tragedy because not all the characters in it are heroes, but there is also a lowly servant, or a peasant who speaks with a coarse voice? A poem would not be beautiful if one were to remove the lesser characters, for the work is fulfilled by the inclusion of all.

<margin>
XII
The seminal Reason of the world sends forth all things from the beginning and nature has produced them; they mingle themselves into the world through a constant flow.
</margin>
->B<-
Reason itself <note>original: "Ratio" / "Logos"</note> suggests that by completely accommodating itself to matter, it created all these things, showing itself as a composite of dissimilar parts; existing as it does from that which came before it, certainly that which has been made could not have anything more beautiful than itself. Reason truly ought not to have been made from parts that are entirely similar, uniform, or identical. In this way, the author is not to be blamed, since this Reason—the craftsman of things—is indeed all things, yet differs in every part. But if Reason had introduced other things into the world from outside itself, such as souls, and had compelled them against their nature to fit into the worldly craftsmanship (and many of them for the worse), how could that be considered a right action of Reason? But truly, we must think that souls also exist as parts of Reason itself; it does not make them worse to accommodate them to the world, but disposes them according to their merit where it is fitting and expedient for them.

<margin>
XIII
There is a shifting change in all things.
</margin>
->C<-
Furthermore, we must not despise what is commonly said: that it is not right to always look only at the present, but also at the past and future cycles of time.

->D<-
For from that perspective, justice is found to be meted out according to merit. A change occurs from masters to private citizens, or into servants in a following life—if indeed they were masters who were useful for good. Certainly, it is expedient for these men to be changed in such a way. Furthermore, if they abused riches, they are transferred into the state of the poor; where indeed, for those who are good, it is not useless to be poor. Likewise, those who have unjustly killed someone will themselves be killed unjustly. "Unjustly," that is, in respect to the one who does the killing, but "justly" in respect to the one who is slain. Indeed, he who suffers this will be brought together with the one who is ready to perpetrate the very things that the victim deserved to suffer.

->E<-
Let no one think that anyone becomes a beggar by reckless chance, nor that one becomes a captive by some accident, nor that the body is violated without a reason: rather, that person once perpetrated in the past what he suffers in the present. And he who extinguished the life of his mother shall in the future be extinguished by a son, having then been born as a woman. And he who had violated a woman, having then been born as a woman, shall himself be violated.

->F<-
Hence arises that oracle concerning Adrastia <note>Adrastia is a Greek name for Nemesis or the inescapable power of Divine Law</note>, which is the incurable power of divine laws. For Adrastia is undoubtedly the establishment of such an order: a truly marvelous judgment, justice, and wisdom. One may conjecture that such an order always exists in the universe from those things which are seen daily in the world: where certainly such an order runs through all things, even the very smallest. A marvelous art appears everywhere, not only in divine things but even in those which one might easily judge to have been neglected by providence because of their insignificance.

->G<-
Such is the skillful and stupendous variety found in even the most discarded little creatures: for this kind of art propagates itself even to the fruits and leaves of plants. In these, one may marvel at how beautiful the forms are, how easily and opportunely they bloom, and how nature’s diverse and beautiful things sprout without labor; nor were they made this way only once, and immediately—

<column-break/>

->A<-
Or if someone were to blame a drama because not everyone in it is a hero, but there is also a servant, and some rustic, and someone speaking foully; yet the beauty consists in this: if one were to take away these roles, the fulfillment that comes from them would be lost. <note>Translated from the Greek: "τὸ δὲ κάλλον ἐστὶν..."</note>

->B<-
If, then, the Reason <note>Logos</note> itself, being sown upon matter, worked these things, the parts would not be uneven because all things are its parts; and this thing which has been generated, being defined, could not have itself more beautifully. But a Reason made of all things similar and most near to one another would not have come into being. Since the craftsman is not to blame, or rather, the parts are not each individual thing, but because he brought other things into the world from outside himself—namely, souls—and forced them to harmonize their nature with the creation; how could he have given thanks, or how could it be right? But it must be said that the souls are also parts of it, and it does not make them worse in fitting them in, but brings them down according to their merit as is fitting for them.

->C<-
SINCE, one must also look at that Reason, not naturally looking at each thing in the present, but toward the prior circuits and into the future; for the transitions and changes of the divine elements are according to merit, and according to what was done in the past,

->D<-
evil masters, and it is not advantageous to them; or if they used wealth badly, they become poor, and it is not disadvantageous for good men to be poor. And those who have killed unjustly are killed: unjustly indeed by the one who does it, but justly for the one who suffers it; and the one who is to suffer is brought together into the same place with the one seeking to do what the other has to suffer.

->E<-
Do not let anyone think that being a beggar happens by random chance, nor that men are taken captive by luck, nor that the body is insulted by chance: but someone did these things at another time, and in turn suffers them. And the one who killed a mother shall be slain by a child, having become a woman. And the one who violated a woman shall entirely be violated, having become a woman.

->F<-
And as the saying goes, Adrastia—for this is the arrangement—is truly Adrastia and truly justice, and a wondrous wisdom. Concerning the things that happen, there is a certain order of the whole, from the things seen in the universe, which one might rejoice in all things, even that which is smallest, for it is wondrous in its nature; not only if someone looks at divine things, but also those whose cause is despised by some as being—

->G<-
—not small in their weakness, even if one looks by chance at animals, where there is a varied and wondrous craftsmanship, even in the parts of plants, fruits, and even the flowers of the leaves, and the smoothness of the base, and how easy and varied it is, and that it has been made—

<summary>Plotinus defends the presence of inequality and "lesser" beings in the world by comparing the universe to a play that requires diverse roles. He argues that suffering and social shifts are the result of reincarnation and divine justice (Adrastia), where past actions dictate future circumstances.</summary>

### BOOK TWO

...at once, and a substance, but it always creates, so that those things governed by eternity <note>original: "aiōn"</note> might remain in the same state. Therefore, things that change are transformed, not by being destroyed, but by taking on other forms <note>original: "schēmata"</note>. 
<margin>Transitional</margin>
But as the powers are beautiful and fitting, they desire to act. For the whole Divine acts according to its nature; and its nature is according to its own essence, bringing together beauty and justice in its activities. For if they were not there, where would they be?

Thus the arrangement follows Intellect <note>original: "noús"</note>, so that it exists without the need for rational deliberation. For if one could use reason most perfectly, they would marvel that the result could not have been otherwise than what Reason <note>original: "logismos"</note> has produced. 
<margin>It is known</margin>
The creator is known in those things where each part exists by nature; for those things which are always coming into being do so more by an intellectual plan than by a calculated arrangement. In each thing, it does not come 
<margin>Having become</margin>
from the thing becoming, but from the offspring. There is no need to demand a cause from the creator, unless one thinks each thing ought to have been made in such a way as those things which are not created. But the cause is found in such things as these, where the cause is in others, directed toward a greater good for the sake of the good. Rather, each divine thing is self-sufficiently healthy in itself; but for those who look at the lesser parts, it was not impossible for reason to have come from them. However, a part is not greater than the whole, nor the parts in the whole; rather, they exist by power, otherwise they would not be a part. For the whole is everything in itself, while the individual parts are as they are, and the collective whole is composed of parts. Or perhaps the whole is in this part, or something else is a part of it, and that too is a whole. But each individual thing, if it is required to be perfect, is so as if reaching a true summit. For by then, it is no longer a part; if it is a part, it belongs to the whole. And indeed, one should look to a greater cause for interpretation, and it is not better to make the whole [the same as the part]. Once adorned, its worth is greater. If indeed the making comes from a similar worth to the whole, it is as if it were conceded to those things before they existed. And so it was arranged in every way, 
<margin>Everywhere</margin>
firstly according to man, something shines out in him. 
<margin>First</margin>
Just as in the divine the highest parts appear, 
<margin>Shines out</margin>
if these are perceived, like a large and beautiful statue, whether it be living or made by art or nature, where stars shine out upon the face, and others are placed elsewhere, and a star was destined to suit the position where it was placed.

Now, each of these things seen individually in themselves may seem thus, but the combination of things that come to be always offers a benefit for themselves. Even if there are threats according to the mutual devouring of other animals, and those human attacks upon one another. And because there are causes of wars, perhaps there would never be a rest or a truce.

<column-break/>

...and immediately cease to be. Rather, it has always been thus, while the higher things are not carried along in exactly the same way. Therefore, whatever things are brought across through various turns are not changed blindly, nor do they take on other forms by chance: indeed, it is just as the beauty of the world requires, and as it befits the divine powers to act. For every divinity acts as its own nature requires; and divine nature acts according to its own essence alone. Its essence truly explains beauty and justice together in its actions; for if they were not present there, they could be nowhere.

<margin>
XIV.
In what nature the discourse of reason occurs; that if it were an effecting reason it would stand by itself in the order of reason, and why those things which are not made but eternal require one perfect good, and why the part must be contained in the whole and cannot be equal to it, and what is to be demanded of the part.
</margin>
Therefore, the order thus established follows Intellect, so that it stands without the discourse of reason <note>original: "rationis discursione"</note>. And yet it so stands that if anyone were able to reason most perfectly, they would be astonished beyond measure that the whole is so disposed, and that reason would not have found or made it otherwise. This is always observed in individual natures, having more of the intellectual form than the order of reason can conceive or produce. In any kind of things that are made, therefore, one should not find fault with the effecting reason, unless one thinks that everything ought to have been made just like those things which are not made, but are eternal—both in the intelligible and the sensible realm (in which some things are also eternal)—demanding, as it were, the greatest possible heap of good, and not thinking the form attributed to each thing is sufficient in itself. It is as if one were to blame nature in man because it did not give him horns, not considering that it was impossible for reason not to spread itself through all things, yet it was necessary for lesser things to be contained in the lower levels, and parts in the whole, and that they cannot be equal, otherwise they would not be parts at all. Every higher thing is all things; but the lower individual things are not all things. And man, insofar as each person is a certain part, is not the whole. But if anywhere in certain parts there is also something else, which is not a part through us, then that too is the whole. Nor should it be demanded that any of the individual things, insofar as it is properly that thing, should have attained the summit of virtue, otherwise it would no longer be a part. Yet a part is not adorned more excellently in dignity as if by envying the whole; for the whole is made more beautiful to the extent that it excels more in dignity. For it is such, insofar as it is similar to the whole, and it is as if it were permitted to be such, and thus ordered at the same time, so that even according to man's place, something might shine forth in him, not otherwise than how the intellectual heavens shine through the divine sky. From this, a certain thought arises, as if a certain huge and beautiful statue, whether living or fashioned by the art of Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and craftsmanship, equivalent to the Greek Hephaestus.</note>, had stars glittering in its face, and others moreover on its chest, and so disposed that they properly create beauty.

<margin>
XV.
In the universal nature, things are necessary and mutually good, so that only those things are good in this world which can represent the universal whole of the world.
</margin>
Therefore, individual things considered in themselves seem to be so: but the combination of these, both those which are made and those which are perpetual, suffers from doubt and objection—both regarding the mutual voracity of brute animals, and regarding the attacks of men against men. Likewise, on account of perpetual war, which indeed can neither be calmed nor easily endured.

# PLOTINUS’ ENNEADS, BOOK III.

<margin>A</margin>
...especially if the very reason <note>original: "ratio", Greek: "logos"</note> of the world itself brought it about that things should be this way, and so it is said to be well-ordered. For that Reason does not support those who speak further against it, but says that as far as it is possible, these things are well-ordered; and that matter <note>original: "materia", Greek: "hyle"</note> is the cause of the fact that things which exist in this way have a lower condition, and that evils cannot be entirely uprooted. Since it was necessary for things to be this way, it is therefore well-ordered. To be sure, matter as it approaches is overcome, but it was brought in so that it might happen this way; indeed, the cause of matter itself was the Reason in this manner. Therefore, the Principle is Reason, and all things are Reason: both the things that come to be, happen through it, and the things that are arranged together in the process of generation are thoroughly held in this state. <margin>B</margin> What then is the necessity of perpetual and natural war among animals and men? Perhaps the mutual devouring of animals is necessary because there are certain successions of animals, which, even if no one killed them, could not remain as they are forever. But if at some time it is necessary to die, then it was necessary to die in such a way that benefit might also come to others from them—why should it be appropriate to begrudge this? And what if those who are devoured are reborn as others at some time, just as if an actor <note>original: "persona"</note> on the stage who is feigned to be killed soon changes his appearance and, putting on the mask of another character, returns to the stage? <margin>C</margin> But perhaps someone might say that this is not truly being dead. Truly, if to die is to change the body, not differently than changing a garment on stage, or if death is to lay aside the body altogether, just as in a comedy the final exit is from the play—where, however, one is to return to the play again at some future time—what then does such a mutual exchange of animals bring of a terrible nature? This is certainly much better than if they had not been born from the beginning at all. For then there would be a void of life, and a certain impotence of life existing in another; but now, since there is much life in the universe, it creates and varies all things in life, nor can it restrain itself from always making beautiful animals, as if they were playthings very pleasing to the sight. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, the weapons of men used against each other—since they are both mortal and fight in a certain decent order in the manner of those who play in the armed dances <note>original: "pyrrhichijs", referring to the Pyrrhic dance, a Greek martial dance performed in armor</note>—plainly declare that all the pursuits of men are play, and that death is not to be thought of as harsh. <margin>F</margin> Those falling in battle, in a short span of time, merely anticipate the death that would have occurred in old age, by departing more quickly, but in turn to return at another time. Therefore, if those living are despoiled of their fortunes, they will easily be able to realize that these were not even theirs before, and that the possession will be a laughingstock to the robbers, since they will in turn be despoiled by another at some time. Even if no one takes it away, the possession would be worse than the loss was to those despoiled. Just as in the scenes of a theater, we ought to look upon slaughters, deaths, the storming of cities, robberies, and spoils in life, as if all things are certain transmutations and alternating turns of characters, and everywhere feigned weepings and wailings. <margin>G</margin> For indeed in each individual act of human life, it is not the soul itself which is within, the true man, but the outer shadow of the man that laments and shrieks, and does all other things on the earth as if on a certain larger stage, in which indeed many shadows of souls jump about, and many shelters for the scenes are built.

<meta>catchword: tenim (For indeed)</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...especially if the Reason <note>original: "logos"</note> has made it so to be, or (as one might say) it is well. For the Reason does not speak to help those looking at the lower parts, to say that it is well or as it is possible to be—the cause being matter <note>original: "hyle"</note>, so that they are deficient, as having less. But as it is possible for evils to be left behind, they have it so. Or it is well thus, and matter did not come in and conquer, but was brought forth. And so it would rather be said that Reason is the cause of it: the principles are Reason, and all things are by Reason, and the things that come to be are according to <margin>Β</margin> it and are arranged together. Upon knowledge, it is entirely so. What then is the necessity of the unannounced war among animals and among men? Or are the mutual eatings of animals both necessary and the required exchanges of animals, as they are able; even if someone does not kill them, would they remain thus forever? But they must go away as something else; it was necessary to depart thus, so that <insert>another</insert> might come to be; for nature has need of them. If it is eaten, <unclear>it perishes</unclear>; like a player of the underlying parts <note>original: "hypokeimenōn"</note>, the one who moves around <margin>Γ</margin> having changed the appearance <note>original: "schēma"</note>, again and again with a <unclear>more useful</unclear> mask <note>original: "prosōpō"</note>... but what? Is it terrible or the truth? If in living it is not just living but a change of body; just as there are [some things] on stage and changes of the body, just as that one from the stage will one day come back again after having competed, what is terrible in this? Or such an exchange of animals with one another, being much better than if they had not come to be in the beginning. For that would be a desert of life, and <margin>Δ</margin> the inability of that which is in another; but now there being many living things in the whole, it makes all and varies the living; and it is not ashamed to make beautiful and fine living playthings. But the weapons of men against each other, being mortals <note>...they act as those fighting on firm ground, as if...</note> <margin>Ε</margin> playing in the pyrrhic dances in armor or in <unclear>rhythmical</unclear> dances (for in the pyrrhic dance they did not work by being called), they show that human pursuits are all plays, both those concerning <margin>Ϛ</margin> <unclear>possessions</unclear>, but that it is also terrible to die in wars. Or those fighting, having thrown <insert>themselves</insert> down for a little while, that which happens is not by old age, or again having drunk, and going again. If they are deprived of money while living, they would know that it was not even theirs. And to those who snatch it, the possession is a joke, they being deprived of it by others. Since even how, to those not deprived, the gain of the deprivation becomes <unclear>worse</unclear>. <margin>Ζ</margin> Just as on the stages of the theaters, so one must view the slaughters and all deaths, and the captures of cities, and robberies, all are changes and re-formings, and the play-acting of dirges and wailings. For here also in each of the acts of life, it is not the soul within but the outer shadow of the man, which wails and laments and does all things on the stage of the whole earth, where stages are made in many places.

# BOOK TWO <note>While the header says Book Two, the content belongs to the famous treatise on Providence in Enneads III.2.</note>

<column-break/>

A Such, then, are the works of man, who knows only how to live for the external world and does not perceive that within his own soul he is merely playing a part, even in his weeping. For only the virtuous man <note>original: "probus", Greek: "spoudaios"—the "serious" or "excellent" man</note> should be taken seriously when performing duties worthy of study; any other sort of man is nothing more than a plaything. Indeed, those who are serious about trivial matters act as though they are doing something significant, but they are ignorant of what is truly worthy of study and how to study it; they are themselves ridiculous. If anyone, while playing along with them, suffers such things, let him recognize that he has fallen into a game of children and set aside the persona <note>original: "persona"—referring to an actor’s mask</note> he has put on. Even if Socrates were to play a part, it would certainly be only the external Socrates who plays. Furthermore, one must remember that we should not argue that things are "evil" simply because people mourn and wail over them; for children, too, weep and lament over things that are not actually bad.

<margin>
XVI. What the seminal reason <note>original: "ratio seminaria", Greek: "logos spermatikos"—the formative principle of the world</note> of the world is, and how it arises from the divine fullness and the four degrees of fullness. Also, how the reasons of things are contained within a common reason even though they are contrary to one another.
</margin>

BUT if these things are said correctly, how can wickedness exist any further? Where is there injustice? C Where is there error? For if all things happen rightly and decently, how can it be that those who act do so unjustly or go astray? And how can they be unhappy if they do not act unjustly or err? Likewise, how shall we say that some things are according to nature <note>original: "secundum naturam"</note> and others are against nature <note>original: "praeter naturam"</note>? For if everything that is done and happens is transacted according to a certain natural order, then can there be any impiety against God? It would be as if a poet introduced a character into his D play who insulted and reproached the poet himself. Let us, therefore, explain more clearly what this Reason is, and prove that it is rightly described this way. This Reason is—if we may dare to say it, for perhaps in this way we shall understand—it is, I say, not pure Mind <note>original: "mens", Greek: "nous"</note>, nor Mind itself, nor a type of pure Soul <note>original: "anima", Greek: "psyche"</note>. Rather, it depends upon these and is a kind of vigor or light emerging from both: namely, from Mind and from Soul. It comes from a Soul affected according to Mind; these together generate this Reason as a kind of life which also possesses a reason within itself. Every life is an act <note>original: "actus", Greek: "energeia"</note>, or at least a most useful life. I mean "act" in the way that fire acts; but the act itself, E even if no sensation is present, is a motion that is by no means random. Whatever happens that participates in this Reason is suddenly affected in a rational way—that is, it is "formed." It is a quality of the act belonging to life that it can form things, and move them as if it were forming them. For this reason, its act is artistic, as if someone were moved in a dance <note>original: "tripudio", Greek: "orchesis"—choral dance</note>. For the dance is very similar to such an artistic life; the art moves the person, and it moves them in such a way F because life itself becomes like that art. Let these things be said so that it may be more clearly known what sort of life this is. This Reason, proceeding from one Mind and one Life—that is, from both in their fullness—is not merely one life or one mind; nor is it full everywhere, nor does it hand itself over in its entirety to the things it shares itself with. Since it has opposing parts within itself, and is therefore in need, it certainly produces the origin of war and strife. And thus G it is a "one-all," even if it is not a simple unity. Having been made, it lacks itself; it is not a single unit, but the last of the parts, each part being full, if...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of "Providence" (the divine plan) and the "Logos" (Universal Reason), specifically addressing how a single, harmonious divine plan can result in a world full of conflict, opposites, and moral evil.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

->A<- Just as a part might be an enemy to itself, so the universe is both a single thing and a friendly one, exactly as if there were one guiding principle for an entire play, whether tragic or comic, which contains many battles within itself. The play itself brings all the conflicting elements into a single harmonious balance, arranging everything like a military formation of combatants. In the universe, however, the conflict of these distant and clashing parts is derived from a single Reason <note>original: "ratio", Greek: "logos"—the formative principle of the world</note>. For this reason, one might better compare this harmony to the sounds produced by conflicting musical notes, and investigate why it is that repelling forces are included within the Reasons themselves. ->B<- If, therefore, these Reasons themselves create the "high" and the "low" notes and breathe together into a single unity—since they are the reasons of harmony within that harmony itself, which is a greater Reason of which they are smaller parts—then we certainly see similar contraries in the universe: white and black, hot and cold, the winged and the wingless, the footed and the footless, the rational and the irrational. All individual animals are parts of one single Universe. ->C<- Now, the whole is in agreement with itself, even though the parts are fighting one another in various places, yet the whole exists according to Reason. It is therefore necessary that this Reason also be one, made from contrary reasons: so much so that this very opposition brings about its constitution and, as it were, its essence. For if it were not multiple, it would not be the "All," nor would it even be a Reason. A Reason, by its very existence, is different even from itself, and the greatest difference appears to be contrariety. ->D<- Therefore, if it is one thing and then another entirely, and if this "other" does something, it does not make it less "other," but more so. It follows that if something produces another thing to the extreme, it must necessarily create contraries. The Reason will be perfect if it produces not only certain differences within itself, but also many contraries.

<margin>XVII. In Providence, all things are prescribed, as well as those things that they subsequently suffer from one another.</margin>
->E<- Since, therefore, Reason is such that it renders itself through the whole, it much more so creates those things that become contrary the further they are compelled to be apart. Truly, the sensible world is "one," just as its Reason is; and for that reason it is more multiple and filled with contraries. Furthermore, the appetite for living is more vehement in individuals, and the love that draws them toward unity is more burning. Yet, those who love often destroy the things they love out of a private greed for their own good, especially when those things are subject to decay. That love, which also draws the part toward the whole, pulls toward itself whatever it can. ->F<- Thus, both the good and the evil are led through contraries as if by the same art of a certain rhythmic dancer <note>original: "saltantis tripudio", Greek: "choros"—referring to the cosmic dance or a choreographed performance</note>. One part of this dance we shall call good, the other bad; and in this way, it maintains its beauty. But then, will it seem that none are truly evil? ->G<- Perhaps nothing here prevents some from being evil; but perhaps it follows that they do not become evil through their own doing. Perhaps also forgiveness will be granted to the wicked, except to those to whom forgiveness should not be given, and for whom Reason itself does not provide it. Indeed, Reason makes it so that such people are not forgiven. Moreover, if one part of it is a good man and another is a bad man, the bad man occupies more parts within it. But certainly, it happens just as in a play: where the poet assigns such roles to the actors, while for others...

<column-break/>

->A<- ...to himself in his parts a state of war, thus it is one and friendly, just as in the logic of a drama. There is one logic of the drama which holds many battles within itself. The drama, then, brings the things that have fought into a single, concordant harmony, like a tension of all those who are fighting. From <gloss>those remaining ones</gloss> remaining. But there, from one Reason, comes the battle of those who stand apart. So you might rather compare it to the harmony ->B<- of those who rejoice together, and you will seek why the fighting elements are in the Reasons. If, then, even here the Reasons make the "high" and "low" notes, and they come together into the reasons of such a harmony—which itself is a greater Reason, while they are smaller parts of it—we see in the whole the contraries. Such as white, black, hot, cold, and winged, wingless, footless, many-footed, rational, irrational. All these are parts of the one whole animal, and the whole agrees ->C<- with itself, even while the parts are fighting everywhere. <gloss>For everywhere</gloss> the whole is according to Reason. And it is necessary that it also <gloss>too</gloss> be a Reason from contraries, since its essence <gloss>and for the</gloss> is the union of them, and its essence brings such contrariety. For if it were not many, it would not be "all," nor would it be Reason. Reason needing ->D<- to make differences of itself, there is a greatest difference, which is contrariety. So that if it makes another thing in another way, it makes the "other." If it makes it most "other," it will make it an "other" by use; so that in making a thing "other" to the extreme, it will also create contraries by necessity, and it will be more than just differences, but will even cause contraries to exist within itself.

->E<- Since it is such as to reach over all things, it will much more make the things that come to be contrary, in as much as they stand further apart. And the sensible world is one. The Reason of the sensible world is one. Within it, it is much more multiple and much more full of contrariety. And the appetite for living is greater in each one, and the desire toward the "only" is more toward the one. By which it will be destroyed, and the <gloss>the one toward</gloss> things that love the beloved often destroy them, since they are singing out of tune with the same good, when they are perishable. The desire of the parts toward the whole pulls toward itself what ->F<- it can. Thus, then, both the good and the bad, as if <gloss>in</gloss> a dance of the same art, are managed through contraries, and we shall say that the part <gloss>for the dancer</gloss> is good, and the other bad. And so it is beautiful. And how then are there still bad people? Either by being bad, they are not destroyed. But if it is a disadvantage, it is because they are such from themselves. But perhaps there is forgiveness for the bad. Unless the matter of forgiveness is not what Reason makes. ->G<- Reason does not make only forgiveness for such things, but they are the part. The man himself is good, but the other is wicked. And the wicked man has more parts, just as in dramas, where the poet assigns some things to them, while for others...

<summary>This page uses the metaphor of a theatrical play and a musical harmony to explain how the universal Reason (Logos) incorporates conflict and evil into a perfect whole. Plotinus argues that true harmony requires the tension of opposites, such as high and low notes or good and bad characters.</summary>

# BOOK TWO

<margin>He already makes use of them</margin>
**A** He makes use of their nature. For he does not himself cause one to be first in virtue within the play, another second, and another third; rather, granting to each their own reasons <note>original Latin: "rationes", Greek: "logous"—the internal principles or characters of the souls</note>, he subsequently assigns an order that is entirely suited to each individual. Thus, a place is designated for everyone that is most fitting, whether for good or for evil. And so, each person proceeds toward either end according to nature and reason as is appropriate, occupying the place they had chosen. Then, one man speaks and acts **B** <margin>It is for each</margin> profane words and deeds, while another does the opposite. For the actors were already disposed in one way or another even before the play began, bringing their own characters into the stories. In the theatrical acts of men, <margin>The poet gave</margin> the poet distributes the lines to each; but the actors possess within themselves, and from themselves, the power to perform well or poorly. For there is an interaction between them that goes beyond the poet’s words. But in the truer poem <note>The "truer poem" refers to the created universe governed by Divine Providence</note>, which human beings represent in part, the soul—which has its nature from the beginning—is equipped for its role. **C** <margin>When they imitate</margin> And just as <margin>Just like those here</margin> actors are equipped by the poet, receiving their masks, their costumes, their saffron robes, or their tattered rags, so the soul, masked by the worldly Poet, undergoes various fortunes not by chance. For these fortunes are according to Reason, and the soul enters into them opportunely. Thus, the soul becomes harmonious with the universal tragedy or comedy of the world, and enters into acts and a universal Reason with which it is in accord. Then, it speaks its actions and all other things just as a soul would do by its own natural disposition, like a kind of song. **D** <margin>Whatever comes from the soul</margin> And just as the voice and the appearance are beautiful or ugly in themselves, and seem to add either a grace to the poem or a defect by the mixing of the voice, this does not make the play itself different than it was, though the voice itself appears discordant. But the author of the poet’s play rejects such a one, censuring him according to his merit and performing the duty of an excellent judge: <margin>But he himself lets go</margin> he promotes one to greater honors and, if possible, to more excellent deeds, while moving another to worse roles if he is able. In the very same way, **E** the soul, entering into this universal poem of the world and making itself a part of the theatrical games, brings with it the ability to perform its gestures well or poorly. Likewise, at its very entrance, it is joined to the order of all other things, and having obtained all other circumstances apart from itself and its own duties, it receives punishments and honors according to its merit. Furthermore, there is something more in such actors, inasmuch as they are equipped in a much grander place than within the limits of a stage. **F** <margin>Such a performance</margin> Especially since the author of the universe has endowed these actors with authority, and there is a greater power to compare many types of characters, gestures, and places. Therefore, <margin>And our punishments</margin> they define the measure of honor and disgrace based also on the fact that they themselves participate in the performance of honor and dishonor; namely, where individual dwellings are suited to individual characters, so that <margin>Toward many things</margin> they agree with the Reason of the universe itself, each one being accommodated according to the judgment of justice **G** to their own lots everywhere. Just as any string in a lyre <note>original: "cythara"</note> is returned to its own proper and fitting place and order according to the principle of sounding, such as the capacity of each one is for this very purpose.
