# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS: BOOK III

**A** is supplied. For in the whole of things, beauty and fitness flourish if each thing is arranged where it belongs, even sounds that are harsh in the darkness and in Tartarus <note>The deep abyss of the underworld in Greek mythology; here used to represent the lowest or most "evil" states of existence.</note>: for in those places, it is beautiful for such sounds to ring out. Consequently, the whole is only truly beautiful if it is not made of just one thing, like a stone, but rather if every part contributes its own proper sound to a single, perfect harmony—echoing life itself, though some sounds are lesser, lower, and further from perfection. **B** Just as in a pipe <note>original: "fistula", a pan-flute or syrinx.</note> a single note does not suffice, but a lower and weaker one is also required to complete the full consonance of the pipe: because the music is divided into unequal parts, and the individual sounds are unequal among themselves; yet from all these, one perfect harmony is produced. In the same way, the entire Reason <note>original Latin: "ratio", Greek: "logos"—the governing principle of the universe.</note> is one, but it is distributed into things that are not equal. Hence, there are different places in the whole, some better and some worse; and thus souls, which are not equal, fit into these unequal places. **C** From this, it follows that places are dissimilar, and unequal souls find these dissimilar places—almost as if according to the different holes of a pipe or another instrument. They inhabit different places according to the variety of the souls, singing their own songs in whatever place they are, yet in accord both with their specific locations and with the whole universe. **D** Indeed, what is sung poorly by any individual soul for itself is sung in harmony with the whole. Likewise, what happens to them against their own nature happens according to the nature of the universe. A lesser tone harmonizes with the whole no less than a greater one, and the one who sings out of tune with himself does not make the whole out of tune. Just as a common, wicked man does not make a city governed by just laws worse, if it is useful to use another example here. For even the use of a wicked man is necessary in a city when circumstances demand it, and such a person is rightly placed.

<margin>
XVIII
Differences
of souls and
confirmation
of the above.
</margin>

**E** SOULS are better or worse partly due to other causes, but partly as if they were not all equal from the beginning. For all things fit the Reason in a fitting proportion, since distribution into unequal parts occurs both in Reason and in the genus of souls. One must consider in the mind the second and third ranks of souls; again, the same soul does not always act according to the same parts of itself. But this must be explained in another way, for the present dispute requires many explanations for the sake of clarity. **F** We must consider, therefore, whether it is perhaps necessary to introduce those actors <note>original Greek: "hypokritas", the source of our word "hypocrite", referring to stage actors.</note> who announce something other than what the poet had written, as if the poet’s composition were imperfect in itself, and they were supplying what remained, filling in the places that the poet had perhaps left empty—as if they were to be mimes, not actors. But rather, the parts belong to the author and poet, who foresaw what the mimes would announce, so that he could rightly connect the rest and what follows in sequence. **G** For all things that follow in the universe in succession, and those things that follow from evil deeds, consist rightly in the Reasons and are dispensed everywhere according to Reason: just as when children are born in the natural order from adultery or a violation committed through theft.

<column-break/>

**Α** of power into the whole and that which is in the whole, the fitting and the beautiful, if each lies where it is placed. Every voice is heard, even the sound of the **wicked in the darkness** and in Tartarus; for there it is beautiful to sound so. And the whole is then beautiful, not if each part were a stone, but if it brings its own sound to contribute to a single harmony, itself voicing a life, though one that is lesser and worse **Β** and more incomplete. Just as the voice in a pipe is not one, but there is also a lesser and dim one that contributes to the harmony of the whole pipe, because the harmony is divided into unequal parts, and all the sounds are unequal; but the perfect one is one made of all. And indeed, the whole Reason is one, divided where things are not equal, and its parts are different, better and worse. Therefore, souls that are equal harmonize **C** in some way with the places, and as they lie or happen to be, they find the places in order. And the souls, not being the same but unequal, have different places, just as according to the inequality of a pipe or some other instrument, the places differ from each other. And each place sounds the same things in harmony both in the specific parts and in the whole. And what is bad **D** for them will be placed well and beautifully according to the whole. And what is against their nature is according to nature for the whole. No sound is lesser, but what it has done poorly, the whole makes use of; further, as it sounds, just as the **executioner** <note>original Greek: "demios", the public executioner or hangman, representing a "necessary evil" in a state.</note> who is wicked, does his work for a city of well-named people, which indeed must be used as an image of something else. For there and then it exists, and therefore even a wicked man is often trusted, and is placed well and appropriately.

->**SOULS ARE WORSE OR BETTER**, some<-
**Ε** from other causes, and others as if from the beginning they were not all equal. For they fit the Reason that divides itself in proportion to the encompassing whole; and one must know this. It is necessary to know the second and third ranks, and that souls do not always act with the same parts of themselves. But again, this must be stated: for the argument needs much for the sake of clarity. For it is not at all necessary to **F** introduce actors who speak things other than what the poet wrote, as if his dramas were somehow incomplete, and they were filling in what was lacking, or as if the creator had left gaps in the middle. Or how could it be that it is not up to the actors, but that the parts belong to the poet, who even knows what they will say, so that he can weave the rest together, and **G** those things that follow may be one? Or even the things that follow in the whole, which come after evil deeds, are in the reasons according to Reason, such as children born according to nature from adultery and the taking of a captive.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the universe is a grand, harmonious "play" where even "evil" souls and sounds have a necessary place, much like the lower notes on a pipe or a villain in a drama. The Divine Reason (Logos) uses even the flaws of individuals to complete a perfect cosmic design.</summary>

BOOK TWO.

...are born, and sometimes perhaps more excellent men: and when cities are overturned by the deeds of the wicked, other more excellent states are established. If, therefore, this introduction of supplementary souls <note>original: "supplementium animarum"; referring to the idea that new souls might enter the world to balance it</note> is absurd—yet these souls do both evil and good things (for we would strip Reason of its authority to create good if we removed from it all connection to evil)—what then prevents us from saying that the actions of the actors are parts of the play? Just as in the stories of a comedy, so it is with the Reason <note>original: "ratio", here translating the Greek "Logos"</note> that exists in the universe: here, both what is done honorably and what is done basely is included. Thus, for each individual actor, a progression is made by Reason itself, so that this worldly craftsmanship is more perfect, and all things are encompassed by it and its Reason. But indeed, for what purpose will the cause of evil effects be granted here? Yet even more divine souls will seem to be nothing more in the universe, but will all be parts of Reason: and either all the Reasons themselves will be souls, or why should some Reasons be souls while others are merely Reasons, even though the universal Reason is itself a kind of Soul?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...better men if it so happens, and other cities are better than those destroyed by wicked men. If, therefore, the introduction of souls is strange—some arriving to do evil and others to do better things—and indeed we shall deprive the Reason of good things by taking away the evil from it. What hinders us from making the deeds of the actors parts, just as in a drama? So too in the <margin>C</margin> Reason of the whole universe, let there be both the bad and its opposite in relation to each individual actor; so that from Reason itself, as this drama is more perfect, all things are directed toward it, and even the bad things are done for a purpose. And as for the souls, the divine ones are no longer anything [special] in the whole, but all are parts of Reason, and all Reasons are souls; or why are some souls, and <margin>D</margin> others merely Reasons, when everything belongs to some Soul?

# P L O T I N I
### ENNEAD THREE,
#### BOOK 3.

->THE SECOND [BOOK] ON PROVIDENCE.<-
->Which is the second book concerning Providence.<-

---

<margin>
I
The nature of the universal, and how easy it is; in the world of ideas, many things are marked as one.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a traveler with a hat and walking stick in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>
WHAT, then, do we think should be said about these matters? Perhaps the universal Reason <note>original: "ratio", the governing principle of the cosmos</note> encompasses both evil and good things at once, of which these are also parts. For this universal Reason did not beget these things alone; rather, the whole exists together with them. For the acts of the Universal Soul itself are the Reasons, and the parts are parts of those parts. But since a single soul has different parts, the Reasons are distributed in a similar proportion: for which reason the works of the final generation are likewise arranged. Souls are indeed in accord with one another, and their works are consonant—consonant, I mean, in such a way that a single entity is constructed from them, even from opposites. For all things, flowing from one certain source, flow together into one by the necessity of nature. Therefore, various offshoots or even opposing things, because they sprout from a single source, are eventually drawn together into one order. For although in individual animals—as in the race of horses—they may fight among themselves, or bite one another, or strive...

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' showing two men in classical or scholarly dress engaged in discussion in an interior setting.</image-desc>
What then is our opinion on these matters? Is it that Reason has embraced all things, both the evil and the good, of which these are parts? And it is not that Reason simply begets these things, but the whole exists with them. For the Reasons are the activities of some universal Soul; and the parts are the parts of the one [Soul] which has <margin>F</margin> differences in its parts. The Reasons are analogous, just as the works are the final offspring. For the souls are in harmony with one another, and the works are in harmony; in such a way that one thing arises from each of them. For all things, having started from one spring, are held together in one by the necessity of nature; so that even different, foreign, and opposing things are drawn together by being from one source; they are pulled into one arrangement. <margin>G</margin> For just as in individual animals, the horses [within a herd] fight and bite one another, and even if...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Universal Reason (Logos) incorporates both good and evil actions into a unified cosmic drama, comparing the world to a play where even the "bad" roles contribute to the perfection of the whole. He suggests that all individual souls and their actions flow from a single source into a necessary natural order.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III

<column-break/>

...they might compete, even if they are moved by zeal and anger, and likewise for all other things that live. And indeed, one must also place human beings among these, and then again join all species to those which were thought to possess life <margin>instead of being</margin>. For since those things that are not living also exist according to their species <margin>such as the non-living</margin> into that which is non-living. Or nevertheless, if you wish, into <margin>things in a place</margin> non-being. Or into that which provides being, or again <margin>material things or bodies</margin> it descended toward manifestation, dividing, or <margin>in the body or in the whole</margin> splitting apart the ability to see well by reaching toward all things and taking them in together, in one composition as a well-ordered living being, many things belonging to that one, or the things truly within it, which are according to their own nature. Yet they are within that whole. Just as fire burns, or the sun performs all its works. And humans, each doing their own things, either flee <margin>the difference of works</margin> or pursue such differences, and then <margin>whether even the base things come from nature</margin> according to their natures and works, they also live both well and poorly.

---

<margin>the principal chances would follow</margin> And as for the self-occurring accidents, <note>original: "αὐτοτυχίαι" (autotychiai); spontaneous events that seem like mere chance but are part of the internal order</note> which are sovereign in how they follow, these too follow in harmony with the things concerning them, and however many consequences are interwoven; and the leading principle <note>original: "ἡγεμονία" (hegemonia); the governing part of the soul or universe</note> interweaves all things, as the individual parts move together according to nature. Just as in military commands, where the general is the leader, but those arranged under him coincide, and the whole is ordered by the general's foresight <term>providence: the Greek word "pronoia" literally means "fore-thought" or "strategic planning"</term>. He seeks out the actions, and the passions, and whatever food and drink are necessary, and indeed all weapons and machines, and from these things being interwoven and flowing together, he ensures that the goal for which they were arranged takes its place here, and that everything is in some way by chance—yet it is impossible for the general's plans to fail, even though he does not explicitly watch over every detail of what the common soldiers were going to do. But if one looks to the rule of the general's authority, or indeed if there is a Great Leader <note>referring to God or the Universal Mind</note> under whom all things are placed, why would anything not contribute to the final result? Why would it not be harmonized?

---

<margin>evil things [traced] to causes, and causes to Reason</margin> For I too am master <margin>the cause of all things</margin>—these things were said, or rather, it asks silently: why is there not more of it in the whole? But we say, why is it such, and from where did such a thing come? There are two things: <margin>if this cause belongs to base passions</margin> the Reason <note>original: "logos"</note> seeks to remain among the qualities of all things, but it deviates back—how does the cause for each person relate to what is happening, or generally if they are even suffering? Just as in the knowledge of plants, is it because they do not perceive, or in other animals, because they are not like humans? And if someone is laughed at for being a human and not like the gods, why is this so, since they were made exactly as they are? We blame the Reason; but in the case of humans, [we ask] why it did not give them the best, or give them "the well" [the good life]. It would be better if everyone were the most excellent...
<note>The Greek text ends mid-sentence, transitioning into Latin notes reflecting on the same theme: "should we blame it in men because there is nothing greater than human [nature]... that man could have been something more excellent."</note>

<column-break/>

**A** ...they act, and they are moved to anger by emulation, and humans act similarly: yet all these species must be gathered into one genus of animals: then also the inanimate things according to the species of things: then into one "non-animal": after these, if it pleases many, to Being itself: finally to that which grants being to each thing. But again, from here, unfolding by division, descend, and contemplate that "one" as if it were pulled apart: because it runs through all things, and at the same time embraces all things in one certain order, so that it is like one animal, manifold and distinct: **B** with each one of those things which are in it performing what is proper to its own nature, yet existing in the universe, just as fire indeed burns, and a horse performs the works of a horse. Humans truly act as they were established by nature, each following their own duties, differing in their differences. And their works follow according to their natures: and again, they live as much well as poorly.

---

<margin>Providence is said to be a turning from that first principle toward itself: from here the connected consequences of things proceed in order.</margin>
**C** Therefore, accidents and fortunes have no authority over the good life, but these too follow, insofar as it is consistent with what preceded them; then indeed the connected consequences of things proceed in order. The leading principle itself connects all things, for it leads all things, while those things which verge on either side according to nature contribute to the same end: just as it happens in an army with the general leading: and those who fight together in a certain order acting in conspiracy. For the whole world is established by a certain commanding providence, [including] the arrangements of the table <note>likely referring to "rations" or "provisions"</note> and passions, and the food, weapons, and machines that must be present: and surely whatever follows from these being connected and conspiring together **D** is foreseen: so that whatever happens from these finds a place where it is well-situated. All things proceed from the general of the army by a certain wise and skillful reason, even though there are external things, alien to him, which enemies are about to bring in. But if he were able to command that army and this one similarly—indeed, if he were the Greatest Commander, to whom all things were subject—what could further lack order? Or what would be empty of connection?

---

<margin>He who says our nature is ordered within the universe. But how this is: to say we are only such as we are by nature is not enough: but we must have a reason.</margin>
**F** And if I am the master in choosing these things or rather those, nevertheless in the choice itself our affairs are ordered with the universe, since our nature is not foreign to the universe, but is numbered in its order as being such a kind or such a kind. But from where comes such a nature? There are two things which are required at present, one of which is: whether it is necessary to refer the cause to the maker (whoever that may be), through which each person is affected by such characters, or to the race [ancestry] itself, or perhaps no cause is to be assigned: just as in the generation of plants, **G** we do not miss a cause for why they do not feel, nor in other animals why they do not behave like humans. For it would be the same as asking why humans are not gods; since in these things we do not rightly accuse the maker himself of why the human species has [its nature]. Perhaps someone will blame nature, because man could have been something more excellent.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the universe is a single, coordinated organism governed by a "Great Commander" (Providence/Reason). He argues that individual differences and even "bad" actions are integrated into this cosmic order, much like soldiers in an army or different species in a biological system, each acting according to its specific nature.</summary>

# BOOK TWO

<column-break/>

A <note>original: "τί οὖν τὸ κρεῖττον" (ti oun to kreitton)</note> If someone judges that a person could achieve something better, they ought to blame the person themselves, not the Creator. But if they desire that something extra be added from the outside by the Maker, it is foolish to demand more than what has been given. It is just as if one were to demand something beyond the natural limits for other animals or plants. We should not ask whether one thing has less than another, but rather whether it possesses what is naturally necessary for it to function. Indeed, it was never intended that all things should be equal. Was there, then, an unequal distribution of things made by <term>Divine Reason</term><note>original: "λόγος" (Logos) / "ratione"</note> through some fitting choice? No, not all things ought to have been equal. Nor was it even B possible; rather, it was the nature of things to happen this way. For this Reason is the follower of another soul, and that soul is the follower of the Intellect. Now, the Intellect is not just one specific thing, but is all things. And because it is "all things," those things are many and diverse. Since they are many, they are not the same; it follows that some must be first in rank, others second, and others third in dignity. C Furthermore, the living beings that are created are not merely "souls," but are rather a sort of "fading away" or diminishment of souls as they proceed into thinner, more fragile forms. For although the "reason" of an animal is animated, it is said to be animated by a different soul, not by the primal one from which the Reason flows. Indeed, this Reason as a whole begins to diminish as it leans toward matter, and that which is born from it comes forth more imperfect. Consider, I pray you, how great a distance now D separates the created thing from its origin, and yet how wonderful it still remains! However, if the thing created is of a certain lowly quality, one should not think its predecessor was entirely like it. For every effect is necessarily more excellent than its cause is when viewed on its own; it is all the more wonderful that it produced something after itself, leaving such traces of its own power. If it provided more than the recipient could hold, that is all the more reason to approve of it. From this, it appears that all fault should be placed on the effects themselves, while the gift of Providence remains more than abundant.

<margin>
III
On the intellect and reason, where they are found, and on the souls of men. Why evil men do not always use reason, why the soul becomes worse, and why this is not the same in beasts.
</margin>

<margin>Where is evil?</margin>
E If man were "simple"—and by simple, I mean if he were only that which he was made to be at the beginning, acting and suffering only according to that nature—then beyond a doubt, every occasion for complaint would be far away, just as we find in other animals. But as it stands, blame finds a place only in the "evil man," and perhaps not without reason. For a human is not only what he was created to be; he possesses another <term>free principle</term><note>original: "ἀρχήν" (archēn) / "principium"</note>, though he does not wander outside the limits of universal Providence and Reason. F For those higher things do not depend on our lower actions; rather, the better things shine upon the worse, and that is the mark of perfect Providence. Now, one kind of Reason is "efficient" (the maker), while another joins the things being made to their better counterparts. The order of those higher things is a Providence acting from above; but there is another Providence from the higher one, connected to that Reason by a second Reason, so that from both a complete <term>interweaving</term><note>original: "πλέγμα" (plegma) / "contextus"</note> is formed—and this is the totality of Providence. Humans, therefore, possess another principle. G However, not all men use all the principles they possess. Instead, some use one principle, while others use another, or even use the worse ones. Yet those higher principles are still present even in those who do not act upon them; nor are the principles themselves sluggish or far from action within their own realm. It is just that the person does not act through them. Perhaps someone will ask how...

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus argues that inequality in nature is necessary for a diverse universe and that human "evil" arises because humans possess a free principle of action that they often fail to align with higher Reason.</summary>

### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD III

If these principles are present, why do they not act? Or is it perhaps that they are not truly present? Indeed, we generally admit they are present everywhere, and that nothing is left abandoned by them. But perhaps we should say they are not present in those things upon which they do not act. Why then do they not act upon all things, seeing as these too are parts of them? I am speaking here of such a principle <note>The "Logos" or Divine Reason.</note>. In other animals, this principle does not belong to them specifically; in humans, however, it is not present in all individuals either. Is it then that this principle is not in everyone? But why is it not in everyone? In those where it alone is present, life is lived according to it; but in others, life is lived according to other things, insofar as necessity compels them. 

Whether such a compulsion occurs because one is cast into a state of turbulence, or because desires overcome the person, it becomes necessary to trace the cause back to the subject itself. But first, it might seem that the cause is no longer found in <term>Reason</term><note>original Latin: "ratio"; Greek: "λόγος" (Logos) — the governing principle of order and intelligence.</note>, but rather in <term>Matter</term><note>original Latin: "materia"; Greek: "ὕλη" (Hyle) — the raw, unformed substance of the universe.</note>. Thus, not Reason, but Matter would dominate. However, the subject exists as it has been formed; or rather, the subject of the principle is Reason, and that which is made from Reason exists according to Reason. 

Therefore, it is not Matter that dominates while the formation simply follows. Rather, one might trace the cause of a person being a certain way back to a "previous life." If that Reason, formed from what came before, has become weak, it is because it is compared to a higher Reason. Indeed, since the soul has become weaker and then shines its light, that Reason itself must be said to contain within itself the "reason of matter" <note>This suggests that the higher principle accounts even for the limitations of the material world.</note>. It will work upon this matter according to its own nature, either molding the matter or reaching a concordant agreement with it. For the <term>Formative Seed</term><note>original: "ratio seminaria" / "λόγος" — the internal blueprint that directs the growth of an organism.</note> of an ox does not exist in any matter other than that of an ox. 

This is why, as he says, a soul may be destined for other animals. When a soul has become different and its internal Reason has turned into something else, the soul of what was once a human may become the soul of an ox. Therefore, by the judgment of Justice herself, such a soul is made worse. But why was the soul made worse from the beginning, and how did it go astray? It has been said many times: not all things are "primary," but those things that are second or third have a nature inferior to those above them. Likewise, even a tiny momentum of "inclination" <note>A leaning toward the material or lower world.</note> is enough to cause us to overstep what is right. Furthermore, the mixing of one thing with another is like a blend that creates a third thing from the two. That which was there is not diminished, but that which is "lesser" was made lesser from the beginning; and it exists as something that was made lesser according to its own nature. If it suffers any consequence, it suffers according to its worth. To all this, we must add that comparisons must be referred back to a "previous life," for subsequent things are drawn from what was done and conceived in that prior state.

<margin>
That there must be different grades of things; that providence distributes to individuals by geometric proportion and not by simple equality; that fate serves providence through free will.
</margin>

**PROVIDENCE** therefore proceeds from the beginning to the end, diffusing itself from above. It does not distribute in equal portions according to a simple count, but rather by a certain comparison of proportion, differently in different places. Just as in a single living animal, where all parts from the first to the last are rightly connected, every limb possesses its own specific duty: the better part has a more excellent action, while the worse part has an inferior action suited to it. They also undergo their own experiences, which are appropriate both to themselves and to the order directed toward the whole.

And indeed, when the soul is struck in a certain way by its own condition, the vocal parts speak out, while other parts suffer in silence, yet follow the movement. Out of all these sounds, sufferings, and actions, a single life emerges—a voice, a life, and a path of existence. Its parts have certain differences and possess different powers. For the feet do one thing, while the eyes do another; the intellect does one thing, and the <term>Mind</term><note>original Greek: "νοῦς" (Nous) — the highest level of reality in Neoplatonism, representing pure intuitive thought.</note> does another. Yet from all these comes one unified <term>Providence</term><note>original Greek: "πρόνοια" (Pronoia) — the divine foresight and care that orders the universe.</note>. <term>Fate</term><note>original Greek: "εἱμαρμένη" (Heimarmene).</note>, however, begins from the lower parts, for that which is above Providence is even greater. In the Intelligible World, all things are <term>Reason</term><note>original Greek: "λόγος" (Logos).</note> and beyond Reason; there, the soul is pure. What comes from that realm is Providence, and insofar as it remains in the pure soul or is distributed among living beings here, it is Reason. Just as in a single living creature, the parts are divided into unequal portions. The things that follow are the actions we see, following skillfully. These are dear to Providence, and this Reason is beloved of God—it is the Reason of Providence. For it gathers together even such works as these. Yet Providence is not the "maker" of human actions; rather, these actions are performed by men or by living beings in general, or by the life of the soul. Whether they are orderly or useful, these too fall under the whole of Providence, which uses all things to maintain mastery, or to rearrange and correct errors. It is like health being restored to a body through the providence of the organism. When an act of daring or a total mistake occurs, the governing Reason once again connects it, or brings in the "medical art" to correct the slip. Thus, evils follow by necessity. They arise either from us as causes, or because Providence uses them under compulsion. But evils do not come from the works of Providence itself <margin>3. themselves</margin>; rather, they are joined to the works of Providence. They are connected according to the will of Providence, or as they happened to occur, or because of the actions of some being, or according to something else in the universe. It is not that Providence itself performed the passion in us. For the same thing does not act the same way on everyone; rather, the same thing acts differently toward different people. For instance, the beauty of Helen <margin>bestows grace</margin> acted one way upon Paris; we see it worked upon him because he was unrestrained, and thus the unrestrained man fell in with the unrestrained beauty. But beauty acts differently upon a temperate man, and a temperate person acts differently toward an unrestrained one. What is done by the unrestrained man is not according to Providence, though it is used by Providence. But the work of the temperate man is according to Providence, for it is in harmony with Reason. It is like someone who performs a good deed through the art of medicine; he acts for the sake of health, even if the doctor originally gave the rules for both the healthy and the sick. The one who is the cause is not—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Now indeed, being struck by its own condition, those parts that are vocal resonate accordingly; others suffer in silence and are moved as a consequence. Therefore, from all these tones, passions, and actions, one vital spirit, as it were, and one life and act is produced. For the parts are diverse among themselves and have diverse actions. For the feet do one thing, the eyes another, thought another, and the intellect another. Yet one thing arises from all, and one Providence. But Fate takes its beginning from a certain lower point; however, that which is superior is Providence alone. <margin>B</margin> For all things that are in the Intelligible World are Reason and above Reason; namely, the Intellect and the pure soul. But what follows thereafter, insofar as it proceeds from there, is Providence; both insofar as it is in the pure soul and insofar as it is propagated from there into living beings. This Reason, distributed into unequal parts, goes forward; therefore it does not make all things equal, just as in any living animal. What follows from this are consequences and companions to Providence; these are the things that occur if one does what is acceptable to the gods, for the Reason of Providence is a friend to God. <margin>C</margin> Let works of this kind also be gathered together: they do not happen by Providence, but are acts already done either by men or by anything else, whether animate or inanimate. If what follows is for the best, they are encompassed by Providence itself, so that virtue may everywhere prevail; specifically, while those who had erred are transformed and their errors corrected. This is no different than health being applied to a single body through the providence that guards the living being. <margin>D</margin> Then, when a cut or a wound occurs, Reason, again dispensing each thing, eventually adapts and joins them together, and once the disease is removed, restores health. Hence it happens that evil deeds exist as a certain necessity of what follows; they are according to causes within us, not indeed compelled by Providence. Rather, they come from us while we adapt our own works to the works of Providence and are protected by Providence, but we are unable to connect what follows next according to the will of Providence. Instead, we attach it according to the will of those who <margin>E</margin> act, or according to some other thing among those in the universe; nor is it Providence itself acting or causing any passion in us. For not every approaching thing does the same thing to every other thing; but that which is the same does one thing to one and another to another. Just as the beauty of Helen toward Paris did one thing, but Idomeneus <note>A Greek hero of the Trojan War; his mention here in the Latin indicates a variant in the manuscript tradition not present in the Greek OCR above.</note> was affected differently. And the intemperate man toward the temperate man, or the beautiful approaching the beautiful, produces one effect. <margin>F</margin> But a temperate beautiful man toward a temperate beautiful man produces another; and he himself does something different toward an intemperate man, and the intemperate man in turn does something else toward him. Now, that which is done by the intemperate man proceeds neither from Providence nor according to Providence. But what is done by the temperate man is not indeed acted by Providence—since it is done by the man himself—yet it is acted according to Providence, for it is in agreement with the Reason of Providence. Just as when someone acts in a way that contributes to health, he himself acts, yet he acts according to the <margin>G</margin> reasoning of the doctor; for the doctor would have handed that down from his art, whether it pertains to the healthy or the unhealthy. <margin>
**VI**
How the consequences of order predict evils from good things. How present things are signs of future events.
</margin>

**A** Whence, then, do prophecies also announce baser things, and why do <term>Astrologers</term><note>In the ancient world, astrology was considered a technical science of reading cosmic patterns rather than just a superstition.</note> pronounce these alongside other predictions? Surely it is because all opposites are woven together as form and matter, just as in a composite living creature—which the <term>world</term><note>original Latin: "mundus"; Greek: "κόσμος" (kosmos).</note> also is. Therefore, he who contemplates its form and <term>reason</term><note>original Latin: "rationem"; Greek: "λόγον" (Logos) — the ordering principle of the universe.</note> also contemplates the thing that has been formed. For he does not merely look upon an <term>intelligible animal</term><note>A "Living Being" existing in the realm of pure thought/forms.</note> in a limited way, nor just a composite animal, but rather the Reason of the living creature which, within the composite, gives shape to even the baser parts.

**B** Since, therefore, this entire universe is a single **living creature**, he who sees what happens within it also sees the elements from which they arise. He sees the Providence reigning within it, which proceeds in an orderly fashion through all things that are and all things that come to be. These things are also living beings, whose actions and sufferings are both mastered by Reason and permitted to <term>Necessity</term><note>original Latin: "necessitati"; Greek: "ἀνάγκῃ" (ananke). Plotinus suggests the world is a mix of divine plan and the "stubbornness" of material necessity.</note>; thus, he contemplates many things, including those that are continually permitted to happen.

**C** And yet, a man cannot by himself discern Providence apart from that which follows Providence, nor can he distinguish what the subject provides from itself versus what occurs within it. Indeed, one might say that to do such a thing is not the task of a man, nor even of a wise or divine person, but rather the gift of God alone. For the purpose of **prophecy** is not to know the *cause* of why something happens, but only to declare that it *will be so*.

**D** The art of foretelling is a kind of reading of <insert>natural letters</insert> which indicate an order that never deviates into the disordered. This is especially revealed by the movement [of the heavens] which announces and brings things to light even before it is apparent in the things themselves what they are or how much they might suffer. For these things concur with those, and those with these in turn, contributing together to the constitution and eternity of the world.

**E** And according to a certain **analogy**—that is, a comparison of proportion—other signs carefully observe these things, since other forms of divination are also made possible by a certain analogy. For it was not necessary for all things to depend on each other in turn, but they ought to have been made like one another in some way. And this is perhaps what is meant by the saying that **"all things are held together by analogy."**

**F** Such an analogy is as follows: just as the better relates to the better, so in turn the worse relates to the worse; as an eye is compared to an eye, so a foot is compared to a foot, one corresponding to the other. Likewise, if you please, as virtue is to justice, so vice is to injustice. If, therefore, analogy reigns in the universe, it is surely possible to prophesy. And if those things act upon these, they act in the way that parts in any living creature operate upon one another—not because one generates the other (for they are born together), but because each is endowed with its own nature, and thus suffers in a way that is consistent with its own properties. And because this thing is of such a kind, and that thing is similar, for so the Reason is also **one**.

<margin>
**VII**
That in the Providence of God, the artistic and natural action is the same which governs the world as it governs plants.
</margin>

**G** FURTHERMORE, because there are better things in the world, there are therefore also baser things. How can there be something worse in a multiform work unless there is also something better? Or in turn, how can there be something better unless there is also something worse?

**WHENCE** then do prophecies announce baser things? And looking toward the movement of the whole, as with other prophecies, how are these things said? It is clear that all opposites are woven together: such as form and matter, since it is a composite living being. When one contemplates the form and the <term>Reason</term><note>original Greek: "λόγον" (Logos).</note>, he also contemplates that which has been formed. **B** ...the Reason forming the baser things in the composite animal. This Providence has traveled through all things that come to be; these are living things, whose actions and sufferings are mixed with Reason and mixed with Necessity. He contemplates these mixed things.

**C** And though they are mixed, they are also distinct. One might distinguish the bodies, the Providence, or that which follows Providence, or the things given to the <term>substrate</term><note>The underlying material or subject.</note> by itself. **D** Or rather, someone might say that the task of the oracle is to persuade; for the prophetic art does not tell the "why," but only tells the "that." And the art is a reading of **natural letters** which reveal order. They are hung together toward that which is not disordered; rather, the movement bears witness and brings things to light even before these or those things appear.

**E** Concerning each thing, as many as are brought together, for these are woven with those and those with these, weaving together at the same time toward the constitution and eternity of the cosmos. Other things signify by **analogy** to the observer. Since other prophetic arts also know by this analogy that all things are hung from one another, it is impossible but that they are made like one another. And this perhaps would be what is said: that **analogy holds all things together.**

**F** Analogy is something like this: as the worse is to the worse, so the better is to the better. For example, as eye to eye, and foot to foot... <note>The Greek text here has some garbled characters: "ζητήτραν πρὸς ζήτραν".</note> and if you wish, as virtue to justice, and vice to injustice. If then there is analogy in the whole, then it is in everything; and if those things act upon these, they act so as parts in a whole living being. It is not as if one thing becomes another, for they come to be at the same time; but as each is born, so it also suffers what is appropriate to its own nature. And because this is such, and that is such, the Reason is **one**.

**G** AND since there are better things, there are worse things; since how could there be the worse in a multiform thing if the better were not there? Or how the better, without the worse?

...so that we should not blame the worse for being in the better, but rather accept the better, seeing that it gave of itself to the worse. In general, those who think the worse should be removed from the whole are actually removing **Providence** itself. For of what would it be the providence? The <margin>Not even into...</margin> Principle, then, is that into which all things are gathered, in which all things are at once, and all things are the whole. Altogether, whoever thinks the worse should be removed from the world, they also remove Providence itself. For of what else will there be providence? Not of itself, nor even of the better: since when we name heavenly Providence, we refer it to that which is lower. For that into which all things are reduced is the Principle, in which all <margin>B</margin> things are together, and all things are the whole. Now, all things proceed from this, while it remains within, as if from a single root resting in itself; they sprout into a very great divided multitude, each preferring the likeness of that principle: but here, one thing is made in another. And some things are indeed near the root, while others, proceeding further, are divided even as far as the branches, and the twigs, and the fruits, and the leaves: and some things always remain, while others, the fruits and leaves, are always being made. <margin>C</margin> And those which are always being made always possess the reasons of the higher things in themselves, as if they wished to be certain tiny shrubs. And if they were to generate before they decayed, they would only generate what is near them: but those empty spaces of the branches are filled again by the root itself, and are naturally held otherwise: from which the extremities of the branches suffer, so much so that the suffering seems to happen only from what is nearby. But that which is according to the principle, this part suffers, while <margin>D</margin> this part acts. The Principle is also itself connected: for things proceeding far off now act among themselves upon each other: but from the principle they come from the same source: just as if brothers should act upon one another, being made similar, as they were born from the same parents.

# MARSILIO FICINO’S COMMENTARY ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, ON DAEMONS.

## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->Summary of the book, likewise on daemons, and on one's own personal daemon.<-

The SUMMARY of this book concerning each person’s own <term>daemon</term><note>In Neoplatonism, a "daemon" is not an evil spirit, but a guiding spirit or a level of the soul that acts as a guardian and intermediary between the human and the divine.</note> is more "daemonic" than divine in this way. Since the **Soul** is all things, and naturally possesses free motion, it can certainly form itself within itself into the likenesses of all things, and consequently shape for itself the bodies of animals and plants. If, therefore, it has lived in the manner of a plant, after this life it forms the body of a plant, in which only the vegetative power acts: but the <term>Sense</term><note>The faculty of perception.</note> presides over such a life like a daemon, not as an actor, but as a constant observer. Similarly, if the soul living as a beast finally becomes a beast, exercising sense with only the vegetative power, the rational power hangs over it idle, like some observing daemon. But he who lives by **Reason** along with sense, has the **Mind** assisting him in the manner of a daemon: finally, he who lives by the Mind seems to have **God** as his presiding daemon. In this matter, Plotinus has partially followed the *Timaeus* [of Plato], which says that the more excellent power of the soul is the leader and daemon of man. He also followed the *Pythagorean Verses*, which pray to God to show us what kind of Daemon we should use: they then declare that within each person there is a certain divinity of their own nature, a "pious daemon," which can reveal hidden things to us. Hence Plotinus and Iamblichus, following the opinion of the Egyptians, place his own **Intellect** over each person, like a daemon always observing all things for the sake of Reason. Plotinus was led to compose this book, as <term>Porphyry</term><note>Plotinus's student and biographer.</note> relates, by the magical works of an Egyptian priest, who promised to show each person's own daemon to their eyes; and he showed to Plotinus, in the presence of many, not a daemon of Plotinus, but a God: because Plotinus [lived] not so much by reason...

...than <term>Intelligence</term><note>Latin: *intelligentia*; here referring to the highest intuitive faculty of the mind rather than just "cleverness."</note> would see, striving indeed through direct insight rather than step-by-step reasoning, and not merely cutting away disturbances, but uprooting them entirely. For this reason, in this book he not only teaches what kind of <term>daemon</term><note>Latin: *daemon*; in the Platonic sense, this is a guardian spirit or guiding genius, not an evil "demon."</note> belongs to each person, but also exhorts us toward God so that we may obtain such a daemon—this is the summary of the book thus far. 

Indeed, Plato and all the Platonists frequently declare that, besides the parts of the soul, there are furthermore external daemons, both in great numbers and as leaders of men. Plotinus himself says this elsewhere, and most notably in his book *On Love*. In this book, however, he chiefly introduces daemons who are parts of the soul, because this had not yet been discussed by others, and because we possess different levels of external daemons according to these internal degrees. 

For where life is arranged according to the <term>imagination</term>, our external daemon is "airy," dwelling in the lowest part of the air and acting upon us through our imagination by means of its own. But where one lives according to <term>reason</term>, a daemon from the middle air directs human reason with its own reason. Finally, where life is <term>intellectual</term>, a daemon from the highest air breathes into our intelligence through its own intelligence; and they do this not so much by choice as by the very way of nature. For even in us, the contemplation of intellectual light naturally moves the imagination toward imagining sensible light, and the imagination in sleep moves the senses, and in waking it frequently moves the emotions by way of nature. Conversely, passion moves the sense, sense moves the imagination, and this naturally moves the reason. Similarly, daemons continually strike our powers with their own; but a more excellent order of daemons acts in a much more hidden and tranquil way, constantly recalling us to the intellect. Such was the daemon that seems to have led Plotinus, and therefore it was called a "God," just like the daemon of <term>Socrates</term><note>Referring to the *daimonion*, the "divine sign" or inner voice that Socrates claimed warned him against certain actions.</note>. For the most excellent daemons are usually called by the name of Gods, just as the lowest are sometimes designated by the name of "spirits."

We have asserted enough in our *Theology* that there are daemons in the air, and that everywhere there are animals endowed with reason—and more so in the air than on the earth. These are as much more excellent and larger as the globe of the air itself is vaster and more excellent than the earth, and especially more akin to the rational life. For that which lives most preeminently in us and obeys our thought is an "airy spirit." Therefore, vast and rational animals dwell in the air, possessing a round shape, just as the shape of the air requires. Their sense is whole throughout their entire body and is most acute according to the nature of the air; their movement is likewise most swift, and the order of their motion is almost like that of the stars. 

Daemons, therefore, are the "stars of the airy heaven," imitating the circuits of the celestial stars according to their powers: proceeding and receding from east to west and back again at appointed times, turning now toward the north, now toward the south, sometimes ascending as if to a peak, and then descending again in a certain order—especially those daemons above the turbulent air. Nor do they act upon us merely by choice, as we said, but mostly by their very nature, like stars, and by their rays, which are hidden yet extremely effective. A <term>Magus</term><note>A practitioner of "natural magic," which in the Renaissance meant someone who understood the hidden medicinal and spiritual properties of nature and the stars.</note> who knows how to gather these rays will be able to see them and show them to others. For just as the sun’s rays, which are not at all discernible by themselves after sunset, are sometimes gathered by certain vapors and are immediately seen in the form of redness or paleness; and just as flames lit far away in the mud at midday are not seen by us, but appear when wood is added, so it seems the Egyptian priest gathered the rays of Plotinus's daemon and (as <term>Porphyry</term><note>Porphyry was Plotinus’s student and biographer; he records this event in *The Life of Plotinus*.</note> testifies) showed its presence to his eyes. Whether he obtained this through the favor of the daemons he worshipped, or whether he poured into the air a certain vapor akin to the daemons, by which the gathered rays of the daemon became visible in a certain way. 

But by what form did the Magus conclude that Plotinus's daemon was supreme? Because, evidently, it did not come with a distorted glow like a rainbow, as the lowest daemons in the thick air usually do; nor with paleness or redness, as the middle ones sometimes do; but with a light entirely pure and most clear, which is the property only of the ethereal and celestial daemons. But if Plotinus’s daemon is the highest, how does it lead him so familiarly? How does that Magus reach its rays? Although a Magus can also act from a distance by the casting of subtle sensory rays and by something like meaningful words, and by this striking, see the innermost spirit of a man, and as if by speaking powerfully, signify and affect something. 

Remember, however, that chains are extended everywhere from the highest to the lowest things. Thus, from each star, certain orders of daemons follow as attendants of the stars in specific ways of duty; and similarly, souls follow their own daemons everywhere. There are, therefore, many in any given sphere, both below the moon and above the moon: <term>Saturnian daemons</term><note>Spirits associated with the planet Saturn, often linked to contemplation and melancholy.</note> under Saturn, <term>Jovian daemons</term> under Jupiter, and others likewise. And among the Saturnians, some are more excellent than others even in the same sphere, and similarly among the Jovians—just as usually happens among men. Therefore, the most excellent daemon among the airy ones leads Plotinus and Socrates, being itself led by a most excellent one among the ethereal daemons, which in turn is led by one of the best among the celestial daemons. Thus, Socrates and Plotinus are found to be connected in a continuous series from the highest. 

But is each person moved by only one in the same sphere? Perhaps not by one alone. For although any daemon may fill a very wide region and, even if it does not change its place, can observe a wandering man in many places and reach him everywhere with its rays like a star, yet it is not probable—when someone journeys from the east to the western region—that a daemon, being far superior in nature, would follow the footsteps of a traveling man like a devoted tutor. What then? Either there is a single daemon that is everywhere, according to <term>Iamblichus</term><note>A later Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized theurgy (ritual magic).</note>, and thus it is not forced to change its place; or, if it is not everywhere at once, it is not just one daemon (one in number), but one in kind that presides over each person. 

Thus, "solar" daemons preside over a "solar" man; wherever he goes, he specifically comes into the domain of solar daemons. I say he himself, and every solar person; and similarly, "Venereal" [of Venus] daemons everywhere influence Venereal people. Yet there are certain differences among solar daemons: just as all the gifts of the sun, which the one sun possesses, are distributed separately among many solar daemons. Many people affected by the sun are also similar among themselves; so much so that even a common man, though he finds his own leaders (that is, common daemons) wherever he goes, finds them less suited in one place and more suited in another. However, he finds the most perfectly suited one, who is unique, in a specific region. 

From this it follows that one person is more fortunate in one place, and similarly in a different kind of work: specifically where his daemon is more powerful and more effective than others. It follows, moreover, that those who are singularly born for a certain task—even many who are under-aged, without teachers or assistants—think out and perform wonderful things by the instinct of their daemons. Then indeed, beyond their own hope and the opinion of others, they happen upon the right times, regions, persons, materials, instruments, and resources. When these are properly supplied, they naturally fulfill the work destined for them. The cause of these various overlapping influences is not natural but "daemonic," connecting them toward a single outcome and directing each thing toward a goal foreknown to itself. Meanwhile, the daemon serves and assists the Heavens—serving, I say, by always providing the means to an end foreknown to the celestial intelligence, and furthermore supplying its own efficacy to carry out that which the celestial motion often does not do, but merely signifies. Hence, sometimes an astrologer will foretell from a certain arrangement of the heavens, as if from a sign, which specific daemon, suited to such an arrangement, acts...

He also addresses the controversial topic of the transmigration of souls.</meta>

<header>ON BOOK IV. ENNEAD III.</header>

*...and the use it can have in us, and in whatever way we can, we effect it. It is clear that after that celestial vision escaped from its own evils, even if it does not return to the same state: from which it appears that it represented our affairs rather than sacred ones. But let us now proceed to the words of Plotinus.*

### How intellect produces soul, soul produces nature, and nature produces matter.

<margin>I</margin> All bodies are always doing something; and by acting outwardly, they soon emit nothing—at least the simple bodies emit things without an inward mutation of themselves. For since each one exists with its whole power in its parts, and they have nothing foreign within them, they deservedly breathe out no substance. In this way, fire provides heat and light without being diminished; similarly, water generates cold and its own quality by flowing, yet its substance is not stolen away. On the contrary, vapors are sent out with some detriment to the substance. Much more do <term>intellect</term><note>Latin: *intellectus*; the highest realm of divine thought in Neoplatonism.</note> and <term>soul</term><note>Latin: *anima*; the mediating force between the divine intellect and the physical world.</note> always propagate something from themselves: intellect produces the soul, and the soul produces the sensual and <term>vegetative life</term><note>The lowest level of the soul's functions, responsible for growth and basic biological life.</note>, which we can call <term>nature</term>. 

But the intellect, after the manner of a simple body, provides the soul without being changed; the soul, however, like a composite body, produces nature while being changed. All things—intellect, soul, and nature—first generate substance, and then quality within that substance. For it is characteristic of a more excellent agent to first generate a substance, and then, as if by looking back at the creator, to affect it with living modes. But in what way does the soul, being moved, produce nature? Certainly not moved by a step-by-step reasoning process. For its offspring would not be its own by some accidental power; rather, through an internal "otherness" reigning within itself, the soul descends from its intellectual power into a sensual and natural faculty far different from the intellect. 

Just as in a composite body the vapor itself, blowing toward the circumference, spreads itself with a certain alteration that does not harm the substance; yet vapor flying further outward seems to represent that passion of the soul with some detriment to the substance. This sometimes promotes the vegetative power beyond itself, beyond the <term>spirit-body</term><note>Latin: *spiritus corpus*; a subtle, "airy" body believed to bridge the gap between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note> most naturally familiar to it, toward composite bodies. For then it is not merely "moved" in a way, but truly changed—that is, it approaches the work of the lowest generation with a certain loss of its own dignity. And just as it has changed within itself, it co-creates such a body from matter for itself, according to its strength. 

Remember among these things that the <term>World Soul</term><note>Latin: *mundi anima*; the soul of the entire universe.</note> itself, if compared with the divine Mind, generates while being moved in a certain way; however, as we have explained, if it is compared with our soul, it completes its generation without being changed—that is, it is in no way distracted from its principal actions. Where it is said that matter is procreated by nature, understand this as being done by the "universal nature" that accompanies the World Soul. Even the intellectual soul (as Plotinus intends) seems likely to procreate matter if it does not find matter already created. He here calls "matter" the lowest part of the universe, the subject for nature itself, which is the last of the divine things; nature fashions bodies out of this utterly undefined matter, applying forms from above. Just as nature, soul, and mind were themselves in a way undefined before they reached their proper form, yet they were never *completely* undefined, because their nature requires them to be referred back to the most absolute Height.

### On the transmigration of the soul: and that it does not pass into beasts.

<margin>II</margin> What Plotinus himself once thought about the <term>transmigration of the soul</term><note>The belief that a soul can be reborn into a new body after death (reincarnation).</note>—unless perhaps he is being poetic like Plato—his writings declare to those who read them. We, however, wish that he (as most philosophers are accustomed to do after more diligent meditation) had changed his opinion in this way, which he seems to have adopted not so much by the necessity of reason as by the custom of the people and the ages. 

Even if a human soul is changed in some way within itself, it is never transformed beyond the certain limits of the **human species**, which also seems to have pleased Iamblichus. He says that the soul preserves its own species in any transformation, since the beginning of its motion comes from itself and is acted out within itself. Where it is said to be "all things," it must be understood that it is all things not in just any way, but in its own way—that is, in the way proper to its own species. Therefore, none shall say: "If the soul is all things by natural power, therefore it sometimes becomes all things." For the soul itself never becomes a bodily form or a body, because the soul is not that kind of form, but exists properly according to its own mode of life. 

Thus, it does not become a beast, since the soul is not simply an "animal," but specifically a **human** one. Furthermore, since we see certain effects arise not from just any causes, but from specific ones—hot things from heat, living things from the living, a lion from a lion—we see that specific species of things do not procreate just any effect, but their own. Surely, we ought not to hope that from the reproductive nature of humans (which is a certain and fixed human species) something else can ever be made, unless perhaps nature itself changes the species, as if a human could sometimes become an ox, which is impossible. Since it is said to be self-moving and eternal, it is never transformed by another, nor would it desert its own species, since all things always strive to preserve themselves. 

Now, from this very fact that the human reproductive nature cannot be bovine, it follows that a human does not come from an ox, nor does an ox procreate a human. For one nature is further distant from another nature than the effects of this nature are from that. In general, other species of things are not accustomed to degenerate into others unless they both lose their internal qualities and take on external ones, coming into a mixture until they gradually cease to be what they were. The Platonists would not concede that this happens to our soul. They would concede, however, that the reproductive property of a human differs in species from the reproductive property of brutes, just as the human species differs from the wild. 

Added to this is that since the soul is said to become "such and such" in Plato through its own choices and actions, if those actions are its own, they are human; therefore, it will not pass beyond the human species. Furthermore, it is vain to say that a soul stained by wicked actions turns into a beast deprived of reason, since such a soul would use no reason at all. For the sharpness of reason does not lie entirely idle in the wicked; rather, it is busily occupied, although it is mostly divided between objects of the senses and the imagination, either to obtain them or avoid them. What is the cause that the wicked often seem sharper and more effective in their works than the good, if not the sharpness and effect of the rational power? Therefore, if a wicked soul must be transferred again into an earthly body after this life, it will return not into a brute, but into a human, with the skill of reason similarly being abused. For the necessity of similarity seems to bring this about. 

For Plotinus himself clearly confesses that man acts not according to one power alone, but according to all the powers of the soul. It will be purged eventually; for by the dispensation of providence, it will eventually fall into such calamities on account of its crimes that it will repent of a life lived basely, while in the meantime being exhorted by a common discipline and a daemon. Finally, no voluptuous man will ever become a plant destitute of senses. As if a voluptuous man neglects the actions of the senses, and in this way becomes a tree robbed of senses! On the contrary, no one uses the senses more than the intemperate man.

Ficino is reconciling the views of Plotinus, Timaeus of Locri, and other Platonists with a more psychological and allegorical interpretation of souls entering animal bodies.</meta>

<page-num>280</page-num>
->COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO<-

If, therefore, the soul is to be turned back again toward earthly bodies, it will return not into a plant but into a human being, whom the violent command of his own senses so agitates, vexes, tortures, and destroys, that at last he becomes weary of a life of pleasure—all while the laws and the <term>divine powers</term><note>Latin: *numinibus*; referring to the guiding spiritual forces or gods in the Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note> call him back to a better life. I pass over the fact that a multitude of the wicked are sent here and there by God, so that those who have committed crimes through perverse pleasure may eventually be punished with cares and sorrows. But he who walks purely and admits every act of reason, who accepts the warnings of care and removes the innumerable things that take away his senses, also takes away the pains associated with those senses. Remember that souls are purged not only in earthly bodies, but also in <term>aerial bodies</term><note>Latin: *aereis corporibus*; in Neoplatonic thought, the "aerial body" is a subtle, invisible envelope that the soul inhabits between its earthly incarnations.</note>: a form of punishment we have explained more clearly in our *Theology*. Furthermore, do not let it disturb you when Plato says that "every soul has care for all that is inanimate"; for it does not follow from this that any soul can be inserted into any body whatsoever—something Plato himself would deny is possible. Indeed, if the rational soul not only rules and moves the earthly body, but also the aerial and celestial ones; if it sometimes lives in the seats poured from above; if it performs various duties similar to the providence of the celestial beings; then it truly seems to have care for the whole of the inanimate world, and puts on various forms within itself without changing its own nature, but rather claiming the likenesses of others for itself, provided its essence remains eternal.

Rightly, therefore, **Timaeus of Locri**<note>A Pythagorean philosopher and character in Plato’s dialogues, to whom a treatise on the soul of the world was attributed in the Renaissance.</note> denies that human souls pass over into beasts; he even denies that they migrate immediately from one human into another. Rather, he thinks they live in the meantime in aerial bodies and are thus purged by the vexation of the mind. He says that sensible tortures—whether they occur in a living body or through water or fire—are "fables" invented to terrify those who cannot be led to virtue by persuasion. Indeed, people affected in this way do not understand spiritual punishments, namely the grief of a soul recognizing it has been deprived of the **Highest Good**, and the narrowness of anxiety which is the very repentance of the soul, by which the sins of this life are paid for even in the aerial body. Timaeus himself would not deny that these punishments are reserved for sinners.

For he thinks that our souls are distinct from one another and immortal. He is a Pythagorean, after all, and highly esteemed by Plato. He even says that God fashioned our soul from the same powers and reasons as the **World Soul**, and sent some down from some stars and others from others to below the moon; again, that the supreme nature of the soul consists of "Identity." It is necessary, therefore, to say according to Timaeus's opinion that the human soul—which by sinning against reason has now fallen into a perverse and more vehement imagination—is tortured immediately after death in the aerial body (which it even now possesses) by that very same perversity and vehemence of thought among the lowest <term>daemons</term><note>Latin: *dæmones*; not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits that can be helpful or punitive.</note> who subject it to similar goads, until, recognizing the cause of such great distress was its own aversion from the **Intellect**, it gradually returns to it. This it can perceive more clearly then, having stripped away a few distractions, than it can now; and so it is raised step by step into a more sublime order of daemons, and finally to the stars themselves along with the celestial body it has possessed from the beginning—each soul to that star or order which it was allotted at the start, or to which it made itself similar by its way of living. Yet everywhere it preserves its human character. For the human being is terrestrial, aerial, and celestial; he is, moreover, solar and Martian. Everywhere, however, "Man" is the rational soul itself, vivifying a body in a certain way: in heaven a celestial body only; in the air an aerial one through the celestial; on earth a terrestrial one through both. At last, however, after certain ages—through a certain relaxation of contemplation and an intention toward generation—Timaeus perhaps thought the soul would subsequently slip back through those same grades of aerial daemons and humans, and finally settle into a terrestrial human. But he did not think this soul—a sibling of the World Soul and a companion to celestial things—would be cast headlong into beasts after a human's death, nor immediately into another equally terrestrial human. For it is more opportunely purged in an aerial body, and more aptly recalled to higher things; but it always returns to a body and a habit of life most similar to itself, whether it revolves among us or above us, until it returns entirely to the same state. For it proceeds from any state to whichever is next. In the meantime, however, it "sleeps" on earth and cannot easily be released; but above the earth it "awakens" and notices its former state, so that through all ages the "person" of the rational mind remains the same.

This is what I conjecture Timaeus perhaps felt, which seems to me more probable among the opinions of the Platonists.

In the second place, however, I would approve of those Platonic views I mentioned earlier: namely, that the human soul is more rightly transmitted from an earthly human into an earthly human than into a beast. Some report that this finally pleased **Porphyry**; although from this opinion it is likely that between terrestrial lives, it also spends a life in aerial bodies. **Proclus**, moreover, along with the common school of Platonists, denies that an intellectual soul can be so fitted to a wild animal's body—which is quite foreign to it—that it could communicate anything to it in life. They think, however, that it "communicates" with brutes sometimes through a certain similarity of life, and that this is what Plato meant. I pass over for now whether, from this very opinion, it should be said that a soul made similar to brutes dwells among them for a time for the sake of punishment, and perhaps is so inserted into the imagination or the imaginations of such beasts—just as many report that lower daemons entering human bodies insert themselves into our imaginations and move them. This is almost like how the Intellect of the Author is said to be infused into souls, or however the matter stands. For where the prophet **Daniel** relates that the **King of Babylon**, on account of his most grave crimes, was "transferred among the oxen" until he recovered his senses through purgation, the **Hebrews** interpret this to mean that the King was overcome by a perverse imagination, to the point that he believed himself to have become an ox, and grieved heavily; just as a magician is accustomed to create <unclear>bewitchments</unclear>. What if the transition of souls in Plato is also like this? It is like this in Timaeus as well, whose opinion I was explaining just now with some ambiguity. For he even seems to have denied any return of souls into a terrestrial body, unless perhaps it be the final return; but that various sins could be variously purged through the affliction of the spirit, provoked by daemons who act as examiners under the judgment of **Nemesis**. Finally, Plato himself warned us not to rashly join any soul to any body when he said in the *Phaedrus* that a soul which is of the form proper to a brute, and which has never glimpsed divine things, cannot enter into a human being. It is as if he meant that the soul of a human cannot descend into the very form of a brute, although it might perhaps descend into a certain similarity and commerce with it.

Since we have frequently made mention of the souls of brutes, it is appropriately asked: if all life is immortal and does not accept its opposite, but flees death (as **Numenius** and **Plotinus** believe); and if, again, the souls of moving animals are both immortal and in some way rational (as **Porphyry** and almost **Iamblichus** want); then what should be said of them? We shall say perhaps according to their opinion, or we shall imagine: that the souls of beasts possessing imagination, and therefore possessing their own motion, subsist in themselves separate from the body and have a certain number from the beginning; and each one is inserted from body to body within its own species, but never confuses species; and in the meantime, until they obtain a more opportune solid body of their own species, they live in their own aerial body. For each has its own...

He emphasizes the psychological nature of spiritual purgation and the soul's eventual ascent back to the stars.</summary>
