<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's *Enneads*, specifically focusing on the relationship between the human soul, the World Soul, and the guiding spirits known as daemons. It bridges the discussion of the soul's descent into lower forms of life with the mechanism by which it is assigned a spiritual protector based on its character and astrological influences.</meta>

<page-num>281</page-num>

<header>ON BOOK IV. ENNEAD III.</header>

He himself also takes up a <term>spirit</term><note>Latin: *spiritum*; referring to the "astral body" or *pneuma*, a subtle vehicle that mediates between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</note>, in which Porphyry believes it obtains a certain gift of art and prophecy by the office of the <term>daemons</term><note>In Neoplatonism, *daemons* are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or guardian angels that guide a soul.</note> to whom they are dedicated. However, he considers the souls that lack their own motion and are devoid of imagination—namely, the vivifying forces of sea creatures and plants—to be certain "enlivening influences" from the <term>World Soul</term><note>Latin: *anima mundi*; the spirit that Neoplatonists believed animated the entire universe as a single living being.</note> rather than individual souls. This is similar to what happens in the hair of animals through the soul of the whole organism; these influences are eventually dissolved back into the life of the world. But where Plato calls souls lower than our own "mortal," those authors I just mentioned explain that they are not mortal in the sense that they perish, but because they depend entirely on something else and seem to have such a great affection and drive toward mortal things. 

After this, where he says that the soul is a "universal" that is both <term>intelligible</term><note>Meaning it belongs to the realm of pure thought and divine ideas.</note> and <term>sensible</term><note>Meaning it belongs to the realm of physical perception.</note>, and that it always acts through the intellect in the eternal intelligible world by a certain intuition of the <term>Ideas</term><note>The divine archetypes or blueprints of all things.</note>, such a great divinity of the soul seems to clash with the idea that it could be confined within a brute animal or a plant. Nevertheless, he tempers this statement somewhat, saying he does not mean that the animal or tree grows from the substance of the soul itself, but from a certain "influx" of it and a specific body. Meanwhile, the intellect does not cease from its own proper work, even though the rational act, habit, and faculty may cease—a point we do not easily admit. For the rational faculty itself is most proper to our soul; therefore, being most natural, it remains in the highest degree. 

Finally, he observes that the <term>generative nature</term><note>Latin: *naturam genitalem*; the power of the soul responsible for biological life and reproduction.</note> is a certain boundary of intelligence: so that what is intellectual at its highest peak is generative at its lowest. Just as what is light at the top is heat at the bottom, and as a visual ray flashes out from a certain axis, so is the generative power in its own sphere. And just as such a visual ray does not depend on anything external at all, but only on the eye—and thus is not extinguished when it does not shine outward, but merely ceases to act externally—so too the generative nature behaves. From the intellectual substance, it shines both within and without. It remains in that intellectual substance without shining outward when the whole mind is turned to the opposite direction, just as the visual ray is retracted rather than extinguished when the eye is turned away.

->Our soul rules the body and feels through attention; the world soul does so without attention.<-

III *Proclus indeed says that the soul, through its own being which is "living" and is everlasting, always vivifies the body, at least in a manner similar to the celestial soul's cognition. Plotinus, however, thinks that the soul will eventually cease even from this activity, which he declares both here and often elsewhere. He believes this happens finally when the rational power itself, along with the imagination, is turned entirely toward pure intelligence. For often, too much intensity in speculation weakens the effect of the generative nature in us, and vice versa. This does not happen to the World Soul, since its power is naturally broader and much more effective; its body is entirely obedient and placed in a safe state. This happens as easily from the living life of the soul as air is ignited by the presence of fire. 

Indeed, it seems to belong to the providence of fate to eventually compensate the soul for those evils by giving rest to a soul that has long been exhausted among us. This will be granted to Plotinus, provided that he also concedes this: a soul that can be raised so far above matter, and can now step beyond the heavens and the duty of the celestial soul, is never confined to a brute or a tree. But since in the World Soul there is no "attention" directed toward the body, is there any sense-perception there? Certainly there is, but it perceives nothing external. For the things it senses are within itself, and it is not distracted by sensing them. For sense-perception there is unique and intimate, and it does not "perceive that it perceives." For nothing foreign happens to it, nothing new. It is entirely necessary, however, that the body—which is most closely joined and related to the soul—be sensed by the soul. But just as it nourishes its body, it senses its body without having a conscious "noticing" attached to this action.*

->How various souls are allotted various daemons, how they change them, and how they come into generation with them.<-

IIII *In the following chapter, he says the mind and soul are allotted such or such a daemon because of a certain choice and change of the soul. I do not mean because of individual choices, but a "type" of choice directing it toward a certain "type" of life. Nor does the daemon change as long as the soul does not change its type of life entirely. Therefore, as long as it leads a "Venereal" <note>Related to the planet Venus; characterized by love, beauty, or pleasure.</note> life, it holds a Venereal daemon. Even if it occasionally abstains from wanton loves, as long as it is easily inclined to love, even if honorably, it does not change the type of its daemon; for it still has a Venereal one, but of a more excellent rank among the Venereal spirits. Similarly, if one moves from commerce to literature, he keeps a "Mercurial" daemon, though a wiser one. If he moves from religion to military service, he changes his daemonic genus and rank. For he passes from a "Jovial" <note>Related to the planet Jupiter; associated with law, religion, and authority.</note> daemon into a "Martial" <note>Related to the planet Mars; associated with war and conflict.</note> one, from which the soul then first emerges as unfortunate. 

Conversely, if he comes from military service to religion, he passes from the Martial to the Jovial, unless he continues to be dissatisfied with his state, in which case he is not particularly fortunate. Most people, however much they may seem to change their mode of life while in this body, nevertheless preserve something of their ancient condition; therefore, they have not yet entirely cast off their old daemon. Accordingly, it appears through what follows that the first affection of the soul—whether natural or chosen—greatly affects the body. Thus, a bad soul eventually brings back bad things, and a good soul good things, from whatever body it is given, and similarly reflects this in its fortune. 

For this reason, the daemon is not changed, nor does it differ because of differences in bodies or fortunes, as long as the movement of the soul itself preserves its ancient "type." When this is changed to the complete opposite, the daemon is also changed, and with the daemon, in truth, so is fortune; for the daemon himself arranges fortune for us. Finally, the "author of life" depends on the quality of the soul: since, according to the difference in the soul's quality, it animates such a daemon, and we cast them off, and fortunes are mostly dispensed through daemons. 

If Porphyry says this is according to the star ruling in the birth chart, or Iamblichus says different daemons are distributed to souls according to the whole harmony of the world then reigning, understand that the celestial motion and aspect are not so much the "cause" of such a distribution as they are the "sign." For the souls of men and daemons, just as they are by nature "before" celestial motions, so they are already such in themselves before those motions. Therefore, Timaeus says that souls first chose their lots and forms of life through their own affections—where I think the daemons were then accepted—and then they reached the fatal motions, reaching them through their "vehicles," namely their celestial bodies, which are contiguous with celestial influxes and motions. 

Think, therefore, of the "Celestial Lyre" which, as <term>Phoebus</term><note>Apollo, the god of music and the sun.</note> strikes it, produces various harmonies for the various hours. All souls, however, are in concord with the Phoebean soul, so that such as they already are in themselves, they are moved by these harmonies rather than those, and some come to dance in one choir and others in another. Thus, from such a state, the soul is allotted a daemon with whom it will act in the choir and how it will dance: where most of this proceeds from the soul, though no small part also happens from the condition of the celestial harmony. In this whole dispute, remember that neither the condition of our affairs nor the order of Platonic words can be rightly maintained, unless besides external daemons...*

<header>COMMENTARY BY MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...some are internal, and in turn, others are appropriately adapted to one another. Likewise, the power and affection of the soul, which is positioned immediately below the innermost <term>daemon</term><note>In Neoplatonism, a "daemon" is not an evil spirit, but a higher guardian or "genius" that guides an individual's soul toward its divine origin.</note>, is occupied with the works of the present life as its own, being the maker of these works. The daemon, however, acts as the <term>charioteer</term><note>A classic Platonic metaphor from the *Phaedrus*, where the soul is compared to a charioteer controlling two horses.</note> and ruler of this maker. This busy making-power does nothing beyond the daemon’s strength, yet it does not perform deeds equal to the daemon's own dignity.

->On the man and the best daemon; how the daemon leads the soul to judgment, and<-
->that souls are able to reach the stars.<-

After this, he says that the soul is especially virtuous in which the powers of imagination and reason are shaped entirely by the intellect, so that the whole life is lived according to the intelligence. In such a case, it is not some daemon that presides over life, but God himself—namely, the divine intellect, then the intellectual unity (which is like the charioteer and head of the intelligence), and then simply the God of the universe, the God of gods himself. 

But then he says that our soul is not always formed by intelligence; for right from the beginning, because of the laborious machinery of <term>generation</term><note>Refers to the process of physical birth and the soul entering a material body.</note>, the activity of the vegetative power is inflamed beyond measure. The imagination is cast down toward this and similar things, and reason too busies itself with them. These things are indeed the opposite of intelligence. Nevertheless, even before we use the discourses of reason, we naturally desire the true and the good through the power of knowing itself. Since this power does not desire something entirely unknown, there is at least a form of the true and good naturally implanted in the mind. 

The daemon rules the soul, not necessarily in an absolute "best" way, but in the best way according to the soul's current quality. After this life in the earthly body, the daemon—now more internal than external—leads the soul to judgment, specifically while it is established in its <term>airy body</term><note>Latin: *aerio corpore*. Ficino refers to the "spirit" or astral vehicle that the soul inhabits after death but before reaching the highest heavens.</note>, before it returns to an earthly body. I say "another" daemon only insofar as there is then a different mode of living in the soul; otherwise, the daemon is the same. 

The state in the airy body is most suited for the judgment of <term>purgation</term><note>The process of cleansing the soul of material attachments through suffering or reflection.</note>. For there, the spirit in sinners suffers affliction, and because there is less distraction, one more easily repents for their fall and expels it; this is a certain projection in the soul from the choice of its future state. For this reason, for the soul to be sent into "brutes" where the imagination is dull is nothing else, as we have said, than to close off that place of power. 

Among these things, I remind you again: it is ridiculous for the soul—if indeed it can exempt itself from the whole world—to be confined within the narrowness of a brute or a plant. You would have spoken more probably along with <term>Proclus</term><note>A late Neoplatonist (5th century AD) who argued that human souls never truly descend into animal bodies, but only into "animal-like" lives.</note>, that the soul neither descends below the human form nor goes outside the celestial body, but retains this constantly. I say "celestial," not meaning that it truly becomes flesh, but that it possesses its own nature elsewhere—at least truly if <term>Plato</term> thinks the soul can eventually be liberated from the universe. He might also have suspected that it could live there perpetually, which they say <term>Porphyry</term> once believed, and which can be justified in the *Phaedo*, when you hear that they shall live without bodies forever. 

But if it ever reaches beyond the condition of this mutable world, it does not seem to use worldly power further; and if you say it will change, it exists at the same time outside the celestial body. For it is also a wonder that a soul contemplating all things as a whole should desire our things, unless perhaps it happens then that they become like people <unclear>fra...olantem</unclear> with free keys and goads. That can only happen to the soul insofar as it is removed from the world, for the sake of which generation occurs. The mind, however, is always granted life by it, at least through the celestial body; otherwise, it would not appear that even a worldly generation placed below the moon could sometimes be "super-lunar."

That the soul is able to reach the celestial realms is proved by this: if all intellectual souls are expressed without an intermediary from the Divine Intellect (the exemplar of the world), and are expressed from the whole—for that is not divided—then they must surely proceed from the whole exemplar. Therefore, both that whole world and these souls exist, not in just any way, I say, but rather in an animate way. 

In our soul, therefore, there are certain powers conformable to the <term>World Soul</term><note>Latin: *anima mundana*. The cosmic soul that governs the planets and the physical universe.</note>, and thus in a certain way congruent with the stars that are around it. So it is not surprising that one who has lived chiefly in contemplation proceeds to <term>Saturn</term> and the gods; he who lived for civic duty to <term>Jupiter</term>; he who lived with magnanimity to <term>Mars</term>; and the others similarly, especially if they were such from the beginning. 

You will note that the generative nature is eternal along with the essence of the soul, even if its effect is interrupted. It is also indivisible in itself, although it seems to be diffused through the body, just like invisible light through the air. That it is indivisible is apparent because the entire seminal power is in every little drop of seed, where many things are generated from a single cast of seed. And entirely all life is in any part of a plant, where a cut-off part preserves life, with the universal celestial nature meanwhile contributing. 

Remember again that the soul's own quality and the daemon domestic to it enter into <term>Fate</term><note>Latin: *fatum*. In this context, the astrological and physical laws that govern the material world.</note> when it enters a changeable body. Besides the common condition of suffering, the soul possesses its own efficacy, so that it does not only suffer in Fate, but acts. For external lot often turns out similar for the dissimilar when it happens to dissimilar characters; and conversely, for souls similar to each other, similar lots turn out very dissimilar. The soul is in Fate by reason of the body: the celestial part as the agent, but regarding other things, more as the sufferer. However, the already mobile body is placed by the fatal revolution of the heavens, having entered into a certain condition of fortune according to a specific order of choice—namely, of reception, infusion, and birth.

<summary>Ficino explains how the soul is guided by a guardian daemon through life and into a post-mortem judgment in an "airy body." He describes the soul's ability to ascend to specific planetary spheres (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars) based on the character of the life lived, while distinguishing between the soul's eternal essence and its role within the laws of Fate.</summary>

<margin>Variant reading</margin>
Of some things, the <term>hypostases</term><note>original: "ὑποστάσεις" — referring to the levels of reality or fundamental substances in the Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note> remain constant while those beings remain as they are. But the soul, being in motion, was brought into being, taking on whatever form it might—be it the sensation found in plants, or <term>nature</term><note>In this context, "nature" refers to the lowest, most automatic level of the soul responsible for biological growth and physical existence.</note> itself. It possesses this nature <margin>within it</margin> within us whenever that part dominates; or rather, it possesses the whole of life in nature. Those parts which are dominated are not seen. This life is in that which it occupies, and is entirely different from it; for after this comes the animal. But that which is produced is not a cause, just as everything generated from that source was at first unformed. If it ever turns toward its generator, it becomes formed, as if it were held fast there. So it is here: that which is generated is not a specific form of the soul, but is something completely indefinite. * If there is any deprivation or indefiniteness, it is not that the soul itself is indefinite, but rather it is indefinite in relation to its own perfection. Now, as it is being perfected, it becomes a body, taking on a shape suited to its potential, as a receptacle for that which generated and nourished it. And this alone of all higher things is held within the body, as the outermost limit of the lower things.

<margin>Care / Concern</margin>
And the saying that "Every soul takes care of the soulless" applies especially to this soul; others behave differently. It wanders through the whole of heaven, sometimes in one form, sometimes in another—whether in a sensory form, or a rational one, or even a vegetative one. For the dominating part of the soul performs the duty suited to it, while the other parts remain idle, having been left outside. In man, however, the lower parts do not dominate, but they exist together. Yet that which is better does not always dominate; for these lower parts also have their own place in him. For this reason, men live as sensory beings, for the instruments of sense are present. Many things in men are also like plants; for the body is increased and generated from within like a plant. Therefore, all these parts work together in action. But according to that which is better, the whole species—

<column-break/>

<margin>I. The Mind generates the soul without alteration to itself, in a certain manner as a source produces.</margin>
THERE ARE things that produce their own subsistent act by remaining as they are; the soul, however, is said to generate by being moved. In its underlying act, it proceeds even unto nature and the plants. For even when it is in us, it possesses a subsistent nature, but it <margin>A</margin> dominates as a part. When it is inserted into plants, however, it prevails as if left alone. Thus it generates nothing, or rather, it generates something <margin>B</margin> entirely different from itself. For after this, life no longer flourishes, but that which has been made is now devoid of life. What then? Perhaps just as everything generated before this was generated unformed, it was then formed by a certain turning back toward its generator, and was thus nourished from that source. Similarly, that which is produced here is no longer a species of the soul. For it no longer lives; rather, it is something entirely indefinite, or indefiniteness itself. In higher things there is indeed an indeterminate nature, but it consists within a certain species. For it is not <margin>C</column> altogether indefinite, except insofar as it relates to its own perfection. But that which is called indeterminate here is entirely indefinite, even indefiniteness itself; which, while it is being perfected, turns into a body, receiving a form suited to its own power—namely, a participation in that which generates and nourishes it. This alone of the higher things is in the body, at the furthest extreme of the lower realm.

THEREFORE, as is said by Plato: "Every soul has care for all that is inanimate," this <margin>D</margin> <margin>II. Transmigration into nature.</margin> applies most specifically to this soul; others behave differently. It is therefore revolved through the whole of heaven, now in some forms, now in others, whether in a sensory species, a rational one, or even a vegetative one. For its dominating part performs the office agreeable to itself; the rest, however, are sluggish, for they seem to have been left outside. In man, however, those parts which are inferior do not overcome him, but <margin>E</margin> exist simultaneously. Yet that which is better does not always overcome; for these also have their own place in him. For this reason, they live as sensory beings, for the organs of sense are present. Many things are also held by men as if they were plants; for the body is clearly increased and generated from within like a plant; wherefore all parts communicate in the acting. But according to that which is better, the whole species—

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD III.

A person is judged. When the soul finally migrates from the body, it becomes that which it possessed in abundance. Therefore, one must flee toward higher things, lest we fall into a sensory appearance by following sensible images, and lest we be plunged into a vegetative life, enslaved to the lust for procreation and ensnared by the sweetness of flavors. Instead, we must rise with all our strength toward the intellectual, toward the <term>Intellect</term><note>The 'Intellect' (Greek: Nous) is the second principle in Plotinus's system, the realm of pure thought and eternal forms.</note>, and toward the Divine. Whosoever, therefore, has preserved their human character is born again as a human. But whosoever B has lived by the senses alone returns as a brute animal. Indeed, those who lived by sense-perception accompanied by anger are born as wild beasts, and the differences between them correspond to the differences in their dispositions. Those who lived by sense-perception through lust and pleasure return as deceptive and gluttonous animals. However, if they did not live so much by sense-perception together with these traits, but rather by a degeneration of the senses, they sprout again as plants. For in these people, only or primarily the vegetative power flourished, and their whole care was to be transformed into plants. Accordingly, those who lived too much charmed by musical C melodies, but were not otherwise depraved, are reborn as musical animals <note>Plotinus likely refers to songbirds or perhaps cicadas, which were associated with music in antiquity.</note>. And those who ruled without reason become eagles, unless they were infected by some other wickedness. Those who, without wisdom, treat lofty things with conceit, often looking up toward the sky, are changed into birds, always seeking higher places in their flight. He who has attained <term>civil virtue</term><note>Political or social virtues, such as justice and temperance, as practiced in human society.</note> returns as a human; but he who has not sufficiently attained civil virtue transforms into a social animal, such as a bee or similar creatures.

D Who then among these shall be called a daemon? And who a God? For it is that which primarily operates in these; for that which operates leads each person, as if it were the principal part there. Is it then the daemon who is allotted to the living being? Perhaps not. Rather, it is that which is above the person: which indeed presides as if in stillness, while that which follows it acts, and we are most especially that which acts. And if we act and live as sensory beings, then reason itself is our <term>daemon</term><note>original: "daemon" / "δαίμων" — In Neoplatonism, this is not an evil spirit, but a guardian or a "higher self" that represents the next level of attainment for the soul.</note>; but if we live by reason, E the daemon is that which is superior to reason, a presiding daemon that leaves the busy office to the other. Thus it is rightly said in Plato: "You shall choose your daemon." <note>A reference to the Myth of Er in Plato’s Republic, where souls choose their next life and its accompanying guardian spirit.</note> For we choose a prefect over us according to our kind of life. Why then does the daemon lead? Perhaps it is not granted to lead one who has finished life; but it was able to do so before, when the person was living. But for one who has finished life, it is necessary to yield the action to another, as one who has already laid down their active life. This [higher principle] now wishes to lead, and that which has surpassed [the previous state] lives itself, having another as its own F daemon. But if the soul grows heavy, with the worse character prevailing, it pays the penalty. In this way, the wicked person falls into a worse state, with that which acts in the human declining into the life of a beast through a similarity of life. But if one were to become superior, living the life of that superior daemon, he would become superior to it, prescribing for himself a presiding power from the more excellent part of himself by which he is led; and beyond that one, another still, until he proceeds to the highest. For the soul is many things—indeed, it is all G things, both the higher and the lower, reaching to every grade of life. For each of us is an intelligible world, and through our lower parts we are joined to this world, but through our

<column-break/>

A A human having departed [from life] becomes that which they have mostly been; therefore one should flee to the things above, so that we do not fall down into the sensory life through sensory images, nor follow the vegetative life through the desire for procreation and the greed for food; but rather flee to the intellectual, to the intellect, and to God. Those who have preserved the human [character] are humans again. Those who lived by B sense alone are animals. If they lived by sense accompanied by spirit <note>original: "θυμοῦ" (thymos) — often translated as "spiritedness" or "anger."</note>, they become wild beasts; and the difference among these depends on the difference of such traits. Those who lived with desire and the pleasure of the appetitive part become intemperate and gluttonous animals. But if they did not live even by sense along with these, but by a dulling of the sense with them, they become plants only. For the vegetative part was most active in them, and their practice was to become trees. Those who loved music but were C pure in other things become songbirds. Those who were unreasonable kings become eagles, unless some other vice was present. Those who were superficial in their study of the heavens, always raising themselves to the sky, become birds that fly high. But he who possessed the civil virtue becomes a human; and he who shared less in civil virtue becomes a social animal, like *bees* or such things.

D Who then is the daemon here? And who is the God here? That which is active leads each person; for it was the leader. * Is this then the daemon to whom the living human was allotted? But it is the one before it, which stands above and is active, while that which follows it and * we are the acting part; or that [higher part] is the daemon and the rational part is us. If we live according to the rational part, E the daemon is that which is above this, standing still and detached, yielding to the one who is working. It is therefore rightly said that we shall choose. For we choose the one who is set before us according to our life. Why then does it lead the one who has finished living? It no longer leads; it led while the person lived. But when life has ceased, the activity proceeds in another way, and it is held by that which lives according to activity. F It wishes to lead, and having prevailed, it lives itself, having another as its own daemon. But if it is weighed down toward the habits of the worse part, it has that [lower state] as a punishment. In this way, the evil person goes to the worse, his likeness having inclined toward that which was active [in life]. But if one is able to follow the higher daemon, he becomes that daemon himself, living that life, and he prevails over the parts by which he was led G until he sets himself apart—and after that daemon, another, until he reaches the top. For the soul is many things, and all things: both the things above and the things below, as far as every kind of life. Indeed, each of us is an intelligible world: by the lower things, we are joined [to this world]...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul's relationship to the higher and lower worlds. On the previous page, Plotinus discussed the soul's migration (metempsychosis) into different animal or plant forms based on its dominant character. Here, he shifts focus to how the soul remains connected to the 'intelligible world' while simultaneously governing the physical body through its lower activity.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR. 283

<margin>A</margin> But concerning those things above, which belong to the intelligible world, we reach them through that part of us which is entirely intelligible, and we remain in that height. However, through the lowest part of the soul, we are bound to the world below, sending down a certain "down-flow" <note>Greek: *aporrhoian*; Latin: *defluxum*</note> from those higher things to the lower, or rather, an activity of the soul that is not itself diminished by the act.

<margin>B</margin> Is it then the case that the activity of the soul is always and entirely in the body? Not at all. For if we turn toward the higher things, that activity is also turned back. What then shall we say of that part of the **World-Soul** <note>The *Anima Mundi*, the soul that governs the entire physical universe</note>? When it is turned toward the higher, is this part also turned away from here? Certainly not: these things belong entirely to the soul's part, and it has neither proceeded nor descended. Instead, while the soul remains still, the body of the world is attached to it and, as it were, kindled and filled with light. Since the world is situated within the whole, and is therefore not disturbed, the soul is rightly not <margin>C</margin> disturbed. What then? Does it feel nothing at all? The world has no sense of sight, as the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe</note> says, because it has no eyes; nor does it have hearing, and therefore no ears, nor nostrils, nor a tongue. Does it then have a certain shared perception <note>Greek: *synaisthēsei*</note>, perceiving what is in itself in the way we experience ourselves? But perhaps, since all things in it always exist similarly according to nature, there is a stillness in it regarding sensation, and no pleasure is present. Thus, the **vegetative power** is present as if it were not, and the **sensory power** likewise. But concerning the world, this has been spoken of elsewhere; for the present, insofar as the doubt was raised, let it be settled.

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, if the soul chooses its **daemon** <note>A guiding spirit or higher principle of the self; not a "demon" in the modern sense</note> and its life there [in the intelligible realm], how are we still masters of any action? Perhaps what is called "choice" there is an obscure way of indicating the soul's disposition and affection universally and everywhere. But if the soul’s choice is the master, and that part prevails which has a greater readiness from the acts of its former life, then the body should no longer be called the cause of any evil for the soul. For if the character of the soul itself precedes the body by a certain prerogative, and it possesses what it chose, and does not change its daemon (as Plato says), then surely it is not here that one becomes good or <margin>E</margin> bad. Perhaps each is so by potential, and becomes so in actuality. What then should be said if someone with good character falls into a bad body, or conversely, if someone imbued with bad character happens upon a good body? Perhaps the things belonging to each soul can, to a greater or <margin>F</margin> lesser degree, affect both bodies in one way or another; since other external fortunes do not entirely force the whole of one's choice. But when it is said that first the "lots" are drawn, then the "examples of lives" are proposed, and after these "fortunes" follow—and again that lives are chosen from the present and proposed options according to one's character—all these things, I say, grant authority rather to the souls that arrange what is given according to their own character. <margin>G</margin> Therefore, this daemon is not entirely external, but is situated as if it were neither bound to us, nor again acting as our own specific self; rather, it is ours because it can be called something of the soul, yet it is not ours in the sense that we are these particular men living such a life under its direction, as the things treated in the *Timaeus* can testify to us; which, if they are understood in this way...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But regarding the higher things which pertain to the intelligible world, we touch the intelligible world and remain in the sublime through that which is entirely intelligible in us. By that part which is its last, however, we are bound to the inferior: as if sending down a certain flow from itself to the lower, or rather an activity of it, without the soul itself being at all diminished.

<margin>B</margin> But is the act of the soul sent down to the lower things always in the body? By no means. For if we are turned toward the higher, that act is likewise turned. <margin>The nature of that which is to be ruled is eternal. The World-Soul rules the body either through attention or service.</margin> What then shall we say of such an act of its part of the **World-Soul**? When that soul is turned to the higher, is this part also turned away from here? Truly it is not fitting: these things are entirely in the soul’s part; it neither proceeded nor descended. But while that soul remains, the body of the world is joined to it, and is, as it were, set on fire and flooded with light. And since the world is placed within the whole, and for that reason is not at all disturbed, the soul is deservedly not <margin>C</margin> disturbed. What then? Does it feel nothing at all? The world indeed has no sight, says the *Timaeus*: since it has no eyes: it has no hearing, and therefore no ears, nor nostrils, nor a tongue. Does it therefore have a certain shared sensation in some way, perceiving the things that are in itself, such as we experience in ourselves? But perhaps, since all things in it always remain similarly according to nature, there is a rest in it as far as sensation is concerned, nor is pleasure in it. Therefore, the **vegetative** is present as if it were not present, and the **sensory** likewise. But <margin>D</margin> concerning the world, this is discussed elsewhere: but for the present, as far as the doubt touched upon it, let it be said.

<margin>E</margin> Accordingly, if the soul chooses its **daemon** and its life there, how are we no longer masters of any action? Perhaps what is called "choice" there darkly indicates the soul’s choice and affection commonly and everywhere. But if the choice of the soul is master, and that part which has a greater readiness from the acts of a former life prevails, the body must no longer be called the cause of any evil for the soul. For if the very character of the soul precedes the body by a certain prerogative, and it has that which it chooses, and (as Plato says) does not change its daemon, then surely it does not become good or bad here. Perhaps each is so by potential, but becomes so in act. What then is to be said if ever one who has upright character falls into a bad body? Or conversely, one imbued with bad character happens upon a good body? Perhaps those things which pertain to each soul can, to a greater or <margin>F</margin> lesser degree, <margin>The soul, according to its changes, changes its daemon, which it holds as chief; one, that is, the presiding power of the soul in the business of its province.</margin> affect both bodies in this way or that: since other external fortunes by no means force the entire choice. But when it is said that first the "lots" exist, then the "examples of lives" are proposed, after which "fortunes" follow; and again, that lives are chosen from the present and proposed ones according to character—all these things, I say, grant authority rather to the souls that compose the things given to them according to their own characters. <margin>G</margin> That this daemon, therefore, is not entirely from without, but is so situated as if it were neither bound up nor, again, properly acting; it is ours, since it can be called something of the soul, yet it is not ours in the sense that we are such-and-such men having such a life under us, as the matters treated in the *Timaeus* can be a testimony to us: which indeed if they are accepted in this way...

<summary>Plotinus explores the soul's dual nature: its highest part remains in the eternal intelligible realm while its lower activity illuminates and governs the physical body. He reconciles the Platonic concept of the "allotted daemon" with human moral responsibility, arguing that our soul's pre-existing character determines how we handle our earthly lot.</summary>

**WHO THEN** is the virtuous man, and what does he do? Perhaps the virtuous man is he in whom that which is better operates: otherwise he would not be virtuous if he did not have the guardian spirit cooperating with him. For the Intellect acts in him; either it is the guardian spirit itself, or it acts according to the guardian spirit; and to such a man, the guardian spirit is a god. Is it then possible that even above the intellect, that which is above the intellect clearly exists as his guardian spirit? But why does one not enjoy this gift immediately from the beginning? Perhaps because of the disturbance heavily brought in from birth itself <note>Latin: *generatione*; refers to the process of entering a physical body</note>. Yet even before the discourse of reason, a certain inward movement is present, seeking those things which are harmonious with it. Does it then entirely correct and direct one toward the best? Perhaps not entirely; since the soul here is affected: for even in such things, it may choose such a life, and have this choice and purpose. Furthermore, this guardian spirit of whom we speak is said to lead the soul to the underworld, and not to remain there entirely, unless perhaps the soul chooses the same things again. But before that, how does it behave? It is said to lead the soul to judgment, to arrive in the same form after a certain end of birth, which it once had before birth: then, as if from another beginning, during the middle space of time that flows between the preceding and following birth, the guardian spirit hangs over the souls paying their penalties, and perhaps their life then is not so much a life as it is judgment and punishment. But what of souls entering the bodies of brutes? Is something less than a guardian spirit present? Perhaps a bad spirit, or one that is sluggish and idle. But for souls that have progressed to higher things, is something of the divine present? Surely from their number, some still lead a life in the sensible world, while others are already outside the world. And of those in the sensible world, some are near the sun, or any other of the planets, while others are in the firmament <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note>: each, clearly, insofar as they directed their actions here by reason. For we must think that in our soul there is not only the intelligible world, but also a certain disposition conforming to the World-Soul itself. Since, therefore, that Soul is distributed into the fixed sphere and also the wandering spheres according to different powers, surely there are powers in us conforming to its powers, and proper actions emanate from each power. You will be able to see that souls which have departed from here to a fitting star follow the character which we used most in acting and living, agreeable to such a god and guardian spirit: where the soul will either use this same power, or something presiding over this power. But we must consider what that "better" thing might be. For souls that have set out beyond the sensible world, we must think they have transcended the demonic nature, and every fate of birth, and all necessity of this world, so long as they dwell in the intelligible world: furthermore, they have retracted with themselves that essence which is in them desirous of generating: which, if anyone should say is that essence which the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the origin of the universe</note> says becomes divisible around bodies, he would be...

# MARSILIO FICINO'S
# COMMENTARY ON THE FIFTH BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, 
# CONCERNING THE GUARDIAN SPIRIT.

### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

> ->Every power, whether of knowing or of generating, rejects the base and strives toward the beautiful: since every power proceeds and is moved from the primary beauty.<-

<margin>I</margin>
**I** believe, Magnanimous Lawrence <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron</note>, that you do not expect a long discussion on love from your Marsilio at this time: both because we have discussed this at length in the *Symposium* <note>Referring to Ficino's "Commentary on Plato's Symposium on Love"</note>, and especially because you have discovered so much concerning love through divine inspiration and have sung of it in elegant poems. Therefore, I shall follow the highest peaks of the matter. Every power of the soul, whether rational or natural, strives with perpetual love to reach and generate the beautiful, because such power proceeds from beauty itself. Therefore, it retains within itself the innate form of beauty and a perpetual instinct toward it as toward the end of love. Whoever is ignorant of this cause cannot express the natures of loves and the passions of lovers. Truly, the Divine Intellect is the primary form, entirely pure and all-forming. The soul's intellect is indeed the secondary form, but similarly all-forming. Nature is the third form, likewise all-forming; led down from these principles, it looks toward them constantly, so that it may wonderfully cover and adorn the formlessness of matter with forms. If, therefore, anything deformed happens under nature, it occurs contrary to the primary intention of God and nature, just as a deformity in a craft occurs contrary to the entire intention of the art. Just as the natural power does, so too the rational power everywhere draws its origin from the primary beauty; it rejects the base as discordant, but accepts the beautiful with all its strength as concordant; it strives to generate a beautiful form and to preserve its own nature perpetually within it. But the rational power brings forth in

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO
<meta>catchword: of them</meta>

...to the beauty of the soul; however, the natural [soul] produces beauty in matter, and both naturally desire a beautiful subject, according to their powers, in which to generate; thus at last beauty is more aptly created.

### The double soul of the world. Two Venuses. Two Loves: which are not passions, but certain modes of existence.

II Since we see intelligence perfected in us to the extent that both the act of understanding and the thing understood are separated from matter and the conditions of matter, we can guess that the first simple Intellect itself is most foreign to matter. Moreover, that the intellectual soul generated immediately from it—and therefore highly intellectual—cannot unite with matter into the common form of a single composite. For this [soul] is both a kind of intellect and simply a soul; however, the life born from this subsequently, like a certain soul and nature in its simplest sense, can now come together as one with matter. Therefore, we call that intellectual soul the first Venus in the world; but let the life infused into the world from there be called the second Venus. In both, a perpetual love flourishes, incited toward the beauty of the divine mind: in the first, toward generating final beauty within itself; in the second, toward expressing beauty in matter according to its powers. Indeed, Plotinus thinks, following the mind of Plato, that while the intellectual soul of the world acts inwardly toward God by understanding and willing Him, it conceives within itself not something imaginary, but something natural and subsisting <note>Ficino means that the thought is not just a passing idea, but a real, existing entity.</note>—imitating, I believe, the mystery of the Christian Trinity in this. He thinks that just as shining and heating are two things in fire, but one thing flowing in the sun, so knowing and loving are different in the rational power, but exist as one act in the intellectual substance. When an act of this kind is innermost in the soul of the world and most effective regarding the innermost, a child suitable to this act is produced within itself. Since this child is born from intelligence, it is something intelligible; since it proceeds from love, it is something amatory—it is not love itself as a passion, but love subsisting as something produced from a certain act of loving. For since there existing and acting are entirely the same, naturally by acting within there exists a certain production within, in which the thing produced is the same essence as the producer, differing only in this: that in the one it is the propagator, and in the other it is the thing propagated from it. It differs further by a certain relationship: since this amatory existence is of both the lover and the beloved. It differs also because in the propagating existence, the vision of beauty itself is placed; in the propagated existence, it is rather the pleasure itself regarding beauty.

### Confirmation of the points above.

III If a pregnant woman often affects the fetus with a certain natural quality because of the wonderful intensity of her imagination and affection—specifically because it is connected to the mother—and if again a similar motion of the mind expresses qualities dwelling in its own body, what wonder is it that something substantial is born in the soul itself from a similar intensity? Especially in the intellectual soul itself, where action is intense, and the affection is not accidental or moving, but entirely natural and firm. And he who sees and rejoices and desires is most effective, and his object is most powerful, and flows in powerfully. These things are confirmed by the fact that if everywhere accidental things are reduced to certain substantial things through a fitting proportion, it is necessary that loves—which are certain accidental passions—be properly referred to substantial loves. After this, one must note again that it is necessary for the world to have two souls: one in a way separate, which is present to the body like a craftsman; the other truly joined, which breathes into the body from there, like a form. It must be present as separate because such a thing shines directly from the pure intellect, and because a craftsman does not absolutely command his craft when mixed with it. Furthermore, a soul must be within the world as joined, both because the first soul is fertile enough to generate this from itself, and because the world must be a most perfect composite. Therefore, it must have the most perfect form for its matter—that is, a living and sensing one. Yet (as Plotinus wishes) the intellectual soul and matter do not become one single thing, because through action and affection intelligence tends toward the opposite of matter. Just as he thinks it does not happen in us; for in us, the intellectual soul does not share with the body in the body's own passions, nor does the body share with such a soul in actions properly belonging to that kind of soul. However, one may say that the intellectual soul is "worldly" when in the world and "human" when in us; and from itself and the animal soul together, one thing is thus produced, because from its influx together with matter a single sensual animal is made, into which that soul always breathes life—which would perish without that continuous spirit. Remember that these twin souls in the world are again two Venuses, which twin similar loves accompany. Remember even that love in this second soul of the world does not only generate all beauty in the world's matter through its generative power, but also, through its effective power of imagining, it both looks up to the divine form and provokes both the world and the things in the world toward that same form according to its powers.

### Two loves naturally implanted in every soul like two "daemons."

IIII He lightly touched upon those loves which, like certain new motions of the soul, are daily incited in us by things offered from the outside as if they were familiar; but he more diligently pursues the "substantial loves"—that is, the essential and perpetual instincts toward beauty naturally implanted in the soul and constantly drawing it toward beauty, even if you do not choose or notice them. One of these is naturally inserted into the power of knowing, the other into the power of generating. And because it leads the soul like a prefect and rules in the manner of providence, it is called a <term>daemon: here used in the Platonic sense of a guiding spirit or inner genius, not a malevolent entity</term>, although the more excellent love is called a god. It is said that the soul generates these not daily, but from the beginning: when, according to its nature (partly handed down to it from eternity and partly contracted from the choice of life at some point), it conceives such instincts that will reign for an age. By their secret nod, many more affections and concepts are daily aroused in us, which certainly neither external sights alone, nor the present state of the body, nor new deliberation provides. And indeed, a certain perpetual tenor of life, directed mostly toward one thing—especially regarding the type of life, knowledge, arts, and the natural faculties proper to each person—is ruled by such a daemon, while being directed in the meantime by a certain external daemon suitable to itself. All rational souls also agree through their own loves of this kind with the loves of the world-soul, insofar as they are sisters of the world-soul; these souls and their loves together depend on the world-soul and its...

...by love, not because they obtain their essence from there, but because the beginnings of that movement are arranged, as if in harmony, with their own motions, and they are moved through their own ends toward the final end of that [First Principle].

### On Demons

We have shown sufficiently in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, *Platonic Theology*</note> that it is necessary for demons to be intermediaries between the stars and humans. If any sphere above us—more excellent and much larger than our own—possesses rational inhabitants suited to their sphere, just as our own sphere does, this must be so. For even Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Platonist famous for his work on the "God of Socrates"</note> proves by the testimony of Aristotle that there are certain "fiery animals." In burning furnaces, specific winged animals have been seen flying about, which spend their entire lives in the fire; they are born with it and are extinguished along with it. Indeed, that which first receives life from the life-giving substance itself—that is, the soul—is fire alone. For fire is the element closest to the soul among all bodies, because it is the most excellent, the most effective, and the most mobile. From this, it follows that individual things live when heat fosters them, and do not live when it does not. Secondly, through fire, the air (which is closest to fire) is seen to gain life and act as the fuel for heat. Through these two, the subtle water is next, being closer to the air; through this, similarly, the subtle earth; and through these four gathered in turn, a body is composed and solid, made not of mere vapors but of thicker materials. It is permitted, however, that what is purer and simpler should shine back everywhere from the composite that follows it.

There are, therefore, five classes of rational animals. The first are those whose body consists of fire alone; and if the stars are visible fire, they are those whom the ancients call the "eternal gods." Orpheus calls all these souls "fiery" or "celestial," holding the place of stars within the planetary circles under a leading planet. For it is not fitting to descend immediately from the innumerable animals in the firmament to the unique [human] below. The second class are those whose bodies are fire and air perfectly mixed; these the same Orpheus calls "ethereal" or "aerial" demons. There are also third animals in which fire and air are composed with a certain subtle water; these he calls "aqueous" demons, who, having become a little denser, can be seen. Nor are the fourth class lacking, which add subtle earth—like a certain earthly vapor—to the three already mentioned. These are called "terrestrial" demons by Orpheus, and sometimes, when condensed a bit further, they may even be felt by touch. These he also calls "subterranean" whenever they enter the caverns of the earth. The fifth class are the bodies of humans, who are like the lowest of the demons. In us, besides that "demonic" mixture of the four subtle elements—which is the demon's own nature but in us is the "spirit," <term>spiritus</term> <note>In Ficino's medicine and philosophy, 'spiritus' is a thin vaporous substance that links the soul to the physical body</note> which first lives and feels—a mixture of more solid materials is joined.

That the spirit is the first to live and feel is clear from the fact that when the spirit is withdrawn from the limbs, sensation and motion immediately desert them, and therefore life does as well. Since that which is first joined by kinship is held more firmly, it seems probable that souls dismiss these later [solid] bodies gradually, while the earlier [subtle] ones are reserved longer. Thus, those who were in a solid body remain longer afterward in the thin body in which they simultaneously existed and in which they primarily felt; because of its kinship, this body easily yields to the corresponding soul. Truly, the more sublime and simple a body is, the more slowly it seems to be deserted by the soul; the celestial bodies are never deserted. For in every genus, that which first becomes a participant is always a participant. And rightly so: eternal life, where it has once naturally animated an eternal body by its very being, never ceases to animate it. The souls of men and lower demons are allowed to change these given bodies because they are composed of discordant things and are therefore dissoluble, and also because they are distracted from blessedness by such a body, place, and service. It is a crime, however, for rational souls—naturally established for the contemplation of absolute things—to be deprived of it for too long. Therefore, when they reach the end, they live for many ages in an ethereal and celestial body. For that which comes from the intention of the "Forms" <note>The Platonic Ideals</note> and their principle is the greatest and most long-lasting.

It is likely that celestial and ethereal demons are both eternal and free from disturbances due to the simplicity of their nature and the purity of their place. Aqueous and terrestrial demons, however, are indeed long-lived but not "impassible" <note>Meaning they are capable of suffering or feeling emotion</note>; they possess harsh disturbances of the soul just as we do. For the proximity of their region and nature brings about a similarity of character. From the first two classes, nothing ever flows out; therefore, they have no need for nourishment, but are delighted and worshiped only by songs, symbols, and lights. Thus they are reconciled to us, especially at those times when the stars they follow are dominant. From the following two classes, since something does flow out, restoration is necessary; but in those where there is nothing earthly, the scent of spices, flowers, and exhaling liquids provides enough reconciliation. The last demons <note>The terrestrial and subterranean ones</note> require thicker odors and vapors, and are nourished by blood and flesh—especially from the ribs—and from things consumed by us.

Therefore, if you believe Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist and student of Plotinus</note>, you would say this [the demons' influence] led us to devour animals: so that they, being near us and within our viscera, might draw in and suck the nourishment from animals that is often already digested and suitable for them. There is innate in them a certain faculty of attracting and sucking, just as there is in the limbs of animals and the roots of plants. We allure them to us with such a "nidor" <note>The smell or steam of cooking meat</note>; whence, as Porphyry says, men devoted to the belly become, as it were, the tools of "unclean demons." Although, as Iamblichus says, if demons need any nourishment, they can supply it for themselves from our efforts everywhere, it is still probable that certain allurements can be offered to them by man. Incontinent <note>Lacking self-control</note> demons mix with incontinent men, and the proud are agitated by prouder demons.

For Porphyry says that pride is the primary thing in them, so much so that they desire nothing more vehemently than to be thought of as the "supreme gods" by us and to be worshiped in their place. Their prince especially contends for this: to be held as the first god of all, inciting us to the pleasures of this body in which they themselves might be delighted in us in a similar way. They provoke us to contentions and battles, by which they themselves sometimes conflict with one another, disturbing the air with their conflict, and they rejoice in constant lies. We, however, cannot resist them except insofar as we diligently expose our minds to the inspiration of higher demons, live soberly and chastely, and humbly commend ourselves to God. For only by purity, holiness, and piety can the human race be defended from the powerful incursion of evil demons. Hence Democritus prayed that he might encounter "good demons"; for as Plutarch says, he thought many demons were evil. He called them all "Idols" <note>Greek *eidola*, meaning images or phantoms</note> walking in the air, emitting voices among themselves, long-lived and difficult to dissolve. Iamblichus asserts that many demons are evil and deceive men under the pretext of being good; but they suddenly flee from the presence of good divinities, and thus a legitimate, religious person cannot be deceived. This is according to the Egyptians and Chaldeans.

Furthermore, Plotinus says that demonic souls exist more prone to bodies because a certain "intelligible matter" reigns in them. This is not only a formable nature (for this is in higher things as well), but a certain intimate essence and disposition, in which identity [does not reside]...

THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

...surpasses otherness, nor stability [surpass] motion, nor the common nature [surpass] the particular, nor the faculty of acting [surpass] the power of being acted upon. Indeed, through this very disposition, such an essence appears suited both to a falling body and to souls prone to disturbance. For this reason, as Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized theurgy and the hierarchy of spiritual beings</note> also asserts, demons do not possess a "common" providence like the Gods, but individual demons are assigned to their own specific actions and provinces.

### On the origin of demons.

¶ I Indeed, Plotinus says in the sixth chapter that demons are generated from the soul of the whole; likewise, Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and editor</note> says in his book *On Abstinence* that demons sprouted from the whole soul. You should not understand this to mean that the very substances of the souls within demons were created from the World Soul. Rather, take the "whole soul" here to mean that "mixing bowl" <note>original: "patera"; a reference to the *krater* in Plato's *Timaeus* where the Demiurge mixes the soul-stuff</note>, or the goddess and common Idea from which the *Timaeus* asserts that, besides the World Soul, the souls of the spheres were produced separately, and then again the souls of demons and men. For as Proclus <note>A later head of the Platonic Academy in Athens</note> says in the *Alcibiades*, demons are generated by the life-giving goddess and by the soul. Plotinus also wishes that from the World Soul itself, and from any rational soul, a certain irrational soul of its own emanates, which he names a "demon." If such demons follow their own souls, they are nevertheless birthed from them under a certain common influx of the World Soul; for it belongs especially to the providence of the World Soul to coordinate the subjects of nature and all of nature toward completing the disposition of the universe. 

In every respect, whatever kind of demons they may be, they are said to depend on the World Soul because the World Soul itself binds their souls—through vital powers—to islands of matter like bait for their bodies. Among these, he places the "intelligible gods," that is, the Ideas and the intellectual souls of the celestial beings. Likewise, he places "sensible gods," namely the stars; and after them the demons, who are invisible, whether they are in heaven or below heaven—since the name "demon" is properly transferred to those who are below the moon. We have described the bodies of demons in the preceding sections with a somewhat freer reasoning, by which we did not depart far from the majority of Platonists. However, we can perhaps say, by a more physical reasoning, that the bodies of sub-lunary demons are for the most part composite. For even the elements in their spheres are mixed everywhere into one. Therefore, there will necessarily be fire in them; for through fire, life and motion flourish. There will also be air as the fuel for the fire—yet not air alone with fire alone, lest they be suddenly dissolved. Let there also be thin water, nor can it subsist without earth; otherwise, it would have the least stability under fire. 

Truly, the spiritual bodies of demons, just like our own spirit <note>Ficino refers to the "pneuma" or "spiritus," the thin vapor that connects the human soul to the body</note>, must be quite tempered so that they may be vessels for that noble life. It is necessary, therefore, that the tyrannical voracity of fire be so tamed in them that from the number of the three other elements—and indeed from a greater quantity of these—the rapacity of the one tyrant [fire] is restrained. However, much earth cannot be there, nor a great deal of water. Let there be, therefore, as much air as possible; in the second place, the thinnest watery moisture; in the third, fire, but in a rare proportion, lest it be perhaps so devouring; and let the most substantial earth hold the fourth place. And although almost all demons are tempered, some are nonetheless the most tempered of all; in others, however, this or that element excels a little more. Their complexions, therefore, will be roughly fivefold just like our own: namely, the tempered one, and four that are not as tempered, which are subject to similar stars and preside by a certain natural justice over humans of the same complexion.

### On subsisting love, and on the eternal intelligence within us.

¶ II In the seventh chapter, where he says: "Reason, therefore, and the other intelligences," he means that for the sake of reason, a seminal power <term>vim seminariam: a formative, "seed-like" force that carries the patterns of higher reality into lower matter</term> flows from the animal intellect into the soul, like a father into a mother, in which it generates a love mixed both from its own abundance and from a certain indigence of the soul. Likewise, he says that the animal intellect begets a perpetual love, both for contemplating the intelligible beauty and in nature for the beauty that can be generated. He judges both types of love to be something essential and "subsisting," because they exist from the soul through its very essence. 

However, those loves which are usually excited recently <note>meaning temporary, earthly passions</note>—since they are not from the soul simply as the actor, but happen to it as a patient from external things and the body—he does not call "subsisting" or "demons," but rather "passions." After this, you should notice that the "common intellect" of all things and the "proper intellect" of each individual differ greatly from one another. Again, the power of knowing which does not have in its essence the very thing which is to be known according to its essence, but only a certain image of it, is deceptive; but that knowledge is certain which holds the object itself within it. If such a power does not hold the object as something imaginary, then it exists as the object itself. Therefore, the most perfect knowledge, such as the Intellect, is the very thing which is called the "object." The most imperfect, however, like the sense-faculties, neither is the things to be felt, nor does it possess them, but it merely turns itself toward them. 

Thought <note>original: "cogitatio"; discursive reasoning</note>, although it is not the thing it thinks, nevertheless possesses it—that is, it possesses the "notions" of things, whether it draws them properly from itself or from its own intellect at will. If you contemplate the intelligible world, there the universal intellect is not only the universal intelligible, but also in any given Idea, a specific intellect is a specific intelligible. Furthermore, the proper intellect of each soul is itself the intelligible. Yet it differs from the simply common intellect in this: that it is not itself the simply universal intelligible, for it is that intelligible in its own particular way. Therefore, our intellect possesses universal intelligence and a "halfway" love, because it both possesses and exists as the universal intelligible itself. And because it exists as this thing here, not simply but in its own way—that is, not in a completely most effective manner—therefore, in any special notion, it does not comprehend individual things as distinctly as the divine mind comprehends them. 

For it is necessary for the intellect to turn toward reason and imagination so that it may know particulars distinctly. That there are others besides the common intellect—not only distinct in classification but knowing in a perpetual state, distinct from the first [intellect]—seems to be confirmed in this way: since the first Intellect is the "first multitude," it is rightly propagatable into many intellects. In it, there is the diversity of the Idea, and there is also identity in the Idea, and this is the more powerful. Since, therefore, it is distributed under diversity into many "discursive" intellects, it is also rightly derived under identity into many "stably knowing" intellects. But in those which are naturally propagated from there, discursive reason is so subjoined to stable intelligence, just as in the first Mind, diversity or "otherness" itself is subjoined to identity. To proceed into an infinite multitude through understanding—that is, to understand individual things—is given to our intelligence when it is joined to reason through the service of the imagination. As for the other things disputed concerning Love and the gods, we seem to have confirmed them sufficiently in our book *On Love* <note>Ficino's *De Amore*, his famous commentary on Plato's *Symposium*</note>.

<summary>Ficino explains the origins of demons from the "Whole Soul" and details their physical makeup as tempered elemental bodies, primarily composed of air. He then explores the relationship between the human intellect and the universal Intellect, defining divine Love as an essential, subsisting force that connects the soul to intelligible beauty.</summary>

### PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. III.

...since it is a most absurd thing to say that one who wishes to produce things beautiful by nature would choose to generate them in something ugly. For those who are moved to generate here in the physical world, it is enough to attain what is beautiful here. This beauty is indeed lacking in images and bodies: for the primary <term>archetype</term> <note>The original divine "blueprint" or "Form" of Beauty in the intellectual realm, of which physical things are only shadows.</note> is by no means present in them, though it is the cause for them of loving even this earthly beauty. Therefore, among those who are called back by this beauty to the <term>recollection</term> <note>reminiscentiam: This refers to the Platonic theory of *anamnesis*, where the soul "remembers" divine truths it knew before being born into a body.</note> of the celestial beauty, this physical beauty is cherished as an image. But among those who, through ignorance of their own passion, do not remember at all, this beauty of ours is judged to be the true beauty. And if they be temperate, their familiarity with this beauty is free from vice. However, the fall of the intemperate into sexual union is a sin. 

Therefore, he who is moved by a pure love of the beautiful is content with beauty alone, whether he remembers the divine or not. But he who also feels a desire for immortality within a mortal thing, seeks the beautiful in perpetual generation and eternal preservation to the best of his ability. And while he proceeds according to nature, he sows and generates in the beautiful, bringing forth toward the eternal; he does so in the beautiful because of a certain kinship with beauty itself. For the eternal itself is kin to the beautiful, and the eternal nature is the primary beauty, and all things that come from it are made beautiful. 

Therefore, he who does not desire generation seems to be more self-sufficient and content with beauty itself. But he who seeks to generate, strives to give birth to something beautiful because of a certain indigence; from this, it appears that he is by no means self-sufficient. He thinks that in his making, he will only produce something beautiful if he generates within the beautiful. But those who strive to generate contrary to law and contrary to nature start their course from a certain natural impulse, but having transgressed the natural path, they slip down through slippery places and lie fallen, ignorant of where love was leading them, and of what the goal of their desire for generation is. Likewise, they are ignorant of how the image of beauty ought to be used, and finally, they are ignorant of Beauty itself. 

Surely those who love beautiful bodies not for the sake of sexual union, love them for the very reason that they are beautiful. Again, those who follow love greatly—I mean toward women—so that perpetuity may be preserved through generation, and do not wander from this path, these desire both beauty and perpetuity at once. Both types of people are temperate, although some are more excellent than others. Among the more excellent, some honor this beauty of ours as if it were sufficient for them; others, namely those who remember the divine, honor beauty itself, yet do not despise this earthly beauty, seeing it as a certain

At the point of reaching for [divine] knowledge, or at least having already escaped by an instinct toward it. To this point must be brought whatever things are discussed in Plato's *Symposium*, where it is written that at the birthdays of Venus, Love was fathered from Want <note>Penia</note> and Plenty <note>Poros</note>. Furthermore, it seems the present dispute requires something concerning Venus. Namely, whether Love is said to be born from Venus, or rather together with Venus: and first, who indeed is Venus? Then, how does she hold herself? Is Love from her, or together with her, or rather does she somehow have Love from herself, born at the same time and together with her? For that which is born directly from the Mind is itself also pure, as it is most powerful according to its own fertility by its proximity to the Intellect itself, and has an inborn appetite to establish itself in its parent. The parent, I say, is powerful enough to keep it sufficiently among the heavenly beings, so that it happens that the soul never falls away, as it hangs by its tracks from the Mind, and it has that gift much more than the light poured around the sun, perpetually proceeding from it and being referred back into it. Following then continuously after Saturn—and if you wish, after the father of Saturn, which is Heaven—she reflected her act toward him, and allied herself to him, and by loving, she fathered love; and with this very love she looks up to him, and the act of this soul produces a substance and essence. Then truly both look thither: both the mother herself and the beautiful Love who was born, a substance indeed always intent upon another beauty,

And truly, Love is the eye of the desirer, providing to the lover that he may discern the beloved through him; yet he himself runs ahead, and before he provides the faculty of seeing through an instrument to that lover, he himself is already full of the sight or the spectacle. He is prior, I say, yet he does not contemplate in the same way, for while he provides the spectacle to the lover, he himself feeds on the fruit, as it were, of the vision of beauty wonderfully poured around him.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III

**A** [The Soul] depends on essence and looks up toward that which is the first essence, and looks up with great intensity. From its first sight of that essence, a "spectacle" or "vision" is formed. It looks upon this as its own good and rejoices in seeing it; and the sight itself is such that what it gazes upon, it does not gaze upon carelessly. Indeed, by its very pleasure and focused intention toward the thing seen, and then by the intensity of the vision itself, something is generated that is worthy of the spectacle. For this reason, both from the fact that it acts most intently upon the spectacle, and from the fact that **B** something flows down, as it were, from the spectacle itself, the eye is imbued—like a vision born together with an image—and this is **Love**. Perhaps it is called *Eros* <note>original: "eros" — Plotinus is using a traditional (though linguistically debated) etymology linking *Eros* to *horasis* (vision).</note> for this reason: because it derives its substance from *horaseos*, that is, from vision. Since love, which is a passion, derives its instinct from this source, the Love which is an *essence* <term>Essence</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, "essence" (essentia/ousia) refers to a fundamental reality, whereas "passion" refers to an emotion or state of being affected.</note> precedes the love which is not an essence. Yet, the passion is also called *eran*, that is, "to love," because it possesses something of this essence, although it is not called Love in the simple sense. Therefore, the love of the supernal soul exists in such a way that it too looks up to **C** sublime things, as a follower of that soul, born from her and remaining with her, content with the contemplation of the gods. Since we say that this soul is "separate"—meaning the first soul that illuminates the heavens—we shall admit without error that this Love is also separate. And if we have said that this soul is most especially celestial, in the same way that we claim our own "best part" is within us, we nevertheless also affirm that it is separate. There, then, let that love remain, where the inviolable **D** soul resides. However, since this [second] Venus belongs to this world—being neither the soul alone nor the soul in its simplest form—she rightly generated Love again while reigning in this world, who now concerns himself with marriages and weddings alongside Venus. Then indeed, insofar as she herself attains a supernal desire, she provokes the souls of **E** youths upward and converts the soul whose colleague she is toward higher things, as much as that soul can naturally be provoked into the memory of them. For every soul seeks the Good, especially that which is mixed with something else and has become part of it; for this soul follows the higher one and emanates from it.
