# BOOK FIVE

**A** <margin>A</margin> Let it be granted that a particular love is attached to a particular soul, and that great Love is attached to the Universal Soul. Just as Love exists in the whole, it thrives everywhere throughout the universe. Furthermore, this single Love branches out into many, appearing everywhere according to its own will, taking shape in its various parts and revealing itself in a kind of image. We must believe that there are many "Venuses" <note>original: "Veneres" — the Latin name for Aphrodite, the goddess of love and beauty.</note> in the world, appearing as spirits <term>Daimons</term> <note>In this context, a "daimon" is not an evil "demon," but a powerful intermediary spirit between gods and humans.</note> born together with Love, all flowing forth from a single, universal Venus. These individual loves depend upon that universal goddess, each with its own specific loves, just as the Soul is the mother of Love. Venus is the Soul, and Love is the active power of the soul that yearns for the Good. Since such love leads each soul toward the nature of the Good, the love associated with the higher soul is a God, for it keeps the soul joined with the Divine. However, the love associated with the "mixed" soul <note>The soul that is more closely tied to the physical world.</note> should be called a daimon.

**B** <margin>B</margin>

**C** <margin>C</margin> <margin>He confirms those who believed that love itself, which is called the "World" by Plato, is actually Venus, who is the World.</margin> AND YET, what is the nature of a daimon, and what is the nature of daimons in general? Plato writes about this in his *Symposium* <note>original: "Convivio" — Plato’s dialogue on the nature of love, where the character Diotima explains Love's birth.</note>. He discusses the nature of other daimons and of Love itself—how Love was born during the birthday celebrations of Venus from the union of *Penia* (Indigence) and *Porus* (Plenty). If anyone thinks that Plato is calling this physical world "Love," rather than saying that love is something born within the world, they will be refuted by many arguments. First, Plato calls the world a "blessed god" who is self-sufficient, whereas he says Love is neither a god nor self-sufficient, but always in need.

**D** <margin>D</margin> Furthermore, it is necessary that if the world is composed of a soul and a body, and if the soul of the world is its own Venus, then the primary part of Love must be Venus herself. Or, if the world is the soul of the world itself (just as a man is truly the soul of a man), then Love must be Venus. Moreover, if Love is a daimon and is the world, why are other daimons—who share the same essence—not also worlds? In that case, the world would merely be a collection of daimons.

**E** <margin>E</margin> Likewise, when Love is called the leader of beautiful youths, how could that description fit the physical world? Finally, Plato says that Love wanders about without bedding or cover, barefoot and homeless. These descriptions cannot possibly apply to the physical world, unless one were to apply them in a very forced and foolish way.

**F** <margin>F</margin> <margin>VI. On the origin of love and regarding daimons.</margin> BUT WHAT should be said about Love and its generation? Indeed, we must explain what Love's mother, *Penia* <note>original: "Penia" — the personification of poverty or want.</note> (meaning Indigence), and his father, *Porus* <note>original: "Porus" — the personification of resourcefulness or plenty.</note> (meaning Affluence), represent. We must also explain how these parents are appropriate to a daimon. It is clear that these parents must also be appropriate to other daimons, for the nature and essence of all daimons—insofar as they are daimons—must be one and the same, unless the name is merely used in a general sense. Let us consider, then, how we distinguish gods from daimons. Although we often call daimons "gods," for our current purpose let us distinguish them as two different classes.

**G** <margin>G</margin> Therefore, we say and believe that the class of Gods is free from passion <term>Passion</term> <note>In Greek philosophy, "passion" (pathos) refers to being "acted upon" by emotions or external changes.</note>. To daimons, however, we attribute passions, though we say they are eternal, occupying the rank immediately following the Gods and standing closer to the human race...

### PLOTINUS' ENNEADS III.

...who are intermediate between the race of gods and humans. It is therefore worthy of consideration why **daimons** <term>Daimon: In Greek philosophy, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but powerful intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between the high gods and mortal humans.</term> did not remain free from passions but descended in nature toward the lower realm. We must also ask whether any daimon exists in the **intelligible world** <note>The "intelligible world" is the realm of pure thought and perfect Forms, existing beyond the physical universe we see.</note>, and again, whether daimons exist only in this world, while God is only in the intelligible world. Perhaps there are gods here as well, and the world (as is often said) is a "third God"; and every being up to the moon is a God.

It is certainly better not to call anyone in the intelligible world a "daimon," but even if a daimon is placed there, to consider it a God. Those who are in the **sensible world** <note>The physical world that we can perceive with our five senses.</note> up to the moon should be called "visible gods," or "secondary gods" following the intelligible gods, depending on them just as the brilliance of light depends on the stars. 

But what shall we say daimons are? Perhaps we should call a daimon the "trace" of the universal Soul as it is joined to the world. I mean the soul infused into the world, because the purer soul generates a God—and we have already said that the love of that soul is a God. But we must ask: first, why are not all daimons "Loves"? And second, how are these not also free from matter? Perhaps those daimons are "Loves" who are born from the soul desiring the good and the beautiful. Indeed, all souls in this world generate this love, but the remaining daimons are also generated by the Soul—specifically the Soul of the whole world—but they are generated by other powers of hers for the use of the universe, filling and managing individual parts for the whole. For it was necessary that the Soul of the whole should sufficiently preside over the entire world, generating powers of daimons suitable and contributing to her whole.

But in what way and of what matter do daimons participate? For they are not corporeal, otherwise they would be sensible animals. For even if they receive bodies of air or fire, their nature must still be different beforehand to become a participant in a body. For that which is entirely pure does not suddenly mix with a body, although many believe the essence of a daimon, insofar as it is a daimon, exists together with some body of air or fire. But why does the essence of daimons have commerce with the body, while the essence of the gods has none, unless there is some cause in that which mixes that contributes to the mixture? What then is the cause? One must posit an "intelligible matter," so that whatever participates in that may also come into this corporeal matter through it.

<margin>
VII
On the composition of love and the distinction regarding the multitude.
</margin>

**PLATO** therefore says that in the birth of Love, **Porus** <note>original: "Porum" — Greek for "Resource" or "Plenty." In Plato's myth, he represents the abundance of the divine realm.</note> was drunk with nectar (since wine did not yet exist), as if Love were born before the sensible world. His mother, **Penia** <note>original: "Penia" — Greek for "Poverty" or "Need." She represents the lack or longing that drives the soul to seek more.</note>, participated in the intelligible nature itself—not merely an image of that nature appearing from elsewhere, but she was present there and joined to it, as if from a specific form and a certain indefiniteness. This indefiniteness is what the soul possesses before it attains the Good; but because it divines that there is something good, it gives birth to the substance of Love according to an indefinite and unlimited image or vision.

<column-break/>

...who are between the gods and our race. How is it worthy to consider why they, being free from passion, have also descended in nature toward the worse? If it must be investigated: whether no daimon is in the intelligible, and again if in the world only daimons are, and God is defined in the intelligible; or if there are gods in this world also. And the world is a God as we are accustomed to say, a "third God," and each being up to the moon is a God.

It is better to say no one in the intelligible is a daimon, but even if one calls it a daimon there, it is a God. And again in the sensible, those up to the moon are visible gods, and gods again after those or according to those, being shadows hanging from the intelligible ones, like a radiance around each, which we call daimons. Or is a daimon a trace of the Soul as it exists in the world, a trace of each? But that which is in the world, because it is pure, becomes a God.

We have already said that the God of Love is this. Why are not all daimons Loves? And how are these also from matter, or those who are born of the soul longing for the good and the beautiful? Or do all those in this world generate this love? But the other daimons are also from the Soul of the universe, but born of other powers, according to the needs of the whole, for the filling or management of individual things. For it was necessary for the Soul of the universe to be sufficient for the whole, having generated powers of daimons suitable for its own whole. But how do they participate in matter? For they are not bodily, otherwise they would be sensible animals. For they do participate in bodies of air or fire, but their nature must first be different so that they may also participate in a body, for that which is pure is not mixed with a body. Yet it seems to many that daimons, insofar as they are daimons, participate in a body of air or fire or something else. Why is it mixed with a body? Its essence is not the cause of the mixing. What then is the cause? One must assume an intelligible matter, so that what shares in that comes also into this matter of bodies through it.

Therefore also in the generation of Love, Plato says that **Porus**, because of his drunkenness with nectar (there being no wine yet), as if Love were born before the sensible world, born upon the essence participating in an intelligible nature; not an image from there, as if appearing from there, but becoming and being mixed there, as from form and indefiniteness, which the soul has before it happens upon the good, but divining that it is something, it gives birth to the substance of Love according to an indefinite and infinite phantom.

### ON THE THIRD ENNEAD, BOOK V. <note>original: IN LIBR. V. ENNEAD. III.</note>

<margin>the</margin> Reason <note>original: Λόγος (Logos)</note>, therefore, coming to be within a reason, but in an indefinite <margin>* subsists</margin> * subsistence <note>original: ὑποστάσει (hypostasis)</note> and a dim substance, made that which was produced not perfect, but deficient—incomplete, as it came from an indefinite desire and an insufficient reason. This is not the pure Reason, <gloss>but</gloss> <margin>most deficient</margin> one having within itself an indefinite, irrational, and infinite desire; for it will never be filled so long as it has the nature of the indefinite within itself. It is dependent upon the Soul, as it is produced from her, <margin>unfillable</margin> being like an outpouring, a mixture consisting of reason and motion within it, but mixed with indefiniteness. It is not <margin>* itself</margin> * self-moving as she is, but [born] of the poverty within her. This Love <note>original: ἔρως (Eros)</note> has become a sort of fruit of this same nature; therefore, even when it attains something, it is in want again. For what it possesses is not fulfilled <gloss>because of its not</gloss> being a pure mixture; for only that which is truly full by its own nature is truly fulfilled. But this [Love], because of its composition as an image, will feel desire, and even if it is never again filled—or if it is filled by all things—it is because of its own helplessness. For every love in [natural] beings exists because of the nature of Reason, and also because of the daemonic nature—for these are my thoughts—and indeed, for the whole and for each individual, in accordance with the ancient [traditions], for whom there are sufficient things and those who desire that [higher] realm. For some, what has been generated is one thing, and for another, everything that is simple is itself, yet desiring some part of being as if it were a good. Whence those who are here [in this world] have love for the good they possess, or simply for the Good which truly exists; those who have a certain love perhaps have other fixed daimons, and different people are fixed to different daimons, those who simply and safely let go of themselves, acting as benefactors. But others are different daimons, whom they chose according to the harmonious part of the soul that acts as a benefactor within them. But those who desire evil things, by the base desires produced within them, have bound all the loves within themselves, just as they are accustomed to block the right reason by the base opinions that arise. Some loves are not [evil] by nature, but are beautiful according to nature. Those belonging to the lower soul are <margin>* otherwise</margin> lesser * in worth or power; but those of the highest soul are the most powerful and beautiful. Those that happen contrary to nature are passions of those who have stumbled, or a mixture of the soul; they are not essential substances, as they arise from the soul as additions, but they co-exist with the vice of the soul, generating similar things in certain * dispositions already. For if it is likely that subsequent things are true, when the soul acts according to nature in defined things, then being is there; but other things do not arise from the soul's own activity, and are nothing other than passions, like false thoughts, which do not have holy essences beneath them, as true, eternal, or defined things do. Thinking and being are together...

<column-break/>

**A** Reason, therefore, is not in [pure] reason, but in an indefinite appetite and a weak subsistence now made; it rendered that which was generated from it neither perfect nor sufficient, but rather unworthy, as it was generated from a certain indefinite appetite and an [insufficient] reason. This reason is by no means pure, since it has within itself an irrational and indefinite appetite; for it will never be filled as long as it possesses the nature of an indeterminate thing. **B** It depends, however, upon the soul, since it proceeds from her as if from a starting principle. It is indeed a certain mixture from reason—not remaining in itself, but mixed with infinity: for it is not reason itself, but what shines forth from it that is mixed with infinity. Love is thus like a needy son by its very nature, and therefore it is rather a thing of want. It does not have a nature that can be filled: since it is a certain mixture, and such a mixture, **C** because of what it does not possess, is not fulfilled: for only that which is already full by its own nature is truly fulfilled. But that which it lusts after because of an inborn indigence, even if it is suddenly filled, retains its defect: since the noble industry of love proceeds from indigence. The faculty of providing or supplying seems to be present because of the very nature of Reason: it is also necessary that every race of **daimons** <term>Daimon: In Plotinus, these are intermediary spirits or powers that bridge the gap between the Soul and the physical world.</term> be constituted from such things. Any of these, toward which it is ordered, has the same nature of **D** providing, supplying, and desiring; and by this logic, Love is a kinsman, being itself not full, but greedy for some particular good. From this it follows that those who are "of the good" here [in this world], the love they have is for the simply true Good itself, and not just any love. But those who are ordered according to other daimons are disposed according to one daimon or another, whom they simply possessed, now allowing for leisure, but **E** acting according to another daimon, whom they chose according to that part of the soul in harmony with the one acting in them. But those who desire evil things through depraved desires already conceived, seem to have hindered and bound all loves in themselves, just as they are accustomed to occupy right reason—if any is innate—with evil opinions contracted at some time. Therefore, the loves that are naturally present and are good according to nature—the loves of the lower soul—are lower in dignity **F** and power; but those of the higher soul are superior: finally, all are placed in essence. But those things which happen contrary to nature are certain passions of those who wander, and are in no way essences, nor are they any essential subsistences: since they are not made by the soul herself, but accompany a vice of the soul, namely, generating certain similar things according to the affection and habit contracted. **G** It is entirely probable that true goods, which the soul performs whenever she acts according to nature in things determined by reason, are essence; but other things the soul does not perform from herself, and therefore they are nothing other than passions. Just as false intelligences behave, not having essences beneath them, such as true, everlasting, and determined intelligences truly possess...

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III

possessing at the same time the act of understanding and the object of understanding, and that the "intelligible" <note>The "intelligible" refers to the realm of pure thought or ideas that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses.</note> exists not only in that which is simple, but also in every individual thing around it which is truly intelligible, and in the intellect within every species. From this arises the love within us, which reaches toward simple and universal things, because such intelligences are present within us. And if the intelligence of some particular thing is present, it seems to be there by accident; just as one understands that this specific triangle has two right angles only insofar as one understands that the "Triangle Itself" <note>The abstract Form or Idea of a triangle.</note> simply has two right angles.

BUT who then is this Jupiter in whose gardens Plato says Plenty <note>original: *Porus*</note> entered? Where are these gardens? We have already agreed that Venus is the Soul. Plenty, moreover, is the Reason <note>original: *Ratio* / *Logos*</note> of all things. It remains for us to reveal what he intends to signify by Jupiter and Jupiter’s gardens. Certainly, it must not be said that Jupiter is the Soul, since we have already conceded that Venus is the Soul. Rather, we should understand "Jupiter" here as Plato names him: in the *Phaedrus*, he is that "Great Leader," though elsewhere he is placed as the third god. But it is clearer in the *Philebus*, when he says that in Jupiter there is a "royal soul" and a "royal intellect." If, therefore, Jupiter is the great Intellect and Soul, and is ranked among the causes, he must be ranked according to that which is most excellent—both for many other reasons and because he is the Cause, the cause of the king and the leader. If this is so, Jupiter is to be understood according to the Intellect; but Venus, who belongs to him, comes from him, and is with him, will be placed according to the Soul—specifically according to that which is beautiful and splendid, and according to that which is sincere, innocent, and delicate within the soul. From all these qualities, the Soul is named Venus. Indeed, if we judge the males among the gods according to the Intellect, we name the females according to their Souls; for since a Soul is joined to every Intellect, for this reason also the Soul of Jupiter will be Venus. This is especially true as the testimonies of priests and theologians support this reasoning. For they take Venus and Juno to be of the same heart, and they call the star of Venus in the heavens the star of Juno.

<margin>

Counsel
from above.

PLENTY <note>original: *Porus*</note>, therefore, being a certain Reason <note>original: *Logos*</note> of those things which are in the intelligible world and the intellect—a Reason, I say, now more widely unfolded—must surely be around the soul and within the soul. For that which is gathered in the intellect, and does not remain in itself but passes into another, is what is signified by "Plenty" being drunk with nectar, representing abundance and fullness. But what is it that is there, filling Plenty with nectar? It is surely the Reason flowing down from a higher principle to a lower one. For this reason, this Reason is conceived by the soul from the intellect when Venus is said to be born; and while it is conceived, it is judged to flow into the gardens of Jupiter. For every garden is a place of splendor and the beauty of abundance. Indeed, the gardens of Jupiter shine with Reason, and the ornaments of Jupiter are the splendors unfolded from his own intellect into the soul.

<column-break/>

A ...possessing the intelligible, and possessing being not only in that which is simple, but also in each thing again, the intelligible is one's own, and the intellect is in each form. In each of us, we must posit the presence of intellection and the intelligible, and that this is not separated or merely simple. From this comes our love of simple things and our movement toward universals, and because in particular things [intellection is present] by accident, just as if one contemplates the two right

B angles of this triangle, it is insofar as it is simply a triangle.
BUT who is this Zeus <note>Jupiter</note>? And where is it said he entered, into whom Plenty <note>Porus</note> went? And what is the garden? If Aphrodite <note>Venus</note> is to be called the Soul by us, and Plenty is said to be the Reason of all things, then Zeus and his garden must be positioned accordingly. The soul is defined by its own traits, and this becomes Aphrodite. It is and

C will be clear in this way, following a certain Platonic Zeus: from the *Phaedrus*, which calls him the "Great Leader," though the goddess is elsewhere said to be the third. Just as in the *Philebus*, when he says there is in Zeus a royal soul and a royal intellect. If Zeus is the Great Cause and Soul, and Intellect is ranked among the causes—and because the "Better" exists through this for

D other reasons, and because it is the Cause, and the Royal, and the Leading—then he exists according to the Intellect. Aphrodite, being his, and from him and with him, shall be ranked according to the Soul, named Aphrodite according to the beauty, the brilliance, the innocence, and the delicacy of the soul. Or, if we rank the males of the gods according to the Intellect, and those called females according to their souls, as each

E intellect dwells with a soul. If this soul is Plenty, or Aphrodite: again, the words of priests and theologians bear witness to this account, for they treat Hera <note>Juno</note> and Aphrodite as the same, and they say the star of Aphrodite is also that of Hera.
Plenty, then, being the Reason <note>Logos</note> of all things there in the Intellect, and being more poured out—as if from the sensible toward the soul—would be around the soul and in the soul. For

F that which is coiled together in the intellect, and not lost, is that which, when he is drunk, brings the quality of fullness. But what would the nectar be that fills him there, if not the Reason falling from a higher principle into a lower one? The Soul is this, and he who says that Plenty is said to have become Aphrodite [meaning the Reason of Aphrodite] has rushed into his garden. Every garden is a thing of splendor, and wealth

G is an adornment; the "uncovered things" <note>The manifest truths</note> of Zeus are splendors. These adornments are the splendors that have come from the Intellect of Zeus into his Soul.

**BOOK SIX.**

<margin>A</margin> What could the things in the garden of Zeus be—or his statues and splendors—except his ornaments, or the reasons <note>original Greek: *logoi*; here referring to the rational principles or "blueprints" of reality</note> that flow from him? Together, these reasons are called "Plenty" <note>original Greek: *Porus*; representing resourcefulness and abundance</note>, or the absence of difficulty, and the wealth of beautiful things already made clear. This is what it means to be "intoxicated with nectar." For what is nectar to the gods but that which the divine nature receives? What is received is the Intellect <note>original Greek: *nous*</note> that underlies it; and the Intellect possesses itself in a state of fullness. One who is "intoxicated" possesses this, and this "intoxication" is the Reason
<margin>B</margin> that is the offspring and substantial reality <note>original Greek: *hypostasis*</note> after the Intellect. These things do not exist within the Intellect itself, but in another—namely, they are said to lie in the "Garden of Zeus." This "lying" occurs when Venus <note>original: *Aphroditē*</note> is said to have her substantial reality. One must take these myths as they are: they divide what they tell into different times, and separate
<margin>C</margin> many things that exist simultaneously, yet differ in their order or their powers. Where "reasons" <note>logoi</note> and lineages are concerned, they create "births" for things that were never actually born, and they distinguish things that exist together. After they have taught as best they can, they allow the one who has understood to bring these elements back together. This gathering together shows the Soul existing with the Intellect,
<margin>unseparated</margin> standing as a reality derived from it, full of Reason and decorated with beauty,
<margin>D</margin> filled with sights so that one may see many splendors and images of all beautiful things within it. This whole is Venus. If all the "reasons" are within her, then "Plenty" <note>Porus</note> is the sum of them, flowing from the heights of the nectar there. The splendors within her, insofar as they lie within Life, are called "The Garden of Zeus." There, Plenty is said to lie, burdened by the life that has appeared. If anyone is among these things, they are called "gods" because they exist in that same blessedness. But what lies outside of that
<margin>E</margin> <margin>perhaps</margin> exists by necessity. From the Soul’s inclination toward what is better and good, Love <note>original: *Erōs*</note> arises. Love is a mixed thing, partaking in need (insofar as it wishes to be filled), but not without resource (insofar as it seeks what it lacks). If something were entirely devoid of the Good, it would never seek the Good.
<margin>F</margin> Thus, Love is said to be born of Plenty and Poverty <note>original: *Penia*</note>. For the combination of defect, desire, and the memory of the "reasons" <note>logoi</note> coming together in the Soul produced the activity directed toward the Good—and this is Love. His mother is Poverty because desire belongs to one who is in need. Matter is itself Poverty, because matter is in need of everything. And the indefinite nature of the desire for the Good is a kind of shapeless thing,
<margin>G</margin> not yet a "reason." In this desiring subject, the desire makes it more like "matter." But the form itself remains only within itself, while the desiring subject seeks to receive it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For what else can the gardens of Jupiter signify, than his images and splendors? What, again, are the splendors and ornaments of Jupiter, if not the reasons <note>original Latin: *rationes* / Greek: *logoi*</note> flowing from him? At the same time, these reasons are called Plenty <note>original: *Porus*</note>, that is, a happy abundance and a treasury of divine and most beautiful things already shining forth openly and clearly. Truly, this is what it is to become celebrated through nectar. For what else is nectar among the gods, but that which a god drinks? That which is subject to the mind drinks the reason of the mind; moreover, the Mind <note>original: *Mens* / *Nous*</note> attains its own fullness.
<margin>B</margin> And since it now possesses this fullness, it is rightly said to be intoxicated—precisely because it contains nothing foreign. Reason, however, is the offspring of the mind, existing after the mind, no longer existing of itself but "lying in another," in the "garden of Jupiter" (as it is said). This happens at the time when the birth of Venus is celebrated—that is, when Venus is born. It is necessary for myths, if they are to be myths and not far from the truth, to divide the times of their narration and to segregate from one another many things
<margin>C</margin> which are actually simultaneous in time, but differ in their order and power. For instance, rational arguments and discourses are accustomed to introduce "births" for things that are unbegotten, and to distinguish things that exist together. After they have taught to the best of their ability, they usually allow those who will understand to reconnect what they had divided. Our highest connection in this present matter is of this kind: the Soul existing together with the Mind and standing as a reality from the Mind itself; being once again imbued with reasons from here, and very beautifully
<margin>D</margin> adorned by its beauties, and luxuriating in abundance, so that within it one may now behold various splendors and the likenesses of all beautiful things. This whole is considered to be Venus herself. All the "reasons" <note>logoi</note> within her are called Plenty <note>Porus</note>—that is, a happy abundance flowing from the celestial nectar. But the splendors in her, insofar as they shine in Life itself, are called "the gardens of Jupiter." It is there that Plenty is said to lie, now heavy with the things with which he is said to be imbued. When Life shines in the order of things—or rather, since it always shines—the gods are judged
<margin>E</margin> by their distinction of union, as those who enjoy such a happy state. Love <note>original: *Amor* / *Erōs*</note>, however, has necessarily always existed for as long as the Soul has, proceeding from the Soul's appetite for the higher Good. It is a mixed thing: participating in indigence, insofar as it affects to be filled; yet not without resource, insofar as it demands the remainder of what it already has. If it were entirely devoid of the Good, it would never seek the Good. For this reason, it is said to have arisen from both Affluence and Penury <note>original: *Penia*</note>. Since
<margin>F</margin> defect and appetite, together with the memory of the "reasons," conspire in the Soul, they have generated the act toward the Good which is called Love. His mother is Penury, because appetite always belongs to the one who is in need. Matter is Penury itself, because matter is destitute of all things. Furthermore, the indeterminate nature of the appetite turning toward the Good declares that very thing which it hungers for, insofar as
<margin>G</margin> the hungering subject takes the place of matter. For neither form nor reason yet exists in that which hungers for the Good; it looks toward it, but is only a species remaining in itself, while at the same time desiring to receive its own nature, which is yet to receive the Good.

# THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO ON
# THE SIXTH BOOK OF THE THIRD EN-
# NEAD: THAT INCORPO-
# REAL THINGS DO NOT SUFFER.

### SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE BOOK.

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial "S" featuring scrolling floral patterns.</image-desc>
THE SUMMARY of this book is to assert that an incorporeal thing cannot "suffer" <note>term: *passio* (passion/suffering). In this philosophical context, it refers to "being acted upon" or undergoing a change caused by an external force, rather than emotional suffering.</note>. He defines an incorporeal thing as that which either includes no quantity in its own definition (even though it may seem to receive it from the outside), such as "matter" <note>term: *materia prima*; the underlying "stuff" of the universe that has no form of its own</note>; or that which entirely excludes quantity, such as the Mind and the Soul. Furthermore, he maintains that "passion" is a change capable of destroying a substance, whether it occurs through division (as happens to physical quantities and things that necessarily possess quantity) or through alteration (as happens between opposing qualities and the forms that such qualities accompany). Therefore, both primary matter and the soul are incorporeal things, claiming for themselves neither quantity nor physical quality, and are thus separated from "passion"—and the soul even more so than matter. For the soul not only refuses to admit destructive forms, but it does not even seem to receive new forms of any kind. Consequently, much is disputed in the following pages regarding the immutable essence of the rational soul and its parts, as well as the essence of the First [Principle], and many things regarding its opposite—namely, primary matter—all to confirm that an incorporeal thing is exempt from being acted upon.

*The Soul neither suffers, nor does it receive forms or qualities. Likewise, on the twofold imagination.*

In the first part of the book, then, which contains five chapters, he shows that the soul is not subject to passion; in the second part, he will then show something similar regarding matter. As far as the first part is concerned, he observes that no impulse or quality from physical bodies falls upon the soul's power of knowing. For if it fell upon the soul in a material way (if I may put it that way), knowledge and discernment would be immediately confused; or if bodies formed the soul through some kind of imaginary condition, it would be a sin to say so: for it is the role of the soul, as the superior, to form bodies, not to be formed by them. Truly, every cognition and affection of the soul, even when reaching toward bodily things, is a certain *action* of the soul regarding such things, and it does not "suffer" or undergo change from them in the meantime. For it is not fitting for the soul to be mixed with bodies in matter, a commotion which usually causes some exchange of "passion" in the agent. What, then, is perception? It is indeed the soul applying its own senses and deploying its power toward those things with which it has a harmonious and naturally fit essence; similarly, to remember is to perform this very same action with great readiness. Therefore, no power of knowing is formed by "new images," but the Intellect is always in a state of "act" <note>The philosophical distinction between "potency" (the potential to do something) and "act" (the actual doing or being).</note> through the very way it knows. Reason and imagination, however, move from a state of potentiality into "act" regarding the things they must think out, becoming in "act" those things that are always in "act" within the Intellect. The external sense perceives things to be sensed, but does not "receive" them. The vegetative power nourishes and moves, yet is not itself moved in the process. All these things are confirmed by Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a major Neoplatonic philosopher.</note>, who shows that when the soul is said to "suffer," this very passion is not any alteration in its nature or some quality, but a certain accommodation and affection of the soul toward this or that thing; it is an action of the soul toward external things, but a "narrow" one—specifically, when the soul itself contracts the affection and amplitude of its powers toward something narrow. Porphyry concludes that all things called "movements" of the soul are not properly movements in the soul, but in the body; in the soul they are actions, while in the body those same things become passions. He adds that the acts of vegetation, sense, and memory are not imaginary, but in a way natural, just as heating, being hot, illuminating, and shining are; Plotinus holds the same view. Note, meanwhile, that virtue in the soul is generally twofold: one kind is, as it were, "private," belonging specifically to one of the soul's parts (this is when any part rightly performs its duty); the other is "public," where all parts harmonize rightly with each other, reason is governed by the mind, and the irrational powers obey the reason (among which desire is subject to boldness). Neither virtue is like a quality impressed upon the soul as if on a subject—likewise with vice—but it is rather like movement, act, and the calling forth of a habit. If there is any "quality" in us, either impressed on the image of the soul by nature or acquired by actions, such a thing is not in the soul, but rather in the body, which is properly affected, and in which forms, unions, and "passions" occur while the soul vegetates, senses, acts, and judges. In short, no change occurs in the soul except a progression from potentiality into act; and this is not from another mover, but from the soul itself; nor is it into an "act" that arrives like a quality, but one that flows forth as an activity. If in any part the soul is called "passive," it is not understood as a subject for bodily passions, but as the *principle* [source] of those passions. Observe again a twofold imagination in us: the first is in the rational soul, capable of discourse and judgment, somewhat similar to reason; the second is impressed by the first into the soul or "life" within us that lacks reason, which surely utilizes "images" not so much by discourse, but is carried by instinct, however intimate; but regarding the passions of the body, which [are] as if...

<meta>catchword: communi (common)</meta>

<summary>This page introduces Plotinus’s argument that the soul and matter are "impassive," meaning they cannot be altered or harmed by physical forces. Ficino explains that while the body undergoes "passion" (being acted upon), the soul only performs "actions" and remains essentially unchanged in its nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plotinus’s *Ennead* III.6. Ficino is expanding on the "impassibility" (the inability to be affected or changed by external forces) of the soul and matter, transitioning into a discussion on how life and intellect relate to the hierarchy of being.</meta>

-> ON BOOK VI OF THE THIRD ENNEAD <-

The common sense <note>term: *communis sensus*; the internal faculty that unifies the data from the five individual senses into a single perception</note> is the principle of the remaining senses. Plotinus sometimes, by a certain metaphor, places imagination even in the vegetative part of the soul <note>The "vegetative" or plant-like soul is the lowest level of the soul, responsible for growth and nutrition</note>; however, this is not a discursive imagination that moves through forms like the first kind, nor is it an intuitive grasp of form like the second. Instead, it is the expression of a form flourishing within itself, and through this impression, it acts upon matter. Here, natural action is like a kind of substantial imagination acting, though not by "imagining" in the usual sense. It is also notable that from the abundant faculty of the soul, the power of desiring sprouts and transcends, just as from the intellect a higher reason flowed forth, and subsequently the first imagination, from which the second also flowed.

### That Life and Intellect are contained in true essence: Also concerning the One which is above essence, and concerning the One which is below it.

In the sixth chapter, you will note that "true being" <note>original: *ens verum*</note> is that which is being in every respect—that is, a thing which lacks nothing necessary for the perfection of its essence. Truly perfect essence includes the intimate and perennial act of itself, which is Life; and indeed, being most intimate, Essence demands this. Such is the case if it be Intelligence: for this is Life reflecting back into Essence. Therefore, from the first Essence, as if from a root, Life and Intellect sprout together into themselves. But a "shoot" of this kind is born to exist only insofar as it possesses fertility from the Good itself, just as two branches of a vine might draw from the sun. Moreover, so that this faculty may be distinguished into Life and Intellect properly speaking, it proceeds from that very Essence—as if from the vine itself—but is determined into two by the power of the unique Sun <note>The "Sun" here is a common Platonic metaphor for "The Good" or "The One"</note>. Thus, the modes of living, understanding, and the like, proceed from the Good itself as the most common principle and end, but they flow from the first Essence itself as their proper root and a kind of formal power. 

Accordingly, Plotinus here accepts as "true being" and "true essence" not only Being itself—the head of all beings—but also every form that has its own being and exists in its own essence, and is therefore separable from matter. In such being, there is no potentiality or inclination toward "not-being," nor any mixture of an alien nature. Nothing necessary for its existence is lacking; the power of the species is always reduced to act, so that, in turn, Life and Intellect are included equally with Essence. All Intellects and intellectual Souls are of this kind, counted within the genus of what is becoming. For sensible forms <note>Forms perceived by the physical senses</note>, which are inseparable from matter, are called "untrue beings" for reasons contrary to those we have stated here. Since matter stands at a much greater distance from the first form of things than do sensible forms, and since even these are called "untrue beings," it is no wonder that matter itself is customarily called "true non-being" by Plotinus and Porphyry <note>Porphyry was Plotinus's student and the editor of the *Enneads*</note>: for it includes nothing formal in itself, but utterly excludes it. 

To be "being," however, is the gift of Form; for the first Essence is the same as the first Form, which is naturally all-formed. To this discussion we must bring the things said of the "One" in the *Parmenides* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the nature of the One and the Many</note>—where it is sometimes denied and sometimes affirmed—and what is said in the *Sophist* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning being and non-being</note> about being and non-being. Therefore, the "One" will be understood in three principal ways: either as that which seems equated with being; or that which is higher than being; or that which is lower. Regarding the One that is equal to being—specifically the first Being itself—all species and properties of things are affirmed equally. For it is the source of all beings and their exemplar. Of this it is usually said: it is the same and the other, stable and mobile, equal and unequal, great and small, and so on. For here reside the ideal "reasons" <note>term: *rationes*; the divine blueprints or Ideas</note> of all things. Regarding the supreme One, however, all these things are similarly denied here: for there, it is not the *form* of these things, but their *cause*. Finally, regarding the lowest One—that is, matter—all these things are equally denied: for it possesses nothing formal in its own nature.

### That natural things are not true beings, and that matter is called non-being, and seems to hold forms like a mirror, which it does not truly possess.

Among these points, where he says that natural things do not so much *exist* in reality as they *seem to exist*, he introduces a certain Epicurean objection <note>The Epicureans were materialists who believed only physical bodies were real</note>. This objection contends that only corporeal things possess true essence, which is evident from two points: first, because by their solidity they resist whatever would divide them, and second, because they strike objects with great force. 

It is answered to the first point that such hard bodies, while they seem to resist, are merely exposed longer to the one striking them and wait for the blow because they are most inept at fleeing. Because of this same ineptitude for motion, they are ineffective by nature; once they are divided into parts, they cannot return to their prior form. Truly subtle bodies <note>e.g., air, light, or spiritual substances</note>, when they seem to yield to a blow, escape the suffering <note>term: *passio*; being acted upon or changed</note> very quickly due to their marvelous efficacy, and by that same efficacy they suddenly return into themselves. Finally, since motion in things is a certain action, and life is most often an indicator of the interior, and there is a vestige of life everywhere, those things which are least corporeal are the most ready for motion. It follows that insofar as things approach an incorporeal nature, they approach a life capable of change and efficacy, and therefore approach true essence; but corporeal things fall away from essence. 

In this part, a similar answer is given to the second point—namely, that corporeal things hurt more when they fall upon something. This is not because they are firmer, but because they are utterly weak, so much so that they cannot sustain themselves; therefore, by their very collapse, they harm whatever is nearby. For those who are most inept at horsemanship are the ones who most press and tire the horses; and fainting bodies are usually the most burdensome to those carrying them. 

After this, remember that matter is an empty shadow of the first essence, while material forms are various images of the Ideas contained in the first essence. These images have no similarity in nature to the Ideas, although in the effect of representation they may seem to have some likeness. Matter is like a mirror: while it receives images—or perhaps does not even receive them but only *seems* to receive them—it actually suffers nothing <note>It undergoes no fundamental change in its own nature</note>. This is especially true because matter, being the ultimate limit, cannot be resolved into anything else, and therefore cannot "suffer" change. Indeed, no form is contrary to matter; it is exposed equally and naturally to all forms. Therefore, it can suffer from none, since things in matter are not acted upon by just anything, but only by their contraries. 

Furthermore, if matter were by its own nature "familiarly" multiform, it would no longer be the most common substrate, equally formable by all things. Just as the subject-substance must remain the same in any alteration while qualities are exchanged, so much more is it necessary for matter to remain permanent in the transformations of the world. Finally, since the goodness of nature by no means allows something substantial to be resolved into nothingness, and simple substances cannot be resolved into anything else, it is right that neither self-subsisting simple forms nor simple matter can ever perish or suffer. Matter, since it is "evil" <note>term: *malum*; defined here as being at the furthest possible distance from the Good</note>—that is, most distant from the Good itself—does not desire the Good so as to claim something natural for itself, but so that it may put on a certain "imagination" as a garment and thus deceive. The more it remains in its own formlessness, the more "evil" it is. Matter itself does not become hot; rather, the composite <note>The physical object made of matter and form</note> becomes hot. Matter itself merely sustains the heat, and when the heat is set aside like a garment, matter's nature is not changed in the least. Again, when something is divided, it is the quantity (and what follows quantity) that is divided, not the matter, which precedes quantity in nature.

Ficino refutes Epicurean materialism, arguing that the solidity of physical bodies is a sign of weakness and inertia rather than true existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, specifically exploring the relationship between matter, form, and the Soul. Ficino here uses the metaphor of light and mirrors to explain how the physical world is merely a reflection of divine reality.</meta>

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

*Just as in the sequence of colors, the last—which is blackness—possesses nothing of the first—which is whiteness—so matter, being the very last in the descent of beings, possesses nothing within itself similar to the First <note>In Neoplatonic thought, "the First" refers to the One or God, the source of all existence.</note>, nor does it behold anything of the nature of the First in its appearance, except for certain empty imitations. And because of its extreme difference from the First, matter does not claim for itself any "flavor" or "scent" of being from the presence of those divine images in a way that is familiar to it; thus, it is equally ready to receive any forms that may arrive in the future, no matter how much they might conflict with previous ones. You will observe this most especially: that natural things, if compared with divine things, have no greater substance than the images of bodies appearing in mirrors. These natural things depend perpetually on the divine in the same way that reflections depend on the objects they mirror. This is the point of that saying of Solomon: "All is vanity" <note>Ecclesiastes 1:2. Original Latin: *Omnia vanitas*.</note>. It is also the point of Paul’s words: "We see now through a mirror, in an enigma" <note>1 Corinthians 13:12. Original Latin: *Vidimus nunc per speculum in ænigmate*.</note>. But because we now see both the bodies and the mirror—on which the images entirely depend—we perceive the vanity of the images themselves within that idea; otherwise, if we did not see the original objects, we could not refute the reality of the reflection. Instead, we would judge the images to be true things. So it is now: because we call natural things "true substances," we believe they are real, since we can see neither the divine things nor the matter from which these things leap forth and bounce back like statues from objects into a mirror. Indeed, either the images in the mirror are real (as the natural philosophers believe), or, as the most skilled teachers pass down, there are no images in mirrors at all, but rather the "rays" of things fall upon the mirror and are reflected from there back to the eyes. This happens when they are reflected at equal angles; then the things themselves are returned to the eyes through these rays in such a way that the sense is deceived, thinking it sees the thing elsewhere than where it actually is. However the matter stands, Plotinus and Porphyry <note>Porphyry was Plotinus’s student and the editor of the *Enneads*.</note> maintain that the relationship of the mirror to visible things and sight is the same as the relationship of matter to divine things and sense. They believe that matter is entirely opposite to Being itself; it does not admit the rays and acts of the first Being into its interior, but because of its "density" and its difference from Being, it is impassable, and it immediately strikes back <note>or "reflects"</note> their acts. By this very reverberation, there appear to the senses things that seem sensible <note>term: *sensibilia*; things that can be perceived by the physical senses</note>, though in themselves they are intelligible <note>term: *intelligibilia*; things that can only be understood by the mind/intellect</note>. We are led to think that those things which exist in the First Being and the Intellect actually "stain" or color matter, and from there they move the soul to know them. Finally, since the lowest parts of Being, while they act upon matter, lose nothing of their nature, nor are they moved from their state, nor do they agree with matter in proportion or character, therefore whatever appears to be given to matter is like a weak and empty void. Matter always needs this "seat" or foundation, and meanwhile, because it never receives anything true, nor even seems to receive anything of any quality (due to its natural falsity), it is never filled; instead, it always provides the occasion for the perpetual urges of transformation.*

-> How much the soul transcends matter, and how a certain quantity of matter follows the mode of any species entering into matter. <-

*When this piece of wood is said to be "outside" that piece of wood, these two are not greatly separated from each other, since they are joined by species <note>i.e., they both belong to the category "wood"</note> and are only separated by external boundaries. Fire is further "outside" water: for they are separated not only by external boundaries but by contrary qualities. However, because they agree in genus and are both made of matter, they can sometimes be mixed. But the soul is separated from matter by its entire genus; therefore, no matter how much it penetrates matter, it remains far "outside" of it. Thus, the soul cannot reconcile matter to itself, nor mix with it, even though it visits the forms it received from the Divine Intellect and translates them everywhere into matter through a "seed-like power" <note>term: *virtus seminaria*; the creative, formative power that allows the World Soul to manifest divine ideas into physical reality</note>. Furthermore, just as matter is by its own nature devoid of all forms, so too is it devoid of quantity; for quantity is itself a certain form. And since quantity is the last of the forms, a certain specific quantity and shape is destined for matter by the Mind and the Soul, following the mode of the species. Therefore, in the "formal reasons" <note>term: *rationes formales*; the internal logical blueprints of things</note> of the species existing in the Mind and Soul, there is included and defined a certain quantity and figure that accompanies each species. In the formal reason of a "man" or a "horse," the quantity of a man or a horse is decreed. This quantity is released into effect because of the power of the formal reason, and a certain specific motion in action, and because of the procession of the natural form emanating from it. This effectiveness and motion produces a mass upon the face of matter, specifically as much quantity as the form itself demands: the world-form produces a world-sized mass, the human-form a human size, the lion-form a lion size. And just as one quantity comes into matter with its own quality and species, so it departs together with that species. Upon the subsequent arrival of a new species, a new quantity is made; just as the specific quality of the species is produced, so an extended quantity is produced in matter according to the distance from the quantity of the acting power and the formal motion. Matter, in its weakness, cannot avoid this kind of motion, nor can it receive forms without such a distension. But the Soul, since it is itself a certain form and a subsisting species, embraces all the species of things as if in a single center. For this form <note>the soul</note> receives those other forms in the "mode of a form": and the mode of forms is such that each one is collected as a simple whole within any part of itself, and all are easily concluded within each other. From this it follows that our reason can comprehend forms both without numerical multitude (in the unity of the species) and separated from the dimension of quantity. But matter always receives forms with a certain extension, because it is drawn everywhere by the motion of the form proceeding divinely upon it; meanwhile, its nature willingly yields to this stretching and is ready for any mass anywhere, since it possesses no mass of its own. And while it is extended through the whole space of the world in dimension, it is not divided into many "matters" but remains unique and continuous—partly because it is not subject to suffering <note>or "being affected"</note> and partly because it follows the power of the one who extends it, which exists from one "reason" toward one form of the universe. This matter is, as it were, the mother of the world, and even less than a mother. But the father is that ancient Mercury <note>Ficino identifies Mercury/Hermes with the mediating reason or *Logos* that shapes the world.</note>, whom they wish to be both the "seed-like reason" of the world within the nature of the World Soul, and also the "ideal reason" of all things in the Divine Mind. In truth, the ideal reason is the father of the universe, but the seed-like reason is the mother, insofar as it has some commerce with matter and is filled from above. Matter, however, is the matrix and the place of generation and the receptacle. You, however, must remember that in the planet Mercury there is both the gift of contemplation from the Divine Mind and the gift of action from the nature of the world; and from this, he gives a genius <note>term: *ingenium*; natural talent or spirit</note> suited either for those who contemplate or for actions and arts, or sometimes one that is vigorous in both. If he looks upon Saturn in a trine or sextile aspect <note>These are favorable astrological alignments of 120 and 60 degrees.</note>, or occupies Saturn’s house, he favors contemplation above all; if he looks upon Mars, he breathes more toward action; if Jupiter, he breathes successfully upon both duties; if he gazes at Venus, he designates a sweetness of talent and eloquence along with ornament.*

<summary>Ficino uses the analogy of a mirror to explain that the physical world is an "empty imitation" of divine reality. He argues that matter has no inherent size or quality but is shaped and "stretched" into specific quantities by the World Soul and the planetary influence of Mercury.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "impassibility" of the soul—the idea that the soul, being a spiritual substance, cannot be physically changed or "wounded" by the material world. Having established that sensations are judgments rather than physical imprints, Plotinus now examines whether moral virtues and vices represent actual changes in the soul’s substance.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD III.
### BOOK VI.

A Since the soul is incorruptible, we must be careful not to grant it passions <note>Original: *passiones* (Latin) / *pathē* (Greek). In this context, it refers to "undergoing change" or "suffering an effect" from the outside.</note> of a kind that might accidentally suggest it is subject to decay. Truly, if its essence is number or reason <note>Original: *ratio* (Latin) / *logos* (Greek). Plotinus is exploring the Pythagorean and Platonic idea that the soul is a mathematical or logical structure.</note> (as we are accustomed to say), how could any passion happen to a number or a reason? Instead, we should consider "irrational reasons" and "impassible passions" to be terms transferred to the soul from the body. These must be understood by opposition B and through an analogical proportion, so that when we say the soul "has" these things, it does not truly possess them, and when it "suffers," it does not truly undergo change. We must reflect on what the nature of such a state actually is.

<margin>II
What virtue is, what depravity is, and that they are not qualities in the soul, but different paths.</margin>
FIRST, we must speak of virtue and vice, and what occurs when vice is said to be present in the soul. We often say that one ought to "remove" something from a wicked person, as if there were some actual "evil" residing within them; likewise, we speak of adding virtue and oratory, replacing C foulness with beauty. If we say that virtue is a certain consonance <note>Original: *consonantia* (Latin) / *harmonia* (Greek). This refers to a musical or structural harmony between parts.</note> and vice is a dissonance, are we bringing forward an opinion consistent with the ancients? Furthermore, will this lead us to what we seek? For if virtue is simply this—that the parts of the soul are in harmony with each other according to nature—and vice is their discord, then nothing "extra" or external comes into us. Rather, each part will enter into harmony by being exactly what it is in itself. Nor will a part enter into dissonance by changing its nature, D just as dancers in a troupe might dance and sing together in harmony, even if they are not the same individuals, or just as a single singer might sing while others are silent. For it is not only necessary for them to sing together, but for each to sing their own proper music correctly according to their own role. Thus, in the soul, harmony exists when each part performs what is E natural to it. Indeed, before this harmony can exist, there must be a specific virtue for each individual part, just as there must be a specific depravity before there is mutual discord. In what presence, then, is a part made "bad"? Perhaps by the presence of depravity. And "good" by the presence of virtue? In the rational part, if one admits that ignorance is its depravity—an "un-knowing" defined by the absence of knowledge—this does not imply the presence of any new thing. But when false opinions are present (which specifically create vice), what prevents something from "becoming" inside the soul, F and thus that part of the soul being changed into a different quality? Furthermore, is the nature of anger not affected differently when it is cowardly compared to when it is brave? Likewise, is the power of desire not disposed differently when it is intemperate compared to when it is temperate? Perhaps, whenever a part is judged to possess virtue, it acts according to that essence by which it exists; and we say this is "to obey reason." G The rational faculty is guided by the intellect, and the remaining parts are guided by reason. Perhaps "obeying reason" is like "seeing": while the part obeys and sees, it is not physically shaped or molded, but it looks upon its object and exists in activity when it sees.

<column-break/>

A Since she possesses incorruptibility, one must be cautious about attributing such passions to her, lest we inadvertently declare her corruptible. If her essence is indeed number and reason <note>Original: *logos*.</note>, as we say, how could a passion occur in a number or a reason? Rather, we should think of her as receiving "reasonless reasons" and "impassible passions"—terms B transferred from the body. Each must be understood as an opposite and by analogy. To "have" is not to possess, and "to suffer" or "passion" must be examined to see what its true mode is.

FIRST, we must speak regarding vice and virtue, and what this becomes when vice is said to be present. Do we say we must "take away" something, as if some C wicked evil were in her, and conversely "add" virtue and order, and "bring in" beauty instead of ugliness? If we say that harmony <note>Original: *harmonia*.</note> is required, and that vice is a lack of harmony, would this be an opinion accepted by the ancients and relevant to our inquiry? Or does the argument suggest nothing unless this temperance is a kind of fitting together of the soul's parts according to nature? If vice is a discord, then each part D must be its own virtue for the harmony to exist. For even in strings, if they do not sound together, it is because one sings what it is while others do not; it is not only necessary to sing together, but for each to sing its own part well with its own music. Thus, in the E harmony of the soul, each part must perform its own task. But before this harmony, there must be another virtue or vice for each part, prior to their discord with one another. By what presence is each part "bad" or "good"? In the rational part, one might say that "folly" is its vice—an ignorance defined by negation. F But when false opinions are also present, which most especially create vice, how can this not be a change in nature? Is it not that the part becomes something else? The spirited part <note>Original: *thymoeides*. This refers to the part of the soul associated with courage, anger, and "will."</note> is in one state when cowering and another when being brave. The desiring part is in one state when it is G intemperate and another when it is temperate. Or is it that when each is in a state of virtue, it acts according to the essence that it is? And we shall say this is "in accordance with reason." The rational part is led from above <note>By the Divine Intellect.</note>, and the other parts are also led from above by their ordering. To be "persuaded by reason" is like seeing: the soul is not shaped into a form, but sees and is in activity when it sees.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul remains "impassible" or unchanged in its essence, even when experiencing virtue or vice. He suggests that moral failings are not "added" qualities but are instead like a musical discord where parts fail to perform their natural functions or "see" the truth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "impassibility" of the soul. Having previously argued that the soul does not "suffer" physical change when it perceives or thinks, he now uses the analogy of sight and memory to prove that mental activities are "actualizations" of the soul’s inherent power, rather than external imprints or physical alterations.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

Just as sight is either in potentiality or in activity, it remains the same in its essence. Its activity is not an **alteration**, but a simultaneous application toward that which it is suited for by nature; it sees and knows without being "affected" <note>Original: *apathōs* (Greek) / *procul à passione* (Latin). This means the soul knows things without being physically changed or "wounded" by the object it perceives.</note>. Even the faculty of reasoning relates to the intellect in this way: it sees, and the power of understanding is such that it does not receive internal impressions as if from a seal. Rather, it "has" what it sees, and yet in another sense, it does not "have" it. It "has" it by the act of knowing; it "does not have" it because no physical thing is brought in from the vision to be imprinted there, as a shape is formed in wax. We must remember that memory is not a warehouse for keeping imprinted shapes, but a power of the soul that awakens itself so that it "possesses" even what it does not physically hold. Why then? Was it one thing before it remembered, and another when it remembers? You may call it "different" if you like, but do not call it **altered**, unless you define "alteration" as the progress from potentiality into activity. For nothing new is added; it simply performs what it is naturally able to do. Generally, the actions of immaterial things do not occur in a way that the acting powers are themselves altered—otherwise, they would perish. Instead, they act by remaining exactly as they are. While it is common for a physical agent to "suffer" or be changed while acting <note>For example, a hammer hits a nail and also feels the vibration/resistance.</note>, an immaterial thing that acts <margin>The soul is not the subject of bodily passions, but their principle.</margin> **has no place to receive such a change.** Just as in the act of looking, while the vision is the "actor," it is the eye that "suffers" the physical effect. Opinions are like these visions. And what of the "spirited" nature <note>The *thymoeides*, or the part of the soul associated with anger and courage.</note>—how is it cowardly or brave? Perhaps it is cowardly because it either does not look toward Reason, or it looks toward a corrupted Reason, or perhaps because of a defect in its "instruments"—that is, a weakness or decay in the bodily "armor" that prevents it from acting or being stirred. It is brave if the opposite is true. In these cases, there is no internal alteration or **suffering**. Likewise, the power of desire brings about "excess" only when it acts alone. Every power sometimes acts alone when the other parts of the soul are not present to take their turn in commanding or restraining it. That which is engaged in seeing sometimes does something else; it does not do everything at once, but pauses in one area to contemplate another as best it can. Perhaps what we call "vice" is mostly just a poor condition <note>Original: *kakexia* (Greek). A medical term for a "bad habit of body," here applied to the soul's moral state.</note> of the body, while virtue is the **opposite condition**. Therefore, no actual addition is made to the soul in either case.

<column-break/>

**A** Just as sight exists both in potentiality and in activity, it is one and the same essence. Its activity, however, is not a change of nature, but a simultaneous application of itself to that which its essence is already suited for; it discerns and knows far removed from any "passion" <note>Here "passion" is used in the technical sense of *passio*—the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>. Furthermore, the faculty of reasoning stands in relation to the intellect just as sight does. The potential for understanding is a thing of this kind: not that it receives impressions from a seal within itself, but that it holds what it sees, and then again does not hold it. **B** It holds it by the fact that it knows, but it does not hold it in the sense that nothing brought from the spectacle is imprinted there, as a form is usually made in wax. It is necessary to remember that memory is also not a kind of guard for imprinted forms, but a certain faculty of the soul that rouses itself so that it "possesses" even what it does not physically have. What then? Was it not different before it remembered, and different again when it now remembers? If it pleases you to call it "different," do not however say **C** it is "altered," unless someone perhaps names "alteration" as a certain progression from potentiality into activity. Nevertheless, nothing is added there; rather, the soul effects what it is naturally able to do. In general, the actions of immaterial things do not happen in such a way that the very powers that act are altered in the process—otherwise they would even be destroyed—but rather they produce their effects by remaining constant. That the "agent" should "suffer" while acting is usually a condition of things that exist alongside matter. But in that which is immaterial, **D** there is no "substrate" in which a change could stay. Just as in the act of looking, while the vision is the acting force, it is the eye that undergoes the physical effect. Opinions are like certain visions. But how is the nature of anger "cowardly," and in what way is it "brave"? Perhaps it is cowardly because it either does not look at Reason, or it looks at a Reason that is already bad, or through a fault of its "instruments" (such as a lack of tension or a breakdown of the bodily weapons), or it is prohibited from acting, or is not incited. It is brave, however, if the opposite conditions occur. In these, there is no alteration, no **E** suffering. Again, the power of desire itself, whenever it acts alone, brings about intemperance. For every part sometimes acts alone, and then the rest are not present—those parts which, when present, are allowed to take turns overcoming and commanding. That which is occupied in seeing sometimes does something else; for it does not do all things, but is at leisure in some respects because it may be contemplating other things as far as it is able. Perhaps a "bad habit" <note>Referring to *kakexia*, a poor physical or mental disposition.</note> of the body is most often the "depravity" of this part, while virtue is the **F** contrary habit. Therefore, no addition is made to the soul from either side.

<margin>The soul is not the subject of bodily passions, but their principle.</margin>
**G** ->THE DISPOSITIONS AND ALTERATIONS,<-
The question was asked: how are harmonies, disharmonies, pains, angers, pleasures, desires, and fears not "permutations" and "passions" that move the inner self? One must certainly distinguish these things by denying they are alterations. That we experience violent sensations is manifest to everyone; what must be sought is what it is that is being "changed." Indeed, if we grant such things to the soul, we will seem to admit something similar to saying the soul itself becomes "red" or "pale," failing to realize that it is *because* of the soul [that the body changes].

<summary>This page argues that the soul’s activities—such as thinking, remembering, and feeling—are "actualizations" of its inherent power rather than physical changes or imprints like wax. Plotinus maintains that while the body may suffer physical "passions" (like turning pale from fear), the immaterial soul remains essentially unchanged and "impassible."</summary>
