<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument that the soul’s essence remains unchanged even when the human being experiences emotions. He is moving from the discussion of memory and perception to the specific mechanics of "passions" like shame, fear, and desire, distinguishing between the mental judgment and the physical reaction.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

Indeed, passions <note>Original: *passiones*. Plotinus uses this term to describe states where something is "acted upon" or undergoes a change, rather than just "feelings."</note> of this kind do occur, but they concern something else which is a composite <note>The "composite" refers to the union of the soul and the body.</note>. Now, shame itself consists in the soul within a certain opinion of disgrace; but because the soul contains the body—to speak precisely so we do not err—we must say it is within the soul that contains it. It is not the same as an inanimate body; I mean, by the very shame of the soul, a change occurs in the blood, especially if it is easily moved. Furthermore, the principle of fear is in the soul, but the pallor is in the body, occurring while the blood flows back toward the interior. Likewise, in sensible pleasure, the manifest spreading and dilation happens in the body. But what then occurs in the soul is not a passion <note>That is, the soul does not "suffer" a physical change; it remains itself while the body reacts.</note>. We must say the same regarding sorrow; since even in the drive of desire, the principle of wanting exists in the soul, hidden at the start, but what proceeds from there is then perceived by the senses. Now, when we say the soul is moved by lusts, by the wanderings of reason, or by opinions, we by no means understand it to be tossed about in these things, but rather that the motions arise *from* the soul itself. Since we say that "to live" is to be in motion, we do not mean a physical alteration <note>Original: *alterationem*. A change in quality, like turning from cold to hot.</note>; for the natural action of each part is life itself, not departing from itself. Finally, this summary will be sufficient: we will not admit that actions, lives, or desires are physical alterations, nor that memories are certain formulas impressed on the soul, nor will we concede that imaginations <note>Original: *phantasias*.</note> are configurations described as if in wax. It follows without controversy that we must confess the soul, in everything called actions and motions, remains the same in its underlying subject and essence. Thus, virtue and vice do not occur in the soul in the way that black and white, or hot and cold, occur in a body; but rather, in the way we have said, the soul relates to both through things that are simply opposite.

<margin>IV. Confirmation of the above, and concerning the double imagination.</margin>

### NOW WE MUST CONSIDER the part
of the soul that is usually called "passive" <note>Original: *passiua* (Latin) / *pathetikon* (Greek). This refers to the part of the soul capable of being "affected" by external things or bodily needs.</note>; although something has already been said about this where we discussed all the passions that arise in the nature of anger or desire, and by what logic they occur. Nevertheless, something more must be said on this very point. First, we must define what exactly it is that is called "passive" in the soul. It is called "passible" <note>Capable of feeling or suffering change.</note> when it is that around which passions seem to revolve; these are the things followed by pleasure or pain. Some passions arise from opinions <note>Original: *opinionibus* / *doxais*. Judgments or beliefs.</note>, as when someone, thinking they are about to die, feels fear, or rejoices when thinking a good thing is coming. In these cases, the opinion is in one part, while the disturbance is incited in another. Other passions are of such a kind that, arising unexpectedly, they create an opinion in that part which is naturally capable of forming opinions. We have already said that the soul allows the opinion, while the one forming the opinion remains unmoved. But an unexpected fear, if it is felt deeply, again draws its beginning from an opinion, as if providing a certain perception to the fearing part of the soul. For what does this fear itself do? It per...

<column-break/>

**A** Indeed, these are the passions, but they occur in relation to another condition. On the one hand, in the soul itself, a shameful opinion <note>original: *doxēs aischras*</note> is carried; on the other hand, the body <unclear>burns</unclear> with what we call shame, lest anyone <unclear>judging</unclear> should think <unclear>we wander</unclear>. * Thus, being in the soul and those things following it, it draws the inanimate part along according to the blood. Generally, in what are called fears, **B** the beginning is in the soul, but the pallor and the retreats of the blood are entirely physical. And regarding pleasures, the "spreading out" occurs in the sensory part **B** around the body; but that which concerns the soul is no longer a passion <note>original: *pathos*</note>. The same applies to grief. Since even in desire, while the beginning belongs to the soul so as to be the thing affected, it receives from that, and the part concerning the senses knows it. And whenever we say the soul is moved in desires, in reasonings, and in opinions, we do not say it is <unclear>shaken</unclear> in itself by doing these things, but that the motions **C** arise from it. For even in calling life a motion, we do not mean a physical alteration; the activity of each of the parts according to nature is life, not departing from its essence. This <unclear>summary</unclear> shows that we do not grant that activities, lives, or appetites are alterations. Nor do we grant that memories are imprints <note>original: *tupous*</note> stamped into us, nor that imaginations <note>original: *phantasias*</note> are impressions as if in wax. **D** In all things called passions and motions, we say the soul remains the same in its substrate and its essence. Virtue and vice do not become like black and white in the body, or hot and cold, but in the way it has been said, both occur concerning all opposites.

CONCERNING the so-called passive part **F** of the soul, we must examine it. This is the beginning of everything concerning that time; for example, what was said about all the passions, those concerning the spirited part <note>The part of the soul associated with anger and courage.</note> and the desiring part. Or how, in each case, the words about these things <margin>* <unclear>passion</unclear></margin> are taken, what exactly we <unclear>say</unclear> the passive part of the soul is. It is said of all things around which passions seem to consist. These are the things accompanied by pleasure and pain. **F** Of the passions, some are produced by opinions, as when someone, having judged that something is about to happen, feels fear; or if a good thing is about to be, pleasure. The opinion is in one part, but the passion, being moved, is in another. Others are such that, arising involuntarily, they cause you—who are naturally fit to form opinions—to hold that opinion. While the opinion exists and remains in the **G** one who opines, the * fear from the opinion is within, and according to the narrative, it stays with all the disturbances of the so-called soul that fears. # BOOK SIX.

<margin>Disturbances of the soul</margin>
**A** They say that disturbance is a stirring and an agitation based on the mental judgment and expectation of evil. It is certain that *Phantasia* <note>original: "Phantasia" – This refers to the soul’s ability to form mental images or representations. In Plotinus’s thought, it is the "mirror" where thoughts become images that the body can then react to.</note> exists in the soul; first, that which we call "opinion," and then that which is born from it. This is no longer a clear opinion, but regarding things below, it is a sort of faint and obscure opinion—a kind of indistinct imagination, much like the "nature" found in plants, acting as a form of energy through which each thing performs its function, as they say, without the need for conscious representation. It is clear that sensible **B** disturbances follow from this and occur in the body, such as trembling, shaking, paleness, and the inability to speak. These things do not occur in any part of the soul; otherwise, we would have to call that part of the soul "bodily." For if a part of the soul suffered these things, they would not then pass into the body. Indeed, the very faculty <margin>naturally *</margin> whose office it is to send these signals would no longer perform its sending, because it would be overwhelmed by the passions <note>original: "passionibus" – In this context, "passions" are not just strong emotions, but states of being "acted upon" or undergoing a physical change.</note> and distracted from itself. Therefore, this "passive" part of the soul is not a body, **C** but a certain "form within matter." It includes the faculty of desire, as well as the powers of nutrition, growth, and generation, which are the root and principle of this desiring and passive form. No disturbance or passion ought to happen to the Form itself; the Form remains as it is. It is the matter that undergoes the passion whenever the presence of a "mover" causes a passion to creep in. For the vegetative power <margin>the Physical/Natural *</margin> does not itself "get vegetated" when it causes growth; nor is it increased when it increases something else. Nor, in general, is it **D** moved by the same motion with which it moves other things. Rather, it is said to be moved in some other way, or by some other logic of motion or action. It is necessary, therefore, that the nature of the Form itself be an "act" <note>original: "actum" / "energeia" – In Greek philosophy, this refers to a thing being fully itself and active, rather than a passive thing waiting to be changed.</note>, and that it produces effects by its very presence, just as if **Harmony** itself could move the strings of a lyre. Therefore, that which is called the "passive" part of the soul is the cause of the passion—whether that motion of passion arises from the sensory imagination, or even apart from imagination. We must further consider whether, when an opinion begins from above, **E** the "Harmony" (the Form) remains as it is, while the causes of the motion are compared to a musician, and the parts struck by the passion are like the strings. For it is not the Harmony itself that suffers, but the string; and the string is not moved correctly—even if the musician wills it—unless the Harmony dictates the movement.

-> WHAT THEN SHOULD WE STRIVE <-
<margin>To purify the soul is not to remove a quality, but to direct the impulse of action.</margin>
**F** for? Should we aim to make the soul free from passion through the study of philosophy? In truth, the soul is not even subject to passion from the start. Perhaps we say this because an image <note>original: "imaginatio" / "phantasma" – a mental picture or representation.</note> falls into the "passive" part of the soul, which then brings about passion and disturbance, joining an "opinionated image of evil" to the physical agitation. Philosophical reason commands us to uproot this kind of passion and not permit it to sprout anywhere. It is as if, wherever it grows, the soul is not yet prospering, but where it does not germinate, the soul is healthy. This is because the imagination, which **G** is the cause of the passion, has not yet fallen into it—just as if someone, wishing to shake off the troubling visions of a dream,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "impassivity" of the soul, moving from how the soul reacts to images (Phantasia) to how it can be "purified" by separating itself from bodily influence. It then transitions into a new inquiry (Chapter VI) regarding the nature of Matter and "True Being."</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEADS III ###

<column-break/>

...recall the soul to wakefulness. Or, if one says that the passions happen because of things sensed externally, then one is saying these passions belong to the soul. But what will the purification of the soul be, since the soul is in no way defiled? Or what will it mean to separate it from the body? Perhaps purification **A** will be to leave the soul alone, not permitting it to share company with others, nor to look toward anything else, nor again to hold foreign opinions—whatever the condition of opinions and **B** passions might be (as has been said)—nor to look upon images, nor to give birth to passions from them. But if it turns from the lower things toward the higher, what prevents this from being a purification and even a certain separation of the soul? That is to say, a soul not yet so enslaved to the body that it becomes the body's own; which indeed is like a light not submerged in the murky <note>original: "turbido" – likely referring to the "muddiness" of material existence.</note>, even though that which is infused in the murky remains unaffected. Moreover, of that which **C** is called "passible" <note>Capable of suffering or being acted upon by external forces.</note>, purification is a kind of awakening from the intuition of absurd and scattered images. Separation, however, is not to be plunged headlong, nor to twist the imagination toward the lowest things. Again, to separate is to remove those things from the middle by which it is somehow distinguished—namely, when it is not permitted to lie in a spirit <note>original: "spiritu" (Greek: πνεύματος / pneuma) – In Neo-Platonism, this "spirit" is a subtle, airy vehicle that carries the soul into the physical body.</note> turbulent with whirlpools, lest it be suffocated by the flesh; rather, that in which it resides is properly thinned out so that it does not kick back against it.

---

<margin>VI</margin>
<margin>
Separate form, or separated from the diverse: from the diverse things said: the account given to matter in things that are not true: finally matter is called true non-being.
</margin>
I BELIEVE enough has been said already about how the intelligible essence <note>original: "essentiam ipsam intelligibilem" – The realm of pure thought and forms, which Plotinus argues is eternal and unchanging.</note> itself must be thought of as devoid of all passion, which indeed is all arranged in its proper species and order. But since matter too is something incorporeal—though it must be investigated in another way—we must ask how it behaves: whether it is passive (as is said) and changeable through all things, or whether it too must be removed from passion, and how it is said to be joined to passion. First, having been led to this, and intending to treat the nature of matter and what kind it is, we must assert: the nature and essence and being of "That which Is" do not behave as many people think. For "Being" is what one might call truly Being—Being that is Being (if I may put it so). This is that which is entirely Being; that which lacks nothing of its own existence. Since it is perfectly Being, it needs nothing to be and to be preserved, but is itself the cause of "seeming to be" for other things that only appear to exist. If these things are true, it is necessary for it to be in life, and in perfect life, otherwise if it failed in this very thing, it would by no means be "Being" any more: for it is Intellect and perfect wisdom. Therefore it is determined and defined and entirely absolute: nothing there exists in potentiality that is not already in such a great power; otherwise it would suffer some defect. For this reason it is eternal, it always behaves in the same way; it never received anything, nor is anything ever brought into it. For if it received anything, it would receive something outside itself, but that must be non-being...

<column-break/>

**A** ...the soul through imagination says it has made the passions, all of which are dramas, saying they are passions of the soul. But what is the purification of the soul itself, which is in no way defiled? Or what is it to separate it from the body? Perhaps **B** purification would be to leave it alone, and not with others, or not to look toward another, nor again to have foreign opinions—whatever the manner of the opinions or the passions, as has been said—nor to see the images, nor from them to work out passions. But if it turns to the things above from the **C** things below, how is there purification and separation? Indeed, for the soul, it is no longer becoming part of the body, as if it were in it... and these things are like light in the murky. And yet it is entirely unaffected <note>original: "ἀπαθές" (apathes) – impassible or incapable of suffering.</note>, even as if in the murky. But for the "passible" part, purification is the awakening from absurd images, and not seeing them. And separation is the not leaning much toward them, and not having imagination about the things below. And again, to separate it is to remove those things from which it is then separated, when it is not in a murky spirit <unclear>breath</unclear> and multitude, or about the flesh. **D** But we know that in which it is, as if upon its own vehicle, staying quiet.

---

The intelligible essence, then, which is all arranged according to the eternal, has been said to be devoid of passion. But since matter too is some one of the incorporeal things, even if in another way, we must examine concerning this also in what way it is: whether it is passive, as is said, and **E** changeable in all things, or whether one should think this too is unaffected, and what is the manner of this lack of passion. But first we must grasp the <unclear>intended</unclear> things concerning its nature which is spoken of—what kind it is—as truly Nature, and Essence, and Being, which are thus... <unclear>determined</unclear>. **F** For Being is that which according to truth is of such a kind, truly Being, which needs nothing, or is entirely Being, from which nothing of Being is absent. Being perfectly, it needs nothing in order to be saved and to be, but is also the cause for others, for those that seem to be, of their "seeming to be." If then this is rightly said, it is necessary for it to be in life and in perfect life; if it were lacking, **G** it would no longer <unclear>be Being but non-being</unclear>. To this belongs Intellect and all Wisdom; it is therefore determined and limited, and in power nothing is not also such a quantity. For it would fail. Wherefore it is also "always" and "in the same way"; it is entirely non-receiving. Or it is nothing other than itself. For if it should receive anything, that would be... but that thing would be non-being, because of itself...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of "Being" and "Non-Being," specifically addressing how physical matter—despite its apparent solidity—is considered "Non-Being" in the Neo-Platonic system compared to the higher reality of the Intellect and the Soul.</meta>

# BOOK SIX. #

<column-break/>

<margin>
To be in all things
</margin>
**A** | ...for Being to exist entirely. It is necessary, therefore, that this <term>Being</term><note>original Latin: "ens"; Greek: "τὸ ὂν" — the fundamental reality or "is-ness" of a thing.</note> comes into existence possessing all things within itself, and all things together as one. If we define Being through these things, then it must be so; otherwise, <term>Intellect</term><note>original Greek: "νοῦς" (nous) — the divine mind or realm of forms.</note> and Life would not emanate from Being itself, but these would be merely accidental additions to it. Furthermore, they could not come from "Non-Being," and Being itself would then be devoid of life and mind. **B** However, that which is not truly Being will possess these qualities in the manner that is appropriate for lower things, which are posterior to Being itself. For that which exists as the "Super-Being" <note>Referring to the "One," the source above even Being itself.</note> grants these things to Being, yet the One itself does not stand in need of them. If, then, Being is of such a nature, it is necessary that it is neither a body, nor that which is subject to bodies, but rather the subject of bodies: for <term>existence</term><note>Latin: "esse"</note> must consist in that which is not merely physical.

<margin>
How the nature of bodies is Non-Being
</margin>
But in what way is the nature of bodies—and in what way is <term>Matter</term><note>original Greek: "ὕλη" (hyle) — the raw, formless "stuff" of the universe.</note>—considered "Non-Being"? For it is in these that mountains and stones exist, and the whole solid earth, and all things that can resist others. Indeed, those things that are struck, being forced by such impacts, seem to confess that their very essence **C** is real. If someone should ask: how is it then that things which neither collide, nor inflict or suffer force, nor resist, nor are seen at all—namely, Soul and Intellect—are truly beings and real existences? We say in response: among those things that are corporeal, the earth remains most at rest, but that which is less heavy is more mobile; and of this very thing, that which is more sublime is also more mobile. **D** Indeed, fire is the most mobile of all, and it already begins to flee the corporeal nature. But (as I think), those things which are more self-sufficient disturb others less and cause less trouble to them. Those things, however, which are more heavy and earthy, to the degree that they are deficient and fall, and cannot lift themselves up, these—falling because of their weakness—seem to inflict collisions on others through their own ruin and, as it were, their inertia. For bodies that lack life fall upon their neighbors more troublesomely and strike and harm them more violently. **E** Truly living things, insofar as they participate more in Being, and the more "existence" they possess, the more they tend to be harmless to their neighbors. Therefore, motion—which is a kind of life in bodies, or an imitation of life—is more present in those things which have less "corpulence," as if a defect of Being causes that thing to become "more of a body." Again, from these things called "passions" <note>The ways in which a thing is acted upon or "suffers" change from the outside.</note>, it can be more clearly known that what is more corpulent is more "passible" (subject to being acted upon). Earth is more so than the rest, and the others follow a similar logic. **F** For other things, when they are divided, return suddenly into one if nothing prevents them. But when that which is earthy is split, the portions remain separated from each other as if they lacked a natural strength; they remain just as they were struck by a small impulse, and so they perish. Thus, that which has become "mostly body," having fallen as far as possible into Non-Being, is least able to recall itself into unity. **G** Therefore, heavy and violent concussions are a kind of "collapse" <note>original: "ruinae" — suggesting a loss of structural integrity or ontological status.</note>, by which things, in their falling, act upon one another in turn. When the weak runs into the weak, it is strong against it; it is Non-Being running into Non-Being. These things are said against those who place "Beings" only within the category of bodies...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 209 regarding the nature of Being and the soul's relationship to the physical world. It specifically moves into a critique of sense perception as a form of "sleep" and introduces a deep philosophical analysis of Matter (Hyle) as a deceptive, "non-existent" mirror of reality.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III. #

...led, evidently, by the testimony of physical impacts and collisions: likewise, by images produced through the senses which they take as proof of the truth. These people are affected in much the same way as those who dream; they believe the things they see are real actions and objects, even though they are merely dreams. For <term>Sense Perception</term><note>Latin: "Sensus"; Greek: "αἴσθησις" (aisthesis) — the process of gaining information through the five senses.</note> is the hand of the sleeping soul; for as much of the soul as is currently within the body is surely asleep. The true awakening and vigilance is a resurrection from the body, not a resurrection joined with the body. For a migration that occurs alongside the body is merely a passage from one sleep to another, as if one were simply moving from bed to bed; but the only true awakening is that which rises entirely away from bodies. Since these bodies possess a nature that is inherently repugnant to the soul, they also possess an essence that is the soul's opposite. This is further proven by their "generation" (how they are born), their constant "flux" (how they change), and their "destruction"—all of which are qualities utterly foreign to the nature of <term>True Being</term><note>Latin: "ens"; Greek: "τὸ ὄν" (to on) — the stable, eternal reality of the spiritual realm.</note>.

<margin>
VII. The conditions of matter as found in Porphyry's "On the Vanity of Matter," and its persistence within matter.
</margin>

**BUT** we must return once more: first, to the underlying <term>Matter</term><note>Latin: "materia"; Greek: "ὕλη" (hyle) — the raw, formless "stuff" of the physical universe.</note>, and then to those things said to exist within matter. From this, it may be clearly understood both that matter is immune to being affected <note>In Neo-Platonic thought, matter is "impassive"; it can be shaped by Forms but its core "nothingness" never truly changes or suffers.</note> and that neither matter nor the things within it truly exist. Matter is therefore incorporeal, because "body" is a later composite thing, and matter itself is what completes a body when joined with something else. It has obtained the name "incorporeal" because both true Being and matter are distinct from physical bodies. Yet, since matter is neither soul, nor mind, nor life, nor <term>Form</term><note>Latin: "species"; Greek: "εἶδος" (eidos) — the ideal blueprint or shape of a thing.</note>, nor reason, nor even a limit—for it is a type of indefiniteness—it is not even a "power." For what could it actually do? Rather, it flees from all these definitions; it certainly should not be called "Being," but is rightly named "Non-Being." However, it is not called "Non-Being" in the same way that "motion" or "rest" are sometimes called non-being; it is, in truth, <term>Non-Being</term><note>Latin: "reuera non ens"; Greek: "ἀληθινῶς μὴ ὄν"</note>. It is a phantom, an imagination of mass, a longing for substance that lacks any real foundation. It is a "staying" that does not actually stand, invisible in itself, escaping anyone who wishes to see it. When one does not look, it seems somehow present, but when one looks at it intently, it is not perceived. Again, it always appears as opposites within itself: it seems small and great, less and more, lacking and exceeding. It is a phantom that neither stays put nor is able to flee; for it has not even the strength to escape, having received no power from the <term>Intellect</term><note>Latin: "intellectu"; Greek: "νοῦς" (nous) — the divine, creative Mind.</note>. Instead, it was formed in the total absence of all Being. For this reason, in every name given to it, it lies and deceives. If it is imagined as "great," it is actually "small"; if it is thought of as "more," it is actually "less." The "Being" that appears in our imagination of it is actually "Non-Being"—a fleeing plaything. Consequently, the things that seem to happen within it are mere toys—phantoms within a phantom—exactly as in a mirror, where the object is situated in one place but appears in another. It seems full, yet possesses nothing, appearing to be all things. Those things which enter and exit it are mere <term>Imitations of Being</term><note>Latin: "imitamina entis"; Greek: "τῶν ὄντων μιμήματα"</note>. They are phantoms surrounding a formless phantom; and because it is formless, they are seen there. They seem to perform some action upon the underlying matter, yet they do nothing, as they are weak and fleeting, possessing no solidity or power of resistance.

<column-break/>

...led by the testimony of physical thrusts through the imagination of the senses, accepting them as proof of truth, just like those who are affected by dreams. Such people believe that what they see is a real activity, even though it is but a dream. But sense perception belongs to a soul that is asleep. For as much of the soul as is in the body, it sleeps; but the true awakening is a true rising from the body, and not a rising together with the body. For a change that happens with the body is a migration from one sleep to another, like moving from one bed to another. But the true rising is entirely away from bodies, which, being of a nature contrary to the soul, also have an essence contrary to it. This is testified to by their birth, their flow, and their destruction, all of which are truly absurd.

But we must return to the underlying matter, and to the things said to be in that matter, from which you will then come to know that neither matter itself nor the things in it truly exist. It is indeed incorporeal, since the body is a later thing and a composite, and matter itself makes a body when combined with something else. Furthermore, it has obtained the name of "incorporeal" because both it and true Being are outside of bodies. Since it is not itself soul, nor mind, nor life, nor form, nor reason, nor limit—for it is a lack of limit—it is not a power. What is it, then, and of what kind? It falls away from all these things, and thus cannot rightly receive the name of "the things that are" (Being). It may be called "Non-Being," not in the sense that motion and rest are called non-being, but truly "Non-Being": a phantom and a ghost of mass, a longing for substance, staying without standing, and invisible by its own nature. It flees from the one who wishes to see it; when one does not see it, it is present, but when one looks, it disappears. It appears as opposites within itself: small and great, less and more, deficient and exceeding. It is a phantom that remains, yet cannot flee; for it has not even the strength for that, having received no strength from the source, but having come into existence in the lack of all things that truly are. Therefore, whatever it promises, it lies; and if it is imagined as great, it is small; if as more, it is less. The Being that appears in it is a phantom, it is Non-Being, like a fleeing toy. Hence the things that seem to happen in it are toys—phantoms within a phantom—just as if something were situated in one place but appeared in another. It seems to be filled, as if it held or received all things, but it has nothing. The things that enter and exit are imitations of the things that truly are—phantoms within a formless phantom—and because of its formlessness, they are seen there. They seem to act with it, but they do nothing, for they are without foundation and without solidity, merely holding a space within it.

<meta>This page continues the deep philosophical inquiry into the nature of Matter (Hyle) found in Ennead III.6. Having previously established that sense perception is a kind of "dream," Plotinus now examines why Matter remains "impassible"—meaning it is never truly changed or harmed by the forms that appear to inhabit it, much like a mirror is not changed by the images it reflects.</meta>

# BOOK SIX. #

<margin>A</margin> Why are they not divided like waters? Or what is the nature of those things said to be forms, such as those concerning the <unclear>shapes</unclear> and the <unclear>shadows</unclear>? Those things that are saved because they appear within them <note>original Greek: "εμφαντάζει" (emphasizes) — referring to things appearing as reflections or phantasms.</note>... one might ask what the nature of bodies is that remain within it, or perhaps they might take something from them through other things. While the things appearing are of one kind, the things seen within are another, <margin>B</margin> and from these one can learn the falsehood of the <term>affection</term><note>Greek: "πάθεως" (patheos); Latin: "passio" — In this context, it means the state of being acted upon or changed by an external force.</note>. Those things seen being false and having no similarity to the one that made them—being weak and false, and falling into falsehood like dreams, or in water, or a mirror—necessarily leave the matter <term>impassible</term><note>Greek: "απαθη" (apathes) — unaffected, undisturbed, or incapable of suffering change.</note>. And in those things previously mentioned, there is a certain likeness to the things seen without the things that see them.

<margin>C</margin> In general, that which is affected must be of such a nature that it exists in contrary powers, and when qualities approach, they produce the "affection." For that which is in heat undergoes <term>alteration</term> by that which cools it, and that which is moist by that which is dry. We say the <term>subject</term><note>Greek: "ὑποκείμενον" (hypokeimenon) — the underlying thing or "substrate" that stays the same while its traits change.</note> is altered when <margin>affection</margin> it becomes hot from cold, or moist from dry. <margin>D</margin> This is also witnessed by the so-called "destruction" of fire, which is a change occurring into another element. For we say the fire is destroyed, but not the matter; therefore, the affections are around the same thing as the destruction. For the path to destruction is the reception of affection, and to be destroyed is to be affected. But it is not possible for the matter itself to be destroyed. How then, having received within itself countless heats, colds, and <margin>E</margin> all qualities generally, does it have them as if they were grown together and alternating? If they were mixed with each other, they would not each be separate; and matter itself, being caught in the middle, would <term>suffer</term><note>Greek: "πασχουσα" (paschousa) — to be acted upon; to experience a change of state.</note> <margin>distinction</margin> from the qualities. But if they mix their own properties with each other, does matter not suffer with them, unless one were to place them entirely outside of it? But whatever is in a subject is present to the subject in such a way that it gives something of itself to <margin>F</margin> the subject.

One must understand "being present," where one thing is in another, not in a single way, but as one thing existing in another. It might be like a presence that makes the other better or worse through a certain change, as is seen in bodies and especially in <margin>G</margin> living beings. But to make something better or worse is for it to "suffer" or "be affected," as was said regarding the soul. Another way is when someone applies a shape to wax, where no "affection" occurs in such a way that the wax becomes something else because of the presence...

<column-break/>

...since matter also possesses no solidity, these things penetrate into it without dividing it, just as images enter into water: or perhaps just as if someone were to send forms into that which is called a vacuum. But truly, if the things that are seen were of the same sort as those from which they come into the matter, perhaps someone would—not without reason—suspect that the matter undergoes a certain force from those things which truly reach it. But since those things that are represented are of one kind, and those seen within are another, one may also understand from this that the "affection" of matter is false: for indeed, we are deceived by what seems to occur within, and it possesses no similarity to the producer. Therefore, being weak and false, and falling into falsehood in a similar way—like in a dream, or water, or a mirror—it undoubtedly allows the matter to remain <term>impassible</term><note>Latin: "impacibilem" — incapable of being affected or changed.</note>, even though in these things I just mentioned, a certain likeness is formed between the things that appear and those to which they are referred.

---

<margin>VIII. Of what nature is it that affection reaches, and what does not reach matter.</margin>
->VIII<-
**ALTOGETHER** truly, that which is affected must be such that there exists a potential in contrary qualities of those things that approach and bring about the "affection": for to that which is inherently hot, an alteration occurs from that which makes it cold. Again, when moisture is present, an alteration happens by a drying agent, and we say the subject is "altered" when it becomes cold from hot, or moist from dry. This is also witnessed by that which is called the "destruction of fire," which happens by a change into another element. For we do not say the matter is destroyed, but the fire: for this reason, the affections are centered around the same thing as the destruction. For the path to destruction is the taking on of affections, and to be destroyed belongs to that which can be affected. But for matter to be destroyed is impossible: for we cannot even conceive into what or how it would be resolved. And truly, since matter receives into itself countless heats and colds and qualities that are altogether innumerable, and is distinguished by these, and has them as if they were innate and mixed with one another—for they are not each separate above it—how is it that the matter itself, left as it were in the middle, does not also "suffer" along with them when the qualities are mutually affected in their mixing? Unless perhaps someone were to place matter entirely outside of them. Yet, whatever is in a subject is present to the subject in such a way that it gives something of itself to the subject.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>

---

<margin>IX. Answer. Since matter neither rules, nor receives, nor sustains, but undergoes: whatever it is that undergoes.</margin>
->IX<-
**IT MUST BE OBSERVED** that when we say one thing is present to another, and one thing is in another, it should not be understood by us in only one way. Sometimes it is such that something, together with its presence, makes the other better or worse by a certain change: which is indeed manifest in bodies, especially living ones. But sometimes something becomes better or worse by the presence of another without "receiving" it: that is, apart from being affected, just as was said regarding the soul. Sometimes it is also such as when one applies a shape to wax, where there is no "affection" through which the wax becomes something else when the shape is present.

<summary>This page explores the concept of "impassibility," arguing that while Matter (the substrate of reality) appears to change when qualities like heat or cold are present, it is actually as unaffected as a mirror or a piece of wax receiving a seal. Plotinus argues that only the "forms" or "qualities" change and perish, while the underlying Matter remains eternally stable and untouched by these reflections.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Matter. The previous page established that the physical world is like a dream or a reflection. Here, Plotinus argues that Matter itself is "impassible"—it remains unchanged and unharmed by the forms and qualities (like heat or color) that appear within it, much like a mirror remains unchanged by the faces it reflects.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD III. #

<column-break/>

its figure; nor, on the other hand, does any defect surely occur when a figure is erased; indeed, light and the illuminated object do not change the figure. Even a stone made somewhat cold by a cooling agent remains a stone, having acquired nothing but coldness. Therefore, what does a line suffer from a color? Or a plane? Perhaps the underlying body is said to suffer, though what it suffers from the color will be specifically designated. For one should not say that to "suffer" <note>original Latin: "pati"; Greek: "πάσχειν" (paschein) — to be acted upon or undergo change from an external source.</note> is simply for something to be present or for an object to be adorned by a form. 

If anyone says that mirrors and transparent things suffer nothing from the images appearing there, they bring a very fitting example: for the forms in matter are also images, and matter itself is even more alienated from passions <note>passions here means "external influences" or "affections"</note> than mirrors are. Therefore, heat and cold arise in it, yet these heats do not warm the matter itself; for getting warm or cold consists in a quality leading the <term>subject</term> <note>Latin: "subiectum"; Greek: "ὑποκείμενον" (hypokeimenon) — the underlying "stuff" or substrate that supports qualities.</note> from one quality to another. 

Among these things, it is perhaps worth considering whether cold is nothing other than a certain absence and privation of heat. Now, qualities occurring together in matter—many of them act upon each other, specifically those that are contrary to one another. For what would a scent do to sweetness? Or a color to a shape? Or what is in one category, to another category? Whence one might most believe that one thing and another can exist in the same place, or one within another, their very presence doing no harm to that which they are in or near. 

Just as that which is harmed is not harmed by just anything, so it is neither changed nor suffers from just anything. Indeed, contraries suffer only from contraries, while other things are not changed by others; clearly, those which have no contrariety suffer from no contrary. Therefore, if anything suffers, it must not be matter, but some composite, or many things existing together. 

But that which is alone, secret by nature from others, and entirely simple, can suffer from nothing; instead, while all things act upon each other, it can stand beneath them as a medium. Just as in a dwelling where several people strike one another, the dwelling itself suffers nothing, and perhaps not even the air within it. Therefore, let the things in matter that meet together act in whatever way they naturally can upon one another; matter itself remains much further removed from "passion" <note>suffering change</note> than any qualities within it, which, because they are not contraries, suffer very little from one another.

<margin>
Confirmation of the previous points: that matter is moved very little from its own state.
</margin>

**IT ADDS** to these points that if matter suffers, it must carry away something from that passion, either the passion itself or be differently disposed than it was before the passion entered it. If, therefore, another quality enters after that one, the receiver will no longer be "matter," but "qualified matter." If the quality itself should depart, leaving something of itself behind because it had already affected the matter, the subject will become even more something else; and proceeding in this manner, the subject will be something other than mere matter—namely, something varied and multiform:

<column-break/>

**A** the shape, like a deficiency when it has departed. But light and the <unclear>activity</unclear> <note>Greek: "γυμνασία" (gymnasia) — likely an error for "appearance" or "form" in this context.</note> do not cause <term>alteration</term> <note>Greek: "αλλοίωσιν" (alloiosin) — a change in quality.</note> in that which is illuminated, nor is a stone that is cooled made less of a stone by the coldness. What, then, would a line suffer from a color? Or a plane? For it is not so, but perhaps the underlying body [is affected]. What has it suffered from color? What could it suffer, unless we must say that to "suffer" is the same as being present or being clothed in a form? 

**B** If someone were to say that mirrors and transparent things suffer nothing from the seen images, he would not be bringing an unlike example. For the things in matter are also images, and matter is even more <term>impassible</term> <note>Greek: "απαθέστερον" (apathesteron) — incapable of being acted upon or changed.</note> than mirrors. Heats and colds, then, come to be in it, but they do not warm it. 

**C** For to be warmed or cooled is for the substrate to be led from one quality into another. It must be considered whether cold is sometimes an absence and privation. When qualities enter into it, most of them—the many—will act on one another rather than on the matter. For would a scent work upon sweetness? Or a color upon a shape? Or that from one genus upon another? From which one might most believe that it is not 

**D** possible for one thing to be another or for one to be upon another without harm, by its very presence, even in that which it is present. Just as that which is harmed is not harmed by any chance thing, so that which is turned or suffers is not affected except by contraries, and the ceasing of contraries. All other things are unchangeable. Those in which no contrariety exists could not possibly suffer by anything. 

**E** It is necessary, then, that the thing suffering is not matter, but the composite, or simply that it is many things. That which is alone and deserted of others, simply simple in all things, would be entirely impassible, set apart from all things in the middle, or from those things suffering from one another. For example, houses are impassible when those inside them <unclear>strike</unclear> <note>The Greek text "παυόντων" (stopping) is likely a typo for "παιόντων" (striking), as mirrored in the Latin "percutientibus".</note> in the same air. And if the air itself [is affected], the things meeting in matter act on each other, especially 

**F** as many as are natural to act. Matter itself is much more impassible than any qualities in it, which, by not being contraries, are least affected by each other.

**G** THEN, if matter suffers, it must have something from the passion, either the passion itself or be in a different state than before the passion entered it. When another quality enters after that one, that which receives it will no longer be matter, but "qualified matter." If the quality itself should depart, leaving something of itself in the product, the substrate would become even more different. And thus, as the process goes on, instead of matter, the substrate will be something of many qualities and many forms.

<meta>catchword: ὥστε (so that)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that Matter (Hyle) is "impassible," meaning it acts as a neutral stage or mirror that remains unchanged by the qualities, like heat or color, that appear within it. He uses the analogies of a mirror and a house to show how things can interact within a space without changing the space itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the impassivity of Matter. Previously, Plotinus used the analogy of a mirror to show that while images appear in Matter, Matter itself remains unchanged. Here, he deepens this by arguing that if Matter were truly "altered" by what enters it, it would lose its nature as a universal substrate.</meta>

# BOOK SIX #
## THE SIXTH BOOK ##

->D<-

Therefore, it would no longer be the common receptacle of all things, since it would have already taken into itself an impediment to many things yet to come; nor would the matter itself remain any longer, and thus it would not be incorruptible. For this reason, if it is necessary for matter to be as it was from the beginning, it must always remain the same. Indeed, to say that this matter has been transformed is to fail to preserve it as matter. Furthermore, if that which is altered must entirely remain in the same species <note>original Latin: "specie"; Greek: "εἴδει" (eidei) — meaning the essential form or type.</note> regarding its accidents, and yet not be changed in its substance <note>original Latin: "substantia"; Greek: "οὐσία" (ousia) — the fundamental "what-ness" of a thing.</note>—if, I say, it is necessary for that which is altered to remain, then that which undergoes the "passion" or affection within it is not that which remains. One of two things must happen: either the matter, being altered, departs from itself, or, if it does not depart, it is not altered at all. If someone should say that it is indeed altered, but not in its capacity as matter, first, they will be unable to explain according to what part it is altered; and second, they will be forced to confess that the matter itself is not altered. For just as in other things which are forms, it is impossible for them to be altered according to their essence—since their essence consists in this very thing—so too, because the "being" of matter is "to be matter," it is not permitted for it to be altered insofar as it is matter, but it must necessarily remain. And just as in the higher realm the form itself is immutable, so too here it is necessary for matter to be immutable.

HENCE I believe the divine Plato, thinking in this way, spoke rightly when he said that the imitations of real beings <note>This refers to Plato's *Timaeus* 50c, where the physical objects we see are called "imitations" or "shadows" of the eternal Forms.</note> entering into and departing from matter do not enter and depart without purpose. Rather, he wished to make us cautious in explaining the manner of this participation—how matter can share in the forms. From this it appears that the Platonic doubt <margin>XI How forms come into matter according to the *Timaeus*: an image into the species.</margin> which asks in what way matter becomes a participant in forms does not tend toward what many before us thought—namely, *how* the forms come into matter—but rather *how* they are *within* it. For truly it seems a marvelous thing how, while these forms are present to the matter, the matter itself remains the same, receiving no passion <note>Again, "passion" here means being changed or affected by an external force.</note> from them, especially since those things which enter into it are acted upon by one another. But indeed, following the Platonic view, we must think that those things which enter into matter expel what was previously there, and that the "passion" exists in the composite <note>The "composite" is the physical object made of both matter and form, like a bronze statue.</note>; yet not in every composite, but only in that which has need of a preceding form or a receding one, and which suffers through the absence or defect of something in its own constitution, but is perfected by its presence. Matter, however, has nothing more in its own nature by anything entering it—for it is not "made" what it is by that which enters—nor again does it have anything less when anything departs; for it remains what it was from the beginning. Truly, an adornment is useful and necessary for those things which stand in need of ornament and order, and such an ornament can be made without transformation, just as when we place a decoration around someone. But if something were so adorned as to have the ornament become innate, it would be necessary for that which is adorned to be transformed from what was previously "ugly" and become different, thus emerging from ugliness into beauty. If, therefore, matter, being ugly, were made beautiful, it would no longer be that same "ugly" thing it had been before.

<column-break/>

Therefore it will no longer be the common receptacle of all, since it would have already conceived an impediment to many things yet to come into itself, nor will the matter itself remain any longer, nor therefore will it be incorruptible. Wherefore if it is necessary for matter to be as it was from the beginning, so it is always necessary for it to be the same; surely to say this has been changed is not to preserve it as matter. Furthermore, if everything that is altered must remain in the same species in its accidents, but not be changed in its substance; if, I say, it is necessary for that which is altered to remain, and that which suffers in it is not that which remains, it is necessary that one of two things happens: either the matter, having been altered, departs from itself, or, if it does not depart, it is not altered in the least. If someone however should say that it is indeed altered, but not by the reason of being matter: first, they cannot explain according to what it is altered; then they will be forced to confess that thus also the matter itself is not altered. For just as in other things which are species <note>forms</note>, it cannot happen that they are altered according to their essence, since their essence consists in this very thing; so because the being of matter is "to be in the manner that it is matter," it is not allowed for it to be altered insofar as it is matter, but it is necessary that it remain. And just as there the species itself is immutable, so also here it is necessary for matter to be immutable.

HENCE I think Plato, having so considered, spoke rightly where he says, the imitations of beings <margin>XI How forms come into matter according to Timaeus—the image into the species.</margin> entering and exiting the matter; for one must not think he meant they enter and exit for no reason, but that he wished to make us cautious in explaining by what means matter can participate in the species. Hence it also appears that the Platonic doubt by which it is asked in what way matter becomes a participant in species does not tend thither, as many predecessors thought, namely how species come into matter, but rather how they are *in* it. For in truth it seems wonderful, how while these species are present to the matter, the matter itself remains the same, receiving no passion from them, especially since those things which enter into it suffer from each other. But indeed from the Platonic opinion it must be thought that those things which enter matter expel the prior things from there, and that the passion is in the composite; nor in every composite, but in that which has need of a preceding form or a receding one, and which through the absence of something suffers a defect in its own constitution, but through its presence is perfected. Matter, however, has nothing more in its nature by anything approaching, for it is not then made what it is by that approaching thing; nor again by anything receding does it have anything less; for it persists as it was from the beginning. For those things an adornment is surely useful and necessary which stand in need of ornament and order, and an ornament can be made without transmutation, just as when we put a decoration around someone. But if something were so adorned that it held the ornament as something innate, it would be necessary for that which is adorned to be changed from that which was previously ugly, and to become different and thus from ugly to emerge as beautiful. If therefore matter, existing as ugly, is made beautiful, it is no longer that same ugly thing which it had been before.

<summary>Plotinus argues that Matter is immutable and "impassible," meaning it remains fundamentally unchanged even when Forms enter or leave it. He interprets Plato’s Timaeus to show that while physical objects change, the underlying Matter acts only as a mirror-like receptacle that does not truly take on the qualities it reflects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the "impassibility" of matter—the idea that the underlying substance of the universe does not change even when it takes on different shapes. Plotinus is specifically addressing how "evil" matter can desire "the good" without being transformed by it.</meta>

PLOTINUS ENNEAD III.

Therefore, while it is adorned in this way, it loses its status as matter, especially if it is considered ugly <note>original: "turpis"</note> not by accident. For if it were so ugly that it was ugliness itself, it could not participate in adornment. Again, if it were so evil that it was evil itself, it would never receive any part of the good. For this reason, participation does not happen as many people think, as if the matter were affected <note>original: "patiente"; meaning undergoing a change or suffering an influence.</note>; rather, there is another reason, namely, that of appearance. Truly, in this way, the doubt is resolved by which it is asked how, if matter is evil, it can desire the good, since by that very participation it does not cease to be what it was. For if participation occurs on this condition—that matter remains the same and is not altered at all, as we say, but remains what it is and always was—it should no longer seem miraculous, even if it is evil, that it participates in the good; for it does not depart from itself. But because it is necessary to participate, it participates in a certain way <note>The OCR 'quadru' likely refers to 'quadruply' or 'in a fourfold manner', though the sense here is 'in some way'.</note>. From the fact that it remains the very thing it is, with the mode of participation aiding it, its essence is not harmed by that which is thus transmitted to it. Indeed, it seems no less evil because of this: because it always remains what it is. For if it truly became a participant and were truly changed by the good, it would not be evil by nature. Wherefore, if anyone says that matter is evil, they will speak the truth if they deny that it is affected by the good; for that is the same as asserting that it is entirely impassible <note>original: "impassibilis"; Greek: "ἀπαθής" (apathes) — meaning unaffected, unchanging, or incapable of suffering outside influence.</note>.

<margin>
XII
Confirmation of the above points: that matter is neither affected in any way in its nature by forms, nor suffers, nor is divided.
</margin>
PLATO, thinking the same thing about matter and judging that participation does not occur in it in the way a form or species enters a subject—so that a "composite" is formed by things that are transmuted, mixed, and affected together—strove to declare how matter, remaining impassible, possesses species <note>original: "species"; Greek: "εἴδη" (eide) — the internal forms or types of things.</note>. He sought an example of "impassible participation," because it is not easy to show what things, by their presence, allow the subject to remain the same. He raised many doubts while reaching for what he desired. Furthermore, he sought to distinguish a certain emptiness of substance in sensible things, and that the "place" <note>original: "locum"; Greek: "χώρα" (chora)</note> of likelihood and image is very great. Proposing therefore that matter, under various figures, brings "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" (passiones/πάθη) refers to external influences or changes acted upon a body.</note> to animate bodies, while matter itself possesses none of those passions, he signified its stability in this way. He challenges the argument, showing that in no way is matter itself affected or changed by these figures. In these bodies that change from one figure to another, one might perhaps say an alteration occurs—namely, the mutation of the figure itself—but you would say such an alteration is "equivocal" <note>meaning the word 'alteration' is being used in a different sense than usual.</note>. Since matter has neither figure nor any magnitude, how could anyone say that the arrival of a figure, however it happens, is an "alteration," even in an equivocal sense? If anyone, therefore, uses the law here and speaks of individual things, declaring that the underlying nature has nothing in the way it is thought to, they will not wander far from reason. Yet, in what way does it "have" them? If it does not please us to say it has them as figures, but the Platonic proposition signifies, as far as possible, that the nature of matter is devoid of passion.

<column-break/>

**A** Thus, in addition to being adorned, it loses its being as matter, especially if it is not ugly by accident. But if it is so ugly that it is ugliness itself, it would not partake of order <note>original: "κόσμου" (kosmou) — meaning world-order, beauty, or adornment.</note>. And if it were so evil that it was evil itself, it would not partake of the good. Thus, participation is not as some think, a being affected; rather, there is another way, like a seeming, perhaps. Or, in this way, the puzzle might be solved: how, if it is evil, it desires the good, so that it does not lose what it was by participation. But if participation is said to be in this way—that it remains the same and is not altered, as we say, but is what it is—it is no longer a wonder how, even being evil, it partakes, or that it does not depart from itself. But because it is necessary for it to partake, the participation is unmixed for it. **C** However it still exists as it is, this participation preserves it, and it is not harmed in its being by that which gives and risks. <note>The Greek text here is somewhat fragmented in the OCR.</note> Therefore, it is no longer what it was if it truly participates by receiving from the giver and being altered by the good; it would not be evil by nature. Thus, if anyone says matter is evil, **D** they would speak the truth if they called the good impassible, for not being affected is the same thing.

Plato, returning to this subject, saw participation as a form occurring in a substrate or as the giving of shapes, so that a composite is not created from things that are poured together and affected together. **E** By this conviction, wishing to show how matter itself remains impassible while holding sensible things, he sought an example of another kind of participation, which is not easy to teach: what things most preserve the substrate by their presence. He fell into many difficulties, seeing what he was aiming at: that sensible things are a "void" of substance, and that "space" <note>original: "χώρα" (chora)</note> is the "place." When he proposed many things under the forms of matter, **F** he suggested that these things produce passions in ensouled bodies, but matter itself has none of these passions, thus indicating its permanence. He leads us to reason that if one were to say it suffers from these appearances and is altered—for in bodies, as they receive one figure after another, one might say an alteration occurs—he would say the word "alteration" is being used equivocally. For how could anyone say that the appearance of a figure in matter, which has no shape or magnitude, is an "alteration," even equivocally? If someone here used the term "by convention" <note>original: "νόμῳ" (nomo)</note>, and said other things were "by convention," naming the underlying nature as having nothing in the way it is thought, they would not be absurd in their reasoning. But how does it have them? If not as receiving figures, the hypothesis indicates that it is as "impassible" as possible.

<summary>Plotinus explains that Matter (Materia/Hyle) is "impassible," meaning it remains fundamentally unchanged even when it takes on the appearance of forms or the Good. He cites Plato to support the idea that Matter is a stable substrate that does not merge with the qualities it displays.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the nature of matter, specifically addressing its "impassibility"—the idea that matter does not truly change or suffer when it takes on forms. It corresponds to Ennead III, Book 6, Chapters 9 through 14.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<column-break/>

...that the presence of forms in it is merely an appearance of phantoms, as if they were present but not truly there. Perhaps we should first speak further regarding its <term>impassibility</term> <note>original Greek: "apatheia"; the philosophical concept that the underlying substance of the universe is not affected or changed by the qualities it takes on.</note>. Therefore, we must train ourselves against the customary use of names, which lead us to believe that matter itself "suffers" or is changed—for instance, when we imagine it being dried, or set on fire, or moistened, and so on, or as receiving the shapes of air or water. For we perceive it receiving the shapes of air and water along with the processes of being fired or moistened. This shows that in receiving shapes, it is not the matter itself that is formed as if the forms had entered its essence; rather, what we specifically call "being fired" is more accurately "becoming fire." For "becoming fire" and "being ignited" are not the same. "To be ignited" implies a state of being affected or changed, but if something is a part of fire, how can it be "ignited"? Such a thing would be as if someone said that because of the bronze, the statue was made, or that fire proceeded through the matter. And if the rational principle <note>original Greek: "logos"</note> approaching it is said to act, how would it "ignite" the matter? Perhaps in its shape? But that which is "ignited" already consists of two things <note>matter and form</note>. How can it be from both if one has not become out of both? Or perhaps, though it becomes one, it is not from two things having mutual <margin>to produce</margin> passions <note>affections or changes</note>, but acting upon something else. Is it because both are acting? Or rather, because one produces and the other does not flee? But when a body is divided, how can it be that the matter itself is not divided? And when the body suffers while being divided, how does the matter not undergo the same passion? Perhaps nothing prevents us from saying, by the same logic, that matter itself is destroyed—asking how, when the body is destroyed, the matter is not destroyed? Surely we should also say that "suffering" and "being divided" only belong to things that have magnitude. But to that which is not magnitude, the passions of magnitude do not belong; and generally, to that which is not a body, the passions of a body do not happen. Therefore, whoever admits that matter can "suffer" is forced to admit that matter is a body.

<margin>circumstance</margin>
<margin>so that if it receives any quality, it is not impassible.</margin>
Furthermore, it is proper to remind them of this: in what way do they say that matter "flees" from forms? For how can stones and other solid things that contain it "flee"? They will say it does not flee at one time and not at another. For if it flees by its own will, why does it not flee always? But if it remains by necessity, there is no time when it is not in some form; therefore, the cause for why the same form does not always contain the matter should be sought rather in the things that enter it. How then is it said to "flee"? Is it not always the same in its nature? And what else can that be, than that it never departs from itself, even while it "has" a shape which it never truly possesses? Otherwise, they will have no way to probably defend what they have said. Furthermore, Plato calls matter the "receptacle" and "nurse" of all generation. Indeed, a receptacle and nurse are something different...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> That the presence of forms in it is only apparent, like images that are not truly present. Perhaps, indeed, the condition of its <term>impassibility</term> <note>original Latin: "impassibili"; the state of being unable to be changed or influenced by external things.</note> should be treated even earlier, and it must be taught that it is necessary to be led by customary names to designate its "passion" in a certain way: for instance, when we think of the same matter being dried and set on fire or moistened (as Plato says) and so on, and as receiving the forms of air and water. 
<margin>B</margin> For what is said later by Plato—that matter receives the forms of air and water—both tempers and diminishes what had been said before, that matter was ignited and moistened. It shows that matter, in that it takes forms, is not itself "formed," but rather that the forms are there as they entered. For what was said about it being "ignited" was not said properly, but rather signified that it "became fire." For it is not entirely the same thing to "become fire" and to "be ignited." For "to be ignited" happens by something else, in which change truly occurs; but that which is a part <margin>C</margin> of fire cannot be "ignited." Otherwise, it would be just as if someone said that the statue proceeded through the bronze itself, or that fire progressed through the matter, and even entered the matter. And yet, even if the "reason" <note>original: "ratio"; the formative principle.</note> itself approaching it is said to act, in what way will it be said to "ignite" the matter? Perhaps in its figure? But that which is ignited already consists of both <note>matter and form</note>. How then can it be from both, if it has not been made one out of both? Or perhaps, although it has become one, it is not from two things having mutual passions, but in other things that are acting. Is it <margin>D</margin> therefore because both are acting? Or rather, because one is the effector and the other does not flee? But when a body is divided, how can it be that the matter itself is not divided? And when the body itself suffers while it is divided, how does it not also undergo the same passion? Perhaps indeed nothing prohibits us from saying, by the same logic, that matter itself is corrupted—asking, that is, in what way, when the body is corrupted, the matter is not corrupted? Surely it would also have to be said that "suffering" and "being divided" are only <margin>E</margin> something that exists in magnitude. But to that which is not magnitude, the passions of magnitude do not belong; and generally, to that which is not a body, the passions of a body do not happen. Because of this, whoever confesses that matter can "suffer" is forced to confess that matter is also a body.
IT is further appropriate to prove by what reason <margin>XIII Constantine follows the above, and proves that matter stands in an unequal way to forms, and to the Divine Mind, just as mirrors stand to images and to the spectacles themselves.</margin> matter is said to "flee" from a form. For in what way does it flee from stones and other solid things that hold it back? They will not say that it flees at some times and <margin>F</margin> at other times does not flee. For if it flees by its own will, why does it not flee always? But if it remains by necessity, no time is given in which it is not in some species; indeed, the cause why the same species does not always contain the matter must be sought more in those things which enter it. In what way then is it said to "flee"? Is it not the same nature always? But what else will that be, than that it never departs from itself, and thus "has" a species <margin>G</margin> which it never truly has? Otherwise, they will have no way to probably defend what they had said. Furthermore, Plato calls matter the "receptacle" of all generation and the "nurse." Surely a receptacle and nurse are something different...

<summary>This page argues that matter (hyle) is impassible, meaning it remains unchanged despite taking on various forms like fire or water. Plotinus uses the metaphor of a receptacle or mirror to show that matter only appears to change while its underlying nature remains unaffected.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 115 regarding the "impassibility" of matter—the philosophical idea that while matter receives various forms (like heat, cold, or shape), it is not itself changed or affected by them. This section specifically employs the famous "mirror" analogy to explain how forms exist in matter without truly being part of it.</meta>

<page-num>116</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK III.</header>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is something other than the process of becoming <note>original Latin: "generatio"; the process of things coming into existence</note>. For that which is altered is caught up in this becoming. And since they have accepted that the "nurse" of becoming precedes the becoming itself, she also precedes any alteration. Truly, that which is called the <term>receptacle</term> <note>original Latin: "susceptaculum"; the "container" or "space" that holds physical forms</note> and the nurse preserves matter as <term>impassible</term> <note>original Latin: "impatibilem"; incapable of being affected, changed, or suffering from external forces</note>. It similarly preserves the description that matter is that in which each thing appears to be made, and from which it then departs. Likewise, he <note>Referring to Plato in the *Timaeus*</note> calls it "place" and "seat." Finally, when he says with right reason that it is, as it were, a "place for forms," he does not describe a "passion" <note>an experience of change or suffering</note> regarding matter, but rather requires another way of understanding. What is this way? Truly, since such a nature ought to be none of the things that exist, but must have escaped every essence of existing things and be entirely different—for the "rational principles" <note>original Latin: "rationes"; the Greek *logoi* or blueprints of things</note> are the things that truly exist—
<margin>B</margin>it is necessary that matter, by this very "otherness," preserves the safety it has obtained. Therefore, it is not only unable to truly grasp existing things, but even if there is some imitation of existing things, matter remains
<margin>C</margin>stranger to any intimacy with it. For only in this way is it entirely different from existing things; otherwise, if it contracted any intimate familiarity with a specific form, it would surely become something else along with that form, losing its distinct "otherness." It would no longer be the "place" for all things; indeed, it would no longer be a receptacle at all, even though it is said to be the receptacle of all things alike. It is necessary that the same matter remains permanent while forms enter it,
<margin>D</margin>and remains impassible when they depart, so that something may always enter and exit. But that which enters will enter as a <term>simulacrum</term> <note>a likeness or "phantom" rather than the thing itself</note>, and it enters into something that is not true at all; therefore, the entry itself will not be true. But will it be truly received? How can something be truly received by that which is forbidden in any way from participating in truth, because it is itself "falsehood"? Perhaps, therefore, it proceeds falsely into a falsehood, and behaves similarly to the images of objects appearing in a mirror, so long as those objects remain 
<margin>E</margin>in view. For if you were to remove existing things from the universe, nothing at all would ever appear—not for a moment—of those things now seen in the world. In our case, the mirror itself is also seen, for it is itself a certain form. But that which is in the world acts as a mirror, but since it has no form, it is not seen in any way; otherwise, it would be necessary for it to be perceived first according to itself. Indeed, it undergoes something like illuminated air, which is hidden from the eyes because it cannot be seen without illumination. For this reason, the things that appear 
<margin>F</margin>in mirrors are believed either not to exist at all, or to exist less than reality, because the thing in which they exist is clearly discerned; the mirror remains while the images depart. But matter is not discerned at all, whether it holds forms or not. If it were possible for the things that fill mirrors to remain there while the mirrors themselves were not seen, no one would ever doubt that the things seen in the 
<margin>G</margin>mirrors were "true." Whether, therefore, there is something in mirrors, the same would apply to sensible things in matter; or if there is nothing in mirrors, but only an appearance, one must similarly say that an appearance occurs in matter. The appearance of this must be assigned to the visible substance of the existing things themselves, which existing things always truly participate in, but non-existing things do not truly participate in.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But becoming is something else than matter itself; and that which is altered is within becoming, coming from becoming. The receptacle and the nurse would also be in this alteration, keeping it as it is—impassible <note>original Greek: "apathes"</note>. And the things that come into being are each a phantom <note>original Greek: "phantazetai"</note>, and again they exit from there. It is a space <note>original Greek: "choran"</note> and a seat; and that which is said and reflected upon <note>*</note> as the whole, when speaking this way, is not said to be a "passion" regarding it. Instead, one seeks another way: how is it then possible for this so-called "nature" to be none of the things that exist <note>*</note>, but to have escaped all the essence of beings, and be entirely other? For those things are "rational principles" <note>original Greek: "logoi"</note>; from these, it is necessary that it be preserved in this "otherness." Its very lack of logic <note>original Greek: "alogia"</note> is its salvation. It is necessary for it not only to stand apart from beings, but also that the imitations of them have no share in intimacy with it. For if it were ever made other, or carried away by some form, becoming something else with it, it would lose its status as "other," and as the space of all things, and the underlying receptacle. But it remains while each thing enters, and remains impassible as they exit, so that the entry and exit of anything may always be into a "nothingness"—the thing entering is like a non-truth entering into a non-truth <note>*</note>. And how can it share in truth at all when it is itself a falsehood? If then it comes falsely into falsehood, it becomes something similar to what is seen in mirrors—the images of things seen there—and as long as one looks at those things and the space <note>*</note>—if the beings themselves were to depart, nothing would appear, no matter how much worse it might seem than the sensible things now seen. The mirror itself is seen, for it is a form; but as for that which is in the world, it is not seen, for it has been made into a formless thing <note>*</note> to be seen by itself. But it suffers something like the air when it is illuminated; it does not appear, and the fire <note>*</note> because it was not seen before being illuminated. In this way, the things in mirrors are either believed to exist, or less so, because that in which they exist is seen, and it remains while the images depart. But in matter, it is not seen itself, whether it has forms or not. If those things from which the mirrors were filled did not remain, and the mirrors themselves were not seen, one would not think they were not true <note>*</note>. And whether the things seen are in the mirrors or in the matter <note>*</note>, sensible things are within; even if they only appear to be there, and we say they appear upon the matter. We assign the cause of the phantom to the substance of the beings themselves, which beings always truly participate in, but non-beings do not. <note>*</note>

<vocab>Plotinus, Enneads, metaphysics, matter, form, mirror, receptacle, becoming, essence, material substance</vocab>
