He argues that Matter must be entirely "other" than Being in order to serve as the "nurse" or "receptacle" for all physical things.</summary>

# BOOK SIX <note>Though titled "Liber Sextus" (Book 6) in this edition, this text is actually from Plotinus’s Third Ennead, the sixth treatise, "On the Impassibility of Incorporeals."</note>

...since it is not right for these things to behave as if they were themselves [independent], in the same way they would have if they existed on their own rather than while they were non-existent.

<margin>XIV.
That matter is in things just as an image is in a mirror; and that matter is empty because it is not such by its own nature, but through the agent; and it is not filled because matter has no life, nor does that which seems to have happened actually belong to it: but it is like an echo.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> What then? If matter did not exist, would nothing at all subsist <note>To "subsist" here means to have a secondary, reflected existence in the physical world.</note>? Nothing at all except for the <term>beings</term> <note>original Latin: "entia"; referring to the eternal, perfect Forms or Platonic Ideals.</note>: just as an image would not exist if the mirror (or anything of that sort) were removed. For this is how its nature is structured: to exist in another. If that other thing does not exist, it could never come to be—for this is the very nature of an image: to be in something else. 
<margin>B</margin> If indeed it departed from the causes themselves, it could certainly exist even if it were not in something else. But since those causes remain, if anything appears elsewhere from them, there must be something else present, providing a "seat" for that which does not truly enter it. This "seat" <note>Matter</note>, by its own presence and audacity—and even, as it were, by its bold indigence—seems to be urged, and urges itself, to grasp [the form]. Yet it is deceived by not truly grasping it, so that its state of indigence persists, compelling it always to beg. 
<margin>C</margin> For once it subsists (as the myth tells us), it always desires <note>Plotinus is referencing the myth from Plato's *Symposium* where Poverty (*Penia*) stalks Resource (*Porus*).</note>. In this regard, its nature is shown to be void of the Good. It desires, yet it does not truly receive the things bestowed upon it; rather, it seems satisfied if it receives a mere semblance, whatever it may be. Thus, it is demonstrated that what appears to us in matter is something different [from the reality]. The name itself, <term>Penia</term> <note>original Greek: "Πενία"; meaning "Poverty" or "Indigence."</note>, declares that matter is never filled. When it is said that Penia consorts with <term>Porus</term> <note>original Greek: "Πόρος"; meaning "Resource" or "Plenty."</note>, it does not mean she unites with Being itself or with fullness, 
<margin>D</margin> but with a certain artful and wondrous thing: that is, with the cleverness of a self-showing image. For since it is impossible for anything that is outside of Being to be entirely devoid of Being—for the nature of Being is to produce beings—and since that which is entirely non-being cannot mix with Being, something truly marvelous occurs: it participates without participating. By its very proximity, it acquires something, even though by its own nature it is incapable of being glued together [with the Form]. 
<margin>E</margin> Therefore, what it receives slips away as if from a foreign nature, like an <term>echo</term> from smooth and flat places. Because it does not remain there, it appears to be there, though it actually comes from elsewhere. But if matter participated in such a way as to actually "take in" the form, as some might think, then whatever approached it would penetrate it as if soaked in. In reality, it appears that it was not soaked in, but remained entirely the same, having gained nothing. It is like a "seat" that reflects a process back into nothingness; it is a receptacle for things that run together in the same place and are mixed with one another. 
<margin>F</margin> This is no different from what happens when people, wishing to catch fire from the sun, hold up certain smooth and solid objects <note>such as glass spheres or "burning mirrors."</note>, which they fill with water so that the flame—held back by the contrary element within—does not pass through, but stays on the outside. In this way, matter becomes the cause of generation, and the things composed within it are established in this manner.

<margin>XV.
On the seminal reason which is in the soul: that it is not mixed with matter; and on the vanity of formative matter and of sensible things.</margin>
In the case of those things that gather fire around themselves from the sun—seeing as they receive flame from a <term>sensible</term> <note>perceptible by the senses</note> fire—they themselves possess the quality of being perceived. 
<margin>G</margin> Therefore they are visible, because the things established there are external, placed one after another and nearby, touching each other. In that case, there are undoubtedly two distinct boundaries. But the <term>seminal reason</term> <note>original Latin: "Ratio seminaria"; the Greek *logos spermatikos*, the formative "blueprint" or "seed" of a thing.</note> in matter...

He uses the myth of Penia (Poverty) to illustrate how matter perpetually lacks the reality of the Good, only ever catching a fleeting reflection of true Being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of matter as a "non-being" that acts as a mirror for forms. It develops the argument that matter is never truly changed or "filled" by the qualities it appears to possess, such as magnitude or shape.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

...it behaves differently so as to be outside of matter. For the harshness of nature <note>The "nature" here refers to the inherent resistance or "otherness" of matter.</note> is sufficient, not requiring a double boundary, but much more than any external boundary it retains a force that resists mixing, because of a difference in essence that is devoid of all kinship. This is the very cause of its remaining in itself: because it does not enjoy what enters it, nor does it in turn enjoy what comes to it. But just as opinions and imaginations in the soul are not mixed, but each one departs again, existing as it was alone, neither dragging anything with it nor leaving anything behind, because it had not been mixed; it has what is said to be "outside," not because it lies nearby, nor is it discerned by sight as if distinct from its foundation, but it is discerned by reason. 

Here, therefore, the imagination constitutes an image, occupying a place. However, since the soul does not naturally become an image—though in many things it seems to lead, and to lead by its own will—it is compared to the soul in a certain proportion as matter. Although, I say, this is the case, the eye of the soul is not obscured, since it is frequently stirred by certain actions proper to the soul. Nor does it ever cause the soul to be completely hidden, even if it spreads itself through the whole soul, although sometimes it appears to be so in a way. For the soul has within itself actions and opposing reasons <term>logoi</term> <note>original Greek: "λογους" (logous); these are rational formative principles or "blueprints" within the soul.</note> through which accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or size that can change without changing the thing's essence.</note> are repelled. 

Matter, however, being far weaker than the soul, has nothing at all of its own, whether true or even sometimes false. Nor does it have anything through which it might appear, since it goes into the falsehood of all things. Rightly is it said to be without cause to appear; nor could it ever say "here I am," even if it is seen the least. But if a deeper reason finds it affected by other beings, it cries out that matter is something destitute of all beings. And although those things that are posterior to beings seem to exist, it is drawn through all these things so that it appears to follow them, and again not to follow them.

<margin>XVI. How reason, acting as form and similar to it, presents forms to matter; which nature presents through all the shapes of forms.</margin>
But some reason <term>logos</term> approaching and extending matter as far as it wishes, makes it "great" <note>Meaning it gives matter the appearance of physical size or magnitude.</note>. It applies a "how much" from itself to matter, which has no quantity by itself; nor is it even made into quantity, otherwise the quantity would be within it. If you take away this form, the subject itself will no longer be "great," nor will it even appear. But if that which has been made great is a man or a horse, then along with the horse comes the magnitude of the horse; and when the horse departs, the magnitude also departs. If someone says that a horse is made in a certain large mass and the magnitude remains, we will say that it is not the magnitude of the horse, but the magnitude of the mass that remains there. However, if this mass is fire or earth, then when the fire or earth departs, the magnitude of the fire or earth departs. For this reason, matter enjoys neither figure nor magnitude; otherwise, something else would not be made from fire, but that fire would remain and never become [not fire].
<note>original Greek fragment: "it escapes notice, or it is not from fire, but whatever it shall be"</note>

<column-break/>

**A** it has another way [of being] outside. But the priority of nature is enough, needing no double limit, but much more it is unmixed around... but separated by the otherness of essence and in no way having any kinship. And for this reason, the cause of its remaining is this very thing: that neither does the thing entering enjoy it, nor does it enjoy the thing entering. But just as...

**B** ...opinions and imaginations in souls are not mixed, but each departs again as being what it is alone, dragging nothing along nor leaving anything behind, because it was not mixed. And it has the "outside" because it is superimposed; and that upon which it is, is not seen as [separate], but reason says it is. Here, then, the imagination is an image, because there are images of things in nature belonging to the soul...

**C** ...even though it seems to lead many things, and to lead wherever it wishes, it nonetheless uses [the soul] as matter or something analogous. However, it does not hide [the soul], being often pushed out by the soul's own activities; nor does it make the soul [an image], even if it should come and be colored by the whole. And yet the things of the imagination [remain]; for the soul has in itself activities and contrary reasons, by which it pushes away the things that are drawn in.

**D** For it is weaker, as compared to the whole power of the soul. Where it [matter] is likewise, so it is both true and not corrupted (*). (*) There, because of its nature, there is a desert of these things, but it becomes a cause for others to appear. It cannot itself rise to the whole of these things, but it is absurdly empty. Yet it is a certain depth from other beings, showing how that which is secluded from all beings is, and of those...

**E** ...things that later seemed to be, it is drawn everywhere and follows as it seems, and yet does not follow.

**F** And indeed some reason <term>logos</term> coming, and leading matter as far as it wished, made it great. And this [reason] itself gave to it the greatness it did not have. For the greatness in it was a magnitude; if you should take away the form, it is no longer [great]. But what appears is a certain subject; for if that which became great was a man or a horse, then together with the horse the greatness of the horse came, and when the horse departed, the greatness also departed with it. But if someone should say that [matter] is in a certain large mass and then it becomes, and the magnitude remains, we will say it is not the magnitude of the horse, but the magnitude of the mass that remains there.

**G** If, however, this mass is fire or earth, when the fire departs, that magnitude of the fire also departs, and that of the earth. If, therefore, it does not [participate] in the shape, nor in the magnitude... but remaining fire, it will become fire <note>original Greek: "εν πυρ γενησεται" - it will become in fire.</note>.

<summary>This page argues that matter is an "empty" receptacle that remains essentially unchanged by the forms it reflects. Using the analogy of mirrors and the soul's imagination, Plotinus explains that qualities like size and shape belong to the rational forms (Logoi) rather than to matter itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of matter, specifically addressing how matter, which is inherently without size or "magnitude," can appear to take on the dimensions of the physical world. It follows the argument that matter is like a mirror that reflects forms without being changed by them.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<column-break/>

Since even now it appears so great, as it seems, when the whole sensible world exists and all things co-existing in it, and after this all quality comes from itself, and the other qualities likewise, it will be left as it was; the living being <note>original Greek: "ζῶον" (zōon); Plotinus often refers to the cosmos as a single living organism.</note> would have been affected by some things being present, and after they have departed from all the recipients <note>original Greek: "λακῶσιν" (lakōsin), likely a corruption of "δεχομένοις" (dekhomenois), the recipients or 'receptacles' of form.</note>—if one did not suffer change, it is no longer like the case of sensible things, where light is present and then departs. If someone wonders how, not having <term>magnitude<note>In this context, magnitude refers to spatial extension or size.</note></term>, it produces something large, and how it produces sound or heat—certainly the same thing is heated, which is itself also a magnitude. Or first, there is an immaterial magnitude, just as there is an immaterial shape; and if it is prior to matter, all such things will participate in it. One part of it is with those sensible bodies: magnitude. Along with the others which are set apart, since it is in a body, the <term>formative principle<note>original Greek: "λόγος" (logos); the rational blueprint or "reason-principle" that gives structure to matter.</note></term> contains also a certain magnitude in the matter, which is either the defined body or simply the body.

But it is not magnitude itself, nor the whole of magnitude, but that which is there, and magnitude in itself. But it leads to an imitation of them, and then it is infinite in extension, so that it will be magnitude; but since it wishes to be in that which is placed with the soul, as far as something is possible—
<margin>in the writings concerning imagination</margin> —since there is not only a desire in it, or a movement toward it, to suffer the same thing. —a subsistence into another; therefore the "great," as if living through imagination, moves toward this very thing: it makes it great by the smallness of matter; it stood apart from that very possession which, when filled, seems to be great. For that greatness is a falsehood, and the falsehood is the not having magnitude; yet extending toward that, it will not appear in its consistency—not all things being as the others, or the other, by their own delimitation—each of the qualified things, as being either the great whole or great in that way. It will not understand the magnitude according to each reason, such as that of a horse or some other animal, occurring before these very things. These things, I think, are an emptying: great toward the "great itself" from the flashes, or each part is something great, or all things together, or it appeared as a form from everything, or the "great," both from each and as if standing by and toward all and everything; or these things are what it is necessary to produce, or if there is a mass or a power which it has made—nothing in it, everything appearing without cause itself, and the color which comes from non-color, or the quality which has its name from those qualities.

<column-break/>

Since even now, as it seems, there is such an effect, as great as this world is, if the heavens and all that are in them should cease to be, all magnitude would likewise withdraw from it at the same time. All those qualities would leave, and there would then be left what was there before, preserving absolutely nothing of those things which they previously possessed around it. Although for whatever things it happens that they are affected by the presence of others, it is also permitted for them to retain something when those things depart; but those which are not affected, retain nothing at all, just as the air, having received light, retains nothing of the light when the light leaves. If anyone should wonder how it is possible that what has no magnitude makes something large, we shall object similarly: in what way does it happen that what has no heat becomes hot? For it is not the same thing for matter to be matter as it is for there to be magnitude, since magnitude is in some parts of matter, just as figure is in material things; and if we preserve matter, we shall say it obtains all things by a certain participation. Indeed, one thing is common: magnitude in bodies, since they are composites, is magnitude together with other things, yet not determined; for in the very <term>account<note>original Latin: "ratione" (ratio); the definition or rational structure of a thing.</note></term> of a body, magnitude is also included; but in matter itself, not even indeterminate magnitude is included, since matter is not a body.

BUT neither will magnitude itself be a <term>species<note>In this context, "species" refers to a Form or an intelligible reality.</note></term> when it is magnitude itself, nor is it ready to be divided: because magnitude exists according to itself.
<margin>XVII. Matter has no size of its own, but it proceeds toward it by subtle steps into itself.</margin>
And if it cannot familiarly reconcile the imitations of beings to itself, certainly it is not magnitude in this way. But because it [matter] wants that which is situated in the intellect or the soul to be great, it therefore handed over to those things which, by proceeding, wish as if to imitate it by a desire or movement toward it, a certain faculty for imprinting their passion in another. Therefore, the "Great," running into a wide space in the progress of the imagination or appearance, brings it about that this "great" concurs with the smallness of matter, making it appear great even in a co-extension that is not filled. For this "great" is false, since, not having this very thing so as to be great, it extends toward it as if co-amplified by the extension. For when all beings act in others or upon another, a specular appearance <note>Ficino uses "apparentiam specularem" to emphasize Plotinus's favorite metaphor: that matter is a mirror where forms appear as reflections but never truly stick.</note> of them and each of the agents occurs by a certain similar reason; and they make it great because it is a whole, and the "great" of each reason concurs after it, such as of a horse or of any other thing. Moreover, the "great itself" stands out, and the entire specular appearance becomes great, namely, shining forth toward the "great itself." Any part whatever becomes something great, and at the same time all things appeared from the universal species, to which the "great" belongs. And also from any part, it was made as if essentially, both the whole and toward all things, and being forced to be that in species, it also produced in mass as much as its power allowed. Whence it happened that what is nothing, again in appearing becomes all things; for this reason, even the color which proceeds from non-color, and the quality which occurs among us from non-quality, [possess] the name.

<summary>This page discusses the Neoplatonic theory of magnitude, explaining how matter—which is inherently dimensionless—can appear to take on size and extension by reflecting the intelligible Form of the "Great." Plotinus argues that this physical extension is a "false greatness" or a specular reflection, much like light in the air or an image in a mirror.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of matter (hyle) and how it interacts with the Forms (eide). It specifically addresses the paradox of how matter, which has no size or "magnitude" of its own, can appear to take on dimensions in the physical world.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.
310

...they have obtained from those things equivocally <note>original: "æquivocâ"; used here to mean that the "size" of matter is not the same kind of "size" found in the realm of True Being.</note>, and magnitude from non-magnitude, or equivocal magnitude. Where certainly those things are considered intermediate between matter itself and the form <note>Latin: "speciem"</note> itself; and they appear indeed, since they shine forth from there in a certain way: yet they deceive, because that in which they appear does not exist. Whatever things are stretched out into magnitude are drawn, evidently, by the power of those things which appear here, and they make a place for themselves. Indeed, the drawing occurs through all things without violence, from the fact that matter is the universe <note>Plotinus suggests that matter provides the underlying "space" or receptacle for the entire cosmos.</note>. Each thing draws through the power it possesses: it has it from there, and that which makes matter great, as it seems, does that by an image of that which is great, appearing here, and that is what is called "the appearing," which is great here. But matter, forced to run together, or in which these things are forced to run together, offers itself all at once and everywhere. For it is matter, and the matter of this universe, nor is it anything <note>In Neoplatonism, matter is often described as "non-being" because it lacks any inherent qualities or independent existence.</note>. But that which of itself is not anything, can through another again become the contrary: and after it has become the contrary, it is not even that, otherwise it would consist only in this very thing.

<margin>
XVIII.
Matter itself has no true form, thus no magnitude: and how, through the effective movement of the form coming into it, it is produced in direction alone, yet it is not pulled apart, but held together.
</margin>
If anyone should possess the intelligence of the great <term>Magnitude<note>In this context, Magnitude refers to the abstract concept or "Form" of size and extension.</note></term>, which indeed has power through which it is not only in itself, but also as if able to go forth outside, and should attain a certain nature not existing in the intelligent being, nor having form, nor any trace of the great, nor of anything at all, what then will it do through such power? Not a horse, not an ox: for other causes will do these things. Perhaps since it comes from the great father <note>original Latin: "magno patre"; original Greek: "μεγάλου πατρὸς". This refers to the Intellect or the One as the progenitor of the Forms.</note>, it proceeds; nothing else can capture that greatness, but this will have it imaginarily. To this, therefore, which has by no means attained greatness so that it is great in its own nature, it remains as far as it can appear great. This, moreover, is not to fail, and if it is propagated everywhere, it does not proceed as if spoken into many, but has related parts in itself, and is nowhere entirely absent. For it could not be that in a small mass there would also be an equal likeness of the great, since it is an image of the great: but insofar as it desired it by the hope of that, it approached, and running as much as it can together with its concurrent [form], being unable to be carried away, it made great that which is not great, and not in such a way that it appears great, and what is seen as great in mass. Matter, meanwhile, preserves its own nature, using this greatness like a garment <note>original: "vestimento"; a common metaphor in ancient philosophy where the physical body or form is a "cloak" for the soul or underlying substance.</note>, with which indeed it is clothed when it ran together with it, while that running led it. If it should ever strip this off, it remains again the same as it was before within itself, namely as large as the present form makes it. Therefore the soul, having the forms of beings, since it is also a form itself, possesses all at once. Since also any form is all at once with you, and seeing the forms of sensible things as if reflected into itself and approaching, it does not [struggle] to capture them with a multitude, but with the mass subtracted from them, it discerns them. For it cannot become anything other than what it is.

<column-break/>

Those things from them, and magnitude from no part, or equivocally considered between them and matter itself, and the form appears to it there, like a shadow <note>original Greek: "σκιά" (skia)</note>. But it deceives, because in that which it appears, it is nothing. For each thing, drawn by the power of those things that will be, and making a place for themselves, is drawn toward all things, which by force * of matter... *
Each according to its own power which it has. It has it from there: and that which makes matter great, as it seems, from the appearance of the great, from that which appears there, that which is great here; but the matter upon which it is forced... all together or everywhere provides itself as matter of the one whole. * and the chance to be greatest... * about itself, can deceive and each... the other from the becoming of the contrary... * for it is again. *

THEREFORE, one who has the intelligence of the great, if the same intelligence should have power, not only to be in itself, but also as if to walk about by power... * to be carried, and would take a nature not being in the thinker; or that which is in the thinker... <unclear>@</unclear> or that which... <unclear>@</unclear> the great, but that which is likely... or which it will make... by power to have—... or itself how it will make its own... those great things from the father come, the power can... to contain the great... which appears, and not truly... greatness, so as to be great in itself... as far as it is possible to appear great * remaining * it is, to not fail, or to remain... many in many places, or if it itself having the accidents... parts, or because of being absent from nothing; or it did not have... in the not-small mass that which is equal to the great... to be an image, and of the great; but as much as you desire... of the hope of that, it approached; or so that also... it was with him... to be taken away and able and has made great; all and... that which is not great, nor if it should so seem, and that which is seen... in mass great; but it nonetheless guards its own nature, using this great [thing], as a garment which ran together with it, * God led her, it was stripped away, or again... if it should take away, it remains again the same, such as it was from itself. And the same, as much as for it the present form makes it; the soul indeed having the forms of beings, being form itself, has all together, and each form being together with it. The sensible forms as if * reflected toward * itself and seeing them going around, it does not feel... to receive the multitude, but being separated from the mass, it sees; for it cannot become other than how it is.

<summary>Plotinus discusses how matter, though inherently void of size, acts as a "receptacle" or mirror for the Form of Magnitude, creating the illusion of physical space and extension. He compares the physical appearance of matter to a garment that covers its true, formless nature.</summary>

### BOOK SIX.

<margin>In another version</margin>
Matter, having no power to "persuade" <note>original: "πείθειν"; here meaning to influence or cast off</note> anything of its own, nor any activity to complete, remains a passive subject for whatever the acting principle wishes to do with it. That acting principle could not be said to exist there <note>i.e., in the physical realm of matter</note>, but rather it possesses the power over things that are to come into being—just as in the imagination <note>term: "phantasia" (imagination/mental representation)</note>, an image is moved by a rational principle <note>term: "logos" (the formative principle or Reason-Scheme)</note> or a motion. Either there is a division under this, or an identity through which it was moved, yet it remains. For all of matter, just like the soul, is unable to exist without structure, otherwise it would not be itself. Since it must receive all things as a whole, yet not in an indivisible way, it is necessary for it to progress through all things in a certain way. If it encountered all things at once, it would be forced to consider a "distance" <note>original: "διάστημα"; spatial extension</note>, because the object of its search is not yet grasped: it grows weary in the face of what is to come. For every thing that does not enter...
<margin>In another version: "it was prevented from being other things; was it not possible to be upon others, or was it not first in one?"</margin>
...the things of every form, so that these are together, even if they are parts. For will life be divided in matter, by the division of living things? If not, the whole would not have come into being according to the rational principle.

---

The things that enter into matter, as if into a mother, do not harm it, nor do they benefit it. For the "blows" <note>The physical impressions left by forms</note> dealt by them do not affect matter itself, but rather the powers affect one another, being directed toward opposites rather than toward the underlying subject—unless one considers the underlying subject together with the qualities collected within it. Heat destroys cold, and black obscures white; or, when mixed together, they produce another quality from themselves. Thus, the things that are mixed are the ones that undergo "suffering" <note>term: "passio" (passion/suffering); in a philosophical sense, this means being acted upon or changed</note>. To suffer, in this sense, is to no longer be what they were. Truly, in living beings, these "passions" occur in the bodies, as alterations arise according to the qualities and co-existing powers. When the constitutions themselves are dissolved, or brought together, or transposed against their natural state, the "passions" are in the bodies; but in the souls, there are "cognitions" <note>conscious perceptions</note> of the more violent passions. Otherwise, they do not recognize them, and matter remains. For matter suffers nothing when cold departs and heat arrives. For none of these things is properly "friendly" or "hostile" to it. Therefore, its most appropriate name is "receptacle" <note>term: "susceptaculum"</note> and "nurse." But for what reason has it also been called "mother"? For matter itself generates nothing. It seems they call it "mother" who believe that matter acts only as a recipient, contributing nothing to those things being born—since the physical mass of a child is sustained by nourishment. If a mother does contribute something to the child, she does so not in her capacity as "matter," but because she is seen as providing a "form" <note>original: "species"</note>. For only the Form is fertile, while the other nature <note>matter</note> is sterile. Hence, I believe, the ancient sages signified this obscurely in their sacred mysteries when they introduced the ancient Hermes <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> as always possessing the "instrument of generation" <note>The phallus, representing the active, formative power of the Logos</note> for the completion of the work...

<column-break/>

But since Matter has no power to shake off <note>original: "excutiendi"</note>, for it possesses no action: and since it is a shadow, it perpetually sustains whatever the cause intends to effect within it. Indeed, that which proceeds from the rational principle <note>original: "ratione"</note> already holds the trace of what is to be made. For just as in the imagination or a certain imaginary appearance, a moved rational principle (or a motion depending on a rational principle) is a "partition." Otherwise, if it were entirely one and the same, no motion would occur there, but it would remain still. Yet matter cannot receive all forms at once as the soul does; otherwise, it would be one of them. Since it is necessary for matter to receive all things, yet not receive them as an indivisible point, it is necessary that it—being the place for all existing things—proceed through all things, meet all things, and suffice for every interval everywhere, since it is not confined by any space, but is exposed to the future. In what way, then, can it be that one thing entering does not prohibit others? Those things which cannot occur simultaneously were perhaps not one primary thing; if that were to happen, that would be the Form of the universe itself. Therefore, all things are indeed together, but in part, whatever you please. For the matter of a living thing is distributed simultaneously with the partition of the living thing itself; otherwise, nothing would have been effected beyond the rational principle.

---

<margin>
XIX
How matter is not changed by the qualities of the forms, and therefore does not "suffer." And how, in the act of conceiving, it does not diminish the form, any more than a shadow might.
</margin>

Therefore, those things which enter matter, as if into a mother, do not harm it at all, nor do they bring it any utility. For the impulses of these things do not pertain to matter, but rather to each other. Since their powers are directed toward opposites, not toward the subjects, unless perhaps one considers the subjects together with the things collected in them. For heat harms cold, and black darkens white: or if they are mixed, they produce some other quality from themselves. Therefore, those things that are mixed "suffer." To suffer is within their power; it is to no longer be what they were. Truly, in animals, the "passions" are in the bodies, while alteration proceeds according to qualities and internal forces. But when the constitutions themselves are loosened, or brought together, or transposed against their natural constitution, the passions are in the bodies, but in the souls there are "cognitions" for those perceiving the more vehement passions. Otherwise, they do not perceive them, and matter remains. For with cold departing and heat arriving, matter suffers nothing. For none of these things is properly "friendly" or "hostile" to it. Wherefore its most proper name is "receptacle" and "nurse." But indeed, for what reason was it also called "mother"? For it generates nothing. But those seem to call it "mother" who judge that matter only receives, but contributes nothing to the offspring—since even the physical bulk of the offspring is maintained from nourishment. If a mother contributes something to the child, she does so not because she is matter, but because she is judged to give a "form." For only the Form is fertile; the other nature is sterile. Hence the ancient sages, I believe, signifying this obscurely in their sacred mysteries, introduce the ancient Hermes <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> as always having the instrument of generation ready for the effect of the work...

<summary>Plotinus argues that matter is an entirely passive "receptacle" that remains unchanged by the forms and qualities it hosts, comparing it to a sterile mother or nurse who provides the space for growth without contributing to the child's essential nature.</summary>

...declaring that the one who generates in the realm of the senses is the intelligible reason <note>original: "intelligibilem rationem"; refers to the *Logos* or the formative principle</note>. By showing the sterility of matter, which always remains the same, they indicate this through those things which are arranged around it but are themselves sterile. For they introduce the "mother of all," as they call it, by taking a principle based on the substrate <note>term: "subjectum/hypokeimenon" (the underlying material)</note> and applying such a name to indicate more clearly what they mean: namely, that matter is not entirely like a mother. This is intended for those who study more deeply to understand the true mode of these things, not being content merely with the surface of reality. I say that they have demonstrated, albeit from a distance and as far as they were able, that matter exists; and that it is not entirely female, but "female" only in the sense that it properly receives. As far as generating is concerned, it does so in no way at all, because that which reaches this point is neither female nor able to give birth; rather, it is separated from all power of birthing. Indeed, such power belongs only to that which remains masculine.

<column-break/>

<margin>Regarding matter</margin>
...of purity <note>original: "Ἀγνείας"; symbolizing matter’s sterile or "untouched" nature</note>, declaring that the one who generates in the realm of sense is the intelligible reason. They show the sterility of matter, which remains always the same, through those things around it which are always sterile. Desiring to make it the mother of all, they took the name from the substrate <margin>In matter</margin> to show that it is not entirely like a mother, wishing to point this out to those who want to grasp the manner of these things more accurately <margin>In the mind</margin> and do not seek only on the surface. Though from a distance, they showed, as far as they were able, that it is sterile; and while it is not entirely female, it is female insofar as it receives, but no longer insofar as it is fertile. For by being separated from itself <margin>In matter</margin>, it is neither able to be made female <note>i.e., to truly conceive</note> nor to give birth, being cut off from all power of generating, which belongs only to that which remains male.

# MARSILIO FICINO'S COMMENTARY ON THE SEVENTH BOOK OF THE THIRD ENNEAD, CONCERNING ETERNITY AND TIME.
## SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->What eternity is, and where it is. What "sempiternity" is. What perpetuity is. How eternity relates to time.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring foliage, scrollwork, and a small figure within the letter's frame.</image-desc>

<margin>Eternity in the Mind, then in other minds and bodies.</margin>
The Platonists place ETERNITY first in the "First Mind" <note>the Divine Intellect</note>; then in other minds; and thirdly in bodies, insofar as something stable is preserved within them. Similarly, they place "Time" first in the primary Soul, then in other living beings, and thirdly in bodies, insofar as motion is found in them. It is asked: what exactly is eternity in the First Mind and in the First Being? Certainly, there are five genera or elements of being there: namely, essence, motion, rest <note>original: "status"</note>, identity, and diversity. There are also the species of things called "Ideas," such as "Humanity" and the like. These genera of being are not predicated of one another; for "rest" itself is neither motion nor is it mobile. Likewise, it is neither diversity nor "the diverse," for these are opposites. Essence itself, in its primary character, seems to have no opposite. Furthermore, the Ideas are not predicated of one another; for the Idea of a lion is neither the Idea of a man, nor is it "human." Eternity, however, is predicated of all things that are there, such that each of them is "eternal." 

Eternity, therefore, is not just one specific genus of being there, nor is it a single Idea. It is a gift common to all, whereas the other things there are distinguished from each other either by incommunicable properties—as individual Ideas are unique among themselves—or by a certain opposition, such as motion and rest, or identity and diversity. Truly, although eternity is a gift common to all, it is present even to motion itself, and to the diversity and multitude existing there; for all these things are "eternalized." It is not primarily designated by "rest," "identity," or "unity" alone, though it is through these that eternity is possessed by the rest. Nor should one think that eternity is strictly the same as "rest." For in the realm of Forms, three things are primarily contained within the concept of eternity: namely, rest, "sempiternity" (which you might call "always-ness"), and identity or unity—or what I might call "lack of distance" <note>original: "indystantia"; meaning a lack of temporal or spatial spread</note>. But "rest" itself does not necessarily include these in its definition. It does not include the "always." For we can conceive of something being at rest, but not "always." Nor does it necessarily embrace unity or "the one," for it can persist in a multitude. Likewise, motion is the opposite of rest, but it is not the opposite of sempiternity. For what prevents that which moves from moving "always"? 

And yet, although sempiternity itself is not the entire definition of eternity on its own, it is the most powerful part of its definition. Since motion is primarily opposed to rest, yet does not oppose sempiternity (the most powerful element in eternity), it follows that eternity is not exactly the same as "rest," which is somewhat distinct from the other things there. Eternity, however, is equally common to all. For eternity is a certain vigor of essential, intellectual life itself, always equally vigorous, possessing all its aspects at once, neither losing anything of itself nor acquiring any new gift over time. Whatever things are there seem to claim such vigor for themselves equally. Meanwhile, you must remember that "sempiternity" is simply like a genus signifying perseverance or life that lacks beginning and end, under which there are two species. The first is "Aeon" <note>term: "Aevum"</note>, which is eternity: life or perseverance that is infinite and remains as a whole all at once. The second is "perpetuity" or time itself: infinite perseverance that proceeds in parts through succession. Hence, as Proclus <note>a late Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says, both are a kind of measure: time measures temporal and mobile things, while eternity measures eternal things. But time measures by frequent repetition and as if by counting; eternity, however, measures by being applied and fitted all at once. The proper definition of eternity is called not so much "essence"...

<summary>This page discusses the metaphysical passivity of matter as a sterile "mother" and introduces Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on eternity and time, defining eternity as a unified vigor of divine life.</summary>
<keywords>matter, hyle, mother, sterility, Marsilio Ficino, eternity, time, five genera of being, essence, motion, rest, identity, diversity, sempiternity, Proclus</keywords>

--- Page 358 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Ennead III, Book 7, specifically focusing on the definitions of Eternity and Time. The previous page established the nature of matter; here, the focus shifts to the metaphysical structure of duration and the soul's relationship to the eternal.</meta>

<page-num>143</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK VII OF ENNEAD III. 143</header>

...essence or intelligence is more than life. It is, therefore, life: but of what extent? Infinite, surely: so that it differs from any portion of time. Again, of what kind? Certainly, it is "whole all at once" <note>original: "tota simul"; a standard philosophical definition of eternity meaning all moments exist simultaneously</note>, so that it differs from the whole of time. The power of eternal life is thus one and whole all at once; and to put it briefly, it is life that is already infinite: whereas time is life proceeding through the infinite. The very "being" of eternity is a presence that is entirely fixed, like a center; for this reason, a single center suffices. Since it never passes away, there is no need for anything to succeed it. 

However, that which is called "present" in time, since it passes away suddenly, requires another successor to take its place, lest the entire nature of time be lost. Time is preserved little by little out of infinite moments succeeding one another; therefore, if it has any essence, it is mixed from "being" and "not being," while the present intervenes between the past and the future, which do not exist. Indeed, time can emulate that eternal "present" through a certain perpetual present of its own, applying itself toward a stable presence, yet it never becomes truly stable. Therefore, what it cannot attain by remaining still, it at least pursues by succeeding itself. By proceeding infinitely through many moments, it matches itself as best it can to that fixed and simple infinity. 

Consider how one remaining moment (if I may call it that), acting as a center, looks upon and encompasses the innumerable moments of time as if they were points on a circumference perpetually running around it, all equally present to its view. Lines and points are indeed distant from one another outside the center, but in the center, they are gathered into one. Similarly, the moments of time and the progressions of temporal things are distant from each other, but in the eternity that saves time—the Principle—they are so reduced to one that there is a single presence for all, the same life, and a single gaze. 

In these passages where Plotinus speaks of the "perfect whole," remember that every "whole" found in art and nature is a common form that follows after individual parts and results from those parts. Therefore, such a whole is not a "whole through itself," but a whole through its parts and through that which gathered the parts together. This, then, is the "First Whole." The First Whole is that which is a simple form and substance, generating parts within itself if it is to have them. And because it generates them, it precedes them in a way; and by the very fact that it precedes the parts, it is entirely indivisible. Now, because it is indivisible, when it inserts itself into individual parts, it inserts its whole self everywhere. This is the "absolutely whole," which is preserved as a whole in any part of itself. 

Such is the Divine Mind in relation to the Ideas; such is the universal vital nature in relation to the "seeds" of things <note>term: "semina rerum" (logoi spermatikoi); the formative principles that guide natural growth</note>; such is the eternity of the Mind and of the first life in relation to its entire presence, remaining always in the One and toward the One. It remains in the One of its own being and active presence; and it is directed toward the One which is the Good to be loved above all essence, committing itself through action. It "remains," I say, because it already possesses whatever it is advantageous to have. It remains likewise through the infinite, yet that infinity is not some quantity external to life. Since the very life of the first being—which is its first and internal act—precedes any quantity, if any duration or quantity of perseverance is attributed to it, you should understand that nothing has been added to the simplicity of that indivisible and present life.

---

### On the conformity of the intellect to eternity. Also, what time is not: namely, that it is not duration in bodily motion, nor a similar measure or number, nor a consequence and companion of bodily motion.

Where Plotinus, after a profound discussion on eternity, descends to the topic of time, you should consider the reason he proves the eternity of the mind: it is because the mind touches eternal things by the act of understanding. Indeed, to understand is, in a way, to touch. Since all the senses perceive a thing to be felt through a kind of touch, much more do the supreme powers of the soul touch things by knowing them through reason and intelligence. This is especially true because they penetrate the inner depths of things by discerning them, which the senses cannot do. Furthermore, their objects come more effectively to be touched—or rather, there is no need for them to "come," as they are never absent. 

The kinship of the intellect to its own eternal objects is thus greater than the kinship of the sense to sensible things. I call it a mutual kinship of intelligence: for insofar as it touches, it is touched and seen. Therefore, just as sense is an agent in time, so the intellect is an agent in the aeon <note>term: "ævo" (the aevum); a state of duration between time and eternity, often associated with angels or celestial bodies</note>. Reason, however, is like a medium between both: for it touches both eternal and temporal things. 

A "middle" can indeed be of this sort. For even the heavens exist in both: through their substance they are in the aeon, but through their motion and action they are in time. Moreover, the universe must not lack such a medium. Between the higher things, which are eternal in both action and essence, and the lower things, which are temporal in both, there must be rational souls. These souls are in the aeon by their essence, but in time by their action and motion. 

Accordingly, it is not without reason that the Platonists find it right that the rational soul should adapt itself to those levels of the universe—the eternal, the temporal, and the intermediate. It unfolds itself into these same levels which are, in a sense, naturally implanted within it, just as our body adapts itself in various ways to any place, composing itself through different figures and modes. 

Now, time is either motion itself, or something belonging to motion: specifically, either the internal span of motion, its measure, or its companion. It is clear that time is not motion, because every motion is performed *in* time; it is as if time were one thing in which motion is carried out, and motion itself were another. Furthermore, if a body that is moving now ceases to move a little later, and then moves again, the motion will have been interrupted, but time is not interrupted. For if we think about how long it moved, we also think about how long it was at rest. Both the cycles of motion and the intervening rest can be measured by the same continuity of time. Even if a body capable of being moved by another ceases to move, time would still remain—at least we can conceive of it in the mover which is "movable through itself"—as if we ought to seek the nature of time above the motion of the body. 

Likewise, in very fast motion, there is a great deal of the nature of motion itself, but very little of time; in very slow motion, the opposite occurs. This shows that time and motion are different things. Finally, the properties of time are brevity and length, whereas the properties of motion are intensity and relaxation (manifested as speed and slowness). Since their properties differ, the things themselves must also differ. It is more probable, therefore, that time is something specifically pertaining to motion rather than being motion itself. 

You might perhaps say that it is a "space"—not of place, which is outside of motion, but of duration and perseverance. This would be an interval internal to motion: the path, the stretch, and the progression of motion. To this, two objections can be made. First, there would be as many such internal intervals as there are motions. But time must be a single, common measure, by which we can measure all motions, however different they may be from one another. Second, such "duration" seems to be nothing other than motion itself—specifically the continuity of motion. If this continuity were removed, motion would not exist if it happened instantaneously. And indeed, this is the highest property or nature of motion: just as an extension through space is either the body itself or the property most belonging to the body.

<summary>This page defines eternity as a fixed "center" where life exists all at once, contrasting it with time as an infinite succession of moments. It also argues that the rational soul serves as a bridge between the eternal and temporal realms and begins a refutation of the idea that time is identical to physical motion.</summary>

<page-num>324</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

Yet, duration itself is not strictly internal to every motion, but is preserved in this or that specific motion. We think of **Time**, however, as being everywhere, and we are accustomed to measuring any duration and perseverance of motion by time. From this, it appears that time is a certain measurable interval <term>interuallum; a span or distance</term>, existing beyond the specific interval of a motion itself, yet not belonging to a spatial interval. Therefore, we must ask about this kind of external interval: what is it naturally in itself, before it performs this act of measurement? For a thing must exist in its own right before it can measure anything else. We also ask whether it measures rest, and in what way. For a thing is "at rest" only insofar as something else is "in motion."

Three propositions regarding time have been put forward by those who say time is "something belonging to motion." First, that it is the space and duration of motion (which we have discussed sufficiently); second, that it is a certain measure of such duration; and third, that it is something accompanying or following motion. But let us return now to the concept of **measure**, toward which we have been gradually descending. We are compelled to answer: what is time in itself before it measures? Is it an external measure, or an internal one? And how does it measure both motion and rest? We further ask why it is called a "numerical measure," as if it were gathered from units. It is more probable, however, given its continuity, to call time a certain "measure" simply, rather than a "number." Yet if it is a measure, it must be a quantity of some sort—a certain "how much" that measures motion as it runs along with it. 

Here we must ask: under what condition does time run with motion? And why does time measure motion, rather than motion measuring time? For we are accustomed to measuring a "length of time" by a "length of motion," and we perceive time through action no less than the other way around. In short, the doubt remains: is time the motion itself measured by a certain magnitude? Or is it a magnitude measuring motion? Or is it a third thing? One might doubt what this "magnitude" uses to measure motion, and indeed doubt the nature of this measurable magnitude itself. For it is as great in itself as the motion it measures. Just as motion is judged to be "so much" because of time, does time itself exist as "so much" because of something higher? Finally, we must investigate what it is before it measures (as we said). Similar doubts arise if we accept the third opinion: that time is something that merely accompanies motion. 

We are forced to conclude that time itself is something real, even if no mind were choosing to use time to measure motion. For the **World Soul** <term>Anima Mundi; the spirit that animates the entire universe</term> generates time by its own natural and internal motion, without using any choice or deliberation to do so.

->Eternity is in the divine mind; Time is in the soul of the world, by which<-
->the world’s motion is driven and measured.<-

In the divine mind, time does not exist in the proper sense. Instead, there is a certain **Idea** of time—a conceptual archetype <note>original: "exemplar conceptum"</note> held there in a likeness of itself. It imitates eternity <note>original: "aeuum"</note>, but meanwhile falls away from it through change. Time, properly speaking, exists in the World Soul—specifically in its vegetative nature <note>original: "vegetali natura"; the most basic level of life that governs growth and existence</note> and its natural imagination, which constantly accompanies that nature. In this dual faculty, I say, the Soul’s action of generating and imagining worldly things is not performed all at once because of its inherent "weakness" <note>Unlike the Divine Mind, which sees everything simultaneously, the Soul must process things sequentially</note>. Instead, it acts step by step: now one thing arises, now another. Though these actions are ordered, they are distinct, turning now to these things and now to those, proceeding according to "before" and "after." This successive procession through such steps is **motion**; the continuity and length of this procession is **time**. 

Now, just as the length of a body differs from the body itself, so does time differ from motion. I mean the "length" of the motion differs from the "acting" of the motion. This length relates to eternity just as a line relates to a point—especially if we imagine a line proceeding from the movement of a point. Plotinus believes that just as a specific body sprouts from the power inherent in a soul's seed, so the physical world sprouts from the natural power of the World Soul breathing into matter. This world is contained, ruled, and moved within the Soul as if in the "place" of the world. It is moved temporally, at certain intervals of time, according to the motion occurring within the Soul; for that Soul, through its own internal motion, created time within itself. Along with this motion and time, it simultaneously produced the world, which is mobile within time.

->The world has but one place: the World Soul. Time is one and everywhere,<-
->since the Soul exercises this vital motion everywhere. Meanwhile,<-
->the motion of the world is governed by the motion of its own Soul;<-
->this, in turn, is governed by its own eternal Intellect;<-
->and that finally by the Divine Intellect and its<-
->primary eternity.<-

<summary>Ficino explains that time is not merely a measurement of physical movement, but a product of the World Soul's internal, successive activity. He defines time as the "length" of the Soul's motion, which serves as a bridge between the physical world and divine eternity.</summary>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. III

...if we are to prevail: and that which is superior to these things should not be described by such names; one might perhaps rightly take the intelligible nature and eternity as the same. Again, both the intelligible world and eternity embrace the same things within themselves. But truly, when we say one is in the other, and we place intelligible things within eternity—and when we declare any intelligible thing to be eternal, just as in the *Timaeus*, where it is written: *The nature of the model is eternal* <note>original: "Exemplaris natura aeterna est." A reference to Plato’s Timaeus 37d, describing the eternal blueprint of the universe.</note>—in these cases, I say, we affirm that eternity is something other than the intelligible nature; yet we admit it exists around it, or in it, or is present to it. However, the fact that both are judged to be venerable does not necessarily prove they are the same. For perhaps one of them has its venerability from the other. Furthermore, regarding the idea that both contain the same things, it must be explained that while the intelligible nature contains its own parts (as components), eternity embraces the whole simultaneously, not as a part, but because all such things are called "eternal" through it.

But should we judge eternity according to the "state" <term>status: translating the Greek *stasis*, meaning rest, stability, or lack of change.</term> existing there, just as we are accustomed to conceive of time here according to motion? First, one might rightly ask about eternity: whether we say it is the same as stability; and perhaps not simply, but the stability that is considered to be around essence. For if it were identical to stability, then first, we would not call stability "eternal," just as we do not call eternity "eternal." For that which is eternal is that which participates in eternity. Secondly, how would motion be eternal? If it were, it would also be stable. Furthermore, how can the notion of stability itself possess "always" within it? I mean not "always" in a temporal sense, but rather the kind we understand when we say "everlasting." If this "always" is contained within the very stability of essence, then we would again be separating the other categories of being from eternity. Added to this is the fact that eternity must be understood not only in stability, but also in the One; and indeed, the quality of being "unextended" <note>original: "indistantis." Meaning without spatial or temporal dimensions; a point-like existence that doesn't spread out.</note> must be preserved for eternity, lest it be the same as time. But stability, by the very reason it is stability, contains within itself neither the concept of the One nor the unextended. Therefore, we preach that eternity "abides in the One." It participates in stability, but it is not stability itself.

### WHAT then, most importantly, will that itself be, through which we say the whole divine world is eternal and everlasting? Or what is everlastingness? Whether it is the same as eternity, or if eternity exists according to it. Perhaps we ought to think of it as a single thing gathered from many—either a single intelligence or a nature—whether it follows the things there, exists alongside them, or is seen within them. All these things, I say, are reduced into that one existing nature, which is also many, and capable of many things. Truly, he who contemplates this manifold power names its "essence" according to that which serves as its subject; but insofar as he beholds its life, he names it "motion"; and then "stability," insofar as it maintains itself in exactly the same way. He sees "alterity" and "sameness" insofar as these many things are simultaneously one. Thus, by composing the "one" back into unity, I say...

<column-break/>

**A** In whatever way we have reached these venerable things, they should not be categorized as if they were merely worthy of this name. For again, both the intelligible world and eternity are both all-encompassing of their own things. But when we say one is in the other, such as things being placed "in the eternal," and when we predicate "the eternal" of them—for he says that *the nature of the paradigm happened to be eternal* <note>original: "παραδείγματι φύσιν ἐτύγχανεν οὖσαν αἰώνιος." From Timaeus 37d.</note>—we are speaking of eternity.

**B** And again, we say that it is something around that nature, or in it, or present to it. Since each is venerable, their identity might not be the same, even if the venerability of one comes from the other. Or it is a matter of fullness: to the one, as being made of parts; to eternity, as the whole together without parts. But we say such things are "eternal" because of it. *But is it according to stability?*

**C** One might say that eternity is the stability there, just as people say time is according to motion. But one might reasonably ask about time if they propose it is stability—not simply, but the "always" stability. For how could it be the same as stability? First, we would not call eternity "eternal," just as we do not call eternity "eternal"; for the "eternal" is that which participates in eternity. Then, how will motion be eternal? For it would then be...

**D** ...stationary. Then how does the concept of stability have the "always" in itself? I mean not the "always" in time, but as we think when we say "everlasting." If it is in the stability of essence, it will again exclude the other genera of being from eternity. For we say eternity is not only in stability, but is also in the One and is unextended, so that it is not the same as time. But stability as such...

**E** ...does not have the concept of the One or the unextended. Rather, we predicate of eternity that it "abides," which would mean it participates in stability, but is not stability itself.

What then is this, according to which we say the whole world there is eternal or everlasting? And what is everlastingness? Is it the same thing, and is it itself eternity, or is eternity according to it? Is it according to...

**F** ...one thing? But perhaps it is a single intuition or nature gathered from many, whether following the things there, or co-existing, or seen within them. All these things together are that one thing, which is many in power. And if you see this many-powered perception... gathering it as it were, one calls it "essence" as the substrate, or "motion" according to its life...

**G** ...then how they are "other" and "same" together. Then, having synthesized these back again into an eternity...

<summary>Plotinus investigates the relationship between eternity and the intelligible realm, arguing that while they are closely linked, eternity is a distinct "oneness" that encompasses the whole of being without being divided into parts. He specifically critiques the idea that eternity is simply "rest" (stability), noting that eternity must also encompass motion and other forms of existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's rigorous definition of eternity (aiōn). Following the previous page's discussion on how eternity relates to the intelligible world, Plotinus now defines it as a "life in stability," contrasting the "ever-present" nature of the eternal with the sequential "now and then" of time. This is a foundational text for the Neoplatonic understanding of timelessness.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<column-break/>

->[The life of the Whole]<-

...being all together. Life, therefore, by gathering into a tension the otherness of its activity, possesses an unceasing nature, and is that which is identical and always the same. It is not a thinking or a life that passes from one thing to another, but seeing all things at once <note>original Greek: "ἅμα πάντα" (hama panta). This is a technical term in Neoplatonism for the simultaneous existence of all things in the divine mind.</note>, always and without distance, it sees eternity. This is found in a life that remains, which is the same and always present, possessing the whole—not now this and later another, but all at once. And not now some things and later others, but an indivisible end, as if in a point all things were together and never flowing away in a stream, but remaining in the same, in itself, and not changing, but being in the present always, because nothing has passed away from it, nor will anything come to be. But that which it is, it is; so that eternity is not the subject itself, but that which shines out from it, its identity, as being always and not otherwise. It does not become something later which it is not already, nor will it be later what it is not now. For there is nothing from which it arrives into the present. That is not something else, but what it must necessarily have now; nor does it have an "it was" around itself. For what is there that was and has passed? Nor does an "it will be" happen to it. For what will be in it? It remains, therefore, in its being as this which it is in itself, which neither was nor will be, but is only this, holding its being firmly by not changing into the future, nor having changed from the past. This is eternity. Thus, the life that concerns being, in being itself, is all together, full and everywhere entirely without distance—this is what we seek, eternity.

**AND** surely it must not be thought that eternity happens to that nature from the outside, but that it is within it, from it, and together with it. For it is seen from deep within itself: since all the other things which we say are there when we look upon them, such as the innermost things, we say are all from essence and together with essence. For those things which are primarily must consist with the first things, and be in the first things, since beauty also is in them, and from them, and similarly truth is in them. And in one way the whole itself is as if in a part, and in another way the parts are as if in the whole, as if that were truly the "all" <term>the "all": referring to the *To Pan*, the totality of the intelligible realm.</term>, not gathered together from parts, but itself generating the parts, so that by this reasoning it is truly the "all." Furthermore, the truth flourishing there is not some harmony toward another, but belongs properly to each thing itself, of which it is the truth. Indeed, all that is true, if it is truly the "all," must not only be the "all" insofar as it is all things: but even the "all" itself must be held so that nothing is lacking to it. But if it were so, nothing will "be" for it [in the future], for if something "will be," it was previously lacking in this part. Therefore, it was not the "all" before this. But nothing can happen to this against its nature, for...

<column-break/>

**A** I say, life alone, contracting in itself otherness, and looking upon the interminable identity of its action, neither ever another, nor passing from one thing into another in intellect or life, but always holding itself in the same way, and standing far from distance. Contemplating all these things, one contemplates eternity, seeing certainly a life remaining in the same, having the whole always present, and not now indeed this something, but later another, but all things at once: nor **B** now indeed some, and later others, but an indivisible end. Where, as in a point, all things are together, not yet proceeding into a flux, but there in the same, that is, remaining in itself, never changed, but always standing in the present: since nothing has passed out of it, and nothing again will be in it, but this very thing which it is, always exists: so that eternity is thus not the subject, but that which shines forth from the subject itself according to **C** that very identity which it claims for itself—not indeed of a future possession, but one already present—promising namely to hold itself so, and never to hold itself otherwise. For what could happen in the future to this which is not now? Nor again will it be something later which it is not in the present. For there is not anything from which it might eventually arrive into the present. For that would not be something else, but would be this very thing, which indeed is not a "future" thing that it does not now possess by necessity, nor **D** does it have around itself what is called "it was." For what is it that "was" and passed away? Nor again does that happen which is called "it will be." For what will be in it? It is left, therefore, to be in itself, this very thing which is "to be." That which, therefore, neither was nor will be, but is only that which has being stably, because it is neither changed into the future, nor has it been changed by the past, is eternity. It is, therefore, the life around being in being itself, all at once and full, and everywhere altogether without distance, **E** eternity itself which we seek.

<margin>
III.
Eternity in essence is first, not an accident, but is from essence: essence is the thing itself and one. Also, in what instant eternal being exists along with temporal being.
</margin>
**NEITHER** certainly must it be thought that eternity happens to that nature from the outside, but that it is that nature, and from it, and together with it. It is perceived as being deeply seated within it: because all the other things whatever we say are there when we look, as if they were internal things, we say are from essence and together with essence: for those things which are primarily must consist in the first things, and be in the first things, since beauty also is in them, and from them similarly **F** truth is in them. And in part indeed the whole itself is as if in a part, and in part truly as if parts are in the whole, as if that were truly the "all," not gathered together from parts, but itself generating the parts, so that by this reasoning it is truly the "all." Truth, furthermore, flourishing there, is not a certain harmony toward another, but belongs properly to each thing itself, of which it is the truth. It is necessary indeed that this "all" be true, if indeed it is truly the "all," not only to be the "all" insofar as it is all things: but even the "all" itself to **G** hold it so, that nothing is lacking to it. Because if it were so, neither will anything be for it [in the future]; for if it "will be," in this part it was previously lacking. Therefore it was not the "all" before these things. <summary>Plotinus defines eternity as a simultaneous, full, and unchanging life that exists within the essence of being, contrasting it with the sequential nature of time. He argues that eternity is not an external quality but an intrinsic "shining forth" of the intelligible nature's identity and completeness.</summary>
