--- Page 363 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Eternity (Aeon) and Time. Plotinus distinguishes between the "being" of eternal realities—which have no past or future—and the "becoming" of generated things, which rely on the future to sustain their existence. This section focuses on the ontological "fullness" of the eternal.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK III.

For it undergoes no change. If, therefore, nothing happens to it, then certainly it will not be anything in the future, nor will it be [later], nor was it becoming, nor has it been made. If you were to take away "it will be" from things that are in a state of becoming <note>original: "rebus quidem generalibus." Plotinus refers to things in the physical world that are constantly changing.</note>, since they exist in a state of perpetual acquisition, they would suddenly cease to exist. However, if you were to add "it will be" to things that are not of that nature [the eternal], they would slip away from their seat of being. For it is manifest from this that "to be" is not innate to them if they exist by virtue of what is to come, or what has been made, or what is to be made in the future.

In generated things, essence seems to be a stretch <note>original: "tractus quidam." A "drawing out" or "extension."</note> from the very beginning of their generation until they reach the extreme limits of time when they are no longer; this is what is meant by "being" in their case: to exist within this span. If one were to cut anything away from this span, their life would be diminished, and thus their "being" would be diminished. The universe must be of such a kind as long as it exists in this way. For this reason, nature hastens toward the future and does not wish to rest; since it draws its being to itself by performing one action after another, moving in a circle out of a desire for essence.

Thus, "being" in these things has been discovered by us. We have also found the cause of their motion toward "always being," as they hurry along with the help of the future. But in the primary and blessed realities, there is no desire for the future; for they are already the whole, and whatever life they ought to have, they already possess in its entirety. Therefore they seek nothing, because for them there is no "future," and thus that in which the future exists does not happen to them. 

The absolute and total essence of being, which is not torn into parts but is whole in its parts, and lacks nothing and has no deficiency, is that to which nothing that is "non-being" can happen. For not only must all things be present to it according to every reason, but nothing of non-being can ever happen to it. This property and nature, I say, is eternity, that is, the *Aeon* <term>Aeon: The Latin *aevum* translates the Greek *aiōn*, representing timeless eternity rather than chronological time.</term>. For *Aeon* is named from that which "always is" <note>This is a traditional philosophical etymology: *aiōn* is derived from *aei on* (always being).</note>.

<margin>
III.
We contemplate eternity itself as a certain eternal presence, which is a kind of infinity beyond all rational calculation.
</margin>

This is best understood when one applies the mind to something and can say of it—or rather, perceive it to be such—that nothing has ever happened regarding it. Otherwise, it would not be "always being," or not always a whole being. Is it then already everlasting? Not unless its nature is also such that it can be believed, without doubt, to be thus and not otherwise in the future, so that if you look at it again, you will find it similarly the same.

But if one never ceases from the contemplation of it, but perseveres steadily, admiring its nature and able to persevere by an untiring nature, perhaps by taking refuge in eternity he may fix his foot there, never turning away, so that he might be invisible and eternal, while he contemplates the eternal by that which is eternal within himself.

If, therefore, that which is thus is eternal and "always being," it never slips into another nature, possessing now the whole of the life it has; it has neither received anything, nor does it receive, nor will it receive. That which is in this state is undoubtedly everlasting. Everlastingness <note>original: "sempiternitas."</note> is a certain constitution of the subject, existing from it and in it at once; but the *Aeon*, that is, eternity, is the subject together with that constitution shining forth within it.

->Which<-

<column-break/>

For it undergoes nothing; nothing would happen to it, nor is it about to be, nor will it be, nor was it becoming. For those things that are becoming, if you take away the "will be" from them as they are always acquiring more, they immediately cease to be. But for those things that are not such, if you add the "will be," they flow away from the seat of being. It is clear that being is not natural to them, or it is not their nature; rather, it has become something for the future, becoming and intending to be later. 

For the essence of things that are becoming seems to be a certain "becoming to be" from the start of their existence until they reach the final time in which they no longer are. This "is" is their being, and it "is" by being present, even if life is diminished. Thus, both being and the whole are as if they were directed toward the future, wishing to be and to will-be, drawing being to themselves, not by doing one thing and then another, but by moving in a circle out of a desire for being. 

Thus we have found "being," and also the cause of the motion toward always being through the future. But for the primary and blessed ones, there is no desire for the future; for they are already the whole, and whatever life is owed to them, they have it all, so as to seek nothing, because the future is nothing to them. Nor, then, is that in which the future exists [time] present in that which truly "is." That which is perfectly auspicious <note>original Greek: "αἰσία" (aisia); likely a variant for "αἰτία" (cause) or related to "divine/eternal portion".</note> and whole, which is not only undivided but will never lack anything, and to which nothing of non-being can be added. For not only must all these things be present to the whole and the all, but nothing of non-being must ever be in it. This disposition and nature is the *Aeon* [Eternity]. For *Aeon* comes from "always being."

ONE MIGHT grasp this in the soul when speaking about the *Aeon*; or rather, one might contemplate it, seeing it as such: that nothing at all has happened around it. If it had anything [added], it would not be the whole, or it would not be the whole at all. Is it not then eternal, that which does not begin, having such a nature that one is persuaded about it, that it is thus and not otherwise? So that if you were to change your view and look back, you would find it the same. 

What if one did not depart from the vision of it, but was always with it, admiring its nature, able to be present to the whole with an untiring nature? Or having run into the *Aeon* himself, he will be there, never leaning away in any direction, so that he may be like that eternal thing, contemplating the eternal by the eternal within himself. If, then, that which is entirely eternal and "always being" does not decline toward any other nature in any way, having its life already whole, neither having taken it up, nor taking it up, nor about to take it up—that is indeed everlasting. Everlastingness <note>Greek: "ἀϊδιότης" (aidiotēs).</note> is such a state of the underlying subject, being from it and in it: indeed the *Aeon* [is this]...

<summary>Plotinus defines eternity as the "always present" life of the divine intellect, contrasting it with the physical world's reliance on the "future" to maintain its fleeting existence. He suggests that through steady contemplation, the human soul can participate in this timeless state.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.

The underlying subject, along with such a state appearing in it—which we call eternity <note>original: "αἰὼν" (aion). If we speak of it as being many, do not wonder; for everything in that realm is many through its infinite power. It is infinite because it never fails, and most properly so because it has nothing to lose. Or, if one defines eternity as an already infinite life, encompassing everything and consuming nothing of itself—since nothing has passed away, nor is there anything to come, for otherwise it would not be "all"—this would be close to a true definition. For the statement that it is "all" and "consumes nothing" is an explanation of it already being infinite.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

it is for the sake of clarity that we always add "always" to it. For "being" is not one thing and "always being" another; just as a "philosopher" is not one thing and a "true philosopher" another. However, because some people pretend to practice philosophy, the addition of "true" was made to "philosopher." In the same way, "always" is joined to "being," and "being" to "always," so that it is called *aion*, which means "always being." <note>original: "αἰὼν, idest ἀεὶ ὤν" (aei on). This is a traditional etymology in Platonism linking the word for eternity (aion) to the phrase for "always being."</note> For this reason, we should understand "always" together with "being" so that it signifies "truly being" to us. Truly, "always" must be understood as demonstrating an indivisible power <note>original: "ἀδιάστατον δύναμιν" (adiastaton dynamin) — a power that does not stretch out or scatter across time.</note> which, besides what it already possesses, lacks nothing; rather, it possesses the whole. Thus, it is the "whole" and "being," and because it is the "whole," it lacks nothing. A nature of this kind is not full in one part and empty in another. For that which exists in time, even if it seems perfect—like a body sufficient for its soul—is made perfect through the soul and yet lacks something of the future, insofar as the time it lacks is still to come. Therefore, even if it is present and concurrent with that future time, it remains imperfect; and for this reason alone, it is said to be "perfect" only in an equivocal sense. <term>Equivocal: When a word is used for two different things, like a "perfect" circle and a "perfect" day; here, Plotinus means temporal things aren't "perfect" in the same absolute way eternal things are.</term> But that which is such that it neither needs the future nor is reduced to some other measured time—nor is it an infinite and infinitely becoming future, but already possesses whatever is necessary for it to be—that is exactly what our intellect desires. To this being, existence does not come from "how much" time it has, but is present even before any "how much." For it is fitting that this being, since it is not a "so much" of anything, should touch nothing that is "so much" or "so great," lest its life be divided and lose its entirely indissoluble nature; rather, it must be indivisible both in its life and in its essence. Regarding what is said in the *Timaeus*, "the maker of the world was good," <note>original: "mundi artifex bonus erat." A reference to Plato’s Timaeus 29e.</note> Plotinus refers this to the Intellect of the universe, signifying that in placing something "above" the universe, we should not understand this in a temporal sense. Therefore, the world did not receive a temporal beginning; for that cause which I have shown is its origin applies the word "was" in a prior sense. However, after Plato had said this for the sake of explanation, he corrects the use of this word "was" in the following sections, as if it is not correctly applied to eternal things.

# BOOK SEVEN.

...of the notion itself, we have now attempted to apply our stated opinion to their concept. But now it is necessary to address the most noteworthy arguments, considering whether our view agrees with them in any way, or if a different account follows from our side. It is perhaps proper first to distinguish the various theories regarding time. For time is said to be either motion, or the thing that moves, or something belonging to motion. Some might say it is rest, or a kind of stability, or something belonging to a state of rest; but this would be altogether far from the notion of time, which never remains the same. Of those who say it is motion, some would say it is all motion, others the motion of the whole universe. Those who say it is the thing moved would point to the sphere of the universe itself. <note>original: "σφαῖραν" (sphaira). In ancient Greek cosmology, the "sphere of the universe" refers to the outermost shell of the heavens containing the fixed stars, whose rotation was thought to drive the cycles of time.</note> Those who say it is something of motion mean either an interval, or the duration of motion; others say it is a measure, others say it is something that follows it, either of all motion or specifically of ordered motion. <note>ordered motion: "τεταγμένης" (tetagmenēs). This refers to the predictable, mathematical movement of the planets and stars as opposed to irregular earthly movements.</note>

### MOTION

It is impossible for time to be the sum of all motions, as if making one out of them all; even in the case of ordered motions, each of these is said to happen "in time." If any motion were not in time, it would be even further from being time itself. For if time were the thing in which motion occurs, it would be different from the motion itself. While other things have been said and could be said, this suffices: that motion can cease and be interrupted, but time never does. Even if one says the motion of the universe is never interrupted, if they mean the circular movement, they must say in what time it occurs and when it returns to the same point. For the movement that completes a half-circle is half the time, and the other is double, even though both are motions of the whole—the one returning to the same spot and the one reaching only the half-way point.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's dialectical investigation into the nature of time. Having already dismissed the idea that time is simply "motion," he now examines the theory that time is the "interval" (diastema) of motion, a view often associated with Stoic philosophy.</meta>

### PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK III.

...if an interval is thought to be time, certainly it cannot be the interval of every motion; for since there are many motions, it would follow that there would be many times existing at once. But if it is the interval of the motion of the universe, and if this interval is inherent in the motion itself, what would it be other than the motion itself? This "so much" <note>The Latin "tantus" and Greek "τοσάδε" refer to the quantitative extent of the motion.</note> will be measured by place, because the place which the motion traverses is of such an extent; and the interval will be called the motion itself because of its continuity, and B because it does not cease suddenly but is continually extended. But if it is nothing other than the multitude or some magnitude of motion—as if someone, observing motion, were to pronounce it to be "much," or if one were to say there is "much heat"—neither does time appear here, nor does it occur to us. Instead, we find motion over and over again, like water flowing again and again. And the interval perceived in it, the repeated outflow, will be a number like a duality or a C trinity; <note>Plotinus is distinguishing between the continuous "stretch" of motion and the "number" we use to count parts of it.</note> but the interval or space will belong to the mass. Thus, the multitude of motion will be like a group of ten, or like an interval seen as if in a mass. This does not possess the rational character of time, but will be something of this sort that occurred *within* time; otherwise, time will not be everywhere, but only in motion as if in a subject, and it would happen again that we call motion "time." For they do not allow time to exist outside of motion, D or they call it the duration of motion; but motion itself is not completed all at once or in an instant. However, when it is said to be "not done suddenly," if we say that something "done suddenly" happens in time, we must ask how that which is "not done suddenly" differs from that which is done suddenly and in an instant. Unless, perhaps, the difference is that it is carried out *in time*; for which reason both the enduring motion and its duration or interval are not time itself, but are fulfilled *within* time. If anyone should assert that the interval of motion is time—not E indeed the interval peculiar to the motion itself, but rather that according to which the motion has extension, as if running alongside it—it has not yet been explained what this actually is. It is considered that this is the time in which the motion occurred. But this was what we were asking from the beginning: what is the nature of time? Since this response is just as if someone, being asked "what is time?", were to answer: "the interval of motion in time." What then is this interval? That which he calls time, who F places it outside the specific interval of motion. For again, even he who places the temporal interval within motion itself will doubt where to place the interval of rest. For as far as one thing is moved, so far does another thing remain at rest; and you will say that the time of both is the same, although they are viewed differently. What then is this interval, and what nature does it have? It cannot be a spatial interval, since that G is something external.

<margin>VIII. Time is not the measure of a body's motion within that motion, nor is it a continuous measure, nor is it like a number.</margin>

**IT MUST BE CONSIDERED** next in what way time can be the number or measure of motion, which would perhaps be more probable than saying it is continuity itself. At the beginning...

<column-break/>

...if of every [motion], at least of such a kind; for these are many, so that many times would exist together with them. And if it is the interval of the whole [universe], if indeed it is the interval in the motion itself, what else would it be but the motion itself, being of such a certain amount? But this "so much" is either by a measure of place, because the light <note>The Greek OCR "φῶς" (light) likely misreads "πῶς" (how), though the Latin text translates the sense as "place it traverses."</note> does not pass through, and the interval will be measured by that of the motion; but this is not <unclear>time</unclear>, but place. And these things—the continuity of motion and its not stopping immediately but taking up more—would be the interval; but how? The "much" of the motion would be if someone, looking at it, declared it to be much, just as if one were to say "much heat," it will not seem to be <unclear>time</unclear>. Light <insert>nor in</insert> now. Nor by manifestation. But motion again and again, like water flowing again and again, and the system viewed upon it; and the "again and again" will be a number, like a duality or trinity; but the interval belongs to the bulk. In this way, the multitude of motion is like a group of ten; or as the interval appearing to the bulk (as it were) of the motion, it cannot be time: but it will be the "where" of things happening, not in time. And motion is not everywhere, but occurs in motion as a subject; why should we again say that motion is time? For if the interval is outside it, but in motion not all at once—but the "not all at once" is not to think of the "all at once." The "not all at once" is defined by something "all at once" and by being in time, so that the definition of motion and its interval is not time itself, but in time. But if someone says the interval of motion is time, or that of the motion itself: but all that belongs to the motion itself, by having extension, will be extended in time, in that [time]. For from where will it be? Or it is clear, indeed, that it will be outside <unclear>time</unclear>, where the motion occurred. Then the argument will not be accepted, or what might time be. Then it does not become something identical, as if someone being asked what is time, should say "the interval of motion in time." What then is this interval, that which is called time, which he who defines it places as existing outside the interval of the motion. For indeed, even if one places the interval in the motion itself, he will be at a loss as to where to place the interval of rest. For as much as something is moved, so much is another thing at rest. And you might say that the time of each is the same, as being another or more. And it will appear neither what it is nor what nature this interval has: since concerning the spatial, it has something besides what happens from the outside.

**NUMBER** of motion or measure, for it is better [to call it] continuous, or as must be examined, beginning <unclear>and</unclear>.

<vocab>
<term>interval (diastema)</term>: a philosophical term for the "stretch" or duration of a thing, often used by Stoics to define time.
<term>number (arithmos)</term>: refers to Aristotle's famous definition of time as the "number of motion in respect of before and after."
<term>bulk (moles/onkos)</term>: refers to the physical magnitude or spatial volume of an object, which Plotinus distinguishes from the metaphysical nature of time.
</vocab>

<summary>Plotinus argues that time cannot be defined as the "interval" of motion, because this would either confuse time with the motion itself or require a pre-existing time to measure the interval. He dismisses the idea that time is just a quantitative "muchness" of movement and begins to pivot toward a critique of Aristotle's definition of time as a "number."</summary>

### BOOK SEVEN.

And here, too, we must raise a doubt similar to the one concerning the interval of motion: whether, that is, we should call the number or measure of *every* motion "time."

Like a line in a certain position, clearly not by motion. But this, by its arrangement, how will it measure things in the same way? <margin>A</margin> Here too there will be a similar doubt as there was regarding the interval: namely, whether we ought to call time the number or measure of every motion alike. For in what way will anyone count a disordered and unequal motion, or what number or measure [would apply]? Or according to what especially does it become a measure? <margin>C</margin> such time is in itself like a number; for in what does it differ from a number like ten or any other gathered from units? A cubit was a standard unit of length; Plotinus is comparing time to a physical ruler.</note>. It will therefore be a magnitude, like a certain line running along with the motion. But how will that which runs along with it measure that with which it runs together? Why indeed should one measure the other rather than vice-versa?
<margin>D</margin> It would be more plausibly placed not in any motion whatever, but in whatever one occurs. <margin>G</margin> was "this much" or "that much." And thus time will be that number of the magnitude accompanying the motion, but not the magnitude itself running together with the motion. But what kind of number is this? Is it made of units, and how...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's critique of the Aristotelian definition of time as the "number" or "measure" of motion. ### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD III.

If something measures, it is necessary to doubt: for if anyone should find a way [to measure], they will not find time itself measuring, but only "a certain amount of time" <note>original: *tempus tantum*. Plotinus distinguishes between the absolute essence of Time and a specific duration used as a yardstick.</note>; however, this is by no means the same as Time itself. For it is one thing to speak of Time, and another to speak of "a certain amount of time." For before we can speak of "how much," we must define what that thing is which is "that much." But is time perhaps a number measuring motion from the outside? Not as the number ten is taken alongside horses, but rather like the number ten *within* the horses. Who then can say what this number is, which exists as itself even before it measures, just as the number ten does? Is it the number that runs along according to the "before" and "after" of motion? But this measure according to "before" and "after" has not yet appeared to us in its true nature. Nevertheless, whatever measures according to "before" and "after"—whether it measures by some mark, like a point on a piece of wood, or by anything else—it will certainly measure according to time. Therefore, this time which measures motion through "before" and "after" will be connected to time and touching time so that it can measure. For one either accepts "before" and "after" according to location, as in the beginning of a racetrack and the starting gates <note>original: *carceribus*. In Roman circuses, the 'carceres' were the stalls or starting gates for chariot races.</note>, or else one must certainly accept a non-spatial "before" and "after," but a temporal one. For that which is called "before" is entirely Time ending at the *now* (the present); and "after" is similarly Time beginning from the *now*. Thus, Time is something other than a number measuring motion through "before" and "after," and this applies not just to any motion, but even to ordered motion. Furthermore, why—when a number is applied, whether according to units of measure or according to a measurer (for perhaps the same thing can be both the measured and the measurer?)—why, I ask, will there be time just because a number is applied? For while motion is already active, and "before" and "after" are occurring within that motion, there would not yet be time [under that definition]; it would be as if one said that a magnitude is not as great as it is unless someone perceives how great that magnitude is. Likewise, since time is said to be infinite, under what condition will there be a number concerning it, unless perhaps someone selects a certain part of time to measure? In that case, it happened to exist even before it was measured. What, then, prevents time from existing before there is a soul <note>original: *anima*. In Neoplatonism, the "Soul" (Psyche) is often seen as the creator or sustainer of time.</note> to measure it? Unless, perhaps, someone says that its generation proceeds from the soul. Yet, through the act of measurement itself, it is in no way necessary that time be created by the soul. For the quantity exists even if no one measures it. As for the suggestion that time is perhaps that which uses magnitude as a measure: if someone suggests this is the soul, we would object that this has nothing to do with the basic concept of time.

TO SAY that time is a certain consequence of motion is not to teach what time itself is; nor is it permitted to say this before explaining what that thing is which "follows" <note>original: *consequitur / παρακολύθημα*. Plotinus is questioning whether time is just a byproduct or "accompaniment" of motion.</note>, for that thing itself might perhaps be time. We must consider this "consequence" itself, whether it happens before, or after, or simultaneously—if indeed there is such a consequence. For in whatever way it is spoken of, it is spoken of *in* time; therefore, if that "consequence" were time, time would be called a consequence of motion in...

<column-break/>

...measure, it is necessary to be at a loss; even if someone finds a way, he will not measure by defining time, but by time measuring time; and this does not come from Time itself. For it is one thing to say "time," and another to speak of it as something distinct. Before doing this, one must say what that thing is, which is "so much." Is it the number that measured motion from outside the motion, like the number ten alongside horses, or taken with the horses? Who could say what the number is? It has not been said. And what does it measure? That which exists, like the number ten, or whatever it is that, running through the "before" and "after" of motion, measured it? But if it measures by "before" and "after"—whether by a point or any other thing—it will measure entirely according to time. Thus, this time which measures motion by "before" and "after" will be time itself, clinging to and touching it so that it may measure. For if one takes "before" and "after" as being in a place, such as the start of the stadium, one must necessarily take something temporal. For "before" and "after" are entirely: the "before" is that which ends at the *now*, and the "after" is that which begins from the *now*. But by the "now" as a number, "before" and "after" are measured. Time measures motion—not just any motion, but ordered motion. Then, why is there time when a number is provided, whether as the thing measuring or the thing measured? For the same thing could be both the measurer and the measured. But if number stays still while time exists, how can motion and "before" and "after" all exist around it, and yet time only exists later? It is as if someone said that magnitude does not exist in its true quantity unless someone takes its measurement. And since time is infinite, how can there be a number concerning it, unless someone takes a portion of it? Everything that measures happens to exist before the measurement; and why must the soul be the one that measures? Unless someone says its birth comes from the soul. But for the sake of measuring, it is not at all necessary for time to exist [only then]. For the quantity exists even if it is not measured. And if someone says the soul uses magnitude to measure, that says nothing about the concept of time.

THE "consequence" <note>Greek: *παρακολύθημα* (parakolouthema), an accompaniment or byproduct.</note> of motion is spoken of, but what this thing is, is not yet taught; nor is it clear, until one says what the "consequence" is. For that itself would perhaps be time. One must examine this "consequence," whether it is after, or simultaneous, or before. For in whatever way the "consequence" is spoken of, it is spoken of in time. If this is so, time will be a consequence of motion in time. But...

# BOOK SEVEN.

But since we are not seeking how long it is, but rather what it is, and since many things have been said about this by the ancients who came before us—which one might go through individually—it would be better to do so later, if we first state those things that are persuasive. First, it is right to mention that even the one who says time is the measure of the movement of the universe <note>Plotinus is referring to Plato's *Timaeus*, but often contrasts this with Aristotle's more mechanical "number of motion."</note> must move past what has already been said and weave in all the other things that have been said about the measure of motion. Aside from the issue of inequality, these other things, which will also fit into the discussion itself, would make it a logical consequence to say: what exactly do we consider time to be?

**W**e must lead ourselves back again to that disposition which we said was in eternity: that immovable nature, entirely present all at once, an already infinite life, unwavering from itself and within itself, standing fast in unity. Time did not yet exist, or at least it did not exist for those eternal beings; but Time was destined to come into being, by the reason and nature of what followed, while those higher things remained in their own quiet. To explain how Time first fell out from Eternity, it would perhaps not be proper to call upon the Muses—though perhaps they were already there then. And however it happened, one might find Time itself once it has been made, seeing how it is manifest and becoming. One might speak of it in this way: before this "before" had been worked out and required a "later," Time lay quiet within Being itself, not yet existing; rather, it also kept its peace within that realm. But a certain Nature <note>The "World Soul" or "Universal Soul."</note>, being restless <note>original: *polypragmōnos*. This famous term implies a meddlesome or over-active nature that desires to produce more than what is simply present.</note> and wishing to be its own master and to belong to itself, and choosing to seek more than what was currently present, was itself moved; and Time also flowed out, always moving toward the "next" and the "later," not staying the same but moving from one thing to another. Having made a length of journey through this movement, we have constructed Time as an image of Eternity. For since there was a certain restless power of the Soul, wishing always to transfer what it saw there [in the eternal realm] into something else, it did not want the whole of it to be present to it all at once; but just as a "seminal reason" <term>seminal reason: *logos spermatikos*, a formative principle that unfolds from a seed into a complex organism</term>, unfolding itself from a quiet seed, makes its way into a great variety (as it thinks), losing the "muchness" by spending it, and showing itself in a weaker length instead of the unity that stayed within itself—so too, the Soul, in making the sensible world, moving with a motion that imitates the eternal one, and wishing to be an image of that realm, first "timified" <note>original: *echronōsen*. A rare verb meaning to bring into the state of time.</note> itself, making this [Time] instead of Eternity. Then, it gave the world of "becoming" over to be a slave to Time, making all of it exist within Time, and encompassing all its various paths within it. For as the Soul moves forward in its journeys...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding Time. But since we are by no means investigating what it is not, but rather what Time truly is, and many things have been said about this by many before us: if one were to run through each opinion, he would be telling a history rather than an inquiry; and insofar as one can scan through them, something has been said about these, and it is possible to refute the one who says time is the measure of the motion of the universe based on what has been said, and to bring further points to the discussion which were just mentioned regarding the measure of motion. <margin>B</margin> For besides the inequality of motion, one can bring up all the other points which will be appropriately applied to them: since, I say, the matter stands thus, it remains now to explain more clearly what time is.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>What remains, namely a certain perseverance of the world-soul in its movements while aspiring toward eternity.</margin> **I**T IS WORTHWHILE to recall ourselves again to that nature which we said in earlier sections was in eternity: a nature, I say, immutable and simultaneously whole, an already infinite life, altogether unwavering, and consisting in one and toward one. But Time was not yet, or at least it was not in those things, but was to follow by a certain reason of a posterior nature. While the higher things were keeping peace in themselves, if anyone should wish to understand how Time first fell away from that principle, he would perhaps not opportunely call upon the Muses for this explanation, as they perhaps did not yet exist. And yet, perhaps it is opportune: since the Muses were also then in existence. And however it may be, one might perhaps find Time itself now that it is made, insofar as it is made and already manifest. <margin>D</margin> Let him speak about this very thing in this manner: Before that "before" itself arose, and required a "later," Time lay quiet, not yet existing, together with Being itself in Being: but in that realm, Time itself also kept its peace. But a certain Nature, prone to many actions, and greatly desiring to be of its own right and to command itself, and choosing always to have something more than what is present; now even she herself was agitated, and at the same time Time flowed out: <margin>E</margin> time thereafter always and into the future, not through the same, but into another thing and then another again. And we, thinking of a certain length of progression produced by this motion, now fashion Time as the image of eternity. For since there was a certain restless power of the soul, wishing plainly to transfer what was inspected there [in eternity] always into another thing, it did not endure having the whole collected together present to itself: but just as a "seminal reason" <term>seminal reason: the Greek *logos spermatikos*, the blueprint that causes a seed to grow into a plant</term> unfolding itself from a certain quiet seed, <margin>F</margin> drives its discourse into many things (as it thinks), meanwhile losing that very "muchness" by a certain partitioning, and spending for one thing that which exists in itself, and consuming it by not remaining in itself, it proceeds into a weaker length: so too the very nature of the soul which we were speaking of, having fabricated the sensible world in imitation of that higher world, agitated by a motion—not the motion that is there, but one similar to the motion that is there—by a motion, I say, affecting to represent the image of that one, <margin>G</margin> first indeed rendered itself temporal, and then gave that which was becoming [the physical world] to serve time: since it had compelled all of this existence to be in time, embracing all the discourses of this world within it.

<summary>Plotinus explains that Time originates from the "restless" activity of the World Soul, which attempts to replicate the unified perfection of Eternity through a sequential, unfolding progression of life and motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of time as a product of the Soul’s activity. ### PLOTINUS ENNEAD III.

For it [time] was set in motion in that [Soul], since there is no other place for the universe than the soul; surely it was also set in motion within the Soul's own time. For by applying its own activity, one after another and then another in succession, the Soul generated the very sequence of "next" along with that activity. It proceeded together with one thought after another, which did not exist before, since such a thought had not yet performed anything. Now, however, the present life is not entirely like the preceding one: therefore, as there is another life, there is also another time insofar as it is different. Thus, the distance and the drawing out of life has been allotted the name "time," and the perpetual extension of life holds an everlasting time, just as past life holds past time. If someone were to say that time is the activity of the soul in a transitory motion proceeding perpetually from one life to another, they would perhaps seem to be asserting something of value. For if eternity <note>original: "æuum" / "αἰών"</note> is life in a state of permanence, in the same and similar habit, being infinite, and if it is necessary for time to be the image of eternity—just as this world is the image of that higher world—then certainly, in the place of the life which flourishes there, we must assert another life here in a certain power of the World Soul. This life is, as it were, homonymous <note>having the same name but a different nature</note> with the higher one, and instead of intellectual motion, it is the motion of some part of the Soul. Likewise, instead of a state of identical habit—similar and remaining—it is that which does not remain in the same state, but executes one thing after another. Again, instead of a property without distance and being "one," it is a simulacrum of the One, possessing unity in a certain continuous succession. Furthermore, in place of that which is infinite and already a whole, this is that which is perpetually propagating itself toward infinity according to what follows next. Finally, instead of that which is a whole all at once, this is that which will be according to parts, and will always be a "whole" only in the future. For in this way it will imitate that which already exists as a whole, gathered together all at once and already immense: namely, if it wishes to obtain its being in a continuous completion of being. For in that way it will best imitate the being of the higher realm. However, one must by no means assume time to be outside the soul, just as eternity is not outside that which is called Being: nor again is it a mere consequence or something posterior, just as it is not so there; rather, it is something seen within, which is both present and exists simultaneously, just as eternity does there.

<margin>
XI
*Confirmation of the previous points.*
</margin>
**IT MUST BE CONSIDERED** from these things which have been said, that time is a nature of this sort: namely, the length of such a life proceeding in changes, progressing quietly and gently in equal and similar stages; a length, I say, having a continuity of activity. But if we were to imagine this power being somehow drawn back and ceasing from this life—which it now leads as an interminable and never-ceasing life because it is the activity of a certain everlasting Soul—if we imagine it not toward itself, nor within itself, but occupied in effecting and generating: if we imagine it, I say, no longer acting, and this part of the soul ceasing, and this soul moreover turned toward the higher things and toward stable eternity, what then will remain besides eternity? What will there be of "one thing after another" when all things remain in the one? What further would there be of "before" or "after," or

<column-break/>

A. For [Time], moving in that [Soul]—for the Soul is the place of this universe—it moved in the time of that Soul. By providing its activity, one after another and again in succession, it generated with that activity the "next" in sequence. It passed along with a different thought after that previous one, which was not the same as the thought previously enacted; thus, it is now another life.
B. Along with this life, it simultaneously held another time. And so the interval <note>original: "διάστημα"</note> of life holds time, and the succession of life perpetually holds time, and past life holds past time. If someone were to say that time is the life of the soul in a transitive motion, moving from one state of life to another, does he not seem to be saying something? For if eternity <note>original: "αἰών"</note> is life in a state of rest, being the same, likewise, and 
C. unbounded, then this eternity must be the model for time. Just as this universe relates to that higher world, so in place of the life there, we must speak of the life of this power of the soul here, being its namesake. Instead of the intellectual motion, there is the motion of a part of the soul; instead of identity and remaining the same, there is that which does not remain the same, but acts in one way and then another. Instead of the partless, there is an image of the one, which now 
D. maintains its well-being through succession. And instead of that which is infinite all at once, there is that which is always "next" toward infinity. Instead of the "all at once" whole, there is that which is a whole by parts and will always be a whole in the future. For in this way it will imitate that which is already entirely 
E. "all at once" and already infinite, if it desires to be always acquiring being in its existence. For in this way its existence will imitate that other existence. One must take [time] as the life of the soul, just as eternity is taken from that which truly is. It must be a consequence, a "later," just as it is observed there, both being within and existing together, just as eternity does.

-> ONE MUST THINK of this nature of time in this way: as the length of life of this kind, always as it were in changes, both smooth and similar, <-

F. proceeding soundlessly, and having continuity of activity. If, then, we were to lead this power back in thought and cause that life to cease which it now has—which is unceasing and would never stop because it is the activity of a certain Soul, directed not toward itself nor in itself, but in making and generating—if we were to suppose this activity no longer acting but ceasing, that part of the soul having turned back toward that which is there, 
G. toward Being, and remaining in silence, what would there be after eternity? Would there be anything other than eternity, with all things remaining in the One? What would be "before," and what would be "after"?

<summary>Plotinus defines Time as the "life of the Soul," representing a transition from the unified, static perfection of Eternity into a sequential, moving imitation of that perfection. He argues that if the Soul's outward-facing activity were to cease and return to its source, Time itself would vanish back into Eternity.</summary>

It must be considered then so that it may

<margin>A</margin> Or longer: By what condition will the Soul
further apply itself to another thing: Unless

<margin>E</margin> to whom the measurement is made? Does it

it may be able to measure, and yet not in the

time will not be the measure of motion
according to what it is, but by accident;
namely, being some other thing prior, it will
reveal how much the motion becomes. Thus
indeed, one motion accepted in such a time,
having been counted often, will lead to the
knowledge of how much time has passed.
Wherefore, if anyone should say that motion
<margin>F</margin> and revolution measure time in a certain way
as much as it can, it is just as much: since it can
neither be accepted otherwise, nor understood,
he certainly will not wander from a fitting
declaration. That therefore which is measured
by the circuit—that is, declared—will be time,
not generated indeed by the circuit itself, but
demonstrated. And so the measure of motion
seems to be that which is measured by a
determined motion, and measured by it as if by
something different from it: since if both that
<margin>G</margin> which measures were one thing, and that
which is measured another, yet measured by
accident, it would have been said just as if
someone said that what is measured by a
cubit is magnitude, yet not saying what the
determined thing itself is...

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. III.

...limiting by magnitude. Again, just as if someone <margin>A</margin> were unable to explain motion itself more clearly because of its indeterminate nature, he might say that motion is that which is measured by space. For by taking the space which the motion has traversed, one will say that the motion is as great as the space was.

<margin>
XII. 
Time is not 
the revolution 
itself, but is 
declared by it. 
Likewise the 
world and its 
motion come 
from the motion 
of the world soul.
</margin>
Therefore, the circular revolution itself makes time manifest, for it is in time that the revolution is performed. However, it is necessary that time itself no longer merely has the quality of being that in which something is carried out, but even more so and primarily that it possesses the very quality of existence <margin>B</margin> in which other things move and rest equally and orderly. Time must shine forth from a certain ordered motion, yet it is not produced by it—whether that motion be at rest or in flux—though it appears more clearly in flux. Indeed, motion seems to contribute more to the knowledge and completion of time than rest does, and it can be more clearly seen how much something has moved than how much it has stood still. For this reason, some have been led to say that time is the "measure of motion" <note>This is a direct reference to Aristotle’s definition of time in his Physics</note>, because they perhaps meant to say <margin>C</margin> it is "measured by motion." Therefore, one must add what it is in its own existence that is being measured by motion, rather than simply stating an accidental quality that happens to it—and even that is stated in a reversed manner. But perhaps those thinkers did not wish for their words to be taken in a reversed sense; rather, we simply do not understand them. Clearly, when they speak of a "measure according to the thing measured," we have failed to grasp their meaning. The reason why we have not understood <margin>D</margin> is this: in their writings, they do not explain what time is in itself, whether it be called the "measurer" or the "measured"—as if they were writing for listeners who already knew these things perfectly. Plato, however, said the essence of time was neither a thing that measures nor a thing measured by something; rather, to make it manifest, the revolution of the world was allotted a very small part for the sake of showing the smallest portion of time. Thus, from this, one can know what kind of thing time is and how great it is. Yet, wishing <margin>E</margin> to indicate its essence, he says it was "born together with the heavens" and that it is a "moving image of the eternal exemplar" <note>original: "imaginem mobilem exemplaris æterni"</note> in relation to eternity <term>Aevum (Eternity): The state of timeless, perfect existence in the Divine Mind</term>. This is because time does not remain still, for life—with which time runs and revolves—does not remain still. It is said to be "born together with the heavens" because a life of this kind creates the heavens, and a single life produces both the heavens and time. Therefore, if such a life could be turned back into unity, time (which exists in this life) would immediately cease, and the heavens <margin>F</margin> would cease, being deprived of that life. If anyone should take the "before" and "after" of this lower life and motion and claim that this itself is time (asserting this is a real thing), while denying that the nature of a truer motion has a "before" and "after," he would be quite ridiculous. Indeed, he would be granting "before" and "after" to an inanimate motion and claiming it possesses time, while refusing to grant it to the motion through which this lower motion is born by a certain imitation. <margin>G</margin> Yet it is from that higher motion that "before" and "after" first flowed, since it is a motion that is effective through itself. And just as it generates its own individual actions, so it produces a continuous succession, and along with this generation, it effects a transition...

<column-break/>

...being measured. And just as if someone, wishing to show motion itself or its power through its indeterminacy, should say: "that which is measured by space." For having taken the place through which the motion has passed, he says that the motion is as great as the place.

Therefore, the circular revolution <note>original: "περιφορά" / "periphora"</note> reveals time, in which this revolution itself exists. But time itself must no longer have its existence only in "that in which" something occurs, but must first be something in itself, in which other things move and stand still smoothly and in an orderly fashion. It must appear and, as it were, leap out from a certain ordered arrangement; not because of that motion, whether in its becoming or in its state, but rather while it is moving. For motion offers a clearer and more evident transition toward time than rest does, and it is more recognizable how much something has moved than how much it has stood still. For this reason, people were led to call it the "measure of motion," instead of saying it is "measured by motion." Then they add that something which is measurable by motion is always present in it as an accident. And these things are said in a confused way. But perhaps those thinkers did not speak confusedly, but we do not understand. Though they clearly speak of a measure according to the thing measured, we have not attained their meaning. The cause of our lack of clarity is this: they do not clarify what it is to measure or to be measured in their own writings, as if they were writing for those who already knew and had heard them. Plato, however, because he called it a "measure," and further "measured by something," does not say that this is its essence, but that for its manifestation, the circular revolution was taken as the smallest part, having been allotted the smallest portion of itself. It is as if someone, in order to know a quantity, were to use a small measure to see what kind and how great time is. For wishing to reveal eternity to him, he says that time was "born together with the heavens" and is a "moving image of eternity" <note>original: "εἰκόνα κινητὴν"</note>. Further, time would not remain if life or motion did not remain, with which it runs. It is said to be "together with the heavens" because such a life also makes the heavens. A single life works both the heavens and time. So if this life were to move toward unity, if it were possible, time would cease along with it, not having this life. But if someone, taking the "before" and "after" of this life and motion, should call it time (for it is a real thing), but should deny that the truer motion which has "before" and "after" is anything at all, he would be entirely absurd. For he gives "before," "after," and time to inanimate motion, but does not give anything to the motion by which the lower one subsists through imitation—from which "before" and "after" primarily come. For as it is the author of motion, and as it generates each of its own activities, so also it generates succession; and along with the generation, it also makes the transition...

### BOOK SEVEN.

<note original: "Βασιν αὐτῶν.../Curnam igitur motum...">Why then do we trace this motion of the universe back to the embrace of eternity and claim it exists within time? Yet, we do not say the same for the motion of the soul, which flourishes within itself and proceeds through a perpetual traversal. Perhaps this is because that which stands above this generated world is eternity, which neither runs alongside motion, nor extends itself with it. Therefore, that primary motion <note>The "primary motion" refers to the internal activity of the Soul</note> regards time and generates it, possessing time simultaneously with its own action. In what way, then, is time <margin>B</margin> everywhere? It is because the Soul and that vital motion are absent from no part of the world, just as the life within us leaves no part of our being deserted. If someone should object that time exists in a state of non-existence <note original: "non-existentia">i.e., that time is an illusion or lacks "being"</note>—for one might speak falsely about time's "being" just as it is said we speak falsely of God when we use "was" and "will be"—we must ask: what shall we say? For "was" and "will be" suggest a location in time where one might say God *will be*. <margin>C</margin> Truly, another method of disputation is required for these matters. However, for the present, we must observe regarding what has been said: when one considers a man in motion, one recognizes how far he has proceeded and how great the movement is. When one judges the motion of, for example, the legs in walking, one simultaneously contemplates the motion itself within the man prior to this outward progress. This internal motion was of such a magnitude that it moved the body through its progression. <margin>D</margin> The body, moved for a certain time, is reduced to a specific proper motion. This internal motion is the cause; time follows it, and this motion follows the movement of the soul, which produces intervals of equal measure. To what, then, shall we primarily refer the motion of the soul? Surely, wherever you wish to refer it, you will eventually reach a point where you must stop. This, therefore, exists here first; it is the very thing in which all other things are contained, while it is no longer contained in anything else. For it cannot have anything else <margin>E</margin> to encompass it. This, then, reigns as the primary principle. In the Soul of the All, the matter stands similarly. Is time, then, also within us? Perhaps it is in every soul of this kind, and exists uniformly in all, and all souls are, in a certain way, one. Therefore, time will not be dispersed, since even eternity, which exists according to another manner, is present in all things that share a uniform nature.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE
## EIGHTH BOOK OF THE THIRD EN-
## NEAD, CONCERNING NATURE,
->contemplation, and the One.<-

->C O M M E N T A R Y.<-
### ->SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.<-

->Natural things are made by a certain life acting through reasons, as if contem-<-
->plative, implanted in it by the divine intellect.<-

<margin>F</margin> **P**HILOSOPHERS of old, some of whom were simply "naturalists," thought that all natural things were generated by some elemental quality. They believed things arose either from the power of the quality flourishing in the agent, or from the efficacy of the motion descending into the matter, and that no <term>reason</term> <note>Ficino uses "ratio" to translate the Greek "logos," meaning a guiding rational principle or blueprint</note> or internal art governed this world. Plotinus, however, wants corporal qualities and motions to be led by an incorporeal form—one not subject to motions, but presiding over them. This he calls "Universal and Primary Nature." I call it a substantial and vital form, which is not merely a quality of bodies, nor does it preside only to procreate, nor does it act by the impulse of motion alone. Rather, it disposes all things with a certain moderation: it acts by its own <term>formal reason</term> and a certain "natural art." It is as if the artistic skill, which is usually an accidental trait in a human craftsman, were instead something subsisting by itself.

# COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

although it exists within matter: it thus acts skillfully by its own nature, just as an artisan acts skillfully by choice. Thus, it will be that Nature acts skillfully by a natural art, just as fire heats naturally by its natural heat. From here, therefore, qualities and motions are open to the Reason of the animal and of Life as instruments. It produces some things through bodily motion, it puts forth bodily movement, and produces the qualities that generate fire. From this, I can clearly know that living things possess essential reasons within themselves in a general sense. For these are the reasons of all things, as we have already proved in our *Theology* <note>Ficino refers here to his own major work, *Platonic Theology on the Immortality of the Soul*</note>. And so, in the present, we briefly confirm that increase and growth—which are types of generation—are themselves simply "generation," which acts in preserved living beings. Since these generations are the works of certain lives or living things, and Nature itself is simply the first common generation, it is simply the work of Life, the common living force of the entire mundane region.

And since certain seeds of physical things are not manifest everywhere in the mass of the world, especially in the earth itself, they instead exist in the Soul as the "living proper reasons" <term>seminal reasons</term> <note original: "rationibus seminalibus">Spiritual blueprints or formative powers that guide the development of physical matter</note> of those things appearing to the senses. For Nature, which acts without choice, acts by the form of the just, and establishes certain forms everywhere as necessary species through these seminal reasons. These reasons serve as principles and rules of motion which, though indeterminate in themselves, define a certain course and tenor. They also define those qualities that act with force and impulse; these are naturally constrained until this moderation leads them to a finished work. Despite the multiform nature of the result, the unity of the soul remains. Nature does not look toward any other certain end than that which art and counsel usually seek, even though Nature itself does not "see" the end. But here, all natural things appear fertile in themselves; while Nature contains natural forms, it is no different than how human art possesses its skills.

On the other hand, things that were in potentiality are always seen by everyone to be brought into actuality only through the life present in matter, but which the Soul comprehends within itself through thought. Nature here is the artisan of all things; it is not a specific matter for the thing, nor does it simply need distinct existence for its work. For as often as Nature renders matter as such-and-such, it moves that matter by a swift command. Indeed, it does not even require this or that quality of matter for its own simple action. For it can generate qualities by means of other qualities, since it is the common principle for generating all of them equally. If it generates living things here and there without manifest seeds, it is even more capable of producing elemental qualities through its own seeds without the exact measure of such elements.

If the "livingness" of matter is affected by certain qualities, it is not by the necessity of the quality it uses, but by accident. This is surely understood by those who judge that a resolution occurs from generation all the way back to "prime matter" <term>prime matter</term> <note>The most basic, formless substratum of the physical world</note>. Therefore, remember that Nature is the strict principle of generation everywhere. For the material form is flawed because it is "formed," and the formal principle generates nothing at all. That which is perfect in any genus begets nothing within that genus. Therefore, material form is not so much the principle of generation as it is a certain affection granted to matter from above by an occult, primeval generating species.

That it generates nothing is confirmed by the fact that generation belongs to Life. But this [material form] lacks life. That it lacks Life is clear from the fact that essence must be present to itself in life, yet it does not prove this by its distance from matter. Indeed, form does not end in quality, and therefore it defines the essence from within, and likewise defines life in Nature, just as it defines qualities in matter.

This Nature is indeed incorporeal. If anyone argues that it is moved, it is meanwhile also moved in its substance. But that which is first moved is that which remains in substance, so that it continues a certain perpetual tenor of motion. If, however, there is an intimate and familiar motion, like a certain form which is Nature itself, it must be that while it moves, it also undergoes a certain movement in one way rather than another—not through a shifting effect. Finally, just as in any living creature it is not an elemental reason but a vital reason that is the principle of what happens in the body, so too in the "universal living thing" (that is, the world), it is not elemental quality or motion that dispenses things so beautiful and diverse, but a certain living Reason. Plotinus says this Reason remains within itself through its essence, although it may be changed in turn from one affection to another. It does not depend equally on matter and on the soul, as a bodily quality does, but depends on the soul alone, like a perennial act of the soul leaning toward matter.

Therefore, Plotinus calls quality and matter "accidents" <note original: "accidens">A philosophical term for a property that is not essential to a thing's nature</note> because they depend on both sides. But life communicated to the body by the soul is not an accident of the body, nor an idle accident of the soul, but an essential act of the soul—a medium between the two, a true substance that proceeds all the way to the intellectual soul. It possesses a certain power by which it sustains and preserves itself in a way, and profits in itself. By this gift, all intellectual essences are said to subsist through themselves and from themselves.

But let us return to Nature, that is, the life depending on the soul. In this are all the reasons that produce natural forms. Any reason within it is not a "notion" conceived through argument or investigation, but an essential property and act of essence, not differing from being such-and-such. There is, therefore, in the soul a certain seminal reason of that which is born from it. Although this is an essential act of nature itself and its very being, it is named by a certain metaphor as an "intuition"—not one acquired over time, but one that is naturally there. It seeks nothing, but possesses from the beginning. It does not notice anything within itself, but is, as it were, "dazed" <note original: "stupidas">Ficino uses this to describe a state of profound, silent absorption or unconscious contemplation, like a trance</note>, much like the state of those standing by, or perhaps like the sense that some attribute to plants. For this is common to every plant: through its own substantial rest and the sensation of enjoying its own life, it conceives natural things. Orpheus attributed this to Nature in his *Hymn to Nature*: a sensation without noise, that is, without the distraction of itself toward another.

In Nature, intuition is nothing other than being such-and-such and doing such-and-such. And since it makes all things as if by a certain intuition and appearance, that which is produced in matter can be called a "spectacle." Furthermore, he calls it the "outward appearance" of Nature, so that if we wish to speak briefly: this inborn sleep is a certain desire and imagination of the mother.

Truly, in neither the intellect nor in nature is there any knowledge, notion, or intuition that differs from "being" in the way that the intuition called "consideration" usually differs—the kind found in those who do not naturally possess the thing they are looking at. But Nature, which depends on intellectual substance, also understands; it naturally possesses all things that are found, and they create by "intending." This essential and effective intuition is what he calls the "seminal reason." He places the first reason in the simple Intellect; the second in the intellectual Soul (which he calls the first soul); the third in Nature (which he calls the second soul); and the fourth in Matter (that is, the material form). Furthermore, the reasons of the first are in the Intellect itself, and there they are contemplations or objects of contemplation. These are called "contemplations" or "spectacles," the notions of all things, or concepts resulting therein, while

<summary>Ficino explains the hierarchical relationship between the Intellect, Soul, and Nature, describing Nature as an "artisan" that shapes matter through "seminal reasons"—unconscious, spiritual blueprints—rather than through conscious choice.</summary>

<header>ON BOOK VIII OF ENNEAD III</header>

...the intellect contemplates and gazes upon itself. Indeed, the secondary forms from the contemplating intellect are naturally expressed into the intellectual soul, and thus these too are certain types of contemplations. Tertiary forms are impressed from there into nature. These, in turn, are also expressed from contemplations and are themselves certain contemplations; to put it all together, I might call them contemplative-products <term>contemplamina</term> <note original: "contemplamina">Ficino uses various Latin forms of 'contemplatio' to distinguish the act of seeing from the resulting formative power.</note>. Finally, the fourth level consists of the concepts of nature's contemplative-products as they are conceived within the matter of the world. And since the aforementioned contemplations follow a certain order and imitate one another, he says that those contemplations—which might also be called "artificial" because they look toward practical use—are produced by intelligences. These intelligences, touching upon craftsmanship, become more and more active through "songs" <note>Here, 'songs' likely refers to the rhythmic, harmonic ratios of the cosmos.</note>, because they strive for a more expressive thought and carry their own power, especially like written words without being spoken.

Therefore, the natural form has this primary quality: that it is so named, and that there are certain intelligences and <unclear>strivings</unclear>, the expressed forces of the intellectual nature, or the "natural intellectualities." For Nature herself, the artisan of things, is like a certain intellectual power of the soul, shaping matter—not as if giving something foreign to it, but giving its own. It does not act like art from the outside, but from within; not by such-and-such a choice, but by such an essence and end, and without reasoning, and always. 

Now, in this, Nature differs from a geometer shaping beauty: for Nature is innate, and acts without instruments or choice, just as a geometer, while he imagines figures intensely and with a certain passion, moves his spirit mostly by imagination and thus shapes them. Plotinus imagines these four—Intellect, Intellectual Soul, Nature, and Matter—as being like four glass panes <note original: "vitra">Can mean glass panes, lenses, or mirrors.</note> arranged in sequence: the very intelligences of the First Intellect pass through them like rays from the sun through the soul, nature, and matter, through a certain continuous conformity. Thus, it can be said in a way that the same "reasoned intelligence" which exists in the preceding levels exists in the subsequent and final ones, but it gradually fails in dignity as it descends from the first. 

But since the contemplation of the First Intellect—and subsequently a certain contemplation in the soul and in nature—is the natural principle, then surely the end and goal of all things is also contemplation. Even if the intellectual level possesses it perpetually, all things happily rest in such an end. This is what rational beings seek, so that they may rest in it; this is what sentient beings imitate to the best of their power through their continuous sensing; this is what all things that generate attempt to reflect, both in the order of nature and in the form of practical use. Finally, the contemplation of divine providence looks toward the highest beauty of the divine mind, and in the whole disposition of things, it consulted ornament no less than—indeed more than—necessity. From this beautiful ornament, it excites wondrous minds to gaze upon the very art of the divine mind and to contemplate its beauty.

# On the goal of intellectual nature, and that in true knowledge the knower and the known are the same; and on the degrees of life and intelligence; and that the First Intellect is all things, and a perfect whole.

In the fifth and sixth chapters of the whole book, you will note that the goal of intellectual power is not simply to "have" the good in any manner, but to understand the Good as a possessed state; for here, "to have" is exactly this: to understand. For this is the action of the intellect from its own nature, the chief method of possession. Likewise, the Good for us is not sensible, but is the highest Intelligible; for this alone is most intimate to us, most quiet, and the same; it is, finally, identical with the power of knowing itself. 

Furthermore, remember that the power of knowing, in the very act of cognition, becomes in a certain way one with the object. The more it becomes one, the more perfect is the knowledge and the vision. For where it is most perfect—indeed, wherever it is true—there, as he says, the power of knowing and the thing known are the same being. Therefore, the Intellect and every intellectual essence, just as it is always all things in act, so also it always understands all things in act. 

The rational nature of the soul, however, wills all that it does, but it does not always have all things "in act" <term>in act</term> <note original: "in actu">A technical term meaning 'currently active' or 'fully realized,' as opposed to 'potential'.</note>. To the extent that it applies itself in act to some "reason" lying hidden within it, to that extent the soul becomes that thing in various ways; through this, it understands those things comprehended in the power of that reason, and by understanding, it becomes them. In short, to truly know something is nothing other than to be or to become that very thing. 

Finally, since the divine Artisan makes all things by contemplation itself, and "speaks" <note>Ficino uses "speaks" metaphorically for the emanation of forms.</note> to herself to be imitated according to her power, surely all things desire and strive for something contemplative or some object of contemplation, whether by understanding, sensing, or even by acting and generating. 

Furthermore, in chapter 7, you will learn that every eternal intellectual power is identical with the Intellect, and in it, "to understand" does not differ from "to be," because it is the highest in the genus of knowledge. The rational power, however, becomes the same as the thing known, but the will is carried outward, as nature tends toward external things. 

Likewise, the first form, from its highest efficacy for movement, is the First Life; and that efficacy is intimate, and the First Intelligence is master of itself. Just as form proceeds through all degrees of things, being made through essence from the first forms, so also the intellectual life proceeds, so that any form can be called a "life" and a certain "intelligence." 

Finally, the First Intellect, just as it is One, is also all things, because it is the first in that genus. It becomes "all-formed" <term>omniform</term> because, by contemplating itself, it beholds itself under a single form as many forms, due to the fertility of its intelligence. Nevertheless, in any form, nature conceives and contains itself so that it recognizes the form of the whole. Therefore, it is a certain "whole," a whole by perfect reason, because the whole is preserved in the individual parts. It is most unified because it is nearest to the divine Unity, though it still falls away from it. 

Because the formal reasons <term>logoi</term> of things differ from one another by formal definition, they are derived by degrees from higher things toward lower ones, and similarly from the better toward the worse. It is concluded that in any genus, that which is "first" is perfectly the whole, and the thing is the whole in any of its parts: thus is Being itself, thus is Life itself, thus is Intellect. But that which "makes" the whole is not composed of its parts in the way that a thing borrows its essence from its parts; rather, it gives being to the parts by its own essence. And a "whole" of this kind, which propagates itself into each individual thing while being preserved in each, is called an "infinite whole." For whatever it receives infinitely within it, the rest follows as well.

## The First Intellect is also necessarily manifold and is all things; therefore, before it is the Principle of all things, which is not all things, but above all things.

These points in the eighth chapter seem worthy of consideration. For the "reason" of the intellect is this: that it is moved and illuminated by that which forms it. Its intelligible properties, however, are opposites. Likewise, it is not necessarily included in the very definition of "intellect" that it be the "intelligible" itself; for no necessity prohibits there being some intellect even if the intelligible were known by no one; conversely, it does not necessarily belong to the definition of the "intelligible" that an intellect exists. For the intellectual power, in the scope of its object, comprehends material and <unclear>immaterial</unclear> things together, and among these, it contains the things to be understood as one...
