<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically Ennead III, Book 8. In the previous section, Ficino discussed how every level of being, from the highest Intellect down to Nature, participates in a form of "contemplation" that results in creation. On this page, he moves higher up the metaphysical ladder to argue that the "First Principle" (the One or the Good) must be even higher than the Intellect itself, because the Intellect possesses a subtle form of multiplicity (the thinker and the thought).</meta>

<page-num>342</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO</header>

...and those things which they do not understand. Therefore, the Intellect and the **intelligible** <term>intelligibile: the object of thought or that which can be understood</term> are distinguished from one another by a certain formal logic; however, the way the "understanding subject" is distinguished from the "thing understood" is, in reality, very close. Indeed, the distinction between them in terms of actual reality is the very last stage of separation. Therefore, that first form in which the Intellect is joined with the intelligible is not a "most simple unity." It is not, then, the first principle of the universe, which is simply one and most simple—just as whatever is first in any category must necessarily be simple. 

That the Intellect is by some necessity **multiple**, and thus not the "First," is confirmed in this way: If the Intellect is the highest form of cognition, it must have the intelligible joined with it—namely itself—insofar as it is not identical in its logical definition. Thus, that which is primarily intelligible according to itself is also, as a consequence, an Intellect. For such an intelligible is a "separate form" <note>A form existing independently of physical matter</note> from a subject, and so, reflecting back upon itself, it carries intelligence. But if a material thing is called "intelligible," it becomes so only insofar as it is transformed into something else and is subsequently understood through that other thing. 

Since, therefore, the Intellect and the intelligible accompany one another—to the point that whatever is one is also the other—and since these differ by formal logic, just as there is multiplicity in the "First Intellect," so there must be a higher "Highest Principle" of the universe. A doubt then arises in this manner: if the Principle itself is not outside the category of the intelligible, it would seem to be unknown to itself; and insofar as it stands above the intelligible category, it can be known in no way at all. To this it is answered: the Principle senses its own excellence by a certain logic through "knowing," or perhaps the soul senses it by a more excellent cognition than the intellectual—or rather, by a certain shared "agreement" <note>original: "pacto"</note> of cognition. 

For the simple Intellect is the highest cognition in us, but it is the **unity formed by the Good** <term>boniforma: a Neoplatonic term for the soul's capacity to be shaped by or united with the Good</term> through which we first enjoy unity and goodness together; just as through the sense being filled with light, we enjoy a luminous object. Therefore, just as one who strives intensely to imagine something ceases to use all other senses, and one who wishes to understand completely sets aside the imagination, so too one who desires to reach that which exists above intellectual and intelligible nature must pass beyond every intelligible thing entirely. One must leave behind their own intellect and impose a total silence upon their intelligence. 

And again, there appears to be something within the "First" itself through which it enjoys the "First" of the universe. One must conclude that a thing knows itself to be different according to different states. The body indeed senses the soul through the senses, but it knows reason not through the senses, but through something better than itself. The Intellect, too, knows itself not through some discourse of reason, but through something more eminent than itself that possesses itself. The "One" and the "Good" are split apart, so that through something more sublime than intelligence and cognition, the "One" may know itself. 

Hence, if we step from the imperfect to the perfect—if we ascend—behold: the imagination, which usually wanders only through certain types of things and over a long time, must be set aside for Reason, which wanders through all things and needs a shorter time. Where Reason is first perfected, it takes the shortest time of all. Above this is the whole Intellect, always existing without time; if it possesses all things perfectly within itself to be seen, it does not have them confused, but distinct and pure—not with a sideways glance, but with a clear, direct, and distinct vision. Above this Intellect, which is necessarily multiple, is the First Principle of the universe. This Principle is not merely "one certain thing among all," otherwise it would not pertain to all things, nor could it be the principle of all; nor is it "all things" in such a way that it is not one and simple, for this is the First. Everywhere, however, there is a prior unity, both unordered and composed; and again, it is simple and "one" equally with "all things." 

If this is conceded by anyone, we distinguish it thus: either it is all things at once, or rather individually. If it were all things together, then every single form would be there with a multitude; but this single form exists before the multitude, and thus it alone is the principle, and there is no need to add a multitude for it to be the principle. Either this one form is with the multitude at once, and thus it is not the "Whole Principle" since it exists united before all things; or this one form is placed after all things, which is the most absurd thing to say. But if we take the other view—that the principle is "all things" in such a way that it can be truly said of each thing seen and discerned individually, "this is the principle"—then it would follow that anything at all is the principle. Since the principle is necessarily unique, there would be only one single thing in the universe; or conversely, the whole would be whatever thing is posited to exist.

->The Good itself is above essence, life, and intellect, and cannot be reached by the intellect.<-

Since we see in the levels of living things that life is most closely joined to being, and that intellect is next to life, we see that the first "passion" <note>In the sense of an attribute or property</note> in the whole order of things is simply "One." I say that the intellect is joined to this; whether you consider it in itself, it is a certain movement toward an identical end; toward another, so that they may be "one" and belong to that "One." Some movement takes this as truth. But both depend upon the Good; thus it was neither essence, nor "to be," but life and intellect that exists, yet it seeks something better than essence—that is, the "Sun of the Good." Indeed, life does not need its own form, nor does the intellect need that which it would lose for the sake of the Good, since it is the Good itself that has no need for any other help. 

Therefore, the mind is the same when it is directed toward the Good, around which it turns. Because that which exists above the intellect and the intelligible is entirely beyond reach, and names are usually imposed from the conception of the intellect, it has no "proper name" in the intellect. It is called "The Good," however, because all things are made from it, and once made, they are perfected. It is also called "The One," because in itself it towers over all things, and it remains unmoved while these things proceed from it; otherwise, nothing would remain anywhere. Nor is it divided into parts, otherwise the "One" itself would cease to be; if that were taken away, all things would soon be lost. Nor is there a multiplicity of forms, otherwise, by being subject to descent or multitude, it would no longer be true unity or found to be simplicity. 

If you proceed through trees, through animals, through the soul, through minds, you will find that what is most simple and most "one" in each of these is the most powerful of all and the principle of the rest. Similarly, you will reduce the Universe to a most powerful unity, about which nothing further can be predicted, since we first conceive of Unity itself or Goodness; otherwise, if anything else were predicated of it, it would be composed of lesser components, making it secondary and subsequent. Do not, therefore, apply "intellect" to this, for the definition of intelligence is one thing, and that of the Good is another. For both do not belong equally to any one thing. 

Intelligence, therefore, creates a connection with the Good that is joined to it. You will not, therefore, apply "Ideas" <note>The Platonic archetypes or forms</note> there, which are seen by the intelligence and are absolutely distant from one another by formal logic—especially the ideas of contrary and opposite things, as is clear from the order of the universe according to the essence and form of what is created. For those things which in this craftsmanship differ in reality and subject, differ in the intellect of the maker of all things by a formal logic; otherwise, he would either confuse forms in an unordered heap or they would proceed from entirely formless matter. 

Plotinus forbids applying formal and absolute distinctions to the First Principle; they even forbid applying "life" or "essence" after "unity" or "goodness." None of these things exist "against" the Good, but they have their first placement above essence and being—just as they judge that matter, which is the opposite extreme under essence, should be placed last. Thus, just as one must descend below...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the nature of the first principle. The previous page established that the Intellect, while high, contains a form of multiplicity (thinker and thought). Here, Ficino argues that to reach the absolute "One" or "Good," we must transcend even formal intellectual concepts.</meta>

<page-num>343</page-num>
<header>ON BOOK VIII. ENNEAD III.</header>

...from all concepts of intelligence which are formal; but to reach that [the One], one must ascend above all such concepts. One must not think that it can be reached by a mobile, multiple, or formal intellectual act, for it stands marvelously above all multiplicity and form.

->The Good itself is the father, whose son is the Intellect, always filled by the father; and the world is the image of this Intellect.<-

Just as sight is one thing and light another—to which the eye is directed in order to receive it, even if we imagine an eye eternally filled with light—so too the Intellect is one thing, and the True and Good itself is another. Toward this the Intellect is born and toward this it strives. Even the Intellect itself differs from that [Good], though by its proximity it always enjoys a most blessed fullness of the Good. Therefore, to enjoy the Good itself, there is no need for "sight" <note>In this context, Plotinus and Ficino mean the dualistic "sight" of an observer looking at an object</note> for the Light itself. Indeed, if anyone could contain the whole beauty of the visible world in one single intuition at once, he would marvel beyond measure. From that image, he might more easily suspect the nature of the **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world: the realm of pure forms and ideas, accessible only to the mind</term> by its help, though the latter is far more beautiful. Again, if someone should behold that realm, in which there is nothing unformed, nothing deformed, nothing immoderate, nothing lacking life or intellect—where all is total splendor, and a sun burns from the opposite side with total purity—he would then guess who its father is, and by what reason he generated such a son. The Father, generating within himself from eternity the pure Intellect and the fullness of all things, is superior to both intellect and fullness.

->On nature, contemplation, and the One. <note>original: "ΠΕΡΙ' φύσεως καὶ θεωρίας καὶ τοῦ ἑνός"</note><-

Supposing we were to play a bit at first before beginning to be serious, and we were to say that all things seek **contemplation** <term>contemplation: from the Greek "theoria," meaning both a mental vision and the creative focus that produces reality</term>, and look toward such an end—not only rational animals, but even those lacking reason, and even the nature of plants and the earth which generates them. Suppose we said that all these things achieve contemplation according to their natural capacity,

<margin>B</margin>
though some contemplate and achieve it in one way, and others in another—some truly, and others through an imitation or an image. If we said this, would anyone accept such a paradoxical argument? Perhaps, if this were discussed among ourselves, we would run no risk of being misunderstood if we "play" in our own territory. Do we not ourselves contemplate while joking or playing at this very moment? Or perhaps we, and all who joke and play, do so because we are striving toward this very thing [contemplation].

<margin>C</margin>
For it seems that whether a child plays or a man plays, or if he studies seriously, the one studies for the sake of contemplation, while the other plays and jokes for the same reason. Indeed, every action strives toward contemplation. ...they might say; that it [Nature] possesses contemplation within itself: and that which it makes, it makes through contemplation, even though it does not possess it <note>Plotinus is exploring the paradox that Nature "contemplates" its own internal logic to create, even though it lacks a conscious, reflective mind like a human</note>, and in what manner it accomplishes this.

<margin>

I. Because, therefore, there are neither hands here, nor feet, nor any instrument, whether brought from outside or innate: but there is need for matter in which it [Nature] acts and which it places into a form: consider the seed of each thing. Nor truly is it to be thought that Nature performs its work by force, as if by pushing and pressing. For what kind of pushing or pressure could produce the many-formed branches and colors and shapes? Since not even the molders of wax and those similar craftsmen whom they call puppet-makers <note>original: "puparios"</note>—whom some have fearfully thought Nature’s own craftsmanship resembles—could produce colors unless they applied them to their works from elsewhere. It was worth considering how, in the practitioners of such arts, something must remain within, according to which they fabricate works through their hands. Similarly, there is something of this kind in Nature, which is indeed a certain power remaining [in itself] and fabricating without the service of hands: remaining, I say, as a whole. For it does not need some parts to remain while others move. For matter is that which is moved there, but in the power itself nothing is moved; otherwise, that which will be moved will not be the primary mover, nor will it be Nature itself, but rather that which consists as an immobile whole. Someone might object that the "reason" <term>reason: translate of "ratio" or "logos," meaning the formative principle or blueprint</term> indeed remains immobile, but Nature is different from reason and is moved. But if they say "the whole," it will similarly be "reason"; but if some part of it is immobile, this itself will be "reason." For it is necessary that this be a "form," <note>original: "speciem"</note> and not be composed of matter and form. For why would it need hot or cold matter? Since the matter subjected to the fabrication brings that with it: whether it be of that kind, or rather even before it takes on quality, it is touched by "reason." For fire does not need to be added so that matter may become fire, but rather the "reason" [of fire] must be added. This is a clear argument in animals and plants, that **seminal reasons** <term>seminal reasons: "seminales rationes," the internal biological and spiritual blueprints that guide the growth of living things</term> are the makers of all things, and that Nature exists as a "reason" which generates another "reason" as its own offspring, while it clearly hands something over to the subject, yet meanwhile remains in itself. Therefore, the "reason" according to the visible form sent forth externally is already the last and lacks life; therefore, it cannot further make another "reason." But the "reason" possessing life within the maker of the form—like a sister, and itself possessing the same power—begets the final "reason" in the result.

<margin>

</margin>
II. In what way then does it make? And in making, how does it touch upon some contemplation? Certainly, if it acts while remaining, and remaining in itself, and is "reason," it is surely contemplation. For action is accustomed to happen according to reason, being clearly different from reason; but reason, assisting and presiding over action, is not action. It follows that it is not action, but reason, and is certainly a certain contemplation. Now truly, in the universal "reason," the last reason proceeds from contemplation, and thus it is called contemplation, as if conceived through contemplation itself and...

<column-break/>

...to be, to have contemplation <note>original Greek: "theoria"</note> in itself, and what it makes, it makes through contemplation, even though it does not have it, and how.
THAT there are neither hands here, nor feet, nor any instrument brought in or innate: and there is need for matter, upon which it will make, and which it makes into a form, is surely clear to everyone. Nor indeed does a lever-like pushing or any kind of prying produce varied and manifold colors and shapes. For not even the wax-molders or puppet-makers—looking at what is available and buying it, as if their own work were like that of Nature—could make colors, unless they brought in colors from elsewhere for their making. But they saw those who think that while in the arts the makers remain, the works are finished; and what the makers do through their hands, they [Nature] do through themselves, to arrive at trust in Nature: that in the same way, the power remains there too, so that the making through hands is trusted because the power remains. For indeed matter requires some things as staying still, and others as moving; matter is the thing moved, but that which moves it primarily is not moved: or it will not be a body, the first mover: nor will Nature be such, but other things that are immobile in the whole. Someone might say that the "reason" <note>original Greek: "logos"</note> is immobile: but Nature is another thing besides the "reason," and it moves. But if we say "all," then it is the "reason": if some part of it is immobile, this also is the "reason." For it must be "form" <note>original Greek: "eidos"</note> itself, and not composed of matter and form. For what does it need of hot or cold matter, or even of matter that is underlying and being crafted? Either it is brought in then, or before the making, not having quality, it is touched by "reason." For fire does not need to be added so that the matter might be fire, but rather the "reason." And the things in animals and the things in plants are a sign or a small proof that the "reasons" are all things, and that Nature is "reason," which makes another "reason" as its own offspring, giving something to the subject but itself remaining in that in which it is "reason"—the one according to the visible shape, which is now the last and dead, and no longer able to make another. But the one having life—which is the brother of the one who has the shape, or itself having the same power—makes in that which is becoming.
HOW then does it make? And since it is making, would it touch upon some contemplation? If indeed it makes while remaining and remaining in itself and is "reason," it would itself be contemplation. For action would happen according to "reason," being clearly different from "reason": but the "reason" being the same as the action or presiding over it, would not be action: if then it is not action, but "reason," it is contemplation, or in every "reason" we have, it is from contemplation. And it is contemplation in this way, as something contemplated.

A What are the things that come to be entirely? That which is not like nature but like soul; they are not things in nature, but things in the soul, and this itself is contemplated. It is altogether in contemplations <note>original: "theoriai"—this refers to the Greek concept of 'theoria,' which means a concentrated looking or mental vision</note>. But even if their activities also produce something, these are not contemplated objects <note>original: "theorema"—an object of study or a mathematical principle</note> themselves, but come from certain contemplated objects. How then does Nature herself possess contemplation? If one possesses it from reason <note>original: "logos"</note>, one might say that contemplating proceeds from reason, 
B being disposed toward the things within her. Being a certain life, reason, and a productive power, is it perhaps that contemplating is not a state of being acted upon, but of acting? And because she possesses something, and is of a certain kind in being the same for all, then that is her acting. Regarding contemplation, the objects of contemplation are also of reason, because she is contemplation, object, and reason all at once. By making some things or the same things, or by making something, 
C contemplation and manifestation are the result of contemplation, while she herself remains. She provides nothing else, but by being contemplation, she is a productive thing.

D AND if someone were to ask her for what sake she creates—if she were willing to listen and speak—she would say: "It was necessary not to ask, but to understand in silence, just as I am silent and not accustomed to speak. What then is there to understand? That what is brought into being is my vision, a silent thing, and a principle of contemplation <note>theorema</note> produced by nature. Because I have come into being from such a contemplation, I have a nature that loves to see; and my act of contemplating produces a vision, just as geometers draw figures while they contemplate. But while I do not draw, 
E but only contemplate, the lines of bodies come into existence as if they were falling out from me. And the disposition of my mother and those who generated me belongs to me: for they too are from contemplation, and my birth resulted from their contemplating. But they did not contemplate with words or theorems; 
F I was born from them." What then does this mean? That what is called nature, being a soul and the offspring of a prior soul that lives more powerfully, possesses a quiet contemplation within itself. It does not look toward the things above, nor again toward the things below, but standing in what it is, and in this understanding and consciousness, it sees what comes after it as far as possible, seeking nothing further, but having accomplished a bright and graceful vision. And if anyone wished to grant her some kind of perception or understanding, it would not be like what people call 
G the perception and understanding of others, but rather like comparing the state of sleep to one who is awake. For while she contemplates her own vision, she rests, cooled by it within herself, and she does not take any part of it herself: but compares it with the knowledge of one who is awake. For contemplating her own spectacle, she is at rest: a spectacle, I say, made in her, from that which remains in herself and with herself...

<column-break/>

A ...perceived. Every Reason <note>original: "Ratio"—referring to the 'Logos' or the rational blueprint of a thing</note> higher than this has some things situated within itself. And one is not like nature, but like soul; the other is in nature, and is nature itself. But does this also happen from contemplation? Entirely from contemplation: but only if it has also contemplated itself in a certain way. For it is the effect of contemplation and of a certain contemplated thing. How then does nature herself possess speculation? 
B She does not possess speculation proceeding from reason <note>i.e., discursive, step-by-step logic</note>; I mean the consideration of those things that are in her, proceeding from reason. But again, she by no means considers her own things, since she is a certain life and reason and an efficient power. Or perhaps because to consider is to not yet possess? But if she possesses these things, does she not create from what she possesses? Therefore, to be what she is, is certainly for her to act; and as much as she is, that much she is also acting. There is, however, a certain contemplation and (if I may say so) a 
C contemplated object <note>original: "contemplamen"</note>, for it is reason. Insofar as there is contemplation, a contemplated object, and reason, to that extent she acts, namely by the reason through which she exists. Therefore, action has now appeared to us to be a certain contemplation: specifically, it is the effect of contemplation, while the speculation remains, not acting in any other way, but creating because the contemplation itself comes to be.

The fullness of the reasons (the "seminary" or seed-powers) in nature is that which nature is. It enjoys these through sense, and generates species in reality, just as that which is already dominant in it reaches into the external action of itself.

D IF ANYONE should ask her for what sake she creates—if only she would wish to hear and speak to the questioner—she will answer: "It was not proper to ask me, but it was fitting for you to understand in silence, just as I am silent and not accustomed to speak out. What, then, was it fitting for you to understand? This, I say, first of all: that what is born is my vision <note>original: "spectamen"</note>, while I remain silent, a contemplated object born of nature. And because I was born from a certain contemplation of this kind, I have, not without cause, a 
E nature desirous of the spectacle. Consequently, that which in me takes the place of a contemplator thus produces a vision, just as geometers describe things by contemplating. However, I do not write; but by contemplating, the lines of bodies emanate from here as if falling out in the meantime. Truly, the affection of my mother and of my parents is preserved in me: for they draw their origin from contemplation. My generation is also derived from speculation. For while they do nothing, but are greater reasons and contemplate themselves, I was born. 
F Of these things, nature is the soul, the offspring of a prior soul living more powerfully, having a quiet speculation in itself, turning neither toward higher things nor toward lower things. This, standing firmly in that in which it is—namely in its own state and, as it were, consensus—through this knowledge and consensus, knows what is after itself as its own nature allows, and does not search 
G further, but has now perfected a splendid and graceful vision. For contemplating her own spectacle, she is at rest: a spectacle, I say, made in her, from that which remains in herself and with herself...

...remains, and let the spectacle itself be quiet; an observation, <margin>A</margin> though darker and weaker. For this is one form of production leading toward intuition: but this is an image of another contemplation. Therefore, by this reasoning, that which is born from it comes forth as a most weak thing, because a weakened perspective produces a weak spectacle <note>original: "spectamen" / "theorema" — the object or result of a mental vision</note>: for indeed, even men, when they become too weak for contemplation, tend to pursue the shadow of speculation and reason, which is action. For when the faculty for contemplating is not at all sufficient, and they are unable to perceive the spectacle sufficiently due to the weakness <margin>B</margin> of the soul—and thus are not fulfilled, yet still desire to see it—they flee toward acting: so that there at least they may see what they were not able to discern with the mind. Therefore, whenever they act, they themselves wish to see it, to contemplate it, and to feel it, and even to have others look upon it with them. When action is set before them, as far as is possible (as they think), we will surely find everywhere that production and action <margin>C</margin> are either a weakness of contemplation or a consequence of it. It is weakness, indeed, where you have nothing beyond the thing that was acted; but it is a consequence if you have something else better than the produced work to contemplate. For who, when they are able to contemplate the truth itself with a certain primary zeal, would turn themselves toward an image of the truth? The dullest of children testify to this <margin>D</margin> who, since they are most inept at learning (and contemplating), slip away into manual arts and physical activities.

<margin>VIII. The intellect of the world-soul is clearly always derived from the contemplation of divine things; just as a pregnant woman gives birth, the soul gives birth to a certain nature of reason as if it were contemplating, and by such observation it generates all things.</margin>

**B**ut since we have now spoken of Nature, and in what way generation <note>the process of bringing things into being</note> is a certain contemplation, let us next proceed to the Soul, speaking as follows. Truly, the contemplation of the Soul and its character—eager for learning, studious in seeking, and furthermore a certain stimulus bringing forth from the things it has known—has now, in its full fertility, brought it about that the Soul itself, having been made through such a great act of contemplation, might produce <margin>E</margin> another object of contemplation. Just as an art also does when it is full, evidently procreating another "miniature art" in a learning boy, who acquires an image of all things; yet he possesses these things differently, as if they were dark and weak, and certain spectacles that from the beginning are not strong enough to defend themselves. Therefore, that higher rational part of the soul remains there, always filled and illuminated by the higher things: but the other part <margin>F</margin> participates in that which participated in the first participation, for life always proceeds from life. For activity <term>actus: the Greek 'energeia,' referring to the actualization or "doing" of a being</term> runs through all things and is nowhere absent: yet as it moves forward, it allows its prior part to remain where it left it, in a way. For if it were to lose the first part entirely, it would no longer be everywhere, but only in that where it ends; yet that which proceeds is not equal to that which stays at rest. If, therefore, it is necessary for it to occur through all things, and for no place to remain where the same activity is not present, then that which is prior is always something different from that which is posterior. But activity proceeds from contemplation or action, yet ultimately from contemplation, especially when action did not yet exist: for it cannot exist before <margin>G</margin> contemplation. If, I say, the matter stands thus, it is necessary that the other form of contemplation be weaker:

<column-break/>

...to remain, and to be a spectacle, and a silent contemplation, though another is dimmer than the one that produced it for contemplation: for this is an image of another contemplation. For these reasons, that which is generated by it is altogether weak: because a weakened contemplation makes a weak object of contemplation <note>original: "theorema"</note>. Since even men, when they are weakened in regard to contemplating, make action into the shadows of contemplation and reason. For because the power of contemplation is not sufficient for them, or being unable to grasp the spectacle sufficiently due to the weakness of the soul, and standing apart unfulfilled, yet longing to see it, they are carried toward action, so that they might see what they did not see with the mind. Whenever they act, they themselves wish to see it, and to contemplate and perceive it, and for others to do so as well, whenever the intention for action is as much as possible for them. Everywhere, then, we shall find that making and acting are either a weakness of contemplation or a byproduct. It is weakness if we have nothing after the thing is done; it is a byproduct if we have something else better than the thing made to contemplate. For who, being able to contemplate the true thing intently, goes toward the image of the true? Even the children of children bear witness, those who are incapable of lessons and contemplations, and are carried down toward crafts and manual labors.

BUT having spoken about Nature, in what way generation is a contemplation, coming to the souls prior to this, let us say how the contemplation of these, and the love of learning, and the searching, and the labor from what it has known, being full, has made it a spectacle and a fertile thing, to make another spectacle: just as art makes, when it has filled each thing, but just as the small arts of children make images of all things: these things are in another way, as if they were dim and unable to help themselves, to make sights and objects of contemplation. The rational part of it, then, toward the things above, being filled and illuminated, remains there: but the other part, by participating in the first participation, participates, for life is always brought forth from life. For activity <note>original: "energeia"</note> reaches everywhere, and there is nowhere it is absent: it stands apart in a way, because the prior part remains as it was before. If it had left [the prior part] to remain, it would no longer be everywhere, but only in that place alone: but the thing proceeding is not the same as the master principle. If it must be everywhere, or else not exist, so that there is not the same activity. Instead of the prior, the posterior; but the activity is from contemplation or action: but action is not yet. For it is necessary that what is produced always corresponds in some way to the nature of its source, yet it inevitably turns out to be inferior, becoming thinner and more diluted as it descends. All things proceed sweetly and quietly because they do not require an external contemplation or an apparent outward action. The Soul indeed contemplates from its highest <margin>A</margin> <margin>B</margin> watchtower <note>original: "specula" — a high lookout point</note>, and because it contemplates in this way—as something rising outward, not in the same manner as that which came before it—it certainly produces what follows it. But if they act out of desire, they act for the sake of what they long for: and that is the object of contemplation and contemplation itself.

<margin>D</margin> **ACTION**, therefore, exists for the sake of contemplation and the object of contemplation; for this reason, the goal of those who act is contemplation. Indeed, what they could not achieve by a direct path <margin>That the goal is contemplation; likewise that Plotinus assumes a certain vital reason <note>original: "rationem" / "logos"</note> and brings it forth in execution, yet it is known by that same reason.</margin>, they strive to grasp through indirect means. The same result occurs when they attain what they desire: for they wished it to be present to them. They do this not so they may be ignorant, but so they may recognize what has been acquired and behold it present in the soul, as if it were placed there for the sake of being seen. Since they always act for the sake of the Good <margin>E</margin>, this Good is not intended to remain outside of them so they possess nothing of it; rather, they act so that they themselves may possess the good that comes from the action. But where is this held? Certainly in the soul. Therefore, action slides back again into contemplation. For that which one receives in the soul—which is a form of reason—what else is it but a silent reason? And the more it is reason, the more it is silent, and vice versa. For then it experiences rest, and being full, it requires nothing further. Contemplation, established in such a <margin>F</margin> state, rests inwardly because of the confidence of possessing its object. And where certainty <note>original: "fides" / "pistis" — here meaning intellectual conviction or trust in the vision</note> is surer, contemplation is quieter; for in knowing the thing itself through reason (as we must now speak seriously), the knower becomes one with the thing known. For if there are two—this thing and that—they will be separate. Therefore, it will seem like something merely adjacent, and being thus doubled, it has not yet contracted a true familiarity <margin>G</margin>—just as when reasons existing in the soul produce no effect. For this reason, it is necessary that reason is not something external, but is united to the soul of the learner until it finds its own home. Therefore, when the soul becomes familiar with reason and is shaped by it, it simultaneously brings it forth; having been made ready, it now proceeds into act. A <note>original: "altera sit à seipsa" — The soul distinguishes itself from the objects it thinks about.</note> ...one part becomes different from itself, and it is known that the other part came from that source; thus, by thinking, it looks upon another thing as if it were itself something else. Yet, this soul is also a <term>rational principle</term> <note>original: "ratio" / "logos" — the organizing blueprint of the soul</note>, and like an intellect, but one that gazes at something else. For it is not "full" in itself, but falls short of that which is above it; nevertheless, it gazes quietly upon the things it brings forth. For those things it has not yet produced, it does not yet bring forth; but those it does bring forth, it pushes into being out of a certain deficiency in its own contemplation, noticing what it possesses within itself.

B But in the realm of practical actions, which are now external, the soul adapts what it holds within. Because it possesses these things more deeply than nature does, it possesses them more quietly; and because it has more, it exists more as a contemplative being. Conversely, because it does not possess these things perfectly, it desires more strongly to have a perception of the thing it looks toward—a vision arising from the wandering path of its own consideration. When it has completely left behind its habit and passed over into other things, and then returns to contemplate again, a part of it is left behind; but the other part, remaining within itself, achieves this less.

C For this reason, the virtuous soul is already the very <term>effect of reason</term>, and it demonstrates to others what it possesses within itself. But when turned toward itself, its vision is already gathered into a single point and into a state of quiet—not only regarding external things, but regarding itself and, finally, all things within.

<margin>VI. It is confirmed that all things are made by contemplation, or by those contemplating, whether they are the reasons that contemplate or those things which act for the sake of contemplation.</margin>

D **JUST AS**, therefore, it is partly established by itself and partly indicated by reason: all things arise from contemplation and are for the sake of contemplation. This includes both the things that truly exist and those generated from them—namely, those things that contemplate, having been made into <term>objects of vision</term> <note>original: "contemplamina" / "theoremata"</note>, whether they present themselves to the senses, to knowledge, or to mere opinion. Furthermore, all actions are directed toward knowledge and toward a final end; even desire seeks knowledge. Moreover, biological generations, taking their start from contemplation, end in a <term>form</term> <note>original: "species" / "eidos"</note>, and they manufacture another form. In short, all things, by imitating their creative causes, produce visions and forms everywhere. The very substances that are created, being imitations of true beings, show that their

E creative causes look toward vision as their end—not toward the making itself, nor the actions, but the work itself, so that it might become a spectacle for those who look upon it. Indeed, even our thoughts deeply desire to see this very thing, as do the senses themselves, whose final goal is knowledge. Again, before these things, nature itself possesses a specimen and a reason within itself, and it generates another reason. Therefore, it is clear that since the very first things consist in contemplation, all other things

F necessarily desire contemplation itself: for if the end is set for all, that end is also the beginning. Indeed, even when animals reproduce, the seminal reasons within stimulate them to give birth; and that whole process is an act of contemplation—a stimulus desiring to manufacture many forms and various spectacles, to fill all things with reasons, and to gaze upon them almost perpetually. For to make something exist is to produce a certain form, and that is the object of contemplation. Furthermore, an unskilled

G craftsman is judged to be like one who creates deformed forms <note>Plotinus argues that "bad" art or "evil" is just a failed or blurry vision of the true Form.</note>.

<column-break/>

A <note>The Greek text mirrors the Latin column, providing the original philosophical terminology of Plotinus.</note> ...becomes other than itself; and being ordered, it sees, as if one thing were seen by another. For it is itself a <term>logos</term> <note>original: "λόγος" — word, reason, or ratio</note> and a kind of intellect, but seeing something else. It is "full," yet it falls short of that which is before it. It sees, however, quietly, the things it brings forth. For what it has already brought forth, it does not yet bring forth again; but what it does bring forth, it thinks it does so because of its own deficiency in possession and its failure to perfectly achieve its aim. In practical matters, it applies what it holds

B to the outside world. Because it does not possess things more than nature does, it is quieter; and by possessing more, it is more contemplative. But by having less, it desires more to have the achievement and vision of that which is contemplated—the vision that comes from inquiry. Even when it leaves one state to become involved in others, and then returns, it contemplates again with the part of itself that was left behind; but the part above, staying in itself, does this less. Therefore, the virtuous <term>logos</term> is already present, and what is within itself, it

C reveals to another. But toward itself, it is vision—for it already exists. It is already directed toward the One and toward the quiet, not only of external things, but toward itself, and all things within.

D **THAT** truly all things—both the things that truly are—arise from contemplation and are contemplation; and the things produced from them, while those beings contemplate, are themselves objects of vision—some by sense, some by knowledge or opinion. Actions have their end in knowledge, and desire is for knowledge, and generations come from contemplation, resulting in a Form and another object of vision. In general, all things being imitations of their makers, they produce objects of vision and forms. The resulting foundations of being, being imitations of true substances, show that the end is the product—not the making, nor

E the actions, but the result, so that it may be contemplated. And this is what thoughts seek in their ideas, and even the senses, whose end is knowledge. And even before these, nature makes the object of vision within itself and its reason, having established another reason; one part it received, and the other it established as irrational <note>original: "ἄλογον" — without its own independent reason, acting instinctively.</note>. For it is clear,

F since it is also clear that it is necessary among the first things, which exist in contemplation, that other things also desire this, which is the end for all. Since even when animals give birth, the reasons within them are moved; and this is an activity of contemplation—a "birth-pang" <note>original: "ὠδίς" — travail or labor-pains of the soul</note>—by making many forms and a multitude of objects of vision, and filling all things with reasons, and being forever in contemplation. For to make something be is to make a form; and this is to fill everything with contemplation. And even the errors in things made, and those in actions, are objects of vision

G arising from a distorted viewer; just as the bad craftsman is like one who produces ugly forms.

Action and physical creation are merely weakened or "fallen" versions of this internal vision, produced when the soul cannot maintain its silent gaze on the higher Truth.</summary>

<meta>This page follows Plotinus’s discussion of how even the "lowest" parts of reality—like plants and nature—possess a silent form of contemplation. He now transitions to the "higher" levels: the Soul and the Divine Mind (Intellect), where the act of thinking and the object being thought of begin to merge into one.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

...and if everyone has seen these things, and how they are described by them.

THESE THINGS indeed, if we ascend in our contemplation from Nature to the soul, and from the soul to the mind—with the contemplations always becoming more intimate and familiar, and becoming one with those who contemplate—then in the case of the virtuous soul, as it moves toward the same goal, the things known are brought back into the same subject. But now, it is clear that in the intellect itself both are one, not through an acquired familiarity, as usually happens in the most excellent soul, but rather through essence, and because there "being" and "thinking" are the same. For there, this is no longer one thing and that another; otherwise, there would again be some other thing in which the two are not distinct.

It is necessary, therefore, that in this state both are truly one: and that is "living contemplation," not merely a "thing contemplated" <note>original: "contemplamen" — Plotinus distinguishes between the act of looking (theoria) and the object being looked at.</note> existing in something else. For that which lives in another is not living by itself. If, therefore, a "thing contemplated" and a "thing thought" is to be alive, it must be life itself—not the vegetative life, nor the sensory life, nor any other animal life (for these others are also "thoughts" in a certain way). This one is vegetative "thought," that one sensory, and another animal. In what way, then, are they "thoughts"? Because, clearly, they are <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "logoi" — the underlying blueprints or formative patterns of reality.</note>.

And all life is a kind of "thought," but one is dimmer than another, just as life itself varies. But the life that is clearer and more powerful is the "primary life," and the "primary intellect," and the "One." Therefore, the primary thought is the primary life, and the second life is also the second thought; finally, the last life is the last thought. Every life of this kind is thus judged to be a "thought." Men might perhaps speak of differences in lives, but they do not speak of differences in "thoughts." Instead, they say that some things are thoughts, while others are not thoughts at all, because they do not seek to understand what life itself actually is.

But it must further be signified that our discourse here shows, perhaps by chance, that all things exist as "contemplations." If, therefore, the truest life is life according to the "thought" itself, and if this is the same as the truest thought, then truly the most perfect thought lives. Thus, contemplation and this kind of living "thing contemplated" are one and the same; and these two are together as one. How, then, is this one many? Perhaps because it does not contemplate just "one." For even when it looks at the One, it does not do so as a single point of contact—otherwise it would not become an <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "Mind" or "Nous" — the realm of divine ideas.</note>. Rather, beginning as a unity, it did not remain as it began, but secretly became a multiplicity, as if already pregnant. It unfolded itself, wishing to possess all things; perhaps it would have been better for it not to have desired that. For from this desire it emerged as the "second" stage of reality—much like a circle unfolding itself becomes a shape, a plane, a circumference, a center, and lines. Some parts are "above" and others "below"—the parts from which the beginning proceeds are better, while the rest are lesser. For that from which the procession begins was not like the destination toward which it proceeds. Nor again was that...

<column-break/>

<margin>
Where understanding thrives as living: that is, it is known: or it is the same. Likewise, it is full of form: as is life: and primary intelligence began: these proceed equally through care: just as intellect is necessary for all.
</margin>

<margin>A</margin> Finally, lovers themselves are primarily in that number who are engaged in looking, and who hurry more eagerly toward beauty <note>original: "speciem" — in a Platonic sense, this refers to the ideal Form or Essence.</note>.

<margin>B</margin> Let this much be said about these things. When, however, contemplation rises from nature itself to the soul, and from the soul to the mind, the contemplations always become more personal and familiar, and they are united with the observers. In a soul already perfected through virtue, the things known are brought back into the same subject, since they hurry toward the intellect itself. Certainly, in this intellect both are now one—not through some acquired familiarity, as is customary in the most excellent soul, but rather through essence, and from the fact that "to be" and "to understand" are the same there. For there, this is no longer one thing and that another; otherwise, there would again be something else in which there is no further "this" and "that."

<margin>C</margin> It is necessary, therefore, for both to be truly one in this state: and that is "living contemplation," not indeed as a "thing contemplated" in another. For what exists in another living thing is not living by itself. If, therefore, some "thing contemplated" (or "thing understood," as they say) is to live, it must be the life itself—not vegetative, nor sensory, nor any other animal life (for the others are also, in a way, "intelligences"). But this one is vegetative intelligence, that one sensory, and another, finally, is animal. In what way, then, are they intelligences? Because, evidently, they are rational principles.

<margin>D</margin> And all life is a certain intelligence, but one is thinner and another is like life itself. But that which is clearer and stronger is the "primary life," and the "primary intellect," and the "One." Therefore, the primary intelligence is also the primary life, and the second life is the second intelligence; finally, the last life is the lowest intelligence. Every life of this genus is therefore also judged to be intelligence. But men might be able to speak of differences in lives, yet they do not speak of differences in intelligences; rather, they say that some...

<margin>E</margin> ...are indeed intelligences, while others are not intelligences at all, because they in no way ask what life itself is. But this must be pointed out besides: that this sermon of ours shows again, as if by chance, that all things exist as contemplations. If, therefore, the truest life is life according to intelligence itself, and if this is the same as the truest intelligence, then surely the truest intelligence lives; and contemplation and this kind of living "thing contemplated"...

<margin>F</margin> ...is life itself, and these two are together as one. Therefore, the "being" itself is one and two. By what reasoning, then, is this one "many"? Perhaps because it does not contemplate the One. For even when it gazes at the One, it does not do so by a simple contact—otherwise it would not become an intellect. Instead, beginning as one, it did not remain as it began, but in a secret way became a multiplicity, as if already pregnant, and it unfolded itself wishing to possess all things. Perhaps it would have been better for it not to have desired that.

<margin>G</margin> For from this it emerged as the "second," not otherwise than a circle explaining itself becomes a shape, and a certain plane, and a circumference, and a center, and lines; and some things are upward, others downward. Those from which the beginning proceeds are better, the rest are worse. For that from which the procession happens was not such as that from which, and into which, it proceeds. Nor again was that...

<summary>Plotinus argues that all life, from plants to the Divine Mind, is a form of contemplation or "thinking," and that at the highest level of Intellect, the thinker and the thought become a single living essence. He uses the metaphor of a circle unfolding from a center to explain how the "One" becomes the "Many."</summary>

from which it simultaneously comes and into which it was such, just as that very thing
<margin>A</margin> from which only the progression begins. And in another way, the mind—not the mind of some individual, but the whole mind. Being the whole, it is also the mind of all things.
It is necessary, therefore, that the intellect <note>The "Intellect" or "Nous" in Plotinus’s thought is the second level of reality, acting as a divine warehouse of all possible forms and ideas.</note> possesses both all things and every part of all things in such a way that each individual part is the whole, and is all things. For if it were not so, it would possess some part which is not intellect; it would be heaped together from things that are not intellect, and would be a sort of accidental pile, waiting for support from all sides to truly become an intellect.
<margin>B</margin> For this reason, it is also infinite in this way; even if something flows from it inwardly, it is not diminished, because that which comes from it is also "all things," or rather, the source from which it comes forth internally was not composed of many parts.

<margin>VIII. Primarily, the intelligible multitude exists before all else, and is all things through itself.</margin> THIS [Intellect], therefore, exists in such a way, and is for that reason not the first; rather, there must be something higher than it. For the
<margin>C</margin> sake of this higher principle, our discourse has been conducted, and for this reason: because a multitude is always secondary to the One. Here there is number; and the principle of number is unity, and specifically a principle that is "one" in such a way. Here, truly, are both the intellect and the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The "intelligible" refers to the objects of thought—the eternal Truths or Forms that the Mind contemplates.</note> together; both together make two. If, however, there are two, it is necessary to grasp something prior to these two. But what must we say this is? Is it intellect alone? But to every intellect there is a joined "intelligible" object; and unless there is a joined object there, there will not even be an intellect. If, therefore, it is not an intellect, but escapes these two, it follows that what is prior to these two is higher than the intellect. But what prevents this from being the "intelligible" alone? For the same reason, clearly: because the "intelligible" also always has the intellect joined to it. If, therefore, it is neither the intellect
<margin>E</margin> nor the joined "intelligible," what will it be? It is certainly that from which the intellect comes, and together with the intellect, the intelligible. What then is this, and how shall we conceive of it? For it will either be something that thinks, or something that does not think. If it thinks, it will be an intellect; if it does not think, it will even be ignorant of itself, and will seem to be nothing venerable. For even if we say that this is the Good itself and the most simple <note>In ancient philosophy, "simple" means "not made of parts"—the ultimate building block of reality.</note>, we do not bring forth anything clear and manifest, even if it is true, as long as we have no point
<margin>F</margin> upon which to fix the gaze of our thought while we speak of it. Furthermore, since the knowledge of other things occurs through the intellect—and those who can know something by thinking possess an intellect—by what sudden intuition shall this principle, which surpasses the nature of the intellect, be perceived? We shall answer this by saying it is perceived through something in us that is as similar to it as possible. For there is something of it in us; or rather, there is no place among things where it is not, at least for those things that have the capacity to participate in it. Truly, wherever you apply something capable of receiving it, you will carry something away from there—just as if a voice were to occupy a desert, or even a desert inhabited by people. Then, in whatever part you apply your ears, you will drink in the whole voice, and yet again, not the whole of it. What then is it that we are prevented from representing as an intellect...

from which and into which, just as the "from which" alone. And in another way the Intellect <note>original Greek: "ho nous"</note>, not the intellect of someone, but also the whole. Being the whole, it is also of all things. It is necessary therefore for it, being all things and of all things, that its part also possesses all things and is all things. If not, it would have some part which is not intellect, and would not be merged into itself, but would be a sort of gathered heap, waiting for some intellect to come into being from all the parts. For this reason it is also infinite in this way: and if anything comes from it, it is not diminished; either that which comes from it is all things and is itself, not that from which it comes, or that from which it comes was not a composition of parts.

THIS intellect then is thus, and for that reason not first: but there must be that which is beyond it, for the sake of which, and toward which we might speak; first, because a multitude is always [secondary], and the whole is a certain number. But number is a principle and a trust, those things that truly are; and indeed the intellect and the intelligible <note>original Greek: "noeton"</note> are together, the whole is two together. But if two, one must take that which is before the two. What then? Intellect alone? But the intelligible is joined to every [intellect]. If then the intelligible should not be joined, there will not even be an intellect. If then it is neither intellect, but escapes the two, that which is prior to these two must be beyond the intellect. What then prevents it from being the intelligible itself? Either because the intelligible is also joined to the intellect. If then it were neither intellect nor intelligible, what would it be? And we shall call the intelligible that which is before it; what then is this, and how shall we imagine it? For again, it will either be thinking or unthinking. If thinking, it is intellect; if unthinking, it will be ignorant even of itself. So what is venerable about it? For even if one says it is the Good and the most simple, clearly we shall also speak the truth clearly, as long as we do not have anything on which to give our thought while we speak. And for again, while knowledge of other things happens through the intellect, and for those able to know by thinking, this thing having surpassed that nature, by what sudden application might it be caught? How then must one signify it, except as is possible by the likeness in us? We shall say, for there is something even in ourselves, or rather there is not anywhere where it is not, for those who can partake of it. For it is everywhere with freedom; wherever you place that which is able to have it, you have it standing there, just as a voice occupying a wilderness, or even with the wilderness, men; and in whatever part of the wilderness you stand, you will receive the voice in its entirety, and yet again not in its entirety. What then is that which we are prevented from setting forth as intellect...

<summary>Plotinus explores the nature of the Divine Intellect, arguing that because it contains a duality of thinker and thought, it must originate from a more fundamental, "simple" source called the One. He uses the analogy of a voice in a desert to explain how this ultimate principle can be fully present everywhere yet not exhausted by any single thing.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section where Plotinus established that the Intellect is a "multitude" of forms. He now moves toward the "One," the absolute source that must exist prior to that multitude. He uses famous analogies—the fountain and the tree—to explain how the source remains whole while generating everything else.</meta>

->BOOK EIGHT.<-

Does it remain? That which is before the mind is as if it were retreating backwards; if one lets go of the mind, which is disputed by those looking behind it, then one sees those things, provided one does not imagine the mind to be the ultimate. For the mind itself is the first life, being an activity in the unfolding <term>Greek: diexodos; the process of thought moving from one idea to another</term> of all things. It exists in that unfolding, or rather by that unfolding. But in that which unfolds—which is both life and equally an unfolding—it holds all things purely and simply as a whole, and not in an unarticulated way, but from all things. But it is necessary that the source itself is no longer in an unfolding, but is the principle of the unfolding; the principle of life, the principle of mind, and the principle of all things. For the principle is not all things, but all things come from the principle. The source itself is no longer all things, nor is it any one of them, so that all things might come to be; and so that it is not a multitude, but the principle of the multitude. For in every case, that which generates is simpler than that which is generated. If, therefore, the things of the mind were generated, then that source must be something simpler. But if someone says that the One itself is all things, either as each individual thing or as all things together—if indeed it were all things gathered together, it would be later than all things. If it is before all things, then all things are one thing, and the source is another thing before them. But if it were simultaneously itself and all things, it would not be a principle. But it must be the principle, and exist before all things, so that all things may exist after it. For if it were each individual thing, it would first be identical to whatever it is compared to, and then it would be all things together without any distinction, and thus it would be nothing of the all, but rather before the all.

What then is it? Is it the power of all things? If it did not hold them, then all things would not exist; nor would they have been filled with life. For what exists above life? The cause of life. For the activity of life, being all things, is the first, but it is as if poured out from a source. Think of a fountain that has no other beginning, giving itself to all rivers, not being exhausted by those rivers, but remaining quietly itself. The rivers flowing from it, before they flow here and there, still remain together for a time, already knowing, as it were, where they will let out their streams. Or think of the power of a great plant <note>Plotinus often uses the metaphor of a tree to describe the "World Soul" or the organic unity of the universe.</note> passing through the whole, while the principle remains, not scattered throughout the whole, but as if established in the root. This provides the whole life to the plant in its many parts, yet it remains itself, not multiplied, but the principle of the many. And it is a wonder how the multitude of life lived from that which is not a multitude; and the multitude would not exist unless that which is not a multitude existed before it. For the part is in the whole, so that it may be divided into the whole. For every loss causes a loss to the whole wherever it is lacking, unless the principle remains within itself, being different from the rest.

<column-break/>

**A** applying [our minds], we receive it. But perhaps it is necessary for the intellect to turn itself as if from the rear, and since it has a face on both sides, to leave itself behind, so that if it is to inspect the Good itself, it must take care not to be entirely "intellect," nor to imagine that the things it understands are all there is. For the Mind itself is the "first life," which is indeed an act in a certain "discursion" <term>Latin: discursio; the movement of the mind as it thinks through complex ideas</term> through all things: a discursion, I say, not one that runs about daily, but one that has always fulfilled its course. If, therefore, it is life and discursion, and it possesses
**B** all things, not in confusion but most exactly—otherwise, if it held them indistinctly, it would hold them imperfectly—it is necessary that it depends on another, which is no longer occupied in discursion, but is the principle of discursion: the principle of life, the principle of mind, and of all things. For the Principle is not all things, but rather all things are from the principle. The source itself is neither all things, nor any one of all things, so that it may generate all things; nor is it a multitude, but the principle of multitude. For that which generates
**C** is everywhere simpler than that which is generated. Therefore, if this Mind was generated, it is necessarily simpler than the Mind. But if anyone should think that the Good itself is the "One" and "All Things," it will either be all things according to each of the singular things, or all things collectively. But if it were all things accumulated together, it would be secondary to all things. For if it existed before all things, all things would be one sort of thing, and the source itself would be something else beyond them. But if the source and all things were the same, it would not be
**D** the beginning. Yet it is necessary that it be the principle, and before all things, so that all things may be after it. But if it were said that the source is individually each one of all things, then first, any thing would be the same as any other thing, and then all things would be together at once, with no distinction. And so, the source itself is nothing of all things, but rather above all things.

### WHAT then is it?

<margin>
**IX.**
*The principle of the universe is the One itself, which is above all things; it is neither moved, nor divided, nor multiplied, since from it the multitude of things proceeds.*
</margin>

Truly, it is the power of all things; if it were not, the rest would not exist. Nor would there be an intellect, which is the first, and every life. For that which stands above life is the cause of life.
**E** For the act of life, which is all things, is not the first itself, but is poured out from the principle like a fountain. Think of a fountain having no other source, giving itself entirely to the rivers, yet not exhausted by any of those rivers, but remaining in itself in quiet. The rivers flowing from it, before they flow this way or that, still remain as one, and as if already knowing where their streams will flow. Or think of the power of a huge tree
**F** with the principle remaining, not divided through the whole, but as if founded in the root. This indeed provides the whole and manifold life to the tree; but it remains itself, by no means multiplied, but the principle of the manifold life. Nor is it strange that it is so.
**G** Perhaps it is even to be wondered at how the multitude of life comes from "non-multitude," and that a multitude could not have existed unless that which is in no way a multitude existed before it. For the principle is by no means divided into the whole; otherwise, if it were divided, the whole would immediately perish. Nor would it ever have been made, unless the principle remains in itself, and is entirely different from this whole.

<summary>Plotinus uses the metaphors of a fountain and a tree root to explain how the absolute "One" can be the source of all life and intellect without being divided or diminished itself. He argues that the source must be simpler than the things it creates and must exist "above" the multitude of the material and intellectual worlds.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "One"—the ultimate, simple source of all reality. Having previously established that the Mind (Intellect) contains a multitude of forms, he now explains why we must look even further back to a single principle that is "beyond being."</meta>

### PLOTINUS’ ENNEADS, BOOK III.

A Therefore, a reduction is made everywhere into the One, and in each thing there is a "one" to which it is reduced: yet the whole of the universe is not reduced to a "one" that is before it simply because one arrives at a simple One. For this One is not referred to anything else, as other things are. Therefore, if you take the "one" of a tree—that is, its remaining principle—or the "one" of a living being, or the "one" of the soul, or the "one" of the universe, you will find in each case that which is most powerful and venerable. But if you take the One itself of those things which truly are—that is, the principle, the source, and the power—shall we then lack faith, B and suspect that it is nothing? It is certainly none of those things of which it is the principle: it is of such a kind that nothing can be predicated of it; it is not being, not essence, not life <note>original: "non ens, non essentia, non vita." This is a core Neoplatonic concept: the source of all things must be "beyond" the categories it creates.</note>, because it is above all these things. But if you should grasp it by stripping away "being" from it, you will immediately be struck with awe; you will direct yourself toward it, and reaching it, you will rest in its very seat. By a single, most powerful and simple intuition, you may now behold it. C Having beheld its greatness, you will recognize its dignity, for the things that come after it exist because of it.

<margin>The Intellect is inferior to the Good; and thus through this connection, it is made good: from this, it glimpses that intelligible world.</margin>

D **FURTHERMORE**, consider it also in this way: since the intellect is a kind of sight <note>Plotinus often uses the metaphor of "Intellectual Vision" to describe how the Mind perceives truth.</note>—a sight, I say, that sees—it is therefore a certain power that has already proceeded into action. It will therefore have one thing in itself as matter, and another as form, just as vision does in its act. I mean, it is "intelligible matter" <term>Intelligible matter: a philosophical concept describing the "substance" or potentiality within the divine Mind before it takes the shape of specific Ideas.</term>. For vision in its act has a double property. Before it saw, it was a certain "one." E Thus, the one became two, and the two became one. For the vision is filled by the sensible object and reaches its own perfection; but for the vision of the mind, the Good is that which fills it. For if the intellect were the Good itself, what would it need to see, or why would it need to act at all? For other things have their action around the Good and because of the Good; but the Good itself stands in need of nothing at all. For this reason, nothing exists for it except itself. Therefore, when you speak of the Good, add nothing else to it in your thought. For if you add anything, it will again be something "added," and you will show it to be needy by its own nature. Therefore, you should not even add "intelligence" to it, lest you add something foreign and make it two—namely, intellect and the Good. The intellect indeed needs the Good, but the Good does not need the intellect. Thus, the mind, by following the Good, becomes "one-form" and is perfected by the Good; while the species which is in the mind proceeds from the Good and is "good-formed" from that source. The kind of trace of the Good that is seen in the mind is the same kind of exemplar you should conceive, judging its truth through the trace impressed upon the mind. F This trace is impressed upon the intellect so that it might see and possess it. For this reason, there is in the intellect a desire; it is always desiring and always attaining. But the Good itself desires nothing—for what could it desire?—nor does it follow after anything. For it has never been in want. Therefore, it is not "intellect," for in the intellect there is desire and a certain application toward its own form. The intellect is surely beautiful, G and the most beautiful of all things, established as a splendor in pure light, encompassing the nature of all beings within itself. Of this intellect, our world here—though beautiful—is but a shadow and an image; but that superior world is positioned in all clarity.

<column-break/>

A Therefore, the ascent is everywhere toward the One, and in each thing there is a "one" to which it is led back; and everything is led to what is before it, which is not simply one, until one reaches the simply One. This is no longer led to anything else. But if you take the "one" in a plant—for this is the remaining principle—and the "one" of life, and the "one" of the soul, and the "one" of the universe, you take in each case the most powerful and the most precious. But if you should receive the One of the true beings, B or take the source and the power, shall we be unbelieving, or suppose it to be nothing? Or rather, it is from these things of which it is the principle; yet it is such that nothing can be predicated of it—neither being, nor essence, nor life—because it is above all these things. But if you take it by removing "being," you would wonder; and casting yourself into it and happening to rest in its presence, you will touch it more closely by your approach to it. C Beholding its greatness, you will see who it is that exists after it.

D And also in this way: since the mind is a kind of sight, and the mind is seeing—a certain power having come into activity—it holds one thing as matter and another as form, just as vision does in activity. I say this is "intelligible matter." Vision in its activity is twofold. Before seeing the One, it was all; E then it became two. There is, on the one hand, the "not seeing," which is the filling from the sensible and its perfection, as it were; but for the eye that is in the mind, it is the Good that fills it. For if it were the Good itself, why should it act at all? For other things have their activity around the Good and because of the Good. But the Good needs nothing; therefore, it does not even have itself within itself. When you utter "the Good," F think of nothing further. For if you add anything that does not belong, you will make it deficient. Therefore, do not even add "thinking," so that you do not make it something else, or make it two: mind and the Good. For the mind needs the Good, but the Good does not need the mind. Whence, the mind, according to the Good, becomes "good-like" and is perfected by the Good. That which is as one upon it, as if coming into the Good, produces a "good-like" quality, and the "trace" of the Good is seen in it—by faith—G but the lower thing is by nature such that the true thing happens to it because of the desire for the trace. This trace of itself upon it, it gave to the mind to have while looking upon it. So that, not in the mind alone is the desire, but the desire is always there, and it is always attaining. It is not, therefore, merely "mind"; or rather, the mind is such because of desire and composition, or its understanding toward its own form. You must perceive all that is beautiful, and H entirely beautiful, lying in pure light and pure radiance, and encompassing the nature of all beings, of which this world is a beautiful shadow and arrival, though that other lies in all splendor.

<summary>Plotinus argues that everything in existence can be traced back to a single source, "the One," which is so perfect and primary that it exists beyond being and thought. He explains that the Intellect (the realm of Ideas) is beautiful but ultimately dependent on the Good, which is the "light" that allows the Intellect to see.</summary>

BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Where nothing is devoid of intellect, nothing is dark, nothing is immoderate, but it leads a blessed life within itself. If anyone should behold this, they will immediately be struck with awe—especially if they immerse themselves into it as they ought and come under its authority. Truly, just as one who looks carefully up at the sky and more intently observes the splendor of the stars immediately thinks of and seeks out the author of the world: so also it is necessary for him who contemplates, perceives, and admires the Intelligible World <note>The "Intelligible World" refers to the realm of pure thought and divine forms, which exists before the physical world.</note> to diligently seek out its <margin>B</margin> maker. Who is He that generated such an intelligible world? Or where and how did He generate such a son—an intellect that is both a child and beautiful, a son, I say, full of the father? Yet that highest father is neither the intellect nor the son or child, but is superior to both the intellect and the child. After him come the intellect and the child, needing nourishment and intelligence; for the intellect is the first thing that comes from Him who needs nothing, nor requires intelligence. By its fullness <margin>C</margin> and intelligence, the son possesses truth, because he possesses it primarily. But that which is superior neither lacks nor possesses; otherwise, it would not be the Good itself.
