# THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO ON
## BOOK IX OF THE THIRD ENNEAD REGARDING
### EIGHT CONSIDERATIONS,
#### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->The first proposition: that the author of the world is the first intellect,<-
->the son of the Good itself.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'Q' featuring scrollwork and architectural elements.</image-desc>

QUITE clearly, eight considerations appear in this book. The first concerns the author of the world: where, if one follows the path of Iamblichus and Proclus <note>Iamblichus and Proclus were later Neoplatonic philosophers who created more complex hierarchies of the divine than Plotinus did.</note>, one will explain that saying of the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> regarding the craftsman of the world: namely, that the craftsman of the world conceived as many distinct species in the world as the intellect understands as ideas within the "living itself." I say he will explain it thus: there are at least three divine substances between the first principle (that is, the Good itself) and the world. The first of these, according to its form, is an essence partaking in the Good, and is moreover life, intellect, and cause. The second, according to its form, is life—a partaker of essence, but the formal cause of the intellect. The third, finally, through its form is intellect—a partaker of life, and the cause of the physical world. He will name the first "Heaven" (*Caelum*), the second "Saturn," and the third "Jupiter." He will consider Heaven to be as much superior to Saturn, and Saturn to Jupiter, as essence is superior to and prior to life, and life to intellect. Indeed, essence is superior to life insofar as it spreads itself more widely, and life, due to a similar amplitude, is superior to the mind. He will say, therefore, that the formal intellect, Jupiter, is the immediate maker of the physical world, having within himself the intellectual ideas of worldly things. He received these ideas from the "vital intellect" (Saturn), in whom the ideas are both intellectual and intelligible equally; Saturn, in turn, has them from the "essential intellect" (Heaven), in whom the ideas are solely intelligible. Thus he will interpret the *Timaeus*. The providence of Jupiter devised the making of as many species in the physical world as he observed the intellect of Saturn contemplating as ideas, living in "Heaven" itself—for essence is the cause of life. 

But according to Plotinus, these three are not separate substances; rather, there is only one substance which is named first essence, first life, and first intellect. For the "first life" is nothing other than the innermost and perpetual vigor and act of the first essence and form, most effective of all in acting. The "first intellect" is also a certain reflection of the first life back into itself, standing most firmly with itself. Therefore, Plotinus calls that substance "intellect" and "form." He likewise calls this substance "intellect" insofar as it regards its vital action arising from itself and reflected into itself; and he calls it "thought" in a certain way, since he establishes that what it sees within, it distributes without. Furthermore, he thinks that in the order of things, motion arises before division; finally, he thinks that the entirely immobile intellect, being a flowing motion, cannot be propagated into many "unparticipated" intellects, but that the genus of the soul, being mobile by its own nature, is multiplied into many souls. And since this genus is a partaker of intelligence, for that reason the intellect is propagated into many "participable" intellects <note>Ficino is distinguishing between "unparticipated" (the pure, singular source) and "participated" (the version of that source that individual souls can connect with).</note>, insofar as the genus of the soul is propagated into many species of soul. He also considers that the intellect, as the craftsman of the world, generates the soul—both the World Soul itself, and the remaining common souls of the spheres and stars, and finally the particular souls of demons and men. And since distribution belongs chiefly to the genus of soul as something mobile and multipliable, he therefore wishes that intellect...

### Second Proposition: How the soul can gather itself into its own intel-
### lect, and through this intellect be formed by the divine. There are also 
### in this chapter three other propositions: two concerning the 
### soul, and one concerning God.

The first consideration of this kind was that which declared the intellect to be the world's maker. The second consideration, however, treats how the soul can transfer itself into this universal intellect. Specifically, just as the soul gathers its multiple senses into the single sense of the imagination, so it should gather widely diverse imaginations into a single common rule of reason. Then, it should bring the various wanderings of our reason back to a stable norm of intelligence. Thus, the soul may be formed as much as possible by its own intelligence, through which it will be formed by the universal intellect—the maker of the whole world. It is possible for the soul to become one with these levels, since it is the same "self" throughout these stages of knowledge. Geometry consists of a thousand propositions; from a prior one, a later one is deduced by necessity; therefore, those that follow are contained within those that preceded them, and all are contained in the first. Indeed, our soul, through its rational faculty, moves from potential to actual power. In another way, if it possesses the whole of geometry, it can hold all the propositions without needing a specific habit or potentiality, as long as it holds one of them in "act" <note>In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic terms, "act" or "actuality" (actus) refers to a state of being fully realized or active, as opposed to "potency" (potentia), which is the mere capacity to become something.</note>. Meanwhile, our intellect also, in whatever it considers according to act, considers through that same reason and possesses all things. We must strive, therefore, so that our rational faculty conforms itself to the intellect as much as possible, so that it may behold all following conclusions in the first principle by that same act with which it beholds the first. 

In the third consideration, Plotinus thinks that the soul of the world—because it once and most powerfully embraced the entire animal form of life within itself, and from there completely occupied the whole body and place—cannot change the form of life within itself, nor can it exchange bodies outside itself. He thinks the situation is similar for the souls of the spheres, stars, and all celestial beings, since they have firmly received universal providence from the beginning. However, he considers that particular souls—which have obtained a particular mode of providence, such as the souls of demons <note>Ficino refers to *daemones* in the Greek sense: intermediate spirits or guardian beings, not necessarily "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> and humans—experience that perpetual providence of the higher beings through a kind of change. Insofar as they change from one form of life to another within themselves, they also change the state of their body and their bond with it. Hence, they seem at some point to "approach" the body, but only after a change has already occurred within themselves. In contrast, the body of the world seems to approach the world soul itself. For while that soul remains firmly in its own state, this body is vivified from the start because it was so affected by the soul—just as the translucent region of the air is always illuminated by the sun. Let it be said, however, that particular souls also "descend" at some point from the soul (meaning the world soul), because from the universal providence of the form of life (which they once possessed together with the world soul), they slip into their own private state, for they did not possess that universal state firmly. 

In the fourth consideration, he divides our soul into three forms: the intellectual, the rational, and the irrational. He thinks that the soul is sometimes transferred entirely to its intellectual form and then dwells with the divine intellect; sometimes it descends from there into itself, that is, into the rational form proper to this soul; and sometimes it descends from here into the inferior form of the irrational, which is the pattern for demons—or rather, it communicates directly with the body to which that life is subject. The last of all is the "image" <note>original: *simulachrum*</note>, that is, matter, which the soul (through its vegetative power) forms by its close proximity with a bodily quality and a certain shape. Then, through this affection, it affects this body (which is now disposed in a certain way) as if with a second nature to be vivified. 

In the fifth consideration, he establishes this: just as in a circle there is a point in itself which is the center, and a point in the whole circumference from any of its parts, proceeding from that which is in itself (or rather, which propagates itself into those parts); and just as there is a "oneness" in any number and its parts flowing from a certain Unity outside the number (conceived simply in itself); so in the whole essence of things there is a certain "unity" as a foundation and a preservation of each thing. This proceeds from the Divine Unity, which remains in itself above all essence <note><term>superessentiam</term>: A Neoplatonic term for the "One," which is so pure and primary that it exists "above" or "beyond" the category of Being or Essence.</note>, and yet sends itself into all things. By its presence everywhere, it procreates from itself a certain unity in every created thing—a "super-essential" producer and preserver of every essence. Now, because this unity is more excellent than essence, wherever it is joined, it is created and preserved by the presence of the Divine Unity.

->On our intellect as well, and how it is always in act.<-

The sixth consideration concerns the soul and the mind together, in this manner: the translucent <note>original: *diaphana*</note> nature of the eye, if it comes mostly from the solar nature and therefore naturally desires light, is easily filled with the light of the sun. Similarly, a translucent nature in heaven proceeds from a certain celestial light which, according to the order of the universe, precedes the translucent and emanates from the intellect and the light. And as soon as the translucent emanates, the producer fills the product; hence the heaven becomes, as it were, a "celestial eye" of the soul, providing for all things through the translucent and the light together. In the same way, the divine mind generates the rational soul by its own light, as if it were a translucent matter beneath that light, and fills it with perpetual light. By this light, the soul always understands both itself (as illuminated by the mind) and the mind (as always illuminating). Indeed, our intellect—the "head" of the soul—does this perpetually. Our rational faculty, however, relates to this intellect just as sight relates to light: not always, but sometimes, the rational faculty acts in an intellectual way. Therefore, when a human understands themselves through reason, if they understand perfectly, they recognize that they are a thinking being; thus, they possess an intellectual nature. This "intellectuality" itself is a kind of intelligence, not so much placed in obvious motion as in a state hidden from us. Indeed, through rational intelligence, the contemplator understands that before "intellectuality" there is life and essence within themselves, which the intellectuality later joins as an "act"—an act, I say, born from a certain fruitfulness of essence and life. Hence, it is necessary that this essence and life be, in themselves, a certain more eminent intelligence. Plotinus here proves that the soul, from its self-knowledge, must first have an eternal knowledge of itself, by which essence and life are fruitful; therefore, it holds the "intelligible things" <note>The "intelligibles" are the Platonic Forms or Ideas that the mind grasps as truth.</note> within itself in a perpetually understood form. The "discourse of reason" is a kind of image of this intelligence when it reaches its peak; whence it is also called intelligence. We confirm the same thing in another way: there are three things in the order of reality that come to our knowledge: a certain singular thing (this specific man), the species shared by individuals (man), and the Idea of man above the individuals. Since these three differ in a certain essential order from prior to posterior, as—

### ON BOOK IX. ENNEAD III.

properly knowing, these things differ among themselves in a similar way: the **imagination** judges what is singular <note>original: "singulare"; referring to specific, individual objects perceived by the senses</note>, while **reason** collects and distinguishes the species <note>original: "speciem"; the general category or "kind" shared by individuals</note> common to individuals, and the **intellect** recognizes the **Idea** <note>original: "ideam"; the eternal, divine archetype that exists before the physical object</note>. Since the Idea differs further from the species (outside of which it exists) than the species differs from the individual (in which it is preserved), the intellect is therefore more distant from reason than reason is from imagination. The stability of the intellect exists within the soul; otherwise, the soul could not divine that Ideas exist through reason, unless reason performed this through a power granted to us by the intellect. And because reason refers individual things to the universal, and the body to the incorporeal, without the help of our imagination—indeed, even when imagination is unwilling and pulls back toward the opposite—it therefore understands by a certain movement of argument. Reason always gazes upon the Ideas, and I say "always." For if it does not reach them by way of argument through the imagination, then the intellect <note>original: "nous"; the Greek term for divine mind or intellect</note> either never reaches them or possesses them always. Fittingly, the soul becomes a medium between eternity and time: for its essence is fixed (and precedes the motion that depends upon it). It is consubstantial <note>sharing the same essential nature</note> that its essence be fixed, from the very sign by which it precedes motion; a certain power is present within it that is entirely immobile and steadfastly watching. Indeed, since this gaze toward essence—tending from a stable power toward an entirely stable Idea—claims stability for itself on both sides. Therefore, just as a mobile imagination is suited to the soul from that which is under eternity, so an immobile acting intellect is suited to it from that which is above time. The act of the intellect is entirely immobile; the act of the imagination is entirely mobile; and finally, the act of reason is mixed. The soul could not be a fitting medium for the universe unless it possessed these things within itself.

### How God is above motion, rest, and knowledge. Also concerning that which is in act, and that which is in potential.

The seventh consideration proves that in the first principle of all things there is no motion, not even a flowing one, nor even a metaphorical one, which is an act tending toward something else. For that which is entirely first and last does not tend toward another. Because of this, "rest" exists there—namely, the quiet toward which motion tends, as opposed to movement. Yet, it does not truly rest in "another" (since it is not moved toward another), nor does it properly rest "in itself" (since it is simplicity itself). For in the first principle, no such distinction falls, by which a "resting thing" is usually distinguished both from "rest" itself and from the "place" in which it rests. It has even less to do with "state" <note>original: "statu"; a condition of standing or stability</note>, for while it keeps its course of motion and power from stability, "state" comes from unity. For to "stand" is nothing other than to preserve one's own unity. The First, therefore, precedes both motion and state. It precedes even the act of intelligence, which is a movement from the <term>potentiality</term> <note>the capacity to become something</note> of understanding toward the "true intelligible" as a good. In every thinking being, even if it understands itself, such a distinction is considered; but in the First, there is no absolute distinction. Finally, the logic of existence is one thing, and the logic of intelligence is entirely another. For not everything that exists also understands. If intelligence were added to the first principle of existence, it would become a composite, and it would be clear that existence itself was not sufficient for its own perfection, since it would have required intelligence to move toward progress.

In the eighth consideration, you will note that the condition of formal <term>act</term> <note>original: "actus"; the state of being fully realized or in operation</note> and formable potentiality are opposed to one another: so much so that this potentiality receives the act, but the act, by the very reason that it is act, does not receive potentiality. Where there is act alone—as in the First—the thing is everlasting, since no potentiality for another form lies hidden there. Likewise, where the entire formal potentiality has been translated into the nature of the form, so that the form there is in no way pulled back to the nature of potentiality, the thing is also everlasting. This is especially true because the potentiality there possesses as much as can possibly be sought or had; such are the intellectual essences and the celestial fire. Fire beneath the heavens, among the lower things, is more perfect insofar as it is most "in act": which is apparent from the pouring out of its form, and from its perpetual motion, and because it does not tolerate being mixed. But because it has matter beneath the act, and is not content with it, it is not forever.

In the ninth consideration, remember that intelligence itself is not chosen for its own sake. For one chooses to know in order to know well and happily, and because it will be as a "good" that is profitable to you. Likewise, the Good itself does not have a "recognition of itself," both because this recognition is one thing and the Good itself another, and because if it is sufficient to itself before recognition, recognition should not be added; if it were not sufficient, it would not be the Good itself. In what way God is neither blind nor ignorant—even if "knowledge" is not added to Him (above which Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher who argued that God is beyond all human categories, including "being" and "knowledge."</note> also places Him)—we shall explain more opportunely in the fifth or sixth Ennead.

<margin>
This world is that first intellect; it consists plainly of what is infused into the earth, etc. See 1: <unclear>corrected</unclear> Plotinus.
</margin>

The Mind (as written in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the creation of the universe</note>) gazes upon the Ideas implanted in that which is the "Living Being" <note>original: "vivens"; referring to the divine, archetypal model of all life</note>. Hence, the Architect <note>original: "artifex"; the Demiurge or craftsman who builds the universe</note> of the world is said to have intended to include in this physical world those things which the Mind contemplates in that which is the "Living Being" or "Animal." Does he not then ask: are the forms <note>original: "species"; the eternal patterns</note> already above the Mind, and does the Mind look upon them as things already existing?

<margin>B</margin>
In the first place, therefore, that which is called the "Living Being" or "Animal" itself must be investigated, to see whether it might not be the Intellect, but something different from the Intellect. For that which contemplates is the Intellect; therefore, we shall call the "Living Being" itself not the Intellect, but rather the "Intelligible" <note>term: Intelligible; that which is the object of thought or can only be perceived by the mind</note>, and we shall say that the Intellect holds what it perceives outside of itself. Yet if this were so, the Intellect would possess only certain images of things, not the true things themselves—if indeed the truth is displayed there. For Plato says that truth is also there, namely in Being itself, where each thing truly reigns. <margin>C</margin> Perhaps, however, although both are different, they are not separated from each other, but only distinct in the sense that one is not the other. 

Furthermore, nothing prevents both from existing as a single unity—as far as the words are concerned—divided only by the act of intelligence. For it holds itself only as Being, and that is partly the Intelligible, and partly also the Intelligent <note>the thinker and the thought</note>. Where it is said that the Intellect gazes upon the Ideas, it does not mean it looks at them in something else, but that it possesses the Intelligible within itself. Or perhaps nothing prevents <margin>D</margin> the Intelligible itself from also being the Intellect, but in a state of rest, unity, and silence. By its nature, the "looking" Intellect—the one that observes—is an act emanating from that resting Intellect, looking back toward its source? And while it looks toward it as if emerging from it, it exists as its Intellect insofar as it understands it. And while it understands it, both the Intellect and the Intelligible exist in another way, because it imitates the original? 

From this, therefore, comes what the Creator devises <margin>E</margin>—to make the four kinds of living creatures in this world based on what he perceives there. Yet there Plato seems to introduce the act of "devising" in a certain hidden way, as if it were distinct from those other two. To others, it will seem that these three exist as one: the Living Being itself, the Intellect, and the one who devises. Or perhaps, as in many cases, Plato proposes it one way, while the reader understands the three to exist in another? Now, two have been spoken of: but what is this third?
<meta>catchword: What</meta>

<column-break/>

Sometimes he says that the Mind sees those Ideas in that which is the "Living Being." Then he says the Creator <note>original: "δημιουργὸς" (demiurge)</note> devised that whatever the Mind sees in the Living Being, this universe should also have. But does he mean that the forms <note>original: "εἴδη" (eide)</note> already exist in that Being, and that the Mind perceives them as already existing? 

First, we must speak of that "Living Being" and seek whether it is not the Mind, but something else. For that which contemplates is Mind; therefore, we shall say that the "Living Being" itself is not Mind, but the Intelligible. And if the Mind holds the things it contemplates outside of itself, it would then have only images and not the true realities, if the truths are indeed there. For he says the truth is there in Being, which is each thing itself. Or are both different, yet not separate from each other? Perhaps they are different only in their "otherness," since nothing prevents them from being both one, yet divided in thought. For if it is only as Being, it is either as Being or as the Living Being. For the specific thing, which he says is one in another, is actually in itself, by having the Intelligible within itself. 

Or perhaps nothing prevents the Intelligible itself from also being Mind, except that it is in a state of standing, silence, or quietude. But he says the one proceeding from it is the "one who sees"—just as the Mind within itself is a certain activity from that source, or as much as that source is. And seeing that source, it becomes a sort of reflection of those things, because it understands that source. And in understanding that source, the Mind and the Intelligible are again different by way of imitation. This is the "devising" part: that what it sees there, it should now make into the four kinds of living beings in the world. 

Indeed, the act of "devising" seems to be introduced secretly as something different from those other two. But to others it seems these three are the same: the Living Being itself, the Mind, and the Deviser. Or perhaps, as he offers it differently in many places, one might understand the three to be different. Two have been mentioned: but what is the third which...

# BOOK NINE.

The judge <note>original: ὁ δικαστὴς; likely referring to the Demiurge or the Mind as the ordering principle</note> labors upon the things seen within the Living Being <note>original: ἐν τῶ ζώω; referring to the Intelligible Living Being, the source of all forms</note>, to work, to create, and to divide. Is it not a wonderful thing that, in one sense, the Mind is the divider, yet in another sense, the Mind is not the one doing the dividing? For either the divider is the Mind itself, acting upon the things divided; or the Mind remains undivided, and the things proceeding from it are divided—these being the souls. In this case, it is the Soul that has divided itself into many souls. For he <note>Plato</note> does not say that the division belongs to the third <note>referring to the third principle, the Soul</note> in the sense that it was already split, which is not the work of the Mind, but rather the function of a Soul possessing a divisible activity within things that are divisible by nature.

Just as a single whole science is divided into individual theorems or powers, so too might we ask: is it by a shared experience? Is the whole present in each power, or is it the same in the beginning and the end? Or must one model it after the principles within itself, or its end? How and in what way do all things lead toward the best of nature? The "best" for each thing is to exist as it is, even if each is deceived; is this within the soul, or does it come from there, or not even from there? Or is it not so, but rather that the body, having come into being, participated in the soul, which is why the soul is not in the body? Nor does Plato ever say that the bodies are within it [the soul]. But they say souls transition: they come from the Soul. And again, they go back and change. Nor could they be from anywhere else, if the Soul is naturally from above. But if he says the whole is like that which is closest to the limit, then the soul that divided itself is illuminated; further, he claims it is a protector. For whatever souls there are, those with them come into the proximity of its nearness. How then is it better? The part that stays with it needs no instruction. Therefore, like something fated, it moves in an indefinite way. And then the image <note>original: εἴδωλον; a phantom or reflection</note> is unclear, entirely dark. For it is irrational, or entirely mindless, and much of what exists seems so. How then, from the middle, are its own things—these images—formed? Like an unseen strike, the image took shape, and everything else comes as they are.

How then does a multitude come from the One? Because the One is everywhere. For the realm there is everywhere. Therefore, the things there are many. For not even all forms are in one. While it remains everywhere, all things are with it; since all things do not fail because of it. Is it everywhere, or most beautifully raised up? And the things under it? Again, he is not himself everywhere, nor does he stay everywhere, but he is immediately everywhere still, concerning which there is no <insert>place that exists</insert>. The inclinations of them going... <insert>and all species.</insert> everything; for if because that exists, it were to be, it would not be because of itself.

**B** through a partition, and in the third, to which the duty of thought has been assigned: however, thought is not the duty of the Mind, but the gift of the Soul, which possesses a divisible action within a divisible nature.

<margin>
II.
This contains three considerations regarding the soul: how it ascends to God, and how it descends to the body.
</margin>
**C** Therefore, just as a single whole science is distributed into individual propositions or notions, yet is not cut or pulled apart into segregated portions, but each part possesses the whole in potentiality, where the beginning and the end are the same: so indeed one ought to compare oneself, so that the principles and ends implanted in oneself are the whole; and finally, all things are reduced into the best of its nature. For when each person has escaped to this, he already dwells there—namely, in this best part of himself—and when he has already insinuated himself, he immediately touches that as well. The universal Soul was never "made," nor did it "proceed": for there was nowhere it could proceed to; but the nearest
**D** and the body, having been created, participated in it. And therefore the soul is not in the body: nor did Plato say so anywhere; rather, the body is added into the soul. But the other souls have a place from which they come: for they come from the Soul itself. They have, moreover, a place to which they descend and pass through: they also have a place from which they return. But the Soul of the whole always inhabits the higher region, where the nature of the soul itself tends to be. Because the universe is willing, it is quickened by this underlying proximity, just
**E** as a transparent body placed under the Sun is illuminated. A particular soul is indeed illustrated when it flees to the higher realm: for then it encounters it there. But when it slips to the lower realm, it falls into non-being: it does this when it descends into itself. For, affecting to receive itself from on high into itself, it already makes that which follows after it its own—namely, its image <note>original: simulachrum</note>, which we also call non-being. For it falls, as it were, through the void and ends up in an indeterminate state. And the
**F** image of this image is indefinite, and entirely obscure. For it is completely devoid of all rational and intellectual nature, and is most distantly removed from Being itself. In the meantime, however, it inhabits its domestic seat as if through the middle: but looking again at the lower things, as if by a second glance of the eyes, it makes an image, and, delighted by this craftsmanship, it enters into it.

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. III.

<margin>A</margin> ...furthermore, nowhere else: for it is necessary that the law <note>original: "ius"; in this context, the governing principle or necessity of nature</note> be one through all things. For this reason, it is necessary for it to fill and create all things, yet it is not all these things which it creates. Furthermore, the soul itself must be as if it were sight, and the Mind <note>original: "mens" / "νοῦς"; the divine Intellect which contains all true forms</note> must be the visible object for it: sight, I say, which is indeterminate before it sees, but is born for seeing and understanding, being of such a nature that it serves as matter <note>The Soul acts as "matter" or a receptive medium for the "form" provided by the Mind</note> for the Mind. When we understand ourselves, we look upon our own understanding nature: otherwise, we would be lying about the act of understanding. <margin>B</margin> If therefore we understand, and we understand ourselves, we surely understand a nature that exists intellectually. For this reason, before this active understanding, there is another understanding that is, as it were, quiet: for there is an understanding of essence, and an understanding of life; therefore, before this, there is another certain essence and life. These things, then, have moved whatever things are acts. But if the intellects themselves are acts, thus constituting themselves in the act of understanding, we truly possess the intelligible <margin>C</margin> within ourselves. Our understanding, however, bears only an image. The first principle of all is the power of both motion and rest: and therefore it exists above these. But that which is second <note>The Intellect/Mind</note> rests around the First, and is moved. To this second principle belongs the Mind. For existing as one thing, it directs its understanding toward another: but that First One does not possess understanding. For that which is understanding is already twofold <note>original: "duplex"; because thinking requires a subject who thinks and an object being thought of</note>, and understands itself: and for this reason it is even needy <margin>D</margin>, because it possesses its own good not in its simple substance, but in the act of understanding. With that which is in act, there corresponds that which proceeds from potentiality into act: which is indeed always the same, so long as it exists. For this reason, it is likewise perfect: and a thing of this kind also belongs to bodies, such as fire, yet it cannot exist forever because it is joined with matter. But that which is pure act, and is not a composite, exists forever. Moreover, that which is in act can also <margin>E</margin> be in potentiality according to something else: but not even the gods in the heights, leaning toward beings, are the First itself: for the Mind is the realm of beings, where there is both motion and rest. Now, however, the First itself is not occupied with anything else, but all other things remain resting around it, and are moved. For motion is a desire <note>original: "appetitio" / "ἔφεσις"; a reaching out or longing for completion</note>, but that First One desires nothing. For what should that which is the highest desire? Will it therefore not even understand itself? <margin>F</margin> Perhaps by the very reason that it possesses itself, it is said in a general sense to understand. Perhaps even more so, not because it looks back at itself as its primary object. For this action is primary and is understanding itself. If therefore this is primary, there must be nothing prior to it. That which provides this understanding, therefore, exists above it: thus, understanding follows after that First. For understanding is not the thing to be primarily venerated. Nor is just any understanding to be venerated, but only the understanding of the Good: therefore, the Good itself is above understanding. Will it not then even perceive itself? What then? Is it the Good before it perceives itself? Or is it not yet the Good? For if it is the Good, it is already the Good before its perception: but if perception makes it the good, then it is not the Good before this perception: for which reason—

<column-break/>

—in this way, or nowhere, because it is necessary for the one to be over all. It must therefore fill itself and make all things: not being all the things it makes. The soul again must be as sight, and the mind must be visible to it: being indeterminate before seeing, but having a nature to think: being as matter unto the mind. We see our own calculating nature, or we would be deceived about thinking. If then we think, and think ourselves, we think a nature that is intellectual. Before this thinking, therefore, there is another thinking, as if quiet: for thinking is of essence and of life. So before this life and essence, there is another essence and life. These then it saw, as many as are acts; if it saw the acts according to the thinking of themselves. We are the truly intelligible, and there <unclear>***</unclear> their thinking carries the image. The first is the power of motion and rest, as being something beyond these. But the second stands and moves around that one. And the mind is about the second. For being something else, it has its thinking toward another: but that does not have thinking. For that which has thinking also thinks itself and is deficient, because it has its "well-being" in thinking and not in its standing-under <note>original: "ὑποστάσει" (hypostasis); its underlying reality or substance</note>. To that which is in act, which comes from potentiality to act, which is always upon this as long as it exists, as something perfect, this also belongs to bodies: as to fire, but it cannot always be, because it is with matter. But that which is simply heat in act, is always. Since the same thing being act, can be in potentiality according to another: but the gods being beyond those things, the mind is the beings, and there is motion already there, and rest. Again, the first itself is nothing [of these], but the others are resting around it and are moved. For motion is desire: but that desires nothing. For what does the highest desire, or does it not even [think] itself? Or that which it has, is entirely called so, or to have itself is called thinking, but by looking toward the first. And this is the first act, and this is thinking. If then this is first, none must be before it. That which provides this, then, is beyond this: so that thinking is second after that. For if the primarily venerable thing is thinking, it would not be every thinking, but that of the good. Therefore the Good is beyond thinking. But will it not follow itself? What? Will it not follow itself being the good? Or we truly know, that the Good is about this following. But if the following makes it so, the Good would not be before this: Or will it not even think itself? What then? Or is it not yet good before thinking itself? Or is it the Good itself? For if it is good, it is the Good even before the thinking. But if the following makes it so, the Good would not be before this:

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic hierarchy, arguing that the Mind (Intellect) is a "second" principle because thinking requires a subject and an object, whereas the "Good" or the "One" is a simple unity that exists above thought and desire.</summary>

BOOK NINE

<note>original Greek: "ὡς τί ἐδ' αὐτῇ ἔσαι..."</note> For what would be in it, if it were not the Good? What then, does it live? Or must we say it does not live, if indeed it is the source that grants life? But to observe itself and to understand itself is a secondary thing: for it follows, or rather, life is present to itself through this activity. It is necessary, therefore, that if it apprehends itself, it must have happened to be unapprehended by itself, and to be deficient in its own nature, but to be made perfect by the act of thinking. Therefore, the act of thinking must be removed from it. For any addition creates a removal and a deficiency.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Otherwise, it would not be the Good itself, since it would not be of the Good. What then? Does it not even live? Perhaps it should not be said to live, if indeed it grants life itself. As for the fact that it observes and understands itself, that holds the second rank: for it observes itself so that, by such an act, it might cling to itself. It must be, therefore, that if it apprehends itself, it happened in some way that it did not apprehend itself at all, and that it is imperfect by its own nature, but is perfected by the act of understanding. Self-apprehension must therefore be removed from the <margin>B</margin> Good itself: for every addition brings about a removal and a deficiency. <note>Plotinus argues that the "One" or "The Good" is so simple and perfect that it does not even need "thought," because thought implies a division between the thinker and the thing thought of.</note>

# MARSILIO FICINO’S COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST AND SECOND BOOKS OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD, CONCERNING THE SOUL.
## SUMMARY OF THE BOOKS.

->The primary Intellect <note>original: "Intellectus"; in Neo-Platonism, this is the Divine Mind or 'Nous,' the first emanation from the One</note> belongs to the first essence, from which and in which other intellects always exist. Likewise, how the soul is simultaneously individual and divisible.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'Q' containing a human face in profile, framed within a circular border with foliate motifs.</image-desc>

*Since we have discussed elsewhere at greater length what Plotinus treats here concerning the soul—especially in the first, third, and seventh books of our "Platonic Theology"—we will touch upon it briefly here. Generation always strives toward being: first toward bare existence, then toward living existence, then toward what is called sensory existence, and finally toward intellectual existence as the highest peak. When the intellectual soul descends into commerce with the body, such is truly the order of essence or being acquired in the stages of generation. Above this order stands the order of essence in the eternal ranks of the universe, in which simple Intellect itself holds the highest place as the principle. From this, the animal soul, descending in generation, holds the highest place in the whole order of generation as its end—not indeed made simply by generation, but adapted to the body to fulfill the providence of the whole. However, simple Intellect is everywhere whole: and in it, souls exist not only through Ideas, but also through their own (so to speak) intellectual existences, according to the intellectual faculty proper to them, even while they are in the body. Just as lines drawn from a center to a circumference do not depart from the center while they touch the circumference, and as rays do not leave the sun while they touch the earth; and just as lines and rays projecting outward are distant from one another in space, yet are together in space at the very principle. So too, the souls among us, according to their bodies or their roles as givers, are all together in the same place according to the intellect in the divine Mind: though they are different from one another according to your individual intellects, just as the ends of lines and rays are different from each other even where they touch the center and the sun. From this, Plotinus concludes that the intellect of a prophetic man, being abstracted, might seem to be only in the East, yet it may perceive things in the West, and from one certain place perform something miraculous in another, moving others by his thought and affection. This is because all intellects are in one another and are everywhere, since they are always in the simple divine Mind, which is always present everywhere in its entirety. By this presence, God perceives prayers, and men may converse most familiarly with God. He also holds that such intellects are the "familiar spirits" <note>original: "dæmones"; here referring to guiding spirits or tutelary geniuses</note> of men, assigned as constant leaders, one to each person. For external spirits perhaps cannot be so closely applied to individual men. He judges that Plato, when he says in the Timaeus that the soul is composed of a certain individual essence and also one that is divisible around bodies, understood the "first essence" to be the intellectual power of the soul, which never declines toward bodies; and the "second essence" to be that nature of the soul which adapts itself entirely to the body, yet is meanwhile called individual. For the soul joined to the body, however much the members of the body are distant from one another, is not distant from itself: since it is the same whole in any member. He states that both faculties of the soul are held in this way, both in our soul and in the Soul of the World. Furthermore, since he says the intellect of both the world and of man is present to all members of its body, and likewise the divine intellect is present to all parts of the world, why is it not said to be divided through the body? Because any intellect grants nothing to the body by its presence except through the soul; thus it seems to be present "at" it rather than "in" it. Moreover, the intellect remains equal in any portion of the body, appearing entirely undivided. The soul, however, exercises one of its powers in this member and another in that, adapting life, sense, and motion through various degrees to the members of its body; thus it seems divided in some way within the body. In the second book here concerning the soul, you will note that Aristotelian <term>Entelechy</term> <note>original: "Entelechiam"; Aristotle's term for the "actualization" or "perfection" of a thing—here, the soul as the "act" of the body</note>, by which the soul is called the act and perfection of the body, can be understood even in Aristotle not only as a form and soul inseparable from the body, but also as that which is separable from the body. Therefore, you should consider that what is properly "divided" is divided in substance; but what is "moved" can indeed be moved properly according to its accidents, qualities, and modes, while meanwhile the substance remains. Therefore, substance is affected and harmed by division rather than by motion. Since in the very descent of things, good begins from the highest and evil from the least, we rightly find things that are properly "more movable" before we find things properly "divisible" as we descend. Therefore, below the divine Intellect, which is both entirely individual and immobile, we find the indivisible soul, which is nonetheless properly movable; then we find bodily form and quality, which is everywhere movable and divided. Finally, there is the body, which is the origin of this division and, being inert, is moved from elsewhere.*

<summary>This page concludes Plotinus's argument that the ultimate "Good" transcends even thought and life, then introduces Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on the soul's nature. Ficino explains how the soul remains unified in the Divine Mind while simultaneously animating and appearing divided within the physical body.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino, Enneads, Soul, Intellect, Entelechy, Divine Mind, Plato's Timaeus, Aristotle, hierarchy of being, emanation</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the preceding philosophical discussion on the nature of "The One" or "The Good" into the Fourth Ennead of Plotinus. While the previous page focused on the absolute simplicity of the divine source, this page introduces the Fourth Ennead, which centers on the Soul. It includes a commentary by Marsilio Ficino (the 15th-century philosopher who translated these works into Latin) summarizing the hierarchy of existence and an index of the books contained within this Ennead.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.</header>

When we say that the soul is "divisible," we do not speak in a strict sense—as we would of a physical body or even a quality—but rather in an improper sense. We mean that it is not divided into sections like a body is, but that it adapts itself to a moving body, distributing its powers, acts, and gifts differently to different members. You should note, meanwhile, that the physical mass and bodily form, which are by nature entirely prone to scattering, can only be held together in us and in the universe by the soul. This soul is not equally divided, but is present as a whole in every single part. Likewise, the World Soul, insofar as it contains a multitude of powers and forms within itself, is in a certain way mobile and adapted to give life to the body of the world. I say "adapted" by the divine mind itself, which is entirely immobile, yet holds a multitude of forms within it. Though in the Soul of the world unity reigns and an eminent simplicity flourishes, all things are governed from that source by a certain intellectual and wise reason. We can conclude that there are five levels of reality here:
1. **The Good itself**: which is purely One in itself.
2. **The Divine Mind**: which is "One-Many" <note>original: "vnum, multa" — a Neoplatonic concept where the mind is a single entity containing many distinct ideas.</note>.
3. **The Soul (both of the world and our own)**: which is "One and Many."
4. **Corporeal quality and form**: which is "Many and One."
5. **The mass of the body**: which is no longer considered "One" in itself, but "Many."
The remaining points are explained in the *Theology* <note>Ficino likely refers to his own major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>, as we have said.

# PLOTINUS
## FOURTH ENNEAD,
### BOOK I.

->ON THE <term>Essence of the Soul</term> <note>original Greek: "οὐσίας Ψυχῆς" (ousias Psyches)</note>.<-
->On the essence of the soul, in summary.<-

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>The first of the <term>entelechies</term> <note>A term for the "actualization" or "perfection" of a thing.</note> is the primary essence, in which the intellect is always in act. Also, the manner in which the soul becomes soul: being one and divisible at the same time.</margin>

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'I' featuring intricate floral and vine-like scrolling patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
In the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the realm of pure thought and forms, beyond the physical senses.</note>, true essence reigns, and its most excellent part is the intellect. Souls are also present there, for from that place they came here into the world. That world indeed holds souls without bodies; but here, they are already implanted in bodies and divided among them. In that higher realm, all intellect is together, neither discrete nor divided; and all souls are together in one world, suffering no distance from any interval of space. Therefore, the intellect is always undivided and inseparable, but the soul in that realm lives undivided and inseparable, yet possesses a nature capable of a certain division.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'E' mirroring the style of the Latin column, with elaborate foliate scrollwork inside a rectangular border.</image-desc>
In the intelligible world is the true essence, and its best part: the mind. Souls are there also, for they come from there. And that world has souls without bodies, but here, they have come to be in bodies and are divided by those bodies. There, all mind is together, not separated nor divided; and all souls are together as one in the world, not in a separation of places. Mind, then, is always undivided and not partitioned; but the soul there is both undivided and unpartitioned, yet it has a nature to be divided.

<summary>This page introduces the Fourth Ennead of Plotinus, focused on the Soul, and provides an index of its nine books. Ficino’s commentary outlines a five-tier hierarchy of reality, moving from the absolute unity of "The Good" down to the pure multiplicity of physical matter.</summary>
<keywords>Enneads, Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino, World Soul, Intelligible World, Entelechy, Neoplatonism, Essence of the Soul, Divisibility</keywords>

--- Page 396 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general introduction of the Fourth Ennead—which focuses on the nature and descent of the Soul—into the second book of that Ennead. The text continues the technical discussion of how the soul can be both "divided" among many bodies while remaining "undivided" in its own essence, transitioning from a commentary or concluding thought into the formal opening of the second treatise.</meta>

**BOOK TWO.**

For the very act of division is to be absent from that higher realm and to exist within bodies. Therefore, the soul is rightly said to be "divisible" in relation to bodies, because in this way it departs or is partitioned. How then is it also "undivided"? Either it has not departed as a whole, or there is something of it that has not descended, which is by nature impossible to divide. Therefore, what is said to be "from the undivided" or "from the divisible around bodies" is the same thing: it is the soul’s descent from the higher and lower vision <note>original: "κορης" — literally 'pupil' of the eye, but used here metaphorically for the soul's power of sight or focal point</note>, being suspended from that higher source, like a flow or a portion extending out, much like a line extending from a center point. Having come here, it sees through this part, yet even with this part it preserves the nature of the whole. For even here it is not merely divisible, but also undivided; for the part of it that is divided is divided in an undivided way. Indeed, it gives itself to the body as a whole, yet it is said to be divided because it is present as a whole in every single part of the whole.

<column-break/>

**A** For its partitioning consists in being absent and distant from that higher realm and being joined to bodies. For this reason, it is not wrongly said to be divisible in relation to bodies. For in this way it is absent and distant, and admits some degree of partitioning. In what way, then, is it also indivisible? It does not depart from that higher realm in its entirety, but some part of it remains above which does not come to the lower things, whose nature can undergo no partitioning. Therefore, what is said in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the world and the soul.</note>—that the soul is composed of a nature divisible among **B** bodies—is the same as saying that the soul consists of a certain essence that partly remains among the higher beings and partly inclines toward the lower things. This essence simultaneously hangs from that source and meanwhile propagates itself down to these lower things, not unlike a line stretched out from a center. Having proceeded to these things through this further part, it clearly preserves the nature of the whole: for even here it is not only partible but also impartible; for that which is said to be divided into parts within it is, in a certain way, divided in an undivided manner. For by pouring itself through the whole body, it is not truly divided, because it is whole throughout the whole; yet, because it is in the whole, it is said to be divided.

# OF PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FOUR,
### BOOK II.

### CONCERNING the essence of the Soul; a treatise which ought to be read before all other discourses on the Soul.
#### On the essence of the soul.

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' within a square frame, depicting a robed figure seated in a high-backed chair, gesturing with hands as if teaching.</image-desc>
**A** SEEKING what the nature of the Soul might be, and having already shown that it is not a body, let us now harmonize it with the incorporeal. Let us set aside the question of whether it is an "entelechy" <note>original: "εντελεχείας" — a term from Aristotle meaning the 'actuality' or 'perfection' of a body.</note> in the true sense as it is commonly said, or if that term truly declares what the soul is. And though we have said it belongs to the intelligible nature and the divine portion, we might perhaps have already brought something clear to light regarding its essence. Nevertheless, it is better to proceed further. We previously made a distinction between the sensible and the intelligible nature, placing the Soul within the intelligible. Now, however, let us investigate whether it is in the intelligible realm, but pursue the specific property of its nature by another path. We say, then, that some things are **C** primarily divisible and by their own nature subject to dissipation; these are things of which no part <margin>*the same.*</margin> is the same as another part or the whole: for their part is necessarily smaller than the whole. These things are the sensible magnitudes <note>Physical sizes and dimensions.</note>.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' within a square frame, filled with dense scrolling foliate patterns and floral motifs.</image-desc>
<margin>It is necessary for the soul to be intermediate between the intellect and the body; likewise, the soul is whole in every part of the body. Again, concerning the levels of the universe.</margin>
**IF**, in seeking what the essence of the soul might be, we have shown that it is neither a body nor, on the other hand, an "attunement" <note>original: "harmoniā" — the theory that the soul is just a balance of physical parts.</note> among incorporeal things; and likewise, if we have set aside what is said concerning the "entelechy"—that is, the soul as a certain act and perfection of the body—as being (as the words sound) not at all true and not declaring what the soul itself is. **B** Furthermore, if we have affirmed that it is of an intelligible nature and a divine lot, we have perhaps brought something manifest concerning its essence into the open; yet it is worthwhile to progress further. Now, therefore, since a distinction has been made between sensible and intelligible nature, and the soul itself has been placed in the intelligible world, let us in the present moment consider it as placed in that world, but let us track down the proper characteristic of this nature by another way. We say, therefore, that some things **C** are primarily divisible and by their very nature subject to scattering: such things are those in which no part is the same as another part or the whole, and in which a part is necessarily smaller than every whole. Such things are surely sensible magnitudes.

H

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the beginning of Book Two of the Fourth Ennead. Having established that the soul is both divisible and indivisible, Plotinus now explores the nature of physical matter versus spiritual essence to explain how the soul acts as a bridge between the two.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV. ###

<margin>A</margin>...and masses <note>original: "moles," referring to physical bulk or material bodies</note>, each of which occupies its own place, and it is not possible for the same thing to exist in several places at the same time. But there is another kind of essence <note>original: "essentia," translating the Greek "ousia" — the fundamental reality of a thing</note> conversely opposed to this one, which is in no way subject to partitioning; it is devoid of parts and therefore indivisible. It does not admit any interval <note>spatial extension</note> even in thought; it does not require a place, nor is it contained within any other things, whether by parts or as a whole. Rather, it rests upon all things at once, not as if supported by them, <margin>B</margin> but because other things are neither able nor willing to exist apart from it. This essence always maintains itself in the same state. It is the firmament of all things that follow it in order, acting like a center in a circle from which all lines are drawn continuously to the circumference, yet the center itself is permitted to remain at rest within itself. These lines have their origin and being from the center and participate in that point; the indivisible is the principle for all of them, and though they proceed from it, the center remains internally harmonious.

<margin>C</margin> Since, therefore, this is the primary indivisible thing and is chief in the order of intelligible beings, and since there is also that which is entirely divisible in the order of sensible things, there exists another nature above the sensible—near it and within it—which is indeed divisible, but not primarily so like bodies. Instead, it becomes divisible within these bodies. Thus, when bodies are cut, the species <note>form or specific nature</note> within them is cut simultaneously, yet it remains in some way a whole in each of the divided parts. <margin>D</margin> I say that the same species now becomes many, each of which is entirely distant from the other; for the species has become entirely divisible, just as colors and all qualities are, or any form that can be present as a whole in many distant things at once, having no part that experiences the same thing as another part. Therefore, this must be considered entirely divisible. <margin>E</margin> Furthermore, beyond that utterly indivisible nature, there is another essence born next from it, which possesses an indivisible duty from its source, but by a certain progression from there, it hastens toward the other nature. It emerges as a medium between both: that is, between the primary impartible nature and the divisible nature that is found around and inherent in bodies. <margin>F</margin> It does not behave exactly like color or every quality, which fill many spaces at once and exist as the same in many physical masses; for the quality in one part is entirely distant from the quality in another part, just as one mass is distant from another. And although the magnitude is one, that which is called the "same" in individual parts has no communion of shared feeling <note>original: "compatiendum," a translation of the Greek "sympatheia"</note>, because this "same" thing is actually one thing here and another there. For this "sameness" is a mere property <note>original: "passio"</note>, not the essence itself. <margin>G</margin> But that which we say exists in this nature according to the indivisible essence, and which proceeds from it, is itself an essence. It joins with bodies, through which it also happens to be divided; yet it does not suffer this until it gives itself to the bodies. When it is present in bodies, even if it is present in the most widely distant parts, it nonetheless adapts itself as a unity—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Those things which, even if conjoined, each has its own place; and it is not possible for the same thing to be the same in several places. But there is another essence opposed to this, not accepting division in any way, being partless and indivisible. It does not admit any extension, even in the mind; it does not need place, nor does it come to be in any of the things that exist by parts or by wholes. It is like that which lies upon all things together, not as if <margin>B</margin> established under them, but because the other things are not able to exist apart from it; nor do they wish to. Again, the things that follow it are judged sequentially, like a center in a circle, from which all the lines reaching to the circumference are suspended. They leave the center to itself, yet they have their origin and being from it; they participate in the point, and we say that the indivisible remains the principle for them even as they proceed from it. <margin>C</margin> Since there is that which is primarily indivisible among the intelligibles and the primary beings, and again that which is entirely divisible in the sensible realm, there is another nature near the sensible and within it. It is divisible, but not primarily so like bodies; it becomes divisible by being in bodies. So when bodies are divided, that which is in them is also divided, though <margin>D</margin> as a whole it is in each of the divided parts, becoming the same thing in many. Each of these is entirely distant from the others, since it has become entirely divisible. Such are colors, and all qualities, and every shape, which is able to be whole in many distant things at once, having no part that suffers the same thing that another suffers. Because of this, it is entirely divisible. And as that divine nature is indivisible, <margin>E</margin> so there is another essence following from it. It holds its indivisibility from the former, but by giving itself to the other nature, it stands as a middle between both: the first [nature] and the divisible [nature] that is around and upon bodies. It does not exist in the same way as every quality, or shape, or color, which is in many physical masses. Rather, it is <margin>F</margin> of its own nature, existing in itself, even though each part is in a mass. And even if it requires nothing, that which is divided in each part has no communion of shared feeling <note>original: "homopatheian"</note> because this same thing is one here and another there. For this sameness is an affection <note>original: "pathema"</note>, not the essence itself. But we say this essence proceeds from the indivisible nature, so that it also comes to be in bodies, through which it also <margin>G</margin> happens to be divided. Yet it never suffers this division until it is toward the bodies; once it is in the bodies and in magnitude and in all that is distant, it remains as a whole within itself, not departing—

<meta>catchword: from itself (Greek: τηι)</meta>

# BOOK TWO. #

<margin>Not out of ignorance <note>original Greek: "οὐ δι’ ἀπειριας"</note></margin>
...it is said that the body is not indivisible. For if the body is a continuous thing, it possesses a multitude of parts, one being here and another there, even if it possesses a single quality. But our nature, which is greatest and indivisible—that which we call the soul—is not "one" in the same way a continuous object is, which has one part here and another there. Rather, it is divisible in the sense that it is present in all parts of that in which it resides, yet it is indivisible because it is whole in all of it, and whole in any portion of it whatsoever. Whoever looks upon this clearly, considering the magnitude and the power of the soul, will understand how divine and wonderful a treasure the soul is, and how its nature surpasses all other existing treasures. For although it is void of physical size, it is present to the entire magnitude of the body; it exists in one place and yet is simultaneously there again—not as something else, but as the very same thing. Thus, it is both divided into parts and, again, not divided. Or rather, it is

<margin>Of nature <note>original Greek: "τῆς φύσεως"</note></margin>
neither divided nor does it become divided. For it remains whole within itself, but it is said to be divided in relation to bodies, since bodies, being divisible, are unable to receive it in an indivisible manner. The result is that this partitioning is not an experience of the soul itself, but an experience of the body.

<column-break/>

**A** ...it does not cease to be one. Nor is it one in the same way a body is one; for a body is one through a certain continuity, whereas its parts are distinct from one another and are situated in different places. Nor, again, is the soul one like a single quality is one. Truly, this nature—which we say is the soul—is both divisible and indivisible at the same time. It is not "one" like a continuum that has different parts in different places; rather, it is divisible because it communicates itself to all the parts of the body in which it resides. It is indivisible, however,

**B** because it is whole in all parts, and it is whole in every single portion of the body. Whoever inspects these matters more clearly and rightly considers the magnitude and power of the soul will understand how divine and how marvelous a treasure the soul is, and how its nature exists above all other treasures. For though it lacks physical size, it is present to the whole of a physical magnitude; and while existing in one place, it exists there again—not as another thing, but as entirely the same. Thus, it is both divided into parts and, again, not divided. Indeed, it is better to say that the soul

**C** is neither divided nor does it become divided. For it remains whole within itself, but it is said to be divided in relation to bodies; for bodies, being divisible, are unable to receive the soul in an indivisible manner. From this, it follows that partitioning is not an affection of the soul, but rather of the body.

<margin>Confirmation of the previous points: how sensation and suffering occur.</margin>
**D** ## THAT it is necessary for the nature of the soul to be such, and that it is impossible for the soul to be anything else—that is, it must not be only indivisible nor only divisible, but must necessarily be both—can be made manifest by the following. First, if the soul were like a body, having one part here and another there, then if one part suffered a sensation, the other part would not experience it at all. Instead, the soul in the finger, being as it were a different soul existing in itself, would feel the suffering there. We would then have many souls governing each of us. This universe would not be ruled by one soul, but by various and innumerable souls separate from one another.

**E** For what someone might argue regarding "continuity" <note>the idea that parts are physically joined like a chain</note> seems vain unless it truly leads to a unified center. We must not accept what many writers say to deceive themselves: that sensations reach the "ruling part" <note>original: "principale," the Latin for the Greek "hegemonikon," the governing faculty of the soul</note> of the soul through a step-by-step, continuous succession. First of to call one part of the soul "ruling" is proposed without due consideration. For how will they divide it? How will they say this part is one thing and that is another, and designate one part as the most "ruling"? By what

**F** standard of quantity will they discern the two, or by what difference will they denote them, where there is only one quality and a continuous mass? Furthermore, will only the ruling part feel, or will the other parts feel as well? If they say only the ruling part feels, then it will only feel if the sensory impression happens to hit the ruling part exactly where it is seated. But if the sensation falls on another part of the soul that lacks the power of sense, that part will not pass the same impression to the ruling part, and no sensation will occur at all. However, if the impression does reach the ruling part, it will hit only one specific section of it;

**G** and thus, while that section feels, the rest will feel nothing. Otherwise, the rest would be superfluous, or there would be many, even innumerable, sensory perceptions, all differing from one another. In such a case, it might be said in one place, "I am the first to feel this," and elsewhere, "I, a different part, am feeling it now."

H i <note>This is a printer's signature mark used to keep pages in the correct order for binding.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul, while remaining a single spiritual entity, manages to animate and perceive through a divisible physical body. It transitions from the primary text of Plotinus to the beginning of Marsilio Ficino’s famous commentary on these ideas.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> ...from its own suffering, and where that suffering was primarily inflicted, any sense will be ignorant of it except for the first one <note>The "first sense" or "principal part" refers to the *hegemonikon*, the ruling part of the soul that processes sensations</note>. Or perhaps every part of the soul will be equally deceived, thinking that the suffering occurred right where that part itself is located. But if not only the principal part but also every other part perceives, why then should this part be the principal one, and that one not at all? Why should it be necessary for the sensation to reach that principal part? And how could things that flow in from many senses, such as through the ears and eyes, come to be known as a single, unified thing?

<margin>B</margin> On the other hand, if the soul existed as a total unity—entirely indivisible and consisting of a single point within itself—and completely escaped the nature of multitude and partition, then certainly no body grasped by the soul would be entirely animated. Instead, the soul, establishing itself as if at the center of a mass, would leave the rest of the physical bulk entirely lifeless. It is necessary, therefore, for the soul to be both one and many, and simultaneously partible and impartible. One should not be skeptical, as if it were impossible for the one and the same thing to be present in many places at once.

<margin>C</margin> For unless we admit this, the universal nature that contains and governs all things would be nowhere—the nature which indeed encompasses all things at once and leads them with wisdom. It exists as a multitude, since there are many beings; yet it also exists as a unity, so that the thing which contains them may be one. Indeed, through its manifold aspect, it provides life to all parts, but through its indivisible unity, it also leads them wisely. In those things where wisdom is not present, this "principal part" is imitated there.

<margin>D</margin> This, therefore, is what is divinely, though obscurely, stated by Plato <note>This refers to Plato's *Timaeus* 35a, describing the creation of the Soul</note> in this manner: The Architect of the World mixed a third kind of essence from both the impartible essence (which always stays the same) and the essence which becomes partible around bodies. Thus, the soul is both one and many in this world; the forms <note>ideal patterns or blueprints</note> that are in bodies are simultaneously many and one; bodies themselves are only many; and finally, that which is supreme is only one.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...would perceive the suffering. But if it saw the suffering in this way, it would be ignorant of each part, belonging only to the first part <note>original Greek: "πρώτης"</note>. Or each part of the soul will be deceived, holding the opinion that the suffering occurred there. But if not only the ruling part <note>original Greek: "ἡγεμονοῦν"</note> but also the other part perceives, why will one be the ruling part and the other not? Or why must the sensation ascend to that part? How could it know anything from many sources of learning, such as ears and <margin>B</margin> eyes? If, on the other hand, the soul were entirely indivisible and remained within itself, or if it entirely admitted multitude and division, it could not grasp any whole thing, even if it were animated. Rather, it would set itself like a center in each part, and leave the rest of the animal's mass soulless. It must be, then, that the soul is both many and divided and undivided. One must not distrust that it is possible for the same thing <margin>C</margin> to be in many places. For if we do not accept this, the nature that holds together and manages all things will not exist—that nature which encompasses all things at once and leads them with wisdom. It is a multitude, since beings are many; but it is also one, because of the unity that holds the many. It is one, and in the parts held by it, it leads wisely through its indivisible nature. In those things without wisdom, it mimics the ruling part. <margin>D</margin> This, then, is what was divinely hinted at: that from the indivisible and always-the-same essence, and the essence that becomes divided around bodies, a third kind of essence was mixed from both. The soul, then, is one and many; the forms in bodies are many and one; bodies are many only; and the highest is one alone.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE
# FIRST BOOK REGARDING THE DOUBTS OF THE SOUL
## COMMENTARY.
### SUMMARY OF THE WHOLE BOOK.

->That our souls differ from the soul of the world, and are not derived from it.<-

**The first** *book on the doubts of the soul contains seven principal questions. First, it asks whether our souls come from the soul of the world, either as parts of it or as something produced by it. Second, how the soul is introduced into the body—specifically by what property, in what different order, and by what law it is arranged. Third, whether the soul, when living outside the body, uses a certain discourse of reason. Fourth, in what way something in the soul is said to be simultaneously impartible and partible. Fifth, whether the soul is in a place in any way, and under what condition it is in the body. Sixth, where the soul is when it is separate from the body. Seventh, whether souls released from here remember human affairs, and simply concerning memory and recollection. Someone might perhaps suspect that our souls are certain parts of the worldly soul, and will assert this from three of Plato’s sayings. First, indeed, what he seems to imply in the Philebus: just as our bodies are parts of the worldly body, so too are our souls parts of its soul. Next, what he seems to believe in the Republic, the Phaedrus, and the Timaeus alike—that our souls follow the revolution of the whole world, and receive their character and fortunes from there. Finally, what he says in the Phaedrus, that every soul of ours takes care of the whole world. Moreover, this common care seems to belong only to the world soul. Furthermore, it seems likely that humans born within the world receive their life from the world and possess certain portions of the total life. For my part, I have removed this suspicion with all my strength in my Theology <note>Ficino refers to his work "Platonic Theology," where he argued against Averroism</note>, where I argue against Averroes. And here, let us proceed similarly with Plotinus to root out the same idea. A form is more excellent...*

<summary>This page presents Plotinus' argument for the soul's unique status as a bridge between the indivisible divine realm and the divisible physical world. It also introduces Marsilio Ficino’s commentary, which outlines key philosophical questions about the soul's origin and its independence from the universal World Soul.</summary>
