<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the soul's nature, moving from the general relationship between parts and wholes to a specific defense of the individual human soul's independence from the universal "World Soul."</meta>

# ON BOOK III. ENNEAD IV.

...than matter, and the whole than its parts: therefore, if a material whole is given, a formal whole is also given. Likewise, if there is a whole made of parts, there must also be a whole made of other "wholes." For since the universe is held together by the highest reason and is perfectly constructed, it is right that whatever true reason concludes to be the best state of affairs already exists in the universe; for it is from the universe that reason draws such inferences. A material whole is spoken of as something like wood: for even if it is multiplied into parts by material division, it is not thereby multiplied into multiple forms. A formal whole, however, is like a tree existing in many parts: for it is divided into forms that are perpetually different from one another. In this formal whole, a material whole is also truly present: for from the fact that they are distinguished into different particular forms, they are also in a certain way different in matter—namely, forms with their own specific differences. Since, therefore, the world is a whole that is absolutely one, it is certainly a formal whole, and a whole made of wholes. However, it will not be a whole made of wholes unless there are many things in it that are not only different in form (as in a tree), but also disjoined according to their existence and separated in their actions: like singers in a choir, where each person matches their continuous duties with the others toward the same goal, yet meanwhile remains an individual, existing by their own right.

That this world must be a true "whole made of true wholes" is demanded not only by its perfection but also by its imitation of its divine model: for that model is also a whole made of wholes. There, in that higher realm, all things exist in each thing, though in different ways; but in this world, the condition of this work further introduces a local separation of things, measuring out spaces and movements subject to time. Finally, where the parts are more perfect, the whole is also more perfect. Parts are truly more perfect when they possess their own existence and their own duty. Thus, the whole is also more "formal" where the parts are more formal. These parts are more formal where they are more distinguished by their forms, their existences, their substances, and their actions. Furthermore, for the whole to be truly one, the order of all things is sufficient—one order from a single source and directed toward a single end. 

From these points, it appears improbable that this world-machine has only one single soul; rather, it is more probable that many souls are present, and many living beings besides the world-soul and the world-animal. Indeed, we infer that there is in us a proper soul—our own substance—different from the world-soul itself, because our own mind possesses its own free movement of choice <note>original: *liberum arbitrij motum*, referring to free will</note>. Regarding this matter, we have dealt sufficiently with it when discussing free choice in our *Theology*. Otherwise, if the soul were merely a part of the whole, it would be snatched away by the sudden impulse of the whole; it would not be capable of the discursive path of reason and counsel, nor could it go astray, since the soul of the world cannot err. Plato, in the tenth book of the *Republic* and in the *Phaedrus* and *Timaeus*, posits free will in us without doubt, and Aristotle confirms it everywhere. To posit that our souls are merely parts of the world-soul is nothing other than saying that your soul is the entire world-soul itself, and mine likewise; for that soul cannot be divided into various portions, but is entirely individual and exactly the same everywhere at once. But since my mind and yours are entirely repugnant to each other in their actions, opinions, affections, and habits, they cannot be the same soul and the same mind. 

Furthermore, if my mind is in some way a part of the world-soul, it lacks its own existence and its own action. It would not, therefore, reflect upon itself, nor could it notice itself; indeed, like some very narrow part, it would not be able to embrace the whole world in thought, nor traverse it, nor think of anything above this world-soul. Consider the human body: it is not merely some continuous portion of the world, but according to its own nature, it has its own shape and motion simultaneously. Since the soul is more excellent than the body and is the origin of this shape and motion, it is far from being a continuous portion of the world-soul; rather, it possesses its own substance. Furthermore, it was not made by the soul of the physical world: for what that soul does, it does with a character of mobility; it makes an essence so changeable that it cannot reach anything immutable. Our mind, however, leaves motion for a state of rest, and subjects changeable things to the unchangeable. Finally, since our mind is a certain intellectual essence, it is rightly produced directly by the simple Intellect itself, from which the world-soul is also born—which is itself a kind of intellect, specifically an "animal" one. From this, it follows that our soul can, like the world-soul, participate in intelligence and rise to those eternal things that are above the world; the remaining parts of the soul, besides the intellectual part, can either arise from or depend upon the world-soul.

### On the dual soul, and that our souls are not parts of the world soul.

In the second chapter, you will note that anything imperfect in any category must be reduced to something perfect placed in that same category, through which it may be reduced to something perfect above that category. Therefore, the soul lacking reason <note>the "irrational" or sensitive soul</note>, being imperfect, which is both a part of a composite and bound to bodily instruments, must be reduced to the rational and intellectual soul, which is independent and perpetually consistent in itself. This must be done both in us and in the demons <note>in the Platonic sense, intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note>, the stars, the spheres, and the world. This opinion is very much in harmony with the Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note>, who rightly place two "movers" in the heavens: one joined to the movable body as its form, which is a movable mover; the other a mover that is in a way separate and immutable, the first principle and end of motion. 

Accordingly, certain "illegitimate" Platonists <note>philosophers who claimed to follow Plato but, in Ficino's view, misunderstood him</note>, who said that the souls of men were parts of the world-soul, meanwhile confessed that the world-soul itself was an individual, eternal, one, simple substance, entirely present everywhere. Consequently, they added that any human soul is conformable to the world-soul, reaching all the same things at once that the world-soul reaches. These people certainly cannot cut the world-soul into our souls in the way that a magnitude is divided into little pieces or a number into units. For in that case, that which is called the "total" soul would perish by such a division, and not remain one. Furthermore, they cannot divide it into these souls in the way that the heat of the whole body seems to be divided into the heat of the parts of the limbs: for they want the soul to be a substance in the body that is not extended in space. Yet heat itself is not properly cut, but rather the dimension in which the heat exists; therefore, the heat of any limb is rather the common heat in a part of the body than a "part" of the heat. Nevertheless, it undergoes division "by accident" in a way, insofar as it is spread equally through the extension of the body; the soul, however, is not like that. For without any extension or dimension of its own, it stands by the dimensions of the body, so as to perfectly equalize and unify things that are divisible by distances. 

Nor, again, can they distribute the world-soul into ours as a teacher might distribute whole branches of knowledge into their specific concepts. For if there were no "total" science besides the specific concepts, there would be no single common soul anywhere; if there were one besides them, it would not be suited to the world, but to us. Finally, they will assert that our souls are called parts of the world-soul just as if someone were to say that our soul in the hand or the foot is a part of our total soul. In dividing it thus, they divide nothing, and they utterly abuse the word "division." For one and the same mind of the soul is present to each thing, entirely and at once, possessing all animal powers everywhere, although it exercises different actions through different limbs as instruments; the "passions" <note>sensations or sufferings</note>, however, are in the limbs themselves.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically addressing the Enneads. Having established that the universe is a "whole made of wholes," Ficino now focuses on the individuality of the human soul against the theory that all humans share a single intellect.</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

The judge of sensory experiences <note>Latin: *passionum*, referring to the passive reception of sensory data</note> is ultimately one, presenting a single judgment by comparing diverse things, sometimes through imagination and sometimes through reason; let it be so, I say, within you. However, it cannot happen in entirely the same way in the world, where it might be imagined that there is only one single soul for every individual. Diverse men can indeed experience diverse things—just as now there are diverse instruments within any one of us—but ultimately a single judgment will be applied, the same opinion, and the same understanding. For these belong to a judge who is free from the experience itself, provided he is a true judge of those experiences <unclear>and of them</unclear>; and therefore he stands in himself somewhat segregated from the experiences, and is thus unique, not made diverse by the various instruments. But since there are contrary judgments among men, these must surely belong to their own understandings and their own substances of souls; for the rational duty is performed not through instruments, but through the intimate faculty of the substance itself.

### There are many intellectual souls besides the world soul, which are distinguished from one another not by external boundaries, but by internal ones.

In the third chapter and thereafter, a certain point is repeated: it is impossible for there to be only one soul in the world. I confirm this again as follows. The supreme Providence of the whole, establishing various kinds of things in order for the highest beauty of the universe, decreed that there would be diverse genera of things and, again, innumerable individuals. Between these, as if across a valley of distance, Providence willed there to be different species in every genus, loving above all else a bounty of species as things of great perfection. Now, if in the lower genera the order of the soul is distributed through many levels of species, why would it not also affect an equal bounty in the higher genus of the soul, and arrange a similar order of levels through different species of souls? This is especially true since the nature of the soul itself—because of its somewhat composite, mobile, and body-adapted condition—is capable of being multiplied and propagated through bodies. Furthermore, the very goal of nature, which concludes one composition with a bond unless it also includes another, might again deviate into minds. But the marvelous number of minds was discussed in the first book of my *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, *Theologia Platonica* (Platonic Theology)</note>, through which the entire world of souls is confirmed. Finally, only the first principle of the universe itself <note>God, or the "One"</note>, because of its supreme simplicity, does not admit a number of natures within itself. The remaining genera of things beneath this—namely mind, soul, nature, and body—both receive a specific number and possess it as something belonging greatly to the common good of the whole. Moreover, the soul does not tend by its own nature toward the first or second rank in the order of things, but necessarily toward the third, as our *Theology* sufficiently proves. Therefore, it is not a single soul, nor should it be, nor, finally, can it be. 

Furthermore, since Plato asserts that the Soul of the World is always in a body and always leads its life there, while our souls are sometimes separated from bodies and, once separated, subsist in a different property and live in a different condition from one another—choosing different bodies again according to their own choices, and finally living dissimilarly by their own will, and after death attaining different levels of living according to the dissimilarity of their lives—how could a Platonist justify there being only one soul? 

What if someone should occasionally suspect, among the followers of Averroes <note>Averroes was a medieval Islamic philosopher who famously argued that all humans share a single, universal "Potential Intellect"</note>, that there is a single intellect in all men? We certainly will not doubt him in the same way we do concerning the soul, nor will we chiefly object by asking how one intellect is in the body and another outside the body, or how there can be intellects of such total confusion in such diverse bodies, as we were just saying about the soul. For souls, as they incline toward bodies, differ not only by intimate differences among themselves but also through various actions concerning various bodies and through the diversity of the bodies themselves. But if it is proved that all intellects—which are separate because they perform the action and property of the soul without bodily instruments—differ among themselves, we shall not flee to the variety of bodies or actions, but rather to the diverse species of understanding and modes of knowing: to the differing modes, understandings, and habits that are at the same time repugnant to one another, which cannot exist simultaneously in a single intellect. For just as in the first Intellect we assign a difference among its many notions only from the diversity of their formal properties, so when we are about to assign the differences of other intellects among themselves, we shall assert them from their intimate properties. 

It is fitting for there to be many species of minds and understandings if the nature of bodies is so rich; just as is <unclear>taught</unclear> here, there are many species of metals, more of plants, and the most of animals. From this it appears that there are many demons <note>In the Platonic sense, *daemons* are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil</note> and minds of whatever kind. Furthermore, it is not fitting to distribute the nature of the soul itself—which is an indivisible substance, perpetually subsisting in itself—into many minds, and then to confuse many back into one, as we divide a great deal of water into parts and then merge them back into the same. Nor should we derive many from one soul as we distribute one light from the sun into many dwellings through windows, only to be resolved shortly after into that same presence. For visible light depends entirely on its source like an accident <note>A philosophical term meaning a non-essential quality</note> and does not retain its own subsistence. But this genus of intellects of intelligible light is far different from this; it is not an accident, but a most absolute substance. Therefore, if it has different levels among itself, it does not receive them from the outside, like accidental forms, but from within; and according to its different properties, it admits many (so to speak) subsistences, and keeps them distinct within the same genus, free from confusion. 

In this genus of intellectual substance and light, you shall place rational souls. And you will recognize how they differ among themselves, and they shall never be merged into one in the manner of cheaper liquids. You must recognize those souls belonging to the life of the world, of which these are certain vestiges of life in animals born from plants. For they will run through the life of the universe by action and transcend it by affection. Nor should you believe that they differ not at all from the World Soul, as if they were certain offshoots of it through the body of the world; nor does my soul differ from yours only because the bodies through which propagation occurred differ; nor does either differ from the World Soul only because that is the root and first plant, while these are offshoots from it. For if it were so, the intellectual soul of Socrates itself would have to be resolved after death into the World Soul (as is imagined), and while it lost its own existence, it would cease to be entirely when it approached perfect being. An intellectual nature does not suffer this: it does not need external boundaries for its distinction, like liquids and light, but being more exact, it is distributed into its own species and existences by internal boundaries. It was sufficiently proven in my *Theology* that the rational soul, insofar as it is intellectual, possesses itself more perfectly the further it separates itself from the body—I say it possesses itself more perfectly according to the peculiar property of its own substance. When it is completely separated from the body at death, then it is necessary that the proper substance of this soul be perfect. Thus, let no one imagine that individual minds are at some point confused into one or suddenly spread apart.

<summary>Ficino argues against the "single intellect" theory (monopsychism), asserting that human souls are individual, distinct substances that retain their unique identity even after death rather than merging into a universal World Soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus's Enneads, Book III, Chapter 4. Having previously argued that individual souls are not merely parts of a single world soul, Ficino now explores the metaphysical mechanism of how souls remain distinct through their essential forms while maintaining a spiritual unity with their source.</meta>

### ON BOOK III OF THE ENNEADS, CHAPTER IIII.

### Intellectual souls are distinguished from one another not by accidental traits, but by their own essential properties; and how the many souls are said to be one, and from one.

Since the first intellect and the first essence are the same, it follows that all intellects are true essences. Therefore, they are distributed among themselves by specific differences—that is, not by accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or location, as opposed to the "essence" or core nature of a thing.</note>, nor by boundaries received from the outside (like the divided parts of a continuous physical object, or material forms), but they are distinguished by the dignity of their own self-subsisting essences through their own internal differences and limits. For a thing is more truly distinguished from another if it differs by a formal property <note>A "formal property" refers to the "form" or blueprint of a being, rather than the "matter" it is made of.</note> than by material division or physical location. Every intellect, therefore, possesses its own essence and being within a certain deep identity and—if I may put it this way—alterity <note>Latin: *alteritate*, the state of being "other" or distinct.</note>. I say identity insofar as it is a most simple form, never falling away from its simplicity; and alterity, in turn, insofar as such a form is distinguished by its very self as its own property from every other thing and every other intellect. If it is distinguished primarily and by itself, it remains forever distinct and far from confusion.

Consider in the divine mind the "great soul"—that is, the general Idea of intellectual souls—in which the various species of souls are conceived. That Idea is a type of intellect there, and these species are also types of intellects there. However, these ideal intellects are distinguished from one another not by having different existences (for so far there is only one unique substance), but by a certain rational principle and formal property. If these essential properties are thought of as proceeding outward, they suddenly become more distinct; they are then distinguished by their existences. For minds are so effective that they act outwardly to produce not something accidental, but substance itself, and diverse substances according to the principles of their diverse forms. These subsistences, proceeding most closely from the primary Intellect, exist primarily as intellects. Because they themselves are highly effective toward an internal conception, each one expresses within itself a property derived from the intellectual beings, though more distinctly divided into many. 

Just as a spark flashes out from a ray, or as a more complex spoken word is produced from a simpler word within the silent imagination, so many souls proceed outward from the one ideal Soul into this world, and even to others. Although these are different substances, they are nevertheless "one" among themselves in three main ways: first, because they are all under the same Idea; second, because they are not separated by space or time; and third, because through their intellectual "peaks" <note>The "apex" or "peak" of the soul refers to its highest, most divine faculty that remains in contact with the higher realms.</note> they are all formed by one and the same divine intellect in action, and they all perpetually contemplate that same intellect. It is right, therefore, that they all naturally refer back to the same universal goals of Providence.

### How every rational soul is all things, and how the species of rational souls differ among themselves.

The supreme principle of all, because of its highest simplicity, is above all things; yet through its power, it immediately effects all things. Therefore, the Intellect, which is its son <note>In Plotinian thought, the "Intellect" (Nous) is the first emanation from "The One."</note>, is the "first all," and it is all things perfectly. For this reason, every Idea within it is all Ideas. The soul, therefore, flowing naturally and closely from its own Idea, draws all things with it: every intellectual soul is thus the universe. However, the first and simplest view of this whole exists there in every genus, and it contains all things in that same place. 

Since the first intellect is the first form, it is measured and uniform, and belongs to the whole universe. Likewise, every rational soul, insofar as it is intellectual, is not only a most simple form but is also the "all" of form—it is all things, I say, in act, just as the intellect itself is all things in act. However, insofar as it becomes an intellectual and then an animal soul, it retains that same duty by which it is still all things, but it retains it less perfectly. It is now the universe "in potential," and rightly so, since God placed it as the middle point of things and tempered it out of everything. 

He tempered the different species of souls in such a way that the soul which was to be the universal life of the world (the World Soul) would always be turned toward the universal Intellect, viewing it universally and with the utmost attention. From this, it came to pass that it carried out a universal providence with wonderful power and universalizing ease—since all power is unifying. The remaining celestial souls after this one would indeed be turned toward the universal Intellect, yet not quite as universally, nor with equal attention; therefore, they perform a providence that is neither as universal nor as powerful. Finally, the lower souls <note>Referring to human souls.</note> are so constituted that they sometimes turn themselves toward the universal Intellect—either more or less universally or attentively—and thus sometimes they contemplate with a greater universal providence, and at other times less so, and with less power. 

Likewise, they sometimes bend themselves not so much toward the universal as toward their own private intellect, and thus they exist less perfectly. Sometimes they turn toward reason, where they see even less perfectly and fall into great variation, becoming worse. Finally, insofar as the rational soul unfolds the universe below, it is admitted into the providence of the universal World Soul; but when it gradually falls from its universal duty into the duty of a "part" and directs itself toward particular care, it enters a particular rank, puts on its own body more fully, and labors more.

### Response to doubts, and proof that rational souls are not derived from the World Soul.

Plato, intending to prove in the *Philebus* that the world is animate, says: "From where would our body, which is composed of parts of the elements, get a soul, unless the world, which is composed of the whole elements, possessed a soul?" That is, the Intellect (the world-maker) was not so unwise as to give souls to us but not to the world. This is especially true because the World Soul, through universal influence, was to prepare the seminal matter of animals to receive their own souls from wherever they might come. Therefore, our body has an intellectual soul from no other source than the world—that is, from the same world-maker. Our sensory soul exists largely because of our intellectual soul, with the World Soul contributing primarily to this. 

Nevertheless, Plato asserts that each rational soul is not from the World Soul, but from the same Author from whom that soul came, and constituted from similar genera. He states that these souls are not the World Soul itself, nor parts or powers of it, but are distinct from it in various degrees by God. This is why he introduces them as falling into bodies and wandering, or departing from them—things that cannot happen to the World Soul. Moreover, in the *Phaedrus*, he says that whenever a particular soul (which is a "whole" in a part) turns itself outside the body or toward the universal form through the act of thinking and loving, it is also to be admitted to the universal providence of the world, being endowed with a celestial body from the beginning. Indeed, even in a decaying body, the philosopher occupies himself with this and experiences the same divine power as much as he is able. Furthermore, wherever Plato seems to suggest that the soul follows the celestial motion, he adds there and elsewhere that it is also possible for it not to follow it. It has also been proven,

From this it appears that if there is a life in us that follows the body like a handmaid <note>Latin: "pedissequa"—literally a female servant who follows behind. Ficino uses this to describe the lower part of the soul that serves the body's needs.</note> and serves fate through this connection, this mundane life can indeed depend on the soul of the body; but that soul in us which is called away from the stirrings of the body and resists its impulses descends from a higher place than the material world. ## How souls differ, and how they are immortal while remaining in their own form, and how the world soul, being everywhere present, leads all things to life.

*In the eighth chapter, these things must be considered first: to what extent our souls harmonize both with each other and with the world soul, so that they are often affected by a similar instinct, and some impulse easily flows from some into others, and particular souls are moved secretly by the universal soul. It is certainly not necessary for our souls to be the offspring of the world soul. For a common progression from the same divine mind and the same general "Idea" <note>In Platonic thought, "Ideas" or "Forms" are the perfect, eternal blueprints for everything that exists in the physical world.</note> of souls is enough to create this harmony and, as it were, sympathy between the world soul and other souls. Furthermore, there are four primary differences among human souls: they differ in a way according to the differences of bodies, since they seem to have movements that are more or less agitated depending on the differences in blood, bile, and spirit. They also differ based on a preceding life: if they possess different capacities for actions among themselves, one might now be more ready for contemplation than another; for one soul might have led a very busy life before birth, while another led a purely contemplative one. The Platonists also think that souls differ in a way by their natural species <note>Latin: "specie"—here meaning their essential "kind" or category.</note> from the beginning: if indeed human souls fall under the same immediate genus, they nevertheless differ among themselves by certain species—even if the difference is as small as possible—by which they are distributed from the highest degree through a second, third, or fourth. Finally, they think souls differ because, although any rational soul is a "universe" in itself, it can nevertheless affect itself in various ways through a certain free movement, as one turns itself toward a contemplative life, another toward an active life, and another toward a life of pleasure. And among those who devote themselves to contemplation, some choose this form of contemplation, and others that form above the rest; and whatever they choose, they soon put on as if it were their nature. Although any soul is "all things," this kind of parity does not make souls equal to one another without any distinction. For in the first Mind, there is a common and ideal rationale <note>Latin: "ratio"—the underlying logic or blueprint.</note> of souls, not merely individual but quite general, and souls possess different ideal grades among themselves, the number and order of lot of which the number of souls follows. And just as in the divine mind one Idea is "all things" in one way, and another Idea is "all things" in another way, so this soul is all things differently than that one, and uses its power differently. Moreover, it is consistent with reason that things composed of the four elements can be resolved back into pure elements: as if the lower elements could not be entirely remade by the more excellent ones, at least the more excellent ones might exist separately from the lower ones in their own purity. Similarly, a soul composed of matter and form, as if from twin elements, is resolved in a way into pure matter, and a form entirely unworthy—one that is pure through itself, which subsists through itself and in itself without matter—even though matter cannot exist far from all form. Just as the formal element (as I said) exists far from the material, even if the reverse does not happen; intellectual souls are numbered among this kind of form. Such a form is a simple essence <note>A "simple essence" is one that is not made of parts and therefore cannot be broken down or destroyed.</note>, possessing its being through itself in itself, in which its "being" is the same as the essential unity of the "one." On the contrary, the essence of bodies "has" being: for in a body, the essence of the form is one thing, and the "being" (which consists in a multitude) is another thing, as is the "unity," which, insofar as it is unity, does not admit multitude; and that "being" follows the union, which the unity precedes. Why say all this? So that you may understand that the form of the soul itself—whose "being" is the same as its essential unity—is entirely indissoluble, just as unity is indissoluble; especially because everywhere in things, existence is through form: it follows that a simple form subsisting in itself always continues its own being in itself. Furthermore, if a simple form were to be lost from mixed matter, it would be reduced to nothing; if it were to be generated, it would be generated from nothing, but physical reason does not allow this. Therefore, the soul is everlasting: especially because, if it were to be fashioned from anything, and yet could not be made from any matter, God its author would be forced to procreate it from his own substance: whence he would be forced to be changeable, especially if he should ever do what he had not done before. Plotinus signifies these things in order to assert that the soul is everlasting; to what extent these arguments should be accepted is sufficiently discussed in our Theology <note>Ficino refers here to his own major work, "Platonic Theology," where he harmonizes these Greek ideas with Christian doctrine.</note>. Among these points, notice that each of such forms is a certain single thing in number distinct from others, not by accident, but by itself—by itself, I say: since souls do not receive their number from the numbers of bodies or of bodily qualities, as if one world soul were propagated into many through different affections of bodies. Now, indeed, any soul so subsists through itself as always one in number, just as in its essence it has its "being," and its "being" is the same as its unity. Therefore, just as the essence of the soul is simply eternal as something simple and subsisting in itself, so also is any singular "being" of that soul: since its "being" is only in its own essence. Likewise, just as being is unity, so is any numerical unity; for there, "to be" is the same as "to be a certain one thing." For a simple essence remaining in itself is distinguished not by external things but by internal ones, so that no one may dream that our souls, having eventually dismissed their personal properties, are to be confused into a certain general soul <note>Ficino is refuting the idea that individual identities vanish into a single "cosmic consciousness" after death.</note>. Indeed, bodily things composed of matter and form preserve a unity of species that is perpetual through succession, but they by no means preserve a numerical and personal unity. And yet they would not even preserve a specific unity in themselves unless they drew this from the perpetual fountain of the soul's generation. Therefore, any soul, as something far more excellent, always retains a numerical and personal unity in itself, not only a specific one; indeed, just as composite things that are dissolved through the soul return at similar recurring times as things entirely similar and of the same species: so the soul, changing form in itself in a way, being more excellent than the body, returns at some time to the same number, and to the same body, and the same person. After this, when it is asked how a simple intellectual form—whether the world's soul or ours—is sometimes called infinite? The answer is: not because it can be divided into infinity, but because it flourishes without end, and can act everywhere and always. Thus, neither is the world soul divided into infinite souls, nor is it stretched out in the manner of a bodily quality as far as the mass of the world extends, but it remains one: and however much of the body can receive anything from it, the soul itself, being whole everywhere, gives it life. Our souls also, just as they do not become exactly as many in number from so many*

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus, specifically addressing how the soul—both the universal World Soul and individual souls—relates to physical matter without being divided or diminished by it. It builds on the previous discussion of the soul's divine origin versus its role in animating the body.</meta>

# ON BOOK III OF THE FOURTH ENNEAD

...with bodily portions and qualities, they are stretched out everywhere into the mass, and are extended across matter in the manner of "whiteness" <note>Ficino uses "whiteness" as an example of a quality that can cover a large surface without the quality itself being "broken" into pieces.</note>; but there are just as many properties in the whole, and however much mass is prepared for their influence, they form that much in a certain half and everywhere in the whole with perpetual vigor. Nor is our soul cut into many souls, whether because of diverse limbs or limbs adapted to whatever purposes: just as the World Soul itself is not divided within itself, nor does it become many souls, even when divided by parts distant from one another. For this soul remains one; however much a living part of the world is separated, it is nevertheless whole at once from both sides because of that one soul. It is also in the middle because of its containment of "prime matter," <term>Prime Matter: the most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical things.</term> and indeed in the "fifth essence," which is the proper vessel of the soul. 

Among these things, if it seems to anyone that Plotinus, in the case of plants and animals born from putrefaction <note>Latin: "ex putrefactione genitis." This refers to the ancient belief in "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise directly from decaying matter.</note>, does not place any soul other than the World Soul, you should not easily grant that; for he himself seems to refute this in the book *On the Immortality of the Soul*. He will say, therefore, that the World Soul itself is indeed present to all such things, and is not forced to become many souls on account of many sections and living beings; but meanwhile, this is not the only life in them, even though it generates life and souls here. Indeed, if these souls are said by some Platonists, and by Plotinus himself in some places, to be eternal according to their own substances, they will not then be generated for the first time by the World Soul, but being generated by its universal influence, they will be infused. 

And someone could say that all life is indeed perpetual, but souls—if there are any such lacking their own ages—subsist after death not so much in themselves as in the common life. Those, however, which use their own motions, especially if they are free, also perpetually preserve their own form through themselves. But perceive with a true mind that the proper lives of living things are subject to the heavens, and that a common vegetative power from the World Soul is everywhere vigorous in <unclear>us</unclear> living things, which both prepares matter for individual souls, confers it at a certain time, and unites all things into one living act. This is what they say Pythagoras meant—as Sextus the Pyrrhonist <note>Latin: "Sexto Pyrranio," referring to the skeptical philosopher Sextus Empiricus.</note> reports—when he spoke of a spirit infused from the soul into all things, which unites humans with the rest of living beings, and unites humans with things from elsewhere. For while this common spirit is vigorous, the rational soul is added to us at birth; but that which, under this common light, thereafter spreads its own peculiar life into the body, is what it draws back into itself at death as its own property, just as the World Soul preserves its own and what is common.

### In how many ways the soul may be introduced into the body, and what the nature of the World Soul is, and how it makes the world and its dimensions, and how it is everywhere.

In the ninth chapter of the book, where the second question begins regarding how the soul is introduced into the body: you will notice that this happens in two primary ways. For it comes into the body either from an incorporeal state or from another body. and this, according to the branch of division, is divided again into four branches: namely, it passes either from a liquid body into a liquid, or from liquid into solid, or from solid into another solid, or from solid back into liquid. Here you will note that if, according to Plotinus’s opinion, it can ever depart from every body, it can be driven to always live outside the body. This is what Plato indicates in the *Phaedo*, and what Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Two influential Neoplatonist philosophers who followed Plotinus.</note> argue for. But if, as Proclus says, it is always in some body, they consequently thought these successions of bodies were eternal. 

But so that you may know how your soul, or rather first how the World Soul, is introduced into its body, think of the intellectual power in the World Soul as being at the top like light, the rational power in the middle, and the vegetative power at the bottom, like heat. Furthermore, consider two things regarding its essence. First, it stands above as something else, and by which those three [powers] are already an influence according to the former three; but truly, of what moment the other is, is in a way obscure, and formless, and cold. Obscure indeed, not yet having intelligence. Thus, the formless light likewise does not yet possess the splendor of reason; finally, the cold light has not yet attained the warmth of the vegetative nature. 

From this essence of its own, therefore, imagine the first "matter" of the world proceeding as something wandering, utterly destitute, and entirely dark, formless, and cold; <unclear>standing</unclear> meanwhile from the essence, insofar as it is already marked by those three powers, contemplate the matter of the world as it begins to be adorned little by little: through intelligence, indeed, by forms that remain inwardly; through reason, by forms that move stably; and finally, through the vegetative power, by forms that move changeably. This happens in such a way that those things which proceed entirely from intelligence and reason flow as naturally from there as those things which are born naturally from the vegetative nature. And thus the World Soul, being endowed with the chief "exemplar" <note>The divine blueprint or perfect model of the world.</note> in forming the world (as Timaeus also suggests), does not look to a changeable and, as it were, generable nature or reason—if only it be a mobile reason—but rather to an intellectual form free from all generation, whether it be the intelligence of a living being or the first intelligence. 

Think again of the soul insofar as it is mobile intrinsically, naturally striving so that it may be moved extrinsically. From this connection, therefore, matter is extended only so far and so wide, so that from the soul’s motion flashing outward, the dimension of matter has arisen, and at the same time the motion of the world; thus, space and time are born there together. Space exists because the soul dwells there by "vegetating" <note>In this context, "vegetating" means the act of giving life, growth, and physical existence.</note>; time exists by which it may move that space (that is, the body) by vegetating. In the intellectual exemplar, a certain dimension of both the world and mundane things was first destined ideally; at which destination such formal efficacy for motion arose in the vegetative nature, which properly provides this great quantity to the world, and such great things to mundane objects, as much and as great as is pre-marked in the very order of things. 

The soul, moreover, can be present as a whole through its essence to any part of the world, however grand, since essence here was made according to how far the soul proceeded, and in proceeding, it made. And the soul itself is neither divided, nor is it a quality resulting from a certain dimension, but is something individual—not like some boundary of dimension marked somewhere by dimension, but rather consisting in itself for the sake of unity, outside the whole category of quantity, overhanging the entire mass in a certain category more than substance by a very long interval of nature and power. Whence this individual part of itself possesses the entire mass everywhere, and is possessed as a whole by it.

### How the World Soul acts within itself, and thus naturally generates the world as "all-formed," just as it is all-formed itself.

The tenth chapter teaches how the highest air is subject to light, and light to the Sun, yet they are always together from eternity; so the World Soul is said to be always subject to the Intellect, and finally to the Good. Likewise, the world always and naturally gushes forth from the "seminal power" of its soul, just as any living thing from its seed; for these things embrace its power in that way. But since no particular nature in any living thing here requires counsel or any machines for motion and generation, much less does this universal nature require them, but rather it makes and moves all things with wonderful ease.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s Enneads, Book IV. Having established the unity of the soul, Ficino now moves into the mechanics of how the World Soul governs the material world and how individual souls descend into bodies, incorporating Neoplatonic allegories involving Dionysus and the Titans.</meta>

COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO

Since the entire mass of the world and its form depend upon it [the Soul], nothing anywhere can resist it: especially because all things depend on it in a subsequent series, such that when stirred or struck by even the slightest nod, all things are immediately moved, and are led toward the action and end of the first mover. Accordingly, things which do not live are ruled from the outside only by the matter of another, for in themselves they are sluggish; but those things which live also act within themselves, and they act perpetually. Therefore, the Soul is the principle of living; the World Soul especially acts always and most powerfully within itself insofar as it is an intelligent being. From this side it forms its own reason; from that side it forms its own nature. But reason naturally discourses within itself and touches all things, and it teems with the seeds of all things, even those of divine bodies. From this soul and its rational movement—through the <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes seminales" — the Stoic and Neoplatonic "blueprints" or formative forces latent in nature that dictate the growth and form of physical things.</note> of things—is born the rational form of the world, which is similarly all-formed; a form, I say, as similar as possible to the soul. For if the reproductive organs which follow strive to generate things similar to themselves, does not the universal and most holy Mother of the world here generate a world as similar to herself as possible?

### Concerning the descent of the soul, Dionysus, Jupiter, the cycles of lives, the order of the world, and the harmony of the universe.

Here he calls nature itself—that is, the vegetative power of the World Soul—Dionysus, whose limbs are the seminal reasons of things within nature itself. When these "limbs" proceed into matter through generation, being more divided among themselves here, they are seen to be torn apart by the <term>Titans</term> <note>In Neoplatonic allegory, the tearing apart of Dionysus by the Titans represents the fragmentation of the One into the Many, or the "scattering" of divine soul into the material world.</note>, who are the overseers of the division of offspring. By them, the limbs of Dionysus—that is, of universal providence—are torn asunder by Typhon, the leader of the generative demons. Therefore, souls living in a certain divine part of the world sometimes, through the imagination (which is the lowest part in them), look forward to the forms lying in the matter of the world. These forms are images of Dionysus and his limbs, glimpsed in matter as if in a mirror. But to see them thus in matter, the soul deflects its affection toward nature in a direct line, and from there toward matter. Wherever the imagination turns itself, there the "fate-bearing reason" diverts itself from the intellect, and both do so not just by looking, but by loving. Love of this kind exists as the principle of descending, and even after the fall, it remains there as long as providence requires the constant attention of our reason. But the intellect meanwhile, which such affection does not touch, keeps itself unmoved in the higher part of the world. 

The kindness of Jupiter instituted the cycles of time: in this laborious life they are generally short; in the life among those above, they are long; and finally, among the highest ones, they are longest of all. Our souls return when they reach the level of the World Soul, where they contemplate its public providence; from the ease of their own governance over their body and their province, they are initiated. Furthermore, the World Soul, like a cosmic Apollo, sings in nature and strikes the lyre in heaven. In nature, the unfolding of all reasons flows in times and movements; it is a universal harmony composed of many and varied melodies. In heaven, similarly, a certain winding arrangement of the stars and movements belongs to the Appollonian sounds; they are sustained by the perpetual concord of that song. If anyone, therefore, through their own disposition, were to sound the continuity of that song, they would continue celestial sounds in a celestial way; and as if now—to speak properly—he would hear them. Moreover, our divine progressions, whether in descent, in habitation, or in ascent, dancing as if on a harmonious <term>tripod</term> <note>A reference to the three-legged seat of the Delphic Oracle, symbolizing rhythmic, prophetic, or divine movement.</note>, adapt themselves to the worldly song. For since they set out from the same place as the World Soul and are its siblings, and inhabit its province, they never dance against its sound; they do not change their "modes" <note>original: "tropas" — musical turns or modes.</note> from there, but willingly and naturally, and at the same time freely, they emulate the worldly order. 

From this it follows that through celestial and human progressions—and these "curves" as if through causes—one is able to guess the "leap" as if through certain signs. This is especially because universal nature and its form contain, by a certain exemplary reason, whatever things are carried out within the world, whether they are led by nature itself, or by the blessed ones, or from anywhere else. Souls live sometimes outside the celestial body, sometimes in the pure celestial body, and sometimes under the celestial. And insofar as the soul puts on a different habit within itself, it also puts on a different figure on the outside. Thus, it sometimes enters a celestial man, sometimes an aerial one, and other times a terrestrial one. And here again, insofar as it degenerates more into the depths, it enters into a man who is either divine, human, or almost beast-like. 

Indeed, we are accustomed to correcting the words of Plotinus in this way: for it is not accepted by the Platonists that a rational soul ever becomes a body or a beast-like form for a man, nor should it have been settled by Plotinus himself, since he had proposed that the change in the soul had its beginning from the imagination, which cannot be changed in its essential species. Just as it was recently accepted that the intellect exists in the human species. However, that our intellect remains happy in the divine while the rational power is plunged into misery, does not seem entirely disagreed upon by Iamblichus; yet it was rejected by Porphyry, the disciple of Plotinus. It is said to have been refuted by Proclus, who argued that the power of the most blessed mind with God would be so great that it would surely retain its contiguous and most similar reason, provided that reason itself did not decline at all, and that in this life we would sin as little as possible. Nor does it seem to agree that the stomach would be very weak as long as the liver remained in such a state. 

Porphyry adds that the fall of the soul did not begin from the imagination or nature, but from the intellect—not a universal one overcome by lower things, but that it exerts its superior power according to a certain measure of its virtue. Therefore, the intention of acting is sometimes relaxed in it, and to that extent, the act of the lower power (that is, of imagination and nature) is permitted to the intellect, since the soul cannot be strained in every direction. Conversely, the acts of the lower powers are relaxed when the act of the higher ones is intensified. But when the philosopher says the intellect acts according to the measure of its virtue, he must be corrected thus: when the intellect is blessed with God, it acts not so much by its own virtue as by the divine virtue, under whose form it now acts. Thus, it must be thought that the soul, having reached that blessed state, will never depart from there. But let those men see to that; for us, it will be enough to have related what the poets would approve, which our Theologians have most strongly confirmed.

### Law, judgment, and the justice of the universe lead souls from within, both by choice and by necessity, to their own end.

Just as someone offering lettuce entices a goose through the exterior sense, so the Great One entices the interior sense through certain internal persuasions friendly to it; and thus the soul is moved here willingly, just like the goose. So again, divine providence draws every will and affection of the mind to the destination suitable for it: namely, through a certain affection and fertility of choices already conceived in the soul, which is thus moved both willingly and so vehemently toward our destination and competent lot, like someone snatched by a secret magic. For God moves the soul...

<meta>This page transitions from Marsilio Ficino’s expansive commentary on Plotinus into a more concise annotative style. Having previously discussed the descent of the soul and its cosmic functions, Ficino now addresses the relationship between the World Soul and the material world through the allegory of Prometheus and theurgy (the animation of statues), before commencing the formal translation of Ennead IV, Book 3.</meta>

...not only more internal than art, but even than nature: and at a certain time, just as nature is accustomed. Therefore, souls from the beginning are moved by their own accord, having been made such by acting in this way: they descend from the state of power from God at certain times, not only by choice but also by the necessity of an unequal law <note>original: "necessitate legis iniqua" — this refers to the "inevitable" descent into the material world which seems "unequal" or "unjust" compared to the divine state, yet leads to a just outcome.</note>; they then arrive at a just lot. Moreover, in the universe, the law is the judgment of justice. For the Law in the divine mind is the very arrangement of all things; they judge in the mind of the World Soul, and according to the norm of divine law, individual things arrive. Justice, indeed, follows by the will of that same soul so willing, and so following individual things, as has already been indicated. Souls also transfer into pure things those which through their own impurity incline downward, just as universal nature drives heavy things toward the center by their own weight; on the other hand, it thinks that by their purity they tend toward the same [height], just as nature drives light things upward by their own lightness. With this brief summary, it is permitted to interpret what Orpheus sings in three hymns concerning the law, judgment, and justice of God: and what Plato, imitating Orpheus in the fourth book of the *Laws*, defined concerning divine law and judgment.

->On the connection of this world to the higher one, and concerning Prometheus and the speaking statues.<-

Within the worldly spheres are many souls, and from here especially their own vital gifts: through these souls indeed, and through animal endowments, as if through certain intermediaries, they obtain certain intellectual gifts consequently from the individual intellects of their own leading prelates <note>Ficino often uses ecclesiastical or hierarchical terms like "prelates" to describe the higher ranks of angelic or celestial intellects that guide the lower ones.</note>: through whom, moreover, they attain some divine gifts of the divine mind itself. To these (as Plotinus and Iamblichus believe) the intellects are inseparably joined, so that it is no wonder that that divine world is thoroughly infused everywhere into this world. After this, you will notice a certain providence of nature reigning in the vital part of the World Soul under the name of Prometheus, who fashions statues—that is, natural things—out of clay (which is primary matter). Part of this workmanship is bound, and part is soluble; and here Prometheus is not "rash light" <note>original: "temeritatem lucam" — likely a reference to Prometheus as "forethought" versus his brother Epimetheus "afterthought," though Ficino's Latin here is slightly obscure.</note>. Likewise, in natural things there are not only animal powers, but also certain intellectual and divine endowments: and all the deities contribute something of themselves to this workmanship—a workmanship, I say, not only of the universe, but of each individual. Among these things, Plotinus alludes to the voice of the clay statue with a just mention of those magicians especially who constructed "speaking statues" <note>Theurgic statues believed to be inhabited by gods or spirits in late antiquity.</note> in which there was neither the proper life of the statues nor the faith of reason, but demons led by the same star under whose command they fashioned the statues. I also think that in that boy, the son of the King, on the day he was born, as Aly <note>Albohazen Haly (Ali ibn Abi al-Rijal), an 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> testifies (who says he was present), it was not the conjunction of the four planets meeting in his horoscope that formed the words, nor did the infant's soul create the words and prophecy concerning the calamity of the father's kingdom that followed shortly after, but rather a demon was placed there: a Martial demon <note>A spirit associated with the planet Mars.</note>. For in the eighth degree of Lyra in the horoscope, which is also the term of Mercury, Mercury itself is said to have been conjoined with Venus, Jupiter, and Mars. But it is not permitted to digress further into the present, or rather, it is not permitted to maintain the manner of observing the sequence from the beginning further. For if we pursue long arguments of this kind, or rather commentaries arranged separately from Plotinus's chapters, the interpretation will become confused and the work will grow to an immense size. Therefore, it shall suffice as we have said until now. It will be enough hereafter to intersperse certain brief little annotations, as we did in [the commentary on] Theophrastus, within Plotinus's chapters.

## ENNEAD FOUR,
### BOOK III.

->First concerning the difficulties of the soul.<-

CONCERNING THE SOUL, as many things as we have found doubtful, we shall either set into a clear way or we shall leave them in the doubts themselves. This must be established: that the genus [of the soul] always remains. It would be right for those attempting a study concerning the genus where there is much discussion and investigation, to be reasonably disposed, both because of many other things and because it gives knowledge of both: the things of which it is the principle, and the things from which it comes. Let us obey as if it were a command from God, who commands us to know ourselves, while making an examination of this matter.

<column-break/>

<margin>How necessary the consideration of the soul is, and how it is [possible] without those things which are listed above for the world.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'P' depicting a figure playing a trumpet-like instrument, possibly representing fame or a messenger, in a circular frame within a square.</image-desc>
IT IS WORTHWHILE to consider whether all doubts about the soul should be resolved, or whether instead our profit should be placed in the doubts themselves. Truly there is no matter about which we ought to investigate and treat more diligently and divinely than the soul: since, besides many other reasons, it also leads to the knowledge of both, namely both those things of which it is the principle, as well as those things by which it is made. Thus we shall obey God when he commands: "Know thyself."

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

### CHAPTER I

**A** Furthermore, while we strive to examine and investigate all other things, we should rightly investigate, first of all, what this investigator within us actually is; especially since we desire to attain that very thing which is lovely and pleasant in the spectacles of contemplation themselves. For in the universal Intellect, the thinker and the object of thought are a twin pair <note>original: "geminum" — referring to the Plotinian concept that in the Divine Mind, the act of thinking and the thing thought are identical</note>. Therefore, it is reasonable that in individual intellects, this aspect is more prominent in one, while that aspect is more so in another. **B** We must also consider how the "receptacles of the Gods" <term>receptacles: *susceptacula*, or in Greek *hypodochas*, referring to how physical things or bodies are prepared to receive divine presence or soul</term> come to be; but we will investigate that more opportunely after we have asked in what manner the soul is in the body. Now, however, let us return to those who say that our souls also are from the Soul of the universe itself.

**C** For perhaps they will object to us that there is not sufficient argument to prevent our souls from being parts of that Soul—since it is said that our souls proceed as far as the World Soul pours itself out, and it is handed down that they have very similar intellectual gifts, even if they concede this: for they will say that parts are usually shaped like the whole. **D** Furthermore, they will bring forward Plato himself, as if he held this opinion, where in proving the world is animate <note>See Plato's *Timaeus* 30b</note>, he says: "Just as our body is a part of the universal body, so also our soul is a part of the whole Soul." Also, it is said and clearly shown that we follow the circuit of the whole world, and from there we have our characters and fortunes; again, being born within the world, we rightly receive our soul from that which contains us.

**E** Moreover, just as every part of us receives from our soul, so also we, by a similar reason, since we are parts of the whole, receive from that Soul of the whole as parts. Finally, what is written—"all soul has care for all that is inanimate"—signifies precisely this: as if outside the Soul of the world nothing of soul is left anywhere. For it is she who cares for the whole inanimate realm.

<margin>
11
The Soul of the world cannot be divided into many parts if it were to have the body, dimensions, and number of a body.
</margin>

**F** To these things, therefore, it must first be said that those who posit that souls are of the same form—because they are allowed to touch the same things—while admitting the same common genus, also cause other souls not to be parts of one. Instead, they would more probably infer that they are one and the same, and any one of them exists in the whole. **G** But by making them one, they will reduce them to something else. This indeed no longer exists as belonging to this one or that one, but as belonging to nothing itself—whether of the world or of another—it performs whatever is judged to be the life of the world and of any animate being. For it seems to be correct that not every soul belongs to someone, since it is an essence; but that some soul exists which belongs to no one at all; and those which are said to belong to someone, become so occasionally by accident <note>original: "secundum accidens" — meaning it is not the soul's essential nature to be trapped in a body, but a circumstantial occurrence</note>—that is, they turn out to belong to someone.

Perhaps, however, in these matters it should be understood more clearly how "part" is said. It is proper to set aside the mode of parts appearing in bodies—whether the body is uniform or multiform—denoting only this: when in bodies of similar parts a "part" is named, it is a part according to mass, not according to species, as we can judge in "whiteness." For the whiteness which is in a portion of milk is not a part of the whiteness which is in the whole.

<column-break/>

**A** To one seeking other things and wishing to find them, we should rightly seek that which seeks within ourselves; what it is, and what we might grasp by observing it. Because of this, even in the Universal Mind there is duality; so that someone might persuasively say that there is a part, one more so, another less. **B** We must look into how the receptacles of the gods are formed; but this we shall do when we seek how soul comes to be in body. Now, however, let us return to those who say that our souls are from the Soul of the All. For perhaps they will say it is sufficient that our souls reach as far as the Soul of the All reaches. Nor are they merely similar in form; even if one grants they are similar, they are not shapes of it, for things of the same form are parts of the whole.

**C** They will also bring forward Plato, who held this opinion when he attempted to say the universe is ensouled: as our body is a part of the body of the All, so also is our soul a part of the Soul of the All. **D** They say it is shown that we follow the rotation of the All, and we receive our characters and fortunes from there, so that by being within it and being contained by it, we receive soul. And just as each part of us receives from our soul, so we too, being parts of the whole according to the same reasoning, participate in the Soul of the All. And that which is said, "all soul takes care of all that is inanimate," means the same thing: that no soul is left outside, after the Soul of the All, but it is the Soul of the All itself that is placed in charge.

**E** Against these things, it must first be said that by making them of the same form and granting they reach everywhere, and giving them a common genus, they make them something other than a part. Rather, they might more accurately say that the same soul is one, or that each is the whole. **F** By making it one, they refer it to something else, which no longer belongs to this one or that one, but belonging to nothing—neither the world nor anything else—it does itself what is judged to be the life of the world and of any ensouled thing. For it is right that not every soul belongs to someone, since it is an essence; but there is a soul that belongs to no one in the whole, and others become so occasionally by accident.

**G** Perhaps it will be clearer how "part" is spoken of. We must set aside the way a part is in bodies, whether it be a uniform body or a multiform one. We should only note that among things of similar parts, when a "part" is spoken of, the part is according to mass or according to form; for example, the whiteness in a portion of milk is a part of the whiteness of the whole.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the soul, specifically addressing whether individual human souls are "parts" of a single Universal Soul. This is a central question in Plotinus's Enneads, Book IV, as it defines how we relate to the divine and the cosmos.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

<margin>A</margin> Regarding milk, whiteness belongs to a part of the liquid, but it is not a "part" of the quality of whiteness itself. This is because whiteness is not a quantity; it is entirely without magnitude or physical size <note>original: "magnitudine carens"</note>. Let that be our starting point. However, when we speak of a "part" in relation to physical bodies, or when we use the term as we do in mathematics—saying that two is a part of ten (speaking here only of pure numbers)—or as a segment of a circle or a line, or even as a specific theorem is called a part of a general science. <margin>B</margin> In the case of units and geometric figures, just as in physical bodies, it is necessary that the whole is diminished when divided into parts, and each individual part must be smaller than the whole. <margin>C</margin> For all such things are quantities, and they possess their existence within that quantity; since they are not the same quantity as the whole, they must necessarily be larger or smaller. But surely, a "part" cannot be spoken of in this way regarding the soul. For quantity does not exist in the soul as it does in a "ten" <note>Plotinus uses the "decad" (ten) to show that if you break a number into units, the units are no longer the whole number</note>, where the whole is the ten and the part is a single unit. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, many other absurdities would follow; for ten is clearly not a single unified thing. Furthermore, either every individual unit would be a soul, or the soul itself would be composed of many soulless parts. Added to this is the fact that it is generally agreed that a part of the soul is "of the same kind" <term>uniform: *uniformis* or *homoeides*, meaning the part has the same nature as the whole</term> as the whole. Yet in a continuous physical object, it is not necessary for a part to be the same as the whole—for example, a part of a circle is not a circle, nor is a part of a triangle necessarily a triangle. Or at least, not all segments are similar to the whole. <margin>D</margin> But philosophers admit the soul is uniform. Likewise, in a line, a part is still a line, but it differs in size. If, in the soul, the difference between an individual soul and the Whole Soul were a matter of size, then the soul would be a quantity and a body, since it would derive its very identity from its magnitude. But all agree that souls are similar and complete in themselves. Furthermore, it is evident that the soul is not divided the way physical magnitudes are; <margin>E</margin> nor would those thinkers admit that the whole is cut into pieces, for otherwise they would utterly destroy the whole itself. If the soul were a single universe from the beginning, it would now be a mere name <note>The author suggests that if the "Whole" is divided, the original unity no longer exists except in name, like wine poured into many cups</note>; as if someone were to say that the wine currently in a specific cup is a "part" of all the wine that was once in a single vat. But could it be that "part" is used for the soul in the same way a single theorem is called a part of an entire science? In that case, the entire science remains whole and intact, while the "partition" is simply the expression or act of a specific part. <margin>F</margin> In this sense, every part has the entire science within it potentially, and the science remains a whole. If this is how the universal soul and other souls are related, then the universal soul—of which the others are parts—would not be the "Soul of the World," but rather just one of the parts. In this view, all parts would be uniform and come from a single source. But how then is one the Soul of the World, <margin>G</margin> while the other is the soul of a specific part of the world?

**BUT** should we perhaps understand "parts" here as one might speak of an animal? For instance, could we say that the soul in a finger is a part of the total soul...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding milk, whiteness belongs to a part, but it is not a part of whiteness; for whiteness is not a quantity, but is entirely lacking in magnitude, and let that be so. But when, in things that are bodies, we speak of a part, or we take a part as we do in numbers, just as two is said to be a part of ten (though let this be said only of pure numbers), or as a part of a circle or a line is usually called, or as a proposition or notion is customarily called a part of a science. <margin>B</margin> In units and figures, it is necessary, just as in bodies, that the wholes themselves are diminished by division into parts, and then the individual parts are smaller than the whole. For since these are quantities, and possess their being in quantity itself, not existing as the same quantity, they necessarily become larger and smaller. Certainly, under this condition, a "part" cannot be spoken of in the soul. For quantity is not in it in such a way that the whole is like a "ten," and the part like a "unit." <margin>C</margin> Indeed, many other absurdities will occur, and undoubtedly ten is not a single thing. Moreover, either each of the units will be a soul, or the soul itself will be constituted from all soulless things. Added to these points is that a part of the total soul is conceded to exist as uniform; but in a continuum, it is not necessary for a part to be such as the whole is, like parts of a circle or triangle; or at least not all small parts are similar in which it is permitted to take a part, such as triangles within triangles. But in these, a specific change occurs. <margin>D</margin> Yet they confess that the soul is uniform. Likewise, in a line, a part indeed has the property of being a line, but here too it differs in magnitude. But in the soul, if the difference is taken in magnitude—namely, of the partial soul to the whole soul—the soul will be a certain quantity and a body; since it would have received the very difference by which it is a soul from quantity. But all souls are conceded to be similar and whole. It is clear, moreover, that it is not divided as magnitudes are divided; <margin>E</margin> nor would they even admit that the whole is cut into parts; otherwise, they are going to lose the whole itself entirely. And if there had been a universal soul from the beginning, it will now be a name only; as if someone, when wine is distributed into many cups, said that what is individually in the cup is a part of the whole wine. But is "part" perhaps taken in the soul just as a certain proposition is called a part of the whole science? The science itself, nevertheless, remains whole and entire, while the partition is like a certain utterance and act of each part. <margin>F</margin> In this matter, each part has the whole science in potential; and this science, meanwhile, is nonetheless whole. But if a part is judged in this way in the soul, both the universal and the others, then surely the universal soul, of which the others are such parts, will become something specific; therefore, it will not be the Soul of the World, but this too will be one of those that are placed in the category of a "part." <margin>III. Is it not, if we imagine a whole and then parts, but that they are contained in the whole, that a part of one member is one part of the whole soul?</margin> Therefore, all parts of the one soul would exist as entirely uniform. But how is this one the Soul of the World, <margin>G</margin> and that other one the soul of mundane parts?

**BUT** should parts be accepted here as if someone might say of one animal that the soul which is in a finger is a part of the whole...
