<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether individual souls are parts of a single Universal Soul. On the previous page, the author argued that the soul cannot be divided like a physical quantity or a number, because a "part" of the soul must still contain the nature of the "whole" soul.</meta>

PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

...of the soul, which is in the whole animal. But indeed this argument either results in no soul being outside the body, or everything not being in the body, but rather outside the body in the manner of what is called the *Soul of the World* <note>original: "mūdi animā" - The Anima Mundi, the divine essence that Neoplatonists believed animated the entire physical universe</note>. This is certainly worthy of consideration; but for the present, we must deal with it as if through an image. For if the whole soul offers itself to all individual living things, and thus each soul is called a part—for if it were divided, it could by no means offer itself to each one—it will surely be the same whole everywhere, one and the same existing in many at once. But in this way, it could not be maintained that one soul is the "whole" and another is a "part," especially in those cases where the same power is present. For even where one function belongs to one thing and another to another, such as with the eyes and ears, we should not say that one part of the soul is present in the eye and another in the ears—for such a division belongs to other kinds of things—but rather that the very same soul is present, though a different power <note>original: "potētia" - the Greek *dynamis*, meaning the specific capacity or faculty of the soul</note> exerts itself in each. For all powers are in both; but because the instruments <note>original: "instrumēta" - the physical organs of the body</note> are different, we must believe that different perceptions occur. Yet all are in the *species* <note>original: "speciē" - likely translating the Greek *eidos*, meaning the formal essence or type</note>, and are entirely capable of being reduced to that species, being formed through all things. This is also evident from the fact that it is necessary for all things to eventually arrive at a unity. It is clear that the nature of the instruments through which this is achieved cannot receive everything; and while the experiences <note>original: "passiones" - the passive reception of sensory data</note> are made different by the instruments, the judgment is carried out by one and the same thing, acting like a judge, attending equally to what is said and what is done. But it has been said that what is one is everywhere, even in those actions which do not differ. If the senses were only there, it would not be possible for each of them to understand, but rather for *that* soul to do so; but if there is a proper intelligence, then surely each soul remains within itself. But when the soul is also rational, and is called rational as a whole, how can it be called a part? It is not a part of the whole, but rather it will be entirely the same.

<margin>
IIII. Agreement: whether the higher souls are distinct in the intellect, and how it ought to happen in the soul, and how some imagine souls to be distinguished for a time; they are in agreement on both sides.
</margin>

### WHAT, then, shall be said, 
if it is indeed thus *one*, when someone asks us from this point—first doubting whether it can be one in all things at the same time, then when the soul is in the body, how it is also outside the body? For perhaps it follows that everything is always in the body, especially the soul of the universe. For it is not said to leave the body as ours is, and even if some say that this body is left behind, the soul will not be entirely outside the body. But if it is entirely outside the body, in what way will this soul desert it, while that one does not, since it is the same? In the Intellect itself, which is distinguished by "otherness" within itself according to its parts (yet these always exist together since the essence itself is indivisible), no such doubt will ever arise. But in the soul, which is said to be "divisible around bodies," this very claim that all souls are one involves us in many doubts—unless one firmly establishes that the One exists in itself, not falling into the body at all. Then one might say that all souls, both the soul of the whole and the others, exist together as one up to a certain point, insofar as they do not become the property of any individual. Suspended by their own limits and "breathing together" <note>original: "cōspirātes" - a reference to the cosmic sympathy or 'conspiration' of all things</note> toward the heights, in the meantime they direct and extend themselves here and there like light; but they remain equally *dependent upon and connected to one another* <note>original: "εξηρτημένας & συνεπας ἀλλήλαις"</note>.

<column-break/>

...and would be a part of the whole animal. But since the argument either makes no soul exist outside the body, or all of it not in the body, but outside the body as that which is called the "Whole." It must be considered less [strictly], and we should examine the arguments as images. For if someone provides the whole of them to all the living things in part, or if each is still a part, if divided, it would not provide itself to each. But the same whole will be everywhere, being one and the same in many at once. In that case, it would no longer allow one to be the whole and another to be a part, especially in those things where the same power is present. And since there is one work for one part and another for another—as for example the eyes or the ears—it must not be said that one is seen by one part of the soul and another heard by another part (for dividing is for other things), but the same soul acts with a different power in each. For all powers are in both. But because the organs <note>original: "ὄργανα"</note> are different, the perceptions are thought to become different. All are in the forms <note>original: "εἰδῶν"</note>, and are able to give form to all things. It is also clear that it is necessary for all things to go toward the one; but the nature of the organs is such that they cannot receive everything. And the experiences become different because of the organs. But the judgment comes from the same source, like a judge. And the reason belongs to the one who has observed both the things said and the things done. But since it is everywhere, it has been said that it is not in the differences of the works, wherever the senses are. Not that each of them thinks, but rather that soul. But if it is likely that there is a thinking, then each remains by itself whenever it is the rational soul. But where it is called the whole rational soul, that which is called a part is also the whole.

WHAT then should we say if it is thus one? Someone will seek the answer from this: first being at a loss as to how it is possible if it were in all things at once; then when it is in the body, or how it is not in the body. Perhaps it will follow that it is always in the body, especially the soul of the universe. For it is not like our soul is said to leave the body; even though some say this one is left behind, it will not be entirely outside the body. But if the same things will be outside the body, how will one soul leave and another not, since it is the same? In the case of the Intellect, which is separated in itself and into parts—for it is indivisible even while being the same—no such difficulty would take hold. But in the case of the soul, which is said to be divisible around bodies, the claim that they are all one would have many difficulties, unless someone says that being is in itself, not falling into the body; and that all those souls—the soul of the whole and the others—are until a certain point contracted, as it were, by not becoming the property of anything. And then again toward the things above, as if also falling upon them like light...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the relationship between the individual soul and the Universal Soul. Having previously established that the soul is not divided like a physical body, he now explores why the Universal Soul remains transcendent while individual souls become entangled in the care of specific bodies.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

<margin>Greatness</margin>...that which is already distributed on earth by dwellings, yet is not separated from itself, but is nonetheless one. The Soul of the Universe always stands above because it does not experience a descent, nor a degeneration into the depths, nor a turning toward the things that follow after. Our souls, however, are less excellent because a specific part in this world is assigned to them, and they bend themselves toward lower things due to the nature of the body, which requires care and worry. Indeed, the <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "anima vniuersi" — the divine soul that animates the entire cosmos</note> through its lowest part is like the life of a massive tree; it governs the plant without labor or worry. However, just as worms might arise in the wounded or rotting parts of a tree, the lowest part of our soul is like those small animals generated in a decaying part of the plant. This is how the body of souls exists within the universe. But another part of the soul, which conforms to the higher part of the Universal Soul, is like a farmer who applies himself to caring for the animals born in the plant and is worried about cultivating it. Or perhaps one might say that a healthy man, running along with other healthy people, is in control of those things to which he has dedicated himself, whether in action or <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: "speculandis" — the act of intellectual or spiritual vision</note>. But a sick man, occupied with caring for his body, is said to be "at the mercy of the body" and has effectively become a part of that body.

<column-break/>

That which is indeed on earth is already distributed by dwellings, yet not disjoined from itself, but is nonetheless one. The Soul of the Universe always remains superior, because no descent happens to it, nor any degeneration to the lower regions, nor a turning toward subordinate things. Our souls, however, are less excellent because a definite part is assigned to them in the world, and they bend themselves toward lower things because of the nature of the body, which requires care and anxiety. Now truly, the World Soul, through its lowest part, is similar to the soul of a massive tree, which governs the plant without labor or anxiety—as when worms arise in wounds. The lowest part of our soul behaves as if small animals were generated from a tiny, rotting part of the tree. This is also how the "body of souls" relates to the universe. But the other soul, which conforms to the sublime part of the Universal Soul, is like a farmer who dwells on caring for the animals born in the plant and is anxious in cultivating the plant. Or perhaps one might say that a healthy man, moving with other healthy people, is focused on those things to which he has devoted himself, whether in acting or in contemplating; but a sick man, occupied in caring for his body, is said to be focused on the body itself, and to have become a creature of the body.

<margin>I. How human souls are propagated in the Divine Intellect, distinct yet joined, and how they remain as many in themselves, and under what ruler they conceive of living beings.</margin>

BUT by what further reason is this soul yours, and this one his, and that one another's? For perhaps this soul belongs to a person according to their own mind, but not this one, but rather that one through the supreme part? But in this way, what will Socrates be when the soul of Socrates itself is in a body? Will it not perish when it is most fully in the best state? But surely none of the things that *are* ever perish; for <term>Intellects</term> <note>original: "intellectus" / "nous" — the second hypostasis in Plotinus's system, the realm of pure thought and Forms</note> do not perish there. They are not joined into one by a bodily condition, but each remains there in its own "otherness," preserving the very thing that is its essence. Thus, in succession, souls are also suspended from there, existing according to each Intellect and as certain <term>Reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes" / "logoi" — the formative principles or blueprints of reality</note> of those Intellects, more unfolded than they are—as if a great deal were made out of a little. Being close to that "little," they seem to wish to be divided among those indivisible things, yet they cannot proceed to the extreme limit of partition. For preserving both the Same and the Other simultaneously, each remains one, and all are one together. It has certainly been said, as far as the summary of the argument is concerned, that all souls are derived from one; I mean that many come from one in the same manner as with the Intellect, divided in the same order, and yet not divided. And indeed, that soul which remains is a single "reason" of the Mind, and from it come partial and immaterial reasons, just as they exist there.

<margin>VI. On the difference of souls, to what extent they are more or less connected to the Intellect, both universal and particular, and to what extent they are connected to the universe or a part of the universe.</note>

BUT why is it that the World Soul, which is said to be of the same form as others, made the world, but the soul of an individual did not, especially since each one contains all things within itself? For it has already been said that it is possible to be in many things at once and still remain. Now this must be explained. For perhaps how the same thing in different places either acts or suffers, or relates to both, will be known from these things. Perhaps it is better to consider this very point: in what way and for what cause did that soul make the world, while others only hold a certain part?

He also explores how souls remain distinct yet unified within the Divine Intellect as formative 'Reasons.'</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the relationship between the individual soul and the Universal Soul. Having previously established that the soul is not divided like a physical body, he now explores why the Universal Soul remains transcendent while individual souls become entangled in the care of specific bodies.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

...govern the world. Perhaps it should not seem a wonder to anyone that among people endowed with the same knowledge, some rule over many things, while others rule over fewer. But if someone should perhaps ask for what reason this is the case, he will answer: that some represent a greater distinction among the souls, insofar as these do not depart from the whole, but resting there, they establish a body around themselves. Others, however, rule over bodies already made and already brought forth; by their favor, these souls have obtained their lots in a certain gradation, as if those [higher souls] had already prepared dwellings for these [lower souls]. Nor is there lacking another <margin>A</margin> difference, through which these indeed look up to the universal <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectū" — in Plotinus's philosophy, the second hypostasis, the realm of pure thought and divine ideas</note>, while others look rather to particular intellects, namely each to its own. Perhaps these too could have made the whole, but since <margin>B</margin> that [Universal Soul] has already made it, the faculty is no longer given to these after that one has first laid the foundations. But in the same way, anyone would wonder if perhaps some other soul had built it first. It is better, however, to say that the primary power and craftsmanship belong to the primary soul for this reason: because it adheres more to the things above. For a greater power arises in the souls that dwell there more attentively. For by preserving themselves in safety, they most easily establish a foundation there; for it belongs to a greater power not to suffer in the things it makes, but the power remains from on high. Remaining therefore in itself, it makes things consequently for others that lie below; but for the others that have approached or proceeded forth, they seem to have descended into the depths. Perhaps as far as the matter is concerned, much is drawn downward, and it draws them with it, so much so that through their thoughts they even seem to have already descended. For what <margin>D</margin> is said in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue regarding the creation of the physical world</note> about the second and third order of souls must be explained: that some adhere closer to the higher things, while others depart further, just as it has already happened among us. For not all souls stand similarly toward the higher realms, but some are, as it were, united to the things above, others finally approach near to the gods, and others finally achieve this less, insofar as they do not use the same things. But these powers use the first, another the second, and those finally even the third, although each soul possesses all the powers.

<margin>
DEVOUT
Responses to
doubts,
especially
regarding why
our souls
are not the
World Soul.
</margin>
Let what has been said of these things suffice for now. But as for what is said in the *Philebus* <note>Plato's dialogue on pleasure and the good life</note>, which we suspect comes to light lest perhaps <margin>E</margin> all souls are parts of the World Soul: he [Plato] does not wish there what one might think, but what was then most useful to argue—namely, that the world is animate. For striving to prove this, he says it is absurd to say that the heaven is inanimate, since we, who have a body that is a part of the worldly body, have a soul. For in what <margin>F</margin> way would the part have had a soul if the whole were inanimate? But the opinion of Plato is most clear in the *Timaeus*, where once the Soul of the World is made, the others then arise in the same <term>mixing bowl</term> <note>original: "patera" — referring to the Crater in which the Demiurge mixes the soul-stuff of the universe</note>; in which they are also mixed and made conformable to it; but he assigns the difference of those through second and third degrees. And as for what is said in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato's dialogue on the soul and beauty</note>, that "every soul has care for all that is inanimate," what wonder is there? For what else governs, forms, orders, and makes the nature of the body, if not the soul? Nor is it said that this soul indeed can do it naturally, while that one can do it nowhere. Whence he adds: "The perfect <margin>G</margin> soul therefore existing itself," namely that of the universe, "elevated more sublimely, neither immersed, but (as I might say)..."

<column-break/>

...administer the cosmos. It is nothing marvelous that those possessing the same science should rule, some over more, others over fewer. But why, someone might say, do things hold this way? It is either the difference of souls, or rather that some have not departed from the whole, but hold their body there around it, while others, when the body already exists, have received their lots as sister souls to ready-made places, as if the former had prepared dwellings for them. There is also the fact that some look toward the whole intellect, others more toward their own particular ones. Perhaps they themselves were in labor to create, but it is not possible for them to create the whole, since another has already received it. They would have made the same things if the whole had been placed elsewhere, but it is better to say that the power of those who have conceived the things above is greater, for they hold themselves in that guard which the middle makes. For it is of a greater power not to be affected by the things it makes; and the power is from above, remaining however in itself, it makes and carries the things that follow. But for those that have stretched into the depth, they are drawn along with their thoughts, and these are the second and third by their proximity, seeking the well-living, just as among us. Not all souls stand the same toward the whole, but some are there, while others descend as they approach, and some have their place according to the powers they exercise. But some use the first powers, others those after them, others the third, though all possess all powers.

THESE things then are so. But the saying in the *Philebus*, which gives the suspicion that the other souls are parts of the whole, means the argument not as one thinks, but as it is resolved. He says it is the same fire of the heaven being animate then and primarily, as it would be an absurd thing to say the heaven is soul-less, when we who have a part of the body of the whole have a soul. For how could the part have it, if soul were not in the whole? It is most clear from his opinion itself, which he makes in the *Timaeus*. The soul of the whole having been born, he later makes the others, mixing them from the same bowl from which the whole was made, making them of the same kind, and the others he calls second and third. And in the *Phaedrus*, he says "every soul cares for all that is soul-less." For what else would it be, which by nature governs the body, and either fashions it or these things, which the soul does and has, either it is of its nature to have the power, or not. The perfect soul, he says, that of the whole, traveling on high, is able, but does not hold [a specific body].

Plotinus reconciles his views with Plato's dialogues, arguing that while all souls share the same essence, they differ in their proximity to the divine Intellect and their resulting governing power.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s relationship to the material world. Plotinus is explaining how individual human souls, though originating from the same source as the Universal Soul, maintain their own distinct identity and agency, even when influenced by the physical "temperaments" of the body or the movements of the stars.</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

...poured out over the world, it also does what concerns the perfect soul, and thus it governs. But the soul that is broken <note>original: "διεῤῥωγυῖα" — referring to a soul that has lost its integrity or "wings" upon descending into a body</note> does not govern the whole, but rather produces the effects of each individual part. These things exist in symmetry <term>Symmetria</term> <note>The mathematical proportion and harmony that Plotinus believes binds the universe together</note> with the eternal movement of the whole, being carried from that source, and ruling over things in accordance with it. For the soul contains a greater number of natural patterns <note>original: "τύπων" (typon) — formative principles or "blueprints" for physical things</note>, sufficient to produce many doctrines, as well as the various dwellings of waters, airs, and cities, or the temperaments <note>original: "κράσεις" (kraseis) — the balance of bodily fluids believed to determine health and personality</note> of bodies. What do we say it is for us, being in the universe, to possess something of the whole soul and to be subject to the celestial rotation? We oppose another soul to these influences, especially one disposed to challenge them. In the end, we are born from these things; even regarding mothers, we say that the soul of the embryo is different from that of the mother.

THESE things, then, might be resolved in this way. And the matter of sympathy <note>original: "συμπαθείας" (sympatheias) — the cosmic "feeling-together" where parts of the universe affect each other instantly</note> does not hinder our argument. For since all souls arise from the same source as the soul of the whole, they are in sympathy with one another. Indeed, it has been said that the soul is both one and many. The individual parts are always chosen by the whole of the rotation. It has been said elsewhere regarding the differences of the soul; and let it be said briefly that they might differ in relation to their bodies, especially in their characters, and in the works of their intellect, or from their previous lives. For according to their previous lives, it is said that the choices are made for the souls <note>A reference to the Myth of Er in Plato's Republic, where souls choose their next lives based on past experiences</note>. But if one takes the nature of the soul as a whole, differences are found there too, where they are called second and third ranks. Furthermore, all these powers are in all souls; but at one time one is active in the path—how it knows, how it desires—while another soul looks toward different things, even seeing into the infinite. And these souls are full and perfect, and this is common to all, but the whole composition in them is varied, in which every rational principle <term>Logos</term> is manifold and varied, just as the souls of living beings have many forms. If this is so, and there is a coordination, and beings are not completely separated from one another, nor is anything found to be made at random in the order of beings, not even in bodies, it follows that there is a certain sequential number. For beings must stand firm, and the intelligible things themselves must be the same, and each must be one in number. For in the case of bodies, which flow according to their nature, they obtain their form by imitating true beings. But among true beings, which are not made from composition, being itself consists in that which is one in number, which exists from the beginning; neither does that which was not before come to be, nor will that which is, cease to be.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Floating above, it acts upon the world, and insofar as it is perfect, it manages it in a similar way. Furthermore, where it introduces the soul with broken wings <note>original: "fractis pennis" — an allusion to Plato’s Phaedrus, where the soul loses its wings and falls into a body</note> as if it were flowing, it clearly shows that such a soul is different from the World Soul <term>Anima Mundi</term>. Therefore, the fact that souls follow the rotation of the universe, and derive their characters and sufferings from it, in no way signifies that our souls are merely small parts of it. For the soul, by the nature of its locations, waters, and air, can repel many things threatening from the heavens; <margin>B</margin> habitation, urban customs, and the temperaments of bodies also resist celestial influences. And even if we say that we, enclosed in the universe, have some life from the World Soul and suffer from the celestial rotation, we have nevertheless introduced, on the contrary, another soul resisting all these things, clearly showing itself to be different by that very resistance. As for the claim that we are born within the world, we respond similarly: a fetus in the mother’s womb has a soul other than the maternal <margin>C</small> soul—namely, one that enters from elsewhere.

<margin>VIII How souls differ: and how they are immortal, remaining in their own form: and how the World Soul contributes to the life of all.</margin>
AND these matters have been resolved for us for the time being. Furthermore, the fact that souls are in sympathy with one another should not hinder our reasoning: for since they all flow from the same source as the World Soul, they naturally feel with one another. Now it has been said that the soul is both one and many. The difference of the part to the whole has been discussed; the difference of the soul has been discussed; <margin>D</margin> and now let a summary also be given. We say, therefore, that besides bodily differences, souls differ among themselves, especially in their morals, in the duties of thought, and even from the settings of a previous life. For it is written by Plato in the *Republic* <note>original: "Republica" — referring to the belief in reincarnation and the soul's choice of its destiny</note> that subsequent lives are chosen by souls according to their preceding lives. If anyone considers the nature of the soul as a whole, he also places differences here, where he arranged second and third degrees. Furthermore, it has been said that all souls are all things, but according to what is active within it, <margin>E</margin> each is a particular thing: that is, one soul strives in action, another in knowledge, another in desire; and they differ further because they look at different things, and the things they look upon, they both are and become. A full and perfect duty belongs to souls, yet not the same for all; but they are situated as if the whole coordination of them were said to be varied. For there is one universal principle <term>Ratio</term>, manifold and varied, like a living being that is both animate and multiform. If this is so, and there is a coordination, then <margin>F</margin> beings are not completely separated from one another, nor is anything found to be made at random in the order of beings, not even in bodies; therefore, it follows that a certain sequential number exists. For beings must stand firm, and the intelligible things themselves must be the same, and each must be one in number: for in this way, each is called "this certain thing." Whereas in the genus of bodies individual things flow back naturally, as those which obtain an accidental form, surely "being" according to form <margin>G</margin> is found here perpetually by a certain imitation of true beings. But among true beings, which are not made of composition, "being" itself consists in that which is "one in number," which indeed exists from the beginning; neither does that which was not before come to be, nor will that which is, cease to be.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the soul. Having previously discussed how the soul relates to the celestial spheres and individual temperaments, he now moves to the mechanics of how a single, indivisible soul can be present in many places or bodies at once without being split into pieces.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

Since if there is anything that the soul itself produces, it certainly A will not create it out of matter; and if this is so, it must add something essential from its own nature. For this reason, there would be a change within the soul itself if it now performs more or less than before. Furthermore, it may be asked why it acts now, and not always in the same way. Moreover, that which is created will not be eternal if it admits to "more" or "less" <note>Plotinus argues that true, eternal being is constant; variation in intensity suggests a temporal, material involvement</note>. Yet the soul is established as being of such a nature. How then will it be infinite if it is limited by something? Perhaps it is infinite in power <note>original: "δυνάμει" (dynamei) — potential or power</note>, because this power itself is infinite, not in the sense B of something that can be divided into infinite parts, since God himself is not limited. This is how it is with souls: for they say they do not exist by a limit, for each soul is what it is not by being "so much" in size, but it exists as much as it wills; nor is it ever led to step outside of itself. Rather, it flows through the whole, for it is so arranged by its nature that it runs through bodies into bodies. Yet it is not pulled apart from itself, even when it is in the finger of the hand and in the foot at the same time. Thus it is in the universe, into whatever C part it runs, appearing in one part and then another, just as in a plant. Even if a part is cut off, the soul remains in the original plant and also in that part which has been separated from it. For the body of the universe is not its owner; rather, the soul is everywhere as if in a single unit. Regarding animals that arise from putrefaction <note>The ancient belief in "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from decaying matter. Plotinus uses this to show that life appears whenever matter is ready to receive it</note>, if many animals should arise from one, the soul of the whole animal is no longer in that body; for the body then no longer has its own proper receptacle, yet the soul has not perished. Those things which, through putrefaction, are made fit D for the generation of animals, receive a soul partly from these and partly from those. Since the soul itself is never absent, yet one thing may be able to receive it while another cannot, those things which thus become living do not force there to be many souls: for they depend on the one, insofar as that one remains one. Just as in us, when certain parts are cut away and others sprout in their place, the soul is absent from the former but present in the latter, so long as it remains one. In the universe, however, it remains always one. The things which are in the universe E partly retain life and partly do not, while in the meantime the powers of that same soul persist.

<margin>
IX
The second question: In what ways is the soul introduced into the body, and how the soul is in the world, and how it creates the world and the elements within it, and how it is everywhere.
</margin>

### We must furthermore ASK how
the soul is introduced into the body: for it does not seem unworthy of wonder and investigation. There are two ways through which the soul enters the body: one occurs when the soul is already joined to a body and is either changing from one solid body to another, or moving from an aerial or F fiery body into a terrestrial one. Many do not call this a "change of bodies" <note>reincarnation or metempsychosis</note> because the source from which the introduction comes is hidden. The other way is that by which the soul falls from the incorporeal <term>Incorporeal</term> <note>Existing without a physical body or material form</note> into any body whatever: which is indeed the first commerce of the soul with the body. It is worthwhile to first consider this fall, and what sort of experience occurs when the soul—still entirely pure and living apart from the body—first takes upon itself the nature of a body. Perhaps it is proper G to begin from the soul of the whole, or rather it is necessary to pursue the truth about it: so that for the sake of a clearer teaching, we may begin to describe its entry and the animation of the body in words; since there was never a time in which...

<column-break/>

...since everything that it will be, it will not be from matter A eternally; it must add something essential from itself, so that there will be a change around that very thing, if it now does more or less. And why now, and not always in the same way? Furthermore, that which is brought into being is not eternal, if indeed it admits of more and less; and the soul is of such a kind. How then is it infinite, if it should have some limit? Or is it infinite in power, in the sense that all power is infinite, but not divisible into infinity, since B God is not limited? And these souls, therefore, in the sense that they are each what they are by no foreign limit, will not be "somewhere" in a limited sense; but the soul itself is as great as it wills to be. And it is never dragged out of itself, but it reaches everywhere, where its nature is to flow upon bodies; it reaches the bodies. On the one hand, when it is by itself, and is in the finger and in the foot, so it is in the total universe, wherever it may reach in one part or another of a plant. And C when a part is cut off so as to exist separately, it is both in the original plant and in the part cut from it. For the body of the universe is not such that the soul is everywhere in it as in a single thing. In the case of animals, if many should come from one, that soul is no longer the soul of the total (for the soul is not in the body in that way), but the body has it, and that part of the soul is its own, where even the imperfections from decay, being suitable for the generation of life, D receive a soul, some from these and some from those. It is never absent from where it can be, but some things are not able to receive it, while others are; and the things that thus become ensouled do not make more souls. For they depend on the one, just as that soul is one, as in our own case. When some parts are cut off and others grow from them, the soul has withdrawn from the former and is present to the latter, so long as the one remains. In the universe, this soul remains one, but the things that exist E, some live and some are set aside, while the same souls remain.

### BUT how does a soul come to be in a body?
We must seek the manner, or how. For surely this was then worthy of wonder and investigation. Now, the manner of the soul’s entry into a body is twofold. In one way, the soul comes to be in a body by being "re-bodied" <note>original: "μετασωματούμενη" (metasomatoumenē) — changing from one body to another</note>, as when it goes from F aerial bodies into a terrestrial one, which they do not call "re-embodiment" because the source from which the entry occurs is unclear. The other way is from the incorporeal into a kind of body, which is indeed its first communion of soul with body. It would be right to examine this, what the experience is that occurs, when G for the first time the soul has communion with a body, being pure before it has anything of the nature of a body about it. Regarding the soul of the whole, it was perhaps more necessary to begin from there. The argument must then, from above, lead to the teaching of the ensouled, thinking that it clearly happens there as well. It is since the sou- <note>original: "ψυ-" — catchword for the next page's first word, "psychē" (soul)</note>

<summary>Plotinus explores the paradox of how the soul can be infinite and indivisible yet present in multiple bodies or parts of a body simultaneously. He explains that the soul is not "divided" like matter but is present wherever a body is fit to receive its life-giving power.</summary>
<keywords>soul, body, infinity, Plotinus, Neoplatonism, animation, universal soul, putrefaction, reincarnation, incorporeal</keywords>

--- Page 414 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on how the soul occupies the body, this page explores the relationship between the World Soul and the physical universe, using the famous analogy of a net in the sea to explain how the soul encompasses and sustains matter.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

The soul animates this whole universe <note>original: "ψυχὴν τήδε τὸ πᾶν"</note>. If the body were self-subsisting, the soul would not be able to grasp it, and the whole would be something immobile. By separating these two in our logic—soul and body—we can analyze the composition of things through our intellect. Truly, the body is like a garment for the soul. Since the body of the universe is what it is by nature, and it moves toward its destination, it creates a place for itself, and thus becomes a body. If its state were observed clearly, it would remain like a great light shining out; yet at the furthest edges of the fire, darkness emerges nearby. Since the soul grew toward something <insert>higher</insert>, it was not right for it to be without reason <note>Greek: "λόγου ἄμοιρον", meaning devoid of the guiding principle of the universe</note>. It receives what is called a dim reflection, but not the dimness of colors. It is built like a beautiful and complex house, which is not unlike its builder. However, it does not mix with the soul, but is deemed worthy of care everywhere, being better for having the soul with it. In this beauty, it participates in the soul's power as much as it can; it remains unharmed by those things that are far off. For eternity remains forever, living through the soul, with the soul entirely governing it. The things produced by the soul are its cause. The body is not something separate from the soul; rather, if it is better for the body, it is like **nets in the water** <note>original: "ὕδασι δίκτυα". A signature Plotinian analogy: the net is the physical world, and the water is the soul that fills and surrounds it</note> which are filled with life but cannot escape the nature of the water they are in. The net, once cast, extends into the sea as far as it can, and even if its parts are moved, it remains in its nature. It is not light, for the body occupies the same space as the light. So, wherever the body extends, the soul is there; but if the body were not there, the soul would have no concern for physical magnitude. For the universe exists only as far as the soul is present. It is defined by eternity for as long as it chooses; it does not belong to itself. And how is it a shadow? It is as great as the *Reason* <note>term: "Logos" — the formative principle or "blueprint" of the soul</note> that comes from the soul. This *Reason* makes a certain light and magnitude, working through the whole as far as the Form has cast its magnitude.

<column-break/>

A. This whole universe would be animated; nor could the body ever subsist if the soul were absent, nor could matter ever prevail as something formless. It is permitted, however, to distinguish these from one another in our thoughts and words. For every composition may be resolved through thought and speech. Now, the matter stands thus: unless there is a body, the soul will not step forward, for there is no other place where it can naturally propagate itself. But if it is to go forward, it will build a place for itself, and therefore B. it will generate a body. But while its status is strengthened in that very state—just like a great light shining at its peak—meanwhile, as if at the very edges of the fire, a shadow results. Looking upon this shadow, the soul, after it stopped, gave it form. For it was forbidden that anything close to the soul should be without reason. Therefore, in that which was made next, something very thin and obscure was received, which is also called "vibrant." Thus the world was made like a beautiful C. and greatly varied building; it is not separate from its maker, nor again did it mix itself with him, but the whole was everywhere judged worthy of care and diligence, so much so that it benefits its very existence and its beauty, as far as it was able to participate in that existence. To the author, however, this same connection is harmless. For remaining in the heights, he presides. Truly, the world is so animated that it does not so much possess its own soul, as it is possessed by the soul; it is overcome, not overcoming; it is held, not holding. For the world D. lies in the soul that sustains it, and nothing in it is devoid of that soul. Just as a **net in the water** is soaked with life, yet is unable to escape the nature of the water in which it is placed; rather, the net is extended as the sea is extended, as far as it can go. For each of its parts cannot be anywhere other than where it is placed. But the soul is by nature so great and so immense E. because it is not limited to a certain size. Thus it can embrace the entire body in one and the same hold, and wherever that body extends, the soul is there also. And if that body did not exist, the soul would have no care to occupy such magnitude, for it is within itself whatever it is. For the universe is only as great as the soul occupies; and the world is determined in size only insofar as the soul, proceeding forward, preserves it. Thus, the vibration is as great as the *Reason* <note>original: "ratio", translating the Greek "logos"</note> depending from the soul. Such was the *Reason* that it created a magnitude as great as its species wished to produce a multitude.

<margin>
x
The World Soul generates the world not by choice, but by a natural fecundity <note>meaning: a natural, overflowing creative power</note>, full of reasons and full of forms similar to those reasons.
</margin>

F. When we have considered these things, we must return again to those who never turn back <note>likely referring to the eternal, unchanging divine principles</note>, to accept all beings together, such as the air, light, sun, or moon. And we must take the light and the sun again all together, yet holding an order of first, second, and third. And here let us consider the soul as always consistent; then the first things, and those following after, like the last bits of fire in the rear—observed G. at first at the edge like the shadow of a fire. Then, this shadow is also illuminated at the same time, so that a Form is, as it were, superimposed upon that which was first made entirely obscure, and clothes it. Truly, it is adorned according to the *Reason* by the power of the soul itself, which possesses itself through the whole as one, through these *Reasons*.

<sig>I 4</sig>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the World Soul creates and sustains the physical universe not through a labored choice, but as a natural radiation of its own power, similar to how light creates a shadow at its edge. He uses the analogy of a net in the sea to illustrate that the world exists within the soul, rather than the soul being "inside" the world.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<column-break/>

A it should adorn: Just as within seeds the <term>formative principles</term> <note>Latin: "rationes"; Greek: "logoi". These are the internal blueprints or active forces that shape biological life.</note> mold and form living beings as if they were certain small worlds. Whatever touches the soul is thus perfected from that source, just as the essence of the soul is naturally disposed. This the soul does not by some external opinion, nor by waiting for counsel or consideration; for if it were, it would not be done by nature, but by an acquired art. For art itself comes later than the soul, and it imitates shadowy and weak copies, fabricating certain playthings of little importance, using many machines to mold these <term>images</term> <note>Latin: "simulachra"; Greek: "eidolon". Plotinus often uses these terms to describe the physical world as a mere reflection of a higher reality.</note>. B But the Soul, through the power of its own essence, is the mistress of the body in such a way that these things are not made or arranged in any way other than how the soul itself directs them. Indeed, even those things which are made from the beginning cannot resist its will. In subsequent things, however, due to mutual obstacles everywhere, the <term>matter</term> <note>Latin: "materia"; Greek: "hyle". The raw "stuff" of the universe which Plotinus views as resistant to the Soul's perfection.</note> is often so hindered that it does not receive its own proper form—that form which the principle lurking in the small seed intended. C There, however, since the whole form arises from it, and those things which are made possess order simultaneously, that which is produced comes forth beautiful without labor or hindrance. Within the Soul itself are established some things as shrines for the Gods, others as dwellings for men, and others accommodated to other beings in like manner. For what should better be made by the soul than those things which it has the power to make? For it is the property of fire to make things hot, and of another thing to make things cold; but the work of the soul is partly from itself into another, and partly within itself. D In inanimate things, that which comes from them lies as if asleep within them; but that which tends toward another thing can perceive what it is able to experience from there, making it similar to itself. Now, it is common to all things to strive toward their own likeness in their actions; but the work of the soul, both what is within itself, is a certain wakefulness and efficacy; and that which tends toward another is very similar. E It brings it about, therefore, that other things live—whatever things do not live by themselves—and that they live by such a life as the soul itself lives. This soul, therefore, living in <term>reason</term> <note>Latin: "ratione"; Greek: "logoi". Referring here to the governing logic of the universe.</note>, also hands over reason to the body, like an image of its own reason. For as much life as it imparts to the body, that is an image of life, and at the same time it imparts bodily forms of which it possesses the principles. It possesses, moreover, the principles of the Gods, and of all things. For this reason, this world also possesses all things.

<margin>
25
The proper function of the soul’s magical power:
To lead a God into these lower realms.
</margin>
AND it seems to me that the ancient sages, whoever wished to have the gods present with them, by fabricating temples and statues, directed the sharp edge of their minds into the very nature of the universe. From this, they noticed F that the nature of the soul is everywhere quite easy to lead and prone to be guided, and can be captured most easily of all if someone fabricates something that can easily be affected by it, and by being affected, can obtain some portion from it. Now, that which is easily affected is that which is in any way suited to imitation, like a mirror capable of seizing a certain <term>form</term> <note>Latin: "speciem"; Greek: "eidos". This refers to the visible appearance or the intelligible essence of a thing.</note>. For the nature of the universe fabricates all things with a certain wonderful artistry in imitation of those things whose principles it possesses within itself. G And since each thing is made in this way, certainly the principle in matter—which was formed according to a higher formative principle of matter—is joined to that God according to whom it was brought forth, and toward whom the soul looked...

<column-break/>

to adorn, just as in seeds the <term>formative principles</term> mold and shape living things, like some small worlds. For wherever it touches the soul, it makes it so, as the making of the soul's nature holds: and it makes it not by an acquired judgment, nor by waiting for counsel or inquiry; for thus it would not make by nature, but by an acquired art. But art is later than it, whereby it imitates, making dim and weak imitations, certain playthings, which are not worth much, using many machines: * molding an <term>image</term>: B But the soul by its essence, in which it is the sovereign power of bodies, has governed the beginnings into that which was easily and as it became good for it; having been opposed to its own will, if those things which come after hinder each other, often happening upon something other than the form of the image. Thus the principle does not wish for a small thing. C But there, the whole form being made by it, and the things that are made having order together, the thing that is made is beautiful without strain and without hindrance, having been prepared. And in it, some are statues of gods, others are dwellings of men: and the other things for others, which must be made by the soul. Or does it then have power for the making? Of fire, indeed, it is to make things hot; and of cold, another thing. But of soul, one part is in itself, the other in another. D And that which is in itself, who would not call soul? One part from them, as if being possible, that which is in them: the other into another, to make it like toward that which is able to be affected. Or is this common indeed, to everything that is, to lead into likeness to itself. And the work of soul is both something of wakefulness, and that which is into another likewise. E Life, therefore, also makes the other things, as many as are not from themselves. And it makes them by living, and always living by living, by which principle it gives principle to the body, an image which it has. Or is it an image of life, as much as it gives to the body: or forms of bodies. Of which it has the principles, and it has also of gods, and of all things through all things, and the world has them.
AND it seems to me that the men of old, as many as wished gods to be present to them, having made temples and statues, looking into the nature of the whole, F took it into mind that the nature of the soul is everywhere easily led. To receive it indeed would be easiest of all, if one were able to be affected by something divine, being made like it or imitating that which is drawn, just as a mirror is able to seize a certain form. For the nature of the whole, having made all things with good craft, into imitation G of those things of which it had the principles. Since each thing had been made, the principle comes to be in matter, which according to the formation before matter, joined itself to that god according to whom it was made: and toward whom the soul looks, and had...

<summary>Plotinus explains that the World Soul shapes the physical universe effortlessly through internal principles ("logoi"), contrasting this natural creation with the "weak playthings" of human art. He also justifies the use of religious statues and temples, arguing that they act as "mirrors" that catch the reflection of divine souls due to a natural sympathy between levels of reality.</summary>

# BOOK THREE.

<column-break/>

A ...as it were. Therefore, it was not possible for anything here to be devoid of divinity, nor again for that divinity to descend into these lower things. For that <term>Intellect</term> <note>Latin: "mens"; Greek: "nous". In Plotinus’s system, the Intellect is the first emanation from the "One," containing all true Being and forms.</note> is itself like a divine sun, which serves as our model of reason. Next after this follows the Soul, suspended from the Intellect; it remains even while moving, for it directs its own limits toward this sun. It acts as a middle point through itself, so that the things following it are bound to the higher realm, acting like an interpreter of the things that are led from there to here, and of the things B that are led back from here to there, as far as a soul can return into the Intellect. For nothing is entirely severed from another, nor is it separated by distance; rather, the difference lies in a certain quality or mission. It exists in a simple state, yet not according to physical location; everything there breathes together, remains together, and yet is distinct. They are diverse only in that they are never abandoned by the higher powers; the "branches" of the soul, as it were, spread themselves out from the beginning all the way to this world. C For this reason, insofar as they exist and are said to look back toward the Intellect, they are called divine; for the soul itself never looks anywhere else but toward that source.

<margin>
XII.
On the difference of souls here, and on their greater harmony, and on the consonance of the world.
</margin>

### HUMAN souls, however, see their own <term>images</term> <note>Latin: "simulachra"; Greek: "eidolon". Plotinus refers to the physical body and the material world as reflections or shadows of the true Soul.</note> as if looking into the mirror of Dionysus <note>This refers to an Orphic myth where the young god Dionysus is distracted by a mirror and then captured; Plotinus uses it to symbolize the Soul being fascinated by its own reflection in matter and thus "descending" into the body.</note>. They rushed down from above, yet even they are not cut off from their own beginning and Intellect. They did not descend in their entirety; rather, they have reached down to the earth, but their "head" remains fixed above the heavens. D It happened, however, that they departed further because their middle power is compelled to care more diligently for the body; for that very thing into which they descend requires constant cultivation. But Jupiter the Father <note>Plotinus uses "Jupiter" or the "Father" to represent the Demiurge or the governing principle of the universe.</note>, pitying the laboring souls, made the bonds in which they toil dissoluble <note>Meaning he made the body mortal so that the soul is not trapped in matter forever.</note>. Thus, he established intervals of rest at certain periods of time, in which they might live free from bodies, so that they too might occasionally be where the <term>Soul of the World</term> <note>The "Anima Mundi," which governs the entire universe without becoming exhausted or trapped by it.</note> always is, never troubled by these cares.

E For the world already possesses what it needs; it is and shall be sufficient unto itself, consisting perpetually according to its nature through cycles of time, and restored perpetually to the same state through certain circuits. This occurs through the measured spans of defined lives, in which these lower things are brought into harmony with the higher ones. All these things are carried out under a single, mutually ordered principle, as far as the descent and ascent of souls and all other things are concerned.

F The fact that there is a harmony in souls according to the order of the universe—yet in such a way that they do not merely depend on it, but rather accommodate themselves to it in their descent, creating a single concord with the world’s revolution—is proven by the way their fortunes and choices of life are signified by the patterns of the stars. It is as has been said: the universe gives forth one harmonious sound, and the whole is G designated through musical consonances. This would not be the case unless the world acted and suffered each thing according to those established revolutions and orders, and through the spans of lives and the types of journeys which souls travel—some indeed there, others...

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Soul acts as an intermediary between the Intellect and the world, and that human souls, while descended into bodies, still have a "head" in the divine realm. He describes mortality as a mercy from "Jupiter" that allows souls to rest from the toil of caring for the material body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the descent of the soul. On the previous page, he established that the Soul acts as a link between the divine Intellect and the physical world. # PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK IIII.

...truly in heaven, but at other times turned toward lower things. The <term>Intellect</term> <note>Latin: *intellectus*; Greek: *nous*. In Plotinus’s philosophy, this is the second "hypostasis" or level of reality, containing all the eternal Forms and ideas.</note>, however, is always in its heights and never falls from its seat; instead, it remains firmly fixed on high, sending down something of itself through the soul even to these depths. The Soul, being closer to the Intellect, is drawn by the <term>Form</term> <note>Latin: *speciem*; Greek: *eidos*. The eternal blueprint or essence of a thing.</note> flourishing there and passes it on to the things that follow. Some things remain always in the same condition, while others change in various ways, though the Soul holds this wandering variety within a certain fixed order. Souls do not always descend equally, but sometimes more and sometimes less, even if they go to the same kind of being. Therefore, each soul falls toward its own prepared place according to the likeness of its own disposition. For according to how it has become similar to this or that state while there, it is then carried into a human being, or into this brute animal, or into another.

<margin>
XIII.
The divine Law implanted in souls leads them both spontaneously and necessarily to their appropriate ends.
</margin>

**T**HEREFORE, what is said concerning the inevitable Law and divine <term>Justice</term> <note>Latin: *iudicio*; Greek: *dike*. Plotinus views "justice" as the natural, cosmic order of cause and effect.</note> is established in nature, which contains and commands all things, so that each thing that is made—every <term>image</term> <note>Latin: *simulachrum*; Greek: *eidolon*. A physical body is considered a mere shadow or reflection of the soul's true form.</note>—proceeds in order according to its prior choice and disposition. Each soul has a form congruent and near to it, toward which it has conceived an affection; the soul looks toward that which then sends it where it must go and introduces it. It does not go into a body, or into a specific kind of body, just because it chooses to at that moment, but when the prescribed limit sends it, the souls descend as if of their own accord to where they must and enter. For each has its own appointed day. When this day approaches, they slide down as if a <term>herald</term> <note>Latin: *precone*; Greek: *kerykas*. A public crier. Plotinus uses this to show that the soul responds to a cosmic "call" when its time for incarnation arrives.</note> were calling them, and enter the body suited to them. They behave almost as if they were being moved and carried by the powerful forces and attractions of the <term>Magi</term> <note>Ancient Persian priests believed to have power over natural and supernatural sympathies. Plotinus uses this as a metaphor for the "magnetic" pull of nature.</note>. Furthermore, they behave like the distribution of parts in a whole living being, moving at a certain fixed time and producing things like hair, the beard, and horns; and at a certain time, impulses and strengths for such things; likewise flowers in plants, which never sprouted before, and other things in these beings distributed by certain ordered rules. Souls proceed neither entirely of their own will nor by compulsion. For their proceeding is not attributed to their will in the sense that they are said to choose deliberately, but rather they leap forth by nature, just as we are often provoked toward sexual desires or toward certain honorable actions by an instinct rather than by the counsel of reason. But such a fate always belongs to such a person; this moment occurs for one, and that moment for another, as decreed by fate. Consequently, the Intellect superior to the world has its fate to remain there continually, and from there to send something down here; then individual things, subject to the common law, are sent down from there step by step. For a common rule is implanted in each, and the law itself receives the power to fulfill its duty not from the outside, but is handed down on the condition that it exists within those who use it, being carried about everywhere by them. Then, when the time approaches that the law itself has decreed, it is acted upon by those who have the law within them, so that they fulfill the law as it moves them, and because it is founded in them, it carries out its decrees more powerfully, as if weighing them down by its own weight, for a long time and with zeal...

<column-break/>

...some indeed in heaven, and some turning toward these [lower] things. Now the whole [Intellect], because it has nothing outside of itself, does not depart from its own, but is established; it sends things here through the soul. The soul, from its proximity, is disposed according to the form from there; it gave what it had, sometimes in one way and sometimes in another, according to the things from of old. It descends, but not always equally; sometimes it is the same, and sometimes less. And how do you [souls] meet the same? Those whose condition always follows each according to the likeness of their disposition; for indeed, according to the likeness, each is carried: some into humans, others into different animals.

For the inescapable [Law] and Justice are thus established in nature, to hold the order for each thing, according to the image that comes to be in each, by choice or as it otherwise receives. Thus, for each type of soul, things are similar to each, toward which it has a disposition. That which is in them sends and introduces them where they must go, not just into a body or into this specific body, but also at the time of their extension, like actions according to their relations. Or in another way, the soul's race arrives, as if heralds were calling them to descend. And they enter the suitable and fitting body, just as each thing comes to be, as if by the powers of magi and some strong attractions they are moved and carried. Just as in each individual, the administration of the whole is completed, moving in a set time and generating things like hair and the growth of horns, and now toward these certain things and perceptions, according to the motion. And again, the administration of trees, which proceeds by certain orders, and these are the petitioners, whether sent or whether the voluntary part falls as if free; but as it is with nature, or natural unions, or certain prior beautiful actions, or motions of reason. But it is always fixed by what came before, and for such a person such a thing, and for this person this, which each world-order has; it has its parts fixed there, which come and are sent. And each thing is sent by the universal law. For the universal is implanted in each. And the law does not have its strength for completion from the outside, but is given to be in those who use it, and is carried about by them; and they desire it, and the divine happens then by those who have it. So that they themselves complete it, as they carry it about and have strength from it being established within them, as if weighing upon them and desiring...

<meta>catchword: stimu- [stimulus]</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the soul's descent into a physical body is governed by a natural, internal law rather than external force or purely conscious choice. This process is compared to biological growth, like the timing of a beard or the blooming of flowers, suggesting that the soul "falls" into the body that best matches its inner disposition.</summary>

...an internal stimulus strikes from within, directing it to go to that place where its own innermost law dictates it should proceed.

### XIV.

<margin>
Concerning the connection of this world through the higher realm, and the gift of the gods descending into the work of the world.
</margin>

**S**ince these things are so, this world, possessing many lights and being illuminated by souls, is adorned according to higher principles. It receives various ornaments from different sources—both from those gods and from other <term>Intelligences</term> <note>Latin: *mentibus*; Greek: *nous*. These are the divine "Minds" or eternal truths that exist above the physical world.</note> who provide souls. Something of this truth is likely indicated by the myth which says: after <term>Prometheus</term> <note>Prometheus represents "Forethought" or the providential power that organizes the material world.</note> had fashioned the woman, the other gods also adorned her. This refers to the story that she was made of earth mixed with water, and that she was given a human voice. Furthermore, because she resembled the goddesses in appearance, <term>Venus</term> <note>Aphrodite in the Greek text; the goddess of beauty and desire.</note> and the <term>Graces</term> <note>The Charites; goddesses of charm, nature, and creativity.</note> bestowed gifts upon her, and each god gave a different gift. She was named <term>Pandora</term> <note>Literally "All-gifted."</note> because of the gifts and the givers. For all the gods gave something to this fashioned creature—a creature already formed by a certain providence. However, the fact that <term>Epimetheus</term> <note>Latin: *Epimetheus*; Greek: *Prometheus* (in this specific manuscript line, though context implies the brother "Afterthought"). Plotinus uses this to show the soul's choice to accept or reject the lower world.</note> refused the gift offered to him, what else does it signify than that the choice of the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The "intelligible" refers to the higher realm of pure thought, which is more excellent than the physical world of the senses.</note> gift is superior? That creator is "bound" because he seems, in a way, to touch his own work; but such a bond is external, and he is eventually freed by <term>Hercules</term>, for there is a power within him by which he is, in a sense, already free. But let each person take these myths as they will. It remains certain that through these stories, the gifts coming down from above into the world are revealed. Therefore, these things seem consistent with what was said previously.

### XV.

<margin>
Concerning the descent of souls, their migration, differences, fate, free will, and how providence connects fate and free will together.
</margin>

**S**ouls proceed by turning away from the intelligible world; first they enter the heavens, and there receiving a body, they glide through it into more earthy bodies, as far as they stretch out in length. Some pass from heaven into lower bodies, and in turn, others pass from some bodies into others. This happens when their power is not sufficient to raise them back up from this place, due to their weight and <term>forgetfulness</term> <note>Greek: *lēthē*. In Platonic thought, the soul "forgets" its divine origin when it becomes too focused on the physical body.</note>, which drags them down so that they are cast headlong through lower things. Souls become different from one another either because of the diversity of the bodies they enter, or because of fortunes, or again because of their education. Or perhaps they carry a difference within themselves from the start, and they vary either because of all these factors or some of them. Consequently, some souls succumb entirely to the <term>Fate</term> <note>Latin: *fato*; Greek: *heimarmenē*. The deterministic chain of cause and effect in the physical world.</note> that rules here, while others yield to fate in some matters but live by their own right in others. There are also those who allow whatever is necessary to be endured, but can nevertheless reserve for themselves whatever belongs to their own duty. These live according to a different constitution of laws that embraces all beings together, turning themselves to another rule. This order is woven together from all the reasons and causes found here, as well as from the movements of souls and the laws depending on them. It is in harmony with the higher realm, taking its beginnings from there and weaving all subsequent things together with them. It preserves all those things unshaken which are able to maintain the character of the higher world. Other things it leads around as their own nature requires, so that in those who descend, there is a cause for their being placed here or there, and for others to be situated differently.

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus uses the myths of Prometheus and Pandora to explain how the physical world is "adorned" by divine gifts and how souls descend into bodies. He argues that while souls are influenced by fate and their physical environment, they retain an internal power to live according to a higher, divine law.</summary>
