<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s journey and the cosmic order from page 483, transitioning from the myth of Pandora to a philosophical defense of divine justice and the mechanics of the soul's descent into the physical world.</meta>

->PLOTINUS’ ENNEADS, BOOK IV<-

<margin>
XVI.
Since it is not in the nature of things for punishments to be carried out unfairly. Whatever happens to good people contrary to what seems just, such as poverty, want, or disease, perhaps occurs because of offenses in a previous life. For these events are woven together and even foreshadowed, since they truly seem to occur according to reason. Might these things happen according to natural laws, and should they not be classified among those things properly called punishments, but rather as consequences of them? For example, if a building falls and someone underneath is killed, should we not see how even in these two things a kind of unity remains, or how one thing is broken or pushed by another? This is discussed more fully regarding what is called "useless": it is not an evil to the sufferer, and it contributes to the harmony of the whole; perhaps it is not even unjust, since individual things are dispensed justly based on what came before. Plotinus, on the differences of fate.
</margin>

**P**UNISHMENTS are carried out justly when they are inflicted by **A** just causes, and they should be regarded as just, as is fitting, and led toward justice. Whatever happens to good people contrary to what seems just—such as being poor, in want, or diseased—perhaps occurs because of offenses in a previous life. For these events are woven together and even foreshadowed, since they truly seem to occur according to <term>reason</term> <note>Latin: *rationem*; Greek: *logon*. In Neoplatonism, this refers to the underlying rational principle or "form" that governs the development of the physical world.</note>. Might these things happen according to natural laws, and should they not be classified among those things properly called punishments, but rather as consequences of them? Just as if, while someone is building, the person **B** who was underneath is killed; in such a case, even in these two events, a kind of unity remains, or one thing is broken or pushed by another as is shown. This is discussed more fully regarding the concept of things called "useless": it is not an evil to the sufferer, and it contributes to the harmony of the whole; perhaps it is not even unjust, since individual things are dispensed justly based on what came before. For it must not be thought that some things are related to each other in an orderly way, while others are diverted here and there entirely by whim. For according to **C** natural causes and consequences, and one reason and one order, it is necessary that all things happen, and we must believe that even the smallest things are coordinated and woven together. Therefore, that which is inflicted as an injustice by one person upon another is indeed an injustice for the one who does it, and yet it is not outside of cause and order: once coordinated within the universe, it is certainly not unjust in that context, nor is it even inflicted unjustly upon the sufferer, but rather it was fitting. For if the one who suffers is good, whatever he **D** suffers ultimately ends in good. It must certainly be believed that this common order of the universe is not devoid of divinity and justice, but renders what is appropriate to each according to a most exact reason, though it keeps the causes hidden within itself, and thus provides an opportunity for those who are ignorant to bring accusations.

<margin>
XVII.
Just as the king's primary household staff is closest to him, so the first orders of souls inhabit heaven, and thus they are animated closest to the entire world, as they are more fit to receive it, etc. But the earthly body is furthest removed from incorporeal nature. Truly all souls illuminate heaven, and give, as it were, the greatest and first part of themselves to the celestial globe, while other things are illuminated by those that come after. etc. But those that descend most deeply illuminate another thing in another way from within. There is surely something like a center, and near this a circle shining from it, and besides these another circle, light from light: beyond these, however, there is no longer a circle of light, but one already in need of foreign light. Let this be the <term>rhombus</term> <note>Latin: *rhombus*; Greek: *rhombos*. Plotinus uses this geometric term to represent the material world or the outermost "skin" of reality that lacks its own light and must be illuminated by the soul.</note>.
</margin>

**F**urthermore, that souls first descend from the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>Latin: *mundo intelligibili*; Greek: *noētou kosmou*. The eternal realm of pure thought and Forms that exists above the physical universe.</note> into heaven can be inferred from these facts. For if heaven is the most excellent thing in the realm of the senses, it is deservedly closest to the last of the intelligible things: from there, therefore, celestial things are first animated and receive [life], since they are much better suited for receiving it. But the earthly body is both the last and thus the furthest removed in degree of origin; it is less able to participate naturally, as it is furthest from incorporeal nature. Truly all souls illuminate heaven, and give, as it were, the greatest and first part of themselves to the celestial globe, while other things are illuminated by those that come after. But those that descend most deeply illuminate another thing **E** in another way from within, though it is not profitable for them to have fallen so far. There is surely something like a center, and near this a circle shining from it, and besides these another circle, light from light: **F** beyond these, however, there is no longer a circle of light, but one already in need of foreign light, due to a lack of its own light. Let this be the rhombus, or rather such a sphere, which receives from the third degree to which it is closest, and shines back by its proximity; thus a great, permanent light illuminates it, and according to reason, a splendor proceeds from it: and it illuminates the rest, **G** partly remaining, and partly [extending] further <note>original: "καὶ κατὰ λόγον ἐξ αὐτῶ αὐγὴ· τὰ δ' ἄλλα συνεπιλάμπεται, τὰ μὲν μένοντα, τὰ δ' ἐπιπλέον"</note>.

<column-break/>

Therefore, the punishments that occur to the wicked are justly rendered according to order, just as they are led from that source by the good toward an agreement outside of justice—such as punishments, or poverty, or diseases—should we say these happen because of previous sins? For these things are woven together and signified, and they themselves and their reasons come to be, and these reasons are natural. Or should those things directed toward punishment be placed among the things that follow from those, such as the fall of a man’s building, or dying in a collapse, or how something happens to someone, or how two things are carried in an order, or how that which falls is wounded or stopped? And the impossibility of evil, which is not useful for the one who suffers but for the whole, will be established there as not unjust. From the preceding things it has been justified, or that the things which are not just are organized in the whole, if indeed they occur according to causes. And natural consequences and reasons, so that in one order, even the things that are beneficial must be organized and thought of everywhere. And the doing of an injustice by one toward another: it is indeed unjust for the one who did it, and the doer is not released from the cause. But when organized with the whole, it is not unjust for that [whole], nor for the one who suffers: but it was necessary thus. And if the one suffering is good, the end of these things leads to good. One must not believe that the organization is without God, nor unjust, but exact in rendering what is fitting, though the causes are hidden, and that they are known to provide causes for blame.

That the souls themselves first descend from the intelligible into the region of heaven, one might calculate from the things believed. For if heaven is the oldest in the sensible realm, and some soul appearing from the last of the intelligibles should come from there: these are the first things it partakes of, as they are more suitable for partaking. But the earthly is the last, and is naturally less able to partake of soul than the nature of bodies. I look around. Indeed, all souls illuminate heaven, and give as it were their first entire self to those things, and the other things are illuminated by the later ones; and those descending below them, for they go as if toward another place below, and it is not better for them to go forward so much. For there is as it were a center, and upon this a circle shining from it: and upon these another, light from light. And outside of these, no longer another circle of light, but one still needing its own light, for lack of a ray. But it is brought by the light itself, or surely from the third person, or surely itself, it is that which is illuminated. The great light, remaining, shines out, and indeed according to reason a ray comes from it: and the other things are illuminated with it, some remaining, some [extending] further...

<meta>catchword: extending-</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that earthly suffering, such as poverty or illness, is not random but is part of a divine, "woven" order of justice linked to past lives. He also describes the soul's descent as an emanation of light, moving from the intelligible center through celestial circles down to the dim material world.</summary>

-># BOOK THREE.<-

Looking at the splendor of the illumination, those things that require more care for their radiance are like the pilots of ships tossed in a storm. These pilots apply themselves more intensely to the task of steering the ships, and in their preoccupation, they forget themselves; they are often unaware that they have been placed in such danger that they may be submerged along with the shipwreck. In the same way, such souls depart from themselves to a great extent. Then, they are held more tightly, bound by the bonds of <term>enchantment</term> <note>Greek: *goeteias*; Latin: *fascinationis*. This refers to the soul being "magically" or naturally attracted to the beauty and needs of the physical world.</note>, being devoted to the care of nature. But if every animal were like the universe—having a perfect and sufficient body, established beyond the dangers of passions—certainly the soul that is said to be present in the body would not be "present" in a burdensome way, but would provide it with life while remaining entirely in the heights.

<column-break/>

**A** turning away from the thorough illumination of the subject. Then, since those things which have been illuminated require the greatest care, just as the pilots of a tossing ship apply themselves more heavily to ruling the vessels, and forgetting themselves, they hardly notice that they are established in such a crisis that they are submerged together with the shipwreck: so also such souls depart from themselves as much as possible. Then they are held more narrowly, bound by the chains of enchantment, clearly devoted to the care of nature. But if **B** any animal were such as the universe is, having namely a perfect and sufficient body, and established outside the dangers of passions: surely the soul which is said to be present to the body would not be present, but would provide life to it, meanwhile remaining altogether in the highest places.

<margin>
XVIII
The second soul according to Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a later Neoplatonist who commented extensively on these themes.</note> is now sometimes joined entirely to the body by light, and then they are the parents of reason from that power of <term>discursive reasoning</term> <note>The process of step-by-step logical thought, as opposed to immediate, intuitive insight.</note> out of ambiguity; so that when they have reached the intellect, they comprehend all things without time, or at least in the shortest time. Likewise, souls converse among themselves in the heavens without speech, as if through a mutual notion from intelligence. In the bodies of the air, souls and dæmons form voices.
</margin>

POSTHAC it must be asked whether the soul uses the discourse of reason before it descends into the body, and after its departure. Perhaps indeed rational discourse **C** happens while it inhabits the body: since it is placed in ambiguity and solicitous with cares, and as if already weakened. For to need the discourse of reason for the function of life and truth happens from a certain <term>detriment of the mind</term> <note>In Plotinus’s thought, needing to "think through" something logically is a sign that one does not have the immediate, perfect vision of the truth that exists in the higher realm of the Intellect.</note>: just as the consultation of reason happens in the arts when the craftsmen are in doubt, as if falling short of perfection. But where no difficulty or defect is opposed, the art immediately overcomes and acts. But if souls live there without ratiocination, how shall they further be called rational? **D** Someone might perhaps respond that they are called rational because they are able to reason, if ever it should be expedient. But it is necessary to accept such reasoning: for if someone accepts reasoning as a stable disposition and action, always flowing from the intellect and existing in the souls, and like a certain flash from there, then certainly souls will use a certain discourse of reason there. However, it is not to be thought (as I believe) that voices are used there, as long as they inhabit the **E** entirely intelligible place. But when they have bodies in the heavens, they do not use speeches there, which they are accustomed to use among us because of need or ambiguity. And since they do all things there according to a certain order and according to nature, they deservedly neither command anything nor consult. But they know their own things mutually among themselves through a reciprocal notion of consciousness, since even here we perceive many things in silence by intuition alone. There, indeed, every body is pure, and each of the inhabitants is entirely like an eye. Nothing there is hidden, nothing is feigned, but before you have said anything to another, the other understands. But it is not absurd for dæmons and souls inhabiting the air to use voices; for such are those animals.

<margin>
XIX
The divine life established from the property of habit or diagnosis. For the divine guidance is around bodies, because it accommodates individual things to their parts without itself. It is also called <term>indivisible</term>, because it is present as a whole to individual things. But the divine reason and mind are simply impartible, because they do not use the weaknesses of the body, and for that reason are separate.
</margin>

**F** WHETHER indeed in the soul "partible" and "impartible" are said according to the same thing, as if these two were tempered with each other: or rather by another reason, and according to another thing this indeed is predicted as impartible, and that as partible, as if different parts were arranged in succession, just as we are accustomed to call this one rational and that one irrational: it will be manifest to us after we have explained what we specifically mean by each. In the first place, **G** "impartible" in Plato is accepted simply, but "partible" not simply, but prepared for the soul.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul relates to the physical body. The previous page used the metaphor of a ship's pilot to describe the soul's care for the body; here, Plotinus refines the technical definition of how a single soul can be "divided" across a physical frame without losing its unity.</meta>

PLOTINUS ENNEAD IIII.

He says <note>Referring to the philosopher Plotinus</note> that the soul becomes divisible in the vicinity of bodies, yet it was not fundamentally made to be that way. Indeed, it is proper to consider the nature of the body—how it is and in what way it requires the soul to live—and that it is necessary for the soul to be present everywhere throughout the body, and to be entirely present to the whole. Every sensing thing, if indeed it is to feel through the whole body, must have reached a state of being <margin>A</margin> divided through the whole in a certain way. Existing everywhere, it is said—not without reason—to be divided. Yet, appearing as a whole everywhere, it is not said to be entirely divided, but rather to "become divisible" in relation to bodies. If anyone <margin>B</margin> should say that it is not divided in the other senses, but only in the sense of touch, the answer must be that it is also divided in the others: for if the body is that which receives the sensation, it is necessarily divided, though less so than in touch. Furthermore, the <term>vegetative power</term> <note>The "vegetative" or "nutritive" power refers to the soul's ability to govern growth and nutrition, a concept from Aristotelian biology.</note> and the power of growth are distributed in a similar way. And if <term>desire</term> <note>Latin: *concupiscentia*; Greek: *epithymia*.</note> flourishes around the liver, and <term>anger</term> <note>Latin: *iracundia*; Greek: *thymos*.</note> around the heart, the principle in these cases is much the same. But perhaps the soul does not receive these things in that mixture, but perhaps in another way, and these things arise from some of the things received there. However, reason and <margin>C</margin> intellect do not surrender themselves to the body. For their work is not performed through a bodily instrument; indeed, the body would be a hindrance if someone were to use it in meditations. For this reason, whether the <term>impartible</term> <note>Original: *impartibile* (Latin) / *ameriston* (Greek). This refers to something that cannot be broken into pieces, like a thought or a mathematical point.</note> (indivisible) and the <term>partible</term> (divisible) are different from one another, they do not seem to be fused into one, but are like a certain whole made of parts—each being pure and separated by their power. Yet if that which is divisible around bodies also possesses an indivisible quality from a higher power, then this same thing can be both indivisible and divisible at the same time, <margin>D</margin> as if it were forged both from itself and from a certain virtue coming down upon it from above.

<margin>
XX
The soul is not in the body as if in a whole, nor as a part in a whole, nor as a quality in a subject, nor as a species in matter, but the body is in the soul, as in that which gives life, encompasses, moves, and stabilizes.
</margin>

### XX
<margin>E</margin> It remains for us to explain whether these and other parts of the soul are in a "place," or whether some are not in a place at all while others are, and where and how; or whether no part at all is in a place. For if we do not assign a certain place to individual parts of the soul—placing nothing anywhere—then we shall judge it to be no more inside the body than outside it, and thus we shall leave the body in the soul. Nor could we explain by what reason those works are carried out which are performed through bodily instruments. On the other hand, if we describe a location for certain parts of the soul, but not for others, then those for which we have not described a location will not seem to be placed within us at all, so that we would not seem to believe that our whole soul is in us. However, <margin>F</margin> we ought not to place any of the parts of the soul, nor again the whole soul, in the body as if in a "place." For a place is something that encompasses and contains bodies. And where each divided thing lies, it lies in such a way that it cannot be the whole in any specific part. But the soul is not a body, and it is that which encompasses rather than that which is encompassed. Nor is it in the body as if in a vessel; for in that case the body would be left lifeless if either the vessel or the place contained the soul—unless perhaps the soul <margin>G</margin> is said to be gathered into itself, and by a certain transmission, sends something from itself into a vessel. And thus, as much as the vessel participates, so much would be taken away from the soul. But a "place," in the way the term is primarily used, is something incorporeal, not a body.

<column-break/>

He says <note>original: "φησὶ"</note> that it becomes divisible <note>original: "μεριστὴν"</note> in relation to bodies, even if it has not fundamentally become so. We must see how the nature of the body, which is to live, depends on the soul, and that the soul must be present everywhere in the body, present to the whole. And indeed, the sensing power, if it is to sense through the whole, must itself reach the point of being divided. For being everywhere, it might be said to be divided; but appearing as a whole everywhere, it would not be said to be entirely divided, but only to become divisible where bodies are concerned. If anyone should say that in the other senses it is not divided, but only in touch, it must be said that it is so in the others as well; since the body is that which partakes, it must be divided within, though less so than in touch. Its natural power, both for growth and in the same way, if desire <note>original: "ἐπιθυμία"</note> is around the liver and spirit <note>original: "θυμὸς"</note> around the heart, others place the rational part within it. But perhaps these things are what is taken up in that mixture. Perhaps in another way, either from something or having been taken up, this [is] reasoning and intellect. For these no longer give themselves to bodies. For their work is not woven through instruments in the body; for it is a hindrance to one, if one should use it in contemplations. But is each then both indivisible and divisible? And not as things mixed, but as a whole from parts, each remaining pure and separate in its power. And again, that which becomes divisible around bodies, because it holds the indivisible from a higher power, is the same whole by power, both indivisible and divided: a thing blended from itself and from the power coming into it from above.

If indeed we must say how these relate to the other parts of the soul, or if these are in some way [in a place], and the others are not in a place, and where, and from where, or how it is not natural for each to have a certain place assigned to the soul, having placed nothing, or rather the bodily things will be inside the soul, or let us make the soul itself that which [acts] in the works of bodily instruments, where we might be puzzled to say we have departed from it. Whether someone [thinks] we shall seem to have parts, so that not all of our soul is in us, we must not say that any of the parts of the soul, nor the whole, is in the body as in a place. For place is encompassing, and encompassing of a body, and each thing being divided is such that it is not the whole in any part. But the soul is not a body; it is that which encompasses rather than that which is encompassed. Therefore, not as if in a vessel—for the body would become lifeless, if it were like a vessel, or if place encompassed it—unless perhaps it were most especially established in itself, gathered together. As much as the vessel received, in that way [it would be] distributed to it; but place in the strict sense is something incorporeal and not a body.

<summary>This page explores the paradox of how the soul can be present throughout the entire body (divisible) while remaining a single, unified entity (indivisible). Plotinus concludes that the soul is not "in" the body like a physical object in a box, but rather the body exists within the life-giving influence of the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the inquiry into the soul's presence in the body. While the previous page discussed the soul's apparent "division" when it animates a physical frame, this section systematically tests various philosophical models for that relationship—asking if the soul is in the body like a liquid in a vessel, a part of a whole, or a pilot on a ship.</meta>

# BOOK THREE.

Therefore, why would the soul have any need <note>original: "ὥστε τί οὐ δέοιτο ψυχῆς;"</note> of the body? Furthermore, the body approaches the soul through its own limit, rather than the soul approaching the body. Many other objections could be raised against those who place the soul in the body as if it were in a "place" <note>Greek: "topos"</note>: for a place is always carried along with the thing placed within it. One would then have to ask what it is that carries the place itself along. Moreover, if a place is defined as an "interval" <note>Greek: "diastema"</note> or a distance, the soul would be even less likely to be in the body as if in a place. For an interval, **B** or space, must necessarily be a vacuum <note>Greek: "kenon"</note>; however, the body is not a vacuum. Perhaps it is said that the vacuum is that in which the body exists, and therefore the body itself is in the vacuum. Again, the soul will not be in the body as if in a "subject" <note>Greek: "hypokeimenon"; a technical term in logic for the underlying thing that possesses qualities.</note>. For that which is in a subject is merely an "affection" <note>Latin: "passio"; a property or quality.</note> of the thing it is in—such as color or shape—whereas the soul is something capable of existing separately. 

Nor is it there as a part in a whole: for the soul is not a part of the body. If someone should say that the soul is like a part in the "whole living being," the same **C** doubt will press upon us: how is it in that whole? For it is not in the body like wine in a jar, nor is the jar in the wine; nor is it in the body in the way something remains within itself. Nor is it there as a "whole in its parts," for it is ridiculous to call the soul the "whole" and the body the "parts." 

Furthermore, the soul is not in the body as "form is in matter" <note>referring to the Aristotelian concept of hylomorphism, where soul is the 'shape' or 'function' of the body's 'matter'.</note>: for a form in matter is inseparable from that matter. Also, the form arrives after the matter already exists; but the soul creates the form within the matter, seeing as the soul is something other than the **D** form itself. But if they say the soul is not a "formed" species but a "separated" one, it is not yet clear under what condition this species exists in the body; the soul would thus remain entirely separate. 

If these things are so, why is it said by everyone that the soul is "in the body"? Truly, since the soul is not visible to the sight, but the body is, we see the body and, perceiving that it is "animated" <note>literally "en-souled".</note> because it moves and senses, we say not without reason that the body "has" a soul. **E** Consequently, we think of the soul as being *in* the body. But if the soul could be seen and felt—existing as something full of life, embracing the body on all sides, and extending itself equally to the furthest extremities—we would never admit that the soul is in the body. Instead, we would say that the less important thing exists within the more "principal" thing <note>original: "principalius"; the governing or higher reality.</note>, and that the "contained" is within the "container," and that the "flowing" <note>the material body, which is constantly changing.</note> is likewise in that which does not flow <note>the eternal soul.</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>
XXI.
The soul is not properly "in" the body, but is distant and rules it only as a pilot in a ship: that is, by way of the oars and the rudder.
</margin>

What then shall we say if someone asks **F** how the soul is present to the body, without offering any explanation of his own? Likewise, if he asks whether the whole soul is in the body at once, or if different parts are there in different ways? Since none of the previously mentioned modes of "being in something" have been proven suitable for the soul's relationship to the body, it is said that the soul is in the body "like a pilot in a ship." This is a correct saying, insofar as it respects that faculty of the soul by which it is able to be **G** separated from the body; yet it does not fully provide the explanation we most desire. For if the soul is taken as a "navigator," the pilot would only be present "by accident" <note>a philosophical term meaning a non-essential or external connection.</note>; but if he is there strictly as a pilot, [how does this fit?] For he is not in the whole ship, in the way that the soul is in the whole body. But perhaps...

<summary>Plotinus critiques various physical and logical models for how the soul resides in the body, rejecting the idea that it is a "part" or "attribute," and suggesting instead that the soul actually contains and governs the body.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, soul, body, pilot of the ship, vacuum, place, hylomorphism, container and contained, metaphysics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the precise relationship between the soul and the physical body, moving from abstract spatial definitions to more organic and functional analogies, specifically comparing the soul's presence to that of a pilot on a ship and light in the air.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>
XXII.
The soul is present to the body in a separable way, just as light is present to the air. The body is in the soul, just as air is in light. The soul was present to the body because their natures are not shared; but the body was present to the soul because the soul's powers act through the body, and the body requires them, nor would the light be sustained by the body.
</margin>

**A** Or it should be stated this way: Just as art is present in its instruments—for example, in a rudder—if by chance the rudder were "ensouled" <note>original: "ἔμψυχος" (empsychos), meaning having a soul or life-force.</note>, so that the art of steering was within it, moving it skillfully from the inside. But there is at least this difference: such an art depends on something external. If, therefore, we place the soul in the body according to that model of the pilot <note>original: "gubernator/κυβερνήτης"; Plotinus is testing the famous Aristotelian analogy of the soul as the pilot of the ship-body.</note> instilling himself into the rudder as if into a natural instrument, the soul moves the body however it pleases. But will we gain anything more regarding our inquiry? Or will we perhaps doubt again how the soul is inside this instrument? Even if this mode is different from the others previously mentioned, we still long to find a clearer explanation and to come closer to the truth.

**B** But should we not rather say that the soul is in the body in the same way that fire, or rather light, is in the air? For light, while present to the air, is also not present to it; it is present through the whole, yet mixed with nothing. The light remains itself, while the air flows through it. And when the air moves outside of that space where the light is, it departs without retaining anything; yet as long as it is under the light, it is illuminated. **C** Therefore, it is correct to say here that the air is in the light rather than the light is in the air. For this reason, Plato, in his account of the generation of the world <note>A reference to the *Timaeus*, where Plato describes the World-Soul.</note>, did not want to say that the soul was placed in the body, but rather that the body was placed within the soul. He says that there is a part of the soul in which the body exists, and another part in which there is no body at all—namely, those powers of the soul of which the body has no need. **D** The same reasoning applies to other souls. We must certainly think that the remaining powers of the soul are not present to the body, but those which the body requires are present; and they are present in such a way that they are situated neither in parts nor in the whole body. For the purpose of sensation, the power of sensing is present to the whole sensing being; but for the purpose of carrying out actions, different powers are assigned to different parts. I speak of it in this manner:

> *Every power of the soul is entirely present in every part of the body, just as the soul itself is. But it is said to act in a specific place when it prepares instruments for itself there; it acts principally where its instrument has its origin. Thus, the acts of sensing and moving are attributed to the head, because that is where the nerves—the instruments of sense and motion—derive from. Similarly, anger is attributed to others around the heart, where its instrument, the "fiery blood" <note>Latin: "sanguis igneus". Ancient physiology often associated emotions with the temperature and quality of blood in specific organs.</note>, is located. Nutrition is located around the liver, where "airy blood" is its instrument. And the power of true reason, even if it has no communion with the body, is attributed in a way to the head, because the act of imagination is close to reason and shares in it.*

**A** Since the living body is illuminated by the soul, we say that different parts of the body receive this illumination differently. According to the fitness of the instrument for a task, it carries with it the power suited to that task. Thus, we name the "visual power" in the eyes, the "auditory power" in the ears, the "tasting power" in the tongue, and the "smelling power" in the nostrils. But we are accustomed to placing the "power of touch" in the whole body. For for this perception, the entire body seems to serve as the soul’s instrument. **B** Furthermore, since the instruments of touch are primarily in the nerves which hold the power for animal movement, and this power adapts itself there—and since the nerves originate from the brain—it is clear that the beginning of sensing and pursuing, and indeed the beginning of the whole living animal, is principally located here. From here, these powers derive to other parts, precisely where the origins of the instruments are located...

<column-break/>

**A** We must say it thus: as art is in its instruments—for example in a rudder—as if the rudder were ensouled, so that the steering motion comes from within through art. But in this case, it is different, because art is external. But if we place the soul in the body according to a model where the thing being steered enters into the rudder as if into a natural instrument, it moves it in whatever way it wishes to act. Has anything more come to us regarding the thing we seek, or will we again be at a loss as to how it is in the instrument? And what manner is it, if it is different from those before? We still desire to find out and to approach more closely.

**B** Should we then say it is this way: that the soul is present to the body as fire is present to air? For the air that has fire does not "possess" it as a fixed presence; rather, it is present throughout the whole and mixed with nothing. It remains itself while the air flows by. And when the air goes outside that in which the light is, it departs possessing nothing; but as long as it is under the light, it is illuminated. **C** So it is correct to say even here that the air is in the light, rather than the light in the air. Therefore Plato also did well when he said the soul is not in the body in every sense, but the body is in the soul. **D** He says that there is a part of the soul in which the body exists, and another part in which there is no body—clearly meaning those powers of the soul that the body needs. And indeed, concerning other souls, the same argument holds: of the other powers of the soul, one should not even say they are present to the body; but those powers which it needs are present—or rather, they are present without being established in the parts of the body, but rather in the whole. And for sensation, the whole sensing power is present; but for activity, it is present to different parts in different ways. I speak of it thus:

-> Chapter XXIII. <-

**A** When the body is illuminated with life by the soul, different parts of it participate in it differently; or, according to the fitness for the work to be done, the soul gives the power appropriate to the work. Thus it is said that in the eyes there is a visual power, in the ears an auditory power, a tasting power in the tongue, a smelling power in the nostrils, while the power of touch is present in the whole. For for this perception, the whole body is present as an instrument to the soul. **B** And the works of touch are primarily in the nerves, which have the power for the animal's movement; here they have this kind of pull. And the nerves beginning from the brain, which is the "source of sources" <note>original: "ἀρχὴ ἀρχῶν" (arche archon); the primary principle or origin.</note> of sensation, or generally of the whole animal, are established there, or it is clear that the origins of the organic...

# BOOK THREE.

->### CHAPTER XXIII<-

<column-break/>

Better, perhaps, to say that the starting point of the activity of that power is located there. For where the instrument <note>original: "ὄργανον" (organon); Plotinus treats body parts as tools or instruments used by the soul.</note> was to be moved, there it was necessary for the power or the "machinery" of the activity to be grounded. And this starting point possesses the instruments. Or rather, it is the starting point of the powers, for power is everywhere; but the activity and the starting point are there where the beginning of the instrument is. Since the power of sensation and that of the desiring soul <note>original: "ὁρμώσης ψυχῆς" (hormō sēs psychēs); the soul that initiates impulse or movement.</note>—which is of a sensory or imaginative nature—has reason positioned above itself, it acts upon what is below. 

Furthermore, because this power was placed by the ancients in the highest citadel <note>original: "arce"; the Latin translator uses the metaphor of a "citadel" for the head.</note> of the whole animal, namely in the head—not because reason is essentially in the brain, but because the sensory power, through which reason appears to be situated in the brain as a medium, is established there. It was necessary to attribute this sensory part to the body, and specifically to that member most capable of receiving such activity. But since reason does in no way communicate with the body, it was necessary for it to communicate entirely with that which is a "form" of the soul <note>original: "ψυχῆς εἶδος"; a specific manifestation or type of soul-power.</note>: that is, a soul-power capable of receiving something from reason. 

For that which is sensory is also, in a way, a judge; and that which is imaginative is like something intellectual. Moreover, impulse and pursuit follow imagination and reason. There, in the reasoning part, it is situated in this way. But how the power of sensation is there, and other things likewise, has already been discussed. Regarding the vegetative, growth-oriented, and nutritive nature—which is never absent from any part of the body—since it is nourished by the blood, and the nourishing blood is in the veins, and the starting point of the veins and blood is in the liver <note>original: "ἥπατι / iecore"; Ancient physiology, following Galen and Plato, held that the liver was the source of the veins and the seat of the "appetitive" soul.</note>, it is not without reason that the desiring portion of the soul was placed there by the ancients. For that which generates, nourishes, and grows must necessarily desire these things. But since thin, light, sharp, and pure blood is the proper instrument for anger, the place from which such blood flows for the act of anger—namely the heart—was designated as the dwelling of anger.

<column-break/>

...having used these things, having been established. It would have been better to place the principle of that power's operation there: for from where the instrument was to be moved, there it was necessary to found, as it were, the power of the craftsman suitable to the instrument. Indeed, power is not localized, for power flourishes everywhere; but the principle of action is there where the beginning of the instrument is. Therefore, since the virtue of sensing and pursuing in the sensory and imaginative soul has reason above itself, as if close to what is lower, it is no wonder that where this is in the highest part, reason was placed by the ancients in the highest citadel of the entire animal, namely the head itself: not because reason is in the brain, but in this sensory part through which, as a medium, reason seems to be placed in the brain. 

It was necessary to attribute this sensory part to the body, and especially to that member which could best receive such an action. But it was necessary for reason, which in no way shares with the body, to communicate entirely with that which is a species of the soul: a power of the soul, I say, able to receive something from reason. For that which is sensory is also, in a way, a judge; and that which is imaginative seems like something intellectual. Furthermore, impulse and pursuit follow imagination and reason. There, then, is the rational part; not indeed as in a place, but because that which is there is in some way a participant in reason. 

But in what manner the virtue of sensing is there, and other things similarly, has been said. Accordingly, since the vegetative nature of growth and nourishment is nowhere lacking in the body, but is nourished by blood, and the nourishing blood is in the veins, and the beginning of the veins and blood is in the liver, from which such power strives, not without reason has the desiring portion of the soul been placed here by the ancients. For that which procreates and nourishes and grows, must necessarily desire these very things. But when thin, light, sharp, and pure blood is the instrument suitable for anger, its place—namely, from where such blood flows out for the act of anger—the heart itself, was designated as the dwelling of anger. <note>original: "σφόδρα ὀργάλε... εὐ ταῦθα γὰ τὸ πεποιηται, εἰκόσις πρέπον." - These fragments suggest the Greek text was echoing the appropriateness of the heart as the seat of the "spirited" or "angry" part of the soul.</note>

---

The soul, which is an incorporeal substance existing in itself, is not determined to any place except through its inclination <note>original: "inclinationem"; a soul's tendency or attraction toward the material world.</note> and action regarding that place. Therefore, once released from the earthly body, if it retains no such inclination, it is nowhere on earth, and yet everywhere, unless perhaps it is in a higher sphere through an inclination toward it. But if it still retains an inclination toward earthly things, it revolves around them in a spirit-body <note>original: "corpore spiritati"; this refers to the *pneuma* or "astral vehicle" that Neoplatonists believed the soul inhabited between incarnations.</note>, in which it also suffers corporeal things. Furthermore, just as among astrologers some fulfill their fate even when unwilling, while in ignorance they choose something through which they fall secretly into fate: so all souls fulfill the divine law in themselves by choosing something, from which they manifest the sentence of the divine laws in what is hidden.

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS: BOOK IV

A [The soul] goes to those places which it is proper for it to reach, even if it is ignorant of them, driven here and there by an unstable movement and by errors. But at last, as if exhausted by the things it resisted, it falls into the place that is suitable for it, undergoing its suffering through a voluntary movement that has become involuntary <note>original: "volutario quodã motu in voluntaria subiens passionem"; Plotinus describes the soul's descent as a "voluntary" choice that results in a state of "unwilling" or fated suffering.</note>. It is ordained in the law how much and for how long it must suffer; and finally, there is a meeting of the release from its sluggishness and the power to escape from those places, a power granted by the harmony that contains all things. B Therefore, souls that possess a body must also endure bodily torments. But those souls which are pure, and carry nothing of the bodily with them in any way, are not confined by any bodily location. If they are not designated for anything of that kind (for they do not have a body in any way), they are undoubtedly there where essence, true being, and the divine consist in God. Here, I say, and together with these things and in this very state, such souls shall dwell. C But if you still ask "where," you must similarly ask where those divine things are. In searching for this, do not seek with your eyes, nor as if you were looking for bodies.

<margin>XXV
In the intellect there is no recollection, since nothing new happens there—whether from outside or inside—that must be preserved or recalled. Nor is there any change there from potential to actual; rather, the function of memory belongs to the soul.</margin>

### IT IS WORTHWHILE to similarly investigate memory: whether souls, when they have departed from these places, remember; and if some remember while others do not. And again, whether they remember all things or rather have memory of only some things; and whether they remember forever, or perhaps only for a time close to their departure. D But before we inquire into this matter, we must first determine what it is that remembers. I do not mean what memory itself is, but in what kind of thing it is most naturally found. For what memory is has been said elsewhere and is often repeated; but we must explain more carefully what is most suited by nature for memory. If the entire faculty of memory belongs to something acquired, whether it be a teaching or an experience, then surely recollection is not at all appropriate for things that are free from suffering <note>original: "passione vacat"; referring to the "impassibility" or unchanging nature of divine things.</note> and are not subject to time. Therefore, memory must not be placed in God or in Being and the Intellect. E For nothing happens to them, and time does not exist around Being, but rather eternity <term>eternity: "aeon" or "aevum," signifying a state beyond the linear progression of time</term>. There is no "before" or "after" there, but it is always as it is, remaining the same, admitting no change at all. How could that which is always in the same and similar state ever use memory? For it does not have or hold one disposition after another which it previously held, nor does it obtain one intelligence after another so that it might remain in one while remembering the other which it had before. F What will prevent this Intellect from knowing the changes of other things—such as the revolutions of the world—while remaining unchanged itself? Perhaps it will understand one thing first and another later, following the changes of the thing it is contemplating. Furthermore, remembering is something other than intelligence, and one should not say that the Intellect "remembers" its own thoughts. For it did not move forward so as to hold onto them lest they escape; otherwise, it would even fear lest its own essence depart from itself. G Nor should we say that the soul remembers in the way we say it "remembers" the things that are innate to it. Rather, while it is here, it possesses those innate things, yet it does not always act according to them—especially when it has traveled far...

<column-break/>

A [The soul is driven toward] ignorance of those things it is proper to suffer: in an unstable movement, hanging suspended everywhere in its wanderings; but wandering, as if weary of the things to which it was assigned, it falls into the place suitable for it, by a voluntary movement, yet having its suffering as something involuntary. It is said in the law how much and how long it is necessary to suffer. And again, there concurs both the relaxation of hesitation and the power of escape from B those places, by the power of the harmony that holds all things. Those possessing a body, even the souls of old, must have a share of bodily sufferings; but for souls that are pure and in no way drag anything of the body with them, they will necessarily live unbound... [The Greek text in this column becomes fragmentary and illegible in the original transcription for several lines].

### CONCERNING memory: whether it belongs to the souls themselves when they have come out of these places to remember; and whether to all or not; and whether they remember always or only for some time close to their departure. It is worth seeking this, D if we are to make our inquiry correctly, we must grasp what it is to remember. I do not mean what memory is, but in which of the things that exist it naturally arises. ### BOOK THREE

The ancients seem to associate memory and recollection with every activity that is already active through its own powers. However, they treat memory as a different kind of faculty because of the passage of time. But perhaps we are too quick to agree on these matters without having investigated the cause of the difficulty: whether this so-called recollection and memory belong to that higher soul, or to another more obscure soul, or perhaps to this joint "animal" <note>Greek: ζῷον (zoon). In Neoplatonism, this refers to the composite of the human soul and the physical body.</note>—and if the latter, from which source does it receive it and how? Or if it is the "animal" itself, we must search for what it is in us that possesses memory, even if it is dependent upon the soul. If it is the soul that remembers, what power or part does it use? If it is the "animal"—just as it seemed to be the thing that perceives—in what manner does it remember? If it is the same entity, would it not appear that the "animal" experiences the perceptions of the same thing? And should it receive the objects of thought <note>Greek: νοημάτων (noematon); refers to intellectual or spiritual concepts rather than sensory images.</note>, or are these something different?

If, then, the "animal" is the union of both soul and body, and perception is a kind of activity, it is because it perceives in a certain way: for it is called a "common" thing <note>Meaning a shared function of both soul and body.</note>, like boring a hole or weaving. In this analogy, the soul acts as the craftswoman and the body as the tool. So if perception is an experience of the body that serves the soul, we must determine whether the soul, once separated from the body, retains the "stamps" <note>Greek: τύπους (typus); the "impressions" or "images" left by sensory experiences.</note> that were in the body, or whether it retains those that came through the body or through the "common" entity. It is likely that the experience belongs to the body; and while perception might be called a common work, it is not necessary for these things to remain common. Once the soul has received the stamp and preserved it, or if it provides the means for discernment, it might be concluded that remembering is a common act. Just as bodies might be controlled, we might become more or less "memorial" <note>Capable of remembering.</note>. But one might also say the body acts as a hindrance, and that remembering belongs specifically to the soul. For how could the "common" entity remember the things we learn in our studies? Or does the soul remember them by itself? If the "animal" is the joint entity in such a way that it is something "other" emerging from both, it would be absurd to say the "animal" is neither body nor soul. For if they change into something else, the "animal" is a different thing; and if they are mixed, the soul is in the "animal" only in a certain way. How then can memory belong to the soul? Just as in a mixture of wine and honey, if there is any sweetness, it remains there because of the honey. What if the soul itself remembers, but because it is in the body, it is not "pure," but rather—being affected in this way or that—it can receive the stamps of sensory things? And it finds a "seat" in the body, as it were, to receive them, unless we think of it as an "outflow." But first, we must ask if these "stamps" have magnitude. And even if they are like seals, or impressions, they are not like...

<column-break/>

<margin>
XXVI.
That it is the soul that receives the form; for he does not say this happens through a mere harmony <note>original: "consonantia"</note>. Then he asks if it is some third partial thing, but rather from the harmony of the body, informing it by act. The form makes it exist as a family <note>original: "famili"</note>. But memory, which is the act of preserving, belongs properly to the soul. It is easy to see it does not belong to the body by this instance: it exists where there is union. For if something is preserved in honey through memory, it is because those things are perceived by the soul together with the body.
</margin>

A [The ancients seem] to have called "memory" and "recollection" the act of operating according to those things which one already possessed; therefore, this is a certain other species of memory. For this reason, the concept of "time" does not strictly fit this memory, but perhaps we conduct ourselves regarding these matters not with careful consideration, but with a light and easy manner. For perhaps someone will doubt whether memory and recollection of this sort belong to that higher soul, or to a lower, viler one, or even to this composite animal. Furthermore, B if it belongs to that other soul, he will wonder when and how it received the things it records; if it belongs to the animal, he will doubt in a similar way. For this reason, we must investigate what in us is primarily endowed with memory, which is what we were seeking from the beginning: whether the soul remembers, and if so, what power or part of the soul, or whether the animal itself uses memory. Just as it appeared to some that it is the animal which perceives, we must ask what the manner of this is, and what should be said regarding the animal itself: C and likewise whether the same entity perceives sensible things, intelligible things, and anything else, or whether one part receives the former and another receives the latter.

If, therefore, the animal is both soul and body together, in the sensory act, it must perceive that such a thing exists. Therefore it is called "common," just as weaving and boring are; so that the soul behaves as the craftsman in perceiving, while the body holds itself as the instrument. While the body indeed suffers and serves, D the soul receives the formation of the body itself, or that which occurs through the body; or at least the judgment which it carries out from the body's suffering. In this case, perception would certainly be called a common action, but memory would not be forced to be so joined; for since the soul has already begun to hold the "figure" <note>Latin: "figura"; equivalent to the Greek "typos" or stamp.</note>, it either guards it or casts it away, unless perhaps someone conjectures that memory is also something common, because we tend to become either mindful or forgetful based on certain temperaments of the bodies. Truly, it can be said that the body E either hinders or does not hinder the effect of recollection, but nonetheless the duty of memory itself is proper to the soul. Now, regarding the memory of the disciplines <note>Scientific or philosophical learning.</note>, how shall this be said to belong to the joint entity rather than the soul itself? But if the "animal" is both together in such a way that a certain third thing arises from both, it will first be absurd to say the animal is neither body nor soul. For the animal is not a different thing because the two are changed, F nor again are they so mixed that the soul is in the animal only as a certain potentiality; and even under this condition, remembering will nonetheless belong to the soul. Just as in a certain mixture made of wine and honey, if any sweetness remains to delight the taste, it has that quality from the honey. What then? If the soul itself remembers, but because it is in the body, it is not "pure," but rather as if already affected in this way or that, it can imprint the figures of sensible things, and use the body as a seat, as it were, G to catch and keep the forms. But first, such figures are not magnitudes; second, they are neither like seal-impressions, nor reflections or certain figurations; since there is no physical pushing there, nor is it an impression as in the case of signets...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the faculty of memory. Having previously questioned whether the soul or the "animal" (the soul-body composite) remembers, he now argues that memory cannot be a physical impression like a seal in wax, but must be an activity of the soul itself.</meta>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEAD IV.

...as is customary to happen in wax, but rather in another **A** mode, such as that of intellection <note>original: "intellectio" / Greek: "noesis". This refers to the highest form of thought, which is direct and non-discursive.</note>, even in things that are perceived by the senses. But in the act of understanding, what kind of "impulse" or "impression" could be spoken of? Or what need is there for a body, or even for a bodily quality, for intellection to be carried out? Furthermore, it is necessary for the soul to remember its own internal movements: such as the things it has desired, and what it has attained or failed to attain. For the thing which is set before us as "desirable" does not reach as far as the physical body. For in what way could the body speak of those **B** things which never reached it? Or by what reason will the mind remember together with the body that which the nature of the body is in no way able to know? But it must be said that some things flow into the soul itself—whatever things come through the body—but other things belong to the soul alone, if indeed it is necessary that the soul itself be something, and that its nature and work exist as a reality. But if this desire is the soul's own property, and the memory of that desire is too, then why not also the remembrance of attainment or of a failed wish? Since even **C** its own nature is not numbered among the class of things that flow away <note>The "flowing things" refer to the material world, which is in a constant state of flux (Heraclitean change).</note>. For unless this were so, we would grant the mind neither consensus, nor consequence, nor conspiracy <note>In this context, "conspiracy" (conspiratio) means a "breathing together" or harmony of parts.</note>, nor a kind of self-consciousness. For unless the soul possessed these by its own nature, it certainly would not acquire them in the body; but it truly has certain actions, the execution of which requires the instruments of the body, and it brings the powers of these with itself; of others, it brings even the actions themselves with it. But as far **D** as memory is concerned, the body is an impediment; since even now forgetfulness occurs from the addition of certain things. But in the removal and purification of these, a certain memory often emerges in us. But while the soul is alone, it is necessary—if the nature of the body that approaches it is mobile and flowing—that this body be considered the "River of Lethe" <note>Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology; Plotinus uses it as a metaphor for the physical body.</note>, and not the source of memory. Therefore, memory belongs to the soul.

<column-break/>

...in wax, but the mode is like intellection, even in the case of sensory objects. But in the case of intellections, what "imprint" could be mentioned? Or what need of a body or bodily quality, with which—but truly also of its own movements—it is necessary for memory to occur in it? Such as the things it desired, and those it did not obtain, or did obtain? For how could the body speak of the "desirable" into the body, concerning things of which it received no perception? Or how will it remember with the body that which the body is not by nature able to know at all? But it must be said that some things end in the soul, those which come through the body, but others belong to the soul alone, if indeed we posit the soul itself as a certain nature and its work. And if this is so, it also has desire and memory of desire, and thus also of success and failure. Since indeed its nature is not of the things that flow. For if this were not so, we would grant it neither shared-perception <note>Greek: "synaisthesis". A key term for self-awareness or the internal sense that coordinates different perceptions.</note> nor following-after; nor any synthesis or, as it were, understanding. For those things which it has from the beginning in its nature, these it carries into the body. But it holds certain activities, the work of which is through the completion of organs. Of some things, it comes bringing the powers; of others, even the activities. But as for memory, it has the body as an obstacle. Since even now, forgetfulness comes by things being added; but through subtraction and purification, memory is often an unfolding. But when it is alone, the nature of the body—being situated and flowing—must be the cause of forgetfulness, but not of memory; for which reason it is the River of Lethe; whether, then, the body belongs to the soul, let these be the experiences.

->*These things are missing in the Greek text up to here, etc. Otherwise, it must be asked: and these are the words of Marsilio.*<-

<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary translator and commentator of Plotinus during the Renaissance. He often added explanations where the Greek manuscripts were fragmented or difficult.</note>

THAT BOTH are eternal, and after death the rational soul can be among the gods, while in the meantime the irrational soul—which is its Image <note>term: "Idolum/Image". In Neoplatonism, the "eidolon" is a lower reflection or shadow of the true soul that remains connected to the realm of generation.</note>—is among men; and this image remembers the things done in this life, mostly its own passions, but less of the things pertaining to the rational soul. Likewise in man—I do not mean the temperate man, but the continent or incontinent man—both souls migrate together and are mindful of human affairs: more easily indeed as long as they live in an aerial body, but more difficultly if they should ever receive an earthly body. It would perhaps be more probable to say that one soul exists in us. And from this, the vital force or life-giving act flowing into this body is called, as it were, a second soul. Which is therefore said to be made from the universal life, because it flows from ours under the Power of the universal life.

---

<margin>
XXVII.
It ought to be asked whether two souls are placed in man, differing from one another by substance. The rational soul indeed from the maker of the world himself, but the irrational from the life of the world.
</margin>

OTHERWISE, it must be asked: of which **A** soul is memory a condition? For one soul is called more divine, according to which we exist; but the other depends upon the universe. Perhaps it should be said that memory belongs to both, but to one as its own, and to the other as a shared memory. And when they are joined, all memories exist together; but if they are separated—provided both exist and remain—the one soul preserves its own things for a longer time, but those which pertain to our lower nature, for a shorter time. This indeed is that which is called the Image (**Idolum**). Therefore, we must consider **B** that the "Simulacrum" <note>term: "Simulacrum/Phantom". Plotinus is referencing Homer's Odyssey, where the hero Odysseus sees the phantom of Hercules in Hades while the true Hercules is on Olympus with the gods.</note> of Hercules among those in the underworld remembers all that was done in life. For this was especially his life. But the other...

<column-break/>

BUT of which soul? Of the one called by us "more divine," according to which we are ourselves? Or of the other, the one from the All? Or must it be said that there are memories of each: some private, some common. And when they are together, all are together; but having become separate, if both should exist and remain, each holds its own for a longer time; but for a short time the things of the other. I think we must consider that the Hercules in Hades remembers all the things performed during his life. For this was especially his life. But the others...

# THIRD BOOK.

...otherwise, the composite <note>original: "το συναμφότερον" (to sunamphoteron) – refers to the union of soul and body</note> will be both, yet they would have nothing more to say than what pertains to this life; and having themselves become the composite, they knew these things because they held onto justice. But Hercules himself would know the things of that place, for it is said he discourse there. But what if another soul is set free and exists alone? For the soul that is drawn along, or even the things it did or suffered as a human, uses what is appropriate at the time of death. From others, memories may appear from previous lives, so that some things are then released or held in low esteem. Becoming purer than the body, the soul will recover things it did not hold in memory here; but when it enters another body, it will be driven out, loving the things outside of this life. And it will say what it has just left. It will also speak of many things from previous times, and from many of all things, yet it will also exist in a state of forgetting. But when the soul becomes alone, what will it remember? Or how does it carry things? By what power of the soul does remembering come to be?

DO WE THEN perceive those things which we learn, or also those things which we desire—the objects of desire—and those things which seem right to the spirited <note>The "spirited" part of the soul (thymos) is the seat of anger, courage, and pride in Platonic thought.</note> part? Or will one part be the <unclear>perceiver</unclear>, as someone says, and another part remember its own affairs? For the desiring part is moved by those things it has enjoyed; again, the <unclear>mind</unclear> clearly moves toward the objects of desire by the memory through which it exists, and not by another. Or is it not so? What about the perception of beautiful and faithful things? Is the name of "desires" always given to the sensory part and to all of them, so that each is named according to what prevails? Or is perception different for each, for instance, if the appetite is mine? Or is desiring one thing, but that desire comes from perception, as if by a transmission? It is as if perception says what it is, but the soul <unclear>suffers</unclear> without awareness; and so with anger, if someone has done wrong, the anger is a perception, but will it act in this way? Furthermore, we might say a dog reacts to a wolf by an impulse or a sound, though I think he may not see it himself? Does <unclear>perception</unclear> rouse us to desire the things we have enjoyed, and does what happens there leave a trace? <unclear>Not</unclear> as a memory, but as a disposition or a feeling. But it is the part that saw the enjoyment itself that holds the memory of what happened. The evidence for this is that the memory is often not pleasant to the part that shares in the desiring, even if their <unclear>traces</unclear> remain.

BUT IF we attribute memory to the sensory power, will the same part of us be capable of both remembering and sensing? But if even the <unclear>form</unclear> is <unclear>another</unclear> that remembers, as was said, the sensory power will be double. And even if the sensory is not the memory, but is in something else, then the memory will be double. Furthermore, if the sensory power also belongs to the retention of lessons, then...

<column-break/>

**A** ...both existing at once, they would have nothing more to say than those things which look toward this life; and having themselves become both at once, they knew these very things: or besides, if anything in some way pertains to justice. But Hercules himself, separated from his image <note>A reference to Odyssey XI.601, where Hercules' "image" or shade is in Hades while his true self is with the gods. Plotinus uses this to show the soul can exist on different levels.</note>, what he might have said has not yet been told. What then would the other soul say when it is eventually separated and lives alone? For the soul indeed, drawn along with this one, recalls whatever the man did and suffered. But as time proceeds at the very **B** moment of death, memories of other things from previous lives arise, so that some of these are let go through neglect. For having eventually become purer than the body, it will recall those things which it did not hold in memory here; but approaching another body, it wanders away, and brings forth the external business of life, and the things it recently left behind: likewise many things from higher realms. But when, through the longer cycles of time, many chance things arrive, it always slides into forgetfulness. But the soul which has now **C** escaped alone, what will it remember? Perhaps we must first investigate to which power of the soul memory itself chiefly belongs.

<margin>
XXIIII.
The power of sensing is something different from the power of desiring, and both of these are excited by sensible objects; however, a more inclined disposition is acquired through frequency, which nevertheless is not memory. For memory pertains to sense and also to reason.
</margin>
**D** DO WE remember by that by which we sense, and by which we learn? Or do we also remember the objects of desire by that by which we desire, and do we remember individual things pertaining to anger by that by which we are angered? For someone will not say that to enjoy is one thing, but to remember those things which another enjoyed is something else. Therefore, the power of desiring, having once possessed certain delights, is moved again through memory if the desired object should ever occur again. Why, however, is it moved by no other object, and in no other way than this? What then prevents us from also attributing a sense of such things to it? And likewise to the sensual part, a desire, and so on through everything, so that whatever prevails, that thing is named? Or perhaps we attribute sense to individual parts differently? Just as vision sees, but the nature of desiring does not. Yet this desire is incited **E** by sense, as if by a succeeding transmission; not indeed so that this says what the sense is like in every way, but it suffers without its own observation. By the same reasoning in those things which look toward anger, vision indeed saw the one doing injury, but the spirit was provoked: just as if a dog were provoked by a shepherd seeing a wolf threatening the flocks, not having seen it himself, but being stirred by a certain impulse or noise. For if the desiring nature once possessed a thing, it retains **F** a mark of what was done implanted in itself, not as a memory, but as a certain affection and passion. But it is another thing which observes the consequence of the one possessing it, and holds in itself the memory of the thing done. The proof of this is that the memory often does not recognize the things which the power of desiring itself participated in, even though they still reside in it.

<margin>
XXIX.
When we place memory in sense, we locate it in the internal sense of imagination. For these repeat and preserve absent things: and the more powerful it is, the stronger the memory is also, especially if the quality of the body and meditation lead to the same end.
</margin>
**G** SHALL WE therefore dedicate memory to the sensory power? And will that which is capable of sensing be the same for us as that which is capable of memory? But if even both images <note>original: "simulachrum" – referring to the layers of the soul, or the shade of Hercules vs. the higher soul.</note> remember, as we were saying, the sensory power in us will be double; and if the sensory power is not the memory, but any other thing is, then even that other thing will be at least doubly mindful. Furthermore, if the sensory power also pertains to retaining disciplines <note>term: "disciplinas" – here referring to branches of knowledge or learned subjects.</note>, then...

<summary>Plotinus explores whether memory resides in the sensory part of the soul or the desiring part, using the figure of Hercules to illustrate how different levels of the soul may retain different memories. He concludes that while desires leave "marks" or "affections," true memory is a distinct observational power often linked to the internal imagination.</summary>
