<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the faculty of memory. Having previously discussed whether the soul remembers its past lives, he now shifts to the technical mechanics of how memory works—specifically, whether there is a single "memory center" for both physical sensations and intellectual thoughts.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin> Will the soul also perceive the thoughts themselves, or will something else instead pertain to both? For if we posit a common perceiver, shall we grant memory of both to this? Truly, if that which perceives both sensible things <note>Objects known through the five senses.</note> and intelligible things <note>Concepts or truths known by the mind alone.</note> is one and the same, something might perhaps be said in its favor. But if it is divided into two parts, there will nonetheless be two distinct things. And if we attribute both to each part of the soul, four faculties will arise. In general, whatever we remember, we should perform both with the same power: <margin>B</margin> and by that which we think, we should also remember those thoughts. However, we see that the same people are not always the most powerful in both thinking and retaining memories; even those who have equally strong senses do not have equally strong memories. Some are quite vigorous in their senses, while others excel more in memory, even when they are not particularly sharp in their perceptions. But again, if each is different, it will also be necessary that one thing remembers what the senses previously perceived, <margin>C</margin> and that same thing must perceive that which it ought to remember. Perhaps, however, nothing will prevent the act of sensing from being a certain act of the **representative faculty** <note>original: "imaginalis" (Latin) / "phantastikon" (Greek). This refers to the mind's ability to form a mental image or representation of an object.</note> for the power of memory. For this faculty is that which defines the sensation; even when the object of the sense is gone or has fled, the vision remains within it. If, therefore, the imagination of the absent thing resides in this power, it certainly possesses memory; and if it remains for a short time, it <margin>D</margin> has a brief memory. But if it is extended for a long time, these people excel more in memory, because this power is held more strongly, so that it is not easily overturned and compelled to lose the memories it holds. Therefore, memory belongs to the representative faculty, and remembering such things is its function. We shall say that souls differ in their ability to remember either because of the differing strengths of that faculty, or because of the frequency of their actions, or their leisure, or because of their bodily temperaments—what is present or absent, what changes might occur, <margin>E</margin> or even what might cause disturbance. But it seems these things must be discussed elsewhere.

There are in us dual imaginations: one in the irrational life, and the other in the rational soul. The former is the limit of the senses, while the latter is the lowest point of thoughts. They are continuous, for the act of perception pertains to both. Just as we see things placed before us, yet we do not notice that we see unless the sensory imagination focuses on it, and unless the vision itself is reflected from there; so too we neither notice that we understand nor that we are moved, unless something of that higher sort touches the imagination continuous with it, and is reflected in it like a mirror. To this imagination also come the acts of the senses and the lower imagination, and in this very place rational memory is situated.

### Chapter XXX.

<margin>A</margin> **BUT** what shall we say of remembering thoughts? Does the imagination itself preserve these too? Truly, if every act of the intellect were followed by an imagination, perhaps while this imagination remained like a sort of image of the thought, there would be a memory of the thing known in both parts; if not, we must seek another explanation. Perhaps, since reason accompanies the act of the intellect itself, a certain transfer and reception into the imagination will constitute memory. For the act of the intellect is impartible <note>indivisible; it happens all at once rather than in a sequence.</note> and has not yet, as it were, <margin>B</margin> proceeded outward, but remains hidden within. But the reason, unfolding and leading it out from the notion of the intellect into the representative faculty, demonstrates that which is called the "intelligible" as if in a mirror, and thus its perception and permanence are achieved...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Will the perceiving part of thoughts be the same as the sensory part, or is it something else from each? Again, by positing a common perceiving part, shall we give to it the memory of both? But if that which perceives both sensible and intelligible things is indeed the same, perhaps it might be so. But if it were divided in two, even then there would be two. And if we give both to each part of the soul, there will be five or more. For in general, we must always <margin>B</margin> remember with that by which we perceive, and both must occur by the same power. Or if we divide them, then we remember thoughts with one part. For if the same thing thinks and remembers the things it thinks about, it would follow that those who are equal in sensing would be equal in remembering. But some have good senses, while others have good memories. And some are sharp and trained in sensation [but not memory]. But again, if each is to be something else, then another part <margin>C</margin> will remember what the senses have already done, and that part must perceive what it is about to remember. Or nothing will prevent the sensation from appearing as something to the one who remembers; to the representative faculty <note>original: "phantastikon"</note>, which is something else, memory and retention belong. For the vision is present to this faculty after the senses are gone and no longer exist. <margin>D</margin> If it stays with this, or even if the imagination is already present, then it would be memory. If it is held for a little, the memory is little. But if it is held much, one remembers more, this power having been made strong so as not to be easily turned away. From these things memory is composed. Memory, then, belongs to the representative faculty, and remembering such things is its function. We may say memories differ either by the powers of the soul involved, or by actions and their lack, or by bodily states—whether they are present or not, or by alterations or not, or by things causing a general disturbance. But those matters do not belong here.

<margin>A</margin> But what of the thoughts? Does the representative faculty hold these too? But if imagination follows every act of intellection, perhaps this imagination—being like an image of the thought—remains, and thus there would be a memory of the thing known. If not, something else must be sought. Perhaps there is a "logos" <note>The Greek word "logos" here refers to a "rational account" or "discursive reasoning" that translates a pure thought into a mental image.</note> that follows the thoughts, and the reception of this is into the representative faculty. For the thought <margin>B</margin> is impartible, and has not yet proceeded, as it were, to the outside, but remains hidden within; but the "logos" unfolding it and leading it out from each thought into the representative faculty, shows the thought as if in a mirror, and thus the perception of it occurs, and its staying...

<summary>Plotinus explains that memory resides in the "representative faculty" (imagination), which acts like a mirror reflecting both physical sensations and intellectual thoughts. He argues that we only become consciously aware of our thoughts when they are "unfolded" into this mental imagery.</summary>

<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, memory, imagination, phantastikon, intellect, dual soul, perception, mirror of the mind</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the faculty of memory within the soul. On the previous page, he questioned whether the higher and lower parts of the soul share a single memory or have separate ones. Here, he distinguishes between the act of thinking and the awareness of that thinking, and explains how the higher soul’s "light" can overshadow the lower soul’s memories.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

And memory. Therefore, because the soul is always moved toward the intellect, whenever it reflects upon this, an awareness occurs within us. For the act of thinking is one thing, and the perception <note>original: "ἀντίληψις" / "animadversio." The distinction between a subconscious mental process and the conscious awareness of that process.</note> of that thinking is another. We are, in a sense, always "seeing" intellectually, but we do not always notice it. This happens because the faculty that receives these thoughts does not only receive intellectual things, but also receives sensations from the outside, and it does so by turns.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And memory. For this reason, since the soul is always moved toward intelligence, as often as it results in this, an awareness is produced in us. For intelligence is one thing, and the awareness of that intelligence is another. We indeed always understand, yet we do not always notice. This occurs because that which receives <note>The "mirror" of the representative faculty.</note> does not only receive intelligences, but also receives senses from elsewhere, and does so alternately.

***

*If our two souls were separated by location, they would possess two distinct imaginations and two distinct memories. But as long as they are together, the inferior soul yields to the more excellent one in the formation of the body, just as a smaller light yields to a greater light. Thus, there are not two separate animals here, because the higher soul acts as the form of the lower one; the lower soul, under the influence of that form, acts naturally within the body. Furthermore, although the representative faculty <note>original: "imaginatio" / "φανταστικόν" (phantastikon). The power of the soul that creates mental images.</note> is naturally present in both, when one imagines more frequently and more powerfully, the other is either idle or acts so weakly that it seems not to see itself, while the imagination is meanwhile laboring more intently on something else. It is fitting and natural that the lower imagination should yield to the higher. Because this higher part comprehends both the marks of intelligible truths and the forms of sensible things at once, it reveals that we are a single living being. When the soul departs from the body, if it has mastered the lower soul through discipline, it consigns vices to oblivion and retains only what is honorable.*

->Chapter XXXI.<-

But if memory belongs to the representative faculty, and each part of the soul is said to remember, then there must be two such faculties. If the souls were separate, each would have its own. But since they are together within us, how can there be two, and in which one does the memory reside? If memory resided in both, the mental images would always be doubled. For we cannot simply say that one part remembers intellectual things and the other remembers physical sensations. If that were the case, there would be two entirely different living beings with nothing in common. If, then, there is an impression in both, what is the difference? Furthermore, why do we not notice this duality? Perhaps it is because whenever the two parts agree or harmonize, the two images become one. Since the imaginative faculties are not separate, the expression of the more powerful soul prevails, and a single mental image <note>original: "φάντασμα" / "phantasma." A mental representation or "vision."</note> is produced; the lower follows like a shadow, or like a small light yielding to a greater one. But when there is conflict and discord, the lower part shines out by itself. However, the duality of the souls often remains hidden from us because they have joined into one. The one part sees all things in the other, and when the soul departs the body, it takes some memories with it and leaves others behind. Just as when we have associated with base companions and then move on to the company of better men, we remember little of the former and much of the latter, who are more excellent and joyful.

->More.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT if memory belongs to the imagination, and each soul is said to remember, there will be two distinct powers of imagining. Indeed, if the souls were separated from one another, they would have double memories. But since they are together in us, how will they have two, and in which of them will the memory-impression be made? For if it is in both, there will always be twin imaginations. It should not be said that one pertains to the memory of intelligible things and the other to the memory of sensible things. <margin>B</margin> For in that way, there would be two animals having nothing in common. If, therefore, an impression is made in both, what is the difference? Moreover, what prevents us from recognizing this? Perhaps it is when one consents to or harmonizes with the other: since the imaginations are not separate, the expression of the more powerful soul then prevails, and one mental image—that is, a vision—comes forth. This is because the other follows like a shadow, and the smaller light <margin>C</margin> yields to the greater. But when there is a fight or discord, then the other also flashes out by itself. However, the fact that it is in the other is hidden, because the duality of our souls is entirely hidden from us. For both have conspired into one, the second being overshadowed. The other, then, has shone forth and seen all things; and as it departs or exits, it keeps some things, while it dismisses others to the second soul—namely, those things that pertain to it. Just as we are accustomed to converse sometimes with viler people, and then if we transfer ourselves to the company of more excellent ones, we retain only a small memory <margin>D</margin> of those former companions, but more of the following and better ones.

***

*In both souls after death, the memory of human affairs remains: but in the lower soul, it remains with perturbation <note>Emotional disturbance or agitation.</note>, especially when it has not fully obeyed the higher soul. In the higher soul, however, it remains without perturbation. Likewise, in the "airy" body <note>The "spirit-vehicle" or astral body that Neoplatonists believed the soul inhabited immediately after death.</note> we remember many mortal things; in the celestial body, we remember few; and beyond the heavens, we remember very few indeed. Remembering fewer things there does not come from a weakness of memory, but from an intense focus on better things, which causes the soul to neglect the lesser, except insofar as the lesser were part of the greater work.*

->Chapter XXXII.<-

What then shall we say of friends, children, and wife? And of one's country, and other such things? Will the soul not remember them? Does the lower part remember them with emotion, while the higher part keeps these memories without passion? For perhaps the higher soul also received the memory of those affections from the start?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> WHAT indeed shall we say regarding friends and children and a spouse; likewise of the fatherland, and similarly of other things which a man of character would be thought to remember honorably? Perhaps that part—that is, the image-soul—remembers each of these with a certain perturbation. But this higher part will retain the memory of them without perturbation; for perhaps the perturbation was in that lower part from the beginning, while certain refined affections were in the more excellent soul.

<summary>Plotinus explains that humans have a dual memory corresponding to the higher and lower souls; normally, the higher soul's light overshadows the lower, but after death, the soul gradually forgets earthly attachments as it focuses on higher truths.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> ...they exist, insofar as it [the soul] has had commerce with the other. It is fitting for the lower soul to desire to retain even the duties of the better one in memory, especially when it is also modest; for it can become better from the very beginning and profit from being educated under the better soul. However, this higher soul ought to willingly consign the trifles of the lower soul to oblivion. It can also happen that when the one is noble, the other, which is by nature inferior, may be restrained by force by the better one. And truly, insofar as it strives toward the higher realms, 
<margin>B</margin> more of these things are also consigned to oblivion by this [lower] soul, unless perhaps its entire life here has been such that it committed only the best things to memory. Indeed, even here it is a noble thing to separate oneself from human pursuits, and this is the duty of absolute virtue; therefore, it is necessarily right to neglect the memory of such things. Wherefore, if someone were to say that a noble soul is forgetful, he would speak correctly in this regard: for it flees from the many, and reduces the multitude into one, dismissing the infinite and the utterly uncertain. For in this way it does not 
<margin>C</margin> live with the many, but considering these things to be trivial, it dwells with itself, having retained only a few things—and even those with difficulty. Since even while it dwells here, as often as it strives to take itself to the higher realm, it entirely omits the rest. Therefore, when it has arrived at the summit there, it will recall few of these things; but he who is in heaven retains more. Now, that [lower] Hercules in the heavens <note>Plotinus is referencing the *Odyssey*, where the "shade" of Hercules is in the underworld while the true Hercules is among the gods. Here, "heavens" refers to the celestial spheres, not the highest intellectual realm.</note> will boast of his fortitude; but that higher Hercules considers such things of little value, having already moved into a narrower <note>original: "angustiorem." Here meaning more concentrated or essential.</note> place and having been 
<margin>D</margin> received into the **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world: the realm of pure Thought and Forms, beyond physical perception</term> itself. And truly, he is superior to Hercules, inasmuch as he has strenuously practiced and abundantly completed the more sacred contests of the wise.

<column-break/>

<note>original: Greek text of the passage above</note>
...noble things, insofar as it shared in the other. It is proper for the lower parts to have been enriched by the things of the other and by memory, especially when they are themselves [noble]. For one could become better from the start, and through education from the superior soul. But it is fitting for the soul to gladly welcome the forgetting of its own inferior traits, if indeed they are noble, or of the other, because the one is by nature inferior, being held back by the other by force. When it hastens toward the above, forgetfulness is greater for it, unless its whole life here was such that its memories were only of its labors. Furthermore, even here, it is good to depart from human concerns. It is necessary, therefore, for the memories to be forgotten as if they had ceased; if one calls the good soul "forgetful," one would correctly state how this happens. Moreover, it flees from the many, and gathers the many into one, letting go of the infinite. For in this way it does not dwell with the many, but is light and stays by itself. Furthermore, even here, when it wishes to be there, while it is here it lets go of all other things; therefore, few things [are remembered]—the things practiced—if it were in heaven, more. But if the shade of Hercules [boasted] of his manly courage to himself, the higher one would consider even these things small, having moved to a more holy place, and having come to be in the intelligible, and having surpassed the strength of Hercules in the contests that the wise contend in.

## ENNEAD THE FOURTH,
### BOOK IV.

### THE SECOND TREATISE ON THE DOUBTS OF THE SOUL.

->The second on the doubts of the soul.<-

-> M A R S I L I O  F I C I N O <-

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'A' featuring architectural motifs and figures in the background.</image-desc>
The **SOUL** <term>anima: the soul as the mediating force between the physical and the divine</term>, once stripped of every body, even a celestial one, and then formed by the divine mind through divine attention, perceives all things simultaneously without discursive reasoning <note>original: "sine discursu." Thinking all at once rather than step-by-step.</note>. Therefore, it is said not to remember human affairs, not because it is ignorant of lower things, but because it contemplates all the causes of lower things while possessing itself most perfectly. But it repeats the smallest things most negligently when it is most attentive to the greatest things; and also because it does not repeat them in a discursive and changeable manner, as human recollection is accustomed to do. It contemplates both through the intellect and through reason whatever it knows in a single intuition without motion, because it sees through a single form of God. Nevertheless, through the very series of ideas—which have levels distinguished from one another not by time, but by order—it discerns that some things are prior to others in that realm. As for the fact that someone among us, thinking most attentively about one thing, cannot meanwhile think clearly about another, this happens both from the weakness of our power and because one does not think of the principle <note>The source or "starting point."</note> of the others, where a single power is both most strong and touches the principles of all. Therefore, in those realms, all things are perceived together, especially because the soul is now entirely separated from motion and time. Finally, after the soul has been formed by the divine mind and the ideas, it reaches the **One** <term>the One: the ultimate, simple source of all reality in Neoplatonism</term> itself, which is superior to the mind and ideas, and yet from there it still contemplates all things: for the power of the One itself, when it is first perceived in another (that is, in the mind or soul), is derived into many things. Chapter I.

# BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial T featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar, in a simple landscape.</image-desc>What then will the soul say, and of what things will it hold a memory when it enters the <term>intelligible realm</term> <note>The "intelligible realm" (noetos) is the higher dimension of pure reality and thought in Neoplatonic philosophy, contrasted with the "sensible" or physical world.</note>, becoming a part of that true essence? Or should we say that it simply contemplates those divine things and acts upon the realities it now lives among? Perhaps it possesses nothing of the things from here, such as the fact that it once studied philosophy, or even that while it was here, it gazed upon those higher things. Indeed, if at any point one's thinking is so intense that it excludes all other thought, then contemplation is not a matter of knowing that one is knowing, but comes later as a conviction of what was recognized. But for one who has already transformed and is among the things that exist purely in the intelligible way, would they have a memory of things here? Perhaps they would not, if indeed each person there seems to be outside of time, possessing all knowledge in <term>eternity</term> <note>Eternity here implies a state where everything is known at once, without the "before" and "after" of human time.</note> and not in temporal succession. Therefore, it would seem there is no memory there, not only of earthly things, but of anything at all, for everything is present to the soul at once. But since there is a progression—a transition from one thing to another, or a division into parts and species, or a descent from the universal to the specific—should we say the higher state is not a simultaneous intellectual act? Yet what is the soul there? If it is truly there, it would solve this doubt, because everything becomes a unified whole. Are these many forms of knowledge caught like prey or perceived like sensory objects? The spectacles there are so diverse that they make the vision diverse as well, containing many forms of knowledge just as the eye sees many movements at once, or as we perceive smells and other senses simultaneously. But let us suppose the vision was unceasing; would the mind then suffer some change? This is more likely in the realm of sense. But what of "before" and "after"? If time does not exist there, how could the intellect create a sequence of earlier and later? It could exist in an order of arrangement, just as someone might observe a plant from its roots to its top; the parts are not seen all at once in time, yet the order of "before" and "after" is present even when the whole plant is viewed together. When the soul looks at one thing, does it still possess the many? Perhaps the primary power was one in such a way that it was also many in another; not all things are according to a single act of thinking. For the energies there are not according to one thing, but through a single power that remains forever, so that many things are produced. For that "One" is not something that does not exist, but is capable of taking into itself the nature of many things that did not previously exist within it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A featuring a tree in a landscape.</image-desc>Therefore, when the soul has set out for the divine world and is established in that essence, what indeed will it say, or what things will it hold in its memory? Perhaps it follows that it contemplates those things in which it now exists, and acts around those same things; otherwise, it would not truly be there. Will it then remember nothing of the things that are here? For example, that it once <term>studied philosophy</term> <note>Latin: "philosophata fuerit." In this context, philosophy is the spiritual practice of purifying the soul.</note>, or even that while living here it looked up toward those higher things? <margin>B</margin> Perhaps, if it is impossible for someone to act or contemplate anything else while they are most intensely focused on understanding one thing—and if in that very act of understanding there is no separate act by which one notices that they have understood, but rather someone might say this later, which signifies a change has already occurred—then it will not be permitted for one who purely enjoys the intelligible world to recall the memory of what happened to them here at any time. <margin>C</margin> And yet, if as it appears, all such understanding is devoid of time (since the things there do not exist in time, but consist in eternity), it is impossible for there to be memory there, not only of our earthly affairs, but of any other things whatsoever. For every single thing is present, and there is neither a discourse nor a change that moves from one thing to another. What then? Will there not be a division from above into species, or from the lowest part to the universal and higher things? <margin>D</margin> Truly, what is said to be "from above" does not happen as a separate, abstracted thing in an intellect that holds all things in action at once; but why should it not exist in the soul that is present there? Yet what prevents this intuition from being made as a whole, gathered into one, just as the things themselves are similarly gathered? Is it not done as if by a single gaze? Or as if all the understandings of many things happened at once? For since the spectacle itself there is varied, it follows that the understanding is also varied and manifold at once. <margin>E</margin> These many understandings are like many senses directed toward a single face, where the eye simultaneously contains the nostrils, the eyes, and the other parts of the face. But when the soul divides and unfolds one thing, what shall we say? Perhaps that distinction exists in the intellect, and there such a thing is more firmly supported and fixed. What is called "earlier" and "later" exists among the species not through a temporal distance; for the understanding of the earlier does not happen before the later in time, <margin>F</margin> but rather in a certain order. It is like the order of a tree, beginning from the roots and reaching to the top; to the observer, it has an "earlier" and "later" only in terms of order, since he perceives the whole plant all at once. But when he looks at one part, if he possesses all the many parts, in what way does he have one as primary and another as subsequent? Perhaps the power itself, which is one, was one in such a way that it was also many in another; and all things do not exist according to a single thought. For understandings there do not relate to one another as single units; nevertheless, they remain there perpetually through the same power, so that they are made many in others. For that which is the "One" is not non-existent; it can take upon itself the nature of many things that did not previously exist in itself.
L <note>Original: "L" is a printer's mark or signature for the page gathering.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul’s journey through different levels of reality. The previous page addressed how the soul, when rising toward the divine, must shed the "trifles" of earthly memory. Here, Plotinus explores whether the soul retains any sense of individual identity (like being "Socrates") when it is fully absorbed in contemplation of the divine Intelligible World.</meta>

### PLOTINUS: ENNEADS, BOOK IV.
<meta>catchword: mationes (formations)</meta>

*The soul, while in this body, is often more attentive to other things and does not meanwhile know itself, because its power here is weak. What it thinks about here is not the true principle of the soul. However, when it contemplates the divine world, having been strengthened and seeing its own origins, it thoroughly recognizes itself, its condition, and its deeds. In this body, the soul is mostly turned toward the <term>imagination</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, "imagination" is a lower faculty that deals with mental images of physical things, distinct from the higher "intellect."</note> and, through it, toward sensible objects. But after death, if it lives in an "airy body," it eventually turns its rights toward reason; and through reason, it turns toward its own intellect, which always contains all things, and it dwells for a time in a temporal measure. But in the "celestial body," reason becomes, as it were, an effect of the intellect; it reduces the discourse of the past to a direct intuition. Here, insofar as it finds the forms within itself, it recognizes itself; and insofar as it sees itself as those forms, it is indeed form itself. Finally, outside the heavens, the soul is so shaped by the divine mind and its ideas—just as the body is shaped by the soul’s powers, or as iron is made fiery by fire. It therefore sees and recognizes itself.*

---

<margin>A</margin> BUT let these matters be so. Does the soul, however, return to the memory of itself? Perhaps it remembers neither itself, nor that it is the one who contemplates—such as Socrates, or another person—nor even that it is a mind or a soul. For how could anyone be mindful of these things in such a state? Indeed, even here on earth, when one contemplates—especially with great intensity—one does not turn back toward oneself through the understanding, but simply possesses oneself. One's activity is directed toward the object of thought, offering oneself as a kind of <term>matter</term> <note>In this context, "matter" refers to the soul acting as a receptive vessel for higher divine forms.</note> to be shaped. The soul is then shaped according to what it sees; <margin>B</margin> it exists then only in potential, for it is only "actually" something specific when it is not thinking of anything else. Or perhaps, if it were only itself, it would be empty of all things when not thinking. But if it is such that it *is* all things, then when it understands itself, it understands all things at once. Therefore, being so constituted, by gazing into itself and seeing itself in action, it holds all things included within. By gazing upon all things, it likewise holds itself included. But if it acts in this way, it would change its thoughts, <margin>C</margin> which we denied in the previous sections. Should we then say that in the intellect itself, this state remains always the same? But in the soul, which is situated at the very edge of the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The "intelligible world" is the realm of pure reality and divine thought, as opposed to the physical world of the senses.</note>, such a change can happen when it is granted the power to recall itself to its innermost parts. For if something is done concerning that which is permanent, that which acts must undergo some change toward the permanent, since it does not remain equally stable. But perhaps we should say there is no change there <margin>D</margin> even when it leans from its own affairs toward itself, and from itself back again. For it is all things, and according to both states—remaining in the intelligible world through another soul—it experiences what is called "one thing and then another" regarding itself and the things founded within it. Or surely, living purely in the intelligible world, the soul also possesses stability. For it is whatever it is; and since it is in that world, it must arrive at a union with the intellect, <margin>E</margin> provided it has turned toward it. Having turned, it suffers nothing in between. Thrown into the intellect, it is blended with it and moves with it; yet it is not dissolved by this, but the two are both one and two. Being in such a state, it will not be changed at all, but will direct itself unchangeably toward understanding, possessing at the same time a consciousness or "consensus" of itself, as one that has now been made one and the same with the intelligible world.

<column-break/>

BUT these things indeed are so. What of the soul itself? Does it then have memory of itself? Does the one who contemplates—for instance Socrates—or the fact that he is intellect or soul, remember these things himself? Does he, especially if he is in the heat of the struggle, turn toward himself in the act of thinking? Rather, he possesses himself, but his activity becomes that thing and that other thing, as if providing himself as matter, taking on the form of the thing seen. He is then himself only in potential; and when is he himself in actuality? Is it when he thinks of nothing? If he were to empty himself of all things when he thinks of nothing, he would be a void. But if he is by nature such as to be all things, then when he thinks of himself, he thinks of all things together. So, by the act of looking toward himself and seeing himself in activity, he holds all things encompassed within him; and by looking toward all things, he holds himself encompassed. But if you act thus, you make thoughts into changes, which we argued against before. Or must it be said that for the intellect, things stay the same; but since the soul has images of the things lying in the intelligible, its power becomes such as to depart from them at times? For if it acts around that which remains, it must have a variation of some middle state, not remaining in the same way. Or should we say changes occur when it goes from its own things to itself, and from itself to other things? For it is all things, and both states exist in "another soul" that is in the intelligible realm. It experiences "this and that" in relation to itself and the things in it; or, being purely in the intelligible, it also holds immutability. For it is what it is. Since when it is in that place, it is necessary to come into union with the intellect—as we have said—for having turned toward it, there is nothing in between. Having entered into the intellect and been harmonized with it, it is not destroyed, but the two are one, yet remaining two. It would not then change, but would hold unshakeably toward thought, having a "con-sentience" <note>Original Greek: *synaisthēsis*. This refers to a shared consciousness or internal perception of one's own state.</note> of itself, as having become the same as the intelligible.

---

*The soul, situated outside the heavens in the divine world, is said to be "one" because it acts only through the intellect. It eventually descends into the celestial body when it unfolds its own inner multiplicity, acting then through intellect, reason, and imagination. At that point, it remembers itself and its affairs in much the same way as is common among humans—namely, through the movement of reason (though very rapid there) and through the formations of the imagination.*

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the soul’s identity and the role of memory. Having established that the soul recognizes itself when it reaches the divine realm, the text now examines how the soul’s focus on different levels of reality—the higher divine realm or the lower physical realm—shapes its very nature and its "memory."</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

...formations and images. But it matters greatly what kinds of things the soul thinks about with affection: for when it thinks by bringing its own hidden forms into action, it certainly becomes those very things it thinks about, and consequently obtains a place and condition suitable to them.

->Chapter III.<-

<note>original Greek: "ΕΞΕΛΘΟΥΣΑ δὲ ἐκεῖθεν..."</note> Having gone out from there <note>The "there" refers to the state of unity with the One or the Divine Mind.</note> as if not remaining a single unity, but loving its own unique property and desiring to be something else—just like something leaping out and leaning forward—the soul assumes, as it seems, a memory of itself. If this memory is of higher things, it still holds the soul back from falling too far; but if it becomes a recollection of our worldly affairs, it plunges the soul down toward our realm. Yet, by a heavenly remembrance, it maintains its standing in heaven. In short, whatever the soul remembers, it becomes and is made into that very thing. <column-break/> <margin>A</margin> For to remember is either to understand or to imagine. This imagination itself does not consist in merely "having" something, but in how the soul sees and is disposed, becoming of such a quality itself. If it perceives sensible things <note>Things perceived through the five senses.</note>, then insofar as it looks upon them, it possesses a certain depth. For although it possesses all things in a secondary condition, it does not even then possess all things perfectly; and since it exists on a border, placed as if on a boundary, it is naturally moved between both realms. <margin>B</margin>

---

*The soul in the supernal world <note>The "higher" or "heavenly" world.</note>, contemplating the ideas of the divine mind: through that mind, as if through a transparent medium, the Good itself wanders like a sun. While the soul exists through these principles, it sees itself; it certainly knows from itself that it is an intelligent being. It recognizes itself entirely. But through that same profound act and divine power, it also recognizes its own nature as its own. Therefore, it is not strictly said to "notice" itself or its prior life and actions, because it does not use discursive reason <term>discursive reason</term> <note>Step-by-step logical thinking, as opposed to direct, instant intuition.</note> or imagination, which are the usual tools of memory and observation. But when it first comes from that state into the sun, and then into the air, these two things happen. Indeed, all the forms of things exist potentially within the soul; they are not merely "accidents" clinging to the soul like letters on a tablet, but are <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>Latin: "rationes seminales." These are "seed-principles" or blueprints that contain the potential for all physical forms.</note>. There are certain essential living principles, the seminal reasons of limbs and bodily qualities in the vegetative power, just as the properties of an entire plant exist within its seed. Therefore, the soul is always all these things, but sometimes it is these things in "potential," and at other times more in "act." The soul is more truly a divine thing if it acts through the intellect alone, rather than if it meanwhile notices itself through the discourse of reason or the figments of imagination; for these latter things distract it.*

---

->Chapter IV.<-

<note>original Greek: "ΕΚΕΙ μὲν οὖν..."</note> Therefore, in the Intelligible World <note>The realm of pure ideas and truth.</column-break/> <margin>A</margin>, the soul also sees the Good itself through the intellect. For the intellect does not hinder it from running all the way to the Good, because the medium between them is not a body that could act as an obstacle—even though even among bodies, the medium often allows a descent from the highest to the lowest things. Consequently, if the soul gives itself over to inferior things, it immediately carries back what it desired, in proportion to its memory and imagination. Specifically, it holds a memory even of the best things, though it is not itself in the best state. <margin>B</margin> We must understand "memory" not only as when someone consciously feels they are remembering, but also when they are presently affected according to the likeness of prior feelings and thoughts. For it is possible that one who does not notice they possess something may hold it more strongly than if they acknowledged it; for if they acknowledge it, they might hold it as if it were "something else," existing as if they were separate from it. But one who does not consider that they have it seems to *be* the very thing they have. <margin>C</margin> This kind of affection moves the soul more vehemently and inclines it further. But if, having already departed from that divine region, the soul reports its memories in some way, the power of memory was already within it there, but the "acts" of those divine things somehow obscured the memory. For we should not say that there were <unclear>àchacétes</unclear> <note>Possibly a Greek-derived Latin term for "clinging" or "adhering" shapes; the OCR is unclear.</note> figures there, lest something absurd follow; rather, the power was there, to be sent forth into action later.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the soul's nature is defined by its focus: remembering divine truths keeps it elevated, while focus on the physical world pulls it down. He distinguishes between conscious memory and an internal state of "being" where the soul becomes one with what it contemplates.</summary>

### PLOTINUS’ ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

When therefore that activity concerning the intelligible realm <note>The world of perfect forms and ideas.</note>, which used to be vigorous, ceases, the soul recognizes itself, having known it before it was there.
<column-break/>
And when the activity in the intelligible realm has ceased, the soul perceives itself, seeing what it had seen before it arrived there. <note>original Greek: "παυσαμένης δὲ τῆς ἐν τῷ νοητῷ ἐνεργείας, ᾔσθετο αὑτῆς ἡ ψυχή..."</note>
<column-break/>

*The soul in this life can know divine things, not through the imagination, nor even through reasoning that takes its principles from the imagination, but through the intellect and reasoning that takes its principles from the intellect. However, when it rises through reason into the mind as if into a mirror—although memory, commonly speaking, is fed by all imagination—nevertheless a certain kind of memory also exists in the reason and the intellect. In the soul above the heavens, the act of understanding occupies its use through the conjunction of reason and imagination; but in heaven, a use of this kind will arise again, through which you remember, as if tangibly, human life and human affairs of old; for the soul has looked out upon these from above the heavens by a certain excellence. Therefore, let souls recognize one another in heaven, especially friends, since we are known through the vivid affections of the souls themselves, and through the bodies which they can have there, possessing a figure similar to this one in a liquid matter, which yields much more to the soul as its shaper than earthly matter now yields to the soul’s affections. Furthermore, if the bodies there are spherical <note>Neoplatonists often held that the sphere was the most perfect shape, and thus the form of celestial bodies.</note>, there will nonetheless be differences—distinct signs and indications of the different souls—whether in shape (as we said), or magnitude, quality, motion, gesture, nod, or light, just as happens in the eyes from the soul's affections, and in various clouds where there are different shapes and colors. There are those who believe the heavenly beings utter voices to one another—for even the heavens can sound—or at least they will converse with one another by mutual nods. In the heavens, they remember divine things more than human ones. But when weary, they can turn back toward the air; however, both when they are in heaven and when they are in the air, they possess a naturally free motion and can remain there for many ages, and return higher from there. Finally, nothing prevents one from always being in the higher realms by an excellent choice, according to Porphyry, Iamblichus, and Julian.* <note>Porphyry and Iamblichus were famous successors to Plotinus; Julian refers to the Emperor Julian, who studied Neoplatonism.</note>

---

->Chapter V.<-

<margin>A</margin> WHAT then? Is it this same power of remembering that now brings those things back into action for us? Perhaps if it does not bring them back, it is done by that memory which we did not see. But if it represents the same things, it does this by the same power by which we saw them there: for it is this which is excited in us whenever we are incited toward those things, and it is this very thing which sees in those things which have been spoken of. For it is not necessary for the soul to show those things by using some likeness or imaginary condition, nor to take its principles from elsewhere through reasoning. Rather, it is permitted to say the same thing about the intelligible world <margin>B</margin> (as it is called) even while existing here—namely, by the very fact that the soul possesses the power to look up at those things. For we must contemplate those things with the same faculty that we excite there, which it is also necessary to excite here. It is just as if someone, ascending a high watchtower <note>original Latin: "speculum" - here meaning a high place or lookout point.</note>, should look out from there with intent eyes upon things that no one else sees who has not ascended with him. When, therefore, it appears from reason that memory takes its beginning from heaven—where the soul has already left the higher region—it is no wonder <margin>C</margin> if, having set out from there into heaven and residing there, it receives the memory of many things that happen among us, of the kind that has been mentioned. It recognizes many souls known before, since it is necessary for them to have bodies around them in similar shapes. But if they should change their shapes and become spherical, they will seem to recognize each other through the very characters and ways proper to each. For this is neither absurd nor wonderful. Granting indeed that they have cast away all passions <margin>D</margin>, nothing prevents them from retaining their character. And if it were also permitted for them to converse, they would also recognize each other in this way. But when they fall from the intelligible world, in what condition do they find themselves? Perhaps they will stir up memory again, yet less than they did concerning those same things when they were there; for they will have other things to remember, and then a longer time will bring about a complete forgetting of many things. But if, having now slipped into the sensible world, they fall here into generation <note>The cycle of birth and physical existence.</note>, what time will be given to memory? Perhaps it is not necessary <margin>E</margin> to be plunged into every depth. For it is possible that souls, having been moved and having progressed to a certain distance, may stand still; nor does anything prevent

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What then? Is that power also present now? And are we led into activity through the act of remembering? Or if we do not wake the memory itself, how is it this very power by which we saw there? For this is awakened in us, both toward those things and toward their interpretation. We do not seem to do this by using mere likeness, nor by a syllogism <term>syllogism: a form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term> taking principles from elsewhere; rather, this belongs to the intelligibles, as it is said, and is <margin>B</margin> here. The same things are said by one who has the power to contemplate the things there. For the same thing had to be awakened in order to see the things there, and so it is awakened. And if he directed the necessity of his eyes toward that watchtower, he would see what not a single one of those who had not ascended before him could see. If, therefore, memory appears to begin from the point of leaving heaven, the soul having already left the regions there, one might <margin>C</margin> say that if it holds power while being there, it is no wonder if it has memory of many things here—such as have been mentioned—and will recognize many of those previously known to it, if indeed it is necessary for them always to have bodies, but in similar shapes. But if the shapes should change, making them spherical, would they recognize each other through their characters and the individuality of their ways? Yes, indeed <margin>D</margin>; for while they have laid aside their passions, their characters are not prevented from remaining. And if they were able to talk to one another, they would also recognize each other thus. But when they descend in some way from the intelligibles, or have moved their memory, they do so less than those who were concerned with the same things; for they have other things to remember, and a complete time has produced a total forgetfulness of many things. But if <margin>E</margin> they fall into these things here? In what time? It is possible to remember, or it is not necessary to fall into the depth. For it is possible for them, having been moved and having proceeded toward something... and nothing hinders them from again [rising]...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of memory within the hierarchy of souls. Having established how human souls retain identity between the physical and divine realms, he now investigates whether celestial beings (the stars, the sun, and the World Soul) possess or require memory in the same way humans do.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

To emerge, and then to return again before they are plunged into the lowest place of generation. <note>original Greek: "ἐκδῦναι... ἔσχατον τόπον." This refers to the soul's ascent and descent between the divine and material worlds.</note>
->To emerge, and from there to return again before they are plunged into the lowest place of generation.<-

*The service of a preserving memory is necessary only where something can pass away and then return, one thing after another. Therefore, memory does not seem necessary for celestial souls; for they do not move about to find or acquire something new, but remain in a state of constant presence.*

->Chapter VI.<-

<margin>A</margin> One might easily assert that souls that move through and change their states would indeed use memory; for memory belongs to things that have happened or passed away. But for souls that remain entirely in the same state, what things would they remember? It is strange for human reason to seek memory in the souls of all the stars, and especially in the Sun and Moon. From here, following a similar line of reasoning, one might move to the Soul of the All, and finally dare to attribute <margin>B</margin> memory to Jupiter <note>Plotinus uses 'Jupiter' (Zeus) here to represent the "Demiurge" or the governing Intellect of the universe.</note> himself. Investigating these things, one will further consider their thoughts and reasonings—if they have any—and what kind they might be. But if they neither seek anything nor doubt (for they lack nothing), and if they do not learn what they previously did not know, what kind of reasonings, logical deductions, or mental schemes would exist within them? Nor will they anxiously consult about the "machinery" <note>original Latin: "machinis," Greek: "μηχαναὶ." Refers to the technical management of the cosmos.</note> by which they arrange human and earthly affairs; for there is another <margin>C</margin> way in which the higher beings munificently dispense all things to the universe.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **SOULS**, therefore, that move about and vary their states can easily be said to use memory; for memory is of those things which have been done or have passed away. But for souls that rest entirely in the same state, of what things will they be mindful? Yet human reason asks for memory in the souls of all the stars, but especially the Sun and Moon. From here, by a similar condition, it transfers itself to the soul of the universe, and finally dares to place memory <margin>B</margin> in Jupiter himself. But inquiring into these things, it will consider besides what their thoughts and reasonings are (if there are any) and of what kind they are. Now if they neither seek anything nor doubt—for they lack nothing—and if they do not learn what they did not know before, what reasonings or logical sequences or mental inventions will be in them? Nor will they anxiously deliberate about the "machinery" by which they might arrange human and earthly things: for there is <margin>C</margin> another way by which the higher beings generously distribute all things to the universe.

---

*For the souls governing the celestial bodies, the service of recollection is not necessary, whether in knowledge, sight, or motion. Their divine intuition, which is never interrupted, is sufficient. They can indeed perceive that they see, but there is no need to repeat that "they have seen," since there is no "having seen" there, but only a "seeing" that is never broken; therefore, it never needs to be resumed. Their life is similar: always the same. So too is their motion—perpetual and continuous in their bodies—and therefore for each of them it is always one, even though it may happen to be, or appear to be, manifold to us. They also look upon changeable things with a gaze that does not change, just as someone might observe a person walking in a straight line for part of an hour with a single, continuous inspection; the observer's view is not changed, even if the person being watched changes position. If the observer judges that the person "is here," "was there," and "will be there," such changes do not happen within the vision itself, even though they are judged to happen within the spectacle.*

->Chapter VII.<-

<margin>A</margin> What then? Do they not remember that they have seen God? Or do they rather see Him always? As long as they see Him, it is not possible for them to say they "have seen" Him, for that would imply they had stopped. That would be a change of state. And what of the fact that they circled the earth yesterday or last year? Or that they lived yesterday and long ago, and have lived since they first began, or have lived forever? To live "forever" is always the same thing. But as for "yesterday" or "last year" in their motion, wouldn't that be like <margin>B</margin> someone who takes a single stride and then divides it into many parts? He makes one motion many, and invents various different ones. For here the motion is one; but for us, it is measured as many, and as different days, because nights intervene. But there, since the day is one, how can there be many? Therefore, there is no "last year." But someone will object that there is not one interval, but one after another, <margin>C</margin> and that there is one part of the zodiac and then another. Why, then, should the celestial soul not say, "I have already passed this part, and now I occupy another"? Furthermore, if they look upon human affairs, how could they not also see human changes, and that there are different people now? If this is so, then different people existed before, and different affairs, from which it would seem they must have memory.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **WHAT** then? Do they not remember that they have seen God? Or rather do they always see Him? As long as they do not cease to see, it is not permitted for them to say they "have seen," otherwise this would be the condition of those who at some time stopped seeing. What then? Neither do they record that they circled the earth yesterday or in the previous year; nor that they lived yesterday and for a long time, and from what time they have lived. Rather, they live always. That which is always the same is always one. But what is said regarding "yesterday" and "last year" <margin>B</margin> in motion is just as if someone should take the impulse and motion made with one foot and divide it into many, and should himself imagine that the one motion is different ones and many. For here the motion is one, but according to us they are measured as many, and as different days because nights fall between. But there, since there is one day, how can there be many? Therefore, there is no "previous year." But someone will object that it is not one, but another and yet another interval; <margin>C</margin> and that there is one and then another portion of the zodiac. Why then should the celestial soul not say, "I have now passed this part; but now I occupy another"? Furthermore, if they look upon human things, how do they not also see human changes, and that there are different men now? If it is so, then other men and other affairs existed before, from which it results that they seem to have memory.

<summary>Plotinus argues that celestial beings and the World Soul do not require memory because they exist in an eternal present. Unlike humans, who experience time as a sequence of passing events, divine beings possess an uninterrupted "seeing" and "living" that makes the concept of "yesterday" or "recollection" unnecessary.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion of celestial souls and their relationship to memory. While the previous page questioned whether the Sun, Moon, or the "governing Intellect" (Jupiter) require memory, this page clarifies that their constant state of contemplation and the "vital" nature of their motion makes human-like memory and imagination unnecessary for them.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

The soul of any star, contemplating the Ideas <note>original: "ideas," the eternal archetypes in the Divine Mind</note> and principles of all things, always possesses within itself a certain knowledge of the universe—whether you wish to call this knowledge intellectual or rational. Meanwhile, through its celestial body, it perceives physical things. Yet, because it perceives all things simultaneously, it does not notice them through imagination, nor does it store them in memory. This is both because it already understands all things from a higher perspective and because these individual details are of no importance to it. Furthermore, because it already perceives all things at once, nothing moves it as if it were a new sensation. Nevertheless, a living being perceives through imagination that it is feeling particular things which are especially necessary to the universe, such as stars, celestial bodies, and elements. Since the purpose of celestial souls is not merely to move through this or that part, or for a specific duration, but to contemplate and to move simply and eternally—and since their motion is perfect at every moment, and all things are fixed in the order of the universe—they have undoubtedly escaped the need for memory. No anxiety or care troubles them regarding any specific place, time, motion, or changeable thing. Thus, even while perceiving such things, they are not forced to apply imagination or focused attention to them. Note that the circular motion of the heavens is neither an "alteration," because it does not change its form; nor is it "local" <note>in the sense of moving from one place to another to find something new</note>, because it does not change its position; rather, it is **vital**—that is, a proper act of internal life, and likewise a natural one. For to act upon oneself and to be moved from within is the defining characteristic of living things. Indeed, the motion of the heavens is of the same kind as the heartbeat in animals or the process of nutrition in plants.

->Chapter VIII.<-

<margin>A</margin> PERHAPS, however, it is not necessary to commit to memory every single thing one gazes upon, nor to gather in the imagination those things that follow entirely by chance. Likewise, to what end does a more certain understanding and knowledge of things reside in the soul if, whenever such things are presented to the senses, the soul must abandon its intellectual knowledge to stare at that which is particular and sensible? This would only happen if one were managing something through action—yet even then, the particular detail would be included primarily within the concept of the whole. <margin>B</margin> I say regarding anyone in this way: in the first place, it is not necessary that someone places what they see within themselves. For when something is of no interest or consequence to a person, the sense alone undergoes the movement of distinguishing what is seen, without our choice; meanwhile, the soul does not receive it into itself. Indeed, that specific difference among visible things is neither a concern for us, nor will it contribute to any necessity or utility. <margin>C</margin> Now, when a person acts entirely toward themselves, or toward certain other things, they do not retain the memory of such past events, just as they do not even perceive the sensation of present ones. Furthermore, it is not necessary for things that occur entirely by chance to be placed in the imagination; or if they are placed there, it is not so they may be guarded and observed. One can perceive that the form of such a thing does not carry one’s consent, if only they take what is said in this way: <margin>D</margin> I say it like this: If it were never our primary purpose to divide this part of the air and then that part as we move through space, or rather to pass through it, we would never think of observing this very thing while walking. For unless it were specifically decreed by us to complete exactly a certain path—and if we were permitted to run through the air—we would never care in which particular stage of the earth we are, or how much space we have already covered. <margin>E</margin> Then truly, if it were required of us to move, but not specifically for a set time, but only to move, we would never relate any other action at all to time, and certainly we would never devise one time after another in our memory. This is most evident from the fact that when thought possesses within itself the whole of what is being done, and trusts that it will be brought to effect, it no longer applies itself to the individual things that happen,

<column-break/>

VIII. It is no longer necessary to place everything one contemplates into memory, nor for those things that follow incidentally by chance to arise in the imagination. If knowledge and understanding are more fluent <note>Greek: εὐερρεστέρα, "well-flowing" or "easy"</note> in the intellect, even if things happen sensibly, there is no necessity for the knowledge of them to be present by focusing on the sensible particular—unless one assigns something in action to that part which is already contained in the whole of the knowledge. I say to each as follows: first, that it is not necessary for something to be placed within oneself. For when it makes no difference, or the sensation is of no value to it at all, the inclinations are moved by the difference of the things seen; the sense alone suffers the sensible things, the soul not receiving them into the interior. It is not a matter of management, nor is the difference itself going to be of use for anything else. When the soul is turned toward itself, or toward other things, or simply exists, it would not "wipe off" <note>Greek: ἀναμάττοιτο, "to take an impression" or "to model," here meaning to record in memory</note> the memory of such passing things, since it does not even recognize the sensation of them when they are present. And indeed, of things happening by chance, there is no necessity for them to exist in the imagination; and even if they do, it is not so that they are guarded or observed. But even if one perceives such things as the senses give, if he takes the meaning thus: I say it in this way: if it never became a primary goal to cut this air and then that air by moving according to place, or even more to pass through it, would you still observe it, would there still be a thought of walking? Since if it did not matter to finish this specific part of the road primarily, we would not even make a concern of the passage; it would not become a care to us at what point we are, or how much we have finished, and in what Form <note>term: 'ἰδέᾳ' (Idea), here referring to the intelligible pattern of the movement</note> we are moved. Nor if we referred any other action to time, would we produce in memory one time after another. We use the fact that the mind holds the whole thing being done and trusts in it, so that it results in every way.

He argues that even for humans, constant observation of trivial details (like the air we move through while walking) is unnecessary for the mind's higher functions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of memory in divine and celestial beings. It argues that the "vital motion" of the stars and the "royal intellect" of Jupiter (the World Soul) operate in a state of eternal presence, rendering the human faculty of memory—which relies on the passage of time and the collection of past experiences—entirely unnecessary for them.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>for them <note>original Greek: αυτοῖς</note></margin>
Therefore, for those who are not in a state of becoming <note>that is, eternal beings</note>, it does not follow that they must observe their own actions, even when one always does the same thing, having learned it and following along with that same repetitive action. As for the stars, they are carried along while performing their own specific duties. Even if they have passed through all these places they traverse, their work consists in the contemplation of what is present to them. Furthermore, as for the past: if the transit through these places were merely accidental, the mind might learn of them; but since they always traverse the same paths, time is not counted by them through calculation, nor by being "in this way" or "in that way." There is no necessity for them to have a memory of the places they have passed. Since they are living beings, and their environment is around them, their movement is not merely "local" <note>concerning physical place</note> but "vital" <note>concerning the internal life of the being</note>; it is the life of a single being acting effectively upon itself. In one sense, it acts upon external things, but in its movement, it is the life within itself, as if it were pursuing its own nature. Nor should one compare their motion to a dance <note>original: χορεία (chorea)</note> that stops; if a dance were to stop, the completion of its performance would fulfill it from beginning to end. But if the motion is simple, or if each part is complete in itself—and if it is the kind of motion that exists forever—then it is always entirely present. It has no "long ago," it possesses no time, and it neither reaches an end nor stands still in a place. Consequently, it would have no desire to stop in a temporal sense, nor would it have measurable memories or any recollection of these things. If the living being lives a blessed life, and their souls always look toward that life, and if the vision of their souls is directed toward that One, and the illumination from them shines into the whole heaven—just like strings on a lyre <note>original: λύρα (lyra)</note> moving in sympathy—then they will care for and sing in a natural harmony. It is not that the whole heaven and its parts move toward themselves, being carried along, while others move differently toward the same point; rather, their positions are distinct. Furthermore, our argument would be even more correct if the life of all things is one and the same.

But Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, who orders all things—of whom Plato says that he possesses a royal soul and a royal intellect <note>A reference to Plato's Philebus 30d</note>—and who possesses providence so that things might come to be, and authority over what has been created, and who administers the order of things, and who has already wound through many cycles and filled them: how could he, in all these things, have a memory of how many cycles of life have occurred and how they might come to be hereafter? Would he be devising, comparing, and calculating all these things through memory? And further, if the Creator is the most wise, he would derive no benefit from memory...

<column-break/>

Furthermore, whenever someone always does the same thing, it is surely useless to observe every single part of one's work. If, therefore, the stars, while they are carried along, perform certain duties of their own, they are not moved simply to pass through these spaces which they traverse. Their work is neither to look at what they pass through, nor at what is already past. Indeed, the transition itself is accidental to them while they are occupied with greater things. Finally, because they always run through the same paths in a similar tenor, time is by no means computed by them as a discrete measure. Even if it were distinguished, it would not be necessary to retain a memory of the places they pass or of the times. This is especially true since they possess entirely the same life always, and they are perpetually revolved around the same place, so that their motion seems not so much local as vital. Indeed, as a single living being, it acts into itself in a state of rest as far as pertains to external things, but in motion through the life that is perpetually awake within itself. Therefore, if anyone should say that the celestial motion is like a dance <note>original: chorea</note>—if indeed a dance that eventually ceases is a complete progression of motion from beginning to end—then each individual part would be imperfect when counted. But if it is compared to a dance that is eternal, it will be forever perfect. If it is always perfect, it will not have a time in which it will eventually become perfect, nor a place. For this reason, it has no appetite for such things; therefore, it is measured by neither temporal nor local conditions. Thus, no memory of these things occurs. Furthermore, by this reasoning, our logic will be even more confirmed: namely, that they lead a blessed life, contemplating life in their own souls. And by the conspiracy <note>agreement or harmony</note> of their own souls toward that One, and by the illumination from themselves into the whole heaven—just like strings on a lyre <note>original: lyra</note>—they wondrously create a melody in a certain natural harmony. And so the whole heaven is turned, and its parts are moved toward it; the whole is agitated in one way, and different parts in another, although toward the same goal. Since their position is different, the life of all is even more unified and very similar.

---

> -> *Jupiter, the ruler of the world, through one simple and all-encompassing form of himself, which is infinite in power and the effecter of infinite things, sees and effects infinite things. He does this not by two separate acts, but by the same act with which he sees, he also effects, and vice versa. It would truly be absurd to say that he gathers knowledge of things from the things themselves; for through a knowledge that precedes the things, he creates the things. Nor could he comprehend infinite things if he were to hunt for knowledge from the infinite. But as it stands, he beholds infinite things through one form of himself, no differently than if the sun, through its one light, were to behold the innumerable shimmering rays resulting from it. Chapter IX.* <-

---

**JUPITER**, however, adorning all things, moderating and disposing them, always possessing a royal soul and a royal mind, and possessing providence for the manner in which each thing is made, and power over those things which are made—likewise disposing each thing in a certain order. Furthermore, unfolding many circuits and bringing many already begun to their end—why would he not have a memory in all these things, having remembered how many and what kind of revolutions have already been driven? And again, as to how they should be in the future: would he be devising, conjecturing, and thinking them out, and thus be the most mindful of all, even more so as he is the more skilled architect? As much, therefore, as pertains to the memory of the revolutions themselves...
