# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

Even in itself, this brings much doubt: namely, what the number [of actions] might be, and whether it is limited. For if it were finite, it would give a temporal beginning to the universe; but if it were infinite, that Ruler would not grasp how many his works are—unless, perhaps, it is said that he always exists in his own knowledge and life, and thus the infinite is there, and there the One consists. This happens not through knowledge falling upon him from the outside, but by constituting the thing itself. Indeed, since he himself is infinite, he always remains a whole at once; or rather, he is accompanied and observed not by an acquired notion. For just as he knows the infinite nature of his own life, so he also knows his action diffused through the infinite universe, especially since it is one, yet not for the reason that it directs itself toward the universe.

*The order of the universe, which unfolds after the highest realm into matter, is as a whole unchangeable; this is true both in the true Jupiter <note>Plotinus uses the name 'Jupiter' (Zeus) to refer to the highest levels of divinity</note>, both in the first, who is the pure Intellect and the segregated craftsman of the world, and in the second Jupiter, who is the intellectual Soul, the joined leader of the world. Therefore, neither Jupiter runs through thoughts or is hesitant about what must be done—especially because the Soul, with a certain focused gaze, looks up at the order of the universe in the first Jupiter and holds it firm. It has the entire matter of the world subjected to it and moves it from within, turning all things most easily from its own life as if from a single hinge, so that nothing resists its action and no ambiguity occurs.*

### Chapter X.

<margin>A</margin> There is, however, a twofold Orderer: for we call one the Artificer <note>original Greek: δημιουργὸν (demiurgon); the divine craftsman</note>, and the other the Soul of the universe. When we name Jupiter, we sometimes mean the Artificer of the world, and sometimes the leader of the whole world. Certainly, we must separate far from the Architect of the whole anything that is called "prior" or "posterior," attributing to him a single, unchanging life that is free from time. <margin>B</margin> But the life of the world, which naturally has this role of leading, seems to require further inquiry and reasoning: might it not also have its life in reasoning, and in searching for what is most especially to be done? For what must be done has already been discovered and ordered—not, indeed, through those very things which are ordered; for the things that are ordered are those very things which are being born, but that which does these things is the "Order" itself. This is the action of a soul depending on permanent wisdom, the image of which is the order that flourishes in the soul. <margin>C</margin> Since that wisdom is not changed, it is necessary that this soul is also not changed. For it does not look up to that wisdom at one time and then not look at another; otherwise, if it stopped, it would immediately be in doubt. But there is one soul and one work. For that which holds the dignity of a single leader always excels; it does not command at one time and then find itself overcome at another, nor does ambiguity arise. Indeed, a single governor always affects the same thing; for what would be the cause for him to <margin>D</margin> desire one thing and then another, such that he would be compelled to hesitate while distracted by many things? Furthermore, even if the one existing Soul of the world were changed in some way, it would still not doubt. For the fact that the world has many parts and many oppositions between parts does not mean it will doubt how they should be arranged. It does not begin from the lowest things, nor from the parts, but starting from the first things, and receiving its way from the First <note>The "One" or the highest principle</note> through a path entirely removed from impediments, it diffuses and adorns itself through all things. Because of this, it dominates and overcomes, since it remains the same in the same work and toward the same goal. But if it wanted one thing and then another, from where would that other desire come?

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Greek original of the preceding Latin text</note>

...and by itself it would hold much difficulty, what the number might be, and if indeed it is finite. For being so, it would give a temporal beginning to the whole; but if infinite, he will not know how many his own works are—unless he knows them as one life. For he is infinite to himself, and the "One" will be in knowledge, but not, I say, as an eternal being... the infinite things are always rather limited and contemplated, not by an external knowledge. Just as he knows the infinite of his own life, so also he knows the activity which is one toward the whole. Because it is toward the whole.

<margin>A</margin> But since the nature of the world-orderer is twofold: one we call the Demiurge <note>Craftsman</note>, the other the Soul of the whole; and when we speak, we are sometimes carried toward the Demiurge, and sometimes toward that which leads the whole. In the case of the Demiurge, one must remove "first" and "later," giving him one unchanging and timeless life. But the life in the world, having the leadership itself, still has a certain "reason" <note>logos</note>, if it does not have it in its life so as to calculate, nor in seeking what it must do. For already it has been discovered and ordered, the things that must be done. And the things ordered are through the things becoming; but that which makes them is the "Order," and that is the activity of the soul depending on the same wisdom, as the order in her is an image. If that is unchanging, it is necessary that this also does not change. <margin>C</margin> For it is not that she looks there at one time, and at another looks toward what she does; for she would then be at a loss. For there is one soul, and one work. For that which leads well is always in control, and is not one part controlling and another part controlled. For from where would there be more [influences], such that a battle or doubt might arise? And that which administers always wills the same thing. For why would it want another and another, so as to be at a loss among many things? And if it were already changing, it would not be <margin>D</margin> at a loss. For even if the whole already has many parts, and oppositions toward the parts, yet it does not doubt from these how it must be disposed. For it does not begin from the last things, nor from the parts, but from the first things; and having received from the first, it goes through an <margin> <insert>* and in whatever way it may be</insert> </margin> unobstructed path to the last things through its power, because it remains the same upon one work, and toward the same. But if it should want another, from where would that other come?

<summary>Plotinus argues that the divine Orderer (the Demiurge and the World Soul) does not use human-like deliberation or memory, as its actions flow from an eternal, unchanging wisdom and a single, unified life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine thought and action. It moves from whether the stars have memory to whether the 'World Soul' or 'Nature' operates through calculation and planning. The text argues that the higher governance of the universe acts automatically and perfectly from an internal principle, rather than through the hesitant, step-by-step reasoning used by humans or doctors.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

...to her, nor the whole. Her work would be in doubt, as if she were uncertain of what to do in her calculations.

FOR the administration of the world is as of a single living being; one part is from external parts, and another from within and from the beginning. It is just as a doctor receives things from the outside and acts piece by piece, being ignorant in many ways and forced to deliberate; but nature acts from the principle, without any need for deliberation. And throughout the whole administration and the one administering, if nature flows to the doctor and he still struggles, how much more is simplicity found there [in the world's nature], insofar as it embraces all things as parts of one living being. It masters all individual natures, and they follow it, being suspended and attached, or as if sprouting out, like branches from a whole plant. But what need is there for calculation, or counting, or memory, when wisdom is always present, acting and ruling, and administering according to the same patterns? For one should not think that because the things produced are varied and different, the producer must act through changes that match the changes in the things produced. For in as much as the things produced are varied, the act of producing remains exactly the same. Indeed, many things happen according to nature in each form of a living being—all the different ages, the growths at their specific times, such as horns or beards, and also the peaks of growth and the birth of others—while the former internal principles <note>original Greek: "logōn"</note> are released and others come to be. This shows that in the living being produced, there is the same and whole principle, and indeed it is worthy to posit the same wisdom there. This wisdom is universal, as if the wisdom in the world were preserved: many and varied things, as of one great living being with many changes, yet belonging to one principle, and all things existing together. For if it did not contain all things at once, then that wisdom would not be the primary one, but would belong to later things and mere parts.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Then, being so affected, she will wonder what is better to be done, and thus her duty in acting will be weakened, if indeed she is distracted by reasoning into the ambiguity of acting.

*By the same proportion that the individual natures of individual parts in any living being depend on a single common nature of the whole living being, so do all natures of things to be lived depend on one common nature of the whole world. Just as the nature of any living being, containing within itself the natural and seminal reasons <note>term: 'seminal reasons' (rationes seminales) are the internal blueprints or 'seeds' that determine how a creature grows</note> of parts and natural effects, neither labors nor consults in acting, nor is transformed while producing diverse things—especially because it acts from the innermost parts, and does not begin its work from many parts, but derives all things from one order of all—so also the nature of the world does not consult in its work, nor labor, nor change. It relates to its work just as we were saying a particular nature relates to its own, and even much more excellently, especially because it is the instrument of eternal and infinite wisdom, led always to the same things in turn, with the same tenor <note>meaning: with a constant and unchanging character</note>, and it presides over all matter. Indeed, when it acts through a habit similar to nature, it acts without consultation, or choice, or attention; for if it were to return to such attention, it would more often be hindered and go astray, as if such attention did not belong to nature. Chapter XI.*

<margin>A</margin> FOR the governance of the world is like that of a single living being. But this governance of the living being itself treats things partly from the outside and through parts; but partly rules from the internal principle. A doctor, indeed, beginning from the outside and proceeding through parts, often moves in doubt and consultation. Nature, however, since it leads its principle from within, does not need consultation. Moreover, the governance of the whole world and its governor must proceed in dispensing things not in the manner of a doctor, but in the manner of nature. <margin>B</margin> Indeed, simplicity is much more preserved there, in that all things are included within, like the limbs of a single living being. For one nature embraces all natures, while the others follow, depending on it and proceeding from it, and thus as if sprouting, just as the natures of branches come from the nature of the whole tree itself. What reasoning, then, or counting, or memory is needed? Since wisdom is always present and acts and dominates, and always governs with the same tenor. <margin>C</margin> For it must not be thought that because the things that are done are varied and diverse, the producer also has a communion with the changes of the things being done. For insofar as the things done are varied, the producer itself remains in the same tenor. For there are many things which are born naturally in each of the living beings, and not all at once. There are different ages and certain sproutings at fixed times, such as horns, beards, and breasts; likewise certain growth <margin>D</margin> and the "flowers" of age, and again the prescribed propagation of offspring by which others are generated, while the prior seminal reasons <note>original: "feminariis rationibus"</note> meanwhile do not fail, but others are produced besides. This indeed is evident from the fact that in the living being generated from it, the same seminal reason is preserved in its entirety. Now indeed it is worthwhile to assert that the same wisdom flourishes here, and that this is universal, like the stable wisdom of the world: many and varied indeed, and again the simple [wisdom] of one greatest of all living beings, which indeed does not become varied from the very multitude of works, but is one reason and all things at once: <margin>E</margin> otherwise, unless it be all things, it will not be itself, but rather a wisdom of later things and parts.

*Thought running through several things in order is a certain motion lacking absolute knowledge, and which, because of need, seeks and consumes truth and wisdom. Therefore such discourse, or consultation, or choice, does not belong to the mind or soul that rules the world, which possesses from eternity a habit full of wisdom, and an entire fullness of both ideas and seminal reasons. By this fullness it anticipates future things in the present, and discerns in what ways they will be, for it is the maker of them, alone dominating all its matter, and not subject to impediments. Therefore it is neither anxious, nor ambiguous, nor restless, but by its own all-forming nature, conforming the universe to itself. Since indeed this nature itself is intelligence and will, it rightly treats the materials of the world not by counsel, but by a wisdom naturally established, and also by a voluntary making.*

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of the World Soul and the stars. Having previously argued that nature acts through internal principles rather than external deliberation, Plotinus now addresses whether the "Leader of the World" (the World Soul) requires reasoning, memory, or calculation to govern the universe.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IIII.

<margin>A</margin> PERHAPS, indeed, someone might think that a work of this kind belongs to nature; but since wisdom exists in the universe, it must necessarily provide for the discourses of reason and memory there as well. However, that is the way of humans, who place wisdom in the lack of wisdom, and who think that seeking wisdom is the same as being wise. For what else is the discourse of reason but the desire to find wisdom, and to find the true reason that is truly master of the mind? For one who reasons is like a person
<margin>B</margin> striking a lyre <note>original Latin: "citharam"</note> for the sake of the striking itself, or practicing to gain a habit, or generally learning for the sake of knowing. For the one who reasons seeks to bring forth that which the wise person already possesses; for this reason, wisdom exists in a certain fixed and stable state. The reasoner himself bears witness to this: for as soon as he finds what he desired, he stops reasoning, and rests, situated within wisdom itself. If, therefore, we were to consider the leader of the world <note>The "Mundi Dux" or World Soul, which Plotinus views as the governing intelligence of the cosmos.</note> to be in the position of students, we would surely
<margin>C</margin> attribute to him the discourses and doubts of reason, and memory, as he compares past things with present and future ones. But if we should rather think of him as one who knows within a stable state that possesses its own boundary, we would rightly judge that wisdom is more suited to him. Furthermore, if he knows the future—for it would be absurd to deny that—why should he not also hold the manner in which future things will come to be? But if he already knows how they will be, what further need is there to investigate by reason, or to compare the past
<margin>D</margin> with the present? Again, the knowledge of future things, if it is granted to be present in him, will certainly not be of the kind usually found in prophets <note>original Latin: "vatibus"</note>, but like that of the creators themselves who know with certainty that it will be so. This is the case for those who possess authority over all things, to whom nothing hesitant or ambiguous happens, and whose judgment, once they have assented to it, rests forever. Therefore, the wisdom regarding the future is the same there as the wisdom regarding the present, according to its stable state. But this is far removed from the investigation of reason; and unless he knows the future
<margin>E</margin> things which he himself is going to do, he will neither know how to act, nor will he act with a view toward something, but he will do whatever happens by chance; but that is nothing other than acting by accident. Therefore, the reason by which he acts remains; and if the reason by which he acts remains, he will certainly not act otherwise than he designs, according to the exemplar <note>The "exemplar" refers to the Platonic Forms or internal blueprints within the Divine Mind.</note> that exists within him: thus he will always act by one tenor and the same reason. For he will not act one way now and another way in the future; otherwise, what will prevent him from wandering far from his purpose? But if the work
<margin>F</margin> itself behaves differently, it will not possess this difference from itself, but insofar as it serves the seminal reasons <note>original Latin: "seminarijs rationibus," translated from the Greek "logoi," the formative principles that direct the growth of the natural world.</note>: these indeed depend on the creator. Therefore, the craftsmanship follows the very series of the reasons. Thus the creator is in no way forced to wander, or to doubt, or to labor in his affairs, as some have thought, believing that the governance of all things is laborious. Truly, to labor in arranging a work seems to be nothing other than
<margin>G</margin> handling foreign materials, that is, materials over which one has the least mastery. But when someone masters the work and commands it, what would he need except himself and his own will? That is his own wisdom; for it is within his power...

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> But perhaps someone might classify such a thing as the work of nature. But if prudence <note>original Greek: "phronēsis"</note> exists in that which is, then the calculative part and memories must also be present. But this is the way of men, who place prudence in the state of not yet being prudent, and in the search for prudence. But what else would calculating <note>original Greek: "logizesthai"</note> be, other than the striving to find prudence and a true reason <note>original Greek: "logon"</note>, and reaching that which is? For the one who calculates is like the one who strikes the strings for the sake of playing the lyre,
<margin>Β</margin> and the one who practices for the sake of knowledge in general through learning. For the one who calculates seeks to learn that which the prudent person already has; so that prudence is in a fixed state. And the one who calculates bears witness to this himself. For when he finds what he needs, he has stopped calculating, and he rests when he has entered into the state of prudence. If, then, we assign to the governor of the universe the rank of a learner, we must give him calculation and
<margin>C</margin> difficulties and memories, as he compares the things that have passed with those that are present and those that are to come. But if he must be considered as one who knows in a stable state that holds its own limit, then he himself must be prudence. And if he knows this and that, and knows the things that are to come—for it is absurd to say he does not know them—then if he must hold them so as to know how they will be, why does he still need to calculate and to compare
<margin>D</margin> the past with the present? And the knowledge of things to come, if it is granted to be present in him, is not such as is present in prophets, but such as is in those who are convinced that they will perform certain things, and that these things will be so. And that which belongs to them, to those with self-governing power, has nothing doubtful or ignored. Wherefore his opinion is fixed, and that which is once decided is his prudence of the future, just as is his prudence of the present, according to the state of stability; but that which comes through calculation
<margin>Ε</margin> is otherwise. But if he did not know the future things he himself will do, he would not even know what he is doing, or perhaps he would act by looking at something, but he would act upon what has passed. But that which is from him is equal. He remains, therefore, according to how he will act; but if he remains according to how he will act, he will not act differently than he thinks he has the exemplar <note>original Greek: "paradeigma"</note> in himself; thus he will act in one way only. And it will be somehow the same now and later, or
<margin>F</margin> what is to prevent him from failing? But if the thing being made will have differences, this difference is not from himself, but from his giving to the reasons <note>original Greek: "logois"</note>; for they depend on the things that will act, so that the blessing follows in the sequence. So that in no way does the acting force him to wander, or to be at a loss, or to have troubles, as some have thought the administration of the whole to be difficult. For to have trouble, as it seems,
<margin>G</margin> is to set one's hand to foreign works; that is, to things over which he does not have power. But of those things which he masters and alone controls, what would he himself need, other than himself and his own will? And that is from them, from his own prudence...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Divine Mind or World Soul governs the universe through perfect, stable wisdom rather than the step-by-step reasoning and memory used by humans. He asserts that the creator does not labor or deliberate because he acts according to internal "seminal reasons" and possesses certain knowledge of the future.</summary>
<keywords>World Soul, Divine Mind, calculation, reasoning, prudence, seminal reasons, Platonic forms, providence, lyre metaphor, creator</keywords>

This page further distinguishes between primary Wisdom (Intellect), the Soul, and Nature.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> *The divine mind, with the seal of its own ideas, imprints forms upon the soul of the world so intensely that it shapes not only the highest part of the soul, which is intelligence, but also its middle part, which is imagination. It even imprints marks of forms upon its lowest part, which is nature. These forms, or "seminal reasons" <note>original Latin: "rationes seminales" — the formative principles or "seeds" that determine how a physical thing grows and develops</note> of things in nature, are the final traces of divine things. Therefore, they lack knowledge, although they do not lack life. They act upon matter like fire and similar forces, and they do so with artifice, because they are the living expressions of a divine intelligence and the words of that intelligence speaking. While nature acts upon matter, it is said to "suffer" <note>In this philosophical context, to "suffer" (pati) means to be the recipient of an action or to be "acted upon" by a higher power.</note> not from the matter itself, but from the soul. The soul, however, does not so much suffer from the mind as it moves itself toward the mind. Chapter XIII.*

In this state, his will is wisdom. Therefore, he lacks nothing for the work of creation, since wisdom is not something added to him from the outside; rather, he is wisdom itself, never using anything external. Thus, he uses neither reasoning nor memory, for these are external additions.

<column-break/>

->Chapter XIII.<-

<margin>A</margin> BUT in what way does such wisdom differ from nature? Certainly in this: that wisdom is primary, while nature is the last. For nature is the image of wisdom. And since nature is the lowest part of the soul, it also possesses the final "reason" <note>original Greek: "λόγον" (logon) — here meaning the rational principle or blueprint</note> shining down from above. This is just as if, when a deep block of wax is pressed, the shape passes entirely through to the other surface; the upper shape is clear and distinct, but the final trace on the bottom is obscure. Because of this, nature 
<margin>B</margin> knows nothing, but only brings things about. For, handing over without choice what it has received from what follows it, nature bestows this upon the bodily and material subject. It possesses only this capacity for action. In the same way, heat offers its own form to what is nearby, making it less hot than the source. For this reason, nature does not possess imagination. But intelligence is superior to imagination, while imagination is the middle ground between natural form and intelligence. For nature has no perception or understanding of anything. 
<margin>C</margin> Imagination, however, provides a knowledge of "foreign" things <note>External sensory inputs or images not native to the soul's own essence.</note> to the one imagining, so that the one who is acted upon may also recognize them. But this production and action depend on the agent itself. Therefore, the mind possesses; but the soul of the whole was always receiving, and always has received, and that is its very life. And what appears and shines within it is always the recognition of the intelligent soul itself. But that which flashes from the soul onto the surface of matter is nature, where beings reach their limit. Or rather, nature precedes that 
<margin>D</margin> which appears; these are the final things of the intelligible order, for after these are only imitations of beings. But nature, acting upon matter, is meanwhile acted upon from elsewhere. The soul, however, which is superior to nature and nearest to it, does not suffer <note>is not passively changed</note> in the act of making. Finally, the mind, standing above, does not act directly upon bodies or matter.

->Chapter XIV.<-

<margin>A</margin> *Universal nature, that is, a certain life-giving power of the world soul full of all "seeds," is present in all bodies born from it—not as a quality merely mixed with them, or belonging to them like heat to air, but as an act of the soul that is in some way separate and present in a separable way, like light to air. Nature relates to the soul as light relates to the sun, but material form relates to nature as heat relates to light generated from light within matter. Chapter XIV.*

<margin>A</margin> ACCORDINGLY, regarding the bodies said to be produced by nature: the elements themselves are these very bodies. But as for animals and plants, do they relate to nature in such a way that they have it as something "adjacent" <note>original Greek: "παρακειμένην" (parakeimenēn) — lying alongside or present without being fused</note> within themselves, just as air has light? Indeed, when the light departs, the air retains no light; the light exists separately, and the air remains separately, as if no mixture had occurred between them. Or does it happen rather as it is accustomed to happen in fire and something that has been heated? For...

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes between the Divine Mind, the Soul, and Nature, explaining that Nature is the "last trace" of divine wisdom—a creative force that acts upon matter without possessing conscious knowledge or imagination. He uses the analogy of light and heat to explain how these levels of reality influence one another without being physically mixed.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

When fire departs from a place, a certain heat remains; this heat is something different from the heat flourishing within the fire itself, and it becomes a "passion" <note>original Latin: "passio"; Greek: "pathos" — in this context, it refers to a state of being affected or a property received from an outside source</note> of the thing that was heated. Indeed, one must consider that the form which nature provides to the thing being formed is a distinct kind of species, separate from nature itself. It remains to be asked, however, whether there is something else acting as a medium between the formed object and nature itself. Regarding the primary difference between nature and the wisdom we have placed within the universe, enough has already been said. <margin>B</margin>

*The internal action of the world soul is not carried out gradually over time, but is fulfilled all at once in a single moment. It is estimated, however—that is, through a certain progression of its power into the world—that the very act of the world is performed through the succession of time. Nature itself, the proper action of this soul, is not in time, but generates time within matter. Chapter XI.*

<margin>A</margin> Regarding all these things we have just said, a doubt may easily arise. If eternity belongs to the realm of the Mind <note>original Latin: "mens"; Greek: "nous" — the divine Intellect or second hypostasis</note>, and time belongs to the realm of the Soul—since we have said that the nature of time is concerned with the action of the soul and depends upon it—how can it be that, while time is divided and possesses a "past," the soul's action is not also divided? And if it were divided, would not the World Soul, by turning toward the past, possess memory? Furthermore, we ought to place "identity" <note>The quality of being the same or unchanging.</note> in eternity, but "difference" or "diversity" in time. Otherwise, eternity and time will be the same thing, provided we remove change from the actions of the soul. <margin>B</margin> Or perhaps we shall say that our own souls, since they admit change, are in time due to their varied states and needs? But shall we say the Soul of the universe generates time, yet is not itself in time? Suppose it is not in time. What, then, is the cause for it to generate time and not eternity? Perhaps because the things it generates are not everlasting, but are encompassed by time. For even the souls themselves are not in time, but rather their "passions" <margin>C</margin> and their works are. For souls are everlasting, and time is a later thing; that which is in time is less than time itself. For it is necessary that what is in time be "contained by time," as the philosopher says, just as a thing is contained by its place or its number.

*The forms of things which are distant from one another in place within matter are distant within the world soul only by a formal difference. Likewise, things which are prior or posterior to one another in time within matter differ in the soul only by a certain order, in which some things yield to others rather than succeeding them. For the soul is, by its all-forming essence, specific to every kind of order, being both the firm exemplar and the effector of the entire future order. As far as it is within itself, it can effect all things at once, if only matter were able to receive all things at once. This soul is said to move toward the Good, because it is turned toward it by desiring it through the medium of the Mind; the Mind, however, rests in the Good, because it uses no medium to reach it. The world, meanwhile, revolves around the soul—or rather, within the soul—through time. Plotinus, in his book On Time, even if he does not define time as motion, places it in the lower part of the world soul, that is, in the trace of the higher soul and in nature. For it is not because the soul acquires or loses forms, but because forms come forth from it at set times like someone waking from sleep. Chapter XVI.*

<margin>A</margin> MOREOVER, if "this after that" is designated within the soul, along with the "before" and "after" of its works; and if it acts in time, it also looks forward to the future. If this is the case, it also looks back to the past. But perhaps this "before" and "past" exist rather in the things being made, while in the soul itself they do not exist at all; rather, all the "reasons" <note>original Latin: "rationes"; Greek: "logoi" — the formative principles or blueprints of things</note> exist simultaneously, as we have said. These reasons are not simultaneous in their temporal effects, just as they are not simultaneous in space, even though they are together in their principles—just as hands and feet exist together in the seed. In things perceived by the senses, however, <margin>B</margin>

<column-break/>

When fire departs, a certain heat remains, being different from the heat in the fire, a certain "passion" <note>original Greek: "pathos" (πάθος) — a state of being affected</note> of the thing heated. Therefore, the form given by the shaping power must be considered a different kind of species from nature itself. But if there is something else after that which is, as it were, between this and nature itself, it must be sought. What the difference is between nature and the aforementioned wisdom in the universe has already been stated. <margin>B</margin>

<margin>A</margin> PERHAPS this is the most important question regarding all these matters: if "eternity" <note>original Greek: "aion" (αἰών)</note> concerns the Mind, and "time" <note>original Greek: "chronos" (χρόνος)</note> concerns the Soul—and we say the substance of time exists around the activity of the soul and from it—how can time be divided and have a past, without the activity also being divided? Or if it turns toward the past, wouldn't it create memory in the soul of the universe? Furthermore, they assign "sameness" to eternity and "otherness" to time. <margin>B</margin> Or will eternity and time be the same, if we do not grant change to the activities of the soul? If we say our souls admit change and are in time, what shall we say of the Soul of the whole? We say it generates time, but is it not in it? Let it be that it is not in time. What is it that it does, to generate time and not eternity? Is it because the things it generates are not eternal, but in time? For not even the souls themselves are in time, but their "passions" <note>original Greek: "pathemata" (παθήματα)</note> which they experience and their works are. For souls are eternal, and time is subsequent, and that which is in time is "less" than time. For it is necessary that what is in time be [encompassed] by time, just as he says of what is in place and in number.

<margin>A</margin> BUT if "this after that" is in the soul itself—the prior and the posterior of its works—and if it acts and thinks in time, then it also looks to the future. And if so, also to the past. Or is the "prior" and "past" only in the things being made? In the soul itself there is no past, but there the "reasons" <note>original Greek: "logoi" (λόγοι)</note> are all together, as was said. But in the things made, they are not together. Since even "togetherness" was in the reasons before it was in the things—just as hands and feet are "together" in the reason [the seed], but in the sensible things [the physical body] <margin>B</margin>

<summary>This page explores the origin of Time, arguing that while the World Soul remains eternal and unified in its essence, its outward activities and the physical objects it creates exist in a temporal sequence of "before" and "after." Plotinus distinguishes between the "seminal reasons" (blueprints) that exist simultaneously in the soul and their sequential manifestation in the material world.</summary>

Having previously established that time is an effect of the Soul’s activity, Plotinus now explores how the World Soul remains unified and eternal in its intent while the physical world it governs moves through time and space. He contrasts this perfect divine governance with the fragmented and often conflicted nature of the human soul.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

...apart, and things there are apart in another way, so that the "other" is also in another way. One thing is apart by its own difference, but the other is as if it did not know the one who orders. Then it will say "this after that." And why? Did these stand together? Or if the one who orders and the order are different, it is as if one were speaking. But if the commanding power is the first order, it no longer speaks, but only acts "this after that." For if it speaks, it speaks looking toward an order, so that it would be something other than the order. How then is it the same? Because the commander is not matter and form together, but form alone, and power and activity; which things are others after the Mind <note>original Greek: "nous"</note> yet in the Soul. But "this after that" occurs in things capable of having these together, for such a soul is a venerable thing, like a circle fitted to a center, immediately expanded after the center, <margin>the most extended</margin> an extension without distance, which each thing somehow possesses. If one were to place the Good as the center, and arrange the Mind as an unmoving circle, and then arrange the Soul as a moving circle, moving by its longing <note>original Greek: "ephesis" — a natural striving or desire</note>, for the Mind immediately possesses and encompasses it. But the Soul longs for that which is even beyond. The sphere of the universe, having the Soul longing in that way or as it is natural to long, is moved; for it is the nature of a body to long to be moved. By always unfolding and going around everything by itself, it thus moves in a circle.

**Α** BUT in what way are the understandings of the soul and its reasons not like this in us? Instead, here what is "after" is according to time, and questions arise here: Is it because there are many things in us which dominate and are moved, and no single thing commands? Or is it also because one thing after another comes to our aid for use and for the present, not defined in itself, but always pertaining to one thing after another from the outside? From this comes a different counsel, and according to the moment, because the need has arisen: and something has happened from the outside, a deception. For because many things rule, it is necessary that there be many imaginations, even those introduced from without, **B** and according to these, some things are impediments to others in their own innate movements and activities. For when the power of desire is moved, there arises an imagination of this, like a sensation announcing and reporting the passion, demanding—

<column-break/>

**A** From this place, they are arranged separately: and if in the seed-bed <note>original Latin: "seminario" — referring to the realm of "seminal reasons" or formative principles</note> it is said to be separated by some other reason, the same will also be prior by another reason. Certainly, what is said to be "apart" will be judged to be apart by a certain otherness: but what is said to be "prior," in what way is it so? Unless the ordainer himself so commands, and commanding, he declares that very thing, namely, "let this be after that": for why should all things not be together? But surely if the ordainer were something other than the order, the matter would be handled as if by speaking. But if the commander himself **B** presiding exists as the first order, he speaks no further, but only acts, making this after that. For if he should speak, he will speak looking at the order; wherefore there will be something else besides the order. By what reasoning, then, is it the same? Because the ordainer is not matter and form together, but the form itself only; and the Soul will be the power and the second act after the Mind. But what is said, "this after that," happens to the works themselves, since they are not able to have all things at once. For such a soul is a venerable thing, namely, like a circle **C** most perfectly fitted to the center, increased immediately after the center, an interval without distance. For in this way individual things are arranged, as if one placed the Good itself for the center, and applied the Mind as if it were an immobile circle, but added the Soul as if it were a mobile circle—a motion, I say, through appetite <note>original Latin: "appetitum" — the desire or striving of the soul toward the divine</note>. For the Mind possesses and conceives the Good placed nearest to it; but the Soul longs for that which is even higher. But the **D** sphere of the world, having the soul longing in that condition—namely, that which by nature it is able to long for—is moved. For it is so arranged by nature that the body may naturally long for that which is outside itself: and this is to pour itself around that thing, and to run around it on all sides, by which it is brought about that it moves in an orbit.

> *In the World Soul, there is no ambiguous deliberation or temporal wandering, because that which is best in it always dominates its other powers from eternity. However, it is present in our soul, since from many parts and powers, now one way, now another dominates. Likewise, because we are ignorant, and also because we are in need of many things, and finally because many passions fall upon us from external things. The rational power in us, if it is not weak by nature, and even if it is not blind, is nevertheless sometimes overcome by the irrational: both because the former is quiet, while the latter is turbulent; and because the former is unified, while the latter is manifold. The worst man is like the worst form of popular government <note>original Latin: "populari gubernationi" — i.e., a degenerate democracy or mob rule</note>; the less bad, to a less bad democracy. The good man is like the government of the best <note>original Latin: "optimatum" — aristocracy</note>, the best man is like a kingdom; perhaps one might say the worst is like a tyrant.*

### Chapter XVII.

**A** But in what way are those understandings, which belong to the soul itself, and its reasons, not like this in us? Instead, here what is "after" is according to time, and questions arise here: Is it because there are many things in us which dominate and are moved, and no single thing commands? Or is it also because one thing after another comes to our aid for use and for the present, not defined in itself, but always pertaining to one thing after another from the outside? And so there is also another counsel, which is present to us according to the opportunity of the time, when necessity demands it. **B** Furthermore, both this and that happen from the outside: because even from the fact that many things dominate in us, it is necessary that many imaginations also occur, both foreign and new, some regarding some things and others regarding others: from which some things are an impediment to others in the promptness of admonition and action. For when the power of desire is moved, there arises in us an imagination of this kind, which, like a certain sense, announces and reports the passion: requiring, namely—

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the Soul's relationship to the material world. While the previous page focused on the Soul’s role in creating time and cosmic order, this page shifts to the internal psychology of the human being. Plotinus examines the conflict between our higher reasoning and our lower physical impulses, using the metaphor of a city's government to explain how different types of people are "ruled" from within.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...the soul yields to desire and provides for its wishes. In such a state, the soul is necessarily drawn into conflict, whether it chooses to indulge and suggest these pleasures or to resist them. Even the impulse of anger, which rouses us to repel an injury, brings the same conflict upon us whenever it is stirred. Thus, the needs and passions of the body introduce various opinions into our minds. Furthermore, ignorance of what is truly good and the failure to find a definitive judgment cause the soul to be pulled back and forth. From the mixing of these elements, other results <margin>B</margin> follow. Even though the best part of us <note>The "intellectual" or "higher" soul in Neoplatonic thought.</note> holds different views than the common failing of the soul and its diversity of opinions, the right reason—transmitted from our best part into our common life—degenerates for this very reason: it becomes weak within the mixture, even though it is not weak by its own nature.

But just as in a crowded and turbulent assembly, even the best of advisors, remaining quiet, fails to persuade; instead, the worse elements prevail because of the sheer number of those shouting and creating a disturbance. <margin>C</margin> That advisor sits in silence, unable to achieve anything, overcome by the tumult of the inferior sort. For in the most depraved man, there is a kind of "commonwealth" made up of all these base elements, much like a city under the worst possible government.

In the "middle" type of man, the situation is like a city where a slightly better element holds sway; it is a form of popular government <note>original Latin: "popularis... gubernatio"; likely referring to a "timocracy" or a mixed democracy.</note> that is not entirely without obedience to law. But in the better man, <margin>D</margin> the form of life is very much like an aristocratic government, because that "common" part of the man now dares to obey the better elements. Finally, in the best man—who separates himself from the common crowd—there is a single ruler, from whom order is extended to the rest. It is as if there were a double city within us: one superior, and the other inferior, decorated in imitation of the superior one.

It has been said that in the Soul of the World, one and the same thing always commands in the same way. But in others, things behave differently, and the causes for this have been assigned. But enough on these matters.

---

*Just as light shines from the Sun and is inseparable from it—not being a quality of the air itself, but heat being generated from that light as a quality belonging to the air—so from our soul shines a life-giving act. This act is not a specific quality of the body, but it generates something vital within the body that becomes the body’s own property. The Soul is substance and life, and that inseparable substantial act of its own is what is life-giving. The quality attributed to the body from this is something accidental, a "vital-like" quality. We call that act the **idol of the soul** <term>idolum animae: a reflection or "image" of the soul that animates the body without the higher soul having to descend fully into matter</term>, in which reside the senses and the vegetative nature. We also call this quality the **image** and **shadow** of the soul. From this and the body, a composite is formed, in which reside bodily pleasures and pains; the sensations of these passions reach the "idol" of the soul, but the higher soul's passions do not. This comparison would be more accurate if we compared the soul's "idol" (which is not severed from the soul) to a visual ray not severed from the eye. When such a ray proceeds from a bloodshot eye, it creates a redness in the object perceived; you might say the shadow of the soul resulting in the body is similar to this.*

### Cap. XVIII.

<margin>A</margin> **IT REMAINS** to investigate whether the body has something within itself, and thus lives by the presence of the soul so that it possesses something of its own, or whether whatever it has is simply the "nature" <note>original Greek: "physis" — the lowest level of soul that governs growth and biology.</note> itself; and whether it is this nature alone that communicates itself to the body. Perhaps the body in which the soul and nature reside ought not to be regarded as something entirely inanimate, like illuminated air, but rather like heated air. Thus, the bodies of animals and plants have a kind of "shadow of the soul" within them; therefore, <margin>B</margin> bodily pains and pleasures concern such a body. To us, however, the suffering of such a body...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...follows that which the desire has hastened towards, but desire becomes a sort of persuasion or necessity; there is anger which rouses one to defense, and again it introduces these same things. Furthermore, the sufferings of the body instill different opinions at different times. Ignorance of the good, and the failure to find that which would cause the soul to stop its wandering, also result from this mixture. <margin>B</margin> But even if the best part of it has other opinions, there is a common state of doubt and a plurality of views. The reason which reaches the common part from the best part becomes weak because of the mixture, even if it is not weak by its own nature. But just as in the great noise of an assembly, the best of counselors cannot lead or prevail, but the worse elements of those making a disturbance or shouting do, while he sits in silence, able to do nothing. <margin>C</margin> The multitude of disturbances of the worse elements prevails. In the most base man, there is a commonality of all these things, like men living under a base constitution. In the middle man, there is something slightly better that prevails, like a democratic constitution, yet not one entirely without order. In the best man, where the best part rules, life is already fleeing from the "common" man <margin>D</margin> and giving form to the better parts, with a ruler who separates and defines the parts. And there is another order: like a double city, where one is above and the other is below, ordered according to the same pattern. But while in the Soul <note>The World Soul</note> everything is well and always the same, in others it is different, and the causes for this have been stated.

<margin>A</margin> **CONCERNING** the senses, whether the body, by the presence of the soul, already possesses something of its own while it lives, or whether what it has is "nature," and whether there is something else that associates with the body, or if it is nature itself and the body in which it is; soul and nature are something. Or is it entirely like an inanimate thing, like illuminated air? Or is it rather like heated air, so that in the body of the living thing and the plant, there is something like a shadow of the soul? <margin>B</margin> Having this, it possesses pain and pleasure. It is necessary that the pleasures of the body are centered around such a body. To us, nature...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the Soul relates to the physical body. # BOOK FOUR.

<margin>being our members</margin>
...and such pleasure comes into a state of knowledge that is free from passion. It tells us that this "other soul" <note>Plotinus distinguishes between the higher, intellectual Soul and a lower "sensitive" soul that deals with the body.</note> belongs to a body that is not foreign to us, but rather <margin>being our members</margin> is one of our own members. Therefore, we care for these parts as our own, which is why we recognize them and why they, in turn, purify us. However, this body is suspended from us and attached to us; we are defined by our "ruling part" <note>The *hegemonikon*, or the rational center of the soul.</note>, while the body is "ours" in a different sense. For this reason, we care for it whether it is in pleasure or in pain. The weaker we are, the more we care for it, and the less we separate ourselves from it, whereas we ought to preserve what is most precious and identify ourselves with the true Human, lifting ourselves toward the heights. We must say that passions of this kind do not belong to the Soul entirely, but to the body—or rather, to the "composite" of the two. For when something is a single, self-sufficient thing, like a body alone, it is soulless and does not "suffer" passion. If it is divided, it is not the body itself that suffers, but the *union* within it that is broken. The Soul alone undergoes no division or passion; it escapes all this. But when two things strive to be one, using a union that is external to them, they undergo the beginning of pain because they are not permitted to remain one. By "two," I do not mean two bodies joined together—for they share one nature—but rather when a different nature seeks to enter into commerce with another kind, and the lower part receives something from the higher. The lower cannot truly "take" the higher, but only a trace or "vestige" of it. Thus, the whole becomes a "two-and-one," a middle state between what it was before and what it cannot attain, placed in a state of difficulty. Because it has entered into an unhappy and unstable partnership, it is always pulled in opposite directions: sometimes turned upward and sometimes downward. When it falls toward the lower things, it reports its torment; when it turns slightly higher, it arouses a desire for communion.

---

### Chapter XIX.

<margin>A</margin> This is what is meant by pleasure and pain: pain is the perception of the body being "led away" or dissolved, as it is deprived of the Soul's image. Pleasure is the perception of life, when the image of the Soul is once again harmonized within the body. Consider the passion itself: the "knowledge" of it belongs to the sensitive soul, which perceives because of its proximity, or rather, it reports what the senses define as pain. For in that specific part...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...pleasure is attained; it arrives in a form of cognition that is free from suffering. We say "to us"—that is, to the "other soul"—as if this kind of body were not foreign to us, but our own; therefore, it is a matter of concern to us, as if it were ours. Yet we are neither the body itself, nor are we totally segregated from it. Rather, it depends on us and is attached to us. We are judged by that which is our principal part, but this body is "ours" in a simultaneous but different way. For this reason, whether afflicted by pain or soothed by pleasure, we <margin>B</margin> have a care for such a body. The weaker we ourselves are, the more diligently we care for it and the more accurately we cultivate it, as we fail to segregate ourselves from it. But this very thing which is most excellent in us—by which we are human—we nearly submerge into such a body. Surely we must not think that passions of this kind belong entirely to the Soul, but to such a body and to something "common" and joined together. For when a thing is only one, it is <margin>C</margin> sufficient unto itself. For example, if a body were alone and inanimate, what would it suffer? If it were divided, the "passion" or suffering would belong not so much to the body itself as to the *union* that exists within it. Furthermore, the Soul alone suffers no division or passion; and being in such a state, it escapes this whole affair. But truly, whenever two things strive to be one and thus employ an external union, they undoubtedly undergo the <margin>D</margin> beginning of pain because they are not permitted to remain one. I say "two," but not as if two bodies were coming together into one; for in those there is a single nature. Rather, it is when a different nature attempts to enter into commerce with another nature and kind: and what is worse, it receives something from the better part. It cannot receive the thing itself, but only its "vestige" <note>original: *vestigium*. In Neoplatonism, the body does not contain the Soul itself, but a 'trace' or 'reflection' of it.</note>. Thus, the whole thing is both two and one, resulting in a middle ground between what it was before and that which it can no longer reach, placed now in difficulty. Indeed, since it has entered into an unhappy and unstable commerce, it is always <margin>E</margin> distracted by different things: for it is revolved upward and downward in turn. When it slides down to inferior things, it announces its own torture; and when it inclines somewhat higher, it awakens a desire for communion.

> *A dissolving passion or a restorative pleasure does not occur in the sense and the soul, but in the body which is already vitally affected through the presence of the soul. In the sense and the soul, however, there is a perception of those passions which is itself entirely free from suffering. The soul is bound to the body by two "knots," as it were: one inclines toward the soul—that is, its life-giving act shining toward the body; the other declines toward the body—that is, the vital quality itself infused into the body through this act. Therefore, the body thus affected and thus bound to the soul belongs to the soul and becomes "ours." Thus we care for it, and when a dissolving or restorative motion happens to it, we perceive this passion through the senses and are inclined either to avoid it or to pursue it. If the destructive passion happened in the sensing soul itself, the sense and judgment would be hindered, and the soul would not be able to discern in which specific member the passion was located. For the soul is indivisible and is simultaneously whole in every part. Therefore, if the soul itself suffered, the passion would occupy the entire soul everywhere.*

---

This, therefore, is what is taught regarding the nature of pleasure and pain: where it is said that pain is a certain perception of dissolution, specifically when the body is despoiled of the Soul's image; and pleasure is the perception in the soul when the image of the Soul is restored in the body. In the body, there is the passion; but the cognition is in the sensitive soul, which by its very proximity feels the passion and reports it to the point where the senses finally end. That indeed is the torment!

<summary>Plotinus explains that while the Soul itself is divine and impassive, it feels the body's sensations because the body is animated by a "trace" of the Soul. Pain is defined as the perception of the body's physical breakdown, while pleasure is the perception of its restoration.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin>
...he says "torment," that is, having suffered, as in a cutting. A "cutting" indeed belongs to the body, and "division" refers to the physical mass. However, "affliction" refers to a mass that is not merely a mass, but a mass of a specific kind. The same must be said regarding inflammation. The Soul, however, perceives this as if by observing a contiguous <note>original: "contiguam"; referring to the soul's close proximity to the bodily event without being merged into it</note> neighbor. The Soul perceives the whole suffering as it arises there, while the Soul itself suffers least of all. For the whole perceiving Soul announces that the suffering is located there,
<margin>B</margin>
where the blow and the pain occurred. But if the Soul itself were suffering, since it is present in the entire body, it would not say or report where the suffering was most intensely inflicted. Instead, the whole Soul would suffer the pain, and it would be distressed by pain throughout its entire being; it would not indicate or declare a specific location of the suffering. Rather, wherever the Soul is, it would say the pain is there too—and it is everywhere. But in reality, the opposite happens: the finger hurts, and the human being hurts for that very reason, because the human's finger is distressed. A human is said to feel pain in the finger in the same way that a human is called "grey-eyed" because of the color
<margin>C</margin>
in the eye. Therefore, that which suffers is also tormented, unless someone perhaps includes the torment together with the sensation that immediately follows as a single concept. If one understands it that way, it clearly signifies that the pain exists in a certain way, and the pain does not escape the notice of the perceiver. Nevertheless, it must by no means be said that the sensation itself *is* the pain, but rather it is the perception of the pain. For true knowledge must surely be free from suffering <note>original: "passionis expertem"; the Greek "apathes" means the soul perceives without being altered by the physical pain</note>, so that it may both know clearly and report honestly. For a
<margin>D</margin>
messenger who is himself caught up in the suffering, while he is occupied by that suffering, either reports nothing at all or arrives as an unreliable messenger of health.

---

*Just as in the body of a wounded thing there is a stimulus toward sensation, in the root toward moisture, and in the leaf toward heat, so in the body through the soul (which is now affected in a vital way), certain natural impulses arise: for a lack, they seek fulfillment; for a fullness, they seek evacuation; for a change of life, they seek the opposite. Meanwhile, the vegetative nature, which generated and preserves the vital affection in the body, labors while it strives when the body suffers; it acts more intensely to preserve or restore the natural state in the body. By this very striving, that desire which began in such a body is said to grow into "nature." When this nature acts more vigorously, the perception of the suffering reaches the senses, and from there, it reaches the imagination and the judgment.*
<margin>Chapter XX.</margin>

<margin>A</margin> It follows, furthermore, that the origin of bodily desires arises from that which is "common" <note>the "common" refers to the composite of body and the lowest trace of soul</note>, and from such a bodily nature. For the beginning of seeking and intensely pursuing something should not be attributed to the body in whatever state it happens to be. Nor should it be thought that the Soul itself desires salty or sweet things, but rather that which is the body strives not only to be a body, but to claim more movements for itself than the soul does. And because of a claim of this
<margin>B</margin>
kind, it is compelled to be moved toward many things; wherefore, being thus affected, it desires salty things, or sweet things; likewise to be moistened, and again to be heated—none of which would be its concern if it existed alone. Just as in the previous case knowledge was born from pain, and the Soul, wishing to withdraw from the thing inflicting the suffering, leads the body away and turns it to flight—which it also warned of, since it first sustained the suffering while also fleeing in a way during that very contraction—so here too a certain sense learns, and the Soul which is nearby, according to that
<margin>C</margin>
which we call the "nature" that grants the traces of life to the body. Therefore, Nature reports the desire when it is already fully grown, as if it were the end of the desire in...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> I say "the blow" is that which has suffered there, as in the cutting of a body being cut; the division belongs to the mass, and the sensation belongs to the mass, which is not only a mass but a mass of such a kind. As in inflammation, it is as if the soul takes it up from what follows, as if by its own suffering it feels the suffering there, yet without suffering itself. For in perceiving the suffering, it says the
<margin>B</margin>
suffering is there, where the blow occurred. But if the soul itself suffered, it would be in the whole body; it would not be in a specific part, but rather the whole soul would have suffered the pain. In the whole being; and it would not have said or shown that it was *there*, but rather "wherever I am." But now the finger is in pain, and the man is in pain, because the finger belongs to the man,
<margin>C</margin>
but the finger is not the man. It is said "painfully" just as a man is called "grey-eyed" because of the grey in his eye. That thing which suffers, then, is in pain, unless one includes "being in pain" with the sensation that follows. If one does include it, it will show that the awareness is like a pain joined with the perception of the pain. But in the
<margin>D</margin>
sensation itself, one should not say it is "pain," but rather the "knowledge of pain." Since it is knowledge, it must be "without passion" <note>original: "apathe"; the soul's ability to remain calm and unchanged while observing the body's state</note>, so that it may know and report healthily. For a messenger who has suffered, being busy with the suffering, either does not report, or is not a healthy messenger.

It follows that bodily desires are ruled by that which is thus "common," and of a certain bodily nature. It must follow upon the body having such a disposition, which is not the beginning of the impulse and desire. It is not for the soul itself
<margin>A</margin>
to seek salty or sweet things, but the body; it wishes not only to be a body, but also to draw movements from this, and even more
<margin>B</margin>
because of the acquisition [of life]. Therefore, when it is in this state, it seeks salty things, and in that state sweet things, or to be moistened, or to be warmed, which would not matter to it if it were alone. Just as there knowledge arose from pain, and the soul, wishing to lead away from that which caused the suffering, turns to flight—and it first taught the suffering part how to flee
<margin>C</margin>
in the contraction—so also here, the sensation having learned, and the soul which is near. Which indeed we call the "nature" that gives the trace [of life]. Nature indeed reports the clear desire, as if...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul perceives bodily pain as an objective observer or "messenger" without actually suffering the pain itself, much as one might recognize a person as "grey-eyed" without being the eye. He further explains that bodily desires (like hunger for salt or sweets) originate in the physical composite's drive for self-preservation, which the soul then perceives and interprets.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the soul's relationship with the body, specifically focusing on the origin of physical desires. In the previous section, the author argued that the soul remains distinct from the body's physical sufferings; here, he extends that logic to appetites like hunger and thirst.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

...of the receiving [soul] if through sensation it receives the mental image <note>original: "phantasiam"; the internal representation of an external object</note>, from which the perfected soul then either pursues, or flees, or endures, or pays attention to that which initiated the desire and to that which desired afterward. But why do we posit two desires, and not rather that the desiring part is simply a body of a certain kind? Or, if nature is one thing and a body of a certain kind is another—though it is produced by nature—it is because nature exists before it forms such a body; for nature itself creates, molds, and shapes a body of this specific kind. It is necessary that nature itself does not initiate the desire, but rather it is the body of a certain kind that suffers those things from which the opposites are known: it suffers either the inflammation of pleasure from certain things, or it suffers from thirst. Nature, acting like a mother <note>Plotinus often personifies "Nature" as a lower, creative aspect of the Soul that cares for the physical world</note>, aims to correct the desires of the suffering part, bringing it back to herself and seeking remedies for its weaknesses. Thus, through this inquiry, she joins with the desire of the suffering part, and the affection <note>the feeling or state of being affected</note> penetrates from the body to the soul. Therefore, one might say that while the body of a certain kind desires by its own nature—perhaps in terms of the initial urge—Nature desires for the sake of something else, and the soul itself is that which either obeys or resists.

> *The incentive to desire bodily pleasures does not arise in the soul’s own power of desire, but in a body of a certain kind through a vital affection of the soul. We conclude this first because since there is both need and suffering in the body, it is right that appetites are stirred here. Second, because as the body differs according to age, health, habit, place, and time, so different appetites creep in, yet the power of desire remaining in the soul is not changed. Third, because sometimes there is a stimulus in the body toward something to which the power of desire does not immediately direct itself. Fourth, because even if the soul soon attends to it, the mind <note>original: "animus"</note> does not always allow it. Fifth, there often arises in a depraved body a stimulus toward something least consistent with nature—such as eating ash <note>original: "cinerem comedendum"; a reference to the medical condition known as pica</note>—which nature, the moderator of the body's condition, does not accept, nor does she adapt it to the body, nor to herself. Finally, the power of desire implanted in the soul is neither filled, nor emptied, nor altered in any way; rather, it is the body that is so affected. Hence, the appetite for such things is stirred from the body, not from the soul.*

<margin>Chapter XXI.</margin>
->**Chapter XXI.**<-

THAT the body is the place where the principle of desire resides is further proven by the differences in age. For the bodily appetites of children, youths, and men are all different; likewise for those who are healthy or sick, while the power of desire <note>original: "concupiscendi virtus"</note> itself remains the same. It is clear, then, that there is something corporeal—a body of a certain kind—which, while being changed in many ways, similarly incites many different appetites. The same is shown by the fact that not every desire is stirred everywhere at once by these incentives, even though the bodily stimulation often persists. Furthermore, even before reason <note>original: "ratio"</note> deliberates on it, the soul often does not want to eat or drink, even while a vehement desire impels the body toward these things. Moreover, nature itself often does not accept, nor wish to bring into the "seat of nature," that which the body is incited toward—as if such a pleasure does not agree with nature. It is the role of nature itself to determine what is consistent with nature and what is not. But if someone should object to the previous point, saying that it is enough for the body to be different...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...already arising from such a body. Sensation, however, produces the imagination <note>original: "imaginationem"</note>, through which the soul (to which it belongs to pursue) either pursues and suggests, or reacts and abstains. It does not always consent either to the beginning of the longing or to that which was desired after such an beginning. But why do we assume two longings, and not just that the body is the thing that hungers? Certainly, nature is one thing, and the body produced by nature is another. Nature exists before such a body <margin>B</margin> is made, since she herself creates the body, shaping and forming it. It is necessary that the soul herself does not start the greed, but rather it is the body that suffers certain things. When it is in pain, it seeks the opposite of what it suffers: it seeks pleasure to cure its weakness, or fullness to cure its need. Truly, Nature, like a mother guessing the desires of a suffering child, must try to guide it and call it back to herself, seeking remedies for its pains. <margin>C</margin> Through this searching, she joins with the desire of the suffering part, and so this affection penetrates from the body to the soul. For this reason, someone might say that the body desires by its own nature (regarding the initial urge), while Nature desires because of something else; but the soul is like a separate judge that either complies or, more often, opposes.

<margin>A</margin> **THAT** the body is indeed the center where the principle of appetite exists is further proved by the different ages of life. For the bodily appetites of children are different from those of adolescents, and those of grown men are different again. The same is true for those in good or bad health, while the power of desire remains the same throughout. It is established, then, that there is a corporeal element—the body, I say—which, while it is changed in many ways, similarly stirs up many appetites. <margin>B</margin> This is also shown by the fact that every desire is not excited at the same time as these bodily urges, even though the physical stimulation often lasts a long time. Furthermore, before reason can even think about it, the soul often does not want to eat or drink, even when a powerful longing drives the body toward them. Indeed, nature herself often does not accept or want what the body is urging; she does not want to bring it into the "home of nature," as if that specific pleasure does not fit her. <margin>C</margin> It is as if it is nature's own job to decide what is in harmony with nature and what is not. But if anyone objects to what was said before, claiming that it is enough that the body is simply different at different times...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-argument; the catchword "concupis-" indicates the next page continues the discussion on "concupiscentias" or desires.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that physical desires like hunger and thirst originate in the body's needs and "affections" rather than the soul's innate powers. He uses the variations in appetite across different ages and health conditions to prove that while the body's urges change, the soul's fundamental capacity for desire remains constant and often acts as a judge or resistor to bodily impulses.</summary>
