<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the nature of desire and sensation, moving from the human soul's relationship with physical appetites to a broader cosmological discussion about the souls of the Earth and the elements. It builds on the previous argument that the soul itself does not "suffer" physical changes but perceives them.</meta>

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...it pertains to the fact that while another part suffers <note>original: "patiente"; referring to the body experiencing a sensation or pain</note>, this very virtue <note>the power of the soul</note> might have different desires for the sake of another, since it is not itself the thing that necessarily experiences them. For it does not belong to the power of desire itself to be nourished, or warmed, or moistened, or changed, or relieved by emptying, or filled by saturation; rather, all these things belong to the specific body.

*Earth, since it generates living beings <note>original: "animalia"; in a Neoplatonic context, this refers to any "animated" or living thing</note>, and is a necessary and by no means contemptible member of the world-animal, is an intellectual and divine living being, possessing sensation. For in the soul, a judicial power <note>original: "vis iudiciaria"; the faculty of the soul that judges and categorizes sensory data</note> flourishes, which, being joined to its body, perceives and identifies the experiences of its own body—and that is what it means to feel. This is true even though Plotinus, out of many options, assigns to each of the elements its own soul. Yet someone might perhaps say, not without reason, that the celestial spheres have souls distinct from one another because they are immutable and remain within themselves without being confused; but the elements, because they were established for the sake of composite things, are changed in sensation, mixed with one another, reduced into a single globe, and bound together harmoniously into one form by appropriate numbers, possess a single soul for all things, which is perfectly adapted to that one complexity of matter—almost like four humors <note>the four fluids of ancient medicine: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>—flourishing mostly in air and fire, and through these simultaneously in water and earth. By the power of this soul, even composite things carry back a vital force, in which portions of the elements are bound to the whole by a certain similar proportion: in earth and water, there are manifest living beings, but in the air, there are spirits <note>original: "demones"; intermediary beings between gods and humans</note> having similarly woven bodies, though they are thin and hidden from us.*

->Chapter XXII.<-

## <margin>A</margin> IS THERE also in plants something distinct that is, as it were, implanted as their own in their bodies, and something else that provides for them? That which in us is called the power of desire is called the vegetative power <note>original: "vegetalis"; the "lowest" level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition</note> in them. Perhaps, however, such a power is in the Earth, since there is a soul within it, and in plants, there is that which proceeds from this power. But someone might aptly ask first: since there is a soul in the Earth, does it shine into the Earth like a sort of radiance from the sphere of the universe itself (which Plato <note>referring to Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus*</note> seems to be the only one to animate primarily)? <margin>B</margin> Or should it rather be said that Plato attributes a soul to the Earth similar to that of the stars, where he again says that the Earth is the first and oldest of all the gods contained within the heavens? For in what way could the Earth be judged a goddess unless she possessed a soul? From this, it happens that it is difficult to find the reason why this matter stands as it does, and a greater—or certainly no less—ambiguity arises from Plato’s words. But certainly, first of all, how can we investigate an opinion that is consistent with reason? <margin>C</margin> In the first place, who could conclude that the Earth has a vegetative soul by observing the things that are born from it? And if many living beings are also seen to be generated from the Earth, what prevents us from judging it to be a living being itself? Since it is such a vast living being, and no small portion of the world, why do we not also say it has a mind, and is thus a God? Now, if we say that any star is a living being, what prevents the Earth also, <margin>D</margin> since it is a part of the whole living being <note>the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul</note>, from being confessed as a living being? For it must not be thought that it is contained on the outside by a foreign soul, but possesses no soul on the inside, as if it alone were unable to have its own soul. For why should fiery bodies be able to, but an earthy one not be able? Surely both are bodies; and there <note>in the stars</note> there are no veins, nerves, flesh, blood, or humor, even though the Earth is furnished with a much greater variety and is constituted of all bodies. If someone should object that the Earth is unfit for motion, one could say that only because it does <margin>E</margin> not move from its own place. Someone will also ask how the Earth can feel; and we shall similarly ask in what way the stars can feel. Now, it is not the role of flesh to feel, nor is it to be attributed at all to the soul...

<column-break/>

...speaks in relation to other things that suffer, it would otherwise have different desires for the sake of other things; since, insofar as it becomes a suffering through necessity, food, heat, moisture, movement, emptying, and filling, and the regret of filling, belong to the desiring part, but not to the same things.

IN the case of plants, is there one thing as it were implanted in their bodies, and another which supplied it? That which is the desiring part in us, is the vegetative part in them. Or does it not come to be, since a soul is in it? If it is of the vegetative soul at some time then. Or does it at some time come to be from its relationship to the whole? In the Earth, is it from the sphere or from this, does it not also seem to be entirely animated as Plato says, like an illumination upon the Earth, or how? Again saying, the first and oldest of the gods, of those within the heaven: and again he gives it a soul, such as he gives to the stars. And how could it be a god without a share of those things? So that it happens to be difficult to find how the matter stands, or not to have an impasse, or not less of one, from the things which Plato has said. But first, how would it be reasonable? Would the matter seem so? That in the Earth one must have a vegetative soul, would anyone judge from the things growing out of it? And if many living beings are seen coming from the Earth, why not say that it is a living being itself? Being a living being of all things and a significant part of the whole. Why will you not say it also has a mind and is thus a god? If indeed each of the stars is too. Why not also the Earth a living being, being a part of the whole living being? For must we say it is surrounded from the outside by a foreign soul, but inside does not have one, as if unable to have its own from itself? For why can the fiery ones, but the earthy one cannot? For each is a body, and in them are no veins, nor flesh, nor blood, nor humor. And the Earth is more varied, and made from all bodies. Or because this is difficult to move, someone might say it does not move from its place, but how does it perceive? For how do the stars? Or is perceiving not of the flesh, nor is it necessary for the body as a whole to be like...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the soul's relationship with the body, specifically focusing on whether the soul requires physical organs for sensation and whether non-human entities like the Earth or plants possess sensory perception. This follows the previous discussion on the "judicial power" of the soul.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
The soul does not take on a body simply so that it might perceive; rather, a soul must be granted to the body so that the body might be animated and preserved. Indeed, since the soul possesses a **power of judgment** <note>original: "vim iudiciariā"; the cognitive faculty that evaluates sensory input</note>, it also has the capacity by which, while it looks toward the body, it is able to judge the **affections** <note>original: "passionibus" / "παθημάτων"; physical experiences or changes acting upon the body</note> occurring within it. But what sort of experiences belong to the Earth? And whose judgment evaluates them? Furthermore, plants, insofar as they are part of the Earth, do not possess sensation. Of what things, then, are there senses? And through what means do they occur? Or perhaps we should not dare to assert that sensation can happen without physical instruments?

<margin>B</margin>
Likewise, for what use does the sensation of the Earth serve? It is certainly not for the sake of knowledge; for perhaps the knowledge that consists in **wisdom** <note>original: "sapientia" / "φρονήσει"</note> is sufficient for those who will gain no practical benefit from the act of sensing. Or perhaps one might not concede this? For even beyond mere utility, there is a certain kind of knowledge found in things perceived by the senses—a knowledge not foreign to the Muses—such as the spectacle of the Sun, the other stars, the heavens, and the Earth. Indeed, to behold these things is inherently pleasant. This matter, therefore, must be considered in the sections that follow.

<margin>C</margin>
For the present, however, we must investigate once more whether sensation exists within the Earth, which animals possess the power to feel, and by what reasoning this occurs. Perhaps it is necessary first to resume the points that were doubted and to understand them collectively: whether sensation can be achieved without instruments, and whether the senses were established for the sake of utility, or if something else results from them beyond mere practical use.

*To sense is not simply to know sensible things, but to perceive through certain "passions" or impressions made either by the things to be sensed near the soul, or by the soul concerning them. The soul, when separated from every body, lives in itself and is turned toward itself; through forms implanted within it, it knows divine things from the Divine, and comprehends those as principles even of sensible things, yet this is not "sensing." For it cannot sense corporeal things at that time because it has no proportion with them through which any impression or expression can be made between itself and them. But when it is joined to a body, it uses the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritu"; here meaning a subtle "pneuma" or intermediary substance between the physical and the immaterial</note> as a middle instrument between itself and external things, creating a proportion between both. In this spirit, qualities or experiences coming from the outside turn into a spiritual and purified **form** <note>original: "speciem"</note> close to the soul, so that through this, the soul excites the forms of sensible things lying hidden within itself. This very excitation is what it means to sense. This entire process is more diligently explained in the book of Theophrastus on the soul, along with the commentaries of Priscianus and Iamblichus.*

->Chapter XXIII.<-

<margin>A</margin>
It must be asserted, therefore, that sensation concerning sensible things is a **perception** <note>original: "perceptionē" / "ἀντιλήψις"; a conscious grasping of data</note> in the soul or the living being. I say perception exists in the power that clings to bodies, perceiving quality and in some way shaping the **form** <note>original: "speciem" / "εἴδη"</note> of those qualities for itself. If this is so, does the soul apprehend sensible things while remaining alone in itself, or rather with something else? If it lives alone and within itself, how could it do so? For while it is in itself, it perceives only the things that are in itself, and it employs only intelligence.

<margin>B</margin>
But if it then perceives other things as well, it must have already possessed these things, either having been made like them, or by joining with something that was at some time made very similar. Indeed, it is impossible for the soul to be like these physical things while remaining in itself. Under what condition could a "point" be made similar to a "line"? Especially since not even an **intelligible line** <note>the abstract concept of a line</note> can fit a **sensible line** <note>a physical, drawn line</note>, nor can an intelligible fire or man fit a sensible fire or man. Indeed, not even the very Nature which generates a man can merge into the same state as the man who has been generated.

<margin>C</margin>
Now, if the soul living with itself could look upon a sensible object, it would immediately be directed toward the knowledge of the **intelligible** <note>the realm of pure thought/forms</note>, while the sensible object would escape it, since the soul would clearly have nothing to receive it with. However, when the soul looks at something visible from a distance, although the form comes into the soul as much as possible, nevertheless, that which begins within the soul—being **impartible** <note>original: "impartibile"; indivisible or non-physical</note>—ends in...

<sig>M 4</sig>

He defines sensation as the "excitation" of latent forms within the soul, triggered by the body's experiences but processed by the soul's unique judicial power.</summary>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK IV.

<column-break/>

...discerning the underlying color and shape, as much as it occurs there. Therefore, it is not enough for only these two to be present—namely, the external object and the soul; for in that case, no **affection** <note>original: "passio" / "πάθημα"; a physical change or impression acting upon the body</note> would occur here. Instead, there must be a third thing which is to be the subject of the affection: this is what receives the **form**. It is necessary, then, for this third thing to meet with the sensible object in a shared experience and in one matter; one part must be affected, while another part comes to know the affection. 

<margin>B</margin>
The affection must be such that it preserves something of the agent that caused it, yet is not identical to it. Indeed, that which is affected acts as a kind of **medium** between the author of the affection and the soul, holding a middle state of affection between the sensible and the intelligible. This medium reconciles the extremes with a fitting proportion on both sides, serving as both a receiver and a **messenger**; for it can be made similar to both. Since it is an instrument of some form of knowledge, it must be identical neither to the one who knows nor to the thing being known, but must easily become similar to both: to the external object because it is affected, and to the internal power because that affection becomes a kind of **species** <note>original: "species" / "εἶδος"; here meaning a mental image or formal representation</note>.

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore, if we speak correctly, senses must operate through bodily instruments. This follows from what we have said: if the soul were entirely outside the body, it would perceive nothing sensible. The instrument must necessarily be either the whole body or some member determined for a specific task, as we see happening in touch and sight. 

<margin>D</margin>
Then, anyone will easily perceive the craftsmanship of the intermediate instruments between those who judge and the things being judged, which signify the property of the underlying things to the one who observes. For a **ruler** <note>original: "regula" / "κανών"</note> adapted to straightness—both the straightness in the mind and that in the wood—being placed correctly in the middle, gives the judge the ability to evaluate the work. 

It would be a matter for another discussion to inquire whether the thing to be judged must be joined directly to the instrument, or whether sensation occurs through some medium at a distance from the object; 

<margin>E</margin>
for instance, if fire is far from the flesh, with the medium itself being unaffected, or if there were a vacuum between sight and color, could one see if the instrument were present? However, it is established that sensation belongs to the soul only while it lives in a body, and is fulfilled through the body.

---

> Since sensation necessarily follows from the soul being joined to the body, the sphere of the world's stars is perceived by the soul. The World senses through one of its parts, and in turn another part; likewise, it senses the parts through the whole. Furthermore, it senses the disposition of the whole through a kind of self-consensus; it contains all things through its vast sphere, especially as if through an eye. For if you see so many things through your eye—because it is animated, transparent, and bright—and you look up at celestial things through its ray reaching toward the heavens, why should the World not see all things through its celestial eye, which is clear, bright, and spreads its rays to all things?

---

->Chapter XXIII.<-

<margin>A</margin>
WE MUST NOW INVESTIGATE whether sensation was granted by nature for the sake of utility alone. Certainly, if sensation is not at all suited to the soul when it lives alone, but senses are employed only in conjunction with the body, it is surely because of the body itself—from which the senses arise—and for the sake of the body's companionship that sensation was given. Either it follows from some necessity, since whatever the body suffers (provided the affection is intense) passes through to the soul; or it was provided as a foresight, so that caution might be taken before an affection grows so strong that it destroys the body, or before that which causes the affection comes too near. 

<margin>B</margin>
If this is so, the senses were given for the sake of **utility** <note>original: "gratia usus" / "πρὸς χρείαν"</note>; for even if...

<column-break/>

...not of an underlying color and shape, seeing as much as is there. 
<margin>A</margin>
Is it then enough for only these to exist, the external thing and the soul? No, for no affection would arise, since there would be nothing to be affected. There must be a third thing, which is that which receives the form. This must be **sympathetic** <note>original: "συμπαθές"; sharing in the same feeling or physical state</note> and of like affection, and of one matter; one part to be affected, and the other to know. 

<margin>B</margin>
The affection must be of such a kind as to save something of the maker, yet not be the same thing. But because it is between the maker and the soul, it holds the affection, lying between the sensible and the intelligible, a middle state by analogy, as if it equalized the extremes to one another. The ruling part is both receptive and communicative; for it must be made like to each. It is an instrument of knowledge in a way, yet by not being the same as either the knower or the known, it becomes like both: to the outer thing by the affection, 

<margin>C</margin>
and to the inner thing because the affection itself is already a form. Therefore we say it is entirely sound that the senses occur through bodily instruments. For this also follows: that if the soul becomes entirely outside of the body, it perceives nothing sensible. The instrument must be either the whole body or a part set aside for a specific work, as in touch and sight. 

<margin>D</margin>
And one might see man-made instruments coming between the judges and the judged, reporting to the judge the quality of the underlying things. For the **ruler**, by touching the straightness in the soul and that in the wood, being in the middle of these, provides the judge with the ability to know the craft. But whether one must join the thing judged to the instrument, or whether those sensible things must be at a distance through some medium—

<margin>E</margin>
for example, if the fire is far from the flesh, the medium suffering nothing, or as if there were a vacuum between the sight and the color—whether it is possible to see when the instrument is present by its power, is another matter. But that sensation belongs to the soul in a body, and is through the body, is clear.

---

->Chapter XXIII.<-

WE MUST CONSIDER whether sensation is for life or for utility only. If for the soul alone there would be no sensation, but with the body there are sensations, they would be because of the body, or something else, or following from necessity, because the body is affected and the affection, being large, reaches the soul. Or it has been contrived because the agent is large or about to be so, so as even to destroy; or to guard before it gets near, if indeed the senses are for utility. For even if...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into whether the universe—the "World Soul" and the celestial bodies—possesses the same kind of senses (sight, hearing, etc.) that humans do. It specifically addresses why a perfect being would need to "perceive" at all if it already possesses total knowledge.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

Knowledge is given to the one who is not in a state of knowledge, but who is ignorant due to misfortune, so that he may be reminded through forgetfulness. This forgetfulness is not explicitly defined, nor is its nature explained; but if someone, because of earthly things, is not only obscured in vision but also loses the sense of the "One" that governs all things and the parts of the world, then perhaps sensation exists for them as a guide. But for that which is a part of the whole and no longer subject to such suffering, would sensation still exist as a present faculty of reason? If it relates to itself, what would it be, since it does not suffer the same things throughout itself? Or through what organ would it perceive? If there is something distinct from the organ that perceives, and that organ were to cease, would not the perceiving self be something else, and the sensation another? Rather, let there be a **self-consciousness** <note>original: "συναίσθησις" / "consensus"; a shared inner awareness rather than external perception</note> of itself, just as we are self-conscious of ourselves. We say that sensation is always of something else. In our case, we perceive some part of our bodies when it deviates from its natural state; we perceive things that have entered from the outside. But just as in us there is not only a grasping of external things but also of one part toward another, what prevents the world from looking through the fixed region at the wandering region <note>The "fixed" stars and the "wandering" planets</note>, and through this, looking at the earth and the things upon it? Even if these parts have different **affections** <note>original: "passiones"; physical impressions or changes</note> from others, nothing prevents them from having different senses. Furthermore, vision in the fixed region might not only be according to itself, but this very region could be like an eye, reporting what it sees to the total soul. For even if it does not admit other affections, what stands in the way of it seeing like an eye, since it is a luminous and living thing? But here Plato will seem to stand in the way, saying that the heaven does not need eyes. Even if nothing is left outside it to be seen, and therefore it did not require eyes of that kind, nevertheless there is that within which may be seen, and nothing prevents it from seeing itself. If someone objects that sensation is not useful because it is vain to see oneself: let it be that this was not established by some primary design for the sake of living in this way, but because it is so arranged by nature that this also necessarily follows; therefore, nothing will hinder it from seeing through a body of such transparency.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Knowledge is granted not to the one who already possesses cognition; rather, it is given to the ignorant as a remedy for misfortune and forgetfulness, so that they might eventually remember. Thus, to one who neither lacks anything nor forgets, such senses were not attributed at all. But if this is the case, we must consider not only the earth but all the stars, and especially the whole of heaven and the world. For to the parts, in relation to other parts that happen to be affected, a sense will be appropriate according to the present reasoning. But for the whole in relation to itself, <margin>B</margin> would it be entirely free of such experience? For if it is necessary that the instrument of the one sensing be one thing, and the thing perceived be something else beyond the instrument, yet the universe is the whole, then surely there will not be in it one thing through which sensation is produced and another which is perceived by the sense. Furthermore, one must attribute to it a certain **consensus** <note>original: "consensum"; a harmony of the parts of a single organism</note> of itself, just as we have a certain consensus of ourselves within us. <margin>C</margin> But sensation that is always directed toward another thing is not present. For we ourselves, when we perceive something in our body that is outside our natural habit, are then touching upon something arriving from the outside. But just as in us there is not only a grasping of external things but also of part toward part, what prevents the world also from looking through the fixed region at the wandering region, and through this, looking down at the earth and seeing those things which are on the earth? If these parts have different affections <margin>D</margin> from others, nothing prevents them from having different senses. Moreover, vision in the fixed region is not only according to itself, but this region itself is like an eye, announcing those things which it sees to the whole soul. For even if it does not admit other affections, what stands in the way of it seeing like an eye, since it is a luminous and animate thing? But here Plato will seem to stand in the way, saying that the heaven does not need eyes. However, even if nothing is left outside to be seen, and therefore <margin>E</margin> it did not need such eyes, nevertheless there is that within which may be seen, and nothing prevents it from seeing itself. If someone objects that sense is not expedient because it is vain to perceive oneself: let it be that this was not established by some primary plan for the sake of living in this way, but rather, because nature is so composed, this also follows by necessity; therefore, nothing will hinder it from seeing through a body of such clarity.

*The souls of the spheres and the stars, and the human world-soul, see and hear; but meanwhile, they do not perceive that they are sensing such things, because the **imagination** <note>original: "imaginatio"; the faculty that translates sensations into mental images</note> to which such observation belongs is always most intently focused on fashioning the marks of the intelligibles within itself. And if they do not perhaps notice that they are sensing us, they nevertheless do good to those who pray to them, through some hidden consensus of nature. This is the opinion of Plotinus among the objections from the faulty text. Someone might say that the imaginations of the celestial souls are so effective that they either derive the marks of the intelligibles into sensible things—and thus sense them inwardly in a way—or they are able to imagine both sensible and intelligible things simultaneously in certain new ways.*

---

### Chapter XXV.

<margin>A</margin> **PERHAPS** it is not enough for an instrument to be present through which action occurs so that it may see and generally sense, but it is necessary for the soul to be disposed in such a way that it "nods" <note>original: "annuat" / "νεύειν"; a metaphorical inclination or turning of attention</note> toward the sensible objects. It is characteristic of the soul itself to always be in the presence of the **intelligibles** <note>original: "intelligibilia"; the higher realm of pure forms and ideas</note>, and if it is possible for it to sense, it is not because it is focused on those intelligibles; for even we, when we are more intensely engaged in understanding...

<meta>This page continues the investigation from page 437 into the sensory capabilities of the celestial bodies and the Earth. While the previous page questioned why perfect beings would need senses, this page explores the mechanics of how they might "hear" human prayers and maintain the unity of the cosmos through a shared "spirit" or sympathy.</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin>
When we are occupied with one thing, other visions and sensations remain hidden from us; and generally, if we focus diligently on one object, everything else is concealed. Furthermore, if the soul should seek to apprehend one part of itself with another—as if it were looking closely at itself—this would be superfluous even in us, and unless done for some specific purpose, it would be in vain. Moreover, to gaze at something else as if it were beautiful is the mark of one who is affected <term>patientis; one who is acted upon by an external force</term> and who is in need. One might suggest that smell, hearing, and the taste of liquids are certain distractions and "ducts" of the soul extending toward the exterior, and that the sun and other stars see and hear only by accident. Yet, if one were to posit that they are converted <note>original: "converti"; turned toward or focused upon</note> through both, the position would not be absurd. Truly, if they are turned toward us, they would also remember human affairs; for perhaps it would be absurd if they did not remember those to whom they diligently do good. Otherwise, if they do not remember, how shall they bestow benefits?

<margin>B</margin>
*The sphere of the world and the stars possess senses, and they hear our prayers. Celestial beings certainly possess sight, though it is different in kind from our sight; yet it agrees in its general nature, being a living nature, clear and luminous. They are also said to possess hearing, but of a kind far different from our hearing, because they frequently fulfill the vows of those who pray, in the manner of those who hear and grant requests. Among all parts of the world, as among the members of a single animal, there is said to be a certain communion, or contiguity, or continuity, or union, of which five foundations are seen. The first is one single **matter** of all things everywhere. The second is the **harmony of qualities**; for just as the elements, although discordant, are nevertheless in harmony through certain neighboring qualities, so too the grades of all things are composed of elements (or not so composed), and though differing among themselves, they touch one another with reciprocating boundaries. The third is the **one spirit** <note>original: "spiritus"; often translating the Greek "pneuma", a vital breath or force</note> everywhere; for just as the heaven is one spirit in the heights, so the earth receives the whole of that one spirit from there. It is infused into all things, and is most similar to the heaven in all things, by which all things are governed in health, and the souls of the world are joined to the lower bodies through the spirit, and all things living through this spirit grow together. I understand this spirit to be similar to our own spirit. The fourth is the **single generative nature** fostering all things through the spirit, bound to the things that follow. The fifth is the **one soul of the world**, everywhere one by its nature, connected to the spirit and all other things. Through this union, therefore, consisting of these five foundations, every most vehement motion reaches the celestial bodies—whether the motion of those making vows—or reaches those making vows from the celestial bodies, especially if not only the soul of the world but also all divine beings are present everywhere, even if they declare their actions more clearly in some places than others. This is what Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus <note>Porphyry and Iamblichus were major Neoplatonist successors to Plotinus; the commentator here is linking their views</note> seem to intend. However, the first God himself, the parent of all and most wide in command, is most present to each individual. The soul of the earth exercises all senses through a spirit that is, as it were, celestial there, and illuminated by the rays of the celestial beings, subject to its own nature, and governing earthly things: it hears prayers.*

->Chapter XXVI.<-

<margin>C</margin>
They also know our vows according to a certain contact and a fixed relationship of all things, tempered together everywhere; and by this same reasoning, effects proceed. Furthermore, in the arts of the magicians, everything is performed through contiguity. These things consist in certain powers, following one another by a certain mutual **compassion** <term>compassione; here meaning "sympathy" or "co-suffering," the idea that distant parts of the universe resonate with one another</term>. If this is so, why should we not say that the earth also senses? But what senses shall we attribute to it? First, why not touch? Whether from part to part, with the sensation being led back to the principal part itself, or whether it senses the whole fire and other elements. For even if the earthly body is unsuited for motion, it is not therefore immobile. It will sense not the smallest things, but the great. But why will it sense? Perhaps because it is necessary, since the soul is present here, that the greatest motions do not remain hidden. Nothing prevents the earth from having sensation for this reason: namely, so that it may well dispose those things pertaining to men, insofar as human duties pertain to it. It will dispose them well through a kind of sympathy or consensus. Nor does anything prevent it from hearing those who pray and nodding to their prayers, though not in the same condition as we are accustomed to. It may use other senses toward itself and other things, as regarding odors and tastes known to others. Perhaps it makes use of the smell of liquids

<meta>catchword: facilitates</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...we know, but other sights and sensations are hidden; and generally, if we are focused, the other things remain unnoticed. Since one part also wishes to perceive another part—for instance, if it should look down upon itself—this would be a functional act even in us, and if not for some purpose, it would be in vain. But in the act of sight, to love a thing as beautiful is the mark of one who is **affected** and in need. As for smelling, hearing, or tasting juices, these are the surroundings and movements 

<margin>B</margin>
of the soul toward the other side. Moreover, the other stars see and hear by **accident** <note>original: "κατὰ συμβεβηκός"; a philosophical term meaning a non-essential property</note>. But if indeed they should turn themselves toward both, the theory is not irrational. But if they turned toward us, they would also remember the affairs of men, for it is easy not to remember. How then do they do good, if they do not remember?

<margin>C</margin>
Knowledge of prayers comes about through **self-consciousness** <note>original: "συναισθήσει" / "sympathy" or "shared awareness"</note>, and by the harmonious fitting together of things that are being taught, and by action, in this way. And in the uses of magic, it is **sympathy** <note>original: "συμπάθεια"</note> that acts. These things work through powers of care and sympathy. If this is so, shall we also grant that the earth senses? But what kind of senses? Or why, or first of all, from what source 

<margin>B</margin>
is the part sent away from the part toward the seat of sensation? Is it the whole of the fire or the other elements? For if the body is difficult to move, it is not therefore motionless. But the sensations will be not of small things, but of great things. But why? Because it is not inevitable, since the Soul is present, that the greatest movements should not remain hidden? Nothing prevents the best sensations from occurring, even if it does something toward 

<margin>C</margin>
men, because human affairs are dependent upon it. And it would be well-placed, as if hearing those who pray through sympathy, and nodding to prayers, but not in our manner. And should it use the other senses toward itself? And regarding other things, such as smells? Or is there a sensation of tastes, as much as provides care for the juices? # BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

[The soul] will provide for the physical body, and we must ask what kind of instruments it requires. For not all animals possess the same organs, such as ears; and those that do not possess them still have the sensation of sounds. But how can there be sight without light? For we must ask this of the body. If we concede this in the vegetative <note>original: "φυτικῷ" (phytikō); referring to the "plant-like" or basic life-sustaining level of the soul</note> part, we must concede it generally. Its spontaneous nature in the vegetative part primarily functions in this way. Instead of a breath <term>pneuma; a subtle spirit or vital "wind" that connects soul to body</term>, let us say it is entirely transparent, or rather a "pneumatic" and transparent substance. Being illuminated by the celestial circle, it becomes transparent, so that it is neither idle nor impossible for the soul of the Earth to see. Therefore, the soul does not belong to a base body, and thus it is a goddess. For it is altogether necessary that the soul itself always exists as good.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> care: thus for the proper care of the body. However, we should not demand such instruments as are found in us. For these are not the same in all animals; for example, ears are not in all of them, yet those which do not have ears nonetheless perceive sounds. But if sight requires light, in what way will it be present in the Earth? Even if eyes are not to be sought there, light nevertheless ought not to be lacking. But if, after it has been granted that a vegetative nature is within it, it must consequently be <margin>B</margin> granted that this very nature is like a certain spirit <term>spiritum; the Latin equivalent of pneuma</term>, and therefore it primarily holds itself thus, why should we doubt that it is also a transparent thing, since it is a spirit? Indeed, it must be confessed that because it is a spirit, it is transparent, and when it is illuminated by the celestial circle, it is transparent in actuality. Wherefore it must be thought neither absurd nor impossible for the soul of the Earth to see. Truly, one must remember that this is not the soul of some vile body, and therefore understand that she is a goddess:

->for it is altogether necessary that the soul itself always exists as good.<-

---

That the Earth has a soul is apparent from plants and stones which grow as long as they remain rooted in the Earth, but not otherwise. Just as teeth, nails, and hair appear in an animal, so the effect of the generative power <note>original: "virtutis genitalis"; the power of reproduction and growth</note> appears in plants clinging to the Earth. However, no power of their own is seen in them; otherwise, even when torn away, they would grow together by their own power. Therefore, this vegetative state is not so much their own as it is common—namely, in the soul of the Earth. Likewise, the masculine and feminine powers—that is, of generating and conceiving—which are distinct in animals, are joined in plants, specifically in the same body. This is because the nature of the plant is inserted into the common nature, just as the body of the plant is joined to the common body. You may see that the masculine and feminine belonging to nature are joined in universal nature, although they are separate in others. Just as sight, where it is perfect, has a piercing power joined with the illuminating light; similarly with the intellect. Thus Orpheus calls the overflowing nature of Jupiter "male" and likewise "female," as does Mercury. By the "flashing of the air," he calls the soul Jupiter, and Juno the soul of the Earth—not only Ceres and Vesta, but he also joined Pluto with Proserpina. Nature joined both sexes in a tree because the tree cannot move toward another for the sake of mating; since it must procreate elsewhere, plants must approach in this way. **Chapter XXVII.**

If in plants he gives the generative power, either he provides the generative power itself, or he preserves it in itself and grants a trace of it to the plants. Thus, the plant will be affected as if it were animated flesh; and under this condition, plants have the generative quality they have drawn from there. Since it is present, it provides for the plant's body that which is better, by which it differs from that which has been cut off. For a cut branch is no longer a plant, but merely wood. But what does the soul itself attribute to the body of the Earth? One must not think that an earthy body cut off from the whole is the same as that which is continuous with the whole. This is demonstrated by the stones themselves, which grow as long as they are rooted in the earth, but remain the size they were when cut off and removed. One must believe that each part has a certain trace in itself. Over this, the universal vegetative power spreads itself, which is no longer the nature of this particular thing mixed with the body, but rather "brooding" or "incubating" over it. Furthermore, there is another soul and mind, which men call Vesta and Ceres, relying on the divine oracle of their own genius when they prophesy such things.

Since it is present, it provides the plant's body with what is better, distinguishing it from that which is severed; for a severed piece is no longer a plant, but merely wood. But what does the soul itself attribute to the body of the Earth? <margin>B</margin> Surely one must not think that an earthy body cut off from the whole is the same as that which is continuous with the whole. The stones themselves demonstrate this, growing as long as they are rooted in the earth; wherefore it must be thought that each part holds a certain trace within itself. Above this, the universal vegetative power diffuses itself, which is no longer <margin>C</margin> the nature of this thing mixed into the body, but rather "hovering" over it. Moreover, there is another soul and intellect, which men call Vesta and Ceres, who, relying on a divine and oracular spirit, prophesy these very things.

The vegetative and generative nature of the soul impresses a certain vital trace upon the complexion of the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health and temperament</note>, from which the body becomes vitally affected. <meta>Continuing the inquiry from the previous page regarding the soul's interaction with the physical body, Plotinus here shifts from the sensory capacities of the "Earth-soul" to the origins of human passions—specifically anger and desire—and how they relate to bodily organs like the heart and liver.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<column-break/>

In passion, at the first movement of sensation, a fiery vigor glows, stirring the imagination and, through it, provoking reason. It happens internally in this way: when reason or the imagination, thinking upon an injury, incites the boiling humors. Furthermore, lust <note>original: "libido"; often used here to refer to the broader appetitive drive</note> has its inclination in the body, and is sometimes raised from the body itself as if swollen with seeds; at other times, it arises from the first affection incited in the body, which moves the imagination or even reason. Sometimes, however, it arises from the imagination or reason itself contemplating a pleasure and thus moving the body. Moreover, the powers of desiring and being angry are like siblings; for those inclined to lust are also more prone to anger, and vice versa—which is why the poets, not without reason, joined Mars with Venus.

### Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>A</margin> Regarding these matters, let it be spoken thus far. We must now return to where we digressed and inquire about the power of anger <note>original: "irascendi virtute"; the spirited part of the soul, or 'thumos'</note> itself. Just as we placed the principle of desire, and pains and pleasures—I do not mean the sensations themselves, but the passions—in a body already affected in a certain way (namely, as if it were made alive), should we also place the beginning of anger there? And should we locate all anger in the whole of such a body, or rather in a certain part <margin>B</margin> of the body, such as the heart or the bile when they are so affected, yet not as if they were devoid of life? Likewise, we must ask: is there something else that grants this <term>animal trace <note>original: "animale vestigium"; the 'ichnos' or impression the soul leaves on matter to animate it</note></term>, or is this spiritedness a single thing not depending on the other powers of anger or sensation? Indeed, in that case, the vegetative power itself, being present in the whole body, imprints a trace upon the whole body; thus, feeling pain and pleasure happens to the whole, and the principle of seeking what is healthful is found in the whole. Regarding the <margin>C</margin> lust of Venus, nothing is strictly defined, but let us say it is centered around the members suited to such a task. Let the region of the liver be the principle of desiring, since the vegetative power acts most strongly there; this provides an <term>animal trace</term> to the liver and the whole body. I say it is there because that is where the action begins. But concerning anger, it is asked: what is it, and what kind of soul does it belong to? Is a trace imprinted by the soul around the heart, or does something else contribute a movement into the "common" <note>the 'common' refers to the composite of body and soul</note> that completes the effect? Or does the soul here provide not a trace, but the very "boiling" of anger itself? First, therefore, we must investigate what this <margin>D</margin> power of anger actually is. It is clear that we are accustomed to being angry not only for what the body suffers, but also for what those dear to us suffer, and generally because of those things which we think are inflicted unworthily upon us or our kin. Therefore, in anger itself, there seems to be a need for sensation and a certain intelligence. Thus, looking at these things, one might judge that anger does not take its origin from the vegetative power, but from some other source. <margin>E</margin> But when a tendency toward anger follows certain physical conditions of the bodies—and when those with boiling blood and bile are more prone to anger, while on the contrary, those who have colder bile or blood are slower to anger—then it seems different. Likewise, brute animals, beyond their bodily compositions, burst into anger merely because someone appears likely to harm them. Again, through these observations, one might easily refer the impulse of anger primarily to a bodily quality and that which contains the constitution of the animal. <margin>F</margin> And when the same men are more prone to anger when they are sick than when they are well—similarly, when they are hungrier they are more irritable than when they are full—it is clear that anger, or the principle of anger, belongs to the body when it is affected in a certain way, and that the bile or blood, as if animated, incites these impulses; and therefore, when such a body suffers...

<column-break/>

And these things, in this way. We must return again to the beginning, from where we must seek concerning the spirited part <note>original: "θυμικοῦ" (thymikou); the irascible or anger-prone part of the soul</note>. Just as we placed the beginning of desires, and pains and pleasures—the passions or the sensations—in the body thus disposed (being a living animal), should we also place the beginning of anger there? Or should we attribute all anger to the body thus disposed, or to some part of the body? For example, the heart being so disposed, or the bile? Or is it in the body, not as something else giving the animal trace, or is anger itself this very thing, that passive and sensory part? And if the vegetative power <note>original: "φυτικὸν" (phytikon)</note> were not in the whole body, would it provide such a trace to every form? If feeling pain belongs to the whole, and feeling pleasure, and the principle of desire—if the desire for sexual things belongs to the whole, then let it be around the parts of such things, as it is said. Let the principle of desire be around the liver, because the vegetative power acts there most of all. Whatever the soul-trace is, it provides it to the whole and to the body. There, I say, is the principle of the activity. But concerning anger, what is it, what part of the soul? Or is there a trace from it around the heart? Or does something else of the movements provide for the completion of both? Or is it these things from a trace? But the act of being angry itself must be considered first. What is it? Is it that the body alone suffers? But it happens when another of our kin [is harmed], and generally as if someone thought their kin were being wronged; either as an opinion or generally in a sensation... from being angry? Looking at these things already, one would not think it comes from the vegetative power. But anger might have its beginning from elsewhere. But when it follows bodily dispositions, the readiness for anger is clear: when they are boiling with blood or bile... they are prone to anger, while those called "bile-less" <note>original: "ἄχολοι" (acholoi); meaning calm or lacking bitter anger</note> or those of good spirit are not. And wild beasts [react] not just from their temperaments, but because of a perceived harm they have anger... again it would be more "body-like" to maintain the nature of the living being, by these angers. Or when the same people are more irritable when sick than when healthy, or when hungry... it is clear that the angers or the beginnings of anger are of the body being in a certain state: if the humors...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the seat of the passions. Having previously discussed the appetitive nature of the "Earth-soul" and its relation to the liver, he now examines the "spirited" part of the soul—the source of anger—and its connection to the heart, blood, and bile.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

...immediately the blood or the bile is moved; once sensation occurs, the imagination also stirs the soul through a bitter bodily disposition <note>original: "πικρᾶ σωματικῆ διαθέσει"</note>. The soul, having already suffered whatever was bitter, then directs the blow toward the causes of its pain. It is clear that this same soul, using reason from above, is moved when an injustice is perceived (or thought to be perceived), causing the whole body to become full of a sinister anger. Because it is natural for corresponding opposites to fight, every such element becomes an ally. That which is roused irrationally also draws reason to itself through the imagination. But that which proceeds from reason ends in that which is naturally prone to anger—which occurs through the vegetal <term>vegetal: the lowest level of soul-function, responsible for growth and nutrition</term> and generative cause—causing the body to seize up, as if it were a faculty for perceiving the pleasant and the painful. By producing something bilious and bitter, a "trace" of the soul <note>original: "ψυχῆς ἴχνος" (psychēs ichnos); Plotinus uses "trace" to describe the soul's faint presence or influence in physical matter</note> is ignited by this bitter movement; it becomes angry because of the harm done to itself, feeling poorly and seeking to make other things similar to itself. A proof that this is a faint trace of the appetitive part of the soul is that those who seek bodily pleasures less and generally disregard the body are less moved toward anger, and their anger is less irrational. It is no wonder that trees do not have anger, even though they possess a vegetal nature, since they share in neither blood nor bile. If these existed without sensation, there would only be a boiling, a sort of irritation; but once sensation is present, an impulse arises toward the thing that caused the offense, so that it rushes to defend itself. But if one were to divide the irrational part of the soul into the appetitive and the spirited <note>The "spirited" part (thymoeidēs) is the seat of courage and anger in Platonic philosophy</note>, making the former the vegetal nature and the latter a trace derived from it near the blood or bile (or something else in the body), the division would not be correctly made. For one is prior and the other posterior. Nothing prevents both from being posterior, or the division being between two things arising from the same source. For this is a division of appetites, or of actions, and of the cause from which they come; that essence is something in itself, not an appetite. But perhaps, by perfecting the appetite and joining its own activity to it, and by considering anger as a trace, it is not absurd to say it is located near the heart. For we do not say the soul itself is there, but rather the principle of that specific kind of blood.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Suddenly the blood or bile is moved, and once the sense is excited, the imagination also awakens. This being awakened, it provokes the soul communicating with such a body to attack the very thing that brought it trouble. It is established, furthermore, that the soul using reason from above is then moved when an injury appears to have been inflicted, even if this disposition—this "spiritedness"—is naturally designed to immediately attack a declared enemy and <margin>B</margin> to fight at the command of reason like a fellow soldier. There is produced in us that which is usually provoked by reason itself, and which, once provoked through the imagination, then calls reason to the same cause. There is also that which begins from reason and ends in that which naturally flares up. Therefore, from the vegetal and generative nature itself, the seeds of anger as well as desire seem to sprout: <margin>C</margin> for this nature has so affected the body that it perceives the pleasant and the painful, and has infused it with bitter bile, and has driven a trace of the soul into a body so affected. Indeed, when it is in such a state regarding painful things, it is irritated into anger; and since it was poorly affected from the beginning, it strives to corrupt the rest and make them similar to itself. That this is a trace of the soul, and not the essence of another trace, can be proven by the fact that those who less desire bodily delights and neglect the body are less provoked to anger and are less carried away by irrational passion. <margin>D</margin> That trees do not have anger, although they have a vegetal nature, ought not to seem strange, since they have neither blood nor bile: for where these are present without sensation, only a "heat" arises, a sort of offense. But when sensation arrives, an impulse then surges to fight off that which caused the offense. Truly, if the irrational part of the soul is divided into the power of desiring and the power of anger, and <margin>E</margin> its trace is located near the blood or the bile (or both), the division will not be correctly made from the opposite side: since one of these is prior and the other posterior. Perhaps, however, nothing prevents both from being posterior, and the division being of two things born from the same source: for it is a division of appetites in the sense that they are appetites, not of the essence from which such things come. For that essence in itself is not an appetite, <margin>F</margin> but perhaps it perfects the appetite, namely by joining to itself the action proceeding from the appetite. Finally, it is not absurd to say that the trace of the soul falling into anger is situated in the chest <note>original: "præcordijs"; referring to the area around the heart/diaphragm</note>: for we should not think the soul is properly here, but rather the fountain of such blood.

***

*In an animated body, there is not only the soul and its continuous life-giving act (like a luminous source emitting light into its own body), but there is also a certain vital trace, like heat beneath the light. I call the natural heat and spirit a vital trace that never perishes so long as the soul is present; but when the soul departs, this vital trace is not immediately lost. To be sure, the natural heat soon ceases to be; the natural spirit is also quickly dissolved. But the vital and animal spirit can survive longer, following the soul as if contained by the soul like a curd <note>original: "coagulo"</note>, acting as a future ferment of the air to be gathered around the body after death, attending to it vitally. If, however, you think there is something in this vital trace besides heat and spirit—something which relates to the soul and its light not as heat, but as a splendor resulting from the light of the soul—that indeed does not perish, but follows as a companion to the departing soul. He opines that light depends in no way on the illuminated object, but only on the luminous source, and that it always follows it together with the splendor resulting in whatever way. This touches upon the opinion stating that the powers and, as it were, the flowers of all colors are in the light.*

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into how the soul departs from the body. Having just discussed the "trace" of the soul in the previous section, he now compares the soul’s presence in the body to light in the air rather than heat in a stone, examining why certain biological processes (like the growth of hair) seem to continue briefly after death.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

...they do not perish, but are rather hidden, only to appear again. In the same way, lights that seem to be extinguished are not scattered, but rather recede into the empty, luminous air, becoming hidden from our sight. Finally, whatever lower life exists within us follows our higher nature and does not perish; a vital trace <note>original Latin: "vestigium vitale"; Greek: "ἴχνος" (ichnos). Plotinus uses this to mean a faint afterglow or remnant of the soul's power.</note> is preserved in the body by the soul—either its own soul or the world-soul—at least for a time after its own individual soul has departed.

<margin>A</margin>But if an animated body is not like a heated object, but rather like an illuminated one, why then does the body have no vital spark after the soul departs? Perhaps it actually does, but only for a short time; for it quickly vanishes, just as heat is quickly extinguished from objects once they are moved away from the fire. <margin>B</margin>Evidence for this is found in the fact that even in the bodies of the dead, hair grows and nails increase. Moreover, many animals continue to move for a time after they have been cut into pieces; this happens, perhaps, because some amount of life still remains. Even if this life exists alongside the other soul, it would not be sufficient proof to show us that it is not a distinct thing. For when the sun departs, not only does the continuous light—which is near the sun and depends upon it—depart at once, but also the radiance which depends on that light, which was cast upon the underlying objects and differed from the sun itself, also departs together with it.

<margin>C</margin>But does it depart along with it, or is it quickly extinguished? This must be investigated in the case of such light, just as we consider the life released from the body, which we judge to belong to the body itself. It is certainly clear that absolutely no light remains in bodies that were once illuminated. But the question is: does it flow back to its source, or is it destroyed? <margin>D</margin>Yet how can it simply cease to be if it was previously something? And what was it, after all? Someone might think that light is a part of the bodies themselves, which is also called "color." And since these bodies are perishable, when they perish, the luminous color is lost with them. Therefore, no one asks where the color of a fire goes once it is extinguished, any more than they ask where its shape <note>original: "figura"</note> goes. Or perhaps shape is merely a certain condition, like a hollow contraction or a dilation? Color, however, is not like that, but is rather like sweetness. What prevents sweetness from surviving after a sweet body is destroyed? Or a scent, after an odorous body is destroyed? These might remain in some other body, yet not be perceived because the participating bodies are not of the sort to transmit the qualities they have received to the senses. <margin>E</margin>Similarly, what prevents light from remaining after its original bodies are destroyed? Yet no light is reflected back to the eyes from anywhere else, as it used to be—unless someone were to say that the mind perceives those things called "qualities" as not being in the subjects at all. <margin>F</margin>But if this is admitted, we will also admit that qualities are incorruptible, and are neither generated in the constitutions of the subjects, nor produced by the "rational principles" <term>rational principles: "logoi" in Greek; the formative blueprints or active forces that shape matter</term> within seeds. Rather, as in birds whose many-colored feathers we see, the colors are already implanted but scattered, and then gathered into one; or perhaps they are even created, but use colors that are in the air. For these colors are in the air, though they do not appear exactly as they do when they are generated in bodies. But let such a doubt rest here for now. <margin>G</margin>However, if the light depends on the body while the bodies remain, and is not separated, what prevents the light from moving together with the moving body?

<column-break/>

How then is the body like something being heated? It is not, but rather like something being illuminated; when the other soul has departed, it ought to have something vital, or does it have it only for a little while? It withers away more quickly, just as the heat of things that have been warmed fades when the fire is removed.

<margin>Chapter XXIX.</margin>

How then is the body like something being heated? It is not, but rather like something being illuminated; when the other soul has departed, it ought to have something vital, or does it have it only for a little while? It withers away more quickly, just as the heat of things that have been warmed fades when the fire is removed. Some evidence for this is the hair growing on dead bodies, and the nails, and animals that move after being cut; this is because the movement of the earth <note>This likely refers to the "earthly" or vegetal soul mentioned in previous sections.</note> was perhaps kindled, and something departs with the other soul, or something remains of that which was bitter, because it is no longer there. Or is it that when the sun has departed, the trace of light remains, or does it depart by stretching back toward it? But also that which is seen then on the outside, in things agreed to be different, departs and is destroyed. And so too with light, it all extends and remains in the life of the body. We say this life belongs to that body. For if there is some light shining in those things that are illuminated, which would either change or be extinguished, it is not simply there. The argument seeks to know how, if someone says it is simply there, it can be infinite. But if it is entirely because of the bodies themselves from which the light comes, it is the so-called "color." For bodies are perishable and changing, and it is a departure when the color of the fire is destroyed, just as with a shape; or is shape one thing, like a contraction or a joy, or a departure? But color is from something, like sweetness or beauty; when the body is destroyed, the sweetness has not perished with the sweet thing, nor the fragrance with the fragrant thing, but it may be in another body, yet it is not perceptible, because the bodies that received it do not communicate it, so that the qualities remain perceptible to the sense-faculty in it; or if some light remains after the bodies are destroyed, why do the more causal things not remain? Unless one says it is seen by law, or that the so-called qualities are not in the subjects. But if they are, they are made incorruptible, not being generated in the constitutions of bodies—those qualities: or rather the "rational principles" in seeds, making the colors, as on the feathers of birds, gathering them together, or making them, but they are mixed with the seeds of such things in the air. For such things are in the air, as they appear when they happen in bodies. But the cause is the difficulty of whether it moves: while the bodies remain, does the light not fall away, or does it prevent the light from moving along with the body as it moves?

<summary>Plotinus argues that the body is 'illuminated' by the soul rather than 'filled' by it, using the analogy of light to explain why life disappears instantly at death while some physical processes, like hair growth, persist briefly.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the soul's "trace" in the body. Having established that a faint remnant of life remains in a body or severed limb for a short time—much like heat lingering in a stone—Plotinus now transitions into a discussion of the celestial bodies (the stars and the Sun), their sensory capacities, and their relationship to human prayer.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> ...hanging closely from what is next to it; and if anything depends on what is near, although it is not seen when it departs, just as it is not apparent when it approaches. Concerning the soul, it will be discussed elsewhere whether subsequent things always accompany preceding things, and whether those that follow are always in the same connection. Or perhaps do individual things stand on their own, even if they are deserted by those that came before, and are they able to persevere in themselves? Or rather, is no part of the soul cut off at all, but are all souls both one and many at the same time, and in what particular <margin>B</margin> manner? But what shall we say of that trace <note>original Latin: "vestigio"; Greek: "ἴχνος" (ichnos). Plotinus uses this term to describe the lowest level of the soul's influence that provides basic biological life to the body.</note> of the soul which is now impressed upon the body as if it were its own? Perhaps if this very thing is the soul, it will follow the principle of the preceding soul, clearly not being segregated from the soul's own logic. But if it is like a life belonging specifically to the body, the condition here will be the same as that which was doubted a little while ago regarding the image of light. For it must be considered whether life can exist without the soul, unless perhaps it happens insofar as a certain soul assists by acting upon another thing.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...hanging closely from what is next to it; and if anything depends on what is near, although it is not seen when it departs, just as it is not apparent when it approaches. Concerning the soul, it will be discussed elsewhere whether subsequent things always accompany preceding things, and whether those that follow are always in the same connection. Or perhaps do individual things stand on their own, even if they are deserted by those that came before, and are they able to persevere in themselves? Or rather, is no part of the soul cut off at all, but are all souls both one and many at the same time, and in what particular <margin>B</margin> manner? But what shall we say of that trace <note>A "trace" or "shadow" of the soul refers to the basic animating force that remains in physical matter.</note> of the soul which is now impressed upon the body as if it were its own? Perhaps if this very thing is the soul, it will follow the principle of the preceding soul, clearly not being segregated from the soul's own logic. But if it is like a life belonging specifically to the body, the condition here will be the same as that which was doubted a little while ago regarding the image of light. For it must be considered whether life can exist without the soul, unless perhaps it happens insofar as a certain soul assists by acting upon another thing.

->THUS FAR in the commentaries of Eustochius <note>Eustochius of Alexandria was a student of Plotinus and a physician who was present at his death.</note> is the second book on the soul, and here the third begins; but in the commentaries of Porphyry <note>Porphyry was Plotinus's most famous student and the primary editor of his works, the Enneads.</note>, the things that follow are joined to the seventh.<-

*The stars possess sight and hearing, but they have no need for memory; furthermore, they hear prayers. Just as one who seasonably exposes his body to the light of the Sun is naturally warmed thereby, so one who applies his soul and spirit to the influences of higher beings through a vow naturally carries away the flowing benefits from those ever-present gifts. Some ancients used to worship the stars in addition to the Sun, but many—especially the Platonists and philosophers of that kind—worshiped only the Sun among the celestial bodies. Julian <note>Likely referring to Julian the Apostate, the Roman Emperor who wrote a famous hymn to King Helios.</note> and Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized theurgy and ritual.</note> composed prayers to the Sun; Plato called the Sun the visible son and image of the supreme God; Socrates was often seen saluting the rising Sun; and the Pythagoreans used to sing hymns to the rising Sun with the lyre. As for the worship of the Sun, let those men see to it: but certainly, God has set his tabernacle in the Sun. Chapter XXX.*

<margin>A</margin> Now, since we have established that memory is superfluous to the stars, yet we have granted them senses—not only sight, but also hearing—we have furthermore conceded that they hear the prayers we direct to the Sun, and indeed, which other men direct toward other stars. For they believe they will obtain many things from them through prayers, and so easily that the stars act as patrons not only for just duties, but often even for unjust ones. Since such doubts arise, we must consider them carefully at present. For <margin>B</margin> these matters hold in themselves the greatest and most common difficulties, especially among those who are distressed that the gods are considered helpers and authors of wicked works, both of others and even of unrestrained love and sexual union. Therefore, both for the sake of these things, and especially for the sake of their memory—of which we spoke from the beginning—it seems that an investigation must be made. For it is certain that if the things we pray for are done, and they do not do them immediately but in the future, and often after a long time, the stars must preserve human prayers in their <margin>C</margin> memory. But our previous reasoning did not allow this at all; rather, as far as benefits bestowed upon men were concerned, it seemed to be such as if they were said to be bestowed by Ceres and Vesta <note>Goddesses of the harvest and the hearth, here used as personifications of the Earth.</note>, that is, the Earth—unless perhaps one says that benefits are bestowed upon men from the Earth alone. We must therefore try to demonstrate both: in what way we may attribute the gift of memory to them—as far as it pertains to us—and not according to how it appears to others who do not forbid giving memory to the stars, and what <margin>D</margin> should be said of those things which seem to be done wrongly by them. This is truly the duty of philosophy.

<summary>Plotinus explores whether celestial bodies like the Sun and stars possess memory in order to answer human prayers, while addressing the ethical problem of why gods might seem to assist in immoral human actions.</summary>
