<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the soul's influence on the body and transitions into a defense of the celestial order. He begins a systematic investigation into how the movement of the heavens affects life on Earth and the nature of "action" and "passion" (being acted upon) in the cosmic hierarchy.</meta>

-># PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.<-

<margin>A</margin> We must consider whether there is some way to resolve the doubts that people have regarding the celestial God <note>The "celestial God" refers to the heavens and the stars, which Plotinus viewed as divine, living beings.</note>; likewise, regarding the whole world, against which similar accusations are directed, as if it were the cause of evil. This is necessary if we are to give any credit to those who believe that even the entire heaven can be swayed to their will by human audacity and art, using certain magic spells. We must further inquire about demons, <margin>B</margin> and in what way they are said to provide such services—unless, perhaps, from the resolution of the former questions, you also receive the resolution for these.

*Some actions are natural, while others are artificial. Natural actions are either of the whole universe toward its parts, of the parts toward the universe, or of the parts toward one another in turn. Artificial actions either end in a work constructed by its own art, as sculpture ends in a statue, or they serve the work of nature, such as medicine, agriculture, and magic—with which rhetorical persuasion and the allurements of poetry and music have a certain similarity. The actions of the celestial bodies upon lower things are not produced through heat or any other quality similar to the elements, but through certain powers far different from innate qualities. For the differences in movements, character, intellects, professions, and fortunes that are either caused or portended by the celestial bodies cannot be attributed to differences in celestial qualities similar to the elements. Nor do the celestial bodies act upon us individually by plan and choice; otherwise, their minds would not always be happy, and they would be daily ministers of evils.* <margin>Chapter XXXI.</margin>

### IT IS WORTH THE EFFORT to consider
generally all actions and passions <note>original Latin: "passiones"; Greek: "παθήσεις" (patheseis). In this philosophical context, "passion" does not mean emotion, but the state of being acted upon by an outside force.</note> that occur in the universe, whether they are accomplished by nature or by art. We should affirm that those which occur by nature happen partly from the whole itself toward its parts, partly from the parts toward the whole, and finally, partly from one part toward another. Furthermore, things which are done by art are performed in two primary ways: either the art provides the beginning of the work and also <margin>B</margin> imposes an artistic end upon it, or arts use natural forces in addition to complete the actions and passions of natural works. Truly, I call "actions of the universe" those by which the whole world-circuit acts upon itself or upon its parts. For while it revolves, it both disposes itself in a certain condition and composes its parts with itself—the parts, I say, which are in the circuit itself, and those which are distributed from there to the earth. Likewise, the actions and passions of parts toward parts are manifest to almost everyone: namely, the Sun's <margin>C</margin> relationship and effects upon other things and even upon terrestrial things. Again, there are the things done in other elements both by the Sun and by others; moreover, there are the mutual actions and passions of those things on the earth as well as those in the other elements, which seem to require individual consideration. Then there are the arts that construct buildings and manufacture other products, which similarly end in such a result. But medicine, agriculture, and others of that kind are the ministers of nature, and they suggest <margin>D</margin> supports to the works of nature so that they may be carried out naturally. It is also useful to consider the art of rhetoric and music, and whatever things entice souls with a certain pleasure; these differ among themselves primarily in that they lead either to the better or to the worse. Among these, we must inquire how many arts there are and what power they have, and if possible, we must treat all these matters in a way that will be useful for our present purpose, seeking the causes in them as far as possible. It is established beyond doubt that the world-circuit <margin>E</margin> itself acts, first by disposing itself in different ways, and then by moderating all the things it contains within itself—including, without controversy, all terrestrial things—not only the constitutions of bodies, but also the affections of souls.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> We should examine, by way of defense, the things said against the god in heaven <note>original Greek: "θεὸν τὸν ἐν οὐρανῷ" (theon ton en ourano). Plotinus refers to the divine nature of the celestial spheres.</note> and indeed concerning the whole world itself, as even toward this the same cause is attributed, if one listens to those who say even the whole heaven is enchanted by the skill of men. And the word about demons <margin>B</margin> will also be sought, how they are said to perform such activities—unless perhaps from the things above, you also find the solution for these.

### UNIVERSALLY, THEN, we must grasp
all the actions and the passions that occur in the whole world, both those called "by nature" and those that occur "by art." Of those by nature, some are said to occur from the whole toward the parts, and from the parts toward the whole, or from parts to parts. Those that occur by art either belong to the arts themselves as a fulfillment for the craftsmen, or they make use of natural powers for the production of natural works. By actions of the whole, I mean those by which the entire revolution acts, as it moves itself and acts upon its parts; it both disposes itself in a certain way, and its parts—both those in the revolution itself and those parts given to the earth. Or the actions of parts toward parts are surely clear to everyone, such as the Sun's relations and productions toward other things, and toward those on the earth. And things in the other <margin>C</margin> elements, both themselves and of the others, and of those on the earth. And for the others, one must always use what is necessary. Some arts make houses and other crafted things, and they end at that. But others, such as agriculture and the like, are subsidiary and provide help for things that proceed naturally, so that they remain according to nature. Rhetoric and music and all "soul-leading" <note>original Greek: "ψυχαγωγίαν" (psychagogian). This refers to the art of "leading" or "persuading" the soul, a term often used by Plato to describe rhetoric.</note> lead either toward the better or toward the worse. It is necessary <margin>D</margin> then to seek how many arts there are and what power they have; and whatever they are, if there is a place for all of them for our present need, and the "why" as far as it can be signaled in these matters. That the revolution acts is certain, first by disposing itself differently, and also the things within it—unquestionably the terrestrial things, not only in their bodies, but also in the <margin>E</margin> dispositions of the soul and each of the parts.

<summary>Plotinus investigates how the universe and celestial bodies influence life on Earth, distinguishing between natural cosmic movements and human arts like medicine, music, and magic. He argues that the heavens affect both physical bodies and the dispositions of the soul, though not through malicious "choice."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's systematic investigation into celestial influence. Having previously discussed magic and demons, he now turns to the mechanism by which stars affect life on Earth, arguing against both purely physical explanations (like heat) and the idea that gods "choose" to make people act wickedly.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

...upon earthly things and generally upon those below, is clear in many ways. But whether these lower things exert any force upon the higher, we shall investigate in what follows. For the present, however, allowing those things which are accepted by all or most people to stand as they seem to be, we must bring forward those arguments that rely on reason, taking up the manner of cosmic reflection from the beginning. For it should not be said that only heat and cold, and other such things—which are called the <term>primary qualities</term> <note>original: "ποιότητες πρῶται" / "qualitates primae"; in ancient physics, these were hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> of the elements—or those things produced by their mixing, are able to act. Nor again should it be thought that the sun does everything through heat, and some other celestial body through cold. For what could be cold in the heaven, which is a fiery body <note>original: "πνεύμα σῶμα" / "igneo corpore"; Plotinus is debating the physical makeup of the stars.</note> and a fire that is in no way moist? Furthermore, by this reasoning, we could not at all grasp the difference between the natures and actions of the celestial bodies. Indeed, there are many things which cannot be referred back to such physical properties as their cause. If one attributes the differences in character to these superior powers according to certain constitutions of the body—claiming such effects arise from an excess of cold or heat—how can one possibly reduce envy, jealousy, or cunning to these same things? Truly, if these qualities had such power, how could they account for better or worse fortunes, for wealth or poverty, for the nobility of ancestors, for one’s own generosity, or the finding of treasures? For anyone can list countless things that are far removed from the efficacy of a bodily quality coming from the elements into the bodies and souls of living beings. Nor should these individual events, which happen to individuals below, be attributed to the deliberate choice or consultations of the stars and the universal mind. For it is a sin <note>original: "Nefas"; a term implying a violation of divine law or natural order.</note> to say that the higher beings plot against humans so that some might become thieves, others might reduce free men to slavery, break through walls, or commit sacrilege; or that others again might be ungenerous and cowardly, behaving like women in their actions and passions, or be devoted to shameful habits. To commit and plot such things is not only beneath the gods, but not even characteristic of moderately decent men. Perhaps, indeed, it is not even the nature of anyone to perpetrate such things from which no benefit would meanwhile come to them.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...of the celestial beings acting upon earthly things and all that follows. Whether these lower things exert any force upon the higher, we shall investigate in the following pages. But for the present, permitting those things which are approved by all or most to remain as they appear, we must bring forth those points which rest on reason, repeating the mode of reflection from the beginning. It must not be said that only heat, cold, and other such things—which are called the primary qualities of the elements—or those which are joined by their <margin>B</margin> mixture, are able to act. Nor again should it be thought that the sun does all things through heat, and some other celestial body performs all through cold. For what is cold in the heaven and in that fiery body, which is fire in no way moist? Added to this is the fact that by this reasoning, we could by no means accept a difference between celestial natures and actions. Now truly, there are many things which cannot be referred to any such things as a cause. If someone attributes the differences in character to superior powers <margin>C</margin> according to certain constitutions of the body, through an excess of cold or heat, in what way will he also be able to reduce envies, emulations, and astuteness to these same things? But if these are valid, how can they refer worse or better fortunes, riches, poverty, the nobility of ancestors, personal generosity, or found treasures to qualities of this kind? For anyone can count innumerable things which are far removed from the efficacy of a bodily <margin>D</margin> quality coming from the elements into the bodies and souls of animals. Nor yet are individual things, which happen to individuals below, to be attributed to the counsel and choice of the stars and the universal opinion and consultations of these. For it is a sin to say that the higher beings plot against men, in what way some might become thieves, others might reduce free men to servitude, dig under walls, or commit sacrileges; others again be illiberal and fearful, and womanish in their actions and passions, and most dedicated to foul morals. For to commit and plot such things is not only not the part of gods, but not even of moderately honest men. Perhaps indeed it is not even the part of anyone to perpetrate such things from which no utility would meanwhile be produced for them.

> *The Heavens act upon all these lower things, not by some choosing counsel to act in such or such a way, nor only by bodily qualities—namely by heating, moistening, rarefying, or the opposite—but by certain natural powers of the vegetative soul. By certain similar powers, which are as if halfway between conscious counsel and bodily qualities, our soul daily restores the humors and members of the body, and their shapes and qualities. Since the world is one single living animal, all bodily things are parts of the world from two perspectives: first, because individual bodies are certain portions of the universal body; second, because in any body there is the soul of the world itself, and a certain efficacy of this soul is distributed to this body. Therefore, insofar as individual bodily things are members of the world-animal, they easily suffer [are acted upon] both by the whole and by one another; for even those places which seem to be distant from one another are near, on account of the wonderful communion of a single nature.*

->Cap. XXXII.<-

<margin>A</margin> SINCE, therefore, we attribute those things which come to us and other animals from the sky, and whatever earthly things there are, neither to bodily causes nor to counsels, what probable cause remains for us? In the first place, this universe must be thought to be one living animal containing all animals within itself, having one soul diffusing itself through its individual parts, insofar as any part is a part of it—and every thing is a part of it.

<summary>Plotinus argues that celestial influence on Earth is neither purely physical (heat/cold) nor a result of the gods' conscious "plotting" of human misdeeds, but rather a natural function of the universe as a single, living organism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of cosmic influence. While the previous page questioned whether purely physical qualities like heat or cold could account for complex human behaviors like envy, this page introduces the Neoplatonic solution: the concept of the universe as a "Single Living Animal" bound together by "Sympathy."</meta>

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> is retained in the sensible order: and certainly, as far as the body is concerned, it is entirely a part; and insofar as it participates in the world-soul, to that extent and by that reasoning it is considered a part of the world. Now, those things which participate in this soul alone are parts in every respect; but those things which possess another soul in addition <note>Plotinus refers to the "rational soul" of humans, which exists alongside the "world-soul" that animates the physical body.</note> have, by this very fact, the quality of not being entirely parts. They nonetheless suffer effects from other things insofar as they possess something of the universe, and they suffer in a manner congruent with those things they possess. 

<margin>B</margin> Indeed, because this universe is one, and one living animal <note>original: "ζῶον ἕν" / "vnum animal"; the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that the cosmos is a single, integrated organism.</note>, it suffers with itself throughout: and that which seems to be remote in it is also near. Just as in any single animal, the nails, horns, fingers, and any other part which are not placed closely together, but are distant by some intervening space: [the part] suffers nothing through a rejection of what is in no way near it. For where things joined together are not continuous in proximity, but are distant with something else intervening, they nevertheless <margin>C</margin> suffer together <note>original: "συμπαθεῖα" / "compatiuntur"; Cosmic Sympathy is the principle that all parts of the universe are interconnected like organs in a body.</note> by their very likeness; and it is necessary that an effect reaches that which is placed far off, even if it is not nearby. But in this universe, which is both an animal and leads everywhere into a unity, nothing is so remote in location that it is not considered near, on account of the very nature of the one animal suffering with itself everywhere. Therefore, that which has a likeness toward that which acts, receives a passion <note>In this context, "passion" means "being acted upon" or "receiving an influence."</note> that is not alien. But if the acting force is dissimilar, it receives an alien and troublesome passion. 

<margin>D</margin> Nor should it be wondered at that in one living being, an action from one part brings harm to another, since even in ourselves, through our own actions, one part is hurt by another; clearly bile and anger <note>original: "χολὴ καὶ θυμός" / "bilis & ira"; Ancient medicine associated bile and the "spirited" part of the soul with physical and emotional agitation.</note> seem to press and sting something else by force. Truly, there is something in the universe very similar in proportion to spiritedness and bile, and similarly from other things: for even in plants, some things are an impediment to others, they consume and destroy. 

But this world is not only one animal, but is also seen as many. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, insofar as each thing is preserved, it is one, and by this very fact it is saved; but insofar as it is many, and many things clash among themselves, it is hurt here and there by opposition. Here, certainly, one thing hurts another for its own use, and they use another for nourishment, since it is at once related and different: namely, everything naturally looking out for itself, it takes into itself as much as is congruent with the other, and as much as is alien, it destroys by its own self-interest. 

Furthermore, while each thing performs its own work, in the meantime—<margin>F</margin> especially that which is able to opportunely admit something into its own coverings—that which cannot sustain the command of the work is either destroyed or affected by detriment. Just as those things which suddenly wither as fire passes by, or as smaller animals are snatched away or trampled by the running of larger ones. Truly, the generation and corruption of all these things, as well as the change for better or worse, perfects the life of the one world-animal itself, a life that is remote from impediment and behaving naturally. 

<margin>G</margin> Since it was not possible for individual things to exist as if they were alone, or as if they were ends unto themselves; but it was necessary to look at them as parts existing, and they must be viewed in relation to that whole as an end, of which they are parts. Likewise, since they ought to be different, it is right that individuals in one...

<column-break/>

...it is to the sensible whole: the body is what suffers, but as much as it has soul by participation, it is also in the whole. In one way, things only participate in this [world-soul] and are thus parts; but as many as participate in another [soul], in that way they are not entirely parts, yet they suffer in the whole insofar as they possess that [body]. And according to that, some things are sympathetic, in that the whole is one, like one animal. And that which is divided far away, just as in each individual thing there is a nail, and a horn, and a finger, and whatever else is not adjacent, but separated by the interval between, if it suffers, that which is near suffers nothing; for that which is adjacent among similar things, even if separated by other things in between, must by similarity suffer together, and it is necessary that it reaches what is far off... <note>The Greek text mirrors the Latin, emphasizing that the "oneness" of the universe allows distant parts to interact through "sympathy" (συμπαθεῖα) rather than physical contact.</note> ...This world is not only a living animal, but also many things to be seen, so that while each thing suffers, it is preserved by the whole... things hasten according to nature, and as much as is related to the other, it takes into itself, and as much as is alien, it disappears within itself... and the generation or corruption of these things, and the alteration toward the worse or better, completes the life of that one animal... for it was not possible for each to be as if they were alone, nor as if they were the final ends, being parts, but toward that [whole] for which they are parts, being differences.

<summary>Plotinus explains the concept of cosmic sympathy, arguing that the universe is a single "world-animal" where distant parts affect each other like organs in a human body. He accounts for conflict and destruction within the world as the natural interaction of parts contributing to the life of the whole.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic discussion of the world as a "Single Living Animal." While the previous page established that all parts of the universe are interconnected through "sympathy," this page uses the metaphor of a sacred dance (tripudium) to explain how the movement of the stars and planets creates a stable, meaningful whole despite constant change.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

life, being always active, in remaining [the same], and its experiences likewise; it is practiced so that the whole remains, holding its stability even while being moved.

->the universe ought to have its own stability within motion.<-

The whole world is one living animal dancing <note>original: "saltans"; Plotinus uses the metaphor of a ceremonial dance to explain how the cosmic bodies move in a complex but ordered way.</note> to a musical reason (must it be admitted that a single purpose follows from the dance?). The universal Soul, in its intelligence, thought, imagination, and nature, leaves things as if it were abandoning them; it draws together all the leaps of the world according to their musical proportions: and it marks things out as if they were coming forth, whether they follow the necessary resolutions in the heavens, or in the way the consequences of place beneath the heavens "breathe." But in the dance of any individual human, they take the marking as if to a melody; their gatherings through emotion follow the revolutions [of the stars], appearing in the world like the gestures of one performing a sacred dance <note>original: "tripudiantis"; a 'tripudium' was a rhythmic three-step dance used in ancient Roman religious rituals.</note>. Indeed, the dancer himself looks with intention, so that he himself is part of such a composition of art. From this, the changes of the world's members flow in a third way through those things which the lord of life himself follows, or has signaled by the dance. And some wise man, acting like a musician, will be able to foresee what kinds of "markings" are united everywhere, and thus what kinds of gestures of the limbs follow among the nations—except where either the inertia of the local matter does not yield to the influence, or the matter is too weak to receive it; in such cases, the matter produces its own manner and choice, though never by mere chance. Just as the sight of a weak human sees only a small part of the whole: God looks upon the spectacle as if in a chorus, where the passion or pleasure of the limbs occurs beyond the rest of the dance.

<margin>A</margin> Concerning the motion, such things are for manifestation. The ratios carried into the living being by Reason, even if they create a harmony, do so toward the being of the whole, and toward the parts within one another; though they may seem to have no relation to specific individual things, yet because the whole living being is one, the parts cannot relate to each other in any other way. Individual spirits may change, or some may move toward motion, while others <margin>B</margin> move toward passions. It is in this way that the parts of the dance are parts of grace; not everyone sees the things that truly are. But the parts of the dance are given to the whole in relation to the melody of the body—these are the "labors" that signify something. In the relation of the part to the whole, and from others, there is labor, but some things are done in return through the motion of the bodies in the chorus. <margin>C</margin> And if the breaths are like those in a chorus, looking toward another thing, these first things will be those that are to come, either from the beginning of the dance, or by cycling through the whole, so that you might use the entire form. <margin>D</margin> Whether it is a labor of the body, it is not everywhere with it, but from an inflow, and the alteration is in all things, just as color is chosen for those things that are formed; the body works upon what truly is. Whence those things which indicate its state, some through form, are acquired by the dance. These things, therefore, are thought to be done by the heavenly bodies, since they manifest the whole world, acting out its entire life within it—the great parts either reshaping themselves or changing their relations. These relations of the parts to one another and to the whole, and their different positions, follow the rest, as the movement of a single animal. <margin>E</margin> In these positions and formations, the things that exist are not the ones being formed as separate lives, but it is the "Former" (the Soul) who is not himself shaped into another body, but is the whole; for he does not act upon another, but is himself all the things that are becoming.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> From life comprehended, they ought not to possess their own identity so entirely and perpetually: nor could it happen that anything should always remain in only one way, if indeed the universe by itself ought to have its own stability in motion.

<margin>Chapter XXXIII</margin>
<margin>A</margin> Since indeed the revolution of the world has nothing accidental in it, but is carried out by some reason toward the animal <note>The "World-Animal" or "Macrocosm."</note>, there ought to be a certain concord and order between the agent and the patient <note>The "agent" is the active Soul; the "patient" is the physical matter receiving the action.</note> which it has already ordered in itself and toward one another: so that according to any state of the revolution, and the substance of that revolution, one disposition or another must happen, as if they perform one dance in a very diverse chorus. In our own dances, who can explain the <margin>B</margin> responses which occur from outside, agreeing with the dances in any single motion? Among those who take note of these things, three elements lead to the chorus: the dance itself, the signs, and the external songs joined together. But it is not easy for just anyone to maintain and declare the parts of the one who performs the dance according to any necessary figure, while the body accompanies and turns away by following a certain reason: in which one part is pressed and restrained, another is relaxed, one <margin>C</margin> labors, and another receives a different "breathing" in the configuration. In the relief of those dancing, one part is watched while the rest suffer following the dance and serve reason, and thus they constitute the whole perfectly. Therefore, the power of dancing is entirely to signify, just as in a dance certain things constituting a limb of the body are raised higher, while another is contracted, another hidden, another meanwhile is pressed to the ground while the dancer himself <margin>D</margin> deliberates on this; but in the dance of the whole body of the universe, he holds this necessary disposition for the part performing the chorus. By the same reasoning, it must be thought that the celestial bodies do whatever they do, and signify most things: indeed, the whole world lives its entire life, moving its great parts, and always transfiguring itself. The habits of the parts, both toward each other and toward the whole, and their different positions, provide the rest of the expression, as if <margin>E</margin> one animal were moved; thus they are according to such habits and positions and figures. It is not as if there are various authors of things who are themselves being shaped, nor does the Figurer himself take on a different face. For he does not act upon something external; rather, he is this world, and he is himself made of all the things that exist.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how human life is woven into the movements of the universe. The previous page introduced the metaphor of the world as a "sacred dance" (tripudium); here, Plotinus and his translator Ficino clarify that while our bodies are subject to the "dance" of the stars, our souls retain a degree of freedom, similar to how a wise servant manages a relationship with a master.</meta>

### PLOTINUS ON THE ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

...there indeed the figures <note>original: "figuras"; in astrology, these are the 'aspects' or geometric relationships between planets.</note> [are found], but here the consequences of those figures [follow] <margin>A</margin> as necessary passions <note>original: "passiones"; here meaning things experienced or undergone by a physical body, rather than just emotions.</note> concerning the living being thus moved. And again, concerning a thing so composed and established by nature, it is both passive and active within itself under these necessary conditions.

*Our body, as a part of the world, follows the fated circuit of the world. The soul also, insofar as it obeys the body, suffers; yet through greatness of mind, it seeks to hold the sufferings of the body in low esteem and to try to avoid them by skill. In various parts of the world's spheres, and in the stars themselves, there are naturally various powers. As many as there are powers, so too are there various figures among the stars firmly established in relation to one another—powers, I say, that are firm. Different powers then arise in succession within different figures, which occur perpetually among the stars due to the diversity of their motion. To these powers everywhere, both of natures and of figures, those things which belong to the Moon follow; partly as if made necessary from there, caught up like those seized by the hand of dancers, but partly as a harmony of the free—like those who act, sing, and dance willingly to the sound of the choral dance. The celestial figures here signify the lower things: but one nature is produced in the figures according to the disposition of matter. Yet the figures signify many things which are not caused by such things but come from elsewhere. Chapter XXXIII.*

<margin>A</margin> WE MUST JUDGE, moreover, that we are only a certain part of these things within us—that which is part of the universal body—and we grant it to that whole; we do not judge that the whole of what is in us belongs to it, even when we suffer things moderated by it. We are like the most prudent of servants, <margin>B</margin> partly yielding to their masters, but partly wishing to be their own masters, and for this very reason they receive more moderate commands from their masters, since they are neither mere chattels <note>original: "mancipia"; referring to legal property or slaves without rights.</note> nor entirely independent. It was necessary for a difference in configurations to occur, as is happening now, because the stars run their courses and do not run with equal speed. Therefore, since they are carried along by reason and result in different habits for the living being—and since the things among us "suffer with" them <note>original: "compatiantur"; a reference to the Stoic/Neoplatonic concept of 'cosmic sympathy' where all parts of the universe feel the movements of the others.</note>—it is reasonable to ask whether we should assert that these things follow those by harmony, or whether the figures themselves have the power of producing effects; and whether it is the figures simply, or rather the figures *of these specific stars*. For the same <margin>C</margin> configuration does not bring about the same effect in one thing as it does in others: since every individual seems to have a nature that differs even in itself. Perhaps it will be rightly said that for some, the configuration is such-and-hers, and the disposition is of this kind; while for others, the configuration being the same, the existence is different. But if this is so, we shall no longer give authority to the figures, but rather to the things configured themselves, or to both together—namely, to those same natures having obtained a different habit. We might even grant <margin>D</margin> different things to the same star simply because it differs by its location. But what shall we grant? Effects, or signs? Perhaps to the conjunction itself—that is, to the configuration of these things—both are proper: both effects and significations in many cases, but elsewhere, significations only. Therefore, this reasoning grants powers to the figures and powers to the things configured: just as those dancing and playing in a choral dance <note>original: "chorea"; a circular dance accompanied by singing.</note> have a certain power, and both the hands and the other members have the figures they <margin>E</margin> assume. But in the third place are the consequences: both the parts of those taken into the dance, and the things from which they are made, or which happen from them—such as the things rubbed together by touching, and the nerves and veins "suffering along" with them.

*The World Soul, having contemplated this universe from eternity within the series of Ideas, chose by one common election that the entire course of the world should be so; meanwhile, the vegetative nature, its image placed beneath it, carries out the entire course of the world without choice. The individual souls of the free stars also hold themselves similarly toward God and the world: to such an extent do they agree with the World Soul, both in will and in nature, that all actions in the world can equally and rightly be called actions of the World Soul. All bodily things are therefore parts of the world-animal: All...*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...there the configurations, but here the things following the configurations, the necessary affections, as if existing in a subject animal; and where this composite [animal] is either acting by nature, it does not suffer while acting toward necessary things.

<margin>A</margin> BUT WE, hearing that we are a part of it and also suffer, insofar as our [body] belongs to that body of the whole, and thinking that its affections are moderate—just as the wise among those who serve, in some things ministering to their masters, <margin>B</margin> but in others being their own [masters], escape the more moderate commands from their masters, since they are not slaves, nor entirely foreign to the whole. The difference of the configurations of the things running [the stars], since they are not of equal speed, must necessarily occur as it now occurs, being carried by reason. If there is a difference of relations toward the things that happen, and if one were to coordinate this with what happens among us—how it ever relates to the things produced—it is reasonable to seek whether one should say these things happen as if having been "marked out" <note>original: "ἐπισεσημάνθαι"; to be signified or signaled rather than caused.</note> in those [stars], or that the configurations have the powers <margin>C</margin> of the things produced; or the configurations simply, or those of these [stars], or by being configured in a certain way. For the same thing in one case, and where it might be otherwise in another, works the same signification or production, since each one also has a nature that differs by itself. It seems perhaps to have reason that the disposition of such a configuration is of such a kind, but that of another, even with the same configuration, is different; but then we shall no longer give [the power] to the configurations, but to the things configured themselves, or <margin>D</margin> to both together—at least to those in which the difference of relation is taken—but also to the same thing alone by its difference toward other things. But what will it produce? A signification? Or both together? By the configuration, both productions and significations in many cases, but elsewhere, significations only. Since, therefore, the argument gives powers to the configurations and powers to the things configured, <margin>E</margin> it is as with a dancer: each hand and the other members have a certain power, and the configurations [of the dance] have more. Third are the things following from them—from the parts of the dancers themselves being taken along with the parts from which these come, as for instance the things of the hand being pressed together, and the nerves and veins "feeling along" in sympathy.

<summary>This page explores the relationship between celestial movements (the "dance" of the stars) and earthly events, arguing that stars primarily signify rather than strictly cause human actions. Plotinus uses the metaphor of a "wise servant" to explain how the human soul can maintain partial autonomy from the "commands" of fate and the physical universe.</summary>

<keywords>astrology, free will, World Soul, cosmic sympathy, Ficino, Plotinus, celestial mechanics, fate, macrocosm and microcosm, sacred dance</keywords>

--- Page 464 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into how the celestial bodies influence the earthly realm. Having established that the universe acts like a choreographed dance, Plotinus and his translator Marsilio Ficino now explore whether these influences result from the "choices" of the stars or from the natural, organic unity of the world as a single living being.</meta>

### BOOK FOUR.

*The actions of natural things are the movements of this living being <note>The "living being" refers to the Anima Mundi, or World Soul, which Neoplatonists believed animated the entire universe.</note>. All the revolutions of the world are its deeds and, as it were, its speeches. Nothing within it, or arising from it, happens by chance; for everything is referred back to the <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes seminales"; these are the formative, "seed-like" principles or blueprints inherent in nature that guide the growth and behavior of all things.</note> implanted here, or even higher to the exemplary patterns. Individual things, therefore, either proceed by an established order or are immediately brought back into that order. The Sun, the heart of the world, possesses and provides much more natural life than the other parts of the world. Because of this, some have placed the soul of the world itself in the Sun, diffused everywhere through its rays. All the powers of natural things exist seminally within the seminal reasons of our shared nature. From these, movements are transmitted into the spheres of the world—the geometric figures of these reasons, which are as mobile as they are firm. From there, they pass into the species of natural things, in which wonderful forces lie hidden beyond the basic elements; and from these very figures, wonderful powers also pass into lower forms. Even our own countenance may possess specific powers in its features to attract or deter, showing that a specific power can exist in shapes no less than in colors. Chapter 35.*

---

<margin>A</margin> How then do these powers work? For we must state more clearly whether a triangle differs [from another figure], or how it acts, or what it accomplishes. If we attribute these actions to their physical bodies, then choice is lost, and we have surrendered their deeds to mere matter. But it is not only the products of a body that are being created; nor can it be from choices, for it would be improper for all the gods <note>Plotinus often refers to the stars and planets as "gods."</note> to act from a constant process of deliberation. But we must remember that we have proposed that the world is **one single living being**, and that being so, it must necessarily be <margin>B</margin> sympathetic <note>original: "sympathes"; the idea that all parts of the universe feel and react to one another, like parts of a single body.</note> to itself. And thus, either the path of its life proceeds according to reason, being entirely in harmony with itself, or there is an order, not just within the animal, but a single harmony and order. The configurations occur according to reason, and each thing according to numbers. And as the parts of a living thing are strung together like a lyre, it is necessary to admit that the activity of the whole is a single work. Just as figures are formed within it, the parts themselves are configured, and other things follow from them. <margin>C</margin> And if someone looks at the whole and its powers in this way—as things that contribute to one another, just as we ourselves are made of many parts under one reason—then the figures are like reasons or proportions, or like the distances, rhythms, and relationships of life. These things are distinct, and the various members are formed like threads; <margin>D</margin> there are other powers of the living being apart from deliberate choice, specifically those in these parts. For what part of choice is in them, or what composition allows them to be living things? By nature, there is one life or one choice of the single living being, but its other powers directed toward itself are many; just as there are many "choices" within it directed toward its own form or universal knowledge. For desires for different things exist in different parts. One part wishes to take something else, or another part feels a lack within itself, and anger arises toward another <margin>E</margin> when something causes pain, or growth happens at the expense of others. These are not merely imitations of some parts. What then of the whole and the specific qualities within it? In what way do they seek the Good? Rather, the whole looks toward it; this is the right choice, which seeks what is above the passions and brings everything together into the same goal. For even among those who serve others, many of their deeds <margin>F</margin> look toward the commands of the master; but the desire for the Good is directed toward that which the master himself looks upon. If, therefore, the Sun and the other stars accomplish anything here, we must believe that they themselves are looking upward. For they are part of one reason...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> In what way, therefore, do these powers hold themselves? For it must be said more plainly: what difference does a triangle have when compared to a triangle, or what does this one do compared to that, and according to what does it act, and to what extent? For we attribute these actions neither to the physical bodies nor to the deliberations of the celestial beings. Not to the bodies, because it has appeared that what happens is not the effect of the body alone; and not to deliberations, because it would be wrong to make the gods work continuously. To this question, therefore, we <margin>B</margin> ought to remember that we proposed above that the world is **one living animal**. Since it is such, it must necessarily be sympathetic to itself: likewise, the course of its life is driven according to a reason that is entirely consistent with itself. Again, in that life nothing is accidental, but there is one harmony and order. Furthermore, all configurations happen according to reason, and each according to certain numbers. The parts of the worldly animal are both, as it were, performing a dance; <margin>C</margin> they are undoubtedly certain acts of the world itself—both the figures that are made within it and its own figured parts, as well as those things which follow from them. And so, by this reasoning, the universe lives and contributes its powers to this very end, just as they were made to be by the one who effects all things through reasons. It must be considered, moreover, that figures are like "reasons" or "speeches," or the intervals of the animal itself, its rhythmic modes, and the habits and gestures of the animal perfected by reason. Those things which are distant and <margin>D</margin> configured are other members; there are also other powers of the living being, separate from choice, acting as parts of the animal itself. For the function of choice there is, as it were, added from the outside, and does not lead the nature of this animal. For there is one institution of choice for the one animal, but its other powers directed toward itself are many. However many choices are in it, they tend toward the same place where the one appetite of the whole tends. For the appetite in those things which are within it is of some things toward others. For they strive to receive something from others—that is, one part from another <margin>E</margin> because it is in need. Indeed, a certain natural anger rises against another when something causes harm. Then growth happens from another, and generation into another of the parts. But the whole itself also does these things in them, yet it seeks the Good itself; or rather, it looks up to it. This, therefore, is also what the right choice—which precedes the passions—longs for, and it conspires toward the same end. For even in those who serve others, many works indeed <margin>F</margin> regard the master's commands; but the appetite for the good looks toward the same thing that the master himself regards. If, therefore, the Sun and the other stars act upon these things here, it must be considered that the Sun itself looks up toward the things above. For in this one instance, what is said of others is given as an example...

<summary>Plotinus explains that the universe acts as a single, sympathetic organism (the World Soul) where celestial movements are like a choreographed dance rather than constant deliberate choices. The geometric "figures" of the stars are expressions of underlying "seminal reasons" that naturally influence earthly life.</summary>
<keywords>Anima Mundi, World Soul, seminal reasons, celestial influence, astrology, sympathy, cosmic harmony, Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino, Sun, geometric figures</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument regarding the organic unity of the cosmos. On the previous page, the text discussed how the Sun and stars act as organs within a vast living body. Here, the focus shifts to the inherent power of shapes, forms, and the "natural soul" that permeates even the lowliest parts of the earth, like stones and herbs, and how these internal "reasons" allow for the practice of natural magic.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV

<margin>A</margin> Consider meanwhile that earthly things grow warm under the influence of the world itself, on this condition: if anything further occurs through a certain transmission of the soul, so far as is possible; for there is a great abundance of natural soul there. Similarly, the rest of the celestial bodies act upon these things as if by illuminating their own power, without deliberate choice, and all things, as a single entity thus shaped by their effect, exhibit one disposition after another, so that the figures themselves also possess power. For according to how it is disposed one way or another, it acts or is acted upon differently. <margin>B</margin> We must think that something occurs through the figures themselves. For one thing happens to these people and another to those. We can see that figures, according to their own nature, have powers even in our own affairs. Why are some figures terrifying to those who see them, even when they have suffered nothing before from those who terrify them, while others do not terrify at all? Likewise, these figures frighten some, but those figures frighten others. <margin>C</margin> Perhaps because these figures act upon a person who is affected in such a way, while others act upon another, being unable to act upon that which is not naturally exposed to this passion. Indeed, a sight shaped in such a way draws the gaze to itself, while in another way it does not draw the same person. For if someone says that beauty is what provokes this, we will object: why does this specific beauty entice this man, while that beauty entices another, unless the difference of figures has power in itself? <margin>D</margin> By what reasoning shall we admit that colors have power and act, but not confess that figures do? It is utterly absurd to say that something is established in the order of things yet has no capacity for anything. For being itself is such by nature that it acts or suffers. To some things, acting alone must be attributed; to others, both. There are powers in subjects beyond figures, and in lower things there are many powers which neither heat nor cold provide, but substances endowed with different qualities and shaped in <term>formal reasons</term> <note>original: "specierationibus"; these are the inner logical blueprints or "forms" that define what a thing is and what it can do.</note>, participating in the power of nature itself, such as the natures of stones and the effects of herbs demonstrating many wonders to us. <margin>E</margin>

*Just as our vegetative life imparts itself to individual limbs, though differently to some than others, and inserts healing powers into some joints and others into others; so, much more excellently, the one World Soul, although it animates different parts of the world differently, being full of innumerable and wondrous virtues—as if pregnant and swelling—overflows into the whole, filling individual members, but especially the superior members of the world, with miraculous powers everywhere. Neither can elementary forces overcome these, nor can we easily express them. Such powers are like the soul's own offshoots, diffused through the members of the entire body of the universe, which the prayers, supplications, and works of <term>magi</term> <note>original: "magorum"; here Plotinus and Ficino refer to "natural magicians" who understand the hidden sympathies of nature, not sorcerers in the modern sense.</note> win over to themselves and can sometimes bring to bear as if through an instrument.*

->Chapter XXXVI.<-

<margin>A</margin> **INDEED**, this whole universe is filled with the greatest variety. Within it are all the <term>reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes"; the divine organizing principles of the cosmos.</note>; within it are innumerable and various powers. Just as they say of man, that the eye contains one power, the bones another, and different parts contain different powers. For the bone of the hand has this power, but the toes of the foot possess a different one, and no part is entirely destitute of power, though not every part has the same one. This is hidden from us, unless someone has perhaps diligently examined such things. <margin>B</margin> Thus surely, and much more so, does it happen in the world; indeed, these things of ours are the footprints of those. It is consistent, therefore, that an inexplicable [power] exists in the world and...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is productive <note>original: "ποιητικὸν"</note>, and to think that it comes from itself just as the process of heating does. And if anything should happen in it from the transmissions of the soul—of whatever amount of natural soul—or of another similar soul, it would produce such things as the brightening of its own parts. Therefore, because all things are in these very configurations <gloss>or "by configurations"</gloss> <note>original: "σχηματισμοῖς"</note>, they grant a disposition in one way or another, so that the shapes also have power. <margin>B</margin> For being thus or so, in one way or another, something occurs through those very things that are configured. For this is one thing to one person, or that is another to him; it is not that the shapes themselves fail to have powers. For one can see this in the same things: why are some shapes terrifying to those who see them, though they have suffered nothing nor were they afraid before, while other sights do not terrify? And why do these things affect one way, and those another? <margin>C</margin> Is it because for such a person, some things are effective, while others cannot be affected by them? There is also a configuration which moves the sight; but it does not move the same person in the same way. And if someone says beauty is what moves us, why does this beauty move some and other beauty not move others, unless the difference according to the shape possesses the power? For why should we say that colors have power and act, but not say the same of shapes? <margin>D</margin> For it would be to altogether give up that anything exists among beings if it does not have some capacity. For being, they say, is itself to act or to be acted upon. And if someone should grant that some things are productive and others are both, even if the power lies in the underlying subject, or in those things where our shapes have long existed, which neither heat nor cold provides, but which arise with different qualities and are given form by <term>reasons</term> <note>original: "λόγοις"; the Greek equivalent of the Latin "rationes," the formative principles.</note>, or participate in the power of nature, such as the natures of stones or the activities of herbs, they provide many wonders. <margin>E</margin>

**MOST VARIEGATED** is the whole, and all <term>reasons</term> are in it, and powers infinite and diverse. Just as they say even in man, the eye has one power and this bone another, and again another has another. This part of the hand has one, and the parts of the finger have another, and there is no part which does not have power, even if we do not recognize it as the same, unless someone has learned such things. <margin>B</margin> And much more so [in the world]. Rather, these are footprints; those things are of the others, if the things everywhere...

<meta>catchword: mirand- (wondrous)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the physical shapes and internal "reasons" of all things—from celestial bodies to stones and herbs—possess inherent powers that act upon the world. He compares the universe to a human body where every organ has a specific function, suggesting that the World Soul's influence is the foundation for natural magic and the sympathies between all things.</summary>
<keywords>World Soul, Anima Mundi, formal reasons, seminal reasons, natural magic, sympathy, Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino, configurations, botanical powers, mineral powers</keywords>

--- Page 466 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 418 regarding how the celestial bodies influence the earthly realm. While the previous page focused on the Sun and stars as organs of the cosmos, this page extends that living connection to seemingly "inanimate" objects like stones, wood, and herbs, arguing that the entire universe is a single, vigilant, and living organism.</meta>

BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin> ...and to possess a wondrous and marvelous variety of powers <note>original: "ἀλλοίην δὲ καὶ θαυμαστὴν ποικιλίαν ἔχειν δυνάμεων"</note>, especially when directed toward celestial natures and their progressions. For it was not fitting for the universe—that is, the grand architecture we see—to be like an inanimate building, especially one so vast and multifaceted, constructed merely from a certain number of stones, timber, or any other materials according to their outward appearance, even if arranged in a number suitable for worldly ornament. Instead, the universe itself must be everywhere vigilant and everywhere living <note>Plotinus argues that the cosmos is not a machine, but a conscious, "wakeful" entity</note>, because otherwise, nothing could exist within it that did not also share in its life. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, the doubt is resolved by which one asks how anything can be inanimate within a being that is entirely animated by a soul. For present reason dictates that different things live in different ways within the whole. We, however, tend to deny that something is "living" if it does not appear to us to move visibly by its own power. Nevertheless, any such thing lives in a hidden way; even that which lives visibly is composed of parts that live secretly, yet these parts bestow marvelous powers upon the living animal for its very life. <margin>C</margin> For it cannot happen that a human is moved to so many and such great actions while the internal powers by which he is moved are entirely soulless. It is likewise impossible for the whole to live in such a way unless every individual part within it lives its own proper life, even if <term>deliberate choice (electio)</term> is not present in them. For in the act of doing, a thing does not always require choice, seeing as natural action is more ancient than choice; thus, the whole often follows the powers of its parts.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...a wondrous variety of virtues, especially in the celestial natures and their progressions. For it was not appropriate for the universe to be constructed like an inanimate edifice, particularly one so great and complex, made of certain stones and wood and other such things, even if they were numbered according to their kind and joined in a fitting number for the adornment of the world. Rather, the universe itself is everywhere vigilant, everywhere living, since nothing could exist anywhere that was not also contained within it. <margin>B</margin> For this reason, that difficulty is solved which asks how, in a living being that is thoroughly ensouled, there can be anything without a soul. For the present reasoning shows that one thing lives in one way, and another in another, within the whole. We, however, say that something does not live if it does not appear to us to move clearly by itself. Yet, everything of this sort lives in a hidden manner: and even what lives visibly is composed of those things which live secretly, which nevertheless grant marvelous strengths to this living being for its life. It cannot be that a man is moved toward so <margin>C</margin> many and such great things, and yet the powers by which he is moved are entirely without soul. It is again impossible for the whole to live thus, unless each individual thing within it lives by its own life, even if choice is not present. For in acting, it does not need choice, as it is more ancient than choice; therefore, it often follows the powers of the parts.

<column-break/>

*Just as our members, both internal and external, receive their power for action and motion from our soul, so do all the members of the world receive power from the Soul of the World itself. The miraculous actions found in small stones, metals, and herbs—which exceed the simple nature of the elements—bear witness that there is a soul in the world, from which even the smallest things possess the greatest powers everywhere. Likewise, the fact that a small fire acts from so far away, and so easily consumes everything into itself, and that it shines, it receives from the soul; as do individual things which generate something within themselves. The very order of movements and forms is governed by the soul, as is the connection of opposites and the motion of the celestial machine, which is so immense. The <term>generative soul (genitalis anima)</term> is most powerfully propagated into this machine as if into its nearest offspring: through this soul into fire, through this into air, and through this into the rest. And this generative life of the world acts not by a "practical" choice, nor by a conscious attention of its actions upon these things, but acts naturally, just as the Sun and fire do—or indeed, as the <term>vegetative soul</term> acts within us. Natural action is more ancient than practical choice, although the contemplative and universal choice of the High Mind itself is more ancient than natural action.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, nothing in the universe is rejected or left destitute by it. Indeed, if anyone among those who now seem wise concerning fire, or any other such thing which we say "acts," were to investigate what this "acting" or "doing" truly is, he would not be able to explain his doubts until he recognizes the effective power in each individual thing as coming from the universe. He would say the same of all things that are in use. But we do not investigate or doubt common things; <margin>B</margin> yet we doubt unusual powers, wondering how each one holds itself, and we marvel only at new things. We would marvel similarly at things that are now familiar to us if, before we were accustomed to them, someone were to bring forth and explain their powers. One must think, therefore, that every single thing has a certain hidden power within itself, having been fashioned and formed within the universe, and is in some way a participant in the World Soul itself—a member of the living whole encompassed by the living whole. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, there is nothing in it which is not a part of it. Some things are more powerful in acting than others, both those on earth and those in heaven. And certainly, the celestial things are the most powerful of all, as they enjoy a more distinct nature. Accordingly, one must judge that many things happen through these powers without any choice being involved, even in those works which often seem to be done by choice. For there is an act of this kind of power in these things as well...

<column-break/>

### Chapter 37.

<margin>A</margin> NOTHING, therefore, is rejected or left destitute by the universe from its own parts. Truly, if anyone of those who currently seem to be wise regarding fire, or regarding any other such things which we say "act," should search out what that "acting" itself is, he will not be able to free himself from doubts until he acknowledges the producing power in individual things as stemming from the whole universe, and says the same thing regarding all things that are in common use. But as for accustomed things, we think we need neither investigation nor <margin>B</margin> doubt. We only doubt regarding unaccustomed powers, as to how each one behaves, and we only wonder at the new—though we would wonder similarly at those things which are now familiar to us if, before we were used to them, someone were to bring the explanation of their powers into the open. One must therefore consider that every single thing has a certain hidden power in itself, shaped and formed within the universe, and is in some way a participant in that World Soul, a member of the living whole contained by the living whole. <margin>C</margin> Since there is nothing in it which is not a part of it, some things are more effective at acting than others, both those on earth and those in heaven. And truly, the celestial things are the most powerful of all, since they enjoy a more vivid nature; therefore, one should judge that many things are done through these powers with no choice being added to them, even in those things whose works often seem to be done by choice. For there is an act of this kind of power in these as well...

<summary>This page argues for the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul, positing that the universe is a singular living organism where even stones and herbs possess hidden, miraculous powers. It explains that natural actions occur through inherent "virtues" rather than deliberate choice, much like how the human body functions without conscious effort.</summary>

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS IV.

which have no choice <note>original: "electionem," referring to conscious deliberation</note>: furthermore, the power of nature itself is not turned into its own act by the strength of its transmission, even if something of the soul itself is brought into effect by causes. For animals are born from animals without choice playing any part in the meantime; nor is the power of procreation diminished or diverted when it is put into action. Otherwise, if the soul possessed choice as the origin of generation, then choice itself would be the thing produced; if it were otherwise, it would not be the producer. But if an animal does not possess choice, it will be much less likely to turn toward itself in its actions.

---

->*The intellectual soul of the world—and of every sphere and star—has a vegetative life <note>term: "vegetative life" (vegetalis vita). In Neoplatonism, this is the lowest level of soul, responsible for growth and automatic biological functions, acting without conscious thought.</note> infused into its body. Through this life, things that follow are generated and moved, and benefits are bestowed upon those capable of receiving them, not by conscious choice but naturally. Whatever flows from such a life is vital and beneficial; yet in some places it turns harmful, either because the matter is not capable of receiving it—just as sunlight and heat affect the weak differently—or because something else results from the mixture of different elements, much as the golden light of the Sun turns red, green, or dark within a cloud. Our own vegetative life is very much in conformity with the life mentioned above; likewise, our spirit <note>term: "spiritus." A subtle, airy substance that connects the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note> is like a ray of that life, both in its approach and its manifestations to those who look deeply. It becomes even more closely related when we are strongly moved toward that life, desiring benefits in harmony with it, and thus transferring our spirit into its rays. This is achieved especially if we employ song and scents agreeable to the deity, such as the Orphic hymns <note>Hymns attributed to the legendary poet Orpheus, used in ancient "theurgy" or divine magic to attract celestial influences.</note> consecrated to the worldly powers. For example: for the Heavens, the scent of burning frankincense; for the Ether, glowing saffron; for the stars, aromatics; for the Sun, frankincense and manna; for the Moon and Night, aromatics; for Saturn and Jupiter, styrax; for Neptune, myrrh; and for Mercury, frankincense. For the spirit, through emotion, song, scent, and light, becomes blood-like in its effect on the deity and draws a more abundant influx from that source.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> WHATEVER things, therefore, are produced by the universe without any mover, are produced by its "other life" <note>This "other life" refers again to the subconscious, vegetative power of the World Soul.</note>, and indeed everything that proceeds from it. But whatever things happen because of another mover—such as voices, whether simple or composed by the art of singing—these should not be referred to any of the higher beings, but to the nature of the thing being done. Now, those things which contribute so much to life and other uses are to be attributed to the gift of those higher beings. Indeed, this gift is poured out from one greater part <margin>B</margin> into another smaller part. But as for what is called "harmful" coming from them into the generation of animals, it must be considered such only because the recipient is unable to receive what is otherwise healthful. For a thing is not produced simply as it is, but as a specific thing in a specific condition. Thus, the subject that undergoes the action must have a certain and definite nature. Also, mixtures themselves produce many results, with each thing contributing something favorable for life to the whole. <margin>C</margin> Something might also happen to someone even if the things are not useful by their own nature. Yet the common order of all things does not provide everyone, everywhere, with whatever they wish. We also add many things ourselves to what is given. Finally, all things are woven together into one, and they produce a marvelous harmony; indeed, some things come from others, even from opposites. For all things are members of one living creature. And if any of the things that exist fall short of the best, as if not fully formed toward their end, <margin>D</margin> it is certainly because matter has not been mastered; just as one who falls away from noble birth and is deprived of nobility sinks into ugliness. Therefore, some things are produced by the higher powers, others are brought into the mix by the underlying nature <note>i.e., the physical properties of matter</note>, and finally, others are added by the things themselves.

---

->*Above the vegetative life of the world, which is called both "nature" and the "nursery" of natural things, there is an intelligence that orders all things more joyfully than nature does. Whatever is born from the "nursery" arises from its intention, appearing beautiful and moving toward action; moreover, these things proceed by a certain accustomed and merely natural tenor toward their own progress. But when things happen to be deformed or weak, it is due to a certain material necessity; and when some things are destroyed by others, or hindered from completing their usual order, growth, and time, and from propagating others by their own seed—this, I say...*<-

...what they have, nor is there a handing over in the giving of power, and something of the soul might come from them in the work, as many things as they do from choice: nor again is it diminished, nor again is the element of choice diverted then, if it should have it, or if the animal should participate in some choice in what they do; even more so for that which does not have the power of choice.

<margin>Chapter XXXVIII.</margin>
SINCE therefore, with no one moving from within it, things arise from its other life, or generally all things that come from it; but as for things where others move it, such as prayers, whether simple or sung with art, these must not be referred back to that individual [the deity], but to the nature of the thing performed. Thus, those things that contribute to life or some other need should be referred from another greater part to a smaller part. And as for what is said to be "difficult" <note>original: "δυσχερὲς," meaning troublesome or annoying</note> coming from them into the births of living things, it is either the inability of the recipient to receive what is pleasant: for the thing produced is not simply produced, but as a "this" and "in this way": and indeed that which is acted upon, and how we are acted upon, depends on what kind of subject or what kind of reception it might have. And the mixtures produce many things, with each part giving what is useful to the living things. But it might also happen to be unfavorable, even if the nature of the gifts is beneficial, in that way it is given to all and to some, but not as much as is always desired by each. And we ourselves also place many things alongside what is given; yet all things are nevertheless woven into one and have a marvelous harmony, and some things come from others, even from opposites, since they are parts of one [being]. And if anything among the things produced falls short of the better, insofar as it was not shaped toward the good, not having mastered the matter: as if falling short of the noble, or being deprived of it, it falls into ugliness. So that some things are made by those [higher powers], others are brought in through the nature of the subject, and others are added by the things themselves.

Yet it is ordered nonetheless, for all things are reduced under one into one. Therefore, through an intelligence superior to nature, such accidents are brought back into control: through that same intelligence, the movements and effects of free will are also arranged in order according to merit. Our prayers are anticipated, as Iamblichus says <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that theurgy (divine ritual) could influence the soul's relationship with the divine.</note>, and are fulfilled, while we in the meantime freely obey, with neither the divine will changed nor the order of things disturbed. Thus, the arrangement of things is wider in the mind than in nature itself: in the mind, I say, not only the primal mind but also the mundane and celestial. Plato, in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politico"</note>, calls the soul's arrangement of things in the primal mind the **Law of Saturn**; he calls the same in the animal intellect the **Law of Jupiter** in the *Statesman* and the *Laws*; finally, in nature, he calls it the **Law of Fate** in the *Statesman* and the *Timaeus*. Indeed, because it is firm everywhere and proceeds inevitably, he names it the **Law of Adrastia** <note>term: "Adrastia." A Greek name for Nemesis or Fate, meaning "the inescapable."</note> in the *Phaedrus*. Now, because he preserves the free efficacy of souls along with the law, he says in the *Laws* that the principle of actions exists in souls, but the limit exists in the law; and in the *Phaedrus* and *Timaeus*, he introduces the decree of the law always with a certain condition, in this manner: *If the soul shall have committed such things, let it report such consequences.* However, when he says in the *Timaeus* that souls did not hear the laws of fate until they were joined to their vehicles <note>The "vehicle" (okhema) refers to the subtle body or "astral body" that carries the soul into the physical world.</note>, he declares that souls are free of themselves, but fate pertains to bodies. Fatal necessity pertains not only to the body, but also to the corporeal life. Whatever life lies hidden in the mundane and celestial body is not a matter of free choice <note>original: "non est Lionis libera," likely a typo for "non est electionis libera"</note>, but by fatal necessity it pours out its influence to the lower things—which indeed shines forth as beneficial even from Mars, or Saturn, and similar stars. Yet a magician <note>term: "Magus." Here used to mean a practitioner of natural magic who understands celestial harmonies.</note> can make it harmful, not unlike one who, with a concave mirror, collects the rays of the Sun and hurls them against an object to burn it. For if someone should force the ten powers of Saturn—necessary and scattered throughout the world and matter—to be joined together into one, he will destroy the one against whom he has gathered them; Saturn, meanwhile, is innocent. By various properties of fertility and reconciliation, he inserts his powers into various things everywhere. The magician, therefore, choosing all materials capable of such powers and applying them (having been collected into one while Venus is reigning) to this or that person, stirs up immoderate love between them, though Venus does not sin. He likewise accumulates the gifts of Jupiter upon others, while the "Jupiter-animal" <note>The celestial body or "living star" of Jupiter.</note> does not notice. Indeed, we call the body of a star a "Jovial animal" or "Saturnian" or "Venereal," living by a vegetative power—the kind of bodies Pythagoras thought of when he said that the invoked Gods flow into us, compelled by a certain necessity.

<margin>A</margin> Since all things are always ordered together, and all things contribute to one, it signifies the things of the One, because of which He dominates, and all things are woven together. <margin>A</margin> SINCE therefore all things have been ordered together always, and lead toward one, it is no wonder that individual things are signified by certain signs, but meanwhile virtue serves no one; nonetheless, the duties of this virtue are woven together with the common order of things. For indeed, since the things that are here depend on that source, namely from those things which are more divine than these things of the universe, that universe is a participant in them. Therefore, those things which happen in the world do not happen only according to seminal reasons, but according to <margin>B</margin> other wider reasons, which comprehend in themselves powers far prior to seminal reasons. For there is nothing in seminal reasons of those things which happen anywhere outside the seminal reasons themselves, nor again anything of those things which are thought to be contributed to the world from matter itself, nor even anything of those things which are brought in turn by created things. Rather, the very reason of the whole is like a reason adorning some city, establishing laws, and certainly knowing what the <margin>C</margin> citizens will do, or for what causes they will act, and for all these things arranging individual institutes, and connecting by laws all their passions and actions. Furthermore, the merits of individual actions, rewards and punishments, are scattered everywhere, while all things meanwhile proceed as if spontaneously into a common harmony. But signification in nature happens not primarily for the sake of this itself—that is, so that a sign might be made—but with things so arranged and born, some things are signified from others, namely that <margin>D</margin> whatever is here, is in a certain way one among itself, and of the One. Therefore, one thing is known from another: the cause from the effect, the consequent from the antecedent, the composite from either part; since one and the other are made at the same time. If these things are said with certainty, those doubts will now be resolved: and especially that one which warned that we must be careful, lest we be forced to confess that the Gods do evil. To this, therefore, we answer first that all these things happen not by choices, but by natural necessities.
