<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of how the World Soul governs the universe. Having previously discussed the "Laws of Saturn and Jupiter" as metaphors for cosmic order, Plotinus now moves into the mechanics of "cosmic sympathy"—how the various parts of the universe, like organs in a single body, react to one another, and how this interconnectedness forms the basis for magic and prayer.</meta>

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin> First, whatever proceeds from that source is transferred from parts to parts, as it were, and follows the life of the One. Second, many things are added to existing objects from the objects themselves. Third, the gifts granted from above are not evil in themselves when considered by their givers, but in the mixture of elements, something else—an evil—occurs. Fourth, life is given and judged not for the sake of each individual part, but for the sake of the whole. Fifth, the underlying nature <note>original: "subiectam naturam," referring to the material or receptive principle</note> receives one thing but experiences or "suffers" another; it cannot always be overcome by the gift itself, nor can it always retain the gift’s own specific power.

Any limb of a living animal has the power to attract its own specific portion of nourishment: the heart attracts aromas, the liver attracts sweets, the veins attract blood, the arteries attract spirit <note>term: "spiritus" (pneuma). In ancient medicine, this was a vital gas or "breath" believed to circulate through the arteries to sustain life.</note>, and the testicles attract seed. There are also medicines that draw out specific humors and seem to seek out certain limbs. The condition of the mundane animal—the universe—is the same. Within it, things are dispersed everywhere that can seize this or that thing for themselves, if they are found gathered together. Through their own prayers or charms, humans can seek things; horses do the same through their own means, as do different types of men, often seeking these things secretly, just as they are openly enticed by the delights of beautiful forms and music. Finally, just as it is well known that a magnet or amber attracts things, so a diligent and fortunate searcher will find the power of attraction in all things. For in every individual limb of the world-animal, a power of "coagulation" <note>original: "coaguli vis," a binding or curdling force that holds things together</note> is implanted, connecting all things into one living being. When this is tempered, it is above nature; but it becomes intemperate whenever forces gathered from everywhere are transferred into something, while the world itself neither suffers nor sins in the process. There are also different powers within this animal, diffused by nature, which are frequently joined by a Mage <note>term: "Mago." A practitioner of magic who understands the hidden connections (sympathies) of the universe.</note> and directed into this or that limb to act more violently or to destroy; in these cases (as I said), the world does not sin. Nor is this a wonder, since there are four things upon which this marvelous power rests: the hidden qualities of species, shapes, harmonies, and prayers. Indeed, those qualities are offshoots of the lives latent within the life of the world, and lower shapes and harmonies often reflect the shapes and harmonies of the heavens. Furthermore, prayer is a certain vehement movement of our soul toward the One, which is its object. If one brings a bit of straw near a fire, even across a distance, the fire draws out a flame and applies itself to the straw. Similarly, a person who is properly prepared can project their soul toward the rays of a star—both the visible and the hidden—which are diffused everywhere and united through that vital force by which the stars claim their existence. Finally, just as all the fixed stars are connected to the firmament, so the lives of all stars and mundane motions are connected to the life of the world, to which our own life is also connected. It is no wonder, then, that the powerful movements of our soul, poured out through the common life that flourishes everywhere, reach even to the mundane divinities, just as the movements of these divinities are brought down to us through that same life. Chapter 40.

### BUT CONCERNING MAGIC
<margin>B</margin> How shall we say these attractions occur? Surely, they arise from a certain consensus <note>original: "consensione," likely translating the Greek "sympatheia" (sympathy).</note> of things in their shared experience, and by a law of nature which ensures that there is concord between likes and discord between unlikes. It also arises from the variety of many powers contributing to a single living animal. For many things are attracted through a kind of magical rite without any other person engineering it; the true magic power in the universe is "Friendship," and conversely, "Discord" <note>note: This refers to the Empedoclean forces of Philia (Love/Friendship) and Neikos (Strife/Discord) which govern the cosmos.</note>. And the first sorcerer and enchanter (if I may put it this way) is Nature itself. Humans, observing this, use Nature's own potions and sorceries upon one another. The effectiveness of the art of love—using philters and charms—is born from the fact that most things can easily love one another naturally and bring about a reciprocal love. The mage applies certain natures to others to reconcile them, possessing an inborn love; they couple one soul to another just as a gardener joins together plants that were distant from one another.

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, they use shapes and figures that possess certain powers. By fashioning themselves according to a specific hidden ratio, they secretly snatch powers for themselves. They do this more easily because they are within the "One" and draw things toward the "One." For if someone were imagined to be "outside" the world, they could not attract anything, nor lead anything down with charms or melodies, nor entangle anything in knots. But as it is, because the mage does not snatch a thing to a foreign place, he gains the power to seize it; he certainly knows the condition by which one thing in the same living being may be drawn toward <margin>D</margin> another. For there is an innate power of transfer in incantations, songs, specific sounds, and shapes.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Whatever comes from there <note>original: "ἐκεῖθεν" (ekeithen), referring to the higher intelligible realm.</note> is as parts to parts, and according to the life of the one. Many things are added by the things themselves in their various combinations. The things given by the individual givers are not evil in themselves, but become so in the mixture. Furthermore, these things do not exist for the sake of the individuals, but for the sake of the whole life and constitution. Nature, having received some things, suffers others.

### BUT CONCERNING SORCERIES
<margin>B</margin> How do they work? By sympathy <note>original: "συμπαθείᾳ" (sympatheia)</note> and by the natural harmony of likes and the opposition of unlikes, and by the variety of many powers contributing to one living animal. Even when no one is plotting, many things are drawn and enchanted by a natural magic. For true magic is the Friendship in the universe, and also the Strife. This is the primary sorcerer and magician. Men, having understood this, use its potions and enchantments on each other. Because things are born to love, and because there are things there that love each other, the arts of sorcery arise from this. They apply touches and join other natures to others, binding one soul to another, just as if they were touching distant plants and joining them together. <margin>C</margin> They also use shapes that have powers in themselves, and they bring things into one, as if they were already one in power. If, therefore, something stood outside of the whole or the world, it could not be drawn or brought down by enchantments or bindings. But now, since it does not lead elsewhere, it is possible for a gift to exist, or for one thing in the living being to be led toward another. <margin>D</margin> For it is natural for this to happen through the incantations of melodies, and the disposition of the person, and the shape...

Such sorcery <note>original: "γοητεία" (goēteia), referring to magic or enchantment</note> is wondered at, as are those things commanded by love, yet it is not the prayers of those using music that are heard. Regarding other prayers, one should not think they are heard by a deliberate choice of the will, any more than those who are charmed by incantations [are chosen]. *Just as there is a perfect weaving of nerves and veins in any animal, so too in the worldly animal <note>The "World Animal" is the Platonic concept that the entire universe is a single, living, ensouled organism.</note> is there a context of natures and lives. Therefore, just as the motion and suffering of the foot in us pertains to the neck, and the neck to the foot, so also in this worldly animal the movements of lower things reach the higher, and vice versa, and almost from any part similarly to its equals. Every movement indeed comes as a healing force from on high, provided that it is captured in the way it comes, and can be captured. Nor does the distance of place stand in the way of movements occurring from both sides in turn, where beyond the common texture, the lower thing has a property—either acquired or natural—that is kindred with the supreme; just as the movement of a nerve in a lyre <note>term: "lyra" (lyre). Plotinus uses the vibration of musical strings to explain "action at a distance" in the universe.</note> reaches another nerve, even if they are far apart, provided they are tuned to the same pitch.*

->Chapter XLI.<-

---

The sun or another star does not "hear" the prayer; rather, the fulfillment of the prayer happens through the sympathy <note>original: "συμπάθει" (sympathei). In Neoplatonism, sympathy is the mechanical/organic link that makes magic possible.</note> of one part with another, just as in a single taut string, if the bottom is moved, the top also feels the movement. Often, when one string is moved, another vibrates as if it perceives the sound, because they are tuned to one harmony. And if in another lyre the movement comes from another, to the extent that there is sympathy, so in the universe one harmony persists. It is made of contraries and of likes, and of all things kindred and opposite. Whatever harms men—such as an angry disposition which, drawn together with bile, enters the nature of the liver—does so not as if it intended to harm. It is as if someone, taking fire from a fire, harmed something else; the one who devised it, or the one who came or took it, performs the action. By giving to everyone, one thing is not transferred into another, and that which has come does not occur unless the receiver was shaken so as to participate in what was there.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But the SUN or any other star does not notice this at all. The power of a prayer's purpose lies in a certain agreement of one part suffering with another part: just as it happens in a certain taut string, where when the lowest part is moved, the highest is soon moved as well. Often also, when some other string is struck, another trembles as if it feels it through concord. And this is most especially so because they are tuned by the exact same consonance. If a movement is also <margin>B</margin> transferred from one lyre to another, one must think that this also proceeds from a certain sympathetic agreement. Therefore, there is also one harmony in the universe, although it be from contraries; for it is also from all similar and kindred things, even those which are contrary. Hence, whatever things harm men—just as a wrathful animal nature together with bile is drawn to the region of the liver—they occurred not as if they were intended to harm men. It is as if someone snatching fire from a fire should hurt another; he in no way plotted <margin>C</margin> for the fire to proceed that far. Perhaps, indeed, the one who receives it acts, because he draws something as if transferred from one thing into another. Indeed, the fire as it proceeds

<note>performs this action where it cannot be captured by that subject into which it is transferred.</note>

---

Many Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests or magicians</note> of old, lovers of this present life and greedy for bodily goods, devised bodily sacrifices and prayers to the living bodies of the stars, in accordance with the living body of the world, so that they might obtain what they desired from there. They seem to have accustomed the people to these same bodily sacrifices dedicated to the stars. Some therefore doubted whether stars have need of sense, imagination, memory, and choice for this very work, in order to fulfill such prayers. Plotinus answers that it is not necessary: for from the living bodies of the world, a certain vigor is derived by its own nature into others. This vigor flows more abundantly into the spirits of bodies when they are more aptly exposed to drink it in through prayer and other suitable things, namely by the proper influx of nature, even if choice is not present. But Plotinus places the intellectual souls of the stars and spheres above their living bodies; these souls are in a way segregated from the body, and no suffering or motion reaches them through the continuous bodily natures. Therefore, such goods are not drawn from there by a kind of magical attraction. Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Successors and commentators of Plotinus who further developed his mystical theories</note> assert the same: they, along with Plotinus, place will and choice in those souls—a great choice not persuaded by lower things, but constituting itself from eternity to imitate the highest God and to provide for all following things. They hear the prayers of suppliants through an intellectual life that imitates the intellectual rulers of the world. In sacrifices, prayers directed from a body to the bodies of the world bring back such goods to men, even for the local body; but more divine goods come through a segregated worship, to divine men only from the divine rulers of the world. Porphyry and Iamblichus add to these that even intellectual vices might refer to certain corporal and external goods.

<summary>Plotinus explains that magic and prayer work through "cosmic sympathy"—a natural resonance between parts of the universe likened to strings on a lyre—rather than through the conscious choice or "hearing" of the stars. The text distinguishes between the mechanical influence of the celestial bodies and the higher, intellectual souls of the universe.</summary>

<keywords>cosmic sympathy, World Animal, Plotinus, magic, prayer, lyre analogy, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Neoplatonism, astrology, harmony of the spheres</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plotinus's fourth Ennead. The previous page discussed how the soul is affected by music and "sorcery" through irrational sympathy. Here, the text further explores the hierarchy of spirits and the mechanism by which stars and magic influence the world without conscious "deliberation."</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

...by the duty of intermediate spirits <note>original: "numinum mediarum," referring to daemons or mediating beings between gods and men</note> who are obedient to superior deities; through their protection, looming evils are often avoided. Abraham the devout <note>likely referring to a pseudo-epigraphical astrological text attributed to the patriarch Abraham, popular in the Renaissance</note>, the astrologer, adds that souls acquire a higher power through their application to God alone, by which they may increase fated goods and diminish fated evils. The Platonists propose pure intellects—or the Divine Intellect—as the governors of the world for intellectual souls, and the Good itself as the father of this Intellect. They establish physical sacrifices for the worldly gods, but they dedicate a set-apart holiness to the superior gods, and a completely secluded sanctity to that God confirmed by Apollonius of Tyana <note>a famous 1st-century sage and philosopher often compared to Jesus or Pythagoras</note>. They choose adoration above all else for the superior beings, and a preserved devotion for the supreme gods, for from them more abundant goods are returned. You may read about these matters at great length in the works of Iamblichus and Porphyry, which we have recently translated.

->Chapter XLII.<-

---

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, the stars will have no need for memory for the sake of hearing a prayer—which is the reason we have treated these matters—nor will they need senses to report the prayers there. Nor should it be thought that the stars nod their assent to prayers as some believe, as if by deliberating; rather, something is effected simultaneously with the prayer itself, and even without a prayer from them, by the very reason that they are parts of one and the same whole. Indeed, there are many powers even without choice, and these proceed into effect sometimes without any contrivance, and sometimes through art. Just as in any single living creature, where one part <margin>B</margin> carries something away from another, and is preserved or harmed by it because they are so naturally constituted; for this reason, the arts of both physicians and enchanters compel one thing to impart something of its own virtue to another. Similarly, the universe both pours out its gifts spontaneously from itself to its parts, and also, when something else attracts it, sends down something inherent in its parts to a specific area, drawn there by the same natural vigor. Indeed, that which it desires is not foreign to it. But if the one who prays is evil, it is <margin>C</margin> no wonder that he obtains his request, for even the wicked draw water from rivers. Furthermore, that which bestows does not know what it bestows; it simply bestows. Meanwhile, however, the gift itself is connected with the nature of the universe. Therefore, if someone receives from those things which are laid out for all, it is not necessary that punishment follow him by law. We must not, therefore, concede that the universe suffers <note>in the sense of being "affected" or "undergoing change"</note>. Perhaps its principal part should be said to exist entirely free from suffering, while <margin>D</margin> passions are inserted into its parts. In those parts, the passion itself remains; but since nothing happens to the whole contrary to its nature, the whole surely remains without passion. Even if passions seem to suit the stars insofar as they are parts, the stars themselves remain free of passion, both because choices exist in them without passion, and because their bodies are naturally far from harm. Furthermore, even if they transmit something to lower things through their soul, the soul is meanwhile not diminished, <margin>E</margin> and their bodies persist as the same. Anything that flows out from them glides away without being felt, and if anything is added to them, it flows in similarly in secret.

<column-break/>

SO THAT there is no need for memory in the stars for this purpose—which is why these things have been discussed—nor for senses to report the prayers so that they might nod assent in the manner some people imagine, as if acting by decree. Instead, something happens alongside the prayer, as if by the parts of a single being. Moreover, there are powers even without deliberate choice, many of which act either without a device or with art, as in a single animal where one part provides to another or is harmed by it, being so constituted by nature. The arts of doctors and enchanters <note>original: "ἐπῳδῶν" (epōdōn), those who use songs or incantations</note> also compel one thing to provide some of its power to another. In the same way, the whole gives to its parts, either from itself or when someone draws something to a part where it resides, toward the parts themselves by the same natural force, so that the things requested are not foreign to it. And if the requester is evil, one should not marvel, for even the wicked draw from rivers. And the giver does not know that it gives, but it only gives; nevertheless, it is always coordinated and given by the nature of the whole. So if anyone takes from what is available to all, it is not necessary to bring punishments upon him by law. It must be granted that the whole is affected unwillingly. And while its leading part must be granted to be unaffected, even when passions occur in its parts, that passion belongs to those parts. But for the whole, since nothing is contrary to its nature, what happens is unaffected in relation to it. For even for the stars, insofar as they are parts, passions occur, but they themselves are unaffected, because their choices are themselves unaffected, and their bodies and their nature exist without harm. Further, even through the soul that gives something, the soul itself is not diminished, and its bodies remain the same; or if anything flows away, it goes out or enters in without being perceived by the senses.

---

> Magical fascination <term>fascination: the power of attracting or enchanting through a gaze or natural sympathy</term> relies on the natural forces of both celestial and inferior things, namely, on both things and words. It therefore most closely touches our spirit, and through this, not only the humors but also the irrational life which depends upon the world itself. However, it cannot touch the rational soul, which is superior to the nature of the world’s corporeal life and depends solely on the divine mind, except insofar as the rational soul consents to the lower life.
->Chapter XLIII.<-

If someone dresses this person in a linen garment and that person in a straw one, he will draw the latter to the former. In this way, those who have investigated magic have uncovered hidden things—not only natural objects, but also words which, pouring out their power from a distance, are able to attract. They secretly apply many things that can be drawn by these—some to a man, others to a woman—and they snatch the woman toward the man. They also apply things that can separate them, just as sailors, by suspending iron, balance it with a magnet so that it is snatched toward the Bear <note>original: "Vrsam," referring to the constellation Ursa Major, used here to explain the magnetic north</note>; and conversely, by staining it with something else, they release that which was so snatched. However, what position of the stars some might use more opportunely for these things, and what images they might fashion, or what materials they might mix together, it is not expedient to tell; nor even...

<summary>Plotinus explains that the universe and the stars respond to prayers and magic through natural, "irrational" sympathy rather than conscious deliberation. He compares this cosmic attraction to medical healing, the flow of a river, and the way a magnet pulls iron toward the North Star.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s commentary on Plotinus’s fourth Ennead. Having previously discussed the influence of celestial bodies on human affairs, Ficino now delves into the mechanics of magic, the power of words (incantations), and how the rational soul remains distinct from the irrational impulses triggered by external spiritual forces.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

By what incantations they are drawn forth. Indeed, Mercury <note>The god of communication and magic</note> presides over words, but Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light and order</note> over the foundations. However, Mercury joined with Phoebus presides over incantations. But to teach where and by what reasoning he is joined to the Sun, and under what aspect of the stars he provides the power of offspring for songs, as well as what harmful counter-charms <note>original: "antiphiltra," remedies against love potions</note> or beneficial incantations he provides, justice forbids. Yet perhaps, just as other mixtures acquire a new power in the blending of qualities, so certainly certain combinations of words—both conceived within the mind and uttered outside the soul—attain a certain wonderful power while still, as it were, "living." This happens either from the present position of the stars or even from the birth-chart of the man himself, in whom this very combination of words proceeded from a singular power of the mind instilled by God. It is intent upon an object as if it were a directed application of virtue from within toward the external; just as the finger of a pregnant woman longing for something marks the cheek of the child, a sign of the force of the thing she saw.

Indeed, the vigor of an incantation proceeds toward a distant object, propagated by a certain motion not only through the air (which is similar to itself, like circles in water once struck), but also through the rays of the exhaling spirit, which a vehement imagination and affection hurl far away. For the radial nature proceeds far into the distance by means of the spirit, and carries with it the ejecting forces. Juno <note>often associated by Neoplatonists with the lower atmosphere or the sublunary realm</note>, imitating all things below the moon, sends forth the powers of her nature and certain vapors like rays, by which distant objects are frequently affected for better or worse according to their nature. This happens more easily since each individual thing is a member of the same "world-animal" <note>term: "world-animal" (anima mundi); the Platonic concept that the universe is a single, living, interconnected organism</note>. The very odors perceived further and longer by dogs declare this.

Consider how much power the demonic sorcerers apply to magical works, which Plato surely confirms in the *Symposium*. By diligent cultivation and soothing, the Magus can even win these beings over to himself, just as a musician might ensnare a noble King with the lowliest of boys, or as certain beasts sometimes fascinate a man. For as a beast stands in relation to a man, or a boy to a mature man, so the Magus seems close in relation to the inferior demons. To this point, perhaps, tends that teaching of Abu Ma’shar <note>a famous Persian astrologer, often called Albumasar</note> and other astrologers: namely, that prayers have the greatest power when the Head of the Dragon <note>term: "Head of the Dragon" (Caput Draconis); the ascending node of the moon, considered an auspicious point in astrology</note> holds the middle of the sky, and Jupiter is either in it or aspects it; and when the moon is either joined with Jupiter or, proceeding from him, pursues a conjunction with the lord of the ascendant; or when the lord of the ascendant seeks a meeting with Jupiter and an affection for the Head of the Dragon. 

For they think that through such loyal alignments, efficacy and prosperity are provided to our spirit to attract the demons subject to Jupiter and the Head of the Dragon. If only they are subjected to these celestial influxes, many things from every kind of sensible object are competent both to this demon and to his star—things which are both laborious to search out and dangerous to observe. A physicist speaking more safely about this will think that the spirit of a man, then more vehemently desiring celestial goods, is exposed by the benefit of Jupiter to drinking more deeply of celestial goods; but that for the sake of moving malignant spirits, divination through the dead must be completed. Ptolemy, in the *Quadripartitus* <note>original: "Tetrabiblos," the foundational text of Hellenistic astrology</note>, thinks it useful to bring together celestial harmony when the Moon is the mistress of the house and inhabits the dwellings of Jupiter, namely Sagittarius or Pisces. 

These things are said in response to that point of Plotinus: where he says that the Magus, in a certain way, ensnares demons and moves inferior things easily through superior ones, openly through the parts of the universe. But I suspect that perhaps the crafty demons merely pretend to be attracted or expelled by certain magical machines. For Porphyry and Iamblichus say that we have command over the lowest spirits properly through God and through the good angels; otherwise, those spirits are frequently accustomed to deceive and harm us. And since they are disturbed and touched (as Plotinus also affirms), Plotinus rightly joins Porphyry and Iamblichus in condemning that superstition which strives to flatter deceptive and disturbed demons with exquisite allurements. 

By what reasoning we are able to pluck vital breaths from the body of the world—which is everywhere alive—using a living star and other parts of the world in the natural manner of farmers and physicians, we have sufficiently discussed in the third book of *On Life* <note>original: "De Vita," Ficino's famous medical and magical treatise</note>. Finally, the Platonists think that the most intense adoration is the most effective of all sacrifices, especially if it is directed toward the superior intellects of the world (namely the angels), and most of all if it is directed toward the superior God. But they hold that nothing is impelled by these beings in a similar way or by a certain natural or celestial motion (whose motion from that source does not pass everywhere), but rather by a certain elevation and conjunction of the mind toward them. Those things which we have related in the previous sections concerning the power of the imagination, fascinations, and magic, we treat more extensively in our *Theology*, and the book *On Love*, and the third book of *On Life*.

->Chapter XLIII.<-

<columns>2</columns>
Is everyone then subject to the power of sorcery and drugs? The soul is indeed unaffected by sorceries in its rational part, nor would its reason suffer, nor would it change its opinion of what is right in the universe. If there is an irrational part in it, it might suffer according to this. Or rather, it might suffer through this; but you do not ask about the love-charms that come from drugs, which are the height of dread and affect the rest of the soul by the suffering of that other part. Just as the irrational part suffers from incantations, so too might the man himself be enchanted and, in turn, he will dissolve the powers there by counter-chanting. He might suffer death from these, or diseases, or whatever is bodily. For a part of the universe might suffer from another part or from the whole, but the man himself remains unharmed. That which is not within, but comes later, would never be affected. But plants and demons are not unaffected, nor are irrational creatures, for they have memory and senses, and through these they are given over to them.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It seems we must ask in what way a good man can be withdrawn by magical machines and drugs. Perhaps he cannot be ensnared through the soul itself, nor does the rational power itself suffer, so that it is changed in its opinion. <margin>B</margin> However, as much as there is of the irrational within him from the universe, he can suffer through this; indeed, he properly can suffer this very thing. But it is not only that, as when one is ensnared by love through potions; for love itself thrives and burns when the one soul consents to the passion of the other soul. Just as the irrational part undergoes passion from the songs of those incanting, so too is he himself enchanted in turn, and the counter-enchanter dissolves the forces there. <margin>C</margin> Consequently, he will suffer death from these, or illnesses, or any detriments of the body without controversy. For a part of the universe easily suffers from another part, or from the whole itself; but he himself, existing as his own master, lives unharmed. That he should undergo passion not suddenly, but after a certain time, is not foreign to the order of nature. Even the demons themselves are not free from passions in their irrational part. Furthermore, it will not be absurd to attribute memory and sense to them.

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic theory of magic, explaining how incantations and astrology work through the "spirit" and the "world-animal," while maintaining that the rational soul remains immune to such sorcery even if the body or irrational emotions are affected.</summary>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, they are naturally soothed and led down, and they listen to those who call upon them. I am speaking of <term>daemones</term> <note>original: "Dæmones"; in Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediate spirits or "rational beings" that bridge the gap between gods and humans</note> among others who are closer to human affairs; they are more affected by us because they exist in closer proximity. For whatever possesses a certain kinship to another is eventually ensnared by it. That to which it relates in this way is captured and drawn away as if by a magical rite; but only that which looks toward itself cannot be trapped or snatched. For this reason, every action and the entirety of the "active life" is ensnared and pulled along; for it is carried toward those things which provoke and charm it. Hence that poetic line: *For the people of great-hearted <term>Erechtheus</term> are most beautiful in countenance.* <note>Plotinus is likely referencing Homer or a similar classic source to illustrate how external beauty acts as a natural charm upon the observer. Erechtheus was a legendary king of Athens.</note> But why should someone be considered to relate to another in a specific way? Truly, it is as if they are drawn not by the arts of sorcerers, but by the "art of nature," which seduces in a marvelous way, reconciling and joining one thing with another—not by physical location, but by <term>love-charms</term> <note>original: "philtris"; from the Greek "philtra," referring to potions or natural attractions that bind souls to bodies</note> applied from the beginning.

---

->*The contemplative life is free; the active life is the servant of actions, circumstances, and fortune; the voluptuous life is the slave of the body. Chapter 44.*<-

---

Since the mind possesses the innate forms of things to be contemplated, and is itself those very forms, it rightly dwells freely within itself insofar as it occupies itself with a natural pleasure in contemplating them. But he who curiously tends to the body and external things serves the body, other men, and fortune. Action and <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passio"; here used in the philosophical sense of "being acted upon" or "suffering" external influence</note> are opposites. Therefore, every movement of ours that takes its stimulus from the body and human passion is a form of suffering and servitude. Finally, nature itself—the life of the world—everywhere fashions images of the Good, the True, and the Beautiful as if they were baits. With these, it deceives souls devoted to this world through pleasure, greed, and vain glory, detaining and dragging them like slaves.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, only contemplation remains which cannot be led away by magical ritual; for no one is attracted "away" toward themselves. For the self is one, and it is itself the very spectacle it observes; it is a reason that is not seduced. Instead, it does what is right to do, and carries out its own life and work. In the active life, however, the soul does not perform what is its own, nor does reason provide the starting point; rather, the beginning is handed over by the irrational part, and the rules of acting are proposed by passion. <margin>B</margin> In the appetite for procreation and the care of children, this "attraction" is clearly visible; it is similar in all things that allure those who desire them with a certain sweetness. Those actions which are moved irrationally through anger, or those incited by lust, as well as the hearing of civil government and the zeal for commanding, signify that a dominant desire, once incited within us, now incites us further. <margin>C</margin> Then truly, the pursuit of command—tending toward this point so that we are not harmed by others—takes its origin from fear; but those pursuits intended to make us gain more than others are led by greed. Finally, those things which serve necessity and utility, attempting to fulfill the deficiency of nature, plainly show the very force of nature reconciling us to the zeal for living. If someone should object that actions concerning honorable things are not "led away" by magical rites, and that the contemplation of beautiful things would then also be ensnared by such a condition, <margin>D</margin> one must respond: if someone follows honorable actions because they are necessary, while looking toward something else that is truly beautiful, he is by no means trapped by magical means. For he knows the necessity, and he does not look toward that which is inherent in our actions, nor is he directed toward other things of this life—unless perhaps through a part

<column-break/>

And to be soothed naturally by harmonies, and to be called by those calling their own [spirits] who are nearer, according to those things of that [world] which relate to things here. For everything that was born toward another is charmed and led back by that other toward which it exists. But only that which is toward itself is un-charmed. Therefore, every action is charmed, and the entire life of the practical man; for he is moved toward those things which soothe him. Whence also [it is said] "the beautiful face of the great-hearted <term>Erechtheus</term>’s people." <note>This column provides the Greek source text for the Latin translation on the left.</note> For what might a man suffer to be held by another? Either being drawn by the arts of magicians, or by all the deception of nature, which embodies one thing toward another, not by locations, but by the love-charms it has given.

ONLY contemplation remains to be un-charmed, because no one is carried toward themselves, for they are one. And the thing being contemplated is himself, and his reason is not being touched, but allowing [him to be], he acts by his own life and his own work. But there [in the active life], he is not himself, and while his reason holds to the body, the beginning is from the irrational [part], and the commands are from it. For the care of procreation, and the pursuit of marriage and children, clearly have this "pull"; because every man is baited by things that become pleasant to the desires. As for action, some are moved irrationally through anger, and others by desires, as if by themselves. Political and ruling appetites, having the desire to lead or to be a tyrant, have an origin in fear; but those for the sake of having more [have an origin in] desire. And those for the sake of necessities, seeking to fulfill the lack of nature, clearly have the force of nature, having made us at home with life. But if someone says that the actions of beautiful things are un-charmed, and that the contemplation of beautiful things is charmed, it must be said: either one must say even the so-called beautiful actions are performed as necessary, but the one who holds to the truly beautiful is not charmed. For he knows the necessity, and does not look toward the things here. Nor is his life toward other things, but by that of nature...

# BOOK FOURTH.

...by an irrational force of human nature, and by a natural familiarity that reconciles us with the life of ourselves or others, such a person might be said to be ensnared. For it seems perhaps rational <note>original Greek: "εὔλογον" (eulogon); meaning reasonable or plausible</note> not to lead oneself out of life <note>A reference to the Stoic or Platonic debates on suicide/leaving the body</note> because of a certain necessity or kinship with life that is most our own, by which we are deeply occupied. If, however, a man devoted to worldly affairs <note>The "active life" of politics or business</note> should be content with the mere beauty of such things and therefore choose those actions, he is already deceived. He is ensnared by the tracks of beauty as if by poisons. <margin>B</margin> For he zealously pursues a beauty that has been grafted into inferior things. Indeed, all such business concerning that which merely *resembles* the truth, and every pull toward it, is a kind of seizure of the mind, deceived by those things that drag the soul toward themselves. This is actually caused by the magical enchantment <note>original Greek: "γοητεία" (goeteia); meaning sorcery or natural bewitchment</note> of nature itself. For a person follows that which is not the Good as if it were the Good itself, while they are lured by its appearance. Driven by an irrational impulse, <margin>C</margin> this is a certain passion of the mind, which is secretly pulled where it does not wish to go. What else shall we call this but a magical rapture? Therefore, only he is least seized by such sorceries who, being pulled by other parts of himself, declares that none of these things which appear good to the world are actually good. He alone knows the truth, being neither deceived nor a mere follower, but already possessing the Good. Such a person is never dragged away.

<column-break/>

->*Man does not only act and suffer many things by fate as if he were merely a part of the world; he also possesses his own substance, which is naturally related partly to higher things and partly to lower things. By his own free movement, he can furthermore take on a disposition and habit that aligns with either the higher or the lower.*<-

->*Such a habit eventually becomes like a second nature to the soul, and by its instinct—under divine judgment—the soul is carried into a lot and a place suitable for either the higher or the lower powers.*<-

### Chapter XLV.

From all that has been said, it is manifest how everything contained in the universe is gifted with a specific nature and disposition, and thus contributes to the whole through its actions and its suffering. Just as in any living animal <note>Plotinus frequently uses the "World Animal" analogy, where the universe is a single, integrated living being</note> every single part, according to its nature and condition, confers something to the whole and provides a service, being valued for its specific order and use. Furthermore, it gives something of itself and receives from others according to its capacity. There is a certain <margin>B</margin> consensus or "shared feeling" <note>original Greek: "συναίσθησις" (synaisthesis); the organic coordination of parts in a whole</note> of the parts toward the whole. If any part were itself an animal, it would have its own animal functions different from its functions as a part. Accordingly, our own condition is also clear: we also do something within the universe. We do not only perform those things which a body does to another body, but we also bring another nature of our own into the mix. We are joined through the kinship inherent within us to those kinships existing outside of us. Indeed, by our <margin>C</margin> souls and our dispositions, we are made—or rather, we are—contiguous with the things placed just below us in the "daemonic place" <note>original: "loco dæmonico"; the intermediate realm between the material world and the purely divine</note> as well as with higher things. Since we are disposed in this way, the kind of people we are cannot remain hidden. Therefore, we do not all offer the same things, nor do we all receive the same. For if we do not possess something, how can we provide it to others as if it were a good? Again, nature in no way...

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the "active life" is a form of natural enchantment where the soul is lured by the reflection of beauty in material things. He concludes by arguing that the universe functions like a single living body where every part, including the human soul, is interconnected by its internal disposition.</summary>
<keywords>natural magic, enchantment, goeteia, active life, world animal, daemonic realm, kinship of souls, free will, Marsilio Ficino, Neoplatonism</keywords>

--- Page 475 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion in Ennead IV.4 (likely chapter 45). On the previous page, he described how the soul can be "bewitched" by the material world. Here, he explains the mechanism of cosmic justice: how souls are moved to different parts of the universe—the "Great Animal"—based on their moral character and internal "pulls," much like the organs of a body are treated to maintain the health of the whole.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

...capable of good: since we just received some good thing? Therefore, each person bringing their own depravity <note>original Latin: "pravitatem"; refers to a soul's moral distortion or vice</note>, and since they are detected in this way, they are driven according to their nature into what they possess, both while among us and after departing from here to another similar place by a certain pull of nature. <margin>A</margin> But a virtuous man receives, gives, and is exchanged in a different way; specifically, each is moved to where they belong by certain natural pulls, as if by ropes. <note>Plotinus uses the metaphor of "cords" or "strings" to describe the invisible sympathetic forces that move souls through the cosmos.</note> This universe possesses such wonderful power and order, in <margin>B</margin> which all things are dispensed justly by a silent and hidden command and path under divine judgment. No one is permitted to escape this sentence; no wicked person understands it, but is merely carried unknowingly to that part of the universe where it is most fitting for them to be moved. But the good man both knows this and approaches the place he ought; even before he arrives, he senses where he must necessarily dwell after his arrival, and he lives in good hope that he will one day dwell with the gods themselves. <margin>C</margin> In a small animal, the changes of parts are also small and the harmonies slight; nor are the parts themselves independent animals, except perhaps for a short time in some. But in that animal <note>Plotinus refers to the Universe as a "Great Animal" or a single living organism (the *Anima Mundi*).</note> in which there are such vast intervals, and where every part undergoes its own inclination and change, and in which many animals dwell, it is necessary that the movements and transfers be <margin>D</margin> greater. We certainly see the sun, moon, and all the stars being moved in a fixed order and changing their positions. It is therefore not contrary to reason that souls also are moved from one place to another, not always keeping the same character, but finally ordered and arranged in fitting proportion as suits their dispositions: where some, clearly, take the place of the head, and others the feet—a place, I say, suitable to the whole. For this world too has differences of better and worse. If any soul chooses neither the better that is here, nor is defiled by the worse, it is moved to another place, and will one day <margin>E</margin> attain the pure state it had chosen. The punishments of souls are such as those of diseased parts of a body, where some are bound with poultices, others are cut away or purged, and others are changed in their qualities so that the whole may be healthy, with each part rightly arranged where it is beneficial. For the health of the whole is the primary concern: this part being bound, that one instead changed in quality, and another expelled from here as if it were languishing, and moved there where
->it may least languish.<-

<column-break/>

Capable of good, are we then considered... whoever has joined wickedness to himself is known, or stands according to his own nature and is pushed to what he possessed, both here and in departures from elsewhere, to another place by the pulls of nature; but for the good man, there are takings and givings, and other changes, as if moved by certain pulls of threads <note>original Greek: "μηρίνθων" (merinthon); meaning cords or packing-threads</note> of nature. The whole is thus wonderfully possessed of power and order; it has judged all that happens by a silent path, from which there is no escape for anyone; the base man is subject to it, but not knowing it; even if he is carried within the whole, the ignorant man does not know where he has arrived, but he will know before he departs that it is necessary for him to dwell in a certain place. He, however, is of good hope, as if he would be with the gods. For in an irrational animal, the changes and coincidences of the parts are small, and the parts themselves are not independent living things, unless one thinks so for a brief moment. But in that [Great Animal] in which the distances are so great, and each thing within it has its own release and a multitude of living things, we see the movements and the transfers are greater. We see the sun, and the moon, and the other stars, moved in order and changing. And so it is not irrational that souls are also moved, not always preserving the same character, but being ordered according to what they have suffered and done in a sequence—some like the head, and others taking the place of the feet and harmonious parts. For the world itself has differences, toward both the better and the worse. But if a soul has neither chosen the better here, nor shared in the worse <unclear>...</unclear> it would have changed to some other pure place, attaining that which it chose. Punishments are like those of diseased parts: for some, applications of medicines; for others, removals or alterations, so that the whole may be healthy while each part is disposed as it must be. The healthy state of the whole <unclear>...</unclear> removing from here what is, as has been said, diseased, or 
placing it where it 
will not be 
diseased.

<meta>This page transitions from the end of Ennead IV, Book 4—which discussed the cosmic justice and the movement of souls within the "Great Animal" of the universe—to the beginning of Book 5. # PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FOUR
### BOOK FIVE

->On the Third Set of Problems concerning the Soul, or on Vision.<-

*TO SENSE is to perceive individual physical things through physical instruments. In sensory perception, it is observed that the qualities or actions of external bodies reach the soul, or affect it in some way; likewise, the power and action of the soul sometimes extend themselves toward physical things. This could not happen unless the soul had a certain proportion <note>original Latin: "proportionem"; a fitting relationship or correspondence</note> to these things. However, the soul does not possess this unless it forms a manifest body—and especially the spirit <note>original Latin: "spiritum"; likely referring to 'pneuma', the subtle material vehicle of the soul</note>—by its own agreement through its vegetative power. Thus, being multifaceted, the soul's power and action may sometimes extend through this body of its own (as if through a tool) toward external things, and the movements of external things may seem to reach the soul by coming to this body. Finally, for the sense of sight to perceive a visible object, there is no necessary need for an external body to act as a required medium for seeing; for the sense of sight and the eye are by nature sufficiently prepared to be occupied with light, and light in turn with sight. But if a medium body is opaque, it hinders sight; if it is transparent <note>original Latin: "diaphanum"; a clear medium like air or water</note>, it only has the property of not obstructing vision as an opaque body does; therefore, it is possible that one might see even without such a medium.*

->Chapter I.<-

---

<margin>A</margin>
Since we have set out to examine whether it is possible to see if there is nothing in between, such as air or any other of the so-called transparent bodies, we must first consider why some say that it is necessary to see through a body—and indeed to sense at all. They say that while the soul is entirely within the intelligible <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the non-physical realm of pure forms and intellect</note> realm, sensation <margin>* actually so</margin> is for her a reception not of things in that realm, but only of sensible things <note>The "sensible world" is the world of matter and physical objects</note>. For every soul, when it becomes joined to sensation, participates in a certain communion of knowledge or experience with things that are like it. Therefore, knowledge also occurs through physical instruments, for through these there are harmonies or continuities of beings, so that they become as one with the sensible objects themselves, a certain shared feeling <note>Greek: "sympatheia"</note> arising toward them, even if no direct contact with the things being known occurs. Regarding how one knows by touch, what he <unclear>says</unclear> is one thing; but regarding sight, and later regarding hearing, we must investigate. Now, regarding sight: must there be a body between the vision and the color, or does the intervening body only happen to be there by accident, contributing nothing to the act of seeing for those who see? If these bodies were dense, like those of earth,

<margin>A</margin>
But since we have decided to investigate whether we can see if there is no medium—such as air or another clear body—between the eye and that which is to be seen, it is worthwhile to pursue this very thing now. In the first place, it has already been said by some that one must see and sense entirely through some body.
<margin>B</margin>
For the soul, without a body, would live entirely in the intelligible world. But since sensing is the perception not indeed of intelligible things, but only of sensible things, the soul must be made somewhat contiguous to sensible things, so that through certain things now familiar to it, it may enter into a certain communion of knowledge or experience with them. For this reason, such knowledge also occurs through physical instruments. For through these, as if they were related or continuous, one must approach the sensible things themselves in a certain way, a certain compulsion toward them
<margin>C</margin>
having already been made. Therefore, that some contact with those things which are to be known is necessary—at least as far as concerns those things perceived by touch—no one perhaps would doubt; but concerning vision, it is more ambiguous. And whether the same is necessary in hearing, we shall investigate in what follows. Now, for the present, we must treat of sight: is it necessary for there to be some intervening body between the sight and the color?
<margin>D</margin>

## ENNEAD FOUR

<margin>A</margin>
...hinder the vision more, whereas the thinner the media are, the more easily we see through them. One might say that these media contribute to sight, or if they do not contribute, at least they do not obstruct it; yet others might call them obstacles. We must ask whether the medium body receives an affection <note>original Latin: "passionem"; a physical impression or state of being acted upon</note> first and is, as it were, shaped by the object. Someone might offer this as proof: if something is before our face, even when looking at a color, that color would not reach us at all unless a certain affection had been impressed upon the medium. 
<margin>B</margin>
But perhaps it is not necessary for the medium to be affected while that which is naturally disposed to the affection—the eye—is being affected. Or, if the medium is indeed affected then, it suffers something else entirely. For the fishing rod held between the numbing fish—called the Narce <note>original: "Narcen"; the torpedo fish or electric ray, famous in antiquity for its ability to deliver an electric shock through a rod or net</note>—and the hand does not suffer what the hand itself suffers. And yet, in this case, unless the rod and the line <note>original: "seta siue capillus"; literally "bristle or hair," referring to the fishing line</note> were positioned in the middle, the hand would not be affected at all. 
<margin>C</margin>
Perhaps this, too, is to be doubted: for if the fisherman is inside the net with the fish, he will still be affected and numbed. It seems this argument leads us toward those "sympathies" <note>original: "compassiones"; the principle of *sympatheia*, where parts of the universe "feel together" due to a shared cosmic soul, regardless of the distance between them</note> we have mentioned. Specifically, if one thing is naturally suited to be affected by another because it possesses a similarity to it, it is not affected *because* of the medium between them—especially if the medium is dissimilar; or certainly, the medium will not be affected in the same way. If this holds true, the thing naturally subject to the affection will be affected much more when there is no medium at all, even if the medium is the sort of thing that can also feel something itself.

---

Between sight and the visible object, the medium is light—either a common external light or the specific light offered by the nature of a very bright thing. A physical body, however, is not strictly necessary as a medium between these two. Let this be part of the argument: just as a visual ray proceeds from the eye to the visible object, or comes from the luminous object to the sight (or both happen at once), it is entirely because both the eye and the visible object are so disposed within the living nature of the world that they have a very similar property to one another. Through this, they are easily moved by each other or mutually affected. Therefore, a body is not necessary in itself to support or carry the ray flashing out from the eye (whether that ray is a substance projected naturally in a straight line), nor to carry the light back (whether it is the eye’s own light or external light), nor even to complete the sympathy between the visible and the sight; they are sufficiently exposed to each other’s influence on their own. Finally, it is not necessary for the medium air to be formed <note>original: "formari"; to be stamped or molded like wax</note> by the object and shaped like wax, through which the eye would then suffer a similar affection. Otherwise, to see an object placed far away, it would not be necessary for the eye to turn toward the object itself; it would be enough for the eye to be touched by the part of the air immediately next to it, which had already been "shaped." In truth, the spiritual forms of visible things <note>original: "spirituales... visibilium species"; the 'logos' or non-material patterns of the objects</note> reach the eye through the light without any physical affection of the air.

---

<margin>Cap. 11</margin>
If vision occurs in such a way that the light of the sight itself joins with the light of the medium all the way to the sensory object, then this medium must be light; this hypothesis requires the medium to be so. But if a colored body affects and changes the medium body in some way, what prevents such a change from reaching the eye immediately, even if no medium intervened? For now, the medium is only necessary because it is "in the way," and must be changed before the eye is changed. Furthermore, those who say we see by a certain "effusion" <note>extramission theory: the belief that the eye sends out rays to "touch" objects</note> of sight itself have no reason to require a medium, 
<margin>B</margin>
unless perhaps they fear the ray itself might fall or fail. But a ray has the nature of light, and light naturally diffuses in a straight line. Those who assign a certain "resistance" as the cause of vision will certainly require a medium. However, those who maintain the theory of images <note>original: "simulachrorum"; refers to the *eidola* of Epicurean physics—thin films that peel off objects</note>—affirming that they pass through a vacuum—require an empty, clear space so that the images are not prevented from arriving. Therefore, if there is much less hindrance where there is no medium at all, then this hypothesis will certainly not be drawn into controversy.
<margin>C</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin>
...prevents us from seeing; and the thinner the intervening space, the more we see. One might grant this: that the intervening spaces are either cooperative or obstructive. These here are obstructive. One might argue that the cause of this is that the medium must first be affected and, as it were, stamped. A sign of this might be brought forward: that if one looks at the color near our eyes, and sees from there, it would not reach us unless some affection occurred in the medium. 
<margin>Β</margin>
Or perhaps it is not a necessity that the medium be affected. If the eye, which is naturally suited to be affected, is affected, or if the body is, it suffers something else. Consider the rod between the torpedo fish and the hand: does it suffer what the hand suffers? And yet, if the rod and the line were not in the middle, the hand would not be affected. 
<margin>C</margin>
Even if the fisherman were in the net, one might doubt this, for he would seem to suffer the numbness by being held. But the argument risks falling back upon the so-called "sympathies." If something is naturally suited to be affected by another through sympathy because of a similarity to it, it would not be a necessity for the medium to be affected. For the medium would not be affected, and much more so if there were nothing in the middle, the thing naturally suited to be affected would be affected—even if the medium were affected, such as if it suffered something itself.

---

If vision is of such a kind that the light of the sight joins with the intervening light as far as the sensible object, then the intervening space must be light; and this is the hypothesis: that the medium must be light. But if the change comes from the colored body itself, what prevents the change from reaching the body <note>the eye</note> immediately, even if nothing were in the middle? For if it is out of necessity, the medium must somehow be affected first. 
<margin>Β</margin>
Those who speak of the "pouring out" of the sight would not be able to explain why a medium is entirely necessary, unless they were afraid the rays might fall. But it is of the nature of light, and light travels in a straight line. Those who blame a "standing-still" <note>resistance or obstruction</note> for the cause would entirely require a medium. But if the theory of images <note>Greek: "eidolon"</note> is fallen back upon, they are said to travel through a vacuum, moving through such things so as not to be hindered. 
<margin>C</margin>
And even more so, nothing would hinder them if there were no medium at all; hope will not dispute this.

# BOOK FIVE.

<column-break/>

Since they say that vision is sympathy <note>original Greek: "sympatheia"; the idea that the universe is a single living organism where all parts resonate with one another</note>, they will either say that if something is in between, it hinders and obstructs, making the sympathy faint; or more logically, they would say it must certainly make it faint, and the medium either suffers the same thing [as the eye] or it does not. If a body is solid deep within and is burned by the application of fire, the part deep inside feels that outside application either less or more. But if the parts of a single living being were sympathetic, would the part not suffer less if there were something in between? Or would it suffer less, yet the suffering would be proportionate as nature wills, and the medium would only hinder the excess? Unless perhaps everything is given [directly], so that the medium does not suffer at all, but the sympathy exists because the being is a living creature, and we suffer because we are within a single whole. When distant things are perceived in this way, there must be continuity, or the medium itself is part of that continuity. Why must it be a living being for there to be continuity, and why should the affection <note>original: "pathos"; a physical impression or state of being acted upon</note> be an accidental property of continuity? Or shall we say that everything is affected by everything else? If this particular medium is necessary, and not just any other or the same one, then a medium would not be required everywhere. If someone says that vision requires [a medium], why should they say so? Since it appears everywhere that acting through air is an affection, making the air [act]. But is it only to divide it, as when a stone falls from above, or does the air endure it in some other way? For it is reasonable to consider "reciprocal displacement" <note>original: "antiperistasis"; an ancient physical theory suggesting that as an object moves, the air it displaces rushes around to the back to push it forward</note>, just as in natural motion. Since fire happened to move upward by reciprocal displacement—but that is absurd; for fire, by its own faster motion, anticipates the displacement of the air. If one says that it is made faster by art than the falling of air, it would happen by accident, and for those things whose impulse is upward (not from the wood [burning]), they are not pushed. And we ourselves, when moving, cut the air, and it is not displacement that pushes us; rather, the air simply follows and fills the space moved by us. If someone could move through such bodies without being affected, what prevents the forms <note>original: "eide"; the intelligible shapes or qualities of objects</note> for vision from passing through the <unclear>medium</unclear> in the same way? If the form does not even suffer as an outflow, why is it necessary for the medium to suffer? And does the affection come to us through the medium because the medium was affected? For if our sense-perception came from the air being affected, we would not see the visible object by looking toward it, but we would receive the sensation from the part of the air adjacent to us, just as in the case of being heated. For there, it is not the distant fire, but the adjacent air that has been heated, which seems to heat us. For that is touch. But if it is through sights, it is not touch; therefore, even the sensible object placed upon the eye does not produce vision:

---

...fire, but the adjacent heated air seems to heat us. But indeed this affection pertains to touch, whereas in vision touch does not occur: therefore neither does the sensible object placed upon the eyes produce vision:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, whoever asserts that vision occurs through a certain compassion <note>original Latin: "compassione"; used here as a translation for the Greek "sympatheia"</note>, will surely say that we see less if some medium intervenes: because this will prohibit and impede it, making the compassion less through imperfection. Indeed, we can say by consistent reason that the medium itself, even if it is of the same kind and experiences the same thing, nevertheless makes that compassion weaker. For even if a continuous body is burned deep within by the approach of fire, nevertheless the part placed in the <margin>B</margin> depths will surely suffer less from the approach to the upper part. But if the parts of a single living being are mutually sympathetic, will they suffer less because there is nothing in between? Perhaps they will suffer less: surely the affection will turn out to be moderate insofar as nature has willed. For since the interposed medium inhibits the excess of the affection, unless perhaps in some place that which is introduced is of such a kind that the medium can in no way suffer it. Furthermore, if the whole is sympathetic because it is one living being, and <margin>C</margin> we therefore suffer because we are in one universe, why should it not be necessary, when something placed far off is sensed, for continuity to be present? Perhaps continuity and the medium itself must intervene in some places, because it is necessary for the animal to be continuous, but the affection is an accidental property of the continuum; otherwise we shall admit that everything is affected by everything. Then indeed, if this is affected by that, but another thing by something else, and they do not suffer the same thing, there will be no need for a medium everywhere. But if someone says that a medium is needed at least in vision, <margin>D</margin> they will have to assign a reason: since it does not appear everywhere that what proceeds through the air brings an affection to the air, but only divides it. Just as when a stone falls from above, nothing else seems to happen to the air except that it does not support the falling stone. For it is not likely that the stone falls through some "reciprocal displacement" <note>original: "subingressum"; the Latin equivalent of the Greek antiperistasis</note> of the surrounding air, as if a natural downward thrust is made for it, since in that way fire would also ascend through a similar displacement of air, which is absurd to say. For fire, <margin>E</margin> by the velocity of its own motion, outruns the succeeding air. But if someone should say that the succession of air is accelerated by that very velocity, nevertheless that will happen according to accident, and not properly upward, since even from logs the impulse is made into the heights, with nothing pushing them as they grow. And yet we, when walking, divide the air, and the succession of surrounding air does not push us then, but the air merely follows and fills the vacuum that we create. Therefore, if the air <margin>F</margin> admits [objects] through its parts, will it suffer nothing else meanwhile as species <note>original: "speciebus"; the visible forms or images of things</note> travel through the distance of such bodies' motion for their passage to the sight? But if the species do not even arrive as if by a certain flow, what necessity requires the medium to be affected? And that the affection reaches all the way to us through the medium, because that medium was previously affected? For if the sense were produced from the fact that the air is first affected, certainly we would not discern the visible object by looking at it, but we would report the sensation from the part of the air closest to us, just as happens in <margin>G</margin> heating. For in that case, it is not the remote...

<summary>Plotinus argues that vision is not a result of the air being physically "affected" or changed, but rather a direct result of the cosmic sympathy within the universe as a single living being. He uses the physics of motion and heat to prove that if we relied on the air to transmit vision, we would see the air next to our eyes rather than the distant object.</summary>

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>But it is necessary for the medium to be illuminated, perhaps because the air is naturally dark. If it were not dark, perhaps it would not need light; for that which is dark, because it hinders vision, must be overcome by light. Perhaps, indeed, it is for this very reason that an object placed too close to the eye is not seen at all, because it brings with it a certain shadow, both of itself and of the air.

*The intervening air is not strictly necessary between the sight and the visible object for the purpose of the object's form being imprinted step-by-step through successive parts of the air until it finally reaches the eye. The first reason for this was assigned a little earlier. Two more follow, one of which is this: When we see a tiny spark from a great distance in the deep of night, we should not think that the form is imprinted gradually from the spark through continuous parts of the air. For the spark cannot "paint" the air in this way unless it also illuminates those same parts, yet it does not illuminate them; otherwise, we would see many other things in that straight line of sight. The second reason is this: If the air were purged of its bodily nature in some way, it would follow that because a tiny part of the air close to the pupil is equal in size to the pupil, it could only show the eye that tiny portion of the whole person it sits in front of; yet, in reality, we see the whole object in any small portion of air. Finally, the air is not affected by that "species" <note>original: "specie"; the formal image or "shimmer" of an object that travels to the eye</note> sent from the object, just as it is not affected by the light itself through which it is sent—I mean by the light in its capacity as light. For in this way, it is present and absent in a moment, and does not remain once the source of illumination is removed, and it is whole everywhere. From this it appears that light does not become a proper quality of the air, nor is it truly corporeal. Thus, this incorporeal thing now proceeds from the world-body. For just as when you see a spark from a vast distance, you hear a tiny sound from that place; and certain animals like bees and ants smell honey from very far away, and shellfish even taste at a distance; and the torpedo fish <note>The torpedo fish is an electric ray known in antiquity for its ability to numb a fisherman even through a wooden rod or spear</note> numbs you through a long rod as if touching you—one must not think, especially in these higher matters, that the tiniest thing cast out is broken across a vast distance and materially affected. Instead, something I might call "spiritual" intervenes, which acts upon the sense across such a long space. That is, it is a specific act proceeding from the visible form's resistance. I say "from the form," not so much because it is in matter, but because it depends on a spiritual and living Idea. I also say "a specific and spiritual act," whether it happens within us in the instrument of sense (as in touch and taste), or outside us in the air (as in sight, hearing, and smell), or even if it proceeds from the sight toward the object. Truly, this act of sensing occurs everywhere through a "compassion" <note>original: "compassio"; here meaning a shared resonance or sympathetic reaction</note> rather than a material change made by the object in the lower air. It happens, therefore, by the power of a common life, by whose benefit all things are bound together so easily that the sense is moved by distant things, and a body of the same nature is affected from afar by its counterpart. This is also apparent in the stars and other celestial bodies which impart their powers to things very far away. Finally, the common life of the world so tempers all these senses to the sensible world that when a sensible object acts, the sense is moved and acts, just as when one string is moved on a lyre, another immediately moves in harmony; and when you shout, the parts shout back in harmony. We treat these matters more diligently in our commentaries on Theophrastus.*

### Cap. III.

<margin>A</margin>**THE GREATEST** argument, however, is that the forms of sensible things are not seen because the air has already received their species through continuous transmission; rather, they are seen because fire and stars, and their forms, are visible even under the dark of night. No one could claim that the impressed species continue through the dark air all the way to the eye; otherwise, it would not be dark everywhere unless the fire handed down its species by illuminating the air. Even when stars and fire are hidden by deep darkness, which completely blocks their <margin>B</margin> light, fire is nonetheless seen from watchtowers and torches, and from the towers that show signals to ships. But if someone were to say that in these cases too the fire passes through [the air], clearly contradicting the evidence of the senses, it would then be necessary for even the smallest things in the intervening air to be seen, and not just the fire. Therefore, if we see what is beyond the darkness despite the intervening darkness, we would discern it much more clearly where there is no medium at all. But <margin>C</margin> here someone will perhaps insist, asserting that where there is no medium, nothing is seen—not indeed because a medium is lacking, but because the animal sympathy <note>The "animal" refers to the universe as a single living organism</note> toward these things would be completely taken away, along with the consensus of parts among themselves in that which consists of one whole. For it seems that sense occurs in whatever way it does because this universal living being resonates with itself everywhere. For if it were not such a being, how could one part receive powers from others, even the most remote? This, therefore, is worthy of consideration: If there were another world, and another

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...but to be illuminated because of the intervening space, either because the air is unformed, or because it is dark; for if it were not, perhaps it would not need light. For the darkness, being an obstacle to seeing, must be mastered by the light. And perhaps for this very reason something placed close to the eye is not seen, because it brings its own shadow and the shadow of the air.

---

### Cap. III.

<margin>A</margin>**THE GREATEST** testimony that seeing is not due to the air being affected, but is a perception of the forms as if by a transmission, is what happens at night in the dark, when fire and the things in the heavens and their forms are seen. For surely no one will say that the forms are created in the darkness so as to reach the eye from the darkness. Or if the fire illuminated those forms, then everything in the dark would be visible. <margin>B</margin> And even when the stars and the fire are hidden, and no light at all shines from them, the fire is seen from beacon-fires and from the towers that signal to ships. But if someone were to say that even through those things the forms of the fire are distributed to the sense, then it would be necessary for everything in the intervening air or darkness to be seen by the sight, even if dimly. But if <margin>C</margin> [we see] those things beyond, then much more would we see if nothing were there; the reason for this is not that the medium is nothing, but that the sympathy of the living being would not exist between the parts of the whole. For perhaps sense exists in this way because the entire living being is sympathetic to itself. If this were not so, how could one part share in the power of another, especially one far away? This must be examined: if there were another world and another...

<summary>Plotinus argues that vision does not require the air to be physically transformed or "stamped" with images, using the visibility of stars and distant fire-signals in the dark as proof. He concludes that perception is possible due to the "sympathy" or interconnected vital energy of the universe acting as a single living organism.</summary>
