<meta>This page continues the investigation from the previous page regarding the mechanics of vision. It specifically addresses whether the air acts as a physical medium that must be physically altered (like wax being stamped) for us to see, or if vision operates through a "sympathy" within the world-soul.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

<margin>A</margin> If there were a living being having no communion with our own, and some power of sight existed on the "back of heaven" <note>This refers to the outer boundary of the celestial spheres in Neoplatonic cosmology.</note>, would such a sight be able to see another world across a moderate distance? Or would there rather be no commerce between this world and that in terms of acting or being acted upon? But we shall deal with that later. For now, one might bring forward this testimony: vision does not occur because the medium is physically affected. For if the air were to be affected, it would necessarily be affected in a bodily way—that is, a form would be imprinted upon it as if in wax. Thus, a specific part of the visible object would be figured in a specific part of the air. It would follow that the part of the air connected to the eye would only be as large as the pupil, and could only receive and pass on a tiny portion of the object's form. In reality, however, the whole object is seen; and no matter where people are in the air—whether directly in front or off to the side—they can see across a great distance. Even those standing behind one another do not block the view of those behind them (provided they aren't physically in the way). From this, it appears that every tiny particle of air contains the entire "face" of the object being looked at. This does not happen through a bodily "passion" <note>original: "passio"; here meaning a physical change or impression made upon a substance</note>, but rather according to higher laws of the soul and the necessity of a single living universe that feels in sympathy with itself.

> *If some medium is necessary between the sight and the visible object, it is indeed not a body, but light—whether it is innate to the eyes or the object, or comes from outside. Not only the "passion" (being acted upon) of the eye contributes to seeing, but also a certain action and light. He touches here upon three opinions regarding vision: One thinks the soul propagates itself through visual rays just as if through hair or hands, and thus touches the sensible object without any reflection. The second thinks the soul is not propagated through rays, but extends them like rods to the object, and the image is reverberated back to the soul from there. The third thinks light is shaped by the object, and the light, thus shaped, reaches the eyes. He plays with the first theory, mocks the second, and rejects the third. Everywhere he strives to prove that there is such a conformity of "sympathy" <note>original: "compatiendi"; the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and react to one another instantaneously.</note> between the sight and the visible object that they move and act upon each other sufficiently even if the medium is not affected. Indeed, the medium does not suffer, or at least not in that way—just as when one string vibrates, another string nearby also trembles; or when one person yawns, another follows; or when a friend imagines something very dear, sometimes his closest friend imagines the same thing.*

->Chapter IV.<-

<margin>A</margin> **BUT** how does the light contiguous to the vision relate to the light near the vision and extending all the way to the sensible object? Perhaps it does not need the air as a medium at all, unless perhaps light cannot be spoken of without air; in that case, the air is only a medium by accident. Light itself is the medium that is least "affected" (physically changed), and there is no need for physical change here at all, but perhaps only for a medium. If light is not a body, then there is no need for a bodily medium. But perhaps someone might say that an external light and medium are not necessary for the act of vision itself, but only so that things at a distance may be perceived. <margin>B</margin> Whether light can exist without air or not, we shall investigate in what follows. Now, however, let us first investigate this: If this light connected to the sight is "animated" (filled with the soul's power), and the soul is carried through it and flourishes in it just as it does in the internal light of the eye, then surely in the act of perceiving—which is what seeing is—it will not need a mediating light. Instead, vision will be similar to the sense of touch; the power of seeing will perceive within the light, while the medium itself is not physically changed, but the sight itself is carried through it. <margin>C</margin> Here we must ask: must the sight proceed because there is an "interval" <term>interval: the empty space or distance between the eye and the object</term>, or because there is a body (like air) filling that interval? If it is because of the body in the interval, then if this obstacle were removed, one would see clearly. But if it is simply because there is an interval, then one must suppose the nature of the visible object itself is idle and doing nothing at all. But this cannot be...

<sig>P</sig>

<summary>Plotinus argues that vision is not a physical process of imprinting images on the air like wax, but a result of "universal sympathy" where the soul uses light as a non-bodily extension to perceive objects. He compares this interconnectedness to the way musical strings vibrate in unison or how friends share thoughts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s argument against the "transmissionist" theory of vision—the idea that the air between an object and the eye must be physically altered or "stamped" like wax. Here, he expands the argument to include the senses of touch and hearing, suggesting that perception relies on a universal "sympathy" or a spiritual connection rather than a step-by-step physical chain reaction.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK 4.

<margin>A</margin> For touch does not only report and touch that which is nearby, but it also reports the specific differences of the tangible thing itself, as if it had experienced them; and unless something stands in the way, it might even sense them from a distance. For at the same moment, both the intermediate air and we ourselves perceive the fire, not waiting for the air to be heated first. In fact, a solid body heats up more quickly than the air does; for this reason, it is heated *through* the air rather than *because* of the air. If, therefore, the sensible object <margin>B</margin> has the power to act, and the eye has the power to be acted upon—or however sight works—why would it need another medium in which to exercise its power to act? For that would be nothing other than requiring some kind of hindrance. Indeed, when the sun's light arrives, it is not necessary for the air to be illuminated first and then us; rather, both are illuminated simultaneously. And often, before the object of sight is near, even while it is still elsewhere, it happens that we see it, as if the air were not affected at all; clearly, this intermediate medium has suffered nothing, and the light has not yet traveled <margin>C</margin> to the point where the sight must be applied. And certainly, under this physicalist supposition, it would be difficult to assign a cause for how and why we see the stars and fire at night. But if the soul remains within itself, yet needs light as a staff <note>original: "virga" / "βακτηρίας"; a metaphor for a tool that extends the soul's reach</note> through which it may extend its perception, it would be necessary for perception to be a violent act caused by a certain reverberation of the extended light, and for the sensible color (insofar as it is color) to have the power of reflecting. For in this way, touch would be produced through a medium. <margin>D</margin> Furthermore, this would occur even before any contact, with no medium then intervening. For then the medium would cause knowledge to happen as if by a kind of memory or rather a logical argument; but in reality, it does not happen that way. But if it is necessary for that which is near the sensible object to be affected, and then for that whole affection to proceed through a continuous transmission to the sight, we will face the same objection as that which claimed the medium is first changed and affected by the sensible object—against which we have argued elsewhere.

> *If any material passion <note>original: "passio"; here meaning a physical impression or a "suffering" of change</note> is carried into the medium by sensible things, because it is certainly different from the incorporeal nature within, it therefore confuses the sense by its own vehemence and is never an accommodated harmony—unless, besides that, something spiritual is present either in the medium or at least in the organ of sense. Indeed, that spiritual element accommodated to the sense also appears in the voice. For the fact that the whole voice is perceived everywhere by many at the same moment signifies that it seems to be something spiritual. The universal cause generates such a thing around every sense, but far away, as the life of the world then acts upon subjects opportunely disposed. This is so akin to the sense that as soon as it flourishes by the act of its own universe, the sense itself is simultaneously awakened regarding that act—just as some men are particularly content with friends, and some things excite others to song and dance. That this sense acts immediately upon the humors <note>The bodily fluids thought to determine physical and mental states.</note> of the sensible things is achieved by the same life of the world everywhere, which primarily provides that they are tempered together from that source: just as by the motion of such a humor, such an imagination and vision are moved. Likewise, according to the various movements and positions of the moon, the humors are moved and affected in various ways; and flame is moved by the movement of sulfur <note>Sulfur was historically associated with the active principle of fire and attraction.</note>. To what end, finally, is the eye aimed in the world, even the left one?*

-> Chapter V. <-

<margin>D</margin> **FURTHERMORE**, regarding the sense of hearing, must it be granted that the air is first affected by motion, and then the air nearest to it is affected by the air first making the sound, and similarly that the air is affected step by step all the way to the ear, and thus reaches the sense? Or rather, is the medium affected in these things by accident, namely because it happens to be in between? So that if it were removed from there, and a sound were made once by two bodies striking each other, the sense of this would be immediately excited in us.

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> For touch does not only speak of what is near and touches it, but it also reports the different qualities of the tangible object; and if nothing divides it, it would sense even things far off. For at the same time, the intermediate air and we ourselves perceive the fire, not waiting to learn of it from the air; for the solid body is heated more than the air is. Thus, it is through the air, but not *because* of the air. And if the sight has power even before [the medium], <margin>Β</margin> at least regarding its being affected, or however the sight works, why does it need something else in the middle? Is it not for the power to act? For this would seem to be a hindrance. Or, when the light of the sun is present, the air does not need to be affected first and then us, but it happens simultaneously. And even before something is near the sight, often we see it elsewhere, such that the air is not affected, while the intermediate space suffers nothing, <margin>Γ</margin> and the light has not yet arrived. Regarding the sight, the fire at night and the stars—which are entirely fire—would also touch it. It is difficult to give an account by this [physicalist] hypothesis. Or does the soul remain in itself, needing light like a staff <note>original: "βακτηρίας"</note> to send its perception toward the light? It is right to ask whether these are affections themselves, or if something of life is sent out, and the sensible object is an act of daring <note>The Greek "τολμημά" (daring) here refers to the soul's outward projection into the material world.</note>. * <unclear>We shall say</unclear> <margin>Δ</margin> they are themselves impressions. For in this way, touches occur through a medium, which if they had occurred near at first with nothing in between, and later one looked through a medium, would produce knowledge through memory or rather by syllogism. But now it is not so. But if that which is at the sensible object must be affected, and then by transmission it reaches the sight, it is the same hypothesis: that the medium must first be turned by the sensible object, which has been questioned in other places.

> *If, however, the intermediate space were to be affected passively toward the sensible object, when this is not the case, the affection would not reach the sense. Furthermore, it is not appropriate for the incorporeal nature to be affected in this way. Thus, the composite is less affected unless by some sympathy, or if some soul were in the intermediate space, or the sense organ received the affection. And the same applies to the voice. For the fact that the same thing is heard everywhere by many is a sign that some soul is also there, or some life below the whole, which by its own sense—directed toward the outside—is affected by the things of others in the same way. Just as in our own parts, some are carried toward the outside and others toward the inside. And while one looks toward the outside, another suffers the affections of the moon; and toward the movement of the divinity, the fire is moved, and all things look toward one end.*

<margin>Δ</margin> **CONCERNING** hearing, should it be granted in this way: that the first part [of air] is affected by motion, and the part adjacent to the sound makes the sound, and the air all the way to the ear is affected in the same way, and thus it arrives at the sense? Or is it by accident that the medium is affected—not indeed *because* of the medium—but once a sound is made, as when two bodies strike together, it immediately meets us as perception...
<meta>catchword: perception</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that senses like sight and hearing do not rely on a physical, step-by-step chain reaction through the air, but rather on a universal "sympathy" or spiritual connection within the World Soul. He uses the example of seeing stars at night and hearing a single voice in many places at once to prove that the medium (air) is not the cause of sensation but merely an accidental presence.</summary>

--- Page 482 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of sense perception. Having previously questioned whether air is strictly necessary for vision, he now applies the same skepticism to the sense of hearing, asking if air is the "master" of sound or merely an accidental medium. The text then transitions into a deeper metaphysical commentary on the nature of light as an "act" of the soul.</meta>

-># BOOK FIVE.<-
->P 2<-

Perhaps, indeed, it is necessary for the air to be struck at the beginning, but that which follows afterward—the medium—behaves differently. Here, the air indeed seems to be the master <note>original: "dominus" / "κύριος"; meaning the primary agent or controlling factor</note> of sound. For it would seem that no sound could occur at the start from the collision of two bodies unless the air, struck and driven out by their swift encounter, passed on such a pulse to the adjacent air all the way to the ears and the sense of hearing. But if air is the master of sound, and sound is the pulse of this agitated air, we must ask: by what principle are the differences between voices <margin>B</margin> and sounds determined? For bronze struck against bronze sounds one way, and other bodies colliding sound another. Yet the air is one, and the pulse within it is one; the differences are not measured solely by whether they are large or small. If it is asserted that the authority of the voice and sound belongs to the air because the pulse inflicted upon the air produces the sound, we must respond that this is not effected by the air's nature *as* air. For the air resonates only when it acquires the stability of a solid body before it is dispersed, remaining, as it were, something solid. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, those things which collide by their own motion are sufficient here, and it must be said that the collision and the pulse are themselves the sound reaching the sense. An argument for this view seems to be the sounds that occur inside the bodies of animals, not in the air, but by one part of the animal striking another. Examples include the flexing of bones or their mutual rubbing where no air intervenes, as well as certain internal ruptures and cuttings. <margin>D</margin> But let this be the doubt concerning this matter, the inquiry of which is similar to the previous inquiry regarding vision. And indeed, concerning both vision and hearing, it must be said that the power of sensing consists in a certain sympathy <note>original: "compassione" / "συναισθήσεώς"; a shared feeling or resonance between parts of a whole</note> and mutual consensus of things, as if they were dwelling within the same living being.

<column-break/>

*Light does not depend on the illuminated object, but on the illuminator. Similarly, all life depends not on the animate body, but on the soul, as its own proper act and vigor, even if every external support is lacking. The first body is the celestial fire; its primary quality is light. Therefore, it is so perfect that it exists as an "act" <note>In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic terms, an "act" (actus) is the fulfillment or active expression of a thing's nature</note> rather than merely an active quality. Indeed, this act is so effective that it extends its presence from its own source without being separated from it. This kind of color is also called fire, which, being diffused everywhere, provides and pours around all colors for the eyes. Furthermore, in whatever body under heaven a certain fiery vigor similar to the celestial prevails, light shines out from there as if it were a familiar color. In the presence of the Sun, light heats the air. This heating indeed requires both: the presence of the Sun and the air. But this appropriate heating is a medium between light and color. Heat, certainly, can remain in the air even without the presence of light. Therefore, light can exist in the Sun without air; but the heat left by light in the air will not remain for long, because it is foreign to it. Light, however, is always around the Sun because it is its own. For that which is "proper" is inseparable. But light is surely the property of the Sun, and not of the "diaphanous" <note>original: "diaphani"; the transparent medium, such as air or water</note>, which can indeed become dark. Therefore, light belongs to the Sun itself and the solar body. And rightly so, for it is a certain form in the order of things consisting in itself, which while it aids another subject, is thus a double act: one is the form of the agent alone, the other is additionally dwelling in the patient <note>the "patient" is the object receiving the action</note>. As for light becoming a proper quality of the diaphanous, we have said elsewhere that it is neither received gradually, nor is it retained, nor is it stained or moved along with the medium; nor are lights confused among themselves; therefore, they are not mixed with other qualities. That they are not confused is apparent from the fact that if a single body is placed against three lights, three shadows result in the opposite direction, because the three lights there remain distinct. Furthermore, if a huge tablet with a hole in the middle is placed against three candles, three lights leap back from there in the opposite direction: one straight ahead, the other two intersecting each other crosswise, yet not confused. Similarly, minds and souls joined to each other are not at all confused. Light is rightly neither captured by a subject nor mixed with anything, because all light is an image of the celestial light; and that light is the act of the celestial soul. For just as a word is sent forth from the soul as an act of the imagination stretched outward, in which three things exist—air, motion, and meaning—so also by the intellectual light, the celestial soul pours out most effective acts through all things, in which three things occur: light, heat, and a hidden power. Light arrives from the brightness where there is no heat, and vice versa. But the hidden power in this act, which is most powerful in it, passes through all things and works wonders, not by formally heating or openly illuminating, but by introducing specific virtues.*

### Chapter VI.

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to investigate whether light would exist somewhere if there were no air; for instance, if the Sun should shine upon the surface of bodies, but the medium...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s examination of the medium of perception, moving from sound to a detailed physical and metaphysical analysis of light. He investigates whether light requires air as a substrate or if it exists as an independent "activity" (actus/energeia) of a luminous body.</meta>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEADS. BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin>
...would be entirely a vacuum. This is indeed what happens now by chance, in that it happens that this medium of the body [the air] intervenes. Or perhaps, is it because of the open air itself that [the eye] experiences something else, and the nature of light exists because of the air itself, of which light is a certain affection <note>original: "passio," translating the Greek "pathēma," meaning a state or quality experienced by a subject</note>? If it were its affection, then surely light would not exist unless the "suffering" air <note>The "patient" or "suffering" subject is that which receives an action or quality</note> existed as well. But light does not belong to the air itself primarily, nor by the very reason that it is air. For there is also a brilliant color in every fiery and shining body, and in similar precious stones; but this very thing that 
<margin>B</margin>
flows from that body possessing such a color into another—will it still exist? If this other thing were a vacuum: surely if light is merely a quality, and a quality of something specific (since every quality must exist in a subject), it is necessary to seek light in that body in which it resides. But if light is an "act" <note>original: "actus," translating the Greek "energeia," meaning an active expression or outpouring of power</note> from another source, why would it stop under that body? If we imagine a vacuum, will it not exist and extend itself even further upward? For since it is focused and upright, what prevents it from passing through even if it is carried by nothing and 
<margin>C</margin>
blocked nowhere? But if it is the kind of thing that "falls," it will be carried down of its own accord: for neither the air, nor anything illuminated, will be what draws this from the illuminating source and compels it to go forward. Since it is not even an "accident" <note>A philosophical term for a property that is not essential to a thing's nature</note>, so as to be entirely in another, or a certain affection of another, there must be something that "suffers" it. Otherwise, when the thing that illuminates departs, the light would have to remain in the thing illuminated. But now it goes away: therefore, perhaps it moves forward. To where, then? Or must there be only space? 
<margin>D</margin>
Otherwise, the body of the Sun would lose its own "act" that depends upon it—and that act is light. It is well known that light will not belong to just anyone. It is an act flashing out from a certain subject, yet not passing into a subject [as a permanent change]: rather, if a subject happens to be present, it will experience something under it. Surely, just as life—which is also an act—is an act of the soul, under which something like a body, if present, experiences something; and even when the body is not present, such an act exists—so nothing seems to prevent light from having the same nature, 
<margin>E</margin>
since it is a certain act of a luminous body. For the darkness of the air does not now generate light, nor does the entirely impure companion of the darkness of the earth procreate light: for that would be the same as saying that something would be sweet if only it were mixed with the bitter. Therefore, if anyone should say that light is a change and an affection of the air, he must say in addition that the air itself must be affected differently in this transformation, and that its dark condition, having been changed into something else, is no longer dark. But in fact, the air remains as it is, as one that has truly suffered nothing. And yet, every affection must belong to that which experiences the affection. Therefore, light is not the color of the air, but it exists in itself, while the air stands nearby. And let so much be said concerning this.

<column-break/>

...being a vacuum, and now by chance <note>original: "τῷ συμβεβηκὸς" (tō symbebēkos)</note>, because it happens to be in the illuminated air. But if because of it [the air] entirely and the others, the existence <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" (hypostasin)</note> of light is through the air: for it is an affection <note>original: "πάθημα" (pathēma)</note>, then the affection would not exist if the sufferer did not exist. First, it is not primarily in the air, nor insofar as it is air. For it is also in each body, bright and shining, and indeed there is a luminous use for certain stones. But that which [flows] into something foreign that has such a color—would it increase if that were not there? But if it is only a quality and of a certain kind, if it is not situated in every quality, it is necessary to seek the light in whatever body it is in. But if it is an activity <note>original: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia)</note> from another, why should it not go forward? Or if a body, but also vacuums in between, if it were possible, that light would also reach the beyond. For being itself upright, why will it not try to advance? But if it is also the kind of thing to fall, it would be carried to the outside. Indeed, the air will not be the illuminated thing at all. That which draws from the illuminator, or forces it to go forward, since it is not an accident—so that it is entirely in another, or an affection of another—so there must be the thing that suffers. Or it ought to remain, but it withdraws and goes away; so, either it must go somewhere, or must there only be place? Or how indeed does it act from itself, how does it not go into that? For that which is of the father? Or the light; but if it is of the thing, if indeed light is a certain activity of some kind, starting from something, yet not into a substrate; but it is present to the substrate if it should be there, and even if it is not present, what would prevent it? And it is through light if indeed it is a certain activity of the luminous thing, for even the darkness is of the air. The light was sufficient, but if they are mixed together, the dark and the truly pure, it would be like saying the sweet exists if it were mixed with the bitter. But if one says light is in the affection of the air, one must say the air itself is turned by the turning. Or it would suffer this, not to have become dark <unclear>...</unclear>, but the air remains as it is, as not having suffered at all. But the affection would be an affection of that thing; therefore, it is not even a color in it, but it is present in itself by itself, and the air is present. Let such things be considered.

---

*Just as other bodies always project something out from themselves, namely vapor, or a power, or an image, so a single and similar body emits its own "act" <note>activity/energy</note> outward. And because it does so effectively, such an act is light at a distance, touching external things indeed, and not leaving its own internal fountain. Between the light that is entirely internal to a lucid body, and the heat now made internal to the air, there is light which is partly internal to the shining source and partly proceeding outside: much like speech <note>original: "sermo" / "logos"</note> stands between thought and the finished work. In the moment that light penetrates a soft transparent medium <note>original: "diaphanum"</note>, it simultaneously strikes through even the hardest transparent thing. It is therefore incorporeal, since the hardness of a body does not resist it. Nevertheless, because it is celestial, the earthly obstacle of nature—even if it is less hard—does not receive the light. Therefore, since it is incorporeal, we ought not to attribute the affections of a body to it—that is, approaching, receding, flowing out, flowing through, contracting, or dilating. Rather, wherever a transparent medium is exposed in the presence of a shining source, light exists there immediately, acting there; otherwise, it does not exist.*

<summary>Plotinus argues that light is an incorporeal "activity" (energeia) of a luminous source rather than a physical substance or a permanent change in the air. He concludes that light does not depend on the air as a substrate but exists immediately in any transparent medium when a source is present.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of light and vision, specifically addressing whether light is a physical substance that travels or an "activity" (energeia) that emanates from a source. It follows the previous page's discussion on whether a vacuum would permit sight.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

*To stand, in that place, is not to cease to act, nor yet simply to cease to be, insofar as it is a luminous body. Similar to light is the radial activity of a sight directed into a mirror. Likewise, the vital activity of the soul is directed into the body. Every vital activity is immortal. And that which is directed from our soul into the body accompanies the soul perpetually. And that which flows into the body from the soul of the world <note>The "Anima Mundi" or World Soul, a Neoplatonic concept of a cosmic force that animates the universe</note> likewise follows this soul continually.*

->Chapter VII.<-

---

Does light perish, or does it run back to its source? Perhaps from this inquiry we might find a path to further understanding. For if we saw light in such a way that it was possessed as something proper to the illuminated object, one might perhaps say it perishes. But if light is an "activity" <note>original Greek: "energeia"; the active expression or outpouring of a thing's power</note>, how could it "flow"? For if it flowed and was poured out everywhere—more so than what proceeds from the acting source—if it changed, it would not perish so long as the source of the illumination remained stable. But when the source is moved to another place, the light exists in that other place; not as if a back-flow or a "running-after" occurs, but because that activity exists or ceases to exist there, provided nothing blocks it. For even if the distance were as great as it is from us to the Sun, the light would reach even to you, with nothing preventing it, so long as no obstacle intervened in the space between. There is, on one hand, the internal activity of the luminous bodies—a sort of life of the shining body, its overflowing principle and fountain of activity. On the other hand, there is the activity beyond the limits of the body, which is a second activity—an image <note>original: "eidolon"</note> of the first—and is by no means severed from it. Indeed, every existing thing has an activity which is a likeness of itself: so that while the thing exists, its activity exists, and while it remains, the activity reaches out to distant points. Some reach further, some less; some are weak and faint, while others are hidden. Others are greater and cast themselves far off. And when they proceed to a distance, one must consider the activity to be present there where the agent is powerful and where the activity reaches. Furthermore, one can see this in the eyes of animals that have shining eyes, where light is produced outside the eyes; or in those animals which have a fire gathered within them that shines out into the darkness when they open their senses; but when they close them, there is no light outside. This light has not been destroyed, but it either is or is not outside. It has not "entered back in," nor is it outside except where the fire is directed outward. Rather, it has withdrawn within. Therefore, the light withdrew from itself? No; but only that part which must strike upon another body so as not to act toward the outside. Thus, the light from bodies is an activity of the luminous body proceeding outward. But light itself, entirely inherent in such bodies—which are primarily of such a nature—is an essence according to the form of the primary luminous body. But when such a body is mixed with matter, it provides a need for the activity alone, yet it gives a sort of coloring, so that even that light is, as it were, set apart; and where the source is absent, the activity is also absent. But light must be judged entirely as incorporeal <note>original: "asōmaton"</note>, even though it is an activity of a body...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It must be asked whether light, when the source that illuminates it departs, vanishes immediately, or rather returns into itself. Perhaps from this we shall make progress toward what was proposed. Certainly, if light were in the illuminated body in such a way that it became its own property, one might say it perishes. But if it is an activity <note>original Latin: "actus," translating "energeia"</note> not flowing out from a fountain—otherwise it would flow around and be possessed within, even more than what proceeded from the agent—it will surely not be destroyed,

<margin>B</margin> insofar as that which illuminates remains in its stability. When, however, the source is transferred, the light also exists in another place: not as if a "re-flowing" or a "trans-flowing" occurs, but because that activity exists and is present insofar as nothing stands in its way. For even if the distance were far greater than the distance of the Sun is from us, that light would fill the whole space from the Sun, provided nothing prohibited it and no obstacle hindered it anywhere. There is one activity in the luminous thing, which is like the abundant life of the shining body, its principle and way of acting outwardly.

<margin>C</margin> There is also another activity beyond the boundaries of the luminous body, which is the image of the interior one, a second activity that is by no means abandoned by the first. Indeed, any existing thing has an activity like a likeness of itself: so that as long as the thing itself exists, the activity exists; and while the thing remains, the activity proceeds to distant parts—some further, some shorter; some weak and thin, others hidden. The activities of some things are greater,

<margin>D</margin> and are poured out far away. And when they proceed to remote places, it must be thought that the activity is there, where the agent is powerful and where it runs. Thus we see in animals whose eyes naturally shine, that light flashes out from their eyes; also in animals that possess a fire collected within, when they open themselves, the light shines out in the darkness; and when they close themselves, no light is left outside. This light does not entirely vanish, but it either is or is not on the outside:

<margin>E</margin> what then, does it return into the animal itself? Or should it rather be said that it is simply not outside? Since the fire has not proceeded to external things, but insinuates itself within. Did the light itself, then, insinuate itself? Perhaps not, but only that part [the activity]. When the source that illuminates hides itself, another body now stands in the way, so that it does not act toward the outside. Therefore, the light emanating from bodies is a certain activity of the shining body proceeding outward; but light <note>Possible footnote marker 'f'</note>f entirely inherent in such bodies, which are primarily of such a nature, is an essence according to the form of the primary shining body. When such a body is mixed with matter, it exhibits color; but the activity alone does not exhibit color, but rather a kind of coloration, since it is of another and continually emanates from it—and when the source is absent, its activity is also absent. Thus one must judge light to be entirely incorporeal, even though it is an activity of a body. Wherefore it is not properly...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the soul's relationship to the body and the mechanics of perception. PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> Concerning this, it is said—and especially whether it approaches or departs—that these things behave differently there, for it is like an activity <note>original: "actus" / Greek "energeia"; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the active expression of a thing's essence</note> of the substance itself. For we must also call the image in a mirror an "activity" of that which is seen in the mirror, acting upon that which is capable of being affected. In this case, nothing actually flows out; rather, it transmits itself, and the image appears there. It is like the image of a color shaped in a certain way. If the object moves away, the transparent body no longer has what it previously held when the <margin>B</margin> sight itself was acting upon the mirror. Accordingly, in the soul as well, insofar as it is an activity of the prior soul, the accompanying activity remains as long as the prior soul remains. But if there is a power that is not an activity of the soul itself, but arises *from* that activity—such as the life we have called proper to the body—is it perhaps like light already mixed with bodies? Perhaps we shall say that this light remains, because that which creates color is mixed; but what of the life proper to the body? Perhaps the body retains this, while another life is seen <margin>C</margin> while the soul is present, for nothing can be devoid of soul. Therefore, when the body perishes and is no longer sufficient for this life—whether it be the life supplied until now or some other that might be present—how does life still remain? What then? Has it perished? Perhaps even this has not perished; for this, too, is a kind of image of an illumination. It must only be said that it is no longer there: <note>original Greek: "της εἰδώλων γὰρ ἐκλάμψεως καὶ τῶν ἐκεῖ οὐκ ἔτι ὄντα μόνον"</note> "for it is only of the radiance of images and of the things no longer there."

Since the world is a universal and sensible body, nothing sensible can truly be placed outside the world. If you were to imagine some body outside that communicated in no way with the world, it would not be perceived by our worldly senses. But if it communicated in any way, it would no longer be outside, but inside. Just as when a toe suffers, the groin immediately suffers with it—and these parts more so than the knees, even though they are further away—this happens because they are in the same living being, and are specifically attuned to one another. Similarly, the stomach suffers when the brain is affected, and vice versa. By a similar logic, even senses that are far apart respond to the gentlest movements of their sensible objects, even if the medium between them does not suffer; this is brought about by the single, continuous nature of the world. Just as with a long, taut string <note>original: "nerui"; literally "nerve" or "sinew," but also used for musical strings or bowstrings</note>: if the lowest part is plucked, the highest part is immediately vibrated. From this it also happens that we imagine a series of events sent down from the heavens, or even future events, or we often imitate them by a certain instinct; and we sometimes anticipate a friend coming toward us through a hidden sense before he arrives.

### Chapter VIII

<margin>A</margin> If there were a body outside the heavens, and an eye from this world were directed toward it—with nothing preventing its sight—it is doubtful whether it could see that body, since it would share no "sympathy" <note>term: <term>sympathy</term> (Latin: compassio / Greek: sympatheia); the Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected like organs in a single animal</note> or communion of experience with it. For now, the communion of experience exists in things because of the nature of the single living being <note>The "Anima Mundi" or World Soul</note> common to all things everywhere. Perhaps if "sympathy" regarding sensible things and the senses themselves are judged to belong to the nature of a single living being, then this world would not see that body at all, unless <margin>B</margin> perhaps that external body were said to be a limb of this living being of ours. For if it were its limb, perhaps it would see it. But if it were not its limb, yet were a colored body and possessed the other qualities that the world has, and were thus conforming to the sensory instrument of this world, someone might think it could be seen. But even so, it would not be seen, provided the hypothesis is correct—unless someone tries to dismiss the hypothesis by arguing it would be absurd if the sight did not clearly behold a color that was present, and similarly if the <margin>C</margin> other senses did not act toward the objects present to them. We, however, shall say why this absurdity appears to us: perhaps because here, being both in one and...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it has departed in the true sense, nor is it present: but these things exist in another way, and it is itself an activity of that soul. For the image in the mirror must also be called an activity of the thing seen, acting upon that which is capable of being affected, without any physical "flowing": but if it is present, that image also appears there, and it exists in such a way as the color of an image, shaped in this way and ending there, if it possesses <margin>B</column> that which is visible and sensible. But once it no longer provides what is needed, the thing seen is gone. But also in the case of the soul, insofar as it is an activity of another soul, while the prior soul remains, the subsequent activity will also remain. But if it is not an activity, but *from* an activity—the kind we call the life of the body—then is it not like the light mixed with bodies, or does it not do the same things as the colors produced by mixing? And regarding the life of the <margin>C</margin> body; or does another soul possess what is modeled after it, when the body is destroyed? For the things that belong to the soul, or come from it, can exist while the body is being destroyed, and it will not be enough for it that it was given, if it still suffices, and life no longer remains: or rather, it was not destroyed, or it is as follows.

<margin>A</margin> If there were a body outside the heaven, and some sight from there, with nothing hindering the seeing, would it not behold that which is not "sympathetic" to it, if indeed "sympathy" exists because the living being is a shared thing? And because the things perceiving and the things perceived belong to one thing? And the senses, in this way, would not exist unless the body were a part of this living being. And if it were, the same things would happen if <margin>B</margin> it were not a part, but a colored body, having the other qualities, just as the things here are of the same kind as the organ. Or even so, it is not a sensible hypothesis, unless someone, by that very fact, were present to remove the hypothesis. It would be strange, he says, if the sight does not see color when it is present, and the other senses, when the sensible objects are present to them, do not act toward them. But how does this strangeness appear <margin>C</margin> to us? Or is it because being here in one and...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into "cosmic sympathy," the idea that the entire universe is a single, interconnected living organism. The author is exploring how perception works across this vast system and whether the parts of the world communicate because they are similar or because they are bound together by a single soul.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

Being of one <note>original: "ἑνὸς" (henos); referring to the One or a single unified principle</note>, we do and suffer <note>original: "πάσχομεν" (paschomen); in a philosophical sense, this means 'to be acted upon' or to experience</note> these things. This, then, must be considered: whether it is because of this, and if it is done sufficiently, it has been demonstrated. If not, it must be demonstrated through other means. That the living being <note>original: "ζῶον" (zōon)</note> is sympathetic to itself is clear. And if it were a living being, it would receive impressions as parts of a single living being. But if someone should say it is through similarity—yet perception according to the nature of the living being, and sensation itself, exists because the same thing partakes in what is similar. The organ <note>original: "ὄργανον" (organon); a tool or bodily instrument of sense</note> is similar to it. Thus, perception will be the soul's apprehension through organs similar to the objects of sense. If, then, being a living being, it perceives not only the things within itself but also those similar to the things within itself, it will apprehend them insofar as it is a living being. However, the objects of sense will not be the things themselves, but things similar to those within it; or perhaps the objects of sense are apprehended in this way as being similar because the soul itself has made them similar, so that they might be fitting. Thus, if the soul there is the creator, there would be other things. And the things hypothesized there to be similar would be nothing to the soul. But indeed, the absurdity <note>original: "ἀτοπία" (atopia); literally 'placelessness' or logical inconsistency</note> shows the contradiction in the hypothesis, as it is the cause of it. For at the same time, one would be calling it soul and not soul, kindred and not kindred, similar and dissimilar. So, it allows for opposites within itself, and it would not even be a hypothesis. For if the soul is in this, so that it places everything in everything, it makes it both another and not another, and nothing and not nothing, and perfect and not perfect. Therefore, the hypothesis must be abandoned, as one cannot seek what follows from it when the very thing hypothesized destroys and annuls itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Being now of one, we act and suffer <note>original: "pati- / mur"; to experience an effect</note> these things. Therefore, this must be considered: whether there is something else to be brought forward besides this. If this satisfies us, it is already demonstrated; if not, it must be demonstrated again through other means. That the living being <note>original: "animal"</note> agrees with itself in its experiences is quite manifest. And if everything mentioned is one living being, it is now enough; all things will be parts of one, and insofar as they are parts of one living thing, they will agree with one another. But if someone should argue <margin>B</margin> that this body perceives the world only because of a certain similarity, the perception itself will nonetheless be according to the nature of a living being and a sense, because it possesses that very similarity: for its instrument is similar. Therefore, sense will be the soul's perception through instruments similar to the things to be perceived. If, then, the existing living being perceives not only those things which are in itself, but also things similar to its own, surely by the reason that it is a living being, it will perceive. However, the things to be <margin>C</margin> perceived will not be perceived insofar as they are its own, but insofar as they are similar. But perhaps rather the things to be perceived will be perceived in this way because of similarity, because that same soul has rendered them similar, so that they might be familiar. Therefore, if the author there is a soul entirely different, certainly the things imagined to be similar there have nothing to do with it. But indeed, the absurdity in the hypothesis declares that there is a contradiction, as if this itself were the cause of the absurdity: for it says that it is <margin>D</margin> at once soul and not soul, kindred and not kindred, similar and again dissimilar. Therefore, since it includes a total contradiction within itself, the hypothesis is not to be judged as correct. For it is also supposed that the soul is in this. Wherefore it posits both a universe and not a universe, and again something else and not something else; likewise nothing and not nothing (namely, outside itself); and finally, perfect and imperfect at the same time. Therefore, such a hypothesis is to be rejected, because it is not permitted to seek a logical consequence from it: for the very thing which is hypothesized is, through that very hypothesis, destroyed and perishes within itself.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how the soul interacts with the physical world. Plotinus is refuting the common ancient idea that the soul is a passive surface that gets "stamped" by external objects.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FOUR,
### BOOK SIX.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FOUR,
### BOOK SIX.

->ON sensation and memory.<-
->On sensation and memory.<-

Sensible forms are not imprinted upon the soul. Our countryman Boethius <note>original: "Boetius"; refers to the 6th-century philosopher Boethius, who discussed this in *The Consolation of Philosophy*</note> proves in his *Consolation* that forms are not imprinted on the soul by sensible objects like a seal in wax; we also prove this in our *Theology* using the commentaries of Themistius <note>Themistius was a 4th-century commentator on Aristotle; the "Theology" likely refers to the translator's own commentary, possibly Marsilio Ficino</note>. Plotinus thinks that if the forms of the soul were thus imprinted, they would take on the nature of a sensible object. Therefore, if the form of the sky were imprinted upon our vision, five absurdities would follow: First, it would not be necessary to direct the eye toward the sky any longer. Second, we would not measure the distance between the sky and the eye—indeed, we would not even think there was a distance. Third, the sky would not appear wider than the eye. Fourth, we would not see the sky itself, but perhaps only this form of the sky within the soul. Fifth, we would not be able to distinguish an object if it were placed directly against the sense organ.
Chapter I.

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial S containing a seated figure, likely a scholar or philosopher, amidst foliage.</image-desc> If we say that sensations are not certain formations or impressions made in the soul, we must consequently say that memory is not the preservation of teachings and sensations, as if certain figures were being kept in the mind, since no such thing was received from the outside in the first place. Therefore, both sensation and memory pertain to the same argument.
<margin>B</margin>
For one must either say that forms are created in the mind and these same forms are preserved (if indeed you remember); or if you deny one of these, you must not admit the other either. We, therefore, who concede neither, are compelled to investigate what the mode of each might be: since we say that no figure of a sensible thing is made in the soul, nor that the mind is shaped, we do not admit that memory is the guardianship of a figure that was once impressed and remains there. If we contemplate what happens in the most clear of the senses <note>Plotinus often uses vision as the primary example of how perception works</note>, 
<margin>C</margin>
perhaps by transferring what we find there to the other senses, we will discover what we seek. It is evident everywhere that when we see something, we look to where the object is located, where the visible thing itself is placed in our sight, as if the perception occurs there, and the soul looks outward. This indeed indicates (as I believe) that no form has been made or is being made in the soul, and that the soul does not see by virtue of receiving an impression, such as wax receives from a seal. 
<margin>D</margin>
For there would be no need to look further outward if the soul already possessed the appearance of the thing to be seen within itself, and if it saw specifically because the species <note>original: "species"; here meaning the visual form or image</note> had entered into it. Furthermore, when the mind applies a distance to the thing it sees, and perceives how far away it sees it, it sufficiently indicates that it does not have within itself the thing it gazes upon; otherwise, since it would be no distance from itself, it would not perceive it as being placed far off. Likewise, it could not judge through a form received within <note>original Greek: "τὰ αὐτῇ, οὐδὲν ἀφεστηκὸς ἀφ᾽ αὑτῆς, ὡς πόῤῥω ὂν βλέποι, τὸ, τὶ μέγεθός αὐτῷ ἐστιν ἐξῆς" — "it would see it as nothing distant from itself, not as something far off, nor would it see its size or what follows"</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial T showing a landscape with figures under a tree.</image-desc> If we do not say that sensations are impressions, nor like seals <note>original: "σφραγῖδας" (sphragidas)</note> produced in the soul, we will speak again of memory in accordance with this: that it is the retention of lessons and sensations, where a "stamp" <note>original: "τύπου" (typou)</note> remains in the soul that does not stay when the object is present; for the same logic would apply to both. Or if we say one is not given, we should not say the other is either. But we who say neither must necessarily seek the manner of each: since we say that no stamp is made in the soul or in what is around it during sensation, we do not say that memory is a collection of images. If we should observe what happens in the most vivid sensation, perhaps by transferring our findings to the other senses, we might find what we seek. It is clear that whenever we receive a sensation through sight, we see there where we direct our vision, or where the visible object is situated. Thus, the evidence of perception occurs there, with the soul looking toward the outside. This happens, I believe, from no stamp being made there in the soul. For if it were by receiving a seal, as one might look at a ring's mark in wax, it would not need to look outside; rather, having the form of the seen object within itself, it would look at the stamp that entered there. But if it indeed adds distance to the vision, and the soul says how great the image is, how could it see it as being far off if it were in the soul itself and not distant from it?

<summary>Plotinus argues that perception and memory do not function like a "wax seal" where objects stamp images onto a passive soul. Instead, he asserts that the soul is an active force that looks outward to perceive objects where they actually exist in space.</summary>
<keywords>perception, memory, soul, wax seal metaphor, vision, distance, Plotinus, Enneads, Neoplatonism</keywords>
