He argues that the soul is not a passive recipient of "stamps" from the physical world but an active judge of external reality.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<language>English translation from Greek and Latin</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<page-num>453</page-num>
<header>BOOK SIX.</header>

How could it be said that the soul is equal to the object, or that it is a portion? For example, the four-footed creature <note>original: "τετραπὸν"; a common philosophical example of a physical category</note>, or the things within it, so that some are powers and others are the greatest of all. If we were to take the form of what we see, we would not be looking at the things themselves that we see, nor would we see them by a void of blood <note>original: "αἵματι δὲ ἐρημώσεως"; this Greek OCR likely contains a transcription error or a corrupted reference to the physical makeup of the eye</note>. Regarding these forms, it would follow that the things themselves are one thing, but the things previously seen are another; and altogether, as it is said, as if vision were something still placed upon the pupil. But by establishing an internal Idea, one must see the colors clearly; it is much more necessary to transfer this concept to the soul. For if we placed the "stamp" or form of the visible object within the soul, that form would be in the bodies, and the bodies would be Ideas. But how can one see if there is no internal image? Is it necessary for the act of seeing to be a "stamp" placed elsewhere, or as something not yet placed, like the heavy tones of a voice, or perhaps they are placed, but vision itself is not a passive placement.

If indeed it is not this way, the soul speaks concerning vision through the powers it possesses. Either it is a "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" (pathos/passio) means being passive—the state of being acted upon by an external force</note> or it is like those who are observing, or spoken of as an "acting" power. For whenever the soul perceives with intensity, it is both the visible and the audible. As if in the spirit <note>term: spirit (pneuma); in ancient medicine and philosophy, this was a thin, vaporous substance that carried sensory information through the nerves</note>, but perhaps these are not even sensations, but activities <note>original: "energeiai"</note> concerning that which they are by nature. For those who lack faith, these things are not pursued, nor is there a change in the power of knowing each thing. It does not "suffer" or undergo a change, but in knowing, each of the things produced nearby is seen, or perhaps in the same manner as the rulers of these things, thinking that perception happens upon it. Or perhaps a "stamp" is made in the air, a certain striking of things being reported: for example, of colors, or things written by the voice, making the powers and the essence of the soul like one who reads "stamps" written in the air, coming close to them, just as those who naturally come to taste and smell. Some are passions, while others are the specific sensations of them and judgments; the sensations are the knowledge of these passions. For the knowledge of things understood by the intellect, it is even more free from passion, not from within like ambassadors, but things from the outside are observed, and those are rather activities, and more sovereign, for they move the soul itself, just as each thing is acted upon. In this infinite way, the soul itself dives in and asks questions; and both things become one in others.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> how great the external thing is, nor even that it is entirely so large, such as how great the heaven is: because the form received within cannot be so great. But what is most significant of all: if we received the shapes of those things we see inside ourselves, it would not be permitted to discern those very things we look upon, but rather their images and shadows. And so it would happen that some things would be what they are in reality, but others would be what appear to us. Truly, it is generally held that we cannot discern an object placed directly against the pupil, but can only see it when it is at a distance; this same principle must be transferred even more so to the soul. <margin>B</margin> For if we placed the shape of the thing to be seen in the soul, it would not see that spectacle at all with which it was being marked. For it is necessary for these to be two distinct things: that which sees, and that which is seen. Therefore, it must be that the thing seeing looks at a shape placed elsewhere, and not placed within itself. For this reason, it is necessary that vision is not something placed *upon* the thing, but rather *not* placed upon it, if there is to be any vision at all.

---

## *To sense is not to be passive toward sensible things, but to act upon them. Chapter II.*

> *The soul, since it is excellently superior to sensible things without any proportion, and does not communicate with them in matter or nature, never receives forms from them. Since it must judge rightly in the act of sensing—and "passion" <note>passive reception</note> confuses judgment—it suffers nothing from the objects. If any passive effect does happen, it reaches the body and the spirit: when this spirit is thus struck or affected by the external world, the soul, being present, immediately perceives such affections. To perceive, however, is not to "suffer," but rather to act—that is, to nourish the spirit in one way or another, and to bring forth the forms of sensible things (as Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the soul's active role</note> says) without being changed. Intellect is even further removed from passion than sense; for it possesses internal forms and does not turn toward the outside.*

---

<margin>A</margin> **IF**, therefore, sensation is such, it remains to inquire how this is so. Does the soul perhaps speak of these things which it does not possess? Surely it does. For this is the property of power: not to "suffer" or be acted upon, but to be strong, and to carry out its own purpose. In this way, I believe, the visible and the audible will be discerned by someone: not indeed if they are certain shapes, but rather if they are not shapes, nor "passions" <note>passive states</note>, but actions concerning that which they were naturally designed for. But we, distrusting that any power can know its object unless it is struck by it, meanwhile make it so that by moving close, the neighbor "suffers" <margin>B</margin> but does not know: a thing which the soul ought to overcome by the gift of nature, not be overcome by. By the same logic, we must judge concerning hearing: a shape, specifically a certain distinct pulse, is made in the air like the articulation of letters written there by the one who brought forth the voice. But the power and essence of the soul reads these shapes written in the air, as it were, by coming very close to them, where they can finally be perceived naturally. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, regarding taste and smell, some things are "passions" (physical effects), but others are the knowledge of those passions—namely, the senses and the judgments of the passions, which indeed differ from the passions themselves. The knowledge of things understood by the mind is even more free from being affected or formed by external things. For these, conversely, proceed as if from the innermost part, whereas sensible things are reached from the outside; therefore, the former are more truly actions, and sovereign actions at that. <margin>D</margin> For they belong to the soul itself, and the soul itself performs each of these. But whether the soul sees itself as two things, and as if another; and the intellect as one, and both as two in one—this must be debated elsewhere.

<vocab>Plotinus, Enneads, Sensus, Anima, Perception, Vision, Iamblichus, Action, Passion, Form</vocab>

<summary>This page argues that perception is an active power of the soul (action) rather than a passive reception of physical impressions (passion). Plotinus explains that if the soul were merely "stamped" by objects, we could not perceive the vast scale of things like the sky.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, perception, active soul, Iamblichus, vision, hearing, sensory judgment, Neoplatonism</keywords>

--- Page 489 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into how the soul perceives and remembers. On the previous page, Plotinus argued against the idea that vision is merely a physical "stamp" on the eye. Here, he extends that argument to memory, suggesting that the soul does not store images like a filing cabinet, but rather uses its own internal power to "reanimate" its knowledge of both the divine and physical worlds.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS IV.

->*To remember and to recollect is not to preserve and repeat the forms of things once impressed upon the soul.* Chapter III.<-

When they say that the soul—being a medium between incorporeal and corporeal things—holds the forms of both within itself, we should not understand these forms as accidents lying hidden in the soul like letters on a tablet, whether they were inscribed at some point or are innate. For the divine nature of the soul neither undergoes new impressions, nor does it merely reserve the principles <term>rationes</term> <note>original: "rationes"; here referring to the "logoi" or the formative, rational blueprints of reality</note> it has from the beginning as if they were distinct from its own nature, like external qualities. Rather, as we have said elsewhere, just as there are natural substantial powers in souls—such as intellect, reason, imagination, sense, and vegetative powers—so too does the soul possess the principles of things to be known as essential powers, much as it possesses the seminal principles of the limbs. Therefore, when the soul meditates on something, it brings itself out from its natural virtue into a natural act concerning that very thing. If it meditates on the same thing more attentively and longer, it conforms itself more strongly to it, and this is what it means to remember; from this, it also recollects more easily.

---

<margin>A</margin> After this, we must speak concerning memory. First of all, it is not to be wondered at—or rather, it is indeed a wonder, yet not incredible—what we attribute to such a power of the soul: namely, that while it receives nothing into itself, it nevertheless notices those things which it did not receive. For the nature of the soul is the reason <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος"</note> of all intelligible things; it is the last of the things in the intelligible realm, but the first of the things in the sensible universe. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, it inclines toward both: from the higher things it is well-affected and brought back to life; by the lower things, it is deceived by a certain resemblance and, as if charmed, it slips away. Since it is situated in the middle, it naturally perceives both. It is said to "understand" the higher things when it is called back into memory, provided it applies itself to them. It knows them because, in a way, it *is* these very things. <margin>C</margin> Certainly, it does not know them by placing them in itself as if in a seat, but by possessing and intuiting them in a certain way. Because the soul is these things more obscurely, it emerges more clearly from a sort of obscure habit as if awakened, and proceeds from potentiality into act. Similarly, by adapting sensible things to itself, it causes them to shine forth and places them before the eyes; for the power of the soul was prepared for this even beforehand, and it distributes these things. <margin>D</margin> When, therefore, it is strengthened toward something it has become accustomed to, it is affected by that thing for a long time as if it were present—and the more it is strengthened, the longer it remains. For this reason, children are said to have better memories, because they do not quickly let go, but keep the object before their eyes for a long time; they are not yet distracted by many things but lean heavily upon a few. However, those whose thought and power are turned toward many things pass over them as if running, never standing still. <margin>E</margin> Furthermore, if the forms of things remained "stamped" in the soul, a great number of them would not diminish memory. Moreover, if the forms merely resided there, we would not need "consideration" to recollect them; nor would we need to recollect them repeatedly after having forgotten them, if the figures remained there. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, meditation itself, which helps in recalling and resuming, shows that what is acquired here is nothing other than a certain strengthening and vigor of the soul. This is just like the exercises of the hands or feet used to perform certain tasks more easily; the ability does not "sit" in the hands or feet, but the limbs are made readier through a continuous habit. Moreover, when you do not remember after hearing something once or twice, but do so after hearing it many times, that which you did not hold when first heard...

<column-break/>

Now that these things have been said, we must next speak of memory. First, we should say whether it is more a matter of wonder—or a wonder indeed, but incredible—that by such a power of the soul, receiving nothing into itself, it perceives things it does not possess. For the soul is the reason of all things, the last reason of the intelligibles, but within the intelligible part of the soul. It is the first of the things in the sensible world, if indeed one might say it holds both in each way. From the higher things, it is itself and is reanimated; by the lower things, it is deceived by a likeness, or as if by a charm. Being in the middle, it perceives both, and is said to "intellect" when it comes into memory of those things which it becomes. It knows by being inclined to perceive; for it knows either by being there with those things, or by having them in a certain way, or by seeing them. And being these things more obscurely, it becomes clearer from that obscurity, as if by awakening more distinctly, going from potentiality into act. And again, in some way, by fitting the sensible things to itself, it makes them shine out from itself. It works to put them before the eyes, ready as it were, and as if the power itself were in labor. When, therefore, it is strengthened toward something currently appearing, it is disposed toward it as if it were present for a long time. and the more it is always so. This is why children are said to be more "mnemonic," because they do not depart, but keep things down before their eyes and are not distracted by many things. But when the intellect and power are directed toward many things, it is as if they run past and do not remain. If the "stamps" <note>original: "τύποι"</note> remained, the multitude of them would not follow or affect memory. Furthermore, if the stamps remained, there would be no need for inquiry in order to recollect, nor would it be necessary to recollect later after forgetting if they remained. In addition to these things, exercises for retrieval show that what is happening involves the powers of the soul. Just as with the gymnastics of the hands or feet to act easily—which does not lie in the hands or feet, but is the result of the coordination that occurs. For why does one not remember after hearing once or twice, but does after many times, and holds what he did not hold when first hearing?

<summary>Plotinus argues that memory is an active power of the soul's vigor rather than a passive storage of "stamps" or "imprints." He explains that the soul, positioned between the divine and physical worlds, remembers by strengthening its internal focus and "awakening" its inherent knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>memory, recollection, soul, intelligible world, sensible world, formative principles, potentiality and act, Plotinus</keywords>

--- Page 490 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus's psychological inquiry from Book Four, specifically focusing on the mechanism of memory. On the previous page, he established that the soul is an active power rather than a passive recipient of physical impressions. Here, he specifically critiques the "wax tablet" model of the mind, arguing that memory is a strengthening of the soul's own internal energy rather than a storage of physical "stamps."</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

->**CHAPTER III (Continued)**<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Memory is necessary not only for things we saw at the beginning, but also for things we recall frequently.</margin>

**A** ...then, after a long time, you suddenly remember. This does not happen because you previously received the individual parts of a shape—for if that were the case, you would simply be remembering those parts—but rather, it is as if the memory is suddenly completed by a final hearing or a specific meditation that carries it through. These instances certainly prove that the power of the soul is being summoned, through which we remember; it is being "strengthened," either in a general sense or toward a specific object.

**B** Indeed, when memory provides us not only with those things we have specifically practiced, but also suggests or returns many other things—accustoming itself, as it were, to certain judgments—whereby from the recovery of one single thing, many other things are much more easily recovered. What other cause can one give for this kind of memory, other than that the soul's own power has been strengthened? Certainly, if the "forms" <term>forms: the mental shapes or concepts of things</term> <note>original: "formae" / "εἴδη"</note> of things merely remained in the mind like physical objects, it would indicate a weakness <note>meaning a passive state of "undergoing" something</note> rather than a potent capacity.

**C** For when something is marked by many impressions, it is shaped in a specific way; and since the "impression" of a figure is a type of passion <term>passion: in ancient philosophy, this refers to a passive state of being acted upon by an external force</term> <note>original: "passio" / "πάθος"</note>, it would follow that whatever has "suffered" the most impressions would be the best at remembering. However, the exact opposite is clearly the case. In no other kind of work does practice make the subject *more* liable to passivity; rather, exercise makes the sense more capable of action. Just as an eye sees not because it is weak, but because it possesses a rich power for acting, so too with the mind.

**D** This is why the elderly are weaker in their senses and also in their memory. Therefore, there is a certain "rigor" or "valor" <note>referring to mental strength or vitality</note> belonging to both sense and memory. Furthermore, since the senses are not merely impressions of shapes upon the soul, how could memory be the "conservation" of things that were never actually deposited within it from the start? But if the faculty of memory is a kind of preparation for being "ready" to think of something, why do we not recall things all at once, but rather one after another? It is because we must apply the power itself and direct it with intention.

**E** We see this same thing happen in other powers, which are prepared to accomplish what they are capable of doing. Some do their duty suddenly, while others must first "collect themselves" before they perform their task. Many people who are intellectually sharp are not necessarily good at remembering, because the power of the two is not the same—just as a boxer is not necessarily a runner. Different "ideas" or capacities dominate in different people. Yet, there is nothing to stop a person with an abundance of soul-power from "reading back" their own thoughts, so to speak.

**F** Finally, the fact that the soul is not subject to "magnitude" <note>physical size or spatial dimensions</note> shows that whatever exists in the soul does not exist through "passion" <note>being stamped/acted upon</note>, but through "efficacy" <note>active power</note>. In general, everything concerning the soul is of a more wonderful nature than is suspected by those who have never diligently investigated these matters. People are often deceived by a superficial similarity to physical things—moving from what they perceive with their senses to conclusions about the soul.

**G** This is why they imagine that letters are inscribed on the soul as if on little tablets or books; they think of the senses and memory in this way. Truly, those who are affected by this view—whether they believe the soul is a physical body or something incorporeal—are entirely ignorant of how many absurdities follow from that false assumption.

<column-break/>

**A** ...then, after a long time, you already hold it. For this does not happen because you previously accepted the parts of the figure—for you would have remembered those too—but rather this is effected as if suddenly, from a final hearing or meditation bringing it to completion. These things surely testify that a power of the soul is being provoked, through which we remember, and it is as if it is being corroborated <note>strengthened or reinforced</note> either simply, or toward something specific.

**B** Then truly, when memory supplies us not only with those things we have meditated upon, but also suggests or restores many things—accustomed, clearly, to certain judgments—whence from the resumption of one thing, many others are also much more easily resumed. What other cause of memory of this kind can anyone bring forward, other than that the power of the soul itself has now been corroborated? Surely, if the forms of things seemed to indicate a weakness in the soul rather than a potentiality...

**C** ...for that which is marked by very many forms is made such in that way. And since the impression of a figure is a certain passion <note>a state of being acted upon</note>, it follows that what has suffered the most is also the most mindful. However, the contrary of this manifestly happens. For nowhere does exercise for a certain task render that which is exercised more subject to passion; since even in the senses, it is not that which is weak that discerns, like an eye, but that in which a more abundant power for acting is present.

**D** Wherefore the elderly are both weaker in their senses and similarly in their memory also. Therefore, there is a certain rigor and valor of sense and memory. Furthermore, since the senses are not certain impressions of figures in the soul, in what way can memory be the conservation of those things which were not even deposited within it from the beginning?

**E** But if the faculty of memory is a certain preparation for readiness, why do we not resume the same things both at once and suddenly, but rather in succession? Because, clearly, it is necessary to apply the power itself and to intend it. For we see this happen in other powers also, which are indeed prepared to perform that which they are able to do. And partly indeed suddenly, but partly truly if they have first collected themselves, they expedite their duty.

**F** Very many people, however, do not seem to be both acute and mindful, since the power of each is not the same: just as the boxer and the runner are not the same. For some ideas dominate in one, others in another. Nevertheless, nothing prevents a man having certain excesses of soul from, as it were, re-reading his own things... finally, the fact that it is established that the soul is not subject to magnitude shows entirely that whatever is in the soul is not there by passion, but by efficacy.

**G** And entirely, whatever things are around the soul, they hold themselves in a certain wonderful manner, otherwise than men suspect, who have never diligently investigated these things, and otherwise than those who manifestly signify as "accessors" <note>those who hold a superficial view</note> passing from those things which are sensed to those [mental things], deceiving themselves by a certain similarity. Whence, just as letters are inscribed in certain tablets or little books, they think similarly of the senses and memory. And indeed, those who are so affected—whether they posit the soul as a body or as incorporeal—are utterly ignorant of how many absurdities follow from that hypothesis.

<summary>Plotinus argues that memory is an active, vital power of the soul ("efficacy") rather than a passive storage of physical impressions ("passion") on a "wax tablet." He uses the example of physical exercise and the failing senses of the elderly to show that memory requires mental strength and focus rather than a capacity to be "stamped" by external objects.</summary>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FOUR
### BOOK VII

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FOUR
### BOOK VII
#### ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL
#### <note>original: "De animi immortalitate" / "ΠΕΡΙ ἀθανασίας ψυχῆς"</note>

->Each one of us is entirely immortal, if indeed the soul itself is immortal. Chapter I.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut headpiece depicting a central face surrounded by elaborate symmetrical scrolls of foliage, flowers, and fruit.</image-desc>

The soul relates to the body in two ways: partly as a certain substantial form <term>substantial form: the essential nature or organizing principle that makes a thing what it is</term> <note>original: "substantialis quaedam species"</note> to matter—since through its presence, a certain balanced temperature of the humors and a vital spirit is born in the body—and partly as a user to an instrument, in so far as it moves the body according to its will; and thus it is separable from the body, and already in a sense separate.

---

<image-desc>Left column starts with an ornamental woodcut initial 'V' featuring scrolling vines. Right column starts with an ornamental woodcut initial 'Ε' (Epsilon) depicting a human figure amidst foliage.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin>
Whether each of us is immortal, or perishes entirely, or if one part is fleeting while another is perpetual—and which part is truly ourselves—one can learn by contemplating the order of nature in this manner. A human being is certainly not something entirely simple, but possesses a soul and a body, whether as an instrument or <margin>B</margin> joined to us by some other condition. It must be proposed and granted that the nature and essence of each are distinct. The body, being composite, is shown by reason to be unable to remain forever, and is perceived by the senses to be utterly dissolved and scattered, since whatever is in it returns to its own kind, changing from one thing to another, <margin>C</margin> and perishing—especially when the soul, which usually holds it together, is no longer present in the physical mass. Indeed, if any body is left alone, it is not yet truly one thing, since it can still be dissolved into form and matter, from which even simple bodies must be composed. Furthermore, since all bodies necessarily have magnitude, they consequently perish when reduced to their smallest parts. Therefore, if the body is a part of us, we are not <margin>D</margin> immortal in every respect; but if it is our instrument, it must be of such a nature as to be granted to us for a time. The principal thing, and the man himself, will be either related to the body as form is to matter—if indeed it is as a form to the body as matter—or it will be like one using the body as a kind of instrument. In either case, the soul is primarily the man himself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Whether each of us is immortal, or perishes entirely, or if some parts of him are eternal and others are not—and if so, which ones—one might learn by examining the matter according to nature. Now, a human being would certainly not be just a body, but the body is his, or he has something about the <margin>B</margin> body, whether as a kind of instrument for us, or attached in some other way; but one must define the nature and essence established for each. Now the body, insofar as it is composite, and according to the reason derived from it, is able to remain [only so long], being subject to dissolution and melting, and undergoing all kinds of destruction, as each of the forms <margin>C</margin> moves toward its own kind, destroying one another and changing into something else and perishing, especially when the soul, which persuades them to be friendly <note>meaning the soul harmonizes the competing physical elements</note>, is not present in the masses. Even if each thing were to become a single unit and be left alone, it is still subject to dissolution into shape and matter, from which even simple bodies must have their compositions. Moreover, having magnitude since they are bodies, they are cut up and go toward nothingness, <margin>D</margin> and in this way they would undergo destruction. So, if this is a part of us, we are not entirely immortal; but if it is an instrument, it must be granted a certain time, being trustworthy in its nature. The most sovereign part, and the man himself, would be either as form to matter—in the sense of the form's relationship to the body—or as the user to the instrument. In either case, the soul is the man himself.

<summary>This page introduces Plotinus's argument for the immortality of the soul by distinguishing the soul's simple, unified nature from the composite, perishable nature of the body. Plotinus argues that whether the soul is the "form" of the body or its "user," the soul constitutes the true essence of a human being.</summary>
<keywords>immortality, soul, body, substantial form, composition, dissolution, Neoplatonism, Plotinus</keywords>

--- Page 492 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus's Fourth Ennead, Book Seven, which is a foundational text regarding the immortality of the soul. The previous page introduced the soul as the "user" of the body; here, Plotinus and his translator Marsilio Ficino argue that the soul cannot be material (a body) because matter lacks the inherent power to organize life or consciousness.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

*No body, insofar as it is a body, possesses its own innate life; however, the soul does. Therefore, the soul is not a body. Could it then be made of a body or bodies, since it is of a more excellent nature? Chapter II.*

*A body by its very nature is capable of being dissolved; the soul, by its own nature, binds the body together and reconciles opposites while mixing them in a certain rational way. It is neither dissoluble nor a body, nor is it conceived from a specific mixture of bodies; rather, the ordered changes in bodies proceed from the soul. We shall be very brief in this book, for we have written most extensively on these same matters in our Theology <note>original: "Theologia" — This refers to Marsilio Ficino’s own massive work, the "Platonic Theology," where he argues for the soul's immortality in much greater detail.</note>.*

<margin>A</margin> This very thing, therefore, which we call by the name of "soul," what kind of nature should we say it primarily possesses? Certainly, if it were a body, it would be entirely capable of being broken down. For every body is a composite <term>composite: something made of multiple parts that can be separated</term>. But if it is not a body, but of a different nature, we must examine this nature, either in the same way or another. First, we must ask into what kind of body we should resolve this body which people call the "soul." Since life is necessarily present in the soul, <margin>B</margin> it would follow that the body imagined to be the soul is composed of two or more bodies—and that either both (or all) possess life in themselves, or that one has life while the others do not, or that none of them have it. If life exists in only one of them, then that one alone would be the soul. But what kind of body is this that possesses life from itself? Surely fire, air, water, and earth are, by their own nature, soul-less; and whenever soul is present in any of these, they make use of a <margin>C</margin> borrowed life. Besides these, there are no other bodies. Furthermore, even those who introduced other bodies as elements <term>elements: the basic building blocks of the physical world</term> did not claim they were souls, nor did they attribute life to them. If someone were to say that, although none of the parts have life, their coming together created life, they would be speaking absurdities. Likewise, if each part had life, then one alone would suffice. <margin>D</margin> Indeed, it is entirely impossible for a gathering of bodies to create life, or for things lacking intellect to generate intellect. Nor will they be able to say that these things, mixed in whatever way, produce either intellect or even the soul. There must, therefore, be something that organizes them and acts as the cause of the mixture. This principle, then, will more rightly hold the authority and rank of "soul." Now, not only would there be no composite body, but there would not even be a simple body in the order of things, unless there were a soul in the universe; for a seminal reason <term>seminal reason: a formative, seed-like power (Latin: "ratio seminalis") that organizes matter into specific shapes</term>...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...approaching matter makes a body, and this reason itself cannot proceed from anywhere except the soul.

---

->...approaching matter makes a body, and this reason itself cannot proceed from anywhere except the soul.<-

---

*Every body creates a distance between its parts, so that when one part is affected, the others do not immediately feel it; however, through the soul, the body possesses a unity so that at the movement or suffering of one part, all are immediately moved. Therefore, the soul is not a body, nor is it a form spread out through the body. Chapter III.*

*It is not a dense body, otherwise it would not easily penetrate the whole; it is not a fluid body, otherwise the most fluid body would not hold together. It is not a form impressed upon the body, otherwise it would not freely command the body to give it life, movement, and cohesion; rather, it would depend on a more excellent form that remains within itself while pouring life through the body. This more excellent form would be the soul itself, which—being indivisible and present as a whole everywhere—easily reconciles opposites and binds together things that are spread out and prone to dissipation.*

<margin>A</margin> If anyone should say otherwise—that atoms or certain indivisible bodies coming together create the soul through their union—they will be refuted by the very consensus of feeling <note>original: "passionio consensione" / "συμπάθεια" (sympathy or shared sensation)</note> and the bond of nature. For a single whole that feels together <note>original: "compatiens"</note> cannot be made from bodies that do not feel, nor would such a union admit life; rather, the soul itself...

<sig>Q</sig>

<summary>This page argues that the soul must be an immaterial substance because physical matter (like the four elements) lacks inherent life and the ability to unify sensations. It introduces the concept of "seminal reasons" as the organizing principles that only a soul can provide to matter.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, Plotinus, Marsilio Ficino, materialism, seminal reason, elements, unity of sensation, atomism</keywords>

--- Page 493 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus's argument from Ennead IV, Book 7, Chapter 3, regarding why the soul cannot be a body. The previous page established that the soul acts as the ruler of the body; this page refutes the Materialist (Stoic and Epicurean) views that the soul is a physical "spirit" or "breath."</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

<margin>A</margin> is entirely sympathetic to itself. Since neither a body nor a magnitude can be formed from indivisible parts <note>original: "individuis" — Plotinus is refuting the Atomist view that the soul is made of tiny, indivisible physical particles.</note>. Furthermore, if one brings a simple body into the discussion, they certainly will not say that its material part has life from itself, for matter is devoid of quality; rather, they will argue that the part which functions as the "form" brings life from outside. If they then say this form is the essence, then certainly not both, but only one of these will be the soul: which indeed is no longer a body. For this is not
<margin>B</margin> also made of matter; otherwise, we would be compelled to break it down again in the same way. But if one suggests that such a form is not an essence but a certain "passion" <term>passion: here meaning a state or property acted upon something, rather than an active substance</term> of matter, it remains for them to explain to us from where this "passion of life" descended into the matter. For matter does not form itself, nor does it provide itself with a soul. There must, therefore, be something that supplies life to it—whether life is supplied to matter itself or to any body whatsoever—and I say this supplier exists outside the body and is superior to every bodily nature. Indeed, there would be no body at all unless the
<margin>C</margin> power of the soul existed. For the body is always flowing, and the very nature of the body is in constant motion, and the universe would quickly perish if all things were merely bodies, even if someone applied the name "soul" to one of those bodies. For such a soul would suffer the same things as other bodies, since the same matter is in all of them; nothing would truly become "one" anywhere, but all things would reside in matter, where the very shaper of matter is absent. Perhaps even this very
<margin>D</margin> matter would not exist at all. This universe will be dissolved if one commits its safety to a physical connection of a body, attributing the order of the soul to it in name only—that is, to a certain "breath" <note>original: "aeri cuidam & spiritui" — Plotinus refers to the Stoic concept of *pneuma*, a physical gas or breath they believed was the soul.</note> and spirit that is entirely capable of being scattered, and which has no union within itself. Since all bodies are divisible, if anyone commits this universe to any body, he will be forced to admit, out of madness, that the whole is agitated by mere chance. What order can there be in
<margin>E</margin> a "spirit" (acting like a wind that requires order from a soul), or what reason, or what intellect? But if the soul is present, all these things immediately assist it in the constitution of the world and the rest of the living beings, while one power here and another there leads everything toward the whole. But if the soul is absent, these remaining things would not only lack order, but they would not be able to exist at all.

---

> The Stoics and Epicureans suspected that the soul was a "spirit" <note>original: "spiritum"</note>, that is, a most subtle body. The former thought it was fiery, while the latter thought it more airy. Both named the soul "spirit," not just any spirit, but one affected by a certain specific property.
<margin>Chapter IV.</margin>

---

> These very words—"property" and "somewhat incorporeal"—which are more excellent than physical things, are not generated by a body, but by a substance that is entirely incorporeal, which should rather be judged as the soul. Since the soul is equally disposed to produce and govern opposite qualities and motions in the body, it is rightly neither a specific body nor a physical thing, nor does it depend on any body or bodies.

---

### EVEN the followers of the physical nature <note>The Stoics</note>, driven and witnessed by the truth, confess that a certain "form" of things belonging to the soul must precede bodies and be more excellent than all bodies, when they bring "intelligent breath" and "intellectual fire" into the discussion—as if the highest grade of nature could not exist in the order of things without fire and breath.

<column-break/>

...herself sympathetic. From indivisible parts, neither a body nor a magnitude could arise. And indeed, if someone says the life belongs to the body, they will not say that the material part has life of itself; for matter is without quality. But they will say that which is ordered according to form has life. If they say this form is the whole essence, then one of these two will be the soul—which would no longer be a body; for if everything is made of matter and a blueprint, we will have to analyze it again in the same way. But if they say it is a "passion" <note>original: "πάθημα" (pathema)</note> of matter and not an essence, they must tell us from where the life, which is the passion, came into the matter. For if matter forms itself, it did not create the soul. But if it is from something else, that which supplies life to the matter must be the source—whether life is supplied to any of the bodies from outside, and beyond all physical nature. Since there would not even be a body, nor any power of the soul, if bodies were all that existed. For the body flows, and its nature is motion, and it would perish as quickly as possible if all things were bodies—even if someone placed the name of "soul" on one of them. For it would suffer the same things as the other bodies, since there is one matter for all of them. Rather, nothing would ever become "one," but all things would be let go into matter, if there were no one to shape it; perhaps even matter itself would not exist at all. This whole universe will be dissolved if one trusts in the cohesion of a body, giving it the name of soul only as far as words go—to the air and the most scatterable breath, which has no power of unifying from itself. For since all bodies are divided, if someone places this whole universe under some body, he will make it without cause and carried along by chance. For what order is in a breath that itself needs order from a soul—or what reason, or what intellect? But when the soul is present, all these things work together with her toward one; both in the world and in each living being, as one power after another contributes to the whole. But if she is not present in the wholes, these things would be nothing, not just lacking order.

---

### THEY ALSO TESTIFY, being led by the truth, that there must be something before bodies that is better than them—a form of soul—even as they posit "breath" and "intellectual fire," as if without fire and breath, the better portion could not exist among beings...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul cannot be a physical body or "breath" (spiritus) because matter is inherently quality-less and divisible. He concludes that an incorporeal soul is necessary to provide the order, unity, and life that physical matter cannot give itself.</summary>
<keywords>soul, body, matter, Stoics, Epicureans, pneuma, incorporeal, essence, Marsilio Ficino, Enneads</keywords>

--- Page 494 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus's critique of materialist theories of the soul, specifically targeting the Stoic belief that the soul is a physical "pneuma" (breath or spirit) in a specific state. It builds on the argument from the previous page that the soul must be an active, incorporeal principle rather than a passive material substance.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

<margin>A</margin> ...to be, and of those things the inquiries are like the accidental, for one ought to seek how it is that bodies are established as they might need something, if indeed the soul is established within bodies. But if they posit nothing else but the spirit <note>original: "πνεῦμα" (pneuma) — often translated as breath or spirit; the Stoics believed the soul was a physical breath pervading the body.</note> as the life and the soul, or their multitude as they are held by themselves—to which they are forced to flee—they posit different things for different bodies, whether a nature that is active or not; or how can the spirit be soul, when there are countless spirits without souls?

<margin>B</margin> But if they say it is "the spirit in a certain state," <note>original: "τὸ πῶς ἔχον πνεῦμα" — a technical Stoic phrase meaning "matter in a certain disposition."</note> does this "state" belong to the spirit by nature, and does this state produce this relationship, or is it one of the natural beings, or is it nothing? But if it is nothing, then it is only spirit. The "spirit in a certain state" will happen to be for them a void name. But if they say it is something else, is it the material and the soul? And is it divine, or are these merely names for that thing alone? But if it is to be either itself, or something else besides the substrate and the matter,

<margin>C</margin> if it must be the matter itself so as not to be accused again of being from matter, it would be a certain reason <term>reason: here "logos," a formative or organizing principle</term>, and not a body, but a different nature. And from this, it appears impossible for the soul to be anything other than a body;

<margin>D</margin> for otherwise it would be hot or cold, or hard, or soft, or moist, or dry, or black, or white, or all those things that are the passions <term>passions: physical properties or states acted upon a body</term> of bodies. For if it only heats, but cools nothing—for the soul also appears to make things light, or produces color; and joy or heaviness or weight and making black things black, or white things white. But if it both cools and heats, these do not come from its essence, but from the soul; and if it produces some effects in some animals and different ones in others:

<margin>E</margin> the same bodies make some things cool, others less so, and some thin, others thick, black, white, light, heavy, and it produces such things according to the bodily qualities of others, and indeed colors, and other things.

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the movements, how can they claim they are different rather than just one, when there would be only one motion for every body? Whether they are purposeful <note>original: "προαιρετικὰς" — involving choice or volition.</note>, or if they blame the reasons, this is correct; but is the purpose a property of a body? Even if the reasons are different, the body being one and simple, either the productive reasons are with it, or they are given to it by that which moves it. Whether it is hot or cold, and to grow in every direction, and to measure until the end—from where could the body itself get the power to grow in an orderly way, so that the growth is uniform, or as much as is left of the matter?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it can, and it would naturally require a certain place where it might be stable, whereas it would be more appropriate to seek where bodies should be placed: since these indeed must truly be placed by the very powers of the soul. Accordingly, if they say that life and the soul are nothing other than a spirit or a wind, it must be asked of them what that common saying of theirs means when they say: the soul is a spirit existing in a certain way. For they are accustomed to flee to this whenever they are compelled to introduce another effective nature besides bodies.

<margin>B</margin> If therefore not every spirit is a soul, since there are innumerable soulless spirits, but only a spirit existing in a certain way, we shall ask whether that which is called "existing in a certain way"—and such a condition—is some real thing, or nothing. For if it is no thing, certainly only the spirit will exist. That which is added, "existing in a certain way," will be a name only. From which it will follow that they concede there is nothing besides matter: and they must confess that the soul and God and all similar things are merely names, but in reality only body exists.

<margin>C</margin> But if that condition is a certain thing, and something else besides the subject and the matter, which is indeed in matter but is nevertheless immaterial (because it is not composed of matter again), certainly it will not be a body, but entirely another nature and a certain reason. Furthermore, it will appear no less from these things that the soul cannot be a body. For in that case, it would be either hot or cold, or hard or soft, or compact or fluid and loose; likewise, it would be proposed as either black or white, and similarly regarding the other qualities of bodies.

<margin>D</margin> And indeed, if it is only hot, it only heats; if cold, it only cools; if light, it only lifts and makes things light wherever it is present; and if heavy, it makes them weighted and heavy. Similarly, black properly produces black things, and white produces white things. For it is not the nature of fire to cool, nor of cold to heat. But the soul produces different things in different animals, and produces contraries in the same one: partly by contracting, partly by pouring out and liquefying.

<margin>E</margin> Likewise, it makes some things dense, others rare, white, black, light, and heavy alike: although it ought to happen not one through another, but only one according to the one quality of the body, and similarly for color. But now it brings many things together.

The soul produces all kinds of movements and effects, both by its vegetative power through seminal reasons <note>original: "rationes seminales" — the inner blueprints or formative principles that guide the growth of living things.</note> and by choice. And it grows the body in a certain order to a certain limit, while it itself remains the same in the meantime. Likewise, the whole soul is in any portion of the soul, whether imagined or real, or in any portion of the body. And the whole power of the soul is preserved in any drop of seed.

These duties, however, cannot belong to a bodily mass or quality. Therefore, the soul is incorporeal. <margin>Chap. IV.</margin>

<margin>A</margin> But how will they be able to assert not just one movement, but different ones, when there is only one motion for each single body? But if they refer the causes of motions partly to choices and partly to seminal reasons, they will indeed assert this correctly. But choice is not a property of the body, nor are the reasons—especially since they are different, while the body here is one and simple—nor can a body be capable of such reason at all, except as much as is granted to it by that which makes it hot or cold. But to grow at certain times and to a certain limit, by what power will this befit a body? To which it indeed naturally befits to be increased, but by no means to increase something else, except perhaps in mass...

<meta>catchword Q 2</meta>

<summary>Plotinus refutes the Stoic materialist view that the soul is a physical "pneuma" or spirit, arguing that the soul's ability to produce diverse effects and hold purposeful "seminal reasons" proves it must be an incorporeal substance.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus's refutation of materialist theories of the soul. On the previous page, he challenged the idea that the soul is a physical "spirit" or "pneuma." Here, he addresses the logical contradictions that arise if one considers the soul to have physical dimensions or "bulk."</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...it serves the matter at the same time, acting like a servant to that which achieves growth through it. For indeed, if the soul—being a body—causes growth, it is necessary that the soul itself also grows, evidently by the addition of a similar body: provided that it is to end up as large as that which is grown by it. Then, truly, that which is added must be either soul or an inanimate body. And if it becomes soul, one must ask from where and how it enters, and under what condition it is applied.

<margin>B</margin> But if that which is added is inanimate, in what way will this be "ensouled" <note>original: "ψυχωθήσεται" (psychōthēsetai) — to be endowed with life or soul</note>, and how will it agree with what came before, and become one, and harmonize with the previous soul in its opinions? Would this new soul not rather be like a stranger, ignorant of what the other knows? And just as the rest of our physical mass suffers—where one part flows out and another flows in—nothing in us would remain entirely the same. How then would memory exist in us, or the recognition of things belonging to us, if we never use the same soul?

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, if the soul is a body, just as the nature of a body consists, it is distributed into many parts, of which no part is the same as the whole. If, therefore, the soul were a certain magnitude <term>magnitude: physical size or bulk</term>, which, if it were somewhat smaller, would no longer be a soul, then surely—just like every quantity—it would be changed from its prior essence by the removal of parts.

<margin>D</margin> If, however, some of those things that are extended in magnitude are at some point diminished in mass but meanwhile remain the same in quality, then surely, by the very reason that it is a body and quantity, it has already become something else; yet in its quality (which differs from quantity), it can meanwhile keep itself the same. What then will they say, those who think the soul is a body? Will they admit that any part of the soul in the same living body is a soul just as the whole is? And again, a part of every single part?

<margin>E</margin> If they admit this, then magnitude would contribute nothing to the essence of the soul, even though it ought to contribute if the soul were a certain quantity. Nevertheless, the whole of the soul itself will be everywhere here, which cannot happen to a body—namely, that the same whole can be in several places at once, and that a part can be exactly the same as the whole. But if they deny that any of the parts is a soul, then surely, according to them, the soul will be composed of inanimate things.

<margin>F</margin> Furthermore, if the magnitude of each soul were defined in this way, it would not be soul if it were stretched toward either direction—either toward the greater or the smaller. When, therefore, twin offspring are procreated from a single intercourse and a single seed <note>original: "σπέρματος" (spermatos)</note>, or as in other animals where even more are conceived (the seed being distributed into several small parts where each part is a whole), why does such an event not warn those who wish to learn? Where the part is the same as the whole, this very thing exceeds the condition of a "mass" in its essence, and it must be entirely removed from quantity.

<margin>G</margin> For only in this way can it remain the same when anything is taken away, as one who has no need of quantity or mass: since its essence exists as something else entirely. Therefore, the soul is void of quantity, and its formative principles <term>formative principles: "rationes" in Latin, "logoi" in Greek; the internal blueprints of life</term> are likewise.

<column-break/>

<note>The right column contains the original Greek text of Plotinus, which mirrors the Latin translation provided in the left column. It covers the same arguments regarding the soul's growth, identity, and indivisibility.</note>

**If the soul were indeed a body and grew,** it would necessarily grow as well, clearly by the addition of a similar body, if it is to be equal to that which is grown by it. And that which is added would be either soul or an inanimate body. If it is soul, from where and how does it enter, and how is it added? If the addition is inanimate, how will these parts be ensouled, and how will it be of the same mind as the previous part, and become one, or share the same opinions as the previous part? Rather, like a foreign soul, it will not be ignorant of what the other knows; and just as our other bulk flows away while another enters, nothing will be the same. How then would we have memories, or how would there be recognitions, if we never use the same soul? And indeed, if it is a body, the nature of a body is divided into many, and each of the parts is not the same as the whole. If then the soul is a certain quantity of magnitude, then if it becomes less, it will not be soul; just as everything, by subtraction, loses its being the same. But if some of those things possessing mass are diminished in bulk but remain the same in quality, then insofar as it is that quantity... it has lost its identity. Therefore, those who say the soul is a body must say, first, that in every part of the soul in the same body, each is the same soul. Or again, the part of the part; for magnitude contributes nothing to its essence, though it ought to have been a certain quantity. But it is a whole everywhere, which is impossible for a body to be present; if they were to say the same whole is both the part and the whole, or each of the parts is the soul. If they say this, the soul will consist of inanimate things for them... Furthermore, each soul will have a fixed magnitude. Neither toward the less nor toward the greater will it be a soul. When, therefore, from one intercourse and one seed twins are born, or as in other animals many are born from the seed being divided into many places, and yet each is a whole, how does this not teach those who are persuaded to learn that where the part is the same as the whole, it has surpassed being a quantity? It shows what it must be. For it remains the same even when something is taken away, as it has no concern for quality or mass, as its essence is something else. The soul must therefore be removed from all [quantity] and reason...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul cannot be a physical body because it maintains identity and memory despite the body's physical changes, and because it can be present as a "whole" in multiple parts (such as in twins), which is impossible for material objects.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, materialism, Stoicism, divisibility, magnitude, quantity, seed, twins, memory, identity, Plotinus</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Plotinus argued that if the soul were a physical body, it would be subject to constant change and flux, making memory and identity impossible. Here, he extends this critique to the faculty of sensation, arguing that a physical soul could never achieve a unified perception of reality.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

->It is necessary that diverse influences flowing through the various senses reach an internal, single, and indivisible sense that correctly compares all things among themselves.<-

->Unless these perceptions are finally gathered into an indivisible point, they cannot be compared by a single, identical judgment. That they are gathered in such a way is apparent, for they are collected in the pupil of the eye in a similar manner. This internal sense can neither be divided according to the divisions of the objects perceived, nor can it be equal to them in physical size. Furthermore, if this sense were liquid, memory would cease; if it were hard, teachability would perish. Altogether, if it were corporeal, the forms of things would obstruct and confuse one another. Chapter VI.<-

***

<margin>A</margin> **T**hat the soul is not a body, and that the capacity for sensation does not arise from a physical nature, may be seen from the following points: it would be clear that nothing could be perceived if the soul itself had to be <margin>* such as a "one" *</margin> a single unit within itself to perceive everything. When many things enter through many sensory organs, or when many qualities exist around a single object—or even when a complex thing like a face is seen through a single sense—it is not as if one part of the soul perceives the nose and another the eyes. Rather, these must all be perceived together. <margin>B</margin> Even if one perception comes through the eyes and another through hearing, there must be a single point where both meet. Otherwise, how could the soul transmit these unless they arrived at the same place? This point must be like a center, and the various senses from every direction must terminate there, like lines converging from the circumference of a circle. Such is the nature of that which truly perceives. But if these points were distant from one another within us, as if the senses terminated at two different ends of a line, they would have to run together again into a single middle point or something similar. <margin>C</margin> If they remained separate, each would have only its own perception, just as if I perceived one thing and you perceived another. Therefore, the sensation—of a face, for example—must be gathered into the same point as it appears. (For we see that perceptions are gathered even within the pupils of the eyes). Otherwise, how could the largest objects be seen? <margin>D</margin> <margin>* It is debated whether the ruling faculty is such *</margin> Furthermore, the ruling faculty <note>original: "ἡγεμονικὸν" (hegemonikon) — the "principal" or "governing" part of the soul in Stoic and Neoplatonic thought</note> would have to be <insert>indivisible</insert> so that things possessing physical magnitude could become indivisible within it. If it were measured out so that one part of the soul perceived one part of the object, no part of us would perceive the whole sensible object as its own; rather, one part would perceive one bit, and how could it ever be divided? For if the soul is divided into parts equal to the object, our ruling faculty could not be equal to every perceived thing. <margin>E</margin> Where, then, would the division occur? Would the soul be cut into as many parts as the perceived object? And would each of those parts of the soul perceive a part of the object? Or would the tiny parts of the soul's parts lack sensation? But that is impossible. Or does every part perceive the whole? If physical magnitude is infinitely divisible, then infinite sensations would occur for every single perceived object. <margin>F</margin> Each image would then be present in the ruling faculty as a countless multitude. Furthermore, if that which perceives is a body, sensation could only occur in the same way that a seal from a ring is impressed into wax—whether the impressions are made in the blood or in the air. And if these impressions are made in liquid bodies—which seems likely—they would be confused and washed away like images in water, and there would be no memory. But if the figures remain permanently, then it would not be possible...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **B**ut if the soul were a body, we would be granted neither the ability to feel, nor to understand, nor to know; indeed, no virtue or anything excellent would exist within us, as will appear from these arguments. For if anything is to perceive, it must itself be one, and it must perceive everything by a certain single and identical power. Even if many things enter through several instruments of the senses, or if many qualities exist regarding a single thing, or if something diverse, such as a face, is seen through a single sense—it is not as if the nostrils see one thing and <margin>B</margin> the eyes another; rather, the same thing sees all at once. Even if one thing penetrates through the eyes and another through hearing, there must be one thing to which both arrive. Otherwise, the mind could not judge the difference between them, unless the intentions of the senses and the sensible objects flowed together into one. It is necessary, therefore, that this be like a center, and that the individual senses be extended toward it from every side, like lines from a circumference to a center. Such a path, embracing all things, <margin>C</margin> is truly a single thing. For if it were something divisible, and if the intentions of the senses reached toward both ends of a line, they would either have to run together again into one and the same point as a middle, or there would be one thing here and another there, and each would have only its own sensation. It would be as if I felt one thing and you felt another, even if the sight—such as a face—were a single thing. Rather, they must be gathered into one. This is apparent: they are gathered even in the pupils, otherwise the largest <margin>D</margin> things could not be seen through them. Therefore, those things that reach the principal part of the soul are much more like indivisible notions; and for that reason, that part itself will also be indivisible. Otherwise, if it had magnitude, it would be divided along with the sensible object. Thus, one part would feel one part of the object, and nothing in us would perceive the whole thing to be sensed. Yet that whole is one: how can it be divided? For if it is divided, it cannot be matched exactly, as equal to equal, since our principal faculty <margin>E</margin> cannot be equal in size to every thing to be sensed. In what, then, shall the division occur? Shall it be cut into as many parts as the sensible object is distributed into? And will every tiny part of the soul feel the same thing? Or perhaps the tiny parts of the parts will lack sensation? But truly, that cannot be. Yet if every part were to feel the whole, since magnitude can be divided into infinity, then surely innumerable sensations would occur regarding each sensible thing in each part—as if there were <margin>F</margin> innumerable images of the same thing in our principal faculty. Furthermore, if that which feels is a body, sensation cannot happen in any other way than if certain images are impressed by a ring into wax—whether they are impressed in the blood or in a certain sensitive air. And if it were as in liquid bodies—which is probable—the images would certainly be confused as if in water, and there would be no memory. But if the figures remain, it will not be permitted...

<sig>Q 3</sig>

<vocab>anima (soul), corpus (body), sensus (sense/sensation), individuum (indivisible), ἡγεμονικὸν (ruling faculty), αἴσθημα (perception), memoria (memory), pupilla (pupil)</vocab>

<summary>This page presents Plotinus's argument that the soul must be an indivisible, non-physical entity to process sensory information into a unified experience. He uses the mathematical analogy of a circle's center to explain how different senses (sight, hearing, etc.) must converge in a single point of consciousness.</summary>
<keywords>indivisibility of the soul, common sense, theory of perception, hegemonikon, ruling faculty, Plotinus, Enneads, sensory convergence</keywords>

--- Page 497 ---
<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Plotinus argued that if the soul were a physical body, perceptions would overlap and blur, making distinct memory impossible. Here, he continues this argument, focusing on how the soul perceives pain and how the intellect must be incorporeal to function.</meta>

PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<margin>A</margin> ...others are formed there while the previous ones remain, and thus other senses will by no means be made; or if others are made, the previous ones will be immediately erased. Therefore memory would cease. If, however, we are able to remember, and to feel one thing after another without the previous ones hindering us, it is impossible for the soul to be a body. <note>Original Greek: ἐμποδιζόντων τῶν προτέρων, ἀδύνατον τὴν ψυχὴν σῶμα εἶναι — "if the prior things were to obstruct, it would be impossible for the soul to be a body."</note>

> *The ruling part of the soul <note>Latin: Principale; Greek: Hegemonikon. The "command center" of the soul in Neoplatonic thought.</note>, as the judge of sensory experiences, suddenly perceives the sufferings of any limb; it distinguishes clearly in which part of the limb they are, and immediately moves the eyes and hands there. It would not be able to do this unless it were entirely present everywhere. Therefore, it is not corporeal. Chapter VII.*

<margin>A</margin> This same point can furthermore be demonstrated from pain and the sensation of pain, as when someone is said to have a "pained finger." In that case, the pain is indeed in the finger, but they will admit that the sensation of the pain reaches the ruling part of the soul. Here, a certain part of the animal spirits <note>Latin: spiritus animati. In ancient medicine, these were believed to be a fine, vapor-like substance that traveled through the nerves to carry sensation.</note> feels the pain, and the ruling part perceives it, so that the whole soul then suffers the same thing in some way. How, then, does this happen? You might respond, I suppose, that it happens by a "successive transmission," meaning that first the animal spirits around the finger suffer, and from here the suffering is passed on to the <margin>B</margin> continuous part, and again to another, until it reaches the ruling part. It is therefore necessary—if the first part to suffer feels it—that there be a second sensation for the second part, if indeed sensation is amplified through a kind of succession. The third part to suffer would also have a third sensation, and many—even innumerable—sensations would occur for the same pain, until finally the ruling part would feel only its own private suffering. Indeed, each individual act of sensing would not <margin>C</margin> perceive the actual suffering of the finger, but only the one following it. For example, <note>original: τὴν ἄλλην — "the other," meaning the part next to the finger</note> the part closest to the finger would perceive the suffering that occurred just after the finger; a more remote part would perceive a more remote suffering, and many pains would occur. In such a case, the ruling part would certainly not feel the suffering that afflicts the finger, but its own; it would then pass judgment while entirely ignoring the others, being completely unaware that the finger is in pain. If, therefore, the sensation of suffering cannot happen through such a succession—and a body, being a physical mass, does not allow <margin>D</margin> for one part to perceive what another part is suffering—then it follows that in any given magnitude, one part is one thing and another part is another. Surely, that which perceives must be such that it is everywhere identical to itself. To achieve this belongs to another class of beings rather than to the body. <note>Original Greek: οἷον πανταχοῦ αὐτὸ ἑαυτῷ, τὸ αὐτὸ εἶναι· τοῦτο δ’ ἄλλῳ τινὶ τῶν ὄντων ἢ σώματι ποιεῖν προσήκει — "As it were, to be everywhere the same as itself; this belongs to some other of the things that exist rather than to the body."</note>

> *The intelligence frequently touches and penetrates incorporeal things, and separates forms from bodies. It is therefore without a body; the intellect, then, is not corporeal. Chapter VIII.*

Since the indivisible can only be touched by the indivisible, the intellect which touches indivisible things is itself indivisible. Where it joins things that are separate, it is separate from the body; and when it separates things that are joined, it most clearly declares itself to be separate.

<margin>A</margin> Moreover, we must demonstrate that if the soul were a body in any way, it would be unable to think. Certainly, if sensing consists of the soul using the body to perceive sensible things, then thinking cannot be an act of apprehending through the body; otherwise, thinking and sensing would be the same thing. If, therefore, thinking is to comprehend without the body, it is all the more necessary that the thing which is to think is not itself a body. Furthermore, if sensation is of sensible things, it follows that intellection is of intelligible things. Even if they do not <margin>B</margin> entirely accept this, there will still be intelligibles...

<column-break/>

...to mark others of those things coming down, so that there will not even be sensations; or if others are produced, those prior ones will perish, so that there will be no remembering. But if there is remembering, and the sensing of one thing after another without the prior ones hindering, it is impossible for the soul to be a body.

->Chapter VII.<-

Look again at the matter of feeling pain, or the sensation of feeling pain—for it is the same thing. When a person is said to have a pained finger, the pain is in the finger, which indeed hinders the pain <note>The Greek text here seems slightly corrupted or differs in nuance from the Latin "prevents the pain"; it likely refers to the localized nature of the injury.</note>, but another experience occurs regarding the sensation and the ruling part. Indeed, most of the parts from which the ruling part is composed perceive it, and the soul suffers the same thing. How then do these things happen? It teaches how it happens to you. For either first the psychic spirits around the finger transmit it in order to the others until it reaches the ruling part. It is necessary, then, if the first part that suffered is to perceive, that the sensation belongs to the second part (if sensation is by transmission), and that of the third to another, and that many or infinite sensations occur concerning the pain. If then the whole character of the ruling part's sensing is to sense only its own state, and not truly that of the other—not the pain in the finger, but the one next to it—then the one that suffered is in pain. Again, the one that follows feels no other thing than the suffering, or rather there are many pains? So that the finger itself perceives the pain, but the ruling part perceives only what is next to it. Or the faculty of knowledge of that thing does not rejoice at all and does not know that the finger is in pain. If, therefore, the experience is such that the sensation becomes a belief in the spirit, being in one thing while another is in another throughout the whole magnitude (for one part is one thing and another is another), then the whole that perceives must be, as it were, everywhere the same as itself. This belongs to some other of the things that exist rather than to the body.

->Chapter VIII.<-

That it would not even be possible for the soul to think if it were a body must be shown thus. For if sensing is the soul using the body to perceive sensible objects, then thinking would not be apprehending through the body, or it would be the same as sensing. If then there is an apprehending without the body, it is much more necessary that the thinking subject itself not be a body. Furthermore, if sensation is of sensible things, and intellection is of intelligible things—even if they do not wish it, there will be at least some intelligibles...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul cannot be a physical body because a body is composed of discrete parts, whereas sensation (like feeling a pained finger) requires a unified, indivisible subject. He also distinguishes between physical sensation and the intellect, which must be incorporeal to grasp non-physical truths.</summary>
