# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>A</margin> ...the understandings of certain things, and the grasping of indivisible <note>original Greek: ἀμερίστων — "indivisible" or "impartible," referring to things that cannot be cut into pieces, like an idea or a mathematical point.</note> things within us. In what way, then, if the intellect were a magnitude <term>magnitude: physical size or spatial extension</term>, would it understand that which is free from magnitude? And how could it grasp the indivisible with a nature that can be divided? Or perhaps it grasps it with some indivisible part of itself? If that were the case, the part that understands would not be a body. For there is no need for the whole to touch the object; it is enough to touch it with a single part. If, therefore, they concede that the primary understandings—which is true—are of things <margin>B</margin> entirely absolute from the body (that is, of each thing in its abstract state, as it is said), it is necessary that the understanding nature also understands to the extent that it either is, or becomes, free from the body. If, however, they say that these understandings deal with forms that are attached to matter, they still overlook the fact that these forms are only understood when they are separated from bodies by the intellect. For it is not the man himself with this specific flesh, nor the circle itself with matter, <margin>C</margin> but the triangle, the line, and the point which stand in the degree to which they are separated by the mind. For this reason, it is necessary for the soul also to call itself away from the body in this state. It is necessary, therefore, that the soul itself does not exist as a body. Indeed, Beauty itself and Justice itself are exempt from all magnitude, and likewise the understanding of these things. Wherefore, these things that come to us are grasped by some partless <note>Latin: impartibili — "without parts." Plotinus argues that if the soul had parts like a physical object, a thought would be split up and lose its meaning.</note> part of the soul, and they will remain in this soul in a partless manner. Finally, if the soul were a body, I do not see how the virtues of temperance and justice could belong to it, which preserve the soul to the extent that they are received by it.

---

*The corporeal essence, being imperfect, depends on the perfect incorporeal essence; since the latter is first made and lives from itself, it is superior to all things of the kind in which the soul is contained.*

### Chapter IX.

*Since the soul is nearby in the divine race, it already seems to see colors during its commerce, from which it attains its best habits. And since it is included in the race of divine things, it continually preserves its nature, or can be recalled to its original dignity.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Truly, it is altogether necessary that there be some other nature besides the corporeal, which has its being from itself, and that such a nature is everything that is judged to be truly being. This indeed neither comes into existence nor perishes; otherwise all other things would slip away, nor would they be formed again if a nature of this kind perished. This nature surely offers salvation to all these things, and even to the universe itself, which is preserved and adorned through the soul. For the soul is the principle <term>principle: the source or beginning</term> of motion, providing motion to others while moving itself in the meantime, <margin>B</margin> and providing life to the animated body. But the soul possesses life from itself, never to lose it, inasmuch as it holds life from its own nature. For not all things use a life that is foreign to them—otherwise there would be a progression into infinity—but it is necessary that a certain nature exists which is primarily living, which must be incorruptible and immortal, as it is the principle of life for others. Surely, in this degree, all that is divine and blessed must consist, living and existing from itself—primarily existing <margin>C</margin> and primarily living—lacking any change in its essence, neither rising nor setting. For from where would it be born, or into what would it be resolved? And if it is right for the true name of "being" to be within this, it ought not to be at one time and not be at another; just as color itself is white through itself, and is not white at one time and then not white at another.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the understandings of certain things, and the grasping of indivisibles within us. In what way, then, if the intellect were a magnitude, would it understand that which is free from magnitude, and grasp the indivisible with a nature that is divisible? Or perhaps with some part of itself that is indivisible? If this were the case, the very thing that understands will not be a body. For there is no need for the whole to touch [the object] in order to reach it; for it is enough to reach it with a single point. If they will therefore concede that the first understandings—which is also true—are of things entirely absolute from the body, <margin>B</margin> namely of each thing as it is said to be "abstracted," it is necessary that the understanding nature also understands to the extent that it either is, or becomes, free from the body. If, however, they should say that these understandings are concerned with forms adhering to matter, they still overlook that these things are only then understood when they are separated from bodies, namely by the intellect separating them. For it is not the "man himself" with these pieces of flesh, or the "circle itself" with matter, <margin>C</margin> but the triangle, the line, and the point, which exist in that same degree by which they are separated by the mind; on which account it is necessary for the soul also to withdraw itself from the body in this state. It is necessary, therefore, that it does not exist as a body. Indeed, Beauty itself and Justice itself are exempt from all magnitude, and similarly the understanding of these. Therefore, the things coming to us are grasped by some partless [aspect] of the soul, and in this very thing they will remain partlessly. Finally, if the soul were a body, I do not see how the virtues of temperance and justice could be its own, which also preserve it to the degree that they are grasped by it.

---

*The corporeal essence, being imperfect, depends on the perfect incorporeal essence; since the latter is first made and lives from itself, it is superior to all things of the kind in which the soul is contained.*

### Chapter IX.

*Since the soul is nearby in the divine race, it already seems to see colors during its commerce <note>Original: "commercium" — interaction or association between the soul and the physical world.</note>, from which it attains its best habits. And since it is included in the race of divine things, it continually preserves its nature, or can be recalled to its original dignity.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Truly, it is altogether necessary that there is some other nature besides the corporeal, which has its being from itself, and that such is everything that is judged as truly being. This indeed neither becomes nor perishes; otherwise all other things will fall apart, nor will they be fashioned again if a nature of this kind should perish; which surely provides safety to all these things, and even to the universe itself, preserved and adorned through the soul. For she is the principle of motion, exhibiting motion to others while moving herself in the meantime, <margin>B</margin> and providing life to the animated body; but she possesses it from herself, never to lose it, as one who has this from herself. For not all things use a life that is borrowed from elsewhere, otherwise there will be a progression into infinity; but it is necessary that some nature exists that is "primarily living," which must be incorruptible and immortal, as it is the principle of life for others. Surely in this rank all that is divine and blessed must be established, living and existing from itself, primarily existing, <margin>C</margin> and primarily living, free from change according to its essence, neither arising nor setting. For from where would it be born, or into what would it be dissolved? And if it is necessary for the true name of "being" to be in this, it ought not at some times to be, and at other times not to be; just as color itself is white by itself, not white at one time and then...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the intellect must be non-physical because it can grasp abstract, indivisible concepts like Justice and Beauty that have no physical size. He further establishes the soul as the self-moving principle of life, which must be immortal to prevent an infinite regress of life-sources.</summary>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

...not white. If, however, "white" itself were Being itself <note>original: ipsum ens — In Platonic philosophy, "Being" refers to true, eternal reality as opposed to temporary, physical appearances.</note>, then surely along with that which is white, it would also exist forever. But as it is, it only has this: that it is white. But that to which Being itself is present from itself, and is primarily Being, undoubtedly exists forever. Therefore, it is not fitting for this primary and eternal Being to lack any nature, such as that of a stone or wood; rather, it must be a living thing and enjoy a pure life—specifically, the best life possible—and yet not lose its own nature, <margin>B</margin> but sometimes resume its ancient state when it returns to its own realm.

*There are two gifts of the divine minds. One is the clarity of the intellect perceiving all things; the other is the habit of the best life. The soul most achieves such gifts when, separating itself from every bodily stain, it returns into itself. From this, it appears that the soul is related by nature to the divine minds. Chapter X.*

*There are two arguments for divinity among us. One is prophecy; the other is the demonstration of miraculous works. Whoever brings back these divine gifts seems to have claimed them for themselves not merely by duty, but because they have recalled the soul from the body back to itself. Whence it is clear that the soul's nature is joined to divinity through itself.*

<margin>A</margin> That the SOUL is indeed related to the divine and eternal nature is evident from the fact that it is not a body, as has been demonstrated to us; it has neither shape, nor color, nor mass, nor quality that is in any way tangible. Therefore, it can also be shown through these things. Truly, since it is established for us that every divine and truly existing being enjoys a good and wise life, we must next consider what the nature of our soul is at its core. Let us take the soul not yet conceiving irrational desires <margin>B</margin> and angers in the body, nor admitting other disturbances; but one which has expelled all these things, and has no commerce with the body, except as much as the utmost necessity compels. Such a soul will undoubtedly reveal to us that the vices and evils of the soul are certain additions, injected into us from the outside; for in a purified soul, the best things are found to be inherent—namely, wisdom and the remaining virtues—as if they were familiar friends. If, therefore, the soul is such a thing whenever it returns into itself, <margin>C</margin> what then hinders it from being in the rank of that nature which we confess to be entirely divine and eternal? For wisdom and true virtue, being divine things, can never exist in any base and mortal nature; rather, it is necessary that such a thing be divine, since it is a possessor of divine things through a certain kinship and communion of substance <term>communion of substance: the philosophical idea that the soul is made of the same essential "stuff" as the divine reality</term>. For this reason, whoever is so affected seems to differ but little in soul from the higher beings <margin>D</margin>: yielding only in this, namely, that he is in a body. Therefore, if even all men, or most, were endowed with such souls, no one would be so incredulous as to ever doubt that the nature of our soul is inwardly immortal. But now, since men perceive the soul in most people to be stained with many vices, they naturally judge it to be neither a divine nor an immortal thing. However, one ought to consider the nature of each thing by looking at its own pure state. For that which is added <margin>E</margin> is always accustomed to hinder the knowledge of that to which it has been added. Consider it, therefore, by stripping away; or rather, let he who strips away behold himself, and he will easily believe himself to be immortal:

<column-break/>

...or white. But if "white" were associated with Being, it would also be something that is, and is forever. But it only has "white"; whereas that to which Being is present—being from itself and being primarily—exists forever. This, therefore, which is primarily and eternally being, is not dead like a stone or wood, but must be living, and enjoy a pure life, as much as remains only in itself. But if it should be mixed with something worse, it has a hindrance toward being at its best, yet it does not lose its own nature; instead, it recovers its ancient state <note>original Greek: ἀρχαίαν κατάστασιν — "ancient state" refers to the soul's original, pure condition before it became entangled with the physical world and sensory desires.</note> when it runs back to its own things.

THAT the soul is related to the more divine and eternal nature is clear from this: that it has been shown not to be a body. This nature is one, and it has no shape, nor any color with it, but even of the things from here, it is unmoved. And it is agreed by all that the divine, that which truly IS, is living, and enjoys a good and wise life; we must then consider after this, from our own soul, what its nature is. Let us take the soul—not the one in the body that has taken on irrational desires and angers and has accepted other passions—but the one that has pushed these away, and as much as possible has no communion with the body. This soul makes it clear that evils are additions to the soul from elsewhere. And in its pure state, the best things exist within it: wisdom and other virtues, which are its own. If then the soul is such when it returns to itself, how can it not belong to that nature which we say is of all things divine and eternal? For wisdom and true virtue, being divine, would not arise in a base and mortal thing, but it is necessary that such a thing be divine, since it is full of divine things through kinship and essential nature. Therefore, whoever of us is such, being diminished only a little from the higher state insofar as he is in a body—if every man were such, or a multitude possessed such souls—no one would be so unbelieving as not to trust that the soul is in every way immortal. But now, seeing the soul in the many full of stains, they do not think of it as a divine or immortal thing. But one must look at the nature of each thing by looking at its pure state. For that which is added is always a hindrance to the knowledge of that to which it was added. Look then by stripping away; or rather, let he who strips away see himself, and he will believe he is immortal...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul’s true nature is divine and immortal, a fact that becomes self-evident when one strips away the "additions" of bodily passions and vices to reveal the soul's inherent wisdom and virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, immortality of the soul, divinity, purification, intellect, virtue, Ficino, Greek philosophy, metaphysics</keywords>

# BOOK SEVEN.

*The animated body possesses, by the benefit of the soul itself, the power to be moved in some way from within. Therefore, the soul possesses life most essentially; thus it has life from itself, and consequently, it has life within itself that does not depend on the body. Therefore, it always lives, even when separated from the body. <margin>Chapter XI.</margin>*

*It is apparent that the mind is moved and lives from itself and in itself, even without the support of the body; furthermore, this is most evident when opposing forces move within the body and when the mind transfers itself to incorporeal things. If any accidental trace of life is impressed upon the body, it must be linked back to the substantial life of the soul existing in itself, just as the heat or paleness of a cloud is related to light; but as light is referred to the sun, so the soul is referred to the mind.*

<margin>A</margin> Regarding this whole matter, someone might be the first to dispute with us, claiming the soul is not immortal. Yet the soul clearly appears to live from itself, as it is impossible for it ever to perish or merely to have "participated" in life <note>original: "vitam metilēphuian" / "vitam participatam" — Plotinus distinguishes between things that "have" life temporarily and the soul, which "is" life.</note>. That which exists from itself is like heat in fire—I do not mean that heat is an external addition to fire, but rather that it is the very underlying nature of the fire. In this way, Plato’s reasoning holds: that the soul has life not as something brought in from outside, but as life inherent within it. <margin>B</margin> It is not an external gift, and every such soul is entirely living, as much as the soul may possess; and they agree that the soul is immortal and proportional to nature. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, as long as it has come into the immortal realm, it is moved by itself (which can never receive a portion of death). Or if they say life is an "affection" <note>term: affection — In ancient philosophy, an "affection" or "accident" is a quality that can change or disappear without destroying the object, like the color of a shirt. Plotinus argues life is NOT an affection of the soul, but its core essence.</term> produced in matter, receiving this state from another, then they will be forced to admit that the source from which this state is given to matter is itself immortal, since it cannot receive a state contrary to its own nature; for there is one nature that is living in its very activity.

*Our soul, imitating the motion of the world-year and the understanding of things, is eternal, just as those things are—especially because by recalling itself to its own innermost depths, it understands reality and declares that it possesses the absolute forms of things born within itself. <margin>Chapter XII.</margin>*

*Finally, if the soul is a simple, indivisible form, not bound to matter, it can neither be dissolved, nor divided, nor destroyed.*

<margin>A</margin> FURTHERMORE, if every soul were by nature perishable, all things would have been destroyed long ago.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Namely, when the soul shall have perceived itself dwelling in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>term: intelligible world — The "Mundus Intelligibilis" is the realm of pure ideas and divine truth, accessible only through the mind rather than the senses.</note> and in a pure place. For it will behold the intellect seeing—not seeing any sensible thing, nor anything of these mortal matters—but rightly considering the eternal by means of an eternal power. It sees all things in the intelligible world, and sees itself having become intelligible and radiant, clearly illuminated by the truth—which indeed flashes forth from the Good itself, which illuminates all intelligible things with truth. Now, therefore, that famous saying will be very fitting for this soul: <margin>B</margin> "Farewell to you. I, truly an immortal God, have now gone forth to the divine" <note>original: "Valete vos. Ego verò immortalis..." — This is a quote from the philosopher Empedocles, suggesting the soul's divine origin.</note>; for it is wholly intent upon the divine likeness. If, therefore, purification itself brings it about that the soul knows all the best things, then surely the sciences lying hidden within shine forth, which are indeed true sciences. For the soul does not run outside of itself to perceive temperance and justice; rather, it sees them within itself in the contemplation of its own being and in the recognition of what it was before. It gazes upon the divine images situated within itself, which previously, through the passage of time, were <margin>C</margin> covered with rust <note>original: "rubigine" — A metaphor for the corrupting influence of the physical world on the soul's purity.</note> but have now been rightly wiped clean. It is as if gold were perhaps alive, and because it was covered with earth, it did not look upon itself as gold and remained ignorant of its own nature; but at last, shaking the earth from itself and perceiving its own purity, it would marvel at itself. It would realize it has no need for external beauty, thinking it best for itself if it were permitted to remain only within itself.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, no person of sound mind, having glimpsed such a thing, will doubt that the soul is immortal, for life is inherent in it from itself and cannot perish. For in what way could it perish, since it is not an added quality? It is not like heat in relation to fire. I do not say this because I think heat is an external addition to fire, but because heat is in the matter of the fire, not the fire itself. For this reason, fire is dissolved; but the soul does not possess life in such a way that matter is the subject and life is an accident <margin>B</margin> of the soul. For either the soul's essence is life itself, and its essence is such that it lives from itself (which is indeed what we seek: the soul), and this they will surely confess to be immortal; or the soul will be dissolved as a composite, and that process will continue until they reach something immortal and self-moving, which it is a sacrilege to suggest could undergo death. Or if perhaps they say that life is a certain "affection" <note>term: affection — here meaning a temporary condition or state.</note> happening to matter, they will eventually be forced to admit that the source from which such an affection was handed down to matter is immortal; since it is unable to receive the <margin>C</margin> contrary of what it brings. In truth, there is one nature that is living through its own activity.

<margin>A</margin> PROINDE if they say that every soul is perishable, it would have been necessary for all things to have perished long ago;

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul is inherently immortal because life is its very essence, not a temporary quality. He uses the metaphor of gold covered in mud to explain how the soul, once purified of bodily influence, recognizes its own divine and eternal nature.</summary>
<keywords>immortality of the soul, purification, intelligible world, Marsilio Ficino, Empedocles, essence vs accident, divine likeness</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the soul's immortality. Having argued that the soul is not a body, Plotinus now addresses whether the soul—specifically the human soul—shares the eternal nature of the World Soul or if it is subject to decay.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD IV.

...but if one part of the soul were indeed perishable <margin>A</margin> and the other not—for instance, if the soul of the universe were immortal while ours were mortal—the cause of this difference must be identified. Both are the principle of movement; both flow from themselves; both reach toward the same things, understanding those in the heavens and those above the heavens, as well as everything that exists according to true essence. Both search for the "whatness" of things, and finally proceed all the way to the highest principle of all. Furthermore, the soul discovers what each thing truly is through its own internal concepts. <margin>B</margin> This is because of the gift of <term>recollection</term> <note>original: "reminiscentiæ" / "ἀναμνήσεως" (anamnesis). The Platonic idea that learning is actually remembering truths the soul knew before birth.</note>, which establishes that the soul lived before the body; and by using eternal sciences, it is proven to be equally eternal itself. Added to this is the fact that everything dissolvable has received its being through composition; thus, it can naturally be dissolved by the same condition through which it was composed. But the soul is a single and <term>simple act</term> <note>original: "simplex actus" / "ἁπλῆ ἐνέργεια". In this context, "simple" means not made of parts, and "act" means a pure expression of being or energy.</note>, a nature consisting in the very act of living; therefore, it cannot perish for that reason. But might it perhaps perish by being divided <margin>C</margin> into parts and scattered? No, for as has been demonstrated, the soul is neither a mass nor a quantity. Or perhaps it will be destroyed by being changed and (as they say) altered? No, for alteration may destroy the form while leaving the matter behind, but this is a passion belonging to a composite thing. Therefore, it can be corrupted in none of these ways; it is necessarily incorruptible.

*Our soul, although it belongs to the class of divine things, nevertheless holds the last rank in that class. It rightly descends into the body—even a perishable one—only to return again to its divine rank.* ->Chapter XIII.<-

*The nature of the intellect is far different from the body; for it acts within itself, fleeing meanwhile from the body. Therefore, between pure intellects and bodies, there are natures having a certain intellectual part and also a "soul-part"—that is, a part verging toward conforming bodies to itself. In these, there are three grades: for in celestial souls, the intellectual part overcomes the animal part; but in ours, there is a turning back and forth, and they possess a <term>dæmonic</term> <note>original: "dæmonicāque". Not "evil" in the modern sense, but referring to "daimons"—intermediate spirits between gods and humans.</note> state of being. It is no wonder then that our soul, insofar as it is divine, descends into a mortal body, since within itself it descends to the third level—that is, beneath the intellect, through reason and imagination, toward the vegetative power.*

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, the <term>intelligible</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and forms, separate from the physical world.</note> itself is separate, by what reason does the soul proceed into the body? Because insofar as the intellect is alone and free from passion in the rank of intelligible things, having only an intellectual life, it remains there always. For there is no impulse in it, nor any appetite. But that which employs appetite, following closely upon that intellect, proceeds quite far by the addition of appetite; it desires to bring order according to the pattern of those things it knows in the intellect. As if pregnant from that source and in labor, it strives to create, and finally it fabricates. Through this zeal, the soul, drawing itself toward the sensible world, now governs it. While it holds the rudder together with the common soul of the universe, it lives as a colleague in the common governance of the whole, presiding as if from the outside, surpassing that which is governed. It then desires to govern a part; it now governs alone, and in that in which it lives, it is not entirely nor wholly of the body, but meanwhile possesses something outside the body. Therefore, the intellect of this soul is not subject to passion. This soul lives at one time in the body, and at another time outside the body; indeed, it begins with a certain impulse from the first things, and having progressed as far as the third things, it descends to our level by a certain act of the intellect. While the intellect itself remains within itself, meanwhile, through the soul, it fills all things with beauty.

<column-break/>

If, however, the things here are not [immortal]—as for example, if those of the light are immortal but ours are not—then the cause of this must be stated. From where does each movement arise? Both are the cause of all and of sacred things, and they grasp the eternal through the same means. They understand the things in heaven and the things before those, and every soul ascends through its own means; or rather, every thing from the soul itself, when it stops within itself, will understand each thing for what it is. And by becoming a result of <term>recollection</term>, it grants the soul to exist before the body; and by having used eternal knowledge, the soul itself is shown to be eternal. And whereas that which is dissolved has taken on a composition, it is by nature meant to be dissolved in that way, or entirely. But the soul is a single and simple activity and a nature found in living; it will not be destroyed in this way. But could it perhaps perish by being divided or cut into pieces? But the soul is not a mass of a certain quantity, as was shown. But again, someone might say it passes into another state; yet while alteration may destroy, it takes away the form and leaves the matter. But that is a suffering of the composite. If it cannot be destroyed in any of these ways, it must be incorruptible.

<margin>A</margin> How then, if the intelligible is separate, does the soul come into the body? Because as far as the mind alone is concerned, it is impassive among the intelligibles, having life only within itself; it will always remain there. There is neither impulse nor desire. But that which has taken on desire, being next in order to the mind, has already moved further because of the addition of desire. Desiring to bring order by itself, and seeing the <margin>B</margin> birth-pangs as if pregnant from those things, it hastens to act and create. In this zeal, as it touches the sensible world, it is managed by itself along with the whole soul of all things, taking part in the care of the universe, not even wishing to govern alone. And having come from there, it is not entirely belonging to the body, but has something outside the body. Through this, the mind is impassive; but the soul is sometimes in the body and sometimes outside the body. Having been moved by the first things, and having gone away toward the third things, it comes into these things here by its activity, while the mind remains in itself; <margin>C</margin> and through the soul, all things are filled with beauty.

<meta>catchword: EXCI-</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues for the soul's immortality based on its simplicity, its pre-existence proven by recollection, and its creative impulse to order the physical world according to divine patterns. He explains the soul's descent into the body not as a failure, but as a result of its productive desire to manifest the beauty of the Intellect in the material realm.</summary>
<keywords>immortality, recollection, simple act, intellect, soul's descent, dæmonic, intelligible realm, creation, governance, Enneads</keywords>

**BOOK SEVEN.**

<margin>The one who provides order <note>original: "ὁ διακοσμήσεως"</note> is immortal through an immortal soul, just as you have profited from the same through unceasing activity.</margin>

->An immortal decorator through an immortal soul: since he himself, also existing forever, dispenses all things through unceasing eternity.<-

*Whatever life shines from our soul into our body accompanies the soul as it departs from here. But that vital spark which had been impressed from heaven into the fetus is preserved by heaven; around this, our soul, if it departs from here in an impure state, turns with love, but if it is pure, it leaves it behind.*

### All souls have their own immortal lives. Chapter 14.

<margin>* Concerning [the soul]</margin>
Regarding the souls of other animals: whichever among them have degenerated from higher states due to their own baseness until they have reached the bodies of beasts, it is necessary that these also be immortal. If there is some other condition of the soul—as if it came from somewhere other than the nature of life—still, the different forms of the soul must provide life to all animals in the same way. This also applies to the souls in plants, as they seem to have originated from the vital images of the first principle itself. Since these souls are incorporeal and indivisible, the question arises whether the human soul, being three-part <note>The "three-part soul" typically refers to the Platonic division: the rational (reason), the spirited (emotion/will), and the appetitive (desires).</note>, will be dissolved when the composite body is broken. We shall say that those souls which depart pure will set aside what was added to them in the process of birth; but others, which have become thick with such stains, will eventually wipe them away through long cycles of time. We say that even that which is set aside as "worse" is not itself destroyed, as long as that from which it draws its origin still exists. For nothing that is considered "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> is ever truly lost.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, a question is asked regarding the souls of all other animals. And indeed, whichever among them are such that they have degenerated from higher states and fallen into the bodies of brutes, these too are necessarily immortal. If there is some other species of soul, it must not depend on anything other than the "living nature," since the soul itself is the cause of life for animals. Similarly, it is necessary that the soul of plants functions the same way. For all souls have proceeded from the same principle, possessing their own life, and these too are incorporeal, indivisible, and essential. If it should be that the soul of man, which exists as three-part, is dissolved when the composite body is broken, we shall say that the souls which depart pure will dismiss that which was joined to them in birth; but others will wipe away such a concretion of stain through long courses of time. We say that even the lower part that is dismissed is not itself destroyed, so long as the source from which it leads its origin remains. For nothing from that which is judged to be "being" is ever destroyed.

---

->*The souls of the deceased remember our affairs, feel them, care for them, and can act for harm or good. Chapter 15.*<-

*As long as souls have a body—whether it be an airy or an ethereal one—they possess their own senses. But if they strip off every body, they judge using a certain eminence of intelligence to discern individual things instead of senses. For imagination, especially when perfected, takes the place of sense; reason drives the imagination and the senses; and the intellect presides over reason and subsequent things in a more excellent way.*

As for those things that were said for those requiring logical proofs, they have been spoken. But regarding those who need a faith mixed with sensory history, we must select from the vast records of such matters. Especially important are those things which the gods have commanded through oracles: ordering that the indignation of souls who were once affected by injury be appeased, and that earned honors be rendered to the deceased, as if they were still capable of perception. This is exactly what all people do for those who have departed. Furthermore, many souls that were formerly in human bodies did not stop bestowing benefits on the human race after they were separated from the body; indeed, having taken up the role of prophecy, they are useful in other ways and demonstrate through themselves and concerning other souls that they have not perished.

<column-break/>

Thus far have been spoken those things which needed to be said to those who demand demonstration. But those things which should be said opportunely to those who rather require a thin faith mixed with history should be selected from the records which abound in such things. This is especially true of those things which the gods have commanded by oracles, ordering that the anger of souls who were once treated with injustice be placated, and that deserved honors be returned to the dead, as though they were still sensing such things. This is consistent with how everyone observes duties toward the deceased. Moreover, many souls, which once led human lives and were then separated from the body, did not cease to affect the human race with benefits; they certainly confer these to us through prophecies and oracles, and thus demonstrate through themselves that the souls of others have not been extinguished.

---

You desire, Great-souled Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the ruler of Florence and Ficino's patron.</note>, a brief summary at last of this long dispute—a dispute, I say, concerning immortality, which has now been drawn out at length both in my *Platonic Theology* and in this present work. Our friend Bernardo Bembo <note>Bernardo Bembo (1433–1519), a Venetian diplomat and scholar, father of the famous Pietro Bembo.</note> also desired the same when, as the orator of the Venetian Senate, he heard us disputing at great length on this subject. Bernardo, I say—a man remarkably learned, a patron of the learned, and my brother joined in a bond of friendship. For you, therefore, and for him as well, this summary will be divided into four chapters: 

First, that the soul is able to rule over falling <note>perishable</note> things and resist the incitements of the body; 

Second, that it frequently thinks of many things separated from bodies, whether it reaches those things that are separate in themselves, or separates them itself; 

Third, that it naturally desires eternal things, and often neglects temporal things through its confidence in the eternal; 

Fourth, that it worships the eternal God for the sake of everlasting life. 

Finally, the whole of natural religion is the firmest foundation of immortality for man.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FOUR.
### BOOK EIGHT.

#### ON the descent of the Soul into bodies.
#### On the descent of the soul into bodies.

> *Our intellectual souls descend into the body through a life-giving nature subjected to their own intelligence, and naturally taking on bodies just as a flame takes to sulfur; similarly, the intellectual souls of celestial beings are joined to their bodies through a medium of this kind. Chapter 1.*

<note>This introductory paragraph is a summary provided by the 15th-century translator Marsilio Ficino, explaining the Platonic view that the soul's entry into the body is a natural process rather than an accidental one.</note>

GOD WILLED, according to the pattern of His own intellect, that in every sphere of the world—both in the heavens and below the heavens—there should be certain intellectual living beings. And lest the intellects be dragged into bodies as if by force, He seems to have reconciled them to the bodies they would willingly take on through a "living nature"—that is, a vegetative power—that grew upon them like a plant.

| Translation of the Latin Text | <column-break/> | Translation of the Greek Text |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| <margin>A</margin> OFTEN indeed, having been awakened from the body into myself, and placed outside other things but centered within myself, I behold a beauty so wonderful that I then feel most confident that I belong to a higher destiny. For I then lead the best life and become one with the divine; being situated within it, I reach <margin>B</margin> that activity through which I establish myself above all other intelligible <note>original: "intelligibile" / "νοητὸν" — the realm of pure thought or the 'World of Forms,' accessible only to the mind.</note> reality. But after this rest in the divine, having descended from the Mind into rational thought, I am uncertain how it is that I am even now descending, and how it was that my soul ever entered into a body, seeing that she is what she appeared to be when by herself, even though she now lives in a body. <margin>C</margin> Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for the idea that "all things flow."</note> therefore urges us to inquire into this diligently; he himself posits certain necessary successions from opposites to opposites, speaking of a "way up and a way down," and says that in this transformation there is rest, as if it were an unbearable fatigue to labor and serve perpetually in the same things. But in discussing these things, he seems to wander through certain similes as if speaking in riddles, neglecting to reveal his meaning clearly to us, so that perhaps we must seek within him just as he himself found by seeking. <margin>D</margin> Empedocles, moreover, says it is a law that souls who have sinned must fall here; he himself, having become a fugitive from God and a wanderer, trusting in "furious strife" and serving it, has (in my opinion) treated the subject only as much as Pythagoras and his followers signified through certain veils, both regarding this and many other matters. | <column-break/> | OFTEN awakening into myself from the body, and becoming external to other things while internal to myself, I see a beauty of marvelous greatness, and I believe then most of all that I belong to the better portion; having realized the best life and having become the same as the divine, and being established in it, I establish myself in that activity above all other intelligible reality. After this standing within the divine, having descended from intellect into reasoning, I am at a loss as to how I am even now descending, and how the soul has come to be inside the body, being such as she appeared by herself, even though she is in a body. Heraclitus indeed urges us to seek this, positing necessary alternations from opposites, and speaking of a "way up and a way down," and that "changing, it finds rest," and that it is "weariness to toil at the same things and be ruled." He spoke in metaphors, neglecting to make the meaning clear to us, as if we ought perhaps to seek for ourselves just as he himself sought and found. Empedocles also says it is a law for souls that sin to fall here, and he himself became a fugitive from God and a wanderer, trusting in "mad strife." He, and I think also Pythagoras and his followers, spoke in riddles <note>original: "ᾐνίττοντο" — hinting or speaking in enigmas.</note> about this and other things. |

# BOOK EIGHT.

<note>original: "τῶ δὲ παρόντι καὶ διὰ πίστεως σαφῆ εἶναι" — "in the present [life] it is clear through faith." This is the conclusion of a sentence from the previous page regarding the certainty of the soul's nature.</note>
We are left with the divine Plato, who said many beautiful things about the soul. He spoke in many places in his five discourses about its arrival <note>Referring to the soul's descent into the body</note>, so that we might hope to receive something clear from him. What then does the Philosopher say? He does not always seem to say the same thing, so that one might easily see his intent. He everywhere looks down upon the entire world of the senses and blames the soul’s communion with the body, saying it is in "bonds" and "buried" within it. He says the statement made in the mysteries <note>The Orphic or Pythagorean "secret" teachings</note> is a great one: that the soul is as if in a "guard-house" or "prison." And the "cave" for him—just as the "cavern" was for Empedocles <note>Empedocles (c. 490–430 BCE) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who described the material world as a dark cave.</note>—seems to me to mean this universe. He says the release from these bonds and the ascent from the cave for the soul is the journey toward the Intelligible <note>term: "Intelligible" / "νοητὸν" — the higher realm of pure thought and eternal Forms, as opposed to the shifting world of the senses.</note>. 

In the *Phaedrus*, he considers the "shedding of wings" to be the cause of the arrival here, and he speaks of cycles that bring the soul back here again after its ascent. He also mentions judgments, falls into these conditions, lots, chances, and necessities; in all these things, he seems to blame the soul's arrival in the body. However, in the *Timaeus*, when speaking of this universe, he praises the world and calls it a "blessed god," and says the soul was given to this whole by the good Creator so that it might exist—for it was necessary for the world to have mind, and it could not have mind without a soul. Therefore, the Soul of the All was sent into it by God for this reason, as were our own souls, to be a part of its perfection. For it was necessary that as many kinds of living beings as exist in the Intelligible world should also exist in the world of the senses.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But here too, on account of his poetic style, he turned out rather obscure. We are left with the divine Plato, who handed down many and excellent things about the soul, and discussed its arrival at our level in many of his books: so that we may hope to receive something manifest from him. What then does this philosopher say? Truly, he does not seem to say the same thing everywhere, such that one might easily perceive his meaning. In the beginning, he everywhere despises the entire sensible world and condemns the soul's commerce with the body, asserting that it is enclosed here in "chains" and <margin>B</margin> "buried" in the body. Likewise, he honors that secret oracle <note>Referring to the Orphic "secret word" or *logos* mentioned in the Greek</note> in which it is handed down that the soul is situated here in a certain "custody" and "prison." Again, the "cave" in Plato, just like the "cavern" in Empedocles, signifies (as I judge) this universe for us. Where also he says the "release from bonds" and the "ascent from the cave" for the soul is its progression toward the Intelligible. 

In the *Phaedrus*, he furthermore considers the "falling of wings" or "loss of feathers" to be the cause of the descent to these things: <margin>C</margin> where certain "circuits" also turn the soul back to our world after it has set out for that other place. In other places, divine judgments, lots, Fortunes, and Necessities cast the souls down here; in all these things, he seems to find fault with the soul's arrival in the body. But in the *Timaeus*, disputing about this universe, he both praises the world and calls it a "blessed god": and he says the soul was handed over to this world by the good Craftsman <note>term: "Craftsman" / "Opifex" / "Demiurge" — the divine architect of the physical world in Platonic thought.</note> specifically so that the world could <margin>D</margin> emerge as an intellectual being. For while it was necessary for this world to be intellectual, the worldly body was not able to attain intellect without a soul. Therefore, the Soul of the whole was infused into all things by God for this reason, and the soul of each of us similarly, for the ultimate perfection of the whole world. For it was necessary that just as many kinds of similar animals as are in the Intelligible world should be contained in the sensible world.

---

->*The conjunction of the soul with the body, even if it is according to a certain nature of the soul and even for the perfection of the universe, nevertheless harms our souls for a two-fold reason: because it both hinders the intellect in some way and fills the soul with disturbances. To celestial souls, however, these impediments do not occur. Chapter 11.*<-

Since through a generative nature the conjunction with the body is natural to the soul, therefore the celestial souls <note>The souls of the stars and planets</note>, which use only this power toward the body, exist happily out of a natural habit. For since their bodies are not to be dissolved, nor subjected to external passions, nor in need of anything, they are easily ruled and moved through the generative power of their soul alone. Nor do these things hinder their contemplation and tranquility. 

But for our souls, it happens by a contrary reason, and yet a return to higher things is granted, if indeed a conversion to higher things occurs at some point. Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says that falling to lower things happens when the soul, like a field, is now corrupted; just as a field that for many years produced wheat might finally yield tares instead of wheat—that is, to produce false intellectual notions and bear imaginal ones. Then, from the "roots" of the soul, he says, the vegetative act sprouts like a bud through which the body of the soul, now extended into a physical body, glues itself together. 

Porphyry here makes the fall of souls similar to the fall of demons introduced by the Hebrews—namely, an effect of a vice of the intelligence or the will, from which followed a mad concupiscence. This is also what Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note> says when disputing about demons: to those who believe that demons are animals <note>In the sense of "ensouled beings" or "living things"</note>, just as Basil and many Greek theologians had thought. Then indeed, if that stern opinion of Damascene <note>St. John of Damascus</note> is true—that only the lowest angels fell and became "animals"—the Platonic fall of souls will be very similar to the demons falling among the Hebrews and Christians. 

Furthermore, where you read in Plotinus and Proclus that "particular souls" undergo particular changes, now to higher and now to lower things, do not understand that a soul will change into infinite bodies: for the mutations of one soul are finite and few in a "Great Year" of the world, and in the following year, as they occur, the same things are thoroughly rewoven. Besides, it is not necessary for every soul to remain in all species, nor for any soul to ascend or descend equally. For there are (to speak Platonically) certain differences between the souls of men that are in some way specific, just as in the stars, which seem similar to the sight: our souls differ from one another, not like a pear from a peach, but like a pear from another pear. Therefore, there are certain progresses determined for each by nature. More excellent souls thus ascend higher and descend less; but the worse ones...

The commentary by Ficino compares these Platonic ideas to Christian and Hebrew traditions regarding the fall of souls and demons.</summary>

### PLOTINUS’ ENNEAD IV.

*...I speak of human souls, and that they descend only into human bodies. For thus we moderate the Platonic opinion, which will be even more moderate if taken from the Hebrews <note>Likely a reference to the Jewish mystical concept of "Gilgul" or the transmigration of souls, which some Renaissance thinkers like Ficino attempted to reconcile with Platonism.</note>, who think the soul comes into a man only three times, and finally will always be either wretched or blessed.*

<margin>A</margin>
While we therefore search in Plato regarding our own soul, it is necessary for us to simultaneously investigate the soul in general: for what reason was it so established by nature that it would have commerce with a body? Likewise, we must ask about the nature of the world, what sort of thing we should chiefly assert it to be, in which the soul is placed to manage bodily things—whether of its own accord, by compulsion, or by some other condition. We must also ask about the maker of these things: whether he acts rightly or otherwise, and whether he <margin>B</margin> acts in a more excellent way than our own souls. For perhaps it was necessary for our souls to penetrate deep into the interior of those inferior bodies they were to govern, if they were to overcome and contain them; for while every individual body tends to dissipate and return to its own place, in the Great Whole <note>original: "in ipso toto" — referring to the Universe or Macrocosm.</note> all things are naturally situated in their own proper seats. Furthermore, our bodies require much anxious <term>providence</term> <note>From "prouidentia" — here meaning the care, foresight, and management a soul must exercise over a physical body to keep it alive and functioning.</note>, for they are subject to many external accidents; they are always in need of many things, and being placed in great difficulty and danger, <margin>C</margin> they require every kind of protection. But the body of the world, since it is perfect, full, and self-sufficient, never suffering anything contrary to its nature, is ruled as if by a certain brief and easy command. And just as the soul is naturally established to will, so it always remains; it is neither incited by desires nor affected by any disturbances, for nothing leaves it, and nothing enters it from the outside. For this reason, Plato says that our soul, if ever it lives with that perfect <term>World Soul</term> <note>The "anima mundana" or Soul of the World is the divine intelligence that Plotinus believes animates the entire universe without becoming "trapped" in it like human souls.</note>, will also be perfect, and will travel through the heights and govern the <margin>D</margin> whole world. For as long as it does not depart from there, nor immerse itself entirely in bodies, nor belong to any specific thing, then it too—like a colleague of the World Soul—will rule the universe with equal ease. It is not an evil for the soul to provide the power of being and well-being to a body in any way; for not every providence exercised over inferior things prevents the provider from remaining in the best state. Indeed, there is a double providence in the universe: common and specific. Common providence, by a certain command free from anxiety, arranges all things with a royal <margin>E</margin> authority. But specific providence, by attending to certain works individually—what I might call "hand-work" or manual labor—fills the craftsman with the condition of his craft and contaminates him. But since the divine soul is said to always govern the whole heaven in the manner I just described—standing above what is inferior yet sending its ultimate power deep within—no one can blame God as if he had placed the soul of the whole in an inferior state. Indeed, this <margin>F</margin> soul is never deprived of its natural office, possessing this very power from eternity and always maintaining it in the same way. This state cannot be contrary to its nature, since it is always present to it and never had a beginning. He <note>Referring to Plato</note> says that the souls of the stars relate to their bodies in the same way as the soul of the whole; for he subjects their bodies to the revolutions of the soul, and in this way certainly preserves a fitting happiness for the stars. For <margin>G</margin> although there are two things for which the commerce of the soul with bodies is chiefly blamed—

<column-break/>

THUS IT HAPPENS to us, while seeking to learn from him about our own soul, that we must of necessity touch upon and investigate the soul in its entirety: how it ever came to have a natural communion with the body, and about the nature of the world in which they place it, where each soul dwells, whether by necessity or in some other way. And about the Creator, whether he acts rightly, or like our souls which manage inferior bodies individually as <term>Forms</term> <note>The Greek "ἰδέᾳ" (idea) refers to the soul acting as the organizing principle or "blueprint" of the body.</note>, being able to enter into them; for these souls were meant to hold mastery, yet individual parts are always carried toward their own place, and the whole does not keep its own parts according to their natural downward tendency <note>original: "φύση κάτω" — the natural inclination of heavy, material things to fall or decay.</note>, unless there were to be much troublesome exertion. For many alien things fall upon them, and they are always held by desires, and they stand in need of all help as if in great difficulty. But that which is perfect, being sufficient and self-sufficient, having nothing in it <unclear>contrary</unclear> to nature, is ruled by a certain brief command through the speed by which the soul is naturally inclined to will; in this way things are held, and it remains ready. For nothing is absent, nor does anything added from outside disturb its nature. Thus he says our soul, if it were with that perfect one, would also be perfected, traveling on high and in this way governing the world; it would not depart to be there <note>in the body</note> nor belong to any specific part, but would easily co-administer the whole with the soul of the universe. For it is not an evil for the soul to provide for a body in any way, giving it power for good, and perhaps the total providence of inferior things does not draw away the strength of the best from that <note>the divine realm</note>. For all care is twofold: on one hand, there is the universal ordering by a royal command and oversight; on the other, there is the specific work done by one's own hand, which, by the nature of the thing being done, fills and infects the doer with its own condition. But the divine soul is always said to govern the whole world in that former way, excelling in that which is superior, while sending its furthest power into the interior. God could not be said to be the cause of this, for he made the soul of the whole not to be lacking. The soul does not depart from its nature, having this state from eternity, and having it always, which is not possible for it to be against its nature; for it exists this way continuously from the beginning. He says the souls of the stars relate to their bodies in the same way as the soul of the universe. For he moves their bodies according to the revolutions of the soul, and thus preserves their fitting happiness. For there being two things because of which the soul's relationship to bodies is found difficult—

<summary>This page discusses the distinction between the World Soul, which governs the universe effortlessly and without contamination, and individual human souls, which often become "trapped" by the needs of the physical body. Plotinus argues that governing a body is not inherently evil, provided the soul maintains its connection to the divine whole.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Plotinus’ Ennead IV.8, moving from the general nature of the Soul to the specific reasons why the human soul descends into a body. # BOOK EIGHT.
R 2

...communion: whether some hindrance to the thoughts arises, or whether it fills the soul with pleasures, desires, and pains. It was necessary to perceive this state of the soul before it was in such a body—that it belongs to no one, nor is it found there <note>original: "ἐκεῖ" — referring to the intelligible realm</note>, but rather the body belongs to it, which is the most certain thing, just as it lacks neither passions nor anything else. Thus, the soul is not filled with desires or fears. For nothing terrible is to be expected regarding such a body. But if some distraction draws it downward, it leads away from the more excellent and blessed vision; yet, staying in the same dwelling, I am able to possess well the things that are there in a state of peace.

*Since every nature beyond the first, most simple nature is infinitely multipliable, therefore in the intellectual genus there are many intellects; in the animal genus there are many souls; in the order of souls there are many intellectual ones: such as the celestial, the demonic, and our own.*

*Our souls, besides the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦς" — the highest part of the soul that eternally contemplates divine truths.</note> which is always active in the intelligible world, possess reason, imagination, sense, and vegetative power, which powers must certainly be used in their proper duties at various times. These, however, are used in the body: therefore, it is consistent that they should eventually descend into bodies.*

<margin>A</margin>
### CHAPTER III.

<margin>A</margin> **A**T present, however, our discourse concerns our own soul, which is said to suffer all manner of evils and to lead a wretched life in the body, being oppressed by pains, desires, fears, and other evils; for her, the body is a bond and a tomb, and the world is a grotto and a cave <note>original: "σπήλαιον κ(αι) ἄντρον" — a reference to Plato's famous Allegory of the Cave in the Republic.</note>. This opinion about the soul, though expressing different views, does not disagree with the truth, since the reason for descending is not the same in every case. In the beginning, since all <term>intellect</term> <margin>B</margin> resides in the very places of intelligence, it is both "whole" and "all," which we consider to be the Intelligible World. Likewise, the intellectual powers and individual intellects are contained therein: for there is not just one solitary intellect, but one and many. Truly, it was necessary that there also be many souls and one soul, and that the many differ from one another though coming from the one, just as species come from a single genus—some being more excellent, others indeed worse; some more intellectual, others less so in their actual state.

For there in the Mind, this one <term>intellect</term> <margin>C</margin> encompasses all other things in potential, like a great living being; but others are each things in act, which potentially encompass the other; just as if some city were animated, encompassing other animated things, the city itself—the common soul—would be more perfect and powerful, yet nothing would prevent the other souls of the city from being of the same nature. Or, just as if from a universal fire, one part were a great fire and others were small fires. For that essence of all fire belongs to the universe; or rather, <margin>D</margin> it is that from which every essence of fire originates. Now, the work of the soul which is more rational is certainly to understand; yet it is not to understand alone—I do not see how it would then differ from the Intellect—but besides being intellectual, it assumes something further, according to which it obtains its own nature and does not remain merely Intellect. It has its own work to do, since whatever is numbered in the order of beings has its own proper work. Now, when the soul looks up to that which is above itself, it understands; but looking back into itself, it preserves itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...it is accustomed to happen, both because intelligence is hindered, and because pleasures, lusts, and pains overwhelm the mind. Truly, neither disadvantage happens to the soul, provided it neither plunges itself entirely into the inner depths of the body, nor becomes "of" any body, nor escapes from the body entirely; but rather, the body belongs to the soul, being of such a kind that it neither lacks anything nor suffers a defect anywhere. Therefore, <margin>B</margin> nothing fearful occurs to the soul in such a body; nor does any occupation falling toward lower things turn it away from sublime and blessed contemplation. Rather, such a soul always leans upon divine things, its power being in no way anxious, nor laboring while it moderates the universe.

---
->*Cap. III.*<-
---

<margin>A</margin> **A**T present, our discourse is of our own soul... <note>The Latin text here repeats the translation of the Greek section provided in the left column above, focusing on the "body as prison" and the "multiplicity of souls."</note>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the soul's descent from the intelligible realm into the physical world. The previous page established that the soul possesses different powers (intellect, reason, sense) and that its movement toward the body is a natural progression of these faculties.</meta>

PLOTINUS ENNEAD IIII.

But truly, turning toward that which is lower, the soul now adorns, governs, and rules it. Indeed, it was not possible for all things to remain at rest within the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The "intelligible world" (cosmos noetos) refers to the realm of pure thought and divine forms, which Neoplatonists believe is the true reality behind the physical world.</note>; for since one thing could be produced after another, and though each subsequent thing must necessarily be lesser, it must still arise as long as that which is superior remains.

*The divine Intellect has imprinted upon our own intellect the form of the universe in all its variety. This form allows the reason—which would otherwise be empty—to gain a subtle utility from within. Therefore, when the reason turns itself completely toward that form and draws the imagination along with it, it remains in the same state as the Soul of the World.*

### Chapter IV.

*That is to say, the soul enjoys the highest contemplation of divine things, and while inhabiting the heaven, it similarly directs its gaze and its affection toward the universal government of the world. But when the reason, together with the universal imagination, neglects the form of the world to gaze more diligently upon some particular part and loves it too ardently, it then begins to affect even that vegetative nature. Then the soul, having become more narrow, produces a narrow body and is subjected to passions. From this point, it is vexed and troubled by innumerable cares.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **IT IS NECESSARY**, therefore, that individual souls—using their intellectual desire in their turning toward their creator, yet possessing a quiet faculty for managing the things that follow—be preserved unharmed and uninjured. They are like light hung from the Sun above, which meanwhile offers itself to lower things without envy. They must be preserved so long as they lead their life in the intelligible world together with the Total Soul. Furthermore, in the heavens, they govern together as if they were colleagues of the whole, just as <margin>B</margin> other kings, gathered with the King of all things, dispense all matters as his associates. They do not descend from their royal seats, for they remain in the same state as the King himself. 

But when the souls depart from the whole to the point that they become a certain part and become "independent" <note>original: "sui juris" / "ἑαυτῶν" — meaning to act on their own authority rather than as part of the divine whole.</note>, as if the time has come to manage things on their own, they then recall themselves to their own private concerns. When the soul does this for a long time, fleeing the whole and departing from it as something separate, it no longer looks toward the <margin>C</margin> intelligible. Having become a part, it is left alone, and as if destitute, it becomes powerless and distracted by business. For it is now devoted to a single part; having been segregated from the whole, it enslaves itself to one thing, fleeing everything else. Having proceeded and turned toward that one thing—which is shaken by all other things—the soul thus degenerates from the whole. It manages its own particular concerns amidst the things that fall upon it from every side, handling and tending to external things. It is not merely present with the body, but has progressed deep within it. 

<margin>D</margin> From this, it is said that souls "shed their wings" <note>This is a famous reference to Plato’s *Phaedrus*, where the soul is described as a winged chariot that loses its feathers and falls to earth when it turns away from divine truth.</note> and are bound in the body after wandering far from the unharmed and innocent habit of governing the better province—a habit which the soul possessed when it was with the Total Soul. That which existed before this was altogether better for the soul fleeing back to it. For this reason, the soul is "fettered"—that is, fallen from on high and bound with shackles—and it uses the senses in its actions because it is prohibited from the beginning from using its <margin>E</margin> mind. It is also said to be "buried" and "hidden in a cave" <note>A reference to Plato’s "Allegory of the Cave" from the *Republic*, symbolizing the physical world as a place of shadows and imprisonment.</note>. But when it turns toward intelligence, it is said to be released from its bonds and to ascend higher, specifically when it begins to contemplate true beings through the gift of <term>reminiscence</term> <note>original: "reminiscentiae" / "ἀναμνήσεως" — the Platonic idea that "learning" is actually the soul remembering truths it knew before it was born into a body.</note>. Nevertheless, it still possesses something that remains above. Thus, souls necessarily experience both lives in turn, leading now that higher life, and then again this lower one, by turns.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...toward that which follows it, which it adorns and administers, and over which it rules. For it was not possible for all things to stand still in the intelligible realm, since another and another could be produced in succession—lesser indeed, but necessarily existing, if that which is before it also exists.

<margin>A</margin> It is necessary for individual souls—desiring the intellectual through their turning toward that from which they were born, yet having power also over the things that follow—just like the light before them, which is suspended from the sun above, but provides itself to all that follows without envy, to remain unharmed by matter while staying in the intelligible. And they govern that world together with the Total Soul; just as if they were with the <margin>B</margin> King of all, beautifully ordered, they would govern with him without descending from those royal places. For even there, they are with the same things. But they change from being the whole to being a part and belonging to themselves. Or, as if weary of being with another, each makes a retreat to its own concern. When it does this for a long time, fleeing the whole and existing in separation and <margin>C</margin> not looking toward the intelligible, having become a part, they sit in isolation and become impoverished. They look toward the part, and when they are with that individual thing, they give themselves to it and flee the alien. Having come there and having been tripped up by turning away from that place, the soul stands apart from its own and from the entire multitude. It governs the particular with much trouble, now touching and serving things from the outside, being present and sinking deep <margin>D</margin> into the interior. 

From this, it happens to the soul that it is said to "lose its wings" and to be in the "bonds of the body," having failed in the harmless administration of the better things, such as it had when it was with the Total Soul. But that which is altogether better must be grasped by all who run back to their own. In this way, it is said to be in "bonds" and "sensation," because it is hindered from acting in the <margin>E</margin> Intellect. The souls are also said to be "buried" and to be "in a cave." But when it turns toward the intelligible, it is "released from its bonds" and "ascends," whenever it takes its beginning from remembrance to behold true beings. For it always has something there, even while it is held above. They become, as it were, "amphibious," living by necessity now the life there and now the life here, living each in turn.

<summary>This page explains the Neoplatonic theory of the soul's descent, using the metaphors of shedding wings and the cave to describe how the soul leaves the divine whole to govern individual bodies. Plotinus argues that while the soul becomes "fettered" by the senses, it remains "amphibious," retaining a connection to the higher intellectual realm through memory.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Plotinus’s fourth Ennead, specifically focusing on the mechanisms of the soul's descent. It reconciles the seemingly contradictory views of Plato, Empedocles, and Heraclitus regarding whether the soul falls by choice, by necessity, or as a punishment.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

**A** Indeed, those souls spend a longer time in the higher life which are more capable of dwelling with the <term>Mind</term> <note>original: *mente* / *νῷ* (nous) - the realm of pure, divine intellect.</note>; but those whose nature or fortune has been the opposite lead a longer life in the lower realm. Plato hints at this when he describes the soul's origins being divided from the "second bowl" <note>original: *secunda patera* / *κρατῆρος* - a reference to Plato's *Timaeus*, where the Creator mixes the substance of souls in a cosmic bowl.</note> and made into parts. At that point, he says it becomes necessary for them to fall into generation, since they have become such parts. 

**B** Where he says that God "sows" the souls, we must understand this in the same way as when he introduces God speaking and delivering a sort of sermon. For these very conditions of existence are produced by the common nature of things, and the order of succession declares how these things are always made and how they consist.

<column-break/>

**A** And indeed, they spend more time in the upper life, as many as are able to be present more with the Mind; but more time here, for those whom the opposite has occurred either by nature or by fortunes. Plato hints at these things as a "mixture," when he divides them from the same bowl and makes them into parts. Then he also says it is necessary to come into generation, since they became such parts. 

**B** But if he says to "sow" them, hear it thus: just as when he makes the Sovereign Creator speaking; but these things are in nature as a whole, and the placement becomes evidence, as it would seem, leading in order, that the things always happening are things that have been made.

---

## The sayings of Empedocles, Heraclitus, and Plato regarding the descent of the soul are in agreement. Chapter V.

*The soul, insofar as it is divine, frequently turns back toward divine things even in this fleeting region. Because it is the final boundary of divine things, it comes into the body through a predestined affection of nature; therefore, it comes by a "natural will," yet is also said to descend by a "choice," because by divine law it is necessary for souls affected in this way to flow out. Consequently, their footsteps follow spontaneously toward all things, where they sometimes happen to fall even into evil. That souls come here pertains to the order of the universe. Where the soul's vice leads to a lower state, the souls that "sin" more lightly are committed to a less happy or unhappy human life—for even these are not without penalty. But those who sin more gravely become <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, "daemons" (dæmonas) are intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, as Hermes <note>original: *Mercurius*</note>, Orpheus, and Iamblichus confirm. Through a youth of "atrocious fate," they seem to be masked as if made of iron. The influences of Saturn and Mars—black bile or anger—and the imaginations of speech vex them. Indeed, the terrifying imaginations of the daemon of Saturn and Mars pass through the mind as if through valleys, such that they can even be afflicted by the movements of the bodily humors.*

---

<column-break/>

**A** Therefore, there is no disagreement between the views that souls are carried into generation for the perfection of the universe, and that they descend as if into a "cave" or a place of punishment. Again, there is no conflict between necessity and spontaneous motion, since necessity also encompasses the voluntary. 

**B** Furthermore, what is said about the soul being in "evil" while in the body does not contradict Empedocles' "flight and wandering from God," nor the idea that they have sinned and thus face judicial punishment. Nor does it contradict Heraclitus' "rest in flight," nor the idea that the condition of descending is both voluntary and involuntary. 

**C** For whatever falls toward a worse state does not arrive there by choice in the absolute sense; yet, because it goes there by its own motion and suffers worse things in the meantime, it is said to receive its "merits" for what it has done. It is necessary by the eternal and perpetual law of nature to do and suffer these things. But if someone says that the soul is "sent by God" to serve some other purpose, having descended successfully from the higher realm, let him be known as one who contradicts neither the truth nor himself. 

**D** For from whatever principle each individual thing is led, it is referred back to that same principle or its ultimate end, even though there are many intermediate steps. Since "sin" is twofold—one in the very cause of descending, and the other in the wrongs committed during this life—the former is exactly what the soul suffers in the act of descending. In this, there is a lesser degree: namely, for some to enter bodies more quickly by a judgment based on their dignity. This act, being done by divine institution, is not labeled as a "judgment" in the usual sense. However, a more immoderate form of wickedness is judged worthy of greater punishment, managed by a certain prefecture of punishing daemons. Thus, although the soul is something divine and originates from higher regions, it is nevertheless immersed in the body. Since it is a "secondary god" <note>original: *Deus quidan posterior* - a being of divine nature but lower in the hierarchy than the ultimate One or the Intellect.</note>, it descends by a certain voluntary inclination and the cause of its power...

<column-break/>

**A** Therefore, the "destructions" into generation do not disagree with one another, nor the "descents" in Plato, nor the "caves" and "caverns," nor the "necessities," nor the "voluntary." Since necessity holds the voluntary, and the "being ill in the body," and the Empedoclean "flight from the gods" and "wandering," and the "sin" for which he sacrifices. 

**B** And the Heraclitean "rest in flight." But entirely, the voluntary nature of the descent, and the involuntary. And at least the one is not a "grace," but because having the greater, it comes to be in the worse, it is said to "have" it. 

**C** On the one hand, since it pursued it in such a way that it either stayed in the same or found some "rest," having causes regarding the forms that precede the descent... and the things in the same, and the worse. 

**D** But to say it is "sent down" and "sent under" and "put to sleep" in itself... and all the greater things, but the last things are referred back to themselves. Since the "sin" is twofold: either according to which the beauty is the cause, or as happening here according to itself or not to the body, and another cause is to deliver the lesser into bodies... faster than judgment or maltreatment... perhaps of the things happening, because I name it "judgment." It is shown. But the immoderate form of vice is deemed worthy of greater things and punishments... they happen to be daemons... and the bodies come to be in the highest places, and as many as are later, which are next to it in power...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "posterioris," indicating the continuation of the discussion on the "secondary" or "lower" nature of the soul as it descends.</meta>
