# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK IV.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...for the sake of adorning it, the soul descends here: and if it flees quickly from here, it is judged to have suffered no harm, primarily because it has arrived at the knowledge of evil and has known the nature of evil itself. Likewise, it has brought its own powers into the light and declared its works and effects. Indeed, if all these things were to remain forever at rest in an incorporeal state, they would be in vain, never coming into their own actualization, and would remain hidden from the soul that possessed them, never flashing forth or proceeding <margin>B</margin> into effect. For everywhere, action reveals power which would otherwise be entirely hidden and obscure—indeed, not even truly existing in that state. Now, everyone admires internal things because of the variety of external ones, guessing what the internal ones are like through these varied and beautiful things that proceed from them.

*The Soul comes into the body not only through a certain weakness that prevents it from remaining further in divine things, but also by the power of a fertile nature sprouting into a seed: for the corporeal form is the offspring of the fertile soul.* Chapter VI.
*By a similar fecundity, the <term>First Good</term> <note>original: *primum bonum* — The One, the ultimate source of all existence.</note> overflows into the all-forming <term>Mind</term> <note>original: *mentem* / *νῷ* (nous) — the realm of divine intellect.</note>; this into the similar <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: *mundi animam* — the life force of the entire universe.</note>; and this into the similarly all-forming world. Likewise, all causes flow into their effects everywhere. Finally, the soul imitates the providence of higher beings by transferring itself to lower things through a certain zeal for providing.*

<margin>A</margin> If, therefore, it is necessary not only for the <term>One</term> <note>original: *vnum* / *ἕν* — the indivisible source of all reality.</note> to exist—otherwise all things would be hidden, lacking their own proper form, and no being would exist at all since it would remain within itself—nor would there be a multitude of those things born from the One, unless subsequent things progressed from it in order, which are allotted to the rank of souls. <margin>B</margin> It is also necessary that souls themselves not only exist, but that their effects appear clearly, since it is inherent in every nature to create something following itself and to unfold it into the light, as if from a certain indivisible seed and principle proceeding toward a sensible end. While that which is prior always remains in its own seat, that which follows is procreated from an ineffable power—as much as is within the superior beings—which it was not fitting to remain as if restrained from generating by envy. Instead, it must always proceed until all things advance to the ultimate limit as far as possible, because of the cause of inexhaustible virtue <margin>C</margin> diffusing its gifts through all things, and not suffering anything to be found anywhere that is devoid of itself. For there is nothing that prevents each thing from being a participant in the <term>Good</term>, insofar as its own nature is capable. Therefore, if the nature of <term>matter</term> <note>original: *materiæ* / *ὕλης* — the physical substrate that receives form.</note> always existed, it was impossible for it not to participate in that which provides good abundantly to all, as much as each can receive. Or, if the origin of matter necessarily followed from preceding causes, even then <margin>D</margin> it was not right for it to be devoid of gifts because of its own weakness, which is noted before one considers a gift descending into it from above; specifically, when it would remain only in itself, which graciously bestows being upon it. The demonstration of those things which are best in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>original: *mūdo intelligibili* / *νοητῷ* — the divine realm of pure forms and ideas.</note> is primarily that which is most beautiful in the sensible world—a declaration, I say, both of their power and their goodness. For in this way, all things are always connected, both those judged to be intelligible and those judged to be sensible: and the former <margin>E</margin> exist through themselves, while the latter always receive being through participation in them, imitating the intelligible nature according to their strength.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to adorn it. Thus it comes and remains. In its flight, it is not harmed. Having gained knowledge of evil and knowing the nature of wickedness, it brings its powers into the open, showing both works and creations. These, if they remained quiet in the incorporeal, would have been in vain, not coming into being, and the soul itself would have been unaware of what it possessed, with these things not being revealed nor <margin>B</margin> manifesting that which everywhere action showed the power to be—wholly hidden or as if not existing, nor truly to be. For now, the wonder of each thing's inner nature is held through the variety of the outer, as these are seen from their polished external forms.

<margin>A</margin> If it were necessary for it [the One] not only to remain well-hidden—for all things would have been hidden, those having form not possessing it—nor would any of the beings have existed if it had remained in itself. Nor would there have been a multitude of beings, those generated after the first, if those after it had not taken their progression, or allotted the rank of souls. Nor should the joys of the soul alone exist, without those things produced through it <margin>B</margin> being visible. Since this is in every nature—to make what follows it and to unfold itself, like a seed, from an indivisible principle, going toward the sensible end, the preceding thing always remaining in its own proper seat, while that which follows is as if generated from an unspeakable power, as much as is in the things above. This power should not have stopped as if cut off by envy, but should always go forth until all things reach the furthest possible point, by the cause of boundless <margin>C</margin> power sending forth from itself upon all things, and allowing nothing to be able to be without a share in it. For what would prevent anything from being of the nature of the good, insofar as each was able to participate? If, therefore, the nature of matter always was, it was not possible for it not to participate, in as much as the good supplies to all as much as each is able. Or if its generation followed <margin>D</margin> by necessity from the causes before it, it should not have been apart from the good through inability before there came into it that which is from the good, even its being—as if the good were graciously giving. It is a proof of the best existing among intelligible things that there is the most beautiful in the sensible, being a sign of their power and goodness. And all things are held together forever: both those beings that are intelligible and those that are sensible. The former exist from themselves, the latter by participation in these, <margin>E</margin> receiving being forever, imitating the intelligible nature as far as they are able.

<summary>This page explains that the soul's descent into the physical world is not merely a fall or failure, but a necessary manifestation of divine power and the "Good" which must overflow and share its existence with all levels of reality. The sensible world is presented as a beautiful, necessary reflection and proof of the power of the higher, intelligible realm.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translation of Marsilio Ficino's Latin version of Plotinus's Enneads, Book IV, Treatise 8, which discusses the descent of the soul into bodies. The previous page established that the soul’s descent is a necessary expression of its inherent power and fecundity.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

> Just as air is a medium between fire and water—being fiery on one side and watery on the other, moving toward both in turn—so the soul relates itself to both divine things and those that are perishable.
-> Chapter VII. <-
All bodies bestow something of themselves upon lower things, but while celestial bodies receive nothing in return from those that follow them, elementary bodies <note>The "elementary" bodies refer to the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> give and receive in turn. Similarly, the celestial souls, in providing for lower things, are by no means stained by them. However, certain demonic and human souls, while they perfect bodies, are in some way stained by them because of a more meddling <term>providence</term> <note>original: *prouidentiam* — the act of caring for or governing the physical world.</note> over a harsher province. Yet, the malice of this place reminds the soul of the happiness of the higher world and warns it to desire that world more vehemently.

---

Since this nature is twofold—the one part <term>intelligible</term> <note>original: *νοητῆς* — relating to the realm of pure thought and divine forms.</note> and the other <term>sensible</term> <note>original: *αἰσθητῆς* — relating to the physical world perceived by the senses.</note>—it is better for the soul to exist in the intelligible realm. Nevertheless, by its very nature, it is necessary for it to participate in sensible things. The soul should not be angry with itself if it is not the very "Best" itself <note>referring to the One or the Absolute Good</note>, for it has been assigned a middle rank among existing things. Being of a divine portion, yet placed at the furthest edge of the intelligible, and standing as a neighbor to the sensible nature, it gives something of its own to the sensible world and receives something from it in turn. This happens unless it governs while safely preserving its own integrity; but if it sinks too deep into the interior with excessive desire, it does not remain a whole soul with the <term>Whole Soul</term> <note>original: *μεθ' ὅλης* — the Universal or World Soul.</note>. Otherwise, it is possible for it to rise again, bringing back the history of what it saw and suffered here, through which it learns. For if there is any benefit there, it is through the knowledge of opposites—for example, it learns that the better things are clearer through the experience of evil, especially where the power of judgment is too weak to achieve knowledge of the good without such experience. Just as there is a descent of the intellectual discourse toward the lowest and worse thing—for it cannot go further upward—it is necessary for the soul, acting out of itself and unable to rest within itself, to proceed by a law of nature toward the soul-level. This is its limit, and its condition is to hand things over to what follows and then run back again. So also is the activity of the soul: on one hand, toward the things that follow by governing them, and on the other, toward the things preceding it by contemplating true beings. Part of this happens in time through a turning toward better things. For the soul said to belong to the All, it does not labor in time nor suffer the proximity of evils, but remains hung upon the divine, which is most wonderful. Both souls receive from above and provide here below, but the way each soul touches these things is most marvelous.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since indeed nature is twofold—one being <term>intelligible</term> and the other <term>sensible</term>—it is better for the soul to live in the intelligible itself. Yet it is necessary, given the kind of nature it possesses, that it also participate in the sensible nature. It should not take it poorly if it is not entirely the "Best" itself, since it holds a middle rank in the order of things. It is a sharer in the divine lot, but placed at the final degree of the intelligible nature, like a relative to the sensible nature. <margin>B</margin> It is thus naturally ordained to offer something of its own to this world and to receive something from here in return, unless it governs while maintaining its own integrity. But if it enters the inner parts of the lower nature with too much affection and zeal, it does not remain as a whole soul with the <term>Total Soul</term> <note>original: *tota anima tota* — a reference to the World Soul or the soul in its universal aspect.</note>. Nevertheless, it can rise up again in turn, carrying back a report of the things it has known and suffered here, from which it learns how blessed is the habitation among the higher beings, and by what comparison of opposites it has perceived the better things more clearly. <margin>C</margin> For the knowledge of good comes forth more clearly through the experience of evil, especially where the judgment is too weak to attain knowledge without the experience of evil. Just as an intellectual discourse is a kind of descent to the final and worse thing—for one cannot progress further upward—it is necessary, as the soul acts from itself and is unable to rest in itself, to proceed by a necessity of nature and law as far as the soul. For this is its limit: to hand over <margin>D</margin> its own conditions to the things that follow, and to return again. Thus is the action of the soul, both toward the following things by governing the body, and toward the preceding things by contemplating the beings themselves. This is fulfilled in most souls by a certain alternation of times, and finally, a conversion from the worse to the better occurs. But for the soul which is called the soul of the universe, it is undoubtedly fitting that it is never occupied with a worse work, nor undergoes evils, but looks forward to the things that follow from a height of contemplation, and <margin>E</margin> always leans back upon the higher things. Indeed, both can be fulfilled in it at once, as it is master of both duties—receiving from above while supplying the lower things. For it could not be, since it is a soul, that it would not propagate itself toward both.

---

> Since our mind has powers and acts similar to the celestial souls, it is probable that at least our intellect always acts concerning divine things, just as the <term>vegetative nature</term> <note>original: *natura vegetalis* — the unconscious biological functions of the soul, such as growth and nutrition.</note> within us is constantly engaged with corporeal things.
-> Chapter VIII. <-
But just as our vegetative actions are hidden from us, so also our intellectual actions are for the most part concealed. No movement made in the vegetative part by the sense of desire is evident to us unless it reaches the imagination and, through it, the reason. Similarly, the act of the intelligence does not reveal itself unless it occasionally passes subtly into the vacant reason and is transferred to a similarly vacant imagination, where notice usually occurs. The celestial souls, having bodies obedient to them, rule them very easily by a mere instinct of nature and a nod of the mind. Our soul, however, occupying itself with the body through imagination and reason, requires a different kind of providence; therefore, it is divinely established that, departing from here at some time, they should return to the celestial realms.

<summary>This page explains the soul's middle position between the divine and physical realms, arguing that the experience of the material world and "evil" serves to sharpen the soul's understanding of the "good." It concludes that while the World Soul governs without being burdened, human souls must eventually return to their celestial origin after their period of earthly care.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's discussion on the soul's descent, specifically addressing the "undescended" part of the soul. It moves from the general necessity of the soul's participation in the physical world to the specific mechanism by which the soul remains connected to the divine realm even while inhabiting a body.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.
### 476

<columns>
<margin>A</margin> ACCORDINGLY, if it is appropriate to speak more clearly, contrary to the opinion of others—as is plainly evident to me—our soul also does not enter the body in its entirety, but there is always something of it in the **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world</term> <note>original Latin: *mundo intelligibili*; Greek: *νοητῷ*. This refers to the eternal realm of pure thought and Forms, as opposed to the physical world.</note> always, and something in the **sensible world**. Indeed, if this [lower part] prevails—or rather, if it is overcome and disturbed—it does not allow us to perceive those things which the highest part of the soul contemplates. For that which is understood only descends into us when it reaches a certain sense <note>meaning a level of conscious awareness</note> by descending. 

<margin>B</margin> For we do not recognize whatever happens around any part of the soul before it reaches the soul as a whole; just as **lust** <note>original: *concupiscentia*</note> thrives in the very nature of desiring, but is only then recognized by us when we notice this very thing by a certain internal power of sensing or even of thinking, or both. For every soul has something both lower toward the body and higher toward the mind; 

<margin>C</margin> and the whole soul (and the Soul of the Whole <note>The World Soul or *Anima Mundi* which governs the universe.</note>) rules the whole by its part directed toward the body. It does this without labor, as it is quite superior, since it does not act by a **discourse of reason** <term>discourse of reason</term> <note>original: *rationis discursione*. Reasoning that moves step-by-step, unlike the immediate intuition of the higher intellect.</note>, as happens with us, but rather by the **intellect** itself, just as a skill or art is not accustomed to deliberate. That [World Soul] adorns the whole through its lowest part, but particular souls—the souls of parts—also have something superior, yet they are too occupied by the senses themselves, and by the perception of many things occurring against nature that afflict 

<margin>D</margin> and disturb them on all sides; since that which is cared for by them is a certain part, needy and deficient, surrounded by many alien and adverse things. It also craves many things, is entangled in many allurements, and is deceived by pleasure itself. But that which is higher is in no way produced by any new delight, but always leads the same life.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> AND if one must dare to speak more clearly that which is apparent, contrary to the opinion of others, the whole soul and our soul did not <unclear>sink</unclear> <note>original Greek: *ἔδυ*. Translates to "enter," "sink," or "plunge into."</note> entirely, but there is always something of it in the **intelligible**, and something in the **sensible**. If [the lower part] dominates, or rather if it is dominated or troubled, it does not permit us to have a perception of the things which the upper part of the soul beholds. For that which comes into us is known then, when it is already descending into perception.

<margin>B</margin> We do not know everything that happens in every part of the soul until it comes to the soul as a whole. For instance, **desire** <note>original: *ἐπιθυμία*</note> may remain in the desiring part, but it is known to us when we perceive it by the sensitive power, or the potential power, or the discursive power, or both. For every soul has something both downward toward the body and upward toward the **Intellect** <note>original: *νοῦν*</note>. And the whole soul, by that part of the whole which is directed toward the

<margin>C</margin> part of the body, adorns the whole. It is superior in a similar way because it does not act from reasoning as we do, but as Intellect or Art intends to adorn its lower part, and that which is in the whole. But those [souls] that have become partial and are a part, they have that which is their own from themselves. But they are occupied with sensation and the apprehension of many things received that are contrary to nature, both painful and disturbing. For they care for a part that is absent [from the whole], being lesser and

<margin>D</margin> having many alien and evil things. It [the soul] desires many things, and is pleased. And there is a wandering of all [these parts]. But that which is always in it, its conduct is similar [to the divine] in the face of temporary pleasures.

</columns>

<meta>catchword: PLO-</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the human soul never entirely "descends" into the body; a part of it remains eternally in the divine intelligible realm, even when our conscious mind is distracted by physical sensations and desires. He explains that we only become aware of the soul's higher activities when they "descend" into our conscious perception, which is often blocked by the disturbances of the material world.</summary>

<meta>This page begins Book IX of the Fourth Ennead. It follows the discussion of the soul's descent into the body by posing a fundamental question of Neoplatonic philosophy: if the soul is an indivisible spiritual substance, are all individual souls actually just one single Soul?</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD IV.
### BOOK IX.

->Whether all souls are one soul.<-

*The opinion of Plotinus is that the world possesses a soul proper to itself, and that all living creatures likewise possess their own individual souls.*

->Chapter I.<-

*Unless the world possessed a single soul, it would not be a truly unified and perfect composite, nor would the other souls in the world easily harmonize in order. Likewise, if we did not have our own individual souls, the feelings, suffering, and actions of one living being would immediately affect all others and the universe itself. Plotinus, exercising his intellect regarding the opinion that posits a single soul in all things, plays with the idea back and forth, while meanwhile working toward another conclusion.*

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring classical figures and architectural elements.</image-desc>
If, just as we say the soul of each individual <margin>A</margin> is one because it is present as a whole throughout the body, and it is truly "one" in this manner—not having one part here and another part there in the body—and if it is whole everywhere in every part, both in the sensing parts and the senses themselves, and also in the **vegetative parts** <term>vegetative parts</term> <note>original Greek: *φυτικαῖς*. These are the faculties of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition, which Plotinus believes are present throughout the organism.</note>, then is it not the case that my soul and <margin>B</margin> yours are one, and indeed all souls are one? And in the universe, that which is infinite is not divided into mass, but is the same everywhere. For why would the soul in me be one, but the soul in the universe not be one? For it is neither mass nor body; and if it were not a body, then both mine and yours would be one with the soul of the universe. And if they must be one, and if both the soul of the universe and mine come from one soul, then all are one. <margin>C</margin> Which one, then, is this soul? But first it must be asked if it is correctly said that all souls are one as each comes from a single source. For it would be absurd if my soul and another's soul were the same. For if it were one, it would follow that when I perceive something, another would also perceive it; when I am good, that person would be good; when I have a desire, they would desire; and in general, we would share the same **feelings** <term>feelings</term> <note>original: *ὁμοπαθεῖν*. This refers to "sympathy" or "co-suffering," the idea that if souls were one, we would experience the same physical and emotional states simultaneously.</note> with one another and with the whole. So that if I suffered, the whole would feel it with me. And how, if there is altogether only one soul, is one part rational while another is <margin>D</margin> irrational? And why is one in animals and another in plants? Yet again, unless we assume them to be one, neither will the universe be one, nor will a single principle of souls be found.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' depicting a figure sitting amidst foliage and figures.</image-desc>
WHETHER, just as we say the soul of each individual is one because it is everywhere whole in the body, and is indeed one in this way—not with one part here and another part there in the body—and just as in those things that sense, there is a sensing soul, and in plants it is whole everywhere in any part likewise; so too are my soul and your soul one soul, and finally all souls one? And in the universe, is that which is in all things one, not as if distributed through a mass, but having the same everywhere? For why is my soul one, but that which is in the world not one? For there is no mass there, nor body, just as there is none in mine. Surely if both mine and yours are from the soul of the whole world itself, and that soul is one, then these must also be one. If, however, both the soul of the world and mine are from a single soul, then again they are all one. We must therefore ask which one this is especially. But first it must be investigated whether it is rightly said that all souls are one, just as each person's soul is one. For it is absurd for my soul and the soul of anyone else to be one. For if it were one, it would certainly be necessary that when I sense, another would also sense; and when I live well, another would live well; and when I desire, another would desire. We would altogether agree in our **passions** <term>passions</term> <note>original Latin: *passionibus*. In ancient philosophy, a "passion" is something the soul undergoes or experiences from the outside world.</note>, both among ourselves and with the whole itself, to the extent that when I suffer, the universe would feel it. But in what way, if the soul is entirely one, is one part rational and another irrational? Likewise, why is one in animals and another in plants? But again, unless we posited one soul, the universe would not be one, nor would a single principle of souls be found.

<summary>This page introduces Plotinus's inquiry into the "Unity of Souls," questioning whether all individual souls and the World Soul are actually a single entity, while acknowledging the logical difficulties this poses for individual experience.</summary>

--- Page 513 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the unity of the soul from page 477. Having established the problem of how one soul can inhabit many bodies, Plotinus now addresses the counter-argument: if souls were truly one, wouldn't we all feel each other's pain? He uses the analogy of a giant sea creature to explain how a single entity can have localized sensations.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.

<page-num>478</page-num>

*Plotinus, while intending to show that souls are indeed distinct, does not easily give in to the reasoning already mentioned—namely, the idea that the suffering of one living thing would immediately pass into another and into the whole universe.* **Chapter II.**

*He would prefer to say that the soul is not corporeal, and therefore does not require distinct souls for individual parts or for the continuous whole; likewise, when the soul of the living being itself is gathered into one, this soul—holding the highest rank in the category of living things—will feel the sensations brought to it from the animals, but will not itself suffer from them in the least.*

<margin>A</margin> **To begin with**, if one person's soul were the same as another's, it would not immediately follow that each is the same in every respect. For the same thing existing in one person and another will not have the same experiences in both. Just as a man—the "same" man—might be moving in me but not moving in you; in me, because I am moving, he is moved, but in you, who are not moving, he is at rest. It is neither absurd nor contrary to common opinion that what is in me is the same as what is in you. Nor is it necessary that if I am sensing something, another person must have exactly the same <margin>B</margin> experience. For even in the same body, one hand does not feel the pain of the other; rather, it is the soul that is in the whole body that feels it. If you were intended to know my suffering, it would be necessary for our two bodies to be fused into one single thing. For only if they were joined in that way would both feel the same thing.

It is worth remembering that many things sometimes escape the notice of the "whole," even those things that happen in one and the same body. This is especially true the larger the mass of the body is, as is said to happen in certain very large creatures <note>original: "vastioribus beluis" — likely referring to whales or Great Sea Monsters.</note>. In these cases, <margin>C</margin> when a part suffers, no sensation reaches the whole because the movement is too small. Therefore, it is not necessary that when one individual suffers, the sensation must immediately reach the whole or be perceived by everyone. 

A shared feeling <note>original: "compar" — used here to mean a sympathetic or shared quality.</note> is indeed not absurd and should not be denied, but it is not necessary for a specific sensory image to be formed in everyone. Thus, it is not surprising that the same soul might have virtue in me but vice in another, since it is not impossible for the same thing to be moved in one <margin>D</margin> place and be at rest in another. 

For we do not say that the soul is "one" in a way that excludes all multiplicity; that is a quality reserved for a higher nature <note>The "higher nature" refers to the One or the Intellect in Neoplatonic hierarchy.</note>. Rather, we say it is "one and many" simultaneously. It participates both in that nature which becomes divisible around bodies and in that nature which remains indivisible. From this, it follows that the soul is once again one. 

Just as a suffering that happens in a part of me does not necessarily occupy the whole, but a suffering that happens to the **principal part** <term>principal part</term> <note>original: "principali," translating the Greek *hegemonikon*, the ruling or commanding faculty of the soul.</note> <margin>E</margin> is somehow diffused even to the parts, so too the things that come from the universe to each individual are more clearly perceived, since the individual parts suffer in sympathy with the whole. But whether the things that happen to us immediately reach the whole remains hidden from us.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is a translation of the Greek column, which provides the original text for the Latin passage above.</note>

First, it would not be the case that my soul and another's are one, such that there is a shared suffering with me, and the same experience occurs in the one and the other. For the "man" in me may be moving, while the one in another is not. It is not paradoxical that the same thing is in me and in you; nor is it necessary that the one who perceives must feel the same things as the other. For even in one body, the experience of one hand is not felt by the other, but by the soul in the whole. If you are to know what I know, there must be one joined body from both of us. 

It signifies that many things escape the notice of the whole which occur in one and the same body, especially when the body has a great size, as is said of great whales. They say that when some suffering occurs in a part, no sensation reaches the whole because of the smallness of the movement. Thus, it is not necessary for an impression of sensible things to exist for the whole, or a mental image for all. We see how we suffer, but it is not necessary that everything follows in order. 

It is not necessary for everyone to be sensory in the same way; for example, the vice in me and the virtue in another are opposites. For we say that in one and another, one may be moved and another remain still. We do not say that souls are entirely without parts, for that nature is superior; but we say they are one and many, participating in the nature that is divided among bodies and the indivisible nature, being one again as is necessary. Just as when we experience suffering in a part, it does not necessarily master the whole, but that which happens to the ruling part reaches the part. Furthermore, the things in the whole are clearer to each individual, as many things sympathize with the whole, but the things in us—it is unclear if they contribute to the whole.

---

->Our Plotinus is still playing.<-
->**Chapter III.**<-

*But just as mutual love between humans signifies a union of souls, so too do the perpetual and dire hatreds between them signify their diversity. For one man is no less divided from another man, or one animal from another animal, than fire is from water; therefore, they are not distinguished by a single power. Indeed, the attraction of magic is largely admitted, and we have declared its causes in the higher realms. Elsewhere we have said that the **formal virtue** <term>formal virtue</term> <note>original: "formalem rei virtutē" — the inherent power or blueprint that makes a thing what it is.</note> of a thing is a "reason" <note>original: "rationem" — often used by Ficino to translate the Greek *logos*.</note> that can be multiplied into many essences, with the sole exception of the First. Therefore, just as the formal reason of a body, quality, or nature is distinct across many bodies, natures, and qualities, so too are there many souls and intellects. Then indeed, if the soul is more excellent in form than a quality, it is certainly established by divine providence that there are many ranks of souls, just as there are qualities formally distinct from one another—not like this heat differs from that heat because of the subject, but like heat differs from cold, or dryness from moisture. Plotinus already hints at this in this chapter, where he says that there are many intellects, and that the individual senses themselves exist simultaneously with the universal ones—that is, with the intellectual souls. This discussion signifies an agreement that there is one soul in all bodies, not a rational one, but a **vegetative** one participating in a certain shared sense; nevertheless, any rational soul can form its own body with irrational life, if it has not already been formed by the Soul of the World.*

<summary>Plotinus argues that the unity of the soul does not require all individuals to share the same physical sensations, using the analogy of a giant sea creature to show how parts can experience things independently of the whole. The commentary notes that while souls share a common nature, they are formally distinct in their individual expressions and ranks.</summary>
<keywords>unity of the soul, individual perception, sympathy, whales, hegemonikon, formal reason, multiplicity, vegetative soul, Plotinus, Ficino</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 478 regarding the unity of the soul. Having previously addressed why individuals do not always feel one another's physical pain, Plotinus now explores the phenomena of "sympathy" and magic as evidence for a single underlying soul connecting all living things.</meta>

# BOOK NINE. 479

<margin><unclear>by itself..</unclear></margin>
ACCORDINGLY, reason dictates that we are affected by one another’s experiences from opposite sides, and that we are touched by mercy at the mere sight of another, and are moved and naturally drawn toward loving. <note>The Greek term *sympathein* here refers to "cosmic sympathy," the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected like organs in a single body.</note> Truly, it is worth considering whether this mutual love arises among us because of a shared nature. Indeed, if certain spells and magical charms draw many people toward a single impulse, and strike a common feeling into those living even far away, it seems this can only be achieved through the agency of a single soul. Furthermore, a word spoken in a low voice 
<margin>A</margin> allures someone far removed and compels them to hear, even across a vast distance. From these examples, one may understand the union of all things, as if they were breathing together through one soul. 

But how can the soul be one if one part is rational, another irrational, and another 
<margin>B</margin> vegetative? <note>The "vegetative" or "plant-like" soul is the level of biological function responsible for growth and nutrition, shared by humans, animals, and plants.</note> Perhaps it is because the part of the soul that is indivisible is attributed to the rational power, which is not distributed among bodies; whereas the part distributed around bodies is also a single existing thing, but 
<margin>C</margin> divided by those bodies. Exercising sensation everywhere, this must be considered another part of the soul. Finally, there is the part that shapes and creates the bodies. Yet the soul is no less "one" simply because 
<margin>D</margin> there are many powers within it. For even in a seed, there are many powers, yet the seed is one; and from this one seed, many things become one. But why then are all these powers not present everywhere? Even in the soul, which is said to be one in any individual, sensation is not exactly the same in all parts; reason is not in the whole body; and the vegetative power is present where sensation itself is absent. Yet they all return and join together in the one body. If the power of nourishment comes from the whole, why then does it not also come from our individual soul? Because that which is nourished is a part of the universe, which is concealed as something sensory through a certain passive condition. Sensation itself is a judging faculty combined with intellect, which did not need to form that which is already formed by the universe. For the soul formed both, unless it were necessary for the creator to be counted within this whole.

---

*He has already refuted the opinion stating that all souls are numerically one; now he touches upon the view that the soul is one in species but distinct in number, and that individual souls are derived from a single divided soul.*

->Chapter IV.<-

---

THESE things have been said so that no one wonders at this reduction to unity. However, the method of our dispute requires us to ask: in what way is the soul one? Are all souls one because they proceed from a single source, or are they all essentially one in themselves? If they come from one, is that source divided, or does it remain whole while nonetheless producing many from itself? And if so, how can an essence that remains whole create many from itself? Let us speak then, 
<margin>A</margin> having first invoked divine help: it is necessary that a "one" exists first if there are to be many souls, and that the many proceed from this one. If this "one" were a body, it would necessarily be divided to become many, becoming a different essence entirely, as if it were 
<margin>B</margin> made of similar parts. In that case, all souls would be made uniform, bearing one and the same form as the whole, but differing only in their bulk or size. But if this difference depends on the bulk of the matter...

<column-break/>

<note>The translator here follows the Latin of Marsilio Ficino, who provided the standard Renaissance interpretation of Plotinus's difficult Greek.</note>

*He refutes this view as well: for the soul is an incorporeal, indivisible substance that exists within itself. Therefore, one common soul cannot be derived into many, as if a continuous thing were cut into parts, or as white color is divided into many whites; nor is it like many impressions made in wax from a single seal.*

---

<summary>Plotinus argues that phenomena like "sympathy," love, and magic prove that all individual souls are connected through a single, universal Soul, though he struggles to define exactly how one essence can remain whole while appearing in many bodies.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Neoplatonism, universal soul, sympathy, magic, rational soul, vegetative soul, unity, incorporeal substance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the unity of the soul. # PLOTINUS ENNEAD IV.
# PAGE 480

<margin>A</margin>
...might have [the property] that they are souls distinct from one another. But if they possess this property instead according to their form, then souls are one in species. This would mean that one and the same soul exists in many bodies, and that before this single soul exists in many, there is another soul that does not exist in many. From this [original soul], the one that is in many depends, like an image <note>original: "simulachrum"</note> carried here and there from a single thing existing in one place: just as if the figure from a single seal <note>original: "sigillo"</note> were impressed upon many sheets of paper. In that way, it would be distributed into many signs.
<margin>B</margin>
However, if the matter stands in the second way, the soul is something incorporeal; and if it were a kind of "passion" <note>In this context, "passion" refers to an attribute or an effect experienced by a subject, rather than an emotion.</note>, it would not be surprising for one quality, produced from a single source, to exist in many. And if the soul were judged according to both aspects joined together, that too would not be strange. But in fact, we consider the soul to be both incorporeal and an essence <note>original: "essentiam"; the underlying "being" or "substance" of a thing.</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...souls are distinct from one another. If, however, this property is such that they are one soul in form, then it follows that one and the same soul exists in many bodies, and prior to this soul which is in many, there is another which is not in many. From this soul, the one in many is derived, like an image cast in many places from a single source, or like an impression made in wax from a single ring. In that manner, it would be shared among a multitude.
<margin>B</margin>
But if the second case holds, the soul being something incorporeal—or even a single shared experience—it would not be at all surprising for a single quality arising from one source to be present in many. And if the soul is both of these things together, it is still not strange; but we are now positing that the soul is something incorporeal and an essence.

---

->Although souls are distinct from one another through their essences, they are all nevertheless in some way one soul, specifically in three ways.<-
->Chapter V.<-

*First, because one general Idea of souls presides over all, and the whole is present in each individual. Second, because any soul is an entirely "all-formed" <note>original: "omniformis"; meaning a form that contains within itself the patterns of all other forms.</note> shape; therefore, any soul encompasses all other souls. Yet this soul differs from that one, because under a differentiated property, both this and that are "all-formed," just as geometric propositions agree with and differ from one another. Third, because all can exist in the same point, just as lights and the images of colors can without confusion. We have already proved in our "Theology" <note>This refers to Marsilio Ficino’s own work, "Platonic Theology," where he argues that there is a unique mind or soul in individuals.</note> that there is a unique soul or mind in individuals. Although this is Plotinus's main point, be careful not to suspect that Plotinus does not distinguish between the essences of souls. For that would contradict all his books, and even this one; for in this Ennead, he creates a specific dispute against those who think the soul is only one. But remember that Plotinus everywhere strives, as much as possible, to reduce all things to a certain unity while preserving the property of their nature. I say "to a certain unity," meaning to a communion of feelings, actions, and experiences: so that a concordant harmony is preserved in the universe, and the transmission of power and action happens mutually and easily through each part—which could not happen unless individual souls, though their essential distinction is preserved, were contained like regions by one form: just as all the powers of the limbs are contained by the power of the heart and the nerves from the neck. He therefore brings forward many signs for judging this union, which he confirms as very strong. He even seems to concede that all souls are of such vigor that they can be led not only to such a union but even to a greater one—almost saying that if anyone could disprove these signs of the union of essence (which I do not approve), we could much more strongly assert through the same signs a union among souls of affection, action, agreement, and compassion.*

<margin>A</margin>
IN WHAT WAY, then, is there one essence in many? Is it one whole in all, or are the many derived from one whole, while that one remains? That one, then, is a unity; but the many are referred to this as one, which gives itself to the multitude and yet, in another sense, does not. For it is enough for it to exhibit itself to all and nevertheless remain one. It can be in all things at once, and is not entirely separated from any one thing. If it were so, it would be thinned out among the many. Nor should one feel any distrust in this: for scientific knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note> 
<margin>B</margin>
is also a whole, and its parts are such that the whole remains while the parts come from it. Likewise, a seed is a whole, and from it come the parts into which it can naturally be divided; yet each part is a whole, and the whole remains diminished nowhere. Someone might say that in the case of matter, a part is not the whole; but here also, that which is most prominent is a part in "act" <note>original: "actu"; in actual practice or manifestation.</note>, insofar as use requires it, and that 
<margin>C</margin>
is placed before the others. Nevertheless, the remaining parts follow as a certain "potential" <note>original: "potentia"</note> lying hidden there, and all things are in the part; perhaps it is by this condition that it is called a whole. The part exists there as if in act, but all things are there together. Therefore, whatever you wish to approach or manage is ready and present. In the part itself, there is what we call "prepared," but it exists in potential...

<summary>Plotinus and his commentator explore how the soul can be simultaneously one and many, using the analogies of a seal's impression, the structure of scientific knowledge, and the potentiality within a seed. The text emphasizes that cosmic harmony and "sympathy" are possible because souls share a unified essence even while remaining distinct individuals.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the final book of the Fourth Ennead and introduces the Fifth Ennead. It transitions from a discussion on how individual souls relate to the universal soul—using the analogy of scientific knowledge where the whole is present in every part—into the famous inquiry regarding why souls forget their divine origin.</meta>

...is judged insofar as it adheres to the whole. One must not think that a notion, in this part of science <note>In Plotinian philosophy, "science" or "knowledge" refers to the structured, unified understanding of the Intellect.</note> we speak of, is empty of other notions; otherwise, it would not be a skillful notion, nor proper to science, but just as if a child happened to speak. If, therefore, it is suited to science, it possesses all parts potentially. Thus, when a man of science focuses on these more inclined matters, starting from one particularly refined point, he subsequently produces the rest through a certain logical consequence. Hence the Geometer 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> in his very resolution <note>original: "resolutione," referring to the process of "analysis" where a conclusion is traced back to its first principles</note> declares that each single thing encompasses all preceding things through which the resolution is made, and also encompasses the consequences which are drawn from there in a certain order. But these things are not believed because of our weakness, and are obscured by the mass of the body; in that higher realm, however, all things are clear, and every single thing is perspicuous.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD V,
### BOOK I.

# P L O T I N I
## ENNEAD V,
### BOOK I.

->On the three principal substances, which have the nature of a principle.<-
->On the three principal substances, possessing the character of a beginning.<-

*The soul in its homeland <note>The "homeland" refers to the divine or intelligible realm (the Kosmos Noetos).</note> lives and acts under the form of the divine mind rather than by its own power, just as the body now lives under the form of the soul. But as soon as the soul applies itself to living and acting under its own form—namely through discursive reasoning—it then slides gradually into the movement of the imagination, and into sensory and vegetative action, so that it now lives as if under a corporeal form.*

->Chapter I.<-

To this soul it finally happens that it thinks of itself as <unclear>corporeal</unclear>; thus, distrusting its own divinity, it neither seeks nor venerates divine things any longer.

<margin>A</margin> WHAT IS IT, then, that has caused the souls to forget God the father, and—though they are portions from that realm and belong entirely to it—to be completely ignorant of both those things and themselves?
<margin>B</margin> The principle of evil for them was audacity <note>original: "audacia" (Greek: "tolma"). In Neoplatonism, this "daring" or "boldness" refers to the soul's desire to assert its own individuality and separate itself from the divine whole.</note>, and generation, and the first "otherness," and the desire to belong to themselves.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> WHAT CAUSE IS IT <note>The OCR "aula" (hall) is a likely mistranscription of "causa."</note> that souls, which are of a divine lot and belong to God, nevertheless forget God the father, being ignorant of themselves and of Him? The principle of evil for souls is audacity, generation, the first "otherness," and because they wish to be their own [masters].

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Ennead V, Tractate 1, one of Plotinus’s most famous works. # PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> ...to be their own masters <note>original: "iuris esse," a legal term meaning to be under one's own authority</note>. Once they began to delight in this freedom or license, making full use of their own power to move themselves and following a contrary path—becoming as remote as possible from their source—they eventually became completely ignorant that they themselves arose from that realm. They are like children who, having been separated from their parents immediately at birth and raised far away for a long time, are ignorant of both themselves and their parents. Since they see neither their father nor themselves, they devalue themselves through ignorance of their lineage <margin>B</margin>; they honor other things, admiring anything that occurs to them more than themselves. Struck with awe and hanging off these external things in wonder, they have surely cast themselves as far away as possible, making themselves subservient to the things from which they turned away, while holding their father and themselves in low regard. Therefore, it seems that an extreme ignorance of the divine results from honoring inferior things and despising one's own self. For as soon as the soul pursues and admires something else, it simultaneously confesses that it is inferior to the very thing it admires and pursues. When it presents itself as <margin>C</margin> inferior to things that are born and perish, and considers itself to be the most dejected and fleeting of all the things it honors, it naturally can conceive of neither the nature nor the power of God in its mind. For this reason, we must address a two-fold discourse to those who are in such a state, if we are to be able to turn them back toward the opposites—the primary things—and lead them back to the supreme One, the First. What then are these two? One surely demonstrates for what <margin>D</margin> reason the soul now honors these lower, internal things; we have discussed this at length elsewhere. The other teaches and reminds the soul of how noble a lineage it was born from, and with what great dignity it is endowed. This second discourse is certainly prior to the first, and once clarified, it will also illuminate the first; it is of this that we must now speak. For this approach seems to come closest to the nature of what we seek and is appropriately placed before the other. That which seeks is the soul itself; therefore, it must first know <margin>E</margin> what it is as an existing being that is searching within itself. It must learn first whether it has the power to investigate such things, whether it possesses the eye with which it can perceive them, and whether it is even fitting to investigate them at all. For if these things are alien to us, why do we search for them? But if they are kindred, it is right and profitable to seek them, and the soul may eventually find them.

> The dignity of the world-soul is demonstrated by the fact that if she were not in the world, the world would be nothing other than formless matter.

->Chapter II.<-

> The soul generates the forms of things, triggers the motions and actions of all, and implants life and growth in everything. She is entirely present everywhere and rules what is born. Her relationship to the body of the world is like the rising sun to the dark air. Our own souls have similar powers and almost the same dignity, especially if they remain within themselves, purified of bodily filth.

<margin>A</margin> **E**VERY soul should first consider that the soul itself produced all living creatures by breathing life into them: I say she made all living things that the earth nourishes, those in the sea, those in the air, and the divine stars in heaven. The soul adorned the sun; the soul adorned this vast heaven and leads it in perpetual order, being herself a nature distinct from the things she adorns, moves, and provides with life. Therefore, she must be more excellent than all these things; for while these things are born,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to be of themselves through their own free will <note>Greek: "autexousio," the power of self-determination</note>. Since they appeared to suffer this [desire for independence], using their own movement to a great extent and running the contrary way, they made a stand far apart. They became ignorant even that they were from that source, just as children who are snatched away from their fathers at birth and brought up for a long time far away are ignorant of both themselves and their fathers. Since they no longer see those parents <margin>B</margin> or themselves, they dishonor themselves through ignorance of their race. They honor other things, admiring everything rather than themselves; being struck by these things and wondering at them, hanging upon them, they have broken away as much as possible from those things from which they turned away in dishonor. So it happens that the honor given to these lower things is the cause of their complete ignorance of the divine, as well as the cause of their self-dishonor. For to pursue and admire another thing is to admit that the one admiring and pursuing is <margin>C</margin> inferior. By placing itself as inferior to things that are becoming and perishing, and supposing itself to be the most dishonored and mortal of all the things it honors, the soul could never take into its mind the nature and power of God. Therefore, a two-fold argument must be made to those so disposed, if one is to turn them back to the opposites and the first things, and lead them up to the highest, the One and the First. What then is each? One shows the <margin>D</margin> dishonor of the things now honored by the soul, which we have treated elsewhere at greater length. The other teaches and reminds the soul what its race and worth are. This is prior to the first, and once made clear, it will also reveal the other. We must speak of this now. For it is near to the object of our inquiry, and it is useful for it. For the seeker is the soul, and she must know what she is while she seeks <margin>E</margin>, so that she may first learn if she has the capacity to seek such things. And if she learns she has a power of her own, and if it is fitting for her. For if they are alien, why bother? But if they are kindred, it is both fitting and she is able to find them.

<margin>A</margin> **LET EVERY** soul then consider, first of all, that it is the soul that made all living things, breathing life into them: those that the earth feeds, those in the sea, those in the air, and the divine stars in the heavens. It is she who made the sun, she who made this great heaven, and she who adorned it, leading it around in order, being herself a nature different from the things she adorns, and which she moves, and which she makes live. And she must be more honorable than these. For while these things are becoming,

<summary>Plotinus discusses the soul's alienation from its divine source due to self-will and its fascination with the physical world. He argues that the soul must be reminded of its own noble origin and its role as the animator of the entire cosmos to regain its true perspective.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the soul's relationship with the divine. Having just discussed why souls forget their origin, he now provides a method for the individual soul to remember its dignity by contemplating the "Great Soul" (the World Soul) that animates the entire universe.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin> ...when the soul supplies life, and they perish when it leaves; but the soul itself exists forever, because it never deserts itself. Now, the manner in which life is supplied to the universe and to individual living beings may be considered in this way: Therefore, let another soul—one that has attained a significant dignity for such contemplation—consider the Great Soul <note>original: "ingentem animam"; Plotinus refers here to the World Soul, the divine principle that animates the entire physical cosmos</note>. This soul must be free from deception and from all the charms that usually fascinate other souls, and so it must be established in a state of the deepest stillness. <margin>B</margin> Not only should the body that surrounds it be quiet, along with the storms of the body, but everything that encompasses it from the outside should also be at rest. Let the earth be still, and the sea, and the air, and the very heavens. Soon, let it conceive in that stillness that a Great Soul flows into this mass from the outside, poured in and penetrating every part, illuminating it just as the rays of the sun illuminate a dark cloud and turn it to a golden appearance. Thus, the soul, having entered the celestial body, <margin>C</margin> gave it life, gave it immortality, and awakened that which was entirely dormant. Being moved by this perpetual motion under the guidance of a wise soul, the world became a blessed living being. The entire heaven attained its dignity as soon as the soul took up its habitation, whereas before it was a body void of life—merely earth and water, or rather, the darkness of matter and non-being <note>original: "non ens"; a philosophical term for that which lacks true reality</note>, which (as Plato says) the gods loathe. The power and nature of the soul will become clearer and more evident if one observes here how <margin>D</margin> it encompasses and leads the heavens by its own will. For it has given itself to this entire mass, however great it may be. Thus, this whole expanse, both great and small, is ensouled, even though one part of the body is situated in one place and another elsewhere; some parts are disposed in one way, some in another, some placed opposite each other, and others connected and mutually dependent. But the soul is not like that. It does not bring life to parts individually by being divided into bits and pieces; rather, it gives life to all things as a whole. It is present in its entirety everywhere, <margin>E</margin> made similar to the Father who generated it <note>The "Father" here refers to the Intellect (Nous) or the One, the higher principles from which the Soul emanates</note>, both in its unity and in its expansive reach through all things. And indeed, though the heaven is manifold and different parts are in different places, it is nonetheless one by the power of that soul. Now, because of this soul, this world is a God; the Sun is also a God because it is ensouled, and likewise all the stars. Whatever excellence we ourselves possess, we have it only because of this. For a body deprived of soul is said to be more contemptible than dung <margin>F</margin>. It is necessary, then, that the soul itself—since it is the cause for the gods being gods—must be a God more ancient than they are. Our own soul is of the same kind. Therefore, whenever you consider it without its attachments, looking at it in its pure state, you will find that very thing which is the soul to be venerable, and far more precious than any body. For without the soul, all things would be merely earth. Even if fire were present, what would its burning intensity be? Or whatever might be composed of these? Even if you added water <margin>G</margin> and air to them, you would still not have found anything venerable. But if the body becomes worthy of pursuit because it is ensouled, why do you leave yourself behind—that is, your own soul—and pursue something else? Come then, having admired the soul in another, admire yourself.
<sig>S 2</sig>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...when the Soul provides life, and they perish when it leaves; it truly exists always, by the fact that it never leaves itself. Now, let the manner of the provision of life to the animal <note>original: "τῷ ζώῳ" (to the living being/animal); in Platonic thought, the entire universe is a single living animal</note>, both in the whole and in the individuals, be reckoned thus. Let the great soul be contemplated by another Soul, one that has become of no small worth for contemplation, having been freed from deceit and the enchantments that have bewitched the others, being in a quiet state. <margin>B</margin> For let there be silence for it, not only from the body that surrounds it and the surge of the body, but also from all that encompasses it. Let the earth be still, let the sea be still, and the air, and the very heavens themselves. Let it think of the Soul as standing outside, flowing in from everywhere into this motionless mass, pouring in, entering from all sides and illuminating it. Just as the rays of the sun, having lit up a dark cloud, make it shine, producing a golden appearance, so the soul, having come <margin>C</margin> into the body of the heaven, gave it life, gave it immortality, and woke it as it lay still. Being moved by the eternal life of the Soul, it became a manifestly wonderful living being. The heaven gained dignity from the soul dwelling within it, whereas before it was a body of soul, earth and water, or rather the darkness of matter and "nothing," and what (as Plato says) has become "something" <note>original: "ὃ γέγονέ τι"; a reference to the Timaeus where matter receives form</note>. This will be made more manifest by the power and nature of the soul if it is considered <margin>D</margin> how it encompasses and leads the heaven by its own wishes. For to all this magnitude, as great as it is, it gave itself, and every distance, both great and small, is ensouled; but whereas one part of the body is here and another there, some in this way and some in that, and some are opposite and others are from everywhere with respect to each other, the soul is not so. It does not give life by being cut into pieces for each part; <margin>E</margin> the soul, being undivided, is not one [piece], but all things live by it, and the whole is present everywhere, having been made like the father who begot it, both in respect to the one and to the whole. And even if the heaven is great and its parts are various, it is one by this power; and this world is a god because of this soul. And the sun is a god, because it is ensouled, and the other stars. And we, if we are anything, are so because of this. For in the case of dead things and dung, <margin>F</margin> it is a loathsome thing; but the cause for the gods being gods must be older than the gods themselves. Our soul is of the same form. And when you look at it, having removed what covers it, looking at it purified, you will find the same honorable thing which was soul, and more honorable than everything. All things that are not bodily—the earth was all [this], and if there were fire, it would be its burning <margin>G</margin> itself. And whatever things are composed of these, and water with the good things, and air; but if it is because it is ensouled that it is pursued, or if it provides something to itself, but it does not pursue, then by loving the soul in another, you love yourself.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion from the previous section (Ennead V, Book 1), where he began instructing the soul on how to recognize its own divine nature. Having established the soul's dignity, he now moves toward the "Intellect" (the second hypostasis in Neoplatonism), explaining how the soul is an image or "word" of that higher Mind.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK V.

*Our rational faculty, being mobile and prone to wandering from the path, depends on something higher; it relies upon our intellect, which is stable and always active. Furthermore, this intellect—as a part of an individual soul—depends upon the Universal Intellect <note>original: "intellectu communi"; referring to the Divine Mind or 'Nous'</note> which exists simply within itself. Chapter III.*

*Our intellect relates to our reason, and the Universal Intellect relates to our own, just as light relates to air and form relates to matter. While our reason is shaped daily by our own intellect, our intellect is always shaped and illuminated by the Universal Intellect. We can therefore estimate the excellence of the Universal Intellect by looking at the high standing of the soul's own intellect.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Since the soul is such a venerable and divine thing, be confident that you can reach God by using the soul as your vehicle; by this very means, ascend to Him. You do not have to wander far, nor are there many obstacles in between. Take hold of that which is most divine within this divine soul—namely, its proximity to the realm above, from which the soul originates and to which it is a neighbor. For as great a thing as <margin>B</margin> reason has shown the soul to be, it is nonetheless only an image of the Intellect itself <note>original: "imago tamen quaedam est intellectus ipsius"</note>. Just as a spoken word <note>original: "verbum in prolatione"; an expression of an internal thought</note> is an image of the word dwelling in the soul, so too is the soul itself the "word" or expression of the Mind (*Intellectus*). The soul is entirely the activity and life which the Mind produces to exist in another form; much like how one kind of heat is innate to fire, while another kind is the heat that fire gives off to something else. We must understand, however, that the life in the soul does not merely flow away from the Mind, but remains partly within it while also extending outward. Therefore, because the soul comes from the Mind, it is intellectual in its nature. The "reasoning" of the soul is its intellect in motion; its perfection comes <margin>C</margin> from the Intellect as if from a father and a nurturer. Indeed, compared to the Mind, the soul was not entirely perfect when it was first brought forth. Thus, the soul’s very substance comes from the Mind, and it becomes "reason" in actual practice—a kind of intellectual expression—whenever it gazes upon the Mind. For when the soul looks toward the Mind, it possesses within itself the things it understands and enacts. It is right to call these "actions" of the soul only when they are intellectual and arise from within its own nature. Those actions which are inferior come from the outside and are merely the <margin>D</margin> passions of such a soul. The Intellect, therefore, makes the soul even more divine, both because it is its father and because it is always present. There is nothing between them except the fact that they are distinct from one another, yet the soul follows and receives from the Intellect, while the Intellect acts as the Form <note>In this context, "Form" or "Species" refers to the organizing principle that gives shape to the "Matter" of the soul</note>. The "matter" of the Intellect itself is beautiful, being something intellectual and simple. How excellent the Intellect is can be seen from this: it is even more excellent than the soul, which is already a thing of great excellence.

<column-break/>

So then, since the soul is a thing truly honorable and divine, trust in such a vehicle to reach God, and by it, go to Him. You will certainly not be cast far away, nor are the distances between you great. Take then the most divine part of the soul, which neighbors the heights, where the soul itself is found. The soul is a thing like an image; just as the spoken word is to the word in the soul, so the soul itself is the "word" <note>original: "logos"; can mean word, reason, or principle</note> of the Mind. It is the Mind's total activity, the life it sends forth to establish another existence. Consider fire: there is its inherent heat, and then there is the heat it provides to others. But we must see this life not as something that has leaked out, but as something that remains in its source while also existing elsewhere. Since the soul comes from the Mind, it is of the nature of mind, and its reasoning is its "Mind." Its completion comes from the Mind, as if from a father who has raised it, though it was not born perfect compared to him. Its existence is an activity derived from the Mind, a "reason-principle" which the soul sees when it looks upon the Mind. For when it looks there, it has within it the things it thinks and does. These alone should be called the soul's own activities: those which are intellectual and home-grown. Lower things come from elsewhere and are the "passions" <note>In ancient philosophy, a "passion" is something that happens *to* you from the outside, rather than an action you initiate</note> of such a soul. The Mind makes the soul more divine because it is its father and because it is present. There is no gap between them, except that they are different; the soul follows in order, while the Mind is like the Form and the soul is like the Matter. But the Mind's matter is intellectual and simple. If one correctly perceives this, one sees that the Mind surpasses even a soul as great as this.

---

*Since the world comes from the Divine Intellect, it is certainly contained entirely within it. And because the Intellect is Being, Life, and the most perfect Mind, everything in the world that is within it is perfect, existing as Being, Life, and Intellect. Chapter IV.*

*The parts of time belonging to worldly things refer to "Total Time," which exists passively in the world. This in turn refers to the time that exists actively in the soul, and that refers back to the Eternity of the Divine Mind itself. However, within the Mind itself, "understanding" and "being understood" differ only by a formal reason. That which understands and that which is understood are the same in substance. There, "understanding" is metaphorically called "motion," while "being understood" is like "moving" and "standing still." Since that Intellect is all-formed and contains some difference and composition within itself, it must ultimately be traced back to something higher and most simple.*

---

<margin>A</margin> One can also recognize this through the following: if someone admires this sensible world, gazing upon its magnitude and beauty and the eternal order of its motion; and likewise the gods within it, some visible and some hidden, as well as the spirits <note>original: "daemones"; in Greek philosophy, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note>, animals, and all plants—let him then look toward the Archetype <note>The original "blueprint" or perfect model in the Divine Mind</note> of this world.

<column-break/>

If anyone admires this sensible world, looking at its size and beauty and the eternal order of its movement, and the gods within it—some seen and some unseen—and the spirits, animals, and all plants, let him then ascend to its Archetype.

<summary>This page describes the metaphysical hierarchy of Neoplatonism, explaining how the human soul is an image or "word" of the higher Divine Intellect (Mind). It encourages the reader to contemplate the beauty of the physical world as a means to recognize the even greater beauty of the spiritual "Archetype" from which it descends.</summary>
<keywords>Soul, Intellect, Reason, Plotinus, Archetype, Divine Mind, Logos, Neoplatonism, Metaphysics, World Soul</keywords>
