<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s explanation of the Divine Intellect (the second principle or 'Hypostasis' in his philosophy). Having discussed how the soul is an image of the Intellect, he now describes the internal life of that Intellect—a realm of eternal, unchanging Being that contains all forms of life and thought simultaneously.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<sig>$ 3</sig>

...within itself, and ascending toward that which is more truly real, he may see all intelligible things there, and the eternal things within it, in its own understanding and life. He may see the pure Mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note> presiding over them, an unblemished wisdom, and the truly "Golden Life" under Saturn <note>original: "Κρόνος" (Kronos); Plotinus identifies the mythical god Kronos with 'Nous' or Intellect</note>, for Saturn is the Intellect. Indeed, it encompasses all immortal things: every intellect, every god, every soul, all standing eternally still. For why should it seek to change when it is well? Where would it move, since it possesses all things within itself? Nor does it seek to grow, being most perfect. Wherefore, all things within it are perfect, so that it is perfect in every way, having nothing that is not so, and having nothing in itself that it does not think. It thinks, however, not by seeking, but by possessing. Its blessedness is not acquired from the outside; rather, all things exist in eternity, and this is the true Eternity <note>original: "αἰών" (aion)</note>. Time <note>original: "χρόνος" (chronos)</note> merely imitates this as it moves around the soul, letting some things pass and reaching for others. For things are always different and successive for the soul: at one moment Socrates, at another a horse; always some single thing among those that exist. But the Intellect is all things. It holds all things together, standing still in the same state. It simply *is*, and its *is* is forever. Nowhere is there a future for it, for it already *is* then; nor is there a past. Nothing there has passed away, but all things exist always, and being such things, they are as if imprinted upon themselves, remaining so. Each of them is both intellect and being, and the whole is every intellect and every being. The Intellect, through the act of thinking, gives substance to Being; and Being, by being thought, gives thinking and existence to the Intellect. The cause of their "being" is something else, or rather, there is a cause that makes both exist together at once. For each individual thing and the whole Intellect exist together, as do the individual beings, yet they are not identical. Rather, the Intellect is Being. Being is the object of thought, and the thinking subject is the Intellect. The Intellect acts through thinking, and Being acts as that which is thought. For if there were no "Otherness" <note>original: "ἑτερότης" (heterotês)</note> as well as "Identity" <note>original: "ταὐτότης" (tautotês)</note>, there would be no act of thinking. These primary categories—Being, Otherness, and Identity—must exist. One must also include Motion and Rest. Motion is required for the act of thinking, and Rest so that it remains the same. One needs Otherness so that there may be a thinker and an object of thought. If you remove this Otherness, the result will become a silent unity. Those things which are thought must also be different from one another, yet the same, insofar as they are within the same whole; the common element is their shared existence, while their difference is Otherness. These factors, as they become many, produce number and quantity. Quality is also produced by the specific property of each, from which, as principles, all other things proceed.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...of this world, its principle and exemplar, he should ascend to the more true world. There, let him behold all intelligible things, and within that realm, let him see the eternal things in their own intelligence and life, presided over by an entirely untainted Intellect and an inestimable wisdom. This is truly the "Golden Life" under Saturn, for Saturn himself is the entirely immaculate Intellect. He comprehends all immortal things in himself: every intellect, every god, every soul, and all <margin>B</margin> these things existing fully within him. For why should he seek to change anything, since he is well? Where would he pass to, since he possesses all things within himself? He does not even require growth, since he is most perfect. Therefore, whatever things are with him are perfect, so that he is altogether perfect, possessing nothing that is not such; nor having anything in in himself that he does not understand. Yet he understands not by searching, but by possessing. Nor does he have a foreign happiness, but he holds all things in an age <note>Ficino uses "aevum" for eternity</note> which is the true <margin>C</margin> eternity. Time imitates this eternity as it revolves around the soul, dismissing some things while attaining others. Indeed, different things follow one after another around the soul. At one time it is Socrates, at another a horse; always one thing out of the many that exist. But the Intellect is all things. It therefore holds all things together, consistent in the same state; it simply is, and is always present, nor is there any way it will be in the future. For it is already then whatever it can be, nor does it have a <margin>D</margin> past. For nothing there passes away, but there all things remain in the present, inasmuch as they are always the same, as if they were content with their present state. Accordingly, any one of them is both intellect and being. And the universe is every intellect and every being. The intellect indeed, because it thinks, claims being for itself; but being, because it is thought, provides both the being thought and the existence to the intellect. However, the cause of thinking is something else, which is also the cause of being for the existent. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, there is another cause for both together. For they both exist at once and never fail each other. But though they are two, this very one is simultaneously intellect and being—both the thinker and the thing thought. The intellect insofar as it thinks, being insofar as it is thought. For the act of thinking could not exist unless there were (so to speak) Otherness and Identity. Therefore, the primary things are Intellect, Being, Otherness, and Identity. One must also join to these Motion and Rest. <margin>F</margin> Motion, indeed, if it thinks; but Rest, so that it remains the same. There must be Otherness, so that there may be a thinker and a thing thought; otherwise, if you take away this diversity, the two will collapse into one and become entirely silent. It is necessary that the things which think and the things which are thought be...

---

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
...diverse from one another here, yet also the same, insofar as they are in the same thing, and share a certain unity common to all. Yet the difference itself is "Otherness" <note>original: "alteritas"</note>. As these become more numerous, they create number and quantity, and finally, the specific property of each of these effects a "quality," from which, as if from principles, the rest of things also proceed.

*The Pythagoreans imagine that in a kind of procession from the One itself, the number two (the Dyad) arises; then, within the limit of the two, the number three (the Ternary) arises, and so on in order. The Platonists judge the primary essence in a similar way.*

### Chapter V.

For since this essence is most perfect, and therefore lives in a similar way, it proceeds inward by a certain vital motion. But since a procession is the opposite of a return or a limit, it surely comes from elsewhere, and it holds that power from above so that it may return, or three... <note>The text ends mid-sentence on the word "tern", a catchword for the next page, likely referring to "ternary" or "threefold".</note>

This state is compared to the mythological Age of Saturn, representing a perfect, simultaneous existence of all Forms.</summary>

PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK V.

...is determined: just as the capacity for reasoning in order to move is derived from the soul, so the movement toward the city <note>The "city" here serves as a metaphor for the intelligible realm or the state of being within the Intellect.</note> is derived from the intellect, or rather from a soul that has already become intellectual. This vital act terminates in the intellect, which is most clear and contains all forms; specifically, it receives its vigor from a divine source in the meantime, just as the eye is affected by a certain native effort, but becomes seeing in actuality and receives its form by the power of light. Finally, since in the first intellect itself—the one that understands itself—the formal principle of the thinker is, as it were, the thing proceeding here and capable of being formed, while the principle of the intellect is that which terminates and forms; therefore, they are opposed to one another. Rightly, then, there is a certain number here, not an accidental one, but one that is entirely essential. There is also a number of ideas there, differing from one another by their formal principle, provided that through them the forms of things that differ from one another are understood and created. Therefore, the intellect is manifold and depends entirely on the simplest principle from the beginning.

---

<margin>A</margin> THUS: God <note>original: "Deus" / "θεὸς"; Plotinus often uses "God" to refer to the Intellect, while "The One" refers to the absolute first principle.</note> exists in great abundance in this soul, coupled with things of this kind within the state of being one, unless perhaps it wishes to depart from there. Drawing near to Him, and having become as if one with Him, the soul thus inquires: Who then is he who begat this one? Who is the simple one that exists before such a multitude, who is the author of its being, and of its being manifold: who procreated number? For number is not primary. For before the "dyad" <note>term: Dyad (the principle of "twoness" or the first step into multiplicity from unity)</note> is the One itself. But the dyad is second, and having been made by the One, it has that One as its definer. By its own nature, however, it is something indefinite. But when it has been <margin>B</margin> defined, it is already number. Number, moreover, exists as an essence; for the soul also is a number. For primary natures are not physical masses, nor are they magnitudes of any kind. For these coarse things are posterior, which the senses consider to be "beings." Even in seeds, it is not the liquid itself that is judged worthy of esteem, but that which is not apparent to the eyes: and that is number and the formative principle <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος" (logos)</note>. Therefore, what is called number and the dyad in that realm <margin>C</margin> is the intellect and certain formative principles: but the dyad is indeed indefinite insofar as it is considered as the subject; but the number which comes from it and from the One is already each specific form <note>original: "species" / "εἶδος" (eidos)</note>, as if the essence of the intellect itself had already been formed by the forms made within it. It is formed in one way by the One itself, and in another way by itself, just as vision is that which is already seeing in actuality. For intelligence is a vision that sees, and both are one.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> THIS God, therefore, exists as many within this soul, joined by being one, unless it should fall away and go out from Him. Having come toward such a one, the soul asks: who then is the one who begat this, the simple one, the one who is prior to such a multitude, the cause of both its being and its being many, he who makes number? For number is not first. For the One is before the dyad. The dyad is second, and having come from the One, it has that One as its definer. But it is indefinite of itself. But when it is <margin>B</margin> defined, it is already number. And it is number as essence. And the soul is number. For the first things are not bulks, nor are they magnitudes. These thick things are later, which sense-perception thinks are real beings. Not even in seeds is the moist part the precious thing, but that which is not seen. These are <margin>C</margin> number and formative principle. And what is there called number and the dyad are certain formative principles. But the dyad is indefinite, taken as the "underlying thing" <note>term: Subiecto / ὑποκειμένῳ (hypokeimenon); the underlying matter or substrate that receives form.</note>. But the number that comes from it and the One is each a Form, as if the thing produced had been shaped by the Forms within it. It is shaped in one way by the One, and in another way by itself, like vision in its actual state. For intellection is a vision seeing, and both are the One.

> *The highest God, without any movement of will or nature, generates the divine intellect as his word, yet differing from the father by a certain otherness: The Intellect, similarly immobile, generates its own word, which is the soul of the world.*

### Chapter VI.

> *If the first principle were in any way changeable, it would completely change all things. Likewise, if it were imagined to generate the substance of the mind through a sort of medium, it would generate by a changing motion; but if it generated without motion, it would then happen as something imperfect, and by accident even the most imperfect of all things, since it could never possess its own parts within itself at once. Therefore, reason dictates that this most perfect substance is generated from God without such an accident, since agents act partly by nature and partly by will, and in the first agent every faculty of acting is contained, and those things which are divided in subsequent things are united in the first: surely God makes things by will as much as by nature. And in Him, nature and Will are the same thing. Thus, even the intellect, turning toward the father by no mere instinct, is filled with the splendor of the ideas. The intellect, therefore, emerges from this as absolutely formed: in a similar way, the soul of the world relates itself to the divine intellect. You will note that prayer will then be most effective when the mind, recalling itself entirely to its own intellect, offers itself alone to God alone, burning with love for that one alone.*

<margin>A</margin> HOW, then, does it see? And what does it see? And how did it essentially exist and proceed from that One, so that it might see? For now the soul holds the very necessity through which these things happen. But it longs to understand again that which is even common knowledge among the ancient sages: in what way, from the One existing as such a thing—as we say the One itself exists—did any substance whatsoever have its existence, whether it be a multitude, or a dyad, or a number; and why did that One not remain within itself, but so great a multitude flowed out from there as is seen in <margin>B</margin>

How one must pray

Generations

**A** How then should we proceed? We believe the order of things must be traced back to that First Principle. Thus, we must speak of it by invoking God himself—not by calling out with spoken words to the ears, but by the soul extending itself in prayer toward Him, for we are able to pray in this way: alone to the alone <note>original: "μόνους πρὸς μόνον" / "soli accedamus ad solum"; a famous Plotinian phrase describing the mystical union of the individual soul with the Absolute.</note>. Therefore, the spectator must behold Him within that inner sanctuary, as if in a temple, remaining quiet and still beyond all things. There, one sees the statues that stand, as it were, outside the shrine—or rather, that first "statue" which is the first to shine forth. **B** We must see how all moving things are ordered; there must be something toward which they move. If that did not exist, we could not posit any movement. If anything is generated after the First, it must be generated while the First is always turned toward itself. Let temporal generation <note>Plotinus warns us not to think of this "creation" as happening at a specific point in time, like a human birth, but rather as an eternal logical relationship.</note> be far from us as we speak of eternal beings. **C** When we attribute "generation" to them in our discourse, we do so to explain their cause and order. We must say that what is born from the First is produced without the source being moved; for if something were generated by the First moving, that product would be the third thing from the source, not the second. **D** Therefore, since the First is entirely immobile, if there is a "second" that comes after it, it must subsist without the First nodding its head, or willing it, or being moved in any way. 

How, then, should we conceive of this "standing" source? Think of a light diffused from it, depending on it while the source itself remains in total stillness—like the brightness surrounding the sun, which runs around it, forever generated from it while the sun remains stable. **E** Indeed, all things, as long as they persist in their nature, necessarily produce from their own essence and present power a surrounding reality that hangs from them; this image is a likeness of the power from which it flowed. Fire, for its part, emits heat; snow does not merely hold its cold within, but shares it with others; **F** this is especially testified by fragrant things, for as long as they exist, something flows out from them into the surrounding air, which those nearby enjoy. Furthermore, everything that has reached perfection generates something. That which is always perfect, therefore, always generates, and it generates something eternal, though lesser than the generator itself. What, then, should we say of the most Perfect? Does nothing proceed from it? On the contrary, from it proceed the greatest things after itself. The greatest thing after the First is the Intellect <note>original: "νοῦς" / "intellectus"; also translated as Mind or Divine Thought.</note>, which is second. For the Intellect sees the First and needs only the First; but the First has no need of the Intellect. It is necessary that what comes from that which is "better than mind" must be Mind itself. The Intellect is the best of all things produced, since all other things come after it. **G** Now, the Soul is the "word" <note>original: "λόγος" / "verbum"; here meaning an expression or manifestation.</note> and a certain activity of the Intellect, just as the Intellect is the word of God. But the word of the Soul is dim. Insofar as it is an image of the Intellect, the Soul must look toward the Intellect; in the same way, the Intellect, as the image of God, looks toward Him.

Every generated thing <note>the "generated" refers to any effect or being that comes from a higher cause</note> longs for its generator and is content in reaching it, especially when the generator and the generated are alone. But where that which generated is the best of all things, the generated necessarily clings to it so closely that it seems to be separated from it only by a certain "otherness," if I may call it that.

->*Just as the intellectual soul depends on the pure intellect, which is not the soul; so too this intellect emanates from the Good itself, which is not intellect but stands above it. Chapter VII.*<-

This intellect flows first from the father like a living essence, but soon, through a natural movement toward that source, it becomes a completed intellect. For the intellect is the very act of "substantial vision" resulting from this natural gaze or affection: its father is simply the One itself. Here, however, we see a "vital unity" where there appears to be a duality <note>The duality of the thinker and the thought</note>, but the gaze adds a third element, making it a trinity. In this trinity, every number—both even and odd—is contained. Similarly, through this natural gaze or affection, the trinity is now formed, and simultaneously all number is brought into being. For by looking naturally toward its source, it is strengthened by the father; thus confirmed, it now grasps its own living essence, in which a fertile and essential power thrives as the mother of all things. Thus, it derives itself into the forms of all things within itself, unfolding its own power by understanding it. It is therefore an effect that takes all forms, coming from the father who nourishes all; and since the father is defined by no single form, He either does nothing (which is a sin to suggest) or He does all things equally, for from Himself—existing as the One above all things—He generates the One that is all forms. This is the "Generated Heaven" <note>original: "Cœlus genitus" / "Ouranos"; representing the first stage of manifestation</note>. He was called Saturn <note>original: "Saturnus" / "Cronus"; the Greek word for Saturn, 'Kronos', was often associated with 'Koros' (fullness) or 'Nous' (mind)</note>, who "swallows" his own offspring—meaning they are kept within him, separated from Rhea (that is, from nature and matter). His son is Jupiter <note>original: "Iupiter" / "Zeus"; representing the World Soul</note>, the Soul of the World, who generates forms in nature and finally produces them into matter.

<insert>A</insert> We say that the intellect is the image of that One. We must explain this more clearly. First, that which is generated must in some way be like its generator, preserving many of its traits and holding a similarity to it, just as light has a similarity to the sun. Yet that generator is not a mind. How then does it beget a mind? Because the generated thing, by a certain turning back <term>conversion: the Neoplatonic concept of "epistrophe," where a being finds its identity by looking back at its source</term>, gazes upon its generator; and this vision itself is the intellect.

<insert>B</insert> For that which perceives another is either sense or intellect. Sense is usually compared to a line, while the remainder of knowledge is compared to a circle. Yet such a circle is, as it were, divisible, whereas the One is not so. Perhaps here, too, there is a "one," but a "one" that is the power of all things. Therefore, the intelligence beholds these things as if they were divided from that power; otherwise, it would not be an intellect at all, since it already possesses within itself a grasp of its own power, realizing its own strength, in which its essence consists.

<insert>C</insert> Therefore, the intellect defines its own being through its own nature, having received a certain power from the One. Here, indeed, it is observed that essence is like a single part of those things which belong to the One and come from the One; it is strengthened by the One and perfected into essence by and from the same. It sees into itself as if a divisible thing coming from the indivisible; it sees its life, its thought, and absolutely everything, because the One is none of those things.

<insert>D</insert> For this reason, all things come from the One: because the One is not circumscribed by any single form. Therefore, the One is none of the things found in the mind, yet all things in the order of reality flow from it; for this reason, these things possess essence. <meta>This page continues Plotinus’s explanation of the Three Primary Hypostases (the fundamental levels of reality): The One, the Intellect, and the Soul. Having established how the Intellect arises from the One, he now uses Greek mythology—specifically the story of Saturn and Jupiter—to illustrate the internal structure of the divine mind and the subsequent birth of the Soul.</meta>

### BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin> It is not to be viewed as something indefinite, but rather as something fixed by a limit and a stable state. In the realm of the intellect <term>intelligibles: objects of pure thought rather than physical senses</term>, this stability is the very definition and form by which it receives its substance <term>hypostasis: the underlying reality or "standing under" of a thing</term>. Therefore, the intellect of this kind is worthy of being called the purest Mind, and we must judge that it is born from no other source than the first principle. Once born, it has generated all existing things along with itself: the entire beauty of the Ideas, and all the intellectual Gods. We must furthermore consider that this Mind is <margin>B</margin> full of all the things it has produced. It is as if it immediately absorbs its offspring, keeping them within itself so that they do not fall into matter or be raised by Rhea <note>In Greek myth, Rhea was the mother of the gods who hid her children from their father, Saturn; here, Plotinus uses the myth to explain how thoughts remain within the divine Mind rather than being lost to the material world</note>, as the mysteries and the myths about the gods hint. They suggest that Saturn <note>Greek: Cronus</note> is the wisest God, born before Jupiter <note>Greek: Zeus</note>; he holds back within himself what he generates, so that he remains full and pure in the completeness of his intellect. After these things, they say he generates Jupiter, who is already a youth—meaning he is pure and vigorous. <margin>C</margin> For the Intellect generates the Soul, and it does so because it is a perfect being. When something becomes perfect, it must generate, and such a great power cannot remain sterile. However, that which is produced could not be better than its generator. Since it is necessarily "lesser," it is an image of the generator and is similarly indefinite at first, but it is then defined and given form by the one that produced it. This offspring of the Mind is a certain "reason" <note>Greek: logos</note> or substance whose existence consists in thinking. This is what moves <margin>D</margin> around the Intellect; it is the very light of the Intellect and a trace that remains forever dependent upon it. On one side, it is joined to the Intellect, and thus it is filled, enjoys it, partakes in it, and understands. On the other side, it touches the things that come after it—or rather, it generates them. It is necessary for these later things to be inferior to the Soul, and we shall discuss them in what follows. Thus far do divine things proceed.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is not to be considered as some indefinite thing, but as something strengthened by a certain limit and state. Stability in intelligible things is their determination and form, through which they obtain their substance. From this point, an intellect of this kind is worthy of the title "purest mind." It should be judged to be born from nowhere else but the first principle, and now, having been generated, it has produced all beings together with itself: the universal beauty of the ideas, all the intelligible Gods. It must be further thought that this mind is <margin>B</margin> full of all that it has fathered, and it is as if it instantly absorbs its offspring: because it embraces all things within itself, it neither allows them to slip into matter, nor to be nourished by Rhea, just as the mysteries and fables about the gods imagine. Indeed, Saturn, the most wise God, was born before Jupiter; he restrains what he generates within himself: to the extent that he is both full and pure in the completeness of his intellect. After these, they hand down that he generates Jupiter as a boy already existing, that is, pure and vigorous, <margin>C</margin> and as if already about to be. For the intellect generates the soul—the intellect, I say, existing as perfect. For when it becomes perfect, it must also generate, so that such power is not sterile. But here also, that which is begotten could not be better than the begetter. Since it was indeed less, it would also be an indefinite image of him in a similar way; but it is defined by the begetter and given form. The progeny of the mind is a certain reason, whose substance consists in thinking. That is the thing which turns itself <margin>D</margin> around the intellect; it is the light of the intellect itself and a footprint always depending from it: on one side, it is joined to it, and so it is filled and enjoys it, and is a sharer in it and intelligent; on the other side, in turn, it touches those things placed below it; or rather, it generates them: it is necessary that these touch upon things inferior to the soul: about which we must speak in the following parts. Thus far, at last, do divine things proceed.

> *From the words of Plato’s Parmenides, it is proved that the Good itself, and the simply One, is superior to Being itself and to the Intellect, which is again a silent longing. Likewise, the divine Intellect is superior to the Soul of the World: since the latter is <unclear>known from itself</unclear> as if already more divided, and exists as an intellect through participation.*

### Chapter VIII.

<margin>A</margin> For this reason, in Plato’s works, all things are arranged in a triple order around the King of all, especially through the first things; then the second things around the second; and finally the third things around the third. Then indeed, he says there is a father of the cause: calling the intellect the "cause." For the creator of the world <term>demiurge: the craftsman or architect of the universe</term> in Plato is the Intellect; he says this Intellect procreates the Soul in that mixing-bowl. But since the cause is the Intellect, he calls the Good itself the "father," which is superior to both intellect and essence. Often he <margin>B</margin> also calls Being itself and the Intellect an "Idea." Wherefore in Plato, one may recognize the Mind and the Idea coming from the Good itself, and the Soul coming from the Mind. And yet, such discourses are not new, nor recently invented, but were said long ago, though perhaps not fully explained. These present discourses are like interpreters of the ancients, and this is confirmed by testimonies, which argue that these opinions are ancient—a fact which can be conjectured from the very books of Plato. <margin>C</margin> Parmenides, therefore, first touched upon this opinion, where he reduced Being and Intellect into the same thing: and he by no means placed Being itself among sensible <note>physical/perceptible</note> things, saying that to think is the same...

<margin>A</margin> ...and to say that being and existing are exactly the same thing; he also calls this "immobile," even though he adds the act of thinking <note>original Latin: "intelligere"</note> to it. He surely removed all bodily motion from it so that it might remain always in the same state. Furthermore, he compares it to the globe of a sphere, because it encompasses all things wrapped within itself, and because intelligence is not sought from the outside but is perfected within itself. However, when he names the "One" in his books, he touches upon <margin>B</margin> the Cause <term>The Cause: referring to the One, the ultimate source of everything</term>, insofar as this is discovered to be many. But Parmenides, speaking in Plato’s dialogue <note>The *Parmenides*, where Plato explores the nature of unity and multiplicity</note>, more precisely distinguishes between: first, the "One" itself, which is primarily One and only One; second, that which he calls the "One-Many"; and third, the "One and Many." In this way, he confirms the three natures we have discussed <note>The One, the Intellect (the One-Many), and the Soul (the One and Many)</note>.

*Anaxagoras, Heraclitus, Empedocles, and Aristotle agree with Plato that the first principle of all things is one and most simple.*

### Chapter IX.

For the fact that all things in the world, however diverse, conspire into one form of the whole, one end, and one effect according to a certain order, arises from the fact that all things are and are led by the One; all things imitate and desire the One. If, once a certain single principle is established, a second were established as equally "first" of all things, the establishment of this second would be superfluous. This would only be called a "principle" by chance, since no reason could be assigned as to why this second thing should also be a principle, or why that first one should be. For it would not be because it is necessary, nor because this comes from that, nor because both this and that come from some third thing. A multitude that does not come from the One is entirely accidental, rash, divided, and impossible.

ANAXAGORAS, when he introduces a pure mind <note>original Greek: "νοῦν" (Nous)</note> free from motion, also posits the "First" as simple and the "One" as separate; however, he omitted a precise discussion because of his antiquity. Heraclitus, moreover, knew the eternal, intelligible One; for he says that bodies are always coming into being and flowing <note>The famous "panta rhei" or "all things flow" doctrine</note>. Accordingly, in Empedocles, "Discord" <note>Strife</note> indeed divides, but in "Concord" <note>Love</note> the One is signified. He also posited this as incorporeal, while the elements take the place of matter. Aristotle, later on, says that the <margin>B</margin> First itself is indeed intelligible and separate; but when he asserts that it "thinks itself," he conversely makes it so that it is not the "First" <note>Plotinus argues that if the One "thinks," it creates a duality between the thinker and the thought, meaning it cannot be the absolute, simple First Principle</note>. Certainly, when he also brings many other intelligibles <term>intelligibles: divine minds or objects of pure thought</term> into the discussion—as many in number as there are spheres in the heavens, so that each may move its own sphere—he arranges these intelligibles differently than Plato does. And since he has no probable reason, he resorts to "necessity." Someone might insist, asking whether this is said with right reason: You will say it is more reasonable <margin>C</margin> that all the spheres and orders of things, contributing together to a single coordination, look simultaneously toward one First. Someone will also ask: are the many intelligibles in Aristotle’s view from the one First, or are there rather many principles among the intelligible things? If all things are from the One, they will be compared by a certain fitting proportion, just as the spheres in the realm of the senses relate to one another: that is, with one encompassing another, and one at last containing them from the outside as a ruler. For this reason, the First there will embrace <margin>D</margin> the rest, and there will be an "intelligible world." Then, just as the spheres here are not empty—rather, the first is full of stars, and each following sphere possesses individual stars—so also there, all things will be in those celestial beings. But if each thing in the number of intelligibles is equally a principle, then the principles will certainly exist by a kind of chance. And one might ask for what reason they conspire...

<column-break/>

...calling it both "being" and "existence," and he says this is "immobile," even though he adds "thinking" to it, removing all bodily motion from it so that it may remain the same. He compares it to the mass of a sphere, because it contains all things within itself, and because thinking is not outside, but in itself. But when speaking in his own writings, he held the "All" <note>The Universe</note>, as if this were found to be many. But the Parmenides in Plato's work, speaking more accurately, divides from one another the "First One," which is more properly the One; and the "Second One," calling it "many"; and the "Third One," which is "one and many." And thus he himself also agrees with the three natures.

(Gap in Greek text corresponding to Latin summary section)

ANAXAGORAS, speaking of a mind pure and unmixed, also posits the "First" as simple and the "One" as separate. He left out the precise details due to his antiquity. Heraclitus knew the One as eternal and intelligible; for he says that bodies are becoming and flowing. For Empedocles, "Strife" divides, but "Friendship" is the One; he also held this to be incorporeal, with the elements acting as matter. Aristotle later says the First is separate and intelligible. But by saying that it thinks itself, he again makes it not the "First." By making many other intelligibles, as many as the heavenly spheres, so that each moves its own, he describes the things in the intelligibles in a different way than Plato, not having a probable reason but positing "necessity." One might reasonably object, for it is more reasonable that all the spheres be completed in one order, looking toward the One, the First. One might again ask about the many intelligibles, whether they are from the one First, or if there are many principles in the intelligibles. And if they are from the One, they will clearly have a proportion, as the spheres do in the sensible world, one containing another, and the one on the outside dominating, so that the First there also contains them, and it will be an intelligible world. And just as the spheres here are not empty, but the first is full of stars, and the others have stars, so also there the movers have many things in themselves, and the things there are more true. But if each is a principle, the principles will exist by chance. And why they will be...

<summary>Plotinus traces the roots of his "Three Hypostases" through ancient philosophy, arguing that Parmenides, Anaxagoras, and others recognized the One as the ultimate principle. He specifically critiques Aristotle's model of multiple "movers" of the celestial spheres, arguing instead for a singular, hierarchical order originating from one First Principle.</summary>

<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

...and they agree that the harmony of the entire visible world works toward a single end. But in what way are the sensible things in the heavens <note>original Greek: "ta en ouranō aisthēta"</note> related to the intelligible movers? Furthermore, how can they be many if they are incorporeal and not distinguished by matter? For this reason, those of the ancients who followed Pythagoras and his successor Pherecydes <note>A 6th-century BCE thinker often identified as the teacher of Pythagoras</note> seem to have investigated this kind of nature with great care. Some left their insights to posterity in books, while others <margin>B</margin> did not leave them in writing but passed them on through oral tradition <note>original Latin: "vna vocis consuetudine"</note>, or let them go entirely.

*The substance of the reasoning soul is separable from the body, because it can reason even without a physical instrument. We discover this both when it reaches conclusions and makes choices against bodily impulses, and also when it perceives forms—either reaching those already separated from matter or separating them itself.* **Chapter X.**

<margin>A</margin> NOW it has been demonstrated that the "One" <term>The One: the ultimate, simple source of all reality, existing beyond all categories of being</term> must be "above-being," just as our argument intended to show—as much as such things can be demonstrated. After the One comes "Being" and "Intellect," and in the third place is the nature of the "Soul." Just as these three exist in nature, we must believe they also exist within us. I do not mean within the things offered to our senses—for the things we are discussing are separate from those—but within the <margin>B</margin> things that exceed the power of the senses and are "outside" of them. They are "outside" in the same way that those three principles in the universal order are entirely "outside" the heavens. Thus, there are three such principles in man—specifically in what Plato calls the "inner man" <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic*, where he distinguishes between our external physical form and our internal rational nature</note>. Our soul is therefore something divine, of a different nature—just as the entire nature of Soul is. It is perfect when it possesses "Intellect" <term>Intellect (Nous): the realm of pure thought and eternal forms, the second level of reality</term>. One part of this intellect is engaged in reasoning, while the other provides the power to reason. <margin>C</margin> This power of reasoning in the soul requires no physical instrument for its own discourse; it keeps its activity in a state of purity so that it can reason clearly. If one places this soul—separate and unmixed with the body—in that first "intelligible" level of reality, they will not be mistaken. We should not look for a physical place to put it; rather, such a power must be established outside of all place. In this way, it can be said to <margin>D</margin> "exist by itself," acting from outside and above matter, whenever it is alone and has nothing of a bodily nature. For this reason, Plato says in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the physical world</note> that God "wrapped" the soul of the world even around the outside of the world, showing the soul's power remains within the intelligible realm. Regarding our soul, he says in the *Phaedrus* <note>A dialogue about the soul's journey and divine madness</note> that it sometimes hides its "head" within the heavens and sometimes "lifts its head" above the heavens. And when, in the *Phaedo* and the *Theaetetus* <note>Dialogues where Socrates discusses the soul's immortality and the pursuit of wisdom</note>, he commands us to "separate the soul" from the body, <margin>E</margin> he is not ordering a separation of physical location (for what is already separate by nature is already distinct), but rather that the soul's movement should not incline toward the body, nor should it become estranged from the Mind through its dealings with the body. Instead, it should strive to lead the lower part of the soul—which is subject to it—upward toward higher things. This lower part is situated here because it is the "architect and shaper" of the body, and it is uniquely focused on this task.

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus establishes that the three primary principles of the universe (the One, Intellect, and Soul) also exist within the human "inner man." He argues that the highest part of the soul is divine and independent of the physical body, citing Plato’s dialogues as historical authority.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how the three primary principles—the One, the Intellect, and the Soul—function within the human person. It focuses on the "Unity" of the soul as the point of contact with the Divine.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS ENNEADS, BOOK V.</header>

### Just as in the universe the One itself is above the intellect, so in our soul the very unity of the soul is more eminent even than the mind, for this higher reason. Chapter XI.

In our Theology and in the first books of Plotinus, we have sufficiently placed the "One" itself <note>The "One" is the ultimate, simple source of everything in Plotinus’s philosophy, existing beyond even being or thought.</note> before "Being" and the "Soul." Likewise, we have shown that in souls, just as in lines, there is a specific unity—acting like a point—through which they can reach the unity of the God of the universe, which acts as a center. Furthermore, we have shown that common notions of things, the rules of the arts, and stable principles always reside in our minds, through which we can reason about similar things at will.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, when the soul consults about what is just and beautiful, and asks whether this specific thing is just or whether that thing is beautiful, there must be something stable—a "Justice" and a "Beauty"—from which the soul's reasoning takes its starting point. Otherwise, it could never move through its logic. And if the soul sometimes reasons about these things and at other times does not, it follows that this reasoning nature is not the ultimate source; rather, there must be a Mind <note>Intellect or *Nous*</note> within us that always possesses the Just and the Beautiful.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, the principle and cause of the Mind, which is God, must be present. He is in no way divisible, but remains entirely consistent—not remaining in a specific place, I say, but within Himself. Yet, He is simultaneously observed in many things, in each of those capable of receiving Him as something distinct, just as a center exists in itself. For all things within a circle have their own point in the center, and the lines provide their own specific point to this center.

<margin>C</margin> For by such a part of the things within us, we also touch the divine, encounter it, and are joined to it. We lean upon it and are bound to it to the extent that we direct our focus and intention toward it.

<column-break/>

Since the soul is said to be concerned with things just and beautiful <note>original Greek: "peri dikaiōn kai kalōn"</note>, and seeks through reasoning whether this is just or that is beautiful, there must be some established Justice from which the reasoning regarding the soul arises. How else could it reason? And since the soul sometimes reasons about these things and sometimes does not, there must be a Mind within us that does not reason but always possesses Justice. We must also possess the cause and principle of the Mind, which is God. He is not divided, but remains fixed. And because He is seen in many things, He is present to each of those capable of receiving Him, as if He were another, just as the center of a circle exists in itself, yet each of the points in the circle has its own sign in the center, and the lines bring their own connection to it.

\* For by such a part of the powers within us, we touch and are with Him and depend on Him \* and we are gathered together with Him by those of us who incline our minds toward Him.

---

### Even if our intellect is always active concerning divine things, we do not notice it, because our reason is distracted by imaginations toward things opposite and varied from the divine. Chapter XII.

<margin>A</margin> But why, possessing such great and powerful things, do we not notice that we have them, but instead remain for the most part idle and separate from such actions? Indeed, there are many who never act concerning these things at all. Yet those higher principles—the Intellect and that which is above Intellect—persist tirelessly in their own activities within themselves. Likewise, the soul has a power that is either immobile or perpetually moving. However, not everything in the soul is immediately felt; it only truly reaches us when it proceeds all the way to our sensation.

<margin>B</margin> When an agent in us, whatever it may be, does not transmit its action into the power of sensing, that action has not yet propagated through the whole soul. For this reason, we do not yet recognize the action, because we identify ourselves with the power of sensing. We are not just a part of the soul, but rather the whole soul. Now, every living thing in the soul performs its own proper duty as long as it lives;

<margin>C</margin> but it only happens that we recognize this when a certain mutual "translation" <note>original Latin: "traductio"</note> occurs, from which awareness arises. Therefore, if we are ever to perceive the things present within us, we must turn our very power of awareness inward, and give effort so that it focuses entirely there. It is just as if someone, wishing to hear one specific voice above all others, might separate themselves from other sounds and strain their ears toward the most desired voice as it approaches. So too here, one must dismiss all things that make noise to the senses, or which interrupt the soul through the senses (except as much as extreme necessity compels), and keep the power of the soul's awareness...

<column-break/>

How is it then that, having such great things, we do not perceive them, but remain uninitiated in most of these activities? For some *do not act at all*. Those higher things are always in their own activities; the Mind and that which is before the Mind are always in themselves. The soul is that which is always in motion, but not everything in the soul is immediately perceptible; it only comes to us when it enters sensation. When each active part does not share its activity with the perceiving part, it has not yet passed through the whole soul. Therefore, we do not yet know it, since we exist alongside the sensing part, and we are not merely a portion of the soul, but the entire soul. And each of the living psychic functions is always active by itself. Recognition <note>original Greek: "to de gnōrizein"</note> occurs when there is a "handing over" and an apprehension <note>original Greek: "antilepsis"</note>. Therefore, there must be an apprehension of the things present within, and the perceiving part must turn toward the interior and hold all its attention there. Just as if someone wished to hear a voice they preferred, they would stand apart from other voices and rouse their ear toward the better of the sounds when it approaches. So must we also here, letting go of sensible hearings, except so far as necessity requires, and keeping the soul's...

<summary>Plotinus explains that while the Divine Mind and the One are always active within the human soul, we often fail to notice them because our conscious awareness is distracted by physical sensations. He uses the analogy of a circle's center to describe how the soul connects to the ultimate source of reality.</summary>

<header>BOOK TWO.</header>

->To receive again a protective power, pure and solitary, a hearing of the sounds from above. 
<note>original Greek: ἐς τὸ αὖ λαμβάνεσθαι δύναμιν φυλακτικὴν καθαρὰν καὶ ἔρημον, ἀκοὴν φθόγγων τῶν ἄνω.</note><-

->A. To be better suited for perceiving higher things, to preserve a deep purity, and to be most ready for hearing heavenly voices.<-

The Christian Trinity affirms this trinity of principles, which is most especially Platonic and Zoroastrian. For the Father's fertility includes the Good itself; the very emanation of the Son, the intellectual one, includes the Intellect <note>In Neoplatonism, the Intellect or *Nous* is the first emanation from the One</note>; and the procession of the Spirit through the mode of will and a kind of vital motion includes the Soul. Furthermore, the firmament reflects the Good itself through the fertility of the stars; Saturn—removed and distant from generation—represents the Intellect; Jupiter—favoring generation—represents the Soul; and Mars—now discordant and warlike—represents the World. Again, the Sun is the Good; Mercury—closest to the Sun in its path—is the Intellect; Venus—desirous of procreation—is the Soul; and this Moon—diverse and changeable within itself—is the World. Furthermore, Fire is the Good; clear and serene Air is the Intellect; Water—supplying moisture for generation—is the Soul; and Earth—composed now from all these—is the World. Finally, individually, a fertile essence is the Good; a firm essence of virtue is the Intellect; and inclination, motion, and action are the Soul. In summary, regarding the soul: fertile memory is the Good; the discourse of reason is the Intellect; and imagination and emotion are the Soul. Therefore, nothing is more certain than this trinity of principles, because nothing is confirmed by greater or more numerous testimonies; rightly does the universe represent the image of its own principles.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD V.
### BOOK II.

# P L O T I N I
## ENNEAD V.
### BOOK II.

->On the generation and order of those things which come after the First.<-

->De generatione & ordine eorum quæ sunt post primum.<-

Just as unity is the principle of numbers but is not itself a number, and a point is the principle of a continuous line but is not a line, and light is the principle of heat and colors but is not itself heat or colors: so the Good itself, the principle of beings, is not any "thing" or essence; therefore, it is neither life nor intellect.
->Chapter I.<-

For it does not produce these things by containing them all within itself beforehand as if pregnant, like the intellect, the soul, or nature; rather, it creates simply by its supreme eminence, just as a unit, a point (or center), or light does. However, that which is procreated most closely from the Good itself—to the extent that it exists immediately from the Good while the Good remains unchanged—is "Being." To the extent that it suddenly turns naturally and is, as it were, moved toward the Good, it becomes "Living." To the extent that it is soon strengthened from there and turns back into itself as if in a circle, it becomes "Intellect." Similarly, from the Intellect remaining as it is, the "Intellectual Soul" comes into being. From this Soul—which does not remain still but flows out through a power running toward the intelligible Intellect and stretching toward things of imagination and sense—its image flows into action; namely, a certain life devoid of reason, endowed with sense and vegetative power. Among these, that which follows eventually perseveres as long as that which is above it exists. Our soul, in the same body and at the same time, acts as a "plant" in those members which it only nourishes; it acts as a "beast" in those instruments where it only feels; it acts as a "human" while reasoning; and it acts as a "spirit" or even "God" while understanding. Again, the same person at different times, although under a human persona, exercises various behaviors of this kind; even within the human species, some lead the life of plants, others of beasts, others of men, and some as gods or spirits. Therefore, whoever has said that our souls—which have already withdrawn from the habit of the higher life—will soon return into a human or earthly form to live similarly, will hold a more probable opinion than if they claimed the human species could freely change into beasts or plants. For such a transformation is both impossible in nature and unnecessary for justice.

<margin>A</margin>
In what way, then, does a multitude proceed from the one simple thing, in which no variety appears, nor any kind of duality or form? Perhaps it is because nothing was in it that all things are from it; and in order for Being <note>The Greek term *on* (Being) refers to the first level of reality that possesses definition and form.</note> itself to exist, the One is not itself Being, but Being is its offspring, its first-born. Indeed, since it is perfect—seeking nothing, possessing nothing, and needing nothing—it has, as it were, overflowed, and its very abundance has procreated another. But that which was made there turned back toward
<margin>B</margin>
the One and was filled; it became such that it looked toward itself, and thus the Intellect <note>original: *intellectus*; Greek: *nous*. This is the Divine Mind or second principle of the triad.</note> came forth. Yet, its state of rest toward that first Being produced its existence, while its gaze toward itself created the Mind. When, therefore, it applies itself to itself so that it may know, it becomes simultaneously Intellect and Being. In this way, Being—just like the One—produces similar things according to its great power of pouring forth. This, too, is its specific form, just as it previously flowed out from the One.
<margin>C</margin>
And here, from this essence, the Soul <note>original: *anima*; Greek: *psyche*.</note> is the active result, made while the Intellect remains unchanged; for the Intellect was likewise produced while that which preceded it remained still. The Soul, however, does not create while remaining still, but having been set in motion, it produces an image. Looking upward to the source from which it flowed, it is filled; but proceeding into a different and opposite motion, it generates its own image: which is sensation in animals and nature in plants. Yet nothing is severed or divided from its superior. For this reason, the human soul also seems to
<margin>D</margin>
reach as far down as the plants. Indeed, it reaches that far in a certain way, because that which is in plants belongs to the soul. However, the soul is not entirely in the plants; rather, it is present in them because it has proceeded downward to that extent, creating another substance by its procreation and its care for lower things. For that which is above this, depending upon the Intellect, allows the Intellect to rest within itself.

<margin>A</margin>
Thus, the procession happens from the beginning to the very last, and meanwhile, each thing is permitted to retain its own proper seat. But that which is created is assigned another order, and a lower one at that. Nevertheless, each thing becomes the same as that which it follows, for as long as it follows it. When, therefore, the soul is inserted into a plant, it is something else, like a certain part in the plant—namely, that which is most reckless and mindless, having wandered down to this point.
<margin>B</margin>
But when it is inserted into a beast, then the power of sensation has dominated and led it. And when it enters a human, then either the motion in the rational nature prevails entirely, or it is a procession from the Intellect, as one having its own mind and a will of its own for understanding, or for moving generally. Now, we may in turn consider ourselves, when someone is in a plant or...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
How then from the one simple being <note>original Greek: πῶς οὖν ἐξ ἑνὸς ἁπλοῦ ὄντος. This begins the Greek parallel of the preceding Latin text.</note>, in which no complexity appears in the same way, nor doubling, nor anything else whatsoever? Or was it that because nothing was in it, all things are from it? And so that Being might exist, for this reason the One is not Being, but is its progenitor, and this is, as it were, the first birth. For being perfect by seeking nothing and having nothing and needing nothing, it has, as it were, overflowed, and its super-fullness has made another. And that which was generated turned back toward it and was
<margin>B</margin>
filled, and became looking toward it, and this is the Intellect. And its rest toward that first principle made Being, but its vision <note>original Greek: θέα (thea)</note> toward itself made the Intellect. Since, therefore, it stood toward itself in order that it might see, it becomes simultaneously Intellect and Being. In this way, then, Being, just like that One <unclear>...</unclear>, makes similar things, pouring forth much power. And this is also a form of it, just as that which preceded it poured it out; and this is the activity from the essence
<margin>C</margin>
of the Soul, produced while the former remains. For indeed, the Intellect was produced while that which was before it remained. But the Soul does not create while remaining, but having been moved, it generated an image. Therefore, looking there to where it was generated, it is filled; but having proceeded into another and opposite motion, it generates an image of itself: sensation and the nature which is in plants. But nothing is cut off from that which is before it, nor is it severed.
<margin>D</margin>
Wherefore the soul of man also seems to reach as far as the plants. For it reaches to them in this way, because the things in the plants also belong to it. Not that the whole soul is in the plants; but having become present in plants, it is so because it proceeded downward to such an extent, making another creation <note>original Greek: ποίησιν (poiesin)</note> by its procession and by its desire for the lower thing. Since that which was before this was hung from the Intellect, it allowed the Intellect to remain in itself.

<margin>B</margin>
it is in an irrational animal, the power of sensing has led by gaining mastery. But when it enters into a man, the motion is either entirely rational, or from the Intellect, as having a proper intellect, or having from itself a will to understand or generally to be moved. <meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the hierarchy of being. On the previous page, he described how the "One" overflows to create the "Intellect" (Mind), which in turn produces the "Soul." Now, he examines how this Soul descends into the physical world—specifically into plants—and how it maintains its connection to the higher realms without being physically "trapped" in a body.</meta>

BOOK TWO.

<margin>A</margin>
...the offshoots, or if one cuts some of the branches, where has the soul that was in them departed, or from where did it come? For it has not moved away in space. It is therefore one with its source <note>original: "archē"; the "beginning" or "principle" from which the soul flows.</note>. But if you were to cut through the root, or burn it, where is that part of the soul that was in the root? It has not gone to another place, but it remains in the same; yet it may be said to be in another if it "runs back" or retreats. If it does not retreat, it remains in another vegetative power <note>original: "phytikē"; the lowest level of soul responsible for growth and nutrition.</note>. For it is not cramped for space. But if it retreats, 
<margin>B</margin>
it will reside in the power prior to it. And where is that? In the power prior to that. This continues all the way up to the Intellect. This is not a matter of physical space, for nothing in that higher realm is in a place. The Intellect is even further removed from being in a place. Thus, the soul’s nature is also not in a place. Being nowhere in terms of location, it is instead in that which is "nowhere," and in this way it is everywhere. But if the soul, while returning to the higher realm, should stop in the middle before
<margin>C</margin>
reaching the highest point, it leads a "middle life" and remains in that part of itself. All these things are both "that" source and yet not "that" source. They are "that" because they come from it; they are not "that" because the source gave them existence while remaining itself unchanged. It is therefore like a great life stretched out in length, where each successive part is different. The whole is continuous with itself, yet each part is distinguished from the other by its own difference, and the prior part is not destroyed
<margin>D</margin>
within the one that follows. What then of the soul that has entered into plants? Does it generate nothing below it? We must consider this by taking another starting point.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...or certain things propagated from there, or if one cuts off certain branches, where does the soul that was in these go? Perhaps back to where it proceeded from. But where is that by nature? For it is not distant in space; it is therefore one with the principle itself. But if you cut the root or burn it, where will that which flourished in the root be? In the soul, not by going away into another place, but it can also be in the same. It will be said to be in another if it has run back; if not, it will be in another vegetative power. For it is not squeezed into a narrow space. But if it
<margin>B</margin>
runs back, it will reside in the superior power. And where is that? In the superior again: and that again in like manner all the way up to the mind <note>original: "mentem"; referring to the Intellect or Divine Mind.</note>, not by any condition of place. For none of these things were in a place. Finally, the Intellect is much less to be situated in any location: for which reason, neither is the nature of the soul itself. It is therefore in no place. But in the fact that it is nowhere, it is meanwhile thus everywhere. If, however, the soul at some point having progressed toward the sublime, should stop meanwhile before it entirely
<margin>C</margin>
reaches the supreme, it leads a middle life, and rests in 그 part of itself. Moreover, all these things are indeed that source, and again they are not that source. They are that, I say, because they are from it: they are not that, again, because that source produced each thing while remaining in itself. There is therefore in the universe something like a certain immense life, produced as if in length, having parts that are indeed distinct from one another in succession, yet meanwhile the whole is continuous with itself, possessing one thing after another 
<margin>D</margin>
by its own specific difference: where surely in that which follows, the preceding is not destroyed. What then of the soul grafted into plants? Does it produce nothing lower? Perhaps it exists only in that in which it is. But indeed, we must consider by what condition that happens, taking a beginning from elsewhere.

<meta>This page begins a new book, continuing Plotinus’s investigation into the hierarchy of being. Having previously discussed the soul's relationship to the physical world and the Intellect, Plotinus now turns to the specific mechanics of how the Intellect—the divine Mind—attains self-knowledge and whether a truly "simple" or indivisible entity can know itself.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD V.
### BOOK III.

# P L O T I N U S
## FIFTH ENNEAD,
### BOOK III.

->ON the knowing substances, and that which is beyond.<-

*That which knows itself is not necessarily forced to be so complex that there is no difference within it at all—as is the case with the "One" itself <note>original: "ipsum unum"; the ultimate, indivisible source in Plotinian philosophy</note>. However, it must be simple in such a way that the whole is contained entirely within every part of it, and its action is completed totally in a single moment. Such is the nature of the Intellect <note>original: "intellectus"; the divine Mind or Nous</note>.*
->Chapter I.<-

*When we say that the Intellect knows itself, we do not divide it into two parts, where one part knows and the other is merely known; otherwise, it would not be a single thing knowing itself, but one thing knowing another. Rather, we mean that the knower encompasses itself along with the object known. Sensation is concerned only with knowing things outside the soul; imagination deals with what is within the soul—namely, the actions of the senses; reason <note>original: "ratio"; the faculty of discursive thought</note> further investigates itself; and finally, the Intellect knows itself. Through a perfect participation in this, even reason sometimes knows itself.*

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'O' depicting a seated figure, possibly a deity or an astronomer with a globe, within a circular frame surrounded by ornamental scrollwork.</image-desc>

In the first place, regarding the claim <margin>B</margin> that something can understand itself because it is composite—and thus one of its parts knows the rest (just as we might know our own form and the nature of our body through the senses)—it does not follow that it truly knows itself. For in such a case, the whole will be known, unless the part that understands also <margin>C</margin> understands itself along with the things joined to it. Otherwise, our goal will not be reached: namely, that a single thing perceives itself. Instead, it would be one thing perceiving another. We must assert, therefore, that it belongs to the simple itself to perceive itself. We must investigate how this happens, if indeed it can; otherwise, we must abandon the opinion that anything truly knows itself. To cast aside such an opinion is not easy, <margin>D</margin> for many absurdities would seem to follow. Indeed, if we do not attribute this power to the soul (though that itself would be quite absurd), it is certainly most absurd not to attribute it to the nature of the Mind—if, I say, it has knowledge of other things but lacks knowledge and science of itself. And...

# BOOK THREE.

### CHAPTER I (Continued)

Sensation is of external things, but if something is to be grasped, and there is will, thought, and opinion, does the Intellect <note>original: "νοῦς/intellectus"; the divine or higher Mind</note> have knowledge of these, or not? These are necessary to the soul. But where they occur, it is clear that the Intellect will know. Or does it not know these things themselves, but rather itself, which knows these? Or does it know the things to be known, or itself, because it knows these things only? Who then would be the one knowing? But if it itself knows that it knows, then who is it that does not know there? Or does it know both its own things and itself? 

Similarly, we must consider what manner and to what extent this takes place.

*The rational power <note>original: "potentia rationalis"</note>, which is always engaged in discourse <note>original: "discurrendo"; the process of reasoning step-by-step from one concept to another</note>, stands as a medium between the imagination and the intellect. It receives certain forms from both sides, composing and dividing them. It adapts the forms recently coming from the imagination to the ancient forms in the mind, or those existing from the mind, and in this adaptation, it becomes intellectual. Chapter II.*

From this, two intellects appear in us: the permanent <note>original: "permanens"; stable and unchanging</note> and the discursive <note>original: "discurrens"; moving from one thought to another</note>, which follows through reasoning.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER II

<margin>A</margin> **FIRST**, then, we must inquire concerning the soul, whether knowledge of itself should be granted to it, what that knowing part in it is, and by what principle. We judge the sensory power, by its very condition, to be concerned only with external things. For although things happening within the body may be perceived, such perception belongs to those things outside the sense, for it then feels the passions that occur within the body beneath it. Furthermore, there is in the soul a power of reasoning <note>original: "virtus ratiocinandi"</note> that judges the images <note>original: "imaginationes/φαντασμάτων"</note> falling from the sense, joining and also dividing them. 

<margin>B</margin> It even looks upon, as if they were figures <note>original: "figuras/τύπας"</note>, those things that descend from the intellect, and it possesses a power regarding them that is entirely the same. It also takes up understanding <note>original: "intelligentiam/σύνεσιν"</note>, in that it weighs and adapts the new and recently arrived figures to the ancient ones; in which matter we believe the recollection <note>original: "reminiscentiam/ἀνάμνησις"</note> of the soul to consist. And indeed, the intellect of the soul stands here by its own power. 

It must therefore be asked, <margin>C</margin> whether this power of reasoning turns back upon itself and knows itself, or whether this should instead be referred to the Intellect? For if we attribute knowledge of itself to this part of the soul, we shall confess this very part to be a "mind" <note>original: "mentem/νοῦν"</note>; and we shall be compelled to seek in what way it differs most from the higher Mind. But if we do not attribute it, reason will lead us to that Mind, and we shall consider how it comes to know itself. 

But if we were to attribute that office to this lower part, we would again investigate how the higher and lower intellect differ <margin>D</margin> in self-knowledge. Especially if this intellect of ours is by no means pure. But then, does the very power of the soul for discourse also turn back into itself? Or does it rather not turn, but instead holds notice of the forms which it obtains from both sides? And surely, we must first ask in what way it attains such notice.

### CHAPTER III

*Reason, with the sense announcing and the imagination indicating, points out that Socrates is approaching. It adds that he is good, just, and wise; it weighs these things and defines them by the rules of goodness, justice, and wisdom, which first shine in the mind, and from there they suggest themselves to the reason as it concerns itself with such matters. Chapter III.*

Since it is proper to reason to act in motion, and motion tends toward another thing, reason rightly concerns itself with other things rather than with itself; therefore, it is not its property to know itself. Most people place three essences in heaven <note>original: "tres in caelo... essentias"; referring to the Neoplatonic Hypostases: The One, the Intellect, and the Soul</note>, namely...
