### PLOTINUS ENNEAD V.

...in the body, matter and form; and besides this, the soul itself is such, and matter is always subject to its own form, just as the body is to the soul. Similarly, there are three essences around our soul: namely, the irrational soul subject to the rational; the rational soul, however, being perpetually joined to the mind, like the heaven of the soul is perpetually coupled to the heaven itself. Plotinus here seems to touch upon this opinion. And yet, Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note>, Themistius <note>A 4th-century statesman and Aristotelian commentator</note>, and Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle</note> seem to have exaggerated such a connection. Porphyry <note>Plotinus's student and editor</note> also interprets Plotinus more in the Platonic manner, saying that the intellect is not the same as the "passive" part of the soul, because it is clearly not a part, but is the power of this substance, by which reason it is called "soul." For it is called soul insofar as it pertains to discourse <note>term: "discursus" (discursive reasoning); the step-by-step process of logical thinking as opposed to immediate intuition</note>, whether it discourses through universals or particulars. But the Intellect is the mental substance itself, to which the power called "soul" is subject. Now, indeed, even the subject itself is named soul insofar as it possesses the discursive power, and it is named Intellect according to the very principle of its substance. For it is the same for it to be as it is to understand, yet it is not the same to be as it is to discourse: therefore, it always understands and remains equal, yet it does not always discourse in the same way.

---

<margin>A</margin>
**SENSE-PERCEPTION** indeed sees a man, and hands over his form to the power of thought <note>Latin: "cogitandi virtuti"; Greek: "διανοίᾳ" (dianoia)</note>. But what does this power say? Perhaps it says nothing yet, but only knows him, and thus rests: unless perhaps it runs through the following within itself, asking "Who is this?" if indeed it has encountered him once before; and it may say of him now, using memory, that this is Socrates. But if it further unfolds and explains the form, it divides what the imagination <note>Latin: "imaginatio"; Greek: "φαντασία" (phantasia)</note> handed over. And if it should say further whether he is good, it then speaks of such a thing through those things which it had known by 
<margin>B</margin>
sense. But what it says regarding these things, it already possesses from itself, for it surely possesses the rule of the good within itself. But in what way does it have the Good within it? It is because it is (if I may say so) "good-form" <note>original: "boniformis"; having the shape or nature of the good</note>, and it has already been strengthened toward the perception of such a thing by the Intellect shining upon it from above. For this exists as the pure part of the soul, and it receives the traces impressed by the Intellect. But why should this itself not be the Intellect? Why is it 
<margin>C</margin>
the soul while the rest is the whole starting from the power of sense? Because it is necessary for the soul to be occupied in a certain discourse of reason. These are all the duties of the discursive power. But why do we not, by attributing the task of knowing itself to this part, make an end of the inquiry? Because, clearly, its highest duty is in considering external things, while it is further distractedly pulled into many things; but we judge it the property of the Intellect to contemplate its own inner things for itself. But if 
<margin>D</margin>
anyone should say: "What prevents that which is distracted from occasionally noticing its own things through some other power of the soul?"—he certainly does not require the power of thinking and reasoning itself, but already accepts a pure Intellect. What then prevents a pure Intellect from being in the soul? We shall say that nothing prevents it. Furthermore, shall we claim that the pure Intellect is something belonging to the soul? Surely we will not say it belongs to the soul, but we will confess it to be *our* intellect: which becomes something else beyond the nature of thought itself, and 
<margin>E</margin>
superimposed upon it, yet it is ours, even if we do not count it among the parts of the soul. Perhaps, indeed, we shall affirm it is ours, and again not ours: for this reason we use it, and again we do not use it; but we use thought always. Therefore, it is ours while we use it, but not ours when we do not use it. But what is meant by "using the Intellect"? Is it perhaps that we pronounce ourselves to have become it, and speak as it does, or at least according to it? For we are not the Intellect; rather, we are 
<margin>F</margin>
according to it, receiving that first power of discourse. For indeed we ourselves perceive through the sense-perception, and we are the ones perceiving. Is it therefore...

<column-break/>

**FOR SENSE-PERCEPTION** indeed saw a man, and gave the impression to the discursive reason <note>original: "διανοίᾳ"</note>. But what does it say? Or does it not yet say anything, but only knows and stops; unless perhaps it should reason with itself, "Who is this?" if it happened to have met him before; and it says again by memory if it were only "Socrates." But if it should also unroll the form, it divides what the imagination <note>original: "φαντασία"</note> gave. And if it should say in relation to reason, "Is he good?", it has spoken the things from the sense-perception, but the things it held concerning this, it already holds within itself, having the nearby rule of the good by itself. How does it have the good by itself? Or is it "good-like" <note>original: "ἀγαθοειδής"</note> and is strengthened toward the perception of such a thing by the Intellect shining upon it. For this is the pure part of the soul, and it receives the sketches of the Intellect. But one must not call this the Intellect, and the other the soul starting from the sensory, except that the life of the soul is to be in reasonings. These things altogether spoken of will be called a "power," but why do we not give to this part the task of knowing itself, and we shall be released from those things peculiar to it which look at the outside and are meddlesome? We deem it the work of the Intellect to look at its own things and the things in itself. But if someone will say: "What then prevents this from looking at its own things by another power?", if he seeks the discursive, he will not seek the reasoning power, but he takes a pure Intellect. What then prevents a pure Intellect from being in the soul? We say nothing, but still one must say: "This belongs to the soul," but we will say: "It does not belong to the soul." We shall say it is *our* intellect, being different from the discursive part, and having stepped upon it; yet it is ours, even if we do not count it with the parts of the soul. Or it is ours, and not ours; wherefore also we use it, and we do not use it. But discursive reason <note>original: "διάνοια"</note> is always, and it is ours when we use it, but when not using it, it is not ours. But what is it to use it? Is it that we ourselves become that and speak as that, or according to that? For we are not the Intellect; therefore, it is according to that with the first reasoning part receiving it. For indeed we perceive by sense-perception, and we are the ones who perceive. Is it then...

### BOOK THREE.

### T 4

...in which we continue to exist, either thinking in this way, or we are the ones who reason, and our thoughts are the concepts within our reasoning. But as for us, some things truly lie above us—just as the objects of our senses shine upon us—these being the true qualities of the soul’s middle power, situated between the worse and the better. The worse is sense-perception, while the better is the Mind <note>original: "νοῦ" (Nous); the higher, intuitive intellect</note>. Though sense-perception always seems to be ours by common consent, whether we are conscious of it or not is currently debated. It is also debated whether the Mind is "us," and whether it is separate from us. It is separate because it does not incline toward us, but rather we look upward toward it. For sense-perception is our messenger, but the Mind is our King.

WE ARE RULED also when we act according to that Mind. This happens in two ways: either by the "letters" or laws, as it were, inscribed within us; or by being filled by it and becoming able to see and perceive it as it is present. We know ourselves through such a vision, learning other things by this light. We may also learn the power that knows such things, learning by that very power, or even by becoming that power ourselves. Thus, the one who knows himself is twofold:
<margin>*</margin>One part knows the nature of the reasoning <margin>**</margin>soul; the other part is above it, knowing himself by having become that higher Mind. In that state, he thinks of himself again, no longer merely as a man, but as something entirely different, having snatched himself upward and drawing along only the better part of the soul. This part alone is able to take wing toward pure thought, so that he may deposit there the things he has seen. Does the reasoning power not know that it is a reasoning power, and that it receives the understanding of external things? Does it not know that it judges what it examines, and that it does so by the rules within itself which it received from the Mind? It knows there is something better than itself which it seeks, and which it possesses entirely. But what is this very thing that does not know itself, being ignorant of its own nature and its own works? If, therefore, it says that it depends upon the Mind, <margin>***</margin> and is second after the Mind, <margin>*</margin>and is an image <margin>**</margin>containing all things within itself as if they were written there—just as there is one who writes and one who has written—will the one who has known himself in this way stop at this point? Or shall we, using another power, behold the Mind in turn, knowing itself and distributing its truths? Or perhaps we assume that Mind as our own, since it too is ours.

<column-break/>

**A** Perhaps we ourselves are those who range through reason, and we ourselves understand the notions of intelligence shimmering within our very thought. For we are this reasoning self. But the actions of the Mind are above us, just as the objects of the senses are below us. We are this very thing proper to the soul, its principal part, located in the middle between two powers: the worse and the better—that is, between sense and intellect. We seem to concede that sense-perception is always **B** ours, for we are always sensing; but regarding the intellect, there is ambiguity, both because we do not always use it and because it is separate. I say it is separate because it does not bow down to us, but rather we look up to it from below. In short, the sense is our messenger, but the Mind is our king.

### *The rational portion by which we exist uses the intellect in two ways: through participation and through form, and thus knows itself. Chapter 4.*

> *Through participation: insofar as it daily receives forms, notions, and rules from the intellect. Here, it knows its own powers through its actions, as if by their effects. It recognizes its essence through these "voices" and realizes that this essence always depends on the Mind for illumination. Through form: when, after frequent use of this reception, it entirely "puts on" the Mind, just as matter takes on a form, and it acts under the operation of the Mind itself. This is like how matter, after receiving heat from a fire, finally becomes a flame. Then at last, the reason perfectly knows itself together with the Mind, as if knowing itself through its cause. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> called this Reason the "possible intellect" and the Mind the "agent intellect" <note>term: "intellectus agens"; the active power of the mind that makes thinking possible</note>.*

**A** Furthermore, we RULE when we act according to that Mind. We act according to it in two ways: either because "letters" and laws are inscribed in us from that source, or because we are filled by it, or because we are able to see and perceive it while it is present. Truly, we know ourselves by such a spectacle, learning other things through it. We might also learn the very power that knows such a thing, being taught by that same power; or we might even become that power ourselves. Thus, that which knows **B** itself now exists as a double entity: one knowing itself as the thinking nature of the soul itself, and the other being superior to this nature, where the one who knows himself has already escaped into that Mind. There, he beholds himself again by that Mind—no longer as a mere human, but having become something else entirely. He carries himself away to the heavens, drawing with him only what is most excellent in the soul. This part alone can fly to the understanding on its grown wings, so that there **C** a person may deposit what he has learned. But does not this power of thinking know that it is the virtue of thinking, and that it gathers the intelligence of external things? Does it not also judge what it judges, doing so by certain rules described for it by the Mind? Does it not know, finally, that there is something more excellent above it, which seeks nothing further but possesses everything? Truly, what is this thing that least knows itself, being ignorant of what it is and what its duties are? If, therefore, it says of itself **D** that it hangs upon the Mind, and is second after the Mind, and is an image of the Mind having all things inscribed within it—just as there is one who writes and one who has already written—will the one who has thus known himself stop his progress there? Or shall we, looking with another power, behold the Mind again as it knows itself? Or shall we indeed take that Mind unto ourselves, since it too is ours?

### PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK V.

and we in turn [perceive] his <note>Referring to the Divine Intellect</note>, and so finally we perceive the Intellect itself. <margin>A</margin> We shall perceive ourselves; indeed, this is necessary if we are to perceive what is the highest Intellect: to know oneself. Therefore, a person becomes the Intellect himself when, letting go of his other parts, he looks upon this very thing with it, and looks at himself with himself, just as the Intellect itself contemplates itself.

->In that which is superior to the rational power—that is, the shifting intelligence—the Intellect, the act of intelligence, and the object of thought are essentially the same. Therefore, it always understands itself. Chapter V.<-

Above the sense-perception which only looks at external things is the internal imagination looking inward. Above this is that which looks only at what is brought in from the outside. Above this again stands **reason**, which additionally works on things closer to home. Above this, again, is that which returns from other known things back to itself to be recognized; this is the **Intellect** <note>original: "intellectus" / "νοῦς" (Nous); the highest form of intuitive, non-discursive thought</note> beginning its vision from itself. While it inspects itself, it contemplates all things—I do not mean the outward shapes of things, but the things themselves, so that they are known in their truest form. If, by touching itself, it establishes all things, then it is surely all things. By the very act with which it contemplates itself, it produces all things, and at the same time, it recognizes that it knows both itself and all things. Truly, the first divine Intellect does not turn to understand anything other than itself; it does not possess accidental knowledge. On the contrary, its essence is absolutely living and understanding. While it enjoys itself through that essential and vital intelligence, it understands itself as existing, living, understanding—completely uniform and yet containing all forms.

<margin>A</margin> Does the Intellect then look at one part of itself with another part? If so, one part will be the "seer" and the other the "seen." But this is not the same as a single thing knowing itself. What then? If the whole is such that it is composed of similar parts, so that the seer does not differ from the seen, then the seer sees that part of itself as identical to itself. In that case, the seer does not differ from the seen. But first, it would be absurd to divide the Intellect this way; for <margin>B</margin> how would the division be made? It should not be divided by mere chance or at random. Furthermore, who is the one who divides? Is it perhaps the one who places himself in the role of the seer, or rather the one in the role of being seen? Moreover, how will that seer know himself while, in the act of seeing, he places himself in the rank of what is being seen? For the act of seeing does not reside in the object seen. Or will the one who knows himself consider himself rather as the seen than as the seer? Therefore, he notices neither <margin>C</margin> the whole nor the entirety of himself. For the one he knows is the "seen," but he does not know the "seer," and thus he will be looking not at himself, but at another. But will he perhaps join the "seer" to himself so that he might perfectly comprehend himself? Truly, if he embraces the "seer," he also embraces the things seen. If, therefore, in the act of seeing, things are perfectly contained, the question is whether the shapes of things or the things themselves <margin>D</margin> are contained. If only shapes, then the things themselves are not possessed; but if the things are possessed, surely he who perceives them does not have them because he divided himself. Rather, even before he divided himself, he was both the contemplator and the possessor. If this is the case, contemplation must be the same as the thing contemplated (so to speak), and the Intellect must similarly be the same as the Intelligible <note>The "Intelligible" is the object of the Intellect's thought; in Plotinus, the thinker and the thought are one at the highest level</note>. Otherwise, if they are not the same, there will be no true truth. For he who is said to possess "beings" will instead have a "shape" of them that is undoubtedly different from them, <margin>E</margin> which is certainly not the truth. For the Truth ought not to be of something else, but what it says, it must also be. Thus, the Intellect, the Intelligible, and Being are one; and this is the First Being, and the first Intellect possessing all beings; or rather, he is the same...

<column-break/>

and we to that [the Intellect], there will be Mind <note>original: "νοῦς" (Nous)</note> and he will know himself, or always knowing himself, if indeed we shall know what is in that same self. And having become that self, because he sees all other things through himself, and himself through himself, just as the Mind sees itself.

DOES IT THEN look at itself with one part of itself and another part? But thus one will be the seer and the other the seen. This would not be [the Mind] itself, or rather it would be as if the whole were made of similar parts, so that the seer differs in no way from the seen; seeing that part which is itself, it would know itself as the same. For the seer is the same as the seen. But first, this is a division of it. For how could it be divided? Surely not by chance. And who is the one who divides? The one who places himself in the position of contemplating, or the one being contemplated? And how will the contemplator know himself if he has ranked himself with the contemplated in the act of contemplating? For the act of contemplating is not in the contemplated. Or, if he knows himself as the contemplated, he will not think of himself as the contemplator. Thus he will not know himself entirely or as a whole. For he knows the contemplated, but he does not know the contemplator; and so he has seen another and not himself. Or will he add everything to himself, including the contemplator, so that he has thought of himself perfectly? But if he adds the contemplator, he adds also the things seen. If they are the things themselves, he does not have them by dividing himself. But even before the division, he was both contemplating and possessing. Therefore, the contemplation must be the same as the contemplated, and the Mind the same as the Intelligible. For if it is not the same, there will be no truth. For the one who has "beings" <note>original: "τὰ ὄντα" (ta onta); the truly existing things/Forms</note> will have something different from the beings, which is not truth. Therefore, the Truth must not be of something else, but what it says, it must also be. If then the Mind, the Intelligible, and Being are one—and this is the First Being—then the first Mind has all beings; or rather, it is the same...

<summary>Plotinus argues that at the highest level of reality, the Intellect (Nous) and the objects it contemplates are a single, unified essence, as self-knowledge requires the thinker and the thought to be identical. He outlines a hierarchy of consciousness moving from outward sense-perception to inward reason, and finally to the unified intuitive Intellect.</summary>

### THIRD BOOK. <note>Although the header reads "Third Book," this text is from the Fifth Ennead, Tractate 3, of Plotinus’s works.</note>

...the wholes. But if the **act of thinking** and the **object of thought** are one, how will the object of thought itself think itself? For either the thinking will, as it were, encompass the object of thought, or it will be the same as the thinking; yet it is not yet clear how it thinks itself. But if the thinking and the object of thought are the same, since everyone who is the object of thought—for that is what is signified—is neither without the object of thought, nor without life, nor again is life something brought in from the outside. Nor is thinking in something else, such as a stone or some inanimate thing, and the first [principle] is the object of thought. If, therefore, the first activity is the first act, and the most beautiful thinking, being essence, then thinking is essence. For thinking is true, but the first thinking, being first and in a primary way, would be the first. This, then, is this **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note>. The other is not in potentiality, where he himself is one thing and thinking another. For in that case, his essential nature would again be a certain potentiality. How, then, is his essence an activity? If his essence and activity are the same, and if the being and the object of thought are the same as the activity, then all will be one: **Intellect**, **thinking**, and the **object of thought**. If, therefore, his thinking is the object of thought, and he himself is the object of thought, then he will think himself. For he will think with the thinking which he himself was, and he will think the object of thought which he himself was. According to each, then, he will think himself, both insofar as he was the thinking itself and insofar as he was the object of thought itself, which he saw through the thinking that he was.

<margin>A</margin> Thus the argument has demonstrated that there is something which primarily and properly thinks itself. It thinks, however, in one way in the soul, which is in a principal state. For the soul seems to look outward because it belongs to another. But the **Intellect** <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note> looks at itself, and what it is, and that it exists from its own nature, and it returns into itself. For in seeing the things that truly exist, it saw itself. And in seeing, it was activity. And the activity was itself. For Intellect and thinking are one. And the whole is that which is not by parts. But let us see how the argument <margin>B</margin> distinguishes this, as having various activities. Necessity requires it thus, but it does not have "passion" <note>In philosophy, "passion" refers to being acted upon by an external force</note>. And the soul is now a necessity, but the soul in its sense-perception. Let us seek, then, as it seems, the truth and the dawn, we who <margin>now</margin> are always hidden in nature and are united to it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the beings of the ideas. But if the **intelligence** <note>original: "intelligentia"</note> and the **intelligible** <note>original: "intelligibile"; the object of thought</note> are one, in what way, on account of this, will the thinker understand himself? For the intelligence, as it were, embraces the intelligible, or it is one with it; however, it is not yet clearly established that the intellect perceives itself distinctly. But if the intelligence and the intelligible are the same—for the intelligible itself is a certain act—then if the intelligible is not merely a certain potentiality, nor lacking in life, and if living is not something added to it from the outside <margin>B</margin> there, nor is thinking in a different subject like a stone or something lacking life, then the first essence is the intelligible itself. If, therefore, I say, the act is there, and it is the first act, then truly the most excellent act is the intelligence, and the intelligence is (so to speak) essential. For the truest intelligence is of this kind, and it is first, existing in a primary way; and therefore, this will be the **First Intellect**. This Intellect is neither in potentiality, nor is he himself one thing and the intelligence another; otherwise, the essential essence would again be a certain potentiality. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, if his essence is an act, and his essence is that act, it will be judged to be one and the same as the act. But since being itself and the intelligible are one with the act, all things will be one at the same time: the **Intellect**, the **intelligence**, and the **intelligible**. If, therefore, his intelligence is the intelligible itself, and he himself is that very intelligible, then surely he will understand himself. For he will understand through the intelligence itself that which he himself is, and he will understand the intelligible <margin>D</margin> which is himself, and himself likewise. Therefore, he will understand himself completely from both sides: both insofar as he is the intelligence, and insofar as he is again the intelligible, which he understands through this intelligence which is himself.

---

*The Intellect itself, since it remains within itself and is not inclined toward other things from the outside or by external effect, rightly acts upon itself regarding the things to be understood—that is, itself. The soul, however, being affected in the opposite way, stands in the opposite relation to knowing. Chapter VI.*

*In the whole order of cognition, the senses hold the lowest position, while the Intellect holds the highest. Since, therefore, the senses remain only on the surfaces, merely touching other things, the Intellect rightly performs a completely circular motion, contemplating itself entirely within its own being. Reason, however, is mostly "oblique" <note>Indirect or step-by-step logic</note>. The forms of things that are in me are entirely essential. Those which are impressed upon reason from the outside are, as it were, essential; those which result from the mind into reason every day are even more essential; and finally, those which overflow into reason from the imagination are the least essential. The soul, therefore, finally knows itself when it fits the lower forms into the higher forms.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, **Reason** <term>ratio: the soul’s ability to think through problems logically and step-by-step</term> has demonstrated that there must be something which understands itself in a proper and primary way. However, it understands itself in one way in the soul, and in another, more primary way, in the **Mind** <note>original: "mens"</note>. The soul indeed knows itself as belonging to another; but the Mind knows itself as being itself, what kind of thing it is, and what it is, and it sees this by its very nature. And in seeing, it is in act, and it is itself the act. For the Intellect and the intelligence are the same, and it beholds the whole of itself as a whole, not discerning part by part. Did <margin>B</margin> reason therefore demonstrate such a thing as holds a believable action? Certainly, it holds necessity; but it does not have a belief drawn from persuasion. For necessity indeed exists in the mind, as it seems, rather to report by persuasion than to perceive the truth with a pure mind. But as long as we remained in the higher region, in the very nature of the Mind, we were sufficiently possessed of ourselves, and content in that state, we then understood.

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic concept of the "Intellect" (Nous), arguing that at the highest level of reality, the thinker, the act of thinking, and the object of thought are a single, unified essence. It distinguishes this perfect self-knowledge of the Intellect from the "oblique" or discursive reasoning of the human soul.</summary>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. V.

...and gathering all things into one, we were contemplating them. For it was the **Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus" / "νοῦς" (nous)</note> that was then thinking, and speaking concerning itself. The **Soul**, however, was then at rest, rightly yielding to the activity and obedience of the mind. But after we have come to this point, we desire in turn to lead the soul by persuasion, as if wanting to contemplate the archetype within an image. Perhaps, therefore, it is necessary to teach our soul in what way the Intellect primarily gazes upon itself: I say, to teach this very nature of the soul, which is in some way intellectual, by positing it as a thinking thing, and by its very name secretly signifying that it is a certain intellect, or a certain power through the intellect, receiving its very function from the intellect. 

It is fitting for the soul to know this: that it also knows whatever it sees and knows what it says. And if the soul were those very things it speaks of, it would surely know itself in that way. But since those things are present, or at least come to it from above—from that place where the soul itself depends—it is surely fitting for this soul, since it is a certain "reason" <note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος" (logos). In Neoplatonism, "reason" is the unfolding or expression of a higher principle.</note> of the Intellect and receives things related to it, to adapt itself to the traces impressed upon it, and thus finally to perceive itself. Let it, therefore, transfer the image into the true Intellect, which is indeed the same as those things that are truly understood, and truly exist, and are primary; since it is established that it is impossible for such an intellect to exist outside of itself. 

Therefore, if it is indeed in itself and with itself, and that very thing which it is exists entirely as Intellect. For a Mind can never be mindless <note>original: "amens" / "ἄφρων" (aphron)</note>; it is rightly necessary that the knowledge of itself be present in it. Especially since it remains within itself, and its work and essence are nothing other than simply being Intellect. For this Intellect does not engage in an action where, looking toward external things out of duty and distracted from itself, it might have a knowledge peculiar to itself but devoted to external things. Nor is it necessary that, if it happens to be engaged in action, it must perceive itself. But for one who is neither threatened by action nor affected in a pure mind—since every obstacle is entirely absent—its turning toward itself is completely direct. This shows that its knowledge of itself is not only probable, but necessary. Otherwise, what would its life be, when it is entirely free from outward action and is placed wholly within the Mind?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and gathering all things into one, we were contemplating them. For it was the **Intellect** that was thinking, and speaking concerning itself. But the **Soul** remained quiet, yielding to the thought from that higher place. But since we have come to be here again, we wish once more to persuade ourselves even in the soul, as if wanting to see the archetype in an image. <margin>B</margin> Perhaps, then, it is necessary to teach our soul how the Intellect ever contemplates itself. And this "intellectual-like" part of the soul will teach this, as we posit it to be a thinking thing, and by the name we imply that it is some kind of intellect, or a power through the intellect, having its cause from the intellect. 

It is proper, then, for this to know that it also knows whatever it knows, and saw what it says. And if it were itself the things spoken of, it would know itself in this way. But since the things it speaks of are realities, it would be known to itself; <margin>C</margin> and it happens also to this, being a "reason," either receiving kindred things or fitting itself to the traces of itself, so as to know itself by transferring the image to the true Intellect, which is the same as the things truly thought, and is truly the first. For it is not possible for such a thing to be outside of itself. So if it were in itself and with itself, this very thing which it is, is Intellect. <margin>D</margin> And being Intellect, it could never be without thought. It would be necessary for it to have knowledge of itself. And because its work is in itself, and not in another, and its essence is nothing other than being Intellect. For it is never "practical" <note>By "practical," Plotinus means oriented toward outward action or doing, rather than pure being and contemplation.</note> in such a way that by looking outward with the practical part, and not remaining in itself, its knowledge would be of external things—which is necessary for the practical person. For the one for whom there is neither outward action nor even desire in the pure Mind, <margin>E</margin> and whose "turning back" <note>original: "ἐπιστροφὴ" (epistrophe). The Platonic concept of a soul or mind returning to its divine source.</note> is toward itself, it demonstrates that knowledge of itself is not only reasonable, but necessary for it. For what would its life be, if it were freed from action and existed in Mind?

---

*Since the Intellect does not turn toward things lower than itself, and is a form entirely in activity, and therefore cannot be vacant from action, it rightly acts always regarding itself and God. Chapter VII.*

*When it is turned toward itself, it knows itself through "form," but God through "effect." When it is turned toward God, it sees God as if through "form," but itself through "cause." Since the vegetative power acts only regarding lower things, and the rational acts regarding lower, higher, and itself, the Intellect rightly acts regarding itself and that which is higher. The things that proceed from the Intellect happen while it remains acting in itself; but those from the Soul happen through a certain motion. But because this soul is the offspring of the divine intelligence, it either turns toward the divine intelligences where it contemplates, or it is occupied with the rules and laws which are images of the intelligences where it governs, or it occupies itself with corporeal forms, which are shadows of the intelligences, where it builds and wanders through the senses.*

---

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> FURTHERMORE, we can assert that the Intellect in that state understands God. But if anyone should confess that the Intellect then understands God, they will be compelled by this very condition to immediately grant that it also knows itself. For whatever it has from God, it will recognize: both what He grants and what He is able to grant. And learning these things and...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT to contemplate God... if anyone should admit that it knows God, they will be forced by this also to grant that it knows itself. For it will know all that it has from Him, and what He gave, and what He is able to do. Indeed, having learned these things and...

<summary>This page discusses how the Intellect (the divine Mind) achieves self-knowledge by turning inward rather than outward. Plotinus argues that because the Intellect is identical to its thoughts, it must necessarily know itself, and that the human Soul can understand this by looking at itself as a "trace" or "image" of that higher Mind.</summary>

# BOOK THREE.

<margin>A</margin> By recognizing this, he shall also know himself through this very reasoning: for he himself is one of those things which have been given; or rather, he truly exists as all things that have been given. If, therefore, he knows that [Source], perceiving also his own powers, he will also recognize himself as having been made from there, receiving from that source what he is able to receive. But if he should be unable to perceive that Source clearly—perhaps because the very act of seeing is said to be the thing seen—then for this reason especially, the remaining vision and knowledge of himself will be his. For indeed, <margin>B</margin> to see is this very thing: namely, to exist as the very thing which is seen. For what else can we attribute to him? By Jove, shall we say "rest" <note>original: "quietem" / "ἡσυχίαν" (hesychian)</note>? But the rest of the mind is not an alienation from the mind; rather, the rest of the mind is its own proper activity, being vacant from all other things. For to all other things to which rest and vacancy from others is given, there remains their own proper activity—especially to those for whom "to be" is not some potentiality, but an activity <note>original: "actus" / "ἐνέργεια" (energeia). In Neoplatonism, a thing's true being is its activity or "doing."</note>. Where being is activity, and nothing remains toward which such a movement is drawn, it surely <margin>C</margin> rests upon itself. Therefore, understanding himself, he thus dwells with himself and directs his activity toward himself. And yet, if anything else depends upon him, it depends because he turns toward himself and rests in himself. For it is necessary first to stand firm within oneself, and then to act upon another, or for another thing to proceed from there, having been made similar to it. Just as it is proper for fire: that it first be fire within itself and have the activity of fire, and thus finally it can print its trace upon another. Now <margin>D</margin> truly, the Intellect is an activity within itself. But the Soul, insofar as it turns toward the Intellect, dwells as it were within; but insofar as it departs from the Mind, it is extended toward external things. From one side, therefore, it turns out similar to that from which it comes; from the other side, although it may proceed as somewhat dissimilar, yet even there it seems to retain a certain similarity, whether it acts or creates. For even while it acts, it meanwhile contemplates; and when it creates, it produces "species" <note>Forms or archetypes</note>, like certain intelligences <margin>E</margin> derived in a long order from the primary Intelligences. Thus all things are traces of the Intelligence of the Intellect, proceeding by degrees according to the first exemplar, and imitating it according to their strength—the closer things more so, but the last things displaying only a certain meager image.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> [Similarly], by recognizing this, he will know himself through this very reasoning. For he himself is one of those things that have been given—or rather, he is all the things that have been given. If he knows that [Source] and learns his own powers, he will know himself as an image that has come to be, receiving what he can. If he is unable to see that Source clearly, because to see is perhaps for him the very thing seen, then he shines most in this way: if he is unable to see himself, or if seeing in this way means that the one seeing and the thing seen are the same. For what else could we grant him? Rest? But this is not a rest of the mind that is a sickness or ecstasy, but perhaps a rest that means taking leisure from other activities. For even in other things where there is rest from others, their own proper activity remains. This is especially true for those whose being is not in potentiality, but is activity. If, therefore, being is activity, and there is no other toward which the activity is directed, it is directed toward itself. He therefore thinks himself, and has his activity directed toward himself and into himself. For if anything of his exists, it is directed into himself; if the first thing is for himself, it is also for another, or something else comes from him that is made like him. For example, if you consider fire: first it is fire in itself, having the activity of fire, and then it might make other things near it such as itself. For again, the Intellect is an activity in itself; but the soul has one part directed inward toward its own intellect, as if inside, and another part directed toward the outside. In one respect it is made like that from which it comes; in the other, even if it becomes dissimilar, it still remains similar even there. Further, it creates—whether it creates while acting, it nonetheless contemplates; or while making certain forms, such as perfected thoughts, so that all things are traces of thought or the Intellect, departing according to the archetype. Being divided, some are closer, while in the furthest things, faint images are preserved.

---

->*Since the soul extends itself outward through growth, sensation, and imagination, but only becomes capable of reflecting upon itself through certain intellectual sparks, it is established that the Intellect is a light perpetually reflected into itself by itself. Chapter VIII.*<-

*If you lightly press the corner of your eye with your finger, an internal light will immediately flash forth to itself. It would achieve this much more easily and abundantly if you had as much light in the eye as the animals that see at night. The Intellect behaves similarly toward itself. Forms in matter are so united with matter that they produce one work and one action; much more so the "seminal reasons" <note>original: "seminales rationes" / "λόγοι σπερματικοί" (logoi spermatikoi). These are the formative principles in nature.</note> of forms in nature; and even much more are the intelligible reasons in the Intellect united to the Intellect, like rays to light, through which the Intellect and the Soul perceive sensible things more piercingly than through the senses. Thus truly Avicenna, and the teacher of the Great Scotus, Henry [of Ghent], following the nature of Plato, think that intellectual forms in the Intellect or the Soul—whether innate to the former or acquired by the latter—exist not just as characters or marks, but as a certain natural habit; by which habit the mind easily turns itself to this or that.*

---

<margin>* What sort of thing is the Intelligible?</margin>
**WHAT** sort of thing is the truly Intelligible, and what sort of thing is it to itself? One must seek it in this way. Just as color or shape upon bodies, before these bodies exist, those things exist, and the Reason which...

<column-break/>

IT MUST, furthermore, be asked, what kind of thing the Intelligible especially sees in the Intellect, and what kind of thing it sees in itself. Perhaps, indeed, one ought not to seek the Intelligible itself as such a thing as is in bodies, whether color or figure. For before these things exist, those exist. And indeed the Reason...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS. V.

<page-num>504</page-num>

...the formative principles <note>Latin: "rationes" / Greek: "λόγοι" (logoi). These are the "seeds" or blueprints of reality in Neoplatonic thought.</note> implanted in the seeds which produce these things are not the things themselves; for these seeds are invisible by their very <margin>A</margin> nature, and much more so are those higher principles. Their nature is the same as the nature of those who possess them: just as the reason which is in the seed is the same as the soul which holds it. 

But the soul does not look upon the things it possesses, for it did not beget them; rather, the soul is itself an image <note>original: "simulachrum" / "εἴδωλον" (eidolon)</note> of the formative principles it sends into matter. That source from which the soul comes is clear, true, and primarily existing; therefore, it belongs to itself and <margin>B</margin> lives for itself. If this were not the case, and it existed only in another, it would not even remain. For an image is connected to its source so that, because it belongs to another, it may exist in another—unless it were to be detached from that source. 

For this reason, the soul does not truly see, because it does not possess sufficient light; and if it does see, since it is made within another, it does not see itself perfectly, but sees something else. But none of these limitations exist there in the Intellect; rather, the vision is simultaneously its own visible object. That which is <margin>C</margin> seen is of the same nature as the vision, and in turn, the vision is of the same nature as the visible. 

Who then can affirm what its nature is? Certainly, it is the one who sees. And the Intellect truly sees: for even with us, when vision itself is light—or rather, when it is joined to light—it sees light. For it sees colors; yet it discerns these not through another medium, but through itself, because it does not look outside. Therefore, by one light it contemplates another light, and certainly not through anything else. Thus, one light sees another light, and therefore it beholds itself. 

This light, reflecting in the soul, illuminates the soul; <margin>D</margin> and this is what makes the soul "intellectual." This light is similarly within itself and is a sublime light. If, therefore, the trace <note>original: "vestigium" / "ἴχνος" (ichnos). Plotinus often uses "trace" to describe the diminished presence of a higher reality in a lower one.</note> of light impressed upon the soul is of such a quality, how much more beautiful, greater, and clearer is the heavenly light when you approach it. You have now come closer to the very nature of the Intellect and the Intelligible. 

For this light provides the soul with a clearer, infused life—a life, I say, that is not merely generative; for on the contrary, it turns the soul back toward itself and does not allow it to be scattered, but causes it to unite the clarity inherent in the mind. Nor does it <margin>E</margin> bring back the life of the senses. For the sensory life looks outward and, for that reason, does not apprehend anything with certainty. 

But he who drinks from that light, the fountain of truths, sees visible things more clearly, though by a different reasoning. It remains, then, that the trace of the mind's life should take on an intellectual life, for there the true things themselves consist. And indeed, the life and activity <note>Latin: "actus" / Greek: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia)</note> in the mind is the first light, shining primarily for itself; a splendor constantly flashing toward itself, both shining and being illuminated at once. 

Truly, the intelligible <margin>F</margin> understands the intellect, and there it remains perceived, needing no other thing by which to be seen, but being self-sufficient for sight: for that which it sees is the very thing that is perceived. Among us, too, it is almost the same, so that our knowledge of it is produced through the thing itself; otherwise, how could we speak of it? In the same way, that higher reality becomes such that it can apprehend itself more clearly, and we, through it, are able to do the same. 

Now it is established by arguments <margin>G</margin> of this kind that we raise our soul to that higher realm—I say the soul, which asserts that it is an image of that Intellect, and that its life is an image and a likeness of it. And whenever the soul understands, it puts on a certain form of that Intellect...

<column-break/>

The reason in the seeds that perform these things is not the things themselves; for these are invisible by nature, and even more so are those higher things. The nature of those principles and those who hold them is the same, such as the reason in the seed and the soul that possesses these things. But the soul does not see them; for it possesses not the offspring, but is itself an image. And the formative principles come from that which is manifest, and again from Being, and from the First, from which it belongs to itself and lives for itself. 

But if it were not something else, and in another, it would not remain; for as an image, it would gaze intently [upon its source]. It exists in another unless it be fixed in that source. Therefore, it does not see, as it does not have sufficient light. And it sees wandering things, if it sees anything else and not itself, but in the act of being perceived... 

But there, it sees its own self; the visible is as the vision. And being mixed with the radiant, it would be itself an image. The Mind sees, since vision will be light, or rather united with light. For it sees colors; but if it attends to itself, it is because it does not look outside. By another light, it sees another light, not through another. Therefore, light sees another light; thus it sees itself. 

The light that shines in the soul illuminates it; but that other light exists for itself. It is similar in itself to its own light. If the trace of light that is produced in the soul is such, how much more beautiful and better is its source, appearing more clearly near its own nature <margin><gloss>variant reading: of nature</gloss></margin>. For this is not a wandering to the soul <margin><gloss>soul</gloss></margin> in the living being; it gave the soul a clearer life, but not the generative life. 

On the contrary, it turned the soul toward itself and did not allow it to be dispersed, but made it love its own splendor. The soul does not see itself as a sensory being, and it perceives more clearly when it has received that light of truths. It sees visible things more clearly, but in the opposite way. It remains then that it leads the soul to truth; for there the true things are. 

This is the life in activity, the first light shining primarily to itself, or the light as its own lamp, shining and being illuminated. Truly, it is the intelligible or the intelligible being understood, seen by itself and needing no other sight, self-sufficient for seeing; because what it sees is itself being known. 

And with us, that same thing occurs, as our life [of the mind] becomes through itself. For how else would we have the power to speak about it? Being such that it can be apprehended by itself, and we through it. Through these reasonings, we lead our soul back to it, as the soul is suspended from it and is an image and likeness of its life. And whenever it understands, it becomes godlike and takes on its form.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Intellect (Divine Mind) is a self-sufficient light that is both the observer and the observed, unlike the human soul which is an image that often looks outward. He argues that the soul becomes "intellectual" and "godlike" only when it turns inward to receive this divine light.</summary>

# BOOK THREE

And if someone asks what the soul is, one understands how it is perfect and how it first knows itself from the primary things beneath it. Having surrendered its own activities, of which it held memory within itself—possessing these, it rouses itself, as if by its own effortless vision it might give form to both [the soul and intellect] through a more accurate likeness to that [Intellect], in so far as a part of the soul is able to attain a likeness to the Mind.

<margin>* .. the</margin> The SOUL, as it seems, even having seen the most divine part of the soul, must [consider] what it is about to meet within itself. <margin>*,* those who.</margin> It would become such as this if you first stripped away the body from the man—clearly, this refers to the shaping of the soul—and then the senses, and furthermore the rhythms and angers, and other such trifles <note>Original Greek: "φλυαρίας" (phlyarias) / Latin: "nugas." Plotinus uses this dismissive term for bodily passions that distract from the divine.</note>, since it inclines too much toward the mortal. All that remains of it is what we called an image of the Mind, preserving that light, much like a sphere of the sun's magnitude, with the light shining around it and from it, as if someone were to allow it for themselves. It must again be from that which moved... remaining around, but falling from another, that which is from it, until it has reached us; but everything around the sun will be one in the open air, so that there is no empty space beneath the sun’s body. But the soul does not become light around it, being suspended from it, and not around another but around the Mind, and it would not have that place where the light of the sun—not the soul itself... <margin>* itself; other qualities</margin> ...of itself or other qualities, or itself around the * Mind <margin>* Mind, reasoners</margin> reasoning, * which having been laid aside, the Mind <margin>* their wisdom</margin> itself is gathered around them. <margin>present to him</margin> It is present to him, and we, when we turn toward it, find our life there, of which there are many lives. But each is nothing of another life, or of others, but as it provides, it provides to others, not to itself, for it does not lack because of these or suffer, nor does it provide less to itself; it possesses the whole, holding the first traces—or rather not holding them, but being these things itself. If anyone is able to have the primary, purely thinking Soul...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is clear again that if anyone desires to know what that perfect Intellect <term>Intellect: The "Nous," the second principle in Neoplatonism, representing pure thought and the realm of the Forms.</term> is specifically, and what that first and all-comprehending thing is, it is necessary first to bring the soul back into the Mind—or at least to surrender its own action to the Mind—to the Mind, I say, as it turns toward those things of which it retains memory. For a soul possessing these things and so disposed, it is possible to demonstrate itself, being able in a certain way to gaze upon that Intellect as if through an image, especially because of the life of the soul, which reflects that [Intellect] with a certain <margin>B</margin> more expressive likeness, in so far as a certain part of the soul can recall itself to the likeness of the Mind.

*If, having set aside the movements of the lower powers from the soul, you take its rational power itself, shining with all its intellectual notions, you will suddenly contemplate the Intellect in this image, just as one sees the sun in a clear hour.*

### Chapter IX.

The rational soul is also naturally an image of the Mind, existing as the nearest light within it, dependent on the sun-like Intellect. As is mentioned in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe.</note> and as Plutarch introduces: the uniform world signifies the infused vigor of ornament; the world is that which is constituted in matter, much higher, which flourishes in action; somewhat more sublime because in the imagination of forms it is sometimes most full; and much more excellent is that which, in a sort of mirror-like reason, excels as a rival of the Intellect, which shines in the Mind. In the world following the preceding one, step by step as if in a mirror, you shall cling to it, and in turn you shall contemplate the lower from the higher as if from a mirror.

<margin>A</margin> THE SOUL, therefore, as it seems, and that which is most divine in the soul, must consider what the intellect is about to know. Perhaps you may achieve this under this condition: if first you separate the body from the man—especially from yourself. Then separate the soul that forms it, and especially the senses, desire, and anger, and other such trifles, as they decline too much toward the mortal. What remains of the soul is that which we said carries before it the image of the Intellect, <margin>B</margin> preserving some of its light, much like the light that glitters nearest to the globe of the sun itself, shining from it and around it. Certainly, no one would grant that the light of the sun, which is within itself and around itself, is the sun itself. Yet, depending on the sun, it remains around it. But one thing after another is continuously propagated from the antecedent, until it descends to us and the earth. Indeed, all the light that is around the sun will be placed in another, lest perhaps the space which lies beneath the sun's body be compelled to be empty. <margin>C</margin> The soul, however, is a certain light produced from the Mind and connected to the Mind around the Mind; nor does it sit in another, but it stands out properly as the Mind. Nor is there any place for this, for there is no place for the Mind. Therefore, while the light of the sun is in the air, the soul itself is so pure that it is perceived in itself, both by itself and by another similarly disposed. And the soul itself is compelled to reason about the Intellect, <margin>D</margin> searching out from itself what kind of thing it is; but the Intellect itself contemplates itself, by no means having reasoned about itself. For it is always present to itself; but we are present to ourselves there when we bring ourselves to the Mind. For our life is divided, and there are many lives; but that [Intellect] is not some other life, nor does it need others, but those lives which it provides, it provides not to itself but to others. For it does not need inferior things, nor does it apply to itself what is less, since it possesses the universe. Nor does it have within it mere traces of primary things; <margin>E</margin> rather, it does not possess these, but it is these things itself. But if someone cannot have the primary soul as such, purely and entirely thinking...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 505 regarding the soul's ascent. The previous text described the soul stripping away bodily distractions to find its "divine part." This page (506) explains how the soul moves from sensory perception to the "First Intellect" where the Forms (divine blueprints of reality) reside.</meta>

PLOTINUS, ENNEADS V.

At least let the soul unite the opinion-forming power <note>Original Latin: *opinatricem*; Greek: *doxastikēn*. This refers to the part of the soul that forms beliefs about the world.</note>, and from there ascend to higher things. But if it cannot even do that, let it at least receive the senses as they assert certain broader forms within themselves—the senses, I say, even within themselves, together with those things they are capable of, already provided with forms. Then, if it pleases someone to descend to lower things, let them turn their path toward the generative power, and reach those final things which it produces; but in turn, let them ascend from these final forms back to the last, or rather, approaching the first.

### In the first intellect, all forms exist: they are the same according to essence, yet distinct by formal reason. Chapter V.

**F**orms <note>The "Forms" or "Ideas" are the eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in the universe.</note> are the primary things there, and therefore they are perfect, and in a perfect manner. Thus they exist essentially, yet they are distant from the intellect by a certain reason. For the intellect is a living intellect, while these forms are many. They differ among themselves by formal reason <note>Original: *ratione formali*. This is a technical term meaning they are distinct in their definition or "blueprint" even if they share the same spiritual substance.</note>, especially since the intellect merely contemplates them; and by contemplating, it understands them distinctly, making all things differ even further among themselves—that is, in reality, in place, and in time. It understands justice and sight as a certain connection and apprehension and discretion; these three are properties of light and fire. Therefore, the intellect, insofar as it turns into itself by understanding, exercises these three toward itself and declares itself altogether multiple. Otherwise, if there were no difference at all within it, it would not be that which attains anything from another, nor would it need application or effort. There would be nothing for it to apprehend or comprehend, neither by apprehension, nor by any union of parts, nor by its own embrace; there would be no place for arrangement. Thus far the Platonists. But the Christians <note>This is a marginal or interpretive addition by the translator (likely Marsilio Ficino), comparing Plotinian thought to Christian theology regarding the nature of God's mind.</note> argue that the first intellect does not have such a multitude of forms, since through its own single form it is one, understanding all things insofar as it relates itself in various ways to all that can participate in it; it sounds its multitude not within itself, but externally.

<margin>A</margin> **O**f these things, let it be spoken in this way. If, however, forms are not only made in the mind—otherwise these forms of ours would not be the last, while those there are the first forms (that is, the efficient causes, and therefore primary)—then it is surely necessary that the forms made there and the maker exist together as one. If not, that intellect will again require something else. What then? Does that which is superior again have need? Certainly not; for this very thing which is in need is the intellect. <margin>B</margin> But does not that supreme being see itself? Not at all; for it does not need vision. But this will be discussed in what follows. For the present, let us treat the same matter again. For the subject now at hand is not to be undervalued. <margin>C</margin> It must therefore be asserted again that this intellect, by the very fact that it sees itself, has a need—or rather, it possesses that very thing continually. Thus, first, it has this from itself: that it is multiple; second, that it belongs to another; then, necessarily, that it is capable of seeing—of that seeing, I say, of which it is also said to exist. Furthermore, its essence itself is vision. For if it were something else, vision would have to exist separately; but if it is not something else, vision would be empty. It is therefore necessary that many things be there to meet with the visible; that which is seen by itself must be a certain multitude, and not entirely one. For that which is purely one has nothing to act upon, but existing alone and singular, it rests entirely. For that which acts by reason <margin>D</margin> results in one thing and then another. Indeed, if there is not one thing and another there, what will it do? Where will it proceed? Therefore, whatever acts must either act concerning something else, or must itself be multiple, if it is to act upon anything within itself. If it does not proceed into another, it will rest. When it rests completely, it will understand nothing at all. For this reason, it is necessary for the thinker, while thinking, to be occupied with at least two things: either one of the two is external, or both are in the same being; and intellection is always occupied with a certain (so to speak) *alterity* <note>Original Greek: *heterotēti*. "Otherness" or the state of being different.</note> and, in turn, with a certain *identity* <note>Original Greek: *tautotēti*. "Sameness."</note>.

<column-break/>

...let it take the opinion-forming power; then, from this, let it ascend; but if not, let it take the sense that brings the forms to itself—the sense, I mean, even in itself with those things it can [attain], or indeed being in the forms. But if someone wishes to descend, let them go toward the generating [power], even down to the things it makes. Then indeed let them ascend again from the final forms to those... back this way; or rather to the first things.

<margin>A</margin> These things, then, are so. But if only the things made [are there], then the last and the first would be the things made, from which they are also primary; such that the makers and the made must be together, and both be one. If not, it will need something else again. What then is beyond that again? For [that would be] of the intellect. Or does it not see itself? Then it needs nothing of vision. But this is for later. Now, <margin>B</margin> let us speak thus. For the inquiry is about the thing sought; it must be said: not again... to be in need of seeing itself. Rather, if indeed seeing itself happens, that which makes must be, so that the other things also are, and by necessity it is capable of sight, and such is the nature of that which comes from it. They said it exists. For it is not of one [nature]... seeing if it is to be; nor into anything... <margin>C</margin> It must therefore be more than one, the things seeing and coinciding with the visible, the visible things. And the things contemplated are the same, being a multitude in the whole. For thus are the things in the whole toward the activity; but being alone and solitary, it will stand altogether. For activity is of one thing and another. And if there were not another, what will the "other" do? Or how will it stand at all? Therefore it is not the active thing, unless it acts concerning another, or is itself many, <margin>D</margin> if it is to act in itself. But if it does not go out toward another, it will be at rest. When there is total rest, there is no thought. Therefore, for the thinker to think, they must not be [simply] one, and either the other is outside, or both are in the same. And always thought is in alterity, and by necessity also in identity.

Plotinus posits that the Intellect contains all eternal Forms as a unified multiplicity, a point where the translator inserts a comparison to Christian theology.</summary>

The previous page (506) established that the Forms (the divine blueprints of reality) exist within the Intellect as distinct but unified entities. Page 507 now explores the "multiplicity" inherent in thought: why the act of thinking requires a division between the thinker and the object of thought, leading to the necessity of a "Simple One" above the Intellect.</meta>

BOOK THREE.
V

Those things that are properly and primarily understood <note>original: "καὶ εἶναι τὰ κυρίως νοούμενα"</note> relate to the mind as being both the same and different. Furthermore, every understood thing brings with it a certain identity and a certain difference. Otherwise, what would it understand, unless it contained one thing and another within itself? For if every rational principle is a certain "word," it is surely already many. Therefore, the mind perceives itself as a <margin>manifold</margin> <note>original: "ποικίλον" (poikilon) - meaning variegated, diverse, or many-colored like a tapestry.</note> manifold eye, or like something marked with various colors. For if it were to apply itself to something entirely one and indivisible, it would be deaf and lack any reason. For what could it say or consider about such a thing?

Indeed, if it were necessary for the indivisible itself to affirm that it is entirely indivisible, it would first have to list the things that it is *not*. In this way, it would still happen that there are many things so that there might be the "One." Furthermore, when it says about itself, "I am that," it puts forward this "that" either as something else besides itself—and thus it lies—or as something accidental to itself, and thus it judges itself to be many. Or perhaps it will say, "I am, I say, I am; I, I say, I." What then? Either only two things will be here—and so it will say of itself "I" and "this"—or it will be necessary for there to be something multiform. Now it will discern these things as different, and by what reason they are different; thus number is already present, and many other things will follow. It is therefore necessary for the thinking subject to receive one thing and another; and that which is understood, as something distinguished within itself by the intelligence, must be diverse. Otherwise, there will be no intelligence of it, but only a "touch" <note>original: "θίξις" (thixis) - a non-discursive, direct contact or "nudging" of the divine, rather than analytical thought.</note> and a kind of strike, such that it can neither be spoken of nor speak. It "pre-understands" (if I may say so) without intellect, because the intellect is not yet born, and the one who reaches there does not yet understand.

It is necessary, moreover, that the thinking subject does not remain simple, especially when it understands itself entirely. For it divides itself, even if someone were to say that intelligence is a form of silence. Furthermore, that which is entirely simple does not require the various care through which it might grasp itself. For what would it grasp when it understood itself? Before it uses the mind to understand itself, it exists entirely as what it is within itself. Finally, knowledge itself seems to be a certain desire, and like a discovery following a search. Therefore, that which has no difference within itself remains at rest everywhere and investigates nothing about itself; but that which unfolds and evolves itself is, of course, multiple within itself.

<column-break/>

Likewise, those things which are properly and especially understood relate to the mind as being both the same and diverse at once. And again, the intellect brings a certain identity and alterity along with itself; otherwise, what does it understand, unless it contains one thing and another within itself? For if each thing is a certain "reason" or "ratio," then it is surely many. It perceives itself, therefore, as a kind of varied eye, or something distinguished by various colors. For if it should apply itself to what is entirely one and impartible, it will be "deaf" and lack reason. For what could it either say or weigh regarding this very thing? And yet, if it were necessary for the indivisible to affirm itself as altogether indivisible, it would first be necessary to number the things which it is not. Wherefore, in this way too, it will happen that there are many things, in order that there may also be one. Moreover, when it says of itself, "I am that": it brings forth this "that" either as something else besides itself (and thus it lies) or as something happening to it (and thus it decrees itself to be many). Or perhaps it will speak thus: "I am, I say, I am; I, I say, I." What then? Either there will only be two things here—and so it will say of itself "I" and "this"—or it will be necessary for there to be something multiform. Now indeed it will discern these as diverse, and by what reason they are diverse; thus number already exists here, and many other things will follow. It is therefore necessary for the one who understands to receive one thing and another: and that which is understood must be diverse in itself, as if distinguished by the intelligence itself. Otherwise, there will be no intelligence of it, but only a certain touch and, as it were, a strike—such that it can neither be told nor tell—and it "pre-understands" (so to speak) without intellect. Indeed, the intellect has not yet been born, and the one who touches there does not yet understand.

But it is necessary that the one understanding does not remain simple, especially when it understands itself completely. For it divides itself, even if one were to say that intelligence is silence. Furthermore, that which is entirely simple does not need various care through which to apprehend itself. For what will it apprehend, if it should ever understand itself? For before it uses the mind to understand itself, it exists entirely as what it is within itself. Finally, cognition itself seems to be a certain desire, and like a discovery accompanying an investigation. That which therefore has no difference toward itself within itself rests on all sides, nor does it investigate anything concerning itself; but that which explains and unfolds itself is, of course, multiple within itself.

***

## *Since in the first intellect there is a number of many things absolutely different from each other, it is necessary that above this there be another principle that is simply one, that is, entirely the most simple.*

->**Chapter XI.**<-

Unless in the first essence, life, and intelligence, there were some distinction between being, living, and understanding, these three things—so different in the order of things—would not easily be maintained; for "being" is the most common of all, "understanding" the least, and "living" holds the middle ground. The intellect itself is nothing other than a certain sight directed toward its first light, just as bodily sight is directed toward its own; by whatever perfection bodily sight is increased, it will always be inferior to the light. Similarly, the intellect, finally perfected by its own light (that is, truth itself), still appears to be a "good" that is fruitful. Essence <note>original: "Essentia" - the basic state of existing.</note>, being the most common of all things, proceeds immediately from Unity after simplicity itself, and besides the "reason" of essence, it offers an image of that unity, which differs in a certain way from the essence. Likewise, by the help of this image, it is turned back toward the One and the Good themselves—not by an intellectual instinct first, but by a natural and vital one. Before this act of conversion, it was already essence and image; in the act of conversion itself, it appears as living; after this, as understanding, while thus turned it receives the gift from the Good itself. And since the Good itself is above all things, holding itself equally toward all, it does not receive something of "all" there, but all things equally, especially since it is the nearest vessel. Therefore, a uniform shape is made from this, having the ideal forms <note>The "Forms" or "Ideas" are the perfect templates of all existing things.</note> of things absolutely distinct among themselves; from which follows a far greater distinction in the process after it. In the same moment, the intellect is made both by these forms and with them. Finally, since the intellect carries a multitude of absolutely different things with it, it rightly depends on a certain superior, most simple principle.

<summary>This page argues that the act of thinking (intellection) requires a split between the subject and the object, meaning the Intellect must be "multiple." Therefore, there must be a higher, "Simple One" (God/The Good) that precedes all thought and division.</summary>
