<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 507 regarding how the "One" (the absolute, simple source of all existence) gives rise to the "Intellect" (the realm of thought and multiplicity). On the previous page, Plotinus argued that for anything to think, it must have an object of thought, which immediately introduces a division. Here, he explores how the Intellect "stretches" toward the One and, in failing to grasp its absolute simplicity, produces the diverse world of Forms.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> Here, therefore, the intellect becomes manifold <note>original: "multiplex" / "ὁ πολὺς". In Neoplatonism, this refers to the transition from the "One" to the "Many."</note> whenever it attempts to understand that which is "beyond." For when it looks toward that One, it tries to reach it as something simple; however, it immediately falls away from that simplicity, receiving it into itself as something multiplied. Consequently, it did not begin its journey as a completed intellect, but rather as a "sight" that does not yet see. It proceeded from the One, carrying away a multiplicity that it generated within itself. Thus, it desired another thing indeterminately, possessing within itself only a certain imaginary reflection <note>original: "imaginarium" / "φάντασμά τι". A phantom or image rather than the thing itself.</note> of the One. But in proceeding from there, it brought forth something else, which it then made into a great multitude within itself.

<margin>B</margin> Now, indeed, it possesses within itself a certain "shape" of the spectacle itself <note>The "spectacle" refers to the vision of the One.</note>; otherwise, it would never have been prepared to receive it. In this way, from the One, it has now become manifold. Thus, as a completed intellect, it notices itself, and the "sight" has finally become a "seeing sight." It is only truly an intellect when it possesses its object and holds it as a thinking mind.

<margin>C</margin> Before these things, however, there was only desire and a formless sight. This intellect directed itself toward that One; having attained its goal, it has now emerged as a completed intellect, forever characterized and formed by "essence" <note>original: "essentia" / "οὐσία". The fundamental reality or being of a thing.</note>. Likewise, the intellect possesses "intelligence" <note>original: "intelligentia" / "νόησις". The act of thinking.</note> after it has thought; but previously, there was no intelligence, since it did not yet have an "intelligible" object—nor was it yet an intellect, since it was not yet thinking anything.

<margin>D</margin> That which exists above these things is their principle <note>original: "principium" / "ἀρχὴ". The starting point or source.</note>. I do not mean that it is a principle *within* them; for the principle from which things come is by no means *in* them, though the elements from which they are composed are within them. That from which individual things arise is not one of those individuals, but is alien to all of them. Therefore, the One is not just one thing among all things, but is *before* all things. Thus, it is also before the mind, for within the mind are all things; and for this reason, it is "above the mind." Furthermore, if whatever exists after the One follows an ordered sequence, then the One is superior to all of them, and it must be that it is none of those things over which it is superior.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, you shall not call the One "Mind," nor even "the Good," if by "the Good" you mean one thing among the many. But if "the Good" signifies that which is above all things, then it may be called so. For if the intellect becomes an intellect by becoming manifold—and if the very act of self-intelligence, even if it proceeds from the One, nevertheless multiplies by the act of approaching—then that which is entirely simple and the first of all must be "above the mind." For if it were to think, it would by no means be superior to the intellect, but would *be* an intellect. Moreover, if it were an intellect, it would also be a multitude.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, this intellect also became "the many" when it wished to think of the "Beyond." If it had wished to see that absolute thing itself, it would have gone out toward it as toward something simple, yet it always receives it as something multiplied within itself. So, it does not go out toward it as a completed intellect, but as a sight not yet seeing. It went out possessing that which it multiplied within itself, so that it desired another thing indeterminately, having only a certain image or phantom of it. It went out from that source, but not by making that source its own; for it has a "stamp" <note>original: "τύπον" (typon). An impression or mark, like a signet ring in wax.</note> of the vision, otherwise it would not have been able to receive the pleasure of it. And because it became something more than one, it became a being that "knew" it, as it were; and then it became a seeing sight, an intellect, an essence, a thought, and a world <note>original: "κόσμος" (kosmos). The ordered universe of the Forms.</note>.

<margin>B</margin> For it is not the case that the intellect has any individual part of this, but it is always the intellect as a whole. But that which is before these things is the principle of these things, and it is not inherent in them. For the "from which" is not inherent, but the "out of which" <note>Plotinus distinguishes between the *source* of a thing (which remains distinct) and the *components* of a thing (which are inside it).</note>. But from where each thing is, each thing has its being, yet the source is before all things. Thus, it is before the mind; for since all things are within the mind, it is for this reason before the mind.

<margin>C</margin> And if those things that come after it have their order relative to all things, then it is also before all things; nor can it be any of those things of which it is the source. You might say it is the Mind itself, but "the Mind" contains all things in their essence. But the One is the same for all, yet before all. And so it is named either "Not Mind" (since the mind is manifold) or simply "Beyond." For if it thinks, it will not be beyond mind, but will be mind. But if it is mind, it will certainly be a multitude.

---

->He argues against those who place one true essence in the first principle, but many acts that are absolutely distinct from one another. Chapter XII.<-

*For either essence and act differ from one another, or they do not. If they differ, the essence is in itself imperfect, namely, needing to be perfected through the act. If they do not differ at all, then even the essence is manifold, because the act is absolutely manifold. This argument of Plotinus does not pertain at all to Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the famous Catholic theologian.</note>, who distinguishes the Trinity by relations. But as for whether it touches the way of Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), another major Scholastic philosopher known for the "formal distinction."</note>, let his followers see and answer: for I hope they may answer very well. Above all multitude, a "One" is necessary, and above any "one thing" is that which is simply the One itself. Since, therefore, essence, life, and intelligence are each "one thing"—that is, one essence, one life, one intelligence—therefore Plotinus here places before them the absolutely One, which precedes all things without any intermediate act or affection, but is itself the end of absolute simplicity. Plotinus denies to God every number that by nature implies multiplication and composition. As for relation...*

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Intellect is a "multiplicity" because the act of thinking requires an object, whereas the "One" (the First Principle) is absolutely simple and precedes all thought. A later scholastic note compares these Neoplatonic ideas to the theological distinctions of Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus regarding the Trinity.</summary>

->### BOOK THREE<-

Indeed, the number found among Christians does not do this at all: it certainly denies every number that can exist within beings and that which has an end. The number placed within the divine unity by Christians is not among created beings. For it is found neither in any of the categories <note>Aristotle’s "Categories," the basic ways things can be described.</note> nor in the transcendentals. Furthermore, whatever number might be imagined, it is not for him; it is neither a number of essences, nor of forms or qualities, nor a likeness. Even if you speak of "persons," you say so by divine authority; however, you will not be able to explain exactly what you mean. Similarly, if you speak of "properties," and someone says they are distinguished by "relation," he himself will admit that he does not fully grasp that mystery. Likewise, anyone who says that absolute things differ will seem to be acting foolishly. It must simply be believed that the mysteries of God are such, a point which Nicholas the Greek <note>original: "Nicolaus Græcus". Likely referring to Nicholas of Methone, a 12th-century theologian who wrote a famous refutation of the Neoplatonist Proclus.</note>, the philosopher, strenuously defended against Proclus.

---

<margin>* as many things, another *</margin>
AND what prevents it from still being a multitude, so long as it is one essence? For the multitude does not arise from composition, but its activities <note>original: "αἱ ἐνέργειαι" / "energeia". In Greek philosophy, this refers to the "active being" or "actualization" of a thing.</note> are themselves the multitude. But if these activities are themselves the intelligible things <note>The "Noeta," the objects of thought that exist in the realm of the Mind.</note>, but it comes from potentiality into activity, then it is a multitude, but an imperfect one, before the essence has acted. But if its essence is itself activity, and that activity is the multitude, then its essence will be as manifold as its multitude. This, however, we shall not grant to that which we have assigned the task of thinking itself. To the beginning of all things, we grant it no longer. For being exists mostly around the "many," from which also comes "muchness," for it stops at number, which is the first. But in the case of number, they say it is so because the subsequent things are compositions. Furthermore, there is already some necessity among beings, and these things do not cease in this way, from which the "many" come. Either the many will be torn apart from each other, <margin>* another thing, that before the composite</margin> or another thing; but not before the composite and the chance thing that goes forth, but from the one. Those who are simple beings will say that the activities have proceeded forth. Now, everything is placed before the activities, but they perceive the activities as intelligible things and as substances <note>original: "ὑποστάσεις" / "hypostases". Here meaning individual realities or "subsistences."</note>. But if they are substances, they will be influenced by those things from which they come. While that source remains simple, that which comes from it becomes a multitude in itself, and is dependent upon that source. For if those were to exist, from where would these substances be benefited, if they were to be so in truth? But if these are the first activities making the second thing, they will make that which was before the activities remain in itself, while the later things, coming from their own activities, will yield to those activities; for the thing itself is one thing, and the activities from it are another. Because the Mind <note>original: "νοῦς" / "nous". The cosmic Intellect.</note> is not itself the first activity. For it is as if it desired to become a thinking thing. Then it became Mind, with the desire being between itself and that which was born. And it was becoming. Nor did it desire at all. For what was simple? And the desire? It did not have anything to desire, nor did it have part of the thing while not having another part. Nor was it envied, nor was there a stretching out, but rather it is as follows. It is later after him; while he remains in the same state, it will already exist, because of which it is something else:
pos: since there is nothing anywhere to which he might turn his affection. But truly, if anything subsists after him, it subsists while he remains in his own proper state.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **SOMEONE MIGHT PERHAPS OBJECT** in this way: what prevents the One from being a multitude, provided that in the meantime it is a single essence? For multitude does not introduce composition into it. For certain activities of it are a multitude. But the response to this is: If its activities are not essences, but it proceeds from a certain potentiality into activity, it will not indeed be a multitude, but it will nonetheless be imperfect in terms of its essence before it acts. But if its essence is activity, and activity
<margin>B</margin> is truly a multitude, then its essence will be as manifold as its activity is manifold. This we concede to the Mind, to which we attribute the cognition of itself, but we by no means concede it to the First Principle <note>original: "principio". The ultimate source, the One.</note>. For it is necessary that before the multitude there is the One, from which the multitude proceeds; for before every number is the one. But some might object here that this is the case in number, since those things which follow the one in sequence are certain compositions; however, in the order of things it does not seem necessary for the one to exist from
<margin>C</margin> which the many proceed. But to these we shall respond: if the one does not preside over the order of things, the many would be dispersed among themselves, perhaps rushing together into a heap from various different places. Therefore, they claim that many activities proceed from a certain intellect that is simple in itself. Yet, they asserted that what exists before these activities is simple; then they will recognize that the ever-existing activities are certain substances, or certain "suppositions" <note>original: "supposita". A technical term for an underlying individual reality.</note>. Since they are indeed certain suppositions,
<margin>D</margin> they will surely be different from that from which they proceed: while that source remains simple, that which proceeds from it has turned into a multitude in itself and depends upon that source. But if, while that source is operating in some way, activities of that kind subsist from it, it too would happen to be a multitude; but if these are the first activities constituting a certain second thing, nothing prevents that which is higher than these activities from consisting in itself, while the second thing
<margin>E</margin> itself flows proximately from there and is composed of those activities; a number of activities is assigned to it. For they proceed while the other is not acting; otherwise, the intellect will not be the first action. For the One did not first desire for the mind to be made, and then the mind was made, as if some such affection intervened as a mediator between the generator itself and the mind being born from it. For there is no affection there. Likewise, that desiring one
<margin>F</margin> would be imperfect, and his zeal would not yet have precisely what it desires; nor again is he partly in possession of his wish and partly not.
It is therefore necessary that something else [subsists] from there.

It argues against the idea that the One's own essence could be a "multitude of activities," as that would imply potentiality or imperfection in the source of all being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between "The One" (the absolute first principle) and the "Intellect" (the first level of being that arises from the One). The previous page explored how the Intellect views the One and, in doing so, creates a multiplicity of forms. Here, Plotinus argues that the One itself is beyond even thought and knowledge.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> ...let it subsist, remaining entirely at rest within itself. Otherwise, it would be moved before it moves, and it would understand before it understands—or at least its first act would be imperfect, being merely a certain impulse. But toward what could such an impulse be directed? Or what could it recently have attained? Indeed, it is more consistent with reason to assert that a certain activity flows from that abiding source, just as light flows from the sun—namely, the Intellect and the entire intelligible nature <note>The "intelligible nature" refers to the realm of pure ideas or forms that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses.</note>—while the source itself remains at the very summit of the intelligible world, reigning over it, <margin>B</margin> not separating from itself that which shines forth from it. Or shall we posit one light upon another light, which indeed shines by always remaining in the intelligible? For that which shines out from it is neither severed from it, nor again is it the same, nor is it of such a kind that it is not an essence, or like something blind; rather, it sees and knows itself, and is the first "knowing thing." But just as that source is superior to the intellect, so too is it superior to knowledge. And just as it needs nothing, so it also has no need for knowledge; <margin>C</margin> instead, knowledge itself is placed in the "second nature" <note>In Plotinian philosophy, the "second nature" or second hypostasis is the Intellect, which emanates from the One.</note>. For knowledge is a certain "one thing," but that source is the One itself, not "a certain one." If it were "a certain one thing," it would no longer be the One itself; for that which is called "itself" stands above that which is named as "something."

## Intellect is not to be added to the Good itself, which indeed can be understood by any created intellect, however high.
## Chapter XIII.

**T**he definition of the Good itself and of the Intellect is as diverse as we have said, so that the former is the most universal, and the latter least so; the former desires nothing, while the latter desires the Good. Likewise, Intellect is the opposite of folly, while the Good is the opposite of evil. Folly and evil are not entirely the same thing; therefore, Intellect and the Good are not the same. Thus, when you add "intellect" to the "Good," you seem to see another and different thing, and you judge the Good to be so far needy, as if you had composed it. This paradox—namely, that the first principle is above essence, life, and intellect—is frequently asserted by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century who adapted Neoplatonic ideas into Christian mysticism.</note>, who adds moreover that the Good enjoys itself in a certain "more-than-intellectual" way, which he names "super-intellectual." Likewise, it "pre-understands" in an ineffable manner beyond and above the intellect, as if it enjoys itself by way of touch rather than vision. For Intellect is a kind of vision; it is not a way of saying something about itself, but rather a way of simply existing as that which it is. If, by some condition, the Good could be imagined in stages by the intellect, let us not imagine some intellect that needs intelligence; let us not imagine intelligence as the act of the intellect regarding the Good, but rather as the Good itself toward which intelligence turns—or perhaps as the light itself which the intellect seeks, in which perfected intelligence finds its end: a light not residing in another, but consisting in itself. This clarity itself is neither "seeing" in the proper sense, nor is it "blind" as if deprived of the good of vision; just as vision itself neither "sees" properly, nor is it blind. Surely the clarity of vision itself is a cause much further removed from the privation of sight than sight itself is, and clarity is not determined by the category of intellection. For that which is the cause of all things is above all things and is defined by nothing from among the number of all things. Therefore, it is not defined by essence, life, or intellect; not by intellectual or intelligible clarity, but by that clarity itself existing simply by itself in itself—the cause of all activity and clarity. It is imagined according to effective power as the height of powers and the flowering of acts. If the Soul lacks hands and feet, yet because it does not need them and possesses the power that generates them in a more eminent way, it is called neither maimed nor lame. By similar reason, the Reason is not "blind" even if it has no eyes, nor is the Mind "irrational" even if it never reasons; for in a single moment it possesses what reason seeks through time. Nor is God "senseless" even if He has no mind; for He is the whole of what the mind strives to possess—or rather, to become.

### FOR WHICH REASON it is truly ineffable. <margin>A</margin>

**F**or whatever you say, you are saying something specific. But that which is above all things and above the most venerable Mind, being set apart from all things, has no other true name, nor is it any among all things. And it has absolutely no name, because nothing can be said of it; but we, as far as we are able, try to signify something about it to ourselves. Furthermore, when we are in doubt, saying for instance that it does not feel itself, <margin>B</margin> or does not notice itself, or does not know what it is at all—then it is surely fitting to consider that whenever we say such things, we are being pulled toward opposites. For it would be a great crime, as far as we are concerned...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...subsisting, it maintains a stillness within itself everywhere. But if it moves before it moves, and understands before it understands, its first activity is imperfect, being only an impulse. Toward what, then, is this impulse directed? Or one might reasonably ask whether a certain activity comes from it, just as light comes from the sun, which then establishes [the intellect] and the whole intelligible nature. But the source itself, standing at the summit of the intelligible, reigns over it, <margin>B</margin> not casting out from itself that which shines from it. Or shall we make another light before the light, or shall we shine while it remains in the intelligible? For it is neither torn away from it, nor again is it the same as it. Nor is it such a thing as to not be essence, or like something blind; rather, it is seeing and knowing itself, and is the first to know. But that which is beyond intellect is likewise beyond knowledge, needing nothing, <margin>C</margin> just as the mind [does not]; nor does it need to know, but knowledge is in the second nature. For "the One" and "knowing" are different; that source is the One itself, not "a certain one," because if it were "a certain thing," it would not be the "itself."

**O**f what sort? What will you say? But that which is beyond all things, and beyond the most venerable things of the mind, is the only truth among all things, not being a name for it but something else, if it is any of all things, because a name belongs to it [only] because nothing is according to it. But as it is possible for us to signify it, we attempt to speak of it. But when we are at a loss whether it has sensation in itself or is already following itself, and does not even know itself, we must remember that in saying these things, we turn ourselves toward the opposites. This page explores why the One cannot possess "consciousness" or "thought" in the way we understand it, as these concepts imply a division between the thinker and the thing being thought.</meta>

### THE THIRD BOOK.
V 4

...for it tries to see knowledge everywhere as a mind. Therefore, let us engage in thinking—not as if the One is thinking of something specific, but rather that thinking already belongs to it. For we are cautious about applying "thinking" to the One at all, lest consciousness <note>original: "συνείδησις" (syneidēsis); here meaning a shared knowledge or internal awareness that implies multiple parts within a single being.</note> should cause it to fall into being a totality of parts. When the mind is truly itself, it is most properly a mind. However, each thing is itself by faith <note>original: "πίστει" (pistei); in this context, it suggests an internal, self-evident certainty of being that requires no external proof.</note>, and I seek nothing else. If thought is directed outward, it is something deficient and not properly "thinking." But that which is entirely simple and truly self-sufficient has no such need. That which is "secondarily self-sufficient" <note>This refers to the "Intellect" (Nous), which is the first thing to emerge from the One. It is self-sufficient compared to us, but deficient compared to the One because it must think of itself to exist.</note> requires itself, and thus requires the act of thinking itself. Indeed, that which is deficient in relation to itself has made itself self-sufficient through the whole; becoming sufficient out of all its parts, it preserves itself and turns its mind toward itself. For consciousness itself is a perception of something that is many, as the name itself testifies. <note>The Greek word "syn-eidesis" literally means "with-knowledge," implying a gathering of multiple things into one awareness.</note> Moreover, thought, being prior, reflects the thinker—who is a plurality—back into himself. Even if the thinker only says "I am Being," he says it as one searching for himself, and he says it truly, for "Being" <term>Being (Ens/On): In this philosophy, "Being" is not simple; it is the collection of all eternal Forms or Ideas.</term> is many. For even when he approaches something simple and says "I am Being," he does not find himself, nor does he find true Being. For he does not mean "Being" as one might say "stone" when speaking the truth; rather, he pronounces many things in a single word.

<margin>A</margin> How then do we speak of it? Either we say something about it, or even while we name it, we have neither knowledge nor thought of it. How then do we speak of it if we do not possess it? Or, if we do not possess it in our speech, do we not possess it at all? Rather, we possess it in such a way that we speak *about* it, but we do not speak the thing *itself*. For we speak of what it is not; but what it is, we do not say. Thus, we speak about it from the things that come after it. We are not prevented from "having" it, even if we do not "speak" it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is. Being itself is many, while we introduce it to be known and we attribute cognition to it: for when we grant it intelligence, we make it so that it *requires* intelligence. And if intelligence were to exist alongside it, it would be superfluous for it to apply intelligence to itself. For the "thinker" seems entirely to be a certain consensus of a whole where many things run together into one, whenever something understands itself—which is indeed the most proper and primary form of intelligence. But whatever is truly one is already a "something" <margin>B</margin> and seeks nothing further. If, however, intelligence is stretched out toward external things, it will be deficient and not a "primary" intelligence. But that which is altogether simple and truly sufficient needs nothing. That which is self-sufficient in the "second degree" but is lacking in itself, this surely needs its own intelligence. Yet that which is deficient toward itself renders itself sufficient by the whole of itself; having obtained sufficiency from all its parts, it dwells with itself and turns toward itself in the act of thinking. For consciousness <margin>C</margin> is itself the sensing of some plurality, as the name itself bears witness. Since the intelligence is prior, it reflects the thinker—who is many—back into himself. For if he should say only this, "I am Being," he says this as if he were discovering himself, and he says it appropriately: for Being is a plurality. For even when he reaches toward something simple and says, "I am Being," he does not attain either himself or the true Being. For he does not speak of "Being" as one might speak of a stone when speaking truly, <margin>D</margin> but in a single word he pronounces many things. For this "to be" which is truly "to be" is not called such because it possesses a mere trace of being; rather, it must be said that just as an image relates to its model, so Being undoubtedly encompasses many things within itself. What then? Shall none of these things be understood? Certainly, if you wish to take it as something remote and alone, you will not understand it, for Being itself is many within itself. And if you have said something else besides, it "has being." If this is the case, if there is something that is the simplest of all, it does not have intelligence of itself: for if it did, it would also have being in some way and in some place. Therefore, it neither thinks itself, nor is there any intelligence of it anywhere.

> *Since the intellect does not exclude multiplicity—which the One itself excludes—and therefore the One itself, being simpler, is more eminent than the intellect, it follows that we are least able to grasp and explain it through the intellect.*

->Chapter XIV.<-

> *Yet we speak about it, as Parmenides and Dionysius <note>original: "Dionysius"; referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist who taught that God is best known through "unknowing."</note> say, through negations and relations. For we "possess" it in a certain way, insofar as we have a certain unity as the head of our mind—a character of the divine unity—by which we then touch the divine unity. When we have been formed by our own mind, and through this have been carried out of ourselves by the divine mind, it now makes us into prophets.* <note>original: "vates"; meaning a divinely inspired seer or poet who speaks in a state of ecstasy.</note>

<margin>A</margin> **IN WHAT** way, then, do we speak of it? Certainly, we say something *about* it, yet we do not speak the thing *itself*; we have neither knowledge nor intelligence of it. But in what manner do we speak of it if we do not "have" it? Because even if we do not have it by way of knowledge, it does not mean we do not have it at all. Rather, we have it in such a way that we can speak *about* it, but we are unable to fully express it. For we are accustomed to pronounce what it is *not*, but what it *is*, <margin>B</margin> never. Therefore, we are accustomed to use words about it based on things that come after it; yet nothing prevents us from "having" it, even if we lack the power to explain it.

Plotinus and his translators explain that we can only speak of the One through "negative theology"—defining it by what it is not.</summary>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, just as those who are inspired by the divine and seized by a trance <note>original: "divinitus afflantur, atq; rapiuntur"; refers to the Neoplatonic concept of 'enthusiasm,' where a person is possessed by a higher power.</note> perceive that they have something greater within themselves, even if they do not know exactly what it is—and from those things by which they are moved, they speak and receive a certain sense of the discovery, though they are distinct from the power that moved them—so we also are disposed toward that One. When we use a pure intellect <note>term: Intellect (Intellectus/Nous); for Plotinus, this is the first level of existence below the One, representing the totality of all forms and thoughts.</note>, we find that this is the innermost mind, the author of essence and of other things belonging to that same rank or order. <margin>B</margin> But we recognize that the One is not these things at all, but rather something more excellent than what we call "Being" <note>term: Being (Ens/On); in this philosophy, "Being" implies definition and multiplicity, so the One must be "beyond Being."</note>. It is more and greater than this very thing we name "Being," because that superior One is more excellent than speech, reason, mind, and sense—providing these things, yet not being these things itself.

->*Being itself, as it understands, is born from the One itself just as the light nearest the Sun comes from the Sun's innermost light. Chapter XV.*<-

*But just as from a nature that has eyes but no feet, more excellent things like eyes and feet are generated, so from the One itself—which does not possess its own essence or the form of life, mind, or intelligence—these things arise by eminence. Since that which is created by Unity itself is indeed something, yet is not Unity itself, it is therefore a certain multiplicity. It is also a "one" in some sense, but less of a "one" than the Source itself, and therefore it is manifold. It possesses something else, and as it simultaneously falls away from that Source, it becomes multiple. Whatever exists after the First is in some way composite; it receives its being and is confirmed in it both by the distinctness of its parts and by their mutual union. Therefore, the First is rightly Unity itself. Nor is the definition of Unity the same as that of Being. For multiplicity is opposed to Unity, but non-being is opposed to Being. Nor is the definition of Being superior to Unity, for if it were, Being would be multiple by participating in Unity. Nor, again, is the definition of Being equal to Unity; otherwise, Being would not become one. Therefore, Unity is superior to Being; indeed, it is (so to speak) its supremacy and its primacy, provided that the definition of Unity and simplicity is the same. The simpler things are in any category, the more primary they are, and vice versa. However, the multiplicity that is most closely received from the Unity of all things is equally primary and all-forming; it is united with itself as much as possible, so that in any of its forms, all other forms are in some way included. Therefore, the Divine Mind is "one-all." The Soul born from this is not so much "one-all" as it is "one-many." Plotinus does not entirely deny that all things are in the First, but they are there as distinct absolute principles, from which distinction can be seen through relative principles. But in the Second [the Intellect], he places the distinction of forms through absolute principles that differ from one another.*

<margin>A</margin> BUT in what way does the One provide such things? Is it by having them, or rather by not having them? But if it does not have them, how did it provide them? If, however, it does have them, it is not simple. If, therefore, it handed these things over without having them, how did multiplicity flow forth from it? Someone might perhaps concede that one thing flows from that which is simple, though even this would be further questioned: how can that even come from what is entirely one? Nevertheless, it is permissible <margin>B</margin> to say that it flows from the One just as splendor flashes out from a light. But how many things come from it will be asked further. Certainly, that which is made by the One ought not to be the same as the One, nor should it be the One itself. If, therefore, it is not the same, and certainly not better (for what is better than the One, or entirely superior to it?), it must be inferior to it, and that means it is more lacking. But what is more lacking than the One, except that which is not one? This, therefore, is already "many," yet it still desires the One; it is, <margin>C</margin> therefore, a "one-many." For the One itself preserves everything that is not one, and everything that exists is whatever it is through the One. For unless it becomes one, even if it is made of many parts, no one can call it "Being." Although one might be able to say what each thing is individually, it is from the fact that it is "one" that each thing exists. And let it be, in some way, the same in itself. But that which does not have many things in itself is no longer "one" by participation in the One, but exists as Unity itself, not derived from another. It is established that this is the very thing from which other things have their unity, some closer and some further away. But that which is closest to it is most especially the same in itself...
<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But just as those who are divinely inspired and possessed would know, at least to this extent, that they have something greater in themselves—even if they do not know what it is—they speak from the things by which they are moved, and in this they receive a certain perception of the mover, while being different from the mover themselves. So it is likely that we also stand in relation to that One: when we use a pure mind, we see that this is the inner Mind, which gave the cause and the other things according to Being. <margin>B</margin> But as for the One itself—since it is not these things, but something better than these, which we call Being, and also more beautiful and greater than what is called Being—it provides these things while not being these things itself, for it is superior to speech, mind, and sense.

<margin>A</margin> BUT how does it provide them? Is it by having them, or by not having them? But if it does not have them, how does it provide them? If, on the one hand, it has them, it is not simple. If, on the other hand, it does not have them, how does multiplicity come from it? For if some simple thing came from it, one might perhaps grant it; indeed, it would be asked how another thing comes from that which is in every way one. Yet it is possible to speak of it as the radiance that comes from light. <margin>B</margin> But how can many things come from it? That which comes from that One must not be the same as it. If then it is not the same, it is certainly not better—for what could be better than the One, or what could be more than many? It is, therefore, many. But still longing for the One, it is not simply many. For everything that is not one is only preserved, or is whatever it is, by being tied together; for if it is not made one, even if it is from many parts, it is not yet that thing which it is said to be. <margin>C</margin> And one might be able to say what each thing is, because each of them is said to "be" by being one; by being itself, it does not have many things in itself, and is already one by participation in the One. But while one thing is one by means of another, it is because these other things are present with them—some by being near, and some by being far. And that which is near...

<summary>Plotinus explores how the "One," which is absolutely simple and beyond Being, can be the source of all complex existence. He uses the analogy of divine inspiration and the radiating light of the sun to explain how the "Intellect" (the first multiplicity) flows from the One without diminishing its source.</summary>

# THE THIRD BOOK.

<column-break/>

Since that which is the same, or that which follows after it, is clearly everywhere by the very fact of its multitude—for if it were a multitude, yet it exists in the same [source], nor can one distinguish how much all things exist together; because whatever comes from it, insofar as it participates in life, is "one-many." For it cannot show itself to be all things in every respect. But that from which this arises is "one-all," because it is led by a Great Principle. For its Principle is itself, in reality and truth, the One. <note>The "One" is the ultimate source in Neoplatonism, preceding even thought or being.</note> However, because it follows from the Principle, it becomes all things in a certain way through a kind of pregnant and overflowing unity, yet meanwhile it remains a participant in the One; and whatever is in it is, in turn, both all things and one. What, then, are "all things"? Surely all things of which that Principle is the source. But how is that the Principle of all things? Is it because the One itself preserves them, clearly ensuring that each of them exists? For did it not also procreate them? But how? Is it because it possessed them beforehand? Indeed, it has been said that it would thus become many; but certainly it holds all things in such a way that they are not yet distinguished from one another. Those things which are in the second rank <note>term: Second Rank; referring to the "Intellect" (Nous), the first level of multiplicity where distinct "Forms" or ideas exist.</note> are distinguished from one another by reason: for they are already perceived in act. That One, however, is the power <note>term: Power (Potestas/Dynamis); here meaning potentiality or the infinite capacity to produce, rather than a physical force.</note> of all things. But what is the mode of this power? For it is not called "in power" in the way that matter is said to be, simply because it receives; for matter suffers what it receives, and thus power is positioned in an opposite way to that which is efficient. In what way, then, does it make what it does not have?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And that which exists after it, is clear for the reason that the multitude of this is one certain thing everywhere. For since it is a multitude, it nonetheless exists in the same [source], nor is it permitted to discern how much all things exist at once; since whatever of those things which are from it, insofar as it participates in life, is one-many: for it cannot show itself to be all things everywhere. But that from which this arises, is "one-all": because it is led from a great principle. For its principle is itself, in deed and in truth, the One.
<margin>B</margin> That which follows from the principle, however, becomes all things in a certain way by the overflowing and pregnant One, but in the meantime it is a participant of the One, and whatever is in it, is again all things and one. What then are "all things"? Namely, all things of which that is the principle. But how is that the principle of all things? Is it from the fact that the One itself preserves those things, while it clearly effects that each of them exists: for did it not also procreate them? But how? Is it from the fact that it previously 
<margin>C</margin> held them? But it has already been said, that it would thus be many: but surely it holds all things in such a way as not yet being distinguished among themselves. Those things which are in the second rank, are distinguished among themselves by reason: for they are already discerned in act <note>original: "actu"; in the sense of being fully realized or manifested.</note>: that One, however, is the power of all things. But what is the mode of the power? For it is not said to be "in power" as matter is, because it receives: for that which receives, suffers <note>original: "patitur"; meaning it is acted upon or undergoes change.</note>, and thus the power is held in an opposite way toward that which is efficient. In what way, then, does it make what it does not have?
<margin>D</margin> For it must not be thought that it happened to make things by chance, nor that it does so by reflecting in its mind on what it is about to do. It has therefore already been said, that if anything flows from the One, it is something other than it: but being other, it is not the One. For that was the One itself. But if it is not the One, it is therefore two, and necessarily now many: for it has in itself the "other," and the "same," and "quality," and the rest. And yet, that which depends on you is not the One itself which pertains to the higher realm, as will perhaps now be seen to be demonstrated. However, whether it be a multitude, a multitude such as is seen in that which follows, is still to be doubted: and the necessity by which the following itself proceeds from there, must be further investigated.

***

The further the cause of the discussion goes, the more things it produces. The First, therefore, effects all things: likewise, in any genus, the first is the simplest: thus the first of all things is so simple that it is not a certain simple thing, but Simplicity itself.

->Chap. XVI.<-

Likewise, just as nature, the mother of the body, is not the body, so the Intellect, the father of the soul, is not the soul; so the Good, the father of the Intellect itself, is not the Intellect, nor the intelligible world, but Simplicity and Sublimity, similarly excelling being <note>original: "excellens ente"; Plotinus famously places the One/Good "beyond being."</note>: For the properties of being are rest and motion: but to be moved is an appetite, not simply, but toward the good: and likewise not simply, but in the good. Therefore, in being itself, rest, motion, life, and intelligence are not the Good itself; but are already something of form, insofar as they turn toward the Good itself, they are filled by it: and in the same they find the greatest rest.

***

<columns>2</columns>

That there must, therefore, be something after the first, we have said elsewhere, and that it is altogether power, and indeed an inestimable power, and this must be asserted from all other things, since there is nothing, even among the lowest things, which does not have the power of generating. At present, however, it must be said that the universe of things which are born does not open toward higher things, but proceeds toward lower things; and this now in such a way that it proceeds step by step into a greater multitude, and therefore the principle of individuals is everywhere

<column-break/>

It establishes that the One is "Simplicity itself" and exists beyond Being, and that all levels of reality (Intellect, Soul, Nature) proceed from it toward increasing complexity and multitude.</summary>

The previous discussion established that the source of all things must be simpler than the things it produces. This page specifically tackles the paradox of how a perfectly simple, non-multiple source can give rise to the "Intelligible World," which is a realm of multiplicity and reason.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin>
...to the simple things, and remaining the same in itself, while a progression into many is granted. For this reason, that which procreated the insensible <note>Original Latin: *insensibilem*. In this context, it refers to the "intelligible" world—the realm of pure thought that cannot be perceived by the physical senses.</note> world is not the sensible world, but is the Intellect and the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The "intelligible world" (mundus intelligibilis) is the realm of Platonic Forms or Ideas, existing within the Divine Mind.</note> itself. Likewise, that which is superior to the intelligible world and its origin is neither the Intellect nor the intelligible world, but something simpler than the Intellect, and simpler than the intelligible world. For a multitude does not arise from a multitude, but this multitude proceeds from that which is not a multitude. For if that source were also a multitude, it would certainly not be the first principle, but <margin>B</margin> something else superior to it. All things must therefore be gathered back toward that which is truly One, beyond all number and any kind of simplicity: if indeed it is truly simple, and in it we must finally halt our progress. Furthermore, we must consider by what reason that which is produced by it is now a manifold <term>reason</term> <note>Original Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. In Neoplatonism, the "Logos" is the formative principle that organizes the universe.</note> and encompasses all things, while the source itself is not that reason. If it is not reason, under what condition does reason arise from non-reason? And in what way does the <term>good-form</term> <note>Original: *boniforme*. This refers to something that possesses the character or "shape" of the Good without being the Absolute Good itself.</note> proceed from the Good, <margin>C</margin> and what does it possess of the Good that it should be called "good-form"? Is it perhaps judged to have a certain good-form because it possesses a certain stability, remaining the same and behaving in a similar way? But what do these qualities contribute to the Good? For we are accustomed to require such a stable state—remaining the same and behaving similarly—only when good things are present. We first desire that from which we should never depart, precisely because it is good; but if it were not good, it would be better to depart from it. <margin>D</margin> Should we then desire it as a good—namely, to live always in the same way, voluntarily remaining in the Good itself? If this is what is most desirable for the Mind—to live in this way—then surely it requires nothing further. It is established that this state is experienced as always being the same because present things are sufficient. But with all things now present to this Mind, living is to be sought as the highest goal; present, I say, in such a way that they are not distinct from it. <margin>E</margin> If, therefore, all life is present to it—a life that is vigorous and clear—then all Soul and all Mind are already perfected in this, and nothing of life or intelligence is lacking. It is therefore sufficient unto itself and desires nothing further. But if it requires nothing, it already possesses it within itself; for if it were not within, the Mind would surely seek it. It possesses the Good within itself—either the Good as such, which we call life and mind, or something else that happens to these things. Yet, if this [Mind/Life] were the Good itself, <margin>F</margin> nothing would be superior to them. But if the Good itself is above these, then life—tending toward that, leaning entirely upon it, possessing its substance from there, and directing itself entirely toward it—will be "good" for the Mind; for that is its principle. It must therefore be that the Good is more excellent than life and mind. For only then can life, flourishing in the mind, turn toward it, as a kind of imitation of that which exists in the One, according to how it lives and follows it. The intelligence of this Mind will also turn as a kind of imitation of what exists in the One, whatever that ultimate thing may finally be.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
The same source is simpler. Therefore, that which made the sensible world would not be the sensible world itself, but Intellect and the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>Greek: *kosmos noētos*.</note>. And that which is prior to these things, which generated the Intellect, is no longer Intellect nor the intelligible world, but something simpler and more impassive than the intelligible world. For a multitude does not come from many, but this many comes from the not-many. For if this [source] were also many, it would not be the principle, <margin>B</margin> but another before it. One must therefore converge into the truly One, outside of all multitude and all simplicity, if it is truly simple. But how is that which is produced from it a "manifold and total reason" <note>Greek: *logos*.</note>, while the source is not reason? And how does reason come from non-reason? And how does the <term>good-form</term> <note>Greek: *agathoiedes*.</note> come from the Good? For what does it have of such a kind that it is called good-form? <margin>C</margin> Does it have the quality of being "according to the same things and in the same way"? And what does this have to do with the Good? For we seek that which is "in the same way" when goods are present, or rather [we seek] that from which we are not separated by bonds because it is good. If it were not, it would be better to leave it. Is it then living "in the same way," remaining in this voluntarily? Or is this life not to be cherished, which is clearly what the One seeks? It seems, then, that "in the same way" is said because present things are sufficient. <margin>D</margin> But when all things are already present to this, life is to be cherished. And indeed, of the things present, they are not as if they were different from it. If all life is these things, and a life that is manifest and full, in Soul and in Intellect, and nothing departs from life—since these are the necessary things—it is self-sufficient <margin>E</margin> and seeks nothing. But if it seeks nothing, it has in itself what we would say it has, if it did not provide it; it has, therefore, the Good in itself. Either it is such as we called life and intellect, or it is something else accidental to these. But if this is the Good, then that [the One] would be nothing of these. But if that is the One, clearly life is directed toward it, and is dependent upon it, and has its substance from it, and lives toward it. For that is its principle. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, that [the One] is better than life and intellect, because [the intellect] has turned toward it, and the life in it is an imitation of that which is in it [the One], according to which this lives. And the intellect in it is an imitation of that which is in it, because it is clearly this.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Neoplatonic metaphysics, shifting from the structural relationship between the One and the Intellect to the experiential process of how the human soul perceives the Good. It bridges the gap between abstract philosophy and mystical experience, using the metaphors of light and childbirth.</meta>

### BOOK THREE.

...being sufficient in itself and most simple. Nor is "to be" desired simply for its own sake, but rather "to be well"; nor is it simply "to live," but to live well; nor is it simply "to understand," but to understand well and blessedly, in a way that is beneficial to you. We do not even desire "truth" simply for its own sake; for truth is not desired if it is harmful, but rather we desire the "true good." Therefore, the Good itself is the goal and the starting point of all these things. The goal of our life is to see the Good itself through its own light. But since this Good is the most stable and most definite of all things, we do not reach it through the back-and-forth movement of logic <note>Original Latin: *rationis discursu*. This refers to "discursive reasoning," the step-by-step process of logical argument, which Neoplatonists believed was inferior to direct, sudden intuition.</note>, nor by the mind’s act of assembling or distinguishing ideas, but by a certain sudden and simple intuition. For us, the sign of this divine enjoyment is when our mind—beyond its usual habit and without any help from the senses—is flooded by a light of steady joy. This is a joyful clarity, a certain splendor of a light that exists within itself, which is God himself. He flows into us whenever His grace grants it, stripping away all other things—that is, our inclinations toward worldly desires, mental images, fantasies, the divisions of reason, intellectual concepts, and the mind's habit of comparing and distinguishing. Plato also speaks sufficiently on these matters in his great Epistle <note>This refers to Plato's *Seventh Letter*, where he describes the spark of truth being lit in the soul after long labor.</note>.

---

<margin>A</margin> What could be better than a life of wisdom, which is free from error and wandering? Even now, possessing all things, we participate in all of life; yet we ask if there is something even more precious, and how it is made. Our logic does not move past it, but stands still before it. Yet we must ascend further, leaving many other things behind, because the quality of being "self-sufficient" <note>Greek: *autarkes*. The ability to exist without needing anything else; a primary attribute of the Divine.</note> is beyond all things.

<margin>B</margin> Each of these things, clearly, is what it is now because it participates in the One. If it were not the One itself, it would have to participate in it. If you allow a thing to be "the whole," it is only self-sufficient because of the presence of the One within that multitude. Thus, the One is clearly the source of all essence and self-sufficiency, though it is not "essence" itself, but is beyond essence and beyond self-sufficiency. Having said these things, let us be released from the labor <note>Greek: *ōdinai*. Literally "birth-pains." Plotinus describes the soul's intense struggle to understand the One as being like the pains of giving birth.</note> of the soul.

<margin>C</margin> Perhaps the soul has not yet given birth; it yearns toward the One, filled with these birth-pains. But we must again find some incantations <note>Greek: *epōdōn*. Magical songs or chants. Here, Plotinus uses it metaphorically for philosophical arguments that soothe the soul's struggle.</note> to soothe these pains. Perhaps from what has already been said, which one might chant to oneself, a new kind of "song" may be found. Let us say that although we participate in all truths, the ultimate truth itself flees

<margin>D</margin> if one wishes to speak of it or think of it. For thought, in order to function, must take up one thing after another; it is caught in a journey of movement. But in that which is entirely simple, there can be no such movement or journey. It is enough to touch it intellectually. But once you have touched it, while you are touching it, you cannot speak, nor do you have the leisure to say anything. Only later can you reason about it. You must believe you have seen it when the soul suddenly receives light.

<margin>E</margin> For this light comes from the Good and is the Good itself. You should believe the Good is present when, like a God called into someone's house, he enters and illuminates it. If he does not enter, he does not illuminate. Thus, the unlit soul lacks that which it sought; but once illuminated, it possesses what it desired. This is the true end for the soul: to touch that light,

<column-break/>

and in a certain way, once he enters, he illuminates it entirely; otherwise, if he has not entered, he does not illuminate. Thus the soul is empty of light and empty of God; but once illuminated, it possesses everything the mind sought. Here, surely, is the soul's true goal: to receive that light and to see the Good by the light of the Good, not by the light of anything else.

<margin>A</margin> What, then, is better than the wisest life, which cannot fall or err? What is better than an intellect that embraces all things? And what is better than the whole of life and the whole of the mind? If we were to answer that what is better is that which created these things, and the manner in which it created them, then our logical reasoning would not proceed further, but would circle back upon itself. Nevertheless, we must progress higher, both for many other reasons and because the sufficiency <term>sufficientia</term> <note>The state of needing nothing else; absolute independence.</note> gathered into these things hangs from something external. In that realm, everything is indeed needy on its own.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, everything is a participant in the "One," yet it is a participant precisely because it is *not* the One itself. What, then, is that in which this thing participates? It is that which makes it so that all these things exist together. For if it makes each thing to be, and if the presence of the One makes the multitude of this speaker sufficient, then the One is clearly the origin of all essence and sufficiency. I say the One itself is not an existing essence, but is higher than essence and higher than sufficiency itself.

<margin>C</margin> Tell me, do these things satisfy us, and can we now put an end to the struggle? Or is the soul still vexed by its birth-pains? Indeed, it is now being stimulated even more vehemently. Perhaps, therefore, it is necessary to prepare our soul, as it is being more ardently stirred and shaken by the many pains of labor. Nevertheless, it is better to assist it again with certain magical songs <note>Original Latin: *magorum carminibus*. A translation of the Greek "incantations" mentioned in the left column; refers to philosophical meditations that calm the mind.</note>, if in some way we might find a chant that aids this birth.

<margin>D</margin> Perhaps if one chants what has been said more often, we shall finally achieve it. But what other kind of "new song" is there? Surely it is the song that transcends all the truths we participate in. It flees immediately if anyone wishes to speak or think it; for it is necessary for thought, in order to say something, to take up first one thing and then another. In this, thought is engaged in a discursive journey. But in that which is entirely simple, no such journey can exist.

<margin>E</margin> It is enough to touch it in an intellectual way. It is necessary that the person touching it, while they are touching it, is neither able to speak nor has the leisure to talk, but only later can they reason about it. We must believe we have finally seen it when the soul suddenly receives light. For this light flows from the Good itself; it is the Good. Then we must believe it is present to us, just as when another God enters when someone calls...

PLOTINUS: ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin>
...in which we should not behold by an external light, but rather look through that very light by which the soul also looks upward. For that by which we are illuminated is the very thing we must perceive. Indeed, we do not usually look at the sun by means of a light that belongs to something else. But if you ask by what reasoning you might achieve this, the answer is: take everything else away. <note>Original: *afele panta* (Greek: ἄφελε πάντα). ...and to behold it by itself, not by another light, but by that very thing through which one sees. For that by which one was illuminated is the thing that must be beheld. For not even the sun is seen through the light of another. How then might this happen? Take everything away.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FIVE.
### BOOK FOUR.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FIVE,
### BOOK FOUR.

->How that which is after the first arises from the first, and concerning the One.<-
->How that which is after the first is produced by the first, and concerning the One.<-

*Things in the universe, though diverse among themselves, would not have concord, order, or union with one another, unless they all proceeded from the One.* <margin>Chapter I.</margin>

*Indeed, this is not "one" in the sense of being this specific thing or that, but the "One" itself in its simple state. Because of its supreme simplicity, it is the first, most self-sufficient, and most powerful. It is the power of all things, through which others have the power to act; the more powerful they are, the more they produce. From this it appears that the first power itself creates all things, holds the widest dominion everywhere, and is most present to all things.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'Q' in a square frame featuring a figure and ornamental vines.</image-desc>
**W**HATEVER exists besides the First must necessarily depend on that First itself, whether directly or through certain intermediaries. There is an order of second and third things: where the second is traced back to the first, and the third to the second. For there must be something above all things, entirely simple and distinct from all that subsists within it, not mixed with those things that follow it, yet present to the rest in another way with the greatest ease.
<margin>B</margin>
This is truly the One; it is not as if it were some other thing first and then became "one," for then "one" would be falsely predicated of it. Furthermore, neither speech, nor reason, nor any knowledge at all can reach it; it is even described as being "beyond essence" <note>Original Greek: *epekeina ousias*. This concept suggests the ultimate principle is so transcendent it cannot even be categorized as "being" or "existence" as we understand it.</note>. Unless it were entirely simple, removed from all conjunction and composition, and purely One, it could not be a first principle. Indeed,
<margin>C</margin>
it is only through this supreme simplicity that it can be most self-sufficient and the first of all things. That which is not first needs what is before it; and that which is not simple needs the simple parts within it so that it may be constituted from them. Now, such a thing must be only one and unique. For if another were said to be of this kind, both would be entirely one;

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'O' (Omicron) in a square frame featuring a figure and foliage.</image-desc>
**B**ECAUSE it is necessary that what comes after the first is from that first, either immediately or through those things necessary to reach it; and there are intermediaries, and an order of second and third things. For some things lead to the first, and others to the things already mentioned, and the third leads to the second. Because this must be simple before all things, and different from all things after it, existing by itself, not mixed with the things that come from it, yet able to be present to other things in a different way, being truly One. Even if it were something else, then the statement "it is" would be false; it is that which neither reason nor knowledge can reach, which is also said to be beyond essence. For if it were not simple, existing outside of all coincidence and all composition, or truly One, it could not be a principle. It is most self-sufficient in being simple, and the first of all. For that which is not first is in need of what is before it, and that which is not simple is in need of the simple things within it, so that it might be made of them. Such a thing, then, must be only one. For if there were two such things, both would be one: for we do not say that these two are some kind of "two bodies."

<summary>This page introduces Ennead V, Book 4, establishing the Neoplatonic doctrine that all reality stems from a single, simple, and transcendent "First Principle" or "One." It argues that for any order or harmony to exist in the universe, there must be a primary source that is entirely unmixed and beyond human reasoning.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition into Book 4 of Ennead V. The previous page established the necessity of "taking everything away" to see the One; this page explores why the One, as the first principle, cannot be a body and why it must necessarily produce something other than itself (emanation).</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

Therefore, if the first principle were a body, it would have to be a simple body <note>original: ἁπλοῦν σῶμα</note>, and a body that is produced, but not the Principle itself. For how could anything come out of it? Bodies will be derived from other things; but those things there would not be in bodies, or if other things are placed before them, then bodies would no longer be the first things. From where, then, do the things after the first come? For if they were to arise by chance, that first thing would be the principle of all. How then do many things come from the first? If the first is the ultimate end of all, it is also the first power, because it is the most powerful of all existing things, and the other powers in turn can follow and imitate it. But we see that the power of other things reaches its peak in the production of offspring; they cannot endure to remain within themselves, but must create another. Not only do those things that have 
<margin>* That the first things do not have a choice, but also those that act by nature.</margin>
choice act this way, but even those that act by nature are always oriented toward imitation, and even inanimate things share something of themselves as far as they are able; for example, fire heats, and snow is cold, and <term>drugs</term> <note>original: φάρμακα (pharmaka). In the ancient sense, this refers to any substance—medicine, potion, or poison—that has a transformative effect on another body.</note> act upon something else, just as all things do, imitating the Principle in its power, toward eternity and goodness. How then could the most perfect and the first Good stay within itself, as if it were envious of itself or lacked power, though it is the power of all things? How then would it still be a Principle? It is necessary that things coming from it should never be false; and other things are established by it. For it is necessary to say that what proceeds from it is the most honorable among the things that follow. It must be that what is produced is the most honorable, and because of its proximity to those first things, it is better than all others.

### *The Intellect depends on the intelligible almost as sight depends on the visible, therefore it is not the first principle. Chapter 11.*

He touches here upon a double intelligible: one joined with the intellect, the other indeed higher. Consider in the eye of an animal seeing itself day and night, the substance of the eye is very bright, and the power of seeing depends on it; this power is indeed formless in itself, but is formed by the bright substance joined to it. Imagine the first intellect in such a way, even where it beholds itself, just as if a very bright eye, pressed in some way by a finger, were to look at itself. The light in the intellect, however, is its own substantial unity; it is its own intelligible, upon which the power of understanding depends, being turned toward it and formed by it. This power, along with its turning, is an <term>indefinite duality</term> <note>original: indefinita duitas. This refers to the Neoplatonic concept of the "Indefinite Dyad," a state of being that is not yet fully formed into the "Intellect" until it looks back at its source.</note>; but defined through its intelligible, it becomes an intellect in act and an all-forming idea. From here it also turns through its unity toward the simply One itself, which is also called the "more excellent intelligible." Plotinus here does not entirely deprive this One of knowledge, but of intellectual knowledge specifically.

If, therefore, that which generates were itself the intellect, it would be necessary for that which is first generated to be something else, and it would be less honorable, and not similar. But if that which generates is beyond the intellect, it is necessary that what is first generated be the intellect. Why? Because the activity of the intellect is thinking <note>original: νόησις (noēsis)</note>; and thinking occurs by seeing the intelligible, and is directed toward it, being as it were brought to completion by it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
...we say, or that the first One is itself a body: since no body is simple: likewise every body comes into being: and therefore it cannot be the principle, since the principle is unbegotten. Since therefore the principle cannot be corporeal, but is truly one and unique, it must surely be the first. If there is, therefore, any other thing besides the first, it will by no means be simple: it will therefore be "one-many." From where, then, does it depend? Surely it depends on the first. For such things
<margin>B</margin>
do not happen or meet by some accidental chance: nor would it thus be the principle of all. In what way, then, does everything else come from the first? Surely if the first is perfect and the most perfect of all, and the first power, it must be the most powerful of all things, and the other powers must imitate it as much as they can, according to their strength. Whatever proceeds from others to its own perfection, we have found, now generates something, and cannot remain sluggishly
<margin>C</margin>
at rest in itself, but makes something else from itself. We have discovered that this is true not only in those things that act by a certain choice, but also in whatever things are born and beget without choice: even things that lack a soul give something of their own to others as far as they can. Thus fire heats, and thus snow similarly cools. Drugs <note>original: Pharmaca</note> and poisons also act on another according to the likeness of their nature. Thus all things finally imitate the first principle to fulfill
<margin>D</margin>
eternity and goodness. Since nature is thus arranged, by what reason should it be believed that the first Good and most perfect of all would keep itself within itself as if through envy? Or perhaps that it could not propagate itself, though it is truly considered the power of all things? Finally, if nothing proceeds from it, it cannot be a principle. Therefore it is necessary for something to be made by it, if indeed anything is made besides it, and for something to be made from those things which are from it. For necessity itself demonstrates that some things are closest to it; then truly it is necessary that what generates the rest be the most excellent of the following things. Furthermore, that which is generated next from there, and holds the second place, is more excellent than the others.

---

<margin>A</margin>
IF therefore the generator were the intellect itself, it would certainly be necessary that what is first generated from it be inferior to the intellect, though close and similar. But since that which first generates is superior to the intellect, for that reason what is first generated is necessarily the intellect. But why is that first generator not the intellect? Because the action of the intellect itself is intelligence—intelligence, I say, looking toward the intelligible and turned toward it, and by it as if defined and perfected.
