<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the emanation of the "Intellect" (Nous) from the "One" (the First Principle). It specifically addresses how the Intellect, while being many, originates from a singular, higher source through the concept of the "Indefinite Dyad."</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin>
By its very nature it is indefinite, like sight, but it is defined by the intelligible. For this reason, as it has been handed down, from the <term>indefinite dyad</term> <note>original: ἀορίστου δυάδος (aoristou dyados). In Pythagorean and Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the principle of "two-ness" or multiplicity that emerges from the One.</note> and the One, the species and numbers are born. This, however, is the **Intellect**; therefore it is not simple, but manifold, exhibiting a certain composition—though an intelligible one—and already beholding many things. Yet it is also itself in turn an object of thought, as well as that which thinks; thus it is already two. There is also another intelligible object beyond this; but in what way does this Intellect depend on that intelligible?
<margin>B</margin>
Indeed, the intelligible, existing in itself, is not in need as that which sees and thinks usually is. I say that the thinking subject is in need relative to the object of thought. That object, resting in itself, is not as if it were devoid of sensation, but all things are its own, both in it and together with it; it is entirely capable of discerning itself. Likewise, life is in itself and all things are in it, and the observation of itself immediately exists, as if with a certain sense and internal consensus in a perpetual state, and with a certain
<margin>C</margin>
intelligence that is different from the intelligence of the Intellect itself. If, therefore, anything is born while that object remains in itself, it is generated from it precisely when that object is most essentially what it is. Thus, while that object remains in its own state, something arises and is generated from it; it is born, I say, while the source remains. Since, therefore, that intelligible object remains permanent, that which is made becomes intelligence. Furthermore, since it is intelligence and understands that from which it is generated—for it has
<margin>D</margin>
no other source—it certainly becomes Intellect, like another intelligible object, and such as that from which it came forth, a certain imitation and image of it. But how does it come to be while the source remains? Truly, one activity belongs to the **essence**, and another activity depends on the essence of each thing. The activity that belongs to the essence is such that each thing is itself that activity. But the activity flowing from the essence is that which necessarily follows every thing, being different from that from which it flowed. Just as
<margin>E</margin>
in fire, one heat belongs to the essence of the fire, while another proceeds from it, as the fire exerts the heat inherent in its essence so long as it remains fire. Thus, then, in that higher realm—and much earlier—while that source remains in its own state, out of the perfection inherent in it and the accompanying internal activity, a generated activity goes forth, taking on a <term>subsistence</term> <note>original: ὑπόστασιν (hypostasin). Here meaning a distinct, underlying reality or individual existence.</note> of its own, as one born from a great power. Indeed, from the power that is the greatest of all powers, it proceeded into being and essence.
<margin>F</margin>
For that which is above is greater than essence, and is the power of all things. But this which we now discuss is already "all things"; therefore it stands above essence. Yet if this is ever all things, but the One exists before all things, then it does not hold an equal condition with all things. For this reason, it is necessary that it be superior to essence—that is, purely superior. Something, therefore, exists that is more ancient than the Intellect. For being itself is not
<margin>G</margin>
something dead, nor is it like something deprived of life and intelligence; therefore, the Intellect and Being are the same. For the Intellect does not relate to the things it understands as the senses relate to sensible things (as if to things that preceded them); rather, the Intellect itself is the very things that exist.

<column-break/>

...and being perfected. It is indefinite in itself like vision, but defined by the intelligible. Therefore it is also said that from the **indefinite dyad** and the One come the Forms and the numbers. For this is the Intellect. Therefore it is not simple, but many, indicating a certain composition—intelligible, to be sure—already seeing many things. It is itself an object of thought, but also the thinker. Thus it is already two. And there is another, the intelligible after it. But how did this come forth from the intelligible?
<margin>15</margin> The intelligible remains in itself, and is not in need, as are the seer and the thinker (and I say the thinker is in need in relation to that object). It is not as if it were without perception, but all things are of it; it is itself and with itself, and possesses the power of its own discernment. It lives of itself, and all things are in it, and its self-awareness belongs to it, as if in a certain sensation, and internal consciousness, and a thinking that is different from the thinking of the Intellect, while it remains eternal. Since it comes from it, how does it come from it when that source is most especially what it is? While that source remains in its own character, that which is produced comes from it; while the source remains, it is produced, since the source itself does not move.
<margin>20</margin> The thing produced is an object of thought, and it becomes Intellect. It stands firm because it also thinks that from which it came forth (for it has nothing else). It becomes Intellect, like another object of thought and like the source itself, both an imitation and an image of that source. But how, while that source remains? There is an **activity** <note>original: ἐνέργεια (energeia). Plotinus distinguishes between the "internal activity" of a thing's essence and the "external activity" that flows out from it.</note>, one of the essence, and the other from the essence of each thing. The activity of the essence is each thing itself. The activity from the essence must necessarily follow every thing, being different from it. For example, in fire, there is one heat that fulfills the essence, and another that is produced from it when that source exerts its inherent
<margin>25</margin> essence to remain fire. So also there, and much more so, while that source remains in its own character, from the perfection within it and its presiding activity, the generated activity takes on a subsistence, having come into being and essence from a great power—the greatest of all. For that source was **beyond essence**, and that source is the power of all things, while these are already all things. But if this is all things, then that source is beyond all things. Therefore it is beyond essence and all things, if all things are the One, but the One is
<margin>30</margin> prior to all things; and in this way it is beyond essence. This, however, is the Intellect. It is therefore beyond the Intellect. For being is not a dead thing, nor is it without life or thought. Intellect and being are the same. For Intellect is not of things in the way that sensation is of sensible objects that pre-exist it, but the Intellect is itself the things.

<summary>Plotinus explains how the Intellect (Nous) emanates from the One without the One being diminished or moved. He uses the analogy of fire and its heat to distinguish between a thing's internal essence and the external activity it naturally produces.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the discussion of how the Intellect (the second principle in Plotinus's system) emerges from the One. Having established that the Intellect is a "manifold" or a collection of many things, Plotinus now investigates whether these things (the objects of thought) exist inside or outside the Mind itself. This is a foundational argument for Neoplatonic epistemology: that to know truly is to be one with the thing known.</meta>

FIFTH BOOK.

Just as it is not brought in from elsewhere—for where else could it come from but from within the things themselves?—knowledge is identical to them, and things without matter <note>Plotinus refers to "immaterial things," which are the pure ideas or forms that do not require physical substance to exist.</note> are not separate from the mind.

But if indeed the mind does not simply drain the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "species". These are the eternal archetypes or blueprints of all things.</note> of things through the act of understanding. For from where would it drain them? Rather, it comes forth together with the things themselves; it is one and the same with them, and vice-versa. Indeed, the things themselves are not "intelligible" (knowable) at all without their own "matter," which in this case is the Intellect itself.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD V.
### TREATISE V.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD V.
### BOOK V.

->That the objects of thought are not outside the intellect: also concerning the Good itself.<-

<margin>Cap. I.</margin>
*Just as sensation, which is the lowest form of knowledge, proceeds only from the outermost parts; so the intellect, which is the highest form of knowledge, looks only at the innermost.*

Therefore, just as in sensation there are only images of the things being perceived, so in the intellect are the things themselves which it understands. Otherwise, if the intellect received mere images from the things it was trying to understand, then knowledge would never equal the things themselves. Such knowledge, being made through images, would be doubtfully inferior to the actual things, and the mind would never be certain of having a sincere judgment about them; for images, when translated into the nature of the one receiving them, do not carry the pure nature of the object. But the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus" (Latin) / "νοῦς" (Greek). In Neoplatonism, this is the Divine Mind containing all eternal truths.</note>, being placed above discursive reasoning <note>Discursive reasoning is the step-by-step logic humans use; Plotinus argues the Divine Mind knows everything instantly and all at once.</note>, holds its objects present before it by its own will. Thus, it possesses within itself not only the principles of arts and things, but it exists within the principles and whatever necessarily follows from them. Nor should you think that these <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibilia". The "knowable things" or pure ideas that the mind contemplates.</note> are merely propositions or some kind of spoken words; rather, they are essential reasons and forms. They are not like separate spectacles set apart from each other, but are forms within a single immaterial form—just as all sensible forms exist in the same unformed matter. Finally, these intelligible forms are much more united with the intellect than sensible forms are with matter, or the stars are with the substance of the heavens. We discuss more extensively in our *Theology* how the forms of things are naturally implanted in our souls.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the objects of thought (the Intelligibles) exist outside of the Intellect. Plotinus is arguing that if they were external, the Intellect could never have certain knowledge of them, as it would only be perceiving "images" of them, similar to how our physical senses work.</meta>

<page-num>520</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD V.</header>

<margin>A</margin>...this is how it must be: since regarding those things offered to the senses, whose reliability seems more certain, doubt is often raised whether their apparent nature resides in the underlying objects or rather in certain impressions <note>original Latin: "passionibus"; Greek: "pathesin". In ancient philosophy, these are the "passive" experiences or sensations produced in the observer by an object.</note> of the soul. In such cases, the judgment of the mind, or at least of thought, is certainly required. For even if it is granted that the natures of perceived things reside in the underlying objects, what is known through sense is a mere image of the thing; sense does not grasp the thing itself. <margin>B</margin> For the thing itself remains outside. 

But if the Intellect, in knowing itself and the objects of thought, knows them as things existing apart from itself, how does it encounter them? For it is possible that it might not encounter them, and thus it might happen that it does not know them. Or perhaps it only knows them at the moment it encounters them, and even then, it would not always possess that knowledge. Furthermore, if some say that the objects of thought are "yoked" <note>original Greek: "sunzeuchthai"</note> <margin>C</margin> to the Intellect, we must ask what that union actually means. 

Moreover, these acts of understanding would be mere shapes or figures; if this were so, they would be external impressions or impulses. But how would the Intellect be shaped? What form would such things take? Finally, understanding would be a perception of external things, just like sensation. How then would these two differ? Perhaps only in that one perceives smaller things? 

Also, <margin>D</margin> how will the Intellect recognize that it has truly perceived something? How can it judge that this is good, or beautiful, or just? For each of these would be different from the Intellect itself; it would not possess the principles of judgment within itself to trust, but these too would be outside, and Truth would be there as well. 

Again, these objects of thought either lack sense, life, and intellect, or they possess intellect. If they possess intellect, then both exist together here, and Truth itself exists here; <margin>E</margin> this would be the primary Intellect. But we must also ask about this: in what condition do Truth, the object of thought, and the Intellect itself exist? Are they in the same place and simultaneous, yet two and distinct, or in some other way? 

But if the objects of thought lack intellect and life, what are they? For they are not merely propositions, nor rules called "axioms" <note>original Latin: "dignitates"; Greek: "axiomata". These are self-evident logical principles.</note>, nor like spoken expressions <note>original Greek: "lekta". A Stoic term for the "meanings" or "sayables" that underlie speech.</note>. <margin>F</margin> For in that case, they would be "about" other things, and not the things themselves; as if they said "the just is beautiful," while the Just and the Beautiful themselves were something else entirely. If they say these are simple things—the Just and the Beautiful each on their own—then first, the object of thought would not be a single thing, nor would it be in one, but each would be severed from the others.

<column-break/>

...it will offer, since even regarding the objects of sensation, which seem to have the most vivid credibility, it is doubted whether their apparent substance is in the underlying objects or in the passive impressions, and requires the mind or the reasoning power to judge. For even if it is granted that the sensory objects exist in the underlying things of which sensation takes hold, the thing known through sensation is an image of the object, and sensation does not grasp the object itself. For that remains outside. 

But if the Intellect, while knowing the objects of thought, knows them as being other than itself, how would it meet with them? For it is possible it might not, and thus it is possible for it not to know. Or, having trusted that it has the knowledge. But if they say they are "yoked together," what is this yoking? 

Furthermore, the acts of thought will be impressions; and if they are impressions, they are imported. How will the shape be imprinted? In what will its credibility lie? Thought will be of external things, just like sensation, and how will it differ, except by perceiving smaller things? How will it know that it has truly grasped them? How will it know this is good, or beautiful, or just? For each of these is other than itself, and the principles of judgment which it would trust are not in it, but they too are outside, and Truth is there. 

Then, those things would be without sensation and lacking life and mind. Or they have mind. If they have mind, both are together here. And Truth is here, and this is the primary Intellect. And concerning this, we shall seek how the truth in it stands. And the object of thought and the Intellect—if they are together, are they two and different, or how? 

If they are soulless and without sensation, what would they be? Certainly not axioms; nor things said here, for these do not speak of themselves, and are not the beings themselves—for example, "justice is beautiful"—but refer to Justice and Beauty as beings. But if they say simply that Justice and Beauty are separate, first, the object of thought will not be a single thing, but each will be torn apart. And where and in what "place of places" <note>A reference to the concept that the Intellect is the "place of forms."</note> would they be? How then will the Intellect coordinate them while running around? How will it remain? Or how does it remain in the same thing? What form or shape will it have at all, unless they are like golden statues or images made of some other material by a sculptor or painter? But then the Intellect which observes the shape will be sensation. We must investigate how it remains...

Indeed, it must be asked where they are, and in what places they are specifically arranged apart from each other: then, in what way the Intellect, running about everywhere, will reach or find them: and how it will remain in them: likewise how it will persist in the same thing: and furthermore what form and figure they will have at all. Unless perhaps they are like images, even if they are golden, or composed of some other material by some sculptor or painter. But if this were so, the mind containing such things would be sensation. Therefore, by what reason among these...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's argument from the previous page (520). He is refuting the idea that the objects of thought—the "Intelligibles" or Platonic Forms—exist outside of the Divine Intellect. He argues that if they were external, the Intellect would only possess "images" or "copies" of reality, rather than reality itself, leading to a loss of certain truth.</meta>

<header>BOOK FIVE.</header>

...of the first things, justice; but the other is something greater. <note>original Greek: "tōn prōtōn dikaiosunēn." Plotinus is discussing the hierarchy of virtues and forms.</note> One might say this of all of them. For if, as much as possible, one says these things are outside, and the thinking of them involves observing them while they are in their own state, it is necessary that he does not hold the truth, and he has been deceived in all things, as it seems. For the true things themselves are not in each act of contemplation; he does not possess them, but has instead received images of them in such knowledge. Therefore, not possessing the true thing itself, but having received images of the truth within himself, he will possess falsehoods, and nothing true. If he knows that he possesses falsehoods, he will admit he is without a share of truth. But if he is ignorant of this, and thinks he possesses the truth when he does not, he will be doubly deceived, which will distance him far from the truth. For this reason, there is no truth in the senses, but only opinion <note>original Greek: "doxa." This refers to a lower level of belief based on physical appearance rather than intellectual certainty.</note>: because in receiving its objects—which is why it is called opinion—it receives something else, and not that original thing from which it has what it receives. If, therefore, truth is not in the mind, we shall ask: do you believe that truth will exist at all? Or will truth be in something else? But if it is not in the mind, it will not be anywhere.

Thus, it is necessary for those seeking the things of the intellect <note>original Greek: "noēta" – the objects of pure thought or "Intelligibles."</note> not to say that there are mere impressions of things that truly exist, thereby depriving the seeker of truth and creating an ignorance of the Intelligibles and a lack of real existence. Furthermore, they should not accept such a denial of reality; rather, if we are to introduce knowledge and truth among ourselves, and preserve the things that exist, and the knowledge of what each thing *is*—rather than just what *kind* of thing it is—we must not hold them as images or traces. We must possess the things themselves, be present with them, and be united with them, just as the true is one with all things. For in this way, knowledge and truth would be known to us, and the mind would not seek the false, and truth would be in it, and the Ideas <note>original Greek: "ideai." The eternal archetypes or blueprints of reality.</note> would exist among the things that are. Or will the act of thinking seek these things elsewhere? Surely these must exist within the most blessed nature. Otherwise, how will there be anything honorable or venerable? For if it is valued in this way, there is no need for faith that it is so, for it will be itself, clearly manifest to itself. Furthermore, it exists of itself, or what could be after it?
<sig>A</sig>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> This indeed is justice, but that is rather something else. Finally, this is the strongest point of all: for if one utterly admits that these are outside, and that the mind contemplates them as they are, it follows necessarily that the mind does not possess their truth, but is deceived and lies in each thing it contemplates. For the things will truly be external; therefore it will look upon them but will not possess the things themselves, but will possess images of them in a knowledge of that sort. Since, therefore, it does not have the true itself, <margin>B</margin> but holds certain images of the true within itself, it will not accumulate all truths, but will instead report falsehoods. If, then, it knows that it has only falsehoods, it will undoubtedly confess that it is devoid of truth; but if it is ignorant of this, and being without a share of the truth, it nevertheless thinks it is in possession of the truth, it will be deceived by a double lie, and will be very far distant from the truth. For this reason (as I believe) there is no truth in the senses, but only opinion: since the <margin>C</margin> condition of sense consists in "receiving," whence "opinion"—*doxa* in Greek—took its name from "receiving" <note>original Latin: "accipiendo." Plotinus often uses wordplay; here he links "doxa" (opinion) to the verb "dechesthai" (to receive/accept), suggesting that opinion is merely a passive acceptance of outside appearances.</note>. Therefore, it receives something other than itself, since that from which it receives what it possesses is also something else. If, therefore, truth is not in the mind, such a mind will neither be truth, nor truly a mind, nor a mind at all; indeed, truth will not dwell anywhere else either.

### The objects of the intellect are not images of things or certain imaginings, but they truly exist as things: since even the objects of sense are certain things.
### Chapter II.

Because the intellect is more excellent and truer than sense, the objects of the intellect are more excellent and truer than the objects of sense, so that they are archetypes <note>original Greek: "ektupa" – here used to mean the original stamps or models.</note>. The Intelligibles are in the very essence of the intellect, since it does not seek them by arguing, nor does it wander outside, but being established within, it gazes steadily as if possessing them. It penetrates and stays within the very substance of each thing. But through images, you could gather nothing other than qualities and external things.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, one should not search for things to be understood outside the intellect, nor admit that figures of things reside in the mind, nor deprive it of truth. For if we grant that the mind does not know the Intelligibles themselves, and that the things offered to be understood do not exist in the order of reality, we would thus sweep the mind itself away. But it is necessary to attribute all things truly to the mind, if we are to introduce cognition and truth, <margin>B</margin> and preserve the beings themselves, and that knowledge which understands *what* each thing is. We should not be satisfied with that knowledge which merely apprehends what *kind* of thing each is—as happens when we only have a phantom or a trace of the thing to be known. In that case, we do not hold the thing itself, nor do we dwell as one with it, nor do we breathe as one with it. For by that former reasoning, the mind will know, and will know truly; nothing will be hidden from it, nor will it ever forget, nor will it wander about searching everywhere. <margin>C</margin> But truth will be in it, as the seat of things; it will live and it will understand. All these things must be present in the most blessed nature, otherwise where would there be anything to be honored and venerated? Furthermore, by this reasoning, it will not need demonstration, nor will it have to be persuaded by faith that it is so. For it is the Intellect itself which is entirely in this state: it is utterly manifest to itself. And if anything before it is similarly discovered, it is because the Intellect is derived from that; likewise if anything is after it.

<sig>X 3</sig>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the Divine Intellect (Nous). In the preceding text, he argued that truth must be internal to the mind; if the objects of thought were outside the mind, we would only possess "images" of truth, not truth itself. Here, he reinforces that the Intellect is a self-contained reality where the thinker and the thought are one.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK V.

...because he himself is this very thing <note>original: "hoc ipsum" — the object of his own thought</note>, and no one is more worthy of trust regarding himself than he is, and he surely has it confirmed that truth is there and truly exists. In reality, therefore, truth itself dwells there, harmonizing not with another but with itself; it says nothing besides itself, and what it is, that it precisely speaks. Who then could refute it? And from where would a refutation be brought? Indeed, any argument brought forward would lead back to the same point as the previous speaker. And even if something different were introduced, it would still refer back to the first speaker’s premise and be entirely one: for nothing is found to be truer than the truth.

<margin>A</margin>

->*Just as the innermost light of the sun pours out light around itself, filled with innumerable rays and powers, so the principle of all things procreates within itself the all-forming Intellect, and this in turn the all-forming Soul. Chapter III.*<-

->*The ancients called that first principle "Heaven," the second "Saturn," and the last "Jupiter." All intellectual souls are able to ascend through their own intellect to the Divine Intellect. Some can and must proceed to the principle of all things, partly through their own unity and partly through the Divine Intellect. <note>Plotinus uses Greek mythology—Ouranos (Heaven), Cronus (Saturn), and Zeus (Jupiter)—as symbols for his philosophical hierarchy: The One, the Intellect, and the Soul.</note>*<-

Therefore, this single nature of the Intellect is all beings: it is truth: it is a certain great God—indeed, not just any god, but all gods. Nor does it unworthily consider itself to be all these things. This nature is therefore God: a fruitful God, I say, revealing himself to those searching, even before they behold that higher One who surpasses him. For that higher One sits more eminently upon this noble throne that hangs from him. It was not fitting for him to arrive in an inanimate chariot, nor even simply upon living creatures, but for an inestimable beauty to shine forth wonderfully before him, just as before the appearance of a great king. For nature is so arranged that as people approach him, smaller things appear first, and then progressively greater and more excellent things offer themselves to those proceeding further; those standing around the king are more "kingly" <note>original: "regia" — meaning more noble or divine</note>, and the rest follow in a similar order. After all these, the great king himself suddenly shines forth: and the others worship the king as suppliants—those, that is, who did not turn back before reaching the end, but progressed to the very last. Blessed are they who consider what shines before the king to be sufficient. In that place, another king rules, and those who appear before him are certainly different from him. Yet that celestial king does not rule as if over strangers, but holds a most just and natural command, and a true kingdom: since he is the king of truth and is by his own nature the master of his entire offspring and the divine assembly: surely the king of kings and the father of the gods, called by a most just name. Jupiter <note>The World-Soul</note> imitated him in this way as well: he did not rest entirely in the contemplation of his father, but proceeded further toward eternity, as if toward his father’s action in the very subsistence of essence (if I may put it that way).

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>D</margin>

->*The principle of all things, which is called "The One" because of its inestimable simplicity and eminence, has no countable number within itself, nor does it agree with things in any common way. Chapter IIII.*<-

For if there were any condition common to this and any other thing, two absurdities would follow. First, that this principle would be composed of that common condi—

<column-break/>

...because he himself, and no one else, is more trustworthy than he is about himself; and because there is luck and reality, and the "really real" truth <note>original Greek: "hē ontōs alētheia"</note>, which does not harmonize with another, but with itself. It says nothing else besides itself, and it is what it is, and what it is, it says. Who then could refute it? And how could a refutation be brought by one who is passing by, and bring something else to the precipice? Thus the hypothesis remains the same from the beginning. And you would find nothing truer than the true.

This one nature for us, then, is Intellect: it is all beings, it is Truth. Or it is a great god—rather, not just "a" god, but "all"—worthy of being these things. And this nature is God: a second God <note>original Greek: "theos deuteros" — the Intellect is the second "person" of the Plotinian trinity</note> making himself visible before one sees the One beyond. He sits and is established upon a beautiful base <note>original Greek: "krēpidos" — like the pedestal of a statue</note> that is hung from the One. For it was necessary that He, in his walking, should not tread upon something inanimate, nor immediately upon a soul, but that there should be an unimaginable beauty proceeding before him, just as before a great king there go the footmen and the lesser ones, and then the greater and more solemn ones after them, and those already around the king, who are more kingly. After all these, the Great King himself suddenly appears, and the others pray and fall down—those who did not depart before him, having been satisfied with the sight before the king. There, then, the King is someone else, and those who appeared after him are different; and even there he is a King, not ruling over strangers, but having the most just and natural rule and the true kingdom, because he is King of Truth. He is lord by nature and truly lord of his own offspring and the divine system. He is the king of kings and of kings, and might more justly be called the Father of the Gods. Indeed, Jupiter imitated him in this respect, not being satisfied with the contemplation of his father <note>Cronus/Intellect</note>, but reaching toward the "outside" of his father, as if toward the activity for the existence of essence.

<summary>This page describes the Divine Intellect as a "Second God" containing all truths and beings, acting as a majestic gateway to the ultimate "King" or "The One." Plotinus uses the metaphor of a royal procession to explain how a seeker must pass through beauty and intellect to reach the highest principle of unity.</summary>

--- Page 558 ---
<meta>This page transitions from discussing the Divine Intellect (Nous) to the ultimate source of all reality: The One. While the previous page established that the Intellect is the realm of true being where thought and object are unified, Plotinus now argues that even the Intellect has a form of multiplicity. To find the absolute beginning, one must ascend further to a unity that is entirely simple and beyond all number.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

...composed by its own condition and its own particular property. According to this, the common nature itself is superior, being simpler and more universal. Furthermore, it does not contain within itself an "essential number" <note>original: "numerum essentialem" — a concept Plotinus uses to describe the structured multiplicity within the Divine Intellect</note>, such as Plotinus devises in the first essence—namely, a multitude of formal principles <note>original: "rationum formalium" — the blueprints or 'Ideas' of things</note> that are absolutely distinct from one another even without an act of understanding. Nor does it contain within itself number as understood in the category of quantity: for number pertaining to quantity, which consists of individual units, is reduced back to the One itself, the proper principle of quantity, which is higher than any specific number. Finally, he likewise reduces the number of essential forms to the essential One, and this, ultimately, to the One that is simply and absolutely itself.

---

<column-break/>

Since we must, therefore, make an ascent toward that which is truly One, and not merely "one" in the way other things are—which, being many in themselves, only participate in oneness—we must not take the One as something shared, nor as something that is more "one" than it is "many." While the intelligible world and the Intellect are indeed more "one" than other things, and nothing is closer to the One than they are, they are still not the pure One itself. Since all things, through their own nature, tend toward unity, and since they exist as they do because they have emerged from it, we must therefore lead ourselves toward it. We must add nothing to it, but place it entirely apart, fearing that if we add even the slightest thing, we might fall away from it. For if you do not do this <margin>* on the phrase "you have two" *</margin>, you will have "two" instead of "one." And if you have two, you do not have the One, but both together. For if we wish to grasp that which is beyond, we must have no hope in any further substance <note>original: "hypostasis"</note>. It is not a number at all, nor a measure; it is not the same as those things which participate in it, nor is it equal to others so as to be counted among them. If it were, those things would still depend on it, and it would be one of the things being numbered. But it is nothing of the sort. And if there is <margin>* but of what kind? </margin> an "essential number" existing by itself, there is also a secondary number following it, which is the number of quantities. The essential number belongs to the act of thinking, providing existence and being. But the quantitative number is that which encompasses "how many" things there are with others, or it imitates others. If, then, number exists there, it is either as a quantity or a count. But the One is not counted among them, for it is the nature that precedes all odd numbers. It is not analogous to the One found in numbers, nor do things divide it up or possess it in such a way; rather, it is only when the "dyad" <note>the number two, or the principle of duality</note> arises that the "monad" <note>the principle of unity or the number one</note> exists before it. And we give it the name "monad" only because we have no better word. Why then should it be more like this or that? If it is neither of these, but that which is beyond, the One remains as it is. How then are those others different? And how is the dyad? Is it not because the same "one" which is in each is the "auto-monad" <note>the Monad itself</note>, or does it participate in the first? We say that it is that by which it participates, but not in the same way.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **ENOUGH** has now been said regarding the fact that we must finally ascend to the One itself, which is truly one, and not one like other things which, though they are many in themselves, are one only by participation in the One. For the One itself must be understood as that which does not become one by participation, as is the case with things that are no more "one" than they are "many." It has also been said that the intelligible world and the intellect are more "one" than all other things, and that nothing is closer to the One than these: yet even they have not existed as purely one until now. <margin>B</margin> At present, however, we desire to contemplate, if we are able, what that pure and true One actually is: that which is one not according to something else, but according to itself. It is worthwhile, therefore, to transfer ourselves entirely to the One itself: and to add nothing further to it, but to rest completely within it, taking total care lest we depart from it by even the smallest distance, and thereby fall from the One into <margin>C</margin> "two." If you do not take this care, you will immediately bring back two, and you will not have the One itself within those two: for both are posterior to the One. For the One does not stand together with any other thing—whether with one other or with however many others one might wish to count it—nor does it allow itself to be numbered at all. For it is the measure itself, and not at all the thing measured. Nor is it equal to any other things, such that it might agree with them in some way; otherwise, there would be something common within it, and simultaneously within those things that are numbered with it, <margin>D</margin> and that common element would be superior to the One, even though nothing can be superior to it. Accordingly, neither "essential number" nor the number that follows it—which properly pertains to quantity—can be predicated of the One. Neither, I say, the essential number (which, by the fact that it is spoken, always shows "to understand" to be "to be"), nor that which looks to quantity (which embraces quantity together with other things). Nor can it be predicated even if it does not run together with other categories, since this is number itself. <margin>E</margin> Since the nature inherent in quantitative number imitates the nature instilled in the prior numbers—which look toward the truly One—it undoubtedly seeks substance for itself by looking similarly toward the one principle of numbers.

---

It claims this substance for itself, neither destroying it nor dividing it anywhere; indeed, even when the "binary" <note>the number two</note> has already arisen, the "unity" <note>the monad</note> itself still stands before the binary. Neither the two units encompassed by the binary, nor either one of them individually, is the "Unity itself." For why should the binary be Unity itself? Or why should one unit of the binary be Unity itself rather than the other? If, therefore, neither both together nor either one alone is Unity itself, then certainly the Unity which is the origin of the whole number is different from all these; and truly, while remaining in its own way, it also seems not to remain. In what way, then, are those other units different from it? And in what way is "duality" <note>the state of being two</note> somehow one? And is it the same "one" that is preserved in each encompassed unit? Perhaps it should be said that both units are participants in the first Unity, but are different from that in which they participate; and that duality, insofar as it is a certain "one thing," is a participant in Unity itself, though not in the same way everywhere.

<summary>This page discusses the philosophical ascent to 'The One,' the absolute source of reality that precedes all multiplicity, including the Divine Intellect and the concept of number. It distinguishes between the pure One and things that merely 'participate' in oneness, cautioning that adding any attributes to the One causes it to fall into duality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the nature of the One as the absolute source of all things. Having established that the Intellect contains multiplicity, Plotinus now explores how "Being" and "Essence" are derived from the One, using both logical analogies and linguistic analysis of Greek terms.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin>Indeed, an army and a house are not "one" in the same way. In these cases, the reasoning is applied to things that happen to be joined together, neither regarding their existence as one thing, nor regarding their quantity as a single unit. Is it not true, then, that the units found in the number five relate to the "one" differently than those in the number ten? Yet, is the "one" itself that is within the five exactly the same as the "one" within the ten? Perhaps if a certain small ship were compared to another large one, or a city to a city, or an army to an army, the "one" in these would also be the same. But if it is not the same there, it is not the same here either. If any remaining doubts about these matters persist, they will be resolved in the following sections.

---

### Chapter VI. That being, essence, and "to-be" proceed from the One itself, as even the Greek name declares, following the nature of the thing itself.

*One might think of "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> as a kind of composite or a duality, in which there is both "essence" <note>original: "essentia"</note> and the act of "to-be" <note>original: "esse"</note>; and that which is "to-be" is called the act of "essence." Therefore, being, having been born from the One, possesses "essence" as a kind of shadow of the One, but "to-be" as an image of the One. Because the One itself is above being—that is, beyond the property of being—it expands its power into being, and thus being was made like matter <note>Plotinus often describes the first stage of "Being" as "Intelligible Matter" before it is fully formed by the One's light</note>. And because of the extreme lack of forms, it is said to be "not-nothing," and afterwards it is called "one." For matter in the world is not a single thing due to a lack of total formlessness. It may even be deceptive to say that any deprivation of the "one" is more "one" than a "habit" or possession; yet a deprivation is judged to be less than a habit. But we have discussed these things elsewhere.*

---

<margin>A</margin>But we must return to that first point: our assertion that the One remains always the same, even though all other things flow forth from it. In the case of numbers, while the "one" remains, a number is created according to it by the action of another. But in that which is above all beings, the One itself remains much more firmly. While it remains, it is not some other thing that makes beings according to it; for the One is sufficient by itself for the making of beings. <margin>B</margin>And just as in numbers, the specific form of the "unit"—the principle of numbers—is preserved in all things in a first and second degree (for the subsequent numbers do not participate in the unit equally), so also in the order of things, each subsequent thing has in itself something of that First Principle reflecting its face. In numbers, the participation in the unit produces quantity. Here, however, the trace of the One itself establishes "essence" <note>original: "essentiam"</note> in things, so much so that "to-be" <note>original: "esse"</note> itself is a trace of the One. <margin>C</margin>Whence, if one were to say that <term>to-be</term> <note>original: "ine", referring to the Greek "einai" (εἶναι)</note>—which is the name declaring <term>essence</term> <note>original: "vsiam", referring to the Greek "ousia" (οὐσία)</note>—is derived from the word <term>one</term> <note>original: "en", referring to the Greek "hen" (ἕν)</note>, he would perhaps not wander from the truth. <margin>D</margin>Furthermore, that which is called <term>being</term> <note>original: "on", referring to the Greek "on" (ὄν)</note> is surely the first thing shining forth from there; and as if not venturing far, it did not wish to proceed further, but turned back toward the interior and stood firm. There, where essence was already made, it displays itself shining in sound and contains itself. Thus was born the term <term>one-being</term> <note>original: "no en", a play on "noein" (to think) and "hen" (one)</note>, declaring by its very pronunciation that it flows from the One itself. Certainly, the word <term>being</term> <note>original: "on"</note> pronounced in this way signifies that very thing as much as it can. Thus, what was made as <term>essence</term> <note>original: "vsia"</note> and <term>to-be</term> <note>original: "ine"</note> imitates the Author according to their strength, flowing from his power. The Mind, noticing these things and led by the spectacle itself, imitating what it knew, suddenly brought forth voices of this kind: <term>being</term>, <term>to-be</term>, <term>essence</term>, and <term>hearth</term> <note>original: "ethian", referring to "hestia" (ἑστία), which sounds like "ousia" and implies the "staying" or "hearth" of reality</note>. For these sounds attempt to express the substance that has been brought forth, with the speaker striving toward that goal, imitating as much as possible the origin of being itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Since an army and a house are not one in the same way, let the continuity still be preserved according to their being one, if anything is one according to the whole. Are the units in the five and the ten the same? Or is the "one" in the five the same as the "one" in the ten? If we say it is the same for all things, then it is the same for a large thing, and a city compared to a city, and <margin>B</margin>an army compared to an army. Is it the same there? If not even there, then not here either. If there are any difficulties about these things, they will be addressed later.

<margin>A</margin>But we must return to that point: they say the First remains the same, and other things come from it, until the whole number remains. It remains, but while another stumbles, the number is made according to it. In that which is always before beings, Being remains much more; while it remains, it does not make another, even if it is Being itself. But just as beings themselves are made, or as <margin>B</margin>in the case of numbers, the first part of the unit is in the things that follow, either primarily or secondarily, or even equally in each—by the rule of it—so if it is established that each participates after the First and has something of it, so it is in that case as well. And there, participation established their quantity. Here, the trace of the One established their essence, so that "to-be" is a trace of being. And "to-be" is the primary naming of essence, so that if one were to say it has come from "one," he might hit upon the truth. For that which is called "being" is the first thing from there, as if having proceeded only a little; it did not wish to rewrite itself by going further, but established essence within. And still seeking, as if the sounds were making it sober by the voice, Being stands. It reveals what comes from the One; and the spoken word signifies it as it is able. All things—essence and to-be—have been made as an imitation, going forth from its power. And the Mind, seeing and being moved by the sight, imitating what it saw, broke out into the voice: "being," "to-be," "essence," and "hearth." For the sounds signify the underlying reality, having generated the spoken words themselves. They have imitated, as far as they are able, the generation of being.

<summary>Plotinus explains that all levels of reality, specifically "Being" and "Essence," are imitations or "traces" of the One. He uses the Greek language to argue that the very words for existence were created by the Mind to reflect their origin in the One.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "One," the absolute and simple source of all existence. Having previously discussed how multiplicity arises, he now explains why the One must be "beyond being" and "beyond form," and why human language—and even the name "the One"—is ultimately inadequate to describe it.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

-> *Since by using the terms "form" or "essence," you are conceiving and defining something through the intellect, know that this is not the true Principle; for the Principle cannot be comprehended in any way. Chapter VI.* <-

The name "the One" or "unity" was introduced by the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who emphasized numbers as the fundamental reality of the universe.</note> to describe, as best they could, the simplicity and transcendence of the source of all things. They did this by denying it had any multiplicity, composition, or even any definition. They were not asserting a specific quality of the Principle, a point they confirmed by using the name "Apollo." Just as the world we see with our eyes has a relationship to our physical senses, the world of ideas <note>original: "intelligibile"</note> has a relationship to our intellect. Therefore, the source of all things, which has no such direct relationship to the intellect, stands above the world of ideas; it is, then, superior to being <note>original: "ente"</note> itself.

***

<margin>A</margin> But let these things be accepted as anyone pleases. However, since the generated essence is a form <note>original: "species"</note>—for no one would call anything else that is born from that source by any other name—and let us say it is not just *a* form, but *every* form, such that no other form is left out, it is necessary that the One itself has no form. Since it is foreign to form, it cannot even be "essence"; for essence must be "this specific thing" <note>original: "hoc aliquid," referring to an individual, defined entity</note>.
<margin>B</margin> But that which is "this thing" is already determined, whereas one cannot think of the One as "this thing"; otherwise, it would no longer be the Principle, but only that which you called "this thing." If, therefore, all things are contained in that which is born from the One, you will say that none of the things within that derivative are truly the Author of all. Since none of these things exist in the Principle at all, it can only be said to be that which exists above them. These things are beings and "being" itself; therefore, that Principle is superior to being. Now, that which is superior to being does not say "this is something"; for it does not posit anything,
<margin>* Being</margin>
<margin>C</margin> nor does it speak its own name. Rather, it only offers this: "not this." In doing so, the mind never fully grasps it; for it is ridiculous to try to embrace that immense nature. Anyone who attempts this removes themselves even further from even the smallest footprint <note>original: "vestigio"</note> of it. Truly, just as we desire to know the intelligible nature, we only come to know what is above the world of the senses when we hold no physical image of a thing in our minds.
<margin>D</margin> So too, he who desires to contemplate the nature superior to the intelligible nature will behold it if he sets aside all that can be understood—learning through this process that it exists, while letting go of the question of *what* it is like. For the word "what" <note>original: "quale," referring to quality</note> actually signifies "not what," because that which does not possess what we usually call "something" <note>original: "quid"</note> does not fit what we usually call "of such a kind." But we, struggling with the narrowness of our minds—like a person in the pains of labor—do not know what is most appropriate to say.
<margin>E</margin> And so we speak and give names to that which cannot be spoken, attempting to signify something to ourselves as best we can. Perhaps even this name, "the One," signifies a denial of multiplicity and an elevation above it, by comparison to the many. For this reason, the Pythagoreans also called it "Apollo" among themselves with a more secret meaning—specifically, the negation of the many <note>A famous Neopythagorean etymology: *a-pollon*, interpreted as "not-many" (Greek: *a* = not, *polloi* = many).</note>. But if this name "One" were to posit and affirm something in its meaning, both the name and the thing named would be more obscure than if one did not discuss its name at all. For perhaps that name was given so that the seeker, starting from that which best signifies simplicity, might eventually reach the point where he denies even this name, as if it were the best a namer could provide, yet still not worthy to describe that nature.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But let these things be accepted as anyone pleases. When, however, the generated essence is a form, for no one would call anything else that is produced from there by any other name: let it be, I say, not a certain form, but every form, so that nothing else of form remains, it is necessary that the One itself does not have a form. Since it is far from form, it cannot even be essence: for essence must be this something: but that is already determined, while that one is not permitted to be thought of 
<margin>B</margin> as "this something": otherwise it would not now be the principle, but only that which you were calling "this something." If, therefore, in that which is generated from it all things are present, you will say that nothing of those things which are in this itself is truly the author of all. And since nothing of these is there at all, it can only be said to be that which exists above these. These, however, are beings and being itself: that, therefore, is superior to being. Now, truly, that which is superior to being does not say "this something": for it does not posit anything, 
<margin>C</margin> nor does it say its name, but it brings forward only this itself, namely "not this." But the one doing that nowhere comprehends it: for it is ridiculous to strive to embrace that immense nature. Whoever, moreover, strives for it, removes himself very far from even the smallest vestige of it: certainly, just as we desire to know the intelligible nature, then finally he will know what is above the sensible genus, when he holds absolutely no image of a thing to be sensed. So 
<margin>D</margin> also he who desires to contemplate the nature superior to the intelligible nature, if only he dismisses everything to be understood, he will contemplate it: through this, I say, learning that it exists: but entirely dismissing what kind it might be. This itself, however, which is called "what kind," signifies in truth "not what kind," for in that which what we are accustomed to call "what" does not exist, neither is it fitting that we should call it "what kind." But we, laboring in our narrowness like someone in labor, 
<margin>E</margin> do not know what it is most fitting to say: and concerning that which cannot be said, we speak and we name, affecting something to ourselves that we can signify. Perhaps indeed also this name which is called "one," through a certain respect to the many, signifies negation and elevation. Wherefore the Pythagoreans also named it Apollo among themselves with a certain more secret significance, namely by the negation of the many. If, however, this name "one" by its significance posits and affirms something, then both the name and the thing named will be more obscure than if someone does not discuss its name at all: for perhaps that name was said so that the seeker, beginning from that which can signify simplicity most of all, may finally arrive there, so as to deny this very thing further, as if it were imposed as well as it could be by the namer: yet nevertheless even this is not worthy by which that nature may be signified.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the "One" is the absolute principle above being and intellect, and that human language, including the names "One" or "Apollo," can only describe it through negation rather than affirmation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion of the "One" or the "First Principle." Having established that the One is beyond form and essence, Plotinus now uses the analogy of light and the eye to explain how the human Intellect (Mind) can experience this ultimate source, even though it cannot be grasped like a normal object of knowledge.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS V.

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, that Principle cannot be reached by hearing, nor can it be understood by anyone who merely listens to words about it. But if it can be revealed to anyone, it happens instead to the one who gazes upon it. Yet, if the observer tries to look at it as if it were a specific "form" <note>original: "speciem" / "eidos". In Neoplatonism, a "form" is a defined, limited idea or object of thought.</note>, they will not see it as a form.

*Just as through light itself the eye is made sharp-sighted and colors are made visible—in which the eye sees the light, though it does not see the light in its pure state—so through the First Principle, the Mind <note>original: "mens" / "nous". This refers to the higher "Intellect," the part of the soul capable of divine contemplation.</note> is able to understand, and truths exist by the act of understanding. In these truths, the Mind understands the light of the Principle itself, though it does not understand the Principle in its own pure state.*

### Chapter VII.

*However, the Mind can withdraw its attention from individual truths and turn it toward the light of the Principle, by which these truths exist and by which the Mind itself understands. In this way, it may enjoy that light. Similarly, if a person calls back their will from loving individual "good things" to loving the Good itself—by which they are a lover and by which those things are lovable—they will immediately enjoy the Good itself, resulting in a certain extraordinary joy.*

<margin>B</margin> ACCORDINGLY, there are two ways of seeing in action, just as occurs with the eye. Certainly, one thing the eye sees is the object itself—the visible forms of things we sense. But another thing is that through which it sees the form; this medium is also sensible to the eye, yet it is different from the form itself. It is the cause by which the form is perceived, existing within the form and seen along with it. For this reason, the light itself is not seen very clearly then, because the eye directs itself more intently toward the illuminated object. 

When, however, there is nothing else besides the light itself, the eye will see it suddenly in a single, total gaze, although even then it perceives the light as something attached to another thing. But if the light were alone, joined to nothing at all, the senses could not grasp it; for the light of the sun, residing in the sun itself, would perhaps escape our senses unless the more solid mass of the sun were placed beneath it. If someone were to say that the sun is entirely light, one might accept this as an explanation of what is being discussed; <margin>C</margin> for that light would be in no other form of the things that are seen, and would perhaps be only "visible" and "radiant," whereas other visible things are not purely light.

In a similar way, the Mind's vision sees the illuminated objects of that First Nature <note>The One or the Good.</note> through another light, and in those objects it truly sees that light. Nevertheless, by turning itself more urgently toward the nature of the illuminated things, it sees the light itself less in the meantime. But if it should eventually let go of the things it sees, and look attentively at that light through which it sees, <margin>D</margin> it will then foresee the light itself and the source of that light. 

But since the Mind must not look at this kind of light as something external, let us return again to the example of the eye, which sometimes does not see an external or foreign light, but before seeing external light, perceives something of its own. It sees a brighter light shining in a certain pure and untouched place, or in the darkness of night it sees a certain ray <margin>E</margin> leaping out from within itself. Or perhaps when it wishes to see nothing of other things, it closes itself with the covering of the eyelids and meanwhile brings forth light from within itself; or when one presses the corners of the eyelids and sees the light that was hiding inside. In that moment, by not seeing, it sees, and then it sees most of all: for it sees light. The other things it had seen before were indeed bright, but they were not light itself. 

So it is with the Mind: by separating and closing itself off from other things and retreating into its interior, seeing nothing, it suddenly beholds the light—not one light within another, <margin>F</margin> but the light itself, alone, pure, and flashing out from itself.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the original Greek text for the section translated above.</note>

...that it is not by hearing, nor must the one who hears understand it to be so. But if it is permitted for anyone to see, but if the one seeing seeks to see a form, they will not see it as that which is sought.

Or since seeing in activity is twofold, as with the eye: for one is a vision for it, the form of the sensible object. The other is its own form, which is also sensible to it, being different from the form; it was the cause for the form to be seen, being viewed upon the form and in the form, wherefore it does not provide clear perception to it, as the focus is always strained toward the illuminated thing. But when there is nothing else besides it, then by a sudden focus... and besides the external thing, something else held by another; let it remain stripped in itself, not toward another, if it is possible to receive some perception. Since even the light in the sun, that which is in itself, might perhaps escape perception, unless its mass were more solid. If someone were to say that it is all light, taken from what comes from it for an explanation of what is said, for it will be light, which saw none of the other things seen, and perhaps vision alone; but the other visible things are that which is light alone. In the same way then, the vision of the mind also sees the things illuminated by the first nature through another light and sees those things in them; consider for me some of the natures of the things shone upon, seeing it less, but if it lets go of the things seen, and into that which it looks, it looks into itself, it would see light and the principle of light. But since not as if from outside, the mind must see a certain light, let us go again to the eye, which once also will see not the outside light, nor the alien one; but before the outside, some personal thing, and rather brilliant in itself... or at night in the dark, from itself leaping out, or when wishing to see none of the others, it wraps the things around it, by the nature of the eyelids, yet carrying the light around, or even pressing them... sees the light in itself. For then not seeing it sees, and especially then it sees; for it sees light. But the others were luminous, but were not light. Thus indeed the mind also, having covered itself from the others, and having gathered into the inside seeing nothing, will behold not another light in another, but it alone by itself, pure upon itself suddenly appearing.

<summary>Plotinus uses the analogy of physical sight to explain how the Mind can perceive the One. Just as the eye sees objects through light but can focus on the light itself, the Mind can turn away from specific truths to experience the pure, internal radiance of the First Principle.</summary>

--- Page 562 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of how the human Intellect (Mind) experiences the "One" or the "First Principle." Having previously established that the Principle is like a light that makes all things visible, the text now explains the "arrival" of this divine light—which is not a physical movement, but a change in the soul's awareness.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE

*Expel three things from the soul: motion, multiplicity, and determination—specifically that through which the soul commits itself to a certain fixed thing, whether by thinking or by desiring. Chapter VIII.*

*Immediately the soul, having been made close to the immobile, simple, and absolute principle, is filled with a new light from that same source; soon it notices that it has suddenly and wonderfully become more beautiful. It perceives this light of new beauty as something deep within, which comes to it from the principle, where it also recognizes the light as something coming from the outside.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If this is the case, it might happen that one wonders from where this light shines: whether from something outside, or rather from within. And when it has departed, one might say: “This was something deep inside,” and then again, “No, it was not inside.” But truly, one should not ask from where it comes, for there is no "where" <note>original: "unde". In the realm of the One, there is no space or location.</note> involved. It does not "approach" us, nor does it "depart" from here to another place, but it either appears to us or it does not appear. Therefore, one ought not to chase after it, but rather to wait in quiet until it shines upon us, <margin>B</margin> preparing ourselves to be spectators of that sight, just as the eye waits for the rising of the sun. The sun, rising above the horizon—as the poets say, emerging from the Ocean—offers itself to the eyes to be seen. 

But this one—this one, I say, whom the physical sun only imitates—from where will he shine from above? What will he transcend to glow clearly for us? Truly, he will illuminate the Mind <note>original: "Intellectus" / "Nous"</note> that looks up toward him. The Intellect, therefore, will hold itself steady in that gaze, looking at nothing else but the Beautiful itself, turning its whole self toward that light and dedicating itself entirely to it. <margin>C</margin> Standing still and as if filled with divine vigor, the Intellect first sees that it has itself been made more beautiful and is now glowing, since it is now very close to the Highest. 

God <note>original: "Deus". Plotinus and his translator Ficino use "God," "The One," and "The Good" interchangeably to describe the ultimate source of all reality.</note> does not "approach" in the way someone might expect, but comes as if not coming. He appears not as one arriving, but as one who was present before all things, even before the Intellect arrived. It is the Intellect that is properly the thing that arrives and departs. The Intellect departs when it does not know where it should remain, or where the Principle <margin>D</margin> stays. For in truth, the Principle remains in nothing. If the Intellect could also be "nowhere"—I mean, not just in a specific place—it would undoubtedly always behold the Principle. Even then, it would not behold it as a separate thing, but would reach it by remaining within it; and even that would not be as two separate beings. 

But now, because it is the Intellect, it seems to "see" when it looks, specifically because the Principle is not within the Intellect. And indeed, it is a wonder how the Principle is present without "approaching," and how, while it exists, it is nowhere, and yet for that very reason, it is everywhere. <margin>E</margin> It is natural to marvel at this because of its unique condition; but for one who has truly known the reality of it, it would be more of a wonder if the opposite were said. In fact, it cannot be any other way, even if one were to wonder at it most vehemently; this is simply how it is.

---

*Since all things depend on God, but he depends on none, all things are in him, but he is in no thing: he contains all, and is not contained. Chapter IX.*

*Because he is contained by nothing, he is nowhere; but because he contains all things, he is present to all. Thus the body of the world is in the Soul of the World; the Soul is in the Mind; and the Mind is in the Good—but not the other way around. Therefore, just as the soul is present to every individual part of the body at once as a free agent, so the Good, which is absolute and free from all limits, is present to all. In general, whatever does not depend on a specific subject or place or a specific nature for its existence is everywhere and nowhere, just like the soul, the mind, and God.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Whatever is made by another is either in its author, or in some other thing, if there is anything else besides the author. For since it is made by another and requires another for its birth, it surely requires another everywhere; therefore, it finds its rest in another.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the divine light of the One is experienced by the Mind not through movement or searching, but through quiet preparation and internal beauty. He establishes that God (the One) is "nowhere" because he is not contained by anything, but "everywhere" because all things depend on him for their existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the "One" (the First Principle). Having previously discussed how the soul waits for the light of the One like an eye waiting for the sunrise, the text now shifts to a metaphysical explanation of how this Principle contains all of reality without being contained by it.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> So it is arranged by nature that the last things are always found within the second-to-last; and these, in turn, are within those that come before them, one thing always being within another, until one reaches the highest point. But the highest principle <note>original: "summum vero principium". This refers to 'the One,' the source of all existence in Plotinus's philosophy.</note>, because nothing stands above it, cannot be inside anything else. Since it is not in another, yet all other things are within those superior to them, it follows that the Principle itself encompasses all remaining things. Though it encompasses them, it is not scattered among them; it possesses them without being possessed by them. And truly, since it possesses them and is not possessed, there is no place <margin>B</margin> <unclear>where it is not</unclear> present. For if it were not present, it would not possess them; and yet, if it is not possessed, it is not "present" in the sense of being contained. It is therefore present and yet not present: it is not present insofar as it cannot be grasped or confined, but because it is free from all things, it is never forbidden from being present anywhere. If it were restricted, it would surely be defined by something else, and the things that follow would be left without its influence. Then God would only rule up to that point, <margin>C</margin> and he would no longer exist within himself, but would instead be a servant to those things outside him. 

Whatever things exist within something else are properly under the jurisdiction of that container. But things that are not "somewhere" in a limited sense are such that there is nowhere they are not. For if a thing is not *here*, it must be encompassed by some other location, and thus it would be "somewhere" after all. Therefore, if it is true that the Principle is not "somewhere," and false that it is limited to a "somewhere"—lest it be trapped in another—then it is clearly absent from nowhere. <margin>D</margin> If it is absent from nothing, yet does not exist in a specific place, it must be everywhere within itself. For it is not as if one part of it is here and another part there, nor is the whole of it only in one spot; rather, the whole must be everywhere. Since it has no specific <unclear>place</unclear> and yet is not absent, it relates to reality in such a way that it possesses it rather than being possessed. Now, consider this world: if there is no other world above it, this world is not "in a world," nor is it in a place. For what place could exist <margin>E</margin> before the world itself? The parts of the world are brought back to it and located within it. But the Soul is not in the world; rather, the world is in the Soul. The body is not a "place" for the soul; rather, the Soul is in the Mind <note>original: "Mens". Here referring to 'Nous' or the Divine Intellect, the second level of reality below the One.</note>, and the body is in the Soul. Finally, the Mind exists in that Other [the One], which does not depend on anything else. Therefore, the Mind rests in nothing else, and in this sense, it is said to be "nowhere." Where, then, are all other things? Doubtless, they are in the Mind. Thus, the Principle is neither absent from things nor is it "in" them; nothing possesses it, yet it contains all things. For this reason, it is judged to be the Good of all: because all things exist through it and are referred back to it. They are referred back in different ways; thus, some things are better than others, because some are closer to it than others.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is the nature of things that the lowest are in those just above them, and those before them are in their own superiors, one in another, until one comes to the First. But that which has nothing before it has nowhere to be. Not being in another, yet the others being in it, it encompasses all things within itself. Having encompassed them, it is not divided among them; it possesses them without being possessed. For it does not remain fixed [as a contained object], but they have it without "having" it [holding it]. <margin>B</margin> There is nowhere it is not. If it were not there, it would not hold them. If it is not held, it is not there; thus it both is and is not. It is not there in the sense of being contained, but because it is free to be in all things, it is nowhere excluded. For if it were hindered, it would be limited, and the things below it would have no share in it. And God would go only so far; he would not be in himself but would be a servant to those after him. Therefore, things in something <margin>C</margin> are there and belong to it. But that which is not "somewhere" is nowhere not present. If it is nowhere [in a specific spot], it is clearly everywhere. Just as it is nowhere not present, so it is not these things themselves, so that "somewhere" is a false description. If "somewhere" is not true, then "anywhere" is also false, lest it be in another... <unclear>it would never arrive</unclear>... and it has been shown to be of nothing... perhaps one might say it is in itself. But not in the sense that one part is here and another there, <margin>D</margin> nor is the whole just here. Thus the whole is everywhere, with no single thing holding it, yet not failing to be held, for we have it without holding it. Look at the world: since there was no world before it, it is not in a world. Nor is it in a place, for there was no place before the world. But its parts are hung upon it. And the body is in the soul, <margin>E</margin> not the soul in the body. But the soul is not in the body's [limitations], but the soul is greater... so in this way, in this stability, how are other things not in it? Therefore it does not stand apart from others, nor is it in them; there is nothing that has it, but it has all things. For this reason, it is the Good of all, because all things exist and are suspended from it, though in different ways. Thus some things are better than others, because some are more [connected] than others.

---

*Composite things are resolved into simple ones: many simple things are resolved into one most simple thing, and this into Simplicity itself. If you ever grasp this Simplicity, you will not receive any single part of it; for it has no parts. Nor will you grasp it by a total reasoning of your own, for then you would be equal to it.*

->Chapter X.<-

*You will grasp it, though not under every aspect, but according to a certain reason and power. You will perceive it through a single and most simple act, whatever and however much you are to perceive. For God himself meets the soul all at once in a single moment, and if you use any composition <note>original: "compositione". Using complex or step-by-step logic rather than direct, simple intuition.</note> in your perceiving, you will immediately separate yourself from that Simplicity.*

<sig>V b</sig>

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic hierarchy of existence, explaining how the First Principle (the One) contains all of reality (Mind, Soul, and Body) without being limited or contained by any of them. It emphasizes that the One is "everywhere and nowhere," serving as the source and "Good" that sustains all things.</summary>
