<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the "One" (the First Principle). Having previously discussed how the soul waits for the light of the One like an eye waiting for the sunrise, the text now shifts to a metaphysical explanation of how this Principle contains all of reality without being contained by it.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

<margin>A</margin> But I pray you, do not look at God through other things; otherwise, know that you will find not God, but His footprint. Rather, reflect within yourself what this might be: something that can only be perceived as standing within itself, pure and unmixed. While all things certainly participate in it, it possesses none of them <note>original: "nihil tamen id habet". The One is the source of all qualities but is not defined by any of them.</note>. Truly, nothing else can be such a thing, and it is undoubtedly necessary that such a thing exists.

<margin>B</margin> Who, then, can grasp all His power at once? For if one could grasp it all at once, in what way would he be considered different from Him? Does he then receive it part by part? No, but you, looking at Him, contemplate Him with a single, total, and unique strike of the mind <note>original: "ictu quodam toto simul & vnico". This describes an intuitive flash of understanding rather than step-by-step logic.</note>. Yet you will not be able to report back the whole to yourself; otherwise, you would be the Intellect <term>Intellect (Nous): the second level of reality in Neoplatonism, representing the realm of pure thought and forms</term> itself, if you were to achieve that. God would immediately escape you; or rather, you would escape God. But when you look, see the whole. And as soon as you have understood Him, whatever you have preserved in memory,

<margin>C</margin> remember that it is the Good itself. For He is the cause of the wise and intellectual life. Since He is the very power from which life and intellect are born, He is surely the author of essence and being, because He is the One itself. He is simple and the first, since He is the Beginning <note>original: "principium", translating the Greek "arche".</note>. For from Him all things flow: from Him the first movement arises, yet it is not in Him. From Him also comes stability, since He Himself lacks nothing. For He neither moves nor rests, as He has nothing in which to 

<margin>D</margin> rest, and nothing in which to revolve. For around what, or toward what, or in what would He primarily move or rest? For He is the First. But He cannot be defined; otherwise, by whom could He be defined? Nor, again, is He infinite in the way an immense mass would be imagined <note>original: "ut immensa moles". Plotinus distinguishes between "infinite size" (which is material) and "infinite power" (which is divine).</note>. For where should He proceed? If He were said to proceed, would it be to bring something back to Himself, He who lacks absolutely nothing? The power itself possesses infinity: He is not infinite in any other way, nor is He ever different, nor will He ever fail; since whatever things do not fail, they have this very quality properly from Him.

<column-break/>

### The first principle, on account of its inestimable simplicity and eminence, by which it is called the One, is limited neither from without nor from within.
### Chapter XI.

> It neither rests nor moves, nor has figure or form. It is infinite in power, not in quantity. Those who think bodies are the most real because of their size are mistaken. For because of that same size, one can learn that a body is never the "whole" itself: neither this part nor that part is the entirety. One can also say infinitely that this part in this thing is small, and that part is small. Therefore, a body is not infinite in itself, and is actually infinitely small. Finally, we distrust the truth of separated things because of too much commerce with matter; souls indeed dream in this body, but are awake outside of it.

<margin>A</margin> And this infinite <note>Greek: "ἄπειρον" (apeiron)</note> is called infinite because it is no more than one, nor does it have anything to which any of its parts might be limited. Truly, from the fact that it is One <note>Greek: "ἕν" (hen)</note>, it is not measured, nor does it proceed into number; therefore it is limited neither toward anything else, nor toward itself, since in that case it would surely be two. Nor does it have a figure, since it has no parts, nor does it have a form. Do not, therefore, seek this with mortal eyes, such as reason proves. Do not, I say, settle on the idea that this can be known in the way someone might think who believes all things that exist are perceptible to the senses; for in doing so, he would remove that which is the greatest of all. 

<margin>B</margin> For the things that someone might think are the most real, these are the most unreal. But that which is great in quantity...

Y

God, Plotinus, infinity, the One, principle, simple, power, intellect, infinite, one

<summary>Plotinus explains that the "One" or "First Principle" is beyond movement, rest, and physical dimensions, being infinite in power rather than size. He warns that the divine cannot be grasped through the senses or as a physical object, but only through a total intuition of its simple unity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion from page 509 regarding the transcendence of the First Principle (the One or the Good). Having established that the One is the source of all but identical to none, Plotinus now addresses the psychological and epistemological barriers that prevent humans from recognizing this ultimate reality, specifically our reliance on physical senses.</meta>

-># PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK V.<-

<margin>A</margin> ...it exists less; but truly, that which is first is the principle of being, and more excellent than essence itself <note>original: "essentiąq; præstantius". Plotinus argues the "One" is "beyond being" (epekeina tēs ousias), a core Neoplatonic concept.</note>. For this reason, we must change our way of thinking, otherwise we shall be left destitute of God. We would be like those who, during the solemn celebration of festivals, gluttonously fill their bellies with feasts—things which it is a sin for those entering the presence of the gods to even taste. Such people think the food for the belly is more <margin>B</margin> certain than the very contemplation of the God in whose honor the festival is held. Thus, they depart without having shared in the sacred rites. Indeed, in such mysteries, as long as the God is not seen, He is thought not to exist by those who believe only that which is tasted and seen by the flesh is real. It is as if someone slept through their entire life, believing the things seen in dreams to be absolutely certain and true. But if someone were to wake them, they would place no faith in the things perceived with open eyes, and would suddenly fall back into a slumber.

---

*As much as the intellect differs from the senses, so much do the things of the mind differ from the things of the senses. To those [materialists], it seems that what is not seen is not true. Therefore, one should not deny the existence of separate, spiritual realities simply because they are not grasped by the senses or by sense-based thinking. Finally, one must know that the Good itself stands even above the intellect and the objects of thought. Chapter XII.*

*All things always and entirely desire the Good; however, not all things desire the Beautiful, nor do they desire it entirely or always. Therefore, by a certain natural judgment, the Good is considered more excellent than the Beautiful itself. Thus, the love of the Beautiful is secondary and follows after the natural appetite for the Good. Finally, while beauty may seem to some to be a primary form where the highest and most uniform shape exists, since the intellect and the object of thought are below it, the Good itself should rightly be judged superior to beauty, just as it excels the intellect and the act of understanding.*

---

<margin>A</margin> **IT IS WORTHWHILE** to prepare oneself to perceive each individual thing with the specific faculty by which it ought to be perceived. For some things are perceived by the eyes, others by the ears, and others by different means. One must believe that the mind perceives things beyond these others, and one must not think that "understanding" is the same as "hearing" or "seeing." It would be as if someone ordered the ears to see, and then denied that voices exist simply because they cannot be seen. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, one must realize that these people have forgotten that which they have desired and longed for from the beginning until this very day. For all things seek that [the Good] by a necessity of nature, as if prophesying that they cannot exist without it. Furthermore, the knowledge of the Beautiful itself comes only to souls that are already awakened and conscious. This beauty brings with it a certain shock and an awakening of love. But the Good itself, because it has been present from the beginning as an innate desire, is present even to those who are asleep. It never strikes those who behold it with such a shock, because it is always there and requires no special act of remembrance <margin>C</margin> to be recognized. Yet, it does not occur to those who do not pay attention to it, since it is present even to the sleeping. The love of the Beautiful, however, when it first offers itself, brings distress and pain, because one must seek the Beautiful through knowledge. Since this kind of love is secondary and belongs to those who already possess intellect, it clearly shows that the Beautiful is secondary. But because the desire for the Good is more ancient and does not require the senses, it testifies that the Good itself is more ancient and superior to the Beautiful. To this is added the fact that all people believe they will have enough and be satisfied if they attain the Good itself, as if they had finally reached their ultimate goal.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is less; but the first things are the principle of being and, again, more sovereign than essence. Thus, one must reverse their opinion; otherwise, they will be left abandoned by God. This is like those who, at festivals, fill themselves to a <margin>B</margin> surfeit with food—things which it is not lawful for those entering the sacred precincts of the gods to take. They think those foods are more pleasing than the vision of the God for whom they chose to celebrate the feast, and so they go away without a share of the sacred rites. Indeed, no one <note>original: "πνοῖά τις" (pnoia tis). This refers to a "breath" or "divine emanation" from the source.</note> who lacks a certain breath from that place believes in it; they think only that which can be seen with the flesh exists. It is as if someone slept through their whole life and thought the things in sleep were clear and real, but if someone woke them up, they would distrust the things seen with open eyes. They would fall back into sleep again.

<margin>A</margin> IT IS NECESSARY to look at each thing with that faculty which is meant to perceive it: some things with the eyes, others with the ears, and so on. One must also desire to see with the mind <term>mind (nous): the intellectual faculty capable of perceiving divine truths</term>, and not think that "thinking" is "hearing" or "seeing." This would be like someone refusing to let the ears see, and saying sounds do not exist because they are not seen. <margin>B</margin> One must realize that these people have forgotten that which they have desired from the beginning until now, and which they still long for. For all things reach out for that [the Good] and long for it by a necessity of nature, as if intuiting <note>original: "ἀπομαντευόμενα" (apomanteuomena), meaning "prophesying" or "divining" instinctively.</note> that they cannot exist without it. The perception of the Beautiful comes to those who are already, as it were, sensing and awake; it brings a shock and <margin>C</margin> an awakening of love. But the Good itself is present as an innate desire even to those who sleep; it does not shock those who see it, because it is always present. There is no "recollection" <note>original: "ἀνάμνησις" (anamnesis). Plotinus notes the Good is so fundamental it doesn't even require the Platonic "recollection" of forgotten forms.</note> of it, and they do not see it because they are asleep. The Beautiful is present to all; but when it appears, it gives pangs to those who have an opinion of it, and to those who are already acting, it makes them feel the Beautiful is of higher rank. But the desire [for the Good], which is more unconscious for most, shows that the Good is perhaps older than the Beautiful and precedes it. All people think that if they grasp this, they will have relief from their disturbances; so it seems to everyone. For as the multitude...

He warns that relying solely on physical senses is like living in a dream, causing one to miss the divine reality that sustains all life.</summary>

Having previously warned against the distractions of the physical senses, Plotinus now distinguishes between "The Good" and "The Beautiful," explaining why the human soul pursues the Good with more urgency and why the Good is ontologically prior to everything else, including Beauty and Being itself.</meta>

# BOOK FIVE.

<column-break/>

As for the beautiful, we believe it also persuades us that the beautiful belongs to itself, but not to them, so that beauty here is also beautiful. For that which possesses ☉ the beautiful ☉ exists, and to seem to be beautiful <note>Plotinus is contrasting 'seeming' with 'being.' Many are content to look beautiful, but no one is content to only 'seem' good.</note> is enough for some, but they do not wish to be so. But as for the good, they wish to possess it in reality, not just in appearance. They claim it especially in the first sense, and they strive for it, and they seek the beautiful. For it is as if they themselves were born from it, like those who come after a king ☉. Just as one who comes after a king might strive to attain an equal dignity, as if coming from one and the same source, not knowing that he himself depends on the king, and even more on that which is before him. But the cause of this wandering is that both participate in the same things. And previously, both were well-off, and because they are bad, the good is given to him, but that beautiful thing is given to the beautiful. And toward the former, it is gentle and refined <unclear>...</unclear> and more delicate. And as someone wishes, * it is present to him. But the beautiful brings awe, and shock, and is mixed with pain, even pleasure. For it draws one away from the good as if they did not know it, just as a younger beloved is drawn from a father. But the older, * or the things of need? But the truth. * It does not have an older power than that which it has. For that which is after it, or all of it. But because it is after him and from him, he is the master of this. And the lord of those things born from him, but also as if standing apart <unclear>...</unclear> because he needed nothing for himself. But since he himself <margin>The Cave <unclear>...</unclear></margin> approached before it happened, since these * were about to happen to him without it being born. Since it was possible for others to be born from him, he knew them, but for him, it is not possible to be one, for he is one, who was not born. The becoming of all things. But he did not need all things, so that he might show him what was next(?) <margin>* <unclear>...</unclear></margin> and so all things * into the things after him. Or to set them in their own order. Always being above them.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, not everyone believes that the Beautiful will fully satisfy them. Furthermore, some even make little of present beauty; likewise, regarding that which is beautiful, they are often content that it is judged beautiful by others rather than being so themselves. Just as they think this beauty of ours belongs properly to the one who possesses it, so most people seem satisfied if they merely *appear* beautiful, even if they are not so at all. But the Good they desire to possess in reality, not merely in opinion. For everyone <margin>B</margin> strives to acquire for themselves that which is the first of all things. What shall we say to this? That the soul, together with the beautiful, competes as if with a certain zeal for victory? As if the soul itself were made from elsewhere, even though others are made from it. It is as if someone who follows a king should study to make another who immediately follows the king equal in dignity—inasmuch as he depends on the same one as the king does—not knowing, of course, that he also depends on the king, and that <margin>C</margin> both are participants in the same thing, and one source is prior to both. It is established, moreover, that the Good itself lacks the Beautiful not at all, but the Beautiful lacks the Good. Therefore, the Good itself is mild, gentle, peaceful, and delicate, and it usually meets anyone just as they wish. The Beautiful, however, renders the soul either stunned or excited by pleasure, which it mixes with pain. Finally, it is often accustomed to turn unwary souls away from the Good, just as a beloved often separates a lover from his father. For the Beautiful <margin>D</margin> is younger <note>original: "iunius". In Neoplatonic hierarchy, 'younger' means further from the source, while 'older' means more primary.</note>, but the Good is more ancient—not indeed in time, but in truth—because it also possesses a prior power. For it possesses *all* power; whereas that which is after it does not possess all, but only as much as is after it and from it. Therefore, that Father is also the master of this power, in no way needing those things which are generated by him, but dismissing everything and the whole which is begotten. Since He needs this in no condition at all, He <margin>E</margin> remains entirely the same as He was before He generated this from Himself. And indeed, it would have made no difference to Him if this had not been begotten; for even if something else could have been generated from Him besides, He would not have envied it the gift of being. But now, nothing further can be produced: for nothing remains that has not already been procreated, since all things are now made. But God Himself is not all things—for then He would be in need of all things—but surpassing all things, He was able to establish all things, and to permit all things to be by themselves, while He Himself remains preeminent over all.

---

### All entities, being more or less good among themselves, end in a certain highest being; this is finally resolved into the Good itself—that is, goodness itself in its simplicity, which is superior to being.
### Chapter XIII.

When you name this very thing, do not think of two things—that is, a certain thing together with goodness. Otherwise, the principle of things will be a composite, and it will not be absolute goodness, but a certain goodness, and like a participant in the good; it would then be referred back to a higher Good, which is not good by participation. That [higher Good] can be predicated of <term>Essence</term> <note>Being or existence</note>, <term>Life</term>, and <term>Mind</term> <note>The Intellect or *Nous*</note> when they are evil, or at least not good, or certainly more or less good. But such things cannot be predicated of Goodness itself in its simplicity. Therefore, the reason for Goodness itself is both different and simpler, and thus prior to the reason for essence, life, and mind. Do not, therefore, imagine that the first God is contained in the common order of beings under the common category of being, and additionally possesses His own goodness; otherwise He will be a composite—not formally, but by a certain participation—and the superior power of the simpler and the good would be made good by another. Finally, the Good itself, which is sought by all essences, lives, and minds, and which perfects and produces them, must not be said to properly have essence, life, or mind, just as we do not say the sun properly possesses in itself those things of which it is the cause in the elements—namely, heat of that kind, growth, generation, and similar forms and figures.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation from page 530. Having established that the Good is the ultimate object of desire, Plotinus now argues for the absolute simplicity of the Good. He explains why the Good cannot "possess" any attributes—not even "goodness" itself—because to possess something implies a division between the possessor and the possessed.</meta>

->### PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK V.<-

<page-num>525</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> Since God is indeed the Good itself, and not merely "good" <note>Plotinus distinguishes between the "Good itself" (the source) and "being good" (a quality something has). If God "had" goodness, he would be a composite of himself plus a quality, which contradicts his absolute simplicity.</note>, he must have nothing at all within himself, as he does not even "possess" the good. For if he were to have anything, he would have either a good thing or something not good. But he does not have the good, for he has absolutely nothing; if he has nothing, he is alone and set apart from all things. If, therefore, other things are good, they are yet not the Good <margin>B</margin> itself; or perhaps they are not good, but he possesses neither of these. Certainly, by having nothing—by the very fact of having nothing—he is the Good itself. Therefore, if anyone adds anything to him, whether **essence**, or **intellect**, or **beauty**, they certainly take away from him, by that very addition, the fact that he exists as the Good itself. By removing all things and affirming nothing about him, and by not lying as if something were present with him, one rightly allows him to be only what he is said to be: nothing of those things which are not present is attributed to him. <margin>C</margin> In this matter, many people are prone to err. Just as those who do not know how to praise someone actually detract from the glory of the person they praise by attaching qualities to them that are lesser than their true dignity, so too do these people fail to apply true praise to the subjects of their acclaim. For this reason, we must be especially careful not to add anything later or lesser, but must strictly observe that the **Mind** <term>Mind: In Greek, 'Nous,' the second principle of reality which contains all forms and ideas.</term> which transcends all these things is the cause of them, yet is not identical to them. <margin>D</margin> Now, the nature of the Good is not to be all things, nor to be any one of all things. Truly, if he were one of all things, he would be under one and the same category alongside the rest. If he were under the same category as others, he would differ from them only by a specific difference or some addition. He would then be two things rather than one: one being that which is "not good" (the part he shares in common with the rest) and the other being "good." <margin>E</margin> Thus, he would be a mixture of the good and the not-good, and therefore he would be neither purely nor primarily the Good. But the "Primarily Good" will be that in which this being also participates, becoming "good" beyond the common condition. This being, then, would be good through a certain participation; but that in which it participates is not one of "all things." Therefore, the Good itself is nothing among the "all." But if the good is within this being—for the "difference" is that by which this composite is made good—this composite must depend on another, which is entirely simple and is the Good alone. <margin>F</margin> This being, as a composite, depends on that which is only good. Therefore, that which exists as the First, and is the Good itself, is established above all beings and is the Good alone; it has nothing in itself, but is mixed with nothing at all, transcends all things, and is the cause of all things. For the beautiful does not come from the evil, nor do beings come from the evil, nor again from things that are indifferent. For the maker is better than the effect; for he is more perfect.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It was necessary that, being the Good itself, he should not have "the good" within himself or upon himself. For if he were to have anything in himself, he would have either a good or a non-good. If he were to have that which is the "Good" in the sovereign and primary sense, he would not "be" what he "has"; he would "have" the good. <note>original: "τὸ ἀγαθὸν τὸ κυρίως καὶ πρώτως." This emphasizes the distinction between possessing a trait and being the essence of it.</note> If, then, he is not a "good thing" and does not "have" a good thing, he would have nothing and possess nothing; he is only the one, isolated from other things which are good. <margin>B</margin> If he is what he is and also something else, then he is not the Good; but he has neither of these. Having nothing, and by the very fact of not having anything, he is the Good. But if someone were to add to him a cause, or essence, or intellect, or some beautiful thing, that addition will take away his very being as what he was. By stripping away all things, and saying nothing about him, and not speaking falsely as if something were with him, one says how he "is." Do not testify to anything present in <margin>C</margin> what he is, lest your knowledge and praise become a diminishment of the glory of the one being praised, by adding things to them that are less than their worth. Those who think they speak truly about the subjects of their discourse often err. For this reason, we should add nothing of the later and lesser things, but look at him as being above these; he is the cause of these, but is not himself these things. <margin>D</margin> And so, the nature of the Good is not to be all things, nor even some one of all things. For if he were any one of them, he would be the same as all; there would be something identical in the "all." He would differ only by his own specific trait or difference. If he is an addition of two things, and if the "common" part is not the Good, then only the other part is the Good. It would therefore be a mixture <margin>E</margin> of the good and the not-good; it would not be purely good. And that which is "primarily" would be that thing in which this participates, and that which becomes good through the common part. We participate in the Good itself. That in which we participate is not one of "all things"; even if it were among all things, it is the Good. But if the Good is in him—for there is a difference by which the "all" is good—or if he is the "all" itself, then it follows <margin>F</margin> that he is good from another. Thus, the One from whom he comes is the only Good. Therefore, the Good is above all things that are, <margin>meta</margin> as it appeared to us; he is the only Good, having nothing in himself, but unmixed with all, above all, and the cause of all. Neither beauty nor beings [come from evil], nor even from things indifferent. For the maker is better than the thing made. For he is more perfect.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Good must be absolutely simple and transcendent, containing no attributes—not even Being or Intellect—because anything that "has" an attribute is a composite and therefore depends on something more primary.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the sixth book of Plotinus’s Fifth Ennead. It continues the previous discussion on the nature of the "One" (the Absolute) by exploring why the highest principle cannot possess "thought" or "intellect," as thinking itself requires a division between the thinker and the thing being thought.</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FIVE,
### BOOK VI.

->On the fact that that which is beyond being does not think; and what is the primary thinker, and what is the secondary.<-

*The Intellect is both united with the object understood and yet remains distinct. Chapter I.*

*If the Intellect knows external things by looking outwards, there is a clear difference between the intellect and the intelligible <note>The "intelligible" refers to anything that can be grasped by the mind or intellect, rather than the senses.</note> object; the intellect takes on a foreign form, even though it is united with the intelligible through that very form. If, however, it understands itself, the essence of the thinker and the object of thought are the same. Nevertheless, there remains an opposition between them in terms of their relationship; they are formally distinct by reason. Furthermore, the nature of the intelligible is superior to the nature of the thinker, just as the nature of light, or the transparent, or a purer light is to a less pure light. For the relationship of the intellect to the intelligible, when it understands itself, is like a preliminary light striving to receive a perfected light, to which it may be equaled according to its capacity.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap T containing a seated figure, possibly a philosopher or personification, holding a staff next to a large celestial globe marked with longitude and latitude lines.</image-desc>
<margin>Itself</margin>
One kind of thinking is of another thing, while the other is of oneself. The latter <note>self-thinking</note> would prefer to avoid being "two," but it is less able to do so. It possesses the power of seeing from itself, but that which it sees is different. If the thinker is not separated by essence from the object, but exists alongside it and sees itself, both become one, yet they are not truly a single thing. Rather, the mind thinks primarily because it "has" or possesses an object, and it thinks primarily because it is a "thinking thing," not simply because it "is." For if the thinker and the thing thought were not distinct, the act of thinking would be something else entirely. It would not be "primary thinking" because it would receive its thought from another; and the primary thinker would be that which does not possess what it thinks as itself. Thus, it would not even be thinking of itself. If it were to possess the object as itself so as to truly think, there would not be "two." Therefore, both must be one. But if it is not itself <note>The One</note>, it is conceived of as following after, so that either there is no thinking at all, or it must be simple. One might choose to believe that such a thing is composed of simple elements when ascending from the soul. For it is easy to divide them, and one might see duality again; for if one were to create a double light, the soul would be according to the idea, and the power of knowing would be according to the duality.

Therefore, if someone ascends upward from the soul, it is easy to make a distinction here, and thus one may more easily detect this duality. If someone, therefore, produces a double light, the soul indeed follows the less pure light, while the intelligible part of the soul follows the...

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap D featuring a profile portrait of a bearded man wearing a cap, framed within the curve of the letter.</image-desc>
<margin>A</margin>
INTELLIGENCE is twofold: for either it understands something else, or it understands itself—which indeed draws it further away through a diversity, by which it becomes two things through the act of understanding. That which understands another also wishes to flee diversity, but it is less capable of doing so; it holds within itself that which it sees, but that object is distinct from itself.
<margin>B</margin>
But that which understands itself is not separated from that which is understood, but coexists with it, and beholds itself. Thus, both existing together are made one. Yet through the "one" it understands more, because it "has" what it understands. It understands primarily because it is necessary for the thinker itself to exist as both one and two. Without this, it does not become one, and therefore if the thinker is one thing and the object of thought is another, it will certainly not be the "primary thinker."
<margin>C</margin>
For by understanding another, it will not be the primary thinker, since it does not possess what it understands as its own; therefore, it does not have it as itself. Or certainly, if it possesses it as itself so that it might primarily understand, these two do not become a single "one," but rather become "two." Certainly, it will not have anything to think; wherefore it will not be a thinker. It is necessary, therefore, that whatever thinks must be simple and simultaneous; it will more clearly comprehend that what it understands is of such a nature.

...purer light of the same kind: then let it act so that the seer itself, in the act of seeing, becomes a light equal <margin>A</margin> to the light it sees. Since there is no longer any difference to separate them, he has made these two into one. This is indeed the "thinking being" <term>intellectus: the mind or higher intellect</term>, because it exists as two; yet it is now "thinking" because it has become one. In this way, he will grasp the intellect and the intelligible <note>The "intelligible" refers to the "object of thought"—the ideal forms or truths that the mind grasps.</note> as one. Therefore, while we, through our human reasoning, attempt to make one out of two, that higher Principle, on the contrary, produces two out of one. This is because it understands by making itself two; or rather, because it understands, it exists as two; likewise, because it is one, it is able to understand.

### *The Intellect, in understanding itself, possesses multiplicity within itself. Chapter II.*

Every intellect is, in a certain way, an object of thought <note>original: "intelligibilis"</note>, but not every object of thought is necessarily an intellect. Therefore, the nature of the "intelligible" is more general and exists prior to the nature of the intellect. Thus, an intellect that understands itself contains different aspects or "reasons" within itself. Furthermore, since the intellect—by its very order of essence—is prior even in time to the act of intelligence, it is rightly prior (at least in its origin) within the first being. Therefore, the essence itself, in its first moment of origin, is not yet "thinking," nor is it "intelligible" in actuality, until there arises within it a power of understanding. This power does not truly "think" in actuality until it is joined with an intelligible object. We must conclude: if the essence of being does not require intelligence for its own perfection of existence (since it precedes intelligence), then much less does that which is *above* being require it. That which is "above" is that in which there is no "first" or "last," nor is there an absolute duality of concepts, such as we find existing in "being" and "intellect."

<margin>A</margin> If, therefore, there is one thing that is the "primary thinker," and another that "thinks in another way," then surely that which is above the primary thinker does not think at all. For it would have to be an intellect in order to think; and if it were an intellect, it would have to possess an object of thought. If it were to think primarily, it would have to hold that object of thought within itself. Yet it is not necessary that every object of thought possess an intellect within itself or perform the act of thinking; if it did, it would be not only an object of thought, but also a thinker. <margin>B</margin> Since it would then be "two" <note>A thinker and a thing thought</note>, it could not be the "First" or the absolute "One." Indeed, the intellect which possesses the object of thought could never exist if there were not a pure essence of that which is the "pure intelligible," which serves as the object for the intellect. By itself, however, this pure essence is properly neither a thinker nor an object of thought; for a thing is only called "intelligible" when it is judged so by another. Moreover, the intellect itself holds its own power—the very strength by which it strives to understand—as <margin>C</margin> empty, unless it has received and grasped the very object of thought which it understands. It does not possess intelligence without an object of thought; it is perfected only when it possesses one. But before it can understand, it must possess a perfected essence within itself. That from which it becomes perfect in its intelligence is the very thing that exists before intelligence. Therefore, this highest Principle has no need of intelligence, since it exists sufficiently before it. Thus, it does not think. There is, therefore, a supreme "Something" that does not think; then there is that which thinks primarily; and finally, there is that which possesses a secondary kind of intelligence. Furthermore, if that first Principle of all things were to think, something would already be added to it. It would no longer be the "First," but the "second"; no longer "One," but many—indeed, as many as the things it thinks. Even if it were to think only of itself, it would once again turn out to be many.

---

### *Until you imagine the intellect—because it thinks either itself or other things—to be so multiform that there are many forms within it, distinct from one another by their very nature, even without external relations, you have not yet found the simplicity of the First Principle. Chapter III.*

Again, wherever many things are composed together, and one thing is made from many, such a multiplicity comes after the "One" itself. Finally, every multiplicity which is something other than Unity itself, and is in some way opposed to the One...

<column-break/>

...purer, then he might make the seer a light <margin>A</margin> equal to the light seen, because that which he still holds separates them as different, so that the two are united; thinking, indeed, because there are two; but having seen, because they are now one. It is both "thinking" and "to think," to perceive. We, therefore, by our reasoning, have made the "one" from the "two." But on the contrary, from the "one" come the "two," because he thinks, making himself two, or rather because he thinks, he is two, and because he is the "One" itself.

<margin>A</margin> If indeed there is the primary thinker, and then another who thinks otherwise, that which is beyond the primary thinker would no longer think. For it would need to think to become an intellect; and being an intellect, it would have to have an object of thought <note>original: "νοητὸν" (noēton)</note>. If it is thought primarily, it has the object of thought in itself. But being an object of thought, it is not necessary for it to think as well. For if it has thinking in itself, it will be not only an object of thought, but also a thinker. And being the first, it is no longer two. For whatever it is that possesses the object of thought, it would not be preserved if there were not a purely <margin>B</margin> intelligible essence <note>original: "οὐσίας" (ousias)</note>. The intellect [will see] the intellect; it will be an object of thought. But the object of thought in itself will not properly be "the intelligible," for the intelligible exists for another. The intellect does not possess the power of thinking that it applies <margin>C</margin> except by taking and seeing the object of thought. For that which possesses the intellect, the object of thought itself, is so much more when it possesses it. But it was necessary, before thinking, to be perfect in itself. From the essence, the "more." From the beginning, for itself therefore, it has that which is before thinking. And for that which thinks, thinking is necessary at that time. Therefore, it is not the object of thought. There is then that which thinks, and that which primarily thinks. And the object of thought is secondary. Furthermore, if the first thinks, it will be concerned with itself; therefore it is not the first. But also because it involves another, it is not one, but already many. And if it will think of itself—for even if it only thinks of * itself—it will be many.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the highest Principle (the One) must be beyond the act of thinking, because thinking creates a split between the observer and the observed, whereas the One must be perfectly simple and unified. He distinguishes between the pure essence of truth and the intellect that strives to grasp it.</summary>

# BOOK SIX.
### T 4

...matter, it is necessary that after the One itself, there is that which participates in the One. The Platonists do not oppose the Christian theologians on these points, for among the Christians, the first principle does not possess multiple forms by understanding many things—no matter how it may understand—but rather, through its own single form, being essentially one and self-sufficient, it perceives all things. That is to say, by considering its own most simple form, it sees how it is to be imitated differently by different things. Furthermore, the divine Trinity (as Dionysius the Areopagite <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-6th century Christian mystic whose writings blended Neoplatonic philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> confirms, and Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop and theologian, known as one of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note> asserts) is the same as Unity itself; truly, just as light and heat are distinct by their rays below the heavens, in the heavens they are one. Moreover, progression and rest are different here; but there, rest is found in progression, and progression in rest. Thus, in the divine nature, because it is infinite, motion agrees with stability: for if you imagine an infinite velocity of motion, you resolve it into a state of rest. Indeed, even infinite slowness and velocity, when they end in a state of rest, agree with one another as one. For an infinite power, being alive, subjects all things to itself and unites itself and others; so it is not surprising to find in Dionysius and Nazianzen that in the divine nature, that which is Unity is also the Trinity itself, and vice versa. For the infinity of power there acts as an internal and equal offspring even unto the Trinity, as they say, while meanwhile preserving Unity. Therefore, the Trinity is not there like a certain multitude participating in unity, which would then have to be referred back to a higher unity: for this is Unity itself. If indeed there is any distinction in divine matters, it is conducted through a certain relation, as most Christians agree, because relation preserves difference without the slightest composition of the "One." The followers of Scotus <note>Referring to Duns Scotus, a major medieval scholastic theologian.</note> add that the only type of multitude unworthy of God is that which is a cause of something through the composition of potentiality and act. But there, a multitude—whether of persons or of ideas—is not considered in that way; rather, all are like certain acts that compose nothing, nor do they emerge from potentiality; on the contrary, they are like certain sacred rays, internal and perpetual births, into which the Light itself simply propagates itself.

<margin>A</margin> <gloss>original Greek: "Εἰ δ’ ἐκ πολλῶν..."</gloss> If someone says nothing prevents the same thing from being made of many, he says that those things which are in the subjects are many in power, but remain one. etc. Or if it is entirely of the One, then these are participants in other things, or taking the One alone by itself, the impulses would be of others, through those things which grasp it. That which is with others, yet is something different from others, should be treated as if it were with others. But then one must seek the subject of the others, no longer with the
<margin>B</margin> others, but itself according to itself. For that which is in others would then be similar to that which is in others, but it must still be itself according to itself, or it is destined to exist in others. Unless someone were to say that its being has its subsistence in the presence of others. For it is possible for it to be once, and the subject from many simply is not. Nor is it itself, for if each of them fails to be, let it be some form of a simple subsisting thing.
<margin>C</margin> But the subject made from many, having no subsistence of its own according to itself, nor being able to, does not provide itself to be with another by not being at all; how then could the composite be from all of them, since it is born from non-beings? Or if not from non-beings, yet let these many not be, for how shall it be of many? Since thinking is a certain multitude, but through the multitude thinking is not.
<margin>D</margin> But in those things where thinking is among the later things, then thinking and the Idea itself exist.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **MOREOVER**, if anyone objects that nothing prevents this first principle from being both the same thing and many things, we shall respond that it is necessary for one subject to agree with these many things. For many things can neither exist, nor produce a "one," unless there is a "one" from which or in which they exist. Or certainly, unless there is a "one" entirely, and that being the first, beyond the number of the rest which are numbered among themselves: which indeed must be accepted only in itself. If, however, it exists together with others, it will be necessary that this "one," accepted
<margin>B</margin> together with others, though differing from the rest, should then allow for the congregation of the others. But one must investigate the subject itself for all things, no longer together with the rest, but rather according to itself. For that which is the same in others will indeed be similar to this, but it will not be this very thing. Truly, it must be itself alone, if it is to be grasped in others as well—unless perhaps someone says that nothing else of it exists except its having substance together with others. But if that were so,
<margin>C</margin> it will never be simple in itself; therefore, there will not be anything anywhere coalesced from many. No one can claim that what cannot be simple will have substance; then, because it is judged to be composed of many, since there is nowhere anything simple, it too will not exist. For since each thing cannot be simple, and no simple thing subsists as a foundation, that which is said to be constituted from many—where
<margin>D</margin> surely none of them can have substance according to itself, nor can it apply itself to the commerce of anything else, because it simply is not—since these things are so, in what way can anything be composed of all of them? Such a thing would be made from those things which do not exist. I do not mean things that are "not something," but things that entirely "are not." Therefore, if anything is a "many," it is necessary for the One to exist before the many. If, therefore, that which is an "understanding thing" <term>intelligens: the mind in the act of thinking</term> is a certain multitude, it is necessary that where there is no multitude, there is also no intelligence <note>The argument is that "thinking" requires a subject and an object, which is a division (multitude). The highest source, the One, must be above even this division.</note>: and that is the first principle itself. Therefore, in those things which follow it, there will be intelligence and intellect.

It is, therefore, entirely simple in itself, and it has nothing added that is not goodness itself. Do not, therefore, by multitude...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

...to imagine such a thing there which creates a composite, or to add intelligence to goodness, would be to create a distance between them within goodness itself. As long, therefore, as you consider the intellect as a Shape, like the Sun, in which the acts of intelligence relate to their own nature just as light relates to the substance of the Sun—which is prior to and far different from the light—so long must you deny that the supreme God is the intellect. Think of God instead as light alone, not existing in any nature other than itself, but remaining within itself; a light from which nothing is ever hidden, since through it all things are everywhere made manifest, even though you must affirm that the supreme God is not any intellect understood by you.

---

<margin>A</margin>
**T**HEREFORE, the Good itself must be simple and in need of nothing; it will in no way require intelligence. For that which is not necessary will certainly not be present to it, since absolutely nothing is present to it <note>original: "nihil adest" / "οὐδὲν παρὸν." Plotinus argues that the "One" or "Good" is so perfectly simple that it cannot even "have" attributes, as having an attribute implies a division between the possessor and the possessed.</note>. Therefore, no intelligence at all exists within it, just as nothing else does. Furthermore, the intellect is one thing, and the Good itself is another. For the intellect becomes "good-like" <term>boniformis / ἀγαθοειδὲς (good-form)</term> by the very fact that it understands the Good. Likewise, just as among two things where one is combined with another, it is impossible for this "one-with-another" to be the primary One; rather, the "One-in-itself" must exist above that "one" which is coupled with another. So it is necessary—as that which is added to the One is joined to it, and that which is added to the simple is joined to it—that the simple itself stands above them, having nothing in itself of those things found in the one coupled with others. For from where would "the other" in a thing come, unless that from which "the other" arises first existed separately? For how can that which is simple be made from another? But that which is manifold, or at least twofold, must necessarily be referred back to another. Now, one may compare the first to light itself, the second to the Sun, and the third to the Moon which draws its light from the Sun. For the Soul possesses an adventitious <note>Coming from outside; not innate.</note> intellect which colors it, making it intellectual; but the intellect possesses within itself its own intellectual light, and is not only light, but that very thing which it is, existing as luminous in its own essence. But that which pours this light here is not something else existing in itself along with the light, but exists as simple light, providing to the intellect the power to exist as what it is. Why then would this require anything? For it is not the same as that which is in another. For that which lies in another is different from that which is entirely through itself and freed from all things.

<column-break/>

FURTHER, if the Good must be simple and without need, it would not even need acts of thought. That which is not in it, would not be present to it; since thinking is not present to it at all. And if nothing is there, because it is nothing else [but itself], then the Good is something different. For to think of the Good is to be "good-form." Further, just as when two things are together, it is impossible for the "goodness" that is with another to be the Good itself. Instead, the "Good-by-itself" must exist before the "goodness-with-another." Let it be then that even if it has goodness by being with another, the simple must be the cause by itself; it does not have in itself that which is in the thing coupled with another. For where would the "other" come from, if the prior did not exist separately? Thus also with other things: for the simple is one thing, and things from another are like it; but if a thing is many or two, it must necessarily be suspended from another. And how should we make the comparison? The light [is] the first; the Sun the next; and the third is the Moon, carrying light from the Sun. For the Soul, by having a borrowed intellect, is itself colored by it, being intellectual. But the intellect has its own [light] in itself, not being light alone, but that which is illuminated in its own essence. But that which provides this light, being no other thing, is simple light, providing to that power [the intellect] its very being; why would it need anything? For the same thing is not the same in another as it is when it is in itself. The causes are by themselves in all cases.

---

> *If you imagine that "understanding oneself" is like returning to oneself, and collecting a multitude known to oneself within oneself, such an action is least suited to the most simple principle of all things. <margin>Chapter V.</margin>*

> *If in any way you think that "understanding" is a certain striving that desires the Good itself, or like a vision seeking light, do not think that such intelligence applies to that which is judged to be the Good itself and the infinite light itself: for the Good does not possess a desire for the Good, nor does the light require a vision hungry for light. Just as numbers refer back to their unity which is prior to number, and continuous things to their superior continuity, so essences are referred to a substantial unity superior to essence. That which is more eminent than essence surely surpasses that intelligence which belongs to high essence; but if you call the existence of the Good and the infinite light "better than intelligence"—treating intelligence as the cause of what is now existing intelligence—you will perhaps not err in so calling whatever is desired by those who possess intellect.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
**F**URTHERMORE, that which is in itself manifold will rightly seek itself, and desire to harmonize with itself, and to mutually perceive itself everywhere. But that which is entirely one, where will it turn toward itself? Where will it receive itself? Where will it need its own innermost sense? For it is the same thing, better than all harmony of sense and all intelligence: since intelligence is not the first thing. For it does not hold the first rank, whether regarding "simply being" or regarding "venerable being"; rather, it occupies the second place.

<column-break/>

FURTHER, the manifold seeks itself, and wants to incline toward itself and be conscious of itself. But that which is entirely one, where shall it go toward itself? Where would it need self-consciousness? Rather, it is the same thing [the Good] and yet better than self-consciousness, and every motion and thought. For thinking is not first, either in being or in being honorable; but it is second,

Plotinus uses the hierarchy of Light, the Sun, and the Moon to illustrate the relationship between the One, the Intellect, and the Soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section, asserting that the "Good" (the One) does not possess intelligence or thought, because thought implies a lack or a movement toward something else, whereas the Good is perfectly self-sufficient.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<margin>A</margin> It [the Intellect] was born after the Good itself existed. As soon as it arose in essence, it turned itself toward the Good. Having been so moved, it proceeded toward that Good and came to know it. This very thing is what it means to "understand": a motion toward the Good, born from a desire for the Good <note>original: "desiderio boni" / "ἐφιέμενον ἐκείνου." Plotinus posits that the "Intellect" (Nous) is not the highest principle, but a secondary one that arises because it "desires" to look back at its source, the Good.</note>. Indeed, this desire procreated intelligence and remains its constant companion. For vision consists of a certain appetite of the sight itself, drawing it toward the act of seeing. For this reason, it is not necessary for the Good itself to understand—neither as an elder nor as anything else. <margin>B</margin> There is nothing else besides itself that could be "the Good" for it. Even when something else besides the Good understands itself, it does so precisely because it is "good-form" <term>boniforme / ἀγαθοειδὲς (having the form of the Good)</term> and possesses a certain likeness to the Good; it understands itself as it becomes something good and desirable, having already attained a kind of image of the Good. If it always holds itself thus, it will always produce the same result. Furthermore, in its own self-knowledge, it perhaps knows the Good by a certain coincidence, for by looking toward the Good, it knows itself. In its activity, it understands itself, and the activity of all things is directed toward the Good.

*Since all powers desire primary acts—that is, forms—as a kind of good, and primary acts desire secondary ones—that is, actions—in a similar way as a good, it is right that the principle of all things, which is most greatly desired by all, is called "Act" <term>actus / ἐνέργεια (actualization or activity)</term>, being superior to any specific form or action.*

### Cap. VI.

*This infinite Act, although it is not strictly said to "act" or to possess a further action, is nevertheless the source from which all things are acted upon and from which all things act. Let me not call this Act "intellect" or "intelligence" as Plotinus defines them everywhere. For with Plotinus, in the intellect (even the first one), the "thinking nature" is one thing, and the "act of thinking" is another; likewise, essence, life, and intelligence are distinct there. Furthermore, the different Ideas <term>ideæ (the eternal archetypes of things)</term> of things are formally absolute among themselves, and differ by reason from the intelligence through which the mind itself understands them. Such differences do not belong to the Platonic or Christian Supreme Reality. God, that highest one, does not understand himself in order to join himself to himself as if he were separate. Nor are there other Ideas through which he might profit by understanding them. For he bestows something better than knowledge upon things—namely, the enjoyment of himself—and he enjoys himself in a better way than by "knowing." Those who enjoy God do so through a unity superior to the intellect, as Dionysius the Areopagite <note>original: "Areopagita Dionysius." A 5th-6th century Christian philosopher who blended Plotinian thought with theology, emphasizing that God is known through "unknowing" or mystical union.</note> asserts.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If these things are said correctly, intelligence has no place in the Good itself. For that which understands must be something other than the Good it seeks. Therefore, the Good itself is entirely free from activity. Why would an "act" need to act? For no act possesses a further act within itself. If we add something more to other acts that are directed toward something else, we certainly must not add anything further to the first of all acts, upon which all other acts depend; rather, it must simply exist as that which it is. <margin>B</margin> Such an act, therefore, cannot be intelligence, for it has nothing to understand. It is the First. Furthermore, it is not intelligence that understands, but that which possesses intelligence <note>Plotinus distinguishes between the faculty/act of thinking and the being that "has" that faculty. The One has no faculties because it is not a composite being.</note>. Thus, two things arise in the one who understands, but the First is in no way "two." Moreover, one will recognize this more clearly by considering how the "thinker" in the universe encompasses this twin nature more certainly. We say that beings are beings, and each is a "one." Those things which truly exist are in the intelligible world <margin>C</margin>, not only because those essences always remain in the same state, while things offered to the senses are in a continuous flux. Perhaps even in the sensible realm there are some things that remain, but it is rather because they [the intelligible things] possess the perfection of "Being" within themselves. For it is necessary that what is first called "Essence" is not a mere shadow of being, but possesses a fullness of being. And Being is full when it receives the form of understanding and living. Thus, all these exist together in the First.*

<summary>This page argues that the Supreme Good (the One) is beyond intelligence and thought, because thinking implies a division between the thinker and the object of thought. Plotinus and the commentator Ficino explain that while the "Intellect" arises from a desire for the Good, the Good itself is a simple, infinite Act that transcends knowledge.</summary>

<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD V.</header>

<margin>A</margin> In being, these three are found: to understand, to live, and to be. If, therefore, being exists, intellect follows; and conversely, if intellect exists, being also exists. There, understanding occurs simultaneously with being. From this, it follows that intelligence is already a multiplicity, not a unity. It is necessary, therefore, that in that which is not of such a nature <note>The "One," which is perfectly simple and unified.</note>, there is also no intelligence. Indeed, if one runs through the individual things in the intelligible world, one everywhere encounters a dual notion: for example, the intelligence of man and man himself; the intelligence of a horse and the horse; and again, the intelligence of the just and justice itself.
<margin>B</margin> All things, then, are double. There, one becomes two; there, in turn, two return into one. But the First itself is neither any of these things individually, nor is it composed of all those things which are double; nor is it double at all. How two arise from one is discussed elsewhere. But since that First is beyond essence, it is rightly judged to be beyond intelligence. Nor is it absurd to say that the First does not know itself at all. Since
<margin>C</margin> it is entirely one, it has nothing at all within itself to learn. Nor does it need to know other things. For it provides something better and greater to them than such knowledge of themselves, which is the good of others. Rather, it grants them the power to reach it within that same state.

<column-break/>

<note>This column translates the Greek text, which mirrors the Latin argument on the left.</note> Thinking, living, and being are in being. If then being, also intellect; and if intellect, then being, and thinking together with being. Thus, thinking is many and not one. It is necessary, then, for that which is not such, that thinking is not there either. And if one looks at things individually: man, and the thought of man; horse, and the thought of horse; justice, and the thought of justice. Why then are all things, even the good, two? And these two themselves come into one. But He is not any of these, nor any individual thing, nor from all the two, nor two at all. How the two come from the one is discussed elsewhere. But since He is beyond essence, thinking also is beyond Him. In that way, He is not ignorant, even if He does not know Himself—for that which loves itself is ignorant <note>The Greek text here implies that the One does not "learn" or "know" in a way that suggests a prior state of ignorance or a separation between subject and object.</note>. Nor does He need to know other things. For He gives them something better and greater than the knowledge of themselves. For the sake of the good of others, they are rather in the same [state], with as much power as possible to touch Him.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD FIFTH,
->BOOK VII.<-

->ON WHETHER THERE ARE IDEAS EVEN OF INDIVIDUALS.<-
->Whether individual things also have Ideas.<-

*As many humans as are born in a Great Year <term>Magnus Annus (a vast cosmic cycle after which the stars return to their original positions)</term> of the world, so many seminal reasons of humans exist in universal nature, and roughly as many ideas of humans in the divine mind.*

<margin>Cap. I.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop-cap 'V' showing a landscape with clouds and architecture inside a square frame.</image-desc>Each rational soul naturally possesses within itself a certain number of lives, corresponding to the various lives it will produce. But just as when we say all heavenly things are in the earth, and conversely all earthly things are in heaven, we understand "all things" according to the nature of the place—that is, in heaven there are heavenly reasons, and in nature, their earthly quality. Thus, when we hear that our soul is "all things," we must understand this according to the property of a human and rational soul. Therefore, your soul will never produce, by itself and in its own form, those things proper to brute animals, but always human things—though they may be somewhat similar to brutes and sometimes to spirits <note>original: "demonibus." In the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary beings, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense.</note>. Your soul can produce only a few changes of life within a Great Year; especially since it leads a very brief life on earth but a very long one above the earth. In the frequent year of the world, there is no change of lives, but rather the resurrection of the exact same humans. Meanwhile, humans differ among themselves not only by matter but also by their own forms, figures, and various modes of generation. This formal difference, since it arises neither from matter nor by chance, depends on certain formal reasons <term>rationes seminales (the "seed-like" principles that direct the growth and form of a living being)</term> which exist both in nature and in the universal mind, and they are not infinite in number. For finite forms are born in a Great Year, and in the following one, the same things return, since the same causes obviously return. But how are there more things in matter than in the soul, and more in the soul than in the mind? Truly, it is because certain things in matter differ from each other in number, either through a defect of form occurring somewhere in the matter (where the form is more perfect elsewhere) or through the division of quantity. But differences that are simply formal are equal to the seminal reasons. There are more such reasons in the soul than there are Ideas in the mind, since in the nature of the soul, there is always an absolute distinction of reason

---

<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E (Epsilon) showing a classical figure holding a book.</image-desc> Is there an idea for each individual? If I and each person have a path leading to the <term>intelligible realm</term><note>The 'intelligible realm' refers to the world of Forms or Ideas, which Neoplatonists believed was more real than the physical world.</note> and our connection is there, then the source of each person is there as well. If Socrates always exists, and the soul of Socrates exists, then "Socrates-himself" will be there in the same way that a soul is an individual there. But if it is said that the same soul becomes a different person at different times—for instance, if it is Socrates at one time and Pythagoras at another—then that specific individual is no longer there. However, if the soul of each person contains the <term>seminal reasons</term><note>Original: "λόγους" (logoi). These are 'seed-like' formative principles or blueprints that guide the development of living things.</note> of all the people it becomes, then all are there. For we say that as the cosmos contains reasons, so too does each soul. If, then, the cosmos contains reasons not only for 'man' in general, but for each individual animal, the soul must also contain them. In this case, the number of reasons would be infinite, unless they return in cycles. Even if one tries to limit this infinity by saying the same things are produced again in a cycle, there must still be reasons and patterns for everything that comes to be in a single period. One 'Man-himself' might seem enough to produce all men, just as a set number of souls produce infinite men; however, different things cannot have the same reason. One 'Man' is not enough to serve as a pattern for many men who differ from one another not only in their matter, but by specific, individual differences. We are not just like images of Socrates copied from one archetype; rather, our differences must arise from different reasons. In a full cycle of the universe, all these reasons are contained. When the cycle repeats, the same things are produced again according to the same reasons. We should not fear an infinite number of things in the intelligible world, because all that multiplicity is contained within an indivisible unity.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V showing a man walking in a countryside landscape.</image-desc> IS there also an idea for each individual? Perhaps if I and each person attain an order for the return to the intelligible realm, the principle of each is also there. Perhaps if Socrates always exists, and the soul of Socrates is Socrates himself, then he exists there as a specific soul. Thus, Socrates and any individual exist there. But if
<margin>B</margin> Socrates does not always exist, but the soul that is now Socrates was previously Pythagoras or someone else, and will be someone else in the future, then each of these people we see here is no longer "there" in the intelligible. However, if the soul of each person holds the <term>seminal reasons</term><note>Original: "seminarias rationes." This is the Latin equivalent of the Greek "logoi spermatikoi," the blueprints for individual existence.</note> for all the lives it completes, then again, all are there. For we acknowledge that the soul possesses as many individual reasons as the world itself does. Therefore, if the world embraces the reasons not only of 'man' but
<margin>C</margin> of individual animals, the soul must also contain those reasons. Because of this, an infinite number of reasons would follow, unless a restoration to the same state occurs in fixed cycles of time. In this way, infinity is avoided when the same things are returned to the world. Otherwise, if the things produced are more numerous than the pattern, there must again be reasons and patterns for everything that occurs in one revolution of the world. It seems that
<margin>D</margin> one 'Man' is sufficient for all men, just as a certain number of souls are enough to produce countless humans; but there cannot be a single reason for distinct things. One 'Man' is not sufficient as a pattern for many men who differ among themselves—not just in their matter, I say, but differing by many unique traits. For this is not a case of many images of Socrates being made from one model; rather, different effects must proceed from different reasons. A single total revolution of the universe contains all reasons; and these same things are regenerated again through those same reasons. We should not worry that an infinite multitude follows in the intelligible world; for there, the entire multitude is contained in a certain indivisible way, and individual things proceed from there only when the world acts.

---

->*Every soul and particular nature contains within itself the seminal reasons of all things that are to be generated from it, which are distinguished from one another by formal differences.*<-
->*Chapter II.*<-

*These things can be distinguished even if they are commonly counted within the same species. Such a specific distinction of forms is prescribed by the very intention of universal nature, because the order, beauty, and goodness of the universe consist in such a distinction. Matter itself brings no unique variety to forms, but rather a defect of form. Furthermore, quantity—by its own arrangement in similar things—creates number in some places, but never variety. Finally, in any one natural order of the world, heterogeneous things are generated that are formally dissimilar to one another, and thus they are created through different reasons. In the following cycle, all the same things are recreated through the same reasons under the same causes.*

---

<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A (Alpha) showing a figure in a landscape.</image-desc> BUT if the mixtures of males and females produce different offspring, then the thing produced is no longer the result of a single reason for each, because each parent—for example, the male—will not produce different reasons, but only one...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V showing a man with a staff.</image-desc> BUT if the mixtures of the reasons of the male and female produce different offspring, then there will no longer be a specific reason for each individual born. And either of the parents—such as the male—will not create through different reasons, but through one...

<summary>Plotinus explores whether individual people like Socrates have unique eternal "Ideas" in the intelligible realm. He concludes that because individuals have unique "formal" differences (not just physical ones), the Soul must contain specific "seminal reasons" for every unique being, though these are all unified within the higher divine Intellect.</summary>
<keywords>Ideas of Individuals, Seminal Reasons, Socrates, Intelligible World, Metempsychosis, Universal Cycle, formal difference, Plotinus</keywords>
