<meta>This page continues the inquiry from Book Seven of Ennead V. While the previous page questioned whether individuals like Socrates have their own eternal Idea, this page expands on how these individual "formative reasons" (logoi) interact with physical matter and the cycles of the universe.</meta>

<page-num>540</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...at least his own, that is, or his father's. But perhaps nothing prevents these from being produced through different causes, because they themselves possess all things, even if at different times some are more prominent than others. But what then, when different children are born from the same parents? Perhaps it is because there is not always an equal dominance or superiority of one parent's influence over the other. But let us consider it this way: even if the difference is not only in outward appearance, and sometimes the male influence dominates and sometimes the female, or perhaps each contributes an equal part, the whole is still transmitted and naturally implanted. However, one part of the <term>matter</term><note>original: "materiæ" / "ὕλης". In Neoplatonism, matter is the 'receptacle' or mirror that reflects the higher spiritual forms, often introducing imperfection or variation.</note> or the other might dominate. But in what way are those conceived in different regions judged to be different? Does matter itself bring about the difference by being overcome in various ways? If that were so, all offspring except one would be contrary to nature. But if variety itself is a beautiful thing everywhere, then it is right that one single species does not exist everywhere. Yet, that which pertains to matter must be attributed to deformity alone. Indeed, in the very Artificer of things, the perfect <term>formative reasons</term><note>original: "rationes" / "λόγοι". These are the spiritual blueprints or 'seed-codes' that organize physical life.</note> are hidden, yet they are transmitted in their entirety. But even if the reasons are different, must there be as many of them as there are things born in one <term>Great Year</term><note>original: "mundi reuolutione" / "περιόδῳ". The 'Great Year' is a cosmic cycle after which all stars and planets return to their original positions.</note>? For it is possible that while the same reasons are applied, different external events may still appear. But it is certainly granted that this happens even when the reasons are transmitted as a whole. The question is whether this also happens when the same reasons are dominant: Is it therefore necessary for there to be just as many reasons? Since the exact same effect can only be repeated in another cosmic cycle; in this current cycle, nothing is ever exactly the same.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...his own, or his father's. Or nothing prevents them from having them according to different causes, though all are present, some are more ready at hand. When different children come from the same parents, is it due to the dominance of the parents? In those cases, the difference is in the appearance. Either it shapes according to the male, or according to the female; or it gives an equal part to each. But the whole was given <margin>B</margin> and is present within. One part of the matter dominates, or the other. How then are those in another place different? Is it not that the matter is different and similarly mastered? One might say that nature would be worse off if variety were not everywhere a beauty, rather than everything being the same. But we must attribute to ugliness only that which deviates because of matter. And while many reasons are hidden, they are given as wholes. But let the reasons be different. Must there be as many as there are things becoming in one period, even if when the same things are given, differences appear from the outside, or if it is granted that they are given as wholes? It is asked whether this happens when the same reasons dominate. Is it not that everything is the same in a different period, but in this period nothing is entirely the same?

---

*Since Nature acts through its own essence—unlike an art or craft which acts through something added to its essence—the Idea rightly contains a variety of things to be generated within its essential reasons. Therefore, the entire arrangement of individual things to be carried out in the cycle of the world was designated from the beginning in the Mind of the World-Maker, and in the mind of the <term>World Soul</term><note>The 'Soul of the World' (Anima Mundana) is the spiritual force that animates the entire physical universe.</note> and its nature. Chapter III.*

*Many believe that the Great Year of the world is completed when all the celestial bodies return to exactly the same position, both in themselves and in relation to each other, as they have today. Some measure this span as thirty-six thousand solar years; others as <unclear>thirty-nine thousand</unclear>; and others measure or think of it differently.*

---

<margin>A</margin> **BUT** in what way shall we say there are different reasons in the case of many twins? And if one were to run through the other animals, especially those that conceive many offspring in a single mating, what shall we say? Shall we perhaps judge that there is only one reason there, where the offspring differ very little from one another? But if that is so, there will no longer be as many reasons as there are individual things. Should we not think that there are as many reasons as there are individual differences—differences, I mean, not resulting from a failure to meet the standard of the species itself? Yet, what prevents us from assigning different reasons even to offspring that do not differ at all, if indeed any are ever born entirely without difference? For the craftsman, even if he makes identical things, nevertheless receives that which is called "the same" with a certain rational difference by which he makes it distinct, applying something different to that which is identical. But in the power of Nature, where the diversity of things comes not from varied reasoning, but only from varied formative reasons, the diversity must be connected to the species itself. We, however, are not strong enough to discern the difference. Certainly, if any randomness were admitted into the generation of things, the reason would be otherwise...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **HOW** then shall we say the reasons are different in the case of many twins? If one goes to the other animals, even the most prolific, or those in which there is no variation, is there one reason? But if this is so, the individuals are no longer as many as the reasons. Or are there as many as there are individual differences, or variety, or in the falling short of the <term>Form</term><note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos). The perfect, eternal shape or Idea of a thing.</note>? Either variety, or as many as are indistinguishable, or if any are entirely indistinguishable. For just as the craftsman may make indistinguishable things, he nonetheless takes "the same" with a rational difference, according to which he makes another. Not that the difference is in the same thing, if it is by nature and not by calculation that the other comes to be, but it is joined only by the reasons, and the difference is by the Form. We, however, are unable to grasp the difference. Or perhaps the production holds the things that are there, and the whole is not another reason.

<summary>Plotinus explores whether every individual person and animal has its own unique spiritual "blueprint" (reason) or if differences are merely caused by the imperfections of matter. He also discusses the "Great Year," suggesting that exact individuals might only repeat when the entire cosmic cycle restarts.</summary>
<keywords>formative reasons, logoi, individual ideas, Great Year, twins, matter, World Soul, Plotinus, Neoplatonism, cosmic cycles</keywords>

<page-num>548</page-num>
<header>BOOK EIGHT.</header>

But if there is a measure of how many things there are, then the quantity is limited; and once the unfolding of the <term>formative reasons</term><note>original: "λόγων" / "rationum". In Plotinus's thought, these are the spiritual blueprints or 'seed-codes' that organize physical life.</note> has reached its requirement, it will cease again, so that when all things have ceased, another beginning starts. For the total span of the world’s existence, and how many stages it will pass through in its own life, is laid down from the beginning in that which contains the reasons. Should we then apply this to other animals as well, where many offspring are produced from a single birth? We need not fear an infinite number in the seeds and the reasons, since the <term>Soul</term><note>The "World Soul" or individual soul which acts as the intermediary between the high realm of pure thought and the physical world.</note> contains all things. Or perhaps the infinity of these things exists in the <term>Intellect</term><note>original: "νοῦ" / "intellectu". The 'Nous' or Divine Mind, the second highest principle in Plotinus's system, containing the Platonic Forms.</note> within the Soul, and these things return again in their cycles from the realms beyond.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But if a limit and measure defines how many things come forth, certainly the quantity and multitude will be determined by the very unfolding and explanation of all the reasons, so that when all things have reached an end, another beginning is woven anew. For how great the world ought to be, and how many things must be transacted in its life, was established from the beginning in that which contains the reasons of all. Shall we therefore bring forth as many reasons in the other animals in which many are procreated in a single birth? <margin>B</margin> Perhaps it is not to be feared that an infinite multitude might occur in the seeds and reasons, since the soul embraces all things. Nor does an innumerable crowd occur in the intellect or the soul: for all the reasons of these things return there by a certain succession, readily coming back into view at the same appointed times.

->*That beauty is natural even in the human intellect is apparent, because it*<-
->*renders raw matter beautiful. Chapter I.*<-

> *Art does not merely imitate the works of nature that it produces, but it does so even more through internal reasons, specifically when it corrects certain defects of nature. From this we conclude that the form of beauty in the mind is more excellent than in any work of art. Add that it is more powerful, because in the work it is scattered, but in the mind it is entirely unified.*

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial "E" featuring a portrait of a bearded man in profile, likely a philosopher.</image-desc> SINCE we say that the one who has become a spectator of the <term>intelligible world</term><note>The "intelligible world" is the realm of pure ideas and perfect forms, accessible only to the mind, not the physical senses.</note>, and who has perceived the beauty of the true Intellect, will then be able to understand its father—the one who is beyond Intellect—let us try to see and to tell ourselves, as far as such things can be told, <margin>B</margin> how one might behold the beauty of the Intellect and of that higher world. Let us imagine two stone masses placed near each other: one indeed unshaped and devoid of art, but the other already adorned by art into a statue of a God or even some human. If of a God, let it be a Grace or some Muse; if of a human, let it not be of any specific person, but rather one whom art has created out of all beautiful features.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial "Q" showing a group of several figures in a classical setting.</image-desc> SINCE we admit that the soul which contemplates the intelligible world, and perceives the beauty of true intellect, is able at some time to observe the father of this world—who is superior to the mind—come now, let us strive with our powers to see, and to express to ourselves <margin>B</margin> as much as such things can be explained, by what specific means we may be able to perceive the beauty of the mind and of that world. Imagine therefore two stony masses placed near each other: one of which is indeed unarranged and lacking the gift of art; the other, however, already sculpted by art into a statue, whether divine or human: and if divine, let it be a statue of some Grace, or a Muse; but if human, let it not be of any particular man, but rather of someone whom art has gathered from all beautiful things.

<summary>This page concludes a discussion on whether the number of individuals in the universe is finite before beginning a famous treatise on "Intelligible Beauty." <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the "formative reasons" (the spiritual blueprints of reality). It marks a transition into Ennead V.8, "On Intelligible Beauty," moving from a general discussion of quantity and Soul to a specific exploration of why we find things beautiful—specifically, whether beauty exists in the material itself or in the Idea (the Form) that shapes it.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> A stone, therefore, which has been arranged by art into the beauty of a **form** <note>original: "speciei" / "εἴδους". In Platonic thought, this refers to the 'Idea' or 'Form' that gives a thing its identity.</note>, will immediately appear beautiful, but not because it is a stone: otherwise, another lump of rock would appear equally handsome. It is beautiful, then, because it possesses the form which art has applied to it. This form was not in the material, but existed in the one who conceived it before it ever entered the stone. Moreover, it was in the craftsman, not by virtue of his having eyes and hands, but because he was endowed with art. This beauty, therefore, was in the art
<margin>B</margin> in a much more excellent way. For it is not the very form existing in the art that comes into the stone; rather, that form remains where it is, while another, lesser form proceeds from it. This latter form does not remain pure within itself, nor is it exactly as the craftsman desired, but is limited by the extent to which the material obeyed the art. If, however, art creates something that is and has such a quality, and creates beauty according to the <term>reason</term><note>original: "rationem" / "λόγον". This refers to the rational, formative principle or 'blueprint' that guides creation.</note> by which it acts, then surely the art itself is more truly beautiful, possessing the beauty of art, which is greater and more excellent than anything that proceeds outward.
<margin>C</margin> For to the extent that a form, in proceeding into matter, is extended, it becomes weaker than that form which remains in the one. Whatever suffers a distance within itself departs from itself: if it is strength, it weakens; if heat, it cools; if power in general, its power diminishes; if beauty, its beauty fades. Now, every primary producer must, in itself, be more excellent than the thing made: for it is not "un-music" that makes a musician, but Music itself, and the music in the sensible sound is generated by the music that exists above the senses.
<margin>D</margin> If anyone despises the arts because they produce by imitating nature, it must be answered, first, that natures also imitate other things. Furthermore, one must realize that the arts do not simply imitate what is seen with the eyes, but they run back to those very <term>reasons</term> from which nature itself consists and acts. Moreover, the arts create many things from themselves and add something extra where anything is lacking in perfection, since they possess beauty within themselves. Finally, Phidias
<margin>E</margin> himself could fashion <term>Jupiter</term><note>The King of the Gods; the Greek text uses "Zeus". Plotinus refers to the famous ivory and gold statue at Olympia.</note>, having imitated no spectacle perceived by the senses, but having imagined what Jupiter himself would look like if he ever wished to appear before our eyes.

---

->*Beauty in a natural work is a certain form, not impressed upon matter at random, but impressed by nature itself at the moment when nature most excellently dominates the matter.*<-

->Chapter II.<-

For this work is not beautiful because of its matter or its size: otherwise, whatever was more material or larger would also be more beautiful. Rather, it is beautiful by reason of a certain more excellent form, which is now rendered almost immaterial. From this, it follows that you are first seized by things as beautiful only when they have entered your vision and have been made spiritual there: and especially when they are contemplated most intensely. Finally, the "form" found in character and in disciplines, which is entirely immaterial, captures us with love because of its beauty. However, the immaterial beauty in nature is far more wonderful than that of art. For nature does not work by some acquired habit or from the outside like art, but by its own internal essence; by dominating with a marvelous ease, it displays beauty to matter.

---

<margin>A</margin> BUT for the present, let us set aside the arts. Let us consider those things whose works art is said to imitate: things made beautiful by nature—namely, rational animals and all irrational ones, especially those among them that are most perfectly finished. In these cases, the sculptor and builder of them, having dominated the matter, has applied the form he desired. What, then, is beauty in these things? For it is surely not the blood and the menses <note>A reference to the Aristotelian view of biological generation.</note>, but a color and a figure different from these, or else it would be nothing, or something without figure and discordant, or like that which contains some simple thing, such as matter.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It would appear, then, that the stone brought into the beauty of form by art is beautiful, <unclear>*</unclear> but not insofar as it is a stone: for otherwise the other stone would be beautiful in the same way. Rather, it is beautiful insofar as it is the form which the art introduced. This form, then, the matter did not have, but it was in the one who conceived it before it came into the stone. And it was in the craftsman, not insofar as he had eyes <unclear>*</unclear> and hands, but because he participated in art.
<margin>B</margin> This beauty, therefore, was in the art, and was much better. For that form which is in the art did not come into the stone; rather, that one remains, and another comes from it, lesser than that one. And that form is not pure in itself, nor as much as the craftsman wishes, but only as much as the stone yielded to the art. If the art makes and produces, and it produces according to the beauty of the <term>reason</term> by which it acts, it is more greatly and truly beautiful, having the beauty of the art, which is greater and more beautiful
<margin>C</margin> than that which is on the outside. For as much as it is poured out into the matter, by so much is it weaker than that which remains in the one. For every distance departs from itself: whether it be strength as strength, or heat if it be heat, or power in general as power, or beauty as beauty. And every primary producer must itself be better than the thing produced. For it is not "the unmusical" that makes a musician, but Music; and the music in the senses is produced by the music
<margin>D</margin> prior to this. But if anyone dishonors the arts because they produce by imitating nature, first we must say that natures also imitate other things. Then, one must know that they do not simply imitate the thing seen, but they run back to the <term>reasons</term> from which nature originates. Further, they also do many things from themselves, and they add to it if anything is lacking, since
<margin>E</margin> they possess beauty. For indeed Phidias, having made <term>Zeus</term><note>The Greek original for the Latin "Jupiter".</note>, did so according to nothing sensible, but having grasped what he would become if Zeus wished to appear to us through our eyes.

---

<margin>A</margin> But let the arts be dismissed by us: let us consider those things which the arts are said to imitate, which are produced and called beautiful by nature—both rational animals and all irrational ones. And especially those among them that are successful, where the one who molded them and crafted them dominated the matter and provided the form he wished. What then is beauty in these things? For it is surely not the blood and the menses: but either a color different from these, and a shape, or it is nothing, or the shapeless, or like that which contains something simple like matter.

<meta>Catchword: Whence (Vnde)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that beauty does not reside in the physical material of an object, but in the "form" or "reason" imparted by the creator, whether that creator is a human artist like Phidias or Nature itself. He posits that the internal idea in the mind of the artist is more perfect and beautiful than the finished physical work.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, aesthetics, form, matter, Phidias, Zeus, Jupiter, beauty, Neoplatonism, formative reasons, art vs nature</keywords>

--- Page 578 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on how beauty is not found in the physical matter itself, but in the artistic or rational "Form" (the Idea) that shapes it. Here, Plotinus moves from the example of a carved stone to the higher beauty of the human soul and the divine intellect.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> From where did the beauty of Helen arise, for which so great a contest was stirred up? From where did all those other forms similar to Venus shine forth? And indeed, from where did the very form of Venus herself rise? Or if any man is entirely beautiful, or a God—whether among those who come into our sight, or those who do not appear but possess a conspicuous beauty within themselves—from where does this come? Is not this **Form** everywhere, descending into that which is born from the very thing that generates it? Just as it was said regarding the arts,
<margin>B</margin> beauty proceeds into the works of art from the arts themselves. What then? Are the works beautiful indeed, and is the <term>reason</term><note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος" (logos). In this context, it refers to the spiritual blueprint or formative principle that gives shape to matter.</note> contained within the material? But the <term>reason</term> which is not in the material, but in the creator—the primary beauty, free from matter—is not [just] the beauty we see, but is reduced into a single unity. However, if a mass were beautiful simply because it is a mass, it would certainly follow that the active <term>reason</term> itself, because it is not a physical mass, is not beautiful. But if the same
<margin>C</margin> **Form**, whether in a small or a large mass, moves and affects the soul of the beholder by its power in the same way, then certainly beauty is not to be attributed to the physical size of the mass. From here again the same argument is taken: since we do not perceive the form insofar as it is outside the soul, nor are we moved by it; but when it is already conceived by the soul, it affects us. Yet the form of things flows in only through the eyes; otherwise, the greatest things could not penetrate through the narrowest passages. Indeed, magnitude itself is contracted, not as a large physical mass, but rather as a "great" **Form**.
<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, the cause of a beautiful effect must itself be either ugly, indifferent, or beautiful. If it were ugly, it certainly would not produce its opposite. If indifferent, why would it make something beautiful rather than ugly? But surely nature, the artisan of such beautiful things, is much earlier and more greatly beautiful. We, however, since we are accustomed to looking at nothing <unclear>clearly</unclear><note>The original text "lotis mus" is a likely OCR error for "totis minus" or "lotius," suggesting a lack of whole or deep perception.</note> and are completely ignorant of internal things, naturally follow external things, being ignorant meanwhile that what moves us lies hidden
<margin>E</margin> within—just as if someone, seeing his own image and not knowing where it came from, should follow that image. But that there is something else which draws those who follow it to itself, and that beauty does not consist in size, is evidenced by the beauty found in disciplines, duties, and throughout the soul: where certainly beauty truly flourishes more, specifically when you contemplate a certain wisdom in the soul. Having contemplated it, you are delighted and you love it, not looking then at the face of the
<margin>F</margin> body—which perhaps might not be shapely—but having set aside the entire form of the body, you follow the inward beauty. But if that soul does not yet move you to call it beautiful, nor do you delight in yourself as beautiful when looking inward at your own self, then you search for that true and internal beauty in vain; for you seek it with something not pure, but shameful. Therefore, words about such matters are not held for everyone. But if you see yourself as beautiful, then from here already remember beauty itself.

---

->*The beauty appearing in matter is a certain image of beauty, which flourishes more excellently in nature: But that image of it which is in the soul is greater than the intellect: This, finally, is the image of that which is first in the divine mind. Chapter III.*<-

->*The splendor of beauty shines out from the divine intellect into the head of the intellect of the soul, just as light from the Sun always shines into a star, and thereafter into the rational virtue of the soul as if into the Moon, insofar as it is turned toward higher things.*<-

Z 4 <note>This is a signature mark used by printers to keep the pages in order during binding.</note>

<summary>Plotinus argues that beauty does not reside in physical size or matter, but in the spiritual "Form" or "Reason" that originates in the Divine Mind and descends into the soul. He encourages the reader to look past physical appearances to find the true source of beauty within their own wisdom and character.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the nature of beauty. Plotinus is moving from the physical manifestation of beauty to its ultimate source in the Divine Intellect (the Nous). He argues that to perceive true beauty, the soul itself must be purified and transformed.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

In vain, however, does the soul seek what beauty itself is if it has not made itself most beautiful through such a conversion <note>original: "conversionem" — a turning inward of the soul's attention from the physical world to the spiritual.</note>. But if it has made itself so, then at some point, looking upon its own beauty, it will look up from there to higher things through its own <term>intellect</term><note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦς" (nous). In Neoplatonism, this is the Divine Mind or the realm of pure thought/forms.</note> now purified—just as one might find gold within a larger mass. It will contemplate the divine intellect as entirely pure gold, not to be sought in any other way. Furthermore, the primary beauty is the fullness of the first intelligence. The gods who are purely intellectual are beautiful gods through their participation in that beauty; through the same participation, the celestial gods <note>Plotinus refers here to the visible stars and planets, which he considered divine living beings.</note>—that is, all those in the world—are also gods. These celestial gods know divine things by a certain direct intuition, while they provide for and govern human affairs through a downward inclination. Finally, the purely intellectual gods, because they exist in the intellectual heaven, are said not to govern those things which exist by reason of them, but rather to contemplate them. Whatever is in the intellectual heaven is likewise entirely intelligible; for all things are there.

<margin>A</margin> THEREFORE, the <term>reason</term><note>original: "ratio" / "λόγος" (logos). Here meaning the formative principle or "blueprint" that gives structure to matter.</note> of beauty in nature is the archetype of this beauty which appears in the body; but the archetype of natural beauty is a certain more beautiful reason in the soul, from which the beauty of nature flowed. This is clearer in a virtuous soul, where beauty is already progressing—namely, adorning the soul and providing light from a greater light, which is also the primary beauty. Thus, I say, its existence in the soul leads one to reason out what <margin>B</margin> the superior principle of beauty might be, which no longer comes to be in anything else nor lies in another, but remains in itself. And so, it is not even a "reason" strictly speaking, but the author of the first reason: since the first reason is a kind of beauty within the soul as if in matter. But the author himself is the Intellect, who is always Intellect and never not-Intellect, since Intellect does not come to him from elsewhere. But what image of the Intellect itself shall we best receive? For whatever is sought from elsewhere will undoubtedly be sought from something inferior. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, the image of the Intellect must be sought from the Intellect itself, so that we do not speak of it through an image, but receive a certain sign of gold from the whole mass of gold. And unless the gold received is already pure, let us purify it either in fact or at least in speech, demonstrating that what we have received is not the whole of gold, but only a certain amount of gold in a mass. So, from this intellect which is in us, now purified, let us ascend to the Intellect itself on high: and if you please, let us proceed from the gods themselves, looking to see <margin>D</margin> what kind of intellect is in them. For all the gods are beautiful, graceful, and venerable, excelling in inestimable splendor. But what is it by which the gods are such? It is surely the Intellect; I say it is the Intellect acting most powerfully in them so that they are seen as such. For it is not because their bodies are beautiful; for even those who have bodies, this very fact is not what makes them gods, but they are gods <margin>E</margin> according to the mind. I say they are not judged to be beautiful gods because beautiful bodies are present to them. For they are not wise at one time and unwise at another, but they are perpetually wise with a tranquil, stable, and pure mind; they understand all things and know not properly human things, but their own—that is, divine things—and as many things as the Intellect itself discerns. Of the gods, those who inhabit the heaven have an abundance of leisure; they continually contemplate, but as if from a distance, the things that are in that first heaven itself, <margin>F</margin> with their heads held high. But those who are in that [Intellectual] heaven, as many as have been allotted a dwelling there, contemplate while inhabiting that whole heaven there. For all things there are heaven: the earth there is heaven; the sea, the animals, the plants, and the men there are heaven. Finally, whatever belongs to that heaven is heavenly. The gods who dwell there do not disdain men, nor anything else of the things that are there, for the very reason that they are of the number of divine beings; for they traverse that whole region and encompass the place while resting.

<column-break/>

THERE IS, therefore, a beauty of the <term>reason-principle</term><note>original: "λόγου" (logos).</note> in nature, which is the archetype of the beauty in the body; but that which is in nature is [derived from] the more beautiful one in the soul, from which comes the one in nature. This beauty in the soul is more manifest when the soul is already good and is greater, being a light flowing from the illumination of life. Since the first beauty exists, it causes one to reason—being itself in the soul—what the one before it is like, which no longer comes to be in another, nor is in another, but is in itself. Therefore, it is not even a reason-principle, but the creator of the first reason-principle, beauty not being in the soul as if in matter. Since the Intellect perceives all things, not as something brought in from outside, what image could one take for it? For all things are held by the inferior [image], but those through the image lead toward the Intellect; as if one were to take a sample not of all gold, but of a certain gold—and if the sample taken is not pure, one purifies it, either in deed or in word, showing that this is not [the whole of] gold, but something in a mass only. Thus also, the things with us having been purified by the intellect—or if you wish, starting from the gods—[consider] what the Intellect is in them. For they are venerable and they look upon beautiful things, and their beauty is immense. But what is it through which they are such, if not the Intellect? And indeed, it is rather because it is active in them so that it is seen. For it is not because their bodies are beautiful; and for those who have bodies, this is not what it is for them to be gods, but they are gods by having Intellect. And indeed, the gods are not wise at one time and foolish at another, but they are always wise in an impassive, stable, and pure Intellect. They know all things, and they know not human things, but their own divine things, and as many things as the Intellect sees. Of the gods, those who are in the [visible] heaven, living in leisure, always behold, as if from afar, the things in that very [Intellectual] heaven, by the excellence of their own "head" <note>This refers to the highest part of the soul or mind reaching toward the divine.</note>. But those who are in that [Intellectual] heaven, as many as have their dwelling upon it or in it, dwell in that whole heaven there. For all things there are heaven—the earth is heaven, the sea, and animals, and plants, and men—everything is heavenly from that heaven. The gods in it do not disdain men, nor anything else there because they are there; they traverse that whole land <margin>and divine things</margin> and the whole of it, while at rest.

<summary>Plotinus describes the hierarchy of beauty, moving from physical bodies to the soul, and finally to the Divine Intellect (Nous). He explains that the gods are beautiful and wise because of their participation in this pure, stable Intellect, which exists in an 'Intellectual Heaven' where all things are divine and interconnected.</summary>

# BOOK EIGHT.

> *Above the physical heaven, there are incorporeal heavens of two kinds: the intelligible and the intellectual. The former are the Ideas; the latter are all the individual Intellects who are blessed by the eternal contemplation of those Ideas.*
->Chapter 4.<-

*The divine <term>Intellect</term><note>original: "Intellectus" / "νοῦς" (nous). The second principle in Neoplatonism, representing the realm of perfect, eternal forms.</note> flows into the <term>Ideas</term><note>original: "ideas." The eternal archetypes or blueprints of all things.</note> in such a way that it is preserved whole within each one, yet with a different character in each. Truly, it should not be said that the Idea is merely in the Intellect, but rather that the Intellect exists as the Ideas themselves—wondrously producing a world of many forms from its own uniform nature. Just as the physical heaven expresses itself in the stars, yet the whole heaven is present in every star, so too are all the stars present in each, though with different qualities. Therefore, when <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher famous for the doctrine that "everything is in everything."</note> Anaxagoras says that "everything is in everything," this does not apply to our sub-celestial world (where unity is minimal) as much as it does to the super-celestial world (where unity is maximal). It also applies in a moderate way to the visible heavens. Here, Plotinus proves that those who contemplate divine things will never depart from them. Consider what <note>Porphyry and Iamblichus were later Neoplatonist philosophers who expanded on Plotinus' work.</note> Porphyry and Iamblichus touched upon: that our own souls can reach a similar state of happiness. "He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved forever." "Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you forever and ever."* <note>original: "Non commouebitur in æternum qui habitat in Hierusalem" and "Beati qui habitant in domo tua domine..." Plotinus’ Christian-era translators often blended Platonic philosophy with Latin Vulgate biblical quotes (Psalms 125 and 84).</note>

<margin>A</margin> For even the living beings there <note>referring to the inhabitants of the Intelligible World</note> are perfect. Truth is their parent, their nurse, and their very essence. All things there are wise and beautiful—not with the fleeting beauty of these physical suns, but with the true beauty that these only resemble. For all things there are transparent; nothing is dark or resistant. Everyone is manifest to everyone else in their innermost being, and all things are clear. For light meets light. <margin>B</margin> Each inhabitant possesses all things within themselves, and in turn sees all things in every other. Thus, all things are everywhere, and everything is the whole. Each individual part is also the whole, and the radiance there is infinite. For each of them is great, since even that which is small is great there. The sun there is all the stars, and each star is in turn the sun and all the stars. A particular quality excels in each, yet all things are visible in every one. Movement there is <margin>C</margin> pure; for as it proceeds, it does not throw things into confusion because it is not distinct from the stability of the motion. Rest is also there, undisturbed by change, because it is not mixed with that which is unstable. Beauty is simply beauty, because it does not reside in something that is not beautiful. Each being walks not as if on foreign soil, but is itself the very place where it exists. As it ascends, its origin follows with it. The being is not one thing while its location is another. For the very foundation is <margin>D</margin> Intellect, and the being itself is Intellect. It is as if one were to imagine this visible, luminous heaven producing and growing stars out of its own light. In physical things, one part does not arise from every other part; each part is only itself. But there, every part arises from the whole, and every part is simultaneously the whole. A part may appear as a part, but to one with keen sight, the whole is visible—<margin>E</margin> just as it is said that <note>Lynceus was an Argonaut in Greek mythology, famous for sight so sharp he could see through trees, stones, and into the ground.</note> Lynceus could see into the very depths of the earth. This myth, I believe, signifies the piercing vision of the higher "eyes" of the soul. Furthermore, we must believe that those who see these things never grow weary of the sight, nor are they ever so satisfied that they stop looking. For there was no emptiness in them that, once filled, would lead to a stopping point; nor is one thing so different from another that the parts of one would be unpleasing to the other. Moreover, everything there is untamed and tireless. If we call it "insatiable," <note>original: "inexplebile." In this context, it means a fullness that never leads to boredom or "having enough."</note> it is because its fullness never causes one to despise that which fills them. By seeing, one sees even more clearly; and

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> This is the goal of the teachings found in Plato’s *Phaedrus*: that the divine beings there lead an easy life, and that Truth itself is their mother, their nurse, their essence, and their nourishment. They see all things—not those things subject to change and "becoming," but those things that exist in true essence. They also see themselves in others. For all things there are transparent from every side. Nothing there is shadowy, nothing is an obstacle; rather, everyone there is visible to everyone else, inwardly and through all things. For <margin>B</margin> light meets light everywhere. Everyone has all things within themselves and beholds all things in another. Therefore, all things are everywhere. Everything there is the whole. There, any part you choose is the universe. An immeasurable splendor shines there. For everything there is great, since even the small is great in that place. The sun and all the stars are there. Every star is a sun, and all are stars likewise. While one quality <margin>C</margin> may stand out in each, nevertheless all things are seen in every single one. Movement there is undoubtedly pure; for it does not confuse the one who moves with a motion foreign to it. Stability is also never disturbed by change, for it is not mixed with an unstable nature. Furthermore, Beauty itself is beauty, because it does not lie within a beautiful object <note>meaning it is the source of beauty itself, not just a beautiful thing.</note>. Truly, everyone remains not as if on a foreign pavement, but each has their own foundation, which is the very thing they are. And as one rises, they coincide with the very source from which they exist. The being is not one thing and its seat another; for the <margin>D</margin> underlying subject is Intellect, and it is itself Intellect. It is as if one were to imagine this heaven, which is visible and bright to our eyes, germinating and growing into stars through its own light. In corporeal things, one part does not emerge from every other part; rather, each part is only itself. But there, any part you choose emerges from the whole, and each part exists simultaneously as the whole. A part appears, but it is also seen as the whole by one who perceives keenly—as <margin>E</margin> Lynceus is said to have been in his vision, who is recorded to have penetrated the depths of the earth with the rays of his eyes. This fable, I think, signified the perspicacity of the higher eyes. Furthermore, it must be understood that those who see those things are never exhausted by seeing, nor are they ever led by any satiety to stop their vision. For there was no void in anyone that, once filled and satisfied, would bring an end to მათი gazing. Nor is this thing one way and that thing another, such that the things in one would be displeasing to the other. Moreover, all things there are uncurbed and indefatigable. <meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the nature of the Intelligible World. Plotinus is moving from the description of the "Intellectual Heaven" to a deeper investigation of Divine Wisdom and how it differs from human reasoning.</meta>

# PLOTINUS' ENNEADS BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> ...beholding its own infinite self and the things it sees, it follows its own nature as its guide. Indeed, this life is never laborious, for it is a pure life; and why should that which lives in the best way feel any toil? Life in that realm is wisdom—a wisdom not acquired through logical arguments <note>original: "nullis argumentationibus comparata"</note>, for it has always been complete, lacking no part that would require a search for answers. This is the primary wisdom, not depending on any other; in that realm, <term>Essence</term><note>original: "essentia" / "οὐσία" (ousia). In Neoplatonism, this refers to true being or reality as it exists in the divine realm.</note> itself is wisdom. It is not that the <term>Intellect</term> exists first and then later becomes wise. <margin>B</margin> For this reason, no wisdom is greater than this. In that place, the very science of the mind is its own companion, as they exist together; just as tradition says, in a kind of imitation, that Judgment and Justice are the companions of Zeus <note>original: "Iouis" / "Διὸς" (Zeus/Jupiter). Plotinus refers to the Platonic idea from the "Phaedrus" that divine qualities are inherent assessors or "colleagues" to the divine mind.</note>. For all things of this kind exist there as if they were statues—or rather, they are the living original archetypes, clear within themselves and everywhere visible, so that the sight of them is a joy beyond even that of the most blessed spectators. <margin>C</margin> One can best consider the greatness and power of this wisdom because it contains and has created all things. For all things that are truly real follow wisdom and exist through it; they arose together with it, and both are one in their essence. Finally, in that realm, essence is wisdom. We, however, do not yet reach this knowledge because we think of sciences as mere speculations, rules, or a collection of propositions—but this is not even true of our own sciences. <margin>D</margin> If anyone doubts our earthly sciences, let us set that aside for now; but it seems worthwhile to start again and discuss that science which Plato <note>A reference to Plato's "Phaedrus" (247e), describing the soul's vision of true knowledge which is not "different in different things."</note> looked upon with awe when he said: "That science is not one thing in one person and another in another." It remains for us to seek and find how this can be, if we consider ourselves worthy of such a name.

->*Since art imitates nature, and nature imitates God, and art acts through a certain wisdom, while God acts through wisdom itself simply, it follows that nature acts through its own indwelling wisdom. Chapter V.*<-

*If all things attain their essence through wisdom, it follows that primary wisdom is primary essence. Wisdom gained through effort, which is human art, depends on the wisdom innate within us and imitates the wisdom of nature. Because these three types of wisdom exist in something else, they must be traced back to the primary wisdom, which exists in itself—where it is seen that wisdom itself is essence. The wisdom of human art is gathered from many acts of meditation and speech; but the wisdom naturally implanted in us, and the wisdom of nature and God, is a single form presenting itself as all-encompassing—like a single face, not like a speech or a long argument. For before the "one" gathered from "many," there is the "One" that unfolds itself into the many, and before this itself is the absolute One.*

<margin>A</margin> **WHATEVER** is made either by art or by nature, it is a certain wisdom that makes it, and wisdom guides the action everywhere. If a certain wisdom is produced anywhere, let such things be called the "arts." But the craftsman himself is, in turn, traced back to natural wisdom, according to which art and every work are performed. I say "according to which" it is no longer a wisdom gathered from speculations, but is a single whole; not composed of many parts into one, but rather a single thing resolving itself into many. <margin>B</margin> If someone, therefore, posits that this wisdom is primary, that will suffice; for since it does not come from another, it will not exist in another. But if someone says that <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "rationem" / "λόγον" (logos). Here meaning the formative principle or blueprint.</note> is in nature, and that nature is the principle of this reason, we shall ask from where nature receives its reason.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...beholding itself as infinite and seeing the things beheld, it follows its own nature. And life has no toil when it is pure. For what would the best life toil at? This life is a wisdom that encompasses all, bringing no calculations <note>original: "λογισμοὺς" (logismous). Human reasoning that moves from point A to point B.</note> because it always possessed everything and lacked nothing that would require a search. It is the first wisdom, not from another. And essence itself is wisdom; it does not belong to essence, as if essence were merely "wise." <margin>B</margin> Because of this, no wisdom is greater. And self-knowledge is there; these things are the assessors of the Mind, appearing together with it, just as they say, by way of imitation, that Justice and Law are the assessors of Zeus, etc. And such things are there, like statues seen within it, making it a spectacle for blessed spectators. <margin>C</margin> One might understand the greatness of this wisdom from the things that exist through it, because it holds all things with it and has made all things. For all things that truly exist are beautiful there, and both are there together. And where there is wisdom, there is essence. We, however, in our own knowledge, are not yet quite there; for we still think of sciences as certain theorems and a heap of propositions—but this also applies to our own sciences. <margin>D</margin> If someone disputes these things, it would be a matter for the present. But concerning the science there, which Plato looked upon and spoke of, saying it is the science that is "not one thing in another," it remains for us to seek and find how it is, if indeed we claim to be worthy of the name; perhaps it is better if we make this our starting point.

<margin>A</margin> **ALL** things that come to be, whether by art or by nature, are made by a certain wisdom, and wisdom is the making and the action everywhere. But if it is wisdom that makes the wisdom [of the arts], let the arts be such. But the craftsman, in turn, comes to the signs of nature according to which he was made. It is no longer composed of theorems, but is a certain whole—not something enclosed from many into one, but rather something being analyzed from many into one. <margin>B</margin> If someone sets this as the first wisdom, it is enough. For it will no longer be *from another. And even if one were to say* <note>The Greek text here is slightly fragmented in the transcription.</note> that reason is in nature, and then say that nature is the principle, we will ask where it gets this one...

<summary>Plotinus argues that divine Wisdom is identical to divine Essence, existing as a complete whole rather than a collection of logical propositions. He explains that human art and natural processes are both reflections of this primary, non-discursive Wisdom which unfolds itself into the multiplicity of the world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Divine Wisdom. The author, Plotinus, is arguing that in the higher realm of the Intellect, wisdom is not a series of logical steps or sentences, but a direct, unified "vision" of reality itself. He uses the example of Egyptian hieroglyphics to illustrate this concept.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT. <note>original: "LIBER OCTAVVS". In this edition, this refers to the eighth treatise of the Fifth Ennead, titled "On Intelligible Beauty."</note>

And if that wisdom is held from another, we shall ask again about that other; but if it holds wisdom from itself, then we shall rest there. Furthermore, if they flee to the <term>Intellect</term><note>original: "mens" / "νοῦς" (nous). The divine or cosmic mind.</note> itself, we must investigate there again whether the Intellect generated wisdom. If they admit this, we ask: from where? If it was conceived from within themselves, it could not have done so unless the Intellect itself were wisdom. Therefore, true <term>Essence</term><note>original: "essentia" / "οὐσία" (ousia). True, unchanging reality.</note> is wisdom, and in turn, true essence is wisdom. The very dignity of essence is claimed by wisdom. For it is certain <margin>B</margin> that true essence comes from wisdom. For this reason, whatever essences do not possess wisdom—though they are indeed "essences" because they were made through a certain wisdom—are not *true* essences because they do not possess wisdom within themselves. Therefore, no one should think that in the <term>intelligible world</term><note>The realm of pure ideas and divine reality, as opposed to the physical world.</note>, either the gods themselves or other blessed inhabitants are contemplating certain rules of propositions; rather, each of the things said to be there offers itself to those who look upon them as certain beautiful models and spectacles—such as one might imagine to exist in the soul of a wise man. I speak not of painted images, but of real existences; for this reason, the ancients called the <term>Ideas</term><note>The eternal archetypes or blueprints of all things.</note> both "beings" and "essences."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But if it is said to be had from another, we shall ask again about that other; and if it has it from itself, we shall rest there. Accordingly, if they take refuge in the mind itself, it must be investigated there again, whether the mind generated wisdom. If they confess this, from where did it come? If it was conceived from themselves, it could not have done so unless the mind itself is wisdom. Therefore, true wisdom is essence; and true essence, in turn, is wisdom. The very dignity of essence is claimed by wisdom. For it is established <margin>B</margin> that true essence is from wisdom. Therefore, whatever essences do not have wisdom are essences in the sense that they were made through a certain wisdom, but because they possess no wisdom in themselves, they are not true essences. No one, therefore, ought to think that in the intelligible world, either the gods themselves or the other more than happy inhabitants there, contemplate certain rules of propositions, but rather that each of the things said to be there present themselves to those who gaze as certain beautiful models and spectacles, such as someone might perhaps imagine to exist in the soul of a wise man. I say, however, not depicted images, but existences; wherefore the ancients called the ideas "beings" and "essences."

> *The Egyptian priests, to signify divine mysteries, did not use the tiny characters of letters, but whole figures of herbs, trees, and animals: because, clearly, God has knowledge of things not as a complex thought about a thing, but as a simple and firm form of the thing.*
<margin>Chapter VI.</margin>
> *The conception of time with you is complex and shifting, saying for instance that time is swift, and by a certain revolution joins the beginning again with the end; it teaches prudence, brings things forth, and carries them away. But the Egyptian comprehends this whole discourse in a single firm figure, painting a winged serpent, grasping its tail with its mouth <note>This refers to the Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of infinity and the cyclical nature of time.</note>; and other things with similar figures which Horus describes.*

---

It seems to me that the wise men of Egypt—whether by a certain perfect knowledge or a natural instinct of the mind—when they decided to signify the mysteries of wisdom to us, did not use the forms of letters which signify the discourses of speech and certain propositions, nor did they imitate the sounds and pronunciations of rules. Instead, they described the individual images of individual things, and by depicting them, they signified the discourse of the thing itself in their temples. For <margin>B</margin> clearly, each image is a kind of science and wisdom, a model and a subject, a whole spectacle collected into one; it is neither a step-by-step thought nor a plan. Afterward, from that model-image or wisdom which is a whole, a likeness is made in something else which is now "unfolded," and which speaks in a kind of discourse, finding the causes why things were so established. For the arrangement of things, because it is so well-ordered, moves us to admiration. Hence <margin>C</margin> he says that one will admire wisdom who considers how wisdom itself—not having the causes of its own essence as to why it is so or acts so—nevertheless provides that it should be so for those things which are made according to it. This very thing, then, which can be called the "order of things" (that is, that things are well-arranged), though it is hardly made manifest by inquiry (for it is clear that things *must* be this way), if someone should find it, I say, this very thing must exist and stand firm in the intelligible world before all inquiry and reasoning. But let us now take this in one "great" thing I am speaking of, which is consistent with all things.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It seems to me that the wise men of Egypt, whether by some refined science or by a natural instinct, when they wished to demonstrate things through wisdom, did not go through discourses of words and propositions using the types of letters, nor did they imitate the sounds and utterances of axioms. Instead, by drawing images and carving an image of each thing in the temples, they manifested the discourse of that thing. Thus, each image is a kind of science and wisdom, a substrate and a whole, not a process of discursive thinking nor a deliberation. Later, from this "whole" image, there is an unfolded representation in something else which now speaks in a discourse and mentions the causes why it has found things to be so. Thus, someone who knows how to wonder at the way things are so well-ordered, he says, would wonder at this wisdom: how, without having the causes of its essence for why it provides things in this way, it nevertheless provides them to those things made according to it. This is well, then, even if it is a matter of faith for them, or <margin>* says, until</margin> as the opinion says, until we say that it must be so; if someone should find it out without questioning and without reasoning, it exists in this way. Let us, therefore, take it in the case of one "great" thing, which I am saying, which will fit all things.

<sig>Z 4</sig>

<summary>Plotinus explains that in the divine realm, wisdom is not a series of logical thoughts but a direct, unified reality. He compares this to Egyptian hieroglyphics, where a single image (like the serpent biting its tail) represents a complex concept all at once, rather than through sentences.</summary>

--- Page 583 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Divine Wisdom. In the previous section, Plotinus compared true wisdom to Egyptian hieroglyphics—direct, non-discursive images rather than a series of logical steps. He now moves to explain how the "Craftsman" of the world (the Demiurge) creates the universe not through planning or effort, but through a natural, unified expression of His own essence.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

### The knowledge of God is not like reasoning or deliberation, but rather like a natural disposition. Chapter VII.

> *For He does not first set down principles and then collect a conclusion through middle terms, nor does He, having established an end, proceed consequently along a path, choosing how to achieve that end and then acting—as those who deliberate do. Rather, because He is by His own nature already disposed toward all things, He therefore exists and acts naturally. Just as a seed is formed in many ways and thus generates a multifaceted offspring, so too that "all-formed" nature of God is His very intelligence. It is the presence of all things at once—not like a tablet with figures drawn on it, but like the sky with stars, which are themselves one. He acts with the greatest ease because He acts by His own nature, and He Himself is the Totality. Our soul acts in much the same way when it recalls itself to its all-formed state.*

---

<margin>A</margin> Do we truly believe that this universe, which we grant was established by another and exists as such, was composed by its craftsman in such a way that he first mentally conceived of the Earth, and that it ought to rest in the middle? And then the water following the Earth, and the other elements arranged in order all the way to the sky? And then all the animals, with the specific forms of each living thing as they now are, and the arrangement of their internal organs as well as their external parts and <margin>B</margin> limbs? And that after he had arranged each thing within himself, he then set about the work of physically arranging them? 

But surely, such deliberation could not have existed in Him. For from where would it have occurred to one who had not yet seen such things? Nor indeed was it possible for him to manufacture them by receiving instructions from someone else, in the way our craftsmen work today, using hands and tools; for hands and feet are later additions to the process of creation. It remains, then, that all things exist within "the Other" <note>The "Other" here refers to the Intelligible realm or the Divine Mind.</note>, and since no obstacle intervenes, by the very proximity of <term>Being</term><note>original: "entis" / "ὄντος". The fundamental reality of the Intelligible world.</note> to something else, its image and likeness suddenly flash forth—whether directly from itself, or through the <margin>C</margin> mediation of the Soul. 

For it makes no difference at present whether it is through a specific Soul; the point is that all these things flowed entirely from that source, and they are more beautiful there than here. For here they are mixed, but there they are pure. This entire universe, proceeding from that source, is encompassed by <term>Forms</term><note>original: "speciebus" / "εἴδεσι" (eidos). The eternal patterns or blueprints of all things.</note> from beginning to end. <margin>D</margin> First, forms appear in the matter of the elements, to which other forms are added, and then others still, so that it is difficult to find matter itself, hidden as it is under so many layers of forms. 

But because matter itself possesses a certain final form, it can easily receive every future form. That Craftsman, in whose power is the "Exemplar" <note>The perfect model or blueprint of the world.</note> of the work, produces all forms. He does this without difficulty or violence, because the acting force there is the Totality, the Essence, and the Form. <margin>E</margin> For this reason, the making was easy and without labor for the Craftsman, and He stood forth as the maker of the whole, just as the Craftsman is Himself the Totality. Therefore, there was no impediment, and even now He reigns freely in the act of making. 

And although elsewhere some things may be an impediment to others, nothing can stand in the way of the making of the universe, even now; for it stands as a complete whole. I believe, indeed, that if we ourselves were the primary models of things—their essences and forms—and if the <margin>F</margin> very form that acts here were our own essence, our "craftsmanship" would rule without labor. However, a human being, because he is now a finished product, crafts a form that is different from himself. For having become a "man," he has ceased to be the Totality. But when he ceases to be a man, as Plato says <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus* (246c), suggesting that the soul, when perfected, "governs the whole world."</note>, he raises himself to the heights and governs the whole world. For having become part of the whole, he also makes the whole. But to return to our purpose...

<column-break/>

<note>The second column contains the original Greek text of the passage translated above. The marginal notes in the Greek column indicate variant readings or clarifications of the text, such as "in all things" or "by proximity."</note>

<meta>catchword: potes</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the creation of the universe by the Divine Mind (the Demiurge) is not a process of planning or labor, but a natural, spontaneous expression of its "all-formed" essence. He suggests that when humans transcend their individual limitations, they can participate in this universal governance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the "Intellectual Beauty" (Ennead V.8). Having previously argued that divine creation is not a result of manual labor or discursive planning, he now explains that the physical structure of the universe—such as the Earth's position and the tilt of the zodiac—arises naturally from the perfection of the Divine Mind. He transitions into a discussion on the nature of Beauty itself as a unified whole.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

You might suggest a cause for all these things—why the Earth is in the middle, and why the zodiac <note>The "oblique circle" or ecliptic path of the sun.</note> is slanted. Even if this reasoning was considered by the Governor <note>The Demiurge or Divine Craftsman.</note> because He so willed it, it is not that He willed it and *then* it became so; rather, because it is good as it exists, it was willed. It is not like a conclusion in a syllogism <note>A formal logical argument.</note> where the result is derived from preceding premises through a sequence of thought. Instead, it exists before truth and before thought. All these things—reason, demonstration, and faith—are posterior to it. Since the Principle is itself the source, all things exist in this way, and it is rightly said that one should not seek the causes of a Principle, especially one so perfect that it is identical with its end. For the Principle and the End are the whole together, lacking nothing.

**The first beauty is a kind of multiform form, suited to the sight; therefore, the first Principle is superior even to beauty.**

### Chapter VIII.

**The Divine Mind is the first "whole," therefore it is whole in every one of its parts. It is also the first beauty, so it is total beauty in every part. Beneath it are three most beautiful goods: the Divine Mind, the Soul of the World, and the Body of the World—just as in the heavens we see the Sun, Jupiter, and Venus. Those captivated by "Venus" <note>Symbolizing physical or lower beauty.</note> do not know what they experience, for they do not realize they admire the lower beauty only because of the higher.**

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> You can indeed assert a cause for why the Earth is placed in the middle, and why it is round, or why the oblique circle <note>The zodiac.</note> was established in a certain region. In the Divine Mind, however, it was not deliberated upon because "it ought to be so." Rather, because it exists as it does, these things are therefore well-ordered. It is as if the conclusion itself stood firm without any propositions, prior to an argument running through causes. For nothing there depends on consequence; nothing is made certain through <margin>B</margin> consideration. Instead, the whole consists before any consequence or consideration. For all these—reason, demonstration, and faith—are later developments. Because the Principle exists, all these things are from it by their own nature and are thus disposed. Now, as for the saying that "one must not seek the causes of the Principle," it is rightly said, especially regarding such a Principle that is perfect, and which is the same as the End. Truly, that which is simultaneously the Principle and the End is the entire universe at once, failing in no part.

<margin>A</margin> This, therefore, is the first beauty: it is the whole, and it is the whole everywhere, so that there is no defect of beauty even in any single part. What, then, shall we call beauty itself? Certainly not anything that is not the "whole" itself, but only possesses a part or possesses nothing of it. Surely, if that is not beauty itself, what else could be? For that which is before it <note>The One, which is above the Divine Mind.</note> does not even wish to be "beautiful." For that which first comes into our sight, <margin>B</margin> because it is a "Form" <note>original: *species* or *eidos*</note> and a spectacle of the mind, is lovely and pleasant to the sight. Wherefore Plato, wishing to signify this to us—bringing the architect of the world <note>The Demiurge.</note> forward as approving his own perfect work—aimed at something more manifest to our minds. Through this, he wished to show that the beauty of the Exemplar <note>The ideal model or World of Forms.</note> and the Idea is lovable. For whenever someone admires a work fabricated according to a model, he primarily admires the model itself. <margin>C</margin> Nor should it seem strange if, in the meantime, the observer is ignorant of what he is experiencing. For even lovers, and generally all who admire this earthly beauty of ours, are ignorant that they are so affected because of the heavenly beauty—and yet, they are indeed affected because of it. Regarding the fact that Plato refers back to the divine Exemplar, saying the architect of the world loved his own work, he declares that He was delighted by the very sight of it. There he purposefully adds: <margin>D</margin> "He was indeed delighted by his handiwork, and even more, he wished to make it similar to the Exemplar itself." By this, he demonstrates what kind of beauty the Exemplar has, because he calls the world an "image." Truly, unless that Model were wonderfully beautiful, possessing an inestimable beauty, what could be more beautiful than this universe visible to our eyes? Therefore, those who disparage the beauty of this world do not judge correctly—unless, perhaps, in their disparagement they mean only that this world is not the heavenly one itself.

<summary>Plotinus explains that the order of the physical world is a natural reflection of the Divine Mind's perfection, not the result of a step-by-step logical plan. He argues that physical beauty is merely an image of a higher, "Exemplar" beauty, which is the true source of our admiration.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the eighth book of Plotinus's fifth Ennead, titled "On Intellectual Beauty." The previous page concluded with the idea that the Divine Mind (the Intellect) is a unified whole where the beginning and end are one. Here, Plotinus provides a famous meditative exercise—the "transparent sphere"—to help the reader transition from perceiving the physical world to grasping the divine, intelligible realm.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

*When you have grasped this whole variety of worldly forms together, and have immediately gathered their forms and motions into one, then strip away their spatial extension. You will then have the Soul of the World, in which all things exist within every form. Next, take away the motions, while keeping the forms in a state of rest; you now have the Divine Mind <note>Also translated as the 'Intellect' or 'Nous.'</note>, where every Idea contains all others. Finally, when the diversity of Ideas is resolved into a single light, you have reached the First Principle.*

->Chapter IX.<-

The corporeal <note>Physical or bodily.</note> world is not truly great, for it depends everywhere on small things. The incorporeal <note>Spiritual or non-physical.</note> world is infinite. One may say it is infinite because all things are present within this Idea. And as all these things are joined together, in any one part there are again all things, and so on in succession. Since primary essence and beauty are the same, it follows that insofar as something participates in beauty, it also participates in essence, and vice versa. Likewise, since the first essence is itself simply the Species <note>The 'Form' or 'Ideal.'</note>, it is by participation in the Species that all things possess their essence.

---

<margin>A</margin>Let us, therefore, take this world of ours and grasp it in our thought in such a way that each part remains what it is, yet they all reside within one another. Let us imagine, I say, all things gathered together into one as much as possible, so that whatever individual thing first presents itself to the eyes—for instance, an outer sphere—there immediately follows the sight of the Sun, and along with it the image of the other stars. Let the earth, the sea, and all living creatures be seen within it, as if in a <margin>B</margin>transparent sphere where everything is visible. In short, let it be possible to see everything within each thing. Let there be in the soul a bright imagination of a sphere that holds all things within itself, whether they are in motion or at rest—or rather, some moving and others stable. Keep this in your mind, but then imagine another thing beside it: strip away the mass <note>Original Latin: 'molem'; Greek: 'ogkos.' This refers to physical bulk or volume.</note>. Remove also the location, and cast far away from yourself every imagination of matter. Do not, however, imagine this second thing to be smaller in mass than the first. <margin>C</margin>Then, calling upon the God who made the world (of which you now have an image), pray humbly that He may come. He will come suddenly, bringing His own world with Him, along with all the gods who are within Him. He will come being one and at the same time all; and each god will come being all, bringing all with them as they gather into one. There, truly, all the gods differ in their powers, but by that one many-powered force, they are all one God; rather, one God is all of them. For <margin>D</margin>that one does not fail so that all those others might be born. They are all together, yet each is again separate from the other in a state that is in no way distant, displaying no form that is subject to the senses. Otherwise, one would be in one place and another elsewhere, and each would not exist as a whole within itself. Nor, again, does any of them have parts different from others or from itself; nor is each thing there a "whole" only as a divine power measured out into <margin>E</margin>as many parts as there are. Rather, the whole is a universal power proceeding into infinity, and infinite in its virtue. Indeed, that world is so vast that its parts also turn out to be infinite. For where can one say anything exists where that world has not already reached? This world of ours is also great, and all powers are within it together; but it would be even greater—inexplicably so—if there were no small power of the body within it. And if someone speaks of the great <margin>F</margin>powers of fire and the other elements, they nonetheless consist of an infinity of true power; and it is through ignorance of this that they seem to be something and to act by destroying, breaking, and serving the generation of animals.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>This world, then—while each of its parts remains what it is—let us confuse <note>In the sense of 'fusing together' (Greek: 'syncheomen').</note> it, and let us take it in our thought as all things together into one as much as possible. So that when any one part appears—for example, if the outer sphere exists—there follows immediately the mental image of the sun, and together with it the other stars, and the earth, and the sea, and all living creatures are seen, as if upon a <margin>B</margin>transparent sphere. For in all parts, all things are seen to be present. Let there be, then, in the soul a certain luminous mental image of a sphere, having all things in itself, whether moving or standing still, or some moving and some standing still. Keeping this, take another for yourself, having stripped away the bulk; strip away the places also, and the phantom of matter within you, and do not try to take another that is smaller in <margin>C</margin>bulk. But having called upon the God who made that of which you have the phantom, pray for Him to come. And may He come bringing His own world, with all the gods in it, being one and all, and each being all, coming together into one. They are different in their powers, but in that one many-powered power they are rather one, all of them. For the whole is one, and they do not live by His life <note>Meaning they do not have a separate life 'borrowed' from Him, but are the life itself.</note>, but each is also separate in turn, in an extension without distance <margin>D</margin>, holding the sensible <note>Objects perceptible by the senses.</note> in a similar state. For one is not in one place, and another in another. Nor again is it divided, or a whole if an age <note>The Greek 'aion' (eternity/age) here refers to the eternal nature of the Intellect.</note> is one thing in some and another in others, or in itself. Nor does a divided power hold each thing as a whole, as if the power were only as much as the measured parts. But it is all, every <margin>E</margin>power, going into the infinite, and being capable into the infinite. And that world is great, so that even its parts become infinite. For it has everything to say. Because it will not be preceded <note>Nothing comes before it or limits it.</note>, this heaven is indeed great, and all the powers in it. But it would be even greater—so much so one could not say—if there were not some small power of body joined to it. And as for the great natures, the powers of fire and the other bodies, they are <margin>F</margin> forms <unclear>glimmering</unclear> by an infinity of true power, and people think they <unclear>perish</unclear> and are altered, and work together toward the generation of animals. But while these are perishable... <note>The text cuts off here mid-sentence.</note>

<summary>Plotinus describes a mental exercise where the reader imagines the physical universe as a transparent sphere, then strips away its physical dimensions to reveal the unified, infinite nature of the Divine Mind. In this intelligible realm, every part contains the whole, and all divine beings exist as a single, multi-powered unity.</summary>
