# BOOK EIGHT.

Physical things pass away and are generated in turn because they are themselves produced. But the power that flourishes there <note>In the intelligible or spiritual realm.</note> possesses only Being, and only Beautiful Being. For where could there be anything beautiful that was deprived of Being itself? Where, again, could Essence <term>Essentia: the fundamental reality of a thing</term> exist if it lacked the presence of Beauty? For if beauty is taken away, essence is removed also. Therefore, Being itself is desirable because it is the same as the Beautiful; and in turn, the Beautiful is lovable because it is also Being. Whether one is the cause of the other is not worth investigating, since the nature of both is one. This false essence of bodies, therefore, requires a certain image of beauty coming from the outside so that it may both appear beautiful and be something at all. For it exists only insofar as it has been made a participant in beauty, which consists of the Form itself. And the more of this small beauty it receives, the more perfect it becomes; for thus a beautiful essence becomes more truly its own, and <margin>B</margin> it finally becomes beauty itself.

<column-break/>

->Together with Jupiter—that is, the Soul of the World—all celestial, demonic, and purified human souls enjoy the whole divine world.<-
->Chapter X.<-

Even if there <note>In the divine realm.</note> individuals contemplate the same whole, some nonetheless attend to different parts more closely and eagerly, toward which the others are, in a way, principally referred. There, Beauty itself is primarily that universal splendor shining from the entire series of Ideas, which are like stars. The power of the entire Intellect, unless a most burning love is added, perhaps reaches only as far as looking upon that beauty as something external. But when love approaches, it transfers the contemplator into that beauty, and vice versa: so much so that the lover-contemplator now sees himself as beautiful—indeed, as having become beauty itself. Plotinus agrees with what Plato says: that philosophers alone walk with Jupiter, sent by Jupiter. For other men are devoted to specific and individual things; the philosopher alone embraces the universe, and Jupiter is the Soul of the Universe.

---

For the reasons stated above, Jupiter himself <note>Zeus/Jupiter here represents the 'World Soul' leading all existence back to the source.</note>, though he is the oldest of the other gods whom he leads, goes forth first to contemplate the intelligible world. He is then followed by the other gods, daemons, and souls who are able to perceive these things. That divine world shines upon them from above, arising from a certain hidden and lofty place, illuminating all the divinities and filling each one with light. Then indeed, it stirs those lower souls, who subsequently turn toward it, though they are not yet strong enough to look upon it as if it were the Sun. But some indeed see clearly, held upright by it and easily enduring its gaze; others, however, are troubled, as many as stand further away from its nature. When each who is able sees, they all look up at it and what belongs to it, yet each one does not always bring back the same vision. But while they gaze attentively, one sees the shining fountain and nature of <margin>instead of <unclear>there</unclear></margin> Justice itself; another beholds Temperance in abundance—not the kind that men sometimes possess within themselves. For our earthly temperance imitates that heavenly one in a certain way; but that one, diffusing itself in all things throughout its entire magnitude, is discerned last, and indeed by those who have already looked upon many clear spectacles. Therefore, the gods see both individually and all together at once. The souls there also see all things, and they become such beings from all those things, so that they too contain all things from the beginning to the end. These souls dwell there, and as much of them as is naturally able to dwell there stays in that place; and often the whole of what is in them dwells there, as long as they are not separated from it. These things, therefore, Jupiter himself sees, and whoever among us loves these things along with Jupiter.

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus explains that in the divine realm, Being and Beauty are identical, and he describes the "procession of Jupiter" where the World Soul leads all other souls toward a vision of the ultimate, intelligible reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of divine beauty from Ennead V, Book 8. The previous page established that in the intelligible realm, Being and Beauty are identical. This page uses the metaphors of golden mountains and divine nectar to describe how the soul transitions from being an external observer of the divine to being internally transformed by it.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> ...happily contemplates, and the final beauty of all things, which shines forth from the whole, and that which partakes of that beauty. For all things there are radiant, and they illuminate those spectators with splendor, so that they themselves also become entirely beautiful: just as often happens to those who climb the highest mountains, where the earth has a golden <note>original: *flauum* / *ξανθὸν*. This refers to a specific quality of light or pure elemental earth described in Plato’s myths.</note> color; for they are immediately imbued with that color, becoming like the earth to which they had ascended. In the divine world, however, that flourishing <margin>B</margin> color is beauty itself, or rather, whatever is there is entirely color and deep-seated beauty. For beauty there does not exist as something else merely blooming on the surface: but among those who are not entirely imbued, only that which glitters on the surface is judged and named as beauty. But those who are thoroughly drenched as if by pure nectar <note>Nectar represents the life-giving, intoxicating joy of divine wisdom.</note> are completely filled, when beauty has poured itself through the whole soul; they do not merely become spectators. For no longer <margin>C</margin> is the spectator on the outside here, and the spectacle likewise on the outside there: but he who sees sharply holds the thing seen within himself, and yet, though possessing it, he often does not know he has it. For he who looks at it as something external does so because he regards it as a visible object, and because he strives to see it in that way. Whatever anyone gazes upon as a thing to be observed, he sees as being outside himself; but it is worthwhile to transfer the divine spectacle into oneself and to look upon it as one, and to gaze upon it as if it were his very self: just as if someone, occupied by God, or Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo, the god of light, music, and prophecy.</note>, or especially seized by some Muse, should produce within himself an image of that God, provided he has the power to behold God within himself.

### *Three stages in divine contemplation, and three preparations for it. Chapter XI.*

*He who is to enjoy God must first conform himself through a common notion and faith in God into a certain divine likeness: then, he must direct his whole thought toward God: thirdly, he must ardently love God alone with his whole will. To one thus affected, God flows in, so that the light, having been spread, is immediately present everywhere. Then indeed the soul does not "suffer" God <note>In the sense of "undergoing" a passive experience.</note>, as long as it is not yet fully joined; it feels and thinks of itself being breathed upon and filled from above. But when it is more closely joined, it looks up at God himself who is breathing into it, and ponders by what reason He flows in. Finally, when it is inwardly united with God, it no longer considers the "occupied" and the "occupier" as separate conditions: but rather, by a simple act, it beholds something one. Nor does it properly "behold," or "hear," or know by limited thought; rather, through a certain inward sense, it enjoys itself living and hidden, together with God as if they were one, and is conscious then at last that it is at its absolute best. This consciousness of self is not a distinct perception, but is almost the same as this state of being at one's best.*

IF, HOWEVER, any of us is unable to see himself, having been thoroughly grasped by that God, he should bring forth into view a sighting or spectacle; he truly brings forth himself, and sees his own image having now been made more beautiful. But laying aside the image, however beautiful, and conspiring together into one, separating nothing further, he exists at once as all things together with that God, who flows in silently and quietly: furthermore, he is with Him as much as <margin>B</margin> he is able and willing. But if he should return to being two <note>The state of separation between the soul and the Divine.</note>, and meanwhile remains pure, he lives next to Him thereafter, so that he may again be present in that way, whenever he turns back toward Him. In that very turning, he carries back this gain: namely, when he first approaches it, he feels himself as long as he is "other"; but when he has penetrated to the innermost parts, he possesses the whole, and having left sense-perception behind, fearing perhaps that he might become "other," he exists there as one: and if he should desire to see anything else as "other"...

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...the first beloved upon all things, such as beauty or that which has partaken of beauty, taking all that is everything. Or one is struck as a spectator, so as to be beautifully and truly moved. As often happens to a person who climbs certain high places, where the earth has a golden color; he is filled with that color, being made like that upon which he had stepped. There, the color <margin>Β</margin> is flourishing and truly exists. Or rather, everything is color and beauty from the depths. For beauty is not something else that blooms on top: but for those who are not the whole, the impact alone is named. For those who are through the whole, as if intoxicated and filled with nectar, and since beauty has come through the whole soul, they do not only exist as spectators. <margin>Γ</margin> For it is no longer the case that one thing is outside and the thing being seen is outside, but he who sees sharply has the thing seen in himself. And having the "other," he is unaware that he has it, and looks at it as if he were outside: because he looks at it as something beloved. And what he wished to see, he sees. And one must see it in the spectator, not looking outside. But one must now transfer it to oneself, and see it as if he were it. And he sees it as himself. Just as if one were possessed by God, "Phoebus-taken," or by some Muse, he would make the vision of the God within himself. If he had the power, he would see God within himself.

IF any of us, being unable to see himself, having been grasped in the act of seeing by that [God], should bring the sight into view, he brings himself forward, and sees his own image having been beautified. But having let go of the image, even though it is beautiful, having come into the same thing and no longer being divided, he is all things together with that God, who is present without sound. And he is with him as much as he can and wishes. But if he should turn back into two, while <margin>Β</margin> remaining pure, he is next to him, so that he may be present <margin>him</margin> again, if he should turn back to him again. And they have a certain gain in the turning back. I accept feeling oneself as long as one is "other": but having run into the interior, he has the whole, and having left sensation behind, fearing to be "other," he is that one. And he will desire to see as if it were another... <meta>catchword: him</meta>

Plotinus explains that true beauty is not surface-level but permeates the soul, ultimately resulting in a state where the distinction between the observer and the observed vanishes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the conclusion of Chapter 11 and the beginning of Chapter 12 of Plotinus’s "On Intelligible Beauty" (Ennead V.8). # BOOK EIGHT.
Aa

<margin>A</margin> ...makes it himself. Therefore, the soul that has been seized by this beauty after these things <note>Plotinus is describing the final stage of mystical union where the distinction between the observer and the observed vanishes.</note>, remains in that state with a certain form, after seeking the rational cause. Since it is always universally in him, it is already a blessed thing to all. This interior power is itself a certain strength, and while it asks "how," it is already quietly there. It is like someone who comes to a realization after a thought has flashed upon them. Thus, he himself is in beauty, though he may not see it; or if he sees it as something other than himself, he is not yet fully in beauty. <margin>B</margin> But having become it, and especially being in beauty, he may weave the external things for himself, appearing as he ought to be, or in this way: as being identical with the object seen. At that moment, a kind of consciousness and self-awareness <term>original: "σύνεσις καὶ συναίσθησις" / "conscientia et consensus" — the internal realization of one’s own state of being</term> of himself arises, taking care lest, by perceiving too much, he might wish to depart from his own state. We must also consider that for evils, the sensations are sharper and their blows are greater; for knowledge, which comes through a strike, causes one to blink. Disease is more of a shock, whereas health, dwelling quietly <margin>C</margin> <margin>It seems not</margin> <margin>And toward</margin> within us, provides a clearer awareness of itself <note>Plotinus argues that we "feel" pain and disease more because they are "alien" to our nature, whereas health and goodness are so natural to us that they feel like silence.</note>. * <unclear>tesia za</unclear> For health is something domestic and is ours, while disease is foreign and not our own; for this reason, the injustice of things truly "other" than us is manifest. But our own things, and we ourselves, being less "perceived" as external sensations, are most of all known to ourselves as our own. It is the same there with our things and ourselves. If things became bad, we would seem to be ignorant of them, despite knowing them best as the same. <margin>D</margin> One waits for a sensation to become a passion, or says he is not satisfied with what he "saw," and if something happens from the outside, it is not led by sensation. This man, looking at something foreign—and, oh father!—even those things will eventually be his own, as he always sees it... the sensations of themselves. But these things themselves, one sees bodies with the eyes.

> What he saw, therefore, let that be: it is sensation. But it is another who saw. Or if that one also stands apart, he will not even believe himself to exist. For he cannot, when he has placed himself outside, look upon himself with the eyes of the body as if he were a sensible object.

<margin>Chapter XII.</margin>
> Whoever enters wholly into his own intellect, through this enters also the divine: which is indeed the son of the Good itself, but the father of the soul of the world.

> Truly, the intellect is generated by the Good, and the soul of the world simultaneously by the intellect; not by a deliberating counsel, but by a fertile nature. In the Good, there is already a will or a pleasure in nature, and in the first intellect, there is its very intelligence. Concerning the creation of the world through will, see elsewhere.

<margin>A</margin> BUT it has been said how one can act as another and how as himself, and how it is one's own. Having seen that he was like another while remaining himself, he might report that he had seen a certain god in labor with beauty, and having given birth to all things in himself, and holding that labor within himself without pain. For having suffered with those things which he loved, and loving his children, he keeps all things to himself and within himself, and provides for all of them and their splendor. <margin>B</margin> Since these things are beautiful, and those staying within are the most beautiful, only Jupiter <note>Plotinus uses the name Jupiter (Zeus) to represent the "Soul of the World," which is the offspring of the higher Intellect.</note>, the son of all these, shone forth. From this last son, as if from a certain image, one can see how great that father is, and how great is the father of Jupiter.
<margin>Plato in the Cratylus.</margin>
* from a certain image of them, he is their own father.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> He puts himself outside. It is necessary, however, for the soul that is to perceive such a divinity to have a certain form of it, and so to persevere while it strives to know it clearly. Thus, recognizing what sort of and how great a thing it is entering, and being confident that it will enter a most blessed thing, it finally immerses itself entirely, to the point that it emerges from being a mere spectator into a manifestation of the other, reflecting from within. But in what way will anyone be in beauty itself unless he sees it? <margin>B</margin> Certainly, if he sees it as something other, he is not yet in beauty; but if beauty itself is the result, then he will be in beauty most perfectly. If, therefore, vision looks toward an external thing, it is not fitting for vision to be there, or to be such that it exists as the same thing as that which is seen. This is like a certain consciousness of oneself, a consensus, guarding lest perhaps if it wishes to perceive more, it might depart from itself. Nor should it escape us that the sensations of evils have greater "pulses" or strikes, but lesser knowledge, <margin>C</margin> since they are excited by a certain force of those pulses. For disease strikes and excites more vehemently; but health, dwelling with us more quietly, provides a clearer notice of itself, sitting silently and peacefully as a familiar thing, conspiring with us into one. But disease has nothing domestic, but is entirely alien; therefore it falls upon us more manifestly, because it meets us as something greatly different. But those things which are ours, and we ourselves, are in us even without manifest sensation. Thus, having ourselves in this way, we are known to ourselves most of all: because we have made our knowledge and ourselves one. Therefore, when we use our divine mind in the world with knowledge to the highest degree, we seem in a way to be ignorant, because we are expecting the passion of sensation; which certainly says it has by no means seen: for it did not see: nor can it ever see such things.

<margin>A</margin> IT HAS BEEN SAID, however, how one can act as another, and how as himself when seeing. He himself, seeing either as another or remaining as himself, what does he principally announce? Namely, that he has seen God as a beautiful son, and that he has generated all things in the son, and held the conception within himself without labor. For God, delighted by these things which he generated, and loving his offspring, contained all things within himself, congratulating himself both on their holiness and their splendor. <margin>B</margin> Since all these things are beautiful, and those which remain inside are more beautiful, Jupiter alone, the son of all, shone forth. From this last son, it is possible to see, as if from a certain image, how great that father is, and how great is the father of Jupiter.

<summary>Plotinus explores the nature of mystical union, arguing that true knowledge of the divine is not an external sensation but an internal state of being similar to health. He uses the mythological relationship between the Good, the Intellect (the Father), and the World Soul (Jupiter) to explain how beauty radiates from the internal to the external world.</summary>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK V.

<margin>A</margin> ...the brothers who remain with the father. Yet it was not without reason that he <note>Referring to the Intellect or the human soul that has ascended.</note> said he came from the father. For there is another world produced from him, which is made beautiful as an image of the Beautiful itself. Indeed, it would be a sacrilege if an image of the Beautiful itself and of true essence were not also beautiful. Therefore, it imitates its archetype in every way. For it possesses life and the gift of essence as a kind of unity; it also possesses beauty insofar as it originates from there. It even possesses eternal existence as an image of that eternity. <margin>B</margin> Otherwise, how could it bear the image of that archetype at one time, but not at another? For an image of this kind was not made by human art. Every image existing by nature persists as long as the archetype remains. For this reason, those who believe this world will perish while the divine world remains are not thinking correctly; they suppose the world was "born" in such a way that its creator at some point deliberated on its construction <note>Plotinus is arguing against the idea that the world was created in a single moment of time after a plan; he believes the world emanates eternally and naturally from the divine.</note>. <margin>C</margin> They certainly do not wish to understand, nor do they know, the manner of this creation: that insofar as the divine world shines, this world flashes forth from it. It will never fail, for since that world exists, this world also exists. That world always was, and always will be. We may use these temporal words for now, compelled by our desire to signify something of the truth.

->The Divine Intellect, who is also called Saturn <note>original: "Saturnus" (Latin) / "Kronos" (Greek). In Neoplatonism, Cronus represents the pure Mind or Intellect.</note>, castrates Heaven <note>original: "Cælum" (Latin) / "Ouranos" (Greek). This refers to the mythological castration of Uranus by Cronus, which Plotinus interprets as the Intellect separating itself from the Higher One to create distinct forms.</note>, that is, the Good itself. Chapter XIII.<-

*For he divides within himself the uniform gift of the father into many forms. He remains, however, within himself without motion, separated from any commerce with the body; for motion generates the worldly administration. He entrusts all things to Jupiter <note>original: "Ioui" (Latin) / "Zeus" (Greek). Jupiter represents the World Soul.</note>, that is, the Soul of the World, whose generative nature is called Venus. The beauty of the corporeal world is a kind of shadow compared to the beauty of the incorporeal world itself. That, in turn, the beauty of the world-soul is an image compared to the wondrous beauty of the First Intelligence. This, finally, is the first splendor of light overflowing outward.*

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, that God, Saturn, who is imagined as being bound <note>The "binding" of Saturn is an allegory for the Intellect remaining fixed and stable in contemplation of the One.</note>, because he always persists in the same state within himself. He is also said to have granted the duties of this empire to his son, Jupiter. It was not fitting for one who was resigning that empire to follow after a younger and later principality, especially since he is filled with the plenitude of all beautiful things. Saturn, I say, having left these things aside, established his father, Heaven, within himself, and raised himself <margin>B</margin> on high toward that place. He established again the things that followed from there, having now taken their beginning from his son after himself. Thus, he holds both middle positions: partly because he cuts away <note>A reference to the "castration" allegory, meaning intellectual distinction or separation.</note> with a certain paternal "otherness," and partly because he abstains from lower things, rising to the sublime. While he is imagined to be held by chains from lower cares, he certainly holds the middle rank between his father, who is greater, and his son, who is lesser. Since Heaven, the progenitor of Saturn and Jupiter, is far greater than what can be called "beauty," <margin>C</margin> Saturn—that is, the Intellect—is the first to stand forth as beautiful. Although the soul is also beautiful, the Intellect is more beautiful than it, because the soul is a vestige <note>A footprint or trace.</note> of the Intellect and exists as beautiful by this very nature. It is more beautiful, however, when it looks toward that Intellect. If, therefore, the soul of the universe (to use more familiar words) and Venus herself are beautiful, of what sort is the Intellect? For if the soul and Venus have this beauty from themselves, how great must the Intellect be? But if they have it from another, from whom does the soul have this beauty, both that which comes to it and that which is naturally planted in its essence? Now, indeed, as often as we are beautiful...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...and the brothers who remained with the father. But he says he does not come from there and belongs to the father, for there is another beautiful world that has come to be, like a beautiful image. For it is not possible for an image of the beautiful not to be beautiful. It surely imitates the archetype everywhere; for it has life and the quality of essence as an imitation, and beauty as something from there. It also has <margin>B</margin> eternity itself as an image. Otherwise, how could he call it an image in one sense but not in another? Or as if the image were made by craft? But every image that exists by nature exists as long as the archetype remains. Therefore, those are not right who destroy it <note>Who believe the world will be destroyed.</note> while the intelligible remains, which is truly living and exists without the creator ever deliberating on the making of it. For such is not the way of its generation; it is as the sun hints at <note>Likening creation to the way the sun radiates light naturally and without effort.</note>. We know that as long as that world shines out, the eternal world never <margin>C</margin> fails. But what is, is the same. Because it is so, we must use these names, for it is necessary to want to signify the meaning.

<margin>A</margin> Why then does the one God remain bound in himself, and concede to his son to rule over all? For it was not right for him who had left the inner rule to follow a younger and later one after himself, since he is full of beautiful things. Leaving these, he established his own father in himself, and reached up to the things above him, and again established the things after him, starting <margin>B</margin> from his son. Thus, he becomes the middle between both, by the cutting off <note>The mythological "cutting" or "division" of the higher realm from the lower.</note> toward the things above, and by supporting the things after him, but being held by a "bond" from the things below—the middle between his father and his son, who is an image and more than an image. But since his father is greater than beauty, he himself remained as the first beautiful thing. And beauty exists in the things of the soul. But he is more beautiful than it, of which she is a trace. <margin>C</margin> She is beautiful by nature, but more beautiful when she looks there. If then the soul of the all—to speak more familiarly—and Aphrodite <note>The Greek equivalent of Venus.</note> herself is beautiful, what is that Intellect? For if she has it from herself, how much greater is he? If from another, from whom does the soul have both its accidental and its innate beauty? Or since...

...since even when one is beautiful in oneself, one would fit into one’s own nature; but when moving toward another, they change their nature. Are the things already said sufficient to lead to a clear persuasion regarding all the intelligible <note>original: *noēta*; these are the "Intelligible" things, the eternal Ideas or Forms that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses.</note> things, or must we again travel another path in this way?

# PLOTINUS’S
## ENNEAD FIVE,
### BOOK IX.

#### ON INTELLECT, AND THE IDEAS, AND BEING.
#### On intellect & ideas & being.

*The soul that contemplates divine things is already in its homeland. Other men and those given to pleasure are exiles: but the high-minded return to their homeland more easily than those devoted to pleasure.*
->Chapter I.<-

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop-cap "P" depicting a seated scholar or philosopher reading at a desk.</image-desc>
ALL men, having come into being from the beginning, use sense-perception before the mind, and necessarily encountering sensible things first, if they remain there, they spend their lives thinking these things are the first and the last. They suppose that the pain and pleasure found in them are respectively evil and good, and they think this is sufficient. They live their lives chasing some things and avoiding others. And they claim to possess wisdom by following this reasoning, being like heavy birds who, having taken much from the earth and being weighed down, are unable to fly high, even though they received wings from nature. Others are raised a little from lower things, moving themselves toward the better from pleasure by the superior part of the soul. But being unable to see what is above, and having no other place to stand, they are carried down, along with the name of virtue, to actions and choices of lower things, from which they first attempted to raise themselves. But the third kind of men is divine, possessing a greater power and sharpness of the eyes. These men, as if by sharp-sightedness, look upon the upper radiance, and are raised to the things there, as if above the clouds and the mist of this world. They remain there, looking down on all things here, delighted by that place which is true and their own, like a man arriving after much wandering into a well-governed homeland.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop-cap "Q" depicting a pastoral landscape with trees and distant figures.</image-desc>
SINCE all men immediately from birth use sense before mind, and necessarily first encounter and apply their affection to things pertaining to the senses, some indeed, persevering in that same habit, pass through life in this way: thinking these things are both the first and the last, and judging what is troublesome in them to be evil, and <margin>B</margin> what is pleasant to be good. And they think they have finally done enough for themselves if they pursue pleasant things throughout their whole life and flee the contrary. Therefore, whoever among them claims any reason for themselves, they judge this to be wisdom: being affected in exactly the same way as heavier birds, which, when they have seized many things from the earth by whose weight they are overburdened, cannot fly further through the heights, although they have received wings from nature. But others are raised a little from <margin>C</margin> lower things, whom the better nature of the soul itself calls back from pleasure to the honorable. But since they cannot gaze upon the supernal, and therefore have nothing else where they may rest, they are carried over, together with the name of virtue itself, to actions and the choice of inferior things, from which they were endeavoring to raise themselves at the beginning. Finally, there is a third genus of divine men, in which are those who, relying on both greater power and perspicacity of the eyes, look sharply up at the supernal light; <margin>D</margin> having perceived it, they raise themselves entirely to it, transcending the lower clouds and darkness, and having ascended, they remain there, utterly despising all these things, being delighted by the supernal region as their true and proper home, not otherwise than a traveler restored at last to his lawful homeland after long wanderings.

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEAD V.

->*That which is primarily beautiful is beautiful by itself and in its entirety, always. Chapter II.*<-

*Therefore, beauty in the body is not primary. For the body is not beautiful through its own whole self, but through a form <note>In Platonic thought, a "Form" or "Idea" is the eternal, perfect blueprint of a thing; physical objects are merely imperfect shadows of these Forms.</note>, and it is subject to change. Nor is beauty primary in the soul: for here, beauty exists through participation in the intellect and is changeable. Rather, the primary beauty belongs to the intellect; and thereafter, it is a kind of image and shape of the Good. <gloss>Plotinus often touches upon the mysteries of the Apostles John and Paul; however, he seems not so much to have sought the mystery of the Trinity as to have perfected it, based on a certain pious conjecture.</gloss>* <note>original Latin: "mysterium tamen Trinitatis... perfecisse." This gloss is likely a comment by the Renaissance translator Marsilio Ficino, who sought to harmonize Plotinus with Christian theology.</note>

<margin>A</margin> WHAT, then, is this region? And in what way can one ascend to it? Certainly, he can ascend there who is drawn by nature especially toward loving beauty, and who is born a true philosopher. Such a man, as a lover of beauty itself, is vexed by a kind of labor of childbirth, yet he is not content with the beauty of the body. Instead, he flees from this toward the beauty of the soul—namely, virtues, sciences, duties, and laws. And from there, <margin>B</margin> he ascends again to the cause of those things which are beautiful in sounds; and if anything exists even higher, he continues until he finally reaches the very first, which is made beautiful by its own self. Upon reaching this, he finally ceases to be vexed, but truly never before then. But in what way shall he ascend there, and from where will such a faculty be given? And by what means especially will reason lead this love, as if by the hand, toward the end? Perhaps reason of this kind is the beauty implanted in bodies, which is foreign to the bodies themselves; for these forms of bodies are within them <margin>C</margin> as if in matter. Therefore, the subject is changed, and from beautiful it becomes ugly; from which reason proves that the body is beautiful only through a certain participation. What, then, is that which makes the body beautiful? In one way, the presence of beauty makes it beautiful; in another way, it is the soul which fashioned it, and in fashioning it, applied such a form to the body. What then? Is the soul by its own nature beauty itself? By no means; otherwise one soul would not be wise and beautiful, while another <margin>D</margin> is foolish and ugly. Therefore, beauty comes to the soul through wisdom. But what is it, above all, that hands down wisdom to the soul? This, surely, is necessarily the Intellect <note>original: *Intellectus* or *Nous*; the divine mind that contains all eternal truths.</note>: the Intellect, I say, which does not at one time become intellect and at another time remain devoid of intelligence, but is rather the True Intellect, which for this reason is beautiful from its own self. But should we rest here as if at the first principle? Or must we rather proceed even above the mind? Indeed, the mind itself meets us first as we proceed on high, before the very first principle of all, as if stationed in the vestibule of the Good itself, announcing and signifying all things within itself—like a certain figure of the Good itself, distributed into a multitude rather than consisting entirely in unity.

---

->*Forms which are in matter, as in a subject, depend on the forms which are in the soul of the world as their source; and these in turn depend on the forms which are in the primary mind as the source of the forms of the soul. Chapter III.*<-

->*If the soul were intellectual by its own nature, then all souls would be equally intellectual; but since it is not so, the soul rightly becomes primary and intellectual through a certain participation in a higher intellect.*<-

<margin>A</margin> WE MUST consider this very nature of the mind, by which reason signifies that it is Being itself and true essence. First, they had asserted (though proceeding by another way) that there must be some such essence and mind. But perhaps it might seem ridiculous to investigate whether Intellect exists in the order of things. Perhaps also some men...

<column-break/>

<margin>α</margin> WHAT then is the place? And how might one arrive at it? He might arrive who is by nature erotic <note>original: *erōtikos*; used here in the Platonic sense of someone driven by a divine desire for beauty and truth.</note>, and who truly possesses from the beginning the disposition of a philosopher, suffering the pangs of labor because he loves the things within the beautiful. He does not endure <margin>β</margin> the beauty in the body, but rather flees toward the beauties of the soul: virtues and sciences, and pursuits and laws. Then again he ascends to the cause of the beauties in the soul, and to the cause beyond that, until he reaches the first—the First which is beautiful by its own self. Having arrived there, he will cease from his labor, but nowhere before that. How then does one ascend? And from where does the power come to him, and what reason will act as a tutor <note>original: *paidagōgēsei*; to lead like a schoolmaster or guide.</note> to this love? It is thus: the beauty upon bodies is something brought into the bodies; for the shapes of bodies are as if shared within matter, by something foreign that rests upon the surface. Thus <margin>γ</margin> things become ugly; therefore, reason says they participate in beauty. What then is it that makes a body beautiful? In one way, the presence of beauty; in another, the soul which molded it and gave it such a shape. What then? Is the soul beautiful from itself? Or is it not? Or would not one soul be prudent and beautiful, and another foolish and ugly? Therefore, beauty is upon the soul by prudence. And who <margin>δ</margin> then is the one who gives prudence to the soul? It must be Intellect. Not an intellect that is sometimes intellect and sometimes not, but the true one. For it is beautiful of itself and is truly the first. But it is necessary that this stands as the first, or must one go even beyond? Intellect is a distance from the first, not giving of itself as if from the first, but as if before the doors of the Good, announcing all its things, like an image; it is there most of all that truth is, and those things which are sensed are staying there.

<margin>α</margin> WE MUST examine this nature of the soul, which reason announces to be true Being and true essence, first confirming it by going another way, with evidence that I recognize. Perhaps indeed it is ridiculous to seek whether Intellect exists among the things that are; yet perhaps some men...

<summary>This page outlines the Neoplatonic "ascent of the soul," describing how the lover and philosopher move from physical beauty to the virtues of the soul, and finally to the divine Intellect. Plotinus argues that Intellect is the source of all form and wisdom, serving as the "vestibule" to the ultimate principle of the Good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the hierarchy of existence, moving from the sensible world toward the "Intellect" (Nous). It follows the previous page's discussion on the nature of beauty by examining how form is imposed upon matter, both in art and in nature, to prove the existence of a higher, divine Mind.</meta>

<page-num>557</page-num>
<header>BOOK NINE.</header>

<margin>A</margin> One might wonder about this, or rather, whether there exists such an intellect as we have described. Is there something separate that truly *is* all beings, and in which the species <note>original: "species"; in Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal "Forms" or "Ideas" that serve as blueprints for all things in the physical world.</note> exist by nature? This is the matter we have decided to debate at present. We observe, therefore, that all things said to "be" are composite, and none of them are simple. This applies both to individual things made by art and to those constituted by nature. For <margin>B</margin> craftsmanship requires bronze, wood, or stone, yet perfected works do not emerge from these until an art acts upon them—one producing a statue, another a bed, and another a house—by applying its own specific form to the matter. Furthermore, those things that are naturally constituted, especially those called "composites" or "mixtures," can be resolved into the form implanted in the composition—just as a human is resolved into soul and body, and the body into the four humors and elements. Since you will find each of these is composed of matter <margin>C</margin> and a forming principle—for the matter of the elements is itself formless—you must ask from where the form of matter comes. You should also ask regarding the soul: is it already simple, or is there something in it acting as matter and something else as form? Specifically, the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectus" / "nous"; for Plotinus, this is the second level of reality, a divine mind that contains all eternal truths.</note> within it; one part being like the form in the bronze, and the other being like the one who created the form in the bronze. Carrying these same principles over to the universe, one will eventually arrive at the Intellect and recognize it as the true maker and <margin>D</margin> craftsman of the whole. One will assert that the underlying matter, receiving forms from there, became fire, water, air, or earth, but that these forms proceed from another source: namely, the Soul. The Soul, in turn, provides form to the four members of the universe. Now, the Mind itself provides the "rational principles" <note>original: "rationes" / "logoi"; these are the formative forces or "blueprints" that organize matter.</note> to the Soul, just as the arts provide the principles of action to the souls of craftsmen. Thus, one <margin>E</margin> aspect of Mind is like the form of the soul (mind according to form), while the other provides the form to the soul, much as the sculptor provides the form to the statue, possessing within itself everything it bestows. And what it bestows upon the soul is close to the truth; but what the body receives are merely images and imitations.

<column-break/>

*Above the souls which proceed from potentiality into the act of understanding, and which undergo some passion and have commerce with the lower world, is the Intellect itself—always understanding in act, free from passion, and separated from the companionship of the body.*
-> *Chapter IV.* <-
*Since mutability happens to things because of matter, surely if there were no things separated from matter, the resulting order and the perpetual succession of similar things in the transformation of the world could not be preserved.*

# WHY, then, after you have come as far
<margin>A</margin> as the soul, can you not rest in it as the primary principle, but are compelled to proceed further? Because, first, the intellect itself is something else and better than the soul. And that which is better exists prior by nature. For the soul does not generate the intellect when it has become "perfected," as many people think. For if something is in a state of potentiality <note>original: "in potentia"; having the capacity to become something but not yet being it.</note>, from where will it eventually become an "act" <note>original: "in actu"; the state of being fully realized or active.</note> unless there is a certain cause standing before it to lead it into that act? For if it happened by chance...

<column-break/>

# FURTHERMORE, why is it that after reaching
<margin>A</margin> the soul, you cannot rest there as if at the first principle, but are forced to go beyond it? Because, primarily, the intellect itself is something different and superior to the soul. That which is superior is prior by nature. Nor, as many suppose, does the soul generate the intellect once it has reached perfection. For if a thing exists in potentiality, how can it ever come to be in act, unless some cause is present to lead it into act? For if by chance...

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic argument for the existence of the "Intellect" (Nous) as a necessary stage above the Soul. While the previous page discussed how forms are applied to matter, this page argues that there must be a primary, "perfect" source for these forms that is always in a state of active reality rather than mere potential.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD V.

<margin>A</margin> ...might proceed into act, it could happen that it might never progress into action at all. Therefore, it is necessary that the first principle exists in a state of **act** <note>original: "in actu"; a philosophical term meaning full, realized existence or operation, as opposed to "potentia" or mere potential</note>, being neither unworthy nor incomplete, but perfect. Those things that are imperfect are secondary to the perfect ones, and are brought to completion by those which produced them—by a certain paternal right, as it were, of the perfectors over the imperfect things they generated in the beginning. Now, that which is generated must first regard its maker as its material, and then be formed. Consequently, if <margin>B</margin> the soul admits some **passion** <note>original: "passionem"; here meaning the capacity to be acted upon or to change</note> within itself, there must exist something far removed from every passion of the senses; otherwise, all things would slip away with time. There must be something higher than the soul. Furthermore, if the soul is in the world, there must also be something outside the world; for this reason too, it is necessary for there to be something above the soul. For if that which is in the world is the same as that in the body and matter, then certainly nothing remains the same; if only such a thing existed, <margin>C</margin> then humanity and all other things would not always remain the same. Therefore, one may understand from these points and many others that the **Mind** <note>original: "mentem"</note> must exist above the soul.

---

*The Intellect, perfect by nature, always understands by itself, since it understands from itself—namely, by being turned inward toward itself. It is of such a nature because, through its essence, it is these very beings which it understands. Chapter V.*

*The perfect Intellect, being a perfect essence, also provides perfect beings. The multitude of these is such that it exists in the first principle of things, and not within matter; it is infinite, and one form is the source of every form. Likewise, since one thing depends on another, there is a multitude of perfect beings within the Intellect. This Intellect does not understand a multitude present outside itself, but rather one proceeding from its own understanding; certainly, nature does not abandon it but follows it, just as words follow a speaker or offspring follow a parent. Perhaps later, the modes of understanding which are diverse in the soul are the same in the Mind: the genus of understanding generates—or rather, it is more an essence—just as fire generates by heating, the sun by shining, and the soul by living. Finally, the **reasons** <note>original: "rationes"; the formative principles or logic of things</note> of objects, which exist in the soul as a mobile nature, are not safe from all change by themselves unless they are traced back to the firm **Ideas** of the Intellect.*

---

<margin>A</margin> We must accept the **Intellect** (if we are to use its true name) not as an intellect in potential, nor as one proceeding from a lack of mind into a state of mind—otherwise we would be forced to seek another higher intellect—but we must accept it as existing in perpetual **act** <note>original: "in actu perpetuo"</note>, so that it always exists as Intellect. If, then, the Intellect does not have its understanding as something added from the outside, whatever it understands, it understands entirely from itself; and if it possesses anything, it possesses it from itself. If it understands from itself and by itself, it <margin>B</margin> truly *is* those very things which it understands. For if its essence were one thing and the things it understands were another, its essence would be void of intellectual power; it would no longer be an intellect in act, but only in potential. It is not proper, therefore, to separate one from the other, even though we are accustomed, led by our experience with worldly things, to separate them in our thoughts. What, then, does it do, and what does it understand? Let us suppose it is those things which <margin>C</margin> it understands. Indeed, since it is intellect and being, it understands and introduces beings through a true mode of existence: it is, therefore, those beings. For it will either understand them as existing elsewhere, or as existing in itself as its own existence, which is indeed the case. For where else could they be? They are, therefore, written and contained deeply within itself. For it does not understand these in the objects of the senses (as many think); for no primary thing is of the kind that is perceived by the senses. For what is in the senses is like form in matter: an image and a shadow of the Being itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is possible for a thing not to enter into **act** <note>original: "energeia"</note>; therefore, the primary things must exist in act, without lack, and be perfect. The imperfect things are later than those, being altered by those which generated them, just as fathers bring to perfection that which they generated as imperfect in the beginning. Therefore, the mover and the maker provide the principles, and in the thing itself, the form is <margin>B</margin> molded, as it were, which requires this; and conversely, there must be something else above the soul. If all things were to perish by the process of "becoming," there must be something before the soul—an Intellect before the soul of the world, and indeed something outside the world. Thus, there must be something for this soul, even if that which is in the world is in body and matter, so that the same thing remains, so that man and all the **Forms** <note>original: "eide"</note> are eternal. If there is a cause, it must also exist above the things of the soul; <margin>C</margin> one might contemplate this from these and many other arguments.

<image-desc>The center gutter contains alphabetical markers A, B, and C used to reference specific sections or lines across the two columns of text.</image-desc>

---

<margin>A</margin> One must grasp this so as to be true to the name: not the intellect in potential, nor that which comes into mind from a state of thoughtlessness (otherwise, we will seek another before it), but the Intellect that is in act and is always Intellect. If its thinking is not brought in from the outside, whatever it thinks, it thinks from itself; and if it has anything, it has it from itself. And if it thinks from itself and out of itself, it is itself the things it thinks. For if <margin>B</margin> its essence were different and its thinking were something else, its essence would be unthinking, and it would be in potential again, not in act, and not inseparable. Therefore, the two are not different, although we, following our own circumstances, separate them in our imaginations. What then does it think, or what does it think primarily, so that it might think those beings? It is clear that being Intellect, it truly thinks the beings and gives them existence. It *is*, therefore, the beings. For it will think them either as <margin>C</margin> brought in from elsewhere, or as being in itself. If they were brought in, they would not be prior to it, yet it thinks them. If they are not there, in what way can they be known, as some believe? For each primary thing is not a sensible object. For the form in those sensible things is truly an image, because it is in matter. Of the...

# BOOK NINE.

...everything that lies in another also depends on another, and is referred back to that thing, and is its **image**. Furthermore, if it is necessary that the **Intellect** <note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦν"; the second principle in Neoplatonism, the realm of pure thought and Forms</note> be the craftsman of this universe, it certainly will not understand those things that exist in that which is not yet in being, so that it might produce it. Therefore, before the world exists, those things must exist—not as figures impressed from elsewhere, but as certain primary **exemplars** <note>original: "exemplaria"; the perfect blueprints or "Forms" upon which all physical things are modeled</note>, the first principles and the essence of the Mind. If anyone should say that **seminal reasons** <note>original: "seminales rationes" / "λόγος φύσεως"; the generative blueprints within nature</note> are sufficient for this, they surely <margin>B</margin> bring forward things that are eternal; and if they are eternal and far removed from all **passion** <note>original: "passione"; the state of being acted upon or changed by outside forces</note>, they must exist in the Mind, and indeed in such a Mind that exists prior to habit, nature, and the soul. For these latter things exist in a state of potentiality, and consist within the power of that Mind. Therefore, the Mind is the **beings** <note>original: "entia"; the true, unchanging realities</note> themselves, according to the true mode of being; it does not understand things that are elsewhere. For these things are neither before it nor after it; rather, the Mind is like a primary legislator—or better yet, it is the Law of existence itself. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, it was rightly said: **to think and to be are the same thing** <note>A famous philosophical principle originally from Parmenides (c. 5th century BCE), meaning that true reality and true thought are identical</note>. Likewise, the knowledge of things that are without matter is the same as the thing itself. Again, I have investigated myself as one of these beings; **reminiscences** <note>original: "reminiscentiæ" / "ἀναμνήσεις"; the Platonic theory that we "remember" innate truths from before we were born</note> testify to the same. For nothing among beings is outside the Mind, nor again in a specific place; rather, they remain perpetually within themselves, undergoing neither change nor destruction. Therefore, they are judged to be beings through the true mode of existence. Otherwise, if they were to arise and perish, <margin>D</margin> they would obtain a borrowed existence; and these would no longer be the beings themselves, but that other thing would be Being itself. Truly, those things which are perceived by the senses exist by a certain **participation** <note>original: "participatione"; the idea that physical objects only exist because they "share in" or "copy" a perfect Form</note> in that which they are said to be. Since the underlying nature receives its form from elsewhere—just as bronze receives its form from the art of the statue-maker, and wood from the art of the carpenter—the bronze proceeds into such materials through an image. Yet the art itself remains meanwhile outside the matter in the same state, and possesses within itself the <margin>E</margin> true statue and the true bed. Thus, therefore, this universe in the category of bodies—which is a participant only in images—manifestly testifies that the beings themselves are different from bodies. For those beings are immutable, while these bodies are changed; those remain firm in themselves, 

<column-break/>

needing no place. For they are not extended by any physical magnitude, but possess an intellectual substance sufficient for themselves. For the nature of bodies always requires some other sustainer. But the Mind, since it subsists by a certain wondrous nature and preserves those things which by their own nature would fall away, is rightly not compelled to seek a place where it may be established.

---

-> The Ideas in the intellect are properly certain powers of it, through which the intellect itself is defined in one way or another. Chapter VI. <-

Because the faculty of understanding and generating is the same there, the **Ideas** <note>original: "ideæ"; the perfect, abstract archetypes of all things</note> do not only behave like various teachings, but also as living and true "seeds" in the soul. On one hand, they are called **exemplars** (the models); on the other, they are called the principles of things, the universal reasons and species. Consequently, entirely material qualities—like heat, cold, and the like—cannot have a mutual relationship without confusion. They either remain separate, or if they are mixed, one either confounds the others or they are all mutually confounded so that something else results from the whole. Qualities that are less material, such as flavors, can be united; like the others, they involve confusion, but not entirely. Smells, however, since they are still less material, are united in the same medium while remaining different, and one confounds the other somewhat less, though they still confound. Different voices are united even more in the medium and are less confounded, because they are less material. But the **species of colors**, even contrary ones, because they are immaterial, are united in the same point and exist there most distinctly without any mutual confusion. From this it is gathered...

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how the Divine Intellect (the second principle of Neoplatonism) contains the perfect Forms or blueprints of all reality. The previous page established that the Intellect is not a passive container but is identical to the beings it contemplates. Here, the text uses the analogy of "seminal reasons" in seeds and the presence of knowledge in the soul to explain how many distinct things can exist simultaneously in a single, unified essence.</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD V.

...the union of forms without confusion—that is, being joined together and yet remaining distinct—is possible in the soul as a certain immaterial essence. This is even more true in the **Mind** <note>original: "mente" / "νοῦ"; the Divine Intellect</note> which is even further separated from matter. Since the union of forms grows step by step as one moves away from matter, and their distinction grows likewise, it follows that in the Mind, things are at once most unified and most perfectly distinct.

---

<margin>A</margin> Let the **Intellect** <note>original: "intellectus" / "νοῦς"</note>, therefore, be essence itself. Let it hold all things in itself, not as if it were a place or a container, but as if it were possessing its very self, existing as one with those things. All things are there together, yet they are nonetheless distinguished from one another. We see this even in the soul, which holds many different branches of knowledge <note>original: "scientias" / "ἐπιστήμας"</note> at once, yet nothing in it is confused. Each branch of knowledge performs its own function when the situation demands it, without dragging the other branches along with it. Every notion acts purely, free from the other internal <margin>B</margin> notions. Thus, and in a much greater way, the Intellect is all things at once, and yet again, not all at once; for in that realm, every single thing is its own specific power. The universal Intellect contains all things just as a **genus** <note>a general category in logic</note> contains its **species**, or as a whole contains its parts. Furthermore, the very powers of seeds, which I was just mentioning, provide an image of this. For in the whole seed, all things are present without being separated; the **reasons** <note>original: "rationes" / "λόγοι"; the formative principles or blueprints</note> are there, collected as if in a single center. Yet within that seed, the "reason" for the eye is one thing, and the "reason" for the hands is another, <margin>C</margin> and it is clear they are different because of the different parts that are born from them. Therefore, the powers implanted in seeds certainly have this quality: each of them is one whole "reason," containing within itself the parts that are necessarily included. Now, that which is corporeal in the seed has matter (such as moisture), but the "reason" itself is entirely **Form** <note>original: "species" / "εἶδος"; the non-physical shape or essence</note>. This reason is the same as the Form of the generating soul, which is itself an image of a higher soul. Some call this the "nature" <margin>D</margin> implanted in the seeds. This nature, descending from those things which are superior—just as light comes from fire—transforms and shapes matter, not by pushing it with force or by using those "levers" so commonly talked about, but by applying its **seminal reason** <note>original: "rationem seminariam" / "λόγων"</note>.

<column-break/>

Let the **Mind** <note>original: "ΝΟΥΣ"</note> indeed be the true beings, and let it hold all things in itself—not as if in a place, but as if possessing itself. It is one with them, yet all things are there together. And they are no less distinct; for even the soul, which holds many sciences within itself, has nothing confused. Each science performs its own task when necessary, without pulling the others along. Each thought acts purely from the thoughts lying within. In this way, and even more so, the Mind is all things together, and again not together, because each is its own power. The whole Mind contains all, just as a genus contains species, and as a whole contains parts. And the powers within seeds also carry the likeness of these things mentioned. For in the whole seed, all are undistinguished, and the **reasons** <note>original: "λόγοι"</note> are as if in a single center. Just as the "reason" of the eye is one thing and that of the hands is another, the fact that they are different is known from the sensory parts that come from them. Thus the powers in seeds are each one whole "reason," along with the parts contained within it. The bodily part is something material, like a fluid; but the reason itself is the whole Form. Being a reason, it is the Form of the generating soul, which is an offshoot of another better soul. Some say that this soul in the seeds is that which, having started from there—as light from fire—turns toward and shapes matter, not by pushing or using much-talked-about mechanical means, but by means of the reasons.

---

->*The notions of sensible things newly acquired or produced in the soul are not the sensible things themselves. But the absolute notions of intelligible things, coming into the rational power from the Intellect, are in a way the intelligible things themselves. Chapter VII.*<-

>*Namely, because the Intellect is intimate to the soul, being both its own property and common to all: in what is "own," the notions and the intelligible things become more the same; in what is "common," they are most identical. The private Intellect (as Plotinus often says) exists in the soul as a Form, while the common Intellect is present to the soul as an active agent. Since the "intelligible" thing relates to the "intelligent" mind almost like a mover—and thus precedes it in a way—we should not say that the Intellect becomes intelligible after it has understood those things, but rather the reverse. Otherwise, acts of understanding would happen by mere chance and would be like mere fictions.*

---

<margin>A</margin> ACCORDINGLY, the sciences which are in the rational soul—those that pertain to **sensible things** <note>objects perceived by the five senses</note>, if indeed our knowledge of these should be called "science" at all, since it is more fitting to call them "opinions"—being later than the things themselves, are merely their images. But those sciences which look toward **intelligible things** <note>spiritual or mental realities</note>, and which are truly sciences, come from the Intellect into the rational soul and understand nothing of the physical world. Insofar as they are sciences, they are the very things they understand; <margin>B</margin> they possess both the "intelligible" and the "act of understanding" from within. For the Intellect is internal; it is the primary things themselves, dwelling with you forever and existing in a state of activity. It does not strain its gaze as if it did not possess what it seeks, nor does it acquire anything new, nor does it travel through a sequence of thoughts...

<column-break/>

And the sciences in the rational soul, those of sensible things—if we must call these "sciences," though the name "opinion" <note>original: "δόξης"</note> is more fitting—being later than the things themselves, are images of them. But those of the opposites, which are truly sciences, coming from the Mind into the rational soul, understand nothing of the senses. Insofar as they are sciences, they are each of the things they understand, and they have within them the nature of the intelligible and the act of thought. Because the Mind is within, it is those primary things themselves, always being with them and existing in activity. It does not apply itself as if it did not possess them, nor does it acquire them, nor does it move through them discursively...

# BOOK NINE.

<margin>...of those things,</margin>
...through those things which it did not previously have at hand: for such conditions <note>The "conditions" or "passions" (pathē) of acquiring knowledge.</note> seem rather to belong to the **soul** <note>original: "animae" / "Ψυχῆς"</note>; instead, the Intellect rests entirely within itself, existing as all things at once. It does not use its intelligence to lead individual things into itself from the outside. For it did not become **God** <note>original: "Deum"; here referring to a divine being or principle</note> when it thought of God, nor did it become **movement** after it thought of movement. Therefore, regarding the statement that "the Forms are the thoughts of the Intellect," if this is meant to imply that the Intellect *becomes* or *exists as* a thing only after thinking it, this is not correctly stated. For that which is thought must exist prior to this act of thinking. Otherwise, how would the Intellect proceed toward the object to be understood? It does not fall upon its objects by chance, nor does it strive toward them in vain or at random.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...through those things which it did not previously have at hand: for such conditions seem rather to belong to the soul; instead, it rests entirely within itself, existing as all things at once. It does not use its intelligence to lead individual things into itself. For it did not become God when it thought of God, nor did it become movement after it thought of movement. Wherefore, regarding the phrase that "the Forms are of the intelligence," if it is said in such a way that it becomes or exists as this thing only after it has understood it, it is not <margin>B</margin> correctly said. For that which is understood must exist prior to this act of understanding. Otherwise, in what way will it proceed to the understanding of itself? For it does not fall upon itself by some chance, nor does it strive blindly or in vain.

---

*The Intellect, taken absolutely, is all the **Ideas** <note>original: "Ideæ" / "ἰδέαι"; the perfect archetypes of all things</note>. Each individual Idea is not the Intellect taken absolutely, but is the Intellect in a specific manner. Likewise, any individual Idea differs from the Intellect only by a certain intellectual reason. However, the Ideas differ among themselves by the nature of the thing and their formal reason.*
->Chapter VIII.<-

*Rather, it is more correct to say: the Idea of a human is Intellect, and the Idea of a horse is Intellect, rather than saying the Idea of a human is the Idea of a horse, even though both fall under a universal. Other Ideas exist in actuality, or by a certain consequence, just as propositions in geometry arranged in order relate to geometry itself and to each other. Furthermore, although the Intellect precedes in a certain natural order, the necessary distinction of **Being** <note>original: "entis" / "ὂν"</note> into its modes of existence rightly and in a certain way precedes the use of intelligence—a distinction which neither the Platonist <note>likely referring to Plotinus himself or his followers</note> nor the Christians willingly admit in the first principle of things. Just as we consider common intelligence in the nature of being, so in any idea we consider a certain proper nature of being and its own proper intelligence. These are like two distinct things, not like matter and heat or transparency and light, but like heat and the act of heating, or light and the act of glowing; both of these are acts, and therefore they are one in reality. Thus, although intelligence is the innermost act of being, it is nevertheless the act of both.*

---

<margin>...highest,</margin>
Since, therefore, that which is understood is internal, this internal reality is itself one thing—both a **species** <note>original: "εἶδος"; a form or specific type</note> and an **idea**. What, then, is this? Truly, it is the Intellect and the intellectual essence, and any idea does not differ from the Intellect, but each is the Intellect itself. Overall, the Intellect is all the species; each species is each Intellect. Just as a whole science contains all its contemplations and notions, and each notion is a part of the whole, not divided by place, but each having its power within the whole. This Intellect, therefore, exists in itself, resting in the same state with itself, the eternal fullness of all things. If the Intellect were thought of as prior to Being itself, one would have to say that the Intellect, by acting and thinking, generates and completes all beings. But since it is necessary to conceive of Being as prior to the Intellect, one must admit that beings themselves are primarily within the one who understands; the act of intelligence comes to the beings, just as the act of fire comes to fire itself. Thus, beings are so deeply implanted in the Intellect that they have it within themselves as their own proper act. Being itself is also an act. Therefore, there is one act for both; or rather, both are one. One nature is Being itself and the Intellect; wherefore beings, the act of being, and the Intellect are one. Such intellections are the species, forms, and acts of Being. Nevertheless, by us who divide such things, some are thought of as prior to others; for one is the dividing intellect, while that other, which is indivisible and does not divide at all, is Being itself and all things.
<margin>...indivisible,</margin>
<insert>it is the dividing intellect; but the other is indivisible and does not divide, and is Being itself and all things.</insert>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, that which is understood is internal, this internal reality is itself one thing—both a **species** <note>original: "species"; here used interchangeably with "Form"</note> and an idea. What, then, is this? Truly, it is the Intellect and the intellectual essence, and any idea does not differ from the Intellect, but each is the Intellect itself. Overall, the Intellect is the common species of all; and each individual species is an individual Intellect. Just as a whole science contains all its contemplations and notions, and each notion is a part of the whole, not divided by space, but <margin>B</margin> each having its power within the whole. This Intellect, therefore, exists in itself, resting in the same state with itself, the eternal fullness of all things. If the Intellect were thought of as prior to Being itself, one would have to say that the Intellect, by acting and thinking, generates and completes all beings. But since it is necessary to conceive of Being as prior to the Intellect, one must admit that beings themselves are primarily within the one who understands; the act of intelligence comes <margin>C</margin> to the beings, just as the act of fire comes to fire itself. Thus, beings are so deeply implanted in the Intellect that they have it within themselves as their own proper act. Being itself is also an act. Therefore, there is one act for both; or rather, both are one. One nature is Being itself and the Intellect; wherefore beings, the act of being, and the Intellect are one. Such intellections are the species, forms, and acts of Being. Nevertheless, by us who divide such things, some are thought of as <margin>D</margin> prior to others; for one is the dividing intellect, while that other, which is indivisible and does not divide at all, is Being itself and all things.

*If the Mind arranges forms in the world through natural intelligence, it embraces those very forms within itself in a natural way.*
->Chapter IX.<-

*Just as the essence of the soul flows into its powers, or as nature contains the seminal reasons <note>original: "rationes seminales"; the formative principles in nature that guide growth</note> of the limbs like species...*
