<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the Divine Intellect. The previous page established that the Intellect does not look outside itself for knowledge but contains all truths within itself. Here, Plotinus (translated into Latin by Marsilio Ficino) explains how the "Ideas" or perfect archetypes within the Intellect provide the blueprint for the physical world, emphasizing that only natural perfections—not flaws—have an eternal origin.</meta>

### PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK V.

...just as fire possesses light, heat, dryness, lightness, and rarity; and in almost this same way, the **Ideas** <note>original: "ideæ"; the perfect, eternal archetypes of all things.</note> correspond to and differ from one another. For it is necessary that the Ideas differ by formal reason; otherwise, the distinction and order of forms in physical things would arise from matter, or happen by chance, or occur because of different agents meeting by accident. But if God acts outside of Himself by free will—as we prove in Theology—like an architect and geometer, He possesses the Ideas of all things.

<margin>A</margin>
BUT what are those things in that one Mind which we ourselves divide when thinking? For it is necessary to bring forth those things that are at rest, and to speak of them as if from a single, abiding knowledge, so that we may more clearly behold the things within. Since this world is a **living being** <note>original: "animal"; Plotinus follows the Platonic tradition of viewing the entire universe as a single, living organism.</note> encompassing all living beings, and receives its existence and its nature from another; and since that source from which it comes is traced back to the Intellect, it is necessary that the universal archetype of the whole exists primarily in the Intellect. This Intellect is the **intelligible world** <note>original: "mundus intelligibilis"; the realm of pure thought and perfect forms.</note>
<margin>B</margin>
itself, of which Plato says in the *Timaeus*: "The Intellect understands the Ideas within that which is the Living Being." For just as when a **formative seed-reason** <note>original: "ratio seminaria"; the internal blueprint or life-force that guides the development of an organism.</note> is present, which is itself a kind of living thing, and matter is present to receive it, it is necessary for a living creature to be generated. So too, since the intellectual nature is present, possessing almighty power, and nothing hinders it (for nothing intervenes between it and its recipient),
<margin>C</margin>
it is necessary for the one to be beautified and the other to perform the beautifying. But that which has been beautified possesses its forms in a divided way—man in one place, the sun in another. The Beautifier, by contrast, possesses all things in a single unity.

->*Every idea is collectively and similarly a living intellectual essence, a species, and an act. However, they differ from one another by their specific properties. Chapter X.*<-

---

->*All formal things in the world—both movements and actions and their effects—proceeding in a certain natural and special order, have their own proper ideas there. However, the defects of natural forms and progressions do not exist there at all, but happen from elsewhere, and are known through the ideas of formal things.*<-

<margin>A</margin>
WHATEVER things exist in the sensible world proceed from there as **species** <note>original: "species"; the perfect forms or types that define a thing's nature.</note>, but other things do not. Therefore, nothing that is "against nature" exists there, just as nothing "against art" exists within the arts, nor is there "lameness" in the seeds. For the condition of lame feet happens during the process of birth, when the formative seed-reason fails to dominate; truly, the loss of the form happens by chance and accident. But qualities consistent with nature itself—
<margin>B</margin>
quantities, numbers, magnitudes, habits, progressions, and natural actions and passions, along with motion and rest in both universal and particular conditions—are among the number of those things that exist there and proceed from there. Instead of time, **eternity** <note>original: "æternitas"</note> reigns there; but instead of place, one thing is found in another through a certain intellectual reason. Since all things are there together, whatever you
<margin>C</margin>
might take from them is **Essence** <note>original: "essentia"; true, unchanging Being.</note>, an intellectual nature, and partakes in life. Thus, "the same" and "the different," motion and rest, the moving and the stable, are all essentially there: essence, quality, and absolutely everything. For each thing is a being not in potentiality, but in **act** <note>original: "actu"; fully realized and active existence.</note>; for this reason, quality is not separated from each essence. But are only those things which are contained in the sensible world present there, or many other things as well? First, it seems we must consider those things produced by the arts; for no evil is there or from there. For evil...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
What then are the things in that Mind, which we divide as we think upon them? For it is necessary to present them as being at rest, as if displaying the things within from a knowledge that exists in unity. This world, being a living creature that contains all living creatures and having its being and its specific nature from another, must be traced back to its source in the Intellect. It is necessary, then, for the whole to exist there in the intelligible realm.
<margin>B</margin>
And the Intellect is that intelligible world which Plato says "contains the living creatures within the Living Being." For as there is a life-giving reason, and at the same time matter which receives that formative seed-reason, a living creature must exist. In the same way, since an intellectual nature exists by itself without any hindrance—nothing being between them, and we have the recipients—
<margin>C</margin>
it is necessary for the one to be ordered and the other to order. That which is ordered has its forms divided—man in one place, the sun in another—but the other holds all things in one.

<margin>A</margin>
Whatever things, then, exist as forms in the sensible world, these come from there; but what are not forms, do not. Therefore, of things against nature, there is no Intellect there. Just as there is nothing against art in the arts, so there is no lameness in the seeds. For lameness is not already in nature, but is a failure of the reason-principle. Rather, it is a ruin caused by chance. But the forms and the qualities that are
<margin>B</margin>
in harmony [with nature] are there: quantities, numbers, and magnitudes, and relations, and motions and rests according to nature. Motions and rests, both universal and particular, are among the things there. Instead of time, there is eternity. Place there is intellectual: one thing within another. Since all things are there together, whatever you may take of them is essence and intellectual,
<margin>C</margin>
partaking in life, both "the same" and "the other," and motion and rest, and the moving and the standing, and essence and quality. For everything there is in activity, and each is a "this." So that quality is not separated from each essence. Are then only those things in the sensible world there, or many others? But first we must consider the arts. For of evil there is nothing; for evil...

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Divine Intellect serves as the "Intelligible World," containing the perfect, unified archetypes (Ideas) of all natural things. He distinguishes between the perfect forms found in this divine realm and the flaws of the physical world, such as lameness or evil, which arise from the failure of matter to perfectly receive the divine blueprint.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Intellectual World"—the realm of pure thought and eternal Forms. While the previous page established that the Divine Intellect contains all natural truths within itself, this page explores whether human arts, crafts, and even individual identities like "Socrates" have their own eternal archetypes.</meta>

### NINTH BOOK. <note>original: "LIBER NONVS"; this refers to the ninth treatise of the fifth Ennead, titled "On the Intellect, the Ideas, and Being."</note>

...here, it happens from indigence, privation, and defect. Evil is certainly a kind of suffering of unfortunate **matter** <note>original: "materiæ"; in Neoplatonism, matter is the lowest level of reality and the source of "evil" because it is a lack or privation of form.</note> that momentarily catches a form: and likewise of that which seems to escape being similar to matter.

<column-break/>

*Works of art which are produced either solely by imitation of natural things or motions, or which proceed from natural and artificial genius, do not have their own Ideas in the divine realm.*
->Chapter XI.<-

*But they are partly reduced to the Ideas of natural things, and partly to the ratios of things—numbers, measures, and modes—innate in the rational soul and dependent on similar Ideas. Philosophical contemplation, however, takes Divine Wisdom as its Idea; the one who governs privately or publicly looks to Divine Providence; and time looks to eternity as its Idea.*

<margin>A</margin> BUT to come now to the arts and crafts: those arts which are purely imitative—such as painting, sculpture, dancing, and the gesturing of hands—since they are produced and exist here in the physical world, use a **sensible** <note>original: "sensibili"; things perceived by the five senses rather than the mind.</note> example, and imitate species and motions. Likewise, they transfer the symmetries they see to their own work. Therefore, it does not seem right that they could be traced back to the higher realm, except through the faculty of human **reason** <note>original: "ratione"; the human mind acts as the bridge between the physical art and the eternal Idea of proportion.</note> itself. 

If anyone considers the habit of symmetry that exists in animals—the general beauty 
<margin>B</margin> found in all living creatures—this will certainly be a part of that faculty which also considers such things in the divine world, and which contemplates the harmony of all things. Furthermore, all music is occupied with harmony and the ratios of rhythm. Insofar as it contemplates certain **intelligible** <note>original: "intelligibiles"; things belonging to the realm of pure thought/Intellect.</note> ratios of numbers and concord, it functions in the same way as that Reason which possesses the intelligible number and concord within itself. 

Whatever arts manufacture physical things—
<margin>C</margin> such as the architect and the carpenter—insofar as they use proportions and measurements, they seem to derive their beginning and some portion of that higher wisdom from above. But when they mix the rules of measurement with physical matter, they do not depend entirely on the higher realm, except perhaps for that part of them that exists in the human mind. 

Furthermore, neither agriculture, which brings aid to physical plants, nor medicine, which cares for human health and provides humans with strength and a firm habit of body, are found there in their physical form. For a different Power and Health flourishes there, through which 
<margin>D</margin> all living things possess sufficient stability. Therefore, the art of oratory, the command of an army, and the discipline of managing a household or a state—if they ever observe the "Honorable" itself in their actions and consider that celestial beauty—derive their share of knowledge from that Science which flourishes there. 

Then truly, **geometry**, which pertains to intelligible things, must be placed there; and likewise **Wisdom**, which is concerned with Being itself in the highest degree. And regarding the arts and the duties of the arts, let this suffice.

---

*In the Idea of rational and intellectual man is contained, in summary, every artificial faculty and the progression of genius.*
->Chapter XII.<-

*All formal differences between individuals that do not happen by chance from the diversity of matter or locations have Ideas there—but rather as powers than as their own distinct acts. This is because within the species themselves, of which there are properly and principally Ideas, are contained various and singular modes of forms that will eventually sprout forth.*

<margin>A</margin> NOW, if the Idea of Man exists there, then the Idea of the "Rational" and the "Technical" <note>original: "artificiosi"; the capacity for art/skill.</note> must also exist there. There are, moreover, arts there which are conceived by the Mind and brought forth like offspring. It must also be said that the **Species of Universals** <note>original: "vniuersalium species"; the general form of "Man" rather than a specific person.</note> exist there—not the Idea of Socrates specifically, but rather the Idea of Man. However, regarding Man, we must specifically consider whether there is also a singular, individual Idea there.

<summary>Plotinus explores how human arts (like music and architecture) and individual identities relate to the eternal Ideas, concluding that while imitative arts belong to the physical world, the mathematical and moral principles they use are rooted in the Divine Intellect.</summary>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK V.
<page-num>564</page-num>

<margin>A</margin>
I mean individual traits, because the individual is not the same as the Form, nor does it possess one thing after another. This person is of this sort, while that one is hooked-nosed <note>original: "aquilinus"; literally "eagle-like," referring to a prominent or Roman nose shape.</note>. Such properties must be placed within the **Form** <term>Form: the eternal, perfect blueprint of a thing in the divine mind</term> of Man, just as there are certain differences of forms, much like an animal has its own distinct differences. But we must consider that some differences—such as why this person is hooked-nosed under this condition and that person under another—proceed from **matter** <note>original: "materia"; the physical "stuff" that resists the perfect imprint of a Form.</note>. Similarly, we should believe that some differences in color consist in the rational principle and form, while others happen due to the diversity of matter and location.

->Any material thing stands in relation to its own Idea as a painted image does to a living substance. Chapter XIII.<-

*But souls, intellects, and their perfected virtues exist as true things outside the Idea just as they do within the Idea; they are called by the same name not merely by chance but because they share the same nature. They do not differ as a painted man differs from a living one, but rather as a boy differs from a man.*

<margin>A</margin>
IT REMAINS to investigate whether only those things contained in the sensible order exist there [in the intelligible world]: or whether, just as our human being here is one thing and the "Human-Himself" <note>original: "ipse homo"; the Platonic Ideal or archetype of humanity.</note> is another, so too is there one soul there that is the Soul-Itself, and another which is this soul; and similarly, one intellect which is this intellect, and another which is the Intellect-Itself. We must say first, then, that one should not believe all things here to be mere copies of archetypes, nor that the soul is a copy of the Soul-Itself; nevertheless, one soul excels another in dignity. The soul is here too, but perhaps it is not the Soul-Itself insofar as it is "here" <note>Plotinus is distinguishing between the soul's essence and its presence in a physical body.</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
Since every soul truly exists, there is also a certain **justice** and **temperance** in the souls dwelling here, and furthermore, true knowledge. These are not merely images or likenesses of the divine virtues as if they were dwelling in a physical place, but those very same things existing here in another manner; for those divine things are not confined to a specific place. Therefore, when the soul emerges from the body, those virtues are in that same place [the intelligible realm]. For the sensible world is determined by only one place, but the **intelligible world** <term>Intelligible World: the realm of pure thought and reality, beyond physical space</term> is everywhere.

<margin>C</margin>
Whatever a soul of such a kind possesses here, it possesses again there. Therefore, if those things said to be in a sensible place are understood to be those numbered among the genus of visible things, then not only are the things in the sensible world present there, but many more flow out from there. But if they are said to be in the world in such a way that both the soul and the things within the soul are included, then surely everything that is there is also here.

->Many things happen by a certain chance through decay, contrary to the Ideas, and are deformed; for the vegetative part of the soul, which is the lowest of divine things, cannot entirely overcome matter. Chapter XIV.<-

*Things that occasionally flow together into one without a certain order directed toward an end do not have Ideas. Under the Idea of Man are contained the ingenious and necessary arts. The soul itself is the Idea of the soul; closest to this is the soul formed into intellects by the understanding. But that same soul stands further away when it takes upon itself the universal providence of the world, and furthest of all when that same soul is finally devoted to particular providence.*

<margin>A</margin>
SHOULD we then believe that this nature, which contains all things in the intelligible genus, is the Principle itself? But how could that be? For the Principle itself is truly and entirely **One** and simple, whereas in the fullness of beings there is a necessary multiplicity. But again, in what way is such a nature and fullness apart from the One itself, yet from the One? And how did this multitude flow from there? Under what condition did all these things come to be? Also, why is the Intellect these things, and from where? Of these matters, truly, we must speak elsewhere, beginning from another starting point.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<note>This column contains the original Greek text corresponding to the Latin translated above. It discusses the "hooked nose" [σιμότης] vs "aquiline nose" [γρυπότης], and the presence of the soul [ψυχή] and intellect [νοῦς] in the intelligible realm.</note>
But the individual [trait] is because one is not the same as another, for instance, one is snub-nosed and another is hook-nosed. Differences in colors and snub-nosedness are in the form of all humans, just as there are differences in the animal. But it also comes from matter: that one person is such and another is such. Differences in colors are partly in the rational principle and partly caused by differences in matter and place.

<margin>A</margin>
IT REMAINS to consider if only the things in the sensible world are there, or just as the sensible man is different from that Man [the Idea], is every soul there, and the intellect of this person there? First, it must be said that not everything here is a copy of archetypes there. The soul must not be a mere copy of the Soul, but one soul differs from another in honor, and it exists here; though perhaps not as the Soul-Itself is here. There is the soul of what each thing truly is, and justice and temperance, and true knowledge in our souls—not copies or images of those things as if in a sensible place, but those very things existing here in another way. For those things are not in a limited place. Whenever the soul is outside the body, those things are there.

<margin>C</margin>
For the sensible world is in one way, but the intelligible world is everywhere. Whatever the soul has here, these things are also there. So if one takes the things in the sensible world to be the visible things, not only are the things in the sensible world there, but even more. But if the things in the world are spoken of as including the soul and what is in the soul, then all things there are also here.

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, this nature which encompasses all things in the intelligible, must this be set as the Principle? And how can it be from that true Principle, the One-Itself, yet be a multitude? How is it a fullness, and how are all these things, and why did they come to be and from where? This must be spoken of by starting from another principle.

He concludes that while some traits come from matter, the soul and its virtues (like justice) are essentially the same in both the physical and spiritual realms, though the "Intelligible World" is the true source of all things.</summary>

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the question of things arising from decay <note>original: "σήψεως" (sēpseōs); refers to the ancient belief in spontaneous generation, where life was thought to arise from rotting matter.</note> and difficult things: whether a Form exists even for those, or if we must call them filth or mud. We must say that whatever one derives from the First <term>The First: The "One," the ultimate source of all existence in Plotinian philosophy</term> is entirely excellent. These lowly things are not among those Forms. Nor does the Intellect <note>original: "νῦς" (nous); the divine Mind.</note> derive from them; rather, the Soul <note>original: "ψυχὴ" (psyche)</note> receives from the Intellect, while also receiving much from Matter <note>original: "ὕλης" (hylēs)</note>. But regarding these things, we shall speak more clearly when we return to the problem: how a multitude arises from the One. It is clear that composite things, which exist by chance or through Intellect but come together as sensible objects by their own impulse, are not contained within the Forms. Furthermore, things from decay arise perhaps from the Soul being unable to do anything else; otherwise, it would have made something according to nature. It does, therefore, what it can. Regarding the arts, those are contained within the human being which refer to the things natural to man. But there is another universal Soul prior to these, and even prior to that universal one is the Soul-in-Itself, or the life in the Intellect before it becomes a soul, so that it might even be called the "Absolute Soul" <note>original: "αὐτοψυχὴν" (autopsychēn).</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But where it is asked whether there might be a species there <note>original: "species"; Ficino’s translation of "eidos" or Form.</note> even of those things which arise from putrefaction, and of difficult and very troublesome things, and likewise of filth and mud, it must be said: that as many things as the Intellect derives from the First are all excellent, in which species these [lowly] things are certainly not present. Nor does the Intellect receive anything from these, but the Soul indeed receives many things from the Intellect, while admitting moreover very many things from matter, in which these [lowly] things happen. But concerning these we shall explain more openly if we return to that doubt <margin>B</margin> which asks: how a multitude flows forth from the One. Now indeed it is established that those composite things which happen randomly and in vain, not by the Intellect but by their own momentum, flow together in this genus of sensible things and are by no means contained by the species themselves. Furthermore, those things which arise by putrefaction happen from a certain chance of the soul, which perhaps was then unable to do anything else; otherwise, it would have undoubtedly made something more agreeable to nature. It makes, therefore, where and how it can. It is also evident that those arts <margin>C</margin> are contained in the higher nature of man itself which are referred to those things that are natural to the human race. But there is a prior universal soul, and prior to the universal is the Soul itself, so that this soul may be formed from it, and it happens that we call that one especially "the Soul itself."

# PLOTINUS
## THE SIXTH ENNEAD
### BOOK ONE.

#### ON THE KINDS OF BEING.
#### <note>original: "De generibus entis"</note>

> *He touches upon many questions regarding the kinds of things; however, he seems to define nothing in this chapter. Chapter I.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V featuring a human face surrounded by floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>IT IS a very ancient question: how many and what kind of things are they which are said to be? Some indeed said that Being <term>Being: "Ens" in Latin or "On" in Greek; the fundamental nature of existence.</term> is only one; others said more than one, but a finite number; others still said they were infinite. Of these, each brought forward different views, whether they proposed one, finite, or infinite things. <margin>B</margin> Since such opinions have already been sufficiently examined by later thinkers, we must set them aside for the present. We must consider only the opinion of those who, through systematic discourse, established certain determined kinds <term>Kinds: "Genera" in Latin; the broad classes or categories into which all reality is divided.</term> of things as the ancients did. These thinkers certainly did not accept that there is only one kind, since they saw that there are many things even among "intelligible" <term>Intelligible: Refers to the realm of pure thought and divine forms, accessible by the mind rather than the physical senses.</term> realities; nor, on the other hand, did they wish to admit an infinite number, since that would be impossible and there would be no science at all. <margin>C</margin> But reducing the finite things to a specific number—since they could not correctly call these "elements" <note>original: "elementa" / "stoicheia"</note> because they contained many things subordinate to themselves—they instead called these "kinds." Some proposed ten, while others proposed fewer. Perhaps there would even be some who might bring still more before us. There is also a difference in these "kinds": for some wanted the kinds to be "principles" <term>Principles: The foundational starting points or causes of all other things.</term>, while others held that the things themselves are ultimately the kinds. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, we must first take up the opinion of those who divided all things into ten <note>Plotinus is referring to Aristotle’s ten Categories: Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Place, Time, Position, State, Action, and Passion.</note>, investigating whether they mean there are ten kinds sharing the common name of "Being," or ten "predicaments" <term>Predicaments: Ways in which something can be described or categorized.</term>. For they themselves admit that "Being" is not used in a single, identical sense across all things, and they are right to admit it. Indeed, we must first ask: are those ten kinds present similarly in both intelligible and sensible <term>Sensible: Things perceived by the five senses; the physical world.</term> realms? Or are all ten in the sensible realm, while only some are in the intelligible? Or are some present in both? No one would say that all ten are present in both realms. But it seems we must investigate which of the ten specifically correspond to the intelligible realm.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or philosopher, within an architectural frame.</image-desc>REGARDING the things that exist, how many and of what sort they are: this is a certain inquiry. Some of the ancients said there is only one; others said there are a finite number. In all these cases, some said one thing and others another. <margin>B</margin> If there are finite things, are they both the sensible ones and all things together with them? Those ancient opinions have been sufficiently and carefully examined and should be left aside by us. We must examine the views of those who have already determined things within specific limits. <margin>C</margin> They proposed these limits because they saw many things even in the intelligible realm, yet they did not want to go toward infinity, since then no knowledge could exist. They reduced the number of things because they saw that the underlying subjects were not correctly identified, nor were they "elements." Some say these are principles, others say they are "kinds." There is also a difference among the kinds, whether the kinds themselves are principles or if they are the things that apply to living beings. <margin>D</margin> First, then, we must take up the view that divides all beings into ten, and we must consider whether they think they are speaking of ten kinds—merely happening to share a name—or ten "categories" <note>original: "katēgorias"</note>. For they say, and say rightly, that "Being" is not a synonymous term applied to all things. Rather, this should be asked first: are these ten found equally in the intelligible and the sensible? Or are all ten in the sensible, but in the intelligible some are found while others are not? For if they were in both, one must examine which of the ten they are.

In these matters which pertain to the intelligible, no one would say they [all ten] are present. But it seems we must investigate which of the ten especially belong equally to the intelligible.

<meta>catchword: ἐπειδὴ (Since/Because)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus begins his critique of the "Kinds of Being," specifically examining Aristotle’s ten categories to determine if they can apply to both the physical world and the higher realm of pure Intellect. He argues that "Being" is not a single, uniform concept that applies to everything in the same way.</summary>
<keywords>Categories, Being, Intelligible, Sensible, Aristotle, Genera, Principles, Plotinus, Enneads</keywords>

--- Page 602 ---
<meta>This page continues the opening of the Sixth Ennead, Book One. In the previous page, Plotinus began his critique of the "Categories" of existence, questioning how many broad classes of things actually exist. Here, he specifically challenges Aristotle’s concept of "Substance" (Ousia), arguing that we cannot use the same word to describe both divine, eternal things and physical, decaying things.</meta>

BOOK ONE.

<margin>A</margin>
Are we then to bring the things that exist there <note>The "intelligible" or divine realm of pure thought.</note> under the same single genus as the things here in the physical world? Or is the word "Substance" <note>original: οὐσία (ousia)</note> used equivocally <term>Equivocally: When the same word is used for two different things, like "bank" of a river and a "bank" for money.</term>, so that the name is common but the nature is not the same, and the term "primary" refers to something else entirely in that other realm? But if one were to say that the word "Substance" signifies the same thing when applied to both sensible beings and those that come after, what would that mean? Is it as if they are in a sequence of "prior" and "posterior," as they say regarding created things and their divisions? Or did they intend for all beings to be divided together, yet in doing so, they left out the most important beings? <margin>B</margin>

---
### *It should not be easily granted that incorporeal and corporeal things, as well as form and matter, and the composite, the singular, and the universal, all meet in one genus of substance. Chapter II.*
---

<margin>A</margin>
Must we then reconsider this? Or how can we say that "Substance" is not a genus covering all things? It is certainly not a single genus, because there can be no common element between the intelligible nature and the sensible nature. If there were, there would have to be something else "above" both of them that is predicated of both—something that would be neither body nor incorporeal. For if that higher genus were a body, then the things called incorporeal would be bodies; and if it were incorporeal, then the bodies would be incorporeal. Rather, we must first investigate the substances here in our world—what is common to matter, form, and the composite <note>The physical object made of both matter and form.</term>. For they say all of these are "substances." Is there something common that holds them together as substance, even if form is called "substance" more than matter is? And they are right to say so, though some might argue matter is more truly substance. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, what do the so-called "primary substances" have in common with "secondary substances"? <note>In Aristotelian logic, a "primary substance" is an individual person or thing, while a "secondary substance" is the species or genus it belongs to.</note> For secondary substances only get their name from the primary ones. More generally, it is not possible to explain what substance actually is among them. Even if one assigns a specific property to substance—such as being a single thing that can admit contrary qualities at different times <margin>C</margin>—that may seem to fit all substances, but it does not reveal the essence itself.

---
### *Those things which the Peripatetics <note>Peripatetics: The followers of Aristotle, who famously walked while they taught.</note> call substances are more likely arranged in a sequence depending on a single source, rather than belonging to the same nature. Chapter III.*
---

<margin>Like</margin> <margin>A</margin>
But should we instead say there is one single category under which we might group intelligible substance, matter, form, and the composite? It would be like if someone spoke of the "Race of the Heraclidae" <note>original: γένος τῶν ἡρακλειδῶν; the descendants of the hero Hercules.</note> as a single group—not because they all share one common characteristic, but because they all descend from a single ancestor. In this sense, the first thing is "Substance" in the highest degree, and the others are substances in a secondary or lesser degree. <margin>B</margin> But what prevents all things that are said to "be" from being a single category? Does everything else derive from Substance? Are other things perhaps just "affections" <note>Properties or qualities.</note> of substance, while the substances themselves are arranged in a sequence, one after another?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
And is it not true that the things there [in the divine realm] must be collected under the same genus as these things of ours, or rather that "essence" is said equivocally of what is there and what is here? Indeed, if the word is used equivocally, there are multiple genera; but if it is used univocally <term>Univocally: When a word is used with exactly the same meaning in every case.</term>, it is immediately absurd that "essence" should signify the same thing in both primary and posterior beings. For there is no single common genus in those things where one is prior and another is posterior; but they do not speak of things pertaining to the intellect according to this division. Therefore, they did not intend to divide all things that exist, but rather they left out the things that most truly exist. <margin>B</margin>

<margin>A</margin>
We must ask again: should these be considered genera, and how can there be one genus of substance? For it seems we must begin entirely from this point. It has been said that there cannot be one genus of substance common to both intelligible and sensible nature. For if so, there would be something else above both intelligible and sensible substance predicated commonly of both, which would be neither body nor incorporeal. Otherwise, if that genus were a body, it would follow that what is called incorporeal under it is a body; or if it were incorporeal, it would follow again that what is called a body under it is incorporeal. <margin>B</margin> Since in those things which are called "substances" by us here, we must ask what is common to matter, form, and the composite. For they say all these are substances, yet they are not equally substances: since form is called substance more than matter is, and rightly so—though others might say matter is more truly substance. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, what will the substances called "primary" have in common with "secondary" substances? Since secondary substances have the very fact that they are called substances from the primary ones. In truth, it is impossible for them to explain what substance is. For even if someone assigns a specific property of substance to us, they have not yet grasped what it is in itself; and perhaps that which is marked as a property of substance—namely, that one and the same thing can receive contraries in turn—seems to apply to all substances.

<margin>A</margin>
But should we say there is one single category under which we commonly understand intelligible substance, and form, and matter, and the composite? It would be just as if someone called the race of the Heraclidae one thing—not as if there were some common quality in all of them, but because they descend from one ancestor. For in the first degree, that is substance; but in the second degree, and to a lesser extent, are the rest. <margin>B</margin> But what prevents absolutely all things from being one category? For what prevents all other things which are said to "be" from being derived from substance? Or perhaps the rest are certain "passions" of substance itself, while the substances themselves are arranged one after another in a certain order?

PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

But indeed, we cannot even in this way halt our progress at substance, nor can we grasp what is most essential to it, <margin>A</margin> so that we might derive other substances from it. Therefore, let all things that are called substances be considered related to one another, having something distinct from the other categories. What, then, is the meaning of this very term, "substance"? What is it to be a "this" and an "underlying subject"? <note>Plotinus is questioning the Aristotelian definition of substance as something that is not "in" another thing like an accident (such as a color is "in" a body).</note> It is said to be that which is not "in" a subject, and that which is not itself a property of something else—in the way that whiteness is a quality of a body, or a specific amount is a quantity of an essence. <margin>B</margin> Likewise, is time a property of motion, or is matter a property of the moving thing itself? Yet, "secondary substance" <note>original: substantia secunda / δευτέρα οὐσία. In Aristotelian logic, "primary substances" are individual things like a specific man, while "secondary substances" are the species or genera, like "Human" or "Animal."</note> is said to be attributed to another. But perhaps this is said of another in a different way than other things are; namely, as a genus that exists as a part, in this way: it belongs to the substance of that in which it exists. Whiteness, however, is attributed to another in the sense that it lies within it as an accident. But someone might call these traits unique compared to others, and thus group them into one and call them substances. <margin>C</margin> However, he would not be correct in saying this is a single genus, nor would he truly explain the concept and nature of substance. But let these matters end here; let us proceed to the nature of quantity.

---

*Number, the continuous, place, and time—which the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for the "colonnades" (peripatoi) where they walked and talked.</note> place in the single category of quantity—do not seem to have a single nature equally common to all: but rather are arranged in a common series by degrees reduced back to a "primary quantity."* ->Chapter IV.<-

---

*Number alone seems to be "how much" by its very self, being quantity itself. In this, the unit defines each subsequent thing as a unit. Compared to this, dimension is weighed to see how great it is: a line or a body is judged by its division.*

---

<margin>A</margin> **NUMBER** is indeed the first thing they call "how much" <note>original: quanta / ποσὰ</note>, along with all continuous magnitude, place, and time. All other things they call "how much," they refer back to these. Thus, they say motion is a quantity because the time in which it occurs is a quantity—though perhaps it should be viewed the other way around, since time receives its continuity from motion. If they say the continuous is a quantity by virtue of being continuous, it would follow that the discrete <note>Things that are separate and countable, like a group of stones.</note> is not a quantity. But if the continuous is a quantity by accident, <margin>B</margin> what will be common to both in the very fact that they are "how much"? In numbers themselves, it may be common that they are quantities; although this very fact—that they are called quantities—is well enough established, it is not yet clear what that specific nature is by which they are so called. Indeed, a line, a surface, and a body are not called "how much" in that same way; they are called magnitudes, but not necessarily quantities. For they only manage to be called quantities <margin>C</margin> when they are reduced to a number—such as when something is measured as being "two cubits" or "three cubits" long. Even a physical body becomes a "how much" only when it is reduced to a measure; likewise, place is a quantity only by accident, not by its own nature. We must not take quantity as something accidental, but rather what is quantity in and of itself. For one should not accept "three oxen" as a quantity, but rather the number itself that is in them. For "three oxen" already involves two categories <note>Substance (oxen) and Quantity (three).</note>. Likewise, a "line of such a length" involves two categories. Similarly, a "surface of such a size" is two categories: the surface itself, and the quantity of the

Let all those things called substances be of the same kind, having something apart from the other genera. What then is this very thing: the primary, the "this," and the "subject"? That which is not in another as in a subject, and is not something else belonging to another—unlike a quality, <margin>B</margin> or motion in relation to time? But "secondary substance" is spoken of in respect to another. One might say that "being in respect to another" is like being a part, or being in a subject, or an entanglement where a part covers something. Or rather, by taking it in respect to other things, I give it a name. But one might say these are specific traits compared to other things, and so bring them into a unity and call them substances. <margin>C</margin> Yet, one would not be saying they are one in the sense of a genus, nor would he reveal the concept of substance and its nature. And these things—let them be as they are. Let us go toward the nature of quantities.

<margin>A</margin> **NUMBER** indeed is the first thing, they say, and all continuous magnitude, and place, and time. And the other things, as many as are called quantities—since they also speak of motion as a quantity because of time, and perhaps conversely of time because of continuity, which it has taken from motion. If they should say the continuous, insofar as it is continuous, is a quantity, then the discrete would not be a quantity. But if <margin>B</margin> they should say the continuous is a quantity by accident, then by what means—if not the other—is the "how much" established? For to say that "how much" exists because quantity is spoken of in relation to itself is to explain nothing. Now, a line, a surface, and a body are not [simply] so called, but are called magnitudes; they are not called quantities except when they are taken in a certain way, such as when they are brought into number as "two cubits" or "three cubits." Since <margin>C</margin> the physical body, once measured, becomes a quantity. Or even the earth [becomes so] by accident, or in whatever way. But one must not take quantity as an accident, but as being quantity in itself. For one does not take "three oxen" as a quantity, but the number in them. <meta>This page marks a transition in Plotinus’s critique of Aristotle’s "Categories." Having previously argued that the category of "Substance" cannot unify the physical and spiritual worlds, he now examines the category of "Quantity" (how much of something there is). He questions whether things like surfaces, numbers, and even speech truly belong to a single category of Quantity.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.
Bb 3

<margin>A</margin> **A quantity:** <note>Greek: ποσὸν (*poson*); Latin: *quantum*. This refers to the category of "how much" or "magnitude."</note> why indeed should a surface itself be considered a quantity? Because when it has been defined by three or four lines, it is judged to be a quantity. What then? Shall we assert that number alone is "quantity" in its truest sense? Certainly, if we admit that numbers exist separately on their own, these are surely judged to be substances—especially since they exist according to themselves. If, however, we take the numbers that are present in the things that participate in them, according to which we count—not indeed the abstract units, <margin>B</margin> but ten horses or ten oxen—first of all, it would seem absurd, if those numbers are substances, that these horses and oxen should not also be substances. Next, it is again absurd if, existing within the subjects, they are "in" them, and yet do not exist outside them while they are measuring, in the same way that certain rules and measures do when they appear to measure. But if they are taken as existing internally within themselves for the purpose of measuring, and not as if they were clinging to some subjects, then surely those things which are the subjects are not "quantities" either, <margin>C</margin> since they do not participate in quantity through themselves.

Why then are these things themselves judged to be quantity? For they are measures. But why are measures "quantities," or "Quantity" itself? Is it perhaps because, existing in the order of things, even if they are not suited to the nature of any other things, they will still be what they are said to be? For the unit itself determines a "one" among them; then it applies itself to another, <margin>D</margin> and number designates how many things are there. And the soul, using number, measures the multitude itself. Therefore, while it measures, it does not measure *what* each thing is; for it says "one" and "two," whatever they may be without that number, even if they are opposites. Nor, again, does it measure what kind of affection each thing has—such as whether it is hot or beautiful—but only insofar as it properly regards "how much" (quantity). Therefore, whether number is assessed according to itself or in the things that participate in it, it is not the participants that are the "how much," but the <margin>E</margin> number itself. Therefore, a "three-cubit" object <note>A cubit was an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> will not be the quantity, but rather the "three" will be this very thing.

If this is so, why then are magnitudes also called quantities? Is it perhaps because they are close to quantity itself, and we call whatever things they are present in "quantities"? Although we do not weigh those things by the "primary quantity" <note>Plotinus distinguishes between the "primary" mathematical quantity (the number 3) and the "secondary" physical quantity (three feet of wood).</note> in that way. Indeed, we call something "great" as if it participates in a large number, and "small" because it participates in a small number. Nevertheless, "great" and "small" themselves are not properly judged to be quantities, but rather "relative" <note>Aristotle placed "Great" and "Small" under the category of Relation (*Pros ti*) rather than Quantity, a point Plotinus is investigating here.</note> to something else. However, we must still consider these matters more diligently. Therefore, there will not be one single genus, but only number; while these other things are in the second place, which relate to one another in a certain way, both those in the first place and those in the second. But we must investigate how numbers that exist according to themselves are substances, and whether perhaps they too are a kind of quantity. In whichever way they relate, they will not have one common thing with these others, unless perhaps in name only.

> *Quantity itself is that through which another thing becomes "how much," but it is through quantity that other things become "how much." <margin>A</margin> **A quantity is:** but why indeed is a surface a "how much"? For which reason, since it is already determined as if by three or four lines, it is judged to be a "how much." What then? Shall we assert that only number is "how much" itself? Truly, if we admit numbers existing separately by themselves to this, these are certainly judged to be substances, especially because they exist according to themselves. If, however, we have accepted numbers which are in those things participating in them, according to which we <margin>B</margin> count—not indeed units, but ten horses and ten oxen—firstly, it will indeed seem absurd, if those are substances, that these also are not substances. Then again it is absurd if, existing in subjects, they are in them, and do not thus exist outside them while they are being measured, in the same way as certain rules and measures, when they are seen to measure. But if they are taken as existing more internally in themselves for measuring, and not as if clinging to some subjects, certainly neither <margin>C</margin> are those things "quantities" which are the subjects, since they do not participate in quantity through themselves.

Why then are they themselves judged to be quantity? For they are measures. But why are measures "quantities," or "Quantity"? Or perhaps because, existing in the order of things, even if it is suited to the nature of none of the others, they will nevertheless be this very thing which they are called? For the unit itself of them determines "one"; then it brings itself to another, and number <margin>D</margin> designates how many things are there. And the soul, using number, itself measures the multitude. While therefore it measures, it does not measure what each thing is; for it says "one" and "two," of whatever sort they are without it, even if they are contrary things. Nor again does it measure what kind of affection each thing has: such as whether it be hot or beautiful, but only as far as it properly regards "how much." For which reason, whether number is estimated according to itself or in its participants, it is not the participants that are "how much," but the <margin>E</margin> number itself. Therefore, neither will a "three-cubit" thing be quantity, but "three" rather will be this very thing.

If it is so, why then are magnitudes also called quantities? Perhaps because they are closest to quantity itself, and we call whatever things they are present in "quantities"? Although we do not thus weigh those things by the principal quantity itself. But we call a thing "great," as if it were a participant in a large number; and "small," because it becomes a participant in a small number. Nevertheless, "great" and "small" themselves are not judged to be quantities properly, but "relative" to something: but even so, these things must nevertheless be considered above all more diligently. Therefore, there will not be one single other genus, but number alone; while these others are in the second place, which are in a certain way among themselves, both those which are in the first and those which are in the second place. We, however, must investigate how numbers which exist according to themselves are substances; or whether perhaps they too are a certain quantity. But in whichever way they relate, they will not have one common thing with these, unless perhaps only the name.

For knowledge is spoken of in relation to the very thing which is to be known; similarly, sensation is in relation to the thing felt. Indeed, knowledge can be said to have a certain actual existence <note>Latin: *subsistentiam secundum actum*</note> toward the specific form of the thing being known, and sensation likewise toward the sensible object. Moreover, that which is called active stands in such a way toward the passive that it can produce a single result, and the measure <margin>B</margin> acts upon the measured to perform the measurement. But what effect does "similar" have when placed against "similar"? Perhaps it does not cause something to happen in that moment, but rather denotes that something already exists—namely, an identity of quality? Nevertheless, beyond the quality lying within each of them, it adds nothing; likewise with equal things. For identity in the "how much" <note>The category of Quantity.</note> precedes the mutual relationship. Is a relationship <note>Latin: *habitudo*; Greek: *schesis*</note> truly anything else besides the judgment of our own minds? This happens when we compare <margin>C</margin> things that exist in themselves for what they are, and we say: "this one and that one have the same magnitude," and "they have the same quality." Likewise: "this person fathered that one," or "this one surpasses that one." Even sitting and standing—what else do they have beyond the person sitting or standing? Now, a "habit" <note>The Greek *hexis* and Latin *habitus* here refer to a state of being or having, not just a routine behavior.</note> which is spoken of according to what it "has" seems rather to signify the act of having; but that which is spoken of according to what is "had" should rather be called a "quality." The same logic applies to "disposition." <margin>D</margin> What, then, will these things be, beyond those that are referred to one another? What are they beyond a certain comparison made by our intelligence? Furthermore, when the "surpassing" is referred to the "surpassed," the former is a magnitude of such a size, and the latter is a magnitude of such a size. This one is one thing, and that one is another; but the comparison is within us, even if it is necessary to them. Likewise, where "right" stands against "left," and "foremost" against "hindmost," perhaps these consist of a certain position, insofar as one is here and the other is there. We are the ones who think of "right" and "left"; in the objects themselves, there is nothing. Likewise, what is called "before" and "after" are in reality two distinct times, but the naming of them as "before" and "after" is placed within our own judgment.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to the similar, the equal, and the unequal, to the acting and the enduring, to the measure and the measured, and finally to knowledge and sense. For knowledge is spoken of in relation to the thing which is to be known. Similarly, sense is in relation to the sensing. For knowledge indeed can have toward the thing called "knowable" a certain existence according to the act directed toward the form of the thing to be known; sense likewise toward the sensible. Furthermore, that which is called active stands toward the passive in roughly this way: it can produce a single work, and the measure performs the measurement <margin>B</margin> upon the measured. But what effect does the similar have then against the similar? Or perhaps it has nothing that "becomes" then, but rather something that already "is"—namely, the identity in quality? Yet, beyond the quality lying in both, it adds nothing; similarly, neither do equals. For identity in the "how much" itself precedes the mutual relationship. But what else is a relationship besides the judgment of our mind? It is when we compare <margin>C</margin> things that exist in themselves as what they are, and we say that "this and that have the same magnitude," and "the same quality." Likewise, "this one begat that one," or "this one surpasses that one." Does "sitting" and "standing" have anything else besides the one sitting or standing? A "habit," however, which is spoken of according to that which "has," seems rather to signify the "having" itself; but that which is spoken of according to what is "had" is rather to be called a "quality." The same reasoning holds for "disposition." <margin>D</margin> What then will there be beyond these things which are referred to one another? What is there beyond a certain comparison made by our intelligence? Furthermore, when the "surpassing" is referred to the "surpassed," this one is a certain magnitude, and that one is a certain magnitude. But this is one thing and that is another; the comparison is in us, though it is necessary to them. Likewise, where the "right" stands toward the "left," and the "earlier" toward the "later," perhaps these consist in a certain position, insofar as that one is here and this one is there. We are the ones who think of right and left; but in the things themselves, there is nothing. Likewise, what is called "before" and "after" are in truth two times, but that which is named "before" and "after" is placed in our judgment.

---

> *He finally concedes that in all things which are called relative to one another, there is some true and mutual relationship, even beyond the effect of our own comparison, although in some places it is firmer and in others weaker. However, he says it is very obscure what this common relationship might be, and he doubts whether its nature is of a single kind.*

->Chapter VII.<-

---

<margin>A</margin> If, therefore, we are saying nothing [real], but are lying when we speak, then none of these things would exist, and relationship would be an empty thing. But if we speak truly when we say "this one is prior to that one," and the other is "posterior," we are taking two times together and saying something other than the subjects themselves—namely, the "prior." The same applies to "right" and "left," and regarding magnitudes themselves, we intend their "how much" to be a certain relationship, insofar as one surpasses and the other is surpassed. <margin>B</margin> Now, if things are this way even if we are not speaking or thinking—if it were perceived that "this is double that," and one "has" while the other "is had"—then they are so before we even notice them, and they are equal to one another before our cognition, and as much as...

<column-break/>

IF, therefore, we say nothing, but lie in the saying, then none of these things will exist, but relationship will be a void thing. But if we speak truly when we say "this is prior to that" and that is "posterior," comparing two times between themselves, we understand that "prior" and "posterior" are something else beyond the subjects. Similarly regarding right and left; and concerning magnitudes, beyond the "how much" itself, we wish there to be a certain relationship, insofar as this one surpasses and that one is surpassed. Now, if the facts are so even if we say nothing and think nothing—so that this is double to that, this has, and that is had—before we even turn our attention to it, and they are equal among themselves before our cognition, and as much as...

Bb 4

<summary>Plotinus questions whether the category of "Relation" (such as being double, similar, or to the left) exists independently in objects or is merely a product of human mental comparison. He concludes that while these relationships are real and exist before we observe them, their exact nature is difficult to define.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the category of "Relation" (Greek: *pros ti*). On the previous page, Plotinus began questioning whether relationships such as equality or fatherhood exist within the objects themselves or merely as concepts in the mind of the observer. He now moves toward defining the specific type of existence that characterizes a relationship.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS: BOOK VI

<margin>A</margin> ...regards quality, it may have a mutual union. In all those things which we say are "relative to something," there exists a certain mutual disposition <note>original: *habitudo*; Greek: *schesis*</note> beyond the subjects themselves, which we perceive as already existing. Similarly, knowledge stands in relation to the thing to be known; in this case, it is even more manifest that there is a certain subsistence <note>The actual reality or "standing under" of a concept.</note> arising from the relationship. If these things are indeed so, we should no longer ask whether a relationship exists in them or not. Instead, we must grant that among such things, in some cases the relationship persists as long as the subjects <margin>B</margin> remain as they were in themselves, even if they are meanwhile separated. In other cases, the relationship is formed when they come together. In still others, the relationship ceases or becomes something else entirely, even while the subjects remain—as happens with "right" and "left," or "near." It is from these latter examples especially that the suspicion arose that nothing truly exists in such things. Having granted this, we must investigate what is the same in all of them, and whether <margin>C</margin> there is a common element there that acts as a genus <note>A primary category or "family" of being.</note> rather than just an accident <note>A non-essential property.</note>. Then, once this common element is found, we must track down what kind of subsistence it has. Now, we must speak of the "relative"—that which is named "toward something"—not if it is simply said to belong to another (such as a certain habit of the soul or body), nor because it belongs to a certain soul or is in something; rather, those things are properly called "relatives" whose very existence <margin>D</margin> is nourished by nothing other than their relationship. I call this existence not that of the subjects, but that which is properly called "relative." For instance, "the double" provides existence to "the half," not to the two-cubit length <note>A cubit was a standard ancient unit of measurement, roughly the length of a forearm.</note> nor to the number two in general, nor to the one-cubit length or the number one; rather, these things being what they are, it follows immediately from their relationship—beyond the fact that one is two and the other is one—that the two is said to be and actually is "double," while the one follows suit by being, in turn, "the half." <margin>E</margin> Both therefore together produce from themselves another state of being: "double" and "half." These are made toward each other, and their being is nothing other than "being toward each other." Being resides in the "double" by the fact that it exceeds the half, and in the "half" by the fact that it is exceeded. Therefore, one of them is not prior and the other posterior, but both exist simultaneously. Furthermore, one might ask whether other relatives also exist simultaneously, or whether some are not simultaneous—as happens with a father and a son, and similar cases. For after the father has died, the son remains; and when a brother dies, the other remains a brother, since we are even accustomed to saying this or that person is similar to one who is deceased.

---

*The common description of a relation is the mutual disposition of two things. But this is so diverse among different relatives that the term is not used in a single, identical sense. Between some relatives, there is a certain action alongside the disposition, as between the one generating and the one generated; in others there is none, as between things that are similar or equal.*

### Chapter VIII.

<margin>A</margin> HOWEVER, we have digressed somewhat. We must first ask from that point: for what cause do these things behave so differently? But now, this very phrase "to be toward one another" ought to declare what common existence it possesses. Surely that common element cannot be a body. It follows, therefore,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> In some cases, being is the identity of things relative to one another; and in those things which we call "relative," there is a relationship <note>Greek: *schesis*</note> between them after the underlying subjects are considered. When we observe them, knowledge is relative to the thing known. These examples make the subsistence of things arising from relationship even clearer. We must, therefore, stop asking if relationship exists. We should note that among all things, in some, as long as the <margin>B</margin> subjects remain as they were, the relationship exists even if they are separated. In others, it is produced when they meet; in others still, the relationship ceases even while they remain, either entirely or it becomes something else, as in "right" and "near." From these examples comes the suspicion that there is nothing real in such cases. Having noted these things, one must seek what is the same in all and if there is something like a genus, and not merely an accident. Then, finding what is the same, we must see what kind of subsistence it has. We <margin>C</margin> should say that "relatives" are all those things said to be in a different way, such as a state of soul or body. It is not just what is in the soul or in the other, but whatever subsistence is derived solely from the relationship. This subsistence is not that of the subjects, but that which is called "relative." For example, the "double" relative to the "half": it gives subsistence to the "two-cubit" length, or the number two generally, or to the "one-cubit" length, or the number one. But these things existing according to their <margin>D</margin> relationship, regarding the "two," its being consists in being called and being the "double," and the other the "half." Having this, it is granted that in their number there is another kind of being, the "double," which is revealed toward each other; and their being is nothing else than "being for each other." To the "double," it is to exceed the half; to the "half," it is to be exceeded. So it is not that one of them is prior and the other posterior, but they are born together. But whether they also remain together [is a question], as in the case of father and son <margin>E</margin> among relatives, where the father perishes but the son exists, and a brother is a brother to one no longer living, since we even speak of the one who is no more.

---

<margin>A</margin> BUT we have digressed into these matters; we must seek from that point why these do not behave in the same way. But this very "being," this having a certain common subsistence toward one another, must be examined. Certainly, that which is common would not be a body. It remains then [to ask] how we speak of it in its pure state.

<meta>The catchword "είλι-" at the bottom refers to "eilikrinei" (pure/sincere), which begins the next page's first word.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explores the category of "Relation," arguing that while some relationships seem temporary or conceptual, true "relatives" (like double and half) have a unique form of existence that depends entirely on their mutual connection. He questions whether such relationships must exist simultaneously or if they can persist after one subject is gone.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation from the previous page regarding the "Category of Relation." Plotinus is currently exploring whether a relationship (like "being a father" or "being double") is a real, independent thing or just a way we describe how two things sit alongside each other.</meta>

# BOOK THE FIRST.

<margin>A</margin> If indeed the relationship is incorporeal: is it contained within the subjects themselves, or does it exist outside them? If the relationship is the same for both parties, we call them **univocal** <note>original: *vniuocam*; having the same name and the same nature, like two people both being "human."</note>. If it is not the same, but one is different from the other, they must be judged **equivocal** <note>original: *equiuocam*; having the same name but different natures, like a "bank" of a river and a "bank" for money.</note>. For it does not follow that just because something is called a "relationship," it possesses the same essence in every case. Should we, therefore, divide relationships in this way? You might say that some have a "resting" or idle relationship—existing, as it were, lying down—and they hold their existence entirely together. Others, however, <margin>B</margin> always possess their relationship through a certain <term>potentiality</term> <note>the capacity to act</note> and <term>act</term> <note>original: *opere*; the fulfillment of that capacity</note>. In these cases, did they have a prepared potentiality beforehand, which then moved into actual existence when they met? Or, to put it simply, should we say that some relationships *produce* something, while others merely *exist*? And does the one that exists merely provide a name to the other, while the one that produces actually hands over a part of its existence to the other? Such is the case with a father and a son, or a person acting and a person being acted upon. These have something like a shared life and action. <margin>C</margin> Is it right, then, to distinguish relationships in this way? That is, to divide them not as if they share some common, identical element with minor differences, but as if the relationship in each party is an entirely different nature? In that case, we would have to call them equivocal. We might call the active side "action" and the passive side "passion," as if they were two parts of a single motion. Or should we posit a different kind of relationship—one that does not "act" itself, but is a third thing acting upon both, such as **equality**, which makes things equal? <margin>D</margin> For it is by "equality" that things are equal, and by "identity" that things are made the same. But where we speak of the "great" and the "small," the former is so named by the presence of magnitude, and the latter by the presence of smallness. However, when one thing is considered "more" and another "less," this is judged relative to those who participate in them: the greater is so because of the magnitude now appearing within it, and the smaller because of the smallness appearing there.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If indeed it is incorporeal: and that is either in the subjects themselves or outside them. If the relationship is the same, it is univocal; but if not, but one is of one kind and another of another, it should be judged equivocal. For it does not follow from the fact that it is called a "disposition" <note>original: *habitudo*; the way one thing stands in regard to another.</note> that it immediately has the same essence. Must we then divide dispositions in this way? You would say, evidently, that some have an idle disposition, as if lying still, and possess their subsistence entirely among themselves at the same time; but others <margin>B</margin> always possess a disposition in some way together with potentiality and act, having previously had a prepared potentiality, and then in their meeting, they also exist in act? Or should it be said summarily that some things effect, and others merely exist? And that which exists only provides a name to the other? But that which effects also passes on existence to the other? Such a thing is surely "father and son," or "the actor and the receiver." For they have something like life and action. <margin>C</margin> Is it then fitting to distinguish disposition in this way? To divide it, I mean, not as if there is something identical and common in the differences, but as if the disposition in each is entirely another nature, which we ought to call equivocal? And should we name that which effects "action" and "passion," as if both were one motion; but set another kind which does not itself act, but is some other thing acting in both, such as equality, which makes things equal? For by equality <margin>D</margin> things are equal, and by identity certain things become the same. But where "great" and "small" are said, the former is so called by the presence of magnitude, and the latter in turn by the presence of smallness. But where this is weighed as "more" and that as "less," it is reckoned according to those who participate: the greater by the act of magnitude already appearing in it, and the smaller by smallness appearing so.

---

-> *Relation is something incorporeal and a certain ratio, which consists either in action, as between the mover and the moved; or in species, as when one thing is more beautiful than another; or in the privation <note>The absence of a quality.</note> of a species, as when one is uglier than another. Chapter IX.* <-

-> *Sometimes it is in the same species, as with similar and equal things; sometimes in opposite species, as with dissimilar and unequal things. It is difficult to place such diverse ratios in the same category, such as habits and their privations, or abstract and concrete things.* <-

---

It is therefore worthwhile in those first cases we were discussing—such as the actor and knowledge—to place a definite and effective relationship, an act, and one that remains within the act. In the remaining cases, however, we should suggest a certain "participation" <note>Taking part in a higher form or idea.</note> of the species and the ratio. For if all things were required to be only physical bodies, it would be proper to say that these relationships, which are spoken of in reference to one another, are nothing at all. But if we grant the primary province of being to incorporeal things and ratios, and we assert that relationships are certain ratios <margin>B</margin> and participations in the "Forms" <note>The perfect, eternal templates of things in Platonic philosophy.</note>, then it is surely consistent to assign causes in this way: the cause of this thing being "double" is the Form of the Double itself. And in turn, for something to be a "half," the cause is the Half. Now, some of these things are of the same species, and others are of opposite species. Thus, at the same time, the "Double" itself happened to this thing, but the "Half" happened to that one; to this one, magnitude, and to that one, smallness. Or perhaps both are in anything: namely, similarity <margin>C</margin> and dissimilarity, and again "sameness" and "otherness." For this reason, the same thing has undergone something that makes it both similar and dissimilar, and both the same and another, all at once.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, it is worthwhile in those things which we were narrating before, as in the effector and in knowledge, to place a certain and effective disposition, and an act, and one remaining in the act. But in the rest, to bring in a certain participation of species and ratio. For if it were necessary that all things be only bodies, it would be fitting to say that dispositions of this kind, which are spoken of relatively to each other, are nothing. But if we attribute the principal province of being to incorporeal things and ratios, and <margin>B</margin> we assert that dispositions are certain ratios and participations of species: it is certainly agreeable to assign causes thus: that this which is double, the double itself is the cause, so that it is double; and in turn that something is a half, the half is the cause. Now indeed, some are of the same species, others of opposite species, even these very things that are spoken of. Simultaneously, therefore, the double itself happened to this one, but the half to that one: to this one magnitude, to that one smallness: or both are in anything, similarity, namely, and dissimilarity, <margin>C</margin> again the same and another: wherefore the same thing has experienced something similar and at the same time dissimilar, the same and another.

<meta>catchword: rurius (again)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explores whether "Relation" is a real, incorporeal force or just a conceptual label, concluding that relations like "double" or "equal" exist through the participation of objects in eternal Forms or Ratios.</summary>
