--- Page 609 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus's critique of the Aristotelian (Peripatetic) categories. Having finished discussing the category of "Relation," he now transitions into a deep investigation of "Quality," questioning whether such diverse things as "habit," "shape," and "capacity" can truly belong to a single family of being.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> What then if this one is ugly, but that one is uglier? Are they called so by participation in the same **species** <note>original: *speciei*; here meaning the "form" or "ideal type" of a thing</note>? Perhaps we should say that if they are ugly, they are entirely equal to one another in the absence of that species. However, if one is more so and the other less, we must say that the one who is less ugly participates in a species that slightly overcomes the underlying matter, whereas the one who is more ugly has a species that is even further overwhelmed by matter. Or perhaps they should be judged by a certain **privation** <note>the lack of a quality that should naturally be present</note>, if someone <margin>B</margin> wishes to compare them to each other as if a species were present within them. Furthermore, a sense-perception is a certain species resulting from both the object and the observer, and knowledge is similarly a result of the species and the combination of both. Then indeed, a **habit** <note>original: *habitus*; a settled disposition or character trait</note> toward that which is held is a certain **act** <note>original: *actus*; the realization of a potential</note>, containing it as if it were a finished effect. Moreover, measurement, which is the action of the one applying the measure to the thing measured, is a certain **ratio** <note>original: *ratio*; a logical proportion</note>. If, therefore, someone places the very condition of relative things as a certain form within a general logic, as if it were a single thing, <margin>C</margin> it would not be out of place for there to be one **genus** <note>a general class or family</note> in these things, and their existence everywhere would be like a certain logical principle. But if the principles are opposed and have the differences we have mentioned, perhaps there cannot be one genus; instead, all things will be reduced to a certain similarity and a single **category** <note>original: *praedicamentum*; one of the basic classifications of being</note>. Indeed, the things said in this way might be reduced to one, yet all the things placed by them under the same category cannot be gathered into a single genus. For even the **negations** <note>the "not-thing," like "not-double"</note> <margin>D</margin> of these things are gathered into one along with the things themselves, as are those named after them—as this or that is called "double" because of "doubleness" itself. But how can the nature of each thing and its negation be gathered into one and the same genus? "Double" and "not-double," "related" and "not-related"—it would be as if someone, having established "animal" as a genus, dared to place "non-animal" in the same spot. Likewise, how are "doubleness itself" and "this specific double thing" numbered in the same genus, or "whiteness" and "the white thing," since the former and the latter cannot be the same thing here?

---

*Having set forth the description of Quality according to the Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note>—namely, that quality is that by which something is named "of a certain sort"—it is argued that whatever things are called qualities cannot be contained under one single, uniform classification. Chapter V.*

*Nor can we easily explain what that thing is in itself by which other things are named as having a quality. For they call something "of a certain sort" based on its substance as well as its weakness; likewise, they use the terms "habit," "privation," and "quality" through opposites.*

---

AFTER THIS, it is proper to consider **quality**, from which a person is rightly named "of a certain sort" <note>original: *qualis*; having a specific characteristic</note>. And first, we must investigate what this quality is that, by its existence, renders other things "qualified." We must ask whether it is one and the same thing existing by a common logic that provides the species for different things, or whether qualities are so diverse among themselves that they cannot form a single genus. Indeed, what can be common between a **habit** <note>a lasting trait like "knowledge"</note>, a **disposition** <note>a temporary state like "health"</note>, an active quality, a **figure** <note>shape</note>, and a <margin>B</margin> **form**? What shall I say of the "thick" and the "thin," the "fat" and the "lean"? For if we say the common element is **potentiality** <note>original: *potentia*; the power or capacity to do something</note>, which fits habits, dispositions, and natural powers (by which the possessor can do whatever it can do), then **impotences** <note>weaknesses or lack of power</note> will no longer fit in the genus with these. Furthermore, in what way is a "figure" or the "form" around any given thing a potentiality? Moreover, if this were so, "being" insofar as it is "being" would have no potentiality until a quality were added to it; but the acts of essences themselves...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What then, if one is ugly and the other uglier? Is it by participation in the same things? Or if one is altogether ugly, is it the absence [of form]? But if one is more so and the other less, the mixtures will involve a participation in the **species** <note>original: εἴδους (eidous); the Greek term for form or idea</note>; regarding the ugly person, the form is either overpowered or being overpowered. Or again, one should look to **privation** <note>original: στερήσει (sterēsei); a lack of what should be present</note> when making a comparison. Whether a certain species exists, or belongs to the things that exist. Sensation is a certain species resulting from <margin>B</margin> both, and knowledge likewise comes from both the composite, or a relationship—the thing held being a species, a certain **activity** <note>original: ἐνέργεια (energeia); being-at-work</note>, and a connective force, like a kind of making. That which is measured [results from] the measuring activity; in relation to the thing measured, it is a certain **ratio** <note>original: λόγος (logos); word, reason, or proportion</note>. If, therefore, someone takes the relationship toward something as a species in a common sense, as a single thing of that sort, he might have its substance by making it a kind of ratio. But if the ratios and the "makings" also have the differences we mentioned, perhaps <margin>C</margin> there would not be one genus, but all things are reduced to a certain similarity and a single **category** <note>original: κατηγορίαν (katēgorian)</note>. But even if the aforementioned things force us to pursue this, it does not prevent them from being under the same category. For one can also reduce their **negations** <note>original: ἀποφάσεις (apophaseis)</note> into one, as well as the things named after them—such as the "double" and the "thing that is double." How again are these in one genus? <margin>D</margin> And the negation, "double" and "that which is double" and "that which is not." It is as if someone made "animal" a genus and did not make "non-animal" a genus. And "double" and "that which is double," just like "whiteness" and "white things," are they the same thing?

---

<margin>A</margin> Regarding **QUALITY** <note>original: ΠΟΙΟΤΗΤΑ (Poiotēta)</note>, from which the so-called "qualified" thing comes, we must now grasp first what it is, and how it provides the things called "qualified." Is it one and the same according to something common, providing the **species** <note>original: εἴδη (eidē)</note> for the differences? Or are the qualities many, such that there might be no single genus? What then is the common element in a **habit** <note>original: ἕξεως (hexeōs)</note>, a **disposition** <note>original: διαθέσεως (diatheseōs)</note>, a passive quality, shapes, and form? And the thin, the <margin>B</margin> thick, and the proportionate? For if we say the common element is **power** <note>original: δύναμιν (dynamin)</note>, it might apply to habits, dispositions, and natural powers (by which the possessor can do what it can do), but **lack of power** <note>original: ἀδυναμίαι (adynamiai)</note> will no longer fit. Then how is **shape** <note>original: σχῆμα (schēma)</note> and form always a power in each qualified thing? Furthermore, would "being" as "being" have no power at all until it receives "quality"? But the activities of...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the Aristotelian categories, specifically moving from the nature of "Relation" (discussed on page 574) into a critique of "Quality." Plotinus is examining whether different types of attributes—like natural abilities, acquired skills, or physical shapes—can all be grouped under a single heading.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

Are they essentially activities of a certain <term>quality</term> <note>original: ποιότης; the attribute that makes a thing "such as it is"</note>, standing by themselves, and reflecting their own internal powers? If we look at the powers mentioned earlier—such as the skill of a boxer, the power of growth, or human nature itself—is the <term>rational faculty</term> <note>the human ability to reason</note> a quality, or is it that which possesses quality? It seems more likely that it is something one acquires through <term>virtue</term> <note>original: ἀρετῆς; excellence or functional perfection</note>. Thus, we must use the term "quality" in several different ways. 

Some are not qualities but powers added to substances to make them "such-and-such" after their initial creation. Others are the essential differences that distinguish one substance from another, and these are called qualities only in an <term>equivocal</term> <note>original: ὁμωνύμως; using the same word for different concepts</note> sense. These are actually <term>activities</term> <note>original: ἐνέργειαί; the state of being "at work" or in action</note> and rational principles, or parts of those principles, which reveal the "whatness" of a thing and seem to define its being. 

But those which are primarily judged as qualities—through which we are made "such" as we are, and which we call "powers"—might be certain principles and forms, such as beauty or ugliness in the soul and body. But how can all qualities be powers? For while health is a quality, so too are sickness, weakness, and total <term>impotence</term> <note>original: ἀδυναμία; the lack of power or ability</note>. Or perhaps, since people are described as being "such" because of these states, we should say they are called so not for a single reason, but because they are causes of things being called "beautifully formed" or the opposite. We should not look at this in only one way, but through all four categories—or at least two: whether a quality is defined by its ability to act or its tendency to be acted upon. 

Thus, the ability to act is judged differently from the tendency to suffer. We are accustomed to calling health, disposition, and habit "qualities," and likewise sickness, strength, and weakness. But if this is the case, the common element among them will no longer be "power" itself; we must seek another commonality. Nor can we call all qualities "rational principles" equally. For how can a sickness, which is a settled condition, be a <term>rational principle</term> <note>original: λόγος; a constructive or defining logic</note>? 

Should we then call the states found in species and powers "qualities," while calling their opposites "privations"? In this way, they would not be a single genus, but rather one category of things—for example, calling knowledge a certain form and power, but ignorance a <term>privation</term> <note>original: στέρησιν; the absence or lack of a quality that should be present</note> and a lack of power. Or is weakness and sickness also a form? 

<insert>
One can do much, but do it poorly. But since these things are nothing more than falling away from the intended goal, in what way should these be called powers?
</insert>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Those things which are primarily activities, acting according to themselves, and the activities of their own powers—insofar as they are what they are—will belong to the category of "quality" in this way. However, according to those powers that exist after the essence of a thing is established, "quality" is considered a faculty; the skill of a boxer is not judged as "man" insofar as he is man, but as a specific power. This rational power is not truly a quality, but rather something one has acquired through industry and practice. Therefore, the rational power is called a "quality" only equivocally.

<margin>B</margin> Quality, therefore, will be a certain power added to essences after the primary definition of that essence, through which things are subsequently named as being "of a certain kind." But those traits through which essences differ from one another are also called "qualities" equivocally; these are actually activities and principles (or beyond a specific principle), yet they declare the very substance of the thing, even if they seem to describe the essence as "having a quality."

<margin>C</margin> But those which are principally judged as qualities, by which we are made "such," and which we call "powers" in a common sense, will perhaps be certain principles or <term>forms</term> <note>original: formæ; the ideal "shape" or definition of a thing</note>—a certain beauty or ugliness found in both the soul and the body. 

<margin>D</margin> But in what way will all qualities be powers? Let beauty and health certainly be "qualities" proper; but how are ugliness, disease, weakness, and impotence qualities? Is it because people are named as being "such" according to these as well? But what prevents those who are called "such" from being named so not by a single definition, but equivocally? And let them be called "such" not only in four ways, but in any of the four modes, at least in a twofold sense. 

<margin>E</margin> Perhaps quality is not judged according to the very movement of acting or suffering. Therefore, that which is able to act is judged and spoken of in one way, and that which is suffering in another. Yet people have been accustomed to calling health, disposition, and habit "quality," and similarly disease, strength, and weakness. 

<margin>F</margin> If this is so, the common element in such things will no longer be "power" itself, but it will be necessary to investigate some other common ground. Nor, again, will it be possible to call all qualities "principles" (*rationes*) equally. For in what way will a disease, which is a confirmed condition, be any kind of principle? Shall we then call the affections that consist in species and powers "qualities"? Their opposite <term>privations</term> <note>the lack of a natural quality</note> we shall not call a single genus, but we will always call them one thing—as if one category. For instance, we call knowledge a certain species and a power, but ignorance a privation and an impotence. Or perhaps impotence and weakness are also a form? And thus both disease and vice—

---

—might be called powers? Perhaps because each of them performs its own specific action, not looking toward the right goal; indeed, a thing would do nothing at all if it had no power to do so. Beauty certainly has a kind of power; does a triangle then have it too? Or perhaps it is not proper to look toward "power" when judging quality, but rather toward the way a thing is disposed or affected? Therefore, quality must be weighed by us according to certain "forms" and "characters."

<summary>Plotinus explores the category of Quality, questioning if it is defined by "power" (the ability to act) or "form" (the way a thing is shaped). He struggles to reconcile positive attributes like health and knowledge with negative ones like disease and ignorance under a single definition.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD. VI.

<margin>A</margin>And in its own order, this common form is a kind of species lying within the <term>essence</term> <note>original Latin: "essentia"; the fundamental nature of a thing</note>, yet arriving after the essence itself. But again, we must investigate how <term>potential</term> <note>original Latin: "potentia"; the capacity to become or do something</note> relates to it. Perhaps even one who is a "boxer" by nature holds this status because they are affected in a certain way; being born for a specific purpose carries a limit, and generally, a "character" is a quality—a sign or a mark—that does not belong to the fundamental essence at all. <margin>B</margin>However, some things seem to contribute to the essence at one time and exist outside it at another, such as heat, whiteness, or any color. In this case, when a thing contributes to the essence, it is like an <term>act of essence</term> <note>original Latin: "actus essentiae"; the essence expressing itself in action</note>. But when it is merely a secondary addition, it is something else: an image or a likeness of that essence existing in another thing. Furthermore, if quality is judged by its formation, its mark, and its <term>rational principle</term> <note>original Latin: "ratio"; the Greek "logos"</note>, how do things signifying <margin>C</margin>impotence or ugliness belong to "quality"? Perhaps we must answer that such things are <term>imperfect reasons</term> <note>original Latin: "rationes imperfectae"; flawed versions of a thing's ideal design</note>, much as a father might see himself in an "ugly" son. But how is there a "reason" in a disease? Perhaps we place the reason of health in this too, but shifted somehow from its proper state. Or perhaps not everything should be placed within this "reason." It is enough to define quality as a common condition involving an <term>affection</term> <note>a state of being influenced or changed</note> or disposition that exists outside the essence and is added after it, so that the quality belongs to the <term>subject</term>. A triangle, for instance, is judged as a quality of the object it is in—not the "Triangle itself" in the abstract, but the triangle that shapes this specific thing. Perhaps even "humanity" shapes a thing, but rather, it provides the very essence itself.

-> Once the Peripatetic <note>the followers of Aristotle</note> description is admitted, it is very difficult to correctly divide what are called qualities among themselves; and it is impossible, when dividing things under the same genus, to collect them with a single, clear definition. Chapter XI. <-

---

<margin>A</margin>**FURTHERMORE**, if these things are so, why are there several species of quality? Why are <term>habit</term> <note>original Latin: "habitus"; a permanent state</note> and <term>disposition</term> <note>original Latin: "dispositio"; a temporary arrangement or state</note> considered different? The difference of a quality does not consist in whether it lasts or does not last; a certain "affection" is enough to make a thing "such-as-it-is," regardless of how long it stays. The "permanence" is merely an external trait added later—unless one were to say that dispositions are like imperfect forms, while habits are perfected forms. <margin>B</margin>But if they are imperfect, they are not yet qualities; if they are already qualities, then "permanence" is just a condition added from the outside. In what way are natural powers a different species of power? If they exist as qualities, do they truly stand apart? For if they are qualities precisely because they are powers, then the condition of "power" does not apply to all of them, as has been said. If we call a man a "boxer" by nature because he is disposed or affected in a certain way, <margin>C</margin>no additional "power" is needed, since power is already contained within the habits themselves. Therefore, why does he who is a boxer by natural power differ from he who becomes a boxer through knowledge? Perhaps in the sense that they are "such-as-they-are," these are not actually different *types* of quality; even if one is stronger by training and the other by nature, the difference is external to the quality itself. But regarding the specific form of "boxing skill," how do they differ? Since some arise from a certain <term>passion</term> <note>an experience or physical state</note> and others do not, do they gain their difference from this? It does not seem to matter...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...and the form that is upon the essence comes after the essence. But again, how do the <term>powers</term> <note>original Greek: "δυνάμεις" (dynameis)</note> and the "natural boxer" relate to being "qualified"? Is it because of being affected in a certain way, or because of a certain <term>impotence</term>? In general, quality is a character, a sort of marking; it does not contribute to the essence. Even if some things seem to contribute, like heat and whiteness and color in general, one part belongs to the essence as its <margin>B</margin><term>activity</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia)</note>, while the other part is derived from it. It is something else in something else—an image or a likeness of it. But if quality is defined by its shaping, its character, and its <term>rational principle</term> <note>original Greek: "λόγος" (logos)</note>, how do we account for things defined by impotence and the disorder of ugliness? Should we say these are instances of disorder, as if the rational principle is present in the ugly or the disordered? Or perhaps health reaches even into these things? Or maybe these are not within the "reason" at all. <margin>C</margin>Rather, we must look for the common element beyond the "being somehow," which exists apart from the essence. These are things that come into being after the essence and "qualify" the underlying subjects. Is a triangle a quality or not? Not the triangle simply, but the one in this specific object, insofar as it has shaped it. But "humanity" also shaped it, or rather, provided its essence.

<margin>A</margin>BUT if these things are so, why are there many species of quality? Why are <term>habit</term> <note>original Greek: "ἕξις" (hexis)</note> and <term>disposition</term> <note>original Greek: "διάθεσις" (diathesis)</note> something different? For "remaining" or "not remaining" is not a true difference of quality. It is enough for the "disposition" to be in whatever state it is in to provide the "quality" to the subject. Staying is almost an external thing, unless one says that dispositions are imperfect forms, while habits are perfect forms. <margin>B</margin>But if they are imperfect, they are not yet quality; if they are already quality, then "staying" is something external to them. As for natural powers, how are they a different species? For those that are called "qualified" according to their powers—if the definition of power fits them all, as has been said. If we say someone is a "natural boxer," <unclear>man</unclear> nothing is added by "power," since <margin>C</margin>powers are also present in habits. Or is it that one is able by knowledge and the other is a boxer by power? If these are differences of quality—one having it by practice and the other by nature—the difference is from the outside. And how does the species of "boxing" itself differ? If some come from <term>passions</term> <note>original Greek: "παθῶν" (pathon); states of being acted upon</note> and others do not, does that difference provide the "quality"?

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's systematic critique of the Aristotelian categories, specifically focusing on "Quality." In the preceding text, he questioned whether qualities are intrinsic to a thing's essence or merely external additions. Here, he examines physical attributes like density and weight, and begins a new chapter on how to properly categorize qualities of the body versus those of the soul.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<columns>
From where does quality arise? I speak of quality in terms of its variations and differences. It might also be a matter of inquiry whether some qualities are <term>passions</term> <note>original Greek: "pathē"; things experienced or suffered by an object from an outside force</note>; if some are in one state and some in another, even if they belong to the same things, how can they be in the same species? And if some arise from having been affected and others from the act of affecting, they would be called qualities <term>equivocally</term> <note>original Greek: "homōnymōs"; having the same name but different definitions</note>. What then is this "shape" that is spoken of? If it is the way each thing exists in itself, or its nature, or its beauty—coming after the <unclear>underlying substances</unclear>, or its generation—it might have a logical basis. But <term>roughness and smoothness</term>, as well as <term>rareness and density</term>, would not be correctly called qualities. For indeed, rareness and density are defined by the distances [of parts] from one another, or their closeness. Roughness and smoothness arise from the unevenness or evenness of their position. Even if quality arises from these, nothing prevents them from being judged as qualities. What then of "heavy" and "light"? It will be clear where these should be placed. But if "light" is also used equivocally, or if it is not judged by weight—of more or less—it would fall into the same order as thinness and slenderness, which are counted as something else, perhaps like feathers.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Whence quality arises: insofar, I say, as it pertains to the change and discrepancy of quality. One may furthermore ask, even if those qualities arising from <term>passion</term> <note>original Latin: "passio"; the state of being acted upon</note> are partly one way and partly another and belong to different things, how they can be placed in the same species. And if it is said that some qualities arise from suffering an effect while others produce an effect, they will be called "qualities" equivocally at the same time. Furthermore, what is the meaning of the "form" mentioned regarding each thing? <margin>B</margin> For if it is the reason why each thing is what it is—whether the species of the subject is called beautiful or ugly—whatever is said can be understood to have some rational basis. But truly, <term>rough and smooth</term>, <term>rare and dense</term>, are not correctly named qualities. For it is not because of certain intense distances or a certain proximity that "rare," "dense," "smooth," and "rough" are indicated; rather, these everywhere arise from the inequality or equality of position. But if they do arise from these, nothing prohibits them from being judged as qualities. Finally, if the condition of "light" and "heavy" themselves is understood, it will be clear to us where these are most especially to be placed. One may furthermore find an equivocal nature regarding the "light": unless perhaps "light" is weighed by some liberation or by the compensation of more or less weight; in which order "meager" and "thin" are also found, which are certainly numbered in a species other than the four [elements].
</columns>

->*It is not permitted to divide qualities in the Peripatetic <note>Refers to the followers of Aristotle</note> manner; nor is it right to place qualities of the body, the soul, and the mind under the same genus.*<-

->### Chapter XII.<-

<margin>A</margin> **BUT** if anyone does not think quality should be divided in this way, by what reasoning could he divide it? We must consider, then, whether it is proper to say some qualities belong to the body and others to the soul; then to divide the body's qualities according to the distribution of the senses—so that some pertain to sight, others to hearing, or to taste, others to smell or touch. But as for the qualities of the soul, since there is no [physical] partitioning, shall we divide them <margin>B</margin> by the faculties of <term>desire</term>, <term>anger</term>, and <term>deliberation</term>? Or by the differences of the actions performed according to them, since these faculties are the producers of those actions? Or shall we divide them according to what is useful and harmful, and then further divide those utilities and damages? Similarly, shall we divide bodily qualities by the very fact that they create a difference, or according to utility or harm? For such differences are characteristic of quality. For utility and harm seem to happen because of quality and the "qualified" thing, or we must <margin>C</margin> search deeply and in another way. We must investigate how it is possible that he who is "qualified" <note>An object possessing a quality</note> according to a quality is properly in that same quality. For is there one genus for both? Likewise, if a "boxer" is in the category of quality, how is he not also an "effector" <note>A producer of an effect</note> in that same category? And if so, how is he not again the "efficient cause" itself? Therefore, it is by no means appropriate to move the "efficient" to the category of Relation, nor again the "patient" <note>The thing being acted upon</note>, if that patient is contained within the order of quality. And perhaps it is better to place the "effector" here, if the effector is judged according to <term>potential</term> <note>original Latin: "potentia"; the capacity for action</note>. For potential is a quality; but if potential exists according to essence—whatever that potential may be—neither is it referred to something else, nor...

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the Aristotelian categories, specifically moving from the internal nature of "Quality" to how quality relates to "Action" and "Relation." # PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> is also reduced to the category of quality. For the active power itself does not behave in the same way as "the greater." Indeed, "the greater" has its <term>subsistence</term> <note>Latin: "subsistentiam"; the state of having real, independent existence</note>, insofar as it is greater, in relation to that which is judged to be "the lesser." An active cause, however, is identified as active because it is already of a certain quality. But perhaps, insofar as it is of such a quality, it is placed in the category of quality; but insofar as it has power over another, and is therefore called "effective," it is rightly numbered among the <term>relatives</term> <note>Things whose nature is defined by their relationship to something else, like "left" and "right" or "father" and "son"</note>.

<margin>B</margin> Why then is a boxer not also counted among the relatives, since his skill defines him as a boxer? For the capacity of a boxer is entirely referred to another person. Indeed, there is no consideration of his skill that is not related to another. Now, we must consider the same regarding the other arts, or at least most of them, and perhaps say: insofar as they dispose and affect the soul, they are qualities; but insofar as they produce something, they are considered "effective," and from this very fact are referred to another and placed in the category of relatives—especially since they are referred to another in yet another way, insofar as they are called <term>habits</term> <note>Latin: "habitus"; a stable, acquired disposition or skill</note>.

<margin>C</margin> But is there perhaps some other existence according to the "effective" itself, since the effective is only effective because it is of a certain quality? For perhaps someone might concede—especially in the case of living beings using <unclear>deliberation</unclear> toward a goal—that there is a distinct existence according to the condition of effective power based on their inclination toward acting. But in <margin>D</margin> inanimate forces, which we called qualities, what exactly is the "effective" part? Perhaps when it encounters something else of such a kind, it receives from it and becomes a sharer in its function. But if the same thing acts upon another and also <term>suffers</term> <note>Latin: "patitur"; to be acted upon or undergo change</note>, how does the "effective" still exist properly as its own thing? For even "the greater," which perhaps exists in itself, usually becomes "greater" or "lesser" only when meeting another. But someone will say that the greater and lesser come to be through a certain participation in magnitude and equality. Perhaps also that which suffers and acts at the same time has a <margin>E</margin> certain participation in both the effective and the passive.

It seems we must also ask here whether the qualities in this world are numbered under the same genus as those in the <term>divine world</term> <note>The higher realm of pure Intellect and Forms in Plotinus’s philosophy</note>. This question is directed at those who place such things there. Or perhaps we must ask similarly even if one does not admit the existence of <term>Forms</term> <note>Perfect, eternal templates of things</note>: namely, if one only admits an Intellect and allows that there is some habit within it, it will be asked whether there is something common to this habit and our own? At least it is conceded that wisdom exists there. Yet if that wisdom is <term>equivocal</term> <note>original Latin: "æquiuocè"; having the same name but a completely different nature</note> to our own, it is rightly not numbered among such qualities. But if it is <term>univocal</term> <note>original Latin: "vniuocè"; having the same name and the same fundamental definition</note>, then the very notion of quality is common to ours and <unclear>those like it</unclear>—unless someone asserts that all things there are <term>essences</term> <note>Substances or fundamental realities</note>, and therefore concedes that intelligence itself is likewise an essence. Truly, this kind of question can be raised about the other <term>predicaments</term> <note>The categories of being, such as quality, quantity, and place</note> as well: whether that which is here and that which is there are different in genus, or rather both are placed under the same genus.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is still a quality. For the "maker" [active cause] is not like the "greater." For the greater has its subsistence <note>Greek: "hypostasis"</note>, insofar as it is greater, <unclear>in relation to</unclear> the lesser. But the active power exists by already being a certain quality. But perhaps according to being a quality, it is a "what" [a sort of thing], or is called a quality from the <unclear>state</unclear> it is in. But according to the power it has toward something, it is "active" or "relative"—for the active is entirely toward another. Indeed, no theory of it exists which is not toward another. And <margin>B</margin> regarding the other arts, or most of them, we must look at it this way. And it should perhaps be said: in the way they dispose the soul, they are qualities; in the way they act, they are active and fall under "relative." And in a way, they are "relative" in another sense, according to which they are called habits. Is there then some other subsistence according to the active, or is the active nothing other than being a certain quality, or insofar as it acts? For <margin>C</margin> perhaps someone, in the case of ensouled beings, and especially those having choice, would grant a subsistence to the active through the impulse to act. But in the case of the inanimate things which we called underlying qualities, what is the active? Is it when it meets another, and that other enjoys and shares in what it has? But if the same thing both acts on another and suffers [is acted upon], how is it still purely "active"? Since even the greater <unclear>exists</unclear> as <margin>D</margin> itself, and becomes greater and lesser in the meeting with another. But someone will say the greater and lesser exist by participation in magnitude and smallness. In this way, there is a participation in the active and passive. We must also seek whether these, and the qualities here, and those there [in the divine realm] fall under the same species, as some assume, or if none of these are here, but are spoken of in Mind [Intellect]; or if someone speaks of a habit, whether it is those there or these others here. Or even if someone, having separated the <term>homonyms</term> <note>Words that sound the same but have different meanings</note> from the things here, should place "Wisdom" there, while we would have only whatever...

</columns>

### **That which among the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>The followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the "peripatos" or colonnade of the Lyceum</note> is named the predicament "When"—that is, yesterday, tomorrow, and similar terms—should properly be understood as time or a part of time according to formal reason. Chapter XIII.**

If therefore it signifies nothing else, they ought not to place "when" in one category and "time" in another. But if it signifies something besides time, then this will no longer be one single category, but a collection of several.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's critical examination of the Aristotelian categories. Having previously discussed Quality and its relationship to Action and Relation, Plotinus now turns his attention to the categories of "When" (Time/Duration) and "Where" (Location), questioning whether they truly deserve to be treated as independent categories or if they are merely sub-types of Quantity and Relation.</meta>

# BOOK ONE. 573

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the category of **When** <note>Greek: *pote*</note>, we must investigate it in this way: if "yesterday," "tomorrow," "last year," and similar segments of time are merely parts of time, or if they are something else existing within time. It is clear that these function just as time does. Since the "now," the "it was," and "yesterday" exist within this thing we call time, it is surely right that they be classified as time. Furthermore, time is said to be a **Quantity** <note>Greek: *poson*; a fundamental category relating to size, number, or duration</note>. Therefore, what need is there for another category? Or perhaps they would say that while time itself is Quantity, "yesterday" or "last year" are specific things falling under time. For these must be subordinated to Quantity, since time is nothing other than time. But sometimes we address time itself, if these "whens" are indeed time. These things—such as "just now," "yesterday" (which is the past)—are a kind of composite. If the "past" is one thing and "time" is another, there will be two categories, and the concept will not be simple. If one says that each "when" is something other than time, how can its meaning be derived solely from the facts of the matter? For example: "Socrates is in the now." Socrates is set forth by himself, and they might have something to say there. But if we say "Socrates was at some time," he will be placed in time, or in a part of it. If they argue that he is in a "segment" of time, and yet they claim that this segment should not be treated as time itself, what are they actually saying? But a past segment of time—one that is "long ago"—is a part or segment that exists in **Relation** <note>Greek: *pros ti*; the category of things defined by their relationship to something else</note> to something else; if one adds "the past" to it, a new charge is brought against the definition. Or is the "now" the same as what was in time, but in an indefinite sense, whereas "yesterday" and "last year" are definite? "Yesterday" would be defined by the "now," and "last year" by "yesterday"; thus, "yesterday" will be a definite time. But this is the same as being "in time," which would make it a superfluous Quantity—specifically, a defined quantity. It is from these elements that it consists. If they say "yesterday," how should we speak of it if not as a past time, a specific defined time? If they insist on adding more, they are dragging in another category from an entirely different genus. If one thing makes another thing, and if these exist in time, we shall find many other categories, making one thing after another. This shall be discussed more clearly in the following sections regarding these matters.

<margin>A</margin> Regarding the category of **Where** <note>Greek: *pou*</note>, such as "in the Lyceum" <note>The school founded by Aristotle</note> or "in the Academy" <note>The school founded by Plato</note>: if "in the Academy" or "the Lyceum" are used, they are entirely places, always either divided or specifically "in the Lyceum" or "in the Academy."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **CONCERNING** that category <note>Latin: *praedicamentum*; the Latin term for Aristotle's Categories</note> which they name "at some time" or **When** <note>Latin: *quando*</note>, it must be considered next. Surely if "yesterday," "tomorrow," "last year," or "long ago," and such things are parts of time, what prevents them from being in the same category as time itself? Inasmuch as "tomorrow," "yesterday," and "now" are species of time, they are not placed anywhere except where time is placed; and time is said to belong to the genus of **Quantity**. Therefore,
<margin>B</margin> why is there any need for a new category for this? If they should say that these things are not merely time—namely "tomorrow" and "yesterday"—and that "yesterday" and "long ago" are placed under time, we must ask where such things as "yesterday" ought to be placed. If they were to say it is not only time, but "time at some point," the response is immediate. First, if it is "time at some point," it is certainly time. Secondly, if "yesterday" is past time, it will be a certain composite; that is, if "past" is one thing and
<margin>C</margin> "time" is another. These would then be two categories, not something simple. But if they say that "at some time" is not time itself, but "in time," then this very phrase "in time," if it signifies the thing itself—as if one said, "Socrates was long ago"—then Socrates existed, which is a different matter, and they are not saying one single thing. But Socrates, or an action in this specific time—what will it be, primarily? Perhaps in a part of time? But since they speak of a "part of
<margin>D</margin> time," and by the reason that it is a "part," they think it is not just time or a part of it simply, but a "past" part of time, they are complicating matters: for they are treating the part, insofar as it is a part, as having a **Relation** <note>Latin: *ad aliquid*; things that exist in reference to something else</note> already attached to it. And "the past" itself would be, in their view, something added on, or the same as the word "was," which is a species of time. But if they say the difference is that "was" is indefinite, while "yesterday" and "last year" are
<margin>E</margin> definite, we will first establish the "was" somewhere; then "yesterday" will be considered as a "was" that is now defined, from which it follows that "yesterday" is a defined time. This, however, is a quantity of time, or a "how much" of time. Therefore, if time is established in the order of Quantity, any of these will be a "quantity already defined." But if they say "yesterday" in the sense of "how many," and we understand that to mean an event happened in a definite past time, they are bringing many things together at once. Finally, if it is necessary to introduce other categories because one thing happens in another, just as in the present case where something is or happens "in time," we shall find many other categories under the same condition, because something exists in another in various ways. But of this we shall speak more clearly in what follows, where we shall dispute this very thing called **Where**.

---

->*It is superfluous to introduce a new category based on the fact that something is said to be "somewhere":*<-
->*For "Where" itself has its own proper place. If we consider something added to this, it does not bring about a new category, but rather some relation or substance. Chapter 14.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> **THEY ARE ACCUSTOMED**, when treating the category they name **Where** <note>Latin: *ubi*</note>, to say: "Where" surely refers to the Academy or the Lyceum, which are entirely places.

This page shifts focus to the category of "Where" (Place) and begins a new chapter on "Action" (Doing).</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

<meta>Catchword: Better</meta>

<columns>

<margin>A</margin> ...and parts of place, such as up, down, and "here" are either species or parts of place. However, the difference lies in the fact that some are more clearly defined than others. If, therefore, up, down, and the center are places—just as the Delphic region is the center <note>The Greeks considered the Oracle at Delphi the *omphalos* or "navel" (center) of the world</note>, and nearby the center is Attica, and the Lyceum, and the remaining regions—why is it necessary to seek anything further beyond "place," especially since we say that each of these signifies a specific location? If we say one thing is in another when we ask "where" <note>Latin: *ubi*</note>, we are not expressing something simple or unified. 
<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, if every time we assert that "this is here," we are not stating something simple, we are creating a specific <term>relation</term> <note>Latin: *habitudo*; a state or relationship between two things</note>—both of this thing being in that, and of the thing received in relation to that which receives it. Why then do we not place this very thing in the category of <term>relatives</term>? For something is generated out of the relationship of each to the other. Likewise, it makes no difference if, living in Athens, you say "I am here" or "I am in Athens." But they concede that this very word "here," since it is a demonstrative sign, signifies a place; therefore 
<margin>C</margin> they will also confess that the phrase "in Athens" designates a place. For this reason, "in Athens" belongs properly to the category of place itself. Again, if being "in Athens" is the same as being "in the city of the Athenians," then surely it is predicated as being something beyond place; yet it should not be so, just as it is not right to assign a category for "quality" that is anything other than the quality itself. Added to this: if what is said to be "in time" or "in place" must be a different category from time and place, why should "that which is in a jar" not introduce another category? Or "that which is under a roof"? Likewise, should "a part in a whole," or "a whole in its parts," or "a genus in its species," or "a species in its genus" similarly be something else? Indeed, we would then be counting a vast number of additional categories.

---

->Perhaps "Effect," "Position," or "Motion" would be more correctly established as a category than "Action." Chapter XV.<-

<margin>A</margin> **I**n that category which they name "Action" <note>Latin: *facere*; literally "to do"</note>, one may consider these points. It is taught, of course, that those things which surround <term>substance</term> <note>Greek: *ousia*; the fundamental reality of a thing</note> must be placed after substance itself, just as quantity and number are. For this reason, they assert that quantity is a different genus <note>A "genus" in this context refers to one of the ten primary categories of being defined by Aristotle</note>. Likewise, because quality exists around substance, the "qualified" is itself placed as another genus. Thus, since "action" or "effecting" also exists around substance, they believe that "Action" itself is another genus.
<margin>B</margin> Is it then "Action" <note>the act of doing</note> that must be posited, or rather "Activity" <note>Latin: *factio*; the state of acting</note> from which "Action" proceeds? Just as Quality is posited, from which the "qualified" similarly arises. Or should "Activity," "Action," and "the Actor"—or perhaps "Action" and "Activity"—be heaped together into one? Now, "Action" signifies the agent more than "Activity" does. Yet "Action" plainly signifies being engaged in a certain effect: and that is to be in a state of <term>actuality</term> <note>Latin: *actus*; Greek: *energeia*</note>. From this it follows that "Activity" or "Actuality" is the more proper category.
<margin>C</margin> Indeed, this "Actuality" is affirmed to be observed around the essence, just as quality is; this Actuality, in turn, is concerned with the essence in the same way as <term>motion</term>. And surely motion exists as one specific genus of things. For why is quality one thing around essence, and quantity similarly one thing, and "relation" likewise because of a certain relationship of one thing to another, but Motion—which is similarly around the essence—should not likewise be a single genus?

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...and parts in a way. Just as "up" and "down," and "here" are species or parts. They differ in that some are more delimited. If, then, up and down and the middle are places—just as Delphi is the middle, and the regions near the middle, such as Athens and the Lyceum and the others—why must we still seek "where" something is outside of us saying these things, or where each of these signifies? 
<margin>Β</margin> But if we say "one thing in another," or "where" we say it, we speak incompletely; whenever we say "here" in this way, we generate a certain relation of "this in that," or of the receiver toward what it pointed out. But why not among the "relative" things, if indeed "where" is a relation of each from both? Since there is no difference between saying "I am here" or "in Athens," some say that "where" is signified by both "here" and "at Athens," so that the "where" is "at Athens," and thus "at Athens" belongs to the "where." But "at Athens" signifies a relation to the place itself and the things there.
<margin>Γ</margin> But it is not so, just as "to be qualified" is not the genus, but only "Quality"; so too these are not categories. Things "in time" would be a different species than "time" and "where," so that "in a vessel" would also make another category, and "in matter" another, and "in a subject" another, and "part in a whole," and "in parts," and generally "in wholes," and "species in a genus"; and generally, if not, there will be many more categories.

<margin>Α</margin> **R**egarding the so-called "Action" <note>Greek: *poiein*</note>, how might one examine it? For it is said that after Substance there are things concerning substance, such as actions and number; that one should call Quantity another genus, and Quality as being around it, and the "Qualified" as another genus, and Action <note>Greek: *poiesis*</note> as belonging to another. But is it "Action" <note>the doing</note>, or the "Activity" <note>the process</note> from which the action comes, just as Quality is that from which the "qualified" comes, or is it both?
<margin>Β</margin> When is there "Conduct," "Acting," or "the Actor," or "the Acted," and "Activity"—how are these to be taken? "Acting" <note>the verb</note> manifests more than "Activity" <note>the noun</note>; but if Activity is not Acting, how is Activity a "how" or an "actuality" <note>Greek: *energeia*</note>, so that Actuality is rather the category?
<margin>Γ</margin> Or is it said to be viewed around the essence, as Quality is there? And this is around the essence just like Motion <note>Greek: *kinesis*</note>, and Motion is a genus of beings. For why is Quality something around the essence, and Quantity something, and Relation because of the relation of one to another, but Motion, being around the essence, shall not be a genus?

</columns>

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Aristotelian categories of Place ("Where") and Action ("Doing"), arguing that "Place" is often just a relationship and that "Action" might be better categorized under "Motion" or "Actuality." He warns that if every specific instance of being "in" something (like in a jar or in a city) were its own category, the list of categories would be infinite.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Aristotelian categories, specifically moving from the category of "Where" (Place) to a detailed examination of "Action" and "Movement." The previous page concluded the analysis of location and relative position, setting the stage for Chapter 16, which explores whether motion should be considered a distinct category or a sub-species of activity.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

Perhaps it would be more correct to place **activity** <note>Latin: *actus*; Greek: *energeia*</note> as the category; and under it, one kind of activity is perfect—such as a habit and a form—while the other is imperfect—such as movement toward a habit and a form. Chapter XVI.

Movement is not called an "imperfect activity" by its own nature; for at the very moment it begins, it is already both activity and movement. Rather, it is so called by reason of something else external to it that is to be completed after the movement. Just as activity and change often occur in an instant, so movement, beginning in an instant, is simply movement already; it enters into time only insofar as it also enters into quantity.

---

If anyone should say that movement is a simple activity, nothing prevents activity from being the primary term, and then assigning movement as a simple form of it—predicating activity of it, but adding "imperfect" as a distinction. For "imperfect" is said of it not because it is not an activity at all, but because it is an activity entirely, yet it possesses a "not yet" or a "repeatable" quality, as if it were always undergoing activity. Further, it is already an activity, but it does not arrive at the "other" which follows it; it is something more than itself, yet it is the thing at which it aimed. For example, walking: from the beginning, it was walking. But if one must finish a stadium <note>A Greek measure of distance, roughly 185 meters</note>, before finishing it, that which was lacking was a lack not of walking, nor of movement, but of a *specific amount* of walking. Walking already existed and had been performed; it was already movement. For the one who is moving has already moved, just as the one who cuts has already cut. And just as what we call "activity" occurs in an indivisible moment of time, so too does movement—but this applies to all movement. If activity is in an indivisible moment, then movement as a whole is too. But if we say movement is entirely in time because we have included the concept of continuity (as in a flow), then vision, which sees without interruption, would also be in continuity and in time. Let the principle of proportion also bear witness: it says one can always take part after part of a movement, and there is neither a beginning of time in which it started, nor a beginning of the movement itself. Instead, the mind can always go further back because of the cause, just as it happens that one has moved for a certain time, and there is an infinite cause for that reception. For this happens because people separate activity from movement. They claim activity happens in an instant <note>original: *in achrono*; literally "without time"</note>, while they say movement requires time—not just a specific amount of time, but they insist that the very nature of movement is necessarily quantitative. Yet they themselves admit that the "quantity" (whether it lasts a day or any other length of time) is accidental to the movement. Therefore, just as activity occurs in an instant, nothing prevents movement also from having begun in an instant. It is called "time" only because it has become a quantity. Even changes are admitted to happen in an instant, as when a total change is said to occur all at once. If it is a change, why is it not also a movement? "Change" is understood here not as the state of having already changed, but as the process itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **IF ANYONE** objects that movement is an "imperfect activity," nothing seems to prevent us from placing activity in the first position and movement under it as a species, subordinate to it as something imperfect. We would predicate activity of movement, while adding "imperfect" as the specific difference. For "imperfect" is said of movement not because it is not an activity, but because it is entirely an activity that acquires a certain repeated succession. This is not so that the movement itself 
<margin>B</margin> eventually arrives at being an activity—for it already exists as an activity—but so that it may produce something else that is beyond the movement itself. In such a case, the movement itself is not being perfected, but rather the thing at which the mover was aiming. For instance, walking was walking from the very beginning. If it is necessary to cross a stadium, and it has not yet been crossed, certainly that which is lacking is not lacking to the "walking" nor to the "movement," but rather to "that much walking." Walking existed even in the smallest degree, and
<margin>C</margin> was already movement. Surely he who is moving has already moved, and he who divides has already divided. And just as that which is called activity does not require time, so neither does movement, except for a movement that is specifically extended. And since activity happens in an instant, certainly movement, which is movement in a total and simple sense, does as well. But if they say movement occurs entirely in time because it claims continuity for itself, the answer is that vision, too, when uninterrupted, has continuity and exists in time.
<margin>D</margin> An argument for this is provided by the power of proportion: it teaches that one can always take part after part from any movement, and there is no beginning of time in which or from which it started; nor is there an initial starting point of the motion. Instead, one can always divide the movement further back, so that it turns out that a movement just begun has already proceeded from an infinite time, and the movement itself is similarly infinite regarding its beginning. This happens because
<margin>E</margin> they separate activity from movement: they say activity occurs in an instant, but they admit movement requires time. I say that they claim not just a specific amount of movement, but the very nature of movement itself is necessarily quantitative; even though they themselves admit that "this much" or "that much" duration is accidental to the motion—whether the movement lasts a day or any other length of time. Therefore, just as activity occurs in an instant, nothing prevents movement also from 
<margin>F</margin> having begun in an instant; it only becomes "time" because the movement has turned out to be of a certain quantity. After all, changes are also conceded to happen in an instant, as when it is said that a change of parts is performed all at once, and in other parts not at all yet. If, therefore, it is a change, why is movement not also performed in an instant? The "change" referred to here is not the state of having already been changed—for it did not need that change—but that which properly consists in the process of changing.

<note>The catchword at the bottom "Cc 4" refers to the signature mark for the book binder.</note>

<summary>This page argues that movement (motion) should not be a separate category but a sub-species of "activity" (energeia). It challenges the Aristotelian view by arguing that movement, like activity, can exist in an indivisible moment and is only associated with time when measured as a quantity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry from page 381 regarding the Aristotelian categories. Having discussed "Place" and the nature of "Movement," Plotinus now examines the relationship between "Action" (doing) and "Passion" (being acted upon), and whether these should be considered part of the category of "Movement" or "Relation."</meta>

# Chapter XVII

*It is more probable to place action and passion under movement as a single genus, rather than as two distinct categories; for their essence is not simply "to be something," but to incline toward something else, since the very thing they are is defined by two substances joined together.*

<margin>A</margin> If someone should argue that neither activity <note>Latin: *actus*; Greek: *energeia*</note> nor movement are categories in themselves, but should be counted within the category of relatives—on the grounds that activity arises from a certain power toward action, and movement from some mobile power through which movement occurs—we must respond. Relative terms always arise from a state of being already present, but they do not originate simply because they are "said toward another." <margin>B</margin> However, when there is a subsisting thing—whether it comes from another or is caused by another—it still obtains its own nature before entering into a relationship. For both of these, activity, movement, and habit exist as something additional to the other; yet the thing does not lack an internal capacity <term>internal capacity: the inherent power (*facultas* or *dynamis*) of a thing to act, independent of external factors</term> through which it is a "thing itself" before the relation. Otherwise, in this way, everything would dissolve into being merely "related to another." For everything has a certain disposition toward something else, which even happens to the soul. Now, the soul performs this action itself; so why are "doing" and "the act of doing" not counted among relations? Either it must be a movement or an activity entirely. <margin>C</margin> But if one places "effecting" in the order of relatives, yet makes "doing" itself a single genus, what prevents movement and the moved from being referred to something else, while "being moved" constitutes a single genus? Yet, do they divide these as if they were one, or are things produced because of two factors—namely, "doing" and "suffering" <note>original: *pati*; in this context, it refers to the state of being acted upon by an outside force</note>? However, it is not permitted for them to exist now as they seem to say: that this genus is "doing," while that genus is "suffering."

# Chapter XVIII

*This seems to be not so much a simple "becoming" as it occurs in fire, in space, and in time. For every action is spoken of in relation to a passion, such as sensing and understanding. Furthermore, movement is an activity, even if movement occurs, is understood, or is the same as other actions which are directed toward something else and stand apart from themselves.*

<margin>A</margin> We must consider, furthermore, whether everything that is "done" occurs within "doing" itself: that some are activities, while others are movements; and that activities are completed all at once, whereas movements are the kind that occur through "dividing" and "being divided." For dividing happens in time. Are all activities perhaps distinct from movement, or are they certainly joined with movement? Likewise, should we say that all "effectings" refer to "suffering" <note>being acted upon</note>, <margin>B</margin> or rather should we affirm that some are absolute, such as walking and speaking? Again, will they call all impulses related to passion "movements," while calling the absolute ones simply "activities"? Or perhaps we place both in both categories equally? Now, they will call walking itself—which is something absolute—a "making of movement"; but they will call "understanding" (which corresponds to a fellow-sufferer) an "activity" or an "action," I believe. Otherwise, understanding and walking would not be distinct. <margin>C</margin> But if these do not fall under a genus of "doing," where should they be placed? Perhaps they will refer "understanding" to the "intelligible," just as they do with "intellection"; for they also direct "sensation" toward the "sensible." But if they direct sensation toward the sensible, why not also refer "being sensed" to the sensible? And yet, the sense-perception which is referred to another does indeed have a relationship to it; but in the meantime, it nonetheless possesses something beyond that relationship—namely, that it is itself a certain activity or a passion. If, therefore, passion exists beyond that which belongs to or falls under something, it is also something else.

<column-break/>

<note>The following is the Greek original of the preceding Latin text.</note>

If anyone should say that neither activities nor movements exist in themselves, but lie within the category of "relation"—on the grounds that there is an active power for activities and a theoretical power for others—it must be said that while the relationship arises from the things themselves, the things are not defined by the relationship. For when there is a substance, it has its own nature before any relationship to another. It possesses its own activity, movement, and habit, and these are not taken away by being related to something else. Otherwise, everything would be a "relation," for everything is in some way related to something else. Regarding the soul's own acting and doing, it is clear these are not merely "relative," for they are certainly either movements or activities. If one places "effecting" among relatives, but makes "doing" a single genus, what prevents one from placing "movement" among relatives while making "being moved" a single genus? Or to say that "doing" is one thing and "suffering" is another.

WE MUST EXAMINE whether we should say that movements are not activities among the things being done—calling activities those things which are complete, and movements those which are indefinite—and what this means. For whether it is "cutting" or any movement, is it always with movement, like something that has passed, or is it all at once, or relative, or absolute? Examples are walking and speaking. And should we call all movements directed toward "suffering" [being acted upon] "movements," but the absolute ones "activities"? Or is each found in both? For they might call walking an absolute movement and a "doing," and "doing" would be its own category, such as walking is. But let it not be forgotten that both are "doings." Perhaps "understanding" is relative to the "intelligible," just as "intellection" is; for "sensation" is relative to the "sensible." But if sensation is relative to the sensible, then "sensation" has a relationship to the other, yet it nonetheless possesses activity or passion absolutely; for being toward another or under something is also something else.

<summary>Plotinus explores whether "Action" and "Passion" (doing and being acted upon) are independent categories or sub-types of "Movement" or "Relation," concluding that things must have an internal nature before they can enter into relationships with others.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Enneads, metaphysics, Action and Passion, Movement, Relatives, Being acted upon, Sensation, Intellection, Aristotelian categories</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the Aristotelian categories, specifically moving from the general nature of "Movement" (discussed on the previous page) into the specific distinctions between "Action" (doing) and "Passion" (being acted upon). Plotinus is here examining whether these are truly distinct categories or merely sub-types of movement.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

...and activity <note>original: ἐνέργεια (energeia)</note>. Walking, too, is of a certain quality, and belongs to the "what" and the "under what" [categories]. Might it be, then, that movements—including thinking—possess within themselves something beyond mere "relation"? Perhaps they are movement itself, or rather, activity.

<column-break/>

...another thing; and clearly the same applies to act and action. For a person walks when that walking belongs to someone; and thus, while it falls under a certain category, it nonetheless possesses the internal character of being a movement. But if intelligence <note>original: *intelligentia*</note> is also a thing independent of its relation to something else, it holds within itself the function of being a certain movement or activity.

---

->*We shall likely set movement as the genus: I am investigating the division between movement that acts internally and movement that falls upon a thing from the outside. Chapter XIX.*<-

---

->*First, names are given to action, whether the transition of movement also passes into another. Second, they are given to passion: whether one thinks these movements—action and passion—differ in reality, or whether they differ only in reason <note>original: *ratione*; meaning a conceptual distinction rather than a physical one</note>.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> We must also consider whether some activities <note>original: ἐνέργειαι (energeiai)</note> appear to be "imperfect" unless they take up a span of time, so that they are joined with movements—such as "living" and "life." For the act of living for each being seems to consist of a completed time. Even happiness <term>happiness: *eudaimonia*, which Plotinus views not as a feeling but as the highest activity of the soul</term> is thought to be a certain activity, not consisting of a single indivisible moment, but rather being a kind of movement. From this, it must be said that both are movements, and that movement itself exists as a single genus. <margin>B</margin> This can be seen from the fact that this genus, in itself, exists beyond the "quantity" that is found in substance, and beyond "quality." Thus, movement is a kind of being that exists around substance. 

If we like, we may divide this common "movement" into two types of motion: some appearing to pertain to the body, and others to the soul. Alternatively, some may remain within the things that move, while others reach into them from elsewhere, under the influence of other things; or some may be proper to the things themselves, while others come from outside. <margin>C</margin> Then, truly, those which come from the things themselves would be "actions," whether they pass into other things or remain independent <note>original: *absolutæ*</note>. Those which depend on other things would be "passions," although movements that pass into other things seem to be the same as the movements said to depend on others. 

For a "division" <note>original: *tmēsis*; often used to mean "cutting"</note>—whether considered from the side of the one dividing or in the thing being divided—is one and the same event; yet "to divide" is something different from "to be divided." Perhaps, however, the division itself is not truly one thing when inflicted by the divider and received by the divided. Rather, "to divide" and "to be divided" might simply mean that from one <margin>D</margin> such action and motion, a second motion follows in the thing being divided. Or perhaps the difference is not measured by the fact of "being divided" itself, but by something else resulting from the motion, such as "feeling pain"—for "to suffer" <note>original: *pati*; the root of 'passion'</note> consists in this. 

What then should we say when no such result follows? What else, except that the act of the agent, falling upon this object, takes the place of pain or passion? For it happens that what is called "doing something" is of such a nature. Thus, "to do" <margin>E</margin> appears to be two-fold: one kind existing not in another, and the other existing in another.

Nor is the division so simple as to say one is "to do" and the other is "to suffer." Rather, the very act of "doing in another" provides the occasion where two things appear: one being the "doing" and the other, by contrast, the "suffering." Consider the logic of writing: although one may admire it in another, it does not bring about a corresponding "passion" in a contrary sense. This is because it effects nothing in the writing process other than the act of the writer himself—which is much like the act of "feeling pain." If someone were to say that it brings about something further—namely, the state of "having been written"—he still does not thereby introduce a "passion" into the discussion.

<summary>This page explores the philosophical classification of movement, action, and passion, questioning whether "doing" and "being acted upon" are two distinct categories or simply two ways of viewing a single movement. Plotinus uses examples like cutting and writing to examine how an activity in one thing can be perceived as a passion in another.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the Aristotelian categories of "Action" and "Passion" (doing and undergoing). Plotinus is examining whether these should be considered separate categories or if they are both subsets of "Movement." He uses the example of walking and the resulting sensations to clarify the distinction.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD. VI.

<margin>A</margin> And yet, even in the act of walking itself, although the ground is beneath and is trodden upon by the gait, it should not be said here that the ground has contributed anything by undergoing an effect <note>original: *perpessam*; refers to the category of "Passion" or being acted upon</note>. But when someone walks upon the body of a living animal, "passion" is then considered, because one perceives the pain arising from it; I say pain is the consideration here, not the walking itself. Otherwise, that walk would have been considered in the same way before. Thus, in all things, "doing" should be called a single genus along with its opposite, which is called "suffering" or "being acted upon." <margin>B</margin> That which is said to be "acted upon" is the very thing that has been produced afterward; it is not an opposite in the same way that "to be burned" is the opposite of "to burn." Rather, "passion" and "being acted upon" refer to the result of the burning—as if, while a single thing exists in reality, there is a resistance, whether that be pain or something else, such as a kind of consumption. What then if someone acts in such a way as to inflict pain? Does not the one act, while the other suffers? And from a single act, two things are confirmed: the one who does, and the one who undergoes. <margin>C</margin> But perhaps in the action itself, the intent of the pain is no longer calculated; rather, he does something else, through which he brings about pain. This, happening within the pain itself and being one and the same thing, also brings it about that the other is affected by a certain pain. What then should be said of that which is a single thing before it even inflicts pain? Or even where no pain is inflicted, is there not a "passion" in the very thing upon which the act is directed—for instance, in hearing? But perhaps hearing is not a passion; indeed, perhaps sensing is not a passion at all. But to be pressed by pain is to be established in a state of passion, which should not be judged as the opposite of the "effecting" or the "doing."

->*Some action is not accompanied by passion, such as intelligence and sense; some is accompanied within, as when a crusher crushes; again, as when heating changes the thing being cooled; some is accompanied from the outside.*<-
->*And this happens in two ways: For either an independent passion accompanies the action*<-
->*from without, such as a person cutting or a blow, as in walking; or in the most hidden*<-
