### Chapter XX.

<margin>A</margin> BUT let it be, if you please, that they are not opposites; nevertheless, since "being acted upon" is something other than "doing," it is not placed in the same genus as "effecting." Or perhaps, if both are movements, they are in the same genus, just as "alteration" <note>original: *alteratio*; a change in quality</note> is a movement according to quality. Is it then the case that when an alteration proceeds from a quality, there is "touching" and "doing," while the quality itself is free from passion? Or perhaps if it is removed from passion, it is occupied in "doing." <margin>B</margin> But if, in acting upon another—as in a mutual beating—one suffers in return, does he no longer "do"? Or rather, does nothing prevent one from suffering while doing? If, therefore, "being acted upon" (such as being worn down) possesses this quality, why is it judged to be "doing" more than "suffering"? Is it because in the act of wearing something down, he is worn down in turn and thus suffers? Shall we then say that because it is a mutual action, there are twin movements around the same thing? But how can there be two? Or is it just one? <margin>C</margin> But in what way is the same motion simultaneously action and passion? It would be called "action" insofar as it flows from one, and "passion" insofar as it flows into another, even though there is only one motion. Shall we then say that the motion is different, and the motion itself, by altering, makes the one who undergoes it? And yet the agent itself does not suffer from the other in the same respect. Wherefore—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And in the case of walking, if ever the ground upon which one walks has suffered anything; but when one steps upon the bodies of living things, the one who assumes there is a "suffering" <note>original: πάσχειν (paschein)</note> perceives a pain, reasoning it out. This is his thought of the walk. And in all cases, regarding "doing" <note>original: ποιεῖν (poiein)</note>, if it must be taken with something called "suffering," these same things are said to "suffer" in this way: that which happened afterward, <margin>B</margin> or the result—for example, "to burn" and "to be burned." But "to burn" and "to be burned" are one thing in the subject, while the "suffering" is that which follows after, whether it be pain or something else like wasting away. What then if he himself should work so as to cause grief? Does not one do, and the other suffer? And from one activity <note>original: ἐνεργείας (energeias)</note> come two things; the one may do, and the other may suffer, either in that activity or in the grieving of the grief. But he does something else, which grieves [the other], and in the grief that has happened, this is the same thing, so that the grieving itself is like that. <margin>C</margin> The thing itself has the one result, and to cause grief or to inflict grief generally is not the same as the "passions" <note>original: παθῶν (pathōn)</note>. Furthermore, there is that—for instance, hearing, or all sensation—where sensing is not entirely [a passion], but to be grieved is something in the "passion," which is not the opposite of "to do."

<margin>A</margin> But let it not be the opposite; nevertheless, being different from "doing," it is not in the same genus as "action" <note>original: ποιήσει (poiēsei)</note>, unless movement <note>original: κίνησις (kinēsis)</note> is both, and they are in the same genus, such as "alteration" <note>original: ἀλλολοίωσις (alloloiōsis)</note>, which is movement according to quality. Is it then that when the alteration comes from the "doing," it is an "action" and the "doing" is without passion? Or if it is without passion, is it in the "doing," but if <unclear>...</unclear> it acts upon another, like <unclear>...</unclear> the striking, where it suffers, it does nothing? And <margin>B</margin> nothing prevents the one doing from also suffering, if not according to the suffering itself—for example, "to rub," as "doing" rather than "suffering." Already it is turned around and he suffers. Is it then because we shall say there are [movements] in both of them around himself, and how both? Rather, there is one; and how is the same thing "action" and "passion" <note>original: πάθη (pathē)</note>? And in this way "action" is that which comes from him, but "passion" is the "undergoing" <note>original: πείσις (peisis)</note>, and is it the same thing? But shall we set it as another? And how is one the other? Or of the one doing <margin>C</margin> it alters, and the one doing is without passion from that. How then is it still called by the name of "passion" and by another of "action," the same thing...

He uses sensory examples like walking, hearing, and the feeling of pain to distinguish between an act and its resulting effect on a subject.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's analysis of the categories "Action" and "Passion" (doing and undergoing). Having previously discussed physical movements like walking, he now moves into more abstract examples—such as a swan turning white or the internal movements of the soul—to determine if "undergoing" requires a change for the worse or simply the reception of an external force.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<note>original: "LIBER PRIMVS"; the first book of the sixth Ennead, focusing on the kinds of Being or the Categories.</note>

For if "undergoing" <note>Greek: *paschein*; Latin: *pati*</note> is defined as that which produces an effect in another, and that other holds the movement within itself, it produces the state of being acted upon. Is the action truly based on the one who acts? Consider a wrestler: the reasoning is that he moves, but he himself is also moved. In practice, he moves, yet he appears to be "undergoing" <note>the effect of the struggle</note> so as to produce the movement. If something later becomes white—for example, a swan coming into being—or if one thing increases and another is increased, shall we say the thing growing is "undergoing" an effect? Or should we place the "passion" only in the *way* it happens? Furthermore, if one thing makes something beautiful, and the other becomes beautiful, does the thing being beautified "undergo" an action? If the old thing becomes worse or fades away, like a piece of tin <note>original: *kyttinos* / *stannum*; Plotinus often compares the weathering of metals</note>, while another becomes better, like bronze, would we say the bronze "undergoes" while the tin "acts"? In nature, nothing is simple. Even when one acts unwillingly, how can it be that every activity of the actor, when entering the subject, does not result in a "passion"? For the act and the passion are one in reality, but they differ in definition. How then can we separate "undergoing" from the reception of something? For learning is not like being struck or hit; learning consists of a certain grasping and discernment, just as seeing is not the same as being struck.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> In what way, then, does a thing "undergo" that very thing which it does in another? Is the cause of "passion" for us the fact that there is movement in another? For certainly, the "passion" was not within the one who performed the effect. But if this thing makes something white (like the nature of a swan), and that thing becomes white (the newborn swan), shall we say the swan "undergoes" something while it is coming into its essence? If, afterward, the grown swan is made white, or if one thing increases and the other <margin>B</margin> is increased, will we affirm that the increased thing "undergoes"? Or rather, shall we place the "passion" in the quality itself? Moreover, if this thing makes something beautiful, and that thing becomes beautiful, shall we confess that the one being made beautiful "undergoes"? If, then, that which makes a thing beautiful also makes it worse or obscures it—like tin—while another thing turns out better—like bronze—shall we say the bronze "undergoes" and the tin "acts"? Finally, how shall we say the one who speaks "undergoes"? It will seem so by the very <margin>C</margin> act of the speaker proceeding into the listener. But how will this be a "passion" when there is only one act? Perhaps the act itself is not the "passion," but the one who receives it is the "patient" <note>the one undergoing the action</note>; since "to undergo" is accepted as belonging to someone else.

---

->Both action and passion can be defined through a certain motion or act. But that which is called "acting" is that whose motion begins spontaneously from itself, whether it passes into another or stays within. That which is called "undergoing" <note>passion</note> is that whose motion happens by chance from elsewhere, whether for the worse or for the better. Likewise, it may come from a separate agent—such as a beating—or from a conjunction, such as an alteration in the body caused by an internal emotion of the soul; the emotion itself is an internal stirring. Chapter XXI.<-

---

<margin>A</margin> By what notion, therefore, shall we properly designate "undergoing" itself? We certainly will not distinguish it by an act that depends on another; for if one has received an act, he has claimed it for himself as his own. But is there a place where there is no act, only "passion"? What if the thing said to "undergo" becomes better, while the act itself is for the worse? Or if someone acts through wickedness and rules another intemperately? <margin>B</margin> Perhaps nothing prevents an action from being wicked and the "passion" <note>the result</note> from being honorable? By what, then, shall we most effectively distinguish them? Shall we not define "doing" as an act passing from any given thing into another? And "undergoing" as an effect resulting from elsewhere into another? What then shall we say if an act proceeds from a thing but does not pass into another? Such is certainly the act of understanding and of opining. What if someone becomes hot from within himself? Whether it happens from intense thought <margin>C</margin> or from anger, where no one else is provoking him, but his own opinion has stirred him up. Perhaps "doing" is an impulse breaking out from itself, whether it remains in itself or acts upon another. What, then, is desire and all appetite? Perhaps if appetite is incited by an object of desire, it is a kind of "passion," even if no one is present to incite it, but the soul has led itself to be excited following that object. Thus, appetite is no different than if someone were pushed, or precipitated like those already in motion. Should we therefore divide appetites, saying that some are actions...

<column-break/>

<note>This column repeats the Latin text from the bottom of the previous section, clarifying the definition of appetite and desire.</note>

...and all appetite, what is it? Perhaps if appetite is incited by something desirable, it is a certain passion, even if no one is present by whom it is incited, but it has followed that which was excited after it. Thus, appetite is no differently situated than if someone had been pushed, or as if one were cast down from those already pushed. Should we therefore divide the appetites, saying that some are actions...

<summary>Plotinus explores the boundary between acting and undergoing, arguing that "passion" (being acted upon) is not defined by whether the result is good or bad, but by whether the movement originates internally or is triggered by an external object, such as desire.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the Aristotelian categories of "Action" and "Passion." On the previous page, he questioned whether physical changes (like a swan turning white) or growth should be classified as "passions" (undergoings) or simply as movements toward a state of being. Here, he explores whether an action that improves an object’s essence can truly be called "suffering" or "passion."</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

<margin>A</margin>...those which remained stayed; but others are passions, where the soul is snatched and dragged along. One "undergoes" <note>Latin: *pati*; Greek: *paschein*—the philosophical term for being the recipient of an action</note> not so much because the effect is brought in by another, but from within itself. For a thing can also act upon itself. However, when nothing changes by its own consent—specifically, a change that does not belong to its essence, but rather leads to a worse state, or at least does not contribute to a better one—we say that such an alteration possesses "passion" and "undergoing" within itself.

<margin>B</margin>But if being heated is nothing other than receiving and having heat, and this heating partly contributes to the essence and partly works against it, then "undergoing" and "not undergoing" would be the same thing. And what prevents heating from being twofold? Perhaps "being heated," when it contributes to the essence, also contributes to the essence of some other thing that is "undergoing." For example, when a certain essence is made from heating—which they call a "statue"—that statue itself is nothing to the heated object, except perhaps by accident <note>The "accidental" properties of an object are those that do not define its core nature, such as its temperature or color.</note>. If, therefore, beauty is made equal by the fact that it is heated, or according to the heating itself, nothing prevents it from appearing to "undergo." For they are accustomed to accept "passion" in two ways, saying it leads either to the worse, to the better, or to neither.

->The same motion, if referred to the agent, can be called "action"; if referred to the patient <note>The "patient" is the entity receiving the action.</note>, it is named "passion." In this way, we distinguish action from affection: we say that after the action, no other work produced from it exists, such as that which came to be through the action, and flowed together.<-

### Chapter XXII.

PERHAPS, therefore, "undergoing" happens because something has a haphazard movement—I mean a movement of alteration—through which it is changed in some way. "Acting," on the other hand, is either having an absolute movement within and from oneself, or putting forth a movement from oneself passing into another, which begins from that very thing said to "act." And yet, movement is indeed in things, but the difference that distinguishes acting and undergoing between themselves is such that "acting" itself remains constant, because acting is devoid of passion.

"Undergoing," however, consists in something being affected differently than before, while the very <margin>C</margin>essence of the "patient" acquires nothing that destroys its essence, but rather undergoes something else in the meantime, while some essence is generated. Wherefore, for the same thing to be in a certain state is "to act," but in another state it is said "to undergo." For according to what consideration do we "act" when the movement is the same? According to the other, it will be "to undergo," because there it is already being affected in such a way. Both, therefore, seem to refer to "the relative" <note>Latin: *ad aliquid*; Greek: *pros ti*—the category of Relation</note>, insofar as the condition of acting relates to the property of undergoing. Indeed, the same thing is "acting" in one respect, but "undergoing" in another. Surely both are considered not so much according to themselves, but together with the agent and the patient; where one moves, the other is moved, and both are two distinct predicates. And yet, this one hands over the motion to that one, and that one in turn receives the motion; therefore, a "giving," a "receiving," and a "relation" occur there. Or certainly, if the one who receives has it—as one is said to "have color"—<margin>D</margin>why should he not also be said to "have motion"? Indeed, even absolute motion, like "walking," has "a walk," and "understanding" has "intelligence." Hence, it is worth considering whether "providing" <note>Latin: *providere*; Greek: *pronoein*—often used in the sense of Divine Providence</note> is "acting," and in turn, to be "governed by providence" is "to undergo"; for it passes into another and concerns another.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...as many as remained; but as for the others, the soul is snatched and dragged. To undergo is what comes from another or from oneself. For a thing can act in itself; but when nothing of itself contributes to an external alteration, it does not lead to the good... and he himself would experience joy... not to his own improvement toward such an alteration, but rather, it is to have "undergoing." But if being heated is to have a certain heat, and if on the one hand it contributes to essence, <margin>B</margin>and on the other not, then "undergoing" and "undergoing" will be the same. And how is being heated twofold? Or is "being heated" whenever it quality-wise affects the essence, and then another thing undergoes... into the quality of essence of the heated things, such as bronze and bodies? But the hearing, or the statue, is not itself heated, except by accident. Or if all the bronze is being heated according to the part being heated, it would also undergo. For "undergoing" is twofold: one being carried toward the worse, the other toward the better, or neither.

<margin>C</margin>### Chapter XXII.

Therefore "undergoing" happens to that thing by movement and by alteration, according to something being otherwise; in which there is a certain quality. "Acting" is what one might have from oneself as an absolute movement from oneself, or that which is completed toward another from itself, the beginning being from itself in what is called "acting." And according to both, there is movement, but the difference or distinction between acting and undergoing is that acting is according to itself, and is passionless. Undergoing is that which becomes different from another than it was before, as long as it possesses essence, with nothing being added to the essence, but another thing having the "undergoing," and some essence being generated. How then does the same thing in a certain relation "act" as it in turn "undergoes"? For it is understood through observation: "acting" is here, for it is in those "undergoing." Since these things are thus divided, just as in each of the two both are "relative," the "acting" toward the "undergoing"... for it then acts on it. If "undergoing" is in it, and each is observed according to itself, but together with the agent and patient, as one moves and the other is moved, there are two categories for each. For one gives movement, and the other receives it; and the "receiving" and "giving" is the relation that was taken. <margin>D</margin>Just as one is said to "have color," why should one not "have motion"? And absolute movement, such as walking, "has a walk" or "has a becoming." Hence we must examine: is "providing" acting, and "attaining providence" undergoing? For it is toward another, or before another, or in itself.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of Aristotle’s categories. Having previously examined "Action" and "Passion," he now moves toward the category of "Providence" (as a form of action) and begins a detailed dismantling of the tenth category: "State" or "Having" (Habitus).</meta>

# BOOK ONE

Providence <note>Greek: *pronoia*</note> seems to be of this nature. But perhaps to provide is not the same as to "make," even if one understands it in relation to something else; nor is being ruled by providence the same as "undergoing" <note>Latin: *pati*; the state of being acted upon</note>. Perhaps even "to think" is not "to make." For the mind does not transfer itself into the object it thinks about; rather, the thought remains concerned with the object. It is not an "effecting" or a "production" at all; nor is it necessary for all activities to be "productions"—such as speaking or doing. However, a "making" can occur there by accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to a thing’s nature, like a person’s location or what they are wearing.</note>. What then should we say? If someone, while walking, leaves footprints, shall we not admit they have "made" something? <margin>B</margin> But because that person is doing or acting or deciding something else, the "making" follows only as a contingency, an action by accident; for the person was not paying the slightest attention to the footprints themselves. We even say that inanimate things "make" or "act," such as fire "making" heat, or a medicine "having made" a result. But enough on these matters.

<column-break/>

->The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, so named because they discussed philosophy while walking in the "peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum.</note> cannot assign a sufficient reason why having clothes should constitute a new category, while having qualities within oneself, or having money, does not. Likewise, "having clothes" or "being armed" signifies not one, but two distinct categories.<-

### Chapter XXIV.

<margin>A</margin> It remains to dispute the category they call "Having" <note>Latin: *Habere*; Greek: *Echein*. This is the last of Aristotle's ten categories, often called "State" or "Condition."</note>. Indeed, if they say that "to have" is meant in many ways, what prevents all modes of "having" from being reduced to this same category? Therefore, "quantity" itself could easily be reduced to this, since a thing "has" magnitude; likewise "quality" could be referred to it, because a thing "has" color. Again, the "father" and similar terms: for a father "has" a son, and a son "has" a father; and in short, all possessions and furniture that are "had." <margin>B</margin> If they should say that all other things that are "had" belong to their own specific categories, but that weapons, shoes, and clothes belong to this specific category of "Having," one might first ask: for what reason is this so? Then, why should the one "having" them create one single new category? If he were burning them, or cutting them, or hiding them, or throwing them away, he would not be creating another new category. <margin>C</margin> If they respond that a category is formed specifically because these things are *wrapped around* the body, it would follow that if a garment is placed on a couch, another category is formed, and yet another if it is draped elsewhere. But if they assert that the category is formed by the act of "containing" and "having" itself, then surely all other things called by the name "having" must be referred here under the same condition. It would not matter what is being "had." Therefore, if in describing such a category, we should not say "having a quality" (since quality has its own place), nor "having quantity" (since quantity has its own place), nor "having parts" (since substance has been properly described), why then is it permitted to say "having weapons," since the substance of the weapons has already been defined? For shoes, clothes, and weapons are all substances. Furthermore, how can "this man has weapons" be a single, simple thing of one category? For that phrase simply means "to be armed" or "to be in a state of being armed."

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Aristotelian category of "Having" (Habitus), arguing that it is redundant because "having" a shoe or a weapon is simply a relationship between two substances, not a unique class of being.</summary>

--- Page 623 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of Aristotle’s categories. Having already addressed the categories of action and passion, he concludes his examination of "Having" and "Position" before launching a significant attack on the Stoic system of four categories.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin>Next, does this category of "having" <note>Latin: *habendi*; Greek: *echo*</note> apply only to a living being, or does it also apply to a statue? For a living being seems to "have" in a different way than a statue does, and perhaps the term is used equivocally <note>Used "equivocally" means the same word is used for two very different concepts, like the "bank" of a river and a "bank" for money.</note>. When we say of a man that "he stands," and we say the same of a statue of a living man, we do not mean "to stand" in the same sense for both. Finally, since this category consists of so few instances and the differences are so minimal, what reason allows us to make it a separate general category?

If one were to be in a certain posture or place, it does not seem to introduce a new category beyond those of shape, place, action, passion, or relation.

### Chapter XXIII.

<margin>A</margin>Finally, there follows the other category which they call "to be placed" or "to be in a certain position" <note>Latin: *situ*; Greek: *keisthai*</note>. This also consists of very few instances with minimal differences, where people are accustomed to say: to recline, to sit, or to be seated. However, they do not mean "to be placed" in a simple sense, but want it to be a new category of "occupying a position" in a certain way—as when it is said, "he is placed in such a figure." In this case, the "figure" is one thing, but the "position" itself, or the "being placed," signifies something else. <margin>B</margin>And indeed, since this signifies being in a certain figure or place, and "figure" and "place" have already been described elsewhere, why is it necessary to pile two categories into one? Furthermore, if one says "he sits," this signifies an act or an action and should be placed in the genus of actions; but if it signifies a passion <note>A "passion" in this sense is not an emotion, but the state of being acted upon by something else.</note>, it belongs in the genus of passions. Next, when something is said to be "suspended," what else does it signify than being "placed upward," just as the opposite signifies being "placed downward," or another being "placed in the middle"? Furthermore, since reclining has been placed in the genus of relations, why are these other positions not also placed there? For since "to the right" is a relation, then "he who is on the right" or "on the left" belongs there too. But enough has been argued regarding these matters.

The four categories should not be placed under one single genus, as many of the Stoics and Cynics <note>The Stoics and Cynics were rival schools to Plotinus's Platonism; the Stoics argued that everything, including the soul, was a type of "body" or matter.</note> have done. Up to this point, Plotinus has toyed with the ten categories of Aristotle and Archytas <note>Archytas was a Pythagorean philosopher; it was traditionally (though likely incorrectly) believed that Aristotle took his categories from him.</note>, exercising the most skilled minds of the nations. From here on, however, he acts more severely against those who placed "matter" in the position of a first principle, and then grouped it together with figures under the same genus.

### Chapter XXIV.

<margin>A</margin>After this, we must speak against those who introduce four categories, dividing reality fourfold into: subjects <note>Latin: *subiecta*; Greek: *hypokeimena*—the underlying "stuff" or matter.</note>, qualified things <note>Latin: *qualia*; Greek: *poia*—things with specific traits.</note>, things in a certain state <note>Latin: *quodammodo se habentia*; Greek: *pōs echonta*—dispositions or arrangements.</note>, and things in a certain state relative to something else <note>Latin: *ad aliquid quodammodo se habentia*; Greek: *pros ti pōs echonta*.</note>. They attribute one common thing to all of them, embracing everything in one single genus. Against them, one may bring many arguments, especially against their claim that one common genus fits all things. <margin>B</margin>For it was introduced by them quite thoughtlessly and without reason when they call this genus "Something" <note>Greek: *ti*. The Stoics used "Something" as the highest category because it could include both physical bodies and "incorporeal" things like time or void.</note>. This cannot be applied to both the incorporeal and the corporeal at once; nor have they left any differences by which they might distinguish what this "something" is. And what is this "something" itself? Is it "being" or "non-being"? If it is said to be "being," then it is just one species among many; but if it is "non-being," it follows that "being" would be "non-being." <margin>C</margin>But these are many things of the same genus. Let us set these aside for the present and consider the division itself. In the first place, by putting the "subject" in the first rank and placing "matter" before all other things, they act quite absurdly by counting the very thing they think is the first principle in the same order as those things which are placed after their own principle. And in the pre...

<column-break/>

...next, whether this applies only to living things, or also to a statue, or generally to these things; for each seems to "have" in a different way, and perhaps homonymously, since "to stand" applies to both, or is the same. Furthermore, it is reasonable that this, being found in so few cases, should not have a category of its own.

### Chapter XXIII.

Regarding "position" <note>Greek: *keisthai*</note>, whether it applies to few things or in itself, such as reclining, or a seat, or "to lie" spoken simply—but how do they lie, and according to the shaping of something? The "shape" is one thing, and the "position" signifies another; or if the "where" and the aforementioned "shape" and the "where" are used, why join two categories into one? Next, "to sit" signifies a certain activity and should be placed among activities; but if it is a passion, it should be placed among things being acted upon. "To recline," or to lie in some other way, is like lying "below" or lying "between." If reclining is among relations, is not "he who reclines" there also? Since that to which "the right" belongs is a relation, "the man on the right" is also there. So much, then, for these things.

### Chapter XXIV.

Against those who propose four qualities <note>Plotinus is referring to the four Stoic Categories.</note> and divide things fourfold into subjects, qualified things, things in a certain state, and things in a certain state relative to something, and who place something common over them and embrace all things in one genus: I do not know how one can take something common over all of them, as many might say. For the term "Something" <note>Greek: *ti*</note> either applies to them or it is applied irrationally; it does not fit both incorporeals and bodies. They have not left behind differences by which they will divide the "Something," and what the "Something" is—whether it is being or non-being. If it is being, it is one of the species; if it is non-being, then being is non-being, and a thousand other absurdities. These things, then, should be left for the present; the division itself must be examined. For having ranked subjects first, and having placed matter before the others, they think it right to rank their first principle along with those things that come after the principle, and...

<summary>Plotinus concludes his critique of Aristotle's minor categories (Having and Position), arguing they are redundant. He then begins a refutation of the Stoic system of four categories, specifically attacking their use of "Something" as a universal genus that mistakenly groups matter with its effects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of the Stoic and Aristotelian systems of categories. After dismissing "Having" and "Position" on the previous page, he now attacks the materialist view that Matter is the primary "subject" or first principle of reality.</meta>

BOOK ONE.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> In the first place, they gather prior things together with posterior things <note>Plotinus is critiquing the Stoic habit of grouping primary things (like substance) and secondary things (like qualities) into the same general categories.</note> into a single group, even though it is otherwise impossible for one thing to be prior and another posterior within the same genus. In those cases where there is a "prior" and a "posterior," the posterior certainly derives its essence from the prior. But in things that fall under the same genus, every individual has an equality of being according to that genus. For a genus must be that which is predicated of its species in terms of "what a thing is" <note>Latin: *quid est*; Greek: *ti esti*. This refers to the essential definition of a thing.</note>. They themselves claim, I believe, <margin>B</margin> that all things have their essence from matter as a cause. Then, when they introduce a single subject instead of counting individual things, they are not really enumerating the things themselves, but are seeking the principles of things. However, there is a difference between naming the principles of things and naming the things themselves. If they want matter alone to be "being," and everything else to be merely "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" refers to modifications or attributes that happen to a subject.</note> of matter, they certainly should not have placed "being" as a single genus for both itself and other things. It would have been better and more correct to define matter as the essence <margin>C</margin> and the rest as its modifications, or as a "universal extension" of its parts. Finally, it is absurd for them to say that some things are "subjects" and others are the "rest," since the subject is one and possesses no difference within itself—unless perhaps they want it divided like a physical mass into parts; though it is not even permitted to divide it in that way,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> in their view, because they believe substance is a continuous thing. It would have been better, therefore, if they had not introduced "subjects" (in the plural) to us, but had introduced "The Subject" (in the singular).

---

->It is forbidden to place Matter, which is formless by itself and capable of being formed from elsewhere, as the principle of things. Chapter XXVI.<-

Especially because all things desire "The Act" <note>Latin: *actum*; Greek: *energeia*. Plotinus argues that the "Good" is activity and form, not passive matter.</note> as the Good—and by "Act" I mean form and action. Therefore, the First Principle must be most beautiful and most simple, containing no potentiality of matter; it is the ultimate end and is "actuality" in itself. By "Act," I also mean the formal essence. For all things desire some other thing beyond their current form. It is ridiculous that, having placed simple matter in the position of a first principle, they then add that matter is continuous and extended. For such a thing would not be simple, but would be mixed with quantity and quality. Finally, whatever consists of many parts, since it exists through the participation of the One, depends on something that is "One" in itself, and is inwardly undivided by ideas.

---

<margin>A</margin> Above all else, it seems most absurd to put matter, which exists only in <term>potentiality</term> <note>Latin: *potentia*; Greek: *dynamis*. The state of "being able to become" something, as opposed to being it already.</note>, before all other things, and not rather to prefer <term>actuality</term> <note>Latin: *actus*; Greek: *energeia*. The state of being fully realized or active.</note> itself over potentiality. For it is impossible for that which is in potentiality to ever proceed into actuality if that which is in potentiality holds the rank of a first principle. For that which is merely in potentiality will never lead itself toward something better; there must be something in actuality existing before it. Thus, matter would no longer be the principle. Or, if they say they exist <margin>B</margin> simultaneously, they would be establishing the principles of things by some random chance. Likewise, if they place them together, why not prefer the Act? And why is this—that is, matter—judged to be "being" rather than the Act? But if they assert that Act is posterior, we must ask under what condition that could happen. Truly, matter does not generate form, because the formless does not generate the beautiful, nor does that which is actually something (or the act itself) ever proceed from that which is only in potentiality. Otherwise, it would have had to exist there previously in some kind of act; and for them, the subject and matter would no longer be simple, and God would be posterior to matter. For they would have to ask where the "form" of the body comes from; unless God also exists without matter, seeing as He is a kind of Reason <note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*.</note> possessing the property of a first principle.

<summary>Plotinus argues that Matter cannot be the first principle of the universe because it is merely passive potentiality; instead, Actuality (Form/God) must be prior to Matter. He critiques the Stoic view that collapses the distinction between the primary essence of matter and its secondary qualities into a single category.</summary>

--- Page 625 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of First Principles. On the previous page, he critiqued the idea of "Being" as a single genus. Here, he specifically targets the Stoic materialist view that Matter or "Body" could be the ultimate origin of the universe, arguing instead for the priority of the incorporeal One.</meta>

PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Surely the active principle is incorporeal <note>original Latin: *incorporeus*; Greek: *asōmatos*</note>. But if they maintain that God has a composite essence without matter—simply because they believe He is a body—they are forced to introduce another kind of "matter" that would be suitable for a divine being. Furthermore, how can matter be the first principle if it is a body? It is impossible for a body not to be a collection of many parts; indeed, every body is composed of both matter and quality.

<margin>B</margin> If they call this body "matter" in an equivocal sense <note>meaning they are using the word "matter" to mean something else entirely</note>, they are merely playing with words. But if they say the common property of a body is its three-dimensional extension, then they are describing a mathematical body rather than a physical one. If they then try to join this three-fold dimension with a certain resistance <term>resistance: translating the Greek *antitypia*, the quality of solid objects to push back or occupy space</term> to give the body its fullness, they are no longer speaking of a single, simple thing.

Moreover, the property of resistance is a "quality," or at least something derived from a quality. We must then ask: where does this resistance come from? Where do the three dimensions come from? What force compelled them to extend? Matter is not contained within the <margin>C</margin> logical definition of three-dimensional extension, nor is three-dimensional extension contained within the definition of matter. Therefore, since matter only participates in magnitude, it is no longer a simple principle.

Furthermore, where does its unity come from? This subject is not Unity itself, but it exists only by participating in unity. It was worth considering that "mass" <note>original Latin: *moles*; Greek: *onkos*</note> cannot be placed before all other things. Instead, we must prioritize something separate from mass: the One itself. We ought to begin from the One and descend into the many; we should start from that which is <margin>D</margin> separate from magnitude and only then arrive at magnitudes. For there cannot be a "many" unless there is a "one," nor can there be magnitude unless there is something free from magnitude.

Magnitude is "one" not because it is the essence of Unity, but because it participates in it. This happens through a kind of meeting—a chance encounter, in a way—with that which is primary and truly "One" before the secondary version can exist. Then we must ask: what is the condition of this meeting? If they had sought this, they would have found the "One" itself, which is not "one" by chance. I call something "one by chance" if unity does not belong to its own nature, but it happens to be one because of something else.

---

->*If first matter is the subject of all moving forces and forms, it cannot be the true first principle.*<-

### Chapter XXVII.

*Matter, being formless in itself, does not give birth to forms. No form existing within matter can stand on its own, since it can never even exist within itself. Nor is their principle some form mixed with matter, for then it could not rule over matter. The most effective mover must eventually be free from material obstacles. If someone imagines matter to be the principle of forms, they either deny it is a subject or affirm that all forms exist through the essence of matter. Ultimately, they would claim that everything truly in the world is matter, while forms are mere imaginings. But in truth, since a form cannot naturally be produced from formless matter—much less a superior form—the most excellent Mind <note>original Greek: *Nous*</note> certainly cannot. God, the principle of material form, is a kind of life that does not sprout from matter, even if it is infused into it. The principle of this life is Life itself, which towers far above matter.*

---

<margin>A</margin> It was proper to regard the first principle of all things in its most venerable seat. One should by no means claim that the first principle is something formless, subject to suffering <term>passion: from the Latin *passio*, the capacity to be acted upon or changed by outside forces</term>, lacking life, devoid of mind, dark, and undefined—and then ascribe the very gift of existence to it. For God is introduced by them merely for the sake of appearances...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If God is incorporeal, then the productive power is also incorporeal. But if He is also immaterial yet has a composite essence, or if He is a body, they are introducing a different matter for God. Then, how can matter be a principle if it is a body? For a body is not one, but many; every body is made of matter and quality. If <margin>B</margin> they use the term "body" for this matter, they use it equivocally. If they mean that which is three-dimensionally extended is common to body, they are speaking of a mathematical concept. If they add resistance to the three dimensions, they are no longer speaking of a single thing. Furthermore, resistance is a quality, or comes from a quality. Where does resistance come from? Where do the three dimensions come from? Who extended them? Either matter is the three-dimensional extension in its definition, or it is not. If it has participated <margin>C</margin> in magnitude, it is no longer simple. Furthermore, where does the union come from? For matter is not union itself, but becomes one by participation in unity. One should have reasoned that it is not possible to have a mass untouched by everything else, but rather the non-mass and the One. One should not imagine things as many do—wandering from the many to the One—but should go from the non-magnitude to magnitudes. For it is not possible for there to be many if <margin>D</margin> the One does not exist, nor magnitude without the non-magnitude. Magnitude is "one" not because it is Unity itself, but by participating in it, and by a kind of meeting. There must therefore be that which is immediately and primarily "One" before that which is "one" by a meeting. How does this meeting occur? If one seeks the manner of this meeting, they might perhaps find the One that is not "one" by accident. I say "by accident" because it is not the One itself, but becomes one through another.

---

<margin>A</margin> It was necessary, when placing the principle of all things in a position of honor, not to suggest that the formless, or the passive, or the lifeless, or the mindless, or the dark, or the indefinite is the principle, and then attribute essence to it. Their "God" is brought in merely for the sake of decency...

<summary>Plotinus argues that Matter cannot be the first principle of the universe because it is composite, three-dimensional, and lacks inherent unity. He concludes that the "One"—a simple, incorporeal, and living principle—must exist prior to any physical mass.</summary>

--- Page 626 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s metaphysical critique of the Stoic belief that matter is the primary substance of the universe. He continues to argue that if matter were the sole foundation, higher realities like the soul and the intellect would be mere secondary "accidents" or "states" of physical stuff, which he finds logically impossible.</meta>

BOOK ONE.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...deriving its essence from matter, it would be both composite and posterior—or rather, it would be matter itself existing in a certain state. Therefore, if matter is the underlying substrate <term>substrate: translating the Greek *hypokeimenon*, the "thing lying under" that supports qualities</term>, it is necessary that there be something else outside of it that acts upon it, making matter subject to the functions it assigns. But if the one who is said to act upon matter is himself within that matter as a sort of substrate alongside it, he would no longer be treating matter as something subordinate. Indeed, he himself cannot be a substrate together with matter. <margin>B</margin> Otherwise, to what would these things be subject? There would be no one further to make them subordinates, since everything would have already been consumed into that which is called the "substrate." For a "subject" necessarily relates to something else—not to what is inside itself, but rather to that which acts upon it. Truly, the subject is set out in relation to that which is not a subject; if this is so, it relates to an external force.

Therefore, this point seems to have been overlooked. However, if <margin>C</margin> they have no need of anything external, but the substrate itself can become all things through its own power—as if it were transformed into various shapes, like a dancer <note>original: *orchēstēs* (Greek) / *tripudiator* (Latin). This is a famous analogy Plotinus uses to describe how the soul or matter might relate to form.</note> who shifts himself into many poses—then it would no longer be a substrate, but rather would be all things themselves. For just as the dancer is not "subject" to his poses (since the poses are merely his own movements and activities), so also that which they call "matter" would not be a substrate for all things if all things come from it. Rather, nothing else would truly exist at all, <margin>D</margin> since everything else would be nothing other than matter itself existing in a certain state—just as a dancer in a performance is simply himself in various poses.

But if other things do not truly exist, then matter itself would not be a substrate; nor would it be the "matter of things," but only matter. Therefore, it is necessary to consider what matter actually is. For matter seems to be a relative term <note>original Latin: *ad aliquid*; Greek: *pros ti*</note>. That which is relative refers to something else and is defined by its relation, like "the double" in relation to "the half." But "being" or "substance" <note>original: *essentia* / *ousia*</note> is not relative to the double. <margin>E</margin> "Being" relates to "non-being" only by accident. But that which exists in itself is "being," and matter itself would be related to "being" as "being."

For if "potentiality" is that which is to be in the future, and that "future thing" is not an essence, then matter itself is not an essence. Thus, it happens that while they criticize those who create essences out of non-beings, they themselves in the meantime turn essence into non-being. For the world, insofar as it is the world, would not be an essence according to them. It is wrong to say that matter (the substrate) is an essence <margin>F</margin> while bodies are not even more truly essences. It is much more absurd to say the world itself does not exist as an essence, but only a single part of it (the matter) is an essence. Furthermore, it would mean that a living creature does not have its substance from its soul, but from matter alone, and that the soul itself is merely a "passion" or a state of matter, appearing later than matter. <margin>G</margin> From where, then, did matter receive the ability to be animated? Where does the substance of the soul itself come from? And how does matter subsist and take form? Surely when matter becomes these bodies, the soul is something other than the matter itself. For if the "form" or "species" came from somewhere other than the soul, the soul would never come into being just because a quality was added to matter; rather, we would have entirely soulless bodies. If something forms matter and generates the soul, it follows that before the soul was created, there was already a "creating soul" <note>Plotinus is arguing for the priority of the Divine Mind or World-Soul over the physical world.</note>.

<sig>Dd 3</sig>

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Stoic view of matter using the analogy of a dancer, arguing that if matter were the only reality, life and the soul would be mere "poses" of dead matter. He concludes that for matter to be organized into a living world, a prior, incorporeal Soul must exist to shape it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of Stoic materialism from the previous page. He is specifically dismantling the idea that "matter" (the substrate) is the most real thing simply because it persists while qualities change. This leads into a discussion of the Stoic categories of being.</meta>

PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

*The more matter remains stable beneath the changes of forms, the more passive it is. Therefore, it is the lowest of all things. If the Mind <term>Mind: translating the Latin 'Mens' or Greek 'Nous', the divine Intellect</term> were secondary to matter, it could neither transcend matter nor even comprehend the small bit of matter present before it.*

<column-break/>

### Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>A</margin> **B**UT since there are many arguments openly opposing this opinion—arguments that could easily be brought forward—we ought to be content with what has already been said, lest it be shameful for us to struggle too long against such obvious errors. Indeed, it is enough to have shown who these people are and how they establish "non-being" <note>original: 'non ens' / 'mê on'. Plotinus argues that matter, being devoid of form, is actually a type of non-existence compared to the "True Being" of the forms.</note> as if it were the highest form of Being, and do not hesitate to place that which is weak in the primary position. The cause of such great error arose because they followed the senses as a <margin>B</margin> guide, placing too much trust in them when establishing principles and other doctrines. Because they thought that only physical bodies were true things, and they feared the mutual transformation of bodies into one another, they came to believe that the thing which remains stable is Being itself. It is just as if someone thought that "place" was more of a "being" than the bodies within it, simply because place is not destroyed. And although matter remains here among them, they should not have <margin>C</margin> judged "Being" to be simply anything that remains; rather, they should have first considered what the qualities of "True Being" are, which, by their very presence, allow the capacity for remaining always the same. Now, even if a shadow remains, continually following something else that is constantly changing, the shadow is not "more" of a thing than that which it follows. Indeed, the sensible object itself, along with many other things, should be judged as "more" of a being—since it is a whole—than any one thing contained within it. But if even that whole substrate is "non-being," how can it <margin>D</margin> be the primary thing?

What seems most marvelous of all is that those who grant the senses the greatest authority over everything have not also affirmed that Being itself can be grasped by the senses. Yet, they did not even correctly attribute "solidity" or "resistance" to it, for that is a certain quality. But if they say they perceive it with the mind, this would be an absurd "mind" which prefers matter to itself, and gives the gift of true existence not to itself, but to matter. Since Mind, according to them, is not "Being," what sort of reliability will it have when it speaks and judges everywhere concerning things that are more excellent than itself, even though it has no kinship with them? But enough has been argued by others concerning this nature and the substrate.

*They established four categories: first, the Substrate; second, the Quality; third, the State; fourth, the Relative State.* <note>These are the four Stoic categories: *hypokeimenon* (substrate), *poion* (qualified), *pôs echon* (disposed/state), and *pros ti pôs echon* (relatively disposed).</note>

### Chapter XXIX.

This very thing which is added, the "Quality"—if it is something simple, as it ought to be if it forms its own category, then it is certainly incorporeal, which is exactly what they do not want. But if it signifies a composite, then it is a single division, dividing things into the "substrate" and then again into the "qualified substrate." And whenever they say that a quality is a "certain state," either they add nothing to the matter beyond it having that state, or they do add something; if they add nothing, then there is in reality only one category. If it is something else, they never explain what it is when questioned. Nor do they ever distinguish between "qualified matter" and "matter in a certain state"—a distinction they would need to make to justify having multiple categories. Finally, if there is nothing in nature except matter in a certain state, the Mind itself will be material, and yet it will be expected to judge both matter and separate things with ease.

<margin>E</margin> **N**OW, those things which they call "Qualities" must be something other than the substrates themselves, which they themselves admit—otherwise, they would never have listed them as secondary. If, therefore, they are different, they must furthermore be simple. If they are simple, they are by no means composite. And if they are not composite, they do not possess matter, which is the very reason they are "Qualities." If, finally, this is true, they must exist as incorporeal and as active powers <note>original: 'efficacia' / 'energeia'. Plotinus is forcing the Stoics into a logical trap: if qualities exist, they must be immaterial, which contradicts Stoic materialism.</note>.

<column-break/>

### Chapter XXVIII.

**B**ut since there are many things said against this hypothesis, we must let them go, lest it be absurd to contentiously fight against what is clearly an absurdity—showing that they have trusted "non-being" as the most real Being, and placed the later thing first. The cause for them was the senses, which became their leader and source of trust in the establishing of principles and other things. For thinking that bodies were "beings," and then fearing the change of these things into one another, they thought that which persists under them—the substrate—was Being. It is as if one thought "place" was more of a "being" than bodies, because place does not perish. But they should have realized that "Being" is not just anything that happens to remain, but they should see what qualities belong to True Being so that it possesses the necessity of always remaining. If a shadow should remain, following that which changes, the shadow is not more real. And the whole itself, along with many other things, would more likely be "Being" than any one thing within it. But if the whole substrate is "non-being," how can that substrate be "Being"? Most wonderful of all is how they refer everything to the senses. Yet it is not by sense, but by the intellect [that they argue]. If it is possible to blame them correctly, their trust is in things grasped by reason; yet the Mind is absurd, which puts matter before itself and gives Being to matter but does not hold it for itself. Since the Mind is not "Being" for them, how can it be trustworthy when it always speaks of things better than itself? It would have no kinship with them, nor would it even be of that nature or of those substrates discussed elsewhere.

### Chapter XXIX.

**A**nd as for "Qualities" among them, if they say they are things other than the substrates—for otherwise they would not have counted them as secondary—what would follow? Clearly they must be simple, and if they are simple, they are not composite. If this is so, they do not have matter, insofar as they are qualities. If they do not have matter, they are incorporeal and are active powers <gloss>energies or activities</gloss>.

<summary>Plotinus critiques Stoic materialism, arguing that identifying "matter" as the highest form of Being is a mistake driven by over-reliance on the senses. He points out that if qualities and the Mind are treated as secondary to matter, the Stoics' own logical categories fall apart.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s critique of the Stoic categories of reality. Having previously argued that matter cannot be the primary "Being," he now examines the Stoic attempts to classify everything else—qualities and dispositions—as mere "modes" of matter.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<column-break/>

For matter is set forth for the purpose of being acted upon; but if it is preserved, then first of all, their division into simple and composite things stands in opposition. Either these things must fall under a single genus, or they must place one of the species within the other, as if someone dividing "knowledge" were to say one part is "grammar" and the other is "grammar and something else." But if they say that "qualified things" <note>original: 'ta poia' / 'qualia'</note> are a certain kind of matter, first of all, their rational principles <note>original: 'logoi' / 'rationes'</note> will be internal to matter. However, by not being born within the matter, they will create a composite. But since they create it before the composite exists, they will consist of matter and form. Therefore, they themselves are not forms, and the rational principles would say that the principles are nothing, or merely matter in a certain state. Clearly, these "qualified things" are "how it is disposed" <term>how it is disposed: a translation of 'pôs echon', the Stoic category describing a state or disposition</term>. And in the fourth category, he blames the "qualified." If the difference belongs to another genus, one must show that these "dispositions" are more of a substance <note>original: 'hypostasis' / 'subsistentia'</note>. Yet, if there is no substance there, why do they count it as a single genus or species? Surely a "being" and a "non-being" cannot be counted under the same category. But what is this "disposition" within matter? It is either a being or a non-being. If it is a being, it is entirely incorporeal. If it is a non-being, it is spoken of in vain. And it is not only that; the "qualified thing" will be nothing at all, merely a disposition. For it is much more a non-being, and the fourth category mentioned is even more so. Therefore, only matter exists. Who, then, says these things? Certainly not matter itself, unless it were itself a Mind—namely, a mind in a certain state—and even then, how could "empty" matter have it? Matter, then, says these things and perceives them! And if it speaks well and wisely, one must wonder how it thinks when it possesses neither mind nor soul. And if it has a soul, it is even more strange. But if it says these things foolishly, asserting so many things it is not and cannot be, to whom should we attribute this foolishness except to matter itself? I say this because whatever says those things speaks with much of the nature of matter within it, being entirely of matter, even if it has a soul. This happens through ignorance of itself and of the power that is able to speak the truth about things that can be trusted.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For among those people, matter is set out for the purpose of receiving passions <note>original: 'passiones'—in this context, it means being acted upon or undergoing change</note>. But if they say that the "qualified things" themselves are composites, first, the division will be absurd, as it distinguishes simple and composite as opposites and yet heaps them into one genus. Furthermore, for this very reason, it is not correct, since it places one of the species within the other: just as if someone dividing "science" were to assert that one part is "grammar" and the other is "grammar and something else besides."
<margin>B</margin> Truly, if they say that "qualified things" are a certain kind of matter, then first, the seminal reasons <term>seminal reasons: 'rationes seminales', the formative, seed-like principles that the Stoics believed organized the material world</term> among them would be material. Not only being placed in matter would they create a certain composite, but having been made by them before the composite, they would constitute species out of matter. Therefore, neither the species themselves nor the reasons would exist. But if they should object that the reasons are nothing other than matter itself being in a certain state, they will be forced to admit that the "qualified things" themselves are "dispositions," and they would have to be placed in the fourth category.
<margin>C</margin> But if they introduce some other relationship, we must ask: what is the difference? Is that which is called "how it is disposed" at this level rather a certain substance? Although, unless there is a substance there, why does he count it as a single genus or species? For one cannot count a "being" and a "non-being" under the same heading. Moreover, what is this thing in matter that is said to be "disposed in a certain way"?
<margin>D</margin> For it is judged to be either being or non-being. And yet if it is being, it is entirely incorporeal; but if it is non-being, it is said in vain, and only matter exists. The "qualified thing" itself would not exist at all; nor even that which is usually called "disposition." For that could seem to someone to be much more a "non-being." Finally, that which is counted as fourth seems much less to be a "being." Therefore, only matter is "being."
<margin>E</margin> Who then says this very thing? For it is not matter itself, unless perhaps matter itself is a mind—specifically, a mind in a certain state. And yet, this very thing which is called "being in some state" is an addition for the one considering it; matter therefore says these things and understands them. And truly, if it spoke rightly and sanely, it would be a wonder how it understands and performs the duties of a soul, since it has neither mind nor soul. But if it speaks foolishly, when it asserts that it is what it is not and cannot be, to whom is it most proper to attribute this foolishness? Truly to no one except itself, if only it could speak. But as it is, it does not speak, and he who speaks such things says it because he has already drunk deeply of matter, being entirely devoted to it even if he possesses a soul. Thus, he speaks from ignorance of himself and of the power which is able to express the truth about such matters.

---

*They do not correctly distinguish between "the qualified" <note>original: 'quale'</note> and "how it is disposed" <note>original: 'quomodo se habens'</note>. For a "qualified thing" is in truth matter disposed in a certain way, and conversely, "how it is disposed" is matter being qualified. Furthermore, "disposition" cannot be a unique genus, nor can anything that exists besides "qualified matter" be designated by this name—namely, as a "disposition."*

->Chapter XXX.<-

Regarding those things said to be "disposed in a certain way," it is perhaps absurd to place them in the third rank, or for them to obtain any order at all: since all things which are handed down as being disposed in some way exist around matter.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Truly, regarding those things which are said to be "disposed in a certain way," it is perhaps absurd to place them in the third place, or to say they obtain any order whatsoever: since all things whatever that are taught to be disposed in some way exist around matter.

---

But they will introduce some difference of those things which are so affected, and say that matter itself is disposed otherwise...

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Stoic categories, arguing that if matter is the only substance, then qualities and dispositions are essentially "non-beings" or must be admitted as incorporeal. He ridicules the materialist view by pointing out the absurdity of mindless matter "authoring" a philosophy that denies the existence of the mind.</summary>

--- Page 629 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s systematic critique of Stoic ontology, specifically focusing on their third and fourth categories: "disposition" (how a thing is) and "relative disposition" (how a thing is in relation to something else). Having argued that matter and quality cannot be merged, Plotinus now questions whether time, place, and action can be reduced to mere "dispositions" of matter.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> To be affected in a certain way, either this way or that, is one thing; however, it is quite another for the remaining things—which are posited as being in whatever state they are—to be affected. Furthermore, even if the **qualities** <note>original: 'qualia' / 'poia'</note> themselves are present around matter as being disposed in a certain way, those things which are properly said to "be in a certain state" are reported to be involved in being affected themselves. But if these qualities exist entirely when they are present, unless the matter is affected in some way, do those things which are "disposed in a certain way" revert back into the matter according to their theory, and thus be occupied with matter? <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, from what perspective can that which is said to be "disposed in a certain way" be a single thing, since there is so much difference in such things? For how can a **three-cubit length** <note>OCR 'tricultatem' is likely 'tricubitalem'</note> and **white** be reduced to one thing, when the former is a **quantity** <term>quantity: the category of 'how much' or 'how many'</term> and the latter is a **quality** <term>quality: the category of 'what kind'</term>? Likewise, what of that which is said to be "at some time," and "in some place"? Again, how is it possible for these to be "disposed in a certain way"—namely, what is said to be "yesterday" or "for a long time," or "in the **Lyceum**" and the "**Academy**"? <margin>C</margin> How, again, can it be brought about that **time** itself is "disposed in a certain way"? For neither time itself, nor the things in time, nor **place**, nor even the things in place, can be that very thing <note>i.e., a mere disposition of matter</note>. Furthermore, that which is said to "act" <note>original: 'facere' / 'poiein'</note> is not what is named as being "disposed in a certain way" or "affected"; since the "act" itself is not "disposed in a certain way," but is rather "acting in a certain way," or simply "acting" altogether. <margin>D</margin> And yet, even the "patient" <note>the one being acted upon</note> is not properly "disposed in a certain way," but rather "suffering in a certain way," or simply suffering in this or that way. Perhaps, indeed, what is called "being disposed in a certain way" will agree with what is usually called "**position**" <term>position: the Stoic/Aristotelian category of 'situs' or 'keisthai', referring to posture or arrangement</term> and "holding a place"; likewise perhaps with that which is named as "having." Nevertheless, in this very thing which is "to have," it is not properly "being disposed in a certain way," but rather simply "having." Therefore, unless they had established the genus of **relation** <note>original: 'relationis' / 'pros ti'</note> as one along with others, there would certainly be another reason for those seeking whether they assign any **substance** <note>original: 'subsistentiam' / 'hypostasis'</note> <margin>E</margin> to such habits; since they assign almost none at all. Finally, what shall we say to the fact that they place a newly arriving thing in the same genus as things that existed before? It is absurd to couple a thing that is adventitious <note>added later or external</note> in the same genus with prior things. For it is necessary that **one** and **two** exist first, so that there can also be a **half** and a **double**. Regarding the rest, whoever else has posited the things themselves or the principles of things differently—whether infinite or finite, whether bodies or rather incorporeal, or perhaps both together—it is permitted for us to inquire separately about each one, taking up in addition those things which were discussed by the ancients against such opinions.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...matter in this way, and in that way, but otherwise in the "being in a certain state," either upon the things after it, and the matter being "in a certain state," but the "affected things" being in a certain state concerning the other things; but those things of the narrow ones being in this way or of the matter being in a certain state, and those well-formed things indeed run through the matter itself, and will be around the matter. But how are the "disposed in a certain way" things, [when there is] a wandering difference in the "being in a certain state" itself, if the <margin>B</margin> **shape** and the **white** [are] into one of the "disposed in a certain way," the one being a **quantity**, the other a **quality**? Furthermore, the "at some time," and the "where" altogether, how are these "disposed in a certain way," such as "yesterday" or "last year" and "in the Lyceum," and "in the Academy"? How [is it] in a certain way that time itself [is]? Furthermore, the "at some time" or the "where" altogether—the "yesterday" or the "long ago" and the **place**, and the things in them? How [can they be] "disposed in a certain way"? Furthermore, is "acting" a "disposition"? But rather, it is "acting in a certain way," or generally being an "actor," but only in a certain way; and the "being acted upon," <margin>C</margin> or "disposed in a certain way," but rather it will be "suffering in a certain way," or generally "suffering." But perhaps these might fit the "**to be situated**" <note>original: 'keisthai'</note>, the "being in a certain state," and also the "**to have**" <note>original: 'echein'</note>; but because of the "to have" and "being in a certain state" <unclear>illegible</unclear> but "having." But the "**relation**" <note>original: 'schesis'</note> in a certain way, and if they did not place it under other definitions, I should speak. And <margin>D</margin> concerning those things, if [one gives] some **substance** <note>original: 'hypostasis'</note> to such and such relations—but they give it in many ways—under the step of a common happening thing, or the later [thing], or the arrangement of the happening thing; and the <unclear>tongue/language</unclear>, how [can it be] the thing before? For it is necessary for **one** and **two** to be, so that there is also **half** and **double**. And concerning the others who placed these things or the principles of beings differently—either infinite or finite, or bodies, or incorporeal, <margin>E</margin> or both—it is necessary to seek concerning each separately, taking up the [sayings] or the principles of the ancients, and the opinions which have been spoken of.

<summary>Plotinus critiques the Stoic categories, arguing that qualities, quantities, time, place, and actions cannot be reduced to mere "dispositions" of matter. He highlights the logical absurdity of grouping distinct concepts like "white" and "three-cubits" or "yesterday" and "the Academy" into a single category of material state.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book 2 of the Sixth Ennead. In the previous book, Plotinus analyzed and critiqued the Aristotelian and Stoic categories (the "ten genera"). Here, he transitions to establishing his own Platonic system of the "Genera of Being," specifically looking at how the "One" relates to "Being" and its various categories.</meta>

# OF PLOTINUS
## THE SIXTH ENNEAD.
### BOOK II.

# OF PLOTINUS
## THE SIXTH ENNEAD.
### BOOK II.

->ON THE GENERA OF BEING (Second Book).<-
->Concerning the kinds of being.<-

*We consider that alone to be true being which is not mixed with its opposite—that is, the lack and deprivation of existence. Chapter I.*

It is necessary, therefore, for that [true being] to be united in itself and whole, and to remain so always. Nor is it fitting to place "false being" together with "true being" under the same species, just as one should not place the image of Socrates alongside Socrates himself. Plotinus will henceforth proceed through the genera of beings in the Platonic manner. You will now receive, O Great-Souled Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the patron of the arts in Florence.</note>, a very brief interpretation of these matters from your Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the translator and philosopher who brought Plotinus to the Latin-speaking West.</note>; for you have heard at times, and perhaps will someday read, your friend and mine, Ficino, treating mysteries of this kind by a certain divine instinct, as he is accustomed to doing in other things.

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a classical figure amidst scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
<margin>* Perhaps indeed.</margin>
SINCE we have already considered the ten [categories] that are commonly spoken of <note>A reference to Aristotle's ten categories: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and affection.</note>, and we have discussed those who reduce all things into one genus or four species <note>Referring to the Stoics, whom Plotinus critiqued in the previous book.</note>: it would follow to say what our own view on these matters appears to be, attempting to bring our opinions into harmony with the doctrine of Plato. If, then, it were necessary to posit that Being is "the One"—as if Being and the One were the same, or as if Being were the sum total of all things—or if the One were the principles <term>principles: the fundamental origins or 'archai' from which all things flow</term>. For if one says that the principles are the same as the One, and then that the One is already the principles, but the genera <term>genera: the highest classes or "kinds" of things that exist</term> are not the principles; or vice versa; or that in each case all are principles and genera, and again genera and principles. Or that in some cases all are both genera and principles, while in others, some are one and some are the other. Since, however, we do not say that Being is "one" [in a simple sense], for the reasons stated by Plato and others, it becomes necessary perhaps to consider these things: how we might, by bringing them into the open, accept a certain number of beings or conduct an inquiry into the nature of beings. It is necessary first to discuss Being itself: what we mean when we say "Being," so that our inquiry may proceed correctly, and what appears to others to be being, but which we call "becoming" rather than truly "being"; or rather, we should see if these things that are "becoming" are the same as those beings about which Plato's doctrine is concerned.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring a figure and ornate foliage.</image-desc>
<margin>A</margin>
AFTER we have considered the ten genera, and then spoke of those who encompass all things under one certain genus as if they were four species: it now remains to explain our own opinion on these things, attempting of course to bring our opinion back to the view of Plato. <margin>B</margin> If, then, it were necessary to posit "Being" as "the One," there would be no need to inquire whether there is one genus in all things: nor again whether the genera are not reduced to one, and whether they should be called principles: nor again whether the principles should also be posited as genera: nor, vice versa, whether the genera themselves are the same as the principles: nor whether all things are indeed principles and genera; or whether genera are not equally principles, or vice versa: or rather, whether in both there are some which are simultaneously principles and genera, and some <margin>C</margin> which are simultaneously genera and principles: or perhaps in some cases all are simultaneously one and the other, and in other cases only some are simultaneously both. Since, however, we do not posit "Being" as one—the reason for this opinion having been assigned by Plato and others especially like him—it is perhaps necessary to consider these things as well: first, what number and in what manner we should bring them forward. Since, therefore, we are inquiring into Being itself or beings, it is necessary in the first place to distinguish these internal things. Namely, <margin>D</margin> what we call Being itself, which we are properly considering at present, and what appears to others to be being, which we nevertheless call not that which "is" at any time, but rather that which "becomes" <note>original: 'fiat' / 'gignomena'. Plotinus distinguishes between the eternal realm of Being and the physical world of Change or "Becoming."</note>. It is worthwhile to understand that these things are distinct from each other, not as if they were one single genus divided within itself. For it is not right to think that Plato distributed them in such a way.

<sig>Dd 4</sig>

<summary>This page introduces Plotinus's own investigation into the "Genera of Being" following his critique of earlier philosophers. He begins by questioning the relationship between the One, Being, and the fundamental principles (archai) of the universe, while setting a clear boundary between eternal "Being" and the physical world of "Becoming."</summary>
