<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "Genera of Being" (the primary categories of existence). Having dismissed the Aristotelian categories for the intelligible realm in the previous book, he now begins to define how "Being" can be both a unity and a plurality of "Greatest Genera" (Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference).</meta>

# THE ENNEADS OF PLOTINUS. BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin> For it would be ridiculous to join Being itself into a single category with non-being; it would be as if someone were to place the actual Socrates and a mere image of him under the same heading. Indeed, to distinguish these things in reality is nothing other than to set them apart and arrange them separately, declaring that what *appears* to be being is actually non-being, while demonstrating that something else exists as truly being. Furthermore, he <note>Likely referring to Plato, particularly in the *Sophist* or *Timaeus*.</note> who always joined "always" to "being itself" showed that true Being must be of such a nature that the essence of being is never found lacking within it. Therefore, regarding those who speak falsely about this being, we shall treat it as if it does not become a single <margin>B</margin> subject. Next, we shall see if we might bring forward something further concerning "becoming" (generation), that which is generated, and the sensible world.

---

*The primary Being is indeed one, but in a certain way it consists of many things, which are both principles and genera. They are "principles" <term>principia; arche</term> because the very nature of being is composed of them; they are "genera" <term>genera; gene</term> because each of them contains many individual species under itself. Nor should these be confused into a single form: for there is a specific and proper order of being there. However, "Being" itself should not be called a genus, for it is not divided into species like a genus, nor is it predicated of them in the way a genus is.* Chapter II.

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, we say that Being is "not one" <note>Meaning it is not a simple, undifferentiated unity like the "One" itself, but a "One-Many."</note>, it follows that we must assert either a specific number or the infinite. In what way do we say "not one," unless we mean "one and many at once"—a certain varied unity encompassing many things within itself? It is necessary, then, that this which is "one" in this way is either a single genus whose species are the individual beings (by which many are thus at once one), or that there are several genera existing under a single head. Or perhaps there are several genera, none subordinate to another, but each containing the things beneath it <margin>B</margin> like a container—whether these be smaller genera or individual species—so that they all coincide in a single nature. From all of these, the entire substance of the **intelligible world**, which we call **Being**, is composed. If this is the case, it follows that these are not only genera, but also exist as the "principles" of Being itself. They are "genera" because there are other narrower genera beneath them, followed by species and individuals; <margin>C</margin> they are "principles" because Being is made of many parts, and the whole exists because of them. 

If, however, there were many parts from which a whole was composed, and these parts did not have other things beneath them, they would be principles but certainly not genera. This is just as if someone were to compose the sensible world from the four elements—fire and the rest. These would be principles of the world, but never "genera," unless one used the term "genus" in a loose or ambiguous sense. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, when we say that these principles are also genera, we must ask: do we mean that each of them is mixed together with all that follows it, creating a total mixture of everything? In that case, each thing would exist there only in **potentiality** <note>original: "potentia" / "dynamis"</note> and not in **actuality** <note>original: "actu" / "energeia"</note>, and nothing would be "pure." Perhaps we will set aside the genera but mix the individuals? <margin>E</margin> But what then will the genera be in themselves? Will they remain pure in themselves? And will the mixed elements not destroy them? How could that be? We shall discuss these things later. For now, since we have admitted that there are certain genera which are also the principles of essence—and principles in a different way through various compositions—we must first state in what sense we call them "genera."

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For it is ridiculous to place being under the same heading as non-being. It is as if one were to place Socrates and his image in the same category. To divide them is to set them apart, saying that this one is being, while that one is not—having pointed out that the other is truly being. By adding "always" to being (since such a thing does not exist in mere opinion), it is shown to never be false. <margin>B</margin> We shall later examine the nature of that which is positioned as "being" in nature, and what we have to say about generation, things that become, and the sensible world.

---

Since we say it is not one, will we perhaps seek to discover how being is either infinite or a plurality, unless we mean a "one-many," a varied thing containing the many in one? It is necessary for this being to either be one in genus (its species being the individual beings), or for there to be several genera under which all things fall. Or perhaps there are several genera, none subordinate to the others, but each encompassing those things beneath it <margin>B</margin>—whether these be other smaller genera or species—and thus, through a chain of causes, all coming together into one nature. From these, the whole composition of the intelligible world, which we call Being, is formed. If so, these are not only genera, but they also function as principles for being. They are genera because beneath them are other smaller things, then species, and finally the individuals. They are principles because Being is made of many, and the whole exists from these. <margin>C</margin> But if there were many parts, and from them the whole was made, but they did not have anything beneath them, they would be principles but not genera—as if one were to make the sensible world from the four elements, fire and so on. These would be principles, but not genera, unless one used the word "genus" equivocally. Thus, if we call them both "principles" <margin>D</margin> and "genera," we must ask: do we take the genera and mix them together with the things beneath them to produce the whole? If we make a mixture of everything, then each thing will be there in potentiality but not in actuality. Or will each thing remain pure? Perhaps we will leave the genera alone but mix the individuals. What then will the genera be in themselves? Will they be pure and independent? <margin>E</margin> And will those things that are mixed not destroy them? How? These things are for later. But now, since we have agreed that there are certain genera, and that they are principles of essence—principles in one way and compositions in another—we must first say in what sense we call them genera...

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes "True Being" from "Becoming" and "Non-being," arguing that Being is a "One-Many" composed of primary Genera. He explores the relationship between "Genera" (categories containing species) and "Principles" (the fundamental building blocks of reality).</summary>

<keywords>Being, Non-being, Genera, Principles, Intelligible World, Potentiality vs Actuality, One and Many, Plotinus, Plato's Sophist</keywords>

--- Page 632 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus's investigation into the "Genera of Being" (VI.2.3). The text transitions from questioning how "Being" relates to its sub-categories to an inquiry into the "Five Greatest Genera" (Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference). Plotinus is arguing that these primary categories cannot be reduced to a single genus because they are the foundation of all reality.</meta>

# SECOND BOOK.

<margin>A</margin> And how shall we distinguish them from one another, and not bring them under a single heading, as if they had been driven together by chance? And if the many things were not to exist, how could it be more rational to bring them under one? If there were something like "Living Being" <note>original Greek: "ζῶ[ον]"</note> which was Being—then all things would be it, and then individuals would follow in order, with nothing outside them, so that perhaps all things would be Being. But since such a position is a destruction of the things themselves <note>The argument is that if everything is simply "Being," then the specific characteristics of individual things are lost.</note>, then what are necessary are species—to have species—altogether many under one. But if all things are one, let no other thing be found outside that specific being. For how could the One become many, just as species are produced, unless there were something else besides itself? And what if the many are not parts into which it is fragmented? But the fragmenting force is also something else. If it fragments itself, then the division itself will be divided. These matters must be considered, and whether the many shall be that which is becoming, or how each thing taken as any sort of thing is to be called Being or Essence <term>Essence; Ousia</term>. But if someone calls it Being, he will say it is so by accident. For example, if he calls "Whiteness" an essence, he speaks of it in the same way as he speaks of "what is white."

<margin>A</margin> We say, then, that there are MANY things, and they are many not by chance. Since they proceed from the One, and those things which are predicated of them belong to their being, it was necessary for each of those things to be a Being <note>original Greek: "ὄν"</note>. Being similar in kind to the other, it would exist as its own genus, which is not outside the genera being produced. It is the cause, yet it is not predicated of the others in their "whatness" <term>whatness; quidditas/ti esti</term>. Or perhaps it remains outside as the One, so as not to be counted among the genera. If the other things are equally among themselves as something that already exists, how can that which was mentioned be remembered? Or are we seeking the Beings <note>original Greek: "τὰ ὄντα"</note> upon which things are imposed? Then there will be the question of what is "counted along with them," and one might wonder how it is counted along with the things that come from it. If they are under one genus, the others are indeed what they are; or if it is counted with those of which it is the cause, as if it were the genus itself and the others were in sequence following it, or if it is predicated of them as a genus while being something else besides them, it is necessary that they themselves come to be under it. Just as if we must consider "walking" as an act, and treat "walking" as a genus. And if I see nothing else besides it as a causal genus, I see the genera that come after it, and the act of walking itself among those things that exist.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And how are we to divide [these things] among themselves, without reducing them to one, as if by some chance they met and formed a single thing? For it would be much more probable that they would be reduced to one. Indeed, if it were possible for all things to be species of Being itself, and if each individual thing followed after these in sequence, and nothing were left outside, then perhaps it would be permitted to achieve this. But since such a position fundamentally destroys these very things—for species would no longer be species, nor would many be gathered into one—on the contrary,
<margin>B</margin> all things would be entirely one, so that there would not be one thing outside another, where all things belong to that One. For in what way did the One come forth and become many, even producing species, unless there were something else besides it? For it does not exist as many in itself, unless one partitions it like a physical magnitude; but in that case, there will also be something else that divides it. But if it is divided either by itself or by another, it will have already been divided—or be indivisible—even before it is divided. For this reason and for other causes, we must be careful not to establish a single genus, especially since it is impossible that whatever you perceive can be called either Being or Essence. For it happens everywhere that a thing cannot be called Being or Essence except by "accident" <term>accident; per accidens</term>—as if someone were to call a substance "white." For in that case, he does not speak of the thing itself, which is white by its own nature, but of that which happens to be white.

---

> *Many things that are in the First Being, since they do not occur there by chance, are necessarily from the One. Again, since there are primary genera of things there, diverse among themselves, they cannot be reduced within to a single genus that is predicated of them as a genus. Rather, they are reduced to a One which is not so much a cause as a nature; a nature which is not constituted from them, but rather constitutes them, propagating itself within them and being preserved entirely in each differing thing. This single nature, because it is a "One" not in a simple sense, but as a "One Being," we trace back to the "Simply One" <note>The Neoplatonic "One," which is above Being itself.</note> itself as its cause.*

->Chapter III.<-

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, we say there are PLURALITIES, and they are not plural by some stroke of fortune. Do they not then come from the One? Certainly. And if they depend upon the One, they do not depend on a "one" that is predicated of them in their very being; therefore, nothing prevents each thing, though it is not identical in form with another, from existing separately as its own genus. Is this One, then, which exists as a cause outside the emerging genera, not predicated of the others in their essence? Perhaps it is indeed outside; for the One itself stands above, as it is not numbered among the genera at all. For through it, other things exist, which are numbered and distinguished equally among themselves so as to be genera. Indeed, in what way is that [the One] not numbered together with them? But truly, we are now seeking the Beings <term>Beings; Entia</term>, not that which stands above. Let this be settled then. But what shall we say of that which *is* numbered with them? Concerning which, surely, someone will marvel: by what condition is it numbered together with its own effects? But if those higher things and other things were numbered together under a single genus, it would be an error. But if it is numbered together with those things of which it is the cause, as if it were a certain genus itself, and the rest follow from it in sequence, and those that follow are different from it—neither predicated of them as a genus, nor spoken of them in any other way—it is necessary that its progression from this point be considered as being under a genus. And unless there were something higher than "walking," as a genus of walking itself, there would still be some things under it, and walking itself would exist as a genus in the order of things.

<summary>Plotinus explores the relationship between the One and the "Many" (the primary Genera of Being), arguing that Being cannot be a single genus because it does not apply to its subdivisions in a uniform way. He suggests that while all things derive from the One, the primary categories of reality exist as distinct, irreducible genera.</summary>

<keywords>Being, One and the Many, Genus, Essence, Species, Accident, Plotinus, Metaphysics, Participation, Categories</keywords>

--- Page 633 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Genera of Being" from the previous page. Plotinus is moving from a general discussion of whether Being is a single genus to a more specific inquiry: how plurality (the "many") can exist within a fundamental Unity (the "One"). This is a central problem in Neoplatonism—how a perfect, simple source produces a complex world.</meta>

<page-num>598</page-num>
# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> Perhaps, however, we should not say that the One is the cause of all the others, but rather that the others are like parts and elements of it, and that all things together are a single nature distributed by our own thoughts. Yet that One, because of its miraculous power <note>original Latin: "mirabilem potestatem"; Greek: "θαυμαστῆς δυνάμεως". Plotinus views the One not as a thing, but as a boundless "power" that overflows into existence.</note> over all things, appears as many and becomes many—as if it were moved, and a capacity for an expansive and multiplying nature brought it about that the One is no longer just one. We, however, presenting certain portions of it, name each one individually as a genus <margin>B</margin>, being ignorant, it seems, that we have not looked upon the whole at once. But by bringing them forth according to parts and individually, we gather them together again, clearly being unable to hold them for long in that way, as they are meanwhile hurrying back to themselves. For this reason, we release them back into the whole, and permit them to become one—or rather, to *be* one. But perhaps these matters will finally become clearer once those other things are known, and we have grasped how many genera there are. For in this way, it will also <margin>C</margin> be more clearly declared how they relate to one another. Since, in treating such matters, one ought not only to introduce negations into the discussion, but also to penetrate into the very notion and understanding of the things being discussed: come now, let us proceed in this way.

---

*Since the mind and soul are separated from matter and quality, and are therefore simple and indivisible, it is difficult to find how unity there has a distinct multitude within itself.* <margin>Chapter IV.</margin>

*In bodies, unity follows after the composition of many parts, and is, as it were, something added to them. Therefore, that unity is rightly dependent on a certain Unity that exists before the multitude, as a principle of generation. Something of this kind is the unity in the Mind and through the Mind—a multitude not made from many parts, but rather the fountain of the many. This, finally, proceeds from that Unity which permits no such multitude within itself.*

---

If we were eager to know what and of what kind it is to be "one" by the very nature of a body in this whole order of things, would we not first consider it in one of its parts? For example, in a stone, we might think that there is one thing that is the subject, another that is the magnitude, and another that is the quality (such as color), and similarly in any other body. And from there, we would immediately say that in the nature of the body, one thing is the substance <term>Substance; Ousia; the fundamental "stuff" or essence of a thing</term>, another is the quantity, and another the quality. All these things exist together, but by a certain reasoning they are <margin>B</margin> distributed into a triad, and it is established that these three are a single body. But if motion were also inherent in the substance, we would count this along with the others. These four would exist as one body, so that the body which is one is composed of and depends upon its own "one" nature derived from all of them. By almost the same reasoning, since the discourse is about intelligible substance <note>The "intelligible" world is the realm of pure thought and reality, contrasted with the "sensible" or physical world.</note> and about its genera and principles, it is fitting to consider such things by removing the "becoming" <margin>C</margin> that is inherent in bodies, and also by taking away the thinking that proceeds from the senses, and furthermore by setting aside physical masses. For in this way, that which is spoken of separately is also a certain intelligible substance, and is Being in a truer and more unified sense. In this, indeed, wonder arises: how that which is so "one" can be at the same time one and many. In bodies, certainly, it is conceded without controversy that the same thing is one and many at once. For the same body is also divided infinitely, and there, color is one thing, and something else—

<column-break/>

Perhaps, perhaps, we should not say that the One is the cause for the others, but that they are like parts of it and elements of it, and that all things are one nature divided by our conceptions. And it, through a miraculous power reaching into all things, appears as many and becomes many—as when it is moved, and the multifaceted character of its nature makes it not be one. We, bringing forward parts of it, speak of each as true, not knowing that we have not seen the whole together. But bringing them forward by parts, we join them together again, not being able to hold them for a long time as they hasten toward themselves. Therefore, we let them go again into the whole, and allow them not to become, but rather to be. But perhaps these things will be clearer when we have grasped how many the genera are; for the "how" will also be known. But since one speaking on these matters should not just speak in negations, but should also enter into the conception and understanding of what is said, this is how it must be done.

<column-break/>

If we wished to see the nature of the body—what kind of thing bodies are in this universe—you would divide each aspect of its nature: the subject underlying it (for example, in a stone), the quantity (its magnitude), and the quality (such as the color). And already these things are different from the body, as the body in its nature is one thing as substance, another as quantity, and another as quality. Even if all are together, the three are divided by reason, and the body would be these three. And if a motion were also present, innate to its substance, there would be four; and the body would be one, from the unity it has, and have the same nature throughout all. In the same way, since the discussion is about intelligible substance and the genera and principles there, one must remove everything relating to the body and to becoming, and the grasp of things through sensation, or magnitudes; and so too color, and those things that are distant from one another. Thus one must grasp a certain intelligible subsistence <term>Subsistence; Hypostasis; an underlying reality or distinct substance</term>, or that which is truly Being, or rather the One, in which there is the wonder of how it is truly one and many. For regarding bodies, it is granted that the same thing is one and many and even infinite; and the color is one thing, and another—

<summary>Plotinus explores the paradox of how the One (the ultimate source of reality) can be a single nature while appearing as many distinct categories or genera to our minds. He uses the analogy of a physical body—composed of substance, quantity, and quality—to explain how we can rationally distinguish parts within a unified whole.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, metaphysics, The One, plurality, substance, quantity, quality, intelligible realm, Neoplatonism, unity, generation</keywords>

--- Page 634 ---
<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "Genera of Being" (Ennead VI.2.5). Having established that Unity can contain plurality, he now examines the human soul as a case study: it is a single, indivisible thing, yet it contains the "many" blueprints (logoi) that give form to the complex physical body.</meta>

<page-num>599</page-num>
# BOOK TWO

...and our own [nature], as a living being might use it forever—finding one soul, indivisible and unmixed, [belonging to] an incorporeal motion. By the first impulse of thought, one might hope to find many things within it again; especially if one considers that in approaching it, one is dividing a living creature into body and soul. The body is clearly seen as multiform, composite, and varied. But the soul is found to be "light" <note>original Greek: "ἐλαφρὰν"; implying something subtle or non-material.</note> and delicate, providing a resting place from the journey when one arrives at this starting point. Let us then take this soul—since it is contained for us within the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" (kosmos noētos) is the realm of pure thought and Forms, as opposed to the "sensible world" of physical objects.</note>, just as the body is in the sensible world—and let us grasp how it is "many" within that unity. We must see how the "many" are there, not as a composite of parts, but as a single nature that is also many. For if this is grasped and made clear, the truth concerning the divine living beings within Being itself <note>Plotinus refers to the "Living Being itself," a Platonic concept representing the totality of all life-forms in their ideal, non-physical state.</note>, which we spoke of, will also be made clear.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...one thing is the shape, but another is the figure; for there these things are separated. But if someone accepts that the soul is a single thing, not separated by distance or size, and entirely simple, how will it appear? At the first glance of thought, how can one hope to find that the soul itself is, in turn, a multitude? This is especially difficult if one believes they have finally reached a state of simplicity—having divided the animal into body and soul, where the body is easily seen to be
<margin>B</margin> multiform, composite, and varied. But meanwhile, one hoped to find the soul as something most simple, and to rest there, as if having reached the end of the process. Therefore, since we have brought forward this soul as something drawn from the intelligible world—just as we previously introduced the body from the sensible world—let us now consider how that "one" is many, and how
<margin>C</margin> the "many" are one. Not "one" in the sense of being made *out of* many...

---

->*Since there is a vast multitude and diversity in a living body, and this is produced most directly by the generative soul, the soul—though it is more truly "one" than the body is—is nonetheless not without a certain multitude. Therefore, the generative soul is a certain single nature, a fullness of "formal reasons" <note>original Latin: "rationum formalium"; Greek: "λόγοι" (logoi). These are the formative principles or "blueprints" that organize matter into specific shapes and functions.</note>, which are its essential acts, just as rays are to an inner light. There is also a multitude within the very essence of the soul, for it does not possess being in a purely simple way, but carries with it a certain essential property of being an animal.*<-

### Chapter V.

<margin>A</margin> In the first place, we must consider how the bodies of animals and plants are structured: each of them is "many"—in colors, shapes, variety of size, types of parts, and in the fact that one part is different from another. Do all these things come from a "One"? Is it from something that is absolutely one, or from something that is "one" in its overall condition, or from something that is "more one" than that which
<margin>B</margin> proceeds from it? For the further one moves away from the One, the further one moves away from Being itself. Since the constitution of bodies comes from the One, but not directly from that which is "absolutely One" (otherwise it would not create such a distant multitude), it remains that this composition of bodies is created by a certain "unified multitude." That which makes bodies is the soul; is the soul, therefore,
<margin>C</margin> a kind of multitude? But what is the primary nature of multitude within the soul? Surely, it is the "seed-reasons" <note>original Latin: "seminariae rationes". These are the generative powers that allow a single soul to produce various physical parts, like a seed containing the potential for roots, leaves, and fruit.</note> of the things produced from it. Is the soul one thing, while the reasons are another? On the contrary, the soul itself is "Reason" <note>original: "Ratio" / "Logos"</note>, the head of all reasons. Its acts, according to its acting essence, are the reasons themselves. Its essence is the very power of these seed-reasons. In this way, this "one" is many.

<summary>Plotinus explores how the soul, despite being an indivisible and incorporeal unity, contains a "multitude" of formative principles (logoi) that allow it to organize the complex physical variety of the body. He argues that the soul is a "unified multitude," serving as the bridge between the absolute One and the diverse physical world.</summary>

<keywords>Soul, The One, Multitude, Seed-reasons, Intelligible World, Formal Principles, Genera of Being, Living Creatures</keywords>

--- Page 635 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 599, where Plotinus explores how the Soul, while remaining a single entity, contains a plurality of "logoi" or rational principles. He is now moving from the example of the Soul to the higher realm of the "Intelligible World" (the world of pure thought), examining how "Being" and "Life" are fundamentally unified.</meta>

<page-num>600</page-num>
# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI

<margin>A</margin>Certainly, this is not the case even with a stone: for the "being" of a stone is not "being" in a simple or general sense, but rather "being a stone." In the same way, the "being" of the soul involves both "being" and "being a soul." But is it perhaps that "being" is one thing, and the remainder which completes the soul’s essence is another? In this view, "being" provides the foundation, while a "difference" <note>original: "differentia"; in classical logic, a "difference" is the specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within a genus.</note> creates the soul. The soul, then, is indeed a certain kind of being—not in the way a "white man" is a combination of two things, but in the way a "man" is himself a being: purely a man. This is the same as saying that the soul does not possess what it has from outside its own essence. <margin>B</margin>

*Essence and life in the soul are indeed one in reality, but they differ in reason <note>original: "ratione"; meaning they are distinct in our logical definitions even if they are one in the thing itself.</note>: for life exists through essence; they are not many by a gathering of parts, but life differs from essence in its mode of being. That vital power does not come to the essence from the outside, but as if from the essence itself: therefore, in the very power of essence, a hidden life flourishes, and from that essence, life is unfolded more clearly in its activity.*

-> Chapter VI. <-

<margin>A</margin>**B**UT does the soul perhaps possess that quality from outside its essence, such that it exists partly according to "being" and partly according to "being of such a kind"? Truly, if it exists according to a "kind," and this "kind" comes from the outside, then the soul in its entirety would not be "Essence" <note>original: "essentia"; the fundamental nature of what a thing is.</note> by the same logic that it is a soul. Rather, it would be Essence only according to one part, and thus Essence would be a part of it, but not the whole. Furthermore, what would its "being" be without the other qualities—would it be like a stone? Or is it rather necessary that this "being" exists within Being itself, as a principle of light? All things that exist, exist as one; therefore, "life" also exists, and both "being" and "life" are simultaneously one in the Intellect <note>original: "intellectu"; referring to the 'Nous' or Divine Mind.</note>. <margin>B</margin> Is it then "one" in the sense of a single definition? Surely the subject is one, and it is "one" in such a way that it is also "two" or even "more"—as many as the primary things the soul is. Therefore, it is either Essence and Life, or it "has" life. But if it merely "has" life, it follows that the thing which has it is not life in itself, and it would seem that life is not within the Essence. But if the one does not merely possess the other, we must say both are one—or rather "one and many," as many as appear within that unity. <margin>C</margin> And it is one to itself, but many to others: truly it exists as one in itself, while meanwhile, as if by its own motion, it renders itself many. It is one, yet by looking at itself as a flowing stream, it makes itself many; just as Being itself seems unable to endure remaining solely one, since it is capable of being all things. Now, for the sake of contemplation, it appears as many so that it may understand. For if it appeared as only one, it would not yet seem to have understood, but would only still be that one thing.

*In the first Intellect, Being, Motion, and Rest are as three genera <note>original: "genera"; the most fundamental categories of reality.</note> of things: there, nature itself is one, differing only in definition.*

-> Chapter VII. <-

*Just as the great diversity of limbs in an animal declares that there is some differing "seminal reason" <note>original: "rationem seminalem"; the formative blueprints or 'seeds' of logic that dictate physical growth.</note> in the seed, so in the Exemplar of the world <note>The 'Exemplar' is the Ideal World or World of Forms that the physical world copies.</note>, Being and Life (that is, Motion) and Rest differ from one another in some way. This is proven to us by the fact that in the physical world, these three are most separated. However, there, Life is an internal, essential, and perpetual motion of Being itself—Being in its full maturity. Yet Being itself is essentially one, and in turn, it is Being in a vital way. Finally, since Rest is opposed to Motion, we gather that there, Rest is not Motion, nor is either of them entirely identical with Being.*

**W**HAT, then, are these things, and how many are seen within? Truly, since we have found both Essence and Life in the soul, and that Essence is common in the soul, and Life is also common; and since Life is again found in the Mind, surely by introducing the Mind and its Life, we shall establish one certain genus: namely, life itself.

<column-break/>

But nevertheless, even there in the case of the stone, "being" for the stone is "to be a stone," not simply "to be." So also here, "being" for the soul includes "being a soul" along with "being." Is "being" then one thing, and the rest which completes the essence of the soul another? And is one "Being," while the "difference" makes the soul? But that which is in the soul, insofar as it is a certain being, is not like a "white man," but as a "man" is a certain being. This is the same as saying it does not have what it has from outside its essence.

*The life and essence in the soul are one in subject, but different in definition <note>original: "λόγῳ"; logos, meaning word, reason, or definition.</note>. For "being" does not create life, but life follows the soul as a being. It is not something added from without, but the life of the essence, life from the essence itself; and the essence is made more manifest by the life...*

-> Chapter VI. <-

**B**UT does it perhaps have its "being" from the outside, and its "being in essence" not according to "being something," but according to being "of a certain quality"? But if it is according to a quality, and the quality is from the outside, then not everything that is a soul is Essence; rather, it is Being according to some part of itself, but the whole is not Essence. Then is its "being" something different from other things, like a stone? Or is it necessary for its "being" to be like a principle within Being? Rather, by being the One, it is all things; and by Being being the One, it is all things and Life, and both together: Being and Life. Is it then "one" as a single definition, or is the subject one while the others are two—as two or even more, as many as the primary things of the soul? Either it is Essence and Life, or it "has" life. But if it has it, the thing possessing it is not life in itself, so it would seem that life is not in the essence. If one does not possess the other, we must call the two things "one and many," as many as are manifested in the One. It is one in itself, but many in relation to other things. And while it is one, it will stay with itself, yet as a kind of motion, as if attempting to see itself in many ways, it makes itself many. For just as Being does not endure to be only one, being able to be all things, so by thought <note>original: "νοήσει"; noēsei, the act of the mind or intellect.</note> it becomes many, even while being one. For if it does not appear [as many], it does not yet seem to think, since it is already that [one] thing.

-> Chapter VII. <-

*In the first Mind <note>original: "πρώτῳ νῷ"; the First Intellect or Divine Mind.</note>, both Being, and Motion, and Rest are three existing genera. For there, nature is one in definition...*
*Just as in a living creature the difference of the limbs manifests that the rational principle in the seed is different, so also in the Exemplar of the world, Being and Life—that is, Motion—and Rest [differ]...*

**W**HAT then are these things, and how many are observed? Since we found in the soul both Essence and Life, and Essence is common, and again the soul's life is common, and Life is again in the Mind; by introducing the Mind and its life, they place some one common thing—all life, motion, and character—at the top.

<summary>Plotinus argues that in the soul and the higher Intellect, "Being" and "Life" are not separate additions but a unified essence that naturally expresses itself as a plurality. He introduces the "three genera"—Being, Motion, and Rest—as the fundamental components of the intelligible world.</summary>
<keywords>Soul, Essence, Life, Intellect, Being, Motion, Rest, Plotinus, Intelligible World, Genera of Being</keywords>

--- Page 636 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation from page 600 into the nature of the Intelligible World. Plotinus is now identifying the primary "categories" or "kinds" of existence that constitute true reality, moving from the unity of the soul to the multi-faceted unity of the Divine Mind.</meta>

# BOOK TWO.

There will be movement, possessing the primary life. Thus, two things must be established as real, even if one does not separate them in thought; yet if finding that which is "not-being" is impossible, or if they cannot be separated, look further. In other things, it is clear that "being" and "movement" (or life) are distinct, even if not in the sense of true being, but rather in the shadow and the namesake of being. For when we speak of the sensory world as an "image," we call it "being," and life is its most authoritative part; for "being" in the senses is a mere shadow, especially when that higher life is withdrawn from the living creature. Yet, one cannot separate "being" from living things as if they were mere imprints, for these are "standing" <note>original: "hestōta"; referring to things that have a fixed, stable existence</note> living beings. Truly, there are many other things; for movement is still under one category, and dependent on being. But after being was found, these were found within it—not as if in a physical subject, but as its very activity. From each of these, the other kinds arise. Or perhaps the two natures are one: this activity, or power. And if you separate them by taking one at a time, movement appears in being; being does not exist by "rest" alone, as if one thing could have the other while remaining separate. Rather, there is a mutual sharing of two natures, an interlacing into each other. A phantom of movement will appear, and from that, its nature; or rather, it attains perfection through being. The things of such a nature are not a reduction of the "standing" nature, for if being does not consist in a "standing still," it must be looked for elsewhere; for the things in the same thought are further removed from stability. The matters concerning movements are those below and likewise, so that they might have as many rational principles as possible. Let there be "rest" as well, if it is something other than movement, which some say is its opposite. It is clear in many ways that truly "being" will differ from the "same," or rather, it is the same as this movement. Why is "rest" the same as "being," while "movement" is not? For movement is a certain life and activity, both of essence and of being itself. But just as we separated movement from it, as being both the "same" and "different" from it, so we spoke of both; and in the same way, we shall treat "rest," and again separate it. We separate this in the mind, in so far as it will be another "kind," or if we should bring these together into the "same" and into "being," saying they differ in no way—neither movement nor rest. But after "being," we shall bring them together into the same, and movement and rest will be for us the—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Movement is common to all life: let us therefore establish essence and movement (which is the primary life) as two primary kinds <term>Genera<gloss>Greek: genē</gloss></term> <note>These are the "Great Kinds" of reality discussed in Plato's Sophist, which Plotinus adopts: Being, Movement, Rest, Sameness, and Difference.</note>. For even if they are one, it is still permitted for the intellect to separate them, which is the very act of discovery; they are so much one that perhaps it is not permitted to separate them. Look also at other things: it is manifest that movement or life is separate from being—and if it is less "true" in those things, it is at least present in the shadow of being, and in that which is called being equivocally. For in the image of a human, <margin>B</margin> many things are said to exist, especially that which is most important: life. So too in things perceived by the senses, "being" is found there, yet it is further removed: as it lacks that which is most vital in being, which is found in the principal form and exemplary life of things. Do we not then learn from this how it is possible to separate "being" from "living," and conversely, to separate "living" from "being" in a similar way? Of "being" itself there are many species, and there is a genus; movement, however, is not to be placed *under* being or *in* being, but <margin>C</margin> *alongside* being. Indeed, it is seen within being, yet it does not lie there as if in a subject <note>A "subject" here means a physical container or a base; Plotinus means movement is part of the very definition of being, not an accidental quality added to it.</note>; for it is the very act of being, and neither exists without the other except in thought. And yet, here are two natures in one: for being itself is not in potentiality, but in act. But if you take each separately, movement will still seem to be in being, and being in movement—just as in a single "being," each taken separately possesses the other. Nevertheless, thought dictates that they are two distinct things, and that each is a species, and each is <margin>D</margin> twofold. When movement appears around being, it does not distract from its nature; rather, because being is perfect, movement is present there, and such a nature is always in this very movement. If being continues in this order, certainly if one does not introduce "rest" or stability here, he will be more absurd than one who fails to include movement. For the notion of the intellect seems more suited to the stability of being, because being does not arise *from* movement. For there <note>In the realm of true Being.</note> that principle flourishes which is said to "always hold itself in the same way, according to the same things, and <margin>E</margin> by one reason." "Rest" is also a kind, in a way diverse from motion, since it can even be seen as its opposite. That it is also different from "being" can be clear from many things; and especially because if it were the same as being, it could no more be the same with being than movement is. For why should "rest" be the same as being, but movement not at all? Especially since movement is a certain life of being, an act, an essence, and of being itself. But <margin>F</margin> truly, just as we separated movement from being (as being both with it and yet not the same), and as we spoke of both as "two" and yet again as "one," by the same condition we may also segregate "rest" from being, and again not segregate it. That is, we separate it by the intellect insofar as it is arranged as another "kind" in the order of things. Otherwise, if we were to join "rest" and "being" entirely into one, saying they differ in no way; and if we similarly melted "being" and "movement" into one, then by the same logic we would join "rest" and "movement" into the same thing using "being" as the middle ground. From this it would happen that movement and rest would be entirely one and the same.

---

*Forms separated from matter are either minds themselves, or they exist in the mind; and there they exist not by accident, but according to an essence that is both intellectual and intelligible. Chapter VIII.*

Thus the first Mind conceives within itself five kinds of things: namely Being, Movement, Rest, the Same, and the Other. In this Mind...

<summary>Plotinus argues that Being, Movement, and Rest are distinct but inseparable categories of the Divine Mind, existing as "Great Kinds" that define true reality. He explains that while they can be distinguished by the intellect, they function together as the internal life and stability of Essence.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "Greatest Kinds" (genera) of reality—Being, Movement, Rest, Sameness, and Difference. Having previously established that Being and Movement are inseparable in the Divine Mind, he now explains how these five categories interact to form the structure of the Intelligible World.</meta>

[his] essence and his intelligence differ in a certain way; otherwise, in the order of things born from there, to the degree that they produced essence, intelligence would also proceed. In that realm, the act of understanding is like a primary movement that rests upon the essence—or the being itself—as if upon a hinge. I say it "rests" in two ways: for it leaped forth from there, and it leaped back there again. Being exists where it is essentially intelligence, and in turn, intelligence exists where it is intellectually being. Furthermore, intelligence arises from a certain inspiration—that is, from the firm vigor of the mind—and it tends toward a state of stability, which is the "Idea," the very limit of intelligence. Therefore, besides being, movement, and stability <note>original: "status"; referring to the Greek "stasis" or rest/constancy</note>, there is also "otherness" <note>original: "alteritas"; the principle that allows one thing to be different from another</note> in that realm, insofar as these things are distinguished from one another by some reason; and again there is "sameness" <note>original: "identitas"</note> insofar as they are all part of the same nature. Now, the four following categories are not properly called "species" <note>In traditional logic, a "species" is a sub-division, but Plotinus argues these are primary "genera" or roots of reality.</note>, but rather certain activities that accompany being itself. Finally, those five are called the "genera of beings" because whatever exists can be reduced to one of them, and all of them are found together in every single thing; to this extent, they can also be called the partial principles of things.

<margin>A</margin>But it is necessary to establish these three things, since the intellect understands each of them separately: but it understands and establishes them simultaneously, provided they have been understood. For since essence in our world is tied to matter, the existence of these material things is not the same as being in the intellect; otherwise, they would be separated from matter. But those things that are truly separate from matter, if they are understood, that very understanding is their actual being. Come now, contemplate the pure intellect, and look deeply into it, not with an external gaze, but fixing your intuition entirely inward. <margin>B</margin>Behold, you now perceive essence there as a vital power and a foundation; you see there an ever-watchful and unquenchable light. You observe, moreover, how the intellect both rests within itself and rightly discerns and distinguishes those things that exist together, while also contemplating a permanent life. You recognize an intelligence that does not act regarding the future, but rather focuses itself on the present—or rather, it already possesses the present and always holds it. <margin>C</margin>There, certainly, the "now" is present and eternal. There, the one who understands does not look at something external, but looks within himself. In the way that he understands, there is activity and movement; but in the way that he perceives himself, essence and being flourish. For he understands because he exists, and he understands himself as an existent being. And that very thing upon which he leans is being itself. <margin>D</margin>The activity directed toward himself is not the essence; rather, that upon which he leans and depends is judged to be being. It is not the act of looking itself, but rather the thing seen that must be called "being." This "being" has existence because that from which it hangs and toward which it tends is being. Since it is not merely a potentiality but exists in actuality, it joins those two into one again; it does not divide them, but makes itself that thing, and in turn, that thing becomes itself. Now, being itself is the firmest of all things, in which all other things are founded; and what it possesses is not foreign, but something it holds from itself and within itself. <margin>E</margin>It is also the point where intelligence reaches its limit—a stability that does not just begin, and from which it breaks out—a stability that does not just erupt. For it is not movement born from movement, nor movement toward movement. Furthermore, the "Idea" consists in stability <note>original: "status"</note>, since it is the goal of the intellect, while the intellect itself is movement. Therefore, all things seem to be one: movement, stability, and those things that exist commonly throughout the whole, which are the "genera." Each subsequent thing is a type of being, a type of stability, and a type of movement. If someone contemplates these three in both—specifically while looking at the nature of being and intuiting being through that which is being within himself—he perceives the others similarly: movement in that realm through his own movement, and stability through his own stability. By matching these to those, and mixing them as if into a single blend, he does not divide them. But after making some distinction, he immediately stops, from which point his intuition rightly discerns being, stability, and movement—these three, and each one individually.

<margin>A</margin>But it is necessary to establish these three, if one is to understand each separately. At the same time, he understands and establishes them, if they are indeed understood. For those things whose being is with matter, their being is not in the intellect itself. But those things that are immaterial, if they are understood, this very thing is their being. See the pure <term>Nous</term> <note>The Divine Mind or Intellect</note>, and look into it intently, not with outside eyes, but as if fixing your vision upon it, either as something being itself, or as one sees the intellect, and as life <margin>B</margin>—thus also as a life that remains, and a thought that does not act toward the future, but toward the present—or rather, already possessing and already being always. And as one thinking in himself and not outside. If, therefore, there is the act of thinking, it is a certain activity and movement; but if there is "being," it is essence and existence. For being, he thinks, or he thinks himself as being, or that upon which he leans as being. For the activity directed toward himself is the <term>ousia</term> <note>Essence or Substance</note>. But that which is as it were <margin>C</margin> the thing seen, is being, not the act of seeing. But the act of seeing also has being, because it comes from and leads toward being. In actuality and not in potentiality, it joins the two again, or rather does not separate them, but makes itself that thing, and that thing itself. Being is the most stable of all things, and around it are the others; by having what it has, it is not something brought in from outside, but from itself. <margin>D</margin>In it is that where thought ends—a stability that did not just begin—and from which it started—a stability that did not just set out. For it would be movement from movement and into movement. But the <term>idea</term> is the stability of the intellect, while the <term>Nous</term> is its movement. So that all things—movement, stability, and the whole—are beings; each of the subsequent things is a certain being, a certain stability, and a certain movement. <margin>E</margin>At the same time, someone seeing these things, having become outside himself <note>original: "en apobolē"; a state of mystical shedding of the self</note> toward the side of nature, sees the other things by the being within himself, and by being itself: movement in that realm by the movement in himself, and stability by his stability. By fitting these to those, becoming together and as if mixing them in confusion, not distinguishing, but as if standing a little back and holding off and distinguishing, he would see and know either movement, these three, or each: being, or stability, or movement—these three or each one.

# BOOK SECOND.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, if someone contemplates these things in this way, does he not consider them to be diverse from one another in some manner, and discern them through "otherness" <note>original: "alteritate"; the principle of difference</note>? Does he not notice this very otherness within being? He would clearly be positing three things—Being, Motion, and Rest—and noting that each one is a unity. Then, seeing all these together as one, and directed toward the one, he gathers and observes them as the same, recognizing a "sameness" <note>original: "identitatem"</note> that has already been established—or rather, that already exists. Is it not necessary, then, to add these two—Sameness and Otherness—to those first three? <margin>B</margin> For this reason, it follows that for all things there are five "genera" <note>The "Greatest Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Otherness.</note>. These five then pass down their own characteristics to the things that follow them, which is why those subsequent things also turn out to be both the "same" and "diverse." For every subsequent thing is "the same" as some things and "different" from others.

People place "The Same" and "The Other" in the order of the genera when they are considered simply and without the additions we usually make when saying something is "the same as" or "different from" something else. Furthermore, these are the "primary genera" because we cannot predicate anything of them that defines what they essentially are. It is true we can predicate "being" of them, for they are beings, <margin>C</margin> but it is not predicated as a genus. For "being" is not predicated of "essence" as if essence were merely a specific type of being. Nor is it predicated of motion or rest in that way; for these are not merely "species" of being.

<column-break/>

->They are: for some beings are like its species, others like participants. They do not walk, nor are they prior to it.<-

### *The One itself, which is superior to Being, is not predicated of any of the genera or beings as a genus. Chapter IX.*

*Because of its utterly indivisible simplicity, the One admits no differences within itself; it allows for no divisions, additions, or compositions through which a "genus" is usually branched out into "species." Likewise, the "One" that is found within being cannot be predicated as a genus for that being, nor can it be predicated "univocally" <note>meaning with a single, identical meaning</note> like a Peripatetic <note>Aristotelian</note> genus. For in the order of these things, one thing is designated in one way and another in another; they are judged to be being and one in degrees of "more or less" or "prior and posterior." Finally, just as in the Moon, that which is on the upper side is simply light, while that which is below is likewise light but not the source, so too being depends on the One itself. Insofar as it naturally tends toward the One, being is rightly called "entirely one" or "unified." However, that which follows after this within being is "one-being" and "many" simultaneously. That first One, by its own absolute unity—since it is indivisible—is not a genus. But this second one, which follows it, does not introduce a new genus above those already mentioned.*

---

<margin>A</margin> That these are the primary genera can be asserted by someone through these arguments, and perhaps through others. But by what reasoning can it be proven that these are the *only* genera, and that there are no others? Why is "the One" not a genus? Why not "Quantity"? Why not "Quality"? Or "Relation" and the other categories that some people have listed? 

As far as "the One" is concerned, if we take it to mean that which is strictly One—to which nothing else is added, neither soul, nor intellect, nor anything else—<margin>B</margin> then it cannot be predicated of anything. Therefore, it will not be a genus. But if you take the "one" that is joined to "being" (which we call "one-being"), that is not the primary One. Furthermore, since the One never admits any differences within itself or toward itself, how could it produce species? Unless it generates species, it cannot be a genus. 

How, indeed, could you divide it? By dividing it, you would create "the many." <margin>C</margin> Thus, the One would end up becoming "many," and if it tried to be a genus, it would destroy itself. To this we add that if you were to divide it into species, you would have to add something else; otherwise, there would be no differences in the One, just as there are differences in essence. How could the mind admit such a thing? Likewise, wherever there is a difference...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the inquiry from the previous page regarding the "Greatest Kinds" of reality. Having established Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Otherness as the primary categories, Plotinus now investigates why "The One" (the Absolute) cannot be considered a genus or category alongside them.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> By positing two things, you destroy the One; for everywhere the addition of unity <note>original: "unitatis"</note> obscures what came before. If someone were to say that the "one" found in Being and the "one" found in Motion and the other categories is a common element, and if he were to reduce this "one" and Being into the same thing, just as he did not allow Being to exist as a genus of the others—because they would not exist as Being itself, but would be called "beings" in a different manner— <margin>B</margin> then in the same way, the One itself will not be a common element among them. Instead, one thing will be "one" in a primary sense, while another will be "one" in a different way.

However, if he should say that the One is not a genus of all things, but is something within itself just like the others—as if he wanted "Being" and "The One" to be the same—then since Being has already been numbered among the genera, he is now merely introducing a name. If he says that the One itself is something different, he is certainly describing a specific nature; and if he adds anything to it, he is bringing forth a "certain one" <note>A specific, limited instance of unity</note>. But if he adds nothing, he is again bringing forth that which is predicated of absolutely nothing at all. 

<margin>C</margin> If he introduces the One as something that goes along with Being, we shall respond that we have already stated that this does not exist as the "primary One" <note>The Absolute source of all</note>. Yet what prevents this from being the primary one, except of course that which is "altogether One"? For we call Being "being" after that source, and we affirm that it is "primary being." Perhaps it is forbidden to say otherwise because that which exists *above* Being <note>The One is "super-essential" or beyond existence in Neoplatonic thought</note> should not be called Being; otherwise, this "primary being" would not be judged as primary. Yet that which is placed above this "One" [of Being] exists as the One itself. 

Furthermore, if the One is separated from Being <margin>D</margin> by the intellect, it admits no differences. Therefore, if the One which is placed within Being is either a consequence of Being (and similarly of all things), it will certainly be posterior <note>Coming after in the order of reality</note>. But a genus ought to be prior. Or, if it occurs simultaneously with Being and the others, the answer remains that a genus ought not to be simultaneous. Or perhaps if it is prior, it will certainly be a kind of principle of that thing alone; but if it is the principle of that thing, it is not also its genus. And if it is not the genus of that thing, it is not the genus of the others either; otherwise, <margin>E</margin> it would be necessary for Being to also be the genus of all the rest. 

In every way, the "one" in Being seems to approach the Absolute One and, as it were, to run alongside Being. Since Being itself leans toward the One, it is "one being"; but that which comes after it is "being," which can also be "many." While the One remains one and refuses to be divided, it certainly does not allow itself to become a genus.

---
->*The One, taken simply in itself, is not predicated as a genus of anything—that is, neither of the genera nor of the Ideas. Chapter X.*<-
---

*For every genus and every Idea is in itself a "certain one," but it is necessarily a participant in a multitude. We are argued with, therefore, and it is by a vastly different reasoning that the first One and these other things are called "one." Multitude is predicated of the genera no less than the One. Furthermore, a genus admits variety within itself, which the One itself does not admit; for as much as it is simply One, it is not the "one of the genera." Now, "one" is present in all beings in common, but it does not exist as their genus for that reason—just as the unit <note>original: "unitas"</note> is not the genus of numbers, nor the point the genus of lines, nor the simple element the genus of composite things. Finally, if the "one" that joins with Essence <note>original: "essentia"</note> is considered without Being, it is not divided by any differences; rather, division happens by reason of Being and within Being. This [Being], therefore, remains the genus, whatever kind of genus it may be.*

<margin>A</margin> In what way, then, is each of those things which are proper to Being itself "one"? Perhaps because it is a "certain one" <note>original: "quiddam unum"</note>, and not the "One itself." For that which is "a certain one" is already many; but each species <note>The Greek "eidos" or Form</note> is "one" only equivocally. For a species is a multitude, as is everything here, like an army or a choir. Therefore, the "One from there" <note>The transcendental One</note> is not in these things, and thus the One is not a common element. Nor can the One itself be considered by means of Being itself, nor by those things which are properly "something,"

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Absolute One cannot be a "genus" (a general category) because it is prior to all things and lacks the internal division or "multitude" that defines a category. He distinguishes between the transcendental "One itself" and the "one" that accompanies being and specific forms.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into whether "The One" (the Absolute source) can be categorized as a "genus" (a general class or category) like Being, Motion, or Rest. The previous page established that if the One is the source of all, it cannot simply be one among many categories.</meta>

### BOOK TWO

As for that which is simply "the One" itself, it is therefore not a **genus**. This is because every genus is defined such that while it is predicated of its members, its opposites are not likewise predicated. However, in the case of the whole of universal Being, wherever we affirm "one," we also find that its opposites can be affirmed. Therefore, whatever is affirmed as "one" in the sense of a genus would have to be judged as something other than a genus. Consequently, it cannot truly be spoken of as a genus even in relation to the **primary genera** <note>The five "Greatest Kinds" from Plato's *Sophist*: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Otherness.</note>.

<margin>A</margin> Since a "one being" is no more "one" than it is "many," and since none of the other genera are "one" in a way that excludes them from being "many," it follows that it is not predicated of those later things which are entirely "many." In short, no genus as a whole is strictly "one." Therefore, if the One were a genus, it would immediately cease to be the One. For the One itself is not a **number**, but it would necessarily become a number if it were a genus.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, it would become a "certain one" within a number. That is, if it were "one" by genus, it would not be the "principally One" <note>The Absolute or First Principle in Neoplatonic thought.</note>.

<margin>C</margin> Moreover, just as in the case of numbers, where the "one" among them is not spoken of as a genus, but is said to be "present in" them without being their genus, so too if the One is present in beings, it does not follow that it is the genus of Being itself, or of other things, or of all things.

<margin>D</margin> Thus, just as that which is a "simple principle" <note>A foundational, undivided starting point.</note> can be the principle of the smallest simple thing without being its genus (otherwise, a simple thing would also be a non-simple thing), so must we speak regarding the One. Specifically, if it holds the place of a principle, it cannot be the genus of the things that follow it.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, it will not be the genus of Being, nor of other things. But if it were a genus at all, it would only be a genus of those things that are individually called "one"—as if someone thought the "one" should be separated from "essence." In that case, it would only be a genus of specific instances. Just as Being is not the genus of all things, but only of the **species** <note>Specific types or sub-categories.</note> that are individually called "beings," so too the One would be the genus of those species individually called "one."

<margin>F</margin> What, then, would be the difference between one thing and another insofar as they are "one," just as there is a difference between one being and another? If the One is divided simultaneously with Being and Essence, then Being exists as a genus both because it is divided and because it is seen as the same within many. Why then should the One not also exist as a genus, since it seems to be present in as many things as Essence and is divided equally?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But surely it is not necessary that if something is present in many things, it must be a genus, either of the things in which it is present or of others. Nor is it required that if something is common, it must also be a genus. Consider a **point** <note>A geometric point, having no parts.</note> which is present in lines; it is not the genus of those lines, nor of anything else. Indeed, as we said, the "one" in numbers is not the genus of those numbers or of anything else.

<margin>B</margin> For it is necessary that what is common and "one in many," if it is to be a genus, must admit its own **differences** <note>Specific characteristics that distinguish one species from another within the same genus.</note> and thus create species, being predicated in the sense of "what a thing is" (*quid est*). But what are the "differences" of the One itself? What kind of species does it produce?

<margin>C</margin> If it is argued that it produces the same species that correspond to Being, then the One would certainly be identical to Being. In that case, "One" would merely be a different name, and "Being" itself would be judged sufficient to describe the reality.

<margin>D</column-break>

<margin>E</column-break>

<margin>F</column-break>

For an army is no less a "being" than a house is, nor is a house less a "being" than a continuum <note>A single, unbroken physical object.</note>; yet an army is "less one" than a house. There is, however, the same ratio between the One and the Good, and insofar as...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the nature of "The One." While the previous page argued that the One cannot be a "genus" (a general category) like Being or Motion, this page explores the intimate link between Unity and "The Good," and how different things (from armies to souls) possess different degrees of unity.</meta>

### PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK VI

...whatever partakes of the One, to that extent it also partakes of the **Good**, and vice versa. It has been said elsewhere that the One is something superior to Being <note>original: "vnum esse aliud superius à quãm ens"</note>, and for this reason, things desire "well-being" even more than mere "being." Indeed, the well-being of each individual thing consists in its union—that is, that the parts of the thing are united with one another, and the whole is united with its beginning and its end. Thus, those things that are more closely united are said to be "nearer" [to the source], while those less united are more distant.

<margin>A</margin> It is worth considering how the One exists within **Being** <term>Ens: The totality of everything that exists, which Plotinus distinguishes from the "One" which is the source of existence</term>, and in what way the so-called "partition" or "division" occurs—and indeed, what the nature of the division of the **genera** <term>Genera: The primary categories of reality, such as Being, Sameness, and Difference</term> is. Furthermore, we must ask whether both types of division are the same or different. First, then, we must think about how any thing at all is said to be "one" and how it exists as such; then we must see if we say the same regarding "One Being," and how it is spoken of in that context. Now, the "one" that is attributed to all things is not the same; for it does not behave the same way in things
<margin>B</margin> perceived by the senses as it does in those perceived only by the intellect. But even among sensible things, it does not exist in the same way. For "one" is not the same thing in a choir as it is in an army, a ship, or a house; nor is it the same in these as it is in a continuous object. Nevertheless, all these things imitate the same One—some from a distance, others more closely. Without a doubt, it is found more truly in the **Mind** <term>Mens: Also known as the Intellect or *Nous*, the highest level of reality below the One itself</term>.
<margin>C</margin> For the **Soul** is one; and the Mind is even more "one," just as Being is one. When we speak of each individual being, do we simultaneously call it "one"? And as it possesses "being," does it likewise possess "oneness"? Or is it rather that while this happens, it does not exist as "one" simply because it is a "being"? It is possible that something which is no less a "being" is nonetheless "less one." For an army or a choir is no less a "being" than a house is, and yet it is "less one."
<margin>D</margin> It appears, therefore, that whatever is "one" in each thing looks toward the **Good** itself. To the extent that a thing achieves the Good, to that extent it is "one"; and a thing's status as "more" or "less" depends on its unity. For every single thing does not wish simply to "be," but to be "with its good" <note>original: "esse cuiu bono"</note>. Because of this, things that are not [fully] one strive as much as they can to become one; and things established by nature desire this by their very nature, coming together into the same thing, clearly desiring to be united to themselves. Individual things do not rush to be apart from one another, but hurry toward each other and toward themselves. Indeed, all souls would choose to merge into one, provided their own essence was preserved in the meantime. And surely, the One reigns over both [the individual and the whole] in the universe.
<margin>E</margin> For the One is that upon which all things depend and toward which all things tend. For they begin from the One and hurry toward the One; for the Good of all things consists in this very thing. Thus, each thing exists in the order of reality. And once it exists, it would not continue to exist unless it hurried toward the One, nor can it restrain itself from rushing toward it.
<margin>F</margin> Those things guided by nature are thus disposed. Every **Art** <note>original: "Ars" (skill or craft)</note> also arranges each thing toward this same goal, as much as the art is able and as much as the individual things are capable of. But **Being** itself attains this most of all, for it is closest to the One. For this reason, other things are only called what they are called, such as "a man"; for when we say "that man is one," we are looking at two things [the man and the number]. But if we speak of "one" in any other way, we do so by clearly adding something. In Being itself, however, we call the whole thing "One Being," and we judge it as one, thereby demonstrating its greatest possible closeness to the Good.

<column-break/>

Whatever partakes of the One, to that extent it also partakes of the Good, and vice versa. It has been said that the One, being something different and superior to Being, exists more fully, and that "well-being" is desired by all beings. The well-being of each thing lies in its union <note>original: "ἐν τῇ ἑνώσει"</note>—that is, in its being in harmony with itself, and the whole being united with its beginning and its end. Those things that are closer [to the source] are said to be more united, and those further away are less so.

<margin>A</margin> We must examine how the One is in Being, and how the so-called "division" occurs—either of the whole or of the genera—and whether each is the same or different. Concerning, then, how any individual thing is said to be "one" and is so: do we speak similarly of the "One Being," or is it spoken of differently there? The "one" in all things is either the same, or it differs between sensible things and the harmony of the intelligible things.
<margin>B</margin> But it is not always the same even among sensible things in relation to each other. For "one" is not the same in a choir, or a phalanx <note>original: "φάλαγγι"</note>, or a ship and a house; in these latter it is by continuity. Nevertheless, all things happen to imitate the same thing; some from afar, others more closely to the truth, in the Mind. For the Soul is one, and even more so is that which is in the Mind;
<margin>C</margin> and in speaking of the things in it, we say that as it has being, so it has oneness. Or does this happen as an attribute, so that it does not exist according to being, but remains no less a "being" while being "less one"? For example, a house, or something in harmony. It seems then that in those cases, whenever one looks more toward the Good, to that extent it is "one"; and the "one" is more or less according to this. For each thing wishes to be not simply, but along with the Good. For this reason, that which is not "one" hastens to become "one" as much as it can. Things by nature, by that very nature, hasten toward the same point, wishing to be fully themselves. For each thing hastens away from being apart, and toward union with others.
<margin>D</margin> And all souls wish to be one, along with their own essence. From both sides there is the One: from which things come and toward which they go. And there, after the One, it hastens toward the One, in which the Good was provided for all. Nothing could exist or stand if it did not [turn] toward the whole
<margin>E</margin> from the One. As for things by nature and those in the arts, each art brings each thing toward the "one," as much as it can or as much as the image allows. Thus we might say that Being is most of all close to the need [for unity]. Hence, other things are either called [one] or are only called so, such as "a man." For when we say "one," we speak in relation to two. And if we say "one" in another way, we say it by adding it to the thing itself.
<margin>F</margin> But in the case of Being, we say the whole is [one] by its existence, or we deem it as "one," showing its exceedingly strong participation <note>original: "συνουσίαν" (communion or association)</note> with the Good. It becomes...

<meta>Catchword: Fu</meta>

Plotinus argues that everything, from physical structures like houses to the human soul, strives for "The One" because unity is the essence of the Good.</summary>
