Having previously discussed how unity is found in various entities, Plotinus now examines whether unity or "the Good" can be considered a "genus" (a general category) and why certain concepts like Motion and Rest are primary, while Quantity and Number are secondary.</meta>

# BOOK TWO

### PLOTINUS ON THE PRIMARY GENERA

<column-break/>

Thus, the One exists in itself as both beginning and end. Yet it does not do so in the same way, but rather differently; therefore, even in this One itself, there is a "prior" and a "posterior." What, then, is this "one" within it? Is it not considered in the same way across all parts and as something common? Perhaps in lines, the point is common, yet it is not the **genus** <term>Genus: In Platonic philosophy, a "genus" is a primary class or category that contains species. Plotinus is arguing that the "One" is too fundamental to be a mere category.</term> of lines. And in numbers, this "one" is perhaps common, yet it is not a genus. 
<margin>B</margin> For the One that exists in itself is not the same as the "one" found in unity <note>original: "vnitate", referring to the mathematical concept of the Monad</note>, or in duality, or in other numbers. Consequently, even in Being <term>Ens/Essentia: The realm of true reality and existence</term>, nothing prevents some things from being primary and others following, some being simple and others composite. But if the One were the same in all things that properly belong to Being—since no difference is present within it to create distinct species—then it logically cannot be a genus.

***
*The Good of even inanimate, discrete, and numbered things consists in a certain union; likewise, each of the five genera is one in itself, and is not divided among those things that participate in it. Chapter XII.*
***

<margin>A</margin> Let these matters stand as they are. But in what way is "the Good" present in numbers, in the sense that each number is a "one," even though numbers are inanimate? Perhaps this is a common trait even in other things that lack a soul. If anyone should object that such things have no share in the Good at all, we shall respond that we have begun to speak of beings insofar as each is a unity. If someone asks how a point can participate in the Good, we will ask in turn whether the point is being considered in itself or not. 
<margin>B</margin> If he accepts it as such, and concedes it is inanimate, we will say he is seeking the same thing we find in other such objects. But if the point is taken in relation to other things, such as in a circle, we will answer that what is "good" for the circle is also good for the point; the point "desires" this <note>The "desire" of a point is a metaphorical way of saying it has a natural orientation or mathematical necessity toward the center or the whole.</note> and tends toward it through the circle. But how are these things "genera"? Are they each divided? Or does the whole exist in each of those things of which it is the 
<margin>C</margin> genus? And how is it still "one"? Perhaps it is one as a genus, like a whole present in many. Is it then only in those things that participate in it? Perhaps not only in them, but also in itself. But perhaps this will be clearer in what follows.

***
*Motion, rest, identity, and difference are the primary genera of things along with Being, since they exist as the primary and most intimate acts of Being itself; number, however, resulted later from these, as did magnitude later still; therefore, these two are not primary genera. Chapter XIII.*
***

<margin>A</margin> We must now investigate why **Quantity** is not numbered among the primary genera, and likewise **Quality**. Certainly, Quantity is not a "primary" alongside the others, because those others exist simultaneously with Being. For **Motion** <note>original: "Motus" / "κίνησις"</note> exists together with Being, insofar as Being exists as an **activity** <term>Actus: The internal energy or "living-out" of a thing's nature.</term>, and Motion is its very act and its life. **Rest** <note>original: "Status" / "στάσις"</note> also coincides within the very essence of Being; or rather, the "to be" is present in them all—in those that are "different" and those that are the "same"—so that these 
<margin>B</margin> are all perceived together. But **Number** is posterior to them, and even posterior to itself; and the very fact that it is "posterior" is something it receives from what is "prior." Therefore, among the primary...

<sig>Ee 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: ...things</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explores why "the One" and "the Good" are not mere categories (genera) but fundamental principles found even in points and numbers. He argues that Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference are the primary pillars of reality (genera) because they are the immediate life of Being, whereas Quantity and Number are secondary developments.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation from the previous discussion on the "One" and the primary categories of being. Here, Plotinus moves into a critical examination of Quantity (specifically Number and Magnitude) and Quality, arguing why they do not hold the status of "primary genera" in the intelligible world.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

### PAGE 608

<margin>A</margin> ...they will by no means be counted among the primary things. We must ask, then, whether number itself is a genus at all. For magnitude <term>Magnitude: In this context, "magnitude" (Greek: *megethos*) refers to continuous quantity, like a line or a geometric shape, as opposed to "number," which is discrete quantity.</term> is even more secondary and composite than number. In magnitude, there is both number and the line, which are two distinct things; there is also the plane, and so there are three. If, therefore, continuous magnitude derives its very nature of being "so much" from number, and if number itself is not a genus, in what way can magnitude be a genus? Furthermore, there is a "prior" and a "posterior" even among magnitudes. 

<margin>B</margin> If the common element between them both [number and magnitude] is the fact that they are "quantities," we must consider what exactly this "quantity" is. Once we have found it, we must place it as a secondary genus, but by no means among the primary genera. And even if it were a genus but not among the primary ones, we must investigate into which of the primary genera it should most properly be reduced, or rather, to which of those numbers that relate to the primary things. 

<margin>C</margin> Perhaps it has been discovered that the nature of quantity signifies a certain "how much," measuring the quantity of each thing and being itself a certain quantity. But if the "quantity" common to number and magnitude exists, either number is primary and magnitude is derived from it, or number is involved in a certain mixture of motion and rest, while magnitude is a kind of motion, or at least depends on motion—insofar as motion proceeds into something indefinite, while rest, by halting what proceeds, produces unity <note>original Latin: "unitatem"; Greek: "μονάδα" (monad)</note>. 

<margin>D</margin> But concerning the generation of number and magnitude, or rather the essence of both and the understanding of them, it seems better to consider these in the following sections. For perhaps number is placed among the primary genera, while magnitude is placed among the composite and secondary ones. And while number belongs to stable things, magnitude is involved in motion. But we shall speak of these things in the following sections.

---

> *Quality is not among the primary rank of things: since quality is secondary to essence itself, and an accident to that which already exists. The primary genera, however, accompany that essence as its indivisible acts. Within the essences of natural things, there are certain natural and inward properties similar to qualities—such as heat in the essence of fire, or the natural faculties of man—which are indeed essential acts rather than qualities. But those things that do not arise from a specific essence, but happen to it from elsewhere—such as whiteness to a man—are true qualities and passions.* Chapter XIV.

---

<margin>A</margin> Why is Quality <term>Quality: One of Aristotle's categories (e.g., color, shape, skill). Plotinus argues that if a property is essential to a thing's nature, it isn't a "quality" in the accidental sense.</term> not among the primary genera? Surely because this too is secondary and is born after essence. It is necessary for the primary essence to possess these subsequent genera within itself, yet not be constituted by them, nor completed through them; otherwise, essence would be secondary to quality and quantity. In composite essences, which are made of many things and in which numbers and qualities exist, these qualities produce their diversity. 

<margin>B</margin> It happens that these are their qualities, and one may observe a certain community among them. In the primary genera, however, it is not fitting to create a division of things that are not simple and composite, but rather of simple things and those that complete essence—I do not mean a *particular* essence. For it is perhaps not absurd for a *particular* essence to be completed by a quality, provided that the essence exists before the quality, and that the "being such-and-such" <note>original: "tale aut tale"; Greek: "οἱονδὲ" (of such a kind)</note> happens to it from the outside. 

<margin>C</margin> But it is necessary for Essence itself to possess whatever it has as essential properties. Although in other cases we have judged those things that complete essence...

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...they would not be counted. We must ask whether Number is a genus at all. Magnitude is even more secondary and composite. For in it there is number and a line (two things) and a plane (three). If, then, continuous magnitude possesses its nature from number, quantity would thus be a genus for number; however, it would not hold the same standing among magnitudes, which have a "prior" and "posterior." 

<margin>Β</margin> If "quantity" is common to both, we must grasp what this is. Once found, it should be placed as a secondary genus, but not as a genus among the primary ones. Even if not among the primary, we must ask to which of the primary it can be traced, or to those things leading to the primary. 

<margin>C</margin> It is clear somehow that the nature of quantity indicates a "how much," and measures the "how much" of each thing, being itself a quantity. But if quantity is common to number and magnitude, either number is primary and magnitude is from it, or number exists in a mixture of motion and rest, while magnitude is a certain motion or from motion—motion proceeding into the indefinite, and rest, in its stopping, acting as the quantifying force and producing the monad <note>original Greek: "μονάδα", the mathematical unit or "the One" in a sequence</note>. 

<margin>D</margin> But concerning the generation of number and magnitude, or rather their essence and thought, we must consider this later. For perhaps number is among the primary genera, while magnitude is later among the composites; or number belongs to the standing things, while magnitude is in motion. But these things we say are for later.

---

<margin>Α</margin> Regarding Quality <note>original Greek: "ΠΕΡΙ δὲ τῆς οὐσίας" - Note: The Greek text here says "Essence/Substance," but the context and the Latin translation "Qualitas" confirm the discussion is about the category of Quality.</note>, why is it not among the primary? Because this too is secondary, and after essence. It is necessary for essence to have these following it as primary things, yet not to have essence derived from these, nor to be completed by these; otherwise essence would be secondary to quality and quantity. In composite essences, which are from many things, both numbers and qualities create their differences and are qualities; and a certain community will be seen in them. 

<margin>Β</margin> But in the primary genera, the division should not be made of the simple and composite, but of the simple and those things that complete essence, or a certain essence. For a certain essence to be completed even from a quality is perhaps not strange, if indeed this quality existed before that particular essence. 

<margin>C</margin> But the "being of such a kind" comes to it from the outside. But Essence itself must have what it has as essential, and as we said in other cases, those things that are completive of essence.

<summary>Plotinus examines the categories of Quantity and Quality, arguing that they are not primary genera of reality because they are composite or secondary to Essence. He suggests that while numbers might be fundamental, physical magnitude and accidental qualities (like a person's color) are derived properties rather than core building blocks of Being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "primary genera" (the basic categories of reality). On the previous page (608), he argued that quantity and magnitude are not primary. Here, he explores why qualities, motion, and identity are essential parts of "Being" itself, while things like "time" and "place" are merely secondary.</meta>

# SECOND BOOK.

<margin>A</margin> We say that "qualities" are named equivocally <note>original: ὁμωνύμως (*homōnymōs*). This means the same word is used for different things, like "bank" of a river vs. "bank" for money. Here, Plotinus means "quality" is used differently for essential traits vs. accidental ones.</note>. Those qualities that exist outside and after the essence are "qualities" in the strict sense; those within the essences are their activities; and those that follow after them are "affections" <note>original: πάθη (*pathē*), meaning things that happen to a substance or passive states.</note>. But now we say that those things that belong to a specific essence do not entirely complete that essence—rather, they are more like additions. For example, in a human being, as a human, they do not constitute the essence itself; for the essence exists from within before arriving at the specific difference <note>original: διαφορὰν (*diaphoran*). In logic, a "difference" is the trait that distinguishes one species from another, like "rationality" distinguishes humans from other animals.</note>, just as "animal" already exists before coming to the trait of "rational."

<margin>A</margin> How then do the four genera <note>The four categories Plotinus is testing: Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference.</note> complete Being, and what kind of Being do they produce? It has already been said that "Being" is first. Motion is not something other than Being, nor is Rest, nor Difference, nor Sameness; it is clear they are the same in that realm. Since motion possesses quality and "being-ness," it is evident. It should be stated more clearly: if motion is the activity of Being, and Being is activity—indeed, the primary things are all activities—then motion would not be an accident. Rather, being an activity, it belongs to that which truly exists in activity. Thus, it should be understood as completing Being, or rather, as Being itself. It does not happen later as an accident, nor does it fall into the category of "quality." They are all ordered together. For "being" does not exist first and then "move." <margin>B</margin> Nor should it be said that being exists first and then "rests." Rest there is not a passive state. Furthermore, Sameness and Difference are not "later" additions, because Being did not become "many" at a later time; rather, it was already "one-many." If it is many, there is Difference. If the many are one from the beginning, then Sameness is also there. These are sufficient for Essence. But when the soul intends to proceed to the lower things, then other categories arise which no longer constitute Essence, but rather "qualified essence" or "quantified essence." These become genera, but not primary ones.

<margin>A</margin> Relation <note>original: τὸ πρός τι (*to pros ti*), literally "the toward something."</note> is like a secondary growth; how could it be among the primary things? For relation is of one thing to another; it is not a state of itself, but always toward something else. Furthermore, "Where" and "When," which are usually numbered among the categories, are distant from that realm. For "Where" signifies one thing inside another, and therefore implies two things. A genus, however, must be a single thing, not a composition. There is no "place" there. We are now speaking of things that truly exist. We must consider if "Time" is there; perhaps it is not. If time is a measure—and not just a measure, but a measure of motion—it is a composite of two things and is "later" than motion. Therefore, it is not distributed equally where motion is.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> We say that things are called "qualities" equivocally: those that come from the outside after the essence are qualities; those that are inside the essences are their acts; and those that follow after those acts are already "affections" or passive states. Now we say that those things which relate to a specific essence do not entirely complete the essence itself. For they are not made as an addition to the essence for a man in the way that a man exists toward essence; rather, the essence is from above before the "difference" is reached, just as <margin>B</margin> "animal" already exists before one descends to the property of "rationality."

->*Just as fire is not first, followed by its light, heat, dryness, and lightness—but these four exist simultaneously with the essence of fire as companion properties of it existing in act—so internal motion, rest, identity, and alterity relate to Being itself.*<-
->Chapter XV.<-

<margin>A</margin> In what way, therefore, do the four genera complete the essence, not yet making it a "specific kind" of essence? For they do not even make it a particular essence. It has already been said that Being itself is first, and that Motion is not a different kind of being, nor is Rest, nor again Difference, nor Sameness; this is well established. Furthermore, it is perhaps manifest that this motion does not bring "quality" to that realm; if it were stated, it would become even more manifest. <margin>B</margin> For if motion is the act of essence, and being is act, and all things that are primary are acts, then motion is deservedly not an "accident" there. Rather, since it is the act of a being truly existing in act, it should certainly not be said to "complete" the essence, but to be the essence itself. Therefore, it did not arrive in the place of something posterior, nor in the stead of a quality, but was established in the order of a certain simultaneous companionship. For Being does not exist first and then move. <margin>C</margin> Nor should it be said that Being is first and afterwards stands still. For Rest is not an "affection" <note>Latin: *passio*. In this context, it means a state that is received or suffered, rather than an active power.</note> there. Moreover, Identity and Alterity (Sameness and Difference) are not posterior, since that Being did not become "many" later, but was already this very thing: a "one-many." If it is many, then Difference was there. And if from the beginning the many are one, Sameness is also there. These indeed suffice for the essence. When, however, there is to be a progress from there to lower things, then others arise, which no longer make Essence, but "essence-of-a-certain-quality" and "essence-of-a-certain-quantity," and such things become genera, but not primary ones.

->*Relation, place, where, when, time, position, habit, action together with passion are neither primary genera, nor exist by themselves. For they are adventitious [added from outside] and signify composition and lack. Chapter XVI.*<-

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, since Relation is like a secondary growth, in what way shall it be placed among the primary things? For relation is of one thing to another; it is not a habit toward itself, but always toward another. Furthermore, that which is usually numbered among the categories as "Where" and "When" is also removed from that realm: for "Where" seems to signify one thing in another, and therefore two things. But a genus ought not to be a certain composition, <margin>B</margin> but something single: and there is no "place" there. Now, however, our discourse is held concerning those things which are truly beings. It must be considered whether "Time" is there; indeed, time is not there. If time be a measure, and not measure simply, but of motion, then it is a certain two things and is a composite, and posterior to motion: and therefore it is not in the same place by equal distribution where motion is.

<summary>Plotinus defines the "Primary Genera" of the intelligible world—Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference—arguing they are internal to Essence rather than accidental qualities. He excludes categories like Time, Place, and Relation from this primary status, viewing them as secondary or derivative.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "primary genera" (the basic categories of reality). On the previous page, he argued that quantity and magnitude are not primary categories because they are derived from more fundamental principles. Here, he examines why "Acting," "Undergoing," "Having," and "The Good" do not qualify as primary genera of Being.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI

Moreover, what is said to "act" or "undergo" <note>original Latin: *facere atque pati*; Greek: *ποιεῖν καὶ πάσχειν*. These are two of Aristotle’s traditional ten categories, which Plotinus is here critiquing.</note> involves motion. Therefore, if acting and undergoing are present there [in the realm of true Being], since acting and undergoing are two distinct things, it is clear that neither will be a "simple" thing. Thus, neither can be a primary genus. Furthermore, even what they call "having" <note>The category of *Habitus* or possession.</note> includes two things within itself [the possessor and the possessed]. Likewise, "position" or "lying down" <note>The category of *Situs*.</note>, which they define as one thing being in another in a certain way, actually includes three components.

---

>*The Good is not among the primary genera. For if it signifies the First Good, it is more eminent than the genera; if it signifies a quality, it is secondary to them. Whatever things are truly called "good" are not so because of a single genus, for they possess their own nature, but because they come from the First Good and incline toward it. The good in the first being is the life and motion that tends toward the First Good. Chapter XVII.*

<margin>C</margin> Why are Beauty, the Good, the virtues, science, and Intellect <note>original Latin: *intellectus*; Greek: *νοῦς* (*nous*). This refers to the Divine Mind, the second level of reality below the One.</note> not also numbered among the primary genera in a similar way? To be sure, if "the Good" is taken as the First itself—what we usually call the very nature of the Good—nothing can truly be predicated of it. Although we speak of this nature as best we can, because we are unable to explain it otherwise, it certainly must not be called a genus of anything. For it is not predicated of any other things; otherwise, each of those things of which it was predicated would be that very thing [The Good] itself. But that Good is not within essence, but *above* essence <note>original: *super essentiam*; Greek: *ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας*. A foundational Neoplatonic belief that the Ultimate Source (The One) is beyond all definitions of "Being."</note>.

<margin>B</margin> If, however, the Good is taken here as a "quality," it must be said that quality is not among the primary things at all. What then? Is the very nature of Being not good? It is indeed good, but in a different way, and not in the same way as the First. It is good not as a quality, but because it has the Good within itself. But we have said that other genera [like Motion and Rest] consist within the nature of Being itself; and for this very reason—because each of them is common and seen in many things—it is reasonable to call them "genera." If, therefore, the Good is seen in every essence or part of Being, or at least in many parts, what prevents it from being a genus and placed in the order of the primary things? This seems to be prevented because the Good is not the "same" in all parts; rather, it is arranged in a first, second, third, and later order.

<margin>D</margin> For in that higher realm, anything is called "good" either because one thing comes from another (the later from the earlier), or because all things depend on the one source above them, participating in it differently according to their own nature. If someone wants to establish the Good as a genus, it will be "secondary"; for it is later than essence. To be "this something" is what it means for it to be good, even if it is always present with it. But the primary genera were said to belong to Being itself insofar as it is Being, contributing to its very essence. From here, one ascends to that which is above essence, since Being and Essence cannot exist without being "many"—it is necessary for these to have these enumerated genera within them, and to be "one-many."

<margin>E</margin> Let us not fear to assert that the "act" of Being, which by its nature tends toward the One itself, is its goodness. Thus, Being becomes "good-formed" <note>original Latin: *boniforme*; Greek: *ἀγαθοειδές*. Resembling or shaped by the Good.</note>. This good will certainly be the activity directed toward the Good itself. That activity is its life, and that life is "motion," which is already numbered as one among the primary genera.

---

>*Beauty, science, intellect, and virtue do not bring new genera, but are in some way reduced to the five already enumerated. Chapter XVIII.*

When we speak of Beauty, if we mean that first, supereminent Beauty itself, we shall give the same or very similar answers as we did for the Good.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Acting and undergoing are within motion; so that in that realm, undergoing and acting are two things. Likewise with undergoing, neither is simple. Furthermore, "having" is two things in a state; but "to be in a certain way" involves another thing, making three. <note>This column translates the Greek text, which mirrors the Latin discussion on the categories of action, passion, and habitus.</note>

<margin>Α</margin> BUT why are Beauty and the Good, and virtues, and sciences, and Intellect not also genera? As for the Good, if it is the First—which we call the nature of the Good, of which nothing is predicated, but we speak of it thus because we have no other way to signify it—it would be a genus of nothing. For it is not said of others; for if it were, each thing would be that thing. But that [First] is not Essence. If it were "good" as a quality, then "quality" as a whole is not among the first things. But what of the nature of the Good? Either the First is different, and that [intellectual Good] is like the first, and as if "upon the Good," not as a quality, but in itself. But we said the other genera are in Being. And if those are in all things, and a genus is seen in many, is the Good not seen in every part of essence?

<margin>C</margin> Either it is this way, or it is spread across the first things, either in all parts or in some. But it exists in a primary, secondary, and following way, or one thing next to another, the later next to the later. Everything would then be made from the One, but each participates differently according to its own nature.

<margin>D</margin> If anyone wants to call this a genus, it is "later," for it is later than essence—the "what-it-was-to-be" <note>term: *what-it-was-to-be* (Greek: *ti ēn einai*). The standard Aristotelian and Platonic term for the "essence" or "definition" of a thing.</note> of the Good, even if always present. But those others [the primary genera] belonged to Being insofar as it is Being, as certain "essences" of the essences. From there, one goes to what is beyond essence, since Being has essence, and it cannot be "not-many" but must necessarily have these enumerated genera and be many.

<margin>E</margin> For if the Good that is in Being is what we call the activity <note>original Greek: *energeia*.</note> of its very nature toward the One, and if that which is from there is "good-formed," then the Good will be the activity toward the Good; and perhaps this is Life itself, and this is either Motion or Intellection, which is one of the genera.

However, if what is "good" here is the "One in Being," its nature tending toward the One itself... [this repeats the conclusion that goodness is an activity or motion toward the source].

AS FOR Beauty, if it is not that first Beauty itself, we shall say the same and similar things.

<summary>Plotinus argues that "The Good" and "Beauty" are not separate categories (genera) of reality; the First Good is above all categories, while goodness within Being is simply the activity or "motion" of reality striving back toward its source.</summary>
<keywords>The One, Primary Genera, Being, Essence, The Good, Beauty, Motion, Intellect, Neoplatonism, Aristotle's Categories</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the "primary genera" (the basic categories of reality). On the previous page, he argued that quantity and magnitude are not primary categories because they are derived from more fundamental principles. Here, he examines why "Acting," "Undergoing," "Having," and "The Good" do not qualify as primary genera of Being.</meta>

# BOOK TWO

<margin>A</margin> ...in the discussions concerning the good. But if we consider the Idea of Beauty, we see it does not appear the same in all things. It also follows after the initial impression. If the Beautiful is nothing other than those things which are the Idea itself, then it resides within the Essence <note>original Greek: *ousia*; the fundamental nature of a thing.</note>. But if it is relative to us who behold it, it is a matter of being affected in a certain way. If this being affected is a movement <note>original Greek: *kinesis*</note> based on an activity <note>original Greek: *energeia*</note>, and if the activity directed toward those things is a movement, then knowledge <note>original Greek: *episteme*</note> will be a self-initiated movement. This is truly an activity, and not a mere habit <note>original Greek: *hexis*; a stable disposition or state of being</note>. Therefore, knowledge itself falls under the category of movement. Yet if one prefers, it could fall under stability, or even both. If it falls under both as a mixture, and if this mixture is something that comes later, then the Intellect <note>original Greek: *nous*</note> does not truly think. <margin>B</margin> And how can it be composed of all things if any of the primary genera are missing from them? Truly, it is not something that follows all things, but is already all beings. Being <note>original Greek: *on*</note> alone, when taken simply, is treated as a genus. <margin>C</margin> In souls, this is how it is: justice, temperance, and virtue in general are all certain activities of the Intellect. Consequently, they are not among the primary things, but come later, acting as genus and species.

*...indeed, temperance and virtue in general are all certain acts of the intellect. For this reason, they are not placed among the primary things, but are posterior in genus, and are designated as species.*

---

->*He raises many questions here; he defines almost nothing.*<-

### Chapter XIX.

Since these four <note>Plotinus typically identifies five primary genera: Being, Motion, Stability, Identity, and Alterity. He is here narrowing his focus to how they interact.</note> are the primary genera, is each one already something existing in itself? Are the things you divide <margin>φ</margin> not independent or separate from the others? Or will the genus contain within itself the differences <note>original Greek: *diaphoras*; the specific characteristics that distinguish one species from another within a genus</note> it has received? On one hand, beings exist, and differences exist. Or perhaps the differences belong to the Being itself. It will be affected and exist, for it is impossible for them to come from non-being. If the remaining three genera clearly arise from these and exist with them, they will be established and justified together, coming into existence at once. These things are always produced together—the "One-All" that is composed of everything. How then do other things remain after that which is composed of all? Or how do all things here become genera? What kind are they? How does movement create species of movement, or stability, and the others? We must investigate <margin>φ</margin> how to take care that we do not make each individual thing vanish within the whole. We must not view the genus as only a separate thing, seen in each individual, but as being both in each individual and in itself simultaneously. It exists as a mixture that is yet pure, and it should not be intertwined in such a way that it loses its own essence. We must consider these matters. Since we have said that each thing is a common element of all beings, and we place the "One" over all things as species and parts, we establish the cause as being the Intellect—the Intellect which is already said to be "posterior" <note>In the Neoplatonic hierarchy, the "One" is the first principle, and the "Intellect" (Nous) is the second, making it "posterior" or secondary to the absolute Unity.</note>. Indeed, we make this investigation useful for our inquiry; and by using it as a model, we shall cast light upon the knowledge of these things themselves.

> *The Divine Intellect relates to the Ideas just as it does to the propositions of its own geometry. For that Intellect, etc.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...regarding those things we have already answered about the good: but if the beautiful is understood as a certain splendor shining within the Idea, it will be objected that it is not the same in all things. Likewise, such a flash of light would be secondary. But if nothing other than the essence itself were offered as the beautiful, then it is already counted within that essence. However, if the beautiful is taken in relation to us who perceive it, because we are affected by a certain condition, it will be established that this very act of affecting us is a movement. And yet, <margin>B</margin> if the act is directed toward that [the Idea], it will similarly be a movement. Knowledge <note>original Latin: *scientia*</note> is also movement itself: since it is an affection of a being, it is not a habit, but an act. Therefore, knowledge itself will be similarly contained under movement. Or, if you wish, it may be placed under stability, or even under both; but if it is under both, it will be something mixed: and what is mixed arrives later. But the Intellect is Being itself understanding itself, and is itself composed of all things, not merely one thing from the genera. For the true Intellect is one Being <margin>C</margin> with all things, and is now all beings. But if Being is taken as something alone and "naked," it is assumed as a genus, and the Intellect is an element of it. Justice indeed, and temperance, and virtue in general, are all certain acts of the intellect. For this reason, they are not placed among the primary things, but are posterior in genus, and are designated as species.

---

->*He raises many questions here; he defines almost nothing.*<-

### Chapter XIX.

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to inquire, since these are the four primary genera, whether any of these genera procreates species, as if becoming divided within itself apart from the others. Perhaps it is not so, because it is necessary to receive differences from outside the genus; and while there are indeed differences of Being insofar as it is Being, the differences themselves are not that very thing. From where, then, will it have them? For it cannot be from those things which are non-beings. But if it is from beings, and there are only three remaining genera, it will clearly receive from these; and with these <margin>B</margin> joined together, it is simultaneously preserved and simultaneously produced. Truly, these things having been established together, they seem to have already completed that which is composed of all things. How, then, do others remain after that which is from all? And how do the genera, since they are all beings, create species? Likewise, how does movement produce species of motion, and stability similarly produce others? That which must be observed in the first place is that each thing is not confused within the species, nor <margin>C</margin> again is the genus merely a predicate, as if considered only in those species. Rather, it exists both in them simultaneously and in itself; it is mixed yet pure and not blended, lest by chance it relates to the essence in another way and loses itself. It is proper, therefore, to consider these things. Since we have said that the Intellect is what consists of all beings, and we have placed Being itself and Essence above all species and as if they were parts, but have not yet called it Intellect, we rightly think that that which already exists as Intellect is posterior. But <margin>D</margin> we have brought this forward as useful: for by using this very thing as a certain model <note>original Latin: *exemplari*</note>, we shall penetrate more effectively into the knowledge of those things we are treating.

<summary>Plotinus explores whether concepts like Beauty, Science, and Virtue qualify as primary categories of reality, concluding they are "secondary" activities of the Intellect. He also discusses how the primary genera (Being, Motion, etc.) combine to form the intelligible world, using an analogy between the Divine Mind and a geometric system.</summary>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEAD VI.

...from itself, this very thing which exists in itself in **actuality** <note>original: "in actu"; the state of being fully realized or active, rather than just a possibility.</note>, and it possesses the **Ideas** <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in the world of the Intellect.</note> in a twofold way: both in actuality, where all exist there together already established, and in **potentiality** <note>original: "in potentia"; the capacity to become or be distinguished, even if not currently active.</note>, where each is soon to be distinguished from the others. Therefore, in turn, each individual thing is in actuality what it is in its own specific property; but in potentiality, it is the whole itself. Furthermore, that which is superior there to the things that follow is like a genus and a cause. In the way that it is a genus, it is in potentiality; but in the way it is a cause, it is again in actuality, and so forth.

Let us then consider the **Intellect** <margin>A</margin> <note>original: "intellectum"; the Greek "Nous," representing the highest level of divine thought.</note> itself as being in such a state that it touches none of those things that are partial; it neither acts specifically upon any one thing, nor does it escape any understanding, but stands just as science does before the specific branches of science, or like a specific science that stands above the parts contained within it. Universal science is indeed none of those things that are partial, yet it is the power of all of them; each specific part is something in actuality, but it is also potentially the whole, just as the science that is universal <margin>B</margin> exists in a similar condition. Now, those things which are in a species are placed within that whole according to potentiality; and those things which are the species itself in actuality are the whole according to potentiality. For the universal is predicated of every universal part; yet it is necessary for the universal itself to consist within itself as whole and simple. Thus, it is right to say that the universal Intellect there is certainly above all things that exist individually in actuality, and above intellects of that kind; <margin>C</margin> while on the other hand, the individual intellects relate differently. These individuals, as those that are partial, are filled with all things, while the Intellect, existing for all, supplies something to each individual. It is their potentiality, containing them in its universals, and they in turn possess the common intellect in their own particulars—just as a specific branch of knowledge possesses the nature of Knowledge itself. Furthermore, the Great Intellect consists according to itself, and again the individuals exist in themselves, <margin>D</margin> and those that are partial are comprehended in that whole, and the whole itself is in turn within the particulars. Each exists both in themselves and again in another, and the whole exists in itself and again in them. Likewise, in that Intellect all things exist—in that Intellect, I say, existing in itself—and those things are there in potentiality, clearly within that which is simultaneously all in actuality. Yet each is also potentially separate. Again, they are in actuality what they are, but they are also potentially the whole. For insofar as they exist as the things they are called, <margin>E</margin> they are in actuality that which they are called; but insofar as they are in that genus, it is established that they are that thing in potentiality. Moreover, in the way that it is a genus, it is the potentiality of all the species that are under it, and is none of them in actuality, but all things are within it as if hidden and quiet. But in the way it is that which exists in actuality before the species, it is the act of those things that do not merely exist individually. It is certainly necessary, if they are to be in actuality as a species, that the act itself, depending on the whole, be the cause of this very species.

<column-break/>

LET US then assume that the one <note>The Intellect</note> must be as if touching the parts, and the other as acting upon anything at all, so that there may be no inquiry—just as science exists before the partial species, or as the science in a species exists above the parts. It is the power of all those things, and that [whole] is those things in their activities; or it is the power of all, and it is the same for the universal. Those in the species lie in the whole power; those which are in actuality in the species, by being parts of the whole, possess their own things as a part of the total. For this is the genus, and the indivisible things exist in the same being; and while the one is simply about all things, the others act upon the particulars. In another way, each of those in the part are filled from the same sources, while the whole provides to all the particulars, being their potentiality, and holds those within the universals. Those in turn, not possessing the particulars, possess the universal. Just as with science and Knowledge, the Great God <note>referring to the Intellect/Nous</note> exists according to himself, and each again exists in themselves, and they are completed as parts in the whole, and the whole is in the part. Each is by itself, and another is by itself, and that [whole] is in them. And in that one, things are such that, being in it, there is power in actuality, and all things are with it together. But the power of each is separate, and they are in actuality what they are, but the whole is the potentiality. And in the way they are called a genus, those things are in actuality what they are called; but in the way they are in the genus, they are those things in potentiality. For insofar as it is a genus, it is the power of all the species under it, and none of them are in actuality, but all its things are quiet; but insofar as it is before the species, it is the activity of the particulars. Thus they will be active, as if the activity from them becomes the cause in the species.

---

### The first Intellect, while in understanding itself it discerns all things among themselves, reveals number there; through its immense virtue it declares magnitude; through the clarity of its intelligence it opens up quality. Chapter XXI.

Qualities and figures are therefore evident there, but through "Alterity" <note>original: "alteritatem"; the principle of Being different or other, allowing for distinction.</note> comes the difference of all qualities and figures, and through "Identity" <note>original: "identitatem"; the principle of being the same, allowing for unity.</note> comes their communion. Since it contains all things through the vivid power of its nature, these are truly the first living intellectual essences. Deservedly, those things understood within are not fictions, but entirely living existences, intellectual in each part. Finally, as the movement of generation <note>The process of physical birth and growth.</note> relates to the generative nature, so does **argumentative reason** <note>original: "ratio argumentatrix"; discursive thought that moves step-by-step, unlike the instant intuition of the Divine Intellect.</note> relate to the Intellect. For the movement of generation strives to generate members little by little, all of which are simultaneously present in the power of the seed; similarly, reason through arguing seeks out beings, all of which are always simultaneously in the mind that never needs to argue. Just as perpetual seeking is a sign of one who does not possess it, so in the mind, seeking nothing is the proof of one who possesses all things.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the Intellect (the Divine Mind) and how it contains both the unity of the whole and the diversity of individual "Ideas" or "Forms." # SECOND BOOK.

<columns>
**A** In what way then does the Intellect <note>Greek: "Nous"; the divine, eternal Mind.</note> itself, while remaining one, produce the parts by its internal reason <note>Greek: "logos"; the formative principle or plan.</note>? This is the same as asking how those things said to follow sequentially are produced from those four primary categories <note>Likely referring to the primary genera of being: Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference.</note>. Come then, contemplate this in this great and unshakeable Mind—not a "talkative" mind, but one "full of mind" <note>A play on words in the Greek text: "poly-lalo" (talkative) versus "poly-no" (rich in thought).</note>. For it is a Mind that is all things, both in the whole and in the part. It is not merely a partial mind. **B** Behold, then, how all things are present within it. It possesses number entirely within those things it contemplates; it is both one and many. And by "many," I mean many powers, and indeed wonderful powers—not weak ones, but because they are pure, they are the greatest, like seals of reality or truly living powers <note>original: "dynameis"; the active capacities through which the Intellect operates.</note>, which are not held back by any limit. Therefore, they are infinite, and they are infinity itself, and greatness itself. **C** Looking upon this greatness, together with the beauty of its essence <note>original: "ousia"; true being or substance.</note> and its surrounding splendor and light, you see "Quality" already flourishing there. Furthermore, along with the continuity of its activity, you see Magnitude appearing to your sight, resting in a state of perfect stillness. Since there are "One" and "Two" there at the start, Magnitude appears as a third, and thus the "Whole" is complete. **D** Likewise, when Quantity <note>Greek: "poson"</note> and Quality <note>Greek: "poion"</note> are observed there, and both flow into one and become as if they were a single thing, you then rightly perceive Shape <note>Greek: "schema"</note>. For as one of these categories falls upon the other, it divides both Quantity and Quality, and so the differences of shapes and other qualities arise. Then, "Sameness" <note>Greek: "tautotes"</note> working there introduces equality, while "Difference" <note>Greek: "heterotes"</note> introduces inequality in both quantity and number, and indeed in magnitude. **E** From these arise circles and squares, and shapes made of unequal parts; likewise, numbers that are similar and dissimilar, odd and even. Since the intellectual life and activity there is never deficient in any part, it rightly leaves nothing out of itself among those things we now find in existence. It leaves out no "intellectual work," but contains all things by its own power. **F** It possesses these things as its own essence, in the same way that an Intellect possesses things. Now, an Intellect possesses through intellection <note>The act of thinking or intuitive understanding.</note>; and this intellection does not wander through steps or "discourse," but has already bypassed nothing of the reasons <note>Greek: "logoi"; the rational blueprints of things.</note>. Rather, it is like a single, massive, perfect Reason, containing all reasons, proceeding in order from its first principles—or rather, always being perfect, so that it is never true to say the Mind "wanders" through its thoughts. **G** Truly, whatever things one might perceive existing in nature through the use of reasoning <note>Greek: "logismos"; discursive, step-by-step logic.</note>, he will find those same things existing in the Intellect without the need for reasoning. Thus, one might think the Being itself, being an Intellect, created things by reasoning in this way, just as it happens with the formative reasons that produce animals. For just as the sharpest mind will reason as well as possible, so all things exist in the divine reasons, preceding all human reasoning. What then should we expect to find in those higher Forms, which precede both nature itself and all the reasons implanted in nature? For in those things where essence is nothing other than Intellect, and where neither "Being" nor "Intellect" is something brought in from the outside, the thing itself exists most easily and perfectly; for there, according to the Mind, all things are exactly as they wish to be, and that "Being" is exactly what the Intellect wills it to be.

<column-break/>

**A** In what way then does the Intellect <margin>A</margin> itself, while remaining one, produce the parts by its very reason? This is indeed the same as if one were to ask how those things said to follow in order are produced from those four principles. Come now, contemplate this in this great and truly inestimable Mind—not a "talkative" mind, but one "much-thinking," thinking many things: a mind which is indeed through all things, and a whole mind. Nor is it indeed a mind in part, **B** nor some specific mind. Contemplate, I say, in what way all things are present there from the Mind itself. It possesses number entirely in those things which it beholds, for it is one and many—"many," I say, meaning very many powers, and wonderful powers, in no part weak, but as they are pure, they are the greatest, flourishing unto the light, and truly being powers, not powerful only up to a certain limit: therefore they are infinite, and infinity itself, and depth of magnitude. **C** Beholding this greatness together with the beauty of essence, and its own splendor and light, which are in the mind, you perceive also "Quality" itself flourishing there. Furthermore, together with the continuity of action, Magnitude shines forth to your sight, situated in a most quiet seat. Since there is "one" and "two" there, and likewise "three," Magnitude occurs as a third, and similarly the "whole quantity." **D** Likewise, when Quantity <margin>D</margin> is inspected there, and Quality, and both flow into one, and are as if they become one, you rightly behold Shape there again; because the "Other" <note>The category of Difference or Alterity.</note> falls upon them from within, it divides both Quantity and Quality, and therefore the differences of shapes and other qualities arise. Then truly, "Sameness" <margin>E</margin> conspiring there introduces equality, but "Difference" introduces inequality in quantity, in number, and altogether in magnitude, **E** from which come circles and squares and shapes constituted from unequals: likewise numbers similar and dissimilar, and odd and even. For since the intellectual life and act is there, never failing in any part, it rightly leaves nothing outside itself of those things which we now find. It leaves out no "intellectual work," but contains all things by its power, **F** possessing these very things as an essence, and in that way in which an intellect may possess them. For an intellect possesses through intellection; and I say that intellection does not "run through" <note>Does not move from point A to point B in a sequence.</note>. Now indeed, nothing has been omitted of those things which are "Reasons," but it is like one Reason, huge, perfect, containing all reasons, starting indeed from its first principles in order, or rather always perfected already, so that it is never true there that the mind "runs through" thoughts. **G** Truly, whatever things anyone may perceive existing everywhere in nature by the use of argumentation <note>Latin: "argumentatione"; the process of logical deduction.</note>, he will find those same things consisting in the mind without argumentation, so much so that it is permitted to think that Being itself makes the mind argue in such a way: just as it happens in the reasons that procreate animals. For just as the sharpest intellect will argue as best as possible, so all things have themselves in the reasons, preceding all argumentation. What then must be thought to be in those superior forms, which precede both nature itself and all the reasons implanted in nature? For in those things where essence is nothing other than intellect, and neither Being nor Intellect is accidental to them, the thing itself very easily holds itself in the best way, since according to the mind all things are there at will, and that Being is what the Intellect also wills.
</columns>

<summary>Plotinus explores how the Divine Intellect (Nous) contains all the variety of the physical and mathematical world (shapes, numbers, qualities) within its unified essence. He argues that the Intellect does not need to "think through" problems like humans do, but possesses all knowledge and forms simultaneously and intuitively.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the Intellect and how the "Living Being" contains all forms and species. It transitions from discussing the qualities of the Divine Mind to how these ideas are perceived and manifested through different levels of reality—from the Divine Intellect down to the World Soul and human reason.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

<columns>
...and it exists and is therefore true and primary. For if it were to depend on another being, that other would instead be the intellect. Since, therefore, all figures appear in being itself, as well as every quality—for there is not merely a single quality there, nor could it be so where "Otherness" <note>original: "alteritas"; the principle of difference that allows for multiple distinct forms.</note> exists, but rather they are many, and yet they are one, for "Identity" <note>original: "identitas"; the principle of sameness that holds the Intellect together.</note> is also there—in which being itself is both one and many. This is so from the very beginning, so that in all species there is similarly one and many: different magnitudes, different figures, and different qualities. For it was neither possible nor divinely permitted for anything to be omitted there; for the universe there is perfect, otherwise it would be less than a universe. Since, I say, life converges there from every side, or rather exists simultaneously everywhere, surely all things have necessarily come forth as living and, in a sense, as "animals" <note>original: "animalia"; in the philosophical sense of "living beings" or "animated entities."</note>. For bodies were not lacking, since both matter and quality were present. And since all things have always been made and remain, and the thing itself is encompassed in eternity by its own being, and each individual thing is precisely what it is, yet they are simultaneously in the one—certainly this very conspiracy and constitution of all things existing in the one is the Intellect itself. Having the beings within itself, it is living, and an animal absolutely perfect through all things, and it is this very thing which is "Living." By showing itself to that which comes from it <note>Referring to the Soul or the human mind.</note> to be seen, and therefore having become an intelligible object to that observer, it allows itself to be rightly called such.

---

*The first essence is called the "Living-itself" and "Animal-itself" <note>original: "ipsum uiuens ipsumq́, animal"; referring to the Platonic "Ideal Living Creature" from the Timaeus.</note> from its own life; its act, reflected back upon itself, is called the Intellect, which in this living substance of its own inspects as many ideas as there are species to be fashioned in the world. Chapter XXII.*

Sensation indeed feels only within itself, but in the imagination it further perceives that it feels. Similarly, imagination imagines in itself; to reason, the thing imagined is perceived. Reason argues in itself; in the intellect, it notices that it is arguing. Our intellect understands in itself; in the divine, it notices its own understanding. But the divine possesses and finds all things in its own living essence. Moreover, this essence is uniform and "all-formed" at the same time; therefore, this world is understood as a whole in itself, and is generated as such. Indeed, forms are there, and they are immediately multiplied into the ultimate species. In the Soul of the World <note>original: "anima mundi"</note> born from it, they are multiplied more, and most of all in "generative nature," which is the last part of this soul. This Intellect calls all of them "ideas," but it names the general idea of souls as the "true Intellect," and also the Soul insofar as it is affected upwards or downwards; similarly, it deems our soul worthy of a triple name for a triple reason.

---

<margin>A</margin> PLATO, therefore, signified this in these words, although obscurely: the intellect, seeing the ideas existing as universals in the "Living-itself," beholds what kind and how many they are. Since even the soul, coming after the intellect, possesses as much as a soul can in itself, yet it looks upward to what is above it more clearly. And our intellect, similarly having things in itself, contemplates them more perfectly in that which is superior. For in itself it only inspects; but in the superior, it further perceives <margin>B</margin> that it inspects. Truly, this Intellect which we say contemplates the ideas, being in no way separated from its own superior, and existing from it (since from the One it becomes many), and having the nature of "Otherness" as its companion, becomes many from one. Since, therefore, it is one intellect and many, and necessarily many in this way, it acts as an intellect, and vice versa. It is absolutely not permitted to find any single thing there by number, such as what is called an "individual." For whatever you take there will occur as a species, for it is without matter. Wherefore Plato, involving this in obscure terms, says: "Essence is torn apart, being led down through infinites." For insofar as one proceeds as if from a genus into another species...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But if, because the first is also true, it were in another, it would belong to that other. Since all figures are carried within Being, and every quality as well—for let no one suppose that if there is one thing, there is only a single union of the "nature of the beast" <note>original: "θηρίου φύσεως"; Plotinus uses "beast" or "animal" to refer to the Living Being of the Timaeus.</note>, but it is one and many. From itself, it is both one and many, and was such from the beginning; so that in all forms, there is the one and the many, different magnitudes, or different figures, <margin>B</margin> and different qualities. For it was not even divinely permitted that anything be left out. The whole is perfect, or it would not be the whole. And it must be a living being <note>original: "ζῶον"</note>, or rather, all things are composed together; all things were necessarily living beings, and indeed bodies, their matter and qualities having come into being. Since all things are always becoming and remaining, and are encompassed in the being of eternity, each thing is separate in what it is—a living being—yet together they are one. Thus, of all things that are, the "weaving together" <note>original: "συμπλοκὴ"; a term used by Plato for the interweaving of Forms.</note> and composition is the Mind <note>original: "νόος"; the Intellect.</note> which has the beings in itself: a living being, both all-perfect and that which is the "Living-itself." By offering itself from itself to be seen, having become "intelligible" <note>original: "νοητὸν"</note> to that observer, it allows itself to be rightly described.

---

<margin>A</margin> And thus Plato hinted at this in those [writings], seeing the ideas existing in the "all-perfect Living Being," what kind they are and how many they are; since even the Soul after the Mind, insofar as it is soul, is in itself, yet it beholds more clearly in that which is before it. And our Mind, having [content] in that which is before it, beholds more clearly; for in itself it only beholds itself, but in that which is before it, it also beholds that it beholds. But this Mind <margin>B</margin> which we say beholds, not being separated from what is before it, being from it (since from the One it becomes many), and having the nature of "the Other" <note>original: "θατέρου"; the principle of Difference in Plato's Sophist.</note> innate within it, becomes many from one. Being one Mind and many, the many are also Mind; of such a kind as they are by necessity. Generally, it is not possible to take the "one" by number as an "atom" <note>original: "ἄτομον"; here meaning an indivisible individual.</note>; for whatever you take is a Form, without matter. Therefore Plato, hinting at this, says that "Essence is fragmented, even unto infinity." For insofar as one goes into another form, as if from a genus...

</columns>

Plotinus explores how different levels of consciousness—sensation, imagination, reason, and intellect—perceive reality and how the "one" essence is divided into many species.</summary>

### BOOK THREE

<columns>
Whenever [it is] infinite <note>original: "ἄπειρον"</note>. But how is that which has been generated bounded? Or is it just as the final forms <note>original: "ἔσχατα εἴδη"</note>, which are no longer divided, and are in another sense infinite? These things, at their furthest limits, are dismissed into the infinite. And they must be content if someone [ascribes] infinity to them, but being to the forms. Thus everything that is within it comes into number. By having the soul with them, as the soul is also in number. Until its furthest parts; and its furthest part is already total infinity. And if indeed a part [is] similar, it also has everything in itself, and the whole [is] in those parts of which it is the activity <note>original: "ἐνέργεια"</note>; neither is the soul a part of itself, but a part of a part. Rather, it is as an activity from it. Within it, the activities are things being activated, but as an issuance into another, it is the cause of the soul. Of the human soul, ours is as a genus, and the other souls as species. And of these activities, some are toward that which is above, while [the soul] itself is toward that which is below; some as powers according to reason, or as many as are already touching and shaping the below; all the rest of it either prevents being, and that which is called the downward-tending faith <note>original: "πίστις"</note> are its images <note>original: "ἰνδάλματά"</note>, not cut off. Or rather like things in mirrors, as long as the archetype is present; but having taken [form] outside, as that which is outside. Or until the first idols. The whole intelligible world <note>original: "νοητὸς κόσμος"</note> is perfect from all intelligible things. And just as this world, small as it is compared to that one, preserves an image of life as much as it is able—living in itself like a painting or a phantom in water—the things concerning opinion and drawings seem to you to be [real]; but the imitation is that in the water and [the] water, or both together, but the one is things formed by the other. Therefore, the images of the intelligibles are the likenesses of the creator, but of the things contained in the creator. Such as man, and every other animal. For the creator is also an animal, but each in a different way. And both consist in the intelligible [world].

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> The infinite <note>original: "infinitum"</note> has not yet occurred. For that which proceeds in this manner is bounded by the generated species: but the final species <note>original: "speciees verò postrema"</note>, which is not divided into further species, is more truly infinite. And this is what is said by Plato: it is necessary for one who has already come close to individual things to yield and surrender them to infinity. But these individuals, as far as they are in themselves, are certainly infinite: but as far as they are encompassed by the One, they come together into a certain number of species. <margin>B</margin> The Intellect <note>original: "Intellectus"; the Divine Mind</note> therefore possesses what comes after it: the soul itself. From this it follows that the soul also exists in certain numbers, up to its very last part. But this last part of the soul is already inwardly infinite: yet it exists as a part of such an intellect; although it possesses all things, and is itself all things, and those things which are parts of it exist as parts of it in actual operation <note>original: "actu"</note>. The soul is a part of a part, but depending upon it as an activity. For when <margin>C</margin> the Intellect acts within itself, these very acts are other intellects; but when it acts outside of itself, as it were, the soul comes into being. Consequently, when the soul acts as a genus or species, other souls exist as species, and of these there are two types of acts. Truly, the act directed toward that which is higher is the intellect: but the act inclined toward the lower reveals other powers that relate according to reason <note>original: "secundum rationem"</note>: finally, the last vigor touches and forms matter itself. <margin>D</margin> Yet that which is the lowest part of the soul does not prevent the rest of the universe from remaining in a higher rank. Perhaps indeed that which is called the "infinite" of the soul is its primary exemplar: but just like images appearing in mirrors, it exists as long as the primary exemplar stands outside. But it is worthwhile to consider how such a thing is said to be "outside." Truly, all the way to that which is the nearest reflection of the soul, the intelligible world <margin>E</margin> is entirely perfect, composed of all intelligible things; just as this world is a certain imitation of that one, insofar as it can preserve the image of that living being as a living thing. It is like a certain likeness appearing either in a painting or in water—namely, of that which is seen to exist above the water and the painting.

---

Therefore, the imitation in a painting or in water is not an imitation of both at once, but only of the one which was formed by the other. Thus, the image of the intelligible world possesses certain likenesses, not indeed of the creator himself, but rather of those things which are contained within the creator; among which number is both man and any other animal. For that which is the creator is indeed a living animal, as is this [world], but each in a different way: and both consist within the intelligible world.

# P L O T I N U S
## SIXTH ENNEAD
### BOOK III

->ON the genera of being, the third part.<-
->On the kinds of being.<-

*Just as in the intelligible world <note>The realm of pure thought and perfect forms, accessible only to the mind.</note>, so in this sensible world <note>The physical world we experience through our senses.</note> five genera of things must be established; yet they are not to be joined under one single genus. Nor should it be thought that these genera in the higher realms agree with those here in the same nature, although they correspond by a certain proportion. Nor should the substance of the intellectual soul be placed among these lower categories. Chapter I.*

---

WE HAVE already spoken about essence <note>original: "essentia"</note>, and what our primary view of it is, and how this view is consistent with the opinion of Plato. But next, we must consider the other nature: whether we ought to place the same genera <note>original: "genera" / "γένη"; the highest categories or "kinds" of things that exist.</note> here as we placed there, or whether we should set forth more categories here in addition to those, or perhaps others entirely? 
<margin>B</margin>Or are they altogether different here and there? Or perhaps some are the same here as there, while others should be arranged differently? However, when we place the same things both here and there, we must accept them as being used equivocally <note>original: "æquiuocè" / "ὁμωνυμίαν"; using the same word for things that are fundamentally different in nature.</note> and by analogy—that is, by a certain proportional similarity. This will become clearer once these things have been examined individually. Our starting point, then, shall be this: Since our discussion concerns sensible things, and every sensible thing is contained within this world, it is necessary for us first to inquire into the world, 
<margin>C</margin>dividing the nature of this world, and by that division, properly arranging the things of which it is composed according to their genera. It is just as if we were to take the voice, which is infinite in its variety, and divide it into a certain fixed number: namely, while we reduce what is the same among many instances into one group, then another, and another similarly, until we place each into a specific number, calling what is found in individual things a "species." 
<margin>D</margin>But regarding what we call a "genus" within those species: in the case of the voice, it would be quite easy to collect every species and all things occurring there into one, and to predicate of them all a "vocal element," a "letter," or simply "voice." But in these matters we are now investigating, it is impossible to predicate in the same way, as we have demonstrated regarding the higher realms. For this reason, we are compelled to seek out more genera, and to assign different ones to this universe than to that one. Since this universe is different from that one, it does not agree with it in a univocal <note>original: "vniuoca" / "συνώνυμον"; meaning the terms have the exact same definition in both cases.</note> way, but is equivocal and an image. Now, since there are different things here in this mixture and composition—for one thing is body, and another is soul—and since the universe is a living being, 

<column-break/>

WE HAVE spoken of essence as it appears to us, and how it may be in harmony with the opinion of Plato. Now we must examine 
<margin>B</margin>the other nature: whether the same genera are to be established as we established there, or whether we must place more here in addition to those, or entirely others, or some the same and others different, or indeed the same? We must take them as being used by analogy and equivocally <note>original: "ἀναλογίαν κ᾿ ὁμωνυμίαν"</note>. This will become clear starting from the things known to us from the beginning: since our discourse is about sensible things, and since every sensible thing is encompassed by this world, it would be necessary to make 
<margin>C</margin>divisions of its nature. And by dividing the things from which it is composed, we should arrange them according to their genera. Just as if we were dividing the voice, which is infinite, bringing it into measurements, putting that which is the same in many instances... then another and another again, until we have placed each of them into a number, calling the "species" <note>original: "εἶδος"</note> that which is over the individuals, and the "genus" that which is over the species. Now, in the case of the voice, each species and all those that appear might be brought back to one thing, to signify the same 
<margin>D</margin>element of voice. But in the things we are seeking, it is not possible to do this, as has been shown; therefore we must seek more genera. And for this universe, a different rule [is needed]. Since this is different from that, it is not univocal, but equivocal or an image. But since here in the mixture and in the composition, one part is body and the other soul, for the whole is a living being,
