<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "genera" or categories of being. While the previous discussion focused on the five genera of the Intelligible World (Being, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Otherness), Plotinus now turns to the Sensible World—the realm of physical matter and change—to see if the same categories apply here, or if this world requires its own unique set of classifications.</meta>

# THIRD BOOK

<margin>A</margin> But the nature of the Soul <term>Soul; original: "Ψυχῆς Φύσις"</term>, existing in that intelligible world, does not belong to the same order as that which is called "substance" here. Therefore, it must be set apart—and although it is a difficult task, it must nevertheless be separated from the present condition of things which we are currently examining. <margin>B</margin> It is as if someone, wishing to organize the citizens of a city into their various classes, honors, and trades, were to leave out the foreigners and temporary residents, keeping them separate. As for the passions <note>Refers to "pathē," the emotions or experiences the soul undergoes.</note> which happen to the soul either in connection with the body or because of the body, we will discuss how they are to be arranged only after we have debated those things which are properly contained within this physical world.

->*In the intelligible world he places true essence; but in this world, an apparent essence, which is really a flux rather than essence. Likewise, he refutes those who do not correctly arrange the genera here, though he has not yet arranged them himself. Chapter I.*<-

<margin>A</margin> AND first, we must contemplate what is called substance <term>Substance; original: "οὐσίας"</term>, granting that the nature of bodies is called substance only equivocally <note>original: "ὁμωνύμως"; used when two things share a name but have different fundamental natures, like a "real person" and a "painted person."</note>, or should not be called substance at all, because the definition fits something that is in flux. Instead, it should properly be called its own kind of "Becoming" <term>Becoming; original: "γένεσιν"</term>. Then, we must distinguish the characteristics of this becoming, both what is unique and what is common. We must gather bodies into one category, <margin>B</margin> § distinguishing the simple from the composite, and their passions, accidents, or consequences from one another. Or perhaps it might seem to some that one part is matter <note>original: "ὕλη"</note> and the other is form <note>original: "εἶδος"</note> imposed upon it, and each should be a genus separately; or perhaps both should be joined into one as "substance," using the name equivocally, or as "becoming." But what is common to both matter and form? <margin>C</margin> And how is matter a genus, or for what things? It is indeed a wonder what the difference of matter might be. Furthermore, in which category should we chiefly place that which is composed of both? If that which consists of both is "corporeal substance," yet neither of the two is a body on its own, how could they produce one thing? And in what way can the elements of a thing be established together with that thing at the same time? If anyone should say that one must begin with bodies, it remains just as if he had commanded that in the study of speech, one should start with syllables <note>Plotinus suggests that studying bodies before matter/form is like studying words before the letters that make them up.</note>. But what prevents us—if we are not permitted to divide according to the same nature—from dividing these things at least according to analogy and proportion? Thus, in place of "Being" itself existing in the higher world, we place matter here; and instead of the "Motion" of that higher Being, we place form here, which is like a certain life and perfection of matter. <margin>D</margin> Then, for that which is "Stability" and "Sameness" there, we have here a certain condition of matter that does not depart from itself. Indeed, in place of "Otherness" itself, we have the great diversity and unlikeness of these things. But truly, matter does not receive form as if it were its own life or act; rather, form enters from elsewhere. Form is more like a state of rest or stillness. Activity and motion are in the higher realm; but here, motion is something else, an accident. Finally, while that realm is defined, this one is indefinite. <margin>E</margin> "Sameness" and "Otherness" are one with themselves there, but here they are different. If the cause exists in later things as it does there...

<margin>\* primary matter, by participation in the higher world, becomes something else, either the same or different.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, the very nature of the soul, consisting in that intelligible world, does not fit into the same order as that which is named "essence" here: therefore it must be segregated. Clearly, although it is an arduous task, it must be separated from the present condition of things which we are currently treating: just as if someone wishing to arrange the citizens of a city by their groups, honors, and crafts, were to leave out the foreigners and newcomers who have been added, <margin>B</margin> keeping them separate. Regarding the passions of whatever kind that happen to the soul alongside the body or because of the body, we will then finally discuss how they are to be arranged, after we have disputed concerning those things which are properly contained in this world.

### THE BEGINNING <margin>A</margin>
Regarding that which is named essence <term>Essence or Substance; original: "essentia"</term>, it seems we must act and concede in the first place that this bodily nature is named essence equivocally, or should be named essence in no way at all, because the notion fits a thing in flux; but it should properly be called "becoming" <note>original: "generationem"</note>. Furthermore, it seems we must say that some parts of becoming are of one kind, and others are of another. And bodies indeed must be gathered into one, <margin>B</margin> both the simple and the composite, along with their accidents and consequences, also dividing these among themselves in the meantime. Or it might seem to someone that this part is matter: and that part is form within matter, and each is a genus separately, or both are to be reconciled into one, as if both were called essence or substance equivocally, or properly becoming. But what is common to both matter and form? <margin>C</margin> And how does matter stand as a genus, or for what things? For it is also a wonder what the difference of matter might be. Furthermore, in what category should we chiefly place that which is composed of both? If that which consists of both is "corporeal substance," and neither of the two is a body, in what way should these two be placed together with the composite in one and the same category? And in what way can the things that are elements of something be established together with it at the same time? If anyone should say that one must begin with bodies, the problem remains just as if he had commanded that in the study of speech, one should start with syllables. But what prevents us—if it is not permitted to divide according to the same nature—from dividing these things at least according to analogy and a certain proportion? Thus, in place of "Being" itself existing there, we place matter here; and instead of the "Motion" of that Being, we place form here, which is like a certain life and perfection of matter. Then, for that which is there "Stability" and "Sameness," we have here a certain condition of matter that does not depart from itself; indeed, in place of "Otherness" itself, we have the great diversity and unlikeness of these things, which overcomes their opposites. But truly, matter does not possess and receive form as if it were its own life or act; rather, form enters from elsewhere, not by chance. Form is rather its state and, as it were, rest. Activity and motion are there; but here, motion is something else, almost a rest. Finally, that higher realm is defined, but this one is infinite, because while there "Sameness" and "Otherness" exist as one, here "Otherness" is spoken of by participation, and in relation to something else, being something "same" and something "other." Nor is it here as it is there in those things that follow it...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of "substance" in the physical world. Plotinus is examining whether matter, form, and the combination of the two (the composite) all share the same defining characteristics of substance, specifically the trait of being a "subject" or foundation for other things—like colors or sizes—without being "in" anything else themselves.</meta>

# THIRD BOOK

<margin>A</margin> quality, motion—or perhaps these are understood through relation <term>Relation; original: "τὰ πρός τι"</term>, for that is a more inclusive category.

->*It is characteristic of a corporeal substance to be the foundation for accidents; yet it is not itself found within anything else as an accident. This property, unique to substance alone, is shared by three types: matter, form, and the composite. Chapter IV.*<-

<margin>A</margin> What, then, is the common element in these three, and what is it that makes them "substance"? Are all three to be considered foundations <term>Foundations; original: "ὑποβεβλημένα"</term> for other things? Matter is certainly a base and a seat; therefore it is the same as matter <note>referring to the underlying substrate of reality</note>, and accidents belong to the composite things, as if added after they are assembled: for example, quantity, quality, and motion. Perhaps, then, substance is that which is not "of another"? For example, "white" belongs to that which was once black; the "whitened" thing is something else, and the "armed" person is so by means of something else. <margin>B</margin> I am not speaking here of relation, but rather of being wood or grain or a father; being a father belongs to something else, as does knowledge, or that in which something exists. Place is the boundary of something else, and time measures something else. But fire is not "of another," nor is wood, as wood, "of another." Similarly, a human is not "of another." Whether we speak of Socrates, or the composite substance in general, or the form according to its essence, it is something else, and not a passion <note>An "accident" or a quality that a substance "undergoes" or experiences, like being hot or cold.</note>. For form is not a part of matter; it is a part of the bodies, and the "human" quality <margin>C</margin> and the human being are the same, while matter is a part of the whole. Or perhaps the whole is not "of another" in the way that "white" is said to be of another. <margin>* To another and to a different thing is its own * to another of which that is said.</margin> It exists entirely by itself, just as a part is something that completes a whole. Each of these is itself. Consider "undergoing" or "passion": we do not speak of it in that way, or if it is a part, it is called something within. <margin>D</margin> It is even itself by nature; in being what it is, it is not said of another. Being a subject <term>Subject; original: "ὑποκείμενον"</term> is common to matter, form, and the composite; but matter is a subject for form in one way, while form is a subject for passions in another, and the composite is a subject for matter. For form is the "perfection" or completion of matter, insofar as it is matter and insofar as it is potentiality. <margin>E</margin> Nor does the form itself exist "in" this; for when something comes together with another to make one thing, one is not "in" the other; rather, both matter and form together are the subject for something else—just as "human" and "a certain human" are subjects for passions, and provide the activity <term>Activity; original: "ἐνεργειᾶν"</term>, and from them come other things, and through them other things, both for undergoing and for acting.

The composite: or rather, the species of matter is not a subject. For the species <note>original: "species"; here used interchangeably with "form" or "eidos"</note> is the perfection of that which is matter, both as matter and as it is in potential. Nor again does the species exist within this: for where something together with another thing creates one single thing, the one will not be in the other there; but both matter and species together are subjects for another, just as a human and a certain human are subject to passions, and they precede actions and consequences. It will seem, therefore, that substance is that from which other things come, and because of which other things exist, and that which undergoes experience and from which action originates.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> quality, motion. Or these will perhaps be encompassed by relation. For relation encompasses more widely.

<margin>A</margin> WHAT then is common in those three: what is it that makes these to be essence or substance? Substance, I say, of the kind that can exist in internal things? Is each of these a substance because it is a certain foundation and a receiver of others? Truly, matter seems to be the foundation and seat of form, but form does not seem to be a seat in the same way: therefore <margin>B</margin> because of form it will not be in the category of substance. The composite also is surely a foundation and seat for many other things: and so form, together with matter, will be a subject for the composite, or rather for all things that follow the composite, such as quantity, quality, and motion. Unless perhaps that which is substance is so for this very reason: because that which it is called does not belong to another. For whiteness and blackness belong to another; namely, to the thing whitened or blackened. A double thing also <margin>C</margin> belongs to another: I do not mean at present that a half is a double, but that wood is double: and a father, insofar as he is a father, belongs to another. Likewise, knowledge belongs to that in which it exists. Again, place is the boundary of another. And time is the measure of another. But fire does not belong to another, nor wood, as wood, belong to another. Similarly, neither a human, nor Socrates, nor any composite substance at all. Yet neither is the form, which exists according to its essence, "of another," since it is the passion of nothing. For <margin>D</margin> form is not matter: yet it is a part of the composite: but the form of a human and the human are the same. Matter also is a part of the whole, and belongs to another insofar as it is the whole—not as if that other exists for which it is said to be: but whiteness is "of another" by its very definition. Therefore, that which exists "of another" and is spoken of differently is not a substance. Substance, then, is that which certainly exists as itself. Or <margin>E</margin> certainly if it is said to be a part of something, it completes the composite itself, while each or both exist for it; but toward the composite, it is said to be "of it" in another sense. Or certainly, by the reason that it is a part, it is spoken of in relation to something else: but because it exists according to its own nature, in that which it is, it is said to belong to no one. To be a subject, however, seems to be common both to matter, to form, and to the composite: but matter is a subject for form in one way, while form is a subject for passions in another, or indeed...

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK VI

> *It is the unique property of substance alone that it does not exist anywhere as if it were inside a subject, nor is it predicated of any subject as if it were something external. Likewise, when we give names to things in the incorporeal world that are specific to the types of physical bodies, we do not apply them according to the same logic and nature; rather, we attribute these names to them through comparison and similarity.*

->Chapter V.<-

<margin>A</margin> These points must be understood as referring to "substance" as it is spoken of here in the physical world. If, however, they also apply in some way to a higher substance <note>the divine or intellectual realm</note>, perhaps they agree through a certain analogy or a shared name used in different senses. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, that which is called "first" is so named in comparison to the things that follow it. For it is not named "first" in an absolute sense, but rather in relation to those things that are lowest; indeed, even those things that follow immediately are similarly called "first" in relation to the things that follow them in turn. Moreover, the term "subject" <term>Subject; original: "subiectum" / "ὑποκείμενον," meaning the underlying foundation or substrate</term> behaves differently here than it does there; it is even doubted whether it is proper to use the term there at all, and if it is, the way it "undergoes" or "receives" things is certainly different there than it is here. <margin>C</margin> It also seems to be a common feature of every substance not to be "in a subject"—provided we define "being in a subject" as something that is not a part of the thing it is in, and which does not combine with it to produce a single, unified result. For that which works together with something else to compose a substance cannot be "in it" as if in a subject. For this reason, neither does "form" <term>Form; original: "forma" / "εἶδος"</term> appear to be in "matter" <term>Matter; original: "materia" / "ὕλη"</term> as in a subject, nor is "human" in Socrates, since it is a part of Socrates. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, that which is not in a subject is judged to be a substance. But if we say that substance itself is that which is neither in a subject nor said of a subject, we must add the qualification "said of a subject" *as if of another thing*. This is so that in the description of substance—where we say substance is not predicated of another—"human" may still be included even when it is predicated of a specific human. <margin>E</margin> For when I predicate "human" of Socrates, I do not speak in the same way as when I say "the wood is white," but rather as if I were saying "white is white." For when I say Socrates is a human, I am confessing that the "human" is everywhere a human, and I am predicating it of the very human who is in the man Socrates. This is the same as if we were to say "Socrates is Socrates," or as if we were to predicate "animal" of a "rational animal" <note>This is a logical identity; Plotinus is arguing that a substance's definition belongs to its essence, not as an accidental property</note>. But if someone objects that it is not a unique property of substance to not be in a subject—arguing that "differences" are among the things not in a subject—he would surely be right if he takes "two-footed" as a part of the essence; he will admit this is not in a subject. However, if he does not take "two-footed" as a core essence, but understands it as "two-footedness" <note>the abstract quality</note>, he will surely not be describing a substance, but a quality; therefore, what is called "two-footed" would then be in a subject. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, neither time nor place seems to be "in a subject." But if time is understood as the "measure of motion" according to the thing being measured, then the measure will certainly be in the motion as its subject, and the motion will similarly be in that which is moved. But if it is understood according to the one who does the measuring, the measure will be in the measurer. As for place, since it is the boundary of the container, it is in that same...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Is it then the case that "Being" <note>original: "ΤΌ ΤΕ ὌΝ"</note> and these other things refer to substance as it is spoken of here? If they somehow apply to the realm "there" <note>the intelligible world</note>, perhaps it is by analogy or by a shared name, or perhaps it is called "first" in relation to what comes after it, and is the same thing in a primary sense. <margin>B</margin> But since those things are the "last" in comparison, the "first" things are also spoken of differently and passively regarding the subject; it is debated whether they are "passive" there in a different way, and whether "not being in a subject" is a universal trait. If "being in a subject" means that which exists not as a part of the thing in which it is, and cannot exist apart from it, yet does not help complete the substance of that thing, <margin>C</margin> then that thing would not have its "form" in "matter" as in a subject, nor would "human" be in Socrates, since it is a part of Socrates. Therefore, what is not in a subject, we call "substance." We must add "as if of another" to the phrase "neither in a subject nor predicated of a subject." <margin>D</margin> This is so that "human," when spoken of regarding a certain human, is included in the definition. For it is a substance by virtue of not being "of another." For when I predicate "human" of Socrates, it is not like when I say "the wood is white," but like "white is white." <margin>E</margin> For in saying Socrates is human, I am saying that a "certain human" is "human," and that the human in Socrates is "the human," and from this, it is like saying "Socrates is Socrates." Similarly, I predicate the same "animal" of "animal-reasonings." But if someone says it is not unique to substance to not be in a subject—for they say all such things are not in a subject—and if he himself takes "two-footed" as a part, then he says it is also in a subject. But if he does not take it as a substance—for it is indeed a substance—but says "two-footedness," meaning a quality, then "two-footed" is in a subject. <margin>F</margin> But time is not in a subject, nor is place. However, if the "measure" is taken of motion according to the thing measured, the measure will exist in the motion as in a subject, and the motion in the thing moved. But if the measure is taken as the "act of measuring," the measure is in the one measuring. And place, being the boundary of the container, is in that...

<summary>Plotinus examines the technical definition of "substance," arguing that true substance cannot be a mere attribute of something else (in a subject). He refines the definition to explain why essential qualities like "being human" are not mere accidents of an individual like Socrates, but are part of his core identity.</summary>

# BOOK THREE.

From the same [source] it will similarly be from the container. On the contrary, the situation is different concerning this essence <note>original: "essentia"; here used interchangeably with substance</note> about which we are currently disputing, regarding which it seems probable that one should receive such a substance according to one of those things said, or several, or all: provided, of course, that those things said are appropriate to matter, form, and the composite.

### Chap. VI.

#### Being is predicated of incorporeal and corporeal substance, as well as of accident, not according to the same definition, but a diverse one, though through a certain similarity.

> *Corporeal substance, when compared to the incorporeal, does not have being from itself, but from the latter; yet when compared to its own accidents, it possesses being in itself, and is prior and simpler. Accidents, however, obtain their being through substance, later rather than substance itself in a certain way. There occurs here a kind of reciprocity: for an accident has being simply through substance, and substance through accidents happens to be "such" or in a certain condition.*

---

<margin>A</margin>
If someone should say that these matters have been considered regarding essence or substance, but what that substance itself is has not been stated, perhaps they require a further inspection of this sensible world. Yet this very thing is, and its being cannot be inspected [directly]. What then? Are fire and water not substance? Is each not a substance? Not at all from the fact that they are seen. Or is it perhaps because they have matter? Not even because of this. But is it because they have a specific form <term>Form; original: "speciem" / "εἶδος," the organizing principle or "whatness" of a thing</term>? Not for this reason either; nor even because there is a composite there.

<margin>B</margin>
By what, then, are they called "substance"? By being itself, surely. But quantity also exists, and quality exists. We shall perhaps say that this very word "is" is spoken of those things and these things equivocally <note>original: "aequiuocè"; meaning the same word is used for different concepts</note>. But then the question arises: what is this "is" in fire and earth and other such things? And what is the difference between this "is" and that "is" which applies to other things?

<margin>C</margin>
It will perhaps be answered that they differ in this: that this one signifies "to be" simply, and a "being" simply; whereas that one signifies "to be white." What then? Is the "being" itself that is applied to white the same as that to which nothing is added? Not at all. But the former exists as a primary being, while the latter exists according to participation <term>Participation; the Platonic concept where a physical thing "shares in" a higher reality</term>, and in a second degree. For white joined to a being rendered it a "white being," and being joined to white made "white being." Therefore, white is an accident to being,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
If someone were to say that these things have been considered concerning substance, but what it actually is has not been said, they perhaps demand to look further into this sensible thing. But this is the thing itself, and it cannot be looked at as "being." What then? Are not fire and water substance? Both are substances—is it because they are seen? Not at all. Is it because they have matter? Not even because of that. Is it because they have form? Not for that reason; nor even because it is the composite.

<margin>B</margin>
By what then are they called substance? By being itself, surely. But quantity is, and quality is. We might say that this "being" is said of them and of these equivocally. But then it will be asked: what is this "being" in fire and earth and the rest? And what is the difference between this "being" and that which belongs to others?

<margin>C</margin>
It will perhaps be answered that they differ in this: that this signifies being simply, and a being simply, whereas that signifies being white. What then? Is the "being" that is added to "white" the same as that which has no addition? Not at all. Rather, the one exists as primary being, while the other exists by participation and in a second degree. For white added to being makes a "white being," and being added to white makes "being white": therefore, it is an accident to the being

<margin>D</margin>
on the one hand, while on the other, being is an accident to the white. We do not speak here as someone might say: "Socrates is white" and "the white is Socrates." For in both cases, Socrates himself is the same; but perhaps "white" is not the same in both. For where it is said, "the white is Socrates," Socrates is included in the white; but where it is said, "Socrates is white," the white is purely accidental. And so, in these matters we are discussing, "white being" has white as an accident. But where it is said "white is being,"

<margin>E</margin>
the white itself has being included in it in some way. Altogether, white has being because it is concerned with being and exists within being; it receives being from that. Being, however, exists as being from itself. It becomes white from white, not because it is itself in the white, but on the contrary, because white comes to be in it. But since even this "being" which is in sensible nature does not exist as being from itself, it must be said that it has being from that which is "truly being" <note>the higher, intelligible realm</note>, but receives "white" from white itself. For even that being there has "being white" according to a certain participation in the white that exists there; and in turn, white itself...

<summary>This page explores how the term "being" applies differently to substances (like fire or earth) and accidents (like the color white). Plotinus argues that while a substance like Socrates has being in itself, a quality like "whiteness" only has being because it "participates" in a substance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the hierarchy of existence. The previous page established that corporeal substances (physical things) derive their reality from higher, incorporeal principles. Here, Plotinus argues that "Being" is not a single category that applies equally to everything; rather, some things (like form) possess more "Being" than others (like matter).</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

...[that they] have their being by participation in the Being reigning there. <note>original Latin: "participatione entis, ibi regnantes"; Greek: "ἐκεῖ ὄντος ἔχοντες τὸ εἶναι". This refers to the higher intellectual realm from which physical things derive their existence.</note>

---

->Both matter and material form depend on a cause separate from themselves, to which form is more similar than matter. Therefore, form is "being," essence, and substance to a greater degree than matter.<-

->Chapter VII.<-

---

Therefore, neither "being," nor "essence," nor "substance" is predicated of matter and form together as if they belonged to a <term>univocal genus</term> <note>A category where the definition applies to all members in exactly the same way, such as "animal" applying to both a horse and a dog.</note>, but rather as an <term>analogous</term> or proportional genus. Furthermore, essence belongs to <term>accidents</term> <note>Non-essential qualities, like color or size, that "happen" to a thing but do not define its core nature.</note> to a lesser degree than it belongs to substance. For to the substances—namely matter, form, and the composite of the two—there would be a certain common future essence. But accidents are merely the "slaves" of substances. Finally, matter depends from above upon that which is least ideal; whereas form is conceived through that which is most highly characterized by quality.

<margin>A</margin> If, however, someone should say that all things here [in the physical world] are in matter and derive their existence from it, we must ask from where matter itself obtains its being and existence. We have stated elsewhere that matter is certainly not the primary thing in the order of reality. But if it is argued that other things cannot exist unless they are in matter, we will admit that this is true for sensible things <note>Things perceived by the senses.</note>. Yet nothing prevents matter itself, which exists before these things, from being "posterior" or lower than many other things, even lower than everything in the intellectual realm. <margin>B</margin> Indeed, matter possesses a dim sort of existence, and it has less "being" than the things that reside within it. Inasmuch as those things are certain <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: "rationes"; Greek: "λόγοι" (logoi). These are the formative blueprints or spiritual patterns that shape matter.</note>, they possess more "being" from the nature of the Supreme Being. Matter, however, is entirely devoid of reason; it is a certain "shadow of reason" and a lapse or fall away from reason. 

But if someone suggests that matter provides existence to the things within it—just as the man Socrates provides existence to the "whiteness" that is in Socrates—we must reply that it is more likely for that which has *more* being to provide existence to that which has *less*. That which has less being can never bestow being upon that which has more. <margin>C</margin> If the "form" or species has more being than matter, then "being" itself cannot be predicated of both as a common attribute. Nor will "essence" be a genus that contains matter, form, and the composite beneath it. Although they may share many commonalities, as we have long said, their actual "being" will be different. <margin>D</margin> For when a greater being approaches a lesser being, it is prior in the order of reality, even if it seems "later" in the sequence of physical development. 

Therefore, unless essence belongs equally to form and matter, and again to the composite, then "essence" can never be a common genus for them. It will relate to them differently than it does to things that come after them, as if it were a common possession that belongs properly to themselves. Just as in the order of life, one life is weak while another is more effective; <margin>E</margin> similarly, in the order of images, one is a faint sketch while another is a more perfect expression. 

<column-break/>

If someone measures "being" by a tiny degree of existence and ignores the greater being in other things, this small degree would again be considered the "common" element. But we must be careful, for perhaps this is not the right approach. Every whole is different. That which is faint and obscure is not a "common" thing in the same way that there is no single "common life" shared by a plant, a sensory creature, and an intellectual being. So too here, "being" is one thing in matter and another in form; both of these depend on a single source, which flows into each in a different way. <margin>F</margin> It is not only true that where a second thing comes from a first, and a third from a second, the first is "more" of that thing and the later things are "less" or worse. Even if both depend on the same source, one can see a similar succession. Just as the potter’s clay, when baked more by the fire, becomes a vessel or a tile; but there will also be clay there that is less baked.

<summary>Plotinus argues that "Being" is not a uniform category; instead, it exists in degrees, with intellectual forms having more reality than the "shadowy" existence of matter. He uses analogies of life and pottery to show that while things may share a source, they participate in existence to different levels of perfection.</summary>

...baked, so that a vessel or tile is by no means produced. Perhaps, indeed, matter and species <note>original Latin: "species"; Greek: "εἶδος" (eidos). In this context, it refers to the "form" or "intelligible blueprint" of a thing.</note> are not from the same source. For there is a difference even in those cases.

---

*When we speak of <term>sensible substance</term> <note>Physical reality that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>, it is better to accept the composite rather than the matter or the form alone. Moreover, it is a general property of these composite substances that they act as subjects, yet they are not "in" subjects. Chapter VIII.*

*Incorporeal substance is pure substance because it does not depend on <term>accidents</term> <note>Qualities like color or size that are not essential to a thing's core existence.</note>; corporeal substance, however, is not pure substance, since it consists of at least certain internal and proper accidents; otherwise, it would not be the sensible and corporeal substance we are currently seeking.*

---

<margin>* plants</margin>
<margin>A</margin> But perhaps it is proper to omit the division into elements for now, especially when we are discussing <term>sensible substance</term> itself. This is something that should be grasped by the senses rather than by pure reason, and we should not necessarily try to join together the parts from which it is composed. For those individual parts are not substances themselves, or at least they are not sensible substances. It seems worthwhile, however, to grasp in a single common genus that which is shared by a stone, the earth, water, and also the things composed of these—namely <margin>*</margin> plants and animals—insofar as they are perceived by the senses. 

<margin>B</margin> In this way, we will not overlook either matter or form, for a sensible substance contains both within itself. For fire, earth, and the elements between them are both matter and form; the composites, then, are many substances reconciled into one. Yet, it is common to all these things that they are distinguished from other categories. For these things are the subjects for everything else, and they are not "in" a subject, <note>In Aristotelian logic, a substance (like a man) is a "subject," while a quality (like "tan") is "in" a subject. Plotinus is testing if physical things meet this definition.</note> nor are they considered to belong to the jurisdiction of another.

<margin>C</margin> And indeed, all the characteristics we have described as proper to substance fit this definition correctly. However, if a sensible substance cannot exist without magnitude <note>Size or volume.</note> and quality, how can we separate the accidents from it? If we strip away these things—magnitude, shape, color, dryness, or moisture—what else can we propose that the substance is? For these qualities are what make the substance what it is.

<margin>D</margin> Yet there is certainly something around which these qualities concur, which together cause that which was merely "substance" to become "such-and-such a substance." In this way, fire would not be entirely substance, but rather some part of it would be judged to be substance. And what would this part be? Perhaps it is the matter. 

Is sensible substance, then, merely a "congeries" <note>A heap or collection.</note> of qualities and matter? Is substance actually all these things mixed together in a single matter? If we take each part separately, one will be a "quality," another a "quantity," or perhaps a collection of many qualities. 

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, whatever exists among these qualities such that its absence would leave the <term>essence</term> <note>The "what-it-is-ness" of a thing.</note> imperfect must be considered a part of that essence. But whatever happens to an already complete essence occupies a different, specific order; it is not included in the mixture that creates said essence. 

I do not mean to say at this moment that such a thing, while present with the rest, is the essence or substance while it completes a specific <margin>F</margin> mass of a certain size and kind. Rather, when it does not complete such a thing, it should be called a quality. 

But I am saying that even there, not every individual part is the substance; rather, the whole, gathered from all these parts, is the substance. Nor should we be distressed if we are building "sensible substance" out of "non-substances" [accidents]; for that whole is not "true substance" or true essence, but rather it merely imitates true essence.

<column-break/>

<page-num>624</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.</header>

That which indeed, without the rest of the things placed around it, possesses being in itself, does so in such a way that other things arise from it, precisely because it truly exists first. Here, however, even that which is cast down as a foundation <note>original Latin: "pro fundamento subijcitur"; Greek: "τὸ ὑποβεβλημένον" (to hypobeblēmenon). This refers to "matter" or "substratum"—the underlying "stuff" of the universe.</note> is sterile; it is not even sufficient to be called "being," let alone for other things to derive their existence from it. Instead, it is a kind of shadow, and upon this shadow a sort of painting is made; it is not true being, but an appearance altogether.

*Species should be counted under the genus of substance either by the distinction of bodies among themselves—such as simple, mixed, or animate. However, one should not say that "this man" is the primary substance while the "universal man" is the secondary. Chapter IX.*

*The species is more universal than the individual, and therefore simpler; thus it is prior by nature, and consequently more perfect in its essence. For "this man"—that is, a man of such a kind and in such matter—comes into being later through a certain participation in the human "reason-principle" <note>original Latin: "rationū"; Greek: "λόγος" (logos). In Neoplatonism, this is the formative force that shapes matter into a specific thing.</note> of the species itself, which exists first and more perfectly in itself, and then imparts itself to others.*

SO FAR we have spoken concerning that which is called sensible substance, and of its one genus. But as for its species, what are the most important ones one can provide? And how shall one divide them? Surely this whole universe must be posited as a body: in which some parts are more material, while others are organic—that is, provided with various instruments. The material parts are things like fire, earth, water, and air; the organic parts are the bodies of plants and animals, distinguished from one another by their forms. Next, one may accept the species of earth and the other elements; and among organic bodies, one may properly divide the bodies of plants and animals by their forms, or even distinguish them by the fact that some are earth-dwellers, while others belong similarly to any other element. Or perhaps some bodies are light, others heavy, and others in between; and while some stand in the middle of the world, others are poured around it from above, and others occupy the middle region. And in each of these, the bodies are already distinguished from one another by shapes, so that there are bodies partly of celestial animals, and partly belonging to the remaining elements. Or first, they may be divided into the four elements as species; then, in another way, they may be mixed with one another, and thus their differences are produced according to locations, forms, and mixtures—such as those which are usually called "fiery" or "earthy" because such an element happens to be abundant or dominant there. As for the claim that some substances are "primary" and others "secondary" <note>This is a direct critique of Aristotle’s "Categories," where the individual (like Socrates) is called primary substance and the species (Man) is called secondary.</note>—such as "this fire" and "fire itself"—it must be thought that they differ from each other in another way (in that one is particular and the other universal), yet they do not admit any difference in substance. For even in the category of quality, there is "white" and "this white"; likewise "grammar" and "a certain grammar." Furthermore, what does "grammar" lack when compared to "a certain grammar," or "knowledge" in general when compared to "a certain knowledge"? For "grammar" is not posterior to "a certain grammar"; rather, because "grammar itself" exists, this grammar is also in you. Indeed, the one in you is "a certain" grammar only because it exists in you; but it is the same as the universal grammar. Likewise, Socrates did not give to one who was not a man the ability to be a man; rather, "Man" gave that to Socrates. For "a certain man" is a man by participation in "Man." Therefore, what else is Socrates than a man of a certain kind? But this very fact of being called "of a certain kind," what does it...

<column-break/>

A ...that which, without the others around it, has its being, while the others come from it; or rather, as they lead the form toward the underlying matter. There, it is sufficient to be "being," because they do not even derive being from it; it is a shadow, and upon the shadow is a painting, existing only in appearance.

A AND concerning what is called sensible substance <note>original Greek: "οὐσίας αἰσθητῆς" (ousias aisthētēs). Physical reality as opposed to the higher world of Ideas.</note> and its one genus, let these things be said. But as for its forms, how would one think it right to divide them? The whole should be posited as a body, and of this, some parts are more like matter, others are organic. The more material are fire, earth, water, air; the organic are the bodies of plants and animals, defined according to their distinct shapes.

B One may take the parts of the earth and the other elements, and among organic bodies, divide the bodies of plants and animals and their shapes, either by their being on the earth or in the earth, or according to each element; or other bodies within it, some light, some heavy, some in between; and some standing in the middle, others heavenly from above.

C And those in between, arranged in each of them by bodies and shapes, so that there are bodies of human animals, and others according to other elements. Or even dividing them this way: the four elements, or weaving them together with one another, or mixing their differences according to places, and shapes, and mixtures—such as "fiery" or "earthy" being so called by their abundance and dominance.

D To speak of "primary" and "secondary"—this fire or fire in another way—they have a difference in that one is particular and the other universal, but not a difference in substance. For even in quality, there is a more common "white," and "a certain grammar" or "grammar." Then, does "grammar" have more than "a certain grammar," or "knowledge" in general more than "a certain knowledge"? Either "grammar" is posterior to "a certain grammar,"

E or rather, "grammar" existing, it is in you; since the one in you is "a certain one" because it is in you, but it is the same as the universal. Or Socrates himself did not give to the non-man the being of a man, but "Man" gave it to Socrates; for "a certain man" is a man by participation. Then, what would Socrates be, other than a man of a certain kind? And what would that "certain kind" produce...

# BOOK THREE.
### G g

<margin>A</margin> ...thirdly, to the end that it might be more of a substance. But if it is said to contribute to this because "man" is the species only, while "a certain man" is the species within matter, it would follow that this individual is "less" of a man for that reason: for the reason-principle <note>original Greek: "λόγος" (logos); Latin: "ratio". In Neoplatonism, this is the formative power or "blueprint" that shapes matter.</note> itself becomes inferior when in matter. But if "man" does not exist according to the species alone, but is also in matter, what then will the species in matter have "less" of, since that very reason-principle is the source of this existence in matter? <margin>B</margin> Likewise, that which is more general is prior by nature; therefore, the species is prior to the individual. That which is prior by nature is also prior in an absolute sense. In what way, then, will it be "less"? Nevertheless, the individual is better known to us, and therefore prior *to us*; but this creates no actual difference in the reality of the things themselves. Finally, if this were the case, there would not be a single definition of substance: for the definition of that which is "primary" would not be the same as that which is "secondary," nor would such things be gathered under one single genus.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...thirdly, toward the goal of it being more truly substance. If, however, it is argued that this is relevant because "man" is the species alone, whereas a specific man is the species embodied in matter, it follows that the individual would be less of a man for this reason: for the internal logic or "reason" itself is degraded when placed in matter. But if "man" is not defined by the species alone but also exists in matter, what exactly will be lacking in that species which exists in matter, given that the very reason-principle is what constitutes this existence in matter? <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, what is more general is "prior by nature" <note>A classical philosophical distinction: "prior by nature" refers to the logical cause (like the concept of 'animal'), while "prior to us" refers to what we perceive first (like a specific dog).</note>, and thus the species comes before the individual. What is prior by nature is also prior simply. How then can it be considered "less"? However, the individual is more familiar to us, and thus "prior" from our perspective; but this does not change the nature of the things themselves. Lastly, if this were so, there would not be one single definition of substance; for the definition of a primary thing is not the same as a secondary thing, and such things cannot be grouped under a single heading.

---

->*The genus of sensible substance, divided into species, can be rightly distinguished through those things which pertain to the senses: namely, by qualities whether simple or mixed, and likewise by forms, figures, and locations. Chapter X.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> WE CAN also divide things in this way: by "hot and dry" together, or "dry and cold" together, or "cold and moist" together, or in whatever pairing one wishes to arrange them. Then, from these, we can create a composition or mixture, and either remain here in the stillness of the compound, or divide them according to whether they are "of the earth" or "living on the land," or according to their shapes and the differences between animals. <margin>B</margin> If animals are to be divided, it should not be by their bodies as if one were merely dividing tools. Indeed, a distinction based on form is not out of place, just as a division based on their qualities—such as heat, cold, and the like—is not absurd. But if someone should object that bodies are formed by these qualities, we shall reply that they are also formed by mixtures, colors, and shapes. Since our discussion concerns "sensible substance" <note>original Greek: "αἰσθητης ουσιας" (aisthetēs ousias). This refers to physical matter that can be perceived by the senses, as opposed to the "intelligible" world of pure thought.</note>, a distinction is not out of place if it is taken from things pertaining to the senses. For this is not "being" in a simple sense; <margin>C</margin> rather, the whole of it is a "sensible being." Indeed, we have said that its apparent existence is a sort of "conflux" <note>Plotinus views physical objects not as solid realities, but as a temporary meeting point or "collection" of qualities like color, size, and weight.</note> of things pertaining to the senses. And it is from the senses that men receive their belief that these things exist. But if an infinite number of compositions confronts us, we may distinguish them by the species of animals: for instance, the "human species" as it exists in a body. <margin>D</margin> For this is a specific quality of the body, and it is not absurd to divide things by qualities. But if it is objected that we previously defined some things as "simple" and others as "composite"—as if we were dividing the composite as the opposite of the simple—we will remind them that we were saying some things are more "material" and others more "organic," without bringing "composite" into the center of the argument. <margin>E</margin> It is possible to assert a difference between the simple and the composite, not as a division of opposites, but by placing simple bodies at the first division and then mixing them according to a different underlying principle.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> WE ARE also able to divide in this manner: namely, through "hot and dry" at once; likewise through "dry and cold"; and again through "cold and moist," or however one pleases to arrange the pairings. Then, from these, one can produce a composition and mixture, and either stay here within the resting compound, or move according to what is "earthy" and "earth-dwelling," or according to the forms and differences of animals. <margin>B</margin> One does not divide the animals themselves, but partitions their bodies as if they were instruments. Nor is a difference based on forms inappropriate: for a division according to their qualities is not absurd—as if one were to speak of heat, cold, and such things. But if someone should reject the idea that bodies are made according to these qualities, we will certainly answer that they are also made according to mixtures, colors, and figures. For when "sensible substance" is being discussed, a distinction will not be absurd if that substance is distinguished by differences belonging to the senses. <margin>C</margin> For this does not exist as "being" in the simple sense, but the whole is a "sensible being": for we have said that even its apparent subsistence is a certain "conflux" of things pertaining to the sense. And indeed, it is from the senses that men have accepted the certainty that such things exist. <margin>D</margin> If, however, an infinite composition should meet us, we may distinguish according to the species of animals: for example, the species of "man" existing in a body. For this very quality of the body is a species of this kind, and it is not absurd to divide by qualities. But if it is objected here that in earlier sections we placed some things as "simple" and others as "composite," as if we were dividing the composite and simple as opposites: <margin>E</margin> we shall point out that we said some things are more "material" and others more "organic," without using "composite" as the middle term. It is even permitted to assert a diversity between the simple and the composite, not by a division of equal opposites, but according to the "primary division": placing simple bodies at the very beginning, and then mixing them from another assumed principle.

<summary>Plotinus argues that universal species are more "real" than individuals, even though individuals are more familiar to our senses. He then explains how to classify the physical world using sensory qualities like heat, moisture, and biological form.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

->*In the category of quantity, there is strictly speaking number and continuity, or dimension; the rest belong to another category.*<-
->*Chapter XI*<-

->*Time, in the respect that it is a measure and a thing measuring, and place, in the respect that it is a container, are categorized as relations. Great and small belong to quantity, beauty to quality, but "less," "greater," and "more beautiful" consist in relation.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin>
CONCERNING what pertains to quantity and the "how much," it has often been said that it should be placed in number and magnitude, insofar as each thing is properly a certain size. This consists in the number of corporeal things and in a certain occupied space. For we are not presently disputing about quantity separated from matter, but about this very quantity which makes a piece of wood "three cubits" <note>original Latin: "tricubitū". A cubit was an ancient unit of length based on the forearm.</note> long; similarly, we speak of the number five which exists in five horses. We have said previously that number and magnitude are the only things that are properly "quantities."
<margin>B</margin>
Place and time, however, are by no means counted in the category of quantity. Instead, time—because it is considered the measure of a moving thing—is placed in the order of "relation." Place also, since its proper function is to be the container of a body, is judged as being in a state of habitude or relation. Even though motion is continuous, it is nonetheless not established within the genus of quantity. But why are "great" and "small" not placed
<margin>C</margin>
under quantity? For that which is great is great because of a certain quantity; yet this magnitude itself is not placed in relation, but "greater" and "less" are rightly thought to belong to relation. For these things are defined by what they are in respect to something else, just like "double" and "half." Why then is a mountain often called "small," while
<margin>D</margin>
a seed of millet is often called "large"? Perhaps when we call a mountain small, we mean for it to be understood as "smaller" <note>Plotinus is arguing that 'small' and 'large' are often hidden comparisons rather than absolute measurements.</note>. Even among those who treat these subjects, it is conceded that a mountain is called small insofar as it is compared with things of the same kind—that is, with other mountains. It is therefore rightly conceded that "small" is used there instead of "smaller." Truly, a "large" millet seed is not judged as simply large, but specifically as a large seed. This is the same as saying it is of a certain size when compared with things of the same kind, compared to which it can be called larger by a natural logic. Next, why is "beauty" not also placed in relation? Truly, beauty itself should not be taken in that way, but as a quality; however, "more beautiful" belongs to those things referred to another. This is true even though what is called beautiful can sometimes appear ugly if it is compared with something else, just as human beauty is ugly when compared with the beauty of the gods. From this comes the famous saying: "The most beautiful of monkeys will be ugly if compared with another genus" <note>original Greek: "πιθήκων φαίνεται κάλλιστος, αἰσχρός" (pithekon phainetai kallistos, aischros). This is a reference to Heraclitus, quoted in Plato’s Hippias Major, illustrating the relativity of aesthetic judgments.</note>. But surely it will be said that a thing is beautiful in itself when considered by itself, but is judged as either more beautiful or uglier when set against another. Therefore, in this genus, something is "great" in itself when endowed with magnitude, but not great in respect to another. Otherwise, if we stop speaking this way, we would be equally forced to say something is beautiful only because something else

<column-break/>

...of composites, either by places or forms, making some heavenly and others earthly. Regarding substance or generation among sensible things, let these things suffice.

<margin>A</margin>
CONCERNING the quantitative and the sensible "how much": it is placed in both magnitude and in the multitude which each thing has in the number of bodies. But the underlying bodies are those in a certain space. For the discussion is not about the abstract concept <note>original Greek: "λόγος" (logos)</note>, but about those things involving bodies: the cubit in the wood and the "five" in the horses. We have already said that these are the only things that are quantities. But place and time are not arranged under quantity;
<margin>B</margin>
rather, time, by participating in motion, belongs to the category of "toward something" <note>original Greek: "πρὸς τι" (pros ti), the standard Aristotelian term for the category of Relation.</note>, which is its definition. Place, being a container for body, is an arrangement in relation, which also belongs to "toward something." Even if motion is continuous, it is not in quantity. But "great" and "small"—why are they not in quantity? If something is great by having a share of magnitude, "the great" is among the "toward something." But while the "less" follows from being "toward something," the "great" follows from itself, just as "the double" exists because of a certain size. A mountain is small and a seed is large
<margin>C</margin>
either because, in the first place, "small" is said instead of "smaller," and it is not agreed upon except in part, just as they themselves admit an order of precedence. In the way that "small" is said in relation, so too is "great" said; it is not called simply "great," but is used for that which is the same among things of the same kind. For among things of the same kind, this would be called "greater" according to nature. This does not apply to calling something "beautiful." For first we say
<margin>D</margin>
that "beautiful" is something in itself and a quality, but "more beautiful" is "toward something." A thing might be called beautiful by its nature, not in relation to another "ugly" thing. For example, the beauty of humans compared to gods; the most beautiful of monkeys appears ugly when it happens to be compared to another genus. But it is beautiful in itself, though against another it is not beautiful, or the opposite. And here, therefore, a thing is great in itself with magnitude, but in relation to another it is not great—otherwise beauty is destroyed if it is only in relation to another...

<summary>Plotinus discusses the categories of Quantity and Relation, arguing that while dimensions and numbers are absolute quantities, terms like "large," "small," and "more beautiful" are actually relations based on comparison. He uses the famous analogy of the monkey, the human, and the god to show how beauty can be both a quality in itself and a relative value when compared.</summary>

# BOOK THREE

... <note>original Greek: καλλίον αὐτὸ...</note> it may appear all the more beautiful to us: but we ought not to deny this. Therefore, it must not be denied that something is "great" simply because something else is "greater" than it: since indeed there would be no "greater" at all unless there were also "great"; just as there would be no "more beautiful" unless there were also "beautiful."

->*Expansion and contraction are opposites. If a number is expanded, it becomes "many"; if it is contracted, it turns out "few." Similarly, dimension becomes "small" through contraction, but "great" through expansion. Therefore, "few" and "many" are opposites, as are "small" and "great." Chapter XII.*<-

->*Just as there is a certain determined definition <term>ratio (Greek: logos)</term> for beauty, so it is for heat and magnitude. Furthermore, in the matter of place, there is an opposition that is properly relative, such as between "above" and "below." Finally, speech belongs to the category of quantity only by accident; in its own nature, it belongs to motion.*<-

<note>The following section translates both the Greek and Latin columns, which provide the same philosophical argument regarding how we perceive size and number.</note>

<margin>A</margin> WE MUST PERMIT, therefore, that opposition <term>contrariety</term> exists within the category of quantity. For our very thoughts admit this opposition when we say "great" and when we say "small," which bring to mind opposing mental images, just as when we speak of "many" and "few." Indeed, similar things happen regarding "few" and "many." For "many" people are said to be "at home," and yet under this name "many," we understand that they are "more" [than usual]. This very thing which is called "more"
<margin>B</margin> is referred to something else <note>This makes it a "relative" term rather than a pure quantity.</note>; often people even say there are "few" in a theater, meaning there are "fewer" [than expected]. It is entirely worthwhile to understand that when we say "many," we mean a multitude that is very large in number. But in what way shall "multitude" be counted among the relatives? This is either the same as saying that multitude is an expansion and propagation of number, while the opposite of this is contraction. The same thing happens in
<margin>C</margin> the very notion of the "continuous" <note>A continuous quantity, like a line or a solid, as opposed to a "discrete" quantity like a number.</note>, as the continuous extends outward to a distance. For quantity seems to arise when a unit and a point move forward. But if both stop their progress quickly, the former turns out "few" and the latter becomes "small"; but if the process of proceeding does not end quickly, the former certainly turns out "many" and the latter "great." What then is the boundary or definition? But what is the definition of beauty? What is the definition of heat?
<margin>D</margin> And yet, in the order of heat there is "hotter"; but "hotter" is referred to something else, while "hot" exists simply as a quality. In general, just as there must be a certain definition <term>ratio (Greek: logos)</term> for beauty, so there must be for magnitude; once this definition is perceived, it makes the thing "great," just as the definition of beauty makes a thing beautiful. Opposition <term>contrariety</term>, therefore, exists according to these terms within quantity. Regarding place, however, there is no longer any opposition, since place does not strictly belong to the category of quantity. Indeed, even if place were in the
<margin>E</margin> category of quantity, that which is called "up" would not yet be the opposite of anything, unless there were a "down" in the universe as a whole. But in specific parts, what is called "up" or "down" signifies nothing other than "higher" and "lower"; and that is similar to what is called "right" and "left." These are numbered in the category of relation. Syllables and speech, however, happen to be quantities and are subject to quantity. For voice is considered a quantity; but voice itself is a type of motion. Therefore, speech should be reduced to motion, just as action is.

<meta>catchword: seems to be</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that "great" and "small" are not merely relative terms but possess an inherent form or "ratio" similar to beauty. He also explains that while speech is often measured as a quantity, it is fundamentally an act of motion.</summary>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK VI

->*A single genus of quantity is common to both numbers and continuous magnitudes; likewise, there is one general type of number for all numbers, and one general continuity for all continuous things. The species of numbers are identified by the difference between even and odd; the species of continuous things are identified by the differences between the line, the surface, and the solid; and so on. Chapter XIII.*<-

<margin>A</margin> The continuous is indeed distinguished from the discrete <note>original: "discreto," referring to "discrete quantity" like individual numbers</note> by a common property, which has already been described as the boundary of their definitions. Next, it must be said that in the case of number, the division occurs through the properties of "odd" and "even." Similarly, if there are further sub-differences within these two, we must decide if such a division is granted to things that already possess number. <margin>B</margin> Or, perhaps we should assign these differences to numbers composed of units <term>monads (Greek: monas)</term>, but not to the "essential" numbers <note>Plotinus distinguishes between mathematical numbers we count with and the "Ideal" numbers that exist in the realm of the Divine Intellect</note>. However, if some reasoning separates the numbers existing in sensible objects, nothing prevents us from understanding those same differences there as well. <margin>C</margin> But how shall the continuous be distinguished? Surely it is distinguished by being either a line, a plane, or a solid; or perhaps it belongs to one, two, or three dimensions respectively. If we divide it this way, we might seem not to be dividing it into "species" but merely measuring the whole. For in every case, the "prior" and "posterior" are contained within the whole, unless some general category is found. <note>Plotinus is wrestling with whether a 3D solid is a "different kind" of thing than a 1D line, or just "more" of the same thing.</note> There is nothing common in the first, second, and third stages of growth except the ratio of its magnitude; in these things there is an equality of "how much" it is, and one is no more a "quantity" than another, even though some possess more parts when divided and others fewer. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, in numbers, insofar as they are all numbers, there could be something common. For perhaps the "unit" does not produce the "duality" <term>dyad</term>, nor the unit the "triad," but rather some identical principle creates all of them. But if these do not exist as such, and we merely think of them as existing, <margin>E</margin> let it be that the smaller is prior and the other posterior, or rather that the other is larger; nevertheless, insofar as they are numbers, they are all bound together into one. For this reason, it is proper to transfer the condition of numbers to the ordering of magnitudes. We should separate these—the line, the plane, and the solid (which is also called a body)—on the grounds that, although they are all magnitudes, they differ in species. If it is necessary to divide each of these, one divides the line into straight, circular, and curved; the plane into rectilinear and circular figures; and finally the solid into solid figures, namely the sphere and figures having straight lines for sides. We shall consider these again in the manner of geometers as triangles and quadrangles, and these again into others, and the conditions by which these are formed.

->*Straightness or curvature applied to a line signifies its property and does not introduce a new composition; likewise, figures should be placed in the genus of quantity, rather than quality. Chapter XIV.*<-

->*When you say a triangle consists of three lines, but held together in a certain arrangement, you signify that they are bounded by a specific limit; such a limit and determination seem to belong to the genus of quantity rather than quality.*<-

<margin>A</margin> ACCORDINGLY, what do we say a straight line is? Is it not a magnitude? Perhaps someone might call "straightness" a quality of a magnitude. What

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Now, it has been well said that the continuous is separated from the discrete by what is common and what is specific. It should be observed that in number, the cut is made by the "even," and again similar differences exist for each of these. Either we must accept all of them, or we must place such differences in numbers made of units; but for numbers in the sensory world, the same logic does not prevent us from seeing such differences there as well. <margin>B</margin> What then? How could the continuous be divided? Either as a line, a plane, or a solid; or by having one, two, or three dimensions. And if it still seems to be divided, it will act to be measured; but if one follows them in the "prior" and "posterior," there is a certain genus among them. <margin>C</margin> There is nothing common in the first, second, and third increase <note>original: "αὔξῃ," referring to dimensional growth</note>, except insofar as the whole is in them; some are not "more" quantities and others "less," even if some have dimensions in more directions and others in fewer. <margin>D</margin> In numbers, therefore, insofar as they are all numbers, you might find something common. It might seem that the unit <note>original: "μονὰς," the Monad</note> generates the duality, or the unit the triad, but the same thing will seem to generate all of these. But if not these, it still makes a mark of recognition; let it be the smaller, or the prior and second, or the larger, but insofar as they are all numbers, they are one. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, one can move from numbers to magnitudes in this way. The separation from each other—line, plane, solid, which is indeed called "body"—is clear because they are species existing through magnitudes. If it is necessary to divide each of these: the line into straight, circular, and spirals; the plane into rectilinear and circular shapes; the solid into either spherical or a sphere, into rectilinear sides. And these again, as geometers do, into triangles and quadrilaterals; one must again examine these in other ways.

<margin>A</margin> What should we say a straight line is? Is it a magnitude? Or would someone say that "straight" is a *quality* of magnitude?

# BOOK THREE

<note>original Greek: "LIBER TERTIVS" refers to the third book of the sixth Ennead in this specific edition's arrangement</note>

What prevents there being a difference <note>Greek: *diaphoran*; Latin: *differentiam* — a distinguishing characteristic that defines a species within a genus</note> of a line, or that "straightness" is not a difference of something else but of the line itself? For we often derive the differences of substances <term>substantia (the underlying essence of a thing)</term> from qualities. If a straight line is a quantity joined with a difference, and this composition is maintained because "straightness" does not exist apart from the line, it acts as its own specific difference. Why is a triangle, which is made of three lines, not placed in the category of quantity? Is it because a triangle is not simply "three lines," but three lines arranged in a specific way? And if a quadrilateral is four lines arranged so, is the straight line not itself a quantity? Or is it that quantity is not the only thing present, and we should speak of the "limit" of the line rather than just its quantity? Is the point the source, and is the finite plane a quantity? Since lines limit a plane, the finite plane belongs even more to quantity, as do squares, polygons, hexagons, and all geometric figures. If we say a triangle or a square is a "certain kind" of thing, why not place it in the category of Quality? Or what prevents the same thing from being placed in multiple categories <note>Aristotle’s "Categories" (Predicaments) were the standard framework for classifying all things in the universe</note>? Insofar as it is a magnitude, it is Quantity; insofar as it provides a specific shape, it is Quality. What then prevents us from calling a sphere a quality as well? If one follows this path, geometry would deal not with magnitudes, but with qualities. But this does not seem right, for the study of geometry is understood to be about magnitudes. Differences in magnitude do not take away the fact that they are magnitudes, just as differences in substance do not make substances stop being substances. Furthermore, every plane is finite, for an infinite plane is impossible. Just as when I consider a quality of a substance, I call it an "essential quality," so too when I consider shapes, I am taking a "difference of quantity." Finally, if we do not take these shapes as differences of magnitudes, what else would they be differences of? If they are differences of magnitudes, then different magnitudes arising from these differences should be placed within their own species.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What then prevents such a difference existing, by which the line is defined? For straightness is not said to belong to anything else but the line; likewise, we frequently derive the differences of substances from quality. If, therefore, a straight line is a certain quantity together with a difference, is the straight line composed of "straightness" and "line"? If something is composed, it is certainly composed with its own specific difference.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, why should a triangle, properly constituted of three lines, not be in the genus <note>category</note> of quantity? Is it perhaps because a triangle is not simply three lines, but three lines having themselves in a specific proper way? A square is also said to be four lines arranged in such a way. Indeed, a straight line possesses both quantity and a certain mode of quantity within itself; that is, if we say a straight line is not only "how much" something is,

<margin>C</margin> what prevents us from also naming a limited line as a "how much"? Indeed, the limit of a line is a point, and that does not exist in any other genus. For this reason, a limited plane is also properly a quantity. Since lines limit planes, they exist much more in the genus of quantity. If, therefore, a limited plane is in the genus of quantity, then a figure composed of many angles will be even more so; certainly, all figures are numbered within the genus of quantity.

<margin>D</margin> But if, because we call a triangle "of a certain kind" and a square "of a certain kind," we therefore place them in the genus of quality, nothing shall hinder us from placing these same things in several categories. For that which is a magnitude (and a magnitude of such a kind) is in the genus of quantity; but that which exhibits such a form is in the genus of quality.

<margin>E</margin> Perhaps even the triangle itself is a certain form of this kind. What then will forbid us from calling a sphere a "quality" as well? If anyone proceeds in this same manner, he would concede that geometry is concerned not with magnitudes, but with qualities. But this does not seem admissible; for this very doctrine is judged to be concerned with magnitudes. Differences of magnitudes do not take away the fact that they are magnitudes: just as differences of substances do not result in substances no longer being substances. Furthermore, every plane is limited: for it is not possible for there to be an infinite plane. Likewise, just as when I take a quality regarding a substance, I call it an essential quality; so much more when I take up figures, I am taking a difference of quantity. Finally, unless we take these as differences of magnitudes, whose differences shall we judge them to be? But if they are differences of magnitudes, then different magnitudes constituted from these differences must be placed within their own species.

---

->Equality and inequality exist only in the genus of quantity; but similarity and dissimilarity are properly in the genus of quality. Chapter XV.<-

*In a certain way we also say that figures are similar to one another not so much by quality as by some other condition. Substance, insofar as it is perceived through the body and through the senses, is a certain gathering of substance and accidents <note>Accidents are non-essential properties, like color or height, that can change without changing what the thing is</note> together. Consider man in four degrees: first, in the Idea of the Mind <note>the divine, perfect template of "Man"</note>; second, in the seminal reason of the soul; third, in this body of ours; and fourth and finally, in a painting. By as much as the fourth is inferior to the third, so the third is to the second, and the second to the first.*

<sig>Gg 3</sig>

<summary>Plotinus debates whether geometric shapes like triangles and squares belong to the category of Quantity or Quality, concluding that while they have qualitative forms, they are essentially differences within the genus of magnitude. The text also introduces a Neoplatonic hierarchy of reality using the "four degrees of man" from the divine Idea down to a physical painting.</summary>
