<meta>Continuing Plotinus's investigation into the categories of Quantity and Quality. This page specifically addresses whether "similarity" belongs to Quality or if it can also apply to Quantity (geometric shapes), and explores the relationship between a thing's form (reason-principle) and its physical appearance.</meta>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> But in what way is it the property of quantity to be called equal and unequal? For even triangles are said to be **similar**. Or perhaps magnitudes might also be rightly called "similar"? And regarding what is called "similarity," does it not exist only so that "similar" and "dissimilar" might be found within the genus of quantity? For perhaps here, in the order of magnitudes, that which is named "similar" behaves differently; not in the same way as it does in the genus of quality.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, if he <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, whose *Categories* Plotinus is critiquing</note> said that "equal" and "unequal" are proper to quantity, it does not follow that "similar" is truly predicated of some of them. However, if one were to say that "similar" and "dissimilar" are proper only to quality, we must speak differently, just as we did previously regarding quantity itself.

<margin>C</margin> But if that which is called "similar" is the same thing and is to be considered in this genus as well, is it not then useful to distinguish the other properties of each genus—both of quantity and of quality? Or perhaps it should be said that the term "similar" is used even in the genus of quantity, insofar as there are differences within it. Generally, however, differences that <term>complete the essence</term> <note>original Latin: *complet essentiam*; Greek: *symplērousas diaphoras*. These are the essential characteristics that make a thing what it is, rather than just accidental traits</note> are joined with the thing itself to which the differences belong, especially when they belong to that difference alone. But if in one case it completes the essence (or substance), while in another it does not, it must be joined with that whose nature it completes. That thing whose substance is not completed by this must be taken only in itself. When he speaks of "filling" or "completing" a substance, he does not mean substance simply, but "of such a kind." In such a case, this very thing which is called "of such a kind" <note>Greek: *poion*, meaning a "qualified" thing</note> does not allow for a substantial addition.

<margin>D</margin> It is worthwhile to notice that we rightly call triangles and quadrangles—and figures in any species, whether flat or solid—"equal." Therefore, "equal" and "unequal" must be placed in the genus of quantity as a proper characteristic without controversy. But we must consider whether "similar" and "dissimilar" belong only to the genus of quality.

<margin>E</margin> Regarding the "qualified" itself <note>original: *quali*; things defined by their qualities</note>, it was said above that matter, along with other things and something mixed with quality, produces the completion of <term>sensible substance</term> <note>Substance that can be perceived by the senses, as opposed to intellectual substance</note>. It seems that the substance which we call "substance" is that which is gathered from many parts: not a "this" in the proper sense, but rather a "qualified" thing. It also seems that the <term>reason-principle</term> <note>original Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*. The formative, organizing principle or "blueprint" of a thing</note>—such as that of fire—signifies a "this" (a specific thing) more clearly; whereas this form which the reason-principle generates signifies "quality" more clearly. The reason-principle of a man is a "this." However, that which is produced from it in the nature of a body, being a mere image of the reason-principle, is rather a "quality." It is just as if this Socrates whom we see is the man himself, but nevertheless his image in a painting—consisting only of colors and pigments—is also called "Socrates." Thus, although the reason-principle according to which Socrates exists is the true Socrates, we nevertheless call this visible person "Socrates." Yet we must call the colors and shapes of this visible Socrates "imitations" of those things that exist in the reason-principle itself. Furthermore, we must judge that this reason-principle stands in the same relation to the truest reason-principle of "Man." Let this much be said on these matters.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But how is "equal and unequal" the property of quantity? For triangles are called **similar**, even in the case of magnitudes. Does the term "similarity" then take away the fact that "similar and dissimilar" exist in quantity? Or is "similarity" in magnitudes categorized differently than in the case of quality?

<margin>B</margin> And if he says "equal and unequal" is a property, does he take away the possibility of "similar" being predicated of some things? But if he says "similar and dissimilar" are qualities, we must speak otherwise—or we say the same as we said regarding quantity. We should investigate if these properties belong to each genus:

<margin>C</margin> both quantities and qualities. Or should we say that "similar," where it is said of quantity, exists insofar as there are differences in it? Generally, in a thing, there must be differences that <term>complete the essence</term> <note>original Greek: *symplērousas diaphoras*</note>. These are differences especially when the difference is unique to it. If a difference does not complete the substance in other things, but only in this one, then those things that do not complete it should be taken by themselves. We say they complete the substance—not substance in general, but the substance of a quantity—by adding "of the quantity" to things that do not otherwise admit it.

<margin>D</margin> And it must also be noted there that things not called triangles and quadrangles—and indeed all shapes, both plane and solid—are called equal and unequal based on the amount of these quantities, but also similar and dissimilar. If one investigates qualities, it was said regarding qualities that they themselves are the matter of another thing, and when mixed with a body, they work toward the completion of sensible substance. There is a risk that what is called "substance" itself is actually this composite of many things, and is not a "this," but

<margin>E</margin> rather a "quality." Or perhaps the *logos* <note>reason-principle or defining formula</note>, such as that of fire, signifies the "what it is" more, while the shape produced by it signifies the "quality" more. Or the *logos* of a man is the <term>essence</term> <note>Greek: *to ti ēn einai*, literally "the what it was to be"</note>, but that which is finished in the physical body, being an image of the *logos*, is more of a "quality." It is just as if Socrates himself is the determined Socrates, but the image of him in a painting—made of color and certain pigments—is also called "Socrates," though not being so in *logos*. The one we call Socrates is not the true Socrates, but the colors and shapes are imitations of those things in the *logos*. And this *logos* itself, in relation to the truest *logos* of "Man," is in the same condition.

<summary>Plotinus debates whether "similarity" is a property of Quality or Quantity, concluding that while "equal" describes size (Quantity), "similar" describes the form or "reason-principle" (logos) that shapes matter. He uses the analogy of Socrates and his portrait to show that physical objects are merely quality-filled imitations of higher essential forms.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: On the previous page, Plotinus examined whether the concept of "similarity" belongs to the category of Quality or Quantity. He now moves to distinguish between incorporeal substances (the soul and intellect) and corporeal substances (physical bodies), and how "Quality" applies differently to each.</meta>

### BOOK THREE

An incorporeal substance is truly called "this particular thing" <note>Latin: *hoc aliquid*; Greek: *tode ti*. This refers to a primary, individual substance</note>, whereas a corporeal substance is called "such a thing." It happens, however, that two things may be of the same "suchness" regarding the qualities of the soul, insofar as those qualities are concerned with matter—both in how it is affected and how it is managed. Conventions regarding common bodies are grouped under the genus of general qualities, while agreements regarding separate qualities are grouped under the genus of separate qualities.

## Chapter XII

Likewise, the qualities within the power of the soul are numbered as "seeds" <note>Latin: *seminaria*; Greek: *logoi*. These are the formative principles or "reasons" that shape reality</note> in the joined genus, even though they are not themselves in matter, but in the separable soul. We do not place the substance of the soul itself in this category, but rather in the genus of separate essence.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But when we consider each of those things that revolve around the aforementioned essence separately, we should not signify the quality existing in them as "this particular thing." Nor should we call quantity or motion "this particular thing." Instead, we should think of them as a certain character, or what is usually called "of such a kind" and "quality." We must think that these things signify for us something "of a certain quality," such as the **beautiful** and the **ugly**, specifically that which exists in the body.

<margin>B</margin> For "beautiful" is an <term>equivocal term</term> <note>A word that has the same sound/spelling but different meanings depending on the context</note> when used for things among us compared to things separated from matter. Therefore, "quality" is also an equivocal term, just as "black" and "white" are different in different contexts. But regarding that which exists in the "seed" and in its formative principle, is it not the same? Or is it rather equivocal compared to what appears to us? And should it be numbered among the separate things, or rather among the lower things?

And as for the **ugly** which is in the soul, should it perhaps be attributed to these lower things? It is already established that the **beautiful** is different. <margin>C</margin> But again, it is doubted whether virtue consists in the soul itself according to a "quality," or if it should instead be computed among these qualities of ours. In truth, we ought to place some virtues in this lower quality, and others in that higher quality.

One might also doubt whether the arts, which are certain rational principles, should be placed in the genus of our qualities. For even if these principles are said to be in matter, the soul nonetheless acts as their matter. <margin>D</margin> But when they exist alongside matter, they seem to be placed here in a certain way—much like a song played on a **cithara** <note>A stringed instrument similar to a lyre, used in ancient Greece</note>. For the song is concerned with the strings, and the song is in a way a part of the art, insofar as it is a perceptible voice; unless, perhaps, one were to call these "acts" rather than "parts."

Nevertheless, they are perceptible acts, since even the **beauty** in a body is incorporeal. Yet, because it is perceptible, we attribute it to those things that concern the body and belong to the body. <margin>E</margin> We should consider **Geometry** and **Arithmetic** as being of a dual nature. Some parts of them, which turn toward this world, should be placed in this genus of quality; others, however, which are the contemplations of the soul itself, should be referred back to that which is intelligible.

Indeed, Plato says that **Music** and **Astronomy** behave in the same way. Therefore, the arts that concern bodies—and use sensible instruments and the senses—even though they are certain dispositions of the soul, we rightly number in this our genus of quality, because they belong to a soul that is already declining toward lower things. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, nothing forbids us from placing there

the active virtues, which perform something here only so that they may act in a civil <note>Referring to the "political" or "civic" virtues of a citizen in society</note> manner. These virtues never separate the soul from this world to lead it toward the heights; instead, they place the perfection of their duty in human affairs. They do not choose such honorable business as a necessity, but establish them as free and primary choices. For this reason, the **beauty** that is in the seminal power—and much more the **black** and **white** that are there—seem to be counted among the inferior qualities. What, then, shall we judge the animal soul to be, in which these principles reside? Shall we place it in the order of essence that is among us? But truly, neither do these bodies...

<summary>Plotinus explores whether qualities like beauty, virtue, and the arts (such as geometry and music) belong to the physical world or the intellectual soul. He concludes that these concepts have a dual nature: a higher intellectual form and a lower form that interacts with the material world.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the classification of Quality. Plotinus is specifically addressing where the "reasons" or formative principles of the soul reside—whether they belong to the realm of Substance or the category of Quality—and how these might be divided into species through the five senses.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK VI

<margin>A</margin> ...as we said: but since the formative principles <note>Latin: *rationes*; Greek: *logoi*. These are the active, shaping principles that organize matter.</note> are concerned with the body and the affections of bodies, we have placed them within this category of quality. However, when we have affirmed that sensible substance is something gathered from all the aforementioned elements, we shall in no way establish an incorporeal substance within it. Moreover, although all qualities of the soul are incorporeal, because there are certain passions <note>Refers to "pathos" or being acted upon/undergoing an experience.</note> in it that decline in some way toward lower things, we have surely numbered them among these, as well as the formative principles that exist for any given soul. <margin>B</margin> For we attribute passion, divided into two—both that which it concerns and that in which it exists—to the soul; this is indeed not a corporeal quality, but nonetheless it exists around the body. Yet we do not adapt the soul itself to this essence, because we have already granted its passion and its affection toward the body to the genus of quality. We attribute the soul itself, considered without such an affection and as a seed-like principle <term>seminary reason: the "seed-like" formative power that generates life and form</term>, to that very source from which it originates, leaving no intelligible essence whatsoever in this lower class of things.

---

->He questions by what reasoning the genus of quality is correctly divided through differences into its species, but in this chapter, he defines almost nothing. Chapter XXII.<-

---

<margin>A</margin> If, therefore, it seems so, the genus of quality must be divided into the qualities of the soul and the body. If someone wishes for all souls to exist in the higher realms, along with their own proper qualities, it will at least be possible to divide the lower qualities through the distribution of the senses: namely, assigning some to the eyes, others to the ears, and likewise through touch, taste, and smell. Similarly, we can distinguish differences within these: assigning colors to sight, voices to hearing, and other things to the other senses. <margin>B</margin> We can further divide voices, insofar as they possess certain qualities, into the sweet, the harsh, and the smooth. 

However, since we divide the differences concerning substance by qualities, and by these same qualities we partition acts and actions—whether they be beautiful or ugly, or existing in any such way—a problem arises. While we rarely or never partition quantity by the differences that constitute species (indeed, we are accustomed to partitioning quantity by its own proper qualities), one may doubt in what manner anyone might divide quality itself. For what sorts of differences will one chiefly use in dividing, and from what genus will he derive them? It seems absurd to divide quality itself by another quality; it would be as if someone were to say that the differences of a substance are again themselves substances. 

By what, then, will one distinguish white and black? By what will one distinguish colors in general from flavors and the qualities perceived by touch? If we assign the differences of these qualities according to the different instruments of the senses, there will be no such difference in the subjects themselves. Furthermore, we must ask how we can discern the difference of qualities belonging to the same sense through that same sense. If a distinction is assigned based on the fact that one quality contracts the sight while another expands it, note that one thing also expands the tongue and another contracts it. First, there will be doubt regarding these passions themselves—whether they are indeed certain contractions and expansions—and then, one might not assign differences to these based on their actual species. If anyone asserts that he has brought forward those things which properly...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...present. But since the principles <note>original: *logoi*</note> are about the body and bodily productions, we placed the essence or the sensible thing in quality as being composed of all the things mentioned; we shall by no means rank the incorporeal within it. While saying all qualities are bodily, <note>The Greek text here uses *somatikai* (bodily), whereas the Latin translation on the left uses *incorporeæ* (incorporeal), reflecting a common tension in interpreting whether the soul's "qualities" remain pure or become "bodily" when acting on matter.</note> certain passions arise in it; and there is the principle of a certain soul, or the passion divided into two: both that which it is about, and that in which it is, which we gave to the soul. <margin>B</margin> Being a bodily quality, and being about the body. But we no longer give the soul to this essence, but rather its passion to bodies; we have already granted it to the "hows" <note>the category of Quality</note>, but the principle remaining without the passion we have given back to where it is from, leaving no intelligible essence of any kind here.

<margin>A</margin> If then it seems so, we must divide: some as soul-qualities and others as body-qualities. As for all the qualities of bodies, if someone wants all the souls to be "there" <note>in the intelligible realm</note>, one must divide the forms of quality by the senses. Some through the eyes, some through the ears, some through touch, taste, and smell, and again the differences of these: colors to sight, voices to hearing, <margin>B</margin> and to the other senses. And voices by the sweet, the sharp, the smooth. 

Since we divide the differences about substance by qualities, and also the activities and actions—beautiful and ugly and such like—one might seek: for quantity either rarely or never makes differences into species, and quantity is likened to its own qualities. One might ask: using what differences, and from what genus? For it is absurd [to use] itself and its like, as if one were to say the differences of essence are again essences. By what then is white and black? By what are colors entirely [different] from flavors and tactile qualities? If it is because these are in different sense-organs, then the difference is not in the underlying subjects. But how is it according to the same senses? Because one is contractive <note>original: *synkritikon*</note> and the other is expansive <note>original: *diakritikon*</note> of the eyes; and another is expansive and contractive of the tongue. First, one would dispute about the passions themselves, whether these are certain expansions or contractions. Then, one would not be speaking of them as different species...

<summary>This page discusses the difficulty of classifying the soul's qualities and how to divide the general category of "Quality" into species. Plotinus explores using the five senses to categorize physical qualities like color and sound but identifies a logical problem in using qualities to define other qualities.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the category of Quality. Having previously discussed how formative principles (logoi) relate to the soul and body, he now moves to the problem of "differences"—the specific characteristics that distinguish one thing from another—and whether these differences are themselves qualities.</meta>

# BOOK THE THIRD.

<column-break/>

...they are able, and it is not unreasonable if they are able; that perhaps we must say that those things which are not seen must be divided by what they are able to do—such as the sciences—whereas those things they produce are sensible. Now, in the sciences, by dividing them according to their powers, and as if the whole powers of the soul were partitioned into others based on what they produce, we are able to grasp their differences through reason. By encompassing a part and seeing their formative principles <note>Greek: *logoi*; Latin: *rationes*. In Neoplatonism, these are the active, shaping "reasons" or blueprints that give form to matter.</note> as the arts, one might ask how, in the principles of their theorems, this or that quality is accumulated, and how it stands regarding the differences of these principles; for it is evident that white things differ from black things, but we must ask in what way they differ.

<margin>A</margin> But indeed, all these points of doubt clearly demonstrate that we must seek the differences of other things so that we may distinguish each from the other. However, to seek the differences *of* differences is both impossible and irrational. For it would either lead to infinity or depart from the nature of quantity—if indeed qualities are distinguished by quality—and to find differences of differences. Rather, it is necessary to concede that things are distinguished by external factors, or by their productive causes, or by their ends. <margin>B</margin> If these are not present—as they say regarding things without color—what shall we say of white and black? What is this difference? Is it an alteration that makes them different, or will sense-perception tell us, just as reason does? Sense-perception speaks because it does not possess the reason itself, but only reports the differences of qualities. Or must we seek these differences in their simple applications, or in reasons everywhere, so that each thing has its own? The mind does not merely oversee their movements, but distinguishes one from the other, <margin>C</margin> and it requires "otherness" for itself. Therefore, one might ask whether all qualities could be differences. Whiteness, or colors in general, or those things pertaining to smell or taste, might be differences of other things, or they might differ by the fact that one belongs to a grammatical soul and another to a musical one. Or especially if they exist by nature, a specific difference <term>specific difference: the characteristic that distinguishes a species from others in the same genus</term> might arise in some way; and a difference would not arise from this genus, or from another, or from this <margin>D</margin> genus among those in the same genus. For example: qualities of qualities, such as virtue and vice. For one disposition <note>Greek: *hexis*; Latin: *habitus*. A stable state or character trait.</note> is of one kind, and another is of another; and insofar as they are qualities, the differences will be qualities—unless one were to say that the differences of differences are themselves qualities, for it is not unreasonable to accumulate these things as well.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...they may be able properly, nor is it beside the point to divide by those things which they can do. Perhaps one should be cautious <note>Latin: *erubescendum*. Literally "to blush," implying a philosophical difficulty or a point where one must be careful.</note> about those things which do not seem to be divisible by what they can properly do, such as the sciences; but let those things which are open to the senses be divided by what they produce. For while we arrange the sciences through various powers of the soul—as if they consist of being diverse based on these things they do—we can meanwhile <margin>B</margin> take their differences by reason, not only looking at what they are concerned with, but looking into their inner principles (*rationes*). Or perhaps we can easily distinguish the arts by certain of their own reasons and notions? But the qualities implanted in bodies—in what way are we able to divide them similarly? And yet, even in the superior nature <note>Refers to the Intelligible realm, the world of pure Forms above the physical world.</note>, one may ask how those very reasons are distinguished among themselves: for it is clear that white differs from black, but we are inquiring into *how* it differs.

*Sensible species of things are distinguished among themselves through differences—internal ones indeed, and in some way even through external ones. But the differences themselves are not distinguished through other differences, but through themselves in turn. Chapter XVIII.*

*Qualities are discerned from one another not through other qualities, but either entirely through themselves or through certain modes of their existence.*

<margin>A</margin> All these things which just now came into doubt for us clearly show that the differences of other things must be sought, by which we may discern individual things from one another. But to demand differences of differences is something we neither can nor should do by any reasoning. For it cannot happen that we investigate the substances of substances, the quantities of quantities, the qualities of qualities, or the differences of differences. Instead, <margin>B</margin> it is necessary, wherever possible, to divide things by what is external to them, or by their effective condition, or by some such factor. Where these are not available, let the distinction be made just as one distinguishes green from pale. But since they say that a thing is also discerned from white and black, what shall we say? These differences among themselves are announced to us by sense or by intellect, even if they do not provide a logical reason. Sense indeed does its part, because it is not its office to provide a reason, but <margin>C</margin> only to bring us the evidence of differences; the intellect, however, can discern them by its own simple intuition. For the intellect does not use logical reasons everywhere, so as to say of each thing, "this is this." There is surely in the very movements of intelligence a certain "otherness" <note>Greek: *heterotes*. One of the "Great Kinds" in Platonic philosophy, the principle that allows things to be distinct from one another.</note> that divides one from another, without that otherness itself needing a further difference. One may therefore ask whether all qualities are differences or not; yet it does not seem so. For whiteness and colors in general, and those things which pertain to touch or taste, can become the differences <margin>D</margin> of other things, even though they exist as species in their own right. But what of Grammar and Music? Perhaps they can be differences because one makes the soul "grammatical" and the other "musical," especially if they are present by nature so that they become specific differences. Furthermore, it must be considered whether a difference is drawn from the same genus or from another. If it is from the same genus, it must be said that for those things within the same genus, the difference is of that kind—just as qualities are the differences of qualities. For virtue and vice are perhaps related in this way: the former is a certain kind of habit (disposition), while the latter is another. Therefore, since habits are qualities, the differences here will be qualities—unless someone says...

<summary>Plotinus explores how we distinguish between qualities (like colors or arts), arguing that while we use 'differences' to categorize things, those differences themselves are ultimately recognized by simple intuition or their own 'otherness' rather than by further sub-qualities.</summary>

<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the discussion from Chapter 18 regarding whether "differences"—the specific traits that distinguish one thing from another—should be classified within the category of Quality. Plotinus is specifically critiquing and refining the Aristotelian categories.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...that a habit <note>Latin: *habitum*; Greek: *hexis*. A stable disposition or state of being.</note> indeed is not a quality without its difference, but that it is the difference which properly constitutes the quality. But if "sweet" is useful to us and "bitter" is harmful, and they are distinguished in this convenient way, they are distributed by a certain relationship <note>Latin: *habitudine*; Greek: *schesei*.</note> rather than by quality. What if someone says that "sweet" is thick, while "harsh" is thin? Perhaps this "thick" quality does not explain what sweetness *is*, but signifies something by which sweetness exists; and the same reasoning applies to the harsh.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, it must be considered whether the difference of a quality is not everywhere itself a quality, just as a substance is not the difference of a substance, nor a quantity the difference of a quantity. Tell me: do five differ from three by "two"? On the contrary, five exceeds three by two, but they do not differ "by two" in a qualitative sense. For in what way is five separated from three by two, when two is also contained within three? Furthermore, neither does one motion differ from another motion by "motion," nor is any other thing distinguished from another in such a way.

<margin>C</margin> As far as virtue and vice are concerned, one must certainly oppose the whole of one to the whole of the other as being diverse, and thus they will be distinguished from each other by themselves. But if someone divides them from the same genus—namely, from the "qualified"—and does not do so by chance, but by conceding that one is concerned with pleasures, another with anger, and another with the care of fruits; and if he admits that they are thus rightly distinguished, it follows that there are differences which are not themselves qualities.

---

->*In the genus of quality, quality itself is primarily placed, such as beauty; secondarily, that which is endowed with quality, in the sense that it is affected by it, such as "the beautiful." Thirdly, qualities of this kind are motions, such as what is expressed by the adverb "beautifully." Negations of qualities or motions toward them are not placed in this genus. Chapter XIX.*<-

<margin>A</margin> Furthermore, we must accommodate to the genus of quality, as has been seen, those things which are named "qualified" <note>Latin: *quales*; Greek: *poious*. Things possessing a quality, like "a white object" vs. "whiteness."</note> through their qualities, insofar as a quality is present in them. Yet we ought not to apply them properly, lest there appear to be two categories; rather, we should call ourselves back from the things to that very quality from which they are named. But regarding what is called "not white": if it signifies another color, it is in the genus of quality; but if it is merely a negation denying the things themselves, or a certain enumeration, it is nothing other than a voice, or a name, or a speech, which also appears to be a certain thing, and the same applies to the thing itself.

<margin>B</margin> And if it is indeed a voice, it will be a certain motion; but if it is a name or a speech, it will verge toward "relation," insofar as these have the power of signifying. But if such an enumeration is not only of things according to their genus, but it is also necessary that both what is said and what is signified separately signify a certain genus: we shall certainly say that some things only establish the objects themselves by declaring them, while others remove things from the middle. Although perhaps it is better not to count negations of things in the same genus as the things themselves, especially since we do not count certain affirmations either, so that we may avoid a composition of many genera.

<margin>C</margin> What then shall we say of privations? <note>Latin: *privationibus*; Greek: *stereseis*. The absence of a quality that should naturally be present.</note> Certainly, if those things whose privations are mentioned are qualities, then the privations themselves are qualities, such as "toothless" or "blind." Yet, in truth, "naked" and "clothed" are neither properly "qualified," but are rather said to be "in a certain state" <note>Latin: *sese habens*; Greek: *pos echon*. One of the four Stoic categories, referring to a relative disposition.</note>;

<meta>catchword: therefore</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...that a habit <note>original Greek: *hexin*</note> is not a quality without its difference, but that the difference makes the quality. But if the sweet is beneficial and the bitter is harmful, is the quality divided by a relation <note>original Greek: *schesei*</note>, or because the sweet is thick and the harsh is thin? Or does the sweet say it is "thick" only insofar as it is sweet, and likewise for the harsh? In this way, there is a reason such that, if the difference of quality is not everywhere a quality,

<margin>B</margin> just as substance is not the difference of substance, nor quantity of quantity, or as five differs from three by two—or rather exceeds by two. A "difference" is not spoken of here; for how could it differ by "two" when two is in three? But neither does motion differ by motion, and in no other case is there such a difference. Regarding virtue and vice, one must take the whole of it as a whole, and thus they are distinguished by their own properties. To make the division from the same genus, not by chance but by the division of the other, is to say that one is

<margin>C</margin> about pleasures, another about angers, and one about the juice of fruit; and if you accept these as well-defined, it is clear that there are still differences that are not qualities.

---

<margin>A</margin> Regarding quality, one must arrange, as it seemed fit, those things called "qualified" <note>original Greek: *poious*</note> according to them, insofar as quality is around them. Or perhaps they should not be arranged with them, so that there are not two categories. Rather, one should go to the quality from which they are named. As for "not white," if it signifies another color, it is a quality; but if it is only a negation of things or an enumeration, it would be nothing unless it were a voice, or a name, or a speech; and it participates in

<margin>B</margin> the things themselves. If it is a voice, it is a motion. If it is a name or a speech, it is a relative, insofar as it is significant. If the enumeration is not only of things and the genus, but it is also necessary that the things said and the things signifying explain what genus each is significant of, some are set down as only manifesting the thing itself, and others as negating them. For it is perhaps better not to count their negations, because of the

<margin>C</margin> definition, but how should we treat privations? If privations are privations of quality, they are themselves certain qualities. But the "blind man," or the "naked," or the "clothed," is neither "qualified" <note>original Greek: *poios*</note>, but rather "being in a certain state."

# BOOK THREE.

<column-break/>

...in a certain relationship looking toward something else. An affection <note>original: *passio*; Greek: *pathos*. In this context, it refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force.</note> that is still in the act of being felt is not yet a quality, but rather a kind of motion. However, that which is derived from the affection—meaning someone has already undergone the experience and now holds the affection as a permanent state—is rightly judged to be a quality. If, however, the affection is no longer present, though the person is said to have "gone through it," it is properly said that they were "moved" or changed. This is the same as saying: "this thing was in motion." One must conceive of motion here simply by removing the element of time; for the present moment is not to be adjusted for this. Furthermore, terms like "beautifully" or "well," and others of that kind, should be reduced to the single notion of the genus. It is worth considering whether we should refer to the genus of quality the act of "reddening" <note>original: *rubere*</note>, or "red," or perhaps "the one turning red" <note>original: *rubescentem*</note> not at all? Certainly, the act of "reddening" is not rightly reduced to that genus. For he who is reddening is undergoing a process or is entirely in motion. But if he is no longer reddening, or even if he is still reddening but is already "red," why should he not be considered "qualified"? We should not define "the qualified" by a specific time, but rather evaluate it by its state. Therefore, when we say someone is "red" or "reddening," we are describing their quality. Otherwise, we would think only stable habits <note>original: *habitus*; Greek: *hexis*</note> are qualities, while temporary dispositions are not; thus, a man would be "qualified" because he is hot, but not while he is in the process of heating up; similarly, a man would be "qualified" because he is weak, but not while he is falling into weakness.

---

*We ought not to define those qualities as contraries only which are furthest apart from each other, but simply those which, while belonging to the same genus of quality, share no similarity in species and offer us opposite effects. Chapter XX.*

*By this reasoning, health and disease—between which there is no middle ground—are contraries. Where middle qualities are set apart from the extremes, they cannot be contrary to those extremes, such as whiteness. However, where there is no comparison, virtue can exist among diseases <note>The text here is difficult to read; it suggests that virtue stands as an absolute</note>. Where a quality consists in a certain individual proportion of truth, it does not admit of "more" or "less," such as harmony, temperance, justice, and health. But where it possesses a scale of degrees, it does admit them, such as heat and cold.*

<margin>A</margin> One must observe whether perhaps every quality does not have another quality as its contrary. Indeed, regarding virtue and vice, a middle quality seems to be contrary to the extremes. But regarding colors, the middle colors do not seem to be contrary in this way. If it were said that this happens because middle colors are nothing other than mixtures of the extremes, then one ought not to divide the middle and extremes so sharply, but rather divide the genus of color by white and black, and consider the others to be certain compositions of these. Or, one might distinguish them so that it is clear we are opposing one quality to another. But if they say middle colors are not contrary to extremes because contraries must not only differ but be as distant as possible, one must ask where this idea of "maximum distance" comes from, since middle states are already positioned between them.

<margin>B</margin> For if one removes such a disposition, I do not know by what standard one would define the greatest difference. But if they say the cause is that yellow <note>original: *luteum*; Greek: *phaion* (grey/dusky)</note> is closer to white than to black, this is certainly what our senses tell us, and we see the same in men.

<margin>C</margin> In the same way, regarding flavors: there is hot, cold, and that which is neither, being in the middle. It is clearly established that we have become accustomed to thinking this way, and perhaps anyone would concede these points to us. But white and yellow, or whatever else is similarly opposed...

they seem to differ among themselves: and since there is a difference, 
<margin>A</margin> such things are like contraries. For it is not properly from the fact that something stands as a medium <note>original: *medium*; a middle ground or intermediate state</note> between these that they are contraries; rather, the specific contrariety between them must be judged on its own. Indeed, between health and disease nothing comes in between as a medium, yet they are nonetheless contraries to one another. Or perhaps they are judged as contraries for this reason: because the things that arise from either one differ to the greatest extent? But in what way 
<margin>B</margin> is it permitted to assert the greatest distance there, where there are no smaller intermediate steps anywhere? It is not possible, therefore, to affirm a "greatest distance" regarding health and disease. From this it is clear that the very thing called a "contrary" must be defined by something other than a "greatest span" or distance. Therefore, if it is determined by "muchness," we must ask whether this "muchness" is taken in the sense of "more" as opposed to "less," or rather as that which is simply "much." If it is taken in the first way, then those things which lack a medium 
<margin>C</margin> will immediately escape the definition of contrariety. But if it is taken in the second way—while it is easily conceded that every nature stands at a "great distance" from another, yet it is not granted that this distance is measured by some specific "more"—we must consider entirely how something is weighed as a contrary. For then, should we not deny that things which have a certain similarity are contraries? I do not mean similarity merely according to genus, nor even entirely because they are mixed with other forms (whether more or fewer of them); rather, I mean that those things 
<margin>D</margin> to which nothing identical is present according to their species are rightly judged to be contraries—but with the addition that they must, of course, be in the same genus of <term>Quality</term> <note>quality refers to the characteristics or "suchness" of a thing, like its color or state of health</note>. Hence one may certainly assert that those things which we encounter as contraries without any medium are those in which nothing appears to be present that contributes to similarity. For there, no other things exist which, by converging toward a single point, might have or reconcile a mutual similarity; rather, they are simply things that do not have it. If this is so, colors in which there is something common will by no means be contraries. Yet nothing will prevent not every thing from being contrary to every other thing, but one thing to another in this way; and similarly among humors <note>the bodily fluids in ancient medicine</note> and flavors. But concerning these matters, the doubt stands thus far. Furthermore, it is usually asked whether quality admits of the "more and the less" or not. And it is certainly conceded that those things which participate in qualities participate in them to a greater or lesser degree. But whether health itself and justice admit of these degrees is still doubted. If, therefore, any of these has its own specific "latitude" <note>original: *latitudinem*; the range or scope within which a quality can vary</note>, it must be granted that these <term>habits</term> <note>original: *habitus*; stable dispositions or states of being</note> also admit of such degrees. But if a quality has no latitude, but each possesses the whole in a certain fixed state, then clearly it admits of neither more nor less.

*We more probably posit <term>Motion</term> <note>original: *motus*; Greek: *kinesis*</note> as a genus rather than <term>Transmutation</term> <note>original: *transmutatio*; change of essence</note>, because transmutation, by changing the nature of a thing, brings forth one thing in place of another. Motion, however, signifies change of this kind, and besides this, it also signifies any progression while the prior nature is meanwhile preserved. Chapter XXI*

---

<margin>A</margin> **W**hether we ought to assert that motion is a genus <note>a primary category of being</note> or not, we may contemplate in this manner: it can certainly be a genus under this condition. First, if it is not fitting to reduce motion into any other genus; second, if nothing higher than motion is predicated of it in terms of "what it is"; furthermore, if, by receiving many differences, it produces species from itself. Come then, tell me: into what genus could you most likely reduce motion? For it is neither substance,

contraries, or if it is by their very being, then there is a medium between them. But the contrariety of these—take health and disease for instance—has nothing falling in between, and yet they are contraries. Or is it that the things arising from each have the greatest variation? And how can one speak of "greatest" when there are no "lesser" things in the middle? It is not possible, then, in the case of 
<margin>B</margin> health and disease, to speak of "greatest." Rather, we must define the contrary by that which is "most." If it is by the "much"—if "much" means their being "more" in relation to one another—again, those without a medium will escape the definition. But if it is simply "much," granted that each thing is by nature far removed, we should not measure the distance by the "more." Instead, we must examine how something is a contrary. Is it then that those things which

These are the issues; but as for qualities themselves: do they admit the "more"? In the things that participate in them, it is clear; but if we consider health itself and justice, do they have it? If indeed each of these has a "latitude," or if we must speak of the "habits" themselves: is each there a whole, or does it also have the "more"?

### BOOK THREE.

->[Translation of the Greek text in the left column]<-

If, then, there is a capacity for acting, and also a capacity for undergoing, there are many motions. But if, again, these exist within the state of undergoing, the motions are still many, namely actions; thus actions and passions <note>The terms "action" and "passion" refer to the Aristotelian categories of *doing* something and having something *done* to you.</note> would be the same thing. But if, on the other hand, motion is a certain "disposition" <note>original: *pōs ti echon*; a state or way of being</note>, then motion exists in and of itself. Quality would be stable, existing at a limit; for how could quality exist except in something? The same applies to quantity. If those things are certain beings and quantities insofar as one thing undergoes something and the other is a "muchness," the same has been said of those cases. How then is motion? Is it a "relation" <note>original: *pros ti*; toward something</note> before it belongs to a specific thing? Or, if it is taken as existing by itself, or not placed in relation to anything at all, it does not exist—unless it is something else, a "subsistence" or "offshoot," then it is spoken of as one thing instead of another through a relationship. For example, the "double" is called "double" in comparison to the "one-cubit" length; it receives its generation and subsistence there. One would think nothing <margin>regarding these *</margin> * exists by nature except in comparison to another. For what is the "being" of that which is not a "this"? Or how do quality and quantity have other states? Or, above all, should we assume that no genus is predicated before it? But if someone says that change <note>original: *metabolē*</note> exists before motion, first, what kind of change do they mean? If they call it a "genus," they would be making it something beyond what was previously stated. Then, clearly, in cases where motion follows, they will establish something else as motion, perhaps "generation." Let every change be a moving thing, but not every change a "motion." Why then is motion or generation distinct? Perhaps some are motions regarding a "how" toward that which is becoming, while others are motions regarding "quality," and these are also changes. Should "generation" still be spoken of? Is it because generation exists, and is something other than "alteration" or "growth," because generation occurs when things are altered or grown? It takes up what exists before the generation. But because of the generation in these, should one take it as something else? If things are altered "passively," then the "becoming" is the generation. <margin>Concerning generation</margin> For example, becoming hot or becoming white. For let us say it has become so, but "simple generation" has not yet occurred. But what is becoming? That which is completed. But when an animal or plant is formed, when it receives a certain form <note>original: *eidos*</note>, which change would one rather name it? Should it be placed in "form" or in "motion"? It requires change, but the "quality of the form" signifies something other than the motion; it has its change in "moving out of the house," just like local motion.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Nor can you reduce motion <term>motus: in this context, change or movement in a broad philosophical sense</term> to action: for there are many motions within passion <note>original: *passione*; the state of being acted upon</note> as well. Nor, again, can you reduce it to passion, since many motions are actions. It is more probable that actions and passions are referred back to motion, but this is not necessary if action is correctly defined. This is because motion is not of itself, nor in itself, but rather belongs to someone and exists in something. In this way, quality would also be placed in the category of relation: for quality belongs to someone and is in something, and quantity is the same way. If, to 
<margin>B</margin>
this, it is responded that those things are properly certain "beings" <note>original: *entia*</note> even if they belong to something—insofar as this one is a quality and that one is a quantity—then by the same reasoning, since motion belongs to something, it must be something before it belongs to anyone. Therefore, we must properly assume that this very thing which exists is, in a way, in itself. Generally, however, a "relative" <term>relatiuum: a category of being defined only in relation to something else, like "taller" or "double"</term> must be properly defined not as something that is first what it is and then belongs to another, but as something that is generated within the relationship itself, with 
<margin>C</margin>
nothing else existing there at all besides the relationship. For instance, the "double" is said to be double in the very comparison to the "half," receiving its generation and subsistence there. Before this, nothing is conceived at all; it only gains its name and its existence in the comparison to the other. What then is this thing? That which, while existing for another, is nevertheless something itself so that it may also belong to another: just like quality, quantity, and essence. But perhaps it is better first to 
<margin>D</margin>
assert that nothing is predicated of it as a genus before itself. But if someone objects that "transmutation" <note>original: *transmutatio*; a general term for change or shifting</note> exists before motion, they will either be saying the same thing entirely, or, by calling that a "genus," they will cause a certain other genus to exist besides those ten categories <note>Referring to Aristotle’s ten categories: Substance, Quantity, Quality, Relation, Place, Time, Position, State, Action, and Passion.</note>. Then, without controversy, they will place motion into a certain species, and setting up something else in opposition, they will oppose it to motion—perhaps "generation," saying that it is indeed a transmutation, 
<margin>E</margin>
but not a motion. What, then, prevents generation from being a motion? For if it is said that it is prevented because that which is being "begotten" <note>original: *gignitur*</note> does not yet exist—and motion cannot exist around a non-entity—we will say it follows from this that generation is not even a transmutation. But if it is asserted, on the other hand, that generation is nothing other than "alteration" <term>alteratio: change in quality, like turning from cold to hot</term> or a certain change and some "increase," because generation belongs to things that have been changed or altered and 
<margin>F</margin>
somehow increased, then surely the one who says this brings to light the things that precede generation. But in these cases, one must accept "generation" as another species: for generation and being begotten does not consist in the fact that something is altered "passively" in some way, such as being heated or being whitened. For it can happen that these things have already occurred, yet "simple generation" was not yet there. And if you ask what we then say is happening, we will answer: this very thing that we say is being altered, or has been altered. But generation only finally occurs when an animal is made, or a plant, or similar things—namely, when a certain "form" <note>original: *species* or *eidos*</note> is taken up there. Therefore, anyone will be able to assert that it is consistent with reason to place transmutation, rather than motion, into a species; for the condition of transmutation signifies one thing becoming in place of another, whereas the nature of motion also involves a certain passage from its own state, just like local motion <note>movement from one place to another</note>.

### PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

If someone should prefer otherwise, at least the act of learning itself, or the striking of the lyre, or in general any movement from a state of rest, will be of this kind. Therefore, change itself—or transformation involving a certain motion—setting aside something of itself, would rather be a species of change.

---

->*Common to all motions is a certain perfection <note>original: "perfectio"; here meaning "completion" or "actualization"</note> from potentiality into act, whether this act is primary, such as a form, or secondary, such as various active states. Motion proceeding into a natural habit <note>original: "habitum"; a settled state or disposition</note> brings it forth; it can be said that what acts upon a habit contrary to nature involves the fall of one thing into what is foreign to another. However, motion is very much like the thing itself; but most truly, the specific property of motion is "otherness"—that is, to hold oneself differently than before—which is consequently also a property of time. Chapter XXII.*<-

---

BUT let this be the notion of transformation or "otherness," insofar as one thing follows after the motion: what, then, must we say motion is? Motion will therefore be—as we have been speaking of this in a certain figure for some time—the exit from potentiality <note>original: "potentia" / "dynamis"</note> into that which is said to be "possible." For when something exists in potentiality, through which it may come forth into some form—just as a statue exists potentially—and again, when something is in potentiality so that it may turn into an act <note>original: "actus" / "energeia"</note>, such as in the case of progressions: when that thing proceeds toward being a statue, the process itself is the motion. And when it carries out the act of progressing, the progression itself is the motion: just as a leap is in one who is able to leap, when they are already leaping. 

Yet, in a certain motion—specifically that which leads to a statue—the form that the motion introduces is one thing; but in another motion, such as in a leap, the leaping itself is a kind of simple form of the "leaping-capable" person, and has nothing remaining after itself once the motion itself has ceased. Why then, if <insert>anyone</insert> should call motion a "wakeful" and "arousing" form—set in opposition to other forms that are, as it were, sluggish—insofar as some are what they are, while others are by no means so; and if they should call it the cause of the other forms, since after it everything here is brought about, they would not be wandering far from the truth of motion. 

If someone, moreover, were to call this motion of which we are currently speaking a certain "vice of bodies," they would not seem to be far from the truth. For we ought to call this motion equivocal to the motions of the mind and the soul. Furthermore, one might persuade oneself that motion is a genus <note>original: "genus"; a primary category of being</note> for this very reason: that it is neither easy, nor perhaps possible, to encompass it in a definition. But how then is motion a species when it slides into the worse, or when motion is entirely a "passion" <note>original: "passio"; the state of being acted upon</note>? Perhaps this is much like how heating under the sun increases some things but diminishes others; the motion itself is something common and the same in both, but it receives a seeming difference according to the subjects. But from this, it seems we must also read the same regarding falling ill and recovering. Truly, insofar as they are a certain motion, they appear to be the same; but in what do they differ? Is it in the subjects, or rather in something else? But these things will be treated in what follows, when we consider alteration; for now, we must observe that something is the same in all motions: for in this way, it could be a genus. But perhaps it is spoken of in many ways, and it holds itself just as if someone were to say that "becoming" is a genus. Looking back again at this—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But if someone should not want this, but rather the act of learning and the playing of the lyre, he who looks at the actual movement would find it to be nothing other than a motion, or rather an "alteration" <note>original: "alloiōsis"</note>, being a certain displacement of motion.

But let there be the same thing understood in alteration, according to the fact that "something else" follows the motion. But what are we to say motion is? Let motion be, to speak in a general outline, the path from potentiality <note>original: "ek dynameōs hodos"</note> toward that which is called potential; for whenever that which was potential in some way becomes a certain form—for example, the statue in potentiality—and again, let it be in actuality <note>original: "energeia"</note>, such as walking. When it proceeds toward being a statue, <margin>B</margin> the progression is the motion; and in the act of walking, the walking itself is the motion, or the prior movement, yet it leaves nothing behind when it is completed. And while in the motion toward the statue another form is added which is the result of the motion, in the other case, such as dancing, the motion is in the potential; it has nothing after it when the motion ceases. If anyone should say that motion is a "wakeful form" <note>original: "eidos egrēgoros"</note> <margin>C</margin> compared to other forms that are standing and not merely abiding, and the cause for other forms when something is made after it, they would not be far from us. 

If someone were to speak of bodies, the same regarding the expectation of motion, and to say that motion is spoken of equivocally with the motions of the soul; yet it is a genus, even if the cause is no more than the fact that it is not easy to grasp it by a definition <margin>D</margin> for its own sake, one might believe it. But how could it be a species, if motion is toward the worse, or when it is a "passive" motion, or similar to heating? For heating by the sun increases one thing but leads its opposite to the contrary; and motion is something common or the same in both, while the underlying subjects have the difference that appears. Healing, therefore, or sickening, are the same insofar as they are motion; but how are they different? Is it by the <margin>E</margin> subjects or by something else? But this we shall consider later when we examine alteration; for now, we must look at what is the same in every motion. For in this way it would be a genus, or again it might be spoken of in many forms, just as if it were "Being" itself. And again, toward—

It transitions from Chapter 22 into Chapter 23.</meta>

# BOOK THREE

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Regarding the doubts that were recently raised, it seems necessary to say that perhaps all motions that lead a thing toward its natural state, or at least act within those things that are according to nature, should rightly be categorized as specific kinds of motion, as has been said. However, transitions toward something contrary to nature <note>original: "praeter naturam" / "para physin"</note> should be categorized by a certain analogy or proportion to the states they lead toward. But what is the common element in alteration, growth, and generation, and their opposites? And again, what is common to change of place, insofar as all these are "motions"? <margin>B</margin>Indeed, for all things that move, this seems to be the primary commonality: that each thing being moved is not afterwards in the same state it was in before, nor does it rest, nor remain entirely idle. Rather, as long as motion is present, it is always being led toward something else. It always has "otherness" <term>alteritas: the state of being different or "other" than before</term> as its companion, <margin>C</margin>precisely because it never remains the same. Otherwise, the motion would immediately vanish if it ever ceased to move from one state to another. For this reason, otherness exists in motion—not because something has already become a finished act and is now at rest in a new state, but in such a way that a perpetual otherness is being carried out. From this, it follows that time is also always "other," since motion generates it. For motion, not resting but being continually measured by its flow, produces time; thus, time runs along with motion itself, as if carried by the very thing that flows. Finally, it is common to all motions to be a certain process and leading-forth from potentiality <note>original: "potentia" / "dynamis"</note>—that is, from what is possible—into actuality <note>original: "actus" / "energeia"</note>. For whatever moves, whatever sort of motion it undergoes, proceeds into that motion because a certain potentiality exists within it beforehand to do or to undergo something.

<column-break/>

---

->*Motion is like a certain stimulus verging toward various modes of action, habits, and various forms; by this variety, living things achieve a likeness to life itself. The knowledge of this motion, like life itself, is invisible.*<-
->*Motion, though resting in itself and invisible, is perceived through variety. Motion depends indeed upon a mover and ends in the movable, appearing as an overflow of the mover. From this, the differences of motions must be understood from both sides.*<-

->### Cap. XXIII.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Now, the motion that concerns sensible things <note>physical things we can perceive with our senses</note> is a certain stimulus or impulse verging from one thing to another, both exciting and impelling it. It allows the participant of the motion not to grow sluggish nor remain in the same state, so that through such a restlessness—and a concern distracted, as it were, by many things—it may achieve a certain image of life. We must not think, however, that the things being moved are themselves the motion. For walking is not the feet; rather, walking is a certain act arising from potentiality concerning the feet. <margin>B</margin>Since potentiality is not visible, it is necessary that we only see the feet in action. I do not mean simply the feet as if they were at rest, but the feet joined with something else—namely, the power of movement—which is itself invisible. Because this power is joined with the feet, we see them occupy one place after another by happenstance, never resting anywhere. Furthermore, we usually notice "alteration" <note>change in quality, like color or heat</note> because something is being altered; we see this because the quality we sense there is no longer the same. <margin>C</margin>In what, then, does motion reside when it moves something else, and when it proceeds from an internal potentiality into act? Does it reside in the mover? But if that were so, how would the thing that is moved and undergoes the change become a participant in the motion? Is it then rather in the thing being moved? But if so, why does it not remain there once it has proceeded? Surely, motion must neither be totally detached from the mover, nor stay entirely within it, but must emanate from the mover into the other.

<column-break/>

nor is it separated from the mover in any other thing; rather, it flows from the mover into the moved like a breath of spirit <note>original: "velut spiritum afflatu"</note>. Therefore, when the power of moving is progressive, it pushes, as it were, so that it constantly changes from one place to another. But when the power is a heating one, it heats immediately, and the motion there is an alteration. When that same faculty is joined to matter, occupying it through a natural state of growth, it is called "augmentation." But when another force takes something away, "decrement" occurs in that which is capable of being diminished. Likewise, where the <margin>C</margin> generative power acts, "generation" occurs; but when this force is sent in such a way that it overpowers the thing and causes it to perish, "destruction" follows—not destruction of what is already finished and completed, I say, but of that which is still in the process of becoming. Similarly, recovery occurs when the power capable of producing health acts and dominates, while illness happens when a contrary power does the opposite. Indeed, every motion seems to exist only in itself, yet it depends on those things in which it occurs, as well as those from which it arises and through which it is transmitted. The specific character of motion itself is a kind of habit, being such as it is within such things.

*Local motions appear to differ from one another either by the fixed boundaries they seek—such as ascent and descent, departure and return—or by the shape of their progression, such as straight and circular. Chapter XXIV.*

<margin>A</margin> BUT regarding linear motion, it is ambiguous how the difference should be understood: whether moving upward is contrary to moving downward, or whether circular motion is contrary to straight motion. For instance, if someone is thrown over the head or beneath the feet, the impulsive power is the same—unless one were to say that the power which pushes upward is one thing, and the power that pushes downward is another. One might have a tendency toward the void, striving for the higher region, while the other moves toward the interior, <margin>B</margin> especially if something moves this way by nature—since in the former there is lightness, and in the latter, gravity. Nevertheless, the common element in these is the same: to be carried to a place not its own. Here, therefore, it appears that the difference in motions is taken from external factors. Indeed, in circular and straight motion, if the same soul acts now straightly and now circularly, how can the motion be different? Or perhaps the difference is taken from the shape of the progression itself? Unless someone were to contend that <margin>C</margin> moving in a circle is a "state of position," as if it were not motion at all since it does not change its place entirely. But in the end, local motion seems to be one thing in itself, taking its differences only from external circumstances.

*Combination and separation are motions differing from all other motions, and even from qualities. From the aforementioned combinations and separations, local motion occurs, as well as alteration, generation, augmentation, and their opposites. Chapter XXV.*

Or should we perhaps reduce these to the aforementioned motions in some way? Or rather, should we assert that from these motions certain different "combinations" exist? If combination consists in one thing approaching and nearing another, and again separation consists in those which were near receding from there, these will be called local motions—namely, while there is either a motion toward one point or a withdrawal from one point. Finally, regarding growth, alteration, and generation, one can distinguish them by whether they occur in a natural or non-natural way, or even by the variety of the subjects involved.

---

Stability exists in eternal things, where there is no motion; in temporal things, it is a certain privation of some motion, or a very slow movement. ### Chapter XXVII.

---

Since, therefore, "quiet" <note>original: "quies"; Greek: "heremia"</note> is a certain privation, it is not a genus in itself. Motion, however, is not simply the privation of quiet; rather, it is an effective act that removes something and brings something new. "Stability" <note>original: "status"; Greek: "stasis"</note> in eternal things is not a privation of motion, for stability does not occur there because motion has ceased, nor are those eternal things naturally suited for motion. Motion has two opposites: another motion that seeks different goals, and rest—especially if rest is considered at the starting point from which the motion has already departed.

---

Regarding "stability" <term>status: refers to the unchanging, permanent state of divine or intellectual realities</term> which is the opposite of motion, or regarding "quiet" <term>quies: refers to the temporary stillness of physical objects in the material world</term>, what ought to be said? Must this also be established as a single genus? Or should it rather be reduced to one of the categories I have already described? It is perhaps better to grant "stability" itself to divine things and to investigate "quiet" here in the physical world. 

Regarding this quiet, we must first investigate what it is: if it is found to be entirely the same as stability, it would seem improper to seek it here in the physical realm, since here nothing remains entirely still; rather, what seems to be standing still is actually being carried along by a slower motion. But if we say that "quiet" is something other than "stability"—because stability concerns a thing that is completely immobile, while quiet concerns a thing that is currently standing still but is naturally suited to move—then we must make a distinction. 

Indeed, if "becoming quiet" is assumed here, the act of "resting" will be said to be a motion that has not yet ceased but is ongoing. If, however, we assume this refers to that which no longer exists around the thing being moved, we must certainly ask if anything among us is entirely unmoved. But if it is impossible for something not to be moved by all motions at once, so that we may at least say this thing which is moved *exists*, what else should be said of that which is not moved in place, but as far as this specific motion pertains is at rest, except that it is "not being moved"? In this way, quiet will be the negation of motion. That which is of this kind is not properly counted as a genus. Furthermore, a thing "rests" only in relation to a specific kind of motion, such as local motion <note>movement from place to place</note>. Quiet, therefore, signifies only the privation of this specific movement. 

If someone should ask why we do not conversely say that motion is the privation of stability or quiet, we shall answer: because motion clearly approaches bringing something with it; it exists as something acting upon and shaking the subject, producing and destroying many things. Quiet, on the other hand, signifies only that the subject does not have motion. But why not consider if, among the things pertaining to the intellect—

Of the motions, are they differences of motions, or are they qualities of motions themselves, and not [produced] by these? And nature seems to be the principle of these, either for those by nature, those by art, or those by choice. By nature: growth, decay. By art: building, shipbuilding. 

<margin>B</margin> By choice: considering, learning, acting in the city. In short, speaking, acting. Regarding growth and alteration, and generation, both according to nature, or contrary to nature. Or generally by the subjects.

<margin>A</margin> CONCERNING stability, or that which is opposed to motion, namely stillness <note>Greek: 'heremia'</note>, what must be said? Whether this too must be placed as a certain genus, or must be reduced to one of the aforementioned genera? It is perhaps better to place stability there <note>in the intelligible realm</note>, and to seek stillness here <note>in the physical realm</note>. As for this stillness, we must first seek what it is. And if it appears the same as stability, perhaps it would not be sought here in the same way, as if it were immobile. 

<margin>B</margin> But things appearing to stand, using a slower motion, if we should call stillness something different from stability—the one, stability, being about that which is entirely immobile, and the other, stillness, being about that which has stood, but is naturally disposed to move when it is not moving—or to say that "becoming still" is a stillness-motion, 

<margin>C</margin> not yet ceased but present; but if it is no longer about the thing moving, when, we must seek if there is anything not moving here. And if it is not possible to be moved by all motions, but certain motions do not move, yes, that regarding place; but as for being a certain thing moving, what else must be said of that which is not moving according to place, but is stilling this motion, than that it is not moving? 

<margin>D</margin> Stillness, then, is a negation; how can it be a genus? It is still by nothing else than according to that motion, such as the local one. It does not even speak of a removal for this. But if someone should say: why shall we not say that motion is a negation of stability? We shall say because motion comes bringing something. It is something else acting and, as it were, pushing the subject, and working myriad things on it, and destroying it. But stillness in each case is nothing besides this, but signifies only that it does not have motion. What then? Is it also among the things of the mind—

[...each of those things pertaining to intelligence, there is nothing besides itself, but this...]

### BOOK THREE.
