...we might call it a denial of motion, or say that stability is the removal of motion; or perhaps it is the same as motion itself, but just as the soul is naturally suited to move, so it is suited for this. Insofar as it does not move there, stability exists; but insofar as stability has taken hold, it stands firm. Yet, insofar as it is a thing in motion, it will move. Therefore, it both stands firm in its stability and moves in its motion. In our world, however, a thing moves through motion, and in the absence of motion, it rests, being deprived of the movement it ought to have. Next, we must see what this stability itself is. We should also observe whether a transition from sickness to health is "health" itself, or whether there is a specific type of rest opposed to this recovery. For if we look at the state from which it departs, that is sickness, not stability; but if we look at the state toward which it goes, that is health. These are identical by nature. But if someone says that health or sickness is a form of stability, they would be claiming that health and sickness are species of stability—which is absurd. But if one admits that stability simply happens to accompany health, then health would not be health before it achieved stability. But regarding these matters, let each person speak according to their own judgment.

## EPILOGUE ON THE PREDICAMENTS <note>The "Predicaments" or "Categories" are Aristotle's classification of all things that can be said about a subject. Plotinus is concluding his review of them here.</note>.

It has been said that acting and being acted upon <note>original: "poiein" and "paschein"</note> must be called motions. We have said that some motions are absolute, while others are actions and others are passions. Regarding the other so-called genera, we have said they relate back to these. Concerning "relation" <note>original: "pros ti"</note>, we noted that it is the reference of one thing to another, and that both must exist together. We also discussed relation in cases where a reference itself constitutes a substance; in such cases, the thing is a relation not because of its substance, but because it is a part—such as a hand, a head, a cause, a principle, or an element. It is also possible to divide relations in the manner of the ancients <note>referring to earlier Greek philosophers like Aristotle</note>: some as productive, others as measures; some based on excess and deficiency, and others distinguished by similarities and differences. Let these remarks on these genera suffice.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> In these cases, we assert that stability is the privation of motion. Because it is not proper to call stability the "privation" of motion <note>Plotinus is careful with the word "privation" (lack), as it usually implies something is missing that should be there; in the divine realm, "rest" is a positive perfection, not a lack of movement.</note>: since stability does not arise simply because motion stops, but when the one exists, the other is motion. Nor is there "rest" there simply because something naturally suited for motion is not moving. Rather, by the reason that stability there grasps the intelligible itself, it remains permanent; but insofar as it moves, it will move forever. Therefore, it both stays firm in stability and moves in motion. 

<margin>B</margin> Corporeal nature <note>the physical world</note>, however, moves in motion, and in the absence of motion it rests, being deprived of its due movement. Furthermore, we must see what stability itself is: for instance, when someone arrives at health from a state of sickness, they recover. What kind of quiet shall we oppose to this recovery? For if the condition from which they depart is that sickness, it is not "stability"; and if the condition they approach is health, that health is not the same thing as stability. If someone were to say that health or sickness is a certain "state" or "stability," 

<margin>C</margin> he would certainly have to concede that health and sickness are species of stability—which is judged to be absurd. But if he confesses that stability merely happens to belong to health, then health before stability would not be health. But regarding these things, let each speak according to their own judgment.

## EPILOGUE ON THE PREDICAMENTS.

We have stated in the preceding sections that "to act" and "to suffer" <note>meaning to be acted upon</note> are motions. Some motions are absolute, while others are partly actions and partly passions. Furthermore, it was said that the other categories we discuss ought to be referred to these ones of ours. We also spoke about relation: namely, that it is the habit or connection of one thing to another, and that both occur simultaneously. Finally, concerning relation, when the connection itself constitutes the substance, then the thing referred to is a "relative" not because of its nature as a substance, but because it is a part—such as a hand, or a head, or a cause, or a principle, or an element. One may also divide relations according to the custom of the ancients: so that some are as if they were productive, others are like measures; some consist in excess and deficiency, and others are distinguished by similarities and differences. But let these things said about these genera be sufficient.

Here, Plotinus shifts his focus to the fundamental Neoplatonic problem of how the Soul or "Being"—which is immaterial and one—can be present throughout the entire physical world without being physically divided or spread thin.</meta>

## ENNEAD SIX.
### BOOK IV.

# PLOTINUS
## SIXTH ENNEAD.
### BOOK IV.

->Concerning the fact that Being, one and the same, is everywhere present as a whole.<-
->That Being, one and the same, is simultaneously a whole everywhere.<-

> *Since the soul neither possesses quantity nor undergoes the qualities of the body, the question is asked how it is diffused through a great deal of space, as it were; whether it exists by itself before the body, or whether it is propagated along with the body and within the body itself to that extent. Chapter I.*

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' used at the start of both the Latin and Greek columns. The letter is surrounded by intricate floral vine-work and flanked by two naked cherubs or putti who appear to be supporting or playing with the foliage.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin>Is the soul present everywhere because it is present to the universe, since the body is called a "whole"? Does its nature, which is divided among bodies, exist everywhere because of itself? Or rather, is it not because it is stretched out by the body, but because the body finds the soul already present everywhere before it? Thus, wherever a body is placed, it finds the soul already existing there, even before that part of the body was situated in a portion of the universe; and the whole body of the universe is placed within a soul that already exists. But if the soul was so widely diffused before such a large body arrived—if the soul, I say, filled the entire interval—what prevents it from having magnitude <note>Magnitude refers to physical size or extension in space.</note>? Or what manner would there be for it to exist in the universe before the universe was made, when this universe did not yet exist? <margin>B</margin> On the contrary, what condition would allow one to admit that the soul itself—which is said to be in parts and yet devoid of magnitude—is everywhere, when it has no physical size? And even if it is said to be extended together with the body, since it is not itself a body, the doubt is not removed by the fact that magnitude is attributed to it by accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has (like being "red" or "large") but which isn't essential to what it is (the "substance").</note>. Indeed, one might rightly ask here as well: in what way can it accidentally become large? <margin>C</margin> For it will not become a quality, like sweetness or heat, which is extended through the whole body: just so is the soul. For these qualities are certain "passions" <note>Affectations or states</note> of bodies; but it would be strange for the body to possess everything it undergoes in this way, while nothing of that sort exists within the soul itself, since the body is one thing, and the soul is known as something else within the body. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, a quality is necessarily as large as the body is. Add to this that the whiteness of one part does not suffer together with the whiteness of another part; and in a white object, the whiteness in this part is the same according to its species <note>Type or kind</note> as the whiteness in the other part, yet it is not numerically the same <note>Meaning they are two separate instances of "white," like two separate white chairs.</note>. But truly, in the case of the soul, the numerically identical thing that is in the foot is also shown to be in the hand. <margin>E</margin> Furthermore, in qualities, the same thing is considered as if divided.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Is the Soul present everywhere because it is present to the body of the whole universe? Does it have a nature such as to be divided among bodies, and is every part of it everywhere? And even if it were removed from the body, would it still touch the bodies, being itself everywhere? So that wherever a part is placed, it will find the soul already there, even before this part was placed, and before the whole body of the universe was placed in the soul? But <margin>B</margin> if it was already so great before the whole body arrived, filling the whole interval, how is it without magnitude? For how could anyone speak of its presence in the universe before the universe came to be, when the universe did not exist? And how can one accept that something said to be without parts or magnitude is everywhere, while having no size? And if it were said to be extended with the body, though it is not a body, <margin>C</margin> how does this not lead to the difficulty of granting it magnitude by accident? For one might similarly ask here with reason, how is it magnified by accident? For it is surely not like qualities such as sweetness or colors throughout a whole body; so also <margin>D</margin> the Soul. For these are affections of bodies, so that the whole thing that is affected has the affection, and no part is itself a body, or known as such. Therefore, it is also of necessity that another part is unjustly [separate], not suffering with the other; and in other parts, while it is the same in species, it is not the same in number <margin>*</margin> <gloss>the same</gloss> <margin>E</margin> but in the case of the Soul, that which is in the foot and that which is in the hand is the same in number, as our sensations show; and yet in qualities, the same thing is seen as divided. Which indeed agreement and observation demonstrate.

<summary>Plotinus begins an inquiry into how the immaterial Soul can be present throughout a physical body without being divided into pieces or possessing physical size. He argues that the Soul is "numerically one," meaning the exact same soul exists in the foot as in the hand, unlike a physical quality like color which is split across a surface.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR.

<margin>A</margin>...is observed; but in the soul, it is the same nature, yet not divided. However, it is said to be divided for this reason: because it extends itself everywhere. Let us speak of these matters again, investigating from the beginning so that it may be clearly revealed to us how the soul, being incorporeal and lacking magnitude <note>Magnitude refers to physical size or extension in space</note>, can be propagated across a great extent, whether it exists before bodies or is extended within bodies to that same degree. For perhaps if it is established that this can happen even before bodies, it will be very easy to admit that such a thing also occurs within <margin>B</margin> bodies.

->*The intelligible world <note>original: "Mundus intelligibilis"—in Neoplatonic thought, this is the higher reality consisting of the Divine Mind and the Forms, which serves as the blueprint for our world.</note>, that is, the first and true being, the universal and great, because it consists of all beings and is a whole in any part of itself, prevails in the universe. And because it is said to be "everywhere," it is that very thing which is called "everywhere." And there are two true sensible things: it is truly small, because "everywhere" consists of small parts. And it is in the higher world, not as if in a containing place, nor as if in some empty interval, but as if in that which is efficient, preserving, sustaining, moving, and comprehending. The world, through any of its parts, reaches that whole everywhere; therefore, it does not move in a straight line toward finding it, but revolves in the same place around that which is found everywhere. Chapter II.*<-

<margin>A</margin> **THERE IS** always a certain universal truth; there is also an image of that universal truth, specifically in those visible things of this world's nature. That which is truly the "Whole," therefore, exists in no part; for no being exists before it <note>Plotinus argues that "True Being" is the source of all, so nothing can contain it or be "before" it.</note>. But that which exists after it must necessarily be in the "Whole," if indeed anything is to exist at all—especially since it depends upon that Whole and can neither remain nor move without it. Indeed, if one were to place this within that Whole, not as if <margin>B</margin> understanding "place" to be a certain boundary of a containing body (insofar as it contains), or some interval that existed previously as a kind of empty nature, but if one were to affirm that this is founded and rests within that; within that, I say, which exists everywhere and entirely comprehends it—whoever has so placed it, letting go of the name of "place," should grasp what is being said through thought itself. <margin>C</margin> This is further said for this reason: because that first and being "Whole" neither seeks a place, nor rests entirely in anything. For since it is the "Whole" through and through, it cannot be that it is in any way lacking to itself; rather, it fills itself and is equal to itself. Nor is there a "Whole" belonging to it there, for it is that "Whole" itself. Entirely, indeed, if anything is founded in the "Whole," it is something else existing besides it that participates in it and harmonizes with it. Likewise, it is <margin>D</margin> strengthened by it, not by dividing it, but by finding it within itself; and it approaches it, while yet that Whole is not placed outside of itself. For it cannot be that being exists in non-being; but if non-being exists in being, it falls into the being as a whole. For it could not be distracted or torn away from itself. And yet, what is said of that "Whole" being "everywhere" must be understood to mean that it exists in being itself, and thus in itself. Nor is it a wonder if that which is called "everywhere" is in being and in itself, for it is "everywhere" in the One. But we, thinking that being is this sensible world, consequently think that it is also "everywhere" here. Likewise, thinking this <margin>E</margin> sensible world to be great, we hardly doubt how that nature can be extended through something so great. But in reality, this which is called "great" is small; and that which is thought to be small is great; since that entire Whole reaches through every part of the universe.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...so too in the soul, it is the same, but not divided. However, it is said to be divided for this reason: because it spreads itself everywhere. Let us speak of these matters then, investigating again from the beginning if by any reason it might be clearly open to us, how the soul, since it is incorporeal and without magnitude, can be propagated into many things, whether before bodies or extended in bodies to that extent. For perhaps if it is established that this can also happen before bodies, it will be very easily possible to admit such a thing in <margin>B</margin> bodies as well.

**THERE IS** always some universal truth; there is also an image of that true universal, specifically in these visible things of the nature of this world. That, therefore, which is truly the "Whole" exists in no part; for no being exists before it. But that which stands after it, it is now necessary that it be in the universal, if indeed anything is to be; especially since it depends upon that, and without it, it can neither remain nor move. For indeed, if someone places this in that, not as <margin>B</margin> understanding "place" as a certain boundary of a containing body, insofar as it contains, or some interval which was previously this, as if of an empty nature and still existing, but if he affirms that this is founded and rests in that; in that, I say, existing everywhere, and thoroughly comprehending it; whoever, I say, has so placed it, now dismissing the calling of this name (that is, of "place"), let him apprehend by thought itself what is said. <margin>C</margin> Moreover, this is said for the sake of this: because that first being and "Whole" neither seeks a place, nor rests at all in anything. For since it is thoroughly the "Whole" from all sides, it cannot be that in any way it is lacking to itself, but it fills itself and is equal to itself: nor is the "Whole" of it there, for it exists as that "Whole" itself. Indeed, entirely, if anything is founded in the "Whole," it—existing as something other besides it—participates in it and conspires with it. Likewise, it is <margin>D</margin> corroborated by it, not dividing it, but finding it in itself: and it indeed approaching it, while yet that is not placed outside of itself. For it cannot be that being is in non-being; but if non-being were in being, it falls into the whole being. For it could not be distracted or torn away from itself. And yet, what is said—that the "Whole" is "everywhere"—is to be understood as existing in being itself, and thus in itself. Nor is it a wonder if that which is called "everywhere" is in being and in itself, for already it is "everywhere" in the One. But we, thinking that being is this sensible world, consequently think it is also "everywhere" here. Likewise, thinking this <margin>E</margin> sensible world to be great, we by no means doubt how that nature is extended through this so great a thing. But in truth, this which is called "great" is small; but that which is thought small is great; since that whole reaches through every part of the universe.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

<margin>A</margin> ...cuts through each; rather, this whole universe, approaching that [intelligible] universe from every side with its parts, finds it everywhere as a whole. It finds it, without doubt, greater than itself. For this reason, as if it could receive nothing more by projecting further—for in that case it might seem to wander outside the universe—it rightly wished to remain within its bounds. Since, however, it could not fully grasp it or insinuate itself entirely within, it considered it sufficient <margin>B</margin> if it obtained a place and order where it could remain near to that which is present, and yet again not present. For that [intelligible] is within itself, even if something else wishes to be near it. Moving toward it, the body of the universe finds the whole, so that it has no need to go further, but finds it better to revolve in the same place, as if the universe were truly that which revolves around it. There, certainly, according to every part of itself, it enjoys that whole. For if that [intelligible] were in a specific place, the universe would rightly move in a straight line toward it; and it would be necessary to reach it in one part through another <margin>C</margin> part, making it happen that it would be sometimes far and sometimes near. But if it is neither far nor near, it must be present as a whole, provided it is present at all. And indeed, it is present as a whole to each of those things to which it is neither near nor far, but is present to those capable of properly receiving it.

->*The intelligible world, by the excellence of its power, diffuses its forces through all parts of the world: and it is present as a whole to every single part, while remaining transcendent above them. Chapter III.*<-

Just as it communicates its powers to all things capable of participating in them, so it is present through its own powers. Where it imparts more powers, it is more clearly present; where it imparts all, it is most clearly present. It does not belong to any specific form or place, even if it seems to; otherwise, it would not nourish the further reaches of the universe, nor would it be commonly present to all. A body is defined by its form <note>original: "specie"</note>, but is divided by its quantity. Therefore, when a division is made, even if the quantity remains the same, the form remains with the true essence. Life and the first Mind are devoid of the quantity of form; if they were divided according to form, they would change the form itself.

<margin>A</margin> Shall we then say that the whole itself is present? Or does it remain in itself, while powers flow from it through all things, and thus it is thought to be everywhere? For some say that souls are like certain "casts" or "rays" sent out from it, so that the source itself rests in itself, while the souls sent out from there become one living thing after another. But surely, to those things to which a certain part of it is granted—because they cannot <margin>B</margin> preserve its entire nature within themselves—it is said to be present to all in such a way that a certain power of it is present. Yet, it is not as if the whole is entirely absent. For even then, it is not separated from that power which it gave to the thing; rather, that which received it could only grasp so much from the whole which is present. Where truly all powers are communicated, the whole itself is most clearly present, yet in such a way that it is simultaneously separate. For if it became the form of this [physical] thing, it could neither be the whole, nor would it be everywhere consisting in itself, <margin>C</margin> but it would exist by accident <note>A philosophical term meaning it would depend on something else for its existence</note>, belonging to another. But since it belongs to nothing (even if that thing wishes to be its own), it draws near to each thing that desires it according to that thing's capacity, yet without becoming part of it. Nor, again, does it belong to another, but is present through desire. Therefore, it is not surprising that it is in all things, since it resides in nothing in a way that makes it become one of them. For this reason, perhaps it is not absurd to say the soul exists "by accident," and thus in a certain way suffers along with the body, even if the soul is said to be within itself and not made of matter or body.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It reaches [all things], or rather, because all things approach the same part from every side, rather than it going to them. As it goes to it, the whole universe finds it to be greater than itself; hence, as if it always holds something of it and will receive something, for otherwise it would become outside and fourth, it wished to return to it. But being unable to encompass it, nor again to pass it by, or because it loves to have it all, it stays in order or a neighboring shape, present to it as it is present. <insert>It is within itself, even if it wishes to be present within it.</insert>
<margin>B</margin> Wherever there is a body, it is the whole that defines it, so that there is no longer any need for distant things, but to be carried around in the same way as being around the whole. For it receives that whole according to every part of itself. If that [intelligible] were in a place, it would have to move toward it, and the two would have to travel, and it would reach it in one part, but in another part it would be far or near. And in order for there to be "far" and "near," it is necessary for the whole to be present
<margin>C</margin> if indeed it is present, and generally if anything has a part of it, to those for whom it is neither far nor near, but for those capable of receiving it.

<margin>A</margin> Shall we then say it is present, or that it is by itself, while a power goes out from it to all things, and thus it is said to be everywhere? Just as they say souls are like rays <note>original: "βολὰς" (bolas) - shots, throws, or rays</note> from it, so that it is established in itself, while those sent out become one living thing after another? Or in those things where the nature of the whole is preserved in that thing, <margin>B</margin> in these we say its power is present, and not that the whole is not present, if indeed some power of it is sent out which it gave to that thing. But how did the one who received it give it, since the whole is present everywhere? But if all the powers are clearly present, yet it remains separate; for if it became the form of this, it would depart, for it must always be the whole, which is in itself everywhere, by accident; or belonging to another? For <margin>C</margin> it does not belong to the cause of the one who wishes it, but to whomever wishes it, it draws near as they are able, becoming like...

<meta>catchword: λαῖ (part of the word "remains" or "shines" in Greek)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Intelligible World (pure reality) is present as a whole to all parts of the physical world because it is not limited by physical space. The physical world rotates because it is trying to stay in contact with this everywhere-present source that it cannot fully contain.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR

But that nature itself <note>original: "ἡ φύσις αὐτὴ" refers to the divine or intelligible nature</note> is immortal and not unable to be present in all things, for it did not have to exist in the same way as physical things do. Therefore, <margin>* sympathetic</margin> what is called accidental "sympathy" <note>original: "συμπαθὲς" – the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected and "feel" together</note> is said to occur with the body; but the soul <margin>* the soul</margin> is not said to exist by itself alone, but as it comes to be in matter and the body. Yet every body is healed or governed throughout by it. One ought to wonder if it is present in the whole, yet not as a part of the whole. It is not a matter for wonder that it is unable to be in a physical place, for where it is present, it is present as a whole; or it is present in such a way that it is not locally present. We say then: what the argument shows is that it is necessary for it to be present as a whole to the place, if "place" is even the right word; it is present to everything as a whole. If one part were here and another there, the soul would be divided like the body. How then could the whole be divided? If the whole were spread out, the parts would be living things; but parts are only parts if they are not in something else. If the whole exists, how could it be said that the body is divided while the parts possess bodies? For this is not a division of the soul, but only of the body, even if each part is called a body.

<column-break/>

A. But the entire body throughout the universe is illuminated, as it were, by the soul. Indeed, nothing ought to seem surprising if that divine whole, since it is not itself in a physical place, is present to everything that *is* in a place. On the contrary, it would be both wonderful and impossible if that which has its own place were present to something else in another place—or if it were present at all in the way we have just described. B. Now, however, reason dictates that it is necessary for it—since it has no place—to be present as a whole to whatever it is present to. To whatever the universe is present, it is present in such a way that it is present as a whole to each individual part. Otherwise, one part of it would be here and another there, making it both divisible and a body. Now, one may ask: how do you divide it? Will you divide life? But if you divide it, and the whole was life, the part will not be life. Will you divide the intellect <note>original: "intellectum," translating the Greek "nous"</note> so that one part is here and another there? C. Truly, neither of those parts will be the intellect. Will you then divide its very "Being"? <note>original: "ens"</note> But then the part will not be "Being" if the whole was "Being." What then? If someone objects that a divided body has parts which are still bodies in themselves, we must answer that the division was not *of* the body's essence, but rather just a division of the physical matter; each body is made and named according to its "form" <note>original: "specie"</note> by which the body exists. But this form, which is what truly matters, does not have a specific "quantity" <note>term: Quantity — in ancient philosophy, this refers to things that can be measured or counted, like size or number</note>, D. nor even any kind of measurable amount.

---

-> The one primary essence, that is, the divine mind, is everywhere as a whole; similarly, the one soul of the world is everywhere as a whole. The multitude of parts in the world does not prevent it from being one and whole everywhere, nor does the primary unity of the mind and soul prevent there being many other minds and souls besides. **Chapter IV.** <-

---

-> The soul is not forced to be manifold or divisible just because the members of the same body are many; nor do many souls arise from the many bodies of the same soul. For indeed, minds and souls, differing among themselves by their own properties, exist even before bodies; they are joined to one another by a certain natural kinship and shared duty, yet they are distinct from one another by the difference of their properties, not by their location. <-

---

But how can these things be if there are many souls? Is the soul many? And are they everywhere, if they are not like the one soul? If some souls do these things and others do those, does this not seem to contradict what has been said? These things are necessary. But those who find it hard to believe that the soul is thus everywhere as a whole might think it better to divide the whole, so that nothing is diminished. If a division has occurred or will occur from it, it is so that they may be better: living in bodies, some will come from that one soul as if they had become parts, now filling all things as souls. But that one soul <margin>* in itself</margin> exists in itself. When it seems paradoxical for it to be whole and everywhere at once, the same argument <margin>* the mind and the souls</margin> is applied to other souls. For in whatever bodies they are said to be "whole," there they shall be placed. But either they will be divided, or they will remain as wholes in a certain part of the body and give their power to the whole. Regarding these powers, the same difficulty exists as to how they are everywhere. Or is it that the soul is in one part of the body while only its power is in the rest? but how

<column-break/>

A. MOREOVER, in what way is it right to speak of Being and beings, and many minds, and many souls? If Being is one everywhere, and not one merely in some similar shape; likewise if Mind is one, and Soul is one—even though we have learned that the soul of the universe is one thing, and the remaining souls are others. This seems to contradict what has already been said. And even if what has been said carries some necessity, it still does not bring total persuasion, since the human mind finds it incredible that one and the same whole can be everywhere. Perhaps, then, it is better to divide that one whole, yet in such a way that the source from which the division is made is not diminished. Or rather, to speak more correctly, let us say that certain things are generated from it, while it is allowed to remain within itself. Those things which are born from it like parts are the souls that fill the universe. But if that Being remains at rest in itself specifically because it seems incredible that one whole should be everywhere at once, the same doubt will surely arise concerning individual souls. For they will no longer be "whole in the whole" of the bodies they inhabit. Instead, they will either be divided, or if they remain whole, they will rest in only one part of the body and spread their powers through the limbs from there. C. Thus, the same ambiguity will arise concerning both the powers and the soul: is it truly "whole" everywhere? Furthermore, one member of the body will have the soul, while another will have only its power. But first, we must investigate how...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Soul and Mind are not physical objects and therefore cannot be divided like matter; they are present as a "whole" in every part of the universe or body they inhabit. He addresses the paradox of how there can be both one universal Soul and many individual souls without breaking the unity of divine Being.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the Soul and its relationship to the physical world. While the previous page discussed the soul’s presence in the body without being divided by it, this page addresses the paradox of how there can be "many" souls if the Soul is fundamentally "one," and how an immaterial entity can "fill" a physical universe.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> From the high origins above, there are many souls, many minds, and many beings besides the One. But those things that flow from the prior ones—which are not physical magnitudes but numbers—similarly bring up a doubt: in what way do they fill the universe? We have found nothing clearly certain from the multitude flowing out in this way that helps explain the doubt. Since we concede that Being itself is many by a certain "otherness" <term>otherness (alteritas): a philosophical term for the principle that allows things to be distinct from one another without needing physical space to separate them</term>, but not by location. For the whole of Being exists at once, even though it is thus manifold; for as Parmenides <note>Parmenides was a pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that "Being" is a single, unchanging whole.</note> says, "Being draws near to Being," <note>original: "ens enti propinquat"</note> and the whole is together at once. Furthermore, the Intellect is manifold by otherness, not location, but is all things at once. Do souls not behave in this same way? Perhaps the soul does as well.

<margin>B</margin> For that which is said to be "partible" <term>partible: capable of being divided into parts</term> regarding bodies is, on the contrary, considered to be "impartible" according to its nature. Bodies, having magnitude, are present to those natures and to the nature of the soul itself. Indeed, since bodies come into existence there, and insofar as they are extended according to every part, that nature of the soul itself appears which is occupied with bodies; thus, it happens that the soul is thought of as divisible regarding them. For it is clearly evident to us that the soul is not distributed into parts along with the parts of the body, but is present as a whole everywhere, because its nature is found to be truly one and indivisible.

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, the fact that the soul is one does not prevent there being many; just as the fact that Being is one does not prohibit beings, nor does multiplicity there conflict with unity. Nor is it necessary to fill bodies with a certain life through multiplicity; nor should it be thought that a multitude of souls arises because of the magnitude of the body; rather, many and one soul exist even before bodies.

<margin>D</margin> For in the whole itself, many already consist—not in potential, but each one already in act <term>in act (in actu): existing in reality or fully realized, as opposed to just having the potential to exist</term>. For that one whole prevents nothing from many existing in it; and in turn, many do not hinder the one.

<margin>E</margin> For they are distant from each other while being not distant, and they are present to one another without being foreign. They are not separated from each other by any boundaries, just as many sciences gathered in a single soul are not; rather, the soul itself is such that it contains them all. Indeed, the lowest nature is exactly of this kind.

-> The Soul of the World, like the Mind, is both indivisible and universal; therefore, it is present as a whole everywhere in the world. Indeed, the Soul, which has no physical quantity, is neither smaller nor larger in quantity than the world, but is in the Mind, which the world cannot even fully contain. Yet the same soul of a larger body suffices for a smaller body because of the greatness of its power. <-

<margin>A</margin> **ACCORDINGLY**, the magnitude of this nature is not to be judged by its bulk; for bulk is a small thing, liable to fall toward nothingness if someone takes away from it. But from that nature <note>i.e., the Soul or Intelligible nature</note> it is not right to take away, nor if you should happen to subtract from it, will it fail in any way. If it never fails, there is no fear that it might ever depart from anyone. For how could it depart from anyone when it suffers no lack, but is an eternal nature that does not flow away? Otherwise, if it did flow, <margin>B</margin> it would proceed as far as it was able to flow. But since it does not flow at all—for it has a place to flow to—it already completely comprehends the whole. Indeed, it is the universe itself, and is something greater than can be judged according to the magnitude of corporeal nature. For it is rightly judged a small thing to attribute to this universe only as much as it is able to carry. It is necessary, however, not to call that upper universe smaller, nor to place it as smaller according to its bulk,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Many souls, and many minds, and the beings; and indeed those things from the prior ones are such that they are not magnitudes, but numbers, and they will likewise provide a puzzle as to how they fill the whole. Nothing further has come to us regarding the multitude that leads to a clear solution to the puzzle. Since we also admit that Being is many, by otherness, not by place. Being is together, manifold, and does not fail. And the whole is together, and all the Intellect.

<margin>B</margin> The souls are also together, since each is all, and souls are said to be divisible in nature because the infinite is divided by bodies, while bodies have magnitude of this soul. It happens by nature, or rather because bodies are resting there where it is divided according to every part, each

<margin>C</margin> nature appearing around the bodies, as if by names or by a mixture. But since bodies must be taken in parts, but not everywhere. It makes clear that Being is truly indivisible in its nature, going out as one into many. Infinity, just as Being is beings, does not fight against multiplicity, there with the one and the multitude,

<margin>D</margin> they indeed fill bodies with life, and the cause is the magnitude of the body, through which it is thought that a multitude of souls is produced. But before bodies there are many and one, in the greater many already in power, but each in act. For neither the one nor the whole prevents the many from being in it, nor do the many prevent the one, or each when separated provide a change or become foreign.

<margin>E</margin> For they know all to be distributed; and the many sciences are in one soul. The one is such that it has all in itself; in this, such a nature is infinite.

<margin>A</margin> **AND** its greatness must be understood in this way, not by bulk. For that which is small is of the kind that falls away if one takes from it; and here, to one who takes away, the subtraction will not fail. But if it were thus, it would fail. Why fear that it might be sent away entirely? Things sent away are those that fail. But it is an ever-flowing nature, or rather not flowing. For if it were flowing, it would stop at some point; as much as it is able, it would never not flow, <margin>B</margin> but it has what is its own, for it has grasped the whole, or rather it is the whole. And it is something greater than the nature of a body, for it would be a small thing to give to each part of the whole as much as one is able to carry. Therefore, one should not call it smaller, nor place it as smaller in bulk.

# BOOK FOUR.

<column-break/>

<margin><unclear>From the...</unclear></margin> As a general rule, so far as is possible for it to be greater, whether in quantity or in a lesser * predicate, or by the bulk of its position, bulk is measured against bulk. It is as if one were to say that the science of medicine is smaller than a five-cubit body <note>A "cubit" was an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of a forearm; five cubits would be roughly 7.5 feet.</note>. And yet, if one considers it greater, every measurable thing is so, but that which belongs to the soul is a "greater" cause, or that "greater" thing which measures bodies. In the greatness of the soul, we have not known the "greater" as something that arrives at every part of it by its own soul, or that which belongs to a smaller bulk. For it is in many ways ridiculous to suggest any addition of bulk to the soul.

<margin>* What</margin> What then happens when every body arrives? Either
<margin>or can</margin> it must be that thing, if it can approach, or having gone around and received it, does one body hold the other body, and thus hold the same soul? Having the soul which it possesses, does it again differ by additions? For how is it the same in the foot and the hand? Is it in one part of the whole, and the same in another? And if the senses are different, and the experiences <term>experiences (passiones): in this context, the passive reception of sensory data or feelings</term> that occur are different, one must speak of them. But the things that lie within are one thing, and that other thing. Or is the judge who decides the same, occurring in different and varied experiences? And it is not the sufferer himself who judges, but the nature of that body. Thus, it is as if we ourselves judge the pleasure concerning the finger, or the pain concerning the head. Why then does the one not perceive the judgment of the other, or is it that there is judgment, but not a shared experience? If it is a judgment according to itself, it says "I have judged," but I have only judged. Just as with us, sight speaks to hearing and to the thing there, so that both are present. But reason <term>reason (logismos): the calculating or rational faculty of the soul</term> is over both. And yet it is something different from both. In many ways, reason also sees the judgment in another, and again there is an experience in the other. But these things have been discussed elsewhere as well.

Truly, we have spoken of this elsewhere too.

<margin>A</margin> lest perhaps you be forced to distrust that it is less able to be amplified through that whole which becomes larger than it. For this very thing which is called "lesser" must not be predicated of it, nor must bulk be applied or compared to bulk in the measurement itself. For that would be exactly as if one said that the discipline of medicine is smaller than the body of the physician himself. Nor, again, should that "greater" be judged according to any measure of quantity, since the magnitude of the soul is not judged to be greater than the body in that way. Indeed, one may best guess the magnitude of the soul from this: that when the mass itself becomes larger, the same soul [remains] through the whole.

### Questions concerning the World Soul and our own. Chapter VI.

> *He asks: If the soul has such great magnitude of power as we were just saying, why does it not also bring life to any body placed near it? He responds that it can, provided the body approaches it—that is, through a formable conformity. Likewise, he doubts: If the soul of the world occupies the whole, does a body animated by its own soul have both its own and the common soul at the same time? And he further doubts by asking how these two souls differ there. He responds that they differ by additions; for although that soul is better, this soul is of one kind, and that of another. Then he confirms that the soul of the world can be the same whole in our bodies, because in us our own soul is the same whole in the foot and the hand at once. He adds that different senses and experiences do not prevent there being one soul in a human, and one in the world; for clearly in any human there is one judge, and so too in the soul of the world. Then he asks, since there are two souls in us—one common and one our own—why does our soul not perceive the judgment of the world soul? He responds: Because no shared feeling <note>original: "compassio"</note> results in us from that judgment. Furthermore, neither does the same power of the soul which judges always notice that it is judging, nor does every power in the same soul communicate its judgment to another. Therefore, it is no wonder if the power of our soul does not feel the judgment of the common soul, nor does that soul communicate its own to ours. But reason in us notices the judgments of the lower parts, and reason in the common soul similarly notices the judgments of its own parts. Our reason is occupied and distracted by sensible things, while the reason of the common soul is collected around intelligible things. Therefore, since they are turned toward opposites, judgment is not easily communicated from one to the other. I pass over for now how through the common soul there is in us a certain community of life and consensus and shared feeling, both among ourselves and toward worldly and celestial things, in which union the power of attraction and magic consists. But take care not to think that Plotinus places only one soul in all things. For this is everywhere repugnant to him.*

---

<margin>A</margin> WHY then does no other body approach? Perhaps truly that body, if it is able, ought to approach: and approaching, it receives from there, and possesses what it has received. What then? Does another body not have the same soul, possessing meanwhile its own soul which it has? How does it differ? Surely it differs by additions. Furthermore, how do we place the same soul in the foot and the hand, but we do not affirm that the soul <margin>B</margin> which is in this part of the universe is the same as that soul which is in another part of the same? But if the senses are different, one must also think that the occurring experiences are different. Therefore, the things being judged are different, but the judge is not another. Surely the same judge decides in different and various experiences, although the one suffering is not the same as the one who judges. But this is rather the nature of such a body. And it is just as if one of us should judge both the pleasure which occurs <margin>C</margin> around the finger, and the pain around the head. Why then does the one not feel the judgment of the other? Perhaps because that is a judgment, not an experience. Furthermore, neither does the power itself which judges say "I have now judged," but it has merely judged. For even among us, sight does not announce to hearing, although both have already judged, but the reason presiding over both is either different from both. Often indeed reason has known what judgment is in another, and noticed the experience of the other.

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI

*The multitude of numbers proceeding from the one, and of lines flowing from a center, do not prevent that one or that center from being indivisible and unique. Similarly, the soul is not forced to become divisible or manifold because of various limbs or bodies. Rather, just as a governing power is present in its entirety in any part of a weight, and the same indivisible light is present in its entirety in any part of the air, so too is the soul.*

### Cap. VII.

<margin>A</margin> BUT let us explain once more how the same thing is present through all things simultaneously: as if we were to ask by what condition each of many senses, scattered and arranged on all sides, participates in the nature sent forth to it. Indeed, it is established that it is a sacrilege to part the "One" itself into many on account of the multitude of things; rather, it is more fitting to collect the many divided things back into the one, which indeed does not "come" to these things. But because these physical things are scattered, they have compelled us to think that the source is also somehow discarded according to them:
<margin>B</margin> as if someone thought that which protects and contains should be divided into equal parts along with that which is contained. Even though a hand can contain a whole body or a piece of wood many cubits long, or any other thing. In such a case, the power itself which is in the hand thrives everywhere that it is held, yet it is not divided into equal parts along with that which is held by the hand: although it appears that as far as the hand reaches, so far is the power of the whole thing. And those internal parts of the hand are defined by a certain quantity, but not by the quantity of the body which is taken up and held:
<margin>C</margin> and yet if another length were added to the suspended body, and the hand were able to sustain it, the power of governing would also rule that part, clearly not being cut into as many parts as the body has. What if someone were to imagine the physical mass of the hand were removed, but it still left behind the same power of support it previously had, so that the same indivisible power remained in the whole weight similarly through any part of it?
<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, if you were to fix a certain tiny luminous body as a center somewhere, and you placed some transparent spherical body around it: so that the light of the innermost small body shone through the whole surrounding mass—wherever the light might be in the external mass, would we not say it belongs to that innermost light? While that light suffers nothing, it remains through the whole external mass, having proceeded from that slightly visible small body to encompass entirely all that stands around it.
<margin>E</margin> But since the light itself did not stand out from the physical mass of that center—for it did not possess light insofar as it was a body, but insofar as it was a *luminous* body, clearly through another incorporeal power—tell me: if someone subtracted the mass of that body, but left the light there, would you still say that the light is specifically "somewhere"?
<margin>F</margin> Would it not rather be equally both within and throughout the entire exterior sphere? No longer would you fix in your thought where it was previously placed, nor would you say further from where or where the light is. Instead, you would be uncertain about these things and utterly amazed. Yet you will see the same light here and there throughout the globe. Now you can also say of the sun, from where the light most powerfully surrounds the whole air, when you look toward the body of the sun and see the light everywhere at once.
<margin>G</margin> Indeed, those things remain which are certain reflections of the light: which surely do not return light elsewhere than from the direction from which the light had flowed, yet they neither cut nor diminish the light.

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> BUT let us speak again of how the same thing is over all things, by being everything, and how it is not without a share in each of the many sensible things, though it is situated in many places. Or rather, that it is correct to say from what has been mentioned, not to divide the one into many, but to lead the many divided things back to the one, as the one has not come to them. <margin>note</margin> But because these things are scattered, it has given us the opinion that the source is divided according to them,
<margin>Β</margin> as if someone were to divide and part the holder and container into the things being held. As if a hand held a whole body, or a piece of wood many cubits long, or something else; since everything that is held is smaller than the hand, or at least is set within the parts of the thing held in the hand. It appears that the power is contained in such a size as it seems, yet the hand is held by its own quantity.
<margin>C</margin> But the divided things are held by a body, and the fall of the body held in the hand—whatever length it may be—the hand is able to carry. The power also holds that, which is not divided into as many parts as the body has. What then? If one were to withdraw the physical bulk of the hand, and the same power were left to support it as before, which was the power in the hand?
<margin>D</margin> Would it not be similarly indivisible in the whole, throughout every part? And if you were to enclose a small luminous mass as if in a center, and place around it a spherical transparent body so that the light within appeared in all the surrounding area, the radiance from elsewhere, from the outside, we would say that the inner light itself suffered nothing, but was extended through the part.
<margin>E</margin> The external mass has come, and that which appears from there in the small mass is understood to be the whole outside as well. Was that light there by the physical bulk, or was it because the body would not have light unless it were a luminous body by another power, other than a physical one? Suppose one were to withdraw the body, but keep the power of light within. Would you still say the light is in a place?
<margin>F</margin> Or would it be equally throughout the whole outer sphere? And you would no longer imagine in your mind where it was previously situated. In this chance of "from where" or "where," you will be at a loss and in wonder. And at the same time, throughout the whole spherical body, you will see the light which is here and there. The sun imitates this trace, from where the light shines and fills all the air, as you look at the body of the sun; and it is the same.
<margin>G</margin> Yet you see light everywhere, and where this is divided, it is clear that the reflections are on the other side from where it has come, which are given to be, but do not divide it.

*Since the soul is prior to all bodies, it rightly depends on none: it needs no place, and is bound to none; it relates to every place indifferently; and therefore it is everywhere in common: and it is everywhere unless each soul, through its own affection, at some time applies itself to something of its own. Ch. VIII.*

*Likewise, since it is indivisible, it is whole everywhere: and whole. Whatever therefore receives it, receives it undivided: in a way, whole: although it may not fully enjoy all its powers. But the soul, that which in bodies does not itself become a body, or a passion, or a form specific to a body, thus does not become multiple, nor is it divided, nor does it suffer: and since it is enslaved to none, it is present to all things unhindered.*

<margin>* continuity *</margin>
And indeed, if the sun were only a power <note>Greek: *dynamis*</note> without a body, and provided light, it would not have begun here, nor would that light have failed to reach there: but it would be everywhere, and the same [light] would originate from both beginnings—from where would it have it?

<margin>* power *</margin>

For such a thing would have its own nature, not having a beginning from which to start, nor from any place, nor does it drink <note>The OCR reading 'πίνει' (drinks) is likely a mistranscription of 'εἶναι' (to be) or similar in the original Greek</note> in a body; how then could it be said to be naturally here or there, or how could it have a place from which it started? If it is said to belong to something, we must say that if anything partakes of it, it partakes of the whole together, and it is not divided in one or the other. For if it were in the body [spatially], it would happen to it by accident. Or in this way it would be called passive and divisible. Since

A **CERTAINLY** since light is something of a body, you can easily say where it came from: indeed, you are able to indicate where that body is. But if something is void of matter and does not need a body—since by nature it is established prior to every body, fixed in itself, or rather not needing such a foundation—this, I say, endowed with such a nature and having no beginning from which to start, nor dwelling within any place, nor belonging to any body, how can you say a part of it is here and a part is there?

For division is a passion of the body, and primarily in that it is a body. If therefore it is divisible in that it is a body, surely in that it is not a body, it exists as entirely indivisible. Therefore, when you say it is one in many, you do not say it has been made into many, but rather you will look upon it as the passion of many things surrounding that one subject, existing in many at once. But that "one" in them is to be understood such that it is the result of neither each of them nor all of them together: but that it is of its own right, and exists as itself. And since it exists as itself, it is nowhere lacking to itself, nor does it admit any defect. Nor, again, must it be thought that it is properly as great as the sensible universe, let alone only as great as some part of the universe: for it is not in any way a quantity <note>Latin: *quantum*</note>.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

...were anywhere. If, therefore, division according to location occurs—that is, when one part of a thing is here and another part is there—it follows that for something to which "being somewhere" does not apply, no manner of partitioning is suitable. For this reason, it is necessary that such a thing remains indivisible <note>Latin: *impartibile*; Greek: *ameriston*</note> in itself, even though many things may be affected by it or even attain it. If, then, many things desire it, it is clear that they seek the whole itself; thus, if any are able, they attain the whole itself according to their capacity. Therefore, those things that participate in it must participate in such a way that they do not take a piece of it, since it has not become the private property of anyone. In this way, it remains a whole within itself, and simultaneously, in the things where it is perceived, it remains and presents itself as a whole. Otherwise, unless the whole remained there, neither would it exist itself, nor would the things themselves participate in that which they desire, but rather in something else which they by no means sought.

*The primary Soul, while exhibiting itself as a whole to the many parts of the world, is neither equalized by multiplication into many souls (for then they would not differ from one another) nor into parts: for it is indivisible. Otherwise, where it ceased to have mass, it would fail, being utterly weakened. Chapter IX.*

*Indeed, it accommodates its powers to the members of the world: but these powers are so essential and proper to it that they are inseparable from it. It is, therefore, everywhere as a whole. Furthermore, if it provides only images of its powers to the world, the Soul itself remains firmly present, destined to reclaim its images everywhere. Finally, just as in us, so in the world: unless the same power flourished everywhere, there would not be such a wonderful consensus and composition of the parts among themselves and toward the whole. Understand that what is said here concerning the Soul of the World <term>Anima Mundi: The Neoplatonic concept of an intrinsic spirit that connects all living things in the universe</term> is likewise said of the Divine Intellect.*

<column-break/>

Or the whole, if division is entirely by places, when one part is here and another is there; thus, to that which "here" does not belong, how can anything participate in it? It will be there, then, as something indivisible, where the whole of it is perceived together, even if many things seek it. And if the whole is desired, and many things desire it, clearly they desire the whole of it. So even if one is able to partake, they partake of the whole; and those things that are received are received according to its traces. Or they partake of it as something that is not their own property, while it remains a whole in itself, and a whole in the things it follows. For if it were not whole, it would not be itself. Furthermore, the desire for it is the participation; but the desire itself is something else.

<margin>A</margin> AND INDEED, if that one common thing <note>original: *unum illud commune*</note> were divided into parts among the many, such that any part was like the whole itself, it would follow that there would be many "First Principles," and each would be a First Principle. Moreover, by what would these many First Principles be distinguished, lest they all be one at the same time? For they will not be separated by their bodies; it is impossible for them to be species of bodies. Indeed, these parts would be similar to that first source from which they flow. But if these so-called parts among the many belong to that common power <note>original: *potentia*; Greek: *dynamis*</note>, then first, each would no longer be a whole. Second, in what way did they proceed from there as divided things, leaving the source behind? For if they desert the source, it is clear they left it <margin>B</margin> in some place, while they themselves proceeded elsewhere. Likewise, it must be asked whether these parts, which have come to be here in the sensible world, still remain in the source or not. If they are no longer there, it is absurd for that common source to become weak and deprived of the powers it previously possessed. It is again absurd and impossible for powers to be segregated from their own essences <note>original: *essentijs*</note>. But if they are both in the source and elsewhere, they will be here either as wholes or as parts. If they are parts, then clearly those remaining there will also be parts. But if they are wholes, and the same as those there, they are here in no way divided. Thus, the same thing will again be everywhere, in no way divided. Or <margin>C</margin> these powers are that whole which has now become many individually, so that each part is a whole, and the powers are similar to one another. And so, each power will be only one along with its essence—the essence itself accompanying it—while the other powers will only be [powers]. Yet it is impossible either for essence to exist without power, or for power to exist without essence. For there, power is substance <note>original: *substantia*</note> and essence, or something even greater than essence. But if there are certain other powers here, <margin>D</margin> as if smaller and thinner ones flowing from there—as if light depended on light, or a glimmer on a bright source—then certain essences are joined to such powers, lest perhaps power exist apart from essence. Certainly, even in such powers which are altogether conforming to one another, it is necessary that either the same one be everywhere...

<margin>A</margin> For even if the part that comes to be in each is a whole, and each thing is from it, like the first things being completed, then each is many firsts, or each is a first. Then these many firsts, how are they different, so that all things are not one at the same time? Surely not by their bodies. For if they think they are because of bodies, then these would be similar to those first things from which they come. But if the <margin>B</margin> so-called parts in the many are powers from them, first, would each still be a whole? Then how did they come to be cut off and left behind? For if they left, they clearly left somewhere; are the powers here empty in it? Or were they generated for the sensible world? It is absurd to suffer anything there, so that they become weak or deprived of what they previously had; for powers cannot be without their own essences. <margin>C</margin> How can they be cut off here? But if they are in that source and are true, they will be either wholes or parts of those here. But if they are parts, then those remaining there are parts; but if they are wholes, they are those which are there and here, divided—and again, equal in this same way—and not divided, or having become many wholes, so that <margin>D</margin> the powers are similar to each other, so that with each essence the power is only one, or safe in the hearth, while the other powers are alone. And yet it is not possible for essence to be without power, or power without essence; for power there is subsistence and essence, or rather something greater. Or if they are other powers, thin and dim powers that are from those: light from light, dim from bright, and the powers are in certain essences, so that power does not come to be without essence. First, even in such powers, it is necessary for all of them to be of the same kind as each other, or the same everywhere...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Soul and the Divine Intellect remain indivisible wholes even as they permeate the physical world. He rejects the idea that spiritual reality is "cut up" into pieces like physical matter, using the metaphor of light to explain how a single essence provides power to many things simultaneously.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of how the soul and the "First Intellect" relate to the physical world. Having established that spiritual reality is not bound by space, Plotinus now addresses objections regarding whether an "image" (like the soul) can exist independently of its "archetype" (the Divine).</meta>

# BOOK FOUR

...to allow it to be, but not everywhere; yet not everywhere at once as the same whole, nor as something divided. Or perhaps the whole exists in the same bodily form, such as that which is in the entire universe. But if you say it is divided into infinity, then those various parts would be weakened by division. Furthermore, if one part exists in one place and another in another, there would be a loss of shared sensation <note>original Greek: *synaisthēsis*; the capacity for the whole soul to feel what happens to a part</note>. Then again, it might be like an image <note>original Greek: *eidōlon*</note> of something, like a weaker light extending outward, which remains dependent on its source. In this way, everything that derives its existence from another is an image of that thing, or is at least capable of extending itself to what is nearby. These powers that come from the source are not "cuttings" or severed pieces. For if they were, the source from which they came would be emptied out. Therefore, the whole must be everywhere at once and not divided.

*Every intellectual soul is an expressed image and power of the first intellect, which is by its essence immobile, since essence exists only from that which is immobile. Similarly, the rays of the sun would persist if the sun itself remained: everywhere there are things and certain powers depending on the Mind, or the first Soul, just like a reflection in a mirror. Therefore, the first Mind is everywhere, and similarly, the first Soul is everywhere. Indeed, here and frequently above and below, you will note through the words of Plotinus that there are many levels of minds and souls, always distinct among themselves, even though the union between them is miraculous. Chapter X.*

<margin>in the colors</margin>
**BUT IF** someone were to say that it is necessary for the image to be present alongside the archetype—for how can an image exist if the archetype from which it comes is absent? Or, like the heat of a fire remaining in a warmed object after the fire has been removed—one might argue this regarding the archetype and the image. If someone mentions a painted image, we would say the archetype did not "make" the image, but rather the painter made it, and the image is not an exact copy of the painter. The painter does not produce the image out of his own substance. Rather, we must say it is the arrangement of colors that produces the image. But this is not "image-making" in the true sense. True image-making is like that found in water, mirrors, or shadows. In those cases, the likeness fundamentally originates from the primary source and is produced by it; it cannot exist if it is severed from its source.
<margin>it happens upon it</margin>
In the same way, the weaker powers <note>The "lower" aspects of the soul that interact with the physical world</note> must be understood to arise from the prior, higher powers. As for the example of the fire: one must say that the heat belongs to the fire, unless one argues that fire is actually *within* the heat, or that the heat is produced separately. But the heat does not stop immediately;
<margin>it cools</margin>
the warmed body only cools once the fire has departed. But if they say these powers [of the soul] can be extinguished, they would first have to claim that only one thing is immortal, and they would make souls perishable, as if they were merely things flowing out from a divine essence. However, it has been stated in many other places that the things of the divine world are not perishable, and that both souls and the All are immortal.

<column-break/>

**A** ...to be within, or if not everywhere simply, then at least throughout the whole, not divided, but as a single whole within one and the same body. If this is so, why not also in the entire universe? But if it were possible for it to be divided infinitely, it would no longer consist of the whole, but would become a mere partition in potentiality. Furthermore, if different powers were in different parts, no mutual communion of sensation would remain. Finally, just as 
**B** a likeness <note>Latin: *simulachrum*</note> or a weaker light is no longer there if it is severed from that which produced it—and generally, whatever depends on another as its image cannot exist without it—so these powers proceeding from the source cannot exist when they are severed from it. If this is the case, wherever these powers are, that source from which they are generated must also be present. Therefore, that whole is everywhere at once and in no way divided.

---

**A BUT IF** anyone should object that it is not necessary for an image to depend continually on its exemplar <note>The "original" or "perfect form"</note>, arguing that an image remains when the model is gone, or that heat remains in a warmed object when the fire is gone: first, regarding the exemplar and the image, we reply: If someone brings up a painted image, we say the exemplar did not create the image, but the painter did; and the painting is not even an
**B** image of the painter himself. Even if a painter chose to paint himself, it is not the painter's body or the form he imitates that actually does the painting; rather, we must consider that a certain positioning of colors creates such an image. But the production of a likeness in the proper sense is not introduced here; that occurs rather in water, mirrors, and shadows. In those cases, the likeness truly arises from the prior thing and is made by it; it cannot exist separately because it is properly made from it. In this way, one will rightly judge that
**C** the weaker powers are produced by the more excellent and superior ones. Furthermore, to the objection regarding fire, we reply: heat is not an "image" of fire, unless one were to say that fire is also in the heat. For if one affirms that, then the heat is not severed from the fire. Indeed, the warmed body will cool down—though not instantly, yet shortly after—once the fire has departed. However, if any should say that these powers are extinguished once they are removed from the universal intelligible world,
**D** they would be forced to believe that only one thing is immortal. They would judge souls and the intellect to be mortal. Moreover, they would be incorrectly granting that essences arising from immobile things could simply "flow away." If the sun itself stood still, it would pour the same light into the same places. And if someone objects that it does not pour the same light, they can easily convince themselves of this by noting that the body of the sun is continually "flowing" <note>Referring to the constant emission of light/heat</note>. But that the things from the immortal world are themselves immortal has been confirmed elsewhere by many arguments.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the soul and intellect are present everywhere as indivisible wholes, using the metaphor of a reflection in a mirror to show that an image cannot exist without its source. He rejects the "painter" analogy, asserting that spiritual "images" like the soul are fundamentally dependent on and inseparable from the Divine.</summary>
