<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding how the soul and the Divine Mind (Intellect) are present within the physical world without being divided or localized like material objects.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

->*Our soul is present as a whole to the entire body and is present with all its powers to any individual limb, even though different limbs receive different powers in greater or lesser degrees. The Soul of the World and the Divine Mind relate to the parts of the universe in a similar way. Chapter XI.*<-

->*Physical bodies are often separated from one another by their external boundaries. Incorporeal (spiritual) things, however, are not separated by external boundaries, but are distinguished by their innermost properties. This is how Ideas are distinguished from other Ideas in the Mind, how branches of knowledge are distinguished in the intellectual soul, how the Mind differs from the soul, and how individual minds and souls differ from one another. A body cannot easily be present within another body, but a body is easily present to a soul; a soul is even more easily present to another soul, and minds are most easily present to the Mind. It is easier for light to unite with light than for light to unite with a transparent object. This union is easier than that of a quality to another quality or to a body, and that in turn is easier than the interaction between physical bodies.*<-

***

<margin>A</margin> BUT if the intelligible realm <note>The "intelligible" refers to the higher reality of pure thought and forms, which Plotinus contrasts with the "sensible" or physical world.</note> itself is present as a whole everywhere, why do all things not receive the intelligible whole? Furthermore, in the intelligible order, how can one thing be "first," another "second," and others follow in sequence? Truly, those things that are more ready to receive it are considered to have it more "present." Indeed, we must judge that Being itself exists everywhere by its very nature, never failing itself anywhere. Whatever is capable of being present to it becomes present, and it is present to that thing only to the extent that the thing is capable—not by moving to a location, but in the way a transparent body relates to light. For in a cloudy or opaque body, we must assume the participation happens differently. Furthermore, how are those "first, second, and third" ranks arranged? Not by steps in space, but according to order, power, and differences that are accommodated step-by-step. Nothing prevents things that differ from being together at the same time: just as the soul, the intellect, and all sciences (both greater and lesser) exist together. For instance, regarding an apple: the eye sees the color, while the sense of smell perceives the sweetness of the odor. Other senses similarly perceive other qualities in the same place, where all qualities exist together and are not separated from one another. But then, would not that intelligible realm be varied and manifold? Certainly it is varied, yet in such a way that it remains simple—a "One-Many." For the Reason-Principle <note>original Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos* — the organizing principle of the universe</note> is both one and many at the same time. Then, truly, every being is one. For even that which is "other" holds its nature from itself, and "Otherness" <note>original: *alteritas*</note> itself is something belonging to Being. It does not belong to non-being. Being itself is constituted from itself, so that the "One" is not scattered or extended everywhere; its own unity is present to itself, and "One Being" in turn consists within itself. For it is possible that what is distinguished by some rational principle may yet exist and be present simultaneously. However, sensible things are present to intelligible things in one way (whenever they are present and to whatever they approach), while intelligible things are present to each other in another way. Just as a body approaches a soul in one way, while knowledge clings to that same soul in another. Knowledge is present to knowledge when both exist together in the same subject. A body, however, approaches another body in a completely different manner.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT why, if the whole is everywhere, do all things not participate in the whole of their intelligible forms?
<margin>• Thought</margin> <note>original Greek: *Noēma*</note> Why is one thing first and another second? That is because the "presence" is judged by the capacity of those receiving it. Being is everywhere, not abandoning itself, but it is present to whatever is able to be present to it.
<margin>B</margin> To the extent that a thing is able to enter in, to that extent is it present—just as light is to the transparent, but participation is different for the turbid. And the first, second, and third ranks are arranged by power and differences of order. It is not necessary that they be separated in space; they can differ without being distant, just as the soul, the intellect, and all the forms of knowledge—both higher and lower—are present together.
<margin>• Form</margin> <note>original Greek: *Schema*</note> Just as the eye sees color and the smell perceives the fragrance, and other senses perceive other things, yet they are all together in
<margin>C</margin> one thing, inseparable. Is that "manifold" then "one-many," or is it "many in one," or "many in a single Reason-Principle"? It is indeed many, just as the One is beyond the same.
<margin>• Otherness</margin> <note>original Greek: *heterotēs*</note> Otherness exists within it. In its unity there is a "twoness" that is not separated. Whenever it is present, the whole is present, and it remains the same within itself.
<margin>• Knowledge</margin> <note>original Greek: *epistēmē*</note> It is present without being divided. Physical things are present to the intelligible in one way,
<margin>D</margin> but the intelligibles are present to themselves in another. A body is present to a soul in one way, but knowledge is present to the soul in another way, where knowledge exists alongside knowledge in the same soul.
<margin>• Body</margin> <note>original Greek: *sōma*</note> But a body is present to another body in a way quite different from the above.

***

->*Just as many ears hear the same voice without it being divided (the whole voice sounds everywhere), so many bodies throughout the world receive their whole life simultaneously from the same World Soul; and similarly, many limbs in us receive life from our one soul. Chapter XII.*<-

->*To say that the bodies of the world were already fit to receive something vital from the World Soul does not prevent these bodies from having their own souls. While the bodies receive and the souls prepare, the bodies are given life by that power through the consent of both souls. The "World of Life" named here signifies the gathering and meeting of all intellects and intellectual souls. Regarding any intellectual soul, it must be understood that its entire substance is present both in the "World of Life" and in the physical world, even if it does not exercise all its powers here. And because it is always everywhere, it exists excellently in this whole; and since it remains here by its essence, the body seems to approach the soul (rather than the soul approaching the body) through a certain fitting accommodation and formable property.*<-

***

<margin>A</margin> OFTEN a voice sounds through the air, and it is grasped as a single word. An ear that is present receives and perceives it, especially in a quiet place. And if another ear is placed in another part of that same region, the word and the voice reach it similarly—or rather, the ear reaches toward the speech and the voice...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> JUST as when a voice is in the air, there is often a word in that voice. It is received in its entirety everywhere, as was said before in the silence; the word and the voice come to the ear, or rather, the ear comes toward the word, and from...

<meta>catchword: and from (Greek: καὶ ἀφ)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the spiritual realm (the Intelligible) is present everywhere as a whole, but physical objects only experience it according to their individual capacity, much like many ears hearing one undivided voice. He argues that spiritual things are distinguished by their internal qualities rather than physical location, allowing many "Ideas" to exist in the same "space" without confusion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into how the One or the Soul can be present in many things simultaneously without being divided into parts. It uses the analogies of sight and sound to explain spiritual presence.</meta>

# BOOK FOUR.

->**HOW BEING, ONE AND THE SAME, IS EVERYWHERE PRESENT AS A WHOLE**<-

And many eyes look toward the same thing, and the entire gaze of each is turned toward it, and they perceive the whole of the sight lying before them, so that the eyes are individually situated; yet those things capable of uniting with a soul receive it, one after another, from the same source. The voice is everywhere its own, and though it seems divided, it is one whole everywhere. That which the sense of sight experiences within itself, possessing the form, it holds it either as a divided thing or not at all; yet there it possesses the form. But though your opinion might grant all this, it must also be said that participation comes from the same source. This is even more effective in the case of the voice, as the act of hearing is whole in the entire air, and the light from its sources is whole for all, even if it does not belong to each individual part of the spoken word; rather, every ear receives the whole. If even here the whole voice is not stretched throughout the whole air such that a part of the voice is with a part of the air, and other parts are according to the location of those parts, why then should the soul not be one? It is not merely contained by things, but it is present everywhere as a whole, present as it was provided. That which is divided, having come into bodies, is essentially proportioned to them, like a voice in the air. But the soul, as soul, exists before the bodies; by the act of "voicing," the phonetic power becomes present in bodies. The soul does not give a piece of itself, but gives all that it has, just as vessels contain what they have received; yet they do not have a likeness of the whole soul, being of a different nature. They receive it as if they have something of it not in the body, but in itself. It appears to many at once. Or rather, the soul is such that it can be received. It appears clearly again, then, as happened with other things—being pierced below—so that they see a part of it toward the illumination. It is said that everything is either in something else or in itself, and that which is in something else is said to be "there." For how did it <margin>* and it came</margin> come? Or rather, it did not even come, but when that which was prepared to receive it was seen, it showed that it was present by itself. It is present to this thing by itself, by "coming" to it. In this way, from those things which truly are, it came to that which truly is, and it came to be in the whole or in each part. But the world of life is in itself. It is taken up into the whole mass—or rather, not a mass. By being drawn into a mass, it participated <margin>* as it happens</margin> as a part of a whole, but it came to the world as a whole, just as the participation happens according to the order in which it is governed; it is present everywhere by number, not divided, but existing as a whole.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Many eyes are also directed toward the same sight, from which all are filled with the vision, although it is situated in a specific location or spectacle. A diverse perception occurs there, because one is an ear, the other an eye. By a similar reasoning, whatever is able to receive the soul receives it, and one thing after another may receive it from the same source. However, the voice is everywhere throughout the air as one, not divided, but everywhere whole: since if the air, as if undergoing the thing to be seen, receives the form, <margin>B</margin> it likewise possesses it undivided. For wherever sight is applied, it receives the form: but not every opinion admits this <note>Plotinus is acknowledging that common sense often struggles to understand how a single thing can be in many places at once.</note>. Therefore let it be said, so that it may be confirmed that participation from one and the same thing is fulfilled in many. But in the voice, what we seek is more manifest, namely that in the whole air and in any part of it, the species <note>original: "speciem"; here meaning the 'form' or 'intelligible essence' of the sound.</note> is whole. For not just anyone would hear the same thing unless the speech expressed through the voice went forth entirely whole everywhere, and every sense of hearing drank it in similarly whole. <margin>C</margin> Accordingly, if the whole voice is not extended through the whole air in such a way that one part of it is joined with this part of air and another distributed with another, why should we not believe even more that the soul is one, instilled into all things, and yet not extended with the extension of things, nor divided with the division of things, but is present everywhere, present as a whole, and exists in any part of the universe without being distributed into parts at all? Now truly when it is poured through bodies, however it <margin>D</margin> approaches, it has a certain proportional likeness with that voice which is already expressed through the air. But while it stands above bodies, it seems to have a certain likeness with the one who is speaking and even the one about to speak. However, once insinuated into the body, it does not cease to play the role of the speaker, for the speaker both possesses the voice and delivers it. But as far as the voice is concerned, it is not entirely the same as those things for whose explanation it was introduced, though it has some similarity. As far as <margin>E</margin> the soul is concerned, since it is of a different nature, it is received in such a way that there is not one soul in bodies and another later in itself: but the whole appears both in itself and in many again. And yet again another lower thing approaches to receive the soul: which itself also receives from the hidden, which certainly existed in others as well. For the matter was not so prepared that a part of the soul placed here would approach it; rather, this very thing which is said to "approach" was in the universe, namely in itself, and it exists in itself: although it seems to descend here—for in what way would it come? If therefore it did not "approach," the soul appeared as now present, nor was it so present that it expected something to participate; it is certainly clear that the soul, existing in itself, is also present to the body. If, however, existing in itself, it is present to this body, this body has rightly "approached" it. If this is so, it follows that since this body was outside that which exists in such a way, it approached that which exists in such a way, <margin>G</margin> and was received into the world of life. But the world of life itself stands in itself, and thus the universe is in itself, so that it is not distributed into any physical mass <note>original: "mole"; meaning the bulk or volume of a material body.</note>. For there is no mass there. Truly, that which has betaken itself there did not betake itself into a mass. It has therefore become a participant of the soul, not indeed of some part, but of the whole. And if anything else should ascend to the world in this way, it will similarly become a participant of the whole. Wherefore if it is said that the soul is in these things, it is similarly again established in any part of the universe. Therefore, the same soul is numerically one everywhere, not divided, but present as a whole in all things.

<summary>Plotinus uses the analogies of multiple eyes seeing one object and many ears hearing one voice to explain how the Soul is present in all parts of the physical world as a single, undivided whole. He argues that the body 'approaches' the soul rather than the soul 'descending' into the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation from page 655 regarding how the Soul and true Being can be present everywhere as a whole without being divided by the physical dimensions of the bodies they inhabit. It moves from the analogy of sound and light to the metaphysical distinction between physical magnitude and spiritual power.</meta>

-># PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.<-

*What appears as the extension of quantity in the corporeal world is, in the world of life, an overflow of power. <note>original: "potestatis excessus" — This refers to the idea that spiritual reality doesn't take up space; instead, its "size" is its power or intensity.</note> And when the Soul is said to be "here and there," we must not imagine any physical location; rather, whatever exists anywhere will immediately find the Soul present as a whole. For by that indivisible vigor, which acts like a glue, all things that are physically dispersed are held together in a perpetual connection. Nor is such a vigor, which rules over all things, merely a part or a single point; if it were, it could not possess the whole of reality everywhere.*

### Chapter XIII.

<margin>A</margin> From where, then, does this extension arise, which spreads through the whole heaven and all living things? Surely that world of life is not itself extended. Our senses—which we often rely on too much, making us doubt these arguments—tell us that life is "here and there." But Reason dictates that these terms "here" and "there" do not mean that the higher nature is physically stretched out; rather, it means that whatever is extended participates in that sublime reality, even though the reality itself suffers no distance or separation within itself. If, therefore, something participates <margin>B</margin> in another thing, it is clear that it does not participate in itself; otherwise, it would not be a "participant," but would be the thing itself. It follows that a body which participates in something must not be participating in another "body," for it already possesses a corporeal nature. Thus, a body will not participate in a body, nor will magnitude <term>magnitude (quantitas/megethos)</term> participate in magnitude, for it already has it. Even if a thing that is already large receives an addition of magnitude, it does not truly "participate" in magnitude itself; a thing of <margin>C</margin> two cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient measurement of length, about 18 inches.</note> does not become three cubits because it "joined" with magnitude, but because the underlying subject, which already possessed one quantity, then received another; otherwise, the number two would actually become the number three. Therefore, that which is dispersed and extended into a mass of quantity must participate in something of a different genus—or something altogether different. It is necessary that the thing it participates in is neither dispersed, nor extended, nor a quantity at all. For this reason, that which is present everywhere as a whole must be present as something indivisible—not "indivisible" in the sense of being a tiny <margin>D</margin> speck, for a speck is still physically divisible and would not fit the whole universe. Nor is it present like a point, for a physical mass is not one point, but contains infinite points. If the Soul were like a point, it would have to be an infinite number of points to touch everything, and it would not be continuous. Therefore, the Soul cannot be like a point. If, then, the entire physical mass possesses the Soul, it must possess it as a whole through every one of its parts.

<column-break/>

From where, then, does the extension come which is stretched out alongside the whole heaven and all living things? Even if the senses—to which we grant total belief—tell us "here" and "there," reason says that "here" and "there" do not mean that the Soul itself has been extended to become "here" and "there," but that every extended thing partakes of it. It does not partake of its distance; for if anything partakes of something, it clearly does not partake of itself, but of the cause of that thing. Whatever partakes of something does so either as a body or through a body; but the body already has its existence as a body. Therefore, magnitude will not partake of magnitude, for it already has it if it is a body. Even if it receives some magnitude, it would be partaking of that which was already magnitude; for a thing of two cubits becomes three cubits because the substrate, having one quantity, takes on another. Otherwise, the two themselves would be three. If, then, that which is divided and extended as a certain size partakes of another genus, or something entirely different, then that which it partakes of must be neither divided, nor extended, nor a quantity at all. Therefore, the thing that is to be present to it must be present as a whole, being everywhere indivisible. And being indivisible in this way does not mean being small, for what is small could still be divided and would not fit the whole of that which it is applied to; nor would it remain the same as the mass increases. It is not like a point, either. For in a physical mass, there are not just points, but infinite points; so there would have to be infinite points in the Soul if it were to fit the mass like a point. Nor would the mass as a whole possess it, even if it were present everywhere.

---

*Beyond the one and primary Soul of the world, there must be individual souls that are both distinct and more excellent, as well as divine souls, which are distinguished from one another not by external or local boundaries, but by their internal properties.*

### Chapter XIV.

*These souls we call "colleagues," together with the Queen Mind—the ruler and leader of the world-soul—and we say they share the same substance in the world of life. They are more united with each other in the higher realms, where they all lean upon the intelligible world (that is, the Divine Mind) as if upon a center, through their intellectual nature. However, they become more divided from one another as they descend and express their rational nature; and soon, through the vegetative power that then takes command, they turn toward the generation of physical life. From the world of life—which is always everywhere as a whole along with all its souls—different bodies receive different lives and souls; just as various bodies daily receive life from the world-soul, and as the various limbs of any individual receive different powers and actions from their own soul.*

<margin>A</margin> But if the same Soul flourishes everywhere, how is it that each person has their own private soul? And how is it that one soul is good while another is evil? Perhaps each person is sufficient unto themselves, yet also possesses all souls and all intellects. For in that higher realm, there is both the One and the Infinite; all things are together, yet each thing is distinct; and again, they are not "distinct" in the sense of being separated, for how then could the Infinite be present? Or it might be said that that nature holds all things together: all life, all soul, and all mind.

<column-break/>

But if the soul is always everywhere, how is there a private soul for each, and how is one good and another evil? Is it that everyone has all souls and all minds within them? For the One is also infinite, and all things are together. And it holds each thing as distinct, yet not divided or separated. For how else could the Infinite be present? Or it could be said that all things are together: all lives, all souls, and all mind.

<meta>continuity: The text ends with the catchword "iter," likely leading into "iterum" or "itineris," continuing the discussion of how the one Soul distributes itself into many lives.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Soul is present in the world not as a physical extension, but as an indivisible power. He explains that while bodies are divided by size and location, the Soul remains a unified whole that provides life and intellect to all things without being fragmented itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation from page 436 regarding the nature of the Soul and the Intelligible World. It explores how individual souls remain connected to the universal Whole and how the human identity exists both in the eternal realm of Intellect and in the temporal realm of the body.</meta>

-># BOOK FOUR.<-

<note>original: "LIBER QVARTVS" — This refers to the fourth book of the Sixth Ennead in Plotinus's arrangement.</note>

...all things; each of them at least, which he defined by limits, because of itself it was necessary for them to have one life, yet an infinite one. And again one, and let that one be one because it has gathered all lives together into one, yet starting from one and remaining where they started—or rather, they never even "started," but were always thus. For there, everything is a single thing coming into being. But it is divided among certain things. Yet it only seems to be divided to the one who receives it; that which is there, has been there from the beginning. That which comes into being approaches and seems to be joined and suspended from that source. But we—who are we? Are we "that" eternal reality? Or are we that which approaches and comes into being in time? Before this birth occurred, we were there as other humans, and some of us were even gods: pure souls, and intellect joined to the whole of essence, being parts of the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The "intelligible world" (noetos kosmos) is the realm of pure thoughts and forms, existing beyond the physical universe.</note>, not defined or cut off, but belonging to the whole. For not even now is any part cut off from the whole. But now, another human has approached that eternal human, desiring to be someone else; and finding us (for we were something of the whole), he wrapped himself around us and added himself to that human who each of us then was. It is as if one voice and one word existed, and someone else from another place applied their hearing and received it; there would then be an "act of hearing" which possesses the voice's power, yet the hearing is not the voice itself. Thus we became both: that which we were before, and that which we added later—the former part often lying dormant while the latter is present to us in a different way.

BUT how does this "added part" approach us? Surely, since a readiness was present in it, it received that to which it was exposed. The body was formed in such a way as to receive the soul. But it is formed so that it does not receive the whole soul, even though the whole soul is present. It is like other animals and plants that take only as much as they can hold. For instance, when a voice signifies a word, some perceive the meaning alongside the sound, while others perceive only the sound and the physical impact. When a living being is created, it has a soul present to it from the True Being, through which it is suspended from the One. Since the body is present—which is neither empty nor lacking soul—it was already lying in a place not devoid of soul, and became even more closely prepared. When it becomes not just a body, but a living body, it possesses a trace of the soul through its proximity. It is not a "piece" of that soul, 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Otherwise all: each of them indeed is distinguished by no boundaries among themselves; and therefore, they exist as one. For it was necessary that the life above should not have only one life, but an infinite one, and yet a single one. And that one is so unified because it contains all lives at once—not huddled together in a pile, but starting from the One and remaining in the One from which they began. Or rather, they never began, but have always been so. For there, nothing is "becoming" <note>original: "fiat" — Plotinus distinguishes between "being" (eternal) and "becoming" (changing/temporal).</note>, and therefore nothing is <margin>B</margin> divided. It only appears divided based on what is received by the body. But that which exists there is exactly what has existed from the very beginning. That which "becomes" merely approaches it, appearing to be contiguous and to depend directly upon it. But what about us? Who are we ourselves? Are we "that" eternal thing? Or are we rather that which approaches it and is made in time? Truly, before this physical generation occurred, we existed there as other humans—pure souls and <margin>C</margin> intellects connected to the universal essence. We were parts of the intelligible world, not segregated or disjointed, but belonging to the whole. Even now, we are not truly severed from it. But now, "another human" has approached that original human, wishing to exist separately. Finding us (for we were not outside the universe), he wrapped himself around us, adding himself to the human that each of us was then. It is as if <margin>D</margin> there were a single voice or speech, and different people in different places turned their ears to hear and receive it. Each "act of hearing" becomes something specific, having the power of the voice present to it. Thus we became both at once: we did not lose what we were before, but we added this second nature, while the former remains dormant or present to us in a different manner.

---

> *If the whole world is a collection of intellectual souls together with the first Mind; and if the first Soul always breathes everywhere as a whole and undivided, it follows that the Soul does not approach bodies through physical movement, but through a certain effect. Nor do bodies approach the Soul, except through a certain formable preparation. It is much like how fire acts on nearby sulfur, or how light acts on a transparent medium.*

### Chapter XV.

> *Bodies affected in certain ways receive vital forces from the Soul of the World. Our body, therefore, first becomes affected in this way, and having obtained such forces from there, it is exposed to the world of life. Thus, the rational and more "proper" soul now inspires a life specific to this body, in which passions and disturbances arise—things which were not previously in the rational soul, nor do they primarily belong to it.*

---

<margin>A</margin> BUT in what way did this "added part" approach? Surely, since a readiness <note>original: "aptitudo"</note> was in it, it rightfully received that to which it was exposed. It was so affected that it could receive a soul. Yet it is made so that it does not receive the *whole* soul. For although the whole is present, it is not "wholly" the body's own. Just as other animals and plants have only as much as they can take. When a voice signifies a speech, some <margin>B</margin> perceive the speech beyond the sound, while others perceive only the sound and the physical vibration. In the meantime, the animal is produced: it has a soul present from Being itself, through which it is brought back to the whole of Being. This happens while the body is present—which is neither empty nor without soul, for it previously lay in a place where soul was not absent—and it becomes even more "near" through a certain preparation. When the body is no longer just a body, but a living body, it relies on a certain "trace" of the soul by its proximity. <margin>C</margin> In this state, it does not receive a "part" of the soul, but rather a certain power flows from the soul,

<summary>Plotinus explains that humans have a dual nature: an eternal, "pure soul" joined to the divine intellect, and a temporal "added" self that joins the body. He uses the analogy of a single voice heard by many to show how the Soul remains a whole even when perceived by many individuals.</summary>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

<margin>A</margin>
...as if a certain heating or illumination already begins to arise within it, becoming the source of desires, pleasures, and pains. However, the body of the animal already formed was not something foreign to it. For the soul remained quiet, stemming from its own divine nature, and according to its own custom, it persisted within itself in its proper state. But the body, because of its own inherent weakness, is in a state of turmoil—partly flowing of its own accord, and partly struck by external blows. It first made a clamor against the "common entity" of the living being <note>The "common entity" (commune) refers to the composite of body and the lower "trace" of the soul, essentially the biological life-force.</note> and transmitted its own disturbance <margin>B</margin> to the whole. This is just as when a senate is sitting and deliberating with a quiet opinion, but a disorderly mob, incited either by hunger or driven by other complaints, immediately disturbs the entire assembly. For as often as those leaders act quietly, and reason reaches them from a prudent man, the people are arranged in a certain order, and that which is worse in the city does not prevail. Otherwise, that which is worse wins out, while that which is better remains idle. <margin>C</margin> Certainly, when the people are disturbed, they cannot look up to the reason of their superior. And this is the wickedness of a city and an assembly; and this again is the depravity of a human being who has, as it were, a "populace" within themselves of pleasures, lusts, and fears that are overwhelming. This occurs when such a "populace" is allowed control over the person so affected. But another person <margin>D</margin> reduces such a crowd to slavery and flees back to that higher self who he once was. He lives according to that higher self—which is his true identity—meanwhile yielding to the body only as much as one might give to something foreign and different. Nor is there lacking one who lives life now in one way, now in another, mixed with a certain good from his own right and his own depravity.
One lives thus, another lives by other means; he is a certain mixture of both. <note>original Greek: ὃ τὸ μὲν ἔτως : ὃ τὸ δὲ ἄλλοις ζῇ . μίκτός τις ἐξ ἀμφῶ</note>

---

# CHAPTER XVI.
<margin>Cap. XVI.</margin>
When our soul does not defend itself or ascend, we must understand that "moving locations" is not meant in the literal sense; rather, to "descend" is to flow toward such a body, and to "ascend" is the opposite—namely, neither to flow into it nor to be afflicted by it. Chapter XVI. Our soul, through the power of the <term>intellect</term> <note>The "Intellect" (Nous) is the highest part of the soul that remains in contact with eternal truths.</note>, is always the whole universe; but through the rational, imaginative, and vegetative powers, it is sometimes the universe and sometimes a part of a single thing. This occurs when one or many or eternal things happen in turn. For when it is not yet affected by this particular body, the soul stands near the universal form of the world by means of reason and imagination. For it is then able to move itself with various expansions. Where our soul is not so engaged, it exists by a particular <unclear>power</unclear>. It becomes a "part" of the universe when it leans toward this body and turns itself away through its own affection. While it is in a particular state in its current action, it is universal in its <unclear>origin</unclear>. Therefore, when it emerges from the universal soul, it does not cease to be particular; for even this property of being a whole is found within its own state. Furthermore, understand the "Idol" <note>The "Idol" (eidolon) or "image" refers to the lower reflection of the soul that animates the physical body, as opposed to the higher, pure soul.</note> of the soul to be the vital breath of the soul generated around the body that is in us: one part from our own soul, another from the soul of the world. Our part cannot be separated from our soul, though it can be free from its effects; but that which comes from the world-soul can be separated from our soul.

---

**TRULY**, that higher nature cannot become evil. This is the manner in which the soul comes into the body and is present. Next, we must ask what the "descent" is, and what the "ascent" is that is restored in certain cycles of time. What are the judgments and the just punishments of souls? Finally, what are the infusions into the bodies of other animals? For we have received these best teachings about the soul from the ancient philosophers. And certainly, <margin>B</margin> an effort must be made to show that the present discourse is either in harmony with them, or at least not in discord. How, then, has this been established—that which is said to participate in that nature, and that the soul does not descend to these things by departing from itself, but rather that this nature comes to be in the soul and becomes a participant in it? This is what they mean when they say the soul "comes" to it. Indeed, it must be asserted that it is the nature of the body to come to be there, and to become a participant in life and soul. And entirely, this "coming" is not to be understood according to physical place, but in another way, whatever the condition of such a communion may be.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
**BUT** it is like a heating, or an illumination that has come, a generation of desires and pleasures and pains within that which receives it. This was already the case for the living beings that were born. The Soul, indeed, from the divine realm, was quiet <margin>Cap. 11.</margin> <gloss>according to its own character</gloss> <gloss>within itself</gloss> standing still. But that which was troubled by the weakness of the body, and something flowing within it, and being struck by external blows, first <margin>B</margin> cried out to the common living being and gave its own disturbance to the whole. It is like an assembly of elders sitting in a quiet council, while a disorderly populace, needing food and complaining of other things they might suffer, throws the whole assembly into a shameful turmoil. If, while such men are keeping quiet out of <margin>C</margin> wisdom, some word inclines toward the people and brings the multitude into a moderate order, then the worse part is not in control. But if not, the worse part prevails while the better part keeps quiet or does not fill the turmoil with the weight of the higher realm. And that is the vice of a city and an assembly. Likewise, the vice in a human is when there is a "populace" within <margin>D</margin> of opinions and desires and fears that overpower their true selves. But in such a case, it is not by being defeated, but as if one could make those who are enslaved run back to that former state; and that man's soul is that man, through whom he gives to the body whatever he gives as to something other than himself. But there is also someone who lives thus in one way, and another who lives differently. He is a certain mixture of both himself and the evil he has used.

---

**BUT** again, that Nature would not become evil. And what is the manner of the soul's presence in bodies—is it a descent, or is it in fixed periods? Or the judgments and the transitions into the bodies of other animals for judgment? For we have received these things from the <margin>B</margin> ancients who have philosophized best concerning the Soul. To demonstrate this, the proposed discourse aims to show our mind's harmony, or at least its lack of discord, with them. Since the soul participates in that nature, its "coming" here is not a departure from the other, but rather by being in that realm, it participates in what is called "white" <note>This likely refers to a metaphor for purity or the "light" of the soul.</note> there. It must be said that the nature of the body comes to be there, or participates in life and Soul. And in general, what he calls "coming" is but this manner of such a communion.

It also distinguishes between the universal intellect and the particular "idol" or reflection of the soul that animates physical matter.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR

<column-break/>

Thus, to "descend"—that is, to come to be in a body—as we say the soul comes to be in a body, consists in its giving something of itself to the realm of the body. To "depart," on the other hand, means that the body no longer shares in the soul at any point, and the soul no longer creates that communion across all the parts of the universe. The soul, having been naturally stationed in the lowest rank of the **intelligible place** <note>The "intelligible place" refers to the realm of pure being and intellect, the true home of the soul in Neoplatonic thought.</note>, gives of herself, just as a light remains steady in itself while casting a radiance onto the shortest distances of nature. Such a communion is considered an evil, and the release from it is a good. Why? Because <margin>in this matter</margin> even if it is not by necessity, the soul, through what is called its "touch," becomes in some way **particular** <note>original: "μερική" - meaning divided or focused on a single part rather than the whole.</note> out of the whole by its own activity. It is no longer directed toward the whole or concerned with the whole, just as if one who possesses a total science were required to act only according to one specific theorem of that science. However, the "good" for the soul is to act according to the science as a whole, through all the knowledge it possesses. Indeed, all the soul’s parts constitute the **intelligible world**; in the whole, the part is hidden, emerging from the whole as a part only when it acts upon a specific thing. It is as if fire as a whole, being one powerful force, were forced to burn some small thing, even though it possesses the power of the whole. For the soul is entirely that higher reality, yet each soul becomes distinct when its activity becomes directed toward a specific part. It is a portion of the whole, and yet it is also the whole; in another way, one should not believe it is anything but the whole, just as it is the whole fire that burns in a single part. Regarding the descent into **Hades** <note>original: "ᾅδου" - Plotinus here plays on the etymology of Hades as the "unseen" or "invisible" realm.</note>: if being "in Hades" means being "apart," it is so named. If it refers to being apart from a place, what is so strange about that? For even now, our body is in a place, but the soul is said to be there too. But when the body no longer exists, what is it for the soul to be in Hades? Perhaps if the **image** <note>original: "εἴδωλον" - a lower reflection or shadow of the soul that remains tied to physical existence.</note> is not entirely torn away, why should we not think the soul is where its image is? But if philosophy should completely release it, and the image departs to a lower region alone, then the soul itself is purified within the intelligible realm, hanging upon nothing. Thus, while an image may be produced from the soul, like a reflection from fire, when the soul shines toward itself, it is drawn back toward the whole; it does not exist in that specific activity any longer, nor is it destroyed. But concerning these things, let this suffice. Let us now resume the argument from the beginning.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Wherefore, it should be said that to "descend" is for the soul to be introduced into the body, just as we have said the soul is in the body; that is, to hand over something from itself to the body, yet in such a way that the soul does not become the body's own. To "depart" from the body, however, is this: it is seen when the body participates in nothing of the soul. Furthermore, one must consider that an order of companionship exists between such parts of this universe: the soul itself, as if placed in the lowest <margin>B</margin> grade of the **intelligible place**, frequently bestows something from itself. Inasmuch as it is near by its power and within the shortest intervals, it contributes by a law of such a nature. Truly, such a "marriage" is an evil, and the "divorce" is a good. But why is that? Because even if the soul was not properly *of* the body, nevertheless, when it is said to become *of* it in any way, it becomes in some manner "particular" out of the whole. For its act is no longer toward the whole, even though it is itself of the whole: <margin>C</margin> just as it happens to one who has a total science, but acts only according to a single notion of it. The "good" of the knower himself was not to act through some single part of that science, but through the whole which he possesses. Now, truly, since the soul itself existed as part of the whole intelligible world and hid its "part" within the whole, it eventually broke forth from the universe into a part: because that into which it drove itself was a part. <margin>D</margin> It is as if fire, though capable of burning the whole, is now compelled to scorch some small thing, even though it possesses all that power. For each soul, when it is entirely segregated from here, is not properly just "each" soul, but is only "separated" not by place, but by activity. Let it be something singular; then it is a certain portion and no longer the whole, although in another way it still consists as the whole. When truly it presides over nothing in particular, it is altogether universal: because then it must be judged as being a "part" only in potentiality. Accordingly, as for what they pass down about the soul proceeding to the **lower world** <note>original: "inferos" - the Latin translation for Hades.</note>, if they want the name of the "lower ones" to signify something hidden, then to proceed among the lower ones is nothing other than to be "apart." But if by this name they designate some inferior place, what wonder is there? Since even now, where our body is, the soul is said to be in that same place. But when the body no longer exists, what is it for the soul to be among the lower ones? Perhaps, indeed, if the **image** <note>original: "simulachrum" - the Latin equivalent of the Greek *eidolon*.</note> of the soul is not entirely plucked away, why should we not think the soul is there where its image is? But if philosophy should dissolve the bond entirely, the image alone goes away into an inferior place—

---

the soul itself lives quite purely in the intelligible world, with nothing of itself then held back or led out of doors. And thus indeed let that stand which is produced as an image from such a source. But when the soul itself shines back into itself, by a certain inclination toward those things which are foreign to this realm, it is then contracted toward the whole; it neither exists in that [particular] act, nor does it perish. But concerning these things, let these spoken words suffice: let us again resume the discussion proposed from the beginning.

<vocab>Plotinus, Enneades, soul, body, intelligible world, image, descent of the soul</vocab>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the "descent" of the soul is not a literal movement but a narrowing of its activity from the universal to the particular. He argues that while the soul animates the body through a lower "image" or reflection, its essence remains part of the divine intelligible realm.</summary>

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD SIX
## BOOK V

->On the fact that Being, one and the same, is simultaneously whole everywhere.<-

*Natural judgment, which cannot be deceived, declares that the one God is everywhere as a whole. Likewise, the natural desire of all things, which calls everything back to the one Good, testifies that the entire nature of beings depends upon the simply one Good, and through it, they possess a mutual union. Truly, the first recipient of the one Good is Being itself; which, indeed, together with the Good, is one and simultaneously whole everywhere. Chapter I.*

<image-desc>The text begins with two historiated decorative initials. On the left, a square woodcut initial 'U' depicts a classical figure seated and holding an instrument. On the right, a square woodcut initial 'T' depicts a standing classical figure draped in robes next to a pedestal or short column.</image-desc>

<margin>A</margin> The common conception of the human mind <note>original: "communis... conceptio" / "κοινὴ ἔννοια". This refers to the Stoic and Platonic idea of "innate notions" shared by all people.</note> indicates that a certain thing, being numerically one and the same <note>original: "numero" / "ἀριθμῶ". In logic, this means a single individual entity, not just a group of similar things.</note>, is simultaneously present as a whole everywhere. This is evident when everyone, moved by a natural instinct, declares that the God within each of us is one and the same in all. And if one does not question them on the manner of this presence, nor <margin>B</margin> strive to dismantle that belief with rational arguments, they will undoubtedly confirm it; having discovered this from their own innate kinship with the divine, they will rest entirely in that knowledge. In this matter, two things strive equally for the same end, and they would in no way wish to be torn away from this union. Now, a principle of this kind is the most firm of all, sounding through the natural spirit of our souls. This principle, I say, is not concluded from individual observations, but comes to our mind before all things are specifically arranged—even before that principle which teaches that "all things desire the Good." For this principle is true: if all things naturally hasten toward the One, and are in some way one, then the One itself exists, and all desire is directed toward it. If this One, proceeding into another part as far as it is possible to proceed, appears to be many, it is still in some way one. But the ancient and primary nature, and the desire for the Good—which indeed has issued from itself—leads back in reality to the One; and in this, the whole of nature strives toward itself. For the "Good" for this one nature is its own existence, namely that it should be itself; and this is to be One. Thus, the Good is very rightly called one's "own" or "domestic" <note>original: "proprium atq; domesticū" / "οἰκεῖον". This suggests that the Good is not a foreign object we seek, but our own true nature.</note>; for which reason it is not to be sought outside. Indeed, where would one be who has fallen outside of Being, here or there? Or in what way could one find the Good in non-being? Rather, it must certainly be sought within Being itself, and not as if it were non-being. But if that Good is Being and is located within Being, then it is certainly within itself in any given thing. We are not, therefore, distant from Being, but are within it; nor, again, is it distant from us. Therefore, all beings are one.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> That which is one and the same in number is simultaneously whole everywhere, as the common notion says, whenever all people, moved naturally, say that the God in each of us is one and the same in all such things. And if a person does not ask "how," or cease to examine their opinion with logic, <margin>B</margin> they would wish, as would everyone, to stand firmly in this thought with an active mind, finding rest in what is their own. They would further wish to enjoy that unity. This would then be the principle for all, I mean, just as our souls speak—not a principle summarized from particulars, but one set forth before all particulars, and before that principle which <margin>C</margin> establishes that all things taste of the Good. For those who say this would again be speaking the truth, if all things hasten toward the One, and are One, and the One is the object of desire. That which proceeds to the other side, as far as it is possible for it to proceed, would appear to be many, and would in some way be so. But the ancient nature and the desire for the Good, which is what they are, truly leads to the One. And toward this <margin>D</margin> every nature hastens: toward itself. For this is the Good for this one nature: its own being. And to be is this: to be one. The Good is rightly called "one's own." Therefore, one must not seek it outside. For where would it be, having fallen outside of Being? Or how could one find it in non-being? But clearly it is in Being, since <margin>E</margin> it is not non-being. If, then, it is in that Being, it is in itself in each thing. We have not, therefore, stood apart from Being, but we are in it; nor is it apart from us. Therefore, all things that are, are one.

<meta>Catchword: Mundus (World)</meta>

# PLOTINUS
## BOOK FIVE

---

### The sensible world is dispersed in three primary ways: by extension and local division, by temporal succession, and by the mutual opposition of qualities. The intelligible world, however—that is, the first fullness of Ideas—admits no such division. Likewise, the "world of life" is not divided, for the assembly of intellectual souls is joined in a marvelous way with the Primary Mind and its Ideas. Chapter II.

However, lest you suspect, on account of the union celebrated here and elsewhere by Plotinus, that neither minds nor souls are plural in number, attend to what I say. For here he says that all beings are one; yet it is established that they are not one by the unity of an individual essence. Rather, he says they are one because they are from the One, and they sink toward and flow together into the One by a certain natural unity. Likewise, they are one because all the separate things he calls "beings" are within one another, with no spatial boundaries preventing them. Furthermore, it is because the lower ranks among the levels of being perform their actions primarily under the form and act of the higher ones. He understands the union of rational souls within the Universal Soul in a similar way. Also, in his book *On Numbers*, he says all beings are one, not as a numerical unit, but as a single collective number, such as "a thousand." This, therefore, is what he means when he says all souls are one. Finally, one must think of the "world of life" <note>original: "mundo vitæ" / "κόσμος ζωῆς". This refers to the realm of living intellect or the Soul of the World.</note> as being marvelously united, not through the kind of reason that argues from the corporeal world, but through the intellect—which is most unified within us—beginning from the very substance of the thing. For whatever is in that world must be judged as substantial.

<columns>

#### <note>original: Greek text of Ennead VI.5.1</note>
If a person attempts to conduct an investigation of what is said <note>regarding the presence of Being</note>, and of how it is divided in everything else, and takes up some of the questions regarding the nature of bodies—deriving their principles from there—they will divide Being, thinking it to be of such a nature. They will lack faith in its unity, having launched the momentum of their search from a starting point that is not mixed with its own proper principles. But we must adopt principles appropriate to a discourse concerning the One and All-Being; these are "intelligible principles of intelligible things" <note>original: "νοητὰς νοητῶν". Ideas that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses.</note>, which hold fast to true essence. For while one thing is in flux, receiving all kinds of changes and distributed across every place—which one should properly call "Becoming" <note>original: "γένεσιν". The world of physical change.</note> rather than "Being"—the other is always distributed in the same way, remaining exactly as it is, neither being born nor perishing. It has no space or place, nor a seat; it does not exit from somewhere, nor does it enter into somewhere else, but remains in itself. When someone speaks of those physical things, they might reasonably argue from that nature and the axioms concerning it. But when a discourse is made concerning the intelligible things, if one accepts the nature of the essence being dealt with, one would rightly establish the principles of the discourse. One should not overstep, as if having forgotten, into another nature, but should think from that essence itself. Since the "what it is" <note>original: "τί ἐστι". The definition or essence of a thing.</note> is the principle for all things, and one is said to define things well by knowing their accidents, in these matters where "everything is everywhere" in the "what it is," one must cling to this principle much more, looking to this, and referring everything back to it.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT since the condition of human reason and discourse, which approaches the discussion of what is proposed here, is not properly a single thing but something divided—and since it accepts the nature of bodies for its investigation, from which it also takes its principles—it naturally divides the thing itself. It judges and considers the matter to be of such a nature, and it distrusts the unity of the thing, especially since its investigation did not begin from its own proper principles. <margin>B</margin> For us, however, in order to conduct the dispute concerning the "One" and the "Universal Being," we must assume principles that are appropriate for the comparison: these are the intelligible principles of intelligible things, which are entirely annexed to true essence. First, therefore, we must consider what this universe is like. It is certainly placed in a state of perpetual transition, changed in every way, and distributed through every spatial location. Therefore, it should not be called "essence" <note>original: "essentia" / "οὐσία". Fundamental reality.</note>, but rather "generation" <note>original: "generatio" / "γένεσις". The process of coming-into-being and passing away.</note>. <margin>C</margin> But Being itself is always undivided, remaining entirely the same way and according to the same things; it is neither rising nor setting, having no receptacle, no place, no seat. it does not go out from anywhere, nor does it enter again into another thing, but remains in itself. For this reason, when someone disputes concerning corporeal nature, they will reasonably argue from this very nature and from those things which are properly attributed to it, weaving together arguments and doctrines very appropriately through things that agree with it. <margin>D</margin> Conversely, when someone disputes concerning an intelligible thing, if they accept the nature of the essence being discussed, they have properly constructed the principles of the dispute from that source. They do not surreptitiously cross over into a different nature, as if forgetting their purpose, but rather think about the thing from the thing itself. Indeed, this very thing called "the what it is" <note>original: "quod quid est" / "τὸ τί ἐστι". The formal definition of a thing's nature.</note> is judged to be the chief principle of understanding and disputing. From this, it is usually said that for those who have correctly defined something, many of its accidents <note>term: accidents. Qualities or characteristics that are not part of the essential nature (e.g., being tall is an accident of a human).</note> are already perceived. In these things, therefore, whose whole consists everywhere in that "what it is," one must rely much more on this principle, looking toward it and referring all things to it.

</columns>

---

### The intelligible world and also the world of life admit no division within themselves pertaining to place, time, or contrariety; nor do they depend on another subject or place. Thus, the whole is rightly always everywhere. Chapter III.

The entire corporeal world necessarily requires the "mode of life" everywhere; therefore, it possesses it everywhere. But so that life may be present everywhere to this world, one must not think of it as being thinned out or divided—passions which belong to the body. Life, therefore, is present to each thing almost as a whole, just like life or light; nor should it be thought of as segregated from any thing by location. For then it would be reduced to a narrow space.

<summary>Plotinus argues that the "One" or "True Being" is present everywhere as a whole because it is not subject to physical division, time, or space. He warns that we fail to understand this if we apply the logic of physical bodies to the realm of the mind and spirit.</summary>

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

<margin>A</margin>If, therefore, this very intelligible realm truly exists as "Being," it always maintains itself in the same manner, never departing from itself. No birth or change <note>original: "generatio" / "γένεσις". Plotinus means that eternal truths do not "become" or "decay" like physical objects.</note> falls upon it, nor is it enclosed in any physical location. It is necessary for it to always dwell within itself, never distant from itself, not having one part here and another there. Nothing of it proceeds outside of itself; otherwise, it would already be in one thing and then another, and generally within something else, no longer remaining in itself nor secure from being acted upon. For it would be "passive" <note>In ancient philosophy, "passive" means being subject to external influence or change.</note> if it lay within another; but it exists in a nature that does not suffer change, not resting in another.

<margin>B</margin>If, then, it is not distant from itself, nor divided, nor changed in any way, yet is simultaneously in many things: surely it must be one whole existing simultaneously as itself. Being identical to itself everywhere, it allows for this very thing: to be said to exist in many. But this is the same as saying that while existing in itself, it is—paradoxically—not confined to itself. It remains, therefore, for us to say that while it is in nothing, other things are "participants" <note>original: "participia" / "μεταλαμβανόντων". This refers to the Platonic theory where physical things "participate" in or mirror the eternal Forms.</note> in it—whichever things are able to approach it, and to the extent that they are able. It is necessary, then, to either do away with those suppositions and principles, admitting no such nature at all, or

<margin>C</margin>certainly, if this is impossible and such a nature and essence necessarily exists, we must entirely concede what we established from the beginning: namely, that a thing is numerically one and the same, not divided, but existing as a complete whole, and not removed from any of the remaining things that exist besides itself. Nor, however, should it be thought to be "diffused" <note>meaning spread out thinly like a mist</note> in a passive way in order to be present to that which receives it; nor, again, should its presence be divided as if portions

<margin>D</margin>flowed out from it. Nor, once more, should we think that while it remains whole in itself, some other thing fashioned by it carries it along and thus proceeds here and there into other things; otherwise, it would certainly be in one place, and that which went out from it would be in another. Yet, if it were already separated from its own effects, it would possess its own distinct location. One may again argue regarding those things that flow from it in this manner:

<margin>E</margin>either each of them represents the whole itself, or only a certain part. But if it is a part, it will not preserve the nature of the whole, as has been said. If, however, each thing is the whole, then either we shall divide the whole into as many parts as there are things in which it remains—and thus it is already divided—or we shall certainly confess that the same whole is able to be everywhere. This reasoning is deduced from the thing itself and from its very essence; it admits nothing foreign, nor does it receive anything from a different nature.

By the common opinion of all, and as reason itself dictates, the soul of the Gods exists everywhere at once. But for God to occupy the entire universe at the same time, He is not forced to be thinned out or divided; otherwise, He would be corporeal [physical], and He would be weakened and perish. Therefore, He is the same whole everywhere. The power of no God suffers any lack; therefore, the spirit is nowhere lacking; God is everywhere. The more excellent a natural power is, the larger the province it occupies. The power of God himself is more eminent everywhere than the most excellent power of nature. The power of the First God is immense. Finally, whatever follows after God cannot be moved or preserved without the presence of God.

<margin>A</margin>If indeed that which is truly being <note>original: "τὸ ὄντως ὂν"</note>, which remains the same and does not depart from itself, does not stay in one place, then it is necessarily within itself, and since it is truly itself and nowhere distant from itself, it cannot be one part here and another part there. Nor can anything proceed from it to another place, for then it would be in one thing and then in another entirely. Perhaps then

<margin>B</margin>if it is in another, it is in a nature that does not suffer change, and it is something else, not having departed from itself, nor having been divided, nor undergoing even a single change. If it is in many things at once, and if it is still at one with itself, then that which is identical everywhere would again have the property of being in many things. It is thus both existing in itself and yet not existing solely in itself. It remains to say that it must be divided. But it is the nature of those things "partaking" in it 

<margin>C</margin>to have an equal share of its power present to them, according to how much they are capable of receiving. It is necessary, then, either to destroy those hypotheses and principles, saying that there is no such nature; but if this is impossible, and there necessarily exists such a nature and essence, it would be ridiculous to deny the original point: that what is numerically the same is not divided, but is a whole, yet is not absent from any of the things that exist after it. It is not there by being poured out, nor

<margin>D</margin>by certain portions of it going out, nor again by not remaining whole in itself while leaving behind something produced by it, so as to be in other things in many ways. For then one part would be in one place and another elsewhere, and that which comes from it would be elsewhere. And it would then be standing apart from the things that come from it. And indeed each would be either a whole or a part. If a part, it will not save the nature of the whole, as is said. But if

<margin>E</margin>each is a whole, then each will be divided into parts equal to that in which it exists, or we shall grant that the same whole is everywhere. Thus, the whole is with the things themselves, and there is nothing foreign to the essence, nor has it been dragged out of its different nature.

<margin>Chapter 4.</margin>
<margin>A</margin>SEE now, if you will, whether we say this God either is not, or is not in one place. For this is the shared belief among all who have an idea of the gods: not only to say it regarding that One, but about all the gods—that they are present everywhere, as reason itself dictates. <margin>thus</margin> It is therefore argued that He is everywhere, but not as something divided. For otherwise He Himself would not be everywhere, but each part of Him would be—this part here, and that part there. Not...

# BOOK THE FIFTH <note>Though the previous page was identified as Book VI, this early edition header marks it as Book V, likely following an older arrangement of Plotinus's works.</note>

<margin>A</margin>...so that it would no longer be one, just as if a certain magnitude <note>original: "magnitudo" / "μέγεθος". In this context, it refers to a physical size or volume that can be sliced into pieces.</note> were divided into many parts. For if it were scattered in such a way, the parts would no longer constitute that original whole. To this, we must add that if God were structured this way, He would possess a body. But if these things are impossible, we find again that which previously seemed unbelievable: that in the whole of human nature, God is thought to be everywhere at once. From this, it is clear that a single, individual thing can be entirely present everywhere at the same time. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, if we say that nature is infinite—for we would not concede it to be finite, as it is primarily infinite—it is so only because it fails nowhere. If it were to fail, it would certainly not be "one" in its existence. For if it could not be present, it would necessarily be absent, and there would be something where it itself was not. Truly, even if we say something else exists after the One, that too must exist together with it. Whatever follows the One must revolve around it and lean toward it, being its offspring and connected to it, so that whatever participates in what follows the One also participates in the One itself. Therefore, since there are many levels in the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" is the realm of pure thought and forms, as opposed to the "sensible world" we perceive with our senses.</note>—a first, a second, and a third—and all knowledge is fixed together as if at the center of a single sphere, they are not separated by any intervals. Rather, because they are all there together, where the third things are, the second and first are equally present. But let us explain this matter more clearly in what follows.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>...that it should no longer be one, just as if a certain magnitude were divided into many: for if it were thus dissipated, not even all the parts together would constitute that whole. Added to this is the fact that God, being so disposed, would also be a body. But if these things cannot be, we again hold as certain what seemed incredible: namely, that in the entirety of human nature, it is understood that God is everywhere at once; from which it is established that one individual thing is everywhere simultaneously whole. <margin>B</margin> Again, if we say that nature is infinite—for we would not grant it to be defined, since it is essentially infinite—it is so only because it never falls short. For if it falls short, it surely does not consist as "one" in its being. If it were unable to be present, it would have to be so, and there would be something where it was not. Now indeed, even if we say something else exists after the one, it must again be simultaneously with it: and that which is after it must dwell around it, and strive toward it, being its offspring connected to it, so that what participates in that which is after it, is also a participant of the One. Therefore, since in the intelligible world there are many things—a first, second, and third rank—and all things by knowledge are as if fixed together at the center of a single sphere, they are not separated by any intervals from one another, but all are there together. Rightly, where the third things are, there the second and first are likewise present; but let us next explain this matter more plainly.

<column-break/>

*> He often takes the "first being" and "intellect" to represent the intelligible world, in which ideas exist like specific centers within a common center. He also frequently takes it to mean what I have said, but one must join to those ideas (as centers) the immaterial forms hanging from them like lines; as they are annexed there, or produced from there, they are many. And this whole heap is the intelligible world, which is more of a "one" than the heap of material forms annexed to matter, which is called the sensible world. The intelligible is more "one" because immaterial forms are more closely and firmly fixed to their ideas, and through ideas to the intellect, than material forms are to their own origins, and through them to matter. Likewise, because that world is one by the highest unity of form, while this world is one by the lowest unity of matter. Also, because here in the material world, union is hindered by lines and brings about the resistance of parts and qualities, making the whole transformation temporal; there, however, these hindrances do not exist. Likewise, the intelligible world is compared to a most vast sphere, within whose circuit are contained other circuits, and to which the centers of immaterial forms are reduced—as if they were spheres contained within the first form, just as smaller spheres are in a larger sphere. This kind of union does not prohibit the distinctions of essences, just as the union of forms in matter does not, nor the connection of lines to centers and a center, nor the collection of spheres within a sphere.*

### Chapter V.

<margin>A</margin> FOR the sake of clarity, it is often said in discourse—as if one had drawn many lines from a single center—that just as these things occur in the sensible world, we must strive to understand that the many things born there <note>i.e., in the divine or intelligible realm.</note> exist simultaneously. One must again realize that just as in a circle it is permitted to take lines that are not entirely distinct from one another as if they were distinct—for the plane is one—so too where there is no interval <margin>B</margin> across the whole plane, but only entirely non-distant powers and essences, all things are not unreasonably thought of in the manner of centers joined to one another at a single point. There, the lines themselves are let go, and only the ends of the lines touching the center are preserved, where all things are truly one. Again, if you join the lines to the points, they will hang from their own centers, which remain individual; nevertheless, each center will be one, not at all separated from the one first center. Thus, while they are together with that center, they are also meanwhile individual, as many as the lines for which they served as ends. Therefore, as many...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> WHAT is frequently said—that just as many lines proceed from one certain center, so too do intelligible things proceed from one source—seeks to conveniently provide an understanding of the multitude generated there. But first, it is necessary to observe this: that all things said to be born as "many" there, exist simultaneously. Again, one must suggest that while in a circle it is possible to take lines that are not completely distinct as if they were distinct (for the plane is one), <margin>B</margin> where there is no interval even according to the whole plane, but only non-distant powers and essences, all things are considered—not without reason—as centers joined to one another in one thing. There, the lines are indeed dismissed, and only the ends of the lines touching the center are preserved, where indeed all things are one. Again, if you join the lines to the points, they will hang from their own centers, which each remain; yet each center will nonetheless be one, by no means separated from the one first center. Thus, while they are together with it, they are also meanwhile individual, as many as the lines for which it had granted that they should exist as ends; wherefore as many...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

where the lines touch the center itself, there appear to be as many points as there are lines. Yet, in truth, the One appears to be all these points at once. If, therefore, we admit that all intelligible things <note>original: "intelligibilia" / "νοητὰ". These are the eternal forms or ideas that exist in the Divine Mind.</note> are similar to many centers—centers, I say, that are reduced into a single center and completely joined—they appear to be many only because of the lines. These lines do not create the centers but merely point to them. Thus, for our purposes, these lines represent a certain proportion in themselves toward that intelligible nature; by touching this nature, it appears to be many and present everywhere.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...where [the center] does not touch the lines, they appear to be so many points. But those points are not in the center; having compared all things there to many points, which are referred back to and united in a center, they appear many because of the lines. These lines did not generate the points but showed them. Let the lines provide for us, for the present, a representation of the things which the intelligible nature touches; thus, it appears to be many and present in many places.

->*On considering all and individual ideas in the first mind, and soon recognizing the full abundance of ideas within any single idea: even if one idea preserves its own unique property from the rest. Likewise, if the intellectual soul forms many bodies in turn, it is one in many; but if it is in the intelligible world, many things are rather in one, or around one. Chapter VI.*<-

---

**INTELLIGIBLE BEINGS**, truly, though they are many, are at the same time one. Again, while they are one, they nevertheless take on the nature of being many; then indeed, there are many in one, and one in many, and all are together. Moreover, they all act toward the whole together with the whole; and again, they act toward the part together with that same whole. The part admits into itself the primary action as a part, but the whole follows afterward—just as if "Man" himself <note>The "Ideal Man" or the universal concept of humanity.</note>, coming into a particular man, should become that man, while still remaining the universal Man. The man who exists in matter <note>A physical, living human being.</note>, derived from the one Man who exists after the Idea, renders those same men many; thus, the same "one" is in many, because a certain identical thing is impressed into many like a seal. But "Man" himself, and each thing in itself, and the entire universe itself, is not in many in that way; rather, the many are in him—or more truly, they are around him. For it is one thing to be present everywhere, as the soul of each individual is the same in every part of the body; it is in this way that Being itself must be judged to be everywhere.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **ALTHOUGH** the intelligible things are many, they are one; and being many by their infinite nature, they are one. The many are in the one, and all are together. Every part acts toward the whole with the whole, and again acts toward the part with the whole. The part receives into itself the first activity as a part, but the whole follows. For example, if "Man" came into a certain man, he would become a certain man, 
<margin>B</margin> while remaining Man. The man in matter, derived from the one Man who follows the Idea, made many of the same men; or, the same thing is in many in this way, as if one impression were made by a seal in many places. But "Man" himself, and each thing itself, and the whole universe, are not in many in that way, but rather the many are in it—or better, around it. For the presence there is of a different kind, 
<margin>C</margin> just as the soul of each is the same in every part of the body. Thus indeed, the whole is everywhere.
