->*Concerning how our nature understands the abundance of ideas—specifically those turned toward its own intellect—and yet does not imagine them through an "image," but is itself the universe through the intellect. Argument: Thus, in the universal form of things, all souls are in a certain way one, even though each is distinct by its own property; insofar as they depart from the intellect, they are distinguished within themselves.*<-
->*Chapter VII.*<-

*In treating these two books, Plotinus does not intend to prove that there can be only one soul, but that one soul can be everywhere, regardless of the size or number of bodies. He argues it is not necessary to place many souls in different parts of the world, as if one common soul were not sufficient to be and rule everywhere. If many souls are posited, they are posited for different reasons than a lack of sufficiency in the One. Rather, many are one through a "blessed union" of state. Likewise, they act under its common power and are reduced to a common Idea of the soul. Every soul contains all the "seeds" of things within itself, just like the World Soul. When it turns into itself, it unfolds itself into all things and becomes equal to that which governs all things equally, contemplating all things equally with the common Mind. Such a soul becomes like the light of all stars within the light of the sun, where all are everywhere and all have equal power to rule all things, yet the others follow in the power of the Sun. Another example is the five senses: they are one, first because they lead from one common sense to the "one" [the soul]; second, because in withdrawing from the body, each of them feels within the common sense; third, if we exercise sight, we feel in the common sense not only visible things, but soon other sensible things as well. All senses first perceive their own objects, then others; and so with the rest. Then each would be one with all others, because all would exist and yet remain distinct. Each can reflect upon its own things as before, and although each pours itself through all things, it begins from a certain source and finally returns to the same. Know that Plotinus, after these books and after the tenth book—where he argues all souls are one—composed three books "On the Doubts of the Soul," where he clearly shows the number of souls.*

---

**INDEED**, our own nature is led back to Being itself, to which we ourselves are led back; we ascend to it, and we exist from it from the beginning. We understand those intelligible things not through their images, nor through any figures that we might possess. But if we do understand them, and yet not through images or figures, it follows that we understand them by being those things ourselves. If, therefore, we are participants in true knowledge, we *are* those things; we do not merely receive them...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **FOR OUR** nature and we ourselves are led back to Being, and we ascend to that, and our first origin is from that. We know those things, not as images of them, nor as possessing types <note>original: "τύπους" / "typos". Often translated as "impressions" or "stamps" in the mind.</note>, or if types, then such as an image has. If therefore we participate in true knowledge, we are those things, not having received...

# BOOK FIVE.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> These things are not in us, but rather we are in them; and since others are also there, or rather we are all those things, we are all one. Therefore, being together with all things, we are those things; thus, we are all one. When we look outward, or toward that from which we are suspended, we are ignorant that we are one—like many faces looking outward, yet having a single crown <note>original: "κορυφὰς" / "vertice". This refers to the top of the head or a common point of origin, suggesting that while individuals look like separate people, they share a single "mind" at their source.</note> on the inside. <margin>B</margin> But if someone were able to turn back—either by their own nature or by some happy fortune of being drawn back—they will see God, themselves, and the All. At first, they will see themselves not as the All. Then, finding no place to set themselves down or to define how far their "self" extends, they will cease to circumscribe themselves from the whole of being; they will arrive at the whole without moving, remaining there where the whole itself stands.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, these things are not in us, but we exist in them. Since not only we are those things, but others are as well, we are certainly all those things. Existing together with all things, we are those things; therefore, we are all one. When we look outward and direct our gaze toward that from which we are suspended, we fail to notice that we are one: just as if many faces were connected in a single circle to a certain vertex <note>The Latin "vertex" implies the highest point or a common center.</note> or a single internal root. <margin>B</margin> But if anyone were able to reflect upon the innermost things—whether by his own nature or by Wisdom <note>original: "Minerua". The translator uses the Roman goddess of wisdom to represent the Greek concept of Athena or intellectual insight.</note> reflecting him—he would see himself as God and the universe. He would see, I say, himself at first not as the entire universe, but then, having no place to stop and determine where he himself ends, he would soon cease to limit himself, and would arrive from his being into the deep, yet in such a way that he never departs, but remains in that very place where the whole consists.

->*The divine mind acts upon matter through its ideas, not from the outside in the manner of human art, but from within in the manner of an artistic nature: nor is it second in place from matter—otherwise it would be assigned its own specific location—nor is it mixed with matter, otherwise it would not rule over it at all. Chapter VIII.*<-

->*But where the idea of fire is, it is everywhere ready to generate warmth: not divided, lest it perish; not extended, lest it become corporeal; not multiplied in number, lest it become innumerable. One is sufficient; one is everywhere whole.*<-

---

I believe that if anyone were to consider how <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "ὕλη" / "materia". In Neoplatonism, matter is the "receptacle" or the lowest level of reality that receives the "form" of higher ideas.</note> participates in the <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "εἰδῶν" / "species". These are the eternal, perfect patterns of things like "Fire" or "Beauty."</note>, they would more easily believe what is being said and no longer doubt it as impossible. For it is probable and even necessary that nature is not arranged so that the Forms are placed in one spot and Matter is located separately elsewhere, with a certain "shining" or "illumination" coming into Matter from above.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> I truly believe that whoever considers the condition by which Matter in some way receives the Forms will more easily grant what is currently being said; they will no longer deny it as impossible or doubt it. <margin>B</margin> For I think it probable and necessary that nature is not so disposed that the species are placed separately here, and Matter is located separately there, with a certain illumination coming into Matter from somewhere above. For we must fear lest this description be ridiculous: what exactly would "at a distance" or "separately" mean in this context? Furthermore, would it not be difficult to explain and full of ambiguity, as we just touched upon regarding the condition of participation? But if this is ever said, it is too easily and promptly brought forward, since one arrives at this knowledge through examples. But whenever we introduce the name of "illumination" <margin>C</margin> into the discussion, we do not mean it as we see in things manifest to the senses, where distant objects are illuminated by other distant objects. But since the things in Matter are images, and the Forms themselves hold the rank of the first patterns, these images seem to flash out from them. We use the term "illumination" because the one who illuminates is not mixed with the one being illuminated. But speaking more accurately now, we must not arrange things as if the Form itself were <margin>D</margin> in a separate place, and then, as if in water, the brightness of the <term>Idea</term> were seen in the Matter. Instead, one must think of Matter as touching the Idea from every side, and yet not touching it; and thus, according to its whole self, it carries away something from the Form, with proximity contributing to this, insofar as it can receive it with no medium intervening. Nor does the Idea run through the Matter or overflow it, but rather remains in itself. For if the Idea of Fire itself does not lie within the Matter, yet we accept that Matter is now subject to the elements, then surely the Ideal Fire [touches] the Matter...

<sig>Kk 3</sig>

<summary>Plotinus explains that humans are fundamentally united with the Divine Mind and can realize this by turning their gaze inward rather than outward. He also argues that the spiritual Ideas (Forms) do not "shine" on Matter from a physical distance but are intimately present within it without being physically mixed or divided.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

Above, and not inherent in matter yourself, you will exhibit the form of fire through the whole of the ignited matter. Let it be supposed that the primary material fire is immediately a large mass. Furthermore, the same reasoning applies to the other elements.
<margin>B</margin>
If, therefore, the Ideal Fire itself is seen in all things, providing an image of itself: it does not provide it as if it were moved from its place—for it is not visible to the eyes—otherwise, this entire fire would already be somewhere in the presence of the senses. If the whole of it is in these parts, it certainly provides images of a certain quality, while its Idea is not circumscribed by place, but rather generates places from itself. Otherwise, if it were not made multiple according to its parts, it would have to 
<margin>C</margin>
divide from itself so that it might become many, and would frequently become a participant in the same thing. Now truly, since the Idea itself cannot be cut, it provides nothing of itself to the parts of matter; and yet, because it is one, it is not powerless to be taken up by that which is not within its own unity. Nor is it compelled to exist in such a way that it forms one part of the universe with one part of itself, and another part with another; rather, it is the whole in any given thing. For it would be 
<margin>D</margin>
ridiculous to introduce many Ideas of fire so that each individual fire is formed by its own Idea—this one by that, and that one by another—for in that case, the Ideas would be innumerable. Furthermore, how would these Ideas properly divide themselves if fire is one and continuous? Then truly, if we add more fire to this matter, increasing it, we must concede that according to that portion of matter as well, the very same Idea has produced the same effects; for no one would say there is a different Idea in that place.

<column-break/>

When it <note>the Ideal Form</note> comes into being in the matter, it will provide a shape to it throughout the whole ignited matter; thus, a large mass of primary fire is produced from the underlying matter. The same logic applies to the other so-called elements.
<margin>B</margin>
Let us not think that the Idea uses that fire for all things by providing an image of itself as if it were separate, or as if we were providing visible reflections. For the fire perceived by the senses is not the whole, and insofar as it is many or parts of itself, it participates in the Idea <note>original: "μετέχοι"</note> in an absurd way, if place were to be generated by it, or if the Idea were contained by the place itself. If it becomes many, it would have to flee from itself and frequently participate in the same thing. It was not necessary for matter to receive something specific from the Idea itself; rather, to the undivided Mind it became impossible for the parts not to be shaped by its unity. It is present everywhere, not shaping one part of the universe with one part of itself and another with another, but rather the whole to everything and to the whole. For it would be absurd for many Ideas to come together, so that for each fire there is another Idea, and these would shape others. These shapes and Ideas would be as if they had become divided, even though fire is continuous; and if we were to add other fire to this matter, making it larger, then according to that part, there would be an impression of the same Idea, and the same things would happen as in the other part.

---

->The single machine of the world <note>original: "mundi machina"</note> was thus fabricated by a single mind, and brought to life by a single soul that is totally present everywhere at once.<-

### Chapter IX.

Just as within one sphere there are many spheres, and lives existing with it both equally and distinctly, so there are many souls within the one Soul. The World Soul <note>original: "Anima mundi"</note> is not like a single point made out of many, but is more eminent; therefore, it does not have a fixed position in a measured dimension. Nor, again, is it one made from many, but a unity unfolding <note>original: "explicans"</note> a multitude within itself. Therefore, it can be present to many parts and bodies at once, and is not distinct from any of them according to place, since it is more "containing" than such things, and it procreates both quantity and place. Finally, however much it is exalted above the machine of the world, it nevertheless sustains it; rightfully, it flourishes everywhere as a whole, and similarly the Mind <note>original: "intellectus"</note> which is the craftsman of the world.

---

<margin>A</margin>
ACCORDINGLY, if someone by reason leads all the elements already made into a single circular figure, they certainly should not say that many authors produced the sphere, such that one was distributed here and another there to produce a specific part. Rather, there is a single cause of the fabrication, completing it as a whole, without one part of itself making one thing and another part making another. Otherwise, there would again be many creators, unless you refer the entire fabrication back to one indivisible <note>original: "indivisibile"</note> source. Indeed, let there be one impartible 
<margin>B</margin>
effector of the whole sphere; yet not in such a way that the author himself is poured out into the sphere, but rather that the whole sphere hangs suspended and clings inwardly to the author. Therefore, one life holds the sphere, and the sphere is located within one life. And thus all things that are in the sphere are reduced to one life, and therefore all souls are, in a certain way, one. But the soul is one in such a way that it is also infinite; for which reason some have said the soul is a number <note>A reference to Pythagorean and Platonic theories that the soul is a "self-moving number."</note>, while others have taught that number increases the nature of the soul. They perhaps thought of it this way because the soul is never lacking anywhere, but stands out through all things, while still existing as itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
AND therefore, if someone by reason brings all the things already brought into shape into one spherical form, one must not say that many produced the sphere, with different ones being sent to different parts to make those parts. Rather, the cause of the production must be one, making the part with the whole of itself. Otherwise, there would again be many, unless you refer the whole composition to one indivisible thing. Rather, let the one who makes the
<margin>B</margin>
sphere be indivisible, not as something poured out into the sphere, but with the whole sphere suspended from the maker. Therefore, the same single life holds the sphere, the sphere itself having been placed in one life. And all things in the sphere, therefore, are in one life. Insofar as all souls are one, they are one in such a way as to be infinite. For this reason, some called it a number, while others said they increase the nature of it... <note>The Greek text here becomes fragmented or abbreviated in the transcription.</note> perhaps imagining it this way, because it fails nothing. But it is over all things, as many as remain and...

<summary>Plotinus argues that the Ideal Forms (like Fire) and the World Soul are indivisible unities that are present as a whole in every part of the physical world, rather than being split into fragments. He concludes that the entire universe is a single "machine" sustained by one Mind and one Soul, which generates space and quantity rather than being contained by them.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the metaphysical investigation of how the Soul and the "One" (the ultimate source of reality) can be present everywhere in the universe at once without being divided into pieces. # BOOK FIVE.

<language>English translation of Greek and Latin parallel text</language>

<margin>A</margin> If the world were even larger than it is, the power of the soul would never fail to propagate itself throughout the whole; it would not merely run through all things, but rather this entire universe would exist within that universal soul. When we speak of "increasing" this power, it should not be understood in a literal sense, as one might speak of stretching a physical object. Rather, although the soul is one, it is never absent from the universe. For the "one" that belongs to the soul is not the kind of unity that can be measured by size or quantity. Such a condition of measurement belongs to <margin>B</margin> a different nature <note>original: "alterius naturae," referring to the material or physical world</note>, which falsely claims unity for itself and only achieves a likeness of being "one" through a certain participation in the true One.

That which is one in true reality exists in such a way that it is not a "one" accumulated from many parts; if it were, the whole would perish if any part were removed. It is also the kind of unity that is not separated by boundaries imposed from the outside. If it were bounded, it might become smaller when other things are present, or <margin>C</margin> it might be dissipated in an attempt to expand through all things. In that case, the "whole" would not be present to everything, but would only touch parts of things with its own specific parts.

Consequently—as is often said—the soul does not know "where" in the world it is, because it cannot be forced into a single point or a specific arrangement that is torn away from itself. If it truly claims this unity for itself, which we may preach as its very essence, <margin>D</margin> then it must be seen as containing multiplicity within its own power—a nature seemingly opposite to its own. It does not borrow this multiplicity from external things, but possesses it within itself and from itself. It is truly one, yet within that Unity, it possesses the quality of being infinite and multiple.

Because it is such a nature, it must be present as a whole everywhere, existing within its own rational principle <note>original: "ratio," often used to translate the Greek "logos"</note> and containing itself. For in containing itself, it also exists as the very thing that contains the world. It is not hidden, but is present everywhere within the world. <margin>E</margin> It is not separated by the limits of space, nor is it disconnected from itself by being in another place; indeed, it exists before all things that are "in a place." The soul does not need places; rather, places need the soul so that they may be founded upon it. Once things are founded within it, the soul does not depart from its own seat—which is nothing other than resting within itself. It is the substantial foundation of all things, supporting them.

<column-break/>

As previously mentioned, the soul is not so foolish as to depart from itself and risk dissolution. While it is preserved entirely within itself, it does not rashly commit itself to the untrustworthy medium of space, which undoubtedly requires the soul's presence in order to be preserved at all.

### These three principles of things are everywhere: the Good itself, the Soul, and the Intellect, which exists through Beauty itself, and whose life is the life of the world. This power, as if by its own pathways, draws all things to itself and collects them into a single desire for the Good, Beauty, and Life. Chapter X.

*The power of heavenly goodness, freedom, and life is present everywhere in its entirety, sufficing for all things; because it is added to nothing, it remains within itself. And even if there were many people, they would not merely enjoy a single light here and there as a whole; likewise, all intellectual souls enjoy the one light of the primary intelligence. This light is present everywhere and divided nowhere, and within it, all souls are one. It is likely that all things feed upon the Good, which is absent from nowhere. Indeed, the distance and discord full of bodies in this world would be nothing if that heavenly world and its inhabitants did not possess a marvelous union. This chapter, and many others, reveals that these "inhabitants" differ among themselves according to their essences.*

<sig>Kk 4</sig>

<vocab>
- **The One/Unity:** In Plotinus's philosophy, the ultimate, indivisible source of all existence.
- **Intellect (Intellectus):** The first emanation from the One, containing the Ideal Forms of all things.
- **Soul (Anima):** The principle that gives life and order to the physical universe.
- **Participation:** The concept that material things only "exist" or have "unity" because they share in the reality of the higher spiritual Forms.
</vocab>

It emphasizes that the three highest principles—the Good, Intellect, and Soul—are universally present and unify all of existence through a shared desire for beauty and life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the "One" and the Soul. ### PLOTINUS ENNEADS VI

That [principle], therefore, remains in itself, overflowing with wisdom, and never clings to anything else. All other things, however, depend continuously upon it, for they find it within themselves through their own desire. And this is that love <note>The "love" described here is the *Eros* of the soul for the Divine, a central theme in Neoplatonic thought.</note> which is said to affect many so deeply that they spend their nights at the gates of the beloved. I speak of a love that stands outside itself, desiring the Beautiful, and considering itself satisfied if it can only participate in it as much as possible. For even the lover of that which is above does not receive the Beauty itself, but experiences it through a certain proximity. Beauty, however, stands firm in itself, and many are lovers of that single One.

<margin>B</margin>
They love the whole, and when they possess it according to their strength, they possess the whole, for it is the whole itself that is loved. What, then, prevents it from sufficing for everyone while it remains within itself? Indeed, it satisfies everyone for this very reason: because it remains [undivided]. It is beautiful precisely because it is present as a whole to everyone.

<margin>C</margin>
Now, in truth, Intelligence itself is present as a whole to everyone; for this reason, it is called "common intelligence." This intelligence does not exist specifically "here" or specifically "there." It would be a ridiculous thing if it required a physical location; surely intelligence does not exist in the same way that whiteness does <note>In ancient philosophy, a quality like "whiteness" is an accident that exists only within a specific body; Plotinus argues Intelligence is a primary reality that doesn't need a body to exist.</note>. For it is not the function of a body to think. Rather, if we are truly participants in intelligence, we necessarily converge into one and the same thing that exists as a whole and at once within itself. We do not receive it in such a way that we take only certain portions of it; nor, again, is it like I have a whole and you have a whole, with one being divided from the other.

<margin>D</margin>
The assemblies and gatherings of seekers imitate this, as if they were converging into one intelligence, for each person on their own is powerless to achieve wisdom. But when, in the gathering itself and through the true bond of understanding, all are joined together, they produce and discover intelligence. For what can prevent the intellect of one person and another from being in the same [source]?

<margin>E</margin>
But truly, although others who are thinking may come together with us toward the same point, they do not appear to us to be coming together at the same time. This is just as if someone, touching the same object with many fingers at once, should think they are touching different things; or as if someone should pluck the same string on a lyre without seeing that they are plucking it. However, we should consider how we reach the Good <term>The Good: The ultimate, supreme principle in Plotinus's system, above even Intelligence.</term> with our souls. For I do not reach one "Good" and you another; rather, it is the same. Nor, again, do we reach the same thing in such a way that one part flows into me and another into you—as if it were located somewhere high above and its gifts descended to us here below. Instead, it is necessary for the Giver himself to be entirely present to those who receive, so that one truly receives from that source; and he who gives should give from his own [being], not from things foreign to him.

<margin>F</margin>
For the gift of the intellect is not performed in the manner of a transmission or the sending of a messenger. Even in physical bodies that are distant from each other in space, a very similar gift is often granted to different people at the same time, and the tradition and effect are directed toward the same end. Indeed, the entire body [of the universe] acts and suffers within itself, and nothing from the outside enters it. If, therefore, nothing from the outside enters the body itself—which by its own nature is always "fleeing" from itself <note>The material world is in a constant state of change and flux ("fleeing"), unlike the stable spiritual world.</note>—how can anything external have a place in a reality that suffers no spatial distance? For this reason, being in the same place, we both see and touch the Good itself. We are together, I say, and we reach it with many intelligible things.

<margin>G</margin>
And certainly, the way of being "there" <note>Plotinus uses "there" (Greek: *ekei*) to refer to the higher spiritual or "intelligible" world, as opposed to "here" (the physical world).</note> is much more unified than it is here...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
It remains, therefore, in itself to be wise, and it could not come to be in another. But those other things are suspended from it, as if looking toward a hearth. The love felt by those outside the gates <note>original: "θυραυλῶν" (thyraulon) - those who sleep at the door</note> is a love always striving from the outside for the prize, and cherishing it in such a way as it is able to participate. For even the lover from that world, who receives beauty from that source, possesses only the traces [of it]. But that [source] remains in itself,

<margin>B</margin>
and the lovers of the One are many. When they possess it, they all possess the whole. For the whole is what is laid out; it is not as if it were hindered. Since it is for this reason that it suffices: because it remains beautiful, as a whole for all. And so, understanding is a whole for all. For this reason, "understanding" is that which defines. If one part were here and another there, it would be ridiculous, for it would require a place to be wise; but let being wise be as it is, and not in the same way

<margin>C</margin>
as whiteness. For if being wise belonged to a body... but if indeed we truly participate in being wise, we all come into the same thing together with it. And whenever we receive from that source, it is not as if we took a part, or as if I took the whole and you took the whole while we were separated from each other. This is what the imitation [shows] in assemblies and all gatherings, as if they were going toward that which is to be wise, though each one is unable to be wise separately. But by contributing to the one whole in the gathering, and even more so in true understanding, being wise

<margin>D</margin>
would come to be. Because indeed understanding, if they were the same... but we do not know. If they do not seem to be together, it is as if someone touching the same thing with many fingers thinks they are touching different things. Or if one should strike the same string without seeing it. And as for the things of the soul, when we touch the Good, we think of it; for it is not that I touch some things and you touch others, but we touch the same things. Or, it is the same thing, but when we approach it...

<margin>E</margin>
...it seems in turn to be in vain. Just as there are some things here, and those things which are with him [the Giver] are here. And the giving and receiving: they do not receive it in every way; he gives, or the giver, or someone deprives. But to all he is still present to himself, or the participation is the gift. Since even in gifts, in other things and all places and bodies, the gift is one thing to one person and another to another

<margin>F</margin>
who is kindred. And the gift and the trust are toward the same thing, and of the bodily things of the whole, you see it was present to him and from there [it came] into it from the outside. If indeed, in the things that are part of him, whether from the outside or from nature, as if bringing it to himself in a thing without distance, how is it from the outside? Therefore, being in the same [place], we either see the good things or we touch it, being together with our own

<margin>G</margin>
intelligible things, and the world is one much more "there."

Plotinus uses the analogies of a public assembly and a lyre string to show that spiritual reality is a "common" source accessible to all without being partitioned.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Plotinus’s Ennead VI, specifically investigating how the "One" or the "Divine Mind" can be present everywhere without being physically divided. The previous page used the analogy of light and the soul's desire for beauty; here, the text shifts to a more technical metaphysical argument regarding "bulk" (physical mass) versus "power" (spiritual presence).</meta>

# BOOK FIVE

->*The Divine Mind, just as it equals and surpasses all time through an indivisible eternity—which is the cause of time—so through its indivisible essence, from which every infinite broad space arises and is exceeded, it is itself present everywhere, preserving space and the things within it. Chapter XI*<-

->*For as all time is related to its indivisible state, so is the whole of dimension [space] related to the surpassing power of the indivisible substance; for there is both persistence there, as well as the immensity of power, and here [in our world] a certain image of both these gifts.*<-

<margin>A</margin>There would be two sensible worlds, divided in the same way, and the intelligible sphere itself would be sensible, if it were not one in a different way than this world of ours. Therefore, it will either excel in unity, or it will certainly be a ridiculous endeavor: if indeed, by some necessity, a physical bulk <note>original: *moles* (Latin) / *ogkos* (Greek). In Neoplatonism, this refers to physical matter that occupies space, as opposed to spiritual substance.</note> were appropriate for this sphere, but that other sphere [the Divine], needing no extension, should stretch itself out and fall away from itself. Finally, what hindrance is there there to prevent all things from coming together into one? For one thing there does not repel another by not granting it a place: just as <margin>B</margin> we see that neither teaching nor universal contemplation, nor indeed all the sciences in the soul, are in the least bit cramped. If someone should object that this union cannot happen in essences <note>original: *essentijs*. The fundamental "being" or "reality" of a thing.</note>, I will respond indeed that it could only be impossible if true essences were physical bulks.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>BUT in what way does that which has no dimension in itself reach through the whole body, being endowed with such great magnitude? Or why is it not dispersed by such propagation, so that one and the same thing is stretched through all things? This is a question we have often brought into doubt, earnestly desiring to put an end to the hesitation at some point. It has already been demonstrated many times that it is so, but it is worthwhile also <margin>B</margin> to bring persuasion, although that very nature—the kind which has been shown—has contributed not a little, but rather a great deal, to persuasion. Similarly, it seems helpful if we consider that it is not like a huge stone <note>original: *saxum* (Latin) / *lithos* (Greek).</note> placed somewhere: which, where it is placed, as large as it is, occupies just as much space, unable to cross those same limits. For since it has a certain measure of quantity, it also has a measure of power within the circumscribed nature of the stone. <margin>C</margin> On the other hand, since that [divine nature] is the primary nature, neither measured nor determined as to how large it ought to be (for by this nature, rather, the other is measured), it exists as a universal power of no specific size. For this reason, it is not in time, but exists outside all time; for time is continuously spread out through intervals, while eternity remains in itself in the same state, containing and surpassing [time]. It is larger than time through its everlasting power, although it may seem to exercise this power in many things. <margin>D</margin> As if a certain line seemed to proceed through the whole, yet was always led back to a point, and ran around that point, and wherever it runs, the point is seen in it: which point does not run at all, but rather the line revolves itself everywhere around it. If, therefore, time has a certain analogous proportion to that which remains the same in essence, and if that nature is infinite not only because of eternity itself but also because of the excess of infinite power, then one must surely return to this infinity of virtue...

<summary>This page argues that the Divine Mind (Intelligence) is not a physical object and therefore is not limited by space or time; it uses the analogy of a circle revolving around a central point to explain how the One remains still while everything else moves around it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 669 regarding the nature of the "One" or the Divine Mind. The previous text established that the Divine is not a physical "bulk" (mass) but a spiritual power. Here, Plotinus (through Ficino's Latin translation) explains how this infinite life is present everywhere simultaneously without being divided into pieces.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI

<column-break/>

...to perceive a certain nature running equally on the other side: which indeed is raised up equally and hangs from that higher nature, while the other power runs through time equally along with the power that remains. And certainly, that power is more ample because it causes the universe to be amplified to its own amplitude according to its strength. Where then is this nature, which participates in this [higher] nature as much as it can? Since indeed this nature is present everywhere in its entirety, yet it is not seen as a whole in everyone because of the weakness of the subject. It is present deep within the universe, not in the same way as a material triangle is in some way the same in many individual instances, but in the way that the immaterial triangle itself is, upon which those in matter depend. But why is the material triangle not everywhere, since the immaterial one flourishes everywhere? Because not all matter is made a participant, but it also has something else: for not everything is adapted to everything. Since not even that first nature immediately applied itself to everything, but first to the primary kinds <note>original: *genera prima* (Latin) / *prote genê* (Greek). In Platonic philosophy, these are the fundamental categories of existence: Being, Rest, Motion, Sameness, and Difference.</note>, and then through these to the rest: yet the superior nature was equally present to the whole.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>B</margin>

> *Life in the world is twofold, namely intellectual and animal: it is both entirely freed from all physical mass, and effective and infinite by its innate vigor; therefore, being itself whole and indivisible, it equally occupies and nourishes all parts of the world's machinery.*

->Chapter XII.<-

> *Your soul also, although it is added to your body through lower powers, is yet the universe through the intellect, but through reason, it is in the middle. Therefore, when reason turns itself and the lower powers toward the intellect, your whole soul becomes the universe. Then you do not doubt that life of the universe reigning everywhere, because you yourself are almost similarly everywhere to it. Everywhere also are all the gods, the rulers of souls and cities, directing all things to the first.*

<margin>A</margin> BUT how is it present? Truly, as one life. For life in an animal does not extend only to a certain point beyond which it cannot progress through the whole; rather, it pours itself through the universe. If someone should ask again, then they ought to remember that the power of life itself is not properly of such a size [finite]; rather, if one allows it to go into infinity in thought, one always encounters the same profoundly infinite power. For life itself does not have matter in it, by reason of which it might fail, falling into parts and then into smallness along with the magnitude of the physical bulk <note>original: *moles*. Plotinus uses this term to distinguish between the "size" of a body (which is limited) and the "greatness" of a spirit (which is infinite).</note>.
<margin>B</margin> If therefore you receive the infinity forever flourishing in it, a nature unfailing and altogether unconquered, failing in no way and nowhere in abundance, like a life truly overflowing, do you think you can look anywhere, or reach anything with your mind, where you do not find it? On the contrary, the opposite will happen to you: for you, in proceeding, will not cross over it, nor again will you stop at some small step, as if it had nothing more to give beyond that, because it fails gradually through small things. But if you are able to run along with it, or rather if, standing in the universe, you require nothing beyond, only then will you attain its presence everywhere: otherwise, if you cannot do that, or refuse, you will immediately fall away into something else, and sink from what is present, and this without noticing, because you are looking elsewhere. But if you seek nothing further, how will you escape being thus affected?
<margin>C</margin> Truly, by the fact that you have approached the whole, and have not remained in a part of it, so that you do not even say, "I am only this much": for when you have entirely omitted this very thing which is properly called "only so much," you have become the whole, although you were also the whole before. But because something else was added to you besides and after the whole...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...giving a nature, being caused or hanging from that one, these things running equally in time, while the power remains. Nor again is it for that one to make itself as much as to be present, by which it is by itself or participates in the things of nature, as much as it is possible for it to participate. The parts...
<margin>B</margin> indeed seen in the whole of everything, which are the subjects in power. And this is present to the whole, like the immaterial triangle in many, being the same in number, but like the immaterial one from which those in matter also come. Why then is the triangle in matter not everywhere, since the immaterial one is everywhere? Either all matter participated, but it has something else somewhere, and all toward all, since neither the first was all toward all, but from which the first of the kinds come. Then toward the others in order. Something was present to the whole.

<margin>A</margin> It is present therefore most distantly as one life; but how is the part in life or life, since it cannot reach into everything but is everywhere again, or since again how, you conceived of the power not as a quantity but as unceasing, and having power through eternity, because the things in it are all at once. And not in life which is in matter, so that with the magnitude of the bulk it might be reduced together into a small lesser thing.
<margin>B</margin> If you do not take the eternal infinity in it, a nature unwearied and untasted, and which is not specialized in itself, like an overflowing life, or that which receives, or the first which does not stumble, to see such a thing... for you have passed beyond and crossed over. Or if again you think it needs to give to a small part, or to fail little by little. But if you are able to suffer this, or rather having become in the whole, and not seeking in part, it was all present, all...
<margin>C</margin> you will go into another, and from that which is present, by looking toward another. But if you seek nothing further, how then will you be in the whole, or because you have come together with the whole, and did not remain in a part of it, nor even were you the whole [initially]? By letting go of "so much," you have become the whole; yet you were also the whole before. But because something else was added to you after the whole...

# BOOK FIVE.

...you turned out smaller by such an addition. For the addition to you was not from the universe: for you will never add anything to that; rather, it was from the non-universe. Now truly, whoever becomes a particular someone, and does so from non-being, you would least desire that. But then one truly exists as the whole, when they have altogether dismissed non-being. Then, therefore, you increase yourself when you dismiss other things; then the universe is present to you as you dismiss the rest. While you are one among the rest, that Divine Light shines for you least of all: but indeed when it shines, it does not "approach" to be present; rather, you had departed from it when it seemed not to be there. Even if you had departed, you did not truly leave it—for it is present everywhere—but neither did you go anywhere else. Instead, while you were still present, you diverted yourself toward contrary things. For the same reason, the other gods also, though they are equally present to many, yet they often appear to only one person: because he alone of all is able to look up and see. But these gods, of every kind and present everywhere, turn cities toward better things; but the cities are finally turned toward that celestial One, and toward it the whole earth, and toward it finally the heaven, everywhere remaining within it and by its power. Furthermore, from it those things which are truly beings <note>original: "τὰ ἀληθῶς ὄντα" (Greek) / "quæ verè sunt entia" (Latin). In Neoplatonism, these are the eternal Forms or Ideas, which possess a higher reality than physical objects.</note> possess being itself, all the way down to the soul and life which are utterly joined to it. And yet that very thing which I just called "being," though it contains an infinite multitude, breathes together into one.

### ON NUMBERS.
#### On numbers.

> If the One itself is the Good, it follows that the farther a multitude departs from the One and from unity, the worse it becomes. Therefore, if a multitude is imagined as either infinite or as lacking any unity, it will be evil itself. <->Chapter I.<-

> Each separate species <note>The "Idea" or "Form" of a thing.</note> and the "idea" of everything is most unified with itself, since its essence is simple and indivisible. A natural species is less unified with itself because it is extended through the parts of a physical body, even while it maintains its continuity; therefore it is a lesser good. A disconnected multitude, occurring through the breaking apart of a continuous whole, has the minimum of unity; therefore it is an evil. That which is imagined to preserve no union at all is called the greatest evil.

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' containing two classical figures, one seated and one standing, in a pastoral or architectural setting.</image-desc>If multitude is a certain departure from the One, and infinity <note>original: "ἀπειρία" (Greek) / "infinitas" (Latin). For each thing becomes "many" when it is unable to remain within itself, and instead flows out and is extended by being scattered. In this way, while it tries to preserve itself through the nature of the One, it becomes a multitude. When there is no other part to unify it with another, if it should continue to happen, it would always be flowing away, and becomes merely a magnitude. But what...

<margin>A</margin> <image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a seated scholar or philosopher figure within the letter's circular frame.</image-desc>IT SEEMS we must first ask whether multitude <note>original: "multitudo" (Latin). Is it for this reason that infinity is evil, and that we are evil when we are a multitude? For then any thing becomes many when it cannot remain within itself, but is diffused and extended until it is dispersed. # PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<column-break/>

**A** For what evil is there in magnitude? <note>original: "magnitudine." Plotinus is discussing physical size or "bigness" as a departure from the simple unity of the soul or the Divine.</note> Surely if it could feel, it would suffer evil. For that thing would sense that it had already departed far from itself. Everything indeed seeks not another, but itself. A movement toward external things is either in vain or certainly forced. Each thing truly exists most, not when it becomes "many" or "large," but when it belongs to itself. Now, it belongs to itself when it looks only toward itself. But that which **B** desires to become "large" in this way does not know what is truly great; it hastens where it should not, and bursts out of itself. 

To turn toward oneself, however, is to remain continually within. This is proved especially by what is produced by magnitude. For if a thing is drawn out further, so that each of its parts exists separately, they will indeed be individual parts, but no longer that specific thing which existed from the beginning. If, however, it is to remain itself, all parts must be turned toward the One, so that it exists when it is in some way "One," not when it is "large." Therefore, because of magnitude itself—and insofar as it consists of size—it loses itself. 

Insofar as it possesses the One, it also possesses itself. Nevertheless, the universe as a whole is great and beautiful; but it is beautiful for this reason: because it is not permitted to escape entirely into infinity, but is instead held together by unity. Now, it is beautiful not by its magnitude alone, but rather by its beauty <note>original: "pulchritudine." Plotinus argues that "size" is just raw material; "beauty" is the form or limit that makes size meaningful.</note>; and yet it stood in need of beauty precisely because it was made large.

**A** <note>This column translates the parallel Greek text provided in the OCR.</note> Is there something terrible attributed to magnitude? If the things within that which is becoming large could perceive, they would see themselves departing from themselves. For each thing seeks not another, but itself; the journey outward is either futile or necessary. Each thing is more truly itself not when it becomes many or great, but when it is its own. It is its own when it belongs to its own kind. The desire for the "outside" as if it were greatness comes from ignorance. **B** ... For the evidence is in that which becomes great: if it is detached, so that each of its parts exists alone, they would be those individual parts, but not the original thing from the start. But if it is itself, all parts remain together... it is through magnitude that it is lost... truly, is the whole great? Or beautiful? Or good? Through the soul it is prevented from fleeing into the infinite, but is instead embraced by beauty. Is it beautiful because of being great? No, it is beautiful because of the beauty within it. Because magnitude by itself, if left desolate, would appear ugly. Greatness is beautiful only when it is ordered; otherwise, the larger it is, the more disordered and ugly it becomes.

Since if this magnitude were destitute of beauty itself, insofar as it is large, it would appear ugly; and thus magnitude itself is the "matter" or raw material of beauty, because it is a "many" that stands in need of ornament. Therefore, that which is large, if separated from beauty, is more unadorned and more ugly.

->If an infinite multitude is imagined, it will not properly be a number. For the number of beings in the incorporeal world is defined <note>original: "definitus." In Neoplatonic thought, the "Intelligible World" or the realm of Divine Ideas is not an chaotic infinity, but a structured, perfect, and therefore limited arrangement.</note>, and from there it is limited in the corporeal world. Nor does the counting soul create number; rather, these numbers exist naturally and are limited on both sides.<-

<margin>Chapter II.</margin>

<column-break/>

### WHAT THEN should be said regarding that
**A** which is called the "number of infinity"? But first we must ask how this "infinite number" could exist. For things subject to the senses are not infinite. Therefore, the number found within them is not infinite either. Furthermore, the one who counts does not count infinity itself; rather, even if he computes doubles, triples, and similar multiples in succession, he certainly defines these. Even if he takes a multiplication toward the future or the past, he seems to define these in the meantime. 

**B** What then should be said? That a certain number is not simply infinite, but is called so only because one may always keep adding to it? But surely the authority to generate numbers does not reside in the person counting; rather, the numbers were already determined and existed entirely. Now, in the intelligible world <term>Intelligible World<gloss>The realm of eternal reality and Divine Mind (Nous), as opposed to the physical world we see.</gloss></term>, just as the beings are determined, so too is the number defined by the "number of beings." 

We, however, just as we make a "man" into many things by often applying to him "beauty" and other such qualities, so too together with every image **C** we conceive an image of number. And just as we multiply a certain city that does not exist, so we are accustomed to multiply numbers in succession. It is as if we were counting in time; using those numbers which we possess, we apply them further to segments of time, while the numbers themselves remain within us.

# BOOK SIX.

## The intelligible world <note>The "intelligible world" (mundus intelligibilis) refers to the realm of pure intellect and the "Forms" or "Ideas," which Neoplatonists believed was more real than the physical world.</note>, since it proceeded from unity itself into a multitude of ideas, is not the Good itself; yet, multiplicity there is not an evil, because it is overcome by the One. For there is one common and indivisible nature of all the ideas, such that any idea is united with all the others. Chapter III.

Infinity itself has no proper being in actuality; otherwise, it would be counted within the genus of beings and designated as something "finite." Therefore, it would no longer be infinity in actuality. Nevertheless, infinity hides beneath a limit, always terminating something. Thus, if you were to remove all forms—which act as limits and boundaries—the remainder that you might imagine is called infinity. If you try to grasp this, you immediately limit it; but if you limit it, you fail to grasp infinity. Finally, if you run through all types of opposites as you please, you will not be able to assign infinity to one side of the opposites alone; otherwise, it would reveal itself to you, and you could again call either of the opposites "infinite" by the negation of the other.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> BUT how did this infinite exist, since it is infinite? For that which has come to be and exists is already encompassed by number. But first, we must investigate whether multiplicity is truly placed in the order of real beings, and how multiplicity might be an evil. In that higher realm, however, multiplicity is united, and is not permitted to escape entirely into a "multitude," because there, multiplicity is a single being. Yet, because of this very fact, it falls away from the One and yields to it; since it possesses multiplicity, and insofar as it looks toward the One, it falls into a lower state. And since it does not possess the nature of the One itself, but has fallen away from it, it deservedly undergoes a deficiency. But by the power of the One itself, it possesses something honorable within it: namely, the multitude is turned back toward the One and stands firm. How, then, can infinity itself exist there? If it has being, it is already defined in the order of beings. Or certainly, if it were not defined, it should not be placed in the genus of beings, but perhaps <margin>C</margin> it will seem to be counted in the order of those things that are "becoming," just as happens with time. Perhaps even if it is defined, it is infinite for this very reason: for it is not the "limit" that is determined, but the "infinite." Nor is anything else placed as a middle ground between the infinite and the limit that might take on the nature of a limit. This infinity certainly flees the very "idea" of a limit, but it is grasped from the outside, being hemmed in. It does not flee from one place to another, for it has no place; but when it is grasped, then for the first time "place" exists. For this reason, we should not think that the motion attributed to infinity in our discourse is local motion <note>original: "motionem... esse localem." Plotinus distinguishes between physical movement through space and the metaphysical "movement" of thought or emanation.</note>, nor that any other of the commonly named motions belongs to it of its own accord. Therefore, it never moves, but neither does it stand still. For where would it remain, since this very word "where" arises later? It seems that motion is attributed to infinity because it is not firmly fixed, but rather remains suspended and revolving. Or rather, <margin>E</margin> is it lifted up to that place and tossed about here? Not at all. For both of these are judged in relation to the same place—both that which is lifted up without turning away, and that which turns away. What, then, will someone think 

---

infinity to be? Surely he will think of it when his intelligence has stripped away the "form" <note>original: "speciem." In this context, "species" or "form" is the defining characteristic that makes a thing what it is.</note>. What then will he understand? Perhaps opposites at the same time, and yet not opposites: for there, both the "great" and the "small" will be understood. For here, both the permanent and the moved come to be because of those things there; but before they come to be, it is clear that neither of them exists there in a determinate way, otherwise you would have already determined them. If, therefore, that nature is infinite, and if—as I was saying—these things are there infinitely and indeterminately, they both clearly appear there in such a way.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

...they were [judging/perceiving]. But if you approach that place closely and do not apply a certain limit by which you can measure it, it will completely escape you, and you will find nothing there; otherwise, it would already be defined. <margin>A</margin> Indeed, if you encounter it as a single thing, many things will suddenly appear. But if you call it many, you will again be lying: for where any part is not truly "one," then "all" are not truly "many" either. This is the very nature of infinity: it is a certain motion of the imagination <note>Plotinus describes how the human mind, when trying to grasp the absolute infinite, experiences a "motion" or flux because it cannot find a fixed point to rest upon.</note>. To the extent that the imagination approaches it, there is motion; to the extent that it has reached it, there is a state of rest. Now, this very fact—that you cannot behold it by itself—is a certain motion and a falling away from the Mind <term>Mens (Nous)</term> <note>Nous, or Divine Intellect, is the second hypostasis in Plotinus's system, the realm of pure thought and the Forms.</note>. However, because the mind touches it but holds it only from the outside, and it seems to the mind that it can cross its boundaries, it must be understood as a state of rest. From this, it appears that we do not merely bring motion to that place, but also rest.

->*He taught that all things—unity and number—possess their own proper logic in the intelligible world, distinct from other things; and if they possess essence, they proceed toward essences, as if they exist within essence, or follow essences by their own nature. He wishes to examine these names in what follows.*<-

<margin>Cap. 1</margin> <margin>A</margin> Since these natures exist in the intelligible itself, it seems they must be considered next. Is unity itself like the other species <note>Species/Forms (Eide).</note>, or is it something that follows them? For example, after a thing is of such a nature as to be "one" there, do we then ascribe unity to it? Then, because they are many—having diverse forms—do we likewise assign number to them? <unclear>If</unclear> we leave to each individual thing its own number, or is it perhaps not so? <margin>B</margin> Rather, is each thing a unity because it is itself, or is unity primarily in Being <term>Ens</term>? Does unity (and how much of it) belong to what comes after it—if indeed there is an order there—and to what extent is it a multitude, just as "ten-ness" <note>Plotinus uses the "decus" or "denarius" (ten) as a classic Pythagorean example of an abstract number being a single "Form."</note> is the number ten itself? Or perhaps it is not so, but number is thought of by itself, and so we must investigate whether it is the first of all things or the last. Plato, therefore, when he said that men learned number from the variety of days and nights, and thus attributed the nature of number to the variety of things themselves, perhaps thought that things to be counted were made <margin>C</margin> because of their diversity. He observes that the soul trusts in the discourse of number when it runs from one thing to another, as if it counts the number of yesterday. The same happens when, running through things themselves, it asserts that this is one thing and that is another; for as long as it thinks of the same thing, it asserts nothing other than "one." Yet, when Plato establishes that <margin>D</margin> true number is Essence, and number belongs to Essence, he retains a certain power of number in itself. He does not say number exists only in the counting mind, but asserts that number lies within [Reality] itself; rather, from the very variety and distraction of sensible being, the concept of number is recalled within our souls.

---

->*Furthermore, he might say that unity and number are not a specific thing, but when any object is placed before us, it is called "one" in the singular; and they have argued about these things in relation to society.*<-

<margin>Cap. 2</margin> From this opinion, we do not have a nature to discern the species of number, nor any specific number. We must look at others; we know the number of men, and number itself will be thought of as even less than an accident <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a property that isn't essential to a thing's nature (like being tall or short), whereas an "essence" is what the thing is.</note>. When we speak of a man as "one," it is asked whether "one" is the same as "good." For "one" itself is not "man," but has the opposite of "multitude," if it is so: since they are predicated commonly beyond the man. Therefore, "one" and number are common to all things in their individuals. But by what reason is one thing more perfect than another? "One" itself is a predicate, but not of being. If he thought of it as being above or below, or opposite to being. Why then should he consider being itself as number, yet restore number to unity? It is right that number should be made prior to beings.
<meta>catchword: Therefore</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...or how, when approaching near, might one not impose a limit, as if by thought, so that there too, things might not be <unclear>undisturbed</unclear>. But for one who gazes upon it, it appears many; and many again, since each is not [just] one, but all are many. This is the nature of it, and there is a certain motion of the phantoms. Regarding the imagination, this is also what <margin>B</margin> cannot see Being <term>on</term> itself; it is a certain motion and a slipping away. Why should it not be able to have a limit? It is received as if in a circle, and not seeing [the end] it has departed. This would be a state of rest, so that it is said to be moved in only one way.

---

<margin>Cap. 1</margin> Regarding numbers, we must examine how they relate to <margin>A</margin> beings. Whether they are something that arises alongside other forms and follows them—as if, since something is such, I first suppose it to be a unit. If, in the case of number, there were also a state of rest, it would be so; and for each of the others, the unit follows. Or does it hold some primary place, <margin>B</margin> so that there are many units for each thing, or the things that come from them, or as great a multitude as is in each, even ten? Or is it not so, but number itself exists by itself, and the "standing" [fixed] number is itself prior to others or later? Plato, however, <margin>C</margin> saying that [man] by good fortune attends to the changes of the seasons and days—does it not seem that he establishes number from the variation of things? Perhaps he says that counting is later than number. And having taken these same things, in the transition of the soul from one thing to another, the soul knows by number. This happens when the soul itself passes through and says within itself "this and that," as if this is one thing and not another with it. But when he speaks of the numbers in <margin>D</margin> sensible things, which is the "one" of number, he again says that number has its own subsistence. And there, number is not just established in the counting of the soul, but the soul brings back into itself the concept of number from the variation surrounding sensible things.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Number and Unity, specifically exploring whether numbers like the "Decad" (the number ten) exist as independent realities in the intelligible realm or are merely labels we apply to groups of objects. It follows the previous discussion on the infinite and the mind's attempt to grasp abstract limits.</meta>

# BOOK SIX

Therefore, when we say "ten men," the number ten itself <note>Original: "decas." In Neoplatonic philosophy, the "Decad" refers to the ideal or essential form of the number ten, rather than just a count of objects.</note> is neither the men themselves, nor is it something that happens to them as a mere accident <term>accident (accidens): a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color or number</term>; otherwise, it could not be used to measure other things equally. Instead, it exists first in itself before it exists in the things being counted as ten. Finally, if someone were to say that "One" itself is joined to beings—whether as an accident or as an element—it still follows that it must exist in itself before it either happens to all things generally or is added as an element.

<column-break/>

What, then, is the nature of these things? Is the "Decad" an accompaniment observed in each essence, such as in "men"? Is "man" both a man and "one"? And are all intelligible things <term>intelligible things: realities that can only be understood by the mind, like mathematical truths or the Forms, rather than sensed by the body</term> each a "one," or is all number like this? But how can there be a "Two" or a "Three," and how are all things categorized under "one"? Or is "the One" itself joined to numbers? Is there a way in which a multitude of units is "one" or a "Decad"? Aside from all things being one, might we say that the thing remains a "Two" rather than something viewed at the very end, which possesses two powers gathered together, like a single composite thing? 

Or is it as the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that numbers were the fundamental building blocks of reality and assigned moral qualities like "justice" to specific numbers.</note> used to say? They seem to speak of number by analogy; for instance, <margin>justice</margin> they called "Justice" the number four, and assigned other numbers to other things. This is based on the condition of the thing that exists, where one might join a number to a multitude, such as a Decad, even if we do not normally define "ten" that way. We are accustomed to saying "ten" when gathering things that are distant from one another. But perhaps we only call it ten when it becomes "one" out of many—a Decad—and then the same logic applies to other things. 

If numbers are treated as actual substances <term>substances (hypostases): independent, self-existing realities</term> observed in the things themselves, could we say they are causes in their own right? Even if they are observed in things through reason, does that mean they have a real existence in those things? For just as motion is observed in being and has a real existence within all being, could number also exist as a kind of "motion" because it is "something"? If it is viewed that way, we might say such an existence is the cause of number—that is, "being is being"—but it acts more like an accident. Or is it an accident at all? For an accident must be something that exists before it happens to something else, and even if it is inseparable, it must have its own nature (like the color white). It is predicated <note>To be "predicated" means to be asserted or stated as a quality of a subject (e.g., in "the man is one," "one" is predicated of "man").</note> of another thing that already exists. So, is "one" something around each thing, or is "one man" the same as the whole man? But "the One" is different from "man," and this applies to each of the other things as well. 

Then, is the "one" in each of the others, or is "man" in each of the others? Does each thing happen to "be," or does it "be" before it is numbered? Furthermore, does that number, which we say exists beyond this, exist in each of the sensible things or each of the intelligible things? I mean the "one" which is predicated of each species. <margin>The second [decad] prior to the individual one which is predicated.</margin> There is something prior to that which is predicated as a Decad; either there is an "Absolute Decad" <note>Original: "autodecas." The pure, divine Form of Ten.</note> or the thing in which the Decad is observed is the Absolute Decad itself. <margin>And therefore</margin> But are these then joined or constituted...

<column-break/>

**A** What then is the nature of number? Is it something that follows as a consequence, seen as it were within each essence—like "man" and "one man"? Likewise, "being" and "each being"? And are all intelligible things thus gathered individually, resulting in a universal number? But if the matter stands this way, how is "Twoness" or "Threeness" there, and how are all things weighed according to the "One"? In what way will such a number be gathered into a single thing? For in that case, there **B** would indeed be some multitude of units, but no number would be reduced to "one" except for the "One" itself—unless someone were to say that "Twoness" is that thing which is considered within it, which has two powers folded together like a single composite. 

Or perhaps it is as the Pythagoreans introduced numbers: they seem to have asserted numbers according to analogy, that is, by a certain proportion, such as calling **C** **Justice the number four**, and similarly for others. Under that condition of the existing thing, one might join unity to a multitude and at the same time a certain number to it—viewing it as a "one" or a "Decad," even though we do not usually define "ten" that way. We are accustomed to saying "ten" when we gather things that are distant from one another. Perhaps we say "ten" in this way, but when a single thing is made from many, we call it a "Decad," and for the same reason there as well. 

However, if it happens this way, will there be any further **D** existence for number, other than its being considered solely in things? Someone might respond that nothing stands in the way; just as whiteness is considered only in things, yet the independent existence of whiteness is rightly weighed within the things themselves. Likewise, because motion is considered in a being, it is established that there is some independent existence of motion within that being. But number does not seem to behave like motion; rather, it is said that motion is something considered as "one" in itself. Furthermore, such an **E** existence would mean that number is not an essence, but rather something "contingent" <note>Something that depends on something else for its existence; a non-essential attribute.</note>—even if it is not entirely contingent in every sense. For a contingent thing must exist as something before it happens to another, and although it may be inseparable, it is still something in its own right with its own nature, like whiteness. This thing, already existing in itself, is then predicated of another. 

Therefore, if "one" is around anything, and if **F** "man" is not the same as "one man," but the "one" is something other than the "man," and if "one" is common to all things, then surely "one" will be prior to "man" and prior to anything else. Thus, both man and any other thing can achieve being "one" individually. Therefore, unity is prior even to motion (if motion is to be one) and prior to being similarly, so that being itself might be "one." I am not speaking here of that "One" which we believe to be above all being, but of this "one" which is predicated of every species. Therefore, the "Decad" itself exists before that of which "ten" is predicated; and this very thing is the Decad itself. For the Decad is not merely the thing in which it is observed. Is it then joined with beings and completely simultaneous with them...

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical nature of number, arguing that concepts like the "Decad" (Ten) and the "One" are independent essences that exist prior to the physical or intelligible objects they describe.</summary>
