<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of Number and Unity, specifically exploring whether numbers like the "Decad" (the number ten) exist as independent realities in the intelligible realm or are merely labels we apply to groups of objects. It follows the previous discussion on the infinite and the mind's attempt to grasp abstract limits.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin>...this "one" itself? But if it is innate, or merely exists as an "accident" <term>accident (accidens): a property that is not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color or its number</term>—just as health is to a man—then it must also be something in its own right separately. Similarly, let that "one" be like an element of some composite thing. If someone says it exists, it must first be "one" in itself <note>original: "secundum se vnum."</note> so that it can also exist with another. Furthermore, if it were first mixed with another so that it became one through that mixture, it would follow that it is "one" only in a false sense, since it would actually be two things made into one. <margin>B</margin> But how would this work in the case of the Decad <note>original: "decade." In Neoplatonic thought, the "Decad" refers to the ideal or essential form of the number ten.</note>? For why would the Decad need such a thing, since it is "ten" by its own great power? But if the Decad forms the object as if it were matter, and the presence of the Decad makes things "ten" and a "decad," then the Decad must first exist in itself as a pure and singular entity, not as anything other than the Decad.

### Chapter VI.

*The species <note>original: "species." Here referring to the Platonic "Forms" or "Ideas," the eternal blueprints of reality.</note> of things precede their essence and order in their genus through a certain intelligence of them, just as objects precede their own acts, and acts precede knowledge. If, therefore, anyone says these species are pre-created by intelligence, they would concede that the species are posterior to it, which is absurd.*

To understand <note>original: "Intelligere." To grasp with the mind or intellect.</note> some ultimate thing—such as justice, rest, motion, and the rest—is nothing other than to declare or discern their species in relation to one another. This definition is not outside the thing itself, nor is it abstracted from the definition in any way. For there is a certain definition that constitutes the true essence of a thing. Finally, every species there <note>original: "ibi." Referring to the Intelligible Realm, the higher world of the Forms.</note> is a property of some essence, existing and remaining as its very own. Thus, it is the kind of thing that depends on essence, and essence is in its possession; since it is intelligence, it differs from essence only by a certain rational distinction.

<margin>A</margin> But if, beyond the things themselves, the One itself and the Decad itself exist, and then the intelligible things <note>original: "res intelligibiles." Realities that can only be understood by the mind, like mathematical truths or the Forms, rather than sensed by the body.</note> exist as something more than just their existence—some being Unities, others Dualities or Triads—what will their nature be? And how are they constituted? We must consider that their generation is fulfilled by a certain reason. First, then, we must generally consider that essence and species do not come forth in such a way that the Thinker first understood individual things, <margin>B</margin> and then his intelligence provided their substance. For one does not come to know what Justice is while remaining outside of Justice. Nor did motion arise because someone thought about what motion is. For if that were the case, the intelligence would have to be posterior to the thing understood—just as the intelligence of Justice would be posterior to Justice itself. And yet, conversely, the intelligence would have to be prior, since it produces the thing by thinking it, provided that the thing understood was something distinct. But if Justice is entirely the same as such an act of intelligence, it would be absurd for Justice to be nothing more than a description of itself. <margin>D</margin> For what else is the understanding of Justice or motion, other than receiving a certain description of what each is? This is the same as if you were to receive a rational account <note>original: "rationem."</note> of things that do not exist, which is truly impossible. Therefore, if anyone claims that in things separated from matter, knowledge and the thing known are the same, this must be accepted on the condition that they do not assert knowledge is the reality itself, nor that the reason contemplating something is the thing itself seen in contemplation. <margin>E</margin> Rather, the thing itself, separated from matter, is an "intelligible" something, and intelligence exists—not, I say, that intelligence which is a mere rational account of the thing or some intuition into it, but the thing itself, consisting in the intelligible world, which is nothing other than intellect and knowledge. For there, knowledge does not look toward the thing to be understood, but...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Who is it but the one with whom it was born? If it is like an accident—such as health is to a man—<margin>*</margin> health would have to exist both in itself and in the composite where it happened to be. But if the "One" is prior and is something in itself before it is with another, or if it is prior to being brought together with another thing that becomes "one" because of it, then they make the "one" unstable; they make it falsely one, making it two. Or how is it with the Decad <note>original: "δεκάδα." The number ten.</note>? <margin>*</margin> Or what need does it have for that Decad? <margin>B</margin> Or for the Decad that exists through such a power? But if it gives form to it as if to matter, and it exists for the Decad itself, either as ten or as a Decad, then there must be some Decad prior to it, existing by itself, being nothing other than the Decad alone.

<margin>A</margin> BUT if, apart from the things, there is the One and the Decad itself, and then the things which, after they exist as what they are, are some of them unities, and others dualities and triads—what would their nature be? And how would it be constituted? We must think that their generation is of such a kind. To grasp it in outline: essence and each species <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos).</note> do not exist because someone thought of each one by an act of will, <margin>B</margin> or because thinking provided their substance. For then Justice would be outside of thinking. <margin>*</margin> Or if, because he thought "there is motion," motion would then be posterior to the thought. Either the things themselves would be posterior to the things thought—this very thinking of Justice itself. <margin>*</margin> And again, motion would be things standing under thinking; if indeed such an essence were to stand under thinking, first it would be absurd for Justice to be nothing but its own definition. <margin>D</margin> For what is it to have thought Justice, or motion, or to have grasped what it is? To take the same definition for a thing that does not exist is to move toward the impossible. And if someone says that among immaterial things, knowledge <note>original: "ἐπιστήμη" (episteme).</note> is the same as the thing, one should not say this in such a way as to mean the knowledge is the thing. Nor that the reason <note>original: "λόγον" (logon)</note> which contemplates the thing is the thing itself. <margin>E</margin> But on the contrary, the thing itself is immaterial, an "intelligible" thing, which is what the thinking is. As if to say that the things are not that which falls upon them from the outside, but the thing itself existing in the intelligible realm is nothing else than intellect <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun)</note> and knowledge. For there, knowledge does not look toward the object, but...

<summary>This page examines the ontological priority of the "One" and the "Decad," arguing that these formal unities must exist in the intelligible realm before they are applied to things. Plotinus further argues that in the realm of immaterial Forms, knowledge and the thing known are identical because the Form is itself an act of Intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how reality is structured in the "intelligible realm"—the higher world of pure thought and Forms. Following the debate on whether numbers like the Decad exist independently, Plotinus now moves to show how knowledge, motion, and the very "Life" of the universe are unified in the Divine Mind, where the act of thinking and the thing being thought of are one and the same.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<margin>A</margin> In that higher realm, the thing itself ensures that knowledge is not distinct from the object, as is usually the case with knowledge of material things. To produce true knowledge is to ensure it is not merely an image of a thing, but the thing itself. Therefore, the intellect’s understanding of motion did not create the motion; rather, the motion itself produced the intellection. For this reason, it conceived itself as both motion and intelligence. Motion in that realm is the intellection of that Being; it is the "first motion" <note>In Neoplatonism, "Motion" is one of the Five Great Kinds of being, representing the dynamic life of the Intellect.</note> because there is nothing prior to it. <margin>B</margin> It is truly motion because it does not happen to something else as an accident; it is the "act" <term>act (actus/energeia): the full realization or activity of a thing's nature, as opposed to mere potential</term> of a being that exists in actuality. Therefore, it is also Essence, though it seems to differ from Being itself through a certain conceptual distinction. 

Furthermore, the intelligence of Justice is not just an idea, but a certain disposition and state of that Mind; or rather, it is an "act" of such a kind that its "face" is truly beautiful—so beautiful that neither the Morning Star <note>original: "Lucifer"</note> nor the Evening Star <note>original: "Hesperus"</note>, nor anything else perceived by the senses, shines so brightly. It is like an intellectual statue <note>original: "statua/agalma." Plotinus often uses the metaphor of a divine statue to describe the radiant, self-contained beauty of the Forms.</note>, standing out from itself and gleaming within itself—or rather, existing entirely within itself.

<column-break/>

*If you were to subtract extended matter from the corporeal world, but preserve the various forms of things within the one living form of the world, you would see one "all-form," where all forms are most united yet also distinct, and all things are living within a single living being.*

## Chapter VII.

*The universe is therefore of this kind, both in its nature and its intellectual soul, and also in the Intellect itself. In this Intellect, the species <note>The "species" or "Forms" are the eternal blueprints for every type of thing in the physical world.</note> exist as true realities, truly understood before any planning of the intelligence. They are as distinct in their activity as they are united in their nature—just as in a fire, the light, the spark, and the heat are all one, yet each is its own act.*

---

One must contemplate those things as existing entirely within a single nature, a single nature that possesses and embraces all things from every side. There, things do not exist separately as they do in the realm of the senses. In our world, the sun is in one place and the moon in another; but there, all things are together in one. This is the very nature of the Mind. Even the Soul imitates the Mind in this way, as does the thing we call "Nature," through which individual things are generated in different places, even while Nature herself remains unified. Although all things exist together in the Mind, each is also distinct. The Intellect that possesses these things sees them within its own essence—not by looking at them from the outside, but by "having" them. It does not need to separate them, for they are already eternally distinct within it. 

To those who marvel at these things, we offer proof from the things that participate in them. We can guess and affirm the magnitude and beauty of that intelligible world by the love the soul feels for it. Indeed, the soul loves those things that strive toward it because of their shared nature, and because through that nature, they achieve a likeness to the divine. It is impossible to admit that a beautiful living animal exists here unless the "Animal itself" <note>original: "ipsum animal/autozoon." This refers to the Platonic Idea of the Living Being, which contains the forms of all possible creatures.</note> possesses a wonderful and inestimable beauty.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> That "Animal" is indeed the universal and entirely perfect Being, composed of all living things—or rather, containing all living things within itself. It is a single being that is simultaneously as many as all things are. In the same way, this physical universe of ours is one, and it is "all that is visible," embracing every single thing that exists in the visible realm.

<summary>Plotinus describes the intelligible realm (the world of Forms) where knowledge and reality are identical. He explains that the "Universal Living Being" or Ideal Animal contains all forms of life in a state of perfect, unified beauty that surpasses anything in the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the metaphysical origins of Number and Being. Having previously established that true knowledge is identical to its object in the higher realm, Plotinus now explores the hierarchical relationship between Essence (Being), the Intellect, and the "Living Being" (the totality of all Forms), and specifically how Number precedes or follows these categories.</meta>

*True essence is a power beyond material mass, established in itself, self-living and supremely intellectual; it is what we call the "Intellectual Living Being," where all numbers exist prior to any intellectual or vital act.*

## Chapter VIII.

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, the "Living Being" <note>original: "animal/zoon." In Platonic thought, this refers to the "Intelligible Living Being," the divine blueprint containing all possible life forms and ideas.</note> exists in the first instance, and since Intellect and True Essence exist around it and through it, this constitutes true reality. This Living Being possesses all other living things within it and contains the entirety of Number; it is the Great Vastness, Beauty itself, and all other things of that kind. In that realm, we speak of "Man himself," "Number itself," and "Justice itself" in a way different from how we speak of them here. It is certainly worth considering how each of these exists and what they are, insofar as such things can be known. To begin, one must set aside all physical sensation and contemplate the Intellect with the Intellect alone.

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, we must observe that even in ourselves, life and intellect do not reside in our physical "mass" <term>mass (moles): the spatial, heavy, material bulk of a body</term>, but in a certain power that is entirely void of mass. True essence is liberated from such bulk; it is a power founded within itself. It is not something thin or weak, but is the most intellectual and vital thing of all. Nothing is more intellectual, nothing more vital, and (if I may say so) nothing more "essential" than this. It is so powerful that whatever touches it attains the same qualities in some measure. One who approaches it closely receives more; one who remains distant receives less. Therefore, if existence is something to be desired, then that which is "more" existent is even more desirable. Similarly, if intelligence is simply to be wished for, then the highest form of Intellect is the most desirable, and Life should be sought in the same degrees. If, then, we must rank them, Essence is taken first (as it is the primary), Intellect second, and the Living Being third—for the Living Being seems to already embrace everything within itself.

<margin>D</margin> Intellect holds the second place, for it is the "act" <term>act (actus/energeia): the active expression or functioning of a thing's nature</term> of Essence. Certainly, Number itself is not thought to exist only because of the Living Being, for "One" and "Two" already existed before it. Nor should Number be placed after Intellect; for before Essence enters the mind, it is already both One and Many.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Since, therefore, the Living Being exists primarily, and for this reason is "Life-Itself," and is also Intellect and True Essence, we say it contains all living things and the whole of Number, and Justice itself and Beauty itself and all such things. For we speak of the "Man-in-Intellect" and Number itself and Justice differently [there than here]. We must again examine how each of these is, and how it is possible to find anything out about them...

<margin>B</margin> ...setting aside all sensation, looking toward the whole as it lies within Life and Intellect. It has power, and true essence contains these things, possessing a power established in itself and not some feeble thing. Rather, it is the most vital and most intellectual of all, so that nothing...

<margin>Γ</margin> ...later it is, whatever touches it possesses these things according to the logic of the touch. That which is near is nearer; that which is far is farther. Desire for the "Desirable" is no more than this, yet it is most intense, just as thinking is in general, and life likewise. In the first instance, one must take the Intellect as being first, while living things already seem to contain everything. But Intellect is the act prior to...

<margin>Δ</margin> ...of Essence, and the Living Being is an effect. Number, indeed, is not [merely] before itself in the soul, but even before the Intellect, before the Intellect itself is the cause and resolves the many.

---

*The One stands preceding; thus Number, consisting in the One, precedes beings—that is, the species and Ideas. And rightly so: through the number that exists in counted things, we see the Number that exists in its own source. It is, surely, that through which the "One" can be seen and derived into multiple beings.*

## Chapter IX.

*Through Number itself, which is an essential power and a certain distinguishing act of Being, it is ordained that Being does not stop at a single level; rather, many beings flow forth from the One. These are distributed in specific numbers and orders. That Number is "enfolded" before the beings exist and "unfolded" within the beings themselves: this is Substantial Number. Number in the category of quantity is merely an image of this higher Number. Beings are founded upon Number, Number upon Being, and Being upon the One, so that it does not immediately scatter away.*

---

<margin>A</margin> It remains, therefore, to investigate whether Essence, by some partition of itself, brought forth Number, or if Number rather partitioned Essence. Indeed, did Essence, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference <note>These are the "Five Great Kinds" (megista gene) from Plato's Sophist, which Plotinus uses to describe the basic structure of the intelligible world.</note> themselves generate Number, or did Number generate them? The starting point of our consideration will be this: Is it possible for Number to exist in itself, or must "two" always be seen in two things and "three" in three things, and must the "one" always be considered as something inserted into numbers? For if Number could exist in itself, apart from the things being counted, it could exist long before Beings. So, can Number exist even before Being? Perhaps for the present, it is better to concede that Being precedes Number, and that Number proceeds from Being.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It remains then to consider whether Essence generated Number by its own division, or Number generated Essence—and indeed whether Essence, Motion, Rest, Sameness, and Difference generated Number, or Number generated them. The beginning of the inquiry is whether Number can exist by itself, or must be seen in two or three things, and likewise "three"... <margin>B</margin> ...and indeed the "One" that is in numbers. For if Number could be independent of the thing counted, it could exist before beings. Is the One, then, before Being? Or is it this [Being]? Let us grant for the moment that Number arises from Being.

<meta>catchword: But (Latin: Verùm)</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explores the hierarchy of the intelligible world, arguing that true reality is a non-material power containing the archetypes of Life, Intellect, and Number. He begins a difficult inquiry into whether Number is a fundamental structure that divides Being into many forms or if it is a byproduct of Being's own nature.</summary>
<keywords>Intelligible Living Being, True Essence, Intellectual Act, Five Great Kinds, Substantial Number, The One, Metaphysics of Number, Plotinus, Enneads</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s metaphysical inquiry into Number. On the previous page, we established that true Essence (Being) is a vital, intellectual power. Now, we examine whether Number is merely a human way of counting things after they exist, or if Number is a fundamental structure that must exist before "Beings" can even appear.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

But if Being is one, and two beings are two beings, then the One must precede Being; and Number must precede Beings. Does this happen merely in our thought and perception, or does it exist in actual reality <term>subsistence (hypostasis): the actual, objective reality of a thing as opposed to a mere concept in the mind</term>? We must consider it this way: when someone speaks of a "living man" or a "one beautiful thing," they think of the "one" as something added afterward to each. And indeed, when one speaks of "being" and "beauty," clearly the "two" is perceived as coming later. But if you were to generate a man, and then generate a horse and a dog—or if you brought forth things already existing within you—would you not say that you must go from one to another, and then another, to make two, and then add another to yourself? Yet, Beings were not simply numbered after they were created; rather, it was already determined how many ought to be created, according to what was most appropriate. Therefore, Number must have preceded Beings. But if it preceded them, then Number was not yet the Beings themselves; rather, it existed already in Being, though it was not yet the number *of* any specific thing, for Being was still "One."
<margin>Being is only one Idea.</margin>
Rather, the subsisting power of Number divided Being into many parts, urging it toward the birth of a multitude. Thus, Number is either the very essence of Being, or its active energy; the "Living Being" <note>the *Zoon*, or the Intelligible Universe</note> and the Intellect are themselves Number. Perhaps Being is "Number unified," while Beings are "Number unfolded"; Intellect is Number in motion within itself, and the Living Being is Number encompassing all. Since Being was generated from the One, it must exist as Number. This is why the ancients called the "Forms" <term>Forms (Ideas): the eternal, perfect patterns of all things in the divine mind</term> both "Unities" and "Numbers." This is what we call "Essential Number." There is another type, called "Monadic Number," which is made of individual units; it is merely an image of the Essential. Essential Number is seen partly within the Forms, helping to create them, and partly it exists prior to them, flourishing within Being itself. In this Number, all Beings have their firm foundation, their source, their root, and their beginning. For the One is the principle of Being itself; without it, Being would immediately dissolve into nothingness.
<margin>It was not possible for Beings to exist as the One.</margin>
Yet the One is not founded *upon* Being, otherwise the One would already be "one" before it even reached unity—just as a "decad" <note>original: "decas." The number ten, symbolizing completion and the full structure of the universe.</note> would have to be a ten before it ever reached the state of being ten.

<column-break/>

**A** Truly, if Being is one, and two beings similarly are two beings, one indeed precedes being, and number precedes beings in the same way. Does this distinction happen only in our thought and perception? No, it also occurs in reality <term>subsistence: the actual existence of a thing</term>. Consider it this way: when someone understands an existing man as "one," and a beautiful thing as "one," they see the "one" as something occurring afterward in both. Furthermore, when they notice a horse and a dog,
**B** they clearly perceive the "two" as something added later. But if you were to create a man, a horse, and a dog—or if you produced them from within yourself—would you not say that you must move from one to another, passing into a second, thus making two, and so on? Now, in truth, even Beings were not merely counted *after* they were made; rather, it was already established how many should be made, based on what was most beneficial.
**C** Therefore, all Number preceded Beings. But if it preceded them, Number was not itself the Beings; rather, it was already in Being, yet it was not the number of any specific Being, for Being was still One.
**D** Instead, the subsisting power of Number divided Being into many, pushing it to give birth to a multitude. Thus, Number is either the very essence or the act of Being; the Living Being and the Intellect are Number. Perhaps Being is "Number unified," while Beings are "Number explained"; Intellect is Number acting within itself, and the Living Being is Number that contains all. Since Being, born from the One, was already within it,
**E** it must necessarily be Number. For this reason, philosophers were accustomed to calling the "Forms" both "Unities" and "Numbers." This is "Essential Number." The other kind, called "Monadic" (that is, gathered from individual units), is only an image of the former. Essential Number is partly seen in the Forms, creating them; but partly it thrives earlier within Being itself, preceding the Beings. In this Number, Beings find their stability,
**F** their fountain, their root, and their principle. For the "One" is the principle of Being itself; in this, Being exists, otherwise it would immediately scatter. However, the One is not based on Being; otherwise, the "One" would exist before it even attained unity—just as that which reaches the "ten" would be a ten before it actually achieved ten-ness.

---

*The nature of the First Being, because it comes after the One, is necessarily manifold in its origin—that is, it is numerical. Through this, Number relates to Beings (the Ideas) in almost the same way that many traditions describe "Matter" relating to "Forms": as a foundation that contains the beginnings of the shapes that will grow within it.*

### Chapter X.

*It is clear that Numbers exist before Beings. If Number only appeared after Beings were already placed in order, then the distinction and order of those Beings would be a mere accident of chance. Furthermore, just as all things that exist through another point back to "Being Itself," so too does anything that is "one" through another point back to "The One Itself." But "The One Itself" cannot be placed under Being; if it were, it would necessarily be manifold, composed of the nature of Being plus an added property. Therefore, it would not be simply "The One." Being is therefore subordinate to the One, just as Beings are arranged under Number. For above the number found in objects, there exists a Number that exists by itself, prior to Beings. Finally, in the formal definition of every species, unity and number are necessarily included. Unity, I say, because in its first state a species is distinct from itself through unity and distinct from all others; Number, I say, because a species has a common nature joined with its own specific property. From this we conclude that Unity and Number precede all species of things, since the formal reasons of all things consist in Unity and Number.*

Ll 4

<summary>Plotinus argues that Number is not a human invention for counting objects, but a divine, "Essential" power that precedes and structures all of reality. Before the many things of the world could exist, Number had to exist within the divine mind to provide the framework for plurality and order.</summary>
<keywords>Metaphysics, Neoplatonism, Theory of Number, The One, Being vs. Beings, Essential Number, Monadic Number, Forms/Ideas, Plotinus, Intelligible World</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether Number is a primary substance that exists before the physical world. Plotinus is arguing against the idea that we simply "invent" numbers by counting objects. Instead, he suggests that Number is a pre-existing blueprint in the Divine Mind that allows things to exist in specific quantities.</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, Being, when it exists as a multitude, emerges as **Number**; it is "aroused" and rises up when it is viewed as a manifold. This was a kind of preparation and pre-figuration for individual beings, providing a place where the "units" <note>original: *vnitates* / *monads*</note> seem to be set out for the things that are to be founded upon them. And yet, even now, someone might say: "I desire a great quantity of gold," or perhaps a multitude of other possessions. Gold is, of course, a single kind of thing; but the person does not wish to turn the gold into a number, but rather to apply a number to the gold. Because they already possess the concept of Number, they strive to apply it to the gold, so that the gold happens to become "this much."

<margin>B</margin> However, if Beings preceded Number—and Number was only observed in them afterward—then the "counting nature" <note>the human mind or the soul that counts</note> would only be moved as far as the objects to be counted were multiplied. In that case, the total number of beings currently in existence would be a matter of mere chance <term>contingency: something that happens by accident rather than by a necessary plan</term>, rather than being the result of a deliberate purpose. If, then, there are "so many" things in existence, it is not by chance; surely Number exists as the preceding cause, determining that there should be exactly this many.

<margin>D</margin> This means that existing Number makes the things that are created "so many" in their very condition. Furthermore, every individual thing participates in the **One** so that it may be "one." But Being comes from Being; since Being is Being from itself, so too the One is One from itself. If several things are individually "one," and yet are "many" when taken together, that which is in them is like a **single triad** <note>original: *trinitas vna*. Here Plotinus refers to the mathematical "Three-ness" or "Triad" as a single Idea</note>, and all beings are "one" in this way. This is not like the "one" we calculate according to a single unit, but rather how we say a **thousand** is "one," or any other number is "one" thing.

<margin>E</margin> Now, if someone counts a thousand things that have already been made, they are not saying that the things are "a thousand" or "ten" or some other name based on themselves, as if they were showing their numbers like a color. Rather, the person judges them so because their own **thought** dictates that number to them. For unless thought dictates it, one cannot know how great a multitude is. How, then, does one speak? Surely as one who knows how to count. And one knows this only if they already know Number itself. They will know it, provided that Number actually exists. Indeed, it would be absurd—even impossible—to suggest that the Divine Nature does not know exactly how many things exist in its own multitude.

<margin>F</margin> Furthermore, if someone speaks of "good things," they either mean things that are good in their own right, or they are predicating "the Good" as an **accident** <term>accident: a property that a thing happens to have, but which is not part of its essential definition</term> of those things. If they mean the former, they are introducing a **primary substance**. But if they bring up things to which "goodness" merely happens to belong, there must first exist a "nature of the Good" so that it can "happen" to other things. There must exist either the Cause itself, which produces goodness in another, or the Good itself, or that which generated the Good, existing in its own proper nature.

<margin>G</margin> A similar condition exists in the order of beings. Whoever speaks of a number, such as a **decade** <note>the number ten as a single entity or "Perfect Number"</note>, is either naming the "Decade itself" as a subsisting reality, or, if they introduce things to which the number ten happens to belong, they would be compelled in turn to place that "Decade itself" within its own realm, existing as nothing other than the Decade. It is necessary, therefore, if one calls beings a "decade," that either the beings themselves are the Decade, or there is another Decade standing above them, which is purely and simply the "Decade itself."

<margin>H</margin> Generally speaking, whatever is predicated of something else either comes into it from another source or is an **activity** <note>original: *actus* / *energeia*</note> of that thing. And when a quality is such that it is not present at one time and absent at another, but is always with the thing, then if that thing is an essence, the quality is also an essence...

<column-break/>

<meta>The Greek text on the right column mirrors the Latin translation provided on the left. It discusses the "pro-upotuposis" (pre-figuration) of number and the "monad" (unit) as the basis for beings. It uses the examples of "chrysos" (gold) and "myrias" (ten thousand/a myriad) to explain how quantity is applied to substance. It concludes with the same metaphysical argument: that if the "Decade" (ten-ness) is a property of things, there must be a "Decade" that exists as a pure form or Idea beforehand.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus argues that Number is not a human invention used to count objects, but a fundamental "pre-figuration" or Idea that exists in the Divine Intellect before physical things are created. He uses the examples of gold and the "Decade" to show that for things to have a specific quantity, the concept of that quantity must exist as a primary reality.</summary>

...the One itself, or rather that [Absolute] or essence itself. But if nothing is the "One itself" <note>original Greek: αὐτὸ ὃ ἔστιν ἕν</note>, then it would not be any of the things that exist. If those things are understood as powers relative to their activities, they must be present; nonetheless, that [One] is placed by us as subsequent to essence in our thinking. But if it is not just in our minds, but exists along with essence, we should not say it is subsequent to it, but rather that it rules alongside it, or even precedes it—if indeed essence exists because of it. We, however, say that the One is prior to the group <note>original Greek: συνομίας - likely referring to a collection or the "Dyad"</note>.

<margin>4</margin> But if someone were to say that the "Decad" <term>Decad: the number ten, viewed by Pythagoreans as a perfect, mystical entity</term> is nothing more than so many units—if they grant that the "Unit" <term>Monad/Unit: the fundamental "one" from which all numbers are built</term> exists, why would they admit that one exists, but not the "ten-ness" of the ten? For if the one has its own substantial existence <note>original: *subsistentia* / *hypostasis*</note>, why not the others? If "Being" must be attributed to existing things, and one unit to each thing, but there is also a common "One" across all things—is this a single nature predicated of many, or do we say it is observed within the many themselves? If it exists in each of these, and is seen again in another, then that single unit will have its own existence. And if there is a multitude of units, do those units have priority? Is it because "Being" is most fully composed in them, or because it is the "One" most fully in all of them? If by the "most Being," then it is just a name like other units; or if the first unit is ranked with them, then number would be composed of dissimilar units, and there would be differences between units even insofar as they are units. But if by the "most One," why would the "most One" need this unit to be one? Either these things are impossible, or it is necessary for the One to be something else—a "naked" or pure One <note>original: *ψιλὸν* / *nudum*</note> that is stripped of the things that come after it, so that each thing can be spoken of or thought of as one. If the thing and the "One" are said to be together, why would it be given existence by something else? And...

<column-break/>

...itself, nor is that more essence than itself. If anyone does not concede that it is essence, at least they will grant it is a Being within a certain order of things. And yet, if that thing can be understood without its own activity, it nonetheless exists simultaneously with it, even if in our own thought we judge it to be subsequent. If, however, it cannot be thought of without it—just as a "man" cannot be thought of without the "one" that makes him a single man—then surely it is not subsequent to it, but exists at the same time, or is even prior to it, so that the thing exists through the One. We, however, confess that the One is prior, and Number similarly.

-> For whatever you might take, whether sensible, intelligible, or an Ideal form, "One" is predicated of it individually. For that which is commonly in each thing is not tied down to any specific thing: indeed, it is the "Super-One" <note>The One that transcends all individual ones</note>, which is in another—that is, the One which reaches even into its opposite, which is the multitude of beings: certainly the One exists by itself outside of others and outside of multitude. <-

-> Chapter XI. <-

Indeed, he is not speaking here of the "One itself" which is primarily "Being" in a higher sense, but of the One which naturally proves itself in the primary Being, and rules in its own order before the multitude of beings and Ideas. From this One, indeed, come all units, and from these come certain numbers that precede the Ideas, and proceed equally from the Ideas: just as this "One" of being exists equally as units. Therefore, the nature of Being, twice-fertile as if with its own seeds, gives birth to Ideas in a sequence of numbers, through smaller and smaller components. Similarly, lower things are born from the Ideas, where the fertility of Being holds the laws of Being within itself through proportions, and then moves outward so that it may never act randomly or in an unordered way. But so that you may understand whose authority Plotinus uses regarding numbers and unity, hear **Pythagoras** <note>Ancient Greek philosopher, c. 570–495 BC, who taught that the universe is built on mathematical ratios</note>: he says that number is the extension and the activity of the "feminine reasons" residing in unity. Likewise, he says number is the first thing consisting in the divine mind, from which and by which all things are composed and remain distributed in certain insoluble orders. **Ippasius** <note>Hippasus of Metapontum, a Pythagorean philosopher</note> the Pythagorean says: Number is the primary exemplar of the world's structure, and the instrument of the world-maker's judgment. **Ecidatas** <note>Likely Ecphantus the Pythagorean</note> says: Number is a certain impression of the eternal perseverance and containment of worldly things, generated from itself. The Pythagoreans say: Unity is the essence through which anything is called "one" as a cause; it is the unity of number and the minimum of parts, from which other eternal reasons and proportions proceed infinitely in both directions like a seminal root—here by multiplying, and from there by dividing. Likewise, Unity is the "Species of species," containing within itself all numbers and the reasons of numbers.

---

<margin>A</margin> Perhaps someone will say that a "Decad"—that is, the number ten—is nothing other than a collection of so many units. But if they concede that the Unit exists, why will they admit one single unit exists but deny the existence of the ten units together? For if that one is granted to have its own substance, why not the others? For it is not necessary that one unit be joined to one specific being; otherwise, no other thing would be "one" anymore. Rather, if it is necessary for every other thing to be one, then "One" is surely common to all. <margin>B</margin> That "One" is a single nature predicated of many, which we have said must exist by itself even before it exists in the many. Since, then, Unity is in this thing, and is seen again in another—if that also exists—it will not be judged that only a single "one" exists, and thus there will be a certain number of units. But if someone thinks only that first unit exists: it would either coexist with that which is "most Being," or <margin>C</margin> entirely with that which is "most One." If it coexists with the "most Being," then the other units will be called units in name only <term>equivocally: having the same name but different meanings</term>; they would be established in the same rank as the first, or else number would be gathered from dissimilar units, and there would be differences between the units themselves, even as units. But if someone says it is coupled with the "most One," why would that which is already "most One" need this extra unit to be one? If, therefore, these things are impossible, it is necessary that "The One" exists—which is nothing other than the "Naked One"—<margin>D</margin> through which each individual is understood and spoken of as one. If, therefore, the "One" exists there [in the divine realm] without the physical thing that is called "one," why shouldn't another "one" also exist there? And...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

...each thing separately are many units <note>original: *monades*</note>, which are also a "one" in plurality. If nature generates things in a sequence—or rather, has generated them—and does not stop at one of the things it has produced, it creates a kind of continuum. Where it marks a boundary and brings the process to a halt, it produces smaller numbers. But if it proceeds further, not into foreign things but within its own movements, it establishes larger numbers. Thus, it fits specific numbers to specific multitudes and to every being, since it knows correctly that unless each thing corresponds to a number, it would either not exist at all or become something disordered and irrational.

->Chapter XII. Whether that which is called "The One" is a real thing in itself, or only a concept of the mind formed about a thing.<-

->*The true notion of the substantial One is innate in the mind, by which we judge this to be more "one," that to be less "one," or again, not one at all.*<-

IF ANYONE denies that the One itself and unity actually exist <term>Substance/Subsistence: In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to a real, independent existence (hypostasis), not just a figment of the mind</term>, asserting that the One is nowhere because there is no such thing as "just one," and claiming that what we call "the One" is merely an affection <term>Affection: A "feeling" or mental state (pathēma) triggered by looking at an object, rather than a quality of the object itself</term> of the soul toward a being: first, what is to stop them from saying that even when they speak of "Being," they are just describing an affection of the soul, and that "Being" itself does not exist at all? If they claim that "Being" exists because it strikes and pushes the mind, creating an image of existence, then we see that the mind is similarly struck every day by the One, and perceives its image. Furthermore, we must ask whether we see this mental affection and notion as "one" or as a "multitude." Indeed, when we say "not one," we do not derive that "one" from the thing itself. For we are saying the One is *not* in that thing. Therefore, we have the concept of the One within ourselves. This exists in the soul without being attached to any specific "something" that is called one. Although someone might object that we possess the One as a kind of understanding or figure received from external things, like a concept formed from the thing itself. Those who introduce such concepts and place "Number" and "the One" in that category would say these have no real substance—if indeed anything of that sort can have substance. One can appropriately argue against such people: if they say that such a "passion" or "notion" is produced in us as something secondary to the things themselves—like the concepts of a "this," a "something," a "crowd," a "festival," an "army," or a "multitude." For just as a multitude is nothing apart from the many things called "multitude," and a festival is nothing apart from people gathered and enjoying sacred rites, so they would argue that the "One" is nothing apart from the one thing, when we isolate it from others in our thinking and call it "one." They would bring up many other examples of the same kind, such as "right" and "up," and their opposites. For what is there (to speak according to their opinion) in that which is called "right" that belongs to real substance, except merely that this person stands or sits in this place, and that person in another? Likewise, in that which is called "up," they would judge the same: that it is merely a certain [position]...

<column-break/>

...each thing separately, many monads <note>original Greek: μονάδες</note>, which are also many, and yet one. But if nature's generation is in a sequence, or rather its generation and its not growing weary in one neighbor, it has created a continuum. By circumscribing the point where it stops, it quickly generates the smaller numbers in its progression; but having moved further, not in other things but in its own movements, it has established the larger numbers. Thus it must fit numbers to each of the things that truly exist, as if it would not fit each thing to a number, each would be nothing, or at least it would happen to be outside and apart from reason.

<margin>A</margin> BUT IF someone were to say that both the One and the Monad do not have a real substance <note>original Greek: ὑπόστασιν</note>, but rather where it does not exist, they are only affections of the soul concerning each of the beings: first, what prevents them, even when they speak of Being, from saying these are affections of the soul and that nothing truly exists? If you say that this is the truth, and that it creates an image of Being, then we see the soul is struck and receives an image regarding the One as well. Should we then say that the affections and the notion of the soul are one, or a multitude? But when we say "not one," we do not have it from the thing itself, yet we have "one." For we say that "one" is <margin>B</margin> itself, so we have "one," and this is in the soul without the "something," which we have in the "something." But having taken a certain notion from equals and certain things of this kind, such as a single notion from the thing—for let it not be of the <margin>C</margin> notions spoken of among them—if they place other things among numbers and the One, they would place such substances as are substantiated among such things. Against whom it might be spoken correctly concerning these matters. But if they say that such a thing as each of the things has become an affection or notion in us, just as the "this" and the "this," and indeed a crowd, a festival, an army, a multitude, and just as the <margin>D</margin> multitude is nothing apart from the many things spoken of; neither is the festival anything apart from those gathered from a purpose for sacred things; or as we think of everything as similar and detached from others when we say "one," and many other such things exist, such as "right" and "up" and the things opposite to these. For what could one show in a real substance <note>original Greek: ὑποστάσει</note> except that one is here and another is there, or is sitting? And indeed in the same way regarding "up": that it has such a [position]...

<summary>Plotinus argues that "The One" and "Number" are not just subjective mental labels but have a real, substantial existence. He refutes the idea that unity is a mere "feeling" or "affection" by showing that our ability to recognize when something is "not one" implies an innate, objective concept of Unity within the soul.</summary>

# BOOK SIX. 681

A position, then, or rather in this universe, which we say is "up" <note>original: *anagein*</note>, as it is said of things of the earth, in whatever way we must speak of them, signifies certain substantial realities <term>Substantial reality: *hypostaseis* in Greek, *subsistentiam* in Latin; referring to things that have their own independent existence</term> in each of these things. Nevertheless, whether this applies to all things—either in relation to one another or in relation to the totality of all things—we must examine these claims separately for each of the mentioned points.

<margin>
Theodorus on Plotinus
</margin>

<margin>
Theodorus: Through
</margin>
Regarding the idea that the forms of subjects arise from the subject itself <note>original: *hypokeimenou*</note> * through motion, and the instances of a man being, or of some other living animal, or even a stone: how can it be argued that while the visible aspects of the man are one thing, all the elements within him are another? For if there were no motion of the man, or if one observed his intellect and then, as if to the right or by some entire movement, moved him; but seeing a difference in position, spoke of "here" <margin>B</margin> and "thus"—all these things are so in truth. For if the experience were not empty, it would not be based on nothing in the argument. * For that which is "between" and "from another" must be in the "itself." But if every "other" or "different" is mentioned, it appears later in relation to the other or to its opposite. Then it is a portion whenever one speaks, or if one speaks alone of the parts of the argument, before the speaking is primarily "this" or "another."
<margin>C</margin>
There is also the matter of things to the right and things that stand within them there, which would likely be toward a deceptive image, whether many or whether one leads them in order. For whenever one speaks truly, one speaks of a "ship" as one, or asserts many parts or portions, and this is the system. For the mind understands that there must also be a multitude. Or rather, and especially here, the mind acts by granting the "one" which the multitude participates in, or entirely seeing the "one" arising from the order, it has brought the "many" <margin>D</margin> <margin>Plotinus</margin> together into one by nature. I, however, even here...

<column-break/>

A position of this kind, and in this part of the universe rather, which we are accustomed to call "upward," signifies that; however, it stands similarly in relation to "downward." Against these points, then, it must first be asserted that in any of these mentioned things, there is some subsistence <term>Subsistence: A technical term for an objective, real existence</term>; yet not the same subsistence in all, whether among themselves or in relation to the one of all things. Nevertheless, we must persist separately against each of the points mentioned.

->When a man is said to be "one," the man is one thing, and "the one" is another, through participation in which he becomes one man.<-
->Chapter XIV.<-

For "one" is predicated of a non-man just as much as of a man, and a man is a certain multitude just as he is a "one." Indeed, "one" predicated of a man does not only negate that he is many—as if it only signified this man and no other—for after you have perceived this man to be truly one, you immediately indicate that there is not another man there, who himself would also be one. Furthermore, the nature of the One itself is so much a "form" <term>Form: In Platonic thought, an ideal essence or blueprint</term> that it unites being; that is, a multitude cannot be understood as one of itself without the One. Rather, all things, whatever they are, consist of a "one," as if the One itself exists most essentially by itself, the highest of all. By right of participation in this, nature willed that the multitude, as it remains and is thought of again with unity, should be something "one"—the discrete being "one" and the continuous being even more "one." Thus, individual things seem most of all to be "one" and to possess their own existence. Furthermore, it confirms the view of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while teaching</term> that "one" signifies something if it encompasses the substance itself entirely and without distance, and is sometimes an affirmation, not a negation. For to this is added the meaning of "being," namely something undivided in itself; in which division a multitude occurs. When combined with privation, it is called "one" because of its essence, and also because, when a multitude occurs, we say by negation: "neither is this that, nor is that this." Since, therefore, the meaning of "one" is opposite to negation, it follows that the meaning of "one" is an affirmation; and the "one" will be so affirmative that it establishes itself by many such things. Finally, listen to those things just said by him in the *Metaphysics*: "The One is perceived and conceived by the intellect before the many," although to the imagination it may perhaps happen otherwise.

<margin>A</margin>
From the beginning, as they say, the notion is formed from the subject—of the subject itself and the man placed in the senses, or of any animal or stone. In what way will this be shown to be consistent with reason? Since the man who is perceived is one thing, but the One itself is another and is in no way the same. Otherwise, the very reason of thinking would never predicate "one" of a non-man.
<margin>B</margin>
Furthermore, just as the thought argued concerning the "right" is not recklessly stirred up, but having gazed upon a different place, says "it is here"; or regarding the "right" and in this matter, when it has inspected something, it pronounces it "one." For this is not some empty affection <term>Affection: A mental state or impression</term>, nor would it rest its case on nothing. Nor should it be thought that it considers the "one" for the reason that this alone is here and nothing else; for in the very act of saying "nothing else," it meanwhile calls the "other" a "one." Then, this very thing which is called "other" and "diverse" falls into place later. For unless the thought strove toward the "one," it would say neither "other" nor "diverse."
<margin>C</margin>
Likewise, when it pronounces that very thing which is named "alone," it then says "one alone." Wherefore it says "one" before it speaks. In addition to these things, you yourself will say that before it speaks of another, "one" exists as "one"; and that very thing of which it speaks, before you say or the mind understands anything about it, is similarly "one." For it is either one, or more than one (that is, many). And if it be many, it is necessary that the "one" precedes it; since even when it says "multitude," it pronounces "more than one"; and when it says "an army is many," it understands "armed men arranged into one <margin>D</margin> order." Truly, the thought of a multitude does not allow the multitude to remain as such: because it reveals in the thing a various subsistence, while it does not exhibit a "one" that the multitude in no way possesses. For that "one" which results from order, the mind perceives very sharply and quickly, and by its own nature reduces the "many" into "one." That, indeed, not even in this matter...

<summary>Plotinus argues that "The One" is a real, affirmative substance that exists prior to the things it unifies. He contends that unity is not just a mental label we apply to objects like humans or armies, but a fundamental reality that allows us to perceive order and count entities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the metaphysical status of "The One." Having previously discussed how number applies to all things, Plotinus now argues that unity is not just a mental label but a fundamental reality that precedes and generates existence itself.</meta>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD. VI

A One is misunderstood and mistaken: just as in a house, something occurs to us as a single thing made of many stones, yet a house is "one" in a greater sense than an army is. If, therefore, unity is more present in a continuous object, and even more so in a thing that is entirely indivisible, it is clearly established that this happens because the "One" itself is a certain nature and possesses its own subsistence <term>subsistence: *hypostasis*, referring to an independent, underlying reality</term>. For it is impossible B for something to exist in "greater or lesser" degrees within things that do not truly exist. But just as we predicate substance <note>original: *substantia* / *ousia*</note> of every sensible object (things we can perceive) and even more so of intelligible objects (things we can only grasp with the mind), we place this very thing we call "substance" most principally within the order of true beings. Thus, substance is more truly found in the intelligible than in the sensible, and more in sensible substance than in other categories. In the same way, we consider "the One" more primarily and fundamentally present: first, among sensible things where it differs by degree; then, most especially among the intelligible beings. We see that in every way, all things are ultimately referred back to the One itself.

C Just as essence <note>original: *essentia*</note> is subtly present in every sensible thing because the sensible participates in the intelligible, so too the One is considered in relation to the sensible through a certain participation. However, it is fundamentally intelligible, and its true kinship is perceived only in the intelligible realm. In perceiving it, the mind understands one thing from another which it does not see. It defines it, then: and if it defines it, it exists as "this certain thing," which is identical to that which is called "existing."

D Furthermore, whenever someone says "a certain one," they are again speaking of unity, just as when they say "a certain two" or "a certain many." If, therefore, it is not possible to understand anything without one, or two, or some other number, it is not permitted to say that a thing does not exist if we cannot even think or speak of it without that unity. It is impossible to deny the existence of that without which we can neither speak nor understand anything. Rather, that which is everywhere necessary for all thought and speech must precede both speech and thought in its generation.

E For in this way, it seems it can be adopted to bring about the generation of these things. If it necessarily contributes to the essence and subsistence of anything—for there is no being that is not also "one"—then surely it exists even before essence and gives birth to essence. For this reason, we usually speak of "one being" <note>original: *unum ens*</note>, rather than "being" and then "one." In that which is "being," the "one" also exists, and therefore many things exist in turn; but in that which is "one," "being" does not exist in the same way, unless perhaps by the leaning of its own generative power it has brought being into effect.

F Consequently, the common habit of saying "this" when demonstrating a thing is not meaningless: for in place of the thing's name, one speaks of a demonstrated substance, a certain presence, whether it signifies essence or any other existing thing. Therefore, the common expression "this" signifies something real to us; it is not merely an affection of thought regarding a non-existent thing, but it places the subject before us, just as if one were providing someone’s proper name.

# BOOK SIX.

*...is essential in incorporeal things, but in corporeal things it is accidental; and even in these [bodies], there is something incorporeal rather than corporeal. Thus, by the presence of unity as a certain nature, anything becomes "one," just as by the presence of any quality, a thing becomes "of a certain quality." Similarly, the fact that there are sometimes "two" is not properly caused by their mutual proximity—for sometimes separation (that is, division) seems to contribute to the same result—but rather by participation in Duality <term>Duality: *duitas*, the abstract essence of being two</term>, which, arising from itself and any other number, is a species in its own right, just like quality and quantity. Indeed, it is more a species than continuous quantity, which is measured by number. There are therefore six successive grades of numbers: the first in the First Being above the Ideas; the second innate in the Ideas; the third in incorporeal substances; the fourth in the powers of such substances; the fifth connected within bodies; and the sixth in bodies as if they were torn apart.*

---

<margin>A</margin> AGAINST those things said regarding "relation," one might reasonably say that the One itself is not the kind of thing that, while something else undergoes a change, it loses its own nature without having undergone anything itself. Rather, it is necessary that if it departs from being "one," the unity must have suffered a "privation" <note>original: *sterêsin*, a lack or stripping away</note> arising from that which was previously there: namely, division. If, therefore, the same mass is divided and becomes "two," it is not destroyed as a mass. Clearly, <margin> * Concerning its nature <unclear>all through</unclear> * From </margin> <margin>B</margin> then, besides the underlying subject, there must be a "One" present within it, which it lost when its unity was destroyed. Now, since this unity is sometimes present in the same thing and sometimes departs, what prevents us from placing it within a certain rank of beings, wherever it may be? We might say that it happens to these things according to their own true existence, appearing both in the sensible and the intelligible <note>original: *noêtois*, things known by the mind rather than the senses</note>. To the later things, it arrives as an accident; but in itself, it is judged to be among the intelligibles— <margin>C</margin> especially among the first of them, since the One exists first, and then Being. But if someone objects that the One itself, while suffering nothing properly, becomes "two" when another is added to it and is no longer one, they would not be speaking correctly. For the One itself has not become "two," nor has that to which something was added, nor that which was added. Instead, each remains "one," just as it was. But "Two" is predicated of both of them together, while "One" remains separately in each. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, the "Two" do not consist by their own nature in some habit or relation, nor does Duality. However, if this happens according to a certain "coming together," and if this very act of "consisting in a coming together" were the same as "making two," then perhaps such a relation would be "Two" and "Duality" itself. Yet now, Duality appears again in the opposite experience <note>original: *pathei*, a state of being acted upon</note>; for it is clear that in a cutting or division, "Two" are produced. Therefore, "Two" is neither a "coming together" nor a certain "separation," such that it would be merely a relation. <margin>E</margin> The same reasoning applies to every number. For when the relation itself is what is thought to generate something, it is impossible for the opposite relation to produce the exact same thing—provided that this thing is properly a relation. What, then, is the primary cause? Truly, the cause by which something is "one" is the presence of Unity itself; similarly, the cause for "two" is the presence of Duality—just as Whiteness makes a thing white, Beauty makes it beautiful, and the presence of Justice makes it just. Otherwise, we could not say that these things even exist; instead, we would have to assign certain relations as causes. For instance, we would think someone is just only because of a certain relation to this or that. Or that a thing is beautiful only because of how we are affected by it, even though there is nothing in the subject itself that would naturally affect us so, nor anything added to it when it appears as beautiful. Therefore, when you see something as "one," and you call it "one,"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> AGAINST those things said by some who place the "One" in a certain relation, one can probably respond that the One itself is not such that, while another suffers, it falls away from its own nature without having suffered anything itself. Instead, it is necessary that if it falls away from that which is "one," it must suffer a certain privation of unity, namely by being divided into two or more. If, therefore, the same mass is divided into two and is not meanwhile destroyed in its nature as a mass, it is <margin>B</margin> plainly evident that besides the subject, there was a "One" present there which it has now cast away, its partition having destroyed it. Now, given that this same thing is sometimes present and sometimes departs, what prohibits us from counting it in some certain order of beings, wherever it may be? We might say that it happens to them to be according to their true selves, when it appears both in the insensible and in the intelligibles themselves, and arrives at the later things as if an accident; but it is judged to exist in itself among the intelligibles. <margin>C</margin> Especially among the first of those, since the One exists first, then Being. But if anyone should object that the One itself—while suffering nothing properly—is no longer one but "two" when some other thing is added to it, he will not be speaking correctly. For the One itself has not been made "two"; neither that to which something was added, nor that which was added. Rather, both remain "one," just as they were. "Two" is predicated of both, but "One" remains separately in each. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, the "Two" themselves do not consist in their own nature in some habit and relation, nor does Duality. But if that should happen according to a certain "coming together" <note>original: *congressum*</note>, and if this very fact of "consisting in a coming together" were entirely the same as "making two," then perhaps that relation itself is "Two" and "Duality." But now, Duality appears moreover in the opposite experience: for "two" are made not only by division of a certain one. Therefore, "Two" themselves are neither a "coming together" nor a certain "separation," such that they are only a relation. <margin>E</margin> The same reasoning applies to every number. For when the relation itself is that which generates something, it is impossible for the opposite relation to effect exactly the same thing—so much so that this thing itself is properly a relation. What, then, is the primary cause? Truly, the cause on account of which something is "one" is the presence of Unity itself; similarly, the cause for "two" is the presence of Duality—just as White is caused by Whiteness, Beautiful by Beauty, and Just by the presence of Justice. Otherwise, one could not even say these things exist; but in them too, certain relations would have to be assigned as causes: as if one must think a person is just only because of a certain relation to these or those things. Or "Beautiful," because we are so affected, even though there is nothing in the subject itself that would naturally affect us so, nor even present as an adventitious quality, if something occurs as "Beautiful." Therefore, when you see something as "one," which you also call "one,"

<margin>A</margin>
...is altogether and in some way great and beautiful, and affected in many other such ways. Just as, therefore, greatness and magnitude are in it <note>the intelligible realm</note>, and sweet and bitter, and other qualities, why should the One <note>the principle of unity</note> not be there as well? For we must not think that quality, of whatever kind it may be, truly exists in its entirety, while quantity does not exist in the very order of beings. Nor should we think that only continuous quantity <note>like a line or a solid</note> exists there, while discrete quantity <note>individual numbers</note> does not—especially since continuous quantity uses discrete quantity as its measure.

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, just as something is "great" by the presence of Magnitude, so it is "one" by the presence of Unity itself, and "two" by the presence of Duality, and others similarly. But if anyone should inquire more curiously into the condition by which things participate in the One and in Number, such a question will be common to all, since participation in other Species <note>the Platonic Ideas</note> is investigated in the same way. Finally, it must be judged that in discrete things, the "ten" <note>the number ten</note> is considered one way when it exists within them, another way in continuous things, and yet another way in the case of many and great powers gathered into one.

<margin>C</margin>
Finally, in the intelligible things themselves <note>the realm of pure thought</note>, it is considered in yet another way, which is easily reached from there. Furthermore, the truest numbers are there—not those seen in other things, but those existing in themselves, like the "Ten-Itself." I do not mean the ten of certain intelligible things, but simply the Ten itself.

*That divine world is therefore a "perfect animal" <term>animal: here meaning a "living being" or "living system," from the Latin *anima* (soul)</term>, because it already possesses the universal number of living beings. Indeed, it has the total number of living beings because it possesses the universal number itself. In that realm, therefore, Number itself precedes both all living beings and all the perfections of the whole world.*

->Chapter XV.<-

*For it produces all forms within itself—the Ideas—by its own specific motion: a numerous motion <note>original: *motu numeroso*, a motion structured by the harmony of numbers</note>. Otherwise, it would not generate the universe at all, namely by conceiving the universe within itself and merely multiplying itself in those things. But since it does not multiply sense-perception except by the power of number, Essence there rightly precedes Number, just as the One is above earlier. Finally, just as the Moon above, being one, is sufficient for all by the light of the Sun, but below generates diverse things with diverse light, so when the Intellect first looks toward the "Simply One" as its peak, and with Number then flashing forth, it brings forth the species of all things.*

---

BUT let us speak again from the beginning after these things already said: that the whole and true being is both Being itself, and Intellect, and the "Absolute Animal" <note>original: *animal absolutum*, the archetypal Living Being</note>, and at the same time all living beings together. This worldly animal <note>the physical universe</note> imitates the unity of that realm with its own unity as much as it can. I say "according to unity," because the nature of this sensible world departs from that "One" because it had to be a sensible thing. Furthermore, that celestial realm must be Universal Number; for if it were not a perfect number, it might suffer the lack of some number; and unless the universal number of animals were in it, it would not be a fully absolute living being. Therefore, Number exists before every living being, and before the Universal Animal. Man, truly, and the other living beings are in the intelligible world insofar as they are living beings; and again, insofar as that realm is the Universal Animal. For even the man among us is a part of the universe; by which reasoning, as a living being, he is part of the whole. Similarly, each thing, insofar as it is a living being, exists there within the "Animal." But in the Intellect, insofar as it is Intellect, all individual intellects are present as parts, of which there is also a number. Therefore, Number is not first in the Mind. But insofar as it is in the Mind, it is considered as a total, just as many acts of the mind as are there.
