# SIXTH BOOK. 687

<column-break/>

...and temperance, and the other virtues and knowledge; for regarding those things which truly exist, how could knowledge not be in something else? Or is it that which is the same and that which is not, either knowledge, the object of knowledge, or knowledge itself? And how again are the virtues there? Or is it because each exists primarily through that from which it happens to be? Or is justice an <term>accident<note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature—for example, a person may be "just," but they could exist without being just. Plotinus argues that in the Divine Intellect, justice is not an accident but an essential reality.</note></term> of the soul, insofar as it is a soul, or is it justice itself? For these exist in potentiality rather than in actuality, except when the soul thinks, or as they exist in the mind. After these things, there is Being itself, and within it, number. After these are living things, <margin>to be added</margin> moving according to number; *and we shall add the numbers of their <margin>hypostasis</margin> <term>hypostasis<note>original Greek: ὑποστάσεως (hypostasis). In this context, it refers to the underlying reality or essential substance of a thing.</note></term>. For just as we view the One itself in relation to Being, in the presence of the First, so too numbers are there, and other things in relation to the First. For the One, when viewed together, is the beginning; but Being, having become number, joins all beings to itself. It is divided, not insofar as it is one, but while remaining what it is, it divides according to its own nature into whatever it willed, and generated those things that are weak in number. Being within it, then, they are like number in their powers, or as they themselves were exhausted; when Being is number, it is the beginning and source of existence for others—the number that is primary and true. Therefore, even here <note>in our physical world</note>, generation occurs for each thing according to numbers. And if one takes another number, either something else is born, or nothing is born at all. And if there are different numbers, some as things to be numbered and others within other things, then both are held; either they are things numbered by these, or then the other things are divided into tenths, either numbering the numbers or the rest. We say there are ten of certain things—is this by the numbers present in them?

---

Regarding these things, then, we say that they are primarily <margin>by what cause</margin> true numbers; or by what cause do we say so? And into what category of beings do they fall? For among all people, they seem to be in the category of quantity, or rather "how many" things there are. In the first things, you made a certain worthiness, similarly in the continuous and the discrete among those things set in opposition; but again you say that they are primary beings, which are numbers for some, and you say there are other numbers besides those, which are used for counting. How then do you arrange these things? Tell us. <margin>limitless</margin> For it holds much uncertainty, since one might speak of sensible things—whether for all, or often if the "one" is a quantity, and not only the beginning of quantity, or a quantity itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...as if the justice of the mind is there, along with temperance and the other virtues; likewise knowledge and whatever the intellect possesses is truly judged to be the intellect. But if knowledge is in it, what prevents knowledge from consisting in another rather than in itself? It is certainly prevented, because the knower there is the same as the thing known, and knowledge and the known exist simultaneously as one, and other things similarly. For this reason, each thing exists there primarily: nor is justice an accident there, although it is an <margin>B</margin> accident to the soul, by the reason that it is a soul. For in the soul, these things seem to exist in potentiality; but in actuality, they exist when the soul rises to the intellect and dwells with it. Beyond this, however, Being itself exists, and number within it with which it generates beings, moved as it is according to number: and thus, placing numbers before the existence of beings, it accommodates them to it. Just as its "one" is set over its existence, joining Being itself to the First Principle; so too numbers do not <margin>C</margin> join other things to the First, for Being itself, being thoroughly annexed to the One, is sufficient for this. But Being, becoming number, reconciles beings with itself. For it is divided not insofar as it exists as one, but its own "one" remains. Once divided by its own nature into whatever it willed, it observed into how many parts it would be divided, and it generated number existing within itself. For it was divided by the powers of number, and it generated as many things as there were numbers. Number itself, the primary and true, is therefore the principle and source of existence for all beings. For this reason, the generation of individual things in this world is driven by certain numbers, and if another number is assumed, either something else is born, or nothing <margin>D</margin> at all is generated. And those primary numbers are as things that can be numbered. But those which are in other things already possess both: for by the reason that they are from these [primary numbers], they are "numbered" things; but insofar as they exist besides them and act according to them, they measure other things, counting both numbers and numbered things. For how could they say "ten" most effectively, unless by the numbers existing within themselves?

*When you happen to count men running past, the number itself creates a new concept within you from the category of quantity. But when you consider ten men arranged for the same purpose in a choir, beyond your own "ten," which is arranged into tens in the category of quantity, the number of parts in any natural thing is essential, and is naturally placed in the category of substance.*

### Chapter XVI.

*Essential number is also in the soul, being harmoniously constituted by its own nature from many parts; essential number is in the divine mind, both in the certain series of ideas arranged there, and in the parts of any of its own ideas, and finally, there is number itself simply above the ideas.*

<margin>A</margin> Someone will perhaps ask us next in this manner: These numbers which you call primary and true, where do you place them? And in what category of things do you especially locate them? Among all people, they certainly seem to be in the category of quantity. You also made mention of quantity in the previous sections, establishing that just as there is continuous quantity, so also discrete quantity <note>discrete quantity refers to things that can be counted individually, like apples or integers, whereas continuous quantity refers to things like lines or time</note> must be established in the very order of beings. But again, you assert that these numbers belong to the primary beings, or <margin>B</margin> even above them, and you say there are other numbers again besides those, used for counting. In what way, then, do you arrange such things? Pray, explain to us; for much doubt arises from this opinion: since even the "one" that is in sensible things comes into controversy, whether it is a certain quantity, or rather, if "one" is assumed repeatedly, it is not a quantity but the beginning of quantity.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 687 regarding the metaphysical nature of Number. Having previously touched upon how virtues and beings exist in the Divine Intellect, Plotinus now investigates the specific origin of "quantity" and distinguishes between numbers used for counting physical objects and "essential numbers" that define the very structure of a soul or a being.</meta>

-># PLOTINI ENNEADS VI.<-

### PAGE 688

Again, where is the principle of quantity? Whether it is innate or foreign? Indeed, you ought to explain all these things to us by right. We must therefore treat these matters, perhaps beginning from this point:

When, indeed? First, this must be examined in the matter of the <term>sensible world<note>The "sensible world" refers to the physical realm perceived by the five senses, as opposed to the "intelligible world" perceived by the mind.</note>: When, I say, you take one thing with another and call them "two"—such as a dog and a man, or even two men, or many, counting up to ten and speaking of a "decad" <note>The number ten.</note> of men—this number is not a substance, nor does it exist within the sensible things themselves, but it is pure quantity. 

Now truly, you are dividing according to the "one," making individual units out of this decad; you are creating the principle of quantity. For one out of the number ten itself is not "the One" in its own right. 

But when you speak of "Man" himself as being a certain number within himself, such as a <term>dyad<note>The number two; in Neoplatonism, the "dyad" often represents the first step away from the absolute unity of the One toward multiplicity.</note></term>—consisting of "animal" and "rational"—this is no longer observed in the same way. Rather, insofar as you move through and count them, you produce a certain quantity. But by what reason are they two, and each "one," if indeed each "one" completes the essence? Since unity is in both, you are pronouncing another, essential number. And this dyad does not occur later, nor does it merely signify a certain quantity outside the thing itself; rather, it exists in the essence and contains the very nature of the thing. 

You do not create number here by counting while you follow things existing by themselves, which are certainly not procreated by your act of numbering. For what could be added to the essence of one man when he is numbered with another? There is no single unity there as there is in a chorus; rather, that "decad" of men exists only in you who are counting. In the ten themselves whom you count, if they are joined by no order into a unity, they will be called a decad, but you yourself make them "ten" by counting, and thus rendering a quantity to that decad. But in a chorus or an army, there is something even outside of you, beyond that which exists within you.

But in what way is it in you? Perhaps the number itself is really implanted in you before the act of counting. For number results from that which appears outwardly; toward that which is in you, there is an act either of those things, or according to those things, while you simultaneously count and procreate number. In this very act, you produce the existence of quantity, just as in walking you produce the existence of a certain motion. 

In what way, then, does that which is implanted in us behave differently? It is surely the number of our own essence, which Plato says participates in number and harmony, and again, that number and harmony exist <note>Plotinus is referencing Plato’s *Timaeus*, where the soul is composed according to mathematical proportions.</note>. Someone might say that the soul is neither body nor magnitude, and therefore the soul is number; if it is an essence, the number of a body is an essence as a body, but the number of the soul's essence is as souls are. 

Now truly, in the purely <term>intelligible world<note>The realm of "Forms" or "Ideas," which Plotinus considers more real than the physical world.</note></term>, if the "Living Being" there is several things—such as a certain <term>triad<note>A grouping of three; here referring to a metaphysical structure rather than the religious Trinity.</note></term>—this very triad which is in the Living Being exists essentially. But a triad which is not called "living," but is simply a triad within Being, is the principle of essence. If, however, you count "Living Being" and "Beautiful" there, each is surely one...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> And from where does the principle come, whether it is related or from another? 
<margin>original Greek: καὶ πόθεν η αρχή... (and from where the principle...)</margin>
All these things I am able to clarify for us... starting from here regarding these matters.
When first, then, we make the argument regarding sensible things. When, therefore, taking one thing with another you say "two," such as a dog and a man, or two men, or many, ten, or a decad of men—this number is not of substance.
<margin>B</margin> Nor as in sensible things; how is number—one being essential, the other quantitative? Rather, it is purely quantitative, dividing according to the "one," or the parts of this decad... not that we make the ten...
But you, by the ten, not from its own self. But when you speak of the men themselves in their own right as a certain number, such as a dyad—"animal" and "rational"—this way is no longer the same. But your traversal and counting makes a certain quantity.
<margin>C</margin> But the subjects are two, and each is something; each completes the essence, and the unity in each is another, essential number.
And this dyad is not later, nor does it signify a certain quantity from outside the thing, but the existence in the essence; not a natural property of the thing. 
You do not make the number here, nor by looking out do you make things that exist by themselves; but by the measurement in the counting.
<margin>D</margin> What then is added to it when it is counted with another? For there is not a "one" as in a chorus; rather, this decad of men would have its <term>hypostasis<note>The underlying reality or actual existence of a thing.</note></term> in you who are counting. If not, the decad is not a number unless it becomes one.
<margin>And the decads: you do not make the number.</margin>
The others being ten are counted... for they will be something ten; but if in a chorus, there is something outside.
<margin>E</margin> How is it in the object of desire, and how is it in you? Having number prior, but otherwise from appearing outwardly toward something; there is an activity either of that or according to that. It is necessary to count... if we do this by activity, we make quantity, just as in walking there is a certain motion. 
How then is the "one" in us otherwise than that of our essence?
<margin>sign</margin> *It participates by nature in number and harmony, and number itself is harmony. For when he says it is neither body nor magnitude, the soul is then number; if indeed it is essence, not as number in a body (as an essence of body), but as souls are.
Indeed, entirely among the intelligibles, if anything there is "Living Being" itself as more than one—for example, a triad—this triad is essential in the Living Being. But the triad which is not of the Living Being, but entirely a triad in Being, is the principle of essence. But if you count "Living Being" and "Beautiful," each is one, and you make a number there.
<margin>G</margin> And the activity of quantity is a dyad. If, however, you call virtue "four," it is a tetrad...

...insofar as you receive the number, it is treated as quantity and a dyad. But if you have said a certain virtue is "four," it is certainly a <term>quaternarius<note>The number four; often associated with justice or the "four cardinal virtues" in ancient philosophy.</note></term>, just as...

<meta>catchword: pactes</meta>

<summary>In this passage, Plotinus distinguishes between "mathematical number," which is a mental construct used to count external objects (like a dog and a man), and "essential number," which constitutes the actual substance or form of a thing (like the two-fold nature of man as an animal and a rational being). He argues that while counting is an act of the mind, the numbers that define the essence of the soul and the intelligible world are real, prior to our counting, and fundamental to existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the metaphysical hierarchy from page 688. Having established that "essential number" defines the essence of a being, Plotinus now investigates how these numbers relate to physical dimensions (length, width, depth) and the concept of infinity.</meta>

-># SEVENTH BOOK<-

...its parts into one; and the quaternary unity <margin>A</margin> <note>original: "partes virtutis conferentes ad unum"</note> the parts of virtue contributing to one: and it is permitted to call the unity a "quaternary" <note>A grouping of four, or the 'Tetrad,' which Pythagoreans held as a sacred number representing the source of all things.</note>, as if it were a certain substrate: and you truly accommodate that quaternary to the one within yourself.

---

*Bodies are indeed resolved into dimensions, and these into numbers. Therefore, in the first archetype, numbers precede dimensions, and these precede bodies. Chapter XVII.*

Truly, before the natural body, there is the "body in itself": therefore, the principles of the latter exist before the principles of the former. Dimensions, which are the boundaries of a body, and numbers, which are the measures of dimensions, are conceived before the specific principles of natural things; for this reason, they are understood without sensible matter <note>Matter that can be perceived by the senses.</note>. A body is certainly not a "body" properly speaking through its matter or its qualities; rather, it is through its quantity, for unless quantity is added, both matter and quality are incorporeal. 

Therefore, since numbers are the principles of quantity, they are probably called the "origins of bodies" by the <term>Pythagoreans<note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed that the universe is structured according to mathematical ratios and that "all is number."</note></term>. For they possess the property of principles: they are established by the first and smallest differences, and they proceed from the simplest unity. This unity precedes the "point" just as a free-standing existence precedes a marked position; indeed, the super-essential Unity itself precedes every essence designated by a specific form. 

In the divine mind, there are certainly Ideas of figures, through which both the sphere of the world and the determined shape of every species are defined. In that realm, however, dimension or figure is limited only by a certain destination of the intelligence. A line there is said to be "infinite" in a rational sense, because the ratio of the ideal line has no quantitative limit; otherwise, it would not fit equally with all lines, whether larger or smaller. The first Essence is considered "One" among the first things, then it is recognized as "Intellectual": or, since it is first Intellectual, it is simultaneously defined as an "Intellectual Living Being," or an "Intellectual Animal." Numbers and figures are found there first, and soon they unfold equally with that Intellectual Animal.

<columns>2</columns>

How then is number said to be "infinite"? For these arguments provide a limit to it, and quite rightly so, if it is to be a number at all; for the "infinite" conflicts with the very definition of number. Why then do we so often speak of an "infinite number"? Is it perhaps in the same way we speak of an "infinite line"? 

We speak of an "infinite line" not because such a thing actually exists, but because it is possible for us to conceive of a line larger than the greatest possible one—for instance, a line larger than the universe itself. So it is with number. After we have understood how great a number is, it is possible for the mind to double it, though not by physically joining this number to that one. For in what way could you join a notion or an imagination—which exists in you alone—with things existing outside yourself? 

Otherwise, we might say there is an infinite line in the <term>intelligible region<note>The 'intelligible region' or 'intelligible world' is Plotinus's term for the realm of perfect, unchanging Ideas or Forms, accessible only through the mind, not the senses.</note></term>; for it would be as great as any line that was there. Truly, if there is no such quantity there, it would be "infinite" in number. But surely, the concept of limits there uses another sort of reasoning, not as if there were a boundary that one is not permitted to cross. 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to explain under what condition a number is called "infinite." For these arguments apply a limit to number, and quite rightly, if a number is to exist; for the infinite is the opposite of number. Why then are we often accustomed to say that number is infinite? Is it perhaps like the way we speak of an infinite line? We speak of an infinite line not because such a thing exists, but because it is possible to imagine a line greater than the greatest line—even the line of the world. So it is also in <margin>B</margin> number. For after we know how great a number is, it is possible to double it in the mind, though not by joining this number to that one. 

For in what way will you couple the notion and imagination which is in you alone with things existing externally? Otherwise, perhaps we shall say that there is an infinite line in the intelligible region: for it would be as great as the line that was there. But if there is no such quantity there, it will be "infinite" in number: but certainly, the boundary there uses another <margin>C</margin> reasoning, not as if it were something that cannot be traversed. 

In what way then is it infinite? Perhaps because in the very "reason" (ratio) of the line itself, no limit is applied by the intelligence. What then and where is the line in that realm? It is surely something posterior to number, for "the one" is seen within it; since it both begins from the one and is produced into a single dimension. 

The quantity of the dimension, however, has no limit. But where is it? This, therefore, exists only in the intelligence as a determining power: or even the thing <margin>D</margin> itself is intellectual. For all things are there in such a way that they are both intellectual and exist as the things themselves are. 

And indeed, regarding the plane and the solid and all figures, where and how they are arranged is pre-determined there: for we do not create figures merely by thinking of them. This is surely testified by the very figure of the world which precedes us, and the other natural figures assigned to things consisting of nature, which necessarily exist before bodies, being "un-figured" and "primary figures" in that realm. For they are not merely forms lying in other things, but they exist in their own right, and therefore they do not require extension: for things which are extended are dependent on others. Therefore, the figure is everywhere one in Being, but the distinction was made either in the "Living Being" itself, or before the "Living Being."

->### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.<-

<margin>A</margin> But I say that each thing was distinct, not because anything was stretched out into a physical mass, but because its own figure was distributed to each living being. Therefore, for the bodies existing there <note>In the "intelligible world," the divine realm of pure ideas.</note>, their own figures are appropriately suited—as for fire, if you like, that pyramid <note>original: "pyramis illa." In Plato’s *Timaeus*, fire is famously composed of tetrahedral (pyramid-shaped) particles.</note>. For this reason, this world also strives to imitate those forms, although it is entirely unable to do so because of the influence of matter. Moreover, other figures exist here and there in the same way, according to a certain analogy and proportion. But do they exist in the living being insofar as it is a "living being"? Or do these figures exist first in the intellect? They are certainly in the living being. If, therefore, the "living being" <note>The "Intelligible Living Being" (*autozoon*), the archetypal model of the universe.</note> encompassed the intellect, they would be in the living being first; but if, on the other hand, the living being is within the intellect, they are first in the mind by order. Indeed, in that utterly absolute living being, there are also souls, and the intellect is prior. But what shall we say to that Platonic saying? "As many [ideas]," he says, "as the intellect perceives in the universal living being," and so forth. If, therefore, the intellect perceives that being, the intellect seems to be posterior—unless perhaps the very thing that is said to be "perceived" is positioned by Plato in such a way that it subsists in the very perfection of the living being itself and the nature of living things. For the one who perceives and the one who is seen are not different, but all are one; the intelligence itself possesses a "naked sphere" <note>A pure geometric form without physical properties.</note>, but the living being itself possesses the sphere of a living creature.

The number of things formally different from one another is determined in the incorporeal world by the ideal number, which is fixed in the divine world; nevertheless, it is called "infinite" there, just as an "ideal magnitude" is, because it possesses the entire fullness of its own nature and of the universe, and is not limited from the outside. Chapter XVIII.

*The beauty of the first essence, flowing by its very nature, is its own intelligence, always turned toward itself and toward the Good itself. Furthermore, every intellect and soul truly contemplating that intellectual life receives from it a light that is both intellectual and vital; as this light approaches, the soul is immediately transformed into it by love. Such effectiveness will be experienced from that being as if from its opposite: for it is the cause of the whole being, and every being in an eminent way, nor is any part of it missing. And since it exists through itself, it is deservedly always, and most fully. Moreover, it depends on the Good itself, while it precedes life and intelligence: for which reason living and understanding are to be desired by us, so that from being we may have the fullest good, or that we may have a "good being." Finally, it is the principle that is sufficient unto itself. The soul indeed is limited and sufficient for what is just; but being is sufficient for itself for its very existence; while the Good itself is sufficient for the Good, and for all things: thus three principles can be seen.*

<margin>B</margin> THEREFORE, every number there is defined: but we imagine a number larger than any given number, and thus the "infinite" occurs in our counting. There, however, a number larger than the one already understood by the Intellect cannot be understood: for it already exists, and none has been left out, nor will any be left hereafter so that another might be added to it. It is lawful, therefore, to also call the number there "infinite," because it has not been measured. For by whom could it be measured? But that which is, exists as a universe, existing as one and at once, and as a whole, not grasped by any boundaries, but consisting of itself and through itself. For none of the beings is circumscribed by a limit: for that which is restrained from sliding into infinity and stands in need of a boundary would be considered limited and measured. But those things are themselves the measures, which is why all things there are beautiful: for insofar as the Living Being itself is, it also exists as beautiful, endowed with the highest life, in which nothing of life is missing, nor does it have a life mixed with death. <margin>C</margin> For nothing there is mortal, nothing is dying, nor again is the life of the Living Being itself thin or weak, but it is the first and most certain, having the full vigor of life, like a primary light, from which souls also live there, and those which come down here derive their life from there. It knows for whose sake it lives, and toward what it lives, and from what it lives.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> I say they are divided, not that they were enlarged in magnitude, but that each was apportioned to each, as if it were so, and was given to the bodies there, and what sort of shape it took, such as the pyramid there, which these things here <note>Physical objects.</note> wish to imitate, being entirely unable to do so. And other things are analogous, as it is said, being the cause before [the effect]; but not in the living being insofar as it is a living being, or in the intellect first. For it is in the living being, unless the art of that thing is always in the living being itself, so that <gloss>so that</gloss> it is in the living being primarily, while those in the intellect are prior according to the sequence. In the [intellect], they are in the all-perfect living being... and prior... but the intellect says "as many" <gloss>so that</gloss> as are in the all-perfect living being. If then you see, it is posterior... it is possible that "he sees" is said as if happening in the nature of the subsistence, or that it is not another, but all things are in the place where the thinking is. It has a bare sphere, but the living being is a sphere of living things.

BUT since the number there is not the cause: we will conceive more, always more, and the "infinite" is thus counted. But there, it is not possible to conceive more than what is already conceived; there are those things which were taken, and all that will be taken, and anyone who adds to it: but not according to the [human] way, because it is not measured, for by what [could it be]? But that which is, is all, in one and together, and whole, not encompassed by a limit at any time <margin>B</margin> being, which is not limited by any of the things that exist at all: for that which is limited is measured, that which is prevented from running into infinity and needs a measure. But those things are all measures, whence also all are beautiful, and for the living being <note>original: *zoon*</note> is beautifully possessing the best life, in which life is not less, nor does it have life mixed with death: for nothing is mortal nor dies. Nor again <margin>C</margin> is the life of those living things weakened, but is the first and most manifest and having the clearest life, just as the first light, from which the souls are there and those that travel here are sustained: it knows for what sake it lives, or toward what, and from what it lives.

<margin>A If then</margin>
If then life—either the whole of it, or the Wisdom <note>original: "phronesis," often translated as practical wisdom or prudence, but here referring to a divine, archetypal intelligence</note> of all things and the Mind of all things—stands present and coexists, then by coloring it and blending Wisdom with it, it makes it better and bestows a more venerable beauty upon it. For even here, Wisdom is a kind of life; it is something truly venerable and beautiful. Although it is seen dimly here, it is seen purely there. For it gives the one who sees both vision and the power 
<margin>B</margin>
to live more fully, and by living more intensely, to see and to become what he sees. Here, indeed, our gaze is very often turned toward inanimate things; and even when it is turned toward living beings, that which is not living in them <note>likely referring to the physical body or material shell</note> is what first presents itself to us. Even the inner life is mixed. But there, all are living beings, entirely alive and pure. And if you take anything there as if it were not a living thing, it immediately shines forth its own life from within itself. The essence passing through them stands as a cause, immovable toward change, 
<margin>C</margin>
presenting both Life and Wisdom. Or rather, everything is within the Cause. For he says <note>referring to Plato</note> that having beheld the body and the whole nature below laughing, he will claim it as a cause, comparing those things which do not have life. But Mind remains fixed, or rather, the things that exist stand out of strength in eternity, even if something turns or moves near it. And there is a grace with it, which touches it. But she <note>likely Nature or the Soul</note> subjects 
<margin>the things of Timaeus</margin> * to her. And those things which are opposed are again impassible in this; they are not themselves contrary, nor is the Being itself which made them, but something else before it in common remains as one, just as in this, it remains 
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>impassible through interpretation</margin> when that Being is correctly there. * And again, it is impassible through its solitude. But because it stands in reason <note>original: "logos"</note> alongside it, it is possible for it to exist. How then could anyone take away Being from it, or anything else, wherever * there is the activity of Being, 
<margin>E * wholly</margin> or as many things as are sent from it? Since it always moves as that does, which exists in the power of beauty, 
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>* by will</margin> it is so great as to * will all things to be hung from it. For it has them with it, having them by itself to love, and after this, to seek the Good. For "to be" is around that which is toward us. Or rather, this whole world—and all life and Wisdom or Will, every soul and every mind—desires to be; but "to be" is self-sufficient for itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Indeed, from that which it lives, it lives again toward the same. The very Wisdom of all and the universal Intellect, standing by, coexisting, and existing together, renders it better as if by coloring it; and by mixing it with Wisdom, it makes its beauty more venerable and more lovely. For even here on earth, a wise life is truly something beautiful and venerable in our eyes, although it is perceived by us obscurely. There, however, it is discerned purely. For it grants to the one who sees the vision itself, and at the same time, 
<margin>B</margin> a fuller life, so that by living more effectively, he may see more effectively, and become the very thing he sees. For among us, the gaze is very often turned toward inanimate things; and when it is turned toward living beings, then that which is not living in them is what first meets us. The life that lies hidden within is already mixed. But there, all things are living beings; they are all entirely and purely alive. And if you should take anything there as if it were not a 
<margin>C</margin> living being, it soon brings its own life into the light for you. Finally, if anyone should contemplate the essence diffusing itself among them and the life it has grasped—utterly immovable—and again the prudence and the wisdom and knowledge proper to them, he will utterly mock this whole inferior nature for claiming essence for itself by common judgment. For from that essence, and alongside it, life remains, and intellect remains. Indeed, essences consist in eternity; nothing departs from there, nothing turns, nothing 
<margin>D</margin> moves it. For there is no Being beyond it that might touch it; and if anything were, it would undoubtedly be beneath it. And if there were anything contrary to it, it would still suffer nothing from that contrary. Moreover, Being itself did not at all make itself into being, but another common thing above it <note>The One</note>, and that would be Being itself. Therefore, for this reason, Parmenides <note>The Pre-Socratic philosopher who argued that Being is one and unchanging.</note> correctly, when he had called Being "one," added for no other reason that it is impassible <note>incapable of suffering or being changed by outside forces</note>, but simply because it is 
<margin>E</margin> Being itself. For this alone possesses "to be" from itself. In what way, then, could anyone take "to be" away from it, or any other of those things which truly exist in act, and which it possesses from itself? For insofar as it exists, it provides its own things to itself; and since it always is, those things are also always there. Indeed, it is so great in power and beauty that it allures and ravishes all things hanging entirely from it to itself, 
<margin>F</margin> which think it a gift to themselves if they can follow even its footprint—things which certainly after this 

---

seek also the Good. For "to be" itself, as far as it concerns us, comes before the Good. Finally, this whole world affects life and wisdom for this very purpose: that it may exist. Every soul and every intellect desires this very thing—to exist. But Being itself is sufficient unto itself.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD SIX
### BOOK SEVEN

->On how the multitude of Ideas arose, and on the Good.<-
<note>original Greek: Περὶ τοῦ πῶς τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἰδεῶν ὑπέστη, καὶ περὶ τἀγαθοῦ</note>

*God, providing for the living being, did not reason in this way: first, that a being placed among contrary forces might suffer; second, that it would need senses to be cautious; and third, the instruments for those senses. Instead, by a single stroke of intelligence and a moment of power, all things were arranged in order within the Divine Living Being simultaneously. Chapter 1.*

*For perfect intelligence and power, which wonderfully precede motion, sense, and sensible objects, do not begin from sense or physical things. Nor is it led in order like a moving thing from one point to another, step by step. Rather, it possesses all things at once in unity. The Idea of any thing—however complex or distracted by movements it may be—is simple within God, possessing in a single presence all those things which, in our world, unfold over time.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C showing a seated figure gesturing, surrounded by foliage.</image-desc>
WHEN God himself, or at least some God <note>Plotinus often distinguishes between the supreme "One" and the "Demiurge" or crafting god who shapes the world.</note>, sent souls down into the realm of generation <note>term: generation (genesis) refers to the physical world where things are born, change, and die.</note>, he fashioned light-bearing eyes in the face and provided the other instruments for the remaining senses. He did this, evidently foreseeing that a living being could only be preserved if it could see and hear things in advance, and finally touch them, so that it might flee some things and pursue others.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
But from where did God foresee these things? For we must not think that he first made living beings which, lacking senses, suddenly perished; and that God, being warned by this failure, then granted them those senses by which humans and other animals might avoid destruction. Perhaps someone will assert that God knew beforehand that the living being would exist among heat and cold and other physical sufferings. Therefore, knowing this, he granted them sense and the organs for those senses to be used, so that the bodies of animals would not be easily destroyed.

<margin>C</margin>
However, we must next ask whether he joined these instruments to souls that already possessed the power to sense, or whether he gave both at once. If he handed over the senses later, then the souls were not "sensory" before, even though they already existed. But if the souls already had these powers when they were made, and they were made specifically to enter the realm of generation, then it must be innate to their nature to enter this physical world.

<margin>D</margin>
From this, it would seem to follow that it is contrary to nature for a soul to leave the world of generation and live in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The eternal realm of perfect Ideas and pure thought.</note>. It would seem they were made to be subject to external forces and to dwell in evil; and that Providence itself schemes to keep them guarded within this evil. Furthermore, this would imply that God uses <term>reasoning</term> <note>original: "logismos." In Platonism, "reasoning" is a step-by-step process used by humans, whereas God is thought to possess "Intellection," an immediate and total understanding.</note>. We must ask: what are the principles of such a logical process? If it comes from other reasonings, one must eventually arrive at something that exists before the reasoning began. What, then, are those first principles? Are they sensory, or are they rather intellectual? But sense had not yet arisen, therefore...

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E showing a standing figure looking up at another figure.</image-desc>
WHEN he sends us, the souls, God placed light-bearing eyes in the face, and gave the other organs to each of the senses, foreseeing that in this way a being might be saved—if it could see and hear ahead, or by touching, flee some things and pursue others. But from where did he foresee these things? Surely it was not that other beings were made first, and then perished for lack of sense, so that he later gave them what was necessary for humans and other animals to guard themselves against suffering. Perhaps the Cause knew that the living being would be among things hot and cold and other bodily affections. Knowing this, so that the bodies of animals might not easily be destroyed, he gave them the power of sensing and the organs of sense. Did he give the organs so that the senses could act, or did he give the organs to powers already present, or both? If he gave them, or rather the senses themselves, then the souls were not sensory before. But if they have them, and are born to enter into generation, it is innate to them to enter generation. Therefore, it is against nature not to be born and to remain in the Intelligible. And they have been made such that they might be saved, as if they were in the midst of evil.

<margin>Providence was in the midst of evil</margin>
Was Providence then a form of reasoning in God? All reasoning has certain principles. For if it comes from other reasonings, it must lead to something prior to reasoning, or to the final results. What then are the principles? Are they sense, or also...

<summary>This page introduces the concept of Divine Providence, arguing that God's creation of the senses was not a reactive "fix" for a dangerous world, but an eternal, unified plan within the Intelligible Realm. Plotinus questions whether the soul's descent into the physical world is a natural state or a descent into a form of "evil" that requires divine protection.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the beginning of Book Seven of the Sixth Ennead, where Plotinus investigates the nature of Divine Providence and the relationship between the Intellect and the physical world. It follows the argument that God's "planning" is not like human reasoning (which moves step-by-step), but is an eternal, simultaneous presence.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

But if the senses belong to their own realm, then... but if the premises are present now, and the conclusion is knowledge, from what source then do we know the sensible? Or is it not that the principle comes from the intelligible, but the majority arrive at thought? How then could we say this Idea relates to sensible thinking? Or is it regarding the providence for a living being? It was not at all the case that the creation of the universe resulted from a process of reasoning, since if reasoning is mentioned at all, it is intended to point toward the most essential causes. It is as if a wise creator were the cause of a structure in later things, and choice were found in the
<margin>* reasoning</margin> things that follow. * For in things that come into being, "pre-reasoning" <note>original Greek: προλογισμός (prologismos)</note> exists; reasoning is useful because of a lack of power
<margin>* because of those coming forth</margin> in that which precedes reasoning. * Choice too is a power for the one choosing, and choice was demonstrated—for there is choice so that these things might happen instead of those, and one fears, as it were, not obtaining the goal. But if choice and reasoning are only for the one who exists simply, they would be the same in form, merely being of the other; for why does he even reason? How indeed could that which is alone, one, and simply simple, admit a correspondence of this to that, so that "this" might not happen "lest that" occur? For "this" was going to happen if "that" did not. And the use of this appeared, as did the preservation of what had been created. Therefore, it was by providence, and "pre-reasoning" is the result. And indeed, what was said from the beginning: why did someone give any powers to every sense, even if the giving causes the greatest difficulty? And every power remained; but if it is necessary for the activity not to be incomplete,
<margin>* but</margin> nor is it right for God to act so, * but because he considers it either a whole or a sum, it is clear that these things exist within that same being. It is clear then that the future must be first, or rather that nothing is "later" in that realm. But what is already present there becomes "later" in another thing, just as the future is not yet present; it must be present as something forethought for what comes after. This means that nothing is lacking at that time. And it is so, with nothing missing. All things, therefore, already were, and always were, and were in such a condition that one could say "this after that" later. For when extended and, as it were, unfolded there, "this after that" is shown. But when existing together, the whole is "this," and in every way it possesses the cause within itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Intellect. But if the intellect is indeed certain propositions, and the conclusion is science <note>In this context, "science" (scientia) refers to certain, demonstrated knowledge or a finished body of wisdom.</note>, it follows that no sensible thing was then consulted. For the principle does not depend on the intelligible while the end descends into something non-intelligible. Then how did it happen that such a habit and deliberation occurred before the sensible world?
<margin>B</margin> For this reason, providence did not occur through any discursive reasoning <note>term: discursive reasoning (rationis discursione) - the human way of thinking that moves step-by-step from one idea to the next.</note> for any animal, nor for this world as a whole: since there is no argumentation at all in God. However, a certain "rational counsel" is sometimes named in God, so that it may be most clearly indicated that individual things were so established by him as a wise man would do by counsel in later affairs. Then indeed, it is called "prevision" <note>original Latin: præuisio (foresight/prevision)</note> in God: because he disposed things just as a wise man would have provided for later affairs. For in those things which are by no means made before argumentation, argumentation contributes on account of the weakness of that power
<margin>C</margin> which precedes the act of arguing. Prevision also contributes, because the one who foresees did not have the faculty through which he would not need prevision. For prevision tends toward this: that this thing, and not that, should happen—where there is a sort of fear lest something foreign might occur. But where not "this or that" is imminent, but "this" alone is present, there is no prevision: indeed, argumentation is accustomed to seek or assume this over that. But where the one alone is present, what
<margin>D</margin> need is there for argumentation? How then does that which is alone, and one, and altogether simple in itself, admit a revolution within itself of this kind: in which "this something" is established lest perhaps "another" should happen? In which it might be said, "unless this is done, that would happen." In which, again, it might be added, "this has now appeared useful, and if this is done, it will preserve the effect." For if it were so thought by God, then he would have foreseen; therefore, he would have
<margin>E</margin> argued beforehand. And yet, as was said from the beginning, he seems to have given sense and powers for this very reason: although whether and how this bestowal happens involves the greatest doubt. Nevertheless, if it is necessary for any action there to be free from defect, and it is not lawful for there to be anything in God which is not whole and universal, it is surely necessary that all things be contained in one. For which reason, since
<margin>F</margin> the future itself is already present there, there is nothing "later" in it: but what is already present there becomes "later" in another. If therefore the future is already present, it must be present as if pre-cognized for the later: that is, so that nothing then has need of anything: that is, so that nothing is lacking at all. All things, therefore, already were: and they were always, and they were in such a way that it was permitted to say "later" that this is after that: namely, when that which is there is unfolded and spread out, then "this after that" appears. But by what reason it exists together with itself, "this" no longer occurs after "that," but rather this "universal": that is, possessing the cause also within itself.

<summary>This page argues that Divine Providence does not involve human-like reasoning or planning, as God is a simple unity where "before" and "after" do not exist. Instead, all things and their causes exist simultaneously in the Divine Intellect and only appear sequentially when manifested in the physical world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into Divine Providence. Having previously established that the creation of the world did not result from a "planning" or "deliberative" reasoning process like that of a human craftsman, Plotinus now explores how the "essence" of a thing (what it is) and its "purpose" (why it is) are unified within the Divine Intellect.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK VI.

Two things are most commonly asked about any subject: namely, *what* the thing is, and *for what reason* <note>original Latin: "propter quid"; Greek: "to dioti". This refers to the "why" or the cause of a thing.</note> it exists. The first is explained by a definition, while the second is made clear by assigning its efficient and final causes; indeed, both are joined together.

### Chapter II.

Sense perception seeks neither of these; reason, however, seeks each one separately; but the intellect <note>term: Intellect (Intellectus/Nous). In Plotinus's philosophy, this is the second reality after "The One," containing all the eternal Ideas or Forms.</note> possesses both simultaneously. Thus, it follows that this realization encompasses both: for as soon as it defines what the nature of a thing is, it immediately discovers within that very definition its efficient and final cause. Conversely, as soon as it grasps such a cause, it understands the very nature of the thing. Furthermore, in any living being—whether it be the universe itself or any individual creature—the members are so connected and emerge as a whole together, that if one inspects a part, its cause is immediately seen, and vice versa. For this whole world is a bond of a divine and single unity, where every Idea is connected to every other. The Mind <note>original: "mens"; Plotinus uses "Mens" and "Intellectus" interchangeably to describe the Divine Mind.</note> itself, holding the *what* and the *why* of everything at once, exists as each Idea itself. Finally, consider fire: the fact that it exists at all, that it behaves as it does, and that it acts or is acted upon in certain ways, draws its cause from elsewhere. However, the fact that it is what it naturally is—namely, a hot, dry, and luminous body—does not come from elsewhere; rather, it is said to be produced from the very fact of being fire, both the "what" and the "why" at once. By this logic, the *what* of its nature and the *for what reason* are not separated; therefore, the definitions of these Species <note>term: Species/Ideas. The eternal, perfect blueprints of things that exist in the Divine Mind.</note> are usually called "necessary and eternal" by the Platonists.

From this, one can discern the nature of the Mind no less—and indeed even more—than other things we see; yet, we still do not see the Mind in its full magnitude. Now, we say that the Mind possesses within itself *what* each thing is, but not at all *why* it is. Or, if we do grant it the "why," it does not hold the one separately from the other. Let us consider "Man," or "the Eye" if it so happens, existing there in the Divine Mind as a sort of image or spectacle, or a part of a spectacle. Such a thing is "Man" there, and again, the "Why" of Man is there. For it is necessary that an intellectual Man and an intellectual Eye exist there, and that the condition of *why* it exists be contained in that intellectual state; otherwise, it would not exist there at all, unless it contained within itself this very thing which is called the *why*. Among us, however, just as the parts are in some way separated from one another, so too is the *why* separated from the *what*. But there, all things are in one; therefore, the thing itself and the reason *why* the thing is so are entirely the same. Often, even in the region of bodies, the thing itself and the *why* pertaining to it are exactly the same: as in the case of what an eclipse of the Sun or Moon is. What, then, prevents each thing from being both the *what* and the *why*? Indeed, it is necessary for this very *why* to be the essence of any thing whatsoever. Thus, it turns out well for those who try to grasp what each thing is in this way. For each thing exists precisely because of *what* it is. I do not say this now simply because the Form <note>original: "species"</note> is the cause of being for each thing—for that is clearly true—but because if you unfold any Form within itself, you will immediately find the *why* inside it. For that which obtains an ineffective and vain essence and life does not possess the *why* within itself. But that which is both a Form and a property of the Mind—how could it receive the reason *why* it is so from anywhere else?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, even here, one might learn the nature of the Mind <note>original Greek: νοῦ (nou)</note>, perhaps even more than we see other things; yet we do not possess it in its full extent. For we know *that* it possesses something, but the *why* <note>original Greek: τὸ διότι (to dioti)</note> we no longer know, or we might know it separately. We see "Man" or an "Eye," if it so happens, like a statue or part of a statue; but there, "Man" exists, or the "Why of Man." For if one must speak of the world itself, there must be a Man there, and an Eye, and a *Why*.
<margin>B</margin> Otherwise, it would not exist there at all, if the necessary things concerning each part were separate, even the *why*. Or rather, from there and into these things, it is so, such that the thing itself and the *why* of the thing are the same. Indeed, often even here the thing and the *why*
<margin>the "why"</margin> are the same, such as what an eclipse is. Or does nothing prevent each thing from being a *why*, either in the case of other things or in
<margin>C</margin> the essence of each? Rather, it is necessary for those who attempt to grasp *what* a thing is in this way; for the being of each thing is because it is a "certain what." And I do not say that the Form of each is the "why" in this way—
<margin>the "why"</margin> for that is true—but that if you were to unfold the Form itself of each thing by itself, you would find the *why* within it. For that which does not truly have life has the *why* poorly. And nothing that truly *is* could fail to receive the *why*.
<margin>D</margin> Wisdom and Mind—I mean the true Mind which is the thing itself—could not have these things lacking in any way, nor could the *why* be lacking. It possesses the *why*, just as each of the things within it; for each of them is itself what it ought to be, such that nothing is needed as to *why* it came to be. Rather, it came to be all at once and has within itself the whole cause of its existence. Since it has come to be in that way, it could have nothing omitted from the *why*.

---

But if someone should say that the *why* is received from the Mind, it is certainly not separate: since the Mind is this very Form itself. If, therefore, it is necessary for the Mind to have these things without any defect, it is necessary that the *why* itself should not be lacking to them in any way. The Mind possesses within itself, most importantly, the reason why the individual things in it are as they are; and those things that are in it, the Mind itself exists as them, both collectively and individually. Thus, none of them needs that which is called a *why* to have been made; instead, it was made and has its own substantial cause within itself at the same time. Since it was not created at random, it has omitted nothing at all that pertains to the reason *why* it exists.

<summary>Plotinus argues that in the Divine Intellect, the essence of a thing (what it is) and its purpose or cause (why it is) are identical and inseparable, unlike in the physical world where they often appear distinct. He uses the examples of fire and eclipses to show that a thing's true definition inherently contains its own reason for being.</summary>

Plotinus is arguing that in the realm of true Being (the intelligible world), the "essence" of a thing and the "reason" for its existence are one and the same, unlike in our physical world where we often have to search for the cause of an object after we have seen it.</meta>

# BOOK SIX.

<margin>A</margin>
But possessing the whole, it possesses at once the reason *why* <note>original: "propter quid" / "dioti". This refers to the rational cause or purpose of a thing.</note> it is so well ordered, pertaining directly to the cause. Furthermore, to those things that participate in it, it imparts nature in such a way that they also obtain the reason why they received it. Just as in this world, which is composed of many bodies, all things are connected to one another; and in the very fact that all things are within them, there is additionally a reason "why" it is so for each one. It is just as in any body where a part is seen to relate to the whole. In that higher realm, it is certainly not a matter of this coming <margin>B</margin> first, and then that following after; rather, they mutually contain the cause and the effect simultaneously. Thus, it is much more necessary there that all things relate to the whole of each individual, and each thing relates to itself. For this reason, if the consistency of all things exists together in such a way, and not by chance, and must in no way be broken, then surely the effects contain their causes within themselves. Each thing is such that it possesses its cause without an external cause. If, therefore, they do not have an external cause for their being, but are self-sufficient in themselves, <margin>C</margin> even if they were solitary in regards to the "partnership" of a cause, they would certainly have the cause within themselves. Furthermore, if nothing there is by chance, and many things exist in each individual, and each is all that it possesses, you will be able to explain the "why" of any thing everywhere. Therefore, the "why" was already present and existed for you simultaneously—not a "why" in the narrow sense, but because the thing exists entirely; or rather, both essence and cause are one. Indeed, if the intellectual <margin>D</margin> concept of the mind—insofar as it is mind—were like some imperfect offspring, it might produce something superfluous. But if the concept is perfect, one cannot be ignorant of where it might fail; nor does it bring forth a "why" for something that is not present. Since, therefore, it is present, you can assert why it is present: in the very substance itself, the "why" is contained. In every notion and action of the mind, the whole occurs at once; just as the mind which pertains to this end shines forth as the "whole man," bringing himself along with it. <margin>E</margin> Possessing all those things which he has from the beginning at once, he is thus placed there as a whole. Now, unless he were a whole, but something additional had to be added, that would belong more to the nature of "becoming" <note>original: "genituram". In Neoplatonism, this refers to the world of change and birth, as opposed to the eternal world of Being.</note>. But that Ideal Man always *is*; therefore, he is a whole by his very reason. He who *becomes* a man, however, is undoubtedly subject to generation.

***

> *Since the intellectual form through which God acts is the very nature of God, and He always acts in the same way, He does not act so much by a specific deliberation as by a natural form expressing itself outward, as if by a natural necessity.*

### Chapter III.

> *In every form divinely created, there are various forms that act as parts of the entire essence. The whole essence exists for the sake of these parts, and the parts are employed for the sake of the essence; and all such parts are the essence itself. You see, therefore, in the formal definition of a thing, that what the thing is and why it exists are declared together.*

***

<margin>A</margin>
**SOMEONE WILL ASK** here what prevents the Intellect from having deliberated about it beforehand. But it must be said that the Intellect is entirely according to that [eternal] state; therefore, nothing is to be taken away and nothing added. Nevertheless, for the sake of our logical hypothesis, the Intellect is imagined to deliberate and argue. For we suppose that these things are "becoming" or being made; and thus a certain deliberation and discourse is applied beforehand. However, from the fact that it is demonstrated that these things are always happening, the need for argument is removed. For reasoning does not apply to that which always exists. If this condition were forgotten—<margin>B</margin> how it acted previously, and whether it produced something better afterward—then its previous works would not have been beautiful. But if they were indeed beautiful, [they must have been eternal].

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus argues that in the Divine Intellect, the "what" (essence) and "why" (cause) of a thing are inseparable and eternal. Unlike human reasoning, which deliberates over time, the Divine Mind contains all causes and effects simultaneously within its own nature.</summary>

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

In the same way, the matter itself stands. For things are truly beautiful if they exist together with their cause; indeed, even now, a thing is beautiful because it possesses all that belongs to it. For this is what a "species" <note>original: "species" / "eidos". In Platonic philosophy, this refers to the ideal Form or blueprint of a thing.</note> is: that it possesses all things, especially if it occupies the matter—and it "occupies" it if it leaves nothing within the matter unformed. It would leave something unformed if any part of the form were missing, such as an eye or any other part. For this reason, when you assign a cause, you are describing the whole. <margin>B</margin> Why, then, are there eyes? Is it so that all parts may be present? And why are there nostrils? Again, so that every single part may be present. Now, if you argue that these are granted for the sake of "salvation" <note>original: "salutis" / "soteria". Here meaning the preservation or survival of the living being.</note>, you are describing a certain guardian of the essence that exists within the essence itself; you would then judge that this "guardian" is something that contributes to existence. Thus, even before this, the essence existed; and in this way, the cause is a part of the essence. And even if it were something else, this very thing which is the cause exists as the thing's own essence. All things, therefore, breathe together <note>original: "conspirant". A Stoic and Neoplatonic concept where all parts of the universe are interconnected.</note>, and the essence is a total, perfect, and universal whole. This very fact—that it is well-constituted—exists together with its cause and is found within the cause. Furthermore, it is proved that the essence, the "what-it-is," and the "wherefore-it-is" are all one. If, therefore, this condition is included within the Form itself (such as the Form of Man), it follows that there is a "sensory man," and that he is sensory by a certain eternal necessity and the perfection of the Mind. If the Mind is perfect, it embraces the causes within itself, so that we may later observe that the matter is rightly arranged. For in that higher realm, the cause is one with the essence, completing the essence. The "Man" who exists there is not merely an intellect to whom the power of sensation is later added when he is sent into "generation" <note>The world of birth, change, and death.</note>. If the matter stands thus, one might wonder what prevents the Mind from still being inclined toward that higher realm. For what would this "sensory" power actually be? Is it perhaps the ability to eventually apprehend sensible objects? If that were so, would it not be absurd for something sensory to exist there eternally, but only perceive things here? It would mean the act of that power is only fulfilled here below, at the moment when the soul has already become inferior.

<margin>Chapter IV.</margin>

### RETURNING to untie this knot of doubt:

<margin>A</margin> we must take up from the beginning what that "Man" is. Perhaps it is better first to explain what this living man here is; and perhaps, not yet fully knowing what this man is, we should investigate that higher Man more curiously, as if we already grasped the one here. For perhaps it might seem to some that our man here and that Man there are the same. Let the starting point of our consideration be taken from here: we must surely ask whether our <margin>B</margin> man here is a certain "reason" <note>original: "ratio" / "logos". In this context, a formative principle or defining formula.</note> differing from the soul that makes this man, providing him with life and the discourse of reason? Or is it rather the soul itself—is such a soul the man? Or, finally, is "man" the soul making use of a certain kind of body? But if "man" is a "rational animal," and an "animal" is that which is composed of soul and body, then this defining reason of man will not be the same as the soul. Yet if the very reason of man consists of a rational soul and a body, how can it be an eternal substance? For such a reason of man only comes into being when the soul and body meet—surely a reason of that kind...

<language>Greek</language>
<margin>A</margin> The beautiful itself and things likewise. Things are beautiful when they are with their cause. Since even now something is beautiful because it is "all things"—that is, the "what it was" and generally all things. And in the case of wholes, it is because it is all things. It would be so if it left no part of itself unformed. It would leave it unformed if any form were missing, such as an eye or something else. Thus, in giving a cause, you say that the cause of why there are eyes is so that "all" might exist, and nostrils so that "all" might exist. <margin>B</margin> If you say it is for the sake of preservation, you are speaking of something protective of the essence which exists in the essence, contributing to its being. So even before this, the essence was. And this cause is part of the essence. And this is another thing: the fact that in the essence, the cause is in all things for one another. And the essence is whole and perfect and all. And the "being well" is with the cause, and in the cause. And the essence, the "what it was to be," <margin>C</margin> and the "wherefore" are contained as one. If one says it is "being sensory," and how it is sensory in the sensible world by an eternal necessity and perfection of the mind. If the mind has this within itself, if indeed it is perfect, it contains the causes in itself, so that we may later see that things are rightly arranged. For there, the cause is in that which completes the whole. And the man remaining there was not just "someone" to whom the sensory part was added when he was sent into generation. <margin>D</margin> How then could that man not incline toward things here? For what would "sensory" be, if not the perception of sensible things? How is it not absurd for the sensory to be there, as it were, but to be completed here? That is, for the activity of the power there to be fulfilled here, when the soul becomes worse?

<margin>A</margin> ### AGAIN, then, regarding this difficulty, 
we must take it from the beginning: who that Man there is, or who this one is. Or rather, before that, we must ask who the man here is, whoever he is as a whole. Perhaps not knowing him perfectly, we should seek him as one who has the things from there. Some say, perhaps, that he is the same both there and here. But we must find the starting point of the inquiry: where is the unique quality? Is this man, you say, <margin>B</margin> different from the soul—the soul that makes this man, either giving him life or providing him with the power to reason? Or is the soul of such a kind the man himself? Or is man the soul using a certain kind of body? But if <margin>gloss</margin> man is a "rational animal," and an "animal" is that which is from soul and body, this "reason" <note>original: "logos".</note> would not be the same as the soul. <summary>Plotinus argues that in the realm of Divine Intellect, a thing's purpose and its existence are identical, meaning even the "sensory" aspects of humanity have an eternal, perfect origin. <meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the definition of "Man." Having established that the "cause" of a thing is part of its essence in the Divine Mind, he now asks whether "Man" should be defined as the soul, the body, or a composite of both, and how the "Reason-Principle" (Logos) forms the living being.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>the not</margin>
<margin>on the simple aspects of the arguments</margin>

A It signifies what is to be, not in the sense of the individual we call "man," but rather it resembles a definition, or a description that does not fully reveal the *essence* <note>original: "to ti en einai". A technical Aristotelian term meaning the "what-it-was-to-be," or the core identity that makes a thing what it is.</note>. For it does not state what a specific person is, but rather indicates the composite whole. Or perhaps "Man" is defined as the essence itself, or according to the *Reason-Principle* <term>Reason-Principle: translating "logos." In this context, it refers to the formative, creative blueprint that flows from the Divine Intellect into matter.</term>. One should not simply say the definition of these beliefs is a composite, but must apply it to each individual case. B One must seek the definition of each thing, especially of simple things, and one must state these definitions alongside their matter. But we must grasp the *Reason-Principle* itself which has created it—taking "Man," for example—or rather, we should demand to define the essence in each thing when they are defined in the strict sense. What, then, is it "to be" for a man? Is it "to be this specific thing"? What is it that creates the essence of Man—is it something inherent or something separate? C Is the *Reason-Principle* itself a "rational animal," or is that the composite? Is the *Reason-Principle* itself a creative "rational life"? Which of the causes is it? Or is it the "Animal itself" providing rational life within the definition? Man, then, is a rational life. But is this life itself a soul, or will the soul provide the rational life? Thus, is "Man" an activity of the soul and therefore a substance, or will the soul itself be the Man? D But if the rational soul is the Man, then when that soul enters into another animal, how is that not also a man?

---

A Therefore, "Man" is a *Reason-Principle* <note>original: "Logon".</note> other than the soul, or perhaps nothing prevents Man from being a composite: a soul situated within a specific Reason-Principle. This Reason-Principle is like an activity of a specific subject. Since the activity is capable of being the acting thing itself, this is also how the Reason-Principles within seeds behave. For they are not without soul—being souls in a simple sense—since the Reason-Principles that create are not soulless. It is no wonder that such substances are Reason-Principles. B If, then, these are the Reason-Principles that create a man, of what soul are they an activity? Is it the vegetative soul, or the soul that creates the animal? Surely it is an activity of a soul that is clearer and more vital. C Such a soul, having entered into such matter—being disposed in a certain way and inhabiting the "shame" of the body <note>A Platonist reference to the body as a "shack" or a source of limitation for the soul.</note>—is Man. But having formed the body according to itself, it creates another "image-man," as much as the nature of the body could receive, just as a painter might create a man, though that is a lesser kind of man.

<column-break/>

A It signifies what is to be, and is not such as when we say "the man himself," but is rather similar to a certain definition—a description, I say, of the sort that does not explain the "whatness" of the thing. For it is not the material form of any species, but rather designates a composite something made at some time. If that were the case, "Man" has not yet been found, whom it is agreed must exist according to a clear *Reason-Principle*. B If someone should say that the definition of such things must be something joined together, but that which is in the thing itself—according to which each thing exists—must be asserted not to exist: this must nevertheless be brought forward, even if the definitions of material forms must be assigned as closely as possible with their matter. Nevertheless, one must grasp the *Reason-Principle* itself which makes a man be a man, especially among those who think that in every single thing, the essence must be fully explained. C What, therefore, is that "itself" of man? It is as if we were to ask: what is it that makes "this" be a man, in such a way that it is not separate, but internal? Is the definition itself, then, a "rational animal"? Or is this rather the composite? Is the *Reason-Principle* itself the creator of the rational animal, being something itself? What does it exist as? Or perhaps in the very definition of man, "rational animal" is placed for a certain rational life? Therefore, man will be a rational life. But is there life without a soul? Either the soul will provide the rational life of the man (which will not be a substance itself, but an act of the soul), or rather the soul will be the man. D But if the soul—namely the rational soul—is the man himself, then when the soul passes into another animal, what prevents it from still being a man?

> *Man is an intellectual and rational soul, simultaneously sensitive. And this condition of the human soul is expressed exactly according to the character of our Idea. Chapter V.*
>
> *Indeed, this Idea is the First Man; the soul, behaving as I have described, is the Second Man; the Third Man is, as it were, no longer man, but a composite of the soul from our body together with a certain life infused into it by the preceding soul. In this third state, sensation is more effective, while in the animal, sensation is dull; but there is a certain human affection which declares that this life of the animal depends not only on the soul but also on our higher nature, just as our divinity always depends and acts.*

A It is necessary, therefore, that "Man" be some other *Reason-Principle* besides the soul. Now, what stands in the way of Man still being something composite? Namely, the soul constituted chiefly in such a Reason-Principle. Here, truly, this Reason-Principle is like a certain activity, and such an activity cannot exist without an agent. For this is how the Reason-Principles within seeds seem to behave: they are neither without soul, nor are they simply souls. For effective Reason-Principles are not entirely devoid of soul. B Nor should anyone wonder that such essences exist as Reason-Principles. But those Reason-Principles which do not make a man—of what soul are they chiefly the activity? Perhaps of the vegetative soul? Or rather of the soul that creates the animal—a soul that is certainly clearer and more effective, and for this very reason more full of life? C Such a soul, being present to such matter, inasmuch as it is this very thing affected in such a way, is judged to be "Man" even without the body. This soul certainly forms something in the body according to itself, and is accustomed to produce another "image" of man, as much as the nature of the body can grasp; it produces, I say, a certain man...
