<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of "Man" and the soul's sensory faculties. It transitions from defining the different levels of human existence (the divine vs. the sensory) into Chapter VI, which explores how sensation exists even in the higher, intelligible soul.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.</header>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is of a lower sort, yet still possesses form, as well as reason-principles <term>Reason-principles: translating "rationes" or "logoi," the formative blueprints of reality that shape matter.</term>, character, affections, and powers—though these are weak and dim. Indeed, everything is dim, because this is not the "First Man" <note>In Neoplatonism, the "First Man" is the ideal, perfect form of humanity existing in the Divine Intellect, while we are reflections of it.</note>. Furthermore, the types of senses there are different, and there are other senses which, though they appear sharp, are actually clouded and mere images compared to the higher senses. But the man who presides over this lower one is counted among the divine beings; he possesses a superior "Man" and much clearer senses.

<margin>B</margin> Perhaps this is the man Plato defines. In his definition, he adds "the soul using the body" <note>original Latin: "animam utentem corpore"</note>, because the soul called "human" rests upon that which most closely uses the body. However, the more divine soul uses the body in a secondary way. For when that which has been made has already become a sensory being, this higher soul follows, providing the inner life—or rather, it does not "follow," but provides a sort of impression <note>original: "plām" / "τύπον" (a seal or stamp).</note>. For it is not distant from the intelligible world, but by touching it constantly, it holds the lower soul suspended from itself, mixing itself with reason-principle toward reason-principle. <margin>C</margin> Consequently, this man, who is dim in himself, becomes more luminous by such an illumination.

### Our soul possesses the sense-faculty so fundamentally that it always uses a certain kind of sense. Chapter VI.

*Even outside earthly bodies, the soul senses through a body in the air, and through a subtle body in the heavens, where the stains of the air do not exist, but only heavenly things. Indeed, even outside this entire sensory world, the soul possesses something of the sort: a reason-principle implanted in its conception and reason-principles received within itself, as well as imaginable reason-principles. Furthermore, our whole human nature possesses certain other reason-principles of the senses, which are connected in a clearer order; some of ours are such that they provide a way of illuminating those things which drive my own being. To the extent that they stand as universal forms, they illuminate—as he says, one is driven by one's own "daemons" <note>Daemon: here, a guiding spirit or a higher level of the self, not a malevolent entity.</note>. Likewise, regarding what power says: the intellectual parts primarily drive the daemon itself across the interval; through it, the power also speaks. And also the reason-principles. After this, Plotinus, with Egyptian-like love <note>A reference to the mysterious or sacred nature of the inquiry, or perhaps Plotinus's own Egyptian origins.</note>, attempts to address the sense-faculty regarding irrational souls; he even questions their transmigrations. Into these, souls do not descend into the nature of a brute beast, which Plotinus himself does not entirely affirm above others, as we have discussed elsewhere.*

BUT in what way does the faculty of sensation exist in that more excellent soul? Surely that power of sensing belongs properly to those things which are called "sensibles" in that realm; thus, there is a sense there, just as there are sensibles. Therefore, the knowledge of sensibles there perceives harmony through sense; specifically, while the sensory man is contained and perceives through sense, he fits what follows—even to the very end—to the harmony flourishing there. Even this fire here agrees with that fire there, which the soul perceived by its own kind of sense—a sense, I say, having a certain proportion suitable to the nature of that fire. If these bodies were there, the soul would also sense and notice them there. <margin>B</margin> Indeed, the man living there is a soul of such a kind, capable of apprehending these things; hence the later man, as a sort of imitation, possesses both his imitation and his reason-principles. And the man who exists in the Mind <note>original Latin: "in mente," Greek: "νοῦς." The realm of pure intellect.</note> precedes all men, shining upon the second man; the second likewise glows upon the third. In a way, the last man possesses all of these—not being made of them, but rather being adjacent to them. <margin>C</margin> This man of ours acts toward the final end; from here, something shines back from the one preceding; for that one, in turn, an action is suggested by the third, higher one. Each person exists according to how they act, although they possess all levels, and yet again, do not possess them. After this third life has been separated from the body, the third man remains without it, if the soul immediately preceding follows it—a following, obviously, that is not at all segregated from the higher realms. Then, wherever one is, the preceding one is also said to be...

<column-break/>

<margin>Α</margin> ...possessing the forms and the reason-principles, the characters, the dispositions, and the powers—all of them dim, since he is not the first, and indeed, [possessing] senses. But those senses are of another kind, and those sensibles are also there, though these here are more dim, being visible images. But this one who presides is a certain being, belonging to the gods, possessing a better man and more distinct senses. And this is the man whom Plato defined. And by adding <margin>Β</margin> "using the body," he showed either that it uses a certain body primarily, or that the secondary soul now uses this body here. For when it became a sensory living being, it gives [life]; but the higher soul does not give it by being present, but as if by a seal. For it does not depart from the intelligible, but it holds the lower soul suspended and joined to it, mixing itself as reason-principle to reason-principle. <margin>C</margin> Whence even the man here, being what he is, became manifest, being illuminated by that one.

### HOW, then, is the sensory faculty in the superior soul? Or is the sensory faculty there receptive of the things in that realm?

Since there are also sensibles there. Therefore, this man also senses his own harmony, and the sensory man, having received it through sense, harmonizes it and holds the harmony that is there, and harmonizes fire to the fire there. The soul possesses a sensory faculty analogous to the nature of the fire there. <margin>Β</margin> If there were bodies there, these would be sensible and perceptible to the soul; and the man who is there, being such a soul as is receptive of these things, and the later man, is a certain imitation, possessing the reason-principles in imitation. For the man in the Mind exists as the man before all sensible things, shining upon the second, who also possesses the third—or how? For he is not set apart from those things, but is active; while the one of us acts according to the <margin>C</margin> last things, and by the one before it, and by the third, that one is an activity according to which he acts; although he might hold all places, yet again he holds [only] what he has. But when the life here is separated from the body, does it sense with the third or with the one before it? But it was together, as he said, since they are separated from those others, but it is called...

He interprets Plato's definition of man as a "soul using a body" to explain how our higher self illuminates our physical existence.</summary>

# BOOK SEVEN.

...it is recovered. But when it is transferred into the body of a beast, it is wondered how the reason-principle of a man will be present; or rather, it is present in all. But it is because it acts according to another principle. As long as it exists in its pure state, before it has been corrupted, it wills to be human, and it is indeed human, even in the higher realms. But that part of the soul which is better produces better things: it also brings forth spirits <term>spirits: translating "daemones" (δαίμονας). In Neoplatonism, these are not "demons" but intermediary beings between gods and humans.</term> of a similar kind to the human. And that which is before this spirit is more divine—or rather, it is a God—and a spirit attached to God is an imitation of God, just as this man here is suspended from that Ideal Man. For it is not called God into which man is most closely raised. There is a difference here, the same difference that souls have toward one another, even if they are in the same rank. One must call these spirits a species of "daemons," just as Plato names them. But when the soul follows a nature it has chosen—even a beastly one—that which was attached to it when it was human remains equal within it. It has given a reason-principle to those animals, for that activity of the soul is of a lower sort.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to be. But when it is transferred into a brute body, it may seem a wonder in what way that reason-principle <term>reason-principle: translating "ratio" or "logos," the internal blueprint that defines a thing's nature.</term> which belongs to the man himself is transferred as well: but truly it was already all things; at other times, however, it acts according to a different principle. Therefore, insofar as it exists in a pure state and has not yet been corrupted, it wills to be man, and it exists as man. For that is better, and it acts upon what is better. It also acts as spirits <note>original: "dæmones"</note> which are prior, but conform to that which acts as man. And that which is before itself is more spirit-like; <margin>B</margin> rather, it is a God. Indeed, a spirit attached to God is a certain imitation of God, just as this man here is suspended toward that [Ideal] Man. For it is not called God toward which man is most closely raised. For the difference here is the same as that which souls have among themselves, if indeed they are of the same order. It is necessary, however, to call these spirits a species of "daemons," whom Plato names as such. When, however, the soul accompanies and chooses the nature of a brute, then that which is <margin>C</margin> attached to the higher soul (even while it acted as man) now provides the seed-like reason-principle <note>original: "seminale rationem"</note> of that animal. For it possesses it, and such an activity is judged to be of a lower quality.

---

> *How Plotinus wishes that the idea of man cannot be mixed with the idea of a horse: likewise that our intellect remains perpetually in divine things: and that reason is governed most closely by the intellect: again, that the divine nature of our soul is by no means cast down to lower things, but rather these lower things strive toward the soul. It followed to say that the human species is by no means transformed into a beastly one. You will note that in our body, beyond the vital "trace" <term>trace: translating "vestigium," a faint impression or mark left by a higher power.</term> impressed by the Soul of the World (which is common to all), there is also impressed a vital trace proper to our own soul; this is different from the Soul of the World, and is changed not by external things, but by the soul itself. From this it follows that by no such change does it entirely cast off its own species. Finally, the soul even in the divine world is said to use the senses, because it perceives corporeal things, though it seems to look forth from a higher watchtower.*

-> Chapter VII. <-

<margin>A</margin> But if the soul, having been corrupted and made worse, fashions a brute nature—which it did not do while it was in its original state—does it create an ox, or a horse, or some other irrational animal? And is the horse contrary to nature, or something less? It is indeed "less" than the original, but in some way it was a horse or a dog from the beginning, from which it might receive its form. If the soul has the power, it produces the better; if not, it produces whatever it can when it is drawn down. It is like craftsmen who know how to make many forms; <margin>B</margin> they then produce either what they were commanded to do, or what the matter requires by its own suitability. For what prevents the power of the Soul of the World—since it is an entire Reason-Principle—from pre-figuring the matter? Even before the individual soul-powers come from it, this pre-figuration is like a preliminary light shining into the matter. Could it be that a soul, following the traces of bitterness <note>original: "pifkrias / πικρίας," here likely referring to a harsh or "bitter" material state.</note>, works out the details? <margin>* if indeed the parts</margin> * And does it articulate the traces <margin>C</margin> part by part, just as we, in each circumstance we encounter, shape ourselves—much like a dancer in a play adapts himself to the role and gestures given to him? But indeed, led by what followed, we have come to this point. Our purpose was to inquire how the faculty of sensation is in man, and how that divine part is not inclined toward generation. Now it has appeared to us, and reason has demonstrated, that those divine things do not look toward these lower things,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> but rather these lower things strive toward those, depend upon them, and imitate them according to their strength; and this man [the physical] depends upon that Man [the Ideal].

# PLOTINUS'S ENNEAD VI.

...to have the powers for those things. Furthermore, these sensible things are consistent with this human being, while those [ideal] things are consistent with that [Ideal] human. For those things are also, in a certain way, sensible; we have named them thus because they are "bodies," but they are perceived differently than these bodies of ours. It has been established, moreover, that the sense here is a dimmer perception than that sense there, which we have called "sense" because it perceives bodies, but we have granted that it is far more clear-sighted. And because of this, we have said that this human being is also "sensible": since he apprehends lower things in a lower way—namely, only the images of those higher things—it can rightly be said that this sense here consists of "dim intelligences," while those intelligences there are "extremely clear-sighted senses."

->*The Intellect, through its exuberant fertility, naturally propagates itself within into as many ideal rays as possible. From this intellectual and natural propagation, the natural forms of things leap forth like lights.*<-

### Chapter VIII.

*There, then, each horse exists; here, let the horse be made. Otherwise, these things would depend on themselves, and the horse would be known there only after it existed here. However, there is no multiplicity there simply because the number of things seems innumerable, insofar as whatever you take as "something" following the whole, it always occurs as a manifold. Furthermore, the Fullness <note>original: "Plenitudo," likely referring to the Pleroma, the state of being full of divine powers.</note> possesses whatever it has within all things equally full.*

<margin>In what...</margin>
**B**UT the faculty of sensing is indeed as it is; however, since that first "Ideal Horse" as a whole, and every individual one of them, does not look back at these animals of ours—if a horse or any other animal is generated here—the Intellect says that the "horse-reason-principle" <term>horse-reason-principle: translating "equinas rationem" (logos). In Neoplatonism, this is the divine "blueprint" that makes a horse a horse.</term> has already come. Even though it is impossible to know how that principle, by prevailing, makes a horse and then makes it most vigorously, for undoubtedly "horseness" existed there if it was to produce a horse. Therefore, it is not the case that the Intellect thought it out later, but it is clear that the nature of it occurred before the future horse here. If, therefore, it existed before the generation and was not created just so it might be born, the Intellect—not looking toward these things of ours—certainly held the "Horse" within itself. Having that Horse there, it did not hold it just to create these things, but because those things are necessary to it. Life is not a solitude; it is not permitted to proceed only as far as those things and then stop. For who could prevent that power from remaining and proceeding equally powerfully?

<margin>How it happens that there are brutes in the ideal world</margin>
Furthermore, what power could there be if these animals were not there? Because these irrational animals live in God, how much honor does such a great irrational multitude of them have? Or rather, does it seem to bring about a kind of disgrace? It is a small thing that the One must be One; it must also be many. Since it comes after that which is entirely One, it does not remain there by chance, but rather follows it.

<margin>The One cannot not have multiplicity.</margin>
But since it is after the One, it cannot happen that it surpasses the One in being "one"; instead, it is necessary to fall short of it. Since the One is altogether the best, it was necessary for this [the Intellect] to be more than one, for multiplicity is found in deficiency. <note>Plotinus argues that the Absolute (the One) is so perfect it is simple. The next level of reality, the Intellect, is slightly less perfect, which is why it breaks into many ideas/forms.</note>

<margin>Whence the binary and number.</margin>
But why is it necessary for "Being" itself to be multiplied only as far as the binary <note>original: "binarium," or the Dyad. This represents the first step from Unity into Multiplicity.</note>? Certainly because each thing placed in the binary is such that it cannot be entirely one. It is necessary for there to be one thing and another, thus at least two existing things. And again, each of them is multiplied in the same way; hence in the first binary there is movement as well as rest. There is also Intellect, and there is life—I mean perfect Intellect and perfect life. It is, therefore, not like one single intellect, but every intellect, containing all individual intellects. It is multiplied to the extent that the intellect...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into how species and "irrational" animals exist in the higher Intellectual realm. It follows the argument that the Intelligible World is a "Fullness" containing the archetypes of all things, not just human beings.</meta>

BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>A</margin> <note>This Greek fragment corresponds to the start of the Latin text below.</note> All acts, or rather, even more extensive. That mind truly lives not as a single soul, but as all souls, possessing a more extensive power for procreating individual souls. It is an "All-Animal," not having man alone within itself; otherwise, only this human being would exist here.

---

->*Since in the first Being the first Number is the origin of things, it is right that the entire number of things exists there. Likewise, since it is the first Form, by right things differ among themselves there by degrees of forms, just as species do. Again, in that perfect life and intelligence, every "Idea" of things—even of things that do not possess life here—is itself a certain life and intelligence. Chapter IX.*<-

->*Similarly, the forms of metals—which do not shine here on their own—all shine in their own planets with a variety of light; and the forms of animals that appear ugly here are beautiful in heaven. Life and intelligence there are wonderfully effective and move within themselves as much as possible; by such motion, by deriving from itself, it divides itself as it were—yet it does not create continuous entities through some material division. Meanwhile, it distinguishes itself by many degrees of forms; and just as the division of the physical world progresses, so too it proceeds into narrower categories, bringing forth the "Ideas" <note>term: Ideas (Ideae). In Platonic thought, these are the perfect, eternal blueprints of all things in the physical world.</note> of smaller things within itself. But since all Ideas there are from one and exist in one indivisible life and intelligence, surely all are contained in every one: just as in any star the powers of other stars are present, insofar as all things in heaven agree in the same light of the Sun, although each primarily displays its own specific property by appearance and effect. Similarly, any Idea brings forth its own nature while containing all the others.*<-

---

<margin>A</margin> But truly, if someone says to you that animals are the things most to be honored, one might ask: in what way do the other animals exist there, especially those deprived of reason? These are surely considered lowly because they lack reason, since we believe an animal is to be honored primarily for its rational virtue. And if a thing is to be honored because of its intellectual nature, then it should deservedly be despised when that nature is absent. Although it is difficult to say how anything there could be lacking in mind or reason, since that in
<margin>B</margin> which (or from which) individual things exist is Reason itself and the "First Intellect." Therefore, before we speak further on these matters, let us entirely agree on this: the man living here is not the same as that "Ideal Man" who exists there. Similarly, the other animals do not exist there as they do here; rather, they are to be understood as existing in a certain more excellent degree. Furthermore, nothing "rational" <note>Plotinus distinguishes between "Reasoning" (a process of moving from thought to thought) and "Intellect" (an immediate, total grasp of truth).</note> exists there in the way we use the word. For here, perhaps, someone might discourse through reasoning; but there, the vigor of "Act" <note>term: Act (Actus). In this context, it refers to the pure, perfected activity of a divine being.</note> is superior to rational discourse. But why then does this human being reason, while the other animals do not? 
<margin>C</margin> Surely because the "Intelligences" there in man and other animals are different, and so too the reason in them differs here: for in some way, the duties of much thought are present in the other animals as well. Why then are they not equally rational? To that objection, one must ask the causes: why do not human beings themselves exist as equal reasons among themselves? 
<margin>D</margin> It is worthwhile to consider that there are many paths and lives, like certain motions, and many intelligences; it was by no means necessary for them to be identical to one another. Instead, there are different lives and similarly different intelligences, and these differences are in some way more or less lucid and clear. That which is closest to the "First Principles" is designated by the first differences; but what is second is designated by the second; the third also by the third. Therefore, in the very order of intelligences, some are indeed gods, while others occupy a second category: in which is contained that which is called "rational" among us. Next follows the nature which we call "irrational." But in that higher realm, even what we call "irrational" is a certain Reason, and what is "lacking mind" there is actually an Intellect. For the being that understands a horse is an Intellect, and the intelligence of a "Horse" is similarly an Intellect. Accordingly, if intelligence alone were there, it would not be absurd for the intelligence of the horse-kind to exist in a state devoid of human-like mind. Now, however, if intelligence and the thing understood are one and the same...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

In what way is this indeed intelligence, while the thing itself is deprived of intellect? <note>original: "quonam pacto hæc quidé intelligentia est. res ipsa vero intellectu privata"</note> Otherwise, the mind would make itself mindless. But surely the thing there <note>referring to the Intelligible realm</note> is not lacking in intellect; rather, it is intellect of a certain kind. For there is also life of a certain kind. Just as any life does not lack that gift by which it is life, so too intellectual life is not far from that similar gift by which it is intellect. Since not even the intellect that thrives there according to each individual animal is deprived of that dowry by which it is intellect, even of all things—such as the intellect of a man. Clearly, whatever part it has received, this itself is all things there, but in a different order and sequence. For in its current act it is a specific part, but meanwhile it is capable of being all things; yet we, in individual things, receive that which exists in act. 

That which is at the very end of the line is the furthest extent: so much so that the furthest point of this intellect is the horse. And in that part where the intellect falls short, that horse arises—always progressing into life at the lowest level. Where the inner part ends, the inner animal also ends. For those powers, while they are being unfolded, continually leave behind what is above. They proceed, always letting go of something, and in letting go, they always suggest other and different things. And because of the neediness of the animal now emerging, they devise another way to apply what it lacks; for example, since there is no longer enough for [pure] life, the claw and the beak appeared, and horns and teeth appeared. Therefore, wherever the mind itself descends, it looks back again at the sufficiency of its own nature from above and emerges; it finds within itself the medicine for the demanding need of that which is deficient.

->Life and the first intelligence, and the most perfect animal, contains all lives, all intelligences, and all grades and species of animals that can possibly be imagined.<-

### Chapter X.

Since the first multiplicity is there, that which is better is rightly multiplied into species; and being united, they are more thoroughly mingled with each other. In the first form, which is most effective and clear at once, all the Forms of things preserve their own properties wonderfully in a common nature, and everything meets them as equally uniform and multiform.

**BUT** in what way is there any deficiency there? Are the horns there for the sake of defense? Truly, such things are there for their own self-sufficiency and perfection, as if of the animal itself. For just as it was necessary for the animal to be perfect, so must it be perfect as mind, and perfect as life; therefore if it lacks this, it must have that. And indeed, the difference itself arises from the fact that one thing is in place of another, and from all these comes the most perfect animal, the most perfect mind, the most perfect life. Individual things, as individuals, are also perfect. Then, even if it consists of many parts, it must again be one, and vice versa; otherwise it is impossible for it to be made of many, yet for those many to be the same among themselves—else the one would exist as self-sufficient. It is necessary, therefore, to come together from things that always differ in species, just as the soul is a composite; yet in such a way that individuals are properly preserved, just as forms and reasons <note>term: reasons (rationes). Used here in the sense of 'logoi' or formative principles that organize matter.</note> are. For forms, such as the form of a man, must display as many differences as they are composed of; although there is one thing in all of them, where certain things are better and others worse than each other—like the eye and the finger—they are nevertheless members of one and the same body, any of which is lesser than the whole. But it is undoubtedly better that things be this way: indeed, "reason" is an animal, and yet something else besides, which is not entirely the same as the animal. A single thing also has something common and something unique within itself, and the whole is beautiful, where that which is common is equally common.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...to the thing, how is there thinking, yet the thing itself is unthinking? <note>original Greek: "πῶς ἡ μὲν νόησις, ἀνόητον τὸ πρᾶγμα"</note> and by the same token the mind makes itself unthinking, and also sensation; but rather this is a living thing, so that whatever life it may be, it is not excluded from thinking. Since nothing is according to its essence which is not also excluded from thinking, and everything is eternal, such as man; if indeed each part, not in proportion, but everything perhaps acts differently with... <margin>B</margin> ...well-minded. And these things are possible; but we take as each individual that which is in act—and what is in act * so that * together the things in so that this certain thing is also the last, since also the deficiency proceeding into lesser animals will rest, then it will cease to be laid down; for the powers, being unfolded, leave behind again, as if they let go and release. And in the act of releasing, they always do so, but because of the deficiency, the animal <margin>C</margin> appears, from that which is lacking, from which it starts to add, as if from what is its own for life, such as by nature a nail and a crooked claw, or also a sharp tooth, or horns. Nature, so that the nail should descend again; again the ends of Nature and all-blessed because it brought to itself the things of the one lacking.

<margin>A</margin> BUT how is there deficiency there? Or are the horns there for defense? Or for self-sufficiency in life, and the perfect, as an animal, since it must be perfect as mind, and perfect as life? So that if not in some way, then in that way. And the difference, by the other and but rather with all things being full, the perfect mind is of life. And the greatest life of each is as each is perfect. And not from many if it takes away the one, or having to be from many, but of the same things, yet either self-sufficient or always. <margin>B</margin> Since not from those but the form just as every composite, and the things of the defined individuals. ### BOOK SEVEN

->Just as the body contains the forms of lower animals as food, even in a living way, for no small reason: so it must be understood that the [Divine Intellect] possesses the forms of the whole world in a more excellent way than the celestial realm. Chapter XI.<-

What, therefore, is it? By the force of order and form, it is impressed by the first mind and wisdom; it possesses these things more expressly in itself—that is, the ideas of these things are more expressive there, which, together with order, manifest the whole more clearly. A more expressive nature belongs to those things which are intelligent. Indeed, if all species in the world, together with their matter, possess something vital and intellectual, it is not without reason that all things seem to exist there. For these material forms are generated most closely by "seminal reasons" <note>original: "seminarijs rationibus"; these are the formative blueprints in Stoic and Neoplatonic thought</note> which live in the life of the world. But truly, they come from those reasons of forms which have life in the divine mind. In all elements there are many living things conforming to the element... the soul is certainly present, and perhaps one soul is in the four elements... like a light flying through the air. Note: intellectual souls are present in bodies not as if enslaved to them, but as the creators of bodily species.

It is said, and it appeared of old, that all the natures of all living things are there. But if someone asks about the bodies there, from where would he have the things he has in himself? He who has made the whole according to <margin>* [missing] the whole</margin> reason or according to opinion. But where there is fire and water there, there must certainly also be plants. But what happens to the plant-like nature? And how does fire live, or how does earth live? Or how does the whole live? For it has what it has, so that everything there lives; or how could it not be so? Therefore, we might adapt these plants to the "Reason" <note>original: "λογω" (logos)</note> of the plant here. It is a Reason existing in life; if indeed the material Reason is that which makes the plant what it is. All life is a certain soul for instruction; the Reason, if it exists, is the primary plant. There are others before it. Either it is the first plant, from which those on earth do not live. These other things must live much earlier there, or that thing itself is a plant from which these come, in a second or third degree. Is there a trace of that life in the earth? Or how? Either it is in being earth, or in having life in all the earth. Or is it prior? Or how is this the whole? Or is the whole of this form there, both the earthly and the plants that follow them? Is it the Reason, or is it not? In the earth, or those receiving <margin>* being made</margin> the most earthy things being made <note>original: "γινόμενα"</note>, or being fashioned in it, we might find here the nature of the earth. Thus, the growth and fashioning of stones, which are not seen to grow, are certain forms growing inside; or how by Reason are they ensouled in the act of creation? If they are being made, we must believe they are coming into being. These are the "form" of the earth that acts, just as in trees there is that which is called "nature," as or in woody trees; by analogy, that which is called earth. It is clear that the stone, entering in, is like the trees in their own specific way, but still grown together, like a part of the plant not yet cut from the wood. How could the creator place a nature in the earth? Living in Reason for men, we might easily find the earth <margin>* still</margin> there. It is much earlier a living thing and <margin>* of irrational earth</margin> a life of irrational earth, the "Earth-Itself" <note>The Platonic archetype of Earth</note>, and primarily earth, from which this earth here comes. Just as fire is a certain Reason in matter, and other such things. For fire does not arise of its own accord.

<column-break/>

It is further handed down that the heavens did not retain any form of all the animals, of which many are admired, as much as this universe possesses all things. But from where did it receive them? Did it not receive whatever it has from on high? Certainly, it has them from there, whatever things were made by Reason and fashioned according to species. But since it has fire, and it has water, and it has plants, in what way are the plants there? And how does that fire live? How does the earth live? For either it found this there, or they lie as if dead, so that not everything there lives. Why are all these things also there? Plants indeed can easily be accommodated to Reason itself: since even among us, a plant is a certain Reason consisting in life. If, then, the material Reason of the plant, according to which it is a plant, is one such thing, and a certain soul, and Reason itself is one thing, is this not itself the "First Plant"? Not exactly: but before this is the First Plant, from which this one is born. For that one is indeed a single thing, but these are many, and necessarily from the one. If, therefore, it is necessary for that to live much earlier, and for this itself to be a plant: from that one, these things exist, hanging in a certain second and third degree, and living according to the traces of that one. But how does the earth exist there? And what is the "being" of the earth itself? And in what way is there an earth there possessing life? Perhaps it is better first to investigate what this lowest earth is, that is, what its "being" is. It is necessary that some Reason be present here at the boundary. Certainly, as far as plants are concerned, the Reason of the plant lives even among us. Does the Reason of the earth itself not also live in this earth? After we have accepted those things which are most earthly, born and made in the earth, we shall find in these also the nature of the earth itself. It must be thought, **therefore**, <margin>* being made * of generation * of the fashioning of the earth **therefore**</margin> that the increments and concretions of stones, and of mountains rising and coalescing, are undoubtedly made through certain inner formations, with a certain "animal Reason" <note>original: "animali quadam ratione"; meaning a soul-like or living principle</note> manufacturing and forming them from within. And this is the species of the earth which makes the earth, just as in trees that which is called "nature" conducts itself. It is similar by a certain proportion to the wood of the tree, which is commonly called earth: yet a stone cut out is like wood that has been lopped off from a tree. But when the stone does not suffer that, but is still annexed, like a branch not yet amputated from a living tree, we surely find a nature implanted in the earth that manufactures it; it is a certain life flourishing in Reason. We will more easily believe from this that the heavenly earth is living much earlier, and that the rational life of the earth is the earth itself—the Primary Earth, from which this earth also proceeds and lives. Just as the Reason of fire is in matter, and other such things; fire is not born by chance or hazard.

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

From where does it come? <note>Referring to the origin of fire and the elements.</note> Surely not from some collision, as one might think. For friction between bodies only occurs when fire is already present in the universe, where the bodies being rubbed together already possess fire. Nor, again, does matter possess fire in such a way that fire is produced by matter itself. If a thing behaves in this way, and if that which produces forms must exist according to a rational principle <note>original: "rationem"; here meaning the 'Logos' or formative blueprint</note>: what then will this be? Surely it is a soul capable of producing fire—that is, a certain life and reason, yet in such a way that both are one and the same. For this reason, Plato says that a soul exists in each of these elements, not otherwise than as an efficient cause, just as it is for this fire manifest to our senses. Therefore, that which produces fire here is a certain fiery life, and indeed a truer fire. The superior fire, since it is more truly fire, is more deeply involved in life; therefore, fire itself lives. The same reasoning seems to apply to the others: namely, water and air. But why are these not also seen as "animated" <note>filled with soul/life</note> just as the earth is? Surely it is established that these also exist within the "Universal Animal" <note>original: "vniuerso animali"; the Neoplatonic concept that the cosmos is a single living organism</note> and exist as parts of that animal; yet life does not appear in them, just as it does not appear [on the surface] of the earth.

Truly, one may argue that the earth is animated from those things which are born within it; similarly, one may conjecture the same regarding fire. For even in fire, living creatures are generated. But this is even more manifest in water; and there are certain compositions of living creatures made of air. Yet individual flames of fire, which are made daily and soon extinguished, pass away while the soul flourishes in the whole. And since this fire has not obtained a permanent mass, it naturally does not reveal the soul inherent within it. The same is true for air and water: for if they cohered naturally into a more constant substance, they would demonstrate the soul infused within them; but since it was necessary for them to be diffused, they do not reveal the presence of the soul at all. And yet these elements seem to behave just like the fluids of a living body, such as blood. For flesh reveals that it possesses a soul; but flesh is composed from blood. Blood, however, not exhibiting sensation, does not seem to have a soul; although it is necessary for the soul to be in the blood as well. Yet this does not appear because nothing violent happens to it; rather, it is most ready to depart easily from the infused soul: just as must be judged to happen in the three elements. Since whatever living creatures coalesce more from "compacted air" have a nature that allows them to perceive without suffering. Just as air does not retain light as something fixed and permanent—insofar as the light remains, the air itself passes through—so the soul is present everywhere in the sphere of air, and yet again it is not present; and it is the same in the other elements.

---

> *In the first life, which is the producer of all things, all things are Living: and since it is the first form because of the marvelous efficacy of life, all living things there are formally distinguished, being entirely propagatable within itself. Moreover, that form is almost to every form as the nature of the Sun is to all the powers of the stars—its light being the rays and all the colors—and as the Vegetative life is to all the forms of the limbs that are to be born from it through seminal reasons.* <note>This italicized section is a commentary by Marsilio Ficino, explaining the relationship between the "First Life" (the Divine Mind) and the physical world using the sun as an analogy.</note>

**Chapter XII.**

BUT we shall say again: since we grant that this world is modeled after the example of that [Higher] world: it is necessary that the Universal Animal also exist there much earlier, and if its existence is to be altogether perfect, all things must be there. Now truly, the heaven there is a living being, nor is it empty of those stars which are gazed upon in this heaven; and the very being of heaven consists in this. It is also clear that the earth there is not empty, but

A certain type is life and reason, both being one and the same. Wherefore Plato also in each of these says there is a soul,

# BOOK SEVEN

A much more vigorous <note>original: "ἐρρωμένην"; referring to a life that is stronger or more robust than physical life</note> life exists there, and in it are all the animals that are called terrestrial and land-dwelling here; clearly, even the plants are rooted in that Living Being. There is a sea there, and all water, existing in life and in a constant flow. All the animals that live in water are there, 
<margin>in water.</margin>
and all those in Nature that exist in every part. The whole of the air is within it, analogous to the terrestrial air, and the animals in the air are there, since those things that are in the air [here] are necessarily there as well. For each of the great parts [of the universe] must necessarily stand in this relation to the animals dwelling within them. And there are the celestial beings there, even if they exist in the air there—they are all celestial. All things are in that Living Being. From where does it have them? Is it because every soul is truly there? For they come from nowhere else. But as for these things, from where do they come, and the "all," and the universe? This is a question that has never ceased to be asked: how all things exist together as living beings of a replenished soul. It is because all things come from her from a single source—not like a single breath or a single heat, but as if from a certain quality that holds all qualities within itself and preserves those qualities: sweetness with fragrance, and the quality of wine, and the power of all juices, and the sight of colors, and everything that the sense of touch recognizes. Let there also be all the things that hearing perceives: every melody and every rhythm.

---

<margin>that [it is] soul.</margin>
It is, therefore, entirely simple, since the whole is the same as the soul; but all things that are simple are also diverse, and they are not composite, but rather dual, and they are actualities. For some things possess an activity 
<margin>every soul</margin>
that is a simple ending, while others are the primary activities of all things. That which is moved is moved in the same way, according to the same things, and is always similar. There is something identical even in a part, but all things are still in a part again, even if there is something then disposed toward the infinite. If we speak of something again, it is directed toward something as an ultimate end. That which is in between is all like a line, or like a circumference—a body that is uniform and without diversity. But what would it encompass there? Or rather, would there be no change at all, for it would all be again

<column-break/>

But much more living there, and full in both ways, all animals are present, whatever are here called walking and terrestrial; plants moreover, clearly founded in life. And there is the sea: all water is there in life and in a stream that does not flow <note>original: "flumine non fluente"; referring to the eternal, stable motion of the divine realm contrasted with physical change</note>. All animals are there. The nature of the entire air is also a portion of that world: aerial animals are in it, clearly adapted to that very air. For why would those things that are in the Living Being itself not be living themselves, both there and here? What, therefore, prevents every animal from necessarily being there? For just as each of the regions and parts is disposed, so too must the nature of the animals flourishing in them be disposed; for how else could it be? There is also heaven there, and so those who possess it are present—whatever animals are in the heaven. Nor could they fail to be present, otherwise they would not even exist. Therefore, he who asks from where these animals come seems to be asking from where the soul is there. But for him to ask that is the same as asking from where the animal comes. It is exactly as if one were to ask from where life comes—all life, and every soul, and where the Mind <note>original: "mens"; the Divine Intellect</note> might be. Where indeed there is no lack, no defect: but all things are full of life and, as it were, overflowing. There is for them (so to speak) an efflux flowing from a single source, not as if from a single spirit, or breath, or from a single heat: but just as if there were one quality possessing and preserving all qualities in itself—sweetness, for instance, together with the sweetness of scent, the vigor of wine, the powers of all juices, transparent colors, and whatever is perceived by touch. Let there also be whatever the voice confesses to drink in: every number <note>musical meter/rhythm</note> and every harmony.

---

->So the Mind is first, since it is all things of all forms, whether simple or mixed, uniform and multiform; and again, most importantly, since it is the principle of all things, for this reason it is also the most loving.<-

->Cap. XIII.<-

Moreover, that form is the most perfect of any form, and for that reason it is known through this true form. It is therefore the act of all things, since, being the greatest act, the first and most efficient of all, for this reason it carries acts within itself. In such great multitude it is most unified; in any part it maintains an undivided unity. All movements introduce a certain variety here into that; but it is clear that this necessarily already possesses its own state, having movement within the Mind. That movement flourishes and exists with time, but in the soul it is present. For movement always has time first; in the Mind alone you find it faster than time, a certain life of motion. For not only in motion and life is it first in the Mind, but also in the variety of its abiding state, just as all life and act are there. Indeed, just as any ray from the wide orb of the Sun proceeds into everything, that which is said to be in a part of its breadth embraces all the Sun’s powers: it especially displays them in everything, and again understands those things through itself and in itself.

But through these acts, any intellectual Mind proceeds, so that again it may say that this is every act of all things, just as it is the life. Each one is indeed exactly in one Idea, like a cone. For how would it be so different from another, if it were turned from others?

---

For there, the intellect is not something entirely simple, nor is the soul hanging from it entirely simple; but all things are far more diverse, insofar as they are simple—that is, insofar as they are not composite, insofar as they are principles, and insofar as they exist as acts. For nowhere is that which is judged there as "last" (an act, as it were, already defining itself) truly simple; but of that which is considered "first," the act itself exists as all acts. The movement of the Intellect is also moved in the same way, and it always shows itself naked, the same and similar. Yet there, nothing is identical and a single thing as if it were a part, but rather it is all things, since that which is in a part is not one single thing, but this too is infinitely divided. We can say that such a process comes from something and is directed entirely toward something, as if toward the ultimate. Is this universe like a line, or some body constituted of similar parts, and not at all diverse? But what beauty would that bring there? For if it has no diversity, neither...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the Divine Intellect. Previously, Plotinus described how all biological and elemental forms exist in their most perfect state within the Intellect. Here, he explores the mechanics of how the Intellect "moves" through these forms, explaining that thought requires a form of "Otherness" or internal wandering to be truly alive.</meta>

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK VI.

If no otherness <note>original: "alteritas"; the principle of difference or distinction that allows one thing to be recognized as separate from another</note> stirs it into living, then surely there will be no actualization. For such a state would be no different from a total absence of activity. And even if there is a movement of this kind, it would be life in only one single way, not in all ways. However, it is necessary that everything there, in every respect, must live, and that nothing should exist there that is not alive. It is necessary, therefore, for there to be movement toward all things—or rather, that there has already been movement toward all things. 

Furthermore, if that which is entirely simple moves, it possesses only that one movement; it remains the same. Thus, it does not proceed or advance toward anything. Or, if it has proceeded and advanced, it has already become something else; consequently, it has become two. If it remains the same as that first thing, it stays as one and has not proceeded. But if it becomes another, it has certainly proceeded with otherness, and has made a third thing out of the "same" and the "other" combined. 

Now, since what has been made is composed of both the same and the other, it rightfully possesses a nature that is simultaneously the same and the other. I say "other," not merely as a specific thing, but as a total and absolute otherness; for even that which is "same" within it is an "all-encompassing same." Therefore, since it is entirely the same and simply entirely other, nothing of those things called "others" has been left out. 

It possesses a nature, then, by which all things are distributed throughout the whole by otherness. If, therefore, all things are "other" above it, it can now be affected by them; but if they are not, then this intellect has generated all things—or rather, it already existed as all things. Wherefore, beings cannot exist unless the mind has operated; and I mean operated upon one thing after another unceasingly, as if wandering through every possible condition of wandering. It wanders, I say, within itself, just as the true intellect is born to wander within itself. It is born to wander among essences <note>original: "essentijs"; the fundamental realities or 'Forms'</note>, while those essences clearly coincide equally with its own wanderings.

But the intellect itself exists everywhere; therefore, it performs a stable wandering <note>original: "peruagantiam stabilem"; a Neoplatonic paradox describing how the mind can move through many thoughts while remaining fixed in its own perfection</note>. Indeed, the wandering of the mind takes place in the very "field of truth," from which it never departs. It occupies the whole, since it has created a place for itself through its own movement; and yet that place is the same as the mind to which the place belongs. Furthermore, this field is diverse, so that the mind may run through it; for unless it were always diverse throughout the whole, the mind would surely come to rest wherever it was not diverse. And if it rests, it does not think; thus, if it has ceased, it has not thought. If it does not do this, it certainly does not exist. 

Therefore, it is Intelligence. The total movement there fills the total essence; and the whole essence, as a total intelligence, embraces total life, always moving from one thing to another. This is especially true since that which is the "same" within it is also "other," so that to one who perpetually divides it, one thing and then another will always occur. 

Progression there is entirely conducted through life and through living beings. Just as for one traveling on earth, whatever things are encountered are found to be earthly everywhere—though they are earthly in different ways—so too there, the life through which one proceeds is the same. 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>* unless everything were so, it would be life in only one way</margin> Lest any otherness <note>original Greek: "ἑτερότης"</note> stir it into living, yet if it were an act <note>original: "ἐνέργεια"</note> again, such a state would be nothing if the act were not different. And if there were such a movement, *it would be one in every way and life would be in only one manner,* but it is necessary for all to be life, and movement from every side. If it did not live entirely, it would not be by movement. <margin>* it moves</margin> Rather, if it moves, something simple moves, and it must have a cosmic order, * and it would not act everywhere toward nothing.
<margin>B</margin> <margin>* and that which has proceeded</margin> * Or if it acts by leaping like two. And the same as it was then, it remains one, and has not proceeded. But if it is other, it proceeded with otherness, and made a third thing out of the same and the other. Since that which has been made comes from the same and the other, it has a nature to be both same and other. It is other, but the whole is other. For even its "same" is the whole. And being entirely the same, from those things of which it is other,
<margin>C</margin> it is because it would leave behind another life. It has a nature, then, to be extended over the whole. If then all the other things are toward the same, it has already ceased. If it is not of them, it does not exist. So that all those things, or rather all the things of that one, must all exist, even without it acting; but when it has acted, it is one thing after another, as if having wandered every wandering, and there being a wandering in itself, such as you now see.
<margin>D</margin> The true [intellect] is born to be in itself. It is born to wander among essences <note>original: "οὐσίαις"</note>, the essences running together with its own wanderings; and it is everywhere, and so remaining, it does not have the wandering. But the wandering for it is in the field of truth <note>original: "πεδίω τῆς ἀληθείας"; a reference to the place of perfect forms in Plato's Phaedrus</note> which it does not leave. It possesses everything by having grasped it, having made for itself its movement like its acting, and all for itself, and the whole place is diverse where there is a certain field, and its passage does not cease.
<margin>E</margin> would be diverse, in as much as it is not more diverse. But if it stands still, the intellect [is such] that the place does not even exist. If it is a type <note>original: "τύπος"</note> and does not exist, yet the intellect exists having thought. The movement filled the whole, every essence, and the whole essence, by every thought, embraced every life. Either one after another, and because it is the same as the other, and the other is divided again and appears. All is a journey through life, and all through life—
<margin>F</margin> just as for one going through the earth, all things are surely earth, even if the earth has differences. And there life is indeed the same, because it is the same but [different], having itself but through the passage of things not itself. Because it does not change, but standing together with the other, so that it is in the same way, and not those things there; for if they were not to be altered in the same way, and according to the same things, they would be entirely idle. The act having acted, or the activity <note>original: "ἐνέργεια"</note>, not at all. But he is the other things, just as he is the whole; both infinite and the whole.

But since indeed that life is always also another, it does not always occur as the same; yet it always performs the exact same traversal through those things that are not identically the same. For it does not change in its traversal; but meanwhile, the condition itself is preserved with diverse things, in the same manner, and according to the same way of wandering. For unless the very tenor of wandering in the same manner and according to the same things were at least distributed around various things, it would surely become entirely sluggish. From which it would follow that what is said to be "in act" would be an act that exists nowhere. But there are other and diverse things that it itself is; wherefore it is itself all things. And if indeed it is itself and also all things: <meta>catchword: otherwise</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explains that the Divine Intellect remains a unity while containing all diversity by performing a "stable wandering" through the "Field of Truth." He argues that thought and life require this internal "Otherness" to function; without this movement through various forms, the Intellect would be stagnant and thus non-existent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Divine Intellect from the previous page, specifically addressing how the "Otherness" within the Intellect does not destroy its unity but rather constitutes its life and completeness. It transitions into Chapter XIV, which uses the analogy of a face and bodily organs to explain how complex forms exist within a singular internal "Reason-Principle."</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN <note>This refers to the seventh treatise of the Sixth Ennead: "How the Multiplicity of Forms Came into Being, and on the Good."</note>

If the totality is not one, and all things are not in all, then it does not exist; for the whole is a completion of all things directed toward something. If it were not both one thing and another, but only its own identical self, it would diminish its own essence—the very nature it provides for its own completion.

Otherwise, it would not even be itself. But if it is entirely itself, it is certainly also "the all," because it encompasses all things. Nothing is found there that does not harmonize with the whole; nor is anything simply itself without also being another. Yet, while existing as another, it is also itself separately. For unless it existed as something else, while remaining fundamentally the same, it would restrict its own effectiveness; indeed, it would fail to adapt its own specific nature to that common harmony <note>original: "conspirationem"; literally a "breathing together" or cosmic sympathy</note>.

*To every part in the world, even the smallest, an ordered distinction is given through forms. This kind of formal and ordered variety does not happen by chance, nor does it arise from dark matter; rather, it depends on the One, because it leads back to the One. Therefore, from the primary divine forms, the power of variety flourishes both in the life of the world and in the Mind.*

### Chapter XIV.

*But both the Mind <term>Intellect: the divine "Nous" or realm of pure thought</term> and the Soul are a certain "one" in themselves—not indeed composed of many parts, but containing many things within. These are directed not toward external things, but back toward the internal, coiling toward the center like a circle. They reduce the wider universes of forms into smaller orbits, finally unfolding themselves into the most specific of species.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> We are able, moreover, to recognize the nature of the Intellect by using intellectual examples. We can see how it was not once empty, but exists as a likeness of unity, entirely free from external diversity. If one wishes, one may take the "reason-principle" <term>Logos: the formative, rational power that shapes matter</term> of a plant or an animal as an example. For if it were merely one thing and not in some way varied, it would not even be a "reason-principle." Furthermore, that which is produced from it would be nothing but matter, unless this principle, which is not merely a single unit, should fall upon the matter everywhere <margin>B</margin> and permit no part of that matter to remain the same. Just as a face is not merely a single mass, but possesses nostrils and eyes; and the nostrils do not possess just one single quality, but something else again, if they are to truly be nostrils. Indeed, if the nose were only one simple thing, it would be nothing but a bulk. And so, truly, in the Mind there are infinite things, because both the Mind itself and whatever is within it are simultaneously one and many. The Intellect is not "one and many" in the way a house is, but rather like <margin>C</margin> a reason-principle containing many things within itself. In a single "mental figure," as if within a boundary, you have internal boundaries and circuits, internal configurations, powers, and intelligences. It possesses a distinction that is not stretched out in a straight line, but is always propagated toward the innermost depths. It is as if, within a universal animal, the natures of great animals were contained, and these in turn branched out into smaller animals and were led down to smaller powers, <margin>D</margin> until they finally end in an indivisible species. Yet, even there, no separation of things lies confused or gaping, even though they have harmonized into one in a wondrous way. Now, such harmony is the "Friendship" <note>A reference to the Empedoclean concept of Philia (Love/Attraction) as a cosmic force of unification</note> which is said to exist in the universe—not, however, the kind that appears in this visible world.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> We are able, moreover, by using intellectual examples, to know what the Intellect is like: how it exists as a sort of unity, yet is not void of diversity. One may take as an example the "reason-principle" of a plant or an animal. For if the principle were just one thing without any variety, it would not even be a rational principle. Again, what comes from it would be mere matter, unless this principle—which is not a simple unity—falls upon the matter, <margin>B</margin> and allows no part of that matter to remain the same as the rest. A face, for instance, is not just a single lump; it has nostrils and eyes. And the nostrils themselves are not just one thing, but have further distinctions, if they are to be nostrils. Indeed, if a nose were just one solid thing, it would be nothing but a mass. This is exactly how the Mind works regarding infinite things: it is itself, and everything in it is, both one and many. The Intellect is not one and many like a house is, but like <margin>C</margin> a reason-principle containing a great many things. Within one mental "shape," as if within a single outline, you have outlines and boundaries within, and internal configurations, powers, and thoughts. It has a distinction that does not extend outward, but is always folded toward the interior. It is as if in a "Total Animal" the natures of huge animals are included, and again others derived from them down to smaller animals and lesser powers, until <margin>D</margin> they finally stop at an indivisible species. Yet no distinction of things there is confused or broken, however much they have moved together into a wonderful unity. Now, this "moving together" is that very "Friendship" which is said to exist in the universe—though not the kind seen in this world.

---

->*It has forged a concord from things that are both standing and discordant. But true Friendship is that by which all things are one, to such a degree that they are never separated from one another. For in this worldly age, things are claimed to be separated or distant.*<-

### *Since the First Intellect is the First Life, only the Intellectual life is true life. Chapter XV.*

The first essence <term>Essentia: Being or Reality</term>, having been turned toward the Good itself through a vital act, becomes "good-formed" <note>original: "boniformis"; shaped by or sharing the nature of the Good</note> and, on account of its own form, becomes multi-formed. It divides the one Good into many forms and derives them into itself, evidently by the power of God. You might imagine these as infinite, glowing "faces" <note>original: "vultus"; the Greek "prosopa" implies both faces and personas or aspects</note> looking at the First, varied among themselves and woven together in an orderly way into a sphere, exceedingly shining and alive. If you then understand that this act—conformed to these various faces and forms—is reflected back as if in a circle, with all spatial distance removed, you will soon understand the First Intellect. You will see it especially if you first become such a being yourself, and then look within yourself.

<summary>Plotinus explains how the Divine Intellect contains multiplicity through the analogy of biological organs (like the nose) that require internal complexity to function, concluding that true unity is a "Friendship" where distinct forms exist without separation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus's exploration of the Divine Intellect (Nous). He argues that the Intellect is "boniform"—shaped by the Good—and that we must eventually look beyond even this sublime beauty toward its source.</meta>

# PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.
<meta>Catchword: the</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
**I**f anyone, therefore, should gaze upon this very life—manifold, universal, primary, and one—he would rejoice in it beyond all estimation, utterly despising every other kind of life. For those other, inferior lives are but shadows: lives that are meager, dark, base, and impure, contaminating the pure lives. As soon as you look toward these lower lives, you no longer see the pure ones, nor do you live according to all of them at once—those in which there is nothing that does not live, and live purely, admitting no evil.

<margin>B</margin>
For evils reign only here <note>meaning in the material, sensible world</note>, since here there is merely a trace of life. Here, there is nothing of the mind but a vestige; however, in that higher realm flourishes the principal exemplar, which Plato calls "boniform" <term>Boniform: "agathoiedes" in Greek, meaning having the shape or character of the Good</term>, because it possesses the Good within its species—that is, its forms. The Good itself is certainly one thing, but here is the "good" one <note>the Intellect</note> who possesses life through contemplation. He contemplates "boniform" spectacles, which he prepared for himself at the very moment he first contemplated the nature of the Good itself.

<margin>C</margin>
The Good itself flowed into the mind, not exactly as it existed there, but as the mind was able to receive it. For that source is the Principle itself, and in this mind, the "good" is derived from it; the mind, as the producer of all these forms, holds this office by virtue of the Principle. For it was not permitted for the mind, while gazing upon the Principle, to understand nothing; nor, on the other hand, was it permitted to behold those spectacles within the Principle itself—otherwise, the mind would not have generated the spectacles itself. Therefore, it received the power to give birth from the Principle, through which it is fully filled with its own offspring. That is to say, the Principle bestowed what it did not possess within itself in a diminished way <note>The One "bestows" multiplicity by being the source of power, though the One itself is simple and lacks the division of the Intellect</note>.

<margin>D</margin>
But from that absolute One, many things fell to this mind. Specifically, since the mind could not properly possess the power it received from there in its pure state, it broke that power into fragments. It caused the one to become many, so that it might at least be able to bear the power part by part. Whatever it generated, it generated from the power of the Good, and that which was born is "boniform." The mind itself is good—a varied kind of good constituted from these boniform things.

<margin>E</margin>
Wherefore, if one were to compare the mind to a living, multifaceted sphere, or if one were to imagine a spectacle composed of faces on every side, shining everywhere with living countenances; or perhaps if one were to think of all pure souls running together into the same point, lacking nothing but possessing all things according to their desire; and further, the entire Mind sitting upon their heights so that the whole region shines with splendor—if, I say, one were to imagine the Intellect in this way, he would surely be looking at it as an observer, as if it were something external. But it is worthwhile for our own soul first to become that very Intellect to be beheld, and then to gaze upon itself as the spectacle already formed within.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
**S**o, if someone sees this manifold life, all of it and primarily one, he embraces being within it, holding all other things in contempt. For the other lives below are darkness and small shadows, dim, faded, and impure, defiling the pure lives. And if you look toward them, you no longer see the pure <margin>forms</margin>, nor do you live those lives that are all together, in which there is nothing that does not live, and live purely, having no evil.

<margin>B</margin>
For evils are here because there is only a trace of life and a trace of mind. But there is the archetype; he <note>Plato</note> says it is "boniform" because it holds the good in the forms. For that is the Good itself. He is the "good" one, having life in contemplation. He contemplates the things seen as being boniform, which he acquired for himself then, when he was contemplating the nature of the Good. It came into him, not as it was there, but as he himself was able to receive it.

<margin>C</margin>
For that is the principle, and from it come the things here, and it is he who made these from that. For it is not lawful for one looking at that to think nothing, nor again to think the things in that <note>the One</note>. Otherwise, he himself would not have generated them. Nor did he have the naked power from that, but it * filled him with offspring, through that One, <margin>* it</margin> things which he himself did not have; rather, from the One they became many, which he received in power, but being unable to hold them <margin>* he shattered</margin> * he shattered them, and made the one into many,

<margin>D</margin>
so that in this way he might be able to bear it part by part. Since, therefore, he was generating good things from power, he was boniform, and he himself was boniform, a kind of variegated good. Therefore, even if someone were to liken him to a variegated living sphere, or if someone should conceive of a thing with many faces, shining with living faces, or if one should imagine all the pure souls running together into the same place, not lacking, but everywhere having their own things, and the whole mind established upon them.

<margin>E</margin>
* so that the place is illuminated as if by an intellectual light. <margin>* some say</margin> Imagining it in this way, being somehow outside it, he sees it as another. But it is necessary <margin>* as a light</margin> for him to become that thing himself and make the vision his own.

> *The primary essence, when it first exists, is turned toward itself from the Good itself, not so much in an intellectual manner as by a vital instinct: just as a plant turns toward the Sun or toward moisture: for this act precedes the other in a certain order. Chapter XVI.*
>
> *But when, directed toward the Good, it is filled there by a certain ray that is equally shining and heating, it immediately conceives within itself all the forms of things—which it perceives as colors—and having been reflected back into its own concepts, it emerges as the Intellect. Finally, just as the sun produces both sight and colors, and joins them to each other, yet is neither sight nor color himself but superior to both; so the Good creates both the Intellect and the things to be understood, and joins them mutually, while remaining more eminent than both.*
