<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the Intellect's relationship to the Good. Plotinus (and his translator Ficino) is moving from describing the "manifold life" of the Intellect to explaining how that life is "filled" and "formed" by looking back toward its source, the One.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN.

<note>original: "LIBER SEPTIMVS"</note>

The Good <note>original: "τὸ ἀγαθὸν"</note>, but marveled at how things were generated from that source. How he did not see each thing individually, but they were situated there, and the ideas were like a mold, being "good-form" <term>Good-form: "agathoiedes," meaning having the quality or shape of the Good</term>, not being the thing that presides over all, yet possessing all. Thus, he holds power over all, and also possesses the living being, for every movement of life belongs to each. Perhaps they are not different things, but insofar as they are good, we are able—what then would this be regarding the investigation of life? It could not be by chance. We proceed from that source; was it because he looked toward the Good that he conceived of the many? It is that source; unless he himself often held himself, living by it, has he not fully traversed the act of thinking within himself? But how was he looking at that source? He looked at all things, or did he have a vision for himself 
<margin>that which is <unclear>not</unclear> he himself <unclear>as if</unclear></margin>
at any time? Rather, he lived toward it and was suspended from it, and was turned toward it. This movement itself, having filled the arena and surrounding that source, fulfilled him. And it was no longer just a movement, but a movement satisfied and full; and thereafter all things were generated, and he knew them by all of them coming together, as they already were. Having been filled, he will see how he possesses them, seeing them himself with light from the one who gave them, and he himself receiving them. Because of this, he is not only said to belong to essence, but also to be the object of desire for him. Thus, he is like that source. For just as the sun is the cause of sensible things to the sight, and the cause of their coming-to-be, he himself is how the vision exists—having heard that vision comes from what is generated—so the Good is the nature of the cause and of the intellectual light. This is a sufficient account of what that source is to the desiring part, for through love all being is asleep, yet he is the cause of these things. He might provide light to himself, into beings and into the mind, for those who are filled; we do not know, but having been filled, how could he not unfold it? He saw there, and that light was already for him, having been filled; but in another way, you receive it as if the filling was from outside—just as what is it that is being filled?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <unclear>If</unclear> he has let go of that which should be let go: he should not only marvel at this, but rather, transcending it, marvel at that source—who the father of that Intellect is, and by what means he begat it. Everything, therefore, existing there is a certain species <note>meaning a Platonic Form or Idea</note> and, as it were, a definite figure. And since that "good-form" quality shines forth everywhere in all things because of something they share in common, it possesses all "good-form" things. It holds, therefore, both being in all things and holds the living being in each one.
<margin>B</margin> It holds a common life flowed into all; it holds perhaps other things as well. But what is that thing because of which they are primarily good, insofar as they are judged to be good? For this contemplation, it will perhaps be most useful to begin from the origin. Did he <note>the Intellect</note> then, when he looked upon the Good, understand that One as if it were many? And since the intellect itself existed as a single being, did it understand that source as many, perceiving it partially within itself because it was unable to understand the whole at once?
<margin>C</margin> But it was not yet "Intellect" while it first looked up at that source. Yet, did it look toward it without intellect? Truly, it must be thought that it had not yet even "seen" it. For it lived toward it, and hung entirely from it, being totally turned toward it. This movement, then, was fulfilled when it was first carried there and was intimately occupied around that source; it filled the Intellect, and its being existed as movement alone at first, but soon became sated and full. Soon, then, Being itself was finally produced, and it recognized that Being by loving it; and for that reason,
<margin>D</margin> it then emerged as Intellect. It was imbued so that it might possess what it could look back upon, being itself such a thing by a certain light received from that same source from which it received all other things. Wherefore, that supreme God <note>The One</note> is handed down as being not only the cause of essences, but the cause of essence appearing to be seen. For just as the Sun is the cause for things which are sensed, both that they exist and that they may be seen—though he is by no means the cause of the vision itself, since among those things he himself is neither the vision
<margin>E</margin> nor the things which are seen—so also the nature of the Good itself is undoubtedly the cause of essence and of the mind. There is also a light in a certain proportion <note>original: "analogia"</note>, by which these visible things and the essence of sight relate to that intellectual essence. It is not that Being, nor is it the Intellect, but the cause of both; and it provides to the mind the understanding of things by its own light, which is diffused above the mind and the mind's reach. Having been filled, the world was then made; but when it was being made, it was simultaneously perfected, and it saw. Its beginning existed as that which precedes its filling. But its other principle is, as it were, external—that which filled it, by which it was formed while it was being filled.

---

->Whatever things exist, from the moment they are and as long as they are, they naturally act toward the Good: from which we argue that the primary essence naturally acts toward the primary Good. Therefore, the Good itself is superior to essence and its act, and to life and intellect. It is not, therefore, properly to be said to "be," to "live," to "act," or to "understand." Chapter XVII.<-

Nor should it be thought that Being properly possesses the forms within itself which it grants to the intellect, just as unity is not "full" of numbers, nor is a point full of dimensions, nor does the light dwelling in the center of the Sun possess within itself those specific rays which, by its power, are emitted ininnumerably from the sun's circumference, ending in an angle from the sphere. Furthermore, the light poured out abroad is full of such rays, sustaining those specific qualities of things which it generates among us through various strikes of the rays. If neither the mind, though it is "all-form" <note>containing all forms</note> in itself, possesses those material forms which it procreates. Now indeed, the primary life arises as a certain indeterminate and unformed act of essence: which certainly turns back toward God himself within the ideal boundaries here—certainly very many of them—on account of its condition being now subject to number and close to precision. At that same moment, life becomes absolute, at the point where it emerges from the intellect. Finally, just as the intellect relates to the soul, so the Good relates to the intellect. For which reason, just as the intellect forms reason in the soul, and is itself separate from rational discourse, so the Good imprints species upon the intellect, yet is ineffably segregated from those species.

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEAD VI.

A
BUT in what way are these things understood, and how does the Intellect itself exist, when they were not in the one who fills <note>The "one who fills" refers to the One or the Good, the ultimate source in Neoplatonism.</note>, nor were they previously in the one being filled? For when the Intellect was not yet imbued with these things, it certainly did not possess them. But perhaps it is not necessary for a giver to possess in himself the exact thing he bestows; rather, in matters of this kind, one must consider the giver to be "greater" and the gift to be "lesser" than the giver.
B
For such is the nature of generation in the order of beings. First, it is necessary that what exists in **actuality** <term>Actuality (Latin: *actu*; Greek: *energeia*): The state of being fully realized or active, as opposed to mere potential.</term> must come first; whereas subsequent things exist in **potential** <term>Potential (Latin: *potentia*; Greek: *dynamis*): The capacity to become something or to act, which is realized by a higher principle.</term> relative to the higher things. Now, that which is first is superior to those things that follow it. And the giver, by the very nature of the gift bestowed, is superior, for he is more excellent. If, therefore, something is prior in actuality, it is superior in actuality. For this reason, **Life** is also superior. If, then, life exists in this [Intellect], certainly the one who gave it, though he bestowed life, is himself judged to be better and more honorable than life. Therefore, he possessed life but did not require a benefactor to give it to him; and life itself appeared as a certain "trace" <note>original: "vestigium," representing the Greek "ichnos" (ἴχνος), meaning a footprint or faint impression of a higher reality.</note> of the giver, though it was not the life of that giver himself.
C
Certainly, when this life first looked toward its giver, it was still indefinite <note>original: "indefinita"</note>; but after it looked there, it was immediately determined by that one who has no limit. For as soon as it gazes toward a single thing, it is defined by that very act, and it brings back within itself a limit, a boundary, and a **form** <term>Form (Latin: *species*; Greek: *eidos*): The essential nature or "look" of a thing that makes it what it is.</term>. This form lies within the thing that has been shaped; however, the shaper is entirely without form.
D
Nevertheless, that limit was not applied there as if it were added from the outside—in the way a boundary is usually placed around a physical object—but rather it was the limit of that entire life, which was manifold and infinite, having already flowed out from such a nature. And yet it was indeed life, though not yet "this" specific life; otherwise, it would have already been determined as if it were a distinct individual; and yet, it was determined.
E
It was therefore determined as the unity of a certain "many"; and each of the many is also determined. On account of the manifold condition of life, many things were determined; and again, on account of the limit itself, they are also "one." What, then, is this "one" that is determined? Truly, it is the **Intellect**. For life, once it has been defined, is the Intellect. And why is it said to be "many" once determined? Because it is, clearly, a "many" of intellects. All things, therefore, are Intellect; and this is the "Universal Intellect," while these others are individual intellects.
F
But does the Universal Intellect, encompassing each individual, contain them as if they were all the same? Not at all; otherwise, it would contain only a single thing. If, therefore, there are many, they must be different; and so we must ask again how each one differs. Perhaps each one perceives its difference in the very fact that it was made "one." For the whole and the individual intellect are not the same. Thus, Life there is all potential, but the vision which flashes from there is the potential of all things. The Intellect that is born there appears as all things themselves. Finally, another principle sits within them, not to be established *in* them, but to establish the form of the primary forms, while remaining far removed from form itself. And this is roughly how the Intellect relates to the **Soul**: it is like a light infused into it, just as the One relates to the Intellect. For when the Intellect defines the soul, it makes it **rational**, exhibiting a trace of the things the Intellect itself possesses. Therefore, the Intellect is also a trace of that higher One. Since the Intellect is a form brought forth in a certain difference and consisting of a multitude, it rightly exists outside of form and species, for it forms the rest into species. But if that one [the One] were a species—

<column-break/>

A But how do these things exist in him and he himself, when they are not there in the one who filled, nor again in the one being filled? Since that which he had was not yet filling—or is it not necessary that everyone who gives must have the mold? <margin>The giver</margin> But in the case of makers, one should consider the giver to be more, and the thing given to be less than the giver. For such is the generation among beings: the first is always in actuality, while the later things are in potential <margin>second</margin> B from them. The first is beyond the things given, and the thing given is that through which it is beyond the things after it. Being is entirely of a certain first actuality. And there are actualities, and that which is beyond life; let life be in him, he through whom he gave life, but he is more beautiful and more honorable than life. He had life, therefore, and from the non-manifold <note>The "non-manifold" (non-poikilos) refers to the absolute simplicity of the One.</note> comes the gift, a mold of life, a certain trace of that one, but not the life of that one.
C Therefore, looking toward that source, it was indefinite. But having looked there, it was defined, though that source has no limit. For seeing toward that source, it is defined in this way. And in itself it has and contains both ideas and the form that is honored. In the light, but that which formed it was formless. And the limit was not placed around it from the outside like a physical size, but it was the whole vision of that life, a life great and infinite, as if shining out from such a nature; a certain life is these things. Defined D as an individual already. But just as if the whole sea, having broken into many parts, each of the many was defined. Because of the multiplicity of life, the whole appeared as many. But because of the limit itself, it is one. Life was defined and limited; that which is a "certain thing" or the "many" are many intellects. And thus every intellect and <margin>of all</margin> each is all. And the individual ones, and the whole, as it contains each. Are they then the same, each being contained? If then they are many, there must be a E difference. Again, therefore, he asks to have a difference, which the whole has and how it becomes as a whole, or in the difference. For it is either the same substance <note>original: "homoousion" (ὁμοούσιον)</note>, or the whole, or not. On the one hand, life is all power. But the vision from there is the power of all things; but the intellect having become, all those things appeared, nor does something sit upon them, not so that it may be established, but so that it may establish form, of the first forms, a manifestation <margin>manifestation</margin> of himself. F And the intellect relates to the soul, as a light into it, as that one [the One] relates to the intellect. And when it defines the soul from the outside, it makes it rational. But that which the soul itself has, it holds as a trace. Therefore, it is a trace of a certain <margin>itself</margin> power. Since the intellect is form, it was unfolded in departure; that one is formless and without species. For in this way, form—

### Chapter XVIII.

*Each of these is good for this reason: since it is from the Good itself, it possesses within itself something of it—though still ineffable—common to all: just as the movement of the tongue, hand, and feet is similarly called "harmonious" because they obtain a similar order from the same musical principle; but that common nature of the Good is much more interior to the mind than musical order is to the limbs.*

FURTHERMORE, regarding those things in the mind, according to what especially are they "good-form" <note>Latin: "boniformia" — having the form of the Good.</note>? # PLOTINUS' ENNEAD VI.

nothing prevents that in their essence that <margin>A</margin> [Good] exists simultaneously, yet it is permitted to grasp it separately by reason: just as "animal" exists simultaneously in both human and horse, or "heat" in both water and fire. But in the former case, it is like a genus <note>In logic, a genus is a general category—like "animal"—that contains various species.</note>; in the latter, it is as if one thing is primarily such, and the other is secondary. Should we then view life and intellect and the rest as "good" individually, or equivocally <note>original: "aequiuocè" — using the same word for things with different meanings.</note>, or rather as being called "good" by a certain analogy? Does the Good then reside in their essence? Or rather, is each thing "good" as a whole? For <margin>B</margin> they are according to the One Good. How then? Are they like parts? But the Good itself is indivisible. Perhaps each thing is the Good itself in a specific way. For the first activity is the Good; and that which is determined within them exists as a Good: namely, from the Good. And that thing is good precisely because it was made by it: this other thing because it is an ornament from it: yet another because it is a reflection. Here, then, all things are themselves and the same: and nothing is the same as if it proceeded from it regarding <unclear>x</unclear> <margin>C</margin> or small fragments or anything else; finally, all are rightly composed. For in these things, all are said to be similarly well-disposed, where order and number reside in all. But what is common among them? You will perhaps say that in these things, the whole being is in each, so that it is rightly ordered from without, though there is a difference concerning the things which the order governs. But in that higher realm, each thing is also individually good. But why is this so? For we must not simply trust that these things are good merely because they come from the One, and leave it at that. For while they are indeed precious because they are from the One, we must further consider by what specific quality their nature is judged to be good.

> *The Good is defined neither by that which becomes desirable, nor by that which becomes the virtue of each thing. For in the first case, a defect or a habit of vice would follow. And because the "desirable" depends on the "desirer," it remains ambiguous whether a true judgment of the Good is being made. In the second case, it remains to be asked why and how a specific virtue, or virtue itself, is a good.*

## Chapter XIX.

SHOULD we then attribute the judgment of the Good <margin>A</margin> to desire and the soul? And by placing full trust in the soul's affection, shall we decide that whatever is desirable to it is the Good? Shall we never investigate *why* it is desired? While we may explain what each of these things is through demonstrations, shall we leave the definition of the Good itself to appetite? However, many absurdities meet us here. First, the Good would be something relative to another thing. Second, because there are many things that feel desire, and they desire different things. How then shall we judge by the mere affection of the desirer which thing is better? Perhaps we will not even recognize the "better" if we are ignorant of the "Good" itself. But is the Good perhaps that state which accords with the virtue of each thing? In that way, we would certainly reduce it to a form and a rational principle—which is a step in the right direction. But once we have arrived there, what shall we answer when it is asked: by what reason are these things themselves good? <margin>C</margin> In lower things, it seems, we might easily recognize such a nature, even if it were not perfectly disposed. But in the higher realm, we cannot judge the primary Good by comparison to lower things. Where nothing is evil, and the things themselves exist as "the better" within themselves, we will be entangled in doubts. Should we then—

—those things which are in their essence <margin>A</margin>, it is nonetheless necessary to grasp the distinction in reason, just as with "animal" in man and horse, or "heat" in fire; and in fire one part is the genus, another is fire primarily, and another is fire in the highest degree. Is each called good for each thing, or again does the Good reside in their creation? Or is there a good for each because of the One Good? How then? Is the Good a part of it, <margin>B</margin> or rather this? Look at it this way: for the first activity is the Good, and the forms upon it are kinds of the Good, and some body? Just as one thing is so because it was generated by it, and another because it is the world <note>original: "κόσμος" — cosmos or ordered universe.</note> upon it, and others because they are connected; these things are not impossible. Is it not like the same light, or walking, and other such movements, or parts, or order and rhythm? What then? If anyone <margin>C</margin> should sing of the whole as being well-ordered from without—since there is a difference in the things which order and number govern—this is in all of them. But these things are through all of them. Or is it that because we must trust in that [the One] as worthy? Or should we grant that those things, being from it, are precious, but our discourse must grasp according to what quality they are good?

Why is it desired? Shall we seek what each thing is, and bring forth demonstrations about them, but give the Good over to desire? But many absurdities appear to us. First, that the Good would be one of those things which are relative. Second, that many things desire <margin>B</margin> different things. How could we speak for the one desiring, if we are ignorant of the Good? But shall we look toward the Good according to the virtue of each? But in this way, we shall lead it back to form and reason, proceeding correctly. But having come there, we shall seek concerning these things themselves: how are they good? If we look toward the lowest things, we might think we have it; <margin>C</margin> but if we look at the primary things, by comparison with the worse? Since nothing there is evil, but the things themselves are the better in themselves, we shall be at a loss. Should we then—

# BOOK SEVEN.

<margin>It appears <note>original Greek: Φαίνεται</note></margin>
<margin>not at all <note>original Greek: ού μή</note></margin>
Since the present reasoning investigates the "why" <note>original: "propter quid," referring to the Aristotelian "final cause" or purpose of a thing.</note> of things, and these things are good in themselves, why does it doubt? Indeed, in that higher realm, the "why" something is said to be is identical to its "whatness" <note>original: "quid est," or essence.</note>. Even if we propose God himself as the cause of these things, as long as our reason has not yet reached that height, the same ambiguity remains. We must, therefore, attempt to pull back our step and see if some clearer path might manifest itself as we travel a different way.

> *For those seeking what the Good itself is, the Intellect <term>Intellect: (Greek: Nous) In Plotinus's thought, the second highest reality, representing the realm of perfect thought and Forms.</term> presents itself clearly to us as a good thing. Through the Intellect, we truly judge between good and evil; from it, the order, species, and life of all things proceed. Even the "fullness of life" that the soul desires is found in the Intellect. However, the Intellect is not the Good itself. Not all things desire the Intellect, yet all things desire the Good. Souls desire the Good before and more frequently than they desire understanding; they do not find their final rest in understanding, but in the Good. They desire to be, to live, and to act—not merely for the sake of being or thinking, but for the sake of the Good. Therefore, the Good is distinct from and superior to all these things.*

---

->Chapter XX.<-

<margin>we were placing <note>original Greek: ετιθέμεθα</note></margin>
<margin>we shall place <note>original Greek: θησόμεθα</note></margin>
<margin>preference <note>original Greek: η προτίμησις</note></margin>
Since we currently distrust our initial impressions regarding what and of what quality each divine thing is, perhaps it is worthwhile to arrive at a different judgment by looking at the oppositions found in things. Consider order versus the absence of order: the balanced versus the uncomposed, health versus sickness, form versus formlessness, essence versus corruption, and stability versus that which vanishes. Who would doubt that the first members of each of these pairs <note>The author refers to the "Table of Opposites," a common Greek philosophical tool where positive traits are aligned in one column and negative in another.</note> are counted within the "species of the good"? If this is so, it is necessary to count the productive causes of these things—such as virtue, intellect, life, and the wise soul—as belonging to the rank of the good. Thus, we also place there those things which a wise life desires.

Why then, one might ask, should we not stop at the level of the Mind and assert that the Mind is the Good? After all, the soul and life are but traces of the Mind. The soul affects the Mind, judges according to it, and in judging, brings itself toward the Mind. It judges that justice is better than injustice and prefers every form of virtue over every form of vice, striving to honor that which it judges most worthy of choice. But whether the soul desires the Intellect alone requires much discussion. We must demonstrate that the Intellect is not the supreme and ultimate end: for not all things desire the Intellect, yet all things desire the Good.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, among those things that lack intellect, not all of them seek to possess a mind; yet those that do possess a mind do not yet rest there, but still strive for a Good that lies further beyond. Finally, the Intellect is sought through a certain "discourse of reason" <note>The logical process of the mind moving from one thought to another.</note>, but the Good is desired even before reason begins. If things desire life, eternal existence, and activity, this is not sought specifically because it is "intellectual," but because it is "good." Life depends upon the Good and is referred back to it; for life is only desirable insofar as it is good.

> *Life, intelligence, and forms are "good-like" and desirable because life is an activity centered on the Good, intelligence is an activity already defined by the Good, and form is the very limit or boundary impressed by the Good. All these things possess a twin light from the Good itself. One light is made specific to each thing as it is born, like a color; the other is a common light that shines upon all things as if from above, glowing more graciously in some places than others. By the first light, things are made good and are sought gently; by the second, they are made "better" and are loved openly and ardently.*

# PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS. BOOK VI.

<column>
<margin>A</margin>WHAT THEN is this one and the same thing existing in all these that makes each thing good? Let us therefore dare to assert that there is indeed an Intellect <term>Intellect: In Neoplatonism, the "Nous" or the second highest reality, containing the eternal Blueprints or Forms of all things.</term>, and that life is undoubtedly "good-like" <note>original: "boniformem," meaning having the form or quality of the Good.</note>. We must say that these things are sought because they are good-like. I say they are good-like because life is an activity of the Good itself—indeed, an activity depending on the Good—while the Intellect is that activity already defined and shaped. These things are surrounded by a certain splendor poured down from above, and the soul pursues them for this reason: because they originate from there. The soul is affected by them again as if by its own proper things, yet not as if they were the perfect Good itself. <margin>B</margin> Although they are good-like, they should not be pursued for that reason alone. For what is familiar and one's own, unless it be good, is indeed "one's own," yet a person might sometimes flee from it. Truly, other things that are far distant and even inwardly polished sometimes draw the appetite to themselves. But a vehement love is incited toward these things not when they exist only as what they are, but when, while being what they are, they receive something else from on high. <margin>C</margin> For just as in bodies a light is naturally mixed within, yet another light is needed so that their color may appear, so that they may be distinguished both from themselves and from any other.

---

## Without the marvelous grace of the first good, no things love nor are loved. Chapter XXII.

*Because an ineffable love of the beautiful seizes us, it is neither matter nor proportion, but a certain vivid glow reflecting from the soul within that proportion. Again, when we are captured by an ardent benevolence for the souls we contemplate, and their virtues and duties, it is a certain intellectual splendor sparkling from the divine Intellect. Finally, while the Intellect contemplates intelligible things, it inflames us with a certain new love; this is a ray flashing from the first Good, on one hand inflaming and exciting the will, and on the other hand bestowing a marvelous grace upon those things we encounter in contemplation. Since all things depend on this by degrees, it follows that even in the senses and bodies, without the specific influx of the first Good, nothing would ever shine with a lovable grace, nor would love be kindled.*

<margin>A</margin>WHENEVER the soul beholds this light, it is stirred toward the divine things surrounded by this light, and encountering the light shining forth in them, it greatly rejoices. Just as those who seem to love these physical bodies do not love the underlying matter itself, but the beauty clearly shining forth in the bodies. For each thing exists as what it is in itself; but it becomes desirable when the Good itself, as it were, colors it, providing <margin>B</margin> grace to the things themselves and infusing love into those who seek them. Now, when the soul has received the influx from there, it is moved; it is filled with a Bacchic frenzy <note>original: "debacchatur," referring to the ecstatic, divine madness of the followers of Bacchus/Dionysus.</note> and incited by stings; and thus love flows into it. Before this, the soul is not even moved toward the Intellect, however beautiful it may be; for the beauty of the Intellect is dormant until it receives the light of the Good. The soul itself falls back on its own, lying flat and sluggish toward everything; even in the presence of the Intellect, it seems to drowse. But after the heat from there has kindled it, the soul is immediately strengthened <margin>C</margin> and awakened, and it is supported by other wings. And while it is vehemently affected toward that which is nearest, it is meanwhile lifted up toward something more excellent by a certain remembrance. And as long as something remains above it, the soul is raised upward by that present higher nature.
</column>

<column>
<margin>A</margin>What then is it in all these that makes each thing good? This much must be dared: either everything in its genus, and that life which we said was good-like, is so because of these things, insofar as they are good-like. I say they are good by that which is gathered after the movement—or rather, from its own activity. And that activity is already defined. It is accompanied by radiance, and the soul pursues it <margin>B</margin> because it comes from there, or toward those things again as being of the same kin; but they are not the Good itself, but good-like. By this they are to be reached. For what is one's own, if it be not good, is indeed one's own, but one would flee from it. Since other things being far off and below would cause a movement. And the love toward them is of a certain kind. It is not when they are merely what they are, but when they are adorned through lack of experience, and take on something else. Just as light is mixed upon bodies, yet they need another light <margin>C</margin> so that the color in them may appear as light. Thus it is with the things there, even though they have much light. They need another and new light for them to be seen either by themselves or by another.
<insert>infused, that is, a light naturally implanted; so also in celestial things, although they have very much light, they have need of a certain more excellent light, so that they may be distinguished both from themselves and from any other.</insert>

<margin>A</margin>Whenever the soul sees that light, then indeed it is moved toward those things, longing for the light that comes upon them and appears on them; just as with bodies here, love is not for the underlying subject, but for the beauty manifested upon them. Since each thing is what it is, it becomes desirable only when the Good gives them color, as it were, giving them graces and putting love into those who desire them. For when the soul receives <margin>B</margin> an outflow from there into itself, it is moved. It is driven into a frenzy and filled with a sting, and becomes love. But before this, it is not moved even toward the Intellect, although it is beautiful. For its beauty was idle until it received the light of the Good, and the soul falls back by itself, and always remains sluggish toward everything. Even when the Intellect is present, the soul is drowsy toward it, until a certain warmth <margin>C</margin> from there is sprinkled into it. Then it awakens and is thus carried, and although it is fixed upon what is adjacent or near, it is nonetheless lifted up toward another thing as if by a memory. As long as there is anything higher than what is present, it is raised upward by nature.

# BOOK SEVEN.

<column>

<margin>the beloved</margin>
A The beloved is that which provides the love. And the mind transcends or is able to seek the Good it sees. <margin>It is intelligible and exists alone</margin> in its underlying subject; as long as it remains upon it, things are beautiful and solemn, but they decrease when one seeks the grace that boils over upon the beauty. Therefore, things are beautiful, but they are not yet the vision, nor that which is longed for, if the grace does not boil over upon the beauty. Therefore, even here, beauty appears more as that which shines upon the symmetry <note>original: "συμμετρίᾳ," referring to the mathematical proportion of parts</note> than as the symmetry itself, and this is what is truly lovable.

B For why is it that in a living face there is more of the beautiful light, while in a corpse there is but a passive trace? And after the face, in the flesh and the divided symmetries, why are the more lifelike statues more beautiful, even if others are more perfectly symmetrical? Or is it that a living person, even if less than ideal, is more beautiful than what is in a beautiful statue? Is it because that which is sought after belongs more to the soul, or because it is more "good-like"? This is the light from the Good itself, coloring it, awakening it, and lifting it up; for everything that is good-like is itself light and awakens the soul.

---

A THERE indeed the soul follows. And where it provides light and has turned toward it, it moves that trace. But why wonder at what power it has, drawing the soul to itself and calling it back from every wandering, so that it may rest within itself? If all things come from that source, and it is better than them, and all things are lesser than it, then what is the best of all beings, and how is it "the Good"? It concerns the nature of the Good to reshape or to be itself, and to be without need—

B <margin>virtues</margin> but not possessing all things, so that it might be different or the same in its seasons. Or is it toward another virtue, or was there not yet any vice? But the evils come later, in which one might not partake even in one of these, or in the furthest things, or in that which is beyond evils toward the worse; then evils would be contrary to it. Or do they not have a middle ground for opposition? But that which is not good belongs to the same realm as the wholly good things. If someone should say it does not exist, or that evil always was, then things would be indifferent toward choice by nature: but this is impossible. Rather, they say these things are "good" toward this end, but that thing is nothing in itself. This I make credible to those who listen.

<column-break/>

A ...it is raised up by him who infused the love: and it indeed transcends the intellect <term>Intellect: The realm of pure thought and eternal forms, one step below the absolute Good.</term>, yet it cannot go beyond the Good: since nothing can be higher than the Good. But if it fixes its gaze upon the mind, it perceives things that are beautiful and venerable; yet it does not yet possess entirely what it seeks. For it is as if it approaches a beautiful face, yet one that does not yet seize the sight for itself: because it still lacks that pleasing grace <note>original: "gratia," translating the Greek "charis," meaning a divine radiance or charm</note> which is accustomed to allure by shining out within beauty.

B Wherefore, even here, we must consider beauty to be that very thing which shines out in proportion <note>original: "proportione," the harmonious arrangement of parts</note>, rather than the proportion itself: and that this is properly what is lovable. For why does the splendor of beauty appear more in the face of a living person, while in the face of a dead one—even if the features are not yet changed—hardly a trace of beauty remains? Why again, among statues, do those which seem more lifelike also appear more beautiful, even though others might be composed with more exact measurements?

C Why does the form of a living person, even if it is less balanced, appear more beautiful than any beauty of a statue? Perhaps because this is truly more to be desired: that it possesses a soul. And again, because this soul is marked by a certain light of the Good itself; from there, being colored, it is immediately awakened, and as if made lighter, it is raised higher, and it renders and excites whatever good it has and is able to grasp.

### The first principle of things is the same as the Good itself. Chapter XXIII.

> *For nothing is better than the Good itself: nothing is likewise better than the first principle of things. Likewise, the Good is sufficient unto itself and is the most truly "being": for it alone can be self-sufficient. Furthermore, evil recedes from the principle through discord, but it shall be joined to the good through approach: since it is guided by it, even evil itself; but the first principle is likewise the Good itself. Finally, since all things desire the Good and profit by participation in it, it is plainly evident that all these things exist and are preserved, are helped by its virtue, and perform whatever they do rightly and naturally.*

A NOR truly should anyone wonder that this which the soul follows, which infuses light into the mind, and whose trace here and there excites us, has such great power; for it draws the soul and the mind toward itself, and recalls them from error everywhere, so that they may finally find rest in its presence. For if that from which all things come allows nothing to be better than itself, and all things are less good, it follows that the best of all things is the Good itself. Furthermore, if it is necessary

B that the nature of the Good be self-sufficient and in need of nothing: what other nature could one find to be more so than this which exists before all other things, when evil does not yet exist? But if evils come later, in these things which participate in nothing of the divine gifts and are the lowest, then there is no evil among the higher beings, nor is there anything worse than evil itself, just as there is nothing better than the Good itself.

C Surely evils stand in a contrary manner to the first principle: having no middle ground for their opposition. Therefore, the Good is precisely this. For either there is no Good at all, or if it is necessary for the Good to exist, it will be this and no other. But if anyone should object that there is no Good at all, he will be forced to admit that there is likewise no evil: from which it would follow that all things are indifferent to choice according to nature; but that is impossible. But other things which are called "good" are referred back to the first principle, while the first principle is referred to nothing else. Since therefore the Good is such, what does it do?

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "Good" (the One). While the previous page focused on the "grace" or "light" that makes things beautiful, this page investigates whether the Good is defined merely by our desire for it, or if it has an intrinsic nature of its own. It also establishes the hierarchy of how the Good "informs" different levels of reality—from matter up to the Intellect.</meta>

### PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

Indeed, it <note>Plotinus is referring to "The Good" or "The One," the ultimate source of all existence in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note> made the mind, it made life, and from the mind it made souls, and absolutely everything else that participates in reason, intellect, or life. What words, then, could possibly express how great a "Good" this is, which is the fountain and principle of all these things? But what does it do now? Certainly, it now preserves those things it has made. For it brings it about that the powers of understanding are able to understand, and that living things live, by breathing into them intellect, breathing into them life—or at least providing a trace of existence where full life cannot be received.

*That being "desirable" is not so much the nature of the Good itself, as it is a condition resulting from the nature of the Good. It is debated what the nature and essence of the Good actually is, and whether those things that follow the Good bring back pleasure alone or other infused qualities, and by what certain sign we are able to discern that the true Good is present. Chapter 24.*

IT REMAINS for us to inquire what the Good performs most especially toward us. But we shall speak again of the light: what that light is by which the mind is illuminated, and in which the soul also participates. However, it is better for the present to defer this until later, and first investigate whether the "Good" is and is called "good" specifically because it is desirable to another; and whether that which is sought after by one is a good for that one; and whether we should assert that the "Good" itself is that which is sought after by all things. 

Or should someone judge this "desirability" to be merely a sign of the Good, while the nature that justly claims such a title for itself must be something else? Furthermore, we must ask: do those who desire it seek it because they receive something from it, or do they simply rejoice in the Good itself? And if they receive something, what is it? If they only rejoice, why this specifically and not something else? 

Here we must also investigate whether the Good is to be weighed by its own unique properties, or by something else? Then, truly, is the Good entirely for the benefit of another, or is the Good also "good" to itself? Or rather, whenever it is "good," is it perhaps not good to itself, but necessarily good to another? Likewise, what is the nature of the Good in the highest sense? For there is some nature for which nothing is "good." <note>This refers to the lowest form of matter, which lacks the capacity to participate in the Good.</note> 

Nor do I think we should pass over in silence what some stubborn and contentious person might object: "O you virtues! Why do you adorn your cause so gloriously by looking up and down? You call life a good, and the mind a good, even though you place the Good itself above these. Tell me, I pray, in what way is the mind itself a good? What good does it possess while it understands the Forms <note>original: "species," referring to the Platonic Ideas or eternal archetypes</note> and contemplates what each thing is?" 

It might perhaps happen that someone, deceived by the delight of these things, calls them "good"; similarly, one might think life is a good simply because it is sweet to them. If one were perhaps placed in such a state that they felt no pleasure, why would they affirm these things are good? Would they perhaps think it is a good merely because they exist? But what fruit would they perceive from "being" itself? What difference would it make to them to be, or not to be at all, unless one asserts that a certain "friendship" or "love" toward oneself is the cause of these things? It would then follow that the estimation of "goods" was only introduced because of this deception naturally implanted in us and the fear of death.

*The Good is the form for matter, the soul for the body, the intellect for the soul, and the principle of all things for the intellect and all else simultaneously. Chapter 25.*

Form provides action and order to matter as a "good"; the soul provides life and motion to the body; the intellect provides virtue to the soul; and the first principle <note>The One/The Good</note> provides vital and intellectual action to the intellect. Just as the nature of fire is followed by an inestimable light, such that at a distance it illuminates, but as one approaches it also warms; or even as the center of a heavy weight draws and holds things, so the nature of the Good is accompanied by this power: it draws distant things through desire, but holds and delights those things that are present.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s examination of the "Good" (the One). On the previous page, we saw the Good established as the ultimate source of life and mind. Here, Plotinus turns to Plato’s *Philebus* to clarify the relationship between the Good, human intellect, and the experience of pleasure, ultimately mapping out how every level of reality—from raw matter to the highest mind—finds its "good" in the level immediately above it.</meta>

# BOOK SEVEN

<column-break/>

**A** Therefore, Plato, when he mixed pleasure with the final goal <note>In his dialogue *Philebus*, Plato explores whether the "Good Life" consists of pleasure, wisdom, or a mixture of both.</note>, did not place the Good itself as something simple or residing solely in the intellect. As is written in the *Philebus*, perhaps he was hesitant to place the Good entirely in pleasure—and rightly so—but he also did not think that an intellect devoid of pleasure should be considered the Good itself. This is because he did not see the "better" state as being entirely without feeling. **B** Perhaps, however, he did not take it quite so simply; rather, he composed the Good in this way because he judged that the Good, since it has such a nature in itself, must necessarily be delightful and desirable to the one seeking it, and delightful to the one who has attained it. Therefore, if joy is not present, the Good is not present; and if gladness is not at the side of the one who first desires it, then the Good is not there either. Thus, he did not compose the Good in this way without reason. For he was not investigating the *Primary Good* <note>The "Primary Good" refers to the One/God, which is beyond all human experience.</note>, but rather only the *human good*. This human good is entirely dependent on another thing and is itself a "mixed" or "composite" thing, as it is inherently deficient. **C** For this reason, he judges that that which is solitary and alone <note>The One</note> possesses no "good" in a human sense, but exists as the Good through a different, more excellent condition and reason. It is necessary, therefore, for the Good itself to be sought after; yet it does not become "good" because it is desired, but rather it becomes desirable because it is "good."

**D** Or is it that, in the order of things, that which precedes is the Good? And it always works upon the senses in such a way that what is superior is present to the thing following it as its "good"—provided that the **ascent** <margin>the ascent</margin> never departs from proportional analogy but always proceeds toward greater things. But finally, the step stops at that which is supreme, beyond which nothing remains that can be accepted as higher. This is the First and truly Good, the chief and greatest Good, and the cause of goodness for all others. Therefore, the good of **Matter** <term>Matter: In Neoplatonism, the lowest level of reality, which has no form of its own and "hungers" for structure.</term> is **Form**. For if matter could perceive, it would undoubtedly rejoice at the arrival of form. **E** For the **Body**, the good is the **Soul**; for without the soul, the body would neither exist nor be preserved. But for the **Soul**, the good is **Virtue**; and even higher than that is the **Intellect**. Finally, for the **Intellect**, the good is that which we are accustomed to call the **Primary Nature**. Furthermore, we must consider that each of these contributes something to the things for which they are "goods." These lower things provide order and ornament, while the higher provide life, wisdom, and the gift of living well. Finally, the Good itself bestows upon the Intellect the gift which we say comes into the intellect from there, making it "good" because it is a direct touch from that Source. And since even now there is that which is called **Light**—from which the entrance into this state is made—we shall discuss what that light truly is in the following sections.

<column-break/>

*Those things endowed with sensation can have this most powerful sign of the presence of goodness: that they are stably delighted by it, rest most willingly in it, and find themselves in a better state because of it. Chapter 26.*

*Just as regarding things subject to the senses there are these two parts—the inclination toward a natural good and its end, and the rest found in that end—likewise, in the natural world, something else occurs beyond the natural good. For there are certain things that perform acts toward the good, or around the good, or in the good. Thus, in things endowed with sensation, desire and pleasure are something different from the Good itself, nor is pleasure alone sufficient. For it is more desirable to be delighted by the presence of the Good which we desire, than to be similarly delighted without it.*

**A** Then, truly, that which can perceive by nature recognizes what approaches it; if ever the Good approaches, it is able to know it and to say that it possesses it. But what should be said if it happens to be deceived? There must certainly be some similarity <margin>that which comes to it</margin> which... <meta>The text cuts off here, continuing with the catchword "ter" for the next page.</meta>

<summary>Plotinus explains that while Plato's "Philebus" discusses a "mixed" human good of intellect and pleasure, the ultimate Good (the One) is the source of a hierarchy where each level of existence finds its "good" in the level above it. He defines the chain of being: Matter seeks Form, Body seeks Soul, Soul seeks Virtue, and Intellect seeks the Primary Nature/The One.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the nature of the "Good" and how it relates to the desires of the soul. Following a discussion of Plato’s *Philebus* on the previous page, Plotinus here examines why pleasure and "familiarity" are insufficient to define the Good, arguing instead that the Good must be something "superior" or "more excellent" that completes a being’s potential.</meta>

# BOOK SIX

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is deceived. If it were known, that thing would certainly be the "good" to him by which he was also deceived; for when that truth arrives, he departs from that which had deceived him. Indeed, the appetite and the yearning <note>The Latin *stimulus* and Greek *ὠδίς* suggest a sharp pang of desire or even "labor pains," indicating a deep, natural striving.</note> of each thing testify that there is some good for every being. In the case of inanimate things, the gift of the good comes from another; but in that which possesses a soul, the appetite itself pursues its own good. Just as bodies that naturally lack life are cared for and tended to by living beings, <margin>B</margin> so do living things provide for themselves as far as they are able. One can undoubtedly believe that they have attained some good when they find themselves in a better state and are not affected by regret, but are instead filled, remaining in that state and seeking nothing else. For this reason, pleasure is not sufficient in itself; for the one who is affected by pleasure does not always desire the same thing. Even if they are said to desire pleasure itself, they cannot be proven to seek the same thing, for the object that provides the delight is always something else. <margin>C</margin> It is necessary for the good—which one desires above all—to be something other than a mere passion or "affection" <note>The word "affection" or "passion" here refers to a state that happens *to* someone, a passive feeling rather than an essential reality.</note> by which the person who attains it is inwardly moved. If the good were only an affection, the seeker might remain "empty" while merely possessing the feeling, just as if they held the feeling of a good without the good itself. For no one would choose to be so affected without actually having a good, just as one would not choose to rejoice as if they had a son when they do not. Nor do those who desire to fill their bellies choose to be delighted as if they were eating when they are not. Nor do those who indulge in love choose as their good the mere soaking in of pleasure without the presence of the beloved or the act itself, as if they were present and acting.

-> Neither appetite nor pleasure makes a thing good; rather, the nature of the Good itself draws the appetite from a distance and, from up close, soothes it with pleasure. Similarly, a mere "familiarity" is not the reason something is its own good. <-

### Chapter XXVII.

*For not just anything similar or nearby is desirable or healthy for you, nor is simple equality enough. Rather, a certain virtue accompanies the nature of the Good, through which it meets us as something domestic and our own, even though its nature is superior to everything else. Therefore, the Good relates to each thing everywhere, either as a specific **Form** <note>Original: *species* / εἶδος. In this philosophy, "Form" is the perfect design or spiritual essence that makes a thing what it is.</note> relates to a subject, or as the **Principle** of that Form relates to both the Form and the subject.*

<margin>A</margin> BUT what exactly must happen for a being to possess what is suitable to it? We shall say it is a certain "Form." For Form is suitable to **Matter** <note>The raw, shapeless "stuff" of the universe.</note>, and the Form of the soul is virtue. But is this Form "good" simply because it is "one's own" and familiar to that being? Does appetite simply lean toward what is one's own? Perhaps not. For what is "similar" is "one's own"; and if someone wants and possesses something similar and rejoices in it, they do not yet possess the Good. <margin>B</margin> If we grant that it is good, shall we not also grant that it is "one's own"? We must tell both seekers that the judgment of what is "one's own" must be referred to that which is more excellent and better—that toward which a thing has a natural **potential** <note>Original: *in potentia* / δυνάμει. The capacity of a thing to be perfected or transformed into a higher state.</note>. For when a thing has a potential for something else, it is undoubtedly in need of it. That "better thing" which it needs is certainly its "good." **Matter** is the most needy of all things, and for it, the final and nearest Form is its good. <margin>C</margin> Beyond matter, one rises step by step to higher things. If a thing is good to itself, its perfection and its Form are much more its good, as is whatever is superior to it. Such a thing is "good" by its very nature, and it brings good to the thing it touches. But why is it the Good? Is it because it is most "one's own"?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...is deceived. If it were known, that thing would certainly be the "good" to him by which he was also deceived; for when that truth arrives, he departs from that which had deceived him. Indeed, the appetite and the yearning <note>Greek: *ἔφεσις* (appetite/desire) and *ὠδίς* (pang/yearning).</note> of each thing testify that there is some good for every being. In the case of inanimate things, the gift of the good comes from another; but in that which possesses a soul, the appetite itself works through it. Just as for bodies that have become corpses, <margin>* care from living beings</margin> <margin>B</margin> there is the care and burial from living beings, so for living things, there is foresight from themselves. It happens for the better when it is filled and remains in that state, and seeks nothing else. Hence pleasure is not self-sufficient; for the one who loves the feeling does not seek the same thing again, for the object of his pleasure is different. Therefore, the Good must be the most desirable thing for him. <margin>C</margin> And the feeling happens to any person and they remain empty if they think the feeling alone is the good. Therefore, the feeling is referred to that which they do not have—for example, if a child is present to them, or not. Nor do I think those for whom pleasure is the good in being bodily filled would choose the feeling of eating without eating, or the feeling of intimacy without being with the one they wanted, or not acting at all.

<margin>A</margin> BUT what things happening to each being shall we say it knows as having what is suitable? Is it that Form is to Matter, and again Form is to the Soul? But as for the Form, is it good to that being because it is "one's own," and is the appetite toward what is "one's own"? Perhaps it is not the similar that is "one's own." <margin>* <unclear>note</unclear></margin> And if a being has and rejoices in the similar, it does not yet have the Good. But we shall say it is "one's own" because we call it "good," or <margin>B</margin> we must say that "one's own" belongs to the superior and the better, toward which the being has a potential. For what is in potential toward something is in need of it. If it is in need of something better, that thing is its good. But **Matter**, though it is the most needy, finds its nearest Form to be its good. After this, one goes upward, where the thing needed is its <margin>C</margin> good within itself. Much more so is its perfection its good, and its Form, and that which is superior to it, if it is such by nature. It is no longer good only because it makes the thing good. But why is it the Good? Is it because it is most "one's own"?

<summary>Plotinus argues that "goodness" is not defined by mere pleasure or similarity, but by the relationship between a being’s potential and the "superior" form that perfects it. He illustrates this by showing that we desire real objects (like food or loved ones) rather than just the subjective feeling of having them.</summary>

They also begin to explore the difficult relationship between "Matter"—viewed here as a formless void—and the "Good."</meta>

### BOOK SEVEN

...but rather to incline toward the Good. Therefore, one should more likely compare this not to the pure beings themselves as if they were the Good, but to those who are more nearly "good." If there is anything in the intellect that is good, let it be the Good itself, just as a divine thing might equal itself by its very nature; and let it not love itself merely *as* a good, but as directed toward the Good that is "beyond" <note>original: "ἐπέκεινα" (epekeina). This is a technical term in Neoplatonism referring to the One or the Good being "beyond being" or "beyond essence."</note>. But if there is absolutely no other, and the "other" must be compared to it, then let it be good to itself. And for this reason, let it be said to be so, and let the "ascent" <note>The journey of the soul back to its divine source.</note> hold the Good, which is the underlying nature. It is not desire that creates the Good, but rather desire is directed toward the Good. And the thing being known becomes pleasant through its acquisition. But even for one whom pleasure did not affect, the Good would still be chosen and sought for its own sake.

<column-break/>

**A** Indeed not; but since there is a certain lot and portion of the good, the familiarity toward oneself and among others is more proper to those who are sincere and better. Now, it is truly absurd to ask why something, since it is good, should be good to itself—as if it were necessary for a thing to stand apart from its own nature, and not love itself as a good. But in this simple reality, one must investigate: whether, when there is no "one thing and another" <note>i.e., no internal division or duality</note> within it, there exists a certain proper relationship to itself, and thus it is good to itself.

**B** In the present case, if what we have said is correct, and the Good stands as a higher degree within a nature, then it is not the appetite <note>original: "appetitio"; referring to the soul's striving.</note> that makes the good, but the appetite arises rather because the thing is good. Likewise, something happens in those who attain the good—a pleasure that accompanies the very achievement of the good. Truly, even if no pleasure followed, the Good would still have to be chosen and sought for its own sake.

---

*Let us consider "prime matter" <term>Prime Matter: The underlying, formless "stuff" of the universe that has no qualities of its own until "Form" is impressed upon it.</term> as a certain power that is indeed formless, but naturally ready to receive form. In the sense that it is formless, it does not yet exist; nor does it properly desire the good in that state. But in the sense that it is a power prepared for form, it is not evil. And if it can desire in any way, it desires the good—that is, it desires Form—especially out of a certain hidden hatred of its own deformity.*

->Chapter XXVIII<-

*Just as the Good itself is lovable to itself and to all, so if one were to imagine "Evil" itself, it would be lovable neither to others nor to itself. To each thing, its "good" is its own particular species, its form, and its perfection, depending on an "act" <note>In the sense of "actualization" or "reality."</note> from above. But the form of a species is always opposed to the formlessness of matter. Therefore, the more a form is separated from matter, the more it is truly a "Species" and the more it is "Good." The most separate species is the best. However, the "Good itself" is no longer a species at all—it is what the divine calls the Good, the author of both species and goods alike.*

**A** Now, regarding the conclusion following from these arguments, which is evident to everyone: they do not see the "Good" as arriving everywhere. It might seem that the Good is even for "Matter," if it desired the Good for itself, as if Matter were itself the "perfect," though this is only a deceptive appearance. For if it desires the Good in any way, it seeks the whole Good. But perhaps <margin>* not all</margin> *not all* of the matter <margin>* but toward</margin> will seek it, but only that part of it which... <margin>* perhaps according to</margin> *perhaps according to* [its nature]. It allows itself to be dragged down by evil. But what is evil? How does it have a striving toward the Good? The argument suggests that desire is in matter by way of a "supposition" <note>A logical premise rather than a literal fact.</note>. But as for sense-perception, it is as if—through the "sale" of matter—when a form approaches like a "dream of the good," the matter comes to be in a better state, which is why matter "hates" evil, as <margin>* rejection</margin> has been said. But if "wickedness" is something foreign, * could sense-perception take hold of it? Is it that, having received what is its own, it will call it "good"? Or is it not the wickedness that chooses, but that which is being "evil-ed" <note>A literal translation of "κακώμενον," meaning the thing suffering or undergoing evil.</note>? If "to be" and "to be evil" are the same for something, how will it choose the Good? Could sense-perception itself take hold of **D** evil and find it lovable? And how can that which is not lovable be loved? Or shall we not define the Good so randomly? These matters stand as they do. But if you grant that the Good is everywhere, the further things ascend, the more they are "Form"; Soul is more a Form than the body's form, and the [Intellect] is more than the soul...

<column-break/>

**A** We now think it necessary to consider what follows from the previous points. If the "Form" <note>original: "species". Ficino uses "species" to translate the Greek "eidos," meaning the intelligible structure or idea of a thing.</note> that is present everywhere is a "good," and if Form is the good for Matter itself, we must ask: if Matter were to become capable of willing, would it want only to become a Form? But if it willed this, it would want to perish <note>Because if Matter became Form, it would no longer be Matter.</note>. Yet all things desire the Good itself. But perhaps it will not specifically choose to be Matter, but simply "to be"; and having that, it will want to cast off its evil. But how will **B** Evil desire the Good? Truly, we do not attribute "appetite" to matter itself; rather, the requirements of the debate have introduced a certain "supposition," attributing a sense-perception to it, if such a thing could be attributed while preserving the nature of matter. And indeed, when Form arrives, as if in a "dream of the good," it causes the matter to be placed in a better order. If, therefore, matter is evil, how the matter stands has already been said. But if there is something else that is—so to speak—"wickedness" itself, and its very being **C** perceives itself, would it still find the Good to be proper and familiar to it? Certainly, it was not "wickedness" itself that was choosing the Good, but rather that which *possessed* evil within it. But if, in that case, "to be" is the same as "to be evil," in what way will it seek the good? Or perhaps it could seem that if Evil perceived itself, it would love itself? But truly, **D** how can that which is unlovable be loved? For we do not believe that the definition of the "Good" should be placed in that which is merely "one's own" or "domestic." And let this be said regarding these things for now.

*But if Form everywhere is the Good itself, and by always ascending higher, Form is more frequently encountered; for the Soul is more of a Form than the form of a body. And in the Soul, Form is even more...*

They explore the paradox of Matter—a formless "evil"—which "dreams" of the Good and seeks Form even though becoming Form would mean its own disappearance as Matter.</summary>

...even more: and finally, the intellect is more of a form <term>species; the Greek *eidos*, referring to the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing</term> than the soul is. Certainly, the Good itself proceeds by a path that is the very opposite of matter; to the Good belongs that which is purified and far removed from matter. According to the degrees of purity, the greatest Good is suited to each thing, from which whatever can be conceived of as matter is far separated. And the nature of the Good itself, fleeing all matter—approaching it in no way and under no condition—undoubtedly escapes into a nature that is entirely vacant of form, from which the first form arises. ->Whether we are usually moved by a deeper pleasure while we are placed outside a perfect state of body or soul during that restoration, which we achieve once we have reached a perfect state: from which it is clear that pleasure, which is a kind of motion, is not the end and perfection of nature. Certainly, in a natural state and a status of perfect life, that "mobile" or changing pleasure ceases. Once the best tranquility is achieved (if I may call it that), a state of health and a natural disposition exists that is more constant, truer, and more desirable than changing pleasure. On the other hand, for those who believe that nothing is good without pleasure or beyond pleasure, Plotinus’s judgment seems to be this: that sensing, understanding, and similar things are "goods" to be chosen, not solely on the grounds that they happen to be joined with a certain manifest pleasure, but because their opposites are naturally shunned as evils.

<margin>A</margin>
BUT unless pleasure follows the Good, and something occurs before pleasure for the sake of which pleasure is accustomed to accompany it, why would the Good not then be encountered as something grateful and lovable? But when we have said "grateful" and "joyful," we have simultaneously already mentioned pleasure. Yet if the Good exists, and it is possible for it to be not "pleasant" even while existing, what shall we say? But perhaps it is so: that even when the Good is present, he who has a sense for the good might not recognize its presence.

<margin>B</margin>
Perhaps, too, nothing prohibits someone from indeed recognizing the Good, yet not being "moved" in any other way after they possess it. This condition is most suitable for one who is exceedingly temperate and in need of nothing. For this reason, an initial "thrill" <note>original: "exhilaratio" (exhilaration or outward joy)</note> does not suit them—not only because the Good is entirely simple, but because only the act of "attaining" (which belongs to one who was previously lacking) is bathed in pleasure. But these things will finally appear clearly once we have purified all other things and driven out the opposing argument.

<margin>C</margin>
Indeed, here is the man who doubts: what fruit does he receive who possesses the Good in his mind to compare it, perhaps, if he is moved by no affect at all while hearing these things? This is because he perceives these things in no way in reality—whether he hears the name, or imagines something else before him in the Latin tongue <note>original: "linguam latinũ". The translator is noting the difficulty of terminology</note>, or seeks something sensible and places the "good" in riches or other things of that sort.

<margin>D</margin>
Against such a person, therefore, it must be said: when he despises these things, he meanwhile confesses that there is something "good" placed within himself. But when he doubts where it is most powerful and by what reason it is placed there, we must then adapt these arguments to that reason which is innate within him. For it cannot happen that one who is entirely unskilled and ignorant of this very thing should ever say: "this or that cannot be horrible." Perhaps even such a discourse prophesies that the Good itself is above the mind. Furthermore, if looking toward the Good itself or toward what is nearest to it he does not discern it, it is useful at least to conceive of the Good from its opposites. Otherwise, he will not even confess that ignorance is bad—although all men desire to understand, and all glory in their intelligence. ### The goal of the intellectual soul is the unhindered and highest act of understanding, entirely focused on the universal good itself.
### Chapter XXV.

An act of this kind is happiness <term>beatitudo; a state of supreme well-being or "blessedness" achieved through the contemplation of divine things</term>, even if no exterior pleasure is added to it, yet it is not itself devoid of pleasure. For the very unhindered integrity and height of the action is pleasure. Then, indeed, a most simple union exists: for the soul rejoices within itself, having already been formed by the light from above. Truly, just as the height of light is already the heat of a white fire, so the height of being is already life; similarly, the height of living is sense, of sensing is imagination, of imagining is reason, of reasoning is intelligence, of intelligence is joy, and of joy is the good. Indeed, one ascends toward the supreme grade of the universe not through division, but gradually through union. Now, just as the elements, by the same thrust of nature, seek and enjoy what is agreeable to them, so the mind, by the same act, when it is at its highest, proceeds toward the ultimate end as the truth, and enjoys it as the good. But we have disputed more extensively concerning the end, intelligence, and pleasure in our *Commentaries on the Philebus* <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue *Philebus*, which examines the relationship between pleasure and wisdom</note>.

<note>The following sections are presented in two columns: a Greek source fragment on the left and a Latin-to-English translation on the right.</note>

**A** AFTER these things, we must investigate whether it is necessary for pleasure to be mixed with the good; otherwise, life might be imperfect, even if one were to speculate upon divine things and their principle. Reaching toward the good, we ought to investigate with the mind. Now indeed, where Plato seems to oppose the good as coming from the intellect (as a subject) and from a certain affection of the soul which follows intelligence, he certainly asserts there that neither the end nor the good itself is a composite. Rather, in that realm, the intellect itself is the good, and we, on the other hand, rejoice in the possession of this good. **B** And this is one opinion concerning the good. The other opinion or exposition is that which mingles pleasure with the intellect, so that it places something from both as the subject, so that we, by comparing or perceiving such an intellect, already possess the good: for a thing that is deserted and alone could neither come to be, nor, if it could, would it be desirable to us as a good. But we must ask under what condition the intellect is mingled with pleasure in a single conspiracy of nature and a common perfection. **C** It is established without doubt that the pleasure of the body cannot be mixed with the mind; nor indeed can any pleasure of the plants be congruent with the soul. But in truth, it is necessary that any action, affection, and life be accompanied [by pleasure], like something overflowing; so long as, clearly, an impediment stands in the way of some act naturally striving, and something contrary is mixed in, which indeed does not permit life to exist in its own right. But for some, the very tenor of the action proceeds pure and sincere, and life flourishes with a serene affection. For this reason, **D** those who judge such a habit of the mind to be the most delightful and most desirable, say in the meantime that it is mixed with pleasure: and they seem to bring this about properly through a lack of a better name, just as those do who transfer other names loved by us to divine things. Wherefore there is that saying: **The Intellect is drunk with nectar.** <note>original: "Intellectus nectare ebrius"</note>. Likewise: **One goes to the banquet and the fodder.** Again, among the poets: **E** **Jupiter himself becomes joyful**; and many similar things. For there, in reality, is the most delightful and most lovable lot of life, and the most to be hoped for of all. And a condition of this sort neither comes to be at some time nor is it turned in motion: <margin>He says they contribute to a single nature</margin> <margin>* for there is something ineffable there</margin> for its cause is that which it colors, illustrates, and sustains.
