The Good itself, the principle of the universe, not only procreates the mind and soul, but also, by infusing a ray of itself like a certain hook of love <note>original: "amatorio quodam hamo" - a metaphor for the magnetic pull of the divine</note>, continually calls them back to itself: where our nature, both in the soul and in the mind, is finally turned toward a vital and gracious abundance; and this is the very happiness of both.

### Chapter XXXI.

The soul is provoked toward celestial beauty not only through divinely implanted love, but also through reason. This occurs when you realize that bodily beauty is necessarily imperfect, as it is positioned in deformity, distance, and instability; therefore, it must proceed from something incorporeal. Thus the soul is finally formed by the divine mind, from which it soon recognizes the Father of the divine mind.

**SINCE**, therefore, all things have been made beautiful by Him who is before all things, and all things shine forth from there: the intellect has indeed received the brightness of intellectual action from that source, with which it then illuminated its own nature; the soul, however, receives from there the power to live, with an abundance of life overflowing into it. Indeed, the intellect was immediately raised toward that place and remained there, considering itself satisfied while it stands near to Him. The soul, having turned toward that same place as soon as it recognized and perceived what it could, rejoices greatly in the spectacle; and insofar as it is capable of seeing, it is immediately struck with awe. It sees, however, as if being struck from there, and having something of that One within itself, it feels within itself the stirrings of a new growth. 

And yet, having been affected in this way, it begins to desire, just like those who are incited by an image of a beloved thing to long for the sight of the thing itself. Just as among us, lovers fashion themselves into the likeness of the beloved—rendering both their bodies more graceful and their souls more elegant to match the beloved's likeness, so that they might not be inferior in temperance <term>temperantia; the virtue of self-control and moderation</term> and other virtues—otherwise they would be utterly despised by those beloved ones who are endowed with virtue. Such are those among the number of lovers who can eventually enjoy the familiarity of the beloved. In the same way, the soul loves the Good itself, having been provoked to love by that very Good from the beginning. 

And truly, whatever soul has a ready love does not wait to be recalled to the memory of the Good by these things which are beautiful among us. Instead, possessing love within itself, even if it is ignorant of what it possesses, it seeks continually; and wishing to approach that Good, it despises all these things of ours. Indeed, considering what appears beautiful in this world, it despises them not without reason, since it sees them lying in the flesh and the body, polluted by their present place and position, and dispersed by dimensions. For even if these things are called beautiful, they are not themselves the true beauties. For it is a sin to believe that those things which are truly beautiful would immerse themselves in the mud of bodies <note>original: "corporum luto" - a common Platonic metaphor for the material world</note>, defiling and destroying themselves. 

But when the soul considers that what we think is beautiful is in a state of perpetual flux, it perceives entirely that the light which shines in them is obtained from elsewhere. After this, the soul is lifted up entirely, being able at last to follow what it loves; nor does it cease until it attains it, unless someone should tear that love away from it. There, at last, it perceives all things as beautiful and truly existing, and being filled with the life of Being itself, it is greatly strengthened. It becomes itself truly Being, dwelling there and truly comprehending, living closest to that which it has sought for so long.

<column-break/>

<margin>A <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ ἐκείνου δὴ τὰ πάντα..." This column contains the Greek source text corresponding to the Latin translation on the left.</note> But since all things belong to Him, to that One who is before all things, and the light is from there—the brightness of intellectual activity—with which He made nature shine. The soul has the power for life, since a greater life has come into it. Now, it is already there, and it remained there having loved it, to be around Him. And the soul, having turned back as we are able, as it knew and saw, was struck with awe at the vision, and as much as it was possible to see. For it was struck as if by a blow, and having something of the One in itself, it perceives it. And being so disposed, we are in longing. 

Just as those who, dwelling on the image of the beloved, wish to see the beloved thing itself. And just as here lovers fashion themselves into likeness with the beloved, bringing both their bodies to be more comely and their souls into likeness, so as not to be left behind, as far as they are able, in the temperance they possess and in all other things, so that they might always be chosen by the souls of the beloved; if they are able to inquire into these things, in this very way the soul loves that One, having been moved to love by Him from the beginning. Either having love ready, it does not wait for a reminder of the beauties here. Possessing something, even if it is ignorant of what it has, it seeks forever. But the soul that yearns for Him looks past the things here. 

And if it <unclear>suspects</unclear> that the beauties in this universe are something, it is because they are in flesh and bodies, and defiled in a certain condition and divided in magnitudes, and are not the beauties themselves. For those things, as they are, would not dare to enter into the mud of bodies, and defile themselves, and disappear where they were, and be corrupted. Indeed, it already knows completely that the divine which is in them is held from elsewhere. Then it is carried there to find what it loves, and does not stop before arriving there, unless someone takes away its love. But there, all things are already beautiful and true beings. It is strengthened more, being filled with the life of being, and truly becoming being for itself; and it is thus with Him, being near, it perceives that which it has long sought.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the soul's ascent toward the ultimate source of all things. Following the discussion of intellectual happiness, the text now focuses on the nature of "The Good" as the source of beauty and the object of infinite love, marking the transition into Chapter 32 of Ennead VI, Book 7.</meta>

-> BOOK SEVEN <-

Whatever exists in the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and divine forms, existing beyond the physical senses.</note> is a **species** <note>original: "species". In Platonic philosophy, this refers to the 'Forms' or 'Ideas'—the eternal blueprints of reality.</note> that is; and that whole world is itself a **species** consisting of many **species**. Each **species**, however, is something deposited within the intelligence. Hence, one is clearly distinguished from another. Again, the universal **species**, consisting of defined parts, is ultimately defined. Likewise, in the multitude of **species**, that one splendor of beauty shines forth.

### Chapter XXXII.

It is necessary, therefore, to go even beyond the defined nature of that world to reach the very immensity of incomparable virtue, and to ascend from beauty—which is like a certain splendor found in many things, such as stars—to the simple light of the **Good** itself, as if to the Sun. This **species** is none of itself, yet it is the very beauty of beauty. And since goodness is infinite toward beauty, it kindles an infinite love in those who approach it. From this we can argue for the eternal happiness of souls.

<margin>How one must ascend to the first beauty. <note>original: "πῶς πρὸς τὸ πρῶτον καλὸν ἀνιτέον"</note></margin>
Where, then, does the one who created these things perceive their structure? Truly, seeing such a life and living essence, you see the beauty running variously over all of them. It is beautiful indeed, but if something comes from those things, one must look to whence these things come and from whence they are beautiful. It must be that he is none of these things; otherwise, he would be a part. He is neither a form nor a certain power. If all these things are there, he is above them all, being the power above all forms. For he must be formless, not as one lacking form, but as the one from whom every form comes. That which becomes what it was becoming had to become something and took a form; but that which was made by no one, who could have made it? Only the source of causes. If all things are becoming, they are later; but all beings are from him, for he is the power that makes all. What magnitude could he have? Or is he infinite? But if he is infinite, he would not have magnitude. Magnitude comes from him as from its source. And he must do this, not having it himself. Then is the magnitude of essence a quantity? He would have magnitude through nothing other than himself. But the great itself can be nothing before that which has no power, nor does it have anything the same as the things it causes. He gives measure to all things, but is he himself without measure? Yes, for how else could he have measured all others, or be the shape of all? If he is the object of desire, and you cannot grasp any shape or form in him, he would be most desirable and most lovely, and love for him would be such as it is, for love is defined here. Because the beloved is not finite, the love then would be infinite, so that his beauty is of another kind than beauty; it is beauty above beauty. For being nothing, what beauty could be lovely? Or being, beauty would be the thing known. He is the power of all beauty, the flower of <margin>The beauty of beauty.</margin> beauty, the beauty-making beauty. <margin>Beauty of beauty.</margin> For he generates it <margin>Beauty-making beauty.</margin> and makes it more beautiful by the abundance of beauty within him. So he is the principle and end of beauty. Since he is the principle of beauty, he makes that of which he is the principle beautiful; he makes it beautiful not in form, but in itself.

<column-break/>

**A** HERE it is now right to inquire in this manner. Come, tell me, O soul, where is he who produced such an immense beauty, who brought forth such excellent life, who created the first essence? Do you see, O soul, beauty itself shimmering in all and various **species**? It is indeed beautiful to remain there. But it is worthwhile for the soul, existing in such beauty, to investigate from where these things come and from where they become beautiful.
**B** It is necessary surely that the author of all beautiful things be none of them himself; otherwise, if he were any of them, he would be only a certain part. Therefore, he is neither a certain form, nor a certain power. Nor again is he all the things that exist there, both forms and powers; but he must stand above all powers and forms. The principle itself is therefore vacant of **species**, not indeed that it lacks form, but rather it is that from which every intellectual form arises. For that which was made was just then
**C** being made; it was necessary for something to be produced and it received its own idea and proper form. But that which is made by no one, clearly, has not become anything. This, then, is none of the beings, and is all beings: none indeed because beings are posterior to this; all because they are born from it. Since, however, he can make all things, what magnitude might he have in himself? Could he perhaps be immense? But if he is immense, he has no magnitude. Magnitude only has a place in the lowest things; it is necessary that the effecter of magnitude not be a
**D** participant in magnitude. That quantity which is commonly called the "magnitude of essence" is not any quantity. He can, without doubt, possess that which is possible for that which is: magnitude. But his magnitude is this: that nothing is more powerful than him, and nothing can be equal to him. For who among his creatures can be equal to him, since none possesses the same nature? Furthermore, what is commonly said—that God reigns through all ages and everywhere throughout the universe—does not signify a measure for God, nor again a vast immensity; otherwise, in what way could he measure anything? Therefore, it is not fitting to imagine any figure in him.
**E** Accordingly, that desirable thing, whose figure or form you cannot grasp, is to be desired and loved above all, and the love for it is more immense. For this love is not finite, since the beloved itself is not finite: but the love for this is infinite. Wherefore its beauty also exists in another way. It is itself the beauty above beauty. Since it is none of the beings, in what way can it be some beauty? Since, however, it is lovable, it is undoubtedly the author of beauty. It is thus the power and the very flower of all beauty, making beauty beautiful: for it generates beauty, and once generated, it makes it more beautiful by the abundance of beauty; for which reason it is the principle and the end of beauty. And since it is the principle of beauty, it makes that of which it is the principle beautiful; it makes it beautiful not in form, but itself

Here, Plotinus means that in the divine realm, things possess form inherently rather than having it imposed on them from the outside.</note>, and it exists in "form" in another way. For that which exists purely as form itself must reside in another; but if it resides in itself, it is considered something without form. Therefore, that which participates in beauty is "formed," but beauty itself is not "formed."

*The beauty of the Good itself is superior to every kind of appearance; the beauty of the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and eternal truths.</note> is a form that encompasses the whole, for nothing there is without form; nothing is so formed that it is not also form itself. The beauty of the physical world is inferior to true form, since it is composed of form mixed with the unformed, and even with deformity.*

### Chapter XXXIII.

*That all-form beauty of the divine world, though it is to be greatly admired, is nevertheless something defined and limited; it is not to be loved above all else, for goodness itself is better than any variety of forms. For even in the divine world, although everything is a certain form, there is still something there compared to another as if it were matter. From this, both this and that are part of a definition. Beauty in the divine world, therefore, acting as the splendor of the Good itself, calls back the soul there—full of wonder—through love to the Good itself. Similarly, beauty in the soul, acting as the splendor of intelligence, secretly invites it through love to the beloved intellect. Beauty in the body, like an image of living beauty, encourages us to desire the beauty within.*

<margin>A</margin> **W**hen, therefore, we speak of "beauty," we must flee far from any specific shape or form; we must not place such things before our eyes, lest we fall away from the truly beautiful into something that is called beautiful only by a meager participation. <margin>B</margin> Truly, the "unformed form" <note>original: "species non formata". This refers to the essence of beauty before it is limited by a specific shape.</note> is what is truly beautiful, provided it remains pure essence. And indeed, as you proceed by separating from matter into every form—as if toward the <term>seminal reason</term> <note>original: "ratione seminaria". The underlying logic or "seed" that generates specific things.</note> of the form itself, in which we say one thing differs from another—just as justice and temperance are distinguished from each other because the intellect understands something unique in them—you will find that although all things there are beautiful, because they are designated as specific things, they are in some way "diminished." This is true even if you grasp all things in the intelligible world together; for if you take each one individually, you will see it has one intelligible form, and if you take them all together, they appear as a single form distinguished by variety. <margin>C</margin> Now, if you have come this far, you must consider more deeply what is most to be thought of—that which is surely higher than this "all-formed" variety, yet is itself not divided by any variety. This is what the soul hungers for, even if it cannot express why it hungers for such a thing. <margin>D</margin> Reason dictates that this is what we must truly love; for the nature of the "best" and "most lovable" consists in that level which surpasses every specific form. Therefore, whatever you show the soul that has a specific form, the soul always seeks something else beyond it which gave it that form. Reason teaches us that whatever has form—and even form and species themselves—is something "measured" and limited. It is neither the whole, nor self-sufficient, nor beautiful by its own nature, but is a mixture. It is necessary, therefore, that these things be beautiful but "measured," while that which is truly beautiful—or rather, "super-beautiful"—is not circumscribed by any limit of measurement. If this is so, it certainly cannot have a "form," nor can it be a specific "species." Therefore, that which is first lovable and exists first of all, surpasses every species; and there, the beauty and grace of the intelligible beauty exists as the very nature of the Good. The passions of lovers testify to this. For as long as one is occupied only with looking at a visible shape, one is not yet seized by love; but as soon as the soul, withdrawing from that shape, conceives a form within itself that is no longer visible or divisible, love is born immediately.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Unformed. In another way, that which is spoken of in form is itself only form, but exists in another. But in itself, the thing that participates in beauty is "formed," but beauty itself is not.

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, whenever beauty is spoken of, one must flee rather from such a form. But that which is productive before bodies exists so that you do not fall away from the beautiful. For that which is called beautiful by a faint participation is one thing; but the unformed species is beautiful, insofar as it is a species. And if there are those [forms] from the source * <note>original: "σωλήνιος", likely a corruption in the Greek transcription for "σωληνώδους" or similar, referring to the flow of forms.</note> upon all things, such as the idea I speak of, or as we say one differs from another—as justice and temperance are different from each other and are beautiful things—you will be moved to understand a specific cause in them, and all things, and the whole, taking each one in the higher realm, and each has one intelligible form. But all together they are like a variety. Still, it is necessary to behold those things that are beyond that "all-beautiful" and "varied" thing toward which the soul reaches, and where its desires are placed. <margin>C</margin> Reason says that this is the "really real," which the one who acts achieves before it. It is natural that this is most lovable. <margin>Isaac of Nineveh <unclear>to the</unclear></margin> <note>This marginal note refers to Isaac of Nineveh, a 7th-century Christian mystic, suggesting a later scholar found parallels between Plotinus and Isaac's views on divine love.</note> * Therefore, as an ascent, the soul is shown to go beyond all other things that it has formed. Reason says that whatever has form, and the form itself, and the species, is all "measured." It is not the whole, and not self-sufficient, nor beautiful through itself, but is somewhat mixed. <margin>D</margin> These things are beautiful, but those things in the realm beyond the beautiful are not measured, nor are they formed, nor are they a species. Therefore, that which is primary and separated is the most beautiful nature of the Good. The passions of * lovers <note>original: "ἐρετῶν", likely a transcription error for "ἐραστῶν".</note> testify to this: as long as one is in that state of having a sensible object, one does not yet love. But when, from that object, the soul itself generates a type within itself—not a sensible one, but in the partless soul—then love is born.

Matter, however, is by its very nature necessarily most remote: since it does not possess from itself even the last of forms. Therefore, if something is lovable to us, it is not matter, but that which is shaped by a "species" <note>original: "specie," used here to mean the defining essence or form.</note>. ### Chapter XXXIV.

> **The Good itself, therefore, is always everywhere present; as soon as it shines upon a soul that is serene, it kindles a wondrous love. This happens when the soul strips away all forms and intentions—not only those that can be imagined, but even the intellectual ones. Then, through the love of the infinite Good, the infinite soul is wonderfully joined together with the Good, filled with ineffable joy. This can happen not only after this present life, but even in this life at times.**

<margin>A</margin> Since things are so, we shall not wonder at those who feel the sharpest stings of love, being far removed from every form, even the intelligible. For this reason, when the soul burns with an ardent love for that Good, it sets aside whatever form it has within itself, even if there is some intelligible form of the Good in it. For it cannot be otherwise: he who holds something else, or acts concerning something else, either sees that other thing or is occupied with it, and cannot be harmonized or joined [to the One]. Rather, one must have <margin>B</margin> nothing else at hand, neither of evil nor of good, so that at last the "alone may capture the Alone." After the soul has successfully obtained this, and the Good has approached it—or rather, is already present and shining over it—it happens when the soul has called itself back from all other present things and prepared itself. It makes itself as beautiful as possible and becomes similar to it. But the preparation and adornment of the soul are known only to those who rightly prepare themselves. <margin>C</margin> After the soul has so prepared itself, it will see God himself suddenly flashing within it. For nothing intervenes between them, nor are they any longer two distinct things, but both are now one; nor can one distinguish them as long as He is present. Lovers and beloveds in our world, who seek to be melted into one, try to imitate this. Now the soul, so dedicated to God, no longer feels its own body, nor does it notice that it is in a body, nor does it declare itself to be anything else—not a man, <margin>D</margin> not a living creature, not a being, not the universe. For the sight of these things is, in a way, unequal and distracting. Nor does the soul then have the leisure to turn its sharp gaze toward those things, nor would it wish to. But when it has sought Him studiously, it joins itself completely to Him as He is present, and sees Him instead of itself; nor is it so free as to recognize who it is that sees. In this state, one is blessed with many things; he would not exchange this present treasure for anything—not even if one were to offer him the entire heaven. For he judges that nothing is more excellent—

Then at last the soul attains a completely true judgment: it recognizes once again that this is the very thing it once longed for with all its strength, and it asserts without a doubt that nothing is more excellent. For there is no deception there; otherwise, it would be possible to find something "truer than the truth."
<margin>B</margin>
What the soul says then, it already *is*; yet it speaks of it later, and speaks of it in silence. And since it is now affected by a blessed sweetness, it is not deceived in its state of being. For it does not say this as if it were a physical pleasure of the body, but as having become that which it once was when it was truly happy. Then, indeed, it recognizes that all other things which it was previously accustomed to delight in—such as power, wealth, ornaments, beauty, or even various branches of learning—are now utterly to be looked down upon. 
<margin>C</margin>

Finally, even if everything else around the soul were to be destroyed, it would gladly accept this, so that it might remain with the Good alone; to such an extent has it proceeded successfully and joyfully in its state of being.

Chapter XXXV.*

In this enjoyment, God himself is the light which the soul beholds, and through which it beholds: and the power of the light is the light itself. Now, in the <term>Intellect</term> <note>The "Nous" or divine mind, which contains all true ideas but is still one step below the absolute unity of the Good.</note>, there is first that direct intuition and contemplation; then it is formed into God, and soon, having been so formed, it becomes contemplation by its very nature. It enjoys God, who is above it; yet it also enjoys itself. In the soul, too, there is a unity superior to the intellect, through which it enjoys God by a vision that surpasses understanding.

<margin>A</margin>
SO TRULY is the soul then disposed toward its desire, that it counts its own intelligence as nothing. Whereas it previously admired its intellect, it now values it not at all; for it clearly recognizes that intelligence is a kind of motion, and the soul itself no longer desires to be moved. Yet it does not even declare that what it sees is the "Intellect," even though the soul has now become intellect to behold it. It is as if the soul were entirely occupied by the intellect and placed within the <term>intelligible realm</term> <note>The spiritual world of perfect ideas, as opposed to the physical world.</note>; being placed within it and surrounding it, it would naturally understand the intelligible. But after it has seen God, it leaves all else behind. It is just like someone who enters a house decorated with many patterns and examines each ornament inside, admiring them before seeing the master of the house. But after they have looked upon the master—who far surpasses the beauty of those images, appearing not as a beautiful image but as beauty itself—they admire him beyond measure. Leaving the images aside, they henceforth gaze only upon him. Fixing their eyes intently on him, they no longer see the visible object as something separate through the continuity of the act of seeing; rather, they blend their vision with the object seen, so that what was previously the "visible" now becomes the "vision" itself, and all other sights are hidden. Perhaps this comparison would maintain its proper proportion if the one who met the observer of the house were not a man, but a God; one not visible to the eyes, but one who fills the very mind of the contemplator.

The soul does not feign this, nor is she lying when she says she is well-off.

For thinking was a kind of motion, but now the soul does not wish to be moved. Indeed, it does not even say that it sees itself while in the act of understanding. It is like one who has been given a place in the intelligible realm, and being in it or around it, understands the intelligible; but once he sees that God, he lets everything else go. It is like someone entering a decorated house, who might admire each of the decorations inside before seeing the master of the house. 
<margin>B</margin>
But having seen him, and being struck with wonder—not at the nature of the statues, but at the worth of the true sight—he leaves those things behind and looks only at the master thereafter. In looking and not turning his eye away, he no longer sees a "spectacle" because of the continuity of the vision. Rather, he has mixed his sight with the object of the vision, so that he now sees something within himself.

This image would quickly preserve the proper analogy if the one who stood before him were not a man, but some God appearing to the contemplator; or rather, not a God appearing to the sight, but one filling the soul of the contemplator.

### BOOK SEVEN.

55. It is necessary for the intellect to have a twin power: one indeed for the act of understanding, by which it gazes upon the things within itself; the other, however, by which it looks toward that which is beyond itself by a certain reaching out and reception, through which it formerly only saw, and by seeing, later
<margin>* healthy, and possessed intellect</margin>
*possessed intellect.* And while that first vision belongs to a sound and temperate mind, this latter is the *loving intellect*, when it becomes
<margin>* It resembles an "overflowing"</margin>
*senseless, intoxicated with nectar.* Then, being filled to satiety, it becomes loving, unfolding itself into a state of blessed well-being. And indeed, *it is better for it to be thus intoxicated* than to live too solemnly as a "sober thinker." In turn, it perceives these things one after another, yet at the same time they are all present; it sees them just as the teaching Word <note>original: *logos*</note> brings them into being. But as for the notion that "it is necessary to understand," the mind endures not understanding something, but rather looking toward that One; and that seeing is the work of the soul, and is kept in silence. As for the separations: I certainly see these things. At least it is said that the intellect has power as long as it remains, but that which is akin to the soul is like a living phantom, a light remaining in it—or rather, a light belonging to it—which it does not see at first. But when the state of arrival occurs, the two become one. The Good thrives upon them, or rather fits itself to the structure of both, an influence and an image of the two, giving them a blessed perception, becoming one and all, so that there is no mark of division, nor is one thing in another, as is natural elsewhere; but the intellect itself retreats toward that which it understands, for there is a place within it, yet it is in nothing else. Therefore, it does not move: for the soul at that time does not move, because that One does not move; nor is it strictly "soul," because it does not strictly "live" in the usual sense, but rather exceeds the function of living. Nor does it "understand," for it must be made like [the One], and the One does not understand.

**A** Therefore, it must be considered that the intellect has a twin power: one indeed for understanding, through which it gazes upon its own internal contents; the other truly by which it looks up to higher things by a certain thrust of intuition and perception. Indeed, by this looking and accepting, it previously only saw, and by seeing, it later received intellect and became one. That first vision belongs to a healthy mind, but this latter is the mind itself in love. **B** For when it is driven "insane," being thoroughly drunk with nectar, then it is seized by love, pouring itself out into a blessed affection and sweetness in its satiety. And truly, it is better for the mind to be occupied by this intoxication than to live soberly and far from such a drink. But does that mind contemplate things one after another, some before and some after? By no means; although the discussion introduces it as contemplating in alternating turns for the sake of teaching. **C** However, the intellect itself is always exercised by the act through which it properly understands; and again, in a proper sense, it does *not* understand, but beholds God by another certain reason. Truly, while it perceived God, it conceived all things from that source within itself, and felt those things now born within it; and while it gazes upon these, it is said to "understand." But it looked up at God by that power through which it was thereafter to become intellect. Accordingly, the soul, as if confusing and erasing the intellect remaining within it, looks up to God. Indeed, the intellect itself is the first to look, but the vision is also translated into the soul, and there the two become one. **D** The Good itself, propagating itself through these things and applying itself to their constitution, flies over them, and joining the two into one, it broods over them, granting a happy sense and a blessed contemplation. Furthermore, it lifts these things up to such an extent that they are no longer in a place, nor in any other thing, whatever the condition might be of one thing being in another; for God himself is not "in" anything. The "intelligible place" <term>Intellectus (Nous)</term> is in Him, but He Himself exists in nothing at all. Therefore, the soul does not move then, because He does not move; nor is it properly "soul," since it does not properly "live" (as we understand life), for He exceeds the gift of living. But neither is it "intellect," since it does not "understand." For it must be made like [the One]; but it does not understand that One, because He Himself does not understand.

> The Ladder by which one ascends to the Principle <note>The "One" or "The Good"</note> has seven steps: first is the **purgation of the soul**; second, the **knowledge of divine works** compared individually; third, the **contemplation of order**, by which lower works are led back to higher ones step by step; fourth, a certain **proportional comparison** bringing oneself from this order to the divine order; fifth, **negation**, through which you separate everything you can conceive from the Principle; sixth, **suppliant prayer** to God, that He, the Father of the intellectual world, might render you an intellectual world in actuality (for by His power this world existed from the beginning); seventh, that when you have emerged as an intellectual world yourself, you might be transformed into the **Good which is superior to intellect**, moved by a more abundant love of the Good and the intellectual breath.

->Chapter XXXVI.<-

> Since the Good is far superior to the intellect, and therefore the enjoyment of it is not correctly called "intelligence," it seems it should not even be named "knowledge." For it is more natural and more desirable than knowledge. Yet we call it so as best we can: sometimes "vision" because of its light and purity, and sometimes "touch" because of the greatest union. It is also called "taste" because of the sweetness thoroughly infused into the soul there, nourishing it healthfully and transforming it wonderfully for the better.

**A** THE REST of these matters are indeed clear. Something has also been said regarding this; nevertheless, we must now add something more, beginning from that point before proceeding through arguments. For either the knowledge or the "touch" of the Good itself is undoubtedly something of the greatest importance: its study Plato called "the greatest," not indeed calling the intuition of the Good itself a "study," but rather a certain notice preceding this intuition. For analogies—that is, proportions—teach us this...

<margin>A</margin>
...of the suitability of actions: likewise, the negations <note>Apophatic theology: a way of describing the Divine by stating what He is not, rather than what He is.</note> of those things which arise from Him are a form of knowledge: and finally, certain ascents that proceed rightly by degrees. We reach Him through purifications, prayers, and the worship that adorns the soul, and by an ascent to the intelligible world <term>Intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure Thought and Reality, as opposed to the physical world of the senses.</note>, and by remaining there; specifically, while the soul feeds upon the banquets of that world, whoever looks upon it becomes at once both the spectator and the spectacle, both of himself and of others. Having become essence, and intellect, and the universal living being, he no longer looks upon these things from the outside; having finally become them, he is now close to the Highest.

<margin>B</margin>
Indeed, that Highest is undoubtedly present there, shining from above throughout the entire intelligible world. There, certainly, once all studies have been set aside and the soul has been led this far and established in beauty, it understands as far as that in which it resides; but being carried out from there by a certain wave, as it were, of that same intellect, and lifted high by the intellect as it swells and overflows, it suddenly perceives, without knowing how.

<margin>C</margin>
But the intuition itself, filling the eyes with light, does not cause another thing to be seen through it; rather, the light itself is precisely what is seen. For in that realm, there is not one thing that is visible and another that is its light, nor is there intellect and the object of intellect: but there thrives the law which generates in the things that follow, allowing them to remain within themselves. Yet that light alone existed, generating the intellect; it is not extinguished by generating, but while the light itself remains, another thing follows from that which the light established. For unless it stood firm in such a way, nothing else would subsist from it.

->Since Plotinus once defined intelligence as a reflected act of a living essence depending on the Good, and such an effort seeks both itself and its cause, and since it lives both through its own parts and through the merit of its cause, he urges that the principle of such intelligence needs supports. Chapter XXXVII.<-

It seems that just as sight is related to light, so is intelligence related to the light of the Good, and they are similarly distinguished: nevertheless, intelligence differs much more from the Good than sight does from light. Indeed, the Good is seen to surpass intelligence in a greater height and breadth than light surpasses sight. Since, therefore, the reasons for the Good itself and for intelligence are so distinct, and are two by nature, you might rightly call the Good "first," comparing it to the simple; thus, being sufficient, do not apply "intelligence" to it, which follows after essence and life, whereas the Good exceeds both. For to be and to live are desired only by reason of the Good. Nor is God "mindless" <note>Plotinus is arguing that while God/The One does not "think" in a human way, He is not "ignorant"; He is above the need for thought.</note> because of a more excellent mind: nor is anything hidden from Him through whom all things are made manifest.

WHOSOEVER, therefore, in their disputations have assigned "intelligence" to the highest principle of things, have utterly taken away the knowledge of all things and of those which proceed from it. Although this seems absurd to some—that God in no way knows other things—those people, finding nothing more excellent than Him, attributed the knowledge of Himself to Him. They did this as if He would become more venerable by the function of intelligence, and as if the function of intelligence were more excellent than the Principle, while this very thing which exists is merely a result: as if the Principle did not provide all dignity to intelligence, but received it from intelligence. Therefore, it must be asked: from what does God rather have His dignity—from intelligence, or from Himself? If He acquires dignity through intelligence, He is certainly not to be venerated for Himself, or at least less so; but if He possesses His dignity by Himself, He is certainly perfect before intelligence, and does not become perfect by the act of understanding. And if anyone should say that because God is not "potentiality" but "actuality," He must therefore understand, we shall distinguish it thus: Either God is an essence that is always understanding, or He is the act of understanding alone. If He is an essence always understanding,

By certain negations, and by the knowledge of those things proceeding from Him, and by certain steps. There, having truly left behind all learning, and having been tutored to this point, and established in the beautiful, he understands as far as that in which he resides: but being carried out by the wave of the intellect itself, and lifted high by it as it swells, he suddenly saw, not seeing how, but the vision, having filled the eyes with light, did not make one see something else through it, but the light itself was the vision.

# SEVENTH BOOK. #

<note>original: LIBER SEPTIMVS. This refers to the seventh book of the sixth Ennead, titled "How the Multiplicity of the Forms Came into Being, and on the Good."</note>

And for this reason they call it "activity" <note>Greek: energeia</note>, yet they speak of two things: essence and thought. They do not posit it as something simple, but rather they add something else to it—just as one might speak of the eye, which possesses vision and activity even when not looking at a specific object. <margin>* Nor was it yet, for...</margin> If they say that God is in a state of activity, it is because activity and intelligence follow one another. But if he does not think in this way, just as motion itself is not moved, [then he is simpler]. <margin>* Nor is this itself moved, for the whole is moved</margin> But here someone among us might object: "Do you not also say that the divine essence and activity are the same?" We certainly admit such things, yet if we confess that these things are many and diverse, then we must assign intelligence to that which depends on another. Through this intelligence, it seeks its own essence, its goal, and its creator, as it were, and turns toward them by contemplating them. But if you do that, we say that it is not yet the Intellect itself. That which is neither created nor has anything else above it, but has always existed as that which it is—we do not see what occasion it would have for the act of thinking. <margin>A</margin> And for this reason, they call it "act," bringing two things together: namely, essence and intelligence. They do not posit it as something simple in this way, but they apply something else to it, just as they are accustomed to adding vision to the eyes according to act, even if they are always looking. But if one says that God exists in act: because act and intelligence follow each other, then in truth, in this way, intelligence would not "think," just as motion itself is not "moved." But here someone among us will object: "Do you not also say that the divine essence and act are the same?" <margin>B</margin> We certainly admit such things; but if we confess these to be many and diverse, then we assign intelligence to that which depends on another, through which it seeks, as it were, its own essence, its aim, and its maker; and in beholding this, it is turned back. But if you do this, we say it is not yet the intellect. That which is neither made, nor has anything else above it, but has always stood forth as that very thing which it is—we do not see what occasion it would have for thinking. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, Plato rightly placed the supreme God <note>The "Good" or "The One" in Neoplatonism.</note> above the intellect. Therefore, if the intellect does not think, it is deservedly judged to be "mindless." For in what else is the nature of an intelligent being required, if it does not think? It is rightly judged insane. But to him who has no need of work, why would anyone assign a work to him, only to then take it away because of the absence of such work? It would be like calling a God "unskilled" in the art of medicine [when he has no need to heal]. Indeed, no work is necessary for God, since it is not <insert>expedient</insert> for God to "act": for he is sufficient for himself, and there is nothing else for him to seek beyond himself, since he exists above all things. For he is sufficient both for himself and for others, while he himself exists as this very thing which he is.

<column-break/>

Therefore, Plato says that the soul goes upward toward the God. For if these things did not exist, the nature of thinking would be mindless. If the First Cause does not have "thinking," it is because it has no "work" or task to perform; furthermore, nothing is imposed upon it to do. Indeed, it is nothing (relative to all things) or rather, it is above all existing things. For it is sufficient to itself in relation to all other things of which it is the cause.

<column-break/>

-> *Since essence, reason, and other things are themselves distinct, and are lower than the "reason" of the Good, it is not correct to say that "being" is predicated of the Good. And if the Good, on account of its supreme simplicity, finds nothing in itself that is "external," it might seem obscure and uncertain to us; nevertheless, it is the clear origin, father, and gateway of all certainty. Chapter XXXVIII.* <-

---

<margin>A</margin> And it "is," yet it is not any specific thing. For even there, "being" is not predicated, but rather all things are directed toward the Good. It is not according to what they are, but according to the fact that they are for all things. The Good may be signified as "that which it is" by someone else. <margin>* We do not say it is the Good itself, but speaking about it...</margin> We do not say it is "the Good," nor do we predicate that it exists, but rather we say this because we deem it worthy to be called the Good itself. <margin>B</margin> <margin>* Nor is this added to it</margin> Not even the word "the" is added to it. But being unable to manifest it, if someone were to remove everything from it entirely—lest we be persuaded that it is "one thing" and then "another"—we should not even say "the Good" is upon it. But if one accepts its nature, there will be perception and knowledge of it. What then will it know? "I am." But it will not say "I am the Good" while it is in that state, or again predicate what it is. It will say only "Good," adding nothing more. For if it thinks, it will think what it is, unless it is predicated of another. <margin>C</margin> But he who thinks of himself as "the Good" will certainly think "I am the Good." Otherwise, he will think "Good," which is present to him, but will not think that he himself is that thought through which the thinking exists.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> *FURTHERMORE, we should not even predicate the word "is" of God: for he does not need it. Since we do not even predicate of him "God is good." Rather, that of which it is predicated "is," and of the same it is predicated "is good." But for God, it is fitting that he is the "Itself" [the Self-Existent]: not as if one thing is predicated of another, but as if it signifies this very thing which it is. We say "the Good" concerning him, not assigning anything to him, nor here predicating <margin>B</margin> that the Good is present to him, but because he stands forth as the Good itself. Furthermore, since we by no means think it should be said of him "he is good," nor should such a phrase as "this" or "that" be placed before him—and yet we are not able to express "Itself" unless one removes everything around it—taking care, clearly, lest we make it "one thing" and then "another." Just as it does not even need this word "is," so we simply pronounce it "Good." Truly, who will admit a nature of this kind, neither feeling nor knowing itself in any way? <margin>C</margin> What then? Will it at least know "I am"? But in what way, since it "is" in the least degree [as a defined being]? Or perhaps will it say "I am good"? But truly, if it only pronounces "Good," what can someone call it without this word "is," unless perhaps he predicates "good" of another? But he who knows himself to be good will certainly understand this very thing: namely, "I am good." Otherwise, he will indeed understand "good," but he will not achieve this: namely, to understand that he himself is this. It is necessary, therefore, if there is an intelligence of the Good there, that it be of such a kind.*

730 PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

...to be as the Good, it might understand. But if intelligence itself is the Good itself, then certainly it will not be the intelligence of itself, but the intelligence of the Good; and it will not even be the Good itself, but rather the intelligence will be something additional to the Good. If, however, the intelligence of the Good is different from the Good, it follows that the Good already exists before the intelligence of it. Furthermore, if the Good itself is by its own nature sufficient before intelligence—and it is certainly sufficient unto itself as the Good—it will in no way stand in need of an intelligence of itself. Therefore, for this reason, the Good does not understand itself at all.

### In the first principle of things there is neither intelligence of self, nor of others: provided that intelligence is a kind of knowledge having certain conditions. Chapter XXXIX. ###

First, that it should have something similar to motion in its unity and stability. Second, that it should admit variety and difference along with unity. Third, that it should discern by opposing things at the same time. Fourth, that the nature whose act is intelligence must be divided within itself <note>original: "difformis"</note>, since it consists of the intellect, the intelligible object, and the act of intellection. Fifth, that it must also be "all-forming" <note>original: "omniformis"</note>, if indeed through this intelligence it is to perceive all things. Plotinus denies a perception full of such variety in God; however, he does not deny a simple certainty, clarity, and light. Similarly, he denies any action or providence that is different from goodness or that wanders outside of it; but meanwhile, he maintains that all things are produced from that source and are disposed by providence.

<margin>A</margin> **I**f God does not understand himself in the manner of the Good, one might ask by what reason he understands at all. And one might answer that nothing else is present to God: but a certain simple intuition <note>original: "simplicem quedam intuitum"</note> exists for him toward himself. Nevertheless, since there is no "interval" there, as it were, nor any difference at all toward himself, this very thing which is called "being aimed at himself" or "beholding himself" exists as nothing other than himself. For this reason, where intellect and essence exist, diversity correctly occurs.

<margin>B</margin> For it is necessary that the intellect, if it is ever to understand, always admits both difference and identity. For it could never distinguish itself from the object of thought <note>the "intelligible"</note> if it did not have a certain relationship of a different nature toward it, nor would it understand all other things if no diversity were present. Moreover, if it brings all things together there, even without the principle of diversity, there would not even be two things there. Furthermore, if it understands, it will not only understand itself if it understands at all: for what prevents it from understanding all things?

<margin>C</margin> Or is it perhaps less able to understand other things than itself? Generally, however, he who understands himself becomes, by that fact, not simple: for it is necessary that the very intelligence of oneself exists as some kind of difference, if one is to be able to understand oneself at all. But we have said that this is not "intelligence" unless one beholds himself as another. He who understands himself necessarily becomes multiple: the thing understood, the one understanding, the motion, and whatever else is suited to the mind.

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, what we have said elsewhere must be considered at present: that any intelligence, if it is to be a future act of thinking, must be something varied. Where there is a simple and entirely identical uniform motion, if it behaves like a "touch" <note>Plotinus uses the metaphor of "touch" (Greek: epaphē) to describe an immediate, non-dual contact that is simpler than the subject-object relationship of thought</note>, it possesses no intellectual condition. What then? Will it know neither other things nor itself? Yet in this way it will retain its dignity intact. Other things are certainly posterior to <note>later than or dependent upon</note> it, and it is itself that very thing which exists before them.

<margin>E</margin> The intellection of those things is an addition; it is not always the same, nor does it belong to things that remain; and even if it should understand permanent things, it nonetheless becomes multiple. For it should not be said that things posterior to it possess essence in addition to intellection, while its own intelligences exist merely as certain empty speculations. Therefore, the principle of providence is sufficiently preserved by the fact that God himself is the one from whom all things come. As for what refers to him, how shall God understand, unless he understands himself, and so persists pure in his majesty? Plato therefore [spoke] of...

<margin>A</margin> ...that it is good <note>Greek: hoti agathon einai</note> * and even if it is not thought, it is the Good itself. For if it were indeed to be thought itself, it would not be the Good insofar as it is good, but rather the thinking. But if the Good is something other than the thinking, then the Good must already exist before * the thinking of it. And the Good would need to be self-sufficient <margin>twofold</margin> apart from the thinking, and it is indeed self-sufficient in its goodness. And it would not stand in need of the thinking concerning itself.

<margin>A</margin> **S**o that if it were the Good according to itself, but in a way where nothing else is present to it, there will be a certain simple application <note>Greek: epibolē, meaning a direct intuition or "striking" of the mind</note> of itself toward itself. As if there were a kind of distance. And indeed, if the application were toward itself as a difference, what would that application or the thing itself be? Therefore, it correctly takes on otherness so that it may also be essence. For through the act of thinking, it always takes on otherness and identity, if it is to think. And how would it distinguish <margin>B</margin> the things related to being thought by the same or the other? If these things were removed and no otherness occurred, which all things are, there would not even be two things at all. Then, if it thinks, it will certainly not think itself alone, if it thinks at all. For why not all things, or will it be unable? Generally, he who thinks himself does not become simple, but through thinking the things around him, they are other; furthermore, the things * within <margin>himself instead of seeing himself</margin> make them other.

<margin>C</margin> And we were saying what thinking is. * And if it should wish to see another <margin>and if another</margin>, having thought itself, it becomes many: the object of thought, and that which moves, and whatever else belongs to the mind. In addition to these, it is also necessary to see that which has already been said in other places: that each act of thinking, just as it is thinking, must be something varied. But that which is simple and the same is like a whole movement. Or by what would there be something like a touch? And one cannot say what preserves <margin>D</margin> the same perception, but it will be majestic. Other things, then, are posterior to it, and that which was before them was [the One], and the thinking of them is an addition. And it is not always the same; and of those that have departed, and those within the mind, there is much. For if indeed the posterior things exist along with the thinking and the being, the thoughts of these things will be only empty contemplations. And providence also consists in it being the same [source] from which all things come. For if it is toward himself, how [can it be] if not himself, but <margin>E</margin> he will be majestic? <meta>This page continues the transition from the end of Chapter 38 and Chapter 39 into Chapter 40 of Plotinus’s Ennead VI, Book 7. The discussion deepens the Neoplatonic argument that the absolute "First Principle" (the One or the Good) is entirely transcendent. Plotinus argues that because the Good is perfectly simple, it does not possess "Intellect" (thinking) or "Essence" (being) in the way lower things do, as these imply a duality between the thinker and the thought.</meta>

### SEVENTH BOOK ###

Speaking about essence <note>original: "οὐσίας" (ousia); the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</note>, he [Plato] says it will either act, or it will be majestic, in the sense that essence does not think; for things that do not think can be majestic, for not having that which could not otherwise be able to tremble <unclear>modestly</unclear> toward that which he thinks is so majestic as to transcend thinking.

**AND** because there ought not to be thinking around it, if it were necessary for those through whom it might touch, or act; he certainly thinks well toward the things through those spoken of, to point out in the argument, through which indeed it has its goodness mixed with passion. Through these things, know and consider how all thinking is from something and toward something; just as life is from which it is, and toward which; it remains within, but the other is outside.
<margin>activity</margin> and as if lying upon it, there becomes an * activity <note>original: "ενέργεια" (energeia); often translated as "actuality" or "divine activity"</note> within it, and a fullness, which lay in potential. This could generate nothing, for that is the perfection of those things alone; and thinking, in turn, with essence and substance <note>original: "ὑποστάσεως" (hypostaseos); the underlying reality</note>, would not have the power to be in that from which it came. For either it would have sought in that, and how the generating comes from power, upon <margin>to be an image to the first</margin> itself it came to be. Or if indeed its essence is that which is in the essence, it is also the first thinking; this essence, and the thinking to itself, the nature, and toward it, but in the word, to the thought and the thinker, a kind of plurality, as has been shown in many ways. This itself is the first activity, and first thinking, and essence, or an image <note>original: "ἴνδαλμα" (indalma); a reflection or appearance</note> of another or of those things of something great, so as to have it also, if that is laid up, which it also possesses there, and it has thinking from itself; but it is the first activity and first thinking, and it would not have an activity or thinking before itself. Therefore, if one passes from this essence and thinking, either to essence or to thinking, those things will have essence and thinking, to the wonderful one, which has neither essence nor thinking in itself, but is solitary in itself, of the things from it; for we need nothing, and for activity was prior, it generated the activity already for they would be thinking before thinking came to be. In general, thinking is for the sake of the good. As toward the good, the proportions are toward the good; it has something which is not the good; it is such, but because in the beginning itself, it would not be thinking, for in that is the good, or thinking is less than it.

<column-break/>

Speaking regarding essence, he says, it will indeed understand, but not because of this will it exist as the most venerable thing. As if essence might understand, but that which does not understand might especially be able to stand as venerable. In these words, Plato says "to exist" or "to consist": because he was not able to express it otherwise. But he considered that which is truly august <note>The Latin "Augustus" here is used as an adjective meaning "majestic" or "holy," matching the Greek "semnon."</note> and venerable to be that which understands: indeed, it stands above all.

He considers every action both to exist from someone and to be concerned with something else: soon he wishes intelligence to be an action: then he considers essence to be the foundation of action and intelligence. Deservedly, therefore, he denies action, intelligence, and essence to the first principle: which indeed is neither subject to an act, nor is it in any way concerned with another. If you grant it either beauty or goodness itself, and soon you attribute intelligence to it: you either think they do not differ at all, or differ by something. If by nothing, you name intelligence there in vain; if by something, it mixes with the highest good and becomes less than good. Let goodness itself, therefore, be not properly "the one who understands," but the cause of intelligence—the light, certainty, and truth consisting in itself: in which the effort of all intelligence is defined as the highest and most desirable end. Finally, there is such power in goodness that intelligence, which exists as its first image, is the first substance. ->Chapter 40.<-

**THAT INTELLIGENCE** ought not to be around the first principle will be understood by those who have touched upon such a thing. It is better, however, to apply certain persuasions to the higher things, on the condition that we may be able to signify what we wish with words. It is certainly necessary to mix necessity with probable persuasion. It must be noted first of all that every intelligence exists both from something and for something. And truly, that
**B** which coheres with that from which it is, has that as its subject of which it is the understanding, and so it is like something inherent, an act of that thing, filling its same power, while generating nothing in the meantime. For it is the lowest, whose perfection it is, so to speak. But the intelligence which is with essence, and through which the substitution of essence consists, cannot be in that from which it was made; otherwise, if it were in it, it would have generated nothing at all. But since it is a certain power of generating, it generated in itself the action of its essence, and it coexists in essence. Nor is intelligence different there from
**C** this essence itself: but this nature understands itself, not as something different, except only by reason, so that there is that which is understood and that which understands, although there is a certain plurality, as has now often been demonstrated. Now, truly, this is the first action generating substance in essence. And since it is the image of another, it is the image of something so exalted that it is also essence: but if it were indeed of that one, and yet nothing else of him were in it
**D** than what was of him, it would not be a substance in itself. Since, therefore, this is the first action and the first intelligence, it surely has no action or intelligence above itself. Whoever, therefore, transcends this essence and intellection, will reach no further toward essence or intelligence, but will ascend above essence and intelligence to something wonderful: which admits neither essence nor any intellection into itself at all: but consists only and purely in itself, needing none of those things which are from it. For
**E** an agent did not first generate action: otherwise, the act would already exist before the act arose. Nor did a thinker generate intelligence: otherwise, he would have understood before intelligence was born. Entirely, indeed, if intelligence is of the good, it is something inferior to the good; for which reason it is not the good itself. I say "not of the good itself," not because the good cannot be understood—for let this be granted for the present—but because in the good itself there is no intelligence: otherwise, the good itself and that which is less than the good, that is, its own intelligence, will be one and the same.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation in Ennead VI, Book 7, specifically Chapters 40 and 41 (labeled as Chapter 31 in this edition). The argument centers on why the "First Principle"—the Good or the One—cannot possess "Intellect" or "Thinking" (nous). Plotinus explains that thinking implies a duality between the thinker and the object being thought, but the Good is perfectly simple and self-sufficient.</meta>

<page-num>732</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.</header>

<margin>A</margin> If, however, there were something inferior, it would exist simultaneously with intelligence and essence. But if the Good itself is more excellent than intelligence, then as soon as it is understood, the "intelligible" <note>original: "intelligibile"; the object of thought</note> will be inferior, and thinking will not exist within the Good. Instead, since thinking is something inferior and therefore stands in awe of the majesty of the Good, it surely dwells apart from the Good, leaving the Good to remain free from thinking, just as it is free from all other things. Truly, since the Good is pure from all thinking, it exists most sincerely as exactly what it is, unimpeded by any presence of intellection from being entirely one and sincere. <margin>B</margin> If anyone should imagine this Good and its understanding occurring at the same time, and imagine essence and intelligence conspiring together with essence, attempting to portray the Good as thinking itself, such a person would certainly require another principle superior to this one. For if the act of intelligence is either a certain perfection of another subject, or if it is (so to speak) a certain "con-subsistence" <note>original: "consubsistentia"; a shared state of being</note>, it still possesses another nature prior to itself, by whose power it rightly happens to understand. <margin>C</margin> Now, it possesses the ability to understand precisely because there is something else above it; for when it understands itself, it then recognizes, as it were, what it previously brought back from a certain intuition of something else. But that which has nothing superior to it, and in which nothing exists from another—what shall it understand? In what way would it understand itself? If it turns toward itself by thinking, it is seeking something: what is it deliberating? Is it perhaps striving to measure how great its own power is? As if that power were somehow outside of itself insofar as it understands it. I say this: if its power were one thing that it learned, and another thing that it spoke. But if it is entirely one, what is it searching for?

->Sight was made, and it strives towards the light of wisdom; light therefore has no need of sight: so neither does the Good itself have need of intellect, or its activity, which by its nature only strives toward this end, that it might receive the light of the Good.<-

### Chapter XXXI.

> *If you say that the Good itself understands, then either it gains nothing by understanding—meaning it understands in vain—or it does gain, and therefore it was not the Good itself previously. If, again, its intelligence contributes to this very thing, so that mutual parts are numbered and the whole is united here, then simplicity does not exist in its intelligence. Where the highest is placed as coming into knowledge as the primary thing, it would have been understood; you do not add reason, imagination, sense, or the eye, lest you add things rashly, or add infinite things to the best. Similarly, where you have granted the immense light of the most sufficient Good, which is the end of intelligence: you ought not to apply intellection to it.*

<margin>A</margin> Now, the gift of understanding seems to have been granted to divine natures—though not the primary ones—as a very grateful lot, like an eye given to those who are by their nature essentially blind. But if the eye itself were light, it would in no way need to look at an object as if it were looking at light. However, he who is in need, being as if dark within himself, seeks light through the eye. Therefore, if the effort of intelligence seeks light, and light does not seek light, then surely the First Nature, since it does not desire light, does not desire to understand. To this Nature, therefore, you ought not to add intelligence; for you will gain nothing from it. <margin>B</margin> And if either the soul or the intellect strives to add it, it is because it itself needs the help of intelligence that it is led to understand. Therefore, the Good neither perceives itself (for it has no need of this) nor is it some kind of duality; indeed, if thinking occurs there, it will be more than two: for the Good itself is not thinking. It would furthermore be necessary for a third to be present—namely, the thing being thought. But if the intellect, the thinking, and the intelligible object are exactly the same, they would certainly be one and entirely confused with themselves; but if they are distinguished, so that one thing is here and another there, then it could not be the First Principle itself. It is necessary, therefore, in considering the best nature, to omit all other things entirely.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> If there is anything inferior, it is with that which has thinking and essence. But if that which is better than thinking exists, the object of thought will be inferior. If thinking is in the Good, it will be inferior, both because it would be contrary to its dignity, and because that which is pure is not in it. Just as with other things and with thinking itself, that which is pure is what it is. But as for the Beginning, we do not even know what it is. If thinking is in it, it is as if it were not pure. What need is there <margin>B</margin> for all things to be together? Perhaps thinking is created as the cause of thought, or it consists in essence, so that it is necessary to make it think something. But even then it will need something beside itself, since the activity of thinking is a certain fulfillment of another thing, or a "con-subsistence." Even before thinking, it has a nature or shame, by which that one also has the power to think, because there is something else before it. It will be in itself, as if learning what <margin>C</margin> it has, coming into itself from another. Where there is nothing else before it, and nothing at all comes to it from another, what will it think or how will it think itself? What would it seek? Or how would it behold its own power, how great it is, as if it were outside <margin>* all things</margin> of itself? According to what it was saying, if it were not another, or if <margin>all things</margin> the power was its own, it would learn; but if it were another, it would have learned. But if it is one, what does it seek?

---

<margin>A</margin> The gift of love seems to be given to those natures which are more divine, yet are the least of them, being like an eye to those who are blind. If the eye were all light itself, why would it need anything? Or if the eye needs something, it has darkness within itself. It seeks light; if it is seeking light, and light is light, it would not have darkness <margin>as a custom</margin> within itself. If the nature itself is light, it no longer needs to think. * <margin>it is necessary</margin> Therefore thinking does not belong to it; for what would it even do? Or what <margin>B</margin> would it add to it? If the intellect needs thinking, it perceives itself and is in need. But that one is rather more than its parts * within itself. <margin>motion</margin> Indeed, thinking is the cause of a third thing—namely, the thought—existing. If these things are known in the intellect, every thing is <margin>for</margin> manifest within itself. If it were divided, it would be another thing again. They would say <margin>* all things</margin> all other things are within it, in the best nature.
