<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the absolute simplicity and self-sufficiency of the "First Principle" (the Good or the One). It further explains why human concepts like "thinking" or "self-knowledge" do not apply to the Good, as these imply a division between the knower and the known.</meta>

<page-num>711</page-num>
<header>BOOK SEVEN.</header>

<margin>
That additions exist in all other things. <note>original: "ὅτι καὶ ἐν πᾶσι προσθῆκαι"</note>
</margin>
...indeed, it requires not a single bit of help. For if "additions" were simply additions, the Good would require nothing. To us, the intelligence within us is a beautiful thing because the soul requires an intellect; but the Good has an intellect—or rather, it is what it is by being the whole, or it is a kind of intellect—or perhaps it does not even "accompany" itself. Nor does "thinking" <note>original: "νόησις" (noesis)</note> reside in it. It would only "accompany" itself by the act of thinking, because to think is to act. If it does not merely act, then it would not have to "receive" anything. For how shall it know itself? It is said that some, because of the multitude within them, have the task of counting themselves and learning how many and what kind of things they are—either they know all things, or nothing, not even what part of them rules or by what criteria they exist. But the Good is itself; it is a matter of greatness <note>original: "μαζωνίας", likely "μεῖζον" (greater)</note>, or according to knowledge, even for those who do not perceive themselves. For it does not even belong to itself, but rather all things belong to it; yet it would only receive itself if it were simultaneously itself and yet something else. For these things are not possible for it. It would not need itself. It would be ridiculous for the same thing to be in need of itself, nor would it look at itself; for that would be a cause of lack, or it would become itself out of the whole. For that which has withdrawn from all things is the source for all things after it. None of the things present in others are present in it. To it belongs all things, just as the one who thinks is the thinking itself, or as essence is in this [thinking], or both together are the first and primary intelligence. Or being, of which there is a word <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note>, just as there is sense or knowledge, because it is not even possible to predicate anything of it as if it were present.

<column-break/>

**A** Indeed, since it requires no assistance: for whatever you might join to a nature that lacks nothing, you would diminish it by the very act of adding. To us, certainly, intelligence is a beautiful thing, because the soul requires an intellect. It is also beautiful to the intellect, because for the intellect, "to be" is the same as "to think," and intelligence itself created the intellect. It is therefore advantageous for the intellect to be joined with intelligence and to always be made conscious of itself, by noticing, clearly, that what is there is one thing made of two. **B** If, however, only a single thing existed, it would surely suffice for itself, and there would be nothing to be received from elsewhere. Now truly, that famous precept, **Know thyself**, only warns those who, because of the multitude implanted within them, are led to enumerate themselves, and to learn how many and what kind of things they possess in themselves which they did not yet know—or perhaps they knew nothing at all: neither what holds the sovereignty, nor by what primary principle they should be judged to exist. **C** If, however, there is something that is "singularly one," it is more excellent than if it had "known" or "understood" itself as a thought: because it is not even "something" to itself. It introduces nothing into itself, but undoubtedly is sufficient in itself. For this reason, it is not "the Good" to itself, but to others. For the remaining things always lack it, but that First thing does not lack itself. That would be ridiculous; for in that way, it would be in need of itself. **D** Therefore, it would not even be necessary for it to look upon itself: for then something would be lacking to it—namely, the very act of looking. All these things, it seems, it has easily granted to the things that follow it, and it appears that nothing of those things which are present to others is present to it anywhere: just as essence <note>original: "essentia", meaning "being" or "substance"</note> is not present to it. Therefore, intellection is not there either: for if essence runs together with intelligence, and both are simultaneously the first and primary intelligence and "being" itself breathing together. For these reasons, Plato says that neither speech, nor sense, nor knowledge can be had of the First: because, clearly, nothing can be predicated of it as an accident <note>original: "accidens"; a logical property that is not part of the essential nature</note>.

---

->*There are three primary principles of things: the Good, the First Mind, and the Soul of the World. Just as the affections in the Soul of the World*<-
->*should not be placed in the members of the world generated from there, and just as the moving discourses and affections of the soul should not be placed*<-
->*in the intellect, so finally the species of intelligence, which are proper to the intellect, should not be attributed to the Good. Chapter 42.*<-

---

BUT whenever you are in doubt about the First, or you seek where these things should be placed, reasoning about them as you are being perfected: put these things aside. Do not consider them as holy things <note>original: "σεμνὰ"</note> among the second things, nor place the second things in the First, nor the third in the second. Rather, place the second things around the First, and the third things around the second. For in this way, you will allow each to stand as it is, and you will hang the later things from the earlier ones, just as those things are revealed, existing by themselves. Therefore, it is rightly said in this way concerning the King of all: all things are around him, and all things are for his sake—all things that exist—as he says "for his sake," since he is the cause of their being, and they reach out for him as something different from all of them. For there is nothing innate that is present in those things [the others], or else it would no longer be "all things." He is the cause of all the other things after him. But is he "all things" in this way? He is the cause of all things, as one who speaks of all beautiful things.

<column-break/>

**A** YOU, however, when you are in doubt concerning these matters, and you ask where these things are primarily to be placed, having been drawn to these things by the discourse of reason—cast away these very things which you think are to be honored in the following levels. Cast them down into the subsequent levels. Neither apply the second things to the First, nor join the third things to the second: but rather place the second things around the First, and the third things around the second. In this way, you will permit each thing to remain as it is in itself, and you will suspend the following things from those [prior ones], as if they were spreading themselves out everywhere around them, while those prior ones meanwhile consist in themselves. **B** Because of this reason, it is also rightly written by Plato: **around the king of all things, all things are; for his sake are all things; he himself is the cause of all beautiful things.** When he says "all things," he understands all "beings" <note>original: "entia"</note>. He adds "and for his sake," and not without justice, since he is the cause of those things which indeed desire him, as one who is so diverse from all of them. **C** Nor does he have anything of those things which belong to them; otherwise, they would not be "above all things," if any of those things which are after him happened to be in him. If, therefore, the intellect is also counted in the number of "all things," it follows that the intellect is not in him. Furthermore, when he calls him the cause, he means the God of all beautiful things.

He establishes a hierarchy where the "First" (the Good) is the center around which "Second" (Intellect) and "Third" (Soul) principles are organized.</summary>

<page-num>734</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS, BOOK VI.</header>

...of all, he seems to place beauty in the **Forms** <note>Latin: *speciebus*; Greek: *εἴδεσι* (eidesi). In Neoplatonism, these are the eternal archetypes of all things.</note>, but the supreme God is properly established above this whole beauty found in the Forms. Therefore, since he placed these intelligible things <note>The realm of pure thought or the Divine Mind.</note> in the second degree, he subsequently transmits the third level of subjects, namely those which come after them. Then, around the third level, he places those things which are born from the third—namely, this world of ours, which depends upon the **Soul**. But since these third things, that is, those pertaining to the soul, are subject to the **Mind** <note>Latin: *mens*; Greek: *νοῦς* (Nous), the Divine Intellect.</note>, and the Mind is brought back to the **Good** <note>The "Good" or the "One" is the ultimate source in Plotinus’s philosophy.</note>, so indeed all things are reduced to it by certain fixed steps: some indeed are most close to it, while others are adhered to those closest things. But among all things, the sensible <note>Physical things perceived by the senses.</note> objects are farthest distant from it, as they are continuously referred back to the soul.

<column-break/>

<margin>the things after these <note>original: *τὰ μετὰ ταῦτα*</note></margin>
<margin>the things dependent on him <note>original: *τὰ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀνηρτημένα*</note></margin>
...he appears to place beauty in the Forms, but he himself is above beauty, and those things then follow; these he says are the "third" things which are hung from them, the things which come into being after them. And concerning the third things, he clearly places those things which come into being from the third—this world—into the Soul. As the Soul is dependent on the Intellect, and the Intellect on the Good, so all things are directed toward that [the Good] through intermediaries: some being near, others being neighbors to those which are near, and finally the sensible things, which are the last of the sensibles, being dependent upon the Soul.

# PLOTINUS
## ENNEAD VI.
### BOOK 8.

# PLOTINUS
## THE SIXTH ENNEAD,
### BOOK VIII.
#### ON the voluntary and the will of the One.
#### CONCERNING the freedom & will of the One.

-> *What is voluntary for us is that which we ourselves do by a free and certain will. Free, that is, compelled by no violence. Certain, that is, slipped into by no ignorance; concerning this, we are truly masters. Chapter I.* <-

<margin>A</margin>
Is it proper to inquire even regarding the Gods, whether anything is placed in their **will** <note>Latin: *arbitrio*; Greek: *ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς* (ep' autois, "up to them"). Refers to free choice or power.</note> or not, or is it rather more fitting to ask such a thing regarding men, on account of their weakness and their doubtful capacity? For it must be granted that the Gods are able to do all things: and that not only is something placed in their will, but indeed all things are so placed. Or perhaps we ought to attribute all power and the free will of all things to the **One** alone: but in the others, some things are this way, and others that way; and in certain cases, one might assert that both states exist equally by reason. Or rather, must these things be investigated? We must indeed dare to search out such a thing even in the first things, and in that which is above all. By what condition, clearly, must that which is usually said be understood: that it is "placed in their power," even though we grant they can do all things. Furthermore, concerning this which we call "to be able," it must be duly considered how it is rightly said, lest perhaps by speaking thus we admit that among the Gods one thing is **potentiality** <term>Potentiality: the capacity to become or do something (Latin: *potentia*).</term> and another is **act** <term>Act: the actual realization or exercise of a power (Latin: *actu*).</term>: and we might perhaps grant a future act. But these things, it seems, should be deferred for later, and the same must first be investigated in ourselves, regarding whom it is usually investigated if anything is placed in our power. First, therefore, we must ask what this very thing is said to be, that which is said to be "in us," that is, established in our own power. We must ask, I say, what the definition of this faculty is: for thus it will be known in a certain way, whether it applies also to the Gods, and even more...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Whether even in the case of the gods, one should seek if anything is up to them, or if it is only among the weaknesses and disputed powers of men that it is fitting to seek what is "up to" whom? Should we grant to the gods that they are able to do all things, and that not just something, but everything is up to them?
<margin>B</margin>
Or should we grant all things to the One, and for the others, some things are this way and others that way? Or should these things also be sought? We must dare to seek even regarding the first things, and that which is highest of all, what "up to him" actually is, even if we grant he can do all things. And yet, this "being able," we must consider how it is said, lest perhaps we say one thing is potentiality and another is act, and an act that is yet to be.
<margin>C</margin>
But these things must be postponed for the present. We must first seek in ourselves if anything happens to be "up to us." First we must ask what it is, this that is said to be "up to us." What is the concept of such a thing? For in this way we might know if it applies to the gods, and even more so...

# BOOK EIGHT.
<sig>Qq 3</sig>

<column-break/>

Whether it is fitting to transfer these concepts to God <note>original: *Deū*; Greek: *θεὸν* (theon). In this context, Plotinus refers to the "One" or the supreme Principle.</note> himself, or not. Or rather, if it is appropriate, it must nevertheless be investigated how something may be placed within their judgment, both in other beings and especially in the highest ones. What then are we thinking when we say something is "in our power" <note>original: *in nobis*; Greek: *ἐφ’ ἡμῖν* (eph’ hemin). This is a technical term in Greek philosophy for things that are within a person's control or moral responsibility.</note>? What is the cause for our inquiry into this? Driven, I believe, by contrary fortunes and joined to adverse necessities, or being snatched away by the violent attacks of perturbations <note>Emotional disturbances or passions.</note> that cloud the mind, B we have certainly come to think that all these things have power over us. Serving them, and being cast headlong wherever they drag us, we have deservedly fallen into this controversy, fearing that perhaps we ourselves are nothing, and nothing stands within our own authority. It is as if "what is in our power" would be that state where, at some point, we are serving neither fortunes, nor necessities, nor violent perturbations, and we may act by our own will, with nothing in the meantime opposing that will. C If this is so, the logic of that which consists in our judgment will be of such a kind that it serves the will, and is either done or not done according to what we ourselves want. Now, a thing is "voluntary" <note>original: *voluntariū*</note> when it is performed both without violence and with knowledge; it is "in our power" if we are the masters of the action. Yet both of these often coincide, even though their definitions differ; sometimes, however, they seem to disagree. Just as if someone were to have the authority D to kill a man, yet it does not become voluntary for him after he has done it if he did not know the man he killed was his father <note>A reference to the tragedy of Oedipus, used here as a classic philosophical example of an act that is "in our power" (the physical act of striking) but not "voluntary" (killing a parent) due to ignorance.</note>. Perhaps, however, this very thing which is called "voluntary" will never be at odds with the judgment of one who possesses true free will. Indeed, knowledge regarding what is called "voluntary" ought to be held not only concerning individual instances, but entirely and simply. Tell me, why should it be judged an involuntary homicide if he is ignorant that the man is his father or a friend? But if he is ignorant of whether it is fitting to commit murder, should that not also be deemed involuntary? But if it is said that such a man is not considered to have acted involuntarily because he *ought* to have learned this, certainly it is not voluntary to be ignorant of what one ought to learn, or even of that which prevents one from learning.

<column-break/>

We do not act as truly free masters of an action insofar as we act according to the movement of the soul incited by the senses and the affections of the senses from external bodies, or even from our own body. Now, when the movement is thus incited, reason either does nothing, or is led by the movement, or leads it. In the first and second stages, we are slaves to bodies and fortune; in the third, while we seem to govern the body and similar things with a certain authority, we still comply with and live by external things, we indulge necessity, and we do not live with that tranquility which we desire. Therefore, we are not entirely free masters.

-> Chapter II. <-

It remains to investigate this very thing which is referred to us as being "in our power," and to which faculty it is most appropriate to attribute it. For we shall say it consists either in impulse and a certain appetite, such as that which is usually done through anger or concupiscence <note>Strong desire or lust.</note>; or you might confer it upon the reasoning process of the mind itself, along with appetite, assigning to it the duty of whether something is done or not done. But if we attribute it to anger and concupiscence, we will be forced to B admit that children and wild animals, as well as the mad and those entirely alienated from their minds—likewise those ensnared by poisons or occupied by sudden hallucinations—possess the gift of free judgment, even though they cannot be masters of the things we are describing. But if we grant free will to the discourse of reason joined with appetite, we must then ask...

<column-break/>

**A** Whether free will belongs to an erring reason, or rather to right reason <note>original: *recta ratio*; the Stoic and Platonic concept of reason aligned with the natural and moral order.</note> and right appetite. Furthermore, one might ask here whether reasoning incites the appetite, or vice versa, whether the appetite incites the reasoning. For if the appetites are according to nature, we may distinguish them thus: If they belong to the "composite animal" <note>The human being as a combination of soul and physical body.</note>, they will follow the necessity of the soul's nature; but if they belong to the soul alone, many things that are now said to be "within our power" will seem to happen outside of it. Furthermore, a certain "bare reasoning" <note>Reasoning stripped of emotional or moral weight.</note> usually precedes the passions; likewise, imagination itself compels us, and appetite—drawn by the demands of necessity—pulls us along. In what way then, in these matters, **B** does it make us masters? Again, in what way are we the masters of that which is called "master"? For that which is in need necessarily desires to be filled; surely it is not the master of that toward which it is entirely led. Finally, how can there be any "choice" <note>original: *arbitrij*</note> in that which depends on another, and has its principle in another, and is produced from there in whatever form? Clearly, it lives according to that principle, and lives exactly as it has been formed. Otherwise, if this were said to have **C** choice, then inanimate things would also be granted the same. For even fire acts exactly as it was generated. But if it is argued that the difference lies in the fact that the animal and the soul know what they are doing, we must distinguish this: if they know it by sense alone, how would this condition help them to act by free choice? For the senses, perceiving only, do not make one the master of an action. But if it is said that something is done freely by some knowledge other than sense, it will further be asked whether this knowledge is of the thing being done; and here too it will be proved that the soul only *knows*, but is led by something else to the *doing*. But if, besides appetite, reason **D** or a certain knowledge acts and dominates, we must investigate to what it primarily refers, and where and how this occurs. And if reason itself creates another appetite, we must assume how it does so. But if someone says that reason consists in itself by calming the appetite, and that free choice is placed in this state, then certainly it will not consist in *action*, but will reside in the *mind*. For whatever is involved in acting, even if reason prevails, is something "mixed," and it does not possess that pure function of choice by which it can be judged to be truly "in our power."

**A** [Translation of the Greek text] ...to reason, or to right reason and right appetite; and one might further inquire here whether reason moves the appetite or the appetite moves reason. For if the appetites are according to nature, one belongs to the animal as a composite, the soul having come to the necessity of nature. But if it belongs to the soul alone, many of the things said to be "in our power" would then be carried outside of us. Furthermore, **B** if a bare reasoning precedes the passions, or if imagination compels the appetite toward *whatever* it leads, dragging it along, how is there *proper action* in these things? Or how are we masters at all, we who are led? For that which is in need, desiring fulfillment by necessity, is not master of that toward which it hastens; for it is led. How can that which is "from itself" exist at all, when it belongs to another and has its beginning from another? And from wherever it has been generated, such it is. And it lives **C** by that, and as it has been molded; so that even inanimate things would follow what is "in their power," acting as they were generated. Like fire. But if it is because the living being and the soul *know* what they do—if it is by sense, what is added to its being "in their power," if the sense has not made the work its own, but only saw it? If it is by knowledge, and if it is knowledge of what is being done, then here too it only knows, but something else leads it to the act. But if reason, beyond the appetite, **D** produces knowledge and prevails: we must seek to what it refers, and how it happens to someone. And if reason itself makes another appetite, how is it to be taken? But if it is by the ceasing of appetite: then "what is in our power" would stand here, not in this action... *but in the standing* <note>original: *ἐν τῷ στῆναι*; a reference to the soul being "at rest" or stable in contemplation.</note> of the soul. Everything of ours that is desirable is entirely and separately reason; but that which is in action is something mixed, and could not purely have "what is in our power."

->*Just as there are two levels of faculty, so there are two levels of liberty. One, however, is the middle between both. Chapter III.*<-

> For he is a slave who follows imagination alone and is incited by our body or by external bodies; likewise, he is a slave whose reason entirely indulges this imagination. He is free in the first sense who lives by the mind alone, content with contemplation, having entirely neglected all other things. He is free in the second sense who, if he does anything else, chooses it only according to the laws received from contemplation, and refers the things to be done back to contemplation. He seems to be a mixture of a certain liberty and servitude who subjects the imagination to right reason, but chooses the active life (otherwise an honorable one) as an end.

But perhaps it is fitting to add: in right reason *including* knowledge <note>original: *scientiam*; Greek: *ἐπιστήμης* (epistemes).</note>. For if someone has acted by having a "right opinion" <note>original: *rectè opinatus*; Greek: *δόξασεν ὀρθῶς*. **A** and those acting of themselves, how should we define self-determination? Indeed, we might say that imagination is the cause of certain things—specifically that imagination which is stirred up by the sufferings of the body, such as the search for food and drink. These needs mold a sort of imagination, a part of which seeks an endless filling; we are even imagined into states by the individual qualities of the fluids <note>original: *humorum*; the "humors" or bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which ancient medicine believed determined a person's physical and mental state.</note> in the body, which stimulate various types of imagination. If we must seek where to place these actions, we certainly do not count them as being in a state of liberty. Therefore, for the wicked who do most things according to these sorts of imaginations, we shall grant neither free authority over their actions nor the gift of the "voluntary." Instead, we shall grant free choice <note>original: *arbitrium proculdubio liberum*</note> to that person who acts through the mind, free from all bodily passions. In this way, we lead the power of free action back to its most beautiful principle: the activity of the mind <note>original: *actum mentis*; Plotinus identifies true freedom with the Intellect (Nous) acting according to its own nature, rather than reacting to external or bodily stimuli.</note>. <margin>The healthy mind. Therefore through action and...</margin> We shall also grant that the propositions and deliberations proceeding from there are free, as well as the appetites <note>original: *appetitiones*; the reaching out of the soul toward an object.</note> stirred by the intellect. We will say that the gods live in this manner, for their life is directed by a mind and a desire that follows the mind.

<column-break/>

->*Since the nature of liberty consists in a certain free movement, so that they are turned toward willing the good, the intellect proceeds freely and with voluntary movement when it moves with certainty toward its own true good, both in acting and in governing.*<-

### Chapter IV.

> Furthermore, if the mind understands, wills, chooses, and acts according to its own nature, it is not for that reason said to be "driven," because this very thing is primarily voluntary to it. Nor is it led to this by anything foreign; nor should the action of the intellect be said to "serve" the nature of the intellect. For there, the action is the nature itself, and it is not compelled by anything, since it is within the Good itself. For since this very thing which is called "existing by its own right" <note>original: *sui iuris*; a legal term meaning "of one's own right" or independent.</note> must be willed by reason of and by the grace of the Good, the intellect is most of all "of its own right" when it is closest to the Supreme Good.

**A** **BUT** someone may inquire here: in what way is that which occurs according to appetite <term>appetite: a desire or inclination toward something</term> made free? For appetite leads toward something external and involves much need. For that which desires is "led," even if it is led toward the good. Furthermore, we must doubt the Mind itself in the same way: if it acts according to how it is naturally constituted, can it be said to have liberty and the principle of action within itself, when it is not within its power *not* to act? **B** Moreover, it is worth asking whether "free choice" is properly judged to exist in those to whom action does not even belong. Yet, for those to whom action does belong, necessity is often introduced from the outside; for they do not act entirely at random or without some proposed end. But how will liberty be preserved for those who are entirely servants to their own nature? On the contrary, one might object: how can that which is not forced to follow another be said to "serve"? **C** And how can something be "compelled" while it is being carried toward the good, since the appetite itself is voluntary, provided it recognizes <margin>To choose the good is good. For the "involuntary" is a turning away from the good.</margin> that it is good and proceeds toward it as toward the good? For the involuntary is, in fact, a certain abduction from the good itself. "Compulsion" or "violence" is said of that which is carried toward that which is not good for it. A thing truly "serves" when it does not have the authority to proceed toward its own good, but is led away from its own goods by some more powerful force, serving that force in the meantime. For this reason, slavery <note>original: *servitus*; here used philosophically to mean being governed by something other than one's own reason.</note> is condemned—not when someone lacks the license to go toward evil, but when they are unable to reach their own good, being dragged meanwhile toward the good of another.

<summary>Plotinus distinguishes between actions driven by bodily needs (not free) and those driven by the Intellect (true freedom). He argues that being "compelled" toward the Good is not slavery, because true liberty is the ability to attain one's own natural good.</summary>

Serving its own nature would make it two: that which serves and that which is served. But a simple nature—a single act—which does not have one part in potentiality <note>original: *in potentia*; the capacity to become something else</note> and another in actuality, why should it not be free? Indeed, it is not proper to say it "works" according to its nature, as if its essence and its action were two different things; in that realm, to be and to act are the same. Therefore, if it does not act for the sake of another, nor exists within another, what prevents it from living freely? And even if it is not proper to say "it is in its own power" in the way we say it elsewhere, the mind here is still something distinct because it is said to "be in itself." It is judged to be in itself because it is not in another, nor is any other the master of its action. Nor is any other the master of its essence, since the mind is a principle. And although the intellect has another principle <note>The "Good" or the "One," which Plotinus identifies as the source of the Intellect.</note>, it does not hold that principle outside of itself, but within the Good itself. And if the intellect is good according to that principle, then much more does this "being in itself" and this freedom belong to it, since everyone seeks freedom and self-possession for the sake of the Good. If, therefore, it acts according to the Good, it possesses even more of what is called "being in its own power" and free will. For it already possesses that which turns toward itself, seen from within itself; it is in itself because it is oriented toward the Good. This is better for it—to be in itself only if it is oriented toward the Good.

### Chapter V.
> The sage knows that many inconveniences—which he would hardly wish for—will often happen to his family, his body, and his mind. He has deliberated to apply timely remedies to these according to his strength. All these things he has arranged in his mind to be voluntary so far as they depend on him; but the actions that follow daily, meeting involuntary troubles, are not so much under his own legal control, but depend in a certain way on opportunity.

<margin>A</margin> Is freedom and free will placed only in the pure and thinking intellect? Or is it also found in the soul when it operates according to the intellect and acts according to virtue? Now, if we attribute this to one who acts, perhaps it should not be attributed to the results of the action. For we are not masters of the consequences. But if we define freedom as the ability to arrange one's duties honorably, perhaps that is correct. But how can that be "within us"? For example, if it is said that because a war breaks out, we exercise the duty of courage. I ask: how can we judge an action practiced at that time to be "within us," since if the battle did not surround us, we would not be granted the chance to use such an action? The same applies to all other actions composed of virtue: virtue itself is always compelled to do this or that according to what happens. Indeed, if one gave virtue the choice of whether it would prefer for disasters to happen—such as looming wars—so that it could demonstrate the duties of courage; or for injustices to be committed so that it could define what is right and settle disputes; or for poverty to oppress so that it could show the gifts of liberality... or if it would rather live in quiet with all things rightly at peace? Without a doubt, virtue would choose a vacation from such actions! It would prefer that no one needed its healing care. It is just as if a legitimate physician, such as Hippocrates <note>The famous ancient Greek physician, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, were to hope that no one should ever need his medicines. If, therefore, virtue consists in actions—

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry into free will and self-determination. While the previous page established that the pure Intellect (the "Nous") is inherently free because it exists within itself and the Good, this page examines how that freedom extends to human virtue and action within the world.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT.

<column-break/>

### Chapter VI.

*Not only should the Intellect, which is satisfied by contemplation alone, be thought to live freely for itself, but reason also—through the virtue it receives from the Intellect—dwells in freedom. This is because it does not set the outcome of outward actions as its goal, but rather moral integrity and internal contemplation.*

*The First Intellect lives with the greatest freedom, for in that realm, to live is to understand. It understands exactly as it wills, for there, will and intelligence are scarcely distinct; indeed, they are essentially the same act. That which is called "will" when turning toward the Good is named "intelligence" when it is drawn by the power of that Good. Just as a ray of light is related to its own brilliance in a clear reflection, and since the Greatest Good is the most voluntary of all things, the Intellect lives most fully as it wills and is free, spending its life within the Good itself.*

<column-break/>

If an action seems to be compelled, how could it be considered pure? How could the power over one's own life consist in such a thing? Shall we then admit that while actions themselves are necessary, the will and the reason that precede the actions are entirely unforced? If we place self-determination <note>original: *autexousion*; the power to act by one's own authority</note> only in what precedes the deed—in virtue itself—then we are surely placing freedom and that which is "up to us" outside of the physical action. 

But what shall we say of virtue itself when considered as a habit <note>original: *habitum*; a stable disposition of character</note> or a state of being? Does it not come to a weakened soul to heal its disturbances and organize its desires? In what way, then, do we say that being good is within our own power, and that virtue "has no master"? <note>A reference to Plato’s Republic: "Virtue has no master; as a man honors or dishonors her, so shall he have more or less of her."</note> Perhaps we should say it is "up to us" because we are the ones who will it and choose it. Perhaps it is because virtue, when present, provides the very freedom and self-governance we speak of, no longer permitting us to be slaves to the things we served before. If virtue is like a "second intellect," a disposition that transforms the soul into a mind, then this "power over ourselves" does not lean toward outward actions, but draws the soul back toward the mind, freeing it from the need to act.

<margin>A</margin> If virtue is compelled to bring help to what is safe, in what way does it possess that gift purely? How can we judge the matter to consist entirely in virtue itself? 

<margin>B</margin> Shall we say that actions are indeed necessary, but the will and the reason that precede them are uncompelled? If we place the choice only in that which comes before the doing, we place freedom in virtue's authority. But what of virtue as a disposition? Does it not approach a weary soul to cure its passions and cravings? 

<margin>C</margin> By what reasoning do we say being good is in our power and virtue serves no one? Perhaps we find it in ourselves when we are willing and choosing. Perhaps because virtue, by its presence, prepares that freedom and "what is up to us," and does not let us serve our former masters. If virtue is like another intellect, a habit transforming the soul into the mind, then that which is "up to us" does not decline toward outward actions, but returns to the mind, released from the stir of deeds.

---

<margin>A</margin> **BUT** by what reason did we previously trace this gift to the will, saying that what is "in our power" is that which happens according to our will? Truly, the answer must be that it was also implied that it might *not* happen. Therefore, if these current points are correct and agree with the previous ones, we shall assert that Mind and Virtue are the mistresses of ourselves, and to them should be referred both freedom and what is "up to us." 

<margin>B</margin> Since two things are preserved here, we must think that the Mind sits within itself, while Virtue wills to rest within itself—meaning the soul presides so that it might be good. Up to this point, the soul remains free, and the mind makes it free. But when necessary passions and actions occur, virtue applies itself to governing them, though it never willed for these troubles to happen in the first place. Nevertheless, even in these trials, virtue preserves the self-determination of the will, provided that it refers every one of these circumstances back to itself. 

<margin>C</margin> For virtue does not follow the event as if it simply wished to save a person in danger; rather, if it judges it better for itself, it casts the person aside and commands them to throw away money, children, country, and even life itself—establishing as its goal not the safety of lower things, but its own moral beauty <note>original: *honestatem*; the Latin translation of the Greek 'Kalon', meaning noble or morally beautiful</note>. 

From this, it appears that freedom and "what is in our power" among the things we do refers neither to the success of the action, nor to the external deed, but entirely to the internal act: the intelligence and contemplation of virtue itself. 

<margin>D</margin> One must consider this virtue to be a kind of mind; it does not include those passions that are enslaved by reason or merely tempered by it. Speaking of these lower things, Plato says that, like the way we care for the body, these are usually corrected and directed through habit and exercise. From this, it is more clearly established that freedom belongs to the reality that is independent of action.

<sig>Q q 4</sig>

<summary>Plotinus argues that true freedom and "what is up to us" do not reside in the success of outward actions, but in the internal state of the mind and virtue. He explains that while we must often react to necessary circumstances, virtue remains free by prioritizing moral beauty and contemplation over physical safety.</summary>

Therefore, whatever things are done from this and because of this, remain within us: and both outside and yet within itself, it is that which it wills and performs, entirely unhindered. ### Cap. VII.

-> *If servitude and chance are concerned with lower things, but liberty and order pertain to higher things, and that which is higher is equally more orderly and more free, surely the Principle of all things is neither accidental nor coerced; since it is the origin of all order and free authority. In which, since the whole nature of the will resides as the highest Good, it is also the whole nature of liberty. Where, if only essence and action could be named, one cannot say that action serves essence: since there is no distinction there. Therefore, just as it exists naturally, so it acts; and conversely, as it acts, so it naturally exists. But of these things we have said enough in our Theology.* <-

The soul, therefore, becomes free through the Mind <note>original: *mens*; the higher rational faculty</note>, moving toward the Good without hindrance. Whatever it does for this reason remains within itself. The Intellect, however, is free through itself. The nature of the Good itself is that which all things desire, and because of it, other things have their own stability. While others may reach the Good without hindrance, the Principle already possesses it. It is the Master of all things, held precious by those below it, sitting on the primary throne. All other things wish to ascend toward it, hanging from it and receiving their power from it, through which they can have the gift of what remains within them. How could anyone reduce this supreme condition to the level of what is specifically called "mine" or "yours"? Since the Intellect itself barely reaches this condition, and seems to be pulled as if by force: unless perhaps some reckless argument, introduced from elsewhere, suggests that the First Nature <note>The One or the Absolute</note> happened by chance to be as it is, and is not the mistress of its own existence; namely, since this very thing which it is does not come from itself, and therefore lacks liberty and self-determination: because it does or does not do what it must do or not do, being already compelled by necessity. This speech is surely turned against itself, and is uncertain; it removes the entire nature and reason of the voluntary, the free, and that which is "up to us." It makes these words empty names for things that exist nowhere. For the author of that speech is compelled to confess that not only is there no authority in anyone...

<column-break/>

the immaterial is free, as is the concept of what is "up to us" <term>up to us: translation of *eph' hēmin*, the philosophical term for self-determination</term>, and this Will is mistress and exists within itself; even if it should command anything regarding external things, it does so out of necessity. If what is "up to us" comes from or through this, then it is external and yet within itself. It wills and acts without hindrance; this is primary in us. The contemplative and first Intellect <note>original: *nous*</note> is thus "up to itself," because its work <margin>not</margin> exists in another in any way, but is entirely turned toward itself. Or rather, its work is itself. Existing in the Good, being without need and full, it lives according to its will. This will is thought. It is called "will" because it follows the intellect; what is called will imitates the intellect. For the will wants the Good. True understanding is in the Good. The Intellect, then, has what the will wants, and by attaining it, it becomes intelligence. If we place what is "up to us" in the will for the Good, being already established where the will wants to be, how could it not have its own self? Or we must assume nothing exists, if one does not wish to ascend to this self-determination.

The soul becomes free through the Intellect, moving toward the Good without hindrance. What it does because of this is within itself. The Intellect is "up to itself." The nature of the Good is the object of desire. Because of it, other things have what is "up to themselves" when they can attain it without hindrance. ### *It is not permitted to imagine that it happened by chance that this very thing which is now the principle of all things is the principle of all things, as if it could have happened that another and differently-disposed thing would be the principle. Chapter IX.*

For the reason of the principle is unique, namely the summit itself, which we can also name infinity; since it imposes stability and necessity upon other things, especially those closer to it, it is rightly not by chance, but by necessity—rather, it is necessity itself. <meta>This page continues the discussion from page 740 regarding the "First Principle" (the One). <margin>
* "That which happened by chance." <note>original: *τὸ δὲ ὅπως ἔτυχεν*</note>
</margin>
In those things that follow from the First Principle, necessity <term>Necessity</term> <note>original: *anankē*; the cosmic force of logical or physical inevitability</note> holds sway; yet even this does not impose violence upon them. This Principle possesses its uniqueness and singularity from itself. This very thing, therefore, is not something else; but it must be as it was appropriate for it to be. It did not happen to be this way by chance, but rather, it *ought* to be thus. This very "ought" <note>the concept of "that which is necessary" or "fitting"</note> is the principle of all things that ought to exist. Therefore, this Principle is in no way a result of chance, for it does not exist as if by a lucky accident; rather, it is what it was necessary for it to be. Indeed, it is not even merely that which it *behooved* it to be. Now, it is fitting for other things to wait for what might appear to them, and for each to assert itself just as it has come to be. Certainly, the Principle does not appear as a mere accident, but as truly King <note>original: *basileus*; a metaphor for the supreme governing principle of the universe</note>, truly Principle, and truly Good. Nor does it act merely *according* to the good, for in that case, it would seem to follow something else; rather, it is this very thing which exists entirely as itself. Thus, it does not act according to the good, but it is, in its very essence, the Good itself. If, therefore, not even within "Being" itself <note>original: *ens* / *on*; the realm of true existence and Intellect</note> is there anything contingent—otherwise, being would be a mere accident <margin>* The vessel <note>original: *τὸ σκεῦος*</note></margin>—and certainly if something were to happen to some being, yet Being itself does not "happen" in any way, nor did it obtain its nature by some stroke of luck. It did not receive its way of being from another, but the very nature of Being is to exist as being. How then could anyone imagine that in that which stands superior to Being, such a condition of "happening" or "chance" could exist? Especially since the Principle itself generated Being. It did not happen by chance, but is as it is: the Essence itself existing as <margin>* Truly <note>original: *ὄντως*</note></margin> that which is Essence, and that which is <margin>* Cause <note>original: *αἴτιος*</note></margin> Intellect <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: *nous*; the divine Mind containing the Forms</note>. Otherwise, by a similar logic, one might say that Intellect also happened by chance, as if Intellect could have been something other than what its nature is. Therefore, that which does not transcend its own nature, nor ever <margin>* So that <note>original: *ὥστε*</note></margin> declines from itself, one might easily call "existing" in the highest sense. What then shall he say who has transcended even this and gazed upon the Supreme? Shall he say that just as he saw the Principle to be, so it also "happened" to be? But surely <margin>* "It did not set it forth" or "It did not offer it" <note>original: *οὐ παρέτι τὶ τοδὴ / ἐξέθηκε*</note></margin> one must not say it "happened" in this or any other way, nor indeed that it happened at all, simply and entirely. Can it then be said to be "only thus" and not otherwise, but "just so"? Nay, not even this "thus" or "in this manner" should be assigned to it; otherwise, you would be circumscribing it and making it into a "this thing." Indeed, he who perceives it ought not to say "thus" nor "not thus," for otherwise you would be naming it as one of the number of things to which the terms "thus" or "in this manner" are usually applied. It is, therefore, something else beyond all things that are said to be "thus" or to have "this manner." But when you have found it to be infinite, you will be able to speak of all things that <margin>* Of Nature / * Properly <note>original: *Φύσεως / * κυρίως*</note></margin> come after it. But you will say that the Principle is none of them, but is like an all-encompassing power truly mistress of itself, existing as it wills. In truth, it projects this very "willing" into the things that exist, while it itself is more excellent than any act of will, and subjects such an act to itself. Therefore, it did not even "will" itself to be "thus," as if it spoke to itself, nor did anyone else effect it so that it would be "thus."

<column-break/>

**A** In those things that follow the principle, necessity dominates: nor does this indeed bring violence upon them. This unique and singular thing it possesses from itself. This itself, therefore, is not another: but that which it was expedient for it to be, it must be. Therefore it did not so happen, but it was necessary thus. This very thing which is called "it was necessary," is the principle of all things that ought to be. This, therefore, is in no way as it happened, for it does not exist as if it fell by chance: but that which it was necessary to be: indeed, not even that which it behooved to be. **B** Now indeed it is fitting for other things to wait for what might appear to them at any time, and only that which exists, that he should altogether assert; certainly not as it appeared by chance, but truly king, truly principle, truly good. Nor indeed acting according to the good, for thus it would seem to follow another, but this one thing itself which is, existing inwardly, so that it does not act according to the good, but is itself entirely the good. If therefore not even in being itself is there anything contingent: otherwise being would be a certain thing, **C** and certainly to a certain being something would happen, yet being itself did not happen in any way, nor by some chance did it obtain that being itself should be thus: nor did it receive from another to be being as it is, but the very nature of being is for being to exist: in what way could anyone think that in that which stands superior to being, this condition—namely that it so happened or turned out—could exist? Since indeed that one generated being itself. Which indeed did not so happen, but is as it is: essence itself existing as that very thing which is essence, and that very thing which is **D** intellect: otherwise by some similar reason he might have said that intellect also happened thus, just as if intellect could have been some other thing besides this which its nature exists as. That which therefore does not transcend its own nature, nor ever declines from itself, one might easily call this very thing which is "to exist." What then will he say who has also transcended this, and looked upon the highest? Will he say that just as he saw it to behave, so also it happened? But certainly **E** it must not be said to have happened either thus or in any way, nay, not even entirely and simply to have happened. Can it then be said "only thus," and not otherwise, but "at least thus"? Nay, not even this very thing which is called "thus," or "in this manner," is to be assigned to it: otherwise in that way you would circumscribe it, and render it "this certain thing." Surely he who discerns it, ought neither to say "thus," nor "not thus," otherwise you would say it is something from the number of things in which this very thing is present, which is usually said "thus" or "in this manner." It is therefore another thing besides all things, which **F** are said to be "thus" and "in this manner." But you, when you have found it infinite, will be able to say all things which are after it. But you will say that it is none of them, but as it were a universal power truly mistress of itself, existing as it wills. Indeed, casting this very thing which it wills into the things themselves, while clearly it is more excellent than every act of will, and subjects an act of this kind to itself. Therefore, it did not even will this very thing, which is said to be "thus," so that it said it to itself, nor did any other person effect that it should be "thus."

*Since the principle imposes form, limit, and order upon all things, and rational order is the opposite of fortune, deservedly if the principle had fallen to things by chance, no order would remain anywhere. Because the principle is uniquely and firmly so, and reminds us that what already exists is not obtained from elsewhere: for this is its very nature. Nor is any weakness the cause, so that nothing else existed, nor could it have proceeded to another. For to be and to remain in immense goodness and power, this is itself the highest liberty as well as power.* ->Chapter X.<-

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the "First Principle" (the One or God). Having previously argued that the One is not subject to external compulsion, Plotinus now addresses the claim that the One might simply exist by "chance" or "accident." # PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

A ONE MAY ASK the person who says that God happened to be this way: under what condition do they think it possible to catch "contingency" <term>contingency</term> <note>original: *contingentia*; the quality of being accidental or not necessarily the way it is</note> being false, if indeed it were ever false? In what way could one take away contingency itself? Yet, if there were a nature that removed contingency from the equation, then surely the condition of the "contingent" would not fit with that nature. For if you commit this very thing—nature—to the hands of fortune, there will never be anything that does not come about by chance. However, the very Principle of all other things removes "fortuitous contingency" <note>original: *fortuitam contingentiam*; essentially "dumb luck"</note> from all things, by bestowing upon each one its species, its boundary, and its form; it is not right to ascribe this sequence of fortune to things so arranged by reason.

B But in assigning the cause to Reason here, we think a cause ought to be provided. However, Fortune <term>Fortune</term> <note>original: *fortuna* / *tychē*; the personification of chance and luck</note> occupies itself with those things that are neither done by a prior purpose nor proceed in a sequential order, but rather fall out by accident. Truly, how could anyone concede that the very principle of all reason, order, and limit could be merged into some kind of accidental lot?

C Fortune is certainly the mistress of many things, but she cannot generate intellect, reason, and order. Indeed, since fortune appears to be the opposite of reason, it can in no way be the mother of reason. If, therefore, fortune does not generate intellect, it deservedly does not generate that which is higher and better than intellect. For it could not have had a source from which to create it, nor did fortune exist at all, nor is it present in eternal things. For this reason, if there is nothing above

D that One, and it existed first, it is best to stop our steps there, and say nothing further about it, but rather to investigate how the things following it were made. As for that Principle, one should in no way search for how it arose, since in truth it was never born. What then if it was not born, but is as it is—not strictly being the "master" of its own essence? For if it is not the master of its essence, but exists as this very thing that it is, not providing existence to itself but using itself however it may be, then this very thing which it is must exist by necessity, and never otherwise.

E But surely it is not in this state because it *could* not be otherwise, but because it is the "Best" <term>The Best</term> <note>original: *optimum* / *ariston*; the Platonic ideal of the highest good</note> to be exactly thus. Proceeding toward the better is not everywhere voluntary; but as for coming toward the worse, it can in no way be prohibited by another. That it has not declined toward the worse, it has from itself that it did not decline, not because it was 

F restrained; but because it is that very thing which never proceeded [downward]. Now, to be unable to decline toward the worse does not signify a weakness in the one who does not decline; rather, it possesses from itself and because of itself this very quality of not going [downward]. And that it is said never to approach another demonstrates the excellence of its power; for while it is not grasped by necessity, it is itself the necessity and the law of all other things. Did necessity itself, then, provide existence for itself? No, indeed, it did not even "come into existence," seeing as all other things which come after the first exist by the power of that First. How then should that which is above existence or subsistence be said to have existed or subsisted either from another or from itself?

<column-break/>

A And therefore, one must ask the person who says "it happened thus," how they would judge "it happened" <note>original: *synebe*; to happen or result by chance</note> to be false, and how they would remove this "happening." If there were some nature where "it happened" fits, it would not fit the nature of other things. But if they attribute it to chance, how would that which is not in chance be described? The Principle of all others removes "as it chanced" <note>original: *hōs etychen*</note>, 

B giving form and limit. And if something is placed according to reason, why should chance be brought in? For chance is in things that do not <margin>* pre-exist <note>original: *proupostēnai*</note></margin> follow an order, but are accidents. How could anyone attribute to chance the very principle of all reason, order, and <margin>* but perhaps <note>original: *isōs de*</note></margin> limit? Fortune is mistress of much, but she cannot generate the order of reason. 

C These things are false, or the opposites are more authoritative. <margin>* because not <note>original: *dioti ou*</note></margin> Chance seems contrary to reason; how could it be the generator <margin>* that the <note>original: *hoti to*</note></margin> of it? If therefore it did not generate the intellect, it did not generate that which is better than intellect. For it could not produce it, nor does chance exist at all among eternal things. One must not speak about that Principle itself, but rather look at what comes after it, <margin>* that perhaps <note>original: *hoti isōs*</note></margin> and how they came to be. But concerning that Principle, one should no longer ask "how," <margin>* this not having happened <note>original: *touto mē gegonos*</note></margin> because it did not "happen." 

D What then if it is held, and is not what it wished to be, since it is, and is not master of its own essence? If it exists without having established itself, but uses itself as it is, it is what it is by necessity and not otherwise. Or rather, it is not thus because it *could* not be otherwise, but because it is the Best. How could it go toward the better, if it is already at the peak? As for going toward the worse, nothing prevents it except

E that it does not go; it has it from itself that it did not go, not that it was prevented, but by being itself that which does not go. And the inability to go toward the worse is not a sign of weakness, but it has this from itself. This not going, and never going toward anything else, has the excellence of power in itself, so that while others are grasped by necessity, it is itself the necessity of others and their law. 

F Did necessity then establish itself? Or was it established by others? The things after it exist through it. How then can we speak of the subsistence of that which is above subsistence, as if it were established by another or by itself?

But once the Principle has shone upon you in its simplicity, do not seek the "what," "where," or "wherefore." Chapter XI. <-

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry from the previous section, where Plotinus argued that the "First Principle" (the One or God) is not subject to chance or fortune. Here, he explores why human language and logic fail when attempting to define the One, specifically addressing the mistake of trying to "place" the Divine within a spatial or causal framework.</meta>

### BOOK EIGHT. 745

> *For if you investigate what it is, you will contract and compose it to the narrowness of your intelligence, and it will immediately slip away from you. Indeed, when reason finds the essence of a principle, it cannot investigate further what it is; for the question of "what it is" is inadequate for the essence. Nor is it lawful to scrutinize the "why" concerning the principle; truly, this question is resolved back into the principle itself. Finally, since you are to deny it essence, and much more so accidents, in what way could you affirm a contingent lot within it?*

BUT why should we not either speak of the cause of the "what," or, remaining silent, depart from here, and placing our thought in it, seek nothing further? For the cause and the inquiry lead toward that which is beyond. The hindrance of every inquiry is the stopping at the other. We use every inquiry either for "what is it to be," or "of what kind," or "why," or "whether it is." We do not say "what it is to be" for that one, but rather from those things which come after it. <margin>*He seeks the principle, but it is already sought.*</margin> But the "why" seeks again for a principle. And of the whole, that is the principle. To seek "of what kind" is to seek the accident <term>accident</term> <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing has but which is not essential to its nature—for example, being "tall" is an accident of a person, but "human" is their essence.</note> which happens to it; but to it, nothing happens. But the "who are you" shows more clearly that one should seek nothing about it, for it is impossible for them to grasp it alone, for in placing nothing in it, one has learned it entirely. We seem to have cast the consideration of this doubt concerning this nature into our mind, if we have first placed a region and a place, like a chaos, then introduced this nature into a place already made by our imagination or existing in our thought. Having introduced it into a place, we ask where it has come from and what kind of thing it is, and how it has come here and how it is present, neither by seeking nor by presence. It is in its essence. Or it is as if someone is outside some depth, or from some height, or cast away. He should remove the cause of the doubt by ascending, making all place outside of his approach toward it, and let him place it in nothing, neither as if it were founded in an infinite space, nor as if it had arrived, but only as being what it is said to be by the necessity of our arguments. But place, like other things, is later, and the last of all. Thinking of this "out-of-place" thing as if it were present, we think either to place things around it as if in a circle, or to encompass it, having as many things as we say happen to it. And yet this "of what kind" is not its form, nor is it any form around it, not even an intelligible one, nor does it relate to another, for it stands by itself before anything else was joined to it or happened to it. Or how shall we speak of "when" and the rest, which are all said of it by way of negation? So that it is truer to say not "so it happened," but "not so it happened," and much more truly: because one should not even say it "happened" at all.

<column-break/>

BUT what must be said of this which does not properly subsist <term>subsist</term> <note>To "subsist" means to have independent existence. Plotinus is arguing the One exists in a way that exceeds our normal definition of "existence."</note> or exist? Truly, it is proper to depart from here in silence with an uncertain mind, nor to investigate anything further. For what could anyone investigate when nothing further lies open where he might proceed? For every question brings itself back to the principle, and finally rests in such a thing. Added to this is that every question either inquires *what* a thing is, or *of what kind*, or *for what reason*, or *whether it is* or is not. We are accustomed to conjecture that it "is" the principle of all things through those things which are from it. But the question "why" (the cause), in considering the principle, looks for another principle: but of the universal principle, there can be no prior principle. Furthermore, to ask "of what kind" it is, is nothing other than to inquire what "happens" to it—to which nothing at all happens. This very fact that we ought to ask nothing about it declares what it "is"; namely, that we can only grasp it by itself, knowing that it is not lawful to add anything to it.

We seem to have thrown the anxiety of this doubt concerning this nature into our soul, because we have first assumed a region and a place like a chaos, and then afterward introduced this nature into a region already fashioned by our imagination or discovered in nature. When we have introduced it into such a place, we are naturally led to ask: from where and by what condition did it arrive here? Treating it as a stranger, we inquire by what reason it is present, and what and of what kind its essence is—as if it emerged here from some depth or descended from a height. Therefore, it is worthwhile, once the occasion for doubt is removed, to separate all place entirely from a vision directed toward God, nor to place Him in anything, whether He be founded in it forever or arrived at some time. Rather, one must think of Him only as existing, just as it is lawful to think He exists by the necessity of reason. Place, like other things, is posterior—the very last of all things.

Therefore, when we understand this very thing to be moving miraculously outside of place, let us understand it however we may; we can move nothing further regarding it, as if we were surrounding it with something. We cannot measure how great it is, nor can we imagine its quality. For there is no form around it, not even a sensible one, nor even any intelligible one. Furthermore, it is not permitted to adapt it to that which is said to refer to another in any way, for it consists in itself, and it existed before anything else existed. Since it is so, in what way can we say it "happened" to be there? Or how shall we dare to utter that, since all other things said of this are said by negation? So much so that it is not true to say of it, "it happened so," but rather the opposite, "it did not happen so," is much truer—since one should not even say that it "happened" in a simple sense.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the "First Principle" (the One or God). Having previously argued that the One is not subject to chance, Plotinus now explores whether the One can be called "master of Himself" or if such language implies a division that does not exist in absolute unity.</meta>

PLOTINUS, ENNEADS, BOOK VI.

*The Supreme God is more rightly called "freedom" by his very nature than "master of his own nature." For in him, action is in no way distinguished from nature; therefore, he should not be described as being the master of his nature in his acting. Rather, he is the simplest act, through which he is more properly called "free," or the principle and end of all actions. From this, freedom is again named in himself; yet he is master not so much of himself as of others. A Being <term>Essentia</term> <note>original: "Essentia"; the fundamental nature or "beingness" of a thing.</note> that exists through an action somewhat distinct from itself can be called the master of its own existence. But the soul, since it is not essence itself in a simple sense but a certain kind of essence, should by no means be called the master of its own essence, although it is in some way the master of itself. The "Form" of the present body, being devoid of essence, has no free mastery over itself. On the contrary, God—through whom higher things are free and hold mastery over those that follow—is simultaneously freedom and supreme mastery.*

### Chapter XII.

---

WHAT then shall we say? Does this very thing which He is, exist? And of His "being what He is," or of that which is superior to His very "being," is God Himself the master? Again, the mind, not yet persuaded by what has been said, remains hesitant. To these points, therefore, we must presently speak in this way: Each of us, according to the body, is far removed from essence; but according to the soul—and that which we most truly are—we are participants in essence, and indeed, we are a certain kind of essence. That, however, is like a composite of difference and essence together. Therefore, we are neither essence in the highest sense, nor are we "Essence Itself," and for this reason, we are not the masters of our own essence. For in a certain way, essence is one thing, and we exist as another. We are not the masters of our essence; rather, essence itself is the mistress of us, since it is this very thing that provides our "difference" <note>In logic, a "difference" is the specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within a genus.</note>. But since we are, in a certain way, also that which masters us, we can nevertheless be called the masters of ourselves in this condition. But that which is entirely "what it is," namely Essence Itself—where it is not one thing and its essence another—surely this very thing which exists is the mastering power. It is no longer referred back to another thing in the way that reason sees it, and in the way essence exists. For again, the idea of being "master of oneself" is set aside; for whatever is primary there is reduced to essence. Now indeed, that which makes essence free—insofar as its nature is to make things free, and is rightly named the "Liberator"—to whom would it be a servant? If indeed it is even lawful to speak of it in any way. This is judged free by its own essence; but even this essence is free because of Him and is posterior <note>Coming after in a logical or causal sequence.</note> to Him; He Himself does not possess an essence. If, therefore, there is any action in Him, and we place Him within that action, He will not for this reason be something other than Himself, nor will He be any less the master of Himself from whom the action is produced; for there, action is not one thing and He Himself another. But if we do not concede that there is any action in Him at all, but rather that other things working around Him possess substance, we shall be even less likely to admit that there is either a "master" or a "ruling power" there; but neither shall we say He is the master of Himself. This is not because anything else rules over God, but because we have already attributed "being master of oneself" to essence. We have placed the Supreme God in a certain more excellent rank than that of "mastering Himself." What then is more exalted than He who is master of Himself? Surely, because in that which is first called "master of itself," essence and action are in some way two things; undoubtedly, He provided the rationale of a master from the action. But this action is the same as essence, and therefore it was made separately so that He might be a master, and was called "master of Himself." But where there are not two things as one, but where there is absolute unity—where there is either only act, or no act there at all—there it is not even correctly said that He exists as the master of Himself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What then remains regarding "being what He is" in that case? Is He Himself the master? For again the soul, though somewhat persuaded by the words spoken, is at a loss. We must say then of our own affairs: that each of us, according to the body, would be far from essence. But according to the soul, as we most truly are, we participate in essence and are a certain essence. And this is a composite, as it were, of difference <margin>B</margin> and essence. Of those things, He is properly [the master]. <margin>* and she being, etc.</margin> Therefore, we are no longer masters of our own essence. But essence itself is our [master], which by itself has also made our difference. Since we are also mastered in a way by ourselves, in this way we are said to be masters of ourselves. But those things which are altogether what they are, and perfectly so—where there is not one thing and its essence another—there, what it is, is the mastering element; it no longer depends on another, nor on its essence. <margin>* that one</margin> <margin>C</margin> <margin>chresis <note>Greek for "use" or "application."</note></margin> In this way, He is also master of His own perception. [He is] the first of essence. Truly, that which has made essence free—being naturally inclined to make it free, and called the Liberator, as it were—to whom could it be enslaved? If indeed it is altogether lawful to say what is said. But it is free by the same essence, yet essence itself is free by Him, having its cause posterior to Him. If then there is <margin>D</margin> a certain activity in Him, and we place Him in His activity, not even for this reason would He be another to Himself. And we are not mastered by Him insofar as there is activity, because the act and He Himself are not different. But if we do not grant that there is activity in Him at all, but that other activities around Him have their subsistence, we shall grant even more that there is neither a master nor a mastered thing there; but neither is He master of Himself. Not because another is master over Him, but because we have assigned "being master of oneself" to essence. But that which is in a more honorable position <margin>E</margin> we have placed [above that]. Or is He not in a more honorable position of the thesis "master of Himself," or because since essence and activity are there, being two in a way, the master is conceived from the activity <margin>* being mastered</margin>; He gave the quality of a master to this essence, and was called master of the same. But where there are not two as one, but one. Either it is activity only, or <margin>F</margin> not activity at all. Nor is "master of Himself" correctly [applied] to Him.

<summary>Plotinus explores the concept of divine freedom, arguing that God (the One) cannot strictly be called "master of Himself" because that implies a duality between a ruler and a subject. Instead, God is described as pure freedom and absolute unity, the source from which all other things derive their own limited mastery and essence.</summary>
