# BOOK EIGHT.

747
<columns>
Rr 2

In whatever way essence, will, and existence may be named in God, they are entirely the same. Therefore, if God wills and acts just as His essence naturally carries Him, then conversely, His nature is exactly as He wills and acts. What He is, is escaped neither by fortune nor by fate, but is by His own will. 

### Chapter XIII.

Insofar as each thing wills itself, it exists by right and justice to the extent that it is aligned with the good. Therefore, the Good itself wills itself entirely, exists as a free being, and if given the option to change, it would never choose to be anything other than what it is. Furthermore, since the wills of all things flow toward the good and find their use in it, certainly within the Good itself, the will is the same as its goodness, which wills to be nothing other than itself. Now, indeed, what it is pleases itself to the highest degree, since things possess the ability to please themselves only by participating in the good. After this, Plotinus says: If to will to be such a thing is the same as the Good, it follows that just as it is in itself naturally, so it wills to be; and as it wills, so it naturally exists. Meanwhile, he considers—in the manner of the Christians <note>Ficino notes that Plotinus’s reasoning here mirrors Christian theology regarding the divine nature and the generation of the Word.</note>—that God, through His own intelligence, generated a certain subsistence <term>subsistentiam</term> <note>A technical term for an independent reality or individual existence.</note> within Himself. Finally, just as he grants the act of will to a more excellent will, he will undoubtedly grant intelligence to the Good in a similar way, through a more exalted intelligence.

---

<margin>And indeed such things hold</margin>
But if someone should again say that these names are introduced because they are not sought correctly, we should reply that while in one sense it is right to remain silent <margin>to himself through his own faith; he holds it</margin> regarding "what kind" or "what" it is—as if the mind were conceiving two distinct things—persuasion is necessary for the sake of the argument. If we grant these as activities, and these activities are like its own essence or its own will, then the affairs of the gods are based on essence. If anyone says that He is as He willed to be, then He wills more so as He is by nature. The activities are as He willed; and for Him, activity is essence. Truly, then, He possesses from Himself those things that are within Himself, including His being, and He is as He is. Each of the things that exist, desiring the Good, wills to be that rather than what it is. And it exists most truly when it partakes in the Good, and in that <margin>... and following upon the will</margin> certainty, each thing chooses for itself to be itself. Or rather, life with the Good is by nature for the Good as it is for itself. As one says, it is much more to be chosen, just as whatever portion is of the Good, it is most desirable in another and is the essence for each. And if essence is the same thing, it will be by will and such as the foundation <term>hypostasis</term> <note>Greek: ὑπόστασις; the underlying reality or substance.</note> of the will. And if the Good should have nothing else, the "by will" is something else. But if He should have it, He wills Himself. And even if such a presence were by chance <margin>this is this</margin> outside of His will, His essence is determined by it, and from this into this; He does not make each thing for Himself. It is clear then that it becomes through Him, as that already becomes through Him for Himself. And He is primarily that which others are for themselves; and He preserves being for Himself by the preservation of the will, which is like being certain. And having heard Him, following the willing for Himself of that which He is, He is a companion to Himself, willing Himself to be, and being this which He wills. And the will and He are one, and in this He is no less one, because He is not one thing that happened to be and another that He willed to be. Or how could it not be by will? And entirely, His immutability becomes because He wills it, and it is impossible for Him to change His nature, as if by another...

<column-break/>

**A** HOWEVER, if we are compelled to introduce these names—even if not strictly correctly, yet as best we can—it seems we must speak again regarding what was asked from the beginning. Part of it was correctly stated, namely that we should not posit two separate things in the Supreme, even if they differ only by reason. Yet partly, in the present case, we must speak more freely for the sake of persuasion, and decline somewhat from the severe rule of the intellect in our speech. If, therefore, we attribute actions to the **B** supreme God, and adapt His actions to His will (for He is not an unwilling operator), and if these actions are, as it were, His very essence, then surely His will and His essence will be entirely the same. Because if this is so, then exactly as He willed, so He exists. Therefore, it is no more the case that He wills and acts as His nature carries Him, than it is that His essence exists as He wills and acts. Entirely, therefore, He is the master of Himself, possessing His own being by His own judgment. Furthermore, consider it this way: of the things **C** that exist, each one, desiring the good, prefers that [the good] over what it currently is. It thinks it "is" most truly when it becomes a participant in the good, and in a certain way chooses its own being; and it approves of its own being more, the more it has from the good. It is as if the nature of the good itself were to be chosen by itself as the most powerful thing long before all else. Indeed, the more chosen and greater the portion of the good attributed to another, the more that being's essence is to be chosen freely and sought after, **D** standing by the will, and existing as one and the same as the will, not subsisting through the will itself. Hence, as long as a thing does not possess the good, it wills something else; but when it possesses it, by that very condition it now wills itself. This kind of presence does not happen by chance, nor is His essence outside of His will; and by this very fact it is determined, and thus He exists of Himself. If, therefore, by this very fact anything makes itself into a particular thing, it is clearly established that He is primarily such a being, **E** through whom others obtain the ability to be themselves. At the same time, the will is joined entirely with His essence, so as to exist as such; nor is it permitted to receive that being without an act of the will approving this very thing which He is for Himself. Thus, God Himself concurs with Himself, willing Himself to exist, and existing as that which He wills; and the will and He are one. From this, He is no less one: since He is not one thing that happened to be by chance, and another thing that He would have willed to be. For what else would He have willed

---

beyond this which now exists? For even if we imagine it brought to His thought that whatever He wills should be done, and that He is permitted to change His nature into something else, it would certainly be established that He does not wish to be anything else.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s exploration of the "One" or the "Good," specifically addressing whether God acts by necessity or by His own free will. On the previous page, the author argued that God’s nature and His will are inseparable. This page moves into a deeper proof of how the First Principle creates His own existence, contrasting the necessary nature of higher beings (like Souls and Ideas) with the accidental nature of physical bodies.</meta>

<page-num>741</page-num>
<header>PLOTINUS'S ENNEADS. BOOK VI.</header>

...or even that it emerged by chance: nor would there be anything in Him that acts as if He had escaped into being what He is through some external necessity, precisely because He is properly that which He Himself always willed, and still wills. For the nature of the Good itself is truly His own will; not in such a way that a portion was assigned to Him, or that He followed some pre-existing nature, but rather that He willed Himself, since there was no other thing to which He could rather be drawn. Added to this is the fact that no other beings include within their own essence a reason for being entirely pleased with themselves; indeed, there might be something in their nature that offends or displeases them. But in the substance of the Good itself, it is necessary that choice and will undoubtedly coincide; otherwise, He would achieve nothing more than the ability to please Himself at some later time—as other things usually please themselves only by participating in, or at least reflecting an image of, the Good. 

For the rest, let pardon be granted for the use of names, if someone speaking of Him is compelled to use certain less fitting terms for the sake of demonstration—terms which a more exact rule of disputation would not normally admit. At least in any such incongruous name, phrases such as *as if*, *just as*, and *as it were* should be understood as applied to each one. If, therefore, the Good itself existed, and at the same time choice and will existed with Him (for without these He will not be), it is necessary that these not be many—namely, the will and the essence—and we must reduce "willing" entirely into a single unity. Since truly the "willing" is from Him, it is necessary that His "being" is also present to Him through Himself. Wherefore, this reasoning finds that He effectively creates Himself. For if His will is from Himself, and is, as it were, His own work, and this will is the same as His substance: surely He thus produced Himself in the very act of existing. Therefore, He is not merely what He happened to be, but rather what He willed Himself to be.

### Confirmation of the previous points. Chapter IX.

Individual things in the realm of bodies can indeed have proceeded into existence contingently <note>In philosophy, "contingent" means something that could have been otherwise—it is not strictly necessary.</note>: in these, besides the necessity of their species, there might also be something accidental. But the Soul, the Intellect, and every Idea <term>Idea</term> <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes of things in the mind of the Divine.</note> is not only necessary according to its essence and species; by this very fact, its existence comes forth from its innermost nature, not by chance, but by necessity. Since these beings follow the Good as proximate principles, the Good above all possesses the power of establishing its own outcome. Furthermore, within a single Idea, remaining the same and substantial, or in a form expressed from a most loving Idea, these two are joined together: namely, *what* a thing is and *why* it exists. Therefore, if you look carefully at the very disposition of nature, you will find that there was a preservation of the parts, and that the whole is the cause of the parts; you will find that those things which have their origin from the First Principle of things possess that same quality even more eminently within themselves. Fortune <note>original: *fortuna*, meaning luck or random chance.</note> is most alien to that realm where the reason for existing is contained within internal causes.

ACCORDINGLY, it is right for us to consider the same thing by this reasoning. Each of those things which is said to "be" is either the same as its very being, or rather it is something else—just as this individual man is one thing, and the "essence of being a man" is another: yet this specific man is a participant in that which is the essence of man. But the Soul and the "being of the soul" are the same, if the soul is simple and not defined by something else. Likewise, the "Ideal Man" <note>The perfect Form of humanity, as opposed to a specific person.</note> himself is the same as the "essence of being a man." And while a person might become a man by a certain chance where he is something other than the essence of man, the "essence of being a man" itself never happens to occur by chance. That is, the Ideal Man is from himself. Wherefore, if this very thing which is called "being a man" is from itself, and does not exist according to fortune, nor happen to be so...

<column-break/>

If anyone is cautious, let him not reproach the One as being what He is under necessity, since He is Himself what He would have willed to be: for the nature of the Good is His own will, and is order itself. But if He trusted His own nature, He did so by choosing Himself, because there was nothing else; nor should anyone say that He was led by that other thing, as if He were an image of other things. He has embraced the reason for being pleased with Himself; for indeed, nothing could be displeasing to Him. But if there is anything in the nature of Goodness, it is necessary that choice and His own will are included within it. For necessity is not the cause of His being pleased with Himself; rather, things that possess a shadow of the Good are pleased with themselves through an image. Wherefore, one must grant the use of the name if one speaks of Him; out of necessity, for the sake of indication, words are pressed into service, though they lack the exactness of the things being described. 

It must be taken that each thing is not merely a product of nature. In His nature is choice and will, and without these He does not exist, since He is not fashioned by another. He is self-acting, existing in the "better," and His essence and His "willable" willing are necessarily with Him, so that His being is from Himself: so that He, in a sense, made Himself, as human reasoning might put it. For if the will is with Him, it is His own work. And since this is the same as His substance, He would be the one who brought Himself into substance; He is not what He happened to be, but what He Himself willed.

### Chapter IX.

Furthermore, one must see whether each of these things that are said "to be" is the same as its "being," or if they are different. For example, a man is one thing, but "to be a man" is another; yet the man participates in "to be a man." But the Soul and "to be a soul" are the same, if the soul is simple and not predicated of another; likewise, the Man-Himself [the Idea] and "to be a man" are the same. And a man might indeed come to be by chance, where he is different from the essence of being a man; but the "essence of being a man" would never come to be by chance. What then is the "Man-Himself" in himself? If the "essence of being a man" is from itself, and is not according to chance, nor an accident, how could that which is above the Ideal Man, and the creator of the man himself, and all beings, be subject to chance?

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the divine nature of the "One" or the "Good." While the previous page established that God acts according to His own will rather than necessity, this page investigates the relationship between essence, causality, and the absence of "chance" in the highest realm of being. It specifically addresses how the "why" (the reason for existence) and the "is" (existence itself) are identical in the First Principle.</meta>

<page-num>749</page-num>
<header>EIGHTH BOOK</header>
<columns>2</columns>

If we were to say that Nature is simpler <note>original: Φύσις ἁπλαστέρα</note> in its absolute being, and that Being, in its entirety, moves toward simplicity, it can no longer carry "chance" along with it. It is proper to remember what we have said before: that each of those things which truly exist possesses its own essence and is the creator of its own foundation <note>original: ὑποστάσεως ὑποστάτην</note>. While in the world of the senses, causes are found in external things, in the intelligible realm, essence and foundation have their own cause within themselves. Therefore, a later observer of any thing must ask "why" each part exists as it does. For example, why is there an eye? Why are there feet for certain creatures? In the sensible world, every part coexists according to a cause, and the reason there are many parts—why feet have a certain length, why the face is such as it is, and why the feet are such—is the general harmony of all parts with one another. This mutual harmony is the "cause." The "why" of a thing is found in its very being; the "what it is" and the "cause" are the same. These things flow from a single source, not through a process of reasoning, but by providing the "why" and the "being" all at once. This source is both Being and the Reason for Being, granting both simultaneously. This is far more certain and true than things in the sensory world which strive toward the best. The Principle from which all things there proceed contains no chance, nor did it "just happen" to be so. All things that have their cause within themselves are governed by Reason <note>original: λόγος</note>, Cause, and Causal Intelligence. This Father is far removed from any chance. If there is a beginning and a model for all things that have no share in chance, it is that which is truly First, unmixed with luck or accidental coincidence, being the cause of Himself. He is from Himself and is what He is through Himself. For He is primarily Himself, and transcendently Himself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Then it can be: especially since nature is simpler than the state of "being human," and since He existed entirely as Being itself. Indeed, for one proceeding in order toward the simpler, it is not permitted to carry the same "fortune" or chance along. Therefore, fortune cannot ascend to that which is the simplest of all. Furthermore, it must be recalled—as has already been stated—that each of those things which truly exist, and which proceed into substance from that nature, possesses within <margin>B</margin> its essence the cause of its own substance or subsistence. If anything among those defined things is such as it is, it is because it depends chiefly upon those higher principles for being so. Consequently, one who later contemplates a thing can assign a reason "why" it is so: for example, why there is an eye, and for what cause feet were given to such creatures. One can prove by reason that any part is in harmony with the whole, and that the parts assist one another in the <margin>C</margin> logic of their cause. Why are the feet extended in length? Because this part is such, and because the face is such; therefore, the feet are also such. The mutual harmony of all things is the cause of each other. Likewise, why is this thing here? Because this very thing constitutes "being human." Therefore, "being" and "cause" are one and the same. These things have flowed from a single source without the use of a <margin>D</margin> discursive train of thought, but by presenting the "why" and the "being" as a single prior whole. Therefore, the source is Being itself and the "reason why" it is said to be; it provides both at once. Such are the things that are made, or rather, the Principle from which they proceed—but in a far more powerful and truer way, surpassing those things that exist by striving toward what is best. Since none of those things which possess their causes within themselves exist by whim, or fortune, or any condition of chance, <margin>E</margin> that first Principle in which all things reside—the Father of reason and (if I may say so) of causal cause—is far removed from fortune in every way. He will surely be the principle and, as it were, the exemplar of all things that have no commerce with fortune. This is the First, who has no mixing with chance or lot, since He is the cause of Himself and from Himself; because of Himself, He is this very thing which is called "Himself." For He is primarily Himself, or beyond being, and (so to speak) transcendently Himself.

---

-> Confirmation of the preceding. Chapter XV. <-

> *If each thing is lovable to itself insofar as it participates in the Good, then surely the Good itself is most lovable to itself; and there, the lover and the beloved are the same. He is, therefore, nothing other than that which always loves its own existence. Furthermore, we are placed outside of accidents and experience true liberty only when, having left all other things behind, we expose ourselves to the single light of the Good that surpasses our intelligence. Therefore, the Good itself is liberty itself, beyond fortune. Finally, since reason is opposed to chance, and since the entire reason of the universe proceeded from the Principle, it follows that He is not only outside of chance, but even above reason—He is existence itself.*

---

And He is the lovable, and Love itself, and the love of Himself, since He is beautiful from Himself and in Himself. For if He exists by being with Himself, where the two are the same, and if being with that which He is with makes them identical, then the one who desires and the object of desire are one. The object of desire, as the foundation or underlying reality <note>original: ὑποκείμενον</note>, would again appear to us as identical to the desire and the essence.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> God is likewise both the object of love and Love itself, and He is the love of His own self, as one who exists as beautiful only from Himself and in Himself. Moreover, this very concept of "being together with Himself" cannot be understood otherwise than that the one who is "with" and the one who is "together" are entirely one and the same. If, therefore, that which coexists and that with which it coexists are one, and that which is there as the "desiring" is likewise one with that which is "desired," and that which is called the "desirable" according to sub-

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section (Ennead VI.8) regarding the nature of the "One" or God. Having established that the First Principle is not subject to necessity, Plotinus now argues that God is the author of His own existence and the very definition of freedom, standing far above the reach of "chance" or "fortune."</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS, BOOK VI</header>

<column-break/>

considered as substance and as a kind of subject. From this, it appeared to us again that desire and essence are the same. If this is the case, it is established once more that God creates himself and exists as his own master, and was not made in such a way as any other thing might have willed, but exactly as he himself wills. Hence, when we say that God neither receives anything into himself nor is held by another, we further separate him by this reasoning from that condition by which some might say he happened to turn out a certain way. This is not only because he acts—or rather, renders himself unique and (so to speak) solitary, keeping himself pure from all things—but also because if we ever behold such a nature within ourselves, having nothing of other things, we will truly experience a life of freedom, far from the accidents that usually happen to us through the things that cling to us. For all other things called "ours" are subservient, exposed to chance, and happen to us as if by accident. But in this alone consists the right of lordship and free existence: through an act of light in the form of the Good <note>original: "luminis boniformis"</note> and a Good that surpasses the mind. I speak of a power that is not external but within him, exceeding all understanding. Therefore, when we have ascended to this and have become this alone, leaving all other things far behind, come now, what shall we say of this state? Surely we shall cry out that we are then far superior to freedom and all choice. For who could then expose us to fortune, or make us subject to the randomness of chance? Especially since we have then become the very life that is true, or have been established deep within that which truly has nothing else but exists entirely as itself. All other things are separated from others and cannot suffice for their own being; but the Principle itself is that very thing which it is, even if it were set apart. Surely the first substance does not consist of a thing without life, nor even in a life devoid of reason. For such a life is weak in its existence, since it is a dispersion of reason and a kind of undefined nature. But insofar as it proceeds into reason, to that extent it leaves fortune behind. For that which proceeds according to reason is by no means involved in fortune. As we proceed higher, we do not encounter the Principle itself as reason, but as something more beautiful than reason; it is so far removed from happening by chance. For it is the root of reason by its own nature, and here at last all things end. It is like the principle and foundation of a certain massive tree living by reason, remaining within itself, but handing over being to the tree through the reason received from it.

->Confirmation of the Foregoing. Chapter XVI.<-

> *If God is neither in time nor in place, he cannot be this very thing which he is by chance, either at some time or in some place. God is not so much "always" as he is Eternity itself; nor does he properly dwell "everywhere," but he certainly is this very thing which we are accustomed to call "everywhere." The Intellect in God—superior to the intellect that is less intelligible—acts so effectively upon itself that it generates existence within itself; similarly, the Will—superior to the desiring will—powerfully produces existence in itself. Since there is nothing in God except himself, he certainly shines forth from himself by understanding and willing in himself, so that his being is neither brought in by chance nor from elsewhere, but he exists as that very thing he is, according to his own intelligence and will. But these matters, and those that follow, we explain more diligently in our Theology.*

A **SINCE** we indeed confess, and it seems probable to all, that God is both everywhere and nowhere, we must also carefully consider what this nature is. From here, we once again investigate what we seek: for if he is nowhere, he is certainly not a body...

<column-break/>

A If this is so, he would again be that which he makes for himself and the master of himself.
<margin>What it means to be oneself</margin>
And he does not possess being as someone else willed him to be, but as he himself wills. Since even now, when we speak of him, we say he is towards himself; if he received anything from another, then that other would be another thing, and he would not be outside of chance.
<margin>The origin of chance</margin>
But rather, chance belongs to those who are such as they are by an external cause, whereas he dismisses chance from himself and sends it down to the things below him.
B When we possess such a nature here, when we are held together by other things, we are subject to passions because many things happen to us by chance. But again, our causes—those which are sons of chance and subject to fortunes—come to us as if by accident. But then, to him alone belongs lordship and self-governance <note>original: "autexousion" - absolute power over oneself</note>.

<margin>Here</margin>
Descending from our inquiry and having become the "One" alone, leaving all else behind, what could we say of him? Or what more could we need? Or how could we increase ourselves? Perhaps the things of evil attach to us by accident, but when one has become the true light itself, and is in this, he has nothing else, but is himself alone. Other things lie elsewhere and do not possess self-willing.
D This is his being: that which he is, whereas a divided foundation <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> and every soul are in this way; the irrational things are weak in their being, because they are a scattering of reason or an indefiniteness. For that which is according to reason, they say, is not by chance; yet even reason is a "why," but he is more beautiful than reason. How far removed is he from happening by chance? For there is no reason in him, but he is the source of reason.

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s investigation into the absolute freedom of the First Principle (the One). Having previously argued that the One is not subject to chance, Plotinus now explores how the One’s very existence is identical to His own will and "awakened" activity.</meta>

<page-num>758</page-num>
<header>BOOK EIGHT.</header>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It is a marvel. If He is everywhere, He is as great as He is in being everywhere. Therefore, if He is everywhere, and this "everywhere" belongs to Him, He exists along with that "everywhere." But He does not merely happen to be there at that time, nor is He simply of the magnitude you might claim; rather, He is present to that "everywhere." Having the highest rank—or rather, being the Highest Himself—He holds all things clearly within Himself. These things happen to Him only in the sense that they depend on Him, or rather, they concern Him because they look toward Him, while He looks toward Himself.

<margin>B</margin> He is carried, as it were, into His own interior, loving Himself as a pure light <note>The Greek text uses "pure land" (γῆν καθαρὰν), while the Latin translation uses "pure light" (puras luce). Plotinus often uses light as a metaphor for the clarity of divine existence.</note>. He is Himself that which He loves; He gives Himself existence through a kind of "super-thought," existing as a persistent activity <term>energeia|the Greek word for 'activity' or 'actualization,' suggesting that God is not a passive thing but a constant 'doing' of being</term>. He is truly the beloved and exists as His own effect. Therefore, He is His own work. Whereas for others, their actions result in things external to their own activity—in which they exist only by accident—He is His own activity.

<margin>C</margin> Since, therefore, His "gaze" toward Himself is, so to speak, a "desire" and a looking toward Himself, and since this looking toward Himself is His very being, it follows that He is not what He "happened" to be, but what He wills to be. His will is not some random impulse, for His will is the Best. It is not by chance that His "birth" <note>Plotinus uses "birth" or "generation" metaphorically here to describe how the One's existence is eternally produced by His own nature.</note> or His activity toward Himself resulted in Him remaining in Himself as He is.

<margin>D</margin> The opposite proves this: if His "generation" looked outward, He would lose the being that He is. Therefore, His being is His activity toward Himself, and since He is His being, He Himself gave subsistence to Himself. If you were to say His activity is not Himself, then He would not be "awakened." But He is the very state of being "awake" or "awakeness" itself—a super-intellection <term>super-intellection|a state of knowing that is above and more unified than ordinary human thought or even the standard Intellect</term> that exists eternally.

<margin>E</margin> Furthermore, since He is "awakeness" itself, He is beyond substance, beyond mind, and beyond the visible. These things are Himself; He is thus the effect, the super-intellection, the wisdom, and the life. From this very essence, these things arise. Everything that belongs to another is actually His and comes from Him. Therefore, He does not exist "as it happened," but He exists exactly as He has willed.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> It happened: again, if He is everywhere, it is beyond doubt that as great as He is, He is so everywhere. Therefore, this very thing which is called "everywhere" and "from every side" is His own existence. Neither is "everywhere" within Him, nor vice versa, but He Himself extended this very thing and grants being to all other things, because they are admitted into that which He is everywhere. Here, however, holding the supreme rank—or rather, not "having" it, but being Himself the Supreme—He has all things placed under Him. He does not even "touch" them <note>This implies that God remains pure and unaffected by the lower world while still sustaining it.</note>, but they "touch" Him, or rather, all things are seen to revolve around Him.

<margin>B</margin> He is carried within Himself equally through the whole, as if loving Himself as pure light. He exists as that very thing which He loves—that is, producing Himself in His own subsistence. He is clearly a remaining act, and where He loves, He is simultaneously there, existing as Intellect. But the Intellect is His own handiwork <note>Latin: "opificium," the work of a craftsman.</note>; therefore, He is His own work. Since He is not the work of another, it follows that He is His own work.

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, He is not as He "happened" to be, but rather as He Himself is. Moreover, He exists primarily from Himself, because He rests upon Himself and looks toward Himself. That looking toward Himself is, as it were, the work of an "effecting." Thus, He is not as He "happened," but as He Himself wills. Nor is His will there rash or vain, nor did it happen by chance. For since His will is the best, it is not empty or accidental.

<margin>D</margin> That such a "nod" <note>Latin: "nutus," a divine command or impulse.</note> toward Himself, being a kind of action and rest within Himself, brings it about that this very thing which is exists, is proven if the opposite of this gift were conceded. Namely, if He looked out or "nodded" outside of Himself, He would first lose what He is. Therefore, to be this very thing which He is, is an action toward Himself, and this action and Himself are one. He, therefore, provides subsistence to Himself, as His action is joined with Him.

<margin>E</margin> If, therefore, His action was not "made," but always existed as a kind of "vigilance" (awakeness), and there the "one who is awake" is not different from the "awakeness" itself—which is indeed a super-intellection always in bloom—then He is exactly as He "stayed awake." This "awakeness" stands as wisdom above the essence of intellect and life. That is what He is. He is therefore an act above intellect, wisdom, and life; from Him these things come, and from no one else. By Him and from Him His own being is produced. Therefore, He does not exist just as it happened, but exactly as He willed.

---

->A Confirmation of the Preceding. Chapter XVII.<-

> *In man, nature (by which he generates his like) is one thing; art and providence (by which he acts with skill) are another. But in the world, both intelligence and nature are present together. Since, therefore, the provident and skillful arrangement is nothing other than an intellectual and natural reason combined, it is necessary that this exists there as His natural form. If, therefore, the form of such a world is far removed from chance, then the Principle of that form is most remote of all from fortune, for by His nature and will He has separated Himself from fortune. Finally, if the Principle creates another thing, it creates its own law.*

...remaining very firmly and with greater certainty. For this reason, those realities are above providence, and above choice and purpose: all things that consist in true Being always persevere firmly in an intellectual state. If anyone, then, should call such a disposition "providence," let them understand it thus: that there is a firmly abiding Intellect over the universe, by which and according to which this whole is constituted. If, therefore, Intellect exists before all things, and if such an Intellect is the principle, it never holds itself as it "happens" to be <note>original: "forte contigit" - Plotinus argues that the Divine does not exist by chance or accident</note>, especially since it is manifold, yet conspiring with itself, and as it were, united into one. For that which exists as a coordinated multitude, and in which all rational principles <term>rationes|logoi; the blueprints or formative principles of reality</term> are comprehended throughout the whole into a unity, can in no way be thought to exist by chance or to have happened by accident. Rather, the recklessness of fortune is far removed from such a nature; fortune itself, wandering in a certain deprivation of reason, is utterly opposed to reason. But if that which exists before such a thing is the principle of all, it is certainly closest to that which is affected in the way described. And that which is so disposed is arranged according to that Principle, participates in it, and exists as that Principle and its powers desire. He, therefore, is God, the ever-present. One single reason <note>original: "ratio" - the Latin translation for the Greek 'logos'</note>, one single number. One who is greater than any spirit <note>original: "genio" - referring to a 'daimon' or guiding spirit</note> and more powerful; nothing is greater than Him, nothing is better. Therefore, He receives neither His existence nor His being such as He is from another. He Himself, then, restores Himself to that which He is, toward Himself and deeply within Himself: so that He does not, even in this state, look outside, or toward any other thing, but rather is wholly directed toward Himself.

### Confirmation of the above. Chapter XVIII.

Nothing outside of God may be imagined. For God is conceived as a power beyond existence; indeed, He is exalted, both existing and encompassing the surface of all things, while His depth penetrates all things entirely. The first Intellect is compared to God just as an inferior circle applies itself to the center of a superior circle, naturally depending upon it; or again, just as light poured forth in many rays returns to the single and solitary sun. Since, therefore, the Intellect is a kind of natural image of the first God, and is entirely and completely Reason, it is clear that the First lives not by nature but by the will of Reason <note>This suggests the Divine is not 'forced' by its own nature but is a free expression of itself</note>: and as the Father, He admits nothing of the accidental from below. Finally, since the whole rational order of what is fitting and opportune is contained as good within the Good itself, the Good itself is rightly called beauty and opportunity. It does not exist by chance, but naturally exists as is fitting through its own natural beauty.

You, therefore, who seek, seek nothing outside of God: but within God find all things that come after God; truly let Him be. For that which is outside is God Himself, the encompassment and measure of all things, or the internal depth of the universe. But that which meets God from the outside, touching Him as if in a circle and suspended entirely from Him, is reason and intellect—or rather, it has become intellect to the extent that it touches Him, and by the manner in which it touches and depends upon Him, since it derives its very nature as intellect from Him. Come, consider a circle touching its center on all sides, and therefore drawing power from the center, being "center-like" and (if I may say so) "center-formed": where the lines of the circle, flowing together to a single center, render their boundary closest to the center such as that to which they are carried, and from which they somehow demand their being. This is indeed more excellent than the condition of the lines and boundaries, which are merely signs of the lines. Yet these are in some way like that center, though obscure and weak, like its traces; for the center contains and generates both the traces and the lines by its own power. These lines...

<margin>A</margin> ...one might be all-ordered, for nothing is many, or a gathered multitude, in which all reasons are encompassed within its own whole... far from the nature of the "why." Here, he extends that argument by using geometric metaphors (the circle and its center) to show how everything flows from the One by a "fitting" necessity and divine will, rather than by accident.</meta>

It lies within him, manifesting through the lines. As if one were to say, like something unrolled and wound up, and the one beyond, to take what is within. Using an image like an outpouring or an unfolding, it is set apart, not from its own intellectual nature. Witnessing it as if in motion, or as the mind extends itself, just as lines extend toward a circle, or rays from a center, the father of the circular lines. Traces

They are in the same, but not in such a way as things here; a certain Mind illuminates them there, greatly scattered from a single source, being transparent in itself. The scattered part is an image, but the source from which it comes is the truth. Or if something else knows it as a scattered image, it is not by chance, but by an individual cause—reason and cause. But that Principle is the cause of the cause. For things that are, as it were, most causal are greater and truer. It is not just as many things as are clear, but those that come from the intellectual cause. And it is generative. It does not hold itself as it happened to be, but as he himself willed; yet his will was not without reason. Nor does it exist as it occurred to him, but as it was necessary. As if he were a single whole there. Plato signified this as far as was possible, desiring to show that it is far from "as it happened." But it is that which is still necessary, and that which is required. These things are not without reason. Or "opportunity" <note>original: καιρός (kairos) - the right or opportune moment</note>, which is the most sovereign thing in those that come after it. And it is prior to him, and not as it happened
<margin>* This</margin>
* as it is. But it is that which he himself willed to be, which is what is necessary; that which is necessary shines forth, and the activity of the necessary is also a substance <term>hypostasis|an underlying reality or actualization</term>, not as a subject, but as a primary activity manifesting itself, which was necessary. For even to speak of him, it was impossible to say what he wills.

<column-break/>

A They have that Principle everywhere: and through lines, it appears everywhere what it is, both as if unrolled, and again not unrolled. By a similar reasoning, contemplate the Intellect <note>original: "intellectum" - the Divine Mind, the first emanation from the One</note> and being itself as generated from it, and as if poured out and unfolded, and suspended from its own intellectual nature. Therefore, think of the Intellect as a witness, like an intellect flourishing in the universe, which yet does not "become" intellect: for it is entirely one. Just as in a circle there is neither a center, B nor any line, nor a circumference: the circumference of the lines is the father, while it offers traces of itself, and by a permanent power produces lines and the circumference. These are not entirely segregated from there, but flow out from there with a very strong vigor. Thus, think of the highest God as the first exemplar of the surrounding intellectual power, and of that power as his image: I speak of God as the Intellect flourishing in the one, whose vigor is moved as if in many ways and through many things, and thus the Intellect emerges there: yet God stands above the mind, and generates the Intellect from his own power. What contingency, then, is there? What chance? What fortuitous event can happen in the presence of such a great power, the procreatress and true effecter of the mind? For such as is that which is in the mind, such is roughly thought to be that which is in D the One, although it is far more excellent: just as if a light widely diffused should proceed from a certain source remaining in itself and being entirely transparent. Where indeed that which is diffused is the image of another. That from which this shines is undoubtedly true light: yet the diffused image is not alien or deformed; it is the Intellect itself: which surely admits no fortune, but whatever is individually in it, is a certain reason in itself and a cause. But God is the cause of the cause. Therefore, in a more powerful degree, God exists as the cause, as if in the E internal work of the cause: I say the cause in a much truer sense, embracing in himself all intellectual causes that will sprout from there at once. And he generates his work not just as it happened, but as he himself willed. But his Will was not devoid of reason, nor was it carried away blindly and in vain, nor did it fall out just as it happened, but rather as it was fitting: since nothing there is rash or vain. Hence Plato called it the fitting and the opportune <note>original: "decens atque opportunum" - referring to the Greek 'prepon' and 'kairos'</note>, wishing in whatever way he could to signify F that God is most remote from fortuitous chance: but that this very thing which he is, is "the fitting" itself. But if this "fitting" exists, it certainly does not exist without reason. And if it is opportunity itself, whose property dominates most in the things that follow, then surely opportunity is present to itself much earlier. Therefore, it does not exist as it happened: but this is rather what he himself willed: since he wills the "fitting," and there the "fitting" or "opportune" itself and the action of the fitting are one. And the fitting is not like a subject, but like a primary action, properly bringing itself into the light, which was also fitting. Our names must be forgiven. For thus we must speak of God, since we are not able to speak of him as we might wish.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 753 regarding the nature of the First Principle (the One). While the previous page focused on the "fittingness" of the One's existence, Plotinus now moves to explain how the One is "beyond essence" and is the source of its own being through pure activity, rather than being a product of chance or necessity.</meta>

<header>PLOTINUS’S ENNEADS VI.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, if someone is moved by the previous arguments toward that highest principle of all things, let them grasp it; and in this way, they will perceive themselves, although they may not be able to express as much as they wish. But seeing that Principle within themselves, having set aside every distraction, they will affirm that it exists of itself, so much so that it possesses its own essence—or rather, its essence serves it, and as it were, flows from it. Because they have contemplated this, they will no longer dare to say that it happened to be as it is, nor will they be able to speak of it in that way at all. <margin>B</margin> For if they dared to pronounce such a thing, they would suddenly be seized with awe. Furthermore, having been raised to this height, they will not even be able to assign a place for where it is; for it reveals itself entirely to the eyes of the soul everywhere. Wherever the mind fixes its gaze, it beholds it—unless perhaps the mind, having let go of God, looks back elsewhere, thinking nothing more of him. Truly, it is worthwhile to consider in this way that mystery of the ancients <note>Plotinus refers to "the ancients" to align his philosophy with older traditions like those of Plato or the Pythagoreans.</note> wrapped in obscure words: namely, that God is "beyond essence." <margin>C</margin> Consider it also for this reason: not only because he generates essence, but because he neither serves essence nor himself. His silence is not the cause of his beginning; rather, he is the principle of essence itself. He did not make essence for his own sake, but having made it, he sent it outside of himself, as one who has no need of that which he has brought into being. Therefore, it is not according to what he is that he performs this very act of being what he is called.

### Confirmation of the preceding. Chapter XX.

Since every essence strives with all its might toward activity <note>original: *actum* / ἐνέργεια (energeia). In Neoplatonism, "activity" is the dynamic expression of a thing's being.</note> as toward something better and higher, it is proper to conceive of the Principle as an activity far superior to essence. And so it is with every essence. Furthermore, if he is said to be "able to be," certainly by the very fact that he is activity, he declares his own existence—not, I say, within essence, but superior to it. Therefore, he does not belong to essence, but is his own within himself, and is thus free. Insofar as he is not preserved by another source, but preserves himself, he is said to generate himself through an eternal generation. Finally, where acting and existing in whatever manner are the same thing, and activity is usually thought of as more excellent, certainly activity can be considered to carry its own existence with it as a companion.

<margin>A</margin>
Someone might ask: "Will it not then follow that God existed before he was made?" For if he determines himself, certainly in the sense that he makes himself, he is said not yet to be; but in the sense that he is said to "make," he is said already to have existed, since he himself is what is said to be made. To this objection, one must answer that God is not to be thought of as a finished product, but as the maker, affirming his "making" as something absolute. Nor is it of such a kind that some other thing is produced from his action; rather, his action does not extend beyond himself, but this whole exists simply. <margin>B</margin> For there are not two things there, but entirely one. We should not fear to place the first activity without essence, but we must affirm this very thing as the "substance" <note>original: *substantia* / ὑπόστασις (hypostasis), meaning a foundational reality.</note>. However, if someone were to posit a substance lacking activity, certainly the principle itself would be deficient and would turn out to be imperfect—yet it is the most perfect of all. And if someone joined activity to substance, they would not preserve it in simple unity. <margin>C</margin> Therefore, if activity is more perfect than essence, and the First is the most perfect, then the First is certainly activity; thus, as the Actor, God already is this very thing. It is not permitted to say he existed before he was made, because he did not exist "before" he was made; rather, he was already the whole of the making. Truly, his activity is not a servant to essence, and this activity is purely and utterly free; thus, God exists of himself. Now, if God were preserved in his being by another, he would not be the First, existing entirely from himself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Let someone, therefore, taking from what has been said and being moved toward that Principle, grasp it for themselves, and they will behold themselves—not being able to speak as much as they wish, but having seen it, and letting go of all reasoning within themselves, they will place that whole Principle beside themselves. If it had an essence, that essence would be a servant to it, and would be as it were beside it. And such a person would no longer dare to say it "happened to be so," nor can they speak of it at all. <margin>B</margin> For they would be struck with amazement if they dared, and they would not even have <margin>and suddenly</margin> a way to describe the flickers that appear before all things concerning it. <margin>Everywhere it is born to him, as it were</margin> <margin>He himself appearing to the eyes of the soul everywhere, before whatever place they gaze upon, seeing him and not looking elsewhere toward anything else; having gazed upon God,</margin> and no longer thinking anything about him, it is necessary perhaps to think of the "beyond essence" in this way, which was spoken of by the ancients through riddles. <margin>C</margin> Not only because he generates essence, but because essence is not for him, nor is he the principle of essence as if he made essence for himself; rather, having made it, he left it outside of himself, as needing nothing from that which he made. Therefore, he is not defined by what he makes.

### Chapter XX.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>* Not because <unclear>his</unclear> especially <unclear>dwelling</unclear></margin>
What then? Someone might say: "Does it happen that he was made before he existed?" For by that which he makes himself, his "being" is not yet present, but his "making" is already himself, since he is the thing that has been made. To this, it must be said that he is not to be ranked among the things that are made, but among the makers, regarding his "making" as absolute. This is not so that something else results from the making, but the whole is this activity. <margin>B</margin> It is not a result, but the whole belongs to that which is, and they are not two things, but one. And one must not fear to place the first activity without essence, but this very thing must be placed as the foundational existence. If anyone were to place a foundational existence without activity, the principle would be lacking, and it would be the least of all things. And if they should add activity to the essence, the activity would not be more perfect than the essence; but the first is the <margin>firstly in activity, in eternal activities</margin> <margin>C</margin> highest. Therefore, the First is activity. Having acted already, he is this, and he is not as if before he was made, because he was not "before" he was made, but was already the whole. Activity <margin>The activity which does not serve is truly free, and truly he was from himself, by himself, for himself.</margin> purely is free. And thus, he is himself from himself; for if he were preserved in his being by another, he would not be the one who is firstly from himself.

Furthermore, as for the tradition that God "contains himself," if this is said correctly, it should be understood to mean that while all other things are held together and sustained entirely by God—existing by a certain participation <term>participation (participatio): the Neoplatonic idea that lower things exist only by "sharing" in the qualities of a higher source</term> in him and being traced back to him—he himself exists by his own power. He requires no connection, containment, participation, or presence from others; rather, he is everything to himself. For you are permitted to touch upon something regarding which you can say or assume nothing else. ## ENNEAD SIXTH.
### BOOK IX.

#### On the Good or the One.
#### <note>original: "De bono vel uno"</note>

->Whatever exists besides the First is composed of many parts or powers brought together into the form of a single whole.<-
->Chapter I.<-

To the extent that unity <term>unity (unitas): the state of being one; for Plotinus, the One is the source of all being</term> thrives within the diversity of each thing, its essence <term>essence (essentia): the core reality or "being" of a thing</term> persists; otherwise, if unity is lost, the essence is destroyed. Therefore, unity preserves essence, and thus unity also creates essence and existence. Certainly, unity, which dominates the diversity opposed to it, does not arise from itself, nor does it emerge from that opposing diversity. Therefore, it comes from pure unity, which exists simply in itself above all diversity of essence. When you say "one body" and "one soul," or "one heat" and "one cold," this predicated unity is not the body itself (otherwise it would not apply to the soul), nor is it cold (otherwise it would not suit heat). By a similar line of reasoning, you will find that the "One" itself is more eminent than any essence; by its power, those things that are more "one" participate more fully in essence. Furthermore, the highest perfection of being itself resides in identity; and this identity is founded upon unity, just as diversity and motion are founded upon number. Therefore, unity, which is the cause of perfection for being, is superior to being. Accordingly, you must either say that "being" is the same as "unity," or that it is different. You will surely admit that unity is the foundation of identity. Therefore, if you say the first—that being is the same as unity—then there clearly exists a prior Unity before this unity, through which being exists. But if you say the second—that unity is distinct from being—then unity itself is prior to being in its own right, before it is distinguished from being. It will be absolutely first in itself by its absolute primacy (that is, by its own nature) before it is related as prior to being. It is not permitted to say that being is so distinct from unity that it is not first in unity; for before it can be said to be distinguished, it must first be identical to itself. And it is identical, I say, through unity. To this is added the fact that nothing can be thought of as superior to simplicity itself, and this simplicity is unity itself. Therefore, unity is not only the first of all things, but is also primacy itself.

<summary>This page concludes a discussion on the One's absolute freedom and self-existence before beginning the final book of the Enneads, which argues that unity is the fundamental requirement for any being to exist.</summary>

...[extrem]ity <note>original: "mitas," likely the conclusion of "extremitas" (extremity) or "proximitas" (proximity)</note>, by reason of which all other things are everywhere prior. From these principles it follows that the [First] itself is thus prior: namely, through a unity joined to itself, and also prior to its own self. Nor should one fear here that "to be one" and "to be one essence" are multiple things. For nothing is "one" in this way—that is, perfectly simple—that is not already in the first [principle]; but the One seems to hold itself thus through unity. Think of "Being" and "the One" occurring together: while "Being" is capable of multiformity, it does not compel itself to be only one; but the One itself is not a composite, whether unique or many. ### NINTH BOOK.

ALL things that are beings are beings by the One, both those that are primary beings and those that are in any way said to be among beings. For what could they even be, if they were not one? Since if they are stripped of the "one" that they are said to be, they no longer exist. For there is no army if it is not one, nor a choir, nor a herd, if it is not one. Nor is there a house or a ship if they do not have the One; for the house is one, and the ship is one, and if they lose this unity, the house would no longer be a house, nor the ship a ship. Even continuous magnitudes <term>continuous magnitudes: physical things that can be measured, like lines or solids, which lose their identity if they are divided into disconnected pieces</term> would not exist if the One were not present in them. At any rate, when they are cut, insofar as they lose their unity, they change their way of being. Furthermore, the bodies of plants and animals, each being a single thing, if they flee from the One, being broken into a multitude, are seen to lose the essence they once had. No longer what they were, but becoming other things, and each of those exists only insofar as it is one. 
<margin>health</margin>
And health exists when the body is coordinated into one; and beauty exists when the nature of the One takes hold of the parts. And virtue of the soul exists when the soul is united into one and into a single harmony. Therefore, since the One leads all things into unity—creating, shaping, forming, and ordering—should we, having arrived at the One, say that the One itself supplies these things, and that the One is [the same as soul], or just as the soul supplies other things to bodies but is not itself what it gives, so also is the One something other than itself? When it supplies, it gives the One, since even a man, considering the idea and the order that leads to unity, when he makes each thing, he is not himself [the thing made] 
<margin>* For the body, being composed of many parts, exists by the One, [as do] the parts by the One.</margin>
<gloss>or a man</gloss> even if he conceives of a man along with the humanity within him, in that which is called the "one." Or is it that each thing is "one," and the soul also is [one]? Thus, those things that have less "being" have less of the One, and those that have more [being] have more [unity]. Or indeed, is the soul something other than the One, having more of it according to reason, and truly having more of "being," but not being the One itself? For the soul is a single thing, and the "one" is in a way an accidental property; these are two things: soul and the One, just as body and the One are two. 
<margin>by the One which is in the body</margin>
That which is discrete, like a choir, is furthest from the One, but that which is continuous is closer. The soul, however, participates even more in the One.

Soul and the One: the One is the prototype by which all other things are individual along with being one; nevertheless it must be asked if,

<image-desc>Decorative initial O with a male figure in a circular frame within a square border.</image-desc>
ALL beings are beings by the One itself, both those that are primary beings and those that are numbered in the order of things in any way. For what would they be, if they were not one? If indeed they are deprived of the "one," they are no longer what they were said to be before.
B Neither will an army exist, unless it has been one; nor a choir, nor any flock, unless they are likewise also one. Then truly neither a house nor a ship will exist, unless they obtain the One; since a house is a certain "one thing" and a ship is one. If indeed they lose this, the house will no longer be a house, nor the ship similarly a ship. Continuous magnitudes, therefore, unless the One is within them, would never exist. When they are divided, they change their being as they lose their unity. Moreover, the bodies of plants and animals, which are each a single unit, if they ever flee from the One—namely, being scattered into a multitude—they immediately lose the essence they had, and they will no longer be what they were before; but immediately they turn into other things, which themselves exist only insofar as they are also one. Furthermore, health flourishes when the body is brought together into one; beauty blooms when the power of the One connects the limbs; virtue reigns in the soul when the soul is united into one and into a single harmony. 
D Since the [Soul] brings all things into one, making, shaping, forming, and ordering at the same time, must we, having progressed this far, assert that the soul provides the "one" to things, while it itself already exists as the One itself? But surely, just as the soul suggests other things to bodies and is not exactly that which is handed over—for example, when handing over a form or appearance, the things granted by the soul are different from the soul itself—so it must be thought that even if it bestows the "one," the One is nevertheless distinct from the soul. The soul itself, looking toward the One, makes each thing "one," just as by looking toward the "man," it rightly fabricates a man.
E At the same time, it assumes the "one" together with the man, that very One which is in the man. Of those things which are called "one," each is "one" just as it possesses that which is within itself. For this reason, those things that have less "being" possess less of the One; but where they are "more" [in being], they are likewise more "one." Now truly, since the soul is something other than the One, yet insofar as it is more and more truly [being], it possesses the One to a greater degree, yet it does not exist as the One itself.
F For in a single soul, the "one" is present as something contingent. And these are two things: namely, the soul and the One, which in the soul are like body and the One together. Surely that which is discrete, such as a choir, is most remote from the One; but the soul is much closer, being itself a participant in the One. If someone should object that the soul is exactly the same as the One, because it does not become a soul unless it is one, we shall respond, first, that other things likewise exist individually and simultaneously exist as "one"; nonetheless, [the One is] something else.

But if he were able to make himself something else <gloss>A</gloss>
than what he made, we would either take away his making 
the good, because he would not make evil. But if power 
there were such that he could do opposites, it would not be like a 
steadfast, immovable power—which is truly the greatest 
power—when it does not depart from the One. If indeed the 
ability to do opposites is a weakness, then it is necessary to 
remain in the best. But we must say that his act of making <gloss>B</gloss>
is at once his being, for it is beautiful, and his 
will would turn toward itself. To the God who uses it, 
the will was the will of nothing existing [prior], but by 
that will, without prior deliberation, the substance stood. 
From where, then, is this will for him? That he is an 
unworking essence? <note>original: "ἀνεργάτης"</note> Or is the will itself his essence? 
If indeed the will is different from the essence, then it is 
nothing of the essence. That which was not, was the 
will. Therefore, the whole was will. And in that he is one, 
he is not one who wills [something else]. But the act 
of pre-willing comes from himself; therefore, the will is himself. 
And the <unclear>non</unclear> inner-spirit of the will was later. Therefore, the whole was will, nor was there anything there not willing, nor therefore was there anything before the will. In the Beginning, therefore, the will itself is God himself. And so on.

<column-break/>

But if he himself is rightly said to contain [himself], surely <gloss>A</gloss>
he must be judged to produce himself as well, if indeed 
that which contains something according to nature 
also made it from the beginning. If, therefore, there had been a time 
from which he began to be, it would be rightly said for this 
reason—in a very proper sense—that he made himself. 
But since God existed even before eternity itself, 
this very fact that he is said to have made himself should be 
chiefly thought of in this way: namely, that his "being" 
and his "making" occur equally together. <gloss>B</gloss> 
For his very being is entirely at one with his making, 
as if by a certain eternal generation. 
Similarly, that which in God is usually called the "supreme 
prince" [or ruler]: if there are two things there, it is 
appropriately assumed; but if there is only 
one, then undoubtedly the ruler is there alone: for 
he has no subject beneath him there. But since he is 
equally called the ruler and master of himself, since there 
is nothing there to which a gift might be referred? Perhaps <gloss>C</gloss>
he is considered the dominator there insofar as he is 
regarded from above, because clearly nothing higher 
exists. But if nothing is higher, this is undoubtedly the 
first—first, I say, not by some order, but by his own authority 
and purely free power. If it is pure, it is not permitted to 
perceive anything there that is in the least bit not free. Therefore, 
the whole is entirely free and willing in itself. 
What then is of him that is not he himself? 
What is there that he himself does not act upon? 
What, finally, occurs there that is not his own work? For if 
anything in him were not his own work, he would by no means 
be purely free or all-powerful. For he would not be the 
master of that, nor all-powerful, since he could not do that 
over which he himself was not the master.

### Confirmation of the preceding. Chapter XXI.

> The Principle is the best and immeasurable power. If anyone, therefore, imagines that this power could or could have behaved otherwise, he imagines it as powerless. For just as it is an evil to be changed from the good itself: similarly, to be able to be changed from the supreme and total power is a pitiable lack of power. Plotinus, both in the preceding and in the present, denies that intellect and will are superior to God in the sense of being an "intellectual intellect" or a "desiring will" [separate from him]. Accordingly, the will in God is the very nature of God. Just as God is considered from his own nature, so too he is said to have come forth by his own will; in him, to exist and to will are the same thing. Note: your mind can reach something regarding God, but only by a certain light shining from above: but you must immediately remove whatever runs beyond that light.

THE QUESTION IS, therefore, whether he could have made <gloss>A</gloss>
himself something other than what he did? However, if 
we were to grant that, we would also deny that he makes the 
good, or at least that he does not make evil; but power 
is not understood there as being able to do opposites. 
Rather, since he enjoys a constant and immutable 
power—which is the highest power—
it never departs in any way from that which is the One. 
For to be able to do opposites is a sign of weakness; 
the truly powerful remains in the best. <gloss>B</gloss> 
It is necessary, moreover, that his "affection" <note>Referring to the "disposition" or "will" of the One.</note> (as we call it) 
should exist simultaneously and once and for all: for it is the best. 
And who could pervert that which is both by the 
will of God and is the very will of God? But 
it is asked: is he made by the will of a God who does not yet 
exist? Again, what shall we say of the will there? 
Is it the will of one not yet willing in his own substance? 
And from where does he get this will? 
From an essence not yet performing anything? 
But the will was in the essence: and thus nothing there is 
different from the essence; otherwise, something would have existed there 
which did not exist as will. Therefore, the whole was will, nor was there anything there not willing, nor therefore was there anything before the will. In the Beginning, therefore, the will itself is God himself. And so on.

# PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> ...is more truly "one" than those things. For a body and "the one" are not entirely the same thing; rather, the body participates in the One. Furthermore, each individual soul, although not composed of parts, exists as a multiplicity within itself. For there are many powers within it: namely, it reasons, it desires, and it perceives or notices; these are certainly contained by the One as if by a bond. The soul indeed passes the One to another, since it is itself one; but meanwhile, the soul also receives this "one" as a recipient from another.

Moreover, our soul is one, and even if it is not made of parts, one can reckon many powers in it—reasoning, desiring, perceiving—which are held together by the One as if by a bond. The soul certainly brings the "one" even into itself, but it also receives the One from another.

### Every essence possesses its own natural multiplicity from the beginning, and yet meanwhile is something one. Chapter II.

A distinction must be granted to the singular whole: this is "being," but that is "the one." <note>Plotinus distinguishes between *Ens* (Being/Existence) and *Unum* (The One). In Neoplatonism, the One is above Being.</note> For insofar as it is being, it is also a certain multiplicity; but in what way can it be a multiplicity? This is possible if the individual nature of any of these things does not creep in; it is itself one thing, and that "one" is another. Nor does it arrange "one and one" as if they were two principles. It happens that it is not "being" where there is something [added] to being; and because it would be manifold, being would not be a participant in the One. Therefore, Being is under the One, especially since primary essence is where all forms naturally exist, and for that reason, it is posterior to pure simplicity. Indeed, while this pure unity is established in its own essence through the One, it is clear through the One that all things have joined themselves to essences.

Furthermore, we embrace the Intellect itself because it seems to be "being"; for we understand not only "being" and "to be," but also that things are beings and exist as "one." For do we not? In the Latin sense, where we think of different properties in a multiplicity, we understand these as "many ones," and the "one" in the whole would be the whole of being; but it is more an indeterminate being toward all species, yet meanwhile determinable toward all. The "one" itself is determinable toward the most simple "one" and thus to the first. Likewise, essence, life, and intellect are certain arts <note>Here "arts" likely refers to the "Logoi" or formative principles.</note> which are distributed through themselves, formally distinct among themselves. Therefore, perfection itself is simple, and before it is divided into three such parts, the Intellect always remains in itself. This very fact—namely, being undivided in itself—is the definition of the One. If it follows that it were "one," then power and wisdom are before them through the One. Although simple perfection and "the Good" are the same as the One, the Good itself is superior to being. Likewise, it will be clear if the One is entirely simple. If the very life of being is that in which the unity and simplicity of essence are set apart, then that essential unity is the effect of being; it takes its "one" from the principle, lest anything appear to be essentially above the One; the One is itself simply unity. If this were posterior to being, it would no longer be unity but a multiplicity, and being itself in its first sign would not be a single thing; therefore, it would be an infinite multiplicity or nothing. 

If you grant some being, or being itself simply, it is divisible into parts, whether infinite or underlying, as it is capable of the nature of some multiplicity. But the unique One admits no such thing. Therefore, it is different and superior. Being is indeed divided and exists as a whole in the parts of being, but unity does not spread itself through division, but by the repetition of the whole into "this" and "that" one. Unity is not mutually given to being; rather, the One is always multiplied against division. Finally, even the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> declare the excellence of unity. Namely, they teach that the nature of form and unity are the same, since insofar as something is "being," it is also "one." Likewise, since a thing is being because of its form, and similarly "one," they rightly say the nature of form and unity are the same. They add that this is different by reason of the former. For since there are three principles, it is the property of form to spread itself through potentiality, but the property of unity is simply to consist in itself, and meanwhile to be one through the rest, both inside and outside. It is established that the reason of unity does not come to them from form—rather, it is different from essence, but even simpler and prior, belonging more to the most exalted principle.

---

<margin>A</margin> IT REMAINS to investigate whether in each of those things which exist individually as "one," the essence of each is not the same as its "one." In the whole of being and essence, is essence or being itself entirely the same as the One, so that he who finds being has also attained the One? Namely, since essence itself is the One—for instance, if essence were the Intellect, then the One itself would exist as Intellect. I speak of the Intellect which is the first being and the first "one." And since it hands down the gift of being to others, in this way and to that extent it also grants the "one." For what else would anyone call "the one" besides being and intellect? For the One itself exists either as the same as being—for "man" and "one man" are the same—or at least as a certain number belongs to anything (as if you were to say "two" of something), so "one" is said of a single thing. If therefore number is something among beings, then "the one" is surely something of beings; what it may be remains to be investigated. But if this whole thing is a certain contrivance of the mind, which approaches and follows the numbering of things, it follows that the One itself does not truly exist in things. Yet the superior reason asserted that whatever loses its "one" simultaneously loses its being. Therefore, it is worthy of consideration whether this being and this "one" are individually the same, and similarly whether being itself and the simply "one" are fundamentally the same: but surely if the being of each thing is a certain multiplicity, and the "one" itself cannot be a multiplicity...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <note>original Greek: "Ἀρ' οὐν ἑκαστῳ..."</note> Is it then the case that for each of the particular things, the essence and the One are the same? And in the whole of being and essence, are essence and the One the same? So that he who has found being has also found the One? And essence itself is the One? For example, if the Intellect is essence, then the Intellect would also be the One, being primarily being and primarily one, and imparting being to other things, and to that extent also...

<margin>B</margin> ...the One. For what would one say it is besides these? <margin>to be a man</margin> It is the same as being; for "a man" and "one man" are the same, or like a number [applied] to each thing, as if you said "two." But since "one" is only of something—if indeed number is among beings, it is clear that the One is also. And we must seek what it is. But if numbering is an activity of the soul following along, the One would be nothing in the things themselves. But the argument said that if each thing loses the One, it will not exist...

<margin>C</margin> ...at all. We must see, then, if "each one" is the same as "each being," and if "the One" is the same as "Being" in general. But if the being of each is a multiplicity, and it is impossible for the One...
