...to be a multiplicity. Therefore, each would be different, even if it becomes "man," both animal and rational, consisting of many parts, or if these many parts are joined together. But is man also "one"? If one part is divisible and another is indivisible, and indeed the whole is one, containing all things that exist within itself, then things that exist are much more themselves. Furthermore, by the sharing of the one <margin>* the one</margin> it would hold and participate in the One. But Being also possesses life and mind. It is certainly not something different. For there are many things within Being, which is the One. So, of necessity, many things exist, and even more so, it would encompass the Forms. Just as an Idea is one, so Number is even more of a distance from the One than the whole. In this way, just as the world is one, so entirely is the One <margin>* first</margin> the first, belonging to no one. But other things, as many as come after it, are each either from many parts or joined together, or are later. If, therefore, each thing exists, it is prior to those others. That the first things are not the intelligible world is clear from what follows; there is a necessity for the intelligible world. Or rather, because it is the best of other things, looking outward, the Mind must turn toward itself as toward its own principle, and indeed it does turn. If there is something in it that thinks or is thought, it is double. But if it looks toward the beginning simply, [it is one]. <margin>* those which look toward the first are different</margin> And it must look toward the first, all looking toward the common principle, and before them something follows even toward the strongest. Let it be the first; and the Mind must be the Forms, as if they were the principles of good things, and in the first. It must look toward that, be present with itself, and think itself, and from these things, think all things. Much more then is the One, though being is many-colored. And if it knows all things, it would be the One, or if indeed it were necessary... and indeed if it knows all things, and these all things exist, and this being all things,

If it does not consist in the one, what nature does it have? Or, by a wonder, it is not easy to say what it is, because it is not even an intelligible thing. Nor is it such that we have knowledge of it, as those things which are similar, but whatever does not lead to formlessness or the soul <margin>*</margin> is breathless to encompass those things not defined as a certain "one." But let it be many. <margin>*</margin> It fears the uniform, and it slips away... <margin>*</margin>

<column-break/>

**A** cannot be, it will undoubtedly be different from each other. Therefore, Man is both "animal" and "rational," and consists of many parts, and many things are glued together into a certain "one." Therefore, man is something different from the "one"; for man is indeed divisible, while the "One" is entirely indivisible. And yet, even Being as a whole, containing all things within itself, exhibits multiplicity even more, and is different from the One, though as a protector it possesses the "one." Furthermore, Being also possesses both life and mind. For it is a sacrilege to believe **B** otherwise. Being, therefore, is also "many." But if Being is the <term>Intellect</term><note>Latin: *Intellectus*; Greek: *Nous*. In Neoplatonism, this is the second level of reality, containing all the "Forms" or "Ideas."</note>, then it is again necessarily many, and much more so if it encompasses the <term>species</term><note>Latin: *species*; Greek: *eide*. These are the eternal archetypes or "Forms" of all things.</note>: for it is not purely one, but rather a certain number, both as individual species and as a whole: and it is "one" only in the way the world is "one." Entirely, however, the One exists as the first: but the Intellect, the Species, and Being cannot be the first. For every species consists of many parts and is a certain composite thing, and **C** therefore comes later: for those things from which each thing is composed are rightly judged to be prior. That the Intellect cannot be the First itself will also be clear through this: it is necessary for the Intellect to consist in the act of understanding. And certainly, the highest Intellect, which does not look at external things, must necessarily understand that which is above it: namely, while it turns into itself, it returns to the **D** principle. Now truly, if it is the same as both that which understands and that which is understood, it already exists as a double; and since it is not simple, it is deservedly not the One. But if it looks to another, it looks up entirely to something better and higher. But if it fixes its gaze both on itself and on that which is more excellent, it thus also seems to hold the second rank. It is certainly necessary to assert that the mind is so affected that it approaches the first good and looks up to it, and besides that, dwells with itself, noticing itself, and thus knowing itself to be all things. Since therefore **E** the Intellect is so varied, it is far from being the One itself. For this reason, neither Being itself nor the Intellect is the One. For in that case, it would again be "all things," since the Intellect itself is all things. Finally, it must not be thought that Being is the One, for Being itself is simply all things.

->The Approach to God. Chapter III.<-

The Soul, however, when it nearly approaches God, suffers from ambiguity. This is partly because the soul is both intellect and form, and is accustomed to leaning upon forms. But God has no form. It is also because the soul then approaches Him as much as it can, when it has itself become <term>godlike</term><note>Latin: *factus est Deus*. Plotinus suggests the soul achieves a state of "henosis" or mystical union where it reflects the divine nature.</note>. It is therefore greatly uncertain whether it encounters itself or another. Whoever retreats toward God, the supreme Good and the One, should depart from opposites—that is, from evil, from the lowest things, and from multitude—and should even exceed the Intellect. For the Intellect is not "Being" in a simple sense, but only intellectual Being. But God is superior to any being, indeed, He is superior even to simple Being. For just as sensible being is bounded by sensible form, so intelligible being is bounded by intelligible form. So finally, Being itself is determined by the form of Being. But the Principle stands above everything determined. It is not said to "stand still," nor is it forced to "become standing." Nor does it do anything by a relationship to things. But things are made by it, becoming what they are without Him "making" them; they are changed without Him being changed.

**F** WHAT, then, is the One itself? And what nature does it have? But truly, it is no wonder that it is not easy to say, especially since neither Being nor Form can be easily expressed; for our knowledge relies on forms. But when the soul is carried toward something formless, since it cannot grasp it—because it is not determined, nor is it shaped by any various shaper—it slips away from there entirely, and fears lest perhaps it...

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI

<margin>A</margin> ...since it finds nothing there to report. For this reason, the soul labors in such matters and often gladly descends from them, falling away from all things until it rushes toward something perceived by the senses, where it might rest as if on solid ground—just as the sight, when exhausted by discerning small things, gladly turns itself toward larger objects. But when the soul strives to see by itself, seeing only by being with itself <note>original: "cum se videat solum"</note>, and because it is made one with the very act of seeing, it becomes one with that object. Indeed, because it is one with it, the soul does not think it has what it seeks, since it is not different from that which is being understood. <margin>B</margin> It is worthwhile, first of all, for the one who is about to philosophize concerning the One itself to prepare himself in this way: since the One is that which we seek—the principle of all things, the Good itself, and the First—it is right that he should not be far removed from those things which are the first, nor should he be cast down in any way toward the extremes of all things. Instead, as he ascends to the first things, he should lead himself back to the heights, away from the things of the senses, which are the last of all. <margin>C</margin> Again, it is necessary to bring a soul purified of all wickedness <note>original: "malignitate purgatum"</note> when one strives to approach the Good. Furthermore, he must raise himself up to his own principle so that he may be with the first things, becoming one out of many, if he is to behold the Principle and the One. At that time, the Intellect <note>original: "intellectum" / "νοῦν" — the Divine Mind or second hypostasis</note> must become the ruling authority, and thus the whole soul must be committed to the Mind and placed deep within it, so that the soul may receive what the Intellect itself sees with an awakened state, and through that Intellect, contemplate both itself and the One. <margin>D</margin> If he brings no sluggishness, nor anything arising from the senses, but contemplates the purest thing with only the pure Mind, the very first part of the Mind. Therefore, whenever one is drawn to contemplate this and imagines some magnitude, or figure, or any kind of mass around this nature, it is certain that the Intellect was not the guide in this speculation, since the Intellect by its own nature does not turn toward looking at such things. Rather, such an action belongs to the senses or to the opinion that follows the nature of the senses. <margin>E</margin> But one must receive the message from the Intellect regarding those things that are in its power. For the Intellect is able to look at what is above itself, what belongs to it, or what is produced by it. Those things in it are indeed pure; but those things above the Intellect—or rather, that which is above the Intellect—are even purer and simpler. For this reason, that which is above the Intellect is not the Intellect itself, but stands before the Intellect. For the Intellect is one of the things that exist <note>original: "ens" — Being</note>; <margin>F</margin> but the other is not "something," but is superior to each thing. Nor is it Being: for Being has, as it were, the very form of Being. But that One is entirely formless, separated even from intelligible form. For since the nature of the One is the generator of all things, it is rightly none of them. Therefore, it is not "something," nor of a certain quality, nor of a certain quantity. Furthermore, it is not Intellect, it is not Soul; it is not moved, nor is it at rest; it is not in a place, nor is it in time. Rather, it is uniform according to itself—or rather,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> What it does not have, because it grows weary in all things, and as if descending it often fails, exhausted by all things, until it comes to something perceived by the senses, in which it might rest as if on solid ground—just as the sight, growing weary of small things, gladly falls upon large ones. But by itself, whenever the soul wishes to see, seeing only by being present with it, and being one, it does not yet think it has what it seeks because it is one, <margin>B</margin> and that which is being understood is not different from it. It is useful for the one who is about to <gloss>philosophize</gloss> <note>original: "φιλοσοφῇ"</note> about the One to act in this way. It will appear how that which we seek is both the principle of all things and the contemplation of the best things. Since it is the First, one must believe that if he must trust in the things concerning the first and the last of all things, he must not stay there, but leading himself away from the first things, he must lead himself back from the sensible things, which are the last. One must be freed from all vice, <margin>C</margin> since he himself is going toward the Good, and he must have ascended to the principle within himself, and from many become one, as one, and as one who will be a spectator. He must entrust the leadership of the soul to the Mind <note>original: "νοῦν"</note>, and having trusted and submitted himself, he will behold the One with that wakefulness which the Mind shows. Just as every sensation is pleasant, so it is for those who receive that vision. <margin>D</margin> But one must behold the One with a pure Mind, the purest part, that which is of the first things. And if the spectator still imagines any superimposed thing, or a shape, or a mass around that nature, then [the Mind] is not the guide of the vision. For it is not likely that he would reach the first things if he were raised up by those things in opinion which follow the senses in their activity. Rather, one must receive <margin>E</margin> from the Mind the announcements of what it is capable of. The Mind is able to see either the things before it, or its own, or the things from it. The things in it are pure. But even purer and simpler are the things before it. Or rather, that which is before it. And that is not yet Mind, but that which is before it is in some way among existing things. For the Mind is "something," but that which is before each thing is not "something"; for the One is, as it were, the form of the things in which it is held. But that is formless, even of intelligible form. For the nature <margin>F</margin> of the One, being the generator of all things, is none of them. It is not "something," nor of a quality, nor of a quantity, nor Mind, nor Soul; it is not moved, nor again standing still; it is not in place, nor in time. But it is of a single form <note>original: "μονοειδές"</note> according to itself, or rather formless, before form and before all movement, before rest. For these things are around Being, which make it many. Why then is it not even moved? <margin>G</margin> Because perhaps, while one of these two—or both—must necessarily be around Being, that which stands still, stands by itself...

But why does it not stand still enough, if it is not moved? Because it is necessary that either one or both of these be present around Being. Furthermore, that which stands, stands by means of stability itself...

# BOOK NINE.

...it is called, nor is it exactly the same as a state: therefore it happens to it, and it no longer remains a simple thing. Indeed, when we affirm that the One itself is the cause of all things, we do not say this because of something happening to it, but rather something that happens to us: since it is absent from us, yet we possess something of it while it remains meanwhile within itself. Therefore, speaking of God with the most exact reason, it is not right to say either "that" or "this": instead, we—wandering around the outside—attempt to interpret our own affections or passions <note>original: "affectiones sive passiones"</note> in whatever way we can. And sometimes we indeed draw nearer to this very thing, while at other times we fall further away in our uncertainty and ambiguity.

<margin>
By not saying "that" or "these things" accurately, but as if we are running around the outside, we wish to interpret our own feelings, sometimes near and sometimes falling away, amidst the difficulties concerning it.
</margin>

->**Access to God. Chapter IV.**<-

*The Principle of all things is entirely incorporeal, immobile, and one. Since, therefore, we cannot reach it through opposites, we rightly do not reach it through the machinations of a bodily imagination, nor by the movement of a changeable mind that never stops thinking of something else, nor by an intelligence that is by its own nature multiple and always meditating on varied things: but we reach it at last by a certain unity of the soul through a higher intellect. This happens when we take refuge in it, having been entirely segregated from the multitude, both internal and external. Then for the first time we have the sign of God, who is everywhere present, now perfectly present to us—especially as a torch, a new light infused from the Mind, an inestimable joy. Two things contribute to achieving this: doctrine, which serves as the path, and segregation, which serves as the preparation of the soul.*

<margin>
The soul experiences its being as a foundation. And concerning its being, it occurs to everyone whenever they receive knowledge. For knowledge is reason, and reason is many.
</margin>

Doubt and a sense of deficiency occur to us regarding the knowledge of God, chiefly because we do not know him through any <term>science</term> <note>In this context, "science" (scientia/episteme) refers to structured, logical knowledge or demonstrative proof.</note> nor through any act of intelligence, as we are accustomed to knowing other things which are called "intelligible." Instead, we know him through a certain **presence** <note>original Greek: "parousia"</note> that is better than science. Indeed, the soul moves far away from the One, and is no longer entirely one, when it takes on the knowledge of something. For science is a certain <term>reason</term> <note>original: "logos"</note>, and reason is many. The soul, therefore, passes beyond the One when it falls into number and multitude.

It is necessary, therefore, to transcend science, and in no way to deviate from that which is to be "one": but one must be called back from science, from the things to be known, and from every other beautiful spectacle. For everything beautiful is later than that One and comes from it, just as all daylight comes from the sun. For this reason, Plato says that the supreme God can neither be spoken of nor written about. Yet we frequently write and speak about him so that we may at least stir our minds by these disputations and direct them toward the **divine spectacle**, as if showing a certain path to someone who desires to see something.

<margin>
*To behold the Reason still, out of these reasons.
</margin>

Doctrine indeed extends its power as far as the path and the journey: but to actually see God is the work of the one who has willed to see. Truly, that person neither reaches the spectacle nor beholds its light—and therefore is not affected by it, nor tastes within himself that **amorous passion** <note>original: "affectionem sive passionem... amatoriam"</note> which usually arises from the intuition of the beloved—unless the lover finally rests in the beloved. There, truly, the true light is received, illuminating the entire soul as it draws nearer. I say that he who struggles to ascend there does not attain such things if he is still held back or hindered by those things which are obstacles to the beholder. Nor does he ascend there alone, but meanwhile draws with him something that distinguishes him from the One; or rather, he has not yet been entirely reduced into one. For God is never absent from anyone, yet in a certain way he seems to be absent from all, so that he is present everywhere, and yet again, not present. For—

<margin>
*He is not only existing as those things which were obstacles to the sight, and has not only ascended, but having the difference from him, or somehow not having been led in, he has been cast out... playing as if being present while not being present.
</margin>

<column-break/>

<summary>Plotinus explains that God (the One) cannot be reached through logic or "science" because these involve multiplicity, whereas the soul must achieve a state of "presence" and absolute simplicity to perceive the divine. He emphasizes that words and teachings only point the way; the final "amorous" union with the light of God is an individual internal experience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Plotinus’s discussion from Ennead VI, Book 9, Chapter 4, regarding the presence of the One. It explores how the soul must prepare itself through likeness and simplicity to "touch" the divine. It then transitions into Chapter 5, which refutes the idea that the universe is governed by chance and begins a systematic proof of the hierarchy of being—from body to soul to intellect, and finally to the absolute One.</meta>

# PLOTINUS, ENNEAD VI.

...it is present only to those who are able to receive it, and who are so prepared that they can harmonize with it, and as it were, reach out to touch it through a certain intimate likeness <note>Plotinus emphasizes that "like is known by like"; the soul must become simple to know the Simple.</note> and power, akin to the gift that was bestowed. This occurs when the soul is completely affected in the same way it was when it first proceeded from that source: and therefore it is now able to see, just as God is by His nature to be seen through Himself. I say that he has not yet arrived there who, because of these obstacles, is pulled back from that place, or even dragged toward earthly things, since there is a lack of the reason and discipline that leads to that point and creates faith concerning divine matters. But truly, as far as other obstacles are concerned, each person could blame themselves: for indeed, one ought to strive to be far away from everything, and to escape alone. As for the reasons which he might perhaps trust less, let him who is about to set out finally think in this way.

---

->Access to the Divine. Chapter V.<-

*In our Theology, and in the book on Love, and in the second book of Epistles, we have more diligently assigned the reasons by which one must ascend step by step from corporeal nature—which is subject to dimension, motion, and number—to the soul, which is already free from dimension. From the moving and multiple soul to the immobile but multiple intellect; and meanwhile, from the intellect proper to the soul itself to the intellect simply; and finally from the intellect, which is necessarily multiform in itself, to the One simply, which is not "the existing One" lest it be multiple: for the ratio of the One and of Being is different. For Being both admits multitude and has "nothing" as its opposite. But the One does not sustain multitude, but rejects it as its opposite. It is therefore not Being, but the entirely absolute principle of Being; and meanwhile the most absolute principle of species. For all species of natural things possess their absolute being in the first things. When we name God "the One," we prophesy and fully indicate simplicity itself, which is far more excellent above essence and the principle of essence than the unity of numbers and the point of dimensions. Truly, just as continuous being and discrete being are referred back to some individual, so the Simply itself is referred to the Simply individual in itself.* <note>This italicized section is a summary provided by the translator and philosopher Marsilio Ficino, explaining the Neoplatonic hierarchy of existence.</note>

---

<margin>C</margin>
**W**HOSOEVER believes that things are governed by fortune and rash chance, and that chance is contained only in bodily things, such people are far from God and the very intelligence of Him is far removed from them. Nor do we address our words to men affected in this way, but only to those who posit another nature besides bodies, and who reach at least as far as the soul. For these, it is useful to diligently observe the nature of the soul, both in how it regards other things, and especially how it proceeds from the intellect, and receiving reason from there, attains virtue. Beyond these things, however, one ought to consider another intellect besides the reasoning intellect, which is called the "rational" one. Likewise, the discourses or arguments of reason, as if already in a certain distance and motion; and also the sciences, which are reasons in the soul of such a kind as are now placed in the manifest, because the intellect has been infused into the soul for the sake of things to be known: which intellect also sees the intellect as if it were sensible: because, clearly, it can be perceived and noticed—I mean the intellect that hangs over the soul, its father, the intelligible world, an intellect entirely quiet, and as if a certain quiet motion having all things in itself, being all things, a multitude indistinct, and again distinct. For it is not discerned just as reasons are accustomed to be in speech, but as if reasons were already thought according to one certain thing; nor again are the things in that mind confused. For each thing comes forth separately, just as happens in the sciences: and although all things harmonize in a certain individual, the individual things are nevertheless discerned from others. This multitude collected together, this intelligible world, stands indeed first and most closely; reason says this is...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
But it belongs to those capable of receiving it who have been prepared, and can fit themselves to it and as it were touch and grasp it by likeness and the power in themselves, akin to it, if indeed any cause came from it to rule. Or if one is unable to see, as that is naturally visible, if he is not yet there, but because of these things is still outside, or lacks the arguments leading there, and faith...
<margin>B</margin>
...concerning the matters, for that reason [one should blame] <unclear>oneself</unclear> <note>original Greek: "ἑαυτὰ"</note>, and surrendering oneself to be alone, but if they should lack faith in the thoughts, let him think thus.

<margin>C</margin>
If anyone thinks these things are governed by chance and spontaneity, and are held together by bodily causes, he is driven far from God and the notion of the One. And the word is not for these people, but for those who set another nature besides bodies, and ascend to the soul; and indeed through these, let them understand the nature of the soul, and other things, and how it is from the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original Greek: "νοῦ" (nous), the realm of pure thought above the discursive soul.</note>, and by participating in...
<margin>D</margin>
...reason from this, it has virtue. After these things, to grasp another intellect than the reasoning one, which is called "rational," which by reasonings, as if in distance and motion, [makes] the sciences [into] reasons in the soul which having appeared, we might now call manifest, the things having become in the soul the intellect, the cause of sciences, or even having seen it as if sensible, to be in a way by the sensible, having ascended to the soul...
<margin>E</margin>
...being its father, the intelligible world, a quiet intellect, which rests in what must be called motion, having all things in itself, which being all things is an indistinct multitude, and again distinct. For it is not distinct like the reasons already thought according to one thing, nor are the things in it confused, for each is separate from each, as even in the sciences all things being in an indivisible thing. Nevertheless, each is separate from them. This therefore is the simultaneous...
<margin>F</margin>
...multitude, the intelligible world. And as for the things near the first, the reason itself says of necessity...

It establishes a hierarchy of existence from the physical world to the soul, and finally to the quiet, all-encompassing "Intelligible World" or Intellect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the soul's ascent toward the absolute. Having established that the soul must be purified of earthly distractions, Plotinus now moves into the metaphysical core of the Enneads: defining the nature of "The One" as the source of all existence, which transcends both being and intellect.</meta>

# BOOK NINE.

<margin>The One, most simple <note>Greek: τὸ ἓν τὸ ἁπλότατον</note></margin>
...if the whole soul is something more sovereign than the body, it must follow that the soul itself is not the First Principle, because it is neither perfectly "one" nor "simple." Yet the One—the principle of all things—is indeed simple. Therefore, that which is before all specific types of things is most honorable. If there must be something before "Being" <note>Plotinus argues that "Being" implies a duality of the thing that exists and its existence; therefore, the source of Being must be even simpler than Being itself.</note>, it wishes to be one, yet it is not "a" being. It seems that "Being" does not scatter itself, but truly holds itself together. Yet that which divides itself to participate in what is near to it feels a sense of lack. And in some way, the thing that fills the "One" is that which exists before it.

<margin>The miracle of the One remaining <note>Greek: θαῦμα τὸ ἑνὸς μενεῖν</note></margin>
It is a marvel that from the One, that which is not one <note>i.e., the multiplicity of the universe</note> exists. And indeed, in this realm, this is so true that there is no name that truly fits it. But if we must name it, it is commonly called "The One"—not as if it were one thing among others, but simply "One." It is difficult to know it through the things we usually know; rather, it is known through its offspring, which is Essence <note>or "Substance," Greek: ousia</note>. The Intellect is a "good" essence, and its nature is such that it is the fountain of the best things, a power that generates all beings while remaining within itself. It is not diminished by the things it creates. Therefore, when we look toward this source, we must call it "The One" out of necessity, so that we may signal it to one another, bringing our souls toward an indivisible concept. When we call the soul "one," we do not mean "one" in the way we speak of a mathematical point or a numerical unit. For that kind of "one" is merely the beginning of quantity, which could not exist unless Essence—and that which is before Essence—preceded it. Therefore, we must fix the sharp point of our thought here.

<margin>Above all essences <note>Greek: ὑπὲρ τὰς οὐσίας</note></margin>
But these matters are always discussed by those people in illogical ways, confusing the "Simple" with the soul's multiplicity and its divisions.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> By necessity, it concludes that if any reason proves the soul also exists, then this source is more excellent than the soul. However, even the soul is not the "First," since it is neither one nor simple. But the One itself, the principle of all things, is undoubtedly simple. Therefore, that which is higher than "Being" itself is the most excellent "One." Clearly, there must be something higher than the Mind <note>Latin: mens; the Intellect</note>, which indeed desires to be one, but is not one, but rather "uniform." This is because the Intellect is not dispersed within itself, <margin>B</margin> but truly harmonizes with itself; nor does it touch itself like something composed of separate joints. Furthermore, that which becomes "one" is closest to it, insofar as it seems to dare to withdraw somewhat from the One. I say that what exists wonderfully above this is like a miracle: the One itself, which surely should not be called "being," lest the One itself be found lacking here as well. No name truly fits it. But if men are forced to name it, it is conveniently called "The One" by common appellation; yet not in such a way that it is first one thing, <margin>C</margin> and then "one." It is certainly difficult to know, chiefly because it is best known through its progeny, Essence: for it leads into the essence of the Intellect. The nature of the One itself is such that it is the fountain of all the best things, a power generating all beings, remaining in itself, neither diminished by what it sends forth in generating, nor resting within the things it has created. Certainly, we name that which exists before these things "The One," compelled by a certain necessity, desiring <margin>D</margin> to designate the first nature of all things among ourselves by a name, leading ourselves into an indivisible notion and striving to bring the soul back to unity. Here, we certainly do not mean "one" and "indivisible" as if we were speaking of a mathematical sign or a numerical unit. For that which is "one" in that way is the principle of quantity—which would never exist unless Essence, and that which is before Essence, came before it. For this reason, we must not fix the edge of our thinking on these [mathematical] things; rather, we must believe that this Unity and this "sign" represent the One itself through a certain analogous similarity, because of a certain quality that is free from multiplicity and division.

---

### Access to God. Chapter VI.

> *By an opposite path, we approach through dimensions and numbers toward their own indivisible point, and among beings, we approach that indivisible point which is the principle of all beings. In the former case [mathematics], one reaches something infinite and smallest; but here [in theology], one reaches the most outward and most ample: I say, the greatest in simplicity and power. For it is always simpler than any simplicity you can imagine, and similarly more powerful than anything can be. The One alone can be the principle of nature; for it alone is entirely self-sufficient. Whatever exists besides it is necessarily multiple and suffers a fourfold lack: for in it, the whole needs the parts, the part needs the other part, the parts need the whole, and finally, it needs the unity that composes it from the outside. But truly, it belongs to the Principle to seek nothing, to receive nothing, to lose nothing. The One alone has this office; otherwise, it would certainly not be "one." When we deny that the One "understands" <note>i.e., possesses Intellect/Thought</note>, we do so lest we force it to be multiple; we do not deny that it is a wondrous light, the creator of intelligence—or even that it is "Intelligence" itself, if only "Intelligence" signifies a light better than ordinary understanding, having within itself (or rather, being entirely) whatever is desirable to those who understand. It is not satisfied with its own uncertainty, nor that of others, but without composition or relation, it shines wonderfully for itself and all others. Finally, as we have said elsewhere, Plotinus thinks no differently than Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian who blended Neoplatonism with Christianity, famously emphasizing God's transcendence.</note>: that the Principle is above intellect, life, and essence.*

---

How then do we say "One," or how is it to be applied to thought, or are we positing many things as one? Or how does a "unit" seem to signify anything here? For in the former case, the soul, having stripped away magnitude and the plurality of number, ends at that which is signified as the outward limit, which is indivisible, yet was once part of divisible things and resided in another.

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin> In what way, then, do we say "One"? By what reason can we most powerfully and appropriately apply our intelligence to it? Truly, we do so if we assert it is "One" in a much more excellent way than we are accustomed to asserting a numerical unit or a sign. For here, the mind, gradually stripping away magnitude and multitude, finally descends into the smallest indivisible point...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence, continuing onto the next page to describe how the soul finds the source of all things by removing every layer of physical and mental complexity.</meta>

--- Page 799 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of the nature of the Absolute (the One). Having previously discussed why the Soul and Intellect cannot be the First Principle due to their inherent multiplicity, Plotinus now defines the One's "infinity" as a matter of power rather than physical size, and establishes its total self-sufficiency.</meta>

### PLOTINUS' ENNEADS VI.

<margin>A</margin>But the One itself resides neither in another, nor in a divided thing; nor is it "indivisible" <note>original: "individuum"</note> in the sense of being some tiny, minimal point. For it is the greatest of all things—not in physical magnitude, but in power. Therefore, when it is called "indivisible," we mean it is indivisible in its power; for indeed, the things that come after it are governed by powers that cannot be dissolved, rather than by physical masses. Furthermore, we ought to call God "infinite," not as if He were some physical size or a numerical quantity that one cannot cross, but because the scope of His power is beyond comprehension.

<margin>B</margin>For however highly you might think of Him—even as Intellect or as God—He still surpasses these concepts and is more excellent still. More accurately: when you have directed your thought to the highest point to reach "the One," even then, He surpasses that very unity you have conceived in its simplicity. For you were trying to reduce Him to the highest unity of *your* understanding; but He surpasses all measure, for He remains within Himself, and nothing ever happens to Him.

<margin>C</margin>Furthermore, one can prove the supreme unity of God through that which is called "self-sufficiency" <note>original: "seipso sufficiens"</note>. For it is necessary that the First Principle of all things should be in no way wanting, but the most self-sufficient of all, and perfectly content in itself. Whatever is not "one," but "many," is necessarily in need: since it is not unity itself, but has become one by being composed of many parts. Thus, its very essence requires unification.

<margin>D</margin>But the One itself does not need itself: for it already exists as itself. Moreover, that which is "many" within itself needs as many things as it contains to exist. And each of the things within it, since it does not exist by itself but only along with the others, certainly needs those others; therefore, such a thing reveals itself to be "in need" both in its individual parts and in its whole. If, therefore, it is necessary for something to be perfectly self-sufficient, it must also be "One": existing in such a way that it is in need neither of itself nor of anything else.

<margin>E</margin>For it does not seek anything to exist in the future, nor to exist well, nor even to find a place to be established; since it is the cause of both existence and well-being for all other things, it rightly does not receive its own existence or well-being from others. For how could "well-being" flow to it from elsewhere? Therefore, "well-being" is not something that happens to it; it is itself this very thing. Likewise, there is no place for it, for it needs no foundation, as if it could not support itself. For that which must be founded in another is judged to be void of life—a collapsing mass, unless it is supported. Other things are stabilized because of the One, through whom they both exist and were allotted a place where they could be arranged in order. But that which seeks a place is undoubtedly in need.

The First Principle, however, has no need of the things that follow it: and so the Principle of all things lacks nothing at all. Truly, that which is "needy" is judged so because it seeks a principle. If the One itself needed anything, it would seek to no longer be the One; it would therefore need a destroyer. Yet whatever is called "needy" is in need of a good condition and a savior. Therefore, for the One, nothing is "good,"

<margin>F</margin>nor does it have a will for anything, but it is (so to speak) "Above-Good" <note>original: "super bonum", Greek: ὑπεράγαθον</note>. It is not a good for itself, but for others, if they are able to participate in it. Nor does Intellect exist within the One, lest there be diversity within it. Again, there is no motion; for the One is superior to both motion and intellect. For what would it think? Perhaps itself? But if that were so, it would be "ignorant" before its act of thinking...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>But if it were in another, or in a part, it would not be indivisible in the sense of being something very small. For it is the greatest of all—not in magnitude, but in power. Thus, that which is indivisible <note>original: "ἀμερέθες"</note> is so in power; and the things that exist after it have their powers in an indivisible way, though they are in physical masses. And one must grasp that He is infinite, not by being "un-traversable" in size or number, but by the incomprehensibility of His power. For whenever you think of Him,

<margin>B</margin>such as as "Intellect" or "God," He is more than that. <margin>* In an equal state of mind and in the same way, it is more than if you imagined him to be God; it is something more unified than your own thought.</margin> And again, whenever you think of Him as something more unified than your own thought, He exists by Himself, with nothing having happened to Him, because He is self-sufficient. And that which is within Him—which is not a "one"—must be the most sufficient of all, most self-sufficient, and least in need. But everything that is "many" and not "one" is in need, being made of many. Whatever it is,

<margin>C</margin>its essence consists in being, and that which it lacks, it lacks within itself; for it is not many, <note>Greek text here is slightly fragmented</note> but is itself to all things. And each thing within it is with the others and in itself; but being one of the others, it shows itself to be in need both in its parts and as a whole. Since, therefore, there must be that which is most self-sufficient, it must be the One, because it alone is such that it is in need neither of itself nor of another. For indeed,

<margin>D</margin>the One did not need anything for itself in order to be established. For why would it, being the cause for others? That which it has from others is what it is; but that which has everything in itself, is itself. So that even "well-being" is not an accident for it: it is itself well-being. And there is no place for it, nor does it need to be established, as if it could not carry itself. That which is not established is centered, soulless, a falling mass, and unless it is established, it will fall. But other things are established through the One, through which they both subsist and have their place, as if in an order of location.

<margin>E</margin>That which seeks a place is in need. But the Principle is not in need of those things that come after it; and the Principle of all is without need of all. For that which is in need, is in need because it longs for a principle. If the One were in need of something, it would clearly be seeking not to be the One, so that which destroys it would be what it needs. But everything that is said to be "in need" is in need of that which is good and which saves it. Therefore, for the One, nothing is "good," nor is there a will for anything; instead,

<margin>F</margin>it is "Above-Good," and it is good not for itself, but for others, if any part of them is able to participate in it. Neither is there Intellect <note>original: "νόησις"</note>, lest there be "otherness" <note>original: "ἑτερότης"</note>, nor is there motion; for it is before motion and before intellect. For what would it even think? Itself? But before thinking, it was already itself...

<meta>The catchword "ignorans" (ignorant) links to the start of the next page's argument: if the One had to think of itself to know itself, it would have been ignorant before that thought, which is impossible for the First Principle.</meta>

<summary>This page defines the Neoplatonic "One" as a principle of infinite power rather than size. Plotinus argues that the One is the only truly self-sufficient being, as multiplicity always implies a need for unification, and it transcends concepts like God, Intellect, and Goodness.</summary>
<keywords>The One, Neoplatonism, Infinity, Self-sufficiency, Above-Good, Intellect, First Principle, Plotinus</keywords>

--- Page 800 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the nature of the Absolute (the One). Having established that the One is infinite in power and self-sufficient, Plotinus now explores why we cannot attribute human "intellect" or "self-knowledge" to the One, as these imply a division between the thinker and the thought. He then moves into a practical "Approach to God," advising the soul on how to strip away external images to achieve union.</meta>

### BOOK NINE.

<column-break/>

**A** If He were ignorant and required intelligence to recognize himself, He would no longer be considered self-sufficient <note>original: "se ipso sibi sufficiens"</note>. Therefore, even if He neither recognizes nor understands himself in a human sense, He is not for that reason in a state of ignorance. For ignorance happens in relation to *another*, when one thing does not know something else. But that which is truly One neither knows anything nor has anything to be ignorant of. Rather, being one with itself—at its most unified—it does not need self-intelligence. **B** Indeed, we should not even apply the concept of "being with oneself" to Him, as if it were a way to preserve His unity. On the contrary, we must entirely remove from Him the notions of intelligence, consciousness, self-observation, self-recognition, and the perception of others. We should not even think of God as an "intelligent being" <note>original: "intelligentis"</note>, but rather as the very act of Intellection itself. Yet, even this Intellection does not "think" in the usual way; it is the cause of thinking for others. The true cause is not the same as that which proceeds from the cause; therefore, the Cause of all things is strictly none of those things. We must not judge Him to be the same as the "good" He provides to others; rather, He is "Good" in a different sense, vastly more excellent than all other goods.

---

-> Approach to God. Chapter VII. <-

Even if God is everywhere, He shines most clearly in the summit of intelligence. To perfectly achieve this light, all forms—not only those we imagine but even those we understand—stand in the way like clouds. Therefore, shake off all of these entirely, and you will happily perceive the divine light with a serene mind.

---

**C** If, however, you find yourself wavering in the indefinite ambiguity of the mind because God is "none of these things," then at least fix your mental gaze upon these things first, and then from them, let your whole mind run back to God. But do not do this by casting your thoughts outward. God is not placed in some specific location so as to be missing from your reach; wherever there is anything capable of touching Him, God himself is present—He simply cannot *not* be present. Just as in other matters, it is not possible for someone who is thinking of one thing and **D** is totally focused on it to think of another thing at the same time; rather, one must bring nothing else to the act of understanding so that the thing itself becomes intelligible. Similarly here: it is impossible for one who holds the image of any other thing in their soul to seek God while that image is still performing its act. Nor can a soul occupied by other things be shaped by a contrary figure. But just as the philosophers say that "prime matter" <note>original: "materiam"</note> must be void of all qualities if **E** it is to receive the forms of all things, so too—and much more so—must the soul become formless <note>original: "informem"; here meaning "stripped of all preconceived images or limitations"</note> if it is to communicate without any obstacle that might prevent it from being illuminated and filled by the First Nature. If this is the case, it is worthwhile for the soul, having separated itself from all external things, to turn itself deeply inward. It should not be pulled back toward anything outside, but should instead become ignorant of all things—first by its disposition, and then even of the very forms themselves. **F** Becoming ignorant even of itself, it should lie down in the contemplation of Him and cling to Him as a familiar. Then, as if it had conversed enough, it may come forth as a messenger (if it can) to declare that divine union to others. It was perhaps by relying on such a union that Minos <note>A legendary king of Crete said to have received laws directly from Zeus every nine years.</note> was once considered the familiar companion of Jove [Jupiter]. Mindful of that conversation, he established laws as an image of it, being filled with the divine through that very touch. Or perhaps, considering civil matters unworthy of himself, he preferred to remain always in the divine height...

PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> He established laws according to that likeness <note>Plotinus is referring to Minos, the legendary king of Crete who was said to converse with Zeus to receive laws</note>, having clearly been instructed by that divine communion to frame legislation. Later, however, a soul might consider civil institutions to be less worthy of its divine familiarity, if it prefers to remain in the heights. This indeed seems to happen rightfully to one who has gazed upon the divine as much as possible. He says, therefore, that God is outside of no one, but resides in all, even if they do not know it. For they themselves flee outside of God, or rather, outside of themselves. Therefore, they are unable to grasp the one whom they flee. And those who have already lost themselves are not strong enough to track down another. <margin>B</margin> Just as a son, placed outside of himself by some madness, will not recognize his father; so too, he who has learned to know himself will also rightly know from whence he came.

### The Approach to God. Chapter VIII.

God is like an individual and immobile center of the universe, upon whom and toward whom all things hang. Similarly, the divine intellect and the intellectual souls created from it have their own certain centers—that is, essential unities higher than the intellect itself. In the divine intellect, therefore, besides such a center, there exists one orbit, which is the intellect's own. In souls, however, beyond their center, there are three orbits: intellect, reason, and imagination. The center is always joined and united to that Center. The intellectual orbit revolves perpetually around the same thing. The rational and imaginative orbits, however, sometimes revolve around their own center and the divine center, and sometimes they are, as it were, "broken" and decline obliquely toward other things; this, we say, becomes the life of brutes when we lead a life by reason not turned toward God in intellect—at least, we still revolve around God. There remains a stillness, even a certain affection in the reason, which will sometimes recall us to God by its own stings. When we are thoroughly joined in union—since we are joined to Him through essential unity—we enjoy Him far more fully within ourselves than one who possesses Him through any kind of knowing. It is probable, indeed, that we who are joined by such a union shall never depart from there. This union is an affection, when the incorporeal is joined to the corporeal, provided that one of them has already set aside the formal diversity <note>original: "formalem diuersitatem"; the distinct individual characteristics that separate one thing from another</note> through which alone it differed from the other.

<margin>C</margin> If, therefore, any soul knows itself at some other time, and recognizes that its motion is not straight—unless perhaps when it suffers some "breakage"—but that its natural motion is, as it were, circular around something, not an external thing, but around a center; and that this is the center from which the circle proceeds. Such a soul will surely move around that very thing from which it exists; and bringing itself toward it from every side, it will apply itself completely to that to which it was fitting for all souls to bring themselves. The souls of the Gods are always carried thither, and for that reason they are Gods, because they are held to that Center: for a God is whatever is joined to Him. But that which stands far off is man—indeed, a "multiple" man and a brute. <margin>D</margin> Is that which is, as it were, the center of the soul, the very thing which is the "Sought-After" itself? But furthermore, one must consider that it is something else into which all centers, as it were, concur. It is necessary to remember that the names of "center" and "circle" are brought forward here according to a certain comparison of analogy. <margin>E</margin> For the soul is not a circle in the sense of a geometric figure; but because the ancient and principal nature is in it and around it. And the soul hangs from such a nature, and even more so when the whole soul is separated <note>original: "separatus"; meaning separated from the body or material concerns</note>. But now, after some part of us is submerged in the body—just as if someone had their feet in the water but the rest of their body above the water—we are raised up by our higher part, and through our center we are joined with Him as the center of all things; just as we are often accustomed to align the centers of many circles with the center of the surrounding and containing sphere. <margin>F</margin> If, therefore, the orbits of the souls were corporeal orbits, they would certainly be revolved by a certain condition of place and a common position. But since souls themselves are intelligible, and that One is above the intellect—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> By doing these things, he was rumored to be pleasing to God, as one who, remembering, enters into all the laws of that nature, being filled with divine laws through contact with God. Or perhaps, having judged political matters worthy of Him, he wishes to remain above; which is what would happen to one who has seen much. As he says, He is not outside, but is present to all who know Him. For those who are "outside" flee from Him, or rather, flee outside themselves; they cannot go there, having fled, or He Himself has departed. <margin>B</margin> Leaving Him, they seek another. But the child who has become "outside himself" in madness does not know his father. But he who has learned to know himself will also know from where he came.

<margin>C</margin> If, then, any soul knows itself at another time, it knows that its motion is not in a straight line, except when it suffers a "break," but its natural motion is like that in a circle, not around something external, but around a center. The center is that from which the circle moves around that from which it is; and it will stand toward it, being brought together with itself toward the same thing from which it came out after all things. The souls of the gods are always carried toward that which they are carried, and they are gods. For a god is that which is joined to Him. <margin>D</margin> But he who stands far off is the "multiple" man and the beast. Therefore, that which is like the center of the soul is the thing sought, or must we think it is something else into which, as it were, all the centers <margin>* the centers</margin> fall together? Or is it an analogy <note>original: "analogia"</note> to the center of a circle? For the soul here is not a circle <margin># not the shape</margin> or figure, but because the ancient nature is in it and around it, and because it comes from such a nature, even more so when it is entirely separated. But now <margin>+ image</margin> a part of us is held down by the body, as if someone had their feet in water but the rest of the body above it. By that part which is not baptized in the body, we rise up, <margin>X like the whole</margin> by this center of ours to that which is like the center of all, just as the centers of the greatest circles remain resting in the center of the containing sphere. <margin>F</margin> If these psychic circles were corporeal, they would be joined to the center locally, both before and now, the centers being around them. But since souls are intelligible, and that One is—

# BOOK NINE.

That [divine being], by other powers than it is natural for the intellect to possess; for it loves by its nature to be joined, as if to become one of many connections. By weaving together, it delivers the act of understanding through likeness and identity. It passes through all things to its kin, if anything should be separated.
<margin>as if through a certain similarity and identity</margin>
They surrender all things, and they exist in that [One] *truly. But bodies are separated by other bodies. The nature of incorporeal things, however, is not separated by such obstacles but by difference. When, therefore, otherness is not present, those things which are not "other" are present to one another. For that One, having no otherness, is always present. But when we do not possess it, it is absent from us—not that the One is gone, but that we have turned away. Just as the One always revolves within itself, we only revolve around it when we look toward it. We are like a choir singing out of tune, even though we are singing around one leader <note>original Greek: "κορυφαῖον" (koryphaion), the lead dancer or conductor of a Greek chorus</note>; if the choir turns toward something outside the spectacle, it falters, but when it turns back, it sings beautifully and truly centers itself around him. So it is with us: we are always around him.
<margin>that is, towards having no tumult</margin>
And when our release from the body occurs in total destruction, *we shall no longer exist. We are not always looking toward him; but when we do look toward him, then we find our goal and our rest, and we no longer sing out of tune, but truly dance a <term>divine dance<note>Greek: "χορείαν ἔνθεον" (choreian entheon), a "god-filled" or inspired dance.</note></term> around him.

<margin>a pure fountain.</margin>
In this dance, one beholds a *pure fountain of life, a fountain of the mind, the principle of Being, the cause of Good, and the root of the soul. These things do not pour out from him in a way that diminishes him. For either the things being born are not perishable, or they are eternal, just as their principle remains the same. It is not divided among them, but remains whole. Therefore, those things also remain, just as if the Sun remained, and the light around it remained. We are not cut off from it. Even if something intervenes or the nature of the body drags us toward itself, we are still preserved in the spirit, through which there is then that ecstasy. But as long as it is present, it does not stop providing. We are more truly ourselves when we understand from that source and look toward it, rather than toward the things here. To stay furthest away is to exist less. Here is the fountain; here the soul finds rest.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> From the higher perspective, it must be considered that by certain other powers—by which the soul, being naturally intelligent, can be moved toward that which is understood—a "coupling" <note>original Latin: "copulatio"</note> is said to occur. This is a certain closeness of a winter's pact, present in likeness and identity. As it is now said, the soul is joined in a certain kinship, with nothing separating them in the meantime. For bodies are prohibited from joining by other bodies, but incorporeal things cannot be separated by the obstacle of bodies. Therefore, they are not distant from each other in space, but rather by "otherness" and difference.
<margin>B</margin> When, therefore, this diversity and (so to speak) otherness is absent, then those things which are not properly "diverse" are present to one another. That One, since it admits no diversity within itself, is always present; but we are present to it only when we have no diversity at all. The One does not crave us so that it is forced to move around us; rather, we crave it, and therefore we ourselves revolve around it. Indeed, we always
<margin>C</margin> revolve around the same center, yet we do not steadily gaze upon it. We are like a choir of singers who, although they revolve around the chief leader, may nevertheless be diverted from the sight of the leader to something else, and thus fall into dissonance. But when the choir turns back to him, it sings rightly and truly turns itself around him. So too we always revolve around God, even when we are entirely dissolved from the body and no longer know him. Yet we do not always turn toward him. But when we look directly into him, then at last we reach our desired end and rest; we no longer sound dissonant, while we truly perform a divine dance around him.

->On the soul alone contemplating God. Chapter IX.<-

> *Just as all good things are from the first principle and proceed from there, so everything that is carried toward any good is naturally an approach toward that same principle. Love toward God is implanted in all, so that by it anyone may become pure. For the ultimate end is the same Good which one had as a beginning. Just as the appetite for the good is naturally excited, so also its enjoyment arises naturally from a single integrity again, and from a certain knowledge—not one placed only in the mind, but such that it works within our very nature. This appears even in plants and the body. To the mature soul, the enjoyment of these first things seems natural and essential; but it must happen not simply by way of the intellect, but by nature. In this state, enjoyment becomes as much more penetrating into the "marrow" as the intelligence is accustomed to penetrate an object more deeply than the senses. Therefore, to enjoy God is not so much to "see" as to "touch"—strictly from the outside at first, but then to glide within, to be affected divinely, and having been so formed, to become God. The soul, having cast aside its vegetative nature, becomes entirely a form of nourishment, or perhaps a way of life. But according to Plato, after the soul had conceived and was subsequently pregnant, having been translated into God, it is not then poured out; the soul, which is naturally filled with love, is converted by the soul into God. Since it is not fitting for God not to be, the soul is eventually transferred into God by its own proper motion.*

For this reason, those things also remain, just as if the Sun remained, the light would also remain.

It is not as if he handed something over to us and then stood apart from us, but rather that he continually bestows it, insofar as he perseveres in being what he is—or rather, insofar as we turn toward him. ### PLOTINUS: ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> The soul is free from evils once it has hurried back to that place which is pure of all evil. There, it truly understands and is no longer subject to any passions; it is there alone that true life happens. For what is called "living" here on earth, without God, is but a trace of life imitating that higher life. Living in that higher realm, however, is an act of the mind. This act also gives birth to gods <note>Plotinus often refers to "gods" as high-level spiritual intelligences or emanations</note> through a certain silent and tranquil touch of the Divine. It generates beauty, it generates justice, and it generates virtue itself. These are the things the soul brings forth when it is pregnant with God; this is the soul’s beginning and its end.

<margin>B</margin> It is the beginning because the soul proceeds from there, and the end because its Good is found there. Reaching that place, the soul becomes what it truly was. For our life here, amidst the things of the world, is a sort of fall, an exile, and a "shedding of wings" <note>original: "alarumq; iactura" / "πτερορρύησις"; a reference to Plato’s Phaedrus, where the soul loses its wings and falls into a body</note>. That our Good consists in that higher place is indicated by the love that is innate to the soul. This is why Love is joined to souls in both writings and myths; since the soul is different from God but also from Him, it necessarily loves Him. Indeed, when the soul lives there, it possesses a heavenly love; but here on earth, its love becomes common and vulgar. For the Heavenly Venus <note>Aphrodite Urania, representing spiritual love</note> reigns there, but here she becomes the vulgar Venus <note>Aphrodite Pandemos, representing earthly or physical desire</note>, as if she has been corrupted. Every soul is a "Venus," as hinted at by the myths of Venus’s birth and the Love born alongside her. Therefore, the soul in its natural state loves God, desiring to be joined to Him, like a beautiful maiden moved by an honorable love for a noble suitor. But when the soul has fallen into the world of generation, it is deceived by various "courtships" and, exchanging its divine love for a fleeting one, it acts wantonly, separated from its Father. Yet, when it learns to hate these earthly outrages and purifies itself of them, it eventually returns to its Father, possessing a blessed affection. If anyone is ignorant of this feeling or passion, let them reflect on it by considering human loves: what great happiness it is to attain what one ardently loves. Yet the things we love here are mortal and harmful—mere images—and our love for them eventually turns to its opposite. This is because what we pursued was not the truly Beloved, nor our true Good, nor that which we naturally desire. But in that higher realm, the truly Beloved flourishes; there we may be joined to it, participate in it, and truly possess it, for it is not wrapped in external flesh. Whoever has known this certainly knows what I am saying: how the soul then leads another life as it moves forward and approaches God. Once it has reached Him, the soul knows with certainty that the Giver of true life is present. At that point, there is no need for anything further; on the contrary, one must set aside everything else and rest in Him alone, becoming God alone <note>original Latin: "Deusq. fieri tantū"; Plotinus describes the "deification" of the soul in union with the One</note>, cutting away all the external things that cling to us. We must therefore hurry to depart from here, grieving that we live bound in part to these earthly things, so that we may embrace God with our whole soul, leaving no part of us that does not touch Him. In that state of living, one may see both God and oneself as it is right to see: oneself illuminated, full of intellectual light, or rather—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> —outside of evils, as if having run up to the place pure of evils, the soul thinks there and is free from passion. And true life is there. For the present life, and that without God, is a trace of life imitating that other life. But living there is an activity of Intellect; and this activity generates gods, in a quiet contact with that One. It generates beauty, it generates justice, it generates virtue. For the soul, filled with God, is pregnant with these things, and this is its beginning and end.

<margin>B</margin> It is the beginning because it is from there, and the end because the Good is there. Having arrived there, the soul becomes itself, that which it was; for life here among the falls and flights is a "shedding of wings." It shows that the Good is there, the Love that is natural to the soul, <gloss>and</gloss> just as Love is yoked to souls in both paintings and myths. Since the soul is different from God, but from Him, she loves Him of necessity; and while she is there, she has heavenly love. But here,

<margin>C</margin> she becomes common. For there is a Heavenly Aphrodite, but here she becomes common and a wanderer. Every soul is an Aphrodite, and this is hinted at by the birth of Aphrodite and the Love born with her. Having her natural state, the soul <margin>\* for the soul</margin> <gloss>the soul</gloss> loves God, wanting to be united as a beautiful maiden to a beautiful Love. <meta>This page concludes the Ninth Book of the Sixth Ennead.
