# BOOK NINE.

<note>original Greek: Φῶς αὐτὸ καθαρὸν...</note>
Light itself is pure, light, weightless; there, one becomes God—or rather, one *is* God. One shines forth in that state, but if the soul becomes weighed down again, it is as if that light withers away.

<margin>*ital*</margin> Why then does the soul not stay there? It is because it has not yet fully arrived or has fallen into total forgetfulness. But there is a way to reach it when the vision is steady. When we are no longer troubled by the body, nothing will disturb us while we are there. It is not the vision itself that is a disturbance, but rather something else <note>likely referring to the physical senses or lower mind</note> that belongs to the one who has seen. For one does not doubt the signs within themselves, or the soul's own reasoning. Knowing and seeing are no longer "reason," but something greater than reason, prior to reason, and above reason—just like the object being seen. 

<margin>*the seer becomes*</margin> Therefore, when one sees oneself at the moment of looking, they will believe in themselves more than anything else. One will perceive themselves having become simple <note>In Neoplatonism, "simple" means unified and without parts, like the Divine</note>. Even if we must use the word "seeing," we should be careful; for "seeing" implies two things: the seer and the seen. But here, they are not two, but both are one. 

<margin>*not by his own power alone*</margin> At that moment, the soul does not even "see" in the usual sense <margin>by means of the intellect</margin>, for it does not distinguish between itself and the vision, nor does it imagine two things. Instead, it is as if the soul has become someone else, no longer itself. It belongs to that higher realm, having given itself over, <margin>*seeing*</margin> joining its own center to the Divine center. For even here on earth, when two things come together, they are one; they are only two when they are apart. This is why the spectacle is so difficult to describe. How could anyone report it as if it were "another" thing, when at the moment of seeing, it was not seen as something separate, but as one with oneself?

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But truly, that light itself is pure, weightless, and sublime. At that moment, the soul is made God—or rather, it is already God—and is then set aflame. But if the soul is weighed down and slips back from that state, it is as if the flame is extinguished.

### The Fruition of God. Chapter X.

*The soul, having finally completed its absolute preparation, draws as close as possible to God. Because the Infinite Good possesses an infinite power of attraction, the soul conceives an infinite love for Him. It sees Him and is transformed into God, so that the whole soul rushes to meet the vision with all its strength. It meets God as one, just as the light is thinned out <note>meaning purified of material density</note>, which perhaps refers to that fire or that saying of our Saint Paul: "He who adheres to God is one spirit." <note>1 Corinthians 6:17</note> Plotinus indeed conceded that our intellect, once placed in God, is never truly torn away. However, it turns back toward the lower intellect when it sets aside its stillness and begins the process of mental argumentation. True conversion means the reason is perpetually turned toward that higher place, especially when it is completely freed from the body, which the leaders of this philosophy seem to have touched upon here.*

<margin>B</margin> **WHY** then does the soul not remain there? Truly, because it has not yet fully emigrated from this life. But there will come a time when the continuity of looking is granted—that is, when the body no longer disturbs the vision in any way. It is not the part that "sees" which is properly disturbed, but something else <note>the lower faculties</note>. And yet, the one who saw is especially free from the vision when they are occupied with "knowledge"—that is, the kind of knowledge involved in demonstrations, conjectures, and the <term>discursive reasoning</term> <note>original: "rationis discursione"; the step-by-step logic used by the human mind, as opposed to the instant intuition of the Divine</note> of the mind. 

<margin>C</margin> But the act of seeing and the seer themselves are no longer "reason," but something more excellent than reason, coming before it. Even if this exists in the reason in some way, it is there as the thing *seen* rather than the act of thinking. Therefore, whoever sees themselves surely inspects themselves as being affected in this way; or rather, they will be joined to themselves in this state and perceive themselves as having become entirely simple. 

<margin>D</margin> Perhaps we should not even say "to see," but rather "to become the vision itself." If we think of these as two separate things—the seer and the seen—then they are not one, though this way of speaking is quite bold. In that moment, the soul does not properly "see," nor does it distinguish itself as a seer, nor does it imagine two things. Instead, the soul, having become "another" and no longer its old self, gives itself over to that realm. Having become entirely His, it emerges as one, just as if one were joining a center to a center. 

<margin>E</margin> For here, things that run together become one, and they are only two when they are pulled apart. This is why we speak of the "other" now. This spectacle is extremely difficult to put into words. For how can anyone announce it as if it were something else, when at the time of seeing, one did not see it as something else, but as entirely one with oneself?

### The Fruition of God. Chapter XI.

*Through the power of the One itself, union happens everywhere. Higher things are more easily unified because they are one in quality. The soul is only then skillfully united with the One—the principle of all things—when the soul itself is most purely "one." This is achieved when the soul strips away the "multitude" belonging to imagination, reason, and intelligence. It emerges as its own solitary unity, and through the affection of love, it enjoys the Divine Unity, coupling its own center with the Universal Center. Plotinus asserts that a soul so affected has transferred its <term>intellectual form</term> <note>the highest part of the human spirit</note> into the Unity. Thus, the rational soul is now held to be intellectual, and remains there perpetually. This is where the soul exists in a state of immobility, having transcended even the primary essences, where it acts without movement or labor. We, certainly, Magnanimous Lorenzo, <note>Marsilio Ficino is addressing his patron, Lorenzo de' Medici</note> now put an end to our labors on Plotinus, with God's help; thus we humbly adore the Almighty God.*

> We give thanks to You, highest God, enlightener of minds and author of all good things, because beyond our merit You have supplied the strength of Your grace to complete so great a work. I pray to You, most merciful God, pour true clarity into the pious reader; and furthermore, grant a light by which they may everywhere discern the true from the false, so that they may never dissent from Your will, whether in meditation or in action.

<summary>This page concludes Plotinus's Enneads with a description of the soul's total mystical union with the One, characterized as a "joining of centers." Translator Marsilio Ficino ends the work with a dedication to Lorenzo de' Medici and a prayer of thanks to God.</summary>
<keywords>contemplation, mystical union, The One, center to center, simplicity, Marsilio Ficino, Lorenzo de' Medici, Neoplatonism, Enneads, divine light</keywords>

--- Page 805 ---
<meta>This page continues the final chapter of the Sixth Ennead, Book Nine. The previous page discussed how the soul, once purified and lightened, perceives itself as divine light. This page elaborates on the metaphor of the religious "mysteries" and the "inner sanctuary" to describe the final stage of mystical union where the seer and the seen become one.</meta>

### PLOTINUS ENNEAD VI.

<margin>A</margin> This, therefore, is what the establishment of such mysteries <note>The "mysteries" refers to ancient Greek religious rites like those at Eleusis, which were secret and required initiation.</note> intends to show, where it forbids revealing them to people who are not yet initiated and purified. Truly, just as it is not permitted to explain what is divine to any other person, it is forbidden to open it up except to that person who has happened to see it for themselves. Since, then, there were not two things, but the seer himself was one with that which was seen (as if it were not properly "something seen" but rather "something unified"), if he who has departed from that state should ever remember it while he was once again thoroughly mingled with it, he will hold within himself an image of that thing.

<margin>B</margin> For he himself was also one, having no difference within himself relative to himself, nor again relative to other things. For nothing moved within him: no anger, no appetite for anything else was present in him once he had been carried up to the heights. Indeed, there was neither reason, nor a certain intelligence, nor—if it is even permitted to say this—was he entirely "himself." Instead, he was as if seized in a rapture <note>original: "raptus"</note>, or like one completely possessed by God, established in a certain safe seclusion and a tranquil state, entirely immovable. He did not decline from his own essence in any way, nor did he turn back around himself, because he was utterly at rest, as if he had already become stillness itself.

<margin>C</margin> Now indeed, he no longer moves around the beautiful, but has already transcended beauty itself, already surpassing even the choir of the virtues. It is just as if someone, having already entered the innermost secret parts of a sacred <term>adytum</term> <note>The inner sanctuary of a temple where the deity's image was kept; a place forbidden to the uninitiated.</note>, should leave behind all the statues arranged in the temple. These statues will be the first things he encounters again upon exiting the sanctuary, after that intimate spectacle within.

<margin>D</margin> After that communion, he does not return to statues or images, but rather to that which the statues and images represent. These should certainly be judged as secondary spectacles. The One itself, perhaps, should not be judged as a "spectacle" at all; rather, there is a different way of seeing there: a certain departure from oneself <note>original: "Exitus... è seipso"</note>, a certain diffusion and a wonderful advancement, a longing for touch, and finally, rest. Every thought of the mind is entirely lost in that coupling, if one truly perceives what is in the sanctuary. But he who perceives it in any other way carries nothing away from there.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, the wise among the Prophets obscurely wrap up such imitations of divine things, indicating the manner in which that God is seen. The wise priest, explaining the wrapped mystery and having entered the sanctuary, achieves true contemplation there. If he has not yet entered, he considers the sanctuary itself to be something invisible, a source and a principle, and he will know it strictly as a "principle." But having entered there, he sees the Principle itself and is joined to it; he perceives the like by the like, neglecting nothing of divine things, as many as the soul is able to attain.

<margin>F</margin> Now, before the vision itself, the soul desires that which remains from the vision. But for the one who has already transcended all things, what remains is the One itself, which surpasses all. For the soul will never naturally arrive at something that is entirely "non-being," but in its fall it will descend into evil, and thus it is judged to rush into non-being—not because it can be plunged into something that is absolutely nothing, but if it ever travels the opposite path, the soul will not arrive at something else, but will arrive at itself.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> <margin>* This indeed is what the mysteries wish to show</margin> THIS indeed is what the requirement of the mysteries wishes to manifest: not to carry out the secrets <margin>* not initiated</margin> to those who are not initiated. Because that thing is not to be made public, <margin>* forbidden to speak</margin> it is forbidden to speak of the divine to another, except to the blessed one who has had the good fortune to see it. Since, then, the seer and the seen were not two, but the seer himself was one with the seen—as if not "seen" but "unified"—one might still have a memory of it, if he were to be mingled with it again.

<margin>B</margin> For he himself was also one, <margin>* one</margin> having no difference toward himself nor toward others; for nothing moved within him, no anger, no desire for anything else was present in him having ascended, nor was there any word, nor any thought, nor was he entirely himself, if one must say even this. But as if carried away or inspired, he came to be in a quiet dwelling-place, in a state of rest...

<margin>C</margin> ...unwavering in his own essence, leaning nowhere, nor turning about himself, standing entirely still and becoming as if stillness itself. Neither was he concerned with beautiful things, but already running beyond the beautiful, having already stepped over even the choir of virtues, like someone who has slipped into the interior of the sanctuary, leaving behind <margin>* the statues in the temple</margin> the statues in the temple. These <margin>* which to one exiting</margin> become the first things seen by one exiting the sanctuary, after the internal vision.

<margin>D</margin> And that communion there is not with a statue or an image, but with the One itself. The other things are merely preliminary sights; but that perhaps was not a sight, but another way of seeing: an ecstasy, a simplification, a giving of oneself, a longing for touch, a stillness, and a focused thought toward fitting together, if one is to see what is in the sanctuary. But if one looks in another way, nothing is present. These things the wise among the prophets hint at through imitations and riddles...

<margin>E</margin> ...hinting at how that God is seen. But the wise priest, understanding the riddle, makes the vision true by becoming present there in the sanctuary. And even if he has not arrived, considering the sanctuary to be among the invisible things, and a source and a principle, he will know it as a principle; he sees the Principle through the Principle and is joined with it, the like with the like, leaving out nothing of the divine things as many as a soul is able to hold.

<margin>F</margin> And before the vision, the soul demands that which remains from the vision. But that which remains for the one who has surpassed all things is that which is before all things. For the soul will not naturally come to something that is entirely non-existent; rather, in its descent, it will come to evil, and thus to non-being, but not to absolute non-being. But running the opposite way, it will come not to another, but to itself.

<summary>Plotinus concludes his work by describing the ultimate mystical union as an "ecstasy" or "simplification" where the soul transcends virtue, beauty, and intellect to become one with the Divine. He uses the metaphor of a priest entering the hidden inner sanctuary of a temple, leaving behind all external images to reach the silent, immovable source of all existence.</summary>
<keywords>The One, mystical union, ecstasy, sanctuary, adytum, initiation, Plotinus, Neoplatonism, soul's ascent, non-being, stillness</keywords>

But to be in itself alone, and not in Being, is to be in That <note>That is, the "One" or the absolute source of all existence.</note>. For the soul itself becomes something that is not essence, but <term>beyond essence</term>, and in this way it * communicates with it. Whoever, then, sees themselves having become such a thing, would hold that as an image of the One. This is perhaps the most famous phrase in Neoplatonic philosophy, describing the solitary soul's return to the singular Source.</note>

<column-break/>

**A** himself: and so since he is not in another, he must not be judged on that account to be in nothing at all, but rather to consist in himself: but to be in himself alone, and not in Being, is nothing other than to be entirely in God. For he himself becomes something that is not essence, but also superior to essence, insofar as he clearly joins himself entirely to God. If anyone, therefore, should ever see himself having become this, he will certainly have himself as a kind of image of that One. And if he should pass over from himself, like an image led all the way to its archetype, he will have already reached the very end of his journey. But if at any time he should fall from **B** <unclear>contemplation</unclear>, again awakening the virtue implanted in him, and noticing himself to be entirely cultivated, he will again be raised to the heights, while he proceeds through virtue into the mind, and through wisdom advances toward God. This, then, is the life of the gods and of divine men—
